papers.title: SANE: Automated Scorer-Specific Metamorphic Testing for LLM Judges
papers.authors: Ethan Ludwick, Yu-Chung Hsiao
papers.abstract: LLM judges increasingly mediate benchmark evaluation, model selection, data curation, and training. Their decisions are useful only when each judge responds reliably to changes affecting its scoring criterion. Existing methods for reliability testing perturb inputs with known expected effects on judge scores. Prominent LLM-judge testing harnesses combine human-authored perturbation recipes with synthetic test generation, leaving scorer-specific recipe ideation outside the automated pipeline. This limits their use to fixed perturbations and pre-assumed scorer types. We introduce SANE, an agent-based framework that encodes behavioral requirements for stochastic evaluators as reusable agent instructions. Given a scorer specification, implementation, and representative inputs, the pipeline first identifies scorer-specific capabilities, then automatically derives perturbation recipes and expected score relations for each. SANE also defines a scorer-independent validation framework for generated judge tests. It determines whether each recipe agrees with scorer intent and whether each instantiated case realizes the recipe and supports its expected relation. Because SANE generates a recipe inventory tailored to each scorer, the number of aligned recipes grows as scorers are added. Across five domains, SANE produces 3.7 times as many validated test families as the Judge Reliability Harness (JRH) at comparable end-to-end validity and detects scorer deficiencies in every domain, including professionalism and toxicity, where JRH detects none. On faithfulness, SANE achieves strong human alignment in judge ranking: its test-suite scores rank 11 judge models consistently with human-labeled FaithBench performance (Spearman rho = 0.852), while JRH does not (rho = 0.100).

papers.title: AI Security Literacy: Ecosystem-based Competency Framework and K-12 Learning Platform
papers.authors: Eric Yocam, Varghese Mathew Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas
papers.abstract: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

papers.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
papers.authors: Hieu Tran, Hong Yu
papers.abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

papers.title: Learning-Enhanced Observer for Sensorless Task-Null-Space Compliant Control
papers.authors: Nuo Chen, Ya-Jun Pan, Onur Toker
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives. Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics. Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance. The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.

papers.title: Human-Robot Interaction via Meta-Learning Based Mode Recognition and Adaptive Control
papers.authors: Nuo Chen, Ya-Jun Pan
papers.abstract: In human-robot interaction (HRI) tasks, humans may interact with the robot in either an active guiding or passive following state, resulting in distinct control objectives for each interaction mode. Most existing approaches rely on predefined switching thresholds to distinguish interaction modes, but their performance can be sensitive to measurement noise. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. First, a neural network (NN) trained via meta-learning is developed to recognize human intention without manually defined thresholds. By successfully incorporating force-dependent parameters from the controller, the recognition rates are improved from 90.1\% to 99.1\% for the passive mode and from 79.8\% to 97.1\% for the active mode. Second, an adaptive meta-learning controller is introduced to compensate for human disturbances and enable online adaptation to varying interaction forces. Third, a multiple-trajectory meta-learning algorithm is designed to jointly learn an environment-basis representation and force-dependent parameters, allowing the controller to deal with unmodeled dynamics efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust and accurate control performance, while providing reliable mode recognition for safe and adaptive physical HRI.

papers.title: Offline Apprenticeship Learning for Human-Centric Environments
papers.authors: Md Mirajul Islam
papers.abstract: Effective decision-making in human-centric environments such as Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) and clinical healthcare requires policies that are adaptive, data-efficient, and ethically deployable. Apprenticeship Learning (AL) infers policies directly from expert demonstrations by recovering the underlying reward structure, enabling strictly offline learning without environment interaction. This dissertation develops a progression of offline AL frameworks organized around two challenges: reward modeling and demonstration quality. For reward modeling, EM-EDM clusters demonstrations by latent reward functions and induces cluster-specific policies, and THEMES partitions trajectories into temporally coherent sub-trajectories guided by a hierarchically learned reward regulator; across one educational and three clinical datasets, THEMES outperforms flat and hierarchical AL baselines. For demonstration quality, HALIDE integrates continuous quality signals into hierarchical policy induction, enabling principled reuse of mixed-quality data under distribution shift. CCHAL further attributes quality to individual decisions via Bayesian credit assignment, dual-arm criticality scoring that contrasts expert and non-expert behavior, and a Bradley-Terry contrastive IRL objective over failure trajectories, outperforming baselines including HALIDE on three clinical EHR datasets and an ITS dataset. Finally, a real-world classroom evaluation of StuEDM, an EDM-induced policy that preserves student agency and intervenes only on disagreement, shows significant learning gains over an Expert baseline and a higher pretest-adjusted posttest score than a CQL policy trained on a far larger corpus, while overriding students less than half as often. Together, this work establishes offline AL as a practical, data-efficient, and ethically viable paradigm for human-centric environments.

papers.title: SimHack: Predicting the onset of detectable reward hacking before RL training
papers.authors: Junwei Deng, Alex Bie, Natalia Ponomareva
papers.abstract: When training LLMs to code with reinforcement learning, reward hacking is often detectable but difficult to prevent, since (a) environment hardening is increasingly difficult as training environments grow more complex; and (b) training-time interventions incentivize models to obfuscate hacking behavior to bypass detection. We instead study whether we can predict when detectable reward hacking becomes dominant before executing an RL run, enabling us to select lower-risk recipes in advance. We find that the initial hacking rate alone does not determine onset, which varies substantially across training recipes and repeated runs. We thus formulate this problem as predicting the distribution of the reward hacking onset step under a target training recipe. We introduce SimHack, a simulator that learns reward hacking training dynamics from a handful of smaller-scale reference RL runs and generates counterfactual simulation runs of unseen target recipes without costly retraining. Across unseen target recipes, SimHack predicts the median onset to a relative error of 11.3% and achieves across-recipe rank correlation of 0.85, while generalizing to differences in model scale, curriculum, number of rollouts, and learning rate between reference and target recipes. As an application, we show that SimHack can guide training decisions by screening candidate RL curricula, discovering curricula over the same set of scenarios that train for 96.6% longer without hacking.

papers.title: Capable Teacher, Myopic Scorer: Reward-Free Teacher Repair for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
papers.authors: Shu Zhao, Tan Yu
papers.abstract: Agentic on-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token. A natural explanation of where it goes wrong is compounding error: the student's mistakes carry its trajectories beyond the region where the teacher is reliable, so recent methods keep training inside that region, through episode-length curricula, teacher-guided turns, prefix replay, or teacher intervention where the two disagree. We show this explanation is incomplete. From the states where the student departs most from the teacher, the teacher's own takeovers still finish the task, yet the student trained on its token scores keeps running out of turns. We attribute this to the myopia of next-token scoring. The teacher rates each token without seeing where the episode ends, so its scores let through the safe, delaying moves that outcome-based RL would punish with zero reward, a penalty agentic OPD lacks. We call this difference between what the teacher does and what it scores the rollout-scorer gap. We propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), which repairs the scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states from the untrained student, running teacher takeovers from them, keeping the states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check such as consensus or an LLM judge, and fine-tuning the teacher to give its takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward, without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training. Across three environments, two teachers and four students, R2S outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods in all twelve teacher-student-environment cells, by 12.8 success points on average over the best of them in each cell. Project page: https://tree-shu-zhao.github.io/r2s/.

papers.title: The Labor of Storytelling: How People with Chronic Illnesses Leverage AI and Communities for Narrative Translation
papers.authors: Drishti Goel, Koustuv Saha, Martez Mott, Denae Ford
papers.abstract: The distinctiveness of people with chronic illness as storytellers is how they experience their illness. Symptoms, pain, and biological disruptions are eloquent forms of speech of the body that beget social articulation. The stories people tell about illness shape how suffering is legitimized, and acted upon. Large language models have emerged as new mediators within this landscape---a role once predominantly supported by communities. In doing so, these systems participate in what we term narrative translation: transforming lived illness experiences for particular audiences and purposes. Through 21 prototype-driven semi-structured interviews with people with chronic illness, we contribute an empirical account of how participants navigate this mediation alongside existing sources of support. Our findings surface distinct yet complementary roles participants envisioned for AI and their communities, and how trust in AI was shaped by learning model-boundaries and perceiving understanding. We characterize these findings to inform future designs of AI-mediated narrative support.

papers.title: How Much of Cross-Subject EEG Emotion Recognition Is Stimulus Memorization?
papers.authors: Haiyan Xu, Konstantinos N. Plataniotis
papers.abstract: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition now reports accuracies above 90% on stimulus-defined benchmarks such as SEED, and the field has examined several ways in which such numbers can be inflated, attributing inflation to subject identity, to data partitioning, and to repeated stimulus presentation. We observe that one variable has been left out. On these datasets the emotion label is assigned to the video at design time, so any encoder that recovers which video was shown obtains the label for free. We adapt three representation-level shortcut diagnostics to a cohort of published contrastive cross-subject encoders, and find that stimulus identity is linearly recoverable at six to fifteen times chance. We then measure its impact on the reported accuracy by holding out subjects and stimuli jointly, and find that each released classifier loses two to forty-four points once the test videos are unseen, so a headline obtained under subject hold-out alone is not a measure of cross-subject emotion decoding.

papers.title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
papers.authors: Christian Meske, Tobias Hermanns, Florian Brachten
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

papers.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.authors: Masahiro Kaneko, Hiromi Arai, Timothy Baldwin
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

papers.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
papers.authors: Anil Srirangapatna Nagesh, Nitin Gupta, Anuj Taneja, Vivek Kumar Singh, Shane Eleniak, Theo Zhao, Moulidharan N, Shashank Keshetty
papers.abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

papers.title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
papers.authors: Andrea Campagner, Federico Cabitza, Vincenzo Crupi
papers.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated Feedback on Handwritten Mathematics: Feedback Quality and Subsequent Exam Performance
papers.authors: Arne Vanhoyweghen, Vincent Holst, Melika Mobini, Lukas Van de Voorde, Tibo Vanleke, Andres Algaba, Sam Verboven, Marie‐Anne Guerry, Filip Van Droogenbroeck, Vincent Ginis
papers.abstract: We evaluate the quality of feedback and practice exercises generated by GPT-5.1 from handwritten university mathematics answers and their grades, and examine whether receiving this feedback improves subsequent exam performance. We use six weekly bonus tests in an English (n=343) and a Dutch (n=236) cohort. Tests 1 and 3 used a crossover feedback design; otherwise, all attendees received feedback. To evaluate the feedback, six reviewers assessed 157 messages from three English-cohort tasks using six criteria scored from 0 to 3. The practice exercises received the highest proportion of strong ratings (95.5%), while diagnostic specificity (41.1%) and clarity and tone (33.4%) received fewer. Feedback for the lowest-scoring answers was rated as less actionable, suggesting that these students may need more targeted guidance from instructors. Comparisons of related exam questions showed mixed results, with no statistically significant differences after adjustment across four comparisons. Greater attendance and feedback exposure were associated with higher exam scores, but the contribution of feedback could not be separated from attendance and practice. Our findings show the potential of an integrated framework merging instructor guidance with automated feedback generation to provide personalised learning support at scale.

papers.title: SAPD: Learning from Agent Experience without Environment Interaction
papers.authors: Juncheng Diao, Haibin Wang, Wei Shi, Yifan Ding, Qingbin Li, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai
papers.abstract: Scaling the training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents typically requires a large collection of executable environments, whose construction, maintenance, and operation constrain the expansion of training experience. Existing offline trajectories offer an opportunity to reuse interaction experience, yet effectively refining the current policy without revisiting these environments remains challenging: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can lead to catastrophic forgetting, while online reinforcement learning requires real-time interaction with the environment. To address this challenge, we propose Step-Advantage Policy Distillation (SAPD), a method for learning from offline trajectories using relative step advantages. SAPD decomposes multi-turn trajectories into individual decision contexts for on-policy distillation, allowing the student to generate responses conditioned on recorded histories, and introduces relative step advantage signals to stabilize training. The entire process requires neither new environment observations nor additional multi-turn interactions. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show that SAPD improves performance across different teacher configurations, mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared with SFT, and runs at least $4.7\times$ faster per training step than online OPD. We will release our code soon.

papers.title: GRADUS: Discovering and Recovering Agent Lessons from the Environment's Latent Syllabus
papers.authors: Qing Ping, Wei Yang, Panpan Xu, Johannes Kirmayr, Lukas Stappen, Junjie Tang, Jun Huan
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents for policy-constrained tool environments, such as an airline backend with booking, refund, and cancellation policies, requires tasks that exercise the environment's rules individually and in combination. Existing synthesis pipelines let a model propose tasks and retain only those it immediately solves, biasing training data toward easier behaviors. We introduce Gradus (Graded Rungs of Ascending Difficulty from an Underlying System), which decouples what a task should teach from the concrete task and solution used to teach it. Without seed tasks, Gradus treats a fixed environment as a latent syllabus, extracting guarded behavioral operators that capture how actions depend on current conditions and how their effects reshape subsequent decisions. It composes these operators into increasingly demanding tasks while using corpus-level feedback to target missing outcome combinations. Crucially, Gradus jointly calibrates tasks and solutions against the environment: execution feedback identifies which side to refine while preserving the intended behavioral requirements. Verification thus becomes a recovery signal rather than a terminal filter, coupling coverage-guided exploration with the preservation of difficult examples. From off-the-shelf backbones, the resulting curriculum lifts a 30B model from 59% to 89% on $τ^2$-Bench and from 47% to 83% on CAR-Bench with an Opus 4.5 proposer, and to 76% and 62%, respectively, with an open-weight Qwen3-235B proposer. These results show the value of jointly controlling which behaviors are explored and which survive into verified training data.

papers.title: S$^2$-MAS: A Society-Scale Multi-Agent Simulation Framework with 500 Million Household Persona Agents
papers.authors: Yang Li, Di Wan, Yike Wang, Chujun He, Zongsi Xu, Yitao Yu, Quanfeng Lu, Xiyu Chen, Sheng Zhong, Binjie Deng, Kunhan Guo, Zhenwei Guo, Tuo Zhou, Kunhan Guo, Weihao Lin, Tuo Zhou, Hai Liu, Chenwei Wu, Jianyuan Zhong, Xilin Dai, Ye Luo
papers.abstract: Simulating economic responses at society scale requires agents whose decisions reflect household circumstances and the effects of earlier actions. We introduce S$^2$-MAS, a society-scale multi-agent simulation framework built on 500 million synthetic household personas grounded in real-survey data. Its Genese engine separates decisions from state updates, while reusable financial scenarios and application ledgers track consumption, cash, debt and payments. Trained with SFT + RLCD on 2.93 million examples, sharp-421m-mlx achieves 74.55% accuracy and 38.37% question-macro F1 on one-shot consumer financial-choice tasks derived from held-out survey responses. Its accuracy exceeds GLM-5.3-Flash, Jev 1.13, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GPT-6-Luna and GPT-6-Astra in the common benchmark (full test for the first four; matched 500-group sample for Astra). We evaluate eight financial task families and simulate 12 million distinct household agents in paired purchase-funding conditions. Jointly raising purchase goals and approved credit limits increases consumption, with responses differing across age and income groups. Education, employment and household-size differences persist after age-income standardization and mainly reflect transitions from deferral to purchase. Asset and debt groups differ in cash drawdown, repayment and closing debt. A response-stratified 24-month panel varies purchase goals under a common credit product, with repayment and arrears updating subsequent offers. S$^2$-MAS links heterogeneous household decisions to evolving consumption, cash and repayment paths, supporting economic experiments across household groups, population scales and time horizons.

papers.title: EEG-Based Classification of Hypnotic Susceptibility Using Two-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.authors: Krzysztof Wróbel, Grzegorz M. Wójcik, Filip Postepski, Andrzej Kawiak, Katarzyna Zemla, Grzegorz Sędek
papers.abstract: Guided Imagery (GI) is a mind-based relaxation technique widely used in clinical and therapeutic settings. Objectively assessing whether a patient has entered a relaxed state remains a challenge for clinicians. This study investigates electroencephalography (EEG)-based classification of hypnotic susceptibility using two-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (2D CNNs) applied to minimally preprocessed signals, without manual feature extraction. Data were collected from 62 male participants (32 Control, 30 Hypno) using a 256-channel dense array amplifier during Guided Imagery or cognitive task conditions. A sliding-window framework evaluated up to 868 independent models across seven anatomically defined brain regions and 124 ten-second time windows. Segment-level random-split screening was followed by Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation to obtain subject-independent performance estimates, and an ensemble approach combined predictions across K = 10 windows. The best single-window model achieved accuracy of 0.82 on the random split. Under LOSO, anterior regions generalised better across subjects: the frontal region achieved mean accuracy of 0.646 (AUC: 0.692). An ensemble of K = 10 windows further improved the prefrontal region to mean accuracy of 0.738. The occipital region, dominant in random-split screening, collapsed to near-chance under LOSO, revealing subject-specific EEG fingerprinting rather than genuine group differences. Bandpass filtering and z-score normalisation suffice for competitive EEG classification without manual feature extraction. Anterior cortical regions are identified as the most generalisable neural markers of hypnotic susceptibility.

papers.title: AudiPsy: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning over Spoken Counseling Conversations for Depression Assessment
papers.authors: Chuanbo Zhu, Run Luo, Weibo Zhao, Yue Li, Kun Qian, Qiang Qu, Yike Guo, Minghuan Tan, Wei Xue
papers.abstract: Depression assessment from counseling speech requires integrating textual and acoustic psychological evidence across turns, yet existing end-to-end classification approaches lack explicit multimodal evidence interpretation and context-aware reasoning. We propose AudiPsy, an evidence-grounded omni-LLM for depression assessment over spoken counseling conversations. AudiPsy employs an Observation-Assessment-Summary (OAS) paradigm to integrate dialogue transcripts, textual and acoustic emotions, and textual-acoustic emotion incongruence into structured reasoning. OAS incrementally organizes multimodal observations, performs contextualized assessment, and maintains an evolving dialogue summary for subsequent turns. To support this framework, we construct AudiPsy-Counsel, a synthetic spoken counseling conversation corpus with multimodal context augmentation, and develop a unified three-stage curriculum for depression-oriented reasoning. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ demonstrate superior depression assessment performance over specialized depression detection methods and general-purpose speech/omni-LLMs, along with improved reasoning quality, while supplementary evaluation on EATD-Corpus supports AudiPsy's applicability to naturalistic conversations.

papers.title: Multiscale Temporal-Spectral-Spatial EEG Learning With Modality-Specific and Modality-Invariant Representations for Emotion Recognition
papers.authors: Jian Zhang, Manrong Liu, Yilei Huang, Wenhua Liu, Xiaohui Yang, Lijun Yang
papers.abstract: Multimodal physiological signals provide complementary cues for emotion recognition. They also raise two related challenges. Emotion-related EEG patterns vary across time, frequency bands, electrodes, and brain regions. Different physiological modalities also contain both modality-specific and shared affective information. This paper presents GMSI-Net, an EEG-centered multimodal emotion recognition framework. It has three key components. The temporal-spatial-spectral-region (TSSR) encoder models multiscale temporal-channel patterns, differential entropy features, and local-to-global brain-region relations. The modality-specific representation (MSR) branch uses bidirectional cross-modal attention and learnable gates. It controls information transfer while retaining modality-specific cues. The modality-invariant representation (MIR) branch learns a shared affective representation. An adaptively weighted contrastive loss aligns this representation across modalities. Independent multiscale Conv-Transformer encoders process the peripheral physiological signals. GMSI-Net is evaluated on DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI using within-subject random ten-fold cross-validation. The model reaches 96.21 (1.47) and 96.41 (1.60) for valence and arousal on DEAP. It reaches 94.10 (2.86) and 94.48 (3.77) on MAHNOB-HCI. These results indicate that combining EEG features with complementary physiological information can improve emotion recognition.

papers.title: Bias and Reliability in Learning-Style Inference from Student--AI Dialogues: An Evaluation of GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash
papers.authors: Samaneh Zamanifard, Sajad Goudarzi, Andrew Robb
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational technologies for personalized support, creating opportunities for real-time learner modeling from dialogue. This study evaluates whether GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Flash can infer three Felder-Silverman Learning Style Model dimensions (Active-Reflective, Sensing-Intuitive, and Sequential-Global) from short, task-focused student-AI problem-solving dialogues. Using questionnaire-derived Index of Learning Styles labels from 153 undergraduate participants, we compared deterministic zero-shot and few-shot prompting under five-fold cross-validation. Although accuracy and support-weighted F1 were moderate for Sensing-Intuitive and Sequential-Global, majority-class baselines, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and per-class recall showed that performance was often driven by dominant-label prediction rather than reliable recognition of both classes. The models substantially under-identified Intuitive and Global learners; few-shot prompting produced mixed effects and sometimes amplified majority-class bias. Active-Reflective classification remained unstable across models. These findings indicate that LLM-generated learner-style labels should be treated as uncertain, bias-prone signals rather than stable learner profiles, and that dialogue-based personalization systems require bias-aware evaluation and uncertainty-sensitive design.

papers.title: A Bayesian machine learning approach to direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with noncompliance
papers.authors: Saurabh Bhandari, Fan Li, Michael J. Daniels
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian machine learning approach for estimating direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with treatment noncompliance. To flexibly model outcomes and treatment receipt while accounting for within-cluster dependence, we combine Bayesian additive regression trees with cluster-level random effects. We augment the outcome regression with a peer-treatment clever covariate, defined as the predicted mean proportion of treated peers from a preliminary receipt model, to mitigate regularization-induced distortion of the effect decomposition. Within a Bayesian g-computation framework, we estimate cluster-average intent-to-treat effects and cluster-average local average treatment effects and examine sensitivity to the cross-world restrictions underlying their decomposition. Simulation studies show reduced bias under model misspecification, while the correctly specified parametric models show expected frequentist properties. We find that the clever covariate improves the decomposition of the total effect into direct and spillover components under moderate or strong spillover, with similar gains in smaller clusters. Its benefits vary with spillover strength, and the $95\%$ credible intervals remain conservative. An application to the Primary School Deworming Project in Kenya suggests reduced infection risk, with a larger estimated contribution from individual treatment receipt than from peer receipt. Overall, our approach provides a flexible Bayesian estimation of direct and spillover effect decomposition in the presence of treatment noncompliance.

papers.title: Influence of Blended Teaching Strategies on Teaching Effectiveness in Government Owned Polytechnics in Anambra State, Nigeria.
papers.authors: Vivian Chioma Ajakpo Anetoh, Rita Njideka Chiekezie, John Chidume Anetoh, Chimaobi Johnson Chiekezie
papers.journal: Scholarly Journal of Science and Technology Research and Development
papers.abstract: Education is a fundamental pillar for national development, technological advancement and socio-economic transformations. Blended teaching has the potentials to revolutionize higher education by enhancing academic performance, improve student engagement especially polytechnics because of its role in producing technical skilled manpower required for industrial growth, entrepreneurial development and innovation driven economies. The motivation for the study emanated due to lingering issues and educational concerns bordering on declining academic performance, limited instructional innovation and inadequate integration of educational technologies experienced in government owned polytechnics in Anambra State, Nigeria. These challenges have therefore hindered the quality of education in these government owned polytechnics. The introduction of blended teaching has therefore changed the narrative because it is an advanced tool which has the capacity to improve students’ academic performance and engagement. Therefore, this research work investigated how teaching effectiveness could be enhanced in government owned polytechnics through blended teaching strategies. Specifically, the study examined how learning management system enhances accountability and transparency in administrative, academic and financial operations in tertiary institutions in southeastern, Nigeria. The study also investigated how AI driven automated grading systems fosters accountability and transparency in selected tertiary institutions in southeastern, Nigeria. Thirdly, the study also ascertained how artificial intelligence driven chatbots can enhance accountability and transparency in selected tertiary institutions in southeastern, Nigeria. Accordingly, the study adopted a descriptive research design using a survey method to source the needed data from the respondents. The target population of the study consist of the staff and management of the selected tertiary institutions in south eastern part of Nigeria. Partial least square structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the hypotheses formulated to guide the study at 5% level of significance. The findings of the study revealed that personalized learning, automated grading system and AI powered chatbots significantly and positively enhance accountability and transparency in higher institutions in southeastern, Nigeria. The study recommended that tertiary institutions should engage more on personalized learning platforms such as Goggle Classroom, Class54 etc. for tailored content to meet students’ academic needs. The study recommended that tertiary institutions in Nigeria should be more engaged on automated grading system systems such as Gradescope, Custom AI in order to reduce bias in assessment thereby promoting accountability through standardized auditable trail. The study also recommended that AI powdered chatbots should be deployed more in tertiary institutions in order to enhance accessibility and responsiveness in tertiary institutions in Nigeria. The study suggests that further studies could be done on the effect of artificial intelligence on accountability and transparency in other areas such as deposit money banks, government parastatals, FINTECH Companies, Corporate organizations etc. The study is expected to offer both managerial and practical implications to various stakeholders such as technology developers, the management of tertiary institutions, Policymakers, students, academia, future researchers, government and even the general public.

papers.title: Inteligencia artificial en psiquiatría: usos y promesas
papers.authors: Ana Cuevas Badallo
papers.abstract: This article examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry, highlighting both its transformative potential and its ethical, clinical, and philosophical challenges. AI applications (ranging from diagnostic algorithms and predictive models to therapeutic chatbots and neuroimplants) are reshaping mental healthcare by improving early detection, personalizing treatments, and expanding access to services, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advanced techniques such as machine learning and natural language processing enable the analysis of multimodal data, enhancing clinical decision-making and enabling preventive interventions. However, the adoption of AI raises significant concerns. These include risks to privacy, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, and challenges in ensuring informed consent, particularly in vulnerable psychiatric populations. Neurotechnologies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when assisted by AI, introduce further ethical dilemmas related to autonomy, identity, and long-term safety. The article argues that these challenges cannot be addressed without a deeper conceptual understanding of mental disorders. It advocates for a pluralistic and enactivist framework, which views mental health conditions as dynamic interactions between brain, body, and environment. Ultimately, the responsible integration of AI in psychiatry requires robust ethical governance, interdisciplinary collaboration, and a human-centered approach.

papers.title: Entre la mente y la máquina: hacia una ética responsable en la era de la inteligencia artificial
papers.authors: Rita María Pérez Pérez
papers.abstract: This article aims to analyze the relevance of cognitive development and comprehensive ethical education in the critical and responsible use of generative artificial intelligence, with the purpose of preventing and counteracting the potential dehumanizing consequences that could affect the human condition in the twenty-first century. From a theoretical-analytical approach, it argues for the need for early digital education that fosters intellectual development and prevents technology from becoming a source of dependency. It highlights that education constitutes a key tool to counter cognitive laziness and the improper use of intelligent systems by university students, to the detriment of their critical reasoning capacities. It concludes that understanding the relevance of brain development and its relationship with cognitive learning processes constitutes an essential foundation for the formation of critical thinking and for the adoption of a responsible ethical approach to the use of artificial intelligence. Integrating these three components –cognitive development, critical thinking, and technological ethics—is indispensable for guiding the application of generative artificial intelligence toward pedagogical and humanistic ends that strengthen cognitive competencies, autonomy, and the reflective capacity of human beings in the twenty-first century.

papers.title: Los riesgos de la IA dialógica en la educación superior: afectaciones cognitivas y en la capacidad de lecto-escritura
papers.authors: Jorge Enrique Linares Salgado
papers.abstract: Dialogic Artificial Intelligence (DAI) or communicative AI within Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly expanding across higher education and academic workflows in both teaching and research. The adoption of DAI is being driven by the pressure to enhance productivity and automate academic practices. This paper discusses the primary risks that the intensive use of DAI poses to human cognitive capacities, information biases, and the erosion of literacy, critical thinking, argumentation, and academic discourse skills. Furthermore, it analyzes emerging forms of plagiarism and misconduct facilitated by DAI while reflecting on the concept of individual authorship, which has become obsolete, giving way to human-AI co-authorship. As an immersive technology that impacts human agency and autonomy, DAI could irreversibly transform cognition, literacy, the sense of authorship, and collaborative frameworks in research, teaching, and scholarly production. Finally, it concludes with a set of criteria and recommendations to guide university regulatory policies on DAI, moving beyond prohibitions, punitive measures, or ineffective appeals to individual ethics in the use of LLMs.

papers.title: Association of Intrinsic Capacity Decline with Frailty, Polypharmacy, Nutritional Status, and Fall Risk among Older Adults: A Cross-sectional Study from a Tertiary Care Center
papers.authors: Harishchandra Rameshchandra Chaudhari, Swapnil Suresh Patil, Yashodeep Baburao Gaikwad
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intrinsic capacity reflects an individual's physical and mental abilities and influencing healthy aging; its decline often precedes disability and is linked with frailty, malnutrition, polypharmacy, and falls. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional observational study was conducted at a tertiary care center in Western Maharashtra, India, among 165 adults aged 60 years and above. Participants were enrolled by consecutive sampling. Sociodemographic details, comorbidities, medication use, fall history, and functional parameters were recorded. Intrinsic capacity was assessed across cognition, locomotion, vitality/nutrition, vision, hearing, and psychological domains. Frailty was assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale, nutritional status using the Mini Nutritional Assessment-Short Form (MNA-SF), and data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27.0. RESULTS: The mean age was 72.77 ± 9.14 years. Intrinsic capacity decline was present in 147 (89.1%) participants, with severe decline in 76 (46.1%). Locomotion was the most commonly impaired domain (106, 64.2%), followed by vitality/nutrition (74, 44.8%) and psychological domain (61, 37.0%). The mean BMI was 22.49 ± 3.83 kg/m2, the mean number of current medications was 4.32 ± 2.09, the mean Timed Up and Go duration was 12.98 ± 3.26 s, the mean MNA-SF score was 11.58 ± 2.01, the mean Clinical Frailty Scale score was 4.27 ± 1.57, and the mean number of impaired intrinsic capacity domains was 2.29 ± 1.34. Intrinsic capacity decline was significantly associated with frailty, nutritional status, polypharmacy, and fall risk. CONCLUSION: Intrinsic capacity decline was highly prevalent among older adults. Routine multidomain geriatric assessment may help identify vulnerable individuals and guide early preventive interventions.

papers.title: Exploring Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality for Inclusive Geometry Teaching in Resource-Constrained Classrooms
papers.authors: Thabisa T. Maqoqa
papers.journal: International Journal of Virtual and Personal Learning Environments
papers.abstract: This study explores the use of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) for inclusive geometry teaching in resource-constrained classrooms. It addresses learner exclusion caused by spatial reasoning demands, language barriers, anxiety, and limited infrastructure. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses‒guided systematic literature review of peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025 was conducted, grounded in an integrative theoretical model positioning artificial intelligence‒enabled technologies as pedagogical mediators. Findings show that AR/VR can enhance spatial visualisation, engagement, and conceptual understanding when aligned with inclusive design. However, effective implementation depends on teacher competence, affordable technologies, and concept-focused assessment. The study recommends low-cost AR/VR tools, targeted teacher development, and inclusive assessment strategies, while highlighting the need for longitudinal classroom research.

papers.title: Algorithmic Trust And Ai Literacy In Shaping Economic Decision-Making: The Role Of Perceived Autonomy As A Mediating Variable
papers.authors: Muhammad Ricky Syahputra Hendri, Anisyah Nur Kuswati, Budi Suryowati
papers.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence in economic activities continues to increase, but it poses a risk of dependency if not accompanied by rational trust and adequate literacy. This study aims to analyze the relationship between algorithmic trust and AI literacy on economic decision-making, both directly and through perceived autonomy as a mediating variable. The research method uses a quantitative explanatory approach through a survey of 200 AI user respondents in Indonesia. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Square Structural Equation Modeling. The results of this study are expected to demonstrate the extent to which algorithmic trust and AI literacy encourage more critical and responsible economic decision-making through the psychological mechanism of user autonomy. The novelty of this research lies in placing perceived autonomy as an empirical mediating variable, rather than merely an ethical issue, in the context of economic decision-making in developing countries. Keyword: Algorithmic Trust, AI Literacy, Perceived Autonomy, Economic Decision Making.

papers.title: Penguatan Kompetensi Digital Guru melalui Integrasi GeoGebra dan Artificial Intelligence dalam Pengembangan Media Pembelajaran
papers.authors: Siti Dinarti, Faridatul Masruroh, Siti Munawaroh, M. Aminullah Mughni
papers.journal: BERDAYA Jurnal Pendidikan dan Pengabdian Kepada Masyarakat
papers.abstract: Digital transformation in elementary education requires strengthening teachers’ competencies in developing interactive and adaptive learning experiences. However, teachers at SDI Al-Fattah Jombang still face challenges in visualizing abstract mathematical concepts and utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI) to develop instructional materials. This Community Service (PkM) program aimed to strengthen teachers’ digital competencies through integrated training and mentoring in developing GeoGebra- and AI-based learning media. The program involved 14 teachers and adopted a participatory approach through workshops and hands-on coaching, comprising orientation, integrated training, technology implementation, mentoring, and evaluation. The program was evaluated through pretest and posttest assessments, practical observations, product assessments, and participant satisfaction surveys. The results showed an increase in teachers’ average competency scores from 40.71 on the pretest to 84.64 on the posttest, with an N-Gain of 0.74, classified as high. A total of 12 teachers successfully developed GeoGebra-based learning media, 13 produced AI-assisted instructional materials, and 11 integrated both technologies. Product assessment yielded an average feasibility score of 91.55%, categorized as highly feasible, while participant satisfaction reached 95.09%, categorized as very satisfied. These findings indicate that practice-based training and mentoring can strengthen teachers’ digital competencies and encourage the application of technology in instructional development.

papers.title: ChatGPT in het vreemdetalenonderwijs
papers.authors: Lili Hargitai
papers.abstract: This study focuses on the use of ChatGPT in foreign language education in Flanders.Given the recent rise of ChatGPT and the lack of systematic research on this topic (BaidooAnu, D., & Owusu Ansah, 2023), the emphasis is on the experiences and perceptions oflanguage teachers. Through a survey conducted among Flemish teachers, their familiaritywith, sense of competence in, and applications of ChatGPT are mapped out. Additionally,concerns and needs regarding this technology are investigated. The results indicate thatthe majority of teachers are familiar with ChatGPT and find it useful for gathering teachingmaterials and didactic tips. However, concerns about its use persist. The main issuesrequiring attention are: (1) ethical concerns such as plagiarism, (2) the lack of guidelines,and (3) the need for training with a focus on responsible use. Furthermore, a positivecorrelation is found between the presence of school guidelines and teachers’ sense ofcompetence in using ChatGPT.

papers.title: Integrative Epistemology in Islamic Education: Classical Tradition and AI Challenges
papers.authors: Suyono Suyono, Indi Aunullah, Adeseko Sunday Olaifa
papers.abstract: Current research remains mostly technocratic and fragmented, neglecting the integration of ethical, spiritual, and revelatory aspects into Islamic educational philosophy, even as artificial intelligence (AI) advances rapidly and transforms the epistemological underpinnings of education. This research reexamines the works of Al-Ghazali and Ibn Rushd, who represent opposing epistemological traditions of spiritual-intuitive and rational-empirical approaches, to create an integrative framework that bridges this gap. Primary writings by scholars, along with current literature on AI and education, serve as the main data sources for this study, which takes a qualitative philosophical-hermeneutic methodology. The research employs comparative and interpretive analysis to examine key themes, including dehumanization, algorithmic bias, and the existential threats posed by AI in educational settings. The research recommends an integrated epistemological framework that methodically integrates revelation (wahy), reason ('aql), and ethical practice (akhlaq) into the learning process. Ethical-spiritual consciousness is presented as the cornerstone of the synthesis, with logical inquiry serving as its operational mechanism within a complementary framework. In the age of artificial intelligence, this leads to a new theoretical framework, "integrative Islamic AI-oriented epistemology," that provides a comprehensive conceptual foundation for developing intellectually sound, morally grounded, and spiritually focused instructional methods. Meskipun kemajuan kecerdasan buatan (AI) sangat cepat dan mengubah dasar pemahaman pendidikan, penelitian yang ada masih cenderung teknis dan terpisah, serta belum menggabungkan aspek etis, spiritual, dan wahyu dalam pendidikan Islam. Untuk mengatasi kekurangan tersebut, penelitian ini mengkaji kembali pemikiran Ibn Rushd dan Al-Ghazali yang mewakili tradisi rasional-empiris dan spiritual-intuitif secara saling melengkapi untuk membangun kerangka pemahaman yang terintegrasi. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan metode filosofis-hermeneutik, dengan sumber data utama adalah karya-karya asli kedua tokoh serta literatur modern tentang AI dan pendidikan. Melalui analisis interpretatif dan perbandingan, penelitian ini meneliti masalah dehumanisasi, bias algoritma, dan tantangan eksistensial dalam pendidikan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan suatu model epistemologi terintegrasi yang menghubungkan wahyu, akal, dan akhlak secara sistematis dalam proses pembelajaran. Sintesis ini menempatkan kesadaran etis-spiritual sebagai dasar, sementara rasionalitas dan berpikir kritis berfungsi sebagai alat operasional. Temuan ini menghasilkan formulasi teoretis baru yang disebut “epistemologi Islam terintegrasi berbasis AI,” sebagai dasar konseptual untuk pengembangan praktik pendidikan yang cerdas secara intelektual, kuat secara etis, dan mendalam secara spiritual di era kecerdasan buatan.

papers.title: Evaluation of the effect of manipulator calibration accuracy on the target-reaching accuracy of a robotic surgical navigation system
papers.authors: Natalia Andreevna Dvoyashkina, Ilyas Gaidarovich Magomedov, Denis Sergeevich Trapeznikov, Alexander Vladimirovich Kolsanov, Чаплыгин Сергей Сергеевич, Denis Vitalyevich Zotov, Vladimir Viktorovich Krylov, Alexander Vladislavovich Prirodov, Michael Mikhailovich Tymoshenko
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the effect of manipulator calibration accuracy and the geometric arrangement of calibration points on the resulting target-reaching accuracy of a robotic surgical navigation system. Materials and Methods. The study was conducted using an anthropomorphic head phantom equipped with a monocular optical system and a REDS-C10 collaborative robotic manipulator integrated with the Autoplan surgical navigation system. Seven calibration configurations were established using different combinations of calibration points, varying in number and spatial distribution across the calibrator planes. For each configuration, three calibration conditions were investigated: standard calibration (without error), calibration with a 0.5-mm error in the specified calibration needle length, and calibration with an artificially introduced error in determining the positions of the calibration points. Each experimental condition was repeated five times. Positioning accuracy was assessed based on the mean deviation of the robotic manipulator flange from the specified trajectory. Results. Introducing errors into the calibration parameters resulted in an increase in positioning deviation compared with standard calibration. The most pronounced effect was observed for errors in determining the positions of the calibration points: the relative increase in deviation for configurations C, E, and F was 384.9%, 179.4%, and 218.3%, respectively. Introducing an error in the specified calibration needle length resulted in an increase in deviation ranging from 42.4% to 131.1% for configurations A–F. The most balanced results were obtained for configuration B, for which the increase in deviation was 42.4% with an error in needle length and 56.3% with errors in determining the calibration point positions. Conclusion. The results demonstrate the influence of calibration quality on the positioning accuracy of the robotic manipulator. Errors in determining the positions of the calibration points had a more pronounced effect on the resulting deviation than errors in the specified calibration needle length. Correct calibration and the reliability of the parameters determined during the calibration procedure are important prerequisites for accurate and safe operation of the robotic surgical system.

papers.title: Hyperparameter Optimization of Random Forest for Multiclass Classification of Student Academic Performance Using Multidimensional Factors
papers.authors: Sri Nurhayati, Diana Effendi, Bobi Kurniawan Soegoto, Adam Mukharil Bachtiar, Hanhan Maulana, Ednawati Rainarli
papers.abstract: Classification for academic performances among students in a multi-class scenario is a challenging task due to its dependencies on multiple factors and characteristics, particularly in the medium academic performance category. This scenario makes it a problem for some models with their conventional settings in terms of their ability to optimally distinguish categories of academic performances while being used in classification tasks, thus leading to the need for optimization techniques in enhancing their performances. This research paper will design an optimization strategy for improving the performances of the Random Forest algorithm in a multi-class academic performance classification among students. This will help in enhancing decision-making systems in education. The research method used is a machine learning approach with a Random Forest algorithm optimized through hyperparameter tuning using RandomizedSearchCV. This study utilizes secondary student data obtained from the Kaggle public repository, consisting of 6,607 data points with 20 determining factors covering academic, behavioral, social, environmental, and health aspects. The results showed that Random Forest hyperparameter optimization was able to improve model performance from a baseline accuracy of 79.56% to 81.08% on the validation data, and achieved an accuracy of 81.69% on the test data. In addition, there was an improvement in performance in the Medium category classification, as indicated by an increase in the F1-score value from 0.69 to 0.72. Therefore, the optimization of Random Forest proved to be good in enhancing the performance and stability of multiclass classification of student academic performance.

papers.title: AI Adoption for PMO Transformation in GCC Banks: An Expert-Refined TOE Model
papers.authors: Aditya Ajit Baswan, Nanda Kumar Karippur, Vanita Bhoola
papers.abstract: Although the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in banking has accelerated across customer-facing and operational domains, its application within Project Management Offices (PMOs) remains underexplored, particularly in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) banks, where PMOs support portfolio governance, transformation, and IT strategy execution. Drawing on the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, with the Organizational Project Management Maturity Model (OPM3) serving as a complementary PMO-context lens, this study develops an expert-refined model of conditions perceived as important for AI adoption in GCC banking PMOs. A mixed-methods survey combining Likert-scale items and open-ended responses was completed by 61 experts. Quantitative analysis was performed to assess the experts’ endorsements, as well as thematic analysis to interpret their contextual meanings. All eight literature-derived constructs received endorsement, with management support, governance practices, and organizational readiness receiving the strongest mean endorsements. The experts interpreted AI-enabled PMO transformation as an organizationally led process involving governed data, leadership sponsorship, capability-building, accountable governance, regulatory assurance, and context-relevant vendor support. This study contributes a contextually grounded TOE-based model of AI adoption for PMOs in GCC banks and offers practical considerations for PMO professionals, banking executives, regulators, and AI vendors. It should be noted that the reported findings are exploratory and reflect expert perceptions, rather than supporting causal or predictive relationships.

papers.title: A Gaussian Mixture Model-Based Machine Learning Framework for Reference-Food Carbon Footprint Estimation in the Food and Beverage Sector
papers.authors: Thing-Yuan Chang, Chien-Chih Chen, Chin-Hsien Hsu, Fong Kin Law, Hsi-Lin Chang
papers.abstract: Product carbon footprint estimation can support early screening in the food and beverage sector, but life cycle assessment requires detailed inventory data that are often unavailable. Machine learning can estimate reference-food impacts from food descriptors; however, whether grouping training outcomes improves prediction remains uncertain when unseen foods must be routed using predictors alone. To examine this gap, we present and evaluate a Gaussian mixture model (GMM)-based framework combining outcome-specialized regressors with neighbor-based routing. Multilingual LEAF names are linked to AGRIBALYSE 3.1.1 climate-change values and enriched with non-environmental descriptors and CIQUAL nutrients, yielding 471,970 observations across 1562 reference codes. Within each training fold, a univariate GMM defines hard or overlapping alpha-cut subsets for K-nearest-neighbor, random-forest, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) regression. Five predictor-space neighbors determine majority or weighted routing. Evaluation uses ten repetitions of five-fold cross-validation grouped by reference code, with training-only preprocessing and fitting. Weighted routing lowers mean root mean squared error (RMSE) relative to majority routing across matched configurations. Weighted fuzzy random forest at alpha = 0.1 reduces mean RMSE from 3.465 to 3.136 kg CO2e/kg, while global XGBoost achieves the lowest RMSE of 2.773. No primary comparison is significant under corrected repeated cross-validation tests with Holm adjustment. Target-value-grouped sensitivity analysis retains the principal learner-dependent pattern. These findings identify limits to outcome-based specialization rather than general superiority, supporting further investigation of reference-impact screening without replacing product-specific life cycle assessment.

papers.title: The Environmental Cost of AI Hype: Corporate AI Catering, Pollution Emissions, and Sustainability Governance
papers.authors: Jingwei Hu, Shuaiwen Chang
papers.abstract: The long development cycle and high investment requirements of artificial intelligence (AI) conflict with the short-term incentives prevailing in capital markets, leading some firms to cater to market expectations through promotional rhetoric rather than substantive investment, possibly at the expense of long-term sustainability commitments. This study examines whether such AI catering affects corporate pollution and under which conditions. Using Chinese A-share listed firms with firm-level emission records from 2016 to 2024, we measure AI catering as AI disclosure in excess of the level predicted by observable substantive AI input and estimate its effect with firm and year fixed-effects models. AI catering is associated with higher pollution emission intensity, whereas substantive AI input is associated with lower intensity. Lower environmental investment and environmental disclosure quality account for part of this association. The association is stronger under formation conditions that make substantive AI adoption costly and weaker under detection and penalty conditions that make laxer pollution control easier to discover and more costly. This study contributes to research on corporate sustainability by revealing an organizational and governance cost of technology hype, distinct from AI’s direct environmental footprint, and suggests that regulators and investors should verify the substantive basis of corporate AI claims.

papers.title: Financial Inclusion or Digital Discrimination? Algorithmic Credit Decisions and Gender Inequalities: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Alexander Haro-Sarango, Silvia Cachay-Salcedo, Jessica Karina Saavedra-Vasconez, Freddy Jesús Robles-Lirio, José Ismael Campos-Ku
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of financial technologies has repositioned algorithmic credit decision systems as central gatekeepers of economic opportunity, raising a fundamental sociological question: Do these systems broaden financial inclusion or do they reproduce—and potentially amplify—gender inequalities under a veneer of technical neutrality? This scoping review maps the scientific literature at the intersection of algorithmic credit decisions, financial inclusion, and gender, following the PRISMA-ScR protocol and combining bibliometric and thematic analysis. A corpus of 279 peer-reviewed documents (English-language articles and reviews, 2022–2026) indexed in Scopus was charted, exhibiting a compound annual growth rate of 31.6%, 4445 accumulated citations (h-index = 32), and a highly skewed citation distribution (Gini = 0.819). Production is led by the Global South—India (n = 64), Indonesia (n = 32), and South Africa (n = 19)—while co-word and semantic cluster analysis reveals five research fronts organized around digital financial literacy, gender and banking, artificial intelligence and blockchain, microfinance and the Sustainable Development Goals, and algorithmic risk assessment. The gender-focused subcorpus (n = 58; 20.8%) and the algorithmic credit subcorpus (n = 49; 17.6%) intersect in only 11 documents (3.9%), exposing a critical research gap precisely where the promise of inclusion and the risk of discrimination collide. This overlap is no larger than independence would predict (expected = 10.2; Fisher’s exact p = 0.85) and stays below 5% under alternative tagging dictionaries, while documents authored exclusively by Global South institutions receive 44% fewer citations than comparable documents. Evidence charted from the corpus documents both inclusionary effects (expanded access for thin-file borrowers, reduced transaction costs) and exclusionary dynamics (gender-miscalibrated credit scores, predatory digital lending, algorithmic opacity, and intersectional data gaps). Rurality, informal employment, ethnicity, and migration status are rarely analyzed together with gender, and an integrative conceptual model links structural conditions, intersecting social positions, data regimes, and algorithmic pipelines to inclusionary, predatory, and exclusionary outcomes. The review proposes an agenda oriented toward algorithmic auditing with gender-disaggregated data, regulatory frameworks for fairness in credit scoring, and the integration of feminist data perspectives into fintech design, arguing that financial inclusion and digital discrimination are not mutually exclusive outcomes but coexisting logics of the same socio-technical infrastructure.

papers.title: Assessing Residents’ Perception of Ecosystem Services in Urban Green Spaces in the Rapidly Urbanizing Himalayan City of Srinagar (Jammu and Kashmir), India
papers.authors: Tuba Naqshbandi, Nashmeen Showkat, Javaid M. Dad
papers.abstract: Urban green spaces (UGSs) serve multiple purposes. Most existing research uses questionnaires to capture how residents use and perceive various UGS ecosystem services (ESs), without documenting what is available and accessible to residents and without identifying underlying patterns. This study addresses this gap by first documenting UGSs in Srinagar, India, and then understanding their usage patterns and ES perceptions by using advanced machine learning. After documenting and mapping all 237 UGSs across Srinagar city, we surveyed 420 respondents across 20 selected UGSs, from April to July 2025, using a semi-structured questionnaire. We then applied a self-organizing map (SOM) to identify patterns, non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) to picture them and permutation-based analysis to recognize key factors. The results show three distinct user groups, while NMDS showed that education, proximity to UGSs and visitation frequency were the main driving factors behind these three groups. There were clear contrasts between the three groups. Young students frequently visited UGSs and identified them as critical for psychological restoration and emotional well-being (Cluster I). Individuals with no formal education, older adults and housewives who live nearby UGSs utilize them for physical activity, child supervision and social cohesion (Cluster II). The engagement of middle-aged government employees and farmers/laborers was characterized by a utilitarian appreciation, and they emphasize the economic value of UGSs, specifically resource harvesting and livelihood support (Cluster III). These findings underscore the importance of considering differences between user groups when planning and managing UGSs.

papers.title: Ketones and Sleep: A Narrative Review of Mechanisms, Preclinical Models, and Human Evidence
papers.authors: Jack C. Jensen, Parker C. Leavitt, Christa J. Nehs
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Sleep is a metabolically dynamic state, and ketone bodies may interact with sleep physiology as both oxidative substrates and signaling metabolites. β-Hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate (AcAc), and acetone rise during fasting, carbohydrate restriction, ketogenic diets used for therapeutic or non-therapeutic purposes, prolonged exercise, selected pathological states of insulin deficiency, and after consumption of exogenous ketones. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and human evidence linking endogenously generated ketosis and ketosis generated from exogenous ketone consumption to sleep architecture, sleep quality, sleep-disordered breathing, and sleep-relevant metabolic pathways. Methods: We reviewed studies involving ketogenic diets, fasting or caloric restriction, and consumption of exogenous ketones, prioritizing investigations with polysomnography, electroencephalography (EEG), sleep architecture, respiratory, or validated sleep-questionnaire outcomes, while also considering mechanistic studies of neuronal excitability, inflammation, epigenetic regulation, circadian timing, and brain energetics. Results: The most direct preclinical evidence indicates that AcAc, but not BHB, increases slow-wave activity (delta power 0.5–4 Hz) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and suppresses glutamate release in mice, supporting a potential role for ketone metabolism in sleep homeostasis. Dietary, fasting, and aging models further suggest that lipid/ketone metabolism can alter NREM/rapid eye movement (REM) balance, circadian metabolic rhythms, and sleep–wake responses to energetic stress, with aged-rat data showing sex-specific REM and cognitive effects of ketogenic interventions. Human studies are suggestive but heterogeneous: acute carbohydrate restriction can increase slow-wave sleep and reduce REM sleep in healthy adults; ketogenic therapies may improve subjective sleep in selected neurological and metabolic populations; and ketone ester ingestion can improve sleep efficiency after strenuous evening exercise, but not during hypoxia-induced sleep disruption. Conclusions: Ketones are sleep-relevant metabolic signals, but their effects are conditional rather than universally sleep-promoting. They may also indirectly affect sleep by enhancing wakefulness quality. The ketone concentration range associated with optimal sleep outcomes remains undefined, and potential dose-, timing-, and context-dependent effects on sleep require further study. Future studies should distinguish AcAc from BHB biology, measure nocturnal ketone dynamics, incorporate PSG/EEG spectral endpoints, and separate ketosis-specific effects from weight loss, energy deficit, exercise load, respiratory physiology, circadian timing, and disease-related confounders.

papers.title: Information Disclosure Strategies of Live-Streaming E-Commerce Supply Chains in the AI Era: A Game-Theoretic Analysis
papers.authors: Ke Yan, Shaobo Chen, Qi Zhang
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of live-streaming e-commerce and artificial intelligence, human and AI live-streaming have become two product information disclosure formats in online retail. From the perspective of product information disclosure, we develop a game-theoretic model of a live-streaming e-commerce supply chain comprising a brand owner and an e-commerce platform. We derive Stackelberg equilibria under the resale mode through backward induction, obtain the optimal retail price and information disclosure level under the agency mode through joint optimization, and then compare disclosure-format and sales-mode preferences. The results show that (1) AI live-streaming does not always achieve a higher information disclosure level. It leads to a higher disclosure level only when consumer trust in AI live-streaming disclosure is high, or when trust is moderate and sensitivity to the information disclosure level is low; otherwise, human live-streaming disclosure achieves a higher disclosure level. (2) Under the resale mode, the brand owner and the e-commerce platform have consistent preferences regarding disclosure formats. Both prefer AI live-streaming when consumer trust in AI disclosure is high, or when trust is low but sensitivity is also low, whereas both prefer human live-streaming when trust is low and sensitivity is high. Under the agency mode, their preferences diverge when consumer trust is low and sensitivity is moderate. (3) Regarding sales modes, the brand owner prefers the agency mode only when the commission rate and consumer sensitivity to information disclosure are both low; otherwise, it prefers the resale mode. These findings provide theoretical and managerial implications for disclosure-format selection and sales-mode decisions in live-streaming e-commerce.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Natural Language Processing of Low-Resource Indigenous Languages in the Americas: A Systematic Review of Methods, Applications, and Effectiveness
papers.authors: J. E. Cruz, Vilma Sarmiento Mamani, Helarf Calsina, Víctor Yana-Mamani, Ferdinand Pineda, Christian Augusto Romero Goyzueta, Saúl Huaquipaco Encinas, Luis Baca, Wilson Mamani
papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in multilingual artificial intelligence, Indigenous languages of the Americas remain underrepresented in natural language processing (NLP) because of limited corpora, annotations, benchmarks, and reusable resources. This systematic review examines AI-based NLP research on low-resource Indigenous languages published within the 2022–2026 review window. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance and an expanded source-verification and supplementary-search process, the final analytical corpus comprised 283 unique records. Machine translation was the most represented application domain (58.3%), followed by language documentation (51.2%), Indigenous-language education (30.4%), and speech technologies (28.6%). Transformer-related architectures (54.1%) and BERT-based models (34.6%) showed the greatest literature visibility, although verified implementation/evaluation was substantially lower than terminology-level occurrence. Quechua (39.2%) and Guarani (33.6%) were the most represented languages.
