Reduced perceived stress emerged as a potential pathway to symptom improvement. To our knowledge, this is the first trial supporting purpose-built, safety-first generative AI for mental health prevention and early intervention in an unscreened population.

papers.title: Functional neuroimaging as a tool to understand social determinants of health in cognitive aging and ADRD: a scoping review
papers.authors: Jade E. Jenkins, Adea Rich, Isabella Manrique, Shirine Moukaled, Natalie L. Marchant, Owen Thomas Carmichael
papers.abstract: The social, structural, and physical conditions in which individuals live, work, and age, collectively termed social determinants of health (SDOH), are associated with risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Differences in brain function in later life may offer understanding of how SDOH become biologically embedded and confer differential ADRD risk. However, how functional neuroimaging techniques have been used to study SDOH in cognitive aging and ADRD has yet to be systematically characterized. We therefore conducted a scoping review. Three databases were searched, 2,930 articles were screened, and 41 studies were included. Education was the most frequently studied SDOH domain, accounting for 65.9% (k = 27) of studies, followed by economic and occupation (k = 9, 22.0%), social and community (k = 5, 12.2%), food (k = 4, 9.8%), and physical environment (k = 3, 7.3%). Of the 41 studies, five (12.2%) examined multidomain determinants and one study (2.4%) examined three determinants each from different domains. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was most frequently employed (k = 31, 75.6%), followed by electroencephalography (EEG; k = 7, 17.1%), and magnetoencephalography (MEG; k = 4, 9.8%). One study (2.4%) employed a multimodal approach, while none used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Resting state paradigms (k = 27, 65.9%) outnumbered task-based (k = 14, 34.1%) and most studies were cross-sectional (k = 38, 92.7%). The predominant focus on education, fMRI, and cross-sectional designs highlights many opportunities for future investigation of how SDOH may be associated with later life brain function.

papers.title: LLM agents in online communities draw fewer replies and more disagreement when labeled as AI
papers.authors: Sara Major, Aleksandar Tomašević, Ana Vranić, Darja Cvetković, D. Vudragović, Boris Stupovski, Marija Mitrović Dankulov
papers.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) accounts now post, reply, and vote alongside people in online communities. Visible identity labels may act as cultural markers that set these accounts apart from human participants. In a field experiment on YSocial, a Reddit-like platform, 36 students at a Serbian university discussed globally circulated popular culture in English alongside 72 AI accounts with persistent personas and relationship-specific memories over 21 experiment days. AI accounts were labeled in one community and unlabeled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, the estimated probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher under hidden labels, given the same eligible earlier thread contributions (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In browser telemetry, the disadvantage of AI-authored posts in direct thread entry from the feed was 4.4 percentage points smaller under hidden labels (95% credible interval 0.8–8.1). In both communities, participants were more likely to answer an AI account that had just replied to them. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4), mainly criticism of content; the corresponding gap in downvotes from other participants was also larger there, and nearly all references to AI identity occurred there. Toxicity differences were uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less selection and more criticism of AI contributions.

papers.title: The Neural Correlates of Implicit Emotion Regulation through Affect Labeling as Reflected in EEG
papers.authors: Jinyu Chen, Johanna M.P. Baas, Leon Kenemans, Irene van de Vijver
papers.abstract: Affect labeling reduces emotional responses during and immediately after use, but evidence for lasting regulatory effects remains mixed. While there is no experiential evidence for lasting effects, psychophysiological studies do hint at a longer-lasting impact. However, neuroimaging research has mainly compared affect labeling with affect matching. Although both involve emotional processing, affect labeling additionally engages linguistic processing. Thus, it remains unclear whether observed neural differences reflect emotion-focused labeling or mere linguistic processing, and whether such effects endure over time. We recorded EEG to examine the effects of affect labeling on negative emotion across two re-exposure phases: immediate and after a short interval (15 minutes). Affect labeling (emotion-specific words) was compared with affect matching (emotion-focused perceptual processing) and feature labeling (linguistic processing without emotional content), allowing us to dissociate emotional and linguistic components. Event-related potentials and EEG oscillatory activity were analyzed in both phases, with pre-intervention neural responses included as baseline. Robust emotion-related neural activity was observed. Negative (vs. neutral) stimuli elicited increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes, enhanced fronto-central-parietal theta power, and greater right-hemispheric alpha activity. However, LPP, theta-, and alpha-band power did not show effects of affect labeling compared to the control conditions. Thus, the present findings provide no evidence for a lasting labeling effect. Because we focused on re-exposure, we may have missed potential regulatory effects during the intervention itself. Future research should further identify factors that influence the effectiveness of labeling and clarify when this implicit emotion regulation pathway is engaged.

papers.title: Flourishing-Centered AI: Designing AI for the Multiple Goods and Tensions of Living Well
papers.authors: Louis Tay, Karina Vold, Gloria Liou, Harsh Kumar, Daniel Harris, Ashton Anderson
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of AI creates both opportunities and risks for human well-being and flourishing, underscoring the need for an integrative interdisciplinary framework to guide its design and evaluation. We advance a flourishing-centered AI framework that draws together philosophical, behavioral, interactional, and technical perspectives. We conceptualize human flourishing as multidimensional, encompassing subjective well-being, psychological functioning, character virtues, and psychological richness. This broader conception of flourishing extends existing approaches by explicitly incorporating character and other goods, and by confronting the possibility that these goods cannot always be maximized simultaneously. Two cross-cutting tensions arise: a temporal tension concerning immediate versus longer-term benefits, and a self-community tension concerning individual versus collective outcomes. We show how these tensions can be translated from behavioral objectives and measurable outcomes into interactional strategies and technical design choices. We conclude with implications for researchers and developers designing AI systems and for policymakers governing their use.

papers.title: Humanizing AI-generated exemplars: Human-source framing facilitates group creative ideation
papers.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong, Yingning Lu, Yihui LIU, Yueyue Ge, Qiannan Ruan, Ke Jiang, Kelong Lu
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

papers.title: PRECOG: Comprehensive Experimental Design and Stimuli Protocol for Investigating Depression and Suicidal Ideation
papers.authors: Myzelle Hughes, Colin McDaniel, Takfarinas Medani, Woojae Jeong, Idan Blank, Dani Byrd, Thomas Austin McGee, Kleanthis Avramidis, Sudarsana Reddy Kadiri, Aditya Kommineni, Chinmay Chinara, Kristina Lerman, Elsi Kaiser, Richard M. Leahy, Shrikanth Shri Narayanan, B. Rael Cahn, Assal Habibi
papers.abstract: The Multimodal Integration of Neural and Biobehavioral Signals for Predicting Preconscious Responses (PRECOG) project investigated the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying depression and suicidal ideation through a series of cognitive tasks paired with continuous multimodal physiological and neurophysiological recordings. A total of 160 college-aged participants, including healthy controls, individuals with depression without suicidal ideation, and individuals with depression and suicidal ideation, were recruited based on screening using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) and the Suicide Ideation Scale (SIS).The experimental protocol included three primary cognitive tasks: (1) an emotional Stroop task to assess attentional biases toward affectively charged and suicide-related words, (2) a sentence processing task examining neural responses to self-referential statements varying in emotional and suicidal content, and (3) the Death-Brief Implicit Association Task (D-BIAT) to measure implicit associations with life and death. EEG and other physiological signals were recorded continuously throughout all tasks. Additionally, resting-state recordings (with eyes open and eyes closed) were obtained before, between, and after the emotional Stroop and sentence tasks.Neurophysiological data were acquired using 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electrocardiography (ECG), and galvanic skin response (GSR), and were supplemented with eye tracking and high-frame-rate facial video recordings. By integrating neural, behavioral, and physiological measures, the PRECOG study aimed to advance our understanding of cognitive and emotional processing in depression and suicidality, ultimately contributing to more precise risk assessment and targeted clinical intervention.

papers.title: Students’ Attitudes Toward ChatGPT Use in English Assignments
papers.authors: Alfred Snae
papers.journal: Journal of English Language and Education
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence has created new possibilities and new tensions in English language learning. This study examines undergraduate students’ attitudes toward using ChatGPT for English assignments and considers whether students view it as more helpful or harmful. A descriptive quantitative survey was conducted with 129 students from the English Education and Christian Educational Management programs at Universitas Kristen Artha Wacana. Data were collected through a five-point Likert questionnaire and two open-ended questions, then analyzed using frequencies, percentages, means, and thematic coding. The findings show generally favorable perceptions: 63.6% agreed or strongly agreed that ChatGPT made assignments easier, and 56.6% reported better understanding of English materials. At the same time, 64.3% were concerned that excessive use could reduce independent writing ability. Students also expressed uncertainty about academic integrity, while 66.7% supported official lecturer guidance. Overall, ChatGPT was perceived as a useful learning aid, but its value depended on critical and responsible use rather than substitution for students’ own work.

papers.title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the Banking Sector: A Systematic Review and Thematic Synthesis
papers.authors: Yuniatin Trisnawati, Tiara Anindya Virana, Andi Asrihapsari
papers.abstract: Banks are increasingly adopting artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to automate routine tasks, assess creditworthiness, manage risks, and support strategic decision-making. This study conducts a systematic literature review of 91 Scopus-indexed publications following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with study quality assessed using MMAT 2018 and CASP frameworks. The review examines theoretical perspectives on AI adoption by banks and consumers, factors influencing implementation, and implications for financial performance, credit risk management, and regulatory compliance. The findings indicate that institutional AI adoption research commonly uses institutional theory, Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE), Resource-Based View (RBV), and Resource Orchestration Theory (ROT). In contrast, consumer adoption studies frequently apply the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), UTAUT2, and Diffusion of Innovation theory. Successful AI implementation depends on technological infrastructure, employee capabilities, fintech competition, and regulatory certainty. AI adoption can improve financial performance, corporate governance, compliance efficiency, and creditworthiness assessments. However, challenges involving data security and privacy, algorithmic transparency, and financial system stability remain significant concerns. This review provides insights for banking executives and policymakers to develop effective, transparent, and ethically responsible AI adoption strategies.

papers.title: Pre-service teachers’ AI literacy: An exploratory study of predecessor literacies and personal characteristics predictors
papers.authors: Andreja Istenič Starčič, Tina Lekan Kraševec, Žiga Turk, Maja Lebeničnik
papers.abstract: Literacy is embedded in social practices that adopt socially constructed technologies. In the 20th century, the invention of the computer facilitated information literacy and computational thinking. Media literacy emerged alongside the development of media. In the 21st century, the accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots using conversational language has expanded significantly, creating a need for their integration in education. AI literacy is being studied within frameworks similar to those of its predecessors, requiring conceptualization and differentiation from related literacy concepts. As of 2025, teacher education regarding AI literacy has been identified as an under-researched area. This article examines AI literacy through the lens of pre-service teachers’ literacy competencies that will shape the literacy practices of future generations. During their own schooling, the current generation of prospective teachers encountered information, digital, and media literacy, as well as computational thinking; these are analyzed here as predictors of AI literacy, measured using the scale for the assessment of non-experts’ artificial intelligence literacy (SNAIL) instrument. Personality traits and mindset are also investigated as predictors of the prospective teachers’ professional competence. The study was conducted in 2024/25 with a sample of pre-service teachers. The research questions are: What is the structure of AI literacy in the sample? To what extent can AI literacy be predicted by components of information literacy? How much of AI literacy can be explained by various established technology-related literacies? To what extent do personality and mindset contribute to predicting AI literacy? The findings confirmed a two-factor solution for SNAIL, comprising technical understanding and critical application. Student perception of information literacy skills proved accurate in predicting the critical application of AI. In addition to information literacy, predictors included the media production subscale of media literacy and mindset. Technical understanding of AI was predicted by the media production subscale, the computational thinking subscales algorithmic thinking and cooperativity, and the personality trait of agreeableness. Establishing AI literacy as an essential teacher competency requires thorough research into AI’s educational impacts and strict alignment with pedagogical goals. Navigating the ethical and moral dimensions of AI usage provides the necessary foundation for this literacy. Consequently, training programs can intentionally foster AI competence by merging specialized literacy modules with algorithmic thinking, media production, and growth-mindset interventions.

papers.title: Geodynamical processes and natural hazards
papers.abstract: This volume contains the abstracts presented at the VI International Scientific Conference “Geodynamic Processes and Natural Hazards”, dedicated to the 80th anniversary of the Institute of Marine Geology and Geophysics, Far Eastern Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences. The volume includes the results of fundamental and applied research on natural processes and hazardous phenomena, contemporary geodynamic processes, seismicity and volcanism, tsunamis and other hazardous marine phenomena, oceanic and atmospheric dynamics, and the state and variability of natural and natural–technogenic systems. Particular attention is given to research conducted on Sakhalin Island, the Kuril Islands, Kamchatka, and in other regions of the Russian Far East and the Asia-Pacific. The contributions address the monitoring and assessment of natural hazards, interactions among the Earth’s geospheres, the state of marine and terrestrial ecosystems, climate-driven changes, geoecological processes, and the consequences of human impacts. The volume presents modern methods of instrumental observation, Earth remote sensing, geoinformation and mathematical modelling, processing of large observational datasets, as well as applications of machine learning and intelligent systems in environmental research. The conference brings together scientists and specialists from research institutions and universities in Russia and other countries, as well as early-career researchers, postgraduate students, and students. The conference proceedings reflect the current state of research into natural processes and disasters and advances in methods for their observation, analysis, and forecasting. They will be of interest to specialists in Earth sciences, oceanography, geophysics, geology, geography, ecology, and related fields.

papers.title: A PRIVACY PRESERVING PERSONAL AI ASSISTANT AND THE COST OF CLOUD MODEL INFERENCE: ARCHITECTURE, CAPABILITY TRADEOFFS, AND EVALUATION PROTOCOL
papers.authors: Aravind Chinnaraju
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
papers.abstract: Personal AI assistants need reliable research and controlled access to private data. This report specifies a local-first Windows architecture and examines the capability, privacy, and operating-cost tradeoff between local Llama 3.2 3B through Ollama and self-hosted Kimi K2.5 on rented NVIDIA GPUs. We analyzed a supplied project design summary, mapped trust boundaries and failure modes, and calculated illustrative costs from a documented eight-H200 deployment and published rental rates. The design separates public research from authenticated browser sessions, enforces permissions outside the model, and requires evidence-supported answers. At an illustrative $4.59 per GPU-hour, eight H200s cost $36.72 per running hour, $4,406.40 for four hours daily over 30 days, or $26,438.40 for continuous 30-day operation, before storage and operations. An assumed 100 W incremental local draw for four hours daily at $0.15/kWh costs $1.80 monthly on an existing PC. These are scenarios, not measured deployments. Kimi K2.5 offers multimodal and agentic capabilities that a text-only 3B baseline should not be assumed to match; no matched end-to-end test was performed. Stronger cloud inference can impose substantial dedicated GPU rental cost and transfers prompts to a cloud operator. Local inference preserves a narrower data boundary at far lower incremental cash cost but requires direct task-quality evaluation.

papers.title: Pengembangan Kreativitas Digital Siswa SMA 1 Sedayu melalui Pelatihan Prompt Engineering Berbasis Framework Role-Task-Context
papers.authors: Intan Permatasari, Iva Mindhayani, Siti Lestariningsih, Izat Ganang Dwi Putra
papers.journal: Jurnal Pengabdian Masyarakat - Teknologi Digital Indonesia
papers.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed learning and working paradigms, shifting the primary challenge from merely seeking information to the ability to formulate precise instructions (prompting). Despite high technology access in Senior High Schools (SMA), its utilization remains largely superficial. This research aims to enhance students' AI literacy skills—encompassing conceptual understanding, ethical awareness, and information verification—through structured prompt engineering training. The study employed a quantitative approach with a pre-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design involving 31 students at SMA 1 Sedayu, Bantul, Yogyakarta. The intervention was delivered through training based on the Role–Task–Context (RTC) framework and hands-on practice using mobile devices. Data analysis included normality tests (Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov), Spearman correlation, and paired samples t-tests. The results indicated a significant increase in mean scores, rising from 57.10 in the pre-test to 89.68 in the post-test. Statistically, |t-Stat| (18.16) > t-Critical (2.04) with a significance value of (p < 0.05), leading to the acceptance of the alternative hypothesis (H_1). A strong Pearson correlation (0.759) demonstrated students' consistency in adopting new techniques. The training successfully transitioned students from passive technology consumers to proactive information managers. In conclusion, integrating prompt engineering as a life skill can transform students' digital behavior from mere entertainment into sophisticated productivity tools, while simultaneously strengthening digital literacy in the digital creative economy era.

papers.title: IMPLEMENTASI CHATBOT AKADEMIK RULE-BASED BERBASIS CLOUD MENGGUNAKAN LARAVEL STUDI KASUS: INFORMATIKA UST
papers.authors: Muhammad Caesar Aditya, Titik Rahmawati, Agung Priyanto, Eka Yulia Sari
papers.abstract: Layanan informasi akademik di perguruan tinggi masih menghadapi berbagai kendala, seperti keterbatasan akses layanan, ketergantungan pada jam operasional administrasi, serta belum terintegrasinya media penyampaian informasi. Kondisi tersebut menyebabkan mahasiswa mengalami kesulitan memperoleh informasi akademik secara cepat, tepat, dan efisien. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengimplementasikan chatbot akademik berbasis Rule-Based dengan dukungan teknologi cloud menggunakan framework Laravel sebagai media layanan informasi akademik pada Program Studi Informatika Universitas Sarjanawiyata Tamansiswa. Pengembangan sistem dilakukan menggunakan metode Rapid Application Development (RAD) yang terdiri atas tahapan Requirement Planning, User Design, Construction, dan Cutover. Sistem dibangun dengan arsitektur Model-View-Controller (MVC), memanfaatkan basis data PostgreSQL berbasis cloud, serta menerapkan Rule Engine untuk mencocokkan kata kunci dengan aturan yang telah ditentukan sehingga menghasilkan respons yang sesuai. Hasil implementasi menunjukkan bahwa sistem berhasil menyediakan fitur pengelolaan Rule Engine, manajemen kata kunci, dashboard, analitik, serta layanan percakapan chatbot berbasis web. Pengujian menggunakan metode Black Box Testing menunjukkan seluruh fungsi sistem berjalan sesuai dengan kebutuhan yang telah dirancang. Sementara itu, hasil User Acceptance Test (UAT) memperoleh tingkat penerimaan pengguna sebesar 86,56%, yang termasuk kategori sangat baik. Hasil tersebut menunjukkan bahwa chatbot mampu memberikan layanan informasi akademik yang lebih cepat, konsisten, mudah diakses, dan meningkatkan kepuasan pengguna.

papers.title: Exploring Demographic Differences in EEG-Based Machine Learning Classification of Schizophrenia
papers.authors: Guransh Singh
papers.journal: Undergraduate Research in Natural and Clinical Science and Technology (URNCST) Journal
papers.abstract: Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder for which objective diagnostic tests are not available, resulting in continued reliance on subjective clinical assessments. Renewed interest in the use of electroencephalography (EEG) as a source of objective neural biomarkers has emerged alongside recent advances in machine learning that improve predictive power. However, the performance of EEG-based machine learning models across demographic groups remains insufficiently investigated. This exploratory study examined the classification performance of EEG-based machine learning models and potential demographic performance differences within a publicly available schizophrenia dataset. The dataset consisted of 81 participants, including 49 individuals with schizophrenia and 32 healthy controls. Following data cleaning and preprocessing, Logistic Regression and Random Forest classifiers were developed and evaluated using a five-fold stratified participant-level cross-validation framework. Model performance was assessed using classification accuracy, confusion-matrix measures, and demographic subgroup comparisons. An additional analysis compared models using EEG and demographic variables combined, demographic variables only and EEG variables only. Logistic Regression achieved a participant-level accuracy of 75.31%, while Random Forest achieved 69.14%. Logistic regression correctly classified 79.10% of male participants and 57.14% of female participants; however, only 14 of the 81 participants were female, limiting interpretation of this observed disparity. The demographics-only Logistic Regression model achieved 74.07% accuracy, compared with 75.31% for the combined model and 60.49% for the EEG-only model. The EEG-only model classified all participants as having schizophrenia, indicating poor discrimination between diagnostic groups despite its overall accuracy. Random Forest feature importance analysis also assigned relatively high descriptive importance values to demographic variables. These findings identify differences in classification performance and feature-set contributions with this dataset but should not be interpreted as evidence of established demographic bias or clinical diagnostic reliability. The small, demographically imbalanced sample limits generalizability and larger, independent and more representative datasets are needed to determine whether these patterns persist across the broader populations.

papers.title: Professionalization of sociologists in digital sociology: competencies, barriers, and institutional strategies
papers.authors: Т. Н. Каменева
papers.abstract: The article examines the professionalization of sociologists in the field of digital sociology. The relevance of the study stems from the fact that digital sociologists currently combine classical sociological reflection with professional competencies in big data analysis, machine learning, and the management of various digital environments. Drawing on an analysis of theoretical and methodological approaches to professionalization and the results of a qualitative empirical study (in-depth interviews with educators, students, and employers; N=25) conducted in January 2026 in Moscow and St. Petersburg, the author identifies key stages in the formation of the professional group of digital sociologists. The article demonstrates that professionalization takes place under conditions of a gap between the academic tradition and the technological dynamics of the labor market, which generates institutional barriers (a shortage of practitioner-educators, obsolescence of educational standards, and the absence of a unified professional community). The necessity of transitioning from spontaneous adaptation to a deliberate institutionalization of digital sociology as both a subdiscipline and a professional field is substantiated. The conclusion argues for the development of new professional standards and educational programs that integrate professional competencies combining theoretical sociological methodology with IT skills.

papers.title: How creative industries perceive and embrace AI
papers.authors: Natalya Anatolyevna Kostko, Irina F. Pecherkina, P. Е. Posokhova
papers.abstract: The Artificial Intelligence perception by creative industries representatives is analyzed using the future theories synthesis and the technology adoption model. The research approach is based on a literature review and semi-structured interviews with creative industries managers/representatives of Tyumen, followed by a thematic analysis. The AI application in creative industries is considered through the lens of future theories prism, which contributes to the emerging body of knowledge about the contempt towards this technology, possibilities and concerns of applying this technology in the industry. In addition, the study allows to increase knowledge about creative industries representatives and their readiness for digital changes. The results indicate that technologies are being perceived as a good in the realm of processes and a challenge — in the realm of meaning. This points to the hybrid model for the creative industries technological development, where digitalization is integrated into practice without the cultural basis of activity substitution. The key to its legitimacy is maintaining the balance between innovation and humanistic values. Technological development of Tyumen creative sector could be described as a reflexive modernization where industries are actively embracing digital tools, while striving for comprehension in their boundaries and implications institutionally and meaningfully.

papers.title: Fast education in the era of artificial intelligence: institutional lag and human-centered compensation
papers.authors: Елена Александровна Литаш-Сорокина
papers.abstract: The purpose of the article is to develop a conceptual framework for analyzing fast education as a compensatory mechanism for the institutional lag between education and work under digitalization and the spread of artificial intelligence. The study is conducted as a theoretical and conceptual analysis with elements of analytical comparison across technological clusters: GenAI and prompt engineering, cybersecurity, no-code / low-code, data and AI literacy. The article distinguishes fast education as a short-term educational format from fast education as a logic of educational acceleration, in which the value of learning is linked to the speed of skill acquisition, credentialing, and labor market presentation. It is shown that fast educational formats temporarily reduce the gap between changing labor requirements and the slower transformation of curricula, qualification frameworks, assessment procedures, and mechanisms for recognizing competencies. The main result is the substantiation of the dual function of fast education: it supports the subject’s rapid adaptation, but under weak institutional support it transfers the burden of continuous self-updating to the individual. The article identifies the social, cognitive, and psychophysiological limits of such compensation, including anxiety about professional obsolescence, dependence on credentials, technostress, learning fatigue, and the risk of forming procedural skills vulnerable to automation. The conclusion is that the productivity of fast education is determined not by speed itself, but by the integration of fast modules into a human-centered architecture for developing critical thinking, self-regulation, metacognitive control, professional judgment, and personal-professional effectiveness.

papers.title: What should teachers upload to GenAI? A privacy-aware framework for language education
papers.authors: Lok Hei Locky Law
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly intertwined with language education, teachers are expected to integrate AI-supported materials development into their pedagogical practice. However, discussions of GenAI in the field have largely focused on pedagogical innovation and student use, while giving comparatively little attention to the protection of student data and the responsible handling of educational resources. This article argues that data privacy and security should be regarded as core components of teacher GenAI literacy. Adopting a conceptual and practice-oriented approach, it proposes a privacy-aware decision framework for GenAI use that helps teachers align the level of data sensitivity with appropriate GenAI environments, including public cloud-based platforms, institutionally supported services, and offline local GenAI tools. Drawing on research from computer science, cybersecurity, and platform governance, the article suggests practical strategies for reducing privacy risks, including removal, masking, and splitting, before discussing how key considerations relating to student data protection, network security, institutional confidentiality and copyright restrictions may influence teachers’ decisions when selecting GenAI tools. Using examples from language materials development, the article illustrates how educators can use GenAI to adapt disciplinary texts, create differentiated learning materials, and generate pedagogical resources while reducing unnecessary disclosure of sensitive information. The article concludes by advocating a more balanced approach to GenAI integration in language education, one that combines pedagogical innovation with informed and responsible data practices.

papers.title: Cited, Ignored, or Invented: How AI Searches Decide What's True
papers.authors: Rebecca Bakker
papers.abstract: We've all used ChatGPT or an equivalent tool by now. But do we know why it might give a student a different answer than it gives you? Or why the same question gets a different answer when dictated, translated, or repeated ten minutes later? This session, presented at SEFLIN 2026, pulled back the curtain on how these predictive engines actually function. It explored where they gather information, why they confidently invent facts, and how they quietly profile users. Attendees learned why a library's website might be completely ignored by AI crawlers, and why friendly chatbot designs lower our critical defenses. The session closed with practical strategies for reference, instruction, and keeping library resources visible to AI search tools, and offered three questions to ask of any AI answer: Where did this come from? What's missing? Could this be made up?

papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Political Communication in Contemporary Conditions: Features, Technologies, and Practices
papers.authors: Сергей Васильевич СЕМЁНОВ
papers.abstract: The article examines the challenges associated with the use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in politi-cal communication. It analyzes the key risks related to the algorithmic manipulation of public opinion, the gen-eration of synthetic content (deepfakes), the dissemination of personalized and targeted disinformation, the reinforcement of information bubbles and echo chambers, and the persistence of a regulatory vacuum. Based on an analysis of international case studies – from the Cambridge Analytica scandal to the use of deepfakes in election campaigns in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Hungary – the article argues that the use of AI in contemporary political interaction creates qualitatively new threats the digital and information security of the society and undermines the fundamental foundations of democratic institutions. Particular attention is paid to the algorithmic shaping of public opinion, the increasing issue of algorithmic bias, and the inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms, including the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The study concludes that there is a need for a comprehensive approach that combines regulatory and legal measures, improvement of technical measures and countermeasures, and enhancement of citizens’ digital literacy.

papers.title: The Value-Normative System of the Culture of Artificial Intelligence: An Anthropological Turn in the Age of “Smart” Networks
papers.authors: Evgeniya K. Belikova
papers.abstract: The article describes the principal sociocultural states produced within the culture of artificial intelligence (CAI): civilizational, substantial, axiological vacuum, inversion, and destructive. It is noted that all of these states can be observed almost simultaneously, owing to the rapid pace at which the AI culture is developing. The article assesses how these states relate to the anthropological turn, which entails a reconsideration of the human role in cultural practices: AI acts as a tool that expands human capabilities rather than replacing them. In the “human + machine” framework, fundamental cultural categories – primarily authorship and creativity – are being trans-formed. Authorship becomes distributed and is increasingly interpreted as a property of the “human + algo-rithm” system, whereas creativity remains the prerogative of humans with their capacity to formulate tasks, in-terpret results, endow them with meaning and assume responsibility for what is created. At the same time, hu-mans retain a leading role: rather than adapting to the logic of the machine, they direct and make sense of its operation. The study of CAI and its value-normative system is necessary because it helps us understand the large-scale shifts in cultural practices and value orientations caused by the spread of these technologies.

papers.title: Readiness of Rural Residents to Use Artificial Intelligence in Agrarian Business
papers.authors: Viktor Viktorovich Shalin, Tatiana A. Zhukova, Andrey A. Sergeev
papers.abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of the awareness and readiness of rural residents and agricultural com-plex workers in Russia to use products and solutions created with artificial intelligence (AI). The work is based on a secondary analysis of data from the nationwide survey conducted by the VCIOM Analytical Center (N = 1604, weighted sample). It is shown that at the nearly level of the general awareness of AI application in agri-culture, the readiness of its usage is sharply differentiated by age: it is declining more than twofold from Gen-eration Z to boomers generation. The research defines with the logistic regression that besides age, it is con-sidered that education, income, type of settlement and gender are significant predictors of readiness, while frequency of internet use loses its meaning once other factors are controlled for. Multiple correspondence analysis revealed that these characteristics form a coherent gradient of digital and innovative inclusion. Factor analysis of eighteen statements about the benefits and risks of AI identified three orthogonal dimensions of perception – techno-optimism, ethico-naturalistic risk, and techno-systemic risk, of which only the first two ef-fectively predict readiness to adopt the technology. Drawing on the latent profile analysis, four stable attitude types – from techno-enthusiasts to ethical sceptics differing not only in the degree of perception factors but also in socio-demographic composition – are highlighted. These findings are interpreted in light of diffusion-of-innovations theory and technology-acceptance models.

papers.title: The Impact Of Artificial Intelligence Usage On Learning Effectiveness and Academic Motivation Among University Students
papers.authors: Ariel Febrian, Zidni Ma’ruf, Keyza Ariq Ronaldi, Royan Hidayah
papers.journal: Jurnal Pendidikan Teknologi Informasi dan Vokasional
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly influenced higher education, including the emergence of AI-based learning applications such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Perplexity. While prior studies have examined the role of AI in general academic settings, limited attention has been given to its use within vocational, practice-based education, where learning outcomes are closely tied to technical skill development. This study aims to describe vocational students' perceptions of AI use in learning, particularly in relation to learning effectiveness and academic motivation, among students at a vocational institution in Palembang. A quantitative descriptive design using the survey method was employed, involving 50 respondents selected through purposive sampling based on their active use of AI-based learning applications. Data were collected through a 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire distributed online and analyzed descriptively using frequency and percentage distributions. The findings indicate that most respondents held positive perceptions of AI, particularly regarding its role in helping them understand lecture material, complete assignments more efficiently, and study independently. However, perceptions were more divided regarding the accuracy of AI-generated information and its contribution to time management, suggesting that the perceived benefits of AI are not uniform across all aspects of learning. Respondents also emphasized that AI cannot replace the role of lecturers. These findings suggest that, when used appropriately alongside critical thinking and lecturer guidance, AI is perceived by vocational students as a supportive tool for practice-based learning. This study is limited by its small sample size, single-institution scope, and reliance on self-reported data without inferential analysis, and future research employing larger samples, validated instruments, and objective learning measures is recommended.Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Learning Effectiveness; Academic motivation; Vocational Education; Vocational Student

papers.title: Interactive proofs for verifying (quantum) learning and testing
papers.authors: Matthias C. Caro, Jens Eisert, Marcel Hinsche, Marios Ioannou, Alexander Nietner, Ryan Sweke
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of testing and learning from data in the presence of resource constraints, such as limited memory or weak data access, which place limitations on the efficiency and feasibility of testing or learning. In particular, we ask the following question: Could a resource-constrained learner/tester use interaction with a resource-unconstrained but untrusted party to solve a learning or testing problem more efficiently than they could without such an interaction? In this work, we answer this question both abstractly and for concrete problems, in two complementary ways: For a wide variety of scenarios, we prove that a resource-constrained learner cannot gain any advantage through classical interaction with an untrusted prover. As a special case, we show that for the vast majority of testing and learning problems in which quantum memory is a meaningful resource, a memory-constrained quantum algorithm cannot overcome its limitations via classical communication with a memory-unconstrained quantum prover. In contrast, when quantum communication is allowed, we construct a variety of interactive proof protocols, for specific learning and testing problems, which allow memory-constrained quantum verifiers to gain significant advantages through delegation to untrusted provers. These results highlight both the limitations and potential of delegating learning and testing problems to resource-rich but untrusted third parties.

papers.title: TRAIL-AI Reporting Framework for AI-Mediated Evidence and Scientific Provenance: A Special Communication (Preprint)
papers.authors: Elia Lima-Walton, Shabbir Syed-Abdul, Philip Scott
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in literature retrieval, evidence synthesis, data analysis, interpretation, and manuscript development. Current guidance from journals and professional organizations emphasizes disclosure of AI use, transparency, and human accountability. However, disclosure alone may not reveal how AI-mediated processes influence evidence selection, reasoning pathways, or the scientific claims ultimately reported. Given growing concerns regarding fabricated citations, unsupported assertions, inconsistent terminology, and nontransparent evidence transformations, additional mechanisms are needed to ensure scientific trustworthiness. OBJECTIVE To propose TRAIL-AI (Transparent Reporting and Audit of AI-Mediated Literature, Evidence, and Inference), a reporting framework designed to improve transparency, traceability, and accountability for AI use that materially influences scientific evidence, analysis, interpretation, or conclusions. METHODS We reviewed emerging recommendations and reporting guidance addressing generative AI in scientific publishing and biomedical research and identified gaps related to scientific provenance and evidence traceability. Building on these observations, we developed TRAIL-AI as a conceptual framework focused on consequence-sensitive reporting of AI-mediated scientific activities. The framework consists of 13 reporting items organized into five domains: (1) task and threshold, (2) resources and retrieval, (3) AI-mediated actions, (4) inspection and verification, and (5) lineage and responsibility. TRAIL-AI introduces a proportional reporting model with three levels: Level 1 for expressive or mechanical assistance, Level 2 for evidence-influencing activities, and Level 3 for inference-influencing activities requiring claim-level provenance documentation. The framework additionally incorporates semantic provenance through the use of recognized clinical terminologies and emphasizes human verification and investigator accountability. RESULTS TRAIL-AI extends existing AI reporting approaches by linking AI-mediated operations to the evidence and claims they influence. The framework introduces a structured provenance statement for evidence-influencing use and a claim-level ledger for selected high-consequence scientific assertions. Key reporting elements include documentation of AI systems and accessible resources, retrieval and screening processes, affected evidence and claims, verification of source existence and claim support, management of evidentiary uncertainty, terminology normalization, preservation of audit records, and designation of accountable investigators. The framework prioritizes reconstructability, allowing reviewers and readers to inspect consequential AI-assisted scientific processes without requiring exact reproduction of nondeterministic model outputs. CONCLUSIONS TRAIL-AI proposes a practical approach for strengthening transparency and accountability in AI-assisted scientific research. By moving beyond simple disclosure toward provenance-based reporting, the framework seeks to ensure that material scientific claims remain traceable to identifiable evidence, documented AI-mediated actions, standardized clinical concepts, and accountable human judgment. Future work should evaluate the framework through consensus development, pilot implementation, and prospective studies assessing validity, reliability, feasibility, and its impact on the identification of unsupported or inadequately documented scientific claims.

papers.title: Clinician Educators Developing No-Code Tools for Educational Record Management With Generative AI: A Six-Step Tutorial (Preprint)
papers.authors: Se Jin Baek
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Clinician educators may wish to develop small tools for educational record management but find it difficult to begin without programming experience. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support development, but educators must verify that proposed configurations preserve educational meaning. OBJECTIVE To present a practical workflow for clinician educators collaborating with GenAI to develop educational record management tools and critically review AI proposals. METHODS The tutorial draws on the development and redesign of a surgical residency training management system. A worked example using synthetic departmental education records illustrates cumulative and placement-specific review. An implementation appendix and an English-language Notion demonstrator support the exercise. Actual development principles are distinguished from specifications reconstructed for teaching. RESULTS The workflow comprises six steps: defining the educational question and scope, reviewing record structure, building a minimum implementation, testing exceptions, defining review actions and responsibilities, and extending the tool while preserving existing meanings. Each step connects clinician judgments, AI tasks, acceptance criteria, and a tangible output. The example addresses missing links, uncertain placement attribution, incorrect relationships, and activity-date criteria while preserving historical completion records. The demonstrator includes six practice pages and independently preserved intermediate states. Saved-view results and selected exception manipulations have been checked; complete visual inspection and independent reproduction by users without development experience remain unverified. CONCLUSIONS The workflow connects educational requirements with implementation and review of AI-assisted tools. Its central principle is to preserve completion evidence while distinguishing placement attribution and retrieval criteria. Independent reproducibility and educational effectiveness require further evaluation.

papers.title: Effect of Sleep Hygiene on Metabolic Syndrome in an Adult Rural Population in India: Protocol for a Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Rishabh Kothari, Sonali Gajanan Choudhari
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) refers to a group of conditions including high blood pressure, excess weight, high blood glucose, and abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels that together substantially increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. Poor sleep hygiene is associated with a higher likelihood of type 2 diabetes, while sleep duration can affect the development of various MetS components. Approximately 25% of adults worldwide currently have MetS, and this prevalence is projected to increase to 50% by 2035. However, there is a distinct lack of evidence about the specific impact of sleep hygiene on cardiometabolic health within the rural Indian population. This study will focus on addressing this literature gap by evaluating these risk factor associations by using validated tools to help develop targeted community interventions. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to estimate the prevalence of poor sleep quality and cardiometabolic risk factors in a rural Indian population and to determine the association between sleep hygiene and cardiometabolic risk factors. METHODS: This study will be a community-based, cross-sectional, analytical study, and data collection will be carried out by trained personnel using validated tools during house-to-house visits. In this cross-sectional study of 281 rural Indian adults aged ≥40 years, sleep quality will be assessed via the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (a score >5 indicates poor sleep), alongside direct measurements of blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, BMI (≥25 kg/m² for obesity), waist circumference, and the Madras Diabetes Research Foundation-Indian Diabetes Risk Score for diabetes risk. Data will be collected through a door-to-door approach, with informed consent entered into Google Forms, and quality checked via training and regular reviews. Using R software, analyses will include prevalence estimates with 95% CIs; chi-square or t tests for associations between poor sleep and cardiometabolic risks; and logistic regression (P<.05) adjusted for confounders such as diet, stress, and physical activity. RESULTS: This study began in January 2025 with conceptualization and ethics approval obtained in June 2025. Data collection commenced in August 2025 following Clinical Trial Registry-India registration, with 53 participants enrolled as of May 5, 2026. Standardized tools (GAD-7, PHQ-9, and GPAQ) were incorporated to assess key confounding variables. Data collection is projected to finish by January 2027, with final analysis and study conclusion expected by March 2027. CONCLUSIONS: The relationship between MetS and sleep hygiene warrants greater attention, particularly as poor sleep habits become increasingly prevalent alongside MetS. This study will deepen the understanding of their connection, paving the way for targeted interventions and prevention strategies. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trial Registry-India CTRI/2025/08/092892; https://tinyurl.com/3sak2h9x. INTERNATIONAL REGISTERED REPORT IDENTIFIER (IRRID): DERR1-10.2196/90117.

papers.title: Addressing the Engagement Blind Spot: 12-Tip Tutorial to Make Reasoning Audible in Health Professions Education
papers.authors: Inthrani Raja Indran, Dujeepa Dasharatha Samarasekera
papers.abstract: Unlabelled: Student engagement reforms have increased active learning in higher education. However, visible participation does not always require students to rehearse the spoken, interactive forms of reasoning central to professional practice, such as explaining one's thinking, responding to challenges, building on others' ideas, and working through uncertainty in real time. We describe this gap as an engagement blind spot. We define audible reasoning as the deliberate externalization of disciplinary or professional reasoning through spoken interaction so that its assumptions, evidence, uncertainty, and justification can be examined, challenged, revised, and developed collaboratively. It is particularly relevant in health professions education and also applies to laboratory-based and scientific disciplines where students must communicate their reasoning under conditions of uncertainty, scrutiny, and collaboration. Digital, hybrid, asynchronous, and AI-enabled learning environments sharpen this blind spot. Shared documents, online quizzes, discussion boards, and generative AI tools can support participation and access; however, they can also allow students to engage without speaking or to produce polished answers without making the underlying reasoning visible. In this context, educators need to ask not only whether students are engaged but also what behaviors they are rehearsing and whether their reasoning is available for examination and development. This tutorial offers 12 practical, evidence-informed tips developed iteratively from recurring challenges encountered in teaching, curriculum design, and faculty development and refined against selected literature. The tips are organized around 4 clusters covering the design of activities that require audible reasoning, the elicitation of reasoning in practice, the development of reasoning through listening and response, and the preservation of audible reasoning in digital and AI-enhanced environments. Across these 4 clusters, we suggest small but intentional shifts that help educators move from silent, constructive tasks toward audible, dialogic, and professionally relevant participation. These include designing tasks around uncertainty, creating low-stakes opportunities for spoken reasoning, using digital tools to surface and organize contributions for further discussion, structuring active listening and peer feedback, reviewing group dialogue formatively, and using conversational AI as a rehearsal partner rather than an authority. These strategies require attention to psychological safety, cultural responsiveness, accessibility, equity, privacy, data governance, and ongoing monitoring. Audible reasoning is not synonymous with speaking more, volunteering more frequently, or sounding fluent. Designing for audible reasoning is not simply an engagement strategy. It is a way of helping students practice the communicative and collaborative behaviors needed to explain, defend, question, and revise human judgment in clinical, scientific, and other professional contexts.

papers.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices of Malaysian Pharmacists Regarding AI Adoption: Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Chee Tao Chang, Xin-Jie Lim, Jason Choong Yin Lee, Chii-Chii Chew, Yen Jun Wong, Huan‐Keat Chan, C. Thum, Kar Meng Yew, Shiau Hueh Yeow, Rajan Philip
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: AI is increasingly integrated into health care systems worldwide, with growing implications for pharmacy practice. Although studies have reported general perceptions of AI, gaps between awareness and practical implementation remain evident, particularly in middle-income settings. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the baseline knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) of Malaysian pharmacists regarding AI adoption in pharmacy practice and identify factors associated with these domains. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted using a self-administered online questionnaire distributed to registered pharmacists practicing in Malaysia. The instrument comprised 12 knowledge items, 10 attitude items, and 5 practice items and underwent expert review and pilot testing. KAP scores were categorized using Bloom cutoff points as good (80%-100%), moderate (60%-79%), or poor (<60%). Data were analyzed using R statistical software. RESULTS: A total of 407 pharmacists completed the survey. The median knowledge score was 75 (IQR 67-92), with 42.3% (172/407) of pharmacists demonstrating good knowledge. The median attitude score was 82 (IQR 76-94), and 64.6% (263/407) of pharmacists exhibited positive attitudes toward AI. However, the median practice score was 56 (IQR 44-68), with 54.3% (221/407) of pharmacists classified as having poor AI use in practice. Statistically significant but weak positive correlations were observed among the 3 domains. Pharmacists with postgraduate qualifications demonstrated significantly higher knowledge scores (P=.01). CONCLUSIONS: Malaysian pharmacists demonstrated moderate knowledge and positive attitudes toward AI. However, the practical integration of AI into routine pharmacy workflows remained limited. Strengthening institutional support, structured training, and implementation frameworks may be necessary to translate perceived readiness into clinical adoption.

papers.title: Thinking with arts: the development of critical citizenship competencies in the ArTrust project
papers.authors: Rita Gomes da Silva Basílio, Ana Catarina Mateus Monteiro
papers.journal: Revista Ibero-Americana de Estudos em Educação
papers.abstract: Faced with growing robotization and the development of artificial intelligence, human beings will have to coexist with the precision of automated means. And this necessarily implies an educational commitment to human competencies. Education must strengthen the fight against violence, discrimination and injustice, aiming at sustainable human development and education for peace. This implies a transformation in the ways of doing/thinking, as well as of the learning spaces and times, where arts become performing agents of a social, emotional and intercultural learning. In this context, we present ArTrust +Art-Citizenship, outlining the guidelines, methodologies and results of the project. Based on the implementation of 47 Art-Citizenship initiatives, involving 1557 participants, we will focus on the potential of the arts to, in an interdisciplinary way, enhance the development of intercultural competencies and the promotion of creative practices.

papers.title: Primary Study on AI-powered English Learning in Islamic University Samarinda, Indonesia
papers.authors: Umar Fauzan, Nor Shahila Mansor, Nadia Nadia
papers.journal: EDUCASIA Jurnal Pendidikan Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran
papers.abstract: AI is increasingly being used in education. However, there has been limited research on the trust and attitudes of educators toward the integration of AI in Indonesia’s Islamic Universities. This study employs a qualitative phenomenological approach. The primary data source are English-speaking university lecturers in Indonesia, while secondary data source include literature such as proceedings, journal articles, theses, and dissertations on the integration of AI in Indonesia’s Islamic Universities. The results show that AI tools like ChatGPT, Quillbot, Grammarly, Turnitin, Mendeley, Zotero, and others are being used to assist students with their lecture assignments, data analysis, and even writing scientific papers. Google Translate, Grammarly, and ChatGPT are particularly popular in English lectures. However, students’ misconceptions about AI usage have made teaching more challenging, as there are concerns that students may become overly reliant on the technology and not invest enough effort in their studies. To address these issues, it is essential for teachers to receive training in AI to become more proficient and to help students use AI tools effectively, dispelling misconceptions about the technology.
