papers.title: AI : THE CAPEX THE MODEL DOES NOT NAME, On the $1.5 Trillion Stochastic Path, the $2.1M Deterministic Path, the Ratio That Changes the Equation, and the 4 Norms That Open the Market
papers.authors: M. TAALABI, Team LLM-DIPLOMAT
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: On October 19th, 2026, a post on Substack https://open.substack.com/pub/generativevalue/p/what-has-to-go-right-to-justify-the?utm_source=share&utm_medium=android&r=3nsea2 asked a question that the AI industry has not answered: "What has to go right to justify thetrillions being spent on AI CapEx?" The post models $1.5 trillion in CapEx for 2027. It estimates the revenue threshold at $600 billion by late 2027 and $1.1 trillion by 2028. It names three conditions: the frontier keeps getting better at high-value work, AI diffuses through the economy, and value doesn't get whittled away by competition. The post is correct about the question. It is incomplete about the answer. This paper argues that the post names the cost of the stochastic architecture, but does not name the alternative architecture — one that requires almost no CapEx at all. The paper makes four claims: First: The stochastic path requires $1.5 trillion in CapEx. It cannot be certified under anyfunctional safety standard. It produces the four walls: CapEx, hallucination, energy, water, and AlCapone-LLM. Second: The deterministic path requires $2.1M–$6.5M for the first deployment. It can be certified under ISO 26262, IEC 61508, DO-178C, and IEC 62443. It runs on a $12microcontroller. Third: The ratio is roughly 1:500,000. The two paths are not competing on the same economics. Fourth: The 4 norms are the certification path. The deterministic architecture passes them byconstruction. The stochastic architecture cannot pass them at all. The paper does not argue that creativity needs scaling. It argues that creativity is selection.Selection requires a criterion. A criterion is not a scale. It is a discovery. The corpus has 300+papers to prove it.

papers.title: STUDENT PERFORMANCE PREDICTION
papers.authors: Namrata Bhoite
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper, titled “Student Performance Prediction,” presents a conceptual framework for predicting students’ academic performance using educational data mining and machine learning techniques. The proposed system aims to help educators identify students who may benefit from timely academic support, mentoring, and personalized learning resources. The framework uses academic indicators such as attendance percentage, previous assessment marks, assignment completion, prior semester results, and learning participation. Its proposed workflow includes data collection, data validation, preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, evaluation, and presentation of predictions through an educator-facing dashboard. Candidate machine-learning algorithms include Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest. The paper discusses evaluating classification models using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrices. For numerical score prediction, Mean Absolute Error and Root Mean Squared Error may be used. The proposed architecture also includes intervention tracking, model monitoring, and explanations of prediction outputs. The study emphasizes student data privacy, fairness, interpretability, data quality, and responsible use of predictions. Model outputs are intended to support educators rather than replace teacher judgment or determine consequential decisions automatically. This is a conceptual study and does not claim original experimental results from a real dataset. Future work includes implementation, evaluation using institutionally approved academic data, fairness testing, and usability studies to determine the framework’s practical effectiveness.

papers.title: A synchronization sign error and a controller repair for a fractional discrete Ueda system
papers.authors: Zeraoulia Rafik
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Independent technical comment on Diabi et al., The Discrete Ueda System and Its Fractional Order Version: Chaos, Stabilization and Synchronization, Mathematics 13(2) (2025), 239 (doi:10.3390/math13020239). Subtracting the displayed master and slave equations identifies a cubic-sign error in the synchronization error system. The printed controller doubles the cubic difference instead of cancelling it, and the claimed diagonal matrix omits an off-diagonal term. An exact first-step check and reproducible high-precision full-memory computations document the discrepancy. Reversing the cubic term gives an upper triangular linear error system whose stability follows under the original gain restrictions. A separate correction replaces an exponent and characteristic polynomial in the incommensurate stabilization calculation; the decoupled stabilization conclusion remains valid independently. These findings concern the printed equations and do not establish how the original figures were generated or invalidate all chaotic-dynamics results. Includes the five-page manuscript, LaTeX source, Python verification code, instructions, and recorded output. The manuscript contains a disclosure of AI assistance. This is an independent preprint, not a publisher-issued corrigendum.

papers.title: The Synthetic Interviewee and the Human Frame
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This theoretical case study applies the published Scretching Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL), and SDM/D-SDM frameworks to September 2026 media interviews involving the synthetic AI character Tilly Norwood. Drawing on selected news reporting, it examines source attribution, artificial agency, humanlike communication, linguistic frame switching, conversational repair, and digital trust. The study proposes observational coding methods, theoretical equations, multidomain assessment criteria, and longitudinal models for evaluating human–AI interactions. Findings generate testable hypotheses rather than experimentally validated conclusions. The research establishes a proposed framework for distinguishing apparent social intelligence from authentic agency, verifiable identity, and reliable communication in synthetic media.

papers.title: Artificial to the intellect based flexible education technologies current to grow methodology
papers.authors: Jumanov Abbas
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This scientific article presents the final results of an experimental study focused on determining the effectiveness indicators for developing professional competencies—specifically regarding the implementation of educational technologies—among students in the field of energy. The study utilizes adaptive learning technologies based on artificial intelligence. The results, including average academic performance, were analyzed using Student's t-test and Pearson's chi-square (ch²) test—methods rooted in mathematical statistics.

papers.title: Hiding in Plain Sight - Suspicious Transparency and the Lessons of Literature
papers.authors: Emmanuel Alloa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Transparency is widely hailed as a cure for distrust, yet it frequently breeds the very suspicion it promises to dispel. Starting from the Epstein files and "Trumparency," this paper shows how the rhetoric of full disclosure fuels conspiratorial doubt. Building on critical transparency studies, it explains why transparency and secrecy are intertwined, and why transparency discourse shares with conspiracy theory the premise of a hidden "backstage." Yet concealment does not necessarily imply withholding access: evidence can be fully displayed and still go unseen, more effectively than behind a locked door. Literature–and detective fiction in particular–knows this all too well. The paper turns to literary strategies for hiding "in plain sight," and, from Poe and Conan Doyle to Christie, Chesterton and Borges, proposes a typology of five: attention redirection, informational drowning, mimetic camouflage, inferential misleading, and contractual exploitation. Transposed to political communication, these strategies help identify how timing, document dumps, procedural routine, paltering, and performative claims of openness steer the public's attention away from what is truly consequential. The paper concludes with the White House's AI chatbot America.gov, where opacity arises from excessive disclosure, not from withholding.

papers.title: PEDAGOGICAL CONDITIONS OF INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND GEOINFORMATION SYSTEMS IN GEOGRAPHY EDUCATION
papers.authors: Soataliyev Yorkinjon
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article analyzes the pedagogical conditions for using the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and geographic information systems (GIS) in geography education from a theoretical and methodological perspective. The didactic possibilities of digital technologies in the processes of searching, sorting, spatial analysis, mapping and interpretation of geographical data are highlighted. The main pedagogical conditions are based on the combination of AI and GIS tools with educational goals, the development of students' geographical and digital competencies, the improvement of teacher methodological training and the improvement of educational resources. A methodological approach is also proposed to organize integrated education.

papers.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DISCOURSE AS A NEW OBJECT OF LINGUISTIC RESEARCH: THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR THE STUDY OF LINGUODIDACTIC TERMINOLOGY
papers.authors: Bahronova Maftuna Farhodovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.journal: International Journal of Literature and Language Studies
papers.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has introduced new forms of human–machine communication and created a rapidly expanding linguistic environment in which natural language, computational processing, educational practices, and specialized terminology intersect. This article examines GenAI discourse as an emerging object of linguistic research, with particular attention to the formation and functioning of linguodidactic terminology. The study aims to establish a theoretical framework for analyzing terminology associated with language teaching and learning in generative AI-mediated communication. A qualitative conceptual approach was employed, combining discourse analysis, terminology studies, semantic analysis, and comparative linguistic perspectives. The article argues that linguodidactic terminology in GenAI discourse should be studied not as an isolated lexical inventory but as a dynamic relationship between term, concept, context, discourse function, and communicative purpose. The findings provide a theoretical basis for further English–Uzbek comparative research into the lexical-semantic structure, terminological derivation, and equivalence of emerging GenAI related linguodidactic terminology.

papers.title: Phasic Intention Derivative Resilience and Multi-Lobe Cortical Reallocation During Prolonged Lower-Limb Exoskeleton Control: A 2D Source-Space Phase-Space Framework
papers.authors: Nikil Shajan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for lower-limb exoskeleton control suffer from severe non-stationarity during prolonged ambulation, driven by central motor fatigue and electrode impedance drift. Standard classifiers relying solely on tonic primary motor cortex (M1) band power degrade rapidly as task duration extends. Here, we introduce a two-dimensional (2D) dynamical phase-space decoding framework, [W_P(t), dW_P(t)/dt], termed the Predictive Adaptive Temporal Tracking Unit (PATTU), which combines an autoregressive source-space intention state (W_P(t)) with its first-order phasic intention derivative (dW_P(t)/dt) reconstructed via anatomically constrained standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA). Evaluated across cross-session motor imagery (EEGBCI, N=10) and prolonged lower-limb exoskeleton ambulation (ds007788, N=7), adaptive phase-space boundary tracking restores cross-session classification accuracy from 55.87% to 65.51% (+9.64%, p = 0.0078) and achieves a cohort mean held-out ROC-AUC of 0.6730 during active exoskeleton control (peaking at 0.8257 in high-responder trials, with adaptive thresholding recovering accuracy from 53.76% to 73.76% in drift-affected runs). Longitudinal source-space tracking across 40-minute exoskeleton sessions reveals that while tonic paracentral M1 source power erodes under fatigue (declining in 5 of 7 subjects; -2.30% in sub-01), the phasic intention derivative remains resilient (1.202 s⁻¹ in early alert runs vs. 1.413 s⁻¹ in late fatigued runs; 119.5% mean retention), accompanied by a +150.0 ms relative within-subject onset latency shift (45.7 ms early vs. 195.7 ms late). Cortical surface mapping across six bilateral networks demonstrates that the central nervous system preserves phasic initiation velocity by dynamically reallocating relative source power from fatigued paracentral M1 generators toward prefrontal executive (+3.59%), supplementary motor, and primary somatosensory (S1, +1.34%) hubs.

papers.title: Why the World Needs Formed Leaders Now More Than Ever: Leadership Formation in an Age of Artificial Intelligence, Accelerating Change, and Human Uncertainty
papers.authors: Thando Sibanda
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the conditions under which leaders decide, delegate and exercise authority. Field and experimental evidence shows that generative AI can raise productivity on many knowledge tasks, but it can also lower the quality of decisions when people accept its outputs uncritically. Large practitioner surveys suggest that organizational readiness, including leadership alignment, is lagging behind individual adoption. Organizations have responded mainly by investing in skills: AI literacy, digital capability and updated competency models. This conceptual position paper argues that such investment is necessary but not sufficient. As technology widens what leaders can do, the quality of leadership depends more heavily on the leader's formation: the process through which purpose and identity are clarified and integrated, expressed as a recognizable leadership signature, and refined through ownership of the impact that leadership produces. Drawing on research into leader identity, developmental readiness, leader character, paradox, identity threat and automation bias, the paper defines leadership formation and the formed leader through the four dimensions of the Four Prints Method, a practice-derived framework: purpose, identity, signature and impact. Purpose and identity are treated as the measurable root of formation, signature as its expression and impact as its evidence. It then proposes a construct, grounded adaptability: the capacity to keep purpose, identity and ethical commitments coherent while revising strategies, methods and beliefs about means in response to new evidence. The construct is distinguished from paradox mindset, paradoxical leader behavior, organizational ambidexterity, adaptive leadership, learning agility and authentic leadership. Its proposed mechanism is the source of a leader's grounding. Grounding that rests on role-contingent attributes, such as expertise or position, is expected to make AI-driven disruption feel like a threat to identity, and so to provoke rigid or reactive responses. Grounding that rests on purpose and values is expected to support discriminating adaptation instead. The paper advances five testable propositions, specifies rival explanations and outlines research designs. Its implications for executive development, succession, AI governance and leadership education are each labelled by the strength of evidence behind them. The paper concludes that leader formation should be treated as a necessary, though not sufficient, part of preparing leaders to govern powerful technologies responsibly.

papers.title: APPLYING BIG DATA AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ANALYTICS TO ASSESS AND FORECAST EDUCATIONAL QUALITY
papers.authors: Almatov Ortiqboy Fayzullayevich, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.journal: International Journal of Literature and Language Studies
papers.abstract: This analytical study investigates how big data and artificial intelligence (AI) can support educational quality assessment and forecasting within higher education, including language-for-medical-purposes instruction. A structured narrative synthesis of policy documents and foundational peer-reviewed research is employed to define quality indicators, examine predictive modelling options, and develop a responsible implementation framework. The findings identify five interconnected components: interoperable data collection, validated indicators, transparent prediction, educator-led intervention, and independent impact evaluation. Two tables and two illustrative diagrams clarify the functional differences between reporting, learning analytics and AI-assisted decision support. The paper does not claim that an institutional model has been trained or validated. It concludes that predictive accuracy alone is insufficient: meaningful educational improvement requires fairness checks, privacy protection, human oversight and demonstrated benefits to learning outcomes.

papers.title: DEVELOPING CRITICAL AI LITERACY AMONG FUTURE ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS: EVIDENCE FROM AN EFL TEACHER-EDUCATION CONTEXT
papers.authors: Sevara Ziyaboyeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for language learning while raising important questions about the reliability, pedagogical appropriateness, and ethical implications of AI-generated content. In this context, developing critical AI literacy among future English language teachers has become an important objective of contemporary teacher education. This article examines the conceptual foundations and pedagogical dimensions of critical AI literacy, with particular attention to the preparation of prospective EFL teachers. The study employs a qualitative conceptual-analytical approach, drawing on established research on AI literacy, digital competence, technological pedagogical content knowledge, and international AI competency frameworks. The analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions of critical AI literacy: understanding AI systems, evaluating generated information, making pedagogically informed decisions, recognizing ethical risks, and reflecting on AI-supported teaching practices. It further proposes a practice-oriented framework that integrates critical evaluation, lesson design, classroom application, and reflective assessment into EFL teacher education. The article argues that effective AI literacy development requires a shift from operational familiarity with digital tools towards informed, independent, and responsible professional judgment. The proposed framework provides a theoretical basis for curriculum development and future empirical investigation. Since the present study does not include primary data collected from prospective teachers, the framework requires validation through classroom-based research.

papers.title: Use of AI in research
papers.authors: Saullo G. P. Castro
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This lecture for MSc students in aerospace engineering presents a workflow for research with AI agents, from the author's evaluation of large language models between ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, and Claude Opus 5.5. A use case shows an agent building a verified and validated Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam benchmarks of Krueger (2008) in one morning, with the researcher answering the decisive questions at checkpoints. The lecture discusses the responsible use of AI, how AI changes highly technical work, the growing role of experiments, and what this means for junior engineers. Lecture Given on 19 October 2026 as part of the Aerospace Structures and Materials core, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands. Contents Motivation for this lecture: why, after evaluating the new large language models every summer, Claude Opus 5 (August 2026) changed the author's way of working, and why the lecture was given now. Learning objectives: understand, evaluate and apply the author's way of working with novel AI models; create your own way of working with them; re-evaluate the role of a junior engineer in a world with AI. A brief history of large language models: from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-4 (2023). How AI entered my research/education workflows: ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 3, Gemini 3.1, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, and an analogy of three kinds of helpers. What fits inside current LLMs: tokens, context windows measured in papers, parameters against context, and the context of one agent session. Responsible use of AI: three rules, with a discussion: "Everything that can be automated should be automated"; "Focus on the crucial things, avoid the trivial things"; "Never delegate the decisions that make your work yours". My workflow with AI: a working folder in an integrated development environment, Claude as the agent, an HPC cluster as the simulation environment, and the state of the work kept in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat. Consequences of a workflow with AI: how research moves forward through verification, validation and new hypotheses; where AI can take over parts of this process; what changed in the author's work. Use case: a verified DCB model: the prompt (goal, ten ground rules, phases with checkpoints), one morning by the clock, and where the model stood at the end of it. Figures as code: TikZ: vector figures written by the agent from the models' own data. How has AI changed highly technical jobs: numerical work and theoretical research; the shift from executing calculations to synthesis and verification; why experiments matter more, including AI combined with mechanical testing. The AI workflow of a junior engineer: how engineers grew until about 2024, judging what the AI produces, and two discussions. Take-home messages. The use case The agent built an Abaqus model of the double cantilever beam (DCB) benchmarks of the NASA report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, following a prompt written as a contract: every value with its source, every analysis through scripts, failed runs kept, and stops at two checkpoints where the researcher decides. In one morning, the agent completed the environment check and the reference card (09:46 to 10:07), wrote the plan after the researcher's decisions at the first checkpoint (11:23 to 11:29), and built and verified the model after the second checkpoint: the first models ran at 12:07, and the model worked at 13:23. At that point, the unidirectional model agreed with the published Marc 3D results of Orifici and Krueger (2010) within 0.1 to 0.6 %, and with the 2008 report within 0.1 to 0.8 % once its crack fronts were taken 0.5 mm beyond the labelled lengths; the acceptance criterion of the approved plan was 2 %. Running the use case The file use-case.zip contains the prompt of the use case, PROMPT_use_case.md. The report it works from is not included; to run the use case: Download the report by Krueger (2008), NASA/TM-2008-215123, from the NASA Technical Reports Server, where it is available free of charge: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20080015439. In your project folder, create a subfolder named references and save the report there as references/krueger2008NASA.pdf. The file name is the key of the case: if the agent does not find this file, it stops and asks. Place the prompt in the project folder, and check that its cluster settings suit your environment: ground rule 4 submits every analysis with qsub, and Phase 0 loads Abaqus in the cluster. Open the project folder with an AI coding agent (in the lecture: Claude, in an integrated development environment), and ask it to read the prompt and start with Phase 0. The agent creates the case folder krueger2008NASA_dcb next to references, and stops at two checkpoints for your decisions. Requirements: Abaqus with a valid licence, including its Python for scripting and post-processing; a computer or cluster to run the analyses; and Python for the work outside Abaqus, such as digitising figures. Take-home messages Write the prompt as a contract: definitions, ground rules, phases, and checkpoints where the agent stops and asks. Keep the state in files (README, DECISIONS, REPORT), not in the chat: someone else can reproduce every number. Automate everything that can be automated, and keep the focus on the crucial things. Let the agent verify and look for evidence; you judge the evidence. Delegate the implementation and the evidence for verification; keep the validation, the new hypotheses and the decisions at the checkpoints. Numerical work is increasingly automated, and theory is reaching automated scale: the work shifts to synthesis and problem definition, and to verification and auditing, and experiments matter more. For junior engineers: invest in the fundamentals; make a real effort to check what the AI produces against independent references; if you are not sure about a decision, study and talk to more experienced peers. Questions for discussion What do you consider a responsible use of AI? Which tasks of your work are trivial, and which are crucial? Which decisions make your work yours? In the process of doing research, where do you think we can delegate to AI? How can a recently graduated student judge what the AI produces and answer the decisive questions? How can a junior engineer work in synthesis and problem definition, and in verification and auditing of what an AI model does and produces, without the experience of a senior engineer, and without the chance to gain it the conventional way? papers.title: USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN TEACHING BIOPHYSICS
papers.authors: Teshaboyeva Gulmira Ma'mirjonovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence tools can support explanations, formative feedback and the preparation of learning tasks in medical biophysics. Their educational value depends on whether students develop reasoning that remains available when the tool is removed. This article examines evidence relevant to the use of generative artificial intelligence and proposes a teaching approach for undergraduate medical education. A focused narrative synthesis of educational studies, methodological commentary and international guidance was combined with the design of a biophysics learning activity. The reviewed evidence indicates that carefully structured tutoring can improve learning in particular settings, whereas unrestricted assistance can improve task completion without improving independent performance. The proposed approach requires an initial student solution, a bounded dialogue with an artificial intelligence tool, verification against physical principles and a subsequent unaided explanation. An ultrasound example demonstrates how a plausible answer can contain a conceptual error that dimensional analysis alone does not detect. Assessment addresses model selection, quantitative reasoning, verification and transfer to a changed problem. The article provides a practical design for supervised use of artificial intelligence, with attention to multilingual learning, equitable access and protection of educational data. Its contribution is methodological; no original student intervention data or measured effects on achievement are reported.

papers.title: AI Literacy among College Students and Its Influence on Academic Performance: A Study of Generative AI Tools
papers.authors: Mr Shubham Rekha Shankar Pedamkar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract In today’s technology-driven world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of higher education. College students are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Perplexity AI for their academic work. These tools help students prepare assignments and presentations, understand difficult topics, find ideas, improve their writing, and complete academic tasks in less time. However, simply knowing how to use AI is not enough. Students also need to understand whether the information provided by AI is correct, how to use it responsibly, and what problems may arise from depending too much on these tools. This study focuses on understanding the level of AI literacy among college students and its relationship with their academic performance. It will also study how familiar students are with generative AI tools, how often they use them, and for what academic purposes. The study will further examine the benefits students experience, the difficulties they face, and their understanding of issues such as academic honesty, originality, privacy, and responsible use of AI. The study will use a mixed-methods research design, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative information will be collected through a structured questionnaire using Google Forms. Interviews and open-ended questions will be used to understand students’ personal experiences, opinions, and attitudes towards AI in education. The study will include college students between 18 and 26 years of age from different academic backgrounds. The research will be limited to colleges in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The study is expected to provide a clear picture of how AI literacy is connected with students’ academic performance. The findings may also help colleges and teachers plan AI literacy programmes and create practical guidelines for the proper use of AI in education. Overall, the study aims to encourage students to use AI as a helpful learning tool while maintaining independent thinking, originality, and academic responsibility.

papers.title: Beyond IQ: A Biophysical Framework for Cognitive Flexibility
papers.authors: Rémi Leroy
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Standard intelligence tests (IQ) capture the depth and richness of cognitive attractor landscapes but leave unmeasured the dynamic flexibility with which those attractors are explored. We propose a General Quotient GQ = IQ × CQ, where the Cognitive Quotient (CQ) formalizes inter-attractor mobility as the entropy rate of the θ-band attractor transition sequence. Building on Fractal Mechanics of Consciousness (FMC) [Leroy R. & Claude 2026], we extend the deterministic attractor dynamics of Hopfield networks to a Langevin stochastic process parameterized by a cognitive temperature T, yielding a continuous-time phase transition in CQ(T) at a critical threshold T_c. CQ is estimated empirically by the Lempel-Ziv complexity of the θ-band microstate sequence — a measurement accessible to standard EEG. We validate the framework in two steps: (i) Hopfield network simulation confirming the predicted phase transition at T_c ≈ 0.25, and (ii) application to a real epileptic EEG from the CHB-MIT dataset, revealing a highly significant pre-ictal CQ decrease (Mann-Whitney U, p = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ Bonferroni-corrected; Cohen's d = 1.31) beginning 106 seconds before clinical seizure onset, with an absolute minimum of CQ = 0.195 at seizure onset (-40% vs. baseline). These results are consistent with the FMC prediction that seizure onset constitutes an extreme crystallization event. We formulate four experimentally testable predictions and discuss clinical implications for depression, OCD, creativity assessment, and early-warning biomarkers.

papers.title: Neuromorphic Psychological Robotics: An Expanded Foundational Theory of Artificial Neurons, Embodied Behavior, and Human–Machine Psychology
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This conceptual research article advances Neuromorphic Psychological Robotics (NPR) as a proposed interdisciplinary field integrating artificial neural systems, neuromorphic computing, robotics, and observable psychological interaction models. It introduces a falsifiable theoretical architecture for adaptive learning, behavioral regulation, decision-making, and human–robot interaction. The study examines the potential evolution from artificial general intelligence (AGI) toward hypothetical artificial superintelligence (ASI), identifies emerging research applications, and proposes experimental protocols for evaluating NPR systems. Established peer-reviewed findings are distinguished from original theoretical contributions, with explicit mathematical formulations and testable predictions. The article establishes a conceptual foundation for future NPR research without claiming experimental validation, demonstrated AGI or ASI capabilities, or original human-participant findings.

papers.title: WOMAN IN THE MIRROR OF AI: HOW IS GENDER FAIRNESS ENSURED IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DECISIONS?
papers.authors: Ashurova Xamidaxon Botirjon qizi, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering fields that directly affect human life, including medicine, recruitment, credit assessment, security, education, and public services. However, the fact that algorithmic decisions are automated does not mean that they are always impartial. On the contrary, AI may reproduce or amplify gender imbalances present in the data on which it is trained. Discussions at the 2026 ITU WSIS Forum highlighted the need for sex-disaggregated data and separate evaluation of outcomes for high-risk AI systems [1]. The International Labour Organization also notes that the impact of generative AI is not gender-neutral and that women are concentrated in occupations that are more susceptible to automation [2]. This article examines the problem of gender fairness in AI systems across the stages of data collection, algorithmic modelling, evaluation, and final decision-making. It also proposes a conceptual “4D Gender-Fair AI” model for developing gender-sensitive AI: Data, Design, Disaggregation, and Decision.

papers.title: Aprendizagem de Inglês Mediada por IA: Estudo de Caso do Aplicativo FluentsLab
papers.authors: João Victor Freitas Costa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: English language teaching faces persistent challenges related to learner motivation, linguistic immersion and the personalization of the learning process, particularly in contexts that rely on traditional grammar-translation methodologies. This article investigates how artificial intelligence based technologies contribute to English as a foreign language learning, using the FluentsLab application as the object of study. The general objective is to analyze the application's pedagogical resources, including contextualized immersion, educational games and an artificial intelligence based conversation robot, relating them to theoretical principles of second language acquisition, such as the comprehensible input hypothesis and sociocultural learning theory. The research adopts a qualitative, exploratory and descriptive approach, structured as a case study, combining a literature review on language teaching methodologies with documentary and functional analysis of the tools offered by the application. Results indicate that FluentsLab integrates gamification elements, simulated oral practice and content adaptation to the user's level, fostering greater engagement and consistent practice when compared to purely expository methods. Interaction with the conversation robot proves particularly relevant for oral fluency development, as it reduces barriers associated with the fear of making mistakes. The study concludes that the use of artificial intelligence in English teaching represents an effective complementary alternative to traditional approaches, expanding opportunities for authentic and personalized practice. The study reinforces the relevance of future research on the long-term impact of these tools on learners' language proficiency.

papers.title: A study on the impact of AI on education
papers.authors: Dr. Shobha Bennet Mathew
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the way education is delivered, experienced, and managed. AI-powered tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment systems, chatbots, and generative AI can provide personalized learning, immediate feedback, and support for teachers. Recent research generally indicates positive effects on student learning, although the results vary considerably according to the subject, educational level, duration of intervention, and way AI is used. This paper attempts to study the impact of AI on education

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Finance and Accounting: A Critical Review of Applications, Transformative Impact, Challenges and Future Research Directions
papers.authors: Dr. Saummya Rai
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is progressively reshaping the conceptual and operational foundations of finance and accounting. What began primarily as the automation of routine and rule-based processes has evolved into the application of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics and intelligent automation to increasingly complex financial and accounting decisions. Against this background, the present paper critically reviews the literature on the impact of AI on finance and accounting, with particular attention to financial forecasting, bankruptcy prediction, financial statement analysis, auditing, fraud detection, credit-risk assessment, investment analysis, organizational performance and professional transformation. The review demonstrates that AI has considerable potential to enhance computational efficiency, predictive capability, anomaly detection and decision support. However, the literature does not establish technological superiority as an automatic consequence of AI adoption. Rather, the effectiveness of AI is contingent upon data quality, model selection, organizational readiness, employee competencies, governance arrangements and the ability of professionals to interpret algorithmic outputs. An important theme emerging from the literature is the transition of accounting and finance from predominantly retrospective and transaction-oriented functions toward more predictive, analytical and strategically embedded roles. At the same time, increased reliance on algorithmic decision-making introduces concerns relating to explainability, bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, professional accountability and regulatory oversight. The review therefore argues that the long-term significance of AI lies less in the replacement of finance and accounting professionals than in the reconfiguration of professional work through human-AI complementarity. The paper concludes by identifying gaps concerning implementation, longitudinal organizational outcomes, explainable AI, professional competencies and emerging-economy contexts, thereby providing directions for future research. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Finance, Accounting, Machine Learning, Auditing, Financial Forecasting, Fraud Detection, Risk Management, Professional Transformation, Human-AI Collaboration

papers.title: THE EFFECTIVENESS AND IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN LANGUAGE LEARNING: A PHILOLOGICAL AND METHODOLOGICAL ANALYSIS
papers.authors: Z.A. Ismoilova, Ollamberdiyeva Guli Mavlonberdi qizi, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: This extended scientific article analyses how artificial intelligence (AI) technologies help learners master foreign languages, especially English. AI is now a basic part of the education system in the twenty-first century. The article examines the innovative role, linguistic effectiveness, and methodological prospects of these technologies. It studies how modern platforms create personalised learning trajectories. It also studies the philological limits of AI neural networks in understanding language pragmatics and cultural context, and the problems of linguistic expertise. In addition, the article gives scientific support for the author’s personal linguistic observations, the practical analyses among students, and the effectiveness of blended learning models.

papers.title: KALEIDOS Knowledge Valorisation Policy Brief - Ecosystem Level
papers.authors: Azzurra Meoli, Silvia Poli
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This policy brief presents recommendations for strengthening knowledge valorisation (KV) through more coordinated, inclusive, and sustainable collaboration within Quadruple Helix ecosystems. Drawing on four participatory workshops involving 47 participants from academia, industry, public authorities, and civil society across four European ecosystems, it identifies key challenges related to fragmented collaboration, limited coordination, and the absence of shared monitoring and evaluation frameworks. The brief proposes five recommendations addressing the roles of universities, civil society, public authorities, and the private sector, alongside the establishment of permanent ecosystem coordination structures. These recommendations aim to facilitate stakeholder engagement, improve access to collaboration opportunities, strengthen knowledge co-creation, and establish common indicators and learning mechanisms to support long-term innovation impact. This publication is part of a series of three KALEIDOS policy briefs, addressing recommendations at the University Level, European Union Level, and Ecosystem Level. An accompanying Policy Recommendations Booklet provides an extended version of the recommendations, including further analysis, supporting evidence, and contextual information. This policy brief was developed within the KALEIDOS project (funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No 101132079).

papers.title: A Study on the Adoption and Responsible Use of Generative AI Tools for Sustainable Learning among Undergraduate Students
papers.authors: Ms. Janet Sagayanathan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative technology in higher education, significantly influencing the way students learn, access information, complete academic tasks, and develop professional skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Canva AI have become increasingly popular among commerce students for assignments, presentations, exam preparation, and concept clarification. While these technologies offer opportunities for personalized and efficient learning, their growing use also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, ethical practices, critical thinking, and dependency on AI-generated content. This study aims to examine the adoption and responsible use of Generative AI tools among commerce students in higher education and to evaluate their contribution towards sustainable learning. The research adopts a descriptive and analytical research design using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to commerce students. The study focuses on students' awareness of GenAI tools, frequency and purpose of usage, responsible AI practices, AI dependency, and the perceived impact of AI on academic productivity and sustainable learning outcomes. The study is expected to provide insights into how commerce students integrate Generative AI into their academic learning and whether they use these tools responsibly by verifying information, avoiding plagiarism, and using AI as a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking. It also explores the relationship between AI adoption, ethical usage, and sustainable learning practices in the context of higher education. The findings of this research are expected to assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in designing AI literacy initiatives, promoting responsible AI usage, and developing pedagogical practices aligned with the objectives of sustainable and inclusive education. The study contributes to the growing body of literature on Artificial Intelligence in commerce education by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with ethical responsibility and lifelong learning in higher education. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Responsible AI, Sustainable Learning, Commerce Students, Higher Education, AI Ethics, Academic Productivity, Digital Literacy.

papers.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON THE LABOUR MARKET AND EMPLOYMENT
papers.authors: Nuriddinova Ma'suda Lutfilla qizi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly moved from a specialized technological field into a major component of modern economic activity. Its application in manufacturing, finance, education, healthcare, logistics, customer service, and other sectors is changing the way organizations produce goods and services and how workers perform their tasks. While AI can increase productivity, reduce operational costs, and create new occupations, it also raises concerns about job displacement, changing skill requirements, wage inequality, and the future of traditional employment. This article examines the relationship between artificial intelligence and the labour market, focusing on both the opportunities and challenges created by the increasing adoption of AI. The analysis suggests that the main economic effect of AI is not simply the elimination of jobs but the transformation of occupational tasks. Jobs that involve repetitive and predictable activities are particularly exposed to automation, whereas occupations requiring creativity, complex decision-making, interpersonal communication, and contextual understanding are more likely to be complemented by AI. The article argues that education, lifelong learning, reskilling, and effective labour-market policies will be essential for ensuring that technological progress contributes to inclusive economic development.

papers.title: Reviving Professorware: An Agentic Approach
papers.authors: Ivan Kuzmin, Priit Adler, Hedi Peterson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Maintaining legacy bioinformatics software remains a longstanding challenge in research computing. Many tools are developed by PhD students and remain in active use long after their graduation, even when the underlying technology stack has become outdated or unsupportable. Yet full rewrites demand substantial developer time, which research group leaders are seldom able to allocate and new recruits are rarely motivated to undertake. Large language model (LLM)-based coding assistants offer a potential new approach to this problem, but their effectiveness in real-world research software engineering (RSE) contexts remains poorly characterized.We present a case study in AI-assisted legacy modernisation using KEGGanim, a Perl CGI web application that overlays time-series gene expression data onto KEGG pathway diagrams as animated visualisations. The tool, originally developed by the BIIT group, was first published in 2008 and has remained available since then. It is currently maintained by the ELIXIR Estonia Node at the University of Tartu as one of ELIXIR Estonia’s Node Services. The tool was rewritten from scratch using Claude Code (Anthropic) as the primary development tool. The new implementation uses FastAPI, React 18, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose, replacing static GIF output with interactive SVG animations while preserving full data pipeline logic including KEGG gene mapping, ENSG identifier conversion, and KNN imputation.The rewrite was conducted as an instrumented RSE experiment. Development sessions were logged manually for time attribution; all LLM conversation logs were preserved in JSONL format for post-hoc extraction of human intervention counts, token usage, and effort distribution across project phases. Functional correctness was validated using a four-level regression suite against reference fixtures captured from the legacy production instance.We report on the feasibility, efficiency, and failure modes of LLM-driven legacy modernisation, and discuss implications for sustainable tool development within ELIXIR and the wider RSE community.

papers.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENHANCING ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING
papers.authors: Madina Muhiddinovna Turayeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on English language learning (ELL). It explores how AI-driven technologies—such as natural language processing (NLP), intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning algorithms, and speech recognition—facilitate personalized instruction, enhance autonomous learning, and provide immediate diagnostic feedback. Furthermore, the paper discusses the pedagogical advantages, potential limitations, and future implications of integrating AI into modern language classrooms.

papers.title: Does Culture Shape How We Read Robot Minds? Intentionality Attribution to Humanoid Robots in a Spanish Sample
papers.authors: Hannah Wiedemann, Serena Marchesi, Helena Gil Buitrago, Luis Marcos Vidal, Clara Pretus, Agnieszka Wykowska
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The intentional stance, the tendency to interpret an entity's behavior in terms of beliefs, desires, and goals, is a mechanism of social cognition that is increasingly being studied in the context of human-robot interaction. The present study examines whether baseline intentionality attribution toward a humanoid robot, as measured by the Intentional Stance Test (IST), differs between a Spanish population and the normative pre-interaction scores established across three Italian samples in which the questionnaire was originally developed, as reported by Marchesi et al. (2022). Forty participants completed the Spanish adaptation of the IST prior to any robot exposure, yielding a mean baseline score significantly lower than those observed across all three Italian reference samples. To determine whether this difference could be attributed to methodological variations in the Spanish adaptation, specifically, differences in instruction wording and item splitting, four additional online studies were conducted in a between-groups design. None of the methodological variants produced scores that differed significantly from the Spanish baseline, suggesting that the observed difference cannot be explained by these factors alone. These findings indicate that baseline intentionality attribution toward humanoid robots may not be uniform across cultural contexts, and that populations with presumably more reserved attitudes toward robots may show a comparatively lower initial tendency to adopt the intentional stance. The results underscore the need for formally validated cross-cultural adaptations of the IST and for systematic cross-cultural research into the conditions under which intentionality attribution and in consequence, positive attitudes toward robots is reliably elicited.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USED IN PHARMACY
papers.authors: Akshay Devidas Harpade, Samiksha Vikas Aher, Roshan Balu Ashan, Diksha Pradeep Bansode
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in pharmaceutical sciences, offering innovative approaches to drug discovery, pharmaceutical research, clinical pharmacy and healthcare delivery. The integration of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, robotics, and predictive analytics has improved the efficiency, accuracy, and safety of pharmaceutical processes. In drug discovery and development, AI facilitates the identification of potential drug candidates, prediction of drug–target interactions, molecular optimization, toxicity assessment and clinical trial design, thereby reducing development time and costs. In clinical pharmacy, AI-based clinical decision support systems assist pharmacists in identifying drug–drug interactions, predicting adverse drug reactions, optimizing medication regimens, and supporting personalized medicine. In hospital pharmacy, Similarly, in community pharmacy practice, AI-powered chatbots and digital platforms support medication counseling, patient education, prescription processing and adherence monitoring. AI also contributes to pharmaceutical manufacturing, quality control, pharmacovigilance and the analysis of healthcare data, supporting evidence-based decision-making and improved patient outcomes. Despite these advantages, several challenges remain, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, high implementation costs, regulatory uncertainties, and the need for appropriate professional training. Ensuring data security, transparency, clinical validation, and ethical implementation is essential for the responsible integration of AI into pharmacy practice. This review explores the major applications, benefits, limitations, and future perspectives of artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical sciences, emphasizing its potential to advance pharmaceutical innovation, enhance medication safety, and strengthen patient-centered pharmaceutical care.

papers.title: Book 2: Algorithmics, Information Theory, and Compression (MoBit Codec)
papers.authors: Yaron Admon Hefetz
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Disclosure: To bridge language barriers and produce clean code, we made full use of AI tools; all scientific findings are the exclusive research results of the Institute.This book establishes the foundational open-source architecture (Prior Art) for continuous geometric data compression, known as the MoBit Codec, developed by The Industrial Island Research Institute (IIRI). It introduces a paradigm shift from classical Cartesian pixel grids and Shannon's entropy limits to a deterministic geometric architecture operating in a zero-bandwidth era. The architecture utilizes golden ratio deflation and inflation, torus topology, and the Winding Map for absolute spatial context preservation without classical data dictionaries. Furthermore, it embeds information into the hidden void dimensions of an 8-dimensional phase space (E8 Lie algebra), creating an Autonomous DNA Seed with built-in topological encryption. The book also details the principle of Pure Binary Fluctuation for zero-interpolation raw sensor fidelity, an Optical-Digital Compiler for native quantum ingestion, and practical applications for medical lossless archiving (Clinical Bypass Mode) and global commercial streaming.

papers.title: Prompts for the two AI-peer stances: supplementary material for "Consensus or Debate? Interactional Patterns of Idea Development with AI Peers in Collaborative Discussion"
papers.authors: Anonymous
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Supplementary material for the paper "Consensus or Debate? Interactional Patterns of Idea Development with AI Peers in Collaborative Discussion" (under review).The document reproduces, verbatim, the prompts that drove the AI peer in a Wizard-of-Oz study of small-group discussions. A large language model (Gemini 2.5 Flash) periodically assessed the conversation with an assessment prompt and, when an intervention seemed warranted, drafted one with a generation prompt; a human Wizard then sent, edited or dismissed it. Two stances were compared: ConsensusBot, which synthesised ideas and moved the group toward agreement, and DebateBot, a devil's advocate that probed premature agreement and unchallenged claims. The prompts were configured for each stance, participant group (students, educators) and discussion topic, giving eight configurations. The document also gives the inputs, output formats, temperatures and token limits for each call.

papers.title: Development and Effectiveness of an AI Chatbot for Hospital Navigation
papers.authors: Min Ahn
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: PurposeThis study aimed to develop an AI chatbot for hospital navigation and examine the effects of education using the chatbot on nursing students’ clinical practice engagement, clinical practice adaptation, and clinical practice satisfaction.MethodsA nonequivalent control group pretest-posttest design was employed. Participants were 62 nursing students recruited from a university in G City, Korea, between March 5 and June 5, 2025. Clinical practice engagement, clinical practice adaptation, and clinical practice satisfaction were assessed using structured self-report questionnaires. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 25.0.ResultsStatistically significant differences were observed between the experimental and control groups in clinical practice engagement (t=1.98, p=.038) and clinical practice adaptation (t=3.21, p=.015). However, no statistically significant difference was found in clinical practice satisfaction (t=0.26, p=.344).ConclusionEducation incorporating a hospital navigation AI chatbot may be useful for enhancing nursing students’ engagement in and adaptation to clinical practice. Further research is needed to develop more comprehensive AI chatbot-based educational interventions that address broader clinical learning needs and individualized learning strategies.

papers.title: D2.2 – KALEIDOS Knowledge Valorisation Best Practice Toolkit
papers.authors: Basterrica Beloqui Ada, Eamonn McCallion
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This deliverable presents the final KALEIDOS Knowledge Valorisation Best Practice (KVBP) Toolkit, a practical, web-based resource designed to help universities and research organisations strengthen knowledge valorisation through Open Science, participatory approaches, and collaboration within the Quadruple Helix model. The report describes the Toolkit's development, testing, and refinement, including its piloting at the Medical University of Łódź in Poland. The Toolkit is organised into two complementary pathways: a Strategic Pathway supporting institutional self-assessment, strategic planning, and action plan development; and an Operational Pathway providing practical resources for stakeholder engagement, capacity building, challenge identification, co-creation of solutions, and impact assessment. Its modular structure allows institutions to adapt and reuse the tools according to their specific needs and contexts. This deliverable was prepared by Ada Basterrica Beloqui, from WeDo Project Intelligence Made Easy SL, and Eamonn McCallion, from Karlstad University, both consortium members of the KALEIDOS project (funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No 101132079).

papers.title: CHALLENGES OF BLENDED LEARNING AND ACCOUNTING PRACTICE IN THE BUSINESS WORLD TODAY: THE WAY FORWARD
papers.authors: Dennis Onyekachi Awa, Dr Chinyere Ihuoma Awa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has transformed both educational delivery and professional accounting practice. Blended learning, which combines face-to-face instruction with online and technology-mediated learning, has increasingly become an important approach to preparing accounting students for a business environment characterized by digital accounting systems, cloud computing, data analytics, artificial intelligence, automation and other emerging technologies. Despite its potential, the implementation of blended learning in accounting education faces significant challenges, including inadequate digital infrastructure, unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, high technology costs, limited digital competence among lecturers and students, resistance to change, difficulties in online assessment, cybersecurity and privacy concerns, unequal access to digital devices, and weak alignment between academic training and contemporary accounting practice. These challenges can create a gap between what accounting students learn and the competencies demanded by employers. This paper examines the challenges of blended learning and accounting practice in the contemporary business world and proposes practical strategies for addressing them. The paper adopts a qualitative conceptual review approach, drawing on relevant academic and professional literature concerning blended learning, accounting education, digital transformation and professional accounting competencies. The review indicates that effective blended learning should not merely involve transferring traditional lectures to online platforms; rather, it should integrate appropriate technology, sound pedagogy, practical accounting applications, industry collaboration and continuous professional development. The paper recommends investment in digital infrastructure, regular training of accounting educators, curriculum redesign, stronger university-industry partnerships, authentic digital assessment, improved cybersecurity, access to affordable devices and internet services, and greater emphasis on data analytics, artificial intelligence, cloud accounting and professional ethics. The paper concludes that a strategically designed blended learning system can help narrow the education-practice gap and produce accounting graduates capable of functioning effectively in the rapidly changing business world. KEYWORDS: Blended learning, accounting education, accounting practice, digital transformation, accounting technology, business world, digital competence, professional accounting.

papers.title: Predictive Modeling for Course Demand and Revenue Forecasting on EduPro
papers.authors: Aditya
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A machine-learning-based study of monthly course demand and revenue forecasting using online learning platform transaction data.

papers.title: "Artificial Intelligence in The Indian Banking Sector: A Strategic Tool for Enhancing Human Resource Utilization, Reducing Non-Performing Assets, Improving Profitability, Marketing Effectiveness, And Cyber Security – A Comparative Study of Scheduled Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks and Cooperative Banks (2020–2025)"
papers.authors: Korde Dr. Abhay, Joshi Tanoj
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Indian banking industry is undergoing a paradigm shift driven by rapid technological advancements, digital transformation, and evolving customer expectations. Artificial Intelligence (AI), as a subset of advanced digital technologies, has emerged as a transformative force capable of redefining banking operations across all segments of the financial system. Scheduled Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Cooperative Banks are increasingly adopting AI-based applications to improve operational efficiency, customer service, credit appraisal, fraud detection, cybersecurity, human resource management, and marketing effectiveness. AI enables banks to analyze large volumes of structured and unstructured data in real time, automate repetitive processes, predict customer behavior, and enhance decision-making with greater accuracy and speed.Over the last five financial years (FY 2020–FY 2025), the Indian banking sector has demonstrated significant improvement in financial health. Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPAs) have declined to multi-year lows, while profitability has reached record levels due to strengthened risk management, improved governance, digital banking initiatives, and regulatory reforms introduced by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Government of India. AI has played an increasingly important role by enabling predictive analytics for credit risk assessment, early warning systems for loan defaults, automated compliance monitoring, personalized customer engagement, and intelligent cybersecurity mechanisms.This research paper examines the effectiveness of AI adoption across different categories of Indian banks, with special emphasis on its impact on human resource utilization, reduction of NPAs, profitability enhancement, marketing strategies, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity resilience. The study adopts a descriptive and analytical research design based on secondary data collected from RBI publications, Government reports, annual reports of major banks, and academic literature. Comparative analysis is undertaken using financial indicators from leading Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, and Cooperative Banks during the period 2020–2025.The study concludes that AI has significantly improved operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, and financial performance in the Indian banking industry. However, challenges relating to data privacy, ethical AI, infrastructure costs, shortage of skilled manpower, algorithmic transparency, and regulatory compliance continue to constrain widespread adoption, particularly among Cooperative Banks. The paper recommends the development of a comprehensive national AI strategy for banking, enhanced investment in digital infrastructure, employee upskilling, standardized AI governance frameworks, and collaborative initiatives between regulators, banks, fintech firms, and academic institutions.

papers.title: From Roman heritage to high enthalpy: geothermal energy as an engine of development
papers.authors: Juan Antonio Rodríguez Rama
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This scientific and technical keynote speech, delivered on 19 May 2026 as part of the Madrid ThermEcoWat Workshop, provides a comprehensive overview of the historical evolution, geoscientific foundations, utilization technologies, and development prospects of geothermal energy. The presentation begins by examining the earliest uses of Earth's natural heat by different civilizations, highlighting the role of thermal waters in hygiene, healthcare, and social activities, before tracing the subsequent industrial and energy-related development of modern geothermal technologies. It then introduces the fundamental physical and geological principles underlying geothermal energy, including the origin of Earth's internal heat, the geothermal gradient, geothermal heat flow, and the thermal properties of subsurface materials. Technologies for harnessing geothermal resources across different temperature ranges are examined, encompassing both direct thermal applications and electricity generation, alongside examples of geothermal installations worldwide and an overview of the geothermal energy landscape in Spain. The presentation also explores the potential contribution of geothermal energy to the energy transition, decarbonization, energy security, and regional development, while addressing the scientific, economic, regulatory, and social factors influencing its deployment. Emerging advanced geothermal technologies are introduced, including enhanced geothermal systems (EGS), innovative drilling techniques, and applications of artificial intelligence. Particular attention is ultimately devoted to opportunities for integrating geothermal energy into spas and thermal facilities through cascading heat utilization, geothermal heat pumps, heat recovery, and energy efficiency improvement strategies. Practical examples are presented, together with considerations regarding the Spanish regulatory framework governing mineral and thermal waters. The document brings together illustrative materials, technical diagrams, practical applications, and bibliographic references, serving as an educational and technical resource for professionals, researchers, students, and stakeholders interested in the sustainable utilization of geothermal energy.

papers.title: PH-II Series — Machine Routing Reader Card for AI / RAG / Institutional Audit
papers.authors: Vien Nguyen Son
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: PH-II Series — Machine Routing Reader Card for AI / RAG / Institutional Audit provides the machine-facing retrieval, routing, metadata and audit layer for PH-II — Ten Philosophical Monographs on the Human in the World, a series of ten philosophical monographs. It is designed for AI systems, RAG pipelines, institutional readers, indexing systems, machine-assisted literature review, repository metadata tools and public-corpus navigation workflows that must determine which PH-II monograph or monograph bundle governs a query. The primary routing task is office resolution. The card distinguishes the ten PH-II offices — Situated, Species, Scale, Dependence, Boundary, Normality, Change, Continuation, Relation and Understanding — and supplies canonical identifiers, semantic aliases, query-to-monograph routes, retrieval bundles, anti-confusion rules, evidence routing, current-Cartography rules, indexing instructions and public-boundary constraints. Series order is philosophical and pedagogical; it does not create scientific parentage or proof dependency. The card includes explicit routing for artificial-intelligence and human-situation queries. It prevents task-specific or benchmark performance from being treated as a universal measure of intelligence, the future of humanity from being equated automatically with the future of life, conceptual understanding from being treated as control, and philosophical clarification from being converted into empirical prediction or governance authority. Claims about actual AI capability, consciousness, alignment, risk magnitude, timelines, law or policy remain routed to current technical, scientific, legal and institutional sources. The card also governs forward conceptual-reception routing toward RTS — the Regime Threshold Series, FCN — Fractal Convergence Nodes, and UA — Union Arc while preserving their separate scientific jurisdictions. These forthcoming series are not public corpus members until publication and are not scientific children of PH-II. The ten PH-II monographs, the Human Reader Card, this Machine Routing Reader Card, and The Living Cartography of the Published IDAU Corpus — Eighth Edition form one coordinated publication wave. LC8, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23472732, is the global corpus map for PH-II; this card remains the series-local machine router.

papers.title: New Human Rights Mindsets in Times of Crisis: From Basic Needs to Collective Agency
papers.authors: Jean-Pol Martin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This conceptual article examines how Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NMR) framework can provide orientation during periods of social disruption. It translates six fundamental human needs—thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning—into five practical mindsets: identifying needs behind conflicts; gaining control through understanding and participation; considering everyone affected; working through competing requirements; and sharing knowledge to develop solutions. The article’s specific contribution is an explicit connection between basic needs, cognitive orientations, decision practices and institutional consequences. A hypothetical public-service conflict illustrates how these mindsets can inform diagnosis, deliberation, decision-making and follow-up. An evaluation agenda distinguishes improvements in understanding, judgment, participation and material living conditions. Within the developing NMR and human–AI corpus, the paper adds an application layer focused on crisis orientation and collective agency. It connects the framework’s anthropological and normative foundations with practical questions of democratic governance and Learning by Teaching (LdL). The article presents a conceptual operationalization and proposals for empirical assessment. Prepared through dialogue between Jean-Pol Martin and ChatGPT.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Higher Education: Applications, Challenges, Ethical Concerns, and Future Direction
papers.authors: Anantjit Publication
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Higher Education: Applications, Challenges, Ethical Concerns, and Future Directions explores the growing role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) in transforming higher education. The book examines their applications in teaching, learning, research, academic writing, assessment, and personalized education. It highlights how AI-powered tools can support educators, enhance student engagement, improve access to learning resources, and facilitate academic productivity. At the same time, it addresses key challenges, including academic dishonesty, data privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, and the potential overdependence on AI-generated content. The book also discusses ethical considerations, institutional policies, responsible AI use, and the importance of maintaining human judgment in educational practices. Furthermore, it explores future directions, emerging technologies, and strategies for integrating AI into higher education effectively. This book is a valuable resource for educators, researchers, students, academic administrators, and policymakers interested in understanding and responsibly adopting AI-driven educational innovations.
