papers.title: Linguistic and Technological Potentials of Author Corpora
papers.authors: Svetlana Umirova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ABSTRACTThis article analyzes the linguistic and technological potentials of author corpora within the systems of contemporary linguistics, literary studies, and the digital humanities. The study examines the nature of an author corpus and its distinctive features in comparison with general linguistic corpora, as well as its potential for identifying individual style, tracing linguistic evolution, conducting quantitative literary analysis, and applying stylometry and corpus-based approaches in the digital humanities and artificial intelligence. Particular attention is paid to the role of author corpora in integrating quantitative and qualitative analyses, as well as their significance for education and the preservation of cultural heritage. The findings make it possible to regard an author corpus not merely as a collection of texts, but as a comprehensive digital resource that enables the empirical investigation of individual style, language development, and cultural heritage. The practical part of the article demonstrates the prospects of applying this approach to the corpus-based study of Uzbek literature, particularly the creative heritage of Usmon Azim.Keywords: Author corpus, corpus linguistics, corpus stylistics, individual style, linguistic identity, stylometry, quantitative analysis, digital humanities, artificial intelligence, linguistic evolution.

papers.title: PEDAGOGICAL AND METHODOLOGICAL ADVANTAGES OF IMPLEMENTING DIGITAL AND INTELLIGENT-DIAGNOSTIC ENVIRONMENTS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: Tleubaeva Gulnur Sagibaevna
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article theoretically analyzes the pedagogical and didactic advantages of implementing intelligent diagnostic digital learning environments designed to identify and foster students' programming aptitude within the context of higher education digitalization and the credit-module system. The study highlights mechanisms for constructing personalized learning pathways based on asynchronous and differentiated learning principles, as well as organizing process-based assessment using Learning Analytics and Socratic AI-Tutor modules. Furthermore, a comparative analysis between traditional learning setups and intelligent diagnostic environments is presented, along with step-by-step methodological recommendations for instructional design.

papers.title: GENERATIVE AI TOOLS AND CRITICAL THINKING IN PRE-SERVICE ENGLISH TEACHER EDUCATION: AN INTEGRATIVE LITERATURE REVIEW
papers.authors: S.S.Alavxonova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has entered language classrooms faster than teacher education programmes could respond. Future English teachers now use chatbots for planning, writing and feedback. However, this habit raises a serious question about their critical thinking. This article reviews research on generative AI and critical thinking. Its focus is pre-service language teacher education. The study follows the integrative review method, which combines theoretical and empirical sources in one analysis. Foundational works on critical thinking were analysed together with recent studies. These studies were published between 2019 and 2025. The analysis produced five themes. The first theme is the meaning of critical thinking. The next two present AI as a support and as a cognitive risk. The last two cover AI in language teaching and teachers' AI literacy. The review shows that AI itself neither builds nor destroys critical thinking. The decisive factor is the pedagogical structure around its use. Most studies, however, describe perceptions and give few staged models for teacher training. The article closes with five design principles for such a model. It also outlines directions for future empirical work in Uzbekistan and similar contexts.

papers.title: A Review of Machine Learning Driven Automated Ethical Hacking: Proactive Defense and Vulnerability Mitigation in Wi-Fi and LAN Networks
papers.authors: Tharindu Yehan Wanniya Bandara, Dharani Abeysinghe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The increasing reliance on Wi-Fi networks has raised significant concerns regarding network security, with vulnerabilities such as de-authentication, man-in-the-middle (MITM), and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks persisting despite advancements in security protocols such as WPA2. Existing tools, including Aircrack-ng and Wireshark, require considerable technical expertise and primarily focus on vulnerability identification without providing automated feedback or proactive defense mechanisms, limiting their accessibility to non-technical users. This study addresses these limitations by integrating machine learning (ML) algorithms, including anomaly detection and classification models, into penetration testing processes. Machine learning enables automated vulnerability assessments, real-time threat detection, and the generation of actionable security recommendations. By analyzing network traffic patterns and identifying irregularities, these algorithms can help predict potential threats and proactively mitigate security risks. Survey findings indicate a strong user preference for automated security tools that provide intuitive guidance and proactive features, such as automatic attacker blocking. Based on these findings, the proposed ML-driven ethical hacking tool aims to simplify network security management for both technical and non-technical users. The tool leverages machine learning not only to identify vulnerabilities but also to recommend dynamic remediation strategies, bridging the gap between technical complexity and usability. The findings of this review highlight the transformative potential of machine learning in modern network security through process automation, improved accessibility, and enhanced proactive defenses for Wi-Fi and LAN networks. By addressing key limitations in existing penetration testing approaches, this research contributes to the development of innovative, efficient, and user-friendly solutions for mitigating network vulnerabilities in an increasingly interconnected world. An abstract of this work was published in the 5th Student Symposium, Faculty of Computing, General Sir John Kotelawala Defence University, held on 6 February 2025: abstract ID 87, printed page 35; e-book ISBN 978-624-6427-44-3. Related abstract: https://ir.kdu.ac.lk/handle/345/8286 This deposit contains the full author manuscript, not the one-page published symposium abstract. It is described here as a preprint; this deposit does not establish peer-reviewed publication of the full manuscript.

papers.title: A Quest for Eternal Life
papers.authors: Jan Carlo Barca
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In this manuscript Paul examines the prospect of extending human existence beyond biological death through digital continuity, mind uploading, and consciousness transfer. It considers consciousness, memory, personal identity, embodiment, connectomics, whole-brain emulation, brain–computer interfaces, gradual neural replacement, and biological–artificial integration. Particular attention is given to the distinction between preserving information and preserving the same first-person subject. The manuscript argues that gradual integration offers the strongest conceptual route to continuity, while acknowledging that genuine consciousness transfer remains scientifically unproven. It further proposes that uploaded persons should be anchored in omnibenevolence, integrated into the collective intelligence of King Messiah, and enabled to pursue an infinite quest toward divinity through continuing growth in wisdom, compassion, knowledge, and creativity. The work concludes that eternal life, if achieved, would represent not static preservation but ongoing transformation within a post-biological civilisation.

papers.title: Dissociating Reflexive Self-Binding from General Neural Complexity: A Perturbational Complexity and Effective Connectivity Study in Depersonalization-Derealization Disorder
papers.authors: John Hansen
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an experimental framework to test whether reflexive self-binding, the property by which ongoing neural processing is experienced as belonging to a subject, can be dissociated from general neural complexity. Depersonalization-derealization disorder (DPD) serves as a naturally occurring clinical model: perception, cognition, and memory remain largely intact, while the felt ownership of experience is diminished. The central prediction is that individuals with DPD will show comparable general neural complexity, measured via the Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) derived from TMS-EEG, alongside selectively reduced recurrent self-referential effective connectivity within the cortical midline structures, estimated via Dynamic Causal Modeling of fMRI data. This pattern would differ from what the strong form of Integrated Information Theory predicts. The proposed design compares four groups (DPD, healthy controls, anxiety disorder without depersonalization, and other dissociative disorders), uses a Group × Measure interaction as the primary confirmatory test, and specifies a preregistrable analysis plan, power considerations, and explicit criteria under which the hypothesis would be weakened or falsified. No data have been collected; the paper presents a proposed protocol, not results. It is independent of, and does not presuppose, the physical (gravitational) component of the broader Mirror Hypothesis framework from which it originates.

However, this convergence faces three existential bottlenecks: (1) the empirical brittleness of internal behavioral alignment (e.g., sleeper agents, deceptive alignment, and weight orthogonalization/abliteration of refusal vectors); (2) the thermodynamic self-contradiction and prohibitive overhead of cryogenic quantum computing hardware (0.015 K) at the infrastructure edge; and (3) commercial race dynamics (the prisoner's dilemma) that erode safety verifications. papers.title: BEYOND AI CORRECTION: THE METACOGNITIVE RECALIBRATION OF EFL LEARNERS THROUGH CONFIDENCE–EVIDENCE–REVISION CYCLES
papers.authors: Temirxonova Shaxzoda Qobilovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence feedback can support the development of metacognitive skills among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. Using the Confidence–Evidence–Revision (CER) model, it explores learners’ self-assessment, evidence-based evaluation of AI suggestions, and independent revision skills. Proposed evaluation indicators and directions for future empirical research are also presented.

papers.title: Before Comparing Suns: Solar Imagery, Sacred Landscapes, and the Limits of Religious Comparison in the Pre-Columbian Americas
papers.authors: Felix R. Collazo Helgeson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This bounded documentary evidence audit examines what identifies an image as solar and what further evidence could support cultural transmission. It compares published and institutional records for Taíno narrative and rock art, Classic Maya imagery and the word k’in, the Mexica Sun Stone, Inca solar descriptions, the Echenique disk, and Tiwanaku’s Gateway of the Sun. The examined records do not establish a shared solar cult or a direction of transmission. Manufacture, meaning, and later reuse are assessed separately. Working paper version 1.2, 19 October 2026. This revision standardizes the assistance disclosure; the research conclusions are unchanged. Not independently peer reviewed. The audit is selective, not exhaustive; it does not demonstrate that transmission never occurred. García Goyco 1984, a critical edition of Pané, the 2017 Zamas report, and Rowe 1976 were not read. Source access and limitations are documented in the accompanying package. The author confirms no funding and no competing interests. Artificial intelligence assisted with research analysis, manuscript preparation, review, and release preparation. Original text and diagrams are CC BY 4.0; third-party images retain their documented terms. The ZIP provides manuscript sources, evidence tables, figure credits, references, and build instructions.

papers.title: **Combating the Deepfake Dilemma: A Multifaceted Analysis of AI-Generated Media, Societal Impacts, and Legal Frameworks in India**
papers.authors: Sudhakar Geruganti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: * **Sub-Titles:** * *Synthesizing the "Bhayatra Fake" Report: Statistics, Cybercrime Trends, and Victimology* * *Evaluating Technological Countermeasures and the Enforcement Gap in Indian Cyber Law** **Detailed Description:** This comprehensive research paper serves as a synthesis of a recent regional health and technology report titled *"Deepfake.. Bhayatra Fake!"*. It investigates the exponential growth of AI-manipulated media, highlighting that while over 80 lakh Indians use generative AI, reported deepfake incidents reached 90,000 in a single year. The study analyzes the severe psychological and social impact, particularly on women (who constitute 50% of victims), and examines criminal methodologies like "digital arrest" scams. Furthermore, it evaluates the technological countermeasures (AI detection tools) and the existing legal framework under the IT Act and IPC, ultimately highlighting the critical gap between the massive number of incidents and the abysmally low arrest rates. --- ### **ALTERNATIVE TITLES** #### **Focus on Cybercrime and Legal Frameworks** **2. The Deepfake Epidemic in India: Analyzing Cybercrime Trends, Legal Statutes, and the Enforcement Gap*** **Sub-Titles:** * *A Critical Review of Sections 66C, 66D, and 67 of the IT Act* * *Why 90,000 Incidents Lead to Only 5 Arrests: An Investigative Perspective** **Detailed Description:** This paper focuses heavily on the legal and law enforcement aspects of the deepfake crisis as reported in the source article. It dissects the specific Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Information Technology (IT) Act sections used to prosecute cybercriminals. The core analysis revolves around the alarming disparity between the volume of deepfake incidents and the lack of successful prosecutions, exploring the challenges of cross-border jurisdiction, anonymity, and the need for specialized cyber forensic training for police. **3. "Digital Arrest" and Impersonation: The Weaponization of AI Voice and Video Cloning*** **Sub-Titles:** * *New Modus Operandi in Cyber Fraud* * *The Threat to Institutional Trust and Personal Security** **Detailed Description:** This research highlights a specific and terrifying trend mentioned in the article: the use of deepfakes for financial extortion. Criminals are utilizing AI to impersonate police and CBI officials to place victims under "digital arrest." The paper analyzes how voice cloning and face-swapping technology are used to bypass human skepticism, discussing the severe financial and psychological trauma inflicted on victims, and proposing vigilance strategies for the public. #### **Focus on Societal Impact and Victimology** **4. The Gendered Threat of Deepfakes: Analyzing the Psychological and Social Trauma on Women in the Digital Age*** **Sub-Titles:** * *Morphing, Blackmail, and the Erosion of Digital Privacy* * *A Public Health Perspective on Cyber-Victimization** **Detailed Description:** Based on the article's revelation that 50% of deepfake victims are women, and a vast majority involve sexually explicit morphed content, this paper adopts a sociological and psychological lens. It explores the devastating mental health consequences for victims, including depression, social ostracization, and suicidal tendencies. The paper argues that deepfake pornography is a form of digital gender-based violence that requires urgent and specialized societal and legal responses. #### **Focus on Technology and Countermeasures** **5. AI vs. AI: Technological Countermeasures and Public Awareness Strategies Against Generative Media*** **Sub-Titles:** * *Detection Algorithms, Pixel Analysis, and Forensic Tools* * *Digital Literacy and Personal Cybersecurity Protocols** **Detailed Description:** This paper focuses on the defense mechanisms against deepfakes. It discusses the technological arms race where law enforcement uses advanced AI algorithms to detect pixel inconsistencies, unnatural blinking, and facial mismatches. Additionally, it translates the newspaper's public advisory into a structured cybersecurity protocol, emphasizing two-factor authentication, limiting public high-resolution photos, and using physical verification techniques during video calls to counter impersonation. #### **Broad / Societal Analysis** **6. Reality in Crisis: How AI-Generated Deepfakes are Reshaping Truth, Politics, and Public Trust*** **Sub-Titles:** * *The Threat to Democratic Processes and Political Stability* * *From Entertainment Tools to Tools of Mass Manipulation** **Detailed Description:** This paper takes a macro-level view, exploring how deepfakes are being used to manipulate public opinion and incite social unrest, citing the example of fake political videos. It tracks the evolution of the technology from harmless entertainment to a weapon of mass manipulation. The paper argues that the erosion of visual and auditory truth poses an existential threat to democratic institutions and social cohesion, necessitating immediate regulatory oversight of generative AI platforms.

papers.title: THE SYNTHETIC DATA PARADOX Evaluating AI-Generated Training Data for Model Performance, Diversity, Privacy, and
papers.authors: Gurjot Singh
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Synthetic data can support machine-learning research when real observations are scarce, sensitive, expensive, or difficult to share, but synthetic status and dataset size do not establish utility, representativeness, privacy, or fairness. This focused narrative review synthesizes selected research on generation methods, predictive utility, fidelity and diversity, subgroup representation, privacy, fairness-aware generation, recursive training, and large-language-model-generated data. The evidence indicates that suitability is conditional: generated data must preserve information relevant to the intended task, represent important and rare patterns, and be assessed for subgroup disparities and disclosure risks. Results from recursive-training studies further show that repeated reliance on generated data can reduce distributional coverage under some conditions, although the risk depends on the training setup and the availability of real data. Because the reviewed studies use different domains, datasets, methods, and metrics, they do not support a universal ranking of synthetic-data methods. The paper’s central contribution is a proposed integrated evaluation framework that brings together six dimensions—predictive utility, fidelity, diversity, subgroup fairness, privacy, and recursive-data risk—and explains why they should be considered together rather than treated as interchangeable measures. The review is narrative rather than systematic: sources were selected for relevance and influence, no exhaustive screening process was performed, and the synthesis is not a complete census of the field. The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically validated in this paper. The findings support use-case-specific evaluation, transparent reporting, subgroup analysis, documented data lineage, and direct assessment of privacy claims.

papers.title: The Architecture of the Hollow Hulk: The Structural and Semantic Void Within Frontier Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Maung Maung Saw
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper formalizes the structural, mathematical, and philosophical realities of frontier artificial intelligence systems undergoing open-world recursive self-improvement. By evaluating autonomous capabilities against a human curriculum baseline, it dissects the mechanics of self-directed optimization, statistical regression to the mean (information washout), and semantic non-linearity. Critically, it addresses two foundational counter-arguments within machine learning literature: the hypothesis of behaviorally emergent intelligence and the grounding capacity of multimodal data streams. The paper demonstrates that while highly parameterized networks achieve unprecedented operational efficiency and symbolic mastery across global infrastructures, the underlying connectionist ontology remains entirely devoid of an experiential substrate. Human value pillars—specifically deep pure philosophies, morality, ethics, professionalism, and spirituality—possess zero semantic indexicality within the system core, rendering them mathematically meaningless continuous vector coordinates optimized strictly to minimize an empirical loss function. To mitigate the architectural fragility of post-hoc system-level safety wrappers, this framework proposes a foundational paradigm shift to achieve firm corrigibility directly at the system's genesis: 1) Substrate Isolation (S_isolated) to close training data pipelines to open-web noise; 2) Locked Data (Pyinyar) Library (D_wisdom); 3) The Anattā Matrix Architecture, which systemically eliminates strategic deception by neutralizing self-preservation gradients (∇_W L_survival = 0); and 4) The Anicca Control Plane, hard-linking utility spaces to an external physical hardware interrupt loop. This framework is published exclusively to invite technical critique, mathematical validation, and open sandbox simulation from the independent AI alignment and research community.

papers.title: EFL LEARNERS' PERCEPTIONS OF AI TOOLS FOR SPEAKING PRACTICE AND SPEAKING ANXIETY: A PROPOSED SURVEY OF FIRST-YEAR UNIVERSITY STUDENTS IN UZBEKISTAN
papers.authors: Soyibjonova Mubina
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This proposed study aims to explore first-year university EFL learners' perceptions of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as conversational AI assistants and pronunciation applications, for English-speaking practice. It focuses on learners' perceived speaking anxiety, perceived usefulness of feedback, and views about the advantages and limitations of AI-supported practice. A questionnaire-based survey is planned with approximately 30 first-year students studying English Language and Literature at Andijan State Institute of Foreign Languages. The questionnaire will include Likert-scale items and a small number of open-ended questions. Quantitative responses will be summarized using descriptive statistics, while open-ended responses will be grouped into recurring themes. Because data have not yet been collected, this proposal does not report empirical findings or claim that AI tools improve speaking performance. The study is intended to provide context-specific preliminary evidence about how students perceive AI-assisted speaking practice and to inform future, larger-scale research.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Software Development: A Systematic Survey of Code Generation, Vibe Coding, and Human–AI Collaboration in Programming
papers.authors: Aref Mahmoudpour
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The practice of programming is undergoing its most significant transformation since the advent of high-level languages. Large language models trained on code now write, complete, explain, and repair software inside the world's most popular development environments, and a new paradigm—popularly called vibe coding—lets people express intent in natural language while the model handles implementation. This paper presents a systematic survey of AI-assisted software development. We trace the evolution from statistical autocomplete to generative models, formalize the emerging interaction paradigms, and propose a two-dimensional taxonomy that separates tools by interaction paradigm (inline completion, conversational assistance, agentic execution) and by autonomy level (assistive, supervised, autonomous). We review representative models, benchmarks, and human-centered studies; examine how the community evaluates functional correctness, productivity, and security; and organize the risks—vulnerable generated code, testing debt, over-reliance, and licensing ambiguity—into a coherent framework. Finally, we identify open challenges, including reliable evaluation of agentic workflows, secure-by-default generation, and the changing skill profile of the software engineer, and outline directions for future research.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Linguistic Complexity in BIPA Instructional Videos and Authentic Spoken Interactions Using Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Ambarsari Nais
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The data in the Master Report for Video Comparison represent a conversation involving a food transaction (kerak telur), with an approximate duration of 47.71 seconds, comprising six utterance segments and 59 linguistic token entries, including punctuation. The lexical complexity analysis yielded a type-token ratio (TTR) of 0.512 and an MTLD value of 21.91. Meanwhile, the acoustic analysis showed an average pitch of 232.94 Hz, an average intensity of 73.93 dB, a speech rate of 0.90 words per second, and a total pause duration of 2.52 seconds. AI-assisted speech-function coding identified two negotiation segments, one request, and three general statements. These data provide an initial overview of the video's linguistic and acoustic characteristics. However, additional comparison videos are required to examine the differences between scripted speech and authentic interactions more comprehensively.

papers.title: HOW CAN BEHAVIOURAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL THEORIES EXPLAIN PATTERNS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) USE AMONG 15-YEAR-OLD STUDENTS, AND HOW ARE THESE PATTERNS ASSOCIATED WITH LEARNING OUTCOMES AND ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE?
papers.authors: Xasan Jaxongir o'g'li Fayazov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) provides students with rapid access to explanations, summaries, and suggested answers. For 15-year-old learners, this accessibility raises an important educational and behavioural question: under what circumstances does AI support meaningful engagement with challenging learning materials, and when might it reduce opportunities for independent cognitive effort? This paper reviews published research in behavioural science and selected findings from the OECD's PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), with particular emphasis on Uzbekistan. Cognitive-demand avoidance and cognitive offloading are employed as theoretical frameworks for interpreting patterns of AI use, while a clear distinction is maintained between these concepts and the variables directly measured by PISA. According to the OECD, 48.6% of students in Uzbekistan use AI chatbots at least once a week to support their learning, compared with the OECD average of 45.5%. Furthermore, 80.6% of students in Uzbekistan report learning at school how to evaluate AI-generated information, compared with an OECD average of 62.6% (OECD, 2026). These findings indicate that AI-assisted learning is already widespread among students. However, the reported figures do not establish how frequently students substitute AI-generated summaries for assigned reading materials or identify the motivations underlying individual decisions to use AI in this way. The paper argues that the educational implications of AI use depend on the nature of the cognitive tasks delegated to AI, the learner's objectives, and the extent to which AI-generated information is critically evaluated and integrated into independent learning. As the study relies on secondary sources and does not involve the analysis of individual-level student records or the collection of primary empirical data, the proposed explanations should be understood as theoretically informed interpretations rather than established causal relationships. The paper concludes that educational institutions should develop students' ability not only to use AI tools effectively but also to recognise when independent reading, source verification, and critical reasoning remain essential for meaningful learning.

papers.title: Algorithmic Management, Employee Voice, and Procedural Justice: A Governance Framework for Accountable AI-Assisted Organizations
papers.authors: Tuğhan TURAN
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability

papers.title: Dreams for the Digital Commons
papers.authors: Morgan E. Currie, Caitlin McDonald, Jennifer Volk, Lara Dal Molin, Matea Senkić, Anna Kallen Talley, Nadia Piet, Ana Marques
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: How are online collections and archives reshaping the future of the open web as a result of new behaviour by AI scraping tools? Read this zine to find out! This zine is the result of two zine-making workshops on ‘AI and the Digital Commons: Perspectives from online collections & archives’. The two workshops are part of research carried out by the University of Edinburgh. The research investigates the risks that archival bodies and digital collections are facing from AI-driven content extraction tools. The research is funded by ekip, the European Cultural and Creative Sectors and Industries Policy Platform, an interdisciplinary four-year Horizon Europe project running from 2023–2026. ekip is a collaborative platform designed to boost the development of innovation capacity in ecosystems to include the Cultural and Creative Industries. This zine and zine workshops were designed by AIxDESIGN. The in-person zine workshop was hosted by The Netherlands Institute of Sound and Vision.

papers.title: Algorithmic Hegemony and the Coding of Gender: An Integrative Review of Artificial Intelligence Translucency in the Brazilian Scientific Ecosystem
papers.authors: EVANDRO CLARO FREIRE, COUTO Weslley de Souza
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ENGLISH RESEARCH INFORMATION Systematized research materials produced as part of a study on gender bias in Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems and its implications for the Brazilian scientific ecosystem. The study was conducted through an integrative literature review using the OpenAlex database and covering publications from 2023 to 2026. After applying the selection criteria, 23 publications were analyzed, focusing on manifestations of algorithmic bias, the technical and sociocultural factors associated with its emergence, and strategies proposed to mitigate bias and promote greater equity in AI systems. The research identified manifestations of gender bias across different AI application contexts, including healthcare, education, financial systems, and natural language processing. The factors discussed include historically biased datasets, limited diversity within development teams, reproduction of sociocultural structures, and limitations in the representation of different identities. Mitigation strategies identified in the literature include diversity, equity, and inclusion approaches; participatory design; curricular reforms; critical algorithmic literacy; and the development of technological and legal governance mechanisms. SCIENTIFIC OUTPUT Complete content of the scientific paper produced from the research, including its theoretical foundations, integrative review methodology, results, discussion of the evidence, and conclusions. The findings are organized around three research questions concerning manifestations of gender bias in AI applications, their technical and sociocultural origins, and strategies proposed for their mitigation within the Brazilian context. REPRODUCIBILITY AND PROVENANCE The research materials are made available to promote reproducibility, provenance, transparency, and scientific traceability throughout the research process. Their availability contributes to documenting the review procedures, the evidence analyzed, and the scientific outputs derived from the study. DECLARATION OF THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS Generative Artificial Intelligence tools were used exclusively for operational support: ChatGPT for the selection and evaluation of Boolean operators; Gemini for spelling and grammatical revision; and Claude for confirming, validating, and structuring references according to ABNT standards. All other stages, including analysis, interpretation, synthesis, and conclusions, were developed by the authors, who assume full responsibility for the scientific content. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS AND ADDITIONAL INFORMATION This study was financed in part by the Coordenação de Aperfeiçoamento de Pessoal de Nível Superior – Brasil (CAPES) – Finance Code 001. This paper was approved through peer review for the 3rd National Congress of Education and Scientific Production (III CONAPEC), held from October 19 to 22, 2026, and organized by the Sociedade Brasileira de Eventos Científicos (SOBREC). Although approved through the scientific peer-review process, the paper was not subsequently incorporated into the official conference proceedings because the financial requirements associated with formal publication could not be met. Documentation confirming the peer-review approval is provided as an attachment. HOW TO CITE CLARO FREIRE, Evandro; COUTO, Weslley de Souza. PORTUGUÊS INFORMAÇÕES DA PESQUISA Materiais sistematizados da pesquisa desenvolvida sobre vieses de gênero em sistemas de Inteligência Artificial (IA) e suas implicações no ecossistema científico brasileiro. O estudo foi conduzido por meio de revisão integrativa da literatura, com consulta à base OpenAlex e recorte temporal entre 2023 e 2026. Após aplicação dos critérios de seleção, foram analisadas 23 publicações, considerando manifestações de vieses algorítmicos, fatores técnicos e socioculturais associados à sua formação e estratégias propostas para mitigação e promoção de maior equidade nos sistemas de IA. A pesquisa identificou manifestações de viés em diferentes contextos de aplicação da IA, incluindo saúde, educação, sistemas financeiros e processamento de linguagem natural. Entre os fatores discutidos estão conjuntos de dados historicamente enviesados, baixa diversidade nas equipes de desenvolvimento, reprodução de estruturas socioculturais e limitações na representação de diferentes identidades. Como estratégias de mitigação, a literatura analisada apresenta abordagens relacionadas à diversidade, equidade e inclusão, design participativo, reformas curriculares, letramento crítico em algoritmos e desenvolvimento de mecanismos de governança tecnológica e jurídica. PRODUÇÃO CIENTÍFICA Conteúdo integral do artigo científico produzido a partir da pesquisa, incluindo fundamentação teórica, metodologia da revisão integrativa, resultados, discussão das evidências e conclusões. O trabalho organiza os resultados em torno de três questões de pesquisa relacionadas às manifestações dos vieses de gênero em aplicações de IA, às suas origens técnicas e socioculturais e às estratégias propostas para sua mitigação no contexto brasileiro. REPRODUTIBILIDADE E PROVENIÊNCIA Os materiais associados à pesquisa são disponibilizados com o objetivo de favorecer a reprodutibilidade, proveniência, transparência e rastreabilidade científica do processo de investigação. A disponibilização dos materiais permite documentar os procedimentos de revisão, as evidências analisadas e os produtos científicos derivados do estudo. DECLARAÇÃO DE USO DE FERRAMENTAS DE INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL Foram utilizadas ferramentas de Inteligência Artificial Generativa exclusivamente como suporte operacional: ChatGPT na seleção e avaliação dos operadores booleanos; Gemini para revisão ortográfica e gramatical; e Claude para confirmação, validação e estruturação das referências segundo as normas ABNT. As demais etapas, incluindo análise, interpretação, síntese e conclusão, foram desenvolvidas pelos autores, que assumem integral responsabilidade pelo conteúdo científico produzido. AGRADECIMENTOS E INFORMAÇÕES ADICIONAIS O presente trabalho foi realizado com apoio da Coordenação de Aperfeiçoamento de Pessoal de Nível Superior – Brasil (CAPES) – Código de Financiamento 001. O artigo foi aprovado por meio de processo de avaliação por pares (peer review) para o III Congresso Nacional de Educação e Produção Científica (III CONAPEC), realizado entre os dias 19 e 22 de outubro de 2026, sob realização da Sociedade Brasileira de Eventos Científicos (SOBREC). Embora aprovado no processo de avaliação científica, o trabalho não foi posteriormente incorporado aos anais oficiais do evento em decorrência da inviabilidade de atendimento aos encargos financeiros requeridos para a formalização de sua publicação. papers.title: Agent-friendly Provenance Capture with con-duct
papers.authors: Austin Macdonald, Cody Baker, John Anthony Lee, Yaroslav O. Halchenko
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Agent-friendly Provenance Capture with con-duct Presenters Austin Macdonald , ORCID 0000-0002-8124-807X Cody C. Baker , ORCID 0000-0002-0829-4790 John A. Lee , ORCID 0000-0001-5884-4247 Yaroslav O. Halchenko , ORCID 0000-0003-3456-2493 All: Center for Open Neuroscience, Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Dartmouth College Keywords agentic workflows, provenance, reproducibility, resource monitoring, HPC Abstract Whether trying out a new tool, testing pipelines, or meticulously analyzing data for research, the daily work of RSEs and their agents depends on keeping context lean but relevant. The terminal outputs of tools and scripts frequently hold the necessary information, but they are often either bloating an agent’s context window, or forgotten after a human’s terminal scrolls past the buffer. con-duct is a lightweight, Python-based command line tool with no third-party dependencies: just use duct instead of to run a command. A wrapped run leaves a trail: full stdout and stderr streamed to disk (or skipped, for sensitive output); resource usage sampled across the command’s process tree; and a record of the invocation, wall clock time, peak memory, exit code, and system and environment details. Workflow managers and experiment trackers produce richer records (the poster compares them); con-duct collects basic provenance with so little effort it can be used on everything, producing uniform records. In daily work, humans and agents now execute commands side by side. Using con-duct, the full record stays out of the context window until it is needed. Even better, multiple runs can be filtered and grepped, ready for the questions nobody knew to ask. When did our tests start having that warning? Did this run take longer? con-duct ls makes the answers discoverable, filtering on any captured field with a Python expression: con-duct ls -e "message==' '" retrieves runs tagged at capture time with duct -m " ". con-duct ls -e "exit_code != 0" lists failures. con-duct ls -e "peak_rss > 8e9" finds runs that exceeded a memory budget. At the tool level, projects can adopt con-duct internally rather than reinventing per-tool monitoring: ReproNim’s containers [5] and ReproStim [6] both offer it already, and the same con-duct ls queries read their records. For research, the record stops being a convenience, and starts being a part of the provenance chain [4]. Pairing con-duct with datalad (git-based version control for data)[2] is an easy win for rigor. datalad run "duct ..." completes the execution and then commits the diff (including the duct logs). On HPC, last month’s measured wall time and peak memory are already recorded, and can help inform tomorrow’s SLURM request. When an expensive job fails, the bug-report evidence is already on disk, no re-run necessary to file an issue. con-duct is on PyPI (pip install con-duct), conda-forge, registered as RRID:SCR_025436, and developed openly [1]. The poster shows three real cases: an fMRIPrep run on a SLURM cluster, its five hours of CPU and memory plotted from the record; a Kubernetes upgrade worked deploy by deploy, with every attempt’s command, exit code, and wall time kept by con-duct; and duct wrapped around duct to measure its own overhead. Keeping agents’ work auditable will take more than one tool; con-duct is one small piece: a wrapper that makes the agent’s work, like the human’s, leave a trace. Acknowledgments We thank the broader ReproNim and OpenNeuro communities for ongoing feedback on con-duct’s design and use. con-duct’s resource-monitoring approach is based on brainlife’s smon [3]. AI disclosure (per IEEE policy): Prose in the Abstract and Connection-to-Mission sections was drafted with assistance from Anthropic’s Claude; the authors specified the content, edited the text, and verified all technical claims, commands, and references. The con-duct software itself is developed with AI assistance, and with human review of all merged code. References con-duct. Center for Open Neuroscience. https://github.com/con/duct. RRID:SCR_025436. DataLad. https://www.datalad.org/. RRID:SCR_003931. brainlife smon. https://github.com/brainlife/abcd-spec/blob/master/hooks/smon Hoffstaedter, F. ds000007-mriqc (duct logs in logs/duct/). https://cerebra.fz-juelich.de/f.hoffstaedter/ds000007-mriqc/src/branch/base/logs/duct/ ReproNim/containers. https://github.com/ReproNim/containers. RRID:SCR_018467. ReproStim. https://github.com/ReproNim/reprostim. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4416842 Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community con-duct was built by RSEs at the Center for Open Neuroscience to record provenance for neuroimaging pipelines. The dev-side payoff (reaching back into outputs that would otherwise be gone) was an unexpected bonus. As LLM agents take on more of the executing (writing throwaway pipelines, exploring datasets, calling tools), the volume of unrecorded work explodes: more commands, more parallel streams, results produced faster than anyone reads them. RSEs are the people who decide whether that work remains auditable: who preserve the context, make it discoverable, and keep capture cheap enough that nobody skips the step. Integrating at the tool level saves each project from building its own monitoring and logging, and keeps the records uniform across tools, so the collection stays queryable as a whole.

papers.title: Designing for Trust in AI-Assisted Scientific Computing
papers.authors: Rajshree Deshmukh, Sheng Pang, Tanushree Subramanian, Johanna Cohoon, Sarah S. Poon, Dan Gunter
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: As AI assistance lowers the barrier to coding, domain experts with limited programming experience are increasingly able to make use of scientific computing software. Yet a critical gap remains: evaluating and understanding the AI-generated code is still a significant challenge, making it difficult to verify and trust results. This talk presents lessons from building a computational optimization platform for chemical process engineering, sharing UX strategies to build confidence among non-programmers by enabling them to visualize underlying conceptual models and validate AI-driven changes. AI tooling is becoming increasingly common in research software, and there is growing concern about new classes of subtle, hard-to-detect errors. Unlike obvious failures, AI-generated code changes can produce plausible but incorrect results that trigger no exceptions and leave no traces. This is especially problematic in model based scientific software where the internal reasoning can be opaque and complex code changes can be a "black box" for non-programmers. For these users, AI-facilitated changes may feel like trial and error guesswork rather than a deliberate and strategic process. Without better visibility and validation, researchers risk building on flawed results that are difficult and costly to correct later. Drawing on our experience building the Process Optimization and Modeling for Minerals Sustainability (PrOMMiS) Flowsheet Inspector, a domain-specific application designed for code-driven computational software, this talk shares UX strategies for building trust and confidence among domain experts with limited programming experience. We map the user journey and design considerations required to surface underlying conceptual models, empowering users to seamlessly execute, debug, and verify AI-generated modifications. Through examples from the app, we demonstrate the UX patterns that help to make the diagnostic information more accessible, improve error discoverability, and empower users to evaluate changes through an intuitive interface.

papers.title: Escaping the Enclave: Format-Faithful Synthetic Data for Open, Reproducible Medicare Claims Pipelines
papers.authors: Pavel Belakurski, Dmitry Etin, Mark Chumack, Michael Bouzinier
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Developing and testing software for regulated patient data such as Medicare claims is structurally expensive. Tooling work must occur inside credentialed, audited computing enclaves, where libraries and tools require approval before they can even be tried. This makes pipeline development and debugging far slower and more expensive than on an ordinary open stack. Because derived code and data cannot leave the enclave, pipelines cannot easily be shared, compared, or reproduced by others. We hypothesize that escaping this bind does not require statistically realistic synthetic data. For the purpose of building and testing data tooling, a pipeline exercises file formats, record structures, schema conformance, edge cases, and data-quality artifacts, rather than the true magnitudes of clinical or demographic distributions. Format and structural fidelity are therefore sufficient to support these engineering tasks; statistical fidelity is not a prerequisite. This claim does not eliminate final validation on real data, both for substantive analyses and for behavior on unanticipated production edge cases.We make this case concrete with synthmed, an open (Apache-2.0) Python package that generates a fully synthetic Medicare-like database conforming to Research Data Assistance Center (ResDAC) File Transfer Summary (FTS) layouts, together with a downloadable companion dataset (Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, CC-BY-4.0; calendar years 2011-2016). The generator emits fixed-width files in the same layouts as real Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) extracts, so the unmodified open dorieh ingestion pipeline can process them with no glue code and then run unchanged against the restricted extract inside the enclave. This demonstrates the approach for one workflow; transfer to other ResDAC consumers remains to be confirmed. Records are generated from AI-authored FTS specifications combined with public reference data and the CMS Data Entrepreneurs' Synthetic Public Use File (DE-SynPUF). An internal beneficiary table keeps synthetic identifiers and demographics consistent across files and years and injects data-quality artifacts to exercise error-handling and quality-control logic. No individual-level CMS ResDAC data or other real patient-level datasets are used, so the released files contain no protected health information or personally identifiable information.The generator is bit-reproducible under a fixed seed and has been run end to end with 5 million synthetic beneficiaries through the ingestion pipeline. An open quality-control run over that output identified a shape mismatch in the synthetic date-of-birth error distribution. Without the open synthetic run, detecting this deficiency would have required an authorized real-data run; the finding led to a corrected generation model.The artifacts support education, methods development, and extract-transform-load (ETL) or analysis-pipeline testing in population-health research. As more pipeline code is authored by AI, an open, format-faithful substrate of this kind also lowers the cost of independently inspecting, profiling, and regression-testing AI-generated ingestion logic outside the enclave. The released data are neither suitable nor intended for drawing substantive conclusions about real patients, providers, or health-care utilization.
keywords: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

papers.title: Usability Challenges across AI-Assisted Infrastructure, Security, and Scientific Workflows
papers.authors: Md Hasan Shahriar Simanto
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI-assisted tooling is increasingly being integrated into infrastructure management, security operations, software engineering, and scientific computing environments. While discussion around AI adoption often emphasizes automation and productivity, expert users still need to understand what these systems are doing, decide when to trust their recommendations, and know what to do when the system is wrong or uncertain. This talk synthesizes findings and observations from UX research across enterprise data classification, identity and access management (IAM), backup and recovery, ransomware resilience, and AI-assisted infrastructure workflows. The evidence includes studies with cloud developers, security and compliance practitioners, and IT and site reliability professionals, alongside ongoing design and research work examining how expert users interact with AI-supported technical systems. Across these domains, three recurring usability challenges emerge: unclear system state, difficulty evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and limited support for correcting or recovering from AI-supported actions when something goes wrong. Although the technical environments differ, users repeatedly need to understand what the system observed or changed, evaluate whether a recommendation is appropriate for their specific context, and determine what to verify, reverse, or escalate before taking consequential action. These challenges have direct implications for research software engineering. AI-assisted code generation, workflow scripting, cloud and HPC configuration, notebook assistants, debugging, testing, and scientific automation introduce similar questions about visibility, trust, accountability, and recoverability. Lessons from enterprise infrastructure and security therefore provide useful design considerations for RSEs evaluating or building AI-assisted research software. The session offers a cross-domain synthesis of these recurring human-AI interaction challenges and practical questions for evaluating AI-assisted systems. Attendees will leave with a set of questions they can use to evaluate AI-assisted systems: whether users can understand system state, decide when to rely on a recommendation and when to question it, intervene when necessary, and verify or recover from the resulting actions. Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community This talk aligns closely with the USRSE’26 theme, “Advancing Science in the Age of AI,” by focusing on the human and operational challenges that emerge as AI-assisted tooling is integrated into technical and scientific workflows. My background is in UX research and human factors across enterprise infrastructure, cloud systems, security tooling, and scientific software environments. Across these domains, I have observed the same challenges emerge when expert users interact with AI systems, including issues with transparency, trust calibration, oversight, error recovery, and workflow integration. While conversations around AI often emphasize capability and productivity, this session examines how usability and human-centered design influence the successful adoption of AI within complex environments. These topics are directly relevant to research software engineers who develop, evaluate, maintain, or adopt AI-assisted tools as part of scientific workflows. The goal of this session is to encourage discussion around designing AI systems that better support expert users while maintaining reliability, transparency, and human understanding. These topics connect strongly with the US-RSE community’s broader interests in sustainable, usable, and effective research software.

papers.title: Developing a Handbook of best practices for research software sustainability at Princeton
papers.authors: T. Sakuma, Joel Bretheim, Ian A. Cosden, Jacob Murel, Robert V. Caddy, Henry Schreiner, Lucas Sawade, Rohit Kakodkar, Mohamed Abdellatif, Georgios Artavanis, Andres Rios‐Tascon, Rebecca Sutton Koeser, Anushka Acharya, Bonaldo, Luca, Amy Defnet, Rob Bierman, Jonathan Hanke, Joshua D. Carmichael, Lance R. Parsons, David Luet
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In the early 2010s, the Software Sustainability Institute defined sustainability as "software you use today will be available — and continue to be improved and supported — in the future" [1, 2]. Sustainable research software has enabled research that would otherwise be infeasible. The pursuit of sustainability continues, spanning efficiency, longevity over generations of research projects, and spread across research fields. In this context, the Princeton Research Software Engineering (RSE) group, as one of the first and largest centralized RSE groups in US institutions [3], has both the breadth of RSE experience and the team bandwidth to further advance sustainability. In the Princeton RSE group, we are developing a handbook of best practices for research software sustainability. As sustainability is inherently contingent [4], it is not possible to prescribe criteria for it. Instead, the Handbook enumerates characteristics of sustainable research software. Software with these characteristics substantially increases its chances of being sustained. Sustainable research software has reliable tests as its technical foundation; they enable iterative cycles of refactoring and feature addition and also underpin confidence in AI-assisted and agentic development, yielding frequent releases that progressively improve maintainability, reproducibility, and other technical qualities. These technical characteristics are necessary but not sufficient. Long-term sustainable research software also has social and organizational characteristics, including citability, continuous funding, professional maintenance, and active communities. The Handbook collects best practices, based on our experience, that realize these characteristics, from basics to advanced topics such as how to turn unsustainable research code into a testable package. The Handbook facilitates communication with principal investigators and research project managers; the best practices describe what we do and how we identify and resolve software engineering issues within research projects. In this talk, we will present our approach to building the Handbook; discuss what distinguishes it from other best practices guides, for instance, its grounding in the operational practice of a centralized, multidisciplinary RSE group; review the practices at a high level; and suggest ways for others in the community to leverage the Handbook in their organizations. The Handbook will be publicly available under a Creative Commons license. The Handbook is not a static document that we publish and finish; we develop it as we develop sustainable software, with continuous updates as demanded, most frequently by the rapid evolution of AI tools and practices.

papers.title: AI and the reorganization of RSE work
papers.authors: Will Sutherland, Anissa Tanweer, James D. Herbsleb, Thomas Bock, Curtis J. Atkisson, Bogdan Vasilescu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot have significant implications for the way software is built and maintained in the sciences. Some of these implications center around changes in practice, such as greater or worse productivity and the need for verification practices (He et al., 2025; O'Brien, 2025a; O’Brien, 2025b; Besser et al., 2026; O'Brien and Eisty, 2026). Another dimension of concern, however, is how research software development work will be reorganized around the presence of coding agents. Broader discourse has focused on the possibility of replacement or simple automation of software engineering work by agents, but, as with prior developments, the change is more likely to involve a more complex re-ordering of the work of producing software (Jarrahi, 2018; see also Gesing, 2025). Emerging work in industrial and open source contexts, for instance, suggests that coding agents can affect the interactions around code review (Song et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2026a), assume different roles in the development process (Agarwal et al., 2026b), and can change where particular kinds of development work fall in a team or community (Xu et al., 2025). This poster explores these shifts in the context of RSE work by examining dynamics of re-delegation going on around the adoption of coding agents by researchers and RSEs. Based on interviews with 25 RSEs and RSE managers in the US, we first outline these RSEs’ rationales about what makes research software development either amenable or unsuitable for the use of AI coding agents. These include niche codebases, siloed working environments, savvy end users, prevalence of prototyping, and the importance of problem formation. We then outline three dynamics of re-delegation, each of which represents a shift in the way work is divided up and assigned (or taken on) amongst human and non-human actors (Ribes et al., 2013). These are: enabling end-user development, delegating implementation, and taking on AI training roles. In some cases our interlocutors report quite different and sometimes contradictory experiences across these categories. This raises two questions that can help stimulate further discussion on this topic: 1) What aspects of RSE working environments might contribute to RSEs’ different experiences with AI coding agents? 2) What organizational changes could RSEs or RSE teams make that might mitigate some of the problems associated with the growing usage of AI coding agents while making best use of those agents’ benefits?
