papers.title: Using AI as an Emotion Regulation Sounding Board in Foreign Language Teaching
papers.authors: Dino Dumančić
papers.journal: Journal for the Psychology of Language Learning
papers.abstract: The aim of the present study was to investigate Croatian foreign language teachers' emotional responses related to challenging situations encountered in their workplace, such as dealing with misbehaving learners, demanding parents, conflicts with colleagues, and unexpected scenarios causing discomfort. By adopting a qualitative, holistic approach, the study explored different facets of teachers’ emotional responses (e.g., behavioral and cognitive), the emotion regulation (ER) strategies employed, as well as the use and perception of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in managing unpleasant emotions. The teachers in the study used an online diary to document their work-related emotional experiences. The findings revealed reports of different unpleasant emotions, predominantly anger, frustration, and irritability tied to varied causes, such as learner misbehavior, colleagues’ unprofessional behavior, and relationship with parents. Emotional experiences were accompanied by various bodily and cognitive manifestations, such as shallow, fast breathing, tension, mental fatigue, and rumination, to name a few. To cope with the unpleasant emotions, the teachers resorted to different types of ER, predominantly those belonging to the response-focused category (e.g., swearing or listening to music), followed by seeking support from others, and cognitive reappraisal (antecedent-focused strategies). The teachers used AI as a sounding board for ER. They received advice emphasizing empathy, calmness, problem-solving, support-seeking, and boundary-setting to address emotional challenges. The participants reported mixed experiences with the advice they received, finding it helpful in some cases but often difficult to apply in practice due to its general nature. Lastly, the teachers observed that AI's lack of empathy and contextual understanding made it a less desirable choice compared to human support when addressing their emotional needs.

papers.title: New and Emerging Sub-Fields of Applied Linguistics: An Introduction to Developing Areas. A Subject Review
papers.authors: Asst. Inst. Lina Salam Farouq
papers.journal: Central Asian Journal of Literature Philosophy and Culture
papers.abstract: New sub-areas have emerged recently next to linguistic fields, which are mostly influenced by digital technology, multilingual classrooms, and attention to the emotional and social learning experience of learners. The current paper aims at exploring ten emerging areas: Generative AI and large language models, Translanguaging pedagogy, Informal digital learning of English, Data-driven learning, positive psychology in SLA, Machine translation literacy, Multimodal literacies, Ecolinguistics, Linguistic landscape studies, and Critical language awareness/Raciolinguistics. The study concluded that the ten areas indicate that applied linguistics is becoming interdisciplinary in its development. Digital technologies link language teaching and learning with computational systems, multilingualism links language pedagogy with research in sociolinguistics and identity, positive psychology links language learning with emotion research, and ecological and critical approaches link language learning with other social issues.

papers.title: Association between Player Perception and AI Disclosure on Steam: An Exploratory Study
papers.authors: Fabian Wiesinger, Johanna Pirker, Denis Helić
papers.abstract: The use of generative AI in game development is growing rapidly and is the subject of intense debate in which player reactions play a central role. This paper contributes to this discussion by analyzing Steam reviews to examine whether games with AI disclosure are associated with different review patterns. Using a dataset across multiple disclosure groups, we apply linguistic analysis including keyword-based, word frequency, and characteristic word analysis to investigate the AI-related discussion on Steam. Our results show that AI-disclosed games are associated with higher levels of AI-related criticism in negative reviews. Our findings provide a first exploratory step towards understanding how players perceive AI disclosure.

papers.title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Shreyas Kulkarni, Uttam Gurram, Madhav Kanda, Krishna Teja Chitty Venkata, Shi Chen, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Supriyo Chakraborty, Sambit Sahu
papers.abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. This can produce inconsistent drafts and reduce acceptance length. Iterative refinement mitigates this limitation by conditioning later predictions on previously committed tokens, though additional passes increase drafting cost. To address this trade-off between draft fidelity and inference latency, we introduce DStill, a two-stage framework that distills a target-conditioned drafter's own multi-step refinement into one-step drafting. We first train the drafter to complete partially revealed blocks, then use its refinement trajectories to train a student to predict the final completion in one pass. Using a curriculum that gradually transitions from partial to fully masked inputs, we successfully transfer the multi-step refinement capabilities into one step. Across reasoning, math, code benchmarks on three model families DStill improves acceptance length by up to 28% and speedup by up to 25% over one-step DFlash, achieving up to 6.45x speedup over auto-regressive decoding.

papers.title: Modeling Authentic Research Trajectories: A Graph View of Research Ideation
papers.authors: Ruochen Li, Zhiyu Chen
papers.abstract: The research idea in a published paper is rarely the project's initial idea. Between the two lies a closed-loop process in which researchers run experiments, derive insights, identify challenges, explore the literature, and revise the idea, with each step motivated by evidence and reasoning they can articulate. We call the path one idea takes through this process, with the evidence and reasoning behind each step, its authentic research trajectory. Although it underlies every scientific contribution, it is rarely recorded. Existing LLM-based research agents generate an idea once, refine it against reviews, literature, or their own experimental results, or search over candidate ideas and experiments. In all of them the text of the idea evolves, while the evidence and reasoning that connected one version to the next are discarded. We propose the Research Progress Graph (RPG), a representation of authentic and complete research trajectories. An RPG records the evolution of an idea as typed research states connected by cognitive transitions, each annotated with a temporal index and the reasoning behind it, which makes this evolution an explicit object of study. We ground the representation in authentic trajectories whose steps their authors justify in annotations and papers. Comparing the representations of thirty-five research agents with the RPG, we find that each is an incomplete RPG; none keeps the state that changed, the evidence that changed it, and the reasoning connecting them as one evolving record. Modeling ideation with the RPG changes how research agents should be designed, evaluated, and trained. Agents predict the next research state instead of a complete idea, ideas are evaluated as trajectories instead of final texts, and authentic trajectories serve as training data. These directions shift research agents from generating static ideas to modeling how ideas evolve.

papers.title: Determination of the Human-Robot Interaction Workspace for Robot Assisted Head Stabilization Control
papers.authors: Xinmin Liu, Alexander L. Van Slyke, Destinee Holloman, Ahmad Sakaamini, Rodney D. Wiersma
papers.abstract: Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.

papers.title: Inspectable LLM-Simulated Participants for Qualitative Interview Rehearsal
papers.authors: Hangyue Zhang, Qiran Hu, Ziyi Zhang, Hyanghee Park, Yun Huang
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly used across research workflows, including research ideation, qualitative analysis, and participant simulation. Within work on participant simulation, prior studies have largely evaluated simulated participants by how realistic or human-like their responses appear, leaving less known about how researchers use and critique these materials when revising interview protocols before fieldwork. We present Rehearsim, an inspectable research probe that treats LLM-simulated participants as materials for methodological rehearsal rather than substitutes for human participants. Rehearsim combines literature-grounded participant construction, interactive interview rehearsal, and traceable thematic review while keeping protocol decisions under researcher control. In a study with 21 qualitative researchers, participants used simulated materials to surface assumptions and gaps, reconsider participant populations, revise target populations, and develop follow-up probes. They also identified risks, including the concealment of weak questions, dismissal of unexpected synthetic details, and interpretive anchoring from generated themes. We derive an inspectable-rehearsal framework emphasizing traceability, contestability, researcher control, and epistemic boundaries.

papers.title: The Differential Effects of AI Abstention on Advice Acceptance
papers.authors: Nicholas Wolczynski, Yotam Liel, Maytal Saar‐Tsechansky, Lior Zalmanson
papers.abstract: AI advising systems are typically designed to always provide a response. Recent work has focused on developing systems that withhold advice in some instances, such as when advice quality is questionable, to improve the overall quality of guidance when it is given; a design paradigm we refer to as AI abstention. While substantial work has focused on optimizing when models should abstain, little is known about how users respond to systems that abstain. In a preregistered experiment, participants made repeated financial decisions, assisted by one of two advising regimes: an AI that advises selectively or one that advises on every decision. We find that the same AI abstention regime produces differential effects depending on the user: it increases advice acceptance among users with high perceived expertise and tends to decrease it among users with low perceived expertise. This differential effect is accounted for by the cognitive burden users face when repeatedly reconciling AI recommendations with their own judgment; AI abstention appears to relieve this burden among users with high perceived expertise, and in doing so increases their receptivity to advice. Further, AI abstention mitigates the decline in advice acceptance observed among expert users over repeated interactions. Exploratory evidence also suggests it increases appropriate acceptance where advice would improve the decision, increasing the downstream accuracy of perceived experts. The AI abstention regime is thus a first-order design property of AI advisory systems, and one that must be calibrated to the users a system serves.

papers.title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
papers.authors: Xiaohang Tang, Rehema Abulikemu, Peng Gao, Yan Chen
papers.abstract: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.

papers.title: AI Misconception and Adoption Among Indonesian K-12 Teachers
papers.authors: Alham Fikri Aji, Afifa Amriani, Rendi Chevi, Ayu Purwarianti, Derry Tanti Wijaya
papers.abstract: Indonesia's fragmented geography and uneven infrastructure pose persistent challenges for adopting new educational technologies. While national initiatives aim to mainstream AI in K-12 schools by 2025, policy readiness does not automatically mean teachers are ready for the classroom. This study surveys Indonesian K-12 teachers to examine: (1) their understanding of AI, (2) how they and their students use AI, and (3) their views on the acceptability of AI in learning activities. Through semi-automated thematic analysis, we identify common misconceptions and use cases. Our findings reveal a notable mismatch: while teachers find AI use in education acceptable and support it for the sake of efficiency, they remain fully aware of the risks to learning depth and academic honesty. We also find that this high level of acceptance is currently coupled with a poor understanding of how AI actually works.

papers.title: Doubly Robust Learning of Heterogeneous Survival Treatment Effects under Time-Varying Treatments
papers.authors: Tomàs Grau Garriga, Munib Mesinovic, Luke De Bretton-Gordon, Gerard Sanz, Axel Brando, Tingting Zhu
papers.abstract: Estimating heterogeneous survival treatment effects (HSTEs) from time-to-event data under time-varying treatments is important in fields such as medicine (e.g., to decide which sequence of treatments is better in terms of survival probability). However, this task is challenging because treatment decisions, patient characteristics, and censoring probability often evolve together, requiring sequential adjustment for both treatments and censoring. Existing survival learners mostly consider a single baseline treatment assignment, while longitudinal treatment-effect learners typically assume uncensored outcomes. In this paper, we introduce a novel doubly robust learner for heterogeneous survival treatment effects under time-varying treatments and history-dependent censoring. Our framework separates the intervention window from the survival horizon, with treatment prescribed for a finite period, after which care follows its natural course. We further establish the favorable theoretical properties of Neyman-orthogonality, rate double robustness and quasi-oracle efficiency. The framework accommodates flexible machine learning models for nuisance estimation and treatment-effect regression. We evaluate our learners through several numerical experiments, demonstrating their effectiveness.

papers.title: SleepPairNet: Learning Multimodal Pediatric Sleep Representations with Random-Pair Cross-Attention
papers.authors: Saurav Raj Pandey, Harlin Lee
papers.abstract: Analyzing physiological sleep signals is important for assessing sleep quality and detecting sleep-related disorders. Learning inter-modal relationships across physiological signals can provide richer representations for downstream sleep analysis. We introduce SleepPairNet, a multimodal self-supervised learning (SSL) framework that learns pairwise interactions between physiological signals through cross-attention. We propose a random modality-pair selection strategy that exposes the model to diverse signal pairs during pretraining, enabling flexibility across modality combinations at test time. Pretrained on the NCH dataset, SleepPairNet outperforms the evaluated SSL baselines on all respiratory tasks while remaining competitive on EEG-related tasks, and shows even stronger results when transferred to the external CHAT dataset.

papers.title: RoboMMT: Learning Stable Tracking of Modulated Expressive and Interactive Robot Motion
papers.authors: Till Hielscher, Kai O. Arras
papers.abstract: Expressive robot motion can improve naturalness, effectiveness, and perceived likability in human-robot interaction. When deployed on dynamically unstable platforms, however, reactive execution of expressive body motion may bring the robot to its stability limits, especially when expressivity is decoupled from physical control. In this paper, we present RoboMMT (Robot Modulated Motion Tracking), a modular control architecture that couples parameterized expressive motion synthesis, physics-based character control, and reactive adaptation to spatial interaction goals. Our approach trains a reference-conditioned tracking policy across a broad domain of expressivity, enabling it to faithfully realize the commanded motions while maintaining dynamic stability. Goal reactivity is achieved by training lightweight, task-specific interaction policies that modulate the reference generator's spatial goal-attraction point, with the stabilizing tracking policy kept in the loop. Evaluations on a quadruped and two humanoid robots show that the learned tracker remains stable and accurate across the entire modulation domain, whereas trackers trained without this coverage lose balance, tracking accuracy, or both. We show that layering closed-loop goal adaptation over this foundation enables interactive facing and pointing behaviors, while maintaining stable execution and comparable reference-tracking fidelity. The robot learns to proactively redistribute its weight and take corrective steps. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated through real-robot experiments on a quadruped under heavy disturbances.

papers.title: LaMER: Language-Conditioned Multi-Expert Routing for Weakly Supervised Referring Expression Comprehension
papers.authors: Yu Yu Chang, Tzu-Hsuan Weng, Youssef Mohamed Amin, Mohaned Ahmed Elsayed, Hung-Hsuan Chen, Min-Te Sun, Sherine Shawky
papers.abstract: Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) localizes the image region described by a natural language expression, underpinning applications such as autonomous navigation, human-robot interaction, and medical image analysis. Under weak supervision, REC is challenged by the visual-linguistic semantic gap and the difficulty of inferring region-text correspondences from coarse image-level signals alone. Moreover, no single visual encoder captures all complementary properties---semantic alignment, fine-grained texture, and boundary awareness---while naively fusing multiple pretrained encoders yields heterogeneous, hard-to-reconcile representations. We propose LaMER, a weakly supervised REC framework that dynamically aggregates four frozen expert encoders through a language-conditioned Cross-Modal Routing Fusion module, adapting expert selection to each referring expression without instance-level bounding-box supervision. A Cell-Text Matching Head with Negative Anchor Augmentation, trained with a multi-objective loss combining contrastive, reconstruction, alignment, and load-balancing terms, further stabilizes optimization. LaMER achieves 77.67\%, 62.81\%, and 69.49\% Acc@IoU\(\geq 0.5\) on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg, surpassing DViN and WeakMCN by up to 16.49 and 14.49 points, with ablations validating each component.

papers.title: Logit Averaging During Training Sets a New State of the Art for Non-Invasive Speech BCI
papers.authors: Miran Özdogan, Gereon Elvers, Michael M. Bronstein, Ōiwi Parker Jones
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces are in practice limited by signal-to-noise ratio, and recent state-of-the-art methods address this limitation by aggregating over repeated trials of the same stimulus. Yet multi-trial aggregation has been treated inconsistently across the literature: some work averages brain signals at the model's input, other work averages predictions at the model's output, and neither treats aggregation as an architectural choice in its own right. We provide the first systematic comparison of aggregation strategies for non-invasive neural decoding, evaluating six paradigms (including logit averaging during training and three attention-based variants we introduce) across three datasets, four tasks, and two group sizes. We find that aggregation choice matters substantially: training-time logit averaging, the simplest method we propose, outperforms all others in 6 of 7 settings. On the phoneme classification setting of the 2025 PNPL competition, it sets a new state of the art, significantly outperforming the competition winner by 17.4 absolute percentage points in balanced accuracy. We further draw a theoretical connection between logit averaging and joint ensemble training, which has been shown to underperform independent ensembling in the deep learning literature; our results call into question recent explanations of why joint ensemble training fails. Together, these findings establish multi-trial aggregation as a key design choice for non-invasive neural decoding and identify training-time logit averaging as a simple, effective default.

papers.title: Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network for Asymmetric EEG-Eye Movement Emotion Recognition
papers.authors: Peijun Shi, Xiujin Zhu, Zhenguo Lao, Chee-Onn Chow, Wei Ru Wong, Zhen Liu, Xiaobing Jiang
papers.abstract: EEG-eye movement emotion recognition can support mental-health monitoring and adaptive interfaces, but most fusion models treat the two signals as parallel features, classify each window alone and degrade when eye data are lost. We propose the Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network (CTD-GNet), in which EEG features form the nodes of an electrode graph, and eye movements and preceding windows modulate its edges, nodes and readout, the edges through electrode-specific prompts. Bidirectional distillation of the graph, node relations and predictions couples this multimodal teacher with a single-window EEG student, improving the teacher and aligning the two graphs 35-fold. In leave-one-subject-out tests on SEED and SEED-IV against 17 baselines, CTD-GNet has the highest mean accuracy, 84.91% and 76.17%, significantly above 9 and 6 of 13 eye-based baselines after Holm correction, the smallest cross-subject spread among multimodal models and the highest worst-subject accuracy. It is the most accurate model at every rate of missing eye data on SEED-IV, keeps 66.1% on SEED without eye data, more than any EEG-only model, and stays 9.3 and 11.9 points above all single-window fusion models under eye-movement noise of one standard deviation. On film clips unseen in training, it leads on SEED with 77.1%.

papers.title: Honeyed Words, Hidden Daggers: Benchmarking and Training LLMs to See Through Mock Politeness
papers.authors: Caixin Kang, Sitong Gong, Tianyu Yan, Kaipeng Zhang, Yoichi Sato, Yifei Huang
papers.abstract: The Chinese idiom "kou mi fu jian" ("honeyed words, hidden daggers") names speech that is polite in form but hostile in function. We present ZhenhuanBench, a 1,592-item benchmark built from expert commentary on Empresses in the Palace, covering speaker intent, emotion-language mismatch, and per-listener uptake. Text-only evaluation covers 34 LLMs. GPT-6 Astra leads the leaderboard at 73.48% overall, while its listener-reaction score is 58.37%. The annotations also supply supervised traces and string-verifiable training rewards. With 338 gold traces, an 8B model outperforms teacher distillation on identical items. Subsequent RL saturates, and chance correction reduces the estimated recoverable performance gap by a factor of 7.5. Our CPR-GRPO loop (Compress-Probe-Replenish) uses this estimate to weight gold supervision, reaching 67.0 on public multiple-choice tasks and 74.5 under the training-matched hidden protocol. Without target-task training, CPR outperforms Base, SFT, and GRPO across six Chinese and English pragmatic and sarcasm evaluations. On three external datasets, training with CPR yields higher mean Macro-F1 than SFT and GRPO.

papers.title: SPLASH: Contrastive Audit Pressure for Detecting and Localizing Security Hallucinations in Generated Code
papers.authors: Mirza Masfiqur Rahman, Ajwad Akil, Imtiaz Karim, Ashish Kundu, Ramana Rao Kompella, Elisa Bertino
papers.abstract: Code generated by large language models often passes every functional test while remaining insecure. These security hallucinations are common, written with high confidence, and repeated across samples, so neither the generator's own uncertainty nor static analyzers reliably catch them. We introduce SPLASH, which is guided by a new measure called audit pressure. It contrasts teacher-forced log-probabilities for the generated program under a security review and a style review. Aggregated to statements and programs, and grounded in a probabilistic model of competing edits, audit pressure allows SPLASH to choose the secure program among a model's candidate programs and locate the vulnerable statement, with no model training, CWE-specific rules, or internal access to the generating model. On 63,684 programs generated by 12 models for 899 tasks, SPLASH picks secure code in 74% of cases, places the vulnerable statement first in 58% of insecure programs, and chooses better than a frontier LLM judge.

papers.title: Correctness-Dependent Asymmetric Target Distributions for Self-Distillation Policy Optimization
papers.authors: Suwan Yoon, Seongryong Jung, Changhee Lee
papers.abstract: Self-distillation policy optimization provides dense token-level supervision for LLM post-training through feedback-conditioned self-teachers. However, directly matching the self-teacher can disrupt successful behaviors on correct rollouts while providing insufficient correction on incorrect ones. We propose Asymmetric Policy Optimization via Self-Distillation (APSD), which constructs correctness-dependent targets by mixing student and self-teacher distributions: interpolation preserves successful behaviors on correct rollouts, while extrapolation beyond the self-teacher strengthens correction on incorrect ones. We analyze APSD through divergence decomposition, reverse-KL barycentric geometry, and gradient analysis, highlighting the importance of gradient flow through student-dependent targets. Experiments under reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and rich feedback show that APSD achieves strong overall performance against reinforcement-learning and self-distillation baselines and matches SDPO performance with 2.6x fewer training steps on average across Qwen3 model scales.

papers.title: OrderGPT: Generation Order as a Learnable Modeling Choice
papers.authors: Chenhe Yang, Yuhuan Lyu, Tianyang Hu
papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.

papers.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
papers.authors: Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu, Hope Yao
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

papers.title: Can LLM User-Proxies Stand In for Humans in Reliance Measurement? Replicating Rel-A.I. with Simulated Users
papers.authors: Shuai Wang, Rui Hua Hu
papers.abstract: Can language-model user proxies reproduce human reliance on an AI answer across contexts? Published simulated-user studies do not establish validity for this partial-answer decision, and Rel-A.I.'s released human record omits trial-level choices. We audit its 90 printed questions and 15 domain-by-marker reliance rates using sampled decisions and counterbalanced A/B probabilities from open models through 72B parameters. A matched crossover varies the printed agent specialty within each question, separating question content, label averages, and their interaction. Mistral Small's strong-marker math-minus-law label marginal is -0.4 percentage points, yet matching the agent label to the question domain raises reliance by 13.3 points on average across the five domains. The best A/B proxy has 22.5-point absolute-rate error and 8.3-point domain-effect error against the human table. A two-sample independent-binomial human replication has 3.5-point expected domain-effect error under the stated working model. The interaction is model dependent, and inference layout changes identical-prompt probabilities. This single-study audit does not establish proxy validity for human effect sizes or general directional screening.

papers.title: PronCFT: Pronunciation Contextual Fine-Tuning for Contextual Biasing of Out-of-Vocabulary Words in LLM-Based ASR
papers.authors: Yifan Xu, Kaixun Huang, Mengzhe Geng, Mingyu Cui, Shen Huang, Shidong Shang, Xunying Liu
papers.abstract: LLM-based ASR systems often replace rare and out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words with familiar words that sound similar. Two factors contribute to this error: the model has not learned how an unseen word's sound maps to its spelling, and it may favor a familiar word over the one spoken, a failure we call prior suppression. Providing candidate pronunciations alone may not help: the model can treat a phoneme annotation as a marker that raises a candidate's output probability without checking its pronunciation against the speech. We propose PronCFT, which uses fixed phoneme sequences and trains the model to transcribe speech into phonemes, match them to context candidates, and output the matched spelling. During training, we alter candidate spellings while keeping their pronunciations unchanged, discouraging the model from choosing a familiar spelling without checking how the candidate sounds. A curriculum then gradually removes intermediate outputs to reduce decoding latency and prevent phoneme transcription errors from affecting the final text. The model's retained ability to use pronunciation cues suggests that this ability can be internalized. On an OOV test set filtered from open-source benchmarks, the final model, PronCFT-C, significantly improves recall from 59.89% to 83.57% (+23.68 pp). Wrong-phoneme and spelling-interference tests indicate that the gain depends on phoneme content rather than the presence of an annotation.

papers.title: A Calibrated Instrument for Detecting Disposition Drift in Language Models
papers.authors: Jerry Kaplan
papers.abstract: Before language models are released, they are tested for harmful traits such as willingness to carry out dangerous requests, deception, power seeking, and sycophancy. The safe behavior these tests certify may degrade as models are modified, by topical fine-tuning, new training data, or changes to settings such as the depth of their reasoning. Most work reports such drift as single summary rates scored by another AI model, without the error analysis needed to interpret them. We adapt a calibrated measurement methodology recently developed for assessing how inference optimizations affect the quality of model outputs. Applying it to several misalignment dimensions in two open-weight models, we first establish the instrument's precision, showing that shifts of a few percentage points can be reliably detected. We then induce drift deliberately by fine-tuning on correct and on subtly harmful medical and financial advice; harmful advice induces a far greater shift than correct advice. Most strikingly, a model that reasons before answering can conceal the shift almost entirely in its answers, even though a direct reading of its internal state shows that its disposition has moved. With reasoning switched off, the same model shifts steadily as the share of harmful advice in its training grows. These results demonstrate the importance of testing safety with reasoning turned both on and off.

papers.title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
papers.authors: Fengfei Yu, Marshall Fisher, Isadora White, Sumanth Varambally, Yasaman Jafari, Shivam Yadav, Samuel M. Bartlett, Shawn Roj, Benjamin J. Moore, Michael D. Warner, Luyu Han, Zhirui Xia, Duncan Watson-Parris, Taylor Berg-Kirkpatrick, Yian Ma, Rose Yu
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Community Medicine, 2015–2025: Transformations in Health Systems, Digital Epidemiology, and Equity-oriented Public Health
papers.authors: Swapnil Namdeorao Patil, Rujuta Hadaye
papers.abstract: Background: Community Medicine has undergone substantial transformation between 2015 and 2025. Global development commitments, changing disease patterns, the expansion of digital technologies, and the COVID-19 pandemic have broadened its scope beyond traditional preventive services towards health-systems strengthening, implementation research, and population-level policy development.Objective: To describe the major advances in Community Medicine between 2015 and 2025, with particular emphasis on universal health coverage, comprehensive primary healthcare, digital health, epidemiological innovation, disease surveillance, non-communicable diseases, environmental health, mental health, and public health governance.Methods: A narrative review was developed using the supplied educational document, Recent Advances in Preventive and Social Medicine (2015–2025), as its primary source. Its thematic content was synthesised around major developments in public health practice and health-system organisation. Selected international frameworks, policy documents, and peer-reviewed publications were used to contextualise the discussion. This was not a systematic review, and no formal database search, study-selection protocol, or risk-of-bias assessment was undertaken.Results: The review identified six interconnected areas of transformation: the transition towards universal health coverage and comprehensive primary healthcare; the integration of digital health and artificial intelligence into public health practice; the evolution of epidemiology and disease surveillance; the growing importance of non-communicable diseases and mental health; the recognition of environmental and social determinants of health; and the increasing emphasis on implementation science, equity, and accountable governance. In India, initiatives such as Ayushman Bharat, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, and expanded telemedicine services illustrate these developments. However, unequal service availability, workforce shortages, financial barriers, digital exclusion, and weaknesses in data governance continue to limit their potential.Conclusion: Community Medicine has evolved into a multidisciplinary, systems-oriented specialty that connects epidemiological evidence with policy, technology, and community participation. Future progress will depend on strengthening primary healthcare, developing a competent public health workforce, improving implementation research, protecting data privacy, and ensuring that technological and policy innovations benefit underserved populations.

papers.title: Remote term consequences of acute peat smoke intoxication during puberty in an animal experiment
papers.authors: Vera A. Vokina, Larisa M. Sosedova, Anna A. Pankova, Вера Александровна Абрамова, Е. А. Титов, Михаил Александрович Новиков
papers.abstract: Introduction. Exposure to peat smoke is a significant environmental risk factor for public health. The period of puberty is characterized by increased vulnerability of the central nervous and reproductive systems to the toxic components of smoke, such as particulate matter (PM2.5) and carbon monoxide (CO). The aim of this study was to evaluate the remote effects of exposure to peat smoke on the central nervous system and reproductive system in white rats under conditions simulating real-world concentrations of PM2.5 and CO.Materials and Methods. Exposure to peat smoke was performed once for 4 hours during the pubertal period in white rats of both sexes. The mean concentrations of CO and PM2.5 in the exposure chambers were 29.3 ± 11.1 mg/m³ and 0.39 ± 0.61 mg/m³, respectively. Examination at adulthood included analysis of behavioral responses in the open field test, electroencephalography (EEG) recording, analysis of DNA fragmentation in blood cells, and histological analysis of brain tissue and testes.Results. A decrease in locomotor and exploratory activity was observed in exposed animals of both sexes. EEG changes were observed only in female white rats and were characterized by a statistically significant decrease in the mean amplitude of the β2 rhythm and an increase in the δ rhythm index compared with the control group. DNA damage in blood cells of exposed animals showed no statistically significant differences when compared with the control. Histological examination of the sensorimotor cortex of the brain and the testes revealed no abnormalities.Limitations. This study is limited to investigating the remote effect of a single exposure to peat smoke during puberty on the central nervous system and reproductive system of white rats.Conclusion. Exposure to peat smoke during puberty potentially contributes to the development of depressive-like behavior in adult white rats while preserving normal histological architecture of brain tissue. No gonadotoxic or genotoxic effects were observed.Compliance with ethical standards. the study was approved by the Local Ethics Committee (LEC) of the East Siberian Institute of Medical and Environmental Research (Protocol of the LEC of the East-Siberian Institute of Medical and Ecological Research No. 7 of 12/15/2023), conducted in accordance with the European Convention for the Protection of Vertebrates Used for Experiments or Other Scientific Purposes (ETS N 123), directive of the European Parliament and the Council Of the European Union 2010/63/EC of 09/22/2010 on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes.Contribution: Vokina V.A. – concept and design of the study, conducting the experiment, processing, analyzing and interpreting data, reviewing publications on the topic of the article; writing and design of the article; Sosedova L.M. – research methodology, writing and formatting of the article, checking of critical content; Pankova A.A. – conducting the experiment, collecting and initially processing the material, statistical processing of data; Abramova V.A. – collecting and pre-processing the material, statistical processing of data, preparing illustrations; Titov E.A. – collecting and pre-processing the material, statistical processing of data, preparing illustrations; Novikov M.A. – collecting and pre-processing the material, statistical processing of data, preparing illustrations. All authors are responsible for the integrity of all parts of the manuscript and approval of the manuscript final version.Conflict of interest. The authors declare no conflict of interest.Funding. The work was carried out according to the research plan within the framework of the state task.Received: April 13, 2026 / Revised: June 2, 2026 / Accepted: July 1, 2026 / Published: October 20, 2026

papers.title: Evaluation of the neurotropism of iron (II, III) oxide nanocomposite in the course of the post-exposure period, based on changes in electroencephalography parameters and behavioral reactions in rats
papers.authors: N. L. Yakimova, Михаил Александрович Новиков, Anna S. Skrynnik, Lizarev Av
papers.abstract: Introduction. Iron oxide nanoparticles (NPs) are widely used in medicine. However, the mechanisms of their toxicity are not fully understood. In particular, due to their ability to accumulate in the nervous system (NS), it is necessary to investigate their remote neurotoxic effects.The aim of the study was to evaluate the neurotoxicity of an iron oxide nanocomposite (NC) encapsulated in an arabinogalactan (AG) matrix over the post-exposure period, based on changes in electroencephalography (EEG) parameters and behavioral responses in male rats.Materials and methods. The experiment was performed on mongrel, sexually mature male albino rats (n = 60). The experimental groups received NC intragastric administration for 10 days at doses of 500 µg/kg (Fe₃O₄AG 500) and 5000 µg/kg (Fe₃O₄AG 5000) body weight. The control groups received 0.5 ml of 0.9% NaCl. Rats’ behavior was studied using the «open-field» method using the EthoStudio setup. EEG recording and analysis were performed using a «Neuron-Spectr-1/V» device. Rats were examined immediately and 6 months after the end of exposure.Results. In the early post-exposure period, the distance traveled increased in the Fe₃O₄AG 5000 group compared to intact animals. In the 1st period, the average power of alpha and beta-1 rhythms increased in the Fe₃O₄AG 500 group in lead Fp1-A1 compared to the control group. In rats, immediately after receiving NC in doses of 500 µg/kg and 5000 µg/kg, an increase in the delta rhythm and a decrease in theta and alpha rhythms were noted in lead C3-A1 compared to the control according to the rhythm index. After 6 months, the number of the supported rearing decreased in the Fe₃O₄AG 5000 group compared to the control group. In the remote period, a decrease in the average amplitude of delta and theta rhythms in lead Fp1-A1 in the experimental groups compared to the control group was more informative. The amplitude of the theta rhythm in the Fe₃O₄AG 500 group was also lower than in the Fe₃O₄AG 5000 group.Limitations. The study was limited to examining behavioral responses in the «open field» and EEG parameters in male albino rats immediately after 10 days of administration of NC Fe₃O₄AG at doses of 500 µg/kg and 5000 µg/kg and a 6-month post-exposure period. Conclusion. During the post-exposure period, NC Fe₃O₄AG at doses of 500 and 5000 µg/kg caused changes in behavioral responses and EEG in rats that were not dose-dependent, which requires further study.Compliance with Ethical Standards. The study was approved by the local Ethics Committee of the East Siberian Institute of Medical and Ecological Research (ESIMER) (Conclusion No. 8 dated December 15, 2023) and was conducted in compliance with the international standards of the European Convention (ETS No. 123) and GLP requirements.Contribution:Yakimova N.L. – collection and processing of material, registration and description of EEG, writing text, editing; Novikov M.A. – the concept and design of the study, implementation of animal studies, editing; Skrynnik A.S. – collection and processing of material, and description of the results of the study of behavior; Lizarev A.V. – collection of material, EEG registration, editing. All authors are responsible for the integrity of all parts of the manuscript and approval of the manuscript final version.Acknowledgments. The authors express their gratitude to L.M. Sosedova, DSc (Medicine), professor, for consultative assistance and editing the article.Conflict of interest. The authors declare no conflict of interest.Funding. The study was carried out within the framework of a government assignment and had no additional sources of sponsorship.Received: April 20, 2026 / Revised: July 10, 2026 / Accepted: September 15, 2026 / Published: October 20, 2026

papers.title: Critical Success Factors for AI Training Robot Adoption in Accounting SMEs: An Integrated Delphi–DEMATEL–ANP Approach
papers.authors: Cheng-Wen, Yutzu, Chung-Kai Lee, Hu, Hsu
papers.journal: Advances in management and applied economics
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotic Process Automation (RPA) are transforming accounting services toward intelligent, data-driven professional services. However, small and medium-sized accounting firms (SMEs) face barriers to AI adoption, including limited resources, technological capabilities, employee skills, and regulatory uncertainty. This study identifies and prioritizes the critical success factors (CSFs) influencing AI training robot adoption in Taiwanese accounting SMEs. The framework integrates the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, Task–Technology Fit (TTF), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Human–Computer Trust (HCT), and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). We used a two-round Delphi process with 15 experts to refine the CSFs, followed by DEMATEL to identify causal relationships and ANP to assess their relative priorities. The DEMATEL results indicate that the Technological dimension is the strongest causal driver (D−R = 1.355), followed by the Organizational dimension (D−R = 0.435), whereas Decision Making is the principal effect dimension (D−R = −1.781). The findings further emphasize task–technology alignment, AI maturity, regulatory conditions, top management support, employee AI competence, and human–computer trust. Overall, AI adoption represents an integrated organizational transformation rather than merely a technological investment. The proposed Delphi–DEMATEL–ANP framework provides systematic decision support for resource prioritization, organizational readiness, capability development, and sustainable AI-enabled digital transformation in accounting SMEs. JEL classification numbers: M15, M41, O33, C44. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Training Robots, Accounting SMEs, Task-Technology Fit, DEMATEL, Analytic Network Process, Digital Transformation.

papers.title: Society Under Deep Transformation: The Judiciary and Algonormative Expectations
papers.authors: Prof. Dr. Diógenes V. Hassan Ribeiro
papers.journal: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
papers.abstract: Observing algorithms, that is, distinguishing algorithms in today's technological and digital society – which is hypercomplex – is indispensable. The emergence of artificial intelligence algorithms has surprised all scientific fields. The education system, for example, is impacted by the possibility of perhaps superficial and certainly very rapid learning of difficult theories that previously took years to master. The science system, on the other hand, besides being impacted by the possibilities, is above all optimistic about the advances. The economic system also sees marked changes. But the legal system is, in a way, apprehensive considering the ethical and normative aspects. The first point relates to decisions. The second point relates specifically to norms and structures of expectations. No one can predict what the consequences will be. But everyone can say that the systems are already revealing great changes and evolutions. Thus, the question arises as to what evolutions have already occurred in the legal system with artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Dampak Konten Berbasis Artificial Intelligence terhadap Literasi Digital Generasi Alpha: A Structured Literature Review
papers.authors: Aliya Marsya As-Syifa, Hitta Alfi Muhimmah
papers.journal: Aksiologi Jurnal Pendidikan dan Ilmu Sosial
papers.abstract: Abstrak: Perkembangan generative AI telah mengubah ekosistem informasi digital secara masif, namun kebijakan literasi yang menyasar Generasi Alpha sebagai konsumen utama konten sintetis masih sangat terbatas. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis tren konten berbasis AI yang dikonsumsi generasi muda, mengidentifikasi dampaknya terhadap literasi digital Generasi Alpha, serta merumuskan strategi mitigasi untuk memperkuat kemampuan kritis generasi tersebut. Metode yang digunakan adalah Structured Literature Review (SLR) dengan protokol PRISMA, melibatkan 15 artikel ilmiah terindeks yang dipublikasikan pada rentang 2021–2025 dan diseleksi melalui kriteria inklusi dan eksklusi yang ketat. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa tren konten berbasis AI berkembang pesat di level pendidikan tinggi namun belum proporsional pada level pendidikan dasar. Dampak konten AI bersifat kondisional: positif dalam setting pembelajaran terstruktur, namun berpotensi memperdalam ketergantungan teknologi dan melemahkan kemampuan evaluasi kritis tanpa pendampingan pedagogis yang memadai. Strategi mitigasi yang efektif mencakup pengembangan kerangka AI literacy pada level individu, penguatan peran institusi pendidikan, dan kebijakan sistemik yang adaptif. Penelitian ini menyimpulkan bahwa literasi digital di era AI bukan kompetensi yang berkembang secara alami, melainkan perlu dibangun secara sadar dan terstruktur melalui pendekatan berlapis. Keywords: Literasi digital; Generasi Alpha; konten berbasis AI; generative AI; misinformasi Abstrak: The rapid development of generative AI has fundamentally transformed the digital information ecosystem, yet literacy policies targeting Generation Alpha as primary consumers of synthetic content remain critically limited. This study aims to analyze trends in AI-based content consumed by young people, identify its impacts on Generation Alpha’s digital literacy, and formulate mitigation strategies to strengthen their critical competencies. A Structured Literature Review (SLR) method with PRISMA protocol was employed, involving 15 indexed scientific articles published between 2021 and 2025, selected through rigorous inclusion and exclusion criteria. Findings indicate that AI-based content trends have advanced rapidly at the higher education level but remain disproportionately underaddressed at the primary education level. The impact of AI content is conditional: positive within structured learning environments, yet potentially deepening technological dependency and weakening critical evaluation skills without adequate pedagogical guidance. Effective mitigation strategies encompass the development of AI literacy frameworks at the individual level, strengthening the role of educational institutions, and adaptive systemic policies. This study concludes that digital literacy in the AI era is not a naturally developing competency but must be intentionally and systematically cultivated through a multilayered approach. Keywords: Digital literacy; Generation Alpha; AI-based content; generative AI; misinformation

papers.title: Epistemic reconfiguration in higher education: Generative artificial intelligence, stratification and the renewal of pedagogical judgement
papers.authors: Aslam Fataar
papers.abstract: This conceptual article contends that generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) is driving an epistemic reconfiguration in higher education. It places AI within the processes of platformisation through which digital infrastructures reorganise how knowledge is produced, accessed and governed. These changes modify the conditions under which knowledge is recognised and learned, potentially weakening the educational relationship between writing, thinking and understanding when AI use bypasses the cognitive and metacognitive work through which understanding develops. The article develops a framework linking platformisation, AI-mediated meaning-making, and the reorganisation of pedagogy. It argues that these processes produce epistemic stratification by unevenly shaping students’ and institutions’ capacity to sustain epistemic ascent. Artificial intelligence is therefore not merely a technological or assessment challenge, but part of a broader epistemic reconfiguration that reshapes the conditions under which knowledge is produced, recognised and learned. Contribution: Situated in Global South contexts, the article examines how these dynamics intersect with historically entrenched inequalities and forms of epistemic dependency. In response, it advances epistemic ascent, understood as the structured development of conceptual understanding, disciplinary reasoning and judgement, as a central educational objective. The article argues that pedagogical judgement and design-based pedagogies are essential for organising AI use in ways that sustain conceptual engagement, epistemic justice and the university’s public-good mission. The article also illustrates two design-based pedagogical tasks through which lecturers can organise AI-supported learning around conceptual reasoning and disciplinary judgement.

papers.title: Predicting travellers’ intentions to adopt generative artificial intelligence for travel planning
papers.authors: Amara Awan, Mahwish Zafar, Kashif Hussain
papers.abstract: This study examines how travelers’ psychosocial factors translate into the intention to adopt GAI tools for travel planning. Accordingly, the study uses an extended TPB framework that incorporates sequential pathways from users’ prior experience with GAI, perceived attributes, and satisfaction, with perceived risk of GAI hallucination as a moderator. Data were collected from 310 travelers in Pakistan and analyzed using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS4. Findings revealed that travelers’ attitude significantly drives prior interaction, which in turn strongly predicts GAI’s perceived attributes, including anthropomorphism and personalization. These perceptions foster satisfaction and, consequently, build intentions to adopt GAI for travel planning. Crucially, this satisfaction-intention nexus is weakened in the presence of GAI hallucination. Theoretically, the study examines sequential rather than direct effects of psychosocial factors. Practically, developers and travel service providers should focus on designing advanced tools to improve customized online services, while policymakers must establish accuracy standards and verification mechanisms to mitigate hallucination-induced distrust.

papers.title: Gold Investment Decisions Under Fear and Uncertainty: A Systematic Literature Review of FOMO and Behavioral Biases
papers.authors: Dian Putra Laroybafih, Andi Wijayanto, Muhammad Agung Baiquni
papers.journal: EKOMBIS REVIEW Jurnal Ilmiah Ekonomi dan Bisnis
papers.abstract: The phenomenon Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) has evolved from social anxiety into a critical driver of irrational investment behavior. While the literature extensively associates FOMO with highly volatile digital assets, its psychological effects on traditional safe-haven instruments remain insufficiently examined. This study seeks to elucidate the relationship between the phenomenon of Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) and decisions regarding gold investment, as well as to assess the impact of psychological pressure on the effectiveness of safe-haven assets.. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach compliant with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 38 peer-reviewed articles from the Scopus and Emerald databases (2016–2026) were thoroughly analyzed. The findings reveal that FOMO operates as a central psychological mediator, bridging cognitive biases such as herd mentality and loss aversion with impulsive investment decisions. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that the safe-haven utility of gold is crisis-contingent rather than absolute; during extreme systemic liquidity panics, FOMO-induced behavior can erode gold's protective attributes, prompting forced liquidations. The study also identifies Artificial Intelligence advisory tools, financial literacy, and religiosity (including Sharia compliance) as significant moderating factors that effectively mitigate speculative hysteria. This study contributes to the development of a behavioral safe-haven model, indicating that the stability of conservative investments is increasingly shaped by collective emotional responses rather than exclusively by their intrinsic economic characteristics.

papers.title: Combined eye tracking and electroencephalography during referential selection in dyadic interaction
papers.authors: Ingmar Brilmayer, Philip Georgis, Petra B. Schumacher
papers.abstract: Understanding language in real-world interaction requires methods that integrate auditory, visual, and neural signals. We present a proof-of-concept study combining mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking to investigate referential selection during dyadic communication. Using a simplified version of the director task, pairs of participants engaged in naturalistic object-movement instructions while EEG and gaze data were recorded and synchronized via LabStreamingLayer, allowing us to calculate overlap-corrected, regression-based event-related potentials (rERPs) time-locked to spoken nouns and to participants' fixations, focusing on the N400/P300 (300-500 ms) and later (500-800 ms) time windows. Our results show that gaze behavior and fixation-related potentials provide crucial information for interpreting language-related ERPs: Targets competing with occluded referents elicited a stronger posterior positivity consistent with greater attentional demands. Fixation timing systematically modulated neural responses. Contrary to predictions, competitors received little visual attention, indicating that participants prioritized task-relevant information. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal data integration for understanding attentional and predictive mechanisms in real-world communication. Importantly, we show that established analytic techniques, such as artifact subspace reconstruction, independent component analysis, and linear deconvolution for ERP calculation, apply to noisy, naturalistic datasets. In addition, we provide a subsampling sensitivity approach to test the stability of the effects across different sample sizes. This study provides a methodological framework linking gaze and neural activity during interactive language processing. All preprocessing and analysis scripts, along with example datasets, are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/5ds4z ; a modified and optimized Python implementation is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/XlinCLab/DGAME ).

papers.title: AI and Media: Challenges, Prospects and Opportunities
papers.authors: Sushmita Kumari -, Atish Prashar, Anand Kumar -
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the media ecosystem by changing how information is gathered, verified, produced, personalized, distributed and monetized. News organisations can use AI for transcription, translation, data analysis, recommendation, automated production, audience analytics, fact-checking support, visualisation and the creation of new formats. At the same time, AI introduces significant risks concerning misinformation, deepfakes, algorithmic bias, privacy, intellectual property, opacity, labour displacement, editorial accountability and the erosion of public trust. These tensions are particularly important in India, where the media environment is linguistically diverse, mobile-first, platform-dependent and characterised by a rapid expansion of digital and creator-led news. This conceptual paper examines the challenges, prospects and opportunities created by AI for Indian media and develops an integrated framework for responsible AI-enabled journalism. Drawing on stakeholder theory, the resource-based view, institutional theory, diffusion of innovations and the emerging literature on algorithmic and automated journalism, the paper conceptualises AI capability as an enabling resource whose value depends on editorial governance, human oversight, professional competence, data quality and regulatory conditions. The framework proposes that AI adoption influences media performance through a mediating mechanism of newsroom capability and workflow transformation, while ethical governance, organisational readiness and regulatory clarity moderate the relationship. The paper argues that AI should be treated neither as a substitute for journalism nor simply as a productivity tool, but as a socio-technical capability that must remain accountable to journalistic values. For Indian media, the most promising opportunities lie in multilingual journalism, accessibility, local and hyperlocal coverage, data-driven reporting, personalised public-interest information, newsroom efficiency and new digital business models. However, these opportunities can be realised only when media organisations establish transparent AI-use policies, verification protocols, disclosure standards, staff training, data safeguards and mechanisms for human editorial responsibility. The paper concludes with implications for media managers, journalists, educators, regulators and technology providers, and proposes directions for future empirical research.

papers.title: A Proposed Model for Teachers' AI Competencies Based on UNESCO and DigCompEdu Frameworks: A Qualitative Study
papers.authors: Marwa Mohammad Al-Baz
papers.journal: Arid International Journal of Educational and physcological sciences
papers.abstract: Teachers’ competencies in artificial intelligence (AI) constitute a fundamental element for achieving innovative and effective education aligned with the demands of the twenty-first century. This study aims to propose a comprehensive model of teachers’ AI competencies based on the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers and the European Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigCompEdu), while adapting them to suit the needs of teacher preparation programs in faculties of education. The study adopts a qualitative approach using focus groups with experts in curriculum and instruction as well as educational technology. The domains, standards, and indicators of both frameworks were analyzed and discussed in order to derive a practical and contextually relevant model. The study resulted in a proposed model comprising five main domains, 15 standards, and 48 performance indicators, covering cognitive, pedagogical, ethical, professional, and assessment dimensions. It also provides practical recommendations for developing teacher preparation and continuous professional development programs, with a focus on integrating artificial intelligence in a responsible and effective manner to support interactive and inclusive learning for students.

papers.title: Psychological and Behavioral Modeling: A Structured Review of Methods, Datasets, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers.authors: Xingxuan Chen, Xinmeng Li, Lujia Yin, Haixiang Zhu, Zixin Xiao, Yong Jun Peng
papers.abstract: Psychological and behavioral modeling turns cognition, emotion, and motivation into computable quantities that can be related to observable behavior. The field has moved from theory-driven rules to statistical machine learning, deep learning, large language models (LLMs), and foundation models of cognition, but methods are fragmented, results are seldom comparable, and the link between opaque predictors and psychological theory is unsettled. This structured narrative review, reported with a PRISMA-style selection flow and an explicit evidence-tier coding, frames the field as a multilevel system. It organizes research into five modeling classes (psychological states, behavioral capabilities, individual–environment interaction, individual dynamics, and group psychology), defined by unit of analysis, target, and direction of inference, and it positions system dynamics, in the stock–flow–feedback sense, as one model family within that scheme rather than as a synonym for dynamical-systems modeling. We score the computational readiness of the theories that supply model ontologies on two rubric-based axes, formal specification and measurement maturity, and compare model families by assumptions, data needs, interpretability, and failure modes. Four claims are defended, each with stated boundary conditions and counterexamples: theory readiness, not algorithmic capability, determines where theory-informed learning is feasible; the dominant use of models shifts from individual-level estimation to collective-level simulation without a parallel shift in validation; multilevel data, not model capacity, constrain cross-scale modeling; and readiness claims must be indexed to a graded evidence base. We catalogue datasets, including small-group, dyadic, and longitudinal-network resources, review applications in mental health, education, decision support, and emergency management with their evidentiary status made explicit, treat military use as an ethically bounded case, and turn five recurrent bottlenecks into research-practice recommendations paired, where possible, with testable predictions.

papers.title: SENSE: A Sensor-Centric Multimodal Evidence Chain for Teaching Evaluation in Smart Classrooms
papers.authors: Lihong Cheng, Xiaohe Liu, Haisheng Yu
papers.abstract: Smart-classroom teaching evaluation increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensing sources, including classroom cameras, microphones, speech-recognition systems, and learning-platform interaction logs. Existing systems often treat these streams as separate analytical inputs, with insufficient attention to cross-modal alignment, missing-sensor robustness, and evidence-grounded large-language-model reasoning. This paper proposes SENSE (Sensor-Evidence Network for Smart-Classroom Evaluation), a sensor-centric framework that organizes classroom evaluation as an end-to-end evidence chain. Visual behavior, acoustic-semantic content, and learning-platform events are aligned in lesson-level time windows and converted into structured evidence packets. Available learning-outcome anchors provide contextual evidence to the semantic evaluator, whereas expert ratings are retained exclusively as external validation references. A DeepSeek-based semantic evaluator then generates engagement, instructional-content, interaction-quality, and teaching-feedback judgments under a fixed output schema. The framework was evaluated using 48 college-English lessons, 48 videos, 48 audio recordings, 4628 timestamped learning-platform interaction logs, and 960 valid student-window observation instances. Compared with a transparent rule-based operational baseline, SENSE reduced the engagement-evaluation error from 12.3% to 5.8%, reduced the content-coverage error from 14.5% to 6.2%, and increased the correlation with the mean expert score from 0.71 to 0.89. Under 30% random evidence removal, the correlation remained 0.80. The results indicate that teaching evaluation benefits from a multimodal sensor-evidence and semantic-reasoning process rather than a single behavior-recognition task.

papers.title: Social Media Influence on Mental Health and Obesity of Adolescents Attending Primary Care Settings in Qatar: A Cross-Sectional Study, 2024
papers.authors: Abduljaleel Abdullatif Zainel, Dana Bilal El Kaissi, Hafiz Ahmed Mohamed, Ahmed Sameer Al Nuaimi, Mohamed Ahmed Syed, Muslim Abbas Syed
papers.abstract: Background: Social media use has become highly prevalent among adolescents and has been linked to both positive and negative health outcomes. However, evidence regarding its relationship with mental health and obesity remains inconsistent, and limited data are available from primary care settings in Qatar. This study aimed to describe patterns of social media use and adolescents’ perceptions regarding its effects and to examine associations between active social media engagement, mental health outcomes, and BMI-for-age among adolescents attending Primary Health Care Corporation (PHCC) health centers in Qatar. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between 5th May 2024 to 30th June 2024 among adolescents aged 11–17 years attending six PHCC health centers across Qatar. Participants were recruited using systematic random sampling. Data were collected through structured face-to-face interviews using a questionnaire that assessed sociodemographic characteristics, social media use, frequency of active social media engagement, and participants’ perceptions regarding the effects of social media. Mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, and anger, were assessed using PROMIS Emotional Distress scales, while anthropometric measurements were used to calculate BMI-for-age z-scores. Descriptive statistics, bivariate analyses, and multivariable logistic regression models were performed. Results: A total of 429 adolescents participated in the study. Overall, 25.3% of participants were classified as overweight and 21.7% as obese. Moderate-to-severe anxiety, depression, and anger were reported by 16.2%, 11.4%, and 10.3% of participants, respectively. TikTok (56.9%), Snapchat (48.7%), and Instagram (47.3%) were the most frequently used social media platforms. While 58.2% of participants perceived social media as having positive effects on communication and relationships, many also perceived it to contribute to obesity (47.6%), mental health disorders (41.7%), and excessive screen time (58.3%). However, these findings represented participants’ perceptions rather than objectively measured effects. Statistical analyses demonstrated limited evidence of associations between the measured frequency of active social media engagement and BMI-for-age, depression, anxiety, or anger. In multivariable analyses, higher household income was associated with increased odds of moderate-to-severe anxiety; however, the overall regression model was not statistically significant, and the finding should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Conclusions: Adolescents attending primary care services in Qatar reported substantial social media use, notable levels of emotional distress, and a high prevalence of overweight and obesity. Although many participants perceived social media as having adverse effects on health and well-being, statistical analyses provided limited evidence of associations between the measured frequency of active social media engagement and mental health outcomes or BMI-for-age. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing perceived effects from observed associations and highlight the need for longitudinal studies using more comprehensive measures of social media use to better understand potential relationships with adolescent health outcomes.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness in Nursing: A Scoping Review of Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice, and Emerging Evidence on Patient Safety Culture
papers.authors: Sarah Hassan Tawhari, Regie Buenafe Tumala, Yahya Hassan Tawhari
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into nursing practice, yet nurses often demonstrate low to moderate AI knowledge, mixed attitudes, and inconsistent practice behaviors. Although individual studies have examined these domains, no review has comprehensively examined AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practice (KAP) together with the emerging evidence on patient safety culture among nurses. This gap is significant because safe AI adoption in nursing depends on both technical competence and a strong safety culture across diverse clinical settings. Objective: To systematically map international evidence on nurses’, nursing students’, and other included participants’ AI-related KAP, and to examine how these factors may relate to patient safety culture. Because several eligible studies included multidisciplinary samples in which nurse-specific quantitative data were not reported separately (China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and three studies from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [KSA]), only studies with extractable nurse-specific results were used to inform nurse-focused conclusions, and multidisciplinary findings were not attributed solely to nurses. Methods: This scoping review followed Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Searches of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (2021–2026) identified studies examining AI-related perceptions among nurses and other healthcare participants when nurse-specific data were reported separately or extractable. Data extraction and narrative synthesis were conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute guidance. Results: Ten studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Studies from China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the KSA, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates showed variable AI knowledge but predominantly positive attitudes. Ethical concerns—privacy, job displacement, and reduced empathy—were common. Younger age, higher education, and prior AI exposure were associated with more favorable perceptions. Nurses across regions emphasized the need for structured AI training. Only one study examined patient safety culture, and it reported that AI knowledge and attitudes significantly predicted patient safety culture, with attitude showing the stronger effect. However, because this evidence comes from a single cross-sectional study conducted in a multidisciplinary sample without nurse-specific results, it is insufficient to establish causal conclusions, and its findings cannot be generalized specifically to nurses. Conclusions: Nurses are generally receptive to AI but lack sufficient knowledge, training, and organizational support for safe implementation. Preliminary evidence suggests a positive association between AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and patient safety culture, but this relationship remains uncertain due to the extremely limited evidence base and the reliance on evidence that is not exclusively nurse-specific. Available studies indicate generally favorable attitudes toward AI alongside variable knowledge, limited formal training, and persistent ethical and organizational concerns, with only one eligible cross-sectional study linking these factors to patient safety culture. The conclusion regarding this association should not be attributed exclusively to nurses because the patient safety culture evidence was derived from a multidisciplinary sample. Future research should explore how AI competencies may interact with safety-related behaviors and organizational systems. Strengthening AI training, ethical guidance, and organizational support remains essential for safe adoption.
