papers.title: Precision Nutrition and Health Outcomes Across the Lifespan
papers.authors: Shi Yang, Alison G. M. Brown, Shilpy Dixit, Eric J. Shiroma, Nicole M. Farmer, Qing Lu, Beena Gaind Sood, Debbie Vitalis, Maliha R. Ilias, Marrah E. Lachowicz-Scroggins, CHARLOTTE A. PRATT
papers.abstract: Precision nutrition is an emerging paradigm that seeks to tailor dietary recommendations and interventions based on individual and population characteristics. Although advances in multi-omics, wearable sensors, and artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) have accelerated discovery, translation into practice remains limited by fragmented evidence across life stages and insufficient integration of knowledge regarding systems biology and other influences on health. Nutritional needs, vulnerabilities, intervention opportunities, and response heterogeneity evolve dynamically from preconception and pregnancy through infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and older age. These life stage-specific processes intersect with (epi)genetic, metabolic and microbiome factors, as well as social, psychological, behavioral, and environmental/geographic influences, contributing to heterogeneity in health outcomes. Addressing this complexity requires not only multimodal predictive models but also frameworks that integrate data standards and harmonization, systems biology, implementation science, and community engagement. To provide a structured approach to this complexity, we developed a seven-pillar Precision Nutrition Framework encompassing prevention for all, data sources, quantitative sciences, qualitative sciences, intervention implementation, communities, and education and workforce training. Using this framework and a lifespan perspective, we examine opportunities for promoting cardiovascular, pulmonary, hematologic, and circadian/sleep health, synthesize evidence on key nutrients, dietary patterns, and emerging biomarkers, and adapt and expand the “precision nutrition plate” for implementation research in clinical and community settings. We highlight critical research gaps, including the need for phenotype-guided trials, standardized data integration, and scalable implementation strategies. By integrating biological, behavioral, and broader environmental dimensions across the life course, precision nutrition can advance more effective, accessible, and sustainable approaches for disease prevention and health promotion.

papers.title: Modeling VIM Concepts Using Large Language Models: An LLM White-Box Study on Metrological Descriptions
papers.authors: Guillaume Bourgeois, Alain Abran, Pierre Bourque
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs), specifically GPT-4, can analyze, explain, and enrich concepts in the International Vocabulary of Metrology (VIM). It uses a white-box approach, in which “white-box” qualifies the input, which is fully known and traceable to a validated normative source, while the model itself remains opaque: the material supplied consisted only of VIM definitions and graphical representations of the relationships between VIM terms, together with the relationship types of the informative Annex A of the VIM. The outputs were analyzed qualitatively by structured expert cross-review against three criteria: fidelity to VIM concepts, terminological consistency, and explanatory quality. Across the seven cases examined (four topology diagrams and three VIM concepts), GPT-4 generated structured descriptions and rendered the hierarchical and functional relationships between concepts. Limitations were also observed: occasional non-normative synonyms and purely qualitative descriptions of quantitative relationships. Output variability, although not measured here, is a known LLM property that calls for expert review. Under the conditions tested, GPT-4 appears to be a promising semantic assistant for studying normative vocabularies, with the controlled input context supporting a traceable assessment of its capabilities and gaps. These observations also suggest future directions, which were not tested here, such as AI-assisted teaching, standardization, and terminological interoperability.

papers.title: The Impact of Multiple Biologic Failures on Surgical Outcomes: A Retrospective Cohort Study of Elective Subtotal Colectomy for Ulcerative Colitis
papers.authors: Yaron Rudnicki, Jaxson R. Jeffery, Donya Derakshani, Kellie Leanne Mathis
papers.abstract: Background: Subtotal colectomy (STC) with end ileostomy (EI) is usually the first surgical stage for patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) who fail medical treatment, most often with biological agents. Is there a difference in surgical outcome after failure of one or two biologicals vs. three or four? Methods: A retrospective study of all patients who underwent STC with EI for UC (5-2018 to 1-2022). After excluding emergent cases, the elective cohort was divided into patients who failed 1–2 biologicals (group 1–2) vs. patients who failed 3–4 biologicals (group 3–4), and surgical outcomes were compared. Data collected included patients’ demographics, preoperative clinical manifestations, and operative and postoperative outcomes. Results: Ninety-eight patients underwent STC for UC, and of them, 53 were elective. Thirty patients failed 1–2 biologics (group 1–2), and 23 failed 3–4 biologics (group 3–4). The groups were similar in average age (37.6 ± 11 vs. 32.7 ± 10), BMI (26.7 ± 6 vs. 27.7 ± 7), number of years with UC (9.5 ± 9 vs. 9 ± 8), rate of steroid dependence (20 (67%) vs. 13 (57%)) but differed in sex; there were 25 (83%) males in group 1–2, and 8 (35%) in group 3–4 (p < 0.01). The operative approaches were similar, as was the operative time (217 ± 74 vs. 210 ± 79 min). The length of hospital stay was 3.2 ± 1 days for group 1–2 and 5 ± 6 days for group 3–4 (p = 0.14). Postoperative complications were seen in 10 patients (33%) vs. 7 patients (30%) (p = 0.82), and of them, two (7%) and two (9%) (p = 0.82) had Venous thromboembolism (VTE), respectively. Only 20 patients (67%) in group 1–2 and 16 patients (70%) in group 3–4 (p = 0.82) progressed to a second stage of an Ileoanal pouch (IPAA) at 11.1 ± 4 and 9.2 ± 2 months, respectively. The overall average follow-up time was 41.1 months. Conclusions: Ulcerative Colitis patients who fail 3–4 biological agents and choose to go to elective STC with EI have very similar surgical outcomes compared to patients who choose elective surgery after failing only 1–2 biological agents in the same time span of known disease. UC patients with severe colitis and poor quality of life who fail two lines of biological agents may be better off electing surgical treatment than failing more biologics and then going to surgery. On the other hand, patients who try 3–4 biologics may expect no worse surgical outcomes than after 1–2 biologics.

papers.title: Disordered Eating Behaviors and Psychological Distress in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Cross-Sectional Study from Tunisia
papers.authors: Rym Ben Othman, Syrine Trabelsi, Ismail Dergaa, Halil İ̇brahim Ceylan, Deniz Öztürk, Nicola Luigi Bragazzi, Yasmine Jallouli, Vаlentinа Ștefănică, H. Jamoussi
papers.abstract: Background: Disordered eating behaviors (DEBs) and psychological distress may complicate type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) care. Objective: To estimate the frequency of DEB screening positivity and examine associated characteristics in a Tunisian T2DM clinic sample. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 400 adults assessed between January and April 2023 using the Sick, Control, One stone, Fat, Food (SCOFF) questionnaire; Bulimic Investigatory Test Edinburgh (BITE); four-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4); and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS). Exploratory analysis estimated crude prevalence ratios (PRs). Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) came from a logistic model including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), diabetes duration, and PSS-4. Separate secondary models replaced PSS-4 with the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale anxiety subscale (HADS-A) or depression subscale (HADS-D). Results: DEB positivity was 26.8% (107/400; 95% confidence interval [CI], 22.6–31.3%). Crude DEB prevalence was higher in women than men (30.4% versus 19.2%; PR, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.06–2.35), in participants with HADS-A ≥11 versus <11 (PR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.64–3.17), and with HADS-D ≥11 versus <11 (PR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.08–2.05). In the primary adjusted model, DEB positivity was associated with younger age (aOR per year, 0.952; 95% CI, 0.922–0.982), higher BMI (aOR per kg/m2, 1.083; 95% CI, 1.042–1.126), and higher PSS-4 (aOR per point, 1.133; 95% CI, 1.067–1.203). HADS scores were positively associated in separate adjusted models. Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was high in both groups (10.36% versus 9.91%; difference, 0.45 percentage points; 95% CI, −0.01 to 0.92). Conclusions: Approximately one-quarter of this clinic sample had a positive DEB screen. Associations with psychological symptoms support attention to eating concerns and emotional well-being in diabetes care. However, cross-sectional data limit causal interpretation, and future longitudinal studies are warranted.

papers.title: The AI Use in Healthcare Anxiety Scale (AI-HAS) for Adult Patients: Development, Validity and Reliability
papers.authors: Özgür Selvi, Ali Yılmaz, Sakine Yalman, Özgen Korkmaz, Halis Altun
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, but concerns about diagnostic errors, data security, reduced human interaction, and opaque algorithmic decisions may cause patient anxiety and hinder acceptance. This study developed and psychometrically validated the Artificial Intelligence Use in Healthcare Anxiety Scale (AI-HAS) for adult outpatients. Methods: Following DeVellis’s eight-step framework, a three-member expert panel comprising two psychologists with PhDs in psychology and an expert in AI applications in education with a PhD in educational technology generated 35 items. Cognitive debriefing and two rounds of formal expert review reduced the pool to 25 items. Participants were recruited by convenience sampling at Kırıkkale University Faculty of Medicine Hospital, Türkiye. Exploratory factor analysis included 369 participants after excluding 13 multivariate outliers identified using Mahalanobis distance (p < 0.001). Confirmatory factor analysis used an independent sample of 225 participants. Test–retest reliability was assessed in 26 participants after approximately 30 days using Pearson’s correlation. Results: Exploratory factor analysis supported an 18-item, four-factor structure explaining 65.80% of the variance: Anxiety Regarding Negative Outcomes, Security Anxiety, AI Integration Anxiety, and Accuracy Anxiety. Confirmatory factor analysis yielded χ2(df, p) = 328.4 (128), p < 0.001; RMSEA = 0.082 [0.074, 0.097]; CFI = 0.930; TLI = 0.916; and SRMR = 0.056. Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega coefficients ranged from 0.83 to 0.91. Conclusions: The AI-HAS showed preliminary evidence of validity and reliability for measuring adult outpatients’ anxiety about AI use in healthcare. Further validation in more representative samples is warranted.

papers.title: Human–AI Interaction and System Usability: A Risk-Calibrated Computational Framework for AI Liability
papers.authors: Yarra Abhinav Reddy, Agama Sony Priya, Katepally Shreya Reddy, Panthangi Ayyappa Deekshith, Dommeti Surya Teja, Maddula Aishwitha Reddy
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly mediate decisions and interactions across healthcare, finance, public administration, education, employment, legal services, and other high-impact domains. Although existing AI accountability research commonly focuses on model accuracy, algorithmic bias, privacy, transparency, and explainability, technically functioning AI systems may still cause harm when users cannot appropriately understand, interpret, challenge, or act upon AI-generated outputs. This paper examines AI system usability as a human–AI interaction and socio-technical systems problem and investigates how usability failures can contribute to legally relevant harm. The study uses doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, HCI and human-factors literature, contemporary AI governance instruments, documented cases, and scenario-based evaluation. It distinguishes AI system usability from algorithmic error and explainability and examines the regulatory contexts of India, Japan, and the European Union. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes a risk-calibrated framework for AI liability based on four principles: control, foreseeability, causation, and capacity to prevent or mitigate harm. The framework allocates responsibility across three principal actors in the AI system lifecycle: developers, deploying organisations, and end users. It further proposes risk-calibrated usability audits as an evidentiary mechanism connecting technical HCI practices with legal standards of reasonable care. The paper argues that meaningful human oversight depends on usable AI systems and that system-level usability should therefore form part of AI accountability without creating automatic strict liability for technical or design failures.

papers.title: Large Language Model Compression for Autoregressive Text Generation: Methods, Evaluation, and Deployment Trade-Offs
papers.authors: Chenhui Zhu, Runhua Zhang, Fangzheng Tian
papers.abstract: Compression changes both the information retained by a large language model and the resources required to complete a request. This narrative review examines quantization, pruning and sparsity, knowledge distillation, low-rank factorization, and token, context, and key–value cache compression for autoregressive text generation, principally with decoder-only LLMs. Its central contribution is a synthesis of changes relative to each study’s baseline, connecting compression mechanisms to capability and deployment choices. Four numerical tables distinguish quality changes at stated compression budgets, distillation gains over same-size students, and paired or independent deployment measurements. Reporting is appraised by source identity, comparison conditions, measurement scope, artefacts, and uncertainty. The reviewed cases illustrate how capacity constraints change the feasible precision choices, how allocating a shared budget changes different task scores, and how compact-model construction and request compression address complementary resource demands. A deployment-validation sequence turns these findings into candidate checks for a target workload. Remaining questions concern transfer across capabilities, delayed use of compressed information, interactions between compression stages, and complete-task cost, including agent interactions.

papers.title: Leakage-Controlled Subject-Aware Graph-Temporal Attention Network (SGTA-Net) for EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
papers.authors: Hyoseong Park, Hyunju Lee, Dongil Shin
papers.abstract: EEG-based emotion recognition results may be artificially inflated due to data leakage from normalization, augmentation, or validation splits. This article introduces SGTA-Net, a Subject-Aware Graph-Temporal Attention Network, evaluated on the DEAP dataset using only EEG features. The approach incorporates feature-space baseline removal, two-stage subject- and fold-aware normalization, window-wise graph convolution over electrode positions, and bidirectional temporal learning with additive attention. Three models—an autoencoder (AE), an AE with graph neural network layers (AE-GNN), and SGTA-Net—are compared under stratified and subject-group five-fold cross-validation for four-class and binary valence/arousal tasks. The primary comparison is the macro-F1 difference between SGTA-Net and the plain AE under identical task and protocol conditions. For four-class group-aware validation, SGTA-Net achieves 73.11% compared to 68.06% for AE (+5.05 percentage points), while binary group-aware differences are minimal (−0.03 points for valence and +0.13 points for arousal). As a secondary robustness analysis, SGTA-Net demonstrates the smallest stratified-minus-group-aware macro-F1 gap (5.33 points for four-class, compared to 15.06 for AE and 12.48 for AE-GNN). A three-seed component ablation reveals that removing the BiLSTM reduces macro-F1 by 2.01 points (significant across subjects but not across folds after Holm correction), whereas removing attention or the graph layers does not result in significant loss. These findings support the importance of window-level temporal modeling and leakage-controlled, protocol-explicit EEG benchmarking.

papers.title: Trust of Pre-Service Teachers in Government Response to Gen AI Generated Deepfakes
papers.authors: Pedro Miralles-Sánchez, José María Campillo Ferrer, Alejandro López-García
papers.abstract: This study examined the perceptions of pre-service teachers regarding the Spanish government’s response to the misuse of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) for creating disinformation, as well as the mitigation of risks associated with deepfakes produced using these digital tools. A quantitative methodology was employed, involving 133 pre-service teachers pursuing a Primary Education degree in the Region of Murcia (Spain) who participated voluntarily. The results revealed low levels of confidence in the government’s response to these online threats. However, a minority of participants expressed greater confidence in the government and focused more on the risk of generative AI being misused to amplify manipulative disinformation campaigns. Raising awareness about the link between pre-service teachers’ knowledge of this issue and the government’s response could prompt educational authorities to take action and establish boundaries regarding the weaponisation potential of deepfakes. Specifically, further research within higher education programs is needed to help students master digital citizenship competencies that enable them to identify tactics of digital political manipulation, evaluate the motivations underlying the sources, and adopt preventive tracking mechanisms to rebuild the trust in authentic political information digitally accessible.

papers.title: Toward Controllable Learner Simulation for Teacher Education: Benchmarking Skill-Profile Control in LLM Answer Behavior
papers.authors: Omri Sasson, Alexander Apartsin, Yehudit Aperstein
papers.abstract: Teacher preparation depends on deliberate practice with learners who have identifiable strengths and weaknesses, yet classroom experience accumulates slowly and is hard to standardize. Language-model-simulated students could offer scalable, repeatable practice, but only if a simulated learner can exhibit a specified answer-performance profile rather than behaving as a uniformly capable assistant. We introduce a benchmark for controllable learner simulation in school mathematics: the target condition is a binary vector of retained and suppressed curricular skill families, and we measure how faithfully a language model’s answer behavior realizes that profile via profile-alignment, retained-versus-forgotten, and cross-skill analyses. Across three models and two grades, selective suppression can be induced and measured, yet higher mathematical capability did not imply stronger controllability among the evaluated models: a model can solve the mathematics well yet be the weakest at selective suppression (bootstrap selectivity index 0.35 to 0.70). Induced errors are systematic: independent models converge on the same wrong answers, and an exploratory single-coder analysis found many compaible with documented error categories. Evidence is answer-level (single turn, multiple choice) at Grades 4 and 5. These results show that answer-level skill-profile controllability can be measured as one prerequisite for studying LLM-based learner simulation in teacher-preparation and assessment research.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Two Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Systems Versus Dental Students in Endodontic Radiographic Classification
papers.authors: Andrea Spinelli, Emanuele Charles, Maria Giovanna Gandolfi, Carlo Prati, Fausto Zamparini
papers.abstract: Objectives: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support image interpretation in dentistry, but evidence regarding their diagnostic performance on endodontic radiographs remains limited. This study compared the diagnostic accuracy of two general-purpose multimodal AI systems with that of undergraduate and postgraduate dental students and evaluated whether image cropping influenced AI performance. Methods: Fifty anonymized periapical radiographs were retrospectively selected, with 10 cases in each of five predefined endodontic diagnostic categories. Reference diagnoses were established by consensus between two experienced endodontists. ChatGPT version 5.2 and Gemini version 3 independently classified each case using both full-size and tooth-cropped images and a standardized prompt. Twenty-five fifth-year undergraduate dental students and 20 postgraduate students in clinical endodontics classified the full-size images. Overall and category-specific accuracies were calculated, and agreement with the reference standard was assessed. Results: Overall accuracy was highest among postgraduate students (84.9%), followed by undergraduate students (78.7%). Gemini achieved accuracies of 72.0% with full-size images and 82.0% with cropped images, whereas ChatGPT achieved 68.0% and 50.0%, respectively. Cropping significantly reduced ChatGPT accuracy (p = 0.0117) but did not significantly affect Gemini performance (p = 0.3018). Diagnostic accuracy varied substantially across categories. Agreement with the reference standard for the AI systems ranged from 50.0% to 82.0%. Conclusions: Diagnostic performance depended on the evaluator, AI system, image format, and diagnostic category. Postgraduate students showed the highest overall accuracy, while AI performance was heterogeneous and did not consistently exceed that of trained human observers. General-purpose multimodal AI may support supervised radiographic interpretation and education, but it should not replace comprehensive clinical assessment or professional judgment.

papers.title: Human Factors in AI-Assisted Interpreter Training: A Design Science Approach to Human-Centred Educational Technology
papers.authors: Adrián Valledor, Francisco Calles-Esteban, Josefa Gómez, Abdelhamid Tayebi
papers.abstract: The educational value of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on technological capabilities and human–AI interaction. This is particularly relevant in interpreter training, which involves high cognitive demands, contextual decisions, and time-sensitive activities. This study examines how Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI) principles can guide AI-assisted educational environments for interpreter training. Using Design Science Research (DSR), an environment integrating AI capabilities across the training cycle was developed and evaluated. Drawing on literature concerning Computer-Assisted Interpreting, HCAI, human–AI interaction, technology acceptance, and interpreting cognition, five design principles were derived: learner agency and human control, transparency and calibrated trust, protection of cognitive resources, contextualised assistance, and AI as a support for learning. A technology acceptance study involving 42 professional interpreters provided contextual evidence on technology use, adoption barriers, and professional practice, informing the specification of these principles. The principles were operationalised in the artefact, and its interaction design was examined through formative heuristic evaluation. Professional evidence therefore informs the design without establishing learner-centred validation or educational effectiveness. The contribution is a human-centred, professionally informed framework linking literature, contextual evidence, design requirements, and implementation to align AI capabilities with educational objectives and the cognitive and interactional demands of interpreter training through explicit and traceable design decisions.

papers.title: Beyond Frequency: Generative AI Engagement Quality, Psychological Well-Being, and Digital Inequality Among Chinese University Students
papers.authors: Zeyuan Cao, Yue Zhai, Rong Zheng
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now embedded in university students’ academic and everyday lives, yet frequency-based measures provide limited insight into why similar levels of use are associated with different psychological well-being outcomes. Using cross-sectional survey data from 3283 university students enrolled predominantly at institutions in Guangxi, China, this study examined GenAI engagement at three levels: overall use frequency, specific use purposes, and engagement quality reflected in self-perceived AI competence, self-reported critical AI literacy, and AI unavailability anxiety. Covariate-adjusted regressions, parallel statistical indirect-path models with 5000 bootstrap resamples, moderation analyses, and family-resource models were estimated. Overall use frequency was not associated with depressive symptoms or life satisfaction in baseline models. By contrast, use purposes showed heterogeneous associations, and engagement-quality indicators were more consistently related to well-being. More frequent use was associated with greater perceived competence and literacy but also with greater unavailability anxiety. Favorable indirect associations through competence and literacy partly offset the adverse association through anxiety, although the total indirect association with depressive symptoms was not statistically significant. The inverse association between self-perceived AI competence and depressive symptoms was statistically significant at low, but not average or high, levels of psychological capital, while family economic, cultural, and network resources showed distinct associations with competence and literacy. These findings direct attention beyond GenAI exposure frequency to the quality of engagement and the institutional conditions supporting equitable access to critical AI literacy.

papers.title: Brain–Computer Interfaces for Cognitive Rehabilitation: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Jessica Cantillo-Negrete, Martín Emiliano Rodríguez-García, Paul ul Carrillo-Mora, Dalia Danely Méndez-Gómez, Ruben I. Carino-Escobar
papers.abstract: Cognitive diseases/disorders are a major cause of disability affecting millions of people worldwide due to pathologies or conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, vascular cognitive impairment, and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. The effects of these diseases/disorders can range from subjective cognitive complaints to mild cognitive impairment and even dementia that can affect multiple cognitive domains, causing disability and alterations in daily functioning and quality of life. Cognitive training has been researched as a potential therapeutic option for treating cognitive disability. In particular, cognitive training delivered using brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) represents a promising technology for cognitive rehabilitation. For this reason, this work presents a narrative review aimed at bridging the clinical aspects of cognition performance and the technical features of BCI systems. Additionally, it reports on the current advances of BCIs for cognitive rehabilitation in the pathologies/conditions that are the main contributors of cognitive impairment globally. Specifically, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, mild cognitive impairment, cerebrovascular diseases, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder were included in the review; other pathologies that can also cause cognitive impairment such as multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury, brain tumors, infectious diseases, and psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia or autism spectrum disorder, or drug or toxin-related causes were outside the scope of the present review. Across the literature, studies have reported that BCI cognitive training can improve cognition performance for mild cognitive impairment, stroke, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, showcasing its feasibility as a complementary therapy. However, the amount of evidence is still scarce, with few reported randomized controlled clinical trials and all of the applications comprising non-invasive systems using electroencephalography, while invasive or other non-invasive approaches remain largely unassessed. Therefore, further research regarding the design of BCIs for targeting specific cognitive domains is necessary to allow for the future introduction of these types of systems into clinical rehabilitation environments, rather than only demonstrating their feasibility, as has been mainly done to date.

papers.title: A Knowledge Transfer Method from Multi-Channel to Single-Channel EEG Toward Real-World Emotion Recognition Deployment
papers.authors: Yanru Gu, Hanzhen Ouyang, Zihua Ouyang, Lishengsa Yue, 毛华娟, Weihui Dai, Yan Kang
papers.abstract: Multi-channel electroencephalography (EEG) provides spatial information for emotion recognition but requires more complex signal acquisition than single-channel EEG. This study proposes a multi-channel-to-single-channel knowledge transfer framework that uses multi-channel recordings during training and one selected physical EEG channel at inference. A 32-channel teacher is pretrained, and Sparsemax-based gating is jointly optimized with a student using classification, logits distillation, frequency-band consistency, and gating regularization losses. The frequency-band objective compares signal-level spectral statistics of the multi-channel recordings and the gated surrogate input. After channel locking, the student is retrained on the selected physical signal. Binary Arousal and Valence classification was evaluated on DEAP using 32-fold leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The proposed achieved higher subject-averaged balanced accuracy and F1-score than Channel-matched CE in both tasks, although component effects varied across tasks and metrics. These findings support the evaluated training approach under single-channel input constraints and provide a methodological basis for simplifying EEG acquisition.

papers.title: The Invisible Watermark: A Pilot Study on the Verifiability Gap in AI Text Watermarking
papers.authors: Selma Bulut, Adem Korkmaz, Selahattin Koşunalp, Vedat Tümen, Erdal Akin
papers.abstract: Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires generative AI providers to mark synthetic content in a detectable format. This obligation is carried out through a mechanism invisible to end users. The resulting gap leaves accountability around disinformation, copyright infringement, and public trust largely unaddressed. This paper reports a pilot study that probes this transparency–verifiability gap through a comparative document analysis of five major providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI) combined with a small-scale empirical robustness pilot of the open-source SynthID-Text method on GPT-2. The document analysis shows that regulatory disclosure does not equate to an independently verifiable detection mechanism for third parties. In this pilot experiment, watermarked texts scored significantly higher than unwatermarked texts (t(38) = 15.94, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 5.04, ROC-AUC = 1.000; Youden’s J-optimal threshold = 0.533, yielding 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity on this intact (uncorrupted) sample; the design was adequately powered (80%) only for effects of d ≥ 0.91 or larger, A calibration/test-separated validation on independent held-out data (n = 320) confirmed this discrimination within the pilot setup (TPR at FPR ≤ 1% = 98.75%), without implying generalization beyond it. This signal, measured with an untrained detector, degraded substantially under a deliberately engineered high-severity stress test (50% word-level corruption), a decline confirmed by Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons across nine of the ten corruption-level pairs (F(4, 56) = 98.39, p < 0.001, generalized η2 = 0.744, r = −0.824). These are preliminary, pilot-scale findings; they indicate that Article 50 guidance should require standardized error-rate reporting and independently auditable detection access, not disclosure alone. They offer an exploratory contribution to the AI ethics literature on transparency and accountability. Given the small open-source backbones (GPT-2, with a replication on Pythia-410M), the primarily untrained detector (a small-scale trained Bayesian detector did not outperform it on intact text), the single watermarking scheme, and the largely synthetic corruption type (only one model-based paraphrase condition was tested), these results remain preliminary, pilot-scale evidence whose generalization to commercial systems, large-scale trained detectors, other watermarking families, and a broader range of realistic paraphrase and translation attacks requires future research.

papers.title: Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Impact on Research Competencies Among Engineering Students in Mexico
papers.authors: José Alejandro Ascencio-Laguna, Armida González-Lorence, Víctor Alberto Gómez Pérez, Ana Lilia Mondragón-Solís, Juan Emigdio Soto-Osornio, Alejandro Jarillo Silva
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence adoption in higher education offers new opportunities for research competency development in engineering programs, yet empirical evidence on student acceptance and its academic impact remains limited, particularly in Latin American contexts. This study examined determinants of undergraduate engineering students’ acceptance of generative artificial intelligence tools and their perceived impact on research competency development. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 50 undergraduate engineering students at a Mexican national technology institute during the January–June 2026 semester. An extended Technology Acceptance Model with seven constructs was operationalized through a 21-item instrument; measurement quality was assessed via composite reliability and average variance extracted. PLS-SEM analysis was conducted in SmartPLS 4 with 5000 bootstrap resamples. Three direct structural paths were confirmed (p < 0.05): trust in AI results and perceived ease of use predicted perceived usefulness; perceived usefulness predicted intention to use. Formally tested indirect effects revealed that trust in AI results exerts a significant indirect influence on intention to use, fully mediated by perceived usefulness (β = 0.257, p = 0.004), constituting the primary adoption mechanism identified in the model. R2 (PU) = 0.396 and R2 (IU) = 0.492 indicate moderate to high explanatory power for the core adoption constructs. Intention to use was not significantly associated with academic performance (p = 0.366), suggesting that adoption intention and course-grade outcomes are governed by distinct determinants in this context. Trust and perceived usefulness are the central drivers of generative artificial intelligence acceptance, with implications for technology integration in Latin American engineering programs. This study contributes an empirically examined extended Technology Acceptance Model with confirmed indirect effects for developing-country higher education.

papers.title: Employee AI Use and Readiness in Applied Higher Education: Awareness, Barriers, and HRM Implications
papers.authors: Shaikhah Alainati, Ahmed A. Al-Hunaiyyan, Salah Al-Sharhan, Abeer Essa Alomairi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in higher education increasingly represents a challenge in workforce development and organizational transformation, rather than a purely technological issue. This study re-analyzed survey data from 311 faculty members, training instructors, and administrative staff at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET), Kuwait, to examine the associations of AI awareness and perceived barriers with AI usage/readiness from a human resource management perspective. AI usage/readiness was treated as a self-reported indicator of AI-related human capital readiness rather than as a measure of demonstrated competence or comprehensive organizational readiness. Ordinal confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were conducted using robust diagonally weighted least squares/weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted (DWLS/WLSMV) estimation. The refined 12-item, three-factor model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity, although model fit was mixed across scaled and robust indices. A near-zero eigenvalue also indicated possible numerical instability, warranting cautious interpretation and independent confirmation. AI awareness was strongly and positively associated with usage/readiness (β = 0.782, p < 0.001), whereas perceived barriers showed a small positive adjusted association (β = 0.117, p = 0.019). Together, the predictors explained 66.0% of the variance in usage/readiness. The positive association with perceived barriers may indicate that employees who engage more extensively with AI are more likely to recognize institutional and technical constraints. Building on these findings, this study proposes two conceptual extensions for future validation: a five-level AI capability maturity model for higher education and a seven-domain AI-enhanced instructor competency framework. The findings emphasize the need to integrate employee capability, institutional support, responsible AI governance, and continuous learning to develop sustainable AI readiness. Given the cross-sectional, self-reported design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: Inhibitory event-related potentials during soccer-specific decision making in collegiate players
papers.authors: Takahiro Matsutake, Hiroki Nakata, Yumiko Yamaguchi
papers.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
papers.abstract: Inhibitory control is a critical component of executive function that may contribute to athletic performance. However, neurocognitive research in soccer has largely relied on general, nonsport-specific tasks. Therefore, this study examined behavioral and neurophysiological indices of inhibitory control, specifically the N2 and P3 components of event-related potentials (ERPs), using visual, auditory, and soccer-specific Go/No-go tasks, and investigated their relationships with physical fitness and technical–tactical performance in amateur collegiate soccer players. Forty-one male collegiate soccer players participated in the study, with analytic sample sizes varying across assessments because of technical problems, artifact rejection, and physical constraints. Participants performed the Go/No-go tasks using a foot-switch response while electroencephalographic activity was recorded. Physical fitness was assessed using a 30-m sprint test, the Arrowhead Agility Test, and the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 2 (Yo-Yo IR2). Technical–tactical performance was evaluated during 4-vs-4 small-sided games using the Game Technical Scoring Chart (GTSC). During the soccer-specific task, reaction time was significantly associated with the peak amplitude of the subtracted No-go-N2 at Fz, with shorter reaction times associated with more negative No-go-N2 amplitudes ( r = 0.552, p < 0.001, n = 37). In contrast, the multiple linear regression model predicting GTSC scores from physical, behavioral, and neurophysiological measures did not reach statistical significance ( F (4, 26) = 2.713, p = .052, R 2 = .294, adjusted R 2 = .186), and none of the individual predictors was statistically significant. These findings suggest an association between inhibition-related ERP activity and response speed during soccer-specific decision making involving complex visual processing and lower-limb responses. Further studies using appropriate comparison groups and better-matched task conditions are needed to determine whether this relationship reflects soccer-specific expertise or more general differences in perceptual, cognitive, and motor demands.

papers.title: Rural digitalization and the multidimensional wellbeing of older adults in China: evidence from the active aging framework
papers.authors: Hubang Wang, Hubang Wang, Qiaohan Liu, Yujie Liu, Shimin Wei, Meihan ZHU, Boyao Li, Hongli Wang, Hongli Wang
papers.abstract: Background Building a more inclusive digital environment is a key strategy for promoting rural digitalization, narrowing the digital divide, and enhancing the wellbeing of older adults in rural areas. However, despite its increasing relevance, research on how rural digitalization affects the wellbeing of older adults in developing countries remains scarce. Objective This study aims to examine the relationship between rural digitalization and the wellbeing of older residents in rural areas, with a particular focus on its underlying mechanisms and heterogeneous effects. Method Grounded in the World Health Organization (WHO) framework for active aging and the multidimensional measurement approach of the Active Aging Index (AAI), this study develops a comprehensive index for evaluating the wellbeing of older adults in rural China while accounting for the specific socioeconomic and contextual characteristics of rural areas. Using matched data from the China Provincial Digital Development Index (2016–2022) and the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), to systematically analyze the relationship between rural digitalization and the wellbeing of the older adults in rural areas, as well as the mechanisms underlying this relationship, and the underlying mechanisms are explored through a double machine learning approach. Conclusions and discussion Analysis indicates that rural digital development significantly enhances self-efficacy, expands social networks, and strengthens social trust among rural older residents. These factors constitute key mechanisms through which digital development is associated with improved wellbeing among rural older residents. The heterogeneity analysis further reveals that the positive impact of digitalization on wellbeing are more pronounced among older adults with lower educational attainment, those with moderate or low income levels, and those living with their children, and the positive correlation is stronger in China’s central and western regions. Overall, this study extends active aging theory to rural digital contexts in developing countries, thereby improving its contextual applicability, while also enriching the existing framework for evaluating the wellbeing of rural older adults and providing policy insights for promoting an inclusive digital society and a more equitable distribution of digital dividends.

papers.title: In-person UCLA-PEERS® program for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in Italy: study protocol for a pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial with pragmatic features and exploratory EEG markers of treatment response
papers.authors: Antonio Narzisi, Maddalena Fabbri‐Destro, Elisa Foti, Chiara Cristofani, Gaia Manetti, Ilaria Accorinti, Rosy Muccio, Stefano Berloffa, Pamela Fantozzi, Elena Valente, Valentina Viglione, Pietro Avanzini, Alessandra Carta, Stefano Sotgiu, Emanuele Bartolini, Milone Annarita, Gabriele Masi
papers.abstract: Background Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Level 1 frequently experience persistent difficulties in peer relationships and social functioning that become more evident as social demands increase. Group-based social skills trainings represent a key evidence-based intervention for this population, yet its availability in routine clinical services is still limited. The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills (PEERS ® ) is one of the most empirically supported interventions for autistic adolescents. In Italy, telemedicine delivery has shown promising results, but the effectiveness and implementation of the in-person format in real-world services have not yet been evaluated. In addition, predictors of individual response to psychosocial interventions remain largely unknown. Methods This study is designed as a two-arm pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial incorporating pragmatic features, including delivery within a routine tertiary clinical service, comparison with Treatment as Usual (TAU), and allowance for ongoing concomitant clinical, educational, and pharmacological treatments. It will compare the in-person Italian adaptation of UCLA PEERS ® with Treatment as Usual (TAU) at IRCCS Fondazione Stella Maris (Pisa, Italy). Thirty-six adolescents aged 11–13 years with ASD (DSM-5-TR) and Full-Scale IQ >85 will be assessed at baseline (T0) and after the 16-week intervention (T1). Randomization will use block allocation with allocation concealment until completion of baseline assessments; outcome assessors and independent ADOS–BOSCC video coders will remain blind to group assignment. The intervention includes sixteen weekly 90-minute group sessions delivered by certified providers, with parallel caregiver sessions and structured teacher contacts to promote generalization. The primary focus of this pilot trial is feasibility, assessed through recruitment, retention, session attendance, and treatment fidelity. Clinical outcomes will be examined exploratorily to provide preliminary estimates of treatment effects. The QSQ-R will serve as the prespecified principal clinical outcome for estimating change in social functioning from baseline to T1. Parent- and adolescent-report versions will be analyzed separately, considering the Social Initiative and Social Reciprocity dimensions as distinct outcomes rather than deriving a composite total score. Key secondary outcomes include social knowledge (TASSK-R), autism-related social responsiveness (SRS-2), social motivation (SSDS), social anxiety (SAS), and observational change in social-communication behaviors (ADOS–BOSCC). Emotional–behavioral functioning (CBCL; YSR) will be explored as additional secondary outcomes. Baseline electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during a gesture–word integration task will be used to derive the N400 congruency effect and to explore whether individual differences in this measure are associated with treatment response. As a pilot and feasibility trial, the study is not powered for definitive efficacy testing and will estimate feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect sizes to inform future multicenter trials. Discussion This study will provide the first evaluation of in-person PEERS ® in the Italian clinical context and test the generalizability of previous telemedicine findings in routine care. The integration of clinical and behavioral outcomes may contribute to mechanism-informed, personalized psychosocial interventions for autistic adolescents and guide the design of future confirmatory studies. Trial registration (ClinicalTrials.gov - NCT07207213 – October, 3, 2025).

papers.title: SDS screen-positive prediction from structured questionnaires in university students: a comparative evaluation of large language model prompting strategies
papers.authors: Xiao Yang, Ying Cao, Haibin Wang, Huan Li, Xin Jiang, Huiying Xu, Tao Yao, Xiaolei Zhang, YeKai Chen, Jiaming Li, Bin Zhou, Lingwei Xu, ZhenDong Chen, Xinzhong Zhu
papers.abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can render structured questionnaire variables as natural-language profiles, but their value in mental-health screening cannot be judged from a single fixed-threshold score. We evaluated LLM prompt conditions in a cross-questionnaire benchmark for predicting screen-positive status on the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) among undergraduates. The intended application was an offline methodological benchmark using previously collected questionnaire data, not a shorter alternative to direct SDS administration. Methods De-identified records were assigned to Development (n=1,951), Test (n=2,186), and Holdout (n=2,258) grade cohorts. We evaluated logistic regression, XGBoost, and 12 model-prompt conditions at the fixed 0.5 threshold and at thresholds selected only in Development-validation. We also examined paired bootstrap differences, ranking stability, scale correlations, grouped ablations, cohort shift, calibration intercepts and slopes, alternative expected calibration error specifications, representative repeated calls at temperatures 0 and 0.1, sex-stratified performance, and per-1,000 screening scenarios. Results At the fixed 0.5 threshold on Test, GPT E1, Gemini E2, and XGBoost achieved macro-F1 values of 0.732, 0.730, and 0.674. At Development-derived thresholds of 0.38, 0.50, and 0.174, the corresponding macro-F1 values were 0.702, 0.730, and 0.660. At the Development-selected specificity target, XGBoost achieved a Test macro-F1 of 0.738. Pairwise intervals showed no clear fixed-0.5 macro-F1 difference among the three highest-ranked LLM conditions. XGBoost yielded the lowest Brier scores. The combined-sample Spearman correlation between SDS and SAS was 0.60. Together with the ablation results, this correlation indicated predictive information distributed across overlapping questionnaire groups rather than dependence on a single measured group. In repeated calls across the complete Holdout cohort, inconsistent-case rates were 23.6% for GPT E1 and 1.5% for Gemini E2. Temperature 0 did not clearly eliminate GPT E1 instability in the representative 400-case subset. Discussion Model conclusions depended on both the threshold and the metric. Certain LLM prompt conditions were competitive at specific operating points, but the evidence did not establish a stable or general advantage over structured-data models. Nor did it establish external validity, clinical diagnostic utility, or reduced questionnaire burden. Threshold choice, calibration, output validity, and repeated-call stability therefore require separate evaluation before prospective use.

papers.title: Perceived artificial intelligence dependence and anxiety symptoms among university students: a three-wave study of experiential avoidance and digital literacy
papers.authors: Xu Liu, Zhenggui Gu, Shi Lulu
papers.abstract: University students increasingly use artificial intelligence tools for learning, decision-making, and academic work, making perceived AI dependence a relevant issue for public mental health and digital public health rather than only for educational technology. This three-wave time-lagged survey examined whether experiential avoidance functioned as a putative explanatory process linking perceived AI dependence with later anxiety symptoms and whether digital literacy moderated the tested pathways. Online survey data were collected from 1,451 university students with AI-use experience; perceived AI dependence, digital literacy, and baseline demographic variables were measured in January 2026, experiential avoidance was measured in March 2026, and anxiety symptoms were measured in June 2026. PLS-SEM results showed that experiential avoidance was strongly and positively associated with later anxiety symptoms (beta = 0.677, p < 0.001), whereas the direct association between perceived AI dependence and anxiety symptoms was not significant (beta = -0.030, p = 0.147); perceived AI dependence was negatively associated with experiential avoidance (beta = -0.114, p < 0.001), producing a statistically significant but theoretically unexpected negative time-ordered indirect association (beta = -0.077, p < 0.001), and digital literacy did not significantly moderate the tested pathways. The findings suggest that anxiety symptoms in AI-mediated learning contexts are closely linked to avoidance-related psychological processes, while the meaning of perceived AI dependence is context-dependent and should not be equated automatically with harmful use or clinical addiction; campus mental-health promotion should therefore integrate responsible AI education with support for psychological flexibility, uncertainty tolerance, and autonomous learning.

papers.title: Repeated prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation improves behavioral regulation and modulates resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with problematic smartphone use: a randomized sham-controlled longitudinal study
papers.authors: Jun Chen, Jianming Cheng, 滕敬华, Hui Liu, Bo Yang, Yanxia Zhu, Enming Zhang, Fan Cheng, Yingying Zeng
papers.abstract: Background Problematic smartphone use (PSU) has emerged as an increasingly prevalent digital behavioral addiction among young adults and is associated with impaired executive control, excessive craving, and altered large-scale brain network organization. Although transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has demonstrated therapeutic potential for addictive disorders, its neurophysiological mechanisms in PSU remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether repeated prefrontal tDCS improves behavioral outcomes and reorganizes resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Methods Eighty participants meeting validated criteria for PSU were randomly assigned to receive active (n = 40) or sham (n = 40) tDCS. Active stimulation (2.0 mA, 20 min/session, three sessions/week for 12 weeks) targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Behavioral outcomes included objectively recorded smartphone use, Smartphone Addiction Scale–Short Version scores, ecological momentary assessment craving, and work and social functioning. Resting-state EEG was recorded under eyes-closed and eyes-open conditions before and after intervention. Canonical EEG microstate temporal characteristics were analyzed using mixed repeated-measures analysis with false discovery rate correction. Results Compared with sham stimulation, active tDCS significantly reduced objectively measured smartphone use, craving intensity, and functional impairment while improving behavioral regulation. Neurophysiologically, active stimulation selectively reorganized resting-state brain dynamics. During eyes-closed recording, microstate C occurrence decreased whereas microstate D occurrence increased significantly. During eyes-open recording, both the occurrence and coverage of microstate B increased following active stimulation. No significant changes were observed in global explained variance, suggesting that repeated tDCS primarily modified the temporal organization rather than the spatial configuration of resting-state brain activity. Conclusions Repeated prefrontal tDCS produced concurrent behavioral improvement and selective reorganization of resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. These findings provide preliminary evidence that repeated prefrontal tDCS is associated with concurrent behavioral changes and alterations in resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Further confirmatory studies are needed to determine the clinical and mechanistic significance of these neurophysiological changes.

papers.title: Patterns of morphology in children’s print: estimates of polymorphemic vocabulary using an innovative, AI-informed database of British and American word families
papers.authors: Clarence Green, Elfrieda H. Hiebert, Averil Coxhead
papers.abstract: Background Morphological complexity is a pervasive feature of the vocabulary children encounter in print, yet resources for investigating morphology remain limited. What morpheme patterns do children encounter in print? Which morphemes cover how many polymorphic words in reading experiences? In this study we introduce the British and American Word Families (BAWF) project, an innovative open database of ∼378,000 words, and use it to address questions such as these. Methods GPT-4.1 was fine-tuned using ∼6000 morphologically-coded words from an existing human-generated database (Morpholex). The fine-tuned LLM coded word-parts in all Wiktionary words attested in large British and American corpora. Performance was evaluated via agreement with existing databases. Classical roots were attributed to a subset of words by mapping a list of roots from Wikipedia to all related entries in Wiktionary. The resulting BAWF database is then used to estimate morpheme patterns across databases of children’s texts and further developed as an online application. Results LLM word part predictions are good and fall within the range of agreement typical of existing databases. Nonetheless, output contains some error/noise. In children’s print, polymorphemic words increase across picturebooks to juvenile fiction and school-reading programs. Greek-Latin root words occur early and commonly. Estimates include that ∼100 prefixes/suffixes may account for nearly all derivations. The BAWF itself is released open-source https://cgg-projects.github.io/BAWF_V1/ , with many lexical, morphological, and psycholinguistic variables, including but not limited to frequency, family size, and morpheme-counts. Discussion The contribution suggests that instruction that prioritizes high-yield morphemes could give children access to large word families. These morphemes are present and common early in print. The BAWF (V1) helps see which may be useful to teach. Users can generate custom wordlists, targeting particular features and families, and access linked dictionary/etymological information. The platform includes AI-assisted searches, explanations, parsing review/corrections, and instructional support. The BAWF project will develop over time, incorporating additional variables (e.g., morphological transparency), improving accuracy and the user interface.

papers.title: Monitoring AI-generated English research texts: lexical-semantic accuracy, source fidelity, and revision performance
papers.authors: Jing Zhao, Lei Chen, Xi Bai
papers.abstract: Introduction Linguistically fluent AI-generated English texts can conceal lexical-semantic shifts, altered concept boundaries, source omissions, and unsupported causal formulations. This study compared English paragraphs generated under general and source-constrained conditions and examined how learners' global judgments and localized problem marking were associated with subsequent written revision. Methods Seventy-three agricultural and forestry students evaluated two English paragraphs generated from Chinese source materials under a fixed sequence of general and source-constrained prompts, then selected and revised one paragraph. The linked corpus comprised 146 AI-generated texts, 73 revised texts, 146 global judgment records, 657 expert rating records, 562 coded terminology units, and 511 participant-marked problems. Expert assessments covered lexical-semantic accuracy, source fidelity, and global discourse organization, while revision analyses examined global judgment discrepancy, localized problem marking, and individual-difference variables. Results Source-constrained texts received higher lexical-semantic accuracy scores (mean difference = 0.846, t = 10.634, p < 0.001, d z = 1.245) and source-fidelity scores (mean difference = 0.855, t = 8.819, p < 0.001, d z = 1.032), while global discourse organization differed little between conditions. Lexical-semantic accuracy was strongly associated with source fidelity ( b = 0.522, p < 0.001), whereas the 5,000-resample bootstrap interval for the product of the adjusted coefficients linking these measures to discourse organization spanned zero. After controlling for selected source-text quality, localized problem marking and domain knowledge were positively associated with revised quality, trust in AI-generated language output was negatively associated, and global judgment discrepancy showed no unique association. Discussion Source comparison and localized problem identification were more closely associated with successful written revision than agreement with expert global judgments. These findings highlight the importance of attending to linguistic form, semantic boundaries, and source information when evaluating and revising AI-generated English research texts.

papers.title: AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education
papers.authors: Xiangyu Wang, Yongwei Wang
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

papers.title: Effects of a somatic dance course on body image, embodied self-awareness, and disordered eating risk in female university students: a quasi-experimental study
papers.authors: 尹佳鸽
papers.abstract: Introduction Body image concerns and disordered eating risk are common among female university students, and contemporary frameworks increasingly emphasize positive body image and embodiment. This quasi-experimental, pre-post controlled study examined whether an 8-week somatic-oriented improvisational dance course, delivered as a non-competitive university body education elective and compared with regular university physical education electives, was associated with changes in body appreciation, embodied self-awareness, disordered eating risk, functionality appreciation, and body surveillance. Methods A total of 128 female undergraduates were allocated to the somatic dance course or comparison condition (64 per group). Post-intervention questionnaires were completed by 115 participants, and the main attention-check-passing analysis sample comprised 103 participants. Group differences were estimated using ANCOVA models adjusted for baseline scores, with baseline BMI as an additional covariate. Results Relative to regular university physical education electives, the somatic dance course was associated with greater post-intervention body appreciation (BAS-2), embodied self-awareness (SBC), and functionality appreciation (FAS) and lower body surveillance (OBCS-BS). Adjusted group differences were statistically significant for BAS-2, SBC, FAS, and OBCS-BS, whereas the group difference in disordered eating risk (EAT-26) was not statistically significant. Exploratory change-score mediation analyses did not support an indirect pathway through change in embodied self-awareness. Conclusion The 8-week somatic dance course was associated with short-term group differences in positive body-image and embodiment-related outcomes among female university students. The group difference in disordered eating risk was not statistically significant, and mediation pathways were not supported, indicating the need for rigorous randomized studies with longer follow-up.

papers.title: The mediating role of artificial intelligence perception and creative idea generation in the impact of sustainable leadership on digital transformation and circular economy awareness
papers.authors: Ceyda Yerdelen-Kaygin, Mustafa Altıntaş, Ethem Topçuoğlu, Onur Oktaysoy, Erdoğan Kaygın, Volkan Tatar, Burcu Turan-Torun, Bilal Kobanoğlu
papers.abstract: Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.

papers.title: Public receptiveness to healthcare AI in Spain: social, political, and regulatory correlates in a surgical scenario
papers.authors: Irene Loureiro-Álvarez, Aliaksandra Savostsikava, Ramón Bouzas Lorenzo
papers.abstract: Introduction The expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare raises questions about how citizens evaluate high-stakes applications. This study provides an initial, bounded assessment of public receptiveness in Spain by examining self-reported comfort with robot-performed surgery. It analyses sociodemographic, ideological, and AI-related attitudes, while addressing the role of AI regulation. Methods Data are drawn from the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS) Study No. 3,495, a nationwide survey designed to represent Spain's adult population ( N = 4,004; 2025). Independent samples t-tests and ANOVA were used to examine dierences across groups. Hierarchical linear regression models were then used to examine the contribution of each factor to comfort. Results Comfort with robot-performed surgery varies between groups depending on factors such as sex, income and educational level. The final hierarchical regression model explained 16.8% of the variance in comfort ( R 2 = 0.168). Perceived AI benefits showed the strongest positive association with comfort (β = 0.244), followed by age (β = 0.207), while gender and ideology were significantly negatively associated with comfort. Discussion The findings identify social, political, and attitudinal correlates of comfort with a specific application. They provide an initial, partial basis for examining inequalities in public receptiveness to healthcare automation and suggest that regulatory visibility cannot be assumed to translate directly into greater comfort or receptiveness in this scenario.

papers.title: The magic of love: gender differences in marriage duration and body mass index
papers.authors: Yuying Li, Panpan Li, Kaichao Shao
papers.abstract: Background The global prevalence of obesity is rising, particularly among married individuals. However, limited research has explored the dynamic relationship between marriage and body weight, and the role of marital satisfaction in this relationship. Methods Using 29,734 observations from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), this study examined the association between marriage duration (MD) and body mass index (BMI), as well as the moderating role of marital satisfaction. The analysis was guided by the health capital model and the Double ABC-X framework. Results We found an inverted U-shaped relationship between MD and BMI, with a stronger association in men than in women. The association was more robust among couples with children and more pronounced in rural areas and northern China. Marital satisfaction buffered the association between MD and BMI in men, but not in women. Conclusion MD has a nonlinear association with BMI, and this association differs by gender, household composition, and region. Marital satisfaction may serve as a protective factor for men's weight-related health. These findings inform the development of marriage-based weight management strategies.

papers.title: The application of brain-computer interface on cognitive function and activities of daily living in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Zijie Luo, Lei Yu, Meiling Wu, Xuan Gong
papers.abstract: Objective Nonmotor dysfunction is a common sequela of stroke, affecting patients across acute, subacute, and chronic recovery stages and significantly impairing their functional independence, psychosocial adjustment, and overall Activities of Daily Living (ADL). Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology has demonstrated effectiveness in motor function rehabilitation. The primary objective of this study was to assess the efficacy of BCI technology on cognitive function (as the primary indicator of nonmotor dysfunction) and ADL in stroke patients through a systematic review and meta-analysis. Methods This review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261453809). Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Google Scholar, CNKI, and Wanfang Data up to March 2026. Statistical analyses and the risk of bias were assessed using Review Manager 5.3. The quantitative synthesis focused on the effects of BCI on the cognitive function and ADL of patients with stroke. Results The meta-analysis reviewed 11 randomized controlled studies (RCTs) involving a total of 559 participants. Compared with conventional rehabilitation, BCI-based training significantly improved cognitive function (SMD = 0.634, 95% CI: 0.214, 1.055; p = 0.003) and ADL (SMD = 1.198, 95% CI: 0.079, 2.316; p = 0.036). Subgroup analyses suggested exploratory patterns of benefit in certain strata. However, subgroup analysis revealed no significant differences for most comparisons (including scale type, region, sample size, stroke type, BCI type, intervention intensity, and intervention duration; all p > 0.05), except for first-episode stroke in the ADL analysis ( p = 0.001). Conclusion BCI-based training shows preliminary promise for improving cognitive function and ADL in stroke patients. Current evidence remains insufficient to recommend BCI for emotion or speech rehabilitation. However, the GRADE certainty of evidence was rated as low for cognitive function and very low for ADL, indicating that further high-quality research is warranted. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/ , CRD420261453809.

papers.title: Linking event-related potentials and structural MRI in the aging brain
papers.authors: Yajya Rishi, Rajpaul Attariwala, Ryan C.N. D’Arcy
papers.abstract: Aging alters both brain structure and electrophysiology, which can be measured non-invasively by structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and event-related potentials (ERPs). On average, gray matter declines steadily from early adulthood, whereas white matter increases into midlife before declining. With respect to ERPs, the well-established P300 response shows reduced amplitude and delayed latency from early adulthood onward. Few studies test whether structural MRI and ERP measures correlate within the same individuals, and those that do disagree over which tissue tracks which ERP change. While ERP changes are not coupled to structural changes in a fixed manner, atrophy in gray and white matter tissue correlate with ERP response decay, and a clear pattern of structure–function coupling emerges with age. This dynamic in turn is magnified by age and disease. Technological advances are now enabling structural MRI and portable ERP to be collected from the same individual in a single visit, with machine learning able to model the two modalities jointly rather than separately. While clinical cohorts have historically been the starting point, healthy normative data sampled across the adult age range represents the foundational baseline. Establishing this coupling directly is the critical first step toward integrating MRI and ERP as mutually informative rather than parallel measures of the aging brain. Accordingly, this brief review assembles the evidence as a conceptual framework for linking MRI and ERP changes in healthy aging to support preclinical detection of cognitive decline, now enabled through recent technological advances.

papers.title: Protein pyruvylation: a potential metabolic checkpoint in tumor immunity?
papers.authors: Ren Liu, Jiamin Yuan, Haigang Jin, Lida Ge, Chunxia Dai, Wei Wang, Pengping Li, 王震宇
papers.abstract: Tumor aerobic glycolysis leads to pyruvate buildup in the tumor microenvironment. Recently, STAT1 pyruvylation induced by PKM2 (pyruvate kinase M2) and pyruvate was shown to suppress type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. In cancer immunotherapy, IFN-I shows a clear acute-versus-chronic paradox. Short-term IFN-I signaling helps antigen presentation and CD8+ T-cell activation. However, long-term IFN-I exposure promotes CD8+ T-cell exhaustion and reduces the benefit of checkpoint blockade. By linking pyruvate to the IFN-I pathway, pyruvylation may help explain this poor clinical response. We hypothesize that lasting pyruvate exposure in the tumor microenvironment keeps STAT1 pyruvylation high in infiltrating immune cells. This may silence endogenous IFN-I signaling for a long time and support tumor immune escape.Zuo et al. recently reported a new post-translational modification. In this process, pyruvate directly modifies amino acid residues. They named it protein Pyruvylation [1]. They showed that high glucose promotes STAT1 pyruvylation at Lys201. This modification stops STAT1 from binding STAT2. As a result, IFN-I signaling is suppressed and antiviral responses are weakened.IFN-I is widely studied, but it shows a basic-clinical paradox in tumor immunotherapy. In preclinical studies, acute IFN-I signaling helps dendritic cells present tumor antigens and activate cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. However, systemic IFN-I treatment often gives low response rates. This opposite phenotype may be related to low-dose IFN-I signaling and microenvironment reprogramming in human solid cancers [2]. In addition, chronic IFN-I exposure can promote immunosuppression. It drives lipid-peroxidation-related terminal exhaustion of CD8+ T cells. It also upregulates transcription factors that form strong inhibitory feedback loops [3,4].Aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect) leads to high pyruvate and lactate in the tumor microenvironment. Lactate can regulate tumor immunity through lactylation [5]. Pyruvate can also support tumor metabolism and immune escape. It has been reported that tumor cells can change pyruvate use and succinate signaling in tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells by remodeling the local metabolic network. This weakens antitumor cytotoxicity [6]. Moreover, pyruvate flux inside T cells also shapes their function. Mitochondrial pyruvate carriers (MPCs) are key regulators of T-cell fate. Short-term MPC inhibition can favor memory T-cell formation through a metabolic-epigenetic axis. In the nutrient-poor TME, effector T cells need MPCs to convert lactate into pyruvate for oxidation to keep antitumor activity [7].Up to now, no immunotherapy cohort has directly measured STAT1 pyruvylation, or global lysine pyruvylation, together with IFN-I treatment response or immune-checkpoint response. The key finding that STAT1-K201 pyruvylation suppresses IFN-I signaling came from antiviral and high-glucose studies, not from cancer trial samples [1]. However, several lines of evidence make a clinical link biologically reasonable. First, chronic IFN-I signaling drives terminal CD8+ T-cell exhaustion linked to lipid peroxidation and reduces anti-PD-1 efficacy. This gives a practical definition of IFN-related immunotherapy resistance [2][3][4]. Second, tumordriven changes in pyruvate use weaken CD8+ T-cell killing, and mitochondrial pyruvate handling shapes antitumor T-cell fate [6,7]. Pyruvate can also regulate PD-L1 and suppress T-cell immunity [8]. Third, another metabolite-driven STAT1 change, lactylation at K193, weakens IFN-gamma-related chemokine programs and helps immune escape. Blocking this change can improve checkpoint blockade in preclinical models [9]. Fourth, STAT1 pathway proteins have already been measured in melanoma cohorts treated with PD-1 blockade. Fifth, Pyruvylation regulators themselves hold effect on prognosis of IBC-treated real word cohort, in which high expression of PKM or HAT1 hold worse overall survival in melanoma with anti-PD1 therapy respectively, while high expression of SIRT3 hold better overall survival in melanoma with anti-PDL1 therapy (Fig. 1). This shows that IFN/STAT1 pathway status can be tested in patients, even though pyruvylation itself has not been measured yet [10]. Therefore, whether IFN-I-related immunotherapy resistance is caused by pyruvylation is still unproven. Current data support a testable working model, not a cohort-proven causal claim. Priority studies include: (i) targeted mass spectrometry of STAT1-K201 pyruvylation in pre-and on-treatment ICB biopsies; (ii) linking glycolytic/pyruvate gene and metabolite scores with IFN-stimulated gene programs and clinical response; and (iii) comparing pyruvylation levels between responders and non-responders.Fig. 1: The prognostic effect pf pyruvylation pivotal regulators in real word cohorts. High expression of PKM or HAT1 hold worse overall survival in melanoma with anti-PD1 therapy respectively, while high expression of SIRT3 hold better overall survival in melanoma with anti-PDL1 therapy. All data from Kaplan-Meier Plotter: https://kmplot.com/analysis/index.php?p=home Systemic IFN-I often shows limited antitumor effects, which differs from many preclinical findings. We propose that high IFN-I activity in a pyruvate-rich tumor microenvironment may trigger feedback inhibition of STAT1/STAT2 heterodimer formation through STAT1 pyruvylation. Here we do not use the uncommon term "immunotherapy fatigue." Instead, we mean early or lasting poor clinical response that reflects chronic IFN-Idriven CD8+ T-cell exhaustion and inhibitory feedback, not a separate formal diagnosis [2][3][4].
