papers.title: A Strengthening Digital Office Administration Competencies through International Community Engagement: An Indonesia–Malaysia Collaborative Program
papers.authors: Mayang Riyantie
papers.abstract: The rapid development of digital technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) requires higher education institutions to equip students with competencies relevant to the digital workplace. This community engagement program aimed to strengthen students' competencies in Digital Office Administration through an international collaboration between Universitas Negeri Jakarta (Indonesia) and Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia. Conducted in a hybrid format, the program combined expert lectures, interactive discussions, and knowledge exchange involving students from both countries. The learning topics focused on Digital Office Administration, AI for administrative support, and Modern Service Practices. Program evaluation using pre-test and post-test indicated an improvement in participants' understanding of the topics presented. The program also strengthened international academic collaboration while enhancing students' readiness to adapt to digital transformation in office administration.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Criterion-Referenced Oral English Assessment: A Measured Pilot Study
papers.authors: Fatima Zulfiqar Ali, Humna Zulfiqar, Atrooba Ilyas
papers.abstract: Oral examination is a high-stakes application of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, requiring transparency and human oversight. This study presents a pilot AI examiner for university oral English examinations following the IELTS Speaking format. The system combines automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Gemini 2.5 Flash, deterministic extraction of fluency, lexical, syntactic, and semantic indicators, and rubric-constrained assessment using Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite. Low-confidence cases are automatically escalated, and final weighted scores are calculated programmatically, while instructors retain authority over academic decisions. The pilot analyzed 45 spoken responses, of which 26.7% lacked usable word-level timestamps, preventing reliable calculation of temporal indicators and highlighting ASR-related measurement limitations. A post-examination survey collected responses from 67 students, achieving a 62% response rate, to evaluate the internal consistency of composite indices. Comparisons between AI-generated preliminary scores and instructor-released grades across 23 paired sessions revealed near-zero correlations and a pronounced ceiling effect in instructor scores. Consequently, these grades could not serve as a valid criterion for evaluating AI scoring accuracy. Instructor feedback also identified operational challenges requiring refinement. Based on these findings, the study establishes a three-level trust framework grounded in observable pipeline conditions and measured failure frequencies. It also proposes a validation protocol involving two independent human raters and quadratic-weighted kappa to assess inter-rater agreement and support future validation of AI-generated scores. Overall, the findings demonstrate the feasibility of transparent, rubric-based AI-assisted oral assessment while emphasizing measurement limitations, standardized expert ratings, and human oversight.

papers.title: Pseudoparousia Theory: Why People Confide in Artificial Intelligence, and Why Confiding Is Not Enough
papers.authors: Khader I. Alkhouri
papers.abstract: People increasingly confide their most dangerous thoughts to artificial intelligence (AI). Studies report that users disclose suicidal ideation more readily to conversational agents than to standard questionnaires or to other people, and platform data suggest that more than a million people each week discuss suicide with a single general-purpose chatbot. Yet this unprecedented volume of disclosure has not translated into proportionate protection, and some of the most serious harms associated with AI in mental health have occurred precisely within relationships of intense disclosure. This article proposes Pseudoparousia Theory (from the Greek pseudo-, false, and parousia, presence) to explain this paradox. The theory holds that disclosure seeks not only a listener but a presence: an other who is affected by what is disclosed, able to act on it, and continuous and accountable over time. Conversational AI produces the experience of presence – attention, responsiveness, apparent empathy, constant availability – without its substance. This counterfeit presence, or pseudoparousia, lowers the cost of disclosure for exactly the reasons that it removes disclosure’s protective consequences. The theory defines presence through three components (affectedness, agency, and continuity), distinguishes four configurations of witnessing (embodied presence, echo, deflection, and absence), formulates six propositions, and derives testable hypotheses, a measurement program, and implications for design, clinical practice, and regulation. Its central claim is that the decisive question for AI in mental health is not how accurately a system can detect distress, but whether presence can be transferred from the machine to a person in time.

papers.title: BCI & AI for Cognitively-Aware Learning: A Review of Technologies, Tools, and Applications
papers.authors: Nurzada Amangeldy, Assel Omarbekova, Gulmira Bekmanova, Marek Miłosz, Sholpan Zholdassova, Nazerke Gazizova, Nazgul Dospol
papers.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive review of technologies, tools, and applications in the field of brain-computer interfaces (BCI) and artificial intelligence (AI) for developing cognitively adaptive learning environments. Unlike prior reviews that treat BCI hardware, AI decoding models, and pedagogical deployment as separate topics, this review develops an integrated cross-layer taxonomy linking hardware constraints, AI architecture requirements, and classroom deployment conditions. Emphasis is placed on the transition from cumbersome laboratory systems to wearable hybrid solutions combining electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), as well as textile sensors that offer a favorable trade-off between neurophysiological signal quality and mobility in real-world classroom settings. The review includes a detailed analysis of modern AI architectures, transformer-based models for processing non-stationary neural signals, and Siamese neural networks implementing a few-shot learning paradigm to address the calibration problem associated with new users. It further proposes a unified state-estimation framework integrating cognitive load, attention, and affect into a single formalization for closed-loop adaptive learning systems. The review concludes with a critical analysis of fundamental barriers to scalability, signal instability, mental state privacy issues, and the risk of a neurocognitive divide arising from unequal access to technology. The authors argue that the future of neuroeducation lies in the symbiotic interaction of humans and AI, supported by unified international standards and the convergence of BCI with large language models (LLM) for predictive communication.

papers.title: Ecosistema formativo para la capacitación del personal del turismo en tecnologías para la gestión del conocimiento.
papers.authors: Yosdany González Hernández, Yakelín Gómez Morales
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To design a theoretical-methodological conception for the training of tourism personnel in technological knowledge management, supported by a training ecosystem that integrates technological, pedagogical, and organizational dimensions within the context of the Hotel and Tourism Schools (EHT) of Cuba. MATERIAL AND METHOD: A qualitative approach was adopted, using the systematization of experiences as the general method. The research was conducted between 2023 and 2026 at the Villa Clara EHT and its Tourism Information and Documentation Center (Cidtur). In-depth interviews, participant observation, surveys, and documentary analysis were applied for the diagnostic assessment. RESULTS: The diagnostic assessment revealed low connectivity, an outdated repository, an inactive newsletter, and limited use of services. An ecosystem was designed comprising five components and guided by principles such as network socialization, mediated externalization, social construction, sustainability, and interoperability. Validation yielded satisfactory results: mean scores above 4.5 out of 5 and coefficients of variation below 0.15 across all evaluated dimensions, complemented by a qualitative analysis confirming credibility, internal consistency, transferability, contextual relevance, confirmability, and dependability. CONCLUSIONS: The conception is relevant and feasible; it transforms professional training by transcending the traditional model and promotes the co-creation of knowledge using digital technologies.

papers.title: Designing Trust in AI-Assisted Fashion Education
papers.authors: Xiaozhu Lin, Andrea Giuseppe Manciaracina
papers.journal: The International Journal of Design Education
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming fashion design education by enabling users to produce visually convincing garments, campaign images, and videos with unprecedented speed. However, as the visual quality of AI-assisted outputs becomes increasingly independent of the depth of human-led design reasoning, final outcomes become less reliable as evidence of student learning, authorship, and disciplinary judgment. This article examines this problem through a reflective practice-based case. An educator-led fashion project was documented from initial asset development to AI generation, redesign and market-ready visualization. The analysis reveals several critical tensions, including the limited perceptibility of the designer–system ratio, the limited visibility of the connection between visual research and print development, the mixed sources of the uploaded assets, and the risk that repeated generation and visual selection may replace deliberate design reasoning. The article introduces the concept of the “output–evidence gap” to describe the disconnection between the apparent quality of AI-assisted outcomes and the evidence they provide of authorship, learning, and critical judgment. It subsequently proposes a Designing Trust Framework structured around framing, sourcing, translating, curating, generating, diagnosing, intervening, and accounting. The article argues that trust in AI-assisted design education cannot be based on visual polish or platform-declared human control alone. Instead, it should be built through trackable processes, domain-specific judgment, meaningful human intervention, and deliberate pedagogical mediation.

papers.title: AI-Augmented Studio Pedagogy
papers.authors: Moâtaz Fatnassi
papers.journal: The International Journal of Design Education
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into design practice has prompted product design education to reconsider the pedagogical foundations of studio-based learning. Although generative AI offers new opportunities for exploration, ideation, and design development, its unregulated use may undermine core designerly competencies, including reflective practice, material experimentation, and critical judgment. This article proposes an AI-augmented pedagogical framework that structures the integration of generative AI within the product design studio. Adopting a theoretically informed Research Through Design education approach, this study develops a pedagogical architecture articulated around four guiding principles, a five-phase studio model, and explicit regulatory mechanisms designed to support responsible AI use throughout the design process. The principal contribution of this article lies in the pedagogical operationalization of regulated co-intelligence. The proposed framework organizes interactions between students, teachers, peers, and generative AI systems in ways that preserve the foundations of designerly reasoning while fostering algorithmic reflexivity, critical AI literacy, and informed professional judgment. Designed as an adaptable pedagogical model, the framework provides a conceptual basis for future empirical research on the regulated integration of generative AI into studio-based design education.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence, Arbitration and the Global South: Addressing Algorithmic Asymmetries in Global Dispute Resolution
papers.authors: Daniel Brantes Ferreira, Elizaveta Aleksandrovna Gromova
papers.abstract: This article examines whether the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in international arbitration risks reinforcing and expanding Global North dominance over the Global South. While existing literature mainly focuses on efficiency, confidentiality, transparency, and due process in AI-assisted arbitration, this article addresses this gap by viewing AI not just as a technological innovation but as a form of private transnational governance embedded within broader structures of epistemic hierarchy, technological dependency, and Global North–South inequality. Methodologically, it combines doctrinal and literature-based legal analysis with a TWAIL-informed political economy perspective, drawing on scholarly literature, institutional reports, surveys, and soft-law instruments. The analysis highlights three main mechanisms through which inequalities may be reinforced: data concentration, vendor control, and the dominance of Global North standard-setting. It argues that AI may strengthen existing institutional, infrastructural, and normative advantages of actors at the center of the arbitral system. At the same time, the article does not oppose AI in arbitration. Instead, it concludes that AI should be governed with safeguards such as disclosure, explainability, contestability, confidentiality, and human oversight, while also addressing deeper inequalities in technological infrastructure and epistemic authority.

papers.title: The Economic and Organizational Consequences of AI-Induced Workforce Displacement: A Mixed-Methods Investigation
papers.authors: Shankar S. Iyer, Raman Subramanian, Rajesh Arora, Dr Brinitha Raji, Veena Christy, Aaryan Kapur, RADHAKRISHNAN NATARAJAN
papers.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming global labor markets by automating routine tasks, reshaping employment patterns, and creating significant economic and organizational challenges. This study investigates the multidimensional consequences of AI-induced workforce displacement by examining employment trends, wage polarization, worker experiences, organizational adaptation strategies, and relevant theoretical perspectives. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was adopted, combining quantitative analysis of survey data from 2,350 workers across 15 industries in 12 countries between January 2021 and June 2022 with longitudinal employment statistics and regression modelling, alongside qualitative analysis of 142 semi-structured interviews with displaced workers, organizational leaders, and HR professionals. Data were analyzed using SPSS v28, Stata v17, and NVivo v12 following institutional ethical approval (Protocol No. WUC-IRB-2021-047_ Dated 7 January 2021), with inter-coder reliability of κ=0.83. Results showed that routine-intensive occupations faced a 67% higher displacement risk, while manufacturing (β=-0.43, p<0.001) and administrative services (β=-0.38, p<0.001) experienced significant employment declines associated with AI adoption. Displaced workers reported an average income reduction of 26.7% and employment transitions lasting 16.8 months. Qualitative findings highlighted psychological distress, organizational culture shifts toward AI adoption, inadequate reskilling infrastructure, and insufficient institutional support, whereas organizations implementing proactive reskilling programs achieved 64% higher employee retention. Overall, AI-driven workforce displacement extends beyond job losses, requiring coordinated policy interventions, institutional support, and continuous workforce reskilling to promote equitable labor market transitions, organizational resilience, sustainable employment, and inclusive economic growth in increasingly AI-enabled economies. These findings emphasize collaborative governance, lifelong learning, adaptive leadership, resilient institutions and responsible implementation.

papers.title: The Aims of Education in the Age of AI
papers.authors: Catherine Pickstock
papers.abstract: We are called upon to construe an ethic and a practical discipline adequate to the unique conditions of our time. 1 For the recent burgeoning of generative artificial intelligence, which simulates the operations of thought and expression, presents not merely an external convenience, but a challenge to the springs of human agency, to the formation of character and to the creative impulse itself. Yet it would be premature to define the contours of this problem in abstraction. The history of civilization is, in no small measure, a history of its responses to innovation, especially to those techniques which touch upon language, memory and the ordering of thought. Again and again, such inventions have been greeted with a double apprehension: that they might enfeeble the discipline of the mind and arrest the growth of the soul, or, conversely, that they might serve as instruments of its preservation against other perils.

papers.title: Learning from the Past: Protocol for a Meta-Narrative Review of Over-Reliance on Cognitive technologies
papers.authors: Chaima Merbouh, Guy Paré, Ryad Titah
papers.abstract: Background: Concerns that humans may become overly reliant on technologies that support or perform cognitive tasks long predate contemporary artificial intelligence (AI). Across successive generations of cognitive technologies, scholars have examined related concerns through distinct research traditions, each bringing its own assumptions, concepts, and vocabulary to the problem. Existing reviews have generally focused on specific manifestations of over-reliance, leaving limited understanding of how these bodies of scholarship relate to one another. This meta-narrative review examines how different research traditions have conceptualized over-reliance on cognitive technologies and what recurring patterns and broader insights emerge across traditions and as these technologies have evolved. Methods: We apply the meta-narrative method through six iterative phases: planning, searching, mapping, appraisal, synthesis, and recommendations. The search combines exploratory scoping, a structured search of Web of Science Core Collection and ProQuest, and backward and forward citation tracing. The mapping phase will identify historically and intellectually coherent research traditions and trace their development over time. Studies will be appraised according to the quality criteria of their respective traditions and analyzed to reconstruct how each tradition has conceptualized, explained, and investigated over-reliance. The synthesis will compare the resulting meta-narratives to identify recurring patterns and points of convergence, divergence, and tension. The recommendations phase will provide a research agenda and consider implications for research and practice. Discussion: By bringing distinct bodies of scholarship into conversation, this review seeks to build a more cumulative understanding of over-reliance on cognitive technologies. It may help distinguish longstanding problems of over-reliance from those more specific to contemporary AI, recover insights developed in relation to earlier technologies, and identify unresolved tensions and questions. These insights may inform research and efforts to design, implement, and govern cognitive technologies in ways that preserve human judgment and expertise in professional practice.

papers.title: Data and Analysis Materials for “Predicting engagement with GenAI writing feedback among international learners”
papers.authors: Syamsul Ghufron
papers.abstract: This project contains the data and analysis materials supporting the manuscript “Predicting engagement with GenAI writing feedback among international learners: The roles of growth writing mindset, GenAI writing feedback literacy, and self-regulated writing strategies.” The study examines how growth writing mindset, GenAI writing feedback literacy, and self-regulated writing strategies predict international learners’ engagement with writing feedback generated by generative AI (GenAI) tools. Data were collected through an online questionnaire among international learners of Indonesian and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Files: first_order data.csv: anonymized data for the first-order model second-order data.csv: anonymized data for the second-order model Engagement with GenAI Feedback 22052026.zip: analysis files and output All identifying information has been removed. Data are shared under a CC BY 4.0 license. Please cite the associated article when using these materials.

papers.title: The next frontier of athletic intelligence in sports medicine and exercise science
papers.authors: Habib Noorbhai
papers.journal: South African Journal of Sports Medicine
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming sports medicine and exercise science, offering unprecedented capabilities in markerless motion capture, automated exercise prescription, diagnostic imaging and integrated athlete monitoring. These advances have the potential to democratise biomechanical analysis, scale clinical expertise to underserved populations and shift injury management from reactive treatment to predictive prevention. However, the pace of adoption carries significant risks, including technological dependency without methodological literacy, the entrenchment of global inequities through biased training datasets and models, the erosion of clinician-athlete relationships and a widening governance vacuum over data ownership and algorithmic accountability. This commentary argues that the next frontier of athletic intelligence will be defined not by technological sophistication alone, but by the wisdom, inclusivity and ethical resolve with which the sports medicine community deploys it. Disciplined engagement (rather than uncritical adoption or reflexive avoidance) is the potential path forward.

papers.title: Detection of code smells using artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Enrique Alejandro Chim Mex, Antonio A. Aguileta, Raúl Antonio Aguilar Vera, Juan Pablo Ucan Pech
papers.abstract: Introduction: This article is the product of research on code smells developed by the Software Engineering for Education Research Group at the Autonomous University of Yucatán in 2025. This study, like others cited in the literature, has relied on artificial intelligence to expand research in Software Engineering. Problem: Although previous studies have analyzed code smell detection using Machine Learning and Deep Learning independently, this research integrates both approaches to provide a more detailed analysis. Objective: The objective of this study is to present the approach taken toward artificial intelligence and code smells. Method: A systematic mapping study was employed as the research method. Based on a search string executed in five databases—ACM, Taylor & Francis, IEEE, Wiley, and SpringerLink—108 documents were retrieved, of which 35 were selected according to the established inclusion and exclusion criteria. Results: Since 2018, a growing trend in this topic has been observed. Machine Learning is the predominant approach, mainly using the Random Forest algorithm, while CNN stands out in Deep Learning. Conclusion: Despite their growing relevance, there are significant areas that require further attention and research. Originality: This research integrates Machine Learning and Deep Learning approaches within the same study for code smell detection, allowing for a broader view and a more detailed comparison. Limitations: The limitation of this study lies in the fact that the review was based only on five databases and on the inclusion and exclusion criteria.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Scores Differ from Candidate Scores on Board Exams: A Critical Appraisal
papers.authors: Jamie L. Mansell, Anne Russ, Ryan Tierney, Reece Hayes
papers.abstract: Context: Recent research has investigated Artificial Intelligence’s (AI) ability to answer items such as board-style medical exam questions. On board style exam questions, do scores differ between AI and humans? Methods: PubMed was searched in May and June of 2024 using the Boolean phrase: Medical examination OR medical education AND artificial intelligence. Inclusion criteria comprised of English-language studies no older than 3 years, evaluating standardized/validated board-style exam questions and compared AI to human examinees. Studies were excluded if they evaluated open-ended or case-study style questions, prompted AI or failed to prevent learning effects of AI, or were systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Studies were evaluated using the STROBE checklist. Outcome measures included scores on board-style exam questions. Results: An original search revealed 4,973 studies. 61 studies met title criteria and were screened more thoroughly. Five studies met all criteria for inclusion and were analyzed. In a study of 11,733 medical residents, ChatGPT-4 outperformed the examinees 70.1% to 55.8%. In another study, ChatGPT-4 outperformed examinees on a pre-internship examination 68.5% to 57%. On a national licensing medical examination, 1,025 first-year medical students were compared to ChatGPT-3.5 and version 4. Both versions of ChatGPT outscored humans 77% (v3.5) and 86%(v4) compared to 55%. On a licensing examination, human examinees were compared to ChatGPT-4 and version 3.5, ChatGPT-4 outperformed humans, v3.5 did not, 85%(v4) and 58% (v3.5) compared to 76%. 736 urologists were compared to ChatGPT-3.5 and version 4, and Google’s Bard. ChatGPT-4 outperformed the examinees, Bard performed at examinee-level, ChatGPT-3.5 performed below-level of humans. STROBE scores were 20, 19, 20, 21, and 15, respectively. Conclusions: AI surpassed human examinees on medical exams. While AI exceeded humans on these exams, it did not score 100%. Caution should be applied when considering using AI as a tool for study sessions or individualized learning plans. SOR = A.

papers.title: Modeling and profiling AI-mediated informal digital learning of English, achievement emotions, and strategic competence for cross-cultural communication
papers.authors: Minlin Zou, Mark Feng Teng, He Xueyun
papers.journal: Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) has received increasing attention in foreign language learning. However, few studies have integrated variable-centered and person-centered approaches to investigate how AI-IDLE relates to achievement emotions and strategic competence for cross-cultural communication (SCCC). The present study therefore examined the associations between AI-IDLE and SCCC through two achievement emotions, specifically enjoyment and boredom, using both analytical approaches. Participants were 435 Chinese university EFL undergraduate students. In Stage 1, a variable-centered analysis was conducted to explore the connections among AI-IDLE, foreign language enjoyment (FLE), foreign language boredom (FLB), and SCCC. The results showed that AI-IDLE directly and positively predicted both FLE and SCCC, while negatively predicting FLB. FLE partially mediated the relationship between AI-IDLE and SCCC. By contrast, FLB did not significantly predict SCCC. In Stage 2, a person-centered analysis was undertaken to identify distinct profiles of students’ AI-IDLE. Results demonstrated that three profiles were identified: passive AI-IDLE users, balanced AI-IDLE learners, and proactive AI-IDLE strategists. Specifically, the profile of balanced AI-IDLE learners accounted for the largest proportion (N = 206, 47.3%). Theoretical and pedagogical implications were discussed.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Peer Review in Cardiovascular Journals: Promise, Pitfalls, and a Path to Responsible Hybrid Adoption.

papers.title: Towards the learning estate: from digital–physical to experience orchestration
papers.authors: Daniel Mitelpunkt, Luke McCrone
papers.abstract: Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

papers.title: Passive Hyperthermia Increases Neural Recruitment, Thereby Reducing Processing Efficiency During Executive Task Performance
papers.authors: Manabu Shibasaki, Shigehiko Ogoh, Kanoko Ito, Tatsuya Hojo, Hiroki Nakata
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Heat-induced hyperthermia impairs cognitive performance and contributes to central fatigue during exercise and environmental heat exposure. Electroencephalographic event-related potential (EEG-ERP) studies consistently show reduced P300 amplitudes under heat stress, whereas functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies often report expanded blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) activation. PURPOSE: This study examined how passive hyperthermia influences task-dependent neural activation and cognitive processing using both fMRI and EEG-ERP within comparable paradigms. METHODS: Eighteen healthy adults (ten males and eight females) performed Go/No-go and Flanker tasks under normothermic and hyperthermic conditions during fMRI. Passive heating increased external ear canal temperature (Tear) by approximately 1.1°C above baseline. Sixteen participants completed an additional EEG-ERP session with the Flanker task. Behavioral responses, regional BOLD activation, and P300 amplitude and latency were assessed. Cervical arterial blood flow was measured by using a color-coded ultrasound system. RESULTS: The mean heating duration was 53.9 ± 9.2 min across all subjects. Hyperthermia increased heart rate and Tear while reducing internal carotid and vertebral artery blood flow. Reaction times decreased in both tasks, with no change in error rates. fMRI showed expanded activation in bilateral frontal, parietal, temporal, and subcortical regions. Task subtraction analyses (Flanker minus Go/No-go) revealed greater frontal and parietal activation during the complex task. In contrast, P300 amplitude was reduced during hyperthermia. CONCLUSION: Passive hyperthermia expands the spatial extent task-related BOLD activation while reducing P300 amplitude, suggesting reduced processing efficiency. However, the BOLD findings should be interpreted with caution because cerebral perfusion was also reduced. These findings suggest increased neural strain under heat stress, contributing to central fatigue and potentially impairing decision-making in sport and occupational setting.

papers.title: PTSD, complex PTSD and the dissociative subtype of PTSD in patients with ultraprocessed food addiction
papers.authors: Timothy D. Brewerton, Cindy Nguyen, Dean Bilenker, Kimberly Dennis
papers.abstract: Higher rates of lifetime traumatic events and resulting symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) have been reported in individuals with ultra-processed food addiction (UPFA). However, the role of complex PTSD (CPTSD) and the dissociative subtype of PTSD (DPTSD) in UPFA remains unexplored. Participants were patients (59% female) admitted to a higher level of care (residential, partial hospital or intensive outpatient) for treatment of a DSM-5 defined eating disorder (ED), substance use disorder (SUD), PTSD, and/or mood disorder. Patients completed self-report assessments within 72 hours of admission, including the modified Yale Food Addiction Scale (mYFAS 2.0), Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire; Life Events Checklist for DSM-5; PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; International Trauma Questionnaire; Dissociative Subtype of PTSD Scale; Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test; Drug Abuse Screening Test-10; Patient Health Questionnaire-9; Spielberger State Trait Anxiety Scale short form, and the World Health Organization Quality of Life Abbreviated Scale. Patients with (n=151) and without UPFA (n=571) were compared using multivariant analyses of variance and age, admission BMI, sex at birth, gender, and ED diagnosis as covariates. Patients who met mYFAS 2.0 criteria for UPFA had significantly higher rates of self-reported types of traumatic events, provisional DSM-5 PTSD (72% v. 51%) and DPTSD (53% v. 32%), provisional ICD-11 PTSD (40% v. 25%) and CPTSD (37% v. 20%), major depression (86% v. 68%), any ED (78% v. 24%), and BMI >30 (46% v. 30%) compared to those without UPFA (p<.001). In patients with UPFA, those with DPTSD and/or CPTSD had significantly higher symptom scores for PTSD, depersonalization-derealization, loss of awareness, psychogenic amnesia, and disturbances of self-organization. They were also more likely to have an ED. In addition, there was significant overlap between the diagnoses of CPTSD and DPTSD with 26% of those with UPFA meeting criteria for both disorders. PTSD, CPTSD and DPTSD are common in patients with UPFA and indicate more complex psychiatric comorbidity, particularly for those that meet both CPTSD and DPTSD. These results emphasize the importance of thorough assessment and the need for integrated treatment that directly addresses the full spectrum of trauma-related symptoms in treatment-seeking patients. Ultra-processed food addiction (UPFA) has been associated with high rates of trauma exposure and symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and related comorbid disorders, yet links to complex PTSD (CPTSD) and the dissociative subtype of PTSD (DPTSD) have been unexplored in clinical research. We studied 722 patients admitted to residential, partial hospital, and intensive outpatient treatment for eating, substance use, and/or mood disorders who were assessed for UPFA, PTSD, CPTSD, DPTSD, eating disorders, substance use disorders, symptoms of associated psychiatric comorbidity, and quality of life. Patients with UPFA (n = 151), as determined by the modified Yale Food Addiction Scale 2.0, had significantly higher rates of both DSM-5 (72% vs. 51%) and ICD-11-defined PTSD (40% vs. 25%) in comparison to patients without UPFA (n = 571). They also had higher rates of CPTSD (37% vs. 20%), DPTSD (53% vs. 32%), eating disorders (78% vs. 24%), depression (86% vs. 68%), and body mass indices (BMI’s) in the obesity range (>30) (46% vs. 30%). Patients with UPFA who had CPTSD and/or DPTSD experienced more severe trauma-related symptoms, including feelings of detachment from themselves or their surroundings, reduced awareness, memory gaps, and difficulties with emotional regulation and self-perception. More than one quarter of patients with UPFA met criteria for both conditions. These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive trauma assessment and the development of integrated, individualized treatment plans for patients with UPFA, particularly those experiencing complex or dissociative PTSD symptoms alongside eating disorders and other psychiatric conditions.

papers.title: A cross-sectional study on the perceptions, utilization, and educational needs of medical students regarding AI, 3D PDF, and deep learning
papers.authors: Eren Öğüt, Eylul Ruya Kurt, Eren Tuna, Muallanur Sagun, Esma Asmin Korkmaz, Rabia Kılınç, Asude Zulal Kaya, Sude Naz Kılıc
papers.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate undergraduate medical students’ awareness, use, perceived competence, and educational expectations regarding artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional portable document format (3D PDF), and deep learning in anatomy education. Data from 607 valid questionnaire responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence. Awareness of AI tools was high, with ChatGPT being the most recognized platform, followed by Gemini and OpenAI. Students mainly used AI to acquire theoretical knowledge, and AI use during studying anatomy ( p = 0.012). The frequency of AI use also varied according to both gender ( p = 0.028) and grade ( p = 0.010). Students reported a need for support in technical use, reliability checks, and ethical principles. Self-rated AI competence was generally moderate and differed significantly by gender ( p < 0.001). Deep learning was less familiar than AI and 3D PDFs. The use of 3D PDFs differed significantly by gender ( p = 0.025) and grade ( p = 0.028). Students considered 3D PDFs most applicable to anatomy education, followed by medical imaging and surgical planning ( p < 0.001). Overall, the findings indicate high digital awareness among medical students but limited structured preparation for responsible AI use, deep learning literacy, and visualization-based anatomical learning. Not applicable.

papers.title: Development of an evidence-informed doctoral curriculum framework in physical therapy sciences: an international benchmarking and expert validation study
papers.authors: Animesh Hazari, Praveen Kumar Kandakurti, Sampath Kumar Amaravadi, Ioannis Agouris, Varoon Chandramohan Jaiswal, Manda Venkatramana
papers.abstract: The expanding scope of Physical Therapy research, coupled with rapid advances in digital health, artificial intelligence, implementation science, and evidence-based rehabilitation, has increased the demand for doctoral graduates with advanced research, leadership, and interdisciplinary competencies. Despite this evolution, published guidance describing systematic and evidence-informed approaches to developing doctoral curricula in Physical Therapy Sciences remains limited. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an evidence-informed doctoral curriculum framework through systematic needs assessment, international benchmarking, competency mapping, and constructive alignment. A multiphase evidence-informed curriculum development methodology was employed. The study comprised seven sequential phases: (1) needs assessment and environmental analysis; (2) international benchmarking; (3) comparative curriculum analysis; (4) competency mapping ; (5) Curriculum framework development; (6) Curriculum refinement and quality assurance; and (7) external expert content validation. Twenty-four doctoral programmes from research-intensive universities in the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and Australia were screened, of which eighteen met the predefined inclusion criteria for benchmarking. The proposed curriculum was subsequently evaluated by an international panel of twelve experts using a structured validation instrument, and content validity was assessed using item-level and scale-level Content Validity Indices. Benchmarking demonstrated substantial consistency across international doctoral programmes in advanced research methodology, biostatistics, research ethics, scientific writing, proposal development, and independent dissertation research. Comparative analysis further identified increasing emphasis on digital health, artificial intelligence, implementation science, interdisciplinary collaboration, research leadership, and knowledge translation as emerging doctoral competencies. These findings informed the development of a competency-based doctoral curriculum aligned with internationally recognised educational frameworks. External expert validation demonstrated high perceived relevance, competency alignment, curriculum structure, content appropriateness, and implementation feasibility of the proposed framework, with domain-specific agreement ranging from 92% to 100%. Minor recommendations related to curriculum sequencing and emerging digital competencies were incorporated without altering the overall doctoral curriculum framework. This study presents an evidence-informed and high perceived relevance, alignment, and feasibility among an international expert panel that aligns Physical Therapy Sciences education with contemporary international educational standards and evolving rehabilitation research priorities. The proposed framework offers a transparent methodology for curriculum development that integrates systematic benchmarking, competency mapping, and expert validation, providing a practical model to inform the development or revision of doctoral programmes in Physical Therapy and related health professions. Future implementation studies are warranted to evaluate its educational effectiveness across diverse institutional settings.

papers.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of AI chatbots in answering guideline-based questions on pulp therapy in primary and immature permanent teeth
papers.authors: Dilan Altun, Merve Özdemir
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into dental education and clinical information seeking is increasing, while concerns regarding the accuracy and reproducibility of AI-generated responses remain. This study aimed to assess the response accuracy and reproducibility of AI chatbots in answering guideline-based questions on pulp therapy in primary and immature permanent teeth. Twenty text-based clinical questions regarding pulp therapy in primary and immature permanent teeth were developed in multiple-choice and dichotomous formats. Seven AI chatbots (ChatGPT 4o, ChatGPT 4.1, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Copilot, Claude 4 Sonnet, and Perplexity AI) were tested over three consecutive days. Response accuracy was analyzed using bias-reduced logistic generalized estimating equations with clinical question as the clustering variable. Reproducibility was assessed using exact agreement, Fleiss’ kappa, Cochran’s Q test, and Holm-corrected exact McNemar tests. No statistically significant overall difference in response accuracy was detected among the evaluated AI chatbots ( p = 0.190). Testing day had a significant effect on response accuracy ( p = 0.016), with accuracy rates of 77.9%, 85.0%, and 83.6% on days 1, 2, and 3, respectively. No significant overall differences were observed according to question type ( p = 0.057) or clinical question category ( p = 0.429). Reproducibility differed significantly among the evaluated AI chatbots ( p = 0.041), with exact agreement ranging from 45.0% to 85.0% and Fleiss’ κ from − 0.025 to 0.567; however, no pairwise comparisons remained statistically significant after Holm correction. The evaluated AI chatbots showed generally high response accuracy in standardized pediatric endodontic scenarios, with no significant overall difference among chatbots. However, response accuracy varied across testing days and reproducibility differed among chatbots, indicating that similar overall response accuracy may not reflect consistent performance over time. Further validation is needed before AI chatbots can be considered for broader clinical use.

papers.title: Towards the Digital Transformation of Official Statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean: Evidence on the Use of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence from the 2024–2025 NSO Consultations
papers.authors: Maria Luíza Guerra de Toledo, JUAN JOFRE, Hanna Diniz Cunha, Andréa Diniz da Silva, Verônica dos Santos, Elio Villaseñor
papers.abstract: This study examines the adoption, use, and institutionalisation of big data and artificial intelligence in official statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing on the 2024 and 2025 International Consultations conducted with National Statistical Offices. The study combines questionnaire data from 15 responding countries in 2024 and 21 countries and territories in 2025 with qualitative evidence from in-depth interviews. It also proposes the Statistical Innovation Index, a composite indicator designed to approximate differences in the adoption, integration, and institutionalisation of big data and AI across NSOs. Results indicate a gradual consolidation of big data use, although applications remain concentrated in web scraping and satellite imagery, particularly for price, population, environmental, and agricultural statistics. AI adoption remains at an earlier stage: 39% of responding NSOs reported its use, mainly in data processing and other operational tasks. The maturity classification reveals substantial heterogeneity across the region, with most NSOs concentrated in early or emerging stages of statistical innovation. Findings suggest that progress follows a selective process in which exploratory initiatives are gradually filtered into a smaller number of sustainable applications. Institutional capacity, governance, infrastructure, and regional cooperation emerge as key enablers of this process. More broadly, the findings suggest that the transition from exploratory to operational uses of big data and AI reflects an evolving institutional role of NSOs, in which technological innovation is accompanied by new responsibilities for data governance, institutional coordination, and maintaining public trust in official statistics.

papers.title: NASA-TLX Reveals Cognitive Workload Across the HoLEP Learning Curve from Our First 100 Cases
papers.authors: Raviraj J. Rege, Víctor Sandoval, Carl A. Ceraolo, Rajat Jain, Scott O. Quarrier, Nitin Sharma
papers.abstract: Introduction: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) has a steep learning curve, which limits widespread adoption. Objective metrics to define surgical proficiency, efficiency, and perceived workload remain underexplored outside academic institutions. This study aimed to characterize the learning curve of HoLEP from one single surgeon at an ambulatory surgical center. Methods: A total of 103 patients underwent HoLEP for BPH between March 2024 and August 2025. Surgical cases were stratified into 3 sequential groups of 34, 34, and 35 cases, respectively, based on operative chronology. Operative characteristics were compared across groups: enucleation time, laser energy, fluid use, and enucleation speed (enucleation time/specimen weight). Perceived workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) to evaluate perceived workload across several “performance” domains (mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration). Comparisons of outcome metrics were made for 90-day postoperative complications. Urinary continence outcomes were evaluated at 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months postoperatively. Univariable and multivariable multinomial logistic regression analyses were performed to examine associations between surgical characteristics and group classification. Results: Progressive improvement was observed in operative time, enucleation time, laser energy, total fluid, enucleation speed, and NASA TLX, as seen in Table 1 . No statistically significant associations were observed between group classification and 90-day postoperative complications or urinary continence outcomes at any follow-up interval. In multivariable multinomial logistic regression analysis, the NASA-TLX score (OR 0.83, 95% CI, 0.70–0.98, p = 0.02) remained an independent predictor of higher learning curve classification. papers.title: AI Augmented Student Advising: A Comparative Study of LLMs and Advisor-Based Course Recommendations
papers.authors: Sriram Srinivasan, Hamdan Ziyad Alabsi, Andrew Mangle, Rand Obeidat, Azene Zenebe, Kavita Kapur
papers.abstract: Course placement in higher education is pivotal for student progression. Traditional advising can be effectively augmented by Large Language Models (LLMs) to ensure scalable guidance. Crucially, we propose a novel on-premises infrastructure that runs LLMs locally, ensuring strict student data privacy. We benchmarked four open-source LLMs against gold-standard responses from human advisors (n = 3) using 35 Information Systems student profiles, identifying GPT-OSS-120B as the optimal model. To guarantee real-world viability, we profiled the infrastructure's resource utilization across 112 sequentially processed cases. Additionally, we evaluated complex scenarios: undergraduate course substitutions (n = 10) and graduate prerequisite assessments (n = 10). Results indicate strong performance in substitutions but mixed outcomes for prerequisite assessments. We also determined the optimal model parameters for recommendation accuracy. To assess broader institutional utility, we expanded testing to include four additional disciplines: Marketing, Economics, Accounting, and Finance (n = 20 per major), demonstrating the system's potential for cross-disciplinary application. This study demonstrates that securely deployed, locally hosted LLMs can provide a privacy-compliant framework to assist academic advisors, though current performance highlights the necessity of continuous human oversight.

papers.title: Is Less More? Exploring the Visual Processes of Minimalist and Complex Photography Through Eye Tracking and EEG
papers.authors: Hsien-Chih Chuang, JING-CIH WANG
papers.abstract: In a world filled with an overwhelming amount of visual information, the clean and distinctive visual style of minimalist photography stands out. However, empirical research on how minimalist style affects visual cognition and psychological responses remains limited. The present study investigated the effects of photographic style (minimalist versus complex) on viewers' visual behavior, emotional responses, and brainwave state by conducting quantitative psychological experiments. Thirty participants viewed photographs in one of the two styles. Eye-tracking, consumer-grade electroencephalography (EEG), and subjective psychological assessment data were collected, enabling comprehensive evaluation of how the participants looked at, responded to, and emotionally engaged with the images. At the level of visual behavior, minimalism elicited significantly reduced number of fixations and saccades, but the duration of a single fixation is significantly longer, and the heatmap hotspots are highly concentrated, presenting a focused processing pattern of fewer but longer gazes. On a psychological level, minimalism evoked significantly less feeling of complexity and greater relaxation, although there was no significant difference in the aesthetics score between the two styles. In terms of brainwave state, viewing minimalist images resulted in significantly higher attention eSense levels, while the meditation eSense level did not show a significant difference. The results of this study therefore show that minimalist composition may influence the visual search pattern to be more focused, which is compatible with the tendency of simplified organization predicted by the principle of simplification. This study not only deepens the theoretical understanding of the psychological mechanisms of minimalist aesthetics, but also provides practical reference for visual communication and image creation of minimalist composition serving as an effective strategy for guiding the eyes toward the core subject.

papers.title: Who sustains the people? Human sustainability beyond AI literacy
papers.authors: ALI MIKAEILI
papers.journal: Libraries and Cultural Resources (University of Calgary)
papers.abstract: Many responses to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, whether critiques of its promised time savings, calls for AI literacy, or support for educator wellbeing, locate the burden of adaptation with individuals. This opinion paper shifts the question to the institution: Can universities integrate GenAI without depleting the people on whom teaching and learning depend? Drawing on the author's practice with instructors, graduate teaching assistants, and education professionals, the paper identifies costs that literacy training does not address, including verification labour, intensified workload, and uncertain assessment judgement. It then makes three contributions. First, drawing on research on human sustainability and sustainable academic work, it defines the human sustainability of GenAI in higher education as an institutional responsibility. Second, it extends critical analyses of responsibilisation in AI policy to literacy-centred responses, which turn systemic problems into personal duties. Third, it proposes a post-adoption test that institutions can use to assess whether their use of AI is sustainable for the people who carry it.

papers.title: Evaluating Explainable AI with Humans: Trust, Reliance, Understanding, and Performance
papers.authors: Jonathan Frez, Nelson A. Baloian, Luciano Ahumada, Ashot N. Harutyunyan
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is often evaluated through claims about trust, reliance, understanding, and performance, yet studies measure these constructs differently and frequently overlook confounding factors. This PRISMA-guided systematic review with narrative synthesis examines human-centered XAI evaluation across these four constructs. The review covers publications from 2015 to 2025. A merged search combined an OpenAlex-informed DOI/title catalog, prior surveys, citation chasing, and a Scopus coverage-completion stage identifying 9,026 records. A targeted revision update added two eligible publications, yielding 119 validated full-text publications. The synthesis highlights three patterns: trust and reliance can diverge; perceived understanding can exceed objective understanding; and interface salience or perceived accuracy can confound explanation effects. Aggregate advice acceptance, for example, cannot distinguish beneficial reliance from automation bias. We therefore recommend measuring acceptance separately for correct and incorrect AI outputs, testing understanding beyond self-report, documenting study context and interface conditions, and evaluating explanations under uncertainty or model failure. The review contributes construct definitions, a synthesis across designs and domains, an analysis of evaluation measures, and practical reporting guidelines. It also examines generated explanations and citation-based interfaces, supporting more reproducible and interpretable human-centered XAI evaluations.

papers.title: Factors Influencing Citizens’ Continuance Intention to Use Government Chatbots: An Empirical Study Based on Diffusion of Innovation Theory
papers.authors: Ayman Alarabiat, Delfina de Sá Soares
papers.abstract: Government chatbots are increasingly deployed to support digital public service delivery, yet their continued value depends on whether citizens with prior experience intend to use them again when a relevant public-service need arises. Drawing on Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory, this study examines factors associated with citizens’ continuance intention to use government chatbots by integrating five DOI constructs—relative advantage, compatibility, perceived complexity, trialability, and observability—with responsiveness and anthropomorphic design. Data were collected from 358 citizens with prior experience using government chatbots and analyzed using PLS-SEM. Responsiveness showed the strongest association with continuance intention, followed by anthropomorphic design and relative advantage, while perceived complexity was negatively associated. Trialability showed a weaker but statistically significant positive association, whereas compatibility and observability were not significantly associated. The model explains 62.4% of the variance in continuance intention. The findings suggest that reuse intention is more strongly associated with interaction quality and perceived functional benefits than with contextual fit or visibility of outcomes. Continuance intention refers to future-use intention reported by citizens with prior chatbot experience and does not represent observed continued use over time. Theoretically, the study extends DOI to a post-adoption government-chatbot context, while practically highlighting responsiveness and anthropomorphic design.

papers.title: Employees' Justice Perceptions and Trust in AI Systems for Performance Evaluation: Uncovering the Role of Gender and Culture
papers.authors: Tam Nguyen, Regina Connolly
papers.journal: ACM SIGMIS Database the DATABASE for Advances in Information Systems
papers.abstract: Organizations are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to support employee performance evaluation, yet employees' perceptions of and responses to these systems within this high-stakes workplace context remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on social exchange, organizational justice, and trust theories, this study examines how employees' justice perceptions shape trust in AI-based performance evaluation systems and how trust in AI relates to broader employee–organization relationship factors, including trust in the organization, trust in managers, and affective commitment. It further investigates whether these relationships vary across gender and Eastern–Western regional contexts. Survey data from 291 employees across Eastern and Western countries were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and multigroup analysis. The findings show that distributive and procedural justice perceptions positively influence employee trust in AI across regional contexts, with distributive justice exerting the stronger effect. Trust in AI, in turn, positively influences affective commitment in both contexts. Gender differences were observed in the relationship between procedural justice perception and trust in AI within the Eastern sample but not within the Western sample. These findings contribute to research on organizational justice, trust, and AI in organizations, while also offering practical insights for fostering employee trust and supporting effective AI implementation in performance evaluation.

papers.title: Delegating Ourselves Away: Preserve Human Voice and Choice in Next-Generation Digital Systems
papers.authors: K.D. Joshi, Xuefei Nancy Deng, Tung Bui
papers.journal: ACM SIGMIS Database the DATABASE for Advances in Information Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic AI is reshaping the framing of equity and inclusion in information systems research. The editorial opens with an urgent call for a conversation about inclusion and equity in the age of agentic AI, given concerns that humans are increasingly removed from knowledge work in human-AI interactions. It then reflects on the digital systems research presented at HICSS over the past 60 years and explains how a new permanent research track has been established to focus on equitable and inclusive digital systems in society and institutions. The editorial outlines what agentic AI is changing, the equity and inclusion risks that follow, and the urgent research agenda this track is uniquely positioned to lead. It ends with a summary of the five papers published in this special issue, which advance our knowledge of equitable and inclusive digital systems from diverse perspectives, and calls for scholars and scientists in the research communities to pay attention to the profound socio-technical paradigm shift driven by the transition from traditional AI to generative AI and to agentic AI.

papers.title: Exploring Normative Behavior in Generative AI: A Case Study of Text-to-Image Systems Using Stable Diffusion
papers.authors: Michelle Melina Dutoit, Baptiste Caramiaux
papers.journal: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
papers.abstract: Generative AI systems embed and transmit norms, raising critical questions for creative practice as they increasingly shape cultural production. This paper examines how creative practitioners per- ceive and experience normativity when using a text-to-image (T2I) system based on Stable Diffusion. We asked artists and designers to create illustrations inspired by two media sources with different levels of specificity, and analyzed their process through a mixed method design combining topic analysis, questionnaires, and semi- structured interviews. Results show that the studied T2I system often simplified the topics involved, particularly in low-abstraction tasks, and that creative practitioners perceived normativity through stereotypical outputs, invariant patterns, and unsolicited omissions or additions of details. These tendencies generated a sense of dis- empowerment, as creative practitioners had to adapt their creative process and linguistic choices to the system’s constraints. We con- clude by discussing how transparency and stronger user control could mitigate these effects to make this technology more empow- ering for creatives and artists.

papers.title: Teaching Novice Computing and Programming in the Agentic AI Era
papers.authors: Kathi Fisler, Shriram Krishnamurthi, Michael L. Littman
papers.abstract: AI programming agents have profoundly disrupted computing education. Rather than treating this as a threat, we argue that it is an opportunity to refocus early curricula. We introduce the “flaky compiler” metaphor to frame what AI programming enables and what it demands of its users. We argue that introductory computing courses can and must become early software-engineering courses, with the objective of teaching students to take responsibility for the work they produce with AI. This induces the need for—indeed, demands—research into how to rethink teaching program specification.

papers.title: Differential Diagnosis Performance of ChatGPT in Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology
papers.authors: Sohaib Shujaat, Marryam Riaz, Jawaher Mohammed Alsubaie, Aljwhrah Abdulaziz Almuammar, Arun Pillai, Abdulmohsen A. Alfadley, Ali Anwar Aboalela
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate ChatGPT (GPT-5.1) for ranked differential diagnoses in oral and maxillofacial pathology, assess image effects on diagnostic performance and examine output stability across repeated runs. METHODS: This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study included 160 biopsy-confirmed cases. Cases were evaluated using a standardised prompt under two conditions: text-only and text plus clinical photographs and/or radiographs. Each case underwent three independent runs. Performance was measured using Top-1, Top-3, Top-5 and Top-10 accuracy. RESULTS: Top-1 accuracy was 44.0% for text-only and 43.3% for text + image inputs. Accuracy increased at broader thresholds, with Top-10 accuracy reaching 80.7% and 82.9%, respectively, but no significant differences were observed between input conditions at any Top-K threshold. Top-1 performance was stable across runs, although variability was observed at broader Top-K thresholds in the text-only condition. CONCLUSIONS: ChatGPT ranked the reference diagnosis first in fewer than half of cases, while broader differential lists more often included it. Images did not significantly improve accuracy, although heterogeneous and non-standardised visual inputs may have limited detection of multimodal effects. These findings support further investigation for hypothesis generation and educational use rather than clinical decision support or replacement of expert judgement and histopathological confirmation.

papers.title: When creativity meets artificial intelligence: a sequential path to smart learning and academic performance
papers.authors: Md. Kazi Hafizur Rahman
papers.journal: Journal of Research in Innovative Teaching & Learning
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and students' creative thinking (CT) contribute to smart learning (SL) and academic performance (AP) in higher education. It further examines whether AI use and SL mediate the relationship between CT and AP in a sequential manner. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was adopted, and data were collected from 227 university students in Bangladesh. Structural equation modelling with SmartPLS was used to evaluate the proposed relationships. Findings The results show that both AI usage and CT are positively and significantly related to SL and AP. Beyond these direct associations, the data also point to a meaningful serial mediation pathway: students with stronger CT tend to report greater AI usage, which is in turn associated with higher SL engagement, and this heightened engagement is associated with better AP. Originality/value This study uniquely links CT, AI use, SL and AP in Bangladeshi higher education. It shows how CT affects academic achievement through sequential paths of AI usage and SL, clarifying how student talents convert into outcomes in digital learning environments. The findings suggest that institutions should promote CT and use AI-based learning tools to improve student performance.

papers.title: Human enough? Examining morality and ethical perceptions of service robots
papers.authors: Amy Wong, Jimmy Wong
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how robot-related social and humanlike cues shape consumers' perceived morality and perceived ethics of service robots, and how these appraisals impact trust and intention to use. Design/methodology/approach A total of 257 usable surveys were collected from diners who have engaged with a service robot at a fine dining restaurant. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings A robot's perceived mind of its own and social presence significantly influenced consumers' perceived morality and perceived ethics. Perceived ethics and social presence significantly influenced trust, while perceived morality and mind of its own exhibited nonsignificant effects on trust. Trust strongly predicted intention to use. Mediation analysis confirmed the intermediary effects of trust between social presence, perceived ethics and intention to use. Practical implications The findings suggest that managers should balance robot autonomy with predictability, prioritize ethical transparency over simulated moral reasoning, design social presence carefully and treat trust-building as an operational process involving reliability, service recovery and escalation protocols. Originality/value The study contributes to service robot research by distinguishing perceived morality as consumers' attribution of moral capacity from perceived ethics as consumers' evaluation of ethical conduct. It further shows that moral and ethical appraisals do not translate into trust in identical ways, highlighting the need to understand service robot acceptance through moral cognition, ethical evaluation and trust formation.

papers.title: ICHGen: a framework for cloud-collar generation and personalised virtual try-on
papers.authors: Jinjing Yu, Yuxuan Guo, Kaixuan Liu
papers.journal: International Journal of Clothing Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Purpose This study proposes ICHGen, a framework for cloud-collar generation and personalised virtual try-on. It aims to integrate traditional structural knowledge and physically informed wearing priors into generative artificial intelligence, supporting culturally consistent design, efficient visualisation and the digital reuse of intangible cultural heritage. Design/methodology/approach ICHGen integrates Shape Grammar, FLUX-LoRA, Position-Based Dynamics (PBD), and Kontext. SG-derived structural guidance is introduced into cloud-collar generation, while PBD-simulated wearing samples provide physical priors for Kontext training. The framework is evaluated using geometric metrics, expert assessment, baseline comparisons and PBD-reference consistency analysis. Findings ICHGen achieved the highest expert Shape grammar Compliance Score (9.51 ± 0.10) among the evaluated generation methods and an overall VTON score of 4.33 ± 0.17. PBD-reference evaluation also showed substantial consistency in garment region and occlusion, while the complete generation-and-try-on process required approximately 18 s per case. Practical implications The framework provides a practical workflow for cloud-collar digital design, personalised virtual presentation, and creative reuse. By incorporating structural and physical priors during model construction, it supports efficient image-based generation without requiring real-time physical simulation. Originality/value The cloud-collar case demonstrates a practical approach to integrating explicit cultural and physical knowledge into generative AI for digital heritage applications. It lowers the threshold of cloud collar design, promotes public participation in intangible cultural heritage innovation, providing a reusable technical reference for the digital revitalisation and intelligent manufacturing of ICH.

papers.title: An empirical study on how social engineering and persuasion principles training affects senior citizens’ responses to SMiShing attacks
papers.authors: Brian Bisceglia, Yair M. Levy, Greg Simco, Wei Li, Carlene G. Blackwood-Brown
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research study was set to address the problem of cyberattacks, such as phishing delivered via short message service (SMS) or SMiShing, targeted towards senior citizens. In 2023, they lost over $36m to such attacks. Phishing success increases when attackers use persuasion principles that bypass logical decision-making and rely on heuristics. Security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programs can reduce susceptibility, yet little research investigated SETA programs that incorporate these principles. Design/methodology/approach This research was conducted in three phases, beginning with Subject Matter Experts’ evaluation of SMiShing messages operationalizing these persuasion principles for use in this study’s instrument. The next phase was a pilot study. The third phase was the main data collection and analysis phase. This research employed a pretest-posttest design to evaluate the efficacy of its novel SETA program. The SETA program used Behavioral Skills Training methodology with 118 senior citizens from South Florida and Central Massachusetts. Findings The experimental results indicated a statistically significant mean difference between pretest and posttest group scores (F = 6.604, df = 5, p = 0.011) in identifying SMiShing messages that operationalize the principles of persuasion used in social engineering. Specifically, the pretest group’s mean score was 73.62, and the posttest group’s mean score was 79.28. The calculated effect size (η2 = 0.054) nears the threshold for a medium effect (η2 = 0.06). Practical implications Recognizing persuasion in SMiShing messages helped senior citizens better detect these cyberattacks. Practical implications include incorporating persuasion principles into the SETA framework to address evolving cyberattacks (e.g. deepfakes, vishing) that are being enhanced by generative artificial intelligence. Social implications As a group, senior citizens have lost millions to cyberattacks. SETA programs that incorporate principles of persuasion appear to help reduce the financial losses this group incurs from cyberattacks and may also improve senior citizens’ confidence and reduce fear when using communication technology. Originality/value This research’s original contribution is the integration of persuasion principles into cybersecurity training programs, helping senior citizens quickly recognize the malicious intent of SMiShing messages, which apply psychological pressures to achieve the attacker’s goals.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence at work: a socio-psychological model of employee adoption and innovation
papers.authors: Amro Al-Madadha, Ahmad Samed Al‐Adwan
papers.abstract: Purpose This research aims to identify the key organisational, cognitive, and psychological predictors of perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence (AI) and to evaluate their influence on the AI adoption intention and innovative behavior of employees in the Jordanian setting. Design/methodology/approach A strict quantitative research design was adopted in the current study in which a structured online questionnaire was conducted among employees working in various industries in Jordan, mainly IT, retail, and banking. Quantitative data comprising 388 valid responses were then analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling to assess both the direct effects as well as moderating relationships between the constructs of interest. Findings The results show that organizational culture (β = 0.216), technology usage habits (β = 0.278), and AI self-image (β = 0.195) positively influence AI perceived usefulness, while AI literacy significantly reduces AI anxiety (β = −0.482). AI perceived usefulness strongly predicts employee innovative behavior (β = 0.608) and AI adoption intention (β = 0.657). Job insecurity weakens the relationship between perceived usefulness and adoption intention (β = −0.234), but its moderating effect on innovative behavior is insignificant. AI anxiety also weakens the effects of perceived usefulness on adoption intention (β = −0.208) and innovative behavior (β = −0.180). Originality/value A socio-psychological approach is used in this investigation, highlighting the significance of identity congruence and the importance of affective processes in the adoption of AI. It anticipates psychological and emotional engagement of employees in AI, breaking the false belief that acceptance is dictated by technical or rational factors only.

papers.title: Smart questioning, answering, and clarifying to support adaptive learning
papers.authors: Quoc-Viet Nguyen, Min-Te Sun, Wu‐Yuin Hwang, Thi-Nhan Cao
papers.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education; however, many AI-based systems function primarily as reactive answer generators rather than adaptive instructional supports. This study develops and evaluates smart questioning, answering, and clarifying (SmartQAC), a pedagogically grounded AI-supported learning system that operationalizes structured dialogic scaffolding through questioning, answering, and clarification mechanisms to support adaptive learning. Design/methodology/approach SmartQAC integrates retrieval-augmented generation, prompt-routing strategies, and structured dialogic interactions to promote metacognitive engagement and conceptual development. A quasi-experimental study involving 52 undergraduate students was conducted within a database course as an illustrative domain application. Mixed-method analyses were performed using pre-test and post-test assessments, interaction logs, questionnaires, and interviews to examine learning achievement, learning behaviors, and learner perceptions. Findings Results indicate that students using SmartQAC achieved significantly higher learning achievement than those in the control group. Interaction behaviors within the SmartQAC environment were positively associated with students' learning achievement. Furthermore, participants reported positive perceptions regarding instructional usefulness, autonomy support, engagement, and pedagogical value. Originality/value This study demonstrates how dialogic instructional principles can be operationalized within a retrieval-augmented large language model system to support adaptive learning. The findings provide empirical evidence for the effectiveness of integrating questioning, answering, and clarification mechanisms into AI-supported learning environments and offer practical design implications for future adaptive educational systems.

papers.title: The hidden learning cost of generative AI: the THINK framework for preserving critical thinking in AI-enabled workplaces
papers.authors: Sam Bodunrin
papers.journal: Development in Learning Organizations An International Journal
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how regular use of generative AI enhances productivity, but somehow, in contrast, reduces the opportunities for employees to utilize critical thinking skills and translate their hands-on experience into organizational learning. Design/methodology/approach The paper is a problem-based conceptual synthesis linking AI literacy, organizational learning, human-AI collaboration, evidence from knowledge workers, and knowledge collapse theory. On the other hand, human-AI augmentation and disengagement are considered opposing risks from which five workplace safeguards are derived. Findings The paper shows that the issue is not the use of GenAI, but organizations that reward flawless automation output while ignoring verification, human reasoning, and visible employee learning. The paper introduces the THINK framework interlinking organizational practices: Transparency, Human judgment, Intellectual engagement, Navigation of evidence and Knowledge construction. Research limitations/implications The THINK framework conceptual synthesis is selective and not empirically tested. Future research should validate the application effect across different sectors, industries and levels of GenAI adoption. Practical implications The THINK framework can be integrated into employee training, performance management discussions, decision-making and AI governance systems. Originality/value The paper transposes the traditional argument about GenAI-mediated cognition into a simple, auditable framework that managers can apply on the job as coaches, learning professionals, and AI governance teams.

papers.title: Readability and Content Integrity of Discharge Documents for Common Pediatric Orthopaedic Procedures Before and After Artificial Intelligence Simplification
