Results showed that intercultural sensitivity was the strongest predictor of willingness to communicate. In contrast, perceived artificial intelligence usefulness had only a minor direct influence. It did not significantly predict intercultural sensitivity, indicating that the hypothesized mediation was not supported. Perceived artificial intelligence usefulness and intercultural sensitivity appear to function as separate, rather than sequential, contributors to willingness to communicate. These findings suggest that language programs should pair artificial intelligence with structured intercultural learning opportunities rather than treat it as a standalone solution. Future research should test alternative mediators and longitudinal designs to clarify the causal pathways involved.

papers.title: Information literacy as an epistemic negotiation of the utilization of artificial intelligence at Institut Pertanian Stiper Library
papers.authors: Helmi Afroda, - Ayuna Meilawati
papers.journal: Daluang Journal of Library and Information Science
papers.abstract: Purpose. This study aims to examine and conceptually explain how information literacy functions as an epistemic negotiation mechanism in AI-mediated academic environments. Methods: This qualitative case study was conducted at the Institut Pertanian Stiper (INSTIPER) Yogyakarta Library using semi-structured interviews with lecturers and students, supported by institutional documents on information literacy and AI-related academic policies. The data were analyzed thematically through transcription, coding, categorization, and interpretative analysis. Findings. The findings demonstrate that information literacy functions as an epistemic negotiation mechanism through which lecturers, researchers, and students critically evaluate, verify, and justify AI-generated knowledge before integrating it into academic practice. The study further reveals that the INSTIPER Yogyakarta Library has evolved beyond its conventional role as an information service to an institutional actor that strengthens AI literacy, mediates institutional AI governance, promotes data ethics and digital information security, and supports responsible knowledge production. Implications. The principal contribution of this study lies in conceptualizing information literacy as an epistemic negotiation mechanism that connects the institutional epistemic role of academic libraries with AI governance and individual scholarly judgment. This conceptual framework extends current discussions beyond AI adoption and AI literacy, providing a foundation for developing evidence-based information literacy programs and institutional AI governance that strengthen academic integrity in higher education.

papers.title: Teaching critical thinking with artificial intelligence: An information literacy training model at the Library of the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing, Universitas Gadjah Mada
papers.authors: Mohammad Riqzazulmi, Fitri Mutia, Sukirno, Tachiyya Nailal Khusna
papers.journal: Daluang Journal of Library and Information Science
papers.abstract: Purpose. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into information literacy training in university libraries, focusing on how AI can foster critical thinking and ethical awareness among students and staff. Methods. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach with data collected through interviews, observations, and documentation at the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing Library of Gadjah Mada University. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns in participants' experiences and in librarians' roles as facilitators. Findings. The training model consisted of three main components: introducing AI concepts and ethical considerations, practicing the use of generative AI tools for literature searching, summarisation, and academic writing, and critically evaluating AI outputs. The training enhanced participants' ability to locate relevant sources, generate summaries, and support administrative tasks. It also highlighted challenges, including difficulties in formulating effective prompts and the need for librarians to upgrade their AI competencies continually. The findings show that AI-based literacy training not only improves technical proficiency but also nurtures reflective and critical engagement with digital tools. Implications. The study concludes that AI-driven information literacy programs in academic libraries can serve as an innovative model for strengthening users' critical thinking, ethical responsibility, and digital literacy. Sustained librarian capacity-building and continuous training are essential to maximize the long-term benefits of AI integration in academic information services.

papers.title: INTEGRATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TO SUPPORT READING COMPREHENSION IN INDONESIAN EFL CONTEXTS
papers.authors: Puspita Mayaratri, Nany Soengkono Madayani
papers.abstract: Abstract The article describes the use of AI-based tools for English reading comprehension teaching among Indonesian EFL learners. This study addresses the perennial reading challenges caused by limited lexical knowledge, inconsistent access to English, large class sizes, and limited individual feedback in the Indonesian university context. Twenty-eight undergraduate students of a Reading class of the Ushuluddin Faculty, UIN Sayyid Ali Rahmatullah Tulungagung, employed 4 AI-based applications for one semester in a mixed-methods classroom intervention: Text Inspector for text and lexical analysis, ReadTheory for an adaptive reading practice, Rewordify for vocabulary assistance, and Quillionz for the automation of comprehension questions. Quantitative results revealed that the post-test mean score was 80.1 (SD = 6.5) as compared to the pre-test mean score of 61.2 (SD=12.3); with a mean gain of 18.9. Qualitative results from students' reflection journals, teachers' observations, and students' focus group interviews found that the tools enhanced students' confidence, strategic reading behaviours, peer interaction, and autonomy in learning. Through interactive reading theory, schema theory, vocabulary learning theory, sociocultural scaffolding, adaptive learning and formative assessment, findings have demonstrated that AI-based tools are educationally beneficial if implemented with teacher mediation, clear instructions on explicit learning strategies, and mindful use of data. This article claims that AI-based reading instruction could offer consistent and individualized scaffolding to Indonesian EFL learners in addition to careful design, digital accessibility and ongoing assessments across educational fields. Keywords: artificial intelligence; reading comprehension; Indonesian EFL; adaptive learning; vocabulary support

papers.title: University Brand Management in the Digital Environment: Faculty as Co-Creators and Brand Ambassadors
papers.authors: Oleksandra Cherniavska
papers.abstract: University brand management in the digital environment increasingly depends on distributed faculty participation because institutional visibility is produced not only by central communication units but also through academics’ professional pages, publications, project communication and external engagement. This study examines faculty members as co-creators of the university brand and as potential voluntary brand ambassadors and identifies the managerial conditions under which favourable attitudes toward institutional positioning are converted into sustained, evidence-based professional visibility. The empirical analysis uses a consent-based sample of 372 faculty members and facilitators from the Erasmus+ SEAL-NR project. Descriptive statistics, contingency analysis, Pearson chi-square tests, Cramer’s V and rule-based behavioural profiling are applied. The results reveal a marked attitude-action gap: 95,1% of respondents use the university brand professionally regularly or sometimes, 61,7% use branded assets, while only 30,4% maintain an active professional page or blog. Digital competence is significantly associated with page status, branded-asset use and co-creation role, but effect sizes are small, showing that competence alone does not substitute for organisational support. A behavioural typology identifies active brand agents/ambassador candidates, potential or limited co-creators and brand sceptics. The study contributes by separating broad faculty brand co-creation from the more intensive voluntary ambassador role and by linking these roles to a differentiated six-layer management architecture integrating capability development, reusable assets, editorial support, recognition, governance and analytics. The findings indicate that universities can strengthen credible digital visibility by reducing participation costs and supporting faculty autonomy rather than imposing uniform promotional obligations. The management implication is a shift from campaign-based communication to a supported participation system in which differentiated faculty roles, reusable workflows and performance feedback connect academic activity with institutional visibility.

papers.authors: Sir-Lord Wiafe, Najme Soleimani, Zening Fu, Robyn L. Miller, Vince D. Calhoun

papers.title: A Hierarchical Framework of the Impact of End-User Machine Learning Tools on Applied Machine Learning Education
papers.authors: Jonathan Niemirowski, David Hall, Krystal Cruse, Mary E. Fendley
papers.abstract: This exploratory study presents an abstraction hierarchy model as a preliminary course design framework for assessing the information and functions associated with applied ML classroom projects from engineering and technology courses.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Engineering Technology: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Outlook
papers.authors: Sabit Ekin, Farid El Breidi, Milad Saadat, Mohammed Metwaly
papers.abstract: This systematic study examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI and large language models, is reshaping Engineering Technology across education, research, laboratory environments, and professional practice.

papers.title: Developing an Industry-Based DevOps Learning Framework Through Microservices, CI/CD, and AI-Driven Bus Scheduling Optimization for Vocational Education
papers.authors: Roni Andarsyah, Cahyo Prianto, Dodi Permadi
papers.abstract: The digital transformation within the public transportation industry demands information systems that are responsive, modular, and capable of supporting data-driven decision-making. This research integrates two previously independent strategic approaches: (1) a DevOps architecture utilizing a CI/CD Pipeline based on Microservices, enhanced with API Logging and centralized monitoring to support the ticketing Dashboard system for bus operators, and (2) a hybrid optimization approach combining Machine Learning and Genetic Algorithms (GA) to optimize airport bus scheduling. Beyond these technical contributions, this research develops an Industry-Based DevOps Learning Framework, a training-oriented framework that can be adapted for vocational education and industry-based learning in DevOps and data-driven optimization. The implementation of CI/CD and Microservices enables rapid, scalable, and zero-downtime deployment, while centralized monitoring using Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana (ELK) Stack and Prometheus–Grafana improves Observability and early anomaly detection. On the operational side, a LightGBM model is employed to predict the probability of passenger occupancy (load factor ≥ 70%), and these predictions are used as a fitness function within the GA to generate optimal schedules. Experimental results show significant improvements: total estimated passengers increased from 478 to 841, and the average load factor improved from 82% to 87%. Furthermore, the proposed integrated system was validated as a project-based training platform through a pilot training involving 22 vocational students, who acquired hands-on competencies in Microservices development, CI/CD Pipeline, and intelligent optimization within a real-world transportation context, showing statistically significant improvement across all six competency domains (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p 0.001) with large effect sizes (r = 0.78-0.94). The integration of these two approaches results in a reliable, adaptive ticketing and scheduling system capable of supporting real-time operational decision-making for bus companies.

papers.title: Beyond the Flag: Preliminary Learner-Centered Design Considerations for AI-Supported Assessment in ODeL Physics Education
papers.authors: Joseph Mesa
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported online proctoring is increasingly used in online and distance education, although its implementation continues to raise questions about anxiety, privacy, fairness, and technical reliability. This exploratory mixed-method case study examined learners’ experiences during the first implementation of an AI-supported online proctored examination in postgraduate physics education within an Open and Distance e-Learning (ODeL) environment. Ten learners participated in the examination, which required interpreting physics concepts and applying them to instructional tasks. Quantitative ratings and written responses were collected concurrently through an anonymous post-examination survey and integrated during interpretation. Eight of the ten learners perceived the system as useful in discouraging academic dishonesty, while six indicated that they would be comfortable using it again. Their responses also showed concerns about monitoring anxiety, technical interruptions, privacy, and the interpretation of AI-generated flags. The findings suggested that learners’ acceptance depended not only on the perceived usefulness of proctoring but also on how the assessment was explained, prepared for, supported and reviewed. Four preliminary design considerations were developed from the integrated findings: Purposeful Assessment, Transparent Procedures, Learner Preparation, and Technical Resilience. These principles offer preliminary guidance for designing AI-supported assessment in ODeL while keeping academic decisions under informed human judgment.

papers.title: What Students and Researchers Think of the Relevance of Academic Libraries in the Age of AI?:: A Survey-Based Study
papers.authors: Dr. Vijay Srinath Kanchi
papers.abstract: Post the introduction of Large Language Models as better substitutes for traditional search engines and as great support for researchers, many critics began to question the very purpose of the continuation of academic libraries in Higher Education Institutions. Certainly, academic libraries have lost the sheen of their yesteryears, where the resources they hosted in the form of printed books and periodicals were considered indispensable for academic pursuits—education and research—thanks to the advent of revolution in information and communication technologies since the 1990s. Search engines, digital databases, institutional repositories, online translation services, etc., have opened access to resources that were once beyond the reach of learners or researchers. But setting aside the critics, what do major, influential organizations around the world think about the future of academic libraries in the AI age? And how do students and researchers look at the usefulness of academic libraries in the digital age? This paper presents a review of the perspectives of major global organizations and the results of a ground survey of postgraduates and doctoral researchers to understand the future of academic libraries in higher education.

papers.title: From Digital Competence Gaps to AI-Enabled Inclusive Learning: A Learner-Centered Framework for Persons with Disabilities in Mongolia
papers.authors: Daariimaa Chuluunbaatar
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence can widen access to learning, but it can also reproduce digital and accessibility gaps when systems are built for an assumed average user. This design study asks which learner needs should shape an inclusive AI-enabled learning environment in Mongolia and how those needs can be translated into an auditable architecture. The empirical base is a mixed-method study of 158 adult (16-35 years old) with vision impairments (n=67), hearing impairments (n=47), and speech impairments (n=44) in Ulaanbaatar. It combined a questionnaire, observation, focus-group inquiry, a five-area DigComp assessment, and an accessibility review of 85 websites and five mobile applications. Aggregate results show that smartphones were the main device for 53%-67% of the three groups, while mean digital-competence scores remained between 2.20 and 2.54 on a four-point scale. Independent participation in online learning ranged from 29% to 49%; average accessibility was 41% for visual access, 47% for hearing access, and 29% across the evaluated mobile applications. Using a design-science process, these findings were converted into requirements for a mobile-first, offline-capable, WCAG 2.2 AA learning environment. The proposed framework combines a consent-based learner model, DigComp 3.0 learning paths, multimodal content transformation, bounded generative AI over approved sources, accessible interaction, human support, and privacy-aware learning analytics. The contribution is a traceable link between disability-specific evidence and a responsible learner-centered AI architecture.

papers.title: From Concept to Production
papers.authors: Kyriaki Kyriakidou, Modestos Stavrakis, Panagiotis Kyriakoulakos
papers.journal: Open Journal of Animation Film and Interactive Media in Education and Culture [AFIMinEC]
papers.abstract: This article examines the potential integration of artificial intelligence tools into the filmmaking process, with a focus on the Pre-Production stage, which includes the design, development, and preparation of production, especially for animated films. Through interviews with experts, literature review, open-source tool testing, and participation in real film projects, the study examines the creative and technical roles that AI can assume during Pre‑Production. The research analyzes how AI technologies influence early production workflows and evaluates their broader impact on the production pipeline through comparative assessments and real‑world applications. Adopting a dual methodological approach that combines a systematic literature review with an applied experimental study, the article moves from a conceptual examination of AI’s capabilities to a collaborative, practice‑based experimental investigation.The first experiment provides a comprehensive review of available AI tools, while the second presents a practical experiment in which students and industry professionals collaborated to create short films using AI‑driven production methods. The study aims to highlight the possibilities, limitations, and challenges arising from AI integration in the pre-production of animated films, contributing to the discussion on the evolution of the film industry and the use of modern technologies in the creative process.

papers.title: Offline social and civic engagement as an ecological correlate of adolescent internet addiction: multilevel evidence from Chinese adolescents
papers.authors: Chengcheng Ma, Yayun Shen, Miao Chen, Yaochen Yang
papers.journal: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health
papers.abstract: Internet addiction (IA) has been a growing mental-health concern during adolescence. Although prior research has emphasized individual and family-related risk factors, less attention has been given to how adolescents’ everyday offline social environments relate to digital well-being. This study examined whether offline social and civic engagement (OSCE) is associated with adolescent IA at both individual and classroom-context levels and whether socio-emotional competence (SEC) helped explain this relationship. Using cross-sectional survey data collected in Spring 2025, we analyzed data from 7,121 secondary school students nested within 329 classrooms across five regions in China. Multilevel modeling was used to examine associations between OSCE, SEC, and IA while accounting for classroom clustering. Machine-learning analyses using accumulated local effects (ALE) plots were conducted to explore nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in the OSCE–IA association across academic pressure, educational aspiration, and parent–child relationship quality. Higher OSCE was associated with lower IA at both the individual and classroom levels. SEC partly explained the association between OSCE and IA at the within-class level. Classroom OSCE climate was also negatively associated with IA, suggesting that broader engagement climates may be associated with adolescents’ digital behaviors beyond individual participation alone. Machine-learning analyses further revealed nonlinear patterns in the OSCE–IA association across academic and family contexts, with stronger negative associations observed under conditions of higher academic pressure and more supportive parent–child relationships. The findings support an ecological perspective on adolescent digital well-being in which offline participation contexts and socio-emotional competencies are associated with lower problematic internet use. Structured offline social and civic engagement may represent an important social-contextual correlate of healthier digital engagement among adolescents.

papers.title: From neural signal to cognitive inference: Legal, ethical, and governance implications of machine learning in neurodata - a case study of cognitive state detection
papers.authors: Sailendra Ramanna, Krishnee Adnarain Appadoo
papers.journal: Journal of Smart Cities and Society
papers.abstract: This paper examines the legal, ethical, and governance implications of Machine Learning (ML) systems applied to neural data, with a particular focus on the emerging capacity to infer cognitive states from brain signals. While advances in neurotechnology are often framed within clinical and therapeutic contexts, the increasing use of ML techniques to analyse electroencephalogram (EEG) data raises broader concerns regarding the extraction and interpretation of highly sensitive neural information. Using a constrained Dynamic Mode Decomposition pipeline for cognitive state detection as a case study, this paper demonstrates how algorithmic analysis of neural signals enables forms of cognitive inference that extend beyond immediate medical purposes. Building on this technical foundation, the paper critically evaluates the adequacy of existing legal frameworks in addressing the unique challenges posed by neurodata. It argues that current data protection and privacy regimes, such as those governing sensitive personal data, are ill-equipped to regulate not only the collection of neural data but also the inferences derived from it. Particular attention is given to issues of informed consent, ownership of neural data, liability for erroneous or harmful inferences, and the distinction between raw data and algorithmically generated insights. The paper further explores the ethical implications of neurodata analytics, including threats to mental privacy, cognitive liberty, and individual autonomy. It highlights the risks of misuse in contexts extending beyond healthcare, such as surveillance, employment, and behavioural profiling. From a governance perspective, the analysis identifies significant regulatory gaps and fragmentation across existing legal regimes, compounded by disparities in institutional capacity in Global South and Small Island Developing State (SIDS) contexts. The paper concludes by proposing the need for a more coherent and anticipatory regulatory approach to neurotechnology and ML, grounded in interdisciplinary collaboration and responsive to both technological developments and socio-legal realities. By situating a technical case study within a broader normative framework, this research contributes to ongoing debates on the governance of emerging technologies at the intersection of law, ethics, and cognitive science.

papers.title: Effects of AI Role and Speech Message Design on Takeover Requests in Automated Driving
papers.authors: Wei-Hsiang Lo, Jingyi Xie, Gaojian Huang
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.abstract: AI agents that provide interpretable messages can support clearer communication between humans and automated systems in situations where drivers need to respond within a few seconds. However, the potential of these capabilities to assist drivers during the takeover process remains unknown. Therefore, this study examined the effects of AI roles, explanation type, and directional semantics in speech-based takeover requests on takeover performance, as measured by decision quality (decision-making time and accuracy), and on subjective ratings. Twenty-four participants took part in a within-subjects SAE Level 3 driving simulator study. Among the three AI roles, Advisor AI was associated with faster decision-making times, and Guardian AI was associated with a lower workload. Co-Pilot AI was associated with the slowest decision-making times, lower accuracy, lower trust than Advisor AI, higher anxiety than Guardian AI, the lowest satisfaction, and the highest workload. The ipsilateral display was associated with shorter decision-making times than the contralateral display. Overall, the findings inform the integration of AI into next-generation automated systems.

papers.title: Integration of emotional intelligence and artificial intelligence for generation Z workforce: A bibliometric analysis and conceptual review
papers.authors: Lopamudra Behera, R. Lathangi
papers.abstract: Background Grounded in conceptual review and bibliometric analysis, this study examines the emerging intersection of Artificial Intelligence adoption and Emotional Intelligence as in the workplace, with particular attention to generation Z employees. Objective The purpose of this research is to examine the mechanism, structural pattern dominating the integrated framework of AI adoption and EI and their relevance to Generation Z work outcomes and well-being. Method This scientific review integrated conceptual review of 45 studies and Bibliometric analysis of 103 Scopus data published during 2015–2026, through secondary data collection from electronic data-bases including Scopus, Science Direct, and Google Scholar. Bibliometrix package and Biblioshiny in R package were used for data visualization and Scientometric analysis. Result The review highlights the emerging themes, contributions, and structural patterns linking AI, EI, organizational support, and workplace outcomes, revealing that context of generation Z remains almost under explored with in AI-EI literature. An integrated conceptual framework proposed based on combined evidences. Conclusion This study provides a theoretical basis for AI-EI workplace literature and identifies generation Z as an under explored contextual dimension and encourage future empirical research while providing actionable advice for HR leaders and policymakers within tech-enabled workplaces.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence empowering mathematics education in higher education: model reconstruction and pathways analysis
papers.authors: Delu Tian
papers.abstract: In tandem with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, the integration of such instruments into higher education sectors has attained escalating depth. As core foundational domains for cultivating the logical reasoning ability, abstract inference capability, and problem-addressing proficiency of students, undergraduate mathematics programs are confronting structural barriers including highly abstract content, rigid instructional approaches, and outmoded evaluation systems. Grounded in the theoretical frameworks of educational technology and curricular reform, the current study has conducted systematic exploration into the potential of AI technologies to drive a paradigm shift of collegiate mathematics instruction via reorganizing teaching processes, optimizing resource allocation, and providing personalized learning support. Based on practical instructional application instances, the present work analyzes application pathways covering intelligent tutoring systems, interactive visualization platforms, AI-assisted problem solving, automatic homework grading, and blended learning models. It further probes the practical challenges from diverse angles, such as the role transition of instructors, assessment innovation, data ethics, and educational equity. Findings indicate that AI does not merely replace traditional teaching tools, but rather fosters a student-centered intelligent educational environment through human-AI collaboration. To achieve deep integration between technical instruments and learning activities, it is essential to strengthen top-level strategic planning, improve the digital literacy of teaching personnel, and refine assessment mechanisms—ultimately serving the goal of nurturing innovative talents.

papers.title: Deep reinforcement learning-based adaptive behavior generation for service robots
papers.authors: Yuting Wang
papers.abstract: In order to improve the adaptability of service robots in complex human-robot interactions, an adaptive behavior generation method based on deep reinforcement learning is constructed. By combining the PPO algorithm with graph convolutional neural network, a behavior generation framework with tight coupling of reinforcement strategy and environment dynamics is designed. The system generates adaptive behavioral strategies through multi-dimensional sensory inputs, such as image features, emotional states and spatial information. The average task completion rates are 94.2%, 91.7% and 87.9% in the three types of tasks, namely guidance service, item delivery and semantic dialog, respectively, and the response latency is controlled within 163.5ms, 179.3ms and 196.8ms, which demonstrates the stability and efficiency of the system in dynamic environments. The impact of perturbation scenarios on the stability of the strategy is further analyzed to verify the high robustness and practical application potential of the method.

papers.title: Information quality, understandability, actionability and readability of large language models for HIV health education: A cross‐platform evaluation
papers.authors: Mengqiu Hu, Zhiqiang Wang, Jinglan Zhang, Xiaoya Li, Mengxia Zhao
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate health education materials, but their suitability for patient-facing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) education remains insufficiently evaluated. We assessed the information quality, understandability, actionability, readability, text structure and source transparency of HIV patient education materials generated by six LLMs or artificial intelligence platforms. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 100 common HIV patient education questions across 10 domains were submitted once in English to ChatGPT 5.4-Thinking, DeepSeek-V3.2, Doubao, ERNIE Bot 5.0 Preview, Ant Afu and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding 600 responses. Responses were evaluated using Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), EQ IP-36, DISCERN, Global Quality Score (GQS), artificial intelligence response quality metric (AIRM), Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmarks and seven readability indices. Platform comparisons used paired Friedman tests with Wilcoxon-Holm post hoc analyses; topic analyses used question-level aggregation followed by Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Holm comparisons. RESULTS: Significant family-adjusted differences were observed across platforms for all prespecified text-structure, quality/understandability/actionability and readability outcomes. At the topic level, five of six text-structure outcomes, PEMAT-P Understandability, PEMAT-P Actionability, the exploratory PEMAT-P composite score and all seven readability indices differed significantly after family adjustment, whereas EQ IP-36, DISCERN, GQS, AIRM and JAMA did not. Overall actionability was limited and readability demands were high. CONCLUSIONS: LLM-generated HIV patient education materials showed substantial cross-platform and topic-level heterogeneity. These findings support the use of LLMs as expert-reviewed drafting tools rather than independent patient education sources. Direct factual accuracy, guideline concordance, hallucination and clinical safety were not assessed.

papers.title: Pilot study of a ChatGPT ‐based educational and counselling tool in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic
papers.authors: Matthew Chung Yi Koh, Jinghao Nicholas Ngiam, Hui Yan Joy Yong, Tiffany Puspita, Joan Quah, Lucinda Mak, Hui Wen Ho, Siok Ching Chia, Timothy Chia, Priscillia Lye, Sean Wu Jiawei, Sai Meng Tham, Brenda Mae Alferez Salada, Nares Smitasin, Dariusz Piotr Olszyna, Sophia Archuleta
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Real-world implementation of large language models such as ChatGPT to enhance patient education remains limited. We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability and attitudes towards a ChatGPT-based counselling tool among patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) in a specialist infectious diseases clinic. METHODS: We conducted a prospective clinical implementation study in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic in Singapore from Jan 2025 to December 2025. Patients interacted with a custom ChatGPT-based chatbot prior to routine counselling by physicians or pharmacists. Responses were reviewed with patients subsequently during consultation. Post-interaction, patients and HCWs completed structured surveys incorporating domains from a validated survey tool: perceived risk, anxiety, technology/social influence and intention for future use. RESULTS: The chatbot was most frequently used for counselling on antiretroviral therapy initiation or switching, and sexual health advice. A total of 35 patients and 35 HCW assessments were analysed. Patients had greater perceived risk with the use of the chatbot compared to HCWs, as indicated by lower median scores (13, IQR 10-16; vs. 18, IQR 15-21), while anxiety scores were similar. Technology/social influence scores were high across both groups (overall median 20, IQR 19-22). Most participants indicated willingness for future use. Qualitative feedback highlighted improved patient understanding and more focused consultations, but concerns included lack of contextual nuance and occasional inaccuracies. CONCLUSIONS: The pilot implementation of a ChatGPT-based counselling tool in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic was feasible and generally acceptable to patients and HCWs. Further studies are required to evaluate accuracy and clinical effectiveness before broader implementation.

papers.title: Ethics and Governance in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Lifecycle Engineering Perspective
papers.authors: Lorenzo Ricciardi Celsi, Junxin Chen
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Trustworthy Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is often treated as a model property addressed through better training data, alignment, evaluation or guardrails. We argue instead that trustworthiness is a lifecycle governance capability that must be engineered, evidenced, monitored and adapted across data acquisition, training and alignment, safe inference, public deployment and post‐deployment use. We develop a lifecycle engineering framework integrating four governance layers – technical, organizational, human‐centred and regulatory – and translate ethical principles and major governance instruments into stage‐specific controls, responsibilities, evidence artefacts, metrics and review triggers. The framework is constructed through a structured conceptual synthesis of peer‐reviewed literature, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894, ISO/IEC 42005, ALTAI, the EU AI Act and complementary security and agentic‐governance guidance. A source register, seven‐field extraction schema, explicit mapping rules, worked extraction example and weighting sensitivity analysis make the construction logic inspectable. A public‐facing retrieval‐augmented generation case and a contrastive agentic‐system stress test illustrate operationalization through measurable indicators, responsible actors, review triggers and capability boundaries without being presented as independent empirical validation. We further address hallucination, prompt injection, privacy leakage, overreliance, unsafe tool use, memory, planners and multi‐agent workflows. The perspective positions trustworthy GenAI as an evidence‐driven, adaptive socio‐technical capability rather than a one‐time model or compliance claim.

papers.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
papers.authors: Elena-Alexandra Diordiev, Valdemar Aksel Stenberdt, Guido Makransky
papers.abstract: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

papers.title: Reinterpreting Sustainability Competencies in AI-Infused Construction Engineering Education: A Human-Centered Systems Design Framework
papers.authors: Daniel Lara de la Fuente, Ruichuan Zhang, Kereshmeh Afsari, Qin Zhu
papers.journal: International Journal of Construction Education and Research
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping infrastructure design, construction and operation amid increasing environmental pressures. Yet sustainability considerations remain insufficiently integrated into AI-focused construction engineering education. Furthermore, existing sustainability competencies are rarely translated into forms that guide technical decision-making regarding ecological and human outcomes. This paper proposes a Human-Centered Systems Design (HCSD) framework, grounded in the capability approach, to address this gap. The framework offers three evaluative lenses – ecological stabilization, environmental conversion, and human sufficiency-, which serve as normative commitments toward sustainable AI to be translated into educational competencies. Using a mid-range normative theory-building approach, the study shows how these lenses, in combination with course-specific contexts, translate broad competencies into assessable course-level learning outcomes. The framework further supports the design of aligned pedagogical activities and assessment strategies, enabling students to evaluate AI-enabled systems in terms of environmental impacts, resource transformations, and stakeholder outcomes. As a result, we provide a structured, context-sensitive approach to prepare future construction engineers to navigate the interrelated challenges of AI innovation, environmental sustainability, and long-term infrastructure performance.

papers.title: From Cause to Innovation: Exploring How Cause-Related Marketing Antecedents Shape Innovative Digital Service Models
papers.authors: Tata Sai Vijay, Shiwangi Singh
papers.abstract: Existing cause-related marketing research examines antecedents in isolation; however, their hierarchical interaction in driving service innovation remains underdeveloped. Addressing this gap, the study employs Modified Total Interpretive Structural Modeling and MICMAC analysis to develop a seven-level hierarchical model. Cause-brand fit and authenticity emerge as foundational drivers shaping consumer and brand identification, cascading through service encounters and co-creation toward innovative digital service models. The research extends the cause-related marketing literature by analyzing hierarchical pathways linking cause stimuli to innovation outcomes. The framework enables managers to prioritize investments in authenticity that systematically drive digital service innovation.

papers.title: A pilot randomized controlled trial of melatonin supplementation on plasma 2-arachidonoylglycerol, ghrelin, and hedonic appetite intensity in females with overweight/obesity
papers.authors: Malihe Karamizadeh, Maryam Parimi, Leila Sadeghi, Marzieh Akbarzadeh, Reza Mahdavi, Bahram Pourghassem Gargari
papers.abstract: Hedonic appetite, the motivation to consume palatable foods for pleasure rather than physiological need, may contribute to overweight and obesity, yet few interventions have targeted it. This pilot randomized, placebo-controlled trial examined the effects of melatonin supplementation on plasma 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), ghrelin, hedonic appetite intensity, dietary intake, and body weight in women with overweight or obesity. Forty-one participants with high hedonic appetite (Power of Food Scale score > 2.5) completed the trial. Participants received either 5 mg/day melatonin (n = 21) or placebo (n = 20) for 8 weeks. 2-AG, ghrelin, and hedonic appetite were assessed at baseline and week 8, whereas dietary intake and body weight were assessed at baseline, week 4, and week 8. ANCOVA or Quade’s ANCOVA was used to compare outcomes between groups. Mean age and BMI were 35.68 ± 7.51 years and 30.36 ± 2.40 kg/m 2 , respectively. At the end of the intervention, plasma ghrelin was significantly lower in the melatonin group than in the placebo group (4.35 ± 0.90 pg/mL vs. 4.78 ± 0.75 pg/mL; p = 0.013). No significant between-group differences were observed for the other outcomes. Melatonin’s effect on lowering ghrelin, without significant effects on 2-AG or hedonic appetite, means that any impact on hedonic appetite remains uncertain. Trial registration : The trial was prospectively registered with the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials ( https://irct.behdasht.gov.ir/trial/70034 ) in 21/06/2023 under the ID number IRCT20080904001197N22.

papers.title: Computer vision, Parkinson’s disease, and the unfinished work of clinical translation
papers.authors: Jane Alty, Maximilian U. Friedrich
papers.abstract: Before a clinical encounter even formally begins, we neurologists watch a foot hesitate at a doorway, a stride shorten on the way to the chair, a subtle change in facial animation during a greeting. We watch for amplitude, speed, asymmetry, overflow, and the countless combinations thereof. We watch in the clinic, in corridors, sometimes as early as the waiting room. This observation fills many of our working hours. And yet, for all the advances in molecular imaging, genetics, fluid biomarkers and artificial intelligence, Parkinson’s disease is still often first recognised through this language of movement - in what the body does, how it does it, and what it no longer quite does. Video has long been part of this practice, helping us teach, document, compare and remember 1 . In their recent editorial in Brain , Ganos, Stanley and Lang argue that video in movement disorders is never just a recording – it is what shapes clinical representation, pedagogy and the visual norms through which human variation is understood. As such, it carries scientific value, but also moral weight: it documents disease, and it documents a person living with it 2 . Artificial intelligence has now arrived at the core of this visual tradition, offering tools that can document and measure movement from an ordinary video, including smartphone recordings, without expensive, complex hardware. Not long ago, this would have seemed an audacious prospect for a field so intimately linked to visual documentation. With the advent of convolutional neural networks, it has become a reality. Computer vision promises to take what neurologists already do – carefully observe movement - and make it measurable, repeatable, and available beyond clinic walls and the constraints of tight schedules. In Parkinson’s disease, this is an attractive proposition: a disease that fluctuates over hours and days, and evolves over years, is still assessed largely through brief, artificial clinical encounters. We ask patients how they have been over weeks or months, then score a few minutes of performance under fluorescent lights, often at a time of day that may not represent their usual function - not to mention the “good day effect”. We know this practice is born of a lack of better tools, and that it is insufficient. Our patients know it too. The literature gives reason for optimism. Recent reviews show that Parkinson’s disease is the most frequently studied movement disorder in computer vision research, that gait is the most common task and that diagnostic accuracies frequently exceed 80% 3 . Open-source and commercial platforms suggest the field is moving from bespoke engineering demonstrations toward shared clinical tools 4 . Several studies, many published in npj Parkinson’s Disease , have further shown that computer vision may inform both clinical decision-making and pathophysiological investigation of parkinsonian bradykinesia across body parts, therapy conditions and care settings 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 . Beyond bradykinesia, computer vision has enabled video-based quantification of tremor amplitude and frequency, the pull test and facial expressivity, often with close agreement to reference methods such as motion capture and accelerometry 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 . A camera in a clinic, home or aged-care facility, it seems, could soon reveal meaningful motor information without wires, markers or specialist hardware 3 , 14 , 15 . Yet the growing number of publications should not be confused with equivalent progress towards clinically valid digital biomarkers. Showing that an algorithm can distinguish patients from controls, reproduce a clinical score or perform well within a selected dataset is an important first step, but it is not sufficient. A video-derived measure intended for clinical use must undergo the same scrutiny as any other biomarker or clinical outcome measure: it should demonstrate test–retest reliability, acceptable measurement error, construct validity, responsiveness to clinically meaningful change and robustness across populations, recording environments and disease stages. Crucially, we need to understand whether a change in the output reflects a true change in the patient rather than variation in camera position, lighting, task execution or model performance. Without this deeper clinimetric work, technical accuracy can easily be mistaken for biological or clinical validity. This may be a reason why the field has produced many models and feasibility demonstrations, but comparatively few, if any, clinically mature digital biomarkers. For all our fascination with these technological advances, and our desire to see them succeed, their potential is clear: better measurement, earlier detection, remote care, trial enrichment and more equitable access to specialist assessment. But realising that potential depends on addressing a pressing challenge: the translation of technical performance into valid measurement, clinical action and patient benefit. Beyond practical issues such as who requests, analyses and interprets video outputs, harder questions follow. A 10% change in finger-tapping amplitude means little until we know what it means for someone’s daily life. Increasing sensitivity may also shift the boundaries of what we call “prodromal” or “pre-symptomatic”, raising questions about disclosure, follow-up, responsibility and reimbursement. Patients must be involved in deciding how they feel about being filmed for diagnosis or monitoring. And any tangible benefit must be legible to both patients and their physicians, not just to a model. These are the implementation questions that separate a research instrument from a clinical tool. Addressing them will require implementation science from the outset, including evaluation of acceptability, feasibility, workflow fit, equity, sustainability and unintended consequences across diverse care settings. For selected motor tasks and recording conditions, the question is no longer simply whether computer vision can extract accurate measures of parkinsonian movement. Increasingly, we know that it can. The more relevant question is whether it can also become useful and valuable . A tool may be technically accurate and still be clinically irrelevant. It may correlate with a rating scale but fail to change a decision. It may add measurement without adding meaning. With the broad availability of wearable technology, medicine is generating a growing number of digital outcomes. Yet despite their technical validity, adoption in clinical studies and guidelines is very limited 16 , 17 . For computer vision to avoid this fate, it must be built around defined clinical decisions and care pathways rather than computational possibility, with explainability taking centre stage. Explainability should be treated not as a cosmetic layer added after model development but as a clinical requirement test with its intended users. Parkinson’s care does not need more numbers in the abstract. It needs help with practical, complex questions - questions such as “Is levodopa still helping?”, “Is gait changing because of Parkinson’s disease, arthritis, cognition, pain or environment?” and “Is this treatment effect large enough to matter to the person living with the disease”? There are harder questions still. If a computer vision algorithm detects deterioration before the patient does, but no effective intervention or care response is available, have we actually helped? Do patients even want this? If a model flags early Parkinson’s disease in someone not yet diagnosed, who carries responsibility for that knowledge? The ethical risks extend beyond the misuse of video data. They include the danger that patients become increasingly visible to health systems without becoming meaningfully better supported by them. Surveillance without response is not care. If a system can detect falls risk, wearing-off, freezing or deterioration, it must be connected to a pathway for timely action. Without such a pathway, computer vision risks becoming a sophisticated way of exposing disease-related need, while leaving that need unmet. This shifts the scientific goalposts away from technical benchmarks, bespoke coding-intensive solutions and clinically meaningless error metrics, and towards deployable, user-friendly and interpretable tools that generate outcomes of value to both doctors and patients. The value of such digital biomarkers extends beyond technical performance: it emerges from rigorous testing against the decisions and outcomes they are intended to inform. This aligns with the broader digital biomarker literature in Parkinson’s disease, which emphasises that digital measures require evidence of reliability, validity, interpretability, regulatory readiness and integration into care pathways before they can become clinically useful biomarkers 18 . More speculatively, computer vision can also inspire us to reconsider how we visually assess our patients. If computer vision can quantify a clinical gesture such as finger tapping - traditionally just a proxy for disease severity - with this much nuance, should we not leverage that precision to measure real-world function directly, i.e. moving towards “ecologically valid neuroscience”? Or, what if a machine’s attention could teach our own, by pointing our eyes to the regions of a video frame it found most informative for a given clinical outcome? 19 In both scenarios, explainability is paramount. Clinicians are more likely to trust and act on outputs that resemble clinical reasoning than “black-box” abstraction: a report visualising reduced amplitude, progressive decrement and increasing irregularity during finger tapping is more interpretable and likely more acceptable than an opaque probability derived from a model that clinicians struggle to understand, let alone explain to a patient. Such explanation must also be faithful to how the model reached its conclusion, rather than merely plausible visualisations generated after the event. The goal is not to replace the neurologist’s eye but to extend it - to slow it down, render it more quantitative and objective, and let it attend to moments it might have missed. This is the “discerning eye of computer vision”. Future directions for computer vision should therefore be ambitious, but not naive. We can imagine movement vital signs: brief standardised videos captured at home or before clinic, summarising gait speed, turning, arm swing or facial expressivity. We can imagine remote specialist augmentation, which rural clinicians, aged-care staff or general neurologists capture structured video and receive an interpretable, clinically governed movement summary - not a diagnosis from a machine, but a better map for human care. Other fields that have already travelled this path already offer us important lessons too. Radiology did not become digital simply because images could be processed; it built PACS, reporting standards, accreditation, quality assurance and clinical governance. Diabetes care did not integrate continuous glucose monitoring merely because glucose could be measured continuously; it became useful when patients, clinicians, devices, reimbursement systems and therapeutic algorithms converged around action. Aviation and other high-stakes contexts emphasise that automation becomes safe when embedded in systems that account for human behaviour, fatigue, error, accountability and trust. In this vein, we argue that the movement disorders field now needs its own infrastructure for visual, measurement-based medicine. That infrastructure must include not only technical standards, but implementation frameworks capable of identifying where, for whom and under what conditions computer vision adds value. The next phase of computer vision in Parkinson’s disease should be defined not by the number of movements that can be extracted from video, but by the number of video-derived measures that withstand rigorous biomarker validation and improve a specified clinical decision. That demands three things. First, standards: consensus protocols for video acquisition, metadata, reporting and validation. Second, proof: prospective implementation studies testing whether computer vision changes clinical decisions, outcomes or patient experience, with outputs co-designed with clinicians, patients and carers, not just delivered to them. Third, governance: bias and failure-mode audits, regulatory and reimbursement pathways matched to real use cases, and explicit responsibility when systems fail or performance deteriorates. Across all three, explainability should be evaluated empirically: can intended user understand an output, recognise its uncertainty and determine what action, if any, should follow? Publication standards should rise accordingly: retrospective performance in a curated dataset should be considered an entry point, not an endpoint. Priority should shift toward studies establishing whether a computer vision-derived measure is reliable, responsive, reproducible, generalisable and clinically actionable. Still, the most important future may be quieter than this: could computer vision help patients feel believed? Many people with Parkinson’s describe changes that are intermittent, subtle or hard to name. They know when walking has become subjectively less automatic, buttoning a shirt feels harder or medication subtly starts to wear off. A sensitive visual tool could make these experiences visible - not replacing the patient’s narrative, but standing alongside it. The measure of computer vision will not be merely its tracking accuracy, but whether it leaves the person in front of us better cared for - and, perhaps, better believed. Now comes the harder work: making computer vision part of medicine, not merely part of research. Just as Parkinson’s disease alters movement in fractions, with a little less amplitude and a little more effort, computer vision allows us to measure those fractions earlier, more sensitively and more faithfully. As a community of clinicians, scientists and people with lived experience, we must now decide what this new way of seeing is for. Its future will be determined not by how precisely algorithms quantify movement, but by whether those measurements improve decisions, transform outcomes, and ultimately, help people with Parkinson’s disease live better lives.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in multidisciplinary and cross-sector public health practice: A scoping review
papers.authors: Han Wu, Ting Yang, Bolin Shi
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This scoping review examined how artificial intelligence is applied in multidisciplinary and cross-sector public health practice, focusing on public health roles, collaborative implementation, and cross-sector governance and equity risks. STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review. METHODS: Following Arksey and O'Malley's framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance, six databases were searched. Sources were included if they examined artificial intelligence or artificial intelligence-enabled decision support in public, population, or community health contexts and provided information on public health functions, collaboration, implementation, equity, or governance. Data were charted and synthesised narratively by study characteristics, artificial intelligence roles, collaborators, implementation conditions, and governance risks. RESULTS: 27 sources published between 2021 and 2026 were included. Most were reviews, evidence syntheses, policy or guidance documents, or conceptual papers, with relatively few empirical or practitioner-oriented studies. Artificial intelligence was mainly used for surveillance and early warning, population risk modelling, health communication, misinformation detection, policy intelligence, participatory co-creation, and routine public health operations. Implementation depended on collaboration among public health practitioners, epidemiologists, data scientists, policymakers, legal and ethics experts, communication specialists, community organisations, and affected populations. Cross-sector governance and equity risks included poor data quality, limited interoperability, workforce gaps, weak real-world evaluation, privacy risks, and unclear accountability. CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence applications in public health are expanding, but the evidence base remains heterogeneous and empirically limited. Routine operational support and AI readiness, together with surveillance and early warning, were among the more frequently represented roles, while empirical evidence on real-world implementation, community engagement and governance evaluation remained limited. Future research should move beyond model performance to examine workflow fit, equity impact, public trust, accountability and population-level outcomes.

papers.title: Associations between positive body image, embodiment, and GLP-1 consideration for weight loss among women in the United Kingdom
papers.authors: Jekaterina Schneider, Kirsty May Garbett, Helena Lewis‐Smith, Nadia Craddock
papers.abstract: Interest in glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications has increased rapidly among the general population in the Global North, yet little is known about the psychological factors that influence consideration of GLP-1 use for weight loss. While recent research suggests that body appreciation may be negatively associated with interest in GLP-1 use, other dimensions of positive body image remain largely unexplored. This study examined associations between body appreciation, functionality appreciation, experiences of embodiment (attuned self-care, positive body connection and comfort, resisting objectification), and GLP-1 consideration among women residing in the United Kingdom (N = 327). Hierarchical multiple regression analyses examined the unique contributions of body appreciation, functionality appreciation, and embodiment subscales on GLP-1 consideration, while controlling for age and body mass index (BMI). Body appreciation, functionality appreciation, and all embodiment variables were negatively associated with GLP-1 consideration, while BMI was positively associated with GLP-1 consideration. When examined simultaneously (controlling for age and BMI), only resisting objectification emerged as a significant and negative correlate of consideration of GLP-1 medications for weight loss, while BMI emerged as a significant and positive correlate. BMI did not moderate the association between resisting objectification and GLP-1 consideration. Findings suggest that resisting objectification may be uniquely associated with lower GLP-1 consideration, independent of other dimensions of positive body image and BMI. These findings extend emerging literature by highlighting the potential importance of embodiment, particularly resisting objectification, in understanding consideration of GLP-1 use for weight loss.

papers.title: The AI gaze and imagined places: Co-creation and negotiation with the generative AI assemblage
papers.authors: Michał Rzeszewski, Phil Jones, Maciej Główczyński, Tess Osborne
papers.journal: Annals of Tourism Research Empirical Insights
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

papers.title: Explaining cyberbullying and cyber violence in the age of AI using individual and contextual factors in Jordan
papers.authors: Khaled Saleh Al-Omoush
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies continue to transform online communication and social interactions, cyberbullying and cyber-violence have emerged as growing concerns that require a deeper understanding of the individual and contextual factors underlying these behaviors. This study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing cyberbullying and cyber-violence in Jordan. Specifically, it examines the effects of individual characteristics and contextual factors, including the legal and policy environment and aggressive social environment, on both cyberbullying and cyber-violence. A total of 472 participants from different demographic groups were included in the study sample. The data were analyzed using Smart PLS software. The results indicate that individual factors such as age, gender, and educational level have varying effects on cyberbullying and cyber-violence. Both age and gender have a significant negative and positive relationship, respectively, with both cyberbullying and cyber-violence. There is no significant relationship between these outcomes and educational level. Contextual factors, on the other hand, have differential effects. The aggressive social environment is positively associated with cyberbullying and cyber-violence, while the legal and policy environment is negatively associated with cyber-violence but not with cyberbullying. This study examines both contextual and individual factors, contributing to a better understanding of factors influencing cyberbullying and cyber-violence. It provides evidence on the impact of age, gender, social context, and legal and regulatory influences, and offers insights that can guide policy, education, and community engagement and inform best prevention practices.

papers.title: A growing challenge: stakeholder perceptions of AI and ML applications in U.S. agriculture
papers.authors: Jennifer Koch, Andrew Fox, Richa Bhattarai, Hank C. Jenkins‐Smith, Jonathan McFadden, Audrey Reinert, Juan Sesmero, M. Z. Walkup, Wolfgang Jentner, David S. Ebert
papers.abstract: Abstract Context The global population is expected to exceed ten billion by 2050 and food demand is projected to increase by up to 100% in the same timeframe. Agricultural management must adapt to meet the increasing global demands. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies can help the agricultural community respond to these needs. Aims An online survey and follow-up interviews were conducted to examine patterns of use, perceptions, and barriers among early adopting stakeholders regarding AI and ML. Methods The online survey with agricultural stakeholders (n=129) included questions regarding the participants’ views on incorporating AI and ML techniques into farming practices and individual follow-up interviews with agricultural stakeholders (n=10) were conducted to better understand their concerns toward technology use and adoption of AI-enabled tools and technologies. Key results Using a mixed-methods approach, four challenges to establishing AI-/ML-enabled technology in agriculture were identified. Namely, challenges related to (1) systems of systems (SoS), (2) sub-seasonal to seasonal weather (S2S) forecasts, (3) precision soil management, and (4) policy and economics. Each challenge was discussed in the context of recent literature. Conclusion Concerns were voiced clustered around four broad research themes. This brief communication brings the perspective of agricultural stakeholders to the discussion of the potential of AI/ML-enabled technology and the direction of their development in the agricultural sector. Implications Data collected in 2021, establish an important baseline for the early phase of AI/ML use in U.S. agriculture, enabling comparison of future perceptions and developments in the sector. Impact This brief communication describes a survey and follow-up interviews conducted with agricultural stakeholders on factors influencing their willingness and reluctance to incorporate AI and ML techniques into farming practices. The findings, summarized and discussed as four key challenges for AI and ML in the agricultural sector, have the potential to streamline research activities.

papers.title: Integrating Sustainability Strategy, Governance, and Outcomes: Reviewing Two‐Decades of ESG Research Through Bibliometric and Content Analysis
papers.authors: Badingatus Solikhah
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study provides an in‐depth literature review on ESG topics. It combines bibliometric mapping of 447 publications from Scopus and WoS, along with qualitative content analysis of 249 papers. The review examines how ESG has evolved from a disclosure‐based measure into a comprehensive framework that integrates sustainable strategy, governance, and finance. The analysis identifies five main research clusters: ESG disclosure and transparency, performance measurement, ratings and evaluation, sustainable finance, and reporting frameworks. The content analysis outlines dominant theories, methods, and variable relationships, showing that ESG can act both as a driver and an outcome in empirical models. It also highlights underexplored areas such as ESG assurance, greenwashing, stakeholder influence, and contextual diversity. Future studies should strengthen conceptual and empirical connections across ESG themes, explore governance in cross‐country contexts, and evaluate the effects of mandatory disclosure regimes. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, and sustainability analytics also offer new opportunities to enhance the credibility and comparability of ESG information.

papers.title: Mental Workload: Physiological Assessment and Validation Using Visual Stimuli
papers.authors: Yamini Gogna, Sheela Tiwari, Rajesh Kumar Singla
papers.journal: Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper provides a notion for the use of electroencephalography (EEG) in the field of cognitive science. In particular, we investigated the brain activity of operators while spotting the differences in similar‐looking pictures at three levels of difficulty. As many practical loads are fundamentally intrinsic, the task was designed to specifically induce intrinsic workload (the productive load as per Cognitive Load Theory (CLT)). The experiment used the task: Spot the Difference to create a workload scenario comprising three difficulty levels: spotting five differences, three more differences, and two more differences (along with retaining the previous differences from working memory). The task was designed intrinsically as the operators are generally occupied with tasks involving working memory and requiring attention towards the varying number of resources. By utilising the brain signatures a mental workload model was developed employing a Support Vector Machine (SVM) as the classifier. The workload levels were classified within an accuracy range of 84% to 98% ( p < 0.05). Moreover, using subjective ratings about the workload on NASA's Task Load Index (NASA‐TLX) rating scale, workload scores were obtained for validation corresponding to the difficulty levels. Finally, a correlation study showed the association of different EEG features with the workload score within a correlation coefficient range of 0.306 to 0.748 ( p < 0.05 2‐tailed). The reported results can also provide new insights into the cognitive workload assessment of the operators at various phases of task loads. Findings of this type may lead to the industrial and professional measurement and improvement of cognitive aptitude soon.

papers.title: When Messages With Persuasive Motives Are AI ‐Enhanced: An Examination of Receivers' Evaluations of the Sender
papers.authors: Magnus Söderlund, Maria Mårtensson
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid development of easily accessible AI‐based tools makes it possible for senders to enhance the text in their messages. Yet, how receivers react to such messages, particularly when the use of AI is not disclosed, is far from clear. This study examines the effects of AI‐enhanced text on the receiver's reactions to the individual sender. The results from three experiments, in which messages from senders with persuasive intent were manipulated (no AI enhancement vs. AI enhancement), show that receivers reacted with reduced evaluations of the sender when the text was AI‐enhanced. Moreover, in each experiment, this effect was mediated by beliefs about AI use and trust in the sender. The results imply that senders (who want to be positively evaluated) should avoid enhancing their texts by means that boost receivers' beliefs about the involvement of AI tools.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Digital Learning Resilience in Higher Education: An Integrative Review and Capacity-Sensitive Framework for Resource-Constrained Universities
papers.authors: Adesegun Nurudeen Osijirin, Nsangaette Asuquo Udo, Khama Valentine Arinze, Irene Chinyere Ezugwu
papers.journal: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
papers.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in teaching, assessment and administration in higher education, simultaneously widening educational opportunity and institutional cyber exposure. This review examines how AI-related and conventional cyber threats affect the continuity of digital learning, how AI can both amplify and mitigate those threats, and which integrated responses are feasible for resource-constrained universities, with Nigeria as the illustrative context. Design/Methodology/Approach: A narrative integrative review following established integrative-review guidance synthesised 60 sources published mainly between 2019 and 2026, comprising peer-reviewed studies, technical standards, policy and legal instruments, and institutional or industry reports. Sources were organised by threat mechanism, institutional vulnerability, educational consequence, response and implementation constraint, and each was classified by the type of inference it can support. Findings: Seven overlapping threat clusters were identified: AI-enhanced social engineering and identity abuse; ransomware and extortion; privacy leakage and surveillance; platform and supply-chain compromise; manipulation of AI-enabled learning systems; synthetic media and assessment-integrity attacks; and human, governance and infrastructure weaknesses. Experimental evidence shows that large language models lower the cost of persuasive phishing, while AI-text detectors and automated proctoring raise reliability and fairness concerns. AI-assisted defence offers measurable triage benefits but introduces false alarms, concept drift, privacy exposure and automation bias. Originality/Value: The proposed AI-Cybersecurity-Digital Learning Resilience (AIC-DLR) Framework adapts NIST CSF 2.0 functions to the educational mission, overlays NIST AI risk-management guidance, and treats usable, equitable recovery of teaching and assessment, rather than system restoration alone, as the protected outcome. A tiered roadmap and a set of operationally defined indicators translate the framework into testable practice. Practical Implications: Priorities for low-capacity institutions are accountable ownership, phishing-resistant identity for privileged users, tested and isolated backups, proportionate data practices, governed AI use and pre-authorised alternative learning channels. The framework is conceptual and unvalidated; comparative implementation studies are required to establish its effect on recovery time and equitable access.

papers.title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
papers.authors: Dmitry Scherbakov, Oleg Chernikov, Victoria Khamash, Kirill Afendulev, Alexey Dontsov, Ivan Oseledets, Elena Tutubalina, Anton Korznikov
papers.abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.

papers.title: Exploring the feasibility of ontology-based educational question generation with an LLM
