Based on these findings and relevant literature, the article proposes a preliminary six-principle Future Minds Framework. The small exploratory sample and self-reported data do not support generalization or causal conclusions about cognition. Further research should evaluate the framework and examine measurable learning outcomes.

papers.title: Effect of a 4-Week Tele-Physiotherapy Exercise Program on Awareness, Acceptance, and Physical Activity Levels among College Students: A Pre-Post Experimental Study
papers.authors: B Vinya Sree, N. Kavitha, M Suresh Kumar, K. Madhavi
papers.journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
papers.abstract: Background: Physical inactivity is common among university students, and tele-physiotherapy offers a low-cost way to deliver supervised exercise. We examined whether a 4-week live, video-delivered exercise programme changed awareness of tele-physiotherapy, acceptance of it, and self-reported physical activity in college students. Methods: Single-group pre-post study using convenience sampling at SVIMS. Participants joined live Google Meet sessions five days a week (30-40 minutes) for four weeks. Physical activity was measured with the IPAQ short form (40 matched pairs); awareness (10 yes/no items) and acceptance (10 five-point Likert items) were measured with study-specific questionnaires (40 matched pairs). Analysis used paired non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, exact McNemar), Holm correction for item-level testing. Results: Participants (mean age 22.7 ± 1.2 years; 31 women, 9 men,) weekly physical activity roughly increased six-fold: median total activity rose from 363 (IQR 278-544) to 2249 (1726-3000) MET-min/week (mean difference 2094, 95% CI 1581 to 2607; p <0.001; rank-biserial r = 1.00). The share of participants in the low-activity category fell from 77.5% to 2.5%, and 25.0% reached the high category. Awareness scores changed from 8.70 ± 1.87 to 9.20 ± 1.42 out of 10 (Wilcoxon p = 0.143), while acceptance scores changed from 39.00 ± 6.42 to 39.58 ± 6.89 out of 50 (Wilcoxon p = 0.081).BMI also decreased where the baseline BMI median was 22.00(IQR21.00-24.00) and the post was 21.95 (IQR 20.80-23.70);p<.001. Conclusion: A short, supervised tele-physiotherapy programme was followed by a large increase in self-reported physical activity in these students, who were already aware of and receptive to tele-physiotherapy.

papers.title: Humanizing Artificial Intelligence for Muslim Community Development: Synthesis of Love-Based Curriculum Practices in Indonesian Madrasahs
papers.authors: Ali Said Al Matari, Adiyono Adiyono
papers.abstract: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into madrasah education offers opportunities to improve personalization, efficiency, and learning quality. It also raises questions about how technology can remain aligned with the moral, spiritual, and humanistic values of Islamic education. The Love-Based Curriculum (LBC) provides a framework that places compassion, empathy, character, and social relationships at the center of education. UNESCO likewise emphasizes human-centered, ethical, safe, and meaningful AI use. This study examines patterns of AI–LBC integration and their contributions to pedagogical transformation and Muslim community empowerment in Indonesian madrasahs. It uses a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA 2020 framework. Of 1,248 identified records, 48 studies met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using descriptive statistics, quantitative synthesis, and bibliometric analysis with VOSviewer. PRISMA 2020 supported transparent identification, selection, and reporting. The three dominant LBC themes were empathy and moral reasoning (34.8%), spiritual awareness and self-regulation (30.4%), and collaborative compassion in learning (26.1%). AI–LBC integration also showed significant effects on teacher–student relationships (d = 0.81) and emotional well-being (d = 0.74). These findings suggest that AI and LBC can support a transformation in madrasah education that advances technological and academic goals alongside character development, spirituality, social relationships, and Muslim community empowerment.

papers.title: Inducting academics into learning analytics in the Global South
papers.authors: M. Zwane
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: Learning Analytics (LA) has become embedded in global higher education policy discourses, yet in the Global South it remains entangled with the afterlives of coloniality, often reproducing technocratic logics of prediction, surveillance, and control. Such logics privilege Eurocentric epistemologies and risk reducing students and academics to data points, undermining the relational, contextual, and ethical dimensions of teaching and learning. Academic induction, currently framed in many South African universities as an administrative exercise, does little to prepare new academics to interrogate these dynamics critically. This article reframes academic induction into LA as a decolonial praxis foregrounding epistemic plurality, relational ethics, and contextual responsiveness. Drawing on the New Academics Transitioning into Higher Education Project (NATHEP) as its project context, it argues that professional learning must move beyond technical competence towards reflexive, ethical, and critically informed engagement with datafication. Building on Mignolo's epistemic disobedience, Moten and Harney's fugitive planning, and Ramose’s articulation of Ubuntu, the article develops a conceptual framework structured around three interdependent principles: ontological re-orientation, epistemic pluralism, and axiological commitment to uBuntu. Through practices such as reflective dialogue, participatory dashboard design, and narrative inquiry, the framework repositions LA as a site of co-creation rather than compliance. This decolonial approach enables academics to recognise and contest epistemic injustices embedded in data systems, and to design learning environments rooted in belonging, relational accountability, and ethical use of student data. Reimagined thus, academic induction becomes an act of decolonial resistance supporting critical, caring, and socially just LA practices across South African higher education.

papers.title: Starting from the margins: Liberation theology as a framework for ethical AI in higher education Authors
papers.authors: Anne S. Lombard, M. H. Jamal
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: The adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) raises ethical concerns in higher-education settings. Current discussions of AI ethics in higher education predominantly emerge in Western secular contexts that fail to adequately address concerns related to marginalisation, lived experience, and Global South realities. This results in a separation between contextual and justice-oriented approaches to AI ethics within South African higher education. To bridge this divide, this qualitative study presents an autoethnographic account authored by a postgraduate lecturer and an academic coach. The article provides a critical analysis of the adoption of AI in the South African higher education context using Islamic Liberation Theology (ILT), under the umbrella of liberation theologies, as a framework for ethically addressing issues of justice, exclusion, and educational equity. The authors' reflections posit three key insights: first, meaningful concern for the marginalised centres on how AI is engaged. Second, ethical formation must stand alongside theological reflection. Finally, through reflections that emerged with the marginalised and engagement with theology, a call for pedagogical action rooted in reclaiming human agency and dignity is presented. This article adds to the growing scholarship on critical AI ethics by focusing on ethical reflection stemming from theological concern grounded in concern for the marginalised, offering a contextual, liberationist perspective informed by South African higher education and theological realities.

papers.title: Beyond adoption: AI, justice, and pedagogical possibility in Global South higher education
papers.authors: Marcina Singh, Michael Samuel, Dick Ng’ambi
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: This article synthesises the contributions to the Special Issue on AI in higher education in the Global South and argues that the key question is no longer whether AI should be adopted, but what happens after adoption in contexts marked by colonial legacies, uneven infrastructures, linguistic hierarchies, and unequal institutional capacity. Moving beyond celebratory and dystopian framings, the article shows that AI in the Global South is always mediated by questions of access, epistemic justice, governance, pedagogy, and power, and that its effects depend on how it is designed, interpreted, regulated, and embedded in local institutional life. Drawing on the articles in the issue, this contribution identifies a shared call for bounded and accountable AI integration, stronger AI literacy, assessment redesign, protection of human judgment, and contextually grounded governance. It also reflects broader sectoral conditions that shape AI uptake, including policy influence beyond formal lawmakers, institutional surveillance, competitive silos, inflated claims of expertise, and the risk that innovation may reproduce exclusion rather than transformation. The conclusion proposes a post-adoption agenda for higher education in the Global South centred on digital and epistemic justice, collective capacity-building, public-interest collaboration, and environmental sustainability.

papers.title: Who owns the story? Perspectives on AI-generated children’s literature in preservice-teacher higher education
papers.authors: Joyce West
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are beginning to play a transformative role in the creation of children’s literature, which presents both opportunities and challenges. In this qualitative exploratory study, 250 preservice teachers conducted a research investigation into the creation of stories for preschool children using large language models such as ChatGPT and other AI illustration tools. Situated within a social constructivist research paradigm, enriched by the theoretical premises of the human-machine teaming (HMT) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study seeks to understand preservice teachers’ experiences and ethical reflections on using generative AI in children’s literature creation, while critically examining broader implications for children’s literature authorship, copyright, and cultural representation. Thematic analysis of preservice teachers’ reflective journals and five key-informant interviews with experts in copyright and publishing highlight the possibilities and dangers of AI-generated children’s literature. The study presents an HMT-TPACK framework as a conceptual map for analysing preservice teachers’ experiences and ethical reflections and presents thematic findings that show how AI-generated story making is enabled and constrained by operational and governance competence, and the capacity to justify authorship through demonstrable human contribution. The findings highlight the need for a reconceptualisation of authorship, concluding that ownership in AI-generated children’s literature cannot be treated as a simple identity claim; rather, it becomes an educational practice grounded in teacher knowledge, ethical legal reasoning, and accountable human design. Recommendations for the use of AI in children’s literature include explicit preservice teacher training on HMT principles concurrent with disciplinary and Pedagogical Content knowledge (PCK).

papers.title: Towards AI learning ecosystems: A domino effect framework for generative AI tutoring in mathematics
papers.authors: Dick Ng’ambi, J. Van der Merwe
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: The Sustainable Development Goal 4 commitment to inclusive and equitable quality education by 2030 requires substantial educational system transformation, including addressing a fifteen-million teacher shortfall in sub-Saharan Africa. Generative AI (genAI) tutoring is increasingly proposed as part of the response, yet institutional approaches to AI in education frequently default to restriction and detection rather than pedagogical integration, foreclosing the conditions under which AI might extend rather than substitute for teachers. This qualitative study examines how curriculum design shapes the pedagogical role that genAI tutoring can play, drawing on classroom-based research in a Grade 9 mathematics class at a South African public high school. Integrating Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, Laurillard's Conversational Framework and a critical AI literacy model (SMART), the study analyses 40 AI-learner chat transcripts through Computational Grounded Theory, contrasting structured learning and problem-based learning contexts. Findings are formalised as a Domino Effect Framework in which initial engagement, sustained dialogue, quality scaffolding and mathematical understanding constitute a sequential cascade activated by problem-based contexts and foreclosed by structured ones. The study argues that institutional transformation toward problem-based curriculum design, supported by critical AI literacy development in both learners and teachers, is a prerequisite condition for AI tutoring to contribute to educational equity in resource-constrained Southern contexts. Implications for curriculum redesign, professional development and assessment are advanced for educational systems navigating the transition from restrictive to integrated AI learning.

papers.title: Graffiti, AI, and decolonial knowledge-making in psychology education
papers.authors: S. M. Auld
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: South Africa’s higher education sector remains marked by structural inequalities that shape access, participation, and the recognition of knowledge. This study explores how carefully constrained uses of artificial intelligence (AI) might support decolonial psychology education while acknowledging that many AI systems reproduce Eurocentric epistemologies, dominant language hierarchies, and neoliberal assumptions that risk reinforcing exclusion. Twelve postgraduate psychology students participated voluntarily in a participatory, arts-based project in which graffiti was documented and analysed as a situated expression of social commentary, emotion, and resistance. Conducted over one academic semester, the study unfolded in three phases: orientation and training, data generation, and collaborative interpretation. A limited set of accessible digital tools and AI-supported features were used to promote inclusive participation, including Google Lens for image recognition, Google Translate for multilingual engagement, Microsoft Word transcription for speech-to-text conversion, and Google Docs and WhatsApp to coordinate asynchronous and synchronous participation. Importantly, AI was positioned as a pedagogical resource rather than an authoritative source of truth. While AI assisted with transcription, translation, and pattern identification, interpretation remained grounded in participants’ contextual, cultural, and historical understandings. AI-generated outputs were critically discussed, accepted, revised, or rejected through collective reflection. Findings suggest that, when used reflexively within a decolonial-critical pedagogical framework, carefully delimited AI tools can support more inclusive and socially engaged psychology education in the Global South by amplifying marginalised epistemologies, fostering critical reflexivity, and encouraging context-sensitive forms of knowledge production.

papers.title: Institutional isomorphism, artificial intelligence, and the structural production of dysfunction in South African higher education
papers.authors: Rubby Dhunpath
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: South African universities share strikingly convergent patterns of institutional dysfunction: governance failures, financial mismanagement, leadership volatility, and the decoupling of policy aspiration from organisational practice. This is prevalent across institutions with profoundly different historical formations, resource endowments, and geographic locations. This article proposes that such convergence is neither coincidental nor solely explicable by apartheid-era inheritance or individual leadership failure. Drawing on DiMaggio and Powell's neo-institutional theory of isomorphism, the article argues that coercive, mimetic, and normative isomorphic processes structurally produce and reproduce the conditions for dysfunction, by compelling universities to adopt similar forms and institutional structures in pursuit of legitimacy, rather than pedagogic performance. Having established this analytical foundation, the article then extends the theoretical argument by examining how artificial intelligence (AI) is likely to intensify, accelerate, and technically embed each of the three isomorphic mechanisms, while simultaneously obscuring them within algorithmic infrastructure that is largely invisible to institutional actors. The analysis builds on the concept of the "algorithmic iron cage" to describe the condition in which isomorphic logics cease to be merely social pressures and become technical constraints inscribed into the systems universities use to manage admissions, assessment, research metrics, and academic integrity. In the South African context, AI-driven isomorphism carries a further dimension: the mimetic adoption of AI models and frameworks built on Global North data reproduces colonial epistemic hierarchies in technical form, constituting what the article terms "colonial isomorphism 2.0." The analysis concludes by arguing that genuinely counter-isomorphic AI deployment, rather than the legitimacy-driven adoption of AI-as-spectacle, is among the most urgent challenges facing South African higher education policy and institutional leadership

papers.title: AI and academic integrity in the Global South: Equity and policy–practice tensions in South African higher education
papers.authors: Eva Gavhaza Makwakwa, Motlokwe Calvin Thobejane
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping assessment practices in higher education, yet its ethical governance in Global South open distance e-learning (ODeL) contexts is complicated by persistent inequalities in digital access, skills, and institutional capacity. This article examines how AI-related academic integrity challenges emerged in a large undergraduate data handling and probability module within a South African teacher education programme offered through an ODeL institution. Framed by Sociotechnical Systems Theory, the study analyses assessment submissions from a cohort of 3,088 students and a purposive sample of 229 submissions, triangulated with written reflections from experienced module markers. The findings identify recurring integrity challenges that cannot be reduced to individual misconduct, including AI-shaped graphical artifacts and procedural calculations, handwritten and scanned submissions that bypass similarity checking, and non-acceptance of End-User License Agreements that weaken accountability. Marker evidence shows how these practices are amplified by weak digital literacies, device constraints, and equity-driven accommodations that unintentionally create loopholes in integrity systems. The article argues that ethical AI governance in resource-constrained ODeL environments requires alignment among policy, technology, and pedagogy, including inclusive integrity pathways, strengthened support for digital and AI literacy, and assessment designs that foreground reasoning, conceptual understanding, and pedagogical interpretation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in health science education in the Global South: A critical autoethnographic inquiry
papers.authors: Rosaley Prakaschandra, Nalini Chitanand
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: This study, situated within Health science education (HSE), drew on critical autoethnography to explore the ethical and pedagogical dilemmas emerging from the increasing unease that I, author 1 (RP) have experienced as a lecturer and researcher while observing my students' overreliance on AI. This unease, when observing polished, yet shallow academic texts and potentially unethical academic practices, prompted a deeper, critical self-reflection on the implications for their learning, the development of complex graduate attributes and my own role within a multicultural, multilingual and historically unequal context. Guided by decolonial theory, critical pedagogy and transformative learning, this study positions AI as embedded within broader historical, epistemic and pedagogical structures. These theoretical lenses also enabled the deep reflexive critique required to confront my vulnerability and complicity within a rapidly evolving digital landscape. Data was generated through the reflexive personal narratives of author 1 (RP), critical conversations with author 2 (NC) and an interview with a student. Together, we explored the cognitive, ethical, and pedagogical implications of AI for HSE in the Global South. Specifically, we examined the challenges of AI integration and the shifting roles and identities of educators within this context and ultimately envisioned a transformative praxis for the field through integrating a decolonial lens. Through the portrayal of three vignettes, “The Unravelling”, “The Recalibration” and “The Revelation”, the analysis traced a reflexive learning trajectory. We show that while AI can democratise access to disciplinary knowledge, it simultaneously risks deepening the epistemic injustices for students in the Global South. In tracing these tensions, through critical autoethnography, we have shown that AI operates within pedagogical border zones, where language, power, identity and epistemic authority are negotiated. In these spaces, AI may function as a pharmakon simultaneously enabling access or threatening epistemic justice. By making visible the ethical and epistemic tensions, this enquiry contributes to higher education scholarship by foregrounding lived experience as a locus for theorising AI integration for HSE in the Global South. The study offers recommendations for AI literacy, assessments redesign, educator professional learning and the development of communities of practice. A key emphasis in this research, through our findings, is the co-responsibility through policy, pedagogy and professional learning, which is essential to prevent AI from amplifying existing inequities under the guise of efficiency or innovation.

papers.title: Toward an Integrated Ecological Listening Framework for Sustainable Communication in Islamic English Language Education
papers.authors: Tetiana Koshlanska, Viktoriia Alperina, Наталія Шевцова, Tetyana SOROKINA, Oksana Petrenko
papers.journal: eJournal of Sunan Gunung Djati State Islamic University (Sunan Gunung Djati State Islamic University)
papers.abstract: Effective listening is essential for meaningful communication in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. However, traditional listening pedagogies often prioritize comprehension testing and task completion over collaborative meaning-making, ethical participation, and sustainable communication. Despite recent innovations in ecological language learning, digital pedagogy, and artificial intelligence that have revolutionized language education, scholarship remains fragmented. There is limited integration of ecological learning, sociocultural mediation, Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), and the Islamic educational philosophy of ta’dib, highlighting a critical gap and an opportunity for a more holistic approach. This study develops an integrated conceptual framework that explains how ecological listening cultivates sustainable communication in Islamic English-language education. Employing a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review, the study systematically synthesized peer-reviewed literature on listening pedagogy, Ecological Language Learning, Sociocultural Theory, digital language education, ESD, and ta’dib. Moreover, the thematic synthesis identified five interrelated dimensions of ecological listening: ecological affordances, sociocultural mediation, digital ecological affordances, sustainable communication, and ethical participation grounded in adab. The findings demonstrate that ecological listening develops through the dynamic interaction of contextual affordances, dialogue, collaboration, learner agency, digital participation, reflection, and ethical engagement; notably, this process is not through receptive language processing alone. Based on these findings, the study proposes the Integrated Ecological Listening Framework (IELF), which reconceptualizes listening as an ecological, socially mediated, ethically grounded, and sustainability-oriented educational process. Consequently, the framework advances ecological language learning theory by integrating contemporary educational theories with Islamic educational philosophy. Additionally, it provides a solid theoretical foundation for designing digitally enriched English language education that, in turn, cultivates communicative competence, adab, responsible participation, and sustainable learning communities.

papers.title: Determinants of Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Construction Project Delivery: Evidence from Large Construction Firms in Nigeria Using the TOE Framework
papers.authors: Sonter John Chen, Aisha P. Abdullahi, Isaac A. John, Precious Aniette Umoren
papers.journal: International Journal of Architectural Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a transformative technology for enhancing construction project delivery. However, empirical evidence explaining the factors associated with its adoption remains limited, particularly in developing-country construction contexts. This study investigated the determinants of AI adoption across construction project delivery functions among large-scale construction firms in Nigeria using the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework. A quantitative survey design was adopted, and data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to construction professionals across 14 purposively selected large-scale construction firms. A total of 288 valid responses were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics and SmartPLS 4. Descriptive statistics were employed to examine respondent characteristics, AI application areas, and construct performance, while Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the hypothesized relationships. The findings indicate that AI adoption remains at a moderate stage, with implementation concentrated in design and BIM processes (50.7%) and planning and project control (38.9%). Organisational factors demonstrated the strongest statistical association with AI adoption (β = 0.404), followed by technological (β = 0.169) and environmental factors (β = 0.158), with the TOE model explaining 30.8% of the variance in adoption. The relatively high organisational readiness score alongside moderate AI adoption suggests that favourable internal conditions do not necessarily translate into extensive AI implementation. By providing TOE-based empirical evidence from these firms in Nigeria, the findings contribute to the growing literature on construction digitalization and offer practical insights for firms seeking to accelerate AI-enabled project delivery.

papers.title: Factors Associated with Research Literacy in University Students: A Systematic Literature Review 2015-2025
papers.authors: Ana Elizabeth Paredes Morales, Marilú Trinidad Flores Lezama, Rolando Rosmer Coronado Orrillo, José Luis Núñez Pesantes, Jacqueline Yovani Palacios Rodríguez, Carlos Alberto Barbarán Villegas
papers.abstract: This systematic literature review analyses factors associated with research literacy among university students based on 50 studies published between 1 January 2015 and 31 December 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, studies were selected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Science Direct databases. The findings reveal research literacy as a multidimensional competency operating through three interconnected dimensions — personal (63%), pedagogical (23%) and institutional (14%), computed over the 35 studies with extractable quantitative data —. Personal factors showed the strongest statistical associations, with information literacy (d = 0.82) and research self-efficacy (d = 0.76) yielding the largest pooled effect sizes. Pedagogical factors, though less represented, were associated with the largest effect sizes, particularly library-faculty collaboration (d = 0.94) and structured instruction (d = 0.78). Institutional factors, including frameworks and technological resources, were consistently associated with larger estimates for personal and pedagogical variables, a pattern compatible with — but not demonstrative of — an amplifying role. The review identified a paradigmatic shift from traditional information literacy toward critical artificial intelligence literacy, with a 410% growth in AI-related studies between 2023–2025. Bibliometric analysis revealed geographical concentration in Europe and Asia (50%), highlighting underrepresentation of Global South perspectives. Methodological limitations include predominance of correlational designs (36%) and scarcity of longitudinal studies (12%). The study proposes an explanatory framework in which institutional conditions operate as contextual antecedents that shape instructional opportunity, which in turn relates to individual research competence through research self-efficacy, with discipline, academic stage and prior digital competence acting as moderators; four testable propositions are derived from it. Because the evidence base is predominantly correlational, these findings should be read as associations rather than causal effects; they provide an evidence-informed basis for designing educational strategies intended to foster critical thinking, information evaluation, and ethical research practices in contemporary higher education contexts.

papers.title: Dose-dependent cardiac autonomic dysregulation under classroom crowding: heart rate variability analysis and machine learning classification
papers.authors: Mohamed Naeem
papers.abstract: Abstract Classroom overcrowding affects hundreds of millions of students globally, yet its physiological impact on cardiac autonomic function remains uncharacterized. This controlled within-subjects experiment enrolled 30 healthy university students who attended standardized 30-min lectures under three calibrated density conditions: low (30 students/150 m 2 ), medium (60/150 m 2 ), and high (100/150 m 2 ), with all environmental parameters held constant. Twenty-five heart rate variability (HRV) parameters spanning time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear domains were extracted from continuous electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings. Subjective workload was assessed via the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), and RoBoSS-SVM (a Support Vector Machine using the Robust, Bounded, Sparse, and Smooth loss function) with Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) classified density conditions from HRV features. Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant density effects on all 25 HRV parameters (all p < 0.001), with 64% demonstrating exceptionally large effect sizes ( η 2 p ≥ 0.50). Parasympathetic markers showed the largest responses: pNN50 declined 52% ( η 2 p = 0.702), HF power declined 51% ( η 2 p = 0.654), and RMSSD declined 32% ( η 2 p = 0.420) from low to high density—while sympathetically influenced indices showed substantially smaller effects, confirming parasympathetic withdrawal as the predominant autonomic mechanism. These suppression magnitudes approach levels associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. NASA-TLX scores increased 74% across conditions ( p < 0.001) and correlated with HRV vagal indices ( r = −0.69 to −0.76), providing corroborating, though not definitive, evidence that crowding engages both subjective and autonomic stress pathways (see Discussion for caveats regarding this association). Temporal analysis confirmed progressive autonomic suppression without habituation across 10-min windows. RoBoSS-SVM achieved 92.2% accuracy for three-class discrimination and 97.2% accuracy (AUC = 0.993) for binary classification, with parasympathetic time-domain features comprising 64% of the optimal feature set. Classroom spatial density produces dose-dependent, mechanism-specific cardiac autonomic dysregulation dominated by vagal withdrawal—consistent with polyvagal theory’s prediction for social-environmental stressors. The excellent classification performance supports feasibility of real-time wearable monitoring for evidence-based classroom capacity management.

papers.title: Virtual reality as a tool to modulate attention and motor activity in functional tremor patients: a pilot study
papers.authors: Silvia Erika Kober, Viktoria Pustelnik, Lisa Maria Berger, Daniela Kern, Maria Schneller, Petra Schwingenschuh
papers.abstract: Abstract Functional tremor is characterized by abnormal attention allocation to the affected body part. The present study aimed to investigate the potential of virtual reality (VR) to guide attentional shifts in patients with functional tremor. Nine patients with functional tremor and nine healthy, matched controls performed various hand movement tasks in VR using their less affected hand or, in the case of the controls, their non-dominant hand. Their virtual hands were depicted either as realistic hand models or abstract hand models (i.e., skeletal hands) to modulate attentional and emotional states. Outcome measures included neuronal responses assessed via electroencephalography (EEG), reaction times, and movement activity of the more affected hand measured using electromyography (EMG). Using the more attention-capturing skeletal hand model resulted in faster reaction times in functional tremor patients during a simple button-pressing task and elicited more pronounced event-related potentials (P300) in the EEG, indicating stronger attentional processing. During a more complex grip task, the skeletal hand model led to greater activation of hand motor areas in the brain when the more affected hand was depicted as an inactive resting hand with no movement, compared to a condition where the inactive hand was not visible in the VR scenario. Additionally, in the condition where the inactive skeletal hand model was visible, the patient group exhibited stronger active inhibition of motor brain areas following the movement task compared to healthy controls. Participants also demonstrated fewer involuntary movements of the inactive resting hand (the tremor hand in the patient group) when the inactive skeletal resting hand was visible. Importantly, the VR interaction did not result in negative side effects, such as cybersickness. These findings suggest that the design of VR scenarios can effectively shift attention in functional tremor patients and may serve as a basis for future VR-based interventional strategies.

papers.title: Differences in perceived influences and educational support needs of generative AI among medical and nursing students across educational levels: a descriptive qualitative study
papers.authors: Guoxin Zhou, Bo Li, Tingmei Wen, Hongyan Wen, Ting Sun, Haitao Zhang, X C Li, L Wang, Yang Wang
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has been extensively integrated into nursing and medical education, significantly transforming the academic practices of students. Nonetheless, the varying impacts of GAI on core competency development across educational stages remain ambiguous, with limited empirical evidence on hierarchical educational support needs. This study aimed to investigate the effects of GAI utilization on critical thinking, research competence, and academic integrity among Chinese nursing and medical students at undergraduate, master's, and doctoral levels, and to identify their specific needs for targeted GAI educational support. Methods This descriptive qualitative study analyzed semi‑structured interviews with 44 students (16 undergraduate, 16 master's, 12 doctoral) from a western Chinese medical university using inductive content analysis, with TAM and AI Literacy frameworks informing discussion. Results GAI usage patterns varied by academic level: undergraduates for coursework, versus postgraduates for literature reviews, experimental design, and data analysis. The dual academic impact featured enhanced critical thinking and knowledge acquisition, counterbalanced by risks of over-reliance, marginal clinical skill efficacy, and cognitive offloading—with research competency gains largely confined to postgraduates. A pronounced demand for systemic support, including teacher guidance and institutional training, pervaded all levels. Conclusion GAI differentially affects nursing/medical students' progression, warranting stage-specific support. We propose a three-stage TAM-extension model (PEOU‑driven, PU‑driven, critical‑reflective) to capture developmental trajectories, offering empirical grounds for tiered AI literacy curricula.

papers.title: Associations between lipid profiles, body mass index, race/ethnicity, and endometriosis diagnosis in a nationally diverse U.S. cohort
papers.authors: Erin Onken, Elizabeth Yi, Kaitlyn McGinley, Cara Satoskar, Maryam Zahid, Anita Register
papers.abstract: Abstract Background/Context : Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory gynecologic disorder associated with pelvic pain, infertility, and systemic metabolic alterations. 1 Despite growing recognition of metabolic involvement in disease pathophysiology, the combined role of metabolic and demographic factors remains incompletely defined. Objective This study aimed to evaluate associations between body mass index (BMI), lipid profiles, and race/ethnicity in individuals with endometriosis using the All of Us Research Program database. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, endometriosis cases (ages 18–45 years) were compared to controls using propensity score matching to adjust for confounders. BMI differences were assessed using Welch t-tests stratified by race, and racial associations were evaluated using chi-square testing and multivariable logistic regression. Lipid analyses — including HDL, LDL, total cholesterol, and triglycerides — utilized matched regression models and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) sensitivity analyses adjusted for age and BMI. Results Endometriosis cases had significantly lower BMI compared to controls (28.97 vs. 30.16, p = 0.004). Stratified analyses showed higher BMI among cases in White (p = 0.010) and Hispanic/Latino (p = 0.034) participants, with no significant differences in Asian or Black groups. Race/ethnicity was significantly associated with endometriosis (χ² p = 0.008); Asian and Hispanic/Latino individuals demonstrated lower odds of diagnosis compared to White individuals. In lipid analyses, matched models showed a significant elevation in triglycerides among cases (β = 10.56 mg/dL, p = 0.049), with non-significant trends toward lower HDL and higher LDL and total cholesterol. IPTW analyses — which achieved improved covariate balance and larger effective sample sizes — demonstrated statistically significant differences across all lipid outcomes: endometriosis was associated with lower HDL (− 1.96 mg/dL, p < 0.001) and higher LDL (+ 5.01 mg/dL, p < 0.001), total cholesterol (+ 5.99 mg/dL, p < 0.001), and triglycerides (+ 8.24 mg/dL, p < 0.001), independent of BMI. Conclusion These findings support a multifactorial model of endometriosis integrating metabolic and social determinants. Race/ethnicity was significantly associated with endometriosis diagnosis, with Asian and Hispanic/Latino individuals showing notably lower odds of diagnosis than White individuals, consistent with well-documented inequities in access to care. These disparities underscore the role of structural and social determinants of health in shaping diagnostic outcomes. Additionally, these findings highlight lipid dysregulation as a potentially important component of disease pathophysiology and long-term cardiometabolic risk.

papers.title: Postoperative TTTG is not associated with PROMs at 12 months following TKA with unrestricted kinematic alignment: An observational case series
papers.authors: Lúcia Almeida, Ramón González-Pola, Jacobus Hendrik Müller, Martin Bafcop, Julien Billières, Philippe Alves
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose The purpose of this retrospective cohort study was to evaluate changes in tibial tuberosity trochlear groove distance (TTTG) among patients who received total knee arthroplasty (TKA) with unrestricted kinematic alignment, and to determine whether these changes are correlated with patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and patient satisfaction at a minimum follow-up of 12 months. Methods The initial cohort of 63 patients (71 knees) received augmented reality (AR)-assisted TKA with unrestricted kinematic alignment between January 2024 and September 2024. Patients completed pre- and post-operative questionnaires for the Oxford Knee Score (OKS; worst, 0; best, 48), the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC Total; best, 0; worst, 96; WOMAC Pain; best, 0; worst, 20; WOMAC Stiffness; best, 0; worst, 8; WOMAC Function; best, 0; worst, 68;), and the Forgotten Joint Score (FJS; best, 100; worst, 0). Patients also rated their level of satisfaction on a 7-point Likert Scale (“Very unsatisfied”; “Unsatisfied”; “Somewhat unsatisfied”; “Neutral”; “Somewhat satisfied”; “Satisfied”; “Very satisfied”). Knees were classified according to their postoperative TTTG using a threshold of <15 mm versus ≥15 mm. Exploratory multivariable analyses were used to assess the association between postoperative TTTG and postoperative as well as the net change in PROMs, adjusting for age, body mass index (BMI), sex, and baseline score. Results Of the initial cohort of 63 patients (71 knees), three did not provide informed consent, three had missing data, two had patellar resurfacing, and two were lost to follow-up. Of the final cohort of 53 patients (61 knees), 50 knees had a TTTG <15 mm, whereas 11 had a postoperative TTTG ≥15 mm. Multivariable analyses revealed no association between continuous postoperative TTTG and postoperative OKS, WOMAC or FJS after adjusting for age, BMI, sex and baseline score. Exploratory multivariable analyses did revealed significant negative associations between postoperative TTTG ≥15 mm and net improvement in WOMAC Total (ß = −8.4; p = 0.046), and Function (ß = −6.9; p = 0.025). Conclusion This single-centre, single-surgeon retrospective study revealed no associations between postoperative TTTG and patient satisfaction or PROMs at 12 months following TKA using unrestricted kinematic alignment. Although TTTG ≥15 mm was associated with reduced net improvement in WOMAC Total and Function, the 15 mm threshold and its potential association with postoperative PROMs need validation in larger cohort studies. Level of evidence IV Clinical trial registration Not applicable.

papers.title: Trust in artificial intelligence at the bedside: a qualitative interview study with neonatologists
papers.authors: Lotte Schuitmaker, Jojanneke Drogt, Sarah Dewi Hartman, Karin Rolanda Jongsma
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) promises to improve patient outcomes, increase efficiency, and reduce healthcare costs. While AI has demonstrated success in imaging fields like radiology, its application is expanding into other data-rich medical domains, including neonatology. Nonetheless, a disparity persists between technical advancements of AI and its practical use in clinical care. A significant obstacle for integrating these systems into bedside decision-making is physicians’ difficulty in determining when AI can reasonably be trusted. Methods We explored the perspectives of neonatologists at a Dutch academic hospital on trust in AI via in-depth, semi-structured interviews ( n = 17). Thematic analysis was used to identify key themes. Results Three overarching themes emerged: (1) Trusting AI in practice, (2) Maintaining control over trusted AI systems, and (3) Limits of trust. Overall, AI in neonatal clinical settings was welcomed. The concept of trust was delineated as being distinct from that of confidence and reliance. For trusting AI, it was deemed important that AI’s role would be supplemental to the role of the physician. Also, AI validation and adequate oversight were considered essential for physicians’ trust. Preserving human expertise while working with AI in clinical settings was deemed important. Concerns about overreliance and incompatibility of clinical intuition with AI in practice were frequently mentioned as reasons to lose trust in AI. Conclusion This study offers practical insights into how trust in medical AI is conceptualized by neonatologists and highlights key considerations for its acceptance. Clarifying what is expected of physicians in terms of reliance on AI at the bedside and formulating concrete guidance for trust in AI is recommended. Trial registration Not applicable. The research protocol was reviewed by the research quality control committee of the University Medical Center Utrecht and was deemed exempt from the Medical Research Involving Humans Act (research proposal no. 23U0364).

papers.title: Why Do You Think You’re More Likely to be Queer? Exploring Autistic Perspectives on the Intersection Between Autism and Sexual Minority Identities
papers.authors: Elle Pemberton, Elizabeth Milne, John R. E. Fox
papers.abstract: Autistic individuals are more likely to be sexual minorities (e.g., gay, lesbian, bisexual, asexual). While several theories have been posited to explain this overlap, the voices of autistic sexual minorities are missing from this conversation. Moreover, there is limited qualitative research exploring the intersection between their dual identities. The co-creation of research by autistic sexual minorities is, therefore, an ethical imperative. This research used semi-structured interviews, facilitated by the shared lived experience of the lead researcher. Fourteen autistic sexual minorities were asked why they think they’re more likely to be sexual minorities and how they experience the intersection between their two identities. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four themes: (a) my identities are interconnected, for better or worse, (b) resisting the influence of social norms on sexual orientation, (c) the intersection between autism and a-spec (asexual and aromantic) identities and (d) being autistic within the LGBTQIA+ community. These findings validate intersectionality as a framework for understanding autistic sexual minority identities and suggest that an indifference to social norms is key to autistic sexual minority identities. Recommendations are provided to facilitate inclusive, LGBTQIA+ spaces and develop educational resources to help autistic sexual minorities navigate attraction, intimacy and consent. Lay Abstract Autistic people are more likely to be sexual minorities (e.g., gay, lesbian, bisexual, asexual). Several theories have attempted to explain why this is; however, the actual voices of autistic sexual minorities are missing from this conversation. In addition, there is very little research exploring how their two identities intertwine. As such, a researcher who is part of this community interviewed 14 autistic sexual minority adults to find out why they think they’re more likely to be sexual minorities and how their autistic and sexual minority identities influence one another. Through analysing these conversations, four main themes were identified: (a) my identities are interconnected, for better or worse, (b) resisting the influence of social norms on sexual orientation, (c) the intersection between autism and a-spec (asexual and aromantic) identities and (d) being autistic within the LGBTQIA+ community. These findings suggest that autistic and sexual minority identities combine to produce a unique lived experience. Participants suggested that they may be more likely to be a sexual minority because they don’t care about following typical social norms. Recommendations are given to create more inclusive LGBTQIA+ spaces and develop educational tools to help autistic people navigate the complexities of attraction, intimacy and consent.

papers.title: AI anxiety among university librarians in Bangladesh: A multidimensional assessment using the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale
papers.authors: Md. Sakib Biswas, Zakir Hossain, Panorea Gaitanou
papers.journal: Journal of Librarianship and Information Science
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into library services, understanding librarians’ psychological responses to this technological transformation has become an important research priority. This study investigates AI anxiety among university librarians in Bangladesh and examines whether anxiety levels vary across demographic and professional characteristics. A cross-sectional survey was conducted using the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS). Data were collected from librarians employed in public and private universities in Bangladesh through convenience sampling. Following data-quality screening, 138 valid responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation analysis, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Bonferroni post hoc tests were employed to examine patterns of AI anxiety and group differences. Overall, university librarians reported a moderate level of AI anxiety (M = 3.00). Anxiety levels were broadly comparable across dimensions, although Sociotechnical Blindness recorded a slightly higher mean score than the remaining dimensions. Educational qualification and professional experience showed limited overall associations with AI anxiety, while gender, age, and professional designation demonstrated little variation. The findings suggest that concerns regarding governance, transparency, professional identity, and organizational readiness may be more salient than technological learning challenges. The study extends research on AI anxiety to a Global South library context and contributes evidence that AI anxiety among university librarians is well understood as an interrelated socio-professional and organizational phenomenon. The findings highlight the importance of professional development, institutional support, and responsible AI governance in academic libraries.

papers.title: Use of artificial intelligence in health education: A bibliometric analysis (2018–2025)
papers.authors: Gamze AĞARTIOĞLU KUNDAKÇI, İbrahim Halil Özdemır, Fırat Sarsar
papers.abstract: Objective: This study aimed to provide an overview of the current state and emerging directions of artificial intelligence research in health education (focusing on patient and public health education rather than professional medical training) through a bibliometric analysis. Methods: Publications indexed in the Web of Science database between 2018 and 2025 that focused on artificial intelligence in health education (encompassing patient education, public health and community health communication) were analysed. 577 articles meeting the inclusion criteria were examined using Biblioshiny and Python to assess annual publication trends, citation patterns, influential journals and authors, collaboration networks, co-citation structures and thematic evolution. Findings were synthesised using descriptive statistics and visual mapping. Results: The findings show a marked increase in artificial intelligence research in health education, particularly after 2023. The literature increasingly concentrates on patient education–related themes, including health literacy, readability, accuracy and the use of conversational agents. Research output and citation impact are dominated by a few countries, notably the USA and China, and are concentrated within a small group of core journals and collaborative networks. Thematic analyses reveal a transition from technology-oriented foundations towards patient- and clinic- applications. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence research in health education now plays a strategic role beyond technical discussions, focusing on patient education and patient–provider health communication. This study maps research trends and highlights areas for future work, especially on the quality, clarity and reliability of artificial intelligence–supported patient information.

papers.title: When Agents Have Faces: Deepfake Avatars, Emotion Signals, and Strategic Trust in Human–LLM Interaction
papers.authors: Konstantin Mortikov, Aliaksandr Karatai, Evgeny Bessonnitsyn, Mikhail Mozikov, Valeria Bodishtianu, Ilya Makarov, Sergey Muravyov
papers.abstract: AI systems are increasingly presented through faces, voices, and emotional displays, making the interface part of the social and strategic context in which users make decisions. While anthropomorphic design is often assumed to increase trust, this assumption is less clear in mixed-motive settings where cooperation, coordination, and bargaining depend on perceived intent. We study this problem in a two-phase incentivized experiment in which participants interact with frontier LLM agents through a text-only interface, a cartoon avatar, or a photorealistic deepfake avatar. The study included 246 participants and focused on three canonical games: the Prisoner’s Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes, and the Ultimatum Game. The agents were powered by GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, or Claude Opus 4.7, with one model fixed for each participant throughout the experiment. In the avatar conditions, agents can autonomously select emotional states that are rendered through speech and facial animation. We find that embodiment does not produce a uniform trust effect: avatar conditions are associated with different patterns of cooperation, exploitation, coordination, and bargaining behavior. Emotional expression is likewise associated with different human responses across the two avatar implementations: negative affect under the photorealistic implementation is associated with a larger reduction in human cooperation than under the cartoon implementation. These results show that avatar implementation and affective display are strategically consequential interface choices, while the present design does not isolate visual realism or emotional display as independent causal factors.

papers.title: From glasswing to fable: AI-scale vulnerability discovery and the governance of selective inoculation
papers.authors: Russell Lundberg
papers.abstract: AI-enabled vulnerability discovery can convert dispersed latent software flaws into concentrated actionable vulnerability knowledge, transforming vulnerability governance from a case-by-case disclosure problem into one of managing large inventories, powerful discovery capabilities and selective access. Existing scholarship retains the individual vulnerability as the practical unit of governance. This article argues that AI-scale discovery strains that assumption and creates a distinct policy category: selective inoculation, defined as the controlled provision of a vulnerability-discovery capability or vulnerability inventory to a limited set of actors for defensive hardening before wider disclosure or diffusion. Using Anthropic’s Project Glasswing and the subsequent Fable episode as illustrative cases, the article distinguishes latent vulnerability from actionable vulnerability knowledge, explains AI-enabled risk activation, and offers criteria for assessing future selective hardening arrangements. The central problem is not that AI creates underlying flaws, but that it can make existing flaws actionable at a scale existing governance frameworks were not designed to absorb.

papers.title: Beyond the Vineyard: Reframing Wine Tourism Ecosystems Through Palm Wine and Indigenous Fermentation Practices
papers.authors: Joy Eghonghon Akahome
papers.abstract: This study explores how indigenous fermentation practices, specifically palm wine production, operate within wine tourism ecosystems and shape visitor experiences and value co-creation. Guided by Wine Tourism Ecosystem Theory and Winescape Theory, it asks: (1) How can palm wine production be understood within wine tourism frameworks? (2) How do these practices influence tourism experiences and community engagement? Using 30 qualitative interviews in Rivers and Bayelsa States, Nigeria, findings show that indigenous knowledge, storytelling, and social relationships create authentic, immersive experiences, highlighting the need to support indigenous practices and community-led, sustainable tourism policies.

papers.title: Understanding the Adoption of AI-Driven Tools Among LIS Faculty, Research Scholars, and Postgraduate Students: Insights from a Survey-Based Study
papers.authors: Mandira Bairagi, Shalini Ramdas Lihitkar, Durgesh R Adamachi
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in AI-driven tools have improved many aspects of research communication and publication, including data analysis, manuscript preparation, and literature search. However, little impact in terms of change is observed in practice due to almost half of the intended users being either ignorant or not convinced of their usefulness. The purpose of this study was to examine the usability and effectiveness of AI-driven tools, awareness, and challenges to adoption by the academic community in the field of Library and Information Science (LIS). A regional study approach was adopted for addressing context-specific challenges, resources, and users’ needs to support equitable adoption of those tools among the LIS community. An online survey was distributed to 250 respondents, and 215 feedback responses were obtained. However, 196 questionnaires were chosen for analysis, and 19 incomplete responses were excluded. Although human activities are overall important to the scholarly work, use of AI is increasing gradually. The wide range of availability can often confuse users and faze them into choosing the right tools. Important barriers to this increased use entail users not possessing adequate skills and training, as well as lack of trust in AI-driven tools. Although the majority of respondents were optimistic about AI, complete trust and integration of variable setbacks did not allow AI to be completely embedded in the research process at the expected level of productivity and trust. These findings imply that there is an urgent need for further investigation into ethical practices in future research involving AI-driven tools.

papers.title: Mapping Generative AI, Consumer Behavior, and Digital Trust in Global Marketing
papers.authors: Gerardo Petroccione, Shaghayegh Asady
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is changing the way consumers search for information, evaluate alternatives, and make decisions in global markets. However, the literature remains fragmented between disciplines, application areas, and geographic contexts, limiting a coherent understanding of consumer responses to GenAI. This study reviews 49 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus and published between 2020 and 2026. Following the PRISMA guidelines, the articles were selected through a systematic selection process and examined using descriptive analysis and thematic synthesis. Five main areas emerge: human–AI interaction and interface design, AI-driven marketing and personalization, consumer psychology and decision-making, predictive analytics infrastructures, and ethics, governance, and responsible AI. Across these areas, trust and perceived control consistently shape consumer responses to GenAI. They can evolve through interaction and influence whether personalization is perceived as useful and engaging or as intrusive and difficult to control. The findings also suggest that TAM and UTAUT provide only a partial explanation of consumer responses to generative AI, given the conversational, adaptive, and increasingly agentic nature of large language models. Based on these findings, the study develops a framework connecting technological, psychological, marketing, and governance factors, with implications for both research and responsible AI deployment across diverse global contexts.

papers.title: From appropriate use to dependency: How AI attitude and use motivations shape university students’ AI dependency
papers.authors: Jianfeng Yin, Yueying Zhang, Runjie Jiang
papers.abstract: Abstract Whether students develop dependence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies largely depends on their attitudes toward using such tools. Existing studies have primarily explained the formation of AI dependence from the perspectives of usage attitudes and technological characteristics, while paying limited attention to the psychological mechanisms through which attitudes exert their influence. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the present study examines how different types of use motivation mediate the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and AI dependence. A total of 405 university students completed a comprehensive questionnaire measuring AI attitudes, use motivations, and AI dependence. The results indicate that: (i) AI attitudes do not directly predict AI dependence; instead, their effects are transmitted through multiple motivational pathways, with intrinsic motivation inhibiting AI dependence, whereas identified regulation facilitates its development; (ii) three distinct AI dependence profiles were identified: dependent, moderate, and conservative users. These profiles exhibited clear stratification, with dependent users showing the highest scores across all dimensions and conservative users the lowest; and (iii) individuals with stronger motivations are more likely to be classified into the dependent user profile, with external motivation playing a particularly salient role. These findings enrich the literature on AI technology dependence and offer practical implications for higher education administrators, tool developers, and educational researchers.

papers.title: Digital application literacy as a mediator of GAI-TPACK among non-STEM teachers after year-long professional development
papers.authors: Yi Min Dai, Zixin Ye, Marie Du, Xuesong Zhai
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can produce and revise instructional content through probabilistic, conversational interaction, creating demands that extend beyond routine use of digital tools. This study examined how digital technology knowledge and skills (DL-S) and digital application literacy (DL-A) relate to GAI-integrated technological pedagogical content knowledge (GAI-TPACK) among 224 Chinese primary and secondary teachers in general-subject settings. Participants completed a year-long professional development program and a post-intervention survey. Structural equation modeling showed positive paths from DL-S to DL-A (β = 0.300) and GAI-TPACK (β = 0.317), and from DL-A to GAI-TPACK (β = 0.453). The indirect effect of DL-S through DL-A was 0.137 (95% bootstrap CI [0.069, 0.219]), consistent with partial mediation. The larger point estimate for DL-A was not tested directly against the DL-S coefficient and is therefore interpreted descriptively. These findings position DL-A as a plausible practice-oriented mechanism linking foundational digital capability with subject-specific GAI integration. Because competence was self-reported at one post-intervention time point, the model does not establish causal development. The study offers a bounded operational account of GAI-TPACK for non-STEM professional development and identifies priorities for multi-wave and performance-based research.

papers.title: Lesions of anterior cingulate cortex disrupt an electrophysiological signature of goal completion in humans
papers.authors: Joyce Oerlemans, Ricardo J. Alejandro, Dimitri Hemelsoet, Eva Genbrugge, Katie Bouche, Luc Defreyne, Veerle De Herdt, Clay B. Holroyd
papers.abstract: Abstract The reward positivity (RewP) is an event-related brain potential (ERP) component associated with feedback and goal completion. Although the component is said to be generated in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), this inference is disputed because of the inverse problem. Recent intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) current source density analyses provided direct evidence that the RewP is generated in caudal ACC, specifically Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’. To further test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of damage to frontal cortex damage on RewP amplitude. Scalp EEG was recorded from 68 stroke patients with frontal lesions while they performed a trial-and-error guessing task used to elicit a canonical RewP. Non-parametric voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping revealed that damage to Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’ significantly attenuated RewP amplitude. These results align with evidence suggesting a single generator of the RewP in the caudal ACC, supporting the role of caudal ACC in motivation of extended behaviors.

papers.title: Performance of large language models in pediatric infectious disease education: a multi-condition comparative study
papers.authors: Kübra Aykaç, Osman Çubuk, Osman Oguz Demir, Young June Choe, Soichiro Kawata, Kamila Maria Ludwikowska, Mike Yat Wah Kwan, Malik Aydin, Yasemin Özsürekçi
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Evaluating how appropriate current large language models (LLMs) respond to common pediatric infectious disease (PID) questions is important for understanding their potential role in education and clinical support. Therefore, we evaluated and compared the clinical quality of answers produced by different LLMs when given professionally written, clinician-style case descriptions, using a purpose-built multi-domain evaluation tool. METHODS: Three different LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, ChatGPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, were investigated using 12 relevant PID scenarios. Each scenario included five open-ended questions: etiology, clinical features, diagnostics, treatment options, and complications. Two PID specialists independently reviewed all responses using a Likert scoring tool. RESULTS: All three models received high overall scores. ChatGPT-5 achieved perfect domain scores (10.0), whereas DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp showed similarly strong results, with only minor reductions in diagnostics (9.83) and treatment (9.92). Gemini 2.5 Flash demonstrated higher variability, particularly in treatment (8.83) and diagnostics (9.75), while matching the other models in clinical findings and complications (10.0) and scoring 9.83 in etiology. However, there were no statistically significant differences across models in domain-level comparisons (all p > 0.05). In addition, model-level analyses similarly demonstrated high accuracy (6.0; 5.98; 5.85), completeness (3.0; 2.97; 2.87), and safety (1.0; 1.0; 0.97) for ChatGPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, respectively (accuracy: p = 0.074; completeness: p = 0.066; safety: p = 0.14). CONCLUSION: Current LLMs performed highly in structured, expert-reviewed PID scenarios and may assist with information organization and early-stage clinical reasoning. However, their optimal use remains within clinician-supervised workflows, where AI-generated outputs complement, rather than replace, human clinical judgment. IMPACT: Current large language models (LLMs) show consistently high-quality performance across pediatric infectious disease scenarios, with no significant differences between models. Our study adds a structured, multi-domain comparison using clinician-style cases and expert evaluation, providing detailed insights into accuracy, completeness, and safety. The findings support the use of LLMs in medical education and early clinical reasoning, while highlighting their role as clinician-supervised tools rather than replacements for clinical judgment. The results demonstrate the reliability of LLMs in organizing clinical information and identifying key diagnostic and management elements in standardized scenarios.

papers.title: SNAP: Spiking neural network-based adaptive data prefetcher via online learning
papers.authors: Chang Ho Ryu, Tae Hee Han
papers.abstract: Data prefetching is crucial for mitigating the widening latency gap between processors and memory. Although machine learning (ML)-based prefetchers surpass traditional heuristics in capturing complex access patterns, their practical deployment is hindered by significant computational overhead and storage requirements. Moreover, most existing models rely primarily on static offline training, limiting their adaptability to dynamic program behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose SNAP, an adaptive spiking neural network (SNN)-based data prefetcher that leverages lightweight synaptic updates for efficient online learning. To effectively process memory streams, we employ selective hashed encoding, which compresses addresses and program counters into fixed-size binary inputs while preserving fine-grained locality. SNAP adopts hierarchical rate–temporal decoding, combining rate and temporal coding to produce deterministic prefetch predictions. We also incorporate spike-based throttling to enable variable-degree prefetching. For weight optimization, SNAP utilizes a hybrid spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) strategy: supervised STDP guided by spiking delta maps ensures rapid convergence during the initial warm-up period, followed by a seamless transition to unsupervised STDP for continuous adaptation. Evaluated on SPEC CPU and GAP benchmarks, SNAP achieves a 43.48% improvement in instructions per cycle (IPC) over a baseline system without prefetching, outperforming Bingo and TransFetch by 6.80% and 1.33%, respectively.

papers.title: Unearthing the impacts of AI-assisted peer assessment on L2 vocabulary acquisition and academic resilience
papers.authors: Hossein Kargar Behbahani, Thomas K. F. Chiu, Sandrotua Bali

papers.title: AI-enabled project monitoring and control: Toward a configurational framework for human–AI collaboration in project leadership
papers.authors: Erik Humberto Araya Aliaga, Adeline Abou-Ali, Costanza Mariani, Mauro Mancini
papers.abstract: As projects become increasingly complex and data-intensive, artificial intelligence is reshaping how project leaders monitor progress, control costs, manage information, and ensure safety. This study examines how artificial intelligence is applied across project monitoring and control functions, consolidating existing knowledge on adoption drivers, functional applications, benefits, and barriers. Drawing on a systematic literature review of 74 studies, in which generative artificial intelligence supported the initial screening of records, the analysis develops a configurational framework. The framework links the antecedents of artificial intelligence adoption, its functional applications (performance prediction, progress tracking, cost control, information control, decision support, and safety control), and their outcomes for project performance and governance. The findings show that artificial intelligence does not merely automate existing monitoring and control tasks but reconfigures control itself, shifting decision-making toward more anticipatory, data-driven, and collaborative forms of human–machine interaction. At the same time, it places new demands on project leaders' judgment, interpretation, and accountability. The study contributes to project leadership research by explaining guidance on aligning technological choices with organizational readiness and control objectives. It also outlines a research agenda to address the gaps identified.

papers.title: Interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention: EEG evidence for joint modulation of late perceptual processing
papers.authors: Thomas Holstein, Jean-Christophe Sarrazin, Bruno Berberian, Andrea Desantis
papers.abstract: Voluntary action shapes our perception through sensory predictions of its consequences. These predictions are thought to inhibit perceptual processing of predicted outcomes, leading to sensory attenuation. However, some studies have reported findings that contrast with this effect, suggesting that the influence of predictions may reflect, or interact with, attentional processes. Here, we investigated the interplay of action-based prediction and top-down attention on early and late perceptual processing, with prediction and attention referring to the likelihood of a sensory event and its behavioral relevance, respectively. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded while participants viewed two sequential gratings. The orientation of the first was either predicted and self-generated or unpredicted and externally generated. Participants judged the tilt direction of the second grating relative to the first but responded only when the grating appeared in a task-relevant color. EEG analyses revealed no modulation of early visual potentials (N1a), but modulations at later processing stages. Specifically, the P3b exhibited reduced amplitude for predicted compared to unpredicted stimuli, but only when they were task-relevant, whereas task-relevance enhanced the P3b only for unpredicted stimuli. Interestingly, multivariate pattern analysis showed significant temporal clusters for decoding the grating's orientation exclusively for predicted and task-relevant stimuli, although decoding performance did not significantly differ between conditions. Furthermore, predicted and task-relevant stimuli elicited faster behavioral responses, with prediction-related P3b latency differences correlating with reaction-time differences. Overall, converging findings from the P3b, multivariate, time-frequency and behavioral analyses provide suggestive evidence that top-down attention and action-based prediction may jointly facilitate late perceptual and decision-related processing.

papers.title: When AI shops for me: How agentic retail representation turns assistance into purchase delegation
papers.authors: Mansour Abdullah Alyahya, Gomaa Agag, Yasser Moustafa Shehawy
papers.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is moving digital retail from recommendation toward autonomous consumer representation. This research develops agentic retail representation capability as the perceived capacity to acquire retail intelligence, adapt choice strategies, preserve consumer goals, and execute bounded actions. The study includes a qualitative pretest, two scale validation samples, three experiments, and an independent category validation study, comprising 4680 quantitative participants and 210 qualitative respondents. Studies 1A and 1B assess four reflective dimensions combined as a formative composite. Study 2 finds higher delegation intention under a bundled capability intervention and statistical indirect associations through perceived diagnosticity and algorithm trust. Study 3 identifies expertise dependent responses across assortments jointly varying in size, priority information coverage, and displayed prices, preventing attribution to complexity alone. Study 4 finds stronger capability related trust under a bundled transparency intervention and higher authorization rates within an experimental shopping task. Study 5 examines measurement transportability and correspondence with independently coded agent activity. These findings concern perceived capability, measured reliance, and task authorization rather than verified commercial purchases. The contribution distinguishes functional capacity from reliance judgments and permission decisions while specifying the limits of measured mediation and bundled interventions. Retail applications require further validation with real payments, delivery, returns, and repeated consumer use.
