papers.title: The hybrid mind: Generative AI and the reconfiguration of cognitive, social, and emotional development in the AI-native child
papers.authors: Claudio Longobardi
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reorganizing the ecology in which cognition, social understanding, agency, authorship, and emotional regulation develop. This critical integrative review treats GenAI as a developmentally consequential interactive artifact: responsive, adaptive, linguistically fluent, multimodal, and increasingly embedded in learning, play, and communication. Drawing on sociocultural, constructivist, ecological, extended-cognition, AI-literacy, and hybrid-learning perspectives, we introduce the Hybrid Mind Framework. It defines human-AI coupling as recurrent, contingent coordination and distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable changes in unaided competence, competence during coupling, trust, support-seeking, or authorship. Four domains are considered: cognitive hybridization, social-epistemic calibration, affective scaffolding and support-seeking, and agency/authorship. The review integrates emerging GenAI evidence with research on earlier responsive technologies and differentiates early childhood, middle childhood, early adolescence, and later adolescence. Existing evidence indicates possible short-term affordances and risks, but long-term developmental effects remain largely untested. Rather than treating GenAI as either a pedagogical miracle or a developmental threat, we propose that AI be designed and governed as part of children's developmental ecology. Testable propositions and age-calibrated implications distinguish observed findings from theory-derived and precautionary claims.

papers.title: GenAI-supported internal feedback intervention for writing improvement: The roles of evaluative judgment and student-AI interaction in a cluster-randomized experimental study
papers.authors: Shijun Cindy Chen, Christian Dieter Schunn, Jie Cao, Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Yizhou Fan

papers.title: The impact of AI on students’ achievement, confidence, and critical thinking in education in Morocco
papers.authors: Fatima Mellouk, Meryem Ouelfatmi
papers.abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant growth in its integration with the field of Education. This has started many concerns about the effect it has on the process of learning, academic integrity and skill development. This paper examines the effects of AI use within the context of higher education institutions, as it investigates Moroccan postgraduate students’ perceptions on their academic achievements. The targeted sample consisted of 15 postgraduate students enrolled in the English departments of two public universities. This research follows a qualitative approach, as it aims to capture the students’ experience of AI use in their academic life. The findings highlight potential risks of heavy reliance on AI, which include a diminished confidence in the students’ performance, reduced engagement in independent learning and more. However, AI also presents many opportunities for enhancing the process of learning and education when used as a complementary tool instead of replacing the whole cognitive process. This study puts an emphasis on the need for a balanced AI integration while focusing on the development of the students’ cognitive skills in the process. This study contributes to the persisting debate regarding the implementation of AI tools in education and examines how they can be used ethically without diminishing students’ efforts or undermining their original contributions.

papers.title: Development and evaluation of eduvate CBT as an integrated artificial intelligence powered assessment ecosystem
papers.authors: Peace Awofesobi, Obiseye Obiyemi
papers.abstract: The growth of digital assessment has intensified concerns about examination integrity, grading efficiency, fairness, and responsible artificial intelligence (AI). This study evaluates Eduvate CBT, an integrated role-based assessment ecosystem combining examination administration, AI-assisted proctoring, automated objective grading, reviewable violation evidence, and learning analytics. A four-week quantitative evaluation covered 250 undergraduate examination sessions across four computing courses, with usability data from 15 instructors and 5 administrators. At the session level, proctoring achieved 94.8% accuracy (95% CI 91.3–96.9), 94.6% precision, 96.6% recall, and an F1-score of 95.6%. Automated grading agreed with instructor consensus for 742 of 750 sampled responses (98.9%; 95% CI 97.9–99.5) and processed the cohort in under 10 s, compared with an estimated 23.1 h of manual grading. The aggregate System Usability Scale score was 87.4 (SD = 5.8; 95% CI 84.7–90.1). Analytics identified six low-performing items in algorithmic complexity, demonstrating how assessment evidence can prompt instructional review. The findings support the feasibility of the integrated workflow, although generalisability is limited by the single-institution design, absence of a competing-system control, and unavailable formal inter-rater reliability estimates.

papers.title: AI content detection in student text assignments, false positive rates, and academic integrity
papers.authors: Mohammad Reza Maghami, Chin Kuan Ho, Camilleri Patrick
papers.abstract: Universities increasingly use AI content detection tools to identify student assignments potentially produced by generative AI, yet concerns remain regarding their reliability and false-positive classification of human-written work. This systematic review examines the causes, consequences, and mitigation of false-positive AI detection in academic contexts. The review covers literature published between 2020 and 2026 and includes 90 eligible studies, comprising 81 Scopus-indexed publications and nine studies identified through Google Scholar. Bibliometric mapping using VOSviewer was combined with Structural Topic Modelling to examine keyword relationships, latent research themes, and temporal development, while qualitative synthesis identified major causes, impacts, and mitigation strategies. The findings reveal three broader themes concerning academic integrity and student assessment, plagiarism and responsible AI governance, and detection accuracy, reliability, and false positives. False-positive outcomes vary substantially across tools and evaluation settings, limiting direct quantitative comparison. Major contributing factors include algorithmic and language bias, limited contextual understanding, surface-level linguistic features, and insufficiently diverse training data. The evidence further highlights risks to assessment fairness, student confidence, and institutional decision-making. Effective responses therefore require transparent detection practices, human review, AI literacy, clear institutional policies, and accessible appeal procedures.

papers.title: Current applications of artificial intelligence for advancing agriculture, sustainability and climate mitigation
papers.authors: Mostafa Farajpour
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping agriculture by enabling data-driven decision-making across crop production systems and supporting the transition toward more sustainable, resilient, and climate-smart farming. This review critically synthesizes advances in AI applications spanning precision irrigation, nutrient and soil management, yield prediction, pest and disease monitoring, computer vision, autonomous agricultural robotics, and large language model (LLM)-based decision support systems. Beyond summarizing technological developments, the review evaluates their practical deployment, emphasizing that successful agricultural AI depends not only on predictive accuracy but also on model generalizability, explainability, economic feasibility, interoperability, and integration with existing agronomic knowledge. Emerging technologies including Vision Transformers, foundation models, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and federated and continual learning—are discussed as important directions for overcoming limitations related to data scarcity, environmental variability, and scalable field implementation. The review highlights that responsible AI adoption requires transparent governance frameworks addressing data ownership, privacy, algorithmic fairness, cybersecurity, and equitable access, particularly for smallholder farming systems. Although numerous AI models report outstanding performance, widespread agricultural adoption remains constrained by cross-region validation, fragmented datasets, infrastructure requirements, and insufficient real-world deployment. Future progress will depend on multidisciplinary collaboration integrating advances in artificial intelligence, sensing technologies, robotics, crop science, and agricultural engineering to develop robust, trustworthy, and farmer-centered decision-support systems. By critically evaluating technological innovations and implementation challenges, this review provides a framework for understanding the current state of AI in agriculture while identifying research priorities that will shape the next generation of sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence literacy: a study of co-occurrence of keywords, research trends, and scientific collaboration networks
papers.authors: Seifallah Andayesh, Zahra Kianrad, Shib Sankar Sana

papers.title: What Can a Representation Support? Generative Artificial Intelligence and Professional Knowing in Practice
papers.authors: Charlotte Arkenback-Sundström, Andreas Stenberg, Martina Wyszynska Johansson
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in professional university work, yet its significance cannot be inferred from individual prompts, outputs or nominal categories of use. This study examines how differently organised professional practices shape what practitioners do with GenAI and what changes, persists, or is reopened as GenAI-mediated work becomes part of continuing professional projects. Drawing on practitioner-led collaborative action research and the theory of practice architectures, we analyse a longitudinal corpus of documented GenAI-mediated interaction embedded in continuing professional projects across assessment and calibration, course development, validation and credit transfer, practicum supervision, academic supervision, and scholarly work. The findings show that professional knowing was practice-specific: what practitioners needed to distinguish and judge differed with professional project and practice architectures. Cross-practice comparison identified recurring but overlapping configurations linking professional grounds, material conditions and situated responsibility, while analytical work could be distributed to GenAI without professional mandate becoming symmetrical. Longitudinally, earlier GenAI-mediated formulations and documents could persist, be reopened, recontextualised or become consequential for later practising. Locally coherent generative work could also cease to serve a wider professional project without becoming factually false. The study therefore complicates accounts of human oversight centred on final output verification. Professional judgement was enacted throughout collaboration through negotiation, restriction, attribution, reopening, and project-level monitoring. The findings further suggest that disclosure categories or preserved chat histories do not by themselves make GenAI participation inspectable, raising implications for scholarly disclosure, student assessment, and the design of accountable AI-mediated knowledge work.

papers.title: Assessing the Potential Cumulative Effects of Longitudinal Interventions for Depression and Deviant Peer Association on Academic Achievement: a Causal Inference Approach
papers.authors: Sarah Mason, Xiao Liu, Karen M. Mason, Alejandra García Isaza, Avia Bateman, J. Mark Eddy, Charles R. Martínez
papers.abstract: In various studies, depressive symptoms, deviant peer association, and academic achievement appear to be reciprocally and cumulatively related across the transition from childhood to adolescence. This study asks a hypothetical question: how much would grade 12 academic achievement improve if a preventive-intervention reduced depressive symptoms and/or deviant peer association across grades 5, 7, and 10? To answer this question, we used longitudinal datasets from 361 students in the LIFT project and employed the Longitudinal Modified Treatment Policies approach, which uses causal inference and machine learning analyses to estimate the total effect of shifting the trajectory(ies) of an exposure(s) while properly handling time-varying confounding. We estimated the effects of reducing depressive symptoms and/or deviant peer association across the grades by a hypothetical magnitude ranging from 10 to 50%. A 50% reduction in depressive symptoms, deviant peer association, or both was associated with improvements in academic achievement of approximately 7.8%, 14.0%, and 17.1%, respectively; the effects remained positive and statistically significant at every reduction magnitude examined. Implications of the findings for identifying key factors across critical developmental windows are discussed.

papers.title: Toward robust, reproducible, and widely accessible intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces: a comprehensive narrative review of neural mechanisms, hardware, algorithms, evaluation, clinical pathways and future directions
papers.authors: Dongyi He, Wai Ting Siok, Nizhuan Wang
papers.abstract: Intracranial speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising route for restoring communication in individuals with severe, chronic, and otherwise irreversible motor and speech impairments who cannot communicate adequately using conventional assistive technologies, but clinical translation remains limited by fragmented and heterogeneous evidence, as well as unresolved design trade-offs across neuroscience, hardware, algorithms, validation methods, and clinical integration. This narrative review synthesizes recent progress across four key domains in intracranial speech neuroprosthetics: i) the neural mechanisms underlying overt, attempted (including silent miming and attempts without observable movement), and imagined speech (speech imagery without an attempt to articulate); ii) decision-oriented hardware comparisons of surgically implanted recording modalities, including microelectrode array (MEA), electrocorticography (ECoG), and stereotactic electroencephalography (SEEG); iii) experimental strategies for cross-subject generalization; and iv) advances in neural decoding, including sequence models, attention-based architectures (e.g., transformers), articulatory intermediate representations, and language-prior-assisted frameworks. We highlight persistent bottlenecks, including limited transfer without individual calibration, long-term non-stationarity and recalibration burden, heterogeneous and non-comparable evaluation practices, limited naturalistic expressivity, and the variable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited temporal alignment of neural activity in imagined speech decoding. Our contributions are threefold: (1) an end-to-end, decision-oriented synthesis that links neural representations to recording choices, experimental design, decoding model architectures, and translational constraints; (2) a structured framework organized around five coupled design questions, accompanied by a unified evaluation framework and a conceptual cross-linguistic, cross-task benchmark template that integrates objective, perceptual, expressive, conversational, and longitudinal metrics; and (3) user-centered translational guidance that includes agency-preserving shared control, verifiable performance priorities, and scenario-specific minimum viable product (MVP) profiles for differentiating between reliability-first home communication and fidelity-first conversational speech restoration. We conclude with a call for larger multilingual, multi-center longitudinal datasets; harmonized benchmarks; adaptive yet interpretable decoders; prospective clinical validation; and transparent data-sharing and reporting practices with robust ethical safeguards. These efforts are essential to accelerate the safe and equitable deployment of speech neuroprostheses.

papers.title: Leveraging extended reality and artificial intelligence for public speaking training in higher education: evaluating the impact of XR MALL on ESL/EFL students
papers.authors: Venus W. M. Chan
papers.abstract: This study examines the potential of XR MALL, an innovative application integrating Extended Reality (XR), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and mobile technologies to enhance public speaking skills among ESL/EFL students in higher education. Grounded in the Constructivist Approach and the Public Speaking Competence Model, a quasi-experimental design was employed with undergraduate students enrolled in an English presentation course at a Hong Kong university. Participants were assigned to experimental and control groups, with the experimental group using XR MALL over a ten-week intervention. Pre- and post-intervention data assessed presentation skills, language proficiency, public speaking anxiety (PSA), and cognitive and affective outcomes. Results indicated that students using XR MALL demonstrated significant improvements in self-perceived English proficiency, presentation skills, vocabulary, listening ability, and reductions in PSA compared to the control group. The experimental group also showed enhanced critical thinking, independent learning, confidence, and motivation. Students reported high satisfaction with the VR practice simulations and AI-powered speech feedback. The findings highlight the pedagogical value of integrating VR-based simulation, AI-driven feedback, and AR-supported vocabulary learning within a mobile-assisted framework. This study contributes to XR research by presenting a theory-driven, purpose-built mobile application that combines immersive practice and personalized feedback for public speaking training in ESL/EFL higher education contexts.

papers.title: Towards the automated identification of data constraints in software documents
papers.authors: Ying Zhou, Miao Miao, Vlad Birsan, Oscar Chaparro, Shiyi Wei, Andrian Marcus
papers.abstract: Abstract Data constraints are important business rules that specify the values allowed or required for the data used in a software system. These constraints are typically described in textual software artifacts ( e.g., requirements, developer documents, user manuals, etc. ). In this paper, we focus on automating the task of identifying data constraints in natural language software documents. In order to automate this task, we first study how data constraints are described in natural language. Specifically, we studied 546 data constraints described in the natural language artifacts of nine software systems. We uncovered and documented nine linguistic discourse patterns that stakeholders use to describe data constraints in natural language. We cast the constraint identification and extraction as a text matching and classification problem. We explore the suitability of traditional machine learning techniques, using the discourse patterns we discovered, together with other linguistic elements, as features, for automatically classifying sentence fragments as data constraint descriptions. The best combination of features and learner achieves 63.63% precision and 61.40% recall (62.34% F1). Automating the extraction of data constraints from natural language text is essential for automating their traceability to code, test generation, compliance analysis, etc.

papers.title: Process, Not Trace: A Theoretical Framework for Agentic AI and Process-Preserving Human–AI Cognition
papers.authors: Michael J. Richardson, M. Paula Diaz Monfort, Ayeh Alhasan, Cassandra Crone, Surbhi Tyagi, Manuel Varlet, Mark Dras, Rachel W. Kallen

papers.title: Harnessing Disagreement: Detecting Correlated Agreement Blindness in Multi-agent Triage
papers.authors: Shay Seiya McDonnell, Avantika Singh, Quoc‐Viet Pham, Vratislav Havlík, Gregory M. P. O’Hare
papers.abstract: Disagreement-triggered escalation can create a structural blind spot in multi-agent arbitration: as base learners improve they tend to converge, weakening safety monitoring exactly where correlated failures concentrate. We term this correlated agreement blindness and present ARAT (Arbitrated Reasoning Agents for Alarm Triage), a directed-star system pairing a Random Forest (RF) agent, a k-nearest-neighbour (k-NN) agent, and a learned routing meta-model. On 82,332 holdout samples from the UNSW-NB15 network intrusion detection dataset, 57.2% of errors occur under agreement and 90.6% of dangerous under-predictions evade disagreement-based monitoring even after a conservative override; strengthening the base learners increases error correlation while reducing disagreement. ARAT delivers a significant reduction in under-prediction from 4.80% under soft voting to 1.70% through a conservative override and a unanimous-Normal safety flag, a gain not reproduced by loss-function tuning nor by single-model uncertainty quantification at equal review budget. The mechanism replicates on the UCI Diabetes readmission data, and the same routing transfers to a cross-family large language model (LLM) committee on cancer staging, cutting dangerous under-prediction for frontier models as well as classical ones. Diversification improves safety only when it yields productive disagreement rather than convergence, and blindness intensifies as agentic pipelines deploy increasingly capable correlated models.

papers.title: Responses of large language models to common questions on premature ovarian insufficiency: A comparative analysis
papers.authors: Jing Zhe, Dan Zheng
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Large language models are widely used in clinical care. Their reliability in specialized gynecological diseases such as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) has not been fully verified. This study aimed to systematically evaluate and compare the accuracy and completeness of three mainstream large language models when answering standardized clinical questions about POI. METHODS: We developed 34 standardized questions covering five core domains of POI according to international clinical guidelines. Two senior obstetricians and gynecologists independently scored responses using a 5-point Likert scale. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient, intraclass correlation coefficient, and mean absolute error. Pairwise between-model score differences were computed and visualized using item-level heatmaps. RESULTS: All three models showed high and steady performance. Accuracy scores ranged from 4.59 to 4.84, and completeness scores ranged from 4.43 to 4.65. Inter-rater agreement was "good" to " excellent", with exact agreement between 91.18% and 97.06% and Cohen's kappa between 0.675 and 0.915. GPT-5.5 performed better in the area of clinical manifestations and treatment. DeepSeek-R1 showed greater stability, defined as maintaining consistently high scores with limited score fluctuation, in etiology- and counseling-related questions. Item-level heatmaps revealed that most individual-item differences were within ±0.5 points, whereas pairwise differences in overall mean scores fell within ±0.5, and some individual-item comparisons exceeded this range, with no obvious systematic bias. CONCLUSIONS: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus-4.7, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrated favorable accuracy and completeness in answering standardized POI questions; overall performance was similar despite deviations across several individual questions. Item-level difference heatmaps further confirmed the consistency and reliability of the three models. These models can serve as reliable auxiliary tools for clinical information retrieval and patient education under professional supervision, meaning that all content generated by artificial intelligence must be checked by qualified clinicians before clinical use.

papers.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Emotional–Cognitive Profiles, and Response to Cognitive Remediation and Emotion Skills Training in Anorexia Nervosa
papers.authors: Paolo Meneguzzo, Elisa Bonello, Alessio Castelli, Anna Marzotto, Elena Tenconi, Patrizia Todisco
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anorexia nervosa (AN) involves restrictive eating and marked difficulties in emotion regulation and cognitive flexibility. Cognitive Remediation and Emotion Skills Training (CREST) targets these domains, but outcomes may vary by psychological profile and adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). This study examined the associations of emotional-cognitive profiles and ACEs with treatment response following CREST in inpatients with AN. METHODS: We studied 198 female inpatients with AN who completed baseline and post-treatment assessments after an 8-week group CREST programme. Cluster analysis of the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Toronto Alexithymia Scale-20 (TAS-20), Detail and Flexibility Questionnaire (DFLEX), and Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) identified subgroups. Outcomes (ΔEDE-Q, ΔDFLEX, ΔTAS, ΔBMI) were compared across clusters. Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) subscales were tested in multinomial regression and moderation models. RESULTS: Three clusters emerged: Cluster 1 (low impairment), Cluster 0 (moderate impairment), and Cluster 2 (globally impaired). Groups differed in age, illness duration, BMI, and adversities exposure (all p < 0.05). Psychological outcomes differed: ΔDFLEX (H = 63.7, p < 0.001) and ΔTAS (p < 0.001), with Cluster 2 showing the greatest gains. Emotional abuse was positively associated with both the moderate and globally impaired profiles, whereas physical abuse specifically predicted the globally impaired profile. Sexual abuse was inversely associated with both impaired profiles. Moderation analyses indicated that associations between ACE severity and psychological change varied across emotional-cognitive profiles, with direction and magnitude differing by outcome and ACE subtype. CONCLUSIONS: Greater short-term psychological changes were observed in the globally impaired profile, although baseline severity warrants cautious interpretation. Adverse childhood experiences were associated with profile membership and heterogeneous patterns of psychological change across profiles.

papers.title: Digital Competencies in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Healthcare Sector
papers.authors: Renata Paukštaitienė
papers.abstract: Background. Artificial intelligence and digital health tools are reshaping clinical workflows, decision-making and remote patient care. In response to this rapid integration, international and Lithuanian institutions provide guidance to support the safe and effective use of digital and AI technologies. These frameworks emphasize the need for strong digital, data governance and AI competencies across health professional roles. Aim. To identify the digital and AI-related competencies required in the era of artificial intelligence and to examine how healthcare professionals currently align with these competencies. Methods. The study consisted of two components. First, key strategic documents were reviewed to identify digital and AI related competencies relevant to modern healthcare. Second, the current competency landscape was analyzed using open data from the Health Technology Competency Questionnaire, developed by the Health Tech Accelerator working group and published on the Lithuanian Open Data Portal (data.gov.lt). A total of 107 respondents were included (55 physicians and 52 nurses-midwives). Descriptive statistics and the Chi-square test for homogeneity were applied to examine differences across professional groups. Results. Strategic documents most frequently highlighted competencies related to digital literacy, data governance, AI literacy, critical evaluation of algorithmic outputs, ethical digital practice and continuous digital upskilling. Respondent data showed strong basic digital skills and moderate understanding of information management, while AI literacy and critical evaluation of results remained limited. All statistically significant differences favored physicians, who demonstrated higher understanding of AI concepts, precision medicine principles, digital system use, digital communication tools and digital transformation processes. No differences were observed in continuous upskilling. Conclusion. The study shows that healthcare professionals have good basic digital skills, but more advanced AIrelated abilities are still uneven, with physicians scoring higher than nurses-midwives; this highlights the need to strengthen advanced digital and AI skills across all roles.

papers.title: Enhancing Linguistic Comprehension in Intermediate ELs Using ChatGPT
papers.authors: Laila Noor
papers.abstract: In this reflection, the author highlights the evolving role of teachers and the integration of ChatGPT in an English language learning classroom setting. Emphasizing both the tool’s benefits and challenges, the author offers teaching tips, including training, setting boundaries, and encouraging critical thinking. The narrative underscores the importance of balancing technology with traditional teaching, advocating for judicious and adaptive use.

papers.title: Teaching with GenAI: Custom GPT as a Scaffolding Tool for Phrasal Verb Learning
papers.authors: Terrence Tianzhi Zhang, Jiqing Xiang
papers.abstract: This study explores a customized ChatGPT scaffolding tool for multilingual English learners studying phrasal verbs. Grounded in sociocultural theory, the Custom GPT followed a seven-step sequence to guide learners in understanding particles’ semantic roles. Four college-level learners participated in five GPT-assisted tutoring sessions. Findings indicate high technical feasibility and strong conversational accuracy, despite occasional glitches and cognitive overload. Students reported that GPT mediation enhanced conceptual understanding and made phrasal verbs easier to remember.

papers.title: Human–Generative AI collaboration and the reconfiguration of academic knowledge work in higher education: A systematic review, science mapping, and integrative framework
papers.authors: Pedro Alejandro Vásquez-Maldonado, Abel Alejandro Tasayco Jala, Elisban Martín Magallanes-Yataco, Aldo Andrés Andrade-De La Cruz
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education by changing how academic tasks, judgement, responsibility, and knowledge production are organised. This study examines how Human–Generative AI collaboration reconfigures academic knowledge work through a systematic review, science mapping, and qualitative integrative synthesis. Following PRISMA 2020, 215 Scopus records published between 2023 and 2026 were screened. A bibliometric corpus of 43 records was retained, while 32 full-text studies informed the qualitative synthesis and framework development. Bibliometric findings show a rapidly expanding but still dispersed field, with concentrated early citations, growing attention to collaboration and agency, and fragmented international collaboration. The qualitative synthesis identified six themes: workload transformation, human oversight and agency, task-contingent collaboration, reconfiguration of academic roles, institutional and capability conditions, and epistemic and integrity consequences. GenAI does not simply automate academic work; it redistributes labour towards verification, supervision, calibration, orchestration, and accountability while reshaping professional and epistemic responsibilities. These findings informed the Academic Knowledge Work Reconfiguration Framework. The study concludes that Human–GenAI collaboration is better understood through task–human role–GenAI role configurations than through a linear logic of automation.

papers.title: Simuladores interactivos y resolución de problemas: Mediaciones pedagógicas para el aprendizaje de la física
papers.authors: Victor Daniel Trillos Miranda
papers.abstract: Problem-solving is a core competency in the education of students and individuals; at the same time, it is one of the challenges encountered when teaching physics. This article reflects on the role of interactive simulators as pedagogical tools to strengthen this competency, integrating recent evidence on PhET, guided inquiry, problem-based learning, digital literacy, artificial intelligence, and virtual laboratories. A literature review of recent research and academic studies was conducted. The findings indicate that simulations facilitate the visualization of abstract concepts, the manipulation of variables, and immediate feedback; however, their effectiveness does not depend solely on the technology itself. Improvement occurs when the use of the simulator, in conjunction with activities proposed by the teacher, guides students to test their own hypotheses, rather than merely observing a result. Limitations related to teacher training, infrastructure, cognitive load, and the risk of purely demonstrative uses were also identified. We conclude that the value of simulators lies in their ability to transform problem-solving into an activity involving modeling, inquiry, and argumentation, provided they are integrated through a deliberate and assessable instructional sequence.

papers.title: La Inteligencia Artificial como mediación pedagógica: una mirada crítica al fortalecimiento de la competencia argumentativa en la educación básica secundaria.
papers.authors: Ronald García Villamizar
papers.abstract: The rapid incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education calls for reflection on its pedagogical meaning, particularly regarding the development of higher-order thinking skills such as argumentation. This article aims to analyze, from a theoretical and critical perspective, the conditions under which AI can become a pedagogical mediation rather than merely a tool for strengthening argumentative competence among secondary school students. The work is developed through a review and discussion of recent research on generative AI, writing, critical thinking, and technological mediation in educational contexts. The findings show that the educational value of AI does not depend on its technical capabilities but on the pedagogical intention guiding its use: when AI is used to challenge ideas, request counterarguments, and demand justification, it can act as an interlocutor that stimulates thinking; when it replaces the student's own textual construction, it displaces precisely the capacity it is meant to develop. Risks related to cognitive dependency, unequal access, and academic integrity are also identified, requiring teacher guidance and critical digital literacy. As a limitation, this analysis is theoretical and does not yet include original empirical evidence, which will be developed in the master's research from which this article originates. Its originality lies in framing AI-based pedagogical mediation as a triangular relationship between student, technology, and teacher, and in linking this framework to argumentative competence in secondary education. It is concluded that the educational challenge is not teaching students to use AI, but forming students capable of critically dialoguing with it, questioning, contrasting, and arguing their own positions.

papers.title: Introducing Coding and Artificial Intelligence to Enhance Teacher Readiness at SDN Cibuntu 01
papers.authors: Dea Andini Andriati, Tri Nur Arifin, Uus Rusmawan
papers.abstract: Rapid technological advances associated with the Fourth Industrial Revolution have heightened the need to cultivate digital literacy from the earliest stages of formal education. Coding and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly recognised as essential twenty-first-century competencies, making teachers’ capacity to incorporate these technologies into instruction particularly important. At SDN Cibuntu 01 in Bekasi Regency, an initial assessment identified substantial readiness gaps: approximately 80% of participating teachers lacked a sufficient grasp of fundamental coding and AI concepts, while 90% had no prior experience using visual coding platforms or AI-supported educational tools. This community engagement programme sought to strengthen teachers’ conceptual understanding, confidence, and pedagogical readiness to integrate coding and AI into classroom learning. It combined interactive training and workshops featuring unplugged activities with guided demonstrations of accessible AI tools. Post-test scores exceeded pre-test scores across all assessed dimensions. Participants also prepared draft lesson plans incorporating computational thinking, while the programme produced a practical guide entitled “Introduction to Coding and Artificial Intelligence for Elementary School Teachers” to support continued implementation. These findings indicate that combining unplugged learning with accessible AI tools can strengthen teachers’ initial readiness for technology-enhanced instruction and generate practical resources that may be adapted by elementary schools facing similar circumstances.

papers.title: Evaluation Of The Impact Of Chatgpt-Driven Instruction On Student Academic Achievement And Critical Thinking Skills In Social Studies Across Varied Iq Levels Within Upper Basic Schools In North East Nigeria
papers.authors: Prof. BANKE SUSAN ADINYA, Assoc. Prof. AMINU SANI, ADEJO-ODAUDU VICTORIA OMOMINE
papers.journal: Web of Scholars : Multidimensional Research Journal
papers.abstract: This study investigated the impact of ChatGPT-driven instruction on academic achievement and critical thinking skills in Social Studies among upper basic school students across low, medium, and high intelligence quotient (IQ) levels in North-East Nigeria. Two specific objectives, research questions, and hypotheses guided the study. A quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test non-equivalent control group design was adopted. The population comprised 38,412 Junior Secondary School Two students in 214 public co-educational schools across North-East Nigeria. A sample of 178 students, comprising 92 in the experimental group and 86 in the control group, was selected using multistage sampling. Data were collected using the Social Studies Achievement Test (SSAT), Social Studies Critical Thinking Scale (SSCTS), and a standardized non-verbal intelligence test. The instruments were validated by three experts, and a reliability coefficient of 0.75 was obtained. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, while two-way Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) tested the hypotheses at the 0.05 significance level. The findings revealed a significant difference in academic achievement between students taught using ChatGPT-driven instruction and those taught conventionally, F(1, 171) = 320.27, p < .001. The experimental group recorded a higher post-test mean score of 75.15 compared with 61.59 for the control group. Similarly, a significant difference was found in critical thinking skills, F(1, 171) = 328.53, p < .001, with respective post-test mean scores of 64.62 and 51.56. Significant interactions between instructional strategy and IQ level were observed for academic achievement and critical thinking skills. The study concluded that ChatGPT-driven instruction was more effective than conventional instruction in improving both outcomes, although its effects varied across IQ levels. It was recommended that Social Studies teachers integrate ChatGPT into classroom instruction and provide guided learning activities that promote academic achievement, critical evaluation, and independent reasoning.

papers.title: Integrating Chat GPT in Modern Education: Enhancing Teaching Strategies
papers.authors: Rujittika Mungmunpuntipantip, Viroj Wiwanitkit
papers.journal: Global Journal of Emerging Trend in Education and Social Science
papers.abstract: This article explores the use of ChatGPT as a transformative tool in teaching and learning processes. It highlights the ways educators can leverage AI for information retrieval, idea generation, literature summarization, article analysis, and crafting critical questions. While embracing this technology, the necessity for educators to possess a strong foundational knowledge in their subject areas remains essential. As we navigate the evolving educational landscape, understanding the implications of integrating such AI tools will be crucial for fostering effective learning environments.

papers.title: Mapping Research Approaches in Islamic Religious Education in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Muhammad Raihan As Syauqi, Arvial Ilham Fahrul Syah, Tedi Priatna, Bayu Bambang Nurfauji
papers.abstract: This article aims to map research approaches in Islamic Religious Education studies in the era of generative artificial intelligence. This study used a literature-based scoping review method presented through descriptive-narrative synthesis. The literature was drawn from Indonesian scholarly publications published between 2021 and 2025 and selected based on inclusion and exclusion criteria related to Islamic Religious Education, research methodology, digital education, artificial intelligence, and generative artificial intelligence. The review process focused on identifying research approaches, dominant themes, data sources, analytical techniques, and research gaps. The findings show that Islamic Religious Education research has developed through qualitative field research, quantitative research, library research, research and development, systematic literature review, bibliometric analysis, and scoping review. The findings also indicate that most studies still discuss AI as a learning and assessment tool, while studies on Generative AI in relation to research methodology, religious source validity, academic integrity, and ethical knowledge production remain limited. Therefore, future Islamic Religious Education research should integrate methodological accuracy, pedagogical relevance, source validity, academic integrity, and ethical responsibility in responding to generative artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Poultry Production: Current Evidence, Challenges, and Implications for Afghanistan
papers.authors: Abdul Khaliq Sahes, Abdul Ghafoor Muradi, Lutfullah Zaheri, Abdul Jamil Ghanizada
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated as a tool for improving poultry production, health monitoring, environmental management, and farm automation. This narrative review synthesizes scientific evidence on AI applications in poultry production and evaluates their potential applicability, infrastructure requirements, limitations, and future opportunities in Afghanistan. Literature was searched using Google Scholar, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, IranMedex, and Magiran using terms related to artificial intelligence, machine learning, poultry production, disease detection, computer vision, Internet of Things, robotics, animal welfare, and Afghanistan. The initial search identified 66 potentially relevant records, and 30 publications were included in the narrative synthesis after screening and eligibility assessment. Current evidence indicates that AI can support early disease and abnormal-behavior detection, environmental monitoring, precision management of feed and production, and robotic farm operations. However, successful implementation depends on data quality, reliable electricity and connectivity, suitable sensors and computing infrastructure, technical expertise, and economic feasibility. Importantly, the available literature does not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that AI is already widely adopted in Afghanistan’s commercial poultry sector. Therefore, AI adoption in Afghanistan should be approached through locally validated, gradual, and economically appropriate applications, beginning with digital record keeping, environmental sensing, computer-vision monitoring, and decision-support systems. Future studies should evaluate these technologies under real Afghan poultry-farming conditions.

papers.title: Beyond Self-Report: A Neurocognitive Approach to UX Evaluation of Greek Municipal Websites
papers.authors: Olga Tsatsani, Yannis Pollalis
papers.journal: SPOUDAI Journal of Economics and Business
papers.abstract: Despite growing investment in e-government infrastructure, the adoption of local municipal digital services remains limited, raising questions about how user experience (UX) is currently evaluated. Traditional approaches, based on expert audits and self-reported measures, capture primarily the conscious and observable layers of interaction, overlooking the underlying cognitive and emotional processes that shape actual user behavior. This study introduces a multimodal, neuroscience-informed framework for UX evaluation and presents, on a pilot basis, an exploratory application of the Neurocognitive Engagement (NCE) Index to three Greek municipal websites representing bad, medium, and good UX quality. A pilot experiment (N=10) was conducted combining electroencephalography (EEG), a Post-Session Recognition Memory Task (PSRMT), eye-tracking behavioral data, and self-reported measures. Findings indicate that while self-reports differentiated UX Conditions, the NCE Index revealed near-identical engagement between medium and good UX (5.20 vs. 5.07), despite substantial differences in audit scores. These preliminary findings suggest that conventional UX evaluation methods may not fully capture the underlying neurocognitive processes associated with user interaction, highlighting the potential value of integrating neuroscience-informed measures into existing UX evaluation frameworks. The study presents exploratory results as a proof-of-concept for a novel methodological framework. Future research with larger, gender-balanced samples is needed to validate and extend these preliminary findings. The study carries practical implications for the evidence-based allocation of public digitalization budgets and the adoption of neurocognitive methods in applied public-sector UX evaluation.

papers.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing English Language Learning
papers.authors: Ergasheva E’zoza Ozod qizi
papers.journal: Spanish Journal of Innovation and Integrity
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing the process of learning English. Specifically, it examines the capabilities of AI-powered tools in expanding vocabulary, strengthening grammatical knowledge, developing writing skills, improving pronunciation, and shaping oral speech. Furthermore, the advantages and challenges of utilizing artificial intelligence are highlighted, including personalized education, instant feedback, over-reliance on technology, misinformation, and academic integrity issues. The study is based on an analysis of existing academic literature. The findings indicate that AI tools create additional opportunities for independent language learning and skill development. However, the effectiveness of these tools depends on their proper application, teacher guidance, and students' critical thinking. The article recommends employing artificial intelligence not as a replacement for the teacher, but as a supporting technology in the educational process.

papers.title: Proven and accepted
papers.authors: Alina Tausch, Daniel Neider, Magdalena Wischnewski, Mustafa Yalçıner
papers.abstract: Mathematical verification is an established mean to ensure reliable functioning of AI algorithms. Nevertheless, does this actually help elicit non-expert users’ acceptance and trust in an AI? Achieving calibrated trust (Lee & See, 2004) requires information on the AI’s reliability that the users can then adapt their evaluation and behaviour to. On the other hand, the process and results of formal verifications are just as incomprehensible as the AI themself to most people operating such systems. Hence, we examine if and how mathematical proofs help achieve calibrated trust and thus appropriate AI use.

papers.title: AI Readiness of Operations & Finance Professionals in a Large Urban Public School District Amidst AI-Driven Digital Transformation
papers.authors: Adetunji Onamade
papers.journal: Digital Commons - URI (University of Rhode Island)
papers.abstract: This qualitative study examined AI readiness among Operations and Finance professionals in a large urban public school district, a public-sector workforce underexamined in the AI adoption literature. Using a grounded theory approach, data from 24 interviews and three focus groups (37 participants) produced 164 codes across 12 themes. Findings converge on a single proposition: AI readiness in this District is an organizational infrastructure problem, not a technology problem. Two theoretical contributions emerged: the Organizational AI Readiness Infrastructure Framework, a three-level diagnostic model, and the AI Readiness Conditions Model, a five-stage prescriptive sequence from governance through systemic transformation.

papers.title: Blue Ocean Strategy in Da’wah: Reconfiguring Public Space and Value Creation in Ngopi Ngaji Trotoar Pamekasan
papers.authors: Ahmad Baikuni, Achmad Fathor Rosyid
papers.journal: Maddah Journal of Advanced Da wah Management Research
papers.abstract: The expansion of da’wah into nontraditional public spaces calls for an analytical framework that can explain changes in da’wah practice rather than merely document a shift in venue. This study examines da’wah innovation in the Ngopi Ngaji Trotoar activity in Pamekasan using the Blue Ocean Strategy framework, particularly the Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create (ERRC) framework, to examine how changes in da’wah practice contribute to value innovation and community engagement. The study employs a qualitative single-case study design based on interviews with eight informants, including organizers, preachers, biker community participants, and surrounding residents, as well as two direct observations. The findings identify three ERRC actions in the practice: the elimination of formal elements such as podiums and hierarchical seating, the enhancement of interaction and accessibility, and the creation of a format that combines religious study with community social activities. The Reduce dimension was not identified in the data. These changes generated five forms of value: religious, accessibility, experiential, relational, and community value. Value creation also involved co-creation, as participants moved beyond attendance to contribute ideas, invite others, assist with activities, and provide feedback, fostering a sense of community ownership. The findings extend the empirical application of ERRC in da’wah studies and indicate that innovation for young audiences can be achieved not only through digital technology but also through adapting space and activity formats to the characteristics of the target community.

papers.title: Komunikasi Dakwah Berbasis Artificial Intelligence: Negosiasi Otoritas Keagamaan antara Dai dan Chatbot AI di Kalangan Muslim Indonesia
papers.authors: Subairi Subairi, Asyaari Asyaari
papers.journal: Dakwatul Haq: Journal of Da'wah and Islamic Communication
papers.abstract: Abstract: The rapid advancement of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of Islamic communication and the ways in which Muslims access religious knowledge. AI chatbots, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Copilot, enable users to obtain instant, interactive, and personalized guidance on issues related to worship, theology, Islamic jurisprudence, and contemporary socio-religious matters. This development has generated a new dialectic of religious authority, as AI chatbots increasingly function as users' initial point of reference before consulting religious scholars (da'i). This study investigates the transformation of AI-mediated da'wah communication and examines the negotiation of religious authority between da'i and AI chatbots among Indonesian Muslims. Adopting a qualitative approach with a digital phenomenology design, the study draws on in-depth interviews with 25 participants who had used AI chatbots for religious consultation, digital observation, and documentary analysis of AI-assisted conversations. Data were analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis through iterative coding, theme development, and interpretive analysis. The findings indicate that AI chatbots serve as a form of preliminary religious consultation by providing rapid, accessible, and context-responsive explanations tailored to users' needs. Nevertheless, for issues requiring authoritative religious legitimacy, most participants continued to verify AI-generated information with qualified da'i or recognized Islamic institutions. These findings suggest that AI does not replace religious authority but instead fosters a collaborative model of da'wah communication through the negotiation of technological capability, scholarly credibility, and users' digital literacy. This study proposes the concept of Hybrid Religious Authority as a conceptual framework for understanding the reconstruction of religious authority in AI-mediated Islamic communication within the digital era.

papers.title: Treating the Trauma Beneath the Violence: A Reappraisal of Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrator Interventions
papers.authors: Huda S Shaikh, Vanessa Cordoba
papers.journal: Index of Texas Archaeology Open Access Grey Literature from the Lone Star State
papers.abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a global public health emergency with little meaningful reduction in prevalence over the past two decades, despite extensive micro-level interventions targeting perpetrators through batterer intervention programs (BIPs) and legal accountability mechanisms (Arce et al., 2020; Babcock et al., 2004; Shetty, 2025; WHO, 2025). Using a macro social work and epistemological lens, this paper argues that the IPV field and judicial systems, particularly in the United States, have relied on an outdated and largely reactive paradigm that obscures the trauma histories of perpetrators, neglects intergenerational and neurobiological mechanisms, and perpetuates epistemic injustice toward both survivors and those who use violence. Drawing on recent global estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO), meta-analytic reviews of BIPs, and literature on trauma, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and children exposed to domestic violence, the paper contends that current approaches have failed to meaningfully reduce the epidemic and may inadvertently increase psychological and emotional abuse while burdening survivors with legal-system-based trauma (Goodmark, 2018; Miller, 2005). It proposes a reimagined macro response that integrates legal accountability with trauma-responsive, brain- and nervous-system-focused interventions for perpetrators, including modalities such as eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) and neurofeedback, as a pathway toward fostering regulation, executive functioning, and genuine behavioral change. The paper concludes by outlining a pilot research design comparing traditional BIPs with integrative rehabilitative models and by advancing an epistemology of justice that treats people who use violence as whole persons with trauma histories, rather than solely as offenders to be managed by the justice system.

papers.title: AI-ENHANCED FLIPPED EFL LEARNING AND VOCABULARY ACQUISITION
papers.authors: Арайлым Тұрусбекова, Arailym Turusbekova, S. G. (Seydalieva) Omarovna
papers.journal: Bulletin of Multilingual education and philology of foreign languages
papers.abstract: Abstract. The article discusses the influence of the "inverted class" model, enhanced by artificial intelligence tools in teaching English as a foreign language, on mastering the lexical stock. The focus on three-stage learning, which is based on independent repetition using artificial intelligence after lessons, recognizing new vocabulary before class, actively using it in the classroom in a semantic context, rather than the model of memorizing words a traditional lesson. The methodological basis of the study was a comparative analysis of the works of Kazakhstani and Russian researchers published in 2023-2025, systematization of the didactic activities of digital tools and pedagogical design of Model tasks for the EFL lesson.The result of the analysis showed that artificial intelligence is more productive as a means of connecting pre-training, level adjusting training, instant feedback and interval repetition than as a separate technology that automatically "trains" vocabulary.In the practical part, samples of identifying new words from the text,creating context, conducting a microdiologue with AI-chat,comparing incorrect answers, forming an individual dictionary map snd deferred verification were presented.

papers.title: Testing Personalization in LLM-Based Mental Health Support: A Proposed Experimental Design for College Students
papers.authors: Tchalim P Agninoube, Greg Williams
papers.journal: Digital Commons - URI (University of Rhode Island)
papers.abstract: Rising student mental health demand has outpaced campus counseling capacity. This paper proposes a 2x2 between-subjects experimental design to test whether a personalized LLM-based chatbot, grounded in just-in-time adaptive intervention principles and cognitive load theory, provides better short-term anxiety reduction than a standard chatbot across stress and neutral contexts. The personalized chatbot uses wearable stress data, sleep quality, self-reported overwhelm, and support preferences to select between low-load and elaborative support paths. The design contributes a practical framework for evaluating personalization in AI-driven mental health tools and informs scalable, responsible institutional deployment.

papers.title: Reimagining Support for DV/IPV Service Providers Through AI Literacy
papers.authors: Vanessa Cordoba, Huda Shaikh
papers.journal: Index of Texas Archaeology Open Access Grey Literature from the Lone Star State
papers.abstract: As Domestic Violence (DV) and Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) organizations work to meet the complex needs of survivors, the realities facing the workforce demand closer examination. DV/IPV advocates must navigate high caseloads, persistent exposure to trauma, limited organizational resources, and extensive administrative responsibilities that often overshadow the relational and advocacy work central to survivor support. Given that 40–75% of DV/IPV staff experience moderate to high burnout (Kulkarni et al., 2013; Slattery & Goodman, 2009), exploration and use of new technological tools, such as generative artificial intelligence (AI), become a consideration in how organizations might offer support to DV/IPV staff in reducing workload, contributing to the discussion on preventing burnout. Research in other sectors suggests that AI technologies can reduce administrative burdens, improve efficiency, and allow workers to focus more on meaningful aspects of their work (Brynjolfsson & McAfee, 2017). While AI integration offers clear benefits, it also raises significant concerns, including deskilling, overreliance, and the marginalization of professional expertise (Pavuluri et al., 2024). Reamer (2025) explains, it is necessary to develop a clear understanding of how AI is being used across the behavioral health settings, the ethical challenges it raises, evidence-informed best practices, and practical risk-management strategies to safeguard both clients and workers. Therefore, as AI integration becomes more prominent in social work settings, a deeper look at the concept of AI literacy among the DV/IPV workforce becomes vital to ensure AI use does not compromise ethics, worker expertise and service delivery (Reamer, 2025).

papers.title: An Adaptive Machine Learning Framework for Predicting and Enhancing Student Performance in STEM Education
papers.authors: B. Fathimamary
papers.abstract: The advent of machine learning in the educational environment opens a number of opportunities for the optimization of the teaching process and the improvement of the results of training in STEM subjects. In this work, we propose a comprehensive application-oriented machine learning framework to predict student academic achievement and apply personalized interventions in STEM education. With the help of a well-crafted dataset consisting of records of academic and behavioral performance of 2,500 undergraduate students for three consecutive academic years, we design and validate a hybrid ensemble approach which uses a combination of Random Forest and Gradient Boosting algorithms. The framework reaches the level of prediction accuracy of 94.2% in detecting at-risk students and an AUC-ROC value of 0.972. Our method outperforms all individual base models. Apart from the predictive task, our framework offers the use of an adaptive recommendation engine suggesting personalized educational resources to students. The proposed framework operates in the form of web-based analytics dashboard for educators. This work highlights how machine learning approaches can be successfully utilized in educational practice, thus bridging the gap between research in education and practical applications of educational technologies.

papers.title: PRE-SERVICE ENGLISH TEACHERS' ACCEPTANCE AND USE OF AI-ENABLED LANGUAGE LEARNING TOOLS
papers.authors: Маржан Дуйсенова, Marzhan Moldakassymovna Duisenova
papers.journal: Bulletin of Multilingual education and philology of foreign languages
papers.abstract: Future language teachers meet AI-enabled language learning tools twice: as learners who use them now, and as professionals who may soon bring them into their own classrooms. This article reports a cross-sectional survey of pre-service English teachers at one Kazakhstani pedagogical university. Thirty-eight third- and fourth-year students took part, and 33 confirmed using AI-enabled language learning tools within the previous twelve months. The questionnaire was adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model and covered perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, an additional block on future professional use, a usage profile, and two open-ended questions. Internal consistency of the multi-item scales was satisfactory (Cronbach's alpha 0.74–0.80). ChatGPT-type chatbots turned out to be the most widely used tools (81.8%), and vocabulary and writing were the skills students practised most often. Perceived usefulness received the highest composite rating (M = 3.80) and perceived ease of use the lowest (M = 3.44). Usefulness correlated positively with behavioral intention (rho = 0.53, p = 0.002), whereas usage frequency showed no significant association with intention. Open-ended responses pointed to infrastructural barriers, distrust of answer accuracy, and the quality of Kazakh-language adaptation. Implications for foreign language teacher education programmes are discussed.

papers.title: A Student-Centered Model for Ethically Evaluating AI Integration in Learning Support Services and Beyond
papers.authors: Cristina Caputo, Bruels, Raymond, III, Alexis Rivera
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes higher education, learning support centers are uniquely positioned to intentionally assess whether if and how to best integrate AI tools into academic services. This session presents a 6-week project framework that was designed to: • Review the literature on critical AI literacy and training • Benchmark current best practices in AI policy, use, and integration alongside human-centered academic services • Examine student AI knowledge and use (needs assessment) • Identify and evaluate relevant AI tools or platforms The framework was developed within the Academic Success Center (ASC) at Nevada State University where Center peer educators (student employees) served as project leads and evaluators. This model offers a practical, research-informed pathway for institutions seeking to lead responsibly in AI-integrated learning support or other student services. Session activities include a walkthrough and discussion of the model structure, tools, challenges, and recommendations. Attendees will leave with: (1) a sample 6-week project roadmap, (2) a student-centered model for AI evaluation and pilot design, (3) learning frameworks grounded in critical AI literacy, (4) adaptable resources for assessment and decision-making, and (5) strategies for positioning students as co-creators in institutional/unit change

papers.title: AI for Everyone: Designing an Introductory AI Course Across Disciplines
papers.authors: Jesse J. Fitts, Waleed Faris
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes virtually every field, universities face a growing imperative to ensure AI literacy is not reserved for computer science majors alone. This panel presents the collaborative design of an introductory AI course built for undergraduate general education — one that serves students across disciplines, regardless of technical background. Two co-designers will share the story of building the course from complementary angles. The first presenter will address the technical foundation of the curriculum: how core AI concepts such as machine learning, data, and algorithms were translated into accessible, hands-on learning experiences for non-specialist students. The second presenter will explore the philosophical framework woven throughout the course — examining questions of ethics, agency, bias, and what it means to be human in an age of intelligent machines. The panelists will discuss how technical and philosophical threads were intentionally integrated rather than siloed, creating a course where students not only understand how AI works, but are equipped to think critically about why it matters. Attendees will come away with practical insights on curriculum structure, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and strategies for making AI education inclusive for students from diverse academic and experiential backgrounds. This session is designed for faculty, instructional designers, and administrators interested in developing or expanding AI literacy offerings at their institutions.

papers.title: Designing with Intent: A Comparative Analysis of Custom AI Chatbots as UDL-Aligned Tools for Multidisciplinary Instruction
papers.authors: Ephraim Quaynor Teye, Clarissa Oteng-Darko, Leping Liu
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: The growing presence of AI in higher education has prompted instructors to move beyond passive adoption, to deliberate theory-grounded design. This session presents two custom AI chatbots (DisneyBot and Rico) developed within a teacher preparation course as the technology-enhanced component of a multidisciplinary instructional unit. DisneyBot is built on the ChatGPT platform to guide learners through an exploration of Disney parks, and Rico, is built on the Gemini platform as an interactive guide to information about Puerto Rico by scaffolding learning across four subject-specific lesson modules – Social Studies, ELA/ENL, Science, and Spanish. Both chatbots were developed to support differentiated and interactive learning for 4th and 5th grade students through a virtual field trip framework, with the broader goal of connecting classroom content to authentic real-world experiences. The design of each chatbot was grounded in UDL principles (CAST, 2018). Rather than serving as static information repositories, the chatbots were intentionally designed to function as interactive instructional mediators which use prompting inquiry, guiding subject-specific exploration, and offering differentiated entry points for learners with varying needs and language backgrounds (Vygotsky, 1978). The differences between the two platforms, in terms of interface architecture, customization depth, persona design, and interaction affordances, form the basis of a comparative analysis that will anchor the session. Participants will interact directly with both chatbots, examine the instructional design decisions behind them, and leave with a working framework for developing purpose-built AI chatbots that can be tailored to their own teaching contexts and disciplines.

papers.title: AI Tutors, Worksheets, and Task Design: Matching AI Tools to Learning Structure
papers.authors: Brock Casselman@unlv.edu
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by students as a learning resource in STEM courses. However, classroom observations and survey data suggest that unstructured AI use may correlate with reduced student achievement. Two concerns are especially relevant: AI systems can produce incorrect responses in tasks requiring precise validation, and students may use AI in ways that reduce active engagement with course material. This session presents two instructional approaches designed to address these limitations: structured AI-generated worksheets and in-chat AI tutors. AI worksheets generate controlled sets of practice problems within instructor-defined course constraints. In-chat tutors provide interactive practice through problem generation, Socratic questioning, and feedback-driven guidance. The usefulness of each approach depends on the structure of the learning task. Drawing from iterative development and testing primarily in introductory chemistry, we examine four types of tasks: (1) conceptual and explanatory, (2) structured tasks with low ambiguity, (3) multi-step quantitative tasks, and (4) highly deterministic symbolic or structural tasks. Examples from chemical nomenclature, dimensional analysis, stoichiometry, Lewis structures, laboratory writing, and mathematical validation illustrate where different AI approaches worked reliably—and where they did not. Participants will receive ready-to-use prompts for both AI worksheet systems and in-chat tutors, along with implementation strategies and observed limitations. The session concludes with a practical framework for selecting AI tools based on the structure of the learning task rather than disciplinary content alone.

papers.title: IT Meets Academia: Giving Students the Tech Tools to Write the AI Rules
papers.authors: Alethea Inns, Beth Rosenberg
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: An AI administrator walks into an Honors English seminar. The assignment: prepare undergraduates to help write the course AI policy. This UNLV case study follows an unusual collaboration between a professor of postcolonial literature and the administrator of the university’s ChatGPT and Claude environments. The administrator also wrote UNLV’s draft institutional AI framework and experiences classroom AI rules as a PhD student. The session asks what becomes possible when the person who sees the systems behind the interface joins faculty and students in the policy conversation. Before students could write the rules, they needed enough technical literacy to understand what they were governing: model limitations, learning tradeoffs, differences between consumer and institutional accounts, data practices, authorship, transparency, and personal boundaries. The presenters will trace how that foundation prepared students to participate in course policy development. Dr. Beth Rosenberg will share why she invited IT into an English seminar, how students responded, and how the policy took shape. Attendees will leave with an adaptable model for combining IT knowledge, faculty expertise, and student agency to create AI expectations grounded in both technology and learning.

papers.title: Building Bots That Teach Thinking: Using Custom AI Chatbots to Enhance Critical Thinking and Decision-Making
papers.authors: Megan Biagi
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly common in education, but its effect on student learning depends largely on how it is used. This interactive session will introduce practical strategies for creating custom AI chatbots that encourage students to think through problems rather than simply ask for answers. Participants will explore ways to design bots that ask learners to explain their reasoning, consider alternative perspectives, identify assumptions, and revise their thinking before receiving feedback. Examples from healthcare education and other disciplines will show how these tools can support guided inquiry, reflective questioning, clinical reasoning, and decision-making. Participants will review and revise sample chatbot instructions, then begin developing a bot for a course or learning activity of their choice. The session will also cover practical considerations such as choosing reliable source materials, setting appropriate boundaries, protecting student privacy, testing the bot before use, and refining instructions based on its responses. Participants will leave with sample prompts, practical design principles, and a plan for using a custom chatbot in their own educational setting. The goal is to help educators use AI in ways that preserve productive struggle, provide a safe environment for practice, and strengthen students’ ability to explain and defend their decisions.

papers.title: AI-Aware Student Recommendations for GenAI in Higher Ed
papers.authors: Neill Stotts
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: What do well-informed students say about the use and integration of AI in their college educations? In Spring and Summer 2026 semesters, students in three sections of ENG 102 at UNR wrote AI-aware white papers with policy recommendations for the integration of genAI into higher education. To develop white paper policies, students read a variety of scholarly, public, and popular sources that show a variety of perspectives on Generative AI and LLMs, including the environmental and cognitive impacts. Then they considered the values and concerns of their audiences—peers, professors, and/or university administrators—to propose “sensible, well-informed, and well-reasoned” policies. This session will discuss their recommendations, insights, and the somewhat surprising classroom experience of teaching sustained, critical enquiry about Generative AI.

papers.title: Crafting Resilient AI policies for Education
papers.authors: Delight Ejiaka, Miranda Hannasch, Branden Cunningham
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into academic spaces requires a shift from passive restriction to resilient, active pedagogical frameworks. This virtual panel explores actionable strategies to protect academic integrity, promote deep critical thinking, and manage AI use, particularly in foundational courses. Panelists will discuss the implementation of high-engagement classroom interventions. The will offer frameworks for transparent student disclosure practices. Attendees will leave with practical templates for syllabus policies, assignment rubrics, and disclosure benchmarks designed to foster a culture of transparency and process-oriented learning in an AI-permeated landscape.

papers.title: Resisting AI with Paper: Possibilities, Concerns and Protest
papers.authors: Laura Evans
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: While there are a number of commercial benefits involved in incorporating AI usage and training into college composition classrooms, to many the perils and problems involved in student AI use outweigh these possibilities. A growing number of composition instructors have chosen to return to requiring assignments to be handwritten on paper as an increasingly viable, and even necessary, strategy to combat the growing use of ChatGPT and other AI text generation software as an essay-writing tool. This strategy has a number of potential benefits – the ability to regulate AI usage, to create better memory retention, and decrease student screen-time – but there are also many potential drawbacks. This panel aims to discuss the viability and sustainability of this option in the AI debate, with special attention to the environmental costs of paper vs. AI, the practicality of implementing paper assignments, and overall where the instructor’s priorities in the modern college composition classroom should lie. The debate might ultimately come down to whether in training for AI usage in the workplace or focusing on the retention of composition skills should be the modern priority. Overall, the question of whether the paper option is a viable solution is a somewhat underdiscussed topic in the AI debate, and this panel aims to consider thoughts from college instructors on the pros and cons thereof.

papers.title: Enhancing the Accessibility of Instructional Content in Higher Education Through AI
papers.authors: Sushma Alphonsa
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into higher education, it presents new opportunities to enhance the accessibility of instructional materials. This session examines how Microsoft Copilot, Adobe AI, and built-in Windows 11 features such as live auto-captions can support more accessible content creation and remediation across Microsoft 365 applications and PDF workflows. Focusing on commonly used instructional formats including Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and PDFs shared through learning management systems, this presentation highlights how AI tools can assist in identifying and addressing accessibility barriers. Examples will illustrate how Copilot can support content development, organization, and alternative text generation, while Adobe AI tools streamline improvements to PDF structure, tagging, and usability. Windows 11 auto-captioning features will also be discussed as a way to enhance access to audio and video content. The session explores practical approaches for integrating AI-supported accessibility strategies into existing teaching and course design workflows. Attention is given to aligning these approaches with accessibility standards and inclusive teaching practices while maintaining efficiency for instructors, instructional designers, technologists, and teaching assistants. Attendees will gain insight into key strategies, considerations, and potential applications of AI to create more inclusive, accessible instructional materials.

papers.title: When the Chatbot is Wrong on Purpose: Using GenAI Role-Play to Build Student Engagement and Critical AI Fluency
papers.authors: Sierra Adare-Tasiwoopa Ápi
papers.journal: Digital Scholarship - UNLV (University of Nevada Reno)
