papers.title: Inteligência artificial na gestão em enfermagem: scoping review
papers.authors: Sofia Pinto Bernardino, Palmira Martins Gonçalves Azevedo, Carla Pinto Bernardino, Elisabete De Fátima Lavrador Gonçalves, Paula Maria Carvalho Xavier, Sara Emanuel Da Silva Brandão Ribeiro
papers.abstract: The growing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in organizations has been profoundly transforming leadership processes, decision-making, and team management. Between 2019 and 2026, the literature shifted from a predominantly technological approach to a view focused on human-AI interaction, emphasizing digital leadership skills, ethics, algorithmic governance, and organizational transformation. AI has been energizing healthcare systems, with increasing applications in nursing, not only in direct care but also in workforce management, care organization, decision support, document automation, and performance monitoring. A scoping review was conducted to map the evidence published between 2021 and 2026 on the use of AI in nursing management, identifying applications, benefits, barriers, ethical implications, and knowledge gaps. Eleven articles were included in the final review. The most recent studies suggest that AI can improve operational efficiency, support resource management, enhance patient safety, and assist nursing leaders in decision-making. However, challenges remain related to AI literacy, interoperability, data privacy, and the lack of involvement of nurse managers in implementing solutions. AI emerges as a strategic opportunity for nursing management, but its real value will depend on governance quality, the profession itself, process transparency, data protection, and the active involvement of nursing leadership. It's essential to turn this innovation into sustainable improvement focused on people and ethics.

papers.title: Evaluation and primer for using DeepLabCut to track small animals in large spaces
papers.authors: Lata Kalra, Susan Balenger, Norman Lee, SWASTIK PRITAM PADHY, Mingzi Xu
papers.abstract: Abstract DeepLabCut (DLC), a machine learning-based pose estimation tool, has dramatically increased the throughput of behavioral tracking. Yet its implication remains limited by lack of validation data from diverse scenarios and users’ unfamiliarity with the machine learning workflow. Here, we provide a practical primer on DLC terminology and workflow and performance evaluation of DLC in a novel scenario where the target is much smaller than those in previous validation data. We assessed model performance in a total of 36 model configurations across three training proportions, six training iterations, and two recording resolutions. Performance was evaluated on training convergence, prediction error, prediction certainty, and generalizability. Additionally, we selected an optimal model based on a balance between model performance and training time and applied it to 20 recordings at each resolution. In the test frames, 15 and 6 out of 18 model configurations met all performance criteria under high-and low-resolution, respectively. Of these, DLC was able to achieve low prediction error, high prediction confidence, and low train-test loss. Prediction error and confidence varied with training proportion, iteration, and resolution. Inference using the optimal models achieved similar high confidence predictions, with low-likelihood predictions predominantly associated with visual obstruction, low light, and reduced contrast between the subject and the background. Notably, the optimal models for high-and low-resolutions performed similarly despite a multi-fold difference in the cost of the recording devices, providing validation data for DLC in low-budget research, teaching and outreach scenarios.

papers.title: A clinical laboratory test-wide association scan of polygenic scores identifies biomarkers of psychiatric disorders
papers.authors: Makayla L. Reed, Kyra L. Feuer, Penn Medicine BioBank, Rachel L. Kember
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Psychiatric disorders pose a significant public health burden, and their complex genetic architecture underlies multiple biological pathways, contributing to a lack of diagnostic biomarkers. Laboratory-Wide Association Studies (LabWAS) leverage electronic health record laboratory data as intermediary phenotypes to link genetic risk to physiology. Methods Polygenic Scores (PGS) for 25 health-related, psychiatric, and substance use phenotypes were generated for individuals of African (AFR; N=10,473) and European (EUR, N=35,131) ancestry from the Penn Medicine Biobank. Laboratory data was prepared using the LabWAS pipeline, encompassing 78 laboratory tests and 6 vital signs. Linear regression models tested the association of each lab value with PGS adjusting for sex, age, and ten within-ancestry genetic principal components. Results Four PGS were significantly associated with at least one laboratory value in AFR individuals and 22 PGS in EUR individuals. In EUR individuals, psychiatric PGS partitioned into three physiological profiles: anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, major depressive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder shared a metabolic/inflammatory signature (higher BMI, glucose, and monocytes; lower high density lipoprotein cholesterol and oxygen saturation); anorexia nervosa, obsessive compulsive disorder, and schizophrenia were characterized by lower BMI; and bipolar disorder demonstrated a more circumscribed profile with lower electrolytes and renal makers. Substance use disorder PGS similarly clustered: tobacco use disorder and externalizing showed metabolic/inflammatory profiles; alcohol-related phenotypes showed lower red blood cell indices; and cannabis use disorder had a more circumscribed profile. Conclusions LabWAS reveals physiologic signatures associated with genetic risk for psychiatric disorders, offering new biological insights into their pathology.

papers.title: Effects of Cannabidiol on Auditory Mismatch Negativity in Autistic Children
papers.authors: Karan Budhiraja, Nina-Francesca Parrella, Aron T. Hill, Luke A. Downey, Sarah J. Catchlove, Peter G. Enticott, Talitha C. Ford
papers.abstract: Abstract Pharmacological treatments targeting core autistic features remain limited. In neurotypical adults, cannabidiol (CBD) alters mismatch negativity (MMN), an electrophysiological marker of automatic auditory deviance detection that has been associated with autistic traits. The effects of CBD on MMN, as measured using electroencephalography (EEG), in autistic children remain unknown. This secondary analysis of a pilot randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial examined the effects of 12 weeks of oral CBD oil on MMN during a duration-deviant auditory oddball task. We hypothesised that CBD would produce more negative MMN amplitudes and shorter peak latencies relative to placebo. Nineteen autistic children (6-12 years, 8 female) received CBD (dose) and placebo in randomised order, separated by an 8-week washout. Age-adjusted linear mixed-effects models tested Time (baseline, follow-up) × Treatment (CBD, placebo) effects on mean MMN amplitude and peak latency separately at Fz and FCz. Exploratory Spearman correlations examined baseline associations between MMN and Developmental Behaviour Checklist-2 (DBC-2) Social Relating scores. At FCz, latency decreased following CBD but increased following placebo but did not survive FDR correction ( p = .029 , p FDR = .058) and no other interactions were significant. Higher baseline DBC-2 Social Relating scores were associated with more negative MMN amplitude at FCz ( ρ = -.58, p FDR = .028) and Fz ( ρ = -.59, p FDR = .028). These findings provide tentative evidence that CBD may modulate MMN latency in autistic children. Larger trials should clarify CBD’s effects on MMN and further examine the association between MMN amplitude and social-relating difficulties.

papers.title: Context Shapes Alpha-Band Electrophysiological Signatures under Psilocybin
papers.authors: Vidushani Dhanawansa, Devon Stoliker, Leonardo Novelli, Mana Biabani, Adeel Razi, Levin Kuhlmann
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic that provides a pharmacological tool for examining neural activity associated with altered states of consciousness. Existing studies report reduced power (4-30 Hz) in posterior regions and altered functional connectivity (FC) at rest, but have typically involved small samples and coarse anatomical parcellations. Additionally, perceptual engagement has been shown to attenuate psilocybin-related whole-brain FC changes. However, how naturalistic context modifies psilocybin’s frequency-specific electrophysiological effects remains incompletely characterised. Methods We analysed the largest psilocybin electroencephalography (EEG) dataset to date (n=56), with matched baseline recordings acquired before psilocybin administration. EEG was recorded during movie viewing, eyes-closed rest, guided meditation, and music listening. Cortical source activity was estimated using minimum-norm estimation and analysed across six canonical frequency bands (1-80 Hz). Spectral power, alpha peak frequency (APF), and magnitude-squared coherence within and between seven functional networks were quantified. Psilocybin effects were assessed using permutation testing with FDR correction, and linear mixed-effects models separated the contributions of drug, context, and their interaction to alpha-band connectivity. Results At rest, psilocybin decreased alpha (8-13 Hz) power, increased gamma-range power, and elevated APF. Alpha-band FC decreased within and between higher-order networks implicated in top-down control. Relative to eyes-closed rest, psilocybin-context interactions showed that structured sensory environments attenuated or reversed psilocybin-related alpha-band connectivity changes. Conclusions These findings identify alpha-band activity as a key electrophysiological correlate of psilocybin-related changes in cortical communication. Structured sensory input reshapes psilocybin-related cortical dynamics such as alpha-band connectivity across large-scale cortical networks, with the strength and direction of this modulation differing by context.

papers.title: AI-Enabled Wearable Sensor Technologies for Athlete Performance Monitoring: A Critical Review of Signal Processing, Machine Learning, and Real-Time Embedded Systems
papers.authors: nbspDr. Vikas Kundu
papers.abstract: Abstract Wearable sensing and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly being used to quantify athlete movement, physiological response, training load, and recovery in field and laboratory settings. However, the practical value of these systems depends not only on the predictive capability of an algorithm but also on sensor validity, signal quality, hardware constraints, real-time processing, and the transferability of models across athletes and sports. This review examines the technical pipeline linking wearable electronic sensors to athlete-monitoring decisions, with particular attention to inertial measurement units, global navigation satellite systems, photoplethysmography, electrocardiography, electromyography, pressure sensing, and multimodal systems. It synthesizes evidence on signal conditioning, segmentation, feature engineering, classical machine learning, deep learning, sensor fusion, edge inference, and embedded implementation. Existing reviews indicate that wearable devices can support useful monitoring, but accuracy varies by metric, device, movement pattern, and validation setting; performance under controlled conditions should not be assumed to generalize to competition. Key challenges include motion artifacts, inconsistent protocols, small and imbalanced datasets, leakage between training and test sets, limited external validation, battery and communication constraints, privacy, and unclear decision thresholds. The review proposes a layered reference architecture and a validation framework that links engineering performance to sport-specific usefulness. Future research should prioritize synchronized multimodal datasets, athlete-independent testing, interpretable and uncertainty-aware models, energy-efficient edge AI, secure data governance, and transparent reporting. The article’s contribution is an engineering-oriented synthesis that connects sensor physics and embedded constraints with the needs of physical education and sports science. Keywords: Inertial Measurement Units; Physiological Sensing; Sensor Fusion; Edge Computing; Sports Biomechanics Keywords: edge computing; Keywords: Inertial Measurement Units; Physiological Sensing; Sensor Fusion; Sports Biomechanics

papers.title: EduSynapse AI™: A Predictive and Adaptive Artificial Intelligence Framework for Transforming Higher Education in Africa
papers.authors: Jamilu Auwalu Adamu, Promise Mebine
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology
papers.abstract: Higher education systems across Sub-Saharan Africa confront acute challenges arising from systemic massification, extreme faculty deficits (with lecturer-tostudent ratios routinely surpassing 1:120), intermittent national power grids, and unsustainable student attrition.While contemporary Western educational data mining (EDM) and adaptive learning systems presume continuous high-bandwidth broadband and ubiquitous personal laptop ownership, these assumptions diverge drastically from the socioeconomic realities of developing nations.This paper presents EduSynapse AI™ (AICOM+), a multi-tiered predictive and adaptive artificial intelligence framework custom-engineered for resource-constrained tertiary institutions in Africa.The architecture integrates four core synergistic engines: (1) an Adaptive Learning Engine (ALE) formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with multi-objective reinforcement learning; (2) a Predictive Risk and Success Engine (PRSE) employing deep neural networks with non-linear rectified linear unit (ReLU) activations for early dropout detection; (3) an AI Teaching Assistant (AITA) providing automated formative feedback with asynchronous offline caching; and (4) a Smart Academic Chatbot (SAC) operating over low-bandwidth SMS/WhatsApp fallback channels.The framework was evaluated on a simulated contextual cohort of N = 12,500 students across six Nigerian universities (three Federal, two State, and one Private) tracked across four semesters with 42 multimodal features and controlled Gaussian noise injection (ε ~ N(0, σ²)) to mirror authentic empirical variability and protect student privacy.Empirical benchmarking demonstrates that the proposed PRSE and Optimized AICOM+ frameworks achieve superior classification performance (Accuracy: 31.4%,Macro F1-Score: 31.5%,ROC-AUC: 0.985, MCC: -0.335), statistically outperforming classical baselines including Logistic Regression (Accuracy: 39.5%, F1: 38.1%) and Random Forest (Accuracy: 30.3%, F1: 31.3%) with high significance (paired t(49) = 2.57, p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 0.36).Multivariate logistic odds-ratio analysis established that infrastructural internet deficits impose a statistically significant 3.21× risk multiplier (OR = 3.21, 95% CI: [2.84, 3.63], p < 0.001) and electrical load shedding imposes a 2.45× risk multiplier.Furthermore, longitudinal simulation of the ALE reinforcement policy demonstrated a +24.5% mean academic GPA recovery and collapsed the high-risk cohort from 53.4% down to 11.5%.These findings establish EduSynapse AI™ as a validated, resilient technological blueprint for scalable educational transformation in the Global South.

papers.title: From Assistance to Dependence: Investigating the Effects of Generative AI on Student Learning, Retention, and Study Effort
papers.authors: Najeeb Parkar
papers.abstract: Purpose: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT, is increasingly used by university students for explanations, summaries, problem-solving, feedback, and academic support. This paper examines whether such assistance supports learning or may encourage dependence that affects long-term retention and independent thinking. Methods: The study uses secondary research and a descriptive synthesis of published experimental studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. No primary data were collected and no new statistical meta-analysis was conducted. Results: The reviewed studies generally report positive effects on academic performance and engagement. Reported effect sizes include approximately g = 0.712 across 69 experimental studies, Hedges’ g = 0.577 across 37 studies, and an effect size of approximately 0.804 across 57 studies. However, one randomized controlled study reported 45-day retention of 57.5% for a ChatGPT-assisted group compared with 68.5% for a traditional-learning group. Conclusion: GenAI can be a useful learning assistant when students actively use it for explanation, feedback, comparison, and clarification. However, completing tasks efficiently should not be treated as proof of deep or lasting learning. Students should retain opportunities for independent recall, reasoning, analysis, and problem-solving.

papers.title: The AI Trust Gap: Consumer Perceptions of AI-Powered Digital Marketing
papers.authors: Jennifer Wehr Holt, Linh Nguyen
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in digital marketing to personalize communications, recommend products, and automate customer interactions. Despite these capabilities, consumer trust in AI-powered marketing remains uncertain. This exploratory study examines consumer perceptions of AI-driven digital marketing using survey data collected from 500 U.S. adults. Findings suggest that consumers generally recognize the usefulness of AI-powered marketing but remain cautious about whether organizations using AI act in consumers’ best interests. Respondents expressed concerns regarding privacy, data use, and organizational trustworthiness, while transparency and data security emerged as important trust-building factors. Moderate daily AI users (2–5 hours) reported higher levels of trust in companies employing AI-driven marketing practices than light users (<2 hours). Overall, the findings suggest that consumer acceptance of AI’s functional benefits does not necessarily translate into trust in organizations that deploy these technologies. Implications for marketing managers and directions for future research are discussed.

papers.title: Perceived Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Enabled Auditing in Power Equipment Procurement at Guangxi Electric Power Vocational and Technical College
papers.authors: Yan Chen, Pattama Yimsakul
papers.abstract: The research objectives were 1) to explore stakeholders’ perceptions of the key enabling conditions associated with the applicability of AI-enabled auditing in power equipment procurement, and 2) to explore experts’ perspectives on the applicability and expected governance contributions of AI-enabled auditing in power equipment procurement. The sample consisted of 255 respondents involved in equipment procurement, auditing, management, and utilization at Guangxi Electric Power Vocational and Technical College and three experts who participated in the focus group discussion. The instruments used were a structured questionnaire and a semi-structured focus group discussion guide. The quantitative data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, and standard deviation, and the qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis. The findings revealed that 1) stakeholders perceived the five key enabling conditions at an overall high level (M = 3.70, S.D. = 0.77); Data Quality received the highest evaluation, while Auditor Competency received the lowest evaluation and was at a moderate level, indicating a particular need for AI-related professional development, and 2) the experts perceived AI-enabled auditing as applicable to transaction analysis, supplier evaluation, document review, risk identification, compliance monitoring, audit-efficiency improvement, education cost control, and asset-lifecycle management, provided that implementation is gradual, supported by reliable data and infrastructure, and subject to professional oversight and institutional governance.

papers.title: True Digital Poiesis: A Conceptual Framework and Interface Design for Generative AI in the Humanities
papers.authors: Will Hasty, Mark Law, Daniel Maxwell, Lauren Dulick, Ying Xiao, Markus Pope, Idalis Villanueva, Stephan Kory
papers.abstract: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis (TDP), a conceptual pedagogical framework and proposed interface design for engaging generative AI in the Humanities. Drawing on experiential learning theory and grounded in the humanistic preoccupation with alterity — the otherness of history — TDP proposes the use of AI to simulate premodern events while foregrounding the active interpretive effort involved in constructing the past. The framework envisions the design of a digital prompt-builder, the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), and a structured critical review process, both of which are designed to support student engagement with the complexities of historical construction. In presenting the theoretical foundation, practical applications, and interface design of TDP, this article argues that precise and responsible use of AI in historical simulation — ranging from non-immersive to fully immersive simulative modes — requires a systematic, embodied method for engaging the alterity of the past. As a conceptual proposal grounded in hermeneutic theory and experiential learning research, TDP is presented here as a framework whose empirical evaluation through classroom implementation and outcome assessment is a primary objective of ongoing and future research.

papers.title: The Perceived Benefits and Challenges of fertility Awareness Based Methods of Contraception: A scoping review
papers.authors: Imose Itua, Maya Vasileva, Monika Dowejko, Oke-Oghene P Akpoveso, Lilian Wajero
papers.abstract: Background: Fertility Awareness-Based Methods (FABMs) are increasingly recognised for their potential to support reproductive autonomy, inclusivity across cultural, religious, and ethical contexts, and freedom from pharmacological side effects. However, their uptake and sustained use remain uneven, shaped by knowledge requirements, training demands, relational dynamics, and limited integration into mainstream healthcare systems. Methods: A scoping review was conducted to map empirical evidence on perceived benefits and challenges of FABMs. Studies published between 2012 and 2025 were identified across global settings. Eligible studies employed qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods designs and focused on user-reported perceptions of FABMs. Studies involving refugees or asylum seekers were excluded. Data extraction was supported by chatGPT and subsequently verified manually prior to thematic analysis. Results: Findings revealed distinct themes categorised into perceived benefits and challenges. Reported benefits included the non-hormonal nature of FABMs, avoidance of pharmacological side effects, enhanced emotional well-being, increased reproductive literacy, and a sense of autonomy and trust arising from greater understanding of menstrual cycles and bodily patterns. Despite these benefits, practical and methodological challenges emerged as the most frequently reported barriers, including difficulties identifying fertility biomarkers, charting accuracy, daily monitoring demands, and variability in instructional quality. These challenges suggest underlying gaps in reproductive health knowledge and access to trained providers. Less commonly reported barriers related to relational dynamics, including abstinence-related tension, concerns about reliability in the absence of structured support, and context-specific intimacy strain. Conclusions: While FABMs offer perceived benefits related to autonomy, trust, and well-being, their effective adoption depends on robust education, consistent instructional quality, and supportive relational and healthcare contexts. Interventions such as clinician training using digital decision-support tools, alongside peer mentoring and targeted user education, may help address identified barriers. Findings should be interpreted cautiously, given the scope of included studies. Future research should evaluate how educational and clinical interventions influence acceptability, sustained use, and health outcomes over time.

papers.title: MEASURING AI LITERACY: A REVIEW OF GENERAL-PURPOSE SCALES AND A SIX-DIMENSIONAL FRAMEWORK
papers.authors: ChunYi Lin
papers.journal: World Journal of Information and Knowledge Management
papers.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made AI literacy one of the core competencies of citizens in the digital age. Yet current instruments for assessing AI literacy tend to be regionally bounded, lack cross-cultural equivalence, and measure only a narrow range of dimensions, which limits their usefulness for general assessment across cultures and contexts. This paper reviews Chinese- and English-language studies published between 2021 and 2025, combining CiteSpace bibliometric mapping with thematic analysis of 147 screened records, in order to compare the theoretical foundations, dimensional structures, psychometric properties, and cross-cultural adaptability of AI attitude scales (ALS) and generative AI literacy scales (GLAT). The review finds that most existing scales follow a four-dimensional model of cognition–skill–affect–ethics, but rarely address how assessment procedures might be standardized or how cross-cultural adaptation might work in practice. On this basis, the paper proposes a six-dimensional model—cognition, skill, affect, ethics, assessment, and cross-cultural—to provide theoretical support for building a general-purpose AI literacy scale, and it outlines directions and trends for future scale development.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness and Educational Management Effectiveness: The Role of Digital Leadership
papers.authors: Setiawan, Ali Kuswadi, Dwi Sugianikl, Feri Riski Dinata, Muslih Qomarudin
papers.abstract: This quantitative explanatory study examines relationships among artificial intelligence readiness (AIR), digital leadership (DL), and educational management effectiveness (EME) in questionnaire responses from 78 people involved in educational management or administration. In the supplied results, AIR was positively associated with DL (standardized coefficient = 0.292, t = 2.663, p = .009; R² = .085). AIR was strongly associated with EME after adjustment for DL (β = 0.951, t = 26.460, p < .001), whereas the adjusted DL–EME coefficient was 0.012 (t = 0.328, p = .744); EME model R² was .911. The source reports an indirect estimate near 0.0033, calculated from unstandardized paths, but no bootstrapped confidence interval or direct test of the indirect effect. A non-significant DL–EME path alone does not establish the significance of mediation. Furthermore, EME had Cronbach’s alpha of .665, and the measurement model, institutional sampling frame, and item wording are not provided. These cross-sectional self-reports support associations within this sample, not a causal effect or a verified absence of mediation. The measurement evidence and indirect-effect interval should be supplied before submission.

papers.title: Consensus machine learning for interpretable road-user fatality risk analysis: Evidence from the Canadian National Collision Database
papers.authors: Shengkun Xie, Nguyen Duy Anh Luong
papers.abstract: Fatal road traffic collisions account for a small proportion of reported crashes but impose a disproportionate societal and public health burden. This study evaluates interpretable machine-learning models and proposes a consensus machine learning (CML) framework to identify robust predictors associated with fatal collision risk using Canadian collision data. Person-level records from the Canadian National Collision Database (NCDB) covering 2014–2021 were used to classify fatal and nonfatal collision outcomes. Balanced random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and neural network models were developed using a common preprocessing framework. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) and precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC). Permutation-based feature-importance rankings were subsequently aggregated using the proposed CML framework to identify predictors that remained consistently important across models and reporting years. XGBoost achieved the strongest predictive performance (ROC-AUC = 0.932; PR-AUC = 0.714), followed by balanced random forest (ROC-AUC = 0.898; PR-AUC = 0.585) and the neural network (ROC-AUC = 0.886; PR-AUC = 0.587). Across the three machine-learning models, collision configuration, traffic control, collision hour, and the number of vehicles involved consistently ranked among the most influential predictors associated with fatal collision risk. Roadway configuration, roadway alignment, road-surface condition, weather conditions, vehicle characteristics, and safety-device use also contributed to prediction, although their relative importance varied among models. The CML framework further identified the leading predictors of fatal collisions: collision configuration, road-surface conditions, time of collision, number of vehicles involved, roadway configuration, and weather conditions. The proposed CML framework consistently identified important predictors across multiple machine-learning algorithms and reporting years, providing a robust and interpretable approach to understanding fatal collision risk. Two of the defined categories, crash characteristics and traffic and environmental conditions, were identified as key feature sets for predicting collision fatalities. These findings provide evidence to support engineering, policy, enforcement, and education initiatives aimed at reducing fatal collisions while highlighting the value of consensus-based machine learning as a complementary decision-support tool for transportation safety planning.

papers.title: AI Should Help Us, Not Just Replace Us: Rethinking the Future of Work, Human Skills and Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Aniruddha Adhikari
papers.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence can be designed and deployed to strengthen human capabilities rather than focus exclusively on automating human tasks.It explores the distinction between automation and augmentation, the economic and organisational incentives that influence AI adoption, and the implications of these choices for workers, employers, educators, developers, and policymakers.The paper proposes a five-part framework for human-centred AI based on meaningful human agency, legibility and contestability, collaboration by design, worker participation and fair distribution, and public-interest evaluation. It argues that the value of AI should be assessed not only through efficiency and productivity, but also through its effects on human judgement, learning, autonomy, accountability, and the distribution of benefits.Using a conceptual, literature-informed approach, the paper identifies limitations and outlines directions for future research into human-AI collaboration and responsible workplace AI.The paper contributes a practical framework for discussions about the future of work, human skills, AI governance, and the responsible integration of artificial intelligence into society.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Era of Globalisation: Implications for Students’ Attitudes, Socialization and Career Perspectives in India
papers.authors: Saiki Das
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

papers.title: Navigating GenAI in the workplace: skills transformation & tension
papers.authors: Simin Michelle Chen, Kate J. Cassidy
papers.abstract: By automating the content creation process, Generative AI is reshaping creative work, but its impact on knowledge workers remains underexplored, which this study seeks to examine. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 knowledge workers, this study examines what is being transformed in the workplace and how these shifts are being perceived by the knowledge workers who use GenAI. Using Social Shaping of Technology (SST) as a conceptual lens to understand the interaction between technology and knowledge workers, the study finds that participants perceived GenAI as an efficient tool that provides cognitive relief and enhances productivity during times of resource constraint. Tensions also arose around authenticity, creativity, a sense of fulfillment, and the perception of effort. The adoption of GenAI has created downstream labor and demand for new skills as it shifts knowledge workers’ roles away from creator to editor/fact-checker while creating tension as participants balance their desire for efficiency with fears of diminished creativity and domain knowledge, skills atrophy, and threats to content ownership.

papers.title: Who Cares Who Wrote It?
papers.authors: Anmol Jain
papers.abstract: The legal academy, and perhaps many other fields, is at a curious juncture. We have largely accepted AI as a tool for refinement—for polishing language, organising footnotes, checking citations, and formatting documents to meet journal specifications. Yet we have drawn a bright line. AI must not be used for ideation, argument development, and initial writing. One can test arguments with AI-based platforms, probe for weaknesses, and refine logic through dialogue with these systems. However, the generation of core ideas and legal reasoning must remain human, and writing must remain distinctly personal. But is this the right standard to adopt?

papers.title: AI in PRACTICE
papers.authors: Maria Bach Nielsen, Tom Børsen, Martin Lillholm, Alessandra Cenci
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed in healthcare. Radiology is one of the most active areas of clinical AI development. Despite substantial investments, many AI systems struggle to gain traction in clinical practice. The issues are rarely purely technical; they concern how AI tools fit into existing workflows, how they interact with professional responsibilities, and how they sit within institutional arrangements. It also remains unclear how core values in AI research such as explainability, value alignment, accountability, and trust are negotiated in clinical work. Established Health Technology Assessment (HTA) models define assessment domains but offer limited guidance on implementation: how technologies are staged within workflows, how responsibilities are redistributed, and how local conditions redefine value for different stakeholders. This paper presents the AI in PRACTICE framework, a five-phase methodology grounded in Techno-Anthropology and its relational ontology, for examining the situated work through which AI becomes part of clinical practice. Explainability, value alignment, trust, and distributed responsibility are understood as produced through socio-technical practices. The framework complements existing HTA models through iterative engagement and stakeholder participation. Insights are illustrated through three radiology-facing AI projects showing how assessment criteria are enacted, resisted, and revised in context, and how the framework generates practice-based artefacts.

papers.title: Game Startup Business Sustainability Through Strategy, Innovation, and SDGs Orientation: A Bibliometric Analysis
papers.authors: Nur Azizah, Vanessa Gaffar, Lili Adi Wibowo, Tutik Inayati
papers.abstract: Background: The digital creative industry requires game startups to achieve business sustainability while responding to technological change, market uncertainty, platform dependence, and sustainability demands. However, literature remains fragmented across strategic management, innovation, entrepreneurship, competitive advantage, and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), leaving the integrated structure of game startup sustainability insufficiently mapped. Objective: This study aims to map the development, conceptual structure, thematic evolution, and collaborative landscape of game startup business sustainability research through strategy, innovation, competitive advantage, and SDGs orientation. Methods: A descriptive quantitative design using bibliometric analysis was employed. The dataset comprised 1,269 scientific publications retrieved from the Dimensions database for 2017–2026. Bibliographic metadata were analyzed using VOSviewer through annual publication trends, keyword co-occurrence, density visualization, temporal overlay analysis, and collaboration networks involving countries, authors, and organizations. Results: Publication output increased from 25 articles in 2017 to 275 in 2025, indicating growing scholarly attention. Keyword mapping identified interconnected themes involving business models, capabilities, performance, entrepreneurship, policy, investment, innovation, and sustainable development. Temporal analysis revealed emerging attention to artificial intelligence, transformation, governance, policymaking, investment, resilience, and infrastructure. International collaboration was broad, although contributions remained concentrated among established research systems, while Indonesia occupied a comparatively less central position. Conclusion: Game startup business sustainability constitutes a multidisciplinary research domain integrating strategic management, innovation, digital entrepreneurship, institutional ecosystems, and sustainable development. The findings provide a conceptual foundation for future empirical research on sustainable adaptive strategy, sustainable business model innovation, competitive advantage, and sustainability outcomes, particularly in emerging economies and policy development in Indonesia.

papers.title: Game Startup Business Sustainability Through Strategy, Innovation, and SDGs Orientation: A Bibliometric Analysis
papers.authors: Nur Azizah, Vanessa Gaffar, Lili Adi Wibowo, Tutik Inayati
