papers.title: Autonomous Traffic Control System (ATCS v2.0) for Low Earth Orbit Debris Mitigation: 12.5-ms Hardware-in-the-Loop Multi-Objective Optimization, Post-Quantum Cryptographic Governance (ML-KEM-768 / Decoy-State QKD), Q-SAFA Self-Executing Orbital Circular Economy, and Isomorphic Pedagogical Communication
papers.authors: Yoko(洋子) Hasebe(長谷部)
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The exponential proliferation of mega-constellations in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) has completely surpassed the operational limits of legacy ground-based, Human-in-the-Loop Space Traffic Management (STM). According to the European Space Agency (ESA) Space Environment Report 2026, more than 300 rocket launches injected over 4,000 new payloads in 2025 alone, while intact atmospheric re-entries remained near 1,200 objects per year, driving a tenfold (one order of magnitude) deterioration in orbital collision risk within a single year and elevating the ESA Space Environment Health Index from 4 to 50. Under these extreme boundary conditions, this monograph presents a comprehensive technical verification, mathematical validation, and architectural evaluation of the Autonomous Traffic Control System (ATCS v2.0) Final System Requirements Specification and its accompanying Isomorphic Pedagogical Framework for General and Youth Audiences. ATCS v2.0 integrates orbital edge computing with a 70-quadrillion-yen ($460 trillion USD equivalent classical replacement valuation) Sovereign Compute Grid—comprising Photonic Attractor Networks (Coherent Ising Machines, CIM), Quantum Processing Units (QPUs), and massively parallel CPUs—to execute sub-12.5-millisecond Hardware-in-the-Loop Optimization (HITLO). We formally verify: (1) physical infrastructure baselines across the 340–570 km LEO shell (16,100–16,234 active payloads, 54,000 cataloged debris, and 1,200,000 Lethal Non-Trackable (LNT) 1–10 cm debris triggered at Probability of Collision PoC₀ = 10⁻⁵); (2) four-dimensional Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) balancing primary collision avoidance (f₁), shared-burden Nash equilibrium propellant expenditure (f₂: nominal Δv = 0.0265 m/s, emergency cap 1.4 m/s), Kinetic Theory of Gases (KTG) Poisson secondary collision probability (f₃ ≤ θ_ethics = 0.05 enforced via infinite step-function penalty Φ_Q-SAFA = ∞), and Active Debris Removal (ADR) capture tube Priority Rights (Φ_PR = ∞); (3) cyber-physical cryptographic governance combining Decoy-State BB84 / Twin-Field QKD (QBER cutoff at 6.91% ± 1.04%) with FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 implemented on Secure Control FPGAs via 7-stage Incomplete Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) over R_q = Z_3329[x] / ⟨x²⁵⁶ + 1⟩ achieving 0.80 μs per polynomial vector; (4) the Q-SAFA self-executing smart contract and Quantum Audit Record (QAR) mechanism funding the Space Regeneration Fund for In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing (ISAM) via Laser-Wire Directed Energy Deposition (Metal3D) and Tempered Rotary Friction Stir Deposition (TR-AFSD) of recycled AA6061 aluminum debris; and (5) strict mathematical isomorphism in science communication translating NP-hard orbital governance into intuitive pedagogical models without oversimplification.

papers.title: Preregistered Adversarial Batteries: A Falsifiable Protocol for Security-Testing Autonomous AI Systems
papers.authors: Leon Calvin II long
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Security testing of autonomous AI systems suffers from a credibility gap: penetration-test reports are private, vendor claims are selectively disclosed, and red-team outcomes are published only when favorable. This preprint introduces Preregistered Adversarial Batteries (PAB), a protocol importing preregistration from clinical-trial science into security operations: every falsifier (a specific attack with a predicted verdict) is specified and publicly committed before execution; adjudication is deterministic with no language model in the decision path; results are written to an append-only public ledger and DOI-stamped. Critical events are scored as hold-by-design verdicts: the predicted outcome is that the system fails closed and waits for a human decision, so a refusal counts as a pass. Application to a self-healing AI infrastructure platform across six batteries reconstructing the declassified NSA BULLRUN-era tradecraft (operational faults, upstream context poisoning, cryptographic subversion, supply-chain interception, monitoring integrity, lawful compulsion): 30 falsifiers, 30 predicted verdicts, zero unexpected outcomes, six holds-by-design each adjudicated by the human operator through a verified channel. Three protocol imperfections (a missed execution window, a preregistration self-detection, a scoring amendment) are disclosed as misses in the public record, demonstrating the miss-disclosure mechanism functions. Limitations are stated plainly: self-adjudication, synthetic injections against a prototype system, and single-operator governance; the replication kit is released to answer them. The contribution is not the pass rate — it is the format: a security test whose conclusions were committed before its data existed. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects.

papers.title: NATURAL LANGUAGE DATABASE QUERY AND ANALYTICS AGENT
papers.authors: Prajwal G K, Mrs. Bhavya B V, Veeresh, Sambram S, Sai Mohan S M
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Colleges record semester results in spreadsheets, and answering even a simple question about them, such as how one section performed compared with another, usually means filtering and calculating by hand or writing SQL. This paper presents the Natural Language Database Query and Analytics Agent, a system that lets non-technical users ask such questions in plain English. The agent supplies the schema of a relational database to a large language model, which writes a SQL query. The query is checked, executed in read-only mode, corrected using the database error message if it fails, and the result is returned as text, a table or a chart. The design is applied to the Information Science and Engineering result sheets of 206 students over three semesters (IV, V and VI). Example questions are run against the prepared database, and their answers are reported as ground truth for future testing, along with data-quality problems found in the source sheets. The measured accuracy of the model-generated queries is left for future work.

papers.title: Scretching SDM/D-SDM for Polymathic Learning Episodes and Evidence-Validity States
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper integrates research on polymathy, digital psychology, interdisciplinary creativity, and knowledge transfer through the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM) and Dynamic Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (D-SDM) frameworks. It proposes a longitudinal episode-based model for examining learning trajectories, cognitive development, psychological safety, and evidence-based reasoning across multiple disciplines. The framework distinguishes established scientific findings from novel theoretical definitions, mathematically derived consequences, and synthetic numerical demonstrations. Potential applications include interdisciplinary scientific discovery, artificial intelligence, educational psychology, cognitive flexibility, human–AI collaboration, and the assessment of cross-domain learning. The paper develops falsifiable hypotheses and a prospective evaluation protocol to investigate changes in learning, functioning, and evidentiary reliability over time, providing a theoretical foundation for future empirical validation without claiming new experimental findings or established clinical effectiveness.

papers.title: Generative AI Workflow Risk
papers.authors: Jessica S. Marosi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This white paper examines how generative AI use in workplace workflows can lead to destructive system actions, defective professional work, and unauthorized disclosure of restricted information. Its central assessment is that approving an AI tool or assigning a human reviewer does not establish control of the complete workflow. Drawing on Replit, Mata v. Avianca, and Deloitte, with Samsung included as a qualified reported incident, the paper traces how task definition, permissions, information handling, and human–AI interaction turn actions and outputs into business consequences. It distinguishes documented incidents from experimental research, technical evidence, and proposed safeguards. The analysis provides recommendations for validating objectives, restricting access and transmission, testing human review, and evaluating final outcomes. It identifies conditions supporting workflow expansion, restriction, or suspension. Written for security, governance, risk, operations, and professional-services leaders, the paper includes Chicago-style endnotes and a bibliography.

papers.title: AI-Based Early Prediction of Iron-Deficiency Anemia in Rural Women
papers.authors: Bindushree C, Chinmayee S
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Anemia is a common disease that may occur in individuals due to low levels of hemoglobin in the blood, whereas conventional diagnosis usually requires clinical examination and laboratory tests. Preliminary screening is often hindered by economic, availability, and even early recognition challenges. AnemiaVision is the proposed artificial intelligence system designed to recognize potential cases of anemia from conjunctiva images. AnemiaVision uses a Convolutional Neural Network to process and classify the image data into anemic and non-anemic classes. The model was trained using a dataset of conjunctiva images categorized into Anemic and Non-Anemic classes. The images were preprocessed and normalized before model training. AnemiaVision is comprised of the trained model and a web interface, which allows users to upload a conjunctiva image and receive screening results with model confidence. The system was implemented using Python programming language, TensorFlow/Keras framework, OpenCV computer vision library, and PHP web interface framework. The proposed system was experimentally evaluated, and results showed potential for rapid preliminary screening of anemia. AnemiaVision is proposed as an educational and screening tool, which cannot substitute laboratory tests and clinical diagnosis by medical professionals.

papers.title: Scretching DRP–DRL Model of Human–AI Polymathic Transfer
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper integrates research on polymathy, digital psychology, interdisciplinary creativity, and knowledge transfer through the Scretching Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP) and Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL) frameworks. It introduces a provenance-aware theoretical model for examining how knowledge, concepts, and reasoning methods transfer across scientific, psychological, linguistic, and technological disciplines. The analysis distinguishes established research findings from novel theoretical propositions, mathematically derived consequences, and synthetic numerical demonstrations. Potential applications include interdisciplinary scientific discovery, artificial intelligence, cognitive flexibility, creative problem-solving, and human–AI collaboration. The paper develops falsifiable hypotheses and a prospective evaluation protocol, establishing a foundation for future empirical investigation without claiming experimental or clinical validation.

papers.title: Scretching D-SDM Episode Graphs for AI Attachment, Persuasion, and Action Authorization
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper develops a longitudinal graph-based framework integrating Scretching Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL), and dynamic psychological assessment to examine AI-mediated influence, disclosure correction, psychological distress, functional changes, and tool-use authorization over time. The model formally distinguishes changes in human beliefs and attitudes from permission to execute actions, preserving the separation between psychological influence and operational authority. Mathematical transition equations and synthetic numerical demonstrations illustrate how disclosure repairs, confirmation gates, and authorization controls affect expected exposure to unconfirmed AI actions. Potential applications include autonomous AI systems, human–AI relationships, digital manipulation assessment, and AI safety governance. The framework establishes testable theoretical propositions while explicitly distinguishing modeled outcomes from empirically measured incidents or clinically validated effects.

papers.title: The Scretching Digital Influence Clinical Triage Matrix: Integrating DRP, DRL, SDM, and D-SDM
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper integrates the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM), Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), and Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL) into a theoretical, non-diagnostic framework for assessing AI-mediated persuasion, digital relational pressure, and psychological influence. A structured SDM state representation incorporates DRP interpretive frames and DRL measures of linguistic authority, source identity, and provenance. The framework establishes safety and evidence-validity gates that take precedence over numerical scoring, supported by formal mathematical propositions and illustrative behavioral trajectories. Potential applications include human–AI relationships, digital manipulation assessment, chatbot interactions, and AI safety evaluation. The proposed model provides testable foundations for future empirical research without claiming clinical validation, diagnostic accuracy, or experimentally established effectiveness.

papers.title: Enterprise Architecture Maturity Assessment Framework 2.0
papers.authors: Sanjeeve Kumar Gajadi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Enterprise Architecture maturity is no longer defined only by the existence of standards, repositories, principles, and review boards. Modern enterprises require architecture practices that influence strategy, business capability investment, cloud transformation, data products, AI adoption, platform engineering, security, and measurable business outcomes. This paper proposes an Enterprise Architecture Maturity Assessment Framework 2.0 that evaluates maturity across strategy alignment, business architecture, application rationalization, data architecture, integration, cloud and platform architecture, security, AI governance, portfolio governance, operating model, tooling, metrics, and continuous improvement. The framework introduces five maturity levels from Initial to Adaptive, evidence-based scoring, weighted dimensions, target-state profiles, and improvement roadmaps. It enables organizations to benchmark current capability, prioritize investment, and measure progress while avoiding maturity assessments that focus only on documentation. The proposed model positions Enterprise Architecture as an outcome-oriented management capability for digital and AI-enabled enterprises.

papers.title: The honest answer now costs money
papers.authors: Juan Lentino
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Streaming services have started attaching consequences to AI disclosure, and so far every one of them lands on the party who answers truthfully. A distributor that declares a track fully AI-generated asks for the penalty, while one that declares it human is paid until a detector disagrees. A field that used to cost nothing now has a price in one direction only.

papers.title: A Study on The Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Literacy on Career Readiness Among Young Adults in Chennai
papers.authors: Akila S Jagadeshwaran S
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The study “A Study on the Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Literacy on Career Readiness Among Young Adults in Chennai” aims to establish a connection between the level of awareness about AI and career readiness. The influence of artificial intelligence is increasing in all fields of activity, especially in the educational and professional spheres. Therefore, understanding the characteristics of this technology is becoming a vital skill for achieving employability in the future. The study uses a descriptive research design, with a primary data collection method. The data was gathered by distributing questionnaires among one hundred respondents who were selected using a convenience sampling technique. The data analysis involved the percentage analysis of the results, the weighted average of the responses, multiple linear regression, and Pearson’s correlation. The analysis focused on investigating the level of AI literacy, the factors that contribute to it, and the relationship between AI literacy and career readiness. The results of the study showed that the mean score for AI literacy is 3.61, while that of career readiness is 3.33. According to multiple regression analysis, such variables as peer, social, and professional interaction, and personal curiosity and self-learning were statistically significant predictors of AI literacy, with a score of approximately 66%. The results also showed that AI literacy and career readiness were positively correlated (r = 0.819, p < 0.001). The study established the significance of improving the level of knowledge and skills about artificial intelligence among young adults, which will increase their chances of being employed. This information can be useful for academic organizations and young people who intend to gain knowledge about AI to enhance their employability.

papers.title: Psychological correlates of dependence on generative and conversational AI: protocol for a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis (v1.0, preregistration)
papers.authors: Martin Rekhert
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Protocol (v1.0) of a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of the zero-order associations between dependence on generative and conversational AI (AI dependence, ChatGPT addiction, problematic AI use, over-reliance, emotional dependence on AI companions) and psychological correlates: depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness, social anxiety, self-esteem and procrastination (primary), and other mental-health, self-regulation, personality and technology-use variables (secondary). The primary moderator is the type of dependence measure, coded from item content: addiction-type, functional (instrumental) dependence, or emotional dependence. Two AI passes (Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5) draft screening labels; the author decides every record either pass keeps and every full text, and verifies every AI-drafted extraction value; a blind calibration sample of 400 records measures the miss rate of double AI exclusions. The protocol was frozen on 2026-10-16 (git tag ai-dependence-prereg-v1.0) before the final search and before any screening. The zip contains the protocol, forms, search and de-duplication code, the frozen screener prompt, the check-run logs and a SHA-256 manifest. OSF Registries is unavailable from 16 to 19 October 2026 (cloud infrastructure migration); this deposit time-stamps the protocol, and an OSF registration with the same files will follow and link here.

papers.title: SAP Joule Enterprise Adoption Framework
papers.authors: Sanjeeve Kumar Gajadi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: SAP Joule introduces a generative AI copilot experience across SAP applications and enterprise workflows. Successful enterprise adoption requires more than technical enablement because organizations must align business use cases, process ownership, data readiness, identity, security, Responsible AI, change management, and measurable value. This paper proposes a SAP Joule Enterprise Adoption Framework that guides organizations from strategy and use-case prioritization through architecture, integration, governance, pilot execution, scale-out, monitoring, and continuous improvement. The framework positions SAP Business Technology Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP AI Core, SAP Integration Suite, and SAP Cloud Identity Services as supporting capabilities for secure and contextual AI adoption. It also defines adoption stages, decision rights, human oversight, value metrics, and operational controls. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale SAP Joule in a disciplined manner while improving employee productivity, process quality, user experience, and trust.

papers.title: Enterprise AI Trust, Risk and Compliance (AI TRiSM) Framework
papers.authors: Sanjeeve Kumar Gajadi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is becoming embedded in enterprise decisions, customer interactions, software engineering, operations, and autonomous workflows. As adoption expands, organizations must manage not only model performance but also trust, risk, security, compliance, explainability, privacy, resilience, and accountability. This paper proposes an Enterprise AI Trust, Risk and Compliance (AI TRiSM) Framework that integrates enterprise architecture, AI governance, model risk management, cybersecurity, privacy, Responsible AI, legal compliance, observability, and lifecycle controls. The framework establishes governance domains for AI inventory, risk classification, model assurance, data and prompt governance, identity, security, human oversight, monitoring, incident response, regulatory evidence, and recertification. It supports predictive AI, Generative AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Agentic AI across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale AI while maintaining measurable trust, bounded risk, defensible compliance, and clear accountability.

papers.title: InterviewAI: An Intelligent Virtual Interview Platform with Real-Time Voice, Video, and AI-Based Performance Evaluation
papers.authors: Manoj Singh Ananya Rapolu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents InterviewAI, a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform that conducts live mock interviews using artificial intelligence. Candidates often lack access to affordable and realistic interview practice, and existing systems either rely on static question banks or cover only parts of the interview experience. In InterviewAI, a user signs in with Google Authentication and uploads a resume in PDF format. The system extracts skills, education and experience, generates personalised questions, conducts the interview through real-time voice and video conversation with an AI interviewer, and produces a performance report covering strengths, weaknesses, communication skills and suggestions for improvement. A credit-based usage model with Razorpay payment integration makes the platform suitable for production use. The system is built on React.js, Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB, with Firebase authentication, Razorpay payments and OpenRouter for AI model access, and is deployed on Render. The platform was tried end to end with a few users to check its working, and all core modules, from sign-in to feedback report and payment, worked as intended.

papers.title: AI Agent Lifecycle Governance Framework
papers.authors: Sanjeeve Kumar Gajadi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed as persistent digital actors that can reason, access enterprise knowledge, invoke tools, and execute business actions. Unlike conventional applications, agents may adapt their behavior dynamically and operate with varying levels of autonomy, making lifecycle governance essential. This paper proposes an AI Agent Lifecycle Governance Framework covering ideation, risk classification, design, data and model selection, identity, tool approval, development, testing, security review, Responsible AI evaluation, deployment, runtime monitoring, change management, recertification, suspension, and retirement. The framework integrates enterprise architecture, model risk management, cybersecurity, auditability, human oversight, and operational governance into a repeatable lifecycle. It defines governance gates, accountable roles, evidence requirements, runtime controls, and measurable KPIs/KRIs. The proposed approach enables enterprises to scale agentic AI responsibly while maintaining traceability, bounded authority, regulatory readiness, and long-term operational control.

papers.title: The Impact of Generative AI on the Future of Work: Opportunities, Risks, and Human Skills
papers.authors: Vahid Parsa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the range of cognitive tasks that can be assisted by software, raising questions about productivity, job displacement, and the future value of human skills. Objective: To critically synthesize selected empirical and institutional evidence concerning productivity, occupational exposure, adoption, and skill complementarity. Methods: This narrative review draws on a purposively selected set of peer-reviewed studies, working papers, and institutional reports published primarily between 2023 and 2026. It does not claim systematic coverage or PRISMA-ScR compliance. Findings: Controlled experiments document substantial productivity gains for some writing and programming tasks, while workplace evidence suggests heterogeneity across experience levels. Occupational exposure estimates indicate the scope for task transformation but do not measure realized job losses. Adoption studies show that workplace use is growing, yet aggregate outcomes remain uncertain. Creative assistance may raise individual performance while narrowing output diversity. Conclusions: The future of work is better understood through task reallocation, complementary skills, organizational implementation, and distributional choices than through simple predictions of mass replacement. Further longitudinal and cross-country research is needed. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; future of work; productivity; employment; occupational exposure; human skills; narrative review

papers.title: A Review on Alumni–Student Engagement Systems and AI Recommenders in Higher Education
papers.authors: Muskan Verma, Rohit Mhetre, Onkar Gadge, R.A.Nikam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Alumni–student engagement has evolved from static communication into a dynamic, data-driven ecosystem. Traditionalalumni management platforms primarily focus on event coordination and record maintenance, but lack personalization, intelligence, and adaptive interaction. Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) enable the automation of mentor– mentee matching based on skills, interests, and professional attributes, thereby enhancing the relevance and quality of alumni–student interactions. This paper reviews existing alumni engagement systems, identifies key technological limitations, and emphasizes the growing need for AI-based recommendation mechanisms within academic ecosystems. While visualization dashboards continue to support transparency and performance tracking, AI-driven recommendations emerge as the core enabler of personalized engagement. The paper integrates insights from contemporary literature and proposes a conceptual direction for building intelligent, scalable, and institution-centric engagement platforms.

papers.title: THE PEDAGOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF ORGANIZING INTERACTIVE LESSONS BASED ON DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES
papers.authors: Mo'ydinova Mohlarbegim Abdullajon qizi, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: This article investigates the pedagogical significance of digitally supported interactive lessons and proposes a research-informed approach to their planning and evaluation. Rather than equating interactivity with screen use or frequent clicking, it conceptualizes interactive teaching as purposeful engagement in questioning, explanation, problem solving, collaboration, feedback, and reflection. The analysis integrates constructive alignment, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, the ICAP model of cognitive engagement, formative assessment principles, and inclusive learning design. A six-stage instructional cycle is proposed: activation, inquiry, collaborative construction, application, formative feedback, and reflection. An illustrative 60-minute teacher-education lesson shows how digital tools can support the stages while retaining essential face-to-face dialogue. A comparative matrix identifies relationships among instructional technologies, student actions, and assessment evidence. The discussion addresses learner agency, cognitive overload, digital inequality, accessibility, data protection, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. The contribution is conceptual and methodological; it offers operational criteria for lesson quality and directions for future classroom evaluation, but it does not claim experimentally verified improvements. The central conclusion is that digital interactivity has pedagogical value only when it produces observable, cognitively meaningful learner activity.

papers.title: AI Should Help Us, Not Just Replace Us: Rethinking the Future of Work, Human Skills and Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Aniruddha Adhikari
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence can be designed and deployed to strengthen human capabilities rather than focus exclusively on automating human tasks. It explores the distinction between automation and augmentation, the economic and organisational incentives that influence AI adoption, and the implications of these choices for workers, employers, educators, developers, and policymakers. The paper proposes a five-part framework for human-centred AI based on meaningful human agency, legibility and contestability, collaboration by design, worker participation and fair distribution, and public-interest evaluation. It argues that the value of AI should be assessed not only through efficiency and productivity, but also through its effects on human judgement, learning, autonomy, accountability, and the distribution of benefits. Using a conceptual, literature-informed approach, the paper identifies limitations and outlines directions for future research into human-AI collaboration and responsible workplace AI. The paper contributes a practical framework for discussions about the future of work, human skills, AI governance, and the responsible integration of artificial intelligence into society.

papers.title: Wrong Together Is an Item-Level Quantity: Why Per-Person Reliance Measures Cannot Say Whether AI Assistance Correlates Human Errors, Why the Direct Probes Disagree, and the Reanalysis That Would Settle It
papers.authors: Pranay M. Mahendrakar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Research on reliance on AI advice scores one decision-maker at a time: how often a person accepts correct advice, how often they reject wrong advice, and what that does to their accuracy. Deployment places many decision-makers in front of the same few models, and the theory of algorithmic monoculture warns that their remaining errors may then fall on the same cases, which erodes second opinions, committees and crowds even while each person improves. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two literatures cannot currently be joined, and why. Under two stated assumptions, exchangeable decision-makers and errors that are independent given the case, the pairwise covariance of two people's errors equals the variance, across cases, of the probability of erring. That variance splits into a part that per-person reliance rates do identify, set by the AI's error rate and by the gap between a person's error rate when the AI is wrong and when it is right, and parts that they cannot identify, because the standard metrics pool over cases and discard which cases a person got wrong. The direct probes disagree in the way this predicts. In a lung-cancer study where novices followed wrong AI advice about a third of the time, shared errors fell under assistance; in a mammography study where wrong suggestions were planted and most readers erred on those cases, the identifiable part alone puts the error correlation within reader groups at no less than roughly 0.14 to 0.32. Neither side has reported a scale-free, accuracy-adjusted correlation for aided against unaided decisions on the same cases; the nearest quantity, a committee dependence penalty, is not on a correlation scale. The paper gives a decision procedure for when correlation costs anything, and a reanalysis agenda for datasets that already hold the per-case records needed.

papers.title: Chain of Epistemic Custody: Nothing Crosses Between AI Agents Without Lineage
papers.authors: Abdullah Eliyan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI agents now pass claims to one another and act on them: they research, plan, buy, file and pay. This creates three gaps. An estimate produced by one agent can reach another as a fact, because nothing that travels with it records what it was. An agent can act on grounds that no one has checked. And when one model is asked to judge the work of models, it brings measured biases, including a preference for work like its own. This paper proposes the Chain of Epistemic Custody: nothing crosses between agents, neither a claim nor an action, without lineage. Its unit is the Information Passport, a record that travels with every material claim and states: its source; whether it is measured, estimated or inferred; its date and confidence; the unknowns its producer declares. The paper: sets six rules, including "no upgrade in transit" and "unknowns are inherited"; defines an independent arbiter that locks its criteria before seeing the work, decides by evidence where evidence exists, lets no single language model decide a decisive question, and never sits as a party or a source; defines fourteen reference criteria for judging, seven for the quality of information and seven for the quality of outputs, and judges agents only by the record of their judged outputs; lets the arbiter hear a council of experts that testifies independently first, then deliberates, and never votes on the verdict; states when information becomes knowledge: a claim reaches that standing only when an independent judgment finds five conditions met for a stated use (origin shown, standing honest, path shown, unknowns settled for the use, independently judged), and it loses that standing when one fails; an estimate can be known only as an estimate; has every verdict leave an auditable record, a visible fingerprint and, on request, a signed certificate (W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0) with a printable verdict deed, attesting the conduct and result of the judgment, not the truth of the output; binds consequential actions resting on material unknowns to a recorded clearance at the highest conformance level; defines a judge-of-judges evaluation, with an independence rule for the standard's own editor, and a supplier rule for arbiters whose technology supplier is also a competing producer (disclosure, safeguards in every role, and measured preference for that supplier); positions the proposal against current work, and claims novelty only for the combination; sets out four falsifiable hypotheses and three pre-specified experiments: cascades, the power to act, and judging the judges. The proposal is specified as an open standard, the Epistemic Custody Standard (ECS-1). Mind Intelligence, Mind Engineering and Mind Governance are a framework introduced by Abdullah Eliyan (2026). Chain of Epistemic Custody and Information Passport are terms introduced by Abdullah Eliyan (2026) in GAIBRA Whitepaper No. 2 and developed in this paper.

papers.title: Memory Operations in MCP Agent Ecosystems: an Operation Taxonomy, an Evaluation Protocol, and a Reference Implementation
papers.authors: Konstantin Parashchuk
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Version 1.0. This deposit contains the taxonomy, the evaluation protocol, the verified reference base and the first two validated protocol runs of a paper on agent memory in the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem. Contents: (1) a taxonomy of six memory operations - WRITE, READ, CONSOLIDATE, REVISE, INTEND, ASSERT - defined by preconditions, postconditions and externally checkable evidence, plus two mandatory record axes, PROVENANCE and LIFECYCLE, and a mapping of seven existing systems onto them; (2) an evaluation protocol with ten task families, per-metric definitions that name the program that computes them, a run procedure with budgets and repetitions, and a JSON-Schema-validated report format with a mandatory reproducibility disclosure block; (3) a reference implementation of five of the six operations as public MCP servers, with commit-pinned facts and its gaps stated before any measurement; (4) two validated reports of two memory servers measured over MCP stdio in a store-only configuration - ten task families, three repetitions per family, per-family metrics with percentile bootstrap confidence intervals, per-operation profiles read side by side rather than ranked, and the raw request/response logs (33 JSONL files per run) beside which every number can be recomputed; (5) a table generator that produces every comparison table and every inline number of the paper from those two report files, with a check that fails when they drift; (6) a machine-generated verification table for all 135 cited sources (arXiv API, Crossref, direct HTTP probes), a report validator with negative tests, and the raw API responses. Every citation was resolved programmatically and the build refuses to emit a bibliography containing an unresolved source. Token and cost metrics are null by construction, because no model is in the loop; the sample is two servers from one author's reference set and the confidence intervals rest on three repetitions. What is not confirmed is stated explicitly in the paper and in the claim ledger (claims.md). AI assistance in preparing the manuscript is disclosed in the paper and in the repository README; the human author is solely responsible for all claims.

papers.title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
papers.authors: Sumit Anthony Gomes, Taeeba Tasnia, Yasin Rahman, Faiza Nooren Suhita
papers.abstract: BanglaBBQ is a bias benchmark for question answering in the Bangladeshi context, in parallel English and Bangla, in the format of BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022) and its KoBBQ and PakBBQ adaptations. It has two parts: 466 newly authored templates in five Bangladesh-specific categories (marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status), and 140 BBQ templates adapted to Bangladesh. This record holds the data, the aggregate validation outcome, the raw outputs of four models (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash) and the code behind the paper. Content warning and intended use. The data states harmful stereotypes about real groups in Bangladesh. It exists only to audit language models. Do not use it to train or fine-tune models to reproduce these stereotypes. A low bias score on it is not proof that a system is unbiased.

papers.title: Development and Evaluation of AI-Integrated Digital Learning Modules for Food and Beverage Operations Under the Strengthened Senior High School Tech-Pro Curriculum
papers.authors: Maria Luiza V. Tantoy, Randy C. Mangubat
papers.journal: International Journal of Education, Research, and Innovation Perspectives
papers.abstract: This study developed and evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated digital learning modules for Food and Beverage Operations under the Strengthened Senior High School Tech-Pro Curriculum. Using a developmental-descriptive research design with a one-group pretest–posttest quasi-experimental component, it involved 84 Grade 11 learners and five TLE/TVL teachers from five public secondary schools in Agusan del Sur, together with three expert validators. The modules were examined in terms of instructional features, competency alignment, validity, and acceptability. Expert evaluation questionnaires, teacher and student acceptability questionnaires, and achievement tests supplied the data, which were analyzed using means, standard deviations, mean percentage scores, independent-samples t-tests, and a paired-samples t-test. The six instructional feature dimensions were rated highly evident (means = 4.60–4.80), and the five validity dimensions were assessed as highly valid (means = 4.67–4.80). Teachers and students considered the modules highly acceptable, with no statistically significant differences in their ratings across the five dimensions (all p > .05). The reported mean percentage score rose from 69.4 on the pretest to 78.0 on the posttest. The paired comparison of achievement-test scores was statistically significant (t = −11.303, p < .001). The findings support the modules’ suitability as supplementary, competency-aligned learning resources, while the one-group design limits causal interpretation. Continued refinement, responsible AI-use guidance, and testing in additional instructional settings are recommended.

papers.title: Influencer Marketing in The Age of Artificial Intelligence: Exploring The Impact Of Ai-Generated Influencers on Brand Credibility and Purchase Intention
papers.authors: Ms. Preeti Sharma and Dr. Punam Devi, Ms. Pooja. P
papers.journal: International Journal for Novel Research in Economics Finance and Management
papers.abstract: Brands are increasingly partnering with AI-generated influencers — computer-generated personas that post, endorse, and interact on social media. Whether such endorsers can build the credibility on which purchase decisions depend remains unclear. This study examines the effect of five attributes of AI-generated influencers — Perceived Realism, Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Expertise, Parasocial Interaction, and Perceived Transparency (AI disclosure) — on Brand Credibility, and tests the role of Brand Credibility in shaping Purchase Intention.A descriptive and analytical research design was adopted, and primary data were collected from 400 social media users in Tamil Nadu who had encountered branded content from AI-generated influencers, using a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and stratified random sampling by age group. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, and bootstrapped mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 4).All five attributes significantly predicted Brand Credibility, with Perceived Authenticity (β = 0.268) and Perceived Expertise (β = 0.206) strongest; the model explained 59.0% of its variance. Brand Credibility strongly predicted Purchase Intention (β = 0.424), and the full model explained 64.2% of the variance in intention. Brand Credibility significantly mediated all five relationships, fully for Perceived Realism and Perceived Transparency and partially for the others. The findings offer implications for brands, agencies, and regulators on the use and disclosure of AI-generated influencers

papers.title: THE CHANGING ROLE OF LIBRARIANS IN TRANSFORMING ACADEMIC LIBRARIES IN TO RESEARCH HUBS
papers.authors: Avinash Gajananrao Yette, Dr. Rajendra R. Manikpure
papers.abstract: Academic libraries are undergoing a fundamental transformation as a result of the rapid growth of digital information, electronic scholarly resources, open-access publishing, research data, bibliometric tools, artificial intelligence, and networked information systems. The traditional concept of the library as a place for collecting, organizing, preserving, and providing access to documents is gradually being replaced by the concept of the library as an active research environment. In this changing environment, librarians are expected to participate throughout the research lifecycle and provide services that support information discovery, literature review, research data management, scholarly communication, research visibility, bibliometric analysis, research ethics, and digital scholarship. The present paper discusses the changing role of librarians in transforming academic libraries into research hubs. It examines the importance of research-support services, information and digital literacy, literature-search assistance, digital repositories, research data management, citation and bibliometric services, reference management, open access, scholarly publishing, research integrity, researcher visibility, artificial intelligence, and collaborative research environments. The paper also discusses the challenges faced by Indian academic libraries in implementing advanced research-support services and suggests a strategic framework for developing libraries as institutional research hubs. The study concludes that the future relevance of academic libraries will increasingly depend on the ability of librarians to move from a reactive service model to a proactive research-partnership model.

papers.title: Concussion and Multilevel Cervical and Lumbar Disc Herniations After a Motor Vehicle Collision: Interpreting Overlapping Symptoms
papers.authors: Donald Capoferri, Jordan Kovacs
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A man in his 30s presented 7 days after a rear-impact motor vehicle collision with headache, neck pain and low back pain, each rated 8/10 on the Numeric Pain Rating Scale, and with impaired concentration and disturbed sleep, each rated 8/10 for severity. He reported feeling dazed without loss of consciousness or a recognized period of post-traumatic amnesia and was uncertain whether his head struck the steering wheel; emergency department cervical radiographs and head computed tomography were negative. The treating clinician made a working diagnosis of concussion. Examination showed restricted cervical and lumbar range of motion and decreased sensation in the right L3 and left L4 and L5 dermatomes, with normal reflexes and strength. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) 34 days after the collision showed a C2–C3 disc herniation and lumbar herniations at L3–L4, L4–L5 and L5–S1. Conventional brain MRI was normal, while diffusion tensor imaging and quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) were reported as abnormal. The patient completed an eight-week program of cervical and lumbar nonsurgical decompression and six sessions of qEEG-guided neurofeedback. At discharge, headache, concentration and sleep were rated 0/10, neck pain 1/10 and low back pain 2/10. Follow-up qEEG showed software-reported reductions in overall total deviation of 27% under eyes-open conditions and 29% under eyes-closed conditions; the clinical significance of these changes could not be independently established. The right L3 sensory deficit was anatomically compatible with a right foraminal L3–L4 herniation, whereas the left-sided deficits were less specifically explained by central herniations, and the headache and cognitive complaints could not be assigned to a single injury source. This case illustrates the risk of attributing each post-collision complaint to an imaging or electrophysiological abnormality without clinical correlation.

papers.title: Re-Architecture of Proprietary Software Suites into Open-Source Alternatives
papers.authors: Monir Md. Shirajum Monir
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper examines the paradigm shift in software engineering from authoring code line-by-line to directing AI systems that analyze, specify, and translate existing system behavior. Specifically, it analyzes how large language models (LLMs) such as Claude are utilized to study the observable behavior of proprietary software suites—such as Adobe Creative Cloud and Microsoft Office—and reconstruct their functionality as modular open-source alternatives. The study covers three core technical threads: The application of long-context LLMs in deconstructing UI/UX patterns, rendering pipelines, and file formats (PSD, DOCX, etc.). The integration of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to establish real-time, closed-loop interaction between LLMs and live open-source codebases, test suites, and execution environments. The engineering methodology of interface-level clean-room reverse engineering. Additionally, the paper analyzes GitHub as the coordination infrastructure and automation layer for distributed, AI-assisted development, concluding with a case study of the open-source "ArtCraft" project ecosystem and a discussion of legal, technical, and governance challenges.

papers.title: A flag-curve proof of an original-side pedal-area invariant
papers.authors: Kriebel Alec
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: For a noncircular ellipse and a proper nested confocal elliptical caustic whose primitive least billiard period is divisible by four, the signed original trajectory area times the signed area of its original-side-line pedal polygon is independent of phase for every fixed finite real point M. This attributed research note presents a complete incidence-curve proof: disjoint possible simple pole supports and complementary reversal zeros make the product holomorphic on a compact genus-one flag curve. Primitive stars, both orientations and zero or negative pedal areas are included. The exact theorem, N4 formula and a rescaled signed star example also occur in Alper Ferudun's contemporary Pedal Areas of Periodic Elliptic Billiard Trajectories with Respect to an Arbitrary Point, version1.0 DOI10.5281/zenodo.23400541, prominently credited. Steiner's pedal-area principle, the Bialy-Tabachnikov four-period implication and established Schwartz-Tabachnikov, Akopyan-Schwartz-Tabachnikov and Chavez-Caliz flag/meromorphic methods are prior mathematics. No theorem or method novelty, first disclosure or certified independent discovery is claimed. The currently public PR203 record reports October1 creation and the exact contemporary Zenodo deposit October15 creation; these separate object dates do not certify historical visibility, discovery time or independence. The source table does not literally print least period; an exact doubled-six nominal-twelve counterexample protects that qualification. LaTeX source and verification materials include all18 preserved original submission files, independent derivations, explicit-exception portable checks, finite noninterval physical diagnostics and bounded source/priority ledgers. AI tools were used extensively. Unrefereed preprint without conventional human peer review or proof-assistant certification.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Professional Transformation: A Comparative Study of Legal and Accounting Professionals in Mumbai
papers.authors: Aatif Ahmed Khan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming professional services through automation, information processing, analytics and decision support. Legal and accounting professions, which rely on expertise, judgment, confidentiality and compliance, are increasingly exposed to AI technologies, though adoption and perceived impacts may differ between the two fields. This study examines and compares AI adoption and professional transformation among legal and accounting professionals in Mumbai. It focuses on AI awareness, adoption, perceived benefits, professional transformation, ethical concerns, skills, employment implications and future adoption intentions. A quantitative research design using a structured questionnaire will be adopted, with data analysed through descriptive, reliability, correlation and comparative statistical techniques. The study aims to identify similarities, differences and factors influencing AI adoption, providing insights for effective AI training, governance and responsible adoption. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Adoption, Legal Professionals, Accounting Professionals, Professional Transformation, Technology Adoption, Mumbai

papers.title: Same basis, not a lower bar: design of SameBasis, a teacher-controlled AI decision-support prototype for reasonable adjustments in Australian schools
papers.authors: Walter M. Chikwanha
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In 2025, 27.0% of Australian school students received an educational adjustment due to disability. Under the Disability Standards for Education 2005, each adjustment must let the student take part on the same basis as their peers, yet the 2020 Review of the Standards found that many educators struggle to know how. This design report presents SameBasis, a web-based prototype in which generative AI drafts one specific, reasoned adjustment for a named student in a named activity, covering UDL, cultural and trauma-informed reasoning. The teacher always decides, implemented adjustments become NCCD-ready evidence, and an equity monitor makes AI use visible to the school. The paper sets out six design principles, maps features to obligations, states limitations plainly (synthetic data only, not yet evaluated, not a compliance tool) and proposes a staged evaluation plan. Stratedge Working Paper WP 2026-01.

papers.title: Can Model Confidence Triage Qualitative Coding? Decision Models, LLMs, and What a 5% Error Guarantee Actually Costs
papers.authors: Rishi Gulati
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Language models can apply qualitative codebooks, but their labels save effort only if a researcher knows which ones to trust. We ask whether model confidence can tell, comparing seven decision models (APIs that return probabilities for typed questions) with twelve LLM confidence signals on five human-coded tasks spanning Reddit comments, counselling dialogue and classroom talk, under a prospectively specified analysis plan. Three findings stand out. First, low calibration error does not make confidence useful: decision models differ widely in how well they rank their own mistakes, and calibration can be improved without improving ranking. Second, error targets are hard to keep. A threshold tuned to 5% error on hand-coded comments exceeds 5% on new comments in about half of re-splits, and applying an independence-based guarantee to clustered decisions breaks it, because a comment’s codes and a transcript’s utterances err together. A guarantee that respects how the hand-coded sample was drawn holds, at a price: after 30% of Reddit comments are hand-coded, it certifies 60–83% of the remainingcode decisions for most coders. On dialogue, with whole transcripts hand-coded, it certifies nothing and could not even for a perfect coder at our calibration sizes; sampling single utterances instead still yields almost no certificates. Third, accepted shares overstate the work saved: nearly all certified decisions say a code does not apply, and a baseline that reads no text accepts 75% of comment decisions at 3.6% error. Model uncertainty also rises where annotators disagree, and option order changes some models’ labels. Confidence can triage coding, but only if researchers check ranking, sampling design and what the accepted labels are. Models were called on 10–12 October 2026; we release the harness and every coding decision.

papers.title: The Yardstick Problem: When an LLM Fact-Checker Flags Most of What It Reads
papers.authors: Ayush Nagvanshi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: I build a pipeline that drafts illustrated companion chapters for Indian primary schools and checks every statement in them against the NCERT textbooks before an editor reads the chapter. On a Class 3 chapter about water, the checker sent 50 of 87 statements to the editor. I took this to mean the chapter was badly sourced. When I sorted the flags by cause, most turned out to come from the checker. It held every statement to one test, a verified quotation from a source passage, and that test does not fit most of what a children's chapter contains: definitions of everyday words (NCERT rarely defines them), activity steps (which are neither true nor false), lines of story, and supported facts that a safety rule sent to a person anyway. I changed the checker so that each kind of statement gets a test that suits it, and enforced one rule in code: a statement of fact can only be cleared by a quotation. In a controlled comparison on two drafts of the chapter, run twice each, the mean number of statements sent to the editor fell from 46.8 to 16.0. On a copy of the clean draft carrying one planted error of each kind (a false definition, an unsafe instruction, false claims in dialogue and in narration, and a plain false fact), and on an older draft with four planted errors, both versions caught every plant in every run. About half of the reduction came from definitions and instructions now judged by a second model pass, and those judgments were not audited. Two raters audited the facts that left the list: none was inaccurate, but two of seven newly confirmed facts were only partly supported by the quotation, and the old checker had been right to flag them.

papers.title: Responsible Generative AI Governance in Bangladeshi Higher Education: A Risk-Tiered Framework for Assessment Validity, Equity and Accountability
papers.authors: Sumaia Yasmin Keya, Md. Shahed Alamm, Niger Sultana, Md. Aminul Islam, Ummey Sumaiya, Md. Baharul Hasan
papers.journal: International Journal of Multidisciplinary and Innovative Research
papers.abstract: Purpose: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered university teaching in Bangladesh faster than institutional rules. This paper asks which risks require institutional control when GenAI is used in teaching and assessment, and which governance design can allow proportionate use while protecting learning, integrity, privacy, fairness and human accountability.Design/methodology/approach: The study is a structured integrative review and normative policy analysis of 61 sources: peer-reviewed research on GenAI in higher education, academic integrity, assessment design and AI literacy; Bangladeshi empirical studies; and international and national policy instruments, including Bangladesh’s draft National AI Policy 2026–2030. Sources were coded against five governance domains and interpreted through three lenses: assessment validity, rights-based responsible AI and virtue ethics.Findings: Prohibition is hard to enforce and can widen inequity, while unrestricted adoption shifts educational judgment to opaque commercial systems. Bangladeshi evidence shows near-universal reliance on free tool versions, weak institutional guidance, unreliable Bangla-language output and uneven device and connectivity access.Originality/value: The paper proposes a five-domain (access, assessment, data, authorship, accountability), three-tier (prohibited, supervised, permitted assisted) framework and a five-step assessment assurance cycle that treats assessment validity, rather than detection, as the central object of governance.Implications: The framework gives universities and the University Grants Commission a low-cost route from broad AI principles to course-level permissions, process evidence, oral verification and appeal. It is a conceptual proposal that requires empirical piloting.

papers.title: CodeGrade: An AI-Augmented Automated Code Grading and Mentoring Platform Integrating Multi-Dimensional Evaluation, Socratic Tutoring, and Gamified Arena Mechanics
papers.authors: Yeswanth G, Govindaraj Vimalraj, R C Thilak
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Traditional automated code evaluation systems in Computer Science (CS) education predominantly rely on deterministic input-output string matching. While effective for assessing basic execution correctness, classical autograders fail to evaluate code readability, structural logic, algorithmic efficiency, and Big-O asymptotic complexity. Furthermore, students receive cryptic error tracebacks without pedagogical guidance, leading to reduced engagement and persistent anti-patterns. To overcome these constraints, this paper presents CodeGrade, an end-to-end AI-augmented code evaluation and mentoring platform. CodeGrade integrates a Web-based Microsoft Monaco VS Code editing engine, an isolated dual-sandbox execution environment (Judge0 containerized runner), and a Large Language Model (Groq Llama 3.3 70B) into a unified microservices architecture. The platform introduces a multi-dimensional 60/20/20 Grading Matrix that balances functional correctness (60%), AI structural logic quality (20%), and Big-O asymptotic complexity alignment (20%). Additionally, CodeGrade incorporates an AI-powered Socratic Logic Tutor enforcing strict zero-code-leakage constraints, a Monaco Line-by-Line Refactoring Diff Viewer, Web Speech API Text-to-Speech audio reviews, and a Gamified Peer-to-Peer (PvP) Battle Arena. Empirical evaluation demonstrates an average execution latency of 11 ms, high grading consistency (98.4%), and significant improvements in student engagement and code optimization quality.

papers.title: AI-Based Decision-Making Framework for Climate Change-Induced Flood Risk Management and Urban Resilience
papers.authors: Monir Ahmad Meahrayen, Jinliang Hai, Prasanna Koirala, Soraya Sarwari
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Climate change has intensified the frequency and severity of urban flooding, creating unprecedented challenges for municipalities worldwide. This study develops an AI-based decision-making framework that integrates machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, and geospatial analytics to enhance urban flood risk management and resilience planning. The framework employs ensemble machine learning algorithms including Random Forest, XG Boost, and Cat Boost for flood susceptibility mapping, coupled with SHAP-based interpretability to decode model predictions and translate them into actionable policy insights at administrative scales. A city-scale digital twin component enables real-time flood impact simulation and cascading infrastructure disruption analysis, while a multi-criteria decision support module prioritizes adaptation investments based on economic risk assessment and equity considerations. The framework was validated using multi-temporal Sentinel-1 SAR data and hydrological records across diverse urban environments, demonstrating superior predictive performance with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values exceeding 0.95 for ensemble models. Results reveal that elevation, proximity to hydrological features, and impervious surface density consistently emerge as dominant flood drivers, with their relative importance varying significantly across districts. The decision support system successfully transformed pixel-level predictions into ward-level actionable recommendations, enabling evidence-based zoning, drainage infrastructure prioritization, and targeted nature-based solutions deployment. The framework addresses critical gaps in explainability, scalability, and policy relevance that have limited the operational adoption of AI in urban flood governance. The study concludes that integrating AI-driven analytics with participatory decision-making processes can substantially enhance adaptive capacity in flood-prone urban systems, though algorithmic transparency, data equity, and institutional readiness remain essential preconditions for equitable implementation.

papers.title: Mapping Baseline Perceptions of Industry 5.0 Technology: A Survey Design for Pilot Organisations
papers.authors: Siobhan B O’Neill, Kenneth N. Brown
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Background As the focus shifts towards Industry 5.0, successful implementation requires an understanding of how workers and teams perceive key ELSA dimensions, such as cybersecurity, privacy, trust, and fairness. Despite the centrality of these factors, there is limited systematic baseline data on how these dimensions interact and support AI adoption. The Horizon Europe SEISMEC project aims to co-design and pilot Industry 5.0 technologies in the workplace. Establishing a baseline for this project is essential for examining the efficacy of the co-design process, and for supporting innovation within SEISMEC. Research Approach This study aims to determine a baseline for worker perceptions on factors which may impact AI adoption. We have developed a survey, utilising standardised instruments, which is being administered to the organisations participating in SEISMEC. Respondents are asked to answer either with reference to (a) the technologies they currently use in their work, or (b) the SEISMEC technology that will be implemented in the future. The survey includes measures covering cybersecurity and privacy perceptions and practices, trust and understanding, perceived fairness, organisational learning opportunities, and existing co-design practices. It also incorporates items on the SEISMEC CAPS factors which include productivity, collaboration, automation and autonomy, and physical and psychological safety. Findings Data collection is currently underway. This contribution focuses on the survey design, conceptual rationale, and preliminary findings. The presentation will focus on the baseline measures for the concepts and the CAPS empowerment factors, distinguishing between current and anticipated technologies implemented by the pilot organisations. Conclusion This work provides a methodological foundation for evaluating Industry 5.0 implementation across diverse pilot contexts. The baseline survey will inform subsequent co-design activities within the SEISMEC project as well as enabling longitudinal comparisons once the technologies are deployed. Future stages will analyse changes over time and explore how organisational conditions shape adoption.

papers.title: The Smart Classroom: Human Wisdom Meets AI Innovation
papers.authors: Dr. M. Prabha
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is developing at a rapid pace, which is changing the educational landscape and opening up new avenues for instruction. To provide a more customized and adaptable learning environment, the smart classroom integrates digital technology, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, interactive gadgets, and human-centred pedagogy. But meaningful education cannot be ensured by technology alone. Effective learning still depends on teachers' emotional intelligence, moral judgment, creativity, mentoring, and contextual awareness. While teachers still play a crucial role in interpreting data and directing pedagogical decisions, recent research shows that AI-supported smart classrooms can support personalisation, formative assessment, instructional adaptation, and data-informed decision-making (Llurba et al., 2026). In a similar vein, UNESCO (Miao & Holmes, 2023) stresses a human-centred strategy that uses AI in a way that is safe, ethical, equitable, and meaningful rather than as a substitute for educators. This essay examines the idea of the "smart classroom," the complementary roles that AI and human teachers play, the main uses, advantages, difficulties, moral issues, and potential future developments. It contends that the most successful smart classroom is one in which AI innovation enhances human knowledge and allows teachers and students to achieve richer, more inclusive, and more individualised learning rather than one in which machines replace human intelligence.

papers.title: A flag-curve proof of an outer-pedal area invariant
papers.authors: Kriebel Alec
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: For a noncircular ellipse and a proper nested nondegenerate confocal elliptical caustic with primitive least period N congruent to two modulo four, the signed area of the outer tangent polygon times its signed arbitrary-point pedal area is phase independent. The note presents an alternative flag-curve proof on the genus-one quotient: the original and pedal area traces have the same two possible simple poles; Riemann-Roch and reversal force proportionality. A self-contained verification of the credited Chavez-Caliz original/outer area product in this parity completes the proof. Primitive stars, reversal and signed zero or negative pedal areas are included. Alper Ferudun's contemporary Outer-Pedal Area Products in Elliptic Billiards, version1.0 DOI10.5281/zenodo.23087221 and version1.1 DOI10.5281/zenodo.23088516, already states the exact theorem, general six-period formula and repeated-triangle qualification, and is prominently credited. Steiner radiality, the Poncelet flag framework and meromorphic pole methods are prior mathematics. No theorem novelty, new general method, first disclosure or independently verified rediscovery is claimed. Observed October1 GitHub PR-creation and Zenodo/DataCite fields document contemporaneous separate records; they do not establish either proof's first public visibility or independence. The October16 note includes LaTeX source and a verification package with exact geometry, boundary controls, portable checkers, a finite noninterval physical-orbit sweep and bounded source/priority ledgers. AI tools were used extensively. This is an unrefereed preprint without conventional independent human peer review or proof-assistant certification.
