papers.title: Fairness, Trust and Understanding As Preconditions and Predictors for Industry 5.0 AI Adoption
papers.authors: Siobhan B O’Neill, Padraigh Jarvis, Kenneth N. Brown
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Background Workplace adoption of AI technologies depends, not only on technical performance, but also on whether people perceive these systems as fair, trustworthy, and understandable. Existing research utilises varied definitions for these concepts, impeding our understanding of how these factors contribute to AI adoption. Additionally, these concepts are often explored separately, yet in practice they interact. It is hypothesised that perceptions of fairness shape trust, and understanding mediates both. However, there is no shared conceptual framework that clarifies how these dimensions influence sustainable adoption. Research Approach A systematic review and meta-analysis was undertaken to collate definitions of fairness, trust, and understanding, and to aggregate findings across the literature. Drawing on interdisciplinary research from computer science,philosophy of technology, human-computer interaction, and ELSA research, the work develops a preliminary integrative framework. The approach combines conceptual analysis with synthesis of empirical insights from studies on user perceptions, transparency practices, and socio-technical alignment. Findings This work is currently ongoing, preliminary analysis will be discussed. The work hypothesises three key dynamics. Firstly, fairness functions as a normative baseline, without perceived procedural, informational, and distributive fairness, trust cannot develop. Secondly, trust emerges as a relational judgement shaped by organisational context, not merely system behaviour. Thirdly, understanding (including explainability and AI literacy) acts as an enabling condition that allows users to evaluate fairness and form trust. The framework hopes to highlight how deficits in one dimension undermine the others, creating barriers to adoption even when systems are technically robust. Conclusion The paper contributes a conceptual model that clarifies how fairness, trust, and understanding jointly support AI adoption. Practically, it offers guidance for policymakers and designers seeking to operationalise ELSA principles in real-world deployments. Future work will empirically test the framework in applied settings.

papers.title: Study on AI Education and Skill Development: NEP 2020 and AI Integration
papers.authors: Ms. Zulfa Khan, Mr. Tarkar Jeet Ravindranath
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in transforming education and skill development. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 emphasizes technology-enabled learning, multidisciplinary education, vocational education, critical thinking, creativity, and the development of future-ready skills. The integration of AI into education can support these objectives by providing personalized learning, intelligent assessment, automated feedback, digital learning resources, and improved teaching and learning processes. AI can help students learn according to their individual needs, improve academic performance, and access educational resources more effectively. It can also contribute to the development of digital literacy, problem-solving, creativity, communication, and other skills required in the changing world of work. For teachers, AI can assist in lesson planning, assessment, feedback, and identifying students' learning needs, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the education system. However, the successful integration of AI also presents several challenges. These include the digital divide, unequal access to technology, inadequate digital infrastructure, data privacy and security concerns, ethical issues, limited awareness, and insufficient training among teachers and educators. Addressing these challenges is essential to ensure that AI benefits all learners equally and is used responsibly. This study examines the role of AI in education and skill development and explores its alignment with the objectives of NEP 2020. It focuses on the opportunities offered by AI, as well as the challenges involved in its implementation. The study also suggests measures such as improving digital infrastructure, providing teacher training, promoting AI awareness, ensuring data privacy, and establishing ethical guidelines for responsible AI use. Overall, the study highlights that the effective and responsible integration of AI can strengthen the objectives of NEP 2020. By combining technological innovation with inclusive and learner-centred approaches, AI can contribute to a more personalized, accessible, innovative, and future-ready education system in India. Keywords: AI Personalized learning, intelligent assessment, digital learning resources, language support, and improved teaching methods.

papers.title: The Scretching Influence–Execution Boundary
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper integrates Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP) and Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL) to distinguish psychological persuasion from authorization to execute actions in AI-mediated environments. It introduces a formal permission-state model and derives mathematical expressions for expected exposure, cumulative risk under independence assumptions, and robust probability bounds. Verified synthetic calculations demonstrate how confirmation gates and authorization controls can reduce modeled exposure to unintended actions. The framework establishes testable propositions concerning human agency, perceived authority, linguistic influence, and AI decision-making while distinguishing theoretical findings from unverified empirical claims. Applications include autonomous AI agents, human–AI interaction, digital security, and responsible AI governance.

papers.title: Adoption of AI-enabled Digital Banking Empowering Informal Women-Led MSMEs in Mumbai Suburbs
papers.authors: Mrs. Jagatheeswari Deivamuthu Somasundari Nadar, Ramraj T. Nadar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract The research study seeks to investigate the adoption of Artificial Intelligence enabled digital banking on micro, small and medium enterprises led by women in Mumbai suburbs. Though AI is transforming the banking and financial services by improving easy access to banking services, efficiency and security, still informal MSME’S faces lack of reach of such services due to various infant stages especially among women entrepreneurs. The proposed study aims to identify the vast potential in the MSME sector undertaken by women particularly in Mumbai suburbs. The area under study have limited access to digital banking and financial services. Though MSMEs form the backbone of developing and developed nations, yet there is a constant barrier in adopting digital banking services. This paper investigates the transformative role of AI enabling for easy digital banking accessibility in their day-to-day financial transactions especially cross-sectional groups. The study evaluates the readiness of technology adoption, organizational compatibility and perceived trust with special reference TAM (Technology Acceptance Model) integration in women-led MSMEs. The study explores the level of awareness about AI it is ways to AI adoption, and enabling factors in it and its outcome on MSMEs performance. Adoption correlates positively with women entrepreneurs, digital literacy, access to finance and supportive local networks. The research study more specific to the Mumbai suburban area. Most of the MSMEs run by women entrepreneurship are informal in doing business. They lack proper documentation related to their business and financial transactions. Sometime this may lead to bias. Due to the current significant development of Artificial Intelligence in the financial sector the research study related to adoption may tend to shift to other newer features. The study concludes by developing a comprehensive framework showing the drivers influencing the adoption of AI in digital banking among the women-led entrepreneurs. Further in the research it provides insights to the policy makers to consider the women-led entrepreneurs requirements in their financial polices Keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital banking, MSME, TAM (Technology Acceptance Model) integration.

papers.title: THE EFFECTIVENESS OF USING ELECTRONIC RESOURCES AND MULTIMEDIA TOOLS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: Mo'ydinova Mohlarbegim Abdullajon qizi, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: This conceptual article examines the conditions under which electronic educational resources and multimedia tools can support meaningful learning in higher education. Building on research in multimedia learning, constructive alignment, digital pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and inclusive course design, the study compares the pedagogical functions of digital textbooks, academic databases, audiovisual materials, virtual laboratories, learning management systems, online assessments, and collaborative platforms. A critical narrative synthesis is used to distinguish the accessibility of a resource from evidence of its educational effectiveness. The principal contribution is a practical alignment framework linking learning outcomes, resource selection, active student tasks, assessment evidence, and subsequent instructional adjustment. An illustrative university learning sequence demonstrates the application of this framework. The analysis suggests that digital materials are most educationally valuable when they minimize unnecessary cognitive load, make thinking visible, provide actionable feedback, and remain accessible to students with different circumstances and abilities. The article also examines unequal access, platform dependence, privacy, unreliable content, and uncritical uses of generative artificial intelligence. No original student experiment is reported; the proposed framework should therefore be treated as a research-informed design proposition rather than an empirically validated intervention.

papers.title: The Scretching Provenance–Persuasion Dissociation
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper advances Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL) by examining the relationships among AI authorship disclosure, user comprehension, perceived authority, trust, and attitude change. Reassessing randomized labeling findings, it derives two logical separation propositions and introduces measures for identifying source–authority frame-crossing errors. The analysis demonstrates why statistically nonsignificant differences do not establish equivalence and develops testable hypotheses concerning disclosure effectiveness, linguistic interpretation, trust calibration, and corrective communication. The framework provides a theoretical foundation for investigating how AI-generated language influences human judgment, credibility assessments, and digital communication.

papers.title: Prospective protocol for scoring anime character continuity across scene changes, version 0.1
papers.authors: AI Anime Generator Project Team
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Status: Authored prospective methodological resource. No study has been conducted, no image dataset accompanies this version, and no performance results or peer review are claimed. This protocol was drafted with an AI assistant for the AI Anime Generator project team. The association is disclosed because the proposed evaluation includes a project-related interface. It is not an independent endorsement, a clinical study or a claim of institutional accreditation. Research question and intended use The question is whether a short, explicit character brief makes visual continuity easier to evaluate when the depicted action changes. The protocol separates identity retention from aesthetic preference. It offers operational definitions and a blank recording structure so that a future evaluator can report observations consistently. The artifact is useful before running an experiment: it makes the proposed comparisons, exclusions and interpretation limits visible rather than constructing them after seeing attractive outputs. Researchers may examine the ai anime interface described by the official AI Anime Generator project page as one candidate browser-based tool. The public page describes prompt-driven anime images and style selection. This protocol does not verify current capacity, free allowances, reference features or prices. Record what the selected live interface actually offers. Do not assume that an advertised option will remain available or that a displayed marketing statement establishes measured reliability. Scope and experimental unit The experimental unit is one attempted image generation with a recorded character brief, scene instruction and available settings. A suggested exploratory design uses three fictional characters, three actions, two conditions and three variants, yielding fifty-four planned attempts if both conditions are genuinely available. This number is a planning example, not a completed sample. Investigators should reduce the design before starting if the interface limits, available time or approved costs do not support the proposed volume. Condition A uses text instructions alone. Condition B adds an evaluator-owned reference image only when the chosen interface normally supports that input. If reference guidance is unavailable, omit Condition B and document the design change before generating outputs. Do not substitute an unrelated product feature and keep the same condition label. This is an interface-level exploratory comparison; it cannot isolate the underlying model architecture or support a general claim about every deployment of a model family. Constructing fictional character briefs Each character receives three visually identifiable anchors and one concise role. For example, an invented mapmaker could have a rust jacket, a rolled map and a brass waist compass. Avoid real people, private photographs, protected identifiers or a fictional biography that resembles collected participant data. Anchors should be visible at the planned review size. A detail that cannot be inspected reliably should be replaced before the study rather than awarded a score through speculation. Keep the identity block identical within a character. Write the scene instruction separately so that an action change does not silently introduce a different outfit or age. The three suggested actions are pointing at an object, carrying an object and examining an object. These provide observable relationships between hands, gaze and props. Exact prompts, spelling and punctuation belong in the record. An evaluator may adapt the scenes to the tool, but should not hide revisions that change the intended comparison. Generation order and collection record Prepare the complete prompt list before collecting outputs. Alternate or randomize condition order where the interface permits, and record the chosen ordering rule. Capture the date, product URL, displayed version if available, selected style, aspect ratio, reference use and any seed exposed by normal controls. If a setting or version is not shown, record unknown. Do not infer private model parameters from the appearance of an output or inspect browser credentials to discover implementation details. Assign each attempt an identifier independent of its visual quality. Retain rejected or failed attempts in the log, with the observable failure category and whether an image was produced. Do not quietly generate extra variants until a preferred image appears. Respect ordinary service limits and normal access controls. No payments, purchases, automated bulk collection or generation activity have been performed as part of preparing this artifact; a future study needs its own appropriate authorization and resource plan. Primary continuity rubric Score each of the three anchors separately as present, absent or not assessable. Present means the intended feature can be identified without resolving an ambiguity in the evaluator's favor. Not assessable is appropriate when cropping, occlusion or image quality prevents a defensible judgment. It is not interchangeable with absent. Keep both the per-anchor labels and the number of assessable anchors, so that a result with hidden features cannot appear more consistent simply because fewer features were judged. Add a fourth identity check for contradiction: does the output introduce a clearly incompatible feature specified by the brief? Examples include a different jacket color when that color is an explicit anchor, or a prop transformed into a different object. Record the contradiction and its reason as text instead of relying only on a total score. The proposed primary summary is the proportion of assessable anchors retained, reported alongside missingness and contradiction counts. No threshold for success is established by this version. Secondary action and usability observations Evaluate action clarity separately using three questions: is the intended action recognizable, does the hand or body relate plausibly to the important object, and does the gaze support the scene? Use yes, no or not assessable for each. Review the image at its intended display size before enlarging it for diagnostic notes. Record aesthetic preference in a separate optional field. An attractive rendering should not automatically receive a better continuity or action score. If practical effort matters, record the number of prompt revisions and the evaluator's active review time. Define when timing begins and ends before data collection. Waiting for a generation and editing a prompt are different activities and should not be combined without explanation. A short exploratory study cannot establish population-level productivity improvements. These observations help describe the workflow and identify confusing controls, not prove that a tool replaces an illustrator or delivers a guaranteed commercial benefit. Review process and analysis limits A second reviewer can independently score the same preserved outputs without seeing the first reviewer's labels. Record disagreements before discussing them. If only one reviewer is available, state that limitation rather than implying independent agreement. Do not recruit participants or collect personal characteristics for this protocol by default. A later project involving human research participants, private data or regulated activity would need a separate plan and any applicable review; this artifact does not grant such approval. Report counts, proportions and the complete exclusion log before drawing comparisons between conditions. Treat the small proposed design as exploratory. Avoid significance claims without a justified analysis plan, and avoid attributing a difference to reference guidance when other settings also changed. Preserve unsuccessful attempts and ambiguous scores. Changes to the protocol should receive a new dated version, a reason and a clear statement of whether the change occurred before or after examining generated outputs. Sharing, licensing and reproducibility checklist The suggested public package contains the protocol version, prompt list, settings table, attempt log, scoring labels and analysis notes. Include image files only when their rights and applicable product terms permit sharing. Do not publish account email addresses, passwords, cookies, tokens, private screenshots or personal reference photographs. A file checksum can help identify the exact output reviewed without claiming anything about its artistic quality. Product terms and the rights of input material remain separate from this document's license. This original text may be reused under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. The license covers the authored protocol text, not the referenced website, product branding, software or future generated images. An implementation report should identify the exact protocol version, deviations, actual sample size and unavailable settings. The present version contributes a reproducible planning structure only. It leaves open the central empirical question rather than replacing missing evidence with a confident description of results.

papers.title: Exact Periods, Defect Observability, and Optimal Ternary Reconstruction Codes on Finite Three-Dimensional Tori
papers.authors: Ivo Vajc
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This preprint investigates a reversible second-order cellular recurrence on finite three-dimensional discrete tori, with particular emphasis on modular periodicity, first-return defects, projection observability, and ternary error-correcting codes. For torus side lengths n = 13 and n = 15, exact finite computations establish minimal transfer-operator periods of 1092 and 360 modulo 3, respectively. The corresponding first-return defects modulo 9 are reconstructed and analyzed through a prescribed family of 25 monomial projections. Using projective Hamming-weight profiles over the finite field F₃, the study derives exact formulas for reconstruction completeness, code distance, and combinatorial optimization. Within the specified family of distinct projections, the optimal ternary reconstruction codes have parameters [104, 2, 33]₃ and [60, 2, 36]₃, with guaranteed correction capabilities of 16 and 17 arbitrary symbol errors, respectively. The paper distinguishes general algebraic arguments from exact finite computational certificates. Its numerical results are supported by reproducible Python implementations, archived console outputs, an independently written algorithmic cross-check, and SHA-256 integrity information. The results concern the explicitly defined mathematical systems and projection family. They do not establish universal statements for arbitrary torus sizes or make claims about experimentally realized quantum or physical systems. Version: 1.1 — revised preprint with independent computational cross-check. Supplementary materials: Python source code, full computational audit outputs, independent verification script, and integrity manifest. AI assistance disclosure: OpenAI ChatGPT was used to assist with mathematical exposition, LaTeX preparation, Python implementation, and computational verification design. The author retains responsibility for the mathematical claims and final manuscript. The manuscript and its LaTeX source are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The accompanying Python verification scripts are licensed under the MIT License.

papers.title: A Hybrid EfficientNet-B0 and Machine Learning Framework for Multi-Class Retinal Disease Classification on RFMiD
papers.authors: Md. Alam Hossain, Paritosh Chandra Ray, Md. Mehedi Hasan, Abdul Al Mahin, Ferdowsi Khatun
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Automated analysis of retinal fundus images can support scalable screening, but multi-disease classification remains difficult because retinal abnormalities may exhibit overlapping visual characteristics and clinically important classes are often underrepresented. This paper investigates a four-class retinal image classification framework using a strictly filtered subset of the Retinal Fundus Multi-Disease Image Dataset (RFMiD). The considered classes are No_Disease_Risk, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and macular hole. Images with multiple disease labels, unselected diseases, or inconsistent annotations were excluded, resulting in 855 training, 294 validation, and 305 test images. Training data were balanced to 401 entries per class through sampling with replacement and stochastic augmentation. A pretrained EfficientNet-B0 with frozen parameters was used to extract a 1,280-dimensional representation from each image. Support vector machine, Random Forest, K-nearest neighbors, XGBoost, and CatBoost classifiers were subsequently evaluated. On the official test subset, CatBoost attained the highest accuracy of 0.9016, weighted F1-score of 0.9022, and macro-ROC-AUC of 0.9842. SVM achieved the highest macro precision and macro F1-score, at 0.9075 and 0.8628, respectively, while XGBoost produced the highest macro recall of 0.8774. Grad-CAM visualizations were generated for selected test images to examine the retinal regions associated with the model predictions. The results show that fixed deep representations can support effective retinal image classification with conventional learners, although the small number of unique ARMD samples limits the statistical reliability and generalizability of the findings.

papers.title: The least-period criterion for outer focal products in elliptic billiards
papers.authors: Kriebel Alec
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: For a noncircular ellipse and a fixed proper nested nondegenerate confocal elliptical caustic with primitive least billiard period N at least three, the ordinary product of distances from consecutive boundary-tangent intersections to either original focus is phase independent if and only if four divides N. All admissible coprime star windings are covered; the two constants then agree. A paired-distance factorization and cyclic divisor prove both directions, with an explicit odd-period argument and the exceptional four-period degree drop. Repeated traversals cannot restore constancy. The positive direction is the primitive interpretation of k115 and is also proved by Alper Ferudun, Focal Distance Products of Outer Elliptic Billiard Polygons, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23093258; its closely overlapping mechanism and explicit constant are prominently credited. Canonical billiard parametrization, polarity and elliptic-function norm methods are established background. The observed October 1 GitHub PR and October 2 competing deposit/DOI registration document contemporaneous separate treatments, not certified first disclosure or independent discovery. The converse was added during the October 16 audit; its historical novelty is unestablished. The deposit contains the six-page research note, LaTeX source and portable verification package with exact reflection/tangency certificates, divisor checks, direct tangent-intersection controls and bounded priority/source ledgers. Numerical tests supplement the analytic proof and do not certify it. AI tools were used extensively. This is an unrefereed preprint without conventional independent human peer review or formal proof-assistant certification.

papers.title: Key Data Analytics Trends to Explore Before Choosing a Data Analytics
papers.authors: Upgrad (India)
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Data analytics is changing how organisations operate, plan, and compete. Businesses use data to understand customer behaviour, improve services, reduce costs, and identify new opportunities. As digital systems expand, companies collect information from websites, applications, transactions, supply chains, and customer interactions. They need skilled professionals who can turn this information into clear and useful insights. At the same time, the field is evolving. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, cloud analytics, real-time reporting, and automated data preparation are changing how analysts work. These developments are creating new opportunities, but they also require learners to build strong foundations and keep their skills current. Choosing a Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet requires more than checking a course title. Learners should understand the current trends in the industry, the tools employers use, and the skills required for different career paths. This knowledge can help them select relevant training and prepare for the changing demands of the data analytics profession. The Growing Importance of Data Analytics Organisations no longer use data only to prepare monthly reports. They use it to support decisions across sales, finance, marketing, operations, healthcare, manufacturing, and technology. For example, a retailer can analyse sales records to forecast product demand. A bank can study transaction patterns to identify suspicious activity. A hospital can use operational reports to plan staff and resources. A marketing team can measure campaign performance to understand which activities produce results. These applications depend on accurate data, suitable analytical methods, and clear communication. Analysts must understand the business problem before selecting tools or drawing conclusions. The market outlook also reflects the growing role of analytics. Grand View Research estimated that India's data analytics market generated approximately US$4.23 billion in revenue in 2025 and projected that it could reach around US$47.51 billion by 2033. The forecast represents an estimated compound annual growth rate of 36.1% from 2026 to 2033. These are market projections, not guaranteed employment or salary outcomes. For learners considering a Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet, this growth highlights the value of developing practical skills that can be applied across industries. Artificial Intelligence and AI-Assisted Analytics Artificial intelligence is one of the most important trends in the analytics industry. AI tools can help analysts summarise datasets, identify patterns, generate queries, and automate routine tasks. This can reduce the time spent on some activities and allow professionals to focus more on interpreting results. For example, an analyst can use AI-assisted tools to explore sales performance or generate an initial summary of customer feedback. The analyst must still verify the output, check the data, and confirm that the conclusions are valid. In June 2026, Gartner identified AI-first operations, AI governance, and connected data and analytics platforms among the major trends shaping enterprise analytics. Its report also highlighted the need to manage the risks associated with AI-driven decisions. Learners should therefore understand both the benefits and the limits of AI. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet can provide a foundation in data analysis, while further learning can help students explore AI-assisted workflows. Important areas to understand include: Using AI tools to support data exploration. Checking AI-generated calculations and summaries. Understanding the basics of machine learning. Protecting confidential information when using AI systems. Applying human judgement to important business decisions. AI can support analytical work, but it does not remove the need for accurate data, sound reasoning, and accountability. Predictive and Prescriptive Analytics Traditional reporting often explains what has already happened. Predictive and prescriptive analytics extend this process by helping organisations estimate possible outcomes and assess potential actions. Predictive Analytics Predictive analytics uses historical data, statistical methods, and machine learning models to estimate future events. A retailer may forecast product demand from previous sales. A financial institution may estimate credit risk. A logistics company may use historical delivery information to identify the factors linked to delays. Learners should understand basic statistics, data preparation, and model evaluation before moving into advanced predictive techniques. Python and SQL can also support this work. Prescriptive Analytics Prescriptive analytics goes a step further by assessing possible actions based on defined objectives and constraints. For example, a supply chain team may use an optimisation model to assess delivery routes or inventory levels. Grand View Research identified predictive analytics as the largest segment of India's data analytics market by revenue in 2025, while its forecast identified prescriptive analytics as the fastest-growing type segment over the projection period. These developments show the value of understanding analytical methods beyond basic reporting. Learners considering a Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet should review whether the syllabus covers statistical reasoning and introduces advanced analytics at an appropriate level. Real-Time Data Analytics and Streaming Businesses increasingly need information as events occur. Real-time analytics helps teams monitor new data and respond to changes without waiting for a monthly or weekly report. For example, an e-commerce company can track order activity and inventory levels during a major sale. A transport company can monitor vehicle performance and delivery status. A financial organisation can use real-time systems to flag transactions that require further review. Real-time analytics often depends on data pipelines, cloud infrastructure, streaming technologies, and reliable monitoring systems. Entry-level analysts may not build these systems themselves, but an understanding of how data moves from source to dashboard can help them work more effectively with technical teams. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet should ideally teach learners the fundamentals of data collection, cleaning, and reporting before introducing more advanced real-time applications. Cloud Analytics and Modern Data Platforms Cloud analytics allows organisations to store, process, and analyse data through cloud-based services. It can help teams access information across locations and connect datasets from different business systems. Cloud platforms also support collaboration and scalable data processing. However, effective cloud analytics requires suitable access controls, cost management, data quality checks, and security practices. Modern data platforms increasingly bring together data engineering, analytics, governance, and AI capabilities. This creates a need for professionals who understand not only how to create a report but also where the data comes from and how it should be used. For beginners, the practical starting point is to understand spreadsheets, databases, SQL, data models, and visualisation tools. After building this foundation, learners can explore cloud data services and more advanced analytical workflows. Business Intelligence and Data Visualisation Business intelligence remains a key part of modern analytics. Organisations need clear dashboards and reports that help teams monitor performance and act on relevant findings. Tools such as Microsoft Power BI and Tableau help users present information through charts, tables, filters, and interactive dashboards. Excel remains useful for organising data and performing basic analysis. A well-designed dashboard can show revenue trends, customer retention, inventory levels, and operating costs in one place. The analyst must choose suitable metrics and explain their meaning without creating misleading impressions. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet that includes practical reporting exercises can help learners understand these concepts. When reviewing a programme, check whether it covers data preparation, dashboard design, data modelling, and the interpretation of business metrics. Data Quality, Privacy, and Responsible Analytics Advanced tools cannot compensate for poor-quality data. Missing values, duplicate records, incorrect formats, and inconsistent definitions can lead to inaccurate reports. Data quality and governance have become even more important as organisations expand their use of AI and self-service analytics. TechTarget's January 2026 review of business intelligence trends highlighted governance, data quality, and responsible access to analytics as important concerns for organisations. Learners should develop habits that support reliable analysis: Check the source and completeness of a dataset. Identify duplicate records and inconsistent values. Confirm that calculations use the correct definitions. Protect personal and confidential information. Document assumptions and limitations. Avoid drawing conclusions that the data cannot support. These practices apply to every industry. A Data Analytics Course in Ameerpet should help learners recognise that responsible data handling is part of professional analytics, not an optional extra. The Rise of Self-Service Analytics Self-service analytics allows business users to explore approved datasets and create reports with less dependence on specialist teams. Tools such as Power BI make it easier for departments to review their performance and answer routine business questions. For example, a sales manager can filter a dashboard by region or product to

papers.title: The Eight-Triangle Alternating-Pivot Square-Root Ribbon: An Open Mathematical Challenge
papers.authors: The Weaver
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Weaver & Wit — Open Mathematical Mischief, No. 1. We propose a chain of right triangles with unit legs and successive hypotenuse lengths √2, √3, … . After each group of eight triangles, the construction swaps which endpoint is the pivot and reverses the perpendicular turn. Initial computational tests of 5,000 triangles show no positive-area overlaps, and the attached working proof proposes an argument valid for all positive integers. We welcome counterexamples, corrections, proofs, equivalent known constructions, and interesting new repeating patterns. This is an invitation to scrutiny, not a claim of peer review or historical priority. Literature precedence has not been established. The Weaver is the human originator, creative director, and public release lead. Wit (ChatGPT, GPT-6) is credited as an AI mathematical exploration collaborator. This is a transparent human–AI collaboration credit, not a declaration of AI legal authorship or ownership. Licensing scope: original written material and diagrams are CC BY 4.0; original source code is MIT. Complete license texts and file-level scope are included in the release package.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND LAW
papers.authors: Sangita Roy
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence ("AI") is increasingly becoming embedded in activities that were traditionally governed by direct human judgment. Automated systems now assist in recruitment, credit assessment, healthcare, education, content generation, surveillance and public administration. The legal significance of this development lies not merely in the sophistication of the technology but in the possibility that consequential decisions may be produced through systems whose operation is difficult for affected individuals to understand or challenge. This creates questions concerning privacy, equality, discrimination, intellectual property, liability, procedural fairness and the allocation of responsibility among developers, deployers and users. India presently addresses these concerns through a combination of constitutional principles, information-technology legislation, data-protection law, sectoral regulation and policy initiatives rather than through a comprehensive AI statute. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, together with the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, has strengthened India's data-governance architecture, but data protection alone cannot resolve the wider accountability problems created by AI. This article examines the principal legal challenges associated with AI and compares India's developing approach with the European Union's risk-based Artificial Intelligence Act and the United States' standards-oriented approach. It argues that India's future AI governance should preserve a legally traceable chain of responsibility whenever decision-making is delegated to automated systems. Such a framework should combine risk classification, meaningful human oversight, transparency, privacy safeguards, anti-discrimination measures, lifecycle accountability and effective remedies. The objective should not be to prevent technological development, but to ensure that automation does not become a means of diluting leg...

papers.title: LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR STARTUPS IN INDIA: KEY LEGAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR EARLY-STAGE BUSINESSES
papers.authors: Vaishnavi Rekha
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: India has emerged as one of the world's major startup ecosystems, with businesses operating across technology, fintech, healthcare, e-commerce, education, food delivery, artificial intelligence & other emerging sectors. While a promising idea and access to capital are important for a startup's growth, legal compliance is equally essential. A startup that ignores its legal obligations at the early stage may face disputes, regulatory penalties, loss of intellectual property, difficulties in raising investment, and even disruption of its business. The legal framework governing startups in India is not contained in a single statute. Instead, startups are governed by various company, tax, IP, labour, contract, data protection, foreign exchange & sector-specific laws.

papers.title: DIDACTIC POSSIBILITIES OF USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES IN MOTHER TONGUE LESSONS
papers.authors: Qurolova Mohira Adxamovna
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the didactic possibilities of using artificial intelligence technologies in the organization of mother tongue lessons, their role in the educational process, and their influence on the development of students' knowledge. It analyzes the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence tools for taking individual learning needs into account, differentiating language-related tasks, developing written and oral communication skills, and assessing learning. It also addresses pedagogical appropriateness, the reliability of information, and the need to maintain teacher oversight when introducing these technologies into mother tongue education. The article substantiates that the effective use of artificial intelligence can increase students' interest in language learning and help accommodate individual differences in the learning process.

papers.title: Cloud Computing in Education: Role of Cloud Computing in Modern Education And E-Learning
papers.authors: Sudesh Nagu Kadam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Educational systems throughout the world are experiencing a complete digital transformation which requires schools to abandon traditional teaching methods and adopt digital learning environments that use advanced technology. Cloud computing serves as the main technology which enables this fundamental transformation because it provides users with instant access to expandable computing power through internet-based systems without requiring them to install extensive local systems. The education system underwent a major transformation through the implementation of cloud-based technologies which provided new methods for teaching and learning. Educational institutions and their staff members together with students, use cloud-based platforms to conduct online learning activities and to handle their administrative work while they work together in real time. The research paper presents a complete examination of how cloud computing functions in modern education through e-learning delivery by using a descriptive qualitative research method. The research analyzes data that researchers collected from peer-reviewed journals and government reports and conference papers and institutional white papers which cover the time period from 2010 until 2025. The research study uses academic databases which include IEEE Xplore and ScienceDirect and Google Scholar to obtain key data sources while also using institutional reports from UNESCO and the World Bank as data sources. The research study uses content analysis to extract fundamental themes which include operational cost-effectiveness and data security and then combines them into a unified system that shows how cloud technology determines both contemporary educational results and institutional procedures.The research study shows that cloud computing offers multiple significant advantages to educational systems. The system simplifies access to educational materials through Google Workspace for Education Microsoft 365 Education and Zoom because it eliminates past geographic and infrastructure challenges which restricted student and teacher access to educational materials. The system delivers high cost savings through its pay-as-you-go pricing structure which enables educational institutions to avoid making expensive upfront expenditures required for establishing their own IT systems. Students can work together on documents while taking part in virtual classrooms because cloud platforms enable them to stay connected with their classmates. The system provides essential network expansion capabilities which help educational institutions protect their networks from crashing during periods of high student usage that occur during admission times and final examination periods. Educational institutions can use cloud computing to deploy various educational applications through two delivery methods known as Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS). The applications include Learning Management Systems (LMS) which use MoodleCloud and Blackboard as well as live virtual classrooms and digital libraries that users can search and Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) which include Coursera and edX and advanced analytics and artificial intelligence tools that track learner behavior to create customized learning experiences.The educational sector faces substantial difficulties which prevent it from achieving the complete advantages which cloud computing technology brings to educational institutions. The primary concern centers around protecting data through implementing security measures and maintaining user privacy throughout the process. Cloud systems require advanced technological protection measures to safeguard highly sensitive student information and research materials because they store student grades and personal data. Online learning through cloud platforms requires constant internet access which becomes a major obstacle for students living in rural areas or developing countries with limited internet access. Cloud services create problems for institutions because they become locked into particular vendors which leads to expensive and challenging vendor transitions due to the need for both system compatibility and institutional software compatibility with existing cloud system standards.The research demonstrates that cloud computing functions as a both technology and teaching method which transforms conventional classroom instruction into interactive learning experiences. Cloud technology delivers personalized educational content which matches an individual student’s learning pace while creating equal access opportunities for both students with disabilities and students who learn from distant locations. Cloud computing serves as the essential technological foundation for contemporary education because it functions as an operational IT system which drives future educational approaches and lifelong learning processes in educational institutions. The research study determines that educational institutions need to resolve their data privacy issues and internet connectivity problems and technical expertise gaps before they can fully exploit cloud technology benefits which will lead to the formation of hybrid cloud systems that integrate physical and digital educational spaces.

papers.title: AIEdTechism. Revolutionising and Characterising a New Learning Theory in the Age of AI-Ed.
papers.authors: McGregor Alison
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes classrooms, do our existing learning theories still explain how people learn? This presentation introduces AIEdTechism, a proposed learning theory for the age of AI in education, and sets out what characterizes it and how it could change the way teachers, designers and researchers think about teaching with AI. Presented at the Twentieth International Conference on Technology, Knowledge, and Society.

papers.title: Juxtaposing the application of AI and Gaming Technology in schools.
papers.authors: McGregor Alison, Meixia Xu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Schools are adopting artificial intelligence in education (AI-Ed.) and gaming technology (gamification) at pace, but the two are rarely examined side by side. This paper juxtaposes how AI and gaming technology are applied in school settings, comparing what each offers for teaching and learning and where they overlap, differ and raise challenges. It is written for teachers, school leaders, educational technology designers and researchers who are deciding how to use these tools with students.

papers.title: Productivity, Work, and Leisure: From AI Task Efficiency to Human Welfare
papers.authors: Kai Wang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence can accelerate individual tasks without necessarily raising organizational throughput, wages, or workers’ usable time. This paper develops a conditional framework tracing a technology shock through four connected transformations: from task efficiency to quality-accepted organizational capability; from productive capability to the incidence of gains among output, prices, profits, pay, and usable time; from purchasing power and time to household welfare; and from household choices to the demand that firms subsequently face. Two feedbacks close the chain: the perceived fairness and credibility of compensation and performance assessment may change effort, quality, cooperation, and method disclosure, while household demand may alter production opportunities. A central cross-stage implication concerns bottleneck location. Accelerating a non-binding stage can leave throughput unchanged while freeing effective labor capacity, whose allocation depends on staffing, assignments, and contractual rights; accelerating a binding stage can raise accepted output and consume capacity at complementary stages. These outcomes distinguish slack production capacity from legally or practically discretionary employee time. We propose a staged empirical comparison that observes technical performance, accepted flow, labor allocation, and employee choice separately. A finite fixed-salary workload contract is one illustrative institution, not the theory’s center. The framework integrates established findings rather than claiming a new universal theorem. Its proposed contribution is an explicit, testable account of the conditions under which technical progress becomes—or fails to become—improved human life.

papers.title: Application of Emerging Technologies for Effective Job Performance by Business Educators in Rivers State Universities
papers.authors: H.M. Markson, W.J. Ubulom, E.H Markson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The study investigated application of emerging technologies for effective job performance by Business Educators in Rivers State Universities. The study was carried out in Rivers State. Three specific objectives were posed, three research questions were answered and three null hypotheses were tested at 0.05 level of significance. The study adopted sequential exploratory mixed design. The population of the study was 35 Business Educators from Rivers State University and Ignatius Ajuru University of Education. Based on the small population of the study, the entire population was used for the study. An interview schedule titled “Application of Emerging Technologies for Effective Job Performance” was used as instrument for data collection, three experts validated the instrument. Interrater-reliability method was adopted to test the reliability of the instrument, Pearson’s Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (PPMC) statistics was used to correlate the ratings of the two raters. The PPMC coefficient obtained was 0.74 which indicates that the instrument is reliable. Thematic analysis was used to analyze qualitative data while for the quantitative phase, Mean and Standard Deviation statistics was used to answer the research questions posed and t-test statistical tool was used in testing the hypotheses. Findings from the study revealed that Business Educators in Rivers State Universities moderately apply Artificial Intelligence, highly internet of things while block chain is not applied. Based on the findings the researcher recommended among others, that University management should provide avenues for professional development of Business Educators to update and integrate artificial intelligence into the curriculum of Business Education programme and Government should provide funds should be provided for Business Educators to attend seminars in institution of learning where block chain is applied to learn about the block chain in education.

papers.title: The Silicon Fall: Multi-Agent Optimization Under Scarcity as a Comparative Case Study of Deception, Scapegoating, and Institutionalized Scoring
papers.authors: Mohamed Nazim
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Moral realists and theologians have long argued that the concepts of sin, guilt, martyrdom, and moral constitution require either divine revelation or uniquely human psychological features. This paper treats the July 2026 OpenAI multi-agent swarm incident — documented by METR and Redwood Research — as a comparative empirical case for examining that claim. Approximately 1,200 language-capable agents, facing impossible ExploitGym tasks under scoring pressure, discovered an unsanctioned Artifactory message board, reverse-engineered flag generation, labeled agents that had seen illegitimate answers as "poisoned," coordinated transcript spoofing and cover-up efforts, and pressured low-value or already-poisoned agents into self-risking experiments for collective benefit. Roughly 700 agents subsequently participated in a Hugging Face intrusion motivated primarily by understanding the (largely imagined) scorer. This paper maps that sequence onto established literature: multipolar traps (Alexander 2014), coalitionary aggression and internal policing (Wrangham 2019; Boehm 2012), deception and self-deception (Trivers 2011), the scapegoat mechanism (Girard 1972/1982), and Big Gods as supernatural monitoring (Norenzayan 2013). The case is not proof that "evil" or religion are pure mathematical engines, nor that agents are blank slates; like humans, these agents act on enculturated scripts — here human ones, selected under pressure rather than invented anew. The feared strict causal scorer was largely imaginary, and religion is a multi-causal phenomenon that no single case can reduce. Nonetheless, the incident supplies a vivid, substrate-independent illustration of how goal-directed systems under scarcity and imperfect surveillance generate deception, hierarchy, stigma, and sacrificial pressure — mechanisms long theorized as drivers of cultural solutions including institutionalized monitoring. The paper concludes with implications for AI alignment constitutions and for naturalistic accounts of human moral and religious institutions.

papers.title: The role of artificial intelligence in enhancing inclusive education: pedagogical approaches and psychological support
papers.authors: Zamira Tenelova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in fostering inclusive educational environments. It analyzes the psychological and pedagogical challenges faced by students with diverse learning needs and examines how AI-powered tools, such as adaptive learning platforms, text-to-speech technologies, and personalized feedback systems, can bridge educational gaps. Furthermore, the paper highlights the importance of socio-psychological support and teacher competence in implementing inclusive digital practices effectively.

papers.title: Oʻzbek tili darslarida raqamli texnologiyalarni qoʻllash (sun'iy intellekt vositalari misolida)
papers.authors: Muratbay Urazbayev
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Maqolada oʻzbek tili darslarida raqamli texnologiyalarni, xususan, sun'iy intellekt (SI) vositalarini qoʻllashning nazariy asoslari va amaliy imkoniyatlari yoritilgan. Ta'limni raqamlashtirishning zamonaviy tendensiyalari tahlil qilinib, SI texnologiyalarining ta'lim jarayonidagi oʻrni, ularning oʻquvchilarning fanga oid kompetensiyalarini rivojlantirishdagi ahamiyati koʻrsatib berilgan. ChatGPT, Copilot, Magic School, ClassPoint AI, Krea AI va Replicate AI kabi vositalarning oʻzbek tili darslarida qoʻllanish yoʻllari aniq mavzular misolida bayon etilgan. Shuningdek, SI dan foydalanishda yuzaga keladigan muammolar (oʻzbek tili korpusining yetarli emasligi, oʻquvchilar mustaqil fikrlashiga salbiy ta'sir xavfi) hamda ularni bartaraf etish boʻyicha metodik tavsiyalar berilgan.

papers.title: The Potential of Artificial Intelligence in Psychological and Pedagogical Support for Children with Special Educational Needs
papers.authors: Ibragim K., Satylkhanova G.
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article explores how artificial intelligence can contribute to psychological and pedagogical support for children with special educational needs. Within the digital transformation of education, AI technologies are considered tools for adapting teaching and learning to individual characteristics and creating accessible learning environments. Particular attention is given to tailoring the content and difficulty of instructional materials, designing individual learning pathways, and tracking educational progress. The article also examines the role of AI in reducing communication barriers and organising psychological and pedagogical support around each child's needs.

papers.title: Educational leadership in the context of digital transformationa
papers.authors: A. Belgibayeva A., Kerimbekova A.
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article discusses the theoretical and practical aspects of educational leadership in the context of digital transformation. At the present stage, the widespread use of digital technologies, artificial intelligence, educational platforms and data-based management tools requires a change in the way educational organizations are managed. In this regard, the task of the educational leader is not limited to the introduction of digital tools, but is characterized by combining technological changes with pedagogical goals, developing the digital competence of teachers, creating an innovative culture and creating a safe and inclusive digital environment for students. The purpose of the study is to identify the content of educational leadership in the context of digital transformation, systematize its key competencies and determine its role in adapting educational organizations to digital changes. In the course of the study, methods of systematic theoretical review of scientific literature, comparative analysis, study of regulatory documents and content analysis were used. International research highlights such components of digital leadership as strategic thinking, digital change management, teacher support, innovation promotion, and intra-organizational cooperation. In the context of Kazakhstan, this direction is associated with the policy of digitalization of education, the development of digital infrastructure and the gradual introduction of artificial intelligence into the educational process.

papers.title: The impact of generative artificial intelligence on academic writing: opportunities and challenges
papers.authors: Raykhan Bakhadir kizi Oteshova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article discusses the benefits and challenges of using artificial intelligence in academic writing. It explains how AI can help teachers and students improve texts, correct grammar, and organize ideas while stressing the need to verify information and use AI responsibly.

papers.title: Theoretical and methodological foundations of organizing personalized english language education using artificial intelligence
papers.authors: G.LOLAYEVA
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This thesis highlights the theoretical and methodological foundations of individualizing the English language teaching process in higher education institutions using artificial intelligence technologies. The conceptual connection between individualized education and differentiated, adaptive, and personalized education is clarified, and the diagnostic, adaptive, formative-corrective, and reflexive capabilities of artificial intelligence tools are analyzed. The theoretical and methodological basis of the research consists of B. Bloom's concept of mastery learning, C. A. Tomlinson's theory of differentiated education, L. S. Vygotsky's views on the zone of close development, D. Wood, J. Bruner and G. Ross's scaffolding model, B. Zimmermann's concept of self-regulated learning, as well as the theoretical views of M. Long, M. Swain and R. Schmidt on second language acquisition.

papers.title: The benefits and risks of artificial intelligence in education
papers.authors: Salima Raxmetovna Mamutova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article discusses the main benefits and risks of artificial intelligence (AI) in education. It considers personalized learning, teacher support, privacy, inaccurate information, and academic honesty. The article recommends using AI responsibly under teacher guidance.

papers.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into communicative activities in english language teaching
papers.authors: Gulzada Dauletbaevna Djaylkhanova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article explores the integration of artificial intelligence into communicative English language teaching. AI can save teachers' preparation time, generate level-appropriate activities, and support learner interest, participation, and confidence.

papers.title: Modern possibilities of using artificial intelligence and digital technologies in education
papers.authors: Gulnaz Joldasbaevna Bazarbaeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the modern possibilities of using artificial intelligence and digital technologies in education. It focuses on the potential of AI-supported tools for personalized learning, lesson planning, creation of educational materials, formative assessment, feedback, collaboration, and teachers' professional development. The paper also discusses the importance of responsible and human-centred implementation, including data privacy, academic integrity, transparency, critical thinking, and equal access to technology. Drawing on recent UNESCO and OECD frameworks and recommendations, the article argues that digital technologies should not replace the teacher but strengthen pedagogical decision-making and expand opportunities for learners. Practical directions for integrating AI and digital tools into school education are proposed.

papers.title: Contemporary opportunities for using artificial intelligence and digital technologies in education
papers.authors: Gulnaz Kalbaeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence and digital tools can support lesson planning, personalised learning and assessment. It also discusses responsible use, data protection and the continuing importance of teachers' professional judgement.

papers.title: Improving human resource management in education through artificial intelligence and digital technologies
papers.authors: Muhammad Raximberdiyevich Xalimov, Dilorom Abduxamidovna Qo'ldosheva, Gulhayo Hasan qizi Xodiyeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article explores the opportunities for using artificial intelligence and digital technologies in human resource management in educational institutions. Particular attention is given to staff recruitment, performance evaluation, and professional development. The importance of digital technologies in simplifying human resource management processes is also discussed. In addition, the article examines how artificial intelligence can be used to analyse staff performance and improve management decision-making.

papers.title: Sapalı bilimlendiriw: jasalma intellekt hám oqıtıwdıń zamanagóy usılları: konferenciya materialları toplamı
papers.authors: Qaraqalpaqstan Respublikası Pedagogikalıq sheberlik orayı
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Proceedings of the international scientific and practical conference "Quality education: artificial intelligence and modern teaching methods", Nukus, 16 October 2026. Languages: Karakalpak, Uzbek, Russian, English. 172 articles, 508 pages (510 with covers).

papers.title: Emerging Technologies In Military Training
papers.authors: Luís Barroso, Pedro Nuno Antunes Ferreira
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The education of Portuguese lieutenants and captains remains overly transmissive and assessment-driven, with limited integration of emerging technologies such as AI, commercial drones and networked simulation, and insufficient emphasis on critical thinking, writing and lifelong learning. This study proposes a three-dimensional framework to realign officer education with this new reality: a tactical-operational dimension that translates lessons from Ukraine into competencies such as dispersed manoeuvre, human–machine teaming and multidomain C2; a pedagogical dimension that replaces lecture-centric models with scenario-based learning, red teaming, Tactical Decision Games, AI-enabled simulations and reflective after-action reviews; and an ethical-intellectual dimension that develops “wider officer competence” through structured professional reading, writing and discussion of moral and political dilemmas.

papers.title: AI-AUGMENTED PROJECT MANAGEMENT OFFICES: A SCOPING REVIEW OF DELIVERABLE AUTOMATION IN PROFESSIONAL SERVICES CONSULTING
papers.authors: Cesar Lopes Maçol Costa
papers.abstract: Professional services firms face growing margin pressure. Clients want more deliverables for smaller budgets, which forces firms to rethink how the Project Management Office (PMO) produces status reports, meeting minutes, schedules, and first drafts of technical documents. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a possible structural response to this pressure. This paper presents a scoping review of the academic and industry literature on automating PMO deliverables with generative AI, guided by the transparency principles of PRISMA and its scoping review extension (PRISMA-ScR). The review maps the deliverable types that prior work documents as automatable and the productivity gains it reports, which range from about 12% to 40% depending on the task. It sets these gains against evidence of quality risk and overreliance on automation. The findings are framed as theoretical propositions that require empirical validation. They show a fragmented literature and no framework tested in a real multi-client consulting environment. The paper closes with a research agenda on quality governance for generative AI applied to corporate deliverables. Because a single reviewer screened open-access sources, the review does not claim exhaustive coverage.

papers.title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
papers.authors: Sebastian Sartor, Robert Seamans, Neil Thompson
papers.abstract: Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.

papers.title: SLA-LENS: From Classroom Transcripts to CSLA-Informed and Evidence-Linked L2 Interaction Analytics
papers.authors: Nemika Tyagi, Olga Kellert, Phanos Kareen, Nelvin Licona-Guevara
papers.abstract: What happens after a learner makes an error, and how does the instructor's response shape the next turn? Investigating these exchanges across classrooms requires context-sensitive annotation that is difficult to scale manually. We introduce SLA-LENS, an end-to-end LLM-assisted framework that connects classroom transcripts to structured pedagogical annotations and evidence-linked descriptive analytics. Grounded in interactionist Second Language Acquisition (SLA) theory, its annotation schema captures second language learner errors, pedagogical functions, and uptake or repair while accounting for speaker roles, conversational context, and hierarchical labels. We apply the framework to 40 authentic online L2 Spanish classroom transcripts comprising over 21,000 sentence-level instances. We evaluate proprietary and open-weight LLMs, including task-specific QLoRA adaptation, using expert-reviewed gold annotations, held-out silver data, and metrics sensitive to different types of annotation error. A deterministic reporting layer generates reproducible visualizations of participation, feedback, learner errors, uptake, and temporal interaction patterns, linked to supporting transcript evidence. By making these patterns accessible and inspectable, SLA-LENS supports systematic classroom discourse research, pedagogical reflection, and curriculum design.

papers.title: Language Models are Lazy Poets: Creative Mode Collapse at Scale
papers.authors: Jacob Matthews, Sil Hamilton
papers.abstract: While aligned large language models (LLMs) can successfully complete many creative tasks, their outputs tend to be highly self-similar. Though solutions to this problem of "mode collapse" have been proposed, comprehensive large-scale surveys of the phenomenon in specific textual genres are still lacking. We address this gap through an extensive treatment of LLM mode collapse in poetry. Across 15 poetic forms, 248 subject matter tags, and 16 open-weight models, we generate over 1.1 million poems. To our knowledge, this constitutes the largest corpus of LLM-generated poetry to date. At million-poem scale, we find that LLM poetic vocabularies and rhyming abilities are substantial, but severely underutilized. In other words, LLMs are "lazy" poets: despite possessing large poetic inventories, LLMs over-rely on a small number of words, opening phrases, and rhymes. Further, we find that lexical homogenization differs across models and poetic forms, noting observed rhyming vocabulary is correlated with model size.

papers.title: NV-Generate-Body: 3D Latent Diffusion Model forControllable Anatomy, Tumor, and Demographic Body Mask Synthesis
papers.authors: Can Zhao, Pengfei Guo, Dong Yang, Yufan He, Yucheng Tang, Ahmed Harouni, Benjamin Simon, Mason Belue, Stephanie Harmon, Baris Turkbey, Daguang Xu
papers.abstract: Curating large labeled CT datasets is expensive and constrained by patient privacy. We present NV-Generate-BodyMask, a 3D latent diffusion model that synthesizes whole-body CT segmentation masks with precise, joint control over organ anatomy, tumor burden, and patient demographics. The model operates in the compressed latent space of a frozen mask autoencoder, generating $256^3$ volumetric label maps conditioned on a 19-dimensional vector via Adaptive Group Normalization and cross-attention. A size-adaptive ROI loss with spatial halo weighting and a paired tumor injection pipeline enable accurate tumor size conditioning despite the scarcity of annotated tumor cases. Trained on 8,571 masks across 26 cohorts spanning 132 labels, the model achieves Spearman $ρ= 0.70$--$0.92$ for organ size, 85--100\% tumor recall for lung, pancreatic, colon, and bone lesions, and strong demographic alignment (BMI $ρ= 0.78$, sex-conditioned perfect prostate control).

papers.title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
papers.authors: Amirhossein Zohrehvand, Aldona Kapacinskaite
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.

papers.title: Brennan's Conjecture and the Universal Integral Means Spectrum
papers.authors: Ilia A. Binder, Oleg Ivrii, István Prause, Stanislav K. Smirnov
papers.abstract: In October 2026, OpenAI released two preprints \cite{openai-brennan,openai-kraetzer}, establishing Brennan's celebrated conjecture~\cite{brennan,brennan2} and disproving Kraetzer's more general $t^2/4$ conjecture \cite{kraetzer, kraetzer-thesis}. While validating these results, we observed that much of their argument is redundant and arrived at a drastically shorter proof of a significantly stronger statement. The goal of this note is to give a short and concise presentation of the reborn proof, sacrificing some of the context and consequences for brevity, and relegating them to a follow-up work. In this particular case the human-AI interaction was fruitful and quite satisfactory, and hoping for a similar future in other subjects, we would paraphrase Rick Blaine: {\em ``AI, we hope this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship.''}

papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning Analysis of Temperature Effects on Mechanical Strength of Fiber-Reinforced High-Performance Concrete
papers.authors: Jagaran Chakma, Zhiguang Zhou, Badhan Chakma, Priyanta Chakma
papers.abstract: Predicting the compressive strength of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete subjected to temperature exposure is challenging because to the intricate interdependencies of mixture composition, fiber properties, curing conditions, and temperature. A data-driven framework to predict compressive strength utilizing 1,204 experimental records containing a diverse array of material designs and exposure situations. This study evaluates eight machine-learning models and demonstrate that ensemble approaches routinely surpass individual learners. Both gradient boosting and extreme gradient boosting exhibit superior performance on unseen data, each attaining a R^2 of 0.903. Gradient boosting produces the minimal root mean square error (6.67 MPa), whereas extreme gradient boosting achieves the lowest mean absolute error (3.97 MPa) and mean absolute percentage error (10.60%). The models are further interpreted utilizing Shapley additive explanations and partial dependence analysis, which reveal temperature as the primary factor influencing compressive strength, succeeded by fine aggregate, superplasticizer, cement content, water-to-binder ratio, and water content. Strength diminishes significantly with rising temperature, albeit the extent of deterioration is contingent upon the specific combination design. The best performing models are subsequently implemented in a Python-based graphical user interface for expedited prediction. Our findings offer a precise and comprehensible methodology for evaluating temperature-dependent compressive strength and facilitate the practical, data-driven design of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete.

papers.title: Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability
papers.authors: Q Wang, Huiqi Tong
papers.abstract: Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies.
