This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

papers.title: "To Boldly Go Where No One Has Gone Before" What Has AI Let Developers Unlock?
papers.authors: Rudrajit Choudhuri, Jenna Butler, Christian Bird, Carmen Badea, Brian Houck, Anita Sarma
papers.abstract: Measuring AI by how much faster developers work is like judging electricity by how much faster it spun a steam-era factory. A fuller measure asks what new work becomes possible. We surveyed 331 software developers at Microsoft about what AI lets them do that they could not do before and analyzed their answers using reflexive thematic analysis with a human-in-the-loop, multi-model AI council. Developers described doing familiar work faster (Faster, 45%), undertaking work previously beyond their reach (Further, 36.9%), and taking on new kinds of work centered on building for and directing AI agents (Afresh, 12.4%). Across these accounts, learning and scaffolding ran in both directions: developers learned new skills with AI while externalizing their tacit knowledge as the context and standards that guide AI's work. Drawing on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, we frame developers and AI as joint learners whose zones meet at the skill-judgment nexus: AI can supply skill faster than it can reliably judge its own work, and developers must continuously bridge that gap. Whether they do sets them on one of two paths. On one, developers' judgment grows alongside AI's skill, and they codify what they learn so the loop keeps turning. On the other, they become hollow orchestrators, approving work they can no longer judge and losing the identity and meaning they once drew from it. Based on our findings, we offer a two-way scaffolding playbook to help developers, teams, and tool builders take the first path.

papers.title: Analyzing Occupational Gender Bias across the LLM Training Lifecycle
papers.authors: Manthan Gadhia, Alexander Hoyle, Karolina Stańczak
papers.abstract: Post-training is widely assumed to reduce the social biases language models inherit from pretraining, yet direct evidence for this assumption remains mixed. In this paper, we examine how gender disparities evolve across the language modeling pipeline. In particular, we study occupational gender bias in OLMo 3, a fully open language model family, across its post-training stages by prompting each checkpoint to generate open-ended narratives about synthetic personas given their occupation and education. We consider two settings, a gender-given setting in which the profile states the persona's gender explicitly and a gender-assumed setting in which it must be inferred by the model. We find that when gender is stated, post-training increases semantic diversity for male-coded profiles, whereas for female-coded profiles the increase is smaller after SFT and not significant after DPO and RLVR. When gender is assumed by the model, post-training affects narratives about female and male personas similarly. The model's own gender assumptions, however, show a consistent female-preferential skew relative to United States labor-force demographics, except for heavily male-dominated occupations. Every successive post-training stage monotonically increases the odds of attributing a female label over the base model. A provenance analysis of the supervised fine-tuning corpus finds only a modest 7.7% female-token surplus, too small to explain the size of these downstream effects. The project code is available under: https://github.com/manthangadhia/llm-lifecycle-bias.

papers.title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents
papers.authors: Jin Ye, Yifan Jiang, Lan-zhe Guo
papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their capabilities in complex tasks. However, scalable skill use requires Selective Skill Exposure (SSE): providing relevant procedural content when needed while avoiding unnecessary exposure that may disrupt reasoning. Existing paradigms fall short in complementary ways. Progressive disclosure exposes metadata for a growing skill library, introducing context pollution; retrieval limits catalog exposure, but static retrieval from the initial task query may be misaligned with capability needs that emerge during reasoning and may still inject unnecessary skills. We propose SkillBrowser, a Meta-Skill-managed framework that enables an agent to identify current capability needs, formulate targeted queries, and selectively load skills on demand. Across six SRA-Bench subsets and five LLMs, SkillBrowser improves aggregate accuracy over static retrieval and LLM-based selection, including multi-step tool use, and mitigates accuracy degradation on already-solvable instances. Benefits remain model- and task-dependent, with under-invocation of useful skills and additional latency as key limitations. These results demonstrate the viability of Meta-Skill-managed SSE for scalable skill repositories.

papers.title: EduWild: How Teacher-Configured Chatbots Fail in Real-World Use and How to Fix Them
papers.authors: Ziqi Liu, Ruiwei Xiao, Yuxuan Li, John C. Stamper
papers.abstract: Teachers increasingly configure educational chatbots through natural-language instructions, but how these bots fail in real-world use remains poorly understood. We introduce EduWild, a dataset of 1,726 conversations with 217 teacher-configured chatbots, each paired with the instructions and configuration behind it, including 900 conversations from the intended end users of 35 deployed chatbots. We develop a 29-code taxonomy covering factual, workflow, diagnostic, and pedagogical failures and apply it using a human-calibrated LLM judge. The most frequent failures are lapses in following teacher intent --- bots skip required workflow steps (53.8% of end-user conversations), omit expectation setup (33.4%), and overload learners with information or questions (37.1%). Guided by these findings, we design a prompt-based harness targeting the six most frequent failure modes. In a study with 200 college students across ten bots, the harness reduces the mean number of target failure codes per conversation from 1.406 to 0.489, a 65.2% relative reduction with bots weighted equally. These findings show how real-world failure analysis can guide practical improvements to educational chatbots.

papers.title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
papers.authors: Songping Wang, Peiyang Li, Yi Huang, Fengting Li, Xuhao Ran, Yueming Lyu, Chao Feng, Caifeng Shan
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. Although prompt injection has been studied in desktop and web settings, its cross-modal properties in mobile ecosystems remain poorly understood, and existing security analyses are still limited. To close this gap, we introduce MobileInject, the first benchmark for evaluating mobile agents against multimodal injection attacks and reasoning-to-action security risks. MobileInject provides a high-fidelity interactive mobile evaluation framework covering 11 scenarios, 9 security-risk categories, and 108 executable risk instances. It further introduces Cross-Modal Consistency Injection to exploit corroboration across modalities, two enhanced attack methods, Multi-Role Collaborative Deception and Reasoning-Camouflage Injection, to intensify trust manipulation and reasoning hijacking, and a Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework for fine-grained failure analysis. Systematic experiments show that mobile agents are broadly vulnerable to multimodal injection, and that many failures stem from reasoning hijacking at early stages. These findings establish MobileInject as a systematic cross-modal benchmark for studying and improving the security of mobile agents. Code release details are provided in the Appendix Open Science section.

papers.title: MultiAgent-OPD: End-to-End Training of Hierarchical Multi-Agent Systems with On-Policy Distillation
papers.authors: Yuhan Sun, Jiaxin Zhao, Yongdong Luo, Yibo Hu, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma, Weixun Wang, weihang Pan, Zhongan Bi
papers.abstract: In a hierarchical multi-agent system, a Leader assigns tasks and subagents carry them out. Jointly training the Leader and the subagents is difficult because a final answer gives only indirect feedback to the subagents. An LLM judge can score the performance of the subagents, but these scores depend on the judge's own assessment of the quality of subagents' responses. We present MultiAgent-OPD, which combines on-policy distillation with reinforcement learning to jointly train a shared-parameter Leader-Searcher-Answerer team end to end. We first train a Teacher in a Searcher-Answerer workflow using answer correctness. During team training, the frozen Teacher scores student-generated search and summary tokens to provide local process supervision for the Searchers, while the Leader learns from team success and the Answerer from candidate correctness. Across seven datasets, the trained system reaches 38.68% macro avg@4, exceeding Prompted Critic by 4.06 percentage points and C-MAS + RL, the trained cascaded multiagent system, by 2.61 percentage points. The team also solves more questions within four attempts.

papers.title: X-MDD: LLM-Based Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis for Unseen Languages with Canonical References
papers.authors: Xintong Wang, Junchuan Zhao, Ye Wang
papers.abstract: Mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) provides phone-level feedback to language learners, but extending it to new languages typically requires collecting and annotating learner speech for each target language. This repeated annotation effort is costly and limits the language coverage of pronunciation feedback. We study whether MDD capabilities learned from annotated learner speech can be applied to languages unseen during MDD training when canonical pronunciation references are available. Our multilingual LLM-based model, X-MDD, uses canonical speech and phones as references to predict the phone sequence actually produced by a learner. It incorporates in-context demonstrations for inference-time adaptation and is further optimized with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using detection F1 and phone error rate. We further analyze how canonical inputs affect prediction and find that (1) canonical speech and phones jointly contribute to actual-phone prediction, and (2) conflicting speech evidence reduces the tendency to copy canonical phones. Trained only on Mandarin and English, X-MDD achieves a detection F1 of 38.07 on Arabic Qur'anic recitation, compared with 44.14 for a supervised challenge baseline trained on Arabic. It also achieves F1 scores of 78.68 and 58.78 on Mandarin and English, respectively, demonstrating effective multilingual MDD within a single model.

papers.title: Designing an AI Agent That Does Not Tutor: Design Rules for Socratic Probing in Introductory Physics
papers.authors: Byungmoon Cho
papers.abstract: Instructors need to know whether a student understands a concept, not only whether the student can produce a correct answer, and the two have come apart: a student can paste a physics question into a chatbot and submit a fluent, correct answer without understanding it. We built a conversational AI agent for introductory mechanics that only probes. It is designed as an instrument that a correct answer alone should not pass. Its key measure is cave detection: identifying a correct first idea that the student abandons when a single variable of the scenario is changed. A single right-or-wrong item cannot see this. The agent asks a student to commit to a prediction about an everyday situation, explain it without physics vocabulary, and defend that explanation against a changed case built from the student's own words. It does not teach, hint, confirm, or correct, and it reports nothing until the end. Such an instrument works only if its replies give nothing away. LLM agents tend to leak evaluation: praise, word choice, reply length, and pacing reveal whether an answer was right, and a student who knows stops reasoning. We report design rules that suppress this leakage, derived from eight versions of the agent and more than 40 scripted simulation runs. The obvious fixes often made leakage worse: listing forbidden praise phrases increased praise, and a single worked example in the prompt spread into unrelated conversations. Each changed case had to alter exactly one variable; otherwise a changed answer could not be traced to a single idea. The evidence is simulation evidence only: no real students have used the agent, and the author wrote both the personas and the scoring rules. This paper reports design findings, not learning outcomes.

papers.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
papers.authors: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar‐Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin
papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.

papers.title: Oh doughnuts, it's the variance! A visual metaphor for the variance, standard deviation, and related quantities
papers.authors: Eugene D. Hahn
papers.abstract: Despite the rise of artificial intelligence, human intuition endures as both a foundation for education and also (for now) a primarily human experience. We re-examine a formula for the sum of squares that is sometimes set aside because of possible numerical issues. The formula can be used to create square doughnuts, a delicious regional favorite. The variance becomes the dough, and we can examine the variance by either comparing doughnuts or by making different sizes of doughnuts with the same amount of dough. In doing so, we provide a new visualization of a cornerstone formula, understandable by students at almost any level. We further provide insight into related topics such as the coefficient of variation as well as a visualization of when numerical issues are likely to be problematic. We also provide a new vocabulary for understanding the variance formula, with `dough' and `hole' taking the place of less edible concepts from the typical recipe.

papers.title: Data Science for the Next Millennium: A Ubiquitous Review
papers.authors: Miss. S. B. Avhad Miss. Warale Tejasvi Narsinha, Prof. J. R. Mahajan
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: Data science has become a practical foundation for understanding complex information and supporting decisions across modern society. Digital services, connected devices, scientific instruments, business systems and public platforms continuously generate structured and unstructured data. This review examines data science as an interdisciplinary process that combines statistics, computing, domain knowledge, data engineering, machine learning and communication. It discusses the typical lifecycle of a data science project, major analytical techniques, commonly used tools, and applications in education, healthcare, business, environmental monitoring, transportation and public services. The discussion is informed by a review of literature published mainly between 2018 and 2023, including the review by Anwar and colleagues, while also drawing on established books and methodological publications. Rather than presenting a new experiment, the paper synthesizes recurring themes and practical considerations reported in the literature. The review highlights that useful outcomes depend not only on advanced algorithms but also on data quality, appropriate problem formulation, reproducibility, privacy, fairness, and communication of uncertainty. It concludes that the future of data science will be shaped by responsible automation, accessible analytical platforms, stronger interdisciplinary collaboration and governance that keeps human needs at the centre of data-driven decisions.

papers.title: Beyond AI Tutors: A Human-Centred Framework for Goal-Driven Learning Agents in Education
papers.authors: Ghodakhe Keshav, Prof. Y.G.Suryawanshi, Dr. H.B.Jadhav
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing education by offering new ways to explain concepts, support teachers, and personalise student learning. However, many conventional educational chatbots focus on answering individual questions rather than coordinating the complete learning process. Students often need more than an answer: they need a learning plan, suitable practice activities, feedback on mistakes, and guidance about what to study next. Agentic artificial intelligence offers a possible way to coordinate these activities around a defined learning objective. This paper reviews selected research published between 2024 and 2026 on pedagogical AI agents, large language model agents, and agentic systems in education. The reviewed literature highlights opportunities for personalized tutoring, adaptive feedback, assignment support, and teacher assistance. It also identifies concerns involving inaccurate outputs, student dependency, privacy, fairness, accountability, and limited real-world evaluation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a human-centred framework that connects learning-goal identification, task planning, trusted educational resources, instructional support, progress evaluation, and adaptive follow-up. The framework centres student independence, teacher judgement, and responsible data use. It is a conceptual proposal and has not yet been experimentally evaluated. Future research should assess its educational effectiveness, reliability, accessibility, and suitability for different learning environments

papers.title: Assessment of Foot Pain and Functional Disability among Traffic Police Personnel in Bareilly: Association with Prolonged Standing, Body Mass Index, and Occupational Factors
papers.authors: Syed Ehtesham-Ul-Huda and Dr. Mahesh Kumar Shou
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: Background: Traffic police personnel are frequently exposed to prolonged standing, repetitive walking, hardworking surfaces, and occupational footwear demands. These factors may contribute to foot discomfort and functional limitations, potentially affecting work performance and quality of life. Aim: To assess foot pain and functional disability among traffic police personnel in Bareilly and examine their association with daily standing duration, body mass index (BMI), age, and occupational characteristics. Methodology: A quantitative, cross-sectional analytical study is proposed among traffic police personnel working at selected locations in Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh. Data will be collected using a structured demographic and occupational questionnaire, a numerical pain rating scale, and a validated foot-specific functional assessment instrument such as the Foot Function Index (FFI). Height and weight will be measured to calculate BMI. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multivariable regression will be used to assess the relationships between occupational variables, foot pain, and functional disability. Expected contribution: The study will provide an evidence-based framework for evaluating occupational foot health and identifying potentially modifiable risk factors. The findings may support preventive education, appropriate footwear selection, and workplace ergonomic measures.

papers.title: Occupational Foot Health Among Traffic Police Personnel: A Review of Foot Posture, Prolonged Standing, Footwear Comfort, and Musculoskeletal Discomfort
papers.authors: Syed Ehtesham-Ul-Huda and Dr. Mahesh Kumar Shou
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: Background: Traffic police personnel perform physically demanding duties involving prolonged standing, intermittent walking, repetitive weight-bearing, and exposure to variable road surfaces. These occupational conditions may contribute to foot discomfort, lower-limb fatigue, and musculoskeletal symptoms. Foot posture, anthropometric characteristics, standing duration, and occupational footwear are important factors to consider when evaluating foot health. Objective: This review examines the existing literature on occupational foot health, with particular emphasis on foot posture, prolonged standing, footwear comfort, body mass index (BMI), foot pain, and functional disability among traffic police personnel and other occupational groups with similar work demands. Review approach: A narrative review approach was used to organize relevant literature on foot posture assessment, occupational standing, footwear characteristics, and musculoskeletal health. Published clinical assessment studies and occupational health reviews were considered. The review emphasizes the relevance of these findings to traffic police personnel in Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh, India. Review findings: The literature indicates that prolonged standing is associated with several adverse health outcomes, including lower-limb discomfort and fatigue. Footwear characteristics, such as cushioning, sole hardness, fit, and insole design, may influence foot comfort and mechanical loading. Standardized tools, including the Foot Posture Index-6 (FPI-6), can support quantitative assessment of standing foot posture. However, static foot posture, pain intensity, and functional disability represent different outcomes and should be assessed separately. The available evidence does not establish that age, BMI, or standing duration necessarily causes a particular foot posture in traffic police personnel. Conclusion: Occupational foot health should be considered an important component of preventive health assessment among traffic police personnel. Future research in Bareilly should investigate foot posture, footwear comfort, standing duration, BMI, pain, and functional limitations using standardized assessment methods. Evidence from appropriately designed studies may inform occupational health screening and further evaluation of preventive strategies.

papers.title: From Rules to Autonomous Agents: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Human-AI Integration, and the Governance of Agentic Systems-A Review
papers.authors: Loso Judijanto
papers.journal: Journal of Engineering and Applied Sciences Technology
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from rule-based symbolic systems into learning architectures capable of perception, prediction, content generation, reasoning, planning, tool use, and increasingly autonomous action. This qualitative literature review examines this transition as more than a technological chronology. It interprets AI evolution through five interrelated dimensions: technological evolution, capability expansion, changing human roles, human–AI integration, and governance. Drawing on contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026, the review identifies seven thematic developments. AI has progressed from encoded rules toward learned representations and goal-directed action; generative AI has expanded AI into a general-purpose content collaborator; agentic AI adds planning, memory, tool use, and iterative task execution; human roles increasingly shift from operator toward collaborator, delegator, and governor; human–AI complementarity remains conditional rather than automatic; effective deployment requires calibrated rather than maximal trust; and governance requirements increase as AI systems acquire greater operational agency. The article proposes the Evolution–Capability–Role–Integration–Governance (ECRIG) framework to explain these relationships. The framework suggests that sustainable benefits from advanced AI emerge when technological capability, human role allocation, interaction architecture, and governance mechanisms develop jointly. The review concludes that the central challenge of the agentic-AI era is not choosing between humans and machines, but designing accountable systems in which increasingly capable artificial agents remain aligned with meaningful human goals, authority, and oversight.

papers.title: ChatGPT Awareness and Utilization Among Undergraduate Biology Education Students at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka: Implications for Mathematics Education
papers.authors: Euphemia Ebubechukwu ONAH, Prince Lazarus NWOTOLO, Winifred Ifeaka Ukwueze, Benson Chukwunonso EZEANYI, Lilian Chioma Ugwuoti, Opeyemi Fadekemi Awosika
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTER RESEARCH
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has created new opportunities for learning while also raising concerns about accuracy, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on automated outputs. This study examined awareness, utilization, challenges, and perceived institutional responses to ChatGPT among undergraduate Biology Education students at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. A descriptive survey design was adopted. Eighty questionnaires were distributed to students across 100–400 levels, and 67 usable responses were returned, representing an 83.75% response rate. Data were collected using a researcher-developed Questionnaire on the Extent of Awareness and Usage of ChatGPT (QEAUC), which demonstrated an overall Cronbach’s alpha of .798. Frequency and percentage were used to analyse awareness items, while mean and standard deviation were used for utilization, challenges, and proposed solutions. The findings showed substantial awareness of ChatGPT: respondents demonstrated awareness on seven of eight awareness items, although only 25.4% recognized that ChatGPT uses natural language processing to understand and respond to queries. Overall utilization was high (M = 2.81, SD = 0.81 on a 4-point scale), with particularly high use for content creation, academic research, education, assignments, brainstorming, and conversation practice. Respondents also agreed that important barriers included inadequate internet access (M = 3.64), training costs (M = 3.46), and rote or superficial use (M = 3.51). The strongest proposed solutions were free internet access (M = 3.85), free Wi-Fi (M = 3.82), curriculum integration (M = 3.76), and guided learning activities (M = 3.58). The study concludes that ChatGPT is already embedded in the academic practices of many participating Biology Education students, but effective integration requires AI literacy, reliable digital infrastructure, explicit institutional guidance, and assessment practices that preserve student thinking and academic integrity.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Business English Training Programs in Corporate Organizations
papers.authors: Varsha Palsule
papers.journal: Contemporaneity of English Language and Literature in the Robotized Millennium
papers.abstract: Effectiveness of Business English training programs is one of the crucial issues in improving the communication skills, professional performance, and workplace productivity of the personnel in corporate enterprises. This study looks into the effectiveness of Business English training, which includes the following aspects of employees’ development: language proficiency, communication skills, confidence level, presentation skills, and overall workplace performance. This study takes into consideration several aspects related to training including duration of training program, number of training hours, teaching methods, participation of employees, and business communication exercises. Quantitative data is processed through statistical and machine learning analysis techniques to establish correlations between training variables and performance results of employees. The results have shown that Business English training can help employees become effective communicators in their meetings, negotiations, and presentations and also while writing professional emails. Regular practice and context-based learning activities will help employees become more confident and proficient in language.

papers.title: Innowacje deliberatywne w samorządzie zawodowym radców prawnych
papers.authors: Mariola Żak
papers.abstract: This paper posits that the professional self-government of attorneys-at-law can serve as a paradigmatic model for transferring democratic (deliberative) innovations beyond the traditional domain of local governance, thereby enhancing the influence of the Bar on public policy-making and the shaping of regulations governing professional practice. Deliberative innovations – such as mini-publics, citizens’ panels, deliberative polls, and hybrid (online-offline) frameworks supporting professional deliberation – introduce mechanisms into decision-making processes that facilitate an in-depth exchange of arguments, a systematic analysis of values and the consequences of decisions, and the integration of expert knowledge with practitioners’ experience. The article examines existing and potential deliberative mechanisms within the professional self-government of attorneys-at-law, encompassing internal regulatory practices, the co-creation of and legislative consultation on draft normative acts, strategic decision-making, and the election of governing bodies. The analysis highlights a qualitative shift in deliberation within the National Bar of Attorneys-at-Law, characterized by greater consistency, transparency, and legitimacy of decisions within the professional community, while fully preserving the autonomy of its statutory governing bodies. The proposed institutional mechanisms, including the Deliberative Panel at the National Bar Council of Attorneys-at-Law (KRRP), supported by the expert infrastructure of the KRRP Centre for Research, Studies and Legislation, demonstrate the practical viability of integrating deliberation into the operations of the professional self-government, thereby fostering a space for reflexive, pluralistic, and accountable decision-making practices.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models’ Responses to Common Queries on Retinal Surgery: Readability and Accuracy Analysis
papers.authors: Erkan Duman, Aydın Maçin, Ayşe Ergin
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIMS: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT-4o mini, ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Microsoft Copilot play an important role in improving health literacy and supporting patient decision making.This study aims to evaluate the clinical appropriateness and readability of responses provided by these LLMs to frequently asked questions about retinal detachment (RD), epiretinal membrane (ERM), and macular hole (MH). MATERIALS AND METHODS:This comparative cross-sectional study did not involve human participants.A total of 121 questions related to RD, ERM and MH were compiled.These questions were presented to LLM interfaces and were categorised into different themes.Inter-rater agreement between two retinal specialists who scored the responses based on their clinical expertise was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).In addition, the readability of the responses was analysed using five readability indices. RESULTS:Response appropriateness rates were similar for ChatGPT-4o mini (100%), ChatGPT-4o (99.2%) and Gemini 1.5 Pro (99.2%), while Microsoft Copilot (90.9%) showed comparatively lower performance.A high level of inter-rater agreement was observed among clinicians.Regarding readability, ChatGPT-4o performed best, whereas ChatGPT-4o mini performed worst.Gemini 1.5 Pro and Microsoft Copilot were intermediate between these two models.The excellent inter-rater agreement (ICC: 0.891-0.938)further supports the reliability of the expert evaluation process.CONCLUSION: Our study showed that the evaluated LLMs provided largely appropriate and comprehensive answers to questions related to vitreoretinal surgery.ChatGPT-4o showed the highest performance in both appropriateness and readability, while ChatGPT-4o mini, despite its high appropriateness, had the lowest readability score.

papers.title: TEACHING ANATOMY BY USING KOLLAR METHOD AS AN AI TOOL FOR LOW ACHIEVERS IN IST YEAR MBBS STUDENTS
papers.authors: Dr. Krishnaveni. C, Dr. Naga Vidya Lakshmi. K, Mehandi.V. Mahajan, Dr. Venkateshu.K. V
papers.abstract: Introduction: This is an acronym, namely KO is for Keys of Originality, L is for Learning, L is for Lecturing, A is for Application of social media and R is for Relaxation. This element of the method helps the teacher focusing on improving the creative skills of the students by applying creative techniques such as divergent thinking, problem solving. The aim of the study is to introduce the KOLLAR method for 1st year MBBS by creating interest in slow learners for their improvement and performance in anatomy. Materials & Methods: The study was performed for 4 years on slow performers/learners in Ist year MBBS students in Department of Anatomy, actively participated in this study after getting ethical approval by the Institutional ethical clearance. After 1st internal assessment the slow learners are identified given assignments (questions) to practice the diagrams. On the same topics they have to prepare by using “KOLLAR method”, later students will do the activity by using their systems/laptops/mobiles any software also they can use and draw a diagram on that topic and save it. KO-they are using normal traditional method by attending regular classes, L-they are learning by dissection methods, drawing diagrams L- normal lecturer classes they will attend and do assignments, A-in initially by using electronic devices and software they will be application of social media. R- it is a playful method. At the end feedbacks will be collected from the students. This study was done only in Hungary nowhere else. Present study is different from Hungarian study by performing on slow learners/low achievers with different methodology adopted by following the concept. Results: By using feedback analysis in Likert’s scale the study was analyzed. The low achievers mentioned that this is useful method in understanding the subjects. So, it is effective in improvising the skills of the slow learners and create interest in the subject and make them successful. Conclusion: By listening the theory classes and performing by this KOLLAR method is better in understanding. Blending of traditional and KOLLAR method it is useful.

papers.title: Magnitude and Determinants of Anemia among the Elderly: A Rural–Urban Comparative, Cross-sectional Study in Bengaluru
papers.authors: Amrita N. Shamanewadi, Sahana Kodagenhalli Suresh, Nithya Madathiparambil Chandran, Bency Naomi
papers.abstract: A BSTRACT Background: Anemia in older adults is frequently overlooked but remains critically associated with impaired physical performance, cognitive decline, increased falls, and higher mortality rates. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of anemia and identify its determinants among the elderly population in both rural and urban areas of Bengaluru. Methodology: A cross-sectional study involved 173 participants from the rural and urban field practice areas of a tertiary care hospital. Data on socio-demographics, medical history, and lifestyle factors were collected, and hemoglobin levels were measured using the Quick-Check Plus Hemoglobin Testing Systems. Statistical analysis utilized Chi-square tests for associations and independent samples t -tests to compare mean hemoglobin levels. Results: The overall prevalence of anemia was 53.8%. Rural participants exhibited a significantly lower mean hemoglobin level (10.02 ± 1.58 g/dL) compared to urban participants (11.39 ± 1.18 g/dL; P < 0.001). Significant associations were found between anemia and dyslipidemia ( P = 0.012), cardiac disease ( P = 0.021), history of blood loss ( P < 0.001), anticoagulant use ( P < 0.001), and BMI ( P = 0.032). Conclusion: Anemia is a major public health challenge among the elderly, with a higher prevalence in rural areas likely driven by nutritional gaps and limited healthcare access. Conversely, the higher frequency of moderate-to-severe cases in urban settings is linked to chronic comorbidities and iatrogenic factors such as anticoagulant use. These findings highlight the necessity for targeted geriatric interventions that address both nutritional deficiencies and the complexities of managing chronic clinical conditions.

papers.title: Implementing AI and Virtual Reality in Elite Sports Psychology
papers.authors: Jian Cao, Weimin Shen
papers.journal: Journal of Cases on Information Technology
papers.abstract: In team sports, psychological regulation is crucial, yet traditional methods lack personalization, rely on subjective assessments, and offer low realism. This study examined the integration of computer-assisted technologies into psychological training. A six-month trial involved 90 professional football, basketball, and ice hockey players, randomly assigned to an experimental group or control group. Data on physiology, psychology, performance, and team communication were analyzed using t-tests. Per the results, the experimental group showed 21.3% lower anxiety, 25.4% higher cohesion, 21.2% faster decision response, 14.3% higher clutch success, 38.7% better communication efficiency; clutch error rate was also reduced from 27% to 11%. However, ~15% experienced virtual reality discomfort, and artificial intelligence overreliance reduced tactical creativity by 19%. Computer-assisted technologies enhance psychological resilience and team performance. Balancing data-driven precision with human-centered coaching is vital. Future work should optimize training models and establish data ethics.

papers.title: Design and Implementation of an Integrated Cross-Platform Privacy Management Architecture Using a Rule-Based Privacy Enforcement Algorithm (RBPEA) for Cross-Platform Social Media Systems
papers.authors: Sabir Umar Danillela
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
papers.abstract: The widespread use of multiple social media platforms has increased user exposure to privacy risks due to fragmented and complex privacy controls. Users are required to configure separate privacy settings across different platforms, often leading to inconsistent configurations, privacy fatigue, and unintended data disclosure. Existing privacy mechanisms remain largely platform-specific and do not provide unified or user-centred control across platforms. This study aims to design, implement, and evaluate an integrated architecture for protecting user privacy across social media platforms. The proposed system employs a Rule-Based Privacy Enforcement Algorithm (RBPEA) to translate user-defined privacy preferences into platform-specific enforcement actions. Using the Design Science Research methodology, a modular, web-based prototype was developed, incorporating secure user authentication, centralized privacy rule management, and cross-platform enforcement through platform adapters. The system was evaluated based on enforcement consistency, usability, and system performance. Results indicate improved consistency of privacy settings across platforms, reduced user effort in privacy configuration, and enhanced transparency through audit and feedback mechanisms. The findings demonstrate that algorithm-driven, integrated privacy management is both feasible and effective for improving user privacy control in multiplatform environments. This study contributes an empirically evaluated architectural model and algorithmic approach for cross-platform privacy protection, addressing a significant gap in existing privacy management solutions.

papers.title: EXPLORING CHATGPT’S ROLE AS AN AUTOMATED WRITING EVALUATION TOOL: A STUDY IN VIETNAMESE HIGH SCHOOL EFL CLASSROOMS
papers.authors: Thi Tuyet Phuong Le, Hoang Minh Trung Bui
papers.abstract: Since its launch, ChatGPT has become a widely used tool by students for classroom exercises and home assignments. This study examines the role of ChatGPT as an automatic writing evaluation (AWE) tool in assisting Vietnamese high school students in self-correcting grammar and vocabulary errors in their descriptive writing assignments. The participants were five 18-year-old students at a private high school in Ho Chi Minh City. Before utilizing ChatGPT to revise original drafts, the participants were tasked with writing seven assignments based on Cambridge English Key (KET) exam picture prompts. Data collection included pre- and post-ChatGPT-usage writing assessments, screenshots of revisions, and some questionnaires exploring feedback engagement and reasoning behind acceptance or rejection of ChatGPT’s suggestions. Results showed improved writing, highlighting ChatGPT’s strengths in correcting grammar and enhancing vocabulary. Students engaged deeply with feedback, selectively accepting or rejecting suggestions based on their writing context and demonstrating enhanced self-assessment and learning independence. This autonomy is noteworthy and valuable in large classrooms where teacher feedback is limited. However, the participants expressed mixed levels of trust in the tool, especially when the suggestions seemed unclear or incompatible with their writing style, and often sought teacher validation. While ChatGPT promotes autonomous learning, it should complement, not replace, teacher feedback.

papers.title: INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL, DOCUMENTAÇÃO PEDAGÓGICA E EDUCAÇÃO ESPECIAL INCLUSIVA
papers.authors: Luiz Fernando Marques dos Santos, Marcilene Moreira Donadoni
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the possibilities and limits of Artificial Intelligence in organizing pedagogical evidence aimed at monitoring the learning pathways of students who are the target audience of Special Education. It develops a bibliographic and theoretical-conceptual study grounded in research on Artificial Intelligence and education, pedagogical documentation, mediating assessment, and Inclusive Special Education. It argues that Artificial Intelligence can contribute to systematizing records, integrating different sources of information, and expanding institutional pedagogical memory, but it cannot replace the ethical, relational, and interpretive processes carried out by teachers and pedagogical coordinators. The analysis indicates that data become evidence only when contextualized and interpreted in light of school experiences. It concludes that the contribution of Artificial Intelligence to democratic and inclusive education depends on its articulation with pedagogical documentation and human decisions committed to students’ singularities and to ensuring the right to learn.

papers.title: AI-Driven Personalization in Digital Marketing: Consumer Trust, Engagement, and Purchase Behavior - A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Raden Ayu Isfiani, Herry Mulyono, Alberta Ingriana
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization has increasingly transformed digital marketing by enabling firms to deliver individualized recommendations, content, and offers based on consumer data and behavioral patterns. However, the growing use of personalization also raises important questions regarding consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. This study aims to conduct a systematic literature review (SLR) of research on AI-driven personalization in digital marketing to examine its implications for consumer trust, engagement, and purchase behavior. Using Scopus as the primary database, the search process identified 2,906 records and, through successive filtering and screening procedures, resulted in 51 eligible studies. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and thematic synthesis were employed to identify publication trends, intellectual structures, and key research themes. The findings indicate a shift from technology-oriented research toward consumer-centered perspectives, with increasing attention to consumer experience, trust, engagement, privacy, transparency, purchase intention, and purchase behavior. The review further demonstrates that the effectiveness of AI-driven personalization is context-dependent and influenced by consumer perceptions and data-related concerns. These findings provide an integrated basis for understanding the evolving role of AI personalization in contemporary digital marketing

papers.title: Reflect-Guard: Enhancing LLM Safeguards Against Adversarial Prompts via Logical Self-Reflection
papers.authors: Lixing Lin, Lixing Lin, Juli You, Lihong Lin, Lihong Lin, Lihong Lin, Yiqing Wang, Zhen Zhang, Moxuan Zheng
papers.abstract: LLM safety classifiers such as Llama Guard detect overtly harmful prompts well but remain vulnerable to jailbreaks that disguise intent via role-play, fictional framing, or indirect requests. We present Reflect-Guard: Llama-Guard-3-8B fine-tuned via QLoRA to generate a distilled, GPT-4o-mini-sourced safety rationale before its verdict. Using only 1000training examples and a five-condition ablation, we isolate reflection’s contribution from that of ordinary supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SFT on verdict labels alone already accounts for most of the aggregate gain over the un-fine-tuned baseline (WildGuardTest F1: 0.770 → 0.860; JailbreakBench guard bypass rate: 10.3% → 0.0%). Adding reflection does not improve these aggregate numbers further (F1 falls to 0.842, guard bypass rises to 1.8%) but reallocates performance toward adversarially framed inputs: adversarial-subset recall rises from 0.845 (SFT-only) to 0.921 (+7.6 pp), at a cost of −7.9 pp precision on that subset. The same direction holds across three training seeds (paired t-tests, p=0.018 for overall F1 and p=0.027 for adversarial recall), though we interpret these values cautiously given the small number of seeds. Measured inference latency is 17.9× the baseline’s, driven by ∼92 additional reflection tokens per prompt. The same checkpoint, without additional fine-tuning, shows promising zero-shot transfer to a 329-example financial-harm benchmark (F1: 0.868 → 0.929; recall: 0.767 → 0.867, zero false positives); preliminary two-seed evidence, however, suggests the SFT-only condition may match or exceed this result, so we treat the finance improvement as evidence toward generalization rather than a settled advantage of reflection specifically. Benchmarked against WildGuard, PromptGuard, and a prompted (non-fine-tuned) GPT-4o-mini reasoning classifier on the same sets, WildGuard leads on aggregate WildGuardTest F1 (0.887), while Reflect-Guard achieves higher adversarial-subset recall than every evaluated classifier, including WildGuard (0.921 vs. 0.827) and the prompted teacher (0.636). Overall, supervised fine-tuning drives most of the aggregate gain over an un-fine-tuned classifier, while the generated safety rationale yields a narrower, latency-costly improvement specifically in adversarial-subset recall, a precision–recall tradeoff relevant to safety-critical deployments that prioritize recall over inference speed.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Corporate Energy Efficiency: A Pathway to Sustainable Manufacturing—Evidence from Chinese Firms
papers.authors: Yahan Shi, Yinchao Zhang, Xizhe Xu, Xiaofeng Xu, Da Tong
papers.abstract: In the context of global efforts to achieve sustainable development and carbon neutrality, improving industrial energy efficiency has become a cornerstone of green transformation. This study examines how corporate AI-related disclosure intensity is associated with sustainable energy efficiency in manufacturing firms. Using panel data on Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2012 to 2024, we measure corporate energy efficiency using energy intensity based on standard coal. AI-related disclosure intensity is constructed from the frequency of AI-related terms in firms’ annual reports and logarithmically transformed. Based on panel regression, process innovation association analysis, moderation analysis, and ownership-based subgroup analysis, this study finds that AI-related disclosure intensity is negatively associated with energy intensity. Higher AI-related disclosure intensity is also linked to a higher share of process innovation, indicating enhanced attention to production process improvement. Data element utilization weakens the negative association between AI-related disclosure intensity and energy intensity, suggesting a moderating effect. The negative relationship persists across both state-owned and non-state-owned firms. These findings contribute to the understanding of how AI-related disclosure intensity reflects corporate energy management and promotes sustainable manufacturing. They offer actionable implications for firms and policymakers seeking to advance green innovation and achieve a sustainable economy.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Development and Worker Employment Quality: Evidence from China
papers.authors: Yunting Wu, Xiliang Feng
papers.abstract: With the continuous development of new technologies, these new technologies have a profound impact on the labor market. This paper uses micro-individual data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) from 2016 to 2022 and provincial-level macro-data on artificial intelligence (AI), employing a two-way fixed-effects model to systematically examine the actual impact and underlying mechanisms of AI development on the employment quality of workers. The study shows a significant positive correlation between the level of regional artificial intelligence development and the employment quality of local workers. However, this overall effect at the regional level cannot directly prove the individual-level effect of enterprises or employees using artificial intelligence. Mechanism testing further confirms that the effect of the regional AI development on improving the employment quality of workers is mainly achieved through optimizing the industrial structure and promoting the intelligentization of workers’ working mode. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the regional artificial intelligence has a greater positive impact on employment quality for male workers, outside-system workers, and workers in the eastern region. Therefore, to achieve higher-quality employment for workers, it is necessary to promote the deep integration of AI with the real economy, build a multi-party collaborative education mechanism involving government, enterprises, and universities, and implement policies to promote digital inclusion and differentiated support.

papers.title: Regulating the Relationship: What the First Sui Generis Companion Chatbot Statutes Achieve for Minors, and What They Leave Undone
papers.authors: YuChao Chen
papers.abstract: AI companion chatbots support extended personal conversations, and many adolescents use them for companionship and emotional support. Two American lawsuits allege that prolonged interactions with these systems contributed to minors’ suicides. In 2025, California, New York and Utah enacted technology-specific statutes addressing companion or mental health chatbots. A close reading of these statutes revisits a longstanding question: should emerging technologies be governed by specialised legislation or general law? The principal contribution of the California and New York statutes is definitional: they recognise the sustained human–machine relationship as an object of regulation. Their substantive duties, however, focus on disclosure and crisis protocols, leaving the design choices that encourage emotional attachment largely unaddressed. Disclosure alone offers limited protection because users can respond socially to machines even when they know they are artificial. The analysis therefore supports a combination of approaches: technology-specific definitions that identify the relationship to be regulated, coupled with duties enforced through established consumer protection mechanisms. This combination provides a basis for regulation, but the enacted duties offer minors limited protection against the commercial design of attachment.

papers.title: Thinking, Feeling, and Acting with Generative AI: Affective, Behavioral, and Cognitive Engagement and Perceived Human–AI Outcomes
papers.authors: Amir Mahmood, Chaocheng Zhou, Xiao Huang, Nadia Rehman, Misbah Shafait Abbasi, Akpaasou Daniel Terver
papers.abstract: Generative AI requires students not only to adopt technology but also to engage critically, behaviorally, cognitively, and emotionally with its outputs. This study develops and tests the AI Engagement ABC+ Model, a domain-specific adaptation of the affective–behavioral–cognitive engagement framework. The model differentiates positive and negative AI affect, three behavioral functions, creation, verification, and community participation, and two cognitive regulatory functions, strategic and critical cognition. A cross-sectional online survey collected data from 1250 students representing 15 nationalities at eight universities in China. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to examine 15 hypothesized associations between seven first-order engagement facets and four self-reported AI-supported outcomes: perceived Output Quality, Creativity, Integrity, and Trust Calibration. Fourteen hypotheses were supported. Verification Behavior had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of Integrity (β = 0.303) and perceived Output Quality (β = 0.269) and was also associated with perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.191). Critical Cognition had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.270), and Community Behavior was positively associated with Integrity (β = 0.290) and Creativity (β = 0.240). Positive AI Affect was associated with perceived Output Quality (β = 0.214) and Creativity (β = 0.139), whereas Negative AI Affect was negatively associated with Trust Calibration (β = −0.137) but was unrelated to Integrity. The model explained 25.7% of the variance in Creativity, 25.2% in Integrity, 20.8% in perceived Output Quality, and 17.6% in Trust Calibration. Positive Q2_predict values provided additional evidence of out-of-sample predictive relevance. The findings support a differentiated view of GenAI engagement in which specific affective, behavioral, and cognitive facets are associated with distinct perceived outcomes. The model offers a theoretically structured basis for further research on responsible GenAI engagement, while its cross-sectional self-report design precludes causal or objective-performance conclusions.

papers.title: Comparing Genetic Algorithms and LLMs for Research-Hypothesis Generation: Mainstream Convergence of LLMs, Wider Hypothesis Exploration by Combinatorial Search, and the Limits of Literature-Distance Novelty Metrics
papers.authors: Akira Otsuki
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based creative AI systems tend to produce plausible rather than novel research ideas. This study compares two ways of generating research hypotheses: a genetic algorithm (GA) that recombines Method, Problem, and Goal elements under a fitness function rewarding distance from the literature and literature support for each link, and free proposals by an LLM. Papers and hypotheses share one embedding space built from 2856 arXiv papers. Over 30 runs with budget-matched baselines and outcome measures on held-out and later-published papers, the selected hypotheses were more distant from the unseen literature than unsearched ones, but the GA matched rather than outperformed random search and hill climbing. Across two LLM families, two prompts, and two temperatures, and even when choosing from the GA’s concept vocabulary, LLM-proposed hypotheses were less diverse and closer to existing literature, whereas combinatorial search explored more widely. On 9755 ICLR submissions, the literature-distance novelty measure was practically unrelated to reviewers’ judgments (Spearman ρ ≤ 0.06), so it cannot establish originality. In controlled manuscript generation, LLM judges proved unreliable, and their order-consistent verdicts more often favored manuscripts built on LLM-proposed hypotheses, which blinded human raters tended to rank as least useful. Code and data are openly released.

papers.title: Generative AI Use and the Verification Gap Follow Opposing Social Gradients in Türkiye
papers.authors: Doğukan Kurç
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) use and online information checking may be socially patterned in different ways. This cross-sectional study analysed the 2025 Turkish Statistical Institute ICT survey of 22,502 internet users aged 16–74 using weighted modified Poisson regression with household-clustered standard errors. Overall, 19.2% reported generative AI use, and 48.3% of respondents who noticed doubtful content did not check it. Conditional non-checking (the verification gap) increased with age and decreased with education and reported digital activity, whereas AI use followed the opposite pattern. Compared with ages 16–24, the adjusted prevalence ratio at ages 65–74 was 1.48 (95% confidence interval 1.30–1.68) for non-checking and 0.10 (0.07–0.16) for AI use. Health information seekers and AI users reported less non-checking among those who noticed doubtful content, but neither group had a lower prevalence of noticing without checking among all internet users. Among non-checkers, 87.3% reported already judging the information or source unreliable and 15.2% reported insufficient skills or knowledge; responses could overlap. These findings distinguish participation in AI use, reported noticing of doubtful content, and subsequent checking. Verification support should address reported difficulty separately from decisions not to investigate content already considered unreliable.

papers.title: Morbidity and Mortality of Statutory Versus Private Health Insurance Patients in Cardiac Surgery in Germany and a Critical Appraisal of the Current Health Insurance Situation
papers.authors: Purevsuren Tsegmid, Filip Schröter, Viyan Sido, Julia Hübner, Martin Hartrumpf, Johannes Maximilian Albes
papers.abstract: Background: In all, 90% of patients in Germany are insured with statutory (SHI) instead of private health insurance (PHI). PHI offers significantly better benefits including earlier and more comprehensive diagnosis and therapy, which can reduce the complication rate and even mortality in fields where patients with high morbidity are treated, yet data on potential outcome differences between SHI and PHI patients in Germany is scarce. Methods: Between January 2023 and December 2025, 144 PHI and 2094 SHI patients underwent heart surgery at one institution. Preoperative baseline characteristics, risk factors, and peri- and postoperative information, including the surgeon’s experience level and distance of the referring hospital, were retrospectively compared. In addition, a propensity score matching (PSM) analysis was performed. Results: The SHI group presented with significantly higher BMI and EuroSCORE II, fewer male patients and higher NYHA states. Significantly more PHI patients were operated on by very senior staff members and none by a trainee, and their hospitalization time was significantly shorter. Neither early mortality (PHI 3.47%, SHI 5.35%, p = 0.432) nor distance levels of referring hospitals differed significantly. After PSM, only differences in the hospitalization time and surgical experience level remained significant. Early mortality came down to 4.86% in the SHI patients after PSM. Conclusions: In a multimorbid patient group, we found no evidence for a difference in outcome depending on insurance status, aside from a shorter hospital stay for PHI patients. Nonetheless, the situation in the pre- and post-hospital phases for SHI patients may have room for improvement. Efforts should be made to give all patients the same rapid and comprehensive access to healthcare services, increasing the system satisfaction of patients with SHI. In cardiac surgery, fortunately, there is no particular need for adjustments regarding the in-hospital phase.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Technical Project Management: A Critical Incident Study
papers.authors: Csenge Kálmán, Barbara Eszter Huszár, András Aschenbrenner
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports project management tasks in technical, technological and innovation-oriented environments. This paper examines how AI is used in technical project management through a qualitative critical incident technique study. The analysis focuses on a technical subsample of five project managers and 26 selected incidents from information technology, vehicle-related technical projects, technology transfer, innovation management and cybersecurity. The findings show that AI mainly functions as a supportive tool in documentation, information processing, data analysis, idea generation and decision preparation. Its strongest value appears in the planning and execution phases, where it improves efficiency, structure and communication. However, the incidents also reveal risks related to data quality, inaccurate outputs, legal constraints, trust and user acceptance. This study concludes that AI can create value in technical projects only when its use remains combined with human validation, professional judgement and clear responsibility.

papers.title: A Lifelong Neuro-Symbolic Explainable AI Twin for Zero-Touch 6G IoE Management Under Non-Stationary Network Dynamics
papers.authors: Walaa M. Alayed, Hassam Ahmed Tahir, Waqar Ul Hassan
papers.abstract: Future sixth-generation (6G) Internet of Everything (IoE) networks require zero-touch management systems capable of autonomously allocating communication and computational resources, satisfying service-level constraints, and providing transparent explanations for their decisions. Existing neuro-symbolic explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) twins improve interpretability by coupling neural prediction with symbolic reasoning; however, most rely on statically engineered causal graphs, fixed rule sets, and immutable knowledge bases. Such closed-world assumptions are unsuitable for non-stationary 6G environments in which radio conditions, mobility patterns, interference relationships, and service requirements continuously evolve. To address this limitation, this paper proposes LL-NS-XAI, a Lifelong Learning Neuro-Symbolic XAI Digital Twin for zero-touch 6G IoE management. The framework integrates three tightly coupled planes: an online implicit learner at the physical edge for time-varying service association and uplink/downlink resource allocation; a dynamic explicit learner in the virtual core for directed acyclic graph (DAG)-based Bayesian reasoning, most-probable-explanation inference, and explainable trust scoring; and a meta-cognitive layer that monitors reasoning residuals, detects parameter drift, structural drift, and ontological emergence, and autonomously revises the causal graph, probabilistic rule sets, conditional probability tables, and knowledge base. Unlike static neuro-symbolic twins, LL-NS-XAI treats realized post-decision outcomes, including achieved channel quality indicator (CQI), measured end-to-end delay, and throughput, as interventional evidence for online causal-model adaptation. Experimental evaluation using a non-stationary 5G-derived dataset with injected parameter drift, structural drift, and emergent IoE service classes demonstrates that LL-NS-XAI maintains higher long-term trustworthiness, lower reasoning residuals, and bounded performance degradation compared with static XAI twins, non-stationary bandits, and pure continual-learning baselines. The framework additionally accommodates a previously unseen IoE service class through autonomous causal-graph expansion, recovering near-oracle performance without offline retraining. These results demonstrate that lifelong causal adaptation can improve the robustness, explainability, and autonomy of AI-enabled zero-touch management in evolving 6G IoE networks.

papers.title: Designing Teaching Materials with GenAI: Perceptions of Cognitive Load and Learner Competencies in Higher Education
papers.authors: Cristina Navas Romero, GANNA ZAKHAROVA, Francisco D. Guillén‐Gámez, Sara Cebrián Cifuentes
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to design instructional materials in higher education, yet limited evidence exists on students’ perceptions of the cognitive demands and learner-related competencies involved. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, this study examined university students’ perceptions of GenAI-supported instructional material design according to gender, age, and admission grade. A quantitative, non-experimental, ex post facto study was conducted with 451 university students enrolled in education-related undergraduate and master’s programmes. The instrument assessed perceived usefulness, beliefs concerning metacognitive practices, prior knowledge, and problem-solving strategies, and perceived intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load. Participants generally reported positive perceptions. Female students reported significantly higher scores on the metacognitive skills, prior knowledge, and problem-solving skills dimensions, although effect sizes were small. These differences should be interpreted cautiously, given that female students represented 82% of the sample. No statistically significant gender differences were detected in the cognitive load dimensions. Age showed only a weak negative association with extraneous cognitive load, whereas admission grade was positively associated with metacognitive scores in both gender groups and with prior knowledge and problem-solving scores among female students. The findings describe students’ beliefs about the practices and cognitive demands associated with GenAI-supported material design and may inform training in the critical review and pedagogical adaptation of AI-generated teaching materials.

papers.title: Bridging the Computational Gap in the Social Sciences: Dual Innovations in Pedagogy and Assessment
papers.authors: Giampiero Giacomello, Fabio Leone
papers.abstract: In a world increasingly dominated by data, graduates in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields are in high demand. This focus often obscures the fact that a significant portion of digital data is social in nature, generated through human–computer interactions. Consequently, experts trained in the social sciences should be equally sought after, yet this is not consistently the case. A contributing factor is the tendency for social and political science departments to adhere to traditional disciplinary boundaries, inadvertently marginalizing their graduates from a growing number of data-centric professions. This paper argues that this gap can and should be addressed. We present a pedagogical project initiated at the University of Bologna, centered on a tailored data literacy and social computing course designed for Political Science students. This study evaluates a dual-case pedagogical investigation evaluating two complementary but empirically independent educational initiatives—conducted across distinct courses, student cohorts, and academic years—unified under an overarching conceptual framework for social science data literacy. This framework combines interactive peer-led learning (Case Study 1) with an instructor-driven, backend Generative AI workflow for multiple-choice question generation utilizing Google Gemini via AI Studio (Case Study 2). Crucially, Generative AI tools were utilized strictly as an offline editorial assistant by the instructor to streamline item creation, maintaining a rigorous human-in-the-loop assessment model, while student examinations remained offline and unassisted. The results and student feedback have been noteworthy, demonstrating improved learning outcomes and high satisfaction, despite methodological limitations including sample size constraints and a quasi-experimental design. We share this experience to encourage colleagues in the social and political sciences to replicate and adapt this model, thereby better equipping their students for the demands of the modern professional landscape.

papers.title: Digital Technologies in Undergraduate Dental Education: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Dimitar Kirov, Ilia Liondev, Мариана Димова-Габровска, Todor Ts. Uzunov, Aleksandar V. Naydenov, Ivet Dzhondrova
papers.abstract: Digital technologies are becoming increasingly embedded in undergraduate dental curricula, with the potential to support learning and skills development. This scoping review mapped recent evidence on the implementation and educational applications of contemporary digital technologies in undergraduate dental education. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify studies published between 2021 and 2025. The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines and included studies investigating digital technologies in undergraduate dental education. A total of 24 studies met the inclusion criteria. The identified technologies included virtual reality and simulation-based learning systems, digital and 3D-printed educational models, digital assessment and feedback systems, web-based learning platforms, artificial intelligence applications, CAD/CAM technologies, and digital clinical devices. Across the included studies, the reported educational outcomes most commonly concerned practical performance, knowledge acquisition, student engagement, self-assessment, and satisfaction, with many studies focusing on short-term preclinical or learner-reported outcomes. Virtual simulation and digital assessment systems were the most extensively investigated technologies. The available evidence suggests that digital technologies may support undergraduate dental education when used as adjuncts to conventional teaching methods. However, the effectiveness of specific blended-learning models requires direct comparative evaluation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal and methodologically rigorous studies examining long-term knowledge retention, clinical competence, educational quality, and the transfer of acquired skills to professional practice.

papers.title: Generative AI and Digital Inequality in South African Higher Education: Students’ Experiences of Access and Meaningful Use at a Rural University
papers.authors: Julius Theledi Nkube, Khashane Malatji
papers.abstract: This study examined the conditions that enable or constrain undergraduate students’ access to, and meaningful use of, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at a rural South African university. Using an interpretivist qualitative case study design, researchers conducted semi-structured, face-to-face interviews with 12 undergraduate students with prior experience using GenAI for academic purposes. Data were analysed thematically following Braun and Clarke’s ix-phase approach. Four interconnected conditions shaped students’ experiences: device and connectivity reliability, the affordability of sustained data access, artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, and institutional infrastructure and training. Students consistently perceived GenAI as useful, but their capacity to realise that usefulness depended on resources and competencies that were unevenly distributed. The study uses this gap to extend TAM’s construct of perceived usefulness with a distinct construct of realised usefulness, and this study argues that generative AI introduces a literacy demand, critical evaluation of machine-generated, plausible-sounding but sometimes inaccurate output. The study contributes to digital-inequality scholarship by extending the access–skills–benefits distinction into the generative AI context and by identifying the gap between perceived and realised usefulness as a mechanism through which existing inequalities may be reproduced. The study recommends that institutional responses combine connectivity, affordable access, structured AI literacy instruction, and explicit academic guidance, rather than treating any one of these as sufficient on its own.

papers.title: Humanizing the Asynchronous Classroom: A Framework for Authentic Online Learning
papers.authors: Somer Matthews, Kristin Krupa Burnette, Amanda R. Casto, Kari Alberque
papers.abstract: Designing asynchronous courses involves attention to students’ relationships, goals, access, and opportunities to contribute to shared learning. This practitioner-focused conceptual article proposes the Authentic Asynchronous Classroom Framework (AACF), informed by relevant literature and two instructors’ experiences redesigning and teaching asynchronous teacher-preparation courses at different universities. A grant-supported, comprehensive course redesign and a multi-year course redesign provided the contexts for reflection and framework development. The AACF organizes humanizing course-design practices into four tiers: Radical Instructor Presence, Student-Centered Utility, Universal and Equitable Design, and Reciprocal Co-Creation. The tier order reflects the instructors’ perceptions of implementation time and effort. Practices may support more than one tier, and instructors can address multiple tiers concurrently. Course examples illustrate responsive feedback, assignments with practical applications, attention to material costs and accessibility, and student contributions to course content and shared resources. The framework offers postsecondary instructors a structure for considering course changes while maintaining course learning expectations. Its contribution is a practice-informed synthesis of instructional priorities, guidelines, and examples. Future empirical research can examine its implementation, usefulness across contexts, and relationships with student experiences and learning outcomes. The AACF frames humanizing asynchronous design as attending to instructor–student relationships, student purposes, access to learning, and opportunities to contribute to shared learning. Its contribution is a practice-informed synthesis of these priorities into a usable framework complete with guidelines and course examples.

papers.title: Baseline AI Economic Literacy and Enacted Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools by Oncology and Critical Care Professionals
papers.authors: Dragoș-Ciprian Negoiță, Ciprian Gîndac, Akhil Akula, Karina Cristina Marin, Adrian Cosmin Ilie
papers.abstract: We examined whether baseline artificial intelligence (AI) economic literacy was associated with sustained use of oncology AI tools. This prospective cohort included 96 oncology and critical care professionals at two centres in Timișoara, Romania, followed for 12 months after institutional roll-out. Participants were classified by AI Economic Literacy Index (AIELI) scores as high (≥14) or low (<14). Sustained use required log-verified activity in at least two of the final three months. Analyses included regression, inverse probability of treatment weighting and exploratory indirect-association analysis through return-on-investment (ROI) confidence. Among 91 completers, sustained use occurred in 29/53 high-literacy participants (54.7%) and 7/38 low-literacy participants (18.4%; risk ratio 2.97, 95% confidence interval 1.46–6.06). The weighted risk ratio was 2.24 (1.15–4.34), and the profession-stratified risk ratio was 2.80 (1.36–5.76). Median time to first use was 5.8 months in the high-literacy group and was not reached in the low-literacy group. Nine participants (eight high-literacy, one low-literacy) had recorded use before the baseline assessment; in a delayed-entry analysis restricted to the 87 participants unused at assessment, the crude hazard ratio for subsequent first use was 2.98 (1.62–5.48) and the crude risk ratio for sustained use after excluding prior users was 3.01 (1.36–6.64); the corresponding covariate-adjusted estimates were less precise (hazard ratio 1.81, 0.89–3.69; risk ratio 2.19, 0.99–4.86) and their confidence intervals included the null. Roll-out-based time-to-first-use comparisons are descriptive because they include events preceding measurement. Sustained use increased across literacy bands. An indirect association through ROI confidence was observed but was not interpretable as causal mediation. Higher baseline economic literacy was associated with earlier and more sustained recorded AI-tool use, although opportunity for use differed by profession, and the adjusted timing-corrected estimates leave the independent contribution of literacy uncertain.
