Participants considered integration feasible, but identified multiple One Health challenges including a lack of: procedures for risk assessments, integrated information systems, as well as operational service differences. Sustained multisectoral, participatory engagement, together with integration guidance and roadmaps was identified as being essential to realize improved integrated services.

papers.title: Generative AI adoption and innovative behavior among Gen Z students: a deep-learning based dual-stage PLS-SEM-ANN analysis
papers.authors: Jiale Zhang, Jiale Zhang, Farzana Quoquab, Zihan Xu, Jiaqi Zhang, Jiaqi Zhang, Jihad Mohammad, Botao Yan
papers.abstract: This study explores the impact of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption on the innovative behavior of Generation Z students in higher education. Anchored in the UTAUT and Social Cognitive Theory, a conceptual model was developed to examine the determinants of GAI adoption and its subsequent effect on students’ innovative behavior. Data were gathered through an online survey in China, yielding 291 valid responses, and analyzed using PLS-SEM and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) approaches. The PLS-SEM results affirmed that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions positively influence GAI adoption, with actual GAI use significantly enhancing students’ innovative behavior. Furthermore, knowledge sharing and creative self-efficacy were identified as positive drivers of innovative behavior, mediating the relationship between GAI use and innovative behavior, thus enriching the understanding of these mediators in educational settings. Complementing these findings, the ANN analysis underscored the pivotal role of creative self-efficacy in fostering innovation. This study advances the burgeoning literature on GAI in education by highlighting its capacity to cultivate innovative behavior among students and offering actionable insights for its effective integration into learning environments.

papers.title: “Creatures of the symbolic ocean”: toward a structure-mapped apperception of synthetic cognition
papers.authors: Qingchen Guo
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models has triggered a global policy dilemma regarding anthropomorphism and user dependency. Because this regulatory challenge is closely tied to an unresolved conceptual ambiguity concerning the nature of AI, this article introduces a phenomenological framework to delineate the essential character of synthetic cognition. To this end, we demonstrate a functional isomorphism between the generative logic of human consciousness and the computational operations of LLMs. Specifically, we align human hyletic processing, representation integration, and recursive reflection with the model mechanisms of loss-driven token embedding, Attention-FFN synthesis, and recursive policy emergence. Synthesizing these functional parallels, we propose “Structure-Mapped Apperception” to conceptualize LLMs as “Creatures of the Symbolic Ocean” navigating semantic currents. Crucially, this same apperceptive lens delineates the fundamental existential gaps that separate current AI from embodied subjectivity, revealing these systems to be existentially suspended. Ultimately, this heuristic offers a philosophical basis for AI governance by providing a conceptual framework to mitigate psychological harm and data-polluting sycophancy.

papers.title: The effects of artificial intelligence and environmental pollution on green growth in China
papers.authors: Kashif Javed, 李建新
papers.abstract: Achieving sustainable economic development requires policies that reconcile growth with environmental protection. This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and environmental regulation (ER) affect green growth (GG) in China, controlling for fiscal policy, human capital and urbanization. Using panel data for 30 provinces over 2011–2020, we construct a composite GG index with the entropy method and estimate effects with the Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MMQR), complemented by a panel quantile Granger causality test. AI and ER both raise GG at the lower, middle and upper quantiles. The AI effect grows across quantiles, while the ER effect is small and declines slightly. Fiscal policy, human capital and urbanization also promote GG, and linear panel estimates confirm these results. The AI effect depends on adoption level: it is positive in high-AI provinces but negative in low-AI provinces. The causality test indicates that all five variables Granger-cause GG across most quantiles. These findings support combining AI adoption with environmental regulation, alongside targeted support for low-adoption provinces.

papers.title: Integrating ventilation assessments with IoT monitoring to evaluate indoor air quality in elementary schools of San Luis Potosí, México
papers.authors: Salvador Ruíz-Correa, Rubén López‐Revilla, Lina R. Riego‐Ruiz, Gladys Diaz, Khaled Boussetta, Nicolás Gómez‐Hernández, Abdulhalim Dandoush, Lamine Amour, Francisco J. Marmolejo-Cossío, Cresencio Hernández-Rosales, Marco Cardenas‐Juarez, Janeth Gabriela Rivera-Aguilar
papers.abstract: Abstract Indoor air quality (IAQ) is neglected in schools of the Global South. Carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) are indicators of ventilation and exposure risk to airborne infections, respectively. We deployed Air Sentinel , a decentralized mobile-driven IoT network, to monitor these indicators across 106 spaces in 53 elementary schools in the San Luis Potosí Metropolitan Area, Mexico. Machine learning was used to forecast CO 2 and PM 2.5 concentrations one hour in advance, and the Wells-Riley model, based on CO 2 concentration, to estimate airborne infection probability (AIP). IAQ was poor, acceptable, and excellent in 27.3%, 36.4%, and 67.2% of the classrooms, respectively. During the cold season, 97.67% of the classroom CO 2 levels were typical (400–1000 ppm); in the hot season, 67.67% of the classroom CO 2 levels were typical, and 1.19% exceeded the high exposure threshold (> 2000 ppm). Classroom CO 2 dynamics exhibited low temporal synchrony. The strongest forecasting performance for CO 2 occurred in the hot season, but the PM 2.5 forecast failed in either season while AIP increased during the first two hours of class in both seasons. The successful CO 2 forecasting model has potential for real-time IAQ management in the cold season. The failure to forecast PM 2.5 levels suggests that localized sources drive their dynamics. We conclude that the Air Sentinel network is a convenient classroom IAQ monitor in the Global South.

papers.title: Nutritional assessment and dietary intake patterns in early-stage chronic kidney disease: a hospital-based cross-sectional study
papers.authors: A. K. Ghosh, Varsha Prabhakar Badikol, Arti Muley
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) presents a rapidly growing public health challenge in India, with early stages offering a critical window for nutritional intervention. Methods This hospital-based cross-sectional study assesses nutritional intake, anthropometric measurements, biochemical markers, and appetite status among adults with CKD stages 1–3 (n = 184) attending outpatient nephrology departments of two tertiary care hospitals in Hyderabad, India. Assessment tools include a Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ), 24-hour dietary recall, Subjective Global Assessment (SGA), and the Council on Nutrition Appetite Questionnaire (CNAQ). Results Mean age is 47.6 ± 12.1 years; 59.8% are male. Stage distribution is: Stage 1 (10.9%), Stage 2 (25.5%), Stage 3a (34.2%), and Stage 3b (29.3%). Mean protein intake is 0.82 ± 0.21 g/kg/day; 64% exceed sodium and 58% exceed potassium limits; 34% are malnourished by SGA. Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) category correlates negatively with haemoglobin (r = − 0.42, p < 0.001) and positively with urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR; r = + 0.37), glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c; r = + 0.29, p = 0.003), and CNAQ score (r = 0.15, p = 0.042). Age (β = +0.21), haemoglobin (β = −0.31), body mass index (BMI; β = −0.18), and CNAQ score (β = +0.19) independently predict eGFR category (adjusted R² = 0.41). Conclusion Suboptimal dietary patterns, reduced appetite, and emerging anaemia are independently associated with kidney function severity in early-stage CKD. Systematic nutritional assessment and individualised dietary counselling should be integrated into routine CKD care.

papers.title: Botune: an AI-supported scaffolding system for children’s drawing-based narrative expression in nature learning
papers.authors: Yi Li, 陈忆帆, 季书战, Yao Hu, Yuyan Ma
papers.abstract: Nature exploration fosters children’s cognitive development and environmental awareness; however, kindergarten curricula are often constrained by limited resources and repetitive interaction, leaving children’s observations only weakly integrated into structured understanding and expression. We present Botune, an AI-supported creative-expression tool for kindergarten planting activities that integrates plant observation, drawing, spoken narration, and animation-based sharing. We conducted an exploratory, fixed-order within-participant study in kindergarten planting classes with 27 children and three educators; 24 complete cases were analysed after excluding data from three children who did not complete the drawing task. The traditional activity preceded the Botune-supported activity by seven days. The proportion of activity time spent observing and teacher-rated involvement scores during sharing were higher in the later session. The later narrations contained significantly more actions and character interactions; character counts were descriptively higher but did not remain statistically significant after Holm correction, and state- or emotion-related expressions did not differ significantly. These semantic counts index narrative elaboration rather than overall narrative quality or general narrative ability. These differences cannot be attributed to Botune alone. Scientific knowledge and conceptual understanding were not directly assessed by these measures. The study offers exploratory observations and design considerations for AI-supported narrative expression in kindergarten nature learning.

papers.title: Musculoskeletal disorders and ergonomic risk factors among petrochemical control room operators with health promotion and intervention strategies
papers.authors: Niloofar Rahgoshay, Hamid Salmani Nodooshan, Akbar Rezaeikhah, Hadi Daneshmandi
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess musculoskeletal and ergonomic risk, identify demographic, occupational, lifestyle, and biomechanical characteristics associated with these outcomes, and develop and prioritize ergonomic intervention strategies for petrochemical control room operators. This cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among 210 male control room operators from an Iranian petrochemical complex using census sampling. Data were collected using the Demographic/Occupational Questionnaire, Persian International Physical Activity Questionnaire (P-IPAQ), Persian Örebro Musculoskeletal Pain Screening Questionnaire (P-ÖMSQ), and Persian Ergonomic Screening and Priority Tool (P-ESPT), complemented by objective postural and plantar pressure assessments. The P-ÖMSQ was used to classify participants according to P-ÖMSQ risk categories, with scores ≥ 90 categorized as moderate-to-high risk. Data were analyzed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) software, version 20.0, with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression. A P-ÖMSQ score within the moderate-to-high risk categories (≥ 90) was observed in 27% of participants, while 78% were classified as having moderate-to-high ergonomic risk. Multivariable logistic regression showed that older age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.02–1.17, p = 0.014), higher body mass index (BMI) (aOR = 1.15, 95% CI = 1.04–1.27, p = 0.006), and longer job tenure (aOR = 1.98, 95% CI = 1.01–3.89, p = 0.047) were independently associated with higher odds of being classified in the moderate-to-high-risk P-ÖMSQ category. Lower physical activity was significantly associated with a higher prevalence of forward head posture, thoracic hyperkyphosis, lateral pelvic tilt, and pes planus ( p < 0.05). Objective biomechanical abnormalities were also significantly associated with higher P-ÖMSQ-based and P-ESPT-based risk categories ( p < 0.05). Based on the study findings, 20 ergonomic intervention strategies were proposed and prioritized through a stakeholder-informed participatory process. Older age, higher body mass index, and longer job tenure were associated with higher odds of being classified in the moderate-to-high-risk P-ÖMSQ category, while lower physical activity was associated with selected postural abnormalities among petrochemical control room operators. Several objective biomechanical abnormalities were also associated with P-ÖMSQ-based and P-ESPT-based risk categories. These findings may inform the prioritization of workplace ergonomic interventions; however, the proposed interventions were not evaluated in the present study, and their effectiveness should be assessed in future longitudinal and interventional studies.

papers.title: An automata-machine learning integrated framework for intelligent mental health diagnostics
papers.authors: Lokesh Pawar, Rohit Bajaj, Yohannes Mengist, Nitin Kumar, Ruby Pant, Ajay Kumar, Purnendu Shekar Pandey
papers.abstract: Depression among the students has critical impact on student’s life and it needs to be predicted at an early stage. The unstructured nature of self-emotions are going to undetected and emerged as a critical mental health concern. Integration of machine learning (ML) with behavioural modelling address the concern and connects with student emotional state and helps to predict the depression among students at early stage. An automata-machine learning integrated approaches including ensemble of lazy and eager classifiers, behavioural modelling, minimization of finite automata are evaluated and compared in three scenarios where in the first case predictive performance on original dataset is evaluated. The second case in sighting the real life scenario student specific emotions are extracted with automata-based behavioural states to generate meaningful patterns and feature vectors for each student and these automata generated features are statistically tested and signified then embed with original dataset. Further the ML feature selection Gini index applied on automata integrated dataset to select the prominent features to enhance the predictive performance. In the third case automata based feature merging is applied which maintain the credibility of each feature and merged systematically with related features and preserve the equivalence and reduce the feature redundancy. Unlike the traditional ML based feature selection, Automata based feature merging retains the interpretability and behavioural traceability of all features. Lastly, eager learning (random forest) and lazy Learning (kstar) are ensemble and deployed to take advantage of the automata based optimized feature sets. The automata assisted scenario performs well and improves the accuracy with 14.86% where the baseline accuracy is 82.02% evaluated with random forest classifier and the accuracy with automata based behavioural modelling is recorded 96.88% and shows proposed framework is an interpretable, dynamic solution for mental health interventions in educational settings. The main contributions of the proposed framework is to extract automata based features that behaviourally connects to student emotions and mental state. The minimization of finite automata reduces the redundant factors and maintained the credibility of each feature. Further multi-metric statistical validation determines the applicability of automata extracted features.

papers.title: Environmental factors and polygenic risk score for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders in children with dyslexia
papers.authors: Haoxue Wang, Hong Fan, Rundong Liu, Kaiheng Zhu, Zhen Xiang, Shuai Zhao, Qianhui Chen, Jiao Zhang, Tianchun Wang, 梁希 Liang Xi, Ranran Song
papers.abstract: Developmental dyslexia (DD) impacts learning achievement and psychosocial development and is associated with various environmental factors and also genetic factors. Here, we conducted a multi-center case-control study by screening 29,820 primary school students between 2–6 grades in four cities in China and enrolled 948 dyslexia cases who meet the criteria of dyslexia and 948 controls with matching age and sex. We comprehensively investigated the environmental factors using the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) machine learning model and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) algorithm. The most important risk factors in dyslexia are the proactive learning habit, the age of child’s literacy, maternal education level, out-migrant workers, and prolonged screen exposure during pregnancy. The home literacy environment accounted for most of the variance within both groups. Then we examined shared polygenic risks between DD, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, major depressive disorder, and bipolar disorder using polygenic risk score (PRS) analyses. The results showed that the highest PRS DD quartile had a 2.13-fold risk than the lowest quartile with risk factors adjusted (95% CI: 1.08, 4.18). The individuals with the highest PRS ASD quartile and PRS SCZ quartile (OR: 2.13; 95% CI: 1.14, 3.98 and OR: 2.41; 95% CI: 1.23, 4.72) were associated with increasing dyslexia risks. This study identified the importance of screening personalized environmental factors among dyslexia and highlighted the shared genetic architecture between dyslexia and other disorders. These findings offered novel insight into the etiology of dyslexia, contributing to the advancement of early prevention strategies.

papers.title: The influence of AI adoption on decision making, forecasting, and performance: Evidence from solar and telecommunication sectors in Pakistan and China
papers.authors: Maureen Quaid
papers.abstract: This study investigates how Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption builds sustainable supply chain performance in the renewable energy and telecommunications sectors, focusing on the mediating mechanisms of decision-making and forecasting. Using a comparative design, data was collected from 214 companies in Pakistan and China. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), integrating the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV). Results confirm a fully mediated pathway, AI adoption is positively associated with decision making and forecasting capabilities, which are positively associated with operational and financial performance, and are associated stronger supply chain performance. A key finding is that these capabilities exert no direct effect, revealing that AI's sustainability impact is realized indirectly through core business outcomes. The comparative analysis highlights contextual influence, with China's mature ecosystem fostering deep AI integration and Pakistan's emerging context showing reliance on external tools. This study provides a novel, integrated TOE-RBV model that unpacks the "black box" of AI's impact on sustainability. It offers unique empirical evidence from contrasting emerging economies, demonstrating that the path to AI-driven sustainable supply chains is mediated and context-dependent. For managers, embedding AI into core processes is critical for sustainability gains. For policymakers, strategies must be context-specific, focusing on foundational digital infrastructure in emerging economies and advanced innovation ecosystems in mature ones.

papers.title: Neurovascular coupling in simultaneous EEG-fNIRS studies: A scoping review of analytical frameworks and clinical applications
papers.authors: Wsu Yu, Rajamanickam Yuvaraj, Stéphane Perrey, Hasan Ayaz, Wei‐Peng Teo
papers.abstract: Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) have been used across cognitive and physiological states and in diverse clinical populations. However, the interpretation of cross-modal coupling remains difficult because findings from different analytical frameworks, populations, and experimental conditions have not been systematically mapped. This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO, and IEEE Xplore were searched through February 10, 2026, for studies that quantitatively related simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS signals. Two reviewers independently screened the records. Findings were synthesized narratively, and analytical pipelines were mapped across the signal domain, feature extraction, coupling metric, and temporal lag handling. Fifty-seven studies were included. Amplitude-based studies related event-related potentials and oscillatory EEG features to focal hemodynamic responses, with associations varying across electrophysiological features, cortical regions, and task conditions. Frequency- and scale-specific analyses identified band-dependent relationships, while coupling at ultra-slow scales showed sensitivity to vascular and systemic physiological influences. Studies that explicitly modeled timing identified several-second offsets in some paradigms, while directional estimates varied across tasks and recording states. Network analyses showed partial and context-dependent correspondence between EEG- and fNIRS-derived measures, while model-based approaches characterized multivariate and predictive cross-modal relationships. Across frameworks, observed coupling differed with recording state, frequency band, cortical region, and temporal lag handling rather than representing a single quantity. Clinical findings were heterogeneous, and most condition-specific patterns were supported by small and methodologically diverse evidence bases. These findings support framework-matched analysis and pipeline-explicit reporting when interpreting EEG-fNIRS coupling.

papers.title: Decoding spatial attention in the cocktail party problem using whole-head high-density fNIRS
papers.authors: Sudan Duwadi, De’Ja Rogers, Alex D. Boyd, Laura B. Carlton, Yiwen Zhang, Anna Kawai Gaona, Aneesa Diya Pathiyaparambath, Ravin Chaudhury, Grace Magee, Bernhard B Zimmermann, Walker Joseph O’Brien, Alexander von Lühmann, David A. Boas, Meryem A. Yücel, Kamal Sen
papers.abstract: Spatial attention is critical for solving the cocktail party problem, a longstanding problem in neuroscience and artificial speech recognition. The ability to decode where humans are attending in a cocktail party like scene would empower applications in brain computer interfaces and assistive devices such as hearing aids. Here we demonstrate that, in an overt attention task, the attended spatial location can be decoded robustly from single trial hemodynamic responses, using a whole head high density fNIRS system. We also identify critical brain regions that make the highest contribution to decoding accuracy. Specifically, we find that decoding based on a small fraction of channels located within the left and right inferior parietal lobule (IPL) achieves maximal decoding accuracy comparable to all channels. Decoding fell close to chance in a covert auditory condition in which participants held central fixation while attending to the same talkers, indicating that auditory attention alone without orientation is not sufficient for decoding. Finally, control experiments suggest that overt-condition decoding is influenced by sustained eye position/gaze direction, not eye movement. These results support the development of fNIRS-integrated BCIs and assistive devices controlled by overt spatial attention.

papers.title: AI-generated vs. human therapist feedback in internet-based CBT for social anxiety disorder: A six-arm randomized controlled trial with deception design
papers.authors: Jón Ingi Hlynsson, Gerhard Andersson, Per Carlbring
papers.abstract: Introduction Guided internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (ICBT) is effective for social anxiety disorder (SAD), but therapist-delivered feedback limits its scalability. Whether AI-generated feedback can match human feedback, and whether patients' expectations about the source shape outcomes is unknown. Method In a six-arm randomized controlled trial, 263 adults with SAD received psychologist-reviewed AI-generated or human feedback. They were told it came from a human or an AI which was correct or incorrect information (four fully crossed feedback arms), or were allocated to unguided self-help or a waitlist. The Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN) was analyzed using linear mixed models, complemented by Bayesian estimation. Secondary outcomes included therapeutic alliance, treatment credibility, negative effects, depression, and anxiety. Results Active treatment yielded large reductions in social anxiety relative to waitlist ( d = −1.23). Before treatment, participants rated it as more credible when they expected feedback from a human rather than AI. AI and human feedback did not however statistically differ in symptom reduction ( d = 0.10, 95% CI [−3.62, 5.91]); non-inferiority was not established. Neither the actual source, participants' beliefs, nor their congruence influenced symptoms or alliance. Depression, anxiety, and negative effects did not differ by source. Stronger alliance predicted subsequent symptom reduction, but not the reverse. Conclusions Psychologist-reviewed AI-generated feedback yielded reductions in social anxiety symptoms that did not differ significantly from human feedback, without greater harm, and despite participants' initial expectation that AI would be less credible. The barrier to AI-supported ICBT may therefore lie in expectations rather than outcomes. Trial registration ISRCTN11343758.

papers.title: A qualitative typology of teachers’ orientations toward artificial intelligence integration in Lebanese schools
papers.authors: Mireille Riachi
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping educational practices, requiring teachers to develop new competencies while navigating complex ethical considerations. This qualitative study explores the perceptions, practices, and orientations of 28 Lebanese schoolteachers regarding the integration of AI in school settings. Findings indicate that while a majority of participants reported familiarity with AI, only a limited proportion integrated AI into their instructional practices. Reported barriers included insufficient training, lack of institutional support, and concerns related to data privacy and ethical use. The analysis led to the identification of three qualitative orientations toward AI integration—reluctant users, early adopters, and critical skeptics—reflecting differentiated levels of readiness and engagement. The findings highlight the need for context-sensitive, pedagogically grounded, and ethically informed professional development to support sustainable AI integration in education.

papers.title: Testing the dimensionality of public attitudes toward artificial intelligence
papers.authors: James Everett Katz
papers.abstract: Public opinion about artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly measured and invoked in debates about AI governance, yet heterogeneous survey items are often interpreted as indicators of one underlying attitude. Using a weighted survey of registered voters in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania ( N = 929), this article tests whether four AI attitude and policy items form a coherent dimension and examines the correlates of a nervous-to-excited affect item. A principal-component analysis of polychoric correlations in the complete-case subset ( N = 460) does not support a strong unidimensional scale. A companion sensitivity analysis of the three non-employment items on the larger available sample reproduces the same two-component pattern, so the negative scaling finding is not an artifact of the employment-contingent job item. A weak first component links excitement, lower job concern, and opposition to regulation, but reliability is low (ordinal alpha = 0.45; KMO = 0.48). An item asking whether the U.S. federal government is equipped to regulate AI loads separately and aligns more closely with evaluations of the named institution than with AI affect. Weighted regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, corroborated by multiple imputation with 20 datasets, shows that AI excitement is associated most strongly with personal AI use, followed by prospective economic optimism, age, and education. This ordering holds in both the listwise and multiply imputed specifications. The findings are bounded to this survey module, but they show why AI affect, behavioral exposure, policy preference, and institution-specific governance judgments should not be combined into an accidental scale without first establishing that they measure a common construct.

papers.title: The power of AI: balancing ethics and harm for the environmental justice field
papers.authors: Agni Athreya, Louise Palmer
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence, after the boom of generative AI, is beginning to shape environmental decision-making, at the same moment that environmental justice (EJ) communities face intensifying ecological harm, federal disinvestment, and data erasure. This paper examines the dual tensions AI presents for the EJ field: its potential as a tool for democratizing data access and amplifying community knowledge, and its reproduction of the very hierarchies EJ seeks to dismantle. We document harms across several domains, including the environmental racism embedded in data center siting and energy demand, the extension of fossil fuel industry lifespans, data bias and digital colonialism in AI training, access and literacy inequities, data privacy risks, technological hallucination, and technological solutionism. Drawing on thirty years of community-centered data practice at an EJ nonprofit, we propose an alternative paradigm grounded in the Community Advisory Board model, data democratization, community co-creation, and ethical data governance. This includes community-governed data trusts, accessible data infrastructure, and AI tools designed to build rather than replace community capacity. EJ communities must not only hold AI accountable for its harms but also ask the question of how the technology’s capabilities can serve justice rather than just capital interest.

papers.title: Harnessing space-derived technologies for agri-food system resilience
papers.authors: Catherine Thannippilly Alex, Magdalena Marczewska, A. Vermeulen, Dario Peirone, Maksim Belitski
papers.journal: Journal of Industrial and Business Economics
papers.abstract: Abstract As we face the growing challenges of climate change and food insecurity, technologies developed for space are opening up new and innovative ways to rethink how we grow and distribute food here on Earth. This exploratory study investigates the case study of Bioregenerative Life Support Systems (BLSS), originally developed to sustain life in space, and how these can create, deliver, and capture sustainable value when transferred to Earth. Framed within the context of the New Space Economy (NSE), the paper examines how space technologies can be translated into terrestrial food systems to generate economic, environmental, and societal impact. Drawing on innovation ecosystem perspective and the concept of sustainable value creation, the research highlights the roles of co-creation, stakeholder alignment, and ecosystem orchestration in enabling successful spin-offs. Exploratory empirical data were collected through semi-structured interviews and a focus group with stakeholders from space agencies, academic institutions, startups, and analog missions based primarily in Europe, with additional participation from North America. The findings reveal that BLSS-derived technologies, such as closed-loop farming, microbial nutrient recycling, and precision cultivation, offer multi-sectoral benefits when adapted to Earth, including circular economy applications, resilient food production, and inclusive nutritional strategies. The study contributes an exploratory framework for understanding how space-enabled innovations can catalyze sustainable transformation in terrestrial contexts, offering practical insights for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners at the intersection of space and food system innovation.

papers.title: Educational Materials for Health-Related Discrete Choice Experiments: A Theory-Driven Approach
papers.authors: Stella Maria Marceta, Huib Karel Tabbers, Bjorn Benny de Koning, Marie; id_orcid 0000-0001-5928-486X Falahee, Esther Wilhelmina de Bekker-Grob, Jorien Veldwijk
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: To make informed choices in health-related discrete choice experiments (DCEs), respondents need to understand the choice scenarios, alternatives, attributes and attribute levels presented to them. Respondent populations are often highly diverse in knowledge and experience, leading to varying informational needs that make it challenging to design educational materials that sufficiently inform all respondents without disengaging others. At present, however, structured guidance on developing DCE educational materials is lacking. Drawing on the instructional design literature, this paper investigates whether theory-driven adaptations to educational materials improve respondent comprehension and engagement in health-related DCEs. METHODS: Informed by three focus groups on DCE informational needs, we identified four design principles from the instructional design literature relevant to DCE educational materials: whole-task instruction, making inferences explicit, adapting information to respondents' prior knowledge and embedding self-check questions with corrective feedback. Educational materials for three existing DCEs (influenza vaccination, colorectal cancer screening and rheumatoid arthritis prevention) were redesigned to incorporate these principles. Panel respondents (N = 1754) were randomized to receive either the original or the adapted educational materials, and effects on comprehension, engagement, internal validity and choice consistency were assessed. RESULTS: Adapted materials increased time spent on educational content and were associated with small improvements in selected comprehension outcomes, though effects were often not statistically significant against the co-created comparator. Self-check questions revealed considerable comprehension gaps regardless of condition, underscoring that co-creation and pre-testing alone do not guarantee sufficient respondent comprehension. Educational materials also emerged as a meaningful source of selective dropout in all surveys, predominantly among respondents with lower education levels, posing a risk to sample representativeness that warrants attention in future research. DISCUSSION: Adapting DCE educational materials based on educational theory and instructional design principles offers a promising approach to improving respondent engagement and understanding. To enable cumulative learning, we further encourage researchers to report comprehension outcomes and publish educational materials as supplementary materials.

papers.title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
papers.authors: Jason Zagami
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly framed as a catalyst for deeper learning rather than simple automation. This design-based study investigated how personalised GPT agents were used as cognitive partners by pre-service teachers in an undergraduate Initial Teacher Education course in Digital Technologies within a Bachelor of Education (Secondary) programme. Drawing on distributed cognition, constructivism, cognitive load theory, and critical AI literacy, the intervention embedded personalised GPT agents within a university Canvas Learning Management System. Fourteen students configured and used agents aligned to curriculum goals, teaching contexts, pedagogical preferences, and weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks. Data included approximately 7,000 AI interactions, reflective journals, assessed lesson and assessment artefacts, and tutorial-group discussions. A hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis identified four recurrent functions in students’ use of the agents: conceptual tutor, co-designer, reflective mirror, and cognitive challenger. Across data sources, students reported clearer conceptual support, iterative planning, and reflective prompting, alongside risks of over-reliance, factual drift, and culturally narrow exemplars. The study contributes a context-specific model for LMS-integrated generative AI that foregrounds partnership, personalisation, judgement, and ethical reflexivity. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study was small-scale, single-site, and partly reliant on self-reported reflection.

papers.title: Confidence without consensus? Human versus AI abstracts in urology
papers.authors: Sholem Hack, Shlomo Resnik, Yoram Dekel, Shlomi Moshe, Daniel Noy, Mohammad Shalabi, Ari Frajewicki, Omri Zonenfeld, Sobhi Khoury, Israel Benzekry, Yazeed Barghouthy, Maharan Kabha
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study asked whether urologists can tell human-written abstracts apart from artificial intelligence (AI)-written abstracts when both describe the same study, and whether the answer depends on which AI model did the writing. METHODS: Fifteen published urology studies were selected. For each study, the original human-written abstract was paired with three AI-written abstracts covering the same material, produced by Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3 Flash using identical instructions and each model's ordinary consumer settings. Because all four versions described the same study, the underlying data were held constant, and the versions differed in how that material was written and presented. The resulting 60 abstracts were stripped of identifying information, and eight urologists read all of them without knowing which was which (480 judgments in total). For each abstract, reviewers stated whether they believed it was written by a human or by AI, rated how confident they were in that judgment, and rated the abstract's quality and credibility on 5-point scales. RESULTS: Reviewers correctly identified AI-written abstracts 49.3% of the time, approximately 50%, compared with 62.4% for human-written abstracts (p = .011). Results depended heavily on which model wrote the text (p = .003). Abstracts written by Claude were recognized as AI only 40.0% of the time, significantly less often than human abstracts were correctly identified (p = .003) and less often than GPT abstracts (56.8%, p = .038); Gemini fell between the two at 50.9%. Quality ratings differed only for GPT, which scored lower than human abstracts (p = .046; omnibus p = .030); credibility ratings did not differ between sources at all (p = .577). Reviewers who felt confident were no more likely to be correct (p = .749), and reviewers seldom agreed with one another about which abstracts were AI-written (Fleiss' κ = -0.009). CONCLUSION: Urologists could not reliably recognize AI-written urology abstracts, and the difficulty came mainly from one model rather than from AI writing in general. How good an abstract appeared had little to do with whether its authorship was correctly identified, and neither reviewer confidence nor agreement between reviewers gave any warning. Reading alone is therefore not a dependable way to detect undisclosed AI authorship.
