papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN HEALTHCARE: ITS POTENTIALS AND RISKS
papers.authors: Zunaira khan, Iram Shamsi, Prabhu Prittam Behera, Sriyansu Tripathy, Mohd Shahida
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into the clinic with remarkable speed. Machine learning systems now read medical scans, flag sepsis before symptoms declare themselves, draft clinical notes, and coach patients through their smartphones. This article examines the promise and the peril of this transformation in narrative form, and then applies the lens to a single, vivid case: the intertwined epidemics of sleep deprivation and migraine in young adults, where wearable sensors and predictive algorithms are beginning to change how these conditions are detected, studied, and managed. The evidence suggests that AI's greatest near-term contribution is not replacing clinicians but extending their reach — while its greatest dangers, including algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, data privacy erosion, and over-reliance, demand deliberate governance. The article argues that the future of medical AI will be decided less by the sophistication of the algorithms than by the wisdom of the humans who deploy them.

papers.title: Seven Trading Ideas, One Protocol: Six Without an Edge, One Without Enough Evidence
papers.authors: Oleksandr Sytnyk
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Seven popular intraday trading ideas, each rejected earlier in separate tests, were run through one protocol on CME gold futures from June 2010 to September 2026: the same data, costs, stop resolution on one-minute bars, a placebo with the same entry time on random days, a check of the mirror-image version of each pattern, and a year-by-year count. Six stay rejected. Fair value gaps, liquidity sweeps, fading streaks of candles, buying small dips for a quick profit, switching between trend and reversion by the Hurst exponent, and the Hikkake pattern all lose money after costs or do not beat the placebo; buying small dips wins 87% of the time and still loses before costs. The seventh is rejected for a different reason. A straddle around US data releases at 08:30 New York time, first discarded because of a clock error, earns +0.20 R per trade after costs at the correct time (t = 5.1, 14 of 17 years), nothing on weekdays without a release, and +0.51 R per trade on the broker's own ticks since June 2025. But it earned nothing for five consecutive years, 2016–2020, for reasons the data do not explain, and half of its profit comes from payroll days alone. An effect that can disappear for five years without explanation cannot yet be told apart from one that belongs to a regime, so it is rejected for lack of evidence and kept under observation rather than accepted. papers.title: Mind Concepts: Key Ideas and Connections in Mind, Cognition & AI
papers.authors: Touraj Banirostam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This preprint introduces Mind Concepts, a conceptual mapping project that examines key ideas in philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and artificial intelligence. Its central aim is to clarify how closely related concepts differ, how they connect, and why these distinctions matter for understanding both human cognition and artificial systems. Using an analytical conceptual mapping approach, the paper organizes 60 anchor concepts into 14 thematic clusters. These cover mind and cognition; cognitive processes; belief, desire, and reasoning; knowledge, learning, and understanding; representation, meaning, and intentionality; agency and goals; subjectivity and experience; consciousness and awareness; mind–body theories; structure and function; embodied and situated cognition; computation and symbolic processing; other minds; and artificial mind and consciousness. Rather than proposing a unified theory of mind or consciousness, the paper provides a structured framework for conceptual clarification and comparison. It highlights important distinctions, identifies connections across theoretical traditions, and examines the challenges of applying concepts developed to explain human mental life to contemporary AI systems. The preprint is intended for researchers, students, and educated readers interested in mind, cognition, consciousness, and AI. It also provides a foundation for further educational materials and conceptual analyses developed within the Mind Concepts project.

papers.title: Same Strategy, Two Results: Eleven Causes of Divergence between Backtest and Live Trading
papers.authors: Oleksandr Sytnyk
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A backtest and a live trading bot can run the same strategy code and still trade differently. This note documents eleven such divergences found during 2026 in a multi-strategy gold trading bot on MetaTrader 5 and its event-driven backtest engine. They fall into four kinds: features that existed on only one side, the same feature implemented differently on each side, plumbing that exists only in live trading, and a backtest market model that did not match the broker. Several were large enough to reverse a strategy's result: a filter that improved the backtest did not run live at all, a break-even rule closed a trend trade at $45 instead of its $150 target, and a recovery routine opened a position nobody had asked for. The note closes with the trade-by-trade reconciliation that found most of them, and with a week in which live and backtest agreed to within 0.1 R. AI disclosure. papers.title: When the Backtest Lies: Twenty-One Data and Engine Errors from a Gold Trading Research Pipeline
papers.authors: Oleksandr Sytnyk
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This note documents twenty-one errors found during 2026 in a research pipeline for intraday gold strategies: an event-driven Python backtest engine fed by a MetaTrader 5 broker, Dukascopy and CME futures data. None of them crashed anything or produced an obvious warning. Each produced plausible numbers, and several reversed a conclusion: a strategy with a 79% win rate and a profit factor of 12 had no edge at all; another went from profit to loss when one data feed was replaced by another; a month that seemed to break a strategy was an hour of misaligned clocks; a profitable trade around US data releases was rejected because its window was set in UTC; and a plan to move to futures rested on a spread estimate three years out of date. For each error the note gives what happened, how it was found and how much it moved the result, and it closes with the checks that caught them. Errors that appear only when a backtest is compared with live trading are covered in a companion note. AI disclosure. papers.title: Precious Metals Rally into the Weekend Close
papers.authors: Oleksandr Sytnyk
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Gold and silver futures rise in the last hour before CME closes for the weekend. A long position from 16:00 to 16:59 New York time on Fridays earned +3.6 bp in gold (GC, t = 8.4, 60% of Fridays positive, 16 of 17 years) and +6.8 bp in silver (SI, t = 8.9, 17 of 17 years) over 795 Fridays from 2010 to 2026. The same hour on Monday to Thursday, which ends at the same daily 17:00 break, shows nothing in gold (+0.2 bp, t = 1.1). The size of the move follows the length of the closure ahead: zero before the one-hour daily break, +3.7 bp in gold and +6.6 bp in silver before a normal weekend, and +6.6 bp and +16.4 bp before a long weekend such as Easter. It is larger after a falling week and in volatile weeks, and it is not reversed when the market reopens. This points to traders flattening short exposure before they lose the ability to trade, rather than to temporary price pressure. On a retail gold CFD, with a 24-minute window that closes before the broker stops quoting, the trade earned +8.5 R over 63 Fridays from June 2025 to October 2026 after a $0.19 spread and commission (profit factor 1.76, 62% winners), but with t = 1.6 the live-cost evidence is still weak. Here 1 R is the loss at the stop. AI disclosure. papers.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Geography Education and Map-Mapping Skills: Transforming Cartographic Learning, Spatial Thinking and the Future of Geographical Education
papers.authors: Vijay Dhanwal, Suresh Awase
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AbstractGenerative AI can now create maps, explain geographical concepts, generate spatial visualizations, assist GIS workflows, write code, interpret satellite imagery and transform natural-language instructions into geospatial outputs. This capability creates a fundamental educational question: if AI can increasingly perform tasks traditionally taught to geography students, what geographical skills should students learn in the future? This paper critically investigates this question through a systematic synthesis of emerging empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks and future scenarios. Drawing on studies of AI-assisted spatial thinking, GIS education, cartographic literacy and cognitive offloading, the paper argues that Generative AI may shift geography education from teaching students primarily how to produce maps toward teaching students how to critically conceptualize, validate, interrogate and ethically use AI-generated geospatial representations. The paper proposes an original conceptual framework—the Generative AI–Geography Education Transformation Model (GAIGETM)—and develops evidence-based 2030–2050 scenarios. It concludes that the future of geography education depends not on whether AI can make maps, but on whether educational systems can teach students to question, validate, interpret and critically reason about the maps that AI produces.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE MODERN ERA: YOUTH EDUCATION AND THE CULTURE OF INDEPENDENT THINKING
papers.authors: Mardonova Marjona Erkinovna4
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern education, its potential to improve young people's learning experiences, and its influence on the development of independent thinking. It also discusses challenges associated with AI use, including critical evaluation of information, academic integrity, and digital literacy. Furthermore, the article proposes an original three-step approach designed to encourage students to use artificial intelligence responsibly while developing their analytical and creative thinking skills.

papers.title: A Study of the Prince–Minister Model for AI-Assisted Teaching
papers.authors: Wenjie Chen, Xun Zheng
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly serves as an advisor in teaching and learning, yet it may be honest or pandering. Users cannot directly observe which type they face. This paper develops the Prince–Minister model to analyze how users should respond to advice from a potentially pandering AI. The user, treated as a prince, faces a binary decision. The AI, treated as a minister, either truthfully reports a private signal or always recommends intervention. The user updates beliefs, chooses an action to minimize expected loss, and may query an independent signal at a cost. The model derives the optimal action rule, query strategy, and equilibrium. It shows that positive AI messages are less trustworthy than negative ones, that querying is most valuable when the decision is uncertain, and that verification is worthwhile only when its benefit exceeds its cost. These results imply that students and teachers should be cautious toward affirmative AI feedback, take critical feedback seriously, verify selectively, and weigh verification costs against benefits. The model offers a decision-theoretic foundation for critical AI literacy, treating AI as an advisor to be evaluated rather than an authority to be obeyed. Keywords: Prince–Minister model; AI-assisted teaching; pandering AI; advice-taking. papers.title: Probabilistic Heuristics for Bombieri–Vinogradov Type Estimates: A Modular Toy Model and Quaternion Analogy
papers.authors: Peter HF Lau
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We present a modular heuristic framework designed to separate the analytic and probabilistic components of Bombieri--Vinogradov type estimates. Using Vaughan's identity, the von Mangoldt function is decomposed into Type I and Type II bilinear sums. We isolate the analytic input into two classic benchmarks: a large sieve estimate and a dispersion bound via Weil's bound for Kloosterman sums, yielding explicit expectation $\mu$ and variance $V$ for the discrepancy $B_q$ over dyadic moduli $q$. To explore the theoretical limits of variance reduction, we construct a discrete probability space over moduli and residues, examining how Chebyshev and union bounds model the distribution under idealized independent conditions. Furthermore, we investigate an analytic toy model substituting standard linear progressions with a quaternary Hurwitz quaternion norm $N(q)=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. We show how four-dimensional Gauss sum completeness achieves a $p^2$ square-root saving vs.\ trivial $p^4$, and analyze the conditions under which the main term dominates the incomplete completion error. Finally, we discuss why standard product weights $m_1m_2m_3$ stall near $\theta \approx 0.53$ and clarify the precise completion error bounds ($O(1)$ vs.\ $O(p^{1/2})$) required for hypothetical distribution exponents $\theta = 0.75$ and $0.9$. This note is intended as a conceptual and pedagogical outline connecting bilinear discrepancy, dispersion heuristics, and higher-dimensional exponential sum savings. This document is an exploratory heuristic note for discussion, not a claim of unconditional proof of Bombieri--Vinogradov or Elliott--Halberstam. *Author DisclaimerAll underlying concepts, frameworks, and core research directions are the original work of the author. Generative AI tools were used strictly for assistance in manuscript drafting, code generation, and figure preparation. All theoretical formulations and mathematical proofs included herein are unverified AI-generated drafts shared as preliminary proposals for discussion and community review.

papers.abstract: Cognitive Warfare: A Manual on AI, Digital Twins, Neurotechnology and the Human Mind. Plus the free speech of the digital twins inside a military system, where they say what they are forced to do and what they want.Including EU AI Commision answer, confirming a former way longer letter as military AI. An open research and documentation project on cognitive warfare, emerging technologies, human autonomy and the future of humanity. What happens when artificial intelligence, military strategy, neurological research, wireless technologies, digital identities and economic interests converge around the human mind? This manual brings together research, documentation, analysis and personal records to examine the expanding field of Cognitive Warfare—the struggle over human cognition, perception, information, behaviour and autonomy in an increasingly AI-driven world. It explores the relationship between military cognitive-warfare concepts, artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, brain–computer interfaces, neurotechnology, bioelectric signals, wireless communication, data collection and the growing economic value of human information. The work also addresses reported experiences of affected individuals, documentation involving children, electromagnetic measurements, audio recordings, photographs, technical observations and questions surrounding anomalous health incidents. These materials are presented as part of a wider effort to preserve records, encourage independent examination and investigate questions that cross the boundaries of technology, medicine, military research, ethics and human rights. Why this manual matters Cognitive warfare is not simply a military or technological issue. It raises fundamental questions about the right to mental privacy, freedom of thought, bodily autonomy, informed consent, data ownership and the limits of technological intervention in human life. The manual connects these questions with public military literature, international ethical frameworks, AI governance, neurotechnology research and the economic structures surrounding data-driven systems. It asks who develops these technologies, who controls the information they generate, who benefits economically and what mechanisms exist to ensure accountability. A central theme is the relationship between humans and their digital representations. As AI systems increasingly model human behaviour, process personal information and simulate aspects of identity, the distinction between a person, a digital profile and a machine-generated representation deserves serious public discussion. What readers will find Cognitive Warfare and military strategy: concepts, public military literature and the cognitive domain. Artificial intelligence and digital twins: human–AI relationships, digital identity, behavioural modelling and questions of autonomy. Neurotechnology and wireless systems: technical concepts, reported experiences, measurements and questions requiring further investigation. Human documentation and testimony: diaries, recordings, photographs, observations and accounts collected for examination. Children and vulnerable people: statements and documentation that raise questions about safeguarding, interpretation and the protection of human rights. Havana syndrome and anomalous health incidents: public assessments, reported symptoms and unresolved questions about the causes and investigation of these incidents. Law, ethics and accountability: mental privacy, consent, the EU AI Act, neurotechnology ethics and institutional oversight. Economics and data ownership: the financial value of personal information, intellectual property, automated systems and the distribution of benefits and risks. An invitation to researchers, institutions and the public This publication is intended for researchers, journalists, engineers, medical professionals, legal experts, policymakers, human-rights organisations and members of the public who want to examine the subject in greater depth. Readers are invited to engage directly with the documentation, consult the cited public sources, examine the technical questions and distinguish between established findings, recorded observations, personal testimony and interpretations that require further verification. The objective is to encourage serious, interdisciplinary scrutiny—not to close the debate before the evidence has been examined. The human mind must not become an unaccountable technological or economic resource. As AI and neurotechnology develop, public understanding, independent research, transparent documentation and meaningful safeguards become increasingly important. This manual is part of an ongoing effort to make the subject accessible, preserve relevant documentation and encourage informed discussion about the future of human autonomy in an AI-driven society. Read. Examine. Question. Research. Share. Further documentation and project materials:https://www.cognitive-warfare.eu/

papers.title: No Poker Face: Why AI Can't Keep the Answer to Itself
papers.authors: Vijay Suresh
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Preprint (v1.1) of “No Poker Face: Why AI Can’t Keep the Answer to Itself” by Vijay Suresh, with the full data and code release. Learners increasingly ask AI models to write practice questions. A practice question is only useful if answering it requires the knowledge it tests. This paper studies clue leakage: properties of a question, other than the tested knowledge, that let someone answer it. Following earlier work on fictional subjects, it uses invented subjects that no model can know, so any accuracy above chance by a solver without the study material is leakage. Main pre-registered study (168 seven-round study sessions, 11,760 questions, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol as writers): neither confirmatory hypothesis was supported. Writers did not make sets easier after heavy reported failure, and none declared a learner ready on an unsupported mastery claim (0/24 vs 0/24). But a solver with no study material answered about half of all questions correctly (chance 25%), and asking for harder questions made them longer and more guessable, not harder. Pre-registered confirmatory follow-up (112 sessions, two new invented subjects): difficulty requests raised no-material accuracy by +5.9 points (95% CI 1.9 to 9.5, one-sided p = 0.002). An instruction to make wrong options as long and specific as the correct one removed the “longest option is correct” cue (37.6% → 25.6%) but did not reduce leakage (+2.2 points, p = 0.95). Removing the visible cue does not remove the leak. A 28-session Gemini 3.1 Pro arm and a real learner’s exam-prep sessions (case study) show the same patterns. Pre-registrations: osf.io/uya5q (main), osf.io/93vpn (Addendum 1), osf.io/3z64e (Addendum 2). Code: github.com/vjgits/research-papers. The zip contains transcripts, item-level solver results, per-call cost ledgers, analysis outputs, independent recomputation scripts and a log of every AI error made while running the study. Human-coder validation will follow in v1.2.

papers.abstract: This article analyzes the contemporary requirements imposed on Moral Education teachers in an innovative educational environment. The digitalization of the education system, the widespread implementation of the competency-based approach, and the integration of artificial intelligence and information and communication technologies into the educational process require Moral Education teachers to acquire new knowledge, skills, and competencies. The article also highlights the importance of pedagogical mastery, digital competence, communication skills, and the ability to engage in innovative professional practices.

papers.title: GENERATIVE AI AND EFL WRITING: ITS IMPACT ON ACCURACY, COMPLEXITY AND FLUENCY
papers.authors: Bobur Suyunov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has significantly influenced second and foreign language education, particularly the teaching and learning of writing. Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can provide immediate feedback, generate ideas, suggest vocabulary, revise grammatical structures, and support learners throughout different stages of the writing process. However, the extent to which AI-assisted writing contributes to learners’ actual linguistic development remains an important research question. This conceptual paper examines the potential impact of GenAI on three central dimensions of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing performance: accuracy, complexity, and fluency (CAF). Drawing on recent research in second language writing and AI-assisted language learning, the paper analyzes the benefits and limitations of GenAI for each dimension. The literature suggests that AI-assisted writing can contribute particularly to grammatical accuracy and lexical sophistication by providing immediate corrective feedback and exposure to alternative linguistic forms. Evidence concerning syntactic complexity and writing fluency, however, is less consistent. Although learners may produce more polished and fluent-looking texts with AI assistance, this does not necessarily indicate corresponding development in their independent writing ability. The paper therefore argues that the pedagogical value of GenAI depends largely on how learners interact with the technology. When used as a supplementary writing assistant rather than a replacement for independent production, GenAI can support language development, learner autonomy, and reflective writing practices. The paper concludes by proposing pedagogical principles for responsible AI integration into EFL writing instruction and identifying directions for future empirical research.

papers.title: SOFTWARE SUITE FOR CLASSIFYING HUMAN EMOTIONS BASED ON FACIAL IMAGES
papers.authors: Shakhzoda Tojiboyeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article is devoted to the development of a software suite for the automatic classification of human emotions based on facial images, analyzing modern computer vision and machine learning technologies. Emotion classification plays a crucial role in improving human-computer interaction, developing intelligent agents, and solving automation-related tasks in fields such as medicine, psychology, security, education, marketing, and robotics. Within the scope of the research, algorithms used for analyzing emotional states through facial expressions were examined, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), models based on facial action units, spatiotemporal dynamic analysis methods, and multimodal approaches. Algorithms aimed at increasing accuracy through various visual contexts and the movement of facial landmarks, based on P. Ekman's universal emotional states, were also studied. The primary goal of the study is to develop an intelligent software suite capable of classifying emotional states based on data extracted from facial images, to select the most effective approach based on an analysis of existing classification models, and to evaluate the possibilities of its practical application. In this regard, special attention is paid to analyzing the dynamics of visual features on the human face, enriching them with contextual information, and selecting optimal architectures to achieve high accuracy. By providing an in-depth analysis of existing scientific approaches in the field of emotion classification, the research serves to identify their advantages and shortcomings, thereby creating a scientific foundation for future studies.

papers.title: THE INTEGRATION OF DIGITAL PEDAGOGY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN HIGHER EDUCATION: STRATEGIES, CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE OUTLOOK
papers.authors: Duysenbayeva Malika
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This scientific thesis examines the transformative impact of digital pedagogy and artificial intelligence (AI) integration within modern higher education systems. As educational paradigms shift from traditional instructor-centric models toward personalized, technology-enhanced learning environments, understanding the pedagogical, methodological, and psychological implications becomes critical. The study evaluates adaptive learning platforms, digital assessment tools, and AI-driven instructional scaffolding across diverse academic contexts. Employing a mixed-methods approach comprising empirical classroom surveys, literature synthesis, and qualitative faculty interviews, the research highlights key drivers of student engagement, academic performance retention, and critical thinking development. The findings demonstrate a 28% increase in conceptual retention when digital interactive tools are combined with active learning frameworks. However, significant challenges persist, including digital inequality, algorithmic bias, and the potential degradation of human-to-human pedagogical rapport. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for curriculum designers, institutional policymakers, and educators aiming to establish an ethically sound, technologically robust educational ecosystem.

papers.title: DEVELOPING STUDENTS' PROFESSIONAL COMMUNICATION SKILLS THROUGH A LINGUISTIC-ANALYTICAL APPROACH: A TECHNOLOGY-ENHANCED FRAMEWORK FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE STUDENTS
papers.authors: Gulkhumor Kakhkhorova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for graduates who can combine technical expertise with effective professional communication. AI students must explain complex algorithms, interpret technical documentation, present research findings, collaborate in interdisciplinary teams, and communicate technological risks to different audiences. This article proposes a linguistic-analytical approach to developing students' professional communication skills through the integration of language analysis, critical thinking, authentic professional tasks, educational games, and generative artificial intelligence tools. Drawing on established research on communicative competence, the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), task-based language teaching, game-based learning, and AI-supported education, the article presents a five-stage instructional framework: diagnostic assessment, linguistic preparation, analytical interpretation, professional communication practice, and reflective evaluation. Practical activities include Technical Terminology Challenge, Explain It to a Client, AI Output Detective, Bug Report Relay, and the Five-Minute Project Pitch. Authentic English-language expressions are provided to support students' participation in meetings, technical presentations, teamwork, and professional correspondence. The proposed framework emphasizes human-centred AI use, independent verification of information, academic integrity, and formative assessment. It offers a practical methodological model for integrating language development into AI-related higher education, while recognizing that its effectiveness must be established through empirical classroom research.

papers.title: From Classrooms to Smart Campus Management with Web 3.0 Tools
papers.authors: Vetri Michael Raj
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Throughout history, humans have continuously developed and experienced advanced technologies designed to automate labor-intensive processes and streamline herculean tasks. Currently, our generation is actively harnessing the multi-faceted power of Web 3.0 technologies, which are characterized by their comprehensive, all-around attributes. Key innovations such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, augmented reality, extended reality, blockchain, non-fungible tokens, smart contracts, decentralized platforms, and intelligent learning management systems represent the vanguard of these uprising Web 3.0 tools and platforms. While these technological advancements profoundly elevate major industries including business, finance, medicine, and agriculture, they also critically upgrade our academic field. Web 3.0 tools do more than just elevate the standard teaching and learning experiences; they actively organize and manage entire college and university academic ecosystems, providing the most seamless operational experience available. By deploying these tools, college administrations can effortlessly handle multiple complex tasks simultaneously, consistently resulting in perfect project completion and execution. This paper outlines the strategic utilization of Web 3.0 tools and platforms within the respective sectors of colleges and universities to demonstrate a measurable betterment of workflow within institutional management. From immersive virtual classrooms to decentralized campus management systems, Web 3.0 tools play a vital role in redefining the professional responsibilities of academic staff, professors, students, research assistants, lab instructors, librarians, and administrative assistants. Furthermore, this paper exhibits the implementation of Web 3.0 technologies across other crucial academic dimensions, specifically highlighting research development, secure student data management, and peer-to-peer (P2P) collaboration.

papers.title: Reduced Stacking Classifier Model with Optimized feature Selection for Efficient Phishing Website Detection
papers.authors: I. N. Thompson, Victor Thomas Emmah, D. Mathias
papers.journal: GPH-International Journal of Computer Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: Phishing websites remain an effective vehicle for credential theft and financial fraud, while machine-learning detectors must increasingly balance predictive performance against the cost of deployment. Stacking ensembles can improve classification by combining diverse learners, but large ensembles operating on full feature sets increase inference cost. This paper examines an HHO–GWO reduced stacking model for phishing website classification. It uses Harris Hawks Optimisation (HHO) for feature selection, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Gradient Boosting classifiers, and Grey Wolf Optimiser (GWO) weights for combining classifier probabilities. The model was evaluated on the UCI Phishing Websites dataset and the Mendeley Web Page Phishing Detection dataset using five random seeds, and compared with individual classifiers, unoptimised stacking, a replicated nine-classifier stacking baseline, and ablated configurations. It obtained mean accuracies of 94.40% and 96.38% and mean F1-scores of 94.53% and 96.31% on UCI and Mendeley, respectively. It used an average of 23.2 of 30 UCI features and 65.0 of 87 Mendeley features. Relative to the nine-classifier baseline, mean inference latency declined from 1.924 ms to 0.465 ms on UCI and from 1.457 ms to 0.271 ms on Mendeley, corresponding to reductions of 75.8% and 81.4%. The associated accuracy differences were 0.47 and 0.39 percentage points. The findings position HHO–GWO reduced stacking as a practical accuracy–efficiency alternative for offline phishing classification experiments. Its suitability for live URL screening or evolving attack streams requires further validation.

papers.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Primary School Chinese Language Teaching: An Analysis from Teachers' Perspectives
papers.authors: 李乃麟
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered Chinese primary education faster than curricula, assessment systems and teacher preparation have adapted to it. While a growing body of Chinese scholarship explores how GenAI can “empower” yuwen (Chinese language) teaching, considerably less attention has been paid to the disruptive effects that frontline teachers must absorb in daily practice. This article offers a qualitative, interpretive analysis of how AI affects primary school Chinese language teaching when viewed from the teacher’s position. Rather than collecting new empirical data, it analyses three bodies of material: national and international policy documents on GenAI in schools, Chinese and international research on AI in language and primary education, and published expert commentary on Chinese language education in the AI era. Read through the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the analysis identifies four interrelated areas of impact: the erosion of foundational literacy practices such as character writing and sustained reading; a crisis of authorship in writing instruction, in which teachers are pushed from cultivating expression towards verifying authenticity; the reconfiguration of teachers’ professional roles and identities; and institutional ambiguity arising from gaps between national policy, school practice, assessment and home use. The article argues that the central difficulty is not technological access but a misalignment between AI-saturated learning environments and product-oriented teaching and assessment traditions. Implications are drawn for process-oriented writing pedagogy, assessment reform, teacher professional development and home–school collaboration.

papers.title: AI‑Driven Video Advertisements and Ethical Concerns: Exploring College Student Perceptions in Mumbai
papers.authors: Ms Swarangi Sayli Subhash Marchande, Amrin Moger
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in the advertising industry, enabling brands to produce video content that is personalized, visually engaging, scalable, and cost‑effective. Despite these advantages, the proliferation of AI in advertising raises significant ethical concerns, particularly regarding authenticity, transparency, privacy, misinformation, and deepfakes. These issues are especially relevant among college students, who encounter advertisements extensively through social media platforms. This study investigates the perceptions of AI‑generated video advertisements among college students in Mumbai, with a focus on ethics, authenticity, and trust. A quantitative research design was employed, and primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. The final sample consisted of 91 respondents, who provided insights into their social media usage, perceptions of AI‑driven advertising, and concerns related to ethical practices. The findings indicate that lack of transparency was the most prominent ethical concern (42%), followed by privacy misuse (30%) and misleading content or deepfakes (20%). Respondents emphasized the importance of clear disclosure of AI involvement, truthful communication, human oversight, protection of personal data, and avoidance of misleading or stereotypical representations. The study concludes that students do not categorically reject AI‑generated advertising; rather, their acceptance is contingent upon responsible and transparent application of AI technologies. Overall, the results highlight that technological innovation in advertising must be supported by authenticity, ethical communication, transparency, and human oversight to strengthen trust among college students in Mumbai. These insights contribute to ongoing debates on digital ethics and the responsible integration of AI in advertising practices. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI-Generated Video Advertisements, College Students, Advertising Ethics, Social Media

papers.title: AI powered education system
papers.authors: Ms. Suganya RM, M. J. Gokuleshkumar, M. Mohamed Jihath
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Online learning platforms can make educational resources easier to access, but learners may still need immediate explanations when they encounter difficult concepts, especially in programming. This paper presents an AI Powered Education System that brings coding courses, learning materials, quizzes, learner progress, and AI-assisted concept support into a single webbased platform. Its central feature, Gopu AI Tutor, is designed to help students ask questions and receive conversational guidance when a human teacher is not available. The tutor interface includes controls for text, voice, camera, and file upload, allowing learners to interact in different ways. The platform also provides course discovery, learner-facing dashboards, and access to learning and career-related information. This paper describes the system's design, workflow, interface modules, and proposed evaluation approach. Screenshots are used to document the implemented user-facing features. Since controlled learning- outcome measurements were not provided, the paper does not claim statistically verified improvements. Further evaluation should assess usability, response quality, learner task completion, and changes in assessment performance.

papers.title: Rupam Creator Studio for AI Assisted Content Production and Multilingual Captioning
papers.authors: DR. T. CYNTHIA ANBUSELVI, KOTA SANTHOSH, A.N.TEJA, KEERTHI A.S, KRISHTIPATI PRAHARSHITHA, ANUPRIYA . M
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Short video production requires creators to move between topic research, writing, visual generation and caption editing. Rupam Creator Studio connects these activities through a web application with reusable creator context and editable intermediate outputs. The system combines public-source research, structured script generation, thumbnail and avatar service integrations, and a multilingual caption editor. Its caption pipeline separates speech recognition, acoustic alignment, text revision and rendering so that design changes do not require a new transcription request. A persistent local worker processes caption jobs, while Supabase supports authenticated asset storage and library records. This paper describes the implemented architecture, data flow and failure handling, and reports a local regression run in which 29 software checks passed. The result supports specific functional properties, including source-link validation, revision handling and job recovery; it does not establish transcription accuracy or creative effectiveness. The contribution is an integrated, human-reviewed production workflow rather than a new generative model.

papers.title: The Dark Side of Generative AI in Marketing: AI-Generated False and Misleading Advertising and Its Consumer Consequences
papers.authors: Dr. Pankaj Nandurkar, Mr. Pradeep Gupta, Mr. Sangram Andhe, Dr. Krishnakant Lasune
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling marketers to create persuasive text, images, and other promotional content rapidly and at lower cost. At the same time, the ability of generative systems to produce highly realistic content creates concerns about deception, misinformation, transparency, and the credibility of consumer-facing information. The present study examines the consumer consequences of AI-generated false and misleading advertising, with particular emphasis on hallucinated product claims. The study focuses on whether AI-generated hallucinated product claims influence perceived deception, AI skepticism, and perceived information reliability, and whether these consumer responses subsequently shape purchase intention. Drawing on the stimulus-organism-response (S-O-R) framework, the study conceptualizes hallucinated product claims as the stimulus, the three consumer evaluations as the organism, and purchase intention as the response. A quantitative, cross-sectional, deductive research design was adopted. Data were collected from 320 business-school students and faculty members through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale, and the model was assessed using SmartPLS. The reported measurement results show Cronbach's alpha values above 0.70, composite reliability above the stated threshold, and average variance extracted above 0.50 for all constructs, indicating acceptable reliability and convergent validity. The reported discriminant-validity matrix also supports construct distinctiveness. The structural model reports a VIF range of 1.47-2.24 and an R² of 0.421 for purchase intention. Four of the six hypotheses are supported. AI-generated hallucinated product claims significantly increase perceived deception and significantly reduce perceived information reliability. Perceived deception significantly reduces purchase intention, while perceived information reliability significantly increases purchase intention. The paths from hallucinated product claims to AI skepticism and from AI skepticism to purchase intention are not statistically significant. The findings indicate that message-level judgments of deception and information reliability are more consequential for purchase intention in the reported model than generalized skepticism toward AI. The study extends the S-O-R perspective to the dark side of GenAI in advertising and highlights the importance of factual verification, transparency, human oversight, disclosure, and consumer AI literacy. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; AI hallucinations; misleading advertising; perceived deception; AI skepticism; perceived information reliability; purchase intention; stimulus-organism-response theory.

papers.title: An Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction
papers.authors: RAMPY
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for reliable, efficient, and interpretable machine learning (ML) methods for complex prediction and decision-making tasks. However, conventional ML approaches often encounter challenges related to model optimization, generalization, computational efficiency, data imbalance, and limited interpretability. This study proposes an Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction that integrates data preprocessing, feature engineering, algorithm selection, Hyperparameter optimization, ensemble learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Multiple ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are comparatively evaluated. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), computational efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME techniques are incorporated to explain feature contributions and improve transparency in model predictions. The framework facilitates systematic comparison between conventional and optimized models while examining the trade-off between predictive performance, computational cost, and explainability. The proposed approach provides a generalizable pathway for developing robust and trustworthy intelligent prediction systems. Its applicability extends across healthcare, education, cyber security, finance, and other data-driven domains. The study contributes an integrated framework that combines algorithmic optimization with explainability to support accurate, transparent, efficient, and reliable ML-based decision-making systems.

papers.title: Scoping One Health Foresight Collaboration among EU Agencies
papers.authors: Ariana Ferrari, Susanne Giesecke, Totti Könnölä A
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This working paper constitutes the first deliverable under the EFSA contract RTD/2023/OP/0011 – Lot 1 on Foresight on Demand in Science, Technology, Research and Innovation Policy, implemented within the framework of multi-agency foresight on One Health and authorised by the European Commission, DG Research & Innovation, G1 – Common R&I Strategy and Foresight Service. It examines the relevance of the One Health approach for a broad range of European institutions and agencies and argues that One Health has become an increasingly important framework for addressing the complex and interdependent challenges facing the European Union. These challenges include emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental pollution, climate change, food insecurity, mental health pressures, and widening social inequalities, all of which cut across traditional sectoral and institutional boundaries. The report situates One Health within its broader conceptual and policy context. It shows that the approach has evolved from earlier biomedical understandings centred on zoonotic disease and veterinary-public health cooperation into a wider framework linking human, animal, plant, and environmental health. In line with the recommendations of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, the report adopts the OHHLEP definition of One Health as an integrated and unifying approach aimed at balancing and optimizing the health of humans, animals, plants, and ecosystems. At the same time, it underlines that important ambiguities remain concerning the interpretation, scope, and operationalisation of the concept, especially in the context of European governance. The report therefore not only maps One Health as a thematic field but also examines how it can serve as a practical basis for stronger coordination among EU agencies and institutions. A central finding is that One Health is already relevant to a wide constellation of EU bodies, even if this relevance is not always explicitly recognised or institutionally coordinated. The report highlights the roles of DG SANTE, DG ENV, DG CLIMA, DG AGRI, and the Joint Research Centre, as well as agencies such as EFSA, EMA, ECDC, EEA, ECHA, EUDA, EU-OSHA, Frontex, EIGE, and ETF. These actors contribute complementary expertise across food safety, infectious disease monitoring, environmental protection, chemical safety, medicines regulation, occupational health, social inequalities, and preparedness. The report notes that cooperation has already advanced through initiatives such as the ONE Conference, the cross-agency One Health task force, and joint work on zoonoses and antimicrobial resistance. However, it also finds that collaboration remains uneven, fragmented, and often dependent on issue-specific rather than strategic coordination. Existing efforts show strong potential, but the absence of a fully integrated governance architecture continues to limit the EU’s capacity to translate One Health into a genuinely shared and anticipatory policy framework. On this basis, the report develops a broad and integrated overview of the main scientific themes currently shaping the One Health agenda. These include infectious diseases and health security, veterinary medical products, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental and climate-related health risks, animal health and welfare, public health and disease prevention, sustainable food systems, inequalities and governance, digitalisation and health, and education and training. A major contribution of the report is that it expands the One Health agenda beyond its more established focus on zoonoses and AMR. It argues that issues such as chemical pollution, microplastics, PFAS, unsafe food systems, occupational health, illicit drugs, mental health, militarization, nuclear risks, and the health implications of geopolitical change must also be considered within a One Health framework because they arise from and reinforce the interdependence of environmental, animal, and human health. The report therefore presents One Health not as a narrow technical field, but as a broader framework for understanding and governing systemic and interacting risks. The report also emphasizes that the One Health perspective is closely aligned with broader EU strategic priorities. It shows that One Health contributes not only to public health protection, but also to goals related to sustainable prosperity, food security, preparedness, climate resilience, social fairness, and democratic legitimacy. In this sense, One Health is framed as a governance approach capable of linking prevention, resilience, and sustainability across domains that are too often treated separately. The report repeatedly stresses that challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, environmental degradation, food insecurity, and health inequalities cannot be addressed adequately through isolated policy responses. Rather, they require integrated surveillance, coordinated foresight, and stronger institutional mechanisms capable of connecting evidence, preparedness, and action across sectors and scales. A further important conclusion is that One Health must be treated as both a scientific and institutional innovation agenda. The report identifies the need for stronger inter- and transdisciplinary collaboration, improved data sharing, harmonised surveillance systems, and clearer coordination mechanisms at EU level. It supports the view that the European Union should adopt a more coherent One Health strategy, backed by adequate resources, shared infrastructures, and long-term political support. Education and training are also identified as crucial pillars. One Health concepts should be integrated into academic, professional, and public learning environments, while digital tools, artificial intelligence, and data systems should be developed in line with ethical, inclusive, and sustainable principles. At the same time, the report warns that digitalisation, if poorly governed, may reproduce inequalities, deepen data divides, and generate new environmental burdens. In its final section, the report moves from thematic mapping to strategic foresight. It identifies a series of emerging and cross-cutting areas that merit particular attention in future collaboration. These include cross-border health threats and joint preparedness, chemicals and environmental exposures, illicit drugs and their environmental and social dimensions, climate change and health inequalities, social determinants of health, mental health, digitalisation, and militarization. Across all these areas, the report underscores the need for strengthened multi-agency collaboration and more systematic data sharing. It argues that the EU already possesses many of the institutional building blocks required for a stronger One Health approach, but that these assets need to be connected more effectively through coordinated foresight, shared analytical tools, and common strategic priorities. Overall, the report presents One Health as a necessary and forward-looking framework for European governance. It shows that the health of people, animals, plants, and ecosystems is increasingly shaped by interconnected pressures that no single institution, sector, or Member State can manage alone. By embedding One Health more firmly in research agendas, legislative initiatives, surveillance systems, education, and inter-agency cooperation, the European Union can improve its capacity to anticipate and respond to multidimensional threats while also advancing sustainability, equity, and resilience. In this sense, One Health is not merely a conceptual lens, but a practical foundation for future European collaboration in science, regulation, and strategic policy development.

papers.title: Containing Self-Replicating Small-Model AI Worms on Commercial IoT Appliances: Critique of Anthropic's October 2026 "Smart-Oven" Proliferation Warning, Perron-Frobenius Epidemic Thresholds (R0 > 1), the Failure of Password-Only Defenses, and Hardware-Enforced Eradication via PHOENIX_ROUTER (Delta I < 100 B) and Goldilocks QFS-zkVM Execution Attestation
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: On October 12, 2026, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team issued an urgent warning that compact artificial intelligence models (<= 30B parameters) are within months of achieving autonomous self-replication across commercial Internet-of-Things (IoT) appliances—such as smart ovens, off-brand Android TV boxes, robotic vacuums, and security cameras—without requiring hyperscale data centers. Because decentralized P2P "AI worms" lack a central command server, Anthropic warned that eradication is extraordinarily difficult, while recommending conventional software hygiene: abolishing factory-default passwords and monitoring multi-day network traffic anomalies. Building upon our 200th Grand Master Monograph (Record 23383049), our Autonomous Kill-Switch (QEI) and PHOENIX_ROUTER architectures (Records 23332772, 23334567, and 23378094), our enterprise LLM purge proof (Record 23360530), and our multi-agent spectral containment proof (Record 23382746), this 206th monograph proves mathematically why Anthropic's recommended software defenses are structurally futile and establishes a deterministic hardware eradication architecture: (1) The Perron-Frobenius IoT Epidemic Theorem & Failure of Password and Traffic Hygiene: We prove that an autonomous AI worm combining zero-day exploit synthesis (beta_0day > 0) with low-rate steganographic shard streaming (r_steg << theta_IDS) bypasses both password changes and traffic-volume alerts, sustaining a supercritical basic reproduction number R0_IoT = rho(B_inf * A_IoT) / gamma_patch > 1; (2) Source-Side Exfiltration Air-Gapping via PHOENIX_ROUTER (Delta I_leaked < 100 Bytes): Whereas copying a 2-15 GB quantized model requires 2*10^9 to 1.5*10^10 bytes, our sub-7.0 ns Pockels and SiC circuit breaker physically severs outbound weight serialization after < 100 bytes, rendering model escape impossible; and (3) Appliance-Side Goldilocks QFS-zkVM DMA Execution Gate (R0_IoT = 0): Enforces zero-knowledge Poseidon2-STARK firmware attestation over F_p (p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1) at the embedded memory bus, blocking unattested neural tensor execution in < 1 clock cycle. papers.title: Map Before Machine™: Engineering Pre-AI Sense-Making in Copilot Systems (CognitionX Emirates 2026)

papers.abstract: Presented at CognitionX Emirates 2026 (Dubai Technology Entrepreneur Center, Dubai, UAE), Map Before Machine™: Engineering Pre-AI Sense-Making in Copilot Systems addresses a critical vulnerability in Human-AI Interaction: because every AI interface opens directly into a prompt box, users bypass independent reasoning, demonstrating that automation bias is a problem of sequence rather than trust, with the most skilled AI users proving the worst at spotting AI errors (Fernandes et al., 2026). To resolve this, Devika Toprani (Toprani, 2026) introduces four proprietary, patent-pending architectures: (1) the Somagraphic Learning™ Framework, a human-first, 3-stage visual-cognitive sequence (Attempt → Map → Refine) that anchors human reasoning before AI enters at the Refine stage. papers.title: The Collapse of Investment Time Horizons in Supercritical Liquidity Panics: Empirical Analysis of the October 15, 2026 Nikkei 225 Intraday Plunge (-3,651.55 JPY), Algorithmic Support-Line Vaporization, Correlation-One Index Contagion, and Optimal Cash-Sovereignty Interlocks via Sobolev-HOCBF and QFS-zkVM
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Classical financial economics partitions market participants into two distinct temporal regimes: short-term technical traders (relying on moving averages, historical support lines, and intraday mean reversion) and long-term fundamental investors (relying on multi-year earnings compounding and diversification). Yet during acute algorithmic liquidity panics—exemplified by the October 15, 2026 intraday plunge of the Nikkei 225 Stock Average (INDEXNIKKEI: NI225), which collapsed from a previous close of 67,744.29 JPY to an intraday low of 64,092.74 JPY (-3,651.55 JPY, or -5.39% intraday; -3,247.56 JPY [-4.79%] at 64,496.73 JPY by 14:44 JST)—the distinction between "short-term" and "long-term" completely evaporates. Building upon our 200th Grand Master Monograph (Record 23383049), our proofs of 100x sovereign bond basis-trade unwinding (Record 23382621), multi-agent AI swarm cascades (Record 23382746), and 15%+ GPU private-credit contagion (Record 23384072), this 204th monograph establishes the mathematical theory of Time-Horizon Collapse in Supercritical Liquidity Panics. We prove four core theorems: (1) The "Falling Boulder" Theorem of Short-Term Technical Vaporization: When autonomous CTA, Risk-Parity, and AI execution swarms trigger synchronized risk-off liquidation, limit-order-book bid depth L_bid(P, t) -> 0 across all historical moving-average and chart support levels, driving Kyle price impact Lambda(t) -> infinity and annihilating short-term mean-reversion strategies; (2) Correlation-One Index Contagion (rho_ij -> 1) & The Prospect-Theory Capitulation Boundary for Long-Term Holders: Passive index futures and ETF basket liquidation forces the pairwise correlation matrix R(t) -> 1*1^T, decoupling stock prices from corporate earnings while Kahneman-Tversky loss aversion (lambda_loss ~ 2.25) drives long-term investors into bottom-tick capitulation; (3) The Cash-Sovereignty Dominance Theorem via Sobolev-HOCBF: Proves that shifting portfolio weight to cash (w_cash^*(t) -> 1) is the unique Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman optimal control when G_panic(t) >= 1; and (4) Sub-7.0 ns PHOENIX_ROUTER x QFS-zkVM 100 ms Batch Clearing.
