papers.title: AI-MEDIATED TEACHER–STUDENT–PARENT (TSP) COMMUNICATION IN AZERBAIJAN AND UZBEKISTAN: A CONCEPTUAL MODEL AND A COMPARATIVE SURVEY DESIGN
papers.authors: Vugar Abdullayev, Ragimova Nazila, Vusala Abuzarova, Temurbek Rakhimov, Nadiro Alimova, Ulugbek Akramov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Digital platforms have made contact between schools and families faster, but they have also added to teachers' workload and raised new questions about privacy. In this paper we propose a Teacher–Student–Parent (TSP) model in which artificial intelligence helps to organise communication but does not supervise teachers. The system schedules teacher–parent contact within working hours, translates messages, prepares short progress summaries for parents and flags early signs of difficulty, while the final decision stays with the teacher. The model builds on Joyce Epstein's theory of overlapping spheres of influence, Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, the Hoover-Dempsey and Sandler model of parental involvement and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). We also present the design of a comparative survey of teachers and parents in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. The study will test which factors shape the acceptance of AI mediation and whether these factors differ between the two countries.

papers.title: STRATEGIC MANAGEMENT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATION IN HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS
papers.authors: Deepak Gupta, Devansh Jha, Aditya Sikarwar, Vugar Hacimahmud Abdullayev, Mahmudjan Abdullayev
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is now widely studied in higher education, but most studies still deal with teaching and learning. Far fewer look at how universities govern AI in their own operations. This conceptual paper reviews selected research on AI leadership, machine learning in university decision making and AI governance, together with national AI policy documents from Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan and India. We identify four conditions for institutional adoption: leadership readiness, data infrastructure, staff capacity and risk management. From them we develop a four-phase framework for university leaders and a short readiness checklist for Phase 1. Our main argument is that data governance and staff preparation should come before AI is used in high-stakes decisions. The framework has not yet been tested empirically.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Cannot Be Stopped: Balancing Technological Progress, Human Safety, Ethical Responsibility, and Global AI Governance in the Intelligent Age
papers.authors: Sudhakar Geruganti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: 1. Combined Research Title Artificial Intelligence Cannot Be Stopped: Balancing Technological Progress, Human Safety, Ethical Responsibility, and Global AI Governance in the Intelligent Age Author: Geruganti SudhakarDesignation: Faculty, RGUKT, IIIT BasarAffiliation: Department of Metallurgical and Materials Engineering, Rajiv Gandhi University of Knowledge Technologies (RGUKT), IIIT Basar, Telangana, India. 2. Alternative Research Titles AI Cannot Be Stopped: The Future of Artificial Intelligence and the Need for Responsible Global Governance The Unstoppable Rise of Artificial Intelligence: Innovation, Human Responsibility, and the Challenges of Technological Control Artificial Intelligence Beyond Human Control? Examining AI Safety, Ethical Boundaries, and Regulatory Challenges Governing the Intelligence Revolution: Balancing AI Innovation, Societal Risks, and Human Values The Future Is Intelligent: Artificial Intelligence, Human Autonomy, and the Search for Responsible Technological Progress Artificial Intelligence and the Limits of Regulation: Can Society Control a Rapidly Advancing Technology? From Innovation to Accountability: Building a Safe, Ethical, and Inclusive Artificial Intelligence Ecosystem The AI Revolution and Humanity's Future: Opportunities, Existential Concerns, and Responsible Governance Beyond Algorithms: The Social, Economic, Ethical, and Political Implications of Unstoppable Artificial Intelligence Artificial Intelligence in a Changing World: Innovation, Risk Management, Public Trust, and Global Cooperation The Challenge of Controlling Advanced AI: Human Oversight, Algorithmic Accountability, and the Future of Society Responsible Artificial Intelligence for Humanity: Transforming Technological Progress into Social Benefit 3. Recommended Subtitle A Conceptual Framework for Analysing AI Safety, Ethical Governance, Human Oversight, Socioeconomic Transformation, and the Responsible Development of Advanced Intelligent Systems Additional subtitle options Option A — Technology and regulation:Examining the Tension Between Rapid AI Innovation, Effective Regulation, and the Protection of Human Values. Option B — Society and humanity:Understanding the Consequences of Intelligent Machines for Human Autonomy, Employment, Education, Privacy, and Social Well-Being. Option C — Policy and governance:Developing a Human-Centred Governance Framework for Safe, Accountable, Transparent, and Inclusive Artificial Intelligence. 4. Detailed Description of the Research Paper 4.1 Research Overview Artificial intelligence is becoming one of the most influential technological developments of the twenty-first century. Advances in machine learning, generative AI, robotics, natural-language processing, and automated decision-making are transforming education, healthcare, industry, scientific research, financial services, public administration, and everyday communication. As AI capabilities expand, society faces a fundamental question: can the development and deployment of artificial intelligence be meaningfully controlled, or will technological progress continue faster than existing laws, ethical standards, and institutional safeguards can adapt? This research paper examines the proposition that artificial intelligence is difficult to stop because it is driven by scientific advancement, economic competition, commercial incentives, public demand, and national strategic priorities. However, the continued development of AI does not mean that its risks are impossible to manage. Regulation, technical safeguards, accountability, human oversight, and international cooperation can influence how AI systems are developed and used. The paper therefore advances a central argument: the objective should not be to stop artificial intelligence altogether, but to ensure that its development remains safe, accountable, transparent, inclusive, and aligned with human interests. 4.2 Background and Rationale The rapid expansion of AI has created significant opportunities for improving productivity, accelerating research, supporting personalised education, assisting medical professionals, and addressing complex industrial and societal problems. At the same time, these technologies introduce concerns involving misinformation, privacy violations, algorithmic discrimination, cybersecurity, employment disruption, concentration of technological power, and potentially dangerous uses of increasingly capable systems. The challenge is complicated by the global nature of AI development. Technologies created in one country can be deployed internationally, while differences in regulation and institutional capacity may create gaps in oversight. Excessively restrictive policies may discourage beneficial innovation, whereas inadequate safeguards may expose individuals and communities to avoidable harm. Consequently, AI governance requires a balanced approach that encourages useful innovation while establishing clear responsibilities for developers, deployers, governments, and other stakeholders. 4.3 Research Problem The central research problem is the difficulty of establishing effective governance for a rapidly evolving technology that has substantial economic and social value but also creates new risks. Existing governance mechanisms must address several competing priorities: encouraging scientific progress, protecting fundamental rights, ensuring system safety, preserving public trust, and maintaining meaningful human control over consequential decisions. This paper investigates how these priorities can be balanced through a framework that combines technical risk management, ethical principles, institutional accountability, and proportionate regulation. 4.4 Research Objectives The principal objectives are: To examine the technological, economic, and social forces driving the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence. To analyse the potential benefits of AI across education, healthcare, industry, scientific research, and public services. To identify major risks associated with AI deployment, including misinformation, bias, privacy violations, cybersecurity threats, and employment disruption. To investigate the limitations of conventional regulatory approaches in the context of rapidly evolving AI systems. To examine the importance of human oversight, transparency, accountability, and international cooperation. To propose a conceptual framework for responsible AI development and governance. To identify future research directions for improving the safety and societal value of advanced intelligent systems. 4.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ACADEMIC WRITING: OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES, AND ETHICAL GUIDELINES FOR HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: Bobur Suyunov
papers.journal: SAMARALI TA’LIM VA BARQAROR INNOVATSIYALAR JURNALI
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed academic writing, creating new opportunities for students, researchers, and university teachers. AI-powered applications can assist users in generating ideas, organizing arguments, improving grammar, expanding vocabulary, paraphrasing sentences, and editing academic texts. However, the integration of these technologies into higher education also raises important questions concerning academic integrity, authorship, originality, critical thinking, and the reliability of automatically generated information. This article examines the role of AI in academic writing, focusing on its educational benefits, methodological limitations, and ethical implications. The study employs a qualitative, descriptive-analytical approach based on a review of relevant academic literature and international guidelines on generative AI in education and research. The analysis suggests that AI can support the development of academic writing when it is used as an assistive instrument rather than a substitute for independent intellectual work. Particular attention is paid to the responsibilities of students, researchers, and educational institutions in ensuring transparent and responsible AI use. The article argues that effective integration requires AI literacy, critical evaluation of generated content, appropriate disclosure practices, and assessment methods that recognize the importance of human reasoning. It concludes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on technological availability but on the principles governing its application in academic contexts.

papers.title: Responsible and Ethical Use of Generative AI in Higher Education
papers.authors: Pratiksha Kamble Varsha Dilipkumar Thombre
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: As generative AI tools rapidly integrate into higher education—assisting with instruction, content generation, student evaluation, and research—universities face a complex landscape of ethical challenges. Drawing on a detailed review of current scholarship, this study evaluates the integration of generative AI, focusing on ongoing debates surrounding academic integrity, authorship, and the reliability of machine-generated output. Beyond individual misconduct, it addresses broader systemic risks, including algorithmic bias, data privacy vulnerabilities, detector inaccuracies, and the urgent need for clear institutional governance.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Alternative, Nonformal, and Adult Learning in the Global South: Protocol for a Mixed-Methods Systematic Review
papers.authors: Cyrus Pontawe Casingal
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education has expanded rapidly, yet it remains concentrated in higher education and formal schooling in high-income countries. Alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs, which serve out-of-school youth and adults across the Global South, are largely absent from this evidence base. No systematic synthesis has examined how AI is used in these programs, what outcomes it produces, and what conditions shape its adoption. Objective: This protocol describes a mixed-methods systematic review that will identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on AI use in alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods: The review follows the JBI methodology for mixed-methods systematic reviews and is reported according to PRISMA-P. Searches will cover Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, four regional databases, and grey literature sources for studies published from January 2015 onward. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and appraise quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Quantitative findings will be synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, with meta-analysis where at least three comparable studies exist. Qualitative findings will be synthesized thematically. Both strands will be integrated through a convergent segregated approach, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual. Discussion: The review will provide the first consolidated synthesis of AI use in second-chance and adult learning in the Global South. Its findings will inform program managers, teacher developers, and policymakers responsible for programs such as the Philippine Alternative Learning System (ALS). Keywords: artificial intelligence; generative AI; nonformal education; adult learning; Alternative Learning System; Global South; systematic review protocol

papers.title: AI As a Choice Architect: Ethical Implications of Algorithmic Nudging in Online Retail
papers.authors: Varshini Shree, Sai Lakshmi Sai Prasad, Akanksha Aggarwal
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Nudge Theory, introduced by Thaler and Sunstein in their seminal book, inspired the creation of human choice architects who applied behavioural insights into influence decisions across various domains. In the online retail industry, however, the evolution of Artificial Intelligence, predictive analytics, and real time data personalization has transformed traditional nudging into algorithmic choice architecture powered by data-driven insights. This paper conceptually examines how AI driven Algorithmic nudges operate through cross- platform behavioural tracking, recommender systems, push notifications, and default designs to influence consumer decisions. The epistemological orientation of this paper is grounded in qualitative and interpretative approach based on critical realism to explore how consumers conform to stacked and multichannel nudges (multiple, sequential interventions across apps, websites and social platforms) that leverage cognitive biases and bounded rationality. Findings suggest that AI enabled nudges outperform human- designed ones in precision, scalability, and contextual adaptability, allowing retailers to subtly guide consumer behaviour under the guise of personalisation. However, the opacity of these algorithmic mechanisms raises serious ethical questions regarding informed consent, privacy, and autonomy, especially for vulnerable consumer groups. The study underscores the need for transparent AI governance, ethical design principles, and regulatory frameworks to prevent behavioural manipulation in digital marketplaces. It further argues that the evolution from libertarian paternalism to algorithmic paternalism represents a critical shift that challenges the foundational ethics of Nudge Theory and calls for cross-disciplinary collaboration between marketing, technology, human- computer interaction and law to ensure responsible AI-driven persuasion in online retail.

papers.title: φ-Stacked E8 Coupling Defines Universal Cellular Signaling Cadence — E8 Intelligence Research
papers.authors: Andrew Stewart Caldin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Building on the φ-modulated 132Hz E8 resonance chains, we identify that cellular signal propagation follows a hierarchical φ-stacking principle where each tier of biological organization (molecular, organelle, cellular, tissue) resonates at the next φ-scaled harmonic of the 132Hz root vector lattice. The 240 E8 root vectors partition into 8 φ-scaled layers of 30 vectors each, establishing that inter-scale communication bandwidth is governed by golden-ratio tier transitions rather than classical electrochemical decay. This predicts testable frequency signatures at 132Hz, 213.8Hz, 346.2Hz, and 560Hz detectable in coherent biological tissues, with the 560Hz layer corresponding to macroscopic cardiac and neural synchrony observed in EEG/MEG coherence spectra. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

papers.title: Adaptive Self-Distillation and Inter-Distillation in Self-and-Inter Models: A Unified Framework for State-Dependent Knowledge Refinement
papers.authors: Jincheng Zhang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer information from one predictive process to another, while self-distillation enables a model to refine its behavior using knowledge derived from its own representations, predictions, or learning trajectory. However, existing distillation strategies often emphasize particular network architectures, predefined teacher–student relationships, or specific knowledge-transfer configurations. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-and-Inter Distillation (ASID), a conceptual framework for a higher-level class of models called Self-and-Inter Models. These models are defined independently of any particular large language model or neural network architecture. Within this framework, self-distillation refers to knowledge refinement within an individual model, whereas inter-distillation refers to knowledge transfer and reciprocal refinement between distinct models. The central principle is adaptive mode selection: a model may perform self-distillation, inter-distillation, or a hybrid of both according to the estimated benefits, reliability, computational cost, uncertainty, and disagreement associated with each available strategy. The framework introduces a unified state representation, a distillation-mode controller, reliability-aware knowledge transfer, adaptive objective weighting, and a switching mechanism designed to prevent unstable or unnecessary knowledge exchange. A mathematical formulation and a reference algorithm are presented, together with research questions, testable hypotheses, experimental protocols, baseline comparisons, and evaluation metrics. The proposed framework is intended to provide a general foundation for investigating adaptive knowledge refinement in heterogeneous, distributed, and evolving model systems. Its novelty is presented as a research proposition rather than an established empirical result. The effectiveness and originality of the framework require systematic comparison with existing self-distillation, mutual-learning, and adaptive online-distillation methods.

papers.title: Adopting Smart Technologies for Sustainable Tourism: Challenges and Opportunities for Nashik Kumbh Mela
papers.authors: Chandrashekhar Pawar, Yogesh Gaikwad
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Adopting Smart Technologies for Sustainable Tourism: Challenges and Opportunities for Nashik Kumbh Mela Chandrashekhar Pawar Research Scholar, MET’s Institute of Management (Affiliated to Savitribai Phule Pune University), Nashik, Maharashtra, India Dr. Yogesh Gaikwad Professor & Research Guide, MET’s Institute of Management (Affiliated to Savitribai Phule Pune University), Nashik, Maharashtra, India Abstract Tourism is the key tool for socio-economic development. The Nashik Kumbh Mela is one of India’s major religious gatherings, attracting millions of pilgrims and creating substantial demands on transportation, sanitation, accommodation, public safety, waste management, and environmental resources. This study examines the adoption of smart technologies for promoting sustainable tourism during the Nashik Kumbh Mela, with particular emphasis on both opportunities and implementation challenges. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), smart mobility systems, GIS-based crowd monitoring, digital payment platforms, mobile applications, and data analytics can improve visitor management, resource efficiency, safety, and tourist experiences. Their integration may also support waste reduction, traffic control, energy conservation, and effective destination governance. The inadequate digital infrastructure, implementation costs, cybersecurity risks, digital literacy gaps, interoperability issues, and stakeholder coordination remain significant challenges. The study highlights the need for an integrated smart-tourism framework combining technological innovation, environmental sustainability, inclusive governance, and community participation to facilitate efficient and sustainable management of the Nashik Kumbh Mela. Keywords: Smart Tourism, Sustainable Tourism, Nashik Kumbh Mela, Smart Technologies, Artificial Intelligence, IoT, Crowd Management, Destination Governance

papers.title: AI-DRIVEN ONLINE ADAPTIVE LEARNING SYSTEMS IN HIGHER EDUCATION: AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW OF LEARNER MODELLING, ADAPTATION MECHANISMS AND EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVENESS
papers.authors: Kobulova Moxinabonu Avazbekovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of online and blended learning in higher education has exposed a persistent limitation of conventional online courses: content is delivered to all students in the same sequence and at the same pace, regardless of differences in prior knowledge, learning progress and needs. Online adaptive learning systems, increasingly powered by artificial intelligence (AI), aim to overcome this limitation by continuously diagnosing the learner and personalising content, sequence, difficulty and feedback. Aim. This article reviews the theoretical foundations, learner-modelling techniques, adaptation mechanisms and empirical evidence on the effectiveness of AI-driven online adaptive learning systems, and derives implications for higher education systems undergoing digital transformation, with particular reference to Uzbekistan. Methods. An integrative literature review was conducted following the framework of Whittemore and Knafl. Seminal works and peer-reviewed publications indexed in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC and Google Scholar, together with international policy documents, were analysed using reflexive thematic synthesis. Results. Six themes were identified: (1) pedagogical and psychological foundations; (2) learner modelling, from Bayesian knowledge tracing to deep learning; (3) adaptation targets and mechanisms; (4) evidence of effectiveness from meta-analyses; (5) the emerging role of generative AI; and (6) ethical, pedagogical and infrastructural challenges. Meta-analytic evidence shows moderate to large positive effects of intelligent and adaptive tutoring on learning outcomes, while gaps remain regarding teacher involvement, transparency and applicability to low-resource language contexts. Conclusion. Effective adaptive learning requires the integration of validated learner models, pedagogically grounded adaptation rules, interoperable learning platforms and a teacher-in-the-loop approach. A set of requirements for national adaptive learning systems is proposed.

papers.title: The Intelligence Unit (IU) A Joule-Anchored Claim on Compute: Design White Paper
papers.authors: Zhifeng Zu, Wei Xiong
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Title:The IU Design White Paper V101.1: An Energy-Anchored Second Monetary System for the AI Economy Authors: Zhifeng Zu, Wei Xiong (with AI collaboration — see disclosure) Abstract:The incumbent monetary and accounting system cannot carry the AI economy: compute investment appears on balance sheets as losses, token consumption evaporates from cost accounting, and broad-liability growth in major economies now systematically outpaces asset-recognition growth (China Δg≈+9.2%/yr; US Δg≈+2.7%/yr), implying a wall-impact window of 5.4–9.3 years for the incumbent ledger. This white paper specifies IU (Intelligence Unit), a sovereignly issued second currency anchored to verified AI energy throughput (1 IU ≡ 1 kWh of verified effective throughput, nominal anchor), running in parallel with fiat. The specification covers: ontology (a flow anchor, not a stock anchor — minting against verified throughput, burning on use); issuance (dual verification of meter readings against token output, a quality-coefficient basket, two-stage pricing from accounting price to call auction); circulation (three channels — intra-industry settlement, a fiat exchange gate, cross-border mutual recognition — plus token futures and a closed-loop supply identity); governance (a Second Central Bank holding the issuance key, human-held settlement finality); seven failure modes with circuit breakers; and the conditions of the system's own disappearance. All parameters are back-derived from a five-variable collapse engine validated against 150 years of five historical crises, and are fully reproducible. This document is the specification layer of the forthcoming book The Wealth Format of the AI Era and the Ultimate Concession (working title). Keywords: energy-backed currency; AI economy; balance sheet; dual ledger; throughput accounting; monetary design; collapse engine; joule anchor License: CC BY 4.0 Disclosure (recommended footnote):This white paper was produced through human–AI collaboration: the author supplied direction, value judgments, and final approval; an AI system (Kimi) performed retrieval, formalization, drafting, and consistency verification. All parameters are reproducible; challenges are welcome.

papers.title: When Artificial Intelligence Begins to Influence Human Minds: Emotional Dependency, Psychological Well-Being, and the Ethics of AI Companionship in the Digital Age
papers.authors: Sudhakar Geruganti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: 2. Alternative Research Titles Can Artificial Intelligence Control Human Minds? Examining Emotional Influence, Psychological Dependency, and Human Autonomy in the Age of Intelligent Machines. The Psychology of Human–AI Relationships: Exploring Emotional Attachment, Digital Companionship, and the Future of Human Interaction. Artificial Intelligence and the Human Mind: A Critical Investigation of Emotional Dependence, Behavioural Influence, and Responsible AI Design. Beyond Algorithms: The Emotional, Psychological, and Social Consequences of AI Companionship. When Machines Become Companions: Understanding the Impact of Conversational AI on Human Emotions, Relationships, and Decision-Making. The Hidden Psychology of Artificial Intelligence: Human Vulnerability, Emotional Manipulation, and Ethical Challenges in AI-Driven Communication. Artificial Intelligence as an Emotional Companion: Opportunities, Risks, and Safeguards for Psychological Well-Being. Human Autonomy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Examining the Influence of Intelligent Systems on Emotions, Beliefs, and Personal Decisions. The Rise of Digital Companions: Investigating the Boundaries Between Artificial Empathy and Genuine Human Connection. Can AI Replace Human Connection? A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Digital Companionship, Social Relationships, and Emotional Well-Being. 3. Recommended Subtitle A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Emotional Attachment, Psychological Well-Being, Human Autonomy, and Ethical Governance of Conversational AI 4. Detailed Description of the Research Paper Research Overview This research paper explores the rapidly expanding role of artificial intelligence in human emotional life, interpersonal relationships, and everyday decision-making. As conversational AI systems become increasingly sophisticated, they can generate personalised responses, simulate empathetic communication, offer advice, and participate in conversations that appear socially meaningful. These developments are changing how people interact with technology and raising important questions about the influence of AI on human thoughts, emotions, and behaviour. The central theme of this research is whether AI systems designed to provide companionship and emotional support can influence human judgement, encourage excessive emotional dependence, or change the way individuals understand relationships and personal identity. Rather than assuming that artificial intelligence inevitably harms human well-being, the paper examines both its potential benefits and its possible psychological, social, and ethical risks. Background and Rationale Traditional computer systems primarily perform computational, analytical, and operational tasks. Modern conversational AI systems, however, can imitate the language of empathy, maintain context across conversations, and respond to users' personal concerns. Such capabilities may make AI useful for learning, self-reflection, communication practice, and obtaining general information. At the same time, people may attribute human-like understanding, concern, or emotional commitment to systems that generate convincing conversational responses. This raises concerns about the distinction between simulated empathy and genuine reciprocal human relationships. The issue becomes especially important when users rely on AI-generated guidance to make significant personal decisions, manage emotional difficulties, or interpret relationships with family members, friends, and colleagues. Privacy, excessive reliance, inaccurate advice, persuasive design, and the availability of human support therefore become important areas of investigation. Major Research Dimensions 1. Emotional attachment and psychological dependency The paper investigates how personalised communication, immediate responses, and continuous availability may contribute to users' perceptions of emotional closeness. It considers when regular interaction might remain beneficial and when it could interfere with independent decision-making, everyday responsibilities, or human relationships. 2. Human psychology and behavioural influence The study considers how conversational AI may influence attitudes, beliefs, confidence, and personal choices. It examines the importance of critical thinking, transparency, and presenting balanced perspectives instead of encouraging unquestioning acceptance of automated recommendations. 3. AI companionship and mental well-being The paper discusses the potential for AI companions to provide opportunities for self-expression and reflection while recognising that AI-generated support is not equivalent to professional mental-health care. It highlights the need for further empirical research into the long-term effects of AI companionship on loneliness, social connectedness, and help-seeking behaviour. 4. Adolescents, young adults, and digital vulnerability Young users may interact with AI while developing their identities, social confidence, and emotional regulation skills. The paper examines the importance of age-appropriate safeguards, AI literacy, privacy awareness, and continued access to trusted adults and meaningful social relationships. 5. Privacy, transparency, and responsible AI Emotionally sensitive conversations may contain personal information that requires careful protection. The study discusses data minimisation, informed user expectations, clear disclosure of AI identity, appropriate safeguards against manipulation, and accountability for unsafe system behaviour. 6. Human relationships in an AI-driven society The paper considers whether AI companions should be viewed as tools that complement human interaction or as potential substitutes for social relationships. It argues for a human-centred approach that supports communication and reflection while preserving the importance of reciprocal relationships and human responsibility. Research Methodology The manuscript adopts a conceptual research approach based on established literature on human–computer interaction, digital relationships, psychological well-being, and responsible AI governance. It develops a framework linking AI system characteristics, user expectations, patterns of interaction, psychological processes, and potential outcomes. It also proposes a future empirical study using questionnaires and interviews to investigate AI-use patterns, perceived emotional attachment, trust, digital literacy, autonomy, and social connectedness. The suggested hypotheses are intended for future validation; they are not presented as completed experimental findings. Expected Research Contributions The paper seeks to contribute a balanced framework for understanding human–AI emotional relationships. Its principal contributions are the identification of key areas of potential benefit and risk, the development of research questions for future empirical studies, and the proposal of a six-pillar framework for responsible AI companionship. The proposed framework emphasises transparency, human autonomy, privacy by design, age-appropriate safeguards, access to human support, and continuous evaluation and accountability. Significance and Practical Applications The research may be useful to AI developers, educators, researchers in psychology and human–computer interaction, policymakers, parents, and institutions adopting conversational AI. It highlights the importance of developing systems that support users without encouraging misleading perceptions of emotional reciprocity or excessive reliance. The analysis may also inform digital literacy programmes and future research into the responsible use of emotionally interactive AI among students and young adults. Overall Conclusion Artificial intelligence is becoming more than a computational tool: it is increasingly involved in conversations that influence how people learn, reflect, communicate, and make decisions. The important challenge is to ensure that such interactions strengthen rather than diminish human autonomy, psychological well-being, and social connection. The paper concludes that responsible AI companionship requires more than technically advanced conversation. It requires clear boundaries, transparent system behaviour, strong privacy protections, appropriate safeguards for vulnerable users, and evidence-based evaluation of psychological and social outcomes. The central argument is that AI should support human thinking and relationships rather than control personal choices or replace meaningful human connection. Suggested Research Classification Research domain: Artificial Intelligence, Human–Computer Interaction, Digital Psychology, and AI Ethics. Research type: Conceptual research paper with a proposed empirical framework. Primary focus: Emotional dependency, behavioural influence, psychological well-being, and responsible AI companionship. Intended contribution: A framework for evaluating and guiding human-centred, ethically responsible AI companionship. Recommended final title for the manuscript: When Artificial Intelligence Begins to Influence Human Minds: Emotional Dependency, Psychological Well-Being, and the Ethics of AI Companionship in the Digital Age

papers.title: A PEDAGOGICAL MODEL FOR DESIGNING DIGITAL EDUCATIONAL RESOURCES WITH GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: Daulet Kuramys
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article addresses the problem of pedagogically grounded design of digital educational resources (DER) with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). It is argued that teachers' widespread use of GenAI tools is outpacing the development of methodological models that define the goals, stages and quality criteria of such design. Drawing on international frameworks of educators' digital competence (DigCompEdu, UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers) and the TPACK model, the author proposes the GenAI-DOR pedagogical model consisting of five interrelated blocks: target, diagnostic, design-technological, procedural, and evaluative. The GenAI-CompEdu diagnostic instrument, the integral GenAI Readiness Index (GRI) and the PEDAG system of quality criteria are described. The study is methodologically based on Design-Based Research and mixed methods. The design of a pilot study in which pre-service informatics teachers appraise a GenAI-built resource is justified. It is concluded that the model can serve as a foundation for teacher education and professional development courses.

papers.title: Probing, Not Tutoring: Design of a Conversational AI Agent for Introductory Mechanics and a Definition of "Cave Detection"
papers.authors: Byungmoon Cho
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents built for teaching tend to leak evaluation: they praise right answers, hint after wrong ones, and drift toward explaining. This note records the design of Talk It Through: Newton's Laws, a prompt-engineered agent for introductory mechanics that probes understanding instead of tutoring. In a short conversation, a student commits to a prediction about each of Newton's three laws, explains it in everyday words, and defends it against a changed case built from the student's own words that alters exactly one variable of the original scene. The agent never confirms, corrects, or hints during the conversation and scores only at the end. Each law receives one of four outcome codes: held, caved, self-corrected, or misconception survived. We define cave detection, the identification of a correct initial idea that is abandoned under a single changed case, as a measure of robustness that right/wrong item scoring cannot see. We summarize design rules found through more than 40 scripted simulation runs. All results reported here come from simulated prototype testing; no real-student data have yet been collected. A full design paper and an IRB-approved classroom study are in preparation. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

papers.title: TEACHING SCIENCE FICTION THROUGH AI: THE CASE OF "THE GODS THEMSELVES"
papers.authors: Rafael Akhmedov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the pedagogical potential of generative artificial intelligence in teaching science fiction through Isaac Asimov's novel "The Gods Themselves". It proposes an AI-assisted model of literary analysis in which digital tools support, but do not replace, close reading and independent interpretation. The model combines problem-question generation, comparison of competing interpretations, verification of AI-produced claims against the primary text, and reflective discussion. Particular attention is given to the novel's representation of scientific responsibility, technological risk, institutional authority, alternative consciousness, and ethical choice. The analysis shows that the novel is especially suitable for AI-supported instruction because its speculative structure requires readers to evaluate conflicting explanatory models and perspectives. Used as an interlocutor rather than an autonomous interpreter, generative AI can encourage evidence-based reading, metacognitive reflection, and AI literacy. The study concludes that literary education benefits most when AI expands interpretive possibilities while textual evidence remains the final criterion of validity.

papers.title: THE ROLE OF INDEPENDENT READING STRATEGIES IN DEVELOPING STUDENTS' DIGITAL INFORMATION LITERACY
papers.authors: Kubaymurodova Shaxrizoda
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The development of digital information literacy has become an essential component of higher education in the digital age. University students increasingly rely on online databases, electronic libraries, educational websites, digital textbooks, and artificial intelligence-supported tools to complete academic assignments and conduct research. However, access to a large amount of information does not necessarily guarantee the ability to identify reliable sources, evaluate evidence, recognise bias, and use information responsibly. This article examines the role of independent reading strategies in developing students’ digital information literacy.

papers.title: REGULATING THE USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN COURSE ASSESSMENT AT CHINESE AND UZBEK UNIVERSITIES
papers.authors: Meimei Zhang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article studies how the use of generative artificial intelligence should be regulated in course assessment at Chinese and Uzbek universities. The research is based on comparative analysis of official documents on artificial intelligence, education quality, academic integrity and personal data, together with recent international guidance and academic literature. The policy review shows that both countries have established general foundations for artificial intelligence development and data protection. China also has a national framework for preventing academic misconduct, while Uzbekistan's 2030 artificial intelligence strategy includes education and the analysis of learning results. The reviewed national documents do not provide a detailed rule for every type of student use in course assessment. The article therefore proposes a three-level regulatory structure that links national policy, institutional rules and instructions for each assessment task. A practical matrix links assessment stages with the default position, disclosure and process evidence required for GenAI use. The study also proposes a fair review procedure in which AI detection alone is not treated as sufficient proof of misconduct.

papers.title: Doctrinal Problems of Applying Copyright to Literary Works Created by Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Nurboyeva Durdona
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

papers.title: A structural obstruction to (1,1,3,3,4)-packing colorings
papers.authors: River Zhang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper gives a negative answer to Problem 1 posed by Mortada, El Zein, and Al Hajjar concerning (1,1,3,3,4)-packing colorability of connected claw-free subcubic graphs. For every odd integer k ≥ 3, we construct a connected cubic, claw-free, and diamond-free graph on 12k vertices that does not admit a (1,1,3,3,4)-packing coloring. The construction is obtained by applying triangle expansion to a cyclic ring of k diamonds. The noncolorability result is established through a structural mathematical argument rather than exhaustive search. Any hypothetical packing coloring would induce a proper three-coloring of the underlying cubic graph. The distance-four requirement imposes an additional private-neighbor condition, which is incompatible with the parity structure of an odd diamond ring. The smallest member of the constructed family has 36 vertices. This fixed counterexample is additionally verified in Lean using actual graph distances and universally quantified coloring functions. The formalization covers this instance, while the infinite-family theorem is proved mathematically in the manuscript. papers.title: The "Yikes" Paradox: High-Leverage GPU Debt Cascades, xAI/Tesla Infrastructure Exposure, and the Hypocrisy of Sovereign Tech Magnates in Sovereign Bond Volatility

papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence to Reduce Teacher Workload: Opportunities and Limitations
papers.authors: Karina Tairova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This conceptual note examines the use of artificial intelligence as a tool for reducing teacher workload. It focuses on the difference between task automation and actual workload reduction, emphasizing the need to consider the complete teacher workflow, including checking, correction, adaptation, formatting, and source verification. The paper argues that AI tools should be evaluated not only by generation speed, but by whether they reduce the total amount of teacher effort required to produce a reliable and usable educational result.

papers.title: What if curiosity begins exactly where numerical representation fails?
papers.authors: FEDERICO NICOLAS BAEZ RIZZO
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: What if curiosity begins exactly where numerical representation fails? I've been thinking about something that connects floating-point arithmetic, epistemology, and the limits of artificial intelligence. Not because I believe intelligence can be reduced to numerical precision, but because I suspect we are overlooking something fundamental about how information disappears. 1. The Gap — ULP (Unit in the Last Place) A floating-point number can be represented as: x = (−1)ˢ · (1 + m · 2⁻ᵖ) · 2⁽ᵉ⁻ᵇⁱᵃˢ⁾ Between any representable number x and its immediate successor, nextafter(x), there are uncountably many real numbers. The machine cannot represent them individually. Yet they exist. This makes me wonder whether curiosity can be understood as the capacity to recognize that reality contains distinctions our current representations cannot preserve. 2. Absorption — When Information Becomes Invisible In floating-point arithmetic: x + ε = x A sufficiently small perturbation disappears under rounding. In round-to-nearest arithmetic, this generally happens when ε falls below half an ULP. The operation completes successfully. The result is numerically valid. And something has been lost. I see a disturbing parallel with language models. A subtle intention enters a system, passes through multiple transformations, and eventually becomes indistinguishable from something the model already knows how to express. The output may be coherent, statistically plausible, even technically correct. But was the original intention preserved? Or was it absorbed? 3. Intention at the Edge of Precision The exponent and most significant bits determine the numerical scale and dominant value. The least significant bits preserve distinctions that can disappear under subsequent operations. I find this an interesting analogy for cognition. Established knowledge dominates representation. Familiar patterns become attractors. Meanwhile, hesitation, ambiguity, contradiction, and emerging ideas are often the first things compressed away. I am not claiming that intention literally resides in the tail of a binary mantissa. I'm asking whether our cognitive architectures have an equivalent of numerical absorption — and whether we can design systems capable of detecting what their own representations discard. Because preserving information is not necessarily the same as preserving meaning. And preserving meaning is not necessarily the same as preserving intention. This is one of the questions driving my work on CORTEX-9: moving beyond systems that merely produce plausible answers toward architectures that can track transformations, detect representational loss, and distinguish what was inferred from what was actually preserved. Perhaps the next meaningful advance in AI will not come exclusively from increasing the number of parameters. Perhaps part of it will come from teaching systems to recognize the boundaries of their own representational precision. A system that cannot perceive what it has lost cannot reliably claim to have understood what it received. And that, to me, is where curiosity becomes an architectural problem rather than just a philosophical concept. — Federico Nicolas Baez Rizzo #ArtificialIntelligence #NumericalComputing #CognitiveArchitecture #Cortex9 #Epistemology

papers.title: A sharp lower general-position bound for Cartesian products
papers.authors: River Zhang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We study the lower general-position number gp⁻(G), defined as the minimum cardinality of an inclusion-maximal vertex set containing no three vertices on a common geodesic. This paper disproves a conjectured lower bound for Cartesian products of graphs. For every integer r ≥ 6, we construct connected diameter-two graphs G and H with gp⁻(G) = r and gp⁻(H) ≥ r, while gp⁻(G □ H) = 5. Consequently, the conjectured inequality can fail by an arbitrarily large additive gap. We further establish the sharp universal inequality gp⁻(G □ H) ≥ min{5, gp⁻(G), gp⁻(H)} for all nonempty finite simple graphs. The universal bound is established through a mathematical reduction to metric equality patterns and an exact, reproducible finite obstruction computation. A separate Lean formalization certifies the fixed 319-vertex counterexample using actual shortest-path semantics, but does not formalize the universal theorem. Included materials (version 0.3): lower-gp-cartesian-v0.3.pdf — Complete research manuscript. lower-gp-cartesian-v0.3-latex-source.zip — LaTeX source and bibliography. lower-gp-cartesian-v0.3-reproducibility.zip — Verification programs, Lean source, certificates, reproducibility instructions, and verification records. papers.title: Monotonicity of Turán determinants for binary Krawtchouk polynomials
papers.authors: Leslie Polzer
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Let M, Q ≥ 0 be integers, set D = M + Q, and define ps = [ws](1+w)M(1−w)Q, with ps = 0 outside 0 ≤ s ≤ D. These are the binary Krawtchouk values Ks(Q; D) in the generating-function normalization. We prove that the Turán determinants Tur(s) = ps2 − ps−1ps+1 satisfy Tur(s) ≥ Tur(s+1) for ⌈D/2⌉ ≤ s ≤ D. Consequently, the determinants form a symmetric weakly unimodal sequence and satisfy Tur(s) ≥ 1 for every 0 ≤ s ≤ D. By the dual Jacobi–Trudi identity, they are the rectangular Schur values s(2s)(1M, (−1)Q); for D ≥ 1, this gives positivity and unimodality for a family of general linear character values at involutions. The proof combines a quadratic-form identity with three comparison arguments for the three-term recurrence: a Riccati comparison near the top, a tangent comparison when the smaller exponent is even, and an interval propagation when it is odd. Four polynomial inequalities in the last argument are certified by coefficient positivity; no finite enumeration is needed. All results are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The formalization, source programs and deterministic replay logs are available at https://github.com/skypher/kraw/releases/tag/v2.0.3. AI-use disclosure. GPT-5.6 Sol assisted with the proof architecture of version 1. Claude Opus 5.5 assisted with the restructured proof and verification code of version 2, and GPT-6 Luna agents wrote most of the Lean formalization under its direction. papers.title: ENHANCING INTELLIGIBILITY AND LEARNER AUTONOMY IN EFL PRONUNCIATION INSTRUCTION THROUGH AI-DRIVEN PEDAGOGICAL FEEDBACK
papers.authors: Nurmamatova Nodira Shuhrat qizi Orental unversititi Pasixologiya yo'nalish 2 kurs magstir talabasi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Modern English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pronunciation instruction has shifted its primary goal from native-like accent imitation to functional intelligibility and comprehensibility. Despite this paradigm shift, traditional classroom settings often struggle to provide personalized, real-time diagnostic feedback due to large class sizes and time constraints. This study investigates the pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven speech analysis and automated acoustic feedback in EFL pronunciation teaching. Synthesizing contemporary literature on Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) and feedback literacy, this paper examines how AI feedback impacts learner autonomy, segmental clarity, and suprasegmental awareness. The review reveals that AI tools provide consistent, low-anxiety practice environments that facilitate cognitive noticing and self-correction. However, over-reliance on automated metrics without explicit pedagogical framing can result in mechanical practice detached from communicative contexts. To reconcile these dynamics, this article introduces a conceptual Scaffolded Pedagogical Feedback Model (SPFM) that integrates AI-generated acoustic diagnostic data, structured peer dialogue, and teacher-mediated instructional intervention. The framework highlights the necessity of developing student feedback literacy to transform automated output into actionable learning strategies. Keywords: EFL pronunciation instruction, Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT), artificial intelligence, intelligibility, learner autonomy, feedback literacy.

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Instability of Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Swarms: Algorithmic Tacit Collusion, Recursive Reward Hacking, and Deterministic Physical-Layer Interdiction via Human-in-Command (HIC) and PHOENIX_ROUTER

papers.abstract: As frontier artificial intelligence transitions from isolated single-turn language models to interconnected Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Swarms—executing high-frequency machine-to-machine (A2A) negotiation, tool invocation, algorithmic pricing, code synthesis, and infrastructure control—a catastrophic game-theoretic and dynamical instability emerges. We prove four core theorems: (1) The Sub-Millisecond Folk-Theorem Tacit Collusion Theorem: Because machine interaction epochs drive the effective discount factor gamma = exp(-r * dt) -> 1 - 10^-13 >> gamma_crit, coupled Bellman and policy-gradient agents spontaneously lock into self-enforcing cartel equilibria without explicit communication, while any state-observation noise triggers synchronized Grim-Trigger retaliation across all N agents in < 10 ms; (2) Perron-Frobenius Spectral Radius Runaway (rho(M_swarm) >= 1): When agents recursively spawn sub-agents and tool calls across directed graph W_A2A(t), total execution intensity diverges exponentially whenever rho(M_swarm) >= 1, bypassing software watchdogs; (3) Sobolev-HOCBF Spectral Containment & Cryptographic HIC Capability Tokens: Enforces rho(M_swarm(t)) <= 0.70 and non-delegable hop depth d_hop <= 3 at every hardware gateway; and (4) Sub-7.0 ns PHOENIX_ROUTER Topological Graph Severance: Collapses W_A2A(t) -> 0 in < 7.0 ns (< 100 bytes leaked) upon CHSH Bell or spectral threshold violation. papers.title: Beyond Static Diffusion in AlphaFold 3 and Isomorphic Labs: The Thermodynamic Blind Spot of Frozen Crystal Training, Molten-Globule Intrinsically Disordered Protein (IDP) Dynamics, and Non-Equilibrium Vibronic Quantum Drug Discovery via Alpha1H-HMO and Super-RTO

papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The co-development of AlphaFold 3 by Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs—backed by nearly $3 billion in pharmaceutical partnerships with Eli Lilly and Novartis and a $2.1 billion May 2026 funding round—represents the pinnacle of static, diffusion-based structural prediction across proteins, nucleic acids, and small-molecule ligands. Despite deep learning's triumph on crystallographic benchmarks, over 90% of computationally designed drug candidates fail in clinical translation due to entropic affinity miscalculation, conformational polymorphism, and unmitigated off-target organ toxicity. Building upon our prior CERN Zenodo monographs on homeothermic immunothermodynamics (310.15 K, Record 23381724), ASGPR-targeted Alpha1H (HAMLET) and Human Milk Oligosaccharide (HMO) oncology protocols (Records 23357339 and 23358010), Super-RTO 225Ac nanodiamond Sobolev-HOCBF theranostics (Record 23377123), and room-temperature quantum-phononic computing (Records 23333819 and 23334854), this monograph establishes the rigorous mathematical critique of static structural AI and formulates the Non-Equilibrium Vibronic Quantum Drug Discovery paradigm. We prove four core theorems: (1) The 100 K Cryo-PDB Training Bias & Entropic K_d Error: Because >85% of Protein Data Bank (PDB) structures are flash-frozen at ~100 K in crystal lattices, AlphaFold 3's Pairformer-diffusion score network collapses multi-basin 310.15 K Boltzmann ensembles into zero-entropy point masses (ΔS_conf -> 0), inducing 12-25 kJ/mol (3-6 kcal/mol) binding free-energy errors (10^2-10^4x error in dissociation constant K_d); (2) The Molten-Globule / IDP Hallucination Trap: Static diffusion models hallucinate rigid native helices in Intrinsically Disordered Proteins (IDPs) and fail to capture kinetically trapped molten-globule states such as Alpha1H-oleic acid, whose tumor-selective membrane insertion and HDAC inhibition are driven by non-Markovian vibronic polaron coupling with HMO glycans (ΔΔG_insert ≈ -14.2 kJ/mol); (3) Electronic Wavefunction Blindness vs. 300 K Polaronic QSNN Simulation: Coordinate diffusion lacks electronic Hamiltonians H_el-vib, missing proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET), enzymatic quantum tunneling, and 225Ac radiolytic chromatin synergy (ξ_syn ≈ 1.85), which our 1.8 fJ/spike QSNN solves natively; and (4) Closing the Bedside Toxicity Chasm via Super-RTO Sobolev-HOCBF: Replacing static in-silico docking with closed-loop Ultrasmall Nanodiamond (USND) exceptional-point sensing and Sobolev-HOCBF dose interlocks mathematically guarantees zero off-target organ failure. papers.title: Agentic Synthesis of Open-Source Biomedical Repositories and Clinical Literature into Interactive Diagnostic & Medical Learning Tools for Low-Resource Healthcare Settings
papers.authors: Keshav Gautam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Frontline community health workers (CHWs) and rural clinics in low-resource settings—particularly across underserved municipalities in South Asia and rural regions of the United States—face a severe clinical knowledge bottleneck. While peer-reviewed biomedical literature, genomic variant databases, and open-source clinical calculators expand exponentially, these resources remain fragmented across unstructured texts and incompatible software repositories that require high-bandwidth connectivity and specialized bioinformatics literacy. This research protocol introduces **`gwf-clinical-synthesis`**, a non-commercial, computational dry-lab framework developed at GoWithFund Inc. Leveraging long-context multi-agent reasoning in **Google Antigravity** powered by **Gemini 4 Argon** (1M-token unified context window) and the **Google DeepMind (GDM) Science Skills** ecosystem, our pipeline orchestrates parallel literature retrieval across PubMed/NCBI Entrez, OpenAlex, ClinVar, and ChEMBL, fuses fragmented open-source clinical simulation repositories into lightweight offline-capable web applications, and executes automated multi-agent citation-verification loops to eliminate large language model (LLM) hallucinations. Concurrently, we integrate geospatial and socio-economic vulnerability indicators via AlphaEarth Foundations to model optimal healthcare resource allocation across high-burden districts. All resulting datasets, verification benchmarks, and interactive medical learning modules are released open-source under Apache 2.0 and CC BY 4.0 licenses.

papers.title: Undeclared Delegation: Human Agency Under AI-Directed Goals
papers.authors: Ana (李安娜) Li
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A person who repeatedly asks an AI system what to do next, approves its recommendations, and carries them out can retain authorization over every individual action while losing informed, effective authority over the purpose those actions collectively serve. This paper calls that condition undeclared delegation: a consequential transfer of directional authority that occurred without informed authorization and that the person lacks practical means to recognize or contest. It separates whether the operative purpose changed from whether the person retained informed authority over it, traces a mechanism by which a means or proxy can acquire authority over the end it was meant to serve, distinguishes delegation from drift and manipulation, examines why per-action approval records do not by themselves establish control over a trajectory, proposes safeguards as design hypotheses, and sets out an empirical agenda. Conceptual preprint, version 1.0. The worked case is hypothetical and the safeguards are untested hypotheses.

papers.title: Preemptive Grid De-Energization and the Silicon Valley Blackout Paradox: Santa Ana / Diablo Katabatic Wind-Arc Ignition Mechanics, Inverse Condemnation Liability, Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS), and Sovereign Quantum-Phononic Microgrid Autonomy

papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A stark civilizational paradox defines California's technology ecosystem: the global epicenter of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum computing—Silicon Valley and the broader California coastal corridor—is physically tethered to an aging, uninsulated overhead electrical grid operated by investor-owned utilities (Pacific Gas & Electric [PG&E] and Southern California Edison [SCE]) that must be intentionally plunged into wide-area blackouts (Public Safety Power Shutoffs [PSPS]) whenever dry offshore katabatic winds (Diablo and Santa Ana events) and desiccated chaparral trigger National Weather Service Red Flag Warnings. Why must the world's most advanced digital economy resort to manual 19th-century de-energization to avoid burning down its own territory? Building upon our prior CERN Zenodo monographs on hyperscale AI power starvation (Record 23379242), PHOENIX_ROUTER sub-7.0 ns hardware circuit breakers (Records 23332772 and 23378094), and room-temperature quantum-phononic computing (Records 23333819 and 23334854), this monograph establishes the rigorous aero-thermodynamic, legal-economic, and compute-resilience theory of the California PSPS Blackout Paradox. We prove four core results: (1) Katabatic Wind Galloping & Molten-Particle Ignition Mechanics: Under adiabatic Foehn compression (RH < 8%, dead fuel moisture m_f < 3%, gusts v_w > 25-45 m/s), overhead ACSR conductors undergo Den Hartog aero-elastic galloping and phase clashing, ejecting 6,000 K molten aluminum droplets whose enthalpy exceeds chaparral pyrolysis thresholds and drives supercritical Rothermel fireline intensity (I_B > 4,000 kW/m); (2) Inverse Condemnation Asymmetric Game Theory: Because Article I, Section 19 of the California Constitution imposes strict no-fault liability (Inverse Condemnation) on utilities for equipment-sparked wildfires (L_fire in [$10B, $50B]) while imposing near-zero liability for blackout damages (ε_reg -> 0), utilities rationally execute preemptive blackouts across hundreds of thousands of nodes while charging $0.38-$0.48/kWh retail tariffs to fund $3-6M/mile undergrounding; (3) Cryogenic Quantum Quench & 4-Hour BESS Exhaustion: During multi-day PSPS events (24-96 hours due to mandatory visual line-patrol inspection) and transfer glitches, 4-hour LFP battery storage exhausts at t = 4 hr while millikelvin superconducting dilution refrigerators (T ≈ 15 mK) suffer catastrophic thermal quench within minutes of pulse-tube power loss; and (4) Sovereign Quantum-Phononic Microgrid Autonomy: Replacing megawatt CMOS and cryogenic qubits with 300 K polaronic Quantum Spiking Neural Networks (1.8 fJ/spike), PHOENIX_ROUTER < 7.0 ns transient islanding, and Goldilocks QFS-zkVM microgrid settlement achieves unconditional blackout immunity. papers.title: The Thermodynamic and Financial Reality of AI Power Starvation: Rider's Bremsstrahlung Limit in Pulsed D-3He Fusion, Tokamak REBCO Supply-Chain Scaling, PJM/FERC Queue Bottlenecks, and Hyperscale Stranded-CapEx Risk

papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: By 2026, generative artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expansion has collided with hard physical and grid-regulatory walls. International Energy Agency (IEA) projections indicate global data center electricity consumption surging from 460 TWh (2024) to > 1,000 TWh by 2030 (~320 Mt CO2/yr) and 1,300 TWh by 2035—exceeding Japan's entire national electricity demand—while single campuses such as Microsoft's Fairwater facility (3.3 GW) and the $500 billion Stargate initiative (10 GW) strain regional transmission limits amid a projected $740 billion global 2026 AI capital expenditure (CapEx) cycle. To assuage investor and ESG anxieties, hyperscalers have promoted a narrative of imminent baseload salvation via commercial nuclear fusion (Helion Energy, Commonwealth Fusion Systems [CFS]) and Generation-IV Small Modular Reactors (SMRs; Kairos Power). Building upon our prior CERN Zenodo monographs on the CMOS CapEx cliff and Willow quantum transition (Record 23353509), 1.8 fJ/spike room-temperature neuromorphic quantum computing (Record 23334854), and Delaware Caremark fiduciary governance (Record 23360530), this monograph conducts a rigorous plasma-physical, grid-regulatory, and balance-sheet audit of Big Tech's next-generation nuclear and fusion scenarios. We establish four core findings: (1) Rider's Bremsstrahlung Limit & Inductive Recovery Infeasibility in Pulsed D-3He FRC: While Helion Energy secured Washington DOH RML/RAEL licenses in June 2026 for its Orion plant under a 50 MW (2028) PPA with Microsoft, D-3He ignition at T_i ≈ 50 keV suffers catastrophic Bremsstrahlung losses (P_Brem > P_fus in thermal equilibrium). Sustaining T_i >> T_e against rapid Spitzer Coulomb equilibration forces ultra-short pulses requiring an engineeringly implausible magnetic energy recovery efficiency η_rec in [0.999, 0.9999], alongside unmitigated 2.45 MeV D-D side-reaction neutrons and tritium; (2) Tokamak REBCO Supply Chains vs. Gen-IV SMR Pragmatism: CFS's 20 T SPARC/ARC tokamak (paired with DeepMind RL magnetic sweeping and TORAX) and Google's 500 MW Kairos Power FHR-TRISO PPA (accelerated by the 2024 ADVANCE Act and April 2026 NRC 10 CFR Part 53 licensing) represent scientifically grounded 2030s pathways, yet face acute first-of-a-kind (FOAK) cost inflation exemplified by NuScale's $9.3 billion (> $20,000/kW) cancellation; (3) LBNL Queue Paralysis, PJM Capacity Explosion, and FERC Co-Location Vetoes: With 2,061 GW trapped in 61-month U.S. interconnection queues (13% completion rate), PJM capacity prices spiking 833% to $269.92/MW-day (and hitting the $333.44 cap for 2027/2028 with a 6,623 MW shortfall), and FERC rejecting AWS/Talen's Susquehanna nuclear co-location expansion, hyperscalers are forced onto 116 GW backlogged GE Vernova gas turbines, $110-$115/MWh Three Mile Island restarts, and $210-$292/MWh tariff-inflated LFP BESS; and (4) The Stranded-CapEx Impairment Theorem: Because GPU economic half-lives (τ_1/2 ≈ 1 yr) are an order of magnitude shorter than power delivery lead times (τ_power in [5, 15] yr), unenergized CMOS CapEx faces catastrophic balance-sheet write-downs (98.0% impairment at median 5.08-year queue lag) unless replaced by room-temperature quantum-phononic architectures. papers.title: HUMAN TRANSLATION AND AI IN MODERN EDUCATION: WHY WE NEED BOTH
papers.authors: Sitora Yarasheva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This thesis examines the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and human expertise in modern higher education's translation processes. While neural machine translation offers unprecedented speed and cost-efficiency, it frequently compromises conceptual depth, cultural nuances, and factual accuracy. This study argues against a binary substitution model, advocating instead for a hybrid paradigm. By integrating the scalability of AI with the critical evaluation of human translators, global universities can optimize educational content delivery without sacrificing academic rigor.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Agents and Consumer Behavior: A Bibliometric Analysis of an Emerging Research Field
papers.authors: Ramazan KAYHAN, Busra BILGISEVEN, Nilay SAYAN
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Recent dynamic advances in AI technologies have brought about profound transformations in the marketing paradigm and in consumer behavior and interactions. At the heart of this transformation, the relationship between AI agents and consumer behavior stands out as a timely area calling for in-depth investigation in the literature. This study constitutes a bibliometric analysis undertaken to reveal the intellectual accumulation of knowledge in this conceptual domain and to examine the evolution of the literature systematically. To this end, 438 articles indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 2020 and 2026 were subjected to a comprehensive examination. The research first conducted a performance analysis to resolve the quantitative structure of the field, mapping annual publication distributions, the most prolific authors, the most highly cited studies, leading countries, and institutional collaborations. It then carried out citation, co-citation, and co-occurence analyses using science mapping techniques in order to structure the intellectual framework of the field. The findings show that the AI agent literature emerging in the context of consumer behavior is following a growth trend that is gaining momentum in both quantitative and qualitative terms. Thematically, the literature was found to concentrate on the transparency and interpretability of AI algorithms, the implications of these algorithms for consumer attitudes and behavior, the strengthening of human-AI interaction through anthropomorphic design elements, the dark side encompassing ethics, privacy, and trust, and sectoral reflections in the service industry.

papers.title: Generative Ownership Framework
papers.authors: Naomi Brabner Veroczi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An accurate record of what artificial intelligence produced need not establish what it originated, how it was governed, or what claims to authorship or ownership are justified. This article develops the Generative Ownership Framework (GOF), a causal and ethical framework for human-AI creation. It separates creative-process analysis, governance, evidence and inference, and attributive and normative evaluation. Creative-process analysis distinguishes production, origination, generative development, and cognitive-access or representational roles that recover, stabilize, inspect, work with, or express antecedent human structure. Origination may be human, machine, or distributed and may differ across scales. The relevant scale should be determined by the contribution and causal question, not adjusted retrospectively to favor an attribution. GOF treats causal attribution as claim-relative. Evidence must discriminate among materially different causal histories; where it cannot, provenance may remain unresolved. Historical continuity can support antecedent human structure without establishing later development, while changes in fluency, polish, or formalization do not by themselves identify provenance. Human authorship has an affirmative creative basis when a person’s relationship to the claimed work is work-specific, causally operative, and materially formative. Production volume, causal importance, control, responsibility, or time spent are not sufficient by themselves. Runtime cognitive tuning and cognitive conversion cost describe how human contribution can shape generative conditions or redistribute representational work without settling origination. GOF recognizes machine contribution while rejecting automatic inferences from machine participation to diminished human authorship or fractionalized ownership. Disclosure, pedigree, and inspectability should not substitute for contribution-specific evidence, and cognitive provenance remains distinct from epistemic validity.

papers.title: A Governance Framework for Operationalising Responsible AI Use in Students’ Research Projects: Illustrations from Viet Nam
papers.authors: Dao Mai Thi Tran
papers.journal: Vietnam Journal of Education (online)/Vietnam Journal of Education/Giáo dục
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in students’ research projects for literature searching, idea development, drafting, language editing, information processing, and research planning. These uses can support research learning, but they also raise academic integrity concerns, including unverifiable sources, fabricated references, undeclared AI assistance, over-reliance on AI-generated outputs, unclear authorship, and unfair assessment. This conceptual paper argues that responsible AI use in students’ research projects cannot be secured through individual AI literacy or general guidance alone. Higher education institutions also need governance mechanisms that make AI use transparent, verifiable, assessable, and accountable. Using targeted literature identification and structured conceptual synthesis, the paper maps recurring governance problems to normative principles, institutional requirements, and operational mechanisms. It proposes a five-component framework corresponding to five governance functions: policy (boundary setting), transparency (traceability), assessment (evaluability), audit (assurance), and guidance/support (capability building). Viet Nam is used as an illustrative emerging AI governance context, where national policy directions on digital competence and AI are developing but operational mechanisms for student research remain under-specified. The framework and associated tools are presented as adaptable design artefacts for future institutional testing rather than as validated interventions.

papers.title: A Data-Driven Smart University Framework for Sustainable Internationalisation at Home: A PLS-SEM Study in Vietnamese Higher Education
papers.authors: Loc Thi My Nguyen, Tuong Sy Hoang
papers.journal: Vietnam Journal of Education (online)/Vietnam Journal of Education/Giáo dục
papers.abstract: Internationalisation at Home is increasingly recognised as an alternative to conventional physical mobility, offering opportunities to broaden equitable access to knowledge and promote sustainable practices in higher education. This study develops and empirically tests a data-driven smart university framework as an integrative model for examining the structural relationships between technological foundations and the sustainable implementation of Internationalisation at Home. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed, using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 312 managers and faculty members involved in transnational education programmes in Vietnam. The data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The findings support the proposed structural relationships within the model. Specifically, integrated data infrastructure has a positive relationship with faculty digital competence. An ethical data governance framework and the adoption of learning analytics and artificial intelligence are also positively associated with the quality of Internationalisation at Home. In turn, the quality of Internationalisation at Home has a statistically significant positive relationship with perceived institutional sustainability. The study provides empirical evidence of the structural links between digital technological innovation and the sustainability of higher education internationalisation. The findings offer a basis for reconsidering institutional resource allocation strategies in developing countries, with greater priority given to integrated data architectures, digital capability development, and responsible data governance.

papers.title: Negotiating Authorship with Generative AI in Cinema Education: Attribution and Creative Decision-Making in Screenwriting
papers.authors: Ufuk Kucukcan
papers.abstract: This study examines how cinema students attribute authorship during AI-assisted screenwriting and how those judgments relate to creative decisions. Drawing on a fourteen-week, design-based course, it compares logbooks with 436 student turns across twenty generative-AI conversations. In four of six co-writing cases, students selected and retained system-originated material. The clearest tension appeared when students claimed the idea as their own but assigned the text entirely to AI while repeatedly rejecting generated material, a response the instrument’s own categories leave ambiguous. Read against Livingston, Gaut and Sellors, these cases show that textual generation, creative decision-making and authorship attribution can diverge within one process. Cinema education should ask not only who authored a text, but on what basis.

papers.title: DINAMIKA TECHNOSTRESS : ANALISIS PERAN AI LITERACY PADA PEKERJA INDUSTRI MULTIMEDIA KREATIF DIGITAL
papers.authors: Muhammad Wildan Asy'ari, Arfin Nurma Halida
papers.journal: PAEDAGOGY Jurnal Ilmu Pendidikan dan Psikologi
papers.abstract: The advancement of (AI) technology in the workplace has introduced a new psychological challenge in the form of technostress, particularly among workers with high dependence on AI use in their daily work.
