The review finds that effective governance of AI requires coordinated multi-stakeholder frameworks that include political oversight, responsible business practices, equitable healthcare policy, and resilient infrastructure planning. Future research should explore comparative cross-national governance models and longitudinal assessments of AI’s socioeconomic and infrastructural impact.

papers.title: AI Adoption and the Digital Divide in Colombia’s Third Sector: Unintended Consequences, Organizational Readiness, and Ethical Tensions
papers.authors: Sara Calvo, Andrés Morales
papers.journal: Canadian journal of nonprofit and social economy research
papers.abstract: This study examines the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in Colombia’s third sector through a mixed-methods study of 104 survey respondents and 20 semi-structured interviews. Findings reveal uneven, largely incremental, task-oriented adoption, constrained by infrastructure, digital skills, governance capacity, and institutional support. While AI offers opportunities for efficiency, communication, and resource optimization, concerns remain around privacy, misinformation, technological dependency, and the erosion of human-centred practice. Drawing on theories of the digital divide, organizational readiness, and unintended consequences, the study conceptualizes AI as both a stratifying and moral technology, highlighting the need for context-sensitive governance, capability building, and equitable institutional support.

papers.title: Operationalizing AI Governance for Defense SMEs: A Modular, Generative-AI-Assisted Framework for NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC Compliance
papers.authors: Rizwan Virani
papers.abstract: This praxis investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) governance can be integrated into the cybersecurity compliance workflows of United States defense small and mid-sized enterprises (SMEs). These firms are navigating the transition to the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) 2.0 program and the foundational requirements of National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP) 800-171. Existing AI risk guidance, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), does not provide implementation-focused direction suited to the resource constraints of smaller firms. This praxis therefore describes a control mapping method consistent with the overlay logic of NIST's Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAIS) concept paper. It uses that method to develop the Modular AI Governance Framework (MAGF), a "comply once, satisfy many" governance framework and toolkit. My research uses a convergent mixed-methods design guided by five research questions. Four ask how practitioners map AI risk categories to control families, which families they identify most often, how feasible they judge lightweight governance artifacts to be, and what barriers and enablers shape implementation. The fifth asks to what extent the resulting framework is practical, scalable, and audit-aligned. In the first phase, 38 practitioners mapped six AI risk categories onto the 14 NIST SP 800-171 control families through a structured survey. They prioritized "auditability gaps" in data integrity and model transparency, yet many reported lacking the specialized staff to document these areas manually. Qualitative analysis of their open-ended responses produced eight empirically grounded design requirements, including control family anchoring, traceability-first evidence, change control for probabilistic systems, and a dual-purpose evidence pattern. Inspired by operational "playbooks," the MAGF defines governance tasks as structured modules with goals, actions, and lightweight evidence artifacts. The modules model the work already required in defense cybersecurity and span the AI lifecycle from initiation and data collection to production deployment and monitoring. A prompt library provides engineered prompts for generative AI chatbot tools like Google's Gemini and Microsoft's Copilot to support human-reviewed drafting of artifacts such as bias assessment records and model/prompt change logs. No output of that prompt library was evaluated in this study. I evaluated the framework through a structured expert review rather than a measured field deployment. A panel of 13 qualified reviewers, six of whom identified primarily as assessors, rated the framework and its artifacts against defined criteria. The results were encouraging but bounded. Reviewers judged the framework relevant, clear, and valuable as assessment evidence. Their reservations centered on the feasibility of the most measurement-intensive artifacts for the smallest firms. Only 30.8% of reviewers were favorable on scalability, which marks the boundary of what this study establishes. An illustrative estimate anchored to published federal compliance cost figures and peer-reviewed evidence on generative writing productivity suggests a meaningful reduction in recurring drafting effort while human review remains constant. The estimate is not a measurement, and it does not assert that any requirement or practice is satisfied. It also shows that careful coordination is needed to keep documentation bloat and fatigue from eroding the benefit and slowing certification. This praxis contributes a method for compliance-aligned and resource-optimized AI governance design and applies it to build an integrated toolkit for defense SMEs. Future work can examine the generative AI assistance in greater detail and apply the framework to other emerging regulatory environments. The method offers a replicable template for integrating emerging technologies into highly regulated and risk-averse operations, helping small firms remain competitive while safeguarding national security.

papers.title: Assessment Validity in Security Programming in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: John C. Mace
papers.abstract: The widespread availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools capable of producing syntactically correct and functionally plausible code is reshaping programming practice in higher education. While these systems offer potential benefits for learning support and productivity, they also challenge established assumptions underpinning programming assessment. In particular, the validity of artefact-centric evaluation becomes uncertain when students can generate high-quality solutions with limited engagement in the reasoning processes that assessments are intended to measure. This paper advances a conceptual analysis of how generative AI disrupts assessment validity in security programming education. Drawing on theories of construct validity and assessment inference, the paper examines how GenAI weakens the evidential relationship between submitted code artefacts and underlying learner competence. These challenges are especially acute in security programming, where competence extends beyond functional correctness to encompass judgement, adversarial reasoning, and context-sensitive evaluation. In AI-mediated contexts, assessments that prioritise implementation quality may risk measuring the appearance of competence rather than the development of security reasoning. The analysis highlights key threats to validity, including incomplete representation of security reasoning, distortion from AI-related factors, ambiguity in interpreting performance, and the risk of illusory progress. In response, this paper outlines implications for assessment design, emphasising approaches that elicit reasoning, critique, and evaluative judgement more directly. Finally, the paper proposes a research agenda to support empirical investigation of validity, learner behaviour, and AI-aware assessment ecologies. By foregrounding validity as a central concern, this paper contributes to emerging debates on generative AI in computing education and highlights the need to reconsider how competence is evidenced and evaluated in AI-integrated learning environments.

papers.title: Teachers' Perceptions of Students' Use of GenAI in Assessments
papers.authors: Y Zhang, JK Wang, Lei Shi, P Bem-Haja, M Lucas
papers.abstract: The emergence of Generative AI (GenAI) in education has led to growing concerns about its use by students to complete assessment tasks. Distinguishing between content that has been genuinely produced by students and content that has been generated by GenAI poses new challenges to teachers. This study explores K-12 teachers’ perceptions of students’ use of GenAI in assessments. It uses text mining techniques and AI-driven topic modelling to analyse posts from 191 teachers in a discussion forum created as part of an online course. The results show that while teachers generally support students’ use of GenAI in assessments, most advocate for its use under specific conditions. Regardless of their initial position, teachers consistently emphasise the need for professional training and support. Several key measures emerge across different positions, such as encourage critical thinking and authentic work, implement monitoring and supervision, establish guidelines and policies, educate on ethics and responsibility, raise AI understanding and awareness and innovate assessment methods. As teachers move from a neutral position to a more proactive engagement with AI, four additional strategies become evident: promote student ownership and collaboration, ensure access to equality and transparency, protect data and privacy, and prioritise the humanistic aspect. In summary, this study provides practical insights into the integration of GenAI in K-12 education and offers guidance for transforming assessment practices.

papers.title: Exploring Differences in GenAI Acceptance and Use in Saudi and UK Universities
papers.authors: Abeer Aziz, Ahmed Kharrufa, Lei Shi
papers.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) tools like ChatGPT and Copilot become increasingly integrated into educational settings, their impact on the academic community remains an open field for investigation. This study explores the adoption and acceptance of GenAI among university instructors and students in Saudi Arabia and the UK, offering insights into how educational cultural contexts shape usage patterns. Using a GenAI-adapted version of the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), we examine key factors influencing acceptance and adoption. Findings reveal significant differences between Saudi and UK participants: for students, Performance Expectancy, Learning Value, and Habit emerged as key differentiators, while for instructors, Social In- fluence, Habit and Trust played a more prominent role. This study con- tributes to the growing discourse on GenAI in education by providing empirical insights into the complex dynamics of GenAI adoption, offer- ing implications for instructional design, policymaking, and AI-driven professional development for educators and students.GenAI, UTAUT2, Culture, Education, UK, Saudi Arabia

papers.title: QUALITY OF HIGHER EDUCATION IN INDIA: CHALLENGES, OPPORTUNITIES AND FUTURE PERSPECTIVES
papers.authors: Anand Katare, Indravesh Arya, Kamlesh Yadav
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Higher education plays a pivotal role in shaping a nation's economic growth, technological advancement, and social development. India possesses one of the world's largest higher education systems, comprising over one thousand universities and thousands of colleges that collectively educate millions of students annually. Despite significant expansion in institutional capacity and enrolment over the past two decades, maintaining quality remains a major concern. Challenges such as inadequate infrastructure, faculty shortages, disparities in access, limited research productivity, employability gaps, insufficient industry-academia collaboration, governance issues, and unequal digital access continue to impede the realization of globally competitive higher education. Simultaneously, transformative initiatives including the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, digital learning platforms, research funding reforms, international collaborations, multidisciplinary education, and the integration of artificial intelligence present unprecedented opportunities for systemic improvement. This review critically examines the current status of higher education quality in India by synthesizing evidence from government reports, policy documents, and contemporary scholarly literature. The paper discusses the multidimensional challenges affecting educational quality and evaluates emerging opportunities driven by technological innovation, quality assurance mechanisms, competency-based curricula, and global academic partnerships. Furthermore, it proposes strategic recommendations to strengthen governance, faculty development, research ecosystems, institutional autonomy, accreditation, digital transformation, and employability. The study concludes that achieving sustainable excellence in higher education requires coordinated efforts among policymakers, regulatory agencies, academic institutions, industry, and society. A learner-centric, technology-enabled, research-oriented, and globally connected higher education system will be fundamental to realizing India's vision of becoming a global knowledge economy by 2047.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Joint Protection Education on Knowledge and Intensity of Pain Among Elderly with Joint Pain in Selected Old-Age Homes, Bengaluru
papers.authors: Ranita Samaddar, Malathi Kota, Routh Boyle
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Joint pain is one of the most common musculoskeletal problems among elderly individuals and significantly affects mobility, functional independence, and quality of life. Elderly residents of old-age homes often have inadequate knowledge of joint protection techniques and non-pharmacological pain management strategies. Educational interventions focusing on joint protection and range-of-motion (ROM) exercises may play a key role in improving self-management and reducing pain intensity among this population. Objectives: To assess the level of knowledge regarding joint protection among elderly with joint pain; to assess the intensity of joint pain before and after joint protection education; to evaluate the effectiveness of joint protection education on knowledge and pain intensity; and to determine the association between knowledge and pain intensity with selected sociodemographic variables. Materials and Methods: A pre-experimental one-group pre-test–post-test design was adopted. Fifty elderly individuals (≥65 years) with self-reported joint pain residing in selected old-age homes in Bengaluru were selected using nonprobability convenience sampling. Sociodemographic data were collected using a structured proforma. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), and knowledge regarding joint protection was measured using a structured 39-item Joint Protection Knowledge Questionnaire. Participants received a single 30-minute joint protection education session (lecture-cum-demonstration) followed by demonstration and supervised practice of ROM exercises for major joints for 14 consecutive days. Post-test knowledge and pain scores were obtained after two weeks. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired t-test, chi-square test, and Fisher’s exact test. Results: All participants (100%) had inadequate knowledge of joint protection in the pre-test. Following the intervention, 60% attained adequate knowledge and 40% had moderate knowledge. Pre-intervention, 68% of participants reported moderate pain and 32% reported severe pain; post-intervention, 56% reported mild pain and 44% reported moderate pain, with no severe pain. The mean pain score reduced from 6.10 ± 0.735 (pre-test) to 3.38 ± 0.667 (post-test) (t = 20.755, p < 0.001). The mean knowledge score increased from 34.60 ± 3.301 to 68.20 ± 5.264 (t = 41.295, p < 0.001). A significant association was found between pre-test pain level and age (p = 0.035), and between post-test knowledge level and BMI (p = 0.033) and history of taking painkillers in the past (p = 0.046). No other sociodemographic variables showed significant association with pain or knowledge levels. Conclusion: Joint protection education, combined with supervised ROM exercises, was effective in significantly improving knowledge and reducing pain intensity among elderly individuals with joint pain residing in old-age homes. The intervention represents a simple, safe, and cost-effective non-pharmacological strategy that can be integrated into geriatric nursing practice to promote self-management and enhance quality of life in elderly populations. Pain intensity was assessed using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), and knowledge regarding joint protection was measured using a structured 39-item Joint Protection Knowledge Questionnaire. Participants received a single 30-minute joint protection education session (lecture-cum-demonstration) followed by demonstration and supervised practice of ROM exercises for major joints for 14 consecutive days. Post-test knowledge and pain scores were obtained after two weeks. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired t-test, chi-square test, and Fisher’s exact test. Results: All participants (100%) had inadequate knowledge of joint protection in the pre-test. Following the intervention, 60% attained adequate knowledge and 40% had moderate knowledge. Pre-intervention, 68% of participants reported moderate pain and 32% reported severe pain; post-intervention, 56% reported mild pain and 44% reported moderate pain, with no severe pain. The mean pain score reduced from 6.10 ± 0.735 (pre-test) to 3.38 ± 0.667 (post-test) (t = 20.755, p < 0.001). The mean knowledge score increased from 34.60 ± 3.301 to 68.20 ± 5.264 (t = 41.295, p < 0.001). A significant association was found between pre-test pain level and age (p = 0.035), and between post-test knowledge level and BMI (p = 0.033) and history of taking painkillers in the past (p = 0.046). No other sociodemographic variables showed significant association with pain or knowledge levels. Conclusion: Joint protection education, combined with supervised ROM exercises, was effective in significantly improving knowledge and reducing pain intensity among elderly individuals with joint pain residing in old-age homes. The intervention represents a simple, safe, and cost-effective non-pharmacological strategy that can be integrated into geriatric nursing practice to promote self-management and enhance quality of life in elderly populations.

papers.title: Digital Transformation in Hospital Pharmacy Services: Effects on Team Performance
papers.authors: Abdulhakeem Mohammed Alshehri, Abdulkarim Abdulrahman Alshehri, Abdullah Ahmed Asiri, Hani Shahir Lafaf Alshammari, Abdulaziz Abdulrahman Alotaibi, Khaled Nasser Almoteri, Nashmi Melfi Mansor Aldafeeri, Abdulaziz Jazaa Sheleweh Alanzi
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has become a fundamental driver of healthcare innovation, particularly within hospital pharmacy services. Technologies such as electronic prescribing, barcode medication administration (BCMA), automated dispensing cabinets (ADCs), robotic dispensing systems, artificial intelligence (AI), clinical decision support systems (CDSS), and integrated pharmacy information systems have significantly reshaped pharmacy workflows. These innovations enhance medication safety, improve operational efficiency, and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. This review examines the influence of digital transformation on hospital pharmacy team performance, emphasizing productivity, communication, medication safety, workload distribution, and patient outcomes. Current evidence indicates that digital technologies reduce medication errors, increase dispensing accuracy, optimize inventory management, and improve staff satisfaction. Nevertheless, implementation challenges— including high costs, cybersecurity risks, resistance to organizational change, and training requirements—remain barriers to widespread adoption. Successful digital transformation requires strategic planning, continuous workforce education, leadership commitment, and robust evaluation metrics.

papers.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT for Myocardial Infarction Health Information: Expert Accuracy Assessment and User Trust Survey
papers.authors: Eman Elsheikh, Abdullah Ahmed Aladsani, Yousef Abdullatif Aljohar, Ghala Abdulaziz Alzahrani, Ali Mohammed Nasser Alsadah, Maryam Ahmed Almuhaysh, Walah Sami Rashid alowaynan, Rehab H. Werida
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence chatbots, particularly ChatGPT, have emerged as increasingly popular sources of health information for the general public. However, concerns persist regarding the accuracy, safety, and appropriateness of AI-generated medical advice, especially for life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction. Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, completeness, and safety of ChatGPT-generated responses and information to public questions about heart attacks, assess user perceptions and trust, and compare AI-generated content with expert-validated sources. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between January and March 2026. A total of 73 commonly asked heart attack-related questions were submitted to ChatGPT (GPT-4), and responses were independently evaluated by two expert reviewers and one external reviewer using standardized rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, clarity, safety, and tone. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients. In parallel, a survey of 352 participants evaluated user perceptions, trust, and behavioral use of ChatGPT for medical information. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlation analyses, and multivariable regression models to identify predictors of trust and satisfaction. Results: Expert reviewers assigned high ratings for accuracy (mean: 4.62 ± 0.62 and 4.48 ± 0.63) and safety (mean: 4.78 ± 0.51 and 4.05 ± 0.50), with substantial inter-rater agreement (ICC = 0.788). In contrast, the external reviewer documented considerably lower completeness ratings (2.59 ± 0.57), revealing deficiencies in information coverage. Remarkably, 40.6% of respondents indicated they had followed ChatGPT's medical recommendations without seeking professional consultation, while 17.6% reported depending on the chatbot during urgent medical situations. Levels of user trust and satisfaction were moderate, showing significant correlations with perceived accuracy, usage frequency, and healthcare-related educational background. Conclusions: Expert assessments confirmed that ChatGPT generally provides accurate and safe cardiovascular health information; nevertheless, considerable inter-reviewer variability—especially the markedly lower completeness scores from the external evaluator—reveals significant gaps in content depth. These results indicate that ChatGPT functions more appropriately as an adjunctive educational resource rather than a replacement for professional medical consultation, emphasizing the necessity for enhanced safety mechanisms, clearer user instructions, and standardized content protocols when addressing high-stakes health topics. ChatGPT should be considered an adjunctive resource rather than a substitute for urgent professional medical assessment in suspected heart attack cases.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND NURSING DECISION MAKING
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a change agent in healthcare and promises to change clinical decision-making opportunities.AI can be used in nursing to increase efficiency, minimize human error, and support evidence-based practice, among other things.Nevertheless, the attitudes, awareness, and desire of nurses to implement AI are still crucial prerequisites to effective integration into clinical processes.Purpose: This research targeted the awareness, perceived advantages, difficulties, and attitudes of nurses to AI as a decision-making tool and determined the reliability and validity of the tool applied.To add to that, the research has also investigated the effects of demographic characteristics like gender, education, and workplace on perceptions and readiness to embrace AI.Methods: A cross-sectional survey design was used, where 237 nurses in 9 hospitals, clinics, community care, and academic institutions were surveyed to gather data.The Likert scale questions (Q620) included in the structured type of questionnaire were demographic data.We used statistical analysis, which is the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, Cronbach's Alpha reliability, KMO, and Bartlett test of validity, independent sampling t-test, one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, Chi-square test, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis.Findings: The data were normally distributed (p > 0.05), and the reliability (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.92) was excellent, as well as the validity (KMO = 0.82; Bartlett's p = 0.001).Cross-group comparisons demonstrated that there was a high level of difference by gender, education, and workplace, and the chi-square analysis indicated that education and AI training were strongly correlated.Pearson correlation also revealed positive relationships between all items in the questionnaire, which showed that there was coherence between awareness, perceived benefits, and adoption.Regression analysis found awareness and understanding to have a strong positive influence on willingness to adopt AI, with age playing a positive but insignificant role.Conclusion: The research concludes that the willingness of nurses to embrace AI is majorly dependent on their awareness and knowledge of the technology, with the educational and workplace context

papers.title: The Importance of Electronic Communication in the Use of Artificial Intelligence Programs and Applications in the Field of Smart Agriculture from the Point of View of Agricultural Extension Workers in Nineveh Governorate, Iraq
papers.authors: Luma Monther Adress
papers.journal: International Journal of Environmental and Agriculture Research
papers.abstract: The study aimed to identify the level of importance of electronic communication among agricultural extension workers in using artificial intelligence (AI) programs and applications in the field of smart agriculture. It also aimed to identify the most frequently used electronic communication means by extension workers in employing AI programs and applications and rank them according to their relative importance; measure the contribution of electronic communication to improving extension workers' efficiency in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture; identify individual differences in the importance of electronic communication and the use of AI applications according to selected independent variables, namely gender, educational qualification, years of service, training courses, level of Internet use, and willingness to use social networking sites concerning smart-agriculture technologies; and identify the obstacles facing extension workers in using AI applications in smart agriculture. To obtain the study data, a questionnaire consisting of five parts was used. The first part concerned the respondents' personal and occupational information. The second part included a scale measuring the importance of electronic communication among extension workers in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture. The third part measured the electronic communication means most frequently used by extension workers in employing AI programs and applications. The fourth part measured the contribution of electronic communication to improving extension workers' efficiency in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture. The fifth part contained 15 items measuring the major obstacles facing extension workers in using AI applications in smart agriculture. After establishing the face validity of the questionnaire, reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, which reached 0.95. The study population consisted of extension workers in the Nineveh Directorate of Agriculture and its 32 agricultural divisions, totaling 256 extension workers. A simple random sample of 128 extension workers, representing approximately 50% of the population, was selected. The data were coded, tabulated, and analyzed using SPSS. The results showed that the level of importance of electronic communication among extension workers in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture was moderate and tended toward high, with a percentage of 48%. The item "Using electronic platforms belonging to agricultural institutions to obtain information related to AI programs and applications" ranked first, with a mean of 4.34. The contribution of electronic communication to improving extension workers' efficiency in using AI programs and applications in smart agriculture was high, with a percentage of 46%. No significant differences were found in the importance of electronic communication according to gender or training courses, whereas significant differences were reported according to educational qualification, years of occupational service, level of Internet use, and willingness to use social networking sites concerning smart-agriculture technologies. The item "Poor compatibility of some AI applications with the nature and needs of agricultural extension work in Nineveh Governorate" was identified as the most important obstacle. The major recommendation was for the Ministry of Agriculture to establish or develop official agricultural electronic platforms affiliated with agricultural and extension institutions and containing updated information on AI applications and their use in different agricultural fields. The main proposed future study was to investigate the obstacles to using AI applications in agricultural extension work in Nineveh Governorate from the perspective of extension workers.

papers.title: Влияние искусственного интеллекта на результаты деятельности фирмы: систематический обзор литературы
papers.authors: Дарья Павловна Степанюк, Олеся Олеговна Ярыга
papers.journal: Известия Дальневосточного федерального университета. Экономика и управление
papers.abstract: This article presents a systematic review of contemporary empirical studies dedicated to examining the impact of artificial intelligence on firm performance. The review findings demonstrate that the influence of artificial intelligence on firm activities is not a direct cause-and-effect relationship but rather constitutes a complex system mediated by organizational capabilities, dynamic capabilities, and contextual factors. Based on the conducted analysis, a conceptual model is proposed, illustrating the interrelationship between formative factors, such as technological, organizational, and external ones, artificial intelligence technologies, and firm performance outcomes, including operational, financial, strategic, and sustainability indicators. The article emphasizes the necessity of transitioning from a narrow technical approach to implementing artificial intelligence technologies to a comprehensive approach that views AI adoption as a complex organizational transformation process, and it identifies promising directions for future research, in particular, exploring the specifics of AI implementation within the Russian business context among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

papers.title: AI-Assisted Mathematics Learning: Jeneponto Salt Production Ethnomathematics And Junior High Students' Problem-Solving Ability
papers.authors: Syaharuddina Syaharuddina, Sumiati Sumiati, Nurqiyamah Hamid, Hasmawati Hasmawati, Muh. Usman Taufik, Adryan Putra Pratama
papers.abstract: Mathematical problem-solving ability among junior high school students remains a challenge in mathematics learning, while the integration of artificial intelligence with local cultural contexts has received limited attention when examined simultaneously. This study aimed to analyze the improvement in the mathematical problem-solving ability of ninth-grade students through Problem-Based Learning (PBL) assisted by an AI chatbot in the context of salt-production ethnomathematics in Jeneponto, both overall and at each problem-solving stage. The study employed a quantitative approach with a one-group pretest–posttest design involving 30 ninth-grade students from a junior high school in Jeneponto Regency who were selected purposively. Mathematical problem-solving ability was measured using an ethnomathematics-based contextual essay test and analyzed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, paired-samples t-test, Cohen's dz, and N-Gain. The mean score increased from 33.13 on the pretest to 80.80 on the posttest. This increase was statistically significant, t(29) = 17.419, p < .001, with a very large effect size (Cohen's dz = 3.18). The N-Gain of 0.707 indicated a high level of improvement. Analysis by problem-solving stage showed improvement across all indicators, with the largest absolute increase occurring at the carrying out the solution stage (D3), followed by the checking the result stage (D4). The findings indicate that the integration of PBL, AI chatbot support, and salt-production ethnomathematics has the potential to support contextual mathematics learning and the development of students' problem-solving ability.

papers.title: Beyond the Algorithmic Scriptor: Generative AI, Reader Interpretation, and the Limits of Barthes’s "Death of the Author"
papers.authors: Kunal UpadhyayG., Dr. Nisha Khan
papers.abstract: Roland Barthes argued that author’s identity and intentions are less important in any text, suggesting that the actual literary meaning is created by the reader of the text. Generative Artificial intelligence (AI) makes Barthes’s concept of "Death of the Author" a reality, by producing brilliant as well as complex prose without biological subjectivity, or human creative intent. However, contemporary literary studies have mainly focused on computational mechanics, disputes regarding copyrights, and stylistic mimicry. This creates a crucial research gap in understanding that how human mind or reader hermeneutics work when the author of the text is a non- human element and is algorithmic. This study addresses this critical theoretical omission. Main objectives of the research include examining how algorithmic generation challenges traditional human written texts, evaluation of the reader’s reaction to authorial absence, and finally, exploration of the fact that why readers are used to ask who or what controls the discourse. Grounded in in post-structuralist critique, this paper focuses on re-evaluation of Barthesian reader-response theory with computational textuality. The findings indicates that readers find it difficult to interpret the text completely due to absence of actual human author or the intention behind it. They naturally look for meanings, purpose, or intention to guide their interpretation. AI shows that readers still expect a human intention behind every text they read, suggesting that meaningful literary interpretation depends upon the connection between reader and the author. People still lack empathy, sympathy and connection towards AI generated works.

papers.title: EVALUATION OF METABOLIC PARAMETERS AND BODY COMPOSITION IN ADOLESCENTS WITH VARIOUS DEGREES OF OBESITY USING BIOELECTRICAL IMPEDANCE ANALYSIS
papers.authors: М.О. Ryznychuk, Т.М. Malinovska
papers.abstract: The rapid rise in the prevalence of obesity among children and adolescents has emerged as one of the most critical challenges in modern pediatrics and pediatric endocrinology. Consequently, implementing highly accurate, non-invasive methods to evaluate body composition – specifically multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis (InBody technology) – is of paramount clinical relevance. The aim – to analyze in detail metabolic parameters and body composition in adolescents aged 11-16 with hypothalamic dysfunction (HD) and varying degrees of obesity, using InBody technology. Materials and methods. The study evaluated 63 children with hypothalamic dysfunction aged 11-16 (mean age: 14.5±1.8 years). The primary group comprised 42 overweight and obese adolescents (21 boys, 21 girls). The control group consisted of 21 healthy peers with normal BMI (11 boys, 10 girls). Inclusion criteria: presence of signed informed consent, verified diagnosis of hypothalamic dysfunction with overweight or obesity or confirmed normal weight (for the control group),as well as the absence of any acute inflammatory or infectious diseases for at least the last month. Exclusion criteria: severe comorbid somatic diseases in stages of subcompensation or decompensation; use of medications with a direct impact on metabolism or water-salt balance (e.g., systemic steroids or diuretics); and presence of metal implants or pacemakers, which represent absolute contraindications for bioelectrical impedance analysis. Body composition was assessed by bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) on an InBody analyzer following a standard morning fasting protocol. The evaluated parameters included total body water (TBW), protein mass, mineral mass, skeletal muscle mass (SMM), fat mass (BFM), percent body fat (PBF), extracellular water-to-total body water ratio (ECW/TBW), and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR). Statistical processing and correlation analyses (Pearson and Spearman) were performed using Statistica and Excel.The study protocol was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of the participating institution (No. 48/6-KE dated March 25, 2024) . The Biomedical Ethics Commission of the State Institution "V.P. Komisarenko Institute of Endocrinology and Metabolism of the National Academy of Medical Sciences of Ukraine" found no violations of moral or legal standards during the study. Informed consent was obtained from all participants and their parents. Results and discussion. Bioelectrical impedance analysis revealed a profound structural and metabolic reorganization of the body as obesity progressed. The dominant pathological process was intensive fat accumulation: body fat mass rose more than 5-fold from 12.36±5.15 kg in controls to 64.04 ±8.26 kg in patients with BMI > 40.0 kg/m2 (p < 0.01). Concurrently, percent body fat in the morbidly obese group reached 49.86 ± 2.90%, demonstrating that adipose tissue accounted for nearly half of the patient's total body weight. During the overweight stage and class I–II obesity, the adolescent body successfully adapted to the increased mechanical load by compensatorily increasing skeletal muscle mass (from 24.66 ±7.07 kg to 31.21 ±5.45 kg, p < 0.05), protein mass (from 8.85 ±2.37 kg to 11.36 ±1.79 kg, p < 0.05), and bone mineralization in response to weight-bearing stress. Correlation analysis confirmed moderate positive correlations between skeletal muscle mass, protein, and waist-to-hip ratio (r = +0.63 to +0.65) in these cohorts. However, once the BMI exceeded the 35.0-40.0 kg/m2 threshold, adaptive mechanisms and anabolic reserves became depleted. In the morbidly obese group, the correlation between BMI and fat-free mass parameters became negative: a moderate inverse correlation was observed between BMI and muscle mass (r = -0.46), protein (r = -0.44), and minerals (r = -0.56). Key insights were also gained from analyzing fluid compartments. The fluid distribution index (ECW/TBW) remained stable across all groups at 0.37-0.38, indicating that genetically determined water-salt balance regulation remains intact. Conclusions: The primary pathological driver of elevated BMI in children and adolescents is progressive lipophilia accompanied by an abdominal fat distribution pattern (WHR>1.0), establishing early risk factors for insulin resistance and cardiometabolic syndrome. The response of fat-free tissues to excess weight is biphasic: an initial phase of physiological compensatory hypertrophy of the muscular and skeletal systems (at BMI < 35.0 kg/m2) is followed by a phase of decompensation and the development of sarcopenic obesity (at BMI > 40.0 kg/m2). These findings highlight the clinical necessity of incorporating multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis (InBody testing) into standard diagnostic protocols for pediatric overweight and obesity.

papers.title: Die Förderung von Critical Digital Literacy im Englischunterricht am Beispiel visueller Repräsentationen von Gender durch künstliche Intelligenz
papers.authors: Subin Nijhawan
papers.abstract: This article examines learners’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) with both languagerelated and subject-specific learning processes in the foreign language classroom. The development of critical digital literacy (#CDL), understood as the ability to critically assess and evaluate digital, including AI-generated content, is focused on in the reported research data, a video-taped double lesson of an upper-secondary advanced English course. In the lesson, learners used generative AI ChatGPT and DALL-E 3) to design their own campaigns for the promotion of gender equality, and discussed and reflected the appropriateness of AI-generated visual representations. The data analysis draws on video and screen recordings, group discussions, the plenary presentation and the subsequently initiated reflection. Focusing on a critical incident, the analysis shows how learners negotiate meaning by aligning with or distancing themselves from AI-generated artefacts, concomitantly developing, testing, evaluating and reflecting upon prompting strategies. In particular, the data reveal the learners’ critical engagement with AI-generated representations of gender in relation to diversity, equality, justice and intersectional equity as well as implicit and contested beauty ideals. Processes of interpretation, appropriation, emotional engagement and the act of developing and defending a position become visible as learners distance themselves from DALL-E 3’s stereotypical visual worlds and the underlying algorithmic biases of ChatGPT.

papers.title: Potenziale und Grenzen einer KI-gestützten filmbezogenen Unterrichtseinheit im Spanischunterricht der Sekundarstufe II
papers.authors: Johanna Lea Korell, Maximilian Irion, Selina Giuseppina Magno, Roland Alexander Ißler
papers.abstract: This study investigates the use of AI applications in film-based learning in upper secondary Spanish classes. It aims to explore learners’ processes, opportunities, and challenges when engaging with language, cultural, and analytical tasks supported by AI. Data were collected triangulatively through videographic classroom recordings, screen captures, and learners’ written products and analyzed using qualitative content analysis. Findings indicate that ChatGPT primarily supports learners in understanding content-related aspects and historical backgrounds, while active engagement with language, film aesthetics, and emotional perspectives remain limited. Learners recognize the limitations of AI-generated outputs and critically reflect on their incompleteness. The study contributes to the research field by empirically examining, for the first time, the intersection of filmbased learning, Spanish instruction, and AI use, providing implications for the didactic design of AI-supported film work.

papers.title: Feedback mit Haken: Was Schüler:innen aus dem KI-Netz fischen
papers.authors: Lena Bukmakowski, Carolyn Blume
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to make it possible to get immediate and personalized formative feedback and correction for grammar and structure in written texts. In this contribution, an exploratory case study examines to what extent the coordination between the technology and the learners fosters a strategic development of the writing process. After first describing the principles of feedback delivered by generative AI, the ways in which learners utilize an illustrative AI-based tool to revise foreign language texts will be analyzed. It becomes clear that the writers intermittently use the feedback to apply metacognitive strategies. At the same time, opaque and vague feedback leads to a rejection of some suggestions. Finally, these findings will be examined in the context of their implications for supporting process-oriented writing in foreign language instruction.

papers.title: A Multi-Agent Chatbot for Heart Failure Self-Management: Mixed-Methods Pilot Study of Feasibility, Engagement, and Patient Experience (Preprint)
papers.authors: Kavita Radhakrishnan, Rachel Tunis, Liya Wang, Yuko Hamajima, Shaked Gofin, Sai Shripad Kolluru, Samara Karthigan, Linda Kim, Ying Ding
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Heart failure (HF) is a chronic condition managed largely between clinical visits, and consistent self-management is a major determinant of hospitalization risk, functional status, and quality of life. Digital health tools—including wearables, apps, and remote monitoring—hold promise for supporting consistent self-management in the contexts of patients’ everyday lives, and large language model (LLM)-based chatbots extend this promise further by generating real-time, individualized content tailored to a patient's questions, health status, and needs. However, the design and evaluation of chatbots for cardiovascular disease remain nascent, and existing chatbots' design and architecture are often reported in insufficient depth to support consensus on future design directions. OBJECTIVE This pilot study aimed to evaluate feasibility, engagement patterns, and patient experience of a multi-agent, psychosocially personalized AI chatbot designed to support HF self-management. METHODS Fifteen participants with HF, recruited from a parent digital health study, were assigned one of three psychosocial phenotypes derived from prior work (Engaged Self-Regulators, Activated Learners, Challenged Survivors) and interacted with the chatbot over a two-week period. The chatbot, a modular multi-agent system routing patient messages to six specialist sub-agents, personalized tone, content, and complexity to each participant. Engagement was assessed via backend logs and usability was assessed via a post-intervention survey. Overall perceptions and experiences were assessed qualitatively through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. RESULTS Thirteen of 15 participants interacted with the chatbot and completed the study period. Participants engaged with the chatbot for a mean of 3.2 (SD 1.8) days, 22.1 (SD 14.3) messages, and 33.0 (SD 26.2) total minutes. Activated Learners showed the highest engagement (4.0 days, 31.5 messages), followed by Engaged Self-Regulators (3.3 days, 19.7 messages), with Challenged Survivors lowest (1.5 days, 11.5 messages). On post-intervention surveys, 11/13 (84.6%) of participants rated the chatbot's self-care suggestions a 4 or 5 out of 5 (with 5 indicating “excellent”), with a mean rating of 4.08 (SD 0.64), and 9/13 (69.2%) rated its support for decision-making around healthy self-care behaviors a 4 or 5, with a mean rating of 3.85 (SD 0.90). Qualitative interviews (n=14) found the chatbot to be approachable, accurate, and supportive of behavior change for several participants, particularly Activated Learners and Challenged Survivors, while Engaged Self-Regulators described a ceiling effect in which the chatbot added little beyond their existing self-management routines. Participants also identified limitations including passivity, limited cross-session memory, and gaps in holistic, multi-condition guidance. CONCLUSIONS A multi-agent, phenotype-personalized chatbot was feasible, usable, and well-received for HF self-management, with the clearest benefit among participants with greater unmet self-management needs. Findings point to specific, addressable design gaps—including memory, supporting sustained engagement, and context-aware reasoning across a user’s full health picture—and support further testing of psychosocial personalization in larger, more diverse samples.

papers.title: The Forgotten Student—Generative AI Use in Medical Education and the Technology-Integrated Educational Design (TIED) Road Map: Scoping Review
papers.authors: Anita Pienkowska, Olivia Ng, Jianlin Hou, Siew Ping Han
papers.abstract: Background: The growing impact of generative AI (GenAI) on medical education has given rise to many reviews discussing AI literacy, trustworthiness, potential uses, and institutional or faculty benefits. However, there has been surprisingly little review-level attention to its impact on students and learning. Objective: This scoping review examines the impact of GenAI-enabled educational interventions on undergraduate medical students. Methods: We followed the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. An electronic search was conducted between September 22 and September 24, 2025, across Ovid (MEDLINE and Embase), PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, with no language or date restrictions, and excluding reviews, commentaries, letters, editorials, preprints, conference papers, and study protocols. Each record was independently screened by two reviewers, who thoroughly discussed and agreed upon its final inclusion in the analysis. We used a modified version of the Kirkpatrick model as an analytical framework for the final dataset. Results: or its sister journals (n=9). The educational interventions described included GenAI used for simulated patient experiences, knowledge or decision support, and content generation. The majority of studies fell under Kirkpatrick level 1 (n=23), focusing on initial user reactions. The studies that fell under Kirkpatrick level 2 (n=16) examined learning outcomes in terms of knowledge gain, skill acquisition, and learning attitudes. No studies were classified as Kirkpatrick level 3. Three studies demonstrated explicit theoretical grounding and therefore were classified as Kirkpatrick level 4 in our modified model. Only 13 studies spanned across levels. Numerous studies fell outside the model, including studies without student-facing interventions (119 studies) and studies focused on GenAI performance (110 studies). Although these studies were not included in the final analysis, they revealed the extent to which other topics dominate the academic conversation on GenAI in medical education. Conclusions: Our review highlights the volume of studies that prioritize tool performance over learning processes, as well as a trend toward the fragmentation of educational design elements in research evaluating GenAI-enabled educational interventions. Therefore, based on our findings, we developed the Technology-Integrated Educational Design (TIED) road map that reimagines the Kirkpatrick model as a tool to guide student-centered, theory-driven, and iterative design of technology-enabled educational interventions. By integrating preinstructional exploration, mechanism-oriented thinking, educational design, implementation, and evaluation within a single student-centered framework, the road map encourages educators and researchers to consider not only whether technology-enabled interventions work and are acceptable, but also how, for whom, and under what conditions they support meaningful learning.

papers.title: Usability and Acceptance of a Social Robot in People With Multiple Sclerosis: Comparative Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Jessica Podda, Alice Bollini, A. Susini, Domenico Presenza, Keven Thomas Kearney, Ester Cecchella, Erica Grange, Mario Alberto Battaglia, Andrea Tacchino, Giampaolo Brichetto
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Socially Assistive Robotics is an emerging interdisciplinary field that integrates robotics, medicine, cognitive and social sciences, and neuroscience to support people across diverse contexts. Despite recent advances, its potential for people with Multiple Sclerosis (MS) remains largely unexplored, even though MS affects sensory-motor, cognitive, and psychological domains where SAR interventions could offer substantial benefits. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the usability of a humanoid robot in people with MS (PwMS), compare their experiences with age-matched healthy subjects (HS) and exploratorily identify potential predictors of usability. Additionally, automated analysis of written language was explored as a supplementary approach to complement the quantitative measures. METHODS: This cross-sectional study was conducted in November 2025 at the laboratory of the Italian MS Foundation (Genoa, Italy). 20 PwMS (M age 51.4, SD 11.0 years; 65% female; M educational level 13.0, SD 3.4 years) and 20 age-matched HS (M age 47.3, SD 10.1 years; 60% female; M educational level 14.8, SD 2.2 years) completed four predefined tasks with the robot Pepper. Usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Attitudes toward robots, robot-related factors, and task-related effort were measured with the General Attitudes Toward Robots Scale (GAToRS), Godspeed questionnaire, and NASA-TLX, respectively. Psychological variables (e.g., personality traits from I-TIPI) and clinical characteristics for PwMS (e.g., cognitive functions via the app DIGICOG-MS, upper-limb difficulties with the AMSQ) were also collected. Written responses to open-ended questions were analyzed using Natural Language Processing (NLP). RESULTS: SUS scores exceeded the standard cut-off in both groups, with no between-group differences (PwMS: M 81.0, HS: M 77.8; P=.392, r=0.14, 95% CI [0.01, 0.42]), indicating high usability. PwMS reported greater negative attitudes toward societal-level robot introduction (GAToRS S-: P=.024, r=0.36, 95%CI [0.08, 0.63]), and judged Pepper as more anthropomorphic (ANTR; P=.007, r=0.42, 95%CI [0.15, 0.67]) and intelligent (INT; P=.020, r=0.37, 95%CI [0.09, 0.61]) than HS. ANTR was strongly associated with visuospatial memory (DIGICOG-MS: ρ= -0.632, P=.003, 95%CI [-0.84, -0.26]), and relatively strong with both verbal memory (DIGICOG-MS: ρ= -0.504, P=.023, 95%CI [-0.77, -0.08]) and Agreeableness (I-TIPI: ρ= 0.491, P=.028, 95%CI [0.06, 0.77]). Exploratory forward stepwise regression showed that Conscientiousness (I-TIPI: B=2.064, 95%CI [0.679, 3.449]), negative personal attitudes toward robots (GAToRS P -: B =0.169, 95%CI [0.033, 0.306]), and perceived upper-limb difficulties (AMSQ: B=0.169, 95%CI [0.033, 0.306]) explained 64% of SUS variance (Adjusted R²= 0.568). Task-related frustration (NASA-TLX: B=- 1.497, 95%CI [-2.276, -0.719]) explained 48% of SUS variance (Adjusted R²= 0.451). NLP analyses revealed no between-group differences in lexical productivity or sentiment-lexicon coverage. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first preliminary evidence that a social robot can be perceived as highly usable by PwMS, with usability ratings comparable to those of HS, suggesting that MS-related challenges may not hinder human-robot interaction. Psychological factors, prior attitudes toward robots, and clinical characteristics were associated with user experience in the MS group. Future research should explore whether integrating these measures alongside language-based approaches may inform the development of tailored interventions in MS.

papers.title: AI-Driven Lifestyle Interventions for Reducing Diabetes Risk: Systematic Review
papers.authors: Obinna Ikechukwu Ekwunife, Tyler Nauta, Raphael André Fraser, Jennifer Annette Campbell, Gloria A. Aidoo-Frimpong, Rebekah J. Walker, Leonard E. Egede
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven lifestyle interventions are increasingly used for reducing diabetes risk. However, whether they produce clinical benefit beyond standard Diabetes Prevention Programs (DPPs) and whether effects vary by AI type, population, or delivery setting, remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of AI-driven lifestyle interventions on clinical, behavioral, and engagement outcomes among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risk and to assess whether effects differed by AI type, population, or delivery setting. METHODS: PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ClinicalTrials.gov, and citation searches were completed on August 3, 2026, for English-language reports published from 2015. Eligible studies evaluated AI-driven digital lifestyle interventions among people with prediabetes or elevated diabetes risks, or healthy participants in feasibility studies. One reviewer (OIE) screened records and extracted data; a second reviewer (TN) independently verified exclusions and extraction. Study quality was assessed with National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute tools appropriate to each design. Given substantial heterogeneity in designs, estimands, and outcome metrics, findings were synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis guideline rather than pooled statistically. RESULTS: Of 8032 records, 11 studies were included: 1 randomized, 1 nonrandomized comparative, 4 observational, and 5 uncontrolled pre-post studies. Seven evaluated AI lifestyle coaching systems, 2 predictive AI platforms, and 2 conversational AI chatbots. Ten of 11 studies used commercially developed platforms. Study quality was rated good for 5 studies, fair for 3, and poor for 3. The randomized controlled trial showed noninferiority of an AI-DPP versus human coach-led DPP for the combined 12-month outcome (23/183, 12.6% vs 23/185, 12.4%; risk difference 0.1%, 1-sided 95% CI -5.5%). Program initiation (171/183, 93.4% vs 153/185, 82.7%; risk difference 10.7%, 95% CI 4.2%-17.3%) and completion (117/183, 63.9% vs 93/185, 50.3%; risk difference 13.7%; 95% CI 3.6%-23.7%) were higher with AI, but this did not translate into superior clinical outcomes. The nonrandomized comparison found no advantage of AI-personalized messaging over static messaging in terms of BMI or physical activity. The remaining studies reported uncontrolled changes precluding causal inference. Evidence was insufficient to determine whether effects differed by population or delivery setting. CONCLUSIONS: One randomized trial supports noninferiority, not superiority, of a specific AI-driven DPP relative to human coaching; the remaining evidence was nonrandomized, predominantly commercially developed, and hypothesis-generating. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to stratify evidence on AI-driven diabetes prevention by AI mechanism-coaching, predictive, and conversational-and by outcome domain, extending prior scoping work that mapped apps without appraising study quality or comparative effectiveness. This structured mapping shows where evidence is the strongest (engagement and weight) and the weakest (glycemic causality and generalizability), giving health systems a concrete basis for deciding where AI-DPP tools may supplement, rather than replace, standard DPP delivery, pending independent, adequately powered randomized trials.

papers.title: SiAman EduBot: Inovasi AI untuk Pelaporan Insiden dan Edukasi Keselamatan Pasien Dalam Satu Platform Digital.
papers.authors: Ronald Winardi Kartika, Sarwoko SITANALA
papers.journal: Sendimas 2021 - Seminar Nasional Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat
papers.abstract: RSUP dr. Sitanala is committed to strengthening patient safety culture toward a smart hospital paradigm through an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven innovation named Si Aman EduBot. This interactive chatbot, integrated via WhatsApp and the hospital's proprietary application, was developed to provide real-time education on safety standards, emergency procedures, and digital incident reporting systems for both staff and patients. This study aims to evaluate the impact of Si Aman EduBot implementation on enhancing safety culture within the hospital environment. The evaluation results over a three-month period demonstrated significant achievements, including over 5,000 user interactions, a 35% increase in incident reporting volume, and a 20% improvement in patient safety culture scores from the baseline. The rapid and responsive nature of the chatbot proved effective in increasing staff awareness and fostering an open, blame-free reporting culture. Through its interactive educational features and digital system integration, Si Aman EduBot holds the potential to serve as a national model for building a sustainable patient safety culture. Future developments will focus on integrating voice assistant capabilities and electronic medical records. Keywords: Patient Safety, Educational Chatbot, Digital Incident Reporting, Blame-Free Culture.

papers.title: The Pemberdayaan Komunitas Kreatif Kampung Batik Semarang Melalui Edukasi AI Motif Batik Berbasis Kearifan Lokal
papers.authors: Bernadeta Lenny Setyowati, Peter Ardhianto, Ekawati Marhaenny Dukut, Krismalita Sekar Diasti
papers.journal: Sendimas 2021 - Seminar Nasional Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat
papers.abstract: This community service program aims to empower batik artisans, particularly female MSMEs in Kemijen and Kampoeng Batik Semarang, by educating them on utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an assistive technology to design Semarangan batik motifs based on local wisdom. An interdisciplinary team spanning Communication Science, Cultural Studies, English, and Visual Communication Design implemented this program. The execution methods included conceptual counseling, practical training on generative AI, project-based creative mentoring, and design evaluations. The results demonstrated a significant increase in digital literacy: 100% of participants understood AI's role as an assistive design tool, and practical AI operational skills rose to 86%. The program successfully produced more than 5 collaborative batik motif prototypes (e.g., Warak Ngendog, blekok, and tamarind tree) and digital promotion copywriting in English. Program outputs include an ISBN-registered interdisciplinary educational module, an Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) registration draft for the educational model, and a scientific article draft submitted to a national Sinta 5 accredited journal. In conclusion, utilizing AI as an assistive technology accelerates visual design exploration without diluting local cultural philosophy and authenticity, thereby strengthening the economic resilience and digital capacity of female batik MSMEs in the creative industry. Keywords--- Artificial Intelligence (AI), Semarangan Batik, female MSMEs, local wisdom, community empowerment.

papers.title: Learning to Stay With Uncertainty
papers.authors: Sigrid Merx, Eva Midden, Annette N Markham, Ani Encheva
papers.abstract: This article reflects on our journey of working to facilitate discussions around the role of Generative AI (GenAI) in education within the Department of Media and Culture Studies (MCW) at Utrecht University during the academic year 2025–2026. What initially appeared to be a manageable question of GenAI’s impact on assessment and writing gradually revealed a complex web of concerns about student engagement, workloads, institutional priorities, and ultimately the purposes and values of higher education itself. Approaching the GenAI moment as a wicked problem, we realized we needed to shift our orientation from finding solutions to creating conditions for collective reflection, imagination, and experimentation. Ultimately, we suggest that responding to GenAI is not so much about finding a way out of uncertainty, but about learning to stay with it by remaining attentive to what emerges, creating space for what might become possible, and continuing to act from the anchor point of the educational purposes and values we care about.

papers.title: Wer trägt die Verantwortung?
papers.authors: Swenja Wütscher
papers.abstract: Bodrožić-Brnić, Kristina; Lucenti Estevam, André & Thiessen, Thomas (Hrsg.) (2026). AI and the Ethics of Innovation. Responsibility in Practice. Springer Nature Switzerland. 301 S., 181,89 €. Wer trägt Verantwortung, wenn KI Entscheidungen vorbereitet, Kommunikation beeinflusst oder Aufgaben übernimmt, die bislang Menschen vorbehalten waren? Die 16 Beiträge des Sammelbandes AI and the Ethics of Innovation nähern sich dieser Frage aus unterschiedlichen Perspektiven. Einig sind sie sich in einem Punkt: Verantwortung lässt sich nicht an technische Systeme delegieren. Die Kapitel zu Desinformation und KI-Kompetenz zeigen das besonders deutlich. ­Eugênio Bucci beschreibt Des­information als kommunikative Umwelt, die eine „künstliche Ignoranz“ hervorbrin­ge. Jan Doria und David Klotz bezweifeln, dass sich die Probleme öffentlicher Kommunikation durch immer präzisere Kontrollsysteme lösen lassen. Sie setzen stattdessen auf AI Literacy. Marco Wedel und Eva Gengler verstehen KI-Kompetenz als gemeinsame gesellschaftliche Aufgabe. Überraschend nah an aktuellen medienpädagogischen Debatten liegen die Beiträge zu TikTok, Generation Alpha und Beziehungen mit ChatGPT. Sie zeigen, wie digitale Systeme Wahrnehmung und soziale Beziehungen beeinflussen und alltägliche Orientierungsprozesse mitgestalten. An diesen Beispielen wird deutlich, worum es den Autor*innen geht. Algorithmen mögen Entscheidungen vorbereiten. Die Verantwortung dafür verschwindet dadurch nicht. Fragen der Transparenz, Haftung oder Verzerrung stehen deshalb im Zentrum. Die Vielfalt der Themen erweitert den Blick, erschwert aber stellenweise den Zusammenhang. Die Zweiteilung in ,Responsibility in ­Society and Organisations‘ sowie ,Governance and ­Normative Frameworks‘ schafft zwar Orien­tierung. Philosophische, rechtliche, organisationsbezogene und medienwissenschaftliche Kapitel bleiben jedoch meist unter sich. Man legt das Buch mit vielen Notizen aus der Hand, ohne genau zu wissen, wie die verschiedenen Verständnisse von Verantwortung zusammenpassen. Aus medienpädagogischer Sicht sind vor allem die Beiträge besonders aufschlussreich, die den Blick auf die sozialen und kommunikativen Folgen von KI für Öffentlichkeit und Bildung richten.
