papers.title: Governance-Aware Human-in-the-Loop AI for Structuring Longitudinal Autism Intervention Evidence and Generating Evidence-Linked Reports: Development and Component Evaluation Study
papers.authors: Ambar Nath Saha, Debashis Patra
papers.abstract: Longitudinal autism intervention review requires specialists to combine observations from caregivers, teachers, and intervention staff across settings and time. We developed a governance-aware human-in-the-loop application that uses AI to organize evidence while keeping intervention decisions with professionals. The system preserves original observations, proposes structured records with Qwen 2.5 7B, requires professional verification or correction before analytics, checks evidence adequacy, supports abstention, and produces traceable reports. Evaluation used archival ASDBank data from 11 children, 85 sessions, and 9,018 behavioral episodes. Two experienced autism specialists created the reference standard, followed by a final-codebook compliance audit. Qwen 2.5 7B achieved 41.3% merged categorical agreement on the 330-segment main batch and remained the strongest evaluated generator. The offline MARS selector returned records for 80.3% of segments but showed no clear field-level advantage over the strongest reviewable generator. A historical generative-reporting experiment failed its full governance contract (0/11), motivating deterministic operational reporting. Final controlled end-to-end testing passed all predefined governance scenarios (77/77 API tests and 9/9 UI scenarios). These findings support a practical architecture in which AI assists evidence organization, while professional review, abstention, provenance, and deterministic controls protect the longitudinal workflow.

papers.title: Chemical Specification and Provisional Novelty Assessment of AIIP BAI 6C DMAE 002 for AI Assisted Immunopharmacology
papers.authors: Angel Justiz-Vaillant
papers.abstract: AI-assisted phytochemical nomination requires independent checks of chemical identity and supporting evidence. This computational case study examines AIIP-BAI-6C-DMAE-002, the proposed 2-(N,N-dimethylamino)ethyl ester of baicalin's glucuronide C-6″ carboxyl group, originating in an author-held AI immunopharmacology book manuscript. The nominated connectivity was reconciled with inconsistent formula and mass entries in that source. RDKit 2025.09.6 generated identifiers, physicochemical descriptors and comparisons with eight related structures. The encoded neutral candidate has formula C25H27NO11, molecular weight 517.49 g/mol, monoisotopic mass 517.1584 Da and InChIKey BIUNXNZQUMPJLF-LYVDORBWSA-N. Relative to baicalin, calculated polar surface area decreases from 187.12 to 179.36 Å², while neutral-form Crippen cLogP changes from 0.1422 to 0.1624. These results do not establish improved absorption. Public literature and patent searching found established esterification and amino-substitution precedents but no individualised exact disclosure in the retrieved evidence; candidate PubChem InChIKey queries returned no matching record. Novelty remains provisional pending comprehensive structure and Markush analysis. The historical AI-generation trace is incomplete, and no synthesis, binding or efficacy is reported. The study provides a reproducible chemical assessment and a validation framework for a phytochemical-derived immunopharmacology hypothesis.

papers.title: Exploring the Advantage, Concerns, and Experiences of Using ChatGPT in Clinical Education and training for pharmacy students: A cross-sectional study in UAE
papers.authors: Ammar Ali Saleh Jaber, Jumana Haider Al Anssari, Ammar Abdulrahman Jairoun
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing educational methods, including the training of pharmacy students. ChatGPT, an AI-based language model, has the potential to support pharmacy education by simulating clinical scenarios, offering real-time feedback, and providing access to extensive medical information. These capabilities could enhance students’ skills in clinical decision-making and understanding drug therapies. Despite its promise, there are concerns regarding the accuracy of AI responses, ethical considerations, and the risk of students becoming overly dependent on such technology. Furthermore, evaluating students' experiences with AI is essential to determine its true effectiveness in education. Striking a balance between the potential benefits and limitations of AI tools is crucial for their successful incorporation into pharmacy training. Methods and Materials: Between August and September 2024, a cross-sectional study was conducted to explore B.Pharm and postgraduate students' perspectives on the use of ChatGPT in clinical pharmacy education and training. The study adopted a convenience sampling strategy through online platforms and utilized a questionnaire to gather data on demographics, perceived benefits, concerns, and experiences with ChatGPT. Data analysis was performed using SPSS software, incorporating both descriptive and inferential statistics. Results: a total of 283 students who participated in the study. A statistically significant association was found between gender and the perception of ChatGPT's advantages, with males reporting a higher mean perception score compared to females (34.41 ± 0.9 vs 31.69 ± 0.52, P = 0.015). Perception of advantages also varied by study year, with second-year students reporting the highest mean score (34.11 ± 5.49), followed closely by postgraduate students (33.57 ± 5.95). These differences were statistically significant (P = 0.007 for t-test and P = 0.009). The oldest age group (>26) reported significantly lower concern scores (13.66 ± 3.71), indicating fewer concerns compared to younger groups, who expressed higher levels of concern. The differences in concern perceptions across age groups were statistically significant (P < 0.001 for t-test and P = 0.003). Conclusion: Incorporating ChatGPT into clinical training presents valuable opportunities, yet many students express hesitation in relying on it for clinical decision-making. This underscores the importance of fostering a collaborative approach where ChatGPT supports, rather than replaces, another expertise of healthcare professionals. It should serve as a tool to enhance human decision-making, addressing areas where human limitations exist.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Related Sentiments and Perceptions on Federated Social Networks: A Computational Text Analysis
papers.authors: Sadettin Demirel
papers.journal: SELÇUK ÜNİVERSİTESİ İLETİŞİM FAKÜLTESİ AKADEMİK DERGİSİ
papers.abstract: This study aims to examine public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) on federated social networks, specifically Bluesky and Mastodon. While existing research focuses on centralized platforms, a significant gap exists regarding AI perception within decentralized networks. This study addresses this gap through computational analysis of AI related posts in Bluesky and Mastodon. A text-as-data approach was employed to analyze 61,285 posts collected from Bluesky and Mastodon between January 1, 2023, and January 1, 2025. The methodology integrated topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and text analysis to identify prevalent themes, sentiment polarity, and discussion patterns within AI-related discourse. Findings demonstrate predominantly positive sentiment towards AI across both platforms, with trust, anticipation, and joy as primary emotional responses, accompanied by underlying fear and anxiety. Platform-specific variations emerged: Mastodon discourse centers on creativity, digital art, and societal-ethical implications including regulation, bias, and disinformation concerns. Conversely, Bluesky posts emphasize economic and geopolitical dimensions, featuring startups, funding, stock markets, and international policy. The analysis reveals significant fragmentation in public AI perception, characterized by discourse division into distinct economic and ethical spheres across platforms. While this fragmentation accommodates diverse social group perspectives, it presents challenges for establishing comprehensive societal consensus on AI governance. The analytical framework provides insights for understanding decentralized social network dynamics and implications for policy makers examining AI perception in federated digital environments.

papers.title: Enhancing Vocational Milling Machine Learning through PowerPoint Hyperlink-Based Interactive Media
papers.authors: Ilham Bayu Haliludin, Marsono Marsono, Yayi Febdia Pradani, Yuli Panca Asmara
papers.journal: Jurnal Pendidikan Teori Penelitian dan Pengembangan
papers.abstract: The advancement of educational technology has led to the development of innovative learning media to improve student engagement and learning outcomes. This study aimed to develop and evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of PowerPoint Hyperlink-based interactive learning media for milling machine material. The research employed the Research and Development (R&D) method using the 4D model, consisting of the Define, Design, and Develop stages. The research subjects were 20 tenth-grade students of the Machining Engineering Department at SMK Muhammadiyah 1 Kepanjen. The research instruments included expert validation sheets, questionnaires, pretest-posttest assessments, and documentation. Data were analyzed descriptively, while the effectiveness of the learning media was evaluated using the Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test and N-gain analysis. The results indicated that the learning media achieved a feasibility score of 87.2%, categorized as highly feasible, based on expert evaluations. The Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test revealed a significant difference between the pretest and posttest scores (p = 0.000 < 0.05). Furthermore, the N-gain score of 0.48 was classified as moderate, indicating that the learning media effectively improved students' learning outcomes. Therefore, the PowerPoint Hyperlink-based interactive learning media is feasible and effective as an alternative learning resource for milling machine instruction in vocational high schools.

papers.title: Per-channel Complex B1+ Mapping for Parallel Transmit Ultra-high field MRI
papers.authors: Ye Yuan, Jianxiang Chen, Christopher T. Rodgers
papers.abstract: Ultra-high field (UHF, B0 ≥ 7T) MRI provides substantial gains in signal-to-noise ratio, spatial resolution, and contrast. Routine clinical deployment has been limited by challenges of transmit field (B1+) inhomogeneity and specific absorption rate (SAR). Parallel transmission (pTx) can mitigate these challenges but it requires per-channel complex B1+ maps to design effective pTx pulses. We review established and emerging approaches to obtain these maps. We begin by summarizing the underlying physical principles and theory. Then we describe methods for magnitude B1+-mapping such as actual flip-angle imaging (AFI), saturation-prepared B1+-mapping (e.g. SatTFL), and dual refocusing echo acquisition mode (DREAM) that are the basis of widely-applied per-channel complex B1+ mapping methods, as well as methods of pedagogical and/or historical relevance. Next, we describe how relative B1+-mapping with low-flip angle gradient-recalled echo (GRE) scans can determine the relative phases (and relative magnitudes) of B1+ for each channel. We recap the important interferometric approach that is now widely used. We explain how magnitude and phase maps are combined into complex per-channel B1+-maps. We discuss remaining arbitrary factors such as the position-dependent transmit reference phase. We discuss recent practical implementations such as Sandwich TFL, 3DREAM, compressed-sensing SA2RAGE, and respiratory-resolved B1+ mapping. We explore the workflow improvements that could accrue if per-channel B1+ maps don’t need to be acquired for every subject. This includes deep-learning-based approaches to synthesize B1+-maps from the normal localizer scans, the Universal Pulses (UPs) approach to pre-calibrate pulses, and variants such as standardized universal pulses (SUPs), and Fast-Online Customized (FOCUS) and machine-learning online customization. We hope to encourage greater openness and harmonization of these critical calibration steps for parallel transmit pulse design. This will become increasingly important as 7T pTx MRI is adopted for multisite cross-vendor clinical research studies and to deliver the full scientific potential of new extremely high field human MRIs.

papers.title: Catheter Cryoballoon Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation: Focus on Men and Women with Chronic Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction
papers.authors: Н. Г. Потешкина, Yavilika R. Shashkina, Ковалевская Елена Анатольевна, M. V. Gorev, A. A. Karasev
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (CHFpEF) are frequently coexisting and mutually aggravating conditions. Data regarding the impact of catheter-based pulmonary vein isolation in AF patients with CHFpEF, particularly among men and women, remain limited. AIM: To study the course of CHFpEF in male and female patients with atrial fibrillation during the early period after cryoballoon ablation of pulmonary veins (CBAPV). METHODS: CBAPV performed in 59 patients with AF and CHFpEF. Patients were divided by gender. Before surgery and three months postoperatively, quality of life (QoL) was assessed using the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ); functional status was evaluated via a six-minute walk test (6MWT); levels of NT-proBNP were measured; ECHO was conducted. RESULTS: There were differences between patient groups based on age: females (n = 34) had an average age of 67.62 ± 6.05 years compared to males (n = 25) who averaged 62.76 ± 7.29 years (p = 0.007). Groups did not differ significantly in terms of body mass index (BMI), duration and type of AF, class of HF, antiarrhythmic therapy, or treatment for HF. In the female group, there was a reduction in MLHFQ scores from 28.00 [25.00; 39.00] to 16.00 [8.00; 23.00] (p = 0.002), an increase in walking distance during the 6MWT from 397.00 [350.00; 440.00] to 425.00 [400.00; 465.00] meters (p 0.001), and a decrease in NT-proBNP levels from 185.00 [69.00; 517.00] ng/L to 126.00 [62.90; 196.00] ng/L (p = 0.015). Among males, the distance covered during the 6MWT increased from 464.00 [402.50; 560.25] meters to 500.00 [450.25; 581.50] meters (p = 0.003), while ECHO showed a reduction in the E/e' ratio from 9.00 [8.05; 9.70] to 8.00 [5.70; 9.00] (p = 0.033). One woman (4.3%) developed hemopericardium threatening cardiac tamponade, requiring pericardiocentesis as a serious complication. CONCLUSION: Three months following catheter cryoballoon ablation of pulmonary veins, female patients with AF and CHFpEF experienced improvements in QoL, increased exercise capacity, and reduced NT-proBNP levels, indicating improvement in their condition. Male patients also increased exercise tolerance and decreased diastolic dysfunction severity over this same timeframe.
keywords: chronic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire

papers.title: Do Malaysian Newsrooms Jump on the AI Bandwagon? Empirical Evidence From Journalists’ Perspectives
papers.authors: Jiankun Gong, Yu Zuo, Izzati Aziz, Mumtaz Aini Alivi, Kunjin Luo, Yuqing Lin
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted as a transformative force in journalism, yet most research on newsroom AI adoption remains concentrated in Western and other well-resourced media settings. This study examines how AI is interpreted, organized, and used in Malaysian newsrooms, offering insight from an emerging Southeast Asian media context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 journalists across six Malaysian news organizations, the article investigates how national AI governance signals are translated into newsroom norms, how organizational resources and managerial priorities shape uptake, and how AI is incorporated into everyday reporting, editing, and verification. The analysis shows that AI adoption in Malaysian newsrooms is uneven and selective rather than uniform. First, national AI momentum has not yet produced strong newsroom-level governance; instead, the practice remains shaped by limited written rules, selective disclosure, and strong human accountability. Second, organizational capacity is patchy, with uneven access to tools, training, and infrastructural support across organizations and roles. Third, AI is used mainly in bounded, assistive tasks such as transcription, translation, summarization, and headline generation, while verification labor is redistributed rather than reduced. The findings identify a typology of newsroom responses—cautious minimalists, experimental pragmatists, and human-gated adopters—showing that Malaysian newsrooms are not simply “jumping on the AI bandwagon,” but engaging AI pragmatically under uneven governance and resource conditions.

papers.title: Independent Human Validation of Two Machine-Coded AI Disclosure Measures in U.S. Bank Annual Reports (FY2021–FY2025)
papers.authors: Werner Girth, Samuel Przeworski
papers.abstract: A longitudinal corpus of annual reporting from 40 publicly listed U.S. banks (FY2021–FY2025, 200 bank-years) has been coded for publicly evidenced AI adoption using two large language models operating under a frozen coding instrument, with adjudication of contested cases. The resulting object register, analytical master v2.19, is frozen and closed. This study tests how far two trained human coders, working independently from the same source packages and under the same frozen coding rules, reproduce the two primary measures derived from that register: whether a bank-year contains at least one qualifying AI adoption object of the bank (participation), and whether at least one such object is in current operation at deployment status DEP03, DEP04 or DEP05 (named-current presence). The draw is made from the 177 bank-years remaining after exclusion of the 23 bank-years previously allocated, within the current panel, to instrument development (3), panel locking (5) and the earlier human reference exercise (15). Those allocations were made before the present validation was planned, and the two cases whose double coding did not complete for want of eligible source material, TD US FY2023 and UBS US FY2024, remain excluded on the same allocation rather than being returned to the frame, so that no bank-year enters the draw on the basis of what it was found to contain. From that frame, 40 bank-years are drawn by a seeded script, stratified on two factors, fiscal year and register participation status, giving ten strata of four bank-years each. The draw therefore reads the register’s participation values; the consequences for the agreement statistics are stated in the analysis plan. The script runs after this registration is submitted, with a seed fixed in advance, and the draw is accepted as it falls. The sample size is fixed on a precision argument stated in the protocol and is not extended on the basis of the observed result. The two coders are independent of the research team, have had no contact with the register, its results or the manuscript, and are blind to the study’s expectations. They receive the source packages and two documents: a coder extract reproducing verbatim every rule of the production instrument that bears on the two judgments, and a procedural instruction sheet. They have no access to the register’s values, to each other’s records, or to the records of the earlier reference exercise. Four bank-years outside the sample are coded first as a pilot, after which the two documents are revised once on wording, dated and locked. A third coder adjudicates disagreements under pre-specified conditions and holds no prior human code on any case in the frame. None of the three is named in this registration; their identities are recorded in the private component, disclosed to the handling editor on request, and published with the data on acceptance. Coding had not begun at the time of this registration.The protocol fixes the sampling frame and draw rule, the unit of agreement, the agreement statistics including chance correction, and the numerical pass thresholds in advance. Results are reported in full whether or not the thresholds are met. The comparison against the register is reported on v2.19 as it stands; the register is not altered before that comparison is complete and written up, and any correction that the comparison triggers afterwards follows the rule in the protocol, with the headline series reported under both versions.

papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Post-Reading Presentations in Improving Secondary School Students’ Attitudes Towards Developing Turkish Vocabulary
papers.authors: Görkem ARSLAN
papers.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine whether middle school students’ attitudes toward developing Turkish vocabulary differ according to the tools they preferred during the preparation of post-reading presentations. The study employed a quantitative comparative correlational design. The participants consisted of 56 fifth-grade students attending a public middle school in Burhaniye, Balıkesir, Türkiye. Within the framework of the Türkiye Century Education Model, students presented the books they had read by using artificial intelligence-supported tools, conventional digital tools, or hand-prepared materials, based on their own preferences. No intervention was made in the natural learning environment. After the presentations, the Attitude Scale for Developing Vocabulary in the Turkish Course, developed by Yaşar and Topçuoğlu Ünal (2016), was administered. Descriptive statistics and the independent-samples t-test were used for data analysis. The findings revealed that students who preferred artificial intelligence-supported tools obtained significantly higher attitude scores toward developing Turkish vocabulary than those who preferred conventional digital tools or hand-prepared materials. The calculated effect size (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.59) indicated a medium effect. The results suggest that students’ attitudes toward developing Turkish vocabulary differ significantly according to the tools they preferred during the preparation of post-reading presentations.

papers.title: Post-Purchase Emotional Collapse: LLM-Assisted Analysis of Online Consumer Complaint Narratives
papers.authors: Eren Temel
papers.abstract: Online shopping environments involve interactions shaped by trust, responsiveness, speed, and personalization. When post-purchase service failures occur, customer reactions may extend beyond dissatisfaction to cumulative emotional disruption, including regret, frustration, exhaustion, perceived betrayal, and trust erosion. Despite extensive research on service failure and complaint behavior, limited attention has been given to progressive emotional breakdowns across digital consumption journeys. Addressing this gap, the study introduces post-purchase emotional collapse (PPEC), defined as a cumulative emotional breakdown resulting from repeated service failures and unresolved negative experiences across customer touchpoints. Using a qualitative content analysis design, the study analyzes 1,000 consumer complaints from sikayetvar.com via Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted emotional coding, touchpoint identification, metaphor analysis, and narrative classification, with human validation on a subsample. Findings suggest delivery failures as the most frequently coded rupture point, with anger, disappointment, and regret as the most frequently coded primary emotions. Complaint narratives include metaphors of deception, battle, and destruction, which are compatible with a reading of cumulative deterioration. The study contributes by conceptualizing PPEC and illustrating the potential and the limits of LLM-assisted qualitative analysis in consumer research; it also offers managerial implications for emotionally responsive complaint management systems.

papers.title: Barriers to and Needs for the Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Radiation Therapy Planning in Saudi Arabia. A Cross-Sectional Survey
papers.authors: Abdulaziz M. Alshaikh, Ghadah AlQarni, Abdulaziz AlGhamdi, Khalid Alrabiah, Nasser Al-Rajhi, Mohammed Aldehaim
papers.abstract: Objectives: To assess radiation oncology physicians' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) in radiation therapy planning in Saudi Arabia and identify barriers to and support needs for its implementation.Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was distributed through the Saudi Association of Radiation Oncology email list to 142 physicians from April to May 2026. We analyzed responses using descriptive statistics and exploratory 2-sided Fisher exact tests comparing residents with nonresidents.Results: Forty-three complete responses were analyzed (response rate: 30.3%). A total of 33 (76.7%) respondents agreed or strongly agreed that AI would improve planning accuracy and efficiency. Nineteen (44.2%) reported no workplace access to AI tools, and 34 (79.1%) reported no formal AI training. The most common concerns regarding AI were output accuracy or validation (n = 28, 65.1%), loss of clinical judgment (n = 22, 51.2%), and legal liability (n = 21, 48.8%). The most requested forms of support were hands-on training or simulation (n = 35, 81.4%), regulatory and legal guidance (n = 30, 69.8%), and vendor technical support (n = 29, 67.4%). Nonresidents more often reported practical implementation barriers, including funding limitations, accuracy issues, and inadequate support; however, these comparisons were confounded by age and experience differences and should remain exploratory and hypothesis-generating.Conclusion: Respondents viewed AI favorably, but gaps regarding access, training, validation, funding, and governance may limit safe implementation. Structured education, local validation, quality assurance, technical support, and clear institutional and regulatory guidance are needed.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness Among Paramedics at the Saudi Red Crescent Authority: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Mohammed Jamaan Alsahli
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate AI readiness among paramedics working within the Saudi Red Crescent Authority (SRCA) and examine demographic and professional characteristics related to their readiness.Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted among SRCA paramedics. Data were collected through a structured online questionnaire covering demographic and professional features and the validated Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (MAIRS-MS), which assesses four dimensions: Cognition, Ability, Vision, and Ethics. Comparisons between groups were performed with the Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests, while correlations were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation, and a multiple linear regression model examined factors independently related to AI readiness.Results: A total of 262 paramedics participated. The mean overall AI readiness score was 72.55 (SD 21.79) on the 110-point scale, reflecting a moderate degree of readiness. The Ethics and the Cognition domains had the highest (3.57/5) and the lowest (3.15/5) mean item scores, respectively. Participants reported greater confidence in AI's ethical and practical aspects than in understanding AI concepts and terminology. Prior AI training was the only factor independently associated with higher AI readiness (B=10.13, 95% CI 3.45–16.81; P=.003).Conclusion: SRCA paramedics demonstrated moderate AI readiness, with greater confidence in AI's ethical and practical application than in its conceptual and technical foundations. Prior AI training was the only independent factor associated with higher readiness, highlighting the potential of structured AI education before the broader implementation of AI in EMS.

papers.title: Large Language Models in the Emergency Department: Fairness Implications for Clinicians
papers.authors: Kasumi Satoh, Manabu Okuyama, Hajime Nakae, Yohei Okada
papers.abstract: Applications of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are rapidly expanding in emergency medicine, but concerns remain regarding their fairness across diverse patient populations. Fairness extends beyond model accuracy and includes equal performance across patient groups, equitable outcomes and allocation of clinical benefits, and procedural fairness throughout the lifecycle of AI implementation. This narrative review aims to provide a practical framework for understanding and evaluating fairness in emergency medicine applications of AI and LLMs. This narrative review organizes fairness risks into three clinically relevant layers. First, datalevel fairness concerns the data used to train, fine-tune, or prompt AI systems. Biased clinical data, including non-random missingness and stigmatizing documentation, can influence model performance. Second, output-level fairness concerns whether the outputs generated by AI systems are equally accurate, safe, and useful across patient groups. In emergency care, subgroup-specific errors in recommendations, predictions, translations, or instructions may arise from aggregation, learning, or evaluation bias, even when overall model performance appears strong. Third, human-interaction fairness concerns whether the benefits of AI are realized equitably in clinical practice and by patients. Even when data and outputs are fair, inequities may arise if clinicians over-rely on or reject useful AI recommendations, or if patients are unable to access, understand, or trust AI-mediated information. Clinicians should consider potential implications for safety, transparency, and fairness alongside overall model accuracy when evaluating AI tools in emergency medicine.

papers.title: Large language models as clinical decision support in emergency medicine: promise, pitfalls, and the risk of uncritical adoption
papers.authors: Chiwon Ahn

papers.title: Scaling Waste-to-Wealth Ventures in Emerging Markets: A Circular Economy Framework for Sustainable Growth
papers.authors: Zwanaka James Mudara, Michael Mncedisi Willie
papers.abstract: The circular economy offers emerging markets a route to growth that does not depend on continued resource extraction, and waste-to-wealth ventures have proliferated in response. Few achieve scale. This paper asks what distinguishes ventures that replicate across markets from those that remain confined to a single site, and develops a conceptual framework in answer. A structured review of four literatures was conducted, covering circular economy theory, waste management in developing economies, the informal recycling sector, and the relationship between circular practice and development objectives. The framework identifies three enablers of scale, namely an adaptive business model, a hybrid capital structure and policy co-creation, and argues that they act through ecosystem orchestration, the alignment of informal collectors, offtakers, municipalities and financiers around a single material flow. Scaling is specified as four stages in which the binding constraint shifts from technical proof to feedstock security, then to offtake, then to policy stability, so support instruments must be matched to stage. Four testable propositions and a set of observable indicators are stated. The framework is offered for empirical testing rather than as a validated model.

papers.title: Toward a Civil Security Orientation: Bridging Research and Practice in Homeland Security and Emergency Management. Insights from the 2nd Pracademic Emergency Management and Homeland Security Summit
papers.authors: Alexander Siedschlag
papers.journal: Journal of Homeland Security and Emergency Management
papers.abstract: Abstract This article synthesizes proceedings and outcomes from the 2nd Pracademic Emergency Management and Homeland Security Summit, hosted virtually by Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Worldwide Campus College of Arts & Sciences and its Virtual Collaboratory for Security and Resilience Education, Research, and Engagement. Drawing on contributions from an international and interdisciplinary group of scholars, practitioners, students, policymakers, and professional organizations representing higher education, government, industry, and operational practice, the summit examined emerging challenges and future directions across homeland security, emergency management, resilience, public health, homeland defense, disaster planning, information disorder, artificial intelligence, ethics, and standards development. Several cross-cutting findings emerged. First, preparedness and resilience increasingly require adaptive, inclusive, and whole-community approaches grounded in trusted communication, social capital, functional needs inclusion, and meaningful stakeholder engagement. Second, while artificial intelligence, remote sensing, and advanced decision-support systems offer substantial operational promise, their implementation demands stronger attention to ethical oversight, interoperability, governance, and consensus-based standards capable of translating technical capability into operational relevance. Third, increasingly complex threat environments reinforce the need for critical thinking, scenario-based learning, ethical reasoning, and career-long professional development to prepare leaders to operate across institutional boundaries and under incomplete information.

papers.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Cognitive Scaffolding, Substitution, and the Risk of Deskilling
papers.authors: Marco Fenici
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

papers.title: Digital twin-assisted edge-local query resolution for privacy–utility trade-off in location-based services
papers.authors: Mohammed Hasan A., Nemi Chandra R.
papers.abstract: Location-Based Services (LBS) generate large volumes of sensitive, location-dependent queries that must be processed under strict and often conflicting constraints of privacy and utility. Existing differential privacy (DP) mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: strong guarantees inject excessive noise and degrade utility, while utility-oriented methods under-protect users. We propose DT-ELR (Digital Twin-assisted Edge-Local Resolution), a framework that jointly optimises disclosure and retrieval utility through two tightly integrated algorithms and an on-device digital twin. Algorithm 1 (SensitivityClassifier) calibrates a monotone geo-indistinguishability budget from a data-derived sensitivity score, validated against a semantic venue-category labelling (AUC 0.81). The digital twin predicts from on-device signals alone whether releasing a query would improve its answer (AUC 0.90); self-sufficient queries are resolved against an on-device venue cache with no release and no budget spent. Algorithm 2 (ClosedFormAllocator) then distributes the remaining budget across released queries in closed form, matching the exact dynamic-programming optimum to within 1%. Experiments on three public check-in corpora - Foursquare-NYC, Gowalla and Brightkite - using an end-to-end nearest-venue retrieval task and three implemented adversaries, show that DT-ELR reduces optimal-inference localization success on sensitive queries from 61.3% to 11.4% on Foursquare-NYC at a matched mean budget, while raising end-to-end retrieval precision from 0.244 under full release to 0.559. Twin-guided release routing outperforms a tuned distance heuristic at every matched release rate, approaching an oracle ceiling of 0.565, and keeps 73% of sensitive queries entirely on the device. Component analysis confirms that each mechanism contributes independently, with edge-local resolution dominant, and the sensitivity model transfers to Gowalla and Brightkite without refitting. Against three recent location-perturbation mechanisms at a matched budget, DT-ELR attains a dominant privacy-utility frontier on all three corpora: higher utility at equal disclosure, and lower disclosure at equal utility.

papers.title: From skills to smart care: The mediating role of digital literacy in the relationship between digital competence and medical artificial intelligence readiness among nursing students
papers.authors: Shaimaa Mohamed Amin, Heba Emad El‐Gazar, Sameer Abdulmalik Alkubati, Mohamed Ali Zoromba, Heba Sobhy Mohamed, Mohammed Adel Abd Elhafeez Elbakry, Ahmed Farghaly Tawfik, Mohamed Hussein Ramadan Atta, Abeer Abdel Aziz Madian, Haitham Mokhtar Mohamed Abdallah, Hanadi Dakhilallah, Azza Abd Elrazek Baraka
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare requires nurses to possess strong digital competence, advanced digital literacy, and readiness to engage with AI technologies. Despite this need, the ways in which digital competence influences AI readiness, and the mediating role of digital literacy, remain underexplored. This descriptive cross-sectional study examined 500 undergraduate nursing students from two Universities for Health Sciences in Saudi Arabia and Egypt using validated measures of digital competence, digital literacy, and medical AI readiness. Results indicated strong positive correlations between digital competence, digital literacy, and AI readiness, with digital literacy partially mediating the effect of digital competence on AI readiness. These findings highlight the importance of integrating ethical, reflective, and AI-focused digital literacy alongside technical skills in nursing education, ensuring that future nurses are prepared to use medical AI effectively and safely, thereby supporting clinical decision-making and improving quality of care.

papers.title: Towards a New Learning Ecology: The Mediator Role of Teachers Facing Generative AI in the University Context of Peru, Chile, and Colombia
papers.authors: Óscar Rafael Boude Figueredo, Jessica Meza-Jaque, Luis Peréz
papers.abstract: Background The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has created an ontological disruption in higher education, challenging traditional pedagogical mediation and academic production. This study examines the transformation of the teaching role in university environments across Peru, Chile, and Colombia, addressing a knowledge gap in Latin American empirical research regarding faculty perceptions and daily practices with Large Language Models. Methods The research employed a descriptive-interpretative qualitative design with an open-ended survey approach interpreted through a hermeneutic lens. A non-probabilistic sample of 48 undergraduate and graduate professors from 20 Higher Education Institutions in the region participated. Data were collected through a validated 18-item structured online questionnaire and analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis assisted by Atlas.ti software. Results The findings identify a transition from traditional instructional roles toward a “mediator-curator” model, where educators act as orchestrators of human-AI co-intelligence. Key applications include pedagogical re-engineering, such as dynamic curricular design, Socratic tutoring, and the shift from product-oriented to process-oriented assessment. Critical dimensions emerged regarding the need for pedagogical re-engineering, ethical challenges in academic integrity, and the development of critical AI literacy. National variations showed Chile focusing on pedagogical equity, Colombia on research productivity, and Peru on didactic agility. Conclusions The integration of GenAI in the Latin American university context requires a situated pedagogical response that transcends instrumental use. The study proposes a new learning ecology where the teacher facilitates critical interaction between students and generative systems. This shift necessitates a reconfiguration of teaching competencies toward epistemic curation and algorithmic responsibility to ensure meaningful and ethical learning.

papers.title: Mapping generative AI in higher education teaching and learning: a scoping review
papers.authors: Michael Pin-Chuan Lin, Daniel Chang, Philip H. Winne, Gervase Michael Bowen, Jeeho Ryoo
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered higher education, but empirical research on its roles in teaching and learning remains fragmented across instructional activities, outcomes, assessment approaches, and stakeholder perspectives. This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines to map 394 empirical studies of GenAI use in higher education published from November 2022 through December 2025. The review examined how GenAI tools were integrated into authentic teaching and learning activities, what outcomes or skills were targeted, how studies assessed those outcomes, and how students and instructors perceived GenAI use. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI was most often used to support existing academic tasks, especially feedback, tutoring, and writing. The most frequently targeted outcomes included engagement, usability and acceptance, critical thinking, disciplinary knowledge, academic performance, writing quality, and AI literacy. Self-regulated learning, ethics, creativity, feedback quality, and equity received less attention. Assessment practices relied mainly on surveys, tests or rubrics, artifact analysis, and interviews, suggesting that much of the evidence base is shaped by short-term and readily implemented methods. Student and instructor perceptions were predominantly mixed, reflecting perceived benefits alongside concerns about pedagogy, integrity, workload, and governance. The review highlights the need for stronger alignment between learning constructs and assessment methods, more process-sensitive evidence, clearer reporting of governance practices, and greater attention to equity in GenAI-supported higher education. Supplementary Information: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00630-9.

papers.title: EEG-biometric authentication system using multi-paradigm neurophysiological measurements and artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Chetan Rakshe, P Sriram Kumar, Christy Bobby Thomas, Mohanavelu Kalathe, Vanteemar Sathyanarayana Sreeraj, Ganesan Venkatasubramanian, John Thomas, Yuvaraj Rajamanickam, Deepesh Kumar, Jac Fredo Agastinose Ronickom
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a promising physiological modality for biometric authentication due to its inherent neural uniqueness and resistance to spoofing attacks. However, reliable EEG-based authentication remains challenging because brain signals are highly non-stationary and vary across cognitive states. To address this limitation, this study proposes a multi-paradigm neurophysiological measurement protocol designed to capture stable subject-specific EEG signatures across diverse brain conditions. EEG signals were recorded from participants during six complementary paradigms, including eyes-open and eyes-closed resting states, left and right-hand motor tasks, working-memory encoding, steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP), and steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEP). The recorded signals were preprocessed and segmented into 2-s epochs with 50% overlap. We extracted 28 quantitative descriptors per channel from time, frequency, time-frequency, and nonlinear domains. These descriptors were used to evaluate several decision models, including Mahalanobis distance-based template matching, logistic regression (LR), support vector machine, random forest, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network. The performance of the proposed measurement system was analyzed under both single-paradigm and multi-paradigm configurations using cross-session validation. Experimental results show that the multi-paradigm measurement protocol reduces the equal error rate (EER) by 2% compared with single-paradigm systems. The LR decision model achieved the best performance with an EER of 1.6% (95% confidence interval: 1.48−1.73), with false rejection rates of 2.06% and 9.01% at false acceptance rates of 1% and 0.1%, respectively. Feature analysis indicated that Hjorth mobility and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients derived from fronto-central cortical channels provide the most reliable neural identity descriptors. These results demonstrate that multi-paradigm EEG acquisition improves the stability of neural measurements across cognitive states and enables reliable biometric authentication in dynamic conditions.

papers.title: When synthetic Delphi panels work: a graph-native methodology for participatory foresight under structural complexity
papers.authors: Ana Bossler, Andrés Fullana, Enric Bas
papers.abstract: Foresight methodology has historically expanded one mode at a time — from supernatural divination through hermeneutic utopias, technical forecasting, emancipatory foresight, and participatory creative futures. The widespread adoption of large language models opens a sixth mode, synthetic foresight , in which participants and evidence bases are computationally generated rather than recruited. We position this mode as the sixth column of an established typology of approaches to the future, extending the participatory tradition. This paper empirically evaluates synthetic Delphi panels and characterises the conditions under which they produce reliable forecasts. We deployed a 60-agent panel — six LLM families across ten disciplinary personas — over a Neo4j knowledge graph of 25,823 circular economy publications, testing eight evidence-base configurations: no grounding, full-text and abstract literature, EU regulatory documents, pre-extracted weak signals, and two graph-derived vocabularies (bridge-term injection via class-based TF-IDF and bridge-author traversal). Rankings were validated against observed 2021–2024 publication growth. The panel converged under every condition (CV reductions of 81–91% across three rounds), matching Delphi benchmarks. However, convergence was independent of coverage of the field’s research communities, indicating that agreement among synthetic panellists is not a sufficient validity criterion. Performance was sensitive to the type of grounding : structured bibliometric context substantially outperformed text-based retrieval on coverage, and the two graph-derived configurations achieved the best balance of coverage and ranking accuracy. We close with a reproducible four-step audit-first, deploy-second protocol and design guidelines, supporting synthetic foresight as a viable extension of the participatory tradition contingent on the quality of the knowledge infrastructure.

papers.title: Poor agreement between measured and perceived body weight status, and determinants of misclassification among adults in Cameroon: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Pavitra Rajesh, Christina Saad, Calypse Asangbe Ngwasiri, Léopold Ndemnge Aminde
papers.abstract: Body weight misperception can adversely affect obesity prevention and control efforts. Despite rising trends in the prevalence of overweight and obesity in Cameroon, limited evidence exists on the magnitude and determinants of weight misperception. This study aimed to examine the prevalence and drivers of body weight misperception, underestimation and overestimation among adults in Cameroon. We conducted a secondary analysis of cross-sectional data collected in 2016 from 1,139 adults in Buea, a semi-urban town in Cameroon. Objective weight status was ascertained via measured body mass index (BMI), while a questionnaire assessed self-perceived body weight status. We evaluated agreement between both methods using the kappa statistic and fitted Poisson regression models to identify sociodemographic and behavioural factors predicting misperception. The prevalence of any misperception in the total sample was 43.0% (95% CI 40.1–45.9), whereas weight underestimation in those with BMI-defined overweight or obesity was 82.8% (95% CI 79.2–85.9). For individuals with a normal BMI, the prevalence of weight overestimation was 4.9% (95% CI 3.4-7.0). Overall, the agreement between the objective and perceived weight status was poor (κ = 0.13). Any misperception was higher among participants aged 45–54 years and those aged 55 years or older, women, married individuals and those who consumed high amounts of alcohol. Overestimation was more prevalent among those aged 55 years or older and among married persons, while underestimation was more common among smokers and those reporting good-to-excellent health status. We found poor agreement between self-perceived and measured body weight in this study, approximately two in five adults misclassified their weight status, and four in five people underestimated their body weight. Public health strategies are needed to improve awareness of weight status and address the related drivers of misperception to optimise health outcomes in Cameroon.

papers.title: Economic evaluation protocol of the Ntshembo (Hope) Trial (RCT) in rural and urban South Africa: an intervention to optimise adolescence body mass index (BMI) pre-conception to address the triple burden of malnutrition
papers.authors: Cyril Bernsah Fonka, Dhyan Saravanja, Shane A Norris, Kathleen Kahn, Stephen Tollman, Chris Desmond
papers.abstract: South African adolescent girls face a triple burden of malnutrition, undernutrition alongside overweight/obesity, and micronutrient deficiencies, heightened risk factors for Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs). The Ntshembo trial is a South African Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) that utilises Community Healthcare Workers to support at-risk adolescent girls (14–19 years old) in improving their body mass index (BMI) through nutrition- and behaviour-based interventions, combined with a household conditional cash transfer. The intervention aims to optimise BMI and, by doing so, reduce both individual and transgenerational risk for metabolic diseases like type-2 diabetes. This protocol outlines the methods that will be used alongside the intervention to conduct an economic evaluation, including a cost-effectiveness analysis, of the Ntshembo (Hope) RCT. The intervention cost will be estimated from the provider and societal perspectives. The cost of implementing the intervention in an RCT setting (scenario 1) and of replicating the intervention in a non-research context (scenario 2) will be modelled. An activity-based approach will be used to identify and cost the activities involved in implementing both the intervention and the comparator (standard of care). The cost components of each activity will be identified and estimated through three sources: (1) expenditure records from the Ntshembo trial, (2) primary data collected through key informant interviews with implementation staff, and (3) participant questionnaires. Additional cost data will be sourced from the Department of Health (DoH) budget reports and published literature to estimate the value of resources used but not directly paid for (opportunity cost). The economic evaluation will consist of three elements: (i) a cost-consequence analysis which compares the cost versus benefits of the intervention, (ii) the incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) using the primary and secondary outcomes, and (iii) the cost per Disability-adjusted Life Years (DALYs) averted by the intervention. DALYs averted over the life course will be modelled using the change in BMI and information on confounders using a Markov model. The long-term benefits, including (depending on the nature and magnitude of benefits observed) later-life labour market outcomes, will be modelled. Probabilistic sensitivity analyses will be performed to understand uncertainty and evaluate the robustness of the results. This economic evaluation study is part of a larger project: The Ntshembo (Hope) trial (see the economic evaluation section of the Ntshembo protocol). The larger study is approved by the Human Ethics Research Committee of the University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa (M211061) and of the University of Cambridge (HBREC.2022.07). The Ntshembo trial is registered with the Pan-African Clinical Trials Registry. identifier: PACTR202201638897606. Registered on 1st August 2022, https://pactr.samrc.ac.za/TrialDisplay.aspx?TrialID=14656

papers.title: Efficacy of arthroscopic technique for rotator cuff tear
papers.authors: 李井杰, 杨秋月, 陆颖辉
papers.journal: Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research
papers.abstract: Rotator cuff tear (RCT) is a common cause of shoulder pain and functional impairment, with its incidence increasing annually due to population aging and rising sports injuries. Arthroscopic technique, due to its advantages of being minimally invasive and allowing for a faster recovery, have become the primary method for treating RCT. However, the rate of re-tearing after surgery remains relatively high, which affects the long-term treatment results of patients. Identifying risk factors that influence surgical outcomes is significant for optimizing treatment plans. It aimed to systematically analyze the clinical efficacy of arthroscopic technique for RCT and explore the key factors influencing functional recovery. 206 patients with RCT who underwent arthroscopic rotator cuff (RC) repair and release were enrolled as subjects. Clinical data (gender, age, BMI, medical history, size of RCT, degree of fatty infiltration around the RC, whether rehabilitation was conducted after surgery, etc.) were collected and recorded. The risk factor analysis was carried out. Patients’ postoperative shoulder score and quality of life (QoL) score were visibly higher than preoperative scores; advanced age, larger RCT, and higher degrees of fatty infiltration around the RC were identified as independent risk factors for re-tear ( P < 0.05). Arthroscopic technique is effective in improving the function and QoL of individuals with RCT. Advanced age, larger RCT, lack of postoperative rehabilitation training, and severe fatty infiltration increase the risk of re-tear.

papers.title: Human–AI interaction in parotid ultrasound diagnosis: a prospective two-phase observer-performance study
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Kim, Seyeon Lee, Hyewon Hwang, Soonho Ha, Yeongmin Kim, Inyong Jeong, Min-Suk Kim, Byungjae Kang, Joon Hong Kim, Sung Jun Hong, Young Hen Lee, Yeon Soo Kim, Seung-Kuk Baek, Sung-Hye You, Hyojeong Kim, Hyun Soo Park, Yeojin Yoo, Thomas J. Kwack, Soon Young Kwon, Hwamin Lee
papers.abstract: Differentiating pleomorphic adenoma (PA) from Warthin’s tumor (WT) — the two most common benign parotid neoplasms — on ultrasound is challenging even for experienced ultrasonographers. Most existing AI systems for parotid ultrasound have been static, retrospective, and tested without prospective reader evaluation. We developed a confidence-aware AI system with a radiologist-editable interface and prospectively evaluated its impact on radiologist performance in an observer-performance study. We developed a confidence-aware hybrid pipeline combining a YOLO detection model with a classification model fallback for parotid ultrasound differentiation, using an internal dataset of 949 images (Korea University Ansan Hospital) and an external dataset of 427 images (Korea University Anam Hospital). We exploratorily evaluated 35 detection × classification combinations to characterize model complementarity, and then prospectively validated a single pre-specified deployment configuration (τ = 0.80, YOLOv12m + ConvNeXt) through a two-phase observer-performance study with three board-certified radiologists on 107 external cases (321 reads total). Standalone detection and classification models achieved external AUROCs of 0.811 and 0.919, respectively. The confidence-aware pipeline outperformed both standalone models in 22 of 35 combinations on external data (highest macro-F1 = 0.838) with the complementary effect most apparent when the two models performed comparably. In the reader study, AI assistance improved pooled diagnostic accuracy from 76.3% to 81.6% (generalized linear mixed model [GLMM] odds ratio = 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12–2.13, p = 0.008) and inter-reader agreement (Fleiss’ κ increasing from 0.475 to 0.611), with larger gains on more difficult cases. Reader response was selective: readers followed correct AI predictions more often than incorrect ones (76.2% vs. 51.1%, p = 0.008), and per-class sensitivity changed in opposite directions for WT (+ 18.1% points) and PA (− 9.3% points), aligning with the AI’s prediction profile. A confidence-aware AI system with a radiologist-editable interface improved radiologist diagnostic accuracy and inter-reader agreement in a prospective observer-performance study. These findings support the system’s potential as a decision-support tool that operates alongside the interpreting physician, and motivate further evaluation in real-world clinical workflows.

papers.title: Construction of a machine learning-based model for predicting specialist nurse transfer tendencies
papers.authors: Gan Wang, Zheng Luo, 吴惠英, Jiaojiao Wang, Wen Ma, Li Luo
papers.abstract: The shortage of specialist nurses poses a significant challenge to healthcare systems worldwide, impacting both patient care and hospital operations. This study explores the application of machine learning to predict the job transfer tendencies of specialist nurses, as well as determining the major causes of the transfer tendencies, aiming to provide hospitals with actionable insights for retention strategies. We applied multiple classification algorithms, such as Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) Classifier, Random Forest Classifier, XGBoost and TabNet Classifier. The final model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) score of 0.766 after cross-validation and hyperparameter optimisation using the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE). To better understand feature contributions, we utilised Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) values to perform feature importance analyses. Our findings identified that key predictors of nurse transfer include whether satisfaction with performance distribution is high, monthly take-home income, number of specialist trainings/continuing education attended, whether working in a specialist nursing outpatient clinic and number of children under 12. However, certain results, such as the unexpected positive correlation between satisfaction with performance distribution and job transfer, revealed anomalies that are likely attributable to class imbalances or data biases. We also discuss the tradeoffs between different data preprocessing techniques, particularly regarding oversampling within cross-validation to mitigate class imbalances. While the performance of the model was moderate, the insights from the SHAP analysis provided valuable directions for future research. Hence, we recommend collecting more representative data and refining feature selection to improve model accuracy. Therefore, this research contributes to the development of predictive tools for hospital management to address the specialist nurse shortage by identifying nurses who are at risk of job transfer. Not applicable. Strengths: • Multiple model comparison: This study explores a wide range of algorithmic approaches to optimise predictive performance by implementing various machine learning models (TabNet Classifier, Random Forest, XGBoost, MLP Classifier, AdaBoost, LGBM Classifier, and CatBoost Classifier). • Cross-validation: The use of cross-validation ensures robust model selection and reduces the risk of overfitting, thus enhancing the generalisability of the results. • Hyperparameter tuning: The application of Optuna’s TPE-based optimisation allows for efficient hyperparameter selection, which leads to improved model performance. • Handling imbalanced data: Our dataset is highly imbalanced. Among the 471 samples collected, 77.9% (367) of the participants intended to transfer while only 22.1% (104) of the participants intended to stay. This study addresses class imbalance by incorporating the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE). SMOTE will oversample the minority class (nurses who do not intend to transfer) until it has the same number as the majority (nurses who intend to transfer), thus ensuring the better prediction of minority cases. • Feature importance analysis: The use of SHAP to interpret feature importance adds transparency and interpretability, which facilitates understanding the decision-making processes of the models. Weaknesses: • Limited interpretability in some models: While powerful, models such as XGBoost and CatBoost can be complex, which makes it harder to interpret the underlying relationships compared with simpler models, such as logistic regression. • One-hot encoding scalability: Using one-hot encoding in preprocessing can lead to high-dimensional data, especially when categorical features have many unique values, which potentially impacts computational efficiency. • Potential data leakage risk: The extensive preprocessing steps, including feature selection and scaling, require careful management to avoid leakage between the training and testing data. • Hyperparameter tuning computational cost: Although Optuna optimises the process, the computational cost of hyperparameter tuning across multiple models can be high, particularly when combined with cross-validation. • SMOTE limitations: While SMOTE helps balance the dataset, it may generate synthetic data that do not perfectly represent real-world nurse resignation patterns, which could introduce noise into the training process.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence ethical awareness and academic integrity among medical students at the University of Khartoum: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Aseel Salah Gabir Muhalil, Abeer Ali Bin Ali Alfaki, Abdelgader Ali Basheer Ali, Yousef Mohamed Ahmed Alslawy, Alaa Alfatih Altaib Albashir, Amna Mohammed Hajhamad Abdelgadir, Aya Eldirdieri Salim Ahmed, HIBA ALZAIN SALIH ABDALGADER, Rafaa Mohammed Abd-Elrahim Abdallah, Yasir Adil Abdalla Mohamed
papers.abstract: Integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical education implies significant opportunities along with significant ethical challenges. Despite the substantial medical student uptake of artificial intelligence globally, little comprehensive assessments of ethical awareness are being conducted. This study aimed to assess artificial intelligence awareness and academic integrity level among University of Khartoum medical students and to examine relationships between the awareness level, demographic factors, artificial intelligence exposure, and tool use behavior. An institutional cross-sectional descriptive study of Years 3–6 medical students at University of Khartoum Faculty of Medicine in 2025 was conducted. A convenience sampling with quota allocation was used, and 349 students responded. The instrument included demographic variables, artificial intelligence exposure measures, and the 32-item Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity Scale. Nonparametric tests were applied. Participants were predominantly female (69.3%) with a mean age of 22.85 years. The median total Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity score was 4.16, indicative of moderate ethical awareness based on sample-derived empirical tertiles. Privacy and Data Protection were highest (median 4.67), with lowest scores in Transparency and Fairness/Non-Discrimination (3.80). Female students were more aware ( P = .01). No year-based differences observed. While 63.9% had minimal formal artificial intelligence exposure, 51.6% had moderate to high informal exposure. ChatGPT usage was prevalent (94.6%), and Google Gemini/Notebook LM usage was strongly associated with higher awareness ( P = .003). Informal exposure was positively correlated with awareness ( P = .01), but formal exposure was not. Multiple regression indicated that gender, informal exposure, and tool accounted for 11.2% of the variance in awareness. University of Khartoum medical students showed moderate-to-high aggregate artificial intelligence, ethical sensitivity, with areas of privacy protection and accountability being of particular strength. Gaps exist for awareness of transparency and fairness. The dominance of informal learning pathways over formal instruction, and gender variability favoring female students are significant findings. Findings highlight the need for institutional policies and conducting longitudinal research to track the evolution of AI ethics throughout medical training.

papers.title: What matters in medical training in Wales: a thematic analysis of Wales-specific responses to the NHS England Medical Training Review Call for Evidence
papers.authors: Ishrat Islam, Thomas Lawson, Caroline Groves, Anton Saayman
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Postgraduate medical education in the United Kingdom is delivered within health services experiencing sustained workforce shortages, workload pressure, and reduced supervisory capacity. National evidence has highlighted concerns around staffing, burnout, training quality, flexibility, and progression, but Wales-specific qualitative synthesis remains limited. This study aimed to identify and interpret key themes arising from the Wales-specific responses to the NHS England Medical Training Review Phase 1 Call for Evidence and to situate these findings in relation to wider UK medical education and workforce evidence. Methods This qualitative study used thematic analysis of Wales-specific free-text responses from the NHS England Medical Training Review Phase 1 Call for Evidence. The dataset comprised responses from 133 respondents who identified with, or commented on, the Welsh medical training context. Analysis involved inductive coding within the broad question-led domains of the parent survey and drew on reflexive principles. Findings were compared at the theme level with the broader Medical Training Review Call for Evidence summary and General Medical Council State of Medical Education and Practice workplace evidence. Results Eleven cross-cutting themes were identified: training capacity and workforce pressures; recruitment, progression, and career development; geographical stability and flexibility; training quality, supervision, and protected educational time; workload, wellbeing, and flexibility; equity and inclusion; curriculum modernisation; service-training conflict; community and interface training; digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence; and system-level reform. The strongest alignment with broader evidence concerned workforce capacity, supervision constraints, service pressure, and structural reform. Wales-specific responses added contextual depth by showing how these pressures were experienced in relation to place-based retention, progression from non-training roles, and the displacement of training by service demand. Conclusions Wales-specific responses to the NHS England Medical Training Review indicate that concerns about medical training in Wales are closely connected to wider UK workforce and training pressures yet shaped by the Welsh service and workforce context. Reform should address training capacity, workforce planning, protected educational time, equitable progression, flexibility, and sustainable working conditions as interdependent features of postgraduate medical education.

papers.title: Body weight following a multidomain lifestyle intervention in older adults at risk of dementia – A post-hoc analysis of the AgeWell.de-trial
papers.authors: Andrea E. Zülke, Adrian Schultz, Melanie Luppa, Solveig Weise, Alexander Bauer, Juliane Döhring, Carmen Wolf, Robert Philipp Kosilek, Jan Ziegler, Christian Brettschneider, Thomas Frese, Hanna Kaduszkiewicz, Jochen Stefan Gensichen, Wolfgang Hoffmann, Hans‐Helmut König, Birgitt Wiese, David Czock, Jochen René Thyrian, Steffi Gerlinde Riedel-Heller
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lifestyle interventions provide a promising approach to address higher body weight as a risk factor for dementia. OBJECTIVE: The AgeWell.de-trial was primarily designed to preserve cognitive function and reduce dementia risk. In this post-hoc analysis, we investigated body weight following the multidomain intervention among older adults with overweight or obesity, as well as the role of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss. METHODS: Analyses used data from the cluster-randomized AgeWell.de-trial, testing a multidomain intervention (dietary counselling, enhancement of physical, social and cognitive activity, medication review, intervention for cardiovascular risk factors, depressive symptoms/grief, if applicable) over 24 months in adults aged 60 to 77 years at risk for dementia. Associations between intervention allocation and body weight at follow-up were analyzed using linear regression, controlling for covariates, based on multiply imputed data. RESULTS: The sample included n = 678 participants with a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m², mean age (SD): 68.9 (4.8), 52.1% female. Group allocation was not associated with body weight at 24-month follow-up (b (unstandardized regression coefficient) = -0.30, 95% CI: -0.51; 1.11). Older age (b = -0.14, 95% CI: -0.25; -0.03) and a high level of education (b = -1.28, 95% CI: -2.55; 0.00) were linked to lower body weight at follow-up, while higher baseline body weight predicted higher body weight at follow-up (b = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.91; 0.98). Levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss remained high but stable in both groups, regardless of group allocation. CONCLUSIONS: In this post-hoc analysis, group allocation was not associated with lower body weight at follow-up. Despite high levels of motivation and confidence regarding weight loss and favorable changes in diet and physical activity in the intervention group, these changes did not translate into measurable weight loss. TRIAL REGISTRATION: AgeWell.de was prospectively registered in the German Clinical Trials Register on December 7th, 2017 (DRKS trial identifier DRKS00013555).

papers.title: Emerging Technologies in Teacher Professional Development Through the Lens of Self-Determination Theory: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: 司乃文, Yingxiong Han (韩映雄)
papers.abstract: Purpose This systematic review analyzed 46 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, revealing eight digital technology types, including Information and Communication Technology, Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Open Educational Resources, Massive Open Online Courses, Learning Management System, and Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality. Design/Approach/Method Technologies are organized across three conceptual layers: Infrastructure, Algorithm, and Application Layer. This study aims to investigate: (a) the key functions and implementation barriers of eight emerging technology types; (b) their impacts on teachers’ autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and (c) their impacts on the equity, quality, and efficiency of scalable teacher professional development. Findings Findings reveal that all technologies demonstrate dual impacts on the three psychological needs, both enabling and constraining, with competence most consistently supported across layers. Equity outcomes prove most challenging. Originality/Value This review concludes that effective technology integration requires human-centered ecosystems that amplify, not replace, teacher agency, advancing a value-rational approach recognizing teachers’ professional flourishing as an intrinsic good rather than an instrumental means.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Valuation Bottlenecks: Why Isn’t a Better Business Enough for a Higher Market Capitalization?
papers.authors: Shumpei Iwao, Vatsal Mitesh Tailor, Qi Wu
papers.abstract: Firms often improve operations, disclosure, governance, or financing capacity without an immediate and proportional market-capitalization response. Could a single unresolved concern limit the market's response to improvements elsewhere in the firm? Classical multifactor and machine-learning models ask which risks or characteristics explain or predict returns. We ask whether the relatively weakest among several coexisting firm conditions receives disproportionate valuation weight. We model equity value as the lower envelope of lens-specific valuations. A hard minimum makes one lens locally binding; a soft minimum assigns continuous, state-dependent weights. We use exploratory factor analysis on 268 accounting characteristics to construct five firm-state lenses, with membership and weights determined by the loading structure rather than by an economic taxonomy, and rank each lens within industry, size, and quarter peers. We document a weakest lens effect : beyond the additive effects of all five lens ranks, a firm's weakest lens carries an incremental association with next-quarter returns, and it survives saturated joint rank-quintile controls. Gating the test at the bottom decile and then the bottom quintile of the peer distribution, the association is concentrated among firms whose weakest lens is weak against peers and not merely lowest within the firm. In baseline soft-min specifications, it fades steadily as the gate is widened. We then investigate whether analyst attention may help explain this pattern. We use large language models on 1.7 million earnings-call questions and find that, in baseline specifications, the weakest lens attracts a larger share of questions, especially when it is also weak among peers; this cross-sectional alignment is consistent with an attention channel as one possible explanation for the observed return pattern. The framework offers managers seeking to maximize market capitalization a new perspective on prioritizing scarce managerial attention.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Changes in Emotional Recognition: A Signal Processing Approach Using Wavelet Features
papers.authors: Beulah Snowin, Philo Hazeena, Lakshmi S. Narasimhan
papers.abstract: Background: motion recognition using electroencephalography (EEG) has gained significant attention in the fields of affective computing and human-computer interaction due to its ability to capture real-time neural responses. EEG signal variations associated with emotional states can be analysed using wavelet-based signal processing within the arousal-valence framework. Purpose: This study aims to analyse EEG signal variations associated with emotional states using a wavelet-based signal processing approach within the arousal-valence framework. Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted on 48 healthy participants. Emotional states were induced using image, video and music stimuli categorised under the arousal-valence model. EEG signals were recorded using the standard 10-20 electrode placement system. The acquired signals were pre-processed and analysed using discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to extract time-frequency features, including energy and entropy. Statistical analysis was performed to evaluate hemispheric differences and gender-based variations. Results: Differences in EEG activity were observed between the left and right hemispheres across multiple emotional states (p < .05). Video and music stimuli produced stronger and more distinguishable EEG responses compared to image-based stimuli. Negative emotions demonstrated higher discriminative patterns than positive emotions. Gender-based variations were also observed in EEG responses. Conclusion: Wavelet-based EEG feature analysis provides meaningful and discriminative information for emotion recognition and may provide a robust feature set for future machine learning-based emotion recognition systems. Further studies incorporating classification algorithms and larger data sets are required to validate their predictive performance.

papers.title: The coercion of care: Compulsory connectivity in assistive communication
papers.authors: Qiutong Meng
papers.abstract: Assistive communication expands autonomy, participation and social life. Under particular conditions, the capacity to communicate becomes a duty to remain available. I describe this configuration as compulsory connectivity. It arises when mediated output functions as evidence of presence, nonresponse attracts an adverse default and refusal threatens care, support or recognition. Advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and locked-in syndrome provide the central case because augmentative and alternative communication may enable speech, environmental control, relationships and access to care. Bringing disability media studies into conversation with deep mediatisation and digital disconnection, the essay identifies three mechanisms: the labour of legibility, recursive interpretation in care and divergence between technical and relational states. Together they make output perform presence and render silence legible as loss. The normative alternative is protected ambient presence: social recognition without continuous communicative production. A two-layer protocol gives that principle operational form: communication status distinguishes engagement from recognised withdrawal, while an independently governed safety channel preserves agreed clinical safeguards. Smartphone messaging isolates availability pressures under weaker dependence; brain–computer interfaces provide a prospective test of the boundary between detectable neural activity, communicative intent and consent. Accessibility becomes emancipatory when control extends beyond how a person communicates to whether communication is owed.

papers.title: Improving the Teaching of Ethics in Tanzania: Pedagogy and Content
papers.authors: Ivan B. Kivinge
papers.abstract: Abstract Ethics is central to human flourishing. Without ethics human wellbeing can rarely be attained. Globally, with developments in scientific research and new technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, ethics becomes even more crucial to guide people in their proper deployment.
