Further, the global economic order and geopolitical landscape are altering dramatically; if not morally guided these unprecedented changes pose a threat to humanity as a whole. Nationally, Tanzania has begun implementing the National Development Vision 2050. For its realisation, ethical leadership of human resource mobilisation and a participating citizenry are key prerequisites. Tanzania’s government has put in place several measures including compulsory moral education at primary and secondary levels. However certain aspects of the curriculum and its delivery need improvement and support. Although Tanzanians may be aware of existing ethical frameworks that are recognised internationally, African ethics would be relevant to their aspirations.

papers.title: Viewpoint on Neural Mechanisms for Multisensory Integration in Speech Perception
papers.authors: Michael S. Beauchamp, John J. Foxe, Edmund C. Lalor
papers.abstract: Abstract This interview brings together perspectives from the authors on the origins, evolution, and future directions of multisensory neuroscience. The authors reflect on their early motivations, tracing the field’s development from studies of intersensory attention and early cortical integration to contemporary investigations of naturalistic audiovisual speech. They highlight landmark empirical and methodological advances — including high-density EEG, BOLD fMRI, intracranial recordings, and analyses of continuous stimuli — that overturned the traditional view of multisensory integration as a strictly higher-order process. Central themes include the role of the superior temporal sulcus in audiovisual speech, the hierarchical and temporally dynamic nature of multisensory binding, and ongoing debates concerning the mechanisms underlying neural responses to naturalistic stimuli, such as evoked-response versus oscillatory-entrainment accounts. The interview also addresses current controversies, including interpretations of redundant signals effects and the neural organization of language, as well as concerns about underpowered studies and reproducibility. The authors strongly advocate open science practices, emphasizing data and code sharing while acknowledging structural challenges. Looking ahead, they discuss the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, invasive human recordings, genetic models, and translational applications, particularly for neurodevelopmental disorders. Collectively, this dialogue situates multisensory integration as a rapidly advancing field bridging sensory processing, cognition, and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Health Literacy and Communication in Stroke Prevention, Management, and Recovery: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
papers.authors: Mulubrhan F. Mogos, Susan E. Maynard, Stacy M Perrin, Mai N. Nguyen‐Huynh, Mona N. Bahouth, Catherine Torrington Eaton, Iris Z. Feinberg, Joyce Sampson, Jared W. Magnani, Kiffon Marie Keigher
papers.abstract: Health literacy is a critical component of high-quality stroke care. Across the continuum from prevention through recovery, health literacy is strongly associated with functional outcomes and stroke-related morbidity. Despite its importance, it is often overlooked, leaving patients and caregivers overwhelmed by communication demands that exceed their capacity. These mismatches are especially pronounced among individuals with stroke-related cognitive or language impairments, limited English proficiency, socioeconomic disadvantage, or limited digital literacy. This scientific statement synthesizes current evidence on the role of health literacy and communication within stroke systems of care and identifies nurse-led opportunities to advance equity and patient-centered outcomes while recognizing this as a shared interprofessional responsibility. Nurse-led interventions, including teach-back-based education, dyadic psychoeducational programs, and tailored digital support, have demonstrated improvements in stroke knowledge, self-efficacy, quality of life, and caregiver preparedness. However, the literature is marked by methodological heterogeneity. Many studies are underpowered and infrequently use validated health literacy or communication measures. Future directions include standardized assessment of health literacy; literacy-sensitive, nurse-led, and interprofessional care models; workforce training in plain-language and culturally responsive communication; and organizational health literacy principles. Emerging technologies, including telehealth and artificial intelligence, offer promise for improving communication and personalization but require rigorous evaluation to minimize bias and ensure equity and usability.

papers.title: An Empirical Analysis of LLM Usage in Software Engineering Course Projects
papers.authors: Hoyeon Jeong, Jindae Kim
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have had a substantial impact on software engineering research and practice, as well as on software engineering education. In Software Engineering (SE) education, prior studies have mainly examined students’ LLM usage through surveys, interviews, or short-term observations, offering limited visibility into their actual development activities. As a result, it remains unclear how students’ perceptions of LLM usage match their actual development practices. To address this gap, we analyze course project data collected over three years from 158 students enrolled in an upper-level SE course, together with students’ experience-sharing presentations, survey responses, and activity logs. We examine LLM integration by jointly analyzing students’ perceived usage and usefulness from surveys and presentations, their actual development activities captured through VS Code activity logs, and their project performance based on evaluation results across different levels of LLM support. By combining these analyses, we connect students’ reported LLM usage with their actual development activities and assess its relation to learning outcomes in SE course projects. Our results show that students utilized LLMs frequently for code-related tasks and generally found them helpful, with frequent usage increasing over the course project while perceptions shifted as project complexity grew. Activity log analysis revealed divergent patterns in LLM usage, reflecting both increasing dependency and deliberate efforts to maintain development independence. Across three years, integrating LLM support did not lead to statistically significant differences in final project achievement as measured by requirement satisfaction, although students with LLM support produced substantially larger software systems and lower-performing teams showed mild benefits, suggesting that LLMs may help reduce the influence of programming proficiency on project outcomes. Our findings highlight both the benefits and tensions of LLM integration in SE course projects and suggest that future SE course designs may incorporate more complex and challenging SE tasks beyond implementation-focused requirements, while also providing explicit education on prompt engineering, supporting students’ code comprehension of rapidly generated LLM-assisted code, and helping students avoid excessive dependency on LLM tools during development.

papers.title: Facial Expression and Behavior Modeling from Digital Avatars to Expressive Humanoid Robots: A Review
papers.authors: Xu Zhang, Longbing Cao
papers.abstract: Endowing humanoid robots with expressive, controllable, and robust facial expressions and behaviors is essential for advancing human-like humanoid-human interaction across social, healthcare, and service domains. However, transforming the semantic richness and flexibility of virtual avatars into the mechanical, real-time, and calibration constraints of physical humanoids remains a fundamental challenge. This survey reviews facial expression and behavior modeling for both and analyzes their virtual-to-physical gaps from a deployment-oriented perspective. Our review is organized along three axes: (i) modeling paradigms , with emphasis on actuator compatibility and transferability; (ii) expression control strategies , assessed for their potential to enable robust robotic deployment; and (iii) deployment dimensions , which examine the challenges of parameter-to-actuator mapping, calibration, and real-time operation. This survey provides a critical synthesis of the trade-offs between expressive fidelity and hardware feasibility. We analyze persistent gaps between algorithmic advances and embodied realization, and review the datasets, metrics, and evaluation frameworks necessary for advancing expressive humanoids and their facial expression and behavior modeling. Finally, we identify open challenges and future research directions, including multimodal coordination, adaptive personalization, and standardized evaluation, providing guidance for next-generation expressive human-like humanoids, and systematically integrating advances in humanoid modeling with actionable deployment of humanoid facial expressions and behaviors.

papers.title: Interaction Patterns and Embodied Design Processes Using an AI Robotics Kit for K–12 Education
papers.authors: Anssi Lin, Henriikka Vartiainen, Anssi Salonen, Matti Tedre
papers.abstract: This multidisciplinary study explores how children interact with a low-cost robotics educational tool designed to teach machine learning (ML) concepts through hands-on making. Artificial intelligence (AI) and ML are increasingly integrated into K-12 education, yet tangible approaches are not extensively studied. We conducted three researcher-led interventions with children aged 10, 11 and 13, each tasked to build an AI-enhanced robot using the robotics kit. Interventions were analyzed both qualitatively and with process mining methods to gain an in-depth view of the interactions. Findings indicate that designing and building were very central throughout the interventions, with the affordances guiding the design process forward. Children exhibited emerging data-driven thinking and ownership of their design process, while still requiring tailored scaffolding throughout the design process. We identify a general structure of the design process from all the interventions and emphasize the importance of building and designing activities. This study provides a new methodological lens to analyzing the interactions between children and embodied AI-educational tools while also contributing to the current body of knowledge on designing and effectively leveraging embodied learning tools.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Explainable Hybrid Machine Learning and True Pareto-Optimal Inverse Design for Strength–Conductivity Optimization of High-Performance Cu–Cr–X Copper Alloys
papers.authors: Aswin Karkadakattil
papers.journal: International Journal of Computational Materials Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: High-performance Cu–Cr–X copper alloys face an inherent trade-off between mechanical strength and electrical conductivity. This study develops a physics-informed, interpretable machine-learning framework for their optimization and inverse design. A literature-derived dataset of 3017 experimental records was compiled, with 2302 records retained after preprocessing and reliability filtering. Metallurgically motivated descriptors, including Aging Severity, Cold Work Index, Cr–Aging interaction, Zener-pinning and Hall–Petch proxies, and source reliability, were incorporated. Random Forest, Extra Trees, XGBoost, and CatBoost were evaluated using a leakage-free 10-fold out-of-fold stacking framework. The stacking model achieved R 2 = 0.895, MAE = 17.3, and RMSE = 48.7, compared with R 2 values of 0.781, 0.802, 0.837, and 0.857, respectively, for the four base learners. SHAP analysis highlighted Cu, Cr, source reliability, aging-related variables, and precipitation-related descriptors as important predictors. Pareto-based inverse screening identified candidates with predicted Strength Index values exceeding 520 and approaching 580, with conductivity reaching approximately 95 %IACS. The framework provides a data-driven route for narrowing the Cu–Cr–X design space, while the predicted candidates require experimental validation.

papers.title: Eating Behaviors, Dietary Intakes, and Other Lifestyle Behaviors as Mediators of Genetic Susceptibility to Obesity: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Simone Lemieux, Laurence Pelletier, Angelo Tremblay, Marie‐Claude Vohl, Vicky Drapeau, Louis Përusse
papers.abstract: Mediation analysis identifies variables that explain the causal pathways linking an exposure (here genetic susceptibility to obesity) to an outcome (here obesity-related traits), offering potential targets for weight management interventions. This review followed the PRISMA guidelines and systematically searched the literature up to August 2024 in four databases (Web of Science, Embase, Medline, CINAHL) to identify studies using mediation analysis with genetic or polygenic risk scores of obesity as exposure and body mass index (BMI) as outcome. Twenty-nine studies focusing on eating behaviors, diet quality, physical activity, and other lifestyle factors were included. Eating behaviors traits emerged as the most influential mediators of genetic susceptibility to obesity. Mediation explained 23%-56% of the genetic effect on BMI for disinhibition, 6%-23% for uncontrolled eating, 4%-19% for susceptibility to hunger, 4%-15% for emotional eating and 8%-10% for satiety responsiveness. For diet quality, fat intake mediated 4%-5% of the effect, while whole grain intake explained 1%-2%. Physical activity accounted for 0.3%-23% of mediation, whereas sedentary time explained 5%-43%. These findings highlight that behavioral and lifestyle factors substantially mediate genetic risk for obesity. Interventions targeting disinhibition, uncontrolled eating, susceptibility to hunger, fat intake, whole grain consumption, physical activity and sedentary behavior could improve obesity prevention and management, particularly for individuals with higher genetic susceptibility.

papers.title: Learning Adaptation in Artificial Intelligence‐Enabled Nursing Education: A Network Analysis of Artificial Intelligence Literacy, Self‐Regulated Learning and Academic Resilience
papers.authors: Xueqing Gong, Xiao Zemei, Dan Chen, Danyan Li, Xiahui Xiao
papers.abstract: AIMS: To examine the interconnections among artificial intelligence literacy, self-regulated learning strategies, and academic resilience in undergraduate nursing students, and to conduct an exploratory comparison of network characteristics between students with and without clinical practice experience. DESIGN: A cross-sectional survey. METHODS: Using convenience sampling, 1784 undergraduate nursing students were recruited from five universities in Hunan Province, China, between March and May 2026. Participants completed a demographic questionnaire and three validated scales. Network analysis estimated node strength, bridge strength, and predictability. Bootstrap procedures assessed network accuracy and stability, and the Network Comparison Test was used to conduct an exploratory comparison between students with and without clinical practice experience. RESULTS: The 10-node network contained 35 non-zero edges and had a mean predictability of 62.6%. Artificial intelligence evaluation showed the highest node strength, followed jointly by monitoring learning strategies and cognitive maturity. Evaluating and revising learning strategies showed the highest bridge strength, followed by cognitive maturity. In the exploratory subgroup analysis, the overall network structure differed between students with and without clinical practice experience, whereas global strength did not. CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence evaluation, monitoring learning strategies and cognitive maturity showed relatively high node strength, whereas evaluating and revising learning strategies and cognitive maturity showed relatively high cross-domain bridge strength. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION: Findings may inform nursing curricula integrating artificial intelligence literacy, learning regulation, and academic adaptation. IMPACT: This study addressed fragmented understanding of these capacities. It identified dimensions with relatively high node strength and bridge strength, providing exploratory evidence for future nursing education research. REPORTING METHOD: This study was reported in accordance with the STROBE statement. NO PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: This study did not involve patients, service users, caregivers, or members of the public.

papers.title: A Fatigue Life Prediction Method Based on Optimized Data Augmentation Algorithm and Adaptive Sampling Model
papers.authors: Lingwen Jiang, Xueshu Liu
papers.journal: Fatigue & Fracture of Engineering Materials & Structures
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Machine learning–based fatigue life prediction is essential; yet their datasets typically contain fewer than 50 samples, severely challenging predictive modeling. This study proposes an integrated framework of simulated annealing (SA)‐guided data augmentation and residual‐driven adaptive sampling (RAS) bagging ensemble. SA optimization identifies augmentation parameters that maximize RAS‐bagging performance, while RAS adaptively reweights bootstrap sampling toward high‐residual regions to enhance ensemble diversity. Repeated nested cross‐validation (tenfold, 30 repetitions with identical splits) showed significant improvements over classical bagging on the CFRP () and DH36 () datasets (Wilcoxon signed‐rank test, all ; large effect sizes, Cliff's ). Mean improved from to and from to , respectively, while mean MAE was reduced by 85.8% and 64.3%, and the standard deviation of decreased by more than an order of magnitude (0.57–0.02 and 1.48–0.13). In addition, the 80% conformal prediction intervals derived from the proposed model achieved an empirical coverage rate of 84%, providing conservative lower‐bound life estimates for reliability‐oriented decision‐making. These results demonstrate that physically bounded data augmentation combined with adaptive ensemble resampling effectively alleviates data scarcity in fatigue life prediction within the studied datasets. Validation on larger independent cohorts, field data, and online learning scenarios is warranted before the framework can be extended to automotive reliability assessment and structural health monitoring.

papers.title: Young Learners' Motivation for AI ‐Supported Extracurricular French Vocabulary Learning: A Q Methodological Study
papers.authors: Xun Lu, Nanlan Pei
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping extracurricular language learning, yet little is known about how young learners construct motivation when using AI to learn less commonly taught foreign languages. This study investigates primary school students' motivational typologies and the factors related to these configurations in AI‐supported extracurricular French vocabulary learning. Twenty learners completed a Q sorting task based on 34 motivational statements, and eight participants were subsequently selected for semi‐structured interviews. Q factor analysis identified four motivational typologies: socially supported learners, future‐oriented learners, enjoyment‐driven learners and mastery‐oriented learners. Thematic analysis further revealed four cross‐cutting factors related to these motivational configurations: human support, AI‐supported autonomy, interactive enjoyment and competence feedback. The findings show that the motivational value of AI is not uniform but depends on how young learners connect technological affordances with interpersonal relationships, personal agency, enjoyment, future goals and perceived progress. By integrating Q methodology with Self‐Determination Theory, this study advances a configurational understanding of young learners' motivation and shows that the same AI‐supported learning opportunities can acquire different motivational meanings depending on learners' social and psychological configurations.

papers.title: Challenges and opportunities in higher education: the use of artificial intelligence in sport management subjects
papers.authors: Jerónimo García Fernández, Ali Sevilmiş, Salvador Angosto Sánchez, Efi Tsitskari
papers.journal: Sport Business and Management An International Journal
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper explores the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on university teaching in sport management subjects. It investigates how AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and other generative systems, are reshaping pedagogical models, fostering innovation in curriculum design, and enhancing the personalization of learning experiences within higher education institutions. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews with 17 professors from eight European universities offering sport management programs. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis with AI-assisted coding through MAXQDA software to identify key dimensions of educational transformation, faculty perceptions, and ethical concerns. Findings Results reveal that AI enhances personalized learning, supports data-informed decision-making, and facilitates real-time feedback in sport management education. Educators view AI as a valuable tool for simulating real-world scenarios, optimizing resource management, and improving student engagement and creativity. However, persistent concerns emerge regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and the potential over-reliance on AI-generated content. The study emphasizes the urgent need to strengthen AI literacy, ethical awareness, and institutional guidelines for responsible adoption. Originality/value This research is among the first to examine AI integration in sport management education from a European academic perspective. It contributes by linking theoretical insights on AI pedagogy with practical applications, highlighting the ethical and professional implications of emerging technologies in a digitally transforming field.

papers.title: From groups to teams: applying Team Academy methodology in organisational development
papers.authors: Nina Swaddle, Heikki Toivanen
papers.abstract: Purpose Team Academy, known in Finnish as Tiimiakatemia, is a well-known method for team-based learning in education, but rarely studied as a tool for organisational development (OD). This article asks whether Team Academy methodology can help organisations move from groups to genuine teams, and whether human collective learning will become a key organisational strength as artificial intelligence changes what individuals can do. Design/methodology/approach The article combines a literature review, drawing on the learning organisation (Senge), knowledge creation (Nonaka and Takeuchi) and selfmanaged learning (Cunningham), with three semi-structured interviews. The practitioners interviewed had each introduced Team Academy methodology inside a large organisation: an industrial technology and logistics company, a telecommunications company and a financial services company. The three cases are discussed together, theme by theme, using thematic analysis. Findings Thematic analysis identified eight cross-case themes, including person-dependent adoption, partial uptake of Team Academy tools, letting go of hierarchical control and middle management as a friction point. Rather than one shared model, the cases show a repeating pattern: a committed individual applies parts of the methodology, meets resistance and builds trust through small steps. A six-phase framework is proposed. Originality/value Team Academy methodology has been widely studied in education, but very little academic work has looked at its use in OD. This article addresses that gap using original practitioner interviews from three sectors, and connects Team Academy to a topic not previously explored: artificial intelligence in the workplace. The resulting six-phase framework offers a new, practical starting point for organisations and researchers.

papers.title: Love as a foundation for global citizenship in human-centred AI-driven higher education institutions – a theoretical exploration
papers.authors: Claude‐Hélène Mayer
papers.abstract: Purpose This article aims at exploring global citizenship in the context of higher education institutions (HEIs) which are increasingly affected by artificial intelligence (AI)-driven interactions. By using AI in a human-centred way, educators can expand ways to create global citizenship, offer personalised and empathetic learning while transcending conventional boundaries of education. AI technologies, including natural language processing, machine translation and adaptive learning systems, enable learners to engage with diverse linguistic and cultural materials in increasingly meaningful ways. These tools facilitate immersive language learning, simulate intercultural interactions and provide real-time feedback connected to individual needs in contemporary HEIs. Design/methodology/approach This research uses a theoretical/conceptual approach. Findings While human-centred AI-driven HEIs are gaining importance, the need to create awareness of character strengths and human-centred new learning environments increases as well. In this article, it is argued that pedagogical love, as a character strength, becomes more important in contemporary HEIs than ever before. By integrating AI thoughtfully and ethically into curricula, educators and institutions can contribute to the education of empathetic, multilingual global citizens. Research limitations/implications This research is limited to a qualitative theoretical and conceptual study and may build the base for future empirical studies. Practical implications Love, as a character strength, might support mental health, well-being and human interconnectedness. Originality/value This approach can strengthen the role of HEIs in creating a more peaceful, integrated world.

papers.title: AI-enabled HR practices and agile talent deployment: the role of trust in AI and digital culture climate
papers.authors: Osama Khassawneh, Tamara Mohammad, Qasim Al-khafaji, Tahir Masood Qureshi
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled human resource (HR) practices foster agile talent deployment within startup firms, particularly highlighting the mediating role of trust in AI and the moderating influence of digital culture climate. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on self-determination theory, the authors propose and empirically test a moderated mediation model using data collected from a three-wave, multisource survey of 298 employees working in three technology-oriented startups in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Structural equation modeling was used to examine the measurement and structural models and to test the hypothesized relationships among AI-enabled HR practices, trust in AI, digital culture climate and agile talent deployment. Findings Results reveal that AI-enabled HR practices positively influence agile talent deployment through increased employee trust in AI. In addition, the mediated relationship is stronger within organizations characterized by a robust digital culture climate, indicating that a digitally supportive organizational context enhances the effectiveness of AI-enabled HR initiatives. Originality/value The paper advances AI-enabled human resource management research by framing trust in AI as a mechanism translating supportive, transparent HR systems into agile talent deployment rather than technology acceptance. It identifies digital culture climate as an enactment condition enabling trust to become adaptive action. Practically, HR leaders should align explainable AI, trust-building practices and digital norms to strengthen workforce agility.

papers.title: AI chatbot integration in fashion e-retail: consumer behaviour shifts and pathways to organizational change
papers.authors: Ying Wu, Malcolm Stewart, Fred A. Yamoah, Fahima Alam
papers.abstract: Purpose AI chatbots are increasingly embedded in customer-facing retail operations, yet research has examined them mainly as tools of individual adoption. This study positions consumer attitudinal and behavioural responses to chatbots in fashion e-retail as micro-level foundations that may create pressures and capabilities for organisational change. Design/methodology/approach Integrating TAM, TRA, TPB and the Uses and Gratifications Theory, an integrative model links technology readiness (TR), perceived adaptiveness (PA), hedonic motivation (HM), symbolic and social value and subjective norms (SN) to attitude and behavioural intention, tested with PLS-SEM on survey data from 776 UK consumers and bias-corrected bootstrap mediation analysis. Findings HM and PA emerge as dominant antecedents of attitude (R2 = 0.736), which strongly predicts behavioural intention (ß = 0.829, R2 = 0.699). Attitude mediates the effects of perceived usefulness (PU) and HM on intention; PA mediates the TR pathway. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, consumer-side design limits causal and organisational inference; longitudinal and cross-industry replication are priorities for future work. Practical implications Managers should treat chatbots as experience-design assets, reconfigure service KPIs around hedonic and adaptive value and address workforce implications of redistributed emotional labour. Social implications This study highlights the societal implications of AI-enabled service transformation, including risks of digital exclusion, job transformation, deskilling and the redistribution of emotional labour. As chatbots become embedded in organisational service infrastructures, firms should balance automation with inclusive, human-centred design. The findings emphasise accessible, ethically governed and culturally responsive AI systems that support equitable participation across diverse user groups while preserving appropriate opportunities for human interaction. Originality/value Recasting fashion e-retail as a distinctive, identity-driven site for theorising AI-enabled change, the study specifies three pathways through which chatbot integration may contribute to organisational change: demand-side expectation shifts, data-enabled organisational learning and the reconfiguration of service work.

papers.title: Addressing challenges of AI implementation in healthcare through business model innovation: insights from collaboration between healthcare professionals and AI experts
papers.authors: Zohreh Yousefi Dahka, Timo Koivumäki
papers.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare, but technological capabilities alone are insufficient for successful implementation. This study examines the implementation challenges that arise in collaboration between AI experts and healthcare professionals (HCPs) and explores how these challenges can be addressed through business model innovation by changing the content, structure and governance of the business model activity system. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the NASSS (non-adoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread and sustainability) framework, a qualitative approach was adopted using semi-structured interviews with four healthcare professionals and five AI professionals in Finland. The findings were then used to define challenge areas and changes in the activity system for business model innovation. Findings The study identifies implementation challenges related to demand-side value, the scope of AI tool use, trust in AI and stakeholder interaction. Interpreting these findings through the activity-system perspective shows how changes in the content, structure and governance of business model activities can address these challenges by improving collaboration between AI experts and HCPs throughout AI development and implementation. Originality/value This study contributes to the business model literature by linking AI implementation challenges to the activity-system perspective of business model innovation. It further contributes by demonstrating how changes in the content, structure and governance of business model activities can practically address these challenges through improved collaboration between AI experts and healthcare professionals.

papers.title: Tail-risk-constrained portfolio optimization with cluster pre-selection and machine learning: risk-adjusted evidence from the S&P 500
papers.authors: David Toscano, Juan Carlos Roca
papers.abstract: Purpose Standard Gaussian risk frameworks underestimate extreme joint losses in large equity universes, exposing investors to unbudgeted drawdowns. This article develops and tests a portfolio-construction pipeline that disciplines tail risk while exploiting forward-looking return signals. Design/methodology/approach The four-stage pipeline integrates a rolling tail-index (Hill) filter, cluster pre-selection, a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) risk-parity optimizer with Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) and extreme value theory (EVT) marginals and a Student-t copula, and an eight-classifier machine-learning ensemble that reallocates weights within the risk budget. It is tested on S&P 500 constituents across 75 monthly walk-forward windows (January 2020–January 2026), net of transaction costs. Findings Among twelve strategies, the pipeline delivers the highest Sharpe ratio (1.106) and monthly win rate (76.0%), surpassing risk parity, Hierarchical Risk Parity and the Gaussian CVaR specification it generalizes; block-bootstrap inference confirms its advantage over passive exposure (resampled mean Sharpe 1.316). Risk parity accumulates greater terminal wealth, a trade-off, since tail constraints curb high-momentum exposure in bull markets. Research limitations/implications The analysis is limited to S&P 500 constituents and a January 2020–January 2026 evaluation period. Results may differ in other asset classes, international markets or under alternative transaction-cost assumptions. Future research could examine adaptive clustering schemes, alternative dependence structures and real-time implementation constraints. Practical implications For investors prioritizing risk-adjusted efficiency over cumulative wealth, the framework is a transparent capital-allocation tool whose tail discipline holds at roughly 97 basis points annually. Originality/value To the authors' knowledge, this is the first to combine tail-index screening, clustering, GARCH-EVT-copula CVaR optimization and a machine-learning overlay within one framework, jointly addressing the dimensionality, distributional misspecification and information-neglect problems that defeat these tools in isolation.

papers.title: Conceptualising Chinese food therapy in tourism and hospitality to facilitate transformative service co-creation
papers.authors: Yanming Jiang, Jörg Finsterwalder, Ning Chris Chen
papers.journal: International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to conceptualise Chinese food therapy (CFT) as a culturally grounded service, a carrier of a non-Western well-being construct, and explores its transformative potential to extend transformative service research (TSR) in tourism and hospitality. It introduces how the core characteristics and principles of CFT are translated into transformative service mechanisms and develops a conceptual bridge that articulates its influence on well-being. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a conceptual approach that synthesises interdisciplinary literature, including CFT’s philosophy, TSR, food well-being and the tourism and hospitality field. Drawing on critical CFT concepts, this study develops a conceptual framework that illustrates how CFT principles are translated into a proposed transformative service cycle. Findings The study shows that CFT entails a balance-oriented well-being concept of harmony among body constitution, food practice and context. It proposes a co-created CFT transformative service cycle in which customers and CFT-informed service providers jointly interpret situated conditions, co-create adaptive transformative service design, use perceived well-being responses to guide re-evaluation and subsequent food practices. CFT’s preventive purpose extends the scope of TSR beyond vulnerability to everyday, population-wide well-being improvement and maintenance. Moreover, CFT’s inherently interactive nature aligns closely with value co-creation and experiential dynamics of tourism and hospitality services. Research limitations/implications The paper contributes to TSR research by reframing CFT as an adaptive transformative service mechanism, establishing a theoretical bridge between non-Western well-being approaches, traditional healthcare and modern experience design. Practical implications This study includes actionable implications for tourism and hospitality providers seeking to design CFT-inspired experiences. CFT presents an accessible pathway for integrating health and well-being intent into daily life and leisure food experiences. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this paper is the first to advance tourism and hospitality studies by positioning CFT knowledge as a unique approach that has not been comprehensively theorised before. It offers a foundation for future empirical research and contributes to a novel lens for reimagining food services and extending TSR.

papers.title: Immigrant earnings and labour-market positioning in a transforming digital labour market: evidence from Canada, 1971–2021
papers.authors: Xingfei Liu, Saba Ranjbar, Tony Fang, Husame Doganay, Arthur Sweetman
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines immigrant earnings trajectories and labour-market positioning across industries and employment arrangements in six Canadian provinces, as well as how industry patterns relate to digital intensity, telework feasibility, and productivity-relevant allocation. Design/methodology/approach Canadian Census microdata, 1971–2021 compare immigrant and native-born earnings across ten arrival cohorts by gender and age at arrival. For two recent cohorts, an earnings-based positioning measure combines industry mean annual earnings with full-time or part-time status multinomial-logit average marginal effects are estimated. The study also maps 2021 industry employment shares to external digital-intensity and telework-feasibility classifications. Individual productivity, artificial-intelligence (AI) adoption, Information and Communications Technology use, and remote-work uptake are not observed. Findings Entry earnings gaps and incomplete cohort convergence persist, especially among women and recent cohorts. Across the two positioning cohorts, immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earnings industries; gaps vary by source region and do not uniformly narrow. Education is associated with better positioning but does not eliminate gaps Immigrant employment is more concentrated in many digitally intensive categories but less concentrated in several higher-earnings, high-telework-feasibility industries digital intensity is not systematically related to immigrant employment shares. Originality/value The paper combines five decades of earnings evidence across ten cohorts with a two-cohort positioning measure and descriptive digital and telework mapping. It complements individual-level careers research by identifying structural differences in opportunity access with possible, unmeasured productivity implications.

papers.title: Trust me, I’m a robot: relational determinants of social robot acceptance among university students
papers.authors: Δήμητρα Παπαβασιλείου, Kleopatra Κonstantoulaki, Ioannis Kostopoulos, Ioannis Rizomyliotis
papers.abstract: Purpose Although social robots are increasingly being used in higher education‚ the relational antecedents of students’ acceptance of these robots remain unexplored. This study re-conceptualises the technology acceptance model (TAM) for social robots by shifting the theoretical focus from utilitarian beliefs toward the relational quality of the human–robot interaction (HRI), positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as main relational antecedents of students’ attitudes and behavioural intentions toward social robots. The study also examines the moderating effects of user motivation‚ empathy‚ risk aversion and technology readiness on the attitude–behavioural intention relationship. Design/methodology/approach Cluster sampling was used to define the sample‚ which comprised 900 university students from six public universities in Greece. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was conducted with AMOS 29 to test the proposed model. Findings Trust‚ satisfaction and rapport are strong positive predictors of student attitude toward social robots‚ which in turn positively influences students’ behavioural intention to use social robots. User motivation‚ empathy and technology readiness motivators (optimism and innovativeness) strengthen the relationship between attitude and behavioural intention towards social robots‚ while risk aversion and technology readiness inhibitors (discomfort and insecurity) attenuate this relationship. Research limitations/implications Despite the contributions achieved here‚ there are some limitations that deserve to be mentioned and suggest promising paths for future research. Because this research used a cross-sectional design‚ it does not allow for causality and the possibility to observe how attitudes and intentions towards social robots develop over time. Future studies with longitudinal designs are needed to test whether the identified antecedents for establishing a relationship with social robots (i.e. trust‚ satisfaction‚ rapport) can increase or decrease with repeated social robot interactions (Donnermann et al.‚ 2022). Practical implications Given the tight connection of trust‚ satisfaction and rapport with students’ perceptions‚ it is important that institutions also consider the quality of the HRI when deciding whether or not to use social robots as teaching assistants. This includes the robots’ ability to build trust through reliable behaviour‚ provide satisfaction through responsive interaction and achieve rapport through attentive‚ empathic and positive communication (Buhmann et al., 2026; Lemon and Dhanesh, 2026). Originality/value This study adds to the literature by being one of the first to conceptualise social robot acceptance as a relational phenomenon‚ positioning trust‚ satisfaction and rapport as core antecedents of attitude and behavioural intention‚ a theoretical move entirely absent from existing social robot acceptance and educational HRI research. Beyond the direct effects‚ this study introduces two theoretically grounded categories of individual-level moderators: psychological-relational moderators (motivation‚ empathy and risk aversion) and technology-related moderators (technology readiness)‚ which collectively provide a coherent and empirically novel account of the boundary conditions governing social robot acceptance among university students.

papers.title: Balancing flexibility and regulatory risk: AI-assisted strategies for non-GAAP disclosures in competitive markets
papers.authors: Hrishikesh Desai
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper develops an optimal control model to analyze how firms optimize their non-generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) disclosure strategies in competitive markets while managing regulatory risks, and examines how artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities in regulatory navigation and operational efficiency influence these optimal disclosure decisions. Design/methodology/approach The study employs an open-loop optimal control framework with a differential-game payoff structure, using a Hamiltonian formulation and Pontryagin's maximum principle to derive closed-form optimal disclosure strategies. Findings The research reveals that optimal disclosure strategies emerge from balancing the valuation benefits of disclosure flexibility against regulatory risk. AI capabilities affect firm strategy through two channels – (1) reduced regulatory sensitivity enables firms to sustain higher equilibrium flexibility levels, and (2) reduced adjustment costs accelerate convergence to target equilibrium flexibility. Comparative statics analysis identifies how competitive intensity, AI capabilities and firm characteristics influence equilibrium disclosure choices. Research limitations/implications The model employs an open-loop formulation and is limited to a two-firm setting. It assumes constant model parameters over the planning horizon and therefore does not capture time-varying market conditions or strategic feedback between firms. Practical implications The framework provides corporate managers with analytical insights into how investments in AI-enhanced regulatory navigation and operational efficiency influence optimal disclosure strategies. It also provides regulators with a theoretical basis for understanding how AI capabilities moderate the marginal relationship between disclosure flexibility and regulatory intervention. Originality/value This paper presents the first analytical model of a non-GAAP disclosure strategy that explicitly distinguishes between AI-enhanced regulatory navigation and operational efficiency, yielding closed-form solutions that facilitate rigorous comparative statics and generate testable empirical predictions.

papers.title: Art-infused fashion, movement of cultural meaning and meaning co-creation
papers.authors: Pielah Kim, Chiara Colombi
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research is to explore the evolution of cultural meanings of visual art, tracing their transformation into a multitude of meanings co-created by consumers through art-infused fashion and its subsequent effect on consumers’ responses toward art-infused fashion. Design/methodology/approach This research examines three illustrative cases: the collaborations between Takashi Murakami and Louis Vuitton, Piet Mondrian and Yves Saint Laurent and Jean-Michel Basquiat and Comme des Garçons. Each case involves a review of published works and photo-elicitation interviews, analyzed using the Gioia methodology. Findings Our research illustrates the significant influence of the market – comprising the fashion system providing art-infused fashion – and consumers, on the development of new and heterogeneous cultural meanings associated with art. Originality/value This research addresses limitations of the Movement of Cultural Meaning model by integrating a processing mechanism – consumer meaning co-creation – and further extends its implications for a specific consumer response, the feeling of ownership over art-infused fashion.

papers.title: Using informatics to understand pediatric allergic diseases
papers.authors: Matthew Grunewald, Robert W. Grundmeier, Stanislaw J. Gabryszewski
papers.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Recent advances in the power, utility, and accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled new methods of investigation in the biomedical sciences and opportunities to transform clinical workflows. As allergic conditions are among the most common chronic diseases affecting children, pediatric allergy represents a promising area for AI-augmented informatics methods to support molecular discovery, early identification, risk stratification, treatment customization, and longitudinal monitoring, as reviewed herein. RECENT FINDINGS: Recent pediatric allergy studies have applied informatics and AI methodologies across various data sources, including molecular and multiomic data, structured and unstructured electronic health record data, environmental exposures, diagnostic images, remote monitoring devices, and patient- and clinician-facing AI tools. Primarily still in the research phase, these approaches include biomarker discovery, disease phenotyping, risk stratification, prediction modeling, remote monitoring, and emerging chatbots for allergy education. SUMMARY: Although still relatively nascent within pediatric allergy, AI-augmented informatics shows promise for extracting usable information from complex data and developing tools aimed at personalizing disease detection and management. Most applications remain investigational, and continued progress will require transparency, rigorous validation, generalizability across diverse populations and health systems, feasibility of workflow integration, privacy protection, and longitudinal oversight to ensure continued safety and effectiveness.

papers.title: Individualized Theta Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation Modulates Mnemonic Discrimination and ERP Responses to Positive Information in Individuals With Elevated Depressive Symptoms
papers.authors: Xinyu Huang, Min Zhou, Chun Wang, Yuxin Huang, Wenchang Wang, Jianfei Shao, Junyu Mao, Jiaqi Li, Zhang Lei, Rong Ye, Chunyan Zhu, Yanghua Tian, Kongliang He, 余凤琼, Kai Wang
papers.abstract: Individuals with elevated depressive symptoms often show impairments in positive memory processing. This randomized, double-blind study investigated whether individualized theta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) using an OFC-oriented montage modulates mnemonic discrimination and ERP responses to positive information. Sixty-one individuals with elevated depressive symptoms received either real or sham stimulation before completing an emotional mnemonic discrimination task. Behavioral results showed that lure discrimination increased following real stimulation but not sham stimulation. EEG results showed that real stimulation modulated ERP responses during positive memory encoding and retrieval, as reflected by increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes during encoding and altered early retrieval-related ERP amplitudes. These findings suggest that individualized theta-tACS may influence both mnemonic discrimination performance and neural responses to positive information.

papers.title: EEG–ECG/HRV associations under multi-stage cognitive stress: characterization and mechanisms
papers.authors: Yanyu 艳羽 Lei 雷, Hongli Yu, Ranlin Zhao, Jiawei Wang, Wenxuan Nie, Tongtong Kan
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Mental stress affects cognitive, emotional, and cardiovascular function, but subjective stress scales are susceptible to individual bias. Brain-heart coupling offers a potential approach to stress assessment. This study examined stage-dependent EEG-ECG/HRV associations during mental arithmetic and Stroop tasks. APPROACH: Sixty healthy adults were recruited, EEG and ECG were recorded during baseline rest, four mental-arithmetic stages, inter-task rest, and four Stroop stages. Stage-specific Spearman correlations characterized between-participant associations between five EEG band-power measures and seven ECG/HRV indices. Mixed-effects models separating within- and between-participant effects tested whether within-participant associations varied across difficulty stages and tasks. MAIN RESULTS: Significant EEG-HRV correlations decreased in number after task onset and partially recovered during inter-task rest. Mental arithmetic showed more pronounced negative high-frequency EEG-vagal HRV correlations, whereas Stroop showed Theta/Beta-HR associations at onset and sustained Alpha-RMSSD associations during middle-to-late stages. Neither task showed FDR-significant stage-averaged within-participant associations. Within-participant EEG × difficulty-stage interactions were FDR-significant for 12 of 35 whole-frontal associations during mental arithmetic and none during Stroop. Combined models identified five significant within-participant EEG × difficulty × task interactions. No linear difficulty interactions survived FDR correction in sensitivity analyses. SIGNIFICANCE: These findings support stage-dependent EEG-ECG/HRV associations in this fixed-order cognitive-stress paradigm. They may inform physiologically interpretable candidate measures for objective mental stress assessment and wearable monitoring.

papers.title: Sleep EEG oscillations and synaptic plasticity in memory consolidation across NREM and REM sleep
papers.authors: Yuxuan Chen, Meimei Zhao, Xue Cao, Gao Zhou, Yu Zhang
papers.abstract: Based on a synthesis of recent advances, this review elucidates the distinct yet synergistic roles of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation. During NREM sleep, cortical slow oscillations (SOs) establish a temporal framework by alternating between UP and DOWN states, facilitating cross-regional communication. SOs phase-couple with thalamic spindles to coordinate hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), thereby driving the reactivation and transfer of labile hippocampal memories to neocortical networks for long-term storage. Concurrent synaptic homeostasis optimises network efficiency through global downscaling while selectively strengthening memory-relevant connections. In REM sleep, theta oscillations synchronise limbic-prefrontal-hippocampal circuits, and ponto-geniculo-occipital (PGO) waves further integrate emotional and procedural memories. The cholinergically dominant, monoamine-depleted neurochemical milieu of REM sleep promotes dendritic spine remodelling and sparse neuronal reactivation, enabling affective decoupling and synaptic refinement. Despite progress, key challenges remain in understanding cross-frequency oscillatory coupling among slow oscillations, spindles, ripples and REM-specific rhythms, glial contributions and clinical translation. Future integration of high-density electrophysiology with computational approaches may yield mechanistic models and clinically relevant biomarkers for sleep-based cognitive monitoring and intervention.

papers.title: Moral Courage vs. Moral Deference: Ethical Leadership and Employee Outcomes During AI-Assisted Internal Crises
papers.authors: James Ndone, Justin F. Willett, Lauren Flaker, Andrea Bergström, Luke W. Capizzo, Yan Jin, Margaret E. Duffy
papers.abstract: This study examines how leadership stance and AI disclosure shape employee responses to CEO communication during an internal, value-based crisis. It further examines the mediating roles of perceived message sincerity and negative moral emotions and the moderating role of employees’ perceived risk. Drawing on ethical leadership theory, workplace courage research, and costly signaling theory, this study employed a 3 (leadership stance: courage-emphasis vs. adaptation-emphasis vs. deference-emphasis) × 2 (AI disclosure: disclosed vs. not disclosed) between-subjects online experiment with 570 participants recruited via CloudResearch. Results showed that courage-emphasis messages generated higher perceptions of ethical leadership, stronger advocacy intentions, and greater perceived organizational READINESS than adaptation- or deference-emphasis messages. Perceived message sincerity significantly mediated these relationships, whereas negative moral emotions did not mediate leadership stance effects. Contrary to expectations, AI disclosure did not produce direct effects but interacted with leadership stance, reducing perceived organizational READINESS for adaptation-emphasis messages. Furthermore, higher perceived risk strengthened the positive effects of courage-emphasis messages on perceptions of ethical leadership and advocacy intentions. The findings contribute to ethical leadership and internal crisis communication research while offering practical guidance for AI-assisted leadership communication during internal, value-based crises.

papers.title: Staging the invisible: tracing public value co-creation through sub-micro infrastructures configured by information coordination organizations in China’s disaster information services
papers.authors: Qingyue Du, Ziqiang Han
papers.abstract: In disaster information services, citizen- and volunteer-generated information arrives as dispersed, uncertain reports rather than usable response information. This qualitative case study examines how Organization Z, a Chinese NGO functioning as an Information Coordination Organization (ICO), makes such information usable for response through sub-micro infrastructures. Data comprise 43 volunteer and 11 coordinator interviews, longitudinal participant observation, and multi-source materials. Four mechanisms emerged: emotional activation makes participation visible; epistemic calibration supports report credibility through traceability and comparability; cross-sector translation makes verified information interpretable and acceptable as a basis for response action; and reflexive learning makes response experience partially reusable. We conceptualize staging as a conditional account of public value formation organized around the four thresholds of visibility, credibility, legitimate actionability, and partial reusability. The study contributes to public value co-creation research by explaining how ICO information work conditions whether information-related participation contributes to disaster response and public value formation.

papers.title: Who reviews the reviews? When AI encounters academic aesthetics
papers.authors: Chen Qu
papers.abstract: This paper focuses on the challenges in digital-era peer review. It explains why an overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in peer review can pose problems beyond legal or ethical compliance. Confronting the hyper-pressure of today’s peer review and research funding systems, moving beyond the debate on whether and how to use AI in peer review, the paper introduces the concept of ‘academic aesthetics’ as an approach to understanding and tackling the challenges posed by digitality and AI.

papers.title: Navigating tensions: an empirical study of ELF teachers’ AI literacy and emotionally mediated responses to artificial intelligence in a Chinese university
papers.authors: Ping Wang
papers.abstract: The emergence of generative AI (GenAI) like ChatGPT constitutes a paradigm shift for language education, particularly for English as a Lingua Franca teachers in China, who face top-down mandates to adopt it. This mixed-methods study of 52 Chinese university teachers examined the interplay between their AI literacy, emotional responses, and professional identity. Findings reveal high awareness but a critical deficit in pedagogical and critical AI literacy. Teachers experienced profound ambivalence, simultaneous enthusiasm and existential anxiety as they grappled with a displaced identity as knowledge authorities. Emotions actively mediated their engagement, leading to defensive, performative, or transformative stances, often exacerbated by institutional ‘AI evangelism.’ The study concludes that support must extend beyond tool training to foster collaborative spaces for ethical sense-making and identity renegotiation, advocating a ‘pedagogy of integrity’ centred on process-oriented assessment and critical human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: When AI Gives the Feedback: Evaluative Outsourcing and Learner Agency in the English Writing Classroom
papers.authors: Anwar Farhan Mohamad Marzaini, Shahazwan Mat Yusoff, Nur Syahirah Ibrahim, Lijie Hao
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to provide feedback and support revision in English writing. Existing debate has largely examined the quality, accuracy, and effectiveness of AI-generated feedback. This conceptual paper argues that such concerns risk overlooking a more fundamental pedagogical issue: the redistribution of evaluative work between learner and system. Drawing on feedback literacy and evaluative judgement, the paper introduces evaluative outsourcing to describe the delegation of interpretive, judgemental, and decision-making work in feedback engagement to AI. It argues that GenAI can enable substantial textual improvement while requiring limited learner participation in the evaluation underlying revision, creating an AI feedback paradox in which better revision does not necessarily indicate better judgement. The paper proposes four principles for retaining learner evaluative agency: making evaluative decisions visible, designing for comparison, preserving consequential decisions for learners, and creating opportunities for evaluative transfer.

papers.title: From digital interaction to social connection: AI virtual humans as interactive learning partners for older adults
papers.authors: WeiCheng Pan, WanQing Zhang, Hong Chen, Qi Guo, Shuyi Wang, Hesen Li
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational and social interaction systems, its potential to alleviate digital exclusion and digital loneliness among older adults has attracted growing attention. Across two independent experiments, this study examined the association between AI-assisted interaction and digital loneliness among older adults, as well as the underlying psychological mechanisms. In Experiment 1, 90 older adults participated in a four-week randomized longitudinal experiment. A 2 (group) × 5 (time) mixed-design repeated-measures analysis of variance was conducted to compare changes in digital loneliness between an AI-assisted interaction group and a conventional interaction control group. The results showed that participants in the AI-assisted interaction group exhibited a more pronounced reduction in digital loneliness over the intervention period. Experiment 2 involved an independent sample of 210 participants and used PROCESS analyses to examine further the roles of perceived social support, evaluative emotional fulfillment, and technology acceptance. After controlling for baseline digital loneliness, perceived social support constituted a significant indirect pathway linking AI-assisted interaction to post-intervention digital loneliness, whereas the indirect effect through evaluative emotional fulfillment did not reach statistical significance. Technology acceptance further moderated the association between AI-assisted interaction and perceived social support. Taken together, these findings suggest that the association between AI-assisted interaction and reduced digital loneliness among older adults is primarily related to the perceived social support pathway. In contrast, evidence supporting the mediating role of evaluative emotional fulfillment remains insufficient. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding older adults’ experiences of social connectedness in inclusive AI-enabled environments. It underscores the importance of enhancing both the acceptability of AI-mediated interaction and its capacity to provide social support within educational and digital learning ecosystems.

papers.title: The Blurring of Reality in the Age of AI: Development of the AI-Induced Reality Perception Confusion Scale and Its Association with Generative AI Literacy and AI Anxiety
papers.authors: BİLAL KAYA, Sezen Ateş Yaman
papers.abstract: This study sought to develop the AI-induced Reality Perception Confusion Scale (AI-RPCS) and investigate the mediating role of AI-induced reality perception confusion in the association between GenAI literacy and AI anxiety. In Study I (N = 355), exploratory factor analysis revealed a single-factor structure, and item response theory indicated that the items displayed high discrimination and suitable difficulty. In Study II (N = 332), confirmatory factor analysis indicated satisfactory model fit indices for the single-factor structure. Significant relationships among the variables supported criterion validity. In Study III (N = 408), structural equation modelling indicated that AI-induced reality perception confusion mediated the association between GenAI literacy and AI anxiety. These results demonstrate the AI-RPCS's initial psychometric validity. Furthermore, this study suggests that GenAI literacy may be associated with lower levels of AI-induced reality perception confusion, which may, in turn, be associated with lower levels of AI anxiety.

papers.title: Measuring Successful Cooperation in Human-AI Teamwork: Development and Validation of the Perceived Cooperativity and Teaming Perception Scales
papers.authors: Christiane Attig, Christiane B. Wiebel-Herboth, Patricia Wollstadt, Tim Schrills, Mourad Zoubir, Thomas Franke
papers.abstract: As human–AI cooperation becomes increasingly prevalent, reliable instruments for assessing the subjective quality of cooperative human–AI interaction are needed. We introduce two theoretically grounded scales: the Perceived Cooperativity Scale (PCS), grounded in joint activity theory, and the Teaming Perception Scale (TPS), grounded in evolutionary cooperation theory. The PCS captures an agent’s perceived cooperative capability and practice within a single interaction sequence; the TPS captures the emergent sense of teaming arising from mutual contribution and support. Both scales were adapted for human–human cooperation to enable cross-agent comparisons. Across three studies (complete N=409) encompassing a cooperative card game (N1=94), LLM interaction (N2=182), and a decision-support system (N3=133), analyses of dimensionality, reliability, and validity indicated that both scales successfully differentiated between cooperation partners of varying cooperative quality and showed construct validity in line with expectations. The scales provide a basis for empirical investigation and system evaluation across a wide range of human–AI cooperation contexts.

papers.title: Adaptive Learning Systems for Children with Special Needs: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Ence Surahman, Zahid Zufar At Thaariq, Deni Darmawan, Élizabeth Gardère, Cecep Kustandi, Memet Karakuş, Nor Laili
papers.journal: International Journal of Disability Development and Education
papers.abstract: The growing emphasis on inclusive education and personalised learning underscores the need for effective educational strategies for children with special needs. While inclusive practices hold promise, their success often depends on individualised support. Adaptive learning systems, powered by advancements in AI and multimodal data, offer significant potential to tailor educational content and methods to the unique cognitive, behavioural and emotional profiles of these children. Hence, this systematic review aims to synthesise empirical evidence on the design, effectiveness and implementation of adaptive learning systems for children with special needs. The review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines. A systematic search of the Scopus database (1 January 2015 – 31 October 2025) identified 50 relevant empirical studies. Data were extracted and analysed using a structured coding form and thematic synthesis, focusing on study characteristics, adaptive technologies, strategies, outcomes and implementation factors. The analysis revealed a diverse landscape of technologies, including social robots for ASD, EEG-guided systems for ADHD and AI-tutoring for specific learning disabilities like dyslexia and dyscalculia. The findings demonstrated significant improvements in academic achievement, cognitive skills, and socio-emotional outcomes, across various disabilities. Future development should focus on disability-specific research, stronger evidence, and ethical, collaborative design involving educators, families, and children.

papers.title: Developing and Evaluating Hikaya: A Bilingual Mobile App for Children with Dyslexia and Dyscalculia
papers.authors: Saadeh Z. Sweidan, Khalid Ahmad Darabkh, Dareen M. Hamdan, Raghad W. Shkukani, Raghad M. Alzaatreh
papers.journal: International Journal of Disability Development and Education
papers.abstract: Dyslexia and dyscalculia are lifelong learning disabilities that affect how individuals process language and numbers. Children with these disabilities often require specialized support, which can be difficult and expensive to provide. Smartphones and their applications (apps) have created opportunities for accessible digital learning support. However, most existing educational apps do not support Arabic language. Motivated by this, we introduce Hikaya, an interactive Android application designed to assist children with learning difficulties, particularly in Arabic-speaking countries. Hikaya provides bilingual support in Arabic and English covering three core subjects: Arabic, English, and Math. Parents can create accounts, add children, and monitor progress through a dedicated dashboard. Children can engage with one of three learning models, including a unique Reading Karaoke feature that allows them to read scripts aloud while the app evaluates their performance. To assess Hikaya’s perceived utility, user satisfaction, and system usability, a perception survey was completed by 200 participants after a one-month test period. The results displayed highly positive user reception and strong satisfaction. As future work, we aim to expand Hikaya’s language capabilities by supporting various Arabic dialects and widely spoken global languages. We also plan to integrate adaptive learning algorithms using Artificial Intelligence and collaborate with educators and speech therapists to enhance the app’s learning value.

papers.title: Beyond performance: ritualized host–guest interaction drives value co-creation in heritage sites
papers.authors: Xin Lei, Wei Guo, Cuiling BAI
papers.abstract: As heritage tourism expands and shifts toward experience-oriented models, understanding how ritualized host–guest interaction generates meaning and contributes to value co-creation has become crucial. This study explores the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which ritualized host–guest interaction influences value co-creation behavior. Based on three scenario-based experiments and a field quasi-experiment at a heritage destination, it proposes and empirically tests a pathway linking interaction, cognition, trust, and value co-creation. The results show that heritage cognition and host–guest trust serve as dual mediators, illustrating the intertwined process of cognitive meaning-making and social relationship formation embedded in ritualized encounters. Furthermore, cultural salience shows a directional tendency to attenuate the cognitive pathway linking ritualized interaction to heritage cognition, while place attachment strengthens the trust-based pathway leading to value co-creation. The field quasi-experiment further supports the ecological validity of the proposed model. This study expands the social-psychological understanding of ritual in tourism and advances theoretical insights into how cultural experiences are transformed into value co-creation behavior. The findings offer practical implications for heritage destination management by emphasizing ritual-based design, cognitive engagement, and affective bonding as key drivers of heritage tourism development.

papers.title: Developing GenAI-Based Feedback Through Iterative Prompt Design: An Exploratory Study of Online Students’ Cognitive, Affective, and Behavioral Perceptions
papers.authors: Meva Bayrak Karsli, Sinem Çilligöl Karabey, Muhammed Guler, Ömer Arpacık, Melike Aydemir Arslan, Engin Kurşun, Ebubekir Kaba
papers.abstract: This study reports the iterative prompt-engineering development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)-based feedback in an online graduate course and examines students’ cognitive, affective, and behavioral perceptions. Grounded in the Student–Feedback Interaction Model, a qualitative case study involved 14 graduate students in a 14-week fully online course on open and distance learning. Students completed forum-based formative activities and received instructor-reviewed GenAI feedback. Informed by expert review, instructor observations, and student reflections, prompts evolved through three stages: checklist-style criterion verification, criteria-anchored synthesized explanations, and personalized diagnosis of strengths and weaknesses. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed through qualitative content analysis. Students reported improved feedback comprehensibility, detail, tone, and timeliness, valuing personalized, explanatory, criterion-based comments. However, inconsistencies between AI comments and instructor scores, limited conceptual evaluation, and lack of emotional presence weakened trust. GenAI therefore functions best as a draft-generation layer requiring sustained, active instructor oversight rather than as a stand-alone source of formative feedback.

papers.title: Three Poems – “My Kyiv,” “Despite Everything,” and “Love”
papers.authors: Oksana Kartavtseva
papers.abstract: The poems were written in Ukrainian in 2026 and translated into English by the author with the assistance of a generative AI tool (see disclosure below). They are original, have not been previously...

papers.title: Artificial intelligence maturity in buyer–seller exchange
papers.authors: Molly R. Burchett, Karen E. Flaherty, Douglas E. Hughes, Avinash Malshe, Ryan R. Mullins
papers.journal: Journal of Personal Selling and Sales Management
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping business-to-business (B2B) buying and selling, yet research has largely examined AI as a unilateral process enabler. While this perspective has generated important insights regarding AI adoption and performance, it overlooks a fundamental characteristic of B2B selling: exchange outcomes depend on the compatibility of buyer–seller decision processes at the exchange interface. To address this gap, the authors advance the concept of AI exchange maturity (i.e. extent to which decision authority within buyer–seller exchange is delegated to AI systems) and theorize its organizational antecedents. Building on this construct, the authors develop a bilateral theory of buyer–seller AI exchange in which value co-creation depends on the configuration of AI exchange maturity across exchange partners. The framework identifies four configurations (buyer AI-maturity advantage, seller AI-maturity advantage, agentic-AI maturity alignment, and pre-AI maturity alignment) and theorizes how each configuration shapes value co-creation through information-processing fit and buyer–seller trust. The authors further identify strategies for selling organizations to manage each configuration to enhance value co-creation. In doing so, the framework shifts the theoretical focus from whether individual firms adopt AI to the distribution of decision authority between humans and AI systems across exchange partners.

papers.title: University students’ engagement in higher education EFL instructional environments: a mixed-methods quasi-experimental study
papers.authors: Merzouk Farahi
papers.journal: Journal of Further and Higher Education
papers.abstract: In an era branded by Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools and high-tech advancements, the shift to distance education has significantly influenced learner engagement, mainly in English as foreign language (EFL) instructional contexts. In online and offline learning environments, skills engagement (SE), emotional engagement (EE), participation/interaction engagement (PIE) and performance engagement (PE) are essential constructs of successful academic outcomes. The present mixed-methods quasi-experimental research examined the role of online and offline teaching formats on learners’ SE, EE, PIE and PE. The study involved 824 Moroccan university EFL learners. Running Paired samples t-tests, One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) revealed statistically significant effects on offline learners rather than on online learners. The study suggests that the major EFL stakeholders should foster supportive learning environments wherein engagement-promoting instructional practices are prevalent, developing accommodated teaching mechanisms that suit distant learners’ needs and nurture effective virtual learning success.

papers.title: Beyond the bluebook: a calibrated framework for redesigning construct-valid assessment in higher education in the age of generative AI
papers.authors: J.M Shalani Dilinika
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has complicated the link between what a student submits as evidence of learning and what that student actually knows and can do. In response, this study advances an AI-resilient approach to assessment design through the development of a calibrated framework for redesigning construct-valid assessment, based on a systematic review and synthesis of assessment frameworks and structured approaches. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting guidance, sixteen primary assessment frameworks and structured approaches were identified. The synthesis brought their complementary components together into three interdependent design constructs: authorisation, verification, and accountability. Messick’s unified validity theory provides the conceptual anchor connecting these components to the inference an assessment is intended to support. The synthesis revealed that the central gap in the literature is not a lack of relevant approaches or components, but calibration. This gap informed the development of the Calibrated Framework for AI-Resilient Assessment (AIRA), which proposes that verification and accountability should become stronger and more diverse as authorised GenAI involvement increases or becomes more consequential to the intended construct. The framework provides educators with a guide for designing assessments and evaluating student learning in AI-integrated environments.

papers.title: Exploring AI-resistant assessments: insights from Large Language Models creating and completing their own research assessments
papers.authors: Joalise Janse van Rensburg
papers.abstract: Higher education institutions have been grappling with the impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) on teaching and learning. LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek, can produce high-quality text with a single prompt. This is particularly concerning in research modules, where students are expected to showcase their work in a text-based format. In this study, ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek were prompted to develop three research assessments that an LLM should not be able to complete and were subsequently prompted with the instructions generated. The purpose was to explore the influence of assessment instructions and characteristics on the ability of these models to generate complete responses. The instructions and characteristics included written text, oral discussions, physical attendance, contextual access, realistic content, lecturer approval, and the inclusion of multiple components. The most influential characteristic was the inclusion of an oral component. Other noteworthy characteristics were requiring students to attend live events and including multiple staged components. These findings contribute to the ongoing exploration of assessment design in the age of AI and LLMs.

papers.title: Dynamic properties and motion reproducibility of a compact pneumatically actuated humanoid upper body for data-driven control
papers.authors: Hiroshi Atsuta, Hisashi Ishihara, Minoru Asada
papers.abstract: Pneumatically-actuated anthropomorphic robots with high degrees of freedom (DOF) offer significant potential for physical human-robot interaction.
