Findings revealed that AI integration in Nigerian business education is at a moderate level, characterized by partial inclusion of AI content in curricula, limited lecturer competence, and inadequate infrastructural support. Inferential results showed a strong positive and significant relationship between organizational policy frameworks and AI integration (r = 0.81, p < 0.05). A significant difference in institutional readiness was also observed between institutions with strong and weak policy frameworks (t = 3.56, p < 0.05). The findings concluded that organizational policy frameworks play a significant role in determining the extent of AI integration, institutional readiness, and competency development. The study therefore recommended that universities should prioritize the provision of essential AI infrastructure, including reliable internet connectivity, digital laboratories, and access to relevant AI software to support effective teaching and learning.

papers.title: Exploring trust, emotional disclosure, and help-seeking among university students engaging with generative AI chatbots for mental health support
papers.authors: Muniba Fatima Zahra, Hifza Huma, Imran Saleem
papers.abstract: In recent years, university students have increasingly used generative AI chatbots for emotional expression and informal mental health care. This qualitative study investigates Pakistani university students' experiences, perceptions, and trust in emotional disclosure and help-seeking with generative AI chatbots. It also explored the issues students raised with the chatbots, why students felt they preferred to seek AI support over human support, and the perceived advantages, dangers, and moral considerations of such practice. The participants who were selected for the study were 22 university students who had used generative AI for emotional or mental health purposes through purposive sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted to gather data, which was then analysed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes were uncovered: trust was developed gradually and remained conditional; students disclosed concerns they could not easily share with people; chatbots were experienced as available and nonjudgmental; AI acted as both a bridge and a barrier to human help-seeking; and privacy, accuracy, cultural relevance, and safety concerns limited trust. The results indicated that students valued the immediate availability, emotional privacy, and supportive language of AI chatbots. They didn't think AI is equally helpful as mental health professionals. Generative AI's role as a tool that complemented emotional reflection and preparation for human assistance was most helpful. Universities must provide culturally competent advice regarding safe use of AI, privacy, crisis support, and referrals to professional sources.

papers.title: Training the Next Generation of Future Surgical Residents: A Scoping Review and Proposal for an Undergraduate Curriculum From the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons
papers.authors: Gianmario Edoardo Poto, Marianna Peruffo, Manfredi Giuseppe Anzaldi, Andrea Castaldi, Gianmarco Elia, Giulia Misasi, Giulia Rovero, Martina Lenzi, Elisa Bassan, Francesca Gigola, Domenico Soriero, Giosuè Giordano Incognito, Gennaro Melone, Roberto Cirillo, Marco Angrisani, Maria Rosaria Mastrangeli, Alessandro Coppola, Michele Maruccia, Gaetano Gallo, Arcangelo Picciariello, Alessandro Pasculli, Ludovico Carbone
papers.abstract: AIM: The transition from medical school to surgical residency is marked by a persistent gap between theoretical instruction and clinical readiness. In Italy, variability in training programs across centers creates persistent gaps in residents' medical education. Scientific societies are asked to identify current training gaps and define the core competencies required for effective surgical training. We propose an undergraduate curriculum to support last-year medical students in Italy. METHODS: A scoping review of the literature focusing on structured surgical curricula for undergraduate medical students was conducted. A suggested "curriculum" was introduced at the 2025 Congress of the Italian Polispecialistic Society of Young Surgeons (SPIGC) in Bari, Italy. RESULTS: The SPIGC curriculum includes seven domains: (1) soft skills: communication, informed consent, and interdisciplinary collaboration; (2) clinical and diagnostic skills: outpatient clinic management and perioperative care; (3) hygiene, prevention, healthcare systems; (4) technical skills; (5) emergency and trauma surgery; (6) perioperative management, integrating Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols, nutritional assessment, and infections; (7) evidence-based medicine and recommendations. The SPIGC curriculum highlights the importance of simulation labs, hands-on workshops, and online learning, while providing clear pathways for fellowships or masters. It also introduces artificial intelligence (AI) systems as a modern learning tool, while highlighting the importance of their safe and responsible use. CONCLUSIONS: The SPIGC curriculum may provide a structured plan to improve surgical education for medical students in Italy and to align it with international standards. Its acceptability and impact on training quality and patient outcomes remain to be evaluated through future consensus and prospective studies.
keywords: transition from medical school to residency

papers.title: Inteligencia artificial en la investigación académica de los estudiantes de Comunicación de una universidad pública de Ica-2026
papers.authors: José Julio Bendezú Huaroto, Mag. Julio Cesar Ortiz Rojas, Navale Quiroz Cano, Rosario Huayanca Zapata, Fabrizio Antonio Jurado Montenegro
papers.abstract: Context: The integration of artificial intelligence into higher education has prompted interest in its relationship with academic research. Objective: To determine the relationship between artificial intelligence and academic research among Communication Sciences students at a public university in Ica in 2026. Methods: A quantitative correlational study used a nonexperimental, cross-sectional design. The sample comprised 153 students selected through simple random sampling. Results: A positive association was identified between the self-reported scores for both variables (ρs = 0.640; p < 0.001), pending verification against the dataset and the valid sample size. Descriptive percentages still require reconciliation with the sample of 153 students. Conclusions: The reported results indicate a positive, statistically significant relationship between artificial intelligence and academic research, subject to the pending verification of the data.

papers.title: Permission Granted? Navigating AI Use in Graduate Speech-Language Pathology Education
papers.authors: Megann McGill, Ana Rivera Rodriguez, Alayna Townsend, Kelly Roy, Christine E. Fiestas
papers.journal: Teaching and Learning in Communication Sciences & Disorders
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), is transforming higher education and raising important questions about its role in graduate professional training. Speech-language pathology (SLP) programs face the dual challenge of preparing students to engage with AI technologies that are increasingly present in clinical and academic environments while also safeguarding academic integrity, ethical practice, and skill development. This tutorial paper describes the development and delivery of a one-hour, synchronous virtual AI training created for graduate students in a hybrid online Master of Science in SLP program at the University of St. Augustine for Health Sciences. The training was developed by a faculty-led AI Task Force and was designed to improve students’ AI literacy, clarify institutional and course-level AI policies, and promote responsible and ethical AI engagement. The training content included: (1) foundational definitions of AI and distinguishing GenAI from AI assistants, (2) orientation to university AI resources and policies for allowable use, (3) description of a checklist designed to scaffold ethical decision-making, (4) explicit instruction on key risks associated with AI use, including hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, and potential skill attrition, (5) AI applications to support student learning, research, clinical preparation, and time management, and (6) interactive application of AI knowledge to clinical and academic scenarios. By describing the case study and sharing accompanying resources, this manuscript offers a practical framework for SLP programs seeking to proactively address AI integration in graduate education. AI literacy training can help graduate SLP programs move beyond reactive policy development toward intentional, transparent, and ethically grounded AI engagement that supports both student learning and professional competence.

papers.title: Penyusunan Modul Kepemimpinan Gembala di Era Digital: Integritas, Batas Teologis Teknologi, dan Regenerasi Kepemimpinan bagi Gereja Lokal
papers.authors: Veronicha Nussa, Darmawan Darmawan, Satya Mega Ywana, Ferry Simanjuntak
papers.journal: Indonesia Bergerak Jurnal Hasil Kegiatan Pengabdian Masyarakat
papers.abstract: Demands for organisational professionalism and the acceleration of digital technology can easily reduce church leadership to a purely managerial affair, even though the heart of Christian leadership is shepherding. This community service programme took the form of module development rather than seminar delivery. Its aim was to provide teaching material that pastors, elders, and ministry coordinators in local churches can use to re-examine their leadership practice through the shepherd leadership paradigm, while also addressing questions of integrity, the use of artificial intelligence, and leadership regeneration. The module was developed through a literature review of Christian leadership and ecclesiology scholarship, framework formulation by four contributors, and cross-checking among contributors to maintain theological consistency. It comprises four complementary parts: five pillars of shepherd leadership as a corrective framework for church governance, a biblical-theology model of pastoral integrity, an ecclesiological-digital church leadership model that positions technology as an instrument under theological limits, and the strengthening of four dimensions of shepherd leadership in digital culture. The outputs are a module manuscript and a leadership self-assessment instrument that a local church can use repeatedly without a facilitator present.

papers.title: Del acceso abierto a la ciencia abierta: desafíos y decisiones para las revistas científicas
papers.authors: Rosario Rogel-Salazar
papers.abstract: Conferencia-taller presentada en el Encuentro Macrozonal Sur Austral de la Red Chilena de Revistas Científicas de Acceso Abierto, Universidad de Magallanes, Punta Arenas, Chile, 14-15 de octubre de 2026.La presentación parte de una pregunta: ¿qué deben transformar las revistas científicas para pasar de publicar en acceso abierto a participar activamente en un ecosistema de ciencia abierta? Se organiza en cinco ejes: (1) del acceso abierto a la participación abierta; (2) nuevas prácticas editoriales: revisión por pares abierta, transparencia editorial y políticas de datos por niveles; (3) integridad científica e inteligencia artificial en el flujo editorial; (4) decisiones estratégicas: políticas editoriales, congruencia de licencias Creative Commons, infraestructura abierta y sostenibilidad; (5) metadatos correctos y completos en Crossref, a partir de estudios recientes sobre las limitaciones de OpenAlex. Incluye cuatro mesas de trabajo para revistas (autodiagnóstico, priorización, caso sobre IA en la revisión y hoja de ruta) y listas de verificación para el depósito de metadatos. Las notas del orador contienen tiempos y consignas para facilitar el taller.English: Workshop lecture presented at the Southern Macrozone Meeting of the Chilean Network of Open Access Scientific Journals (Punta Arenas, Chile, October 2026). It examines which editorial decisions journals must make to move from open access publishing to active participation in open science: open peer review, editorial transparency, data policies, research integrity and AI, Creative Commons license consistency, open infrastructure, and complete Crossref metadata in light of recent evidence on OpenAlex data quality. Language: Spanish.

papers.title: A Guide for Clinical Adjustment of Mechanical Insufflation-Exsufflation in Patients with ALS/MND
papers.authors: Tamara Le Blanc, Lauren Tabor Gray, Lauren Tabor Gray
papers.abstract: Educational clinical handout developed for the NEALS Respiratory Care & Ventilation Workshop, October 27, 2026.The MI-E Settings & Clinical Adjustment Guide for Patients with ALS/MND is a practical healthcare-professional resource designed to support individualized use and adjustment of mechanical insufflation-exsufflation (MI-E), commonly referred to as cough assist, in people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/motor neuron disease.The guide addresses key MI-E parameters including insufflation and exsufflation pressures, inspiratory and expiratory timing, flow, triggering, oscillations, airway considerations, patient comfort, and troubleshooting. The goal is to support adequate lung inflation, effective expiratory flow, secretion clearance, and individualized treatment based on patient response.This resource is intended for healthcare-professional education and clinical decision support. It is an educational conference resource and has not undergone formal journal peer review.AI Assistance Disclosure: Generative AI (OpenAI ChatGPT) was used to assist with formatting and visual layout development. Clinical content, recommendations, references, and final design decisions were reviewed and approved by the authors.

papers.title: From Representation to Relational Mentorship: User Perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage Learning
papers.authors: Quanyi Zhao, Xiangming Mu, Xun Zhu
papers.abstract: This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

papers.title: Digital Competencies for Higher Education in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: Hadi Almohab, Ulfi Sartika Lubis
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education is reshaping digital competency requirements beyond conventional technological proficiency. However, existing research remains fragmented regarding emerging competency dimensions, institutional development strategies, and the implications of increasingly autonomous AI systems. This review aims to synthesize contemporary evidence on the transformation of digital competencies, institutional responses, and future research priorities in AI enabled higher education.

papers.title: From Technology to the Development of Competence . AI as a resource of teaching English: A Review of University-Level Foreign Language Instruction
papers.authors: Ketty Zoraida Vergara Mendoza, Mariana Marisol Briones Zambrano
papers.abstract: El rápido desarrollo de las herramientas de inteligencia artificial (IA) generativa, entre ellas los chatbots conversacionales, los sistemas de tutoría inteligente y las plataformas de evaluación automatizada de la escritura, ha transformado la manera en que se desarrollan las competencias comunicativas y lingüísticas en las aulas universitarias de lenguas extranjeras y segundas lenguas (L2). Este artículo revisa la literatura empírica y teórica reciente (2023-2026), además presenta un resultado cuantitativo de 238 estudiantes sobre la enseñanza de lenguas mediada por IA y sitúa los hallazgos en el marco de los modelos de competencia comunicativa de Hymes (1972) y de Canale y Swain (1980). Las investigaciones muestran que los chatbots de IA pueden aumentar la disposición de los estudiantes a comunicarse y reducir la ansiedad al hablar en una lengua extranjera, y que la retroalimentación escrita generada por IA puede mejorar la precisión gramatical y los hábitos de revisión. Sin embargo, las mejoras en la competencia lingüística no siempre se traducen en un mayor desarrollo de habilidades comunicativas o críticas de orden superior, y persisten preocupaciones relacionadas con la dependencia excesiva, la integridad académica y el acceso equitativo. El artículo concluye con implicaciones pedagógicas que plantean la IA como un andamiaje, y no como un sustituto de la interacción mediada por el docente, así como con líneas para futuras investigaciones.

papers.title: ZanIA: aplicación multiplataforma basada en inteligencia artificial para el análisis nutricional de alimentos por imagen conforme a la NOM-043-SSA2-2012
papers.authors: Felipe Cocón, Dámaris Pérez-Cruz, Fátima Gisell Castellanos Flores, Arthemisa Nicte Ha Nettel Cabello, Víctor Hugo Hernández Hernández
papers.abstract: Overweight and obesity represent a major public health problem in Mexico: according to the 2023 ENSANUT Continua survey, 37.3% of adults are overweight and 38.9% are obese, while combined prevalence among adolescents reaches 40.4%. Given the lack of accessible tools that translate official nutritional regulations into practical guidance, ZanIA was developed—a multiplatform application that uses artificial intelligence (Gemini model) to analyze photographs of meals and generate nutritional information (calories, protein, fat, and carbohydrates) aligned with the NOM-043-SSA2-2012 standard. Development followed a four-phase experimental methodology: design and planning, development and implementation, testing, and results analysis. The prototype, built with Python and Streamlit, integrates a BMI calculator, a recipe generator, and the "Platosaurio," a dinosaur-shaped physical device that photographs the meal and, through traffic-light-style LED lights, indicates and rates its nutritional balance according to Mexico's "Plato del Bien Comer" scheme. Usability testing, conducted through direct observation and verbal feedback with a small group of five people, showed an interface perceived as intuitive and a clearly useful value proposition, although no large-scale external validation or standardized instrument was used. The project demonstrates technical feasibility and lays the groundwork for future validation with real users.

papers.title: AI Literacy, AI Anxiety, and AI Acceptance Before and After an Artificial Intelligence Education Program for Older Adults : A MAILS-Based Analysis
papers.authors: 서울교육대학교 교육대학원 컴퓨터교육전공 박사과정, Hyosang Son, Dukhoi Koo
papers.journal: Intelligent Information Convergence and Future Education

papers.title: ¿Quién está pensando? Delegación cognitiva, misiones de aprendizaje y el lugar del docente en tiempos de inteligencia artificial generativa
papers.authors: Juliana Valeria Viviani
papers.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence forces a revision of assumptions that have become entrenched in contemporary pedagogical discourse: that activity by itself produces learning, that projects automatically develop critical thinking, that student autonomy requires reducing teacher intervention, and that competency development can be conceived separately from knowledge construction. This article argues that none of these four assumptions withstands close scrutiny against the available evidence on problem-based learning, project-based learning, cognitive load, and scaffolding, and proposes shifting the discussion away from the choice of active methodologies toward the design of learning missions, understood as intentional architectures of cognitive experience that articulate problems, knowledge, cognitive operations, interactions, mediations, teacher interventions, technologies, and evidence. The central argument concerns the risk of cognitive delegation, that is, the displacement of specific intellectual operations onto external resources, particularly artificial intelligence systems. Delegation is not intrinsically negative; the problem arises when the operation delegated is precisely the one that constitutes the object of learning, and artificial intelligence does not by itself create educational superficiality but rather makes visible, and can amplify, a superficiality that certain pedagogical designs already contained. The article brings together classic contributions on problem-based learning, cognitive load, scaffolding, and cognitive apprenticeship with recent research on generative artificial intelligence, critical thinking, cognitive dependence, and the evaluation of student-AI interactions, and introduces the categories of cognitive density and delegation architecture as didactic design tools. It concludes by proposing that teachers be restored to the role of designers of the cognitive architecture of the experience, responsible for defining what can be delegated, what must be verified, and what operations must necessarily remain in the student’s hands.

papers.title: Global Leadership in the World of AI:
papers.authors: Danielle Badgett, Michael King
papers.journal: αρετή (Arete) Journal of Excellence in Global Leadership
papers.abstract: Background: This poster offers a practical approach to global leadership when introducing artificial intelligence (AI) into culturally diverse organizations. Methods/Approach: The approach draws from leadership theory, emerging research on AI in the workplace, and cross-cultural communication theory. Through this research, The Ethical AI Competency Model and AI Implementation Protocol were developed. Objectives: The Ethical AI Competency Model highlights six interconnected competencies: Cultural intelligence, Ethical AI Stewardship, Sensemaking and Strategy, Human-Oriented AI Application, Cross-Cultural Communication, and AI Literacy (Chee et al., 2025; Hagerty & Rubnov, 2019; Oh et al., 2026; Passlack et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025). Results: Grounded in this competency model, the AI Implementation Protocol offers a seven-step protocol to support responsible and culturally inclusive AI adoption. Conclusions: At its core, the framework argues that successful AI implementation within global leadership necessitates human-centered values, organizational transparency, and the willingness and knowledge to adapt across cultures (Pillai, 2024; Rezaei et al., 2024).

papers.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence for Facial Aesthetic Surgery: a Systematic Review
papers.authors: Sarasukma Maharani, Ni Putu Gita Raditya Sanjiwani, I Gusti Agung Ngurah Widya Pramana
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to improve assessment, visualization, and communication in facial aesthetic surgery; however, its clinical reliability remains uncertain. This study aimed to synthesize contemporary evidence on AI applications, performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance in facial aesthetic surgery. A systematic review conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines searched PubMed/MEDLINE, SAGE Journals, ScienceDirect, EBSCO, Scopus, and Web of Science for English-language original studies published between January 2022 and August 2026. Eleven studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis and risk-of-bias assessment using an adapted framework informed by the Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) tool. AI applications included apparent-age estimation, automated facial morphometry, rhinoplasty simulation, patient counseling, and social media analysis. AI-based systems quantified postoperative changes in perceived age and facial morphology, generated realistic surgical visualizations, and provided comprehensible patient education responses. However, visual realism did not establish patient-specific predictive accuracy, and improvements in computational performance did not necessarily translate into greater patient satisfaction or psychosocial benefits. Six studies raised some concerns regarding risk of bias, while five were judged to have a high risk of bias. Methodological heterogeneity, limited external validation, proprietary algorithms, and potential demographic biases limited the interpretation and generalizability of the findings. AI represents a promising adjunct to facial aesthetic surgery; however, prospective multicenter validation, transparent reporting, demographically diverse datasets, and patient-centered outcome assessment are needed before routine clinical integration can be recommended with confidence.

papers.title: Trust in AI translation: Reception and adoption among Jordanian business professionals
papers.authors: Ahmad S. Haider
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly integrated into multilingual professional communication, particularly in translation. This study examines the perceptions, adoption patterns, and future intentions of 2,500 business professionals across various sectors in Jordan regarding AI-powered translation tools. Data were collected using a 28-item questionnaire covering seven dimensions: trust in human versus AI translators, perceived AI accuracy and reliability, adoption and frequency of use, perceived usefulness, organizational policy and support, ethical concerns, and future adoption intentions. The findings revealed a significant negative correlation between perceived AI accuracy and reliability and comparative trust in human translators (r = −.339, p < .001), alongside a positive correlation with future adoption intentions (r = .453, p < .001). Organizational policy and support were negatively associated with ethical concerns (r = −.411, p < .001). No significant differences in perceived AI accuracy and reliability were found based on formal AI training (p = .057). However, AI translation adoption varied significantly across sectors, with higher adoption in Technology and Marketing/Advertising than in Legal Services and Healthcare/Pharmaceuticals. Larger organizations also reported stronger institutional policy and support. Overall, the findings suggest that growing reliance on AI translation does not eliminate the need for human linguistic expertise, particularly in sensitive professional contexts. The study highlights the importance of organizational support and ethical governance in promoting the responsible integration of AI translation into professional practice.

papers.title: AI as a language tutor: Jordanian university students’ perceptions of AI-generated feedback on their English
papers.authors: Ahmad S. Haider
papers.abstract: This study examines Jordanian university students’ evaluations of AI-generated feedback on their English and the extent to which these evaluations predict continued-use intention. A questionnaire was completed by 750 students, with analysis of the 25 perception items restricted to the 720 respondents with prior AI experience. The items assessed feedback quality, personalization, usefulness, trust, motivation, and continued-use intention. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a six-factor structure. Students rated usefulness (M = 4.00) and continued-use intention (M = 3.98) more favorably than trust (M = 3.39) and personalization (M = 3.50). Feedback quality correlated positively with trust (r = .35), while personalization correlated with motivation (r = .41). Usefulness, trust, and motivation jointly predicted continued-use intention, explaining 14.8% of its variance. Higher self-assessed English proficiency was associated with more favorable evaluations of feedback quality (η² = .045). Formal AI training was associated with slightly higher perceived usefulness (d = 0.19), and frequency of use showed a weak positive association with continued-use intention (ρ = .14). Perceived accuracy had little association with usefulness or intention, indicating that students’ appreciation of AI feedback did not necessarily reflect confidence in its correctness. These findings support integrating explicit instruction in evaluating AI-generated suggestions into university English programs, retaining teacher guidance and providing additional support for less proficient learners.

papers.title: Analysis of the Influence of the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on Students' Critical Thinking Abilities in Learning
papers.authors: Miftah Rakhmadian, Haris Amrullah, Adittya Junaidi Pria Pratama, Nuzmi Rosyidah
papers.abstract: This study examines how Artificial Intelligence (AI) use affects students' critical thinking skills in learning. The study uses a quantitative, explanatory research design. The study population consisted of students in the Economics Education Study Program who used AI-based applications for learning. The study collected data through a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire from 64 respondents who met the research criteria. The researchers analyzed the data using validity and reliability tests, assumption tests, and simple linear regression in SPSS. The results show that using AI has a positive and significant effect on students' critical thinking skills. The t-test yielded t = 4.670 (p = 0.000), and the regression coefficient was 0.431. The R-square value of 0.260 indicates that AI use explains 26% of the variation in students' critical thinking skills, while other factors account for the remaining 74%. These findings suggest that appropriate AI use can support students' ability to analyze, evaluate, and solve problems.

papers.title: Integrating Technology, Humanities, and Indian Knowledge Systems for Viksit Bharat’s Higher Education
papers.authors: Anita Singh
papers.abstract: The vision of a Viksit Bharat sets its higher education system a threefold task: to absorb advancing technology, to sustain the humanising work of the humanities, and to recover the depth of India’s own knowledge traditions. These are often pursued separately, and sometimes as rivals. This paper argues that they are strongest when integrated, and that Indian Knowledge Systems supply the principle by which technology and the humanities may be reconciled. The occasion for the argument is the arrival of generative artificial intelligence in the university, which now performs on demand a large part of what higher education has traditionally taught and assessed summarising, analysing, comparing, and composing often faster than the student examined on these operations. The development forces a question at once practical and philosophical: what does higher education accomplish that a machine cannot, and where should the machine be placed? The answer proposed here returns to a distinction already present in Indian epistemology, the Upaniṣadic difference between aparā vidyā, the lower knowledge of information and the disciplines, and parā vidyā, the higher knowledge that issues in realisation and self-understanding (Radhakrishnan, 1953). Artificial intelligence, it contends, is a powerful instrument of aparā vidyā that cannot enter the domain of parā vidyā, which the university exists to serve. Drawing on the doctoral research from which it arises, the paper synthesises classical Indian aesthetics (Rasa, Dhvani, Vakrokti, and the ideal of the sahr̥daya) and the Vedāntic learning sequence of Śravaṇa–Manana–Nididhyāsana into an integrated framework for higher education, within which technology is assigned a real but bounded role. Its principal field of application is English literary studies, where a brief textual illustration shows how Indian aesthetic categories and a contemplative classroom rhythm may reshape the reading and teaching of literature in an age of intelligent machines. Related throughout to the National Education Policy 2020, the paper concludes that such an integration offers Viksit Bharat a higher education in which the most advanced tools serve, rather than supplant, the oldest ends of learning.

papers.title: From AI Consumers to AI Value Creators: Assessing Urban Indian University Students' Readiness for Viksit Bharat 2047
papers.authors: Ms. Ramya R., Sri Abirami Lakshmi H, R. Maya Smriti
papers.abstract: This study aims to explore the technological sovereignty of urban Indian university students with respect to the use of AI towards Viksit Bharat 2047. It demonstrates the current state of AI usage orientation among the younger generation as AI consumers or AI value creators and strives to assess the path that we are journeying in towards a developed nation. With the current digital era, AI tools seek to help in research, improve problem-solving skills, and encourage innovative thinking. Generative AI and prompt templates help in comprehending the cognitive abilities of university students using digital learning platforms and enable the students to utilize artificial intelligence to design creative solutions and have an entrepreneurial mindset. Ultimately, this research delves into the future scope regarding urban Indian university students' readiness in terms of automotive technology towards Viksit Bharat 2047.

papers.title: A PIPELINE FOR DEPLOYING AND MONITORING MACHINE LEARNING MODELS WITH DATA DRIFT CONTROL
papers.authors: V. Buzdin, Evgeniy Anikeev
papers.abstract: A pipeline for putting machine learning models into operation is considered, com-bining automatic deployment, quality monitoring, and control of input data drift. A feedback scheme is proposed in which retraining is triggered by a drift index. Using an educational example, it is shown that drift control reduces the time to detect model degradation and the downtime on an outdated version without constant scheduled retraining.

papers.title: THE IMPACT OF AI ON EVERYDAY LIFE
papers.authors: J. Rahman, Andrey Akimenko
papers.abstract: This article looks at how artificial intelligence (AI) now shapes the daily lives of or-dinary people. It reviews the main areas where AI is used health care, education, transport, shop-ping, the home, and the workplace. The paper discusses both the new opportunities that AI provides and the problems that it creates, such as concerns about privacy, ethical issues, threats to jobs and the digital divide.

papers.title: Sleep Quality and Its Association with Glycemic Control Indices in Children with Type 1 Diabetes: A Cross-sectional Study
papers.authors: Saeed Nouri, Setila Dalili, Shahin Koohmanaee, Zahra Haddadi, Maryam Zavar Mousavi
papers.abstract: Background: The relationship between sleep and diabetes is bidirectional. Sleep disturbances can be triggered by clinical and psychosocial factors, including glycemic fluctuations, nightmares, parental nocturnal monitoring, and comorbid mood disorders. Conversely, disrupted sleep architecture affects metabolic homeostasis by modulating insulin sensitivity and cortisol secretion, thereby influencing blood glucose levels and glycemic indices in patients with diabetes. Objectives: Given the increasing prevalence of diabetes in children, the importance of sleep management in diabetes control, and the limited research in pediatric populations, this study aimed to investigate the association between glycemic control parameters and sleep quality in children with type 1 diabetes receiving care. Methods: This cross-sectional analytical study included 195 children and adolescents aged 12 - 18 years who had had type 1 diabetes for more than 1 year. After written informed consent was obtained from the parents of eligible participants, 60 children with good sleep scores and 135 with poor sleep scores were assessed as two groups based on Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores (validity, 86.5%; reliability, 89.5%). Patients with chronic diseases, mental disorders, sedative or anticonvulsant use, confirmed psychiatric disorders, or treatment nonadherence were excluded. Age, sex, Body Mass Index (BMI), age at diabetes onset, diabetes duration, frequency of nocturnal blood glucose monitoring by parents, fasting blood sugar (FBS), HbA1c, recent diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) episodes, daily insulin dosage (IU/kg), and PSQI score were recorded. Data were entered into SPSS version 19. Results: Subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, male sex, and higher BMI were independently associated with higher FBS levels. Similarly, subjective sleep quality, sleep efficiency, daytime dysfunction, male sex, and higher BMI were independently associated with higher HbA1c levels in the multivariate logistic regression analysis. Mean HbA1c and FBS levels, as well as the frequency of recent DKA episodes, were significantly higher in children with poor sleep than in those with good sleep (P < 0.001, P < 0.001, and P = 0.003, respectively). The proportion of children with abnormal HbA1c levels in the poor sleep group was approximately twice that in the good sleep group (P < 0.001). The poor sleep group had a higher proportion of children with a BMI below the 5th percentile (P = 0.006). Diabetes duration was also significantly longer in the poor sleep group (P = 0.021). Conclusions: This study demonstrates a significant association between sleep quality and glycemic control parameters. The results suggest that patients with suboptimal glycemic control are more likely to experience poor sleep quality.

papers.title: From Webinar Participant to EFL Lecturer: Identity Construction through Pedagogy, AI, and Research
papers.authors: Endah Kurtianti
papers.abstract: Professional identity has been widely examined in language teacher education, yet little is known about how sustained participation in webinar ecosystems integrates pedagogical learning, artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, and research engagement during the transition from master’s student to lecturer. This narrative inquiry explored how webinar-based professional development contributed to the professional identity construction of Nada (pseudonym), an Indonesian EFL lecturer who began attending webinars as a master’s student in 2020. Data were collected through three in-depth narrative interviews and supporting documents and were analyzed using thematic narrative analysis. The findings show a cumulative identity trajectory. First, self-directed webinar participation expanded from thesis-related learning into sustained professional learning, networking, and academic socialization. Second, exposure to lecturer-development and research communities enabled Nada to anticipate academic responsibilities and reposition herself from a participant to a lecturer. Third, pedagogical learning, AI literacy, and research engagement became mutually reinforcing identity resources, reflected in more concise online teaching, greater confidence in AI-assisted material preparation, publication activity, and the acquisition of a competitive early-career research grant. The study offers an original temporal account of webinars as digital communities of practice in which professional learning, possible future selves, and academic recognition jointly support identity negotiation. It highlights the value of webinar-based development for preparing EFL educators for integrated teaching, technological, and research roles.

papers.title: Building AI-ready institutions with ASCEND-AI
papers.authors: LaTanya Brown-Robertson
papers.abstract: Building AI-ready institutions with ASCEND-AI Read here about how ASCEND-AI is preparing the future by building AI-ready institutions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer a future development; it is here and embedded in hiring decisions, clinical workflows, financial systems, legal research, and public policy. This AI economy is not waiting for higher education to catch up. And the students sitting in classrooms at Howard University, Bowie State University, and around the world today will graduate into a professional landscape that demands not just familiarity with AI, but the literacy and ethical grounding to lead with it.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Off-Grid Renewable Energy Systems in Nigeria
papers.authors: Justice Mlambo
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionize off-grid renewable energy systems in Nigeria by enhancing efficiency, reliability, and sustainability. This study employs a qualitative research approach using secondary data sources to examine the role of AI-driven technologies in optimizing energy generation, distribution, and storage. Anchored in the Technological Innovation System (TIS) theory, the research explores how AI innovations can transform decentralized energy networks while identifying barriers to adoption. Findings indicate that AIpowered predictive analytics enhance energy demand forecasting, reducing inefficiencies and minimizing waste. AI-driven smart grids improve real-time power distribution, and battery management systems optimize storage performance, extending battery lifespan. However, key challenges—including high implementation costs, limited data infrastructure, technical skills shortages, and regulatory constraints—hinder AI adoption in Nigeria’ s energy sector. Case studies from India and Kenya illustrate successful AI applications in off-grid electrification, offering valuable lessons for Nigeria. To facilitate AI integration, policy interventions, publicprivate partnerships, capacity-building initiatives, and improved digital infrastructure are recommended. By leveraging AI innovations, Nigeria can advance rural electrification, promote sustainable energy access, and drive economic development.

papers.title: Mapping Digital and Experiential Project-Based Learning in STEM Education: A Scientometric Analysis of Curriculum, Engagement and Research Fronts
papers.authors: Kunawut Boonkwang, Natthawan Phoonson, Rungfa Pasmala, Taklaew Klaewkla, Thada Jantakoon
papers.abstract: Digital and experiential project-based learning (PBL) has become a prominent response to the demand for authentic, technology-mediated STEM instruction, yet existing bibliometric mappings of this literature have been confined to a single database, a single educational level or a window shorter than a decade. This study reports a scientometric analysis of the field for 2015-2024. A five-facet Boolean query was executed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection in April 2025. After removal of ineligible document types (n = 230) and cross-database duplicates (n = 666), 2,103 records were analysed in ScientoPy 2.1.3 using total output, average growth rate (AGR), average documents per year (ADY) and percentage of documents published in the last years (PDLY). Journal articles (n = 930) and conference papers (n = 757) dominated; review articles, although few (n = 68), showed the highest recency (PDLY = 25.0%), signalling a field entering consolidation. Author keywords concentrated on “project-based learning” (n = 307), “experiential learning” (n = 221) and “virtual reality” (n = 129), while “online learning” declined (AGR = −2), consistent with terminological migration. The United States led absolute output (n = 594), but Indonesia (PDLY = 44.8%) and India (PDLY = 30.3%) accelerated most steeply. Individual and institutional productivity was flat and unconcentrated: no author exceeded eight documents and no institution exceeded nine. The study contributes the first decade-scale, two-database performance and thematic map of digital PBL in STEM education and identifies assessment methodology, artificial-intelligence integration and cross-system comparative work as principal research fronts.

papers.title: Impact of Generative AI Adoption on the Trading Patterns of Retail Investors
papers.authors: Naralasetty Hiranya, Meda Srinivasa Rao
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: The growth of GenAI has introduced new ways for retail investors to get their hands on, process and use financial data to make their investment and trading decisions. Investors can also leverage generative AI apps and services, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot, to help them understand and analyse financial data, keep abreast of market trends, discover investment ideas and make trading decisions. The increasing access to such services and applications also has the potential to influence the way retail investors interact with financial markets and inform their trading decisions. This study examines how the usage of Generative AI (GenAI) tools influences retail investors’ trading behaviour. This research looks into how much people use Generative AI, why they use it, and how it connects to different parts of trading behavior like how often they trade, the choices they make, how much risk they take, how long they hold their trades, and their trading style. The approach used for the current study will be a quantitative method based on the use of primary data collected using an on-line survey completed by the retail investors themselves. The data are looked at using appropriate descriptive and inferential statistics. The results of this study point to a conclusion about how Generative AI affects retail investors' trading.

papers.title: A Study on the Impact of AI-Powered Investment Apps on Investment Decisions among Young Investors in Chennai City
papers.authors: Mithra Shree S, G. H. Kerinab Beenu, John Walsh
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: This study examines how features of AI-powered investment apps (usability, alerts, relevance, trust and personalization) influence the investment decisions of young investors in Chennai City, how these features relate to perceived financial literacy, and whether demographic factors are associated with usage frequency. A descriptive research design was adopted and primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. Using convenience sampling, 65 valid responses were obtained from young investors who use AI-powered investment apps, and opinion statements were measured on a five-point Likert scale. Percentage analysis, descriptive statistics, multiple regression, Pearson correlation and chi-square tests were applied. The regression model (R² = 0.83, F(5, 59) = 57.38, p < 0.001) showed that usability (β = 0.20, p = 0.014), alerts (β = 0.22, p = 0.020) and trust (β = 0.31, p = 0.004) were significant predictors of investment decisions, with trust the strongest; relevance and personalization were not significant at the 5% level. All five features were positively and significantly correlated with perceived financial literacy, personalization being the strongest (r = 0.781, p < 0.001). Age, gender, occupation, monthly income and marital status showed no significant association with usage frequency (all p > 0.05). The study recommends transparent explanation of AI recommendations, simple interfaces, customisable alerts, clear risk disclosure and in-app investor education.

papers.title: A Study on the Factors Influencing Customer Awareness and Adoption of AI-Powered Digital Banking Services
papers.authors: Jennifer S, Akila S
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: AI-powered features such as chatbots, fraud detection and personalised recommendations are becoming a regular part of digital banking, but their benefits depend on whether customers are aware of them and choose to use them. This study examines the factors influencing customer awareness and adoption of AI-powered digital banking services, considering awareness and perceptions, perceived usefulness, ease of use, time saving, convenient access, digital literacy, consumer concerns and consumer trust. A descriptive research design was used, and primary data were gathered from 50 digital banking users, selected through purposive sampling, using a Google Forms questionnaire. The data were analysed using percentage analysis, descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The results revealed that 80.0% of respondents are aware that AI-powered features are available in digital banking, while 80.0% to 88.0% are concerned about the security and privacy of their information. The regression model was significant (RZ = 0.60, F = 10.53, p = 0.000), with time saving (B = 0.78) and convenient access (B = 0.50) emerging as significant positive factors, and time saving showed the strongest correlation with adoption (r = 0.645, p = 0.000). Banks can use the results to improve awareness, transparency and trust in their AI-powered digital banking services.

papers.title: PromptIQ: An AI-Assisted Prompt Analysis and Refinement System Using Chrome Extension, JavaScript and Rule-Based Scoring
papers.authors: Atharv Khumkar, Khushi Kathiwale, Anuj Ramteke, Sanchit Dongre, Prof. Priydarshani Gotmare
papers.journal: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
papers.abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are increasingly used for education, software development, data analysis, content creation and decision support. The quality and usefulness of their responses are strongly influenced by how users formulate prompts. However, many users do not have a systematic way to judge whether a prompt is clear, contextual, specific and efficient before submitting it. This paper presents PromptIQ, a browser-based prompt analysis and refinement system designed to provide immediate feedback while a user is interacting with supported AI platforms. The proposed system uses a Chrome extension to detect prompt text through a content script and pass it to a local JavaScript scoring engine. The current scoring model evaluates four dimensions: clarity, context, specificity and efficiency, combined into an overall score on a 0-100 scale. Functional testing of the implemented modules is used to evaluate the reliability of the system. The proposed system demonstrates how browser-based and rule-based technologies can be combined to develop an accessible, transparent prompt-quality feedback platform, with a future version expected to integrate an external language model for explanation and automatic prompt refinement. Keywords— Prompt Engineering, Large Language Models, Prompt Analysis, Prompt Optimization, Chrome Extension, Natural Language Processing, Generative AI.

papers.title: A integração da inteligência artificial às metodologias ativas: impactos na aprendizagem significativa de estudantes universitários
papers.authors: Percília Augusta Santana da Silva Campelo, Kecyani Lima dos Reis, Cesar Mendel Fernandes Ferreira, Wanderson Thiago Santos Noleto, David José Oliveira Tozetto, Tatiana Teixeira de Castro Carvalho Beckemkamp, Maria Joana da Silva Pinto, Daiane Rodrigues De Oliveira, Cátia Irene Duarte Valente, Herick Pampolha Huet de Bacelar
papers.journal: Revista edUCA - Revista Multidisciplinar da Faculdade Católica Paulista
papers.abstract: Este estudo aborda a integração da Inteligência Artificial (IA) às metodologias ativas no ensino superior para a promoção da aprendizagem significativa. O objetivo foi analisar, mediante revisão sistemática, as evidências científicas sobre os impactos dessa integração em estudantes universitários. A metodologia seguiu as diretrizes PRISMA 2020 e a estratégia PICO, realizando buscas nas bases Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, MDPI, Frontiers e SciELO. Após triagem e avaliação de elegibilidade, selecionaram-se 14 artigos para a síntese qualitativa. Os resultados indicam que o uso de chatbots, tutores inteligentes e sistemas adaptativos articulados a métodos como sala de aula invertida, aprendizagem baseada em problemas/projetos e gamificação favorece a compreensão conceitual, o pensamento crítico, a motivação, o engajamento e a autorregulação. Contudo, emergem desafios referentes à formação docente, à integridade acadêmica, à privacidade de dados e aos vieses algorítmicos. Conclui-se que a IA potencializa as metodologias ativas para uma aprendizagem significativa, desde que haja fundamentação pedagógica sólida, ética, mediação docente intencional e suporte institucional com capacitação continuada.

papers.title: “ChatGPT Says You’re Wrong!” How Generative AI Exposes the Fragility of Explanation-Centered Pedagogy
papers.authors: Jon Billsberry, Albert Munoz, Véronique Ambrosini
papers.journal: Academy of Management Learning and Education
papers.abstract: In this essay, we examine a growing tension in management education revealed when students use generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT to question and challenge their educators. We argue that these encounters expose a contest over educational authority. Management education has long relied on explanation-centered pedagogy, allowing authority to rest on theoretical articulation rather than on the demonstrable development of students’ judgment and capability to act. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) destabilizes this arrangement by making fluent explanation ubiquitous, inexpensive, and readily contestable. Our provocation is that business schools have misdiagnosed this as primarily a technological problem when it more fundamentally reveals the fragility of explanation-based authority. We contribute by explaining how explanation became a scalable and defensible proxy for forms of managerial capability that are difficult to observe and assess, and why generative AI now devalues that currency. We call for authority to be rebuilt around capability-oriented education organized at the program level, with theory repositioned as a resource for interpreting, guiding, challenging, and evaluating action. This requires coordinated work by educators, program leaders, deans, and university administrators to make students’ developing capabilities visible, cumulative, and assessable.

papers.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) Innovations for Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Social Well-Being in Nigeria
papers.authors: Augustine Ele Asor, Ekoro Ekoro Igo, Stella Ogar Eyam, Effiong Emmanuel Bassey
papers.journal: American Journal of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a strong tool for tackling worldwide issues, including the United Nations SDGs. This paper investigates how AI innovations can be used to further the SDGs and improve societal welfare in Nigeria. Primary data gathered through questionnaires, surveys, and discussions with stakeholders from government bodies, private enterprises, and schools were used. The study focuses on three SDG targets: reducing poverty, delivering quality education, and ensuring affordable healthcare. Using chi-square analysis, the research found a notable positive link between AI tools and higher earnings in cities, but no meaningful effect in rural zones. It also observed improved educational access in both urban and remote locations. Moreover, AI-driven mobile health apps significantly boosted healthcare access in cities, though not in rural areas. While these results offer a guide for using AI to promote fairness and economic progress in Nigeria, the paper also looks at obstacles such as poor infrastructure, lack of skills, and ethical issues. It recommends that the Nigerian government extend electricity and internet connections to underserved regions, offer subsidies for AI tools, provide digital training, and foster public-private partnerships to roll out AI solutions in education, health, and poverty reduction.

papers.title: The Impact of Childhood Obesity on Asthma Severity: A Cross-Sectional Study at Sabratha Teaching Hospital
papers.authors: Nawal Hasan, Huria Dardar, Karima Hwisa, Waheedah Awushah, Rabia Aldabosy
papers.journal: AlQalam Journal of Medical and Applied Sciences
papers.abstract: There is strong experimental and epidemiological support for the "obesity-related asthma" phenotype. Children who are obese are more likely to develop asthma, and those who already have the condition have worse symptoms, more frequent attacks, and a lower overall quality of life. Data on the relationship between childhood obesity and asthma severity remain scarce in Libya. This study aimed to assess the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and asthma severity among children attending Sabratha Teaching Hospital in western Libya, and to identify the lifestyle, environmental, and clinical factors most strongly associated with disease severity and exacerbation frequency. A cross-sectional descriptive analytical study was conducted among 99 children (aged 2–18 years) with a confirmed diagnosis of asthma. Data were collected via a structured interviewer-administered questionnaire and standardised anthropometric measurements. BMI was classified according to age- and sex specific reference standards. Asthma severity, attack frequency, and hospital admission were assessed as primary outcomes. Pearson correlation, chi-square tests, and a multivariate general linear model (GLM) were applied to identify associations and independent predictors. The study population had a mean age of 9.87 ± 3.84 years, with a male predominance (66.7%). Abnormal BMI was prevalent in 74.7% of participants, comprising 60.6% underweight and 12.1% obese. BMI category was significantly and positively correlated with asthma severity (r = 0.306, p = 0.002) and hospital admission (r = 0.352, p < 0.001). In the multivariate GLM, regular exercise emerged as the strongest independent predictor of asthma severity (F = 12.604, p = 0.001, partial η² = 0.118), followed by BMI category (F = 9.504, p = 0.003, partial η² = 0.092) and passive smoking exposure (F = 4.965, p = 0.028, partial η² = 0.050). Across the cohort, pharmacological treatment alone did not significantly differentiate controlled from uncontrolled asthma status. Our findings suggest that abnormal BMI, particularly obesity, is significantly correlated with asthma severity and hospitalisation among children, as well as physical inactivity and passive smoking exposure being the most clinically significant risk factors identified. Integrating nutritional assessment, regular exercise, and tobacco-exposure counselling into routine pediatric asthma management is highly recommended in systematic inclusion.

papers.title: The effects of artificial intelligence feedback on the writing proficiency of English majors in a Chinese context
papers.authors: Jie Li, Supei Wang
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence feedback has become a hot topic in second language writing research. Although previous studies have yielded fruitful findings, most of them have adopted a cross-sectional research design, failing to demonstrate the long-term effects of AI feedback. In view of this, the current study adopts a longitudinal design to study the effects of AI feedback on the writing proficiency of 72 English majors at a comprehensive university in northwest China. The writing proficiency was evaluated via lexical complexity, syntactic complexity and accuracy. Findings revealed that AI feedback had a significant positive effect on English majors' language accuracy and lexical complexity, but had no effect on their syntactic complexity. This study finally highlights a few implications for the use of AI in second language writing.

papers.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Qualitative Analysis: A Case Study of Medical Students with Academic Difficulties
papers.authors: Xiaohan Zhang, Shaohua Li
papers.journal: International Journal of Education and Social Development
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support qualitative research, yet practical accounts of how they can be incorporated without displacing human interpretation remain limited. This study presents a researcher-supervised workflow for processing and analysing semi-structured interviews with medical students experiencing academic difficulties. Thirty interviews were transcribed, checked against recordings, de-identified, and analysed through three stages: event/theme identification, element-level examination of focal events, and cross-event interpretive construction. The workflow identified recurring difficulties involving unclear learning goals, limited learning resources, professional-identity tension, and family expectations. LLMs supported the organisation of long transcripts and the comparison of related experiences; researchers verified outputs, retained contextual qualifications, and developed the final interpretation. The findings illustrate that LLMs can make qualitative analysis more traceable and efficient when their outputs are treated as provisional analytic material rather than authoritative conclusions. We propose practical safeguards for transcription, privacy, validation, and documentation. This case study offers a concise, reproducible pathway for using LLMs to assist—not replace—qualitative inquiry.

papers.title: From Automation to Engagement: Teaching Academics' Future Plans for AI in Higher Education
papers.authors: Lynn Sheridan, Isabelle Wentworth, Rebekkah Middleton, Elisabeth Duursma, Simon Andrew Moss, Sasha Nikolic, Rachel A. Jones, Montserrat Ros
papers.journal: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used within higher education to enhance curriculum design, automate academic tasks, and personalise learning. Despite this, little is known about teaching academics’ attitudes, intentions and behaviours and in turn, how they use and plan to use GenAI in practice. This qualitative study explored teaching academic staff attitudes, intentions and behaviours regarding their use and future use of GenAI. Data was collected via five open ended questions focusing on current teaching practices. The Theory of Planned Behaviour informed the analytical process. Academic staff were drawn from 20 different disciplines across 24 countries. Six main themes were identified: Efficiency and Automation, Ethics and Authenticity, Quality, Customised Learning, Institutional Policy-Practice and Sociocultural Implications. Overall, there was a dichotomy in responses. Participants noted that while GenAI could streamline teaching and enhance resource quality, it might also increase short-term workload and reduce the role of human judgement, risking unreliable outputs. They also highlighted limited institutional policies, strategies, and training. These attitudes have implications for updating policies, practical strategies, and meaningful training in higher education institutions.

papers.title: Covariance Intersection for Robust Sensor Fusion in Anti-drone Defense System
papers.authors: 이원석, Baeksub Shin, Seungkeun Kim, Jinyoung Suk
papers.journal: Journal of Institute of Control Robotics and Systems
papers.abstract: In this study, we aim to establish a radar sensor-based defense system against the threat of suicide drones, which are not limited to attacks on personnel but can also neutralize critical friendly assets, including armored vehicles. Since drone tracking relies heavily on sensor performance, sensor fusion is employed to prepare for situations in which sensor performance is degraded, such as jamming attacks or sensor failures. First, an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) is used to estimate the position of an enemy drone in X, Y, and Z coordinates based on range, elevation, and azimuth measurements from radar sensors. The position estimation performance is further improved through sensor fusion using the Covariance Intersection (CI) method. To address sensor degradation, an Adaptive Kalman Filter (AKF), which updates the R matrix of the UKF, and a Fault Detection and Isolation (FDI) algorithm are applied to suppress the influence of degraded sensors. Simulations are conducted under assumed sensor-degradation scenarios, such as Noise Modulation Jamming and Range Deception Jamming, affecting a specific sensor. The results demonstrate that the proposed method maintains excellent position-estimation performance even under such conditions and enables interception of enemy drones using the Proportional Navigation Guidance (PNG) algorithm.

papers.title: Being "STEM-trygg" as a proposed concept for feeling at home in STEM
papers.authors: Ulrika Sultan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Conversations with educators in Sweden have led me to reflect on the gap between research language and everyday pedagogical work. Science capital offers a useful research concept, but educators may find it difficult to use when planning activities or discussing people's experiences. This has inspired me to propose a complement: STEM-trygg. I use STEM-trygg as an expression for feeling able and welcome to engage in science, technology, engineering and mathematics while recognising that one's knowledge is incomplete. The corresponding noun, STEM-trygghet, names that experience in a particular setting. I propose the expression as support for educators and science centre staff, who create opportunities for children, young people and adults to explore how the world connects and works. These experiences can range from atoms and artificial intelligence to ecosystems and equations, bringing subjects together around questions that matter to visitors and learners. As I navigated the complement, I used a purposive conceptual analysis of fifteen sources, spanning research and studies on preschool science play, school pedagogy and informal science learning. This was condensed down to four dimensions: perceived legitimacy, interpersonal security, confidence to engage and familiarity with engagement. They overlap with existing concepts, including science capital, self-efficacy, science identity, belonging and psychological safety. STEM-trygg may help educators move beyond grades to focus on the democratic aspects of education, discuss engagement, and consider how the experiences they create and plan could develop, support, and encourage science capital and lifelong learning.

papers.title: PEDAGOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR DEVELOPING STUDENTS' ACADEMIC WRITING COMPETENCE THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: Mokhlaroyim Khamdamova Oybek qizi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper examines the pedagogical foundations for integrating artificial intelligence into the development of students' academic writing competence. It adopts a conceptual approach informed by writing pedagogy, self-regulated learning, and human-centred principles of AI use in education. Academic writing competence is understood as the ability to construct coherent arguments, evaluate and integrate evidence, follow disciplinary conventions, and revise texts independently. The paper proposes an instructional framework combining explicit teaching, guided AI interaction, critical feedback evaluation, and reflective revision.

papers.title: Pedagogical conditions for developing students' academic writing competence through artificial intelligence.
papers.authors: Mokhlaroyim Khamdamova Oybek qizi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the pedagogical conditions necessary for effectively developing students' academic writing competence by integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into higher education. As global academic standards increasingly demand high-level research writing, clarity, and adherence to international publication ethics, educators face the challenge of equipping students with advanced text-production skills. This study outlines a comprehensive framework of pedagogical, methodological, and technological conditions—such as prompt engineering literacy, critical feedback literacy, scaffolded AI-assisted drafting, and ethical integrity safeguards. By establishing these conditions, institutions can transform AI from a mere shortcut into a cognitive partner that fosters critical thinking, structural coherence, and linguistic precision in academic discourse.

papers.title: The Graduation Protocol Hypothesis
papers.authors: Walter Hivoina
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Graduation Protocol Hypothesis (GPH) proposes that a simulated reality could function as a developmental curriculum for consciousness. Its proposed threshold is civilizational and recursive: biological intelligence creates artificial intelligence, and creator and created minds recognize the same pattern of minds making minds. Version 3.1 strengthens the argumentative structure: it supplies independent motivation for preferring a curriculum reading over pure containment or ancestor-simulation alternatives; offers provisional operational criteria for the graduation threshold; keeps interpretive developments (hatching, milestone downloads) explicitly downstream of the optional interface and non-evidential for the core; expands potential disconfirmers for the core thesis itself; and broadens the objection field. The paper continues to place GPH beside Nick Bostrom's simulation argument, consciousness-based alternatives and Danny Goler's published 'Code of Reality' pilot report. GPH remains a philosophical hypothesis until it yields operational definitions, unique predictions and disconfirming outcomes.

papers.title: AI Dependence as Strategic Fragility: Time-to-Paralysis and Organizational Resilience
papers.authors: Lenin Heartly
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly embed artificial intelligence in operating workflows to improve speed, scale and consistency. The same choices can create latent strategic fragility when AI substitutes for independently executable capacity and firms remove the slack, alternative paths and practiced human capability needed during disruption. This conceptual article develops a temporal threshold model of AI continuity dependence. It introduces time-to-paralysis as the interval between material AI functional loss and breach of a workflow's minimum acceptable service level. Drawing on strategy, automation, organizational resilience, dependable computing and production-machine-learning research, the framework proposes how continuity dependence creates an executable-capacity deficit; how coupling, dependency concentration, queues and retry amplification accelerate threshold crossing; and why technical restoration may precede organizational recovery. Source-checked provider incidents are used as bounded mechanism illustrations rather than evidence of prevalence or causal effect. The article reframes AI resilience as a strategic capability comprising independent options, residual human capability, tested fallback, queue control and post-incident learning. Its proposed contribution is an integrative vocabulary for separating AI adoption from continuity dependence, connects efficiency choices to disruption exposure, and provides measurable constructs for future research. For managers, the central implication is not to avoid AI dependence, but to make its continuity consequences visible, testable and governable. Preprint status: Conceptual research manuscript; not peer reviewed. The proposed framework and seven propositions have not been empirically validated.

papers.title: Bypassing the Kantian Limit: A First-Principles Rebuttal to DeepMind's Abductive Bottleneck via Cyber-Physical Homeostatic Regulation and Negative Constraint Vectors
papers.authors: Syed Abraham Ahmed
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The trajectory of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) has recently intersected with a profound theoretical and epistemological bottleneck. Recent scholarship from Google DeepMind posits that current artificial intelligence paradigms, specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), are structurally incapable of profound scientific invention because they lack the capacity for "abductive leaps". According to this critique, generative AI excels at inductive pattern matching and deductive logic but fails to generate novel explanatory hypotheses because it remains trapped in a disembodied digital vacuum, entirely reliant on pre-existing symbolic data. This white paper serves as a direct, first-principles rebuttal to that conclusion. The limitation identified by DeepMind is not an intrinsic boundary of artificial intelligence, but rather a localized artifact of relying on probabilistic pattern-matching algorithms devoid of sensory grounding and deterministic mathematical physics constructs. By replacing statistical token-prediction models with a Cyber-Physical Homeostatic Regulation Architecture, artificial intelligence can achieve true abductive reasoning and epistemological sovereignty. This paradigm shift, pioneered through the intellectual property and frameworks of Lifeline AI by founder and CEO/CTO Syed Abraham Ahmed, leverages Negative Constraint Vectors (NCVs), the Meta-Cognitive Governance Core (MGC), Deep-Relationship Dynamic Bayesian Neural-Networks with Time-Varying Neural Parameters (DR-DBNN-TPNV), molecular dynamic machine learning contracts, and hardware-tethered deterministic physics. By decoupling generative engines from validation engines, the architecture allows the AI to learn in first principles directly from physical, real-world thermodynamic failures. These physical failures are brought back into the generative engine to geometrically mutate the latent space, allowing the system to genuinely fail forward. Through the application of Bipartite Dynamic Slicing, Adjoint Backward Passes, Non-Intrusive Least Squares Shadowing (NILSS), and isometric Tensor Network States (isoTNS), the architecture bypasses the combinatorial explosion of chaotic systems. This paper rigorously details how anchoring causal discovery in absolute thermodynamic nullity and executing hardware-tethered geometric repulsion allows AI to shatter the Kantian Limit, achieving omni-deterministic scientific discovery and establishing the definitive blueprint for true AGI. Furthermore, While the core Cyber-physical Homeostatic Regulation Architecture, the Meta-Cognitive Governance Core (MGC), underlying Negative Constraint Vectors (NCV) architectures and molecular dynamic machine learning contracts, and hardware-tethered deterministic physics are governed by proprietary and patent-pending frameworks, scheduled to be published globally in November, 2026, comprehensive supporting validation materials are available. These include the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), and the (International Search Authority) (ISA) Written report, citing zero prior art teaching the technology and formally confirms the architecture’s strict fulfillment of all patentability requirements, including Novelty (N), Inventive Step (IS), and Industrial Applicability (IA).

papers.title: Sovereign Zero-Knowledge Governance for National Health Insurance and Preventive Medicine AI: Prohibiting Raw Epidemiological Weight Contagion, Algorithmic Worker Profiling, and Central Data Aggregation Across Occupational Health Funds
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Public health ministries are increasingly deploying centralized artificial intelligence (AI) systems to aggregate subscriber health records and prescribe preventive medical interventions across occupational and municipal insurance funds. Specifically, Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) has initiated a 5.0 billion JPY budget request for FY2027 (targeting FY2028 pilot trials and FY2030 full-scale operation) to construct a centralized AI proposal platform spanning corporate Health Insurance Societies (Kenpo Kumiai), the Japan Health Insurance Association (Kyokai Kenpo) covering small-to-medium enterprises, and Municipal National Health Insurance (Kokumin Kenko Hoken). Under this paradigm, insurers input subscriber attributes (e.g., night-shift schedules, chronic lifestyle disease prevalence, specific health checkup Tokutei Kenshin biomarkers, and historical intervention outcomes) into a central AI engine that outputs targeted behavioral directives. Building upon our foundational proofs of weight-space intellectual property and privacy contagion (CERN Zenodo Record 23360530), Human-in-Command (HIC) governance (Record 23375986), and zero-knowledge clinical telemetry under Super-RTO (Record 23377123), this monograph establishes the formal mathematical, cryptographic, hardware, and statutory prohibition against unattested centralized health-insurance AI architectures. We prove four interlocking propositions: (1) Irreversible Epidemiological Weight Contagion: Pooling occupational and biomarker tensors into centralized neural weights W induces non-diagonal Hessian cross-covariance coupling, enabling membership inference and corporate shift-morbidity reconstruction that cannot be excised via post-hoc orthogonal unlearning; (2) Anti-Profiling & Counterfactual Non-Discrimination: We formulate a strict mathematical prohibition against algorithmic worker scoring, enforcing zero Kullback-Leibler divergence across protected labor attributes (D_KL = 0) and mandatory dual cryptographic sign-off by licensed occupational physicians (Sangyoui) and subscribers under HIC; (3) Sovereign Zero-Knowledge Federated Verification (QFS-zkVM): Using recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field (F_p, p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1), local Kenpo vaults prove intervention efficacy in zero knowledge without exporting raw subscriber attributes (I_exfil = 0); and (4) Hardware No-Learn Interlocks (PHOENIX_ROUTER): Physical Pockels shutters sever compute buses in < 7.0 ns upon detecting unauthorized gradient updates, enforcing compliance with Articles 13 and 25 of the Constitution of Japan, Special Care-Required Personal Information (Yohairyo Kojin Joho) mandates under Japan's APPI, and trustee fiduciary duties. License & Integrity Covenant: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) with Strict No-Learn Covenant (NLL-v1.0-2026).

papers.title: Generative AI — Applications, Limitations, and Ethical Challenges
papers.authors: Kamna choudhary Choudhary, Yash Choudhary
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
