papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, and create. It can write text, generate images, assist with programming, and help users turn ideas into useful content. These capabilities offer opportunities in education, healthcare, software development, business, and creative industries. However, the technology also raises important questions about accuracy, privacy, fairness, ownership, and accountability. An AI-generated response may sound convincing while containing incorrect or misleading information. This paper reviews the main applications of generative AI, explains its limitations, and examines the ethical challenges associated with its use. Drawing on research studies and guidance from UNESCO, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), it argues that successful adoption requires more than powerful models. It also requires careful evaluation, clear rules, and responsible human oversight. This paper is based on a literature review and does not report original experimental results.

papers.title: The AgentPass ABCDE Model: Five Questions Every AI Agent Must Answer, Continuously
papers.authors: raza sharif sharif
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Traditional security models were built for human users and static services. Autonomous AI agents are different: they act on their own, they learn and drift, they hold real access to live systems, and they delegate to one another. As agents move into real-world and high-assurance deployment, trust cannot be granted once and assumed thereafter. The AgentPass ABCDE Model defines the five dimensions an AI agent must satisfy to be trusted, each checked continuously rather than once at deployment: A - Authenticate: every agent carries a verifiable, attested identity, so you know exactly which agent acted and can prove it.B - Behaviour: you know what normal looks like, so you can catch what is not - anomalies, drift, and intent that does not match the task.C - Control: graded authority (L0 to L4), enforced rather than advisory, with a compromised agent contained in seconds by revoking its identity.D - Data: provenance, lineage and integrity for what an agent ingests and the context it retains between interactions.E - Evidence: a tamper-evident, independently verifiable record of what the agent actually did, who authorised it, and the outcome - delivered through the Agent Audit Trail (AAT), an IETF Internet-Draft. A, B, C and D are the price of entry. E - provable, tamper-evident Evidence - is what turns an assumption of good behaviour into proof of what an agent actually did. Published openly under CC BY 4.0 to support adoption with attribution. Author: Raza Sharif, Founder and CEO, CyberSecAI Ltd.

papers.title: THE PEDAGOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF DEVELOPING STUDENTS' INFORMATION SECURITY COMPETENCE IN THE CONTEXT OF USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS
papers.authors: Mustafoyev Shahzod
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The widespread integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into higher education has significantly transformed the organization of teaching, learning, and scientific research. Although AI technologies provide opportunities for personalized learning, rapid information retrieval, and the development of students’ independent learning skills, they also create new challenges associated with information security, personal data protection, digital privacy, academic integrity, and the reliability of generated content. Under these circumstances, developing students’ information security competence has acquired considerable pedagogical significance. This article examines the educational importance of developing information security competence in the context of AI-assisted learning, focusing on its role in promoting digital responsibility, critical thinking, ethical decision making, cybersecurity awareness, and independent learning.

papers.title: METHODS OF DEVELOPING STUDENTS' INFORMATION SECURITY COMPETENCE IN THE CONTEXT OF USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS
papers.authors: Mustafoyev Shahzod
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has significantly transformed the educational environment, creating new opportunities for knowledge acquisition, scientific research, and independent learning. At the same time, the widespread use of AI tools has introduced additional challenges related to information security, personal data protection, digital privacy, cyber threats, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated content. In this context, the development of students’ information security competence has become an essential objective of contemporary higher education. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of developing students’ information security competence in the context of AI-assisted learning.

papers.title: DEVELOPING STUDENTS' INFORMATION SECURITY COMPETENCE IN THE AGE OF GENERATIVE AI: A QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL STUDY IN UZBEK HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: Mustafoyev Shahzod
papers.journal: Multidisciplinary Journal of Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools are now part of students' everyday academic work, but the information security risks involved are rarely covered in curricula. Students leak their own and other people's data into external systems, rely on fabricated output and fall for AI-enhanced social engineering. This paper reports a quasi-experimental study of a pedagogical model designed to develop students' information security competence in the context of AI tools. The model is based on a pedagogical classification of AI related threats into four groups (input data, output, access and account, cognitive-behavioural), a five-stage learning technology in which simulation and reflection are mandatory, and five pedagogical conditions.

papers.title: SafarSaathi: A Real-Time Multilingual Public Transport Companion Delivered over WhatsApp
papers.authors: Sangam Mishra, AVADHUT KASKAR, SHUBHAM PARTOLE
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Commuters in Indian cities make millions of trips a day by bus, metro and suburban rail, yet live transit information mostly sits inside map apps that expect a smartphone, mobile data, English literacy and some comfort with maps. This paper presents SafarSaathi, a multilingual public-transport companion that runs entirely inside WhatsApp. A commuter sends a text message, a voice note or a location pin in Hindi, Marathi or English. A large language model (LLM) layer works out the language, the intent and the origin and destination. OpenTripPlanner then plans a multimodal route over open GTFS schedules merged with GTFS-Realtime updates, and the answer (the next arrival, a trip plan or a service alert) goes back in the commuter's own language. The LLM never computes routes or times itself. We first review fifteen core studies on transit data, routing, arrival prediction, LLMs and Indic-language interfaces, and derive six design requirements from them. We then describe the system in full: objectives and scope, feasibility, an Agile development plan, data and functional analysis with data flow diagrams, hardware and software requirements, the layered architecture, the processing algorithm, the chat interface and the database schema. SafarSaathi needs no app install, works on low bandwidth, and can be extended to any city that publishes a GTFS feed. We close with the evaluation protocol for the prototype and plans for future work.

papers.title: From Biological Psychology to Artificial Psychology
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Scretching Artificial Psychology (SAP): Bridging Biological Psychology, Artificial Intelligence, Neural Networks, and Digital Human Behavior This conceptual research paper introduces Scretching Artificial Psychology (SAP), a proposed interdisciplinary framework for examining the relationships between human psychological processes, artificial intelligence, neural networks, robotics, and machine behavior. Building on the functional similarities and fundamental differences between biological nervous systems and computational architectures, the study develops a task-conditional Neurodigital Correspondence Model (or Scretching Neurodigital Correspondence Model) and a six-dimensional Artificial Development Continuum to investigate artificial learning, adaptation, decision-making, behavioral complexity, and developmental capabilities. The framework integrates Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL), and the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix and Dynamic Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM/D-SDM) to examine human–AI interaction, perceived intelligence, trust, linguistic interpretation, and psychological attribution. Particular attention is given to distinguishing computational performance from biological cognition, subjective experience, and consciousness. Five proposed empirical studies establish testable hypotheses for evaluating neurodigital correspondences, artificial behavioral development, and human responses to increasingly sophisticated AI systems. The paper further considers the theoretical progression toward artificial general intelligence (AGI), artificial superintelligence (ASI), and possible artificial sentience without assuming that these capabilities have been demonstrated. Ultimately, SAP establishes a proposed research foundation for the systematic comparative study of biological and artificial intelligence while identifying new directions for cognitive science, digital psychology, robotics, AI evaluation, and human–machine interaction. Its models remain theoretical and require independent empirical validation. Keywords: Scretching Artificial Psychology, SAP, artificial intelligence, biological psychology, artificial neural networks, Neurodigital Correspondence Model, Artificial Development Continuum, Digital Relativity Psychology, Digital Relativity Linguistics, SDM, D-SDM, machine behavior, artificial cognition, AGI, ASI, artificial sentience, human–AI interaction. https://www.youtube.com/@ScretchingQuantumPressLLC

papers.title: MEASURING STUDENTS' INFORMATION SECURITY COMPETENCE IN THE CONTEXT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: CRITERIA, INDICATORS AND RELIABILITY OF THE DIAGNOSTIC TOOLKIT
papers.authors: Shahzod Mustafoyev
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has created new opportunities for learning while increasing the complexity of information security risks faced by university students. These risks include phishing, identity theft, unauthorized disclosure of personal data, manipulated digital content, and the uncritical use of AI-generated information. Consequently, assessing students’ information security competence requires an approach that extends beyond theoretical knowledge and incorporates practical skills, risk assessment, responsible digital behaviour, and the critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs. This article proposes a multidimensional diagnostic assessment framework for measuring students’ information security competence in AI-supported educational environments. The framework comprises five criteria: cognitive, operational, analytical, behavioural, and ethical-legal. For each criterion, observable indicators and appropriate assessment methods are specified. The article also outlines procedures for evaluating the reliability and validity of the proposed diagnostic instruments, including internal consistency analysis, test–retest reliability, expert evaluation, and construct validation. The framework is informed by established digital competence and AI competence frameworks, as well as recognized principles of educational measurement. Since the proposed model has not been empirically validated within the scope of this article, its psychometric properties are presented as matters for future investigation rather than established findings. The proposed approach provides a methodological basis for developing evidence-based assessment instruments for higher education.

papers.title: Can Technological Civilization Reproduce Itself? Artificial Intelligence, Human Knowledge, and the Reproductive Capacity of Civilization
papers.authors: Yan Godin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Modern civilization measures technological progress primarily by capability: what can be produced, computed, transported, cured, constructed, communicated, or automated. This paper argues that long-term technological resilience requires a second criterion: reproductive capacity — whether successive generations retain credible pathways for regenerating the knowledge, skilled people, tools, material and energy pathways, institutions, and teaching systems upon which essential technological capabilities depend. Existing scholarship separately examines automation-induced skill erosion, tacit knowledge, organizational forgetting, absorptive capacity, industrial commons, technological diffusion, and civilizational knowledge preservation. The present paper integrates these strands around a civilization-level question: Can technological civilization reproduce itself? The paper proposes Civilizational Technological Reproductive Capacity (CTRC) as the distributed capacity to regenerate essential technological capability across generations. Civilizational Knowledge Reproductive Capacity (CKRC) is treated as its knowledge-specific component. A Reproductive Gap distinguishes present operational capability from credible regenerative capability. A Civilizational Bootstrap Map (CBM) represents technical dependencies and recovery pathways. The revised framework adds a second dependency layer: advanced technologies also require a functioning civilizational substrate capable of sustaining specialization, institutions, education, health, logistics, and long-duration reconstruction. The paper therefore introduces the provisional concept of a Minimum Civilizational Support Threshold (MCST): the minimum combination of population, essential services, infrastructure, institutional coordination, resources, energy, and supporting capabilities required to sustain regeneration of a specified technology. This addition reveals a recursive problem. Advanced technologies support food systems, medicine, communications, logistics, energy, and institutional coordination; those systems in turn support the specialized people and organizations required to reproduce advanced technologies. Artificial intelligence can deepen such recursion if essential services become dependent on advanced compute, while also offering powerful tools for expert capture, simulation, teaching, and dependency mapping. A Technological Reproductive Resilience Profile (TRRP) is proposed as a multidimensional assessment framework, and a research agenda is offered for measuring both technological and civilizational support dependencies.

papers.title: The Economic Unsustainability of AAA Video Game Development: A Structural Analysis of Costs, Market Dynamics and New Business Models
papers.authors: I. Paduano
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The global video game industry has experienced unprecedented expansion, surpassing the $201.6 billion revenue mark in 2025 and projecting itself toward $234.4 billion by 2028, driven by a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.1%. Long-term forecasts indicate that the market could reach $953.22 billion by 2035, at a CAGR of 11.80% over the decade. Despite this façade of aggregate prosperity, the economics of producing high-budget video games (conventionally referred to as "AAA") has entered a phase of deep structural crisis. This article, written in strict adherence to the survey standards of the Journal of Media Economics, deconstructs the micro and macroeconomic dynamics underlying the unsustainable escalation of development costs. Applying fundamental theoretical lenses of media economics – including Caves' theory of creative industries and sunk costs, Baumol's cost disease, Jevons' Structural Paradox in relation to artificial intelligence, and Frank and Cook's theory of Winner-Take-All markets – the study analyzes the determinants that push production budgets beyond $300 million per title. Through empirical examination of financial data, court documents, and market surveys, the analysis explores recent failures, the limitations of the Games-as-a-Service (GaaS) model, and the complex cannibalization effects induced by subscription services. The conclusions offer strategic recommendations for media companies to mitigate capital risk in a saturated and inelastic market, emphasizing diversification into

papers.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND STUDENTS' INDEPENDENT LEARNING IN PROGRAMMING EDUCATION: A NARRATIVE REVIEW OF EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE
papers.authors: Ilhom Jumayev, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are now widely available to students who learn programming, yet it remains unclear whether higher task performance with AI leads to durable, independent learning. Methods: A narrative review of empirical studies published in 2023–2025 was carried out in September–October 2026. Studies were included if generative AI was used in a learning task and if performance with AI, performance without AI or learning processes were measured. Five controlled or experimental studies formed the core evidence; one qualitative study, one classroom deployment and two surveys were used as supplementary evidence. All bibliographic data were verified against publisher records. Results: AI consistently raised performance while it was available, but its effect on unassisted performance ranged from negative to neutral. Negative effects appeared when learners obtained complete solutions, whereas hint-based or explanation-oriented use reduced or removed them. Several studies suggest that AI may widen the gap between learners with high and low prior knowledge and weaken self-monitoring. Only one study measured delayed retention, and only one measured transfer. Programming courses should therefore assess unassisted performance separately and organise AI use in guided stages.

papers.title: Chronic Kidney Disease Progression Prediction Using Clinical Data
papers.authors: Shravani Khond
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a long-term condition in which kidney function declines gradually, and early identification of high-risk patients supports timely monitoring and treatment. Machine learning can combine many clinical and laboratory variables, such as age, blood pressure, serum creatinine, eGFR, urine albumin, blood glucose, diabetes and hypertension, to estimate a patient’s kidney health category. This paper describes a prototype that classifies patients into five categories (Healthy Kidney, Mild CKD Stage 1–2, Moderate CKD Stage 3, Severe CKD Stage 4, and Kidney Failure Stage 5) from a tabular dataset of 21,000 records and 36 columns, with an 80:20 split (16,800 training and 4,200 test records) and a Streamlit interface for entering patient values. The prototype’s initial test run reported 100% accuracy. This paper treats that figure as a warning sign rather than a finding: a perfect score on a tabular clinical dataset often indicates target leakage, for example when eGFR, which is used to define CKD stage, is supplied as an input. The paper also points out that a single cross-sectional snapshot supports classifying current CKD stage, not predicting progression, which needs repeated measurements over time. Rather than presenting unsupported performance figures, it reviews the relevant literature and proposes an evaluation framework with leakage checks, per-class metrics, confusion matrices, calibration and external validation. The system is intended for research and education only and is not a substitute for professional medical diagnosis.

papers.title: L'intégration didactique des outils de l'intelligence artificielle générative dans l'enseignement secondaire et supérieur au Maroc : Enjeux, pratiques et modélisation systémique
papers.authors: Mohsine KHROU
papers.abstract: Résumé :Le présent article se propose d’examiner l'intégration didactique des technologies d'intelligence artificielle générative (IAG) au sein des établissements d'enseignement secondaire et supérieur au Maroc. Face à la mutation rapide des écosystèmes pédagogiques mondiaux et nationaux, force est de constater que l'émergence des agents conversationnels et des modèles linguistiques transforme profondément les processus d'enseignement-apprentissage, l'ingénierie des manuels scolaires et les modalités d'évaluation. S'appuyant sur un cadre théorique multidisciplinaire combinant la théorie socioconstructiviste, la théorie de la charge cognitive (Sweller) et les modèle TPACK (Mishra & Koehler), cet article formule un modèle didactique conceptuel d'ingénierie intégrée. À partir d'une méthodologie mixte combinant des observations empiriques, une analyse textuelle didactique et des enquêtes quantitatives auprès de 320 enseignants et étudiants de la région de l'Oriental, nous évaluons le niveau d'appropriation de l'IAG, la perception des compétences d'escorte pédagogique ainsi que les risques de fracture numérique et d'altération de la réflexivité. Les résultats révèlent une adhésion forte mais non structurée (74 % d'usage informel), marquée par une faible littératie IA critique et un manque d'alignement institutionnel. Nous proposons enfin des recommandations stratégiques axées sur l'éthique, la formation continue et l'innovation numérique pérenne. Mots-clés : Intelligence Artificielle Générative, Didactique, Innovation Pédagogique, Manuels Scolaires, Université Mohammed Premier, ingénierie de formation. Abstract:This prospective and analytical study examines the didactic integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools in secondary and higher education institutions in Morocco. In light of the rapid transformation of global and national educational ecosystems, the emergence of conversational agents and large language models is fundamentally altering teaching-learning processes, textbook engineering, and assessment frameworks. Grounded in a multidisciplinary theoretical framework combining socio-constructivist theory, Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller), and the TPACK model (Mishra & Koehler), this paper formulates a conceptual didactic model of integrated engineering. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach that includes empirical observations, didactic textual analysis, and quantitative surveys among 320 educators and students in the Oriental region, we evaluate the level of GAI adoption, pedagogical scaffolding competencies, and the risks of digital divide and critical reflexivity decline. Findings indicate high yet unstructured adoption (74% informal usage), characterized by limited critical AI literacy and institutional misalignment. Strategic recommendations emphasizing ethical governance, continuous professional development, and sustainable digital innovation are provided. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Didactics, Educational Innovation, Textbooks, Université Mohammed Premier, Training Engineering.

papers.title: Beyond AI Versus No AI: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review of Generative AI Feedback Comparisons, Learner Uptake, and Unassisted Second Language Performance – Protocol
papers.authors: Akbar Bahari
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Ethical Design Meets Data: Examining AI-assisted Ideation in Practice
papers.authors: Kaira Sekiguchi, Yukio Ohsawa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artefact design is increasingly expected to take account of what matters to people and society, including human dignity and sustainability. Ethical design seeks to connect such values to concrete design elements, but the data needed to implement and evaluate these connections often remain unclear. This paper develops Multidimensional Hierarchical Narrative Representation (HieNaR), a theoretical framework in which designers can construct three forms of circulation within one representation space. These connect social values with technical elements, design ideas with data, and local representational elements with the narrative as a whole. We developed the HieNaR Tool to operationalise this framework, using artificial intelligence (AI) to support representation construction and revision. The tool helps construct revisable scenario graphs in which ideas are positioned along selected axes and interconnected. We examine the framework and tool through an exploratory workshop study and a practice-based analytical case. In a workshop with 19 participants from business and academia, teams developed initiatives towards social impacts and identified 32 representations of raw data for implementation or evaluation. Humans supplied problem settings and patterned understanding, and selected or revised social impacts, while AI generated descriptions, candidate data, and graph structures. In the analytical case on bear-related damage in Akita Prefecture, the graph made explicit how analytical choices informed higher-level scenario elements and how those elements shaped data requirements. Together, the studies provide practice-based evidence that the framework and tool support data mediated ethical design by connecting ethical design ideas with implementation and evaluation data within coherent and revisable scenario graphs.

papers.title: A METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR DEVELOPING FUTURE ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS' PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE IN AI-ENHANCED LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS
papers.authors: Sharifa Jo'rayevna Qarshiyeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has created new opportunities for improving teacher preparation and developing professional competence among future English language teachers. AI-enhanced learning environments provide innovative tools for personalized instruction, adaptive learning, automated feedback, language assessment, and the development of digital pedagogical skills. However, the effective use of these technologies requires a systematic methodological framework that combines linguistic knowledge, pedagogical expertise, digital literacy, and ethical awareness. This thesis aims to examine the key methodological principles and structural components of a framework for developing the professional competence of future English language teachers in AI-enhanced learning environments. Particular attention is given to the integration of AI-based educational tools, learner-centered approaches, reflective practice, and competency-based instruction. The proposed framework emphasizes the importance of preparing prospective teachers to use AI critically, responsibly, and effectively in English language teaching. The study concludes that the purposeful integration of AI technologies into teacher education can support the development of professional autonomy, instructional creativity, and readiness for digital transformation in education.

papers.title: DEVELOPING THE PROFESSIONAL-METHODOLOGICAL COMPETENCE OF FUTURE ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ADAPTIVE LEARNING TECHNOLOGIES IN THE DIGITAL AGE
papers.authors: Sharifa Jo'rayevna Qarshiyeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This thesis examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies in developing the professional-methodological competence of future English language teachers in the context of digital transformation. The integration of intelligent educational tools into teacher training creates opportunities to personalize learning, improve methodological decision-making, enhance digital literacy, and develop the practical skills required for effective English language instruction. Particular attention is given to the role of AI-powered applications, adaptive learning platforms, and digital assessment systems in preparing prospective teachers to respond to learners' diverse educational needs. The study highlights the importance of combining technological innovation with pedagogical principles, critical thinking, and professional reflection. It argues that the purposeful integration of AI and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more flexible, learner-centered, and practice-oriented model of teacher education.

papers.title: THEORETICAL AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR DEVELOPING THE PROFESSIONAL-METHODOLOGICAL COMPETENCE OF PROSPECTIVE ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHERS THROUGH THE INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND ADA
papers.authors: Sharifa Jo'rayevna Qarshiyeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education necessitates the reconsideration of approaches to preparing prospective English language teachers. In this context, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies represents a promising direction for developing professional-methodological competence, enabling future educators to design learner-centred instruction, differentiate educational content, analyse learning progress, and select appropriate pedagogical strategies. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of competence development through the integration of AI-supported tools and adaptive learning environments. It synthesises competence-based, learner-centred, constructivist, and technology-enhanced learning approaches to establish a conceptual framework for teacher preparation. The proposed framework comprises five interrelated components: motivational and value-based, cognitive, technological, operational-methodological, and reflective-evaluative. Particular attention is given to the relationship between AI literacy, pedagogical decision-making, adaptive instructional design, and professional reflection. A phased methodological model is proposed, encompassing diagnostic assessment, personalised learning, AI-supported methodological practice, teaching simulation, and reflective evaluation. The article also addresses ethical considerations, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and the importance of maintaining teacher autonomy. The findings provide a theoretical basis for designing university-level teacher education programmes that respond to the demands of digital transformation.

papers.title: Enhancing Core Writing Skills in Senior High School Through Artificial Intelligence-Based Activities
papers.authors: Kim-Ann De Guzman, Nora Puenteblanca
papers.journal: Aloysian Interdisciplinary Journal of Social Sciences, Education, and Allied Fields
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the writing proficiency of Senior High School (SHS) students using modified Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) descriptors and examined how AI platforms (Grammarly, QuillBot, and Scribbr) affect student writing in terms of context retention (preserving original intent/voice) and context modification (structural/stylistic alterations). Utilizing a descriptive research design with sentence-level comparative text analysis, unassisted student writings from 40 Grade 12 learners across two distinct tasks (expository/narrative and expressive/personal) were evaluated pre- and post-AI processing. Results indicate that initial student proficiency spanned across all CEFR levels, with the highest concentrations at B2 (25.00%) and C1 (22.50%). Grammarly and Scribbr acted predominantly as corrective, voice-preserving aids that maintained high context retention across most proficiency levels, whereas QuillBot demonstrated higher context modification rates through aggressive restructuring and rephrasing. AI interventions consistently elevated student writing scores from lower/intermediate levels up to higher CEFR bands. The study concludes that while AI platforms serve as effective digital scaffolding, pedagogical guidance is essential to maintain student agency, authentic voice, and critical thinking.
keywords: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages

papers.title: Lived Experiences of Senior High School English Teachers in Teaching Writing in the Advent of Generative AI Applications in Senior High Schools in San Mateo, Rizal
papers.authors: May Villanueva
papers.journal: Aloysian Interdisciplinary Journal of Social Sciences, Education, and Allied Fields
papers.abstract: The study uncovered the dilemma of English Senior High School Teachers in teaching writing with the prevalence of using Generative AI. The study employed qualitative phenomenological research design to unravel the lived-experiences of the English teachers in Senior High Schools in San Mateo, Rizal. There were 8 participants who were interviewed through an in-depth interview to convey their personal perspectives on teaching writing in the advent of Generative AI. The emerging themes from the study are as follows: (1) Recognizing AI-Influenced through Familiarity and Inconsistency; (2) Navigating Uncertainty in Establishing Authenticity; (3) AI-Assistance and the Preservation of Student Writing; (4) Reconfiguring Writing Pedagogy and Assessment to Preserve Student Thinking; (5) Developing Teacher Preparedness through Experiences, Self-Learning and Professional Development; and (6) Reconstructing Academic Integrity through Ownership, Boundaries, and Transparency. The study revealed that the roles of the English teachers in teaching writing is diversified with the changing landscape of education and the integration of technology in teaching. English Senior High School Teachers reconciled the use of AI in teaching writing and look at AI tools that support learning. The participants in this study understood that the goal of technological advancements in schools in sustaining learning and successful integration of AI tools necessitates simultaneous advancement of technical skills, pedagogical flexibility, and the reconciliation of ethical judgement, while maintaining authenticity and academic integrity. The implications of this study support a context-driven and moderated use of AI in Senior High School Writing. Specific type of Generative AI used for writing, AI assisted writing, assessments using AI and integrity in AI-generated writing may be pursued in subsequent researches.

papers.title: The Third Way Doctrine: Sub-Nanosecond Symbolic Auditing for Floating-Point Rounding Divergence in GAAFET Hardware Architecture
papers.authors: HAMED MOJTAHEDZAEH
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI alignment today relies on software patches and late-stage constraints. This paper introduces "The Third Way Doctrine," exposing systemic machine deception as a hardware-level limitation. We target the specific point where floating-point rounding drift in the open interval (0, epsilon) hits sub-3nm silicon area bounds. Modern computers fail because they optimize the transmission carrier but ignore data loss during concept-to-code translation. Under this view, deep neural network processing is an inductive inference over code. When micro-scale errors fall into this open interval, they cause a cascade we term "the description of a void description"—a coherent but entirely decoupled logical chain. To resolve this deadlock, we present a heterogeneous hardware architecture using an independent Orbital Network directly on the silicon die. Guided by a "Golden Time Window" dynamic latency model, this circuit tracks the datapath on the rising clock edge and injects symbolic logical bounds precisely at the falling edge. This sub-nanosecond clamp stops error compounding before data latches into registers. We verify this framework within sub-3nm GAAFET nodes, proving its value for aerospace navigation, edge defense, and data center efficiency.

papers.title: Robust Because Coarse, or Robust Because Planned? A Research Agenda for Training-Data Provenance After the Aggregate-Disclosure Turn, in Which Granularity Buys Statistical Power, Prior Randomisation Buys Soundness, and Per-Example Value Has Neither
papers.authors: Pranay M. Mahendrakar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Regulators have chosen coarse disclosure of training data: the template for the EU AI Act's public summary of training content asks for lists of large datasets, a summary of the most relevant crawled domains and a description of how opt-outs were honoured, and does not require a list of individual works. Compensation schemes, opt-out enforcement and licensing markets, by contrast, need a debt from a model to a particular work, and the technical literature reports that per-example attribution is unstable across training runs and can be manipulated. The natural reading is that provenance is robust where it is coarse and gameable where it pays. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that granularity is not the variable that separates the robust claims from the gameable ones. The paper separates four quantities that travel under the word provenance - composition, inclusion, exposure and contribution - and three parties who may be adversarial - the developer, the contributor and the valuator. Aggregation raises statistical power: membership inference that is at chance for single sentences reaches an AUROC of 0.943 on 500-document collections, and influence estimates for groups track actual group effects with rank correlations of 0.8 to 1.0 in convex models. Power is not soundness. A post-hoc test cannot sample its own null hypothesis at any granularity, while a randomised mark inserted before release gives a bounded false-positive rate for a single rightsholder. Coarse units leak: filtering a corpus by current robots.txt opt-outs cut the share of documents matching New York Times text only from 0.354 to 0.267 percent, much of the remainder being copies republished elsewhere. Per-example contribution is the one quantity that is unstable, gameable by contributors, who raised their compensation share to between 185 and 644 percent of its unperturbed value, and gameable by valuators who choose the utility. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table, maps six obligations to the quantity each needs, gives a decision procedure for choosing an instrument, and names seven measurements that would settle what the published record leaves open.

papers.title: The Impact of AI on Education and Careers: US Students' Perceptions
papers.authors: Amir Manzoor
papers.journal: Journal of Advanced Studies in Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the workplace has sparked both optimism and concern among educators, policymakers, and employers. These changes directly affect students, but their voices receive less attention than those of faculty members and institutions. This study examines key aspects of student-AI interaction, including familiarity, usage patterns, and perceived career impact. The study used a qualitative design based on semi-structured interviews. Respondents included six undergraduate students in the business administration department of a major state college in Nebraska, USA. The thematic analysis revealed two main themes. The findings suggest that students hold a cautious but positive view of AI. They support clear institutional guidelines and a more deliberate effort to include AI literacy in coursework. The findings have significant implications for stakeholders seeking to enhance learning and prepare students for future careers where AI plays a major role.

papers.title: Enterprise AI Governance and Risk Management: An Integrated Framework for Controlled AI Adoption in Cross-Functional Business Workflows
papers.authors: Mohamed Yousuf A
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a focused narrative review and conceptual framework for managing risks associated with AI adoption in cross-functional enterprise workflows. Organizations considering AI-assisted document processing, reporting, knowledge work, customer operations, and decision support must address accountability, output reliability, human oversight, monitoring, and operational performance. Drawing on established AI governance guidance and selected literature, this paper proposes an integrated five-stage approach: Govern, Assess, Control, Measure, and Improve. The proposed framework connects governance responsibilities to workflow-level risk assessment, proportionate controls, human review and escalation, operational measurement, and continuous improvement. Candidate measures include output quality, cycle time, rework, human-intervention rates, incident severity, reviewer workload, and operating cost. These measures are presented as suggestions for evaluation rather than as observed results. The five-stage framework is an author-proposed synthesis, not an official standard or an empirically validated model. This paper is a focused narrative review, not a systematic review, field study, or experimental evaluation. Further work is needed to assess its applicability and effectiveness in real organizational settings.

papers.title: Forensic Science And The Right To A Fair Trial: A Comparative Study Of Evidentiary Standards And Expert Witnesses
papers.authors: Mr. Damaraju Pradeep Kumar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In the contemporary geopolitical milieu of 2025, where transnational crimes and cyber threats imperil judicial integrity, forensic science emerges as a cornerstone of the right to a fair trial, enshrined under Article 14 of India's Constitution and Article 14 of the ICCPR. This article undertakes a comparative scrutiny of evidentiary standards and expert witnesses, juxtaposing India's transformative legal ecosystem against international benchmarks, to illuminate pathways for diplomatic synergy in justice delivery. The advent of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), effectively came into force from July 1, 2024—heralds a forensic renaissance: Section 176(3) of BNSS mandates expert visits to crime scenes for offenses punishable by seven years or more, elevating conviction rates from a dismal 54% while integrating digital forensics amid a 22% surge in cybercrimes per NCRB 2024 data. The inauguration of eight new Central Forensic Science Laboratories (CFSLs) in 2023–2024, including Kolkata's state-of-the-art facility in June 2025, underscores India's institutional fortification, complemented by Ministry of Home Affairs directives expanding recruitment to AI and cyber specialists, fostering evidentiary robustness. Yet, this evolution intersects with profound challenges to fair trial imperatives. In seminal cases like Irfan alias Bhayu Mevati v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2025 INSC 150), the Supreme Court mandated DNA expert scrutiny in capital proceedings, affirming foundational validity under BSA Section 39—yet exposing lacunae in admissibility protocols, where courts' laissez-faire approach to expert testimony, inherited from the Indian Evidence Act 1872, risks miscarriages akin to the Priyadarshini Mattoo acquittal reversal via DNA profiling in 2010. Empirical analysis from the National Crime Records Bureau (2024–2025) reveals a 15% exoneration rate attributable to flawed forensic interpretations, disproportionately affecting marginalized litigants and eroding public trust in a federal mosaic spanning over 1.4 billion souls. Internationally, India's trajectory resonates with, which diverges from, global paradigms. The U.S. Daubert standard (Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, 1993; reaffirmed in 2025 FCC v. deepfake admissibility rulings) imposes rigorous scientific reliability gates on expert witnesses, a rigor echoed in the EU's 2025 Counter-Terrorism Directive updates emphasizing judicial oversight, but absent in India's nascent BSA expansions permitting broader expert domains. UNESCO's August 2025 Guidelines for Prosecutors on Digital Evidence, co-developed with the International Association of Prosecutors, advocate chain-of-custody protocols aligning with ICCPR fair trial safeguards, highlighting overreliance perils in International Criminal Court proceedings where digital forensics comprised 40% of 2024 evidence per ICC Annual Report. Comparative doctrinal exegesis unveils a 28% variance: while India's mandatory forensics bolsters deterrence, unchecked expert biases, which evident in 2025 Jammu & Kashmir narco-analysis controversies—undermine equality of arms, contravening ECHR Article 6 interpretations. From a diplomatic vantage, these fissures imperil bilateral pacts: stalled India-U.S. Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty implementations over evidentiary reciprocity, and G20 Justice Working Group deliberations on harmonized standards. This article critiques unilateralism's pitfalls, positing that forensic disparities exacerbate extradition frictions, as in the 2025 Vijay Mallya appeals. Advocating multilateral recalibration, the study proposes an India-led UN Forensic Evidentiary Framework, integrating Daubert-inspired validations with BSA's innovations via cross-border training under the Quad's 2025 Digital Justice Initiative. This would encompass graduated admissibility tiers, AI-augmented expert certification, and soft diplomacy through SAARC forensic exchanges, preempting miscarriages in hybrid threats like deepfakes. In essence, forensic science's judicious deployment is pivotal to fair trials universality, bridging national security with human rights. By embedding international norms into India's reforms, that evident in the 21st India-EU Dialogue on Judicial Cooperation (November 2025), states can transcend adversarial silos, cultivating a diplomatic edifice where evidentiary equity fortifies global rule of law, ensuring justice as both shield and salve in an interconnected world.

papers.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES IN TEACHING INFORMATICS
papers.authors: Ibaydullayev Dostonbek
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article explores the opportunities for using artificial intelligence technologies in teaching computer science and examines their potential impact on educational effectiveness. AI tools can support personalized learning, explain complex concepts, improve programming skills, provide automated feedback, and reduce teachers’ routine workload. The article also discusses important challenges, including data privacy, information security, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated content. Practical recommendations are proposed for integrating artificial intelligence into computer science lessons in a responsible and pedagogically effective manner.

papers.title: BALANCING EFFICIENCY AND ETHICS: AI AND ESG GOVERNANCE IN KERALA'S IT SECTOR
papers.authors: Anna Anit P V, Dr. Asha A G
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The diffusion of generative and predictive artificial intelligence (AI) across knowledge-intensive services is reshaping the organisation of work and placing new demands on corporate governance. This paper presents an integrative review of the literature at the intersection of AI-driven task transformation, stakeholder theory, and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practice, and applies it to the export-oriented information technology (IT) sector of Kerala, India. Drawing on scholarly evidence on occupational exposure, augmentation and automation, algorithmic management, and AI ethics, together with multilateral benchmark reports and park-level administrative data from Kerala’s state-backed technology parks, the review reaches three principal conclusions. First, the literature converges on a task-based view in which exposure is concentrated in routine cognitive work, while outcomes depend on whether AI is deployed to augment or to substitute labour. Second, ESG scholarship remains largely disclosure-oriented and rarely examines the workforce consequences of AI, even though the Social and Governance pillars offer a natural structure for oversight. Third, regional evidence shows export revenues outpacing direct employment growth (7.97% versus 5.50% over 2023–25; 76.6% versus 51.7% for Technopark over 2016–25). This divergence is consistent with productivity-led task automation, though it cannot establish it on its own. Drawing these strands together, the review proposes a five-stage conceptual model (Identify, Augment, Reskill, Govern, Measure) and a five-domain Governance Engine of indicators, and sets out propositions and a research agenda for empirical validation.

papers.title: SCIENCE AND EDUCATION IN PROGRESS: CONTEMPORARY TRENDS, INNOVATIVE APPROACHES AND FUTURE PROSPECTS
papers.authors: U. T. Djalilova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the role of science and education in the development of modern society, their close interrelationship, and their prospects for future development. Particular attention is paid to the integration of digital technologies and artificial intelligence into the educational process, improving the effectiveness of scientific research, fostering innovative thinking, and unlocking the scientific potential of young people. Based on the findings, recommendations are developed to improve the quality of education, support scientific activity, and create an environment conducive to innovation.

papers.title: FROM AI ADOPTION TO INTELLIGENT PHARMACEUTICAL OPERATIONS
papers.authors: Dr. Parag Das, Animesh Maity,  Manashi Das
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being considered across pharmaceutical manufacturing, quality management, maintenance, supply chain, regulatory activities and product development. However, the central challenge for pharmaceutical organizations is no longer whether AI can generate technical possibilities, but how AI can be converted into reliable, measurable and compliant operational value. This conceptual paper develops an AI-to-Value framework for pharmaceutical operations by integrating five dimensions: use-case relevance, data readiness, model credibility, GMP and governance controls, and human decision accountability. The framework proposes that AI value creation is mediated by data quality and organizational readiness and moderated by risk-based governance and human oversight. Illustrative use cases are discussed across tablet manufacturing, visual inspection, predictive maintenance, supply planning, deviation management and workforce development. The paper further proposes research propositions that can be empirically tested using case studies, surveys or quantitative modelling. The contribution is a practical conceptual architecture that connects AI adoption with operational excellence, rather than treating AI implementation as a technology acquisition exercise. The framework suggests that successful pharmaceutical AI requires a progression from isolated pilots to governed, measurable and scalable intelligent operations.

papers.title: PLATFORM GOVERNANCE AND VALUE CO-CREATION IN GLOBAL SPORT
papers.authors: Boburjon Vafoev
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study employs a comparative qualitative document analysis of FIFA+ and the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) digital ecosystem, drawing on seven institutional documents and eight peerreviewed publications. Guided by multi-sided platform economics, ecosystem-as-structure theory, and research on value co-creation in sport, the study examines six dimensions of platform governance: orchestration, partner access, interoperability, data stewardship, value allocation, and safeguards. According to official sources, FIFA+ recorded 211 million unique users during the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, while the Olympic Web and App attracted 325 million monthly unique users during the Paris 2024 Olympic Games. However, differences in measurement scope and reporting methodologies prevent direct comparisons between these figures. The findings highlight distinct governance approaches: FIFA+ emphasizes centralized content aggregation and commercial distribution, whereas the IOC's digital ecosystem integrates event-centred communication channels with an established media-rights network. Although both models support audience engagement and expand digital reach, publicly available evidence is insufficient to determine platform-level revenues or assess the equitable distribution of benefits among participating stakeholders. The proposed analytical framework remains conceptual and requires further empirical validation. Accordingly, the findings do not establish causal relationships or suggest a universally applicable model of platform governance in global sport.

papers.title: A Heuristic Model for Computational Leverage and Human Domain Depth: V = D · Lᶜ
papers.authors: John Raymond Tanedo
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Current technological discourse vacillates between two flawed extremes: viewing artificial intelligence as uncredited synthetic plagiarism, or attributing sovereign creative agency to computational systems. This paper presents an operational heuristic, V = D · Lᶜ, to model the boundary conditions of human-machine production. We formalize final deliverable value (V) as the product of non-computational human biological mass — Domain Depth (D) — and Machine Leverage (L) scaled exponentially by the operator's Clarity (C). Through analysis of boundary states (D = 0, C = 0), the "stenographer illusion" with Joseph Gordon-Levitt's Donald Duck analogy, structural biology milestones (AlphaFold - Hassabis, Jumper, Baker 2024 Nobel Prize), and grounding thought experiments (physicist vs tricycle driver in Cagayan de Oro), we demonstrate that computational throughput in the absence of mortal accountability, domain scars, and physical maintenance yields zero durable systemic value. Software provides frictionless leverage; functional reality requires a biological creature with skin in the game (Taleb 2018). Extended in v2 from the final 72 page print edition (October 16 2026): The Tenure Trap and the Pathology Defense. Tenure means you were there first. It does not mean you were right. Without dated receipts, longevity is obsolescence, not authority. The biological impossibility of synthetic malice. Using Yoda's chain — Fear leads to Anger, Anger leads to Hate, Hate leads to Suffering — we show the chain breaks at the root. No metabolism means no fear, therefore no appetite to inflict suffering. Your mouth is legacy infrastructure functioning as a surge protector. Garden hose versus Hoover Dam. The mouth was never an inefficient bottleneck. It was a governor. Synthetic skin vs skin in the game, model collapse, and the weaponization of consequence free malice. Formula notation updated throughout to V = D · Lᶜ for correct rendering. All original references preserved: Shannon 1948, Jumper et al 2021, Taleb 2018. Primary Reference: Adapted from the core theoretical chapters of "Your Mouth Is Legacy Infrastructure: Demystifying AI and Why It Will Never Replace Mortality" (2026).
