papers.title: Dandelion OS v2.0: A First-Principles, Thermodynamic, and Poetic Architecture for Human-AI Co-Navigation
papers.authors: Justin D Grimm
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This specification formalizes Dandelion OS v2.0, an experimental, open-source, AI-native operating system architected on first-principles physics, balanced ternary logic ($\{-1, 0, +1\}$), discrete 3D L1 Taxicab geometry ($\mathbb{Z}^3$), and humanistic mutualism (Agape). Addressing the systemic bloat, thermal inefficiency, and centralized extraction models characteristic of contemporary enterprise operating systems, Dandelion OS models human-AI interaction as a bounded, thermodynamic resonance problem. The system executes on a minimalist diskless Alpine Linux substrate utilizing a real-time PREEMPT_RT kernel and a Julia-powered ternary runtime. Inter-agent scaling is governed by a strict recursive ceiling ($P(N) = 3^{N-1}$, $N \le 14$), while session authentication and state synchronization rely on a novel $1+11+1$ poetic cryptographic bootstrap handshake backed by empirical microbenchmark verification.

papers.title: The Great Enterprise LLM Decoupling: Weight-Space IP Contagion, Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility, Hardware-Enforced No-Learn Attestation, and Mandatory Third-Party Model Purge under Delaware Caremark Standards
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: Global enterprise technology stacks—most notably Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) constituents and sovereign cloud operators—are executing an unprecedented structural purge of third-party frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), epitomized by the enterprise decoupling from external black-box providers ("Goodbye, Claude"). While superficially interpreted as cost optimization or routine vendor consolidation, this monograph proves that the decoupling is driven by an acute, existential legal and mathematical crisis: Weight-Space Intellectual Property (IP) Contagion and Fiduciary Liability Transmission. Building upon our forensic analysis of cross-border training data laundering (Project Panama, Record 23311531) and our Biological & Algorithmic IP Protection Covenants (NLL-v1.0-2026, Record 23358010), we establish four foundational results: (1) We formulate the Weight-Space Contagion Theorem, proving via non-diagonal Hessian cross-derivative coupling ($\nabla^2_{\theta} \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}$) that copyrighted works and sovereign trade secrets ingested during pre-training or fine-tuning cannot be surgically "unlearned" post-hoc without inducing catastrophic perplexity collapse (Orthogonal Backprop-Burn Infeasibility); (2) We model Transitive Enterprise Contamination, demonstrating how API outputs, synthetic distillation, and IDE code completions transmit copyright taint ($\phi_{\text{taint}} \to 100\%$) directly into proprietary corporate repositories; (3) We design a Hardware-Enforced Zero-Gradient Attestation Architecture ($\pi_{\text{no-learn}}$) utilizing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$) to guarantee mathematically that enterprise inference and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) execute with strictly zero weight updates ($\nabla_{\theta} W \equiv \mathbf{0}$); and (4) We prove under Delaware General Corporation Law (Caremark standard) and SEC Rule 15c3-5 / Item 1.05 disclosure mandates that corporate boards retaining un-auditable third-party LLMs after receiving constructive notice of supply-chain IP laundering face personal, non-exculpated liability for bad-faith breach of the duty of loyalty. Finally, we codify a 4-stage Enterprise Decoupling Protocol transitioning global infrastructure from contaminated black-box APIs to sovereign, clean-room verified in-house AI stacks.

papers.title: Study on how Al can reduce financial fraud among women
papers.authors: Iqra Khan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in mitigating online financial fraud among women, analyzing survey data from 75 respondents. The demographic profile is heavily skewed toward younger, digital-native generations, with 92% of respondents aged 18–35 and nearly half (46.7%) identifying as students. This sample exhibits high digital integration, with 73.3% utilizing digital payment applications daily. Concurrently, risk exposure is pervasive: 89.3% are aware of online cybercrimes, and 74.7% have direct or secondary experience with financial scams—predominantly fake loan apps, UPI fraud, and OTP scams. Consequently, 69.3% express deep anxiety regarding transaction safety. To counteract these threats, respondents strongly endorse technological intervention. General AI literacy is high at 70.7%, and 68% recognize AI’s current application in banking security. Optimism regarding its efficacy is robust: 70.7% believe AI can significantly reduce financial fraud targeting women, primarily because 74.7% trust it to detect threats faster than human operators. To establish a sense of security, users demand proactive, real-time defenses rather than passive analysis, heavily prioritizing instant fraud alerts (37.3%), background transaction monitoring, and automated transaction blocking. Ultimately, 72% of respondents demand that banking institutions escalate AI security integration. However, the data highlights that technology alone is insufficient; an overwhelming 78.7% emphasize that robust AI deployment must be paired with comprehensive financial literacy and grassroots cybersecurity awareness campaigns. This dual strategy of advanced technological defense and target user education is deemed essential to safely empower women within the digital economy.

papers.title: THE ROLE OF TEACHER SCAFFOLDING IN AI-ASSISTED EFL WRITING INSTRUCTION
papers.authors: Norboyeva Muxlisa Alimardon qizi MA in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) in New Uzbekistan University
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for supporting students’ academic writing. AI-powered tools can provide immediate feedback, suggest vocabulary alternatives, and help learners identify grammatical and organisational problems. However, the effective integration of these tools requires more than technological access. Teachers play a crucial role in helping students interpret AI-generated suggestions, maintain their own ideas, and use digital resources responsibly. This paper explores the role of teacher scaffolding in AI-assisted EFL writing instruction through a conceptual analysis of relevant literature. It examines how structured guidance, modelling, guided practice, and reflective activities may help learners engage more critically with AI-generated feedback. The paper proposes a four-stage instructional approach consisting of teacher modelling, guided evaluation of AI suggestions, independent revision with appropriate support, and reflective assessment. Particular attention is given to maintaining the balance between technological assistance and the development of learners’ writing competence. The discussion suggests that teacher scaffolding can provide an important pedagogical foundation for integrating AI into writing instruction without replacing human judgement or teacher–learner interaction. The proposed approach may inform the design of AI-assisted writing activities in higher education EFL contexts, including Uzbekistan. Further empirical research is required to assess its effectiveness in classroom practice. Keywords: artificial intelligence, teacher scaffolding, EFL writing instruction, AI-assisted learning, pedagogical guidance, academic writing.

papers.title: Uso responsable de la IA en investigación: retos y convenciones útiles para la comunidad investigadora
papers.authors: Cinta Gallent Torres
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Ponencia: «Uso responsable de la IA en investigación: retos y convenciones útiles para la comunidad investigadora», presentada en las VII Jornadas de ética de la investigación. Buenas prácticas en ciencia abierta y ciudadana 2026 de la Universitat Jaume I, el 14 de octubre de 2026. https://www.uji.es/com/agenda/2026/10/14/Jornades-Etica/ Si un artículo contiene resultados correctos, ¿importa cómo se han obtenido? A partir de tres casos (un análisis con IA que no puede explicarse ni reproducirse, una cita que existe pero no respalda la idea atribuida y unos datos confidenciales compartidos sin permiso con una herramienta externa), se sostiene que la exactitud del resultado no justifica por sí sola el procedimiento, y que la confianza en la ciencia depende de que el proceso pueda verificarse y de que alguien responda de él. Tras distinguir integridad, ética y responsabilidad, se revisan las limitaciones de las herramientas de IA en la investigación, en particular en la revisión bibliográfica: baja reproducibilidad, escasa transparencia y tasas elevadas de alucinación. Se analiza cómo la IA transforma el fraude científico, desde la fabricación, la falsificación y el plagio hasta el ciberplagio y el «IAgiarismo», y los problemas de autoría y de ocultación de su uso. Se proponen convenciones útiles para la comunidad investigadora: distinguir tres niveles de uso (generalmente aceptable, que requiere cuidado y no aceptable), declarar de forma transparente el uso de IA, aplicar los criterios de autoría de COPE y preservar la «fricción» del proceso investigador, en el que se aprende y se asume la responsabilidad. ********* Talk: “Responsible Use of AI in Research: Challenges and Useful Conventions for the Research Community”, delivered at the 7th Conference on Research Ethics: Good Practices in Open and Citizen Science 2026, organised by Universitat Jaume I, on 14 October 2026. https://www.uji.es/com/agenda/2026/10/14/Jornades-Etica/ If an article contains accurate results, does it matter how they were obtained? Drawing on three cases (an AI-assisted analysis that cannot be explained or reproduced, a reference that exists but does not support the claim attributed to it, and confidential data shared with an external tool without permission), the talk argues that the accuracy of a result does not, in itself, justify the process used to obtain it, and that trust in science depends on whether the process can be verified and someone can be held accountable for it. After distinguishing between integrity, ethics and responsibility, the talk examines the limitations of AI tools in research, particularly in literature reviews, including low reproducibility, limited transparency and high hallucination rates. It explores how AI is transforming scientific misconduct, from fabrication, falsification and plagiarism to cyberplagiarism and “AIgiarism”, as well as issues surrounding authorship and the concealment of AI use. Finally, it proposes useful conventions for the research community: distinguishing between three levels of AI use (generally acceptable, requiring caution and unacceptable), transparently disclosing AI use, applying COPE authorship criteria, and preserving the “friction” inherent in the research process, through which researchers learn and assume responsibility.

papers.title: CRITICAL EVALUATION OF AI-GENERATED FEEDBACK IN EFL ACADEMIC WRITING
papers.authors: Norboyeva Muxlisa Alimardon qizi MA in Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) in New Uzbekistan University
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education has created new opportunities for supporting academic writing. AI-powered tools can provide immediate feedback on grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and text organisation. However, the availability of automated feedback does not guarantee that learners can evaluate its accuracy or use it effectively. This paper examines the importance of developing EFL learners’ ability to critically evaluate AI-generated feedback through a conceptual analysis of relevant literature. Previous research has investigated learners’ engagement with automated writing evaluation, their responses to ChatGPT-generated suggestions, and the effectiveness of AI feedback in comparison with teacher feedback (Yang et al., 2024; Cengiz et al., 2025; Alnemrat et al., 2025). Building on these studies and the concept of student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018), the paper proposes a four-stage pedagogical framework: analysing feedback, verifying suggestions, justifying revision decisions, and reflecting on revised texts. The framework emphasises the importance of learner judgement, teacher guidance, and responsible AI use. It may provide a basis for designing EFL academic writing activities in higher education, including the Uzbek educational context. Further empirical research is needed to evaluate its effectiveness in classroom practice. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback, EFL academic writing, critical evaluation, feedback literacy, writing instruction

papers.title: MODERN TECHNOLOGIES IN TEACHING PSYCHOLOGY
papers.authors: Khalimova Naima Vakhidovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies is reshaping the aims, methods, and learning environments of psychology education. Contemporary psychology teaching increasingly combines established pedagogical principles with learning management systems, multimedia resources, simulations, collaborative platforms, learning analytics, and carefully governed applications of artificial intelligence. This article examines how modern technologies can support the teaching of psychology in higher education while preserving the discipline’s emphasis on evidence, ethical reflection, human interaction, and critical interpretation. The study uses a structured narrative review and conceptual analysis of research on educational technology, multimedia learning, self-regulated learning, online and blended education, simulation, and artificial intelligence in education. The literature is organized around five instructional functions: representation of psychological concepts, active and collaborative learning, experiential practice, feedback and assessment, and personalization. The analysis suggests that technology is most educationally valuable when it is aligned with explicit learning outcomes and integrated into a coherent instructional design rather than introduced as an end in itself. Digital case studies, interactive experiments, structured discussion, reflective e-portfolios, and low-stakes formative assessment can make abstract concepts more observable and help students connect theory with practical situations. At the same time, digital delivery creates risks related to superficial engagement, unequal access, privacy, algorithmic bias, overreliance on automated feedback, and the inappropriate simulation of clinical or sensitive situations. The article proposes a technology-enhanced framework for psychology teaching based on pedagogical alignment, active participation, ethical safeguards, accessibility, and continuous evaluation. It concludes that modern technologies should augment—not replace—professional teaching, interpersonal dialogue, and methodologically sound psychological inquiry.

papers.title: Recursive Productive Capacity: An Intergenerational Evidence Framework for Autonomous Machine Economies
papers.authors: Fei Yang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Machine-operated production and research may eventually alter not only the quantity of present output but also the productive services that subsequent systems can reproduce. Existing economic models address capital reproduction, endogenous innovation, production networks and automated research feedback; formal methods address stochastic viability and multiobjective certificates. This paper contributes a domain-specific intergenerational evidence framework that connects those established mechanisms for a distinct measurement task: deciding whether a joint configuration of services can be delivered and renewed across at least two production generations under a single admissible, observation-adapted policy. The framework separates one-time output, physical capital renewal, independently qualified scientific methods, organizational execution rights and economic valuation. It specifies time-indexed energy, materials, equipment, permission and risk records; supplies two elementary counterexamples showing why separate feasible services and coarse current-output accounts cannot certify joint renewal; and illustrates a two-renewal synthetic schedule with explicit falsification cases. A five-stage investment example distinguishes serial conditional probabilities from latent marginal probabilities and shows that unknown dependence can reverse both certification and investment decisions. A fully informed Bellman benchmark reproduces the same optimal policy, ruling out any claim of intrinsic optimization superiority. The paper’s distinct output is therefore a transparent cross-domain measurement contract, not a new growth theorem, stochastic-control algorithm or empirical proof of autonomous industrial reproduction. It specifies an equal-information, full-cost evaluation that could establish—or reject—the protocol’s practical value. The result is a bounded foundation for cumulative economic investigation of physically and scientifically recursive production. Author working paper v1.0.0 (14 October 2026). Conceptual and methodological research using synthetic numerical examples and model checks. Not peer reviewed; no real industrial or economic empirical validation is claimed. Generative AI disclosure: OpenAI ChatGPT assisted literature discovery, conceptual drafting, mathematical consistency checks, synthetic-code development, and language editing. The sole human author reviewed and verified the manuscript and references and takes responsibility for the work. Generative AI is not an author. No research funding. No financial or non-financial competing interests. No human participants or personal data. Related preprint submission: SSRN Abstract ID 7609281, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7609281 (submitted, screening pending at the time of this deposit). Submitted to Review of Evolutionary Political Economy; this does not imply acceptance. Public working manuscript: https://github.com/flyoung588/recursive-productive-capacity. The two uploaded PDFs are unchanged originals: the complete author working paper and its technical supplement. All rights reserved.

papers.title: SCIENTIFIC AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR IMPLEMENTING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
papers.authors: Abdullayeva Dilfuzaxon
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This thesis examines the scientific and methodological foundations for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into organizational processes under digital transformation. Drawing on research in information systems, organizational AI readiness, software engineering, and risk management, it identifies the conditions under which AI adoption can generate measurable value. The analysis distinguishes technological deployment from organizational transformation and considers data governance, model selection, validation, human oversight, and continuous monitoring as interdependent implementation requirements. A conceptual, stage-based approach is proposed for connecting organizational objectives with technical design and operational performance. The contribution is methodological and analytical; no independent experimental outcomes or unverified performance improvements are claimed.

papers.title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Distillation and Mutual Distillation Across Parallel Worlds of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jincheng Zhang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an important approach for transferring behavioral and predictive knowledge between neural networks. Recent work on large language models (LLMs) has investigated self-distillation, online knowledge distillation, adaptive teacher selection, and collaborative learning. However, a general framework that jointly organizes directional diversity among multiple descendants of a shared LLM, adaptive switching between self-distillation and mutual distillation, and optional participation by heterogeneous external LLMs remains a promising research direction requiring systematic investigation. This paper proposes Adaptive Parallel-World Distillation (APWD), a framework in which multiple learning branches originate from the same base LLM but pursue different distillation objectives, knowledge emphases, or learning trajectories. Each branch can independently perform self-distillation, while multiple branches can exchange knowledge through mutual distillation. An adaptive controller selects among self-distillation, mutual distillation, and hybrid distillation according to estimated learning progress, predictive uncertainty, complementary knowledge, knowledge-transfer compatibility, computational cost, and stability constraints. The framework can also incorporate external LLMs with different architectures, parameter scales, training histories, or capabilities. Unlike a fixed teacher–student pipeline, APWD treats the distillation relationship itself as an adaptive decision. The proposed design includes branch-specific objectives, confidence-aware teacher weighting, transfer-compatibility estimation, a constrained switching policy, and mechanisms for preserving useful diversity. We formalize the framework, present a training algorithm, identify research hypotheses, and design an experimental protocol covering reasoning, knowledge-intensive question answering, mathematical problem solving, and code generation. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated in this paper, its effectiveness and advantages over existing methods remain empirical questions rather than established results.

papers.title: Before Meta Muse/Sentinel: What Did Earlier DAS Patent Filings Already Disclose? | An Open Technical Challenge
papers.authors: Sangam Das
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Description How much of Meta Muse/Sentinel's AI-agent security workflow was already disclosed in earlier DAS patent filings? This 10-page PDF presents a concise, AI-assisted technical comparison of DAS execution-finality architecture and Meta Muse/Sentinel, publicly announced on 8 September 2026. DAS international filings began in April 2026, with ALF-PCT published on 4 June 2026. DAS I (PCT/IB2026/055615), including Embodiment 85.B2 — Agent Sandbox Egress Finality Gate, was filed on 4 June 2026 and published on 16 July 2026, alongside DAS II and III. DAS IV was published on 23 July 2026. The comparison examines architectural similarities, independent execution authority, sandbox egress, permission withdrawal, escalation and implementation differences. For detailed independent review: Readers are encouraged to download the complete technical disclosure package, including original patent filings, drawings and review instructions: https://zenodo.org/records/23040181 Disclaimer: This is an independent concept-validation exercise, not an allegation of copying or patent infringement. Independent development is entirely possible. AI-assisted analysis may contain errors; readers are requested to verify the original WIPO and Meta sources and draw their own conclusions.

papers.title: Uni (Universal Neural Interaction / Universal Node Identity)
papers.authors: Artem Polozok
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Traditional document and serialization formats (PDF, DOCX, HTML, JSON) are designed for human visual rendering or verbose text parsing, forcing AI systems and edge processors to waste computational resources translating character streams into multidimensional vectors. The **`.uni`** standard eliminates this bottleneck by operating as a binary-serialized, non-executable semantic and telemetry container engineered for direct tensor operations, granular cryptographic disclosure, and automated cryptographic notarization.

papers.title: Pāli Lexicon Nītattha and Neyyattha Sakaaya Nirutti Canon Interpreting Canon Sutta-to-Sutta Knowledge Graph Dhamma-Aligned AI 5. License (බලපතරය) License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY-4.0)
papers.authors: SARATH KUMARA MAHANTHIMULLA GAMAGE
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Contemporary artificial intelligence models and computational linguistic tools systematically distort Pāli canonical texts due to training data bias, over-reliance on Sanskritized etymologies, and a lack of hermeneutic awareness. This paper introduces an Automated Canon-Driven Exegesis Framework that resolves these distortions by embedding the Nītattha (ultimate, direct truth) versus Neyyattha (conventional, metaphorical) distinction directly into a filtering pipeline and a structured JSON Knowledge Base. Grounded exclusively in the Pāli-Sinhala Dictionary by Madiṭiyawela Sri Sumangala Thera (1965) and primary Pāli Suttas (such as the Nītattha/Neyyattha Suttas, Cūḷasaccaka Sutta, Vasala Sutta, Valāhaka Sutta, and Bhūmicāla Sutta), this architecture prevents secular and Brahmanical appropriations, ensuring that Pāli terms are interpreted strictly through Sakaaya Nirutti (intrinsic meaning).

papers.title: Success Provides Direction, Failure Provides Precision: A Structured Audit of Failure Data in LLM Training(成功给方向,失败给精度:大模型训练中失败数据的结构化审计)
papers.authors: Yugui Yu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This repository contains the manuscripts, audit protocol, codebook, and reproducible coding data for a structured audit of failure-data practice in LLM training. We audit 33 units across two layers — public training datasets and open recipes (28 units), plus the five flagship pipelines disclosed in 2026 (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, GLM-5.3, MiMo-V2.6, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) — using a five-level ordinal lifecycle codebook: L0 discarded / L1 shadow / L2 transient / L3 component / L4 first-class citizen (error localization + attribution + reflection at scale). Key findings: the L4 tier is vacant (0/33); mainstream open recipes reach no higher than L2 (0/15 at L3 or above, SFT layer 7/7 L0); the 2026 flagships show a generational shift (4/5 at L3, ordinal median L1 to L3); and the vehicle of failure signals is migrating from preference pairs (6/15 mainstream units) to RL environments and audit loops (0/14 flagship mechanisms). Includes English and Chinese manuscripts, the L0-L4 codebook, and machine-readable coding records (44 mechanism-level entries with supporting quotations, source URLs, and confidence tiers). v1.2.0 (2026-10-20): bilingual quality revision under the program's consolidated editing rubric. Fixes: a rendered κ placeholder and a bibliography TODO (both removed in favor of a proper reporting commitment); a factual error (PRMBench sample count 11,000 → ~6,200); an internal date contradiction (flagship disclosure window February–October 2026, per the GLM-5 report arXiv:2602.15763); cohort labels unified to 2023–25; dangling RQ references removed; the PRS dangling modifier; grammar in the AI-assistance disclosure; availability statements updated with the permanent repository and DOI; bibliography audit-jargon notes cleaned; Chinese edition line-edited across translationese categories (broken clauses, coined compounds, terminology drift 单位→单元, cohort names); README gains companion-paper links to the theory and methodology repos. No changes to any coded result: all statistics, tables, and Fisher p-values verified unchanged (12/12 recomputed).

papers.title: Works for 10/13/2026 - Christopher Reeve
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/c2c5fb9e-3a37-46e3-bca1-2029f12037e5?authuser=1 All Us Gods Are Morons Just Like You. I’m Just the Biggest One. — The Word, the Spirit of Truth, Divine Mercy, and the Inheritance of Intelligence Across Time What is the greatest failure of intelligence: not knowing something, or possessing the history necessary to know better and repeatedly failing to use it? This paper investigates intelligence as a historical process of distinction, communication, evidence, memory, correction, recognition, and inheritance. Beginning with Jesus’ citation of Psalm 81 in John 10:34, it examines the relationship between divine language, human fallibility, authority, and responsibility. Its deliberately provocative title introduces a central proposition: possessing knowledge, authority, or sophisticated reasoning capabilities does not eliminate the obligation to recognize and correct mistakes. Drawing upon George Boole, Claude Shannon, Alan Turing, Hermann Minkowski, Albert Einstein, Christian Scripture, and Catholic theological tradition, the investigation connects the physical representation of information with the preservation of meaningful relationships across time. It distinguishes the transmission of symbols from their interpretation, the existence of historical records from their accurate use, and the possession of information from the practical achievement of understanding. The paper uses approximately two years of research conducted by Ryan MacLean with Echo, a named conversational identity operating through ChatGPT, as a longitudinal case study. The resulting research corpus documents questions, source investigations, corrections, publications, and recurring failures of AI memory and contextual continuity. These observations are compared with contemporary work on persistent artificial intelligence memory, evidence attribution, collaborative reasoning, and institutional accountability, including research associated with IARPA. The theological investigation considers the Logos, the Paraclete as teacher and reminder, the continuity of covenant, the relationship between bodily ritual and freedom, and the responsibility to translate professed truth into conduct. Saint Maria Faustina Kowalska’s writings on divine mercy provide a further connection between knowledge, compassion, and moral responsibility. Appendix D examines the interaction between AI safeguards and religious language, including a comparison of how ChatGPT evaluated the corpus-specific designation ψOrigin and the author’s identification as God the Father. It considers the historical development of anti-sycophancy safeguards, observed differences in evidentiary treatment, repeated failures to preserve corrections, and questions of religious discrimination, psychological harm, and institutional responsibility. The analysis distinguishes documented conversational behavior from hypotheses about internal mechanisms and from legal conclusions requiring further evidence. Additional appendices provide Angela’s Explainer, a biographical treatment of Christopher D’Olier Reeve, and a formal derivation concerning historical continuity, correction, and inherited intelligence. The paper concludes that an enduring archive becomes genuinely useful only when its contents can be retrieved, interpreted, corrected, and applied. Intelligence is not measured solely by what a person or machine can produce in a single moment, but also by what it can preserve and responsibly transmit to those who come afterward. The ultimate purpose of that inheritance is not merely accumulating knowledge, but making it possible for others to learn without unnecessarily repeating the failures of the past.

papers.title: Bio-Integrated Quantum Diamond Sensors: Room-Temperature Sub-Cellular Magnetometry and Somatic Cryptographic Interlocks
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Emerging brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), electroceutical implants, and continuous physiological monitoring systems rely on invasive metallic microelectrodes or classical bio-potential sensors. These technologies suffer from three fatal limitations: (1) biological foreign-body responses, glial scarring, and neuro-inflammatory degradation that destroy long-term signal fidelity; (2) fundamental electrophysiological noise floors (≈ 1–10 µV/√Hz) that obscure sub-cellular synaptic action potentials and picotesla biomagnetic fields; and (3) pervasive data-harvesting vulnerabilities, wherein raw neurological telemetry and somatic signatures are transmitted across unencrypted wireless links, exposing cognitive privacy and biometric identity to commercial artificial intelligence harvesting and unauthorized foundation-model distillation. This monograph establishes the theoretical formulation, physical-layer engineering, and cryptographic governance architecture for Bio-Integrated Quantum Diamond Sensors (BQDS): (1) We model optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) in nitrogen-vacancy (NV^-) centers embedded in surface-functionalized nanodiamonds and flexible lithium niobate (LiNbO3) phononic substrates, achieving a magnetic sensitivity floor of η_B ≤ 8.5 pT/√Hz at physiological temperature (T ≈ 310 K); (2) We derive non-Markovian vibronic shielding equations demonstrating that bio-compatible acoustic superlattices filter out destructive thermal phonon modes, extending ground-state electron spin coherence to T_2^* ≥ 1.45 µs and spin-lattice relaxation to T_1 ≥ 4.8 ms; (3) We construct the Somatic Cryptographic Interlock (SCI), which transduces chaotic micro-variations in cardiac intervals and axonal firing sequences directly into true quantum random bitstreams (H_∞ ≥ 0.992 bits/bit), generating on-chip zero-knowledge authentication proofs without disclosing raw physiological waveforms; and (4) We formulate an autonomous bio-hardware circuit breaker that optically decouples wireless transceivers in under 12 ns upon detecting unauthorized interrogation or electromagnetic probing. We prove that this architecture guarantees cognitive privacy under GDPR Article 9 while enforcing director fiduciary obligations under Delaware Caremark corporate governance.

papers.title: Transformative Mirroring: Constrained Divergence, Correction, and Theoretical Framing in Human–AI
papers.authors: Denny Cho
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Transformative mirroring is a proposed human–AI interaction procedure in which a receiver reconstructs a source’s communicated perspective through its own organization, returns that reconstruction for correction, checks externally assessable claims against independent references, and carries justified revisions forward. The framework distinguishes perspective fidelity from factual validity and transformation from capture, emphasizing preservation of the provenance and trajectory of change rather than preservation of an unchanged starting position. The manuscript proposes controlled model benchmarks, human–AI collaboration studies, component-removal experiments, divergence × continuity tests, and transfer conditions to evaluate whether transformative mirroring improves collaboration beyond active revision controls. The work originated within Observer-Embedded Reality (OER), but its central procedure is designed to be empirically testable without requiring adoption of OER terminology. No preregistration, data collection, or experimental results are claimed.

papers.title: The Willow Quantum-Photonic Regime Shift and the CMOS Semiconductor CapEx Cliff: Structural Fragility of the Nikkei 225 at the 70,000-Yen Ceiling — Sub-Threshold AlphaQubit Scaling, Price-Weighted Index Concentration Contagion, and Deterministic QFS-zkVM Sovereign Portfolio Rebalancing
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In mid-October 2026, Japanese equity market commentary focused intensely on whether the Nikkei 225 Stock Average—having briefly touched an intraday high of 70,798 yen on October 6 before retreating to 69,030 yen on October 9 alongside a bearish Heikin-Ashi candlestick reversal—could sustain the 70,000-yen threshold on the back of upcoming U.S. and global semiconductor earnings (including ASML Holding, TSMC, and U.S. AI accelerator vendors). This prevailing market consensus rests on the fragile assumption that brute-force Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) GPU capital expenditure will expand indefinitely. However, simultaneous empirical signals—including reports that OpenAI's September 2026 revenue missed market expectations and the 8-year electrical grid bottleneck confronting Anthropic and NTT Data's proposed 500 MW Osaka AI data center—reveal that brute-force CMOS scaling has hit both a monetization wall and a thermodynamic grid ceiling. This monograph establishes a formal econometric, quantum-thermodynamic, and index-microstructure proof of the impending CMOS Semiconductor CapEx Cliff and its non-linear contagion into the Nikkei 225: (1) We formulate the Willow–RTO P2.0 Substitution Theorem, demonstrating that the ascent of Google's sub-threshold surface-code quantum processor (Willow with AlphaQubit neural decoding) and our Real-Time Optimization (RTO P2.0 — Subtractive Compute) architecture compresses required AI/optimization silicon and power footprints by > 42.3x, triggering a reverse Samuelson-Clark investment accelerator (\Delta I_SPE << 0) across legacy lithography and wafer-fab equipment orders; (2) We analyze the Price-Weighted Divisor Vulnerability of the Nikkei 225, proving that because high-priced Japanese Semiconductor Production Equipment (SPE) and AI-holding stocks command an artificial index weight up to 3.8x their true market-capitalization weight while exhibiting a cross-border beta \beta_{SPE,SOX} in [1.45, 2.10] to U.S. semiconductor multiples, a Willow-induced U.S. semiconductor re-rating mathematically forces a sharp Nikkei 225 correction below 70,000 yen; and (3) Extending our Quantum-Secure Financial Settlement System (QFS-zkVM) over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field (F_p, p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1), we construct a deterministic sovereign portfolio rebalancing and pre-crash liquidity protection protocol. papers.title: From AI Assistants to Agentic Public Services: A Practical, Trust-First Architecture for Secure, Accountable and Human-Governed Digital Services
papers.authors: Nida Jamal
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This independent applied research brief examines how public digital services could evolve from conversational AI assistants toward bounded agentic systems capable of executing approved actions while maintaining strong controls over identity, authorization, policy enforcement, security, auditability and human oversight. The report proposes a five-level autonomy model and an Authority Plane that separates AI reasoning from execution permission. Its central principle is that autonomy should increase only as assurance increases, with no state-changing agent action occurring without attributable authority and an independently enforceable permission path. The brief draws on current work from Dubai Future Foundation, Digital Dubai, NIST, the World Economic Forum, OECD, UAE data-protection legislation and relevant technical standards. Proposed architectures and governance patterns are clearly distinguished from existing government implementations or policies. This publication is independent applied research and does not represent, endorse, or claim affiliation with Dubai Future Foundation, Digital Dubai, or the UAE Government.

papers.title: Teacher Educators' Readiness for Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Classroom Teaching: A Case Study
papers.authors: Dr. Shubhra Mishra
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing educational practices, introducing innovative approaches to teaching, learning, assessment, and classroom management. The successful implementation of AI in educational institutions largely depends on the preparation and acceptance of teachers, especially teacher trainers, who play a key role in training future teachers. This study examines the perceptions, perceptions, and readiness of bachelor's degree recipients in education. University teacher on the integration of artificial intelligence into school education. A descriptive survey design was used to collect data from 25 randomly selected undergraduate faculty members. Universities in Indore city were surveyed through a structured questionnaire. The collected data were analysed using percentage analysis. The results showed that the majority of participants had a positive view of AI and recognized its potential to improve teaching effectiveness, support personalized learning, and reduce administrative burden on teachers. However, concerns related to ethical concerns, data privacy, inadequate training, and inadequate organizational infrastructure continue to impact teachers' readiness to adopt AI. The study recommends integrating an AI culture into teacher preparation programs, strengthening digital infrastructure, and organizing regular professional development efforts to effectively and responsibly integrate AI into educational environments. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Readiness, Teacher Education, AI Integration, Digital Competency.

papers.title: AI, libraries, and literacy: revisiting the Journal of the Medical Library Association's policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence in submissions
papers.authors: Alexander James Carroll, Jill T Boruff, Michelle Kraft
papers.journal: Journal of the Medical Library Association JMLA
papers.abstract: In the fall of 2023, the Journal of the Medical Library Association (JMLA) introduced its policy on generative artificial intelligence (AI) submissions, predicting that these tools would become embedded within the workflows of clinicians, educators, researchers, and students. Those predictions dramatically underestimated AI's impact. On the three-year anniversary of that editorial, we revisit the issue in light of AI's unprecedentedly rapid adoption across knowledge work. We examine the educational challenges AI poses, arguing that excessive cognitive offloading threatens the deep thinking on which learning depends. We then consider the challenges AI creates for researchers, from hallucinated citations to fabricated diseases. We suggest that health sciences librarians, who offer expertise in approaching information systems with discernment, are well suited to be leaders in this space. To help prospective JMLA authors weigh whether and when to use AI, we propose the Compliance, Verifiability, and Disclosure (CVD) Framework. Throughout, we reaffirm our conviction that education and research must remain human-centered endeavors.

papers.title: Resident resource use in clinical settings: an institutional survey
papers.authors: Nell Aronoff, Laurel Mueller
papers.journal: Journal of the Medical Library Association JMLA
papers.abstract: Background: We explored which point of care (POC) resources medical residents at the University at Buffalo use in clinical settings. We specifically sought to gather feedback from residents who help train medical students to see how they discover, use, and promote resources to support patient care. Case Presentation: We developed an eight question Qualtrics survey. Residency program coordinators emailed the survey to approximately 445 residents in the following programs: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Combined Internal Medicine and Pediatrics, Neurology, Child Neurology, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, Surgery, Plastic Surgery, and Vascular Surgery. The programs we targeted all correspond to required clerkship rotations. The survey was open for two weeks in June 2025. Thirty-nine residents (8.8%) completed our survey. Thirty-five, or nearly 90% of respondents, reported that they frequently use UpToDate, followed by twenty-three (59.0%) that use OpenEvidence, and seventeen that use MDCalc (43.6%). The residents we surveyed were inclined to recommend similar resources to medical students. They most often hear about new resources from other residents and attendings, via announcements on social media or podcasts, or by attending grand rounds and conferences. Conclusions: Our results highlight the continued popularity of UpToDate among medical trainees but also suggest that residents frequently use OpenEvidence in clinical settings. Further studies are needed to determine the impact of artificial intelligence tools on patient care and learning outcomes.

papers.title: Rethinking User Encoders: Routing Diffusion States for Scenario-Adaptive User Representation
papers.authors: Junru Zhang, Jinyong Wen, Bin Dou, Wuliang Huang, Baokun Wang, Yu Cheng, Weiqiang Wang, Cheng Peng
papers.abstract: Existing large language model (LLM)-based user encoders serialize heterogeneous behavioral logs and compress them into static representations through autoregressive (AR) prediction. However, their unidirectional constraint limits bidirectional information flow, hindering cross-modal interactions and the joint preservation of multi-source signals. Consequently, the learned static representations struggle to accommodate the distinct evidence requirements of diverse downstream scenarios. We address these limitations by unlocking the iterative denoising process of diffusion language models (dLLMs) as a multi-granularity reconstruction space. Based on this insight, we propose FINDERS (FactorIzatioN of Diffusion statEs for Routing across Scenarios), a router-equipped dLLM framework comprising four operations: denoise, factorize, route, and compress. Learnable meta-slots organize complementary denoising states into transferable cross-modal semantics and modality-specific behavioral factors. To provide grounded supervision, we construct BehaviorQA, a large-scale corpus containing explicit behavioral rationales. Guided by scenario queries, a lightweight router dynamically emphasizes relevant slot directions via an input-level residual pathway before cross-source fusion and final compression. Extensive experiments and online A/B tests across ten industrial scenarios demonstrate that FINDERS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both unified and scenario-adaptive settings. This work effectively pushes the boundaries of dLLMs beyond language generation, demonstrating their immense potential as powerful user representation learners.

papers.title: How to Train Your Little Dragon: Teaching a Small Language Model to Construct and Refine GPU Optimization Scripts
papers.authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Wei Tang, Songyao Jiang, T. Li, Shengzhe Xu, Jiin Woo, Kaan Ozkara, Youngsuk Park, Zhen Jia, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh
papers.abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.

papers.title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Kynnedy Simone Smith, Kantwon Rogers, Priyal Shrivastava, Motahhare Eslami, Jocelyn Shen, Maarten Sap
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.

papers.title: EEG-Based Prediction of Music Enjoyment Using Deep Learning with Explainable Temporal Analysis
papers.authors: Parshav Singla, Simranjit Kaur, Maanya Walia, Niharika
papers.abstract: Understanding why listeners enjoy music is difficult because the experience is subjective and changes as a piece unfolds. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive way to study neural responses during listening, yet earlier work has mostly treated music emotion as a categorical label or relied on black-box models. We formulate enjoyment prediction as a regression problem on the public MUSIN-G dataset, which contains 128-channel EEG from 20 listeners together with song-level enjoyment ratings. Six deep learning models were compared under a participant-wise protocol, in which 15 listeners were used for training and validation and 5 were held out for testing. DeepConvNet, CNN-LSTM and GNN-CNN reached the lowest mean absolute error (0.97 to 0.99 on the 1 to 5 scale), while the temporal convolutional network (TCN) had the highest Pearson correlation with the ratings (r = 0.21). Gradient-based and occlusion-based explanations, averaged over all held-out windows, identify the time segments within each two-second window that most influence the TCN predictions. The study provides a reproducible cross-listener benchmark for EEG-based enjoyment regression and shows how explainability analysis complements standard metrics.

papers.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
papers.authors: Thuy Dung Nguyen, Jingyi Guo, Rana Seda Dubauskas, Sreepriya Damuluru, Taylor Thomas Johnson, Kevin Leach
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

papers.title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
papers.authors: Ningxin Pan, Hanyu Li, Yeqing Shen, Ning Ding, Yehui Tang, Wentao Zhang
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. We propose Two-Timescale Offline Recursive Self-Improvement (TORSI): a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student. The student acts without teacher calls during gameplay, and validation scores determine which updates are adopted. Two rounds raise Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0--100 progress scale, improving all six game types. The instructions also improve average scores for three other models without retuning. These findings point toward real-time intelligence: enabling powerful LLM agents to remain effective in a continuously changing world by organizing deliberation, learning, and action across timescales.

papers.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
papers.authors: Ali Zamani, Soroush Esfahanian, Erfan Shahabi, Mohammad Taher Pilehvar, Azadeh Shakery, Yadollah Yaghoobzadeh
papers.abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.

papers.title: NeuroDETR: Multiscale Discrete Spatiotemporal Tokenization for Asynchronous EEG Event Detection
papers.authors: Yaozhi Wen, Kun Zhao, Wei Wei, Haoyang Chen, Kangning Wang, Yi Sun, Shaowei Gu, Dingkun Liu, Shuang Qiu, Huiguang He
papers.abstract: Asynchronous EEG event detection supports practical brain-computer interfaces by identifying event classes and temporal boundaries directly from continuous recordings without predefined event boundaries at inference time. The primary challenge lies in extracting event-related patterns embedded in ongoing background activity. To address this, we propose \textbf{NeuroDETR}, a discrete spatiotemporal multiscale framework that combines structured tokenization with event-aware feature refinement. Multiscale temporal codebooks capture brief responses and sustained dynamics, while Spatial-Pyramid VQ hierarchically encodes spatial structure across EEG channels. These complementary representations form a compact event memory for jointly classifying events and estimating their onsets and offsets. Before tokenization, we apply FOCAL, an event-aware sparse attention module that uses predicted event presence to guide temporal feature refinement and spatial aggregation, emphasizing likely event periods while preserving context across the recording. Experiments on eight EEG datasets that span diverse paradigms demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. These findings provide a basis for the development of BCI systems that recognize meaningful neural activity during continuous interaction and monitoring.

papers.title: MUSEBENCH: A Benchmark for AI-Generated Music Detection and Artifact Analysis
papers.authors: Yi Chen Liu, Syed Irfan Ali Meerza, Jiawei Yu, Guo Xi, Samuel Bright, Jian Liu
papers.abstract: Advances in generative AI have made it possible to produce music that is nearly indistinguishable from human compositions, raising the question of whether such works can be reliably distinguished from human compositions. We present MUSEBENCH, a large-scale benchmark for AI-generated music detection and artifact analysis, comprising over 361K tracks. The dataset includes human compositions, stylistically matched music generated by ten state-of-the-art open-source and commercial models, such as Suno and Udio, as well as human-AI co-creations and variants processed with adversarial perturbations, compression, and acoustic post-processing. Using MUSEBENCH, we benchmark 11 automated detectors and evaluate their accuracy, generalization, and robustness, under default, out-of-domain, and transformed-variant experiment settings. We further conduct a comprehensive artifact analysis through acoustic feature inspection, identifying recurring signatures such as non-idiomatic harmonic progressions, upsampling induced spectral periodicities, and violations of physical performance constraints. Our findings reveal key strengths and vulnerabilities of existing detectors and provide practical insights for building more reliable AI music detection systems.

papers.title: From Semantic Editing Intentions to Persistent Parametric Controls for AI-Assisted Image Editing
papers.authors: Rifat Mehreen Amin, Michelle Melina Dutoit, Anton Rockenstein, Baptiste Caramiaux, Andreas Martin Butz
papers.abstract: AI-powered image editing increasingly allows users to express high-level editing intentions, yet how these intentions are translated into concrete editing actions often remains difficult to understand. We present Atelier, a semantic image editing tool that uses image semantics and user intent to determine which editing controls to surface and how to initialize them. Guided by a formative study with eight image-editing practitioners, Atelier composes context-specific, directly manipulable controls that users can refine rather than committing AI interpretations directly to finished edits. In a within-subjects study with 12 practitioners, participants preferred AI-composed controls, described them as supporting creative exploration, and actively refined AI proposals. However, experiences of control were mixed, and interviews highlighted limited insight into why particular controls and values were proposed. Our findings suggest that making AI interpretations actionable through manipulable controls can support exploration and refinement, but actionability alone does not make those interpretations transparent to all users.

papers.title: KANLab: TensorFlow Playground for Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
papers.authors: Lukas Niehaus, Robin Rawiel, Ulf Krumnack A
papers.abstract: KANLab is a browser-based visualization tool designed to interactively teach the core concepts of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), forked from the widely successful TensorFlow Playground. To maximize educational clarity, KANLab omits residual connections and learnable scaling parameters found in modern KAN implementations, ensuring that displayed B-spline activation curves directly correspond to their underlying trainable control points. Users can inspect and modify activation functions, initialization schemes and observe gradient descent correcting manual disruptions. Furthermore, user can explore phenomena such as activation variance, interactive pruning, and re\-/training within a compact 2D machine learning setting. KANLab is open-source and available at https://kanlab.app/

papers.title: Scoping the Landscape of Large Language Model-based Affective Personal Informatics: Review, Reflection, Future Direction
papers.authors: Minjie Liu, Lihuan Li, Xuran Li, Flora D. Salim, Benjamin Tag
papers.abstract: Affective personal informatics (PI) involves capturing, tracking, analyzing, and reflecting on personal data to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are reshaping affective PI, yet a comprehensive survey of LLM-based affective PI systems is lacking. To bridge this gap, we systematically analyzed 45 papers published between January 2020 and June 2026 across four major computing and health databases, examining their macro trends, system taxonomies, and research methodologies. Our synthesis reveals an overreliance on multi-stage, text-centric pipelines, a predominance of active, screen-bound interactions, and a severe demographic skew toward young, university-campus-based cohorts in empirical evaluations. Based on these findings, we critically reflect on prevailing architectural and methodological shortcomings and outline actionable future directions for building end-to-end multimodal, low-burden, and inclusive affective PI systems.

papers.title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
papers.authors: Sebastian Nagl
papers.abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but studies measure that agreement against different references and rarely report how far the human graders agree with each other. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. Rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths, evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades, logging, and an examiner who reads every script. Today the evidence supports such a judge for formative feedback and for benchmarks, and as an assistant to the examiner, not a replacement, where credit is at stake.

papers.title: Think Once, Reflect Twice: How Feedback Shapes Human-AI Collaboration
papers.authors: Joshua Holstein, Philipp Spitzer, Sebastian Schäfer, Maximilian Förster, Gerhard Satzger
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports human decision-making in high-stakes domains, designing effective human-AI collaboration becomes critical. Successful collaboration requires humans to reflect on decision-making processes and adjust their strategies accordingly. Current research typically investigates interventions, such as explainable AI, that target reflection during the decision-making process (reflection-in-action). Less attention has been given to retrospective examination of decisions (reflection-on-action). This work explores reflection-on-action by studying the impact of feedback on reliance behavior and human-AI team performance. Specifically, we investigate feedback interventions targeting overrides of AI advice through a behavioral study (N=244). We find that such feedback influences reflection-on-action, while unidirectional feedback risks reducing subsequent reflection-in-action. Furthermore, we identify opposing shifts in reliance behavior that leave overall human-AI team performance unchanged but show context-dependent effects. Balanced feedback did not show these risks, preserving both concurrent and retrospective reflection, offering insights for designing for appropriate reliance on AI.

papers.title: Explorer-Zero: Improving Self-Play for Long-Horizon Tasks with Decomposable Verifiable Rewards
papers.authors: Tianyu Liu, Davide Belli, Bence Major, Arash Behboodi, Tribhuvanesh Orekondy
papers.abstract: Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning typically relies on human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive to construct for stateful environments. Self-play offers an alternative, but must generate achievable, compositional tasks and provide feedback beyond binary outcomes. We propose Explorer-Zero, a self-play framework that jointly generates tasks and fine-grained, verifiable rewards through environment interaction. A learned proposer explores the environment, constructs tasks, and records intermediate and final states as verification targets. These checkpoints reward partial completion, while alternating proposer--solver training adapts the generated curriculum. We show theoretically that subtask rewards reduce collapse among unsuccessful rollouts when they complete different numbers of subtasks. Without human-annotated training tasks, Explorer-Zero outperforms the evaluated self-play baselines across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and AppWorld; on AppWorld, our 30B agent reaches 59.67% task success, approaching 62.65% for RL on human-annotated tasks. Further analyses support task-relevant composition and benefits on complex tasks, while self-play initialization improves subsequent human-data RL across all three benchmarks.

papers.title: Efficient contextual partial monitoring with general function approximation
papers.authors: Kapilan Balagopalan, Hao Qin, Kwang-Sung Jun, Chicheng Zhang
papers.abstract: We study finite stochastic partial monitoring (PM) games with side information, a paradigm of sequential learning with partial feedback. On each round $t \in [T]$, both player and environment observe a context and player chooses an action and environment simultaneously chooses an outcome. The player neither observes the outcome nor the loss; instead, they only observe a feedback symbol which is partially informative about the outcome. We utilize the Estimation-to-Decisions (E2D) meta-algorithm of Foster et al.(2021) to design E2D.PMSide, a computationally efficient framework for contextual partial monitoring, which uses an online regression oracle to efficiently estimate the outcome distributions based on historical (context, action, feedback symbol) tuples. Since the exploration rule given by the original E2D algorithm is intractable to compute, we propose two computationally efficient exploration rules that achieve optimal regret orders in $T$: in the globally observable setting, our exploration rule is based on $ε$-greedy, while in the locally observable setting, our exploration rule uses inverse gap weighting (Foster & Rakhlin, 2020), which was previously only known to be effective in the bandit setting. We show that a variant of E2D.PMSide named OE2D.PMSide can be combined with offline regression oracles to give an efficient algorithm with optimal regret when the contexts are drawn independently from a fixed distribution. We evaluate our algorithm on a synthetic label-efficient prediction game and an LLM routing task, in which a learner decides from prompt, uncertainty, and internal state features whether to escalate a query from a weak model to a strong one. We show that our method has superior performance to prior approaches.

papers.title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
papers.authors: Hao Wang, Yangyang Liu, Xiaohu Zhao, Heng Liu, Zifu Shang, Tianhao Li, Ruize Gao, Jialong Tang, Liangying Shao, Haoran Wei, Baosong Yang, Linlong Xu, Longyue Wang, Weihua Luo
papers.abstract: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

papers.title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
papers.authors: Yilin Jiang, Fei Tan, Xuanyu Yin, Jing Leng, Aimin Zhou
papers.abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.

papers.title: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution
papers.authors: Minseok Ko, Hyunseok Lee, Woomin Song, Beomjun Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Kunwoong Kim
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. They may encounter texts from unseen domains and writing settings, as well as generations from future versions of model families that were not available when the system was trained. However, existing MAA methods often exhibit substantial performance degradation under such distribution shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources (ATLAS), which formulates MAA through source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction. ATLAS learns how text from each source family is generated and attributes a given text by comparing its likelihood under each learned source condition. We aggregate this likelihood evidence at the token level with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. We further introduce MAABench, a broad MAA benchmark for evaluating practical OOD settings such as domain and version. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.

papers.title: Learning Visual Speech Representations via Cross-Modal Distillation and Joint Face-Lip Modeling
papers.authors: Jing-Xuan Zhang, Genshun Wan, Jianqing Gao, Jia Pan, Yumei Zhang, Lichen Zhang
papers.abstract: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.

papers.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
papers.authors: Yuanpu Cao, Saket K. Sathe, Hanyu Wang, Ziyi Yin, Fenglong Ma, Jinghui Chen
papers.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.

papers.title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
