Therefore, the 36 participants provided insight into their households’ dietary practices and food decision-making processes. All focus group discussions were audio recorded to ensure accuracy and authenticity of participants’ narratives, then directly translated into English within a few days of being conducted. Each transcript was cross-checked by at least two team members. Data were analyzed thematically using Braun and Clarke’s approach: codes, categories, themes, and subthemes were iteratively refined through collaborative team review and organized within the socioecological framework. Results: The analysis identified two overarching themes at the individual, family, community and structural levels. Attachment to traditional and ethnic foods functioned as important cultural and health-related anchors. Participants shared their preference for ethnic foods as healthier, more natural, tastier and central to identity and continuity after migration. Sustaining healthy dietary practices at the individual and family levels was shaped by complex factors such as: work and caregiving demands, stress, time constraints, and changing family dynamics and roles. Intergenerational differences were especially salient. Children adopted American foods faster, increasing reliance on fast and convenience foods, creating household tensions, and sometimes requiring separate meal preparations. Community and structural factors further shaped dietary choices. High costs, limited availability of cultural foods, distance to ethnic stores, and transportation barriers constrained access, while highly processed and sugary foods were easily accessible. Participants also described reduced routine physical activity and migration-related stress as contributors to perceived diabetes risk. Ethnic grocery stores, halal markets, community networks, recipe adaptation, and the continued consumption of traditional foods were perceived as protective resources amidst these challenges. Overall, the findings appear to demonstrate that food and dietary acculturation are not a linear process in which immigrants shift from a traditional to a Western-based diet. Rather, it is shaped by complex interactions across individual, family, community, and structural factors. The study limitations, and implications for practice and research are discussed in the paper.

papers.title: Hybrid Vulnerability Discovery in the Wild: Automated Screening, Fine-Tuned LLMs, and Four Published CVEs
papers.authors: Sai Teja Erukude, Lior Shamir
papers.abstract: Automated security scanners produce many alerts, but disclosure requires evidence of attacker control, reachability, impact, and reproducibility. We present an evidence-gated workflow that screens recently updated Python AI/ML and data-science packages then uses two separately fine-tuned open-weight agents to distinguish vulnerability plausibility from CVE worthiness: the first tests attacker control and reachability, and the second assesses novelty and impact before human proof-of-concept validation and coordinated disclosure. In a targeted campaign covering 400 packages, screening yielded 1292 clustered signals; the agents retained 96 vulnerability hypotheses, including 65 provisional CVE candidates. All 13 Critical or High candidates were reproduced with benign proofs of concept and acknowledged by a CVE Numbering Authority as valid security findings. As of 30 September 2026, four had published CVEs affecting OpenMed, Python StateMachine, uproot, and SpeechBrain; five had maintainer-acknowledged patches in progress; and four awaited maintainer response. Field detection accuracy was not measured.

papers.title: Neuro-Trust and System Trust: A Dual-Track Trust Structure and Antecedent Patterns in EEG-BCI Attention Training
papers.authors: Xiaolin Zhou, Hancheng Cao, Minjian Hong, Qingling Du, Fang Hao
papers.abstract: As brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) move toward training, rehabilitation, and consumer use, users must judge both whether a system is technically reliable and whether it credibly represents their own neural or attentional state. This study tests whether trust after an initial EEG attention-training session is better represented by two related yet distinguishable targets: Neuro-Trust (NT), trust in the system’s representation of one’s internal state, and System Trust (ST), trust in the overall device–algorithm–training system. Candidate antecedents were generated from interviews with 18 users and comments from five platforms; survey data from 300 young adults yielded 274 valid cases. A nine-factor confirmatory factor analysis fit better than an eight-factor model merging NT and ST (Δχ2(8) = 327.155, p < 0.001; HTMT = 0.411). Structural equation modeling showed that perceived feedback explainability (PFE) related positively to both NT and ST, whereas perceived attention-regulation value (PARV) related to NT only (Δχ2(1) = 21.655, p < 0.001; bootstrap Δβ = 0.388, 95% CI [0.168, 0.607]). Out-of-fold SHAP analysis under repeated nested cross-validation reproduced this pattern: PARV ranked first for NT but fifth for ST, whereas PFE ranked second and first. BCI trust may thus comprise related but distinguishable dimensions with shared and limited track-specific antecedents.

papers.title: Development of a Machine-Learning-Based Predictive Model for Burnout Among Senior High School Teachers
papers.authors: Jun Peng, Yilin Jiang, Xiaoyu Liu, Shuhua Guo
papers.abstract: Teacher burnout is a persistent problem characterized by psychological exhaustion and occupational stress, posing serious constraints on teachers’ professional development, the improvement of teaching quality, and the stable functioning of the educational ecosystem. Conventional questionnaire-based surveys, which dominate teacher burnout research, primarily assess prevalence and bivariate correlations, often at the expense of predictive precision. Such approaches often have limited predictive accuracy and generalizability, making it difficult to identify teachers at risk of burnout with precision. To develop a more effective predictive model for burnout among senior high school teachers and clarify its key underlying mechanisms, this study recruited 2441 in-service teachers from 42 senior high schools in Guangdong Province and the Macao Special Administrative Region of China. The performance of logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost was compared to identify the optimal predictive framework. Interpretable machine learning methods were then employed to investigate the key factors associated with teacher burnout and the mechanisms through which they operate. The results showed that CatBoost achieved the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 0.815, a specificity of 0.836, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.817, the highest among the five models. This superior discriminatory capacity (AUC = 0.817) suggests that gradient-boosted decision trees are more adept than linear classifiers at capturing the multivariate complexity inherent in teacher burnout. Using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), an interpretable machine-learning technique, we analyzed factors associated with teacher burnout and identified several variables showing significant correlations with burnout among senior-high-school teachers. Depression, neuroticism, surface acting, family–work conflict, and high perceived stress emerged as positive correlates of teacher burnout. By contrast, work engagement, deep acting, psychological need satisfaction, social support, psychological resilience, teacher self-efficacy, high conscientiousness, and openness to experience were negative correlates of teacher burnout. Based on the machine-learning framework, this study constructed an interpretable prediction model and a visual predictive tool for teacher burnout, and unpacked the association patterns between each variable and teacher burnout. The findings of this study can provide robust theoretical evidence and practical support for educational administrative authorities to conduct cross-sectional association screening for teachers with high-burnout profiles and formulate tiered and differentiated psychological intervention strategies.

papers.title: Identifying Barriers to Using Generative AI in Education Through AI-Assisted Literature Mining of arXiv Articles
papers.authors: Jianhua Yang, Kerem Öge, Hoang Van Pham, Chidi Okorro, Youn Affejee
papers.abstract: This study presents an exploratory, generative AI (GenAI)-assisted full-text analysis of barriers to using GenAI in education within an arXiv corpus. A total of 19,756 records were retrieved using a keyword search and then screened for relevance using three large language models (LLMs), GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.0 flash-lite, and Llama3-70B (Groq), through a voting mechanism. This yielded a corpus of 1998 education-relevant full-text articles. Using GPT-4o, learning and teaching scenarios (LTSs) were extracted using a structured 6As framework (Actor, Activity, AI Role, AI Interface, Assessment, Achievement) developed for this study. Barrier themes were derived separately by clustering a total of 4729 barrier descriptions, embedded using OpenAI’s embedding model. The descriptive results indicate: (i) STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) vs. non-STEM distributions of GenAI use cases are broadly comparable; (ii) approximately 75% of reported GenAI intervention outcomes were classified as non-negative across the different disciplines; and (iii) reported barriers show different descriptive patterns between STEM and non-STEM disciplines. STEM use cases more frequently report performance constraints, while non-STEM ones more frequently report privacy and workflow integration concerns. The observed disciplinary differences in extracted barriers suggest that approaches to supporting GenAI use may need to vary by disciplinary context. However, the findings are limited by arXiv coverage and limited human validation; future research should broaden source coverage and strengthen robust validation.

papers.title: Children’s Perception of Parental Body Size and Its Association with Their Desire to Be Like the Parent
papers.authors: Abdullah Kaan Kurt, Serdar Karakullukçu
papers.abstract: Background: Childhood obesity is a major and growing public health challenge worldwide. Although parental misperception of children’s weight is well documented, how children perceive their parents’ body size and whether parental body size is associated with children’s expressed desire to be like the parent have received little attention. We examined children’s perception of parental body size and whether parental BMI was associated with their expressed desire to be like the parent in a primary care sample. Methods: This single-center, cross-sectional study included 229 parent–child pairs consecutively recruited from a family medicine outpatient clinic in Türkiye between January and March 2026. Children aged 4–8 years rated the accompanying parent’s body size and reported whether they wanted to be like that parent, while parents independently rated their own body size. The BMI-based Body Size Guide was used for all figure selections, and the classification derived from objectively measured parental BMI served as the primary reference. Agreement was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa coefficients, associations were examined using multivariable logistic regression, and the children’s spontaneous explanations were examined using qualitative content analysis. Results: Parents showed moderate weighted agreement with the BMI-derived classification (weighted κ = 0.536, 95% CI: 0.456–0.612; exact agreement: 59.4%), whereas children showed fair weighted agreement (weighted κ = 0.315, 95% CI: 0.231–0.392; exact agreement: 42.8%). After adjustment for child age, child sex, child weight status, parent sex, and parent age, parental overweight (aOR = 0.353, 95% CI: 0.170–0.733) and parental obesity (aOR = 0.133, 95% CI: 0.057–0.307) were associated with lower odds of the child reporting a desire to be like the parent. After adjustment for child age, child sex, parent sex, and parent age, parental overweight (aOR = 2.818, 95% CI: 1.101–7.211) and parental obesity (aOR = 4.774, 95% CI: 1.816–12.546) were associated with higher odds of child overweight/obesity. Among the 53 children who provided an explanation, responses referred to body size, weight, health, appearance, affection, and identification with the parent, illustrating the broad interpretation of the question. Conclusions: Children aged 4–8 years were able to rate parental body size, although their agreement with the BMI-derived classification was limited. Children’s expressed desire to be like the parent varied according to parental BMI; however, this broad question may reflect emotional, relational, behavioural, and appearance-related considerations rather than bodily resemblance alone. The open-ended responses provide context by showing that only some children spontaneously referred to body size or weight. These findings support further research using developmentally validated and stigma-sensitive measures to clarify how young children perceive parental body size and interpret questions about identification with a parent.

papers.title: A Multimodal AI and Visual-Programming Framework for Sketch-Based BIM: Formalization and Empirical Validation
papers.authors: Tahir Akkoyunlu
papers.abstract: Early-stage architectural design is still dominated by hand-drawn 2D floor-plan sketches, and converting these sketches into object-based Building Information Modeling (BIM) models remains a manual bottleneck that delays downstream simulation, costing, and coordination. Recent advances in multimodal artificial intelligence (vision-language models, code-generating large language models) and visual programming for BIM (Dynamo, Grasshopper, Refinery) have not yet been unified. Objective: We present and empirically evaluate a semi-automatic framework in which a vision-language model (VLM) emits executable visual-programming code (Dynamo-compatible DesignScript) that is wrapped into a node graph and executed in Dynamo to drive Revit, producing native BIM elements; the IFC export is independently validated in BlenderBIM as a visual sanity check. This is a proof-of-concept evaluation (n = 5 case studies), not a claim of production-scale deployment. Methods: The seven-module pipeline (sketch input, preprocessing, VLM interpretation, code-to-graph translation, Dynamo + Revit execution, IFC export with a BlenderBIM sanity check, and human-in-the-loop review with a feedback loop) is formalized mathematically—a line-sharpness function, a probabilistic AI-success model, and a closed-form architect-effort expression—and evaluated on five case studies (a Medipol student sketch, a public RPLAN sample, a tablet-drawn two-story house, a CubiCasa5K sample, and a real Istanbul apartment) against three baselines: a CNN recognizer (MuraNet), a JSON-emitting LLM pipeline (Sketch2BIM), and a hand-coded visual-programming framework. The primary VLM is Qwen-VL 9B (open-weight, Apache 2.0); GPT-4V and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are ablated on Case A only as closed-weight sensitivity checks. Results: Across the five cases, the framework achieves wall/opening F1 of 0.84–0.91 (mean 0.88), IFC schema validity of 100% in every case, a 56–61% reduction in time-to-editable-BIM, and 58–74% fewer architect edits than fully manual modeling, outperforming all three baselines on the architect-edits-required metric. The closed-form model predicts a 72% effort reduction under nominal parameters but overestimates the observed 56–61% by 11–16 percentage points; once the empirically observed architect-edit time is substituted, the calibrated model matches the observed range. Numbers are means over three runs per case. Conclusions: Unifying multimodal AI code generation with visual programming for BIM produces a more robust, editable sketch-to-BIM pipeline than the JSON-schema approaches in the current literature. Caveat: the evidence is a proof-of-concept scale (n = 5); broader validation (≥20 cases, cross-practice) is a key objective for future research.

papers.title: Social Media Fatigue and Depressive Symptoms Among Chinese University Students: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety as a Statistical Mediator and Subjective Socioeconomic Status as a Moderator
papers.authors: Manlin Wu, Huimin Ma, Song Zhou, Lixian Yang
papers.abstract: As social media and artificial intelligence (AI) become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning and daily lives, fatigue arising from established digital platforms and anxiety surrounding emerging AI may constitute interrelated forms of technology-related distress. However, how these experiences are jointly associated with depressive symptoms, and whether these associations vary by subjective socioeconomic status (SSES), remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and research on status maintenance, this cross-sectional study examined AI anxiety as a statistical mediator of the association between social media fatigue and depressive symptoms and further tested whether SSES moderated the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms. Survey data from 1108 Chinese university students were analyzed using regression models with heteroscedasticity-consistent type 3 (HC3) robust standard errors and percentile-bootstrap confidence intervals. Social media fatigue was positively associated with AI anxiety, which in turn was positively associated with depressive symptoms, yielding a significant statistical indirect association. As SSES increased, the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms became stronger, and the corresponding conditional indirect association also increased. Overall, these findings suggest that understanding university students’ digital mental health requires attention to both distress arising across different technological environments and the subjective social positions from which these experiences are evaluated, offering a more context-sensitive perspective on how established and emerging forms of digital stress may be jointly associated with psychological well-being.

papers.title: HexaClus++: Uncertainty-Aware Hexagonal Supervised Spatial Clustering
papers.authors: Yameng Guo, Seppe vanden Broucke
papers.abstract: Due to the heterogeneity and uneven distribution of geospatial data, predictive geospatial techniques are often required to provide both accurate target predictions and uncertainty quantification. However, existing approaches typically only provide post-hoc uncertainty estimates, rather than using uncertainty to guide the spatial model training process itself. To address these limitations, we introduce HexaClus++, a supervised, uncertainty-aware, spatial-clustering-based approach that integrates both accuracy and uncertainty to guide local model training on clustered spatial hexagonal regions. To evaluate the performance of our technique, we conduct experiments on property valuation datasets using diverse machine learning approaches. The results demonstrate that HexaClus++, when combined with different base learners, achieves competitive accuracy while also delivering well-calibrated uncertainty, reliable prediction intervals, and enhanced interpretability through regional uncertainty maps and spatially varying feature importance.

papers.title: Evaluation Bias in Cross-Context Generalization of EEG-Based Affective Computing: A Simulation Study
papers.authors: Morteza Fani Tazekand Kahlan, Mohammad Mahdi Rasoul Amini, Sina Samadi Gharehveran, Kimia Shirini, Arya Abdolahi, Ahad Shahhoseini
papers.abstract: Cross-context accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG)-based emotion recognition is usually reported without the model-selection rule, chance-level test, or reliability reference needed to interpret it. We quantify the consequences in simulations with known ground truth and on real EEG features with randomly assigned labels. Selecting a linear classifier’s regularization parameter on the test set gave mean cross-context accuracies of 0.706 (two classes; chance 0.500) and 0.212 (seven classes; chance 0.143) on data without signal, while nested cross-validation stayed at chance. Real EEG features from 89 participants gave 0.640 and 0.207. Because the offset is shared by all participants, group-level t-tests were falsely significant in 95–100% of groups of 10–60 participants. The offset was nearly constant across true effect sizes and appeared for every model class tested, for pooled feature selection, and for repeated test-set reuse. Representational similarity analysis was less sensitive than decoding when conditions shared mean patterns across contexts, and it alone detected structure that was shared relationally but carried by different features. A single condition carrying a power artifact produced a spurious cross-context geometry. An exact permutation test was falsely significant in about one-third of realizations, whereas a conditional permutation test and condition dropping remained calibrated. We derive five reporting items from these results.

papers.title: Teaching computational toxicology as new approach methodologies in the era of next-generation risk assessment
papers.authors: Shengnan Liu, Jin Li, Dawei Tang, Kan Shao, Qiao Xue, Paul Lawford Carmichael, Jingbo Pi, Qiang Zhang
papers.abstract: The global initiative toward non-animal chemical testing methods has recently gained significant momentum, requiring developing new approach methodologies (NAMs) as transformative solutions for next-generation risk assessment (NGRA). NAMs refer to any in chemico, in silico , and in vitro technology, methodology, or combination that do not rely on animals. A range of computational toxicology methods are becoming critical components within the NGRA framework across multiple testing tiers. These approaches are needed to support hazard characterization and prioritization for further testing, calculate points of departure, identify modes of action, and bridge the data gaps between in vitro assays and in vivo exposures as well as apical health endpoints. The core technologies of computational toxicology include (i) quantitative structure activity relationship, (ii) benchmark dose modeling, (iii) bioinformatic analysis of omics data, (iv) physiologically based kinetic modeling, (v) quantitative adverse outcome pathway modeling, (vi) molecular docking and dynamics, and (vii) more recently, machine learning and artificial intelligence tools. The NAM community, in academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, are facing increasing demand for training current and future professionals to master these skills. In this article, we described our perspective, experiences, and challenges in disseminating these computational toxicology techniques. Unlike established disciplines, the curriculum of computational toxicology and associated software tools are constantly evolving, requiring instructors to adapt in a timely manner. Challenges abound, we are embraced with an unprecedented opportunity that educating next-generation toxicologists is a critical effort of this revolutionary movement of chemical toxicity testing and safety assessment.

papers.title: Creating common ground: integrating transformative agroecology and extension research in undergraduate education
papers.authors: Karen L. Nordstrom, Victor M. Izzo, Emily Hoyler, V. Ernesto Méndez
papers.abstract: This paper examines the Agroecology Extension (AX) summer Research Fellowship at the University of Vermont, a 5-year USDA-funded undergraduate program that intentionally integrated extension research with agroecology education within a land-grant university context. Drawing on predominantly qualitative evaluation of five cohorts (2021–2025, n = 47), we identify enabling and constraining pedagogical factors for creating common ground between two domains that remain institutionally separated at most land-grant universities. The study contributes to the emerging signature pedagogy for sustainable food systems education by documenting how three interconnected pedagogical dynamics—integrating political agroecology with extension, centering equity as a sustained commitment, and supporting participatory knowledge co-creation with students—shaped program design and evolution across 5 years. Findings demonstrate that transformative education at the intersection of agroecology and extension requires explicit engagement with the political dimensions of agroecology and extension history, relational infrastructure for equity work, and deliberate structures for co-learning. This case study offers practical pedagogical insights for land-grant universities seeking to develop sustainable programs that bridge agroecology and extension while preparing graduates to address complex agricultural and food systems challenges.

papers.title: Physiological characterization using standardized submaximal treadmill responses in professional male soccer players
papers.authors: Ágnes Sziva, János Pórszász, Zsuzsanna Kívés, Zsolt Szelid
papers.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
papers.abstract: Objectives Submaximal treadmill variables are increasingly used in professional soccer, but their practical interpretation remains limited. Therefore, we aimed to determine whether standardized submaximal treadmill-derived variables provide a more informative characterization of positional differences than maximal exercise variables and to examine their associations with maximal exercise performance. Methods In this retrospective cross-sectional study, professional adult male soccer players ( n = 206), including midfielders, defenders, and forwards performed an incremental treadmill test until exhaustion, with enhanced speed-dosing above 4 mmol·L⁻ 1 blood lactate (4L). Absolute and relative heart rate (HR) and speed variables at 4L and exhaustion, together with their associations were analysed during this incremental treadmill test. Results Midfielders reached the highest 4L-related values, including speed (V 4L : 15.6 ± 1.3 km/h, p < 0.005 vs others), HR (HR 4L : 177.2 ± 9.0/min, p < 0.05 vs others), V 4L as % of maximal speed (V 4L/Max ratio: 77.6 ± 4.9%, p < 0.005 vs. forwards), and HR 4L as % of HR reserve (HR 4L/Res ratio: 87.1 ± 4.9%, p < 0.05 vs. others). Positional differences at maximal exercise were inconsistent. V 4L correlated moderately with HR 4L in all players ( r = 0.364, p < 0.001), largely with HR 4L/Res ratio ( r = 0.609, p < 0.001) and while HR 4L/Res ratio correlated very largely with V 4L/Max ratio ( r = 0.795, p < 0.001), without positional differences. Between 4L and exhaustion, correlations were larger for HR, than for speed, being very large for HR in all ( r = 0.739, p < 0.001), while large in forwards ( r = 0.661, p < 0.001), and for speed large in all ( r = 0.575, p < 0.001), across playing positions. After adjustment for age, BMI, club, competitive division, testing phase, and testing year, positional effects remained significant for V 4L ( p = 0.003) and HR 4L ( p = 0.007), but not for V Max ( p = 0.077) or HR Max ( p = 0.147). Conclusions Submaximal treadmill-derived variables differentiated playing positions more consistently than maximal exercise variables, while remaining strongly associated with maximal treadmill performance. These findings highlight 4L-related heart rate and running speed variables as informative submaximal markers for the physiological characterization of professional soccer players.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for astrobiology investigations (AI2): an open-source graphical user interface
papers.authors: Floyd Nichols, Grant Major, Ryan C. Felton
papers.journal: Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences
papers.abstract: A growing number of studies in astrobiological research have utilized and shown the potential in applied machine learning. However, the number of these studies are still quite limited. Furthermore, educators, students, and researchers often do not have the time and/or resources for developing machine learning knowledge and skills. To facilitate the use of applied machine learning for astrobiology, we developed an open-source and freely available web-based graphical user interface (GUI) for teaching and developing machine learning models called Artificial Intelligence for Astrobiology Investigations (AI 2 ) . Our project enables educators, students, and researchers to make use of explainable machine learning models most amenable to tabular (i.e.csv files) astrobiology datasets. The application is an interactive tool and serves as an entry point for educators, students, and researchers who are novices in machine learning. By providing an easy to follow and standardized machine learning workflow, the GUI highlights how certain machine learning approaches work, and how to reliably utilize machine learning Furthermore, the application can serve as a means of rapid prototyping of machine learning models, with or without the need for technical expertise, thus freeing up time for researchers to investigate and explore their data. Accordingly, the AI 2 project aims to serve as a stepping stone towards more advanced implementation of applied machine learning by building the foundation and intuition necessary for technical expertise.

papers.title: Multimodal wearable biosensors in sports: integrating physical and chemical sensing for performance and health
papers.authors: Burhan Adıgüzel, Mansour Ghorbanpour, Begüm Sarac, Seydanur Yücer, Fatih Çiftçi
papers.abstract: Wearable technologies have emerged as essential tools for monitoring athletes’ performance and physiological states in real time. This review systematically examines advances in biosensing and wearable systems for sports applications, highlighting their design, sensing modalities, and integration strategies. Athlete tracking and data acquisition form the foundation for personalized training, injury prevention, and performance optimization. Biopotential sensors, including electrocardiography (ECG), electromyography (EMG), electroencephalography (EEG)/electroneurogram Electroneurography, and biopotential electrodes, provide insights into cardiac, muscular, and neural activity. Physical sensors, such as temperature, piezoresistive, piezoelectric, balance and acceleration, pressure, optical, and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors, enable real-time assessment of movement, mechanical load, body posture, stress, and environmental interactions. Chemical sensors, including sweat and glucose sensors, facilitate non-invasive metabolic monitoring, supporting hydration and energy management. Integrated and hybrid biosensor systems combine multiple sensing modalities, offering comprehensive real-time feedback and personalized analytics for athletes. Despite these advances, challenges remain in sensor miniaturization, power efficiency, data accuracy, wireless communication, and user comfort. Future directions focus on artificial intelligence-driven data analysis, flexible and durable materials, multi-modal integration, and fully personalized wearable platforms. Collectively, wearable biosensing technologies present a transformative approach to sports monitoring, enabling enhanced performance evaluation, injury prevention, and long-term health management.

papers.title: Global variability in dental unit waterline safety standards: bridging the gap between guidelines and practice
papers.authors: Kimia Sadat Kazemi, Yalda Anvari, Michelle F. Siqueira
papers.abstract: Background Dental unit waterlines (DUWLs) are a recognized yet frequently underappreciated source of microbial contamination in dental environments. Their narrow tubing, intermittent water flow, and internal surface characteristics create favorable conditions for rapid biofilm growth. These biofilms can persist and release microorganisms into the water used during dental procedures, potentially increasing the risk of infection. Methods This review synthesizes global guidelines, regulatory frameworks, and emerging evidence related to DUWL contamination, with particular attention to regional variations in standards, compliance expectations, and monitoring practices. Results Although most guidelines converge on potable-water quality for nonsurgical procedures and sterile water or saline for surgical care, substantial international variation persists in implementation and enforcement. North America generally provides relatively consistent guidance, though adherence remains uneven, while Europe and the Asia–Pacific region exhibit marked differences in microbial thresholds, surveillance practices, and regulatory oversight. Beyond bacterial contamination, emerging evidence highlights the clinical relevance of fungal colonization and the potential role of DUWL biofilms as reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance. These issues remain insufficiently addressed in many regulatory systems. Inadequately controlled DUWL contamination can contribute to preventable infections, inflammatory complications, and diagnostic uncertainty, which may lead to unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions. This highlights the importance of incorporating environmental infection control into dentistry's antimicrobial stewardship efforts. This review also explores the persistent gap between knowledge and practice among dental professionals. It identifies opportunities for future advancements, including artificial intelligence–assisted monitoring, nanotechnology-enhanced antimicrobial materials, and environmentally sustainable disinfection strategies. Conclusions Overall, the findings underscore the need for harmonized international guidance supported by enforceable monitoring standards and adaptable implementation pathways for resource-limited settings. Strengthening DUWL management through evidence-based protocols, technological innovation, and enhanced professional education is essential to reducing contamination risks and promoting safe, high-quality dental care globally.

papers.title: Generative AI in aging societies: the risk of a double divide
papers.authors: Alexander Seifert
papers.abstract: Population ageing and the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence are two defining transformations of the twenty-first century, yet they are rarely considered together. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) is moving from a technological novelty to an everyday infrastructure. It drafts emails, summarises documents, translates services, produces images, answers health questions and increasingly mediates first-line interactions with organisations. Public debate has focused heavily on schools, universities, workplaces, productivity, misinformation and regulation. Much less attention has been paid to how this transformation intersects with population ageing and the increasingly digital organisation of later life. This omission matters because generative AI is not simply another digital tool. It is becoming part of the infrastructure through which people search for knowledge, assess risks, access services and imagine social groups.Older adults (people aged 65 and older, in line with the statutory retirement age in Switzerland) are not a marginal user group; they are a growing share of the population in many countries and are increasingly expected to navigate digital welfare, health, financial and communication systems. Yet research and design practices often continue to position older adults as late adopters, vulnerable users or recipients of technological solutions rather than as citizens whose agency, knowledge and social representation matter in the future AI ecosystem (Mannheim et al., 2023;Choi et al., 2026).Existing concepts illuminate different aspects of this problem. Research on digital inequality has long conceptualized the "digital divide" as multidimensional, encompassing inequalities in access, skills, use, and outcomes (Dijk, 2020;Bentley et al., 2024). Research on digital inequality has long understood the digital divide as multidimensional. It encompasses inequalities in material access, digital skills, forms and quality of use, and the benefits or disadvantages resulting from use. Research on digital ageism, in turn, examines how age-based assumptions and inequalities are embedded in and reproduced through digital technologies (Mannheim and Köttl, 2024). The two mechanisms underlying the proposed framework, unequal participation and biased representation, are thus already established in the literature, but neither has been specifically applied to generative AI. The doubledivide framework's contribution lies in examining how these mechanisms operate together and may reinforce each other in this context.The proposed double-divide framework distinguishes inequality in engaging with generative AI (Wang et al., 2025) from inequality in being represented by it (Chu et al., 2022): First, older adults may face an AI Participation Divide: inequalities in the ability to access, use, interpret and critically evaluate AI-generated information. Second, they may face an AI Representation Divide: inequalities in how ageing and older adults are represented through AI-generated text, images and decisions. These two divides are distinct but connected. Together, they may shape who benefits from AI and how ageing itself is understood.The promise of generative AI for older adultsGenerative AI can offer substantial benefits in later life. Its natural language interface may lower the barriers that made earlier digital technologies difficult to use. A person who struggles with search engines, online forms or administrative language may ask a chatbot to explain a letter, draft a response, translate information or compare options. Such functions could support autonomy and participation when they are reliable, accessible and embedded in meaningful social contexts. Unlike many earlier digital technologies, generative AI does not require users to navigate complex menus or predefined categories. Its conversational form may allow older adults to start with questions in their own words. In health, AI-driven tools may help explain medical information, support appointment preparation, make complex instructions easier to understand and offer new forms of communication support. For older adults with sensory limitations, low digital confidence or limited formal education, conversational interfaces could be more approachable than menu-based systems. Emerging work on AI-based health technologies and assistive technologies suggests that older adults often see potential benefits, especially when technologies are useful, understandable, trustworthy and aligned with their everyday lives (Enam et al., 2025;Wong et al., 2025). This promise matters. If generative AI is well designed, it could become an important tool for inclusion. The problem is that benefits do not flow automatically from availability. Access to an AI system does not mean that people know what to ask, how to interpret answers or how to judge the accuracy of the output. This is where the first divide begins.In the age of generative AI, the crucial question is not only whether older adults can access generative AI but also whether they have the competence to use it effectively and critically. We define the AI Participation Divide as the unequal capacity to access, use, interpret and evaluate AIgenerated information. Age alone does not determine AI competence. Inequalities within later life reflect accumulated differences in education, income, health, prior occupational exposure to technology, social support and opportunities for digital learning (Enam et al., 2025;Suárez and García-Mariñoso, 2025).The first layer is access and use: Generative AI may be freely available through search engines, smartphones and apps, but this does not mean that its use is evenly distributed. Evidence on AIrelated competencies shows that vulnerable user groups with lower AI knowledge and skills are more likely to be older, less educated and less equipped with privacy-protection skills (Wang et al., 2025).Behavioural evidence on ChatGPT use likewise points to generational and educational differences in adoption (Kacperski et al., 2025). These findings suggest that AI may extend rather than erase established inequalities in digital participation.The second layer is meaningful use: Generative AI requires a new repertoire of practical skills. Users need to know what AI can do, which tasks it is appropriate for, how to formulate prompts, when to provide context and when not to disclose sensitive information. These are not trivial skills. They are learned through experimentation, social support and prior digital confidence. Existing digital experiences can therefore spill over into relationships with AI: People who have felt excluded from digital technology may approach AI with lower confidence, fewer positive experiences and less trust (Bentley et al., 2024).The third layer is interpretation: AI outputs often sound fluent, confident and authoritative, even when they are incomplete, biased or wrong. Older adults, like all users, need to understand that generative AI produces plausible responses rather than verified truth. This distinction is especially important when AI is used for health information, financial questions or legal guidance. The danger is not only non-use but overtrust: a person may use AI and still be disadvantaged because they cannot recognise the limits of the answer.The fourth layer is evaluation. This may become the defining competence of the generative AI era.Evaluation competence includes more than checking whether a statement is factually correct. It also involves recognising when an image, voice, recommendation or personalised message may have been synthetically generated, manipulated or designed to exploit trust. For older adults, this is particularly crucial in domains where trust relationships matter, such as health advice, social communication, banking and public services. Users increasingly need to detect hallucinations, misleading summaries, manipulated images, synthetic voices, scams and AI-generated fake content. Older adults are often framed as vulnerable to online misinformation (Brashier and Schacter, 2020;Li et al., 2025), yet the question should not be reduced to individual deficit. The information environment itself is becoming harder to evaluate, especially for older adults with limited familiarity with generative AI. As services, media and interpersonal communication are increasingly saturated with synthetic content, the critical evaluation of AI becomes a basic condition of social participation. The result is not merely an individual skills gap, but a societal divide in the ability to judge the credibility, authenticity and trustworthiness of AI-mediated information.The AI Participation Divide thus refers to unequal opportunities to access, use, interpret, and evaluate generative AI, and to participate in its design and evaluation. These inequalities do not arise solely from individual abilities, but from the interaction of personal resources with interface design, accessibility, affordability, institutional practices, and available support. Participation is therefore relational, depending on both users and the conditions under which AI is designed, provided, and supported.The second divide concerns representation. The divide lies between the diversity of later life as it is lived and the restricted repertoire through which AI systems often make it visible. Generative AI does not merely help people retrieve information; it also produces text, images and narratives that circulate through society. When people ask AI systems to describe older adults, design services for ageing populations, generate images of later life or summarise what ageing means, the outputs participate in shaping cultural understandings of age. This matters because ageism is already embedded in technology design and AI systems (Martens et al., 2025;Osinga et al., 2026). Reviews of digital technology design show that older adults are frequently framed through assumptions of decline, dependency and lack of competence (Mannheim et al., 2023). Work on sociotechnical ageism shows how AI in care and ageing contexts can reproduce narrow ideas of old age as a problem to be managed through technical solutions (Neves et al., 2023). A scoping review of agerelated bias in AI further shows that age bias may enter AI systems through data, design, modelling and deployment, including through underrepresentation of older adults and biased evaluation of system performance (Chu et al., 2023). Generative AI intensifies this issue because it makes representation scalable. Repetition gives such representations social weight. When similar ageist framings appear across chatbots, image generators, search interfaces and administrative tools, they may come to look less like stereotypes and more like common sense (Martens et al., 2025) Avoiding a double divide requires more than giving older adults access to AI tools. First, AI literacy initiatives must include later life and move beyond basic awareness. These need to teach practical prompting, interpretation of uncertainty, privacy protection and critical evaluation of AI-generated content, including health misinformation, scams, deepfakes and synthetic media. Second, AI systems should be evaluated for age-related bias not only in technical performance but also in the narratives and images they generate. Third, older adults should be involved as co-designers of AI systems and not merely as test users. A recent scoping review shows that older adults are still inconsistently engaged across the design, implementation and evaluation of AI systems (Choi et al., 2026).Participation must include heterogeneous groups of older adults and should address power imbalances in design processes. Fourth, essential health, welfare, financial and public services should retain accessible non-AI alternatives. Age-inclusive AI cannot mean making participation conditional on the ability or willingness to interact with automated systems. Fifth, AI governance should treat age as a core dimension of fairness, inclusion and representation. This includes audit practices that examine whether AI systems exclude older adults from benefits or reproduce ageist assumptions in outputs and decisions. The proposed policy and design recommendations are normative proposals informed by the preceding evidence and conceptual analysis. Their effectiveness should be examined empirically across different populations, settings, and generative AI systems.Age-inclusive AI therefore requires both the capacity to act within AI-mediated environments and the right to be represented by them in ways that reflect the diversity, agency and complexity of later life.Without such efforts, generative AI may widen a double divide in ageing societies, one that limits older adults' capacity to act in AI-mediated environments and narrows how ageing itself is seen.

papers.title: AI use and risk disclosure by investment advisers
papers.authors: Samir Chincholikar, Robin Chawla
papers.abstract: Introduction Investment advisers increasingly report using artificial intelligence (AI), but little is known about what they disclose about it in fiduciary filings. The SEC brought its first AI-washing enforcement actions in 2024, so regulators and researchers need a reproducible measure of AI disclosure. We provide large-sample evidence on AI disclosure in Form ADV Part 2A brochures and show how the estimate depends on measurement design. Methods We drew a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered investment advisers from a population of 16,223 firms, crossing adviser type (private-fund vs. wealth/retail) with 2024 assets-under-management (AUM) quartile. A large language model (LLM) classified the 388 available brochures under a prespecified five-label typology: investment-process use, operational or client-service use, AI-related risk, explicit non-use, and named AI vendors. We treated the LLM as a measurement instrument and validated it three ways: same-family reproducibility, blinded cross-family recoding of 180 brochures, and human verification of 158 cases. Secondary analyses compared brochures with 283 matched firm websites and applied a screen derived from SEC enforcement orders. Results AI use is disclosed in 23.7% of brochures (22.7% survey-weighted), while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The within-brochure difference is significant (McNemar p = 0.036). Disclosure rises from 10.4% in the smallest AUM quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and is higher among private-fund advisers. Against human coding, the composite any-use measure achieves precision of 0.76 and sensitivity of 0.81. The same corpus yields estimates of 9.9%, 13.1%, and 23.7% under alternative constructs, adviser universes, and weighting schemes. A literal keyword rule misses or mislabels roughly a quarter of cases. A raw 17.3-percentage-point brochure–website gap disappears after conditioning on document length. None of the five enforcement-screen matches was adjudicated as an unsubstantiated promotional claim. Discussion Advisers present AI at least as often as a risk as a capability, and disclosure is concentrated among larger and private-fund advisers. AI-disclosure prevalence reflects measurement design as much as adviser behavior, so estimates should be reported with their construct, universe, weighting, and validation. The validated framework and an open reproducibility capsule provide a baseline for monitoring AI claims and AI-washing in investment management.

papers.title: Landscape and training opportunities in artificial intelligence for biosciences in Latin America: the BiotrAIn project
papers.authors: José Arturo Molina-Mora, Flavio Ezequiel Spetale, Túlio de Lima Campos, Pedro Eduardo Romero, Lucas Inchausti, Adrian Gustavo Turjanski, Ignacio Alcántara, Maria Fernanda Ribeiro Dias, Carla Valeria Filippi, Matías Dominguez, Juan Antonio Bizzotto, Daniela Senra, Jorge Noé García-Chávez, Claudia Hoepfner, Cleidy Osorio-Mogollón, C. Paola Rangel-Chávez, Valeria Foronda, Alejandra Rougon‐Cardoso, Nelly Selem Mojica, Yesid Cuesta-Astroz, Cindy Marié Aguilar-Bartels, Rebeca Campos-Sánchez, Lizzie Tchongwe Divala, Kim Gurwitz, Cath Brooksbank
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is redefining biosciences by enabling the analysis of complex, large-scale biological and medical data. Latin America has demonstrated remarkable potential through studies applying AI to biomedical sciences often using locally generated data and addressing regional needs. However, the integration of AI into research and healthcare in this region faces several structural challenges, including insufficient infrastructure, lack of specialized training, fragmented research systems, and continuously constrained funding. To overcome existing limitations, capacity building at the regional level is crucial. This includes developing localized AI training programs and the reinforcement of a collaborative research framework. Collaboration across institutions and countries, along with engagement from industry and government, is key to fostering an enabling environment for the responsible and effective use of AI. One promising response to these challenges is the BiotrAIn project, a partnership involving EMBL-EBI, the University of Costa Rica, and CABANAnet, with support from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. The project is structured around three pillars: knowledge exchange, curriculum development, and regional training. BiotrAIn exemplifies how strategically designed, regionally adapted programs can build AI capacity in biosciences and foster more equitable scientific development across Latin America. Strategic efforts like BiotrAIn serve as essential building blocks toward a more robust, ethical, and sustainable AI ecosystem in the region, while offering a model that could be adapted by other regions globally. Ultimately, with coordinated investment, inclusive policies, and collaborative networks, Latin America can position itself as a significant contributor to global AI-driven bioscience.

papers.title: Teaching AI, teaching bias: addressing gender inequality in public health education
papers.authors: Andrea Dietrich, Karolina Czok, Karina Ilskens
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes healthcare, public health and health professions education. However, predictive and generative systems can reproduce or amplify longstanding inequalities embedded in data, institutions and established knowledge structures. Public health education therefore needs to connect technical approaches to identifying and mitigating algorithmic bias with their broader social, population health and institutional contexts. This conceptual article presents the sociotechnical Bias literacy for public health education framework (SBL-PHE), developed through a theory-informed conceptual synthesis drawing on conceptual framework analysis. A focused supplementary literature search in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ERIC and the ACM digital library was conducted to examine and refine its theoretical foundations. An evidence-informed composite case of AI-supported cardiovascular risk assessment traces algorithmic gender bias from knowledge production and data representation through modeling and implementation to monitoring. The framework comprises five interconnected competency dimensions concerned with recognizing, explaining, evaluating, addressing and reflecting on algorithmic bias. For master’s-level public health education, these dimensions are linked to learning objectives, learning activities, assessment methods and a prospective evaluation strategy. Sociotechnical Bias literacy is proposed as a foundational competency for public health professionals who use or interpret AI. Sociotechnical fluency describes an advanced, role-dependent capability, particularly for responsibilities in implementation, evaluation, translation and governance. SBL-PHE provides a theoretically grounded framework for integrating technical understanding, health equity, professional judgment and institutional responsibility into public health education. The framework and its proposed educational application have not yet been empirically validated.

papers.title: Self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward artificial intelligence in pediatric healthcare in a children’s hospital in China: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Siyu Chen, Yang Li, Qi-Gang Ding, Dong-Xin Huang, Qiuyu Tang, Xue Kong
papers.abstract: Objective To investigate the self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in pediatric healthcare in a children’s specialty hospital, and to compare differences between the two groups. Methods This single-center cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted at Fujian Children’s Hospital from January 2026 to June 2026. A self-designed questionnaire was used to assess healthcare workers’ and caregivers’ self-reported understanding, trust, risk perception, and willingness to accept AI applications in pediatric healthcare. Respondents were divided into groups according to their identity. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, while continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Results A total of 261 respondents were included, comprising 159 caregivers and 102 healthcare workers. Healthcare workers had a higher level of self-reported understanding and a higher frequency of use of AI applications in pediatric healthcare than caregivers ( p < 0.01); however, they also showed stronger perceptions of data security risks ( p < 0.001). Caregivers reported greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making than healthcare workers ( p < 0.001). Most respondents believed that AI could not replace pediatric healthcare workers, with no statistically significant difference between the two groups ( p = 0.166). Regarding potential advantages, healthcare workers were more likely to agree that AI could reduce human error ( p < 0.001). Regarding potential limitations, healthcare workers expressed greater concern about the risks of misdiagnosis, lack of humanistic care, and data privacy and security issues ( p < 0.001). Conclusion In this single-center children’s specialty hospital, healthcare workers reported greater self-rated understanding and more frequent use of AI, together with stronger awareness of several potential risks, whereas caregivers showed greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making despite lower self-rated understanding. These findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger multicenter studies before being generalized to broader populations in China.

papers.title: Physical activity and body dissatisfaction among female university students: a three-wave study of psychological flexibility and resilience
papers.authors: Youshan Zhang, Zhigang Liu, Chang Hu, Laibing Lu
papers.abstract: Objective Body dissatisfaction (BD) is a common psychological concern among female university students. Although physical activity (PA) has been associated with more favourable body-related evaluations, the psychological factors that may account for this association remain unclear. This study examined the independent and theoretically ordered indirect associations of psychological flexibility (PF) and psychological resilience (PR) in the prospective association between PA and BD. Methods A three-wave prospective study was conducted among 1,086 first- and second-year female university students from three universities in China. Assessments were administered at 6-month intervals over 12 months. The hypothesised statistical model included T1 PA, T2 PF, and T3 PR and BD. PF was operationalized as lower experiential avoidance, with lower experiential avoidance representing greater PF. Only-child status, BMI category, and self-rated health were included as covariates. Indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results T1 PA was positively associated with T2 PF ( β = 0.419, p <.001) and T3 PR ( β = 0.239, p <.001), while T2 PF was positively associated with T3 PR ( β = 0.434, p <.001). T1 PA, T2 PF, and T3 PR were each negatively associated with T3 BD ( β = −0.127, −0.225, and −0.355, respectively; all p <.001). The total indirect association was significant ( β = −0.243, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.280, −0.206]). Significant specific indirect associations were observed through PF ( β = −0.094, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.121, −0.069]), through PR ( β = −0.085, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.109, −0.061]), and through the theoretically ordered PF–PR sequence ( β = −0.064, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.081, −0.050]). Conclusions Higher PA was prospectively associated with lower subsequent BD, with significant theoretically ordered indirect associations involving lower experiential avoidance, operationalized as greater PF, and greater PR. These findings highlight the potential relevance of adaptive psychological resources in understanding the prospective association between PA and BD among female university students.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence literacy profiles differ in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being among adolescents
papers.authors: Ja-Yeoung Lee
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly important for adolescents, yet variation in literacy across multiple dimensions and its associations with educational and psychological outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study identified generative AI literacy profiles among Korean adolescents with generative AI experience ( N = 3,959) using K-means cluster analysis based on information evaluation, communication, creative use, and ethical use. Two profiles were identified: Higher AI Literacy and Lower AI Literacy. The profiles differed primarily in their overall literacy levels rather than in qualitatively distinct patterns across the four dimensions. Adolescents in the Higher AI Literacy profile reported greater generative AI education experience and higher academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being than those in the Lower AI Literacy profile. Differences in academic self-efficacy and subjective well-being remained significant after adjustment for gender, school level, academic achievement, and economic status. These findings demonstrate meaningful level-based variation in generative AI literacy among adolescents with generative AI experience and suggest that such variation is associated with educational experience and academic and psychological outcomes. A person-centred perspective may complement variable-centred approaches and inform future research and educational approaches that consider differences in students’ generative AI literacy levels.

papers.title: How generative AI becomes embedded in design learning: a 14-instructional-day intensive longitudinal study of reciprocal dynamics between AI use and self-efficacy
papers.authors: Yang Li, Yi Yang, Silu Bao
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in design education, yet little is known about how students’ daily engagement with generative AI is dynamically associated with their learning-related capability beliefs across successive instructional days. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examined the reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between daily generative AI use in design learning and daily design-learning self-efficacy, and further investigated whether baseline hassles were associated with individual differences in these dynamics. A 14-instructional-day diary study was conducted with 260 Chinese undergraduate design students, yielding 3,558 observed person-day assessments out of 3,640 possible assessments. Daily generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy were assessed throughout the diary period, whereas hassles were measured at baseline. The data were analyzed using bivariate dynamic structural equation modeling within a Bayesian estimation framework. The results showed significant autoregressive effects for daily generative AI use ( β = 0.198, 95% CrI [0.154, 0.237]) and daily design-learning self-efficacy ( β = 0.138, 95% CrI [0.100, 0.175]). At the within-person level, higher-than-usual generative AI use on one instructional day positively predicted design-learning self-efficacy on the subsequent instructional day ( β = 0.043, 95% CrI [0.006, 0.077]), while higher-than-usual design-learning self-efficacy also positively predicted generative AI use on the subsequent instructional day ( β = 0.059, 95% CrI [0.023, 0.095]). At the between-person level, greater baseline hassles were associated with higher average generative AI use ( β = 0.135), lower average design-learning self-efficacy ( β = −0.254), and a stronger cross-lagged association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy ( β = 0.458). Gender did not significantly predict the main random effects. These findings indicate modest reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy, suggesting that the two may reinforce one another across instructional days. The stronger association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy among students reporting greater baseline hassles further suggests that contextual demands may shape how generative AI becomes integrated into students’ day-to-day design learning.

papers.title: Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance
papers.authors: Usman Rehman
papers.abstract: Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

papers.title: Academic emotions and perceived learning outcomes in GenAI-supported learning: the serial mediating roles of AI acceptance and learning behaviors
papers.authors: Huaruo Chen, Gefan Wang, Zhentao Peng, Wanru Song, Jie Xu
papers.abstract: Objective With the widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, academic emotions play a vital role in students’ learning processes. This study aims to examine the associations between positive and negative academic emotions and college students’ perceived learning outcomes, and analyze the serial mediating roles of AI acceptance and learning behaviors within GenAI-supported learning environments. Methods A total of 526 college students with GenAI learning experience were recruited via convenience sampling. All participants completed four standardized scales measuring academic emotions, AI acceptance, learning behaviors and perceived learning outcomes. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, confirmatory factor analysis and bias-corrected Bootstrap mediation tests were conducted using SPSS 26.0 and AMOS 27.0. Results All variables were significantly correlated ( p < 0.01). Positive academic emotions exerted a significant direct association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.176), whereas the direct association of negative academic emotions was non-significant ( β = −0.098, p = 0.049, 95% CI [−0.205, 0.007]). AI acceptance and learning behaviors had significant independent mediating effects. The serial mediation effect value was 0.020 for positive emotions and −0.037 for negative emotions, with all 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. Indirect pathways dominated the influence of negative academic emotions. Conclusion This study identifies a pattern of associations consistent with the hypothesized emotion-cognition-behavior-outcome pathway in GenAI-supported learning. The findings offer empirical evidence for developing targeted academic-emotion-informed intervention strategies, improving students’ AI acceptance and learning engagement, and promoting the high-quality development of intelligent education.

papers.title: Needs and current status of generative artificial intelligence use among college students: a cross-sectional survey based in China
papers.authors: Rong Zeng, 雷春涛, Qian Jiang, Xueqin Gan, Xiaoguo Zhang, Yu Feng, Qin Xu, Yan Huang, Yang Qian
papers.abstract: Objective This study aimed to investigate the current status of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) usage needs among vocational college students from China, explore their relationships with learning engagement and academic resilience, and identify variables associated with GAI usage demand. Methods Using convenience sampling, 3,876 students from five vocational colleges in Sichuan Province were enrolled. Surveys were conducted using the Generative Artificial Intelligence Application Status and Usage Demand Scale, the Learning Engagement Scale, and the Academic Resilience Scale. Results The average GAI needs score among vocational college students was 58.23 ± 12.77. Correlation analysis revealed positive relationships between GAI needs and both learning engagement and academic resilience ( p < 0.01). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that gender, academic year, availability of GAI learning devices at home, level of GAI understanding, enrollment in GAI-related courses, frequency of active GAI use, student-reported frequency of teachers’ use of GAI in teaching, learning engagement, and academic resilience were independently associated with GAI usage demand (all p < 0.05). The model explained 24.4% of the variance in GAI usage demand [ R 2 = 0.244, adjusted R 2 = 0.241, F (14, 3,861) = 88.932, p < 0.001]. Conclusion Vocational college students’ GAI usage demand was slightly above the theoretical midpoint of the scale. Greater GAI usage demand was independently associated with male gender, earlier academic year, better availability of GAI learning devices at home, a higher level of GAI understanding, enrollment in GAI-related courses, more frequent active GAI use, more frequent student-reported teachers’ use of GAI in teaching, higher learning engagement, and greater academic resilience. Because of the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal relationships.

papers.title: Comprehensive artificial intelligence-assisted mental health program for university students in China (CAMPUS): study protocol for a multi-center prospective cohort with planned embedded randomized intervention trials
papers.authors: Guang Yang, Rongxun Liu, Chuansheng Wang, Rongxin Zhu, Shisen Qin, Jinnan Yan, Yan Wang, Hongbo Pei, Lijuan Liang, Yingying Su, Shuai Wang, Weidong Wu, Guangjun Ji, Fei Wang, Wei Yange
papers.abstract: University students face a rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and suicidal ideation that exceeds the capacity of conventional, resource-constrained campus support services. Although artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools have emerged, many have evaluated selected modalities or isolated prediction tasks, and their integration with prospectively evaluated intervention pathways remains limited. This protocol describes the Comprehensive Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Mental Health Program for University Students in China (CAMPUS), a multi-center research program comprising a five-year prospective cohort, eight planned embedded randomized controlled trials, and exploratory multimodal AI and multi-omics studies across seven Chinese universities. Longitudinal cohort enrolment commenced at Henan Medical University in September 2025 and is planned to expand across seven participating universities. Multidimensional screening integrates psychological self-report (PHQ-9, GAD-7, ISI, BSI-CV, and others), physiological measurements (EEG, MRI, fNIRS, HRV, eye tracking, facial-expression analysis, ERP, voice acoustics), and an exploratory biospecimen component for multi-omics profiling, potentially including genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and microbiome analyses, subject to the finalization and approval of layer-specific protocols. Students identified through cohort screening as potentially eligible for an intervention trial will undergo trial-specific eligibility assessment. Those who meet the eligibility criteria and provide trial-specific informed consent will be individually randomized in a 1:1 ratio to the intervention or its comparator within one of eight separate two-arm, multi-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trials. A Transformer-based multimodal AI framework with SHAP-based feature attribution will be developed and internally evaluated for questionnaire-defined risk stratification and exploratory treatment-response prediction. The initial Henan Medical University cohort recruitment and university-student mental-health assessment were approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Henan Medical University (XYLL-20250484), and written informed consent is obtained from participants before enrolment. Each additional participating center will obtain local ethics approval before study activation. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, scientific conferences, and policy briefs, providing evidence that may inform the design and prospective evaluation of youth mental-health programs in other university settings. Clinical trial registration The two clinical trials were registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR). The registration details and URLs are as follows: ChiCTR2500113527: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298271 ; ChiCTR2500113613: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=298268 .

papers.title: The study of Chinese EFL teachers' emotions in the digital transformation of education
papers.authors: Feng Wu, Youjie Hua
papers.abstract: Introduction The rapid and continuing development of digital technologies has significantly reshaped the educational landscape, generating diverse emotional experiences among teachers. This study examined the emotional experiences of Chinese EFL teachers and the major antecedents of those emotions. Methods This study employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. First, questionnaire data collected from 296 university EFL teachers identified five primary emotions (love, joy, anger, sadness, and fear). Secondly, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 participants to explore the antecedents underlying these emotional experiences. The qualitative findings were subsequently integrated with the quantitative results and presented through a joint display. Results The findings showed that EFL teachers experienced positive emotions more frequently than negative emotions. Of the five primary emotions, joy and love had the highest mean scores, followed by fear, anger, and sadness, respectively. The findings further showed that teachers' emotions were closely associated with their professional goals and students' performance. Several antecedents were found to shape these emotional experiences. The flexibility, interactivity, and innovative opportunities introduced by digital transformation enhanced EFL teachers' sense of love for their work. Likewise, the efficiency and abundance of resources provided by digital tools and platforms contributed to their sense of joy. In contrast, students' misconduct and dishonest behaviors often provoked feelings of anger. Teachers experienced sadness when confronted with students' lack of critical thinking and when they felt inadequately supported in their work. Fear was primarily driven by peer pressure, time constraints, and the threat of being replaced by artificial intelligence. Discussion The study discussed the implications of these findings and proposed recommendations for emotion regulation and emotional support for EFL teachers in China and comparable educational contexts.

papers.title: Can large language models reproduce humans’ perspective-dependent judgements of gratitude? Evidence from Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Doubao
papers.authors: Wenjun Chen, Yujie Chu, Xiaoming Jiang, Yan Li
papers.abstract: Human social interaction is full of episodes of help, and the person giving it and the person receiving it may not interpret the same episode in the same way. Against a background of reports that large language models match or exceed human performance on social reasoning tasks, this study asks whether they reproduce this asymmetry between the two sides. Forty-eight Chinese university students read 24 everyday helping scenarios, each in four situational versions, from either the beneficiary’s or the benefactor’s side, and rated the helper’s willingness, the recipient’s need, the difficulty of helping, and the recipient’s gratitude. The identical Chinese materials were then given to 12 models, the flagship and the light model of three providers based in English-speaking countries and three based in China, with 30 independent runs per text, followed by two further prompt conditions: the same scenarios in English for the six models of the Chinese providers and a stated identity prepended to the prompt for all 12. Bayesian mixed models showed a dissociation. On what the situation called for, the models mostly matched the humans or exceeded them: the contrast between a pressing need and one already met was 1.325 scale points in the humans and 1.159 to 1.825 across models, above the human value in 11 of 12. On which side the episode was judged from, most fell short: the humans rated gratitude 0.756 points higher from the beneficiary’s side, the models 0.047 to 0.727, with 11 of 12 credibly below the human estimate. Only Doubao-2.1-Pro matched the humans on gratitude, and it departed from them on willingness and difficulty. Capability tier ordered the 12, though the contrast did not exclude zero, while the provider’s country did not order them at all. Among the six models of the Chinese providers, writing the scenarios in English raised the effect in five, though not to the human estimate. Likewise, across all 12, stating an identity raised it in 10, by 0.10 on average against a mean shortfall of 0.44, and 11 of 12 still sat below the human estimate. Our results suggest that large language models, at least those surveyed here, read what a situation calls for at a level comparable to human readers, but that they show markedly less sensitivity to perspective, namely to the asymmetry with which benefactors and beneficiaries evaluate one and the same act of help.

papers.title: Stress-related helplessness is independently associated with reward-driven eating in adults with BMI-defined normal weight and obesity
papers.authors: Imke Schamarek, Peter Louis Kovacs, Michael Stümvoll, Matthias Blüher, Anke Tönjes, Kerstin Rohde‐Zimmermann
papers.abstract: Background Accumulating evidence indicates that stress is associated with reward-driven eating, yet the stress dimensions underlying this relationship remain insufficiently understood. Inconsistent findings may partly reflect conceptualizing stress as a unitary construct and insufficient consideration of weight status. This study examined the independent associations of perceived stress dimensions (Helplessness, Self-Efficacy) with hedonic hunger, trait food craving, and uncontrolled eating in adults with BMI-defined normal weight and obesity.
