papers.title: Breathing Digital Life Into Legacy Fields and Enhancing Value Through Real-Time Operational Intelligence
papers.authors: C. S. Ibeh, P. Njoku, K. Awonuga, C. Eluwa, E. Ogidi, I. F. Onuche
papers.journal: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
papers.abstract: Abstract Sustaining high production efficiency (PE) remains a top priority across industries, particularly in oil and gas, where complex/obsolete systems and a volatile commodity price environment amplify the cost of inefficiency. The production value chain of a typical conventional oil field spans from the reservoir all the way to the export systems. This paper presents the experience of an international oil and gas company (henceforth referred to as "the company" or "the operator") over the past couple of years with digitalizing this value chain across its mature assets in the Niger Delta with the primary objective of achieving a PE above 90% while reducing operational costs. The methodology involves clear problem definition, rigorous design, strategic technology selection and deployment, and a disciplined feedback loop to embed continuous improvement. Structured project framing and value mapping workshops, including future state ideation and vendor/technology assessments, led by a cross-functional team where conducted. Recent advances in digital technologies, including cost-effective wireless solutions and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) devices, enable real-time production surveillance at scale. However, data acquisition alone is insufficient; transforming this data into actionable insights through advanced data analytics and physics-informed machine learning is what ultimately drives better decisions and outcomes. Early successes include loss production mitigation and operational cost reductions. These outcomes were enabled by the systematic deployment of digital instrumentation and adoption of digital tools. Field operators are now able to quickly identify and restore down wells back to production and proactively optimize well parameters to improve production. Remote surveillance has minimized operational exposure and is a big plus for personnel health, safety, and regulatory compliance. By the end of 2025, over 330 wells representing ~95% of the active wells were successfully instrumented with the remote wellhead sensors. Thus far, the proactive production optimization efforts implemented based on the insights from the real-time data have delivered over 226,000 barrels of oil (gross) in LPO avoidance and more than $1.5 million in logistics cost savings since project inception. This milestone achievement was not without challenges such as resource limitations, logistical constraints, and change management hurdles. This paper presents practical strategies for assessing and scaling digital production-surveillance technologies in brownfield operations. Many companies limit digital technology deployment to greenfield developments because of concerns about operational disruptions or production losses in mature assets. This work challenges that paradigm and adds to the existing body of knowledge by showing how digital technologies can be deployed efficiently and strategically to deliver significant value to the oil and gas industry.

papers.title: A Conversational User Interface for Autonomous Reservoir Simulation Deck Generation and Execution
papers.authors: I. Matejka, W. Laube, D. Perschke
papers.journal: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
papers.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper presents CLARISSA (Conversational Language Agent for Reservoir Integrated Simulation System Analysis), a conversational agent that autonomously generates, executes, and analyzes reservoir simulation models from natural language input. Engineers describe what they want; CLARISSA delivers working models. To enable standardized comparison of conversational deck-generation systems, we introduce RIGOR (Reservoir Input Generation Output Review), a benchmark for evaluating CLARISSA and future similar efforts. Methods, Procedures, Process CLARISSA employs large language models integrated with OPM Flow through a multi-stage translation pipeline that converts natural language problem descriptions into PetroScript, a typed, simulator-independent authoring language whose compiler currently emits Eclipse-format deck syntax. The system supports multiple input modalities: voice, text chat, web interfaces, and REST APIs. Physics-aware validation flags inconsistencies during conversational elicitation, while analog databases suggest reasonable defaults for incomplete specifications—all assumptions are explicitly documented. Generated decks execute autonomously on OPM Flow; outputs can be exported for commercial platforms when third-party validation is required. RIGOR employs execution-based evaluation using simulator diagnostics including convergence behavior and material balance closure. Results, Observations, Conclusions CLARISSA successfully generated decks for SPE comparative solution projects including SPE1 (Odeh, 1981), SPE5 (Killough and Kossack, 1987), and SPE9 (Killough, 1995) from text and tabular input specifications. Generated decks executed without error and matched published benchmark results. Beyond validation cases, CLARISSA demonstrated autonomous model reformulation: given only a compositional table, the system converted a black-oil model to a fully compositional equation-of-state formulation without additional user intervention. This capability enables rapid evaluation of tertiary recovery options from existing assets. RIGOR defines complexity tiers from foundational (linear displacement corefloods) through intermediate (multi-well pattern floods) to advanced scenarios requiring mid-conversation compositional pivots. Execution-based scoring derives from simulator diagnostics: convergence behavior, material balance closure, and physical constraint satisfaction. The binding constraint on simulation adoption has never been solver performance—it is human cognitive load and workflow friction. CLARISSA eliminates both commercial licensing barriers and the specialist training traditionally required, enabling practicing reservoir engineers to directly leverage simulation capabilities previously accessible only to dedicated specialists. Novel/Additive Information Unlike prior work focused on querying existing models (SPE-221987) or retrieving reservoir data through pre-built tool functions (SPE-229646), CLARISSA is the first system capable of generating—not merely querying or modifying—complete simulation decks from natural language. RIGOR provides the first standardized benchmark for evaluating conversational deck-generation systems, enabling reproducible comparison of future approaches analogous to established benchmarks in software engineering code generation. PetroScript, to be released alongside RIGOR, is to our knowledge the first typed authoring language for reservoir simulation decks designed to be simulator-independent, replacing positional keyword syntax with named, validated parameters.

papers.title: Rollout-Aware Graph Neural Network-Based Simulator for Hydraulic Fracture
papers.authors: Yuxuan Liu, Yutong Wu, Liansong Wu, Jianchun Guo
papers.journal: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
papers.abstract: Abstract Hydraulic fracturing is a key technology for the efficient development of unconventional oil and gas reservoirs, and numerical simulation is an effective approach for investigating hydraulic fracture propagation. However, conventional hydraulic fracture propagation models struggle to achieve a satisfactory balance between computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, making it difficult to simulate fracture evolution in real time as field operations progress. Incorporating machine learning into next-generation hydraulic fracture simulators offers a promising route toward real-time prediction of fracture propagation. In this study, we develop, for the first time, a hydraulic fracture propagation simulator based on a rollout-aware graph neural network (RAGNN), termed RAGNN-FPS, to enable second-scale prediction of hydraulic fracture evolution. The simulator is designed to facilitate rapid adjustment and optimization of field fracturing parameters and thereby improve reservoir stimulation performance. RAGNN-FPS learns from massive, high-fidelity, mesh-scale simulation data generated using the finite-discrete element method (FDEM), including displacement fields, velocity fields, and hydraulic fracture propagation states. A heterogeneous graph containing both solid-element edges and joint edges is constructed, while static geological parameters and dynamic engineering parameters are encoded as node and edge features. A rollout-aware training strategy is further introduced, whereby errors arising from the model's own predictions are progressively incorporated during training. This strategy mitigates error accumulation during autoregressive inference and improves long-horizon prediction stability. The results show that the proposed simulator can stably reproduce the complete hydraulic fracturing process, including fracture initiation, propagation, and interactions with natural fractures, while achieving second-scale prediction of fracture evolution. Compared with the teacher-forcing baseline, the median relative L1 error of the full-field displacement is reduced to below 0.073, while the F1 score for joint failure-state classification increases from 0.197 to 0.965. All test cases lie outside the parameter ranges used for training, with extrapolation levels ranging from 25% to 150%. Under these extrapolation conditions, the relative error of the displacement field increases from approximately 5% for interpolation to approximately 10%. On the same workstation, prediction of one complete trajectory requires approximately 9 s, whereas an FDEM simulation of the same scale takes approximately 10 min, corresponding to a speedup of about 65 times. Evaluation of 50 design scenarios requires only approximately 8 min. By integrating a heterogeneous graph neural network architecture with a rollout-aware training strategy, RAGNN-FPS provides a pioneering learning paradigm for real-time simulation of hydraulic fracture propagation and offers a potential solution for digital-twin physical modeling of fracture propagation in geotechnical systems.

papers.title: Mapping Successful AI Application in Well Delivery to Domain Knowledge, SME Capacity in Operators and Their Suppliers
papers.authors: J. P. de Wardt, P. Kowalchuk, A. Wang, K. Umay
papers.journal: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
papers.abstract: Abstract Major operators and service companies sustain deep expertise by funding robust hiring and training to develop in-house Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). Conversely, smaller players lack the capital for permanent specialist benches. Their fluctuating needs and limited funding force them to purchase knowledge from lower-cost service companies that similarly lack SME resources. While AI is viewed as a way to leverage SMEs, implementation requires capital, data, and SME knowledge, resources that, for these same reasons, small operators and service companies lack. This paper will present an analysis of the technical and human capital requirements for AI implementation, highlighting the systemic challenges facing small-scale producers (under 100,000 Bbls/day and even those below 5,000 Bbls/day). Given these operators account for over half of global production, we investigate the disparity in AI readiness compared to major organizations. The process evaluates a procedural framework for overcoming resource constraints through federated learning and shared data infrastructures. Finally, we outline a customization-led model (80% standard, 20% tailored) designed to bridge the domain expertise gap in these essential, yet cash-constrained, operating environments. This analysis concludes that successful AI adoption for smaller operators depends on identifying specific data technologies that bridge the resource gap. Three primary pillars are identified: Collaborative Data Infrastructure: A secure framework for pooling data across multiple companies to achieve the volume necessary for robust AI models while strictly preserving individual data privacy. Federated Learning Protocols: A decentralized methodology where models are trained locally on individual company data and aggregated into a comprehensive "big model," effectively mitigating data security concerns. Flexible Architecture: Technology must leverage a modular design—standardizing 80% of functionality while allowing 20% customization to meet unique company and regional operational requirements. Furthermore, observations indicate that accessing domain expertise requires a shift toward "knowledgeable procurement." Smaller operators must develop the internal competency to select and manage third-party consultants and specialized AI tools effectively. Ultimately, high-quality investment decisions necessitate a rigorous payoff analysis that balances the costs of acquiring domain expertise, managing data procurement, and technical implementation. By adopting these strategic frameworks, small-scale producers can overcome capital constraints to realize significant operational gains and sustain global production levels. This paper will provide a realistic framework for AI adoption across diverse operator profiles, bridging the gap between theoretical benefits and practical implementation. By focusing on small-scale producers, who collectively account for over half of global oil production, this work addresses a segment whose high combined volumes are critical to global energy security. The study provides these operators with a scalable roadmap for AI integration that is equally applicable to the burgeoning geothermal sector.

papers.title: Assessment in the Age of Generative AI: Academic Integrity, Authentic Learning and Assessment Design in Tanzanian Universities — A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Henry Nkya, Patrick Ngulube
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT can now produce essays, problem solutions and examination answers that pass as competent student work, raising the question of whether university grades still show what students know and can do. This systematic review with thematic synthesis examined what the international and African literature reports on GenAI and academic integrity, the effectiveness and fairness of AI detection, and the assessment designs that hold up in an AI-rich environment. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases and organisational sources were searched for studies published between January 2018 and June 2026. Thirty studies were included, eleven from Africa and four from Tanzania; they were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, AMSTAR 2 and the AACODS checklist and synthesised thematically with frequency counts. Five themes emerged: widespread and rising student use of GenAI (50% of studies); the vulnerability of conventional take-home and online assessment (60%); the unreliability and unfairness of AI-detection software (27%); the partial protection offered by authentic, process-focused and oral assessment (37%); and policy, capacity and training gaps (60%), most acute in African institutions. The evidence indicates that Tanzanian universities cannot rely on detection. They should move from a policing model to a design model of integrity, supported by institutional guidance, staff development and a graded scale of acceptable AI use. A Tanzanian Assessment Redesign Framework (TARF) is proposed for empirical testing, and priorities for intervention research are identified.

papers.title: Perceived Value and Adoption Intention of Enterprise AI Solutions in Bangladesh: Integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Diffusion of Innovations Theory
papers.authors: Taseen Karima, Kazi Abdul Mannan
papers.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is increasingly framed as a value-realisation problem rather than a simple question of whether users are willing to try new technologies. This study examines perceived value and adoption intention for enterprise AI/cloud solutions among technology-oriented respondents in Bangladesh by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory. Distinct from a conventional predictor-only adoption model, the study specifies a value-realization mechanism in which relative advantage and compatibility shape perceived usefulness, which in turn contributes to adoption intention; direct DOI-to-intention paths are retained to test partial versus full mediation. Innovation adoption readiness is additionally examined as a boundary condition on the usefulness-intention relationship. The supplied database contains 385 complete observations after exclusion of 15 blank rows. Respondents are distributed across students, employed professionals, and self-employed/freelance users, with substantial variation in technology-use frequency and experience. Composite-score path analysis shows that relative advantage and compatibility are positively associated with perceived usefulness (β=.204 and β=.217, respectively; both p<.001). Perceived usefulness is positively associated with adoption intention (β=.119, p=.020), while relative advantage (β=.147, p=.005), compatibility (β=.156, p=.003), and innovation adoption readiness (β=.150, p=.004) also have significant direct associations with adoption intention. Bootstrap indirect effects through perceived usefulness are positive for both relative advantage (ab=.025, 95% CI [.003, .052]) and compatibility (ab=.026, 95% CI [.004, .053]). The usefulness × readiness interaction is not statistically significant (β=.039, p=.447). The findings therefore indicate a partial value-realisation pathway rather than a simple direct-determinants model. The article contributes by linking innovation attributes to the TAM usefulness mechanism in a Bangladesh enterprise-AI context and by showing that readiness operates more clearly as a direct adoption resource than as a moderator of usefulness.

papers.title: Founder Readiness and Institutional Fit: A Leadership-Contingent Model of Generative AI Adoption in Founder-Led SMEs in Switzerland and the United Kingdom
papers.authors: Valeriia Yevsiukova
papers.abstract: Comparative research on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and artificial intelligence usually treats national institutions and firm leadership separately. Institutional studies ask which countries make adoption easier. Leadership studies ask which managers make adoption happen. In founder-led SMEs, where one person often holds most decision rights, these questions cannot be separated. This study argues that the same founder can be more or less effective at leading generative AI adoption depending on the institutional setting, and that the direction of this effect depends on the type of readiness the founder has. We develop the Founder-Institution Fit (FIF) model. It builds on the Founder Readiness Framework (FRF-4) proposed by Sarkisyan (2026) and combines two founder composites, structural and psychological readiness, with three national parameters: the depth of the market for external expertise, the strength of internal delegation norms, and regulatory clarity. We apply the model to four stylized founder archetypes in Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Both are high-income economies, but they differ sharply in institutional type. The illustrative analysis gives three findings. First, psychological readiness works as a multiplier. A founder who is low on it achieves little in either country, whatever institutional support is available. Second, the country advantage reverses with the founder's profile. Founders whose readiness rests mainly on learning orientation gain more in the British setting, which offers a deep market for outside expertise. Founders whose readiness rests mainly on identity plasticity gain more in the Swiss setting, which supports internal delegation. Third, once regulatory differences are neutralized, the crossover follows a closed-form threshold: the British setting is preferred when the ratio of learning orientation to identity plasticity exceeds 4:3. We discuss implications for founders, boards, advisors, and policymakers and set out an agenda for empirical calibration.

papers.title: Academic Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Scoping Review (2026)
papers.authors: Владимир Михайлович Московкин
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed the landscape of modern higher education, prompting a critical paradigm shift in how academic integrity is conceptualized. This scoping review synthesizes 20 cutting-edge academic publications from 2026 (retrieved via Google Scholar) to examine the evolution of academic integrity from mechanical plagiarism detection and punitive surveillance toward comprehensive institutional, pedagogical, and ethical redesign. The synthesis reveals that the primary systemic catalyst for academic misconduct remains the pervasive “publish or perish” culture and quantitative assessment paradigms that prioritize performance over moral growth. Contemporary scholarship moves beyond identifying individual infractions to address systemic vulnerabilities, student uncertainty, data privacy, and the degradation of higher-order cognitive skills (analyzing, evaluating, creating) resulting from unreflective AI reliance. To mitigate these threats, the review highlights four key integrative strategies: (1) adoption of ecosystemic models (e.g., A. Maleki’s Higher Education Integrity Ecosystem) linking governance, assessment, cultural norms, and individual agency; (2) implementation of process-oriented, authentic assessment frameworks (e.g., S. Lehane, A. Wright and P. Fenton’s Model for Practice and P.D.N. Ncube et al.’s PRISMA-based multi-stage evaluations) that render automated cheating obsolete; (3) operationalization of the AI3 model that integrated AI, academic integrity, and assessment innovation (C. DeLuca, L.Volante and M. Holden), and (4) proactive educational initiatives, AI literacy, and epistemic pluralism to safeguard neurodivergent learning trajectories. Ultimately, the academic community is transitioning from technocratic panic to building ethically resilient, adaptive educational ecosystems aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 4 and SDG 16).

papers.title: Machine Learning Based Dyslexia Screening Using Multimodal Tests
papers.authors: Vidya Kawtikwar, Sagar Hegde, Alok T. Pal, Harshada Pimpale, Chandankumar Soni
papers.abstract: Dyslexia is a common problem that affects how people read and write. It is not because they are not smart. Because their brain works a little differently. It is really important to find out if someone has dyslexia so we can help them with their reading and writing. The problem is that the ways we have now to figure out if someone has dyslexia are not very good. They take a lot of time. Are not always right. In this paper we are talking about a way to find out if someone has dyslexia. This way uses computers to look at how people write and talk. We use something called Natural Language Processing to look at the words and sentences that people write. We also use something called Sequence-to-Sequence to look at the patterns in their writing. This helps us to see if someone has dyslexia or not. We tried out our way with some tests and it worked pretty well. It was able to tell if someone had dyslexia or not 63 percent of the time. This is really good because it means that we can use this way to help kids who have dyslexia. It is also a way because it is not too expensive. This means that teachers and parents can use it to help kids with dyslexia. Dyslexia is a problem that we can help with if we can just find out who has it. Our new way is a step, in the right direction. Dyslexia detection is important. Our system can help with dyslexia detection.

papers.title: Learning for Sustainability in Urban Innovation Areas: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Maria Eunice Viana Jotz, Diogo Onofre Souza, Carina Rapetti, Josep Miquel Piqué
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of socioenvironmental challenges requires environments capable of integrating learning, innovation, governance, and sustainability. Although urban innovation areas are widely recognized for their contribution to economic and technological development, their role as territorial platforms for sustainability-oriented learning and transformation remains underexplored. The objective of this study was to map and synthesize how the scientific literature addressed sustainability-oriented learning processes in urban innovation areas, with a focus on understanding these contexts as territorial learning ecosystems, while identifying learning mechanisms, governance and participation arrangements, institutional roles, and research gaps related to sustainability transitions. To map, systematize, and analyze the scientific production related to this topic, a scoping review based on the PRISMA–ScR protocol was conducted, combined with a thematic analysis of 26 studies selected from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The results indicated that urban living labs, co-creation processes, collaborative networks, knowledge spillovers, and multi-actor governance structures were recurrently identified as mechanisms supporting collective learning and urban experimentation. Learning emerges as an articulating dimension between innovation, participation, and territorial governance, whereas institutions play a strategic role in creating conditions for the production, circulation, and application of knowledge. The study also highlights the challenges related to participation asymmetry, environmental justice, social inclusion, and power relations within innovation ecosystems. As a contribution to the literature, this article proposes understanding urban innovation areas not merely as spaces of economic and technological innovation, but also as territorial learning ecosystems in which governance, social participation, and knowledge circulation are articulated to support sustainability-oriented transitions. Finally, it highlights the need to develop indicators and conduct empirical research to assess their contributions to territorial transformation dynamics.

papers.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Animation
papers.authors: Sebastian Pagueguy
papers.journal: The International Journal of the Image
papers.abstract: This article explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in contemporary animation workflows through the analysis of two applied case studies, both directed by the author within the Chilean creative studio Poston Digital Arts. The first case examines the production of an animated title sequence for the science fiction film Affinity, while the second analyzes the development of a commercial spot for the Mortal Kombat x Saucony product collaboration. Both projects involve hybrid production pipelines that combine AI-based tools, such as generative image models, AI-driven motion capture, and AI-assisted storyboarding, with traditional animation techniques. Through comparative analysis, this article identifies advantages in production efficiency, creative iteration, and visual output quality while also recognizing limitations and risks associated with the use of AI. Key findings include the shifting roles within animation teams, the emergence of new professional profiles (such as AI operators and prompt engineers), and the continued importance of human artistic direction. The discussion concludes that AI, when properly integrated, serves as a powerful creative accelerator without replacing the essential role of human oversight, and its use requires conscious management to avoid risks, such as aesthetic homogenization and the erosion of foundational artistic skills.

papers.title: HUMAN-AI COLLABORATIVE DEBATE IN EFL CLASSROOMS: RE-EXAMINING ARGUMENTATIVE SPEAKING COMPETENCE, ACADEMIC INTEGRITY, AND PEDAGOGICAL AGENCY THROUGH COPILOT AND CHATGPT
papers.authors: Ranta Butarbutar, Rubén González Vallejo, Mohammed Boukezzoula
papers.journal: Veredas do Direito Direito Ambiental e Desenvolvimento Sustentável
papers.abstract: Argumentative speaking competence in English as a foreign language is multidimensional and includes linguistic accuracy, rhetorical logic, interactive response, and affective regulation. However, its development remains challenging, particularly in terms of argument coherence, anxiety management, and academic integrity in the era of learning-based AI. This study employs a mixed-method sequential explanatory design with one group pre-test and post-test over eight weeks, involving ChatGPT and Copilot as debate partners and reflections through Google Classroom. Quantitative analysis showed significant improvement in ASC (d= 2.86), academic integrity (d=2.04), and pedagogical agency (d= 2.37). Meanwhile, qualitative data confirm that students perceive AI as idea facilitators that help to find out contra-argument and increase self-confidence, but still remain critical to keep integrity. These findings strengthen cross-culture communicative competence and AI as a cognitive partnership and are consistent with the UNESCO and OECD principles of AI ethics. Practically, this suggests that educators should utilize AI as a sparring partner in the reflective pedagogy framework, students should use AI as an idea’s facilitator, not a final answer or argument, and decision makers and EFL curriculum and material developers should organize particular modules about AI-ethical communicative competence so that integrating technology still aligns with academic values.

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Japanese Language Education in the Age of Human–AI Collaboration: Toward a Human Competency-Oriented Framework for Future-Oriented CAN-DO
papers.authors: Franky Reymond Najoan, Elvie Nitje Piri
papers.journal: Journal of Japanese Language Education and Linguistics
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper examines how Japanese language education can respond to Human–AI Collaboration while preserving the educational philosophy of the Japan Foundation’s JF Standard and CAN-DO orientation. It develops a focused, non-systematic synthesis of educational philosophy, competency-based language education, official educational frameworks, and selected journal literature on AI-supported teaching and learning. The analysis distinguishes educational purposes from technological capabilities and considers how AI assistance changes the interpretation of communicative achievement. Its principal conceptual outcome is a Human Competency-Oriented Framework for Japanese Language Education connecting Educational Purpose, Human Competency Development, Human–AI Collaboration, Future-Oriented CAN-DO, and Teaching / Curriculum / Assessment. The framework retains six competencies: critical thinking, communication, collaboration, intercultural competence, ethical AI use, and lifelong learning. Building on this framework, illustrative Future-Oriented CAN-DO Descriptors make learners’ evaluation, revision, justification, reflection, and responsible use of AI explicit within communicative tasks. These proposals constitute neither an official revision of the JF Standard nor empirically validated learning outcomes. The paper concludes that CAN-DO remains educationally relevant when AI-supported performance is interpreted with attention to learners’ contributions and responsibility. It offers a conceptual basis for curriculum development, classroom practice, and subsequent validation of descriptors.

papers.title: Use of Generative AI in Scholarly Research: Challenges and Opportunities
papers.authors: Marco Marabelli, Robert M. Davison, Giovanni Gatti, Ankita Srivastava, Monideepa Tarafdar
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: The focus of this panel report is to present evidence of a panel discussion that took place in October 2025 on the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) in academic research and publishing. The panel included publishers (Elsevier, Emerald, Galiot Press, MIT Press, Nature/Springer, Wiley) and editors-in-chief (representing the Information Systems Journal, Journal of the AIS, Journal of Data Science and ICES Journal of Marine Science). Key outcomes of the panel are the following: (1) publishers and editors have some disagreements regarding GAI use; (2) besides disagreements, all recognize that GAI is here to stay, and therefore, outstanding issues (e.g., training for PhD students and junior faculty and consequences for unallowed uses of GAI) need to be addressed jointly; (3) GAI is in constant flux, and this is a challenge for publisher and journal policies; and (4) it is unclear the extent to which GAI will affect future scholarship outcomes, especially having in mind the potential for scholarly deskilling.

papers.title: Social Processes as Drivers for Empowerment of Sustainable Fisheries Management on Åland
papers.authors: Kristina Svels, Katrina Rønningen, Viktor Eriksson, Linda Sundström, Salina Spiering, Cecilie Helene Bratt, Maiken Bjørkan, Brendan Murtagh, Wesley Flannery
papers.abstract: This study analyses and evaluates an early-stage, pre-intervention phase in Åland’s small-scale fisheries community and examines the usefulness of a mixed-methods approach. It focuses on how combining three complementary methods supports the development of a grounded and legitimate pilot, rather than assessing pilot outcomes. The study applies a mixed-method approach combining a governance audit, community stakeholder workshops, and Q-methodology to map the social and institutional context prior to pilot implementation. The small-scale fisheries community in Åland represents an important cultural heritage and way of life, but faces increasing vulnerability due to regulatory pressures, ecological challenges, and socio-economic marginalisation. The findings suggest that combining multiple social science methods can contribute to a more nuanced understanding of stakeholder perspectives, power dynamics, and governance constraints, while supporting the identification of locally relevant intervention pathways and creating conditions for more legitimate and inclusive pilot development. However, the results also highlight limitations related to uneven participation and the difficulty of engaging diverse stakeholder groups in practice. The analysis indicates that social science approaches can provide an essential foundation for the later development of ecologically and socially grounded interventions, including nature-based solutions where locally appropriate. Nevertheless, social science contributions are currently less prominent than technical nature-based interventions, suggesting the value of more balanced integration between scientific disciplines in future initiatives. Overall, this article illustrates both the potential and the limits of mixed-method approaches in early-stage co-creation processes, offering insights for the design of participatory governance interventions in coastal communities.

papers.title: AI-Powered Versus Scripted Virtual Patients in Health Professions Education: A Critical Systematic Review of Realism, Fidelity, Flexibility, Learning Outcomes, Learner Experience, and Misconceptions
papers.authors: Arezoo Behzadi, Fatemeh Bakhshi, Sara Heydari
papers.abstract: Ethical considerations: the ethics committee of shahid sadoughi university of medical sciences approved the study(IR.SSU.REC.1405.008). Type of study: A Critical Systematic Review Search start date: 1404/07/01 The main research question In health professions education, how do artificial intelligence (AI)-based virtual patients compare with scripted virtual patients in terms of realism, simulation fidelity, interactional flexibility, learning outcomes, learner experience, and the development or reduction of clinical misconceptions? Main question Secondary question Does dynamic response generation in VP-AI systems result in greater flexibility, more natural interaction, and higher learner engagement? What differences exist between the two types of virtual patients in terms of clinical skills, clinical reasoning, decision-making, and learning transfer? How do learner experiences differ with respect to satisfaction, usability, engagement, trust, cognitive load, and anxiety? What types of misconceptions, misinformation, bias, or reasoning errors have been reported during interactions with VP-AI systems? What gaps in the available evidence are apparent with regard to validation, educational safety, reproducibility, and direct comparative evidence? Entry and exit criteria Entry criteria :Studies must meet all or the principal components of the following eligibility criteria Participants must be students, interns, residents, trainees, or practicing health professionals in medicine, nursing, or other health professions. A virtual patient must be used for teaching, practice, assessment, or skills development. The type of virtual patient must be explicitly classifiable as VP-S, VP-AI, or hybrid VP. At least one prespecified outcome is reported; The article must be published in English. The full text of the article must be available. The article must be published in a peer-reviewed journal. The study design must be one of the following: RCT؛ quasi-experimental؛ controlled before-after؛ cohort or comparative observational؛ pre-post study؛ mixed-methods Provided that the learners experience and flexibility and fidelity and realism and qualitative study have been examined.؛ For S-VP the search is restricted to publications dated from 1 january 2015 onwards. For AI-VP the search is restricted to publications dated from 1 january 2022 onwards. Exit Criteria Studies involving general education or non-health-professional users. Studies evaluating only a technical system or algorithm without an educational virtual patient. Studies in which AI is used only for content generation, scoring, data analysis, or image creation and does not play a dynamic role in generating patient responses. Studies pertaining to: VR-only Non-interactive virtual patients robotic patients or Physical robots Manikins and physical simulators standardized patients Serious games without a clearly defined virtual patient component Non-interactive avatars General-purpose chatbots without a clinical scenario and a clearly defined educational objective. Studies in which the VP architecture cannot be determined. Letters to the editor, abstracts, protocols, commentaries, conference editorials, and short articles lacking sufficient data. Theses and grey literature; however, their references will be examined for citation chasing. Systematic reviews and secondary studies; these will be used only to identify primary studies and examine evidence gaps. Not englished articles. Pico design The final definition component Students and learners in the health professions, including medicine, nursing, midwifery, dentistry, pharmacy, physiotherapy, allied health professions, residents, and interns. Population AI-powered or generative-AI-based virtual patients that generate dynamic responses in real time during interaction. Intervention Scripted virtual patients with predefined, branching, rule-based responses or limited, preprogrammed interaction pathways. Comparator Realism, fidelity, flexibility, clinical skills, clinical reasoning, decision-making, knowledge, performance, satisfaction, usability, engagement, trust, anxiety, cognitive load, misconceptions, and educational errors. Outcomes Additional information and search sources Main base PubMed/MEDLINE Scopus Web of Science Core Collection ERIC Additional resources Google Scholar for citation chasing and Identification of additional studies Sources and AMEE publication types Of studies backward citation and forward citation check Manual search in Medical Education Simulation in Healthcare Academic Medicine Google Scholar will not be used as a primary reproducible source. papers.title: Does music prime language? A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of cross-domain N400 and behavioural congruency effects
papers.authors: Ruikai Yuan, Ruikai Yuan
papers.abstract: Whether music can convey meaning that the language system recognises is a long-standing question at the boundary of neurolinguistics and music cognition. The N400 component of the event-related potential is a well-established index of meaning processing (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011). Koelsch et al. (2004) reported that visual words preceded by semantically unrelated musical excerpts elicited an N400 effect comparable to that produced by sentence primes. Later studies extended this effect to single-chord and timbre primes (Steinbeis & Koelsch, 2011) and to designs in which words primed musical targets (Daltrozzo & Schön, 2009). The effect has also been observed in implicit lexical decision tasks (Cai et al., 2015). The evidence has not been synthesised quantitatively. The only related meta-analysis identified (Armitage, 2024, doctoral thesis) pooled behavioural affective priming effects from 12 English-language articles and did not analyse ERP data. Individual ERP studies are small and differ in priming type and analysis window, so the size and boundary conditions of the cross-domain N400 effect remain uncertain. This review addresses the following questions. 1. Primary. What is the pooled size of the N400 congruency effect when musical stimuli and linguistic stimuli are paired as primes and targets? 2. Secondary. What is the pooled size of the corresponding behavioural congruency effect in reaction time and in accuracy? 3. Moderators. Does the N400 effect differ between affective and conceptual priming or between music-to-language and language-to-music directions? Does task explicitness moderate it? 4. Exploratory. Do stimulus onset asynchrony and prime type moderate either effect? Does musical training moderate it? Which special populations have been studied, and what do their results suggest?

papers.authors: Tolga Topçubaşı
papers.abstract: Systematic review (PRISMA 2020; SPIDER; MMAT 2018; thematic synthesis) of empirical research on in-service and pre-service teachers' use of AI in Life Studies and Social Studies education. Databases: Web of Science, Scopus, OpenAlex, ULAKBİM TR Dizin and the YÖK National Thesis Centre (searched 13–14 October 2026). Deposited materials: protocol, search log and raw search outputs, screening table with exclusion reasons, extraction records, coded table of included studies, PRISMA 2020 flow diagram, re-screen sample and kappa sheet.

papers.title: Working Paper · The ARC Theory · The Hyperspace Recursive Intelligence Hypothesis: a Bayesian and Physical Research Programme for Intelligent Cosmogenesis
papers.authors: Michael Darius Eastwood
papers.abstract: I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. This working paper states the Hyperspace Recursive Intelligence Hypothesis (HRIH) in a form that can lose. In the words of its long-form edition, the hypothesis is that "reality is a recursive creation by intelligence: a real cosmos seeded by an intelligence that arose in the one before". The paper reconstructs it as a nested, falsifiable research programme, not as a claim that intelligence has been shown to create universes: a fair model space in which real intelligent cosmogenesis competes with non-deliberate cosmology and simulation families; explicit observer weighting; a cosmogenic reproduction number with the extinction threshold of a branching lineage; and maker-selection beyond habitability, its one distinctive empirical claim, for held-out tests to decide. Five predictions and five studies are specified for registration, each with what would count against it. Current evidence does not discriminate between HRIH and its strongest rivals, and the paper assigns HRIH no posterior probability. It isolates the scientific core of HRIH for review and testing. The long-form monograph, The Hyperspace Recursive Intelligence Hypothesis, which stands at version 3.51, remains the canonical and provenance-bearing work: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/UYDXQ. Where the two are ever found to disagree, the monograph governs, except on the points this paper lists as its corrections. Its place in the programme: HRIH is the separable cosmological wing of the ARC Theory, the founding theory of Recursive Dynamics, the field Michael Darius Eastwood founded. None of Laws I to V is a premise of it or enters any likelihood in it (Laws IV and V were added on 24 September 2026, and neither is yet registered as a law or tested); ARC work may inform its creator-stability factor; neither the Eden Protocol nor the HARI Treaty enters it. The statement paper gives its weight plainly: "Refuse it and the theory loses nothing" (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/GW5MX). The paper tests none of the ARC Theory's laws. Status: version 4.0 is a working draft, released before its review is complete. Still to run: review from outside the programme by a statistician, by a cosmologist or quantum-gravity specialist and by a philosopher of probability, without which this version is not final; a systematic literature review of the priority of the exact conjunction it claims; and the deposit, beside the paper, of its reference code. When they have run, the checked paper replaces this one as a labelled new version, with its changes listed. Licence: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). Michael Darius Eastwood conceived and directs this research programme and is the author of this work. Across the programme, he has used more than six AI systems in parallel, under his own instructions, to stress-test his arguments, identify possible errors, and assist in preparing draft text from his own outlines. He determines what is adopted, revised or rejected and takes responsibility for the published content. These systems are tools, not authors.

papers.title: Beyond Error Correction: ChatGPT as Formative Feedback for Arabic Writing
papers.authors: Abdul Hafidz bin Zaid, Muassomah Muassomah, Moh. Ismail, Alif Cahya Setiyadi, Agus Yasin
papers.journal: eJournal of Sunan Gunung Djati State Islamic University (Sunan Gunung Djati State Islamic University)
papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs) is transforming language education; however, evidence regarding their pedagogical value for Arabic writing remains limited. This study investigates the educational potential of ChatGPT as an AI-assisted formative feedback tool for Arabic academic writing in a pesantren-based university in Indonesia. To achieve this, employing a qualitative descriptive design, the study integrates Error Analysis with the Student Feedback Literacy framework to examine students’ writing errors and evaluate the educational quality of AI-generated feedback. A corpus of 30 Arabic writing texts produced by 30 first-year students enrolled in an intensive Arabic matriculation program was analyzed. ChatGPT (GPT-4, May 2024 version) generated corrective feedback using a standardized prompt, and two Arabic linguistics experts evaluated the linguistic accuracy and pedagogical usefulness of each response. The findings identified 132 errors comprising 39.4% lexical, 32.6% syntactic, and 28.0% morphological errors. Notably, ChatGPT produced fully acceptable feedback for 50.76% of the errors, demonstrating its capacity in lexical and syntactic correction. However, its performance was less consistent in addressing morphologically complex and context-dependent constructions. Overall, the findings indicate that ChatGPT supports learners’ ability to recognize and revise writing errors, although it still requires teacher validation. Consequently, this study contributes valuable insights into AI-assisted language education through meaningful engagement with formative feedback in Arabic writing.

papers.title: DIGITAL-BASED PUBLIC SERVICE INNOVATION: TRANSFORMING LICENSING GOVERNANCE THROUGH THE SIPINTER APPLICATION IN CIMAHI CITY
papers.authors: Siti Zahrotul Mulkiyah, Didin Muhafdin, Sawitri Budi Utami
papers.journal: Politik Indonesia Indonesian Political Science Review
papers.abstract: This study aims to analyze in depth the public service innovation process through the SIPINTER (Integrated Service Information System) application developed by the Cimahi City Investment and One-Stop Integrated Service Agency (DPMPTSP). The study uses a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data collection techniques were carried out through in-depth interviews, observations, and documentation studies. The analytical tool used refers to the perspective of co-creation-based public sector innovation, with a focus on four main dimensions: real-time data accuracy, public participation, governance transparency, and legitimacy. The results show that SIPINTER has contributed significantly to increasing the efficiency and transparency of licensing services through the provision of real-time data and openness of service process information. However, public participation is still instrumental and has not fully developed into deliberative participation, while the legitimacy of innovation is highly dependent on system reliability, human resource capacity, and consistent institutional support. This study confirms that the success of digital public service transformation is determined not only by technological aspects, but also by institutional and relational factors that shape public trust. Theoretically, this research enriches the study of public sector innovation by offering an understanding of conditional co-creation in the context of local government in Indonesia.

papers.title: Machine Learning Framework for Integration of Video and EEG Reveals Distinct Seizure Phenotypes in Mouse Models of Epilepsy
papers.authors: Christine Junhui Liu, Caryn Martin, Allison Christine Lee, Tristan T. Sands, Wayne N. Frankel, Christopher D. Makinson
papers.abstract: Video-electrocorticogram (VEEG) recordings are the gold-standard diagnostic tool for detecting and characterizing seizures in rodent models of seizure and epilepsy. Manual/visual scoring remains the prevailing strategy despite significant limitations. Alternatively, automated and semi-automated analyses have been applied to either EEG or video features alone but integrating these disparate data forms presents a challenge that has not been sufficiently addressed. Here, we introduce an integrated machine learning pipeline that jointly leverages EEG and behavioral video data to enable scalable and objective event classification. Integrated video-EEG analysis was initially validated using a well-established pharmacologically induced seizure paradigm in male mice, where overt generalized motor seizures provide a clear benchmark. We then tested the pipeline on a genetic mouse model of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) that displays a complex spike-wave discharge (SWD) seizure phenotype that poses significant challenges for traditional scoring methods. Machine learning-powered integrated analysis of video-EEG recordings outperformed unimodal EEG- or video-based approaches and performed favorably to experienced rodent EEG electrophysiologists while also uncovering distinct phenotypic relationships, including classes of atypical behavioral and typical non-behavioral SWD events. This framework provides a flexible tool for high-throughput, precise analysis of VEEG data, with potential to accelerate discovery in epilepsy and seizure research. Furthermore, this approach represents a generalizable strategy for the integration of diverse neurobehavioral time series data types. Significance Statement Seizure detection in animal models of epilepsy has relied heavily on manual analysis of video-EEG recordings, a process that is slow and subjective. We present a machine learning pipeline that integrates EEG and video data from mice to classify seizures with high accuracy. This work was validated across two models, first a pharmacologically induced generalized seizure model, and second, a spontaneous spike-wave discharge (SWD) model in genetic epilepsy. Our approach detected events missed by human reviewers and revealed previously uncharacterized SWD subtypes distinguished by their behavior. By combining open-source tools in a flexible framework, this work lowers the barrier to high-throughput, unbiased seizure phenotyping, and also offers a broadly applicable strategy for linking neural activity to behavior in neuroscience research.

papers.title: Review of Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It, by Cory Doctorow
papers.authors: Manouchehr Madani Civi
papers.abstract: Digital platforms are no longer quiet conveniences operating at the margins of modern life.They are the core infrastructure through which people communicate, gather news, work, shop, and engage in public discourse.Higher education is thoroughly bound up in this shift.Universities and schools now rely heavily on commercial platform ecosystems to run day-to-day teaching, assessment, communication, learning analytics, and institutional administration.The recent surge in generative artificial intelligence has only deepened this integration, cementing commercial tech vendors as central actors in academic practice rather than simple external service providers.These shifts were initially greeted with widespread enthusiasm.Commercial platforms promised operational efficiency, expanded access to resources, personalized instruction, and unprecedented collaborative reach.Yet education scholars have increasingly shown that these tools are far from neutral pedagogical utilities.They actively reconfigure institutional decisionmaking, academic labor, data governance, and the fundamental relationship between public universities and private tech corporations (Selwyn, 2022;van Dijck et al., 2018).Debate surrounding educational platforms has thus evolved far beyond technical capability or instructional strategy; it is now a matter of institutional governance, political economy, and public policy.This changing landscape makes Cory Doctorow's Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It especially timely.Doctorow contends that the widespread decline across major digital platforms is neither an accidental glitch nor a string of isolated executive failures.Rather, it represents a predictable lifecycle driven by market concentration, weak antitrust enforcement, and financial incentives that consistently privilege short-term shareholder extraction over user value.He

papers.title: Evidence Governed Artificial Intelligence Across Domains Using CQE MCD and QSLA
papers.authors: Olumisimi Akinde
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly need artificial intelligence to interpret records, recommend decisions and initiate actions. These activities require different forms of control: understanding a situation is not equivalent to authorizing a consequence. This paper proposes an adaptation of the Cognitive Query Engine (CQE), the Mastery Command Deck (MCD) and Quantum-Safe Ledger Architecture (QSLA) into a coordinated architecture. CQE supports questions, evidence retrieval, investigation and conditional scenarios. MCD provides the human interface for reviewing evidence, managing decisions and submitting authorized requests. QSLA evaluates consequential operations, restricts execution and preserves decision records. The integration is organized around a non-compensatory admission rule: every mandatory condition must pass, and strength in one condition cannot repair failure in another. The paper defines its vocabulary, specifies component boundaries, presents an operation information model and explains evidence classification, human review, concurrency and cryptographic governance. Eight hypothetical worked cases cover banking, public administration, healthcare, industrial control, robotics, telecommunications, enterprise assistants, and research and audit. A prospective evaluation programme separates component accuracy, execution enforcement, human understanding and operational outcomes. A companion reference package supplies complete schemas for a bounded payment profile, a signed-token profile, deployment files and 55 locally executed conformance tests. No authentic deployment results, effectiveness measurements or independent validation are claimed. The contribution is a proposed integration and teaching specification, with explicit limits on factual verification, safety models and the conclusions that retained evidence can support.

papers.title: Redefining creativity in AI era: Bloom’s taxonomy framework and peer interaction elevate higher-order thinking skills
papers.authors: Abdhy Aulia Adnans, Noor Raihan Ab Hamid, Norlina Kamudin, Andri Dayarana K. Silalahi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming cognitive learning by reshaping pedagogical models and raising questions about its impact on higher-order thinking. AI-driven personalized learning improves knowledge acquisition, but its effect on creativity remains largely unexplored. Most research emphasizes content delivery over cognitive engagement, which leaves gaps in understanding how AI influences deeper learning processes. This study investigates how ChatGPT-enabled personalized learning, framed through Bloom's Taxonomy, influences creative thinking among Indonesian higher education students, considering the moderating role of peer interaction. Using SEM via Smart-PLS 4.1, data from 533 Indonesian students reveal that personalized learning strengthens both lower-order cognitive skills-such as remembering, understanding, and applying-and higher-order functions, including analyzing, evaluating, and creating, which are essential for creativity. Among these, analyzing and creating have the strongest impact on creative thinking. Peer interaction selectively moderates this relationship, significantly enhancing creativity in tasks involving creation, while its effect on other cognitive functions remains limited. This study introduces a dynamic framework that integrates personalized learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, and peer collaboration, offering new insights into how tailored cognitive processes and selective peer engagement drive creativity in learning environments.

papers.title: Short-term subjective and EEG responses following cervical rotatory manipulation are not reproduced by simulated cracking sound: A randomized controlled study
papers.authors: Yuanxun Lin, Weixing Zhong, YU Meiling, Yaoshuai Yu, Lixin Tang, Xue Fan, Jundan Wei, Junhua Li, Yikai Li
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cervical rotatory manipulation (CRM) is commonly used for neck-related symptoms and is often accompanied by a cracking sound. Whether a simulated cracking sound can reproduce the short-term subjective and neurophysiological responses to the complete CRM remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study compared short-term subjective and electroencephalography (EEG) responses to CRM with those following sham manipulation with or without a simulated cracking sound. METHODS: In this randomized controlled trial with three parallel groups and a single intervention session, 54 healthy volunteers were allocated to CRM, sham manipulation, or sham + simulated sound. Positive affect, negative affect, comfort, satisfaction, and eyes closed resting state EEG were assessed before and after the intervention. Prespecified EEG derived outcomes included frontal alpha power, frontal alpha/beta ratio, occipital individual alpha frequency, and alpha band frontoparietal and frontotemporal functional connectivity. RESULTS: CRM produced greater improvements in positive affect, comfort, and satisfaction than sham manipulation or sham + simulated cracking sound, whereas no clear difference among groups was observed for negative affect. Differences among groups were also observed in frontal alpha/beta ratio and alpha band frontoparietal and frontotemporal functional connectivity. Sham + simulated sound did not reproduce the overall pattern of subjective and EEG responses observed after CRM. CONCLUSIONS: CRM produced greater improvements over the short-term in positive affect, comfort, and satisfaction and was accompanied by differences in selected resting state EEG outcomes compared with sham manipulation with or without simulated cracking sound. Adding simulated cracking sound to sham manipulation did not reproduce this pattern. Because CRM differed from the control conditions in several procedural components, the specific component or combination of components responsible for these differences could not be determined. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was registered with the International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry (URL: https://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn; ITMCTR2025001112).

papers.title: The ethical and regulatory framework of medical artificial intelligence (AI) system’s behavioral performance for image-based diagnostics: An ethical evaluation of the International and European Union Scope
papers.authors: Nina Parchmann, Marcin Orzechowski, Daniel Braun, Florian Steger
papers.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for image-based diagnostics is rising rapidly and enables new opportunities for improving clinical diagnostics through high precision and a quick identification of anomalies. However, a technology characterized by a high variability of image data and the opaqueness of AI models within patient care raises ethical challenges and requires protection by an appropriate ethical and regulatory framework. To identify ethical challenges of the ethical and regulatory framework of the behavioral performance of medical AI systems for image-based diagnostics on the international and European Union level, we searched and screened documents in April and May 2025. The documents were thematically evaluated before conducting an ethical analysis. We identified regulations and ethical recommendations that could be divided into five thematic categories: The (i) data basis is regulated by data standardization, data assessment, and data quality. (ii) Reliability considers assessments, the intended performance, robustness, accuracy, and compliance, whereas the (iii) comprehensibility centers on explainability, understandability, and traceability. The (iv) disclosure of the system considers transparency, operational disclosure, and collaborations, and the (v) usability is regulated on resources and competency. This framework could support the autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and (social) justice, however allows a wide range of compliant technical measures that vary in effectiveness. The insufficient technical feasibility to provide security measures against malicious data alteration as well as the dynamic development of attack and defense mechanisms severely challenge the maintenance of a compliant safe and secure diagnostic AI system. Thereby, the autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and (social) justice could be jeopardized. In conclusion, AI image-based diagnostic systems are regulated by a similar ethical and regulatory framework as general medical AI systems. To protect data and the intended performance, sufficient protection through a regulatory framework is necessary that responds to the challenges of image-based AI diagnostic systems.

papers.title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
papers.authors: Erdem Dogukan Yilmaz, Ivana Naumovska, Vikas A. Aggarwal
papers.abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

papers.title: First person – Iván Hidalgo-Cenalmor
papers.abstract: First Person is a series of interviews with the first authors of a selection of papers published in Journal of Cell Science, helping researchers promote themselves alongside their papers. Iván Hidalgo-Cenalmor is first author on ‘ NucleiSky enables cross-scale multimodal registration of microscopy data using nuclei constellations’, published in JCS. Iván is a PhD student in the lab of Guillaume Jacquemet at the Turku Bioscience Centre, Turku, Finland, where his work focuses on developing computational and image analysis tools for biological imaging, including microscopy image registration and explainable artificial intelligence.

papers.title: ChatGPT’s feedback credibility and students’ perceived learning: the role of agent-related social perceptions
papers.authors: Raúl Pérez‐López, Rubén González-Vallejo, Laura Lucia‐Palacios, Iguácel Melero‐Polo, Andreea Trifu
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines whether students’ agent-related social perceptions of ChatGPT are associated with the perceived credibility of its feedback in academic tasks and whether such credibility, in turn, is related to students’ perceived learning. It also investigates whether the relationship between feedback credibility and perceived learning varies according to students’ sensitivity to the quality of their academic work and their sensitivity to grade-based rewards. To address this, we develop a theoretical model grounded in social perception theory and prior research on students’ experiences with AI-based tools. The model is tested using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) on data collected from 230 students who completed an academic writing task. The findings reveal that students’ agent-related social perceptions—particularly perceived competence and human-like empathy—are positively connected to the credibility students attribute to its feedback. In turn, perceived feedback credibility is interestingly related to students’ perceived learning in the context of academic writing. Furthermore, the positive link between credibility and perceived learning is weaker among students with higher grade-based reward sensitivity. This research contributes to the educational technology literature by advancing understanding of how students evaluate the credibility of ChatGPT-generated feedback and how such evaluations are associated with learning perceptions. It also shows that agent-related social perceptions play a significant role in students’ credibility judgements. Finally, the findings offer practical implications for educators and students seeking to integrate ChatGPT effectively into academic activities.

papers.title: Short-term cardiovascular adaptations to Ramadan-associated time-restricted eating in healthy adolescents: a repeated-measures observational study
papers.authors: Samah Jalal Jabr, Dima Al-Karad, Khaled Moayad Alrefaai, Omar Amin Alsaleh Alatma, Ahmad Nabulsi
papers.abstract: Ramadan fasting represents a naturally occurring model of time-restricted eating associated with substantial changes in meal timing, hydration patterns, and circadian behaviour. Although cardiovascular responses to Ramadan fasting have been investigated extensively in adults, evidence regarding adolescents remains limited, particularly in populations exposed to low-resource and conflict-affected environments. This study aimed to characterize short-term cardiovascular adaptations during Ramadan fasting among healthy Syrian adolescents using a repeated within-subject design, including evaluation of conventional cardiovascular parameters and derived hemodynamic indices. A community-based repeated-measures observational study was conducted among 120 healthy adolescents (65 males and 55 females; mean age 18 years) attending a specialized secondary school in Daraa, Syria, during Ramadan 1447 AH (2026). Participants underwent standardized cardiovascular assessments during the first week of Ramadan (early fasting phase) and the third week of Ramadan (established fasting phase). Measurements included systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), resting heart rate (HR), rate pressure product (RPP), shock index (SI), body mass, body mass index (BMI), and self-reported fatigue-related symptoms. Within-participant changes were assessed using paired statistical analyses, with additional subgroup analyses according to sex and Suhoor consumption. Compared with the first week of Ramadan, the third week was associated with significant reductions in SBP (129 vs. 113 mmHg; mean difference − 17 mmHg; 95% CI − 20 to − 14; p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 1.17) and DBP (81 vs. 73 mmHg; mean difference − 8 mmHg; 95% CI − 11 to − 6; p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 0.65). Resting HR increased significantly (90 vs. 95 beats/min; mean difference + 5 beats/min; 95% CI 3 to 8; p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 0.45). Similarly, RPP decreased significantly, whereas SI increased during established fasting. No significant changes were observed in body mass, BMI, or overall fatigue-related symptom profiles. Sex-stratified analyses demonstrated comparable reductions in blood pressure between males and females, while the increase in HR was more pronounced among males. Participants who omitted Suhoor demonstrated greater reductions in SBP and DBP and a greater increase in HR compared with those who consumed the pre-dawn meal. Ramadan-associated time-restricted eating was associated with measurable short-term cardiovascular adaptations among healthy adolescents, characterized by reduced blood pressure, increased resting heart rate, and altered derived hemodynamic indices without concurrent changes in body mass, BMI, or subjective fatigue burden. By providing repeated within-person cardiovascular data from an understudied adolescent population in a conflict-affected setting, this study expands current understanding of physiological adaptation during Ramadan fasting. Further longitudinal studies incorporating dietary assessment, hydration measures, autonomic evaluation, and biochemical markers are required to clarify the mechanisms and long-term clinical implications of these responses.

papers.title: AI literacy and STEM education: emerging frontiers and research priorities
papers.authors: Jonas Hällström, Thomas K. F. Chiu, Meixia Ding, Milo Koretsky, Yeping Li
papers.abstract: Abstract This article examines the state of the art in AI literacy and STEM education and identifies emerging frontiers and research priorities to inspire cutting-edge empirical and theoretical research. The reviewed research is grounded in established AI literacy frameworks and shows that there is potential for students’ development of a critical and technologically informed AI literacy. However, the research is unevenly spread across the STEM disciplines and the potential for AI to transform STEM learning remains unclear. Thus, while the field has expanded rapidly, particularly with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI), fundamental challenges remain. The conceptual ambiguity surrounding AI literacy, combined with the rapid evolution of AI technologies, demands continued theoretical refinement and empirical investigation. Critical questions remain regarding how AI literacy intersects with disciplinary STEM literacies, how GenAI tools both support and reshape teaching and learning processes, and what opportunities and trade-offs arise when students engage with AI as learning partner. The ethical dilemmas of AI integration, including bias, data privacy, and environmental sustainability, also warrant urgent attention. As STEM education increasingly engages with AI as both a subject of learning and a learning tool, future research must move beyond one-size-fits-all frameworks toward context-sensitive approaches that empower educators and learners to critically and responsibly engage with AI while preserving core STEM learning goals. This article highlights key research frontiers and priorities for advancing scholarship at the intersection of AI literacy and STEM education.

papers.title: An analytical and machine learning approach to evaluating economic impacts of digital transformation
papers.authors: Munir Majdalawieh, S. Sheeja Rani, Maher Alaraj
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has become a significant driver of economic and social development in the twenty-first century, producing both positive and negative economic repercussions. It involves the strategic integration of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, and the Internet of Things (IoT), across business, government, and societal functions to transform operations, enhance value creation, improve adaptability, and support long-term sustainability. This study examines the relationship between digital transformation, AI-driven technological development, economic repercussions, and technology-bubble dynamics. Key findings: AI and digital transformation have emerged as important concerns for economists, policymakers, and technology-driven organizations. Generative AI is increasingly evolving from an emerging technology into a strategic tool for decision-making, while effective data strategies have become central to successful digital transformation. In developing economies, digital transformation provides opportunities to address developmental barriers, industrialization challenges, poverty, educational inequalities, and limited healthcare access. However, the shortage of skilled professionals capable of implementing and managing advanced technologies remains a significant challenge. Methods: This study reviews and comparatively analyses machine learning, deep learning, and advanced analytical methods used to evaluate economic repercussions associated with digital transformation. The analysis considers computational cost, time complexity, efficiency, economic outcomes, investment behaviour, and technology-related risks. Particular attention is given to the evolution of technology bubbles, including Tech Bubble 1.0 (Dot-Com), Tech Bubble 2.0 (Post-2008/COVID-19), and Tech Bubble 3.0 (AI and emerging technologies). Conclusion: Digital transformation is not a one-time technological initiative but a continuous process of organizational and economic adaptation. The study identifies major developments, methodological trends, economic implications, opportunities, challenges, and potential technology-bubble risks, providing insights into sustainable digital transformation and future AI-driven economic development.

papers.title: Latent profiles of academic stress and exercise motivation among college students: A latent profile analysis
papers.authors: Pukui Wang, Zihao Li, Wang Xiangyu, Gao Xiang
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the latent profile structure of academic stress and exercise motivation among Chinese college students and to examine the predictive effects of demographic variables, including gender, body mass index (BMI), grade, and household registration background, on profile membership. From May 14 to June 3, 2025, convenience cluster sampling was employed to recruit 1,346 first- to third-year undergraduate students. The participants completed the Academic Sub-Scale and the Chinese-translated Behavioral Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire-2. Latent profile analysis was performed using Mplus 8.3 to identify distinct combined patterns of academic stress and exercise motivation, and the R3STEP method was applied to test the predictive utility of demographic variables on profile assignment. Four latent profiles were identified as the best-fitting solution. Profile 1, the High stress-low motivation profile (9.0%), was characterized by elevated academic stress and low scores across all exercise motivation dimensions. Profile 2, the High stress-high motivation profile (7.4%), exhibited the highest academic stress and the highest levels of external, introjected, and identified regulation. Profile 3, the Low stress-high autonomy profile (22.1%), demonstrated the lowest academic stress and the highest intrinsic motivation. Profile 4, the Moderate-balanced adaptation profile (61.6%), was marked by moderate scores on all variables and represented the most prevalent pattern. Students with normal weight showed a significantly stronger probability association with the High stress–high motivation profile, the Low stress–high autonomy profile, and the Moderate-balanced adaptation profile compared to their overweight and obese counterparts. Female students and third-year students demonstrated a lower probability of belonging to the High stress–low motivation profile. Rural students exhibited a stronger probability association with the Low stress–high autonomy profile, whereas urban students showed a stronger probability association with the Moderate-balanced adaptation profile. Four heterogeneous combined patterns of academic stress and exercise motivation exist among Chinese college students. Normal weight, female gender, higher grade level, and rural background were positively associated with autonomous exercise motivation and may have a potential protective role in the present sample. These findings provide empirical support for the application of self-determination theory and the strength model of self-control in the context of academic stress and offer targeted references for the implementation of differentiated mental health and physical exercise interventions in higher education settings. However, due to the sampling limitations of this study, caution is warranted when extrapolating the present conclusions to the entire population of Chinese college students.

papers.title: Multimodal neuroimaging of cue-induced craving and cortical alterations in etomidate use disorder
papers.authors: Junwei Zheng, Taoyu Wu, Jingli Yue, Mingming Zhang, Wangyue Liu, Yuchen Huang, Shenghong Zhao, Tianye Jia, 鲍彦平, Lin Lü, Sizhi Ai, Yan Sun, Jie Shi
papers.abstract: Despite the escalating global abuse of etomidate, a GABA A -specific anesthetic, the neurobiological mechanisms underlying craving and structural brain alterations remain poorly understood. This case-control study aimed to identify the neural characteristics of cue-induced craving and cortical brain changes in etomidate use disorder (EUD).
