Right-hand males aged 18–45 years meeting DSM-5 criteria for EUD and age-matched healthy males for controls (HC) were recruited in Guangzhou, China, between June 2023 and October 2024. Within a cue-reactivity paradigm, spatiotemporal neural dynamics of drug craving were investigated using multimodal neuroimaging, including electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in independent cohorts. Effective connectivity was analyzed with dynamic causal modeling (DCM), and structural MRI (sMRI) was further employed to assess cortical thickness. EEG analyses demonstrated amplified frontocentral late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes in response to drug cues in the EUD group, which correlated with subjective craving. FMRI analyses revealed cue-induced hyperactivation in the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC). Signed cue-modulated DCM parameters indicated abnormal VLPFC-to-TPJ inhibitory modulation in the EUD group, with weaker inhibitory modulation associated with higher subjective craving. Furthermore, sMRI identified widespread cortical thinning across prefrontal, parietal, occipitotemporal, and limbic regions among EUD individuals. These findings suggest that chronic etomidate exposure is associated with altered VLPFC function, maladaptive top-down inhibition within the VLPFC-TPJ connectivity, and heightened salience attribution to drug cues. These findings highlight the VLPFC-TPJ circuit as a promising neuromodulation target for treating EUD, underscoring its clinical potential in addressing this growing public health issue.

papers.title: Scenario-based artificial intelligence education and professional identity in nursing students: a qualitative futures study
papers.authors: Gönül Bodur, Piril Panayir Bohur
papers.abstract: To explore nursing students’ future-oriented perceptions of professional identity and autonomy in AI-mediated nursing futures through structured scenario-based foresight, with SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats) incorporated as a framework for developing alternative 2050 scenarios. Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming healthcare systems and nursing practice. Preparing future nurses requires not only technological literacy but also the development of ethical reasoning, professional identity, and autonomous decision-making in AI-mediated environments. Qualitative descriptive study using scenario-based foresight methodology. The study was conducted with undergraduate nursing students enrolled in an AI elective course. Students developed individual written scenarios envisioning nursing and healthcare in 2050 using a structured scenario development form supported by SWOT prompts. Fourteen students voluntarily participated. Scenario narratives were analysed using thematic analysis, and the resulting themes and subthemes were subsequently classified under the four predefined SWOT dimensions. Students articulated a dual trajectory regarding AI integration in nursing. On one hand, AI was associated with risks such as algorithmic dominance, ambiguity in professional accountability, and the potential weakening of relational care. On the other hand, students envisioned opportunities for strengthened professional agency through expanded roles including ethical stewardship, digital advocacy, and decision-support partnership. Across scenarios, autonomy and human-centred care emerged as central values guiding students’ evaluations of AI in nursing. Scenario-based AI education may support nursing students’ critical reflection on professional identity and autonomy. Educational approaches that integrate foresight activities with ethical and professional discussions may better prepare future nurses to navigate AI-mediated healthcare environments.

papers.title: Development and validation of the AI literacy questionnaire for health professions students using Rasch analysis
papers.authors: Yue Li, Qin Ye, Wei Qin, Ning Liu
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and creating new competency requirements for health professionals. However, assessment instruments tailored to this population remain limited, and item-level measurement evidence is scarce. This study aimed to develop and validate an AI literacy scale (AILS) for health professions students using an integrated theoretical framework. The item pool was informed by UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Students, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge model, the Kirkpatrick evaluation model, a literature review, and qualitative interviews. Items were refined through Delphi method, content validation, and pilot testing. Data were collected from 473 students. The sample was divided into two subsamples for exploratory factor analysis ( n = 241) and confirmatory factor analysis with Rasch rating scale analysis ( n = 232). The final 33-item AILS comprised four dimensions: Technical Understanding, Ethical Awareness, Practical Ability, and Social Impact. The four-factor solution explained 63.676% of the total variance. The total scale demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.979), and CFA showed acceptable model fit (χ²/df = 2.175, IFI = 0.917, TLI = 0.908, CFI = 0.916, and RMSEA = 0.071). In the Rasch analysis, person and item reliabilities were 0.96 and 0.95, respectively. The person–item map showed that the mean person measure was 1.66 logits above the mean item difficulty of 0.00 logits, indicating limited upper-end targeting. This mismatch may reflect insufficiently difficult items, sample characteristics, previous AI experience, limited curricular emphasis on advanced competencies, or a combination of these factors. The AILS demonstrated evidence of validity and reliability for assessing AI literacy among health professions students. The combined use of factor analysis and Rasch measurement illustrates the potential value of Rasch analysis for evaluating item functioning and person–item targeting. The current scale appears better suited to group-level assessment of foundational and intermediate AI literacy than to distinguishing advanced competence. Further research should develop more challenging items and validate the AILS in independent, multicentre samples. Application in other professional education domains would require discipline-specific adaptation and validation.

papers.title: Association between self-efficacy and AI dependence among medical postgraduates: a multicenter cross-sectional study with exploratory prediction
papers.authors: Meng-Pan Li, Meng-Jian Ren, Jiang-Peng Wu, Zhaohui Li, Tong-Tong Liu, Hao-Ran Chen, Heng-Yi Guo, Wencai Liu, Yafei Jiang, Ling-Feng Yu, Xiao-Jun Ma
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in postgraduate medical education and research, but the relationship between self-efficacy and dependence-like reliance on AI remains insufficiently characterized. We examined the association between continuous self-efficacy and AI-dependence scores and separately explored prediction of sample-relative higher AI-dependence scores. This multicenter cross-sectional online survey included 1,546 valid questionnaires from medical postgraduates at six participating Chinese universities between January and March 2026. Self-efficacy was assessed using a five-item study-specific academic measure, and AI dependence was assessed using a direct Chinese translation of the 22-item Artificial Intelligence Addiction Scale for Researchers. Analyses used multivariable linear regression with HC3 standard errors, restricted cubic splines, model diagnostics, and item-overlap sensitivity analyses. Exploratory prediction used the sample median score of 70 as a non-diagnostic boundary and a fixed 70:30 training/test split for internal validation. Among 1,546 participants, 938 (60.7%) were women and 579 (37.5%) studied clinical medicine. In the primary adjusted model, each 5-point higher self-efficacy score was associated with a 5.296-point lower AI-dependence score (95% CI, -5.918 to -4.674; P < 0.001). Restricted cubic splines supported the overall association (chi-square = 287.10; df = 3; P < 0.001) and modest nonlinearity (chi-square = 8.79; df = 2; P = 0.012). After removal of clearly overlapping items from both instruments, the Model 3 estimate changed by 2.1% (beta = -5.187; 95% CI, -5.800 to -4.575). The exploratory model achieved an AUC of 0.875 (95% CI, 0.845–0.906) in the held-out internal test set. Higher self-efficacy was inversely associated with continuous AI-dependence scores among medical postgraduates. These findings suggest that AI-literacy education may need to support autonomous task engagement and critical verification of AI outputs, but the cross-sectional design precludes causal interpretation. The exploratory prediction analysis was internally validated only, used a sample-relative boundary, and requires independent validation before practical use.

papers.title: From chatbots to chairside: how artificial intelligence understands molar incisor hypomineralization in pediatric dentistry
papers.authors: Esra Düzyol, Semanur Özüdoğru
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, yet their utility in pediatric dentistry remains unclear. This study evaluated and compared the clinical quality, readability, and specificity of responses generated by four contemporary LLMs to questions regarding Molar Incisor Hypomineralization (MIH) from dentists and parents. A standardized set of 50 open-ended and true/false MIH questions was administered to ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and DeepSeek-V3.1. Two independent pediatric dentists evaluated response quality using the Modified Global Quality Scale (MGQS), and the mean score served as the primary outcome. Readability was assessed using the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES) and the Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). Data were analyzed using a repeated-measures design: MGQS scores were compared via the Friedman test, and readability metrics were compared using repeated-measures ANOVA or the Friedman test based on normality (Shapiro–Wilk test); multiple comparisons were evaluated using the Bonferroni-corrected Conover test. Inter-rater agreement across all 200 responses was determined using unweighted Cohen’s kappa (κ = 0.662; 95% CI, 0.565–0.758). Significant differences in MGQS scores persisted among the models for open-ended questions directed to both parents (Friedman χ²(3) = 32.52, p < 0.001) and pediatric dentists (χ²(3) = 18.03, p < 0.001); DeepSeek-V3.1 scored significantly higher than the other three models in both subgroups (Bonferroni-corrected Conover test, all p < 0.05), while ChatGPT-5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and ChatGPT-4o did not differ significantly from one another in most pairwise comparisons. No significant differences were found for true/false questions (both subgroups p > 0.10). Readability differed significantly among models in every subgroup: Gemini 2.0 Flash and DeepSeek-V3.1 generally produced more accessible content (higher FRES, lower FKGL) than ChatGPT-5 and ChatGPT-4o, although the least-readable model varied by subgroup rather than being uniformly attributable to a single model. DeepSeek-V3.1 demonstrates a clear clinical quality advantage for open-ended queries in pediatric dentistry, while Gemini 2.0 Flash and DeepSeek-V3.1 provide more readable text overall. LLMs exhibit heterogeneous, subgroup-dependent performance and should be used with caution as adjunctive tools in MIH-related education and clinical care. Readability profiles should not be broadly generalized across different question formats.

papers.title: Performance of LLM-based systems in a national dental specialty examination: a multi-system benchmark study
papers.authors: İdris Onur YALÇIN, Gizem Yüksel, Cemre ÇELİK YALÇIN, Oğuz Tavşan
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated in healthcare and medical education, particularly for examination-based tasks. However, their performance in dental specialty examinations and across languages remains uncertain. This study compared response accuracy across LLM-based systems using Turkish and researcher-translated English versions of a retrospectively assembled DUS-sourced question set in Türkiye. A retrospective DUS-sourced item set was assembled across nine examination administrations (2020–2025). Question texts were obtained from archived booklets and commercial preparatory compilations; final answers and cancellation status were verified against ÖSYM materials. After exclusion of 17 image-dependent and 3 officially cancelled questions, 1,060 source questions were retained. Six LLM-based systems were evaluated: ChatGPT, ChatGPT Pro (Pro-tier access condition), ChatGPT Dentistry (third-party custom GPT), DeepSeek, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini. Each system was evaluated in both Turkish and English, yielding 12,720 system–question–language responses. Binary response accuracy was analysed using generalised estimating equations with source-question clustering to account for repeated evaluations of the same questions. System × language, system × discipline, and system × question-format interactions were evaluated, together with the overall effect of examination period; Holm adjustment was applied to relevant pairwise comparisons. Overall accuracy ranged from 31.5% for Copilot to 71.7% for ChatGPT Dentistry. The system × language interaction was significant (Wald χ²(5) = 158.73, p < 0.001), indicating system-dependent language effects. Accuracy was lower in Clinical Sciences than in Basic Sciences across all systems, with a significant system × discipline interaction (Wald χ²(5) = 101.06, p < 0.001). Combination-type multiple-choice questions were associated with lower odds of a correct response than standard multiple-choice questions (odds ratio = 0.79, 95% confidence interval 0.67–0.94, p = 0.008), whereas the system × question-format interaction was not significant ( p = 0.307). Accuracy also varied across examination periods ( p < 0.001) without a consistent temporal trend. This study provides an examination-specific benchmark of LLM answer-selection accuracy in DUS, with performance varying across systems, languages, disciplinary domains, and question formats. It does not provide evidence that LLM use improves learning outcomes or establishes clinical competence or patient safety.

papers.title: A leakage-controlled multimodal model integrating 18F-FDG PET/CT radiomics, deep-learning features, metabolic parameters and haematological inflammation–nutrition indices for preoperative prediction of axillary lymph-node metastasis in invasive breast cancer
papers.authors: 赫 聂, Huarui Tan, Zhen Cao, Xiaozheng Cao
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The status of the axillary lymph nodes (ALN) guides staging and the extent of axillary surgery in invasive breast cancer, yet confirmation still depends on sentinel lymph-node biopsy or axillary dissection. This exploratory study developed and internally evaluated, by cross-validation, a model combining five complementary streams of information available at staging ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT radiomics, deep-learning (DL) imaging features, volumetric metabolic parameters, routine clinicopathological variables and blood-count-derived inflammation–nutrition indices) within a machine-learning pipeline designed to avoid information leakage. Methods Sixty-three women with histologically confirmed invasive breast carcinoma who underwent baseline 18 F-FDG PET/CT at a single centre were analysed retrospectively (42 node-positive, 21 node-negative); 40 (63%) subsequently received neoadjuvant systemic therapy. Features were extracted from the tumour volume delineated on co-registered PET and CT: 2,167 IBSI-compliant radiomics features, 12,288 ResNet-50 transfer-learning features, 11 volumetric metabolic parameters, 7 clinicopathological variables and 7 inflammation–nutrition indices. Median imputation, variance filtering, standardisation, univariate AUC screening, collinearity pruning and LASSO selection were fitted only within the training folds of repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation (10 repeats). Five single-block models and three fusion strategies (stacking, feature concatenation and a parameter-free probability mean) were compared across four base learners, and the complete choice of block, fusion strategy, learner and decision threshold was repeated inside a nested cross-validation. Uncertainty was estimated by patient-level bootstrap, models were compared by paired bootstrap, and calibration, decision curves, the incremental value of imaging over clinicopathological variables, the handling of missing data and robustness to contour perturbation were assessed. Results The nested cross-validated AUC of the whole modelling procedure was 0.711 (95% CI 0.609–0.805). The probability-mean fusion, the most frequently selected strategy, reached 0.795 (0.678–0.891) on the same splits, indicating a model-selection optimism of about 0.08; its sensitivity and specificity at training-fold thresholds were 0.80 and 0.60, and calibration was imperfect (slope 1.53). Single-block AUCs ranged from 0.590 (inflammation–nutrition; 95% CI including 0.5) to 0.750 (DL). Adding PET/CT-derived information to the clinicopathological variables (AUC 0.681, 0.544–0.805) increased the AUC by 0.107 (− 0.023 to 0.247; P = 0.12), and net benefit exceeded that of a treat-all strategy only at threshold probabilities of about 0.4 or higher. Discrimination was poor in patients who received neoadjuvant therapy (nested AUC 0.561). Under a stringent one-voxel contour perturbation, 23% of radiomics features had an intraclass correlation coefficient of at least 0.75, and restricting the radiomics block to these features did not reduce performance. Conclusions In this small single-centre retrospective cohort, combining PET/CT-derived and routinely available clinical information under leakage-controlled, nested cross-validation gave moderate discrimination of axillary nodal status, with imperfect calibration and no statistically demonstrable incremental value of imaging over clinicopathological variables. The work should be regarded as a proof-of-concept framework; prospective multicentre external validation, including comparison with routine PET/CT axillary assessment, is required before any clinical application.

papers.title: Feeling of loneliness and determinants of health as correlates of cardiometabolic syndrome: a population-based US study
papers.authors: Saja Hamad, Abdelrahman Shehadeh, Hani Tamim, Marwan Refaat, Miran A. Jaffa
papers.abstract: Loneliness is an emerging social health factor that has been linked to cardiovascular outcomes and early mortality. Cardiometabolic syndrome is characterized by a combination of metabolic disturbances, including impaired glucose regulation alongside abdominal obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, and is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. While prior research has linked loneliness to individual CMS components, some studies have also examined its association with metabolic syndrome as a cluster; however, this association has not been extensively examined in large, weighted samples of U.S. adults spanning a wide age range. Moreover, the biological, social, and behavioral factors associated with both loneliness and CMS have not been examined together. Therefore, this study investigated whether loneliness is associated with CMS, while examining biological, social, and behavioral factors associated with both conditions. We conducted a secondary analysis of 160,223 adults across 24 U.S. states using data from the 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). The main exposure was self-reported loneliness, and the outcome was cardiometabolic syndrome (CMS), operationally defined in our study as the presence of self-reported type 2 diabetes plus at least two of the following: hypertension, obesity (BMI ≥ 30.0 kg/m²), or self-reported high cholesterol, based on the available BRFSS data. Additional predictors included biological, social, and behavioral factors. Survey-weighted chi-square tests and survey-weighted logistic regression models were used to examine associations between loneliness, CMS, and other study variables. An additional analysis examined the association between loneliness and CMS after adjustment for depression. Among respondents, 7.55% ( n = 14,362) had CMS and 3.02% ( n = 2,725) reported always feeling lonely. In the fully adjusted model ( N = 84,939), always feeling lonely was associated with higher odds of CMS (aOR = 1.61, 95% CI: 1.09–2.36; p = 0.015). Male sex, older age, Black race, lower education and income, former smoking, and physical inactivity were also associated with higher odds of CMS. Adjustment for depression attenuated the loneliness-CMS association, which remained significant when income was excluded ( N = 100,238 ); (aOR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.03–2.01; p = 0.031), but not in the fully adjusted model ( N = 84,659); (aOR = 1.41, 95% CI: 0.96–2.07; p = 0.079). Loneliness was associated with cardiometabolic syndrome, although the association was attenuated after accounting for depression, suggesting potential overlap among psychosocial factors. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporality and determine whether addressing loneliness may influence cardiometabolic health.

papers.title: Feasibility of intraoperative resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy for assessing the effects of propofol anesthesia on frontal cortical activity and network organization
papers.authors: 曹乃晗, Xinlong Cui, Li Zhao, Yi Liu, Jie Xiang
papers.abstract: The neurological mechanisms of general anesthesia have been studied extensively using electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The current study evaluated the feasibility of using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to evaluate the effects of propofol-based general anesthesia on frontal cortical activity and functional connectivity (FC) during surgery. Seventy-eight patients scheduled for elective colorectal cancer resection were recruited. Frontal fNIRS signals were recorded before anesthesia and during stable anesthesia following resection. Analyses focused on changes in fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (fALFF), resting-state (rs) FC, and graph theory network metrics. Significant reductions in frontal fALFF, rsFC, and Eg (global efficiency of the frontal network) were detected during anesthesia, particularly among components of the executive control and dorsal attention networks. Characteristic path length (Lp) was longer during anesthesia. The small-world metrics sigma and gamma were also weaker during anesthesia, but network small-world properties (σ > 1) were preserved. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy can detect hemodynamic correlates of anesthesia-associated changes in cortical activity and network organization, providing indirect signatures of altered cortical states and providing evidence for the future development of complementary intraoperative monitoring approaches and investigation of anesthesia-related cortical mechanisms. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, identifier: ChiCTR2200063584, Date: 12/9/2022.

papers.title: Beyond the Finish Line: Value Co-Creation and Value Co-Destruction in City Marathons From a Spectator Perspective
papers.authors: Ruowei Zhang, Shuhua Zhou
papers.abstract: City marathons are often positioned as tools for urban branding and socioeconomic development, yet their value is negotiated through stakeholder experiences. This study investigates the 2025 Wuhan Marathon as a communication ecosystem where value co-creation and value co-destruction coexist. Drawing upon value co-creation, value co-destruction, and sport event research, this study examines how spectators’ event-related engagement and perceived disruptions are associated with event satisfaction, perceived city image, and perceived socioeconomic impact. Survey data from 431 spectators were analyzed using regression-based moderated mediation models. Results showed that value co-creation was positively associated with event satisfaction and indirectly with more favorable evaluations of Wuhan’s city image and the marathon’s socioeconomic impact. In contrast, value co-destruction was negatively associated with event satisfaction and indirectly with less favorable urban evaluations. Spectator identity did not significantly moderate these indirect associations. The findings position spectators as interpretive actors whose event-level experiences were associated with how favorably they appraised the very claims — city image, social value, economic worth — that anchor official accounts of marathon success.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Continuous Glucose Monitoring in Non-Intensively Managed Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
papers.authors: Ayman Al Hayek, Wael M. Al Zahrani, Haifa F. Alotaibi, Manal El Jammal, Mohammed A. Al Dawish
papers.journal: Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Background: The effectiveness of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) not receiving intensive insulin therapy remains incompletely established, particularly regarding glycemic metrics beyond glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating real-time CGM (rtCGM) or intermittently scanned CGM (isCGM) in adults with T2D managed with non-intensive insulin regimens or non-insulin therapies. Databases were searched from inception to February 2026. Primary outcomes included HbA1c, mean glucose concentration, time in range (%TIR), time above range (%TAR), time below range (%TBR), body mass index (BMI), and patient-reported outcomes. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using Stata 17. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias tool, version 2, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Results: Twenty-five RCTs were included. Continuous glucose monitoring significantly reduced HbA1c (mean difference [MD] −0.34, 95% confidence interval [CI], −0.46 to −0.23), mean glucose concentration (MD −13.97 mg/dL, 95% CI, −23.13 to −4.81), and %TAR (MD −6.75%, 95% CI, −10.81 to −2.70), while significantly increasing %TIR (MD +7.85%, 95% CI, 4.32-11.38). No significant effects were observed for BMI (MD −0.16 kg/m 2 , 95% CI, −0.45 to 0.12) or %TBR (MD −0.11%, 95% CI, −0.31 to 0.08). Benefits were generally more pronounced in non-insulin-treated populations. Patient-reported outcomes were heterogeneous but suggested improved treatment satisfaction and glucose-monitoring experience with CGM. Certainty of evidence was moderate across outcomes. Conclusions: Continuous glucose monitoring probably improves glycemic control in adults with T2D not receiving intensive insulin therapy, particularly by reducing hyperglycemia and improving TIR, with limited effects on hypoglycemia or body weight.

papers.title: Corpus-Based Modeling of Second Language Acquisition Trajectories: A Multidimensional Analysis of English Grammar Development Among Chinese Learners
papers.authors: Xin Yin
papers.abstract: In the context of the growing global demand for English learning, it is crucial to understand the systematic patterns of grammar acquisition by Chinese learners. Traditional cross-sectional studies and teaching methods, focused on static rules, fail to capture the dynamic, nonlinear trajectories of development and the profound influence of first language (L1) typology. This study addresses these gaps by integrating Dynamic Systems Theory with machine learning algorithms to model the developmental pathways of three core grammatical domains: articles, prepositions, and verb collocations in Chinese learners of English. Utilizing a multi-source longitudinal corpus and applying mixed-effects models alongside random forests, we uncover stage-specific transitions, demonstrate how L1 typology differentially shapes the acquisition of grammatical structures, and establish a hierarchy of difficulty among grammatical items. Methodologically, this research introduces a novel analytical framework that effectively captures the heterogeneity and nonlinearity inherent in L2 grammatical development. Theoretically, it provides empirical evidence for the nuanced role of L1 typological transfer in shaping developmental trajectories. These findings offer a scientific basis for stratified pedagogy and the design of adaptive learning systems tailored to learners’ developmental stages and L1 backgrounds.

papers.title: Integrating Cultural and Family Resilience Into Health Promotion Programs With Black Families
papers.authors: Mary J. Quattlebaum, Timothy Simmons, Dawn K. Wilson, Pamela Davis Martin
papers.abstract: Growing evidence shows that cultural and family resilience resources may serve as a protective buffer of the deleterious impacts of racial stress on psychosocial and health-related outcomes among Black adolescents. Thus, we sought feedback from Black adolescents and parents on their use of resilience resources to cope with stress. Specifically, Black facilitators conducted qualitative in-depth interviews with 16 Black adolescents and parents (adolescents: ~63% male, M age = 15 ± 2.45, M BMI percentile 97.0 ± 3.31; parents: 100% female, M age = 49.19 ± 9.19, M BMI = 39.76 ± 6.84) to assess their experience with cultural and family resilience and to gather recommendations for integrating these resources into future resilience-based health promotion trials. Findings showed that families endorsed leaning on the core resilience resources of racial socialization (egalitarianism, preparation for racial bias, racial coping, cultural pride), racial identity (positive affirmations, Black history), cultural assets (spirituality, kinship, traditions around food), and family resilience (family meals, family bonding) to cope with stress. Families provided insightful recommendations of culturally relevant curriculum to integrate into future trials, including engaging in discussions and activities focused on family traditions and values of managing stress, racial coping skills, positive affirmations about Black identity, leaning on social support, and preparing for experiences of racial bias. Findings highlighted the value of core resilience resources as a critical buffer to stress among families. Participant insights guided the curriculum development for future resilience-based health promotion programs with Black families.

papers.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Language Models on Critical Thinking in Theoretical and Practical Aspects of Learning among Undergraduate Nursing Students: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Erandima Sandamali, W.H.M.S. Samarathunga
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) language models are increasingly used in higher education. Many students use them for learning, often without proper academic policies or guidelines. Nursing undergraduate curricula include both theoretical and practical aspects of learning, in which critical thinking is essential, especially for clinical decision-making. This review explores the effects of AI language models on the critical thinking skills of undergraduate nursing students. Sixty-seven articles published between 2020 and 2025 on AI in nursing, medicine, or higher education, and its impact on learning and cognition, were analyzed and synthesized. Findings revealed that AI language models offer benefits, limitations, and ethical concerns. Benefits include improved academic writing, rapid access to information, and support for self-directed learning. Limitations include overdependence, biased content, and reduced social learning. Ethical concerns include confidentiality and plagiarism. In nursing education, AI models affect critical thinking both positively and negatively, enhancing simulated clinical decision-making but potentially reducing independent analysis and interactions with real patients. Studies recommend developing guidelines, training, and balanced integration to maximize benefits while minimizing risks.

papers.title: Fostering Agile Mindsets in Management Education: A Systematic Literature Review of Agile Teaching Strategies and Their Implications for Educators
papers.authors: Alina Enge, Patrizia M. Ianiro Dahm
papers.abstract: Management education has increasingly adopted agile frameworks such as Design Thinking and Scrum, yet a growing distinction separates doing agile – teaching in an agile manner, the visible enactment of practices – from being agile , the underlying agile mindset. Recent psychometric work has established the agile mindset as a valid construct predicting workplace performance and innovative work behaviour. This raises the question of whether current teaching designs actually engage the mindset dimensions underlying agility. Drawing on 69 peer-reviewed studies published between 2012 and 2024, this systematic literature review uses the four-dimensional agile mindset construct (Learning Spirit, Collaborative Exchange, Empowered Self-Guidance, Customer Co-Creation) as an analytical grid to map which mindset dimensions teaching designs address, and which they leave aside. Findings show a strong emphasis on Design Thinking, while iterative approaches such as Scrum remain underutilised. Collaborative Exchange dominates the coded mechanisms across studies, whereas Customer Co-Creation is comparatively neglected. Critically, although many studies report student outcomes, these rarely concern change in the agile mindset dimensions, and none employ a validated multi-dimensional measure of the construct. We therefore frame our synthesis as evidence about reported alignment and pedagogical mechanisms, not verified mindset change, and derive implications for curriculum design and faculty support.

papers.title: Predicting the industry income of the top 20 universities worldwide based on key performance indicators using a machine learning approach
papers.authors: Yones Romiani, Maryam Sadat Ghoraishi Khorasgani
papers.abstract: In recent years, university-industry collaboration has emerged as a critical factor in the success of universities. This partnership can play a significant role in ensuring stability and securing additional resources for higher education. On the other hand, due to changes in the environment and the transformation of universities from third-generation to fourth-generation, their functions have also undergone change. Among these transformed functions, one of the most pivotal is industry income. In this context, the objective of this study is to forecast the indicators for industry income in the top 20 universities worldwide. This study draws upon the databases ( https://www.timeshighereducation.com ) and ( https://www.topuniversities.com ). Utilizing regression models, including Ridge, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and Elastic Net, as well as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), we have analyzed the indicators of industry income within the studied universities over the past 12 years (2011 to 2022). The results reveal that, among the regression models, the LASSO model excels in predicting industry income. The ANN model, boasting a higher coefficient of determination (R2) and lower values of Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), outperforms penalized (PR) and linear (Ordinary Least Squares) models considerably, showcasing greater accuracy in this context. Overall, the findings underscore that research indicators, international outlook, and financial sustainability possess a greater predictive capability for augmenting industry income in the top 20 universities worldwide. This study adds to the readers’ knowledge about the industry income of universities as well as the factors that can help in increasing this type of income. Universities can pay attention to the results obtained in this study in order to diversify their incomes and also to strengthen the university-industry collaboration.

papers.title: Tools versus rules: School leaders as protectors of collective professional capital under the shock of generative AI
papers.authors: Jess L. Gregory
papers.abstract: This qualitative study of 17 educational leader candidates interrogates how future administrators negotiate generative artificial intelligence's (GenAI) disruptive insertion into P-12 school activity systems. Framed by the integrated lenses of Professional Capital theory and Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), the research traces systemic contradictions between rapid algorithmic capabilities and lagging institutional rules, professional norms, and layered, entrenched divisions of labor. Data were generated via open-ended pre and postcourse surveys during a graduate leadership preparation course in summer 2025, intersecting with an acute macrohistorical shock: the public popularization of an MIT Media Lab preprint warning of GenAI causing student “cognitive debt.” Baseline findings reveal severe primary and secondary contradictions characterized by an acute fear of automated deprofessionalization, curriculum deskilling, and the depletion of teacher decisional capital under rigid district policies. However, post-intervention reflections indicate microlevel movements along an expansive learning cycle. When leadership preparation intentionally mobilizes social capital through collaborative theoretical reflection, candidates shift from defensive, rule-bound policy enforcement toward critical AI literacy. Ultimately, this article offers a conceptual framework for leadership preparation programs to buffer school ecosystems against external narrative panics, resolve institutional friction, and sustain human professional capital against automated erosion.

papers.title: Data-Driven Governance and Digital Learning Systems as Catalysts for Safeguarding Democracy in Africa
papers.authors: Philip Okposo
papers.abstract: Africa’s democratic systems are increasingly influenced by digital technologies, data infrastructures, social media, and artificial intelligence. These developments provide opportunities to improve electoral administration, evidence-based governance, civic education, and citizen engagement, while also creating risks related to misinformation, exclusion, surveillance, and declining public trust. This study examines how data analytics and Learning Management Systems (LMS) can work together to support electoral integrity and responsible citizenship without replacing established democratic institutions. The study adopts a documentary secondary-data research design, drawing on peer-reviewed studies and authoritative institutional evidence. Selected democratic, digital access, and electoral participation indicators are examined descriptively to identify key democratic pressures and their relationship to potential technological interventions. The findings indicate a significant gap between democratic aspirations and citizens’ experiences. Across 39 African countries, 66% of citizens express a preference for democracy, while 45% describe their countries as mostly or completely democratic and 37% report satisfaction with how democracy works. Although 75% support fair, open, and honest elections, only 39% report trust in their national electoral commission. Internet use in Africa reached 38% in 2024, highlighting both the potential reach and limitations of digital interventions. Electoral participation also varies considerably across selected countries. These findings do not establish a causal relationship between digital learning and electoral participation but demonstrate the importance of context-sensitive approaches. The study therefore proposes the Data-Driven Democratic Resilience Framework (DDDRF), comprising data acquisition, analytics and assurance, LMS-enabled civic learning, citizen feedback, and safeguards relating to privacy, transparency, accessibility, human oversight, and redress. The study contributes an information-systems perspective to research on African democracy by integrating data governance and civic learning within a common framework for strengthening democratic resilience.

papers.title: Fairness in the Eye of the Beholder: How Gender Bias Alignment Influences Fairness Perceptions and Reliance in Human–AI Teams
papers.authors: Domenique Zipperling, Luca Deck, Julia Lanzl, Niklas Kühl
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems
papers.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is increasingly relevant in consequential areas where AI recommendations support human discretion. However, human-AI teams’ effectiveness, capability, and fairness highly depend on human perceptions of AI. Positive fairness perceptions have been shown to foster trust and acceptance of AI recommendations. Yet, work on confirmation bias highlights that humans selectively adhere to AI recommendations that align with their expectations and beliefs—despite those recommendations not being necessarily correct or fair. This raises the question of whether confirmation bias also transfers to the alignment of gender bias between human and AI decisions. In our study, we examine how gender bias alignment and the presence of explanations accompanying the AI recommendation influence fairness perceptions, human self-confidence, and reliance on the AI system. Findings from two 2 \(\times\) 2 between-subjects studies underscore the relationship between gender-bias alignment, fairness perceptions, and reliance, demonstrating that merely constructing a “formally fair” AI system is insufficient for optimal human–AI collaboration. Ultimately, AI recommendations are likely to be overridden when the system's biases do not align with those of its users.

papers.title: Fostering Virtual Heritage Experiences for the Elderly: Design Considerations for Inclusive Digital Heritage
papers.authors: Stella Sylaiou, Angeliki Antoniou, Vasileios Arampatzakis, Panagiotis Dafiotis, Konstantinos E. Evangelidis, Kyriaki Kostoglou, Fotis Liarokapis, Theofilos G. Papadopoulos, George P. Pavlidis, Vasileios Sevetlidis
papers.journal: Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: This paper presents the results of a study which draws on a desk/ literature review, as well as on extended reality (XR)-related experiments with regard to fostering virtual heritage experiences for the elderly (FIREFLY project). Its main aim is to inform design considerations in relation to the adaptation of the XR applications’ user experience (UX) for the elderly. It ventures to achieve this goal, firstly, by reviewing (and revisiting) existing perceptions, methodologies and theoretical underpinnings that condition research on older users’ engagement with cultural heritage-related XR experiences. This study is moreover informed by experiment-based investigations on technology related issues that are seen as inextricably related to conceptual frameworks in this field. Thereby, this paper addresses methodological issues through applied research, mostly in two areas: identification of optimal XR UX features for elderly people, as well as optimization of data gathering methods, such as use of electroencephalography (EEG) experiment setups and emotion-related multimodal data collection for the evaluation of said XR applications’ effectiveness. This paper contributes towards a paradigm shift in perceptions of this demographic’s profiles, needs and strengths, as a fulcrum for more inclusive design approaches in digital heritage.

papers.title: Lightweight 3D Convolutional Networks for Biomechanical Motion Analysis in Martial Arts Training
papers.authors: Hongling Li, Zerong Mao
papers.journal: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
papers.abstract: To reduce the subjectivity of traditional martial arts training assessment and avoid the deployment requirements of wearable devices, the study develops an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted analysis system based on a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D CNN). This study adopts a 3D CNN as the backbone network and develops optimization strategies from four aspects. Spatiotemporal decomposition convolution factorizes standard 3D convolution kernels into a combination of spatial convolution and temporal convolution. The temporal attention mechanism adaptively computes the importance weight of each frame, enabling the model to focus on key action frames. A dynamic inference mechanism determines whether computation should be terminated early based on the confidence of intermediate-layer outputs, thereby reducing redundant computation. Knowledge distillation uses only the class-similarity soft distribution of a large teacher model to supervise the lightweight student model. This reduces the loss of feature representation caused by network compression and helps maintain recognition accuracy with fewer parameters. Experimental results are obtained on the Chain-of-Thought Action Form Assessment (CoT-AFA) and Martial Arts, Dancing and Sports Dataset (MADS) public datasets. The results show that the proposed method achieves a Top-1 accuracy of 74.2% on the CoT-AFA dataset, which is close to the 75.3% achieved by Video Swin Transformer. Meanwhile, the proposed method reduces the number of parameters by approximately 52.3% (14.2M vs. 29.8M) and decreases Floating Point Operations per Second by approximately 43.7% (52.4G vs. 93.0G). In addition, the mean squared error (MSE) for quality evaluation is reduced to 1.48. On the MADS dataset, the Top-1 accuracy reaches 68.9%, while the mean per-joint position error is reduced to 60.5 mm. The results support the use of the system for video-based analysis in martial arts training.

papers.title: Toward AI-Enabled Precision Exercise: Neurophysiological Effects of Acute Moderate-Intensity Resistance Exercise on Executive Function in College Students with Different Motor Skill Backgrounds
papers.authors: Dong Wang, Shu-Hui Lin, Bo-Siang Huang, Chun-San Chou
papers.journal: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and intelligent healthcare technologies, integrating neuroimaging with exercise interventions has emerged as a promising strategy for promoting cognitive health and precision medicine. This study investigated the immediate effects of acute moderate-intensity resistance exercise on executive function in college students with different motor skill backgrounds and explored the underlying neural mechanisms using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Furthermore, the multimodal behavioral and neurophysiological data generated in this study provide a valuable foundation for future AI-assisted cognitive assessment and precision exercise prescription. A total of 36 healthy male collegiate athletes were recruited and assigned to either an open-skill group (n = 18) or a closed-skill group (n = 18). Participants completed a 30-minute acute moderate-intensity resistance exercise session at 70% of their 10-repetition maximum (10RM). Executive function was assessed before and after exercise using the Stroop task, 2-back task, and More-odd shifting task to evaluate inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility, respectively. Simultaneously, changes in oxygenated hemoglobin (ΔHbO 2 ) within the prefrontal cortex were continuously recorded using fNIRS. Data were analyzed using paired-sample t-tests and two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance. The results demonstrated that acute moderate-intensity resistance exercise was associated with significant improvements in selected executive-function outcomes within both groups. In the open-skill group, reaction time decreased in the Stroop task, while accuracy increased and reaction time decreased in the 2-back task. In the closed-skill group, reaction time decreased in the 2-back task. Both groups showed improvements in selected outcomes of the More-odd shifting task. However, no significant Group × Time interactions were observed for any behavioral outcome, indicating that the magnitude of behavioral change did not differ significantly between groups. fNIRS findings revealed task- and channel-specific changes in prefrontal ΔHbO 2 following exercise. Moreover, significant Group × Time interactions in ΔHbO 2 were observed at selected prefrontal channels during the Stroop, 2-back, and More-odd shifting tasks, suggesting that motor skill background may be associated with different patterns of prefrontal hemodynamic response following acute exercise. In conclusion, acute moderate-intensity resistance exercise was followed by improvements in selected executive-function outcomes in young male collegiate athletes. The integration of behavioral assessments with fNIRS-derived neurophysiological data provides additional evidence regarding behavioral and prefrontal hemodynamic responses to acute resistance exercise. Although the behavioral changes did not differ significantly between groups, exploratory fNIRS findings indicated task- and channel-specific differences in ΔHbO 2 changes between the open-skill and closed-skill groups. Further studies incorporating a non-exercise control condition, larger and more diverse samples, and appropriate correction for multiple channel-level comparisons are needed to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Developing a generative AI chatbot to support students’ higher-order thinking in STEM education
papers.authors: Lindsey E. Richland, Shuyuan Yu, Banu Karyagdi, Hongyang Zhao, Shayan Doroudi, Joseph T. Wong, Ella Rose, Maryam Cheraghi, Katherine Trieste Rhodes
papers.journal: Journal of Microbiology and Biology Education
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Higher-order thinking is a key component of science, technology, engineering, mathematics (STEM) reasoning and supports students’ ability to reflect on their ideas, make connections, and generalize across contexts. We report a new approach to the use of generative AI in STEM education, in which we are developing a chatbot that aims to engage students in higher-order thinking, rather than giving instructional content. We describe a proof of concept test of whether interaction with our generative artificial intelligence chatbot could elicit students’ higher-order thinking talk (HOTT) in conversation as they reflected on their solutions to proportional reasoning problems. Thirty-three fifth- and sixth-grade students received a 30-min lesson on symbolic and number line strategies for comparing ratios and completed an assessment following the lesson. Students then engaged in dialog with the UCI Math ThinkBot (afterward Math ThinkBot ) to explain their solutions and compare strategies. These transcripts were examined qualitatively and quantitatively for HOTT, revealing that HOTT appeared in both chatbot prompts and children’s responses—which is important because eliciting student HOTT can be a challenge in classroom discourse. In addition, children’s HOTT was positively associated with the HOTT produced by the chatbot. These findings suggest that human-artificial intelligence dialog can lead to instructional HOTT discourse and may offer a promising approach for supporting higher-order thinking and STEM reasoning.

papers.title: “Tension Suspension” Remnant‐Preserving ACL Reconstruction Promotes the Early Maturity of the Graft Ligament
papers.authors: Jiamin Liang, 黃亙亘, Wenhan Yang, Junming Wei, Yingzhen Yang, Zirong Huang, Weimin Zhu
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: The clinical application of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) remnant preservation remains controversial, and conventional remnant-preserving techniques cannot fully maximize the biological potential of ACL remnants. To compare graft ligamentization, femoral tunnel enlargement, and clinical functional scores between "tension suspension" remnant-preserving anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and single-bundle anatomical ACLR. METHODS: Forty-eight patients enrolled from December 2021 to June 2023 were divided into non-preserving remnant (NPR, n = 18) and preserving remnant (PR, n = 30) groups. At 3 and 6 months postoperatively, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the knee was performed to measure graft signal noise quotient (SNQ) of the region of interest (ROI) and femoral tunnel diameter changes. Lysholm, IKDC, and Tegner scores were assessed at 6 months. Demographic and preoperative data were analyzed; intergroup comparisons of graft SNQ, femoral tunnel diameter changes, and clinical scores were conducted. Spearman correlation analysis evaluated the relationship between graft SNQ and knee function scores. RESULTS: No intergroup differences were noted in age, sex, BMI, or graft diameter. At 3 months, significant differences were observed in graft SNQ (most prominent at the distal end) and femoral tunnel diameter changes (p < 0.05). At 6 months, no significant differences were found in SNQ (except near-significant proximal SNQ, p = 0.058) or femoral tunnel diameter changes; clinical scores showed no intergroup differences. Tegner scores were moderately to significantly positively correlated with 6-month SNQ (< 0.05). CONCLUSION: "Tension suspension" remnant-preserving ACLR has significant advantages in early graft ligamentization and inhibiting femoral tunnel enlargement. Subjective knee function may be related to graft signal intensity.

papers.title: Using Robots in Nursing Care: An Explorative Study Into the Perspectives of Nurses and Hospital Managers
papers.authors: N. J. E. De Beer, N. Wiersma, Peter de Winter, Harmieke van Os‐Medendorp
papers.abstract: AIM: The growing mismatch between care demand and system capacity is driven by ageing and rising pressure on healthcare resources. As a result, the fundamentals of care are increasingly under strain. The use of robots is viewed as a possible solution. This study aimed to investigate the perspectives of nurses, policymakers, and managers regarding the use of robots in hospital settings and factors influencing their acceptance. DESIGN: Sequential explanatory mixed methods. METHODS: A cross-sectional questionnaire based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology was administered to 121 nurses in spring 2025 to identify attitudes, acceptance, and digital skills toward care robots. Findings from this phase informed the subsequent qualitative phase: in-depth exploration interviews with 4 nurses and 8 hospital staff members. RESULTS: Robots were seen as potentially useful in reducing workload and physical strain, but nurses stated that robots cannot replace human interaction in care. Facilitating conditions were perceived as supportive, and fear related to robot implementation was low. Drivers and barriers to robot implementation highlighted the importance of communication, nurses' involvement, and clear responsibilities during implementation. CONCLUSION: Nurses and hospital staff expressed a cautiously positive stance toward the utilisation of robots in the context of hospital nursing care. They are considering care robots as a potential solution to alleviate nurses' workload. However, there are concerns regarding the impact of robots on the fundamental responsibilities of nursing, particularly with regard to patient interaction, emotional support, and the potential loss of the human aspect of care. This requires nurses' awareness and ethical judgement. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND PATIENT CARE: Nurses are key when considering the implementation of robots, ensuring its alignment with the fundamentals of care and maintaining patient-centred values. Nurses' unique position allows them to voice patient needs; their involvement shapes the successful implementation of robotics in hospitals. NO PATIENT OR PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT: This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting. REPORTING METHOD: GRAMMS guidelines for Reporting Mixed Methods Research were used.

papers.title: Assessment of Dental Students' and Recent Graduates' Knowledge of Artificial Intelligence Applications in Dentistry
papers.authors: Tuğba Ayvacı, Burcu Kanmaz, Pınar Meriç
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming dentistry by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, clinical efficiency and personalized treatment planning. This study evaluates the awareness and perceptions of AI applications among dental students and recent graduates to support AI integration in dental education and practice. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This cross-sectional study included third, fourth and fifth-year students, along with dentists who graduated within the past 5 years. A total of 452 participants completed a 26-item online survey via Google Forms between July 1 and September 1, 2024. The survey comprised demographic data and AI awareness assessment. Data were analysed using SPSS (version 21, IBM, Chicago, USA), with reliability analyses and descriptive statistics conducted. Fisher-Freeman-Halton Exact Test was used for group comparisons (p < 0.05). RESULTS: Participants were evenly distributed by academic year, predominantly female and aged 20-30. No significant differences were found between educational levels and gender. Most participants acknowledged AI's transformative potential but did not view it as an immediate threat. Fourth-year students disagreed with 'I see AI as a partner, not a competitor' (p < 0.05). Similarly, recent graduates strongly opposed concerns regarding AI replacing dentists, while fourth-year students expressed higher agreement (p < 0.05). Most participants supported integrating AI education into undergraduate curricula. CONCLUSION: This study highlights dental students' and recent graduates' perceptions of AI in dentistry. While AI's potential is widely recognized, its presence in dental curricula remains limited. These findings emphasize the need for comprehensive educational programmes to facilitate AI integration in dental practice.

papers.title: RobotFuse: Real-Time Robot Pose and Joint Angle Estimation From a Single RGB-D Image
papers.authors: Nianfeng Wang, Yizhang Wu, Jingxin Lin, Kaixiang Zhang, Zhibin Lai, Xianmin Zhang

papers.title: The ongoing evolution of Airbnb
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to review the latest management developments across the globe and pinpoint practical implications from cutting-edge research and case studies. Design/methodology/approach This briefing is prepared by an independent writer who adds their own impartial comments and places the articles in context. Findings Though business model innovation (BMI), firms have become better positioned to broaden their horizons and engage in new or complementary activities. Exploiting network effects and enhancing efficiency are likewise essential, along with strong emphasis on trust, governance and compliance with regulations. Originality/value The briefing saves busy executives, strategists and researchers hours of reading time by selecting only the very best, most pertinent information and presenting it in a condensed and easy-to-digest format.

papers.title: Advancing multidimensional enterprise risk management with artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Yee Shuang Poa, Elaine Yen Nee Oon, Zarina Zakaria
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a conceptual framework designed to assist organizations in understanding and promoting the adoption of a multidimensional Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) enterprise risk management (ERM) that integrates artificial intelligence (AI). The proposed framework serves as a tool to improve organizational risk governance, stability, and resilience within an evolving digital landscape characterized by increasingly complex, rapidly changing, and interdependent risks. Design/methodology/approach This study creates a conceptual framework by expanding upon the conventional technology-organization-environment (TOE) model through theoretical integration and tailored ERM contextualization. The methodology includes an extensive review and synthesis of literature on COSO ERM, multidimensional risk perspectives, AI-driven risk management, and technology adoption frameworks. Findings This paper conceptually extends the TOE framework by maintaining its core dimensions while introducing two novel ERM-specific constructs: security and privacy (SnP) and organizational multidimensional risk–technology awareness (ORTA). It also reconceptualizes three existing TOE constructs to better align with COSO ERM realities: organizational compatibility is embedded within organizational readiness (ORD), top management support is operationalized as tone at the top (TtT), and cost is reframed as value for money (VfM). These additions and refinements enhance the explanatory power of the original TOE framework by demonstrating how both traditional and ERM-specific factors shape organizational perceptions of readiness, trust, and strategic alignment in a digital risk environment. Research limitations/implications The proposed framework improves our theoretical understanding of ERM transformation in the digital era by providing a more integrated explanation of how adoption decisions are shaped within complex governance environments. Unlike previous fragmented explanations of technology uptake, this framework demonstrates how interconnected determinants simultaneously influence ERM transformation, especially in AI-enabled settings. Practical implications From a managerial perspective, the framework offers a structured approach for evaluating adoption readiness and designing interventions that facilitate successful COSO ERM transformation. It allows risk leaders to systematically assess internal preparedness across key governance and capability dimensions, with a particular focus on the awareness of multidimensional risk, leadership commitment, and organizational trust in AI-enabled risk systems. Social implications This study has broader societal implications by promoting stronger organizational resilience and more effective risk governance in an increasingly complex and interconnected world. Adopting a multidimensional COSO ERM integrating AI can enhance an organization's ability to anticipate and respond to emerging risks, including financial, operational, cyber, and ESG-related challenges. Originality/value This study addresses an important gap in the literature by investigating the organizational adoption of a multidimensional COSO ERM integrating AI. The interplay between ERM-specific determinants, technological enablers, and managerial adoption intentions in this context remains largely unexplored. By expanding the TOE framework with novel and refined ERM-focused constructs (e.g. ORTA, ORD, VfM, TtT, and SnP), the proposed conceptual model offers a theoretically robust and practically applicable tool for understanding how organizations address strategic, cultural, and governance challenges in digitalized risk management.

papers.title: Automating the understaffed library: a framework for low-code workflow automation in colleges of education libraries
papers.authors: Ronald Andoh-Kwaw, Martha Baidoo, Franklin Gyamfi Agyemang
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address the problem of chronically understaffed academic libraries, using Ghanaian Colleges of Education as the case, and develops a practical framework for using low-code and no-code workflow automation to lift routine work without new hires. Design/methodology/approach The framework is developed through a conceptual synthesis of the general automation, library-practice and African library-technology literatures, adapted to the resource-constrained College of Education setting. Findings The paper sets out a four-stage framework – identify suitable workflows, select a tool, build along a maturity model, and govern the result – supported by a task taxonomy, an impact-and-effort prioritisation method, a tool-selection guide, a maturity model, and explicit boundary conditions for when not to automate. Originality/value Existing work is either not about libraries, code-heavy, tied to costly subscription platforms, or frames automation as expensive artificial intelligence. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first framework to treat low-code workflow automation as a deliberate, affordable strategy for the understaffed, resource-constrained academic library, built on self-hostable tools and within reach of a single capable librarian.

papers.title: AI in education: boosting productivity or challenging cognitive effort?
papers.authors: Lucia Šatková, Paula Puškárovà
papers.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. Findings Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. Research limitations/implications The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity. Practical implications The results provide actionable guidance for universities seeking to integrate AI into teaching and assessment practices. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. Given that daily users show higher critical evaluation but lower perceived accuracy, teaching practices should incorporate reflective assignments that require students to justify, critique and revise AI-generated content. Assessment formats may need redesign to ensure transparent AI use while still requiring independent reasoning, analytical justification and domain-specific understanding. Social implications Policies should balance the productivity benefits of AI-supported learning with safeguards that promote independent thinking, academic integrity and equitable access. Addressing disparities in AI literacy and access is essential to prevent the widening of the existing academic inequalities. Originality/value This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-assisted learning by examining students’ perceived productivity gains alongside several concurrent dimensions of their AI-supported academic experience, including time efficiency, perceived academic performance, academic self-efficacy, changes in cognitive effort and AI dependency. Rather than proposing these dimensions as new constructs or causal mechanisms, this study brings them together within a single analytical framework. Particular attention is given to whether perceived productivity gains and growing reliance on AI coexist with self-reported changes in cognitive effort, an interplay that remains insufficiently explored in the existing research. Empirically, this study provides exploratory evidence from Vietnam, an underrepresented higher education context in Southeast Asia.

papers.title: Philosophical foundations of AI-mediated inquiry: filling the gap in automated knowledge production
papers.authors: Zubair Ahmed Pirzada, Syed Muneer Ahmed Shah, Shoukat Ali Mahar
papers.journal: Journal of Information Communication and Ethics in Society
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine these philosophical dimensions within Sindh’s academic community by employing a convergent parallel mixed-methods design. Design/methodology/approach A structured online survey of 120 faculty and graduate students across ten institutions (e.g. University of Karachi, University of Sindh, Mehran University, NED University) quantified AI adoption at key research stages where literature screening (85%), qualitative coding (60%), hypothesis generation (40%) and drafting (46%), and measured participants’ ontological, agency, validity and ethical-concern stances. Findings Inferential analyses revealed that the use of AI for hypothesis generation significantly increased acceptance of AI agency, that senior faculty exhibited lower trust in AI outputs compared to graduate students, and that broader AI usage correlated positively with trust. Concurrently, semi-structured interviews with 10 authors whose recent publications explicitly acknowledged AI assistance surfaced four themes: AI as an efficiency collaborator, epistemic uncertainty and trust negotiation, contested agency with researcher oversight, and ethical dilemmas around bias and data privacy. Integration of quantitative and qualitative findings highlighted a model of “hybrid scholarship,” wherein AI accelerates routine tasks, but human interpretation and moral responsibility remain central. Originality/value Drawing on these insights, this paper proposes a modular philosophical framework that delineates human and machine roles at each research stage and offers actionable guidance for training, institutional policy and ethical oversight in Sindh’s academic research.

papers.title: The perception of craft construction workers on the application of artificial intelligence in health and safety in UK construction
papers.authors: Victor Asiku, Emmanuel Itodo Daniel, Christiana Ada Adah
papers.journal: Journal of Engineering Design and Technology
papers.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is starting to play a bigger role in health and safety (H&S) in UK construction. While most studies today are concerned about managerial perceptions, technological possibilities and organisational readiness, there is a dearth of research on the use of AI based on the lived experiences of construction workers. This research aims to explore how craft construction workers perceive the application of AI in construction H&S. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was used to garner the data to achieve the research aim. Overall, 20 craft construction workers with 5–20 years of experience were purposively selected from the UK (England, Scotland and Wales) and interviewed. The data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings The findings revealed a slow but gradual uptake of AI-enabled H&S tools, and AI is mostly used for hazard warning on construction sites. Some workers view AI as a beneficial modern addition; others perceive it as a form of surveillance. In addition, workers’ age influenced their attitudes towards AI, and the clarity of AI tools’ functions influenced how workers accepted them. One benefit of AI is hazard detection, but workers lack trust in its reliability. Practical implications The findings reported in this study will assist the construction industry, policymakers and technology developers in addressing concerns about AI in H&S while leveraging the benefits associated with their usage. Originality/value This study is among the first qualitative studies to empirically explore the perspective of key stakeholders (frontline workers−craft construction workers) in the UK on the application of AI in construction H&S management. This study contributes to future AI adoption in construction H&S management in the UK.

papers.title: Sufficient and necessary conditions in the adoption of generative artificial intelligence by entrepreneurs: findings in Spain
papers.authors: Jorge de Andrés Sánchez
papers.journal: Journal of economic and administrative sciences.
papers.abstract: Purpose This study assesses the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) among entrepreneurs in Spain, examining both sufficient and necessary conditions for different levels of use. Design/methodology/approach The study uses survey data from the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas. Ordered logistic regression is applied to identify sufficient conditions, while Necessary Condition Analysis is used to detect bottlenecks for higher levels of GenAI use. Findings Knowledge of GenAI and perceived economic usefulness are the main predictors of more intensive use. However, the NCA shows that technological optimism and the absence of very high scepticism operate as necessary conditions, especially at regular levels of use. Research limitations/implications The assessment relies on cross-sectional, self-reported data from Spanish self-employed workers. Future research should distinguish between different entrepreneurial profiles and types of GenAI use. The analytical framework may be applicable across different contexts, although the specific associations and bottleneck thresholds observed here should be validated through cross-country research. Practical implications Support policies should combine awareness-raising, applied training, and practical guidance on how GenAI can generate value in entrepreneurial activity. Social implications The findings suggest that responsible GenAI adoption among entrepreneurs requires not only favourable attitudes towards technology but also knowledge, perceived usefulness, and clear guidance on its business applications. Originality/value The study contributes by combining sufficiency and necessity logics to explain actual GenAI use among entrepreneurs, rather than focussing only on behavioural intention, while indicating that technology-readiness dispositions and GenAI-specific behavioural factors may fulfil distinct roles at different levels of use. By distinguishing probabilistic drivers from necessary bottlenecks, the study provides a more complete account of entrepreneurial GenAI adoption and generates more actionable implications for training and policies aimed at increasing effective use.

papers.title: Sociolinguistic compatibility in AI adoption: extending DoI–TOE in public relations
papers.authors: Shadi Abu-Ayyash
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how AI adoption in public relations (PR) unfolds in the Arab region and positions that experience against global industry discourses, with attention to the linguistic and cultural conditions that shape adoption trajectories. Design/methodology/approach Guided by Diffusion of Innovations (DoI) and the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, the study combines 20 semi-structured interviews with senior Arab-region practitioners, association leaders and academics across six countries with a directed content analysis of professional guidelines and industry reports of global, cross-regional and regional scope. Findings Adoption is early-stage and selective, concentrated in content assistance, media intelligence and reputation monitoring, driven by efficiency gains and client expectations and inhibited by skills gaps, limited Arabic-language tooling and unclear governance. International discourses converge on augmentation under norms for disclosure, oversight and capability building, while ethical risks are compounded in Arab settings by cultural–linguistic fit and uneven institutional support. Research limitations/implications Interview evidence is concentrated in the Arab region and drawn from a senior, purposively selected sample; cross-regional comparison rests on documentary sources. Practical implications Editorial review should be organized as a staged production sequence; training should target the specific sociolinguistic labour the technology cannot perform; and localization should be approached as an organizational process rather than a tool feature. Global PR associations should incorporate sociolinguistic review as a named component of human-in-the-loop protocols. Social implications Framing sociolinguistic compatibility as organizational work makes visible the human labour behind AI outputs in underserved languages. This supports more equitable AI integration across linguistic communities and strengthens the case for investment in Arabic-language AI capability, protecting culturally attuned communication in Arab public spheres. Originality/value The study contributes a structured comparative positioning of adoption trajectories and a DoI–TOE extension that models how organizational investments produce sociolinguistic compatibility under technological constraints, identifying levers for responsible, context-responsive AI integration in PR.

papers.title: When emotions matter: the contextual effectiveness of emotional expressions in AI agents
papers.authors: Peng Liu, Xingwei Lu, Weizhen Zhou
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) agents’ emotional expressions (positive or neutral) interact with service task types (subjective or objective) to shape consumer service satisfaction, and explore the mediating roles of mind perception, including perceived agency and perceived experience, in this process.
