Design/methodology/approach This work uses four studies, including a secondary data analysis of relevant Weibo posts and three scenario experiments involving a total of 587 participants, to underline the interaction effect between AI agents’ emotional expressions and service tasks on service satisfaction, and demonstrate the dual-path mediating effect of mind perception. Findings Across four studies, the authors find that the effectiveness of AI agents’ emotional expressions depends on service task characteristics. The secondary data analysis of Weibo posts first documents consumers’ differential responses to AI emotional expressions across subjective and objective service contexts. Three scenario experiments then establish that positive emotional expressions are more effective for subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotional expressions are more effective for objective tasks. Further analyses show that these effects operate through distinct psychological pathways: positive emotions enhance perceived experience in subjective tasks, whereas neutral emotions strengthen perceived agency in objective tasks, ultimately increasing consumer satisfaction. Research limitations/implications This study, while strong in internal validity, faces external validity limitations. It focuses on AI communication in commercial service texts, neglecting other domains like education and health care, and overlooking the nonverbal emotional expressions of embodied AI. In addition, the research primarily uses service satisfaction as the sole dependent variable, thus missing a broader spectrum of consumer responses such as repurchase intentions and word-of-mouth. Practical implications This research informs managers that AI service agents should be designed as social actors with mind perception rather than as purely functional tools. Firms can leverage emotional expressions to shape consumers’ social evaluations of AI. But emotional design should align with service task types: positive emotional cues are more effective for subjective, experiential tasks, whereas neutral styles better support objective, data-driven tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the emotional AI literature by uncovering critical situational factors that shape the effectiveness of AI emotional expressions and advances the authors’ understanding of the underlying mechanisms through a dual-path mediation framework of mind perception. The findings also provide practical implications for the strategic deployment of emotional AI in service design.

papers.title: From office to living room: linking AI awareness and career sustainability from a work–family boundary perspective
papers.authors: Weiqi Pan, Shan Wang, Chenhong Hu, Shanshi LIU
papers.abstract: Purpose Drawing upon work–family boundary theory and the significance of employees career sustainability amid widespread artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, this study examines the impact of AI awareness on two indicators of career sustainability (i.e. well-being and productivity) via work–family conflict and the moderating role of work–family segmentation preference in this relationship. Design/methodology/approach We collected data from 421 subordinate-supervisor dyads across multiple industries using a two-wave design and tested the hypotheses with structural equation modeling in Mplus. Findings The results indicated a negative effect of AI awareness on career sustainability (i.e. subordinate-rated well-being and supervisor-rated productivity) via work–family conflict. Additionally, work–family segmentation preference functions as an important boundary condition, weakening the positive relationship between AI awareness and work–family conflict and attenuating the indirect negative effect of AI awareness on both well-being and productivity. Research limitations/implications This study offers three key theoretical contributions. First, it identifies AI awareness as a novel antecedent of career sustainability, extending research within socio-technical organizational contexts. Second, drawing on work–family boundary theory, it reveals a cross-domain spillover mechanism through which AI awareness undermines career sustainability via work–family conflict. Finally, it highlights work–family segmentation preference as a boundary management strategy that buffers the negative effects of AI awareness, enriching understanding of individual-level moderators in AI-related career research. Practical implications This study offers several practical implications. First, organizations should mitigate the negative impact of AI awareness on career sustainability by fostering balanced human–AI collaboration through clear job design, AI literacy training, and supportive feedback systems. Second, promoting work–family boundary management – such as, encouraging segmentation preferences and family-supportive policies – can reduce work–family conflict and enhance employee well-being. Finally, integrating boundary management skills into recruitment and development practices helps organizations sustain both employee happiness and productivity in AI-driven workplaces. Social implications As AI becomes increasingly embedded in workplaces, its influence extends beyond productivity to employees' family life and long-term career sustainability. This study suggests that unmanaged AI-related stress may erode well-being and work effectiveness through work–family conflict. The findings highlight the broader social need to promote healthier human–AI collaboration, clearer work–life boundaries, and more sustainable career development. By encouraging AI literacy, boundary management, and supportive organizational norms, organizations can help reduce the unintended social costs of technological disruption and foster employee well-being, family harmony, and sustainable employment in the AI era. Originality/value Our study contributes to career sustainability research by identifying AI awareness as a novel antecedent in socio-technical workplaces. Additionally, we reveal a cross-domain spillover mechanism through which AI awareness undermines employees' career sustainability via work–family conflict. Furthermore, we identify work–family segmentation preference as an individual boundary management strategy that buffers the negative spillover effects of AI awareness.

papers.title: Design, implementation, and reflections on delivering machine learning workshops for medical microbiology and infection science
papers.authors: Benjamin Ryan McFadden, Mark A Reynolds, Timothy J. J. Inglis
papers.abstract: Increasingly, machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) methods are being applied in medical microbiology and infection science. With this comes a need to provide domain professionals with practical opportunities to develop ML literacy while introducing the foundational concepts required to use and critically evaluate these methods. This article outlines the design, implementation, and reflections on delivering “Using Data Science and Machine Learning for Infection Science: A Hands-On Introduction”, a recurring one-day workshop created to introduce data science and ML concepts to infection science and medical microbiology students and professionals. The workshop provides participants with the opportunity for experiential learning using Orange, a no-code, open-source, and free-to-use data mining software application, where participants are exposed to the fundamentals of the ML lifecycle. By the conclusion of the one-day workshop, participants gain experience developing end-to-end analytical pipelines for tabular datasets, with a specific example focused on blood culture outcome prediction. The workshop emphasises transparency, reproducibility, and open science, promoting critical awareness of how data science can be applied within participants’ own domain specialty. This article details the curriculum design, practical implementation, and delivery of the workshop. Additionally, we reflect on the lessons learned and directions for future iterations of the workshop.

papers.title: Exploring Policy for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Nursing Education: Student and Faculty Perceptions
papers.authors: Helena M.H. Nadder, Barbara J. Patterson
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education, creating opportunities and challenges related to academic integrity, educator readiness, and policy clarity, particularly in nursing education. PURPOSE: To examine nurse educator and student perspectives on GAI use, institutional policies, syllabus language, and best practices in nursing education. METHODS: A descriptive quantitative survey was completed by 211 nurse educators and 89 nursing students (N = 300) across diverse nursing programs. Data were analyzed by program type, learning model, and degree level. RESULTS: Findings revealed widespread uncertainty and inconsistent communication of GAI policies and expectations. Students reported greater confusion regarding acceptable use and institutional guidance, while educators described decentralized and inconsistent approaches. Demographic factors were not significantly associated with perceptions. CONCLUSIONS: Nursing education requires clearer, more accessible, and unified approaches to GAI governance to support ethical, effective, and pedagogically sound integration.

papers.title: Symptoms of anxiety are linked to N3 sleep and lower dissipation of slow-wave activity during nocturnal sleep
papers.authors: Mikko Heimola, Maija Orjatsalo, Paavo Laitinen, Katinka Tuisku, Henna Pitkänen, Jussi P. Toppila, P. E. Simola, Antti‐Jussi Ämmälä, Pekka Räisänen, Kai I. Parkkola, Jussi Virkkala, Anniina Alakuijala, Tiina Paunio
papers.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) is vital for brain health, memory, and emotional resilience. Slow-wave activity (SWA) reflects homeostatic sleep pressure, which dissipates across successive sleep cycles. Impaired SWA dissipation has been linked to depression. We examined whether reduced SWA dissipation is associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression in healthy conscripts. METHODS: Seventy conscripts (67 males, aged 18-24) undergoing compulsory military service participated in overnight polysomnography. SWA dissipation was assessed by comparing normalized delta (0.5-4.0 Hz) electroencephalogram power between first and third NREM sleep episodes. This was complemented by full spectral analysis of sleep stages. Psychological measures included Overall Anxiety Severity and Impairment Scale, Beck's Depression Inventory, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale. RESULTS: Conscripts with elevated anxiety (24%) exhibited weaker SWA dissipation and greater proportion of N3 sleep. Similarly, anxiety was negatively correlated with SWA dissipation and positively with proportion of N3. Additionally, conscripts with elevated anxiety but without elevated depressiveness had less REM sleep than those with both anxiety and depression, as well as those without symptoms. Findings related to sleepiness or depression without anxiety were limited. In full spectral analysis individuals with higher anxiety exhibited elevated alpha power during REM sleep, potentially reflecting cortical hyperarousal. CONCLUSIONS: Higher proportion of N3 sleep and lower SWA dissipation were associated with greater anxiety rather than depression. These findings highlight the importance of adequate SWS in emotion regulation. Impaired SWA dissipation may contribute to preservation of negative emotional memories during sleep. Another possibility is that hyperarousal increases need for recovery sleep.

papers.title: UEFA consensus guidelines on anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in Women’s football – part one: risk factors and prevention
papers.authors: Katrine Okholm Kryger, Amelia Joanna Hanford Arundale, Zoran Bahtijarević, Chris Brogden, Meredith Chaput, Sebastian Rilk, Naomi Datson, Allison M. Ezzat, Eva Ferrer, Ventura Ferrer-Roca, Stephanie Rose Filbay, Frank Barnett, Celeste Geertsema, Martin Hägglund, Gino M. M. J. Kerkhoffs, Christina Y. Le, Gary Lewin, Xavier Linde, Jelle P. van der List, Lawrence Mayhew, Carly D. McKay, Christian Moen, Grethe Myklebust, Tania Nilsson, Elke Van Den Steen, Matthew Whalan, Javier Yanguas, Gabriel Monthuley, Evert A.L.M. Verhagen
papers.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are among the most burdensome injuries in women's football, carrying significant consequences for players and the football community. To develop practical, evidence-based guidelines for ACL injury prevention, UEFA convened a multidisciplinary expert panel of 31 doctors, sports scientists, physiotherapists, and a player. Using the RAND-UCLA Appropriateness Method, 101 evidence statements were synthesised from existing literature and subjected to a modified Delphi process with three rounds of confidential voting. Consensus was reached on 88 statements. Through online and in-person discussions, this evidence was integrated with expert and clinical and practical judgement to produce actionable recommendations tailored to women's football. The guidelines conclude that ACL injuries in women's football typically occur in non-contact situations during high-intensity movements such as cutting, pressing, or landing, and may be influenced by a combination of modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors. Proposed modifiable factors include deficits in neuromuscular control, strength, and movement quality, which can be addressed through multicomponent prevention strategies. These programmes were identified as the most effective, incorporating plyometric, strength, and proximal control exercises performed two to three times per week for 15 to 20 minutes, with evidence showing they can reduce non-contact ACL injuries when adherence is high. Successful implementation requires context-specific tailoring, embedding programmes into routine training, and addressing barriers such as limited resources, time constraints, and lack of coach education. The guidelines recommend enhancing buy-in through co-creation with coaches and players, integrating prevention into existing practice, and strengthening organisational and policy support to sustain long-term adoption.

papers.title: Real versus AI-generated war videos: comparative effects on viewer attitudes, emotional arousal, and behavioral intentions
papers.authors: Ravi Kumar
papers.abstract: With the advent of generative AI technology, the massive production of synthetic imagery and videos of war that convincingly mimic the images of real wars is made possible through rapid dissemination through social media, posing critical concerns regarding the potential psychological implications of this form of media content. Studies on deepfake technology reveal that these kinds of media content can contribute to uncertainty, distrust in news, and even negative impacts on democracy, despite being less “persuasive” compared to other forms of media. Furthermore, continuous exposure to the disturbing image of war on the internet is linked to trauma, fear, and perception of danger. In the research study social media users were randomly assigned to watch either a real or an AI-generated war video pertaining to the Middle East crisis or the Russia–Ukraine war. Participants completed pre-exposure measures of media literacy, prior conflict attitudes, and psychological baseline, followed by postexposure assessments of perceived authenticity, trust, emotional arousal, agenda-congruent attitudes, behavioral intentions (sharing, policy support, donation willingness) and psychological distress.

papers.title: Empathy, embodiment, and expanded auditory performance in the age of AI
papers.authors: Pierre Jolivet
papers.journal: International Journal of Performance Arts and Digital Media
papers.abstract: This article explores empathy through experimental sound art and digital performance, drawing on over three decades of practice spanning industrial music, spatial sound, and biofeedback technologies. It asks how embodied listening can generate empathic encounters beyond visual representation and narrative identification. Focusing on EEG-driven installations and immersive multi-channel performances, including work with 4DSOUND and CMMAS, it examines how physiological data, spatialisation, and perceptual feedback loops create conditions for shared sonic presence. Machine learning and self-generative processes are considered as mediators of these encounters, with attention to their aesthetic potential and ethical limitations. Grounded in sound studies, affect theory, and critical posthumanism, the article develops sonic empathy as a situated, bodily, and relational process rather than a measurable emotional outcome. Its practice-as-research approach combines iterative biofeedback mapping, spatial composition, audience response, accessibility-led adjustment, and reflexive documentation. The discussion addresses algorithmic bias, sensory overload, unequal access, and the risks of affective manipulation. It argues that digital performance can support empathic listening when technological mediation remains intelligible, participation accommodates difference, and listeners retain agency in negotiating the encounter.

papers.title: Make or buy AI? Evidence on AI sourcing decisions and workforce outcomes
papers.authors: Oscar Stålnacke, Ebrahim Bazrafshan, Amin Sofla
papers.abstract: We examine how firms acquire artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities and how their AI sourcing decisions relate to workforce outcomes. Using Swedish enterprise surveys from 2019 and 2021 linked to financial statements and employer–employee data, we directly observe whether firms adopt AI and whether they outsource AI-related activities. AI adoption is concentrated among larger firms. Among adopters, pre-existing cost pressure is associated with outsourcing. Relative to non-adopters, both in-house adopters and outsourcers have higher subsequent employment and persistently higher shares of university-educated and computer-science (CS)-educated workers, with no further change in workforce composition in the year after adoption. Workforce outcomes are statistically indistinguishable between in-house adopters and outsourcers.

papers.title: Algorithm or Assembly? An Experimental Study of Recommendations by AI Versus Deliberative Mini-Publics in Democratic Decision-Making
papers.authors: Nuri Kim, Myojung Chung, S. Mo Jones-Jang, Sangwon Lee, Jihyang Choi
papers.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) renewed debates about who—or what—can legitimately contribute to democratic processes. While both AI and deliberative mini-publics can supplement citizens’ efforts to form judgments about issues, little is known about how citizens evaluate policy advice from these sources. In an online survey experiment with U.S. adults (N = 502), participants read a mock news story reporting a policy recommendation, attributed either to an AI system or a deliberative citizens’ assembly. Opinion climate was orthogonally varied to assess contextual influences. Results were split: citizens’ assemblies were rated fairer and more satisfying, but AI was perceived to be more useful. Opinion climate cues had no moderating effects. Further analysis indicated that acceptance of AI versus citizens’ assembly recommendations depends on individual factors, such as prior attitudes toward the issue and trust in AI. Findings offer theoretical and practical implications for designing democratic decision support systems.

papers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in Personal Health Contexts: Investigating Information Seeking Motivations, Information Processing Behaviors, and Behavioral Responses During and After Interaction with GenAI
papers.authors: Sihui Chen, Jingyi Li, Cindy Sing Bik Ngai, Tien Ee Dominic Yeo
papers.abstract: Following the advent of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), seeking health information on GenAI has become a more common and flexible approach. However, laypeople's health information seeking and processing (HISP) motivations and behavior on GenAI platforms remain underexplored, particularly given the current shift from search-based activities to more interactive and conversational processes. This study addressed this gap by exploring laypeople's HISP motivations, behaviors, and behavioral responses during and after interaction with GenAI. Using the risk information seeking and processing model as the theoretical framework, the HISP process was explored from a risk reduction perspective to understand how laypeople interact with GenAI to address their health concerns. Think-aloud protocol and retrospective interviews were employed to capture participants' real-time and reflective HISP interactions. Participants were mainly young individuals in Hong Kong. Through systematic thematic analysis using both inductive and deductive coding, we found that participants' GenAI-based health information seeking was shaped by multifaceted factors, including relevant health experiences, perceived health characteristics, affective responses toward health risks, and personal factors such as relevant channel beliefs. Trust played a critical role in shaping how participants processed the provided information and was associated with indicative heuristic and systematic processing patterns, given the information characteristic (medical vs non-medical) and perceived acceptance risks. Emotion sufficiency, information overload, and information affordance were identified as emerging variables and discussed in the GenAI-mediated HISP context. Finally, participants may choose to follow, reject, or integrate the GenAI-provided health advice into future health consultations, considering information characteristics and implementation difficulty.
keywords: risk information seeking and processing model

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Teacher–AI Partnership in Inclusive Education: A Multi-Level Socio-Educational Psychology Framework
papers.authors: Chohra Faycal
papers.journal: International Journal of Disability Development and Education
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into inclusive classrooms presents opportunities for personalised support alongside risks of deepening educational inequities, particularly for students with disabilities. Existing frameworks address AI in education and inclusive pedagogy largely in isolation, lacking theoretical integration that explicates psychological mechanisms through which AI systems may support or undermine belonging, participation and wellbeing of learners with diverse needs. This conceptual article addresses this gap by developing a multi-level socio-educational psychology model of teacher–AI partnership, synthesising theoretical and empirical work across disability studies, inclusive education, teacher professional agency and technology-acceptance literatures. The proposed framework connects three interdependent levels: (a) school-level conditions, including climate, governance and resources; (b) teacher-level processes, encompassing beliefs, emotions and instructional practices and (c) student-level outcomes, comprising learning, participation and wellbeing. The model positions AI as a socio-technical mediator that can function as either protective or risk factor for inclusion, contingent upon implementation conditions and disability-responsive governance structures. The article derives testable propositions and offers evidence-informed guidance for special education practice, teacher education, school leadership and participatory AI governance that safeguards children’s rights and promotes educational justice.

papers.title: Institutional and academic determinants of ChatGPT adoption in higher education: evidence from a resource-constrained university context
papers.authors: Cuc Thi Doan
papers.abstract: This study examines the determinants of students’ use of ChatGPT as a learning support tool at a public local university located in a resource-constrained, mountainous region of northern Vietnam, characterised by socioeconomic disadvantage and limited access to educational resources. Drawing on survey data from 906 undergraduate students, the study investigates how individual digital readiness, academic context, institutional support, and economic constraints jointly shape students’ engagement with ChatGPT. The findings indicate that students’ use of ChatGPT is influenced more strongly by academic and institutional conditions than by individual digital competence alone, while economic barriers remain a significant constraint on sustained use. By situating generative AI adoption within a structurally disadvantaged higher education context, this study extends technology acceptance research and underscores the importance of context-sensitive, institution-led strategies to ensure equitable and responsible integration of generative AI in public universities.

papers.title: Generative AI in Global Marketing for Sustainability: A Systematic Review of Creativity, Cultural Adaptation, and Governance
papers.authors: Mohamed Nassar, Osama Sam Al-Kwifi, Amr El-Alfy, Georgia Sakka, Zafar Uddin Ahmed
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has emerged in global marketing amid intensifying sustainability regulation and scrutiny. Yet the same generative capabilities that can support the detection of greenwashing may also facilitate its production and dissemination. This systematic review examines how GenAI in marketing is governed for sustainability, integrated into marketing operations, and shaped by cultural context. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched five databases for English-language studies published between January 2020 and May 2026, yielding 77 studies for analysis. Three findings emerge. First, GenAI functions simultaneously as verification and persuasion infrastructure. Because both functions draw on the same generative capability, this duality is structural; its sustainability implications depend on the governance conditions surrounding deployment. Second, cultural adaptation remains underdeveloped: only 9% of studies provide strong evidence on this dimension, Sub-Saharan Africa is absent from the corpus, and Latin America and the Caribbean are represented by a single study. Third, although 77% of studies engage themes relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), only 10% explicitly identify specific goals, with the largest gap concerning SDG 12. By integrating governance, operational deployment, and cultural context, this review identifies the conditions under which GenAI may support or undermine sustainable marketing.

papers.title: Evaluation of Outcome of Corpus Callosotomy in Management of Intractable Generalized Epilepsy
papers.authors: Ali Abdel Hamid Abdel Aziz Maarek, Magdy AbdelAziz Elmahallawy, Mohammed Amer Ibrahim, Esam Abdelhay Mokbel, Ahmed Fathi Saleh, Essam Ahmed Abdelhameed
papers.journal: Arquivos Brasileiros de Neurocirurgia Brazilian Neurosurgery
papers.abstract: Abstract Epilepsy can remain uncontrolled despite multiple medications, making corpus callosotomy a practical palliative option for generalized or non-localizing seizures. It may reduce seizure severity, especially drop attacks, although it is rarely curative and carries some risks. To evaluate callosotomy outcomes and techniques, and also the advantages and limitations in managing intractable generalized epilepsy. The present study included 20 patients with medically refractory generalized seizures, unresponsive to 2 or more appropriate antiepileptic drugs, and without a resectable seizure focus. All patients underwent comprehensive evaluations, including detailed history (seizure onset, duration, frequency, family history, previous neurological events, drug history, seizure characteristics, drop attacks, and injuries), thorough physical and neurological examinations, neuropsychological assessment, and relevant investigations including video-electroencephalogram (EEG) and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with Harmonized Neuroimaging of Epilepsy Structural Sequences (HARNESS) protocol. In this series, children developed seizures early in life and underwent corpus callosotomy after prolonged drug-resistant epilepsy. Despite frequent, predominantly atonic seizures, surgery, mainly anterior callosotomy, resulted in seizure freedom or near-freedom in 70% of patients at approximately 15 months of follow-up, with few, mostly transient complications and no clear predictors of outcome. Corpus callosotomy is a practical and feasible palliative option for patients with intractable generalized epilepsy, particularly for controlling atonic seizures (drop attacks). It significantly reduces seizure-related injuries, activity limitations and caregiver dependence. An initial anterior two-thirds callosotomy is recommended for safety and to minimize cognitive risks, with completion to total callosotomy reserved for cases with inadequate seizure control.

papers.title: Stress-testing consentAI: a pipeline for evaluating a conversational educational adjunct to surgical informed consent
papers.authors: Anthony Abou Mrad, Jayanth S. Pratap, Aviona Conti, William Azar, Paola Vargas, Natalie Moreno, Joseph Cheaib, Mansour Riachi, Lisa Marie Knowlton, David P. W. Rastall, Gabriel A. Brat, Melissa S. Camp, Lilah F. Morris, Anne Ehlers, Dana Alexa Telem, Peter Najjar, Andrew MacGregor Cameron, Jeffrey K. Jopling
papers.abstract: Informed consent is delivered inconsistently, and the comprehension it should produce is often poor. We built ConsentAI, a conversational educational adjunct that guides patients through a surgeon-authored consent form and gates progression on demonstrated understanding. Before any patient-facing trial, we asked how such an agent can be evaluated at scale, and which methods can be trusted. Eight clinicians scored 50 simulated laparoscopic cholecystectomy sessions on a 10-item rubric. We tested four LLM judge architectures against this clinician reference under a pre-specified, imbalance-robust plan. No single judge reproduced clinicians’ failure calls. Only jury aggregation improved sensitivity (0.421; 95% CI, 0.26–0.61), and no architecture reached a usable triage point. A constant pass-everything labeler topped raw agreement and AC1 yet scored zero on Matthews correlation and Cohen’s kappa. Evaluating clinical conversational agents therefore requires multiple clinician ratings and imbalance-robust metrics, treating clinician adjudication as a measurement layer, not ground truth.

papers.title: From compliance to competence: a multi-level model for AI governance in undergraduate medical education
papers.authors: Juan José Gualda-Gea, Lourdes Estefanía Barón-Miras, Maria Jesús Bertran, Alberto L. García‐Basteiro, Guillermo Mena, Marta Aldea, Gemina Santana, Jaume Grau, Andrés Prat Marín, Isabel Torá Rocamora, Antoni Trilla
papers.abstract: AI's fast-paced irruption in medicine and education has challenged undergraduate medical colleges, with institutions documenting policies emphasizing immediate conduct restrictions, while strategic oversight, infrastructure and evaluation remain less consistently developed. We propose a multi-level framework for AI governance in undergraduate medical education based on accountability, competence and co-responsibility across institutions, educators and students, designed to turn a fast-evolving technology from a threat into an opportunity for collective progress.

papers.title: From research to clinical practice: Expert consensus on Neuroimaging AI tools for the Memory clinic (Neuro-AIM)
papers.authors: Natasha Clarke, Mathias Huybrechts, Jay Amin, Lewis Hotchkiss, James Leighs, Matthew Leming, Usman Saeed, Catherine J Scott, Dirk Smeets, Angela Tam, Stefano Tamburin, Geert Vanhooren, Meike Willemijn Vernooij, Jennifer Camaradou, David J. Llewellyn, Timothy Rittman, Rose Bruffaerts
papers.abstract: Abstract Although AI tools for neuroimaging show considerable promise in the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of neurodegenerative disorders, their uptake in memory clinics has been limited. A key barrier is lack of consensus on their effective design and implementation. Here we establish expert consensus on the specific goals, usage and challenges of AI tools for neuroimaging in the memory clinic using a Delphi process. Sixteen experts from clinical, academic, and industry backgrounds participated in three rounds of questionnaires, coordinated by the Imaging Working Group of the Deep Dementia Phenotyping (DEMON) network, with support from a patient and public involvement representative. Consensus was reached on eight statements covering four themes: purpose, quality, interactions with clinicians and memory clinics, and privacy and ethics. Implementation of these recommendations will further the adoption of AI neuroimaging tools from research to clinical practice, improving diagnostic and care pathways for patient benefit.

papers.title: Development of ethical evaluation indicators for educational artificial intelligence based on the “Life-Practice” pedagogy
papers.authors: Q Chen, Hui Jing, Ruijun Zhao
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has ushered in a new era of educational artificial intelligence (EAI), bringing both immense potential and significant ethical challenges. To promote responsible development and effectively mitigate potential ethical risks, there is an urgent need to establish clear evaluative criteria for ethical practices involving EAI. However, current generic frameworks often prioritize technical safety over pedagogical generativity. This study addresses this imperative by developing an ethical evaluation model and corresponding system of indicators for EAI. Guided by the core principles of Professor Ye Lan’s “Life-Practice” Pedagogy, this study developed a set of ethical evaluation indicators across two critical perspectives: design and usage. These indicators were refined through two rounds of Delphi surveys, and their importance was quantitatively determined using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). The resulting ethical evaluation framework comprises two perspectives, encompassing 8 first-level indicators and 32 s-level indicators. These indicators offer theoretically informed guidance that requires further empirical validation, thereby potentially supporting the ethically informed development and responsible integration into educational contexts.

papers.title: Course-embedded AI-augmented teaching is associated with engagement and performance in software education
papers.authors: Zhe Gai, Junjun Wang, Jinyong Wu
papers.abstract: AI-augmented teaching may reduce feedback delays in software courses, but semester-long classroom evidence remains limited. This course-level quasi-experimental study evaluated a course-embedded AI-augmented teaching (AIT) model in an undergraduate Python course. Two intact classes participated: 60 students in the AIT class used a large language model teaching assistant restricted to course-specific materials and instructional rules for question answering, code diagnosis, personalized recommendations, and teacher monitoring, whereas 60 students in the conventional-instruction class received the same course instruction without access to the AIT platform. Student-level analyses, interpreted cautiously because of the class-level design, showed higher posttest, programming assignment and final composite scores in the AIT class after baseline adjustment. Learning engagement also showed clearer gains, especially overall and behavioral engagement. AI usage intensity was moderately associated with engagement but weakly associated with academic performance. Mediation analysis provided clearer evidence for an indirect engagement pathway for project practice performance than for final composite performance. Open-ended feedback indicated that students valued immediate feedback and debugging support but remained concerned about accuracy, dependency and ethical boundaries.

papers.title: Sex- and age-related heterogeneity in obstructive sleep apnea phenotypes in a predominantly Afro-Caribbean population
papers.authors: Moustapha Agossou, Salvatore Metanmo, Nadine Simo, Marion Edoh Coffi, Jocelyn Inamo, Mathilde Andreu, Berenice Awanou, Mathilde Provost, Nelly Ahouansou, Marion Dufeal, Maturin Tabué-Teguo, Moustapha Dramé
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) shows wide variability in clinical presentation. Sex-related differences in symptom expression are increasingly recognized, but the contribution of age and respiratory event composition remains insufficiently explored in underrepresented populations. To describe sex- and age-related heterogeneity in clinical and respiratory phenotypes of OSA in a predominantly Afro-Caribbean population referred to a tertiary sleep center. We conducted a cross-sectional study of consecutive adults evaluated for suspected OSA at a tertiary sleep center (July 2024-June 2025). Clinical characteristics, symptom profiles, and respiratory indices were compared by sex and age (< 65 vs ≥ 65 years). Multivariable models adjusting for BMI and age assessed whether sex differences were independent of these factors. Among 213 patients evaluated, 189 had OSA (women: 61.4%, n = 116). Women had a higher BMI than men (31.4 vs 27.6 kg·m −2 , p < 0.001) and a lower respiratory event burden, with a lower apnea index and oxygen desaturation index but a higher relative contribution of hypopneas to the AHI (all p ≤ 0.045). Women also reported more insomnia (68.1% vs 49.2%, p = 0.02) and higher fatigue scores ( p = 0.02), with no significant difference in daytime sleepiness. After adjustment for age and BMI, these sex differences in respiratory indices persisted (all p ≤ 0.002), while the fatigue association was attenuated ( p = 0.08). Age ≥ 65 years was independently associated with a higher AHI, apnea index and ODI, a lower hypopnea/AHI ratio, and lower odds of excessive daytime sleepiness (adjusted OR 0.32, p = 0.002), patterns masked in unadjusted comparisons. A sex × age interaction was significant only for insomnia ( p = 0.007): the sex difference was confined to patients ≥ 65 years (adjusted OR 9.12) and absent in younger patients (adjusted OR 1.20). OSA phenotypes in this Caribbean population show marked heterogeneity by sex and respiratory event composition, largely independent of BMI and age. Age modulated daytime sleepiness, respiratory composition, and the sex-related difference in insomnia, which was concentrated among older patients. Reliance on daytime sleepiness alone may underestimate OSA burden in women, older patients, and hypopnea-dominant phenotypes, supporting a more phenotype- and age-based approach to screening.

papers.title: A low-cost environmental monitoring framework for climate-sensitive disease surveillance in the Peruvian Amazon
papers.authors: Bryan Fernandez-Camacho, Edson J Ascencio, Antony Barja, Luis C. Revilla, Diego Villa, P. Brou, Yomali Ferreyra, Lucia Bartolini-Arana, Rachel Lowe, Gabriel Carrasco‐Escobar
papers.abstract: Abstract Malaria, dengue and leptospirosis are endemic in the Peruvian Amazon, where routine surveillance operates without village-scale environmental observation. We report the yield of that monitoring framework, the completeness of its meteorological record, and its cost, operated at village scale alongside notifiable disease surveillance. Across ten villages along the Iquitos–Nauta Highway, we operated drones, automatic weather stations, low-cost particulate monitors and acoustic recorders, inspected terrain and geolocated cases. Co-creation with the regional health directorate and villages governed deployment and data handling. Streams were harmonized into a spatial database at daily to annual resolution. Nine quarterly campaigns between March 2023 and March 2026 covered 14 flight areas, 14 km 2 per round, and produced 756 orthomosaics from 1.16 million images. Sensors returned 678,564 meteorological and 2,778,363 air-quality records and 4349.75 h of audio. Completely missing outdoor-temperature weeks ranged from 5.1 to 61.4% across sites. Of 10,883 notified individuals, 1489 (13.7%) were georeferenced, with coverage of 8.3% in 2010–2015 and 31.1% in 2021–2025. Capital outlay was about USD 22,050, each campaign about USD 3660. The harmonized series is intended to inform vector control and case detection for local health authorities and stakeholders.

papers.title: MassNet: billion-scale AI-ready mass spectral corpus empowering scalable deep learning in proteomics
papers.authors: Jun A, Xiang Zhang, Xiaofan Zhang, Jiaqi Wei, Te Zhang, Yamin Deng, Pu Liu, Zongxiang Nie, Yiwen Yu, Yi Chen, Nanqing Dong, Zhiqiang Gao, Siqi Sun, Tiannan Guo
papers.abstract: Here we present MassNet, inspired by large-scale data corpora of text and images; MassNet is an artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data corpus for mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics. The corpus contains 1.5 billion tandem MS spectra from high-quality data-dependent acquisition (DDA) MS data across 35 species. Approximately 1.7 million peptide precursors are from human samples. We further present an AI-ready DDA data format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT) for compact and standardized storage, curation and reuse of data from multiple sources, which can be optionally converted to a Lightning Memory-Mapped Database for accelerated input/output in deep learning. On the basis of MassNet, we develop XuanjiNovo, a nonautoregressive transformer model that leverages a curriculum learning strategy for de novo peptide sequencing. XuanjiNovo achieves 38.35–143.57% improvement over state-of-the-art methods on human Astral data. MassNet also supports additional downstream tasks, including retention time prediction and PSM rescoring. MassNet represents a foundational MS-based proteomics data resource, marking a critical milestone for AI proteomics research. This Article presents MassNet, a large-scale AI-ready corpus of 1.5 billion MS/MS spectra spanning 35 species, paired with a standardized storage format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT). Built on this resource, XuanjiNovo is a nonautoregressive transformer for de novo peptide sequencing that substantially outperforms previous methods.

papers.title: Large language models in STEM education: Opportunities, pedagogical shifts, ethical concerns, and future research directions
papers.authors: Ahmad Subhi Salem Mufleh, Muza A. E. Abunamous, Loubna Hussain Rashid Alajmi, Shadi Majed Alshraah, Amani Bin Jwair, Aashir Waleed
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming STEM and engineering education, yet their pedagogical value and responsible adoption depend on task design, systematic verification, and human oversight. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizes evidence from 98 peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2026, identified through a systematic search of major academic databases, to examine pedagogical applications, instructional transformations, ethical considerations, and research directions for LLM use in these disciplines. The findings indicate that LLMs can support a broad range of educational activities, including scalable tutoring, formative feedback, bilingual conceptual learning, programming, technical writing, assessment, and project- and capstone-based learning. However, the literature also highlights persistent challenges—academic integrity, output reliability, data privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, and institutional governance—that underscore the need for carefully designed and appropriately governed integration. In the Saudi Arabian context, LLM adoption aligns with Vision 2030 and the National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI), yet realizing these benefits will require stronger institutional policies, faculty development, AI literacy, and assessment reform. The review proposes a multi-level conceptual framework that links national priorities, institutional governance, pedagogical integration, and student learning outcomes. Key research priorities include multimodal learning support, standardized prompt scaffolding, rubric-guided feedback, trustworthy tool-augmented systems, discipline-specific benchmarking, and longitudinal evaluation of educational outcomes. Overall, the review synthesizes current evidence to inform educators, policymakers, and researchers about the opportunities, challenges, and governance requirements associated with LLM integration in engineering education, while identifying priorities for future empirical validation.

papers.title: Sleep underestimation and subjective sleep appraisal: Limited value of routine polysomnographic and electroencephalographic features
papers.authors: Chunyan Long, Junyi Chen, Xiaolan Xu, Dandan Mao, Tao Zhang, Lisha Zhong, Ling Li, Chunrong Liang

papers.title: High-dose cerium dioxide nanorods induce behavioral and electroencephalographic abnormalities through 5-HT1B receptor signaling disruption with an evaluation of anpirtoline's therapeutic potential
papers.authors: Mingshan Liu, Yuedong Li, Chunhao Shen, Hongyi Huang, Quanlei Liu, Bin Fu, Bihan Wu, Xiaomin Wu, Yumin Luo, Yongzhi Shan, Xuegang Niu, Guoguang Zhao
papers.abstract: Cerium dioxide nanorods (CeO 2 NRs) have drawn extensive research attention in the past few years for their exceptional generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and intrinsic catalytic properties. The two ends of the biological effect show a dose-dependent difference: protection of cells at low doses and damage to cells at high doses. Although the above processes are well documented in other biological contexts, the neurotoxicity induced by acute exposure to CeO 2 NRs, as well as its mechanism and possible prevention strategies, have yet to be elucidated. In the present study, we have found that CeO 2 NRs at a concentration of 300 μg/mL or higher induced neuronal apoptosis and reduced cell viability in vitro. After intranasal instillation in mice, CeO 2 NRs accumulated in the lysosomes and nuclei of neurons in the hippocampus and striatum. There was an increase in these abnormal exploratory behaviors, heightened seizure susceptibility, and altered electroencephalographic (EEG) oscillations. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic profiling further indicated disruption of serotonin (5-HT) metabolism, caused by a downregulation of the 5-HT1B receptor, and thus provided a possible molecular mechanism for the behaviors and EEG abnormalities observed. Considerable changes also occurred in the various serotonergic mediators, neuronal excitability indicators, and inflammatory markers. Pharmacological activation of the 5-HT1B receptor with anpirtoline partially reversed the behaviors and EEG changes induced by CeO 2 NRs.

papers.title: Affective and cognitive resources for engagement in AI-assisted language learning: A self-determination theory perspective integrating SEM and random forest
papers.authors: Fan Zhang, Fanfan Hou
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping language learning in higher education, yet students’ engagement in AI-assisted language learning depends on more than access to technological tools. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as an overarching theoretical perspective, this study examined how emotional intelligence and metacognition were associated with engagement directly and indirectly through enjoyment and self-efficacy, while also evaluating their predictive value. Survey data from 847 university students in China were analyzed using structural equation modeling and random forest analysis with repeated nested cross-validation. The SEM results showed that emotional intelligence and metacognition were positively associated with engagement, enjoyment, and self-efficacy, while enjoyment and self-efficacy were also positively related to engagement. All four indirect effects were significant. The extended random forest model achieved an out-of-sample R² of .472, improving R² by .081 over the baseline random forest and by .069 over the extended linear model. Emotional intelligence showed the highest permutation importance and revealed potentially nonlinear predictive patterns across individual learners. These findings highlight the complementary value of explanatory and predictive approaches for understanding engagement in AI-assisted language learning.

papers.title: Effects of an e-health enhanced multicomponent outpatient intervention for children and adolescents with overweight or obesity in routine primary care (STARKIDS): a cluster-randomized controlled trial
papers.authors: Katrin Ziser, Rebecca Sarah Erschens, Stephan Zipfel, Peter Martus, Johann Jacoby, Anne Herschbach, Annalena Wels, Isabelle Mack, Alisa Weiland, Inga Krauß, Constanze Greule, Gorden Sudeck, Ansgar Thiel, Guido Zurstiege, Andreas Hoell, Hans Joachim Salize, Wolfgang Andreas Bethge, Monika Ums, Torben Sammet, Maren Reyer, Olaf Schliesing, Katrin E. Giel, Stefan Ehehalt, Florian Junne
papers.abstract: Background Pediatric obesity is a major global public health challenge, associated with increased risk for numerous sequelae, persistence into adulthood, and growing economic burden. STARKIDS is a stepwise, tailored, e-health-enhanced, family-focused intervention in primary care. It integrates nutritional counseling targeting dietary energy density reduction, physical activity promotion, behavioral strategies, and psychosocial support. Methods We tested whether STARKIDS improves weight development and quality of life (QoL) compared with usual care. A cluster-randomized controlled trial was conducted in pediatric/family practices enrolling children/adolescents with overweight/obesity. Practices were stratified and block-randomized (no blinding) to STARKIDS or one-time counseling (optimized treatment-as-usual, TAU-O). Outcomes were assessed at baseline, 12, and 18 months. Primary outcomes were changes in BMI z-scores and QoL. Trial registration: DRKS00022813. Findings 89 practices were cluster-randomized (44 intervention, 45 TAU-O). Between April 2022 and July 2023, 379 families were assigned to STARKIDS and 232 to TAU-O. 343 and 216 families were included into the intention-to-treat analysis. After 12 months, 114 (33%) participants in the STARKIDS group and 47 (22%) in the TAU-O group achieved a BMI z-score reduction ≥0.2 (risk difference=0.11, 95% CI 0.03, 0.20, p = 0.0256). After 18 months, no group differences in BMI z-score reductions were found ( p = 0.6940). No significant differences in QoL were observed between study arms at either time point among adolescents. Among parents/guardians, a statistically significant between-group difference was observed at 18 months (−2.10, 95% CI −4.13 to −0.06; p = 0.044), though not considered clinically meaningful. No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported. Interpretation STARKIDS improved BMI z-score over 12 months with effects comparable to more intensive programs. The German Federal Joint Committee recommended transferring step 1 into routine care for children/adolescents with obesity. Effects were not sustained at 18 months, indicating a need for adaptations including additional contact hours to reinforce achieved outcomes, followed by a gradual reduction. Funding Innovation Committee of the German Joint Federal Committee (G-BA).

papers.title: Domain-adversarial anatomical graph networks for cross-user human activity recognition
papers.authors: Xiaozhou Ye, Kevin I‐Kai Wang
papers.abstract: Cross-user variability remains a fundamental challenge in wearable Human Activity Recognition (HAR), as differences in body morphology and movement styles cause significant distribution shifts across users. Existing approaches typically focus on feature-level alignment while overlooking the biomechanical invariants—shared anatomical constraints governing human movement that persist across individuals. Moreover, current Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based HAR methods rely on single-type edge relationships (e.g., physical adjacency) with static edge features, limiting their capacity to capture the diverse and dynamic biomechanical dependencies essential for cross-user generalization. We propose Edge-Enhanced Graph-Based Adversarial Domain Generalization (EEG-ADG), a novel framework that explicitly encodes multi-relational anatomical knowledge into graph-based representation learning with probabilistic edge modeling. Unlike prior work that treats sensor relationships as fixed and homogeneous, EEG-ADG constructs a unified graph capturing three complementary biomechanical priors: Interconnected Units, Analogous Units, and Lateral Units. To handle the inherent uncertainty in these relationships across users, we introduce a Variational Edge Feature Extractor that learns probabilistic representations of inter-sensor correlations—a capability absent in deterministic edge-based GNNs. An adaptive edge attention mechanism further modulates relationship importance based on activity context, while adversarial training on graph-structured representations disentangles activity-relevant features from user-specific biases. Comprehensive experiments on the OPPORTUNITY and DSADS benchmarks demonstrate that EEG-ADG achieves state-of-the-art cross-user generalization performance, outperforming existing domain generalization methods. Our findings highlight the value of integrating biomechanical prior knowledge with probabilistic graph learning for robust, generalizable HAR systems.

papers.title: Crisis translation: A student-led crowdsourcing initiative of a disaster relief term-base after 2023 Türkiye-Syria earthquakes
papers.authors: Fazilet AKDOĞAN ÖZDEMİR, Hüseyin Mergan, Abdullah Sadık Kuralay, Ahmet Ergün, Betül Mulbay
papers.journal: International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction
papers.abstract: Large-scale disasters generate acute multilingual communication needs that often exceed the reliability and governance capacity of automated translation alone. The February 2023 Türkiye–Syria earthquakes exemplified this challenge: while international search-and-rescue teams arrived and volunteer language support surged, high-stakes crisis communication still required dependable, domain-specific terminology and carefully coordinated translation and interpreting. This paper studies a case-based response through TermQuake, a student-led crowdsourcing initiative establishing a disaster-relief term-base at Boğaziçi University in Türkiye. Drawing on crisis-translation scholarship, it reframes translation and interpreting as communicative mediation that supports disaster risk reduction by bridging expert-to-expert and expert-to-non-expert communication, where domain-specific terminology competence is decisive for preventing harmful misunderstandings. While machine translation and LLM-based systems can reduce latency, their limitations—restricted language and resource coverage, infrastructural constraints, and risks of context insensitivity—support a hybrid approach requiring human post-editing and terminology verification for accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and institutional trust. The paper documents TermQuake’s development from an initial terminology resource into a mature platform, including terminology creation and verification, community-building through crowdsourcing, mobile-app development, and ongoing project governance. The case demonstrates that—despite expanding AI-enabled capacity for fast content generation—crisis settings continue to require human expertise, offline-accessible infrastructure, and robust terminological foundations to ensure semantic accuracy and cultural appropriateness. The study also highlights interdisciplinary collaboration as a driver of effective crisis translation, advancing resilience-focused evidence for preparedness planning, capacity-building, and policy development.

papers.title: Location-aware artificial intelligence historical narration for cultural heritage learning: A conceptual design perspective
papers.authors: Boaventura DaCosta
papers.abstract: Historical interpretation often separates voice from place. Visitors may stand where events occurred, yet the voices they encounter are often fixed in signs, audio tracks, tours, or exhibits. This work asks what might change if a historical figure could answer questions based on where visitors are standing. It presents a conceptual design for location-aware Artificial Intelligence (AI) historical narration, using a narrator based on Sarah Osborn at Yorktown Battlefield as an illustrative case. Osborn’s 1837 pension deposition serves as the primary-source foundation for the proposed narrator. Research on AI-generated historical characters and mobile, location-based games in cultural heritage (CH) frames the design problem, pointing to the importance of bringing conversational AI, archival sources, and movement through a site into relation. A design narrative follows several waypoints to show how dialogue, location, and historical limits shape the proposed experience. The work then proposes design principles for combining primary-source-based narration with site-based interaction. It contributes to digital heritage applications, human-heritage interaction, and heritage education by showing how conversational AI can be bounded by primary sources and physical location. Together, the conceptual design and principles guide location-aware AI historical narration in CH settings, where primary sources can be connected to specific places through interactive dialogue.

papers.title: A biophysically-inspired framework with spatiotemporal graph diffusion for EEG-based mental workload assessment

papers.title: Combined pharmacologic and lifestyle intervention for breast cancer prevention: Results of the randomized phase II TOLERANT trial in high-risk women
papers.authors: Davide Serrano, Matteo Lazzeroni, Roberta Rizzo, Patrizia Gnagnarella, Gaetano Aurilio, E. Colombo, Aliana Guerrieri‐Gonzaga, Harriet Ann Johansson, Stefania Zovato, Mariateresa Nardi, Anna Matteraglia, Matilde Pensabene, Simona Buccolo, Luigi Pistelli, Giorgia Giancarli, Alessio Carbone, Valentina Aristarco, Debora Macis, Chiara Arianna Accornero, Davide Merli, Emanuela Omodeo Salè, Andrea DeCensi, Sara Gandini, Bernardo Bonanni
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Breast cancer (BC) prevention strategies include lifestyle modification and preventive agents such as selective estrogen receptor modulators and aromatase inhibitors. Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is a breast cancer risk-associated biomarker; however, it is not a validated surrogate endpoint for breast cancer risk reduction. METHODS: Population: women with hereditary BC risk, a ≥ 5% 10-year BC risk, or a history of intraepithelial neoplasia were enrolled. TRIAL DESIGN: a four-arm randomized phase II biomarker trial: Tamoxifen 10 mg every other day (LDT); LDT + Intermittent Caloric Restriction (ICR); Lifestyle intervention with a step counter (LI); LI + ICR. PRIMARY ENDPOINT: Post intervention levels of circulating SHBG. Secondary endpoints: modulation of IGF system, adipokines, inflammatory markers, quality of life. Main analysis was LDT+ ICR vs LI+ICR. RESULTS: One hundred and ten participants were randomized to: LDT, LDT plus ICR, LI, or LI plus ICR, for 6 months. Mean age was 52 years and mean BMI was 25 kg/m²; 62% were unaffected carriers, and 65% were postmenopausal. LDT±ICR significantly increased SHBG and IGFBP-3 and decreased IGF-I (absolute change p < 0.0001, p = 0.004, and p < 0.001, respectively). ICR arms showed higher adiponectin than non-ICR arms (p = 0.003). Furthermore, in adherent subjects (>90%), LI plus ICR was significantly associated with higher SHBG compared with LI alone (p = 0.045). No differences in adverse events between arms; LDT demonstrated a mild, although significant, worsening in quality of life. CONCLUSIONS: LDT favorably modulates BC risk-associated biomarkers, and ICR adds a complementary metabolic effect, supporting further investigation of these combined strategies.

papers.title: CNPY3 variants associated with a recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy affect inflammasome and TLR function
papers.authors: Vera Garloff, Mona Grimmel, Reza Maroofian, Stéphanie Efthymiou, Sven Stengel, Dolores Bello, Carolin Tille, Mohamed Ghait, Oliver Ohlenschläger, Andrea Dieckmann, Heike de Vries, Matthias Waginger, Seba Nadeef, Ehsan Barkhordari, Rauan  B. Kaiyrzhanov, Sarah Bühler, Irisa Pjeci, Stefanie Beck‐Wödl, Javeria Raza Alvi, Tipu Sultan, Anna Chassevent, Constance L. Smith‐Hicks, Irina Mishina, Agustí Rodríguez‐Palmero, Evangeline Wassmer, Julie Vogt, Christopher Manuel Meudt, Rami Abou Jamra, Mohammad Reza Abbaszadegan, Naser Ajami, Reza Azizimalamiri, Hamid Galehdari, Niloofar Chamanrou, Mina Zamani, Gholamreza Shariati, Pardis Nourbakhsh, Farhan Bahadar Ali, Ambrin Fatima, Sohana Nadeem Hashmi, Zafar Iqbal, Sidra Kaleem, Mathias Toft, Erum Afzal, Shazia Maqbool, Fatima Rahman, Vincenzo Salpietro, Margot Grisval, Caroline Racine, Louis Januel, David Cheillan, Cécile Acquaviva, Chadi Al Alam, Majid Alfadhel, Muhammad Umair, Barbara Oehl‐Jaschkowitz, Shahzad Haider, Vivek Jain, Bhuvandeep Narang, Fawzia Amer, Nour M. Elkhateeb, Carolina Alvarez, Eduardo Pérez‐Palma, Loreto Ríos‐Pohl, R. Møller, Debangana Baruah, Lokesh Lingappa, Ahmad Farooq, Maha Saad Zaki, Gulnara Svyatova, Alexandra Murtazaliyeva, Asem Burabayeva, Kamran Salayev, Ulviyya Guliyeva, Kimia Kahrizi, Hossein Najmabadi, Anya Revah‐Politi, Maureen Mulhern, Tristan T. Sands, Hafiz Muhammad Mustafa, Hani Akbar Rao, Gabriela E. Oprea, Abolfazl Rad, Mohammad Miryounesi, Ali Mardi, Vykuntaraju K. Gowda, Varunvenkat M. Srinivasan, Rola Mohammed Alanazi, Iman Sabri Abumansour, Bader Alhaddad, Khadijah Bakur, Michael W Bauer, Fowzan Sami Alkuraya, Peter Huppke, H Houlden, Tobias B. Haack, Ignacio Rubio, Ralf A. Husain
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. METHODS: 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. FINDINGS: Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. INTERPRETATION: CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment.
