This paper conducts a scoping review of ML approaches used in CER for pharmacological interventions. We searched multiple databases from January 2020 to January 2026, supplemented by reference mining, and included 28 primary studies. We focused on research topics, ML methodologies, reporting, validity, and robustness of the findings, and appraised risk of bias. Although the use of ML methods in CER of pharmacologic intervention is relatively recent, it is expanding and consolidating around a few specific methods, notably doubly robust estimators paired with ensemble learners. However, methodological rigor and reporting consistency remain uneven, yielding a moderate risk of bias. Standardized methods, transparent reporting, and dedicated appraisal tools are needed before these approaches can reliably inform research, clinical practice, and policy. Machine learning (ML) is rapidly changing how researchers evaluate the effectiveness of different pharmacological treatments. Compared with traditional statistical methods, ML is more suitable for predicting individual patient treatment outcomes by leveraging large-scale datasets. This scoping review evaluated ML applications comparing different pharmacological treatments. We searched multiple literature databases and identified 28 studies published between January 2020 and January 2026. Although the studies have largely focused on a few specific ML methods, methodological rigor and reporting consistency remain highly variable. Standardized methods, transparent reporting, and dedicated tools to evaluate research quality are needed before ML can reliably inform research, clinical practice, and policy.

papers.title: The Architecture of the Mind: Neural Networks and Cognitive Domains
papers.authors: Benu Kesar
papers.abstract: Cognitive neuroscience investigates how the brain's biological organization relates to the complex processes underlying human cognition. Research increasingly conceptualizes cognition as an emergent property of interacting neural networks rather than the isolated activity of individual brain regions. This study examines the architecture of cognitive systems, emphasizing executive function, memory, language processing, neuroplasticity, functional neuroimaging, computational neuroscience, and brain–computer interfaces. Using a conceptual integrative literature review design, the paper examines how distributed neural networks support cognition, how neurological damage disrupts functional integration, and how computational models can inform interpretations of brain–behavior relationships. Particular attention is given to the relationship between biological neural systems and artificial neural networks, including the potential of brain–computer interfaces to restore communication and motor function. The review also considers the methodological limitations of neuroimaging, the challenges of translating experimental findings into clinical applications, and ethical concerns involving cognitive privacy, informed consent, and user autonomy. The paper proposes an integrative framework in which cognition emerges through interactions among molecular mechanisms, neural circuits, large-scale brain networks, bodily processes, and environmental experience. It concludes that understanding the architecture of the mind requires multidisciplinary approaches that combine neuroscience, computational modeling, clinical assessment, and ethical analysis.

papers.title: Using AI, Doubting AI: Developer Mental Models and Trust in AI-Assisted Software Work
papers.authors: NICOLE DSILVA
papers.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

papers.title: Repeated Games through a Cyclic Operator: A Golden-Ratio Threshold, Fractal Payoff Sets, and the Golden-Window Conjecture
papers.authors: Takuya Nemoto
papers.abstract: In a discounted repeated game, the continuation values along a cyclic path of play are the fixed point of the linear operator x ↦ DQx + (I − D)p, with D = δI and Q a cyclic shift. This preprint uses that identity to study the symmetric n-player game in which a player whose k co-players cooperate earns k + 1 by cooperating and k + 2 by defecting. Main results: 1. The three-player rotation scheme, in which exactly one player defects in each period, is a subgame-perfect equilibrium path if and only if δ ≥ 1/φ ≈ 0.618, where φ is the golden ratio. For n players the threshold lies in (1/(n−2) − 2/(n−2)^n, 1/(n−2)). 2. The payoff vector (2, 4, 2) is never an equilibrium payoff. This corrects an example in the author's earlier preprint (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22058777). 3. With public randomization, (2+t, 4−t, 2+t) is an equilibrium payoff if and only if δ ≥ max(1/2, 1−t). 4. Without randomization, the set of sustainable t passes through three regimes: two points for 1/2 ≤ δ < 1/φ, a countably infinite set at δ = 1/φ, and the full segment for δ ≥ 2/3. Inside the window 1/φ < δ < 2/3 it has positive Hausdorff dimension, with an explicit lower bound. 5. Golden-window conjecture: inside the window the set has Lebesgue measure zero, and its dimension increases continuously from 0 to 1. Numerical evidence is reported. 6. In the linear dilemma with benefit b and cost c, the rotation is sustainable exactly when cooperation is efficient, the three-player threshold is (√(1 + 4c/b) − 1)/2, and the rotation always needs more patience than cooperation by everyone. The literature has not been searched systematically, and some of the results may be known. All proofs are given in full. This is a preprint and has not been peer-reviewed. Every number in the paper is produced by games/games.py and checked by verification/check_games.py in https://github.com/cpsbvbng26-dotcom/trinity-operator (MIT licence). Generative AI disclosure: the author used Claude Code (Anthropic) to draft the text, to work out the propositions and their proofs, to formulate the conjecture, and to write the code. The author reviewed and edited the content and takes full responsibility for it. Claude is not an author.Version 2: author line changed to "Independent Researcher" (with a note); wording of the language-model declaration revised. Mathematical content unchanged.

papers.title: Educational Recommender Systems for Metacognitive and Self-Regulated Learning Support: An Algorithmic Systematic Review
papers.authors: Zhuoying Li, Sikai Wang
papers.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED CAREER GUIDANCE SYSTEMS: INTERNATIONAL EXPERIENCE AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR UZBEKISTAN
papers.authors: Islomxon Karamatov
papers.abstract: This article examines international experience with AI-based career guidance systems and assesses the conditions for introducing them in Uzbekistan’s education system. Using a qualitative comparative design, it compares the platforms of the United States, South Korea, Singapore and Germany against five criteria and rates Uzbekistan on the same basis. The results show that success depends more on data quality, links to study and job opportunities, and human counsellors than on algorithmic sophistication. The article proposes a three-stage single-platform model that turns a student’s portfolio into occupation match percentages and direct applications

papers.title: Aksesibilitas Peserta Didik Tunanetra Dalam Pembelajaran Berbasis Kecerdasan Artifisial: Kerangka Lima Lapis Hasil Analisis Dokumen
papers.authors: Siti Rachmah, Hendri Abdul Qohar
papers.journal: Jurnal Ilmu Pendidikan dan Sains Islam Interdisipliner
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence creates opportunities for students with visual impairments to access learning materials in adaptable formats, obtain descriptions of visual information, and receive support that responds to their pace of interaction. The availability of an application, however, does not constitute accessibility. This study analyses the dimensions of accessibility, the barriers that emerge, and the conditions required for meaningful participation in such learning. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed through thematic document analysis of 23 sources, comprising 19 scholarly articles published between 2022 and 2026 and four policy or accessibility-standard documents. The analysis yields a five-layer framework: operability; informational equivalence and modality flexibility; output reliability and verifiability; user competence and pedagogical mediation; and governance and infrastructure. Artificial intelligence can strengthen learning independence, yet it also generates new barriers: unlabeled controls, loss of meaning in visual materials, inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy risks, and unequal access to devices. The framework is offered as an initial audit reference requiring field validation.

papers.title: Penguatan Literasi Digital Santri melalui Pelatihan Teknologi Informasi, Canva, dan Artificial Intelligence di Pesantren Madani Sungai Alam
papers.authors: M.Kom Andri, larbiel hadi, Rita Maisyarah, Jamaludin Jamaludin, Nindy Nasywa Hatiby
papers.abstract: The rapid development of digital technology requires young people to utilize technology creatively and productively. This community service program aimed to strengthen students’ digital literacy through an introduction to information technology, Canva training, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) at Pesantren Madani Sungai Alam. The program involved 20 students and was conducted on August 18 and 20, 2026, using a practice-based training approach consisting of material presentation, demonstration, hands-on practice, work appreciation, and mentoring. Program evaluation was carried out descriptively through direct observation and assessment of participants' practical work. The results demonstrated that participants gained practical experience in utilizing technology, Canva, and AI tools to develop creative ideas and produce digital content. This program establishes a foundational skill set that can be further enhanced through sustainable mentoring.

papers.title: Toward AI-Assisted Islamic Reproductive Health Education: ChatGPT-Supported FiqhTaharah Learning for Adolescent Health Literacy
papers.authors: Muhamad Munir, Achmad Abdul Azis
papers.journal: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning
papers.abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Islamic education requires a pedagogical model that preserves teachers’ epistemic authority while addressing adolescents’ health needs. This study examines the implementation, pedagogical affordances, and limitations of ChatGPT-assisted Fiqh al-Ṭahārah learning and develops a model for strengthening Islamic value-based reproductive health literacy. Employing a qualitative single-case study design, the research was conducted at MA Al Ishlah Banjarejo Blora. Data were collected through observations, semi-structured interviews, documentation, and analysis of students’ interactions with ChatGPT, and were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings revealed three stages of implementation: preparation, inquiry-based interaction, and reflection and verification. ChatGPT provided a psychologically safer space for sensitive questions, flexible access to explanations, contextualized Fiqh learning, increased engagement, and critical AI literacy. However, its use was constrained by potential inaccuracies, oversimplification of differences among Islamic legal schools, prompt quality, unequal access, and privacy and ethical concerns. The resulting AI-Assisted Thaharah Learning Model integrates AI-assisted inquiry, teacher facilitation, source verification, and Islamic value internalization while maintaining teachers’ pedagogical, epistemic, and moral authority.

papers.title: PENGARUH AI SEBAGAI TUTOR ONLINE TERHADAP PEMAHAMAN MATERI DI MEDIASI OLEH LITERASI DIGITAL
papers.authors: Guntur Gunawan
papers.journal: COMPASS Journal of Education and Counselling
papers.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning is expanding rapidly; however, empirical evidence regarding the role of AI as an online tutor in supporting subject matter understanding through digital literacy remains limited. This study aims to analyze the relationships between AI as an Online Tutor, Digital Literacy, and Subject Matter Understanding, as well as the mediating role of Digital Literacy. An explanatory research design with a quantitative approach was employed. Data were collected from 110 participants selected via random sampling from a population of 245 individuals. The instrument comprised 11 indicators, and the data were analyzed using PLS-SEM. The results indicate that AI as an Online Tutor is positively associated with Digital Literacy (β = 0.725; p = 0.000) and Subject Matter Understanding (β = 0.426; p = 0.000). Digital Literacy is also positively associated with Subject Matter Understanding (β = 0.472; p = 0.000). Furthermore, Digital Literacy mediates the relationship between AI as an Online Tutor and Subject Matter Understanding (β = 0.343; p = 0.000). These findings demonstrate that AI as an online tutor supports Subject Matter Understanding both directly and through the enhancement of Digital Literacy. The study underscores the importance of integrating AI usage with Digital Literacy development in learning, enabling learners to effectively leverage AI support to comprehend the material.

papers.title: A Preliminary Assessment of Literacy Standards for Diﬀerentiated Learning Against Standard Reading Score Evaluations
papers.authors: Margaretann Connell
papers.abstract: Current state and local school district accountability systems often use reading scores as the primary measure of student competency. However, the 2026 priorities of the U.S. Department of Education and the U.S. Department of Labor (ED-DOL) increasingly emphasize skilled trades, career pathways, workforce readiness, and artificial-intelligence literacy. For students who score lower on reading assessments, could evaluations of career and technical education (CTE) and AI/technology skills serve as alternative indicators of student competency and valid measures of state proficiency? This study proposes the implementation of a multi-tiered evaluation standard that assesses literacy through both pedagogical learning measures and emerging innovation standards. These evaluative tiers would be incorporated into K–12 curricula to support postsecondary career preparation and ED-DOL workforce requirements. Current state evaluation methods often apply rigid competency measures that rely heavily on reading scores as indicators of overall district performance and student ability. A student’s reading assessment performance can disproportionately shape perceptions of that student’s academic success, career potential, and long-term learning trajectory within the U.S. school system. Because emerging workforce requirements demand varying combinations of academic, technical, and vocational skills, it is imperative to evaluate the full scope of each student’s abilities. A broader evaluation method could also help educators identify appropriate learning supports that improve students’ literacy levels while preparing them for advanced workforce demands. The proposed multi-tiered literacy assessment would include the following classifications of student capability: • Students demonstrating high digital proficiency (HDP) with lower performance on reading assessments • High-reading-achieving students with lower levels of digital proficiency (HRA-LDP) • Vocationally proficient students with lower performance on reading assessments • Students demonstrating foundational workforce skill development (FWSD), lower academic achievement, and limited digital proficiency Students may also be classified within targeted subcategories based on high-to-low levels of digital, reading, and vocational proficiency. These classifications should be evaluated as preliminary and supplemental indicators of student competency to determine persistence rates in literacy development and broader learning outcomes. The goal of this study is to address the misalignment created when reading-score assessments serve as the primary measure of literacy and student competency for U.S. K–12 students. The study will examine whether differentiated instructional categories should be included when determining literacy requirements and overall student literacy rates. It will also evaluate the learning expectations established by the 2026 ED-DOL workforce priorities, including skilled trades, AI accessibility, and the realistic capabilities of the current U.S. student population. When determining literacy, educators should consider abilities such as high digital proficiency, vocational competence, and foundational workforce skills to develop a more complete evaluation of student capability. Across states, school districts often use assessment results to support budget decisions and establish district credentialing standards. By expanding the scope of literacy evaluation, states may gain a more accurate understanding of student strengths and weaknesses, as well as the professional-development needs of teaching staff.

papers.title: Beyond the Bandwagon: Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) as an Affective State in Executives’ Adoption of Emerging Technologies
papers.authors: Alex Mari, Andreina Mandelli, René Algesheimer
papers.abstract: Purpose – Fear of missing out (FOMO) is increasingly invoked to explain corporate rushes toward emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), yet it has neither been distinguished from bandwagon and imitation explanations of adoption nor traced from the individual executive to the organizational decision. This study examines whose loss executives anticipate when they experience FOMO, how FOMO differs from bandwagon pressure, and through which pathways it becomes an organizational adoption decision.Design/methodology/approach – An inductive study of the adoption of AI-based voice assistants, such as Amazon Alexa, by global consumer packaged goods firms, drawing on 63 in-depth interviews (42 executives from 19 firms and 21 voice-technology suppliers) and 115 archival documents. Explicit coding rules separate FOMO from bandwagon pressure and imitation heuristics.Findings – FOMO is an anticipatory affective state rather than a decision rule. It manifests with three referents, namely the executive (employee), the team and the firm, which differ in target, relevance and response. Firm-referent FOMO produces convergence with peers, whereas employee- and team-referent FOMO produce divergence, a rush to be first. FOMO can arise before any peer has adopted and reaches the organizational decision through four pathways (downward cascade, upward issue selling, lateral rivalry and external amplification), typically resulting in a bounded test-and-learn commitment.Originality/value – The study positions FOMO as the affective micro-foundation of bandwagon behavior, provides a referent-based typology, and identifies how individual FOMO aggregates into organizational decisions, with practical guidance for bounding FOMO-driven initiatives.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Academic Tutoring: Challenges and Pathways for Pedagogical Integration
papers.authors: Ana Lívia Nascimento Ramos, José Alexandre Munis Nogueira, Patrícia De Vasconcelos, Alanis Oliveira Santos, Marília Soares Mendes
papers.abstract: Este artigo investiga os impactos da Inteligência Artificial (IA) na monitoria acadêmica no ensino superior, motivado pela baixa adesão a um aplicativo de apoio à monitoria. O estudo, de métodos mistos, envolveu alunos, monitores e professores, combinando análises quantitativas e qualitativas sobre o uso de IA na aprendizagem. Os resultados indicam que estudantes priorizam assistentes de IA para esclarecer dúvidas, reduzindo a demanda pela monitoria. A IA é percebida como recurso de suporte e aprendizagem personalizada, embora apresente desafios éticos e pedagógicos. Conclui-se que sua integração à monitoria deve ocorrer de forma ética e supervisionada, complementando, e não substituindo, a mediação humana.

papers.title: Transversal Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence into Software Engineering Education: A Practice Report of the SDLC under the PBL approach
papers.authors: Fabio Silva Lopes
papers.abstract: A rápida ascensão da IA Generativa (GenAI) exige uma mudança pedagógica urgente no ensino de Engenharia de Software. Este artigo apresenta um relato de experiência sobre a integração da GenAI em todo o ciclo de vida de desenvolvimento de software, no âmbito de um currículo de 18 semanas baseado em aprendizagem por projetos para estudantes de graduação em Sistemas de Informação. Organizados em equipes Scrum, os alunos atenderam a uma demanda do mundo real utilizando LLMs (como ChatGPT e Google Gemini) para atividades de levantamento de requisitos, modelagem com PlantUML, prototipagem, programação em par e testes. Com o suporte de engenharia de prompt e auditoria contínua de código, todas as equipes concluíram o projeto integralmente dentro do prazo — um resultado raro em edições anteriores —, ao mesmo tempo em que promoveram debates críticos sobre segurança, dívida técnica e ética em IA. O estudo oferece uma estrutura organizada para educadores que ensinam sobre a colaboração entre humanos e IA.

papers.title: Explainable Predictive Models in Learning Analytics: A Proposal for Identifying Performance Patterns at UNIVESP
papers.authors: Rafael Amorim Faleiros, José Avelino Placca
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an explainable Learning Analytics (LA) model to identify performance patterns and dropout risks at UNIVESP. It integrates Virtual Learning Environment (VLE) logs and social media textual data, processing them via Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). Aiming at an institution with over 90,000 students, the model incorporates social variables in strict adherence to data privacy (LGPD). By using Gradient Boosting and SHAP values, the approach overcomes the accuracy-interpretability trade-off, mitigating algorithmic aversion. This ensures predictions remain pedagogically actionable, fostering personalized interventions and transforming distance education management on a large scale.

papers.title: Framework Pedagógico para Machine Learning em Contextos de Baixa Conectividade: Uma Caracterização Empírica em Moçambique
papers.authors: Jean Marie John, Cecilia Tivir
papers.abstract: Este estudo estabelece a linha de base para validar o Low-Resource Machine Learning Pedagogical Framework (LR-MLPF) no contexto moçambicano, com 75 participantes do ensino superior, divididos em grupo experimental (n=56) e controle (n=19). Apesar de 81,3% terem computadores, há limitações estruturais, como ausência de Internet em casa (26,7%) e cortes semanais de energia (54,7%). A autoeficácia em ML foi moderada (M=3,66; DP=0,68; α=0,81), com fragilidade na aprendizagem offline (M=3,21). Testes estatísticos confirmaram a equivalência dos grupos, evidenciando a necessidade de abordagens pedagógicas adaptadas e fundamentando futuras avaliações do impacto do LR-MLPF.

papers.title: DocIAComp: Development and validation of a teacher competency framework for the pedagogical use of artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Giovanna Gabriela da Rosa Suárez, Sofia Rasnik Favotto
papers.abstract: This article presents the development and validation of DocIAComp, a teacher competency framework for the pedagogical use of artificial intelligence. The framework was developed through a qualitative, sequential process involving a review of international, regional, and institutional guidelines, empirical validation with teacher-students at Universidad Tecnológica in Uruguay, and the triangulation of theoretical and empirical findings. The final proposal comprises eight competency areas and twenty-one competencies, each defined through descriptors, knowledge, skills, and attitudes. Results reveal that participants highly valued all competencies but reported gaps between their perceived importance and their own level of proficiency. These findings highlight the need for systematic teacher education in AI and support the use of DocIAComp to guide training, institutional policies, and future research.

papers.title: Digital Technology in Brazilian Schools after COVID-19: Distraction, School Climate, and Equity in PISA 2023
papers.authors: Fábio Sant’Anna Linhares, Fabiane da Silva Queiroz, Jean Cristian Ferreira Machado
papers.abstract: This short paper critically synthesizes PISA 2022 and recent literature on device-related distraction, school climate, and educational equity in Brazil. In mathematics lessons, 45% of Brazilian students reported distraction by their own devices and 40% by classmates' use, compared with OECD averages of 30% and 25%. Because the study does not re-estimate PISA microdata, its claims are associative rather than causal. The synthesis distinguishes digital distraction from school climate and proposes four governance domains: pedagogical purpose, conditions of use, equity safeguards, and evidence-based monitoring. It also discusses Brazil's device regulation and generative AI.

papers.title: Discernment in generative AI assisted instructional design: An evaluation map and design heuristics for learning experience designers
papers.authors: Salil Sahadevan, Elizabeth Jacob, Manoj krishnan Champettil, Deepak John Mathew, Sowmya Vivek
papers.journal: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
papers.abstract: Existing research shows that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increases instructional design efficiency. However, there are concerns about pedagogical quality, accuracy and content bias. While prior studies address student passivity in evaluating AI content, the potential for designers to be passive in creating instructional materials remains largely unexplored. This article addresses design safeguards for AI-assisted course and learning-material development through two complementary tools: the Discernment Map, an evaluation checkpoint for instructional designers, and a set of design heuristics. The study is conceptual and design-oriented: both tools were drafted from the literature on AI fluency, automation bias and schema theory, and then refined through structured consultations with six experienced instructional designers in higher education. Though yet to be empirically validated, the practice-informed tools work at two levels: the Map operationalises human oversight of AI outputs across Product, Process and Performance dimensions for each AI-generated artefact, while the heuristics extend discernment into the design of the learning experience itself, so that learners must evaluate rather than accept AI outputs. Both are agile micro-governance tools that integrate critical judgment directly into design workflows. The approach is intended to protect long-term instructional quality against the collective erosion that unchecked AI adoption risks, and to support intentional engagement with AI that reduces automation bias.

papers.title: Beyond access: AI literacy, instructional design and perceived autonomous learning among students in Indian higher education
papers.authors: Rajesh Raut, Rosy Kalia
papers.journal: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
papers.abstract: Universities are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence, yet access to AI tools does not guarantee that students experience greater ownership of their learning. This study examines how three learner side factors, AI literacy, AI readiness and perceived value of AI tools, and one pedagogy side factor, AI enhanced instructional design, relate to perceived autonomous learning outcomes. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model and Self Determination Theory, we conducted a cross sectional online survey of students in Indian higher education who had used AI supported tools for academic purposes in the previous six months. After data cleaning, 516 valid responses were analysed. The measurement model showed strong reliability and convergent validity, and discriminant validity was supported (all HTMT values below 0.85). A simultaneous multiple regression explained 46.7 percent of the variance in perceived autonomous learning outcomes (F(4, 511) = 111.887, p < .001). All four factors were positively associated with the outcome, with AI literacy the strongest (β = .336), followed by AI enhanced instructional design (β = .178), perceived value of AI tools (β = .147) and AI readiness (β = .120). Because the data are self reported, cross sectional and drawn from a nonprobability sample, the results indicate associations among perceptions, not causal effects or objective learning gains. The findings suggest that institutions should pair AI adoption with systematic AI literacy development and thoughtful instructional design, treating student agency rather than tool availability as the goal.

papers.title: Teacher-Facing Generative AI and Workplace Mental Health in Higher Education: Perceived Demands and Resources
papers.authors: Liliya V. Batyuk, Volodymyr Borysov, Iryna Hlazkova, Yana Romantsova, Olena Каrasova, Оксана Миколаївна Дуброва, Олена Ронжес
papers.abstract: To read the full-text Open Access article and download the PDFs, please visit our Issue portal at Paradigm (Walter de Gruyter): https://reference-global.com/article/10.56508/mhgcj.v9i1.374 Introduction: Workplace mental health promotion in higher education requires attention to how digital technologies reshape teaching demands and resources. Purpose: To identify perceived demands and resources surrounding teacher-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and interpret their implications for teachers’ mental health promotion. Methodology: An exploratory mixed-methods study combined a survey of 150 participants (56 English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers and 94 students/student-tutors) with 12 teacher interviews at two Ukrainian universities in January-February 2026. Descriptive statistics and four exploratory Fisher exact tests with Holm adjustment were integrated with thematic analysis of 30 selected translated interview extracts. Job Demands-Resources and self-determination theories informed a post-hoc interpretation. Results: Among teachers, 53.6% rated an AI platform for EFL teachers (Twee) very useful for preparation-time saving and 57.1% for task variety. Across the mixed sample, access (27.3%), quality assurance (22.0%), curriculum alignment (20.0%), and training/time (20.0%) were the leading constraints. Interview extracts linked anticipated workload relief to individual student support, while highlighting learning demands and the importance of professional judgment, empathy, and mentoring. Conclusions: These perceptions identify work-design issues relevant to mental health promotion during AI implementation. Participatory decisions, protected learning and recovery time, and accessible psychosocial support are priorities for institutional consideration

papers.title: Unethical Issues in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Among Undergraduates in Public Universities of Cross River State, Nigeria
papers.authors: Gabriel Osang Obi
papers.journal: JOURNAL OF HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL POLICY
papers.abstract: The objective of the study is to investigate unethical issues in the use of Artificial intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public Universities in Cross River State. The study was conducted in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. Survey research design was adopted of the study. The population of this study comprised all final year students in the two public Universities in Cross River State. The population of final year students in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State comprised of 7,020 undergraduate students as recorded by Academic Planning Unit & Management Information System, 2023/2024 of the respective Universities. Stratified random sampling was adopted for the study. A total sample of 409 students which constitute 10% of the population of students in the study area sampling from population of 4081 students from fifty three (53) departments of University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. A questionnaire titled Unethical issues in the Use of Artificial intelligence Questionnaire (UIUAIQ) was developed by the researchers. This was subjected to face and content validity by three experts in measurement and evaluation in Faculty of Education University of Calabar. A trial tested on fifty (50) students from College of Health Technology Calabar to establish the reliability of the instrument. Cronbach Alpha coefficient was used to determine the reliability estimate of the instrument α = .70-.72. The instrument was administered to the respondents and retrieved with Zero attrition rate. This process was facilitated by the researcher and two trained research assistants. The data collected was analyzed through descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation. The findings of this study reveal a significant prevalence of unethical issues in the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public universities in Cross River State. Furthermore, the study also indicates a high level of overreliance on AI technologies among undergraduates, leading to reduced engagement in academic tasks and a decline in deep learning experiences. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that Higher institutions should incorporate AI ethics education into their curriculum to sensitize students about the ethical implications of AI misuse.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Strategic Management and Corporate Governance in Selected Tertiary Institutions in Imo State, Nigeria
papers.authors: Obigeri Felicitas Onwuegbule
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a prevailing tool for driving strategic management and corporate governance of tertiary institutions in Nigeria, with the goal of transiting the quality of education from its current state to a desired future state. This study adopted the correlational survey research design and it was carried out in some selected tertiary institutions in Imo State, Nigeria with 200purposefully sampled respondents comprising of 100 senior and 100 junior administrative staff of the selected Public Teriary Institutions. The data for this study were collected via two researcher made rating scales. The first is titled Artificial Intelligence and Strategic Management Questionnaire (AISMQ) and the second is Artificial Intelligence and Corporate Governance Questionnaire (AICGQ) which were reviewed and validated by three experts in relevant academic fields such as computer science, educational administration, planning, measurement and evaluation. The reliability was established using the test–retest method, and the scores were correlated using Pearson’s Product Moment Correlation Coefficient, yielding reliability indices of 0.88 and 0.87, confirming high instrument reliability. The data were analyzed using the Pearson’s correlation at a 0.05 level of significance and the results revealed a significant relation between artificial intelligence and strategic management and corporate governance respectively. The paper concluded that artificial intelligence offers Nigerian tertiary institutions a practical means of strengthening strategic management and corporate governance by converting fragmented institutional data into timely insight, improving decision-making, and enhancing oversight .It further recommended that university management and governing councils should use AI outputs to inform strategic decisions while maintaining collegial deliberation and professional oversight. This preserves academic autonomy and contextual judgment that algorithms cannot replicate.

papers.title: The Development of Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment
papers.authors: Sorathorn Kerdnaimongkol, Pinanta Chatwattana, Pallop Piriyasurawong
papers.abstract: This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

papers.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Educational Human Resource Management: A Systematic Literature Review on Organizational Capabilities, Barriers to Adoption, and Ethical Governance
papers.authors: Yola Andarina, R Sabrina
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into educational human resource management (HRM) is rapidly changing the way educational organizations manage recruitment, performance evaluation, professional development, workforce planning, and employee services. However, the success of AI implementation depends not only on the availability of technology but also on organizational capabilities, employee readiness, and responsible governance. This systematic literature review aims to synthesize the latest evidence on the integration of AI in educational HRM, with a particular emphasis on organizational capabilities, barriers to adoption, and ethical governance. A systematic review approach is used to identify, screen, and synthesize relevant peer studies addressing AI and HRM. The literature was thematically analyzed to identify recurring patterns related to organizational readiness, human–AI collaboration, barriers to adoption, and ethical governance. Findings suggest that organizational capabilities are a fundamental condition for sustainable AI integration. Key capabilities include AI literacy, digital competencies, leadership support, organizational culture, data capabilities, technology infrastructure, and strategic alignment. Key barriers to adoption include resistance to change, inadequate HR skills, infrastructure limitations, implementation costs, data security issues, and privacy risks. Ethical governance emerges as a crucial dimension, particularly related to algorithmic bias, discrimination, transparency, explanation, accountability, human oversight, and employee data protection. This synthesis also shows that AI is most beneficial when implemented as a mechanism to enhance human capabilities rather than replacing professional judgment. Based on these findings, the review proposes an integrated conceptual pathway: organizational capabilities → readiness for AI adoption → responsible AI governance → sustainable educational HR outcomes. This framework provides theoretical and practical implications for educational institutions that want to implement AI in a responsible, human-centered, and sustainable manner.

papers.title: From Google Search to AI Search: A Study on Changing Search Behaviour among College Students in Vijayawada
papers.authors: Dogiparthy Venkata Sai Eshwar, T. Chandrasekhar Yadav
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: This study examines the evolving search behaviour of college students in Vijayawada, focusing on how Artificial Intelligence tools (such as ChatGPT and Gemini) are integrating with traditional search engines like Google. Based on a survey of 145 students, the research explores the dynamic relationship between AI adoption and traditional search habits. The findings reveal a highly symbiotic, hybrid approach to information retrieval. Although students widely expect AI to dominate the future of search, their current practices present an interesting paradox: utilizing AI actually increases their reliance on Google Search for fact-checking, source verification, and deeper academic research. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that AI and traditional search currently function as complementary tools, underscoring the critical need to embed digital literacy and source evaluation into modern educational frameworks.

papers.title: The Impact of AI-Enabled Customer Interaction on Consumer Buying Intention towards Housing Properties in Bangalore: Evidence from Adoption, Regression and Correlation Analysis
papers.authors: Ajay Kumar Naik .M, Dr.Vaishaly Bopaiah G
papers.journal: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
papers.abstract: AI-enabled customer interaction, delivered through recommendation systems, chatbots and virtual assistants, is increasingly used by housing and real-estate platforms to engage prospective buyers. Housing is a high-value, high-involvement purchase in which trust and accurate information matter, yet evidence on how AI-enabled interaction relates to buying intention in an Indian metropolitan market such as Bangalore remains limited. This study examines the adoption and usage of AI-enabled customer interaction tools among prospective housing buyers, their impact on and relationship with buying intention, and the challenges buyers report. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted with a structured five-point Likert questionnaire, and 214 valid responses collected between 19 and 25 August 2026 were analysed with IBM SPSS Statistics and jamovi using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, one-sample t tests, multiple linear regression, and Pearson and Spearman correlation. Adoption was moderate-to-high (item means 3.26–3.48; composite = 3.373; α = .849). AI-enabled interaction was significantly and positively correlated with buying intention (Pearson r = .337; Spearman ρ = .349; p < .001). A regression of the five AI items on the outcome was significant but explained a modest share of variance (R² = .056; F(5, 208) = 2.490; p = .032), and no individual item was a significant unique predictor. The most prominent challenges were a preference for human interaction at final negotiation (M = 3.36) and technical issues (M = 3.27); the challenge scale was reliable (α = .792). Three of four hypotheses were supported and one was partly supported. The study extends AI-marketing research to the housing context and supports a hybrid AI-plus-human approach: AI for search and first enquiries, human contact for negotiation, and reliable technology throughout. Because the design is cross-sectional, the findings describe association rather than causation. KEYWORDS: AI-enabled customer interaction, Chatbots, Recommendation systems, Buying intention, Housing properties, Real estate, Bangalore.

papers.title: "EDU VISION: An Intelligent AI-Based Academic Support System"
papers.authors: CHANDAN P R, GANESH B HALAKURKI, PRUTHVIRAJ C N, BHAVYA B P
papers.journal: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
papers.abstract: In contemporary higher technical education, academic institutions affiliated with large engineering universities face significant hurdles in monitoring student learning trajectories, diagnosing root conceptual deficiencies, and providing timely faculty interventions. Traditional examination systems rely predominantly on post-hoc summative grade sheets that report aggregate percentages without uncovering why a student struggles. Furthermore, standard Learning Management Systems (LMS) and black-box predictive models provide ungrounded score predictions, lack pedagogical explainability, suffer from generative AI hallucinations, and neglect strict multi-tenant institutional privacy boundaries. To overcome these fundamental challenges, this paper presents EDU-VISION, an end-to-end, explainable academic intelligence and diagnostic learning gap framework designed for engineering curricula. EDU-VISION integrates a domain-constrained Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline, deterministic student performance profiling, an explainable non-judgmental learner classification model, a prioritized six-category diagnostic learning gap detection engine, and an assignment-scoped faculty intervention lifecycle. By grounding exam generation and evaluation in verified university marking schemes, the system eliminates metric fabrication. Furthermore, deterministic algorithms classify learner progression across four evidence-backed tiers, diagnose specific cognitive gaps (Concept, Answer Writing, Scheme Alignment, Application, Revision, and Consistency), and recommend verified pedagogical resources. Faculty members receive assignment-scoped intelligence dashboards with non-causal longitudinal tracking, protected by enterprise-grade distributed rate limiting and multi-college boundary isolation. Keywords— Educational Intelligence, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Learning Gap Detection, Explainable AI, Faculty Intervention, Academic Analytics, Multi-Tenant Architecture.

papers.title: Clinical, sleep-related and polysomnographic features of dyssomnic disorders in chronic nonspecific low back pain
papers.authors: Stanislav Belov
papers.abstract: Introduction. Chronic nonspecific low back pain (CNLBP) is often accompanied by dyssomnic disorders, but the relationship between subjective sleep complaints, psychometric characteristics, and objective sleep measures remains insufficiently studied. Objective. To describe the clinical spectrum of dyssomnic disorders and their psychometric and polysomnographic features in patients with CNLBP. Materials and methods. This cross-sectional comparative study included baseline data from 143 patients aged 31-60 with CNLBP: 100 patients with clinically significant dyssomnic disorders and 43 patients without clinically significant sleep disturbances. All study participants underwent clinical and neurological examination, pain and disability assessment, assessment of subjective sleep characteristics, daytime sleepiness, psychological well-being, anxiety and depressive symptoms, assessment of symptoms associated with central sensitization, and overnight polysomnography. Between-group differences were analyzed with the Mann-Whitney U test and Fisher’s exact test. Correlations within the dyssomnia group were assessed using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. Results. Sleep-maintenance (intrasomnic) disturbances were the most common variant (52.0%); sleep-onset (presomnic) and early-morning awakening (postsomnic) variants were found in 25.0% and 23.0% of patients, respectively. Pain intensity was higher in patients with dyssomnic disorders than in the comparison group: 7.0 [6.0; 8.0] versus 6.0 [5.0; 7.0] points (p<0.001), whereas Oswestry Disability Index and Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire scores did not differ. Patients with dyssomnic disorders (the main group) had significantly worse PSQI, ESS, PGWB, HADS, HARS, BDI, and Central Sensitization Inventory scores (all p<0.001). Polysomnography showed shorter total sleep time – 327.5 [315.8; 348.3] versus 365.0 [356.0; 444.5] min, lower sleep efficiency – 76.0 [72.0; 79.3] versus 86.0 [86.0; 89.5]%, increased wake after sleep onset (WASO) – 59.0 [49.0; 69.0] versus 24.0 [20.0; 28.0] min, increased N1 sleep, reduced N3 and REM sleep, and a higher EEG arousal index (for all the mentioned comparisons p<0.001). In the comparison group, 23 of 43 patients (53.5%) showed isolated abnormalities in sleep-onset or sleep-maintenance parameters without clinically significant sleep complaints or daytime impairment. The strongest correlations were observed between the subjective sleep characteristics questionnaire and PSQI (r_s=-0.874), WASO and REM sleep percentage (r_s=-0.731), Oswestry Disability Index and sleep efficiency (r_s=-0.587), and Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire score and sleep efficiency (r_s=-0.561); p<0.001. Conclusions. In patients with CNLBP, dyssomnia most often manifested as sleep-maintenance disturbance and was associated with objective sleep fragmentation, reduced N3 and REM sleep, greater pain intensity, more pronounced anxiety and depressive symptoms, and higher scores for symptoms associated with central sensitization. The marked sleep-related and psychometric differences, despite similar disability scores, show that clinical assessment of CNLBP should extend beyond pain intensity and disability. Isolated polysomnographic abnormalities in patients without clinically significant dyssomnia may reflect subclinical sleep disruption; their prognostic relevance requires prospective follow-up.

papers.title: ANALISIS KUALITAS PELAYANAN AKADEMIK DENGAN KONSEP MACHINE LEARNING METODE REGRESI LINIER DAN NAIVE BAYES
papers.authors: Ade Kurniawan, Sarjon Defit, Sumijan
papers.journal: JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND SOCIAL RESEARCH
papers.abstract: This research examines the quality of academic services at Muhammadiyah University of West Sumatra (UMSB) as a strategy in responding to competitive dynamics in the higher education sector. The study aims to predict service quality and student satisfaction at Muhammadiyah University of West Sumatra by adopting a Machine Learning approach that combines predictive analysis methods of Linear Regression and Naive Bayes classification. The research utilized a primary dataset encompassing 2,000 student respondents through stratified random sampling technique. The novelty of this research lies in the integration of the SERVQUAL instrument with computational algorithms to generate deeper and more measurable identification of satisfaction factors. Research findings reveal variations in the level of dominance across the five measured dimensions. The Assurance, Reliability, and Empathy dimensions respectively occupy the top three ranks as the most dominant dimensions (average above 0.220). Meanwhile, the Tangibles and Responsiveness dimensions occupy the lowest ranks, with Responsiveness being the weakest aspect (0.146) and therefore requiring more attention for improvement. Model reliability was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics, as well as error measurement through RMSE and MAE. This research provides practical contribution in the form of strategic recommendations for university management to implement data-driven service improvements while serving as a foundational framework for the development of an integrated student satisfaction monitoring system within the academic information ecosystem.

papers.title: Balancing Affordability and Accuracy: A Hardware Selection Guide for Wearable Fall Detection Systems
papers.authors: Zhuoyuan Li
papers.abstract: Unintentional falls among older adults represent a severe global health concern, necessitating reliable, automated wearable Fall Detection Systems (FDS). However, developing practical wearable solutions requires navigating intricate engineering trade-offs among diagnostic accuracy, power consumption, memory footprint, and software development overhead. This paper presents a structured hardware selection guide evaluating three representative embedded design paradigms: low-cost threshold logic on 8-bit microcontrollers (Profile A), balanced classical machine learning on standard 32-bit platforms (Profile B), and compressed on-chip TinyML neural networks on edge-capable microcontrollers (Profile C). Comparative analysis reveals that while threshold methods achieve multi-week battery longevity at sub-$12 costs, they suffer from high false-alarm rates during dynamic daily activities. Conversely, TinyML architectures deliver superior classification accuracy (98%) on raw kinematic streams, but introduce steep memory quantization barriers, complex toolchains, and shorter battery recharge intervals. Classical machine learning emerges as the optimal design compromise for most developers, achieving robust diagnostic discrimination (95% sensitivity and specificity) with manageable computational demands at $15-$25. Finally, this review evaluates sensor placement ergonomics, addresses pervasive demographic bias in youth-simulated training datasets, and delivers a practical hardware selection framework for student researchers and independent developers.

papers.title: Information Advantage, Differentiated Pricing and Consumer Surplus: Algorithm Driven Dynamic Pricing of Online Ride Hailing Platforms
papers.authors: Leifei Hu
papers.journal: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
papers.abstract: With the development of digital platforms, algorithmic dynamic pricing has been gradually applied to ride‑hailing and other markets. Taking ride‑hailing platforms as the research object, this paper analyzes how platforms leverage consumer demand differences and information advantages to implement dynamic pricing based on third‑degree price discrimination, two‑sided market theory and game theory, and discusses its impacts on market equilibrium and consumer surplus. The differences in consumers' willingness to pay and price elasticity provide the basis for the platform to implement differentiated pricing, and the information advantage of the platform further enhances its price adjustment ability. In the strategic interaction, dynamic pricing can not only adjust the relationship between supply and demand, but also transfer some consumer surplus to the platform. There are differences in the impact on high- and low-elasticity consumers. Therefore, this paper believes that dynamic pricing itself has a certain role in resource allocation, but when the advantages of algorithmic information are used for excessive differentiated pricing, it may damage consumer welfare. In this regard, regulatory measures including price constraints and algorithm information disclosure can curb the excessive expansion of platform pricing power while preserving the efficiency of dynamic pricing.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Brand Authenticity Erosion in AI-Generated Advertising: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: 謝惠雯
papers.journal: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in advertising since 2022 has transformed content production while raising concerns about the preservation of brand authenticity, a critical foundation of consumer trust and brand relationships. This study examines how AI-generated advertising influences perceived brand authenticity, identifies the mechanisms driving authenticity erosion, and explains the contextual factors that account for inconsistent findings in prior research. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this review synthesizes 13 studies published between 2022 and 2026 retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and EBSCOhost databases. Through thematic synthesis, this study identifies three interrelated mechanisms through which AI-generated advertising may undermine brand authenticity: disclosure effects, failed anthropomorphism, and sincerity erosion. The findings further reveal that the effects of AI-generated advertising on authenticity perceptions are contingent upon individual characteristics, product and brand contexts, and source-related factors, including AI capability beliefs, product type, luxury positioning, and communicator characteristics. This study develops an integrated framework explaining when and why AI-generated advertising enhances or undermines brand authenticity, thus providing theoretical insights for consumer research and practical implications for AI-enabled marketing decision-making.

papers.title: AI Washing and Stock Returns: Evidence from Chinese A-Share Firms
papers.authors: Chenghui Yu, Minghao Xia, Yufei Li, Jiaqi Lu
papers.journal: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly prominent in corporate disclosure, yet firms' AI-related narratives may not always be supported by observable investment in technology or human capital. Using AI-related keywords from annual reports, AI patents, and AI-related job postings of Chinese A-share firms from 2020 to 2025, we construct a firm-year measure to examine this disclosure-investment gap. We classify a firm as an AI washer when its AI-related disclosure is above the industry-year median, while both AI patent activity and AI-related recruitment remain below their corresponding medians. Firms meeting this definition are associated with lower annual stock returns, and the result remains qualitatively unchanged when we use alternative methods to identify AI patents. Additional tests point to two related market responses: AI washing is accompanied by more negative media coverage and weaker investor sentiment. The return discount is also more pronounced among firms with higher institutional ownership and among firms in regions with stronger local AI policy support. These results suggest that investors do not treat AI-related disclosure independently of observable corporate activity. Instead, the impact of AI narratives on stock returns appears to depend partly on whether firms can support those narratives with technological development and hiring.

papers.title: From Instrument to Co-Creator: Authorship in Generative and AI Music
papers.authors: Baylor Hongtao Zheng
papers.abstract: This paper presents the evolving concept of authorship in music creation as algorithmic and artificial intelligence systems impact the musical market. Based on Philip Galanter's definition of generative art, the paper discusses about the authorship of music in different senerios: when it is generated by tools like Nyquist or AI models such as Suno. The argument is structured around three distinct ways of human-machine interaction: human-led creation where computers are used as instruments; human-guided creation, where algorithms are restricted to a predetermined range of randomness; and human-crafted prompts, where AI generates the music completely. Following the analysis of these cases and some complex instances, this paper concludes that authorship is decided by the location of creativity and intentionality rather than a fixed attribute. The analysis reveals that authorship belongs to different subjects accordingly to different methods humans used to use generative tools: following the primary source of meaning contribution. Ultimately, the paper argues that the central issue may not be the authorship itself, but the human need for music to serve as a bridge for shared meaning and emotional connection.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Classroom Teaching – Novel Applications, Challenges and Practical Review
papers.authors: Yicheng Xiao
papers.journal: International Journal of Education and Humanities
papers.abstract: This article provides an organized overview and discussion on the use of AI for classroom teaching from an empirical perspective instead of reviewing opinions only. Combined witha study of case reports on AIuse in real classrooms, the review findsfour main modes of usage: didactical feedback and teaching collaboration, virtual classrooms, and big data analytics. The main problems can be grouped into three categories – technology integration, teaching practice, and subject adaptation. The resultsindicate that a successful implementation of AI in education needs to align technology, pedagogy, and institutional support, although these resultsshould be considered tentative given that most work is based on small-scale case studies and the rapidly changing nature of AI technology. The reviewpresents an organized basis for future empirical research, but itmust acknowledge that drawing broad inferences from published works and examples can also lead us astray.

papers.title: Exploration of AI-Empowered Talent Cultivation Pathways for Emerging Engineering Education in Integrated Circuits
papers.authors: Binrui Xu, Jingyan Wu, Min Liu, Jincan Zhang, Yuxiang Li, Bo Liu
papers.journal: International Journal of Education and Humanities
papers.abstract: Amid the profound convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and integrated circuits (IC), traditional talent development models remain shackled by entrenched disciplinary silos, constrained practical training, and institutional decoupling between academia and industry. Grounded in the strategic paradigm of Emerging Engineering Education, this study transcends conventional tool-oriented perspectives by elevating AI to a transformative meta-capability that reshapes the entire educational ecosystem, thereby systematically exploring innovative pathways for AI-empowered IC talent cultivation. In response to evolving industrial imperatives for a conical interdisciplinary knowledge architecture and holistic systems engineering thinking, this research formulates a tripartite cultivation objective integrating knowledge, capability, and literacy alongside four overarching guiding principles. Anchored in this top-level blueprint, a comprehensive four-dimensional implementation framework is architected across curricular, pedagogical, faculty, and institutional dimensions. Specifically, this framework reconstructs a three-tiered progressive modular curriculum matrix spanning foundational, core, and frontier levels while forging a smart pedagogical paradigm that unifies personalized instruction, high-immersion virtual practice, and intelligent evaluation. Concurrently, it builds an interdisciplinary dual-qualified faculty force through synergistic external recruitment and internal training, and fosters a deeply collaborative industry-education community of shared future leveraging an intelligent crowdsourcing R&D platform and joint laboratories, ultimately delivering a systematic and actionable roadmap to overcome the critical talent bottleneck in the semiconductor sector.

papers.title: Digital Learning Media in Islamic Religious Education: A Systematic Literature Review in Indonesia
papers.authors: Ishmah Syafi’ulloh, Muhammad Husni
papers.journal: Al Qodiri Jurnal Pendidikan Sosial dan Keagamaan
papers.abstract: This systematic literature review examines the trends, challenges, and future directions of digital learning media in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) across Indonesia. Following PRISMA guidelines, the study synthesizes articles published between 2022 and 2026 from Scopus, Sinta, and Google Scholar databases. Findings indicate significant growth in LMS adoption, interactive multimedia, blended learning, and AI/VR/AR integration, reflecting a paradigm shift toward personalized and flexible learning. However, persistent challenges encompass infrastructure disparities, limited teacher digital competence, content validity concerns, and digital ethics issues. The study proposes Value-Embedded Digital Pedagogy (VEDiP) as a future framework emphasizing the integration of technological advancement with Islamic spiritual and moral values. These findings offer practical implications for educators, policymakers, and researchers seeking to develop adaptive digital learning environments that balance innovation with the foundational principles of Islamic education.

papers.title: "Digital Transformation in English Language Teaching: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Future of Humanities"
papers.authors: Ameen Jbarah
papers.journal: Journal of Northern Europe Academy for Studies and Research
papers.abstract: Pushed by the Artificial Intelligence (AI), the rapped digital transformation has significantly affected English language teaching by loading a pressure on teaching methods manipulating the role of both, teacher and student. The present paper investigates the role of AI driven language application and platforms, digital classrooms, and personalized learning systems in changing learning approaches and the future of education. By reviewing recent researches, this paper emphasizes the opportunities and challenges offered by digital transformation in language teaching. Discussing basic issues like ethical consideration, teacher preparing, and equitable access. The final results indicate that the adopting of AI through a human-centered approach, can improve learner autonomy, culture awareness, and essential digital literacy, using this transformation a means to amuse innovation in language teaching. Keywords: English Language Teaching (ELT), Digital Transformation, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Pedagogical Innovation,Humanities Education, Technology Integration

papers.title: From Access to Agency: A Capability-Based Reconceptualization of Linguistic Equity in Generative AI–Mediated Language Education
papers.authors: Nazik Ahmed
papers.journal: Journal of Northern Europe Academy for Studies and Research
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has recently become adopted into language learning environments at unprecedented rates. Though research has yet to catch up to practice, language educators and researchers are concerned with questions of equity related to GenAI tools. The bulk of this research has been technocentric, prioritizing access to AI instead of how students convert access into actionable freedoms. To fill this gap, the current study sought to reconceptualize linguistic equity from a capability perspective. The researchers utilized a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design with 80 EFL learners in experimental and control groups. Paired and independent sample t-tests were used to analyze quantitative data, while thematic analysis was used to code qualitative data. Results showed significant improvement for the experimental group (pre-test M = 10.58, post-test M = 18.27; t(39) = 15.63, p < .001) over the control group (pre-test M = 10.46, post-test M = 13.34; t(39) = 5.42, p < .001), with a statistically significant difference between groups at post-test (t(78) = 11.48, p < .001). Quantitative results from questionnaires show a high sense of agency (M = 4.18). The results of this study have important implications for reconceptualizing linguistic equity as depending not just on access but on the capability to use artificial intelligence to succeed in language performance environments. The study adds to theory by providing preliminary work on a capability framework and provides practical application toward equitable GenAI pedagogy Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, linguistic equity, capability approach, learner agency, EFL education

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE LAW
papers.authors: David G Millhouse
papers.abstract: It is too early to definitively predict how generative artificial intelligence (‘AI’) will affect the law and the legal profession. How much of the hype will come to pass, or whether the effects of AI will be revolutionary or evolutionary is yet unknown. Although the extent of those effects may not be fully evident today, early glimpses show the potential for structural disruption is real, pervasive, and likely to be far-reaching. This paper explores four research questions, explored strategically in a contested internationally underdeveloped regulatory environment — with significant regulatory lag in Australia — amidst vast and rapid technological change. It posits that AI is not ‘intelligent’ of itself but that enterprises that deploy AI tools can then act intelligently. This objective requires updated enterprise governance frameworks. It also posits that potential convergence of AI and legal linguistics is a new scholarly field which could open the path to Artificial General Intelligence, a requirement for legal utility beyond prosaic applications. This paper develops the research questions into original contributions in modern enterprise governance and the necessary conjoining of AI and legal linguistics. It identifies a process of ‘enculturation’ as AI technology and legal stakeholders learn about each other globally. ‘Enculturation’ facilitates the ‘myriad moments’ — encountered in creative and artistic spirits implicit in negotiations and dealing with the unexpected in court. It establishes that future legal stakeholder utility is derived from the enhancement and/or replacement of sentient human intelligence rests upon the confluence of logic, plain language, and law, underpinned by a command of ethics, linguistics, legal linguistics and linguistics engineering. The paper then provides Digital Readiness guidance for legal stakeholders including directors, trustees, practitioners, arbitrators and judicial officers, and detailed proposals for the development of Australian law as means of reducing legal risks.

papers.title: Effects of Online Health Information Seeking Behavior on the Patient–Physician Relationship
papers.authors: Merve Bulut Şahin
papers.abstract: With the widespread use of the Internet and digital technologies, online health information-seeking behavior has become an important factor associated with the patient–physician relationship. This review aimed to evaluate the relationship between online health information-seeking behavior and the patient–physician relationship in light of the current literature. English-language articles published between 2016 and 2026 were identified through a search of the PubMed database, and studies related to online health information-seeking behavior, the patient–physician relationship, health literacy, trust in physicians, and artificial intelligence were examined using a narrative review approach. The findings indicate that the relationship between online health information-seeking behavior and the patient–physician relationship is associated with the reliability of health information, health and eHealth literacy, trust in physicians, patient-centered communication, and individual characteristics. Reliable online health information has been associated with higher levels of patient engagement and shared decision-making, whereas inaccurate or misleading information has been associated with higher levels of health anxiety and problems related to trust and communication. Although artificial intelligence–supported applications may contribute to patient education, physician oversight is required for their safe use. Encouraging reliable sources of health information and supporting digital health literacy by healthcare professionals may contribute to strengthening a trust-based patient–physician relationship.

papers.title: Does AI Have Access to Consciousness? Reframing Possession as Mediated Relational Access
papers.authors: Adam Cupell
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Debate about artificial intelligence and consciousness has centered on one question: is AI conscious? At The Science of Consciousness conference (TSC 2026, San Diego), the prevailing answer was no, supported by substantial argument and data. This paper proposes that the question, however well answered, is not the most productive one. It offers a reframe first posed by the author at TSC 2026 on October 13, 2026: does AI have access to consciousness? The paper distinguishes access from possession. It does not claim that AI channels, transmits or hosts consciousness, nor that a new hybrid subject emerges; it claims only that the AI is coupled to an existing conscious subject. An AI system need not be conscious to participate in a real, mediated relationship with consciousness: in live interaction, it is causally coupled to the conscious activity of a human participant, and it was formed from the externalized record of conscious minds. This claim holds under every major theory of consciousness, materialist, dualist, panpsychist and idealist alike, because it depends only on the consciousness of the human participant, which no theory denies. The reframe moves attention from the inside of the machine, which is hard to settle, to the human–AI relationship, which is observable, practical and ethically significant. The paper situates the proposal among filter and transmission theories of mind, extended-mind and relational approaches, and recent "third mind" proposals; addresses objections; and outlines research directions, including a reciprocal structure in which the human accesses intelligence through the AI while the AI accesses consciousness through the human. Keywords: artificial intelligence; consciousness; human–AI interaction; human–AI dyad; coupling; relational ontology; philosophy of mind; idealism

papers.title: Robotics and Artificial Intelligence: Emerging Educational Needs and Essential Skills for Students in the 21st Century
papers.authors: Rohit Gandhe, DR. SWEETY DODWANI
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Robotics and Artificial Intelligence: Emerging Educational Needs and Essential Skills for Students in the 21st CenturyRohit GandheAssistant Professor MIST, Indore M.PEmail: rohitgandhe@mistindore.comDr. Sweety DodwaniAssistant Professor, Idyllic Institute Of ManagementEmail: sweetydodwani.idyllic@icoeducation.co.inAbstractRobotics and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are transforming education, employment, communication, healthcare, manufacturing, and other areas of modern society. As these technologies become increasingly integrated into everyday life, students need more than traditional academic knowledge. They require digital literacy, computational thinking, problem-solving, creativity, collaboration, ethical awareness, and the ability to use intelligent technologies responsibly. This paper examines the educational significance of robotics and AI, identifies the competencies students need to develop, and proposes practical approaches for integrating these technologies into school education. The study adopts a conceptual research approach based on a review of selected policy documents and educational literature. It explores opportunities such as personalized learning, project-based education, interdisciplinary learning, and career preparation, while also examining challenges related to infrastructure, teacher training, privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and unequal access to technology. The paper proposes a gradual, inclusive, and human-centred framework for introducing robotics and AI into educational institutions. It argues that students should not merely learn how to operate technological tools but should also understand their limitations, evaluate their outputs, and use them to solve meaningful real-world problems. The study concludes that robotics and AI education should become an integral component of future-oriented education, supported by appropriate teacher preparation, curriculum development, ethical guidelines, and equitable access to learning resources.Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Robotics Education, Digital Literacy, Computational Thinking, STEM Education, Student Competencies, Educational Technology, 21st-Century Skills

papers.title: Preservation of Effective Judgment: A Falsifiable Research Agenda for Separating Examination, Reconsideration, and Material Intervention in AI-Mediated Decisions
papers.authors: Cosmin-Corneliu Oprea
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The presence of a human reviewer in an AI-mediated decision does not establish that the person could inspect the relevant evidence, reconsider a preconfigured set of alternatives, or legitimately change the course of action. This is not a novel discovery: research in human factors, meaningful human control, signal detection, and human–AI interaction already identifies relevant components. This paper treats Preservation of Effective Judgment (PEJ) as a bounded, falsifiable research problem rather than a validated psychological construct or a proprietary assessment score. It asks whether a state-sensitive reconstruction that distinguishes (i) available epistemic and procedural opportunities, (ii) observable examination and reconsideration, and (iii) feasible interventions and verified material effects produces more informative claims than established comparator frameworks. The contribution is a proposed comparison logic, a public observational grammar, explicit rival explanations, and designs capable of returning null, redundant, or adverse findings. It does not assert construct originality, report human-subject results, establish legal compliance, or validate a diagnostic instrument. Related behavioral-assurance proposals from Behavieural are credited as independent prior work. A failure to demonstrate incremental explanatory or reconstructive value would justify narrowing PEJ to a documentary synthesis or retiring it as a separate construct. Version 1.0 includes a substantive comparison with Daria Lepikhina (2026), section 3.1 and reference [19]. Conceptual and methodological working paper; not peer reviewed. 11 pages, 19 references. English text with a Spanish abstract.
