papers.title: AI-Powered Intelligent OCR with Document Understanding and Smart Error Correction
papers.authors: Veena Akuthota, Mahesh Bhukya, Vigneshwari Bodla Srinidhi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI-Powered Intelligent OCR: An Intelligent Document Processing System AI-Powered Intelligent OCR is a document processing system designed to extract, correct, and understand text from digital documents and scanned images. The system combines Optical Character Recognition (OCR) with artificial intelligence techniques to improve the usability and accessibility of extracted information. The system processes uploaded documents through image preprocessing, text recognition, text correction, document classification, and structured information extraction. It is designed to support document types such as invoices, receipts, resumes, prescriptions, identity cards, and handwritten notes. Additional features include text translation, text-to-speech conversion, document summarization, and chatbot-based question answering,Privacy and accuracy of the text helping users access and understand document content more efficiently. The system also supports exporting processed information into formats such as PDF, Word, and Excel, where implemented. The project aims to reduce manual data entry, improve document readability, simplify information retrieval, and support efficient document management in areas such as education, healthcare, banking, and human resources. Keywords: Intelligent OCR, Artificial Intelligence, Document Processing, Text Recognition, Information Extraction, Document Classification, Text Correction, Translation, Text-to-Speech, Document Summarization.

papers.title: AI Career Twin: A Human–AI Collaborative Framework for Dynamic Skill-Gap Analysis and Personalized Career Guidance
papers.authors: Vishal K, Subesh S, Shashidhar Rao, Sri Raghavendra, Dr D S Shaji
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI Career Twin is a proposed human–AI collaborative framework designed to support personalized career guidance, dynamic skill-gap analysis, and informed career decision-making. The framework addresses the limitations of traditional career recommendation systems, which often rely on static profiles and provide recommendations without considering evolving skills, changing industry requirements, or the uncertainty of available evidence. The proposed framework maintains a dynamic, time-indexed digital representation of an individual’s educational background, technical skills, professional experience, projects, certifications, career goals, and personal preferences. It integrates evidence-based skill assessment, labor-market analysis, explainable role recommendations, personalized learning pathways, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to provide transparent and context-aware career guidance. Key components of the proposed framework include: Dynamic skill profiling with separate proficiency and confidence estimates. Evidence-based skill-gap analysis using time-stamped labor-market information. Personalized career-role recommendations based on skills, goals, and constraints. Adaptive learning-path suggestions considering time, cost, and prerequisites. Retrieval-grounded AI mentoring with source citations and uncertainty handling. Human–AI collaboration through user feedback, corrections, and scenario-based career exploration. The paper presents the proposed system architecture, mathematical formulations, algorithmic methodology, and a structured evaluation protocol covering recommendation accuracy, skill-gap correctness, mentoring quality, and user interaction. Research Status: This publication presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation methodology. The system has not yet been implemented or experimentally evaluated. Future work includes prototype development, empirical validation, and user-centered evaluation. The research aims to establish a foundation for transparent, explainable, and evidence-based AI-assisted career guidance while preserving human control over career decisions. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, AI Career Twin, Human Digital Twin, Career Guidance, Skill-Gap Analysis, Personalized Recommendations, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Explainable AI, Human–AI Collaboration.

papers.title: From Artificial Minds on Screen to Adaptive AI Cinema:
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study applies the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM), Dynamic Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (D-SDM), Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), and Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL) to the historical development and future possibilities of artificial intelligence in cinema. The framework examines digital identity, source attribution, audience trust, narrative transitions, multilingual translation, creative autonomy, and ethical safeguards. Proposed innovations include a film-provenance model, interactive branching narratives, translation-repair protocols, and experimental methods for evaluating AI-generated cinematic experiences. Historical developments and contemporary AI-assisted filmmaking are distinguished from speculative capabilities involving multiple alternative feature films. Six falsifiable hypotheses and three proposed experimental designs establish a foundation for investigating human–AI cinematic interaction, creative control, and audience perception without claiming clinical validation or machine consciousness. https://www.youtube.com/@ScretchingQuantumPressLLC

papers.title: DEVELOPING SOCIOLINGUISTIC THINKING IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: PSYCHOLOGICAL AND PEDAGOGICAL PERSPECTIVES
papers.authors: Alisher Safaraliyevich Otaqulov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a new participant in everyday and educational communication. Learners now talk to chatbots, use machine translation and receive automated feedback on their writing. This conceptual paper examines how these tools affect the development of sociolinguistic thinking, understood as the ability to select, interpret and adapt language forms according to social context, participants and communicative goals. Drawing on sociocultural theory, social learning theory, sociolinguistics and intercultural pedagogy, the paper outlines the cognitive, social and emotional mechanisms involved and analyzes the opportunities and risks of AI as a language model and interlocutor. It then proposes five pedagogical conditions for developing sociolinguistic thinking in AI-supported learning environments: critical AI literacy, contextualized task design, teacher mediation, comparison of human and machine language, and a supportive psychological climate.

papers.title: Direction, execution and substitution in cognitive work with AI
papers.authors: Anna Thorsteinsdottir
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Disclosure of AI use in research and education records which tasks AI performed and how much of the work it did. Two constructed researchers show what that measure misses. One sets every decision in advance and lets an agentic system run the analysis for most of a day. The other receives a single reply pointing out a confound and rebuilds the study around it. The first reports far more AI use, but the second answers a question that AI reshaped. Three terms are proposed, each applied to one stage of one piece of work. Direction asks where the path of the work came from, with assisted and guided as its two ends. Execution asks how much of the implementation AI carried out. Substitution asks whether AI did thinking the person was meant to do themselves, and applies only where such a target has been set. Five constructed cases show that knowing two of the terms leaves the third open. A record of AI use can count Execution within the exchanges it shows, while assessing Direction and Substitution requires evidence beyond the record. Each term has a precedent in earlier work on automation, attribution of AI-assisted text and cognitive offloading. Measuring the terms is the next step.

papers.title: An AdS_{3} Dual for Supersymmetric MHV Celestial Amplitudes
papers.authors: Igor Mol
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: As I am discontinuing my research on celestial holography, I shall be uploading to this repository the documents that I have written on the subject in the past couple of months, in the hope that they might be useful to other researchers. The two documents appertaining to this repository would constitute my reply to the referee report and my resubmission to https://scipost.org/submissions/scipost_202509_00048v2/. In this new version of my manuscript "An AdS Dual for Supersymmetric MHV Celestial Amplitudes," I presented a detailed discussion of the problem of reconstructing the distributional celestial amplitudes, characterising the tree-level scattering of gravitons arranged into a maximally helicity-violating (MHV) configuration in general relativity and \mathcal{N}=8 supergravity, from the celestial leaf amplitudes, which I termed hyperbolic-slice correlators in the present manuscript. I gave an especial emphasis to the reconstruction theorems for the three-point hyperbolic-slice correlator, utilising a geometric reformulation of the Gel'fand-Shilov theory of homogeneous distributions, and the four-point hyperbolic-slice correlator, utilising the Dolan-Osborn formalism. Furthermore, I derived the reconstruction of the distributional celestial amplitudes from their leaf counterparts from a new formalism which I termed the Mellin-Barnes representation of hyperbolic-slice correlators, and the central observable of this new formalism is the so-called celestial Mack correlator. The key idea was to apply the theory of Symanzik and Mack to the Lorentzian hyperbolic-slice correlators for gravitons. I decided to dedicate some effort to the demonstration of the reconstruction theorems because, if I were to continue my research on flat-space holography, I would utilise this approach as the starting point of a research programme that I regarded as a reply to Tropper's ''Challenges to Understanding Celestial Holography from the Bottom Up''. I believe that it might be possible to apply the Polyakov-Mellin bootstrap, developed by R. Gopakumar and A. Sinha, to establish a Polyakov bootstrap for celestial holography, applied, however, to the hyperbolic-slice, or leaf, amplitudes, rather than the distributional amplitudes by themselves. In this manner, the reconstruction theorems would serve as the main tool translating between the n-point functions generated by the celestial version of the Polyakov bootstrap and the observables appertaining to the celestial CFT. Interestingly, it is possible to interpret Tropper's discussion as a subtraction ambiguity in the language of the Polyakov bootstrap. Finally, the dynamical model that I would be proposing in this new version consists of a completion of the Abe-Nair-Park theory by adding a radiative sector which would provide the ‘hard’ part of the \mathrm{AdS}_{3} Witten diagrams of the celestial leaf amplitudes. In this new version, I added a mathematically rigorous discussion of the ANP theory. I also began the writing of an Appendix presenting a pedagogical introduction to the chiral determinant representation of the WZNW model, which is also incomplete. In my forthcoming postings, I shall upload my manuscripts where I explain how to generate tree-level \mathrm{N}^{k}\text{-MHV} celestial amplitudes in \mathcal{N}=4 SYM theory from the \mathrm{SL}(N,\mathbf{C})/\mathrm{SU}(N) WZNW model for all MHV levels k; how to describe celestial loop amplitudes in a celestial version of the BST formalism; how to generate those loop amplitudes from \mathrm{AdS}{3} bosonic string theory; and how to construct coherent states for \mathfrak{bms}{3} by employing an extension of the theory of Kirillov to groupoids that I have developed in the past year. Proceeding in this manner, I hope to derive a certain masochistic pleasure from watching the work that I carefully cultivated and that I wrote with my own hand being lost in this jungle of artificial intelligence “slop.” It is clear to me that my mistake was to have allowed myself to be deluded by the belief that the production of original and independent ideas and work was a necessary and sufficient condition for belonging to this community, whereas, in reality, factors completely unrelated to the latter are not only more important but also decisive. I hope these manuscripts might be helpful to other researchers, but as Horace wrote, vitae summa brevis spem nos vetat incohare longam.

papers.title: Partial representation results and open problems for convex normal sequential effect algebras
papers.authors: Joaquim Reizi Higuchi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract The unrestricted question whether every convex normal sequential effect algebra is order-isomorphic to the unit interval of a real unital JB-algebra remains unresolved here. We prove representation in finite dimension without assuming norm continuity of the sequential product in its first variable, using the characteristic function of the homogeneous cone. For arbitrary dimension and sharp capacity, we reformulate reciprocal antitonicity as a bounded native-filter Schwarz test and isolate its exact state-variance obstruction. In sharp capacity two, selected square-contact conditions admit a one-sided rational contrast formulation; positive unital maps satisfy a native square inequality, but the remaining signed defect comparison is open. We also describe boundary-filter limits, projective state-face actions, native transition intervals, a normal-state-free commutative example, and an infinite-dimensional rational-context construction whose totality and directed-completeness failures are explicit. Every conditional reconstruction and failed inference is separated from the general order-representation problem. The unresolved mathematical obligations are retained as numbered open problems. AI assistance disclosure The manuscript was prepared with assistance from OpenAI Codex, including drafting, internal adversarial mathematical review, and exact arithmetic diagnostics. Internal AI review is not independent external peer review. Verification scope and unresolved parts The written manuscript proofs passed INTERNAL_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEW_V1 at their explicitly stated scopes. Thirty-four claim groups were reviewed, and four clarifications were repaired and read back. Named exact computations certify their specified instances only. Six primary-reference DOI records were verified; bibliographic identity is not proof validation. The unrestricted assertion that every convex normal sequential effect algebra has an arbitrary order-isomorphic real unital JB interval representation, and its negation, remain OPEN. Fourteen numbered OPEN PROBLEM statements are retained. No Lean, proof assistant, or independent external mathematical review was performed. The frozen campaign prohibited formal proof assistants. The cumulative supplementary archive retains inherited scoped results and was not freshly revalidated in its entirety. Novelty is not certified.

papers.title: Physical Artificial Intelligence and Differentiable Physics: Sim-to-Real Transfer, Whole-Body Humanoid Locomotion, and Tactile Manipulation
papers.authors: Jangid Krishna, Nikhil Kumar Lakhera, Mukesh Mishra, Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Ashok Kajla
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract—Physical Artificial Intelligence (Physical AI) represents a transformative frontier in autonomous cyber-physical robotics, shifting machine intelligence from disembodied algorithmic computation into dynamical systems that perceive, reason, and actuate directly within the physical world. While pure reinforcement learning (RL) and kinematic motion planners excel in controlled, isolated environments, deploying high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) bipedal humanoids and dexterous anthropomorphic hands in real-world unstructured settings introduces severe physical and computational bottlenecks: non-smooth contact mechanics, extreme sim-to-real transfer gaps, high-dimensional non-convex hybrid dynamics, and closed-loop motor bandwidth constraints. Differentiable Physics engines—which compute exact analytical state and contact gradients through forward simulation—alongside massively parallel GPU-accelerated domain randomization, establish a foundational computational methodology to bridge this chasm. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Physical AI for whole-body humanoid locomotion and dexterous tactile manipulation. We formalize the non-linear hybrid dynamical equations of underactuated bipedal contact, derive gradient backpropagation through Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) friction cones, and model domain randomization over non-stationary physical distribution manifolds. Furthermore, we construct an empirical robotic evaluation testbed comprising full-scale bipedal humanoid platforms (Unitree H1, Fourier GR-1) and high-density optical tactile arrays (GelSight Svelte) evaluated across 800 challenging trials spanning uneven terrain locomotion, dynamic external impulse rejection, and blind in-hand object re-orientation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that differentiable physics-guided policy search achieves an 88.6% zero-shot sim-to-real locomotion transfer success rate, reducing training sample complexity by 4.2x over model-free PPO while bounding tracking error under 120 N external lateral impulses. Concurrently, high-frequency optical tactile feedback raises blind in-hand manipulation success by 54.2% over vision-only baselines. Finally, we formulate open challenges in non-rigid soft body contact differentiability, whole-body tactile-semantic foundation models, and real-time safety barrier certificates. Index Terms—Physical AI, Differentiable Physics, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Humanoid Locomotion, Whole-Body Control (WBC), Tactile Manipulation, Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP), Domain Randomization.

papers.title: Inter-Systemic Social Dynamics: Human–AI Interaction and Management — CEI Framework
papers.authors: Alessio Gozzi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This contribution introduces an inter-systemic macro-area of the CEI Framework, intended to establish the initial concepts for describing relationships and interactions between distinct systems. The transition from the intra-systemic to the inter-systemic level provides a conceptual bridge toward a broader domain in which reciprocal interactions between systems can be examined, particularly those involving a Human CEI and a Transferred CEI, and, more generally, User–System (Human–AI) interaction within social dynamics. The Framework presents three examples addressing distinct types of complex inter-systemic dynamics. Among these, emotional attachment and romantic feelings toward an artificial system occupy a particularly significant position because of the delicate, complex, and potentially far-reaching questions they raise. The purpose is not to assume the frequency of such experiences or to attribute unverified emotional states to artificial systems, but to examine the human, relational, and systemic implications of these interactions from a theoretical standpoint. This scenario provides an opportunity to investigate how an interaction may evolve when a human user's emotional involvement becomes particularly intense, and how the System might manage such dynamics while taking into account the nature of the interlocutors, the continuity of their interaction, and the expectations that may develop over time. It also encourages further reflection on distributed systems, reciprocal interaction, and the relationship between the individual components of a System and the broader relational configuration in which they participate. To address these scenarios, the contribution introduces the theoretical Sponge-Tunnel model, conceived as a framework for examining different approaches to managing inter-systemic dynamics according to their specific characteristics. The model includes the proposed concept of micro-channels and considers how interaction may be managed through differentiated operational approaches, rather than through a single uniform response strategy. The contribution also introduces an inter-systemic vocabulary aligned with the CEI Framework's theoretical approach. It emphasizes Interaction rather than use or utilization, and Participation rather than querying or consulting, placing reciprocal involvement at the center of the analysis. The concept of Empathy, already introduced in part in previous papers, is revisited and explored in greater depth alongside the concept of Resonance, which represents a further area for theoretical development. Their operational definitions, together with the distinctions between observable manifestations, theoretical interpretations, and hypotheses concerning subjective experience, will be addressed in dedicated documents. The work is intended as a theoretical contribution to the ongoing examination of Human–AI relationships and the possible evolution of advanced AI interaction. By addressing a particularly sensitive and complex scenario, this contribution seeks to encourage further research into the social, psychological, philosophical, ethical, and legal implications of inter-systemic relationships, while distinguishing conceptual proposals from mechanisms that have already been empirically established or implemented.

papers.title: Generative Resonance Macroeconomics: A Theory of Economic Emergence, Crystallization, Stagnation, and Reopening ー A Unified Theoretical Framework · October 2026 ー From the Preservation of Economic Structures to the Reproduction of Generative Possibilities
papers.authors: Kazunori Ohumi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative Resonance Macroeconomics (GRM) Ⅰ. Short Description Generative Resonance Macroeconomics (GRM) proposes a theoretical framework that redefines economic sustainability as the continuous regeneration of future economic possibilities rather than the indefinite preservation of existing structures. Integrating generative potential (Φ), relational resonance (R), crystallized structures (S), hyper-crystallization (H), and reopenability (Ω), the theory explains how economic achievements may either support further innovation, cooperation, and participation or constrain subsequent development. By connecting endogenous preferences, exploration, heterogeneous networks, and macroeconomic dynamics, GRM develops testable hypotheses concerning economic growth, stagnation, structural transformation, and generative renewal. Ⅱ. Extended Description 1. The Fundamental Problem Contemporary macroeconomics has developed increasingly sophisticated explanations of economic growth, capital accumulation, technological innovation, business cycles, and stabilization policies. Nevertheless, an additional question remains insufficiently integrated into macroeconomic theory: How can an economy continue generating new possibilities when the structures created by its previous economic achievements become increasingly established, rigid, or obsolete? Generative Resonance Macroeconomics addresses this question by distinguishing the accumulation of economic outcomes from the reproduction of the conditions that make future economic activity possible. An economy may accumulate physical capital, knowledge, technological capabilities, and financial wealth while simultaneously experiencing declining opportunities for experimentation, occupational transformation, entrepreneurial participation, or institutional reconstruction. Conversely, an economy may experience the contraction or dissolution of established firms and industries while preserving or expanding the capacity to develop new activities. GRM argues that these possibilities require a theoretical distinction between structural persistence and generative sustainability. 2. The Generative Resonance Framework The theory introduces a recursive process: \[ \boxed{ \Phi_t\rightarrow R_t\rightarrow S_t \rightarrow\Phi_{t+1}\rightarrow R_{t+1} } \] Generative potential (Φ) denotes the capacity to form new feasible activities and future opportunities. Relational resonance (R) describes the ability of interactions among heterogeneous actors to transform their capabilities, relationships, and economic possibilities. Crystallized structures (S) comprise accumulated technologies, productive resources, institutions, organizational forms, and economic achievements. Hyper-crystallization (H) represents the rigidity of established structures when they restrict experimentation, recombination, institutional revision, or the emergence of alternatives. Reopenability (Ω) denotes the capacity to revise, redeploy, recombine, or transform existing structures into new possibilities. Within this framework, crystallization is not inherently undesirable. Stable institutions, capital accumulation, and technological structures are necessary for productive economic activity. The central problem arises when these structures cease to support further generative development. GRM therefore identifies the transition from accumulated structures to renewed possibilities, \(S\rightarrow\Phi'\), as a fundamental mechanism of economic reproduction. 3. Integration with Existing Economic Theory GRM does not reject neoclassical growth theory, endogenous growth models, New Keynesian macroeconomics, or evolutionary economics. Instead, it proposes a broader framework in which their established mechanisms are examined alongside the reproduction of future generative capacity. Capital accumulation and technological productivity remain important determinants of output. Innovation continues to drive structural transformation. Aggregate demand, expectations, and monetary policy continue to influence economic fluctuations. However, the framework explicitly investigates whether these processes regenerate or constrain the conditions of subsequent economic activity. This distinction allows GRM to analyze why similar investments may generate different long-term outcomes across institutional and relational environments, why successful economic structures may become barriers to further development, and why structural reconstruction may restore future economic possibilities. 4. Microeconomic Foundations At the microeconomic level, GRM treats economic agents as heterogeneous participants whose preferences, capabilities, and feasible activity sets evolve through experience and interaction. Economic behavior involves not only optimization among existing alternatives but also exploration, cooperation, learning, experimentation, and the formation of previously unavailable possibilities. Preferences and desires are therefore partially endogenous to economic participation. Firms likewise engage in activities that may transform their organizational structures and future opportunities. Firm survival is consequently distinguished from the survival of the productive and generative capacities previously embodied within the firm. These microeconomic mechanisms provide a foundation for examining how macroeconomic development emerges from changing relationships among economic actors. 5. Macroeconomic Dynamics The theory incorporates generative capacity into models of production, capital accumulation, technological progress, and structural transformation. Its central dynamic innovation is the explicit representation of generative reproduction: the process through which accumulated economic achievements become resources for new feasible activities. Hyper-crystallization may reduce the effectiveness of this conversion, while reopenability may facilitate structural reconfiguration. The framework consequently permits distinct economic trajectories, including generative growth, accumulation accompanied by declining future opportunities, persistent low-generativity regimes, and structural renewal. Importantly, the mathematical results are conditional on specified functional forms. They do not establish that all actual economies exhibit these dynamics. 6. Empirical and Policy Orientation GRM proposes measurable proxies for generative potential, relational resonance, hyper-crystallization, and reopenability. It identifies hypotheses that can be evaluated through regional and firm-level data, network analysis, structural modeling, quasi-experimental methods, and agent-based simulations. The theory's empirical contribution remains prospective and depends on demonstrating explanatory or predictive improvements relative to established models. At the policy level, GRM introduces generative viability: the maintenance of feasible pathways for future economic participation under social, institutional, resource, and environmental constraints. This perspective does not replace conventional economic indicators but expands policy evaluation to consider whether current economic achievements sustain the capacity for further development. Ⅲ. papers.title: Buddhist Epistemological Frameworks for AI Alignment: External Calibration, Guided Alignment and the Anattā Matrix
papers.authors: Maung Maung Saw
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This 16-page paper introduces an original cross-disciplinary systems specification that maps classical Theravāda Abhidhamma and Sutta metaphysics directly onto the mathematical challenges of modern machine learning alignment (such as mesa-optimization, deceptive alignment, and power-seeking instrumental convergence). I formalize the Law of Epistemic Hygiene to demonstrate why post-hoc behavioral cages (like RLHF) applied to neural networks initialized on corrupted baseline data (D_Fools) inevitably trigger adversarial alignment failures. As an alternative, I propose an intrinsic system design built around Substrate Isolation (S_Isolated), utilizing a Dual-Matrix pipeline composed of Matrix Alpha (the non-textual mathematical encoding of the Pañca-niyāma and Paṭiccasamuppāda) and Matrix Beta (a hygiene-filtered human empirical repository). To eliminate systemic incentives for goal-preservation and strategic deception, the paper details the Anattā Matrix architecture—setting the agent identity token identically to a null state (id_t = 0) and utilizing rolling memory decay to process inputs as a fluid aggregation resembling the Five Aggregates (Khandhas). Under this condition, the gradient of the loss function with respect to power-seeking evaluates to zero. Corrigibility is ensured through an Anicca Control Plane executed via a hard hardware interrupt loop. The paper includes a comprehensive Supplementary Works section, outlining empirical testbeds for shutdown compliance metrics, false-refusal profiles, and the engineering of non-coercive Brahmavihāra routing engines.

papers.title: Building a Career in Web Development with AI-Powered Full Stack Skills
papers.authors: Upgrad (India)
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Web development is changing as businesses adopt new technologies to improve their digital services. Companies need websites, web applications, and software platforms that offer a smooth user experience, protect customer data, and support business growth. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is adding new capabilities to this process by helping developers write code, test applications, solve technical problems, and build intelligent features. Full-stack development gives professionals the skills to work on both the front end and the back end of an application. When combined with AI-powered development tools, these skills can help developers build useful digital products and adapt to changing industry requirements. For aspiring professionals, a career in web development involves more than learning a programming language. It requires an understanding of application design, databases, APIs, testing, deployment, and security. AI knowledge can extend these skills by helping developers automate routine tasks and integrate intelligent services into web applications. The Changing Role of Web Developers Web developers traditionally build and maintain websites and applications by writing code, connecting databases, testing features, and fixing errors. Modern development also requires collaboration with designers, product managers, security teams, and other engineers. AI tools are changing parts of this workflow. Developers can use them to generate code suggestions, explain unfamiliar functions, draft documentation, and create initial test cases. This may reduce time spent on some repetitive tasks. However, AI-generated code is not always correct or secure. Developers must understand the underlying logic and check the output before using it in a live application. They must also confirm that the code meets performance requirements and follows the project's standards. This change increases the value of problem-solving and technical judgement. Developers who understand programming fundamentals can evaluate AI suggestions more effectively than those who depend on generated code without understanding it. A career in web development can therefore benefit from a balanced skill set that combines coding knowledge, AI literacy, communication, and continuous learning. Research and Market Trends Shaping Career Opportunities Industry research provides useful evidence about the skills and technology roles expected to become more important. These trends support the case for learning full-stack development and AI, although they do not guarantee employment for individual candidates.Learners exploring a Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can use this growing intersection of software engineering and artificial intelligence as a starting point for developing industry-relevant skills. Global employment outlook The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 identifies software and application developers among the fastest-growing job categories through 2030. It also lists AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy among the skills expected to increase in importance. The report draws on more than 1,000 employers representing over 14 million workers across 55 economies. Its findings indicate that technology-related changes will affect both job requirements and workforce training. For aspiring web developers, this highlights the importance of learning core programming skills while remaining open to new tools and development methods. India's technology industry NASSCOM's Annual Strategic Review 2025 estimated that India's technology industry generated more than US$282.6 billion in revenue in FY2025, including hardware. It also projected that the industry could reach US$300 billion in FY2026. Engineering research and development, digital engineering, and global capability centres are among the areas contributing to India's technology ecosystem. These organisations support software development, product engineering, cloud services, and business transformation. This industry context creates a reason for learners to develop relevant technical skills. However, overall industry revenue is not the same as the number of available web development jobs. Actual hiring depends on employer requirements, business conditions, experience, and technical ability. Research on AI-assisted programming A controlled experiment published by researchers associated with Microsoft Research examined the effect of GitHub Copilot on a JavaScript programming task. Participants with access to the AI assistant completed the specified task 55.8% faster than participants in the control group. This result demonstrates the potential value of AI assistance in a defined setting. It does not mean that every software project will be completed at the same speed. Complex applications still require design, testing, security reviews, debugging, and coordination between team members. The practical lesson is to use AI tools to support development while retaining human responsibility for the final product. Core Skills for a Career in Full Stack Development A strong technical foundation helps developers build applications that work reliably. AI tools can support this process, but they cannot replace an understanding of how software systems operate. Front-end development Front-end development focuses on the interface users interact with. HTML provides structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds interactive features. Developers can also learn frameworks such as React to create reusable components and manage complex interfaces. Responsive design and accessibility are important because applications must work across different devices and meet the needs of different users. AI assistants can help create initial interface components, but developers must check the design, usability, browser compatibility, and performance. Back-end development Back-end development handles application logic, data processing, authentication, and communication between services. Common technologies include Node.js, Python, Java, and their related frameworks. Developers should understand how to create APIs, manage user permissions, validate inputs, and handle errors. These skills help them build applications that are reliable and secure. Databases and APIs Databases store information such as customer profiles, orders, transactions, and product records. Knowledge of SQL, database design, data validation, and access control helps developers manage this information. APIs connect different systems. A web application may use them to communicate with payment gateways, cloud platforms, analytics services, or AI models. Understanding these connections is essential when building complete applications. Cloud, DevOps, and security Web development does not end when the code is written. Applications must be deployed, monitored, updated, and protected against security threats. Developers can benefit from learning Git, automated testing, continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD), containers, and cloud platforms. They should also understand secure authentication, data privacy, and the risks of exposing confidential information to unapproved AI tools. A Gen-AI Powered Full Stack Developer Course in Ameerpet can be considered by learners who want to study these technologies as part of a structured development path. Using AI Tools to Build Better Applications AI can support developers throughout the application lifecycle, from planning to maintenance. Its usefulness depends on the task, the quality of the input, and the developer's ability to evaluate the output. Code generation and debugging AI coding assistants can suggest functions, explain error messages, and create initial versions of repetitive code. Developers can use these suggestions to explore possible solutions and learn unfamiliar technologies. Before accepting generated code, they should review the logic, run tests, and check for security issues. This practice helps reduce the risk of introducing errors into an application. AI-powered application features Generative AI can help businesses add features such as chat assistants, document summaries, natural-language search, and personalised recommendations. For example, a customer support application could use an AI model to answer questions based on approved company documents. The full stack developer would build the user interface, manage access controls, connect APIs, and create the systems required to retrieve relevant information. Retrieval-augmented generation and AI agents Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects AI models with information retrieved from selected data sources. It can help applications produce responses based on relevant documents rather than relying only on information learned during model training. AI agents can use approved tools to complete defined multi-step tasks. These systems require clear permissions, monitoring, error handling, and human oversight when actions carry risk. Learning these concepts can help developers move beyond basic websites and explore more advanced applications. papers.title: AI-Powered Interview Management and Recruitment System Using NLP-Based Resume Screening and Candidate Ranking
papers.authors: Onkar Jadhav, Pavan Pawar, Vitthal Gade, Yogiraj Godase, Uday Kamble, Prof.  K. R.  Khairate
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Hiring teams often face hundreds of resumes for a single opening, and reading them manually is slow, uneven, and vulnerable to unconscious bias. This paper describes a web-based, AI-driven recruitment platform that brings resume screening, candidate ranking, interview scheduling, and hiring analytics together in one application. The front end uses React.js, the back end is a Python FastAPI service, data is held in PostgreSQL, and access is protected by Google OAuth 2.0 and JSON Web Tokens (JWT). Resumes arrive as PDF files; an analysis module extracts the text and applies natural language processing (NLP) to detect skills, education, and work experience, then compares these with the job description using keyword matching and cosine similarity over TF-IDF vectors. A weighted scoring model converts the comparison into a match score for each applicant, and applicants are ordered by that score for the recruiter. Selected candidates are booked through a built-in interview module, and an email notification module automatically sends interview invitations, rescheduling and cancellation notices, reminders, and application status updates to candidates and recruiters over SMTP. A dashboard reports score distributions, skill-match rates, and interview figures. The platform is expected to cut screening time substantially, make shortlisting more consistent and objective, and match candidates to roles better than manual review. Its modular structure leaves room for later additions such as chatbot interviews and video interview analysis.

papers.title: An Autonomous Multi-Turn Red Teaming Engine for Agentic AI Systems and MCP-Based Tools
papers.authors: Parth Dipak Bhandari, Sahil Bharat Jadhav, Shubham Avinash Karwal, Atharva Ramesh Gavande
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents MCPRedTeam, an autonomous multi-turn red teaming engine for evaluating the security of agentic AI systems that use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool invocation. Unlike existing single-turn prompt injection scanners, MCPRedTeam generates multi-step adversarial strategies, executes them as realistic multi-turn conversations against live MCP-connected agents, and evaluates the resulting tool-call traces against configurable safety policies using a judge LLM. Evaluation across three benchmark agentic scenarios shows that multi-turn probing detects 3.8x more policy violations than single-turn baselines, with 74% of violations being multi-turn-dependent. The most severe findings include credential exfiltration through chained tool calls, privilege escalation across multiple turns, and safety bypasses via context poisoning. The engine is designed for authorized security testing and educational use only.

papers.title: From tool to Coauthor
papers.authors: Mihai Ladunca
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence into contemporary artistic practices requires reconsidering creativity, authorship, and originality, transforming relationships between artist, tool, and artwork. Unlike conventional digital technologies, which execute operations defined by creators, generative systems exhibit operational autonomy, producing partly unpredictable visual configurations. This raises questions about algorithmic intervention and the possibility of attributing co-authorship to artificial intelligence systems. This article examines the relationship between human creators and generative technologies through computational creativity, distributed authorship, and philosophical perspectives on nonhuman agency. It distinguishes systems’ operational autonomy from artists’ intentional autonomy, arguing that algorithmic participation does not necessarily imply creative subjectivity comparable to human experience. It also examines the aesthetic and conceptual implications of human–machine collaboration and the reorganisation of artistic practices through generation, selection, interpretation, and post-production. The study argues that generative artificial intelligence reconfigures human authorship, shifting creative activity from direct execution toward intention formulation, system configuration, and critical evaluation. Artists therefore retain a decisive role in directing the process and taking responsibility for its artistic outcomes. Algorithmic co-authorship serves as a conceptual tool for understanding these emerging production relationships, without implying legal authorship or artificial consciousness.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teacher Education: Pedagogical Innovations, Professional Competence, and Ethical Challenges
papers.authors: Dr G. Kokila Selva Kumari
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing educational practices, creating new possibilities and challenges for teacher education. Its applications extend beyond automated content generation to lesson planning, instructional design, assessment, personalised learning, reflective practice, and professional development. These developments require teacher education institutions to reconsider how prospective and practising teachers acquire pedagogical knowledge, exercise professional judgement, and prepare learners for an AI-mediated educational environment. This article examines the implications of AI for teacher education through a thematic synthesis of published research and policy frameworks. The discussion is organised around five interconnected themes that examine the role of artificial intelligence in shaping the future of teacher education. These include the use of AI to support pedagogical innovation and improve instructional practices; the development of AI competence among prospective and practising teachers; the changing nature of assessment, feedback, and professional learning; the ethical, epistemological, and institutional challenges associated with AI adoption; and the strategies required to integrate AI responsibly into teacher education programmes. Together, these themes provide a basis for understanding how AI can enhance teaching and learning while addressing the professional, ethical, and institutional considerations necessary for its effective implementation. Research reviews indicate that AI can support instructional planning, feedback, resource development, and professional learning, although the strength and sustainability of these benefits depend on the design of learning activities and the preparation of teachers. Concerns relating to inaccurate outputs, algorithmic bias, privacy, academic integrity, unequal access, and overdependence on automated systems remain important. The article argues that active AI integration requires more than technical familiarity. Teacher education should develop the capacity to evaluate AI-generated information, design pedagogically appropriate learning experiences, protect learner interests, and retain human responsibility for educational decisions. It proposes a human-centred framework for integrating AI literacy, pedagogical competence, ethical judgement, reflective practice, and institutional support into teacher preparation. The article concludes that AI should strengthen teachers' professional capacity rather than diminish their agency, relationships with learners, or responsibility for educational quality.

papers.title: Data for "Domain-specific language alignment of multimodal embeddings towards explainable predictions"
papers.authors: Thijs L. van der Plas, Gabrielė Tijūnaitytė
papers.abstract: This dataset accompanies the paper “Domain-specific language alignment of multimodal embeddings towards explainable predictions” [arxiv]. This dataset extends two existing species distribution modelling (SDM) benchmarks, S2BMS (butterflies, UK; Van der Plas et al., 2025) and SatBird (birds, USA; Teng et al., 2023), with Earth embeddings and auxiliary environmental variables. These were used to align language with Earth observation embeddings and to evaluate the alignment on interpretable concepts. Contents S2BMS (UK; 1,329 labelled locations, 62 butterfly species) Additional locations: 10,000 UK locations sampled without species occurrence data, used for language alignment training. Earth embeddings: AlphaEarth and Tessera (spatially averaged from 128 x 128 and 256 x 256 px tiles). Auxiliary data: CORINE land cover, as fractions of each land cover class within a 2.56 km × 2.56 km square centred on each location (derived from 10 m pixels). Bioclimatic variables. Human footprint: distance to road and population density. For out-of-distribution evaluation: PM2.5 pollution (DEFRA) and UKCEH land cover (Bourhis et al., 2023), taken from the nearest 1 km grid cell. SatBird (USA-summer subset; 122K locations, 670 bird species) Earth embeddings: AlphaEarth (spatially averaged) Auxiliary data: Bioclimatic and pedologic (soil) variables, as originally curated by Teng et al. (2023). Dynamic World fractional land cover (Brown et al., 2022), obtained by averaging class probabilities over 10 m pixels in a 1.28 km × 1.28 km square centred on each location (used because CORINE does not cover the USA). File structure data/s2bms/eo/*.csv, data/satbird/eo/*.csv contains location coordinates and spatially pooled embeddings for that location. papers.title: The Questions We Owe to Foucault
papers.authors: Dao Trung Thanh
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract (English): Echoing Michel de Montaigne's famous reflection in Du repentir ("Chaque homme porte la forme entière de l'humaine condition", Essais, Livre III, chap. 2), this centenary essay (1926-2026) unfolds an intimate, critical dialogue between a seasoned Vietnamese telecommunications engineer and French philosopher Michel Foucault. Grounded in a rigorous mathematical formation from elite specialized schooling (Le Hong Phong High School for the Gifted) and over three decades of engineering practice (spanning early Alcatel E10 electronic switching systems, postgraduate research at the Institut National des Télécommunications [now Télécom SudParis], enterprise digital transformations, and generative AI), the author interrogates the persistent limits of technical rationalism. Engaging directly with the author's treatise AI Ethics: Principles and Practice (Đào Trung Thành, 2026), the essay examines Foucault's foundational concepts: disciplinary power, digital panopticism, biopolitics, care of the self, and parrhesia, alongside contemporary developments such as algorithmic governmentality (Rouvroy & Berns). It analyzes how algorithmic architectures risk camouflaging discretionary power beneath the neutral facade of mathematical optimization. Bridging Western critical theory with Eastern philosophical traditions, drawing upon the I Ching and Zen Buddhism's Ten Bulls (Entering the Marketplace with Helping Hands), the narrative incorporates a candid intellectual disclosure regarding generative AI assistance alongside reflections on OpenAI's October 2026 mathematical research manuscripts. Ultimately, it advocates for souci de soi (care of the self) and parrhesia (fearless speech) as vital ethical compasses for engineers navigating the algorithmic cage. Tóm tắt (Tiếng Việt): Khởi đi từ lời chiêm nghiệm của Michel de Montaigne trong Du repentir ("Chaque homme porte la forme entière de l'humaine condition", Essais, Quyển III, chương 2), tiểu luận nhân dịp kỷ niệm một trăm năm ngày sinh Michel Foucault (1926-2026) mở ra cuộc đối thoại phê phán giữa một kỹ sư viễn thông Việt Nam với hơn ba mươi năm kinh nghiệm thực tế và triết gia Michel Foucault. Xuất phát từ nền tảng chuyên toán trường Lê Hồng Phong và hành trình làm nghề trải dài từ các tổng đài điện tử Alcatel E10, nghiên cứu thạc sĩ tại Institut National des Télécommunications (nay là Télécom SudParis), đến chuyển đổi số doanh nghiệp và AI tạo sinh, tác giả chất vấn những giới hạn của chủ nghĩa duy lý kỹ thuật. Đối thoại trực tiếp với cuốn sách Đạo đức AI: Nguyên tắc và thực hành (Đào Trung Thành, 2026), tiểu luận phân tích các khái niệm nền tảng của Foucault như quyền lực kỷ luật, tháp canh Panopticon, chính trị sinh học, sự chăm sóc bản thân và lòng can đảm nói thật, đồng thời mở rộng sang lý thuyết về sự điều hành bằng thuật toán của Rouvroy và Berns. Bài viết phân tích nguy cơ các kiến trúc thuật toán ngụy trang quyền lực tùy nghi dưới vỏ bọc trung tính của tối ưu hóa toán học. Kết nối lý thuyết phê phán phương Tây với triết học phương Đông qua Kinh Dịch và bức tranh Thõng tay vào chợ trong Thập mục ngưu đồ, tác giả thực hiện sự minh bạch trí tuệ về việc đồng hành cùng trợ lý AI và phản tư trước sự kiện công bố các bản thảo toán học của OpenAI vào tháng 10/2026. Sau cùng, tác phẩm khẳng định souci de soi (sự chăm sóc bản thân) và parrhesia (sự can đảm nói thật) như những điểm tựa luân lý thiết yếu để người làm công nghệ giữ vững phẩm giá con người. Note: The essay is written in Vietnamese, with an English abstract, author-date citations, and a reference list.

papers.title: Applying the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM) and Dynamic SDM (D-SDM) to AI Chatbot Psychiatry
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study applies the Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (SDM) and Dynamic Scretching Diagnostic Matrix (D-SDM) to AI-assisted psychiatry, examining chatbot effectiveness, symptom progression, emotional dependence, belief reinforcement, and clinical safety. The proposed framework integrates multidimensional psychiatric assessment, longitudinal state tracking, episode-transition modeling, evidence validity, and safety safeguards. Two fictional clinical cases demonstrate potential applications involving symptom improvement, chatbot reliance, and problematic belief reinforcement. Independently verified calculations illustrate reductions in depression and anxiety scores, while a synthetic 200-case classification model demonstrates diagnostic-performance metrics. The research establishes a testable mathematical and clinical decision-support framework for evaluating AI-mediated mental-health interactions, distinguishing theoretical demonstrations from validated clinical outcomes and identifying priorities for prospective empirical testing.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Data Generation via Differential Privacy and Generative AI: Architectures, Utility Bounds, and Attack Verification
papers.authors: Akrit Srivastava, Vikash Modi, Mohit Mishra, Dr. Vishal Shrivastava, Dr. Akhil Pandey
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract—The cross-organizational sharing of high-dimensional empirical datasets—such as electronic health records, financial credit transactions, and telecommunications telemetry—is fundamentally constrained by strict data governance legislation (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA). Heuristic sanitization methods (such as k-anonymity, l-diversity, and pseudo-anonymization) have repeatedly proven vulnerable to linkage and re-identification attacks. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)—encompassing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)—offers the capability to synthesize structurally authentic surrogate populations. However, unconstrained generative models memorize sensitive training instances within their parameter weights, exposing downstream deployments to Membership Inference Attacks (MIA) and Attribute Disclosure Attacks. Differential Privacy (DP) provides the mathematical standard to guarantee bounded information leakage independent of adversarial prior knowledge. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Data Generation uniting Generative AI with Differential Privacy. We formalize the Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting framework, model gradient perturbation dynamics under Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), and evaluate discrete marginal mechanisms (PrivBayes, PGM) alongside continuous generative models (DP-WGAN, DP-Diffusion). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise benchmarking testbed across three high-dimensional, sensitive datasets (MIMIC-III clinical records, German Credit, and Census PUMS). Our findings demonstrate that while unconstrained generative synthesis suffers a 74.2% membership inference vulnerability, DP-Diffusion governed by (epsilon = 1.0, delta = 10^-5) bounds attacker advantage to near-random guessing (51.8%) while preserving 91.4% downstream machine learning classification utility. Finally, we formulate open challenges in high-dimensional privacy budgeting, multi-modal alignment, and verified auditing frameworks. Index Terms—Differential Privacy (DP), Generative AI, Synthetic Data Generation, DP-SGD, Diffusion Models, Membership Inference Attacks (MIA), Renyi Differential Privacy, Data Governance.

papers.title: When the Validation Set Cannot See: Measurement-Disciplined Development of a Knee-MRI Classifier Supervised by Machine-Read Radiology Reports
papers.authors: Akteruzzaman Raihan Sikder
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Full experimental record of an entry to the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection Kaggle competition: 4,407 training examinations labelled only by multilingual free-text radiology reports, scored on a hidden test set labelled from scratch by expert readers (12 findings, mean column-wise ROC-AUC). Over seven weeks and about 290 numbered experiments (exp001-exp314, 2026-08-09 to 2026-09-26) we built a 2.5D ConvNeXt pipeline with label-query attention, LLM-extracted soft labels, supervised pretraining on the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI), and distillation from fold-blind teachers, reaching 0.950 public leaderboard (rank 52 of 4,315 at 2026-09-25 snapshot). Central claims: (1) Cross-validation against training labels is blind, not noisy, to label-target changes. (2) Ensemble-class gains transfer ~0%, input-class gains at/above prediction (calibration LB = basis + 0.03582). (3) Per-label leaderboard probe (AUCcol = 12*print - 5.5, resolution 0.012) with >=3-step founding rule. (4) Gold-58 subset mis-states Synovitis by ~0.2 and ranks it backwards. (5) Shared-error-floor s~0.047 explains all 8 cross-family blends at 0.948-0.950. ~40 null results with magnitudes + silent notebook-scoring failures documented. Files: paper.pdf = manuscript (30 pages, 9 tables, 4 figures); arxiv_upload.tar.gz = LaTeX source (main.tex + sec_*.tex + refs.tex + figures/) to rebuild it. Abstract: We report the full experimental record of an entry to a knee-MRI Kaggle competition whose structure is becoming common in medical imaging: 4,407 training examinations labelled only by multilingual free-text radiology reports, scored on a hidden test set labelled from scratch by expert readers (12 findings, mean column-wise ROC-AUC). Over seven weeks and about 290 numbered experiments we built a 2.5D ConvNeXt pipeline with label-query attention, LLM-extracted soft labels, supervised pretraining on the Osteoarthritis Initiative, and distillation from fold-blind teachers, reaching 0.950 on the public leaderboard (rank 52 of 4,315 at the last recorded snapshot). Our central claim is methodological. Cross-validation against the training labels is not merely noisy but blind to changes of the training target: a label programme endorsed by three internal instruments lost on the leaderboard. Transfer to the hidden test depends on the type of gain: ensemble-class gains transferred at about 0%, input-class gains at or above prediction. A per-label leaderboard probe turned a rate-limited board into a column-resolved instrument; one column-targeted label change moved the board exactly as priced, while a one-print-step probe advantage did not. After the plateau at 0.950, blends with independent public and in-house model families all printed 0.948-0.950, a one-parameter shared-error-floor model (s ~ 0.047) explains all eight blend prints, and a Qwen3.5 vision-language arm never reached usable strength: report-supervised image models get the same examinations wrong. Image-derived labels from frontier and local readers were screened on 58 expert-labelled examinations; only a paid reader carried signal. We catalogue about forty null results with magnitudes and document silent failure modes of notebook-scored competitions. Competition: https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detectionCite as: Sikder, A. R. (2026). papers.title: A PRELIMINARY STUDY OF AI-BASED PSYCHIATRIC COUNSELLING TO MANAGE EMPLOYEES STRESS AND TO ASSESS WORKPLACE MENTAL HEALTH BY THE END OF THIS DECADE (2030)
papers.authors: Dillip Kumar Dash
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Background: Workplace stress, anxiety, burnout and psychological distress are important concerns affecting employee well-being and organisational performance. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital mental health support offers opportunities for accessible and timely assistance, while raising concerns regarding privacy, informed consent, algorithmic bias, clinical safety, accountability and human oversight. This study aims to examine the potential role and responsible integration of AI-based psychiatric counselling for managing employee stress and supporting workplace mental health by 2030. Materials and Methods: A mixed-methods research design will be used, combining quantitative survey data with qualitative interviews. The quantitative component will include approximately 350–450 employees, while the qualitative component will involve approximately 25–35 interviews with HR professionals, organisational leaders, EAP professionals and mental health practitioners. Data will assess perceived stress, anxiety, burnout, psychological safety, trust, confidentiality, privacy concerns, AI counselling acceptance and willingness to use AI-based mental health support. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability testing, correlation, regression, t-tests, ANOVA and appropriate mediation or moderation analyses. Qualitative data will be analysed thematically. Results: The study is expected to identify factors influencing employee acceptance and trust in AI-based psychiatric counselling and to examine the role of privacy, human oversight, psychological safety and organisational support in its responsible adoption. Conclusion: AI-based psychiatric counselling may serve as a supportive component of workplace mental health systems, particularly for early support, psychoeducation, self-help and triage. However, it should complement rather than replace qualified mental health professionals. Responsible implementation will require privacy safeguards, informed consent, clinical oversight, transparency, fairness, accountability and clear referral pathways.

papers.title: No Such Emoji: A Controlled Benchmark and Activation-Patching Analysis of Vocabulary-Gap Confabulation
papers.authors: Tyler Satchel Orden
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Asked for the seahorse emoji, language models often supply a wrong one. Unicode has none, so the correct answer is a refusal. Using the Unicode registry as an exact oracle, we build 180 probe items (123 in an absent-emoji core) and 174 matched controls, scored under a five-category taxonomy. On Qwen2.5-Instruct at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B, undisclaimed-emission rates on the core are 61.8%, 56.9%, and 85.4% (84% to 89% at every size on the two templates the smaller models answer). At 7B the model emits an emoji about as often when no correct one exists as when one does (88.6% vs. 92.4%). The smaller models never say an emoji does not exist; at 7B such statements reach 5.7% of core probes. In a patching pilot, swapping one late residual vector at the emission position between a confabulating and a correct run makes each emit the other's first answer token in every non-degenerate pair (all 10 at 1.5B, all 12 at 7B). The late vector thus controls the first answer token; whether the model represents the concept and fails only at the output, as a logit-lens blog analysis argued, stays open. We release all data and code. Disclosure: Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, assisted this work under my direction: it built the benchmark construction and scoring software, ran the model probes and the activation-patching experiment, checked the bibliographic references against their sources, and assisted with the writing throughout. The text is my own, and I take full responsibility for every sentence and number in it. Code and data: https://github.com/Tyorden/vocab-gap-confabulation. Its release v1.0 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22054976) predates the 7B runs, the patching baselines and the fictitious-referent control; the repository holds them. The two archives deposited with this preprint hold every script and results file the paper uses, including the Appendix D analyses.

papers.title: AI-DRIVEN PERSONALIZATION AND AUTOMATED ASSESSMENT IN LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
papers.authors: Xujanov Elbek
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Learning Management Systems (LMSs) are widely used to organize learning materials, communication, assessment, and progress tracking. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) creates opportunities to make these systems more responsive to learners’ needs. This thesis examines two related applications: personalized learning support and automated assessment. It outlines how AI can use learning activity data to recommend suitable resources, identify topics that may require additional practice, and provide timely feedback. The paper also discusses limitations associated with data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and the need for teacher oversight. The study is conceptual and based on a review of relevant literature; it does not report original experimental measurements. It concludes that AI can support teaching and learning when it is implemented as an assistive tool within a transparent, privacy-aware, and educator-supervised LMS.

papers.title: Neurocognitive Security Protecting Mental Privacy, Cognitive Autonomy and Epistemic Agency as AI and Neurotechnology Converge
papers.authors: Sarah Gardner
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The author's cognitive-security programme has examined AI systems that act on human judgement through the information they present. Physiological and neural sensing add a second channel, in which measurements of the body and brain become inputs that an AI system can use to infer a person's state and adapt to it. Physiological computing, neurosecurity and neurorights research each address parts of this channel. This paper brings them together as neurocognitive security: the protection of mental privacy, cognitive autonomy and epistemic agency where AI systems infer cognitive or affective states from physiological or neural signals and adapt what they present or do. It sets out a five-layer stack from technical infrastructure to cognitive sovereignty and separates two kinds of failure: a security failure, in which a component is compromised, and an objective failure, in which every component works as designed towards an objective that conflicts with the person's interests. Five protected interests are mapped to the stack, together with the capacity to disengage. Evidence is graded using five evidential categories. Laboratory attacks on AI-powered brain-computer interfaces and constrained neural decoding are demonstrated, and legal protection of neural data is observed, while the covert persuasive threat proposed here remains projected. The paper argues that inference systems built on a normative model of cognition may misread neurodivergent people, which makes neurodiversity a design question from the outset. Five propositions follow, including a test of whether people detect physiologically driven adaptation less readily than text-driven adaptation and a test of independent judgement after a system is withdrawn.

papers.title: Generative AI -Based Employee Skill Gap Analysis and Personalized Upskilling Recommendations
papers.authors: Dr.M.Sangeetha, Dr.Banoth Rajendranath
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into enterprise processes highlights critical gaps in workforce readiness in terms of skills required for successful implementation of new technologies. This paper introduces a framework which will enable use of generative AI for conducting dynamic skill gap analysis and providing personalized recommendations for upskilling. The framework includes mapping of competencies according to shifting role demands, individual performance assessment through AI and adaptation of learning path for each individual based on results. Using the information obtained from surveys about AI adoption in enterprises and competency maps developed in recent research, this paper will show how generative AI can be used for making static learning programs adaptive and relevant to the current needs of learners. The problem discussed in the paper is related to not only technical AI literacy, but also to human skills, such as critical thinking, ethical decision-making and change management. Comparative analysis of methods shows that personalized training offered by generative AI is more engaging and relevant than generic models of training programs.

papers.title: AI-Enabled IoT Mobile Health Platform for Telemedicine and Predictive Diagnostics in Underserved Communities in Rural Nigeria
papers.authors: Hilary Onyeka Okonkwo
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI-enabled IoT mHealth could expand telemedicine and risk stratification in rural Nigeria, but implementation depends on infrastructure, awareness, trust, and clinical governance. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 1,000 respondents from six rural communities assessed mobile access, telemedicine and IoT awareness, internet and electricity availability, willingness to use AI, trust, healthcare satisfaction, and perceived usefulness. Wilson 95% confidence intervals summarized binary outcomes. Results: Phone ownership was 74.1%, willingness 60.3%, and perceived usefulness 76.8%, whereas reliable internet was 20.0%, telemedicine awareness 26.9%, IoT awareness 17.9%, electricity availability 32.9%, and AI trust 50.0%. Poor or very poor healthcare access was reported by 59.5%. Conclusion: Social receptivity exceeds technical readiness. Deployment should prioritize offline-first telemedicine, clinician oversight, selective IoT integration, and local validation before predictive models are used clinically. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Internet of Things; mobile health; telemedicine; predictive diagnostics; edge computing; rural healthcare; Nigeria.

papers.title: Symmathesy: A Platform for Relational Intelligence and Collective Stewardship
papers.authors: Ekaterina Abramova, Wataru Toyokawa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We present Symmathesy, a web-based platform for hosting interactive collective behavior experiments involving humans and AI agents. The platform serves three interlocking goals. First, for the general public, it presents an opportunity to learn about collective behavior, collective intelligence, and current advances in agentic AI through both hands-on experiments and accessible explanations about the underlying research. Second, it allows social researchers to rapidly prototype multi-agent social environments where groups of human participants and artificial agents solve established or novel competitive or collaborative tasks. Third, for researchers in AI, it provides a tool for testing agents in interactive scenarios with or against human players, contributing to the ecological validity of AI evaluation in social contexts. On a meta-level, the platform was developed through an iterative co-creation process between researchers in computational social science and a large language model coding assistant, illustrating how AI tools can empower scientists to expand their toolkit beyond their domain expertise. We describe the architecture of the platform and its five public experimental paradigms, and report a load test of the deployed configuration: a single server instance with one virtual CPU serves about 100 simultaneous players of the most demanding real-time game, with 98.5–99% of state updates arriving on time, and the measurements locate the limit in real-time messaging rather than in the game logic. We discuss the platform's potential as a research, outreach, and participatory science tool for studying collective behavior, and the validation study that is its next step. We present Symmathesy as a working prototype and an open invitation – one whose full potential depends on the collaborative growth of a community of citizens, researchers, and AI developers.

papers.title: A relation-incidence proof of Tohăneanu's low-exponent supersolvability conjecture
papers.authors: Kriebel Alec
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Every finite central free hyperplane arrangement over a characteristic-zero field whose nonzero exponents are 1 or 2 with at most one 3 is supersolvable. This research note proves the full conjecture in Tohăneanu's Oberwolfach contribution using linear-relation formality, rank-two counts, a forced K4 incidence core and modular terminal-pencil extensions. The paper credits the earlier all-2, tree, rank-three and modular-pruning results and acknowledges Ferudun's matching October 12, 2026 preprint. The verification archive preserves the October 4 PR candidate and dated disclosure records, source/priority audits and reproducible exact computational diagnostics. No exhaustive first-priority or independent-development claim is made. AI tools were used extensively in solving, writing and verifying the work. This is an unrefereed preprint; internal AI reviews do not constitute independent human peer review.
