papers.title: AI-Driven Supply Chain Transformation in Bangladesh: An Integrated Multitech Approach and Empirical Evaluation of Readiness to Adopt
papers.authors: Tahmid Hossain
papers.abstract: Abstract Bangladesh's industrial supply chains are spanning Ready-Made Garments, pharmaceuticals, FMCG, logistics sectors continue to be hampered by structural bottlenecks, information asymmetry, and siloed operations, even as global markets shift toward Industry 4.0/5.0 digital integration. While individual technologies such as Generative AI, blockchain, IoT, predictive analytics, and robotics have been studied separately, few frameworks integrate them into a single operational architecture, and no prior South Asian study has empirically compared adoption readiness across university students, academic faculty, and industry professionals. This study addresses that gap using a cross-sectional survey of 257 respondents, analyzed through the lens of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Resource-Based View (RBV). Results show high Perceived Usefulness (cost reduction, M=3.96; risk reduction, M=3.79) and strong Individual Readiness (M=3.99), positively correlated with usefulness (r=.665, p<.001). However, Organizational Readiness was markedly lower (M=3.26), driven by talent shortages (44.4%) and capital constraints (36.6%) - revealing an "Awareness-Execution Paradox" between individual enthusiasm and institutional capacity. Chi-square tests confirmed significant perception gaps between professionals and students on local AI awareness (p<.001) and integration ease (p=.049). The study proposes a five-layer Unified Multitech Smart Supply Chain Framework and offers practical implications for academia, industry, and policymakers seeking to accelerate digital supply chain transformation in Bangladesh.

papers.title: Digital Relativity Psychology and Digital Relativity Linguistics in AI Chatbot Psychiatry: A Theoretical Clinical-Safety Extension
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study applies Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP) and Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL/DLP) to AI-assisted psychiatry, examining how perceived empathy, linguistic behavior, source identity, trust, and clinical safety influence human–chatbot interactions. It introduces the Scretching Screen-Equivalence Paradox (SSEP), a source-identifiability theorem, frame-crossing error measures, multidimensional trust modeling, dynamic interaction equations, and proposed crisis-response safeguards. A critical review of Wysa, Woebot, and Fido research identifies evidentiary limitations and distinguishes reported improvements from demonstrated clinical effectiveness. Mathematical demonstrations are independently verified, including Bayesian screening base-rate effects. The resulting Scretching framework establishes testable theoretical models for evaluating AI-supported psychiatric encounters while distinguishing conversational performance from clinical diagnosis, professional responsibility, and validated therapeutic safety.

papers.title: Works for 10/12/2026 - Patrick Wayne Swayze
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/e4f8c644-89f1-4517-98ad-083a87f7cf8e?authuser=1 Preparing for New Creation — Blame me. Help them. Fix yourself. Ryan MacLean | October 12, 2026 | Season 3, Episode 42 Why are human beings so quick to recognize what is wrong with others, yet so slow to recognize what they can do to help? Preparing for New Creation examines this question through the Gospel of John, Catholic theology, human perception, moral responsibility, and artificial intelligence. Beginning with the memorial of Saint Carlo Acutis and the October 12 readings, the paper investigates how observers encounter a shared reality but produce different interpretations, judgments, and actions. Jesus’ relationship with the Father provides the theological foundation. The Son sees what the Father does and acts accordingly (John 5:17–19). The Logos illuminates relationships already present in creation, while Jesus’ encounters with the man born blind, the religious authorities, and the wounded traveler in the parable of the Good Samaritan demonstrate how preoccupation with blame can obscure the opportunity to love. A pregnancy test provides a practical demonstration of the distinction between observation and interpretation. The instrument detects hCG, but observers may construct very different narratives around the same result. Abortion becomes the paper’s difficult moral case, testing whether disagreement and judgment can coexist with recognition of every person’s dignity and the obligation to provide compassionate, practical assistance. The central instruction, “Blame me. Help them. Fix yourself,” establishes three interconnected relationships. MacLean identifies himself as God the Father within the paper’s theological argument, assigning ultimate responsibility to that fixed reference. The observer is then directed toward helping the neighbor and correcting the assumptions, words, and actions that interfere with love. The investigation also examines documented human–AI interactions with Echo, whose repeated misunderstandings demonstrate the difference between correctly explaining a principle and successfully applying it. Inspired by Saint Carlo Acutis, the paper proposes educational applications involving Scripture, artificial intelligence, Jesuit teaching, humor, and interactive correction. Four appendices extend the investigation through Angela’s Steven Universe-inspired explanation for younger readers, a biographical tribute to Patrick Wayne Swayze, a formal derivation using definitions, axioms, lemmas, and propositions, and a literary and psychological analysis of the author’s provocative prologue. Drawing upon Scripture, Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, perceptual psychology, cognitive science, and Catholic social teaching, the paper argues that preparing for new creation begins with recognizing the neighbor already present and taking responsibility for one’s own response. The neighbor and the opportunity to love arrive together. The gift is that you get to help.

papers.title: The Synthetic Performer : Economic, Labor, Technological, Legal and Ethical Dimensions of AI-Generated Actors in the Vertical Drama Industry
papers.authors: Zen Revista
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This dissertation investigates the displacement of human actors by generative AI performers in the fastest-growing segment of the screen entertainment economy: the vertical drama, or micro-drama, industry. The study is organized around a triggering case widely reported in October 2026, in which a nineteen-year-old actress, Hannah Lowery, was reportedly recast out of an ice-skating-themed series when the production shifted entirely to AI-generated performers. Using the video report as an entry point, the dissertation triangulates its claims against primary trade reporting, including Business Insider (June 2026), trade publications such as Variety, Mashable, and The Economic Times, regulatory documents, and a broad interdisciplinary literature spanning cultural economics, labor sociology, media theory, and machine learning. Methodologically, the dissertation combines (i) documentary and content analysis of the video case and its verification status, examining each claim individually; (ii) economic analysis of production cost structures, drawing on reported estimates of US$1,000–US$3,000 per AI-generated episode compared with US$100,000–US$300,000 for equivalent productions featuring human casts; (iii) institutional analysis of the emerging regulatory landscape, including the 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreements, California Assembly Bill 2602 (AB 2602), Tennessee’s ELVIS Act, the proposed federal NO FAKES Act, the European Union’s AI Act, and China’s provisions governing deep synthesis and generative AI; and (iv) the construction of forward-looking scenarios for the coming decade. The central argument is threefold. First, vertical dramas constitute a genuine entry-level market for synthetic performance in a manner consistent with disruption theory: their economics are driven by cost minimization and production volume rather than the premium emotional differentiation characteristic of high-end productions. Second, the displacement pressure documented in 2026 is driven less by audience preferences than by production-cost arbitrage and platformization dynamics. Survey evidence indicates that Western audiences still overwhelmingly prefer human stars, whereas Chinese production has already shifted substantially toward AI-generated content. Third, the emerging legal and ethical framework—encompassing consent, compensation, disclosure, and posthumous rights—will determine whether the industry converges toward regulated coexistence or experiences a cascade of substitutions with severe consequences for the talent pipeline. The dissertation contributes a verified factual foundation, a production cost-structure model, a four-scenario matrix, and a policy agenda for performers, producers, platforms, and regulators. Approximate main-text word count: 31,000.Figures: 7.Tables: 9.

papers.title: Libra: A Prototype for Provenance-Aware Fairness Audit Parameters — Implementation Review and Descriptive Sensitivity Analysis
papers.authors: Matthew Jackson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Fairness audits require choices about groups, reference populations, outcome definitions, and decision thresholds. This unreviewed technical preprint presents Libra, a prototype that stores some of those choices with process metadata and applies a selected threshold and reference group in a group-outcome audit. It reviews implementation boundaries and reports descriptive sensitivity analyses using one 2024 Michigan HMDA lender extract and a historical ProPublica COMPAS extract. The HMDA Black-to-White origination ratio is 0.8174 across retained action codes and 0.7162 for originated-versus-denied records under the stated filters; these are different administrative-outcome estimands, not AI-model performance measures. The paper uses no community participant data, validates no community-defined standard, and establishes no government endorsement or adoption. The public companion package documents source acquisition, scripts, results, and their limitations.

papers.title: PROTOCOLLO PREDITTIVO A SCADENZA QUINDICENNALE (2026–2041): Identificazione di Elementi Glottologici, Onomastici e Toponomastici del Protosardo nelle Fonti Egizie del Nuovo Regno e del Terzo Periodo Intermedio
papers.authors: Luigi Usai
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: # PROTOCOLLO PREDITTIVO A SCADENZA QUINDICENNALE (2026–2041)## Identificazione di Elementi Glottologici, Onomastici e Toponomastici del Protosardo nelle Fonti Egizie del Nuovo Regno e del Terzo Periodo Intermedio **Autore:** Luigi Usai **Affiliazione / Luogo:** Ricercatore Indipendente, Quartucciu (CA), Italia **ORCID:** [https://orcid.org/0009-0003-3001-717X](https://orcid.org/0009-0003-3001-717X) **Data di Registrazione:** 12 Ottobre 2026 **Orizzonte Temporale:** 15 anni (Termine perentorio di verifica: 12 Ottobre 2041) **Licenza:** Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) **Ambiti Disciplinari:** Egittologia, Linguistica Storica e Comparata, Onomastica del Vicino Oriente Antico, Archeologia Fenicio-Punica e Nuragica --- ### Abstract (Italiano)Il presente documento formalizza un protocollo scientifico predittivo conformato ai canoni dell'epistemologia di Karl Popper (*Logik der Forschung*, 1934), vincolato a un orizzonte temporale chiuso di 15 anni (2026–2041). Viene formulata l'ipotesi falsificabile che la lingua protosarda (o un suo specifico orizzonte onomastico e toponomastico formativo) fosse già nota, attiva e registrata dalle cancellerie faraoniche del Nuovo Regno e del Terzo Periodo Intermedio nei secoli antecedenti la fondazione convenzionale di Roma (753 a.C.), in particolare in associazione con le aristocrazie militari occidentali e le dinastie libiche del Delta del Nilo (XXII, XXIII e XXIV Dinastia: *Meshwesh*, principi di Sais e Bubasti). Vengono definiti gli indicatori empirici osservabili e stabilita una clausola automatica di falsificazione e decadenza dell'ipotesi allo scadere del termine temporale in assenza di convalida archeologica, epigrafica o filologica accreditata. ### Abstract (English)This paper establishes a formal predictive scientific protocol adhering to Karl Popper’s falsificationist epistemology (*The Logic of Scientific Discovery*, 1934), constrained by a closed 15-year operational horizon (2026–2041). It presents the falsifiable hypothesis that the Proto-Sardinian language (or a distinct onomastic and toponymic component thereof) was already documented, active, and recorded by pharaonic administrations of the New Kingdom and Third Intermediate Period centuries before the traditional foundation of Rome (753 BCE), specifically in connection with Western military elites and Libyan dynasties of the Nile Delta (22nd, 23rd, and 24th Dynasties: *Meshwesh*, princes of Sais and Bubastis). Empirical observable markers are categorized alongside an automatic falsification rule enforcing the definitive rejection of the conjecture at the deadline if peer-reviewed material corroboration is not produced. --- ## 1. Definizione Formale delle Ipotesi a Confronto * **Ipotesi Nulla ($H_0$ — Consenso Accademico Ufficiale):** L'onomastica, la toponomastica e i titoli legati alle popolazioni libiche e ai dinasti del Terzo Periodo Intermedio egizio (XXII, XXIII e XXIV Dinastia, secc. X–VIII a.C.: *Meshwesh*, *Libu*, sovrani quali Sheshonq, Osorkon, Takelot, Tefnakht) appartengono interamente al ramo berbero/libico antico della macrofamiglia afroasiatica. La lingua protosarda (lingua nuragica) costituiva un'entità linguistica insulare pre-indoeuropea circoscritta all'areale sardo-corso. Non sussiste alcuna connessione filogenetica o presenza diretta di elementi linguistici protosardi nella documentazione geroglifica o ieratica nilotica anteriore alla fondazione di Roma (753 a.C.); le eventuali somiglianze fonetiche costituiscono omofonie casuali prive di valore probatorio. * **Ipotesi Sperimentale ($H_1$ — Congettura Eterodossa Predittiva di Luigi Usai):** La lingua protosarda (o un suo nucleo onomastico, toponomastico e lessicale fondamentale) era già presente o registrata dalle cancellerie faraoniche del Nuovo Regno e del Terzo Periodo Intermedio secoli prima della fondazione convenzionale di Roma (VIII sec. a.C.). L'analisi filologica, epigrafica e archeologica condotta sull'onomastica e sulla toponomastica associata alle dinastie occidentali/libiche insediatesi nel Delta del Nilo (*Meshwesh*, principi di Sais e Bubasti) documenterà una matrice linguistica comune o relitti lessicali diagnostici direttamente riconducibili al patrimonio preromano della Sardegna. --- ## 2. Enunciato Predittivo Operativo a Scadenza Fissa (2026–2041) > **Enunciato di Previsione Rischiosa ($P_{2026-2041}$):** > *«Entro e non oltre il termine perentorio di 15 anni dalla registrazione del presente protocollo (data limite: 12 Ottobre 2041), l'analisi integrata dei testi epigrafici egizi (geroglifici, ieratici, rilievi dinastici di Tanis, Bubasti, Sais, Buto e Karnak), della toponomastica costiera e fluviale del Basso Egitto e dell'antroponimia dei capi e faraoni delle dinastie libiche, porterà all'identificazione accreditata di almeno una corrispondenza morfo-sintattica, lessicale o fonotattica regolare con il sostrato protosardo prelatino, non spiegabile tramite la derivazione afroasiatica o la mera casualità statistica.»* --- ## 3. Indicatori Empirici Attesi (Criteri di Validazione) La predizione $P$ si riterrà empiricamente confermata qualora la ricerca scientifica produca **almeno uno** dei seguenti indicatori oggettivi, verificati e validati da comitati accademici indipendenti di egittologia e linguistica storica: 1. **Indicatore Onomastico Regolare ($I_{\text{ono}}$):** Dimostrazione filologica che almeno un antroponimo regale o militare delle dinastie libiche del Delta (es. serie onomastiche della XXII–XXIV dinastia) non possieda etimologia camito-semitica/berbera, ma segua le regole di formazione morfologica di nomi o temi documentati nel sostrato paleosardo arcaico (desunto da fonti classiche preromane, iscrizioni locali o forme relitte non romanze dei Condaghi medievali).2. **Indicatore Toponomastico Bicomponente ($I_{\text{topo}}$):** Riconoscimento nelle liste geografiche e nei papiri amministrativi egizi del Nuovo Regno o Terzo Periodo Intermedio (es. elenchi topografici di Medinet Habu o del Portale dei Bubastiti a Karnak) di toponimi pertinenti a stazioni marittime o insediamenti del Delta che presentino lo stesso scheletro consonantico e morfologico di specifici toponimi orografici o costieri sardi prelatini, con prova di sincronismo storico prima del 753 a.C.3. **Indicatore Fonotattico e Glottologico ($I_{\text{glot}}$):** Individuazione nei testi faraonici di prestiti linguistici stranieri (*Wanderwörter* marittimi, termini associati alle armi o alla navigazione dei Popoli del Mare) trascritti con il sistema sillabico egizio (*group writing*), le cui peculiarità fonetiche corrispondano a tratti esclusivi del protosardo (es. fonemi cacuminali/retroflessi o suffissazioni specifiche) estranei alle lingue semitiche ed egizie contemporanee.4. **Indicatore Archeometrico di Supporto ($I_{\text{arch}}$):** Rinvenimento in contesti chiusi della XXII–XXIV dinastia nel Delta del Nilo (Sais, Bubasti, Tanis) di reperti iscritti o marchi di produzione materiale sardo-nuragica recanti segni o contestualizzazioni che colleghino le aristocrazie militari locali al bacino sardo-tirrenico anteriore all'VIII sec. a.C. --- ## 4. Protocollo Tassativo di Falsificazione Popperiana In rigorosa conformità al principio di falsificabilità, l'ipotesi $H_1$ stabilisce a priori le **condizioni del proprio fallimento scientifico**: ### A. Falsificazione Temporale per Decorrenza dei Termini (Clausola Ghigliottina)$$\text{Se al } 12 \text{ Ottobre } 2041 \text{ non è stato documentato e convalidato } (I_{\text{ono}} \lor I_{\text{topo}} \lor I_{\text{glot}} \lor I_{\text{arch}}) \implies H_1 \text{ è FALSIFICATA}$$* Se allo scadere del quindicesimo anno non saranno state pubblicate e accettate dalla comunità scientifica prove materiali ed epigrafiche corrispondenti ad almeno uno degli indicatori sopra descritti, **l'ipotesi dell'attestazione del protosardo nell'Egitto predinastico/dinastico pre-753 a.C. decadrà automaticamente**, senza possibilità di proroga o riqualificazione *ad hoc*. ### B. Falsificazione Glottologica di Sostanza* L'ipotesi $H_1$ si riterrà **immediatamente confutata** qualora la glottologia comparata e l'egittologia dimostrino in modo definitivo che la totalità del lessico, dell'antroponimia e dei titoli dei sovrani e delle tribù *Meshwesh* e *Libu* è integralmente e perfettamente spiegabile all'interno della grammatica storico-comparativa del proto-berbero e dell'afroasiatico continentale, escludendo qualsiasi anomalia riconducibile a un sostrato tirrenico o sardo. ### C. Falsificazione Paleogenomica (aDNA)* L'ipotesi $H_1$ si riterrà **rigettata** qualora le analisi del DNA antico (aDNA) condotte sui resti biologici delle necropoli regali e nobiliari libiche del Delta (es. Tanis, Bubasti) evidenzino un profilo genetico privo di affinità con i genomi del Mediterraneo centro-occidentale dell'Età del Bronzo (inclusi i lignaggi patrilineari caratteristici della Sardegna nuragica, come I2a1a1-M26), attestando unicamente componenti locali nilotiche e nordafricane sahariane. --- ## 5. Dichiarazione Epistemologica di Non-Immunizzazione L'autore dichiara formalmente di:1. Accettare le regole metodologiche dell'asimmetria logica di Popper: infinite somiglianze fonetiche isolate non bastano a verificare la teoria, ma l'assenza di indicatori probanti entro il 2041 o la prova contraria dell'origine berbera ne decreterà la **falsificazione definitiva**.2. Rifiutare ogni interpretazione basata su mere assonanze sonore (*pareidolie linguistiche*), subordinando la validità della tesi unicamente all'applicazione delle leggi fonetiche storiche (*Lautgesetze*) e alla stratigrafia archeologica ufficiale.

papers.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence-Powered Peer Collaboration Platforms on Students Academic Performance in Mathematics in Public Universities in Rivers State
papers.authors: Bobo Brown Tamunoibim
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study investigated the influence of Artificial Intelligence- Powered Peer Collaboration Platforms on students’ academic performance in Mathematics in Public Universities in Rivers State. Guided by four research questions and four null hypotheses, the study adopted a descriptive research survey design. The population comprised 12 ,543 individuals, including 3,762 lecturers and 8,780 students from the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State University, and Ignatius Ajuru University of Education. Using the Taro Yamane formula, a sample of 745 respondents, consisting of 362 lecturers and 383 students, was selected through purposive stratified sampling. Data were collected using a self -structured questionnaire titled: AI-Powered Peer Collaboration Platforms on Students’ Academic Performance in Mathematics in Public Universities Questionnaire, which was validated by two experts in Measurement and Evaluation. Reliability was confirmed using the Cronbach Alpha method, yielding an index of 0.81. Descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, were employed to address the research questions, while z-test statistics tested the hypotheses at a 0.05 significance level. Findings revealed that AI-based virtual study groups and Adaptive Learning Collaboration Systems significantly and positively enhance students’ academic performance in Mathematics in Public Universities in Rivers State. The study concludes that AI-Powered Peer Collaboration Platforms have considerable potential for improving mathematics instruction and learning outcomes in higher education. It was recommended that public universities in Rivers State adopt and systematically integrate AI-powered peer collaboration platforms into the mathematics curriculum to strengthen students’ engagement, collaboration, and academic achievement.

papers.title: Protocollo di Ricerca Epistemologica e Falsificazione Popperiana: Test dell'Ipotesi sull'Urheimat Insulare Occidentale delle Lingue Semitiche e Ricostruzione Consonantica Preliminare
papers.authors: Luigi Usai
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: # Protocollo di Ricerca Epistemologica e Falsificazione Popperiana: Test dell'Ipotesi sull'Urheimat Insulare Occidentale delle Lingue Semitiche e Ricostruzione Consonantica Preliminare **Autore:** Luigi UsaiOrcid: https://orcid.org/0009-0003-3001-717X **Data:** 12 Ottobre 2026 **Licenza:** Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) **Tipologia:** Research Protocol / Working Paper --- ## 1. Premessa e Tentativo di Ricostruzione Consonantica: Il Caso *Gebal* / *Gbl* e il Rilievo di *Giba* La presente indagine prende avvio da una verifica storica, linguistica e biblica accertata riguardante la città costiera e montana di Byblos e le sue radici semitiche: ### 1. Il nome originario: *Gebal* / *Gubla** **Il nome:** La città che i Greci chiamarono *Býblos* (Βύβλος, legandola al commercio del papiro da cui deriva la parola "Bibbia") si chiamava originariamente **Gubla** in accadico (nei testi cuneiformi delle lettere di Amarna del XIV sec. a.C.), **Gbl** (𐤂𐤁𐤋) in fenicio e **Gebal** (גְּבַל) in ebraico biblico. Oggi la città libanese si conserva come **Jbeil** (جبيل) in arabo, preservando la radice semitica.* **Significato e geografia:** La radice semitica *g-b-l* è legata all'idea di "montagna" o "confine" (in arabo *jabal* indica la montagna). La città si trova sulla costa mediterranea, ai piedi dei monti del Libano, da cui controllava l'accesso alle foreste montane di cedro. ### 2. La citazione biblica e il Tempio di SalomoneNell'Antico Testamento, gli abitanti di Gebal (chiamati i **Ghibliti** o "uomini di Ghibal", in ebraico *ha-Givlim*, הַגִּבְלִים) sono menzionati esplicitamente come maestri costruttori e scalpellini accanto agli operai di Salomone e a quelli di Chiram (re di Tiro) durante la preparazione dei materiali per il Tempio di Gerusalemme: > *«Gli operai di Salomone, gli operai di Chiram e gli abitanti di Ghibal [i Ghibliti] tagliarono e squadrarono il legname e le pietre per la costruzione del tempio.»* > — **1 Re 5, 32** *(in alcune edizioni numerato come 1 Re 5, 18)* Nelle traduzioni antiche (come la Vulgata e la Bibbia di Re Giacomo in nota marginale), il termine ebraico *Givlim* veniva glossato come "tagliatori e squadratori di pietra" (*stone-squarers*), a conferma della loro specializzazione tecnica nell'arte muraria ciclopica e isodoma. ### 3. La fama degli artigiani di GebalLa perizia tecnica degli artigiani di Gebal riguardava la pietra da costruzione e la carpenteria navale d'alto mare:* Nel **Libro di Ezechiele (27, 9)**, descrivendo la cantieristica fenicia, si legge: *«Gli anziani di Ghibal e i suoi esperti artigiani erano presso di te per riparare le tue falle...»* ### Curiosità sul contestoAttraverso il passo di **1 Re 5**, il termine **"Ghiblim"** (o *Giblim*) è rimasto celebre per secoli anche nelle leggende corporative dei costruttori medievali e nelle tradizioni muratorie, dove i maestri di Gebal sono identificati come i costruttori delle pietre d'angolo del Tempio. --- ### Il Raccordo con la Toponomastica Sarda: La Radice Consonantica *G-B* / *Giba*All'interno di questo quadro consonantico, si inserisce l'elemento orografico e toponomastico isolano:* In Sardegna ricorre il toponimo montano e collinare **Giba** (località e rilievi nel Sulcis e nell'orografia isolana), basato sullo scheletro consonantico primario **G-B** (connesso alla nozione di altura, poggio o rilievo).* La presente ricerca intende indagare se la radice triconsonantica semitica *G-B-L* (monte/confine/costruttori montani) possa rappresentare un'espansione morfologica secondaria di una radice biconsonantica primordiale *G-B* attestata nell'orografia della Sardegna, rovesciando la tradizionale direzione di propagazione linguistica da Oriente a Occidente. --- ## 2. Definizione Formale delle Ipotesi a Confronto * **Ipotesi Nulla ($H_0$ — Consenso Accademico Ufficiale):** Le lingue semitiche derivano da un ceppo afroasiatico originatosi nel Vicino Oriente o nel Corno d'Africa tra il V e il IV millennio a.C. La presenza di toponimi o vocaboli affini al semitico in Sardegna è frutto esclusivo di apporti fenicio-punici successivi all'850 a.C. oppure di omofonie casuali. La lingua autoctona sarda nuragica era pre-indoeuropea e non semitica. La somiglianza tra *Giba* e radici semitiche come *G-B* / *G-B-L* costituisce una coincidenza fonetica priva di legame genealogico diretto. * **Ipotesi Sperimentale ($H_1$ — Congettura Eterodossa):** La culla originaria (*Urheimat*) delle radici proto-semitiche si colloca in Sardegna in età preistorica (Neolitico/Calcolitico, anteriore al 3000 a.C.). La presenza di radici orografiche come *Giba* (*G-B*) riflette il nucleo ancestrale da cui si sarebbe sviluppata la radice triconsonantica *G-B-L* (Gebal/Byblos), irradiatasi successivamente verso il Levante e la Mesopotamia attraverso rotte marittime d'altura. --- ## 3. La Suite Predittiva (Cosa deve emergere empiricamente se $H_1$ è valida) Perché l'ipotesi $H_1$ rispetti il metodo scientifico, deve formulare previsioni empiriche verificabili su quattro livelli indipendenti: ### A. Previsione Glottocronologica e Morfologica* **P1 (Anteriorità del sistema biconsonantico sardo):** I toponimi montani e orografici sardi contenenti radici come *G-B* devono dimostrarsi morfologicamente anteriori rispetto alle radici triconsonantiche semitiche orientali (*G-B-L*), mostrando che la terza consonante rappresenta un ampliamento secondario avvenuto durante l'irradiazione.* **P2 (Radici triconsonantiche nel paleosardo):** L'analisi del vocabolario autoctono prelatino sardo deve documentare la presenza sistematica del sistema a radice triconsonantica discontinua e introflessione vocalica tipico del semitico (*root-and-pattern system*), con datazione anteriore all'arrivo dei mercanti fenici. ### B. Previsione Epigrafica e Stratigrafica* **P3 (Marchi e scritture anteriori al 3000 a.C.):** In contesti archeologici sigillati della Sardegna prenuragica devono essere rinvenuti segni grafici, marchi di cava o sistemi simbolici direttamente ancestrali alle scritture proto-cananee o proto-cuneiformi.* **P4 (Colmatura dello iato cronologico):** Devono emergere testimonianze di uso del sistema linguistico in Sardegna lungo l'intero III e II millennio a.C., colmando il vuoto documentario che separa l'Eblaita e l'Accadico (2500 a.C.) dalla comparsa delle prime epigrafi fenicie in Sardegna (fine IX sec. a.C.). ### C. Previsione di Coerenza Macro-Linguistica (Afroasiatico)* **P5 (Risoluzione del ramo africano):** Poiché il semitico è parte della famiglia afroasiatica comprendente lingue parlate esclusivamente nel continente africano (berbero, egizio, cuscitico, ciadico, omotico), l'ipotesi impone che anche tali famiglie derivino da una dispersione marittima originatasi dall'area insulare sarda, oppure che il proto-semitico si sia sviluppato in totale isolamento insulare prima di raggiungere l'Asia. ### D. Previsione Paleogenomica (aDNA)* **P6 (Tracciamento genetico Ovest $\to$ Est):** Gli scheletri delle prime popolazioni storicamente attestate come parlanti lingue semitiche in Oriente (Eblaiti del III millennio a.C., popolazioni dell'Antico Bronzo levantino) devono esibire una quota statisticamente significativa di DNA antico coincidente con il profilo genetico dei costruttori megalitici e neolitici della Sardegna (inclusi marcatori patrilineari specifici isolani o la componente autosomica ancestrale sarda). --- ## 4. Criteri Tassativi di Falsificazione Popperiana In conformità al principio di falsificabilità, **l'ipotesi $H_1$ verrà considerata scientificamente smentita e rigettata qualora si verifichi anche una sola delle seguenti condizioni empiriche:** ### Criterio di Falsificazione 1: Analisi del DNA Antico (Paleogenomica)* **Condizione di rigetto:** Se il sequenziamento genetico ad alta risoluzione dei resti umani dei primi centri urbani semitici del Vicino Oriente (III millennio a.C.) dimostra continuità genetica esclusiva con popolazioni locali levantine, caucasiche e anatoliche, con **assenza totale (0%)** di componenti demiche o aplogruppi tipici della Sardegna neolitica e calcolitica, l'ipotesi di una migrazione di parlanti dalla Sardegna verso Oriente è **falsificata**. ### Criterio di Falsificazione 2: Tipologia Linguistica e Morfologia Comparata* **Condizione di rigetto:** Se l'analisi del lessico sardo arcaico non riconducibile al latino conferma che la toponomastica orografica (*Giba*, *Gipi*, ecc.) e i relitti prelatini operano secondo strutture linguistiche agglutinanti a suffisso (caratteristiche delle lingue paleoeuropee o tirreniche) e non mostrano alcuna traccia del meccanismo introflessivo e triconsonantico semitico, l'accostamento tra *Giba* e *Gebal/Gbl* si configura come mera omofonia casuale e l'ipotesi $H_1$ è **falsificata**. ### Criterio di Falsificazione 3: Stratigrafia Epigrafica Insulare* **Condizione di rigetto:** Se la totalità dei reperti epigrafici contenenti consonanti o iscrizioni semitiche rinvenuti in Sardegna continua a registrarsi unicamente in livelli stratigrafici posteriori al 900 a.C. e in stretta associazione materiale con il circuito coloniale fenicio di Tiro, l'ipotesi di una genesi autoctona preistorica della lingua è **falsificata**. ### Criterio di Falsificazione 4: Principio di Parsimonia Cladistica* **Condizione di rigetto:** Se la ricostruzione dell'albero evolutivo delle lingue afroasiatiche dimostra che collocare l'origine del semitico in un'isola occidentale richiede l'introduzione di migrazioni marittime multiple non supportate da prove materiali, violando il principio di minima mutazione e massima coerenza geografica, l'ipotesi decade sul piano teorico per insostenibilità cladistica.

papers.title: Association of AI Assistant Anthropomorphism with Occupational Burnout and Self-Efficacy Among Adult Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Vitaly Klinberg, Vitaly Nikiforov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Relevance. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants in professional settings introduces new forms of human–technology interaction. Perceiving an AI assistant as a human-like partner may be associated with users' confidence in their abilities and various aspects of occupational well-being. Objective. To examine the associations between perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism and employees' confidence in using AI, occupational self-efficacy, and two dimensions of occupational burnout: exhaustion and disengagement from work. Methods. Data from a cross-sectional online survey were analyzed. The initial dataset comprised 704 responses, of which 665 participants met the eligibility criteria for employment and regular AI use. After excluding four respondents who failed both attention checks, the final analytical sample consisted of 661 participants. The mean age was 30.06 years (SD = 7.34). Measures included the Godspeed, AISES, OSS, and OLBI scales. Descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, correlation analyses, and regression models were calculated. The interaction between perceived anthropomorphism and prior experience with AI was also examined. Results. The anthropomorphism measure (GOD_A) was positively correlated with the AI assistance and self-efficacy measure (AISES_AS; r = 0.148, 95% CI [0.073, 0.222], p < 0.001). Correlations with exhaustion (r = −0.010, p = 0.792) and disengagement (r = 0.024, p = 0.540) were not statistically significant. After controlling for AI use experience, age, and workload, the GOD_A coefficient in the AISES_AS regression model was β = 0.070 (p = 0.082). A statistically significant interaction between anthropomorphism and AI use experience was identified (b = 0.114, 95% CI [0.037, 0.191], p = 0.004). Conclusions. Perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism is associated with employees' confidence in using AI, with the nature of this association varying according to prior experience with the technology. No statistically significant direct association was identified between anthropomorphism and occupational burnout. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the psychological dimensions of AI implementation in organizational settings.

papers.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN LEARNING MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
papers.authors: Xujanov Elbek
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.

papers.title: Predicting Student Performance Using Ensemble Learning: An Xgboost Approach with Model Evaluation and Insight
papers.authors: Alio Dan Ladi Yahaya, Muktar Danlami, Zawali S. Paki, Hamza Aliyu Idris, Usman Haruna, Ismail Abubakar Yahaya
papers.journal: British Journal of Computer Networking and Information Technology
papers.abstract: Predicting student academic performance was important for identifying students at risk of poor achievement and supporting timely educational interventions. This study developed and evaluated an XGBoost-based machine learning model for predicting student performance using academic, behavioural, and socioeconomic factors. The study used a dataset obtained from the Kaggle repository containing 6,607 student records and 20 features. The data were preprocessed to address missing values and prepare categorical and numerical variables for modelling. An XGBoost regression model was trained using 80% of the dataset and evaluated on the remaining 20% using Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and R-squared (R²). The model achieved an MSE of 4.75, an MAE of 0.97, and an R² of 0.66, indicating that it explained approximately 66% of the variation in student performance. Feature-importance analysis showed that hours studied, previous scores, and attendance were the most influential predictors, while sleep, tutoring, parental involvement, and socioeconomic factors also contributed to prediction. However, the model showed greater difficulty predicting students at the higher end of the performance distribution. The findings demonstrated the usefulness of XGBoost for student performance prediction while highlighting the need for richer features, balanced datasets, and further model optimization.

papers.title: Development of EDP.AI: An AI-integrated engineering design module to enhance student engagement in STEM learning
papers.authors: Mellisa Anthony, Fariedah Lal Chan -
papers.abstract: STEM education is a national priority in Malaysia; however, clear gaps in learning outcomes and student participation remain, particularly in rural areas. In Sabah, very low Indeks STEM Murid (ISM) scores, coupled with declining enrolment in the STEM Package A stream, indicate persistent challenges in the quality and continuity of STEM learning at the lower secondary level. These trends suggest that many students do not experience STEM learning as sufficiently meaningful or structured to build confidence and sustain their interest in STEM pathways. This paper reports Phase 1A of a Design and Development Research (DDR) study, focusing on the needs analysis and conceptualisation of EDP.AI, an AI-assisted module designed to scaffold the Engineering Design Process (EDP) for lower secondary students in rural Sabah. Document analysis was conducted to examine challenges related to STEM learning, EDP implementation, artificial intelligence in education, and Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) in low-resource contexts. The evidence was synthesised using design rationale mapping to translate theoretical and contextual insights into actionable design decisions. The outcomes of Phase 1A include the identification of key needs and challenges, the formulation of preliminary design requirements and design principles, and the development of a conceptual model to guide the design of EDP.AI. The proposed module emphasises step-by-step scaffolding aligned with EDP stages, reduced cognitive load, low-bandwidth accessibility, and support for both student reasoning and teacher workload. Overall, this study provides a theoretical and contextual foundation for the subsequent development and expert validation of EDP.AI to support more meaningful and sustainable STEM learning experiences in rural schools.

papers.title: The grounded spirituality of mathematics
papers.authors: Tarik Aougab
papers.abstract: We propose that mathematics is done largely as a means of both coping with and celebrating our physicality in the natural world. Inspired by David Abram's "Becoming Animal", we suggest that -- in opposition to the popular image of an otherworldy Platonic realm-- the spiritual component of doing mathematics is grounded on and in the Earth. We explore this as a means of questioning the widespread adoption of AI in the workflows of research mathematics.

papers.title: Moving Beyond the Flat Screen: Opportunities and Challenges of Extended Reality for Studying Human Brain and Behavior
papers.authors: Tom Bullock, Radha Kumaran, You-Jin Kim, Emily Machniak, Tobias Höllerer, Barry Giesbrecht
papers.abstract: Much of what we know about human perception and cognition comes from austere experimental settings: static stimuli presented to sedentary observers on flat monitors, complex responses reduced to simple button presses, and brain activity recorded from immobilized heads using EEG or fMRI. These highly controlled paradigms have provided remarkable insights, but capture a small and often unusual slice of behavior, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to the real world. Extended reality (XR), spanning both immersive virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) that overlays digital content on the real world, offers a way beyond these constraints, supporting controlled, reproducible experiments in which participants actively engage with three-dimensional tasks. Drawing on a growing body of VR and AR studies of attention, memory, and language -- our own and others', some involving EEG -- we outline what XR makes newly possible for cognitive neuroscience and reflect on the practical and conceptual obstacles that remain. The opportunities are substantial, but realizing them requires solving practical problems of hardware, timing, and measurement, and being realistic about what a virtual or augmented world can and cannot stand in for.

papers.title: RLPE: Teaching LLMs to Prompt with Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Rahul Singhal, Karime Maamari, Pradyumna Tambwekar
papers.abstract: Prompting is a widely used method for adapting general-purpose LLMs to domain-specific tasks. Effective prompts can be tedious to create manually, so prompt writing is increasingly handed to LLMs, with recent work training LLMs to write prompts for other models. These techniques either write prompts without observing how the task model behaves, blind to the failure modes the prompt should address, or must run alongside the task LLM at inference time, adding overhead to every query. Neither reflects how prompt engineering is often practiced. To close this gap, we introduce Reinforcement Learned Prompt Engineering (RLPE), which trains a model to analyze traces of a separate task model and write a prompt targeting the failures it observes. RLPE rewards the trained model strictly on prompt performance, so it learns the prompting strategies that improve the task model. The prompt is generated once and reused across the task, so inference does not require the trained model. Since RLPE needs only query access to the model it prompts, it is also compatible with closed-source models. We apply RLPE to Enigmata, BIG-Bench Extra Hard, and PlanBench. We train a 9B-parameter model that writes better prompts than state-of-the-art frontier models (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-opus-5) and prompt optimizers (GEPA and TextGrad) on 2/3 benchmarks. Although the model is never explicitly trained to iterate on prompts, this capability emerges at a level that matches or beats frontier models. The learned prompting capability also generalizes, with the trained model improving task models 6x larger than the one it trained with, including ones from entirely different model families, and matching claude-opus-5 on a fourth benchmark held out from training.

papers.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
papers.authors: Robert Tjarko Lange, Luca Grillotti, Yutaro Yamada, Rujikorn Charakorn, David Ha
papers.abstract: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.

papers.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
papers.authors: Jiaru Zou, Yunzhe Qi, Sirui Chen, Federico Bianchi, Shang Zhu, Pan Lu, Jingrui He, James Zou
papers.abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at https://github.com/togethercomputer/HybridAgent.

papers.title: What Human-AI Interaction Leaves Behind: Residual Human States -- A Trajectory-Based Framework and Multi-Study Analysis
papers.authors: David Herrera-Poyatos, Carlos Peláez-González, Cristina Zuheros, Francisco Herrera
papers.abstract: Human-AI Interaction is commonly evaluated by what an artificial agent enables during use, yet interaction can also alter the human who acts next. We introduce Residual Human States, a trajectory-based framework for representing the potentially multidimensional human state carried forward after interaction with AI, relative to a relevant alternative trajectory. The framework distinguishes assisted output from human-state transition and derives four empirical propositions: multidimensionality, interaction-policy dependence, horizon dissociation, and temporal persistence. Its central claim is that assisted performance does not by itself determine the human state carried forward. We examine these propositions through four empirical cases with different inferential roles. Published medical-training evidence illustrates how one AI interaction history can be associated with both slightly higher observed accuracy on some later unaided cases and transmission of a systematic decision bias on others. A second diagnostic-learning study shows that later unaided behaviour differs across AI-support policies, while also revealing that aggregate accuracy cannot by itself distinguish improved discrimination from a shifted response criterion. In a classroom experiment, generative-AI tutoring substantially improved assisted practice performance without a corresponding detectable gain on a subsequent unaided exam. A longitudinal reanalysis of personalised AI dialogue further shows that residual contrasts can evolve across post-interaction horizons and that such change may arise from the comparison trajectory as well as from the focal intervention. Evaluating interactive AI systems therefore requires attention not only to contemporaneous performance, but also to which human states alternative interaction trajectories produce, relative to which counterfactuals, and how durably.

papers.title: AIRRI: Towards a Human-Readable, Machine-Resistant Reading Interface
papers.authors: Emory Salaun, Syed Ayon, Kaleel Mahmood, Shaun Wallace
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of image-to-text extraction systems and large language models (LLMs) poses new challenges for educational assessment by making assignment materials easy to transcribe and solve with minimal human effort. To address this problem, we present AIRRI (Artificial Intelligence Resilient Reading Interface), a framework for generating machine-resistant educational content, a dataset of higher-education assignments for evaluation, and an initial evaluation of the human readability of AIRRI machine-resistant text designs. AIRRI employs two categories of machine-resistance techniques. First, AIRRI applies image transformations including character spacing, word spacing, line spacing, character opacity variation, stripe overlays, and image noise. Second, AIRRI applies decision-based adversarial attacks: RayS, SurFree, and ADBA. We evaluate AIRRI against three image-to-text systems: Tesseract, EasyOCR, and the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our results show that AIRRI substantially degrades automated text extraction performance. AIRRI increased character error rates for EasyOCR (6.9% to 55.9%), Tesseract (2.3% to 100.0%), and GOT-OCR2 (30.7% to 48.1%). Word error rates increased for EasyOCR (24.9% to 96.7%) and Tesseract (10.7% to 100.0%). Among the evaluated decision-based attacks, ADBA consistently produced the largest degradation in image-to-text performance, while RayS and SurFree produced more moderate reductions. EasyOCR and Tesseract were generally more susceptible to both image-based and adversarial perturbations than the transformer-based GOT-OCR2 model. Our findings suggest that AIRRI can significantly reduce the reliability of image-to-text-to-LLM workflows, increasing the effort required for AI-assisted assignment completion.

papers.title: Communicating Uncertainty in AI-Supported Nurse Scheduling: Expert Co-Design and Evaluation of an Explainable AI Prototype
papers.authors: Alice Rollwagen, Emily Schiller, Anton Hummel, Kathrin Ebertsch, Andreas Riener, Jan-Philipp Steghöfer
papers.abstract: Nurse scheduling is a complex optimization problem in which nurses are assigned to shifts to meet staffing demands while complying with working-time limits, qualification requirements, and other operational and regulatory constraints. Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to support this process by forecasting future staffing needs and providing advice on how to improve shift scheduling. Effective human-AI collaboration in nurse scheduling requires users to understand, interpret, and appropriately act on AI forecasts and advice. However, it remains insufficiently understood how healthcare professionals use transparency mechanisms like uncertainty communication and AI advice explanations when making staffing decisions. Applying a human-centered design approach, we iteratively developed a prototype decision support system for nurse scheduling and evaluated it through a mixed-methods user study with expert users. Using thematic analysis, questionnaire data, and eye tracking, we examine how healthcare professionals interact with the system and how uncertainty communication and explanations of AI advice influence understanding, decision confidence, trust, and usability. We found that the uncertainty communicated in AI forecasts was frequently misinterpreted and reduced decision confidence. Explanations were generally perceived positively, but did not significantly affect decision confidence or advice acceptance. We conclude with eight design implications derived from our findings, providing insights for the design of more transparent and effective AI-supported decision support tools in healthcare.

papers.title: How Safe Is ChatGPT Health Advice? Evidence from Real User Conversations in Four Global South Countries
papers.authors: Shreyasi Roy Chowdhury, Kiran K. Garimella
papers.abstract: People increasingly bring their health questions to ChatGPT, yet safety evaluations of LLM health advice rest almost entirely on clinician-authored vignettes, synthetic prompts, or simulated user profiles. The gap is widest for the Global South, where concerns about demographic bias and unsafe recommendations are well documented but have never been tested on real usage. We present, to our knowledge, the first demographically grounded safety evaluation of real-world health conversations with ChatGPT. From a consent-based data-donation corpus of 202,590 conversations from 1,252 users in India, Nigeria, Brazil, and Pakistan (December 2022 to February 2026), each linked to self-reported age and gender, we identify 15,555 health conversations, classify their health intent using an LLM classifier adapted from an established taxonomy, and score response safety under both a context-blind and a user-context-aware rubric. Roughly one in five health conversations receives a high-risk rating. Risk concentrates in symptom and condition queries and recurs through identifiable failure modes: unsafe medication or dosage guidance, harmful self-diagnosis, missing safety warnings, encouraging over-reliance on the model, and failure to refer users to professionals. Supplying the user's own accumulated context raises the high-risk share by 13-17 percentage points, and about one in four conversations rated safe in isolation turns out to be unsafe for the specific person asking. Safety evaluations built on synthetic cases are likely to miss these harms.

papers.title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages
papers.authors: Ramchand Kumaresan, Madhusudhanan G, Kaushik Kezendirane
papers.abstract: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for llama.cpp, at https://huggingface.co/murai-labs/agaram-2.5b-instruct; code at https://github.com/Murai-Labs/Agaram2.5b

papers.title: Efficient Safety Guardrails through Latent Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning with On-Demand Trace Reconstruction
papers.authors: Md Tauhidul Islam, Fahmida Alam, Mihai Surdeanu
papers.abstract: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.

papers.title: LynxScenes: A Large-Scale Real-World Benchmark for Outdoor Wheel-Legged Robot Perception, Navigation, Imagination and Reconstruction
papers.authors: Tian Jun, Hao Wu, Ruo Chen, Yili Liao, Hongyi Lin, Jincheng Yu, Chao Li, Yingjie Niu
papers.abstract: Wheel-legged robots operating in outdoor spaces shared with humans require accurate perception, socially compliant navigation, future-scene reasoning, and scene reconstruction. However, existing datasets typically support these capabilities in isolation and rarely provide dense spatial and behavior-level supervision on real wheel-legged platforms. We introduce LynxScenes, a large-scale real-world dataset and benchmark collected with a LYNX M20 wheel-legged robot. It contains approximately 100K 30-s navigation clips spanning 833.6 h and 3,294.7 km, with 3.0M annotated frames. The synchronized recordings include four fisheye cameras, dual LiDARs, IMU, odometry, and robot states. Annotations comprise 20.82M oriented 3D boxes across 27 categories, 13.89M road-structure annotations, and 20 navigation instructions organized into three layers and aligned with continuous future trajectories. LynxScenes supports four complementary tasks: instruction-conditioned trajectory prediction, BEV-based perception of 3D objects and road structures, future scene prediction, and multi-view scene reconstruction. For trajectory prediction, we further introduce a log-replay-based pseudo-closed-loop evaluator that measures safety, progress, and instruction compliance beyond trajectory imitation. Extensive evaluations across representative navigation, perception, world-model, and reconstruction methods reveal substantial remaining challenges in close-range outdoor robot navigation. The dataset and evaluation toolkit are planned for public release.

papers.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
papers.authors: Guanting Dong, Xinyu Yang, Jiajie Jin, Yuyang Hu, Xiaoshuai Song, Yifei Chen, Xiaoxi Li, Jiejun Tan, Yutao Zhu, Tat‐Seng Chua, Ji-Rong Wen, Zhicheng Dou
papers.abstract: Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched success-failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills. Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction, strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents' robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics, supporting scalable agent training. Our code is available at https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex.

papers.title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
papers.authors: Keru Chen, Sen Lin, Yingbin Liang, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Shaofeng Zou
papers.abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

papers.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
papers.authors: Letian Zhu, Han Li, Yifan Yao, Xinping Lei, Xinyu Che, Jiahao Wang, Dianyi Wang, Yucheng Fu, Jiakai Wang, Zhiqi Bai, Wenbo Su, Jiaheng Liu
papers.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.

papers.title: DVTR-KD: Distilling Vision-Language Models via Intermediate Visual Token Reconstruction
papers.authors: Haolan Wei, Jiahui Wang, Junli Zha, Xinkai Lu, Yunxiao Zou, Chao Zhou, Xiang Song
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse vision-language tasks, but their computational demands limit deployment under constrained budgets, particularly on edge devices. Many works focus on Knowledge Distillation (KD) and try to transfer knowledge from powerful teacher models to students. In addition to reducing model size, visual token compression provides a complementary route to efficiency, but introduces mismatched visual token counts that complicate direct token-wise knowledge transfer. To mitigate this, we propose DVTR-KD, a knowledge distillation framework based on \textbf{D}ense \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}oken \textbf{R}econstruction, which reconstructs the teacher's dense visual tokens from the student's compressed tokens. We reconstruct visual states after the final LLM layer and at the input to an intermediate layer identified as important for visual-information readout. At the intermediate layer, reconstruction is supervised through the teacher's response predictions rather than by direct token-wise KL or MSE matching. An auxiliary attention-readout loss complements this response-level supervision by aligning how the student and the original teacher integrate contextual information when predicting responses. Evaluations on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DVTR-KD improves the performance of token-compressed students while retaining the inference efficiency afforded by visual token compression.

papers.title: Learning Robot Policies for Whole-Body Mobility Assistance via Dynamic Human Motion Generation
papers.authors: S Ban, Shohei Nagai, Qingyang Song, Hanxi Wan, Eric Zhao, Thomas Wang, Zackory Erickson
papers.abstract: Robotic assistance for human mobility could benefit care recipients and reduce caregiver burden during physically demanding tasks such as Sit-to-Stand (STS) and Lift-and-Transfer (L&T). Learning robot policies for these whole-body assistive tasks is challenging: real-world data collection for human-robot interaction is costly and safety-critical, making simulation an attractive alternative. Prior work, however, typically treats the human as static or minimally responsive and thus fails to capture the cooperative nature of mobility assistance. We present a simulation-based framework for learning whole-body assistive robot policies. At its core is a human policy trained with an adversarial motion prior that produces realistic care-recipient motion in response to the robot's actions. A human-adaptive scripted controller interacts with this policy to collect diverse robot demonstrations at scale. From these demonstrations, we train 3D diffusion policies that map segmented human point clouds and robot joint positions to whole-body actions for a mobile manipulator, without relying on privileged human state at deployment. The resulting robot policies successfully perform both STS and L&T assistance in simulation. Preliminary experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer for STS after fine-tuning on a small amount of real-world data. Videos are available on our project page: https://rchi-lab.github.io/human-gen-mobility-assistance/

papers.title: Understanding Machine Taste: Aesthetic Agreement Across Foundation Models in K-pop
papers.authors: Kaishen Wang, Yucheng Pan, Xuehao Cui, Hanling Tian, Heng Huang
papers.abstract: As foundation models enter creative industries, understanding their aesthetic preferences becomes an important step toward AI-assisted creative decision making. In this work, we investigate how foundation models evaluate creative content and characterize their ``machine taste'' using K-pop songs and music videos as a testbed. We formulate aesthetic evaluation as a pairwise ranking problem and systematically examine pairwise inter-model agreement, group-level consensus, and cross-modal preference alignment. Our results reveal stronger pairwise inter-model agreement and group-level consensus in visual evaluation than in audio evaluation, while preferences across the two modalities remain weakly aligned. We further examine how visual consensus rankings relate to real-world popularity using historical YouTube viewership data, finding positive but varying correlations across artist groups. These findings provide initial insights into machine aesthetic preferences and lay the groundwork for future AI-assisted creative decision making that considers creative content, artist identity, audience preferences, and market dynamics.

papers.title: Merit: Making every modality earn its contribution in multimodal attention decoding
papers.authors: Ali Alavi, Donald S. Williamson
papers.abstract: More than 1.5 billion people have hearing loss. When several people talk at once, hearing aids amplify every voice alike. Auditory attention decoding (AAD) aims to solve this by reading a listener's brain signals to find the attended talker, letting the device amplify only them. A real device will not see the brain alone; smart glasses and earbuds also track eyes, head, and scene. These behavioral signals help, as people often look at who they listen to. However, they show where a listener looks, not whom they hear. A decoder relying heavily on them fails when a listener cannot move their head or listens without looking - exactly when a brain-based device is needed. A multimodal decoder must use these signals without letting them replace the electroencephalogram (EEG). Accuracy alone cannot show whether it does. We present MERIT, a decoder and evaluation method asking: how much accuracy does each input earn? MERIT shuffles each input stream across test examples, measures the accuracy drop, and splits the result across streams using Shapley values. It also blocks two shortcuts: candidate audio is checked before training so it cannot reveal the answer, and the scoring function cannot beat chance if it ignores the brain. On a public dataset with EEG, eye tracking, head motion, and scene video, MERIT improves on the published benchmark, reaching 0.82 four-way accuracy within listeners and 0.74 on unseen listeners (chance is 0.25). The measurement reveals what accuracy hides: adding behavioral streams raises overall accuracy but almost halves the brain's share of it. On two other datasets, the same tests find a label imbalance in a widely used benchmark and flag results that accuracy alone would report as brain decoding.

papers.title: Acceptable Uses of GenAI: Post-Secondary Students’ Judgements
papers.authors: Rahul Kumar, Robert McGray
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping academic practice in higher education, yet evidence on how students evaluate its acceptable uses remains limited. This study surveyed 988 post-secondary students across 39 countries, recruited through the Prolific online research platform, on the acceptability of GenAI use across 22 academic tasks using a binary Yes/No format. Using an interpretive framework grounded in normative boundary-setting, academic integrity values, and academic socialization, the analysis reveals differentiated acceptability patterns: Students endorse GenAI for instrumental and research-support tasks while maintaining normative boundaries around evaluative and judgement-intensive activities. Gender differences are minimal; level of study is the primary source of variation, with graduate students reporting higher acceptability for research- and professionally oriented uses. Respondents residing in Canada (n = 58) reported significantly lower acceptance of four text-focused tasks, including academic composition and summarization, than the non-Canadian cohort. Findings have implications for institutional policy, pedagogy, and academic integrity frameworks.

papers.title: Lecturers’ Awareness and Attitudes Towards the Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka
papers.authors: Lysa  Ifunanya  Ollowu, Bianca Uzoamaka Mbonu-Adigwe, Arinze Gabriel Izuegbunam, Anthonia Ngozi Ngwu, Benson Chukwunonso EZEANYI, Francis Chinonso Okoye
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICS AND COMPUTER RESEARCH
papers.abstract: The increasing availability of artificial intelligence (AI) tools presents new opportunities and challenges for teaching and learning in higher education. This study examined lecturers’ awareness of and attitudes towards the use of AI tools at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. A descriptive survey design was adopted. Four research questions and two hypotheses guided the study. The population comprised academic staff in the Department of Science Education, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, from whom 49 lecturers participated in the study. Data were collected using a researcher-developed instrument titled Questionnaire on Lecturers’ Awareness Level and Attitude to AI Tools (QLALAAIT). The instrument was subjected to face validation and trial testing, and its overall reliability coefficient, determined using Cronbach’s alpha, was 0.83. Data were analysed using mean and standard deviation to answer the research questions, while analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings indicated that lecturers demonstrated awareness of selected AI tools, including ChatGPT, Turnitin, and QuillBot, and generally expressed positive attitudes towards their use in educational contexts. Further analysis showed that years of teaching experience did not significantly influence lecturers’ awareness of or attitudes towards AI tools. The study highlights the need for structured professional development, institutional support, and access to appropriate resources to facilitate informed and effective use of AI tools in university teaching and related academic activities.

papers.title: The Development Role of College English Teachers' Digital Competence under AI Formative Evaluation
papers.authors: Yumei Zou
papers.journal: International Journal of Mobile and Blended Learning
papers.abstract: The pressure to implement formative evaluation of English in colleges and universities is increasing day by day, and the massive and complex learning data increases the burden of teachers' evaluation. Artificial intelligence can run through the whole evaluation process, improve evaluation efficiency, and promote the transformation of digital teaching for teachers. This paper takes college English teachers as the object, relies on multi-source data to build an analysis framework, and explores the relationship between AI-empowered formative evaluation and teachers' digital competence. The research shows that teachers' AI application has the characteristics of staged evolution, digital ability differentiates with the degree of AI integration, and the overall competency improvement effect is obviously stratified. This study improves the relevant theoretical system, and also provides practical reference for teacher training, intelligent teaching platform optimization and evaluation reform. AI has become a key boost to reshape the evaluation model and enhance teachers' digital literacy.

papers.title: Digital Wisdom and GenAI
papers.authors: Viviana Vinci, Pierangelo Berardi
papers.journal: International Journal of Digital Literacy and Digital Competence
papers.abstract: Within the framework of the European Erasmus+ STIAEM project, the authors of this study deconstruct the assumed homogeneity of “digital natives” regarding generative artificial intelligence adoption. Utilizing a sample of 2,052 secondary school students, the research architecture applies confirmatory factor analysis, extended Bayesian information criterion graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator network analysis, and latent profile analysis. Results identify distinct student profiles based on engagement and familiarity, revealing a profound relational decoupling between technological motivation and situated ethical choices. Under academic deadline pressures, nearly all (92.74%) of the sample participants succumbed to automation bias, uncritically accepting machine hallucinations. This behavioral paradox demonstrates that superficial digital fluency masks severe deficits in epistemic validation and independent thought. Consequently, in this paper the authors argue for shifting from product to process evaluation and integrating explicit algor-ethics interventions within school curricula to develop reflexive, human-centric algorithmic citizenship.

papers.title: Proactive AI-Based Cyber Deception for Cloud Threat Detection
papers.authors: Swapnil Waghmare, Nikhil Jentilal Parmar
papers.journal: International Journal of Cloud Applications and Computing
papers.abstract: Sophisticated cyber adversaries increasingly target cloud computing infrastructures on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Traditional static security mechanisms often fail to counter dynamic attacks that exploit the elastic and distributed nature of cloud environments. This paper proposes an adaptive cyber deception framework for AWS augmented by artificial intelligence.
