The framework deploys realistic honeypots across EC2, S3, and Relational Database Service, supported by AWS Secrets Manager for secure credential handling, to emulate high-value assets. Real-time telemetry is analyzed using random cut forest and XGBoost models deployed through Amazon SageMaker to detect anomalous behavior. An adaptive orchestration layer using AWS Lambda dynamically modifies deception strategies, including elastic Internet Protocol (IP) rotation, S3 bait updates, and adaptive Relational Database Service schema enrichment. Experimental results show improved detection accuracy, reduced false positives, and effective adversarial engagement.

papers.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Personalized Learning on Korean Language Performance
papers.authors: Chencen Lin, Guang Liang
papers.journal: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence: Ethical Considerations and Its Impact on Students’ Cognitive Skills
papers.authors: Tamanna Jena, Surya Prakash Devara, Disha Jatania
papers.journal: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, influencing how students learn, produce knowledge, and engage in assessments. This study examines the ethical implications of AI integration in university courses and its perceived impact on students’ cognitive skills. Using a mixed-methods secondary data analysis, survey data from 23,218 students across 109 countries and 252 teachers from China, Romania, India, and Brunei were analyzed to explore perceptions of AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, behavioral intentions, and cognitive outcomes. The results have shown that although students are aware of the potential of AI in improving the efficiency and content creation and assistance in the learning process, there are still concerns about overdependence, plagiarism, and lack of critical thinking. The views of faculty underline moral direction and the necessity of systematic assimilation. Developing upon these insights, a theoretical framework is developed that connects antecedent variables, behavior intentions and institutional context to two outcomes the cognitive impact and institutional influence. This framework offers a guide on how universities should introduce generative AI in a responsible manner, and strike a balance between ethical principles and training higher-order cognitive abilities.

papers.title: All Talk and No Action?
papers.authors: Kristian Heinrich Träg, Miriam Mulders, Dominik Evangelou
papers.journal: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
papers.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) has been proposed as a promising tool to enhance social competences in higher education, especially in resource-constrained counseling seminars. This study investigates the effects of a single-session VR-based training on university students’ counseling competence and self-efficacy. Forty-five students took part in a standardized counseling scenario delivered through a realistic social VR environment, interacting with a trained actor in real time. Pre- and post-training questionnaires assessed changes in self-efficacy and counseling competence, alongside measures of presence, realism, cognitive load, and perspective-taking. Results showed small, non-significant improvements in both outcome variables. Regression analyses revealed that perceived realism significantly predicted counseling competence, while presence and extraneous cognitive load influenced perspective-taking. However, the limited duration of the intervention and the absence of a control group constrain causal inferences. Despite these limitations, the study provides initial empirical support for the integration of VR technologies into counselor education and outlines key factors for effective implementation. Future research should explore adaptive, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced VR environments that allow for repeated practice and personalized feedback to fully realize the potential of VR in social skills training.

papers.title: Visualized Empowerment Nursing Pathway for Nutritional Outcomes in Lymphoma with Chemotherapy-Induced Oral Mucositis: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.authors: 吴爱军, Wenjun Wang, Yun Yin
papers.abstract: This study examined the effect of an empowerment nursing model on the nutritional status of patients with lymphoma who developed oral mucositis during chemotherapy and further developed a visualized implementation pathway. A total of 133 patients with lymphoma who received chemotherapy and developed oral mucositis between March 2024 and October 2025 were included. Based on previous nursing records, 62 patients who had received an empowerment nursing model centered on "assessment-identification-goal setting-training-implementation-feedback-continuing management" were assigned to the study group, while 71 patients who had received routine nursing were assigned to the control group. After baseline adjustment, the study group showed more favorable Patient-Generated Subjective Global Assessment (PG-SGA) and Nutritional Risk Screening (NRS) 2002 scores, body weight, body mass index (BMI), serum nutritional markers, dietary intake, self-management, symptom burden, and quality-of-life outcomes than the control group, while the change in oral mucositis grade and the visual analog scale (VAS) pain score also favored the study group. After false-discovery-rate correction, ulcer duration, mucosal healing time, and length of hospital stay remained shorter in the study group, whereas the differences in malnutrition rate, oral nutritional supplement use, and medication-use duration were no longer significant. These findings suggest that the visualized empowerment nursing pathway was associated with better nutritional status and oral intake, faster recovery from oral mucositis, and stronger self-management ability.

papers.title: System analysis approaches for the development of advanced architectures
papers.authors: Г. В. Горячев
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established a new technological and organizational landscape across all industries, yet the process of creating AI architecture remains disjointed, intuitive, and domain-oriented. The proposed study introduces a System-Analytical Framework of Artificial Intelligence Architecture Design (SA-AI Framework), a collection of principles from systems analysis and multi-criteria decision-making intended to harmonize architectural design processes across heterogeneous AI domains. The paper is based on twenty-five current studies in explainable AI, neural-symbolic architectures, human-centered robotics, agentic systems, and domain-specific applications, such as healthcare, finance, energy, and education, that inform a comparative synthesis of architectural design principles. A Research Design Science Research (DSR) approach is used to model and test the SA-AI Framework conceptually across four stages: requirements analysis, identification of architectural alternatives, multi-criteria evaluation, and model validation. Results show that the framework offers a systematic, defensible method for constructing AI architectures, enabling greater exposure, flexibility, and decision-making effectiveness. It has cohesively unified the different models of AI, including the agentic AI, Explainable AI (XAI), Human-Centered AI (HCAI), and safety-driven architectures, providing both theory and practice to AI engineering and policy design. This paper concludes that system analysis helps design AI systems that integrate both technical and socio-technical systems to enhance the governance, reliability, and sustainability of intelligent architecture in the next generation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in English Language Learning: Student Perspectives on AI Literacy, Academic Integrity, and Dependency at Universidad Tecnológica de Tijuana
papers.authors: Gilda Torres Román, Blanca Román Ortiz
papers.abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created new opportunities for English language learning while also raising concerns regarding academic integrity, student dependency, AI literacy, and institutional regulation. This study aims to analyze university students’ perceptions of these four dimensions in the context of English language learning at a technological university in Mexico. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, and correlational research design was employed. Data were collected from 214 university students through a 16-item questionnaire organized into four constructs: Academic Integrity, AI Literacy, AI Dependency, and Institutional Regulation. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson’s correlation coefficient, and Kruskal–Wallis tests were used to analyze the data. The results showed relatively high levels of AI Literacy (M = 3.77, SD = 0.88) and Academic Integrity (M = 3.61, SD = 0.86), whereas AI Dependency obtained a lower mean (M = 2.61, SD = 0.78). AI Literacy was positively correlated with Academic Integrity (r = .684, p < .001), while Academic Integrity and AI Literacy were also positively associated with Institutional Regulation. AI Dependency showed weak negative correlations with Academic Integrity and AI Literacy. Significant differences according to frequency of AI use were found for AI Dependency and Institutional Regulation, but not for Academic Integrity or AI Literacy. The findings suggest that responsible AI integration in English language education requires more than regulating access to technology; it also requires developing students’ AI literacy, maintaining academic integrity, and promoting learner autonomy through clear institutional guidance.

papers.title: From AI-generated health information to medication action: Trust, risk recognition, and physician/pharmacist verification among university students
papers.authors: Talal Aburjai, Ahmed S.A. Ali Agha, Lujain Nemer, Hayat Aljammal, Dalin Said, Natasha Osama Marji, Nadeen Al-Shwyiat, Abdel Aleem Bello
papers.abstract: Publicly accessible conversational artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly informs self-care, yet research among university students has primarily examined awareness, acceptance, and information seeking rather than the progression from AI output to medication action and safety experiences. This cross-sectional study examined 504 University of Jordan students who had previously used AI for self-treatment or self-medication. A 39-item questionnaire assessed symptom consultation, professional verification, medication-related behaviors, and self-reported adverse effects. We derived attitudinal domains using exploratory factor analysis, and modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs). AI was the first source consulted for new symptoms by 36.5% of participants; 42.5% reported purchasing medication following AI advice without consulting a physician or pharmacist (19.0% frequently), 20.0% selected antibiotics following AI-generated information or recommendations, 36.9% reported adverse effects following an AI-recommended medication, and 35.7% modified physician instructions because of conflicting AI advice. Per one-standard-deviation increase, trust/personalization was associated with higher prevalence of all five evaluated outcomes, including any unconsulted purchasing (aPR 1.49, 95% confidence interval 1.33–1.66), whereas risk recognition showed consistent inverse associations (aPR range 0.73–0.80). Physician/pharmacist verification, reported by 64.7%, was associated with lower prevalence of frequent unconsulted purchasing (aPR 0.57, 95% confidence interval 0.40–0.83), reported adverse effects (aPR 0.78, 0.64–0.96), and modification of physician instructions (aPR 0.74, 0.60–0.91), but not with any purchasing or antibiotic selection. Cross-sectional self-report precludes causal attribution. By identifying output appraisal and professional verification as distinct correlates of medication action, this study extends adoption-focused research to clinically relevant behaviors.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence Tools into English Language Teaching: Opportunities and Challenges for Teachers
papers.authors: Amir Abdulhussein Hashim Albuhmedee
papers.journal: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has shifted from supportive digital tools to more sophisticated systems with an active learning and teaching function. The present study discusses literature between 2021 and mid-2025 on the use of AI tools in English Language Teaching (ELT), with a specific concentration on teachers' attitudes, potential, and concerns. A PRISMA-guided methodology drove the search and screening of 65 peer-reviewed papers, case studies, and practitioners' reports from around the globe. The review classifies main categories of AI applications, including adaptive learning systems, automatic evaluation systems, conversational agents, translation and multimodal tools, and AI literacy tools. The evidence points to potential benefits, such as personalized learning, productivity gains for teachers, enhanced learner engagement, and enhanced access for students from low-resourced environments. Simultaneously, key issues are flagged concerning pedagogy, infrastructure, teacher education, ethics, privacy, and professional identity. Case studies report on actual teacher and student experiences using ChatGPT, Duolingo, and Grammarly, illustrating possibilities as well as dangers for classroom adoption. The review further points towards the incorporation of AI literacy in teacher training, provision of ongoing professional development, and building critical digital literacy. The findings first and foremost signal that the successful use of AI in ELT should appropriately weigh teaching methods and technological innovation, moral rights, and contextualization in their upholding of fairness and longevity.

papers.title: TEACHING PRACTICES OF GRADE 8 SCIENCE TEACHERS EMBEDDED WITH AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE LEARNING SYSTEM IN SCIENCE INSTRUCTION
papers.authors: Jenny M. Santiago, Sonny De Leon
papers.journal: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to personalize science instruction, yet evidence regarding teachers’ AI-supported practices and learners’ cognitive engagement remains limited. This study examined Grade 8 Science teachers’ practices embedded with AI-driven adaptive learning systems at Bongabon National High School, Nueva Ecija, during school year 2026–2027. Specifically, it described teachers’ profiles and practices across planning and preparation, classroom environment, instruction, and professional responsibilities, and investigated relationships and differences in respondents’ perceptions. A descriptive survey design with quasi-experimental designation, involved six Grade 8 Science teachers and 499 students. Teacher respondents were covered through complete enumeration, while student respondents were selected through simple random sampling. Questionnaires provided data analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t-tests, and Spearman’s rho. Findings indicated that AI-embedded teaching practices were “Always Practiced,” with an overall grand weighted mean of 3.60. Classroom environment obtained the highest combined domain mean (3.64), followed by instruction (3.62), planning and preparation (3.59), and professional responsibilities (3.55). Teachers’ educational attainment showed significant negative relationships with planning and preparation (rho = −0.892) and classroom environment (rho = −0.874), whereas other profile variables showed no significant relationships. Teachers’ and learners’ perceptions did not differ significantly across domains. The study concluded that AI-supported teaching practices were consistently reported and recommended targeted professional development and activities to strengthen comparatively less-practiced areas. These findings may guide context-responsive integration of adaptive learning tools in junior high school Science instruction while supporting reflective teaching practice and student engagement. This supports responsible implementation.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in functional gastrointestinal disorders: From symptom recognition to personalised management
papers.authors: Han-Run Wang, He-Lei Wang
papers.abstract: Functional gastrointestinal disorders, now termed disorders of gut-brain interaction, are heterogeneous conditions shaped by psychological, physiological, microbial, and environmental factors.Diagnosis and treatment remain difficult because symptoms overlap, trajectories fluctuate, and no single objective biomarker exists.This minireview synthesises human evidence for artificial intelligence (AI) in symptom classification, digital phenotyping, microbiome and multi-omics prediction, treatment-response estimation, wearable monitoring, and language-based care.Targeted PubMed searches were updated through September 20, 2026.Current studies show feasibility, but most use small, single-centre cohorts, retrospective designs, or internal validation; calibration and prospective impact evaluation are uncommon.The most plausible near-term role of AI is therefore clinical augmentation: Identifying longitudinal patterns, supporting shared decisions, and detecting changes that require reassessment while preserving human oversight and patient autonomy.Large language models may improve education and communication, but disorder-specific evaluations reveal imperfect diagnosis and treatment recommendations with marked overconfidence.Translation requires representative cohorts that include overlapping organic disease, explicit endpoints despite the absence of a diagnostic gold standard, external validation, calibration, equity assessment, and prospective evaluation of patient benefit.AI should be judged by outcomes and care experience, not discrimination alone.

papers.title: Rethinking “In-The-Loop” Approaches in Educational AI: A Learning Sciences Perspective
papers.authors: Prajakt Pande
papers.abstract: In educational AI, “In-the-Loop” framings (e.g., human-in-the-loop) are presented as systems that secure human-technology balance in enabling timely feedback and personalization. This learning sciences perspective-piece argues that the critical issue is not whether humans participate sufficiently in educational processes, but how the educational loop is rendered actionable. When educational activity is organized around cycles of data capture, computational interpretation/inference, and probable responses, pedagogical action is reconfigured around what computational systems can detect, compare, and act upon. In higher education, these operational requirements can create tensions between promises of meaningful human participation and the conditions under which participation occurs. Actual enactments of educational AI often rely on epistemically simplified proxies that shape what counts as evidence, constrain interpretation, redistribute agency, and impose system-defined temporality on natural educational cycles. In the context of assessment, this poses risks where predictive indicators of learning drift toward a kind of deterministic practice that normalizes data overreliance and trajectory-prescription. Such tensions persist even with increased human oversight/automation, because they arise from the loop’s operational commitments to closure and actionability. Through learning sciences perspectives, I caution against treating loop operability as compatible with how learning, as a process, happens, and as a sufficient pedagogical condition. Finally, I outline implications for learning-theoretically grounded approaches to educational AI.

papers.title: Dual Transition Organization of EEG Microstate Dynamics During Naturalistic Emotion Processing
papers.authors: Wanrou Hu, Duan Xujun, Zhiguo Zhang, Jinming Xiao, Shuyue Xu, Huafu Chen, Zhen Liang

papers.title: Omotenashi in Service Marketing and Festival Tourism
papers.authors: Gustavo Lunardelli Trevisan
papers.journal: International Journal of Sustainable Competitiveness on Tourism
papers.abstract: This article examines omotenashi as a cultural and organizational orientation in service marketing and extends its application from lodging to festival tourism through the Fukushi-kyosan Sapporo Odori Beer Garden 2026. The study adopts an integrative literature review supported by a documented platform-based search strategy focused on omotenashi, Japanese hospitality, customer experience, service management, event quality, festival experience, co-creation, trust, personalization, and intercultural interaction. The analytical corpus includes fifteen substantive academic studies that met the relevance criteria, complemented by official documentary sources used to examine the 2026 event. Thematic analysis identifies four service manifestations anticipation of needs, personalization, attention to detail, and human relationships supported by organizational consistency and conditioned by functional quality and cultural context. The Sapporo application shows how these categories can interpret reservation design, tourist-specific Omotenashi Seats, multiple service environments, information, ordering, seating, and host–visitor interaction without treating institutional communication as evidence of satisfaction or loyalty. The findings position omotenashi as an analytical framework for service marketing across hospitality and festival settings and identify contextual appropriateness as the principle linking service design to visitor experience.

papers.title: Generative AI Use and the Student Well-Being Paradox in Higher Education: Efficiency-Gain Retention, Performance Escalation, and Relative Competition
papers.authors: Weida Zhang, Heng Wang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce the time and cognitive effort required for university learning, yet technical efficiency does not necessarily translate into improved student well-being. This article develops and tests a conversion account of this paradox by distinguishing efficiency gains that remain available as student-controlled resources from gains that are associated with perceived increases in performance expectations, competitive pressure, verification work, and dependence. A sequential three-study mixed-methods program was conducted with undergraduates in Jiangxi Province. Study 1 used codebook thematic analysis of 42 interviews to identify six mechanisms linking immediate efficiency to resource retention or perceived pressure. Study 2 surveyed 1268 students across eight universities. GenAI use was strongly associated with perceived efficiency gains, but also with perceived performance-standard escalation and verification burden. Positive retention and negative competition pathways were similar in magnitude, yielding a nonsignificant total association with well-being; working-time retention strengthened the efficiency–well-being association. Because Study 2 was cross-sectional, these pathways are interpreted as indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Study 3 used a 2 × 2 experiment (N = 320) and found that AI access improved task quality and reduced completion time under both performance-norm conditions, whereas gains in autonomy, retained time, and state well-being were evident under the stable norm but not statistically distinguishable from zero under the escalated norm. The findings distinguish technical affordance from context-dependent conversion and suggest that responsible AI integration should consider whether efficiency gains remain available for learning, recovery, and student-directed use alongside productivity.

papers.title: Co-Creating Experiential Tourism in Community Contexts: A Participatory Approach to Designing Professional Skill Development Toolkits for Local Interpreters
papers.authors: Sunanthra Kamnuanthong, Watcharee Phetwong, Thitithana Trisit, Junphen Wannarak, Pimpan Amphanthong, Monnapat Bunyaburana
papers.abstract: Experience-based tourism has grown in importance within the current tourism environment, with a focus on providing meaningful, authentic and immersive experiences that are jointly created by visitors and the destinations in question. In this regard, local interpretation plays a vital role in turning the resources of the community into engaging and memorable experiences. However, limited research has systematically connected community identity, co-creation processes, and the skills required by local interpreters, particularly in community-based tourism. The present study has two aims: (1) to examine the assets associated with community-based experiential tourism and (2) to develop a prototype competency-development toolkit for local interpreters based on the qualitative findings. A qualitative research approach was employed, involving in-depth interviews, participant observation, and participatory workshops with key parties including local interpreters, community leaders and practitioners. The data were analyzed using content, thematic, and interpretive analysis to identify recurring patterns, themes, and context-specific meanings. The results revealed three main findings. First, seven dimensions of destination identity were identified: natural resources, organic agricultural production systems, community lifestyles, local wisdom, community culture, experiential activities, and community products and economy. These dimensions contribute to the formation of community identity. Second, the findings identified stakeholder participation, knowledge exchange, and experience design as central components of the co-creation process within the community context. Third, these findings informed the development of a prototype competency-development toolkit comprising five modules: understanding local identity, introduction to local interpreters, storytelling techniques, experience design, and communication tools and skills. Theoretically, the study contributes a context-specific explanation of how community identity, co-creation, and interpretation competencies can be integrated within community-based experiential tourism. Practically, the study provides a context-specific prototype toolkit intended to support future capacity-building for local interpreters and the development of community-based experiential tourism. Its effectiveness and longer-term contributions to visitor outcomes and sustainability require further empirical investigation.

papers.title: Personal and Academic Factors in Teachers’ Perceptions of Educational Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Inmaculada Serrano-García, Ramón Chacón Cuberos, Amador Jesús Lara-Sánchez
papers.abstract: (1) Background: The aim of this study was to analyze how teacher trainees and teachers relate to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education across socio-emotional, attitudinal, competency-based, and ethical dimensions, considering the influence of personal, academic, and professional variables. The study was conceptually framed by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), complemented by DigCompEdu as a broader reference for teacher digital competence. (2) Methods: A quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive, cross-sectional design was developed with a sample of 1292 participants from Andalusia, consisting mainly of university students, along with teachers. The ACISE-IA scale, consisting of 39 items developed by Serrano-García et al. (2026), was used for data collection. (3) Results: The results showed that age and teaching experience are negatively associated with favorable attitudes and digital competence, while academic performance is positively related to greater openness, critical reflection, and perception of competence. Likewise, significant differences were identified according to the branch of knowledge, employment status, and academic year, with more positive assessments among students and in social science areas. (4) Conclusions: Overall, the findings show that the relationship with AI is not homogeneous, but rather modulated by educational and professional trajectories, underscoring the need to design flexible teacher training models that integrate technological development with pedagogical, emotional, and ethical reflection. These findings also contribute to educational sustainability by highlighting the importance of developing teacher training strategies that support the responsible and sustained integration of AI into educational systems.

papers.title: A Latent Profile Analysis of Coping, Psychological Inflexibility, and Health-Related Quality of Life in Adult Regular Exercisers
papers.authors: Walter Sapuppo, Antonietta Monda, Davide Giacconi, Rita Polito, Fiorenzo Moscatelli, Girolamo Di Maio, Giovanni Messina, Daniele Saccenti, Mattia Ferro, Claudia Maria Mineo, Antonietta Messina, Vincenzo Monda, Regina Gregori Grgič, Giovanni Michelini, Marco La Marra, Sergio Chieffi, Maria Giovanna Tafuri
papers.abstract: Background: Regular physical activity is generally associated with better health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and lower psychological distress, yet regular exercisers may differ in how coping strategies, psychological inflexibility, and cognitive fusion relate to perceived health and functioning. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of adult regular exercisers based on coping, psychological inflexibility, cognitive fusion, HRQoL, psychological distress, age, body mass index (BMI), and years of regular physical activity. Methods: A total of 591 regular exercisers (358 males, 60.6%; 233 females, 39.4%; mean age = 32.46 ± 13.72 years) completed the COPE-NVI-25, SF-36, GHQ-12, Acceptance and Action Questionnaire–II (AAQ-II), and Italian Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire (I-CFQ). Results: Latent profile analysis was performed using age, BMI, years of physical activity, five coping subscales, eight SF-36 domains, three GHQ-12 domains, and AAQ-II and I-CFQ scores. A three-profile solution was retained as the preferred substantive solution based on the joint consideration of statistical fit, class representation, entropy (0.87), parsimony, and interpretability. Class 1 (35.5%) showed high avoidance, poorer HRQoL, and higher distress; Class 2 (43.0%) showed near-average coping and better HRQoL; Class 3 (21.5%), comprising older, longer-term exercisers, showed the most adaptive coping and psychological flexibility profile alongside favorable HRQoL. Conclusions: These findings support person-centered approaches in sport and exercise psychology.

papers.title: Multimodal Sensing and Digital Biomarkers in Virtual Reality-Based Cognitive Rehabilitation: Clinical Validation, Adaptive Systems, and Real-World Translation
papers.authors: Francesco Rundo, Sabrina Musso, Serafino Buono, Marilena Recupero, Raffaele Ferri
papers.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is evolving from a platform for cognitive exercises into an instrumented rehabilitation environment capable of simultaneously delivering treatment and quantifying behavior. This critical narrative review examines how behavioral, ocular, kinematic, physiological, and neurophysiological signals can be transformed into clinically meaningful digital measures, candidate biomarkers, adaptive interventions, and real-world functional outcomes. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched from database inception to 20 September 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching and targeted searches. Clinical, methodological, validation, and directly relevant technical studies were considered, including studies in healthy participants when methodologically informative. Of 690 records identified, 145 duplicates were removed; 545 unique records were screened and 303 formed the candidate evidence pool for critical narrative appraisal. Behavioral and interaction-derived measures are the most established, while eye tracking, kinematic sensing, autonomic monitoring, EEG, and fNIRS provide complementary information on attention, strategy, workload, and engagement. Quantitatively, combined hand- and eye-tracking features distinguished mild cognitive impairment from healthy controls with 93.3% accuracy, 100% sensitivity, and 83.3% specificity, while immersive VR life-skills training produced real-world functional gains of d = 1.00 post-training and d = 1.12 at 1-week follow-up. However, most sensor-derived variables remain digital measures or candidate biomarkers rather than clinically validated biomarkers; physiology-informed closed-loop adaptation is uncommon, and evidence that such adaptation produces sustained ADL or assisted-living benefits is lacking. Progress now depends on standardized reporting, external and multicenter validation, clinically interpretable adaptive models, and objective demonstration of real-world transfer.

papers.title: Risk-Aware Predictive Maintenance for Aero-Engines via CVaR-Guided Reinforcement Learning and LLM-Based Risk Abstraction
papers.authors: Bolin Song, Yingqing Guo, Zaiyang Yu, Yao Ni, Wangyu Wu
papers.abstract: A fundamental limitation of current predictive maintenance is the inability to transform prognostic uncertainty into actionable decisions, which often leads to either wasteful early interventions or catastrophic failures in aero-engines. To address this, we propose the Risk-Aware Predictive Maintenance (RAPM) framework consisting of four integrated components: a probabilistic stacked sparse autoencoder that extracts degradation features while providing distributional remaining useful life (RUL) predictions; a Monte Carlo Dropout module with Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) that summarizes lower-tail predictive risk and produces a conservative RUL estimate for decision making; a locally deployed large language model (Qwen2.5-3B) that abstracts numerical uncertainty into discrete semantic risk levels, enabling interpretable reward shaping; and a Proximal Policy Optimization agent trained with curriculum learning to handle long-horizon sparse-reward maintenance optimization. On the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 benchmark, RAPM achieves a 96.0% optimal stopping rate with no late interventions or failure events compared with 90.2% for the strongest independent maintenance baseline. Under controlled substitution with LSTM-MCD, Transformer-MCD, CNN-MCD, and Deep Ensemble prognostic backbones, the same CVaR-LLM-PPO decision architecture maintains optimal stopping rates of 92.4–95.2% with no late interventions or failure events. Within the matched Rule-PPO ablation, CVaR increases the mean optimal stopping rate from 92.0% to 95.0% under unperturbed conditions, which is a gain of 3.0 percentage points. Under Gaussian sensor noise (σ=0.05), the gain reaches 9.0 percentage points, from 73.0% to 82.0%. These results demonstrate that the decision benefit of RAPM extends across independently trained prognostic models.

papers.title: FPGLNet: A Lightweight Frequency Prior-Gated Network for EEG Emotion Recognition
papers.authors: Yue Yuan, BI Yingzhou, Shanrui Liu, HUO Leigang
papers.abstract: Although deep learning-based electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition methods have achieved promising performance, they generally depend on complex network architectures and high computational costs, which limits their deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. Meanwhile, existing approaches mainly focus on local spatiotemporal feature extraction while insufficiently exploiting global frequency-domain dependencies and dynamic information selection during feature propagation, resulting in inadequate spectral information utilization and redundant feature representations. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Frequency Prior-Gated Lightweight Network (FPGLNet) for EEG emotion recognition. First, a Mixed Aggregation Convolution (MAC) module is introduced at the input stage to jointly encode EEG spatiotemporal characteristics through temporal and spatial convolutions. Subsequently, a Fused Fourier Convolution Mixer (FFCM) module is developed to model global frequency-domain dependencies through Fourier transform and integrate multi-scale depthwise convolutions for collaborative frequency-spatial feature representation. Furthermore, a Prior-Gated Feed Forward Network (PGFN) is proposed to dynamically generate prior-guided gating weights based on feature responses, enabling adaptive selection and recalibration of discriminative features across different brain regions and temporal segments. This mechanism enhances emotion-related representations while suppressing noise and redundant information. Owing to the lightweight architecture design, FPGLNet achieves an effective balance between feature representation capability, model complexity, and computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that FPGLNet achieves classification accuracies of 96.22% and 92.69% on the public SEED-IV and SEED-V datasets, respectively. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed frequency prior-gated strategy in improving EEG feature representation while maintaining competitive recognition performance and deployment efficiency.

papers.title: AIDCare: A Technical Proof-of-Concept for Integrating Personalized Nutrition, Physical Activity, and AI-Assisted Care in Diabetes Lifestyle Management
papers.authors: Adnan Kavak, Muhammad Jamil, Halil Bahadır Arın, Alpaslan Burak İnner, Hossein Fotouhi, Emre Gezer, Özlem Alkan, Zeynep Cantürk, Alev Selek, Gautam Srivastava
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Medical nutrition therapy and structured lifestyle self-management are fundamental to diabetes care, yet conventional mobile health tools typically track diet, physical activity, and glucose measurements in isolation, with limited connection to clinical oversight. This study presents AIDCare, an integrated mobile health platform that connects camera-based nutritional assessment, wearable physical activity tracking, physiological monitoring, and clinician-supervised conversational artificial intelligence (AI) to support personalized dietary and lifestyle self-management in diabetes. Methods: AIDCare links a patient mobile application with wearable sensors, backend analytical services, and an interactive clinician portal. Dietary assessment uses smartphone camera imaging to identify foods and estimate meal contents, specifically carbohydrates, protein, and dietary fiber, against nutritional reference data. Physical activity and energy expenditure are captured through smartphone and smartwatch motion sensors. To support contextual lifestyle guidance, an open-access medical conversational language model was adapted using 24,612 structured digital health and diabetes educational articles. A clinician-in-the-loop mechanism allows healthcare providers to inspect AI-generated recommendations and adjust personalization parameters. System feasibility was evaluated through benchtop and system-level testing without patient recruitment, using synthetic patient profiles across 400 data-acquisition pipeline trials and an intent-classification benchmark spanning nutrition, activity, glucose monitoring, and physician consultation. Results: Across the 400 software-pipeline trials, the platform achieved data acquisition, transmission, and processing completion rates of 97.5%, 96.5%, and 95.5%, respectively, with backend response times under 1.8 s. In the recommendation-intent benchmark, the medical language model achieved 81.0% accuracy, 83.5% precision, 79.0% recall, and an F1-score of 81.2%. The platform successfully linked image-based meal nutrient estimates (carbohydrate, protein, and dietary fiber) with physical activity metrics and physiological tracking within a unified interface under clinician supervision. Conclusions: AIDCare establishes the technical feasibility of a unified digital platform that integrates dietary nutrient estimation, physical activity tracking, and clinician-guided AI decision support for diabetes self-management. By bridging daily nutritional intake with metabolic tracking and professional oversight, the architecture provides a functional framework for personalized lifestyle care. Prospective clinical trials in patient cohorts are required to establish nutritional estimation accuracy against weighed food records, long-term user adherence, and clinical efficacy on glycemic control.

papers.title: How Underdog Brand Biography Mitigates Consumer Skepticism Toward AIGC: Evidence from AI-Generated Agricultural-Product Advertisements
papers.authors: Wen Luo, Peixuan Luo, Yijing Zhang, Mineo Keito, Yuan Feng
papers.journal: Journal of theoretical and applied electronic commerce research
papers.abstract: While AIGC can improve operational efficiency in marketing, it may also erode consumer trust owing to widespread skepticism toward AIGC. Therefore, this study examines agricultural product advertisements to explore the impact of Underdog Brand Biography (UBB) disclosure on consumers’ purchase intentions. It also investigates the mediating roles of cognitive trust and affective trust, as well as whether these effects differ across product-price levels and production-background conditions. We conducted three experiments to investigate these relationships. The data were analyzed using t-tests, analyses of variance, and moderated mediation models. The findings indicated that UBB disclosure significantly increases purchase intention and that this effect is mediated by both cognitive trust and affective trust. The indirect effects via both pathways differed across product-price levels: both were significant in the high-price condition, whereas in the low-price condition only the affective pathway remained significant. Additionally, both trust pathways were amplified in the cultivation-scene background condition relative to the plain background condition. Given that our samples were drawn from an online consumer panel, the present findings and their implications should be interpreted with respect to online consumer populations. These findings provide preliminary insights that may inform trust-based theories of AI disclosure and offer practical considerations for marketers designing AIGC advertising strategies.

papers.title: One Voice, One Impression: Why Customers Perceive the Service Quality of AI Voice Bots Holistically and What It Means for Electronic Commerce
papers.authors: Oren Dayan
papers.journal: Journal of theoretical and applied electronic commerce research
papers.abstract: AI voice bots are a standard channel for post-purchase service in electronic commerce, yet conversational-agent research has centered on text chatbots, and whether the quality dimensions of a voice agent are perceived as separate remains open. This study argues that customers experience the agent as one unified impression, because a voice-first encounter is a continuous spoken dialogue without a visual interface, so customers respond to the agent as a single social actor. Perceived quality is theorized as a higher-order construct, building on information systems success theory, technology acceptance theory, and social responses to computers, and tested on a cross-sectional survey of 295 voice bot users in Israel across eight service categories, with partial least squares structural equation modeling and competing measurement models. The quality facets remain distinguishable, yet one general factor accounts for most of their common variance, supporting a single higher-order construct. Perceived quality is the strongest predictor of overall service quality, directly and partly through perceived usefulness, while interaction complexity shows no significant moderating or predictive effect. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, these relationships are associations, not demonstrated causal effects. The study extends success and acceptance theory to the voice-first service encounter.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Growth: Adaptive Human Intelligence, Emotional Dynamics, and Willingness to Write in Artificial Intelligence-Mediated Informal Digital Learning of English (AI-IDLE)
papers.authors: Chenghao Wang, Lanfang Sun, Bin Zou, Yunyan Zhang
papers.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is expanding AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE) from predominantly receptive and conversational activities to cognitively demanding productive tasks such as academic writing. Yet little is known about how learners’ motivation and technology-related emotions develop over time, or how sustained interaction with GenAI may engage human capacities for evaluation and adaptation. Grounded in Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), this study investigated the longitudinal development of willingness to write (WTW), technology-related enjoyment (ENY), and technology-related anxiety (ANX) among Chinese undergraduates learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL) in teacher-supported AI-IDLE embedded within an 11-week English for Academic Purposes writing course. Twenty-six participants with complete records across 11 measurement occasions were included in the longitudinal analysis. Trajectory analysis, change-point analysis, and exploratory moving-window correlation analysis were combined with thematic analysis of learners’ reflections. WTW followed a nonlinear trajectory, declining during the middle period before a potential late-stage transition and subsequent increase, whereas ENY remained comparatively stable and ANX generally declined. The relationships of WTW with ENY and ANX also varied over time. Learners’ reflections revealed increasing recognition of human–AI complementarity and more selective, critical, and strategic engagement with GenAI. From a human-intelligence perspective, these patterns illustrate adaptive and metacognitive capacities involved in evaluating AI-generated information, adjusting strategies, and coordinating human and artificial resources. Rather than treating WTW or emotions as measures of intelligence, the findings position AI-IDLE as a context in which such human intellectual capacities may be exercised and expressed.

papers.title: The Influence of Neurotic Disorders and Neurobiological Basis on Eating Behavior in a 21-Year-Old Patient: A Case Study—Diagnostic Difficulties: Is It PANDAS/PANS in Relation to an Elevated ASO Level and the Diagnosis of OCD?
papers.authors: Agnieszka Zygo, Kamila J. Regin, Aleksandra Purkiewicz
papers.abstract: Background: Anxiety and obsessive–compulsive disorders can co-occur with disordered eating behaviors and difficulties in emotional regulation. This article presents the clinical case of a 21-year-old female student whose complex neuropsychiatric profile required the simultaneous consideration of psychological, psychosocial, and somatic factors. The aim of this case report was to examine the coexistence of psychopathological symptoms, eating disturbances, psychosocial experiences, and somatic findings, while considering the potential role of post-infectious factors. Methods: A retrospective analysis of the patient’s medical and psychiatric history was conducted, including childhood infections, psychiatric diagnoses, psychosocial experiences, eating behaviors, and available laboratory findings. The assessment also included quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG) brain mapping performed under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. Particular attention was given to the retrospective hypothesis of PANDAS/PANS (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections/Pediatric Acute-onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome), while distinguishing documented clinical findings from unconfirmed etiopathogenetic hypotheses. Results: Retrospective history revealed recurrent upper respiratory tract infections and bilateral pneumonia in early childhood, followed by increasing anxiety and social withdrawal from peers. The patient was diagnosed with obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) at the age of 13, while psychiatric records from 2023 also documented depressive disorders and social phobia. Within the family system, the patient experienced relational trauma, including systematic verbal and psychological abuse by her father. Blood tests performed on 11 June 2025 revealed an elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) level of 436 IU/mL, which may indicate previous streptococcal exposure but does not confirm active infection, PANDAS/PANS, or a causal relationship with neuropsychiatric symptoms. The available documentation lacked microbiological confirmation of streptococcal infections or evidence substantiating a PANDAS/PANS diagnosis. QEEG brain mapping revealed elevated fast HiBeta activity in the frontal regions under both recording conditions; however, incomplete methodological documentation precluded definitive interpretation of this finding as evidence of persistent cortical overactivity or specific cognitive deficits. Somatic and metabolic findings included morning cortisol of 7.7 µg/dL, dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-SO4) of 163 µg/dL, prolactin of 513.0 mIU/L, and total cholesterol of 138 mg/dL. A previously recorded glycemic value of 45 mg/dL was also noted, although insufficient information was available to confirm reactive hypoglycemia. The patient reported a dichotomous eating pattern characterized by appetite suppression during acute stress, followed by episodes of increased food intake aimed at regulating emotional tension. However, the absence of standardized assessment prevented confirmation of formal binge-eating episodes. Food avoidance and restriction were associated with contamination fears and obsessive–compulsive rituals. The patient also expressed marked body image dissatisfaction and a desire for an extremely thin physique, although no formal diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder was documented. Conclusions: This case highlights the complex coexistence of obsessive–compulsive and anxiety symptoms, disordered eating behaviors, psychosocial trauma, and somatic findings. Although retrospective clinical history and elevated ASO levels raise the possibility of a post-infectious contribution, the available evidence does not establish an autoimmune mechanism or confirm PANDAS/PANS. The findings emphasize the importance of distinguishing documented clinical observations from etiopathogenetic hypotheses and support an interdisciplinary approach integrating psychiatric care, psychotherapy, nutritional assessment, and appropriate somatic diagnostics.

papers.title: Skin Color Representation Within Podiatric Medical Education Materials
papers.authors: Chiara Edlin, Elizabeth Gajardo-Stitt, Erica Preblich, Ashley Dikis, Kevin Smith
papers.journal: Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association
papers.abstract: Background: The ability to accurately diagnose dermatologic conditions in patients with various skin tones is an essential skill for the podiatric physician, as many lower extremity pathologies present differently depending on skin pigmentation. Our study sought to evaluate diversity of skin color representation in images used in lecture material within podiatric medical education at a single institution, as well as within commonly utilized textbooks. Methods: Images presented throughout the curriculum at our academic institution and those found in widely utilized podiatric textbooks were evaluated by three independent coders. Images were categorized based on skin tone via the Massey–Martin skin color scale. Results: A total of 5276 images were evaluated using the Massey–Martin skin color scale. Interrater reliability was assessed using a subsample of 90 images independently coded by all three raters, yielding a strong ordinally weighted Krippendorff’s alpha (α = 0.905). Among those images used within our institutional podiatric curriculum, 86.34% of images were within the lightest skin color range (0–2), 11.7% were of medium skin color (3–5), and 1.96% contained darker skin tones (6–10). The average between the textbooks evaluated showed 82.1% were light, 15.4% were medium, and 2.5% were darker skin tones. Conclusions: Despite the growing diversity of the U.S. population, there remains a notable lack of darker skin tone representation in medical education, including disseminated course materials at our institution and within commonly used podiatry textbooks. This gap in diversity within educational resources can hinder the ability of healthcare professionals to provide comprehensive and equitable care, particularly when it comes to conditions that present differently across various skin tones. Declarations and Disclosures: No financial disclosures or conflicts of interest. No generative artificial intelligence was used in the writing of this work.

papers.title: Hybrid Explainable Artificial Intelligence Architecture for Transparent Learning Outcome Prediction in Outcome-Based Engineering Education
papers.authors: Wai San Leong, Wai Yie Leong
papers.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a critical enabler for deploying trustworthy AI systems in higher education, particularly in course assessment and learning outcome prediction. While advanced machine learning models such as gradient boosting, neural networks, and ensemble methods achieve high predictive accuracy, their opaque decision-making processes limit adoption by educators and accreditation bodies. This study proposes an efficient XAI framework that integrates interpretable modeling techniques with high-performance predictive algorithms to enhance transparency, fairness, and pedagogical alignment. The framework combines feature attribution methods, including SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations), with hybrid predictive models to generate both accurate and interpretable insights into student performance and outcome attainment. Experimental evaluation on academic datasets demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves competitive prediction accuracy while significantly improving interpretability and stakeholder trust. The results show that key predictors—such as continuous assessment scores, engagement metrics, and assignment submission patterns—can be clearly explained and mapped to learning outcomes. The framework supports evidence-based decision-making, facilitates Outcome-Based Education (OBE) compliance, and enables instructors to design targeted interventions. Overall, efficient XAI models provide a scalable solution for transparent, accountable, and data-driven assessment in modern higher education systems.

papers.title: Human–AI Collaboration Systems: A Multi-Layer Computational Architecture for Behavioral Analytics and Social Identity Modeling in Hybrid Work Environments
papers.authors: Wai San Leong, Wai Yie Leong
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into hybrid work environments has transformed organizational structures, collaboration patterns, and employee identity formation. Human–AI collaboration enables enhanced productivity through automation, decision support, and data-driven insights. However, it also reshapes how individuals perceive their roles, social belonging, and professional identity. This paper investigates the socio-technical dynamics of Human–AI collaboration, focusing on its impact on social identity formation in hybrid work settings. A multi-layer framework combining AI-assisted workflows, social interaction modeling, and identity perception analysis is proposed. Experimental findings indicate that AI integration improves efficiency and collaboration quality, but introduces challenges related to trust, role ambiguity, and identity shifts. Survey results reveal that employees’ acceptance of AI is strongly influenced by transparency, perceived fairness, and organizational culture. The study concludes that successful Human–AI collaboration requires balanced integration of technology and human-centric design to support identity stability and organizational cohesion.

papers.title: Intelligent Human–AI Collaborative Architecture for Adaptive Teaching and Learning Analytics in Higher Education
papers.authors: Wai Yie Leong
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has led to the emergence of Teacher–AI co-teaching models, where human educators collaborate with intelligent systems to enhance teaching and learning processes. These models leverage AI for adaptive content delivery, real-time feedback, and data-driven decision-making, transforming traditional pedagogical practices. However, their adoption depends heavily on social acceptance, trust, and perceived usefulness among educators and students. This paper investigates the socio-technical dynamics of Teacher–AI co-teaching, focusing on pedagogical transformation and user acceptance in higher education environments. A hybrid framework combining AI-assisted instruction, human facilitation, and learning analytics is proposed. Experimental results demonstrate improved student engagement and learning outcomes, while surveys reveal varying levels of acceptance influenced by trust and digital literacy. The study concludes that successful implementation requires a balanced integration of technology, pedagogy, and institutional governance to ensure ethical, effective, and inclusive AI-enhanced education.

papers.title: An AI Integration Framework for Social Innovation: A Cross-Case Analysis of AI System Configurations for the Triple-Zero Agenda
papers.authors: Thai Son Chu, Nitirajsingh Sandu, Bhargavi Goswami, Shakir Karim
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly being applied to complex social and environmental challenges, but their implementation across different application domains requires appropriate combinations of computational techniques, data sources, deployment environments, user interfaces, and responsible-AI mechanisms. This study proposes an AI Integration Framework for examining and configuring AI-enabled social innovation systems in support of the Triple-Zero Agenda: zero poverty, zero unemployment, and zero net carbon emissions. The framework is derived from a qualitative multi-case analysis of five social enterprises operating in agriculture, healthcare, education, clean energy, and employment. The analysis examines the AI technologies employed, their development and deployment environments, accessibility mechanisms, data-collection approaches, privacy mechanisms, explainability practices, human-in-the-loop controls, ethical review mechanisms, and measurable impact indicators. The cases demonstrate the use of heterogeneous AI configurations, including predictive machine learning in mobile and cloud environments, natural language processing in application and SMS-based systems, adaptive learning algorithms in web platforms, AI-based energy optimization integrated with IoT and edge devices, and AI-driven skill-job matching through mobile applications. The cross-case analysis indicates that effective AI deployment depends not only on the choice of AI technique but also on the configuration of supporting data, infrastructure, interaction, privacy, explainability, and human-oversight mechanisms. Based on these observations, the study organizes these dimensions into an AI Integration Framework that provides a structured basis for analyzing and configuring AI systems for socially oriented applications. The framework also connects system configurations with operational, social, economic, and environmental outcomes, thereby providing a computer science-oriented perspective on the design, deployment, and scalability of AI-powered social innovation.

papers.title: Governing Generative AI in Higher Education: A Cross-National Analysis of Policy Framing and Student Maneuvering
papers.authors: Zhiru Sun, Anna Møller, Nina Bonderup Dohn
papers.abstract: Universities promote generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a pedagogical resource while regulating it as a risk to academic integrity and fair assessment. This study examines how differentiated policy framing varies across substantive policy dimensions and national contexts, and how students interpret and navigate such guidance in practice. Using a convergent mixed-methods design with quantitative priority, we analyzed GenAI policy documents from 36 universities in Denmark, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the Netherlands, complemented by eight semi-structured interviews with graduate students at one sampled university. Aspect-based sentiment analysis and mixed-effects modeling show significantly positive sentiment in teaching-related statements and significantly negative sentiment in GenAI- and ethics-related statements, while student- and assessment-related statements do not differ significantly from neutral. Neither country nor the policy-dimension-by-country interaction is statistically significant. The interviews contextualize these policy-level patterns: participants described uncertainty around acceptable use, disclosure, and instructor expectations, with responses ranging from cautious experimentation to avoidance. Together, the findings show how differentiated GenAI guidance can coexist within university policy and illustrate the interpretive demands students may face when applying such guidance in practice. Clearer programme- and course-level guidance, consistent disclosure expectations, and stronger support for GenAI literacy may help connect institutional policy more closely with teaching and learning practice.

papers.title: AI Tutor, Online Course, or Both? A Randomized Experimental Pilot Study for Evaluation Capacity Building
papers.authors: Lendel Kade Narine, John M. Diaz
papers.abstract: Extension lacks literature comparing standalone generative artificial intelligence (AI) with structured professional development for capacity building. Guided by Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, this study evaluated the effects of an asynchronous online course and a custom AI tutor on evaluation knowledge and self-efficacy among Cooperative Extension professionals. We conducted a randomized 2 × 2 factorial pilot study crossing access to an evaluation certificate course with access to a custom Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). Of 144 registrants, 78 provided matched pre- and post-test data, with attrition differing across conditions. Data were analyzed using a three-way mixed factorial ANOVA. Course access and GPT access each increased objective knowledge, with post-test means around 91% across treatment groups. No statistically significant additive effect was detected for knowledge gain. However, given a possible ceiling effect and limited statistical power, this result is inconclusive. Course access and GPT access each increased self-efficacy, but the combined condition produced the smallest self-efficacy gain among treatment groups. Because these estimates are based on participants who completed the study, findings are preliminary. If replicated, results suggest that Extension should combine AI tutors and coursework only when each modality provides known complementary value.

papers.title: Generative AI-Guided Versus Human-Guided Learning from Errors in Higher Education: A Comparison of Student Perceptions
papers.authors: Orly Barzilai, Ronit Shmallo, Rina Zviel-Girshin
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support programming education, but its use in learning-from-errors activities has received limited research attention. This quasi-experimental study compared AI-guided and human-guided support in a structured learning-from-errors programming activity, focusing on students’ perceptions and their variability. A total of 59 college students completed the JavaScript error-detection and correction activity under AI-guided or human-guided support. Following the activity, students completed a questionnaire measuring perceived learning experience, satisfaction, general motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL), and self-efficacy. Between-group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests, and differences in variability were examined using Levene’s tests. Students in the AI-guided condition reported significantly more positive learning experiences and greater satisfaction than those in the human-guided condition. They also reported significantly higher overall SRL and greater use of SRL strategies. No significant differences were found in general motivation, SRL motivation, SRL planning and organization, or self-efficacy. The AI-guided group showed significantly lower raw variability in satisfaction and self-efficacy. However, a sensitivity analysis did not establish that these variance differences remained after accounting for mean-related constraints on the bounded response scale. The findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a scaffold for error analysis when integrated in ways that maintain students’ active cognitive engagement.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education—Ethical Policies Mapping
papers.authors: Kalin Penev, Vladislav Slavov, Radoslav Deliyski
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is transforming numerous sectors, and education is no exception. The adoption of generative AI tools in higher education presents significant opportunities for enhancing teaching, learning, assessment, accessibility, and administrative processes. At the same time, their widespread use raises critical ethical concerns related to academic integrity, bias, transparency, data protection, and the possible erosion of critical thinking and creativity. In response, higher education institutions worldwide are beginning to formulate ethical guidelines to govern the use of AI by students, educators, and administrators. However, institutional responses remain diverse across different contexts. This study examines how academic institutions across different countries conceptualise ethical AI use, define risks, and operationalise principles in practical policies through mapping 55 higher education institutions, complemented by an extended analysis of 87 documents. Across the six analysed thematic categories, transparency and disclosure, academic integrity, data protection and privacy, accountability, and risk mitigation are more consistently addressed than accessibility and inclusion. The analysis identifies practical guidance and recognised legitimate AI uses. The discussion considers the interpretation of AI and recommends aligning its use with ethical standards. The article concludes with a summary of the results and directions for future research.

papers.title: Clinical Effectiveness, Safety, and Implementation of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Insulin Management Systems in Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
papers.authors: Victória Dogani Rodrigues, Virgínia Maria Cavallari Strozze Catharin, Mauro Audi, Eliana de Souza Bastos Mazuqueli Pereira, Jesselina Francisco dos Santos Haber, Débora Audi, Vitor Cavallari Strozze Catharin, Maria Angélica Miglino, Lucas Fornari Laurindo
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into insulin management through decision-support systems, adaptive bolus calculators, conversational platforms, and automated insulin delivery (AID) technologies. However, the clinical effectiveness and safety of AI-assisted insulin management remain uncertain. Objective: To systematically evaluate evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating AI-assisted insulin management systems in individuals with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched for RCTs evaluating AI-enabled insulin management interventions in insulin-treated individuals with diabetes. Eligible studies compared AI-based systems with standard care, clinician-guided insulin titration, conventional bolus calculators, or other AID algorithms. Outcomes included glycemic control, insulin titration, safety, and implementation-related measures. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively. Results: We included seven RCTs published between 2020 and 2025. Interventions comprised clinical decision-support systems, adaptive bolus calculators, conversational AI platforms, neural-network-based artificial pancreas algorithms, and exercise-aware AID systems. AI-assisted interventions consistently demonstrated favorable safety profiles, with no increase in severe hypoglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or serious adverse events. Some systems, particularly fully automated closed-loop platforms and conversational AI-guided insulin titration, showed improvements in time in range, glucose control, adherence, and insulin optimization. User acceptance and adherence emerged as important determinants of effectiveness. Conclusions: Current randomized evidence suggests that AI-assisted insulin management systems are safe, feasible, and capable of achieving glycemic outcomes comparable to conventional care. Although certain technologies demonstrate promising clinical benefits, the evidence base remains limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up durations, and heterogeneity across interventions. Larger, long-term randomized trials are needed to establish comparative effectiveness, optimize human–AI interaction, and support broader clinical implementation.

papers.title: Predicting MCI-to-Alzheimer’s Conversion: A Systematic Benchmark of Classical, Machine Learning, and Deep Survival Models
papers.authors: Nathalia Arias Santa, Genaro Daza Santacoloma, Walter Serna Serna
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Predicting time-to-conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a critical clinical challenge. Most survival analyses rely on static baseline variables, ignoring the temporal dynamics of serial neuroimaging. We benchmark seven survival model families using a novel temporal MRI descriptor pipeline on ADNI. Methods: A cohort of 661 MCI patients (250 conversion events, 37.8%, median follow-up 42.0 months) was constructed from ADNI. FreeSurfer volumetrics of six brain regions were summarised into three time-based descriptors each (atrophy rate, trajectory variability σ, and time-weighted cumulative mean μ) under strict anti-leakage constraints, yielding 18 neuroimaging features which, combined with six clinical variables (age, sex, education, MMSE, ADAS-13, and APOE-ε4), form a 24-dimensional covariate vector. Cox PH, Weibull AFT, Exponential, RSF, GBST, DeepSurv, and DeepHit were evaluated under stratified 5-fold cross-validation and assessed on an independent OASIS-3 cohort (n=78) as an exploratory analysis. Results: All seven models achieved C-index 0.853–0.863 (Δ=0.010), with Cox PH reaching 0.863±0.027 using only routine structural MRI. Time-dependent AUC ranged from 0.856 (12 months) to 0.938 (48 months). Risk stratification by quartile yielded highly separated Kaplan-Meier curves (log-rank p<0.001). On OASIS-3 (n=78, exploratory), classical models showed preliminary cross-cohort consistency (Weibull AFT 0.760±0.063, RSF 0.759±0.049), while deep learning degraded substantially (DeepSurv 0.551±0.116); these results are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as confirmatory given the small per-fold sample size (EPV ≈ 1). Conclusions: The temporal MRI descriptor pipeline achieves a C-index of 0.863 using only routine structural MRI, without PET or CSF biomarkers, demonstrating strong discriminative performance on ADNI MCI-to-AD conversion. The narrow performance band (Δ=0.010) suggests that, within this feature-engineering paradigm, no clear performance separation was observed among the evaluated model architectures; this convergence may reflect feature-level rather than architecture-level constraints, although the underlying cause cannot be established from discriminative performance alone. Classical models showed more stable cross-cohort behaviour under data-scarce conditions; prospective validation on larger cohorts with full covariate parity is required before clinical translation can be considered.

papers.title: Transformational Leadership and Heterogeneity in Teachers’ Readiness for AI Integration: A Complementary Variable- and Person-Centered Approach
papers.authors: Yaxuan Geng, Kangjie Geng, Kai Wang, Qianqian Ruan
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in education has attracted increasing global attention. Existing studies have mainly examined teachers’ AI adoption intention in relation to technology-related perceptions and broader school-level conditions, but the role of transformational leadership remains underexplored. Drawing on complementary perspectives from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this study examined transformational leadership in relation to teachers’ readiness for AI integration using complementary variable- and person-centered analyses of data from 596 Chinese in-service K-12 teachers. The variable-centered results showed that transformational leadership was positively associated with teachers’ behavioral intention to use AI tools, with indirect associations involving willingness to develop AI competence and constructivist teaching beliefs. The person-centered analysis identified four readiness profiles: (1) Favorable Orientation but Behavioral Hesitation, (2) Limited Orientation and Behavioral Hesitation, (3) Low Orientation and Weak Behavioral Inclination, and (4) Favorable Orientation and Behavioral Inclination. Profiles 1 and 4 both showed relatively high constructivist beliefs and willingness to develop AI competence, but Profile 4 reported stronger behavioral intention to use AI tools. Profiles 2 and 3 were below the sample average across all three indicators, with Profile 3 showing the lowest behavioral intention. Relative to Profile 1, higher transformational leadership was associated with greater odds of membership in Profile 4 and lower odds of membership in Profile 3. These findings suggest that teachers’ readiness for AI integration varies in both level and configuration, highlighting the need for differentiated leadership and professional support.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Employee Innovation: A Literature Review
papers.authors: Xi Cun, Liangbo Zhang, Jifan Ren
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly embedded in knowledge work, creative work, customer service, product development, human resource management, and organizational decision systems. Although research shows that AI can raise productivity, support creative output, accelerate searching, and reorganize innovation work, the evidence remains fragmented across innovation management, organizational behavior, information systems, human resource management, economics, human–computer interaction, and behavioral sciences. This framework-based review synthesizes high-quality English-language journal articles on AI, human–AI collaboration, employee creativity, innovative work behavior, algorithmic management, and innovation management. Building on established models of individual innovation, it develops a worker-centered framework linking four innovation stages with three higher-order AI functions: task execution, knowledge support, and organizational governance. The evidence is strongest for searching, idea generation, creativity, and short-term task performance, and remains limited for idea promotion, implementation, diffusion, and realized innovation outcomes. The synthesis identifies three central tensions: performance equalization versus capability differentiation, short-term quality versus long-term capability development, and individual improvement versus collective homogenization. AI can enhance innovation-related work through cognitive expansion, search acceleration, productivity release, recombination, feedback, and learning, but it can also reduce output diversity, weaken expertise development, intensify work, increase dependence, and shift managerial control over creative labor. The review positions AI as both a cognitive resource and an innovation-governance mechanism and outlines directions for future research on mechanisms, heterogeneity, novelty, capability accumulation, and responsible governance.

papers.title: Twins Discordant for Parkinson’s Disease: A 10-Year Longitudinal Follow-Up of Mortality, Clinical and Lifestyle Features, Nutritional Status, and Dietary Habits
papers.authors: Michela Barichella, Antonio Natale, Elena Contaldi, Luca Magistrelli, Emanuele Cereda, Carlotta Bolliri, Maria Carmela Macchione, Federica Invernizzi, Daniela Calandrella, Ioannis U. Isaias, Gianni Pezzoli
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Twins discordant for Parkinson’s disease (PD) share genetic background and early-life exposures, offering a model for non-genetic determinants of disease. We aimed to evaluate longitudinally the mortality, clinical and lifestyle features, nutritional status and dietary habits of a cohort of PD-discordant twins, with specific attention to the monozygotic (MZ) subgroup. Methods: One hundred and eight subjects from 54 PD-discordant twin pairs (26 MZ, 28 dizygotic [DZ]), with genetically confirmed zygosity, were assessed at baseline (T0) and after 10 years by telephone interview (T1; 33 pairs), using Kaplan–Meier/Cox survival analyses, a clinical and lifestyle history questionnaire, body mass index (BMI), and a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). Results: Ten-year mortality was markedly higher in PD (31.5% vs. 5.6%; HR 6.83), with all MZ deaths occurring in the affected twin.
