The framework further considers how digital storytelling, visual communication, online communities, tourism, and digital commerce may contribute to cultural, educational, social, experiential, and economic value. At the same time, these processes require mechanisms that balance accessibility with contextual depth, participation with cultural authority, and commercialization with continuity. The article contributes a conceptual perspective for understanding how place-based cultural heritage can remain culturally meaningful while engaging with contemporary digital environments.

papers.title: AI-Driven Urban Heat Island Monitoring and Mitigation Planning: A Beginner-Accessible Streamlit Dashboard with Automated Real-World Data Acquisition (Preprint)
papers.authors: Mansi Morey
papers.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Background: The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, in which built-up areas record higher temperatures than surrounding rural regions, affects public health, building energy demand, and outdoor thermal comfort. Machine learning is widely used to predict UHI severity, but most published systems are evaluated offline and assume that every input feature is already known, which leaves a gap for non-expert users such as students, civic technologists, and local planners. Objective: This study aimed to develop and functionally evaluate an end-to-end UHI monitoring and mitigation-planning prototype that predicts a three-class Heat Level (Low, Medium, High), explains the contributing factors, recommends mitigation measures, and fills its own inputs from a single typed location. Methods: A Random Forest classifier (200 trees) was trained on a synthetic dataset of 1,000 records from 25 cities with 15 environmental and urban-structure features, and deployed in an interactive Streamlit dashboard. The dashboard returns class-probability gauges, a rule-based explanation, a feature-importance chart, and severity-tiered mitigation recommendations. An automated data-acquisition layer geocodes a free-text location, retrieves live weather and air-quality data from public APIs, and estimates urban-structure features from OpenStreetMap using documented heuristic formulas. Results: On a 200-record hold-out set, the classifier achieved an accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score of 1.0000. Because the label is derived from temperature, which is also an input, this result validates the pipeline and not real-world predictive skill. Replacing a single global temperature distribution with per-city climatological baselines moved the Low/Medium/High thresholds from 31.9/39.3 ◦C to 27.6/34.9 ◦C. Training took 366 ms and single-sample inference averaged 11.6 ms. Six operational failure modes of free geospatial services (including HTTP 406, 429, and 504 errors and a failure-caching defect) were identified and corrected. A qualitative case study of two Pune, India neighborhoods agreed with independently retrieved weather data. Conclusions: The prototype shows that prediction, explanation, mitigation guidance, and automated data acquisition can be combined in one accessible tool. It is a preliminary decision-support prototype and not a validated urban climate assessment. Validation on real satellite-derived data, removal of label leakage, and a formal usability study are the main next steps

papers.title: An AI-Powered Career Development Assistant Using Large Language Models and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Preprint)
papers.authors: Bhushan Dagwar
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Abstract—Few decisions shape a life as much as the choice of what to study and which career to pursue, yet good guidance remains unevenly distributed. Personal mentoring is scarce and costly, while the tools most job seekers actually reach for—aptitude quizzes, keyword-driven job boards and generic advice columns—seldom account for who the individual really is. Large language models (LLMs) can hold fluent, mentor-like conversations, but on their own they fabricate facts, fall behind a fast-moving labour market and reason only shallowly about a person's background. This paper describes a career development assistant that closes these gaps by pairing an instruction-tuned LLM with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The assistant indexes a curated knowledge base—occupation profiles drawn from the National Classification of Occupations (NCO-2015), skill taxonomies, learning resources and current job postings—and retrieves supporting passages to ground every reply. Four capabilities sit behind a single retrieve-then-generate core: skill-gap analysis, learning-path recommendation, resume and interview feedback, and job-fit explanation. We present the architecture, the profile-aware retrieval and grounding strategy, and a serving design suited to interactive use. Across offline evaluation and a user study, grounding raises answer faithfulness and recommendation relevance while sharply lowering hallucination relative to an LLM-only baseline, indicating that retrieval is a practical foundation for career guidance that people can actually trust. Index Terms—Large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, career guidance, recommender systems, personalization, question answering, natural language processing OBJECTIVE What to study, which skills to build, which roles to chase—these choices follow a person for years, shaping their earnings, their stability and their sense of purpose. Access to sound advice about them, however, is deeply unequal. One-to-one mentoring is expensive and in short supply, and the resources that fill the gap for most people—static aptitude quizzes, keyword-driven job boards and one-size-fits-all articles—rarely reflect an individual's history, constraints or the reality of the market they are trying to enter. The problem is sharpest in smaller towns and colleges, where trained career counsellors are often unavailable altogether. METHODS What to study, which skills to build, which roles to chase—these choices follow a person for years, shaping their earnings, their stability and their sense of purpose. Access to sound advice about them, however, is deeply unequal. One-to-one mentoring is expensive and in short supply, and the resources that fill the gap for most people—static aptitude quizzes, keyword-driven job boards and one-size-fits-all articles—rarely reflect an individual's history, constraints or the reality of the market they are trying to enter. The problem is sharpest in smaller towns and colleges, where trained career counsellors are often unavailable altogether. RESULTS Matching people to work is a long-studied problem, and recent efforts increasingly lean on learned representations of resumes and occupations. Decorte et al. [19] predict career paths from resume embeddings combined with skill-based matching; Du et al. [20] derive language-based occupational representations from LLMs; and skill-aware encoders such as CareerBERT [21] align resumes with occupations through taxonomy-grounded embeddings. Our aim is complementary rather than competing: instead of understanding queries or ranking candidates for a matching engine, we advise the seeker directly, and we ground that advice in retrieved evidence instead of trusting the model's parameters alone. D. Retrieval-Augmented Generation CONCLUSIONS Matching people to work is a long-studied problem, and recent efforts increasingly lean on learned representations of resumes and occupations. Decorte et al. [19] predict career paths from resume embeddings combined with skill-based matching; Du et al. [20] derive language-based occupational representations from LLMs; and skill-aware encoders such as CareerBERT [21] align resumes with occupations through taxonomy-grounded embeddings. Our aim is complementary rather than competing: instead of understanding queries or ranking candidates for a matching engine, we advise the seeker directly, and we ground that advice in retrieved evidence instead of trusting the model's parameters alone. D. Retrieval-Augmented Generation

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Ebola Disease Preparedness and Response: Public Health Priorities (Preprint)
papers.authors: Simon Pistrosch, Sunil Munthumoduku Krishna Murthy, Björn Wolfgang Schuller
papers.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Ebola disease causes recurrent humanitarian and public-health emergencies that demand rapid decisions under uncertainty. Outbreak control is complicated by incomplete surveillance, limited diagnostic and treatment capacity, mistrust, and constrained healthcare infrastructure. Artificial intelligence (AI) could support preparedness and response, but its value depends on reliable data, disease-specific validation, and adaptation to local conditions. This viewpoint examines five application areas: zoonotic surveillance, adaptive outbreak management, public health communication and education, clinical decision support, and therapeutics discovery. We review AI and related computational research, separating Ebola disease–specific findings from opportunities inferred from other diseases and settings. Existing studies have investigated applications in ecological risk mapping, outbreak forecasting, social-media sentiment analysis, clinical prognostic modeling, and drug and vaccine candidate prioritization. However, many proposed applications remain unvalidated in Ebola disease settings, and evidence of improved clinical or public-health outcomes is limited. Using the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease emergency in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda as context, we distinguish research priorities relevant to the ongoing response from longer-term priorities in zoonotic surveillance and countermeasure development. We outline the challenges of integrating outbreak data under clear data governance arrangements, evaluating models across outbreaks and healthcare settings, and assessing performance across population groups. We also discuss infrastructure constraints, ethical oversight, and community participation as requirements for responsible deployment. We argue that AI research should prioritize clearly defined public-health needs and demonstrate measurable benefits. Progress will depend on systems that support human expertise, strengthen existing response capabilities, and remain usable under the conditions faced by affected communities.

papers.title: Predicting Measles Vaccination Defaulting in Uganda and Kenya: Comparative Evaluation of Custom Soft Voting and TabNet Stacked Ensemble Architectures
papers.authors: Bartha Alexandra Nantongo, Josephine Nabukenya, Peter Nabende
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Measles is a major cause of death among infants despite free routine immunization (RI) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Vaccination defaulting contributes to measles outbreak occurrences. Conventional immunization defaulter identification methods are expensive to implement, prone to data falsification, reactive, and overestimate uptake. Several machine learning studies leveraged the use of child and maternal characteristics as predictors of immunization defaulting, overlooking community, demographic, and socioeconomic factors. Similarly, there is limited research regarding the use of interpretable deep learning and advanced ensemble methods to improve model performance in predicting RI defaulters and establishing significant predictors at the national level in the LMIC context, like Uganda. Objective This study predicts infants at a risk of defaulting on measles vaccination in Uganda and Kenya using advanced ensemble learning architectures. Methods The study benchmarked classical and deep learning models using Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) datasets (2016-2022) with child, maternal, community, social-economic, and demographic characteristics as predictors. The robust modeling pipeline began with feature selection according to the literature and the expert domain. It was followed by vaccination eligibility, missing value handling, and feature elimination using the phi-k correlation framework. To mitigate class imbalance, synthetic minority over-sampling technique for nominal continuous features was used in a training pipeline after the RobustScaler. Nine baseline classifiers, including Tabular Network (TabNet), multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest (RF), gradient boosting (GB), adaptive-boosting (AB), among others, underwent stratified k-fold cross-validation and hyperparameter optimization via grid search. Custom soft voting was evaluated alongside TabNet stack architecture for superior ensemble prediction. Models were evaluated for accuracy, precision, recall, and F 1 -score. Model explainability was decoded using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), while Streamlit and SQLite formed the tool architecture. Results The proposed TabNet+GB+RF custom soft voting achieved significant, nonrandom performance over tuned base models with an F 1 -score of 0.7111, area under the curve (AUC) of 0.8847 for Kenya. Conversely, for Uganda, the TabNet hybrid ensemble (GB+RF+ AB→TabNet) was the best with AUC of 0.8862 and F 1 -score of 0.6756, which was statistically insignificant. SHAP identified child’s age and vitamin A1 as universal key predictors in both countries; others varied. In Kenya, time to water source, respondents’ education, district lived previously, and current district were the most influential global features, respectively. In Uganda, Polio inactive, Pentavalent3, current district, and respondents’ education were the most influential factors to defaulting, respectively. Conclusions The proposed advanced ensemble learning models improved the classification of measles vaccine defaulters compared to individual models. The study recommends distinct country-tailored strategies. In Kenya, outreaches are recommended to areas with low literacy, distant water sources, and mobile populations. Conversely, in Uganda, the study recommends reminders to avoid missing preceding vaccines and outreaches to high-default districts.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning–Derived Nomogram Model to Predict Population Health Literacy: Cross-Sectional Development and Validation Study
papers.authors: Xuehai Zhang, Haojie Jin, Zhiming Xie, Yan Li, Zishuo Huang, Chenkai Zhang, Yue Xu, Dingming Yao, Xiujing Hu, Yuyang Zhu, Xuebo Zhu, Chishuang Wang, Chun Chen
papers.abstract: Background: Health literacy (HL) is a major factor associated with population health. However, no visualized predictive model has been developed to identify populations with low HL in a cost-effective manner. Objective: This study aims to identify key determinants of HL and develop a predictive nomogram model for population-level HL screening. Methods: This study analyzed cross-sectional data from 56,340 residents (aged 15-69 y) in Zhejiang Province (2023) And used the Chinese Health Literacy Scale to measure HL. We used 3 complementary analytical approaches: logistic regression (LR) analysis to identify HL-associated factors, machine learning models (gradient boosting decision tree [GBDT], extreme gradient boosting [XGBoost], LR, and random forest [RF]) with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to quantify predictor importance, and nomogram development using 2023 data with external validation on 2024 data. In the nomogram, model 1 used all the predictive variables, while model 2 used the 5 core predictive variables determined through SHAP analysis. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. Results: The nomogram models designed for predicting HL demonstrated robust stability, with good results in external validation. The area under the curve (AUC) values for both the test and validation sets of the machine learning models exceeded 0.75. At the 0.5 threshold, the sensitivities of the GBDT, XGBoost, LR, and RF test sets and validation sets were all >60%. The specificity of the test sets and validation sets of all 4 machine learning models was >75%. The positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were both >60%. The AUC value of nomogram model 1 developed using the data from 2023 was 0.821, and the AUC value of the externally validated nomogram model 1 was 0.814. Similarly, nomogram model 2 had AUC values of 0.819 in the internal validation and 0.812 in the external validation. The PPV and NPV of both the internal validation model 1 and model 2 were all >60%. The integration of GBDT, XGBoost, LR, and RF models, along with the SHAP method, highlighted education level, age, annual household income, smoking, and occupation as the 5 most critical determinants. Conclusions: By using the GBDT, XGBoost, LR, RF, and nomogram models, a predictive model with substantial efficacy was effectively developed and validated for forecasting the HL levels of the population. This comprehensive model not only exhibits a commendable predictive capacity but also identifies the pivotal factors influencing HL. Such insights are crucial for shaping health policies and fostering healthier behaviors across the population.

papers.title: Association of Noise Exposure, Perceived Noise Impact, and BMI on Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Among Chinese Seafarers: Nationwide Population-Based Survey
papers.authors: Ruizi Shi, Shuai Zhou, Zhitao Yang, Erzhen Chen, Hanbing Shang, Ying Zhou
papers.abstract: Background: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a global public health challenge, yet its relationship between occupational noise exposure and perceived noise impact remains unclear. Objective: We characterized maritime noise exposure patterns and examined the associations of noise exposure, perceived noise impact, and BMI with NAFLD among seafarers. Methods: A population-based survey was conducted from March to May 2024 through the China Shipowners' Association. Participants completed a structured online questionnaire. Noise exposure was assessed via self-report, and NAFLD presence was determined by self-reported physician diagnoses based on the 2018 updated NAFLD guidelines. Results: A total of 8143 male seafarers was included, with an overall NAFLD prevalence of 18.5% (n=1503). The prevalence was significantly higher among seafarers with a BMI of 24.0 kg/m² or above (25.9%, n=1261), chronic noise exposure (19.4%, n=1293), and higher perceived noise impact (slightly: 16.9%, n=589; moderate: 19.1%, n=359; significant: 22.5%, n=511). Among seafarers with a BMI of 24.0 kg/m² or above, chronic noise exposure and higher perceived noise impact were significantly associated with an elevated risk of NAFLD. After full adjustment, the combined association of chronic noise exposure and higher perceived noise impact remained significantly associated with increased NAFLD risk, with consistent patterns observed across both workplace and rest area settings. A significant interaction was also observed between rest-area noise exposure and perceived noise impact in this BMI subgroup. Conclusions: Noise exposure, perceived noise impact, and BMI were significantly associated with NAFLD among seafarers. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing occupational health benefits, especially among those with metabolic disorders.

papers.title: Balancing Support and Deskilling
papers.authors: Christopher Klupak, Elmar Dammann
papers.abstract: Context: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers accessible task support, but the implications for independent learning remain uncertain. This paper examines perceived support, possible cognitive offloading, and self-regulated learning in vocational education and related higher education settings. Approach: A structured narrative synthesis examined six unpublished empirical bachelor’s and master’s theses completed at the University of Hamburg between 2023 and 2025. Four studies concern vocational education and two provide complementary higher education perspectives. Surveys, a task comparison, an uncontrolled pre-post study, and qualitative accounts were compared while retaining their methodological differences. Findings: Surveys reported substantial AI familiarity and use among respondents, perceived benefits, and concerns about uncritical reliance. In a small task comparison, AI-assisted responses more frequently met the completeness criterion, whereas responses produced without AI more frequently met the study’s transfer and independent-wording criteria. A vocational intervention found increases in self-reported self-regulation, motivation, and self-efficacy; its design cannot isolate an AI effect. Qualitative findings highlighted difficulties in organising problem-solving and evaluating understanding. Conclusions: Perceived usefulness, task-product quality, and independent competence are distinct outcomes. The studies do not establish long-term deskilling or a causal role of self-regulation in AI effects. The synthesis motivates instructional approaches that combine AI assistance with explanation, verification, and independent application, and identifies priorities for controlled and longitudinal research.

papers.title: Beyond AI Skills
papers.authors: Andrey Felipe Sgorla
papers.abstract: Context: Current debates on Vocational Education and Training (VET) increasingly emphasise the need to equip learners and workers with artificial intelligence (AI) skills, particularly in cultural and creative sectors. European policy initiatives often frame this challenge through competence development, qualification reform, and employability agendas. While important at system level, such perspectives provide limited insight into how vocational learning is enacted in everyday work settings where knowledge is socially, materially, and historically situated. Research on work-based learning has long demonstrated that vocational competence develops through participation in occupational practice, mentoring relations, and engagement with workplace affordances (Billett, 2001; Lave & Wenger, 1991). This perspective is particularly relevant in artisanal and creative occupations, where learning relies on embodied judgement, tacit knowledge, and situated problem-solving (Sennett, 2008; Marchand, 2016). Against this background, the study examines how generative AI is entering work-based learning practices in Tuscany’s craft and creative sector. Approach: This first-stage study adopts a qualitative exploratory multi-source design with focused ethnographic elements. Data were drawn from focused workplace observations in artisanal settings connected to VET pathways, including informal conversational encounters with craft practitioners, field observations at the Mostra Internazionale dell’Artigianato (MIDA) in Florence, and documentary and digital materials. A prior empirical mapping of hybrid craft and digital workplaces in Tuscany (Sgorla, 2025) provided the basis for purposive site selection. Data were analysed through iterative thematic coding informed by sensitising concepts from work-based learning, situated learning, and sociomaterial theory. Findings: Early findings indicate that generative AI is being incorporated unevenly across craft settings, used more frequently for ideation, marketing and design support than for core manual production. Learning about AI occurs informally through self-directed experimentation and peer exchange rather than formal training. Tensions emerge between innovation narratives and concerns regarding authenticity, authorship, and occupational identity. The notion of “the hand” (la mano) functions as a boundary marker between tasks where AI may support the creative process and those where embodied execution remains non-negotiable. Craft practitioners evaluate AI-generated outputs through sensory, aesthetic, and practical judgement developed over years of material engagement, positioning AI as raw material to be filtered rather than as a replacement for craft knowledge. Conclusions: The study contributes to VET research by moving beyond competence-based framings of AI and examining how technological change is mediated through situated vocational practice. Conceptually, it advances the notion of hybrid learning ecologies (Sgorla, Melacarne & Banchetti, 2025), understood as learning environments shaped through the interaction of embodied workplace practice, mentoring and peer relations, institutional training arrangements, public sectoral networks and events, and AI-mediated knowledge resources. The Tuscan case reveals that the critical capacity for craft workers is not the ability to use AI tools, but the evaluative competence to contextualise and integrate AI outputs within situated practice.

papers.title: Towards an Inclusive VET Ecosystem
papers.authors: Evelyn Ansah Karkkulainen, POON CHUN YIN, Kuen Fung Sin, Daniel Kwasi Ahorsu
papers.abstract: Context: Several countries have endorsed the United Nations agencies' mandate on inclusive vocational education and training (VET) for learners with special educational needs (SEN). Despite these robust international commitments, empirical evidence supporting inclusive VET remains dispersed across disciplines, national contexts, and thematic areas, thereby limiting the synthesis of cohesive policy and practice. This systematic review examines the evidence on inclusive VET across four domains: (1) pedagogy, (2) institutional support, (3) school-to-work transition, and (4) digital tools and mental health. Approach: Following PRISMA guidelines, a search was conducted across five databases (ERIC, Web of Science, PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus) and through manual searches of four principal VET journals from January 2008 to April 2026. Findings: The review included 38 peer-reviewed empirical studies from 18 countries across four analytical domains: pedagogy and life skills (n = 18), institutional support (n = 16), school-to-work transition (n = 21), and digital tools and mental health (n = 4, both with partial focus). Data across the studies were primarily from (1) learners with SEN, (2) parents of learners with SEN, (3) VET teachers/staff, and (4) SEN–VET specialists. Across the studies, four cross-national themes emerged: (1) a universal gap between policy and practice, in which inclusive VET is widely mandated but inadequately implemented; (2) the VET teacher serves as the de facto inclusion system, with institutional support fragile because it relies on individual teacher commitment rather than structural design; (3) a pre-VET bottleneck, in which the transition from school to VET is the strongest predictor of the long-term risk of not in employment, education, or training (NEET) for learners with SEN; and (4) a critical oversight in digital and mental health, with no primary-focus studies addressing artificial intelligence, assistive technology, or mental health specifically within VET for SEN students. VET systems vary across countries; however, some consistently yield better results. Conclusions: Achieving inclusive VET requires a systemic approach rather than relying solely on individual efforts. The evidence points to four priority actions: (1) addressing the universal policy and practice gap through accountability mechanisms; (2) easing the burden on VET teachers by strengthening institutional support structures; (3) mitigating the pre-VET bottleneck through early transition planning that engages employer and VET providers; and (4) closing the critical evidence gap in digital and mental health, by funding targeted research on assistive technology, AI tools, and well-being interventions in VET contexts.

papers.title: AI-Mediated Vocational Pedagogy in Transition
papers.authors: Steinar Karstensen, Leif Christian Lahn, Svanhild Kristine Berntsen, Nina Aakernes
papers.abstract: Context: Generative AI has diffused into vocational education and training (VET) faster than teacher education systems have developed institutional strategies for pedagogically meaningful integration. While individual AI pioneers drive innovation, collective institutional capacity has not kept up, and pedagogical configuration, not access, emerges as the critical moderator of learning outcomes. Approach: An exploratory case study purposively selected pioneering teachers in the Norwegian upper-secondary Information Technology and Media Production (ITMP) programme across two schools. Data sources include semi-structured interviews (N=5), field observations and documentary material, analysed using an abductive thematic approach. In this paper we reflect critically on the empirical study and outline a study protocol for the AIVOCPED research project and its intersection with the National Network for AI in VET (NAIVET). Findings: Five interlocking patterns emerge: AI-mediated vocational didactics with project- and production-oriented learning environments; reconfigured assessment practices shifting from product to process; teacher roles in transition towards facilitation and co-learning; ethical and epistemic challenges requiring integration with field-specific didactics; and individualised teacher competence development against weak institutional support. Pedagogical design emerges as the analytical core distinguishing strengthening from inefficient uses of AI. Conclusions: Sustainable AI-mediated vocational pedagogy requires institutional anchoring across levels and must involve teacher professional communities. Eight principles for a participatory, design-based and longitudinal AIVOCPED–NAIVET study protocol are proposed. With Article 4 of the EU AI Act entering enforcement on 3 August 2026, the loop from research to collective practice must be shortened.

papers.title: Emerging Researchers as AI Pioneers: AI Use and Ethical Competences in Vocational Education and Training Among Young Professionals
papers.authors: Lisa Meyne, Susanne Peters
papers.abstract: Context: The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education and vocational education and training (VET) fundamentally changes research practices, academic writing and collaborative knowledge production, particularly for emerging researchers at the beginning of their careers. While several European and international frameworks now define AI-related competences for educators, there is still limited conceptual work that addresses the specific professional requirements of VET research and connects AI competences explicitly to ethical reflection, research practice and work-process orientation. Approach: The paper presents a narrative compilation of recent policy documents, framework papers and project outputs on AI in education, with a particular focus on ethical issues and competence development. It analyses these contributions from the perspective of international VET research and combines them with concepts of work-process and action-oriented learning. On this basis, the paper outlines a design for an interactive, international workshop format to strengthen these competences. Findings: The analysis suggests that AI-related competences for emerging researchers in VET can be clustered into three domains: Technical and methodological competences (e.g., understanding AI systems, data and tools), ethical and critical competences (such as fairness, transparency, bias, academic integrity) and collaborative and professional competences (e.g., interdisciplinary cooperation, peer learning). These domains are mutually dependent and only in their integration enable a responsible use of AI in research and teaching. Several unresolved questions are identified, for example around independent academic achievement, fair assessment in AI-supported contexts, bias in AI detection tools and distributional fairness regarding access to AI. Conclusions: The competent use of AI should be regarded as an important element of professionalisation for (emerging) VET researchers rather than as an optional add-on. The paper argues for work-process-oriented, case-based and international peer-learning formats and proposes the further development of guidelines for VET research, that can be empirically validated in future research.

papers.title: Embodied AI Customer Role-Play in XR for Retail Apprentices
papers.authors: Martin Berger, Stefan Greuter
papers.abstract: Context: Professional communication is a core competence for Swiss retail apprentices and is assessed in the final practical examination, yet role-play practice is hard to scale because it depends on trained actors and expert feedback. Generative AI and immersive XR offer a possible route to repeatable practice in routine classroom settings. Approach: We implemented an AI-supported customer role-play and reflective coaching system on XARA and evaluated it in a single immersive XR condition using Meta Quest 3. Nine Swiss retail apprentices completed one approximately 11-minute session, followed by a group interview analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings: Apprentices described the XR experience as engaging and potentially useful for practising difficult interactions. They also identified limited conversational flexibility, insufficient situation-specific coaching feedback, and practical requirements for classroom deployment. Conclusions: The study provides early design insights into AI-supported communication training delivered in XR. Because no non-immersive condition or learning measures were included, the findings describe initial learner perceptions and do not establish effects of the XR modality, learning outcomes, or scalability.

papers.title: Schumpeter's Innovation Theory and Technopreneurial Character Development Among Industrial Electrical Engineering Graduates in the Age of Automation
papers.authors: Arif Wibowo, Jessen Bakoh Trantoko, Chairul Nur Yasin, Muhammad Habibullah, Fakhruddin Mangkusasmito, Dista Yoel Tadeus
papers.abstract: The rapid development of automation, artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things, and smart manufacturing has transformed the competency requirements for Industrial Electrical Engineering graduates. Technical proficiency alone is increasingly insufficient, as graduates are also expected to identify technological opportunities, develop innovative solutions, and create economic value. This study aims to examine the integration of Joseph Schumpeter’s Innovation Theory into the development of technopreneurial character among Industrial Electrical Engineering graduates in the automation era. A descriptive qualitative literature review was employed by synthesizing scholarly literature on Schumpeterian innovation, creative destruction, technopreneurship, automation, and engineering education. The analysis focused on translating Schumpeter’s five forms of innovation into the context of electrical engineering and examining their implications for technopreneurial character development. The findings indicate that Schumpeter’s innovation framework provides a relevant conceptual foundation for transforming technical competencies into entrepreneurial value creation. The five forms of innovation new products, new production methods, new markets, new sources of supply, and new forms of industrial organization can be applied to electrical engineering through the development of smart monitoring systems, efficient engineering processes, affordable automation solutions, alternative technology resources, and technology-based service models. This study proposes an integrative pathway from technical competence to problem identification, innovative recombination, prototyping, market validation, commercialization, and value creation. The study contributes a Schumpeterian perspective for strengthening technopreneurship education and repositioning Industrial Electrical Engineering graduates as technology creators and value creators in the era of automation. Keywords: automation; creative destruction; engineering education; electrical engineering; schumpeter; technopreneurship

papers.title: Generative AI Use and Learning Productivity Among Google Gemini Users in Bangladesh: An Integrated TAM-Self-Regulated Learning Model
papers.authors: Khan Rifat, Kazi Abdul Mannan
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p < .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p < .001) and PU (β = .218, p < .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p < .001) and SRL (β = .202, p < .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

papers.title: Best Administrative/IT Practices When Rolling Out Custom Agents
papers.authors: Anurag Mathews, Coco Shen, Edward Zeng, Asad Malik
papers.abstract: Educational institutions recognizing the widespread value of artificial intelligence agents may desire to adopt the emerging technologies within their own organizations. However, the deployment of custom agents involves risks for the institutions in the form of prompt injection attacks, hallucinations, embarrassing responses, data leaks, RAG poisoning, and more. Accountability structures, proper identity and access management, and legal compliance standards (FERPA, AI Disclosure Laws, and ADA accessibility) must be maintained on an administrative level to ensure the institution can safely and efficiently deploy agentic technology. When it comes to the initial deployment of the agent, technical teams should implement guardrails, RAG databases, and rate limiting to protect against many of the associated agentic-specific risks, excluding traditional software risks. Finally, subject matter experts can review existing metrics and agent traces to adjust RAG database documents, token limits, tools, and more to ensure optimal agentic output.

papers.title: Seeing and Unseeing the City: Photography, Power and Spatial Justice in Urban Co-Creation
papers.authors: Jorge Gonçalves
papers.abstract: Photography occupies a prominent and contested place in contemporary participatory urban planning. This research develops a critical-interpretative framework that rejects celebratory narratives of visual participation, whilst recognising the genuine possibilities that participatory photography can offer under appropriate political and institutional conditions. Drawing on recent literature, we examine four interrelated issues: i. access to participation and the exclusions it reproduces; ii. control over the production, selection, interpretation and circulation of images; iii. divergent spatial experiences and conflicts of use; iv. and the gap between representation and material change. The evidence gathered and analysed reveals tensions that methodological refinement alone cannot resolve, namely: researchers limit participants’ autonomy even in ostensibly co-produced projects; visual literacy and technological access remain unevenly distributed; images are selectively appropriated to legitimise predetermined institutional agendas; and emerging AI technologies risk intensifying these dynamics through algorithmic bias and a growing loss of trust in evidence. Participatory photography is understood here as a contested terrain, whose emancipatory potential depends on power relations, institutional conditions and the community’s control over the production and use of the images themselves.

papers.title: Psychological Mechanisms of Forming Trust in Generative AI: A Critical Review of Definitions and an Integrative Model
papers.authors: V. O. Otchertsova, Olena Ye. Blynova
papers.abstract: Aim . To conduct a critical analysis of existing definitions of trust in generative AI, identify key contradictions in the conceptualization of the phenomenon and propose an integrative definition that considers the specifics of human interaction with intelligent agents. Methodology . A systematic critical review of trust in AI from sources in 2020–2025 has been conducted including large-scale empirical studies, systematic reviews, theoretical works. The analysis was carried out according to the criteria: structural components, antecedents, typology, levels of analysis, cultural specificity. The method of theoretical research included the selection of sources according to the criteria of empirical validity, theoretical reflexivity and relevance, systematization of definitions, comparative analysis of key dimensions, identification of contradictions and synthesis of integrative definitions. Results . There is a lack of consensus in definitions: trust in generative AI is conceptualised as a psychological attitude, a multilevel social phenomenon, or reduced to technical characteristics. Ten key paradoxes have been discovered: transparency, experience, anthropomorphism, prejudice towards automation versus rejection of algorithms, cultural and others. Trust in AI differs from interpersonal trust in seven unique ways: opacity, anthropomorphism, explainability, epistemic versus social trust, compensatory trust, and the U-shaped dynamics of experience. Research implications . An integrative review of trust in AI is proposed. It combines three components (cognitive, affective, behavioural), four levels of factors (individual, system, context, society) and it is aimed at reasonable trust. Critical gaps in research and priority areas have been identified. The results are significant for the development of reliable AI systems, effective regulatory frame-works, and AI literacy programs.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Psychological Effects on University Teaching
papers.authors: Sergey M. Grigoriev
papers.abstract: Aim . To identify GenAI‑specific psychological mechanisms through which LLMs reshape academic teaching work, and to compare effects in content creation versus assessment. Methodology . The study combines a transparent integrative review (2015–2025; Scopus, WoS, PsycINFO, ERIC, RSCI; 56 sources with PRISMA‑style tracking) with a qualitative pilot (16 semi‑structured interviews with Russian university instructors; thematic analysis) using an integrated JD‑R and SDT framework. Results : GenAI acts both as a resource and a work‑redesign driver, generating AI‑specific demands: epistemic uncertainty, verification workload, trust calibration, accountability / responsibility anxiety, norm acceleration and “silent” intensification, and a role shift toward surveillance in assessment. A domain asymmetry is found – content work is mainly burdened by hidden cognitive verification, while assessment amplifies emotional and normative risks related to fairness and conflict. Research implications : a model linking GenAI properties to job demands / resources and basic needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) is proposed; recommendations include formal time for verification, a human‑in‑the‑loop standard for high‑stakes assessment, clearer academic integrity policies, and safeguards against intensification.

papers.authors: Patrick Baert, Ella McPherson, Isabelle Higgins, Shannon Philip

papers.title: Bioconstitutionalism as a Manifestation of Adaptive Constitutionalism: The Transformation of Constitutional Values under conditions of Biotechnological Challenges
papers.authors: S.Yu. Poyarkov
papers.abstract: In the context of the rapid development of biotechnologies capable of radically transforming the biological and cognitive foundations of human existence, there is an urgent need to develop a new constitutional law paradigm capable of safeguarding the anthropological core of the legal order. The study substantiates the concept of bioconstitutionalism as a specialized form of adaptive constitutionalism aimed at preserving biological integrity, cognitive autonomy, and human dignity in an era when human nature itself has become an object of technological design. The paper demonstrates that traditional constitutional values require ontological reconsideration and an expansion of their substantive scope in response to the challenges posed by gene editing, neurotechnologies, reproductive innovations, and the commercialization of genetic data. Particular attention is paid to germline genome editing, the consequences of which are irreversible and heritable and affect the rights of future generations. In this context, the human genome is conceptualized as a bearer of a person's constitutional identity, while any unauthorized intervention is regarded as an infringement of human dignity. The author introduces the concept of cognitive integrity, defined as the right to protect one's mental processes from external reading, recording, or modification through neural interfaces. Such protection is becoming a necessary condition for the exercise of freedom of conscience, freedom of expression, and freedom of will. The article emphasizes that bioconstitutionalism is not a prohibitive mechanism intended to restrict scientific progress; rather, it establishes constitutional limits on biotechnological interventions on the basis of the principles of intergenerational justice, the prohibition of dehumanization, and the primacy of bioethical norms.

papers.title: How customer preconceptions appear to shape value co-creation: The identification of four customer archetypes in a boutique ice cream service encounter.
papers.authors: Brice Smith
papers.abstract: Abstract: This study examines how customer preconceptions appear to shape frontline interaction and value co-creation in a boutique ice cream service encounter. Drawing on Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and customer journey theory, the study investigates how prior expectations, environmental cues, and employee interaction influence perceived value across pre-consumption, consumption, and post-consumption touchpoints. Using structured participant observation in an artisan creamery setting across two trading seasons, the study analyses approximately 10,000 anonymous customer transactions within a retail setting designed to combine familiar core flavours with rotating novelty offerings. The findings indicate four recurring customer archetypes—Predictable, Cautious, Indifferent, and Adventurous—each associated with distinct non-verbal cues, choice behaviours, and emotional trajectories across the service encounter. Predictable customers tend to value speed and confirmation, Cautious customers are more vulnerable to choice anxiety, Indifferent customers prefer simplicity and low-friction guidance, and Adventurous customers respond positively to storytelling, sampling, and novelty. The study contributes a practical typology of customer preconceptions and suggests that flexible service scripts, adaptive sampling, and strategically deployed surprise can support value co-creation more effectively than uniform frontline service design. The findings are bounded by a single-site qualitative design and should be interpreted as context-specific.

papers.title: A Relational Inquiry into AI Generativity: The Historical Formation of Judgment and Its Role in Value Recognition
papers.authors: Wanhong HUANG
papers.abstract: This theoretical discussion paper examines how artificial intelligence participates in cognition, judgment, and generative activity through historically constituted relations among models, humans, other artificial agents, institutions, and environments. It distinguishes equal access to foundational technical capability from equality of situated performance, evaluative and generative judgment, practical opportunity, social recognition, and authority. A preliminary Generative Relational Theory (GRT) perspective treats historically conditioned AI configurations as candidates for relational reality where sufficiently stable causal efficacy can be established, while suspending claims about consciousness and ultimate ontological status. The analysis considers how interaction histories, conversational practices, memory, feedback, aesthetic preferences, and normative criteria may shape the realization of AI capabilities. It also investigates coordination conventions and rule-like practices among interacting AI agents, their uncertain normative authority, and the distinct processes through which generated contributions acquire recognition and institutional influence. Findings from existing experiments and field studies are interpreted within their task-specific limits, including evidence concerning heterogeneous productivity, creative diversity, contextual accommodation, and collective coordination. A comparative research program is proposed to distinguish historical causal contributions from prompt effects, unequal information, institutional selection, and other rival explanations. Relational differentiation may coexist with convergence or the reduction of existing disadvantages. The paper neither reports new experiments nor establishes a general law of AI-mediated inequality; questions of legitimacy and justice require normative arguments in addition to causal analysis.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Readiness Among Nursing Students: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Aamer Aldbyani
papers.abstract: This scoping review aims to systematically map and synthesize the existing literature on artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and readiness among nursing students in educational and clinical learning contexts. The review will examine how AI literacy and readiness are conceptualized, defined, and measured among nursing students. It will identify the levels and dimensions of AI-related knowledge, skills, competencies, attitudes, confidence, and preparedness reported in the literature, as well as factors associated with students' readiness to engage with AI technologies in nursing education and future professional practice. The review will also explore the educational strategies, training initiatives, assessment instruments, and institutional factors discussed in relation to the development of AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The review will be guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and structured using the Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework. Relevant evidence from quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies will be considered, subject to predefined eligibility criteria. A systematic search of relevant bibliographic databases and supplementary sources will be undertaken, followed by transparent study selection, data charting, and descriptive and thematic mapping of the available evidence. Findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), where applicable. The anticipated outcome is a comprehensive overview of the scope, characteristics, measurement approaches, educational applications, and research gaps relating to AI literacy and readiness among nursing students. The findings may inform future research, nursing curricula, AI-related educational interventions, and the development of relevant competencies and assessment frameworks.

papers.title: Fewer Visits, Deeper Audits? Structural Change in Japan's Tax Audit Activity, 2010–2024
papers.authors: 勉 矢作
papers.abstract: Japan's National Tax Agency (NTA) publishes annual counts of field audits and "simple contacts" (written, telephone or office-visit requests to review a return, without visiting the taxpayer), together with the additional tax assessed. This study assembles these published statistics for corporations and for individual income taxpayers for business years 2010–2024 (each business year runs from July to the following June), adds the share of staff working days spent on audit-related work from the Ministry of Finance's annual performance evaluation of the NTA, and tests whether the series changed at three points fixed in advance: the codification of audit procedures in the Act on General Rules for National Taxes (in force January 2013, business year 2012), the COVID-19 period (business year 2020), and the NTA's adoption of AI-based case selection. The question is whether Japanese tax audits shifted from visiting many taxpayers to selecting fewer cases and spending more time and obtaining more tax per case.

papers.title: Beyond Engagement: A Scoping Review of Algorithmic Governance, Learner Agency, and Digital Inequality in AI-Augmented Gamification in Higher Education
papers.authors: Lenin Omar Lara Castro, Willam Esparza, Wilson Herrera
papers.abstract: This preregistration describes a scoping review examining the sociotechnical implications of AI-augmented gamification in higher education. The review will map how artificial intelligence techniques are integrated with gamification mechanisms and analyze their relationship with learner autonomy, learner agency, digital inequality, privacy, surveillance, datafication, algorithmic bias, transparency, algorithmic governance, and human control. The review will follow JBI methodology for scoping reviews, report according to PRISMA-ScR, and document database searches in accordance with PRISMA-S. Eligible studies will include peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings published in English or Spanish between 2011 and the final search date in 2026. Searches will be conducted in Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library, complemented by backward and forward citation searching. The objective is to provide an integrated sociotechnical synthesis of how AI-augmented gamification shapes learning, institutional decision-making, learner agency, and equity in higher education.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in EFL teaching: teachers’ practices, perceptions and professional development needs
papers.authors: Claudia Bernabeu Díaz, Víctor González Calatayud
papers.journal: Revista Internacional de Lenguas Extranjeras / International Journal of Foreign Languages
papers.abstract: Given the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) –and, particularly, of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)–, and its growing presence in the educational field, it is crucial to understand how teachers are responding to these changes to provide appropriate support and promote the effective use of these technologies in the classroom. Therefore, this study aims to explore, by means of a Google Forms questionnaire, how Primary English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers in the Region of Murcia use and perceive AI in their teaching, as well as to identify their training needs for its successful integration. The results show that most of the participants are familiar with and use tools like ChatGPT, mainly for elaborating didactic materials, searching for information, and planning teaching sequences, although their frequency of use is generally occasional. More interactive and student-centred applications are less common. Furthermore, teachers recognise benefits such as time saving and increased student interaction, discussion, collaboration, and motivation, but also express concerns about a potential diminishment in critical thinking, technological dependence, and risks related to privacy, misinformation, and equity. Even though many feel relatively prepared to use AI in their classes, they stress the need for ongoing training to ensure the responsible and effective use of these tools.

papers.title: AI Laboratories and the Future Academic Library: A Framework for Assessing User Perceptions and Acceptance of AI-Driven Services in the Indian Institutes of Management
papers.authors: Abhishek Kumar Gupta (Dashora), Dr. Rakesh Kumar Khare
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping teaching, research and scholarly communication, and several Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) are now building AI schools, centres and laboratories.This paper examines the importance and future role of AI laboratories in IIMs and asks what this institutional shift means for users' perceptions and acceptance of AI-driven library services.Drawing on official institutional sources and recent literature on AI in academic libraries and technology acceptance, the paper (i) maps AI laboratories and AI-focused units across the 21 IIMs, identifying four IIMs (Ahmedabad, Calcutta, Lucknow and Udaipur) with an identified AI laboratory or unit; (ii) proposes an AI Lab-Library research-support framework; and (iii) sets out a research design for assessing user perceptions at IIM Udaipur, covering awareness, perceived usefulness, ease of use, trust, privacy and ethical concerns, satisfaction and behavioral intention.The paper is conceptual and design-oriented and reports no primary survey results.It argues that AI laboratories should be treated as research-support infrastructure that creates new scholarly information needs, that libraries are well placed to provide a human-centred and ethical layer between AI infrastructure and users, and that acceptance cannot be assumed from the availability of technology alone.Practical recommendations for IIM libraries and testable propositions for future empirical work are provided.
keywords: perceived usefulness and ease of use

papers.title: Sharenting jako praktyka rodzicielska a uznawanie podmiotowości dziecka w perspektywie analizy transakcyjnej
papers.authors: Agnieszka Iwanicka
papers.abstract: This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Statistical analyses (Welch's t test, Pearson's χ² test) revealed a digital privacy paradox: despite widespread endorsement of children's right to privacy, as many as 61.6% of parents of children aged 6–15 do not always ask their children for consent before publishing their image, or do not always respect their answers. This practice illustrates the discounting of the child's digital sovereignty from a paternalistic life position. Mothers were more likely than fathers to approach sharenting relationally, seeking digital strokes through the Child ego state. Higher self-assessed knowledge co-occurred with stronger concerns about artificial intelligence and with a propensity for corrective action (41.7% of parents had deleted previously posted photos of their child). The shift toward a position that recognizes the child as a subject occurs in response to adolescents' resistance or to parental self-reflection. The pedagogical implications point to the need for workshops on relational digital maturity and for promoting digital consent from the earliest years.

papers.title: Sharenting as a Parenting Practice and the Recognition of the Child's Agency: A Transactional Analysis Perspective
papers.authors: Agnieszka Iwanicka
papers.abstract: This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. papers.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Optometry: Awareness and Perspectives Among Scandinavian Optometrists
papers.authors: Alberto Domínguez Vicent, Signe Krejberg Jeppesen, Lene A. Hagen, Abinaya Priya Venkataraman
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Optometry and Visual Science
papers.abstract: The awareness and perspectives of Scandinavian optometrists regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in eye care was evaluated through a web-based questionnaire. Responses from 421 optometrists were analyzed for familiarity, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to engage with AI technologies. Most participants expressed familiarity with AI and support for its inclusion in education and practice, though concerns regarding diagnostic accuracy and potential impacts on the patient-optometrist relationship were noted. These findings are critical for informing educational strategies and facilitating knowledge exchange aimed at addressing uncertainties and optimising the benefits of AI in eye care.

papers.title: Fostering team learning for educational innovation: An academic development initiative on genAI and assessment
papers.authors: Franziska Zellweger, Tobias Röhl, Sabine Binder, Jacqueline Egli, Mònica Feixas i Condom, David Gavin, Thomas Matti, Luca Moser, Bernadette Spieler, Saskia Waibel, Markus Weil, Tobias Zimmermann
papers.journal: Journal of Adult Learning Knowledge and Innovation
papers.abstract: Abstract Drawing on the notion of workplace learning this study examines how academic development can design and facilitate team learning in the academic workplace to support co-constructive educational innovation. Based on a qualitative case study at a Swiss University of Teacher Education, it analyses a participatory initiative addressing generative artificial intelligence (genAI) in assessment. The staged process combined SWOT-based collective sense-making, a design sprint, selective project funding, and facilitated reflection during project development. Data consisted of process documentation and collaboratively generated written reflections, which were analysed and refined through iterative feedback and co-writing. The findings show how structured formats, shared artefacts, and deliberate facilitation enabled participants to make distributed expertise visible, develop shared problem understandings, form project teams, and move from exchange towards co-construction and coordinated experimentation. At the same time, public pitching, funding decisions, time pressures, and institutional constraints created tensions between collaboration and competition, openness and focus, and participation and decision-making. The study suggests that academic development can support educational innovation by acting as facilitator, trust-building broker, and co-learner. Its contribution lies in conceptualising participatory innovation processes as workplace-learning arrangements that connect emerging team-learning processes with local experimentation and wider institutional conversations, while recognising that organisational learning requires further institutional uptake.

papers.title: Desafíos y retos en la Encíclica Magnifica Humanitas
papers.authors: José Ignacio Torres Araya
papers.abstract: The encyclical Magnifica Humanitas of H. H. León XIV reflects on the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to human dignity, emphasizing that technological progress acquires meaning only when it serves the human person and the common good. The document warns about the risks of the technocratic paradigm, the dehumanization of relationships, information manipulation, educational inequalities, and the impact of automation on work. It also proposes a culture of love, solidarity, and justice as the foundation for guiding scientific and technological development. From the perspective of Christian humanism, it highlights the need for an integral education that fosters critical thinking, ethical discernment, and the responsible use of new technologies. Finally, it argues that artificial intelligence should complement, rather than replace, moral responsibility, freedom, and the transcendent vocation of the human person, thereby promoting an authentically human and inclusive form of development.

papers.title: Community Engagement for Ethical Digital Justice: Practical Standards for Online Hearings and Electronic Evidence
papers.authors: Volodymyr V. Shekhovtsov, Юрій Богданович Гофман, Юлія Олександрівна Фідря, I. O. Bylytsia, Інна Володимирівна Ковальчук
papers.journal: Jurnal Pengabdian Hukum Indonesia (Indonesian Journal of Legal Community Engagement) JPHI
papers.abstract: The rapid digitalization of judicial systems has transformed legal practice by expanding the use of online hearings, electronic evidence, and digital communication, while creating new ethical challenges for judges and lawyers. Existing ethical frameworks in Ukraine provide only general guidance and do not adequately address the complexities of digital justice. This study aims to identify the principal ethical issues arising from digital litigation and to develop a unified framework of digital ethics for judges and lawyers based on international best practices and the Ukrainian legal context. The research employs a qualitative methodology combining doctrinal legal analysis, comparative legal analysis, and general scientific methods, including analysis, synthesis, induction, deduction, analogy, and generalization. National legislation, judicial ethics codes, international standards, and relevant case law were examined to assess current regulatory gaps and identify effective approaches to digital judicial ethics. The findings reveal significant shortcomings in the regulation of online hearings, electronic evidence, lawyer–client confidentiality, digital competence, transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence in judicial proceedings. The study proposes a unified minimum standard of digital ethics that integrates procedural safeguards, ethical principles, and comparative international practices to enhance consistency, fairness, and public confidence in digital justice. The novelty of the research lies in developing an interdisciplinary framework that systematically links ethical challenges with practical regulatory solutions through a problem–solution–impact model, offering a comprehensive basis for the modernization of judicial and legal ethics in Ukraine. The proposed framework supports the development of a transparent, accountable, and technologically resilient justice system. The framework also identifies the institutions responsible for implementation and links digital-ethics reform to access to justice, public legal education, and inclusive participation in remote proceedings.

papers.title: Використання цифрових технологій та психологічного благополуччя: огляд доказових даних і каузальна модель для персоналізованої підтримки прийняття рішень
papers.abstract: Digital information technologies (IT) have become deeply embedded in everyday life, transforming communication, education, work, and social interaction and raising pressing questions about their psychological consequences.This review synthesises current evidence on measurable IT-related factors (screen time, social media use, smartphone use, information overload, online social support, digital gaming, remote work, interactions with artificial intelligence, cyberbullying, and technology-related sleep disturbance) and their relationships with psychological well-being.It also surveys the statistical approaches used to quantify these relationships, including specification-curve analysis and multilevel modelling.The evidence indicates that associations between overall technology use and well-being are small in aggregate and highly heterogeneous across individuals and contexts, whereas cyberbullying and sleep disturbance show more consistent negative associations.Building on these findings, the paper proposes a causal framework for personalised decision support, in which recommendations are based on the expected effect of actually changing a person's digital behaviour rather than on observed correlations, and favour small, achievable changes that preserve the benefits of technology use.The review concludes that progress requires longitudinal, experience-sampling, and experimental designs, more consistent measurement of IT-related factors, and reporting of how sensitive findings are to modelling choices.

papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence for Academic Vocabulary Acquisition during University Studies: A Case Study of International Students in Northern Ireland
papers.authors: Duc Phuong Vu

papers.title: Artificial intelligence transparency statements and publication governance in medical literature: cross-sectional analysis of 97,916 articles, 2015–2026
papers.authors: Philip C. Jarrett, Samia Farooqi, Gabriella Quinn, Wendy W. Chapman, Andrew Jamieson, Dazhe Cao
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across scholarly writing, peer review, and editorial workflows, creating new research integrity questions about attribution, accountability, and disclosure. We measured how explicit artificial intelligence (AI) transparency statements are appearing in published medical literature and whether scalable full-text methods can monitor their adoption across journals and specialties. We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of 97,916 English-language medical journal articles published from 2015 through April 2026 across 14 medical and surgical fields. Full text was retrieved from PubMed Central XML or publisher-hosted article files and classified with a large language model for positive AI-use disclosure, explicit statements of non-use, named tools, use cases, and statement location. Validation used pre-ChatGPT specificity, second-model agreement in 10,979 articles, and blinded human review of 300 stratified cases by 2 independent reviewers with adjudication. All rates were recalculated excluding Frontiers journals, whose submission workflow applies a standardized AI declaration. Any AI transparency statement increased from 1.4% in 2023 to 22.4% in January-April 2026, or 9.9% excluding Frontiers journals. Positive disclosure reached 7.3% (6.2% excluding Frontiers), while negative disclosure reached 15.1% (3.7% excluding Frontiers). Frontiers contributed 6.1% of articles but 71.1% of negative disclosures. Health Informatics and Digital Medicine had the highest positive disclosure rate during 2023–2026 (11.1%; 10.5% excluding Frontiers). Among 91 journals with at least 20 classified articles in 2025–2026, statement rates ranged from 0 to 100%, and all 3 journals at 100% were Frontiers titles. Language refinement was the most common disclosed use (72.8%). Inter-model agreement was high (Cohen kappa = 0.96 positive, 0.98 negative), and blinded human review confirmed 93.3% and 97.3% of these classifications, respectively. AI transparency statements are becoming a measurable publication-governance signal, but their prevalence is driven substantially by publisher submission infrastructure rather than author initiative: one publisher accounted for 71.1% of all negative disclosures. Near-universal declaration capture is therefore achievable through workflow design, and low observed disclosure rates may reflect missing declaration fields more than author reticence. Scalable full-text monitoring may help editors, publishers, and research integrity stakeholders evaluate policy implementation and distinguish assistive from generative AI use.

papers.title: Comprehensive assessment of nutritional status in colorectal cancer patients before surgery: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Zohre Abdolahi, Abbas Abdollahi, Maryam Emadzadeh, Mohammad Moeini Nodeh, Nafiseh Alizadeh, Mahsa Chaji, Fatemeh Shahabi, Sara Movahed
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Malnutrition is a prevalent and clinically significant problem among patients with cancer, affecting 20–70% of cases, with the highest rates in gastrointestinal malignancies. In colorectal cancer (CRC), preoperative malnutrition is particularly concerning, as it increases postoperative complications, prolongs hospital stay, impairs treatment tolerance, elevates healthcare costs, and reduces survival. Tumor-related inflammation, metabolic stress, and surgical trauma further exacerbate nutritional deterioration, making early identification essential. There are few studies that have exclusively examined the nutritional status before surgery in CRC patients, specifically in Iran. Given the importance of nutrition screening and the comprehensive evaluation of malnutrition in patients at risk of malnutrition before surgery, this study aimed to evaluate the comprehensive nutritional assessment of these patients before surgery. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted from October 2023 to January 2025 at the surgical department of Ghaem Hospital, Mashhad, Iran. Hospitalized patients with confirmed CRC were included. Demographic and disease-related information was collected. Nutritional status was assessed using the patient-generated subjective global assessment (PG-SGA). Anthropometric measurements, body composition analysis, dietary intake evaluation, nutrition impact symptoms, handgrip strength, and laboratory tests were assessed. Logistic regression was used to identify independent factors associated with critical nutritional risk (PG-SGA score ≥ 9). Results A total of 105 patients (mean age 57.5 ± 13.3 years) were included. 54.3% had moderate-to-severe malnutrition (PG-SGA Category B or C), including 21.9% with severe malnutrition (Category C), and 40% had critical nutritional risk (PG-SGA score ≥ 9). Low muscle strength was observed in 78.1%, and reduced muscle mass in 26.7%. Common symptoms included abdominal pain, indigestion, bloating, constipation, and anorexia. Inadequate energy and protein intake were reported in 48.6% and 83.8% of patients, respectively. Older age (> 65 years), low economic status, cancer unawareness, tumor pathology, anemia, lower serum albumin, and insufficient energy and protein intake were associated with higher PG-SGA scores ( p < 0.05). PG-SGA scores negatively correlated with BMI, Karnofsky performance status, mid-upper arm circumference, total body water, and fat-free mass index ( p < 0.01). FFMI (fat-free mass index), serum albumin, and non-adenocarcinoma pathology ( n = 5; imprecise estimate) were independently associated with critical nutritional risk (PG-SGA ≥ 9) in the exploratory multivariable logistic regression analysis. Conclusion A substantial proportion of patients awaiting CRC surgery had moderate-to-severe malnutrition or critical nutritional risk. These findings highlight the importance of timely nutrition screening to identify at-risk patients, followed by comprehensive nutrition assessment to guide individualized interventions, optimize preoperative care, and improve clinical and functional outcomes.

papers.title: Application of the MoCA score, sociodemographic and health-related factors to evaluate interpretable screening models for geriatric cognitive disorders in Chongqing: a cross-sectional survey study
papers.authors: Feiya Cai, Yalan Cai, Qiming Luo, Xiaolin Tan, Bo Tian
papers.abstract: Geriatric cognitive disorders (GCDs) exhibit a significant age dependence. As global populations age, China, with its substantial demographic, must prioritize the increasing incidence of cognitive disorders among older adults. Notably, the prevalence rate of cognitive disorders in Chongqing is the highest in the country. Social and health-related factors have drawn considerable attention as predictors of cognitive decline because they are noninvasive and readily available. In this context, this study uses MoCA score, sociodemographic and health-related data to develop and validate machine-learning models that predict cognitive disorders in the elderly in Chongqing city and assess individual classification. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of older adults in Chongqing using stratified cluster sampling to collect sociodemographic data (4 items), health-related variables (13 items) and MoCA score. We then trained nine machine-learning algorithms to build screening models for GCD. The aims were to clarify the predictors associated with prevalent GCD and to develop early screening models for GCD. We evaluated model performance by area under the curve (AUC), calibration curve, decision curve analysis, sensitivity, specificity, and validation cohorts. The Shapley additive interpretation (SHAP) method is used to rank the importance of features and interpret the final model. The prevalence of cognitive disorders among the elderly in Chongqing (32.8%) significantly surpasses the national average. Through feature selection, 11 variables were identified as independent predictors of GCD. Prediction models were developed based on these factors through nine distinct machine learning methods. Among the nine ML models, the XGB model achieved a relatively high AUC value (0.9397, 95%CI 0.9136–0.9658). External validation further confirmed the validity of the XGB model, with an AUC value of 0.9349 (95%CI 0.9139–0.9558). According to SHAP analysis, age, high education, MoCA score, hyperglycemia, hypertension, marital status, cerebral infarction, and cerebral atrophy are the key predictors for screening the likelihood of cognitive disorders in the elderly. We developed a machine learning–based prediction model that indicates potential screening utility to assess the risk of cognitive disorders in older adults.

papers.title: What influences patients’ perspectives on the fairness of AI decision-making tools in healthcare? A cross sectional survey in the UK
papers.authors: Elizabeth Remfry, Giulia Tomba, Michael R. Barnes, Tapabrata Chakraborti, Robin Mitra, Christopher Banerji, Bastian Greshake Tzovaras
papers.journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Whilst the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is growing, with promises that AI will reduce costs and improve efficiency, there is also concern that AI systems can perpetuate health inequalities. Prior work has explored patients’ trust in AI, but less attention has been given to how patients conceptualise the fairness of AI decision-making in healthcare and which factors influence these views. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of UK patients, recruited through public and patient involvement and engagement (PPIE) networks, exploring perceptions of fairness across two AI vignettes: a patient-facing symptom checker and a clinician-facing cancer treatment decision-support tool. Respondents rated the perceived impact of 13 factors on the fairness of AI decisions and completed free-text responses to identify any additional factors.
