Demographics and survey variables were reported using descriptive statistics, along with Pearson’s chi-square test for differences in attitudes. Associations were estimated using ordinal logistic regression. Free-text responses were analysed thematically. Results A total of 149 respondents from the UK completed the survey. The factor perceived to most strongly undermine fairness of AI decisions was the absence of human supervision, with 89.9% of respondents reporting that AI decisions that could not be questioned by patients or clinicians would negatively impact fairness. This was followed by AI tools developed without clinician input (89.3%) and incorrect data in electronic health records (86.6%). Perceptions were consistent across both vignettes. Thematic analysis identified additional concerns not captured in the structured survey, including accessibility, the complexity of long-term conditions, ongoing maintenance of AI systems and the loss of human empathy. Conclusions Patients hold nuanced, wide-ranging concerns about fairness which span the AI lifecycle from development and deployment to maintenance. We offer design considerations, including the need for human-in-the-loop systems designed with end users and that can adapt to professional input, to support the development of fair AI systems in healthcare.

papers.title: Evaluating the constructiveness and professional tone of AI-generated corrective feedback for medical learners
papers.authors: Bonnie C. Desselle, Emma Simon, Amy Prudhomme, Christy Mumphrey, Leslie Reilly, Margaret Huntwork, Shubho Sarkar, George C. Hescock, Zhide Fang, Jessica Patrick Esteve, Kelly Gajewski, Amy M. Creel
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Faculty feedback is vital for the professional growth of learners. Barriers such as faculty’s confidence in their feedback skills and time limitations may inhibit the provision of quality feedback. Generative large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have the potential to support faculty in providing high-quality corrective feedback by producing effective narrative feedback scripts for faculty to reference. Objective This study explores the quality of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated text in the context of corrective feedback, based on standardized scenarios of learner deficiencies. Methods Six medical education leaders blindly rated two narrative feedback scripts for eighteen learner deficiency scenarios; one script for each scenario was authored by educators, the other script was generated by ChatGPT. The raters scored each script in four domains (behavior-centric, balanced between positive and negative, non-judgmental, and focused) using a 3-point scale (0–2), where 0 = No, 1 = Somewhat, 2 = Yes. The mean scores of the educator authored scripts and the ChatGPT-generated scripts were compared by domain. An overall score was also generated for the educator authored script and the ChatGPT-generated scripts using descriptive statistics. Results Across all four domains, ChatGPT-generated scripts received high mean scores, with all rated higher than the educator authored scripts. Also, ChatGPT-generated responses achieved higher overall scores than those authored by educators for 17 of 18 scenarios. Conclusion AI-generated responses can be of high quality and may provide a useful tool for faculty who are preparing to give corrective feedback. Further studies are needed to explore the utility of AI in supporting feedback delivery.

papers.title: The experiences of bereaved family caregivers in end-of-life wish fulfilment interventions: a qualitative evidence synthesis using realist principles
papers.authors: Yuying Li, Zhenhong Han, Qiuyan Liu, Xue Dong
papers.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) family caregivers face substantial psychological burdens. End-of-life wish fulfilment interventions such as the 3 Wishes Project offer a low-cost, humanising approach, yet the mechanisms through which they shape bereaved families’ experiences remain poorly understood. This qualitative evidence synthesis, informed by realist principles, aimed to identify context-dependent generative mechanisms underlying family caregivers’ experiences of end-of-life wish-fulfilment interventions. Following ENTREQ and RAMESES publication standards, we conducted a qualitative evidence synthesis informed by realist principles. We systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and PsycINFO (inception to April 2026) and included eight qualitative or mixed-methods studies reporting bereaved family caregivers’ experiences of the 3 Wishes Project. From these studies, we extracted 45 unique family caregiver quotations (52 quote entries after accounting for six quotations supporting multiple mechanisms). Thematic synthesis was used to generate descriptive and analytical themes, which were subsequently organised into Context-Mechanism-Outcome (CMO) configurations. We used the CASP checklist to assess methodological quality and the GRADE-CERQual tool to evaluate confidence in the review findings. Based on the evidence, six intervention-oriented CMO configurations were identified: narrative re-personalization, role liberation and relationship reshaping, emotional release and continuing bonds, partnership and institutionalized compassion, spiritual substitution and meaning-making, and co-creation and restoration of agency. All six configurations were rated as moderate confidence. The evidence base was limited to a single intervention programme (the 3 Wishes Project) and relied entirely on retrospective, post-bereavement interviews. In the ICU setting, end-of-life wish fulfilment interventions appear to support patient dignity and restore caregiver agency through six interrelated psychosocial processes. However, the evidence is confined to one programme and consists entirely of retrospective designs; future independent real-time evaluations are needed to validate these provisional, context-dependent mechanisms.

papers.title: Development and validation of a nomogram for predicting postoperative lymphedema risk in breast cancer patients
papers.authors: Jinting Sun, Juan Xu, Yanxia Han, Juan Ji, 商丽云, Yongmei Zhao, Ying Jiang, Yuanfei Chen, Siying Zhou
papers.abstract: Breast cancer-related lymphedema (BCRL) is a common long-term complication after breast cancer treatment that impairs upper-limb function and quality of life. Early identification of high-risk patients enables timely risk-adapted surveillance and rehabilitation support. To develop and internally validate a nomogram incorporating clinical, surgical, and postoperative recovery-related factors to predict BCRL risk. This retrospective cohort study included 751 patients who underwent breast cancer surgery at a tertiary hospital between January 2022 and December 2023. Patients were randomly divided using outcome-stratified sampling into a training cohort (n=525) and a validation cohort (n=226). LASSO regression was used for predictor selection, followed by multivariable logistic regression to construct the prediction model. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and bootstrap validation with 1,000 resamples. BCRL developed in 212 of 751 patients (28.2%). Independent predictors included age, BMI, clinical stage, hypertension, ALND, postoperative radiotherapy, drainage duration, wound complications, breast surgery type, and weekly exercise duration. The model showed high discrimination, with AUCs of 0.936 (95% CI, 0.915–0.958) in the training cohort and 0.939 (95% CI, 0.910–0.968) in the validation cohort. The optimism-corrected AUC after 1,000 bootstrap resamples was 0.925 (95% CI, 0.902–0.949). Calibration and decision-curve analyses indicated satisfactory performance and potential clinical utility. This study developed a postoperative nomogram for individualized BCRL risk prediction, with high apparent discrimination and satisfactory calibration in a single-center cohort. The model provides a practical tool for identifying patients at elevated risk who may benefit from intensified postoperative surveillance and rehabilitation support.

papers.title: The impact of disparities in social determinants of health on adverse neonatal outcomes among women with gestational diabetes mellitus: The role of gestational weight gain trajectories in a multicenter cohort
papers.authors: Dan Luo, Xiong Liu, LokChong Huang, Koubihan Hu, Qianyin Pang, Qinquan He, Jie Mei, Jing He
papers.abstract: Disparities in multidimensional social determinants of health (SDOH) significantly exacerbate the risk of adverse neonatal outcomes among women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). While optimal gestational weight gain (GWG) is a critical, modifiable determinant of perinatal health, its role in linking structural social vulnerabilities to neonatal complications remains unclear. This multicenter cohort study aimed to evaluate whether longitudinal GWG trajectories may partly account for the association between SDOH profile and adverse neonatal outcomes. In this multicenter cohort of women with GDM, SDOH profile was assessed as the primary exposure, GWG trajectories as a dynamic weight-management phenotype, and composite adverse neonatal outcome as the outcome. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the associations of SDOH profile and GWG trajectories with composite adverse neonatal outcomes, whereas multinomial logistic regression was used to assess the association between SDOH profile and GWG trajectory membership. Mediation analysis, interaction analysis, body mass index (BMI)-stratified analyses, and sensitivity analyses excluding women with pre-existing endocrine disorders were also performed. Among 1,916 women with GDM, 482 neonates (25.2%) experienced a composite adverse neonatal outcome. The disadvantaged versus advantaged SDOH profile was associated with adverse neonatal outcomes (aOR 1.703, 95% CI 1.314–2.214) and high GWG trajectory membership (aRRR 2.162, 95% CI 1.560–2.997. High GWG trajectory was associated with adverse neonatal outcomes (aOR 2.196, 95% CI 1.660–2.902). Mediation analysis estimated that 25.6% of the association may be accounted for through GWG trajectories. Among women with GDM, the disadvantaged SDOH profile was associated with higher neonatal risk and a greater likelihood of high GWG trajectory membership. GWG trajectories may partly account for SDOH-related differences in neonatal outcomes, supporting more equitable, risk-stratified GDM care.

papers.title: Differences in disability-free life expectancy among Chinese older adults by combined body mass index and waist circumference categories
papers.authors: Yiru Jiang, Shimin Su, Weiqiang Su, Qian Wang, Huiling Dong, Tingting Xu, Bingyi Wu, Yu Bi
papers.abstract: Weight management is an important component of strategies to promote healthy aging. However, the associations of body shapes and fat distribution with disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) among older adults have not been adequately evaluated. Data were obtained from the 2011–2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). Participants were categorized according to a combined classification of body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC). Microsimulation was used to estimate life expectancy (LE) and DFLE across the different BMI–WC categories. Subgroup analyses were further conducted by sex and, within each sex, by urban-rural residence. Z tests were used to assess whether differences in DFLE between groups were statistically significant ( P < 0.05). At baseline, the mean age of the participants was 85.49 ± 10.98 years. At age 65, DFLE was 14.25 years (95% confidence interval (CI): 13.38–15.05) in the low BMI group, 15.47 years (95% CI: 14.72–16.37) in the appropriate BMI with central obesity group, and 15.82 years (95% CI: 14.27–17.20) in the high BMI group; all were lower than that in the appropriate BMI with normal WC group (16.02 years, 95% CI: 15.32–16.74). Among participants aged 73–95 years in the appropriate BMI with central obesity group, men had significantly shorter DFLE than women ( P < 0.05). Among women aged 76–95 years in the low BMI group, those living in urban areas had significantly shorter DFLE than their rural counterparts ( P < 0.05). Older adults with low BMI or appropriate BMI with central obesity had shorter DFLE, suggesting that weight management in later life should consider both BMI and fat distribution. Although older women had longer LE, they spent a smaller proportion of their remaining life disability-free. In particular, urban older women with low BMI may experience a greater burden of disability.

papers.title: Comparison of Deepseek-V3, ChatGPT-4o, and online medical platforms in addressing chronic pancreatitis related questions
papers.authors: Wanshun Li, Zhicheng Yang, Guotong Qiu, Xinyi Su, Zhenghui Yang, Hanbin Zhu, Chao Liu, Deyu Zhang, Haojie Huang, Zhendong Jin
papers.abstract: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a complex, progressive inflammatory disorder characterized by irreversible damage to the pancreatic parenchyma, leading to exocrine and endocrine dysfunction. Patients with CP frequently experience debilitating symptoms including chronic pain, malabsorption, and diabetes mellitus, significantly impacting their quality of life. A critical challenge in CP management is the limited accessibility to accurate, up-to-date medical information, which is essential for informed decision-making. In recent years, advanced large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek have emerged as potential sources of medical knowledge, offering rapid responses to health-related queries. However, the reliability and clinical utility of these AI-driven platforms in the context of CP remain underexplored, particularly in comparison to established online medical resources. This study aimed to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the performance of two leading AI models DeepSeek-V3 and ChatGPT-4o alongside conventional online medical platforms in addressing CP-related inquiries. The assessment focused on two key domains: (1) guideline-based knowledge derived from the 2020 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines, and (2) patient-specific concerns extracted from real-world clinical follow-up records. By comparing AI-generated responses to physician-curated information, this research sought to determine the potential role of LLMs in supporting CP patient education and clinical decision support. We conducted a two-phase evaluation comprising 21 guideline-derived questions and 40 patient-derived questions. In the first phase, two blinded gastroenterologists independently assessed responses from DeepSeek-V3 and ChatGPT-4o for accuracy, completeness, comprehensiveness, and safety. Their ratings were averaged for each question and model. In the second phase, responses from both models were compared with physician responses from online medical platforms. Forty patients rated responses from all three sources for empathy and satisfaction. Comparisons used paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests or Friedman tests followed by paired Wilcoxon tests with Holm adjustment. Because participant-level ratings were unavailable for reanalysis, patient-reported outcomes were analyzed using matched question-level aggregated means. DeepSeek-V3 and ChatGPT-4o performed similarly across accuracy, completeness, comprehensiveness, and safety when answering guideline-based questions. For patient-derived questions, the three information sources showed comparable accuracy and safety. Although completeness differed in the omnibus analysis ( P = 0.015), none of the pairwise comparisons remained significant after Holm adjustment. Comprehensiveness also differed across sources ( P < 0.001), with DeepSeek-V3 receiving lower scores than both online medical platforms (Holm-adjusted P = 0.020) and ChatGPT-4o (Holm-adjusted P = 0.009); ChatGPT-4o and online medical platforms did not differ significantly (Holm-adjusted P = 0.499). Question-level mean ratings showed no significant differences among sources in perceived empathy or satisfaction. Across all sources, empathy was rated relatively favorably, whereas satisfaction remained comparatively modest. DeepSeek-V3 and ChatGPT-4o provided generally accurate and safe responses to chronic pancreatitis-related questions. However, DeepSeek-V3’s descriptively higher completeness did not translate into broader clinical coverage, as its comprehensiveness scores were lower than those of ChatGPT-4o and online medical platforms. LLMs may supplement patient education, but their responses should complement rather than replace professional clinical assessment, particularly when individualized interpretation and broader clinical context are required.

papers.title: NAFLD/MASLD, including cirrhosis: Burden from 1990 to 2040, GBD decomposition, CDC WONDER analysis, and machine-learning attribution
papers.authors: Luna Zhao, Bingjie Li, Xi Zhang, Jinbao Liu, Jingkun Li, Hanwen Zhang, Kexin Cui, Junhao Ma, Fangyi Zhao, 朱庆峰
papers.abstract: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)/metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), including cirrhosis, is an increasing global health concern, yet long-term trends, drivers, and subnational disparities remain inadequately characterized. We assessed the global burden and U.S. subnational variations using machine-learning-based attribution. Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, we analyzed global incidence, prevalence, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), temporal trends, decomposition, inequalities, and Bayesian age-period-cohort projections through 2040. For complementary U.S. analyses, we used CDC WONDER data, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)–SHapley Additive exPlanations attribution, and autoregressive integrated moving average/Prophet forecasting. Globally, incident cases, prevalence, and DALYs approximately doubled from 1990 to 2021. Age-standardized incidence and prevalence increased, whereas DALY rates remained stable (estimated annual percentage change = 0.04), with population growth and aging identified as the main drivers. Absolute inequality, measured by the slope index of inequality (SII), widened from 20 to 36 per 100,000. High-burden regions included North Africa and the Middle East, Latin America, and Eastern Europe. In the U.S., the South and Midwest had the highest and fastest-growing mortality rates. XGBoost identified diabetes prevalence as the dominant state-level predictor, showing a nonlinear positive association above approximately 10–12%, whereas higher educational attainment showed an inverse association above approximately 90%. A sharp inflection in mortality occurred in 2020. Mortality is projected to increase through 2035, particularly in the Southwest and Appalachia. The absolute burden of NAFLD/MASLD, including cirrhosis, continues to rise despite stable age-standardized DALY rates. Global trends and U.S. machine-learning evidence indicate that prevention should shift toward systemic metabolic risk management, with liver fibrosis screening integrated into routine diabetes and obesity care.

papers.title: Cognitive Impairment Detected Using the Mini-Cog Screening Tool Among Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes: A Study from South India
papers.authors: Vaishnavi Vijay, Manjula Arunraj, Satyavani Kumpatla, Vijay Viswanathan
papers.journal: International journal of clinical metabolism and diabetes.
papers.abstract: Background and Aim: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) increases the risk of cognitive decline in older adults. Evidence from India on cognitive impairment in this population remains limited; hence, this study assessed cognitive impairment using the Mini-Cog screening tool among older adults with T2DM. Materials and Methods: A total of 204 participants aged ≥60 years with T2DM were enrolled at a tertiary care centre in Chennai from February to May 2024. Cognitive status was screened using the Mini-Cog tool. ‘Scores of 0–2’ indicated a positive screen for cognitive impairment, whereas ‘scores of 3–5’ indicated a negative screen for cognitive impairment. Anthropometric, clinical and biochemical information was collected. Results: Among the 204 older adults with T2DM screened using the Mini-Cog, 20.6% screened positive for cognitive impairment. Among those who screened positive, the proportion of women was significantly higher than that of men (61.9% vs. 38.1%, P = .04). The mean BMI was significantly higher among women than men (28.7 ± 5.3 vs. 26.7 ± 3.9 kg/m², P = .003). The combined presence of hypertension and dyslipidemia was significantly higher among screened positive participants compared to screened negative participants (61.9% vs. 38.3%, P = .005). Binary logistic regression analysis showed that HbA1c > 9% (odds ratio [OR] = 2.4 [95% confidence interval {CI} = 1.01–4.98); P = .04] and the presence of hypertension and dyslipidemia [OR 2.4 (95% CI 1.09–4.13); P = .02] were significantly associated with those who screened positive for cognitive impairment. Conclusion: The study findings highlighted that a significant proportion of women with T2DM screened positive for cognitive impairment as assessed by the Mini-Cog tool. Poor glycemic control and the presence of comorbid conditions such as hypertension and dyslipidemia were independently associated with those who screened positive for cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Gamma transcranial alternating current stimulation prevents scopolamine-induced damage to EEG activity and spatial memory
papers.authors: Yuan Yuan, Shu Xing, Ping Ren, Zhuangfei Chen, Yu Fu
papers.abstract: BackgroundDementia is a serious public health concern, primarily caused by Alzheimer's disease (AD). Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) can improve cognitive function by modulating neural oscillations. While tACS shows therapeutic potential for dementia, its preventive effects remain unknown. Because tACS has long-lasting modulatory effects, we propose that these offline effects may help prevent dementia.ObjectiveThis study aims to determine whether pre-administered 40 Hz tACS prevents scopolamine-induced impairment of electroencephalogram (EEG) activity and spatial cognition. Scopolamine induces cholinergic dysfunction in animal models, mimicking AD-related behavioral and EEG abnormalities.MethodsScopolamine (3 mg/kg, i.p.) was administered to induce a mouse model of dementia. Prior to induction, tACS targeting the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and/or hippocampus (Hip) was performed for five days (40 Hz, 300 μA, 20 min/day). EEG activity was recorded from the PFC and Hip during spontaneous and task-related (Y-maze) states. In addition, spatial memory was evaluated using the Barnes maze test, and general activity including locomotion and anxiety was evaluated using the open field test.ResultsScopolamine reduced spontaneous EEG activity in gamma frequency band and task-related PFC EEG activity across multiple frequency bands. Prior Hip tACS prevented these EEG reductions. Behaviorally, scopolamine induced spatial memory deficits and increased locomotion and anxiety-like behaviors. Notably, dual-site tACS reversed memory impairment and PFC tACS reduced locomotion. In addition, tACS had little effect on anxiety.ConclusionsPrior gamma tACS exerts region-specific protection against scopolamine-induced EEG and behavioral impairments, providing first evidence for its potential as a preventive strategy for dementia-related deficits.

papers.title: Generative AI as a Catalyst: Transforming Digital Literacy Practices in English Language Teaching
papers.authors: Yuwei Wan, Benjamin Luke Moorhouse
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in English language teaching calls for an immediate and thorough response from language teachers. Employing an exploratory qualitative approach, the study explores how 10 English language instructors at a Chinese university integrate GenAI tools in language teaching through lesson study. Data were collected through classroom observations, recordings of collaborative lesson preparation/reflection sessions, teaching materials, and three rounds of in-depth interviews. Our analysis centres on the transformative impact of GenAI on teachers’ digital literacy practices, conceptualised as doing, meaning, relating, thinking, and “being.” The study contrasted the participants’ new digital literacy practices with their previous practices in various professional practice domains and traced the sustainability of these practices over time. Findings reveal that GenAI catalysed a transformation of teachers’ practices across lesson planning, instruction, and assessment. However, the sustainability of these practices varied due to multiple factors. We argue that sustainable GenAI integration requires viewing digital literacy as a situated social practice shaped by utility and professional risk. The study offers insights for developing collaborative professional development programmes that support teachers’ critical and sustainable engagement with GenAI.

papers.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education: Insights from ASLP students
papers.authors: Komal Aggarwal, Rohit Ravi, Dhanshree R Gunjawate, Krishna Yerraguntla, Kaushlendra Kumar
papers.abstract: BackgroundEmerging artificial intelligence-based technologies are increasingly influencing teaching and learning practices in healthcare education, offering new opportunities for student engagement, learning, and skill development.ObjectiveThe purpose of this study was to explore utilization of artificial intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education based on insights from students. Further, to explore their awareness, use, perceived benefits, barriers, and attitudes toward the integration of artificial intelligence.MethodA cross-sectional online survey of 17 questions was distributed to 483 audiology and speech-language pathology students enrolled in undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes across multiple institutions in India through social media platforms. The questionnaire was developed following a review of previously published studies examining students' perceptions of the implications of artificial intelligence in education. Descriptive analysis was used to analyse the findings.ResultsA total of 286 students participated in the study (mean age = 21.73 ± 2.33 years), of whom 82.2% were females. Most participants (96.9%) were aware of artificial intelligence technologies, and 89.9% indicated using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. Regarding the future role of artificial intelligence in education, 75.1% disagreed that it could replace human lecturers. Students primarily used it for assignments and exam preparation, while limited institutional acceptance was a major barrier to its implementation.ConclusionsStudents expressed an optimistic view regarding the application of artificial intelligence in education. Students reported concerns about inaccurate artificial intelligence-generated information, while limited acceptance, inadequate knowledge, and ethical concerns hindered its effective integration into education.

papers.title: AI adoption and employees’ physical and cognitive ergonomic outcomes in the information technology sector: The mediating roles of trust in ai and workload
papers.authors: KDV Prasad, Shivoham Singh, Ankita Pathak, Ved Srinivas, Hemant Kothari
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the information technology (IT) reshaping the work design, with significant consequences for employee well-being and ergonomics. While AI enhances efficiency through task automation, its influence on workload dynamics and ergonomic consequences remains not sufficiently understood, particularly in emerging economy contexts.ObjectiveGrounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework and informed by Sociotechnical Systems Theory, this study investigates the relationship between AI adoption and employees' physical and cognitive ergonomic outcomes while examining the mediating roles of trust in AI and workload among information technology professionals in India.MethodsTo assess this, seven reflective constructs were measured. The AI adoption construct has three sun-dimensions: performance expectancy, effort expectancy and usage behavior/intention. Employee ergonomics has two sub-dimensions: physical ergonomics discomfort, cognitive ergonomics/digital fatigue, which are modeled as higher-order constructs. However, trust and workload dynamics are modeled as lower-order constructs. The higher-order constructs were assessed along with the lower-order constructs. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were carried out to unravel the structural relationships among the constructs, and hypothesis testing was performed using structural equation modeling.ResultsThe findings indicate that AI adoption significantly enhances trust in AI and reduces workload, Trust in AI is negatively associated with workload, while workload positively influences both physical ergonomic discomfort and cognitive fatigue. AI adoption also demonstrates a significant direct effect on employee ergonomics. The mediation analysis revealed that trust and workload fully mediated the relationship between AI adoption and ergonomics, whereas trust partially mediates the relationship between AI adoption and workload. The serial mediation results reveal partial mediation on role of trust and workload in the nexus among AI adoption and ergonomics.ConclusionConsistent with the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework, the findings demonstrate that AI functions simultaneously as a job resource and a source of new job demands. Trust in AI serves as an important psychological resource that reduces workload and enhances employees' physical and cognitive ergonomic outcomes. Trust in AI emerges as a vital psychological mechanism that mitigates workload and enhances ergonomic outcomes. The outcome contributes to the development of human-centric AI implementation strategies by highlighting the importance of trust-building and workload management in designing sustainable, ergonomically sound workplaces.

papers.title: Trust and adoption maturity: An analysis of industry perceptions on the generative AI competency gap among business graduates
papers.authors: Weli Weli, Sylvia Diana Purba, Syarief Darmoyo, Katherine Olivia Josephine
papers.abstract: This study maps the importance, perceived needs, and competency gap of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across four domains—Technical, Strategic, Ethical, Adaptive—and examines their associations with trust, adoption maturity, and industry context. Data were collected from 389 industry professionals in Indonesia using purposive and snowball sampling. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests. The results indicate relatively high perceived GenAI competency needs across all domains, with the largest perceived gaps in the Technical and Strategic domains. Trust in GenAI was positively associated with perceived competency needs across all four domains and with perceived competency gaps in the Technical, Strategic, and Adaptive domains, but not the Ethical domain. Adoption maturity was associated with differences in several dimensions of industry perceptions, particularly industry-perceived graduate readiness to adopt GenAI and perceived needs in the Adaptive and Strategic domains. Sectoral differences were limited, with significant variation observed only in industry-perceived graduate readiness. The study contributes an integrated perspective linking trust and adoption maturity with perceived GenAI competency needs and gaps in Indonesia, highlighting curricular areas that warrant greater attention to applied Technical and Strategic capabilities across organizational GenAI adoption stages.

papers.title: Governing Large Language Model Services for Confidential Microdata: A Decision Framework for National Statistical Offices
papers.authors: Hanan Ather, Mohammed Haddou, Saeid Molladavoudi
papers.abstract: National statistical offices increasingly face requests to provide large language model (LLM) capabilities in secure research environments. The governance problem is to determine which service configurations, if any, can be supported safely on confidential microdata. These services challenge traditional statistical disclosure control because interaction is adaptive, systems may retrieve documents or call analytical tools, and outputs may appear plausible without being grounded in approved data. This paper proposes a governance framework that organizes each request as a sequence of decisions: whether an LLM is needed, which service mode is justified, which threat model applies, which controls are required, and what evidence must be reviewed before release. The framework spans deterministic pipelines, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), tool-using agents, code-execution agents, linkage configurations, and fine-tuning.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Across the Surgical Research Workflow: A Stage-Specific Framework for Benefits, Failure Modes, and Oversight
papers.authors: Isaac H. Lies, Alexander Urevick, Lynch Major, Kay B Buerster, Addison Stewart, Meredith G. Rippy, Syamal Dave Bhattacharya
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, particularly large language models (LLMs), have rapidly integrated into surgical and biomedical research, prompting fundamental questions about their appropriate role. This review presents a stage-specific framework mapping each phase of the surgical research workflow (literature review, data analysis, manuscript preparation, and research synthesis) to the role AI plays, the benefits it provides, the failure modes it introduces, and the oversight it requires. Artificial intelligence-powered query systems are designed to speed literature synthesis across thousands of publications. In data analysis, LLMs paired with statistical environments can perform regression modeling and generate auditable code, while specialized architectures support automated image segmentation and histopathology analysis. Each stage's benefits, however, are matched by characteristic failure modes: LLMs are prone to error and hallucination, reproducibility is threatened by model versioning and run-to-run variability, fabricated citations and paper-mill submissions endanger the integrity of the literature, and over-reliance risks eroding trainee competencies in critical appraisal and biostatistical reasoning. Because these failure modes are stage-specific, governance must be stage-specific as well: the framework pairs each risk with a matched oversight mechanism, and these mechanisms translate into practical implementation recommendations for surgical departments, residency programs, research groups, and journals. The integration of AI into surgical scholarship should be viewed as augmentation rather than replacement, supported by standardized disclosure frameworks, AI literacy in graduate medical education, and institutional governance structures that preserve the integrity of surgical research.

papers.title: Decoding object categories from electroencephalography during free viewing reveals early information evolution compared to passive viewing
papers.authors: Carmel R. Auerbach-Asch, Gal Vishne, Oded Wertheimer, Leon Y. Deouell
papers.abstract: Object processing is central to visual perception, and its neural substrates inform cognitive and computational models of vision. Electroencephalographic (EEG) research has increasingly adopted multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode distributed neural representations, moving beyond average signal changes and predefined electrodes. Yet, most MVPA studies use passive viewing paradigms that constrain eye movements and evoke brain activity by external stimuli presentation, creating an artificial dissociation between perception and action. Here, we examine object category representations during active vision by combining MVPA with a deconvolution method for overlapping fixation-related responses. By decoding category information from single fixations, we compare the temporal dynamics of object processing between free viewing (active) and rapid serial visual presentation (passive) conditions. We find that categorical information, across multiple levels of abstraction, can be decoded from individual fixations during natural viewing, and that object representations generalize across passive and active conditions. Notably, representational dynamics time-locked to fixation onset emerge earlier than those time-locked to stimulus onset. We discuss the possibility that object processing begins parafoveally, aligned with saccade onset, rather than foveally at fixation. Thus, information about what and when to expect new information, available in free viewing, facilitates processing. These findings underscore the importance of studying vision in naturalistic settings and highlight key methodological considerations for combining MVPA with deconvolution in overlapping neural data. Object processing is fundamental to visual perception and to cognitive and computational models of vision. Although MVPA has advanced EEG research by enabling the decoding of distributed neural representations with high temporal precision, it has been applied primarily in passive viewing paradigms that constrain natural eye movements. The current study bridges the gap between passive and active vision research by combining MVPA with overlap deconvolution to decode object category information from EEG during natural fixations in free viewing. This approach reveals that category-specific representations emerge earlier in active viewing, likely reflecting processing that begins during saccade planning or execution. The findings underscore the importance of studying vision under ecologically valid conditions and introduce a novel methodological framework for capturing neural dynamics during active perception.

papers.title: Structuring Local Triple Helix Alliances: Evidence from Student Innovation Programmes
papers.authors: Kaspars Steinbergs, Renāte Cāne, Anna Strazda, Emils Liepnieks
papers.abstract: Abstract The purpose of this study is to explore how student-centred innovation projects affect local Triple Helix interactions in a small national innovation system. Even though the role of universities in regional development is increasingly stressed, there is little evidence about the role student-centred activities may play in fostering collaborative relations. A qualitative, multiple-case design was applied, with cases selected among Latvian Innovation Grants for Students programme experiences. Sources of empirical data included document analysis and semi-structured interviews with university and business actors. According to the results, while talent-related value logics, which include gaining access to students and potential for recruiting them, are crucial for university-industry collaboration, the innovation and co-creation value logics focus on coordination capacity and preparedness for interaction. This paper contributes to knowledge with an exploratory conceptual model of local Triple Helix interaction, based on four ideal-type alliances that depend on coordination infrastructure and value logics.

papers.title: A Large-Scale Privacy Analysis of Android Education Apps
papers.authors: Rakibul Hasan
papers.journal: Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society
papers.abstract: Mobile apps pose significant privacy risks to their users as they collect, process, and share sensitive personal data. Prior studies investigated apps in domains like health and gaming, but similar research remains scarce for apps used in educational settings. Education apps raise unique privacy concerns due to regulatory requirements and a large user base of minors. In this paper, we report results from a large-scale (N=33,023) static analysis of Android education apps. By analyzing binary application packages and decompiled source trees, we uncover pervasive trackers and data brokers. We find that most apps request highly sensitive data (e.g., location) that is seemingly unnecessary for their functionality. We further discover embedded third-party machine learning libraries and AI APIs. Trackers and data brokers were ubiquitous, potentially violating laws such as COPPA and GDPR. Analyzing privacy policies, we find widespread practices of data collection and sharing for advertising and personalization. While many of these findings align with past studies on general apps, the stricter legal protection for minors and education records suggests more frequent privacy violations with severe consequences.

papers.title: Reverse Prompt Engineering in Generative AI: A Baseline for Deepfake, Deception and Disinformation Mitigation
papers.authors: Jongkil Jay Jeong, Ashish Nanda, Sai Gautam Mandapati, Fokke Heikamp, Robin Doss
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has democratised content creation while scaling systemic threats in Deepfakes, Deception, and Disinformation (D3). As traditional content detection and watermarking are increasingly bypassed, this paper presents a position and baseline synthesis of Reverse Prompt Engineering (RPE) as a defensive capability. RPE inverts the generative pipeline to infer plausible instruction prompts and support, rather than definitively proving source-model attribution. Grounded in threat telemetry, we synthesise representative RPE frameworks while explicitly delineating the evidentiary limits of prompt recovery, attribution, and content provenance. We further evaluate RPE across public information, legal, and policy/governance viewpoints, analyse key technical limitations such as cross-modal generalisation, and outline a research roadmap to establish RPE as a cornerstone of digital provenance and AI accountability.

papers.title: Beyond Deepfake Detection: MOSAIC, a Confidence-Aware and Counter-Deception Framework for Synthetic-Media Operation Attribution
papers.authors: Yuval Sinay
papers.abstract: Synthetic media forensics can detect manipulation and attribute generators, but the operations require a higher-level judgment: whether an artifact can be linked to a coordinated campaign, an operator, or a sponsor. MOSAIC is an integration and decision-control framework with five bounded stages - Media, Origin, Systems, Activity, and Identity - and cross-cutting Confidence and counter-deception controls. An evidence ledger records provenance, quality, diagnosticity, spoof resistance, freshness, dependence, contradictions, and chain of custody; competing hypotheses include false flags, shared tooling, compromised infrastructure, proxies, AI-enabled actor emulation, and unknown actors. Minimum sufficient attribution (MSA) links the lowest defensible attribution level to the consequence and reversibility of a proposed response. A structured integrative synthesis, requirement traceability, adversarial stress cases, and a retrospective 2022 Zelenskyy surrender-deepfake example evaluate the design structurally. MOSAIC is confidence-aware rather than probabilistically calibrated; empirical calibration, inter-analyst reliability, and campaign-level validation remain future work.

papers.title: Recognition of Cognitive Intervention Effects and Modeling of Learning Behavior Patterns in Second Language Acquisition Using a Multimodal Intervention-Aware Temporal Graph Network
papers.authors: Wei Wang, Weifeng Liu
papers.journal: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: To distinguish between “text improvement” and “cognitive gain” in generative-AI-assisted second language learning, this study proposes a Multimodal Intervention-Aware Temporal Graph Network (MITG-Net). The method integrates human-AI dialogue, revision trajectories, behavioral logs, and learner attributes. Through intervention-conditioned dynamic weighting and heterogeneous temporal graph modeling, it captures the relationships among prompts, feedback, revisions, and transfer, and jointly performs intervention-effect recognition and learning-behavior-pattern discovery. Experiments were conducted on 744 learning sessions collected from 186 undergraduates at three universities. MITG-Net achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.816 and a weighted Kappa of 0.854, outperforming the strongest baseline, HGT, by 3.4 percentage points in Macro-F1. Removing behavioral logs and revision trajectories reduced Macro-F1 by 0.054 and 0.045, respectively. The model identified five behavior patterns. Among them, the strategy-transfer application pattern achieved an average effect level of 2.78 and a transfer score of 0.82, substantially higher than the 1.36 and 0.31 obtained by the AI-dominated direct-adoption pattern. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively recognize cognitive intervention effects and provide interpretable evidence for personalized support in second language learning.

papers.title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review
papers.authors: David Chen, Ayden Blayne, Tony Ning, Inaam Chattha, Majid Afshar, Jasmine Chiat Ling Ong, Julian C. Hong, Nan Liu, Leo Anthony Celi, Karel G.M. Moons, Professor Gary S. Collins, Danielle S. Bitterman
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-research analysis. DATA SOURCES: Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis-LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. RESULTS: The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare. CONCLUSION: Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.

papers.title: Service Recovery in Chatbot‐mediated Environments: Trust Dynamics and Customer Loyalty Intentions
papers.authors: Wilson Ozuem, Silvia Ranfagni, Michelle Willis
papers.abstract: Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

papers.title: Balancing explainability strength and privacy in counterfactual explanations for insider threat detection
papers.authors: Naila Naila, George Loukas, Manos Panaousis
papers.journal: Greenwich Academic Literature Archive (University of Greenwich)
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) methods, such as counterfactual explanations, help make model decisions more transparent and actionable. However, they can unintentionally reveal sensitive information, which is a critical concern in security settings such as insider threat detection, where both transparency and privacy are vital, particularly when explanations are shared with external analysts or decision-makers. We propose a privacy-aware counterfactual framework that integrates Differential Privacy (DP) to add only the minimum adjusted noise required to satisfy user-defined privacy caps, reducing information leakage while preserving explanation fidelity. Two task-specific metrics are introduced: XAIStrength, which measures how faithfully a counterfactual follows the model’s decision boundary, and XAILeakage, which quantifies privacy risk based on movement into sparse feature regions. Experiments on the CERT insider threat dataset show that initially generated counterfactuals were highly faithful for most users but frequently violated privacy requirements. After optimisation, leakage was reduced to meet strict, moderate, and lenient privacy caps (τ = 0.05/0.10/0.20) while maintaining practical fidelity. More than 60% of users retained Sopt ≥ 0.70 under strict privacy constraints, while over 60% maintained Sopt ≥ 0.85 under moderate privacy settings. Comparative evaluation against standard and privacy-aware baselines shows that the proposed framework achieves a stronger balance between explanation utility and disclosure risk. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to formally quantify and optimise the XAIStrength–XAILeakage trade-off in counterfactual explanations using statistically grounded risk measures and DP-calibrated optimisation.

papers.title: Strengthening customer relationships in omni-channel retail: omni-channel service quality
papers.authors: Mengjia Gao, Lin Huang
papers.abstract: Purpose Service quality plays a pivotal role in shaping customer engagement and loyalty across physical stores, virtual stores, and omni-channel retailing. However, the differential impacts of specific service quality components on consumer decision-making remain poorly understood. Grounded in the elaboration likelihood model, this study aims to investigate how the three components of omni-channel service quality – integration, physical store, and virtual store qualities – differentially impact customer engagement and loyalty, with customer engagement's mediating role tested under a value co-creation framework. Design/methodology/approach Consumer responses were collected through online questionnaires from two major Chinese retailers. After establishing measurement invariance across the two subsamples, the datasets were combined into a single sample of 310 responses. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was then employed to analyze the pooled dataset and examine the hypothesized relationships. Findings The results indicate that the three components of omni-channel service quality have different effects on and causal relationships with customer engagement and customer loyalty. The results confirmed that channel integration quality has an indirect effect on customer loyalty via customer engagement. In contrast, physical and virtual store qualities had no significant effect on customer engagement but positively impacted customer loyalty. Research limitations/implications This study contributes to the omni-channel retail service literature by elucidating the components of omni-channel service quality and how these components contribute to customer engagement and customer loyalty. Practical implications Retailers should adopt asymmetric strategies by optimizing physical and virtual store quality for single-channel customers, while deploying cross-channel integration features to enhance interaction and engagement for omni-channel customers. Originality/value This study advances omnichannel retailing literature by demonstrating that customer loyalty is shaped through two distinct pathways. Channel integration quality fosters customer engagement via central route processing but does not directly affect loyalty. Instead, loyalty is primarily driven by physical and virtual store quality through peripheral route processing. Customer engagement mediates the integration–loyalty relationship, suggesting that retailers should balance integration efforts with physical and virtual store quality to optimize retention.

papers.title: Understanding AI visual search adoption in secondhand fashion retail
papers.authors: Zihua Li, Minyi Yuan, 尹前进, 차민성, Yoon-Jung Lee
papers.journal: International Journal of Retail & Distribution Management
papers.abstract: Purpose Secondhand fashion markets are characterised by high uncertainty, heterogeneous products and fragile trust, complicating consumers’ search and evaluation processes. This study employs the technology acceptance model while incorporating consumer trust to explain AI visual search adoption in a high-uncertainty secondhand C2C retail context. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained from 299 Chinese consumers, and the model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Findings Perceived intelligence and perceived enjoyment enhance perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness and consumer trust, indicating their roles as core cognitive and affective drivers of adoption. Perceived risk negatively influences consumer trust, whereas perceived complexity reduces perceived ease of use. Perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness and consumer trust collectively shape adoption intention. Additionally, technology-related discomfort attenuates the effect of perceived ease of use on perceived usefulness. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of accurate AI-powered visual search, trust-building interface design and user support in facilitating adoption of AI visual search under conditions of high information uncertainty. Originality/value This research extends the TAM by demonstrating that consumer trust plays a central role in AI visual search adoption under conditions of high information uncertainty, whereas technology-related discomfort constrains the translation of perceived ease of use into perceived usefulness.

papers.title: Place-based industrial policy and firm-level skill upgrading: evidence from China's demonstration bases for new industrialization
papers.authors: Tao Zhang, Ridong Hu, Xiaoyu Li
papers.abstract: Purpose Industrial policy can influence not only how much firms produce but also the types of workers they employ. This study examines whether China’s National Demonstration Bases for New Industrialization reshape manufacturing firms’ educational and occupational composition. Design/methodology/approach We compile approval records from over 500 official documents and match them to A-share listed manufacturing firms at the county level for 2005–2023. Staggered difference-in-differences models, supplemented by double machine learning and robustness checks, estimate changes in two dimensions of workforce composition. Findings The policy increases the share of employees with a master’s degree or above and the technical-to-nontechnical personnel ratio. Effects vary across industrial and institutional settings, with clearer evidence for occupational composition than educational attainment in several specifications. Further analysis associates policy implementation with increased customer and industry concentration, while evidence for supplier concentration is inconclusive. Originality/value The study connects research on technological change and skill demand with the institutional setting of place-based industrial policy. By distinguishing educational from occupational composition, it identifies workforce adjustments that aggregate employment and firm performance measures may overlook. The concentration results also motivate further research on supply-chain relationships, market structure, and skilled labor allocation.

papers.title: Beyond access and algorithms: a curricular model for inquiry-driven student-AI engagement
papers.authors: Scott Ko
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper proposes a pedagogical framework for cultivating inquiry-driven agency in student engagement with artificial intelligence (AI). It addresses a gap in the AI-in-education literature, in which substantial scholarly attention to material access and algorithmic fairness has been accompanied by comparatively less sustained attention to the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. The paper offers three connected contributions: a cyclical model of inquiry-driven learning, a four-phase curricular sequence for student-AI engagement, and an operational assessment counterpart that remains diagnostically meaningful in AI-mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach The paper employs an integrative conceptual approach in the tradition of model-paper scholarship (Jaakkola, 2020). It synthesises five bodies of literature: AI in education and AI literacy frameworks, critical scholarship on educational technology, foundational work on curiosity, dual-process cognition, and adaptive expertise, constructive-developmental theory, and research on question-asking in learning and authentic assessment. Sources were identified through targeted citation tracing supplemented by database searches. Theoretical resources are justified at the point of use rather than methodologically up front. Findings The analysis demonstrates that material access and algorithmic fairness, while necessary, do not on their own account for the learner-side capacities that determine whether AI is engaged with critically or passively. It argues that inquiry-driven agency, the capacity to ask productive questions of AI rather than receive its answers, is a worthwhile object of pedagogical design. The Student-AI Learning Trajectory Model presents this development as a four-phase curricular sequence (AI as Tool, Machine, Object, and Partner), with progression understood as a curricular design decision made by educators rather than a developmental trigger inside the learner. Research limitations/implications The model is conceptual rather than empirically validated, and its applicability to younger learners, neurodiverse learners, and low-literacy contexts has not been fully worked out. The paper signposts several lines of empirical inquiry: longitudinal studies of SALT-informed curricula, methodological development of inquiry-sequence assessment instruments drawing on the Objective Structured Clinical Examination tradition, and comparative studies across institutional contexts and learner populations. The contribution is bounded to the pedagogical dimension and does not address the structural reforms that critical scholarship has identified as necessary for genuine educational equity. Practical implications The paper has implications for curriculum design, educator development, and assessment practice. Curricula can sequence student-AI engagement across phases of increasing sophistication rather than treating AI literacy as content to be covered. Educator development requires sustained investment in pedagogical capacity, particularly the modelling of inquiry-driven engagement in front of students. Institutions should treat the redesign of assessment for the AI era as a pedagogical question rather than an integrity question, with inquiry-sequence assessment offering one operational direction. Equity-oriented investment should prioritise educator capacity over the mass distribution of adaptive learning software. Social implications The cultivation of inquiry capacity in AI-mediated learning environments matters for the kinds of learners that schools and universities send into a world increasingly shaped by automated systems. Without deliberate pedagogical design, AI risks becoming a multiplier of existing educational divides rather than a neutralising force. The model locates responsibility with institutions and educators designing learning environments, not with individual students, and identifies the risk of a pedagogical Matthew Effect in which inquiry-driven pedagogy becomes available primarily to already advantaged students absent institutional investment in educator capacity. Originality/value The paper brings together three conversations that have developed largely in parallel: AI literacy as a set of competencies, evaluative judgement as a response to generative AI's destabilisation of assessment, and curiosity as a driver of self-directed learning. Its distinctive contribution is the articulation of phase progression as a curricular sequence informed by a cyclical model of inquiry learning, complemented by an operational assessment counterpart. The paper offers vocabulary and tools for educators, curriculum designers, and assessment scholars responding to the question of how AI should be integrated into the work of cultivating independent learners.

papers.title: Beyond the white cube: a practice-oriented theory of the art museum
papers.authors: Steven Chen
papers.abstract: Purpose This article develops a practice-oriented theory of the art museum to address the tension between traditional institution-focused theories and the need to attract a diverse public. It posits that a museum's function emerges dynamically from visitor practices, with value co-produced through the interplay of visitor behavior and service design, rather than being institutionally predetermined. Design/methodology/approach A structured, participant observation study was conducted across 30 geographically and typologically diverse art museums. Data from field notes, visual documentation and archival materials were analyzed using a three-stage grounded theory approach (open, axial and selective coding) to identify and categorize core visitor practices. Findings The analysis reveals four distinct, co-existing visitor practices: (1) Aesthetic Wandering (contemplative exploration), (2) Goal-oriented Learning (structured education), (3) Social Performance (identity performance and sharing) and (4) Community Use (utilizing the museum as a “third place”). These practices emerge through interaction with service design: Aesthetic Wandering is facilitated by white cube spaces, Goal-oriented Learning by interpretive technologies, Social Performance by immersive installations and Community Use by amenities and policies. The white cube service design partially supports the first two but is largely incompatible with the latter two. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on a sample of museums primarily from Los Angeles and Seoul, limiting generalizability. Future research could examine museums in other regions and adopt a temporal perspective covering pre- and post-visit experiences. Practical implications The typology provides a blueprint for museums to evolve beyond the white cube. It advocates for a modular service design that creates distinct zones and phygital integrations to simultaneously support all four practices, transforming museums into dynamic, multi-modal platforms. Originality/value This study moves beyond institution-centric and broad “edutainment” models by offering an empirically grounded typology of visitor practices. It reframes the visitor as an active co-producer of the museum experience and extends service-dominant logic by operationalizing co-creation through four distinct practice types. The typology provides a diagnostic framework linking practice observation to service architecture, enabling museums to design services that support the full spectrum of co-existing practices.

papers.title: Challenges in using online assessments to measure student understanding in the era of generative AI
papers.authors: David P. Smith, Paula R. L. Heron, Peter S. Shaffer

papers.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: Do large language models utilize the clinical practice guidelines?
papers.authors: Michaela Dukes, Behrad B. Sirjani, Ethan Blackburn, Luke Robinson
papers.abstract: Background: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a common entrapment neuropathy, and as patients increasingly seek health information online, the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in providing accurate medical advice is gaining attention. This study evaluates the responses of two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Google Gemini, regarding CTS management, comparing their outputs to established clinical practice guidelines in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability. Methods: Seven questions related to CTS treatment were developed and posed to both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The generated responses were assessed by eight fellowship-trained hand surgeons, who independently classified each answer as “appropriate,” “appropriate but incomplete,” or “inappropriate.” Readability was determined as grade level using a standardized online calculator that assessed multiple readability formulas. Results: Out of 112 total responses evaluated, 76 were deemed appropriate, with ChatGPT providing 46 appropriate responses compared with 30 from Gemini. Readability analysis indicated that ChatGPT’s responses averaged at a 12th-grade reading level, while Gemini’s averaged a 10th-grade level. Notably, 24 responses were graded as “appropriate but incomplete,” emphasizing the need for comprehensive information. Conclusion: This study demonstrates the potential of AI-driven platforms in enhancing patient education on CTS management. ChatGPT outperformed Gemini in accuracy, but both models showed limitations in completeness. The findings highlight the importance of ensuring that AI-generated health information is not only accurate but also accessible to patient populations. Future research should focus on improving the integration of AI with health care provider insights and quality resources to enhance patient outcomes and understanding.

papers.title: Treatment Failure After Laparoscopic Radiofrequency Ablation Compared With Myomectomy
papers.authors: Katherine S. Brito, Michael Schembri, Ram Parvataneni, Shira Varon, Naghmeh Salamat-Saberi, Craig J. Sobolewski, Soyini Hawkins, Nicole Williams, Shawn Tassone, Antoinette Allen, Vanessa L. Jacoby, L. Elaine Waetjen
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare treatment failure and factors associated with failure between laparoscopic radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of leiomyomata and laparoscopic myomectomy. METHODS: We analyzed data from the multicenter prospective ULTRA (Uterine Leiomyoma Treatment with Radiofrequency Ablation) study, which investigated laparoscopic RFA and laparoscopic myomectomy for symptomatic uterine leiomyomata. Our primary outcome was receipt of any subsequent procedure (surgical failure) for leiomyomata within 2 years of the procedure. Our secondary outcome was composite failure (surgical failure or any self-reported failure, eg, continued leiomyomata symptoms affecting quality of life) within 2 years of the procedure. Odds ratios (ORs) were generated from multivariable logit models adjusting for a priori selected covariates. RESULTS: We identified significant baseline differences between our groups. The RFA group (n=231) was older and had higher body mass index (BMI), gravidity, and parity than the myomectomy group (n=110). In the RFA group, 15.2% experienced surgical failure compared with 3.8% in the myomectomy group (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 4.17; 95% CI, 1.39-12.50), and 46.4% experienced composite failure in the RFA group compared with 25.5% in the myomectomy group (aOR 3.18; 95% CI, 1.80-5.60). Submucosal leiomyomata were associated with failure in the RFA group (OR 2.76; 95% CI, 1.21-6.28); there was a nonsignificant trend toward failure in the myomectomy group (OR 3.00; 95% CI, 0.99-9.05). Lateral leiomyomata were associated with higher odds of RFA failure (OR 2.49; 95% CI, 1.32-4.69), but no leiomyoma position was associated with myomectomy failure. CONCLUSION: Laparoscopic RFA of leiomyomata is associated with higher odds of surgical and composite failure compared with laparoscopic myomectomy at 2 years, even after adjusting for baseline differences between groups. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02100904.

papers.title: Multimodal Evidence for Large-scale Network Imbalance in Etomidate Use Disorder
papers.authors: Juan Le, Xingmin Wang, Ying Tang, Hao Chen, Xinxin Chen, Xuhao Wang, Yunde Tang, Lishun Zhao, Lin Zhao, Hongxian Chen, Qiuping Huang, Zhenjiang Liao
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Etomidate use disorder (EUD) is an escalating public health issue in East and Southeast Asia, yet its neuroimaging features remain poorly understood. This study used simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to examine multimodal functional connectivity alterations in individuals with EUD. METHODS: A total of 54 individuals with EUD and 46 healthy controls (HCs) were recruited and underwent simultaneous resting-state EEG and fNIRS recordings. Psychological dimensions including impulsivity, aggression, and craving were evaluated using standardized and validated scales. Source-level EEG functional connectivity and fNIRS hemodynamic connectivity were analyzed to identify group differences. Associations between altered connectivity features and clinical measures were examined within the EUD group. Machine learning analyses were conducted as exploratory assessments of the discriminative information contained in multimodal connectivity features. RESULTS: In unadjusted exploratory analyses of BIS-11 and BPAQ subscales, the EUD group showed higher cognitive impulsivity, non-planning impulsivity, physical aggression, anger and self-directed aggression (t=2.32 to 4.54, p<0.05), but lower motor impulsivity, compared with HCs. Source-level EEG analysis revealed significant group differences only in the delta band, with reduced large-scale connectivity in EUD involving default mode, dorsal attention, visual and sensorimotor systems. fNIRS analysis showed reduced hemodynamic connectivity across multiple frontal subregions and motor-related areas. Weaker connectivity between the primary motor cortex and the triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus was associated with stronger negative reinforcement craving (rho=-0.471, p_FDR<0.05). Exploratory machine learning analysis showed preliminary discriminative performance, with the random forest model producing the numerically highest test-set AUC (0.80) in this particular data split. CONCLUSIONS: Convergent EEG-fNIRS findings suggest delta-band network decoupling and reduced frontal hemodynamic connectivity as multimodal neural features of EUD. These findings provide preliminary evidence for the neural mechanisms of EUD and may inform future objective assessment and treatment-monitoring studies.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in mathematics education: a systematic review of pedagogical impact, cognitive outcomes, and ethical implications
papers.authors: Mohammad Nurwahid, Meita Fitrianawati, Nurmaningsih, Fazrina Saumi, Rosmaiyadi Rosmaiyadi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping mathematics education, yet reviews remain fragmented by tool, level, or outcome. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC (2015–2025) and included 46 of 4,475 records, all published from 2022 onward and appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (κ = 0.762). Generative AI accounted for half of the studies. AI use was associated mainly with procedural, engagement, and self-regulation gains, whereas support for deep reasoning and proof remained fragile. Teachers acted as designers, supervisors, co-creators, and AI literacy mentors; ethical risks included hallucination, academic integrity, over-reliance, and a Global South gap. We propose a Pedagogical–Cognitive–Ethical (PCE) framework in which teachers mediate these interdependent dimensions.

papers.title: AI-enabled assessment: framework, perspective and educational outcomes
papers.authors: Bayode Ogunleye, Olakunle Olayinka, Kudirat Ibilola Zakariyyah, Oluwaseun Ajao, Hemlata Sharma
papers.abstract: The development and use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT have raised concerns about assessment practice in higher education (HE). Prior studies have discussed the need to re-imagine and re-design assessment instruments; however, there is limited empirical evidence on how to effectively deploy this in practice. This paper proposes the TSD (task, scaffolding support and deliverable) framework to guide academics and education providers on how to effectively integrate AI and reflective practice into assessment design. By doing so, we adopt a mixed-method approach to investigate educational outcomes, tutors’ and students’ perspectives on the reflective AI-enabled assessment. This study collected data from UK University students (22 respondents) and tutors (24 participants) using a survey questionnaire and semi-structured interview questions, respectively. This study provides empirical support for positioning reflective practice as evidence of learning rather than being treated as a mere assessment activity. The findings show that AI output verification specific tasks need to be incorporated into AI-enabled assessment design. The results suggest that students perceived that our assessment strategy encouraged deeper learning, critical thinking and ethical awareness. Similarly, tutors were mostly positive with the adoption of the strategy, but some highlight the need for caution and multimodal approach .

papers.title: Following freshman footprints: early student activity & academic performance
papers.authors: Thomas 1960- Gößl, Luis Rumert, Kerstin Schneider
papers.abstract: Study performance in the first semester is highly predictive for study success. Hence, early interventions targeted at students-at-risk are called for. This study examines the potential of first-semester system activity data for student at-risk classification. By incorporating login data from the learning management system Moodle and information on registered exams, we aim to improve outcome forecasts even before exam results are available. Using machine learning techniques, we demonstrate that including this data significantly enhances classification accuracy for all three outcomes: dropout, (in-) activity, and first semester retention. Moreover, classifying student activity levels can be done under stricter data availability constraints, making it a potential alternative to traditional study success or failure predictions. Our regression analysis reveals a strong relationship between learning platform activity and study performance. Additionally, it suggests that learning activity later in the semester is more important for academic performance than activity during the first month.

papers.title: Youth as co-researchers in child-friendly urbanism: insights from a civic lab in Budapest
papers.authors: Anna Keszeg, Lili Kriston, Zsuzsanna Kiss-Gál, Katalin Vasali, Rita Szerencsés, Ádám Molnár
papers.journal: International Journal of Urban Sustainable Development
papers.abstract: Contemporary scholarship on urban mobility acknowledges differentiated urban experiences, yet perspectives of young people navigating the transition between childhood and adolescence remain underrepresented in research and planning. This article examines spatial experiences, mobility practices and emerging agency of youth aged 10–15, positioning them as co-researchers through an Urban Youth Civic Lab in Budapest within the CONIFER project. Drawing on participatory workshops in two schools with contrasting socio-spatial contexts, the study integrates design thinking, co-creation and photovoice methodologies. Findings reveal that youth understand the „15-minute city” through social nodes, emotional attachment and informal spatial practices rather than proximity to services. Mobility is shaped by perceived safety, cultural mentality and permission culture, extending accessibility beyond distance to encompass confidence, autonomy and social norms. The paper introduces mobility literacy – the capacity to read, interpret and navigate urban space – arguing that its cultivation through co-creative processes can support inclusive, child-friendly urban futures.

papers.title: Adapting to Disruptions: Strategies of Mathematics and Science Teacher-educators Towards Maintaining Assessment Credibility in Transitioning from Face-to-face to Online Modalities
papers.authors: Lawan Abdulhamid, Ajayi Eyitayo Julius, Herman Tshesane, Judah Paul Makonye, Eunice Nyamupangedengu, Monde Kazeni, Portia Mabenge, Caleb Mandikonza, Magdeline Mmapaseka Stephen
papers.journal: African Journal of Research in Mathematics Science and Technology Education
