papers.abstract: This paper explores the challenges faced by Mathematics and Science teacher-educators at a South African university in maintaining assessment credibility during the transition from face-to-face to online modalities. It utilises a Professional Learning Community (PLC) framework and authentic conversations amongst nine PLC members as a means of documenting scholarship of teaching and learning. The study delves into the challenges relating to disruptions to traditional assessment practices and the strategies employed to navigate them. The research is guided by the substitution, augmentation, modification and redefinition model, which provides a theoretical lens for understanding the evolution of technology in teaching and assessment. The findings reveal four key challenges: assessment integrity issues, load shedding disruptions, technical glitches and limited lecturer expertise in designing and administering higher-order online tasks. While the transition initially involved substitution and augmentation, with online assessments often deemed ‘too simplistic’ and prone to issues of academic integrity, efforts to move towards the modification phase showed promise. Modifications, in the context of assessment, included adapting the assessment task to ensure Mathematics and Science concepts are effectively assessed in an online, non-invigilated settings, as illustrated in the paper. Despite these advancements, progress towards the redefinition phase where assessments are fully integrated and technologically sophisticated to mitigate unethical usage of artificial intelligence remains limited. The paper argues that achieving this phase requires sustained and deliberate training for teacher-educators in advanced technological integration, emphasising the need for continued professional development in the post-COVID era.

papers.title: The impact of ChatGPT-assisted instruction on speaking performance, motivation, and self-regulated learning: a quasi-experimental study of intermediate EFL learners in China
papers.authors: Yan Chang
papers.journal: Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: Purpose: This study examined the effects of ChatGPT-assisted speaking instruction, compared with conventional communicative instruction, on the speaking performance, motivation, and self-regulated learning (SRL) of intermediate Chinese EFL learners. Design/methodology/approach: A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control-group design was conducted with 143 intermediate EFL learners across four private language institutes in Chongqing, China. Over a 12-week period, the experimental group engaged in 10 ChatGPT-assisted speaking sessions featuring interactive practice and automated formative feedback, whereas the control group received conventional communicative speaking instruction. Data were collected using validated speaking assessment rubrics, an EFL motivation questionnaire, and a self-regulated learning scale. One-way analyses of covariance (ANCOVA) were performed to assess post-intervention differences while controlling for baseline pretest scores. Findings: After controlling for pretest performance, the ChatGPT-assisted group demonstrated statistically significant improvements over the control group in speaking performance (F (1,140) = 32.06, p < .01) and self-regulated learning strategies (F(1,140) = 505.32, p < .01) However, the between-group difference in motivation did not reach statistical significance (F(1,140) = 3.29, p = .072, ηp2 = .02), though adjusted descriptive means favored the intervention cohort. Originality/value: While generative AI tools have attracted considerable attention in language education, empirical research evaluating their concurrent impact on linguistic output and psychological/metacognitive attributes remains limited. This study contributes empirical evidence regarding how interactive generative AI can foster autonomous, regulated learning behaviors alongside oral proficiency development, providing practical and pedagogical insights for curriculum designers and EFL educators integrating AI into communicative language classrooms.

papers.title: Making GenAI revision accountable: learner evaluation, uptake, and revision quality in source-based academic writing
papers.authors: Huican Huo, Yanfan Cheng, Yue Peng, Weiwei Xie
papers.journal: Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can provide fluent revision suggestions, but source-based writing requires learners to judge whether those suggestions preserve source meaning, evidence, attribution, task requirements, and intended stance. This classroom-based study examined 40 second-year English majors completing two source-based writing tasks. The dataset comprised 160 drafts, 80 reflections, 793 traceable revision episodes, and independent ratings of 80 D1–D2 pairs. Cross-classifying 131 reflection-linked rationales with uptake showed that language-clarity reasons were concentrated in local language uptake, trust or uncertainty frequently accompanied checked uptake, and efficiency or time was concentrated in weakly checked uptake. Excluding 34 risk-unclear episodes, substantive-risk suggestions were more often associated with visible checking than local-only suggestions (32.5% vs. 18.9%; participant-clustered GEE, OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.48, 2.91], p < 0.001), although the authorial-stance contrast was not robust. Within substantive-risk episodes with determinate consequences, visible checking was associated with higher odds of local improvement (84.6% vs. 39.6%; adjusted OR = 8.11, 95% CI [4.88, 13.47], p < 0.001) and lower odds of degradation. D2 texts were rated higher than D1 texts, but absolute rater agreement was moderate, ICC(A,k) = 0.625, and no participant–task-level uptake proportion was significantly associated with whole-text gain after multiplicity correction. The findings are consistent with risk-calibrated accountability as an observational design principle; they do not establish a causal effect of visible checking.

papers.title: Mobility wearable devices in older adults: a scoping review of hardware, artificial intelligence software and socio-ecological influences on device use
papers.authors: Harjot Suri, Areeya Hillman, Ashely Chan, Chukwuebuka Prince Onyekere, Peace Kumapayi, Ethan Chan, Ambika Mehta, Michael Ebe Kalu
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: This scoping review maps mobility wearable device hardware and artificial intelligence(AI) software and synthesise socioecological factors influencing device use among older adults aged 65 years and older. METHODS: We followed the Arksey and O'Malley five-step framework and searched five databases and one data interface (OVID) between January 2010 to December 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data in Covidence© using predefined eligibility criteria. Data were analysed in pairs and synthesised using the socio-ecological framework and an AI taxonomy (unsupervised, semi-supervised, supervised, deep learning and reinforcement learning). RESULTS: We included 197 studies from 27 countries, predominantly quantitative (97.0%). Mobility monitoring relied on accelerometers (63.5%), plastic (87%) and worn at the hip/waist. Fourteen studies employed AI-enabled analytics, of which 13 used supervised learning and one used both supervised and deep learning approaches. A socioecological framework guided us to derived 22 themes, 10 opportunities and 12 challenges, across individual, interpersonal, environmental and policy levels. Real-time mobility monitoring with feedback was the unifying opportunity, while privacy, data governance, trust and digital literacy inequities were recurring constraints, underscoring the need for inclusive, equity-oriented design. Level-specific opportunities included cognitive and mental health benefits (individual), social motivation (interpersonal), workforce efficiency (organisational) and reimbursement evolution (policy). Level-specific challenges included acceptability (individual), autonomy and dependence tensions (interpersonal), standardisation and integration barriers (organisational) and regulatory gaps (policy). CONCLUSION: The evidence base remains methodologically fragmented, with limited longitudinal real-world evaluation of AI models. Progress will require addressing multilevel implementation, integration and equity barriers that shape real world adoption among older adults.

papers.title: Machine learning in comparative effective research of pharmacological interventions: a scoping review
papers.authors: Zhen Wang, Bijan J. Borah
papers.journal: Expert Review of Pharmacoeconomics & Outcomes Research
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Machine learning (ML) is rapidly transforming the evaluation of the comparative effectiveness research (CER) of pharmacological interventions. It offers an attractive data-driven alternative to traditional statistical causal inference methods for estimating heterogeneous and individualized treatment effects and is particularly well-suited for high-dimensional real-world data. While a variety of ML algorithms have been applied in CER, methodological challenges and limitations remain, and recommendations for conducting, reporting, and evaluating such studies have only recently been proposed. AREAS COVERED: This paper conducts a scoping review of ML approaches used in CER for pharmacological interventions. We searched multiple databases from January 2020 to January 2026, supplemented by reference mining, and included 28 primary studies. We focused on research topics, ML methodologies, reporting, validity, and robustness of the findings, and appraised risk of bias. EXPERT OPINION: Although the use of ML methods in CER of pharmacologic intervention is relatively recent, it is expanding and consolidating around a few specific methods, notably doubly robust estimators paired with ensemble learners. However, methodological rigor and reporting consistency remain uneven, yielding a moderate risk of bias. Standardized methods, transparent reporting, and dedicated appraisal tools are needed before these approaches can reliably inform research, clinical practice, and policy.

papers.title: Digital involution in AI-assisted academic writing: revisiting educational innovation through empty competition in a postgraduate course
papers.authors: Jie Zhang
papers.journal: Innovation The European Journal of Social Science Research
papers.abstract: This research note reconsiders the conceptualisation of innovation in the era of generative artificial intelligence (AI). Based on observations from an academic writing course, this research identifies a pattern of excessive textual production with limited intellectual gain. The note interprets this phenomenon as digital involution, in which generative AI lowers the cost of output yet intensifies empty competition among students. The underlying logic aligns with theories of symbolic capital, performativity and algorithmic scale, suggesting that the efficiency of generative AI may increase peer pressure toward quantifiable output at the expense of substantive learning. Rather than defining innovation through productivity and efficiency, this note argues that AI-assisted writing risks a degenerated form of competition through the accelerated production of inflated content and reduced cognitive engagement. The research calls for redesigned assessment and pedagogical practices grounded in the Literacy of Refusal. Future study should prioritise meaningful learning outcomes and the development of critical thinking over textual expansion in AI-assisted environments.

papers.title: When less is more: anthropomorphic cue configuration in embodied AI travel agents
papers.authors: Dahye Kim, 강유림, Youngjoon Choi

papers.title: When AI Delivers the Message: Emotional and Relational Consequences of AI-Generated Feedback in Marketing Education
papers.authors: A. Banu Elmadag, Aisha Ghimire
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in instructional feedback processes in marketing education, yet little is known about how students psychologically process feedback when it is attributed to AI rather than a human instructor. To clarify the state of the field, we first conduct a systematic literature review of 25 peer-reviewed studies on AI use in higher education, revealing a dominance of technology adoption and performance-focused models and a limited integration of emotional and relational mechanisms in AI-mediated feedback contexts. Building on source credibility theory and affective appraisal perspectives, we then test a moderated serial mediation model using a 2 × 2 experiment with undergraduate marketing students (N = 371). Results show that feedback valence significantly influences positive emotional responses, and this effect is amplified when feedback is attributed to AI rather than to a human instructor. Emotional responses subsequently shape perceived feedback clarity, instructor likability, and perceived instructor benevolence, which in turn predict engagement intentions. The findings demonstrate that AI-generated feedback is not processed as a neutral delivery channel but as a socially interpreted evaluative source. By integrating systematic synthesis with experimental evidence, this study advances a process-oriented understanding of the emotional and relational consequences of AI-mediated feedback in marketing education.

papers.title: Teaching Generation Z: The Pedagogical Innovation Pentagon For Hybrid Introductory Marketing Education
papers.authors: Oula Bayarassou
papers.abstract: This study examines how pedagogical innovation can support Generation Z students in post-COVID marketing education, where hybrid learning and artificial intelligence are reshaping course design. It introduces the Pedagogical Innovation Pentagon, an evidence-informed model organized around five interrelated dimensions: hybridization, digitalization, artificial intelligence, responsibility, and harmonization. The model was developed and evaluated through a mixed-methods exploratory study conducted with first-year students enrolled in a bilingual introductory marketing course within a multi-campus business program. The model was implemented through an Instructional Capsule, a structured learning environment combining bilingual content development, guided activities, feedback mechanisms, sustainability-focused case studies, and shared assessment practices across campuses. Student self-reports and course analytics were used to explore how this instructional approach supported engagement, clarity, feedback, ethical awareness, and coherence in students’ learning experiences. Findings suggest that effective innovation in marketing education depends less on technological sophistication than on the meaningful integration of digital tools within a human-centered and ethically intentional learning environment. The study contributes to marketing education by offering a transferable approach for integrating digital transformation, AI, and responsible pedagogy into course design and continuous improvement.

papers.title: ChatGPT as cognitive scaffold: computational thinking and metacognition in AI-embedded instruction
papers.authors: Tanya Chichekian, Joel Trudeau
papers.abstract: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

papers.title: From Representation to Relational Mentorship: User Perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage Learning
papers.authors: Quanyi Zhao, Xiangming Mu, Xun Zhu
papers.abstract: This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

papers.title: Using AI, Doubting AI: Developer Mental Models and Trust in AI-Assisted Software Work
papers.authors: NICOLE DSILVA
papers.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

papers.title: Design Implications for Teacher-Configurable Generative AI Writing Tools: A Participatory Design Study with StoryBot
papers.authors: Ariel Han, Shenshen Han, Zhenyao Cai, Joey Huang, Franceli L. Cibrian, Kylie Peppler
papers.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) tools become accessible, their integration into K–12 writing presents opportunities and challenges. This study partnered with 21 primary school teachers in a participatory co-design process to develop StoryBot, a teacher-configurable GenAI story-authoring platform. Teachers identified instructional needs and learning outcomes that informed system features, including genre-specific writing scaffolds, configurable prompts, and constraints on full-text generation to preserve student voice. The platform positions educators as co-designers of AI behavior rather than passive users. We conducted a pilot writing workshop with 13 youth (ages 8–12) and a focus group with six educators to examine how the platform influenced students’ writing behaviors and classroom integration. Findings demonstrate the value of teacher co-design and configurable AI systems in aligning GenAI tools with pedagogical priorities and practices. We present design implications for teacher-configurable GenAI writing systems that support student agency, ethical safeguards, and instructional alignment in human–AI coauthoring environments.

papers.title: Educational Recommender Systems for Metacognitive and Self-Regulated Learning Support: An Algorithmic Systematic Review
papers.authors: Zhuoying Li, Sikai Wang
papers.abstract: Recommender systems (RSs) increasingly support self-regulated learning (SRL) through personalized resources, feedback, and strategy recommendations. However, traditional content based and collaborative filtering approaches suffer from cold start problems, while machine or deep learning methods raise interpretability concerns and LLM-based recommenders require evaluation of explanation faithfulness and hallucinations. This systematic review examines SRL-oriented recommender algorithms from an algorithmic and pedagogical perspective. Six databases were searched using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, yielding 25 eligible studies published between 2020 and 2025. The review traces the evolution from traditional filtering methods to machine or deep learning and emerging LLM-based approaches. Three major challenges were identified: cold start, limited explainability, and LLM hallucinations, alongside gaps in learner system interaction and metacognitive scaffolding. Future SRL-RS research should compare algorithms under controlled data sparsity, evaluate explanation faithfulness and source curation, preserve learner agency, integrate SRL strategies across three phases, and longitudinally assess SRL skill maintenance and transfer.

papers.title: Negotiating Algorithmic Branding: Consumer Interpretations of AI-Generated Advertising in a Heinz Campaign
papers.authors: Tao Papaioannou
papers.abstract: This study examines how consumers interpret AI-generated advertising through Heinz’s “A.I. Ketchup” campaign. Drawing on reflexive thematic analysis of 36 stimulus-based interviews, the findings conceptualize consumer responses as a process of legitimacy negotiation in which creative agency, procedural transparency, brand continuity, and ethical responsibility are evaluated together rather than as separate concerns. AI familiarity and perceived AI literacy shaped the interpretive resources participants used in making these judgements, but frequent AI use did not necessarily imply critical understanding. The study contributes to global marketing by showing how generative AI can reinforce brand salience while making algorithmic brand power, creative authorship, and responsible brand communication ethically contested.

papers.title: AI-Powered Teaching and Learning in Health Education: Navigating Innovation, Engagement, and Ethics
papers.authors: Kristen M. Ford, Julie M. Knutson, Teri Langlie
papers.journal: Journal of Physical Education Recreation & Dance
papers.abstract: This article is connected to THE FUSED Health Education Series and explores the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), in health education. As educators face increasing demands in planning, assessment, differentiation, and student engagement, AI offers tools that can improve efficiency, creativity, and instructional effectiveness. GenAI can generate text, visuals, feedback, and interactive learning experiences, allowing teachers to save time and focus more on student learning. Key applications discussed include curriculum development, lesson planning, assessment creation, personalized feedback, and differentiated instruction for diverse learners. AI can also increase student engagement through simulations, virtual tutors, creative prompts, and real-time support. In multilingual and under-resourced settings, AI may help improve access and educational equity through scalable, personalized resources. The article also addresses AI’s role in professional growth and collaboration by helping educators access resources, co-create materials, and stay current with best practices. At the same time, ethical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, AI scales, and overreliance must be carefully considered. Ultimately, AI is presented as a tool that can support and enhance teaching and learning when used thoughtfully, ethically, and with a continued focus on human connection.

papers.title: The power of framing AI: preliminary evidence on hybrid intelligence and future work perceptions
papers.authors: Lau Holgersen, Janet Frances Rafner, Patrycja Julia Rogozińska, Michail J. Beliatis, Dominik Dellermann, Jacob Friis Sherson
papers.abstract: As generative AI diffuses across organisations, individuals encounter competing frames of AI as autonomous automation or human–AI collaboration. We examine framing as an early interpretive condition that may shape whether people understand AI as a replacement for human labour or as a collaborative system supporting human co-adaptation. Two exploratory experiments tested whether competing AI frames influence master's students' perceived automation risk and sensemaking about AI's role in future work. In Study 1, a randomised repeated-measures experiment with Business Intelligence students (N = 35), introducing a hybrid intelligence (HI) counter-frame after an AI-capability frame was associated with lower perceived job displacement expectations than in the control condition. In Study 2, a randomised framing-primacy workshop with Digital Design students, numeric automation estimates did not differ significantly (N = 31), but in the written-response sample (N = 35), participants exposed to an HI-first frame expressed significantly more augmentation-oriented interpretations of AI's role. The studies suggest that AI frames may influence perceived automation risk and the language used to make sense of human–AI collaboration. We discuss implications for managers and educators and position HI-TAM2 as a preliminary theoretical agenda for research on framing and contextual antecedents in HI acceptance rather than a validated model extension.

papers.title: Examining the impact of COVID-19 on student mathematics achievement across countries: A multilevel machine learning analysis of PISA 2022
papers.authors: Xue‐Lan Qiu, Jin Yuan, Jinran Wu, Weide Li, Jiesi Guo, Frederick K. S. Leung
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic caused significant disruptions to education globally. This study examines and compares the impact of COVID-19 on students’ mathematics achievement across eight countries/regions, namely, Australia, Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong (China), Japan, Korea, Macao (China), Singapore, and the United States, using data from PISA 2022. It uses multilevel machine learning models that explicitly account for hierarchical data structures and incorporate a comprehensive set of national-, school-, family-, and individual-level predictors. Results show that school closures had the strongest negative effect on mathematics achievement, whereas school support and students’ self-directed learning exerted positive influences. Substantial cross-country and subgroup differences were also observed. Education systems with shorter school closures and more effective remote instruction were better able to mitigate pandemic-related learning losses. Male students, students from higher SES backgrounds, and second-generation immigrants generally demonstrated higher mathematics performance. The study concludes with methodological and practical implications.

papers.title: Traveling with Darwin in the Age of AI: Handwritten Historical Imagination and Evolution Learning in Introductory Biology
papers.authors: Jordan A. Smink
papers.journal: The journal of college science teaching
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has complicated writing assignments in college science courses by making it easier for students to produce polished explanations without necessarily engaging deeply with course concepts. Rather than focusing only on preventing or detecting AI use, instructors need assignments that preserve the work of student thinking when AI is readily available. This article describes “A Letter from the HMS Beagle,” a low-stakes assignment used in a large introductory Biology II course. Students imagined themselves as traveling companions of Charles Darwin and wrote a one-page, handwritten letter explaining natural selection through scientific evidence and a historically framed narrative. AI use was permitted during preparation, but the final response had to be handwritten on a provided sheet and submitted in person. The assignment combined scientific explanation, evidence use, historical imagination, and a deliberate procedural constraint. Rather than attempting to make student writing AI-proof, the design emphasized explanation, interpretation, and personal engagement. The activity offers a practical model for preserving scientific thinking and student engagement in AI-mediated science classrooms.

papers.title: Enriching the EuSO ontology through GenAI-based terminological selection and conceptualisation
papers.authors: Helena Ortiz-Garduño, Esther Castillo-Pérez
papers.journal: Terminology International Journal of Theoretical and Applied Issues in Specialized Communication
papers.abstract: Abstract In academic and institutional contexts, the management and structuring of specialised knowledge are essential to support effective communication and internationalisation. Traditionally, ontology development and ontology-driven terminology work have relied on expert-based manual processes and corpus analysis techniques. However, recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) have opened new possibilities for supporting knowledge representation tasks. In this context, this study explores the use of a customised GenAI-based chatbot for assisting ontology development in the domain of European higher education. Specifically, The Ontology Assistant, built on ChatGPT-5.2 and enriched with a domain-specific corpus, was designed to support the identification and structuring of ontological categories within the EuroScholar Ontology (EuSO). The model’s performance was evaluated through six experimental runs using a gold standard derived from a selected ontological category. Precision, recall, and F1-measure were used to assess category retrieval. The results show consistent behaviour across runs, characterised by high recall and low precision, reflecting the exploratory capacity of the chatbot to identify candidate ontological categories. These findings suggest that GenAI chatbots can function as useful support tools within ontology development workflows, provided that expert intervention is applied to verify and maintain alignment with the EuSO.

papers.title: Functional specialization and dynamical interaction in human amygdala subregions support fearful-expression processing
papers.authors: Dan Cao, Jiachen Cui, Xinyuan Yan, Xinru ZHANG, Yuanyuan Dang, Hulin Zhao, Jin Li, Jianning Zhang, Yanyang Zhang
papers.abstract: Fearful-expression processing supports adaptive responses to potential threats, requiring both rapid threat evaluation and face-related information processing. However, how human amygdala subregions contribute to these complementary processes remains unclear. Here we record intracranial electroencephalography from twelve patients with epilepsy during an emotional face-matching task, sampling 58 amygdala contacts with balanced hemispheric distributions. Condition-specific analyses reveal separable theta/alpha dynamics between the lateral and medial amygdala within fearful-face and neutral-face matching conditions, but not shape matching. Between-condition contrasts further reveal earlier lateral amygdala engagement and stronger lateral-to-medial directional interactions for fearful-face versus neutral-face matching, whereas later medial engagement and stronger medial-to-lateral interactions emerge for neutral-face versus shape matching. Control analyses preserve the main neural effects. In a separate cohort of seven patients, intracranial stimulation produces dissociable behavioral effects, with lateral stimulation impairing fear matching and medial stimulation facilitating neutral-face matching. Together, these findings reveal a condition-dependent functional differentiation within the human amygdala during fearful-expression processing.

papers.title: Realizing the value of the divergence event in clinical human-AI interaction
papers.authors: Florence Xini Doo, Gabriel A. Brat, Sarah Collins Rossetti, Robert Klitzman, Charles E. Binkley
papers.abstract: When a clinical AI system’s output differs from a human clinician’s judgment, what follows is consequential and underspecified. Current AI interfaces offer only a narrow lane for what happens next: they present the AI output (and its associated potential divergence) as an adjudicative choice for a human to accept, override, or modify. In practice, collapsing this human-AI interaction into a single output inadvertently obscures what happens in a potential divergence event (Fig. 1 ) which can be characterized along three axes: What the workflow and interface allow the clinician to see and do ( structural axis), what information each side brought to the interaction ( informational axis), and how the clinician engaged with the AI’s reasoning rather than only its output ( behavioral axis). When clinical judgment and AI output diverge, clinicians must ultimately decide what to recommend and how to explain their recommendation to the patient, consider their autonomy, accountability, and liability, and bear moral responsibility 1 . A recent systematic review of AI ethics in nursing and midwifery found that AI challenges the role of health professionals not through replacement, but through subtle reconfiguration of the activities that count as care and that emphasis on AI efficiency may risk certain relational aspects of care less visible and valued 2 . Because clinicians often cannot see how an AI system reached its output, they are left to choose between that AI output and their own judgment. Clinicians are told to be the “human in the loop” but are typically given no method for doing so beyond “exercising their judgment” 3 . Efforts to make AI output both more technically explainable and human interpretable - have not directly correlated with improved clinical decisions and have sometimes created false confidence in incorrect AI output 4 .

papers.title: The effect of appearance features of sidewalk autonomous delivery robot on perception of pedestrian
papers.authors: Fan Xu, Duanduan Liu, Chao Zhou, Jing Hu, Zheyuan Zhang, Shan Sun
papers.abstract: Sidewalk autonomous delivery robots (SADRs) are increasingly appearing on urban sidewalks and sharing public space with pedestrians. This study aims to investigate how different appearance features of SADRs influence four dimensions of human perception: Likeability, Competence, Perceived Safety, and Existence Acceptance. In Study 1, an affinity diagram method was used to classify the appearance features of existing SADRs into four categories—contour, proportion, facial features, and color scheme—which were then used as the design variables in Study 2. In Study 2, 100 participants completed an online questionnaire after viewing AI-generated videos of SADRs and evaluated the robots on the four perceptual dimensions. The statistical results showed that rounded contours and the presence of facial features significantly increased Likeability, Perceived Safety, and Existence Acceptance. White–black and yellow color schemes generally received higher ratings for Likeability, Perceived Safety, and Existence Acceptance than black–gray and red color schemes. In addition, a tall proportion significantly reduced Likeability. Study 3 used online semi-structured interviews to further examine the reasons underlying these evaluations and to explore participants’ subjective perceptions of SADRs. The findings provide practical guidance for designing SADR appearances that can foster more positive pedestrian perceptions and acceptance.

papers.title: An explainable AI framework using wearable IMU-based motion sensing for estimating and explaining motor skill improvement in school-based Baduanjin education
papers.authors: Jiaqi Li, Ye Zhang, Yuanhang Sun
papers.abstract: Estimation of individual skill improvement within specific school-based physical education units remains methodologically underdeveloped, with existing approaches typically lacking external validation and interpretability. Because the full model incorporates training-load features aggregated across the same temporal window as the outcome, it is epistemologically retrospective; readers should not interpret it as a prospectively deployable prediction tool. This study aimed at developing and externally validating an explainable machine learning ensemble to retrospectively explain and estimate standardized skill gain (Δz) in Baduanjin (eight-section brocade) qigong, a mandatory traditional martial arts skill in the Chinese national PE curriculum, among students from four schools ( n = 727). A stacking meta-learner composed of five candidate algorithms, including XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest, LASSO, and MLP, was trained using biomechanical, psycho-cognitive, and semester-aggregated training-load features obtained from the development cohort (Schools A + B, n = 486) and then validated against two geographically independent but regionally situated cohorts (Schools C + D, n = 241). Because the training-load features were aggregated across the full 16-week semester, the model functions as a retrospective semester-level estimation framework rather than a prospective early-warning tool. The model yielded an external validation R² of 0.691 (95% CI: 0.661–0.718), with robust subgroup performance across gender, initial skill quartiles, and sport types. SHAP-based interpretability analysis identified exercise self-efficacy as the highest-ranking modifiable feature in model-derived importance, with its predictive contribution predominantly associated with the training-response component rather than baseline level. A baseline-only sensitivity model excluding semester-aggregated training-load variables retained moderate external validity (R² = 0.573), indicating that prospective application at semester onset is feasible in principle but at substantially reduced precision. These findings suggest that, within this dataset and model specification, psycho-cognitive features contributed more strongly to model estimations than biomechanical features.

papers.title: Machine learning-based association analysis and cross-sectional classification of physical exercise behaviors and mental health among vocational medical students
papers.authors: Saisai Tian, Shuai Meng
papers.abstract: Psychological distress is common among vocational medical students, yet how multidimensional exercise behavior relates to their mental health remains coarsely described. This cross-sectional study surveyed 1,127 students at three vocational medical colleges in China between September and November 2024, applying machine learning to two analytically separate tasks: describing association patterns between exercise profiles and psychological status, and classifying concurrent psychological risk. Exercise behavior was measured with the IPAQ Short Form plus purpose-written items on modality, motivation, social context and temporal regularity; psychological status with the GAD-7, PHQ-9, PSS-10 and SWLS, combined into three ordered categories that are operational rather than diagnostic. Random forest ranking, Apriori rule mining and K-Means profiling agreed on three points: weekly frequency carried the most information among behavioral variables; frequent moderate-intensity aerobic activity co-occurred most often with low anxiety and depression; and four partially overlapping profiles emerged. XGBoost classified best on an internal hold-out test set of 226 students, one fifth of the full sample (accuracy 0.889, 95% CI 0.842 to 0.924; macro-averaged AUC 0.943), yet reached only 0.769 sensitivity for severe distress, and accuracy fell to 0.858 under leave-one-college-out validation. Because the design is cross-sectional and validation internal, these findings describe associations rather than supply a screening tool.

papers.title: Human–artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time
papers.authors: Zack Goldblum, Haoer Shi, Zhongchuan Xu, William K.S. Ojemann, Carlos A. Aguila, Kevin W. Long, Kevin Xie, Kerry C. Nix, Katherine G. Walsh, Ellie Chang, Sarah B. Lavelle, Brandon Bach, Kathryn A. Davis, Nishant Sinha, Lauren H. Hammer, Erin C. Conrad, Brian Litt
papers.abstract: One-third of the world’s 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions. A small epilepsy monitoring study shows that a moderated, large language model-based chat interface lets patients converse with their electroencephalography monitoring in real time, using a smartphone, and patient feedback cut seizure-detector false alarms by about 80% without clinician input.

papers.title: How L1–L2 typological distance moderates the interplay between cognitive resources and LLM predictors in L2 reading
papers.authors: Zhizhuo He, Cheng Yang, Shiyi Lu, Sun Rui
papers.abstract: Abstract This study investigates how L1–L2 typological distance moderates the predictive validity of large language model (LLM)-based metrics in L2 reading, alongside the compensatory role of cognitive resources. Eye-tracking data from Chinese learners with L1 Lao, Burmese, Thai and Vietnamese revealed that surprisal predicted processing difficulty across all groups, whereas contextual entropy effects were group-specific and qualified by cognitive differences. Cognitive abilities explained unique variance only in Vietnamese learners, with verbal short‑term storage (VSTS) showing an independent effect. Additionally, VSTS and reading comprehension accuracy showed significant interactions with typological distance, such that higher learner-level memory and comprehension-performance indices were associated with reduced processing burden under greater L1–L2 divergence. These findings demonstrate that LLM metrics’ validity is constrained by typology and modulated by cognitive resources, supporting adaptive L2 processing models and the Cognitive Resource Coordination Model (Robinson [2001, Second Language Research 17(4), pp. 368–392]).

papers.title: Governing sustainable co-creation in business–NGO collaborations: Institutional logics and innovation outcomes
papers.authors: Annabeth; id_orcid 0000-0002-6213-0682 Aagaard, Lise Andersen Lodsgård
papers.abstract: This study examines how governance in business-NGO collaborations conditions co-creation for sustainable innovation under institutional plurality. Drawing on institutional logics theory, we conduct a qualitative cross-case study of five Scandinavian retail firms and their NGO partners. We identify three recurrent governance configurations: separated coexistence, assimilated coexistence, and logic blending. The configurations differ in how partners manage organizational boundaries, allocate decision authority, integrate knowledge, and establish accountability. In the cases studied, separated coexistence was recurrently associated with regulative innovation, where protected organizational distance supported credible monitoring and verification. Assimilated coexistence was recurrently associated with inclusive sustainable business innovation, where NGO knowledge entered bounded parts of firm-led innovation. Logic blending was most evident in social impact innovation, where joint problem framing, shared interpretation of evidence, and relational accountability supported long-term societal outcomes. These relationships represent empirical tendencies rather than necessary, sufficient, or exclusive associations. Different configurations may coexist across activities and may evolve as collaborations mature. The study extends institutional logics research by showing how responses to plurality are operationalized as interorganizational governance arrangements that structure decision rights, knowledge interfaces, boundaries, and accountability. It contributes to sustainable co-creation research by explaining why different innovation tasks call for different combinations of governance practices.

papers.title: From digital skilling to sustainable performance: How climate entrepreneurship and attitudes toward artificial intelligence shape the future of SME technological transitions
papers.authors: Fazal Ayaz, Guoping Chen, Shah Abbas, Zohaib Hassan
papers.abstract: Digital technologies are reshaping how small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies respond to environmental pressure, yet two questions remain open. Research linking digital skilling to sustainability has largely tested direct effects without tracing the behavioral pathway such an effect would have to travel, and attitudes toward artificial intelligence have rarely been examined as a condition governing whether green entrepreneurial activity converts into performance. This study addresses both. Integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, and Contingency Theory into a single explanatory sequence, it models climate entrepreneurship (CE), green entrepreneurial behavior (GEB), and green entrepreneurial intention (GEI) as the mechanisms linking digital entrepreneurial education and training (DEET) to sustainable environmental performance (SEP) and sustainable organizational performance (SOP), with commitment to the environment (CTE) and attitude toward artificial intelligence (ATAI) as boundary conditions. Survey data from 648 Pakistani SMEs are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with a random forest robustness check confirming that the modelled relationships are linear and compensatory. DEET directly predicts organizational performance but has no significant direct effect on environmental performance; its environmental influence is transmitted entirely through the three behavioral mechanisms. Environmental commitment and favorable attitudes toward artificial intelligence each strengthen the conversion of green entrepreneurship into sustainability outcomes, though the interaction effects are modest in magnitude. The findings suggest that digital skilling initiatives are unlikely to yield environmental returns unless paired with entrepreneurial agency and technological openness, with implications for the sequencing of digital and AI-readiness policy in resource-constrained economies.

papers.title: The AI dilemma in L2 writing: Is AI literacy associated with willingness to write through self-efficacy, anxiety, or both? A serial mediation investigation
papers.authors: Yanyu Yang, Bingwei Li
papers.abstract: This study investigates the psychological mechanisms through which artificial intelligence (AI) literacy relates to L2 learners’ willingness to write (WTW). It proposes a serial mediation model wherein L2 writing self-efficacy (WSE) and L2 writing anxiety (WA) sequentially mediate this relationship. Grounded in social cognitive theory and control-value theory, the research employed a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design with 303 Chinese EFL learners. Quantitative results from structural equation modeling indicate that: (1) L2 WSE fully mediates the relationship between AI literacy and L2 WTW; (2) AI literacy is indirectly linked to L2 WTW through a sequential pathway: by first positively predicting L2 WSE, which in turn negatively predicts L2 WA; and (3) the direct effects of AI literacy on L2 WA and L2 WTW are non-significant. To explain these quantitative pathways, qualitative interviews with 16 participants further elucidated how AI tool usage corresponds to higher L2 WSE through strategic partnership, reduced startup burden, and task scaffolding support. Furthermore, the qualitative narratives revealed that while AI usage can initially be associated with anxiety (e.g., fear of exposure, tool-related frustration), the heightened L2 WSE linked to AI literacy effectively serves as a protective factor against these affective barriers. The study concludes that AI literacy positively correlates with L2 WTW through a fully indirect mechanism, in which heightened L2 WSE serves as a vital prerequisite for lowering L2 WA. These findings contribute to theory by integrating two major psychological frameworks and offer practical implications for leveraging AI to cultivate more willing L2 writers.

papers.title: Welfare regimes and the adoption of artificial intelligence in healthcare
papers.authors: Ritumbra Manuvie, Jeanne Mifsud Bonnici, Mirjam Plantinga
papers.abstract: This paper examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare through the analytical lens of the political determinants of health (PDOH), arguing that AI is not a politically neutral technological innovation but a domain in which longstanding distributive logics of welfare regimes are reproduced and potentially intensified. As a conceptual, theory-building contribution, this paper develops a set of testable propositions about how welfare-regime logics may condition the adoption, regulation, and distributive effects of AI in healthcare. While existing scholarship on AI in healthcare has largely centred on ethical risks, algorithmic bias, privacy, and data governance, these discussions often overlook how political systems shape both the speed and equity of AI adoption. Drawing on Navaro et al.’s typology of political regimes —social democratic, Christian democratic, liberal, and ex-dictatorship—the paper argues that welfare state traditions and power resource configurations may structure how AI is developed, regulated, and what are its distributive consequences. Social democratic regimes, with strong universalist commitments, are likely to adopt AI cautiously but equitably; Christian democratic systems may integrate AI through corporatist negotiation and regulated pluralism; liberal regimes may accelerate market-driven AI innovation at the cost of uneven access; and ex-dictatorship states may face the dual pressures of modernization and institutional fragility, leading to uneven but politically charged trajectories of adoption. The paper concludes by arguing that regulatory progress on AI must be conceptualized in light of the political frameworks it comes to operate within and therefore, for AI in healthcare to be inclusive it may require a reaffirmation of the values of universal access.

papers.title: Openness to experience modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing
papers.authors: Bing Li, Chih-Mao Huang, Qiduo Lin, Hsu-Wen Huang
papers.abstract: Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to Experience (openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes increasing as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences.

papers.title: Clinical summarization from FHIR bundles using model context protocol–orchestrated large language models: A scenario-based physician validation study
papers.authors: João C. Ferreira, Luís Maia, Ricardo Correia, Alberto Vilas, J A Martínez Matos, Nuno Vila‐Chã, Maria Carlos Pereira
papers.abstract: Objective To develop and evaluate a provenance-bounded architecture for generating narrative patient summaries from Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) bundles while reducing hallucinations, medication distortion, and unsupported temporal inference. Unconstrained large language models applied directly to fragmented FHIR bundles have been reported to fabricate diagnoses, invent medication changes that were never documented, and infer disease progression not supported by the underlying records [11], [23], [24]; the architecture evaluated here was designed specifically to prevent this class of failure by separating deterministic data preparation from generation. This separation was informed by prior work on FHIR structural mapping and terminology interoperability [27], [28] and on tool-grounded LLM orchestration for auditable clinical decision support [12]. Methods We implemented an end-to-end summarization pipeline in which a large language model (LLM) was restricted to validated context produced through deterministic preprocessing, including patient-specific FHIR (Release 4, R4) retrieval, terminology normalization against SNOMED CT, ICD, and LOINC, medication reconciliation, and structured context packaging. The orchestration layer was implemented using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to expose auditable FHIR-aware tools, each invoked by a single LLM backend (Llama 3.2 3B Instruct, quantized to 4-bit precision, deployed locally through Ollama; exact decoding parameters are reported in Section 4.8). The architecture was evaluated as a proof-of-concept, safety-oriented study using 10 clinician-curated synthetic FHIR bundles representing Parkinson's disease cases with multimorbidity and polypharmacy. Three neurologists with subspecialty expertise in movement disorders and post-residency clinical experience ranging from several years to approximately two decades (further detailed in Section 4.3, including disclosure of the two reviewers who also participated in bundle curation) independently performed blinded assessments across six validation scenarios, scoring diagnostic accuracy, completeness, medication fidelity, longitudinal coherence, and hallucination presence (the first four dimensions rated on a five-point Likert scale), the last operationally defined as any narrative statement that could not be traced to, or was inconsistent with, the source FHIR bundle. Results Mean evaluation scores were 4.6/5 for diagnostic accuracy, 4.5/5 for completeness, 4.8/5 for medication fidelity, and 4.6/5 for longitudinal coherence. No hallucinated diagnoses, medications, laboratory values, or temporal distortions were identified in the reviewed summaries. Inter-rater agreement was strong overall (Fleiss' kappa 0.82; 95% CI 0.70–0.91) and observed agreement on hallucination absence was 100% (kappa not estimable because all ratings were identical; see Section 4.6). Stable performance was observed across scenarios involving polypharmacy, sparse laboratory data, acute events, deep brain stimulation, and cross-domain multimorbidity. Conclusion In this proof-of-concept architectural evaluation, hallucination-resistant clinical summarization was achievable when deterministic semantic harmonization preceded generation and the LLM operated only on provenance-linked validated context. The findings support MCP-orchestrated, tool-grounded summarization as a promising design pattern for safer FHIR-based clinical decision support. However, broader validation using real-world multi-site datasets and direct comparisons with unconstrained and retrieval-augmented baselines remains necessary, and a protocol for executing that comparison, sharing the same dataset, physician panel, and scoring instrument as the present evaluation, is specified in Section 4.4.

papers.title: eHealth literacy levels and associated factors among nursing students: A global systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Xin Zhang, Yan Qiaoyun, Jixuan Hou, Jiao Wang, Wang Li
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The rapid digital transformation of healthcare highlights the importance of electronic health literacy (eHealth literacy) for nursing students. However, existing global evidence regarding their eHealth literacy levels and associated factors remains fragmented. OBJECTIVE: To determine the overall level of e-health literacy among nursing students worldwide, analyze its associated factors and associations with health outcomes, and provide evidence-based support for nursing education reform in the digital age. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in eight Chinese and international databases, including PubMed, for cross-sectional studies published from the inception of each database through June 1, 2026. Study quality was assessed using the AHRQ scale, and random-effects meta-analyses and meta-regression analyses were performed using Stata 19.0. This systematic review protocol was registered in advance with PROSPERO (Registration No.: CRD420261418156). RESULTS: = 99.4%, P < 0.001). Senior-year students demonstrated significantly higher levels of literacy than junior-year students (SMD = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41-0.59, P < 0.001); gender had no significant overall effect on literacy (SMD = -0.04, 95% CI: -0.35-0.27, P = 0.803). Regression analysis showed that living in an urban area (β = 4.24, P < 0.001) and having good economic conditions (β = 0.79, P < 0.001) were exploratory study-level indicators associated with higher literacy. Digital health literacy was moderately positively correlated with health-promoting behaviors (r = 0.42, 95% CI: 0.35-0.49, P < 0.001) and was significantly associated with lower levels of anxiety (OR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.92-0.99, P = 0.006). CONCLUSIONS: Overall, the digital health literacy of nursing students worldwide is acceptable, but regional digital divides remain prominent. Systematic nursing education may help enhance digital health literacy, which is associated with more positive health behaviors and mental health outcomes. Institutions need to refine their digital health curriculum systems, focusing on cultivating students' abilities in information evaluation and AI-assisted decision-making to meet the evolving demands of digital healthcare and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Prevalence and clinical associations of sleep-disordered breathing in multiple sclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Dwiti Jatin Ponda, Florence Olivia Wong, Laura J. Edwards
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), including obstructive and central sleep apnoea, may contribute to fatigue, cognitive impairment, and reduced quality of life in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). Reported prevalence varies widely, and the influence of MS-specific factors on SDB risk remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting objective measures of SDB in adults with MS. Databases were searched up to July 2025. Pooled prevalence and mean apnoea-hypopnoea or respiratory event index (AHI/REI) were estimated using random-effects models. Meta-regression examined associations with demographic and MS-related factors. Case-control studies were pooled to compare SDB odds in PwMS versus controls. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. RESULTS: 29 studies including 1167 PwMS were included. Pooled prevalence of SDB was 30% (95% CI: 21-40%), with a mean AHI of 7.2 events/hour (95% CI: 4.2-10.2), indicating predominantly mild SDB. Meta-regression identified higher body mass index (BMI), longer disease duration, greater disability (EDSS), and a higher proportion of people with progressive MS in the population studied as predictors of elevated AHI. Case-control studies (n = 7) did not show significantly increased odds of SDB in PwMS versus controls; however, case-control participants had relatively low EDSS scores. Heterogeneity was substantial, and certainty of evidence was very low across outcomes. CONCLUSION: SDB affects a considerable proportion of PwMS, particularly those with more advanced disease or higher BMI. Although most SDB identified was mild and fatigue in MS has multifactorial origins, the potential contribution of SDB to sleep quality and cognitive function supports targeted screening approaches. Further research should evaluate whether MS-adapted assessment strategies improve detection and whether treatment of SDB improves MS-related outcomes.

papers.title: Seeing prosperity, confronting crime: Infrastructure inequality and perceived wealth in Chinese cities
papers.authors: Ziwen He, Wenlin Zhao, Jin Rui
papers.abstract: Cities increasingly rely on infrastructure investment and streetscape upgrading to improve urban conditions, yet how macro-scale infrastructure inequality and micro-scale street environments relate to different dimensions of urban experience remains insufficiently understood. This study develops a geospatial learning framework to examine their associations with two distinct outcomes across Chinese cities: recorded crime rates and perceived wealth. The framework combines network-based accessibility measures for infrastructure systems, within-city inequality indicators, street-view-derived environmental and perceptual measures, and interpretable machine-learning analysis. The results reveal divergent spatial patterns. Recorded crime rates are most strongly associated with inequalities in telecommunications and educational infrastructure accessibility, together with selected streetscape characteristics. Telecommunications accessibility inequality shows a strong positive association with recorded crime rates, with its contribution becoming more pronounced at higher levels of inequality. By contrast, perceived wealth is explained predominantly by directly visible streetscape characteristics, particularly greenness, complexity, and openness, while infrastructure, socioeconomic, and security-governance variables contribute less. These findings show that recorded crime and perceived wealth capture different dimensions of the urban environment: the former is more closely associated with infrastructure accessibility inequality and selected street conditions, whereas the latter is primarily structured by visual streetscape cues. This distinction highlights the need to consider both spatial inequality and street-level environmental quality in evaluating urban conditions. For urban policy, strategies focused on beautification alone may overlook underlying vulnerabilities, while more equitable infrastructure provision may better address persistent spatial disparities in recorded crime rates.

papers.title: Using emojis to uplift emotion: Effects on mental health chatbots’ performance
papers.authors: Zhaohua Deng, Xiangqian Yan, Guorui Fan
papers.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
papers.abstract: As AI-based chatbots increasingly expand access to mental health support, understanding how text-based systems convey emotional attentiveness without face-to-face nonverbal cues is important. Emojis may serve as lightweight paralinguistic cues, yet their effects in mental health support remain unclear. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and psychological ownership theory, this study examines associations between emoji use and users’ emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Two scenario-based online experiments were conducted in China using random sampling through Credamo, yielding 459 valid responses (59 in the pretest and 400 in the main study). Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26 and the PROCESS macro. Across the experiments, emoji use was associated with more favorable emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Mediation analyses supported an indirect pathway through perceived warmth and psychological ownership, whereas the corresponding competence-based pathway was not supported. AI literacy strengthened the perceived warmth–psychological ownership association but, contrary to predictions, weakened the perceived competence–psychological ownership association. Moderated mediation analyses provided preliminary support for AI literacy strengthening the warmth-based indirect effects of emoji use on emotional well-being and continuance usage intention. The corresponding effect on satisfaction was not supported. These findings extend research on AI-mediated mental health support by identifying a warmth–psychological ownership pathway and the differentiated role of AI literacy. The study also offers preliminary, context-bounded guidance for the strategic and context-sensitive use of emojis in supportive, non-clinical chatbot interactions.

papers.title: An explainable patient-independent machine learning framework using visibility graph representations for EEG-based AD diagnosis
papers.authors: Vandana Padmakumar, Neethu Mohan, O.K. Sikha, S. Sachin Kumar
papers.journal: Journal of Computational Mathematics and Data Science
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a gradually developing neurodegenerative condition marked by substantial cognitive decline, underscoring the importance of early and precise diagnosis for optimal management. EEG has emerged as a valuable, non-invasive modality for detecting AD-related alterations in brain dynamics. In this work, we propose an end-to-end explainable machine learning framework for patient-independent AD diagnosis. The temporal EEG signals are converted into graph representations, in which each time point is mapped as a node, allowing the graph to directly encode the intrinsic complexity of EEG signals. A comparative study of seven visibility graph (VG) variants for EEG-based AD classification is conducted. By extracting and analysing topological metrics, measures of connectedness, and higher-order statistics, our study highlights the effectiveness of VG-based approaches in capturing distinctive characteristics of AD without the need for prior decomposition into frequency bands. The extracted features are evaluated using SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost, and Extra Trees. Despite its simplicity, SVM consistently achieved the highest accuracy across all VG variants. The study confirms patient-independent classification, achieving 95.2 % and 95.8 % accuracy for AD classification under EC conditions in dataset-1 and dataset-II, respectively. When both datasets were combined, the model further improved to 97.7 %, demonstrating promising patient-independent classification performance under the evaluated limited-data conditions. To ensure transparency, ANOVA is applied as a statistical test to validate feature significance, and SHAP is used to explain the model’s decisions. The results underscore the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed framework for AD classification and its possible uses in neuroscience and clinical domains.

papers.title: From assistants to auditors: opportunities and challenges of using general-purpose AI for auditing responsible AI systems
papers.authors: Javier Del Ser, Pedro A. Moreno-Sánchez, Emília Gómez, David Fernández Llorca
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence Systems (GPAIS) has introduced new capabilities and significant governance challenges. As regulations impose stringent transparency, accountability and auditability requirements, evaluating responsible AI systems –namely, AI systems with built-in auditability and accountability mechanisms that support their lawful and ethical operation– becomes increasingly complex and resource-intensive. This paper examines GPAIS as enablers of scalable, evidence-based auditing of such systems, while recognising that their own risks and limitations constrain their suitability as auditors. Our primary contribution is GRAAF, a structured framework for integrating GPAIS into responsible AI evaluation pipelines, conceptualised as a multi-level fusion problem spanning data, models, agents, and audit judgements, and formalised through reliability-, disagreement- and uncertainty-aware fusion operators. GRAAF progresses from GPAIS as assistants to human auditors towards semi- and fully automated auditing agents. Through a taxonomy of use cases, operational metrics, and governance safeguards, we show how GPAIS can augment explanation generation, bias detection, robustness testing, and compliance monitoring. We also address risks of overreliance, adversarial manipulation, and audit capture, proposing mitigation strategies and a roadmap for safe adoption. We further instantiate GRAAF in a clinical triage drift-monitoring case study, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) auditor, meta-audited against deterministic reference rules, met all predefined success criteria while exhibiting limitations that preclude autonomous certification. Scalable AI auditing thus hinges on fusing heterogeneous evidence, multi-agent reasoning, and multimodal signals, with GPAIS as orchestrators; within layered oversight architectures, this fusion can make auditing more trustworthy and scalable without compromising human accountability.

papers.title: Student perceptions of generative AI in accounting education: A thematic analysis
papers.authors: Ümmügülsüm Zor, Oğuzhan ARI
papers.journal: The International Journal of Management Education
papers.abstract: Generative AI has outpaced pedagogical and ethical guidance in accounting classrooms, leaving students and educators uncertain whether it supports or undermines the discipline's dual emphasis on procedural accuracy and professional judgment. To address this problem, this study examines how 92 business undergraduates perceive generative AI tools, notably ChatGPT, in accounting education, drawing on in-class, handwritten survey responses. Findings show that students view AI as a useful yet uncertain resource: valuing its speed, accessibility, and support while raising concerns over cheating, fairness, unclear institutional policies, and overreliance. Four interconnected themes emerged: Practical Affordances and Engagement, Ethical Tensions and Integrity, Curricular and Institutional Context, and Reflective Learning and Active Engagement. These results suggest student perceptions are shaped less by technology alone than by the pedagogical and ethical conditions of its introduction. Theoretically, the study identifies an augmentation–formation paradox specific to disciplines that combine codifiable procedure with professional judgment, which is advanced tentatively as extending the boundary conditions of paradox theory in education, a proposition that requires further empirical testing. Thematic analysis using a hybrid inductive–deductive coding strategy served as the primary analytic approach, supported by supplementary lexical analyses. The study contributes to management and accounting education by demonstrating that responsible AI integration requires clear guidance, reflective learning, and explicit alignment among AI use, assessment design, and academic integrity.

papers.title: Causal representation regularized heterogeneous graph neural network for robust EEG-fNIRS bimodal emotion recognition
papers.authors: Yushun Xiao, Cheng Lu, Tao Zhao, Xinxun Jiang, Hailun Lian, Shuo Shan, Jiateng Liu, Yuan Zong

papers.title: Beyond the equations: Integrating political economy into modelling green-growth pathways for low- and middle-income countries
papers.authors: Gerald Emmanuel Arhin, James Dixon, Lucas Somavilla Croxatto, Pietro Lubello, Jennifer Cronin, Leonhard Hofbauer, Fatima Afifah, Giulia Ragosa, Elena Pierard Manzano, Gregory Ireland, Steve Pye, Julia Tomei, Yacob Mulugetta
papers.abstract: Energy system models are increasingly used to guide infrastructure planning and energy and climate policy in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Yet these models are predominantly built around technical and economic assumptions that inadequately account for the political and institutional realities that shape whether modelling outputs are adopted and implemented. This perspective addresses that gap by presenting structured guidelines for integrating political economy analysis throughout the energy system modelling process. The guidelines focus on what needs to be considered at each stage, and signposts to theories and frameworks that can guide implementation. Drawing on the complementary expertise of political economists and modellers, and grounded in experiences across diverse LMIC settings, the guidelines inform seven stages of the modelling process: 1) problem definition, 2) model selection and world view, 3) data collection, 4) assumption setting and scenario development, 5) calibration and interpretation, 6) policy recommendation development, and 7) communication and engagement. The guidelines encourage iterative, reflexive and collaborative practices rather than a mechanical procedure. They emphasise stakeholder co-creation and transparency in model assumptions, along with sensitivity to power dynamics, institutional constraints, and political feasibility. We contend that the purpose of modelling is not solely to identify optimal solutions but to facilitate dialogue, build shared understanding, and support coalition formation around feasible pathways forward. Our contribution offers context-specific guidance that is responsive to the political realities of LMICs. These guidelines aim to strengthen the legitimacy and contextual relevance of modelling analyses in support of climate-compatible development.

papers.title: Operator workload responses to a VR-based cognitive and motor task before and after a 30-day simulated ICE mission: A multimodal ergonomic assessment
papers.authors: Jing Qu, Xiaoyi Zhou, Si Li, Kaili Yin, Jun Ding, Xinyi Wang, Lingguo Bu, 顿志平
papers.abstract: In isolated, confined and extreme (ICE) environments, prolonged sensory monotony, limited space and sustained task demands may affect operators’ cognitive performance and workload state, with potential consequences for mission safety and system reliability. This small-sample exploratory longitudinal repeated-measures study involved seven male participants in a 30-day simulated ICE mission and examined operator responses to a virtual reality (VR) cognitive and motor task at the pre-isolation and post-isolation measurement windows. The experimental factors were the pre-isolation and post-isolation measurement windows and the pre-VR and post-VR task phases. At each window, participants completed Stroop, Vigilance and reversed digit memory tasks, while cognitive task performance, subjective scales, VR movement behavior, electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) signals were recorded. After Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) correction, the clearest changes occurred in the Stroop task. Compared with the pre-isolation measurement window, the post-isolation window showed a higher Stroop completion count, a lower average reaction time and lower EEG Delta-band wavelet amplitude in the left occipital lobe, right occipital lobe, left motor cortex and left prefrontal cortex. In the pre-VR versus post-VR comparison, Stroop completion count increased and average reaction time decreased after VR. Other results from EEG effective connectivity, fNIRS, subjective scales, VR behavior and cross-modal associations did not show similarly stable corrected differences. The findings indicate that cognitive performance and neurophysiological measures describe different aspects of operator-state changes during confined, high-demand operations and may inform operator workload assessment, multimodal state monitoring and VR task design in ICE and similar operational environments.

papers.title: Hacking adaptation: What role can policy hackathons play in understanding and adapting to climate change impacts?
papers.authors: Sadie McEvoy, Marjolijn Haasnoot, Harm Albert Zanting, Ferdinand Diermanse, Karin de Bruijn, Vitória Alencar Passos, Beatriz Carneiro Menezes Silva, Renske de Winter
papers.abstract: Planners and policy makers face complex and pressing decisions under climate change. To complement traditional planning processes, new tools and methods are needed to make rapid and integrated assessments of climate change impacts and adaptation options. In this perspective, we reflect on the potential of policy hackathons to support climate adaptation planning and policy development.
