Drawing on five hackathons conducted in Brazil and the Netherlands, we illustrate how these short, intensive, co-creation events enabled first-order assessments of climate risks and adaptation options, fostered interdisciplinary collaboration, and catalyzed action. We argue that policy hackathons are a promising approach for exploring urgent and emergent questions, identifying knowledge gaps, and generating momentum within planning and policy-making processes. Hackathons also support the continuous learning and innovation required by adaptation. Most importantly, within planning and policy processes, hackathons can contribute to accelerating climate action.

papers.title: Adaptive visual feedback in VR displays: Modulating sense of agency and frustration during motor imagery interactions
papers.authors: Songyue Yang, Kang Yue, Haolin Gao, Mei Guo, Yue Liu

papers.title: Teaming or friction? Human–AI collaboration with a Multimodal Digital Intelligent Assistant in assembly manufacturing
papers.authors: Nicolò Sabetta, Filippo Bianchini, Marco Calamo, Francesco Costantino, Letizia Lorenzo, Massimo Mecella, Jacopo Rossi, Silvia Colabianchi
papers.abstract: The transition toward Industry 5.0 promotes human-centred production systems in which digital technologies augment human capabilities rather than replace them. Within this paradigm, Digital Intelligent Assistants have emerged as promising tools to support operators during complex industrial tasks. Moreover, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including Large Language Models and Vision Language Models, enables the development of such systems by combining natural language interaction with visual perception. This exploratory mixed-methods pilot study investigates the impact of a multimodal Digital Intelligent Assistant (M-DIA) designed to support operators during a manual assembly process. A controlled laboratory experiment involving 60 participants compared four conditions: multimodal interaction (voice and camera), voice-only interaction, camera-only interaction, and a manual baseline. The analysis considered process performance, perceived cognitive workload, usability and user experience, and operator behaviour. The results show that M-DIA improves assembly quality by reducing product errors compared with the manual condition, although no reduction in total process time is observed due to interaction-related delays. From a human perspective, the assistant reduces perceived cognitive workload, while higher frustration levels emerge in configurations involving voice interaction. Usability and user experience evaluations are overall positive across all experimental conditions. Behavioural observations further indicate that operators maintain an active supervisory role, critically assessing system outputs and avoiding systematic overreliance on the assistant. These findings provide preliminary empirical evidence on the role of GenAI-based multimodal assistants in human-centred manufacturing and highlight key design implications for their industrial deployment.

papers.title: Interpreting aberrant testing events in remote assessments: Innocuous or malicious?
papers.authors: William C. M. Belzak, Yigal Attali, Basim Baig, Rose Hastings, Connor Brem, Liberty Munson, John Kleeman
papers.abstract: Remote assessments are increasingly utilized in education and professional certification due to their accessibility and convenience. However, ensuring test security in these environments presents significant challenges, particularly in distinguishing between innocuous activity and more malicious behaviors. To address this, we introduce the Continuum of Deception (COD) framework, which ranks aberrant testing events along three dimensions: malicious intent, risk to score integrity, and verifiability. This framework guides empirical investigations across three complementary studies. Study 1 examines expert rankings of aberrant events and finds strong agreement on malicious intent and risk but less agreement on verifiability. Study 2 analyzes score changes among repeat test takers and finds that some flagged events, particularly speaking-related ones, are associated with large score gains. Study 3 evaluates proctoring agreement and finds that events detected with machine or AI assistance, such as plagiarism, are identified more consistently than events based on human observation alone, such as looking away excessively. We use these findings to develop a four-tier system of consequences for test takers, based on the severity of an event and how reliably it can be verified. By integrating theoretical and empirical insights, this research provides a structured approach to balancing test integrity with fairness in remote assessments.

papers.title: From lex ferenda to lex lata? AI and international law: converging existing principles with emerging standards
papers.authors: Alesia Zhuk
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has outpaced efforts to establish binding global regulation, leaving AI governed by a fragmented patchwork of national laws, regional instruments, and soft-law guidance. This paper advances two connected arguments. First, a complementarity thesis: in the absence of comprehensive AI-specific global standards, the established norms of international human rights law, international humanitarian law, and international criminal law supply a binding, near-universal baseline that fills regulatory gaps, guides interpretation, and disciplines the design of new instruments. Second, and more distinctively, a crystallisation thesis: the striking convergence of soft-law instruments – from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Principles (OECD) and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Recommendation to consensus General Assembly resolutions and the Council of Europe Framework Convention – around a recurring core of principles, notably transparency, accountability, and human oversight, indicates that general principles of law specific to AI are already forming, even as attempts to conclude binding instruments advance slowly. On this view, a court confronted with an AI dispute need not declare a non liquet: existing international law, thickened by these crystallising principles, precludes a legal vacuum. The paper substantiates these claims by examining the regulatory efforts of the United Nations, OECD, European Union, and standard-setting bodies, the obstacles to global harmonisation, and the application of existing legal principles to AI, arguing that a unified framework should consolidate this emerging normative acquis.

papers.title: Negative and positive emotional eating and food cravings related to weight loss during weight management
papers.authors: Michael Orwin, Gemma Traviss‐Turner, Robert West, Andrew J. Hill
papers.abstract: Emotional eating and food cravings are common among adults living with overweight or obesity. This study investigated these in relation to weight-management success and reports on strategies for managing emotional eating. A quasi-prospective study design was used including an online survey completed by 3,834 adults on a community weight management programme. Measures included negative and positive emotional eating (BEES) and food craving (CoEQ). Additionally, objectively measured body weight over the previous 12 weeks was obtained and participants were grouped into Higher (>10%, N=962), Moderate (5-10%, N=2156), and Lower (<5%, N=716) weight loss groups. Open questions were used to explore strategies for managing emotional eating. Between-group differences were tested using univariate ANOVAs, with Tukey post hoc comparisons where significant effects emerged. Open ended responses were analysed using inductive thematic analysis and mapped onto the Behaviour Change Taxonomy. Respondents were mostly female (92.0%), mean age=57.2 years, and BMI=32.1 kg/m 2 . Results showed participants had lost 3.7 BMI units over the previous 12 weeks. Higher weight loss was strongly associated with lower negative and positive emotional eating, fewer food cravings and eating control difficulties. Prominent themes for managing emotional eating were distraction (31.7%) and physical activity along with healthier food substitutions, planning and positive mindset. Group social support was also highlighted. These data highlight the perceived importance of psychological and group-based social support in weight management.

papers.title: AI literacy for AI natives? A four-country comparison
papers.authors: Caroline Cohrssen, Parian Madanipour, Cristina Guarrella, Mia Yue Chen, Somin Park
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly mainstream in children's homes and everyday lives. Using neo-ecological theory as a conceptual framework and Yang et al.'s (2026) five-component AI literacy progression model as an analytical lens, this document analysis examined core ECEC curricula and related guiding documents currently in use in Australia, China, Japan, and South Korea to determine whether early childhood education and care (ECEC) guiding documents are keeping pace with the rapid development. The analysis reveals that the curricula of Japan and South Korea contain no explicit reference to AI literacy, prioritising human-to-human relationships and offline safety. China's national ECEC guidelines similarly contain no AI references. However, Shanghai's strategic action plan explicitly positions kindergartens within broader AI education initiatives, though without specifying pedagogical progressions for young learners. Australia demonstrates limited and uneven alignment across AI literacy components, with the strongest alignment in “Interacting with AI Agents” and no alignment in “Understanding Human-AI Relationships”. Young children’s development of AI literacy is thus likely to remain contingent on the home environment, where they may be interacting with AI agents and creating artefacts more than developing awareness of ethical considerations and risks. Wide differences in children's foundational AI literacy capabilities may entrench educational disadvantage along the lines of AI literacy as it becomes increasingly mainstream in society. We argue that curriculum-guiding documents should be strengthened by articulating explicit AI literacy learning priorities and developmental expectations for young children, accompanied by culturally responsive resources to equip educators to facilitate equitable learning.

papers.title: A fuzzy decision support system for monitoring student academic performance and supporting early intervention
papers.authors: Xiaoxiao Liu, Kewei Wen
papers.abstract: In digital learning environments, monitoring of students’ learning behavior is challenging due to the uncertainty, incompleteness, and gradual changes in student learning behavior. Current prediction models may achieve good performance but offer little interpretability and limited support for timely academic intervention. This study proposes an interpretable Fuzzy Decision Support System (FDSS) for monitoring student academic performance and supporting early intervention strategies. It combines academic, behavioral, and engagement measures from the xAPI-Edu-Data dataset with a Mamdani fuzzy inference mechanism, triangular and trapezoidal membership functions, and centroid defuzzification. The FDSS was assessed using classification measures, early-warning analysis, sensitivity testing, and comparison with baseline machine learning models. The proposed system achieved an overall accuracy of 0.86, a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.84, an AUC of 0.91, and a High-Risk recall of 0.89. The results indicate that the FDSS is a viable tool for predicting academic performance and for providing rule-based academic intervention support that is transparent to the user.

papers.title: Towards clinical communication training with LLM-based conversational virtual patients and automatic evaluation systems
papers.authors: Andrea Bayona, Rubén Manrique, Christian Grévisse
papers.abstract: Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” ( $$\rho = 0.64$$ ) and lowest for “Completeness” ( $$\rho = 0.09$$ ), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.

papers.title: Guidelines for AI-supported virtual laboratories in science museums
papers.authors: Jorge Sanabria-Z, Pamela Olivo, Amadeo Argüelles, Inna Artemova
papers.abstract: Abstract Science museums are increasingly positioned as spaces for non-formal sustainability education, yet systematic frameworks for integrating AI-supported virtual laboratories into these environments remain scarce. This review article proposes a preliminary conceptual framework for the design of AI-integrated virtual laboratories in science museums, with a focus on citizen science participation and socioecological challenges. Through a Delphi-oriented, internal designer-led consensus process combining two rounds of multidisciplinary reflection with LLM-assisted synthesis, the study identifies thirteen dimensions: contextual understanding, operational sustainability, research support, educational design, audience personalization, technological infrastructure, physical-digital interaction, operability, ethics, participation, accessibility, interculturality, and international collaboration. Each dimension is characterized by possible AI capabilities and intended outcomes. Developed in connection with LúmiaLab, a virtual interdisciplinary laboratory currently in its conceptual design phase with the Museum of Environmental Sciences in Guadalajara, Mexico, the framework is contextually grounded but has not yet been independently or empirically validated. It contributes a structured theoretical-practical reference for subsequent co-design, piloting, and external validation rather than evidence of educational effectiveness or generalizability.

papers.title: Multiclass neurodegenerative disease classification framework based on explainable ensemble learning using cerebrospinal fluid proteomic data
papers.authors: Laxmikantha K., Ashok Kumar P. S., Anupkumar M. Bongale
papers.abstract: Early and accurate stratification of Alzheimer Disease (AD) is a key requirement in the field of neuroscience. This article presents a machine learning framework for multiclass AD classification across three classes: Control, Asymptomatic Alzheimer’s Disease (ASYMAD), and Alzheimer’s Disease using Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) proteomics data. A publicly available dataset comprising 393 CSF samples with 62 synaptic peptide features was utilized in this study. We used six base classifiers—Elastic Net, Random Forest, XGBoost, Linear SVM, LightGBM and CatBoost—trained and evaluated with nested stratified 5 fold cross validation with inner loop randomized hyperparameter search. Based on their complementary linear and nonlinear inductive biases, an ensemble consisting of Elastic Net, CatBoost, and Linear SVM as base learners with a logistic regression meta learner was designed, and was benchmarked against an equal weight soft voting ensemble. The stacked ensemble achieved the highest point estimate for accuracy of \(0.832 \pm 0.052\) and the highest macro one-versus-rest ROC-AUC of \(0.952 \pm 0.012\) , with a macro F1 of \(0.826 \pm 0.059\) ; however, its improvement over the best single model , Elastic Net at macro \(\hbox {F1} = 0.827\) , and over the simpler soft voting ensemble at macro \(\hbox {F1} = 0.828\) was small and not statistically significant after a Friedman omnibus test and Bonferroni corrected pairwise Wilcoxon tests. Model calibration was additionally quantified using reliability diagrams, the multiclass Brier score, and Expected Calibration Error. Through eXplainable SHAP analysis consensus candidate peptide features were identified that are consistently selected across Elastic Net, Random Forest, and XGBoost, including ELDVLQGR, AQALEQAK, and ELQAAQAR, offering biologically interpretable signals that warrant independent validation before clinical use.

papers.title: Enhancing Prehospital Emergency Care Through Reliable Assessment of Consciousness Levels: A Structured Narrative Review
papers.authors: Joao C. Ferreira, Pedro Faria, Filipa Barros
papers.abstract: Altered level of consciousness (ALOC) is among the most frequent and most consequential presentations in prehospital emergency care. Registry data from unselected ambulance populations indicate that approximately one in eight transported patients has a reduced Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, and that even mild reductions carry substantial 30-day mortality. Assessment of consciousness governs airway management, transport destination, and activation of stroke and traumatic brain injury (TBI) pathways. The GCS and the AVPU scale (rendered AVDS in Portuguese-language services) are the instruments in routine field use, yet both were developed and validated predominantly outside the prehospital environment. This review addresses four questions: (i) the clinical importance of consciousness assessment in prehospital care; (ii) the reliability and validity of the GCS, AVPU/AVDS, and FOUR score, with specific attention to performance in EMS provider cohorts; (iii) the operational and human-factor determinants that degrade assessment accuracy in the field; and (iv) the current evidence for objective adjuncts to subjective scoring. We conducted a structured narrative review reported in accordance with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026, combining controlled-vocabulary and free-text terms across four concept blocks: consciousness; assessment instruments; prehospital/EMS setting; and reliability, validity, accuracy, and inter-rater agreement. Records were screened independently by two reviewers. Where a prior review was identified, its reference list was hand-searched and the underlying primary studies were retrieved and cited in preference to the review, so that evidence is not double-counted. Thirty-six sources form the synthesis corpus. A narrative rather than systematic design was chosen because the eligible literature is heterogeneous in design, population, and outcome metric to a degree that precludes meaningful pooling; the trade-offs of this choice are stated explicitly. Field GCS correlates with arrival GCS ( r = 0.67; n = 12,882) and the change between the two independently predicts mortality. The GCS is the most granular instrument, but its reliability is component-dependent, with the motor component consistently weakest; after structured training, weighted kappa reached 0.85–0.96 across components, motor response remaining lowest at 75.1% agreement. For AVPU/AVDS, large prehospital datasets localise disagreement precisely to the Verbal and Pain categories: in 4.3 million paediatric EMS encounters, overall AVPU-GCS accuracy was 0.95 (kappa = 0.61) but intraclass F1 fell to 0.37 for Verbal and 0.50 for Pain, against 0.98 for Alert; in 2,900 prehospital trauma activations, GCS differed significantly between all AVPU categories except Verbal versus Pain ( p = 0.18). The FOUR score shows modestly superior reliability and validity to the GCS in ICU and ED settings but has not been validated prehospitally. Substituting GCS-motor for total GCS increases undertriage in patients over 65 ( n = 4,480,185). Automated pupillometry substantially outperforms manual pupil examination (ICC 0.99 versus 0.92), and low Neurological Pupil Index (NPi) values are consistently associated with adverse TBI outcomes, though prognostic accuracy in isolation is moderate (AUC 0.66–0.68). Ambulance-based EEG recording is feasible but remains at proof-of-concept stage. The evidence supports specific, bounded recommendations rather than broad prescription. Calibration training should target the GCS motor component and the AVPU/AVDS Verbal-Pain boundary, which are the empirically identified loci of disagreement. Total GCS should be retained over GCS-motor for field triage, particularly in older patients, and all three components should be documented and handed over alongside the total. Automated pupillometry is the most mature adjunct and warrants piloting in defined high-yield scenarios. The central evidence gap remains the principal research priority: no study has directly compared GCS, AVPU/AVDS, and FOUR score reliability within a prehospital provider cohort under field conditions.

papers.title: Obesity and Early Biologic Failure in Psoriasis: An Italian Multicentre Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.authors: Jacopo Tartaglia, Massimo Donini, Carlo Garbo, Alessandro Gatti, Paolo Gisondi, Niccolò Romagnolo, Lorenzo SCHIESARI, Stefano Piaserico
papers.abstract: Introduction Obesity may reduce biologic effectiveness in psoriasis, but its effect on specific reasons for treatment discontinuation is less well defined. We evaluated the association between obesity and biologic drug survival, with particular attention to primary failure and therapeutic class. Methods This retrospective multicentre cohort study included patients with plaque psoriasis treated with biologics at five Italian dermatology centres. Analyses were conducted at the treatment-line level using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards models. Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m2. BMI was also examined continuously and using a natural cubic spline. Logistic regression and Cox models with standard errors clustered by patient were used as sensitivity analyses. Results Overall, 573 patients contributed 770 treatment lines; 193 of 562 patients with available BMI data (34.3%) were obese. Primary failure occurred in 17.0% of treatment lines from patients with obesity and 5.8% of treatment lines from patients without obesity (log-rank p < 0.001). In the adjusted Cox model, obesity was associated with a higher risk of primary failure (hazard ratio [HR] 2.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.59–4.77). Each 5 kg/m2 increase in BMI was associated with a 37% higher risk (HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.14–1.65), with evidence of non-linearity (likelihood ratio p = 0.0018). Compared with tumour necrosis factor-α inhibitors, interleukin (IL)-17 inhibitors (HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.24–0.97) and IL-23 pathway inhibitors (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.24–0.93) showed lower primary failure risks. Obesity was not associated with secondary failure or safety-related discontinuation. Conclusion Obesity was associated mainly with early biologic failure in psoriasis. The association was most evident with tumour necrosis factor-α inhibitors.

papers.title: From the operating room to the cloud: the evolving continuum from live surgical broadcasting to remote tele-surgery
papers.authors: Priyank Yadav, Husam H. Balkhy, Mohan S. Gundeti
papers.abstract: In the last four decades, the transmission of a live surgical operation to a remote audience has evolved from closed-circuit educational broadcast into a fully remote, robot-assisted surgery performed across different continents. This review maps that journey systematically, defining a six-rung Digital Surgical Spectrum - from passive live broadcast to artificial-intelligence-augmented autonomous surgery - grounding each stage in published clinical evidence across multiple surgical domains. We demonstrate that each rung of this spectrum is no longer theoretical. Live broadcasts have reached audiences across multiple countries. Tele-proctoring was validated at scale during the COVID-19 pandemic, and tele-mentoring has been shown in systematic review to produce a safety and efficacy profile broadly comparable to on-site supervision. True remote tele-surgery has been accomplished over distances exceeding 8,000 km with latencies well within established procedure specific safety thresholds. We also present a case timeline and an Institutional Readiness Framework specifying the technical, regulatory, and other prerequisites for each rung, organized visually as a Digital Surgical Spectrum. Importantly, nuances such as the performance paradox of observed surgery, consent frameworks, cybersecurity risk, regulatory fragmentation, and the threat of entrenching rather than correcting global surgical inequity are examined. As the field advances, the growth of tele-surgical technologies will depend on international regulatory harmonization and equity-centered deployment, supported by prospective multi-specialty outcome registries.

papers.title: Developing computational thinking in teacher education: a brief experience with coding, robotics, and machine learning
papers.authors: Susana Sánchez Castro, María Ángeles Pascual Sevillano, Rogelio Buceta Otero, Javier Fombona Cadavieco
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines post-intervention self-reported outcomes associated with a short intervention designed to introduce coding, educational robotics, and introductory concepts of machine learning into initial teacher education for Primary Education. The proposal is grounded in Papert’s principles and the Creative and Computational Problem Solving model, combining active learning methodologies with accessible technologies. A quasi-experimental design with a non-equivalent control group was employed. A total of 144 first-year students from three Spanish universities participated (105 in the experimental group and 39 in the control group). The intervention consisted of a two-hour workshop with hands-on stations and technological challenges, designed as a feasible microintervention within regular teacher education contexts. Assessment was carried out through an ad hoc questionnaire focused on three dimensions: knowledge of programming and machine learning, block-based programming and game engines, and active learning, all assessed through self-reported perceptions. The results showed statistically significant post-intervention differences in favor of the experimental group, with a small effect size for knowledge of programming and machine learning and large effect sizes for block-based programming and game engines and active learning. Item-level analyses revealed that favorable overall perceptions coexisted with lower self-reported familiarity in specific technical areas, particularly machine learning, prior experience with block-based programming, and programming in game engines. Three exploratory response profiles were also identified: reluctant, intermediate, and enthusiastic. The findings suggest that well-structured microinterventions may support higher self-reported knowledge of programming and machine learning, greater familiarity with block-based programming and game engines, and more positive perceptions of active learning in teacher education.

papers.title: Concept-Based Explainable AI in Retinal Imaging: Core Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
papers.authors: Mohadeseh Mollapour Papkyadeh, Koorosh Aslansefat, Bhupesh Kumar Mishra, Tejal Shah, Zhibao Mian, Mehran Hosseinalizadeh
papers.journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
papers.abstract: In high-stakes domains like healthcare, establishing trust in AI-assisted decisions is critical for fostering confidence among experts and researchers. However, standard explanation methods may not fully meet clinical needs, offering raw data, such as saliency maps, rather than human-readable text and auditable, transparent reasoning. To bridge this gap, researchers are increasingly adopting concept-based approaches that express model reasoning through human-readable concepts grounded in expert-backed clinical knowledge. Although this field has advanced rapidly in recent years, retinal C-XAI remains methodologically heterogeneous, with limited agreement on taxonomy, evaluation, and clinical validation. This review identifies recurring reliability gaps in retinal C-XAI and synthesises potential directions for addressing them, including independent concept-level auditing, robustness testing, and clinician-informed validation. As an illustrative example, we discuss how the established SMILE methodology could be adapted for concept-level auditing in retinal C-XAI; this is presented as a candidate research direction rather than a new or clinically validated framework.

papers.title: Preoperative pain and achievement of the minimal clinically important difference for physical function one year after total hip arthroplasty: a prospective cohort study
papers.authors: Rubén Eduardo Gajardo-Burgos, Ricardo Arteaga San Martín, Jorge Fuentes, Manuel A. Monrroy Uarac, Cristhian Saavedra-Santiesteban, Claudio Bascour–Sandoval, Eduardo Sáez de Villarreal
papers.journal: Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To examine the association between preoperative social, clinical, and biological variables and the achievement of the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) on the WOMAC-function subscale one year post total hip arthroplasty (THA). METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, 85 patients (aged ≥ 65) completed baseline preoperative assessment, and 53 completed the 12-month follow-up (32 lost to follow-up; 66.0% achieved MCID). The outcome was achieving WOMAC-function MCID (≥ 26.54 points). Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for baseline pain, age, sex, and BMI were performed. ROC curves evaluated discriminative capacity. RESULTS: An exploratory ROC analysis identified a baseline pain threshold of 6.5 on the Numerical Rating Scale yielded an AUC of 0.740 (70% sensitivity, 77% specificity). CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative pain intensity independently associated with clinically meaningful functional improvement post-THA. An exploratory pain threshold of 6.5 on the NRS may provide an exploratory benchmark for future risk stratification.

papers.authors: Christoph R. Landolt, Tobias Lorenz, Marta Kwiatkowska, Mario Fritz

papers.title: Theorizing future phenomena: Metaverse, wearables, and humanoids
papers.authors: Andy Wu, Ronald Wang
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

papers.title: Understanding Early Attitudes Towards Generative AI Regulation in Higher Education: The Role of Academic Scientists’ Experience and Risk Perceptions
papers.authors: Jinghuan Ma, Tipeng Chen, Rong Zuo, Timothy P. Johnson, Eric W. Welch, Ashlee Frandell, Wenceslao Arroyo‐Machado, Lesley Michalegko
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology rapidly permeates higher education, it creates opportunities to transform teaching, research, and workforce preparation while raising ethical, social and environmental concerns. Academic scientists have a unique role in this transition as their early exposure to publicly accessible GenAI tools shapes emerging practices, norms, and institutional responses. Existing research often treats AI‐related risk as a single construct, limiting understanding of how distinct risk dimensions shape regulatory preferences. This study investigates how academic scientists’ experience with GenAI relates to risk perceptions over agency loss and data breach, and how these perceptions are associated with their regulatory attitudes during its formative stage. Using survey data collected between September and November 2023, shortly after ChatGPT became widely accessible, we find that greater GenAI experience is associated with lower perceived risks. Meanwhile, different risk perceptions are linked to distinct regulatory preferences: perceived risk of agency loss is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation and a lower likelihood of supporting academic self‐regulation, whereas perceived data breach risk is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation but not associated with the likelihood of supporting self‐regulation. These findings provide an early baseline understanding of faculty attitudes toward GenAI regulation in academic contexts.

papers.title: An Explainable Self‐Supervised Temporal Transformer for Participant‐Level Classification of Depressive Symptoms From Resting‐State EEG
papers.authors: Pushpamala Ramaiah, Ibtesam Nomani, Hayam Ibrahim Asfour, Mirza R. Baig, Maksudjan Yuldashev, Ibrokhim Sapaev, Zein Bassam Bani Younes, Sumit Sharma, Mahesh Manchanda, Mohamad Ahmad Saleem Khasawneh, Majid S. Jabir
papers.journal: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive modality for investigating depressive symptoms; however, conventional deep-learning methods often require large labeled datasets and provide limited interpretability. We developed an Explainable Self-Supervised Temporal Transformer Network for participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG. METHODS: The framework employed masked temporal modeling for self-supervised pretraining followed by supervised fine-tuning. Model performance was evaluated using repeated nested participant-wise cross-validation and compared with conventional machine-learning and deep-learning baselines. Explainability was investigated through transformer attention maps and SHAP-based channel attribution. RESULTS: The proposed model achieved a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.73-0.90), a precision-recall AUC of 0.69, balanced accuracy of 0.75, sensitivity of 0.72, and specificity of 0.78. The positive predictive value was 0.57, indicating a substantial false-positive burden in the evaluated cohort. The proposed model showed the highest point-estimate ROC-AUC among the evaluated baselines, with a 0.07 improvement over EEGNet; however, the overlapping uncertainty intervals and the small elevated-symptom cohort warrant cautious interpretation of comparative superiority. Performance decreased from an ROC-AUC of 0.82 in Run 1 to 0.78 in Run 2 and to 0.72-0.73 under cross-condition transfer, supporting interpretation of these analyses as internal reproducibility and condition-shift assessments rather than independent external validation. Removing self-supervised pretraining reduced the ROC-AUC to 0.74. Explainability analyses identified distributed temporally relevant intervals and frontal-midline to centro-parietal channel contributions, with attribution interpreted as model-relevance evidence rather than causal biomarker evidence. CONCLUSION: Overall, the findings provide preliminary internal evidence that self-supervised temporal representation learning can support participant-level classification of BDI-defined elevated depressive symptoms from resting-state EEG under the evaluated experimental conditions. The findings do not establish clinical diagnostic validity, screening readiness, or independent external generalizability.

papers.title: Peer Effects in Digital Finance Usage and Rural Household Consumption: A Double Machine Learning Approach
papers.authors: Hanxiao Li, Shaozhe Li, 陈思琪, Liqiong Lin
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Using data from the China Household Finance Survey (CHFS), this study develops a simplified intertemporal household consumption‐saving model and uses double machine learning to examine peer effects in digital finance usage and their influence on rural household consumption. The results show significant peer effects in rural households' digital finance usage. The estimates further show that peer households' digital finance usage is positively related to consumption among focal households. The positive relationship is more pronounced among households with greater wealth, higher education levels and lower degrees of ageing. Mechanism analyses suggest that peer households' digital finance usage is linked to weaker liquidity constraints and lower precautionary saving motives among focal households. Further analysis indicates that peer households' digital finance usage relates to both survival‐oriented consumption and development‐oriented consumption, as well as greater breadth of consumption‐category participation. Accordingly, this study argues that strengthening the social learning effect of digital finance usage is crucial for enhancing rural households' consumption capacity and fostering sustainable rural economic development.

papers.title: Are AI Recommendations Less Green? The Effects of AI Recommendation Sources and Green Product Attribute Framing on Consumer Responses
papers.authors: Li Ayong, HE Ai-zhong, Weisha Wang
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Extant research has reported mixed evidence regarding the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) recommendations in promoting green products, leaving it unclear under which conditions such recommendations are more (or less) effective. Drawing on Self‐Determination Theory (SDT), this research addresses this ambiguity by proposing a congruence effect between AI recommendation sources (substitute versus augmented AI) and green product attribute framing (utility‐based versus sustainability‐based). Using four scenario‐based online experiments (total N = 1114)—including one product choice task, one preference evaluation, and two studies measuring purchase intention and willingness to pay—this research demonstrates that substitute (augmented) AI recommendations are more effective for utility‐framed (sustainability‐framed) green products. Furthermore, consumers' sense of control mediates this congruence effect, and providing attribute‐based post hoc explanations eliminates the disadvantage of substitute AI under sustainability framing by shifting consumer responses toward sustainability‐framed green products. These findings advance understanding of human–AI interaction in green consumption and offer actionable insights for businesses seeking to leverage AI recommenders to increase the market share of green products.

papers.title: Changing Food Environments and Behaviours
papers.authors: Lucy Cokes
papers.abstract: Session: Young People Changing the Food System – Restorative Practice and Behaviour Change This practice research addresses a critical public health challenge: the high consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPF) among adolescents, who currently derive approximately 70% of their daily energy intake from UPFs. Recognising that traditional, information-based health education rarely produces sustained dietary shifts in young people, this project investigates how co-created creative advertising, choice architecture, and behavioural science can be integrated into secondary school environments to drive positive, long-term behavioural change. Developed as a collaborative project between be.good (Falmouth University’s in-house agency led by Lucy Cokes), local GP Dr Rhiannon Day-Thompson, and undergraduate Creative Advertising students, the inquiry culminated in a live, whole-school pilot intervention deployed at Camborne Science & International Academy (CSIA). The research offers a novel, youth-centric co-creation model that bridges academic research, clinical expertise, and student graphic design. The design and implementation of the intervention are grounded in theoretical frameworks from implementation science and policy development, including the COM-B Model of Behaviour Change (Michie et al., 2011), The Balm Behavioural Model (Balm, 2002) and. The EAST Framework (Behavioural Insights Team, 2014). Presented at the Sustainable Food Cornwall Summit 2026 to regional public health leads, educators, policy makers, and food sustainability partners, this presentation effectively shared initial insights, real-world pilot findings, and theoretical approaches from the CSIA rollout. The research establishes a scalable, evidence-backed methodology for secondary schools across the region, serving as the blueprint for an expanded, funded multi-school research study launching in September 2027.

papers.title: Σχεδίαση και ανάπτυξη προσωποποιημένης διαλογικής διεπαφής για εφαρμογή "Fantasy football"
papers.authors: Ιγνάτιος Παναγιώτης Τουβλέλιος
papers.abstract: Fantasy Premier League (FPL) is one of the world’s most popular online fantasy sports games, in which millions of managers worldwide are required to make a series of critical decisions regarding their virtual teams every gameweek, in order to accumulate as many points as possible from the real-world performances of the footballers they select. However, the official platform primarily provides raw statistical information and limited decision-support capabilities, while existing third-party applications are mainly targeted at experienced users and frequently organise information through dense tables and long lists of metrics. Managers are therefore forced to switch between multiple websites and tools to analyse players, compare alternatives, and manage their squads, frequently through subscription-based services. They are left with a fragmented and demanding environment that imposes a considerable cognitive load and requires substantial time to learn, and that becomes difficult to use for those without much experience. This thesis presents the design, development, and evaluation of a complete full-stack Fantasy Football web application with a personalized conversational interface (AI chatbot). The central contribution is twofold: first, it implements the game itself and comprehensively redesigns the overall user experience (UI/UX) compared with both the official Fantasy Premier League application and existing third-party platforms, bringing together team management, data analysis, player-performance predictions, and decisionsupport functionalities within a single coherent and user-friendly environment. Second, it integrates a conversational Artificial Intelligence coaching assistant that personalises its recommendations according to each manager’s preferences, playing style, and current squad status, providing tailored explanations and decision support through natural language interaction. Underneath runs a machine-learning pipeline that forecasts points, minutes played and likelihood of appearance for the next gameweek, using gradient-boosted tree models with rolling-origin cross-validation and an acceptance check that retains the previous model whenever a retrained one performs worse. The resulting predictions are utilised by a hybrid recommendation engine that combines machine-learning techniques with heuristic rules, as well as by an integer linear programming optimiser for constructing the initial squad. A Large Language Model layer then turns these structured numerical recommendations into natural, explanatory dialogue. The platform is supported by a complete backend, a relational database, an automated data-synchronisation mechanism, a job-scheduling system, and user authentication. The implementation employs the Next.js and Express frameworks with TypeScript, Python for the machinelearning pipeline, and PostgreSQL for data management. The system was evaluated with respect to the accuracy of its predictive models, the quality of its recommendations, and the usability, clarity, and overall user experience delivered by the application.

papers.title: Da resposta da IA ao julgamento próprio: pensamento crítico e autonomia do estudante
papers.authors: Juan de Jesús Alvarado Ortiz, Oralia Mercedes Moguel Morales, Francisco Jesus Vieyra Gonzalez, Onelia Hernández Torres
papers.abstract: Introduction: The growing integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has transformed the way students access, process, and produce information, creating new learning opportunities while also raising risks associated with cognitive dependence. The objective of this study was to analyze the relationship between the use of generative artificial intelligence, critical thinking, and student autonomy, identifying the conditions that foster independent judgment and those that may promote excessive delegation of reasoning. Materials and methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, considering publications from 2021 to 2026 in high-impact academic databases. After the identification, screening, and eligibility stages, 24 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. The results revealed four main thematic areas: AI as cognitive support, critical thinking and evaluation of AI-generated responses, self-regulation and student agency, and cognitive dependence or cognitive offloading. Conclusions: It is concluded that AI does not automatically strengthen or weaken student autonomy; its effect depends on the degree of cognitive control retained by the learner. When AI-generated responses are contrasted, verified, and critically reflected upon, AI can enhance learning; when they are accepted uncritically, the risk of dependence and loss of independent judgment increases.

papers.title: MAIN DIRECTIONS AND RESULTS OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN THE FIELD OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: Utkirbek Mutalibjonovich Muxtarov
papers.journal: International Bulletin of Engineering and Technology
papers.abstract: This scientific article highlights the main directions of scientific research in the field of artificial intelligence, the results achieved, and their significance in the development of modern society. It analyzes the developmental characteristics of areas such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence. Opportunities arising from the application of artificial intelligence technologies in the fields of education, medicine, industry, economics, and information technology will also be considered.

papers.title: 4Cast Lab: Open-Source App for Machine Learning & Statistical Analysis
papers.authors: Periklis Gogas
papers.abstract: 4Cast Lab is a free, open-source application for machine learning, econometrics and statistical analysis that runs on the user's own computer, with no installation, no programming and no data leaving the machine. It was developed at the E|M|E|F Lab, Department of Economics, Democritus University of Thrace, for researchers, analysts, instructors and students in any field. Its Forecasting mode trains eight learning algorithms (with three kernels for SVM/SVR), implemented from scratch, under leakage-safe validation for time-ordered data; it selects models by cross-validation, compares the selected model with every alternative and with naive benchmarks through formal tests of predictive accuracy, and documents each run in a methods report and a Python script that the user can export. Its Estimation mode covers the core of applied econometrics, from OLS with robust inference to ARIMA, ARDL, VAR/VECM and GARCH. This paper describes the design, the interface and the workflow of version 4.6.2, reports a validation of 1,234 numerical results against statsmodels, linearmodels, arch, scikit-learn and NIST certified values, illustrates the workflow with three examples, and discusses current limitations.

papers.title: More Than Memes: Recognition, Justification, and the Work of Understanding
papers.authors: Joanne Irving-Walton, Helen Tidy, Giulia Bini, Maria (Masha) Wald, Marina Gazzini, Stefano Bertacchi
papers.journal: Research in Digital Learning in Higher Education
papers.abstract: This short paper emerged from a multidisciplinary collaboration investigating the use of memes in higher education across Biology, Education, Forensic Science, Mathematics, Medieval History, and Russian Studies. As colleagues compared examples from different disciplines, it became clear that the most interesting questions were not about memes themselves. Instead, the project highlighted a broader issue concerning how learners encounter meaning through digital artefacts and how moments of recognition relate to deeper disciplinary understanding. What began as a study of memes ultimately led to a wider exploration of interpretation, justification, and the work of understanding in digitally mediated learning environments. This short paper explores how digital artefacts - including memes, diagrams, AI-generated summaries, visual explanations, and discussion formats - shape interpretation within higher education. It argues that such artefacts often make ideas recognisable before they are fully justifiable within disciplinary frameworks. Students may identify patterns, coherence, or intended meaning before they are able to explain, critique, or defend those interpretations through disciplinary reasoning. This distinction has become increasingly significant in the context of generative AI, where fluency and coherence can easily be mistaken for understanding. Drawing on examples from practice and insights from edusemiotics, digital pedagogy, and disciplinary learning, the discussion reframes digital artefacts not as simple engagement tools but as sites of interpretive and intellectual work. The paper concludes with practical reflective questions and open-access resources designed to support colleagues in working more intentionally with digital artefacts in their own teaching.

papers.title: University students’ perceptions of technology-enhanced education in the Albanian context: Opportunities and concerns
papers.authors: Lenida Lekli, Ardita Dylgjeri, Lumnis Çela, Fatos Gjata, Ornela Çoku
papers.abstract: This article deals with university students’ perceptions of digital technology within the Albanian context. Conducted as part of a project, funded by the National Agency of Scientific Research and Innovation in Albania, the research adopted an integrated qualitative-quantitative design based on a questionnaire with 835 students across the five faculties of “Aleksandër Xhuvani” University. The findings revealed large access to personal digital devices for educational engagement, alongside institutional infrastructure generally rated as moderate. Students reported predominantly positive perception of digital technology, associating it with improved study quality, motivation and task facilitation, although its role was mostly viewed as supportive rather than transformative. Notably, students drew a distinction between general digital technology which was viewed more favorably, and artificial intelligence which raised concerns related to potential intellectual laziness and limitations to creativity and critical thinking. Based on the research, the findings suggest that Albanian higher education requires a digital integration model which balances technological accessibility with responsible digital literacy, ongoing institutional support, and meaningful human engagement in the learning process.

papers.title: Penguatan Literasi Kecerdasan Buatan (Artificial Intelligence) bagi Mahasiswa untuk Meningkatkan Adaptasi di Era Digital
papers.authors: Ifnu Wisma Dwi Prastya, Lisa Aminatul Mukarromah, Mula Agung Barata
papers.journal: Karsa Bhakti Journal of Community Service
papers.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology in the digital era has changed students' learning patterns, but its utilization has not been fully accompanied by adequate conceptual literacy and ethical understanding. Students generally have used various AI-based platforms, but this is still limited to practical use without understanding the working principles, information validity, and academic limitations. This community service activity aims to improve students' artificial intelligence literacy as an effort to adapt to the demands of learning and the working world in the digital era. The implementation method of the activity includes the preparation stage, socialization, practice-based training using Giri AI, and evaluation through pretest and posttest. The activity was held on February 23, 2026, at the Faculty of Sharia and Adab Building of Nahdlatul Ulama Sunan Giri University, involving 30 students from UNUGIRI, IKIP, UNIGORO, and Universiti Malaysia Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah. The implementation results showed a significant increase in participants' AI literacy, demonstrated by the average score rising from 58.8 in the pretest to 86.0 in the posttest, an increase of approximately 46%. This training not only enhanced the skills in using AI academically but also built ethical awareness and critical thinking abilities among students in responsibly leveraging technology in the era of digital transformation.

papers.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
papers.authors: Yangfan Lu, Yang Zhang, Hongwei Ding, Yi Lin
papers.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

papers.title: Enhancing Students' Learning Effectiveness through the Integration of Differentiated Instruction and Modern Digital Technologies

papers.abstract: This article analyzes the pedagogical potential of integrating differentiated instruction with modern digital technologies in the context of general secondary education, taking into account students’ individual educational needs, level of knowledge, pace of learning, and cognitive abilities. It substantiates the potential for increasing the degree of individualization of the educational process through the integration of traditional forms of differentiated instruction with digital educational tools, adaptive learning systems, educational platforms, electronic assessment, multimedia resources, and artificial intelligence-based technologies.

papers.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Translation: Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for Future Translators
papers.authors: Muhabbat Alisher kizi Safarova
papers.journal: Spanish Journal of Innovation and Integrity
papers.abstract: In today’s world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an increasingly influential technology in the field of translation, transforming both professional translation practices and translator education. The development of neural machine translation, large language models, and generative AI systems has provided translators with new opportunities to improve productivity, manage terminology, generate initial translations, and perform post-editing tasks. At the same time, the growing use of AI raises important concerns related to translation accuracy, cultural and contextual interpretation, ethical responsibility, data privacy, and the changing role of human translators. Recent research indicates that AI-assisted translation should not be viewed simply as a replacement for human translation. Instead, it increasingly requires translators to develop technological literacy, critical evaluation skills, post-editing competence, and the ability to make context-sensitive decisions. This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence in modern translation, focusing particularly on its opportunities and challenges for future translators.

papers.title: Modeling Student-Centered Feedback Mechanisms: ChatGPT-Supported Feedback in the Feedback Orientation Scale for Secondary Chinese Reading
papers.authors: SIYI ZHU Augustine
papers.abstract: This study addresses the underexplored role of ChatGPT-supported feedback within secondary Chinese reading contexts in mainland China, characterized by constrained persistent teacher-centered instruction, limited AI-related research and access to transnational AI systems. Conceptualizing the Feedback Orientation Scale (FOS) as a student-centered model, the study examines how ChatGPT-supported and conventional human-generated feedback differentially influence underlying processes and overall learning gains. Psychometric evaluation preceded a quasi-experimental pre–post design (N = 200) employing multi-group SEM and ANOVA to examine model fit, structural pathways, and developmental changes. Results indicate substantial between-group differences, with ChatGPT-supported feedback producing greater gains in feedback, feedback orientation, and reading outcomes, demonstrating excellent model fit and a feedback orientation mediation-dominant structure. In contrast, except for good effect size gains in reading outcomes, two feedback-related variables show significant decline and negative effect size in conventional feedback group, with weaker FOS model fit and fragmented pathways. These findings highlight how, within the student-centered FOS framework, ChatGPT-supported feedback more effectively contributes to overall learning gains and demonstrates its capacity to integrate feedback, feedback orientation, and reading outcomes into a unified student-centered learning mechanism for instructional practice in secondary Chinese reading instruction.

papers.title: Analisis Etika Penggunaan AI Generatif (ChatGPT) dalam penulisan Tugas Kuliah Studi Kasus : Mahasiswa Teknologi Informasi Untara
papers.authors: Saryani Saryani
papers.journal: JOURNAL INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ENGINEERING AND SCIENCE (JITES)
papers.abstract: This study explores how effective and ethical the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, especially ChatGPT, is in helping students complete their academic assignments. The research was conducted with 32 students from the Information Technology Study Program at Universitas Tangerang Raya, using an online questionnaire (Google Form) as the main data collection method. The findings show that almost all students (96.9%) have used AI in their coursework. Most of them use it to find references (93.8%), write or organize content (31.3%), and check grammar (21.9%). In addition, 78.1% of students always review the AI-generated results before submitting their work, which indicates a good sense of academic responsibility. However, 62.5% of respondents were neutral about whether using AI is ethical, suggesting that many students are still unsure about the ethical boundaries of AI use. In general, the study concludes that tools like ChatGPT are effective learning aids that can make writing tasks easier and faster. Yet, their use needs to be balanced with ethical understanding and critical thinking skills, so students can use AI responsibly and wisely in academic contexts.

papers.title: Navigating Artificial Intelligence ethics: A comparative study of medical undergraduate and post graduate students of public sector medical institutes of Lahore
papers.authors: Muhammad Awais, Dua Imtiaz, Eisha Tariq, Eiman Waheed, Hafiz Hamdoon Bin Saleem, Hafiz M. Umair Younas, Mobeen Rathore
papers.journal: Journal of Society of Prevention Advocacy and Research KEMU
papers.abstract: Introduction: The huge usage of artificial intelligence in healthcare has raised numerous ethical dilemmas, which needs to be understood between different educational levels. Objective: To compare the knowledge about ethical dilemmas regarding AI usage among undergraduate and post graduate students of public sector medical institutes of Lahore. Methodology A literature-validated survey (June-July 2024) examined AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practices, focusing on privacy, consent, ownership, attitude, and accountability. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used to analyse responses and determine significance. Results We include 134 participants including both undergraduates and post graduates. Undergraduates made the majority of respondents (52.2%), followed by postgraduates(47.8%).Undergraduate students expressed higher concerns about AI-driven privacy breaches (41.4% vs. 35.9%) and unauthorized data access (60% vs. 54.7%) than postgraduates. While, Both groups agreed that data breaches are unacceptable (undergraduates 74.3%, postgraduates 62.5%). Undergraduates (60%) were more sceptical about broad consent for future research than postgraduates (57.8%). Undergraduates (72.9%) showed significantly higher concern about ethical risks in data management than postgraduate(51.6%). Postgraduates (54.7%) were slightly more concerned about economic inequality from AI than undergraduates (40%), with differences in regulatory awareness significant between the groups. Conclusion Our study looked at what undergraduate and postgraduate students at public sector medical institutes of Lahore think about using Big Data and AI in healthcare. We found that undergraduate students worry more about privacy and data protection and postgraduate students worry more about AI making healthcare unfair and increasing health inequalities We recognise creating guidelines and rules for using AI in healthcare, protecting patient data and privacy, watching AI systems closely to make sure they’re working correctly. Our study helps us understand the benefits and risks of using AI in healthcare, and how we can use it to improve patient care while avoiding potential problems.

papers.title: Expert-Owned Validation of Enterprise RAG Assistants: An Exploratory Study of Test-Suite Adequacy and Feedback- Driven Refinement
papers.authors: Muntasir Adam, Maab Mohammedali
papers.journal: Gothenburg University Publications Electronic Archive (Gothenburg University)
papers.abstract: Background: Many organizations are deploying retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) question-answering systems for internal use. However, there is limited empirical guidance on how expert-owned test suites and user feedback can support the structured assessment and improvement of such systems, and help organizations judge when testing is “good enough” in practice. Objective: This thesis investigates how an expert-owned validation setup can be used to evaluate an enterprise RAG-based question-answering assistant in an industrial setting. The study examines how formal test material, expert review, automated harness indicators, and user feedback contribute to judgments of answer acceptability, test-suite adequacy, and trust in practice. An HR knowledge-base chatbot deployment at Getinge serves as an exploratory setting for these broader software-engineering questions. Method: The study followed a Design Science Research approach in an industrial setting. The studied validation artifact consisted of a formal 57-case expert-owned test suite with preferred answers, an expert accept/decline review process, a test harness, user feedback, and a feedback-to-action workflow. The research team designed the study, organized and conducted the empirical evaluation, moderated three focus-group sessions involving six employees and one HR validation expert, analyzed the available expert material and harness export, reviewed 34 logged user-feedback items, and examined project and stakeholder documentation. The employees represented roles or responsibilities related to UX, HR, training, analytics, AI, and product or business development. The concrete setting was a Danish HR knowledge base; the study focused on the validation process rather than on country-specific policy content. Results: The findings indicate that test-suite adequacy depended primarily on the composition of the test material rather than on the number of test cases. Important characteristics included realistic employee phrasing, high-risk and ambiguous scenarios, and cases that exposed weaknesses in the underlying knowledge base. The formal 57-case test suite was executed five times per case, resulting in 285 harness executions. The harness reported an overall Average Quality in Agreement of 72 %, calculated from embedding-based cosine-similarity comparisons between generated answers and expert-defined preferred answers. In parallel, the HR validation expert accepted 55 cases and declined 2 cases, highlighting differences between automated similarity indicators and expert judgments of answer acceptability. Expert review and user feedback also informed candidate test-suite refinements and identified broader improvement needs related to knowledge-base content, interface design, scope communication, and system performance. Conclusion: Based on this exploratory study, the thesis provides practical guidance for the validation and improvement of enterprise RAG assistants. The study suggests that effective validation depends on expert-owned test suites that evolve through expert review and user feedback, with adequacy judged by scenario realism, risk relevance, and coverage of ambiguous cases rather than by test count alone. Automated harness indicators provided descriptive monitoring information, while expert review assessed policy consistency, completeness, grounding, scope, and potential consequences for employees. The thesis also formulates an empirically grounded Expert-Owned RAG Validation Refinement Workflow for reviewing, classifying, and routing observed issues to test-suite refinement, knowledge-base clarification, interface or source-presentation changes, scope communication, or technical-performance action. The findings are exploratory and context-dependent and do not provide a general measure of RAG reliability.

papers.title: Digital Transformation of Museums in Bukhara: Innovative Technologies, Management Efficiency, and Tourism Attractiveness
papers.authors: Rahmonov Sherzod Axtamovich
papers.journal: Intersections of Faith and Culture: American Journal of Religious and Cultural Studies (2993-2599)
papers.abstract: This article examines the opportunities for improving the effectiveness of museums in Bukhara through digital transformation, the introduction of innovative technologies, and the modernization of museum management. Particular attention is paid to the digitization of museum collections, the development of unified electronic catalogues, the use of QR codes, multimedia installations, three-dimensional (3D) modelling, virtual and augmented reality (VR/AR), and the establishment of virtual museums. The article also considers the application of artificial intelligence, digital marketing, interactive visitor services, and modern conservation technologies. In addition, it highlights the importance of cooperation between museums, higher education institutions, research centres, and tourism organizations. The proposed approaches aim to improve the accessibility of cultural heritage, strengthen the educational role of museums, enhance the visitor experience, and increase Bukhara’s attractiveness as a cultural tourism destination. The article concludes that digital transformation should be implemented through an integrated strategy that combines technological innovation, professional staff development, heritage conservation, and systematic evaluation of results.

papers.title: LLT AI Use Disclosure Checklist for Reviewers
STRUCTURAL-SEMANTIC AND PRAGMATIC FEATURES OF NEOLOGISMS RELATED TO ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE
papers.authors: Rizayeva Xurshida Ravshan qizi
papers.abstract: This study examines how English-language expressions associated with artificial intelligence (AI) are formed, how their meanings become specialized, and how speakers deploy them for explanation, persuasion, evaluation, and risk communication. A purposive, illustrative set of twenty widely recognizable AI-related expressions is analysed through morphological classification, semantic component analysis, and pragmatic interpretation. The study distinguishes established lexical items undergoing semantic extension from recently popularized compounds, blends, derivatives, and initialisms. In the selected set, compounding accounts for 11 of 20 items (55%); these proportions describe the analytical selection only and do not estimate the frequency of neologisms in English. The findings suggest that AI vocabulary performs dual functions: it provides operational labels for technical workflows and frames public judgments about agency, reliability, creativity, and responsibility. Particular attention is paid to metaphorical expressions such as hallucination and to socially evaluative forms such as AI slop. The article proposes a replicable coding scheme for future corpus-based inquiry and discusses implications for terminology management, translation, and critical AI literacy.

papers.title: GENERATIVE AI AND ENTREPRENEURIAL MARKETING PERFORMANCE IN E-COMMERCE FIRMS
papers.authors: Muhammad Asif Noor, Muhammad Muzaffar, Mahmood Rahmani
papers.abstract: With the arrival of generative AI, most e-commerce businesses have shifted from seeing it as a novelty to a necessity, but it remains unclear how to fully leverage its marketing potential. This study examines Generative AI as a strategic asset with implications for Entrepreneurial Marketing Performance that are mediated by a sequence of organizational capabilities, based on Dynamic Capability Theory. Specifically, it builds and tests a model in which generative AI adoption increases Content Capabilities and Market Sensing, which in turn leads to greater Brand Visibility and ultimately to even better marketing outcomes as generative AI adoption is translated into these capabilities; and Digital Orientation conditions the extent to which Generative AI Adoption is translated to Content Capabilities and Market Sensing. The model is tested using a cross-sectional survey of owners, managers and marketing professionals from e-commerce companies in Pakistan and using PLS-SEM with direct effects, serial mediation and moderation tests. The results indicate that Generative AI Adoption has a significant impact on Content Capabilities and Market Sensing, which in turn have a significant impact on Brand Visibility, which in turn, along with a direct effect of AI adoption, has a significant impact on Entrepreneurial Marketing Performance. There are two confirmed serial pathways and the capability building effects of AI adoption are additionally enhanced by Digital Orientation. The study contributes to the Dynamic Capability Theory in the era of Generative AI and provides an evidence-based roadmap for entrepreneurs in emerging digital markets to transform the investment in AI into customer engagement and competitive advantage, through the indirect pathways. Keywords: Generative AI Adoption; Entrepreneurial Marketing Performance; Content Capabilities; Market Sensing; Brand Visibility; Digital Orientation; Dynamic Capability Theory; E-Commerce.
