papers.title: AI and Legal Language Education: A Review of Pedagogical Applications, Writing Development, and Emerging Challenges
papers.authors: N. Polraj alias Goutham, K. Gurusamy, A. Pradheepa
papers.journal: International Journal of Scientific Research in Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Generative AI now writes passable legal prose, and law schools are still deciding what that means for the teaching of legal English. This systematic review maps how artificial intelligence has been used in legal language education between 2020 and 2026, with attention to pedagogical applications, writing development and the problems that recur across studies. The review draws on Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SpringerLink and ScienceDirect. Studies were coded for context, design, AI tool, pedagogical use, writing-related outcomes and reported limitations. The evidence base is small, recent and uneven. Most studies appeared after the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, and they concentrate on exam performance, legal vocabulary and instructor perceptions. Controlled evidence on legal writing development is scarce, and the few experiments available suggest that benefits depend on prior skill and on whether students receive structured guidance. Reported challenges include fabricated legal authority, shallow issue-spotting, over-reliance, academic integrity and low instructor preparedness. Studies from India and from learners using English as an additional language are almost absent. The review closes with a research agenda centred on longitudinal designs, validated writing rubrics, and tools built on verified legal corpora.

papers.title: AI-Mediated Organizational Communication and Crisis Management: Trust, Transparency, and Stakeholder Perception
papers.authors: Ilham Bangsim Mohammed, Temiloluwa Paul Adetola, Nawas Abubakar
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming embedded in organisational communication through message generation, conversational agents, monitoring systems, decision support, and automated service recovery. During crises, these functions offer speed, scale, consistency, and continuous availability, but they also change how stakeholders infer agency, competence, care, responsibility, and authenticity. This critical narrative review integrates crisis communication, organisational trust, human–automation trust, artificial intelligence-mediated communication, public relations, and service-recovery research to examine when AI-mediated communication is likely to sustain or erode stakeholder trust. The evidence indicates that no uniform ‘AI effect’ exists. Stakeholder responses depend on whether AI assists a human communicator or appears to replace one, whether the task is informational or relational, whether the crisis demands empathy and moral accountability, whether AI involvement is disclosed, and whether human responsibility remains visible. Technical or process transparency can strengthen perceived accountability and system trust, while simple disclosure that a message was produced with AI may reduce perceived legitimacy, authenticity, or credibility in some contexts. Anthropomorphic cues can increase social presence and perceived empathy, yet they may also raise expectations that become costly when the system fails. Evidence from crisis-response experiments, organisational studies, chatbot research, and service recovery therefore favours calibrated human–AI orchestration over indiscriminate automation. The review proposes that trustworthy AI-mediated crisis communication requires fit among task, crisis responsibility, stakeholder vulnerability, disclosure purpose, system reliability, and accountable human oversight. Current confidence is constrained by a literature dominated by short-term experiments, consumer and convenience samples, hypothetical crises, and limited longitudinal or field evidence. Research should move towards preregistered factorial studies, live crisis simulations, cross-cultural and multi-stakeholder designs, longitudinal trust measurement, and explicit testing of governance and escalation arrangements.

papers.title: Diagnostic Challenges in Seronegative Section Autoimmune Limbic Encephalitis Presenting as Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures: A Case Report
papers.authors: Tejo Varshini Paleti, Srija Sura, Shivam Gupta, Sagar Ashok Patil, Nirmala Devi Chandrasekaran
papers.journal: JOURNAL OF CLINICAL AND DIAGNOSTIC RESEARCH
papers.abstract: Faciobrachial Dystonic Seizures (FBDS) are sudden brief seizure-like episodes, which are highly characteristic for Autoimmune Limbic Encephalitis (AIE), mostly associated with Voltage-gated Potassium Channel (VGKC), classically Leucine-Rich Glioma Inactivated-1 (LGI1). Timely diagnosis in seronegative patients poses a big challenge, often leading to delay in intervention, causing irreversible neuronal damage. A 66-year-old male with a history of hypertension for seven years on regular medications presented to neurology Outpatient Department (OPD) with one week history of recurrent brief involuntary dystonic movements involving left face and upper limb, along with neuropsychiatric manifestations. Initial assessment revealed mild hyponatraemia. Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) analysis, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Electroencephalogram (EEG) were unremarkable. Fluorodeoxyglucose-Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography (FDG PET-CT) revealed hypermetabolism in right mesial temporal cortex, bilateral caudate nuclei and putamen. Despite the fact that antibodies were absent in CSF, patient was still started on pulse intravenous corticosteroid therapy and Anti-Seizure Medication (ASM) along with immunotherapy resulting in significant improvement of the patient. The present case highlights the limitations in presently used diagnostic criteria, which rely heavily on MRI and CSF analysis. Advanced imaging techniques like FDG PET-CT are more sensitive, and hence support the diagnosis, when diagnostic criteria are not fulfilled. Timely initiation of immunotherapy based on strong clinical suspicion and advanced imaging is very important to prevent irreversible cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Generative AI-Supported Learning, Cognitive Offloading, and Metacognitive Awareness: Examining Changes in Students’ Learning Regulation
papers.authors: Mashal Maqsood, Nisar Ahmad, Sidra Hussain
papers.abstract: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

papers.title: AI Ensemble Framework for OSINT-Based Social Media Crime Prevention in Kenya
papers.authors: Alfred Ngala, Shem Mbandu, Anthony Mile
papers.abstract: Criminal networks increasingly exploit social media to organize, recruit, incite, and coordinate unlawful activities, whereas law-enforcement monitoring in Kenya remains largely manual and English-centric. This study aimed to design, implement, and rigorously evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) ensemble framework for open-source intelligence (OSINT) classification of crime- and threat-relevant content in Kenya's trilingual (English, Kiswahili, and Sheng) and code-switched digital environment. A corpus of 6,212 documents was assembled from six sources: Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and two Sheng-language corpora. The corpus was weakly labelled using a 214-term trilingual crime-and-threat lexicon. Label noise was quantified against a manually annotated stratified validation sample (n = 320), yielding Cohen's κ = 0.350, silver-label precision of 0.525, and recall of 0.750. Combined word- and character-level term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features comprising 25,831 dimensions were used to train a hyperparameter-tuned, weighted soft-voting ensemble consisting of multinomial naive Bayes, a calibrated linear support vector machine, random forest, logistic regression, and XGBoost. The decision threshold was calibrated using cross-validated out-of-fold probabilities. The optimized ensemble achieved 98.3% accuracy, 80.6% precision, 62.5% recall, 70.4% F1-score, 0.907 ROC-AUC, 0.724 PR-AUC, 0.702 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and a 0.50% false-positive rate. The ensemble outperformed the best single learner and a frozen multilingual transformer baseline (F1 = 26.2%). Ablation analysis demonstrated the contribution of the Sheng-normalization layer, while comparison of class-imbalance strategies showed that cost-sensitive learning combined with threshold calibration produced the strongest overall performance compared with SMOTE-based resampling. The findings demonstrate that linguistically inclusive classical machine-learning ensembles can provide an accurate, auditable, and computationally deployable approach to proactive social-media crime prevention in low-resource, code-switched settings. The study also derives policy implications concerning threshold-calibrated triage, expert annotation, data-protection impact assessments, and safeguards against dual-use misuse.

papers.title: ASSESSING GENERATIVE AI'S IMPACT ON SUSTAINABLE URBAN DESIGN IN VICTORIA ISLAND, LAGOS, NIGERIA
papers.authors: MIKE ADEBAMOWO, ADEFEMI USMAN AFOLABI, Paul Obi
papers.journal: Journal of Environmental Management and Construction Research
papers.abstract: This study assesses the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on sustainable urban design, exploring its potential benefits and limitations. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining qualitative and quantitative data collection and analysis. A comprehensive literature review was conducted to identify the current state of research on generative AI in urban design, and a questionnaire survey of 100 urban design professionals and stakeholders was administered to gather quantitative data. The survey revealed that 85% of respondents believed generative AI has the potential to promote sustainability in urban design. The top benefits identified included improved design efficiency (75%), enhanced design creativity (65%), and reduced environmental impact (55%). However, limitations such as lack of transparency (60%), bias in AI outputs (50%), and limited contextual understanding (40%) were also noted. The study's findings suggest that generative AI can be a valuable tool for promoting sustainable urban design,but its development and implementation must be carefully managed to address the identified challenges. To realize the benefits of generative AI, it is essential to develop transparent and explainable AI models, address bias in AI outputs, and improve contextual understanding. The study's conclusions have implications for urban planning and design practices, highlighting the need for a multidisciplinary approach to AI development and implementation. The findings of this study can inform policymakers, urban planners, and stakeholders seeking to harness the potential of generative AI in promoting sustainable urban design.

papers.title: THE FUTURE OF MILITARY ENGLISH LANGUAGE TRAINING: AI, PERSONALIZATION, AND INTELLIGENT EDUCATIONAL ENVIRONMENTS
papers.authors: Наталія Демченко
papers.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming approaches to foreign language education and creating new possibilities for organizing personalized, adaptive, and continuous learning.Recent research demonstrates that the use of AI in language education is expanding from individual applications, such as chatbots and automated feedback systems, toward more complex forms of human-AI interaction and technology-supported learning environments [1; 2].These developments are particularly relevant to military English language training, which requires a high degree of professional relevance, adaptability, and alignment with the communication needs of military personnel.Military English represents a specialized area of English language education associated with professional communication, international cooperation, and interoperability.A recent scoping review of three decades of research in Military English identified a wide range of research themes, including learner needs, motivation, teaching and learning practices, testing, and the development of contextspecific language competence.At the same time, the authors emphasize that Military English remains a relatively under-researched domain and that more evidence-based and context-specific approaches to language education are needed [3].The future development of military English language training should therefore involve not only the introduction of individual digital tools but also a transformation of the educational environment in which these technologies are integrated.The transition can be described as a movement from isolated digital applications toward intelligent educational environments that combine learning content, learner data, adaptive technologies, AI-supported interaction, assessment, and teacher guidance.One of the most significant components of this transformation is personalization.Traditional language instruction generally provides the same sequence of materials and

papers.title: Beyond Technocentrism in AI-Supported Special Education: The PAISEN Model of Teacher-Mediated Inclusive Learning
papers.authors: Zaheril Zainudin, Nurmuma Kamarina Jamil
papers.journal: Journal of Research Innovation and Strategies for Education (RISE)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new possibilities for inclusive teaching and learning for students with special educational needs (SEN), yet AI-in-SEN research remains largely technocentric, often describing system capabilities without explaining how outputs become pedagogically meaningful. This conceptual paper develops the PAISEN Model (Pedagogical Artificial Intelligence for Special Education Needs) through an integrative synthesis of AI in education, inclusive pedagogy, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and assistive technology. The model proposes a non-deterministic sequence in which AI Teaching Support Systems provide data and adaptive affordances, Teacher Pedagogical Mediation interprets and contextualises them, and an Inclusive Learning Environment translates decisions into accessible participation opportunities. SEN learning outcomes are treated as proposed consequences rather than established effects. Teacher AI competency, institutional support, digital infrastructure, and learner characteristics function as boundary conditions, while an adaptive feedback loop links learner evidence to teacher reflection and instructional adjustment. The novelty of PAISEN lies in making teacher judgement the central explanatory mechanism and separating technology, pedagogical processes, learning conditions and moderators. Theoretically, it bridges AIED and inclusive education; pedagogically, it clarifies differentiated and UDL-aligned AI use without replacing teacher agency; practically, it provides a testable structure for implementation and evaluation. The proposed relationships require empirical validation in authentic SEN settings.

papers.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Generative AI: Institutional AI Policies and the Potential for Student Inequality
papers.authors: Bright Mleta, Emelia Owusu–Ansah, Naomi Mpata, Ursular Koranteng
papers.journal: Journal of Education Learning and Management
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, prompting institutions to develop policies governing its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Although existing discussions have emphasized academic integrity, assessment practices, and technological access, less attention has been given to the knowledge and competencies students may need to interpret and comply with institutional AI policies. This study examines how institutional GenAI policies establish explicit and implicit expectations for students and identifies potential pathways through which policy-navigation demands may contribute to educational inequality. Using comparative qualitative content analysis, publicly available policies and guidance documents from 20 purposively selected higher education institutions across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and South Africa were examined. The analysis considered policy permissiveness, disclosure requirements, instructor discretion, student responsibilities, AI-literacy guidance, accessibility, equity, and implicit navigation demands. Findings indicate that acceptable AI use is frequently determined at the course, instructor, or assessment level, requiring students to interpret context-specific rules, understand disclosure requirements, verify AI-generated outputs, and reconcile varying instructor expectations. However, explicit consideration of differences in technological access, language, accessibility, and institutional knowledge was less consistently evident across the reviewed documents. Drawing on hidden-curriculum and digital-inequality perspectives, the study identifies AI policy-navigation burdens and proposes the concept of a potential policy-navigation divide. While the findings do not establish unequal student experiences or educational outcomes, they highlight institutional conditions through which inequalities could emerge. The study recommends clearer policy communication, transparent assessment-specific expectations, accessible AI-literacy support, and greater attention to equity in institutional AI governance.

papers.title: The Application of AIGC in Empowering Talent Cultivation for Cross-border E-commerce Live-streaming in the Business English Major: A Case Study of Huainan Normal University
papers.authors: Xiao Ling
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has fostered innovative pedagogical models and propelled sectoral reform. Concurrently, cross-border e-commerce, as a rapidly expanding industry within economic globalization, has intensified the demand for specialized talent. Consequently, Business English education must evolve to cultivate professionals better aligned with the competencies required by the cross-border e-commerce sector. Based on artificial intelligence, business English students need to cultivate qualities and skills that are suitable for the new era. To provide high-quality business English talents and ensure the alignment of supply and demand, this project, under the background of artificial intelligence, interprets and analyzes the solutions for business English talent cultivation through methods such as literature research, case study, and questionnaire survey. It explores innovative strategies for the cultivation of business English professionals in combination with the needs of cross-border e-commerce live streaming, and integrates artificial intelligence technology into business English teaching to cultivate business English talents suitable for the new era of the digital economy. It promotes the development of cross-border e-commerce live streaming and the development of the new era of the digital economy.

papers.title: Nutrient Knowledge, Self-Care Behaviour, and Nutritional Status of In-Patients with Diabetes Mellitus at Ekiti State University Teaching Hospital, Ado Ekiti, Nigeria
papers.authors: Oladiran Isdaiah Olagunju, Adesina Dorcas, Adegoke Latifat Olamide, Esther Olufunke Ademola, Olatise Bintu Omolayo, Olagunju Oladiran Isaiah
papers.abstract: Background: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a growing non-communicable disease crisis in Nigeria, with rising prevalence among older adults and escalating complications burden on health systems.Nutritional knowledge, dietary self-care behaviour, and nutritional status are critical, interlinked determinants of glycaemic control, complication prevention, and quality of life for people living with DM.Despite the critical role of these factors, systematic assessment among hospitalised DM patients in South-Western Nigeria remains limited. Methods:We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional study among 161 inpatients with diabetes mellitus at Ekiti State University Teaching Hospital (EKSUTH), Ado Ekiti, using purposive and multistage sampling.A semi-structured interviewer-administered questionnaire assessed socio-demographic characteristics, nutritional knowledge (24 items), dietary self-care behaviour, and anthropometric measurements (BMI and WHR).We analysed data using SPSS version 25 with descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression.Results: Respondents were predominantly aged 61 and above (44.7%),female (54.0%), married (85.7%), and Yoruba (95.7%).While 85.7% correctly identified that untreated diabetes raises blood sugar, only 9.9% correctly refuted the myth that kidneys produce insulin, and 56.5% held the misconception that

papers.title: Explainable Generative AI for Personalized E-Commerce Decision Support: Integrating Customer Behaviour, Trust and Purchase Prediction
papers.authors: Dr. S Afsar Ahmed
papers.abstract: E-commerce systems increasingly predict which products a customer may click or purchase, but a ranked list rarely explains why an item fits a person's needs or which trade-offs deserve attention.Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates opportunities for conversational product comparison, review summarization, and personalized guidance; however, fluent output can contain unsupported claims.This paper proposes a conceptual decision-support framework integrating customer-behaviour modelling, purchase-propensity prediction, explainable machine learning, and retrieval-grounded generation.The framework combines searches, views, cart activity, purchases, returns, and review interactions with current product attributes, price, availability, delivery, and return-policy information.A predictive model estimates purchase propensity, an explanation layer identifies relevant evidence, and a generative layer converts it into concise answers with source links and uncertainty disclosures.Trust is treated as an outcome to evaluate-not an automatic benefit of AI-and is supported through transparency, privacy safeguards, user correction, and control over personalization.The paper presents an architecture, research questions, an experimental protocol, and metrics for prediction, calibration, explanation faithfulness, factual grounding, and user understanding.No dataset or user study is claimed; this is a research framework, not a report of measured performance.Its goal is to help shoppers make informed decisions rather than simply maximize conversion.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness and Integration in Teaching Practices among Secondary School Teachers in Katsina State Nigeria
papers.authors: Muhsin Mustapha Inuwa, Muhammad Sani Umar
papers.abstract: This study examines associations between technological self-efficacy, pedagogical readiness, ethical AI awareness, perceived relevance, institutional support, overall, AI readiness and self-reported AI integration among secondary school teachers in Katsina State, Nigeria.A supplied questionnaire dataset was analyzed using construct means, Cronbach's alpha, correlations and exploratory linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors.The Google Forms export contained 68 submissions recorded from 10 to 21 September 2026, all with affirmative participation consent and distinct timestamps.All 68 submissions were analyzed; 67 distinct structured-response patterns were examined separately as a sensitivity analysis.Mean readiness was 3.42 (SD = 1.36) and mean integration was 3.41 (SD = 1.39) on a five-point agreement scale.Institutional support had the lowest construct mean (3.00).64.7% of records selected limited connectivity, while 65.7% of those answering the training-needs question selected basic AI literacy.Readiness and integration were strongly correlated (r = .954;95% CI .926-.971).In the readiness model, pedagogical readiness and institutional support remained statistically distinguishable from zero after Holm adjustment across seven hypotheses; perceived relevance met the unadjusted threshold only.In the full integration model, readiness had a positive but imprecise coefficient (B = 0.586; 95% CI

papers.title: Equity in the Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Facilities Among Urban and Rural Public Secondary Schools in Benue State
papers.authors: Donatus Peter Ochai, Lawrence Linus Bodams, OJonoka Victoria Attah
papers.abstract: This study investigated equity in the availability and utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) facilities among urban and rural public secondary schools in Benue State, Nigeria. The study was guided by two research questions and two hypotheses. A descriptive survey design was adopted. The population comprised 3,726 teachers in 128 public secondary schools, from which 361 teachers were selected using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using the Equitable Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (EUAIQ), validated by three experts in the Faculty of Education, Veritas University, Bwari, Abuja. The instrument yielded a Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficient of 0.88 based on a trial test involving 30 teachers. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, with a 2.50 decision criterion, while independent-samples t-test was used to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed significant differences between the mean ratings of respondents from urban and rural public secondary schools regarding both the availability and utilization of AI facilities for teaching and learning in Benue State. The study concludes that disparities exist in the availability and utilization of AI facilities between urban and rural public secondary schools. It recommends equitable provision of funding, reliable internet connectivity, stable electricity and AI-enabled digital resources by government and relevant stakeholders, alongside continuous capacity-building programmes for teachers on the effective use of AI facilities.

papers.title: The Interplay of Copyright and Personhood Rights in the Age of Digital Creation
papers.authors: Ms. Shreya Goswami, Apoorva Dixit
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed the creation, distribution, and protection of intellectual property, raising important questions about the relationship between copyright law and personhood rights. Traditionally, copyright has focused on safeguarding the economic interests of creators; however, in the digital environment, creative works are increasingly intertwined with personal identity, dignity, reputation, and self-expression. This paper examines the interplay between copyright and personhood rights in the age of digital creation, emphasizing the role of moral rights, particularly the rights of attribution and integrity, in protecting creators’ personal and professional identities. It explores key challenges arising from unauthorized reproduction, digital remixing, data mining, privacy violations, cross-jurisdictional enforcement, artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content, and deepfakes. The paper further examines the limitations of existing legal frameworks in addressing the complex relationship between creative ownership and individual identity in an increasingly interconnected digital landscape....

papers.title: Unveiling the Lived Experiences of Senior High School Teachers in Adopting Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Instruction in Humanities and Social Sciences: A Phenomenological Study
papers.authors: Maria Cristita Bucayu-Cuerdo
papers.journal: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming part of teachers’ instructional work, yet its use in Humanities and Social Sciences raises concerns beyond convenience. This descriptive phenomenological study explored the experiences of eight Senior High School teachers adopting AI-enhanced instruction in selected campuses of Las Piñas City National Senior High School. In-depth, semistructured interviews were analyzed using Colaizzi’s seven-step method. Eleven theme clusters described workload relief, resource access, material construction, activity design, contextual adaptation, professional learning, verification, access and content limitations, teacher agency, learner thinking, and emotional reassurance. Participants used AI to organize lessons, prepare materials, and develop activities while continuing to verify, revise, contextualize, and sometimes reject outputs. Difficulties included prompting, inaccurate or conflicting information, limited local context, language concerns, connectivity, subscription costs, and uneven preparation. Teacherperceived learner interest coexisted with concern about copying, dependence, and reduced independent reasoning. Teacher responsibility remained central to deciding what was accurate and meaningful for particular lessons and learners. All eight participants confirmed the final fundamental structure without requesting revision. The experience involved assistance alongside scrutiny, growing familiarity alongside uncertainty, and technological support alongside teacher agency. A proposed six-component framework was derived to inform instructional practice, with teacher agency operating throughout. The framework remained conceptually developed and untested. The findings provide a context-bound account of teacher experience; they do not establish improved learner outcomes or instructional effectiveness.

papers.title: Attenuated alpha state transitions and disrupted repetition-dependent temporal adaptation in mild cognitive impairment
papers.authors: Xuan Wang, Ying Zhu, Jian Zhang, Zheng Zheng, Ming Yu
papers.abstract: Abstract Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) may involve impaired dynamic regulation of brain states that is not captured by conventional resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). We quantified occipital alpha (8–12 Hz) transitions during three repeated eye-opening/eye-closure cycles in 60 healthy controls (HC) and 77 participants with MCI. Eye-state events were refined from frontal ocular artifacts. Transition magnitude was measured by the log-transformed post-/pre-event energy ratio, and transition success by the expected direction of alpha change. For canonical transitions meeting prespecified fit-quality criteria, mono-exponential fitting yielded transition onset (t onset ) and the post-onset time constant (τ). MCI showed weaker alpha suppression during eye opening, weaker alpha enhancement during eye closure, and lower odds of transition success. No significant group difference in τ was detected within the canonical quality-controlled subset. In contrast, t onset showed significant Group × Trial interactions in both conditions: HC developed later onset during eye opening and earlier onset during eye closure across repetitions, whereas MCI showed no comparable change. These findings suggest reduced alpha state-transition capacity and altered repetition-dependent temporal organization in MCI.

papers.title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm
papers.authors: Fran�ois Fricker, Vincent Dornier, Giulia Buzi, Maelys Morantin, Franck Doidy, Patrice Clochon, Annabelle Goujon, Emmanuel J. Barbeau, Thomas Hinault
papers.abstract: Abstract Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.

papers.title: Nicotine and Cathinone Use, Dietary Habits, Physical Activity and Gender Disparities Among Saudi University Faculty: A Cross-Sectional Analysis
papers.authors: Ibrahim Metaan Gosadi, Jamilah Albalawi, Reem Alsalman, Adnan Altalhi, Abdullah Babour, Thana Aldulayqan, Leen Alghamdi, Dona Babour, Ayman Mahrat, Tahani Alhawsawi, Ali Albraih, Layan Almohsen, Alaa Alanazi
papers.abstract: Background: Gender-based variations in health-related behaviors persist even in highly educated populations. Understanding these differences among university faculty in Saudi Arabia is crucial for developing effective, gender-sensitive wellness policies in academic institutions. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate lifestyle behaviors among Saudi university teachers and examine gender-based differences in these patterns. Methodology: A cross-sectional study was conducted from May 2023 to May 2024 among faculty members at Jazan University, Saudi Arabia. Data were collected via validated questionnaires that included sociodemographic (age, income, marital status), lifestyle behaviors (diet, physical activity, smoking, khat chewing), and satisfaction metrics (weight, eating habits). Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, and chi-square tests. Results: This cross-sectional study of 516 Jazan University faculty teachers (274 female, 242 male) revealed significant gender disparities. Males were more likely to smoke (12% vs. 2%) and chew khat (3% vs. 0%) (p < 0.01). Females were significantly more likely to consume low-fat products (51% vs. 40%; p < 0.05), though other dietary habits (whole grains, fruits/vegetables, low-fat meats, sugar avoidance) showed no significant differences. Physical activity levels and BMI were comparable between groups (p > 0.05), though males had significantly higher height and weight (p < 0.01). Regarding lifestyle satisfaction, females were more dissatisfied with their eating behavior (46% vs. 33%; p < 0.01) and weight (50% vs. 42%; p < 0.1), while physical activity satisfaction did not differ significantly. Conclusion: Gender disparities persist in academic settings, influenced by cultural norms and socioeconomic factors. Findings highlight the need for gender-sensitive workplace wellness policies to address inequities in health behaviors and satisfaction. Future research should expand to national samples and incorporate longitudinal designs to inform institutional and public health strategies.

papers.title: MathemAfrica: A Multilingual Explainable Artificial Intelligence Ecosystem for Adaptive Mathematics Education in Resource-Constrained African Learning Environments
papers.authors: Jamilu Auwalu Adamu, Muhammad Bello Sadiq, Professor Promise Mebine
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology
papers.abstract: Secondary mathematics education in developing and resource-constrained contexts confronts systemic bottlenecks, including overcrowded classrooms, acute teacher shortages, frequent electrical blackouts, prohibitively expensive cellular data, and linguistic dissonance between official English instruction and students' indigenous home languages.To address these interconnected challenges, this study developed and evaluated MathemAfrica, an innovative digital learning platform integrating Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, Multidimensional Item Response Theory (M-3PL IRT), offline optical handwriting verification, and multilingual scaffolding in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, and Swahili.Employing an ADDIE-based design science methodology and a 16-week quasi-experimental non-equivalent pretest-posttest control group design, the intervention was evaluated across six public secondary schools in Kano State, Nigeria, with 1,428 Grade 10 students.Expert reviews confirmed high content validity (97.06%) and media quality (94.56%), while students reported exceptional practicality (96.13%).Analysis of Covariance revealed statistically significant and substantial gains in mathematical proficiency, with adjusted posttest scores of 73.84% in the intervention group versus 57.22% in conventional instruction (F (1, 1425) = 148.92,p < .0001,Cohen's d = 0.94).Furthermore, the platform closed 80.4% of the indigenous language achievement penalty, while maintaining real-time adaptive sequencing at merely 38.4 kB per session.The results provide empirical evidence that combining edge-native computation with culturally responsive multilingual scaffolding strengthens secondary mathematical achievement under severe resource constraints.

papers.title: Graduate Admissions Testing Perceptions: Results from the ETS/NAGAP February 2025 Survey
papers.authors: Reginald M. Gooch, Sara Haviland
papers.abstract: Higher education admissions have been undergoing significant disruption, with a variety of social forces impacting it including the rise of generative AI and the decline of race-based affirmative action. In this report, we reflect upon the current state of change in graduate admissions, drawing upon insights from ETS’s February 2025 pulse survey of members of NAGAP, The Association for Graduate Enrollment Management (GEM). We also present survey data on factors influencing graduate application requirements across institutions, including the role of the U.S. Supreme Court’s Students for Fair Admissions affirmative action decisions. We conclude with a discussion on the implications of these findings for GEM policies and practice. Suggested citation: Gooch, R. M., & Haviland, S. B. (in press). Graduate admissions testing perceptions: Results from the ETS/NAGAP February 2025 survey (Research Notes). ETS. https://doi.org/10.64634/37f75641

papers.title: AI-Based Personalized Travel Planning and Recommendation System: A Unified Framework for Intelligent Trip Planning
papers.authors: Shubham Pandey, Satyam Anand, Sujal Das, Raushan Kumar Tiwari
papers.abstract: A growing number of travel planning activities involve managing multiple pieces of often competing data about destinations, budget, weather, attractions' availability, transportation options and personal preferences that are typically distributed across a number of isolated online services. Traditional travel-planning tools tackle these issues one at a time: choosing or navigating, and rarely include personalization, predictive analytics, and multi-constraint reasoning within a single interface. We propose a unified framework for personalized travel planning that integrates personal preferences, context-based destination recommendation, budget- and weather- aware filtering, and route and distance analysis, and AI-assisted itinerary generation. The framework is inspired, and to some extent generalized, from the design of the ongoing academic research prototype TripCraft, an AI-powered agent for trip planning. We build upon the state of the art of recommender-systems theory, context-aware recommendation, tourist trip design (route optimization) literature, and recent large language model-based agents for travel-planning to develop a system-level description, a hybrid AI/ML approach, and a step-by-step algorithmic process for creating personalized itineraries that take preference, budget, weather and route constraints into account. We provide preliminary proof of concept based on a synthetic evaluation on fabricated records using baseline comparisons and constraint-compliance metrics. The findings are only indicative of the possible effectiveness, but do not constitute proof of concept. The expected contribution is the conceptual and methodological foundation for unifying preference-, budget-, weather- and route awareness in intelligent travel planning.

papers.title: Transforming Mathematics Education in the Era of Generative AI: From Problem Solving to AI-Supported Mathematical Reasoning
papers.authors: Baharuddin
papers.journal: International Journal of Technology and Education Research
papers.abstract: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has brought significant changes to mathematics education, particularly in problem-solving processes and mathematical reasoning. This study aims to analyze the transformation of GenAI utilization from an answer-generating tool into a facilitator of mathematical reasoning. The study employed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of relevant studies published between 2023 and 2026. The data were analyzed thematically to identify patterns of AI utilization, the role of AI in mathematical thinking processes, and the implications for mathematics education. The findings indicate that GenAI can be used not only to generate solutions but also to function as a cognitive scaffold by providing guiding questions, alternative strategies, feedback, error detection, and support for reflection. These findings suggest a shift from conventional problem solving toward AI-supported mathematical reasoning, in which learners remain the primary agents of their thinking processes while AI serves as a supportive tool. This transformation necessitates changes in teachers’ roles, instructional design, and assessment practices, with greater emphasis on mathematical reasoning, argumentation, verification, and reflection. Therefore, the integration of GenAI should be directed toward enhancing the quality of students’ mathematical reasoning rather than replacing their thinking processes.

papers.title: Inteligencia artificial y razonamiento clínico en educación médica: una revisión sistemática
papers.authors: Rafael Emiliano Sulca Quispe, Juan Miguel Purilla Janto, María del Rosario Jáuregui-Figueroa, María del Rosario Figueroa Bejarano De Jauregui
papers.abstract: Context: Artificial intelligence has transformed learning environments in the health sciences and prompted debate about its role in developing clinical reasoning. Objective: To analyze the role of artificial intelligence in developing clinical reasoning in medical education. Methods: A systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Twenty-two publications, including primary studies, reviews, and reflective papers, published between 2021 and 2026 were selected. Results: The included meta-analysis by Takita et al. (2025) reported an overall diagnostic accuracy of 52.1% across 83 studies. In Gordon et al. (2024), 6.8% (13/191) of articles/innovations focused on teaching or assessing clinical reasoning. Arcos Huaman et al. (2025) reported 31% regulatory barriers in Latin American cardiovascular diagnosis, without assessing their curricular prevalence. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence is a valuable complementary educational resource whose curricular integration requires active faculty supervision, explicit ethical frameworks, and ongoing empirical validation.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and University Students' Critical and Higher-Order Thinking Outcomes: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Review and Thematic Analysis
papers.authors: Yunardi Kristian Zega, Rini Sumanti Sapalakkai, Yuireishang Shithungdang, Luiramsing Zimik
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot into higher education has raised urgent questions about their effects on students' higher-order cognitive abilities. While these tools promise unprecedented access to information and cognitive support, growing concerns have emerged regarding the potential erosion of critical thinking skills among university students who adopt them uncritically. Despite increasing scholarly attention to artificial intelligence in education, systematic evidence on how generative AI relates to distinct dimensions of higher-order thinking remains limited. This systematic literature review, guided by the PRISMA 2020 reporting guideline, aims to identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on the relationship between generative AI use and university students' analytical, evaluative, and creative thinking outcomes, using the higher-order cognitive processes of Bloom's Revised Taxonomy as an organizing framework. A comprehensive search across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar yielded 847 initial records, of which 42 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria after screening. Thematic synthesis revealed heterogeneous outcomes: analytical thinking outcomes were generally positive under structured prompting conditions, evaluative thinking appeared most vulnerable in the absence of deliberate pedagogical design, and creative thinking outcomes were most frequently reported as positive. Across themes, the quality of pedagogical integration was the condition most frequently associated with favorable outcomes. This review contributes a dimension-level synthesis of generative AI and higher-order thinking, identifies the pedagogical conditions associated with favorable and unfavorable outcomes, and documents the heterogeneity of outcomes across studies, offering an evidence-informed framework for educators, curriculum designers, and policymakers seeking to use generative AI as a cognitive scaffold rather than a cognitive replacement.

papers.title: Perceptions of Academic Staff on the Integration of AI and Digital Connectivity for Transformative Educational Management in Bayelsa State
papers.authors: Ebimiere Akosubo – Ogori
papers.journal: African Journal of Humanities and Contemporary Education Research
papers.abstract: The study assessed the perceptions of academic staff on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital connectivity for transformative educational management in tertiary institutions in Bayelsa State. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, guided by two research questions. The population comprised academic staff from selected public universities and colleges of education in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 350 respondents was drawn using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity in Educational Management Questionnaire (AIDEMQ), validated by experts and yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.89 via Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to answer the research questions. The findings revealed that academic staff generally perceived AI as enhancing administrative efficiency through improved decision-making, error reduction, transparency, and time management, although challenges such as inadequate training and limited practical application constrained its full potential. Similarly, digital connectivity was perceived as effective in improving communication, collaboration, information dissemination, and the quality of teaching and learning, though gaps in infrastructure and system functionality limited its impact on administrative planning and scheduling. The study concluded that while AI and digital connectivity hold significant potential for transforming educational management, targeted interventions including capacity building, infrastructure enhancement, and strategic system integration are necessary to fully realize these benefits. Recommendations included providing regular staff training, investing in robust digital infrastructure, and implementing supportive policies to optimize the integration of AI and digital tools in tertiary institutions.

papers.title: Universities as Engines of AI Sovereignty
papers.authors: Akintayo AKINRINSOLA, Omowonuola Okunnu, Ololade Periola
papers.journal: African Journal of Humanities and Contemporary Education Research
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping governance and economic systems worldwide, yet many countries in the Global South remain dependent on technologies, infrastructures, and governance models produced elsewhere. This dependency reflects deeper patterns of digital colonialism, including data extraction, reliance on foreign cloud systems, and limited capacity to shape AI on local terms. Grounded in African empirical evidence with broader application across the Global South, this paper argues that universities are critical but overlooked institutions in efforts to strengthen AI sovereignty. While governments, firms, and civil society face persistent capability gaps, universities hold mandates that position them to build research capacity, cultivate technical and governance expertise, and coordinate innovation ecosystems. Drawing on political economy and higher education scholarship, the paper develops the Capability–Alignment–Impact (CAI) Framework to explain how universities can contribute to autonomous AI development through three pathways: strengthening foundational knowledge; improving coordination across government, industry, and civil society; and translating expertise into societal impact. The paper concludes by outlining practical implications for policymakers, development agencies, and university leaders seeking to support sovereign AI ecosystems in the Global South.

papers.title: Cybersecurity Responsibilities in Enterprise Generative AI Adoption: A Qualitative Documentary Analysis of Delegated Authority and Organizational Oversight
papers.authors: Xiaohang Li, Chengzhi Cai, Haizhou Wang
papers.journal: Academic Journal of Management Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: Enterprise generative artificial intelligence assistants can retrieve organizational information, recommend decisions, and initiate actions through connected tools. These capabilities make cybersecurity a question of how authority and responsibility are distributed across systems and organizations. This study examines how public guidance translates security responsibilities into controls over enterprise AI assistants. A purposive corpus of 12 documentary units from public bodies, a security community, and technology providers was retrieved on 28 September 2026. Focused qualitative document analysis combined six initial coding categories with cross-document comparison, producing a register of 27 evidence records. Four interpretive themes were developed: responsibility is allocated at different organizational and technical levels; permission inheritance requires contextual judgment about appropriate access; human oversight depends on enforceable intervention points; and incident accountability requires continuity across organizational and temporal boundaries. Counterevidence matters: the corpus contains explicit oversight, authorization, and incident-management provisions, so it does not support a general claim that AI security guidance lacks responsibility requirements. The analysis instead identifies an implementation translation problem between broad obligations, application-level controls, and locally assigned decision rights. A proposed governance framework links retrieval, recommendation, and action capabilities to permission boundaries, intervention conditions, accountable owners, and retained decision evidence. The framework is an analytical synthesis, not an empirically validated maturity model. The study contributes a focused account of responsibility at transitions between AI capabilities and offers an auditable structure for enterprise deployment decisions. Its conclusions concern the selected documents and do not establish organizational compliance, control effectiveness, or industry-wide prevalence.

papers.title: Technology-Based Interventions for Autistic Children: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies
papers.authors: Sridevi S
papers.journal: International Journal of Interdisciplinary Approaches in Psychology
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition marked by difficulties in social interaction and communication and by repetitive behaviours, which affect a child’s socio-emotional growth and adjustment, especially in educational settings. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, mobile applications, wearable devices and robotics are increasingly used in educational and therapeutic settings to support children with ASD. This systematic literature review analyses the effectiveness and application of such interventions and their outcomes. Eight empirical studies were included, their characteristics were tabulated and major themes were analysed. The findings indicate that technological interventions provide a structured, engaging and adaptable learning setting suited to children with ASD, and that virtual reality and robotics offer immersive experiences that promote skill development.

papers.title: Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) Laboratory Manual: Fundamentals and Practical Industrial Automation
papers.authors: Elaf A. Saeed
papers.abstract: This PLC Laboratory Manual is an educational and practical resource designed to support undergraduate learning in Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) and industrial automation. The material combines fundamental theoretical concepts with laboratory-oriented procedures to help students understand PLC architecture, programming principles, input/output systems, control logic, and practical automation applications.The manual introduces students to PLC hardware and software environments and provides structured laboratory activities that emphasize practical implementation, testing, simulation, monitoring, and troubleshooting. It also supports the development of essential skills in ladder logic programming, digital and analog I/O handling, control sequencing, timers and counters, and the integration of PLCs with industrial devices and automation systems.Each laboratory activity is organized to connect theoretical concepts with hands-on engineering practice, enabling students to gradually develop the ability to design, implement, test, and evaluate PLC-based control solutions. The material is intended to strengthen students’ understanding of industrial control systems while promoting problem-solving, logical thinking, and practical automation skills.This resource is suitable for undergraduate students, instructors, and learners in Automation, Artificial Intelligence, Systems Engineering, Control Engineering, Mechatronics, and related engineering disciplines who are interested in gaining practical experience with PLC-based industrial automation.The laboratory material can be used as a teaching resource for university laboratory sessions, practical training, and introductory study of programmable control systems and modern industrial automation.

papers.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) For Job in Emerging Economies: Evidence From Nigeria's Technology and Education Sector
papers.authors: Mary  Ala Nandi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (Al) is a set of technologies that enable computers to perform a variety of advanced functions, including the ability to see, understand and translate spoken and written language, analyze data, make recommendations, and many more. It is often assumed that artificial intelligence would eliminate jobs and raise unemployment. The same was assumed when the Internet was in its early stages,. but the internet opened far more new doors and provided individuals with new work prospects that no one could have imagined at the time. With the progress of Artificial Intelligence, we can say the same thing is possible. This paper shall examines the concepts of artificial intelligence and the place of job creation, it shall discuss the relevance of job creation and Al perspectives, examine criticism from different scholar regarding the two concepts and the role of artificial intelligence and job creation will be mention which are; skill transformation, job displacement, debate, organizational productivity, entrepreneurship development in generating new employment opportunities, while enhancing productivity. However, the effective utilization of Al for job creation requires adequate training, digital literacy, and supportive government policies that encourage innovation and workforce development. Recommendations are; emerging economies should prioritize, Strengthen Technical and Vocational Education (TVET), Promote Inclusive Al Policies, Invest in Digital Infrastructure, Support Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs, Encourage Public-Private Partnerships, Foster Entrepreneurship and Startup Ecosystems. SBTC theory was adopted as a frame work this paper. So therefore, embracing artificial intelligence while investing in human capacity building is essential for maximizing its potential to generate sustainable employment opportunities and contribute to national development KEYWORDS: Artificial Intelligence (Al), Job Creation, Employment Opportunities, Digital Skills, Entrepreneurship.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Enhancing Students' Academic Performance in The University of Calabar, Nigeria
papers.authors: Mary  Ala Nandi
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has significantly transformed the and learning process across the globe. Artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly being adopted in universities to enhance learning outcomes, support academic research, and improve students' academic performance. This paper examines the role of artificial intelligence in enhancing students' opinion-based academic performance in the University of Calabar, Nigeria. Using an analytical and foundations of approach artificial grounded in contemporary literature, the study explores the conceptual student learning outcomes. intelligence, its applications in higher education, and its implications for students' academic The paper argues that artificial intelligence has the capacity to improve technologies, automated performance through personalized learning systems, intelligent tutoring feedback mechanisms, and Al-assisted research tools. These innovations enable improve students the quality to access educational resources more efficiently, enhance critical thinking skills, and education also of academic research. However, the adoption of artificial intelligence in higher considerations, raises important concerns relating to academic integrity, digital inequality, ethical experiences and the risk of overdependence on automated systems. Drawing from global and the Nigerian educational context, the study concludes that artificial intelligence can significantly systems. The improve paper students' academic performance if properly integrated into institutional learning recommends that Nigerian universities should develop institutional policies invest regulating in digital the ethical infrastructure use of artificial intelligence, integrate Al literacy into academic curricula, and that supports innovative learning environments. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Academic Performance, Higher Education, University of Calabar, Nigeria. Download Pd

papers.title: Impact of Auditory and Visual Information on Corticospinal Excitability and Vividness in Mental Practice Using Motor Imagery: A Pilot Study in Healthy Adults
papers.authors: Nakashima Akira, Naoki Iso, Toshio Higashi, Akira Sagari, Kengo Fujiwara, Takefumi Moriuchi
papers.abstract: Purpose/Aim: Observation of task-related videos during motor imagery (MI) is frequently incorporated into mental practice as a strategy to enhance imagery vividness. However, the effects of auditory and visual information obtained from task videos on MI generation during complex, task-oriented activities of daily living remain unclear. Materials and Methods: This pilot study of eight healthy adults examined the effects of sensory information from a video of an activity of daily living on MI under four conditions: no information, auditory information, visual information, and combined auditory and visual information. The MI task involved cutting paper with scissors. Corticospinal excitability during MI was assessed using motor-evoked potentials elicited by transcranial magnetic stimulation, and subjective MI vividness was evaluated using a visual analog scale. Results: Corticospinal excitability differed significantly across the four conditions (no information, auditory information, visual information, and combined auditory and visual information); however, post hoc analyses did not reveal significant differences between individual conditions. In contrast, subjective MI vividness differed significantly across conditions, with the combined auditory and visual condition yielding the highest vividness ratings. Visual information tended to facilitate MI more effectively than auditory information. Conclusions: These findings suggest that combining visual and auditory sensory information enhances the subjective vividness of MI during mental practice for activities of daily living. Incorporating task-related sensory information may therefore support more effective implementation of mental practice in rehabilitation, particularly in occupational therapy practice.

papers.title: Logic or Emotion? The Impact of Persuasion Strategies on Human-AI Trust
papers.authors: Tianhao Li, Yue Qi
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly engage in persuasive and socially interactive roles, understanding how users calibrate trust toward AI versus human persuaders, and how persuasion strategy shapes this process, has become critical for human-AI interaction research. Prior work has examined preferences for human- versus AI-produced content, yet little is known about how persuasion strategy and persuader identity jointly influence trust during interactive communication. This study investigates how logical versus emotional persuasion, delivered by either human or AI sources, shapes two task-specific outcomes in a multi-turn social reasoning context: round-level credibility evaluations and final accept/reject choices. We treat these outcomes as complementary indicators of trust-relevant evaluation and reliance-related choice. We developed an online interaction paradigm in which participants evaluated persuasive messages under varying identity disclosure conditions. The empirical program included two human-participant studies and two exploratory LLM-based extension studies. Across four studies, AI-generated persuasive messages produced under standardized prompting constraints were evaluated differently from human-authored scripted messages under the present task constraints. In the human-participant studies, results showed a message-source-contingent pattern: AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher credibility ratings in several conditions. under explicit identity disclosure, AI-generated logic-framed messages received higher ratings than human-authored logic-framed messages, whereas human-authored emotion-framed messages received higher ratings than AI-generated emotion-framed messages. Under identity ambiguity, differences between AI and human persuaders were attenuated. The exploratory model analyses examined whether the same manipulations produced convergent or divergent output patterns in GPT-4o and Qwen-Max. Both models assigned higher ratings to logic-framed messages; the logic-over-emotion difference was stronger for Qwen-Max, whereas GPT-4o produced a more balanced pattern. These findings provide a structured account of how identity transparency conditions source-strategy fit in trust calibration and offer design implications for aligning AI persuasion strategies with different identity-disclosure contexts.

papers.title: Effects of Transparent Robot Intentions on Human Trust and Compliance in Decision-Making: The Role of Benevolent and Ulterior Intentions of Robots
papers.authors: Arndt Schäfer, Bettina Kubicek
papers.abstract: Humans are more commonly relying on the assistance of advanced robots in decision-making processes and may follow robots’ suggestions depending on their understanding of how such suggestions are generated. To enhance human understanding, robots can communicate their (simulated) intentions, influencing the trust placed upon them. However, it remains uncertain whether and under what conditions robots’ simulated intentions could also negatively impact trust and compliance. Therefore, we conducted a laboratory experiment with 182 participants, exploring whether information about a robot’s potential benevolent intentions and ulterior motives increased or decreased trust and compliance with the robot’s suggestions, while also altering participants’ involvement levels in a decision task. The results of two 2x2x2 ANOVAs revealed that, regardless of the involvement level, the robot’s simulated ulterior motives decreased trust and compliance, while benevolent intentions did not significantly affect these outcomes. Thus, simulated intentions should be considered in the design of collaborative decision-making between humans and robots.

papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Electronic-Entrepreneurial Intention: Mediating Role of Entrepreneurial Self Efficacy: A Study from District Haripur Pakistan
papers.authors: Shahzad Khan, Ubaldo Comite
papers.journal: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The use of AI has been increased in all areas of life. Among these areas, entrepreneurship is one major area. The study investigates the role of literacy of artificial intelligence in electronic-entrepreneurial intention. The study has measured the mediation role of entrepreneurial self-efficacy between artificial intelligence literacy and electronic-entrepreneurial intention. The study has used a probability sampling technique from the university of haripur students. A sample of 200 were chosen on simple random sampling to assess the data. The Study results indicates that AI Literacy positively contribute towards E-entrepreneurial Intention. Furthermore the result also shows that entrepreneurial self-efficacy positively mediates towards electronic-entrepreneurial Intention. The study results indicate that there is strong need for AI-Ethics development among Entrepreneurs E-entrepreneurial Intention.

papers.title: The Impact of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence on Public Sector Financial Reporting: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.authors: Nur Izzati Kamaruddin, Nur Anis Md Sahibudin, Muhammad Amirul Malikee Mohd Zakee, Yusri Huzaimi Mat Jusoh, Rosliza Bahari, Samsuria Abd. Rahman
papers.journal: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming public sector financial reporting by enabling greater efficiency, accuracy, transparency, and accountability. This paper examines the impact of digitalization and AI on public sector financial reporting in Malaysia, with particular emphasis on the opportunities and challenges associated with their adoption. Using a conceptual and literature-based approach, the study synthesizes existing research and Malaysian policy initiatives to identify the key implications of emerging technologies for public financial management. The analysis indicates that digitalization and AI provide significant opportunities through enhanced process automation, improved transparency and accountability, stronger fraud detection and risk management, data-driven decision-making, and long-term cost efficiency. However, their effective implementation is constrained by several challenges, including shortages of skilled personnel, fragmented legacy systems and data silos, cybersecurity and privacy risks, regulatory and ethical gaps, and high implementation costs, particularly among smaller public agencies. The paper therefore proposes targeted upskilling and reskilling programmes, a unified data governance framework, strengthened cybersecurity infrastructure, clear ethical guidelines for AI adoption, and greater utilisation of scalable cloud-based solutions. The study contributes to the emerging literature by highlighting the need for a balanced digital transformation strategy that integrates technological innovation with institutional readiness, governance, and human capabilities. Addressing these issues is essential for Malaysia to realise the full potential of digitalization and AI in achieving more efficient, transparent, accountable, and sustainable public sector financial reporting.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness, Whistleblowing Systems, and Professional Skepticism in Higher-Education Fraud Detection
papers.authors: Tryas Chasbiandani, Gunawan Baharuddin, Hindradjid Harsono, Muhammad Rafli Kristianto, Elsa Rahma Kartika
papers.journal: Journal of Business Social and Technology
papers.abstract: Background: Digital transformation has increased the complexity of fraud risks in higher education institutions, requiring governance mechanisms, professional judgment, and technological capabilities to operate in combination. Objective: This research investigates the influence of Whistleblowing Systems and Professional Skepticism on Fraud Detection Effectiveness while examining the direct and moderating roles of Artificial Intelligence Readiness. Methods: A quantitative methodology was employed through a cross-sectional survey involving internal auditors, members of Internal Supervisory Units (Satuan Pengawasan Internal [SPI]), and university staff engaged in governance and fraud prevention across Indonesian higher education institutions. The collected data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: The findings reveal that Whistleblowing Systems, Professional Skepticism, and Artificial Intelligence Readinesseach have a positive and statistically significant effect on Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Artificial Intelligence Readinessalso significantly strengthens the relationship between Whistleblowing Systems and Fraud Detection Effectiveness but does not significantly moderate the relationship between Professional Skepticism and Fraud Detection Effectiveness. Conclusion: These results suggest that artificial intelligence supports fraud detection not by replacing auditors' professional judgment but by strengthening organizational preparedness to integrate intelligent technologies into governance frameworks. Therefore, effective fraud detection in higher education depends on the synergy among organizational governance, human expertise, and Artificial Intelligence Readiness.

papers.title: PERCEIVED BENEFITS OF AI-ENHANCED TEACHING AND RESEARCH: A GENDER-BASED COMPARISON AMONG STUDENT OF TEACHER TRAINING PROGRAM
papers.authors: Nadia Razzaq, Muzammila Akram
papers.abstract: The introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is penetrating our environment and education as well, resulting in potential benefits for teaching preparation and research activities. Therefore, this study aimed to help investigate the perceived benefits by student-teachers towards an AI for teacher training and how perceptions may be different from each other based on gender. The methodology, which includes the target population, participants, sampling method and data collection procedure with instrument details consisting of a self-developed questionnaire was made up of two dimensions: AI-enhanced teaching benefits and AI-enhanced research benefits that were collected from student-teachers. The data was analysed using both descriptive and inferential statistical techniques. The results indicate that student-teachers generally perceived AI positively for research and teaching purposes but more so concerning research activities. In teaching, the highest perception of benefit was for developing assessment questions and feedback; whilst in research, it was speeding up access to academic information. The results also highlighted some notable gender differences across both domains, with female student-teachers perceiving greater potential benefits of AI-enhanced teaching and research compared to male student-teachers. Overall, the study anticipates that AI is considered an entry point for assisting student-teachers in term of professionalism and academic works. It advises on embedding applied AI training into teacher education programmes, especially regarding lesson planning, literature reviews and the critical evaluation of information provided by AI tools as well as responsible use of these technologies. These findings highlight the importance of strengthening AI literacy to prepare future teachers for the responsible and effective integration of AI into educational practice.

papers.title: PAI Students’ Perceptions of Ethics in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Learning
papers.authors: Afif Michel Hariya, Deswalantri
papers.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.

papers.title: The unbearable (and unsustainable) social impact of AI-generated “cultural monism” and the EU digital legislation
papers.authors: Francesca Rotolo
papers.abstract: The increasing use of generative AI (genAI) across cultural and (re)creative sectors is indisputable in contemporary times. Within the EU, these systems are classified as “general-purpose AI” models (Recital 99 of the Artificial Intelligence Act – AI Act) and are expected to deliver a wide range of economic and societal benefits, as affirmed in Recital 105 of the Act. Yet, significant concerns have emerged regarding their potential impact on individuals, civil society, and democracy. In the cultural domain, genAI technologies are widely employed to generate outputs often perceived as original. However, scholarly debate has increasingly highlighted the risk that their widespread diffusion may lead to a form of cultural impoverishment – understood as the depletion of cultural pluralism and diversity of artistic expression resulting from the pervasive use of these systems and their underlying architectures, as well as, ultimately, an increasing standardization of the outputs of the algorithmic creative process. These systematic risks are not merely social or political but also carry significant legal implications. The potential effects of genAI on freedom of (artistic) expression and cultural pluralism may, in fact, infringe upon fundamental rights enshrined in international human rights charters. Yet, the role of legal scholarship in addressing such risks remains uncertain. A promising conceptual instrument for tackling this issue is the notion of systemic risk, recently introduced in two key pieces of EU digital legislation: the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the mentioned AI Act. This article examines the advantages and limitations of employing this concept to address the risk of cultural impoverishment. The analysis focuses primarily on the EU legal framework, with particular attention to the AI Act, while adopting a functional and comparative perspective, given that the principal challenges stem from US-based AI systems. It also situates the inquiry within the broader dynamics of the data economy, specifically the logic of knowledge capitalism.
