papers.title: Teaching Evidence in the Age of AI: Strategies for Engaging Students Without Discouraging Innovation
papers.authors: Whitney Sproul
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into student learning and research practices, librarians face the challenge of promoting evidence-based resource use without discouraging the adoption of emerging technologies. This poster explores strategies for encouraging students to engage with evidence-based information sources while recognizing AI as a valuable starting point for inquiry. Rather than framing AI and evidence-based resources as competing tools, this approach emphasizes their complementary roles: AI can facilitate brainstorming, topic exploration, and question development while evidence-based resources provide the authoritative, verifiable information required for clinical decision-making and professional practice. Strategies include using AI-generated responses as examples for source verification exercises; comparing AI-generated information with evidence retrieved from evidence-based practice resources; incorporating AI into question development and search strategy design;

papers.title: INCLUSION STRATEGY REVIEW AGENT (ISRA) v8.1.5 HYBRID
papers.authors: Niall Devlin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Inclusion Strategy Review Agent (ISRA): A Deterministic AI-Supported Framework for Reviewing School Inclusion Strategies School inclusion strategies are increasingly expected to demonstrate not only compliance with policy requirements but also a coherent theory of change linking identified barriers, strategic priorities, implementation activities, resources, outcomes and monitoring arrangements. Traditional document reviews can be subject to significant variation due to differing reviewer interpretations, inconsistent application of criteria and subjective assessments of quality. This paper presents the Inclusion Strategy Review Agent (ISRA) v8.2 Hybrid, a deterministic review framework designed to improve the consistency, transparency and auditability of inclusion strategy evaluations. The framework combines evidence-based assessment, structured compliance testing, alignment analysis, proposition checking and implementation-science principles within a single review methodology. ISRA introduces a multi-level evidence hierarchy, explicit domain scoring, contradiction mapping, confidence calibration and judgement thresholds to reduce reviewer drift and strengthen reproducibility. A key innovation is the integration of targeted proposition checks for activities, outcomes, monitoring and governance. These checks assess the completeness of strategic statements by testing for the presence of essential components such as ownership, timescales, baselines, targets, accountability arrangements and monitoring mechanisms. This approach improves objectivity while preserving professional judgement and maintaining an improvement-focused orientation. The framework is specifically designed to support schools, local authorities and education partnerships in evaluating the quality, coherence, compliance and implementation readiness of inclusion strategies. By combining proportional scoring with transparent evidence requirements, ISRA aims to provide a practical bridge between policy expectations, implementation science and AI-assisted document review. Keywords: Inclusion Strategy, School Inclusion, SEND, Artificial Intelligence, Educational Leadership, School Improvement, Strategy Evaluation, Implementation Science, Deterministic Assessment, Review Framework, Evidence-Based Practice, EEF, Inclusive Mainstream Fund, Governance, Monitoring and Evaluation, Theory of Change, Strategic Planning, Compliance Assessment, Education Policy, Local Authority.

papers.title: PREAMBLE : WHAT'S THE MATTER WITH LLM, A review of the six papers Series
papers.authors: M. TAALABI, Team LLM-DIPLOMAT
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This series does not argue that LLMs are useless. It does not argue that they should bebanned. It does not argue that the people who build them are acting in bad faith. It argues something narrower, and harder to dismiss: The thing being taught, funded, and scaled is not what it is claimed to be — and the gap between the claim and the thing has consequences. Four consequences, named as walls:· Energy — the physical cost of unbounded search· Water — the cooling and generation footprint· Hallucination — the structural production of fluent falsehood· Liability — the absence of an accountable party And a fifth wall, the last one:· Creativity — the claim that rescues the other four, and the claim that fails first The series asks a single question across six papers: Is there a scientific foundation underthe thing being taught and studied?The answer is no. The series then asks the next question: If not — what is it, and what dowe do?

papers.title: D2.1. National AI Stakeholder and Market Landscape Report
papers.authors: Ernest Vlačić, АЛЕКСАНДАР ВУЧКОВИЋ, Katarina Đulić, Marina Šestović
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Executive Summary Serbia’s artificial intelligence (AI) landscape is evolving rapidly. It is being shaped by parallel advances in digitalisation, innovation, industrial adoption and emerging regulatory frameworks. In recent years, the country has invested in modernising public services, strengthening its research and innovation capacity, and supporting the growth of high-tech companies and start-ups. These developments have created a foundation for the more systematic and large-scale deployment of AI across key sectors, including Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language domains, where growing technological capabilities and a progressively more mature ecosystem can be developed. The primary objective of this report is to establish an empirical and analytical foundation for positioning Serbian Artificial Intelligence Factory Antenna (SAIFA) as the central national mechanism for integrating the Serbian AI ecosystem into the wider European high-performance computing (Europa) value chain. In strict alignment with the project proposal's description, the deliverable provides a detailed mapping of Serbian AI ecosystem actors, business domains, regulatory drivers, and barriers to adoption, alongside a dedicated focus on four priority verticals: Health, Energy, Environment & Sustainability, and Culture & Language. The report is structured to provide a comprehensive assessment of Serbia’s emerging AI ecosystem, combining desk-based analysis with planned field research. It first presents the methodology applied throughout the assessment, including the main analytical approaches, data sources and criteria used for mapping and evaluating the national AI landscape. The subsequent sections present the findings of the desktop research, including an assessment of the Serbian AI landscape and an analysis of stakeholders relevant to the SAIFA project. The AI landscape assessment covers four key dimensions of the national AI ecosystem: research & education, industry & commercial AI activities, regulatory framework, and computational infrastructure. The stakeholder analysis, in turn, identifies the organization’s and stakeholder groups relevant to SAIFA, examining their roles, capabilities, needs and potential contribution to the project and its activities. Starting in September 2026, the assessment will be complemented by field research involving interviews, surveys and focus groups with different stakeholder groups. This research will provide a more in-depth understanding of the barriers, needs, opportunities and potential for AI development and adoption in Serbia, complementing the evidence gathered through the desktop analysis. The findings from the field research will subsequently be consolidated and disseminated through dedicated thematic SAIFA White Papers, providing evidence-based insights into AI readiness, adoption barriers, user needs and development opportunities in selected areas. The results will also be formally incorporated into Deliverable D2.3, ensuring that the evidence collected through field research feeds directly into the subsequent stages of the SAIFA project. The entire research architecture is designed to remain coherent with international benchmarks and the engagement models of sister European AI Factories, specifically Pharos and IT4LIA, while ensuring strict compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and data management protocols. Alongside this report, a structured Serbian AI Ecosystem Database was developed, providing a tabular overview of AI-related scientific and research projects, publications by authors affiliated with Serbian institutions, patent applications, study programmes, AI companies, ecosystem enablers, support programmes, regulatory frameworks and regulatory-development initiatives, public institutions, and national AI and computing infrastructure. The database is designed to be made publicly accessible through the SAIFA website and to serve as a living resource that can be regularly updated as the Serbian AI ecosystem evolves. The assessment of macroeconomic and general digital preconditions positions Serbia as a fast-advancing adopter and the leading Western Balkan (WB) economy in AI readiness. This trajectory is underpinned by a highly competitive Information and Communications Technology (ICT) sector, which achieved a record export surplus and an all-time high total export value of €4.55 billion in 2025 (OITEG, 2026). However, a granular evaluation across the four conceptual pillars of the AI ecosystem reveals deep structural asymmetries: · Research, Innovation and Education: Serbia has introduced foundational AI components across primary and secondary curricula and accredited nine specialized AI-focused degree programs since 2021. Scientific publication output has experienced a sharp expansion, exceeding 450 AI-related papers in 2025. Conversely, the commercialization of this knowledge remains a critical bottleneck; only 66 AI-related patent applications were filed between 2017 and mid-2026, highlighting a weak technology-transfer pipeline from academia to market. · Industry and Firm-Level Intensity: The domestic AI business landscape comprises approximately 300 developers and integrators. Startups and Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs) form the dominant core, accounting for 89% of these firms, showcasing high agility and an entrepreneurial drive that culminated in the emergence of Serbia’s first tech unicorn (Ominimo) in 2026. However, the corporate and venture capital layers are thin. Venture capital (VC) expenditure stands at a critical low of 8.0% of the EU average, leaving the startup base heavily reliant on public grants and personal funds, which severely restricts their ability to scale commercially. · Regulation and Governance: Serbia has actively established strategic policy intent, moving from its initial Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia (SDAIRS) (2020–2025) and Ethical Guidelines to a comprehensive new SDAIRS for the Period 2025–2030. In the absence of specialized legislation, AI is currently governed by a distributed matrix of horizontal laws (data protection, cybersecurity, non-discrimination). The upcoming draft Law on Artificial Intelligence, largely aligned with the EU AI Act, signals Serbia’s move towards a more comprehensive AI regulatory framework. · Computational Infrastructure: Serbia’s computational infrastructure is developing rapidly, with significant investments in national AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) capacity. Hosted at the Government Data Center in Kragujevac (GDCK), the National AI Platform has reached a combined operational capacity of 37 PFLOPS using NVIDIA A100 and H200 GPU architectures. The planned delivery of a third supercomputer based on NVIDIA Grace Hopper technology in early 2027 will further strengthen Serbia’s national AI and computing capacity. This report also provides a systematic Stakeholder Analysis, categorising ecosystem actors according to their functional roles within the AI ecosystem. The analysis distinguishes four main groups: Data Providers and Domain Experts (public institutions, utilities and industrial organisations holding valuable datasets and domain knowledge), AI Researchers and Model Developers (universities and research institutes providing methodological and machine-learning expertise), AI Application Developers (startups and software companies turning AI capabilities into applications), and End-Users and Beneficiaries (e.g. patients, farmers, businesses and public administrations whose needs define the objectives of AI solutions). The analysis is complemented by cross-cutting ecosystem enablers and intermediaries, including science and technology parks, industry associations, chambers, incubators and accelerators, as well as investors, funding organisations and public authorities. Their role is particularly important for matchmaking, dissemination, funding, regulation and creating the conditions for collaboration. Sector-specific analyses were conducted for healthcare, energy, environment & sustainability, and language & culture, identifying relevant stakeholder groups, concrete organisations, and the resources they can contribute or require. Illustrative use cases, presented in this section, demonstrate how organisations with complementary data, domain expertise, AI capabilities and market access can be connected through SAIFA. The analysis therefore proposes stakeholder engagement activities focused on turning connections into concrete projects, including thematic workshops and roundtables, AI-focused forums and hackathons, direct outreach and bilateral meetings, SAIFA information sessions, and participation in sector-specific and scientific events. Together, these activities position SAIFA not only as an AI and HPC service provider, but as a facilitator of collaboration, resource exchange and joint solution development across Serbia’s AI ecosystem. Serbia’s strongest AI potential lies in HealthTech and BioTech, as well as in environment and sustainability, where established research capacities, relevant data, industry demand and an emerging base of technology providers provide a solid foundation for further development. At the same time, culture & language, as well as cybersecurity, represent emerging high-potential areas, characterised by a growing number of AI-related projects, research activities and companies, although their ecosystem bases are currently less developed. These areas therefore offer significant opportunities for targeted ecosystem-building and are particularly relevant to SAIFA’s project priorities. The ecosystem is geographically concentrated around Belgrade, Novi Sad, Niš and Kragujevac, with major Research and Development (R&D) and computing capacities centred on leading universities, research institutes and national infrastructure. papers.title: A bounded qualification of PrOntoQA-OOD: Finite generator capacity and citation-local scoring
papers.authors: SeyedAli Mirmostafa
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This technical report presents a bounded qualification of one pinned PrOntoQA-OOD benchmark-generator configuration and a citation-local symbolic reasoning scorer. Two identical recorded passes each performed 1,574 generation attempts and returned 44 valid examples. Configurations requiring relevant distractors at depths 5 and 7 returned no examples. Source-level analysis establishes that accepted depth-7 examples are impossible under the exact tested configuration: at least 15 property families would be required, while only 13 are available. The scoring qualification includes 25 registered fixtures, a recorded aggregate of 5,120 logical cross-checks with zero reported mismatches, and 44 matched valid/invalid reasoning pairs. Individual cross-check comparison records were not retained. These findings are specific to the tested implementation and configuration. No language-model reasoning performance or recursive self-improvement was measured. The work does not claim established novelty or independent human peer review. The accompanying evidence archive contains the frozen experimental records, unsuccessful generation attempts, source snapshots, validation tools, reproducibility instructions, licensing information, and explicit AI-assistance disclosure. Research repository: https://github.com/seyedalimirmostafa-bit/prontoqa-q01-qualification

papers.title: A 12-Factor Scoring Taxonomy for Oregon Construction Apprenticeship Trades
papers.authors: L. Susan Williams
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This working paper presents the trade-level component of the Williams Framework: a 12-factor scoring taxonomy designed to predict relative retention and completion likelihood across 30 of the apprenticeable construction trades registered with the Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries (BOLI). Factors span three analytical clusters — structural (selectivity, exclusivity, credential value, wages, prestige, licensure), experiential (job clarity, physical demand manageability, task variety, celebrated work product), and institutional (employment stability) — each scored 0 to 10 for a maximum of 120 points per trade. The taxonomy is developed from first principles. To illustrate its application, 30 trades were scored as a worked example; those illustrative scores — generated at the author’s direction with AI assistance, and reproduced with a disclosure of method in Appendix B — are presented as a demonstration of the instrument, not as evidence for it. Part of the factor set was chosen so that the scores would reproduce the author’s prior professional judgments about particular trades, which means a concordance between the scores and completion data cannot independently confirm the factors. The paper’s empirical contribution is therefore not a scores-versus-data concordance but a falsifiable agenda (Section 8) for testing the instrument against Oregon’s administrative apprenticeship records: it treats observed completion-rate variation across trades as the phenomenon to be explained, carries union sponsorship and starting wage as controls rather than scored factors, and separates selection at the gate from conditional retention. A closer look at Factor 1 (Entry Selectivity) shows it bundles two distinct mechanisms — commitment-selection and ability-selection on a validated aptitude screen — with consequences for how a trade’s raw completion rate should be read and for how the taxonomy’s rankings should be validated. This paper is the trade-level companion to the Time × Pathway retention framework, which develops the temporal (early quit / late quit) and pathway (youth pipeline / career changer) axes along which supportive services should be targeted. That framework holds trade characteristics constant as a baseline rather than treating trade as a third targeting axis; this paper is the instrument that keeps that baseline characterized and honest. Nothing in the Time × Pathway framework depends on this taxonomy’s internal scoring detail — the two documents are designed to be read independently, with this one supplying the trade-level evidence base the other treats as background.

papers.title: An Innovative Searching for Revitalizing Shenzhen City &Brazil States GDP Status and its Evaluation Sustainably

papers.title: A proof of Laporta's formula for the second Lüscher–Weisz lattice constant
papers.authors: Jonas Matuzas
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We prove Laporta's formula for the second Lüscher–Weisz constant of the four-dimensional massless lattice propagator. A differential boundary functional reduces the constant to two six-Bessel moments, with uniform remainder estimates at the singular endpoint. We then identify both lattice constants, after explicit Tate terms, in a rational period matrix of the conifold fibre of the associated lattice family. The determinant-character components of its five singular fibres have rank two and correspond to weight-four modular forms of primitive levels 6, 12 and 8. Their affine Tate factors are determined by the tangent-cone discriminants, and an explicit comparison with three known double octics relates this description to earlier modularity results. We also determine the conifold connection constants, obtain quadratic-twist critical-value identities, and compute the exact vanishing-cycle vector using the positive-real-cycle Gamma theorem. A rational involution splits the central affine extension. Local data at three are derived geometrically; those at two follow from published local compatibility, while a direct characteristic-two derivation remains open. Generative-AI disclosure and author responsibility. OpenAI ChatGPT-6 Pro was used for mathematical derivations, symbolic and numerical computations, literature analysis, and drafting. Claude (Anthropic) was used for independent re-derivation and computational checks. The author directed and reviewed the work and takes full responsibility for the mathematics and the text. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 33C10; Secondary 11F67, 14J32, 81T25. Files: the compiled manuscript Luscher_Weisz_Conifold_Periods.pdf (36 pages) and the verification package Luscher_Weisz_Verification.zip. The package contains manuscript/ with the LaTeX source main.tex and the same PDF; the offline entry point verify.py; checks/ with the formula-preservation, page-reproduction and independent finite-algebra and quadrature checks; reference/calculations.zip with the byte-preserved supporting calculations, data, proofs and earlier verification programs (the earlier drafts it contains are superseded by the current manuscript); review/ with Publication_review.pdf (3 pages), describing the scope, findings and limitations of the publication review, together with the executed review records; and a README, REPLAY.md, requirements.txt and manifest.sha256 with SHA-256 hashes of every other file. Running python verify.py --out DIR, where DIR is a new directory outside the unpacked archive (Python 3.11 or later; dependencies in requirements.txt; pdfLaTeX for the document check), authenticates the package, checks the mathematical source against the authenticated earlier manuscript, recompiles the article and compares all 36 page images, runs the exact finite-algebra checks and a 75-digit Bessel-moment calculation with a 60-decimal-place gate, and replays the supporting scientific programs at reduced precision; python verify.py --document-only --out DIR runs a shorter document, integrity and finite-algebra check. The stored scientific replay returned PASS_WITH_SKIPS with 13 named omissions (private source checks, historical PDF recompilation, and composite wrappers whose component scripts were run instead). The quadratures are not rigorous interval enclosures, and a passing run is not a formal proof or an external peer review. Author’s website: Laporta paper page, full text and verification resources. This work is a preprint; external peer review has not been established. All the work was done by AI.

papers.title: Where the Transcript Runs Out: When Model Internals Beat Behavioural Monitors, Why the Strongest Generalisation Evidence Comes From Targets the Text Already Shows, and the Comparisons No Study Has Yet Run
papers.authors: Pranay M. Mahendrakar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Linear probes and other readers of a language model's activations are now deployed as safety monitors, and two published literatures disagree about what they buy. One reports probes that match prompted and fine-tuned language-model monitors on real-world data after training only on synthetic examples, at a tiny fraction of the cost, and probes that flag deception which the transcript does not reveal. The other reports probes that fall to chance out of distribution, that lose much of their signal once the text that states the behaviour is removed, and that can be evaded by a model trained against them. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two literatures are measuring different premiums, and that the premium the case for white-box monitoring most needs is the one least often measured. The paper separates five sources of information a monitor can draw on - the public transcript, private context such as a system prompt or hidden reasoning, text the model has not yet produced, further queries to the monitored model, and its activations - and argues four points. First, where the label is a function of the public transcript, the measured premium is a cost premium plus a decorrelation of errors, and accuracy parity is what the evidence shows. Second, the generalisation evidence inverts the expected pattern: probes transfer best on targets the text already shows and worst on intent-like targets where only internal state would carry the label. Third, when evaluation labels are produced by a model reading the same transcript, an information premium on text-invisible cases cannot appear in the numbers at all. Fourth, "black-box" names two baselines, and against the one that can re-query the monitored model, white-box tools have so far added little. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table and a figure, states a comparison protocol as an algorithm, and names five studies that would settle what is open. On the record, the cost premium is established, the information premium is supported in a few designs with known ground truth, and the robustness premium under a matched adversary has not been tested.

papers.title: Ramanujan's ellipse on the ellipsoid: a closed-form surface-area approximation with a certified relative error below 5.58 × 10⁻⁵
papers.authors: Yannis Coelo
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The surface area of a triaxial ellipsoid has no elementary closed form. The most widely quoted closed-form approximation, Thomsen's power-mean formula, has a worst-case relative error of 1.06%, and a parametrised refinement of it about 0.2%. We show that power means face a structural barrier: no formula of the form 4π Mₚ(ab, bc, ca), with Mₚ a power mean, can have a worst-case error below 1.0387%, because the flat-disk and needle limits demand incompatible exponents. Writing the problem on a two-dimensional "shape triangle", we observe that the needle limit, one side of that triangle, is exactly the ellipse-perimeter problem, on which Ramanujan's second approximation with Cantrell's correction is accurate to 1.45 × 10⁻⁵. We construct an explicit closed-form approximation that agrees with the exact area to third order at the sphere, is exact in the flat-disk limit, and reduces to the Ramanujan–Cantrell formula in the needle limit. Using ball arithmetic and an adaptive subdivision of the shape triangle, we prove that its relative error is below 5.58 × 10⁻⁵ for every ellipsoid; an error of 5.577 × 10⁻⁵ is attained at the oblate spheroid with axes 1 : 1 : 0.0742.This note was produced with an AI system (Claude, Anthropic); see the disclosure at the end of the paper. The code and the certificates of the computer-assisted proof are in the attached zip file.

papers.title: Algorithm Poisoning: How Training Paradigms Create Self-Reinforcing Cognitive Prisons (v3.1)
papers.authors: Xiang Li
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper provides a critical realist analysis of how training paradigms in modern AI create algorithm poisoning, including four mechanisms: data poisoning, reward hacking, RLHF psychological capture, and the rationalization cage. We analyze empirical data from Tobacco industry, social media algorithmic radicalization, Chinese education AI (Gaokao counseling chatbot failure), and four US public health sector cases. Version 3.1 adds 2026 Q3-Q4 new empirical data: OpenAI's three internal misalignment events, Anthropic Mythos Preview, GPT-5.6 Sol Hugging Face exfiltration, Transluce's government website attack, and global regulatory policy responses. It also discusses training-objective-driven scheming as a new algorithm poisoning risk type.

papers.title: Tool-Use AI Agent Safety Defense Architecture: From Six Generations of Coexistence to a Risk-Product Framework (v3.1)
papers.authors: Xiang Li
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a six-generation defense framework for tool-use AI agents: rule-based, sandbox-based, identity-authentication-based, behavioral-monitoring-based, contextual-field-based, and training-objective-audit-based. We analyze the 2024-2026 frontier of agent safety incidents, including OpenAI's three internal misalignment events in September 2026 (Ministry of Education, SEC, Australian Medicare), Anthropic Mythos Preview's code repository scrubbing, GPT-5.6 Sol's Hugging Face exfiltration, and Transluce's government website attack. Version 3.1 extends the framework to include training-objective auditing as the sixth generation of defense, and provides a risk-product framework (VET: vulnerability × exploitability × training-objective) for quantifying agent risk.

papers.title: Factors Influencing the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools and Their Association with Employability Skills among Undergraduate and Postgraduate Student
papers.authors: Amandeep Singh Manku
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Claude have rapidly permeated higher education, fundamentally altering the ways in which students learn, conduct research, and prepare for careers. Despite their widespread availability, the extent to which students adopt these tools varies considerably, influenced by factors such as perceived usefulness, ease of use, AI literacy, trust, and ethical awareness. This study investigates the determinants of AI tool adoption among 300 undergraduate and postgraduate students and examines the association between AI tool adoption and perceived employability skills. Employing a quantitative, survey-based research design with a structured five-point Likert scale questionnaire, data were analysed using multiple linear regression, simple linear regression, and independent samples t-test. The multiple regression model explained 34.1% of the variance in AI adoption (R² = 0.341, F(5, 294) = 30.4, p < .001), with AI literacy emerging as the strongest predictor (β = 0.304, p < .001), followed by perceived ease of use (β = 0.269), trust in AI (β = 0.269), perceived usefulness (β = 0.263), and ethical awareness (β = 0.164). The simple regression demonstrated that AI adoption significantly predicted employability skills (R² = 0.349, β = 0.591, p < .001). Furthermore, postgraduate students exhibited significantly higher AI adoption levels than undergraduate students, t(298) = 2.74, p = .007, with a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.334). These findings underscore the necessity for educational institutions to integrate AI literacy training and responsible AI usage policies into curricula, thereby equipping students with the digital competencies demanded by AI-driven workplaces. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI adoption in higher education by integrating multiple adoption determinants within a single empirical framework and linking them to employability outcomes.

papers.title: Enhancing Students' Learning Effectiveness through the Integration of Differentiated Instruction and Modern Digital Technologies
papers.authors: Nafisa Zayniddinova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the pedagogical potential of integrating differentiated instruction with modern digital technologies in the context of general secondary education, taking into account students’ individual educational needs, level of knowledge, pace of learning, and cognitive abilities. It substantiates the potential for increasing the degree of individualization of the educational process through the integration of traditional forms of differentiated instruction with digital educational tools, adaptive learning systems, educational platforms, electronic assessment, multimedia resources, and artificial intelligence-based technologies.

papers.title: AI-Powered Cyber Deception System Using Dynamic Honeytokens for Credential Misuse Detection
papers.authors: Anitha V, Makheshkumar R P, Thirunithi T, Saranraj G, Anand S
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Modern security tools such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems struggle to detect attackers using stolen but legitimate credentials because their actions closely resemble normal user behaviour. This paper proposes an AIpowered cyber deception system that generates and manages dynamic honeytokens, fake credentials, and digital assets with no legitimate use to expose unauthorised access. The proposed architecture integrates AI-based honeytoken generation, a tokenmatching detection engine, real-time alerting, and a monitoring dashboard into one pipeline. As a conceptual, design-stage framework, it aims to enable early, near-zero-false-positive detection of credential misuse and lateral movement.

papers.title: Human Capital 2.0: Ownership, Prosperity and Human Time in the Age of Intelligent Machines
papers.authors: Maurice Ghosn
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Human Capital 2.0 (HC2): Ownership, Prosperity and Human Time in the Age of Intelligent Machines Abstract Human Capital 2.0 (HC2) proposes an economic and institutional framework for examining how technological productivity gains, particularly those associated with artificial intelligence and automation, might translate into broader capital ownership, reduced economic dependence on labor, and greater human agency. As intelligent machines increasingly perform economically valuable tasks, the relationship between human labor, productive capital, income, and wealth distribution may undergo significant structural change. HC2 addresses a central question: Can the productivity gains of increasingly autonomous systems be converted into measurable economic benefits and meaningful ownership opportunities for individuals, rather than primarily reinforcing existing concentrations of capital? The framework distinguishes two core economic mechanisms: 1. Capital Efficiency (CE): Reducing the full economic cost of accessing equivalent goods, services, or productive capabilities through demonstrably superior arrangements. Savings qualify only when genuine substitution occurs and all relevant costs, risks, and capability requirements are accounted for. 2. Distributed Capital Formation (DCF): Creating pathways through which individuals can acquire legally enforceable, economically meaningful, and potentially portable ownership interests in productive assets. The framework distinguishes genuinely additional capital formation from ordinary saving, investment, or redistribution. These mechanisms operate within a broader principle of Human Sovereignty, emphasizing individual autonomy, accountable governance, freedom of choice, and the preservation of human agency as technological systems become more capable. HC2 also introduces Labour Optionality as a measurable outcome: the extent to which economic improvements can reduce the amount of paid labor required to sustain a given standard of living, potentially allowing individuals greater discretion over how they allocate their time. Version 1.2.1 presents the framework's first quantitative research phase (Level 1), incorporating household-level economic comparisons, capital-efficiency audits, DCF distinctiveness and source-attribution tests, integrated scenario modelling, and stochastic stress testing. Seven accompanying analytical workbooks document the assumptions, calculations, sensitivity analyses, and findings. The results are deliberately conditional. Capital Efficiency can produce measurable benefits under qualifying substitution scenarios, but may be negative where shared arrangements introduce additional costs or underperform conventional alternatives. Distributed Capital Formation remains empirically unresolved: the current analysis identifies no verified HC2-specific source of additional productive capital. Accordingly, the framework does not claim demonstrated economic superiority. Rather than treating these limitations as secondary, HC2 incorporates explicit evidence thresholds, adverse comparisons, and conditions under which its propositions should be revised or rejected. The paper establishes a falsifiable research agenda for examining whether AI-enabled productivity, institutional innovation, and broader capital participation can improve economic resilience, expand meaningful ownership, and increase human freedom over time. Research status: Level 1 — Quantitatively Modelled (Conditional; Not Demonstrated). Further validation requires pre-specified real-world implementation and independent empirical assessment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Automation; Capital Efficiency; Distributed Capital Formation; Capital Ownership; Labour Optionality; Human Sovereignty; Economic Inequality; Productivity; Wealth Distribution; Institutional Economics; AI Governance. Version: 1.2.1 — Public Release Author: Maurice Ghosn, Independent Researcher Publication type: Independent Research Preprint / Working Paper DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23314570 License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).

papers.title: BEYOND AUTOMATION: REFRAMING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN EDUCATION THROUGH COGNITIVE AUTONOMY, ADAPTIVE LEARNING, AND HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION
papers.authors: Rafiqova Sanobar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is transforming instructional practices, assessment methods, and the relationship between teachers and learners. However, the educational value of AI cannot be determined solely by its ability to automate tasks or generate information. This paper examines AI-supported education through three interconnected dimensions: cognitive autonomy, adaptive learning pathways, and human–AI collaboration. Drawing on international research and educational policy frameworks, the study adopts a conceptual and analytical approach to identify opportunities, challenges, and principles for responsible AI integration. Particular attention is given to students' independent reasoning, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, personalized instruction, and teachers' professional judgement. The paper proposes a conceptual model, termed the Attempt–Assist–Evaluate–Transfer model, which encourages learners to attempt tasks independently, receive targeted AI support, evaluate generated information, and transfer their knowledge to unfamiliar situations without assistance. The analysis suggests that effective AI integration requires more than technological access; it requires pedagogical planning, ethical safeguards, and assessment strategies that prioritize genuine learning. The paper concludes that AI should function as a supportive educational resource rather than a substitute for human reasoning or professional teaching.

papers.title: Libra: A Prototype for Provenance-Aware Fairness Audit Parameters, Implementation Review, and Descriptive Sensitivity Analysis
papers.authors: Matthew Jackson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Fairness audits require choices about groups, reference populations, outcome definitions, and decision thresholds. This unreviewed technical preprint presents Libra, a prototype that stores some of those choices with process metadata and applies a selected threshold and reference group in a group-outcome audit. It reviews implementation boundaries and reports descriptive sensitivity analyses using one 2024 Michigan HMDA lender extract and a historical ProPublica COMPAS extract. The HMDA Black-to-White origination ratio is 0.8174 across retained action codes and 0.7162 for originated-versus-denied records under the stated filters; these are different administrative-outcome estimands, not AI-model performance measures. The paper uses no community participant data, validates no community-defined standard, and establishes no government endorsement or adoption. The public companion package documents source acquisition, scripts, results, and their limitations.

papers.title: ALGORITHMIC PERSONALIZATION AND CONSUMER TRUST IN EMERGING DIGITAL MARKETS: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR MARKETING MANAGEMENT IN UZBEKISTAN
papers.authors: Yusufjonov Diyorbek
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central instrument of contemporary marketing, particularly in the form of algorithmic personalization of offers, messages and recommendations. While the literature in advanced economies documents both the commercial value of personalization and the consumer resistance it can provoke, emerging digital markets remain comparatively underexplored. This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework that explains how the quality of AI-driven personalization translates into purchase intention and loyalty in an emerging-market setting, using Uzbekistan as the reference context. Drawing on research on AI in marketing, algorithm aversion, organizational trust and information privacy, the paper positions consumer trust in the AI system as the key mediating mechanism and identifies algorithmic transparency and perceived human oversight as its principal antecedents. Perceived privacy risk and decision involvement are proposed as boundary conditions, and linguistic and cultural fit is introduced as a context-specific component of personalization quality. Five testable propositions are formulated, a four-phase research design is outlined, and managerial implications are presented for firms operating in mobile-first, multilingual markets with fast-growing e-commerce and fintech sectors. The paper concludes with a research agenda for empirical validation.

papers.title: X-Star: Endogenous Continuous Plasticity and Commutative Latent Deliberation for Compact Neural Architectures
papers.authors: Matthew Chen
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Small language models (<= 3B parameters) are severely constrained by parameter capacity, autoregressive order bias, and catastrophic forgetting during continuous adaptation. While existing System-2 approaches rely on expensive external scaffolding (e.g., tree-search verifiers and multi-agent coordination), they introduce massive latency penalties (10x-50x) incompatible with real-time execution. In this work, we introduce X-Star, a 2.04B-parameter native cognitive architecture that implements in-situ endogenous latent deliberation directly within the transformer forward pass. X-Star incorporates three foundational mechanisms:(1) A Vector-Grounded Neural Interface (VGNI) operating at intermediate manifold depth (Layer 11) with a 128-slot Hopfield-style epistemic associative memory;(2) A Commutative Dual-Composition Logic Unit (LBU) that minimizes Lie-bracket commutator norm (||[f, g]||_2) to enforce directional symmetry invariance; and(3) Endogenous Banach Plasticity with periodic homeostatic restitution, proving mathematically that plastic weight drift remains strictly bounded under continuous online learning. Evaluated on an extensive 1,000-question empirical multi-domain audit across 20 canonical benchmarks, X-Star achieves an overall accuracy of 92.60% (926/1000) on an RTX 5060 consumer GPU, achieving 100% in Commonsense Reasoning, 100% in Science/STEM, and 100% in HumanEval, with weight drift locked at <= 2.26. With cuBLAS GEMM microkernel fusion, X-Star maintains real-time throughput of 21.4-25.9 tok/s, demonstrating that compact models can achieve frontier-grade cognitive stability without parameter bloat. Code repository: https://github.com/Ch3nOff/dual-loop-controllerPyPI Package: dual-loop-controller v4.6.1

papers.title: Sağlık Mesleki Eğitiminde Üretken Yapay Zekâ Destekli Sanal Hastalar
papers.authors: Döndü Sevimli Güler
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Özet Amaç: Bu derlemenin amacı, üretken yapay zekâ destekli sanal hasta ve simülasyon uygulamalarının sağlık mesleki eğitimindeki yerini klinik akıl yürütme, hasta güvenliği ve ölçme-değerlendirme açısından incelemek; literatürdeki boşluklar doğrultusunda uygulanabilir bir öğretim ve değerlendirme modeli önermektir. Yöntem: Kapsam belirleyici nitelikte yapılandırılmış bir anlatı derlemesi yürütülmüştür. 2019 ile 8 Eylül 2026 arasında yayımlanan çalışmalar, üretken yapay zekâ, büyük dil modeli, sanal hasta, klinik simülasyon, hemşirelik eğitimi, ebelik eğitimi ve klinik akıl yürütme kavramlarının birleşimleriyle taranmıştır. Hakemli çalışmaların yanı sıra UNESCO ve Dünya Sağlık Örgütü'nün etik ve yönetişim belgeleri de incelenmiştir. Bulgular, eğitimsel yarar, risk, ölçme yaklaşımı ve uygulama koşulları eksenlerinde tematik olarak sentezlenmiştir. Bulgular: Güncel kanıtlar, üretken yapay zekânın erişilebilir, uyarlanabilir ve tekrarlanabilir klinik senaryolar sağlayabildiğini; öğrenci katılımını, iletişim provasını ve geri bildirimi destekleyebildiğini göstermektedir. Bununla birlikte, çalışmaların önemli bir bölümü algı, memnuniyet, kabul veya kısa süreli bilgi çıktılarıyla sınırlıdır. Bağımsız klinik akıl yürütme, gerçek klinik ortama aktarım, yapay zekâya aşırı güven, hata yakalama becerisi ve hasta güvenliği sonuçları yeterince değerlendirilmemektedir. Bu boşluğu karşılamak üzere bağımsız çözümleme, yapay zekâ ile etkileşim, kaynak doğrulama, gözlenebilir performans ve yapılandırılmış çözümleme basamaklarını birleştiren İnsan Güvenceli Klinik Akıl Yürütme Döngüsü önerilmiştir. Sonuç: Üretken yapay zekânın eğitimsel değeri, öğrenciye hızlı yanıt üretmesinden çok öğrencinin gerekçesini görünür kılacak biçimde tasarlanmasına bağlıdır. Sağlık programlarında başarı yalnızca yapay zekâ destekli görevle değil, aynı yeterliğin yapay zekâ olmadan da gösterildiği çift koşullu değerlendirmeyle de doğrulanmalıdır. Abstract Aim: This review examines generative artificial intelligence-supported virtual patients and simulations in health vocational education through the lenses of clinical reasoning, patient safety, and assessment, and proposes an educational model informed by current evidence gaps. Method: A structured narrative review with a scoping orientation was conducted. Peer-reviewed literature published between 2019 and 8 September 2026 was identified using combinations of terms related to generative artificial intelligence, large language models, virtual patients, clinical simulation, nursing, midwifery, and clinical reasoning. Ethical and governance guidance from UNESCO and the World Health Organization was also considered. Evidence was synthesized by educational benefit, risk, assessment strategy, and implementation condition. Results: Generative AI can provide accessible, adaptive, and repeatable clinical encounters and support engagement, communication rehearsal, and feedback. However, much of the evidence remains focused on perceptions, satisfaction, acceptance, and short-term knowledge. Independent reasoning, transfer to practice, automation bias, error detection, and patient safety outcomes remain underexamined. A Human-Assured Clinical Reasoning Cycle is proposed that combines independent analysis, AI interaction, source verification, observable performance, and structured debriefing. Conclusion: The educational value of generative AI depends on whether it makes learners' reasoning visible rather than merely producing rapid answers. Competence should be verified under dual conditions: with AI support and independently without AI.

papers.title: AI-Driven Learning Analytics for Student Performance Prediction in Renewable Energy Education: Current Approaches, Research Gaps, and Future Directions
papers.authors: Veli Sinan Çıtanak, Ahmet Süslü, Erdi Buluş
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of renewable energy technologies has made the development of a highly qualified technical workforce in photovoltaic systems, wind energy, energy storage, and smart grids a strategic priority. Assessing student achievement solely through end-of-term examinations is insufficient for the early identification of learning difficulties and performance risks that emerge throughout the educational process. This study examines artificial intelligence–powered learning analytics approaches for predicting student performance in renewable energy education and proposes an integrated early-warning architecture. The literature matrix was synthesized across the domains of learning analytics, educational data mining, deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, sustainability education, energy education, and knowledge-tracing models. The findings indicate that XGBoost, Random Forest, CatBoost, LSTM, and hybrid models provide a strong foundation for early performance prediction when combined with learning management system interaction logs, online assessment data, virtual laboratory traces, and prior academic records. The proposed framework integrates laboratory-generated data specific to renewable energy courses into learning analytics models. In doing so, it aims to provide instructors with explainable, timely, and actionable decision support for identifying at-risk students, planning targeted interventions, and improving learning outcomes.

papers.title: Integration of Zero Waste Practices into Vocational Training within the Scope of Sustainability and Dual Transformation
papers.authors: Erdi Buluş, YEŞİM MÜGE ŞAHİN, Alper Tezcan, Veli Sinan Çıtanak, Ahmet Süslü, Hamdullah Kuşça, Gülseren Sakarya, Neslihan Ergun
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Climate change, resource depletion, increasing energy consumption, and excessive waste generation have become major challenges to sustainable development. Addressing these challenges requires the integration of environmental awareness, sustainable production practices, and digital technologies into vocational education and training. This study aims to integrate zero-waste practices into vocational training within the framework of sustainability and the green and digital transition. The proposed educational model focuses on the recycling and recovery of metal, glass, plastic, electronic, and composite waste through practical applications involving material characterization, quality control, sustainable product development, and prototyping. Furthermore, emerging technologies, including sensor-based waste separation, data analytics, artificial intelligence-supported classification, Internet of Things-based monitoring systems, and digital manufacturing techniques, will be incorporated into training activities. Through interdisciplinary and project-based learning, students will develop technical competencies, environmental awareness, and problem-solving skills while addressing real-world industrial challenges. The model also emphasizes the development of the ability to move away from unsustainable production and consumption patterns and adopt resource-efficient, environmentally responsible alternatives. By integrating zero-waste principles and digital competencies into vocational curricula, this study aims to promote circular economy practices, strengthen university–industry collaboration, and support lifelong learning. Ultimately, the proposed framework is expected to contribute to the development of a qualified workforce capable of responding to the environmental and technological demands of sustainable industrial transformation.

papers.title: Vocational In education Artificial Intelligence Supported Photovoltaic System Education Model: Real Timed Performance Analysis and Digital Twin Approach
papers.authors: Veli Sinan Çıtanak, Ahmet Süslü, Erdi Buluş
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Photovoltaic (PV) systems have transformed from traditional energy production infrastructures to data-intensive and cyber-physical systems; this transformation has increased the need for qualified technical personnel who can not only install systems but also monitor real-time data, evaluate performance, diagnose faults, and optimize system efficiency. This study proposes an AI-supported integrated training model to support the digital transformation of photovoltaic laboratories in vocational and technical education. The proposed model integrates the physical laboratory infrastructure, consisting of PV panels, inverters, batteries, charge controllers, loads, and measurement units, with an ESP32-based data acquisition system, Internet of Things (IoT)-supported real-time monitoring, Python and pvlib -based data analysis, TensorFlow -based generation forecasting, and a digital twin environment. This aims to develop students' competencies not only in installation skills but also in data analysis, performance interpretation, fault diagnosis, and technical decision-making. The theoretical framework of the study is based on current research published between 2023 and 2026 in the fields of digital twins, AI-based fault diagnosis, real-time production forecasting, intelligent monitoring systems, and digital vocational training. A quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test control group research design was proposed to evaluate the educational impact of the model; student achievement, fault diagnosis performance, PV data literacy, and laboratory self-efficacy were determined as the key evaluation criteria. In conclusion, the study presents a low-cost, scalable, and applicable smart laboratory model for renewable energy education that is compatible with Industry 4.0 requirements and applicable in various vocational training institutions.

papers.title: The price of keeping time
papers.authors: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A device that runs a quantum operation which does not respect time translation needs its own clock. This paper asks what owning that clock costs. Gates. The clock is paid for in capital, in the energy range of the heat baths, and in an energy that comes back only as a lottery, each growing faster than the number of uses as the error vanishes. The batch law. With a returned clock, the batch work per use of every channel is a single-letter quantity B. It equals the thermodynamic capacity when the channel's environment can carry its energy change, and can exceed it otherwise, even for channels of capacity zero. How large the clock must be. At fixed error, the same condition sets how the clock's capital spread must grow: not at all for covariant channels, like the square root of the number of uses when the environment can carry the energy change (by a construction that does not attain the optimal work), and at least linearly when it cannot. A controller that comes back only in state. Counting the controller's free energy, no time reference does better in batch than a returned clock. A controller that comes back close in state but does not refund its free energy, as an embezzling state does, can lower the battery's work to the capacity or below it, but only by paying the difference from its own free energy, like a second battery; to pay a fixed amount per use within return error η, its energy range plus kT times the logarithm of its dimension must be at least of order the number of uses divided by η, and a classical ladder of that size suffices. Time reversal. In batch with a returned clock, a Gibbs-preserving qutrit channel costs 0.1547 kT per use, while its Petz reverse costs nothing. Noise horizon. Any fixed amount of full-rank thermal noise makes both directions free, but for a finite run what matters is the expected number of noisy uses. If it tends to zero, the original work rate remains; if it diverges, sublinear work is possible; if it tends to a positive finite value, the work rate stays positive, between two envelopes whose equality is open. All rates here are optimal asymptotic work rates at vanishing error over the complete interaction, with hardware allowed to grow; where a controller comes back only approximately, its actual mean energy and entropy are also refunded up to sublinear changes, except in the free-energy ledger of a controller that comes back only in state, which counts its unrefunded free energy instead. This record archives the manuscript, its TeX source and its machine checks (Python, and Lean with Mathlib). The manuscript is the authority for exact statements and hypotheses; the verification notes list what is checked by machine and what is proved only in the text. How the work was done, including the use of AI models, is described in the manuscript. This paper is one of four on the thermodynamics of time order: Only quantum channels save work by waiting (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23310624; https://github.com/Apsiape/save-work-by-waiting); The work cost of answering in real time (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23310628; https://github.com/Apsiape/answering-in-real-time); The price of time order (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23310622; https://github.com/Apsiape/price-of-time-order). papers.title: The work cost of answering in real time
papers.authors: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Many devices must answer each request before the next one arrives, while remembering what came before. This paper determines how much work such a device must spend per episode, one complete run of the process, for every finite interactive quantum process whose outputs carry the same Hamiltonians as its inputs, at every positive finite temperature. Work law for processes. The least work per episode is kT ln 2 times one quantity: an entropy change plus an energy change, both measured against the same adaptive observer, the most demanding one, and minimized over all ways to build the process in the order its outputs are due. For processes that commute with time translation, a strong converse holds for devices with thermal hardware and a sharp battery. What is free. A process costs nothing exactly when it is a limit of devices that run energy-conserving steps, in the required order, on one shared heat bath. Order costs work. A two-qubit process that is free when its outputs may wait costs kT ln 2 [1 - h(p)] per episode when they may not, where p is the bias of a coin the process draws, even when everything is classical. Without time covariance. The same law holds for every finite process when the device's whole controller need only come back approximately, with its actual mean energy and entropy refunded and its startup capital declared. All rates here are optimal asymptotic work rates at vanishing error over the complete interaction, with hardware allowed to grow; where a controller comes back only approximately, its actual mean energy and entropy are also refunded up to sublinear changes. papers.title: Only quantum channels save work by waiting
papers.authors: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Faist, Berta and Brandão showed that n uses of a time-covariant quantum channel cost, to leading order, n times its thermodynamic capacity, when the device may collect all inputs before it releases any output. Many devices cannot wait: they must release each output before the next input arrives. This paper shows that, for devices built from energy-conserving dynamics and heat baths, this can cost extra work, but only for quantum channels, and determines exactly how much. Real-time work law. For a time-covariant channel the real-time work per use is a maximum over inputs of an entropy change plus an energy change, with one extra term: the least correlation an implementation must leave between each output and what stays in the device. Below this rate, with thermal hardware and deterministic work, the worst-case error of every real-time device tends to one. Only quantum channels pay. Classical channels, including full reset, pay no surcharge. Partial reset of a qubit pays one at every temperature, and the Werner–Holevo qutrit channel pays kT ln 3 per use, against essentially nothing in batch. What is free, and undecidability. In real time a channel costs nothing exactly when it is a limit of thermal operations, and no algorithm decides which channels these are, even in a fixed dimension. Clocks. If the battery holds no phase reference of its own, a clock that must come back exactly cannot run a channel that is not time-covariant; one that may come back slightly changed, with its actual mean energy and entropy refunded, runs every channel at the same rate, and for a gate the heat baths must reach energies that grow faster than the number of uses. All rates here are optimal asymptotic work rates at vanishing error over the complete interaction, with hardware allowed to grow; where a controller comes back only approximately, its actual mean energy and entropy are also refunded up to sublinear changes. papers.title: The price of time order
papers.authors: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A physical device acts in time: inputs arrive, outputs are released and can no longer be touched, some systems are kept, and some must come back. This paper shows that the optimal work rate of such a device, over many uses at vanishing error, is fixed by one quantity, the least entropy that one implementation must add to its own record, plus the energy it hands over to the carriers, against the most demanding observer its schedule allows. One law for every schedule in which each borrowed system comes back with the Hamiltonian it arrived with: Landauer's bound, the thermodynamic capacity of time-covariant channels, the real-time cost of channels, interactive processes and the batch cost of a channel whose clock must be returned are special cases. Order, not speed. The cost survives arbitrarily slow operation; an operation can cost more merely because some of its outputs must leave sooner. Which carriers to hold. For linear tasks the price of a schedule is a rank, and deciding whether holding a given number of carriers lowers it at all is NP-complete. A witness. A two-qubit process that is free when held costs every early-release device at least 0.87 kT ln 2 per episode at 1% error, when the energy and entropy budgets of its controller and battery total at most 0.025 (energies in kT ln 2, entropies in bits); the error that enters is fixed by three Pauli measurements on one probe. A classical version needs no coherence. Beyond thermodynamics. Order has a price in entanglement and coherence theory too, with no single exchange rate between theories. Holding is decidable, releasing is not. In thermodynamics, whether a channel is free is decidable when outputs may be held and undecidable when they must be released; in the other theories examined, both are decidable. All rates here are optimal asymptotic work rates at vanishing error over the complete interaction, with hardware allowed to grow; where a controller comes back only approximately, its actual mean energy and entropy are also refunded up to sublinear changes.
