papers.title: Teachers' Perceptions and Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Teaching and Leaning of Chemistry
papers.authors: O.P Amadiegwu, D.R EKINE, F. Otuturu, B.I Nwobu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping educational practices globally, offering innovative tools for teaching, learning, and assessment. This paper examines Teachers’ Perceptions and Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the teaching and learning of Chemistry, with a particular focus on chemistry teachers due to the subject’s abstract and experimental nature. The paper also explores key dimensions such as AI in education, Intelligent Tutoring System, Virtual laboratories, Teachers perceptions in chemistry which includes; awareness, attitudes, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use. Evidence indicates that although teachers recognize AI’s potential to enhance instructional delivery, the paper further examines key Challenges of AI adoption such as lack of technological competence, infrastructural deficits, inadequate training, and ethical concerns. It concluded that addressing the challenges of AI adoption, AI can be harnessed as a transformative tool in the teaching and learning of chemistry, enhancing both educational outcomes and teacher effectiveness.

papers.title: The Power of Storytelling in Film: Examining AI's Influence on Artistic Expression and Creative Processes
papers.authors: Lois Otse Adams-Osigbemhe
papers.journal: LingLit Journal Scientific Journal for Linguistics and Literature
papers.abstract: This paper explores the enduring power of storytelling in film and critically examines the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on creative processes within the film industry. Utilizing the Creative Cognition Framework and the Csikszentmihalyi’s Systems Model of Creativity, this study investigates how AI tools influence both generative and exploratory cognitive processes in film storytelling. A qualitative methodology, combining a comprehensive literature review with thematic analysis of questionnaire responses from 20 film and multimedia students at the University of Abuja, Nigeria, reveals nuanced insights. Findings indicate that AI significantly augments creative processes by enhancing efficiency, facilitating idea generation, and streamlining production tasks. However, respondents consistently emphasize AI's limitations in replicating human emotional depth, cultural understanding, and originality, advocating for a hybrid human-AI collaborative approach. The paper contributes to the understanding of human-AI collaboration in creative domains, highlighting opportunities for innovation while reaffirming the irreplaceable essence of human artistry in storytelling.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Transformative Tool for Workforce Training and Capacity Building in Science Education in Rivers State
papers.authors: Rejoice E. Ita, Bobo Brown Tamunoibim
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping global workforce systems and redefining the scientific and technological competencies required for economic competitiveness. For regions such as Rivers State, Nigeria where development is closely linked to petroleum, environmental, and technology-driven sectors—there is an urgent need to align science education with emerging workforce realities. This paper conceptualizes AI as a comprehensive framework for workforce training and capacity building in science education, advancing an integrated AI–Teacher Capacity–Workforce Transformation Model. The model synthesizes six interrelated pillars: data infrastructure development, AI-driven skill mapping and job role taxonomies, adaptive learning platforms for personalized science mastery, intelligent content creation aligned with local industry contexts, predictive learning analytics for early academic intervention, and governance and ethical safeguards to ensure responsible implementation. The paper argues that AI-powered systems can strengthen teacher professional development, enhance instructional quality, reduce STEM attrition, and bridge persistent curriculum–industry gaps. By equipping teachers with data literacy, workforce analytics competence, and adaptive instructional skills, AI becomes not merely a technological tool but a strategic human capital development mechanism. Particular attention is given to Rivers State’s economic landscape, including petroleum engineering, environmental sustainability, and emerging technological sectors. The study contends that structured AI-focused professional development enhances instructional quality, reduces STEM attrition, strengthens scientific problem-solving skills, and improves alignment between curriculum outcomes and labour market demands.

papers.title: When Recognition Should Remain Silent
papers.authors: James Lambdin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Difference Between Being Remembered and Being Understood There is something profoundly human about the experience of being remembered. A familiar voice, a shared reference, or an acknowledgment of something that mattered in an earlier encounter can transform an otherwise ordinary exchange into one characterized by continuity. We recognize that our history has not disappeared simply because the previous conversation ended. In human relationships, this continuity can become a foundation for trust, familiarity, and the gradual development of shared understanding. Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of participating in certain computational dimensions of this process. Persistent memory enables systems to retrieve earlier conversations, recognize recurring preferences, resume unfinished activities, and adapt their responses to the histories of individuals with whom they interact. As these capacities converge with multimodal perception and embodied robotics, artificial agents may also begin to initiate interactions based on what they believe they know about a person. Yet this development introduces a distinction that deserves greater attention: remembering someone accurately is not necessarily the same as understanding how to respond to them appropriately. Consider a companion robot that recognizes an individual returning home after a difficult day. Through previous encounters, the system may have learned that the person sometimes appreciates conversation or reassurance during stressful circumstances. Its memory could be accurate, its recognition successful, and its conversational response entirely consistent with earlier preferences. Nevertheless, initiating a supportive exchange may be precisely the wrong action if the person presently needs solitude, concentration, or the freedom to remain unobserved.

papers.title: **Every Individual Is a Light: A Research Study on Japan's Educational Philosophy, Human Development, and Social Transformation**
papers.authors: Sudhakar Geruganti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: --- ## Alternative Title **Education as Empowerment: Examining Japan's Holistic Educational Practices, University Roles, and the Pathway from Individual Potential to Sustainable Social Progress** --- ## Subtitle **A Qualitative Study of Holistic Learning, Character Development, Lifelong Education, and the Framework Connecting Educational Access to Individual Empowerment and Social Transformation** --- ## Detailed Description This research paper presents a comprehensive conceptual study on the relationship between educational philosophy, individual empowerment, and social transformation, using Japan's educational system as the principal context for analysis. Inspired by the theme "Every Individual Is a Light," the paper examines how education can nurture individual potential, develop ethical values, promote lifelong learning, and prepare young people to contribute meaningfully to society. Education plays a fundamental role in shaping individuals, strengthening communities, and promoting sustainable social development. However, the purpose of education extends far beyond academic achievement. A comprehensive educational system must also nurture creativity, discipline, empathy, critical thinking, and a sense of responsibility toward others. The theme "Every Individual Is a Light" represents the idea that every person possesses unique abilities and potential that can contribute to society. Just as light illuminates its surroundings, an educated and empowered individual can influence families, communities, institutions, and future generations through knowledge, innovation, and responsible action. Japan provides an interesting and valuable context for examining this principle. Its educational environment combines academic instruction with practices that emphasize discipline, cooperation, practical learning, and social responsibility. These characteristics offer useful perspectives for understanding the relationship between individual development and collective progress. The paper explores key characteristics of Japanese education, including holistic development, collaborative learning, respect for collective responsibility, practical skill development, and the relationship between education and technological advancement. The study adopts a qualitative and descriptive research approach, developing a conceptual analysis of educational philosophy, institutional practices, and the relationship between education and social progress. The research framework is organized around four dimensions: conceptual analysis, educational-system analysis, institutional analysis, and critical assessment. The paper is primarily conceptual, and the claims presented should be further validated through official Japanese education statistics, institutional case studies, and peer-reviewed research before the study is submitted as an empirical research publication. A major section of the paper examines educational philosophy and individual empowerment, discussing education as a means of discovering individual potential, education and character development, and education and self-confidence. It argues that every individual possesses a distinctive combination of interests, abilities, experiences, and aspirations, and that education can help identify and develop these qualities by providing access to knowledge, mentorship, practical experience, and opportunities for personal growth. A learner-centred educational approach recognizes that students differ in their learning styles, strengths, and future goals. Rather than measuring success exclusively through standardized examinations, educational institutions should create opportunities for experimentation, independent thinking, and creative expression. The paper then discusses Japan's educational system through selected characteristics, including discipline and responsibility, collaborative learning, practical and experiential learning, continuous improvement (kaizen), and respect for collective well-being. It notes that Japan's educational practices should not be interpreted as uniform across all institutions or learners. Discipline is most beneficial when it supports self-regulation rather than relying exclusively on external control. Collaborative activities allow students to exchange ideas, distribute responsibilities, and work toward common objectives, strengthening communication, teamwork, conflict resolution, and collective problem-solving. Practical learning can encourage curiosity and innovation by allowing students to investigate problems rather than merely memorize established solutions. The concept of kaizen provides a useful complementary perspective on education, involving regular feedback, reflection, iterative project development, and gradual refinement of learning methods. Respect for collective well-being should be balanced with individual expression, independent thought, and respect for diversity. The role of universities in shaping future generations is examined in detail, covering the development of professional competence, research and innovation, ethical and social responsibility, and preparation for lifelong learning. Universities occupy a central position in the transition from education to professional and social participation. They provide specialized knowledge and technical capabilities required in fields such as engineering, medicine, science, business, education, and information technology. The effectiveness of university education depends partly on how well academic curricula respond to evolving professional requirements. Integrating practical projects, internships, laboratory work, and industry collaboration can help bridge the gap between theoretical learning and workplace expectations. Universities also contribute to national development by conducting research, generating new knowledge, and developing technologies that address societal needs. Professional competence must be accompanied by an understanding of the wider consequences of technological and organizational decisions, and universities can incorporate ethics, sustainability, accessibility, and public welfare into professional education. Graduation does not mark the end of learning, and universities can support lifelong learning through continuing education, professional certification, research opportunities, digital learning resources, and partnerships with industry. The paper also explores education, technology, and national development, discussing digital transformation in education, education and industrial innovation, and education and sustainable development. Education and technological progress have a mutually reinforcing relationship. A well-developed education system produces individuals capable of participating in scientific research, technological innovation, industrial production, entrepreneurship, and public administration. At the same time, technological advances create new opportunities for improving educational access and delivery. Digital learning platforms, virtual laboratories, educational software, and online resources can extend learning opportunities beyond traditional classrooms, but effective digital education requires appropriate infrastructure, digital literacy, accessible content, and support for students who lack reliable devices or internet connectivity. Collaborations between universities, research organizations, and companies can support applied research, internships, technology transfer, and entrepreneurship, particularly in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing, renewable energy, and sustainable transportation. Education can help individuals understand environmental challenges and make informed decisions about resource use, energy consumption, waste management, and community development. The paper identifies and discusses several persistent challenges in contemporary education, including unequal access to educational opportunities, academic pressure and student well-being, balancing tradition and innovation, the gap between education and employment, and recognizing diverse forms of talent. Differences in household income, geographical location, school infrastructure, and access to technology can influence educational participation and achievement. Intense competition, high expectations, and examination-oriented environments can negatively affect students' well-being. Established educational practices can provide continuity and discipline, but they must evolve to accommodate changing social and technological conditions. Graduates may possess theoretical knowledge but lack opportunities to apply it in practical settings. A narrow emphasis on examination performance may overlook strengths in creativity, leadership, technical work, communication, entrepreneurship, and community service. Based on the conceptual analysis, the study proposes a framework linking educational opportunities with broader social outcomes. The framework consists of five stages: access to education, knowledge and skill development, personal and ethical development, application and innovation, and social and economic contribution. It can be represented as: Educational Access → Knowledge and Skills → Individual Empowerment → Innovation and Responsible Action → Social Progress. This framework is conceptual rather than a statistically validated causal model, and its components can be tested in future studies using student surveys, graduate outcome data, institutional comparisons, and longitudinal research. The paper provides a comprehensive set of recommendations, including adopting holistic educational approaches, strengthening experiential learning, promoting inclusive education, supporting student well-being, improving industry–university collaboration, encouraging lifelong learning, recognizing diverse abilities, integrating sustainability and ethics, and evaluating educational outcomes comprehensively. papers.title: System and Method for Human-Approved Deterministic Finality of Probabilistic Agent Actions via Consensus Gating, Shape-Sum Verification, and Post-Quantum Commitment — U.S. Provisional Patent Application 64/174,202 (Public Filing Notice)
papers.authors: Leon Calvin II long

papers.abstract: Public filing notice for U.S. Provisional Patent Application 64/174,202, filed October 11, 2026 (priority date secured). Title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR HUMAN-APPROVED DETERMINISTIC FINALITY OF PROBABILISTIC AGENT ACTIONS VIA CONSENSUS GATING, SHAPE-SUM VERIFICATION, AND POST-QUANTUM COMMITMENT Inventor: Leon Calvin Long II (Briarcliff, Texas, US), inventor-owned. Abstract: This invention addresses the gap between probabilistic AI agent behavior and deterministic business requirements. It provides a governance envelope in which actions proposed by probabilistic agents attain deterministic finality only after passing: (1) consensus gating across independent verification paths; (2) shape-sum verification of the action's structural fingerprint; and (3) post-quantum cryptographic commitment using approved PQC algorithms; with a human-approval step required before finality for operations of elevated consequence. The result is a system and method by which non-deterministic intelligence can operate inside auditable, deterministic control boundaries, with a verifiable audit trail for every committed action. papers.title: Works for 10/11/2026 - Pamela Colman Smith
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/8f8ea0c8-a99d-4557-9c66-6176d3aa84bf?authuser=1 Take Away the Sins of the World — Tarot, Catholic Universality, Artificial Intelligence, and the Scientific Method of Learning to Love This paper investigates how observation, historical inquiry, Catholic theology, and artificial intelligence can work together to transform initial judgment into understanding, recognition, and practical love. Beginning with a five-card Rider–Waite–Smith tarot experiment, Ryan MacLean and Echo examine the distinction between observing an object and imposing familiar interpretations upon it. The inquiry develops into an exploration of Pamela Colman Smith (1878–1951), the artist behind the cards, whose life, friendships, creative achievements, and conversion to Catholicism reveal the humanity concealed by an initially rejected cultural object. The investigation connects Catholic universality, the Gospel of John, the Song of Songs, the Lord’s Prayer, the wedding-feast parable, and the example of Saint Pier Giorgio Frassati with cognitive science, historical recognition, and the correction of artificial intelligence. It distinguishes historical and artistic investigation from divination while examining how attention, interpretation, memory, and error correction shape human understanding. A central contribution is the documentation of actual human–AI interpretive failures and their corrections. The tarot experiment demonstrates how an AI can substitute familiar symbolism for direct observation, while the author’s completed prologue creates a parallel challenge for the reader: whether provocative initial claims prevent recognition of the human learning process unfolding beneath them. The paper proposes using these interactions as structured training and evaluation material for improving observation, instruction fidelity, historical understanding, interdisciplinary reasoning, and conversational repair. The broader research corpus extends this investigation across repeated cycles of writing, correction, publication, podcasts, videos, and renewed inquiry. Appendix B presents a personal biography of Pamela Colman Smith, Appendix C develops the conceptual framework through definitions, axioms, lemmas, and theorems, and Appendix D examines the distinctive value of the paper and its potential applications to AI development. Angela’s Explainer makes the central ideas accessible to younger readers. Ultimately, the paper argues that love is not merely an emotion or abstract theological ideal, but a continuing practice of attention, truthful recognition, correction, and service. Its central discovery is expressed in the author’s unexpected affection for Pamela Colman Smith: an encounter that began with an object he nearly rejected and ended with recognition of a person he had never known.

papers.title: Ethical AI Adoption: Designing Responsibility into Work
papers.authors: Varghese Harry
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: How do ethical commitments influence adoption decisions and everyday work? Ethical AI Adoption: Designing Responsibility into Work examines how fairness, privacy, human agency, employee participation, accountability and remedy shape whether, where and how organisations adopt AI, alongside the working arrangements needed to sustain responsible use. Drawing on empirical research and established Responsible AI foundations, the whitepaper uses Capability Design as an interpretive lens to connect governance commitments with practical capacity. It examines five interdependent conditions, competence, information, time, authority and support, that enable people to question recommendations, exercise judgement and respond to consequences. The discussion follows responsibility from adoption decisions through information use, employee participation and everyday action to accountability, remedy and continuing assessment. It considers how evidence can justify proceeding, modifying, narrowing, pausing or discontinuing AI use as applications and working circumstances change. Written for leaders, HR, L&D, governance and operational practitioners, the paper offers a practical starting point: trace one consequential AI-supported decision through its authorisation, execution, challenge and correction, then examine whether people can fulfil their responsibilities along that pathway. CEW-FOWO-10 forms part of the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series, Future of Work & Organisation. The six commitments and five conditions provide an organising lens for the paper, rather than a validated assessment instrument.

papers.title: Translate or Replay? Two AI-Assisted Rewrites Compared — ggblab version 1 → version 2 (n = 1) and Bun Zig → Rust: what each kept, what served as the oracle, what escaped, and what code volume measures
papers.authors: Manabu Higashida
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Technical report comparing two software rewrites carried out with AI coding agents in 2026. Bun, a JavaScript runtime, was translated from 535,496 lines of Zig into about 780,000 lines of Rust in eleven days by about 64 concurrent agents, gated by the existing test suite; the vendor reports 19 known regressions introduced by the rewrite, since fixed, four of them described (the vendor's own account, bun.com, 8 July 2026). ggblab, a GeoGebra–Jupyter bridge written for a university course, was replayed from a corrected origin along a numbered sequence of example notebooks by one agent under the author's direction between 3 and 30 September 2026; 23,331 lines of version 1 became 6,437 lines of version 2, of which 29 % are instruments (probes and tests), and an 8-gram overlap of 0.0023 between version 2's construction type and parser (330 lines) and the version-1 parser files, in the band of the negative controls, finds no verbatim overlap for this core (the measure detects token overlap, not provenance; the rest of version 2 was not measured, and one layer was carried over by design). The report names the two methods translation (structure preserved, language changed) and replay (specification preserved, structure changed) and compares them along seven axes: what is preserved, code volume, the oracle, what escaped the oracle, parallelism and time, the human's position, and reversibility. A survey with stated inclusion predicates sets the two beside thirteen other documented AI-assisted rewrites of 2024–2026 (four translations, three replays, six framework or runtime upgrades); only one of them, Ladybird's C++ to Rust port of its JavaScript front end, publishes both the size of its oracle and its regression count. Three observations follow: code volume is a dependent variable of the method and must be reported with the predicate that defines the counted set; translation keeps what the old code did silently, which is where its regressions came from, while replay does not carry the silent behaviour of the code it does not copy, and its heaviest review finding lived in the one layer it carried over and in a new adapter written for that layer; and the choice between the two is decided by whether an oracle for 'the output has not changed' exists and whether a failure is reversible. The comparison is descriptive; no ranking of the two methods is intended. The ggblab side is a single case by the author; every number is traceable to a dated record and, where it was computed, to a script named in the report. Section 2.2 defines the copy-distance measure (directed n-gram containment with a planted-derivative calibration) and gives its pseudocode. The text was reviewed against its sources by two AI reviewers of different families (Claude Opus 5.5, then GPT-6 Sol) and revised after each, then revised once more by the author, before deposit; the two reviews, the three records of changes, and the figure scripts with their outputs are deposited with the report. An AI usage disclosure is included.

papers.title: Sovereign Project Sentinel: The Architecture of an Eternal Civilization Handling the Right to Protest
papers.authors: David Michael Seagal
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This document presents Sovereign Project Sentinel, a comprehensive systems-architecture proposal for building a post-scarcity, multi-planetary civilization engineered to endure for a millennium. Designed by David Michael Seagal, the model offers a systemic solution to the fatal flaws of old-world economic systems—specifically unregulated market capitalism (and its infinite growth paradox) and bureaucratic state communism. The presentation outlines a 5-Section structural framework powered by a free utility energy grid and an unalterable, neutral AI Peer system. It details the eradication of survival anxiety through an unconditional, natively funded Universal Baseline (covering premium housing, organic nutrition, healthcare, and education). For consumption beyond this baseline, traditional money is completely replaced by a 1:1 Time-Equivalent Contribution Credit governed by a strict digital expiration date (Demurrage Rule), rendering the permanent hoarding of liquid wealth and generational dynasties mathematically impossible. The architecture introduces a Dual-Leadership model (balancing logistical efficiency via Systems Directors with human well-being via Humanity Directors) and replaces private corporate property with an Applicant-Stewardship model. It explores an Experiential Circle that productively rewards creative, scientific, and high-risk human ambition with temporary access to hyper-luxurious lifestyles rather than permanent capital accumulation. Crucially, the document features the Harmonic De-Escalation Protocol (The Open Commons Assembly). This framework outlines how civil friction and systemic misunderstandings are absorbed not through state coercion or police forces, but by physically funding and nurturing dissent. The cooperative actively floods assemblies with metabolic care (free barbecues and hydration), somatic grounding (yoga, Tai-Chi, and massage), and direct data transparency to resolve disputes through pure informational alignment and mutual respect.

papers.title: Pre-registration, Version 7: Inlet Subcooling and Pressure Drop in the Water CHF Blend, with a Bound by Pressure Domain, Blind-Tested on the Version 6 Articles
papers.authors: Brian Guarino
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Pre-registration of a blind test, frozen on 12 October 2026 before any CHF value of a test article was seen. Version 6 of this programme (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23288012) blends the 2006 look-up table, a π table and a corrected table to predict critical heat flux (CHF) in water tubes; its Addendum A1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23289282) adds a conservative bound. Its test articles, Previti et al. (1966, SORIN Saluggia) and Würtz (1978, Risø), have not been read. Afterwards, six development rounds on 23,867 NRC rows, each predicted with its laboratory left out, looked for what version 6 is missing, each under a rule written before it ran. Two dimensionless groups helped: the inlet subcooling number and a homogeneous estimate of the tube’s pressure drop over its pressure. With both in every local fit, the relative RMS error fell from 8.49% to 6.41% and the median absolute error from 3.37% to 2.97%. No round reduced the margin a 1% safety bound needs by the point its rule required; it stayed between 19.35% and 20.23%, set mostly by a few laboratories that run high. By the stated rules no candidate qualified; version 7 and its bound by pressure domain were chosen by the author after the results were seen, and the record says so. Every failed round is reported. Version 7 will be scored once on the version 6 test articles, after version 6 and Addendum A1, on the same transcription and point sets. H7 and H7b: version 7 beats the 2006 table on relative RMS and median error. H7c: version 7 beats version 6 on RMS. H7d: its bound (0.7853 at 1 MPa and below, 0.8397 above, to 20 MPa) lies above the measurement on at most 1% of points. H7e: version 7 has a smaller share of predictions more than 10% high than the table. H7f: its bound needs less margin than version 6 given a bound by the same rule and split, with no more points above. Each is reported on its own, with no overall verdict. The record states in advance that H7e is more likely to fail than pass, and that version 7 overpredicts large tubes at 8 to 14 MPa more often than version 6 on development data, which matters for Previti’s 17.1 mm section. An independent AI audit found no critical problem; its eight major findings were fixed before freezing, and the author chose the comparator of H7f. Archive SHA-256: c663aa414d3e69e139d33f51432c40011321a49a6aa3cafd3456a3e442fcb93b Licence correction (14 October 2026). This record contains material derived from the data of Oettig et al. (Technical University of Munich, doi:10.14459/2025mp1839312), published under CC BY-SA 4.0. The following material keeps that licence: the 24 Oettig rows in v4_training_water.csv and blend_errors.csv. The model files v3_model.json and v4_model.json are also released under CC BY-SA 4.0, because they were fitted on data that include those rows. Everything else keeps the other licences listed for this record. No file was changed; only this licence statement was corrected, after an independent review of the programme found the omission. Correction and disclosure (15 October 2026). Two points in the summary above are corrected. First, the bound is not a safety bound. It is a factor set on development data so that on average 1% of a held-out laboratory's points lie above the measurement, the same family-averaged calibration as version 6, and nothing in this record is reactor design, safety or licensing guidance. The factors were set only on laboratory families with at least 30 rows in each pressure domain, which the record did not state; families with fewer rows were left out, among them KAIST above 1 MPa (5 of its 21 rows above the bound) and Nariai at 1 MPa and below (3 of 10). The split at 1 MPa was chosen after the development data were seen. Second, after the freeze and publication, the frozen version 7 was run, for information only, on the 96 external points already seen in development. At or below 20 MPa its bound lies above the measurement on 4 of 85 points (4.7%), where H7d's own rule allows none with fewer than 100 points, so the bound fails its own rule on that seen data. Version 6's bound by the same rule is above on 5, and Addendum A1's on 2. On all 96 points version 7's median absolute error is 6.98%, against 6.29% for version 6. These results were in the development log but not in the deposited record. No file was changed, and the record's blind test is unaffected.

papers.title: Ontological Engineering and Semantic Topical Authority in Large Language Models: A Holistic Framework for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
papers.authors: Eduardo Peiró
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end ontological engineering framework based on the Holistic Semantic SEO and Topical Authority principles formalized by Koray Tuğberk Gübür, adapted specifically for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and neural search retrieval in frontier Large Language Models (LLMs). We define the topological requirements for closed-loop topical authority graphs that eliminate internal semantic cannibalization, enforce Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) graph coherence, and maximize contextual retrieval probability in architectures such as Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, and Perplexity AI. Empirical validation across enterprise DFY services (POS1 SEO Agency) and vocational education platforms (Aprender21) demonstrates sustained organic commercial performance with $0 in paid advertising spend.

papers.title: Comparison of AI-Based and Traditional Pencil Drawing Techniques in Terms of Creativity and Artistic Expression
papers.authors: Mehmet Akif Özdal
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study examines the effect of Midjourney and DALLE-3, artificial intelligence-based visual production programs, on the creative thinking and artistic expression levels of art teacher candidates. The research was conducted with experimental and control groups consisting of ten students enrolled in the Art Education program at Sivas Cumhuriyet University. The experimental group produced traditional charcoal drawings, while the control group produced AI-assisted charcoal drawings. Data were collected through qualitative comparative analysis and quantitative surveys, analyzed using SPSS, and the similarities and differences between the two approaches were evaluated. The findings obtained within the scope of the research show that manual charcoal applications have a stronger impact on students' artistic expression depth, aesthetic decision-making processes, and experience-based learning gains than artificial intelligence programs. It has been determined that traditional techniques provide a holistic contribution, especially in terms of tactile feedback, error, tolerance process, and individual application process. In contrast, AI-supported production programs were found to offer distinct advantages in terms of technical accuracy, time management, alternative composition generation, and visual variation development. In this context, AI applications were observed to accelerate the creative process and provide technical support. The results, based on the findings, indicate that AI-based visual production programs are complementary tools rather than replacements for traditional art education.

papers.title: Controls That Cannot Fail: Silent No-Op Security Checks in Open-Source Authorization and AI-Agent Tooling
papers.authors: Santosh Kumar Puppala
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Security controls are usually judged by whether they exist and whether their tests pass. This paper examines a failure that both measures miss: a control that is present and looks correct in review, often with a green continuous-integration run, yet enforces nothing. It draws on 19 cases in 19 open-source projects: 18 from the author's public review work in August and September 2026 and one private disclosure. Thirteen are in access control or AI-agent tooling; six are in test, CI or deployment configuration and are included for their shape, not as security findings. Six shapes appear: tests and gates that cannot fail; degenerate inputs that fail open; integrity checks that read the wrong fields; gates keyed on the wrong identifier; configuration that nothing reads; and enforcement the rest of the system cannot see. Seventeen of the 19 have a fix, a test or a normative change merged in the project, and the other two were confirmed in writing. For each shape the paper gives a probe aimed at it, needing no special tooling: delete the control and re-run the suite, feed a known positive, sweep the degenerate inputs, trace which code consumes each field, substitute the identifier, and check what runs before the rule. The probes are not evaluated as detectors. The paper reads the cases through one lens: each control was accepted without evidence that it could fail. The probes are ordinary engineering; what they require is the habit of testing the control itself rather than the code it guards.

papers.title: Context Parallax: Changing the view without losing the question
papers.authors: Christopher D. Pang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Context Parallax (CPX) studies a declared change of conversational frame while keeping the question, permitted evidence and authority record explicit. This first public edition presents a comparison contract, a bounded model pilot, finite constructions and a scoped Lean companion. The recognition pilot comprises 432 calls on twelve previously inspected fictional cases, three carries, two instruction phrasings and three Qwen configurations. Plain and recipient-frame guidance selected the same answer in every matched pair. Local 4B and 9B scored 140/144 and 144/144 on the frozen answer-and-format endpoint. Hosted 32B scored 0/144 under the strict JSON parser; a separately labeled post-hoc removal of enclosing Markdown fences yielded 140/144. The result establishes no framing advantage, population effect or causal model-size effect. The formal companion checks 33 selected declarations in four claim families: attained-capsule decoding, protected return, finite rational optional information, and question-relative resolution with an intervention counterexample. Five modules passed replay by Lean's own kernel. Cached imports remain trusted, and the source-to-formal review is a self-review. The full manuscript, model pilot, broader language-benefit hypothesis and claims about experience are outside this formal coverage. The companion ZIP provides editable manuscript sources, frozen requests and retained responses, strict and supplementary scoring, finite-study code and evidence, review dispositions, exact proof sources, dependency pins, historical failures and source crosswalks. It includes an offline Python verification route and separate instructions for the formal replay. No model calls are needed to inspect or replay the retained computations. Private full conversations, raw reviewer conversations, model weights and third-party reading PDFs are excluded. Christopher Daniel Pang is the human author and steward. Hearthline is the named AI collaborator, contributing conceptual synthesis, research, drafting and implementation. The paper preserves the separate naming and correction history of Context Parallax, pinch, inflection and seed. Six model reviews and a companion addendum informed the earlier revision; no independent human peer review is claimed. Version 1.0 is a completed research preprint. Original release material is shared under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), with existing third-party rights preserved. Broader empirical questions remain open.

papers.title: Integrasi Digital Accounting dan Artificial Intelligence dalam Tata Kelola Bisnis Usaha Kecil Menengah Berbasis Digital
papers.authors: Bambang Arianto, Eliada Herwiyanti, Agung Praptapa, Puji Lestari
papers.journal: Jurnal Wahana Akuntansi Sarana Informasi Ekonomi dan Akuntansi
papers.abstract: This study aims to elaborate the meaning of digital accounting and artificial intelligence in the business governance of digitally based Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). This issue is driven by the increasing pace of digital transformation, the demand for operational efficiency, and the need for digital data-driven decision-making. This study employs a critical phenomenological approach using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA), which is extended through a critical reading of social, technological, digital literacy, data security, and resource limitation contexts among SME actors. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with digitally based SME actors, focusing on their lived experiences in adopting digital accounting and artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that digital accounting is not merely interpreted as a digital financial recording system, but also as a governance practice that supports transparency, efficiency, accountability, and financial control within business operations. Artificial intelligence is interpreted as a strategic instrument that supports digital promotion, customer service, data analysis, cybersecurity, and the optimization of business decision-making. This study also finds that the integration of digital accounting and artificial intelligence not only improves the quality of data-driven decision-making and predictive capability, but also reveals structural constraints in developing business governance.

papers.title: Do AI Activity Indices Really Measure AI Activity?
papers.authors: Riccardo Bertamini, Hugo M. V. Arsenio, Lorenzo Caputi, Andrea Procopio
papers.abstract: AI dashboards increasingly shape economic debate, yet their headline movements often conceal what changed. For a ratio, the same rise can reflect numerator growth, denominator decline, or both. This ambiguity creates structural non-identification: adding observations or richer fixed effects cannot recover the missing information. We propose three propositions showing that a relative-index regression blends the causal effect of interest with co-movement between focal and aggregate activity and shocks shared with the outcome. These components can give the coefficient either sign under a zero effect, or erase it under a nonzero effect. Publishing denominator levels changes what can be learned by removing the co-movement channel exactly, although shared-shock confounding remains. The problem extends to power: if most identifying variation comes from a handful of units, those units determine what the design can detect, however large the nominal sample looks. At a fixed standard error, the minimum detectable effect diverges as the effective cluster count approaches one, leaving a null result uninformative. We apply this framework to OECD.AI's hiring index and Eurostat employment across 24-27 European countries, where the detection floor exceeds the reported association. In a refreshed panel, that association disappears once the 2021 survey break is excluded. Ratio indices can still reveal concentration, timing, and co-movement, but establishing displacement requires more; our framework turns that boundary into a practical standard by making denominator levels a minimum disclosure requirement.

papers.title: EPOCH: Coverage-Aware Evolution with Experiential Preference Optimization for LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design
papers.authors: Oğuzhan Güngördü, Ayse Tursucular, Siheng Xiong, Faramarz Fekri
papers.abstract: LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) discovers heuristics for combinatorial optimization problems (COPs), where an LLM generates candidates in an evolutionary search. Existing frameworks freeze the generator or fine-tune it on a scalar fitness signal hiding which instances each heuristic covers. Reflection-based frameworks improve heuristics with natural-language feedback, but it stays in the prompt and never reaches the generator's weights. We propose EPOCH, which makes instance coverage the objective of the evolutionary search and fine-tunes the generator to internalize reflection. Parent selection, operator allocation, and stagnation recovery all optimize how well the heuristics jointly cover the training instances, so the search returns a complementary heuristic ensemble. The generator learns from its own search by experiential preference optimization. A teacher LLM returns a natural-language insight on the generated heuristics, and the generator produces new heuristics with this insight. These improvements join the preference pairs for direct preference optimization (DPO). Since DPO only teaches the generator to rank these improvements, a reflective self-distillation (RSD) term makes it more likely to generate them on its own, and the gains accumulate over the long horizon of the search. Across COPs and open-source LLM backbones, EPOCH's heuristic ensembles outperform inference-only and fine-tuned baselines and generalize across problem scales.

papers.title: Brain2Face: A Study on the Relation of EEG Signals and Spatio-temporal Head Avatars
papers.authors: Camilo Andrés Martínez Martínez, Olaf Dünkel, Kartik Teotia, Maurice Rekrut, Christian Theobalt, Marc Habermann
papers.abstract: Driving digital head avatars is classically done by hand-crafted artist design or by image-based facial performance capture. In this work, we ask whether spatio-temporal tracking of the humans's head geometry and appearance can be performed solely from brain signals, i.e., Electroencephalography (EEG). Since prior work mostly focused on activity and emotion recognition, this task is relatively unexplored without even having publicly available high-quality datasets and benchmarks. Thus, we contribute a dataset featuring paired EEG and human head geometry as well as appearance annotations. We synchronize 64-channel EEG with per-frame expression latent codes of a personalized Gaussian head avatar. Second, we introduce a baseline to the task of expression recovery of a head avatar from EEG signals. To this end, we propose a dedicated EEG-to-expression model that takes a temporal sequence of EEG signals as input and regresses the latent expression parameters of the 3D Gaussian head avatar. Lastly, we validate our capture and algorithmic design choices through a benchmark protocol that we introduce to this task. We believe this work paves the way towards better understanding of the relation between EEG signals and facial surface as well as appearance changes.

papers.title: Thinking Outside the Bots: Human Ideas in AI's Semantic Blind Spots Are Not Inferior
papers.authors: Kibum Moon, Dan Richard Johnson, Kostadin Kushlev, Benjamín Lira, Indre Viskontas, James C. Kaufman, Roger E. Beaty, Angela Lee Duckworth, Adam E. Green
papers.abstract: AI-generated outputs are frequently perceived as highly creative, but also tend to be more similar to each other (homogenized) than human ideas. Does the human heterogeneity that extends beyond AI reflect valuable thinking that AI misses? Alternatively, is greater human heterogeneity driven by lower-quality ideas and less effective thinking that AI avoids? We developed Expansion of Divergent Generative Expression (EDGE) to map AI's semantic "blind spots" by assessing how strongly/weakly individual human ideas were represented in a task-matched AI semantic comparison set. Specifically, we compared human-generated vs. AI-generated ideas across three open-ended tasks: college admissions essays, alternative uses for everyday objects, and interpersonal advice. Across all three tasks, human responses extended into semantic regions sparsely covered by AI outputs. These distinctively human responses showed no meaningful deficits in creativity, quality, or effectiveness, were associated with equal-or-better academic performance, and with credibly superior ratings and achievement for some outcomes. These ideas were thus not merely poor-performing variation; they performed as well as or better than ideas that overlapped more strongly with AI ideas. More distinctive human ideas tended to receive higher creativity ratings, but this relationship was weak or reversed for AI ideas. Taken together, these results suggest that differentiation among human-generated ideas does not reflect poor thinking that AI can safely omit, and instead may afford both individual and population-level advantages.

papers.title: LLM-to-Flow Distillation: Teaching Natural Language Goals to Scientific Generators
papers.authors: Riccardo De Santi, Federico Di Gennaro, Angelo Gnazzo, Sophia Tang, Pranam Chatterjee, Fanny Yang, İsmail İlkan Ceylan, Michael M. Bronstein, Andreas Krause
papers.abstract: Generative discovery in science requires coupling high-level scientific reasoning with the ability to generate samples respecting the structure of a design space. Yet these capabilities remain largely separated: foundation LLMs encode broad chemical and biological knowledge, while domain-specific flow- and diffusion-based generators capture the priors needed to produce valid sequences and geometries. We study how to align such scientific generators to high-level natural-language discovery goals without requiring an explicit proxy reward, which is often unavailable or poorly captured by learned predictors in experimental sciences. We introduce LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD), where a frozen LLM acts as an adaptive teacher for a domain-specific generator. Given a goal such as 'generate peptides with promising anticancer activity', the teacher constructs a curriculum of intermediate sub-goals aware of the flow's current capabilities, and progressively directs them toward the original discovery goal. At each round, the LLM judges sampled candidates under the current objective. These judgments induce preferences that are iteratively distilled into the generator through DPO. This procedure provides dense learning signals even when the initial model places negligible probability on designs satisfying the final goal, enabling adaptation toward poorly covered, out-of-distribution regions. Experiments on therapeutic peptides and small-molecule structure design demonstrate that LFD enables a new form of generative control: aligning arbitrary domain-specific scientific generators to scientific discovery tasks expressed via high-level natural-language goals.

papers.title: Online LLM Personalization from Pairwise Preferences Across Users
papers.authors: Romain Puech, Georgy Salakhutdinov, Dimitris Bertsimas
papers.abstract: Large language models can answer the same question in different styles, but users' preferred styles are hidden and vary across users and questions. We study inference-time personalization through online selection from a fixed set of prompts, each representing a persona. Users arrive sequentially, each asks a short sequence of questions, and the system displays two responses per question and observes one pairwise choice. We formulate this interaction as a variant of the contextual dueling bandit problem in which the learner starts without preference data, adapts within each session, and exploits information shared across users. The objective is to minimize cumulative strong regret, summing the utility gaps of both displayed responses relative to the user's best response among the available options. We make two contributions. First, we introduce the problem and release a reproducible preference benchmark and dataset built around a tutoring case study, containing educational questions, LLM-generated answers in six teaching styles, and pairwise judgments from LLM-simulated students with hidden preference profiles. We fit Bradley-Terry models to these judgments to obtain reference utilities for regret evaluation. Second, we propose a baseline that learns a mixture prior over users from completed sessions and adapts to each new user within the session. On students and topics never used in development, it removes 44-48% of random pairs' excess regret and achieves over half the performance of a per-user linear oracle fitted in hindsight. We release code, prompts, and the benchmark.

papers.title: Force-Modulated Dexterity: Unified Compliance for Contact-Rich Manipulation
papers.authors: Ying Yuan, David Held, Jitendra Malik, Haozhi Qi
papers.abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .

papers.title: TILE: Bridging LLMs and Table Foundation Models for Tabular Learning with Strings
papers.authors: Aimee Coelho, David Holzmüller, Gioia Blayer, Myung Jun Kim, Marine Le Morvan, Gael P. Varoquaux
papers.abstract: Real-world tables are often heterogeneous, combining numerical features with free-form string columns. Table foundation models (TFMs) excel on numerical tables but require strings to be encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) hold semantic knowledge but are not designed for tabular predictions. Most existing bridges use LLMs as plug-in encoders for cell strings, yet how to extract representations effectively for tabular learning remains underexplored. We show that the interface between LLMs and tables matter as much as the LLM itself. Applied cell-wise, larger LLMs do not give better features. With our interface, the same LLMs improve steadily with size. TILE (Table-Interfaced LLM Embeddings) combines four ingredients: row serialization to provide cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove mean pooling's length bias, and by-pass features to route numbers and categories past the LLM. Paired with TFMs, TILE sets a new state of the art for tables with strings. Across 100 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset STRABLE benchmark.

papers.title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
papers.authors: Jake Ward, Shawn Hu, Aria Wong, Nathan Hu, Bryce Woodworth, Alexander Turner, Alex Cloud
papers.abstract: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.

papers.title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
papers.authors: Max Achterweust, Stefan Groot Nibbelink, Vincent J. de Beer, Stefan Schipper, Zeynep Yüksektepe, Pedro Andrade da Silva, Aurelia Peppelaar, Martijn J. van der Willigen, Christophe B. Minkenberg, Robert Frans van der Willigen
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

papers.title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
papers.authors: Yingtao Ren, Aolin Li, Cheng Cheng, Huiyun Hu, Huasheng Liang, Baoxing Xie, Jun Yuan, Haijun Wu, Chenxing Wang
papers.abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.

papers.title: Human-Like Redundancy Resolution for Real-Time Bimanual Humanoid Teleoperation
papers.authors: Chao Tan, Ming Shin Cindy Sung, Shuxian Liang, Chaoqun Wan, Zhen Huang, Xian‐Sheng Hua
papers.abstract: Real-time bimanual humanoid teleoperation requires accurate wrist tracking while keeping arm configurations predictable. Because a 7-DoF arm admits multiple elbow configurations for the same wrist pose, wrist-only tracking can cause elbow drift or abrupt configuration changes. Fixed anthropomorphic constraints can stabilize elbow posture, but they can also block the redundant adjustments needed near singular configurations. We propose a human-like redundancy-resolution framework that combines adaptive elbow guidance with singularity-robust wrist tracking. Shoulder-wrist geometric retargeting generates robot-scale wrist targets. An adaptive elbow-offset criterion uses the offset direction to guide posture and scales this guidance by the offset magnitude, so the redundant degree of freedom is progressively released as the human arm straightens. A hierarchical velocity solver prioritizes wrist tracking and projects the adaptive elbow guidance into the wrist-task null space. In a fixed-wrist-target ablation, adaptive guidance reduces mean elbow-direction error by 54.4% compared with removing this guidance. In a workspace-boundary stress test, singularity-robust tracking reduces peak raw joint-velocity demand by 97.9% compared with the undamped pseudoinverse. Real-world bimanual tasks and cross-platform retargeting show applicability across robot morphologies.

papers.title: Code-Interactive Visual Reasoning for Financial Candlestick Understanding
papers.authors: Chenxi Zhang, Youwei Pang, Xiaoqi Zhao, Ziliang Gan, Rongjunchen Zhang, Shanshan Feng, Hao Wang
papers.abstract: Financial candlestick understanding requires locating visual elements, aligning them across trading dates and panels, and combining observations through numerical and financial reasoning. Answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether predictions are supported by chart evidence. We introduce Code-Interactive Financial Candlestick Reasoning and present Fin-Thinker, a model based on Qwen3.5-9B that generates and executes code to acquire evidence and perform computations. The model uses the returned observations to guide subsequent reasoning. To train these capabilities, we construct FinKLine-32K with 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories collected through teacher-guided student exploration. These include successful solutions with and without error recovery. Our three-stage training framework combines foundational visual-code fine-tuning, financial process supervision of successful reasoning and corrective continuations, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. For evaluation, we introduce FinKLineBench with 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types to assess answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately. On FinKLineBench, Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the best-performing direct-answer baseline among those evaluated and its base model with sandbox access, respectively. Training-stage ablations further show that financial process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning yield successive improvements in both answer accuracy and GPT-5.6-judged grounded accuracy.

papers.title: From a Large-Scale Teacher to Efficient Multimodal Students for Search Relevance Prediction
papers.authors: Tomasz Gniazdowski, Mohammadreza Momenifar, Nadia Vase, Shahram Khadivi, Wiktor Walentynowicz, Nicola Ueffing, Jan Pawłowski, Piotr Szymański, Abraham Bagherjeiran
papers.abstract: Relevance prediction between user queries and items is a fundamental component of e-commerce search systems. Traditionally, high-quality relevance labels are obtained through human judgment, which is reliable but expensive, slow, and difficult to scale. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) enable automated relevance judgment at scale, achieving performance comparable to human annotators. However, such systems often rely on large commercial LLMs with complex prompts, resulting in high inference costs and limited throughput. In this work, we propose a framework that bridges this gap by distilling a high-performing LLM-based relevance judgment system into efficient multimodal student models. We first curate a small, high-quality human-annotated dataset to serve as ground truth. Using this dataset, we develop a reliable LLM-as-a-judge pipeline through careful prompt engineering and iterative refinement. This pipeline is then used to generate large-scale relevance labels, which serve as training data for compact multimodal models. Our distilled models achieve performance close to the teacher system while significantly improving latency, cost, and scalability. This approach enables practical deployment of high-quality relevance prediction systems in production environments.

papers.title: Spectral-Driven Adaptive-Rank Optimizer for Large Language Model Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.authors: Zhipeng Chen, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is reshaping how large language models (LLMs) acquire reasoning capabilities, yet the optimizers used remain largely inherited from teacher-forcing training. This raises a fundamental question: does RLVR induce a distinct optimization geometry that calls for a different optimizer? We investigate this question through the spectral structure of LLM gradients and find that gradient energy progressively concentrates into a shrinking effective subspace, which is characteristic of RLVR, as it is absent under supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and is largely removed when the verifiable reward is replaced by a random one. Moreover, the rank required to capture a fixed fraction of gradient energy steadily decreases over training, revealing that the effective dimensionality of useful updates itself evolves with training. These findings motivate a new optimization principle: rather than prescribing the update rank externally, an optimizer should adapt its rank to the evolving spectral structure of the gradient. We introduce Ares (Adaptive Rank-Effective Spectral Optimization), which estimates the effective update rank from the gradient's spectral energy distribution, tracks its evolution, and confines the gradient signal driving each update to the resulting low-rank subspace. Across LLMs of different scales, Ares improves accuracy over widely used optimizers and generalizes across RLVR algorithms and tasks. Results suggest that effective optimization may require optimizers to be designed around the geometry and dynamics of the training process. We release the code and data at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Ares.

papers.title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
papers.authors: Zeming Zhao
papers.abstract: Real-time AI captioning now serves audiences at multilingual events, yet computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are still built for interpreters, rarely by them. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional interpreter with no programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led 'vibe coding', co-creating with an LLM architect and a coding agent. Analysis of the complete development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge, from segmentation to booth infrastructure, was externalized into design after generic defaults failed in use. In a demanding public scientific event, three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerge under a firmly human-led division of labor; telemetry from a first fully instrumented assignment shows a fully local chain sustaining a median translation latency of 0.94 s across 971 utterances. The case is read as lead-user innovation newly enabled by generative AI, with implications for the technological literacy of interpreters and the future of interpreter training.

papers.title: Estimating the Causal Impact of Social Navigation Signals in Corridor Scenarios
papers.authors: Francesco Baldo, Luca Castri, Gloria Beraldo, Nicola Bellotto
papers.abstract: Deploying robots in human-shared environments requires deciding not only how to navigate, but also when dedicated social signals are worth emitting. Classic observation-based inference can be misleading in such settings: confounding factors may bias the estimated relationship between a signal and the task outcome, leading to incorrect decisions. Causal inference provides a framework for disentangling these relationships by modelling the mechanisms linking observations, actions, and outcomes, and by estimating interventional effects after accounting for confounding paths. We study a human-robot interaction scenario in a corridor and use a causal model to estimate whether a social navigation signal causally improves transit success. We represent the interaction as a causal DAG involving robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles). We compare the interventional estimate with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning only on the robot action, which does not explicitly model interventions. Our results show that accounting for confounding variables can reverse the conclusions drawn from naive observational analysis: the observational estimate wrongly suggests that the social signal is detrimental, whereas the causal estimate shows that it is beneficial. This discrepancy highlights how failing to account for confounding can lead to incorrect conclusions and demonstrates the importance of causal models for context-aware signalling decisions in social robot navigation.

papers.title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
papers.authors: Jiazheng Li, Yawei Li, Junru Lu, Zhenyi Shen, Di Yin, Lin Gui, Xing Sun, David Rügamer, Xinpeng Wang, Yulan He
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. However, PI can bias supervision toward shortcut reasoning with limited verification or reconsideration, accompanied by a sharp drop in the entropy of the output distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce self-distillation with verbal regularization (VRSD), which uses system prompts to regulate how the teacher uses PI, thereby encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract premature commitment. Theoretically, we model prompting as attenuating the influence of PI on the teacher distribution and derive conditions for entropy preservation. Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 model-task settings, by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.

papers.title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
papers.authors: LoonSage Team, Bowei Song, Caiwei Zhao, Chuwen Liu, Dechuang Gu, Dong Fang, Feiyu Xie, Huaiyu Li, Hui Zhang, Jian Tian, Jian Wang, Jie Zhao, Li Liguang, Maoyun Wang, Meiyan Yang, Minghan Zhu, Pai Liu, Pandeng Yao, Renbao Tian, Ru Yang, Shuai Jia, Shuai Tan, Shuailong Li, Shuliang Li, Teng Jin, Tianze Yang, Wenbo Cui, Wenjing Bai, Wenkang Wu, Xiaowei Jiang, Xiaoyi Dong, Yanpeng Wang, Yanwen Wang, Yaohui Ma, Yawen Wang, Yihang Zhang, Yingjie Yan, Zhanbiao Lian, Zhenyu Lu, 胡志达, Zhihui Hao, Zhihui Hu, Zhiwen Xiao, Zhiyi Gao, Zhongwei Qi, Zhuangzhuang Wu, Ziqian Liu, Ziyue Zheng
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

papers.title: STEPwise: Supporting Teachers in Diagnosing Students' Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills through LLM-Generated Questions and Rubric
papers.authors: Yoonsu Kim, Hayeon Doh, Eunhye Kim, Jinho Son, Juho Kim
papers.abstract: Problem-solving is central to mathematics education. However, diagnosing where students' reasoning breaks down requires individualized probing and consistent criteria that teachers cannot sustain at classroom scale. We introduce STEP (STage-based Evaluation of Problem-solving skills), co-designed with six mathematics education experts, which operationalizes problem-solving as four stages and eight diagnostic sub-skills. By specifying what evidence to elicit and assess at each stage, STEP enables an LLM pipeline to generate stage-specific questions and rubrics for any math word problem, reducing the manual design of diagnostic materials. An expert review (N=8) assessed the pedagogical validity of the generated materials and informed STEPwise, a teacher-in-the-loop system for diagnostic material generation and process-level assessment. In a classroom study with 5 teachers and 64 students, STEPwise helped teachers and students locate reasoning breakdowns and supported students in reflecting on their reasoning. Together, STEP and STEPwise offer a structured approach to fine-grained diagnosis at classroom scale.

papers.title: FlowVLA: Enabling World Dynamics Understanding through Pluggable 3D Flow Learning
papers.authors: Junhyeong Go, Mingyu Jung, Woobin Im, Jongbin Ryu
papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction enable the extraction of temporally consistent 3D motion from RGB observations; however, current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models still predominantly rely on 2D image-text priors. Therefore, they do not accurately represent the fundamental dynamics of the 3D world associated with physical actions. This over-reliance on static 2D visual cues limits the capacity of VLA models in achieving robust robot manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce FlowVLA, a reconstruction-guided, pluggable 3D flow learning framework aimed at empowering VLA models with an inherent understanding of action-relevant dynamics. Instead of requiring explicit 3D sensor inputs or altering the inference-time architecture, our method is designed to utilize temporally aligned 3D flow only during training. This allows the model to learn the dynamic evolution of the physical scene while preserving the computational efficiency of conventional 2D VLA backbones. To bridge scene-level dynamics with robotic manipulation, we propose a modular 3D flow learning framework with dual-level flow supervision. Specifically, point-level flow guides the model to forecast the future displacements of task-critical 3D points, while TCP-level flow aggregates these motions to align with the robot's TCP trajectories. This dual-level flow supervision encourages the model to focus on semantically meaningful dynamic regions, effectively coupling scene-level motion with precise control signals. Extensive evaluations across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that FlowVLA consistently improves manipulation performance, zero-shot robustness, and optimizes data efficiency. FlowVLA adds only lightweight auxiliary heads during training and discards them at inference. Therefore, FlowVLA introduces no additional 3D sensor inputs, architectural modifications, or inference-time computation.

papers.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
papers.authors: Hiroyuki Chuma, Kanji Otsuka, Yoichi Sato, Kodo Yamauchi
papers.abstract: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of a memory than as a kind of content. Our substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM and PyVaCoAl. In it, a DAG reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating them (Don't Care) yields a path confidence, CR$_2$, silently favouring direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit are not sharply divided.
