Chatbots trained and validated predominantly in high-resource, English-language settings may perform less reliably for populations with the greatest unmet need -the same populations digital public health is meant to prioritize under SDG 3, 9, and 11's emphasis on inclusive infrastructure and sustainable, resilient communities. A chatbot that reduces cost-per-contact for a health system does not automatically reduce disparities in outcomes; without equity-explicit design, deployment, and evaluation, it may simply reallocate existing advantages to those already best served by digital tools, echoing patterns already observed in AI-enabled primary care and telemedicine expansion (Elangovan et al., 2025).The third tension is the sharpest. The same generative capacity that lets an AI chatbot deliver personalized, conversational health guidance also lets it generate fluent, plausible-sounding health misinformation, and do so faster than human fact-checkers can respond. A 2025 opinion piece in this journal warned that generative AI tools function as de facto triage systems and informal health advisors in low-and middle-income countries, where their fluency can be mistaken for authority even when their outputs are unreliable. A parallel systematic review of generative AI and health misinformation catalogued mechanisms of production, propagation, and mitigation across text, image, and synthetic media, underscoring that the problem is not hypothetical but already observed at scale (Saeidnia et al., 2026). Mitigation research is advancing in step. Retrieval-augmented generation has been used to improve the factual reliability of LLM-based COVID-19 fact-checking tools (Li et al., 2025), and thematic-analysis pipelines have been proposed to detect and "inoculate" audiences against circulating misinformation narratives (Malek et al., 2026). A recent risk taxonomy specifically for public health LLM adoption (Zhou et al., 2025) offers a structured way for practitioners to reason about failure modes before deployment rather than after. Conversational AI for vaccine communication, an earlier and instructive precedent, showed both promise for addressing hesitancy and clear risk of amplifying inaccurate claims when systems were insufficiently curated (Passanante et al., 2023). The lesson across this literature is consistent: the communicative power of conversational AI is not neutral infrastructure like a water pipe; it actively shapes the epistemic environment it operates in, for better or worse, depending on design choices made well upstream of any individual conversation.Evidence highlights Population-level implication Efficacy vs. evidentiary depth ~82% of behavior-change comparisons favorable, but only ~1/3 with moderate+ effect sizes; RCTs a minority (Fu et al., 2026) provenance, and risk taxonomies (Zhou et al., 2025) prior to releaseNone of this argues against conversational AI in public health; the direction of the evidence is cautiously positive, and the WHO's own experimentation with S.A.R.A.H. reflects institutional recognition that this technology will be used regardless of academic ambivalence. The argument is instead for treating conversational AI the way public health has learned, sometimes painfully, to treat other infrastructure: as a shared resource whose design choices carry population-level consequences, and which therefore warrants governance commensurate with its reach. Three concrete commitments follow. First, funders and health systems evaluating AI chatbot interventions should require reporting of architecture (rulebased versus LLM-based, retrieval-augmented or not), population stratification by digitalaccess indicators, and effect durability beyond the intervention period -the absence of which currently limits comparability across the field (Fu et al., 2026). Second, deployment in low-resource or multilingual settings should be preceded by equity-focused validation rather than assumed from high-resource pilot data, consistent with behavioral-access frameworks that treat dissemination and sustainment as distinct design stages, not afterthoughts. Third, any public health-facing conversational agent should be built on retrieval-grounded, provenance-transparent architectures and evaluated against a structured risk taxonomy before release, rather than relying on post hoc misinformation cleanup. WHO's 2024 guidance on large multimodal models already articulates comparable principles -transparency, accountability, and human oversight -for governments and developers; the task now is operationalizing them at the level of individual chatbot deployments rather than treating them as abstract commitments.The digital public health field has an opportunity, still open but narrowing, to shape how conversational AI is integrated into population health promotion before deployment patterns harden into path dependency. The evidence reviewed here suggests genuine, if still shallow, behavioral benefit; genuine, if unevenly distributed, gains in access; and genuine, dual-use communicative power that can either strengthen or corrode public trust in health information depending on how it is engineered and governed. Framing conversational AI as infrastructure rather than as a discrete clinical tool has practical consequences: it shifts evaluation from short efficacy trials toward equity-stratified, durability-tested, misinformation-resilient deployment standards, and it shifts responsibility from individual developers toward the institutions, including public health agencies, research funders, and journals such as this one, that decide what counts as sufficient evidence for scale. A reasonable objection is that infrastructure-level governance risks slowing beneficial innovation, particularly in settings where any accessible health guidance outperforms none. That concern is legitimate and argues for proportionate, tiered oversight rather than uniform restriction -lighter validation for low-stakes wellness nudges, more rigorous requirements for agents addressing vaccine hesitancy, chronic disease self-management, or crisis-adjacent mental health support. What the evidence does not support is treating conversational AI's current trajectory as selfcorrecting. Left to consumer technology incentives alone, generative health chatbots are likely to continue optimizing for engagement and fluency rather than for population-level epidemiological benefit or equitable reach. The digital public health community is well positioned, through funding priorities, publication standards, and partnership with bodies like WHO, to redirect that trajectory toward public-interest design before it further consolidates around existing digital and geographic advantage.

papers.title: The synergistic effect of internet-based health communication on health promotion: the chain-mediating effect of health literacy and health education
papers.authors: Xuezhen Chen, Ziqi Zhang
papers.abstract: Next-generation internet technologies, represented by artificial intelligence, are reshaping the nationwide health information distribution system; this study examines the synergistic benefit effect of online health communication on health promotion. The analysis utilizes 5,333 data points from the 2023 China General Social Survey (CGSS), which employed a nationally stratified, multi-stage sampling design. Using the Hayes PROCESS Model 6 serial chain mediation model, 2,000 bias-correction Bootstrap samples were generated to conduct baseline OLS regression, mediation effect decomposition, multidimensional heterogeneity analysis, and an IPW inverse probability weighting robustness test. The baseline OLS regression reveals a significant positive overall association between online health communication and health promotion. The chain mediation model identified three indirect pathways: a single health literacy mediation pathway, a single digital health education mediation pathway, and a core serial synergistic pathway (“Online Health Communication → Health Literacy → Digital Health Education → Health Promotion”); the confidence intervals for all three pathways do not include zero. The heterogeneity analysis uncovered the distribution pattern of the digital health gap: the serial chain effect is slightly higher in urban areas than in rural areas, and slightly higher among women than among men (though the intergroup difference is not statistically significant); the strongest effect is observed among the middle-aged population aged 31–60 years, while the serial transmission chain tends to weaken among groups with lower educational attainment. Multiple robustness tests, including IPW inverse probability weighting, support the reliability of the core findings. The positive association between online health communication and residents’ health promotion can be explained through the independent and serial mediation statistical pathways involving health literacy and digital health education; this observation reveals a “progressive synergy” relationship among the three factors.

papers.title: Behavioral differentiation during the AIGC image generation waiting period: effects on creativity in conceptual design
papers.authors: Ziliang Zhu, Jiang Xu
papers.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) offers new ways to generate inspiration for conceptual design, yet limited attention has been paid to the waiting period between prompt submission and AI image output. This study examined behavioral differentiation during this interval and investigated how the task relevance and cognitive load of waiting-period behaviors affect creativity in conceptual design. Methods Three experiments were conducted with design students. Experiment 1 identified and classified core waiting-period behaviors ( N = 30); Experiment 2 measured the cognitive load of representative behaviors using the NASA-TLX ( N = 24); and Experiment 3 employed a behavior-based 2 × 2 conceptual framework ( N = 60), in which four representative waiting-period behaviors were selected to represent different combinations of task relevance (high/low) and relative workload (higher/lower), and their creative performance was compared. Results The results showed that the AIGC generation waiting period was not a passive interval but involved multiple identifiable behavioral patterns. Creative performance differed across the four representative behavioral conditions. Specifically, the overall creativity score in the GP condition was significantly lower than the scores in the RS, DB, and RB conditions, whereas no significant differences were observed among the latter three conditions. These findings further suggest that the subsequent influence of waiting-period behaviors on creativity may depend not only on the level of cognitive demand but also on whether cognitive resources remain directed toward the ongoing creative task. Discussion This study further interprets AIGC generation waiting-period behaviors from three interrelated functional perspectives: task continuity, cognitive expenditure, and temporary disengagement/incubation. This functional account provides an empirical basis for understanding the cognitive role of the AIGC generation waiting period and for optimizing AI-assisted conceptual design workflows.

papers.title: Knowledge, attitudes, and practices among users of GLP-1 receptor agonists in Saudi Arabia: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Abdullah Ali Alshehri, Mohammed K. Al-Osaimi, Nawaf N. Al-Saeedi, Osama M. Al-Wagdani, Sultan S. Al-Zahrani, Fareed A. Alharthi, Ghadah H. Alshehri, Fahad Hassan Baali, Saeed Saad A. Alghamdi, Wael Y. Khawagi
papers.abstract: Background The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists has increased rapidly in Saudi Arabia for weight management and glycaemic control. However, concerns remain regarding inappropriate use, medication safety, and misconceptions surrounding these therapies. This study assessed the knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) of GLP-1 receptor agonist users in Saudi Arabia and identified factors associated with these domains. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among adult GLP-1 receptor agonist users in Saudi Arabia between December 2025 and March 2026. Eligible participants were aged ≥18 years and had used semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, or tirzepatide within the previous 12 months. Participants were recruited through purposive snowball sampling via social media platforms. Descriptive statistics and binary logistic regression were used to assess KAP levels and associated factors. Results A total of 310 participants were included. The median age was 33 years (IQR: 16), and the median BMI was 33.9 kg/m 2 (IQR: 7.1). Tirzepatide was the most frequently used medication (46.1%). Good practices were reported by 54.8% of participants, whereas only 25.8% demonstrated good knowledge and 33.2% reported positive attitudes. Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores were positively correlated (ρ = 0.278–0.395; all p < 0.001). Participants aged >50 years were less likely to demonstrate good knowledge (aOR = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.04–0.82) and positive attitudes (aOR = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.09–0.91). Postgraduate education was independently associated with positive attitudes (aOR = 6.51, 95% CI: 2.23–18.99) and good practices (aOR = 4.47, 95% CI: 1.37–14.60), while female sex was associated with good practices (aOR = 2.06, 95% CI: 1.28–3.33). Conclusion GLP-1 receptor agonist users demonstrated generally favourable medication-use practices but suboptimal knowledge and attitudes. Higher knowledge was associated with more positive attitudes and better practices, highlighting the importance of patient education and healthcare professional counselling to support safe and informed use.

papers.title: Wave-function formalism for evolving neural dynamics: a mathematical framework informed by EEG
papers.authors: Madelyn Klebba
papers.abstract: The organization of distributed neural activity remains one of the central challenges in computational neuroscience. Contemporary frameworks, including Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, entropy-based approaches, and electromagnetic field theories, have advanced our understanding of neural coordination but employ different mathematical descriptions of large-scale brain dynamics. This study investigates whether wave-function formalism provides a useful mathematical framework for representing evolving neural dynamics measured using electroencephalography (EEG). Rather than introducing a new electrophysiological measure or proposing a new mechanism of consciousness, the framework represents complementary EEG observables within a common state-space description of neural activity. Mathematical inspiration is drawn from Everett’s representation of evolving state spaces, although no claims are made regarding quantum computation or quantum processes in the brain. Electroencephalographic recordings from interictal, preictal, and ictal seizure states (150 EEG segments) were analyzed using complementary measures of signal amplitude, spectral organization, entropy, phase dynamics, cross-frequency coupling, and recurrence quantification. Statistical comparisons employed nonparametric analyses, effect-size estimation, confidence intervals, and post hoc testing. Significant differences were observed across all major electrophysiological domains. Ictal recordings exhibited increased signal amplitude, redistribution of spectral power toward lower frequencies, reduced entropy, altered phase organization, changes in cross-frequency coupling, and increased recurrence structure, indicating coordinated changes in evolving neural dynamics during seizure progression. These findings are interpreted within a mathematical framework that treats established EEG observables as complementary descriptors of a single evolving neural state. The principal contribution of this work is the proposal of a mathematically grounded and experimentally testable representation of evolving neural dynamics. Whether this formalism provides new insight into cognition or conscious experience remains an empirical question for future investigation.

papers.title: Case Report: Longitudinal evaluation of cerebrospinal fluid Alzheimer’s disease core biomarkers in a case of refractory late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology
papers.authors: Takafumi Wada, Akira Kuzuya, Kazuma Koda, Sakiho Ueda, Atsushi Shima, Nobukatsu Sawamoto, Akio Ikeda, Ryōsuke Takahashi, Riki Matsumoto
papers.abstract: In recent years, late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU) has increasingly been recognized as a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other forms of dementia. We present a case of refractory LOEU with progressive cognitive decline, longitudinally evaluated over more than 20 years using neuropsychological tests, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) AD core biomarkers (Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau), electroencephalography, and neuroimaging. The CSF AD core biomarkers were consistently positive, indicating the presence of both amyloid and tau pathology; however, CSF Aβ levels markedly decreased in parallel with improved seizure control. Notably, the addition of low-dose perampanel (1 mg/day) led to improvement in both cognitive function and seizure control, while 18 F-flutemetamol positron emission tomography remained visually negative despite exceeding the predefined quantitative Centiloid threshold. Two years later, seizure frequency increased again, cognitive function deteriorated, and amyloid PET became visually positive, accompanied by an increase in the quantitative Centiloid value. This longitudinal observation suggests that chronic epileptic activity may modify or confound the interpretation of CSF AD biomarker profiles and contribute to cognitive decline, while concomitant early or slowly progressive AD pathology cannot be excluded. The overall biomarker trajectory, including persistently positive CSF AD biomarkers and progressive amyloid PET findings, is compatible with evolving AD pathology, although the marked decline in absolute CSF Aβ concentrations during improved seizure control suggests that chronic epileptic activity may also influence biomarker dynamics. Careful interpretation of AD biomarkers is therefore essential in patients with LOEU, particularly in the era of anti-amyloid therapies.

papers.title: Current status of medical students’ use of large language models for graduation thesis writing: a comparative cross-sectional survey
papers.authors: Xuexiu Liu, Junyang Luo, Yanhan Chen, Jianjun Zhu, Yi Liu, Zhengjie Wang
papers.abstract: Objective Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a conceptual framework, this study explored medical students’ use of large language models (LLMs) in graduation thesis writing, focusing on application patterns, perceptions, and potential risks. Methods A comparative cross-sectional questionnaire survey using convenience sampling was conducted among medical graduates from medical schools in China in 2024 and 2025. The self-designed 25-item questionnaire included five-point Likert items on perceived advantages and disadvantages of LLMs. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's α , exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was performed, and univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were used to identify factors associated with LLMs use. Results A total of 341 valid questionnaires were collected. Overall, 54.25% (185/341) of respondents reported using LLMs in graduation thesis writing, with use reported by 27.37% (52/190) in 2024 and 88.08% (133/151) in 2025. ChatGPT was the most frequently used platform in 2024 (82.69%, 43/52), whereas Deepseek was the most frequently used platform in 2025 (88.72%, 118/133). LLMs were used primarily during the literature review stage (74.05%, 137/185), mainly to provide writing suggestions (82.16%, 152/185). Cronbach's α was 0.720 for perceived advantages and 0.650 for perceived disadvantages, and exploratory factor analysis identified a two-factor clustering pattern consistent with the predefined grouping of perceived advantages and disadvantages. Among LLMs users, 68.65% (127/185) believed that LLMs use would not compromise academic integrity, whereas 47.57% (88/185) remained concerned about potential academic misconduct. The main perceived disadvantages included the risk of academic misconduct, limited content accuracy, and data privacy and security concerns. The findings were discussed with reference to TAM-related concepts as an interpretive framework. Conclusion LLMs use was substantially higher in the 2025 survey than in the 2024 survey. Although LLMs improve writing efficiency and provide valuable writing support, concerns regarding academic integrity, content accuracy, and data privacy remain important considerations. The TAM provides a useful framework for interpreting students’ adoption patterns and may inform the development of AI education and governance strategies in medical education.

papers.title: Sex differences in sleep and memory relationships in older adults at risk for Alzheimer’s disease
papers.authors: Negin Sattari, Abhishek Dave, Ivy Y. Chen, Kitty K. Lui, Miranda G Chappel-Farley, Destiny E. Berisha, Kate E. Sprecher, Brady A. Riedner, Stephanie Jones, Barbara B. Bendlin, Bryce A. Mander, Ruth M. Benca
papers.abstract: Introduction Biological sex is an important modifier of aging and Alzheimer’s disease risk, yet the sleep-related mechanisms through which sex and genetic risk interact to influence memory remain poorly understood. We examined whether associations among non-rapid eye movement sleep physiology, overnight memory retention, and apolipoprotein E ϵ4 ( APOE ϵ4) status, a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease, differed by sex in cognitively unimpaired older adults enriched for Alzheimer’s disease risk. Methods Eighty participants completed overnight polysomnography with high-density electroencephalography, and 65 also completed an evening encoding/immediate recall and morning delayed recall word-pair memory task. Results Overnight memory retention did not differ by sex. However, exploratory analyses of the proportional overnight retention measure suggested a sex × APOE ϵ4 interaction, such that female APOE ϵ4 carriers may exhibit reduced overnight forgetting relative to female non-carriers and male carriers. Although counterintuitive, this pattern may reflect compensatory or resilience-related sleep-memory mechanisms in cognitively unimpaired women at genetic risk for Alzheimer’s disease rather than a protective effect of APOE ϵ4 itself. Women spent more time in N3 sleep and had higher non-rapid eye movement delta and slow sigma power than men. Sleep-memory associations also differed by sex: greater N2 duration was more strongly associated with better overnight retention in men, whereas greater frontal slow sigma power and fronto-central fast sigma power were positively associated with retention in women. Exploratory APOE-stratified analyses suggested sex-specific differences in sleep stage-memory relationships, with more positive N2-memory associations in male than female APOE ϵ4 carriers and more positive N3-memory associations in female than male carriers; both differences remained significant after FDR correction. TFCE-corrected analyses further identified positive associations between NREM delta and sigma activity and overnight memory retention in female APOE ϵ4 carriers. Discussion These findings highlight sex-specific patterns in NREM sleep physiology and sleep-memory relationships in cognitively unimpaired older adults at risk for Alzheimer’s disease. More broadly, the results suggest that sex and APOE ϵ4 status may jointly shape the neurophysiological pathways linking sleep and memory, underscoring the importance of considering sex as a biological variable when studying sleep, cognitive aging, and Alzheimer’s disease vulnerability.

papers.title: Digital translation practices in university English learning: adoption, disciplinary variation, and AI-assisted revision
papers.authors: Kevin Mario Laura-De La Cruz, Astrid Camila Milagros Palacios-Mamani, Sebastian Alejandro Flores-Maquera, Pilar Valeria Zapana-Aguilar, Paola Milagros Paredes-Machaca, Lucia Esperanza Caceres-Ramos, Enrique Jose Quispe-Mello, Gina Maribel Valle-Castro
papers.abstract: Introduction Machine translation and generative artificial intelligence (AI) are now common resources in English as a foreign language learning, yet evidence from Latin American higher education remains limited and often conflates tool use with learning impact. This study characterized translation practices, tool preferences, print-dictionary use, and AI-assisted text revision among university students in southern Peru. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 435 students from 37 degree programs and seven faculties at a public university. Questionnaire items were analyzed as separate indicators rather than combined into a latent scale. Valid percentages with 95% Wilson confidence intervals were estimated, paired exact McNemar tests were used for within-participant comparisons, faculty differences were assessed using Monte Carlo chi-square tests with false-discovery-rate adjustment, and an exploratory logistic regression was fitted. Results Use of AI or automated translators was reported by 94.7% of respondents, and 92.4% used translation applications or websites. Both were more prevalent than print-dictionary experience (65.4%; paired odds ratios 9.86 and 7.88, respectively; both p < .001). Google Translate predominated across questionnaire contexts, whereas ChatGPT accounted for 7.7% of responses to the general-use item and 34.0% to the AI-focused item. AI-assisted revision was reported by 74.1% and varied across faculties (52.2%-96.8%; Cramér's V = .274, q < .001). Although 75.0% reported using print dictionaries rarely or never, 78.0% supported their continued promotion. Discussion The findings describe a heterogeneous institutional translation ecology in which widespread digital-tool adoption coexists with disciplinary variation, context-dependent tool preferences, and continued endorsement of print resources. These findings do not establish learning effects. They support pedagogical attention to verification, post-editing, and independent language production, whose effectiveness requires direct evaluation.

papers.title: Financial literacy in digital and AI-supported educational contexts
papers.authors: Drnovšek, Nika, vzgoja in izobraževanje, Stanislav Avsec, Francka Lovšin Kozina
papers.abstract: In an era of expanding digital finance, fintech innovation and AI-supported decision-making, financial literacy has become a critical educational priority for informed, inclusive and responsible participation in contemporary financial systems. This study examines financial literacy in digital and AI-supported educational contexts through bibliometric mapping and a PRISMA-based systematic review. A bibliometric analysis of 3,105 Web of Science and Scopus records identified the broader conceptual structure of the field, followed by thematic synthesis of 29 studies with educational relevance. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. The findings show that financial literacy and financial inclusion form the main conceptual hubs, while fintech and digital finance act as bridging themes. AIrelated research is visible, but is mainly linked to prediction, decision-making, fintech adoption and digital services rather than direct pedagogy. The review further shows that digital tools are used across diverse educational and assessment contexts, with the more consistent evidence emphasizing structured instructional design and pedagogical integration rather than technology exposure alone. AI-related evidence remains limited and is predominantly analytical, diagnostic, advisory or supportive rather than directly pedagogical. The main research gap lies in the limited empirical evidence on pedagogically grounded AI-supported approaches to financial literacy education. Overall, the study provides an integrated framework for identifying conceptual structures, emerging digital and AI-supported trends, and critical pedagogical gaps relevant to evidence-informed and inclusive financial literacy education.

papers.title: Financial literacy in digital and AI-supported educational contexts: a bibliometric and PRISMA-based systematic review
papers.authors: Nika Drnovšek, Stanislav Avsec, Francka Lovšin Kozina
