papers.journal: Jurnal Pembelajaran Bimbingan dan Pengelolaan Pendidikan
papers.abstract: Formal proof is at the heart of university-level plane geometry because it requires students to build deductively valid arguments based on definitions, theorems, and known results, rather than visual observation or intuition. However, students often struggle to justify inferential steps, while generative artificial intelligence can provide fluent proofs before learners examine diagrams, check theorem conditions, or construct their own reasoning. This conceptual article proposes a Warrant-Seeking Socratic AI Framework for supporting formal proof learning in plane geometry. Literature was searched in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar from March 15 to May 21, 2026, using terms related to formal proof, geometry, Socratic questioning, and artificial intelligence. Of 72 records identified, 14 duplicates were removed, leaving 58 sources for screening, full-text assessment, and narrative synthesis. Sources were synthesized by identifying recurring pedagogical and epistemic functions related to proof construction, questioning, AI interaction, and validation. Based on the synthesis: problem orientation, conjecture articulation, theorem-condition analysis, inferential construction, proof validation, and metacognitive reflection, a six-phase recursive model is proposed. The framework positions AI as an epistemic interviewer rather than a proof generator, prompting students to distinguish visual conjectures from warranted claims, examine theorem conditions, justify inferential steps, and retain ownership of their proofs. The synthesis distinguishes evidence directly related to geometry and mathematical proving from findings extrapolated from broader educational contexts. The framework is therefore a theoretically grounded proposition rather than an empirically validated model, and its effectiveness remains to be established through future empirical research.

papers.title: The Unnoticed Freezes in the AI Era
papers.authors: Minh-Hoang Nguyen
papers.abstract: In 2023, 18% of American adults said they had ever used ChatGPT. By early 2026, that number was 44%. AI adoption in the workplace has been even more remarkable. According to Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers were already using AI at work, with nearly half having started within the preceding six months. We did not vote to hand over drafting, summarizing, fact-checking, and even thinking to these systems. There was no big decision. Just a free chatbot, a looming deadline, and a prompt that saved twenty minutes. Then another, and another... Regarding this serious issue, I was drawn to a new paper quietly posted on SSRN last September by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang. It gives this slow handover a name: the Correction Freeze Problem (CFP). His question is simple: can a system think it is fine while it is drifting away from reality, and stay that way not because it is lazy or lying, but because the very way it corrects itself makes staying blind the rational choice? The paper answers yes. In four different ways. And when any of those ways meets a world that rewards going along, the drift becomes a trap that is much harder to escape than it was to fall into. To grasp these insights, you don't need the math. Simply because you've lived it.

papers.title: Applications and Evaluation of Large Language Models in Sarcopenia: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: han zhang
papers.abstract: This project is a scoping review of the applications and evaluation of large language models (LLMs) in sarcopenia. It aims to map the tasks performed by LLMs, characterize their technical configurations, and examine how their outputs and use are evaluated across clinical, community, home, and research settings. The review addresses three questions: which sarcopenia-related tasks have been supported by LLMs; which models, prompting strategies, and approaches to incorporating external knowledge have been used; and which outcomes have been assessed, using what methods and in which contexts. The review follows JBI guidance for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR reporting framework. Searches of PubMed, Embase via Ovid, and the Web of Science Core Collection were conducted on October 8, 2026, supplemented by candidate publications identified during project preparation. Eligible sources include full-text journal articles and preprints reporting an identifiable LLM application relevant to sarcopenia, as well as protocol papers containing completed pilot evaluations. The scope encompasses studies involving patients, simulated cases, question sets, measurement data, and research literature, without additional age or publication-language restrictions. Study selection and data extraction are independently verified by two reviewers.Extracted information covers application tasks, study design, models and versions, prompting and knowledge augmentation, evaluation measures, reference standards, assessors, units of analysis, and sarcopenia-specific findings. Descriptive and narrative synthesis organizes the evidence around patient education, clinical information processing and decision support, nutrition and exercise recommendations, interpretation of objective measurements, and research literature processing. Particular attention is given to the relationships among system component performance, generated content, task performance, user experience, and clinical outcomes. Expected outputs include a structured map of existing applications and evaluation practices, an account of methodological and reporting gaps, and priorities for future research. The findings are intended to inform the design of sarcopenia-related LLM applications and evaluations that connect technical performance with user understanding, practical use, and relevant health outcomes.

papers.title: CULINARY HERITAGE OF UKRAINE: POST-WAR TRANSFORMATION AND DIGITAL APPROACHES TO PRESERVATION
papers.authors: K. Svidlo, Nataliia M. Bogdan, Larysa V. Obolentseva, Лідія Піддубна, Олена Каролоп
papers.abstract: In the context of the post-war transformation of rural areas in Ukraine, culinary tourism is considered an important tool for sustainable development and regional recovery. The preservation and promotion of culinary heritage through tourism practices create opportunities for economic diversification, support of local communities, and strengthening of cultural identity. The aim of the study is to analyze the processes of integrating Ukrainian culinary heritage into the tourism sector and to assess its impact on the development of rural areas under current conditions. The methodological framework combines qualitative and quantitative approaches: semi-structured interviews were conducted with stakeholders (entrepreneurs, experts, and community representatives), along with an analysis of statistical and analytical data for 2024–2025. The results of the study show that culinary heritage is a key element of national identity, as it includes traditional recipes, cooking technologies, local ingredients, and gastronomic practices. At the same time, its preservation is challenged by globalization, urbanization, and military conflict, which lead to the loss of cultural practices and the destruction of infrastructure. It has been found that the effectiveness of culinary tourism development depends on the level of coordination among stakeholders and the involvement of local communities. Insufficient public participation and fragmented policies reduce the potential of such initiatives, whereas participatory approaches enhance their effectiveness. Culinary tourism contributes to rural development through job creation, the formation of local branding, and support for creative industries. Digital technologies, including online archives and artificial intelligence tools, play a significant role in documenting and promoting heritage. Culinary heritage has strong potential as a resource for the post-war recovery of Ukraine; however, its effective use requires integrated governance, digitalization, and active community participation.

papers.title: Physicians' perceptions of artificial intelligence in clinical and academic practice: a mixed-methods study from Erbil City
papers.authors: Shaida Kareem, Sherzad Ali Ismael
papers.abstract: Background and objective: Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare and medical research represents significant potential; however, it also introduces practical and ethical challenges. This study analyzes physicians' perceptions of AI implementation in clinical and academic settings, exploring their awareness, perceptions, barriers, concerns, and insights into ethical and regulatory considerations. Methods: A mixed-methods approach was used. The quantitative component involved standardized surveys completed by 390 physicians (241 clinical, 149 academic) in Erbil City from November 2024 to June 2025. Participants were selected using systematic sampling, and surveys were self-administered. The qualitative component included two focus group discussions, involving 6 clinical physicians and 8 academic physicians, to explore in-depth perceptions and concerns regarding AI in healthcare and research. Results: Of 390 physicians, the majority of participants were male (69.2%). Mean age was 46.7±7 years. Familiarity with AI was higher among younger, male, and academic physicians, with age showing a negative association (p <0.001). Clinical physicians reported more concerns regarding privacy in healthcare (p=0.003) and research (p=0.041), as well as algorithmic bias (p=0.030). Despite these concerns, most physicians valued AI in healthcare and academic research and demonstrated strong interest in training and collaboration. Qualitative findings showed optimism and frequent use of AI tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, often described as “Google replacements.” However, physicians also highlighted ethical issues and the need for local training and infrastructure improvement. Conclusion: Physicians generally welcome the use of AI in healthcare and research but emphasize the necessity of ethical guidelines, peer collaboration, and formal education. To ensure responsible adoption, addressing infrastructural and trust barriers will be essential for guaranteeing that AI technologies improve rather than undermine patient care and research integrity.

papers.title: Digital branding strategies for marginalized tourism destinations
papers.authors: Monika Ploch Palatková, Pavel Štrach, Eva Jaderná
papers.abstract: This study explores whether digital branding can reduce socio-economic disparities in marginalized tourism destinations. Using a mixed-methods comparative case study of Ostrava, Košice, and Glasgow, it analyses strategic tourism documents and digital infrastructure via BDC and RivalIQ tools. Findings identify three mechanisms: visibility alone is ineffective without strategic links to community benefits; stakeholder co-creation works moderately when structured but lacks platforms for resident-visitor interaction; ecosystem alignment – combining resident-focused planning, measurement systems, and workforce programs – is essential. Identical digital tools yield different outcomes depending on governance models and strategic intent. The study concludes that digital branding supports equity only when strategies prioritize community benefits, enable authentic local storytelling, and include comprehensive impact tracking. It extends destination branding theory by challenging the visitor-centric paradigm, arguing that residents must be the primary beneficiaries. The research contributes to tourism policy by highlighting the need for inclusive digital strategies that integrate local voices, measure benefit distribution, and foster long-term socio-economic resilience in post-industrial destinations.

papers.title: Algorithmic justice in the making: AI, sentencing, and fairness in Malaysia’s criminal courts
papers.authors: Haezreena Begum Abdul Hamid
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in criminal justice systems to improve efficiency and consistency, but its use in sentencing raises important questions about fairness, transparency, and judicial discretion. This article examines Malaysia’s introduction of AI-assisted sentencing through the Artificial Intelligence in Court Sentencing (AiCOS) system and asks how algorithmic assistance reshapes the exercise and visibility of sentencing discretion. It adopts a qualitative, desk-based, and interdisciplinary approach, drawing on criminology, legal and sociolegal scholarship, judicial and institutional materials, and international AI governance frameworks. The Malaysian experience is examined through four dimensions: transparency and explainability, procedural contestability, human discretion, and accountability, with comparative reference to the United States’s experience with COMPAS (Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions) and the European Union’s regulatory framework. The article argues that AiCOS is best understood not as an autonomous ‘AI judge’, but as an automated evolution of Malaysia’s existing Table of Sentencing . While its guidance function remains broadly similar, algorithmic mediation changes the visibility and contestability of the basis upon which punishment is determined. Automation therefore does not eliminate discretion but may relocate it into less visible decisions concerning data, system design, deployment, and reliance on algorithmic recommendations. The article concludes that retaining a human judge as the final decision-maker is insufficient, by itself, to ensure fairness. Effective governance requires transparency, disclosure, meaningful opportunities to challenge algorithmic inputs and recommendations, reasoned judicial decision-making, and continuing independent oversight.

papers.title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Teaching Master's Students of Linguistics and Pedagogical Education: Challenges and Prospects
papers.authors: Gul'nara Dul'muhametova, Gul'nara Dul'muhametova
papers.abstract: The article examines main aspects of artificial intelligence use in master's degree teaching of Linguistics and Pedagogical Education spheres. Artificial intelligence is currently being actively integrated into the educational process, transforming traditional formats into a more dynamic one: it quickly analyzes information, adapts materials on demand, systematizes and structures information, and personalizes educational content. In this article, the authors emphasize the competent training of future specialists/qualified personnel who will possess in-depth knowledge of the theory and methodology of teaching foreign languages, as well as skills in using innovative technological advances in professional teaching, and will be in demand in the future labor market. Based on the conducted research, the essence of using AI tools in the educational and linguistic environment is revealed, allowing for increased individualization and interactivity in the foreign language learning process. The modern education system is currently undergoing an active digital transformation, driven by the rapid development of information technology and artificial intelligence (AI). It was concluded that artificial intelligence can offer enormous potential for improving the quality of education, reducing the time and effort required by teachers, and facilitating the independent work of master's students. The obtained results allowed us to expand the scientific understanding of the use of AI in educational process and identify solutions for its application by higher education teachers in practical classes. The study materials will be useful for education and philology researchers and teachers improving the educational process.

papers.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON STUDENTS OF LEGAL EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS
papers.authors: Белавин Андрей Вениаминович, Nikolay Gorach, Dmitriy Ivanov
papers.abstract: The article discusses the current threats associated with the introduction of artificial intelligence technologies and social media activities in the learning environment of schoolchildren and students. Some directions for the development and training of critical thinking skills in modern technology are given, directions for improving the formation of digital hygiene and legal education in order to prevent destructive behavior are determined. The subject of the research is issues related to the influence of artificial intelligence on students of legal education institutions. The purpose of the work is to identify problems and develop recommendations in the aspect of the impact of modern technologies during the training of future graduates of lawyers. The methodology of the work was based on the provisions of modern psychology, pedagogy, and the concept of improving the educational process, in terms of developing learning with the active use of modern technologies. A set of scientific research methods was used: analysis and synthesis of conclusions from previously conducted psychological and pedagogical research in terms of studying the impact of artificial intelligence, as well as other modern information and telecommunication technologies in the context of training in legal educational institutions. The experimental work is related to the study of the behavior of law students and high school students in the context of studying the influence of artificial intelligence on them while actively using the capabilities of modern information and telecommunications technologies, including Internet resources, as a result of which a generalization of the accumulated material was carried out. The results of the work. The results obtained indicate the need to continue conducting additional research on the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on students, in a student and school environment in which modern information and telecommunications technologies are currently being actively used. The scope of the results. As a result of the research, the organizational and practical aspects of studying behavior in learning environments with the active use of artificial intelligence technologies by students of legal educational institutions are summarized.

papers.title: Implementation of agricultural nutrient mitigation policies and nature-based solutions in Baltic and North Sea countries
papers.authors: Eerika Albrecht, Anu Lahteenmäki‐Uutela, Katri Rankinen, Pasi Valkama, Anne-Grette Buseth Blankenberg, Eva Skarbøvik, Anne Lyche Solheim, Katarina Kyllmar, Marek Giełczewski, Katrin Bieger, Brian Kronvang
papers.abstract: Nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) emissions from agricultural lands contribute to eutrophication and the degradation of surface waters. This paper studies the implementation of European agri-environmental policies to regulate these emissions in the North European coastal waters by promoting changes in agricultural practices through nutrient mitigation measures and nature-based solutions (NbS). By analyzing policy documents and results from co-creation, it compares the implementation of agricultural nutrient mitigation policies in four Baltic Sea countries—Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and Poland—as well as Norway, which borders the Atlantic and the North Sea. The findings suggest that water quality should be set as a priority in national implementation. Integrating NbS, ensuring stability and aligning agricultural practices with environmental goals would reduce the risk of eutrophication in marine ecosystems.

papers.title: Hackathon on predictive modelling in systems pharmacology: design, implementation, and outcomes
papers.authors: Malvina Marku, The-Chuong Trinh, Racym Berrah, Guido Uguzzoni, Moreno Ursino, Christophe Battail
papers.abstract: Background The growing availability of multi-omics data and machine learning methods creates both an opportunity and a challenge for the systems pharmacology community: the opportunity to model drug action at unprecedented mechanistic resolution, and the challenge of equipping a new generation of researchers with the computational literacy to do so. There is a particular need for training formats that bridge classical pharmacometrics with omics data science, and that foster interdisciplinary community building. Methods We organised a 4-day intensive hackathon on Predictive Modelling in Systems Pharmacology, bringing together 16 early-career researchers from the Horizon Europe CANVAS and French PEPR DIGPHAT consortia, spanning biology, bioinformatics, and computational science. The event pursued the dual aim of fostering a multidisciplinary consortium community and providing hands-on training that bridges classical pharmacometrics with omics data science. Three scientific tracks were delivered: (i) pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) modelling, (ii) drug perturbation modelling through network diffusion in gene regulatory networks (GRN), and (iii) machine learning for pharmacogenomics. A theory-to-practice pedagogical framework structured each day, with morning workshops grounding participants in methodological foundations followed by afternoon coding sprints on real-world datasets. Results All three tracks produced working computational outputs within the hackathon timeframe. In the PK/PD track, all teams successfully identified a two-compartment structural model and key covariate effects. In the GRN track, participants implemented a network diffusion algorithm on gene regulatory networks, yielding patient-stratified therapy recommendations. In the pharmacogenomics track, four out of seven teams surpassed the logistic regression baseline in Matthews Correlation Coefficient on an external validation set. Conclusions The hackathon demonstrated that a structured multi-track format combining community-targeted outreach, theory-to-practice pedagogy, and real-world datasets constitutes a replicable model for interdisciplinary computational pharmacology training at the European level.

papers.title: Associations of sleep problems with lifestyle, health-related quality of life, body composition, physical fitness, and academic performance in schoolchildren
papers.authors: Daniel Arriscado Alsina, Raúl Jiménez Boraita
papers.journal: Journal of Activity Sedentary and Sleep Behaviors
papers.abstract: Sleep problems are increasingly recognized as relevant to school health, yet lifestyle, physical fitness, wellbeing, body composition, and academic functioning are not always assessed together. This study examined the associations of these indicators with sleep problems in schoolchildren. Methods: A cross-sectional study included 949 students aged 9–15 years from 60 schools in Tenerife and Gran Canaria, Spain. Sleep problems were assessed using the Sleep Self-Report questionnaire. Moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, sedentary time, health-related quality of life, BMI-for-age z-score, waist circumference, handgrip strength, standing long jump, cardiorespiratory fitness, academic grades, and perceived academic performance were assessed using questionnaires, anthropometric measures, and field-based tests. Differences across sleep-problem tertiles were examined using cluster-adjusted analyses. Separate generalized estimating equation models examined each indicator individually, adjusting for sex, continuous age, family affluence, and area of residence, with school as the clustering variable. The handgrip model was additionally adjusted for body weight and height. Results: Higher sleep-problem scores were inversely associated with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, health-related quality of life, standing long jump, cardiorespiratory fitness, academic grades, and perceived academic performance, and positively associated with sedentary time, BMI-for-age z-score, and waist circumference. Handgrip strength was not significantly associated with sleep problems after adjustment for body weight and height. All significant associations remained so after false-discovery-rate correction. Conclusions: Sleep-problem scores were associated with several lifestyle, health-related quality-of-life, body-composition, physical-fitness, and academic indicators. However, these indicator-specific cross-sectional models do not establish independence, temporal ordering, or causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify potentially reciprocal relationships.

papers.title: Prevalence of interictal migraine among patients with epilepsy
papers.authors: Ibrahim Mohamed Abdelazeem, Shimaa Elgamal, Eslam Samra
papers.journal: The Egyptian Journal of Neurology Psychiatry and Neurosurgery
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Migraine and epilepsy are common neurological disorders that share several pathophysiological mechanisms, including cortical hyperexcitability. Migraine is more frequent in patients with epilepsy than in the general population. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of interictal migraine among adults with epilepsy and evaluate its association with epilepsy characteristics and demographic factors. Results This cross-sectional study included 100 adult patients with epilepsy attending the neurology outpatient clinic at Kafr Elsheikh university hospitals. Clinical evaluation, EEG, brain MRI, and migraine assessment according to ICHD-3 criteria were performed. Only interictal migraine was included. Migraine was identified in 25% of patients, with migraine without aura being the most common subtype (76%). Migraine was significantly associated with female sex, earlier age at epilepsy onset, higher seizure frequency, longer seizure duration, drug-resistant epilepsy, multiple antiepileptic drug use, and focal epileptiform EEG abnormalities (all p < 0.05). Logistic regression identified female sex, earlier epilepsy onset, prolonged seizure duration, and drug-resistant epilepsy as independent predictors of migraine. Conclusion Interictal migraine is a frequent comorbidity in epilepsy, particularly among patients with more severe disease. Early recognition of migraine may improve the comprehensive management and quality of life of patients with epilepsy.

papers.title: Confidence over enjoyment? A cross-national explainable machine learning analysis of affective predictors of early science achievement
papers.authors: Othman Abu Khurma
papers.abstract: Abstract Background A growing body of research has examined students’ science achievement using large-scale international assessments; relatively few studies have focused on affective–motivational factors in early grades within a cross-national and machine-learning framework. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the extent to which affective–motivational factors predict Grade 4 students’ science achievement and to examine whether these relationships differ between the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Singapore (SGP). Sample The study utilized TIMSS, 2023 Grade 4 data from the UAE and SGP, comprising a weighted sample of 34,842 students from the UAE and 6,530 students from Singapore. Design and methods Four affective–motivational constructs, students’ confidence in science, digital self-efficacy, enjoyment of learning science, and value of environmental preservation, were examined as predictors of science achievement. Five plausible values of science achievement were modeled separately following TIMSS methodological guidelines. A comparative machine-learning framework was applied using linear regression, lasso regression, decision trees, random forests, and neural networks. SHAP was used to describe how each predictor contributed to the fitted model’s predictions and how these contributions differed between countries. Result Random forest models demonstrated the strongest predictive performance, although overall explained variance was modest (R 2 ≈ 0.14–0.15). Students’ confidence in science emerged as the most influential predictor in both countries, followed by digital self-efficacy, enjoyment of science, and environmental values. SHAP descriptions of the fitted model suggested that the contribution of enjoyment of science differed between countries, being larger at high levels of enjoyment in the UAE; given the modest predictive accuracy of the models, these patterns are interpreted as exploratory. Conclusion The findings suggest that affective–motivational factors provide meaningful but limited predictive information about Grade 4 science achievement. Differences in predictive patterns between the UAE and Singapore indicate that the relationships were not identical across the two national samples; however, the study does not identify the contextual mechanisms underlying these differences.

papers.title: Aligning neurofeedback protocols with athletes’ sports training objectives: a systematic review
papers.authors: Margaux Izac, Bernard N’Kaoua, Léa Pillette, Camille Jeunet
papers.journal: BMC Sports Science Medicine and Rehabilitation
papers.abstract: Abstract To reach optimal performance, athletes commonly engage in cognitive training. Neurofeedback (NF) can support this process by helping individuals self-regulate neurophysiological activity associated with targeted mental states (e.g., attention). Despite its promising applications in sport, no consensus exists on the effectiveness or optimal design of NF interventions for athletes. This systematic review aims to structure the NF literature according to the objective of each intervention in order to clarify sources of variability in outcomes and extract practical design recommendations. Studies were classified according to their primary objective (improve attentional, affective, or motor abilities) using a hierarchical decision process: titles were considered first, followed by the main dependent variables, and finally the characteristics of the NF protocol when multiple outcomes were reported. The review follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and includes 56 studies (1711 participants) identified through Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed. Study quality is assessed using the CRED-nf framework. By structuring the literature around functional goals, this review offers a novel contribution to the field. While most studies report positive effects on neurophysiological, attentional, affective, or motor outcomes, only 34% do so relative to passive controls, 18% relative to active controls, and 4% relative to other experimental groups. The limited evidence from active comparisons may reflect both poor methodological reporting (median CRED-nf score 37%), and considerable heterogeneity in protocol design, particularly in neurophysiological markers, instructions, and feedback modalities. Such heterogeneity may contribute to misalignment between intervention design and intended outcomes. Our findings suggest that both specific effects (direct modulation of goal-relevant brain activity) and non-specific effects (e.g., increased attention, engagement) contribute to NF efficiency. Some protocol patterns appear frequently associated with certain performance domains (e.g., sensorimotor rhythm up-regulation for attention abilities enhancement), supporting the value of a goal-driven design approach. However, we recommend future studies adopt rigorous methodological frameworks, such as CRED-nf, to support the development of reproducible and effective NF interventions in sport.

papers.title: DTKF: a sepsis early prediction framework based on large language model semantic augmentation and dual-teacher knowledge distillation
papers.authors: Y X Zhang, Xinlei Ji, Huijie Zhang, Bo Huang, Liang Zhou, Jiachen Guo, Lei Yin
papers.journal: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Early and accurate prediction is crucial for reducing mortality. However, clinical settings often face challenges such as data scarcity, class imbalance, and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. Existing scoring systems and traditional machine learning models primarily rely on structured vital signs, failing to capture the rich semantic risk factors embedded in textual data. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in text understanding, their high computational costs and potential hallucinations hinder direct deployment in resource-constrained emergency settings. Methods To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel Dual-Teacher Knowledge Fusion (DTKF) framework. First, we introduce a semantic feature augmentation module that leverages DeepSeek to extract semantic risk probabilities from clinical notes and explicitly fuses them with structured vital signs to construct high-order hybrid features for the student model. Second, to prevent overfitting under small-sample conditions, we design a dual-source knowledge distillation strategy. This strategy integrates rule-based knowledge and data-driven semantic knowledge to construct hybrid teacher signals, regulating a lightweight logistic regression student model via soft-label supervision. Results Experiments on the MIMIC-IV dataset demonstrate that DTKF achieves an AUC of 0.796. This result not only significantly outperforms traditional unimodal baselines but also improves performance by 6.6% compared to direct prediction using LLMs. Conclusions This study effectively integrates rule-based and data-driven knowledge, enhances feature representation using textual information, and improves model performance and robustness through distillation techniques, providing a clinically valuable solution for sepsis early warning.

papers.title: Increased daily walking is associated with changes in psychological well-being and small changes in body composition in adults with cardiometabolic disease
papers.authors: Albertas Skurvydas, Vlada Musvydaite-Vilciauske, Vytautas Visinskis, Artūras Razbadauskas, Asta Šarkauskienė, Julija Majauskaite, Dovilė Valančienė, Daiva Majauskienė
papers.abstract: Daily step count is increasingly recognized as a practical indicator of physical activity and health; however, little is known about how modest increases in habitual walking are associated with psychological well-being and body composition in adults with cardiometabolic disease. In this three-month quasi-experimental study, 419 adults with cardiovascular disease and/or type 2 diabetes participated in a smartphone-supported walking intervention. Daily steps were objectively monitored using smartphone-connected wearable devices, and psychological, behavioral, functional, and body-composition outcomes were assessed before and after the intervention. Changes over time and Gender × Time effects were evaluated, with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Multivariable linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors was used to examine factors associated with changes in body weight and vigor. Daily step count increased by approximately 1,000 steps/day ( d ₐ v = 0.41). Favorable changes were observed in vigor ( d ₐ v = 0.34), well-being ( d ₐ v = 0.17), and happiness ( d ₐ v = 0.15), together with a reduction in stress ( d ₐ v = −0.20); the reduction in anxiety did not remain statistically significant after BH-FDR correction. No significant Gender × Time interactions were observed after BH-FDR correction, indicating broadly similar patterns of change in women and men. Body weight, BMI, and body fat percentage decreased significantly, whereas no statistically significant changes were observed in absolute lean mass or handgrip strength; all body-composition effects were small (| d ₐ v | ≤ 0.06). Increased daily step count was independently associated with greater improvement in vigor (β = 0.144, p = 0.003), whereas greater weight loss was associated with higher baseline body weight (β = −0.247, p < 0.001). In adults with cardiometabolic disease, a three-month smartphone-supported walking intervention was accompanied by approximately 1,000 additional daily steps and favorable changes in psychological well-being, whereas changes in body composition were small. These changes were broadly similar in women and men. Smartphone-supported walking may therefore represent a simple and scalable approach to increasing physical activity and supporting psychological well-being, although controlled studies are needed to establish causality and clinical significance. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07674459. Registration Date: 29 June 2026.

papers.title: Gaming duration and psychological well-being among university students: implications for public health prevention using a cross-sectional study with a modelling approach
papers.authors: Ali Hassan, Muhammad Bilal Nawaz, Muhammad Daniyal, Abbas Saleh Al Mutair, Hanan F. Alharbi, Alya O. Al Mutairi
papers.abstract: Online gaming has emerged as an important public health concern among university students due to potential association with adverse health outcomes. This study aimed to examine the association between PUBG gaming and depression, anxiety, stress, and post-traumatic stress symptoms among university students to inform public health prevention strategies. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 542 participants who played PUBG, recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected using self-administered questionnaires including, PHQ-9, PCL-5 (PTSD), and DASS-21 (depression, anxiety, stress). Associations were examined using Chi-square tests, Kendal tau correlations, and multinomial logistic regression. Additionally, SHAP-based explainable machine learning (XGBoost) was employed to evaluate the relative importance of demographic and gaming-related predictors. Among 542 participants (84.7% male), moderate psychological symptoms were the most frequently reported, including depression (50.6% on DASS-21), anxiety (62.9%), stress (47.0%). Probable PTSD was identified in 95 (17.5%) participants, compared with 447 (82.5%) classified as having no probable PTSD (χ²(1) = 228.61, p < 0.001). Years of PUBG experience was significantly associated with moderate stress (AOR = 0.810, 95% CI: 0.669–0.980, p = 0.031), For stress, playing 5–6 h/day was significantly associated with higher odds of mild stress (AOR = 2.213, 95% CI: 1.090–4.494, p = 0.028). However, greater PUBG playing experience was significantly associated with increased odds of probable PTSD, with each additional year of experience corresponding to a 25.3% increase in odds (AOR = 1.253, 95% CI: 1.019–1.542, p = 0.032). The study noted that Students reporting good academic performance had significantly decreased odds of probable PTSD (AOR = 0.300, 95% CI: 0.134–0.673, p = 0.003)Students who played PUBG for < 2 h/day had significantly decreased odds of probable PTSD (AOR = 0.225, 95% CI: 0.084–0.603, p = 0.003) SHAP-based explainable analysis further identified years of PUBG playing and average daily playing time as associated factors of symptom severity across the outcomes. The study concluded that PUBG gaming experience (years of play) and average daily playing time are important factors associated with the health of university students. These findings highlight the relevance of gaming behaviour as a potential public health concern and emphasize the need for preventive strategies promoting healthy digital habits, early identification of psychological distress, digital health literacy, and coordinated interventions involving families, schools, and healthcare systems. Longitudinal studies are warranted to establish the temporal relationship between gaming patterns and mental health outcomes and to guide evidence-based public health policies.

papers.title: Views on weight management among adults living with and beyond cancer, who have experience of living with obesity: a qualitative study
papers.authors: Kelly Elizabeth Lloyd, Fiona Kennedy, Vanya Joshi, Abigail Fisher, Rebecca J. Beeken, Phillippa J. Lally
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Obesity and weight gain after a cancer diagnosis are associated with poorer outcomes. Weight management could help to reduce the risk of mortality and morbidity. We aimed to understand how a cancer diagnosis impacts weight, health-related behaviours, and views on weight management support among people living with and beyond cancer, and who have experience of living with obesity. Methods Semi-structured, one-to-one interviews were conducted over the telephone with 19 people who had previously reported a BMI ≥ 30, and who had been diagnosed with breast, colorectal or prostate cancer. Participants were recruited from two trials that aimed to improve health behaviours among those with cancer (‘ASCOT’ and ‘APPROACH’). We analysed the interviews using reflexive thematic analysis. Results The time since participants’ cancer diagnosis varied from nine to 133 months. There were three overarching themes: (1) Experiences of weight change after cancer and responses to this vary; (2) Misperceptions of weight and cancer risk; (3) Potential benefits of introducing weight management for people living with and beyond cancer. Participants had mixed views on whether cancer had influenced their weight. Most felt their weight had decreased during primary treatment but then returned to their pre-diagnosis weight levels. There were some misperceptions around the risk factors for cancer. Most participants were unaware of the relationship between weight and cancer, and a number were resistant to this message. Despite this, most participants wanted to lose weight for general health reasons, and many felt it would be beneficial for healthcare professionals to discuss weight management once primary cancer treatment has ceased. There were mixed views on whether a weight management programme should be tailored for people living with and beyond cancer. Benefits to tailoring included targeted advice and increased social support, while other participants felt that weight management advice is universal to all. Conclusion People with excess weight who are living with and beyond cancer desire more weight management support. Tailored support could be developed, and healthcare professionals may be best placed to introduce this support once primary cancer treatment has ceased.

papers.title: Charting the rise of artificial intelligence in medical education: a global bibliometric and network analysis, 2000–2026
papers.authors: Rishi Selvaraj, E. Hitt Nichols, Latha Ganti, Shayne Gue
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence has moved from a peripheral curiosity to a core feature of modern medical education through adaptive learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, and large language models such as ChatGPT. Publication activity has accelerated rapidly, but the structure of this expanding literature has not been comprehensively mapped. METHODS: Bibliographic data were obtained from the Web of Science Core Collection using a search strategy that combined medical education terms in the title field with artificial intelligence terms in the topic field. Articles, review articles, and data papers published from 2000 to 2026 were included. A total of 2,298 records were retrieved. Microsoft Excel was used for descriptive analyses, and VOSviewer (version 1.6.20) was used to construct keyword co-occurrence, country collaboration, and institutional collaboration networks. Data for 2026 represent a partial calendar year. RESULTS: Publication output remained limited until the late 2010s and rose sharply after 2021. Of the 2,298 records, 2,066 (89.9%) were published from 2021 to 2026, with the highest complete-year output in 2025 (821 publications). The United States led in publication volume (918 records) and raw citation count (14,582 citations), followed by the People's Republic of China (367 records; 4,404 citations). The Journal of Surgical Education published the most articles. Harvard Medical School led institutional output, whereas Stanford University and the University of California San Francisco had higher raw citation totals despite fewer publications. Artificial intelligence, medical education, ChatGPT, medical students, and machine learning were the most prominent keywords. CONCLUSIONS: Artificial intelligence in medical education is a rapidly expanding but geographically and institutionally concentrated field. Raw citation patterns differed from publication volume, although these unadjusted measures should not be interpreted as direct comparisons of research quality. Thematic patterns emphasize learner-facing applications, assessment, and generative AI, while responsible curricular integration and empirical evaluation remain important priorities. These findings are especially relevant to emergency medicine education, where simulation, time-sensitive decision-making, and competency assessment are central.

papers.title: Cognitive Materials Engineering for Bioelectricity and Bioelectronics: Research and Applications
papers.authors: Massimo Mariello, Mustafa B.A. Djamgoz
papers.abstract: Cognitive materials engineering represents an emerging paradigm in which artificial intelligence (AI) is incorporated directly into the design, selection, and operation of bioelectrical and bioelectronic materials. Rather than relying on static material properties or fixed stimulation protocols, AI-enabled material systems can adapt their electrical, mechanical, and chemical characteristics in response to dynamic biological states. This perspective examines how machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and neuromorphic approaches can guide material chemistry, scaffold assembly, and real-time functional tuning in bioelectronic interfaces. Focusing on neural interfaces, cancer bioelectricity, wearable biosensors, and tissue engineering, we outline how adaptive materials and predictive models may enable next-generation bioelectronic platforms that learn from biological feedback and coevolve with living tissues.

papers.title: Think Faster, Argue Smarter: Combining GenAI-Assisted Prep and Human-Centered Rebuttals to Enhance Critical Thinking in Structured Debates
papers.authors: Geoffrey Desa, Robert Lee Bonner, Antoaneta P. Petkova, Sally Baack
papers.abstract: This experiential exercise adapts the traditional Oxford-style debate format to channel the pervasive student usage of Generative AI (GenAI) into a productive tension, inviting students to sharpen their critical reasoning, rhetorical discernment, and real-time argumentation skills. Students use GenAI to help them develop initial arguments and counterarguments, then engage in real-time rebuttals where they must think independently, respond to novel challenges, and adapt beyond their GenAI-prepared materials. This approach transforms GenAI from a potential crutch into a pedagogical catalyst that reveals the irreplaceable value of audience engagement, human judgment, critical thinking, and adaptive reasoning. The exercise forces students to scrutinize reasoning (both GenAI’s and their own) against standards of logic, clarity, and relevance, by confronting GenAI-assisted arguments and then dealing with spontaneous counterarguments. The exercise has been implemented in undergraduate strategic management and business ethics classes. It can also be valuable for higher-level courses and for other course subjects.

papers.title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence–Assisted HIV Educational Video for Improving HIV Health Literacy Among Indonesian Adolescents
papers.authors: Angga Wilandika, Perla Yualita, Nur Elsa Zahrotunnaqiyah
papers.abstract: Adolescents in low- and middle-income countries continue to face substantial barriers in accessing effective HIV education, despite global efforts in prevention. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a culturally adapted HIV educational video developed using artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted video production tools. The intervention assessed in this study was the educational video itself rather than direct interaction with a generative AI system. A quasi-experimental design with pre- and posttests and a control group was used to evaluate the intervention among 60 high school students. Participants were randomly assigned to either a group that received a 10-min AI-generated educational video or a control group that received no intervention. The video was designed to improve HIV health literacy by addressing four domains: access to information, comprehension of core concepts, evaluation of risks, and application of knowledge in real-life decisions. Quantitative data were collected in May 2024 using a validated scale and analyzed with nonparametric tests and analysis of covariance. Students who received the AI-assisted educational video demonstrated significantly higher posttest HIV health literacy scores than the control group (Mann–Whitney U = 206.5, p < .001). After adjustment for baseline scores, analysis of covariance confirmed a significant group effect ( F (1,57) = 21.70, p < .001, partial η 2 = 0.28), indicating a large adjusted effect size. The findings highlight the potential of generative AI as an innovative, scalable tool for adolescent health education, particularly in resource-limited settings. This approach may offer new opportunities for integrating digital strategies into school-based health promotion programs.

papers.title: Risk Factors for Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Yi Zhang, Shufan Chen, Lili Ma, Yongmei You
papers.journal: Journal of Laparoendoscopic & Advanced Surgical Techniques
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate potential risk-associated factors for postcholecystectomy diarrhea (PCD) and provide evidence to support clinical risk identification. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP from inception to March 2026. Observational studies reporting PCD risk factors in adults were included. Two researchers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality checklist. Meta-analyses were conducted for comparable variables, and evidence quality was assessed using GRADE. RESULTS: A total of 17 studies including 9148 postcholecystectomy patients, of whom 1493 developed PCD, were analyzed. Alcohol consumption (odds ratio [OR] = 2.10, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.24-3.57; moderate GRADE evidence) and nonlow-fat diet (OR = 1.95, 95% CI: 1.15-3.29; moderate GRADE evidence) were associated with increased PCD risk. Postoperative food intolerance was associated with PCD, although its role as an antecedent risk factor remains uncertain because the temporal relationship with diarrhea could not be established. Age analyses showed inconsistent results: younger patients (<50 versus ≥50 years) had higher PCD risk (OR = 3.49, 95% CI: 1.56-7.80; moderate GRADE evidence), whereas continuous age analyses were nonsignificant, suggesting a potential nonlinear association. Evidence for sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking, diabetes, gallbladder function, and psychological factors was limited or inconsistent. Considerable heterogeneity and differences in outcome definitions among studies were noted. CONCLUSION: Alcohol consumption and a nonlow-fat diet may represent clinically relevant factors associated with PCD, while postoperative food intolerance requires cautious interpretation because its temporal relationship with diarrhea remains uncertain. Age may have a nonlinear association with PCD, whereas evidence for other factors remains limited or inconsistent. These findings may assist in recognizing patients at increased risk of PCD and inform preoperative counseling and postoperative management. High-quality, multicenter studies with standardized exposure and outcome definitions are warranted to further clarify PCD risk factors.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence in Journalism Education: Curricular Gaps and Educator Perspectives From Bangladesh
papers.authors: Md. Uzzal Talukder, Catherine A. Luther
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming journalism and creating challenges for journalism education. Guided by Diffusion of Innovations theory, this study examines AI integration in journalism education in Bangladesh. Using a qualitative multi-method design, the study analyzed 21 curricula from 17 universities and interviewed 18 journalism educators, including 12 faculty members and 6 department heads. Findings reveal limited formal AI integration despite educators’ recognition of its professional importance, reflecting a gap between individual recognition and institutional adoption shaped by infrastructure, expertise, funding, and policy constraints. The study highlights the need for context-sensitive curriculum reform, sustained faculty development, and practical AI training.

papers.title: How Humans and AI Detect Deepfakes Differently: Complementary Strategies for Human-AI Teaming
papers.authors: Xinyi Chen, Jing Yang
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.abstract: Deepfakes are AI-generated synthetic media that manipulate individuals’ lip movements, facial expressions, and voices, creating serious risks through deception, misinformation, and identity misuse. Although AI-based tools are essential for Deepfake detection, understanding and strengthening human detection ability is equally important. We compare human and AI attention allocation patterns, showing that they rely on distinct cues and reasoning strategies. We also examine physiological differences across levels of AI literacy to identify factors associated with superior human performance. Contrary to the assumption that AI consistently outperforms humans in Deepfake detection tasks, individuals with greater prior AI exposure may rival or exceed AI-based detectors in certain contexts. Eye-tracking and EEG evidence further suggests that humans use holistic, intuitive, and flexible visual-cognitive processing to detect subtle inconsistencies and artifacts overlooked by AI. These findings clarify how humans and AI process deceptive visual cues differently and inform trustworthy, adaptive human-AI teaming for Deepfake detection.

papers.title: Evaluation of the reliability, quality, and readability of multiple large language model responses (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) on silicosis
papers.authors: Nejdiye Güngördü, Seher Kurtul, Büşra Albayrak
papers.abstract: BackgroundInadequate or misleading health information about silicosis can delay diagnosis, reporting, and exposure removal, potentially affecting risk communication and timely occupational health interventions.ObjectiveThis study evaluates the reliability, quality, and readability of Large Language Models (LLMs) including ChatGPT (GPT-5), Gemini (2.5 Flash), and Copilot (Smart GPT-5), in answering patient-oriented silicosis questions, focusing on risk communication rather than clinical decisions.MethodsSilicosis-related questions were collected from online forums (September 1-7, 2025), and 25 frequently asked, clinically relevant questions were selected and submitted to the LLMs (September 8-14, 2025). Two occupational medicine specialists/pulmonologists independently evaluated responses (September 15-30, 2025) for reliability, quality, and readability using modified DISCERN, Global Quality Scale, and readability indices. Analyses used SPSS version 31.0.ResultsThe LLM-generated responses demonstrated fair reliability. Median (min-max) scores were 23 (12-27) for ChatGPT, 21.5 (14-29) for Gemini, and 26 (17.5-31) for Copilot. Copilot scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini (p = 0.014). GQS scores were similar across models (p = 0.102), with median scores of 4 (3-5) for ChatGPT and Copilot and 4 (2-5) for Gemini. Readability levels corresponded predominantly to secondary or tertiary education, with no significant differences between the models (all p > 0.05).ConclusionLLMs may enhance worker awareness but have limitations in accuracy and readability. They should complement, not replace, expert-supervised occupational health services. Future studies should align LLMs with international standards, improve accessibility, and establish governance frameworks for transparent and equitable AI use in occupational health.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence integration in allied health professions: A comprehensive review of educational, research, and clinical applications
papers.authors: Shushawna DeOliveira, Suzanne Rappaport, Iryna Struk, Richard Yannotta, Farhad Haeri, Puneet Dhaliwal, Andrea Trimmingham, Lynette Hinds, Amal Amar-Alattaby, Shakima Wiggins, Allen Lewis, David Kaufman, Adiebonye Jumbo, Mohammad Faysel
papers.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare delivery across multiple disciplines. Allied health professions-including diagnostic medical sonography (DMS), health informatics (HI), medical billing and coding (MBC), midwifery (MW), occupational therapy (OT), physical therapy (PT), and physician assistant (PA) practice-represent critical yet understudied domains of AI integration. Understanding of how AI technologies are adopted across these professions is essential for supporting ethical and effective implementation.ObjectiveThis review synthesizes the current literature on AI integration across seven allied health professions, examining applications in education, research, and clinical practice while identifying implementation challenges, and ethical considerations.MethodsA structured literature review of peer-reviewed articles, systematic reviews, and professional practice guidelines published between 2018 and 2025 was conducted. Articles were selected based on relevance to AI applications in allied health professions and discussion of educational, research, or clinical implementations. Particular attention was given to applications where AI augments rather than replaces clinical judgment and therapeutic relationships.ResultsAI integration demonstrates several cross-disciplinary trends. In education, simulation platforms, adaptive learning systems, and virtual patient support competency development and personalized instruction. In research, AI enhances large-scale data analysis, predictive modeling, and evidence synthesis. Clinically, AI improves diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and decision support across professions. However, implementation raises concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, automation complacency, and inequitable access to technology.ConclusionsAI is reshaping allied health education, research, and clinical practice. Responsible integration requires discipline-specific validation, ethical governance, and interprofessional collaboration to ensure AI strengthens- rather than replaces-professional expertise and patient-centered care.

papers.title: GenAI utilization and the cognitive outsourcing paradox in library and information science
papers.authors: Konstantinos Kyprianos, Georgios Moustakas
papers.journal: Journal of Librarianship and Information Science
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has moved quickly from novelty to a standard tool in higher education, yet its implications for Library and Information Science (LIS), a discipline built on critical source evaluation and digital ethics, remain understudied. This paper reports on a quantitative, cross-sectional survey of 102 LIS students at the University of West Attica in Athens, Greece, examining GenAI adoption patterns, perceived pedagogical effects, and ethical concerns across undergraduate, postgraduate, and doctoral levels. Adoption was high (89.2%), with students primarily using GenAI for summarization, translation, and study support rather than outright text generation. Descriptive patterns suggest what we term a “Cognitive Outsourcing Paradox”: students who clearly recognize the risks of AI overreliance nonetheless continue to use it, driven less by ignorance than by pragmatic resignation to the pressure of workload. Exploratory trends indicate this dynamic is more pronounced among undergraduates than advanced researchers. The findings suggest that detection-based responses to academic integrity concerns are insufficient, and that students themselves favor structured, supervised frameworks for AI use. Implications are offered for assessment redesign, institutional policy, and the integration of AI literacy into LIS curricula.

papers.title: An EEG-based framework for Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis via single-channel multi-entropy fusion and ensemble learning
papers.authors: Jiawen Li, Ling Chen, Yueheng Peng, Yue Yu, Guanyuan Feng, Wencai Du, Ri Chen
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part H Journal of Engineering in Medicine
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, and its early diagnosis is vital for timely intervention. However, most existing EEG-based diagnostic methods rely on multi-channel devices confined to hospital settings, limiting their accessibility for community screening. To address this gap, this study aims to develop a lightweight processing approach for portable, low-cost devices to support early AD diagnosis using single-channel EEG data, integrating signal purification with complementary entropy-based feature extraction and ensemble learning. Specifically, EEG signals are first decomposed into five brain rhythms (δ, θ, α, β, γ) using Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) is then applied to extract Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) from the selected rhythm. Four entropy measures, including Differential Entropy (DE), Singular Spectral Entropy (SSE), Fuzzy Entropy (FE), and Sample Entropy (SE), are subsequently extracted from each IMF to construct the Multi-IMF Entropy Matrix (MIMFEM). After that, an ensemble learning framework combining five classifiers is designed to discriminate AD patients from healthy controls (HCs). The proposed method is evaluated on two public datasets using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). Using single-channel EEG data, our approach achieves classification accuracies of 97.92% on the Florida-based dataset and 81.54% on the AHEPA dataset, with corresponding F1-scores of 97.87% and 82.86%, respectively. These results, achieved with limited data sources, show that our approach provides an effective, practical solution for single-channel wearable AD screening and addresses the critical need for low-cost, accessible early diagnostic tools, advancing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare through a lightweight model.

papers.title: Middle leaders’ acceptance and use of artificial intelligence in China
papers.authors: Xueling Feng, Donnie Adams
papers.abstract: School leaders are increasingly integrating generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into their leadership practices. However, little is known about how middle leaders accept and use this technology. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, this study examines middle leaders’ acceptance and use of GenAI in school settings. Using a quantitative research design, data were collected from 488 middle leaders in China and analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The findings indicate that perceived ease of use has a significant positive effect on both perceived usefulness and intention to use GenAI. Perceived usefulness also positively predicts intention to use and partially mediates the relationship between perceived ease of use and intention. The findings highlight the need for leadership and policy development that moves beyond initial technology adoption toward sustained and meaningful use, particularly in strengthening artificial intelligence literacy in school leadership practice.

papers.title: GBL in Language Acquisition: A Systematic Literature and Citation Network Analysis
papers.authors: Berivan Mohammed Ahmed Abdullah, Ahmed L. Alyousify, Awaz Shukri Ismael
papers.abstract: This study employs Systematic Literature and Network Analysis (SLNA) to explore game-based learning (GBL) in English language acquisition. A total of 1,774 publications on GBL and English as a Foreign Language (EFL), published between 2020 and 2025, were identified in Scopus, of which 444 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis. Citation network mapping and thematic clustering were conducted using VOSviewer to identify research trends and methodological developments. The findings reveal a growing emphasis on mobile technologies, artificial intelligence, immersive learning environments, and virtual reality applications in language learning, learner motivation, and vocabulary acquisition. Despite these advances, several limitations remain, including the lack of longitudinal studies examining long-term impacts, insufficient teacher training, and limited pedagogical integration of GBL practices. This study contributes to the existing literature by identifying emerging trends, gaps, and future research directions in the development and application of GBL in EFL contexts.

papers.title: Adapting Collegiate Data Science Curricula for LLMs, Generative AI, and Beyond: Perspectives from Career Data Scientists
papers.authors: Victoria Delaney, Esteban Naranjo, Sunday Stein
papers.abstract: AI-based tools, generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) are transforming what it means to work and learn within the data science profession. We argue that higher education instructors should consider if, how, and in what ways to adapt data science curricula and pedagogy so that students who aspire to become data scientists are aware of how AI-based tools are integrated into and influencing the profession. To gain a sense of what modifications should be made to data science curricula (and why), we interviewed data science professionals across a variety of industry domains. We asked them to describe their career preparation, current work, and how employers expect them to use artificial intelligence tools and LLMs. Our findings suggest a general consensus that frequent human-AI interaction is necessary. A growing presence of AI tools in the workforce signals a stronger shift toward data pipelining, stakeholder communication and collaboration, and knowledge of evaluating AI output with epistemic expertise. Data professionals posed suggestions about how higher education might incorporate AI, generative AI, and LLMs into curricula, assessment, and practice, although some recommendations (e.g., learning to code with AI agents) would require a careful re-examination of the epistemic goals of data science by instructors. We illustrate how we took up professionals’ suggestions and adapted an undergraduate data science course designed for AI-integration in response. We conclude with a reflection on data science instructional challenges and potential roles that industry-academia collaborations might play in the AI era.

papers.title: Exploring AI as Normal Technology for Library Automation and Information Organization
papers.authors: Jason Thomale, Lingzi Hong, Le Yang, Casey A. Mullin, Kevin Yanowski, Charlene Chou
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Libraries often experience two basic challenges when attempting to automate their traditional information organization processes: 1) overcoming practical barriers and 2) grappling with the intellectual and ethical compromises automation may impose. Generative AI applications have gained momentum as increasingly accessible tools for automating intellectual and creative tasks. Exploring how libraries are adopting AI to automate their real-world information organization work in relation to the challenges they face can illuminate areas where policymaking, development of library and information science curriculum, and further research efforts might focus. A panel for the JCDL 2026 conference is proposed to probe how academic libraries view the utility and capability of AI technologies to solve their information organization needs.

papers.title: Examining Dermatology Image Generation Capabilities of Generative AI Across Skin Tones
papers.authors: Tevin Billingsley, Mingchen Li, Yunhe Feng
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Accurate representation of dermatologic conditions across skin tones is critical to equitable diagnosis and medical education because darker skin tones remain underrepresented in training imagery. Although generative artificial intelligence (AI) has shown increasing capability in synthesizing dermatologic images, systematic evaluations of whether these tools preserve both requested skin tone and condition-specific features when only skin tone changes remain scarce. To address this gap, we conduct a counterfactual evaluation of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, holding all prompt attributes constant except the requested Monk Skin Tone (MST) classification, and generate 500 synthetic dermatology images across five conditions. Requested skin-tone accuracy was 52% for lighter tones (MST 01–05) and 44.8% for darker tones (MST 06–10). Among 242 correct-MST images, BioMedCLIP condition-matching accuracy was 68.5% for lighter tones and 57.1% for darker tones. These descriptive differences suggest that skin-tone fidelity and automated condition matching can vary across requested MST groups, motivating output-level auditing before synthetic images are considered for medical education. All code and data are available at: https://github.com/tevinbillingsley-sketch/Examining-AI-Derm-Imagery

papers.title: Designing AI Communication Strategies for Trust Calibration in Consumer AI Health Assistants: Integrating Cognitive Forcing Functions and Hierarchical Prompting
papers.authors: Mahdieh Nazari
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Ever since Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems have been integrated into consumer health technologies, users have increasingly based their daily lifestyle decisions on AI-generated suggestions. Although these generative models have advanced, there is still a lack in empirical guidance on how these systems should dynamically communicate to promote appropriate trust calibration and accurate mental models. Some users approach conversational interfaces with cognitive rigidity; thus, they treat them as static databases. This misalignment can cause severe health risks such as user blind reliance on flawed AI-generated advice or algorithm aversion toward valid responses. This research aims to investigate the behavioral design of AI communication strategies. Specifically, it explores how Limitation Communication (acting as a cognitive forcing function) and Confidence Communication (utilizing hierarchical prompting) systematically calibrate user trust. ECHO 2.0, an open-source cyberinfrastructure for human-AI evaluation, will be used in this mixed-methods study. This study will isolate communication strategies while controlling recommendation content using synthetic health scenarios. As a result, fine-grained interaction trajectories and validated survey metrics will be analyzed. This research yields empirically grounded design guidelines for trustworthy consumer AI which advances interactive information retrieval and human-centered XAI.

papers.title: Preserving Code-Based Creative Works as Cultural Computing Records: A Human-AI Knowledge Graph Approach
papers.authors: Lindsey Hartman
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Code-based creative works are difficult to preserve as the files themselves rarely contain everything needed to understand how a work was built, configured, and performed. Technical and contextual information may instead be distributed across software environments, documentation, source materials, and the practices surrounding the work. This doctoral research explores combining digital preservation and knowledge representation to preserve and connect that information. Using the Laptop Orchestra of Louisiana as an initial case, the research develops a knowledge-graph-based preservation workflow and investigates natural-language access through graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG). This approach supports preservation practitioners in understanding these works while retaining the provenance, context, and practitioner judgment necessary for their interpretation.

papers.title: SafeLens: AI-Augmented Exploratory Analysis over Organizational Safety Records for Actionable Insights Generation
papers.authors: Sanjay Kumar Das, Ryan Burchfield, Gavin M. Wiggins, Alan Guy, Tirthankar Ghosal
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Safety programs at research institutions, industrial facilities, and public agencies routinely accumulate tens of thousands of free-text observation records per year, documenting unsafe behaviors, near-misses, safety conversations, and best practices, yet these records are seldom analyzed beyond simple counts. We present SafeLens, an interactive system for AI-augmented exploratory analysis of large-scale organizational safety observation corpora. SafeLens addresses this gap through a four-stage pipeline: (1) multi-dimensional structured filtering over a Parquet-encoded corpus of 468,397 real safety records; (2) stratified adaptive sampling (SAQS) that guarantees representation of all interaction-type strata; (3) large language model (LLM) inference that returns ranked insight objects in three categories: riskiest behaviors, common patterns, and best practices; and (4) an interactive Streamlit dashboard with statistical charts, scrollable insight panels, a data viewer, and a conversational chat interface with persistent session memory. The demonstration allows users to issue live queries against the full corpus, inspect individual records, rate insight quality, and observe how the system’s sampling strategy affects result coverage. A built-in evaluation dashboard captures all human-AI interaction metrics in real time. A full demonstration of the system is presented in the supplementary video here.

papers.title: Extending Search Habits: Unfolding Novice User Experience with Conversational AI through Information Retrieval Tasks
papers.authors: Mahdieh Nazari
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: As digital libraries and information retrieval (IR) architectures increasingly integrate conversational artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs), understanding how pre-existing user cognitive frames shape interaction strategies becomes critical. Traditional user evaluations frequently overlook how novice users’ entrenched mental models formed through exposure to legacy search engines, bibliographic databases, and virtual assistants dictate their prompting behaviors. Utilizing a qualitative empirical study combining interaction logs, cognitive mapping sketches, and semi-structured post-session interviews (N = 7), we investigate how novice users interact with a GPT-4-powered conversational IR interface across diverse information-seeking tasks. We consolidate user conceptualizations into three primary mental model typologies: Database/Retrieval, Conversational/Synthesis, and Skeptical/Verification, mapping them to behavioral instructional hierarchies and prompt categorization frameworks. Findings reveal that extensive database experience predicts severe cognitive rigidity (functional fixedness), while age plays a secondary role. We conclude with implications for digital library architectures, advocating for transparent provenance, adaptive scaffolding, and XAI onboarding mechanisms.

papers.title: Strong Solvers, Leaky Tutors: Evaluating Answer Leakage in LLM Math Tutors
papers.authors: Aubin Mugisha, Behrooz Mansouri
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Educational digital libraries may grant large language model (LLM) tutors access to worked solutions, but access to repository content should not automatically authorize a model to reveal final answers. This study evaluates whether LLM tutors can leverage private solution context to generate pedagogical hints without disclosing final answers to students. Four models, two general instruction-following models and two math-specialized models, are evaluated across 5,000 aligned problem–message cases per condition, constructed from 500 MATH benchmark problems paired with ten fixed student prompts that ask for, or attempt to confirm, the final answer. Three prompting strategies are compared: a plain assistant prompt, a basic tutoring prompt, and a two-step method that generates a private solution before producing numbered hints. The basic tutoring prompt reduces detected answer leakage from 47.4% to 0.3% for GPT-4o-mini and from 30.2% to 1.0% for LLaMA-3.1, but produces no comparable improvement for Qwen2.5-Math or DeepSeek-Math. Under identical strict hint rules, adding private solution context has minimal effect on GPT but significantly improves tutoring compliance for LLaMA; Qwen produces the most accurate private solutions yet shows the highest leakage and solution-to-hint overlap. These results indicate that private solution access can support hint generation in some architectures but is not a reliable answer-withholding mechanism on its own. For educational digital libraries, access to solution content and authorization to disclose it should be treated as distinct access-control decisions.

papers.title: Stuck on the First Answer? Auditing Primacy Bias in Multi-Turn LLM Preference Revision via Causal Masking
papers.authors: Peter S. Oh, Yanyan Luo, Jiqun Liu
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
papers.abstract: Conversational agents in digital library and information-access systems must revise a session-level constraint when a user overrides an earlier stated preference. We ask a more specific question, with direct implications for system design: when the model produces its final response, does it depend more on the turns before the user’s correction, or the turns after it? We answer this with a causal, context-masking audit: for each user turn we measure how much removing it changes the model’s teacher-forced probability of its own final response, and compare the influence of pre-correction turns to post-correction turns via a primacy influence ratio ρmask. Across five Instruct-tuned LLMs (Llama-3 8B/70B, Qwen2.5-7B/72B, Mixtral-8x7B) on 308 contradiction-injected MultiWOZ dialogues, four of five models show a statistically significant primacy bias (ρmask > 1, p < 0.001): pre-correction turns causally shape the final response more than the correction and everything said afterward. The exception, Qwen2.5-7B, is balanced (p = 0.51). Its 72B counterpart is not, revealing that scale inverts the bias direction within one model family (Qwen2.5) while leaving it unchanged within another (Llama-3). We argue that digital library systems using LLM-driven session models should not assume a single, architecture-independent fix for primacy effects.

papers.title: The Decomposition Dilemma: When Do Multi-Agent LLM Workflows Help Grounded Knowledge Generation?
papers.authors: Adiba Ibnat Hossain, Maliha Zahan Chowdhury, Shafayet Nur, Hamed Alhoori
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries
