Experiments on the BCI Competition IV dataset 2a (four-class) and 2b (binary-class) show that STGCAN-MI achieves average best classification accuracies of 83.17% and 87.50%, respectively, outperforming several representative baseline models. Ablation studies and visualization analysis validate the effectiveness of each core component. This research provides a new approach for developing high-performance decoding methods for motor imagery EEG.

papers.title: An interpretable machine-learning signature predicts early triple-negative breast cancer recurrence but adds no prognostic value beyond clinicopathological factors in external validation
papers.authors: Haocheng Nan, Rong Di, Xiaorong Kou, Gang Ma
papers.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype that lacks targeted therapies and carries a high risk of early distant metastasis, yet interpretable tools for predicting early recurrence remain scarce. We develop an end-to-end, leakage-safe machine-learning framework that predicts 3-year distant recurrence from the gene-expression profiles of 101 TNBC patients in GSE58812, and evaluate it in an independent, clinically annotated cohort—the triple-negative subset of METABRIC ( \(n=320\) ). Supervised feature selection is embedded within every fold of repeated stratified cross-validation, so that seven classifiers are compared on honest out-of-fold predictions; an \(\ell _2\) -regularised logistic regression on a fifty-gene panel attained a mean per-fold cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.689 (standard deviation 0.137) and a repeat-averaged out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.738 (95% CI 0.626–0.837), with good calibration (Brier score 0.171). The two are not interchangeable: 0.689 estimates the discrimination of one fitted model and is the primary, more conservative figure, whereas 0.738 describes the repeat-averaged ensemble and is the value to which the calibration, decision-curve and internal survival analyses correspond. Both retain the optimism of having chosen the reported learner as the best of seven on the same resampling: nested selection of the learner gives 0.648. The panel size was fixed a priori; nested tuning did not improve honest discrimination (0.648), and performance was flat for panels of 30–100 genes. Coefficients and SHAP attributions agreed almost perfectly, which for a standardised linear model holds by construction and is reported as an internal consistency check; a model-agnostic explainer applied to three non-linear learners gave much weaker cross-model agreement (Spearman \(\rho \) 0.54–0.94, median 0.62). Functional annotation showed natural-killer-cell-mediated cytotoxicity and antigen presentation, with proliferation up (E2F targets, NES \(+2.23\) ) and interferon- \(\gamma \) response down (NES \(-2.77\) ) in early-recurring tumours. Because GSE58812 records no clinicopathological variable beyond age, METABRIC was used to test the signature against, and on top of, the routine factors that govern treatment decisions. A clinicopathological Cox model discriminated relapse-free survival well (concordance index 0.673), driven chiefly by nodal burden, whereas only 20 of the 50 genes are quantified on the Illumina array, so what could be scored externally is the cross-platform-transferable component. It carried only a weak univariable signal (hazard ratio 1.23 per standard deviation; 3-year AUC 0.55) and did not improve discrimination over clinicopathological factors (combined concordance index 0.652; likelihood-ratio \(p=0.13\) ). Re-deriving the panel within the gene universe common to both platforms yielded a fully scoreable signature that separated relapse-free survival externally (hazard ratio 1.30 per standard deviation, \(p=0.004\) ) but still added nothing ( \(p=0.09\) ), and ComBat changed the external AUC by less than 0.01 while a within-METABRIC refit reached only 0.56–0.57. The endpoint mismatch does not account for this: the signature performs no better against a metastasis-dominated cause-specific endpoint, and even if three first relapses in ten were local the corrected concordance index would rise only to 0.58. A transcriptomic signature can therefore be developed and interpreted reliably, but clinicopathological variables remain the dominant determinants of recurrence risk. The signature is best regarded as a hypothesis-generating molecular adjunct rather than a clinically ready tool.

papers.title: Mapping the Molecular Universe
papers.authors: Dan Hannah, Yumin Zhang, Stanley Whittingham, Martin Winter, Ying Shirley Meng, Qichao Hu, Kang Xu
papers.abstract: Abstract The success of large-language-models highlighted the importance of datasets, whose quantity, quality, and diversity dictate the accuracy and creativity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in learning and inferring. However, in scientific domains, such datasets required for domain-specific AI/machine-learning (ML) models do not exist most of the time. In this perspective, by examining the logics and rationales behind the construction and mapping of a universe for small organic molecules (108–1012), we explore what new capabilities AI can bring to the materials discoveries. We identify the elusive structure–property relationship as a core challenge for new materials design and explore the possibility AI tools could enable us to design based on targeted properties instead of the structural derivation. In a broader context, we further discuss what challenges and limitations AI-driven material sciences still face and envision possible avenues into the future of AI4Materials.

papers.title: Stepping into the Machine Chemist: An AI Vision-Driven Titration Robot for Learning by Creating
papers.authors: Hao Zhang, Shanyong Dong, Meng Li, Yawen Tang, Yizhou Ling, Gengtao Fu
papers.abstract: Abstract In the era of deep integration between artificial intelligence and scientific research, the machine chemist has emerged as a new paradigm for chemical experimental research. Grounded in the philosophy of learning by creating, we have designed an AI vision-driven titration robot (hereinafter referred to as AI-TitroBot) that students can build autonomously. Serving as an entry-level machine chemist, AI-TitroBot is capable of fully automated titration operations. It precisely identifies the titration end point through AI vision, automatically controls the peristaltic pump to cease titrant addition, and calculates both the consumed titrant volume and the concentration of the analyte solution based on calibrated flow rate and titration duration. Experimental results demonstrate that the device exhibits good repeatability. While the accuracy of the redox titration is relatively high, the acid–base titration still shows a systematic negative deviation of approximately 5%. The AI-TitroBot effectively strengthens students’ understanding of chemical principles while integrating interdisciplinary knowledge and skills from artificial intelligence, electronics, programming, and engineering design, thus exploring a feasible pathway for innovation in intelligent chemistry education.

papers.title: Public acceptance of autonomous flying cars in urban air mobility: The mediating role of trust
papers.authors: Ying Yang, M. Xu, Jiahao Zhan, Zhe Zhang, Yang Liu, Xiaobo Qu
papers.abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous flying cars relies heavily on artificial intelligence, making public trust in AI a prerequisite for willingness to fly. However, how AI-related attributes shape this trust and adoption willingness remains underexplored. Based on the integrative model of trust, this study investigates how negative AI attitudes and AI literacy shape public willingness to adopt autonomous flying cars, with trust playing a key mediating role and AI self-efficacy acting as a moderator. Based on survey data collected from 420 respondents, mediation analysis demonstrates that trust plays a predominant mediating role in the relationship between AI attitudes and willingness to fly. AI literacy is examined along various dimensions, such as technical understanding and critical appraisal, which yield divergent effects on trust. While technical understanding is positively associated with trust, critical appraisal shows no significant effect. This suggests that in early-stage adoption, trust is driven more by prior knowledge than by cognitive evaluation. Moreover, an Artificial Neural Network coupled with explainable machine learning is further employed for nonlinear insights, revealing significant nonlinear relationships between these factors and willingness to fly, particularly the opposing effects of critical appraisal. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for UAM policymaking and sustainable urban mobility.

papers.title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
papers.authors: Kjetil Rustenberg, Bjørn Erik Munkvold, Kristine Steen‐Tveit, Jaziar Radianti, Terje Gjøsæter
papers.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

papers.title: Beyond curricular inclusion: An indigenous knowledge sovereignty framework for South African technology teacher education in the AI era
papers.authors: Benjamin Seleke
papers.abstract: Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) are increasingly visible in curriculum policy, yet visibility can coexist with weak community authority over how knowledge is selected, interpreted, digitised and assessed. This conceptual article develops and theoretically grounds RELATE as a community-accountable framework for evaluating and designing Indigenous knowledge engagement in South African Technology teacher education. A bounded critical integrative conceptual synthesis connected 21 substantive sources across four domains: IKS in science, STEM and Technology Education; epistemic justice and decoloniality; culturally sustaining and Indigenous methodologies; and Indigenous data and artificial-intelligence governance. Sources were purposively selected for conceptual relevance, South African specificity where available, traceability and evidentiary contribution; policy, legal, empirical and conceptual claims were coded separately. The synthesis identifies four recurring deficits: representation without epistemic parity; contextualisation without community authority; digitisation without governance; and innovation without ecological or distributive accountability. RELATE responds through six interdependent dimensions: Recognition, Ethical reciprocity, Local authority, Apprenticeship and agency, Technological translation, and Ecological responsibility. The framework treats these dimensions as a non-linear governance architecture rather than causal stages. It extends adjacent approaches by integrating curriculum, pedagogy, community decision rights, technological mediation and ecological accountability within one Technology-teacher-education framework. RELATE is a theoretically derived proposal, not a validated intervention or measurement instrument. Its contribution is to make authority, permission, benefit, restriction and contestation assessable features of programme design and future empirical inquiry.

papers.title: A spatio-temporal attention convolutional network with topology-preserving channel embedding and transformer for EEG decoding
papers.authors: Wenqi Sun, Shuo Fu, Jinhua Zhang, Aibin Zhu, Jing Wang, Shuai Yin, Gang Liu

papers.title: Enhancing large language model-based systems for end-to-end circuit analysis problem solving
papers.authors: Liang‐Liang Chen, Weiyu Sun, Huiru Xie, Yongnuo Cai, Ying Zhang
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in data-rich domains such as programming, yet their reliability in engineering tasks remains limited. Circuit analysis, requiring multimodal understanding and precise mathematical reasoning, highlights these challenges. Although Gemini 2.5 Pro has improved capabilities in diagram interpretation and analog-circuit reasoning, it still struggles to consistently solve problems containing both textual descriptions and circuit diagrams. This paper presents an enhanced end-to-end circuit problem-solving framework using Gemini 2.5 Pro as the backbone model for scalable engineering-education applications. We systematically evaluate Gemini 2.5 Pro on undergraduate circuit-analysis problems and characterize two key failure modes: 1) circuit-recognition hallucinations, particularly incorrect source polarity detection, and 2) reasoning-process hallucinations, such as incorrect current direction assumptions. To address recognition errors, we integrate a fine-tuned YOLO detector and OpenCV-based processing to isolate voltage and current sources for polarity re-identification. To mitigate reasoning errors, we introduce an ngspice -driven verification loop that triggers iterative solution refinement with optional human-in-the-loop feedback. On 83 problems, the proposed pipeline achieves 97.59% accuracy versus Gemini’s 79.52% baseline. On four hand-drawn diagram variations, accuracy improves from 60.61%—71.21% to 89.39%—92.42% with statistically significant gains ( p < 0.005 ). An additional evaluation on 43 problems from a different textbook improves accuracy from 58.14% to 83.72%, providing further evidence of cross-textbook generalizability. Error analysis indicates that circuit recognition remains the dominant source of remaining failures, particularly for different diagram representations. These results demonstrate the robustness, scalability, generalizability, and practical applicability of the proposed framework for engineering education and real-world circuit analysis.

papers.title: Value co-creation under hierarchical constraints: Enterprise-led rural tourism development
papers.authors: Fan Zhou, Ben Wu, Chen-Wei Tao
papers.journal: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Management
papers.abstract: This study explores how cultural and tourism enterprises enable emerging forms of value co-creation in rural tourism development, drawing on a community-based rural revitalization project in eastern China. Using value co-creation as the primary analytical lens and a multistakeholder governance perspective to examine participation structures and power relations, this study adopts a qualitative approach grounded in 17 semi-structured interviews with representatives from four stakeholder groups. The findings reveal that stakeholder engagement in this project operates within an enterprise-led and hierarchically structured governance arrangement, where participation is role-differentiated and strategically bounded. The enterprise functions as the central coordinator, integrating different resources, connecting stakeholders, and enabling operational participation while retaining control over key decisions. Value co-creation therefore develops unevenly across levels, with consultation, feedback, and operational co-planning coexisting with centralized strategic decision-making. Conflict management follows a similarly differentiated pattern: high-salience disputes are resolved through centralized authority, whereas lower-salience tensions are addressed through consultation and incremental adjustment. The study contributes to tourism research by showing how value co-creation can unfold under asymmetric authority within a transitional hybrid governance structure and offers practical insights for destination managers and policymakers seeking to support incremental and context-sensitive rural development initiatives.

papers.title: Emotion regulation in euthymic bipolar I disorder: an exploratory multimethod pilot study using self-report, ERPs, and facial EMG
papers.authors: Kornelia Gentsch, Philipp Kanske, Michèle Wessa
papers.abstract: Background Emotion regulation (ER) disturbances and heightened emotional reactivity may persist during euthymia in bipolar I disorder (BD-I). This exploratory multimethod study examined two ER strategies—distraction and distancing-based reappraisal—in euthymic BD-I without psychiatric comorbidity and matched healthy controls, using self-report, ERPs (P300, LPP), and facial EMG (corrugator, zygomaticus). Methods Participants (n BD-I = 22; n HC = 22) viewed positive, negative, and neutral IAPS images and were instructed to view, use distancing-based reappraisal, or distract via mental calculations. Emotion ratings were collected after each trial. Event-related potentials (ERPs) and facial electromyography (EMG) were recorded concurrently. Trait ER was assessed using the Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (CERQ) and the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ). Results During passive viewing, BD-I patients rated neutral images more positively, whereas ERP and EMG responses were similar to HC. During ER, both strategies reduced self-reported affect in both groups; BD-I reported higher positive affect overall and more negative affect during regulation. For LPP, regulation did not differ between groups for negative affect, but for positive affect HC showed attenuation during distraction and reappraisal whereas BD-I did not. For EMG, regulation did not differ between groups. BD-I reported more rumination, catastrophizing, and less positive reappraisal than HC. Limitations Small sample size and post-experimental-only arousal assessment limit interpretation and generalizability. Conclusions Findings provide preliminary evidence for response-system-specific differences in ER in euthymic BD-I, most clearly in reduced LPP modulation during positive affect regulation. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to establish their robustness and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Attenuated attention engagement and sensorimotor resonance to social events in first-episode adolescent depression: Evidence from EEG oscillations
papers.authors: Enze Tang, Shiyi Zhang, Weijie Qin, Yiyang Xu, Jiewei Zheng, Xuanqiang Chen, Ruihan Wu, Haoyang Zhao, Yao Fu, Ciyun Zhao, Wenbo Song, Jian Li, Chengying Liu, Yueyao Liu, Jun Yin, Manli Huang, Hui Chen

papers.title: Sharing blame with me: How AI anthropomorphism encourages individual unethical behavior
papers.authors: Xianzheng Fei, Yinghao Yu, Yaoyue Li
papers.abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents.

papers.title: Club research: A review and research agenda
papers.authors: SoJung Lee, Na-Young Choi
papers.abstract: Private clubs constitute a distinctive hospitality context defined by membership-based governance, shared authority, and long-term relational exchange, yet existing scholarship remains theoretically fragmented. This study systematically reviews 67 SSCI-indexed journal articles published through 2025 to examine the thematic evolution, theoretical foundations, and methodological patterns of club research. Using multi-layered bibliometric and content-based analyses, the review shows that research has expanded from managerial competency and member satisfaction toward innovation, governance, and digital engagement, but remains divided between consumer-experience and organization-centric management perspectives. This fragmentation under-theorizes clubs as hybrid governance-service institutions, especially at the member–management interface where authority, legitimacy, accountability, and value co-creation intersect. Methodological reliance on cross-sectional quantitative designs, U.S.-centric samples, and single-stakeholder perspectives further constrains cumulative theory building. Grounded in an institutional governance lens, the review advances a hybrid governance perspective and proposes future research on member–management dynamics, multi-role members, and access-sensitive, multi-stakeholder methods suited to private club settings.

papers.title: The impact mechanism of AI streamer characteristics on consumer purchase intention
papers.authors: Zhongya Han, Dengsheng Yu, Lei Yan, Zhongya Han
papers.abstract: AI streamers are increasingly being deployed as service agents in livestream shopping. Although prior research has examined various AI streamer characteristics, existing explanations have tended to focus on social, relational, or affective evaluations and have not systematically explained how different characteristics are associated with purchase intention through a technology-oriented evaluation or why these relationships vary across consumers. Using the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) framework as its overarching structure, this study draws on the cue logic of anthropomorphism theory to select four consumer-perceivable characteristics and organizes them into two categories: attractiveness and vitality as form-related characteristics, and professionalism and responsiveness as behavior-related characteristics. Drawing further on innovation diffusion theory, consumer innovativeness is specified as a boundary condition. Survey data from 405 Chinese consumers with experience of AI streamer-led livestream shopping were used to examine these relationships, together with the mediating role of perceived novelty and the moderating role of consumer innovativeness. The results showed that all four characteristics were positively associated with purchase intention both directly and indirectly through perceived novelty. Consumer innovativeness strengthened the direct relationships of vitality and responsiveness with purchase intention and the indirect relationships of attractiveness, vitality, and responsiveness with purchase intention through perceived novelty, but did not significantly moderate relationships involving professionalism. These findings highlight perceived novelty as a technology-oriented evaluative mechanism linking AI streamer characteristics to purchase intention and reveal the characteristic- and pathway-dependent boundary role of consumer innovativeness, offering practical implications for differentiated AI streamer design and consumer targeting.

papers.title: Does artificial intelligence improve social stability risk performance in China?
papers.authors: Jinrui Zhang, Ruilian Zhang, Chen Yin
papers.abstract: This paper examines whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to improving the social stability risk level in China. Against the backdrop of rapid digital transformation and increasingly complex governance challenges, AI has been widely adopted in areas such as public security, social management, and risk monitoring. However, its actual effectiveness in mitigating social stability risks remains underexplored. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions in China, this study constructs an empirical framework to evaluate the impact of AI policy on social stability risk levels. The analysis integrates indicators of technological capacity, governance performance, and socio-economic conditions, and applies quantitative methods to identify both direct and indirect effects. The findings suggest that AI policy significantly reduces social stability risks by promoting digital economy development, increasing wage levels and investment in education. At the same time, the results reveal notable regional heterogeneity. The AI policy significantly reduces social stability risk in the central and western regions, and areas with moderate digital economy development, but has no statistically significant effect in economically developed and digitally advanced areas. The study also highlights potential challenges, including data governance concerns and uneven technological access, which may offset some of AI's benefits. This research contributes to the literature by linking technological innovation with social governance outcomes and provides policy implications for leveraging AI to promote social stability. It suggests that policymakers should not only invest in AI infrastructure but also address institutional and regional disparities to ensure inclusive and effective risk management.

papers.title: Optimal sound-color matching scheme of five-element music and lighting colors for emotional responses in patients with GAD: A randomized, two-factor mixed-design trial
papers.authors: Jing Gao, Mengni Zhang, Huan Chen, Xiaohui Dong, Fei Wang, Chaoming Hou
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sound-color matching offers a novel approach to enhance music therapy, but the optimal combinations for emotional dysregulation in generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) remain untested. OBJECTIVE: To identify the optimal sound-color matching scheme for emotional responses in GAD patients using Five-Element music and different lighting colors. METHODS: A randomized two-factor mixed-design trial was conducted between June 2024 and February 2025 at Grade-A tertiary hospitals. Lighting color (cyan, red, yellow, white, black) was the between-subjects variable, and musical emotional valence (positive, neutral, negative) was the within-subjects variable. 210 eligible GAD patients were randomly assigned to five lighting color groups. The audiovisual stimulation combined calibrated LED lighting and validated Five-Element music segments in a standardized laboratory environment. Primary outcomes were subjective valence and arousal scores (Self-Assessment Manikin). Secondary outcomes included skin conductance (SC), skin temperature (ST), heart rate (HR), and electroencephalography (EEG) power spectral density (PSD). RESULTS: All 210 patients were included in the subjective data analysis, with 205 providing valid physiological data and 204 yielding EEG data. Significant interactions between lighting color and music valence were observed for valence scores (F=2.02, p < 0.050), arousal scores (F=2.77, p < 0.050), ST (F=51.18, p < 0.050), and HR (F=39.77, p < 0.050). Cyan lighting with positive music produced the highest valence scores (7.79 ± 0.81) and optimal physiological regulation (lowest HR: -15.44 ± 1.89 beats per minute (bpm); highest ST: 0.84 ± 0.09°C). Red lighting with positive music induced the highest arousal (6.83 ± 1.23). EEG analysis revealed a significant interaction only in the theta band (F=1.98, P = 0.024), with positive music showing lower PSD across all bands. CONCLUSION: Among the tested pairings, positive Five-Element music with cyan lighting elicited the most favorable immediate emotional and physiological responses in patients with GAD, supporting further investigation of sound‑color matching as a multimodal adjunctive strategy for emotional regulation. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This clinical trial was registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (clinical trial number: ChiCTR2400079878).

papers.title: Verifier-guided knowledge distillation of large language models for auditable thermal comfort reasoning
papers.authors: Moein Younesi Heravi, Inbae Jeong, Youjin Jang, Hyosoo Moon
papers.abstract: Occupant-centric building operation requires models that can not only predict thermal sensation, but also justify predictions through auditable reasoning. Traditional mechanistic models, such as Fanger’s predicted mean vote (PMV), often show limited field accuracy, whereas advanced machine learning models can improve prediction but typically remain opaque to facility managers and building operators. This study proposes a verifier-guided knowledge distillation framework for auditable thermal comfort reasoning using a lightweight LLaMA-3.2-3B student model. The framework consists of three sequential stages: (1) knowledge distillation from a teacher model, GPT-4o, to transfer domain-specific explanatory patterns; (2) supervised fine-tuning with ground-truth anchoring and a TSV-weighted loss to improve thermal sensation vote (TSV) prediction while limiting teacher-error propagation; and (3) verifier-guided direct preference optimization using an automated claim-consistency verifier. The verifier extracts factor-direction claims from generated explanations, such as high air temperature or low air speed, and checks them against comfort-centered percentile thresholds derived from the ASHRAE Global Thermal Comfort Database II. On the held-out test split, the final model achieved 42.7 % exact TSV accuracy and 79.9 % ±1 accuracy, comparable to standard tabular baselines on the same split. More importantly, the verifier-guided alignment stage reduced the any-incorrect-claim rate from 52.3 % to 16.5 % and improved linked claim accuracy to 78.3 %. Robustness tests showed reasonable directional consistency under perturbation without strong dependence on PMV or SET proxies. At the hot and cold tails, 81 % of explanations named an HVAC-controllable factor, so compact language models can pair thermal comfort predictions with verifiable, operator-actionable explanations for building operation.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence use for academic writing in English among Kuwaiti nursing and health sciences students in a mixed methods study
papers.authors: Abdullah M. Alazemi
papers.abstract: Abstract Research on generative AI use in EMI nursing and health sciences contexts in the Gulf region remains limited. This study investigated the uses, experiences, and perceptions of generative AI among nursing and health science students at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET) in Kuwait. Using a single-institution convergent mixed methods survey design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected from 241 undergraduate students. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. The findings showed that 94.6% of participants reported previous use of generative AI tools and 83.4% reported using them for academic purposes at least occasionally. Four interrelated themes emerged: (1) AI as a facilitator of English academic writing; (2) AI as a cognitive and academic efficiency tool; (3) AI as a confidence-building resource; and (4) students’ awareness of opportunities and risks associated with AI use. Students primarily used AI to improve grammar, vocabulary, idea generation, and writing organization. Participants also reported greater perceived confidence and reduced writing anxiety. Furthermore, participants expressed awareness of concerns regarding overreliance, inaccurate information, and academic integrity. The study contributes to emerging research on AI in higher education by highlighting students’ reported use and perceptions of AI in EMI health science contexts in Kuwait. The findings suggest the need for AI literacy frameworks that promote responsible and ethical use of AI in academic writing.

papers.title: Effects of AI-assisted speaking practice on spoken English performance in higher vocational education
papers.authors: Yang Zhang, Ying Zhou
papers.abstract: Abstract With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-assisted tools are increasingly integrated into language education. However, empirical evidence on their effectiveness for spoken English in higher vocational colleges remains limited. This quasi-experimental study examined whether AI-assisted speaking practice using iFLYTEK Spark, a generative AI platform with speech recognition and real-time feedback capabilities, was associated with higher post-intervention spoken English performance among 92 first-year vocational college students in China. Two intact classes were assigned to an experimental group ( n = 46) receiving 12 weeks of AI-assisted practice plus conventional instruction and a control group ( n = 46) receiving conventional instruction only. Post-intervention speaking performance was assessed by three trained raters using an analytic rubric covering pronunciation, language use, fluency and coherence, and interaction. The experimental group achieved significantly higher overall posttest scores (M = 3.69, SD = 0.76) than the control group (M = 3.19, SD = 0.82; t(90) = 3.011, p = 0.003, Hedges’ g = 0.63). Medium-to-large effect sizes were found in language use (g = 0.49), fluency and coherence (g = 0.50), and interaction (g = 0.75), whereas the difference in pronunciation was smaller and non-significant (g = 0.38, p = 0.071). Semi-structured interviews with one teacher and three students provided supplementary insights into perceived benefits, including increased practice opportunities, reduced speaking anxiety, and enhanced motivation. While the intact-class design and coarse baseline proficiency measure limit causal claims, the findings suggest that AI-assisted tools can serve as a valuable supplement to conventional spoken English instruction in higher vocational settings. Implications for pedagogy and future research directions are discussed.

papers.title: A scoping review of trust in firsthand and secondhand communication involving humans and artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Kohei Yamamoto, Tomohiro Tanikawa, Hideaki Kuzuoka
papers.abstract: Conversational and generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly create and pass information between people. This can make it hard to see who created a claim, whether it was changed, and whom to trust. Many studies examine firsthand human-human and human-AI communication, but less is known about secondhand communication, in which AI or another actor passes on a claim made elsewhere. In these cases, a human decision maker must evaluate the claim and the people or systems that created or passed it on. We present a scoping review built around six minimal motifs that represent firsthand or secondhand communication routes. Humans or AI systems may serve as the source or intermediary, while the decision maker remains human. We screened 3810 records and coded 124 studies to identify 21 trust factors in four dimensions: Decision Maker, Messenger, Message Property, and Environment. Qualitative synthesis also identified four recurring route-level patterns: distorted trust calibration, trust transfer, extremity amplification, and accountability diffusion. These patterns guide future research on AI-mediated communication. Overall, this review provides shared terms and a route-based framework for studying trust in multi-party human-AI communication and designing AI-mediated communication systems.

papers.title: An extended theory of planned behavior model of generative AI use intention for music composition among Chinese music students
papers.authors: Li Pan, Qihuan Chen, Yannan Liu
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly being used in music composition, reshaping how musical ideas are generated, modified, and developed. Music students are an important group because their willingness to incorporate AI into future composition remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, the present study extends the Theory of Planned Behavior by incorporating task-technology fit, AI trust, and AI anxiety to examine Chinese music students’ behavioral intention (BI) to use generative AI (GenAI) for music composition. A total of 892 undergraduate music students with prior hands-on experience using GenAI tools for composition-related tasks were recruited from five provincial-level regions in China, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and artificial neural network (ANN) analysis. PLS-SEM showed that AI trust and attitudes had the strongest positive associations with BI, while AI anxiety was negatively associated with BI, and the model explained 56.2% of its variance. From a predictive perspective, ANN ranked AI trust highest in relative predictive importance for BI, followed by attitudes, task-technology fit, AI anxiety, perceived behavioral control, and subjective norms. Overall, AI trust and attitudes showed comparatively prominent relationships with BI, whereas perceived behavioral control and subjective norms showed more limited roles in this predominantly low-frequency user sample. These findings suggest that educators could support students in developing calibrated judgments of GenAI reliability, evaluating its suitability for specific composition tasks, and addressing AI-related anxiety while preserving authorship and creative agency.

papers.title: Cohort-level growth modeling of ethical engagement with artificial intelligence in education
papers.authors: Musa Adekunle Ayanwale, Christian Basil Omeh, Lindelani E. Mnguni, Folasade Mardiyya Oyeniran
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet limited evidence explains how students’ ethical engagement develops over time. Existing research is largely cross-sectional and often treats ethical awareness, reflection, and responsible use as a unified competence. This study examined cohort-level changes in AI Ethics Awareness (AEAw), Responsible AI Use (RAIU), and AI-Driven Reflection on Decision-Making (AIRD), including relationships among their initial levels and growth rates. Transformative Learning Theory provided a heuristic interpretive lens, while a socio-technical perspective situated ethical engagement within institutional, pedagogical, cultural, and technological conditions. A rotating-cohort longitudinal design involved 350 undergraduate computer science students from two Nigerian public universities across three annual measurement occasions. Confirmatory factor analysis evaluated the theoretically specified measurement structure, while univariate and multivariate latent growth curve models estimated construct-specific trajectories and their interrelationships. Results revealed statistically significant and practically substantial cohort-level increases in AEAw, RAIU, and AIRD. However, relationships among their initial levels and growth factors were predominantly weak and mixed, providing little evidence of a unified developmental sequence or compensatory-growth process. Theoretically, our findings refine Transformative Learning Theory by showing that awareness, reflection, and self-perceived responsible practice may develop asynchronously rather than through a deterministic progression from knowledge to action. Practically, universities should complement ethics-awareness initiatives with explicit AI-use policies, authentic ethical tasks, disclosure requirements, behavioural assessment, and institutionally supported opportunities to translate reflection into responsible practice. These findings represent aggregate cohort trends and do not establish individual development or causal instructional effects.

papers.title: Silk Fibroin-Based Flexible Electronics: A Mesoscopic Pathway Toward Human–Machine Interconnection
papers.authors: Jing Li, Shuyi Gao, Changsheng Wang, Jianbing Xiahou, Xiangyang Liu
papers.abstract: Silk fibroin, a natural textile material spun by silkworms over millennia, is emerging as a transformative platform for integrating human intelligence with artificial intelligence. Its core innovation lies in the meso-functionalization strategy, which precisely programs protein refolding and hierarchical assembly. This strategy groundbreakingly resolves the long-standing performance paradox among biocompatibility, mechanical compliance, and high-fidelity signal acquisition in bioelectronic interfaces, thereby providing a solution that is difficult to achieve with other material systems. This transformation elevates the traditional fiber into a programmable electronic material, capable not only of conformal and seamless skin contact but also of constructing dynamic conductive networks, and even pioneering the fabrication of neuromorphic memristors that emulate synaptic plasticity. Furthermore, silk fibroin systems, reshaped through meso-engineering, are poised to catalyze a novel paradigm for deep integration between biological systems and artificial intelligence. When coupled with AI-driven intelligent analytics and closed-loop feedback control, the system can decode human physiological states in real time into machine-interpretable command signals, while simultaneously delivering adaptive regulatory responses back to the body. This bidirectional interface breaks through the conventional boundaries of human–machine interaction, with application prospects spanning frontier domains such as wearable health monitoring, invasive brain–computer interfaces, and cognitive augmentation technologies. Ultimately, while honoring its heritage as a natural textile, silk fibroin opens a pathway toward deep biointegration that is both sustainable and exceptionally biocompatible. Along this pathway, ancient material wisdom collides with future artificial intelligence to spark synergistic innovation, ultimately empowering human intelligence to reach new heights through human–machine co-evolution.

papers.title: Externalizing Epistemic Governance from Stateless Clinical LLMs: Why It Is Necessary and Why It Must Be Constrained
papers.authors: Stefano Natangelo
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models are increasingly embedded in clinical decision support, but they are stateless. They preserve no epistemic commitments across contexts, identical cases can yield divergent outputs, and fluent generation can acquire de facto authority over what counts as evidence without any matching structure of responsibility. We argue that whether clinical AI can be trusted and held accountable depends on where epistemic authority sits and who governs it, not on how well the model performs or how fluently it generates. From this it follows that epistemic governance has to be externalized from the model. It also has to be constrained, because relocating authority into a second generative layer reproduces the original problem. We make the claim concrete with a non-agentic, constraint-based architecture, instantiated in oncology. Context classification, evidence authority, and truth-state assignment are settled by dedicated, inspectable layers before any generation occurs; the language model is confined to bounded extraction and summarization. The central move is to keep deontic authority, what is permitted and reimbursed, distinct from epistemic authority, what the evidence supports, so that a reimbursement or jurisdictional constraint is represented as an allocation decision rather than collapsed into an apparent clinical fact. Uncertainty, disagreement between authoritative sources, and clinician overrides are preserved as explicit, inspectable states. By settling authority before generation and keeping it inspectable, the architecture restores the structure of responsibility that fluent generation erodes: the exercise of authority becomes attributable, and the resulting recommendation can be contested rather than absorbed as plain clinical fact.

papers.title: Walking the Middle Path
papers.authors: Liam C. Kelly, Anna Istratoaie, Lachlan J. Dowling, Sarah A. Ward
papers.abstract: The arrival of publicly-accessible generative-AI tools, such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, has significantly disrupted standard practice in education, research, and publishing. Academic publishers and journals, in particular, have responded by adopting policies which reflect both how they perceive the problems that generative-AI tools pose, and what kinds of solutions address these issues while remaining consistent with key scholarly values: integrity, transparency, and the primacy of human authorship. This article surveys the current state of generative-AI in academic publishing-including relevant policies at the publisher and journal-level-in anticipation of the JBI's forthcoming policies concerning generative-AI disclosure in manuscript submission and peer-review. Mirroring the emerging policy consensus concerning generative-AI use in academic publishing, this paper proposes that 'AI-disclosure statements' constitute an adaptive 'middle path' between prohibition and unrestricted permissiveness. Beyond this, though, we argue that AI-disclosure statements are valuable for their potential to codify desirable norms governing generative-AI use in publishing, and so to subtly influence the underlying 'academic form of life' for the better. We conclude by discussing one possible outcome of this influence, suggesting that it may represent a solution to problems raised by recent criticism of AI-disclosure statements.

papers.title: Combining multiple and boosting regression analyses to identify factors predicting achievements on mathematics national assessments
papers.authors: Daniel Doz, Bor Bregant
papers.journal: Educational Research for Policy and Practice
papers.abstract: Abstract Numerous factors are related to students’ performance on standardized mathematics tests, including teacher-assigned math grades, gender, socio-economic status (ESCS), origin, geographic location, and school type. Typically, the influence of these factors on students’ outcomes on standardized mathematics tests is analyzed using classical regression analyses, which might not be able to handle complex, high-dimensional datasets and capture non-linear relationships. Boosting regression, a machine learning approach, was employed to overcome these limitations, allowing for more robust estimation of variable importance, detection of interaction effects, and provision of insights that are directly relevant for educational policy and intervention. Therefore, in this paper, we investigate the significance of these factors in predicting students’ achievements on the Italian national assessment of mathematical knowledge, INVALSI, through both multiple regression and boosting regression analyses. Results indicate that school type and teacher-assigned grades emerged as the most influential predictors, contributing approximately 42% and 30% of the relative importance within the predictive model, respectively, followed by macroregion (19%), gender (6%), and ESCS (3%). Students’ origin accounted for less than 1% of relative importance. These values reflect predictive contributions rather than causal effects and should be interpreted as indicators of the strength of association within the model rather than direct proportions of explained variance. This study demonstrates that the combination of multiple regression and boosting regression analyses can offer educators and policymakers clearer insights into the determinants of students’ performance in the national mathematics knowledge assessment.

papers.title: Who Is Using Pornography Generated by Artificial Intelligence? Correlates of AI-Porn Use and Familiarity in an Australian Adult Sample
papers.authors: Joel Anderson, Lily Moor
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are rapidly transforming how people create and experience sexual content, including the emergence of AI-generated pornography (AI-porn). Yet little is known about who is engaging with this evolving medium. This study presents findings from a cross-sectional survey (data collected in 2025) of 367 heterosexual Australian adults (age range = 19-87 years, M = 39.07, SD = 13.43; 52.5% men, 44.8% women [and 2.2% non-binary, excluded from inferential analyses due to small cell sizes]) examining demographic, ideological, and relational correlates of AI-porn familiarity and use. Overall, 26.0% of participants reported having used AI-porn and were moderately familiar with it. Regression analyses showed that men and younger participants were significantly more likely to be familiar with and to have used AI-porn. Ideological factors (religiosity, political orientation) and relational factors (relationship status, relationship and sexual satisfaction) were not associated with use. These findings suggest that engagement with AI-porn is emerging most prominently among digitally curious younger men, yet appears ideologically broad and not linked (in this data set) to relationship dissatisfaction. As AI tools enable new forms of personalized, creative sexual expression, understanding who is exploring these technologies can help researchers and clinicians track evolving norms around intimacy, fantasy, and sexual media in the digital age.

papers.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Fostering Inclusive and Culturally Responsive Education for Multilingual and Multicultural Learners
papers.authors: Salma Gehad Waly
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background of the Study Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the way teaching and learning occur in formal and informal settings. Simultaneously, classrooms across global contexts continue to welcome students from various linguistic and cultural backgrounds due to the shifting global dynamics around us. With a wide range of AI platforms currently utilised worldwide, the question of whether AI is creating inclusive spaces for multilingual and multicultural students remains unanswered. AI tools can support multilingual and multicultural students by personalising learning journeys, enhancing efficiency and access to resources and differentiating instruction. Despite that, AI tools are influenced by social, cultural and institutional factors, and there is growing concern that AI might cause further inequalities among traditionally marginalised students, especially when dominant languages and cultures are privileged and algorithmic bias is embedded. Objectives This study critically examines the extent to which AI supports or undermines equity, diversity and inclusion in multilingual and multicultural educational settings, grounded in culturally responsive pedagogy, translanguaging theory and critical digital pedagogy. Methods Utilising a systematic literature review informed by PRISMA guidelines, the study examines how AI use overlaps with issues of equity, diversity and inclusion in multilingual and multicultural settings. Results Findings identified recurring concerns across literature related to monolingual design bias, cultural misrepresentation in AI‐generated content, algorithmic representational harm and constraints on learner agency and access. These findings informed the development of the IHSAN Framework (Identity, Humanity, Safety, Access and Nuance), presented as a conceptual model in the Discussion. Conclusions The study recommends shared accountability among educators, AI developers, educational institutions and policymakers through culturally responsive AI design, equitable implementation practises and governance structures that protect linguistic diversity and learner access.

papers.title: Aspects of Improving the Risk-Based Internal Audit System in Higher Education Institutions
papers.authors: Ibragimov Inomjon Ilhomovich
papers.journal: American Journal of Economics and Business Management
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the current state of the risk-based internal audit system in higher education institutions and develops scientific and practical proposals aimed at improving its efficiency. In the course of the study, risk factors associated with tuition-contract funds, scholarship payments, business travel expenses, and the accounting of material assets were examined, and mechanisms for mitigating them were proposed. Furthermore, the study substantiates opportunities for enhancing the efficiency of internal audit by strengthening integration between the Billing, HEMIS, and UzASBO information systems and by employing artificial intelligence, data analytics, continuous auditing, and continuous monitoring technologies. As a result of the research, proposals were developed for introducing a risk-based automated analytical module for internal auditors within the UzASBO information system, as well as for implementing a three-tier control mechanism for financial transactions. The practical application of these proposals will contribute to improving the internal control system in higher education institutions, reducing financial risks, and ensuring the effective use of public funds.

papers.title: Corpora & Datasets — Acquisition & Provenance Log
papers.authors: Tristen Pierson
papers.abstract: Acquisition and provenance log for the corpora and datasets the program works from (Phase-107 acquisition audit, 2026-10-05; canonical copy: reports/phase107_acquisition_log.json in glossa-lab). INGESTED (with provenance): - Holdat corpus — 1,670 seals / 7,002 tokens / 390 Mahadevan-numbered signs (public GitHub source recorded in CITATIONS.md A.13). - ICIT (Wells & Fuls, Interactive Corpus of Indus Texts) via the public Lipi export (field-cady MIT mirror) — 5,679 source inscriptions / 19,942 tokens; converted working layer 1,007 inscriptions / 2,238 tokens (Wells to Mahadevan numbering via the canonical registry + M-P crosswalk v2.1). Internal research use; provenance caveat recorded. - CISI Mohenjo-daro subset — 179 inscriptions already in-repo, re-verified against the crosswalk (7/179 fully convertible via crosswalk v2.1). FOUND, NOT OBTAINABLE (blockers recorded, not circumvented): - RMRL Mahadevan concordance (indusscript.in) — online and searchable (2,906 objects) but no bulk export; license is research-use, contact required. - Official ICIT scholar access — request by email; the program's governance bars agent-sent email. - CISI print volumes / CISID — paywalled; no public digital release verified as of 2026-10-05. - Wells sign list — no standalone public digital form. - Dixit et al. 2025 seal-imaging dataset — no public sign-sequence release. - Tamil Nadu graffiti database (Rajan & Sivanantham 2025) — search-only; held as a comparative layer by design, never pooled into the Indus training corpus. SEARCHED, NOT FOUND: a CDLI Indus corpus (CDLI is cuneiform only); OSF/Figshare Indus epigraphy datasets; downloadable Dilmun/Gulf seal corpora; Harappa.com datasets; 2025-conference data releases. UPDATE 2026-10-08 — datasets added in Phases 121/122/124 (statistics and the program's own documents are published in Zenodo v4.3.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23250395; third-party source data is NOT deposited): - Soviet positional dataset (Phase-121): Kondratov 1965 Tables 1-4 and Proto-Indica 1973, extracted from in-copyright research copies held locally (Zide & Zvelebil 1976; Knorozov ed. 1973).
