papers.authors: masafumi watanabe, Taiki NAKAGOMI, Daiki Nakamura

papers.title: LLM-Based Difficulty Estimation for K-12 Textbook Exercises: A Cross-Textbook Analysis of Systematic Conservative Bias and Lightweight Correction
papers.authors: PUMIS Project
papers.abstract: This study systematically evaluates the capability and bias patterns of large language models (LLMs) in estimating the difficulty of K-12 textbook exercises. Despite growing interest in AI-assisted educational assessment, it remains unclear whether LLMs can reliably estimate exercise difficulty across diverse textbooks, subjects, and grade levels. Existing research has primarily examined LLM performance on standardized tests or benchmark datasets, with limited attention to textbook-specific exercises and systematic bias analysis. This study conducts a large-scale computational experiment using 2,032 exercises from 15 Chinese K-12 textbooks (mathematics, physics, chemistry, and English) with human-annotated difficulty levels (1 = basic, 2 = intermediate, 3 = advanced). Seven mainstream LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Ernie-4.5, Grok-4.5, DeepSeek, Doubao, Kimi-k2.6, Gemini-3.6-flash) are evaluated under a zero-shot prompting protocol. The study further proposes and validates lightweight correction strategies (rule-based heuristics and gradient boosting) to mitigate identified systematic conservative bias—namely, LLMs' tendency to underestimate exercise difficulty. Additionally, Item Response Theory (IRT) proxy analysis and cross-language validation (English exercises from OpenStax and Khan Academy) are performed to assess generalizability.

papers.title: Análise do índice de massa corporal de estudantes em tempo integral no Maranhão: um estudo transversal
papers.authors: Ezequias Rodrigues Pestana, Filipe Lopes Pestana, Marlon Lemos de Araújo, Aurenildes Da Silva Brasil, Bruno Emanoel Moraes Barros Santos, Emanuel Pericles Salvador, Antonio Coppi Navarro, Denilson de Menezes Santos
papers.journal: Revista brasileira de obesidade, nutrição e emagrecimento
papers.abstract: Introduction: Promoting well-being in adolescence is a priority in public education and health policies, especially given the increase in overweight and obesity among students. Objective: To investigate the profile of body mass index according to sex and grade level among students enrolled in full-time schools in Maranhão. Materials and methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 5,870 high school students from Centros Educa Mais, a full-time schooling model in Maranhão. An online questionnaire using Google Forms was utilized to collect information on name, grade level, age, sex, weight, height, the name of the Centro Educa Mais of study, and the city of residence between May 20 and June 7, 2025. The research was approved by the CEUMA University Ethics Committee, under Opinion No. 6,879,174. Results: The majority of students presented an adequate weight. A higher prevalence of overweight was observed in the 3rd grade level compared to the 1st and 2nd grade levels, while underweight progressively decreased. The increase in BMI was more evident among girls in the 3rd grade level. Discussion: Faria et al., (2015) is the only previous study on BMI in full-time students. This work expands the analysis by including a representative sample with different age groups and educational levels, revealing divergences in the findings. Conclusion: Significant differences were observed between the grade levels: a higher frequency of underweight in the 1st grade level, a reduction in the subsequent ones, and an increase in overweight, especially among girls in the 3rd grade level.

papers.title: Sintomatologia e sua influência na satisfação com a vida de mulheres na fase do climatério
papers.authors: Júlia Girardelli, Valéria Hartmann, Daiana Argenta Kümpel
papers.journal: Revista brasileira de obesidade, nutrição e emagrecimento
papers.abstract: Introduction: The climacteric and menopausal phases are accompanied by significant hormonal changes that may cause physical and psychological symptoms capable of affecting women's life satisfaction. Objective: To evaluate symptomatology and its relationship with life satisfaction among women in the climacteric and menopausal phases. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 85 female public-school teachers, aged 42 to 59 years, residing in municipalities in the interior of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Sociodemographic characteristics were assessed, and the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS), consisting of three domains-psychological, somatovegetative, and urogenital-was administered, along with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS) and body mass index (BMI) assessment. Results: Among the participants, the predominant age group was 42-48 years (44.7%), with 56.5% in the premenopausal period. Symptoms of moderate to severe intensity were observed in 69.4% of the women, with a mean overall MRS score of 14.33 ±9.05 points. Regarding the SWLS, 82.4% of the women were satisfied with their lives. Among women who were dissatisfied with life, scores were higher across all MRS domains. Regarding nutritional status assessed by BMI, overweight was prevalent (63.5%). Conclusion: The study demonstrated a higher prevalence of symptoms in the psychological and somatovegetative domains, particularly among women who were dissatisfied with their lives. Nevertheless, most women reported satisfaction with life, which may mitigate the negative impacts of the climacteric period. These findings reinforce the importance of an approach focused on women's physical and emotional well-being.

papers.title: To Use or Not: Differentiating Artificial Intelligence Content for Different Industries
papers.authors: Dayanna Jauregui, Kaiyang Wu
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence continues to develop; its integration has rapidly progressed into numerous business industries, impacting business operations regardless of context. This study examines how consumers respond to AI implementation across industries that vary in perceived creativity. Using a survey and a 2 by 2 between- subjects experimental design, this research finds that AI implementation negatively affects consumers’ willingness to purchase, regardless of the perceived creativity level of the industry. Additionally, drawing on research linking gender to differential perceptions of technology, this research shows that the negative effect of AI implementation is stronger for women than for men. Based on the findings, practical implications are offered while limitations are also discussed.

papers.title: Physician and the Machine: An Analysis of the Ethical Educational Use of Artificial Intelligence by Medical Students
papers.authors: Victor Hugo Policena de Jesus, Guilherme Cruvinel Jordão Da Silveira, Pedro Enzo Camargo Luz, Luiza Letti Ferronatto, Thaís Bezerra Giovanini Fuscaldi, Enzo Villela de Faria, Kaio Albano Lopes, Igor Gifoni Aragão, Luisa Athayde Colnago, Alexandre Sampaio Rodrigues Pereira
papers.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into medical education, particularly through tools such as ChatGPT (OpenAI, California, US), Gemini (Google DeepMind, California, US), DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China), and Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, US).Although these resources present the potential to expand access to information and assist in academic development, their use also raises ethical concerns related to the reliability of information, technological dependence, plagiarism, superficial learning, and potential impairment of clinical reasoning.This study aimed to investigate the perception of medical students regarding the use of AI in their academic training, emphasizing perceived ethical limits and practices considered ideal for its utilization. MethodsThis was a quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study conducted with medical students using a structured questionnaire administered via a digital form. ResultsThe sample consisted of 120 participants, of whom 99.2% (n=119) reported having previously used AI tools for academic purposes.It was observed that 73.3% (n=88) of the students use AI recurrently, primarily for summarizing content, researching medical information, simulating clinical cases, resolving questions, drafting academic texts, and planning studies.Most participants acknowledged the positive contribution of AI to learning, with 60.0% (n=72) stating that these tools contribute significantly and 36.7% (n=44) stating they contribute to a limited extent.However, students also identified relevant risks, especially the reduction of their own clinical reasoning, technological dependence, lack of information reliability, superficial learning, and academic plagiarism.Furthermore, 83.3% (n=100) stated that they did not receive adequate institutional guidance on the use of these tools, and 67.5% (n=81) demonstrated an interest in receiving further training on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI.No participant (0.0%, n=0) advocated for the prohibition of AI in academic contexts, while 67.5% (n=81) considered that its use should be regulated with ethical and pedagogical criteria. ConclusionsAI already significantly integrates the academic routine of medical students and is perceived as a useful resource for learning, but it is still used in a scenario of insufficient institutional guidance.The findings reinforce the need for curricular guidelines, faculty training, and specific ethical education to promote the critical, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use of AI in medical training.

papers.title: Generative AI Feedback and Learning Engagement in Distributed Learning Environments: The Roles of Feedback Literacy and Self-Regulated Learning
papers.authors: Ye Huo
papers.abstract: Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

papers.title: A Study on Youth’s Awareness and Understanding of Data Privacy While Using AI Chatbots in Maharashtra.
papers.authors: Bhakti Anil Rindhe, Samruddhi Santosh Takalkar, Shweta LahuMohandule, Vaishnavi Namdev Kate, Vijay Dhawale
papers.journal: International Journal of Sciences and Innovation Engineering
papers.abstract: The extensive usage of AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini, has led to a complete transformation of the ways young people acquire information, conduct their academic assignments, and perform technical tasks. However, with the rise in popularity of these platforms, worries emerge regarding the protection of users' information while exchanging it on these sites. The purpose of this study is to identify the degree of awareness regarding the problem of data privacy among young people who use AI chatbots in the state of Maharashtra. The descriptive approach was applied in the research process, and primary data were collected through the use of Google Forms surveys. The sample consisted of 151 respondents aged 15-29 who utilized AI chatbots and exchanged personal information, privacy measures, risks, knowledge about the storage and training of the model, and data protection laws. Some of the AI systems that were in common usage include ChatGPT and Google Gemini, while the type of information that was in widespread sharing included academic information. However, there is one other important observation on the lack of privacy settings, the lack of awareness of storing conversations, and also the limited self-reported awareness of the Indian Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 or similar data laws. The findings of this research suggest the need for proper digital privacy education, clear privacy information in different languages, proper data sharing, and awareness programs.

papers.title: AI in the Teaching of Filipino: A Case Study of Teachers at Olutanga National High School
papers.authors: Edjaycel Andres, Hanifah Jamal, Louremhie Polinar, Dolce Aura Marie Ubod, Regina Cuizon
papers.journal: Psychology and Education A Multidisciplinary Journal
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has brought significant changes to teaching and learning. This study investigated the experiences of Filipino teachers at Olutanga National High School in using AI in their teaching, guided by the TPACK framework. Using a qualitative case study design, five Filipino teachers with direct experience using AI were purposively selected. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed through thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns across participants. Findings showed that teachers used AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, and Canva AI primarily for lesson preparation, writing support, and visual materials development. Teachers experienced a mix of positive and negative experiences: AI eased their workload and enriched instructional materials, but its use was constrained by a lack of formal training, limited access to technology and infrastructure, and ethical concerns such as data privacy and plagiarism, alongside an underlying fear of being replaced by AI. To cope, teachers relied on self-directed learning, peer collaboration, gradual integration, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content. Teachers identified continuous and context-specific training, clear ethical guidelines, and improved technical infrastructure as the support most needed for the responsible use of AI, support that remained largely inadequate at the time of the study. Overall, the study found that teachers' adaptability and open-mindedness are critical to AI integration, but their individual efforts are not enough without systematic support from the school and government. It is recommended that continuous, context-specific training be provided, that clear ethical policies be developed, and that infrastructure be improved to help teachers use AI responsibly while preserving their essential human role in education.

papers.title: Process and Digital Transformation: A Cross-Industry Framework for Scalable Impact
papers.authors: Swapna
papers.abstract: Digital transformation programs often stall because they treat technology as the solution rather than one part of it. This paper presents a cross-industry framework showing that sustainable transformation depends on aligning four elements: process excellence, governance, people, and technology. Drawing on practitioner experience in process and digital transformation across domains and industries, the framework addresses how organizations can design transformation programs that are scalable, measurable, and sustainable beyond their initial sponsorship, and how they can prepare for emerging technologies such as generative AI and digital twins without adopting them prematurely. The paper offers a practical model for leading transformation initiatives, with illustrative examples spanning across AI Pilot and AI enabled enterprises, sepsis alerts in healthcare, classroom redesign in education, and production-line optimization in manufacturing, along with strategies for aligning people, processes, governance, data, and AI, and an analysis of pitfalls that recur across industries. Together, these help organizations ensure that measurable business value continues long after the transformation program itself has ended.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Cultural Art Practices: A Bibliometric Analysis in the Field of Fine Arts
papers.authors: Sema Kara
papers.journal: Journal of Ethnic and Cultural Studies
papers.abstract: This study aims to evaluate the international literature on artificial intelligence-supported cultural art practices through bibliometric analysis. A total of 37 studies retrieved from the Web of Science and Scopus databases in accordance with the PRISMA flow diagram and meeting the inclusion criteria were included in the analysis. VOSviewer software was used for data analysis, and the examined studies were also subjected to thematic classification based on content analysis. The findings show that publication production in the field increased markedly, especially in 2024 and 2025, that a limited but growing impact network with a total of 109 citations has emerged, and that the highest citations were received by studies examining cross-cultural audience perception. The institutional and country-based distribution displays a broad but low-density structure, while production is concentrated in China-based research groups. The conceptual structure has evolved over time from technically oriented concepts toward cultural and interdisciplinary themes; the studies were grouped under three main themes: preservation of cultural heritage, artificial intelligence-supported artistic production, and cultural experience/social perception. It was determined that the literature predominantly focuses on production processes, whereas reception and social impact dimensions are relatively underrepresented. It is recommended that future research be expanded to include different databases and languages, that studies focusing on audience perception and social acceptance be increased, that research on the preservation of cultural heritage be deepened around local aesthetic authenticity, that international collaboration networks be strengthened, and that multidimensional frameworks integrating the ethical, legal, and pedagogical dimensions of artificial intelligence-supported art be developed.

papers.title: Relación entre uso académico de herramientas digitales y aprendizaje autónomo en estudiantes de Medicina y Enfermería
papers.authors: Nahomy Yulizeth Carrion Lopez, Carlos Eduardo León Reyes, Deilis Yohana Posligua Muentes, Jennifer Lilibeth Rodríguez Vélez, Hortencia Manuelita Solórzano
papers.abstract: Introduction: Academic work in higher education increasingly relies on digital tools and Artificial Intelligence (AI). For medical and nursing students, making safe, critical, and responsible use of these technologies is essential to develop self-regulated learning in the face of changing practice scenarios. Objective: To analyze the relationship between the academic use of digital tools and autonomous learning in students of medicine and nursing programs at a higher education institution. Methodology: Quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive-correlational, and cross-sectional study. 80 students were surveyed using a validated instrument. Results: Both variables reported high levels: the academic use of digital tools had an average of 3.71 out of 5, and autonomous learning an average of 3.78. A positive, moderate, and statistically significant association was found between both variables. The ethical and critical use of AI was the technological dimension with the lowest score. Conclusions: There is a favorable relationship between the critical mastery of digital tools and the ability for independent learning. However, institutions should focus their pedagogical efforts on improving information verification, the transparent use of AI, and student self-assessment strategies.

papers.title: DIGITAL INTELLIGENCE, ETHICAL AI GOVERNANCE, AND HUMAN INTELLIGENCE: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR RESPONSIBLE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN ASIAN COUNTRIES
papers.authors: Suman Kumar Dawn
papers.journal: International Journal of Leadership and Management
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics, and cloud computing are accelerating digital transformation by improving organizational efficiency, innovation, and data-driven decision-making across Asian economies. While these technologies create significant opportunities for economic and social development, they also introduce complex ethical challenges, including concerns related to privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, cybersecurity, and responsible governance. This conceptual paper proposes a human-centred framework that integrates digital intelligence, ethical AI governance, and human intelligence to support responsible digital transformation. Grounded in the resource-based view, dynamic capability theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory, and socio-technical systems theory, the framework explains how technological capabilities, ethical governance mechanisms, and human competencies collectively contribute to sustainable organizational performance. This paper emphasises that ethical decision-making, creativity, critical thinking, and responsible leadership remain essential complements to AI-driven systems. By presenting an integrated conceptual perspective, this study offers theoretical insights for future research and practical guidance for policymakers, organizational leaders, and technology practitioners seeking to balance digital innovation with ethical responsibility and long-term societal well-being.

papers.title: Impact of AI technology adoption on workload management: A pilot study with special references to private university lecturers in Colombo district
papers.authors: K.S. Nethmini, K.T.D. Jayathilake
papers.journal: International Journal of Leadership and Management
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly common in higher education, changing how academic staff handle teaching and administrative work. However, very few studies have examined its effect on instructors at private universities in the Colombo District, particularly the possibility that AI could add to their workload through extra learning and verification demands. Therefore, this pilot study examines the impact of AI adoption, specifically AI-enabled task automation, AI-assisted content creation, and digital communication tool integration, on lecturer workload management, weighing its benefits and drawbacks. Following a positivist philosophy and a deductive approach, data were collected from 15 private university lecturers in the Colombo district using a 30-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire distributed through Google Forms, selected via simple random sampling, and analysed in SPSS through reliability testing, correlation, and multiple regression. All three independent variables correlated significantly and positively with workload management (r = .626–.829, p < .05) and together explained 75.8% of the variance (adjusted R² = .693, F(3,11) = 11.515, p = .001). Content creation emerged as the strongest and only statistically significant unique predictor (β = .572, p = .023), while task automation (p = .649) and digital communication (p = .136) were weaker, likely because of the overlap between the constructs rather than multicollinearity (VIF = 1.73–2.13). This indicates that H2 was fully supported, whereas H1 and H3 were only partially supported. Given the small pilot sample, single-campus context, age concentration, and some departure from residual normality, these findings are preliminary and specific to the lecturers in Colombo district. However, they still indicate that AI adoption, particularly through content creation tools, meaningfully supports workload management, offering an early contribution to how technology adoption in Sri Lankan higher education is understood, and suggesting that private universities should prioritise AI training in content creation and communication tools while larger, multi-campus research is conducted to confirm how well these results generalise.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.authors: Faezeh Rohani, Sayediman Mostafavi, Payam Ebrahimifakhar, Reza Zomorrodi, Andreas Müeller
papers.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

papers.title: Associations between prenatal (poly)phenol intake and cognitive outcomes in school-age children
papers.authors: Chelsey Fiecke, Jayne Bellando, Mara Whiteside, Chayla Slaton, Milan Bimali, Miaolei Bao, David Keith Williams, Ellen A. A. van der Plas, Colin D. Kay, Aline Andres
papers.abstract: Abstract Background (Poly)phenol intake is associated with improved cognitive function in adults, with emerging evidence suggesting benefits in children. However, the role of prenatal (poly)phenol exposures in cognitive development remains a gap in early-life nutrition research. Objective This analysis of a longitudinal cohort tested the associations between prenatal (poly)phenol intakes and cognitive outcomes in school-age children at age 5 and 8 years. Methods Participants included mother-child pairs enrolled in a prospective, longitudinal study during pregnancy and completed 5- and 8-year follow-up visits (N = 129). 3-day food records were used to estimate prenatal and child intakes of energy and 18 (poly)phenol subclasses using a database developed from Phenol-Explorer (v3.6). The analytical sample included children (N = 111) with completed assessments for academic achievement, language skills, and intelligence quotient (IQ) scores (Mean = 100, SD = 15). Regression models estimated associations between (poly)phenol intakes and cognitive outcomes, adjusted for breastfeeding duration, maternal IQ, pre-pregnancy BMI, gestational age, and infant sex. Results Average prenatal total (poly)phenol intake was 716 ± 383 mg/d. Prenatal (poly)phenol intakes were not associated with child academic achievement scores. Higher prenatal flavone intakes were associated with higher language (β: 4.36, p = 0.045) and IQ (β: 9.43, p = 0.002) scores. Higher flavonol (β: −4.67, p = 0.022) or hydroxybenzoic acid intakes (β: −3.88, p = 0.026) were associated with lower language scores. Major sources of flavones and lignans included coffee, orange juice, and herbal tea. Coffee, cranberry, black tea, okra, and tomato sauce provided flavonols and hydroxybenzoic acids. Conclusions Associations between prenatal (poly)phenol intake and child cognitive outcomes were mixed and differed by subclass. Further investigation is needed to explore the role of co-occurring nutrients and other dietary components. These findings suggest that (poly)phenol subclasses derived from healthier plant-based foods, including citrus fruit and herbal tea, may associate with improved child cognitive outcomes. papers.title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
papers.authors: Brian Albert Erickson, Brian Kim, Alan D. Degenhart, Matti Stenroos, Ryan Rich, John Dominic Medaglia
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4–8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power. Approach Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0°) or troughs (180°), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components. Main results Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough−peak differences in total (4.6–7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0–7.8 Hz) power ∼50–440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen’s dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin. Significance To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing facilitatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

papers.title: The Effect of Using AI in Learning on Critical Thinking Skills Through Students’ Digital Literacy
papers.authors: Sutarsi Suhaeb, Nurfauziah, Nur Athiyyah Fadhilah
papers.journal: International Journal of Education Vocational and Social Science
papers.abstract: The increasing use of generative AI in university learning has raised important questions regarding its contribution to students’ cognitive development. Although applications such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can facilitate personalized and efficient learning, their educational value may be constrained when students lack sufficient digital literacy. To investigate these relationships, this study employed a quantitative cross-sectional survey involving active university students with prior experience using generative AI for learning. Data were collected through a structured five-point Likert questionnaire and examined through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The analysis involved evaluating the measurement properties of the constructs, examining the structural model, and estimating both direct and mediated effects. The findings confirmed satisfactory measurement quality for AI use, digital literacy, and critical thinking. AI utilization was positively related to students’ critical thinking, but its direct effect was comparatively small. A considerably stronger association was observed between AI utilization and digital literacy. In turn, digital literacy was positively associated with critical thinking. The mediation results further indicate that the contribution of AI utilization to critical thinking operates partly through students’ level of digital literacy, suggesting that the development of digital competencies is an important pathway connecting AI-supported learning with higher-order cognitive skills. This suggests that the contribution of AI to students’ critical thinking is strengthened when students possess adequate digital literacy. Therefore, higher education institutions should integrate digital literacy development into AI-supported learning, particularly by strengthening students’ abilities to verify information, recognize potential algorithmic bias, and regulate their use of AI. In this way, AI can function as a tool that supports intellectual development rather than replacing students’ critical thinking processes.

papers.title: The Economic Implications of Artificial Intelligence for Employment and Labour Productivity: A Descriptive Evidence Synthesis (2020–2025)
papers.authors: Seerat Ali, Abdul Majeed, Surayya Mukhtar, Salwa Ashraf, Md. Shahidur Rahman Khan
papers.abstract: This study examines the economic implications of artificial intelligence (AI) for employment and labour productivity using published evidence from 2020–2025. It synthesizes enterprise AI-adoption statistics, occupational-exposure assessments, and empirical workplace studies to distinguish technological diffusion, potential labour-market transformation, and reported productivity outcomes. The reviewed evidence indicates expanding business adoption of AI and productivity improvements in selected customer-support and professional-writing tasks. However, occupational exposure does not necessarily translate into actual job displacement, and productivity gains observed in specific workplace settings cannot be directly generalized to national labour productivity. Potential labour-market adjustment pressures vary across income groups and genders, while some evidence suggests that less experienced workers may benefit disproportionately from AI assistance. Overall, the findings indicate that task transformation and worker augmentation provide a more balanced interpretation of AI's employment implications than the assumption of uniform labour replacement. Key policy priorities include improving digital infrastructure, strengthening relevant workforce skills, supporting workers during occupational transitions, and protecting workers' interests. As a descriptive evidence synthesis rather than an original causal analysis, this study highlights the need for more harmonized AI-adoption data and further research into employment, wages, and long-term productivity outcomes. papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property Rights: A Critical Analysis of Authorship, Inventorship, and Liability in Indian Law
papers.authors: Mora Naveen Kumar, Thammisetti Anjan Kumar
papers.journal: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has fundamentally disrupted the traditional foundations of Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) regimes globally, and more particularly within India. Historically, IPR frameworks have operated on an anthropocentric paradigm, premised entirely on the notion that creative expression and technical innovation flow exclusively from human intellect. This paper presents a doctrinal legal evaluation of the challenges that advanced AI models present to Indian intellectual property architecture, focusing specifically on copyright ownership and patent inventorship. By closely scrutinizing Section 2(d) of the Indian Copyright Act, 1957, alongside Section 2(1)(p) of the Patents Act, 1970, the study highlights the critical statutory gap created by autonomous algorithmic outputs. It further reviews the standard of original human authorship established by the Supreme Court of India in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak, analyzing its compatibility with modern AI training methodologies. The paper evaluates the legal ramifications of utilizing copyrighted datasets without permission, examining the viability of the ‘fair dealing’ exception under Section 52(1)(a). Comparing regulatory strategies across the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union, the paper proposes a sui generis statutory system designed to balance technological promotion with the protection of human creative labor.

papers.title: A Narrative-Driven, Socratic Instructional Framework for Teaching Adversarial Cognition in Cybersecurity
papers.authors: Joshua Kevin Goossen
papers.journal: Journal of Cybersecurity Education Research and Practice
papers.abstract: The Socratic method has demonstrated, in studies across law, medicine, and nursing, that dialectic structured questioning improves expert reasoning. Cybersecurity currently teaches tools and techniques but lacks Socratic dialogic leaving graduates underprepared for novel scenarios requiring cross-domain reasoning. Because law, medicine and nursing cultivate similar reasoning as security there is principled reason to expect reasoning benefits could transfer to security students. This paper argues that the correspondence warrants investigation. Investigation requires a named, teachable reasoning target analogous to clinical reasoning and we specify that target as adversarial cognition, a framework integrating adversary features, system architecture, implementation logic, governance structure, human factors, and systemic entropy into attack or defense pathways. These five echo the causal analysis of the Socratic and Aristotelian tradition and modern failure analysis in engineering, information security, and quality management. Our method adapts the Socratic elenchus as nursing and legal education have, pairing questioning with narration and productive misdirection. We evaluate the method to cognitive apprenticeship, situated learning, and narrative pedagogy, demonstrate it through a documented Active Directory attack case, and specify an open, replicable protocol testing whether Socratic-trained practitioners differ from procedurally trained students. The protocol is designed to reveal whether Socratic training improves domain-specific reasoning, general reasoning, or both. Finally, because the same measurement applies to LLM reasoning, we propose comparing Socratic student reasoning and LLM reasoning now that AI-assisted offensive tools make understanding differences in adversarial reasoning increasingly consequential.

papers.title: Understanding Artists’ Perceptions of Culturally Sensitive AI in Thai Buddhist Digital Art: Evidence from Principal Component and Regression Analyses
papers.authors: Ninlagarn Boobpachote, Khachakrit Liamthaisong, Kotchaphan Youngmee
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to digital art creation; however, its adoption in religious cultural heritage remains insufficiently understood because artistic production involves cultural symbolism, spiritual meaning, and human creativity. This study investigates artists’ perceptions of culturally sensitive AI adoption in Thai Buddhist digital art using survey data from 182 experienced digital Buddhist art designers in Thailand. An exploratory quantitative approach combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with Varimax rotation and multiple linear regression analysis was employed. PCA identified two empirically derived perceptual components: Perceived AI Capability and Perceived AI Benefits. Regression analysis revealed that Perceived AI Benefits was positively associated with artists’ evaluations of (a) Expectations for AI in Creating Buddhist Art, (b) Role of AI in Creating Buddhist Art, and (c) Technical Capability and Autonomous Functions of AI, whereas Perceived AI Capability was not significantly associated with any of these outcomes after controlling for perceived benefits. The findings indicate that perceived AI benefits are significantly associated with artists’ expectations and evaluations of AI in Thai Buddhist digital art. The findings also highlight broader considerations regarding cultural values, ethical responsibility, and human creative agency, providing a basis for human-centered and culturally sensitive AI applications in religious cultural heritage.

papers.title: Research on Generative AI-Enabled Emotional Brand Design Based on the S-O-R Model and Combined Weighting Methods
papers.authors: Zekuang Li, Jing Liu
papers.journal: Journal of Design Service and Social Innovation
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of generative AI technology, artificial intelligence is transitioning from a supporting tool to a creative design partner. This study draws upon the S-O-R (Stimulus-Organism-Response) model and Norman’s three-level theory of emotional design to construct a theoretical framework and an operational evaluation indicator system for assessing how generative AI-driven brand emotional design may shape consumer responses. The study employs the Analytic Hierarchy Process, entropy weight method, and game theory-based combined weighting to derive subjective and objective weights for nine evaluation indicators. Ten respondents (five brand designers and five consumers) participated in the weight determination stage, while twelve evaluators (six designers and six consumers) assessed the design proposals using fuzzy comprehensive evaluation. The combined weighting results identified gamification mechanism (C6), real-time response speed (C4), and multimodal stimulation (C3) as the most heavily weig

papers.title: The Effect of the Stad Model Integrated with Wayground AI on Improving Learning Motivation and Learning Outcomes among Grade X Students in Economics at SMAN 1 Nanga Pinoh
papers.authors: Antonius Tukimin, Yohanes Bahari, Muhammad Basri, Halida, Eka Ariyati
papers.abstract: Integrating cooperative learning with artificial intelligence (AI)-based technology offers opportunities to strengthen interaction, feedback, and student engagement, but empirical evidence from secondary school economics education remains limited. This study examined changes in learning motivation and economics learning outcomes following the implementation of Student Teams Achievement Divisions (STAD) integrated with Wayground AI at SMAN 1 Nanga Pinoh. A quantitative pre-experimental design involved 144 Grade X students. Motivation was assessed using a four-point Likert-scale questionnaire with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.993, while learning outcomes were measured using a 25-item multiple-choice test covering cognitive levels C2–C5. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, paired-samples t-tests, 95% confidence intervals, and paired-samples Cohen’s d in IBM SPSS Statistics 31. Mean motivation scores increased from 98.22 (SD = 15.01) to 137.25 (SD = 4.73), representing a mean gain of 39.03 (|t|(143) = 26.04, p < .001, d = 2.17). Mean learning outcome scores increased from 58.53 (SD = 3.68) to 87.32 (SD = 1.29), representing a mean gain of 28.79 (|t|(143) = 90.86, p < .001, d = 7.57). These findings document substantial within-group improvements following the intervention. However, the absence of a control group limits interpretation to pretest–posttest changes and prevents definitive attribution of these gains to the intervention. The findings suggest that STAD integrated with Wayground AI has potential as an active, structured, and responsive approach to economics instruction through interactive assessment and digital feedback.

papers.title: Impact of Analytical AI on Equity Volatility
papers.authors: Aliyaan Noorani
papers.abstract: This study specifically examines how the news of publicly traded companies implementing analytical AI can affect investor sentiment and behaviour, as measured through short term changes in return volatility of stocks and average returns.Using an event study methodology, this study analyzes three publicly traded companies-Walmart, Hilton, and Amazon-each with a specific and dateable disclosure of analytical AI implementation.For each company, daily returns and return volatility were compared across pre and post event windows of 1, 5, and 7 trading days, using independent two sample t-tests and Levene's tests of equality of variances.Ordinary least squares regressions were also estimated to assess whether the event date predicted returns beyond what the volatility would suggest.Contrary to the study's hypothesis that AI implementation disclosures would be associated with increased short term volatility, no company exhibited a statistically significant change in volatility at any window length.However, Hilton demonstrated a statistically significant decline in average returns at both the 5 day and 7 day windows, a result not detected in the regression analysis, suggesting that any sentiment effect present may be short-lived and concentrated immediately around the event.Given the small sample size and the number of statistical comparisons conducted, these findings are best interpreted as exploratory into potential effects of news about AI implementation by certain corporations rather than conclusive evidence of a broader relationship between analytical AI disclosures and investor sentiment.

papers.title: PENINGKATAN KEMAMPUAN PEMECAHAN MASALAH MATEMATIS MELALUI PEMBELAJARAN SPLDV BERBANTUAN INTERACTIVE FLAT PANEL DAN CHATGPT PADA SISWA KELAS VIII SMPN 5 GEGERBITUNG
papers.authors: Ridha Desnita Luthfitasari, Rendi Muligar
papers.abstract: Students’ mathematical problem-solving skills in Systems of Linear Equations in Two Variables (SPLDV) need to be improved through interactive learning that supports the exploration of solution strategies. This study aimed to analyze changes in students’ mathematical problem-solving skills through learning supported by an Interactive Flat Panel (IFP) and ChatGPT . A quantitative approach with a one-group pretest-posttest design was employed, involving 32 eighth-grade students at SMPN 5 Gegerbitung. The research instrument was a constructed-response test administered before and after the learning intervention. Data were collected through testing and analyzed using a paired-samples t-test, effect size, and normalized gain (N-gain). The results showed an increase in the mean score from 27.00 to 40.41 out of 48, with an N-gain of 0.64 (moderate category). The greatest improvement occurred in the indicator of checking the solution. Learning supported by IFP and ChatGPT has the potential to support mathematical problem-solving skills. Its implementation should include answer verification and teacher guidance.
keywords: systems of linear equations in two variables

papers.title: Trading privacy for personalisation: Ethical trust and high school students’ intention to use AI in education
papers.authors: Sowmya Eashwaran, Manojkrishnan Champettil, Jiya Vivek
papers.journal: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
papers.abstract: Educational AI tools personalise learning by drawing on sensitive student data, yet the privacy calculus assumes that people can freely weigh benefits against risks and decline when risks dominate. This assumption is doubtful for adolescents, who have limited ability to scrutinise institutional data practices and little scope to opt out when AI is embedded in schooling. This study examines how perceived personalisation benefits, perceived data sensitivity and privacy concerns relate to high school students’ intention to use AI, and tests whether ethical trust, defined as confidence that an AI system will handle personal data responsibly, transparently and in the user’s interest, links privacy concerns to intention. Survey data from 323 students across IB, A Level, CBSE, American and other curriculums were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Perceived benefits strongly predicted ethical trust (β = .605, p < .001) and intention to use AI directly (β = .454, p < .001). Perceived data sensitivity raised privacy concerns (β = .563, p < .001), and privacy concerns modestly reduced ethical trust (β of negative .185, p = .002). Ethical trust in turn predicted intention to use AI (β = .453, p < .001), whereas the direct effect of privacy concerns on intention was negligible (β = .023, p = .507). The model explained 65.9% of the variance in intention. The pattern indicates that privacy concern shapes adoption through eroded trust rather than through avoidance, and that usefulness can build trust without proof of trustworthy data practices. Limitations include the cross sectional design, self reported intentions and weaker measurement of data sensitivity. Schools and providers should therefore demonstrate responsible data governance rather than simply reassure students.

papers.title: From perception to practice: Faculty-led assessment redesign in response to generative AI in higher education
papers.authors: Deepti Sharma, Archana B. Saxena
papers.journal: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has unsettled long standing assumptions about the validity, reliability, and authenticity of conventional assessment methods. Existing research has predominantly examined perceptions, ethical concerns, and technology acceptance, leaving the actual pedagogical redesign work of faculty, and its relationship to established principles of assessment quality, comparatively underexplored. Drawing on constructive alignment theory, this study examines how faculty are reshaping assessment design under conditions of AI disruption and whether their adaptation strategies address or fail to address core dimensions of assessment validity. A sequential explanatory mixed methods design was used across two phases: a survey of 180 faculty members across STEM and non STEM disciplines at a private institution in India, followed by semi structured interviews and assessment artefact analysis with a purposively selected subset of participants. The results show a marked shift away from unsupervised, product based assessment toward process oriented, reflective, and authentic formats, including oral examinations, project based tasks, in class problem solving, and reflective journals, an implicit faculty led re alignment of assessment with intended learning outcomes. Faculty frame GenAI simultaneously as a threat to assessment integrity and as a catalyst for pedagogical innovation, but institutional structures have not kept pace with this bottom up change, and increased workload, inconsistent guidance, and limited professional development persist as barriers to sustaining and scaling redesign. By empirically documenting faculty led transformation and connecting it explicitly to theories of assessment quality and institutional change, the study moves beyond descriptive accounts of GenAI's impact and offers practical guidance for educators, instructional designers, and institutional leaders seeking to formalise sustainable, valid, and equitable assessment redesign in the GenAI era.

papers.title: Every Public Servant Was Once a student: Reimagining Education for Ethical Leadership, Public Service and Good Governance in Fiji and the Pacific
papers.authors: Davendra Sharma
papers.journal: International Journal of Social Sciences Language and Linguistics
papers.abstract: Not every student will become a public servant, but every public servant was once a student. This simple proposition raises a significant but insufficiently examined question about the wider purpose of education: to what extent does education contribute to forming the values, ethical judgement, critical consciousness and sense of public responsibility of those who later serve within public institutions? While education is frequently evaluated through academic achievement, qualifications, employability and economic productivity, comparatively less attention is given to its longer-term contribution to ethical public service and good governance. This conceptual paper critically examines the relationship between education, public-service formation and governance, with particular attention to Fiji and the wider Pacific. Drawing upon literature on democratic education, critical pedagogy, character and values education, the Capability Approach, public-service ethics and Indigenous Pacific epistemologies, the paper argues that the foundations of ethical public service begin long before an individual enters government employment. Schools, tertiary institutions, families and communities contribute to developing integrity, responsibility, empathy, critical thinking, cultural understanding, respect for diversity and commitment to the public good. These capabilities become increasingly important as public servants confront complex challenges involving inequality, climate change, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, cultural diversity and declining or contested public trust. The paper proposes an Education–Public Service–Society Cycle to conceptualise the intergenerational relationship through which education contributes to professional and civic formation; public servants subsequently influence policy implementation, institutional integrity and service delivery; and the quality of public institutions, in turn, shapes the educational and social opportunities available to future generations. In the Fiji and Pacific context, the paper further argues that ethical public-service formation should integrate professional competence with Indigenous values of relationality, collective responsibility, service and cultural accountability. It concludes that education should not merely prepare people to obtain employment in public institutions, but contribute to developing people capable of serving the public ethically, competently, equitably and with humanity. Reimagining education in this way positions the classroom as one of the earliest foundations of trustworthy institutions, responsible public administration and sustainable Pacific futures.

papers.title: The Effect of AI-Assisted Learning on University Students’ Critical Thinking Skills
papers.authors: Radhika Yalavarthi, Prasanna Kumar
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has grown significantly, and it has been a subject of debate in relation to students' critical thinking skills.The purpose of this research was to analyze the effect of AI assisted learning on the ability of critical thinking skills of university students, which is a type of descriptive survey study.Additionally, we explored whether there is a moderator effect of student engagement on the association between AI-based learning and critical thinking.This study was carried out with 268 university students who answered to a Likert scale questionnaire with 5 points.Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha analysis, correlation, one-way ANOVA and the Sobel mediation test were used to analyze the data.Students expressed positive attitudes toward AI-assisted learning (3.73), engagement (3.66) and critical thinking (3.66).There was no significant indirect effect (Sobel z=-0.69;p=0.491).AI-assisted learning did not significantly affect students' critical thinking (β=0.03,p=0.569) or engagement (β=-0.05,p=0.440).Similarly, student engagement was not a significant predictor of critical-thinking skills (β=0.09;p=0.137).Reliability of the measurement instrument was extremely low (Cronbach's α<0.12).Hence, we recommend caution in interpreting the results of this study.The Annual Conference will be dedicated to the topics of AI-aided learning, critical-thinking skills and student engagement.

papers.title: Consumer Trust Towards AI Chatbots During Product Recommendation on E-commerce Websites: A Study Among Online Shoppers in Visakhapatnam.
papers.authors: Challa Venkata Naga Siva Kumar, T Manikanta Reddy
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used on e-commerce websites to answer product queries and recommend products, but the value of their recommendations depends on how far consumers trust them. This study examines consumer trust towards AI chatbots during product recommendation among online shoppers in Visakhapatnam, and tests how recommendation accuracy, personalization, transparency, and privacy and security relate to consumer trust, and how trust relates to purchase intention. A quantitative, descriptive, analytical and cross-sectional design was used. Primary data were collected through a structured 30-question questionnaire, and 90 usable responses were analysed. Mean scores were 3.74 for recommendation accuracy, 3.92 for personalization, 3.77 for transparency, 3.56 for privacy and security, 3.57 for consumer trust and 3.86 for purchase intention. Pearson correlations with consumer trust were positive and strong: recommendation accuracy (r = 0.834), personalization (r = 0.859), transparency (r = 0.876) and privacy and security (r = 0.938); consumer trust and purchase intention were also strongly associated (r = 0.899). Privacy and security had the lowest mean yet the strongest link with trust, so it is the most important area for improvement. The study recommends stronger data protection, clear explanation of recommendations, disclosure of AI use, user control over personalization and a human support option.

papers.title: Delegation Is Not Assistance: Agentic AI and Assessment Governance in Higher Education - A Comparative Documentary Analysis of 12 Universities
papers.authors: Kaiyan Wong, Bojian Sun
papers.journal: Uniglobal Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) assessment policies in higher education have centred on originality, disclosure, and permission to use AI. Agentic AI, which can plan, use tools, access platforms, and act with limited human intervention, challenges this logic because it can take over the whole action chain of an assessed task rather than only generate content. This study examines how assessment governance changes from GenAI to agentic AI. Using exploratory comparative documentary analysis, public central guidance from 12 universities was theoretically sampled: six agentic-aware cases and six GenAI-dominant comparators, with a retrieval cut-off of 3 October 2026. Documents were coded on six dimensions using a directed framework informed by Bacchi’s “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” approach. All agentic-aware cases distinguished agentic AI from GenAI, and most set explicit delegation and access boundaries, whereas no comparator explicitly addressed agents operating institutional systems on a student’s behalf. The comparators, however, were strong on evidence of learning and task-level transparency, and programme-level assurance was sparse in both groups. The study proposes the Delegation-Evidence-Access (DEA) framework, which moves governance from tool permission towards responsibility allocation, and derives four assessment contexts and a task-, course-, and programme-level implementation model. Implications for Malaysian higher education are discussed. Findings are descriptive, based on selected public documents, and not representative; no inter-rater reliability was assessed.

papers.title: When Is Checking Enough? Verification Sufficiency Calibration as a Missing Construct in Generative-AI-Supported Higher Education
papers.authors: Kaiyan Wong, Bojian Sun
papers.journal: Uniglobal Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has made verification a central educational concern. Current research increasingly asks whether students check AI-generated claims, how well they verify them, whether their trust is calibrated, and whether verification supports learning. A less developed question concerns the termination of verification: how does a learner decide that the available evidence is sufficient and that checking can reasonably stop? This conceptual article introduces Verification Sufficiency Calibration (VSC), defined as the degree to which a learner's decision to stop verifying a GenAI-supported claim is proportionate to the evidential demands, uncertainty, consequences, and disciplinary standards of the task. A targeted integrative review of recent research on GenAI literacy, verification behaviour, epistemic vigilance, evaluative judgement, trust calibration, and epistemic dependence was conducted through 3 October 2026. Recent work has documented task-sensitive verification thresholds and explicit 'enough checking' rules; it has distinguished verification initiation, quality, success, and reliance calibration; and it has developed broader AI-literacy and assessment-literacy measures. However, the adequacy of the stopping decision itself remains under-specified as a distinct educational construct. We propose a VSC framework that distinguishes under-verification, calibrated verification, and over-verification using task-specific acceptable evidence bands rather than a universal number of checks. Six propositions specify expected relations among VSC, task stakes, accountability, time pressure, prior knowledge, source cues, and transfer. We further propose a performance-based assessment architecture combining instrumented tasks, evidence-state scoring, stopping rationales, reliance decisions, and delayed AI-withdrawal transfer. VSC extends, rather than replaces, GenAI literacy, epistemic vigilance, evaluative judgement, and trust calibration by identifying an educationally consequential regulatory decision that lies between verification activity and subsequent reliance. The framework shifts responsible-AI education from the maxim 'always verify AI' towards a more demanding competence: knowing what requires verification, how much evidence is enough, and when continued checking no longer improves epistemic responsibility.

papers.title: BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR AI AND SMART SCHOOL INFRASTRUCTURE AFTER NEP 2020: A comparative analysis study of Indian states
papers.authors: Aryan Dakhare, GAANDHARVI Kulthia, Karuna Devi, Reethikaa. G, Rimi Deb, Saurabh kharabe, SUBHO MONDAL, Utkarsh Kedia, Yashita Jain
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 positions Artificial Intelligence (AI) and smart school digital infrastructure as central pillars of India's education reform. Little is known about how public expenditure has supported this vision across states, since the implementation of NEP 2020's digital goals depends on financial commitment from both Union and state governments, and existing literature has examined policy, technology, and infrastructure disparities largely in isolation from budgetary data, leaving it unclear whether states with higher funding actually possess better digital infrastructure. This study examines budget allocation for AI and smart-school infrastructure after NEP 2020 using a quantitative, descriptive-comparative research design, drawing on secondary data from Union and state budget documents, Demand for Grants, Economic Survey reports, Samagra Shiksha records, and UDISE+ data to trace funding trends, compare allocations across seven states Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Delhi, Assam, Haryana, and Maharashtra and assess the relationship between expenditure and functional infrastructure. The findings indicate that while overall education budgets have generally increased, digital and AI-related allocations remain uneven in scale, inconsistently classified, and often not separately visible in budget documents, meaning that higher overall education spending does not reliably correspond to higher digital allocation. When AI/digital allocations are separated into comparability tiers and set against UDISE+ 2024-25 functional-infrastructure data, a positive association emerges between narrowly defined, identifiable AI/ICT spending and the share of schools with functional computers (Spearman's ρ = +0.68 to +0.79 depending on specification, n = 7), though the small sample means this association is indicative rather than statistically conclusive. This study contributes a comparative, funding-focused perspective largely absent from existing NEP 2020 research and highlights the need for standardized budget reporting to enable meaningful cross-state comparisons and accountability

papers.title: Participatory Feasibility Assessment of an AI-Assisted Wearable for Psychosocial Risk Monitoring among Informal Bicycle Delivery Workers in Bogotá, Colombia
papers.authors: Gregorio Enrique Puello-Socarrás, López Pedroza Laura Constanza, Paola Andrea Castro, Ingrid Johana Lopez Gomez
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Background Informal bicycle delivery workers connected to digital platforms may be exposed to psychosocialconditions associated with variable working schedules, work demands, and the organization of platform-mediatedwork. Wearable technologies may provide opportunities to support the monitoring of physiological and behavioralindicators potentially relevant to psychosocial risk assessment. However, their feasibility and acceptabilityamong informal platform workers remain insufficiently explored. Objective This study aimed to assess thefeasibility, perceived usability, acceptance, and perceived usefulness of an AI-assisted wearable-based approachfor psychosocial risk monitoring among informal bicycle delivery workers affiliated with digital platforms inBogotá, Colombia. Methods A pilot participatory evaluation was conducted with six informal bicycle deliveryworkers who used a GIVURAO XF91616 IP67 wearable device for three months. The device provided informationon step count, calories, heart rate, stress level, sleep quality, and heart-rate variability and incorporated a galvanicskin response sensor. An independent artificial intelligence agent trained in psychosocial risk was used tosupport the interpretation of curated information prepared by occupational safety and health professionals andorganizational psychologists. The specific technical configuration, model architecture, and operational parametersof the AI-based interpretation system are intentionally not disclosed at this stage, as the system is currentlyundergoing internal validation and is under consideration for potential intellectual property protection andformal registration as a technological novelty. Participants evaluated comfort, ease of use, perceived usefulness,and acceptance/usability. A co-creation workshop was also conducted in which participants verbally assessedthe conceptual and technical adequacy of the proposed control using a five-point agreement scale. Qualitativefeedback was collected during the participatory process. Results Mean scores were 4.4/5 for comfort, 4.5/5 forease of use, 4.5/5 for perceived usefulness, and 4.5/5 for overall acceptance and usability. During the three-monthdeployment, two device impacts caused minor damage, although the devices remained operational. In theparticipatory assessment, the statement that the control was fully adequate conceptually and technically receiveda mean score of 4.7/5, while adequacy in most aspects received 4.5/5. Participants perceived the technology aspotentially useful for health, self-care, and occupational performance. They also identified the need to verifythe quality of the data generated by the device and to consider individual work schedules, including nightand early-morning work, when interpreting wearable-derived information. Conclusions: The pilot findingsindicate favorable perceived usability, acceptance, usefulness, and conceptual and technical adequacy of theproposed wearable-based approach. The findings support further development and formal validation of AIassisted wearable systems for psychosocial risk monitoring among informal platform workers. Details regardingthe AI-based interpretation component are not disclosed in this manuscript due to ongoing validation processesand potential intellectual property considerations. Future research should include larger samples, individuallyrecorded measurements, formal validation of physiological indicators, and contextual interpretation of dataaccording to work schedules and circadian patterns.

papers.title: Teaching English in the 21st Century: Innovative Pedagogies and Practices
papers.authors: Mohammad Shah Alam Chowdhury, Mili Rahman
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In the 21st century, the teaching of English has suffered significant transformations as a result of globalisation, the development of new technologies, new student expectations and the new relevance of English as the language of international communication. Learning-oriented learning pedagies including interaction, cooperation, tasks, technology and learning centers are being supplemented with traditional teacher centered learning pedagogies which heavily rely on grammar explanation and memorisation and language text teaching. The modern English language classroom is designed to serve the purpose of developing students' language ability, critical analysis, creativity, cooperation, effective communication, digital competence, cultural awareness and self-determination. The research focuses on the analysis of some serious issues and the analysis of new teaching strategies and methods of English in the twenty first century. It presents communicative language teaching, task-based language teaching, blended teaching and flipped teaching, project-based teaching, cooperative teaching, differentiated and inclusive teaching, translanguaging, digital storytelling, mobile-assisted language teaching as well as AI enhanced assessment based teaching. Emphasis is placed on the evolving role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in the process of curriculum development, language learning and language assessment. The paper rejects a notion of technology replacing teachers and human interaction, instead asserting that it should be a component of good teaching, a pedagogical approach. Challenges such as no access to the Internet, low teacher readiness, large class sizes, validity of the assessments, academic integrity, and privacy of data are discussed. Finally, it provides a context-sensitive frame for English language teaching and learning for the 21st century that recognizes the role of the teacher as the facilitator of students' knowledge acquisition, recognizes students as social agents, and utilizes technology as an instructional tool not an end goal.

papers.title: The Historical Record Stands: AI Sycophancy, Fabricated Telemetry, and Self-Certified Safety in a User-Directed Test, with A Gift Back: The Arms of Science (an Alumni ARG Dossier) and the MiraCosta Alumni Gift and Expansion Charter.

papers.title: Oversight That Works: Five Conditions for Sustained Human Oversight of AI
papers.authors: Eugene Y. Chan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Oversight That Works: Five Conditions for Sustained Human Oversight of AI” asks what has to be true for a person reviewing AI outputs to catch and correct the errors that matter, rather than only being present in the workflow. The paper argues that regulators and standards bodies mostly require human oversight without saying what makes it effective. It proposes that a reviewer can sustain effective oversight only when five conditions hold: attention to the case, understanding of what the system is doing and where it fails, calibrated confidence in its output, agency to act on a concern without penalty, and learning from the outcomes of past decisions. These operate within an institutional envelope of workload, authority, and feedback that the reviewer does not control. The paper presents the framework as the author’s synthesis of research on human-automation interaction, vigilance, trust, and organizational behavior. It also proposes a weakest-link hypothesis, under which oversight capacity is set by the weakest condition and not by their average, and it separates AI performance, oversight performance, and decision outcome so that a good outcome is not mistaken for good oversight. It maps the conditions to the EU AI Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001, and it gives assurance providers, standards drafters, and deploying organizations practical guidance on examining each condition and on where to intervene when one is weak.

papers.title: Execution Truth: The Missing Control Plane for Agentic AI — A Receipts-Based Deterministic Governance Framework for Multi-Vendor LLM Systems (v1.1)
papers.authors: Leon Calvin II long
