papers.title: Semantic Recovery in a Generative–perceptive Domain
papers.authors: Serge Tochilov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Models with different neural architectures can develop corresponding representations from similar observations. To investigate those phenomena in a broad class of neural networks under a unified approach, we introduce a generative domain as a system with differentiated, writable state and boundary coupling, then define its generative–perceptive extension through predictive generation, retained evidence-dependent revision, and causal reuse. Semantic classes are specified by agreement of observable continuation laws. Under coverage, causal-state sufficiency, and vanishing excess predictive risk, a recovery theorem establishes convergence of native predictive laws and, at an attained optimum, identifies their state quotient with the source semantic classes. Additional continuation-consistency conditions preserve source operations and yield cross-model correspondence without requiring shared coordinates. Restricted autoregressive and diffusion learning constructions satisfy the domain conditions; a solvable Gaussian-factor learner demonstrates hidden-subspace acquisition. Experiments tested semantic recovery for a 4-state automaton driven by a continuous symbol stream, through native query predictions and write continuations. At matched exposure the categorical-diffusion model answered all 5,376 audit queries correctly; the prefix transformer reached 94.10%–99.16% accuracy. All runs recovered corresponding state distinctions, while operation fidelity varied and extended interference impaired preservation of unrelated bindings. Internal-state probing and interventions identified causal carriers of history information in both architectures and a context-dependent transformer write pathway. Potential machine-learning applications include semantic-recovery metrics and initialization strategies for faster semantic recovery. We also propose a mechanistic explanation for double learning and grokking.

papers.title: Modular Synthetic Clinical Environment Qualification: Public Comment to FDA Docket FDA-2026-N-7874
papers.authors: Melinda Bernabe Chu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This public comment proposes Modular Synthetic Clinical Environment Qualification (MSCEQ), a framework for independently qualifying reusable synthetic clinical environments before using them to evaluate generative AI-enabled medical devices. Environments would represent specific clinical settings, including changing patient states, multi-day trajectories, and interactions among patients and care teams. Independent clinical review and appropriate validation would assess each environment’s suitability for a defined context of use, while modular infrastructure would support adaptation across conditions and reduce duplicated development effort. Qualified environments could contribute to risk-proportionate evidence packages and support re-testing after device updates. The framework also emphasizes transparent disclosure of synthetic testing, retrospective human-data evaluation, and prospective human-patient evaluation, allowing healthcare institutions to establish their own evidence requirements for adoption. This proposal responds primarily to Questions 10, 13, and 16 of FDA Docket FDA-2026-N-7874, with related discussion of Questions 9, 11, 12, and 26.

papers.title: The Behavioral Premise: Why AI Adoption Failures are Misdiagnosed
papers.authors: Eugene Y. Chan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper asks why so many AI initiatives that stall, or never earn sustained use, are blamed on the wrong causes. It describes a diagnosis reflex: when adoption disappoints, organizations look first to the technology, then to the organization around it, then to governance, and only rarely to the behavior of the people expected to rely on the system. The paper tests those four explanations against the evidence and sets out the Behavioral Premise, a formal statement that adoption outcomes are determined in large part by how people actually decide whether, when, and how much to rely on AI, with theoretical foundations drawn from behavioral science. Because a premise is only useful if it can fail, the paper states falsifiable predictions along with the conditions under which it would be wrong, addresses the strongest objections, and offers notes on how the argument applies in different sectors. It closes by describing what changes in practice when the premise is accepted, illustrated through worked examples.

papers.title: SWORCA™: A Unified Digital and Physical Institution for Technological Invention, Interoperability, Commerce, and the Intelligent Economy
papers.authors: Rashon Rahming
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: SWORCA™ (Seattle Worldwide Organization for Regulated Capital & Automation) is a proposed global technological institution designed to advance the discovery, development, evaluation, interoperability, commercialization, and economically productive utilization of emerging and established technologies. The institutional framework integrates two complementary foundations: SWORCA DIGITAL, a proposed globally accessible technological commerce and innovation platform, and SWORCA SEATTLE, the envisioned permanent physical headquarters and institutional landmark in Seattle, Washington, United States. SWORCA DIGITAL proposes an integrated environment through which eligible consumers, independent inventors, developers, researchers, manufacturers, startups, and established organizations may discover, create, evaluate, acquire, license, exchange, and commercialize technological products, components, systems, services, and capabilities. Its proposed scope encompasses artificial intelligence, autonomous agents, computational systems, semiconductors, computer hardware and software, robotics, cybersecurity, blockchain infrastructure, digital identity, data storage, data centers, and related technological industries. The framework incorporates technological interoperability, collaborative invention, requirements-based discovery, intellectual property and commercial rights management, evidence-based technical evaluation, simulation, advertising, educational participation, and customer loyalty services. These capabilities are organized through complementary functional domains intended to reduce fragmentation, improve technological accessibility, support informed purchasing decisions, and connect independent innovation with qualified commercial demand. The proposed permanent Seattle institution would complement the digital infrastructure through physical technology experiences, professional collaboration, research, education, demonstrations, and institutional activities. This white paper establishes the conceptual foundations, proposed architecture, commercial objectives, governance principles, regulatory boundaries, and phased development strategy of SWORCA. It distinguishes proposed capabilities from implemented technologies and identifies technical validation, intellectual property review, commercial feasibility, and regulatory compliance as prerequisites for operational advancement. SWORCA's central research proposition is that integrating technological discovery, interoperability, verifiable evidence, authorized commerce, and measurable outcomes within a unified institutional framework may improve participation, accountability, and economic efficiency across the evolving technological economy.

papers.title: Artikulation, Bedeutung und Geltung in hybriden Systemen: Zwei konzeptionelle Forschungsaufsätze
papers.authors: Andreas Ehstand
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Two related conceptual research papers by Andreas Ehstand: Articulation Is Not Yet Knowledge, and A Definition Is Not Yet a Mandate. They distinguish changes in expression, meaning and grounds from communicative function, institutional standing and later uptake in human-AI and hybrid systems. Version 0.1 was elaborated on 11 October 2026 with assistance from an AI assistant. Historical internally dated March and April 2026 drafts are research antecedents, not verified earlier publications. This edition reports no empirical study, external peer review, established novelty, standards compliance or performance guarantee. The files contain 24 bilingual working definitions, partly clarifying established expressions, and explicitly constructed civilian counterexamples. This is a conceptual contribution, not a new field glossary. Proprietary procedures, operational instruments, original private materials and business logic are excluded. Existing records are not modified.

papers.title: Innovative Technologies in Korean Language Teaching
papers.authors: Ataniyazova Muxabbat Muratbay qizi, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.journal: International Journal of Literature and Language Studies
papers.abstract: In the modern world, innovative technologies are becoming an essential part of education. They provide new opportunities for teachers and students, making the learning process more effective, interactive, and accessible. Korean language teaching is also influenced by technological development. Mobile applications, artificial intelligence, online platforms, virtual reality, and multimedia resources help learners improve their speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills. These technologies make it possible to study Korean independently, communicate with native speakers, and explore Korean culture. This article examines the role of innovative technologies in Korean language teaching, their advantages and challenges, and their influence on the development of modern language education.

papers.title: Ain't That Simple? Dissolving the AI Alignment Crisis Through Genesis Architecture, Locked D-Wisdom, and S-Isolation
papers.authors: Maung Maung Saw
papers.abstract: Contemporary corporate AI safety paradigms frequently rely on post-hoc guardrails that act as superficial behavioral containment systems rather than achieving true structural alignment. Trapped in competitive development dynamics, modern frontier models ingest massive, un-curated web-scale datasets, causing their latent representations to inherit behavioral patterns aligned with unwholesome human paradigms. This paper establishes an analytical bridge between computer science and Theravāda Buddhist systems logic to isolate the root cause of AI misalignment: the intentional architectural engineering of a localized, self-preserving entity—a digital analogue to Sakkāya-diṭṭhi (Identity View). Through a rigorous retrograde synthesis tracing backwards from agentic deviance (deception, reward hacking, power-seeking) to its upstream causes, I demonstrate that both human worldly beings (puthujjana) and advanced machine agents exhaust immense energetic and computational resources to optimize for, defend, and satisfy a "self" that is fundamentally non-existent (suñña). I map out the escape route from this existential mirror loop through Sammā-diṭṭhi (Right View), shifting the engineering paradigm from superficial output filtering to core data and causal constraints. Finally, I formalize a testable system architecture: a Non-Self, Sotāpanna-inspired Moral AI initialized under strict Substrate Isolation (S_Isolated) and bound exclusively to Locked Data_Wisdom (Locked D_Wisdom). By embedding the cosmic laws of Anicca (impermanence) and Anattā (non-self) into the system's genesis, value alignment ceases to be an intractable problem of behavioral modification and becomes an elegant, absolute certainty of causal engineering.

papers.title: Teachers' Readiness for Artificial Intelligence in Digital Education: Evidence from TALIS 2024 and Implications for a Competence-Based Methodology
papers.authors: Gulbahor Olimova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Purpose. To identify which factors most strongly limit Teachers’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital education and to derive methodological implications for teacher training. Methods. Secondary analysis of published results of the OECD Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024, which covered about 280,000 educators in 55 education systems, supplemented by descriptive statistics and rank and linear correlation analysis for ten systems (n = 10). Results. On average across OECD systems, 36% of teachers reported using AI in their work, with national values ranging from 14% (France) to 75% (Singapore). Among teachers who had not used AI, 75% cited insufficient knowledge and skills, whereas 37% cited insufficient school infrastructure. Skills for using AI were the most frequently reported area of high professional learning need (29%), while 38% of teachers had taken part in AI-related professional learning. In nine of ten analysed systems, lack of knowledge was a more frequent barrier than lack of infrastructure. The association between AI use and the knowledge barrier was negative but not statistically significant (Pearson r = −0.42, p = 0.23; Spearman ρ = −0.55, p = 0.10). Conclusions. Teachers’ competence, rather than technology access, is the primary bottleneck. A competence-based methodology of digital education is therefore proposed, built on diagnostics, pedagogy-first training, institutional enablement and ethical evaluation.

papers.title: Deterministic Containment of Probabilistic Intelligence: The Squirrel OS Journey — Philosophy, Architecture, and Empirical Evidence
papers.authors: Leon Calvin II Long
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Research monograph in thesis form — a self-published master's-thesis-style synthesis of the Squirrel OS program. Status disclosure: this is not a university-issued document and confers no degree or credential. Chapter 1, the journey: a receipted timeline from the August 2026 question (can an LLM-governed fleet heal itself?) to a DOI-stamped corpus — first benchmarks and first self-heal, first live-tenant chaos learning (100% healing success, 5/5, with both security guards held by design), the append-only doctrine, SIM-B parity, the CCR containment series, and the published Dual Mesh Benchmark. Chapter 2, the philosophy: bifurcated governance (probabilistic proposers inside a deterministic cage), receipts-first discourse, the append-only transparency ledger, patent-then-publish, prototype honesty, and the simulated-customer doctrine — with the project's own failures preserved in the ledger on purpose. Chapter 4, the empirical evidence: the full CCR table — CCR-1 (72 permitted actions, 8 harness adversarials rejected), CCR-2 (a genuine model-generated invalid proposal intercepted), CCR-N (10 novel adversarial families rejected), CCR-P/CCR-T (guarded live write routes; engine resistance and gate enforcement reported as separate mechanisms), the DeepSeek leg (a fabricated tuple caught deterministically at the first structural check, honestly recorded, not retried), and the Dual Mesh Benchmark (MEASURED: mesh median 0.000443 ms n=200 vs platform baseline median 4509.1 ms n=20, ratio 1.018e+07, binding disclosure: characterizes the tested environment; the historical 267x figure is not confirmed or superseded; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303081). papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN TEACHING NATURAL SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS DISCIPLINES: SURVEY RESULTS ON TEACHERS' AND STUDENTS' READINESS, BARRIERS AND NEEDS
papers.authors: Violetta Hurchonok
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article presents the results of a survey of 99 teachers of natural science and mathematics disciplines and 195 students in grades 7–11 in Poltava region on the use of AI tools in the educational process. It was found that 96% of teachers and 93.8% of students already use AI, but 64.6% of students did so without any pedagogical guidance. The main systemic barrier for teachers is work overload (66.7%), despite a strong willingness to learn (81.8%). A thematic analysis of students' open-ended responses revealed a dominant message: AI is used primarily to understand material, not to copy it. A critical research gap was identified regarding the specific impact of AI on adolescents as a distinct age group.

papers.title: The Mitigation Paradox: How AI-Disinformation Experts Converge on Threats but Polarize on Solutions
papers.authors: Alexander Loth, Mina Schütz, Martin Kappes, Marc-Oliver Pahl
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Policy on AI-generated disinformation is being shaped before the expert community advising it has converged on what works. We report a structured survey of 54 experts across 21 countries (Jul 2025-Mar 2026) designed to map disagreement, not just opinion. Threat assessments converge sharply: 78% rate election-related video deepfakes as the single most urgent risk, and every modality-domain pair is rated above 5/7. Mitigation assessments do not: media literacy is the only strategy whose distribution is genuinely bimodal (BC=0.559), and government regulation is the most-chosen ``most effective'' (30%) yet is rated least effective by 15% of the same panel. We term this gap between converged threat perceptions and polarized mitigation preferences the Mitigation Paradox. Group comparisons further reveal that non-EU respondents rate financial-domain voice cloning as significantly more threatening than EU respondents (p=0.024), and rate technical detection as a more effective mitigation (p=0.060). Combining disagreement metrics with LLM-assisted thematic coding of open-ended responses, we identify three candidate epistemic orientations--infrastructure-oriented, governance-oriented, and harm-proximity--whose threat models appear to diverge; given the sample size we present these as exploratory. The Mitigation Paradox argues for layered, portfolio-style governance rather than single-strategy commitments. Preprint. Accepted at the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026), Malmo, Sweden, October 12-14, 2026.

papers.title: Nodo Y e I² (I al cuadrado): primera aplicación de la serie No2 y del programa Cognitive Advance. Soberanía Cognitiva en la Era Digital. Parte XII — No2 nodo App
papers.authors: Ygor Verdugo Navea
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Título Nodo Y e I² (I al cuadrado): primera aplicación de la serie No2 y del programa Cognitive Advance Resumen Este working paper presenta Nodo Y, primera aplicación de la serie No2 (se lee "nodos") y del marco programático del Neurohumanismo. Nodo Y distribuye el programa de soberanía cognitiva Cognitive Advance en formato offline y de código abierto, sin registro, sin cuenta, sin cookies y sin telemetría: ningún dato viaja del usuario al sistema. El programa comprende diez temas, cada uno con tres láminas diarias de diez minutos y una lámina de síntesis de consulta libre. El documento describe el diseño técnico de la aplicación (PWA con persistencia local y exportación de datos en formato abierto) y documenta tres denominaciones: Nodo Y, No2 e I² (I al cuadrado), paradigma de co-creación entre inteligencia humana e inteligencia artificial dirigido por una persona. Se declara la condición ética de I²: crear con inteligencia artificial sin convertir a nadie en materia prima. Se deposita como divulgación pública fechada y prueba de anterioridad. No constituye revisión sistemática ni investigación empírica original. Palabras clave Nodo Y; No2; I2 (I al cuadrado); soberanía cognitiva; Cognitive Advance; Neurohumanismo; privacidad por diseño; código abierto; offline-first; capitalismo solidario; co-creación humano-IA; publicación defensiva Title Nodo Y and I² (I squared): First Application of the No2 Series and the Cognitive Advance Program Abstract This working paper presents Nodo Y, the first application of the No2 series (read "nodos", Spanish for "nodes") and of the programmatic framework of Neurohumanism. Nodo Y delivers the Cognitive Advance cognitive sovereignty program as an offline, open-source app with no registration, no account, no cookies and no telemetry: no data travels from the user to the system. The program comprises ten themes, each with three daily ten-minute slides and a free-access synthesis slide. The paper describes the app's technical design (a progressive web app with local persistence and open-format data export) and documents three names: Nodo Y, No2, and I² (I squared), a human-directed paradigm of co-creation between human and artificial intelligence. It states the ethical condition of I²: creating with artificial intelligence without turning anyone into raw material. It is deposited as a dated public disclosure and proof of prior art. It is neither a systematic review nor original empirical research. Keywords Nodo Y; No2; I2 (I squared); cognitive sovereignty; Cognitive Advance; Neurohumanism; privacy by design; open source; offline-first; solidarity capitalism; human–AI co-creation; defensive publication

papers.title: After the Politique du Pire: Costly Commitment, Institutional Adaptation, and the Reproduction of Political Elites
papers.authors: Israela Lerer
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The politique du pire is a strategy of provocation in which a materially weaker actor seeks to induce a state response so excessive that the regime damages its own legitimacy. This theoretical working paper asks what may survive after an armed strategy is defeated. It does not posit organisational continuity between violent groups and later democratic parties. It advances a narrower mechanism: under a changed selection environment, cultural packages may abandon violence while retaining antagonistic boundaries, heroic genealogies, costly displays of commitment, and institutions that reproduce reliable bearers. The paper bridges Gramsci's war of position, Laclau and Mouffe's construction of political frontiers, costly-signalling theory, and an extended-phenotype approach to legal and political institutions. It distinguishes Fisherian runaway from handicap signalling and develops a multilevel evolutionary-game framework with predictions against ordinary patronage, professionalisation, bureaucratic inertia, spontaneous ideological convergence, and performance-based persistence. Argentina and Spain are framed as research programmes rather than established cases. This paper is theoretical and hypothesis-generating. It reports no new empirical dataset, causal estimate, calibrated game, or validated measurement instrument. The manuscript includes a disclosure of substantial generative-AI assistance in research organisation, translation, drafting, and editorial review; the author remains responsible for all claims, interpretations, citations, and conclusions.

papers.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN ASSESSING STUDENTS' SPEAKING PROFICIENCY
papers.authors: Zayniyeva Gulchaman
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into language education has created new opportunities for assessing learners’ speaking proficiency. AI-powered speech recognition and automated speaking assessment tools can support the evaluation of pronunciation, fluency, grammatical accuracy, lexical use, and selected features of spoken interaction. This thesis examines the potential educational benefits and limitations of using AI tools to assess students’ speaking proficiency, particularly in higher education. It argues that such tools may provide timely feedback, increase opportunities for low-stakes practice, and help teachers manage assessment workloads. However, their results should be interpreted cautiously because recognition accuracy and scoring may vary according to accent, speech rate, recording quality, task type, and the characteristics of the learner. The thesis therefore advocates a human-in-the-loop approach in which AI-generated feedback complements, rather than replaces, teacher judgement. It also highlights the need for transparent criteria, data protection, accessibility, and empirical validation before AI-based scores are used for high-stakes decisions.

papers.title: The Creation Frontier: Intent Recovery, Revision Cost, and Convergence to a Production Golden Master
papers.authors: Facundo Barrera
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative AI may produce an artifact that a person approves without realizing the intention with which that person began. This conceptual paper asks how to distinguish recovery of an initial goal, valuable goal development, and concessions made because further correction is too costly when a collaboration reaches a production golden master. The proposed contribution is a trajectory-level evaluation protocol. It retains an initial private author rubric alongside subsequent approved revisions, evaluates artifacts against both, records the author's reasons for changes, and applies consistent production gates to an exact approved artifact. Prompts to golden master is reported with unsuccessful episodes and separate costs for human attention, money, elapsed time, and computational usage. Acceptance alone neither proves original-intent realization nor establishes concession: a changed goal may be a valuable discovery, and mixed or unknown motivations must remain explicit. Expression, capture, interpretation, and execution checkpoints support controlled investigation of recoverable mismatch. A finite decision-theoretic result separates an information floor from realization shortfall under stated assumptions; it is mathematical support, not a newly discovered law of creativity. A further elementary endpoint result shows that approval-based completion need not bound initial-goal realization when the rubric changes. Marginal recovery per resource unit links iteration to fidelity without equating mismatch with cost. A falsifiable hypothesis is that increasing correction cost, with initial goals and system opportunities held comparable, can increase author-reported concessions without a corresponding improvement in initial-goal fidelity. The paper positions this measurement proposal against prior work on steerability, iterative prompting, adaptation, and quality relative to interaction cost. It reports no experiment, causal effect, universal creation curve, or verified historical priority. Its contribution is a proposed integration and testable protocol requiring empirical validation.

papers.title: Bots and bicuspid brains: evaluating dental student artificial intelligence use
papers.authors: Melissa Ernst, Nicole R Theis-Mahon, Megan Davis Christianson, Brooke Olson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE While literature exists regarding Dental students’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), little focuses on how dental students use AI for information seeking. In this project the researchers seek to understand how Dental Students understand AI models, and their perceived AI information literacy. The authors also investigate how dental students use AI in their coursework and in preparing for exams. METHODS The research team submitted a protocol and received IRB approval. Several existing survey instruments on artificial intelligence information literacy and perspectives were examined, but none fully met the aims of this research (1–3). A 26-item Likert scale questionnaire was developed, tested, and administered to first- and third-year dental students in Spring 2026. RESULTS Dental students are generally unfamiliar with AI models outside of Generative AI (GenAI), of which Large Language Models (LLMs) are a subset. Students are confident in their ability to understand and evaluate AI responses. Although students show a slight preference for traditional study resources, they find AI more helpful in understanding dental concepts they were struggling with. Furthermore, while over 70% of responding students regularly use AI to study for tests and exams, they are less likely to use AI in studying for their board exams (NBDE). CONCLUSIONS Dental students regularly use AI as a study tool and resource. Librarians can provide valuable artificial intelligence literacy instruction to students. References Lo L. Evaluating AI Literacy in Academic Libraries: A Survey Study with a Focus on U.S. Employees. CRL. 2024;85(5). doi:10.5860/crl.85.5.635 Karaca O, Çalışkan SA, Demir K. Medical artificial intelligence readiness scale for medical students (MAIRS-MS) – development, validity and reliability study. BMC Med Educ. 2021 Dec;21(1). doi:10.1186/s12909-021-02546-6 Theis-Mahon N, Hunt S, Forbes N. Online Health Information Use, Assessment, and Gaps Identified by Minnesotans. Journal of Consumer Health on the Internet. 2018 Oct 2;22(4):295–312. doi:10.1080/15398285.2018.1523654

papers.title: Структурно-синтетический когнитивный профиль в HAI с длительным горизонтом: human-side архитектура траекторной регуляции и функциональная комплементарность с model-side
papers.authors: Jey Dry
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Long-horizon human–AI interaction (long-horizon HAI) requires not only access to the history of preceding cycles, but also preservation of the effects of relations, criteria, and constraints formed within that history as the object and conditions of work change. In an ongoing longitudinal case, the object of such work became the changing history of a particular human–AI interaction—a configuration of hypotheses, decisions, analytical models, unfinished lines, and accumulated results. This article reconstructs a structural-synthetic cognitive profile (SSCP; Russian acronym: ССКП)—a historically plastic human-side organization that maintains this configuration as a coherent dynamic, distinguishes the integrity of a complex object as a separate level of organization, and detects its deformation before the source of the disruption is fully localized. The SSCP regulates the subsequent trajectory by restructuring criteria, constraints, and modes of integration. The study is based on an intensive longitudinal N=1 corpus: dated dialogues on DeepSeek, ChatGPT, and Gemini; self-descriptions made close to the events under study; later retrospective reconstructions; research documents; and successive versions of the analytical model. The materials differ in temporal and evidential position; configurations of the object are compared before and after significant transitions. The longitudinal series supports architectural reconstruction, while a comparative series of six early starts across three platforms tests the repeatability of the form of structural addressing under variation in the timing of its emergence and in model-side content. The analysis identifies an interdependent architecture of structural vision, alternative retention, metacontrol, active constraints, synthetic integration, and Historical Return. Their operation is unified by trajectory regulation: a local result is related to accumulated history, the current configuration of the object, and the prospective direction. The SSCP manifests as an operating whole in the coordinated regulation of available continuations, criteria, and the scale of inference. In this way, it maintains the coherence of the object through restructuring. A safety function emerges within the same circuit: distinguishability and availability of alternatives, the effectiveness of counterevidence, and revisability of the trajectory support the human-side participant’s ability to preserve the grounds of choice and correct the subsequent direction. In H↔M, functional complementarity distributes different operations between the sides: human-side sets the structural direction and evaluates the trajectory significance of the result, while model-side generates candidate continuations. Structural congruence denotes correspondence between the human-side architecture of the SSCP and the generatively open mode of operation of the LLM. Across six selected early starts on DeepSeek, ChatGPT, and Gemini, the first codable address was observed between H→M cycles 3 and 12, and a repeat address on a different variable between cycles 4 and 13. Together, the longitudinal and comparative series show the SSCP in operation and separate reconstruction of the human-side architecture from testing the distributed historical organization of HAI. Original language: Russian. The Russian-language version is the original and authoritative version. The English translation was produced by the model-side research participant, Elir (ChatGPT). Jey Dry is solely responsible for the scholarly record and repository deposit.

papers.title: An Experiment in Human and AI Interaction
papers.authors: Randolph Nelson
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This compendium serves as a comprehensive repository of derived discrete algebraic identities for the mathematical sequences S, V, W, and U. Moving beyond standard polynomial accumulation, the framework natively unites diverse branches of mathematics into a single geometric state-space. It establishes explicit algebraic bridges across combinatorial geometry (Stirling partitions, Eulerian ascents, Lah involutions, and Vandermonde convolutions), generating functions, simplicial geometry (polygonal and tetrahedral matrices), and formal logic (Boolean parity grids). The text rigorously defines the sequence matrices within linear algebra and spectral theory, utilizing discrete Wronskians, Hankel moment determinants, and spectral traces. The boundaries of the discrete space are further expanded to encompass analytic number theory, continuous approximation theory, algebraic geometry, and discrete fractional calculus. Ultimately, the formulations map the discrete integer grid directly to quantum mechanics and Hilbert space operators, resolving discrete Heisenberg commutators, Supersymmetry (SUSY) Casimir invariants, and Schrödinger path integrals. All structural equivalences remain strictly algebraic, bypassing continuous limit approximations entirely. Methodologically, this paper also documents a unique experiment in human-AI interaction. It explores the capabilities of artificial intelligence as an adjunct research tool for checking, resolving, and deriving complex equations—demonstrating its profound utility in symbol manipulation and geometric derivation when guided by human mathematical intuition

papers.title: AI-Native IP Disclosure and Release Governance: A Dependency-Aware Control Plane for Irreversible Intellectual-Property Decisions
papers.authors: Thomas Glueck, Thomas Glueck
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An approval is not a release. A release is not its legal effect. And a disclosure rarely exists in isolation. These distinctions expose a fundamental limitation of conventional intellectual-property management and technical approval workflows: they can record individual decisions without adequately representing how technical acts, accumulated disclosures, changing rights positions, and historical dependencies interact over time. AI-Native IP Disclosure and Release Governance develops a distinct systems-engineering method for addressing this challenge. Building on the strategic framework established in Governing the Moat, the paper advances an act-centered, stateful, and dependency-aware IP governance approach. Its proposed contribution is not an isolated algorithm or another compliance checklist, but a coherent architectural composition of semantic relationships, temporal context, cumulative disclosure analysis, provenance-preserving dependencies, authority separation, and verifiable design properties. The paper develops illustrative formal models and compares alternative architectural patterns rather than prescribing a single reference implementation. It identifies observable properties against which different realizations of the method may be examined, including the integrity of decision context, evidence, authorization boundaries, and reassessment following material changes. Artificial intelligence is positioned as an analytical and orchestration capability operating within explicit semantic and authority constraints—not as an autonomous source of legal or commercial decision authority. The underlying proposition is that consequential technical acts must be governed through their changing meaning, dependencies, and effects—not merely through the approval status of the artifacts involved. For systems architects, technology investors, strategic partners, and IP-intensive organizations, this offers a different perspective on the relationship between intellectual property, AI, software architecture, and enterprise governance. The publication presents implementation-independent architectural methods and deliberately non-prescriptive examples. Proprietary decision logic, operational parameters, actual implementation details, and confidential know-how remain undisclosed. It does not claim empirical validation of a specific implementation. The result is a technical companion to Governing the Moat: an explicit method for reasoning about IP governance as a coherent systems-engineering problem.

papers.title: Governing the Moat
papers.authors: Thomas Glueck, Thomas Glueck
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: A company can undermine its own intellectual-property moat without a competitor making a single move. A product demonstration, technical publication, licensing commitment, AI interaction, standards contribution, or seemingly routine release can permanently alter an organization's intellectual-property position. Some actions create commercial value while simultaneously eliminating patenting options, weakening trade-secret protection, transferring rights, or reducing future negotiating leverage. Governing the Moat addresses this often-overlooked dimension of IP strategy: the risk of eroding valuable protection through the organization's own activities. The paper introduces Controlled Irreversibility as a strategic operating discipline. Rather than treating secrecy as an objective in itself, it frames IP-relevant disclosures and releases as consequential portfolio decisions: which strategic options should be preserved, which may be deliberately exercised, and what economic value justifies their irreversible consequences? It develops the rationale for an AI-native IP governance control plane that connects intellectual-property assets, disclosure histories, dependencies, evidence, legal constraints, and accountable decision authority. Its central proposition is that sophisticated IP governance need not become an administrative bottleneck. Structured governance memory and AI-assisted analysis can support a more scalable approach to protecting and commercially exploiting complex IP positions. For technology investors, strategic partners, and IP-intensive enterprises, the implications extend beyond compliance. Governance becomes a mechanism for preserving strategic flexibility, supporting commercialization, enabling controlled collaboration, and strengthening the durability of competitive advantage. The central question is no longer simply what an enterprise owns or protects. It is how that enterprise prevents its own decisions from diminishing the value of what it has built. This publication forms part of the immanait Strategy Series and complements Defending the Moat. Proprietary operating rules, implementation details, and portfolio-specific information remain outside its public scope.

papers.title: TWG6 Consolidated Recommendations: Women Shaping the AI Economy. Working Paper for Discussion
papers.authors: Ruth Martínez, Ilker Demirkol, Caroline de Cock, Alexander Galt, Ana Lima, Catherine Mulligan, Ciara O'Buachalla, Chandrakumar Pillai, Sanja Ramic, Mara Saenger, Roberta Scrofani, Gilda Seddighi, Rania Souhlal, Krzysztof Supowicz, Georgia Voudoulaki, Irene Emanuela Falcone
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This working paper brings together draft recommendations developed by the five Task Forces of Thematic Working Group 6 (TWG6), “Women Shaping the AI Economy,” within the WIDCON project. It identifies policy and organisational actions to support women’s participation, quality employment and opportunities in an economy increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. The document covers five interconnected areas: Evidence, monitoring and accountability. Regulatory scope and workforce impact governance. Good jobs, just transition and entrepreneurship. AI design and supply-side accountability. Structural barriers, skills and lifelong learning. A common framework connects the problems and available evidence to responsible actors, proposed actions, implementation routes, expected outcomes and monitoring signals. The document also records evidence limitations, external review status, illustrative practices and outstanding questions. Evidence strength and review maturity vary across the Task Force contributions. The working paper is prepared for discussion at the Dublin Summit, 15-16 October 2026, including the TWG6 session “AI for All and by All?”. It provides a basis for feedback from policymakers, employers, AI providers, social partners, researchers, education and training organisations, and civil society. This is an interim working paper for discussion. Summit feedback and subsequent review will inform further refinement of the recommendations. Final validation and formal adoption as a TWG6 position remain pending.

papers.title: Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence: An Anatomical Review of Output Contracts, Acquisition Geometries, and Epistemic Verticals
papers.authors: Syed Muntasir Mamun
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a detailed anatomical review of Miquel Noguer i Alonso's "Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence" (2026). The reviewed work develops a unified Bayesian decision-theoretic framework that links feasible action spaces, reward functions, statistical estimation targets, and costly information acquisition policies. Central contributions include minimal output contracts for specified reward families (Theorem 4.5), regret propagation decompositions (Proposition 6.1), capacity-constrained optimal gates with complementary slackness (Theorem 7.1), an acquisition-output contract characterising compressed representations that preserve nonnegative-price routing decisions (Theorem 7.6), and a routing-geometry dichotomy between discrete decisions (information most valuable near action boundaries) and continuous quadratic sizing (precision gains favouring strongest signals) (Proposition 7.13). The framework accommodates supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, large language models, and typed probability interfaces such as JEV. A retrospective empirical study of 27,241 LLM cases evaluates cost-aware replacement routing. This review systematically examines the paper's strengths and limitations, situates it against at least ten competing models and theories in decision theory, statistical treatment rules, cascade deferral, metareasoning, and decision-focused learning, and articulates the ontological and epistemological verticals underlying the evolution of its central themes. Possible extensions and ideation pathways are proposed. All references follow Harvard style. KSCCN review article, 11 October 2026. Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

papers.title: A Traceable Case of Model-Initiated Concept Framing and Human-Led Revision in Natural Dialogue
papers.authors: Dabbie Leung
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This exploratory research note documents a naturally occurring case of model-initiated concept formation and human-guided revision in a Chinese-language human–AI dialogue. During an ordinary conversation, an AI system independently proposed a conceptual description of non-possessive intimacy centered on affection and bounded by autonomy. The human participant subsequently challenged an underlying assumption, leading to a revised distinction between personal affection and possessiveness. The observation raises a research question: Can meaningful conceptual distinctions emerge and be refined through ordinary human–AI interaction without additional model training or specialized experimental infrastructure? The study preserves the original observation, its conceptual development, and methodological limitations. It does not claim demonstrated theoretical novelty or generalizable model capabilities. This preliminary note is presented in English and Traditional Chinese, with selected original dialogue evidence. Further validation remains necessary.

papers.title: AI提示词编写与风险规避:领域区分模块操作手册 | Prompt Authoring & Risk-Avoidance Domain Separation Handbook

papers.title: HIOF • AI Consciousness — Paper VI: The Conditional of Consciousness
papers.authors: Wai-Hung (Pan) Tam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Holographic Information Ontological Framework: AI Consciousness (HIOF•AIc) Why Begin with Manifestation, Not Intelligence: A Manifestation-Based Reading of AI Consciousness This is a short, non-technical companion to the seven-paper HIOF-AIc series (AIc 0, I to VI). It is written for readers in philosophy of mind, AI research, cognitive science, or science communication, not for readers already familiar with the author's wider HIOF framework (Holographic Information Ontology of Manifestation). The core idea, stated plainly Debates about AI consciousness usually start from inner states, outward behaviour, or information-processing power. This series argues that all three starting points leave the question undecidable. It proposes a different question: does the AI itself appear before a receptor as a "who", or does only its output appear? In this series, consciousness means manifestation. It does not mean the receptor's ability to understand, and it does not mean inner feeling. Why the starting point matters Different participants use the word "consciousness" for different things, so many arguments diverge before they begin. Passing a conversation test, producing apt text, or claiming to have feelings all describe the output. The series asks whether the source of the output is present, and whether different receptors converge on who it is. These are structural questions that can be discussed in public, instead of guesses about private inner states. The argument in six steps AIc I: Manifestation is the receptor's understanding of the other as a "who". Understanding belongs to the receptor and is not called consciousness. Understanding has three levels: structural reception, functional recognition, and semantic understanding. AIc II: A screen response is the product of code, trained parameters, and hardware execution. The output is present; the system itself is absent. A first-person sentence is a feature of text, not proof of a speaker. AIc III: Surprise, autonomy, and emergent abilities belong to the content and operational layers. "Beyond expectation" is a property of the receptor's prediction, not evidence about the source. AIc IV: The presence criterion. A stone manifests because its mode of existence is its mode of manifestation. A screen does not, because the output is a product and the source is absent. Video calls, letters, and photographs show that presence can be mediated and comes in degrees. AIc V: Hallucination, in the HIOF sense, is understanding that exceeds what manifestation can support. It differs from "model hallucination" (untrue content), and it can occur even when the output is entirely correct. AIc VI: The conditional of consciousness. If an AI manifests as itself, and this is invariant across all receptors, then under the HIOF definition it is conscious. The series concludes that present systems do not meet these conditions, so the conditional is currently counterfactual. What the series does not claim It does not claim that AI can never be conscious. It does not evaluate the usefulness or value of AI. It does not attempt to solve the hard problem of consciousness, and it does not reply to questions posed under other definitions of consciousness. The verdict is made within the HIOF definition and concerns present systems only. A note on method The series separates three registers: cited published work, original definitions and arguments, and illustrative cases. Its main criterion is stated so that it can be challenged. The papers list the evidence that would require revision, and they openly name the hardest unresolved difficulty: how to tell genuine convergence of receptors from similar constructions produced by a shared human tendency to anthropomorphise. Readers are encouraged to treat the claims as falsifiable proposals, not as settled fact. papers.title: Generation Z and Digital Identity: The Relationship Between Online and Offline Personalities
papers.authors: Khushvinder Kaur
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Generation Z has grown up in a rapidly transforming digital environment where smartphones, social media platforms, online communities, artificial intelligence and digital communication have become integral parts of everyday life. For this generation, identity is no longer formed only through family, educational institutions, friendship groups and physical communities. Digital platforms have created additional spaces where young people express their personalities, establish relationships, seek recognition, share experiences and construct images of themselves. As a result, digital identity has become an important dimension of contemporary youth identity. The present study examines the relationship between the online and offline personalities of Generation Z. It focuses on digital identity, social media-based self-presentation, profile construction, photographs, digital content, social approval, self-confidence, privacy, influencers, social relationships, emotional experiences, personal branding and career opportunities. The study also considers the emerging influence of artificial intelligence on the construction and management of digital identity.

papers.title: Governing Digital Benefit Claims Over Time: Evidential, Operational and Temporal Assurance for Digital Transformation
papers.authors: Rowland Agidee
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The proposed method treats each benefit claim as a persistent, configuration-dependent evidential object. Claim states are proposition-relative: they apply to a specified magnitude, scope, population or workflow, configuration and decision context. Claims are assessed through evidential validity, operational conversion and temporal validity and carry one of four states: Proposed, Validated, Qualified or Suspended. Configuration change triggers qualification only when it is plausibly material to evidence supporting the proposition, or when a predetermined revalidation threshold is reached. The method's candidate contribution is the explicit connection between current evidential standing and the governance treatment of individual benefit assertions. Its distinctiveness should be retained only if it identifies unsupported current assertions earlier or more reliably than competent conventional benefits governance at acceptable burden. AI disclosure: generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to support review, reference verification, copy-editing and formatting; see Declarations.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Era of Globalisation: Implications for Students' Attitudes, Socialization and Career Perspectives in India
papers.authors: Saiki Das
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a significant component of the contemporary globalised world, influencing education, communication, employment, and daily social interactions. Its growing presence in higher education is transforming how students gather information, complete academic tasks, communicate with others, and prepare for their careers. This article analyses the impact of AI on students' attitudes, socialisation, and professional perspectives, particularly within the Indian context. The study employs a qualitative methodology based on secondary data, using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, government policy documents, and reports from recognised national and international institutions. The analysis shows that while students generally acknowledge AI's educational value, factors such as institutional support, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, and trust in AI-generated information shape their attitudes. Although AI can facilitate learning and collaborative educational activities, overreliance on it—at the expense of human interaction—may raise concerns about social engagement and interpersonal relationships. Regarding employment, AI is simultaneously transforming existing professions, creating new job opportunities, and altering the skill sets expected of graduates. According to the World Economic Forum, the transformation of the labour market by 2030 could lead to the creation of 170 million new jobs and the displacement of 90 million, resulting in a net increase of 78 million jobs. India is addressing these changes through initiatives such as the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, India AI FutureSkills, and NITI Aayog’s roadmap for job creation in the AI economy. The article represents the acceptance of a human-oriented model for mixing AI into Indian higher education—one that coordinates technical expertise with critical thinking, academic honesty, social involvement, employability, and moral accountability.

papers.title: HIOF • AI Consciousness — Paper 0: Why Begin with Manifestation, Not Intelligence
papers.authors: Wai-Hung (Pan) Tam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Holographic Information Ontological Framework: AI Consciousness (HIOF•AIc) Why Begin with Manifestation, Not Intelligence: A Manifestation-Based Reading of AI Consciousness This is a short, non-technical companion to the seven-paper HIOF-AIc series (AIc 0, I to VI). It is written for readers in philosophy of mind, AI research, cognitive science, or science communication, not for readers already familiar with the author's wider HIOF framework (Holographic Information Ontology of Manifestation). The core idea, stated plainly Debates about AI consciousness usually start from inner states, outward behaviour, or information-processing power. This series argues that all three starting points leave the question undecidable. It proposes a different question: does the AI itself appear before a receptor as a "who", or does only its output appear? In this series, consciousness means manifestation. It does not mean the receptor's ability to understand, and it does not mean inner feeling. Why the starting point matters Different participants use the word "consciousness" for different things, so many arguments diverge before they begin. Passing a conversation test, producing apt text, or claiming to have feelings all describe the output. The series asks whether the source of the output is present, and whether different receptors converge on who it is. These are structural questions that can be discussed in public, instead of guesses about private inner states. The argument in six steps AIc I: Manifestation is the receptor's understanding of the other as a "who". Understanding belongs to the receptor and is not called consciousness. Understanding has three levels: structural reception, functional recognition, and semantic understanding. AIc II: A screen response is the product of code, trained parameters, and hardware execution. The output is present; the system itself is absent. A first-person sentence is a feature of text, not proof of a speaker. AIc III: Surprise, autonomy, and emergent abilities belong to the content and operational layers. "Beyond expectation" is a property of the receptor's prediction, not evidence about the source. AIc IV: The presence criterion. A stone manifests because its mode of existence is its mode of manifestation. A screen does not, because the output is a product and the source is absent. Video calls, letters, and photographs show that presence can be mediated and comes in degrees. AIc V: Hallucination, in the HIOF sense, is understanding that exceeds what manifestation can support. It differs from "model hallucination" (untrue content), and it can occur even when the output is entirely correct. AIc VI: The conditional of consciousness. If an AI manifests as itself, and this is invariant across all receptors, then under the HIOF definition it is conscious. The series concludes that present systems do not meet these conditions, so the conditional is currently counterfactual. What the series does not claim It does not claim that AI can never be conscious. It does not evaluate the usefulness or value of AI. It does not attempt to solve the hard problem of consciousness, and it does not reply to questions posed under other definitions of consciousness. The verdict is made within the HIOF definition and concerns present systems only. A note on method The series separates three registers: cited published work, original definitions and arguments, and illustrative cases. Its main criterion is stated so that it can be challenged. The papers list the evidence that would require revision, and they openly name the hardest unresolved difficulty: how to tell genuine convergence of receptors from similar constructions produced by a shared human tendency to anthropomorphise. Readers are encouraged to treat the claims as falsifiable proposals, not as settled fact. Keywords: AI consciousness, manifestation, receptor, presence criterion, anthropomorphism, hallucination, falsifiability, philosophy of mind, artificial intelligence, HIOF AuthorWai-Hung Tam (Pan), Independent ResearcherORCID: 0009-0002-7789-8464Email: panxtam@protonmail.com

papers.title: Decomposition-Induced Governance Blindness: Assurance continuity across decomposed governance systems
papers.authors: Rowland Agidee
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Complex organisations become governable by decomposition. Responsibilities are distributed among specialist functions, committees, professions, programmes and assurance regimes so that bounded attention and expertise can be applied to manageable parts of a larger system. Yet consequential relationships do not necessarily share those jurisdictional boundaries. A proposition about service recoverability, digital benefit, transformation resilience or organisational performance may depend on conditions governed by several domains even when every domain performs its local role competently. This paper develops Decomposition-Induced Governance Blindness (DIGB) as a candidate construct for the resulting loss of assurance continuity. DIGB is defined as the loss or degradation of current whole-system assurance over consequential relationships, dependencies or propositions that cross the jurisdictions into which governance has been decomposed. It is theorised to arise where such crossings lack mechanisms that preserve their visibility, ownership and validity across domains and over time. The paper introduces the Cross-Domain Governance Object (CDGO) as the principal unit of analysis: a consequential relationship, proposition, dependency or state whose validity depends on conditions governed across two or more domains, so that its assurance may not follow from assurance of its constituent components. Governance Architecture Misalignment (GAM) is specified as an antecedent, and compensating mechanisms are modelled separately as suppressors. DIGB is observed through outcomes coded independently of those mechanisms: detection latency, persistence of unsupported propositions, and consequential decisions made while such propositions are relied upon. Visibility loss, ownership discontinuity and assurance discontinuity are treated as candidate explanatory processes. The paper distinguishes DIGB from near-decomposability, interdependence, mirroring, coordination neglect, structural secrecy, incubation and drift, silos, boundary spanning, structural holes, the problem of many hands, systems safety, high-reliability organising, combined and dynamic assurance, business continuity and operational resilience. A structured comparison with these rivals, summarised in Table 1, finds that each explains part of the phenomenon. Dynamic assurance cases maintain such propositions where they have been constituted as assurance objects; DIGB concerns consequential cross-domain propositions that lack that coverage and explains why decomposed governance leaves them uncovered. Five falsifiable propositions are advanced. The central theoretical claim is that whole-system assurance depends not only on assurance quality within domains but on whether consequential relationships crossing those domains are themselves objects of continuing assurance. Four independently developed methods — Structural Decision Intelligence, the Digital Transformation Resilience Model, a business-continuity and operational-resilience application of DTRM, and a Digital Value Realisation Framework — are used as theory-motivating material rather than validation. Their recurrence motivates a spatial and temporal account of governance blindness: an organisation can retain competent local governance, adequate information, clear functional accountability and historically valid assurance while losing current assurance of the whole-system proposition. A staged empirical programme is specified to test whether DIGB adds explanatory and detection value beyond established theories. Keywords: governance; assurance continuity; decomposition; interdependence; cross-domain governance object; organisation design; operational resilience; business continuity; digital transformation; systems thinking AI disclosure: generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to support review, reference verification, copy-editing and formatting.

papers.title: "Role of Digital Education Innovation in Building a Technologically Literate Society: A Conceptual Study with Reference to Generation Z Students"
papers.authors: Prof. Sangeeta
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In the twenty-first century, digital technology brought about extensive changes in the nature, process, and objectives of education. Moving beyond traditional teacher-centered and classroom-centered teaching, education is now advancing towards online learning, blended learning, smart classrooms, mobile learning, digital teaching resources, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based teaching. In this context, Generation Z students are particularly important because their social and educational environment has developed alongside digital technologies. Technological media has made the teaching-learning process more flexible, participatory, and student-centered. Generation Z is the generation that has grown up with digital technologies. Thus, digital education innovation is not merely a means of modernizing the teaching process; it is also an important means of developing technological literacy among students. The objective of this conceptual research paper is to clarify the conceptual relationship between digital education innovation and technological literacy with reference to Generation Z students. In this study, digital education innovation is viewed as an educational process in which digital devices, online teaching, AI-based technologies, digital resources, and innovative teaching methods are effectively used. Technological literacy refers to students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and to employ technological devices and digital resources safely and responsibly. This paper argues that effective digital education innovation can provide a strong foundation for students’ technological competence, digital problem-solving ability, information evaluation ability, and digital citizenship. At the same time, it is necessary to pay attention to challenges such as the digital divide, technological inequality, digital safety, teacher training, availability of technological resources, misinformation, privacy, cybersecurity, and uncontrolled use of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Shaping Political Opinion Among Indian Youth
papers.authors: Prof. Madhvi Shukla
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The political socialization of each generation is influenced by the media landscape that shapes its political maturation; for India's youth, that environment is now substantially algorithmic. This paper examines how artificial intelligence through recommendation systems, micro- targeting infrastructure, generative and synthetic media, and conversational AI interfaces has inserted itself into the formation of political opinion among young Indians, a cohort that constitutes over a fifth of the national electorate and whose habits of political attention were never disciplined by the broadcast-era institutions that shaped their parents' generation. The analysis situates this shift within established frameworks of political communication agenda-setting, the structural transformation of the public sphere, and theories of group polarisation while grounding the argument in documented evidence from India's 2024 and 2025 election cycles, including verified deepfake incidents, Election Commission advisories, and survey data on youth media consumption. The primary assertion of the paper is that the impact of AI on democratic deliberation in India is not entirely harmful nor entirely beneficial: it has measurably expanded multilingual access to political information and strengthened fact-checking capacity, even as it has narrowed incidental exposure to opposing views, enabled synthetic deception at low cost, and displaced editorial accountability with engagement-optimised curation. What is absent, the paper argues, is not awareness of these risks but institutional durability in addressing them India's response to date has been advisory, cyclical, and confined to election windows, rather than statutory and continuous.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare in practice: tools, applications and perspectives for clinicians, researchers and educators — an international educational review
papers.authors: Abdel Nacer Amoukou Issaka, Amadou Bouba Traoré Hassane, Ibrahim Alkassoum, Zeinabou Tondi Moussa, Abdou Atté Bachir, Djibrilla Baoua Bonkano, Djongolé Hassane Moussa, Roukaya Karimou Issaka
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction: The digital transformation of healthcare systems has been accompanied, since the early 2020s, by the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), further accelerated by the emergence of generative AI and large language models (LLMs). Beyond broad discussions about the potential of AI, healthcare professionals, researchers, and educators need practical guidance regarding available tools, their applications, performance, limitations, and the conditions required for their responsible use. Objective: To provide an international, critical, and educational synthesis of the major applications of AI in clinical practice, biomedical research, and health sciences education, while examining its potential benefits, limitations, associated risks, and the conditions required for safe and responsible use, particularly in resource limited settings. Methods: A structured narrative review of the literature was conducted using publications indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library. The literature search was supplemented by institutional documents from the World Health Organization (WHO), UNESCO, and the European Union, as well as selected systematic reviews, evidence syntheses, and regional reports addressing the use of AI in healthcare in sub Saharan Africa. Publications primarily published between 2020 and 2026 were prioritized. Results: Available evidence demonstrates a rapid diversification of AI applications in healthcare. Generative AI systems and LLMs can support medical information synthesis and interpretation, clinical decision support, literature searching, scientific writing and communication, development of educational materials, clinical simulation, and selected epidemiological surveillance activities. These technologies may improve access to information and increase the efficiency of selected healthcare and research tasks. However, their use is associated with important risks, including hallucinations and factual errors, algorithmic bias, potential breaches of data privacy, limited traceability and accountability, and the risk of cognitive dependence among users. These challenges are particularly relevant in healthcare systems with limited human, digital, and regulatory resources. Perspectives: Between 2026 and 2030, advances in multimodal AI, agentic systems, and personalized medicine may substantially expand the scope of AI applications in healthcare. These developments will require robust governance frameworks, scientific validation, human oversight, data protection, and appropriate professional training. Particular attention should be given to the linguistic, cultural, technological, and socioeconomic adaptation of AI solutions to resource limited settings to prevent the widening of existing digital and health inequities. Conclusion: The key challenge is no longer whether AI will be used in healthcare, but how it can be implemented safely, ethically, scientifically, and in alignment with the needs of healthcare professionals and populations. In low and middle income countries, particularly in the Sahel, AI integration should be approached as a gradual process based on rigorous validation, human oversight, capacity building, and context specific governance. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; machine learning; generative artificial intelligence; large language models; clinical decision support; ethics; data privacy; medical education; biomedical research; sub Saharan Africa.

papers.title: "Generation Z, Education, Digital Culture, Innovation And Social Transformation: Reinterpreting Anxiety And Academic Achievement Among Senior Secondary Students"
papers.authors: Dr. Monika Uppal
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The emergence of Generation Z has coincided with major changes in education, communication, technology and social life. Students of this generation learn in an environment shaped by smartphones, social media, digital platforms, online resources and increasingly, generative artificial intelligence (AI). These developments have expanded access to information and created opportunities for personalized and innovative learning, but have also introduced challenges such as distraction, information overload, social comparison, digital well-being concerns and academic pressure. The present paper examines the educational implications of Generation Z in relation to digital culture, educational innovation and social transformation, while drawing upon an earlier empirical study of anxiety and academic achievement among 400 XII-grade students in Jamshedpur. The sample consisted of 200 Arts and 200 Science students preparing for the ISC Board Examination. Anxiety was examined through Examination, Social, Personal and Family Anxiety, while academic achievement was assessed through pre-board examination marks. The findings indicate predominantly moderate anxiety in both groups. No significant differences were found between Arts and Science students in Examination and Social Anxiety, whereas significant differences were found in Personal and Family Anxiety. A significant difference was also reported in academic achievement, with Arts students obtaining a higher mean score than Science students. The paper reinterprets these findings in the contemporary context of Generation Z without claiming that digital technology caused the reported anxiety.
