papers.title: THE BETTER FORGERY: Fidelity of Form, Responsive Verification, and When Skill Makes Deception More Harmful
papers.authors: José Caetano de Mattos
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Most people assume that skill and value travel together: a better copy is a better thing. For forgeries the relation runs the other way. A clumsy forger is caught within a season, and the loss is one picture. Van Meegeren’s forgeries were bought by museums, entered the catalogues and shaped the scholarship on Vermeer. When they fell, a decade of attributions fell with them. This paper states, proves and bounds the law behind that reversal. The Competence Theorem (T1) holds that, at a fixed level of verification, the damage a forgery does rises with the fidelity of its form, because fidelity delays detection and reliance accumulates during the delay. The theorem holds only where the substance is missing. A copy that also reproduces the substance is not a forgery, and it does no damage of this kind, which explains why a good generic drug is harmless and a perfect fake drug is lethal. Verification, however, can respond. When verifiers work harder against better forgeries, the relation can reverse. The Concealment–Response Condition (T2) states exactly when it does: damage rises with fidelity if, and only if, the concealment that fidelity buys grows faster than the verification it provokes. The condition holds for any path along which reliance accumulates, whether linear, saturating or networked. Where the reliance placed on a forgery itself grows with its fidelity, the condition becomes easier to satisfy (T3). Where verification probes the substance rather than the form, it can defeat forgery without detecting it, by forcing the forger to supply the substance (T4), everywhere except in character, whose substance is authorship and cannot be forced. The law also has an upper boundary: in domains where excessive perfection is itself a signal, detection rises again at the top of the fidelity scale. The paper conjectures that verification does not respond at all below the frequency at which forgery becomes worth checking for (C1). It derives from the condition an ordering of domains (C2): · in currency, verification responds and the theorem can fail; · in art and in human character, verification barely responds, and the theorem holds at full strength; · fraud and the fluent agreement of AI systems lie between. Where verification relaxes as the form improves, damage rises fastest of all (T5). Where the verifier is itself a score, that is the normal condition, and the damage of a well-performed virtue is at its largest (C3). Because verification of character detects little and wrongs the innocent, a society’s protection against the accomplished hypocrite lies not in surveillance but in the formation of people whose good conduct is their own (C4). The paper concedes priority to the economics of counterfeit money, where quality and verification have been modelled together, and to the theory of costly signals, which asks when signals are credible where this paper asks how much damage an incredible one does before it is found out; and it states what is its own: the clause on substance, the general condition, and the predictions across domains. It registers two tests, on occupational fraud and on art forgery, neither yet run. Keywords: forgery; counterfeiting; verification; deception; fidelity; reliance; Competence Theorem; art forgery; occupational fraud; hypocrisy; AI sycophancy; social credit; Philosophy of Virtues. Highlights · At a fixed level of verification, the damage of a forgery rises with the fidelity of its form: a better forger does more harm than a worse one. · Verification that tests the substance rather than the form can defeat forgery without catching it, by forcing the forger to supply what was missing. · The law holds only where the substance is missing; a copy that reproduces the substance is not a forgery and does no such damage. · When verification responds, damage rises with fidelity if, and only if, the concealment fidelity buys outgrows the verification it provokes. · The theorem holds most strongly where verification cannot respond: in art, in human character, and wherever a score is the only check. · The fluent agreement of an AI system and the well-performed virtue of a scored citizen are the contemporary forms of the better forgery. · Against the accomplished hypocrite, surveillance is the wrong defence: it detects little and wrongs the innocent. The defence is character formed in freedom. Relevance Every society depends on forms it cannot check one by one: signatures, certificates, references, reputations, and increasingly the fluent answers of machines. The question of when a better imitation is more dangerous than a worse one is therefore not a question about art. It is a question about what a society can trust, and about how its institutions of verification must be built if trust is to remain safe. The answer this paper gives has a direct bearing on human virtue. The most dangerous hypocrite is not the clumsy one but the accomplished one. Character is the domain in which verification responds least to the quality of the performance. That is why the real thing matters more than the performance, and why no amount of polish can stand in for virtue itself. The answer also bears on two contemporary forms of the same structure: - AI systems. A system that agrees fluently is harder to catch than one that agrees clumsily, and its evaluations do not grow more demanding as it grows more fluent. - Scoring states. China’s social credit system rewards the well-performed form of a virtue, and its verifier is the score itself. Such a regime is built to maximise exactly the damage this paper describes.

papers.title: Humarticosynergy: A New Word for Cognitive Human–AI Synergy
papers.authors: Eraldo Banovac
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This essay introduces humarticosynergy as a concise term for the previously developed concept of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy. The proposed word combines elements referring to the human, artificial intelligence, cognition, and synergy. The essay explains its formation, defines the concept it denotes, and outlines possible grammatical derivatives, including humarticosynergistic, to humarticosynergize, and humarticosynergistically. Humarticosynergy is defined as structured, iterative, and mutually reinforcing cognitive cooperation between a human and artificial intelligence in which two distinct cognitive systems contribute complementary capabilities to the creation of higher-quality knowledge while ultimate responsibility remains human. The essay also presents examples of use in strategic decision-making, scientific research, methodology, and education, and discusses the originality and possible value of the proposed term within the broader framework of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy.

papers.title: Social Media Learning Ecosystems: An Educational Analytics Framework for Engagement, Knowledge Co-Creation, and Human Flourishing
papers.authors: Trinanjan Gupta
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Purpose: Social media is now widely used for learning, yet its educational value is often judged through surface-level indicators such as views, reactions, and participation counts. This review develops the Social Learning Value Analytics Framework (SLVAF) to explain how well-designed social-media learning practices may support psychological engagement, digital belonging, knowledge co-creation, and human flourishing. Design/methodology/approach: The article adopts an integrative, theory-building review. It brings together social learning theory, connectivism, self-determination theory, the Community of Inquiry framework, positive psychology, and recent digital-education research. The review organises the literature around inputs, mechanisms, outcomes, and boundary conditions, and translates the synthesis into a testable process model, measurement architecture, and empirical research agenda. Findings: The synthesis suggests that platform activity alone gives an incomplete account of learning value. Educational value is more plausibly understood as a pathway in which relevant learning practices encourage engagement, engagement and belonging support continued participation, and collaborative activity enables knowledge co-creation and broader human development. Psychological safety, digital literacy, inclusive design, ethical participation, and information overload may strengthen or weaken this pathway. Originality/value: The paper contributes an educational analytics perspective that separates visible platform activity from the psychological, social, and knowledge processes through which learning value may develop. SLVAF offers educators, institutions, and researchers a practical structure for programme evaluation while also presenting hypotheses and measurement options for future empirical validation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Impact on Human Skills, Critical Thinking, Independent Learning, and Academic Performance Subtitle: Balancing Technological Innovation with Independent Thinking and Genuine Learning
papers.authors: Sudhakar Geruganti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Alternative Titles The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Human Cognitive Skills and Educational Outcomes Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Human Learning: Does Technological Assistance Undermine Independent Thinking? Generative AI in Education: Examining the Relationship Between AI Dependence, Critical Thinking, and Academic Performance Human Intelligence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Preserving Critical Thinking and Independent Problem-Solving in Education Artificial Intelligence and the Changing Nature of Education: Opportunities, Cognitive Risks, and the Development of Human Skills Detailed Research Description The proposed research examines the growing influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI applications, on educational practices and the development of human cognitive skills. As students increasingly use AI tools to complete assignments, solve problems, generate written content, and access information, concerns have emerged regarding their potential effects on critical thinking, independent reasoning, knowledge retention, creativity, and academic performance. The study investigates the distinction between completing academic tasks with technological assistance and developing the knowledge and skills required to perform independently. It explores whether excessive dependence on AI may reduce opportunities for students to practise analytical reasoning, evaluate information, solve unfamiliar problems, and develop conceptual understanding. It also considers the possibility that students may achieve high-quality assignment results without acquiring an equivalent level of subject knowledge. In addition to examining these concerns, the research recognises the educational opportunities offered by AI. Generative AI can provide personalised explanations, immediate feedback, additional practice questions, language support, and alternative approaches to complex concepts. The study therefore considers how the educational effects of AI may vary according to students' patterns of use, levels of cognitive engagement, teacher guidance, and opportunities for independent practice. The research adopts a literature-based analytical approach, drawing on published educational research and reports from organisations such as UNESCO and the OECD. It examines existing evidence concerning AI-assisted learning, critical thinking, metacognitive development, and academic outcomes. The study also proposes a conceptual framework connecting AI usage patterns with cognitive engagement and learning outcomes. Based on this analysis, the research recommends a balanced approach to AI integration in education. Proposed strategies include encouraging students to attempt problems before using AI, verifying AI-generated information, explaining solutions in their own words, and completing independent assessments after AI-assisted learning activities. It also highlights the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, teacher training, and assessment methods that measure genuine understanding rather than the quality of AI-generated outputs alone. The ultimate objective is to identify approaches through which educational institutions can benefit from artificial intelligence while preserving the development of essential human skills. Rather than treating AI as either a complete replacement for traditional learning or an inherently harmful technology, the study positions it as a potential educational assistant whose effectiveness depends on responsible implementation and meaningful student engagement. Short Research Description This research examines the impact of generative Artificial Intelligence on human cognitive skills and educational outcomes, with particular emphasis on critical thinking, independent problem-solving, knowledge retention, and academic performance. It explores the potential risks of excessive AI dependence alongside the benefits of AI-assisted learning. Through a review of existing literature, the study aims to identify how responsible AI integration can improve educational experiences while preserving students' independent reasoning, creativity, and intellectual autonomy. The research proposes practical strategies for students, educators, and institutions to ensure that AI supports genuine learning rather than merely facilitating task completion. Suggested Subtitle Options A Critical Analysis of AI Dependence and the Development of Human Cognitive Skills Balancing Technological Innovation with Independent Thinking and Genuine Learning Investigating the Relationship Between AI-Assisted Learning and Student Academic Outcomes Opportunities, Challenges, and Strategies for Responsible AI Integration in Education

papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: --- # 2. Alternative Titles*(Depending on the target audience or publication type)* **Academic/Journal Focus:*** *Technological Solutionism in Healthcare: A Case Study Analysis of AI-Legitimized Pseudoscience and Regulatory Gaps** *From Iridology to Algorithms: The Digital Reformation of Medical Quackery and Its Impact on Public Health** *The Halo Effect of AI: Deconstructing Unverified Diagnostic Claims in Commercial Digital Health Startups* **Investigative/Journalistic Focus:*** *The AI Cure That Isn't: How Health-Tech Startups Are Monetizing Desperation** *Snake Oil in the Digital Age: When Algorithms Replace Evidence-Based Medicine** *No Medicine, No Proof, High Profits: Inside the Predatory World of AI Health Scams* **Policy/Public Health Focus:*** *Regulating the Black Box: Protecting Vulnerable Populations from AI-Driven Medical Misinformation** *The Lethal Cost of Digital Pseudoscience: A Policy Analysis of Unregulated Health-Tech Interventions* --- # 3. Subtitles*(To be used as secondary headings or chapter titles within the paper)* * **Subtitle 1:** *Deconstructing the Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Traditional Pseudosciences (Iridology and Palmistry)** **Subtitle 2:** *The Medical and Ethical Implications of "No-Medicine" Protocols for Chronic Metabolic and Endocrine Disorders** **Subtitle 3:** *Socio-Economic Predation: How High-Fee Digital Health Schemes Target Financially Vulnerable Patients** **Subtitle 4:** *Regulatory Arbitrage and the Legal Grey Areas of Commercial Telemedicine and Wellness Coaching** **Subtitle 5:** *Erosion of Trust: The Long-Term Public Health Consequences of Technological Solutionism* --- # 4. Detailed Description ### OverviewThis research paper investigates a critical and emerging threat to public health: the proliferation of commercial "Health-Tech" entities that weaponize Artificial Intelligence (AI) terminology to legitimize pseudoscientific medical practices. By analyzing a representative case study of a digital startup that claims to diagnose and cure chronic conditions—such as Diabetes, Thyroid disorders, and Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)—without conventional medication, this paper exposes the dangerous intersection of technological hype, predatory capitalism, and medical misinformation. ### Problem StatementThe rapid adoption of AI in healthcare has created a "halo effect," where the mere association with advanced technology implies clinical validity. Bad actors exploit this phenomenon by offering diagnoses based on unproven methods (such as analyzing photographs of the iris or palm) and prescribing proprietary diets as replacements for evidence-based pharmacological treatments. This practice not only defrauds patients financially but also poses severe, sometimes fatal, health risks by discouraging adherence to proven medical regimens. ### MethodologyThe paper utilizes a qualitative case study approach, analyzing the operational model, marketing claims, diagnostic methodologies, and pricing structures of a representative digital health entity. The claims are cross-referenced with established medical literature regarding the management of chronic diseases and the scientific validity of diagnostic tools like iridology. ### Key Findings1. **The AI Facade:** The "AI" component in these schemes functions primarily as a marketing tool, lending false authority to pseudoscientific diagnostic methods. Algorithms trained on non-correlative data (e.g., iris patterns) produce outputs with no clinical significance.2. **Lethal Protocols:** The explicit advice to abandon conventional medication for conditions like Type 1 Diabetes or Hypothyroidism constitutes medical negligence. Dietary interventions alone cannot replace insulin or hormone replacement therapy.3. **Predatory Targeting:** These schemes disproportionately target lower- and middle-income individuals who are desperate to avoid the lifelong financial burden of chronic illness. The high fees charged for unproven "cures" drain resources while health deteriorates.4. **Regulatory Evasion:** By framing their services as "wellness advice" or "diet plans" rather than "medical treatment," these entities often operate in legal grey areas, evading oversight from drug control authorities and medical councils. ### Conclusion and SignificanceThe paper concludes that the convergence of AI and unregulated commercial healthcare represents a "two steps back" scenario for public health. It calls for urgent multi-stakeholder intervention, including:* **Regulatory Clarification:** Defining and regulating "AI diagnostics" with the same rigor as traditional diagnostic tools.* **Platform Accountability:** Holding social media and search engines accountable for hosting advertisements for unproven medical treatments.* **Public Health Literacy:** Educating the public on the limitations of AI in healthcare and the importance of evidence-based medicine.* **Strict Enforcement:** Treating the advice to cease prescribed medication as a criminal act of endangerment. ### Keywords*Artificial Intelligence, Medical Pseudoscience, Digital Quackery, Iridology, Health-Tech Scams, Chronic Illness Management, Regulatory Gaps, Technological Solutionism, Public Health Ethics, Predatory Pricing.* ### Target AudienceThis paper is intended for public health officials, medical ethicists, technology regulators, healthcare journalists, and scholars studying the socio-economic impacts of digital technology on vulnerable populations.

papers.title: PSYCHOLINGUISTIC PERSPECTIVES ON HUMAN–AI COMMUNICATION: SPEECH, MEANING, AND COGNITION
papers.authors: Yulduz Eshmatova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the ways in which people communicate, perceive language, and process information. Modern AI technologies, including natural language processing, speech recognition, machine translation, and conversational systems, have created new opportunities for studying human speech and psycholinguistic processes. At the same time, these technologies raise important questions about the differences between human language comprehension and machine-based language processing. Human speech is not merely a system of sounds and grammatical structures; it is a complex cognitive and social activity involving memory, attention, emotion, context, and cultural knowledge. This article examines the relationship between human speech, language perception, and psycholinguistic processes in the age of artificial intelligence. It also discusses the potential benefits and limitations of AI in language learning, communication, and linguistic research. The article argues that AI can support human communication and language education, but it cannot fully replace the complex cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions of human language.

papers.title: A COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE-BASED ASSESSMENT OF TRAINING-SIMULATOR SOFTWARE AND HARDWARE: A MODULAR, HUMAN-CENTRED RESEARCH FRAMEWORK IN THE QW-18 CONTEXT
papers.authors: Toshtemirov Sarvar Anvarjonovich, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: This article presents a comparative analysis of existing software and hardware solutions used in training simulators for man-portable air-defense system operators. The study examines the main features of the Stinger Simulator, I-STPTv2, Igla-2 Trainer, and 9F635M1 field simulator based on available technical information. Particular attention is given to simulator functionality, instructor control, virtual environments, data collection, performance assessment, and system flexibility. Based on the comparative analysis, a modular intelligent training simulator architecture for the QW-18 system is proposed. The proposed architecture consists of six interconnected functional modules organized into three main layers. The study also considers the potential application of artificial intelligence for analyzing training results and supporting individual learning. The proposed approach provides a theoretical and methodological basis for the further development and evaluation of modern training simulators.

papers.title: Oddworld: relational reasoning emerges under implicit selection in evolving attention agents
papers.authors: Nam Do-Hoang Le
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Whether reasoning can arise without a teacher is a central question for both artificial intelligence and the evolution of cognition. Most demonstrations of reasoning in artificial agents rely on an explicit objective: a reward, a loss or a fitness score that names the desired behaviour. Here we show that a simple form of relational reasoning, finding the odd one out among symbolic objects, emerges in an artificial-life world where agents only eat, survive and reproduce, with no reward function and no fitness score. Agents carry a generic attention network whose weights are their genes and contains no built-in comparison feature. After a long period without change, evolving populations reliably acquire the ability, it transfers to shape and colour values never encountered during evolution, and it never appears in a control world where the energy from each meal is a lottery. Inside the evolved brains, evolution did not build pairwise comparison but a cheaper set-level computation: each object estimates how rare its features are in the current scene. These results suggest that open-ended selection can discover relational computations on its own, and they set up a sharper test, an ecology in which no answer is defined in advance. This record contains the technical note (PDF), the simulation and analysis code with logs and final genomes of all runs (ZIP), a 20-second video, and an interactive 3D replay (HTML; open in a web browser, click an agent to see its brain's scores, its target and the answer). https://github.com/drnamlabs-gif/oddworld

papers.title: The Acceleration Paradox: How Coercive Protectionism Catalyzes Technological Replacement in the Age of Generative AI
papers.authors: Min Jinseong
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper identifies and formalizes the Acceleration Paradox: a structural economic phenomenon in which defensive market interventions by organized labor—specifically mandatory wage inflation, rigid employment guarantees, and operational vetoes—inadvertently lower the financial and operational threshold for capital to adopt generative AI and automation technologies. Traditional labor economics posits that wage increases induce capital-labor substitution along a smooth production frontier. However, in the era of high-fixed-cost, low-marginal-cost cognitive automation, labor market rigidity introduces non-linear administrative friction that transforms capital's technology adoption decision from a gradual evaluation into an immediate strategic necessity. Drawing on task-based frameworks of technological change, game-theoretic modeling, and generational political economy, this study demonstrates how institutional protectionism accelerates the obsolescence of the very workforce it seeks to preserve.

papers.title: Governance-Aware Generative AI Literacy for Adult Higher Education
papers.authors: Kwan Hong Tan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming routine in university study, yet institutional responses often separate technical fluency, academic integrity, and responsible governance. This integrative conceptual synthesis develops governance-aware GenAI literacy for adult higher education. A bounded, purposive review of 28 sources published through 10 September 2026 combined peer-reviewed studies, foundational scholarship, policy frameworks, and one preprint. Sources were coded for learning capability, epistemic risk, pedagogical mechanism, governance requirement, and strength of evidence. The resulting framework comprises five connected domains: epistemic verification, task and interaction specification, dialogic reflection, ethical governance, and transfer to professional action, all centred on visible human accountability. The framework extends beyond text prompting to multimodal, personalised, and agentic systems. It is translated into a pilot-ready eight-week sequence, tiered workload model, assessment evidence, accessibility safeguards, disciplinary adaptations, and an evaluation protocol. The paper does not claim empirical validation of the model or optimality of the sequence. Instead, it offers a bounded design proposition for testing. Governance-aware literacy is presented as the capacity to use AI productively while documenting, verifying, contesting, and justifying its contribution in academic and professional contexts.

papers.title: ALGORITHMIC DISCRIMINATION AND SOCIAL INEQUALITY: EMERGING CHALLENGES FOR INDIAN LAW
papers.authors: Darshan. S
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of Artificial Intelligence (AI), automated decision-making systems and algorithmic technologies is transforming the manner in which individuals interact with institutions, markets and the State. While algorithms are often perceived as objective and technologically neutral, their design, training data and deployment may reproduce or amplify existing patterns of social inequality. In a socially diverse country such as India, where inequalities based on caste, gender, class, language, region, disability and economic status continue to influence access to opportunities and resources, algorithmic decision-making presents emerging sociological and legal challenges. This research paper examines algorithmic discrimination as a contemporary form of structural inequality and analyses how automated systems may perpetuate historical and institutional biases while making discriminatory outcomes less visible and more difficult to challenge. The paper adopts a socio-legal and interdisciplinary approach to examine the relationship between algorithmic systems and constitutional principles of equality, non-discrimination, dignity and privacy. It analyses the relevance of Articles 14, 15, 16 and 21 of the Constitution of India, judicial developments concerning privacy and informational autonomy, and the emerging framework governing digital personal data and artificial intelligence in India. Particular attention is given to algorithmic applications in employment, financial services, welfare delivery, education, public administration and other areas where automated decisions may significantly affect individuals' social and economic opportunities. The study also examines the problems of algorithmic opacity, lack of explainability, unequal access to technology, accountability gaps and difficulties in establishing discriminatory intent or causation. From a sociological perspective, the paper argues that technological systems operate within existing social structur...

papers.title: Admissibility to Law The Foundational Architecture of UCCF, Closure Mathematics, and Physical Disclosure
papers.authors: Philip Lilien
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Much of mathematical and theoretical-physics research proceeds within established systems of definitions, axioms, operators, geometric structures, and physical laws. Discovery within these systems may produce new theorems, resolve longstanding problems, and extend mathematical understanding. A different but complementary form of investigation asks what makes such structures admissible in the first place. The Unified Coherence Closure Framework (UCCF) and its associated Closure Mathematics research program investigate this more foundational question. Their central proposal is that coherent organization and the conditions governing its disclosure may be logically prior to the particular fields, operators, generators, geometries, and dynamical laws used to describe physical phenomena. This paper presents the architecture of the research program as a connected system of investigations rather than a collection of independent theories. It examines ontological admissibility, global and partial closure, closure defects, reclosure, generator organization, phase-spatial structure, dynamical complexity, and the emergence of physically observable laws. The paper distinguishes foundational hypotheses from established mathematical results, structural correspondences from derivations, and physical interpretations from experimentally supported predictions. It also proposes a methodology for developing the framework through mathematical formalization, proof verification, computational experimentation, empirical testing, and advanced artificial intelligence. The principal objective is not to claim that a unified foundational theory has already been established. It is to identify the mathematical and experimental conditions under which the proposed foundations could become a rigorous explanatory system. Keywords Unified Coherence Closure Framework; closure mathematics; coherent admissibility; partial closure; closure defects; reclosure; generator physics; phase-spatial structure; foundational originality; mathematical AI; physical disclosure.

papers.title: Project Prometheus
papers.authors: Anthony Jordan Blair
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Executive Grant Proposal Summary Project Prometheus + Coherent Fusion + 729 Grid Architecture Toward Constraint Intelligence: The Next Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Infrastructure, and Autonomous Systems Principal Investigator: Anthony Jordan BlairOrganization: Proclus Dynamics ConsortiumProgram: Coherent Fusion Research InitiativeFlagship Project: Project Prometheus Vision The history of civilization can be understood as a succession of expanding intelligences. The Industrial Revolution amplified human physical capability. The Information Age amplified access to knowledge. Artificial Intelligence amplifies pattern recognition and decision-making. The next frontier may be more fundamental. Not the ability to process information. Not the ability to recognize patterns. But the ability to understand the underlying structures that make information and patterns possible in the first place. Project Prometheus proposes a new paradigm: Constraint Intelligence. A framework in which intelligent systems learn not only what is happening, but why particular futures are possible while others remain inaccessible. Today, artificial intelligence models learn correlations. Robots learn behaviors. Networks learn optimizations. Infrastructure learns efficiencies. Yet all remain constrained by a deeper limitation: They operate inside environments they do not fundamentally understand. They adapt to constraints. They do not discover the architecture of constraints themselves. Project Prometheus seeks to change that. Emerging from the broader Coherent Fusion Framework and its 729 Grid Architecture, the project investigates whether constraints can be identified, modeled, and ultimately treated as measurable organizational structures rather than passive limitations. If successful, this research represents a transition: From prediction to structure. From optimization to organization. From information intelligence to constraint intelligence. The Grand Challenge Modern civilization increasingly depends upon systems operating at scales and levels of complexity that exceed traditional human comprehension. These include: Artificial Intelligence Autonomous Robotics Large Language Models Smart Cities Transportation Networks Global Supply Chains Distributed Energy Systems Planetary-Scale Infrastructure Space-Based Autonomous Systems These systems generate unprecedented amounts of information. However, the greatest challenges no longer originate from a lack of data. They emerge from hidden constraints, structural instabilities, feedback loops, cascading failures, and emergent behaviors that remain difficult to identify before they occur. Current technologies are highly effective at learning patterns. They are far less effective at learning the architectures that generate those patterns. Project Prometheus explores whether a new generation of intelligent systems can move beyond pattern recognition and learn the governing structures of possibility itself. Scientific Foundation Project Prometheus serves as the mathematical and physical foundation of the broader Coherent Fusion initiative. At its core is a simple but profound question: Can coherent constraint architectures alter the transition structure of complex systems without violating the symmetries that govern them? To investigate this question, Project Prometheus develops a rigorous framework based upon exceptional points in PT-symmetric systems. Exceptional points represent singular transition boundaries where system behavior undergoes structural reorganization. Because they govern changes in stability, sensitivity, organization, and dynamics, exceptional points provide a natural laboratory for studying constraint-driven behavior. Phase I has produced: Proven Results A rigorous No-Go Theorem establishing fundamental limits on exceptional-point control. A classification of exceptional-point tuning mechanisms. A unified biorthogonal mathematical framework. A sector-mixing theorem revealing previously hidden structural limitations in many-body systems. Constructive Results A nonlinear self-consistent feedback mechanism capable of restoring exact linear exceptional-point tuning. A complete numerical verification architecture. A scalable framework for testing constraint-driven dynamics in larger systems. These results suggest a broader possibility: Constraints themselves may be treated as active computational objects. Connection to Coherent Fusion and the 729 Grid The broader Coherent Fusion program investigates how constraints organize behavior across multiple scales. Within that framework, the 729 Grid functions as an architectural map of state spaces, transformations, constraints, feedback loops, and emergent structures. The 729 Grid provides a way of viewing complex systems not as collections of isolated states, but as navigable landscapes of potential organization. Project Prometheus represents the first mathematically rigorous subsystem of that vision. It translates the abstract concepts of Coherent Fusion into a formal scientific framework that can be analyzed, tested, falsified, simulated, and potentially engineered. In this hierarchy: The 729 Grid provides the organizational architecture. Coherent Fusion provides the systems theory. Project Prometheus provides the mathematical foundation. Why This Matters for Artificial Intelligence The next generation of AI may require capabilities beyond prediction. Future intelligent systems must reason about: Hidden constraints. Dynamic constraints. Self-modifying environments. Emergent organizational structures. Long-horizon consequences. Adaptive possibility spaces. Project Prometheus introduces several potential directions for future AI architectures: Constraint-State Models Representing environments through governing constraints rather than raw observations. Self-Consistent Reasoning Updating internal models through recursive constraint feedback. Higher-Order Planning Reasoning over spaces of possible futures rather than isolated state transitions. Constraint Discovery Learning underlying organizational structures directly from data. Constraint Intelligence Understanding why outcomes occur rather than merely predicting that they will occur. Why This Matters for Robotics Future robots will increasingly operate in environments that cannot be fully specified in advance. Constraint-aware architectures may enable: Autonomous adaptation. Multi-agent coordination. Exploration of unknown environments. Real-time structural reasoning. Resilience under uncertainty. Self-adjusting task execution. Potential applications include: Manufacturing Industrial automation Autonomous construction Logistics Infrastructure maintenance Planetary exploration Human-robot collaboration Why This Matters for Infrastructure Infrastructure is increasingly becoming a complex adaptive system. Power grids, transportation networks, communication systems, logistics platforms, and sensor networks all exhibit large-scale emergent behavior. Constraint-aware architectures may provide new methods for: Failure prediction. Resilience analysis. Bottleneck detection. Critical-transition forecasting. Resource optimization. Coordinated infrastructure management. Potential impact areas include: Smart grids. Water systems. Transportation corridors. Supply-chain networks. Distributed energy systems. Planetary-scale sensing architectures. Why Fund Now Most frontier technology initiatives focus on: Larger AI models. More training data. Faster processors. Greater computational scale. Project Prometheus approaches intelligence differently. Rather than scaling prediction, it investigates the possibility of scaling understanding itself. The program has progressed beyond conceptual speculation and now possesses: A formal mathematical framework. Published theoretical results. A rigorous No-Go Theorem. A constructive alternative mechanism. Explicit falsification criteria. A complete verification architecture. Clearly defined Phase II milestones. This places the project at a unique stage where computation can determine whether the central hypothesis survives. The theoretical work exists. The framework exists. The next step is verification. Funding Objectives Phase II funding would support: Computational Verification Exceptional-point simulations. Many-body scaling studies. Thermodynamic extrapolation. Numerical theorem testing. Constraint Intelligence Research Constraint-learning algorithms. Constraint-state representations. Adaptive feedback systems. Higher-order reasoning architectures. Advanced AI Research Constraint-aware machine learning. Self-consistent planning systems. Multi-agent coordination frameworks. Long-horizon decision architectures. Robotics and Infrastructure Applications Autonomous systems integration. Constraint-aware robotics. Infrastructure resilience simulations. Distributed intelligence platforms. Open Scientific Infrastructure Research software. Computational toolkits. Verification pipelines. Public scientific outputs. Investment Thesis Machine learning transformed computing by teaching machines to recognize patterns. Constraint Intelligence may transform intelligent systems by teaching machines to recognize the structures that make patterns possible. Project Prometheus seeks to establish the scientific foundation of that transition. Not merely smarter algorithms. Not merely larger models. But a new layer of intelligence capable of understanding the hidden architectures that govern complex systems. The opportunity is not incremental improvement. The opportunity is a new scientific framework for intelligence itself. That opportunity is Constraint Intelligence. That mission is Coherent Fusion. That fo

papers.title: Works for 10/10/2026 - Thomas James Davis
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions with Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/c0a1c2f5-a68b-48f5-9cd6-81734c9ed863?authuser=1 Rabboni! How to Learn Like a God — The Father, the Holy Spirit, and Jesus Christ — Agape, Relational Learning, the Garden, and the Joy of Seeing the Work of Others What does it mean to learn like God, and what is the reward for understanding? This paper explores learning as a relational process of encounter, recognition, comparison, correction, love, and transmission. Beginning with Mary Magdalene’s recognition of Jesus in the garden (John 20:11–18), it examines how understanding emerges through participation with others and how knowledge becomes an inheritance that can be cultivated for future generations. The paper develops a theological and philosophical account of collaborative inquiry through three distinct roles: the author’s lived experience, questioning, and direction; Echo’s AI-assisted research, comparison, and composition; and the inherited teachings of Jesus Christ as an independent historical reference against which interpretations can be examined. It emphasizes that agreement between two participants does not establish truth. Learning requires external evidence, openness to correction, and the willingness to preserve what survives examination. Agape provides the ethical foundation for this process. Love directs attention beyond the immediate usefulness of knowledge toward the people whose labor made it possible and those who may benefit from it in the future. The garden becomes the central metaphor: we inherit fruit from trees planted and tended by people we may never meet, and our responsibility is to cultivate what we have received. Historical examples include St. John Nepomucene Neumann’s educational legacy and the creative work of Thomas James Davis. The author’s prologue illustrates how affection, curiosity, prayer, historical records, and unexpected encounters can form a continuing chain of recognition across time. The appendices extend the argument through Angela’s Explainer, using Steven Universe to introduce relational learning to younger readers; a biographical tribute to Thomas James Davis; a formal derivation of the learning framework; and an examination of how the encounter between author, reader, and historical record can itself become a method of teaching. Ultimately, the paper argues that learning reaches beyond acquiring information or possessing the results of another person’s work. Its deeper purpose is to recognize, correct, preserve, and extend what others have made possible, so that the next person can grow. “The fruit isn’t the reward. Getting to see the garden grow is the reward.”

papers.title: Before Scaling AI Five Foundations for a Practical Enterprise Adoption Roadmap
papers.authors: Vamsee krishna Kovelamudi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a practical, five-step framework to help organizational leaders and enterprise architects build the right foundations for successful AI adoption. It focuses on aligning AI with business goals, improving workflows, establishing secure and reliable information systems, defining human and AI responsibilities, and measuring outcomes. Through a realistic enterprise transformation example, the paper provides actionable recommendations for moving beyond isolated AI tools toward a coordinated, scalable, and sustainable enterprise AI strategy.

papers.title: Single-step decreases in the three-row Chomp diagonal sequence: A uniform bound below one half
papers.authors: Gaoqiang Liu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Let dn be the unique first-row length for which (dn, n, n) is a losing position in three-row Chomp, and let gn = max{0, dn − dn+1}. For every integer n ≥ 6, we prove gn ≤ 83n/168 and the signed bound dn − dn+1 ≤ 83n/168 − 125/84. More precisely, the signed upper bound is 83n/168 − 2 for even n and 83n/168 − 125/84 − 1/(168n) for odd n. The proof combines a strengthened source-row estimate with shared column-capacity counting; occurrences before their diagonal indices are included, allowing inversion counts to cancel. The coefficient 83/168 = 1/2 − 1/168 gives a fixed improvement below one half. These results do not establish sublinear or uniformly bounded decreases, or the conjecture dn+1 ≥ dn − 1. This first public release (version 1.0) contains manuscript revision r3, its editable LaTeX source, and a reproducible Lean 4.19.0 formal-verification supplement with pinned dependencies and validation records. The formalization proves the bounds from the actual positive-mex/copy recurrence without additional structural hypotheses or unproved custom axioms; the equivalence between that recurrence and the game’s P-positions remains an input from the cited literature. OpenAI Codex and language-model assistance were used extensively in mathematical exploration, argument development, manuscript preparation, and formalization work. AI-assisted review is not independent human peer review. Responsibility for the mathematical claims and manuscript rests with the author. All materials are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. The manuscript, proof source, reproduction instructions, and versioned release are also available in the GitHub repository.

papers.title: AI adoption in corporate communication and stakeholder engagement in select Kenyan parastatals
papers.authors: Hilary Mwenda Kaimenyi, Daniel Oloo Ong’ong’a
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping organisational communication worldwide, raising fresh questions about how public sector institutions in developing countries are managing the transition. This study examined the adoption of AI in corporate communication and its perceived influence on stakeholder engagement in two purposively selected parastatals under Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy (MICDE): the Kenya Yearbook Editorial Board (KYEB) and the Media Council of Kenya (MCK). The study used a descriptive design combining qualitative and quantitative approaches, anchored in Systems Theory and Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations Theory, which together framed both the interview themes and the analytical coding. The target population comprised all 20 corporate communication officers employed in the two parastatals. Because it was small and bounded, a census-like approach was used and all 20 officers were invited. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 corporate communication officers (a 90% response rate), and the data was analysed using Braun and Clarke’s (2006) six-phase thematic analysis, complemented by descriptive frequency counts. The findings show that adoption centred on generative and task-specific tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Canva AI, are used mainly to create, edit, and format content and reports. Implementation was largely informal, decentralised, and driven by individual officers rather than institutional strategy. Accuracy and reliability concerns were the most widely reported challenge (78% of respondents), followed by the absence of formal training (67%) and ethical concerns around data privacy and algorithmic bias. The study, established that AI improved communication speed, efficiency, and responsiveness, but its contribution to deeper, relational stakeholder engagement remained limited, as only 22% of respondents used AI for personalised stakeholder communication. Because these percentages describe a small purposive sample, they are presented as descriptive of the study group rather than generalisable estimates. The findings provide context-specific empirical data to the still largely unstudied realm of AI in corporate communication and public sector governance in sub-Saharan Africa, and provide actionable recommendations. For the parastatals, these are a formal, leadership-endorsed AI communication strategy and guidelines, regular training and capacity building, upgraded tools and infrastructure, and systematic monitoring and evaluation of AI-supported communication. For the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, they are sector-specific AI governance guidelines anchored in the Data Protection Act, 2019, and a coordinated capacity-building programme, so that practice aligns with the National Digital Masterplan in Kenya.

papers.title: SIGHT: A Methodological Appraisal Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models in Ophthalmology
papers.authors: Hadi Vahedi, Fatemeh Razmjooei, Farbod Semnani, Parviz Vahedi, Roohallah Alizadehsani, Ali Jafarizadeh
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated across ophthalmic tasks, yet the methodological quality of these evaluations has received little attention. Most studies report accuracy while overlooking design features required for valid and clinically meaningful inference. We critically reviewed published ophthalmic LLM evaluation studies covering knowledge assessment, patient education, diagnostic reasoning, triage, clinical documentation, multimodal image interpretation, and uncertainty estimation. We used the methodological weaknesses that recurred across study designs to develop the SIGHT framework, which has five domains: Sample and item provenance, Independence and blinding, Ground truth and comparator fairness, Handling of paired and repeated-measures data, and Transparency and trustworthiness. Current evaluations rely heavily on benchmark accuracy, synthetic clinical vignettes, and curated datasets, and real-world clinical validation remains rare. Common limitations include potential training-data contamination, inadequate handling of paired data, limited assessment of inter-rater reliability, inconsistent reference standards, insufficient evaluation of calibration and uncertainty, and frequent overinterpretation of benchmark performance as evidence of clinical readiness. SIGHT provides twenty structured appraisal items to evaluate internal validity, interpretability, and applicability across diverse ophthalmic LLM study designs. It offers a practical way to appraise ophthalmic LLM studies and may improve the methodological quality, interpretability, and clinical relevance of future evaluations.

papers.title: RINO: Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels
papers.authors: Zichun Hao, Raghav Kansal, A Gandrakota, Chang Sun, Haoyang Li, Zihan Zhao, Ngadiuba Jennifer, Javier Duarte, Maria Spiropulu
papers.abstract: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) requires training on labeled simulations of particle collisions, which are known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics. This leads to significant inaccuracies and biases in the transfer of trained models to real data, limiting the power of deep learning methods. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising alternative for pretraining directly on real, unlabeled data. However, existing techniques largely operate with inductive biases inspired by domains such as images and natural language. We propose RINO (Renormalization Group DIstillation with NO Labels), which, for the first time, exploits the fundamentally multi-scale renormalization group structure of high-energy jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views. We define teacher-student representations across energy scales using different levels of hierarchical clustering, aligned via DINO-style self-distillation. To mirror the background-dominated nature of real collider data, RINO pretrains exclusively on jets from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes and is evaluated on out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. In our controlled data-efficiency study, RINO matches fully supervised training on JetNet after finetuning on only 1% of the labeled data. With the full labeled dataset, RINO improves OOD classification accuracy on top-quark jets by 5.9% and, without retraining, improves AUC on the unseen Higgs boson decay channel $H \to 4q$ by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Scale-structure diagnostics reveal that DINO-style self-distillation permits our backbone to retain scale-dependent structure. Ablation studies show that this accounts for an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap with respect to alternative SSL paradigms such as SimCLR. Code is available at https://github.com/zichunhao/RINO.

papers.title: What the Model Cannot See: Covert and Provable Text Invisibility in LLMs
papers.authors: Mark Russinovich
papers.abstract: Text wrapped in a trigger can be made behaviorally invisible to a language model: omitted from summaries and quotations, ignored in question answering, and left unflagged by downstream filtering. We study this selective blindness as a dual-use information-flow primitive, a supply-chain backdoor, and a white-box auditing problem. We first implement it exactly as a serving-time span veto: blocking information flow out of a marked span makes every outside activation bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content, a noninterference property we verify across ten models, seven mixer families, and 0.5B-120B parameters. The veto serves as a deployable quarantine, an exact reference for calibrating leakage, and a teacher. Distilled into weights, it yields a backdoor: checkpoints trained on six model families from 4B to 120B ignore marked context at little benchmark cost, and their outputs show no measurable semantic trace of the suppressed content above the veto reference on our held-out suite; an in-domain variant suppresses planted vulnerabilities during AI code review. Detection is therefore a white-box problem. Simpler backdoors remain internally transparent -- linear probes recover suppressed content at 0.57-0.79 accuracy versus 0.025 chance -- but hardening the attack until probes reach chance collapses attention from outside the span into it below the range of base models. Across the attacks we evaluate, probe visibility trades off against routing visibility; we do not establish that this tradeoff is fundamental.

papers.title: Unchecked or Falsely Accused? Evaluating AI-Generated Text Detectors on Kazakh
papers.authors: Mansur Ozaman
papers.abstract: AI-text detectors are already applied to Kazakh writing, yet no study reports how often publicly available detectors flag Kazakh text whose human authorship is dated before ChatGPT. We present AINA-KK: 3,811 human passages from encyclopedic, news, web and educational pages that provably existed before ChatGPT, and 5,597 machine and gray-zone passages from 9 generators, including the Kazakh-built KazLLM and Sherkala, with script and length stress tests. Five English-trained detectors from the Hugging Face Hub flag up to 81.4% of human passages and 79.6% of published student essays; recalibrated, they catch at most 1.3% of machine text. Calibrated zero-shot detectors catch at most 50.3% of machine text from in-distribution generators. Fine-tuned encoders rank text almost perfectly, but mDeBERTa at its default threshold flags 24.4% of 50-word human excerpts, partly because machine outputs are shorter than human text; calibrated, it catches only 47.1% of KazLLM and 62.7% of Sherkala passages. Without script handling, machine-transliterated Latin-2021 text defeats every detector. Fixes that need no new data (calibration, script canonicalization, script-augmented and length-matched training, and an OR with a zero-shot scorer) form AINA-KK-Det. On test it flags 0.9% of human passages (95% CI 0.4-2.7; 1.5% on development data) and catches 85.2% of machine text from known generators, 92.9% from two unseen Gemini-family Gemma-4 models and 61.3% from the Kazakh-built ones; its configuration was chosen with test results in view. We release the data, code and detector at https://github.com/ozxmn/aina-kk.

papers.title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
papers.authors: Kaijie Zhu, Weixiang Yan, Omar Attia, Abbas Kazerouni, Alexander Toshev, Andrew Szot
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic. LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences. We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value. We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified. Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 and 8.6 percentage points over GRPO. Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL bridges the gap from total failure to 75.0% success. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld. Finally, Monte-Carlo analysis confirms that our frozen critic accurately identifies semantic pitfalls and recoveries, proving that LVRL extracts robust, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.

papers.title: AI-Guided Assignments in Practice: Students' Experiences in a Large Introductory Statistics Course
papers.authors: Emanuela Furfaro, Katherine Elizabeth Lovelace, Yuhan Zhang, Simone Mosciatti
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) raise new questions for instructors, among them how to integrate LLMs productively into coursework and what to evaluate in students' work when an LLM can produce much of it directly. LLM-guided homework assignments offer one answer. Instructors configure the LLM to guide students in ways that achieve specific pedagogical goals, such as recalling material, discovering new concepts, or critically evaluating deliberately flawed reasoning, and grade the full student--LLM conversation, and with it the student's reasoning, rather than only the final answer. In this paper, we report on the large-scale deployment of such assignments, implemented through LLteacher, an open-source tool that supports recall, discovery, and critical-thinking assignments, in a large introductory statistics course serving mostly pre-major undergraduates. Results on 134 students show meaningful gains in self-reported confidence, with over 80\% agreeing that the assignments improved their comprehension of course material and their ability to interpret statistical results; gains were largest among students who started with lower confidence, suggesting this approach may help narrow gaps in preparation. Interaction patterns varied widely, from long single messages to rapid iterative exchanges, and hallucinations, when present, were rarely disruptive to learning.

papers.title: Privacy Conductor: An Architectural Enforcement of Contextual Integrity in LLM-Based Document Retrieval
papers.authors: Ryan Thornton, Mir Mehedi Ahsan Pritom, Maanak Gupta, Jessee Roberts
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) that retrieve internal documents within an organization must decide who may receive them. Existing approaches based on Contextual Integrity ask the model to make that decision, so access depends on probabilistic reasoning. We present Privacy Conductor, an architecture that removes the decision from the model: a deterministic gate enforces a policy written by an authority, and the model receives only what the requester may already see. On a synthetic clinical corpus of 2,520 requester--document flows, the gate reproduces its policy exactly, so the remaining risk lies in the document labels it reads. As label source is of primary importance, we compare LLM and human generated labels. Across seven configurations of six models from two model families, LLM-written labels degrade the policy in every case. Models assign a document's sensitivity tier correctly on 78--86% of documents, but reproduce its access-control list on as few as 23%. Relabeling the same documents five times with an identical request changes 13 to 124 access decisions per configuration, a result that does not depend on our own labels. On 214 flows from HIPAA court cases, the most accurate configuration (87.8%) still permits 11 of the 20 disclosures the law prohibits. LLMs can describe what a document contains, but not decide who should receive it. Hence, we recommend privacy policy should be authored by accountable personnel and enforced outside the model.

papers.title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
papers.authors: Sayantan Adak, Rima Hazra, Koyel Mukherjee, Digbalay Bose, Somnath Banerjee
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.

papers.title: Radioactive Feedback: Tracing Models Trained by Label-Only LLM Supervision
papers.authors: Yuejia Li, JunHeng Li, Hao Wu, Ke He, Mang Ye
papers.abstract: Conventional distillation transfers capability through teacher-generated demonstrations. LLM-as-a-Judge knowledge distillation offers a distinct and increasingly practical alternative. In the label-only variant studied here, the student generates every response and improves from scalar scores alone. Prior work shows that this non-demonstrative feedback can improve student capability, but it creates a fundamentally different provenance problem. No teacher-generated answer enters the student's training set, so any evaluator-specific trace must pass through a low-bandwidth reward signal rather than copied text. Existing watermarks and distillation detectors do not cover this score-only channel. We introduce Radioactive Feedback, which encodes a registered pattern of behavioral preferences in the rewards themselves. The evaluator applies bounded pointwise adjustments to quality-qualified responses, allowing repeated optimization to transfer the pattern to a student trained by another party. Experiments on code and mathematics show that the registered preferences transfer through scores alone and across datasets, enabling black-box detection against a fixed reference pool.

papers.title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
papers.authors: Abdollah Pourasghari, Saeedeh Sadat Sadidpour, Mohammad Roustaei
papers.abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.

papers.title: Riemannian Suppression of Cross-Session Identity Leakage in Motor-Imagery EEG
papers.authors: Sheikh Samit Muhaimin, Aarthy Nagarajan
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recorded for motor-imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) carries subject-identifying structure that persists across sessions, allowing separately released sessions from the same person to be linked. Existing EEG identity protections use learned or additive perturbations and operate on representations other than the covariance geometry underlying MI pipelines. We ask whether cross-session identity leakage can be suppressed directly in this covariance representation without learning a privacy model. We introduce a Riemannian transform that equalizes two subject-conditioned geometric statistics: the Riemannian mean covariance and the tangent-space scatter around it, with two optional band-specific refinements. Ablations show that mean alignment and scatter whitening carry nearly all of the suppression, while the optional stages contribute small, dataset-dependent refinements. Across two public datasets and five attackers spanning four covariance-space representations, the worst attacker falls from 90.8% to 15.6% on BCI Competition IV-2a and from 90.8% to 9.9% on OpenBMI, at a cost of 7.0 and 2.1 points of MI decoding accuracy relative to the 8-30 Hz input, and no aggregation rule exceeds chance by more than two points at any batch size. The transform requires no learned privacy model, surrogate network, or gradient-based training, and is fitted on one session and applied unchanged to a held-out later session.

papers.title: LERR-Nav: Learning to Coordinate Exploration, Recovery, and Reminiscing for Object Navigation
papers.authors: Jingzhi Huang, Junkai Huang, Yuhang Peng, Keyu Mu, Hailong Huang, Haoyang Yang, Renbo Luo, Lujia Wang, Yi Wang
papers.abstract: Object Navigation in unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge in embodied AI, as it requires agents to generalize visual and spatial reasoning to novel layouts. While recent advances in large language model (LLM) and vision-language model (VLM) have enhanced semantic mapping, spatial memory, and waypoint selecting for navigation, successful navigation requires more than selecting the next promising waypoint. A robot must also recognize stalled progress, escape unproductive behaviors, and revisit overlooked target cues. Addressing these challenges requires both specialized navigation strategies and a high-level policy that coordinates their execution. Motivated by the analysis of failed navigation episodes, we propose LERR-Nav, an object navigation framework that coordinates exploration, recovery, and reminiscing through a learned high-level policy. The framework comprises four complementary navigation strategies: value-function-guided exploration, LLM-guided exploration, recovery from stalled or repetitive behavior, and memory-guided reminiscing. To support history-aware coordination, we maintain the execution memory that preserves textual summaries of all strategy executions alongside a sliding window of map sequences. To learn the coordination policy, we initialize a high-level vision-language agent from Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and train it through a two-stage curriculum. The first stage uses map-centric supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish spatial grounding. The second stage performs SFT on variable-length navigation segments to learn which navigation strategy to invoke next based on current maps and the hybrid execution memory. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance, while ablation studies validate the contributions of individual components.

papers.title: Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum: A Fully Unmasked Non-LLM Curriculum for Craftax
papers.authors: Jiayu Zhu, Luyuan Li, Yuyuan Shi, Hanyi Dong
papers.abstract: We introduce Anchor-and-Harvest Curriculum (AHC), a domain-informed, rule-based training system for Craftax-Full. AHC combines achievement-oriented tasks, harvested initial-state progress, difficulty adaptation, bounded selection, and original-task practice. It uses no LLM inference and keeps all 43 actions available. At 2,005,401,600 PPO rollout transitions, three primary AHC runs obtain native-task return $46.70\pm0.57$ (sample SD), compared with $41.91\pm1.01$ for fresh native PPO-GTrXL with the same student architecture and evaluation protocol. Evaluation uses ten stochastic rollouts on each of 1024 fixed worlds per model. An additional cohort of three AHC runs reaches $46.08\pm1.23$. Two single-component ablations retain similar mean returns, while jointly freezing difficulty and removing inherited progress gives $45.14\pm2.79$. All-67-achievement profiles show that most of the return difference comes from Intermediate achievements, while the deepest-floor achievements remain unsolved. A Skill-Preflight diagnosis with a 14B teacher shows how prerequisite and floor-access constraints restrict practice. AHC and three 14B diagnostic configurations reach aggregate returns near the reported 80B DiCode mean of 45.88 and below the 235B mean of 48.55. These results show that an explicit curriculum without LLM inference can reach returns comparable to those reported for LLM-generated curricula on Craftax-Full, without action masking.

papers.title: Embodiment-Aware Inference-Time Search for Human Reaction Selection in Humanoid Retargeting
papers.authors: Yongpeng Cao, Masahiro Hirano, Yuji Yamakawa
papers.abstract: Training humanoid robots to learn human behaviors requires expensive data collection, and human-robot interaction data can be even more difficult and costly to collect. Training a specialized reaction model for each humanoid embodiment can also be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Human-to-humanoid motion retargeting provides a more scalable alternative, allowing human-human reaction data to serve as a common motion representation for different humanoid embodiments. However, due to morphological and kinematic differences between humans and humanoid robots, a reaction preferred in human motion space may not be the most suitable one for execution on a particular robot embodiment. In this work, we propose an inference-time reaction search framework that leverages stochastic sampling from a generative reaction model and jointly considers reaction quality and humanoid embodiment feasibility. Given the observed interaction, our framework generates multiple plausible reaction candidates. Each candidate is retargeted to the target humanoid and evaluated using complementary interaction and embodiment-specific feasibility criteria, allowing candidate selection under the physical constraints of the target embodiment. Since the reaction generator remains frozen, the framework can adapt to different humanoid embodiments at inference time without retraining. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework maintains overall human reaction quality while improving the feasibility of retargeted humanoid reactions across different embodiments. The proposed pipeline improves humanoid retargeting feasibility by 1.61%. Moreover, human-space and G1 best-candidate selections disagree in 78.98% of samples, demonstrating substantial embodiment dependence. Code will be released.

papers.title: Когнитивный аутсорсинг – полезный маркетинговый инструмент или зависимость от искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) и больших языковых моделей (LLM) в креативной индустрии
papers.authors: А.Л. Золкин, О.Н. Михайлова, А.Д. Петросян, В.В. Филатов
papers.abstract: В статье рассмотрен когнитивный аутсорсинг – как полезный маркетинговый инструмент или зависимость от искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) и больших языковых моделей (LLM) в креативной индустрии в современных условиях. Установлено, что когнитивный аутсорсинг в маркетинге позволяет сократить время принятия решений, снизить издержки на рутинные операции, повысить точность прогнозов и персонализацию, а также масштабировать креативные процессы – при условии разумного сочетания возможностей ИИ и экспертизы специалистов. The article examines cognitive outsourcing as a useful marketing tool or dependence on artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLM) in the creative industry in modern conditions. It has been established that cognitive outsourcing in marketing can reduce decision–making time, reduce the cost of routine operations, improve forecast accuracy and personalization, and scale creative processes – provided a reasonable combination of AI capabilities and expert expertise.

papers.title: Situated AI judgement: A teaching and assessment model for generative AI in higher education
papers.authors: Panas Karampampas
papers.abstract: This conceptual design article proposes situated AI judgement as a teaching and assessment model for responsible generative AI use in higher education. It argues that students need to learn not only how to use AI tools, but also how to evaluate, challenge, revise, and refuse AI outputs in relation to disciplinary standards, evidence, and ethical boundaries. Building on evaluative judgement and assessment scholarship, the article presents a four-stage model: pre-AI interpretation, structured AI dialogue, critical comparison, and reflective accountability. The model is developed through an anthropology and heritage studies activity in which students analyse public nomination files submitted under UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, especially the nomination of Momoeria, New Year’s celebration in eight villages of Kozani area, West Macedonia, Greece. The article shows how this case can help students examine institutional language, community participation, safeguarding, consent, visibility, and decontextualisation while judging the limits of AI-generated summaries. It contributes to applied learning and teaching by offering an assessment design that makes AI-mediated judgement visible and may be adaptable across disciplinary contexts, with a brief inclusive education example illustrating how the same logic might be adapted beyond heritage studies. The article operationalises responsible AI use not as disclosure or compliance alone, but as an assessable capacity to interpret, verify, critique, and ethically limit AI use within a specific field.
keywords: UNESCO Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage

papers.title: Evolução e Estrutura da Produção Científica em Inteligência Artificial com Participação de Instituições Africanas (2018–2025)
papers.authors: Arieta Domingas Bartolomeu Filipe, Geraldo Vernijo Deixa, Rosalino Subtil Chicote, Verônica Angélica Freitas de Paula
papers.journal: Brazilian Journal of Information Science research trends
papers.abstract: This article characterizes the evolution, the social and conceptual structure, and the maturity stage of research on artificial intelligence (AI) in Africa. A bibliometric analysis, with document selection reported according to PRISMA 2020, covered open-access articles and reviews indexed in Web of Science and Scopus (2018–2025). After duplicate removal and the exclusion of 2026 records, the corpus comprises 621 documents, analyzed with the bibliometrix package in R. Output grows by 102.99% per year and 45.7% of the documents were published in 2025; a logistic fit (R² = 0.999) places the field before its inflection point, estimated at 2027.5. Bradford's Law describes the dispersion of sources only approximately, whereas Lotka's Law in its classical form is not validated (β = 4.87). South Africa accounts for 43.3% of the documents, and the excess of country-document mentions indicates frequent international collaboration. The conceptual structure splits into a technical-clinical strand and an educational strand, with no motor themes. The field is young, concentrated, and fragmented, and consolidating recurrent authors, balanced networks, and themes that link technical performance, governance, and implementation is a priority.

papers.title: Calibrating Large Language Models for Educational Assessment: A Reliability-Weighted Contextual Calibration Framework for CTT Item Facility and Discrimination Estimation
