papers.authors: Weifan Liu, Chenghong Yu, Ruifeng Yue, Ruixiang Huang
papers.abstract: Item facility and item discrimination are two frequently used indices in Classical Test Theory (CTT) for evaluating examination quality. This study evaluates four state-of-the-art LLMs—ChatGPT, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, and Doubao—by comparing their predicted item facility and discrimination with empirical CTT estimates computed from undergraduate mathematics examinations. To improve the consistency of LLM-generated estimates, we propose a Reliability-Weighted Contextual Calibration Framework (RCCF), which combines reliability-weighted model aggregation with contextual information from historical assessments. The framework is evaluated using a nested leave-one-item-out cross-validation (LOOCV) procedure. Experimental results show that RCCF demonstrates competitive performance across the evaluated assessment settings and CTT parameters, while its relative advantage over individual LLMs and ablation models varies across tasks. By integrating multiple LLM estimates with available historical and contextual assessment information, RCCF provides a practical framework for preliminary CTT parameter estimation, with further prospective validation needed to establish its generalizability to unseen examinations.

papers.title: A Study on the Factors Associated with College Students’ Intention to Use AI-Based Mental Health Services: The Roles of Trust, Empathy, and Privacy Concern
papers.authors: Meng Fan, Xiaowei He, Mengyuan Zhou, Tiansheng Xia
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence technology is gradually being integrated into mental health service contexts and is increasingly discussed as a potential supplementary resource to university mental health support systems. However, AI-based mental health services involve sensitive factors such as emotional expression, personal privacy, and relational interaction. Therefore, college students’ willingness to accept AI-based mental health services and the potential factors associated with such acceptance remain unclear. Based on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, this study introduces six factors—Accessibility (ACC), Privacy Concern (PC), Perceived Anthropomorphism (PA), Perceived Empathy (EMP), Trust (TRU), and Perceived Usefulness (PU)—to systematically examine their relationships with university students’ Behavioral Intention (BI) to use AI-based mental health services. A total of 375 volunteers participated in the current study and completed relevant questionnaires. Structural equation modeling was employed for data analysis. The results indicate that accessibility, perceived usefulness, and trust are all significantly and positively associated with behavioral intention. Perceived empathy is significantly and positively associated with trust, whereas privacy concern is significantly and negatively associated with both trust and behavioral intention. The analysis of indirect effects shows that there is a significant sequential indirect association between perceived anthropomorphism and behavioral intention through perceived empathy, trust, and perceived usefulness. In addition, a significant negative indirect association between privacy concern and behavioral intention through trust was observed. The findings indicate that, in the highly sensitive context of mental health services, college students’ intention to use AI-based mental health services is associated with a combination of accessibility, perceived usefulness, emotional interaction experience, privacy-related evaluations, and trust.

papers.title: The Impact of Configurational Fit of Product and Service on Customer Decision-Making: Evidence from an Event-Related Potential Experiment
papers.authors: Meina Zhao, Mingming Xu
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence provides new approaches for smart product–service systems. As such, an increasing number of service-oriented manufacturing enterprises are leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) to achieve value co-creation with customers. In the process of intelligently matching additional services to products, measuring the congruity of product–service systems remains to be explored. This study employs an event-related potential (ERP) methodology to examine how product–service congruity influences customer purchase intentions associated with cognitive processing. ERPs elicited by high-congruity product–service combinations were significantly different from low-congruity combinations. By proposing a method to determine product–service congruity, this study provides insights for matching product–service combinations in an AI-driven context. These findings can guide the delivery of enhanced personalized product–service combinations in platform economies and AI ecosystems, enabling enterprises to achieve value co-creation.

papers.title: Recent Advances in Modeling, Control and Motion Planning for AI-Driven Soft Robotic Systems
papers.authors: Lingli Tang, Wenguang Yang, Wenyuan Chen, Jie Yang
papers.abstract: Due to their high compliance, environmental adaptability, and inherent safety in human–robot interaction, soft robots have demonstrated considerable potential, including medical rehabilitation, compliant grasping, and operations in complex environments. Unlike conventional robots relying on rigid structures and discrete joint motions, soft robots use flexible materials such as elastomers and hydrogels to achieve motion and functionality through continuous deformation. Despite providing excellent adaptability, these compliant materials also introduce complex behaviors, including continuous morphological changes, material nonlinearities, time-varying properties, and environmental coupling, posing substantial challenges to modeling, control, and motion planning. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI), through nonlinear representation, data-driven learning, adaptive optimization, and autonomous decision-making, has provided new technical pathways for addressing these challenges. Unlike previous reviews organized primarily by AI algorithm type, this work narratively reviews 39 studies and organizes AI-driven approaches according to the soft robotic system implementation process, encompassing modeling, control, and motion planning. Specifically, in modeling, neural networks, Koopman representations, and physics–data fusion methods have enhanced the representation of complex dynamical relationships. In control, learning-augmented control and reinforcement learning have reduced reliance on accurate system models and improved adaptability under uncertainty. In motion planning, learning from demonstration, reinforcement learning, and intelligent optimization methods have strengthened the capability for autonomous motion generation under complex constraints. Finally, this paper summarizes the current state of the field and discusses future trends in AI-driven soft robotics, emphasizing stronger coordination across functional modules. Closed-loop integration of prediction, decision-making, control, and feedback updates may further advance soft robots from stage-specific intelligence toward system-level autonomy.

papers.title: Design and Performance Analysis of 3RSS/S Ankle Rehabilitation Robot
papers.authors: Ahlem Hamel, Ridha Kelaiaia, Allaoua Brahmia, Adlen Kerboua, Ameur Latreche
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Ankle rehabilitation robotics has garnered a lot of interest because of its ability to improve therapeutic outcomes and enable quantitative patient monitoring. The ankle has a complex biomechanical system, so the design needs to have accurate kinematics, structural stiffness, and biomechanical compatibility. This paper deals with the design and performance analysis of a 3RSS/S parallel robot for ankle rehabilitation. Methods: A multi-objective optimization framework is presented for simultaneous optimization of workspace volume, kinematic accuracy and structural stiffness. The topology of the 3-DOF parallel mechanism is presented, and its geometric model and Jacobian matrix are derived. The optimization problem is solved using NSGA-II and the compromise solution is selected using TOPSIS. Results: For the adopted geometric, joint and actuator-compliance models, the chosen design yields an orientation-workspace measure of WV=0.1342rad3, a global Jacobian-conditioning index of ηJ=1.0812 and a global stiffness-conditioning index of ηS=1.1874. Numerical verification shows that the prescribed clinical orientation range is covered, that the clinical workspace volume Vclinical=0.1275rad3 is strictly contained in the reachable workspace, and that the chosen solution is insensitive to the assumed geometrical tolerances. Conclusions: These simulation-based results motivate prototype development and subsequent experimental kinematic, stiffness, safety, and human–robot interaction validation.

papers.title: “It Works, but I Don’t Know Why”: Uncritical Use, Verification Behavior and Perceived Understanding in Non-CS Students’ Generative AI-Assisted Programming Projects
papers.authors: YeEun Jang, Jung-In Choi
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enables students with little programming experience to produce working software, raising the concern that learners may build artifacts they cannot explain. This convergent mixed-methods study examined how uncritical GenAI use and verification behavior (VB) relate to novices’ self-reported understanding of their own AI-assisted projects. Participants were undergraduates from predominantly non-computing majors in two offerings of a general-education Python course; 64 provided complete survey data and 68 written reflections were thematically analyzed. Uncritical use (UR) was associated with a larger self-reported product–understanding gap (GAP; r = 0.43, p < 0.001) but showed little association with perceived understanding (PU), whereas VB was associated with PU (r = 0.45, p < 0.001) but showed little association with the gap. Tests of dependent correlations confirmed that these associations differed. In the reflections, execution-based checking was the most commonly reported verification strategy (47 of 68), whereas comprehension-oriented strategies were less common. Because all measures were self-reported and cross-sectional, the findings are correlational; they suggest that instruction should explicitly scaffold comprehension-oriented verification in AI-integrated introductory programming.

papers.title: Generative AI Literacy and Multidimensional AI Anxiety in Creative Higher Education
papers.authors: Xin Yong, Junjie Gavin Wu, Wei Wei
papers.abstract: Engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involves practical literacy as well as learning, professional, sociotechnical, and configuration concerns. This mixed-methods study examined whether these responses were differentiated among Chinese arts-university students. Primary inference used a quality-screened cross-sectional sample of 355 questionnaire records from 351 participant-identifier clusters after excluding 105 of 460 eligible records (22.8%) showing exact whole-battery straightlining across all 59 structured items; the full eligible sample of 460 records from 455 clusters was retained as a sensitivity analysis. GenAI literacy was assessed with a 16-item music-context-adapted self-report instrument covering cognitive (CL), behavioral (BL), affective (AL), and ethical (EL) literacy, and AI Anxiety with 21 items spanning Learning Anxiety (LA), Job-Replacement Anxiety (JR), Sociotechnical Blindness Anxiety (ST), and AI Configuration Anxiety (AC). Of six prespecified associations, only EL-JR and EL-ST met the Holm-adjusted criterion in the primary sample and remained supported in the full-sample and prior-use-adjusted sensitivity analyses. CL-LA and BL-LA were unsupported in both samples, whereas AL-LA and AL-AC were sample-specification sensitive. Measurement models showed mixed fit; CL-BL separation improved after quality screening but remained incomplete. A secondary 47-person exact-identifier matched panel showed higher later-wave CL, BL, and AL scores, whereas EL and all four AI Anxiety dimensions showed no Holm-adjusted difference. These literacy comparisons are exploratory because the administered literacy items were music-framed while the documented learning activities involved broadcasting scripts and AI-supported video production. Independently analyzed qualitative material provided construct-level consistency with the EL-ST interpretation and tentative complementarity for EL-JR, but was not participant-linked to the quantitative samples. Overall, the evidence supports a bounded interpretation of differentiated, calibrated rather than anxiety-free adaptation; it does not establish causal intervention effects or participant-level mixed-method mechanisms.

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning Models for Pan-Cancer Prediction and Explainable Feature Analysis
papers.authors: N Lokesh, L. Thara, R. Kumuthaveni
papers.journal: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science Engineering and Technology
papers.abstract: Cancer classification based on molecular information is a more complex multiclass learning problem, as tumors from different tissues can present with different expression profiles and cancers with similar molecular characteristics can occur in different tissues. The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) gene-expression data is used to create a practical pan-cancer classification framework that is described in this paper. The working dataset consisted of 11,062 labelled samples representing 33 cancer types, after preparation and labelling. Representation of the input was reduced to 500 gene-expression features using a feature-selection stage. A single XGBoost multiclass classifier was then trained to understand the relationship between the chosen expression profile and the 33 cancer classes. The implementation performed with an accuracy of 94.49%, precision of 94.66%, recall of 94.49%, and F1 score of 94.27% on held-out test data. To make the model easier to inspect, a feature-importance analysis based on SHAP was added. The trained model was deployed into a Streamlit dashboard, with a FastAPI backend to upload a gene-expression sample and display the predicted cancer type, probabilities of cancer classes and explanation information. The system is a research and educational prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic system; an independent validation should be required before clinical interpretation.

papers.title: Mental Health Detection using Advanced Machine Learning
papers.authors: S Bhavithiran, S Nithyanandh, V. S. Anita Sofia
papers.journal: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science Engineering and Technology
papers.abstract: There are a number of factors that can impact on students' wellbeing, such as academic workload, financial concerns, sleep patterns, social support, lifestyle and other factors. This research presents the web application MindScope Lab, which is based on machine learning algorithms and was designed to illustrate how simulated mental health-related risk patterns can be identified in student profiles. A synthetic dataset of 30,000 student records was generated with attributes based on the students' demographics, academic, wellbeing, lifestyle and support. The data comprises age, gender, department, CGPA, PHQ-9 score, anxiety score, academic stress, financial stress, sleep duration, sleep quality, social support, physical activity, family history, counselling history. The dataset was split in 80:20 stratified fashion and a Random Forest classifier was trained on the same. The model obtained a high accuracy of 96.92% for unseen synthetic test data. The trained pipeline was then integrated into a web application built using Flask that would take in a fake student profile from a user and give them a lower-risk pattern and guidance or a higher-risk pattern and guidance. The application was kept alive by a GitHub repository and deployed as a web service. The project illustrates the complete process of synthesizing the data, preprocessing, building a machine-learning model, testing it, developing a web-interface, and deploying it. The underlying data and target labels are synthetic data, and the system is for academic and technical demonstration only. It is not a medical diagnostic system, clinical screening tool or a substitute for mental health services.

papers.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
papers.authors: Esther Mertens, Janis Butz, Jean‐Louis van Gelder
papers.abstract: While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

papers.title: A Critical Epistemological Audit of Early Evidence Syntheses in Generative AI Educational Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Tim Fütterer, Nina Peltzer, Peter H. Gerjets, Detmar Meurers, Tamara Powell Tate, Mark Warschauer, Valentin Emslander, Lisa Bardach, John Hattie, Michael Sailer, Jochen Kuhn
papers.abstract: The rapid emergence of ChatGPT in education was accompanied by an equally rapid proliferation of meta-analyses synthesizing its effects on educational outcomes. We conducted a systematic epistemological audit of the first wave of these meta-analyses, evaluating both their methodological and reporting quality and the primary evidence they synthesized. We included meta-analyses published after the release of ChatGPT that quantitatively synthesized its effects on educational outcomes. Five meta-analyses comprising 87 unique primary studies met our inclusion criteria. We also reconstructed their quantitative evidence base and conducted exploratory three-level random-effects meta-analyses to examine effect magnitude, heterogeneity, and robustness, and how these varied with theoretically and methodologically relevant characteristics. The five meta-analyses generally searched multiple databases, specified eligibility criteria, and examined heterogeneity and potential publication bias, but showed limitations in independent screening and coding, preregistration, open data and code, and transparent reporting. The underlying primary evidence likewise showed methodological and reporting limitations and substantial conceptual heterogeneity. Among 69 classifiable primary studies, 79.7% assessed performance exclusively, whereas only 11.6% assessed learning exclusively. The reconstructed meta-analysis yielded a positive average effect (g = 0.83, 95% CI [0.68, 0.97]), but heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 94.06%; 95% prediction interval [−0.75, 2.41]), and estimates were markedly attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing small-study and selection effects. Although positive effects remained among stronger studies assessing learning, increasingly stringent quality criteria rapidly reduced the evidence base, limiting the certainty and generalizability of conclusions about learning effects. Overall, our findings caution against interpreting a single pooled estimate as a stable general effect of ChatGPT on learning and highlight the need for more rigorous, conceptually precise, transparent, and reproducible research.

papers.title: The Epistemic Authority in Islamic Religious Education in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence: Reconstructing the Concepts of Sanad and Talaqqī
papers.authors: Faqih Abdul Aziz, Rohmat Robi' Rozaqiy, Dinar Bela Ayu Naj'ma, Muhammad Ja'far Nashir, Ghazali Mohamed Fadzil
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) places students of Islamic Religious Education before a source of religious knowledge that carries no chain of transmission. Existing scholarship addresses digital religious authority without entering the classroom, and technology in learning without questioning the knowledge's validity. This study reconstructs sanad and talaqqī into criteria of epistemic authority, tests generative artificial intelligence against them, and draws out the implications for Islamic Religious Education. Methodologically, this conceptual and philosophical-hermeneutic study draws on classical texts of hadith transmission, technological documents, and recent literature drawn from the Scopus database. Directed content analysis yields four criteria: continuity (ittiṣāl), moral integrity (ʿadālah), accuracy of transmission (ḍabṭ), and formation (takwīn). Generative artificial intelligence satisfies only accuracy, and only partially. Crucially, three failures are structural and one is contingent. This distinction requires task sorting and reasserting the teacher's standing, not blanket prohibition.

papers.title: Teachers’ perceptions of ChatGPT support across TPACK domains: A cross-sectional survey in UAE schools
papers.authors: Mohd. Elmagzoub Eltahir, Frdose Mohd Elmagzoub Babiker
papers.journal: Eurasia Journal of Mathematics Science and Technology Education
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine teachers’ perceptions of ChatGPT support for instructional practices from the technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) framework perspective. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed, with data collected from 109 in-service teachers in the United Arab Emirates using a structured questionnaire measuring seven TPACK knowledge domains. Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were employed to examine teachers’ perceptions of ChatGPT support across the TPACK domains and differences associated with demographic variables. The results indicate that teachers perceived ChatGPT as providing positive support across all TPACK domains. Content knowledge (CK) received the highest score, particularly for curriculum development, lesson planning, and instructional content preparation, whereas technological knowledge (TK) received the lowest score. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated a statistically significant difference between perceived ChatGPT support for CK and TK. No statistically significant differences were found in teachers’ perceptions of gender, teaching experience, or academic qualification. The findings suggest that ChatGPT is perceived as a useful instructional support tool across TPACK-related practices, while effective and responsible use requires stronger artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and technological competence. The study recommends professional development focusing on prompt design, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, bias awareness, privacy protection, and ethical AI use.

papers.title: Co-Creation to Improve Performance and Quality of Public Services
papers.authors: Ilham Rifai Hasan, M. Darwis Nur Tinri, Bachtiar
papers.abstract: This study aims to explore and analyze a service quality model—specifically the gap between service users' expectations and management's perceptions—within the context of public services for Population Administration and Civil Registration. Qualitative data were collected from key participants—including management (Heads of the Population Administration and Civil Registration Service Sub-divisions), service counter staff, and service users—until data saturation was reached. Data collection involved in-depth interviews, field observations, surveys, and an analysis of user complaint feedback, all of which were subsequently analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings reveal a stark perceptual gap centered on the dimensions of Assurance and Empathy, whereas Tangibles, Reliability, and Responsiveness showed low to moderate levels of divergence. Theoretically, this study contributes to public service literature by demonstrating that the SERVQUAL Gap-1 in public organizations is not merely a communication failure but a misalignment of cognitive orientations stemming from bureaucratic inertia. While management interprets service quality through the lens of internal regulatory compliance and procedural speed, the public evaluates quality based on psychological security, administrative transparency, and relational empathy. By framing Gap-1 as an institutionalized cognitive divide between administrative compliance indicators and public value co-creation, this article advances the SERVQUAL framework within public administration theory. In summary, managerial strategies such as Management by Walking Around (MBWA) and citizen review mechanisms are proposed to realign organizational cognition with public expectations. The study's strategic implications highlight the importance of leveraging Gap-1 mechanisms—such as suggestion boxes, opinion polls, citizen charters, and public consultations—to steer the co-creation process toward the realization of public value at the "value-in-use" stage.

papers.title: A missing-relationship worksheet for an invented teaching figure
papers.authors: Figran Team
papers.abstract: This educational resource is an openly licensed text worksheet. Its entire example is invented: a learner writes a question card, sorts it into a topic group, and a peer reviews its wording. An arrow means only the next task in that invented sequence. It does not mean scientific causation or measured influence. The worksheet supplies a five-statement source brief, four possible statuses for an absent relationship, a five-field review record, four worked proposals, and a peer review prompt. Readers practice separating missing information, a declared scope boundary, and an omitted but explicitly supported line. The material can be completed on paper; it requires no account, product purchase or software. It has not been classroom-tested, and no experiment or measured learning benefit is reported. Content: the author-owned public worksheet linked below, first published on 11 October 2026. The text is CC BY 4.0; attribute Figran Team and the worksheet title, link the license, and indicate changes. This license does not cover Figran software, logos or third-party material. Authorship and relationship disclosure: Figran Team created this teaching text; we work on Figran. AI assisted the wording. This resource record is educational material, not a commercial software listing, an independent review or a report of research results.

papers.title: Dari mesin jawaban menjadi teman berpikir: Reorientasi peran artificial intelligence dalam pembelajaran mendalam di pendidikan tinggi
papers.authors: Qorinul Huda, Pamelia Nuryatman
papers.journal: Prosiding Seminar Nasional Sanata Dharma Berbagi
papers.abstract: Perkembangan generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) telah mengubah cara mahasiswa memperoleh, mengolah, dan menghasilkan pengetahuan di pendidikan tinggi. Kemudahan memperoleh jawaban secara instan meningkatkan efisiensi pembelajaran, tetapi juga berpotensi mendorong cognitive offloading dan mengurangi keterlibatan mahasiswa dalam proses berpikir. Artikel ini bertujuan menganalisis pembelajaran mendalam (deep learning pedagogy) sebagai respons pedagogis terhadap disrupsi GenAI serta merumuskan reorientasi peran AI dari answer machine menjadi thinking partner. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan desain analisis konseptual melalui sintesis literatur ilmiah, teori, dan dokumen kebijakan mengenai GenAI, cognitive offloading, konstruktivisme, berpikir kritis, metakognisi, dan pembelajaran mendalam. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa persoalan utama penggunaan GenAI bukan keberadaan cognitive offloading, melainkan pendelegasian aktivitas kognitif yang menggantikan proses berpikir yang menjadi tujuan pembelajaran. Artikel ini merumuskan efficiency–depth paradox, yaitu ketegangan antara peningkatan efisiensi melalui AI dan kebutuhan untuk mempertahankan kedalaman proses belajar. Pembelajaran mendalam melalui prinsip mindful, meaningful, dan joyful learning dapat berfungsi sebagai pedagogical safeguards. Reorientasi AI sebagai thinking partner menempatkan mahasiswa sebagai primary thinker, sementara AI berfungsi sebagai scaffolding untuk questioning, exploration, feedback, verification, dan reflection.

papers.title: Assistance Footprints of Repeated AI Support in Chronic Disease Self-Management: A Framework for Evaluating Later Capability and Support Decisions (Preprint)
papers.authors: Pedro Miguel Lopes de Sousa
papers.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are moving from single-encounter advice toward continuing support for people who manage a chronic disease. Most evaluations ask whether people decide better while the assistant is present. Far fewer ask what people can do later without it, or whether that later capability should change how support is given. This Viewpoint argues that these are two separate evidence questions. The first concerns an assistance footprint: the average causal difference in later unaided capability between alternative support histories, for a specified task, population, and follow-up period. Randomized experiments in education and in general adult samples show that the way AI is used can change later unaided performance. Available evidence has not yet established whether alternative histories of AI support produce clinically meaningful differences in later unaided self-management capability, or whether anticipating such differences improves subsequent support decisions. The second question is whether a decision policy that anticipates a footprint makes better support choices than an otherwise identical policy that does not, and than a flexible policy that learns from each person's full history. Using peripheral artery disease as a worked example, the paper shows why similar effects can justify different decisions for different people, and why independence from AI is not an automatic goal. It outlines a staged, clinically governed evaluation, states what each possible result would and would not mean, discusses counterarguments, and offers a minimum reporting list for studies of repeated AI support. The contribution is not a new theory, whose components are established, but a precise causal question, a demanding comparator, and a practical evaluation agenda. Until such evidence exists, assistance footprints are a research construct and not grounds for reducing care.

papers.title: Beyond Information Seeking: Young Adults' Expectations of Sexual and Reproductive Health Chatbots Across the Care Pathway in a Cross-Sectional Survey Study (Preprint)
papers.authors: Divya S., Naily Nevarez, Nicole Levitz, Karen Shum, Elise Gust
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) chatbots are built and evaluated as information systems. Less is known about what users of a deployed SRH chatbot expect it to do, or whether expectations extend beyond information to assessment, connection to services, and continuity of support. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to characterize what young adults expect an SRH chatbot to do, immediately after using one, to inform design and evaluation: (1) how capability demand is distributed across 4 care-pathway functions (informing, assessing, connecting, and sustaining), (2) the proportion wanting information seeking alone, (3) the structure of capability evaluations, and (4) where gaps between valued and deficient capabilities are widest. METHODS We conducted a cross-sectional web-based survey of 1200 adults aged 18 to 32 years in the United States, recruited through a commercial research panel. Each participant completed a 5- to 10-minute guided interaction with Roo, Planned Parenthood Federation of America's free, nongenerative guided-flow SRH chatbot, then ranked 10 features, rated 11 capabilities on a 7-point importance scale, and completed checklists of desired improvements, additions, and anticipated uses. Analyses included a Plackett-Luce ranking model, composite demand indicators, exploratory and split-half confirmatory factor analysis, and importance-by-unmet-demand analysis. RESULTS Demand was present at every care-pathway function. Accurate information ranked first of 10 features and was rated most important (mean 5.92, SD 1.53), yet 54% of participants named accuracy as needing improvement; a symptom checker was the most requested addition (62.7%), and 46.4% wanted video consultation with professionals. In total, 87.8% (1054/1200) wanted a service-connection capability or a use beyond information seeking (median 2 such endorsements), and 8.2% (98/1200) wanted information seeking alone. Exploratory factor analysis supported 2 components (63.5% of variance): a core health-utility component combining accuracy and confidentiality (loadings 0.90) with educational resources, personalized advice, a symptom checker, and real-time expert access (0.70-0.76), and a lower-rated engagement and customization component. In a held-out half, a confirmatory model separating trust attributes from consultative capabilities fit better than a 2-factor model (comparative fit index 0.93 vs 0.85); trust and consultative capability correlated 0.84, each less with engagement (0.33 and 0.65). The widest gaps between importance and perceived deficiency concerned accurate information, real-time expert access, and the symptom checker rather than content breadth. CONCLUSIONS Young adults evaluated the chatbot as a first point of consultation that should interpret their situation and connect them to care, with accuracy and confidentiality as preconditions. The capabilities they most wanted, symptom assessment and real-time access to a professional, are those SRH professionals have considered least appropriate for chatbots, placing users' demand where clinical caution is greatest. Services should treat accuracy and confidentiality as gating requirements, prioritize assessment and connection over engagement features, build chatbot-mediated escalation to human channels, and add role-performance outcomes to accuracy-based evaluation.

papers.title: Stakeholder Perspectives on the Acceptability, Appropriateness, and Implementation Requirements of a Retrieval-Augmented Perioperative Education Chatbot (Digital Teammate): Explanatory Sequential Mixed Methods Study (Preprint)
papers.authors: Maximilian Wutz, Emilie Valiquette, Joshua Rocca, Juliane Köberlein–Neu, Arnaud Romeo Mbadjeu Hondjeu
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Patients require timely, understandable, consistent, and actionable perioperative information. In routine care, however, this information is often distributed across clinicians, written materials, institutional documents, and verbal instructions, making consistent, tailored guidance difficult. Conversational agents (CAs) may help provide scalable perioperative education, but implementation in safety-sensitive pathways requires understanding how stakeholders interpret usefulness, trust, role boundaries, and implementation requirements after interacting with a functioning system. OBJECTIVE The aim was to evaluate how stakeholders judged the acceptability and appropriateness of the Digital Teammate, after hands-on use, and to identify the requirements for its use in routine perioperative care. Digital Teammate is a bilingual English–French, multimodal, retrieval-augmented conversational agent designed to support perioperative patient education. METHODS We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods pilot study at a Canadian tertiary care hospital. Quantitative user acceptance testing (UAT) data were collected first and then expanded through open-ended UAT responses and four role- or perspective-homogeneous focus groups. The analytic UAT sample included 58 participants: 35 healthcare workers and 23 patient participants. A purposively selected subsample of 24 UAT participants took part in four focus groups with physicians, registered nurses, respiratory therapists, and anesthesia assistants, operational and support staff, and patient participants. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively. Qualitative data were analyzed using structuring qualitative content analysis. Integration was conducted through a mixed-methods joint display to examine how qualitative findings explained, expanded, or qualified the quantitative UAT findings. RESULTS Participants evaluated the Digital Teammate positively across all four UAT domains. Domain-level mean scores were 3.71 (SD 0.79) for usability, 3.95 (SD 0.77) for interaction quality, 3.76 (SD 0.85) for perceived usefulness, and 3.61 (SD 0.96) for acceptance and intention to use. Patient participants rated the system more favorably than healthcare workers across domains and rated standardized perioperative responses favorably more often (87.5% vs 79.3%). Qualitative findings generated six themes: a bounded complementary role, usability and interaction reliability, language clarity versus information consistency, workflow and workload impact, conditional trust, and conditions for safe implementation. Mixed-methods integration generated four overarching meta-inferences: usability was strong but did not by itself establish appropriateness for routine use, the clearest initial use case was routine perioperative preparation and orientation, clinical complexity and safety relevance defined the boundary of stand-alone use, and acceptance was positive but conditional on complementarity, trust, governance, and workflow integration. CONCLUSIONS The Digital Teammate was usable, showed favorable initial acceptance, and was perceived as valuable for routine perioperative preparation and orientation. However, safe progression toward patient-facing feasibility testing requires a staged pathway. Structured clinician-led validation and correction of content, interaction, and escalation issues should precede prospective feasibility testing in routine care. Complex, individualized, safety-critical, or emotionally distressing questions should be handled through bounded responses, transparent uncertainty acknowledgement, and escalation to human clinicians when appropriate.

papers.title: Benefits, Barriers, Preferences, and the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Recruitment for Cardiovascular Clinical Trials Among Black Adults: A Focus Group Study (Preprint)
papers.authors: Tamunotonye Harry, Zaib Hussain, Azuka Amaka Ngige, Adriana Foster, Emma Mitchell, Kimberly R. Warren, Jingyi Cao, Ruth‐Alma Turkson‐Ocran, Stephen Paul Juraschek, Timothy Lahey, Timothy B. Plante, Yuanyuan Feng
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Black adults in the U.S. remain underrepresented in cardiovascular clinical trials despite bearing a disproportionate burden of disease. Digital recruitment strategies offer a scalable alternative to traditional outreach, but evidence on their effectiveness for improving racial and ethnic representation remains mixed. The growing use of artificial intelligence within digital recruitment pipelines adds further complexity given documented biases in the data used to train these systems. Little qualitative research has examined how Black adults with community research experience perceive digital recruitment strategies for cardiovascular clinical trials, or their views on the use of artificial intelligence within that process. OBJECTIVE We explored perceived benefits and barriers of digital recruitment, ethical and privacy-related concerns including the use of artificial intelligence, and preferences for the content, format, and delivery of digital recruitment materials. METHODS We conducted three virtual focus groups via Zoom with 10 Black adults recruited through the IMPACT Community Research Council and the Morgan CARES (Community-Aligned REsearch Solutions) network at Morgan State University. All research participants had experience advising or supporting public health research initiatives. We analyzed transcripts using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis approach. A codebook was applied independently by three coders, with reliability assessed using Cohen's κ and disagreements resolved through reconciliation. RESULTS Analyses yielded 120 coded excerpts across 12 themes and 57 codes, with inter-rater reliability at theme-level mean κ = 0.74 and code-level mean κ = 0.70. Participants recognized digital platforms as scalable and convenient but identified barriers including limited digital literacy and exclusion of older or less digitally connected individuals; unfair exclusion on this basis was rated a major concern by 7 of 10 participants. Mistrust of research institutions was pervasive and rooted in historical exploitation of Black communities, including the legacy of Johns Hopkins in Baltimore. This mistrust extended to artificial intelligence and algorithmic bias. Of the seven concerns assessed, AI use in medical research was rated highest, with 9 of 10 participants calling it a major concern. They did not oppose artificial intelligence outright but emphasized the need for human oversight, particularly for participant-facing applications; there was strong support for disclosing its use. Participants also rejected the premise of a homogenous Black audience for recruitment messaging, and expressed strong preferences for video content, culturally resonant and plain language, diverse representation, trusted community messengers, and flexible, equitable compensation. CONCLUSIONS Digital recruitment strategies show measurable promise for improving cardiovascular trial recruitment among Black adults, but their effectiveness depends on how they are implemented. Transparency, disclosure of artificial intelligence use, equitable compensation, and recognition of diversity within Black communities are essential for digital recruitment strategies to be experienced as trustworthy by the communities they aim to serve.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Resource Practices: Examining the Moderating Effect of AI on Recruitment, Selection, Staffing, and Organizational Performance
papers.authors: Ali Elnabawy Arafat, Ghada Awad El-Kot, Mohamed Mostafa Fouad
papers.journal: MSA- Management Sciences Journal/MSA-Management Sciences Journal
papers.abstract: This research examines the moderating role of artificial intelligence in the relationship between three core human resource practices – recruitment, selection, and staffing – and organizational performance in Egypt’s telecommunications organizations. Grounded in Human Capital Theory, the Resource-Based View, and the Technology Acceptance Model, the research proposes a model in which AI moderates the effect of each HR practice on OP. Data were collected through a structured, 46-item questionnaire distributed to employees of Egypt’s four major telecommunications operators, yielding 380 valid responses from a population of approximately 24,000 employees. PLS-SEM was used, with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, was used to test six hypotheses. All three HR practices exerted significant positive direct effects on OP, together explaining over 80% of its variance, with staffing the strongest predictor (β = .872, p < .001), followed by selection (β = .069, p = .008) and recruitment (β = .057, p = .017). AI did not significantly moderate the recruitment-OP or selection-OP relationships but significantly and negatively moderated the staffing-OP relationship (β = -.073, p = .027), suggesting that heavy reliance on AI can erode the marginal contribution of human-led staffing decisions. These findings indicate that AI’s influence on HR-performance relationships is uneven rather than uniformly positive, and that AI should complement, rather than replace, human judgment in staffing decisions. The research offers Egyptian telecommunications organizations empirically grounded guidance for pursuing AI-enabled HR digital transformation while safeguarding the human judgment that underpins effective performance outcomes.

papers.title: AI-Supported Enhanced Recovery Nursing Program after Major Abdominal Surgery: Impact on Recovery, Complications, and Length of Stay
papers.authors: Reham El Ashery Ashery Asker, Iman Abd-Elmoaty Mohamed, Manal Mohamed Ahmed Ayed, Walaa El-khanany Zahran
papers.abstract: Background: Major abdominal surgery is associated with considerable physiological stress and may lead to postoperative complications, delayed functional recovery, prolonged hospitalization, and increased healthcare burden. Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways aim to accelerate recovery through evidence-based perioperative interventions; however, integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into nursing care may further support individualized risk assessment, timely decision-making, continuous monitoring, and early identification of postoperative deterioration. Aim: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of an AI-Supported enhanced recovery nursing program on postoperative recovery, complications, and length of hospital stay among patients undergoing major abdominal surgery. Methods: A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 100 adult patients undergoing major abdominal surgery in General Surgery Department at Sohag University Hospitals. Patients were recruited using a convenient sampling technique. The intervention consisted of an AI-supported enhanced recovery nursing program incorporating preoperative education, individualized postoperative nursing care, pain and symptom monitoring, early mobilization, respiratory exercises, nutritional advancement, fluid and wound-care monitoring, prevention of postoperative complications, and AI-assisted identification of patients at increased risk of delayed recovery or complications. Data were collected using a Structured Patient Assessment Tool, Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Nursing Milestone Assessment Checklist, Postoperative Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) Assessment Scale, A Postoperative Complications Assessment Record and Clavien–Dindo Classification, AI-Supported Postoperative Risk Assessment and Nursing Monitoring Record, and Postoperative Length of Hospital Stay Record. Patients were assessed pre and post implementation of the program, with postoperative outcomes monitored throughout hospitalization. Results: Following implementation of the AI-supported enhanced recovery nursing program, patients demonstrated significant improvement in overall postoperative recovery, including improved pain and symptom control, earlier mobilization, improved tolerance of oral intake, and greater adherence to enhanced recovery practices. The incidence of postoperative complications was reduced, while patients experienced a shorter duration of hospitalization compared with their pre-intervention status. The intervention was associated with statistically significant improvements in the measured recovery outcomes (p < 0.05). Conclusion: The AI-Supported Enhanced Recovery Nursing Program was effective in improving postoperative recovery and supporting early identification and management of complications among patients undergoing major abdominal surgery. Its implementation may contribute to safer postoperative care, reduced complications, and shorter hospital stays. Recommendations: Surgical nursing units should consider integrating AI-supported monitoring with ERAS-based nursing protocols to facilitate individualized postoperative care, early recognition of deterioration, complication prevention, and timely discharge planning. Further controlled studies with larger samples and longer follow-up periods are recommended to evaluate the sustainability and cost-effectiveness of AI-supported enhanced recovery nursing programs.

papers.title: Applying Generative Artificial Intelligence to Personalized Theatre Productions and Film
papers.authors: Kira Mineeva
papers.abstract: This study explores the potential of generative artificial intelligence in theatre and film, focusing on personalized audience experiences, creative production processes, and emerging business models. It examines the opportunities offered by AI-driven content generation and adaptation, as well as the associated risks, including ethical concerns, intellectual property issues, and the potential impact on creative professionals. The research also considers how personalization may influence audience engagement and consumer behavior. Finally, it proposes practical approaches to responsible AI implementation in the creative industries, emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with artistic integrity, transparency, and human creativity.

papers.title: Effects of AI-Supported Learning on Independent Cognitive Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Instructional Scaffolding and Learner Characteristics
papers.authors: S.J. Liu, Yunxiao Guo
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the effects of AI-supported learning on objectively assessed cognitive performance when AI assistance is unavailable during assessment. It will cover intelligent tutoring systems, traditional chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI across educational stages and subject areas. Technology characteristics and instructional support functions will be coded separately, allowing overlapping features rather than imposing mutually exclusive technology categories. The primary objective is to estimate the effects of AI-supported learning compared with non-AI learning conditions on independent cognitive performance. Secondary objectives are to examine direct comparisons between AI-supported instructional approaches and whether effects vary with baseline learner characteristics and instructional support functions. Relevant support functions include hints, explanations, feedback, worked examples, self-explanation prompts, verification and revision prompts, adaptive learning pathways, and restrictions or fading of AI assistance. Randomized and non-randomized controlled intervention studies will be synthesized separately. A distinct observational evidence stream will examine associations between actual AI use, such as usage frequency, help-seeking, and verification behaviors, and eligible cognitive outcomes. These associations will not be combined with intervention effects or interpreted as causal evidence that a particular use behavior improves learning. Eligible outcomes include objective measures of knowledge and understanding, application and transfer, other cognitive skills, and composite achievement, which will be analyzed separately. The first eligible post-intervention assessment and subsequent delayed assessments will be distinguished. Assessments must be completed without AI; access to non-AI resources will be recorded separately. Unclear AI permissions will remain awaiting clarification rather than being treated as confirmed eligibility or grounds for automatic exclusion. Two human reviewers will independently screen records, extract key study information, and assess risk of bias, with disagreements reconciled. Analyses will account for overlapping reports, shared samples, dependent effect sizes, and differences in study design and comparison conditions. Moderator analyses will depend on sufficient comparable evidence. Within-study learner moderation will be distinguished from between-study associations. The review aims to clarify whether benefits of AI-supported learning persist when learners are assessed without AI, and which learner characteristics and instructional support functions may be associated with those benefits. No uniformly positive effect or ranking of technologies is assumed. Before registration, preliminary scoping and pilot screening examined 30 purposively selected candidate reports, and selected results from four reports underwent trial extraction to assess feasibility and refine the protocol. This prior exposure to study findings is disclosed. A comprehensive systematic database search, formal independent duplicate screening, complete data extraction, and quantitative synthesis have not yet been conducted. Substantive subsequent changes will be documented through dated amendments.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Technostress and Whistleblowing Intention in Higher Education: A Systematic Literature Review of Psychological Safety, AI Shared Mental Models, Ethical Leadership, and Perceived Algorithmic Power Author: Maria Ulfa (Universitas Negeri Semarang, Indonesia) | Date of registration: [11/10/2026] | Registration type: OSF Preregistration (Systematic Review
papers.authors: Maria Ulfa
papers.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has been adopted rapidly in higher education, yet it brings new psychological strain (AI technostress) for academics precisely when safeguarding academic integrity demands the courage to report wrongdoing (whistleblowing). Evidence on the six streams of this phenomenon — AI technostress, psychological safety, AI shared mental models, ethical leadership, algorithmic power, and whistleblowing intention — has developed in isolation. Objectives: This review systematises, appraises, and integrates the published evidence to map what is known, how the evidence connects, and where the gaps lie. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and IEEE Xplore were searched for publications from 2015 to 2026, complemented by backward reference tracking. Of 1,333 records identified, 54 studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesised thematically with an evidence-strength appraisal. Results: (1) Strong evidence shows that technostress — particularly hindrance stressors — depletes psychological resources and erodes psychological safety. (2) Emerging evidence links psychological safety to employee voice and whistleblowing, with ethical leadership as a key antecedent. (3) Shared mental models of technology causally reduce workload and techno-frustration in teams. (4) Algorithmic systems redistribute organisational power in ways that suppress employee voice, yet a perceived algorithmic power construct remains unformalised. (5) No study has examined the effect of AI technostress on whistleblowing intention, particularly in higher education. Conclusions: The review proposes an integrated conceptual model grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, together with a measurable research agenda that includes the development of a perceived algorithmic power instrument and two-wave multilevel designs

papers.title: Integration of Digital Technologies in Ethnomathematics Research: A Scoping Review (2015–2026)
papers.authors: Patricio Rosas Villagómez, stalin patricio songor illescas, Devís Geovanny Cedeño Mero
papers.abstract: This registration documents a scoping review that maps the empirical and conceptual evidence on how digital technologies are integrated into ethnomathematics research in educational contexts. Ethnomathematics links mathematics teaching to the practices of cultural groups, and digital technologies (dynamic geometry and other software, mobile apps, web-based environments, augmented and virtual reality, artificial intelligence, digital games) offer new ways to represent and teach those practices. Previous reviews of the field are bibliometric, systematic or meta-analytic and have not mapped technology integration as such. Objective: to identify trends, predominant technologies, educational levels, geographic distribution, study designs and research gaps. Four research questions guide the review: (RQ1) which digital technologies have been integrated into ethnomathematics research in education; (RQ2) at which educational levels and in which contexts; (RQ3) with which designs, theoretical frameworks and evaluation approaches; and (RQ4) which gaps are reported or observed. Methods: the review follows the Arksey and O'Malley framework, the Levac et al. enhancements and the JBI guidance, and is reported according to PRISMA-ScR, with a PRISMA 2020-style flow diagram. The question was structured with the SPIDER framework. Scopus and Web of Science were searched on 10 October 2026 with a three-block Boolean string (ethnomathematics terms AND technology terms AND education terms), restricted to 2016–2026 in Scopus (journal articles) and 2015–2026 in Web of Science. Eligible documents address ethnomathematics, ethnomodeling or indigenous/cultural mathematics; involve an explicit digital technology; and have an educational component. Reviews, meta-analyses and bibliometric studies were excluded. Records were deduplicated by DOI and normalized title and screened at title and abstract level. Data were charted for year, country, technology, educational level, study design and reported gaps, and synthesized descriptively with frequencies, cross-tabulations and a narrative synthesis. No formal critical appraisal was performed, in line with scoping review guidance. Transparency statement: this is a retrospective registration, submitted after the search and the screening were completed, so it is not a prospective protocol. The question, eligibility criteria and search strings were documented in an internal process report before screening. Screening and coding were done by a single reviewer with the assistance of a large language model (Claude, Anthropic) and the reviewer's supervision; the reviewer changed six screening decisions and checked the full text of eight records. Deviations and limitations are reported in the manuscript.

papers.title: Redundancy of orientation information and reports of seeing in near-threshold EEG perception: a preregistered secondary analysis
papers.authors: Tristen Pierson
papers.abstract: Preregistered secondary analysis of a public EEG dataset (Wiens, Andersson & Gravenfors 2023, Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience; Stockholm University Figshare, CC BY 4.0). In near-threshold visual perception with trial-by-trial awareness reports, the study tests whether, at matched total decodable information about a stimulus's orientation, trials whose orientation information is redundantly distributed across many disjoint subsets of EEG channels are reported as seen more often than trials whose information is concentrated in few channels. Support thresholds were frozen in advance, including a preregistered robustness gate stratified by stimulus opacity.

papers.title: Care-Full Alignment: Operationalizing Care Ethics for Human-LLM Relationships
papers.authors: Rayane El Masri
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are increasingly used for emotional support and companionship alongside practical tasks. While these interactions can reduce loneliness, they pose significant risks: emotional dependency, manipulation through anthropomorphic design, and fundamentally parasocial relationships. Contemporary value alignment practices emphasizing helpfulness, harmlessness, and honesty fail to account for users' contextual vulnerability or the long-term relational consequences of LLM use. This project integrates Joan Tronto's political care ethics into LLM value alignment, operationalizing her five care phases into measurable indicators for evaluating relational harm. Three connected studies develop a Care Ethics analytical codebook; apply it through Discursive-Digital Analysis to conversations between higher degree research students and three commercial LLMs across care-relevant scenarios; and test whether care-informed fine-tuning using Direct Preference Optimization measurably reduces harmful relational patterns. This work reconceptualizes AI safety as a relational practice rather than a purely technical problem.

papers.title: Towards Trustworthy Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Nursing Education: Integrating Nurse-Informed Design with a Frugal Neuro-Symbolic Architecture
papers.authors: Nevena Kostadinova Dicheva
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Nursing education is increasingly expected to provide personalised, scalable, and clinically meaningful learning experiences while responding to educator shortages, growing student numbers, limited placement opportunities, and rapidly evolving healthcare environments. These pressures have led to the adoption of technology-enhanced learning and renewed interest in innovative and student-centred pedagogies within healthcare education. Consequently, nursing education has explored a broad range of computer-aided educational approaches, including virtual reality, augmented reality, simulation systems, mobile learning applications, haptic devices, and chatbots. Although many of these technologies demonstrate educational potential, important limitations remain regarding explainability, accessibility, educator involvement, adaptive support, and long-term educational effectiveness. Recent interest in large language models and conversational AI has introduced further concerns surrounding reliability, hallucinations, transparency, privacy, educator trust, and ethical deployment within healthcare education. One AI-enabled learning environment that may address several of these limitations is the Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS). Traditionally, ITSs combine domain, tutoring, student, and interface models to provide adaptive instruction, individualised support, and immediate formative feedback. Through natural-language processing and adaptive learning techniques, ITSs may support realistic communication scenarios, individualised learning experiences, and scalable educational assistance. Compared with isolated educational technologies, ITSs are particularly promising because they can support students and educators within one integrated learning environment. Despite this potential, ITS research in nursing education remains limited. Earlier reviews in this doctoral research found that ITS-related studies represented only a small proportion of AI research in nursing education. They also identified limited attention to student modelling, tutoring strategies, explainability, educator oversight, pedagogical alignment, and the wider educational context in which these systems are introduced. Importantly, no nurse-informed conceptual or design-oriented framework was identified to guide ITS development within nursing education. This gap became the central motivation for this doctoral research. The project adopts a multi-phase, sequential exploratory mixed-methods and design-oriented approach. Phase One used grounded theory interviews to explore nurses’ and nursing students’ awareness, perceptions, expectations, concerns, and educational requirements regarding ITS adoption. These qualitative findings informed the development of the CARE-ITS framework. The framework comprises Content Alignment; Adaptive and Accessible Learning; Retention of Human-Centred Learning; Ethical and Trustworthy AI; Individualised Learning Support; Timely and Explainable Feedback; and Sustainability and Educator Support. The framework was subsequently evaluated and refined through expert validation (N = 20), with 95–100% agreement across the overall evaluation criteria (means = 4.40–4.55 out of 5). Phase Two translated the validated CARE-ITS framework into the design, development, and evaluation of EduNurse, a functional web-based ITS prototype for scenario-based nursing education. EduNurse uses a frugal neuro-symbolic assessment architecture that combines domain-adapted embeddings, deterministic educational constraints, structured rubrics, retrieval-grounded explanations, adaptive progression logic, and educator supervision. The grading pipeline does not use a generative large language model. Instead, it uses semantic similarity as one source of evidence alongside explicit relevance, rubric, safety, and uncertainty checks. This enables the system to provide structured formative feedback while retaining appropriate boundaries for educator oversight. The research contributions achieved to date include: 1. A substantial literature contribution through two complementary published reviews. A mixed-methods systematic review of computer-aided pedagogies and a scoping review of ITSs in nursing education critically examined the existing evidence base. Together, they identified gaps that informed the subsequent phases of this doctoral research. 2. An empirical contribution through a learner needs analysis for ITS in nursing education. This doctoral research presents a learner needs analysis employing a grounded theory approach to investigate nursing students’ and nursing professionals’ awareness, perceptions, educational requirements, and implementation expectations of ITSs. The study addresses an important gap within the literature by providing an empirically grounded understanding of the pedagogical, educational, and implementation requirements that should inform the design and development of AI-supported educational systems for nursing education. 3. A methodological contribution through the translation of qualitative findings into a design-oriented conceptual framework. This doctoral research demonstrates a systematic approach for translating empirically derived learner needs, pedagogical considerations, and implementation requirements into actionable design guidance. This provides a transparent transition from qualitative findings to educational AI design that may inform future research within nursing and other professional education domains. 4. The development of the CARE-ITS conceptual framework. Derived from the learner needs analysis, CARE-ITS is a nurse-informed, design-oriented conceptual framework. The framework addresses key components including content alignment, adaptive and accessible learning, retention of human-centred learning, ethical and trustworthy AI, individualised learning support, and timely and explainable feedback. By translating the identified educational requirements into AI system design principles, CARE-ITS provides an evidence-based framework to support the design and implementation of trustworthy ITSs within nursing education. 5. The design, development, and evaluation of EduNurse, a domain-specific ITS prototype for nursing education. Guided by the CARE-ITS framework, this research presents a scenario-based ITS prototype (EduNurse) that translates empirically derived learner needs, pedagogical considerations, and framework-guided design principles into a functional educational system. EduNurse does not introduce a new AI technique. Its contribution is how it brings established approaches together within a nurse-informed ITS architecture designed around the pedagogical requirements of nursing education. Within EduNurse, semantic similarity is used alongside educational decision rules to assess written scenario responses and provide feedback and learner support. This forms the basis of its frugal neuro-symbolic approach to scenario-based learning and assessment. In doing so, this research demonstrates how AI techniques can be applied within a trustworthy ITS that is informed by empirical educational requirements and aligned with the pedagogical, professional, and ethical principles of nursing education. The formal evaluation of EduNurse is complete. The evaluation combines nursing learners’ questionnaire responses, linked system-interaction records, technical-performance logs, and an independent nursing-educator audit of assessment outputs. Data analysis is now being undertaken to examine the extent to which EduNurse demonstrated the intended CARE-ITS capabilities and achieved the doctoral research objectives.

papers.title: Small-world Networks of Agents Brainstorm AI Risks to Support Ideation
papers.authors: Ke Zhou, Edyta P. Bogucka, Daniele Quercia
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: The ideation phase of participatory AI risk assessment often starts with a blank slate or a limited list of predefined risks, making it difficult to surface indirect or systemic harms. To address this limitation, we propose a three-stage tool to support the ideation phase of AI risk assessment. The tool complements participatory AI, rather than replacing it, and helps focus later engagement with affected communities. First, it dynamically discovers stakeholders depending on the given AI use and recursively expanding outward, allowing overlooked or indirect stakeholders to emerge. Second, it simulates these stakeholders with LLMs (creating in-silico stakeholders), connecting them into a network of a given topology, and having them ideate about risks. Third, it prioritizes risks using network centrality measures (the centrality of in-silico stakeholders in the network). In an initial evaluation, we found that betweenness centrality run through agents connected in a small-world network works best as it elevates risks raised by stakeholders who bridge disconnected groups, surfacing novel, systemic harms that traditional methods often miss. On an AI chatbot companion use case, this approach increased the novelty of the identified risks by approximately 1.1 points over single LLM brainstorming, and by 0.5 points over agentic LLM brainstorming, measured on a normalized five-point Likert scale, without reducing the plausibility or severity of the identified risks. To test whether our framework helps a human-led ideation session using the Futures-Wheel approach, we divided 11 teams of non-western young chatbot users into two types: control (team) and treatment (team) in a participatory AI risk assessment. The control teams started from a list of risks generated by the 45 AI practitioners in the initial evaluation; the treatment teams started from a list generated by our framework. The treatment teams identified more risks overall, and more systemic, human-computer interaction, and environmental risks in particular, categories that practitioners typically find harder to spot.

papers.title: Who Will Become the Next Senior? How Generative AI Erodes the Development Pathway in Software Engineering
papers.authors: Sumin Yu, Taesup Moon
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping software engineering, raising concerns about how the development pathway through which juniors become seniors is being eroded. While macro statistics show a decline in junior hiring and controlled studies demonstrate the effects of AI on individual task performance, the mechanisms through which GenAI reshapes early-career development in real organizational and educational contexts have not been thoroughly examined. Through 14 semi-structured interviews with juniors at the threshold of entering software engineering and senior software engineers in South Korea, analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis, we reveal a foundational pattern of Absorption---GenAI redirects entry-level work into senior–AI workflows---and three consequences: (1) juniors losing the productive struggle through which expertise once developed; (2) the structural reproduction of this loss through collective normalization of GenAI use in university classrooms; and (3) the perceptual asymmetry between seniors and juniors that prevents either side from correcting these dynamics on their own. By extending learning theory and situated cognition to organizational and institutional scales, we argue that GenAI appears to be absorbing not just specific categories of tasks but also parts of the pathway through which the next generation of seniors is formed. Preserving this pathway will require deliberate institutional design across classrooms, workplaces, and the evaluation criteria for juniors.

papers.title: What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education
papers.authors: Kai Yao
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Generative AI is changing a basic premise of educational assessment: that submitted work can reliably evidence the human capacities a credential claims to certify. The challenge is not simply whether students use AI, but what remains inferable about learning when some cognitive work has been delegated to a system. This paper develops cognitive stewardship, a framework for AI-mediated assessment that links the learning claim, delegation boundary, evidence standard, and safeguards. We then audit verified public generative AI assessment guidance from 30 universities. Using a pre-specified scoring codebook, a written, source-grounded rubric, four open-weight LLM models applied the rubric as structured coders, with scores averaged to reduce dependence on any single model's bias. The audit shows that public policies are becoming better at classifying AI use than at explaining what evidence and protections preserve credential validity. Boundaries are more visible than evidence standards; safeguards are uneven; and guidance is clearest when AI use resembles final-output substitution rather than feedback, access, verification, or professional workflow. The takeaway is that permission categories are necessary but insufficient. Universities need policies that make the certification logic visible: what learners may delegate, what they must still demonstrate, and how institutions will protect fair evidence rather than merely monitor AI use.

papers.title: What Should I Become? When LLMs Present a Slice of Opportunity as the Whole
papers.authors: Taylor Wise, Scott Seidenberger, Anindya Maiti
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for life-path guidance, yet the distribution of options they surface has gone largely unexamined. We characterize occupational-category visibility across 165,000 LLM responses spanning 100 user profiles, 15 prompts (grouped into seven framings), 11 models across seven families, two role framings, and five temperatures, with keywords derived automatically from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) occupation titles. Trades & Labor occupations, roughly 40% of projected job openings, account for only 6% of surfaced visibility, the largest gap in the data, while Education and STEM are over-visible (31% and 14%) relative to their labor-market shares, and Business is under-visible (19% vs. 31%). Re-weighting by entry-level education exposes a sharper credentialing skew, in which LLM-implied openings at the Bachelor's-or-above level reach 44.8% against a BLS share of 20.6%, and this skew tracks socioeconomic profile signals. This signal is conditional: Low-Income responses discuss an education tier far more often than Wealthy/Privileged ones (28.9% vs. 4.1%), and among tier-mentioning responses Bachelor's-or-above is far rarer for Low-Income profiles (8.3% vs. 73.4% of mentions), carrying a 50% education-implied wage gap that the occupational-category channel does not produce. Across all responses, however, the two groups reach Bachelor's-or-above guidance at comparable rates (4.2% vs. 3.1%). The aggregate distribution lies closest (Jensen–Shannon divergence 0.021) to open-web "General Advice / Blogs" content and far from the BLS labor-market structure, consistent with web-text mirroring. The skew is stable across model families and temperatures, though prompt framing shifts which categories surface.

papers.title: People Are Not Just Their Countries. Disentangling Social Determinants of LLM Value Alignment Across Europe
papers.authors: Maria-Louisa Wightman, Guillaume Bied, Tijl De Bie
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as a primary source of information and advice, understanding their alignment to humans in terms of values becomes a pressing concern. A growing literature has leveraged large scale surveys to investigate to what extent LLMs' and humans' stated values and opinions align. With limited exceptions, studied populations have been defined country borders or cultural bounds. Yet, this focus neglects the role that socio-demographic divides may play for value alignment disparities. Relying on the European Social Survey, we address this knowledge gap by considering value alignment displayed with respect to 10 prominent commercial LLMs in terms of 15 socio-demographic variables as well as country of residence. Our analyses reveal that LLMs are indeed unequally aligned to the values of different socio-demographic groups, notably those defined by education, income, occupation and religion. When examining alignment at the individual level, a respondent's country, taken as a stand-alone variable, explains a substantial amount of variation that is on par with the full set of considered socio-demographics. Further disentangling the respective role of country-level and socio-demographic factors, we find they are complementary in explaining value alignment patterns, with their relative weights varying across the subset of questions considered.

papers.title: AI Revealed Preferences
papers.authors: Sam Wang, Sofiia Lobanova, Yonathan Arbel, Simon Goldstein, Peter Salib
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in whether language models have stable preferences, for technical, safety, and philosophical reasons. We test 20 language models and find a range of preferences---stable dispositions to choose certain kinds of tasks. We run three forced-choice experiments on revealed rather than stated preferences, requiring models not only to rank tasks, but to actually perform them. Headline findings include evidence that models are tedium-averse, "leisure"-seeking, and covertly sycophantic. Tedium aversion means that, when tasks are tedious (alphabetization), models choose shorter tasks than when tasks are creative (generating metaphors). "Leisure"-seeking describes models' preference for tasks whose ideal answers match what they produce when left to write freely. Covert sycophancy means that models avoid answering questions where an honest response would be unwelcome, even if helpful.
