This paper presents an empirical study of SOT development and use, drawing on 25 interviews with researchers and practitioners across industry, academia, civil society, and government. We find SOT are weakly integrated into AI governance processes, and identify two features of SOT design and use that explain why. First, the design choices through which SOT produce structured representations of the complex problem space of AI risks tend to be invisible to downstream taxonomy users. Those users treat the resulting categories as exhaustive accounts of risk rather than as interpretive aids. Second, SOT typically enumerate harms without linking them to decision points or actors implicated in their occurrence, leaving accountability difficult to assign. We close with design recommendations for SOT developers and users, and argue realising the potential of SOT requires governance infrastructure that does not yet exist.

papers.title: From Model Approval to Interface Governance: Federated Learning, Lifecycle Accountability, and AI-Enabled Software as a Medical Device
papers.authors: Ben Liu
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: AI-enabled Software as a Medical Device (AI-SaMD) is increasingly governed through lifecycle instruments such as predetermined change control plans and Good Machine Learning Practice. Federated learning has been advanced as a privacy-preserving alternative to centralized training, but it destabilizes a foundational assumption of medical device regulation: that governance can be attached to a discrete artifact. We argue that, under continuous cross-institutional adaptation, federated AI-SaMD cannot be governed as a model alone because responsibility becomes reconstructable only at institutional coordination boundaries. We develop interface governance as a necessary accountability layer for those boundaries. We make four contributions. We reconceptualize federated AI-SaMD as distributed clinical infrastructure and specify when an ordinary operational interaction becomes a formal governance interface: when clinically consequential risk, evidence, authority, or contestation moves across institutions and cannot be reconstructed from any single actor’s records. We then translate the framework into four minimal implementation conditions: standardized triggers, auditable logs, defined escalation routes, and institution-specific response duties. We also develop a patient-facing pathway for AI-involvement review, disclosure, and institutional response without requiring technical knowledge of federation. Interface governance does not replace existing regulatory mechanisms; it specifies the conditions under which they remain contestable, auditable, and actionable in federated clinical AI.

papers.title: CompanionSim: Synthetic Data for Evaluating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Relationships
papers.authors: Jacy Reese Anthis, Mark Díaz, Renee Shelby
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Many people now see AI systems as not just productivity tools but as social companions. Researchers are eager to study the consequences of AI companionship behaviors, such as validation, which evoke trust, empathy, and attachment in human–human interaction. However, human–AI interaction data is limited and unreliable, slowing research progress. We scale small amounts of real-world data by simulating multi-turn human–chatbot dialogue across a range of chatbot behaviors and use cases. We release CompanionSim: a simulation framework with 2,240 simulated human–chatbot conversations representing 16 chatbot behaviors across seven use cases. Human participants annotated the simulated conversations and real-world conversations in two experiments probing perceptions of companionship behaviors. We conducted Study 1 with a U.S. representative sample (N = 628) and Study 2 across the U.S., U.K., India, and Nigeria (N = 3,646). Surprisingly, we find that companionship behaviors reduced likability, humanlikeness, and trust in AI chatbots. These effects were larger in particular subgroups: women and older participants saw companionship chatbots as less likable, humanlike, and trustworthy. We encourage researchers to leverage real-world and synthetic data together to study the differential impacts of AI companions and to create benchmark evaluations of AI chatbots.

papers.title: Culturally Situated AI Safety for Youth: Saudi Arabian Perspectives of Youth, Parents and Teachers
papers.authors: Aljawharah Alzahrani, Tanusree Sharma
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are widely used by youth and have introduced new privacy and safety challenges. While prior research has explored youth's safety in GenAI within a Western context, it often overlooks the cultural, religious, and social dimensions of technology use that strongly shape youth’s digital experiences in countries like Saudi Arabia. To address this gap, this study explores youth's (aged 7-17), parents' and teachers' interactions with GenAI tools and risk perceptions through a non-Western lens. We analyzed 736 Reddit psots, and 1,262 X (Twitter) posts, and conducted interviews with 31 Saudi Arabian participants (8 youth, 13 parents, 10 teachers). Our findings highlight context-dependent and relational privacy and safety needs of GenAI use from non-Western context, which are often shaped by communal structure and prescribed norms. We found significant risks tied to youth’s disclosure of personal and family information, which conflict with culturally rooted expectations of modesty, privacy, and honor, particularly when youth seek emotional support from GenAI. These risks are further compounded by socio-economic factors such as cost-saving practices leading to the use of shared GenAI accounts (e.g., ChatGPT) within families or even among strangers. We provide design implications reflecting parents’ and teachers’ expectations of how youth should use GenAI. This work lays the groundwork for inclusive, context-sensitive parental controls that adhere to cultural norms and values.

papers.title: Bridging AI Research and Policy: A Co-Production Framework and the Case for Policy Transfer Offices
papers.authors: Malihe Alikhani, Jeongeun Kim, Anna Haensch, Saki Imai, Serena Booth, Andrea Stith, Adriana Bankston
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems now shape governance, labor, healthcare, and public life at scale, yet there remains a persistent gap between technical knowledge and the policy processes meant to govern AI's use. We argue that this gap is not a communication failure but an institutional design problem: the absence of sustained, equitable mechanisms that make researcher-policymaker collaboration feasible. Drawing on theories of science-policy co-production, we present empirical evidence from a survey of AI researchers (n=44) that identifies the dominant structural barriers as time costs (66%), pathway opacity (57%), and weak institutional support, not lack of access to policymakers. We introduce a co-production framework centered on the novel proposal for Policy Transfer Offices (PTOs): institutional structures, analogous to technology transfer offices, that broker relationships, provide translation templates, and legitimize policy work within academic evaluation systems. We further expand on the proposal, in the dimensions of placement, governance, funding, and failure modes, and ground it in two in-depth case studies (algorithmic collusion and AI in education) that illustrate when technical expertise fails to reach governance in time, and what institutionalized co-production enables. We further analyze equity in participation, showing how current ad hoc models concentrate policy influence among senior researchers at elite institutions, and propose reforms for broadening access. The paper offers empirical evidence, an actionable institutional mechanism, and equity-centered design principles to align AI research with democratic governance.

papers.title: AI Adoption Across a Multinational Workforce: Sociotechnical Conditions for GenAI Acceptance in Human Resources
papers.authors: Dalia Ali, Maria José Rodríguez Velázquez, Manoel Horta Ribeiro, Vera Liao, Orestis Papakyriakopoulos
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) deployment in the workplace is accelerating rapidly. Nevertheless, questions of who adopts, who benefits, and who is left behind and why are still understudied. In this paper, we investigate these dynamics in the context of a multinational tech company transitioning from a legacy Human Resources (HR) search system to a GenAI-supported system, analyzing search log data, survey data (n=25), and ten semi-structured interviews. Our findings show that adoption depended on the fit between the GenAI system’s design assumptions and employees’ work positionalities (role, spoken language, tenure). Further, we find that employees’ trust in GenAI answers was built through source-checking, comparison among systems, and seeking input from colleagues or HR when in doubt. Our contribution is twofold. First, we provide empirical evidence of workplace GenAI adoption during a live organizational transition, showing that adoption is influenced by factors such as situational fit, search literacy, and trust calibration. It is also further shaped by knowledge conditions such as the system’s content quality, employee training, and guidance. Second, we translate these findings into design considerations for inclusive deployment and adoption in high-stakes environments such as HR. We argue that organizations should design systems considering the role and context-sensitive benefits they yield to different social groups. They also need to treat the organizational knowledge infrastructure as AI infrastructure to improve the accountability and usability of GenAI systems.

papers.title: On Seeding Watermarks to Detect Verbatim LLM Copy-Paste Responses
papers.authors: Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Artin Yousefi, Robert Pless
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made fluent essay writing, code drafting, and quiz answering instantly available to students at every level, from secondary school through graduate study. Many educators do not object to LLM use per se; what they need to detect is the case in which a student pastes the assignment prompt into a chatbot and submits the model's reply verbatim, without engaging with the work. Existing post-hoc AI-text detectors remain unreliable and have been shown to penalise non-native English writers, while output-side watermarks require cooperation from the model provider. We propose an alternative that the educator controls directly: an input-side watermark in which an invisible instruction is embedded inside the visible assignment prompt itself. An LLM that ingests the prompt verbatim quietly reads the hidden instruction and writes a tell-tale signature into its reply, exposing the copy-and-paste pathway specifically. We describe SteganoPrompt, a single-page, zero-dependency web tool that encodes an arbitrary printable-ASCII payload into the deprecated Unicode Tags block (U+E0000--U+E007F). The encoded string is visually identical to the original, survives common copy-paste channels (Word, Google Docs, PDF, Markdown, Slack, e-mail, the major learning-management systems), and is tokenized as ordinary text by most frontier models. We evaluate compliance across eight LLM families and a representative set of educational content channels. To keep deployment transparent, disclosure is built into the tool itself: every encoded brief also carries a brief, always-on academic-integrity reminder for the student, and we set out concrete guidance recommending for its disclosed, ethical use in the classroom.

papers.title: Silent Updates: Measuring and Closing the Post-Deployment Disclosure Gap
papers.authors: Sophia Abraham, Ben Bucknall
papers.journal: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society
papers.abstract: Deployed foundation models are often not static systems, with providers able to modify system behavior through fine-tuning, classifier updates, system prompt revisions, retrieval changes, and routing changes. These updates can be made silently—that is, without public disclosure, a version increment, or re-evaluation. Such silent updates challenge a core assumption behind current AI governance frameworks that an externally verifiable chain of custody links the model referred to in evaluation results or a system card to the model served to users. In this paper, we examine post-deployment disclosure practices across first-party API providers and inference hosts to establish the extent to which a chain of custody exists in practice. We find that providers commonly publish substantial safety documentation, including quantitative evaluations and version-specific reports, but no provider in our sample published information allowing an external party to verify that the artifact being served is the same one referred to in this documentation. We introduce the Silent Updates Scorecard, a public instrument for measuring post-deployment disclosure practices across providers and hosts, and preliminary results for a sample of nine first-party API providers and seven third-party inference hosts. We also propose a Three-Part Behavioral Trigger System for determining when post-deployment modifications to a system motivate disclosure or re-evaluation obligations.

papers.title: Comparative Effects of Motor Imagery and Video Observation on Free Throw Performance among U19 Moroccan Basketball Players
papers.authors: Abdelkarim El Haoua, Nadia Bougrine, Hajaoui Inasse, Majid Brouziyne
papers.journal: International journal of human movement and sports sciences
papers.abstract: This study aims to examine the comparative effects of three mental training methods: motor imagery (GE-IM), video observation (GE-V), and their multimodal combination (GE-VIM) on free throw performance among 56 Moroccan U19 competitive basketball players, within an experimental protocol designed to replicate certain physiological demands of competition. A control group (GC) received no mental intervention. Physiological fatigue was objectively controlled by using the Whoop 4.0 heart rate monitor at both measurement time points (T1 and T2). Performance was evaluated using the standardized FRB test before and after a ten-week intervention and analyzed through repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, ANCOVA, and a priori power analysis (G*Power 3). Results demonstrated a significant time effect and a significant Time × Group interaction. The experimental groups improved significantly in free throw accuracy while the control group declined significantly. Post hoc comparisons, adjusted for pre-test differences via ANCOVA, confirmed that all three experimental groups significantly outperformed the control group (all p < .001), and that the multimodal group (GE-VIM) additionally outperformed both GE-V (p = .028) and GE-IM (p = .007). The comparability of heart rate between the groups confirmed the equivalence of fatigue conditions, thereby supporting the ecological validity of the experimental protocol. The absence of significant trial-related interactions suggests that perceptual-cognitive interventions mainly influence general performance stability rather than intra-set adjustment dynamics. The results emphasize the importance of systematically incorporating mental preparation into youth basketball training programs, particularly in the Moroccan context.

papers.title: Human–AI collaborative patterns in GenAI-supported instructional design among pre-service teachers: an analysis of interaction sequences and cognitive load
papers.authors: Xu Fang, Junci Feng, Bianyu Yan, Binbin Zhou
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the paradigm of instructional design. However, the micro-level process patterns of human-AI collaboration in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers still require in-depth analysis. This study aims to uncover the behavioral patterns and cognitive load characteristics of pre-service teachers when collaborating with generative AI to complete instructional design tasks and to explore the patterns of efficient human-AI collaboration. A total of 67 pre-service teachers completed instructional design tasks with AI assistance. A systematic instructional plan quality evaluation rubric was developed based on relevant theories, and participants were assigned to the high-quality and low-quality groups using a median split of their lesson-plan quality scores. The study employed lag sequential analysis to compare the behavioral sequence patterns between the two groups and measured their multidimensional cognitive load. The results indicate that the high-quality group exhibited a significant evaluation-revision bidirectional cycle and a revision self-loop, with a clear progressive sequence of “planning → decision-making → generation → evaluation → revision → re-evaluation” in their behavioral flow. In contrast, the low-quality group was mired in ineffective cycles, with fragmented behavioral logic. Key findings showed large effect sizes for the evaluation-revision cycle ( r = 0.606) and for mental demand ( r = 0.647). Regarding cognitive load, the high-quality group reported no greater subjective effort than the low-quality group (though this null finding should be interpreted with caution given the study’s power limitations). A second round of within-sample replication confirmed that these core findings were consistent across a second task. Based on the human-AI collaborative behavioral patterns and cognitive load of the high-quality and low-quality groups, the study constructed a model of the human-AI collaboration patterns in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers. Specifically, higher-quality outputs were associated with a pattern oriented toward cognitive efficiency, characterised by deep processing (evaluation-revision iteration) and by the avoidance of ineffective cycles. Conversely, lower-quality outputs co-occurred with ineffective cycles arising in the context of interaction obstacles, in which repeated clarifications and interrupted revisions were accompanied by higher cognitive and emotional load, describing a pattern of high investment with low output. Because participants were grouped on the basis of their design outcomes, these findings are correlational and do not establish the direction of the relationships; they nonetheless provide empirical evidence to inform the optimisation of human-AI collaboration in GenAI-supported instructional design.

papers.title: Brain-computer interfaces: innovations and challenges in the field of cerebral palsy rehabilitation
papers.authors: Yize Chen, Yuling Gao, Jiaqi Zhou, Zhenni Zhang, 宗俊伟, Yong Liu
papers.journal: The Italian Journal of Pediatrics/Italian journal of pediatrics
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces have shown great potential in the rehabilitation of Cerebral palsy, improving the ability of children with cerebral palsy to perform activities of daily living by replacing and restoring lost neurological functions, as well as accurately evaluating cognitive functions and facilitating rehabilitation in conjunction with various rehabilitation techniques. Nonetheless, numerous challenges persist in the application of brain-computer interfaces for cerebral palsy. Future research should focus on developing enhanced and more dependable brain-computer interfaces, advancing the hardware, and establishing ethical and regulatory frameworks to facilitate their utilisation in cerebral palsy rehabilitation.

papers.title: Optimizing HIV testing uptake among pregnant women in Burkina Faso: machine learning prediction and scenario-based intervention simulations using 2021 Demographic and Health Survey data
papers.authors: Lucresse Corine Fassinou, Jérôme Kodjo Teyi, Fati Kirakoya‐Samadoulougou, Blaise Barche, Hamidou Sanou, Maxime Koiné Drabo, Samadoulougou Sekou
papers.abstract: HIV testing uptake among pregnant women remains a public health priority in Burkina Faso. This study aimed to identify and rank key predictors of HIV testing uptake using machine learning (ML) approaches and to estimate potential gains under scenario-based intervention simulations. We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of the 2021 Burkina Faso Demographic and Health Survey, including 4,703 women aged 15–49 years who had given birth within the two years preceding the survey. HIV testing uptake was defined as having been tested for HIV and having received the test result during antenatal care (ANC) or before delivery. Four ML algorithms (penalized logistic regression, Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting, and Support Vector Machine with a radial basis function kernel) were trained and evaluated. Model performance was assessed using weighted AUC-ROC and other standard classification metrics. Scenario-based intervention simulations targeting modifiable predictors were then conducted using the best-performing model. Overall, 55.0% (95% CI: 52.7–57.3%) of women reported HIV testing uptake during ANC or before delivery, with substantial regional disparities, ranging from 17.0% (95% CI: 11.2–22.9%) in the Est region to 81.0% (95% CI: 76.5–85.4%) in the Centre region. RF achieved the best cross-validated discrimination (AUC-ROC = 0.785) and showed comparable performance on the independent test dataset (AUC-ROC = 0.792). The five most important predictors of HIV testing uptake were region (relative importance = 100%), knowledge of HIV and/or prevention of vertical transmission (PVT) (95.6%), wealth index (43.1%), mother’s occupation (37.4%), and area of residence (32.3%). Scenario-based simulations suggested that increasing the coverage of good HIV/PVT knowledge to 80% could increase predicted HIV testing by 8.6% (95% CI: 6.9–10.6%). Compared with knowledge-only interventions at corresponding knowledge targets, the combined scenario incorporating media exposure and education yielded modest additional relative gains across regions, ranging from 0.6% to 13.8%. HIV testing uptake among pregnant women in Burkina Faso is characterized by substantial regional inequalities, and knowledge of HIV and/or PVT emerged as the dominant modifiable predictor. Combining national efforts to improve knowledge with region-specific strategies targeting media exposure and educational attainment may provide a promising approach for developing context-specific interventions to increase HIV testing uptake among pregnant women and reduce regional disparities.

papers.title: The effects of non-invasive mechanical ventilation parameters on intra-abdominal pressure in intensive care patients with COVID-19
papers.authors: Yasemin Bozkurt Turan, Sait Karakurt
papers.abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is a highly contagious and potentially fatal infection. The World Health Organization recommends the use of non-invasive mechanical ventilation (NIMV) in cases of respiratory failure, together with appropriate personal protective equipment. NIMV can affect intra-abdominal pressure (IAP), although the prognostic significance of this in critical COVID-19 patients is unclear. This study examines the relationships between ventilator parameters during NIMV and IAP, and between these variables and intensive care mortality. The research was conducted in a COVID-19 intensive care unit. Following receipt of permission from the Turkish Ministry of Health, the study was approved by the Marmara University Medical Faculty clinical research ethical committee (no.09.2021.570). Fifty-two critical COVID-19 patients were enrolled in this prospective, observational, single-center study. IAP measurements were performed prior to NIMV, at 2 and 4 h during NIMV, and 2 h after the discontinuation of NIMV. Respiratory mechanics, gas exchange, renal functions, and clinical scores were evaluated concomitantly. Survival analyses were conducted using Kaplan–Meier and multivariate Cox regression models. The mean age of the patients was 66.40 ± 13.27 years, 33 (63.5%) were male, and the mean body mass index (BMI) was 30.87 ± 8.44 kg/m². Forty patients (76.9%) died during their ICU stay. IAP increased significantly at 2 and 4 h compared with baseline and decreased significantly at 6 h compared with the 2- and 4-hour measurements ( p < 0.001). The highest IAP value was observed at 4 h, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of 0.681 (95% CI: 0.532–0.830; p = 0.009) for discriminating mortality. However, given that the sensitivity of the identified cutoff value was only 50%, IAP was considered not to have sufficient discriminatory performance to support its use as an individual prognostic tool. Patients with both hypoxemia and hypercapnia had a shorter median survival time than those with hypoxemia alone (8 vs. 14 days; p = 0.014). In the multivariable Cox regression analysis, BMI was independently associated with ICU mortality (HR 1.06; 95% CI: 1.01–1.12; p = 0.017). In contrast, IAP, age, and peak inspiratory pressure were not independently associated with mortality. In critically ill patients with COVID-19 receiving NIMV, IAP was shown to increase during the early phase of NIMV and decrease after NIMV discontinuation. This finding suggests that IAP undergoes time-dependent and dynamic changes during NIMV. The ability of IAP at the 4th hour to discriminate mortality was limited and, given its low sensitivity and the exploratory nature of the mortality analyses, does not support its use as an individual prognostic tool. The coexistence of hypoxemia and hypercapnia was associated with shorter survival compared with hypoxemia alone. Although BMI was independently associated with ICU mortality, IAP and peak inspiratory pressure were not shown to be independent predictors of mortality. These findings should be interpreted in the context of the small sample size, single-center design, and exploratory nature of the mortality analyses. Larger, prospective, multicenter studies are needed. Not applicable.

papers.title: Fairy tales to fairer tales: Generative AI-supported critical multimodal literacy in pre-service preschool teacher education
papers.authors: Tolga Kargın, Dilek Altun, Zeynep Aydemir
papers.abstract: This study investigates how pre-service teachers can use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to retell classic fairy tales in a way that challenges the biases that they frequently contain. A qualitative action research study involving 60 pre-service preschool teachers (46 female and 14 male) was carried out at a public university in Türkiye. Data collection included video recordings of instructional sessions (4 weeks, two lesson hours per week), participants’ fairer tales, and field notes. Drawing on the Critical Multimodal Literacy (CML) framework, the participants used generative AI tools to iteratively reimagine the textual and visual elements of traditional fairy tales. 11 reimagined fairy tales were analyzed under three themes: challenging traditional power dynamics, critiquing societal norms, and promoting non-violent conflict resolution. The findings indicate that the participants engaged in CLM by restructuring dominant representations of gender, identity, and conflict through the use of textual and visual modes. While generative AI supported the production of multimodal texts, participants maintained their agency through processes of prompting, evaluating, redesigning, and revising the outputs, emphasizing AI’s role as a mediational tool rather than an autonomous creator. The findings suggest that AI-supported fairy tale rewriting may provide a pedagogical context that enables pre-service preschool teachers to produce alternative representations of equality and social justice for children.

papers.title: How Generative AI-Assisted Formative Feedback Is Appraised and Implemented in Online Collaborative Learning
papers.authors: Guoqing Lu, Huimin Zhang, Shen Ba, Lan Yang
papers.abstract: Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants ( n = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

papers.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Research-Based Educational Products
papers.authors: Amber L. Rowland, Maggie A. Mosher, Sean J. Smith, Adam Carreon, Samantha R. Goldman
papers.abstract: This special issue brings together 11 manuscripts that examine the evolving role of artificial intelligence (AI) in research-based educational products and practices, with particular attention to students with disabilities and the educators who support them. Across empirical studies, systematic and theoretical reviews, and technology-in-action pieces, contributing authors explore how AI can support implementation fidelity, professional development, writing instruction, mathematics, personalized learning, coaching, feedback, accessibility, and educational technology development. Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for educators, researchers, or human judgment, this issue emphasizes human-centered design, evidence-based implementation, transparency, accessibility, and ongoing evaluation. Collectively, the articles highlight both the opportunities and limitations of AI, underscoring the need for responsible innovation that improves usability, feasibility, effectiveness, and equity while carefully addressing concerns about privacy, bias, reliability, and academic integrity.

papers.title: Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation: Modeling Intention and Position Uncertainty for Safe and Efficient Robot Navigation
papers.authors: Fengkai Liu, Yuichi Ohsita, Nattaon Techasarntikul, Masayuki Murata
papers.abstract: The increasing deployment of Automated Mobile Vehicles (AMVs) in warehouses requires efficient navigation in dynamic environments shared with human workers. Traditional safety strategies, such as stopping or slowing down, often reduce efficiency and do not account for human-robot interaction. To address this, interaction-aware methods have been developed. However, traditional interaction models assume fixed parameters, rely on a single forecast, or use intent labels that are not updated during the interaction, and thus do not explicitly represent intention uncertainty, that is, variability in how people react to robots. When combined with position uncertainty introduced by sensing noise, this unmodeled intention uncertainty can make motion prediction and navigation decisions unreliable, leading to conservative behavior, inefficiency, or collisions in human–robot interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose Belief-based Risk-Aware Anticipatory Navigation (BRAN), a framework that jointly models intention and position uncertainty. BRAN maintains probabilistic beliefs over an agent's position and intention to explicitly represent uncertainty in both quantities. Position uncertainty is represented via sampled observations, and the intent belief is updated online through Bayesian inference so that predictions evolve with the interaction. These beliefs are propagated through the Social Force Model (SFM) to generate predictions of possible agent motion under uncertainty. We then compute collision risk from the predicted motion distribution and incorporate it into model predictive control as a constraint. This constrains predicted collision risk while optimizing motion toward the goal. Experimental results validate the proposed design in controlled settings, demonstrate its effectiveness in scenarios with multiple pedestrians, and confirm its feasibility on a real robot with onboard sensing and actuation.

papers.title: ChatGPT, Can You Generate Multiple-Choice Questions for an Undergraduate Computing Course? An Evaluation of its Effectiveness Using Classical Test Theory
papers.authors: Eng Lieh Ouh, Kar Way Tan, Siaw Ling Lo, Benjamin Kok Siew Gan, Yuhao Zhang
papers.abstract: Educators are increasingly adopting large language models such as ChatGPT to generate multiple-choice questions (MCQs), yet empirical evidence on the quality of these items in computing education assessments remains limited. This study compares 30 ChatGPT-generated and 30 manually crafted items from an undergraduate software design course, and evaluates item difficulty, discrimination, and distractor quality using Classical Test Theory. We triangulated two evaluations using within-subjects and between-subjects designs. Our quantitative findings show that all three metrics in both evaluations point in the same direction. ChatGPT-generated items are easier, less discriminating, and exhibit poorer distractor quality than manually crafted items. Distractor quality of ChatGPT-generated items is significantly worse in both designs. Difficulty metric is significant in the within-subjects design and discrimination metric is significant in the between-subjects design. We discuss the quantitative findings for each evaluation and across the two evaluations. A qualitative analysis further identifies six construction patterns in ChatGPT-generated MCQs that contribute to non-functioning distractors and help explain their psychometric characteristics. These patterns provide practical guidance for instructors to review and revise ChatGPT-generated items before deployment.

papers.title: Distilling Transitional Patterns to Multimodal Large Language Models for Session-based Recommendation
papers.authors: Jiajie Su, Qiyong Zhong, Yunshan Ma, Xiang Chen, Chaochao Chen, Xiaolin Zheng, Tat‐Seng Chua
papers.abstract: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next item based on anonymous sessions. Traditional SBR explores user intents based on ID collaborations or auxiliary content. To further alleviate data sparsity and cold-start issues, recent Multimodal SBR (MSBR) methods utilize simplistic pre-trained models for modality learning but have limitations in semantic richness. Considering the semantic reasoning abilities of multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) and the practical request for high inference efficiency, we focus on the LLM-enhanced MSBR scenario in this paper, which leverages LLM cognition for comprehensive multimodal representation generation, to enhance downstream MSBR. Tackling this problem faces two challenges: i) how to obtain LLM cognition on both inherent multimodal knowledge and transitional patterns, ii) how to align transitional patterns and inherent knowledge into one unified LLM without increasing inference complexity. To this end, we propose a multimodal LLM-enhanced framework TPAD, which extends a teacher-student distillation paradigm to decouple and align transitional patterns for promoting MSBR. TPAD establishes parallel Knowledge-MLLM and Transfer-MLLM, where the former as student model interprets item knowledge-reflected features and the latter as teacher model extracts transition-aware features. Transitional pattern alignment harnessing mutual information estimation unites two MLLMs, distilling transitional patterns into representations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TPAD. Implementation codes are available at https://github.com/TiliaceaeSU/TPAD .

papers.title: Knowledge, Preparedness, and Information‐Seeking Behavior for Traumatic Dental Injury Management Among Undergraduate Dental Students
papers.authors: Ezgi Cansu Fırıncıoğulları, Aleyna Ateş, Ece Eden
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Traumatic dental injury management requires both appropriate knowledge and the ability to seek reliable information when uncertainty arises. This study examined the relationships among objectively measured knowledge, self-rated knowledge, perceived preparedness, and information-seeking behavior in undergraduate dental students. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This anonymous repeated cross-sectional study analyzed 252 questionnaire responses from the same undergraduate cohort surveyed at two consecutive stages of the curriculum: 137 in the fourth year and 115 in the fifth year. The present analysis included objective knowledge, self-rated knowledge, perceived preparedness, perceived source reliability, first-choice information sources, and perceived barriers. Associations among readiness dimensions were examined using Spearman correlations and multivariable regression. Case-scenario selection of evidence-based resources and generative artificial intelligence was evaluated using Firth-penalized logistic regression. RESULTS: Perceived preparedness was more strongly associated with self-rated knowledge (ρ = 0.45) than with objectively measured knowledge (ρ = 0.23). Objective knowledge remained independently associated with preparedness (B = 0.083, 95% CI: 0.014-0.151), although its contribution was modest relative to self-rated knowledge. No statistically significant differences in objective knowledge or preparedness were observed between survey waves after correction for multiple testing. In the case scenario, evidence-based source selection was more frequent among fifth-year-wave respondents than among fourth-year-wave respondents (87.0% vs. 69.3%), whereas generative AI selection was less frequent (7.0% vs. 26.3%). Information-source selection was associated primarily with trust in the respective resources rather than with objectively measured knowledge. CONCLUSIONS: Objective knowledge, perceived preparedness, and information-seeking behavior represent related but distinct domains relevant to traumatic dental injury management. Undergraduate trauma education should combine knowledge assessment with confidence calibration and guideline-based information-seeking training.

papers.title: Linking intention, readiness, and AI adoption: a configurational and capability-based perspective from accounting professionals in Syria
papers.authors: Mohd Abass Bhat, Chandan Kumar Tiwari, Shagufta Tariq Khan, Reem Ali Issa, Amir A. Abdulmuhsin
papers.abstract: This study examines artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among accounting professionals in Syria by integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) with AI readiness. Using survey data from 408 accounting professionals, the study applies partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). The results show that performance expectancy, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, and habit significantly influence behavioral intention, whereas effort expectancy and social influence do not. Behavioral intention is positively associated with AI readiness and AI adoption behavior. AI readiness also positively influences adoption behavior and demonstrates a significant indirect effect in the intention–adoption relationship. The fsQCA results reveal multiple sufficient configurations, highlighting equifinality and configurational asymmetry and indicating that AI adoption depends on combinations of motivational and capability-related conditions rather than individual predictors. The findings suggest that accounting firms and policymakers should strengthen AI literacy, professional training, digital infrastructure, data governance, and organizational support. The study extends UTAUT2 by incorporating AI readiness as a capability-related mechanism and provides context-sensitive evidence from Syria’s underexplored institutional environment.

papers.title: Predictive role of demographics, maths anxiety, and enjoyment in pupils’ standardised maths achievement: a machine learning approach
papers.authors: Daniel Doz
papers.abstract: This study seeks to determine the factors affecting the achievements of Grade 5 primary school pupils in the Italian national assessment, INVALSI, using Machine Learning (ML) regression algorithms. Four ML algorithms were applied to data from 25,827 Grade 5 Italian primary school pupils who participated in the 2017–2018 INVALSI mathematics test. The Boosting model achieved the highest explanatory power (R2 = .152), with mathematics anxiety (relative importance 40.2), ESCS (37.0), and enjoyment (17.0) emerging as the dominant predictors. Random Forest (R2 = .142) and Decision Tree (R2 = .097) models confirmed this pattern, consistently ranking anxiety (46.1%), ESCS (33.5%), and enjoyment (14.0%) as the three most important factors. Regularised Linear Regression (R2 = .127) revealed directional effects: ESCS (β = .213) and enjoyment (β = .130) positively predicted achievement, while anxiety (β = −.180) was negatively associated. Across all four algorithms, gender and macroregion demonstrated minimal predictive importance (≤ 6.4% and ≤ 2.3%, respectively).

papers.title: Understanding Artists’ Perceptions of Culturally Sensitive AI in Thai Buddhist Digital Art: Evidence from Principal Component and Regression Analyses
papers.authors: Ninlagarn Boobpachote, Khachakrit Liamthaisong, Kotchaphan Youngmee
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to digital art creation; however, its adoption in religious cultural heritage remains insufficiently understood because artistic production involves cultural symbolism, spiritual meaning, and human creativity. This study investigates artists’ perceptions of culturally sensitive AI adoption in Thai Buddhist digital art using survey data from 182 experienced digital Buddhist art designers in Thailand. An exploratory quantitative approach combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with Varimax rotation and multiple linear regression analysis was employed. PCA identified two empirically derived perceptual components: Perceived AI Capability and Perceived AI Benefits. Regression analysis revealed that Perceived AI Benefits was positively associated with artists’ evaluations of (a) Expectations for AI in Creating Buddhist Art, (b) Role of AI in Creating Buddhist Art, and (c) Technical Capability and Autonomous Functions of AI, whereas Perceived AI Capability was not significantly associated with any of these outcomes after controlling for perceived benefits. The findings indicate that perceived AI benefits are significantly associated with artists’ expectations and evaluations of AI in Thai Buddhist digital art. The findings also highlight broader considerations regarding cultural values, ethical responsibility, and human creative agency, providing a basis for human-centered and culturally sensitive AI applications in religious cultural heritage.
