papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded in teaching, learning, research, assessment, and employment, making AI literacy an increasingly important component of higher-education readiness.Awareness of AI tools does not necessarily imply the ability to understand their limitations, evaluate outputs, protect privacy, recognise bias, or use AI ethically.Gender adds another layer to this problem because access to digital resources, confidence, patterns of technology use, institutional support and perceptions of risk may not be evenly distributed.This critical integrative review examines the relationship between AI literacy, gender and future readiness among women in higher education.The review synthesises conceptual scholarship on AI literacy, recent evidence on gender differences in higher-education AI engagement, international digital-inclusion data, and policy frameworks concerning AI competencies and responsible educational use.The analysis treats AI literacy as a multidimensional capability comprising AI knowledge, functional use, critical evaluation, ethical judgement, and future-oriented agency.Recent systematic evidence indicates that gender differences in AI engagement exist, while also showing that female students may approach AI more cautiously and express stronger concerns about privacy, dependency, reliability, and critical thinking.Such patterns should not be interpreted automatically as technological deficiency; they may also reflect different risk perceptions and expectations concerning responsible academic use.Global digital-access data further show that the gender digital divide remains present, with women representing 65% of Internet users compared with 70% of men globally in 2024.The review proposes a Women's AI Readiness Framework linking awareness, literacy, critical evaluation, ethical competence, confidence and future participation.The paper argues that

papers.title: Bridging Total Quality Management and Internal Quality Assurance Cells in Indian Higher Education Institutions: An Integrative Review of the TQM–IQAC Linkage
papers.authors: Shoubhanik Saha
papers.abstract: Indian higher education has entered a phase of intense quality scrutiny, driven jointly by the massification agenda of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the tightening benchmarks of the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC).Within this environment, Total Quality Management (TQM) -a management philosophy born in industrial manufacturing -and the Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC) -a statutory mechanism unique to the Indian accreditation ecosystem -have increasingly been discussed together, yet the conceptual and empirical linkage between the two is rarely made explicit in a single, integrative account.This review synthesises 43 peer-reviewed articles, institutional reports, and policy documents published between 2021 and 2026 to examine how TQM principles are operationalised through IQAC structures in Indian higher education institutions (HEIs).Using a PRISMA-informed screening process, the review develops an integrated TQM-IQAC conceptual framework, maps Malcolm Baldrige-derived TQM vectors on to the seven NAAC assessment criteria, and traces the empirical evidence linking IQAC functioning to accreditation grades and National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) performance.The review finds consistent evidence that leadership commitment, stakeholder (student) focus, and continuous-improvement routines are the TQM dimensions most strongly embedded in NAAC's evaluative architecture, while documentation burden, uneven regional capacity, and a persistent compliance-over-culture tension remain the principal obstacles to converting IQAC activity into genuine quality culture.The paper also considers the emerging role of artificial intelligence in accreditation data processing as a potential accelerant of the TQM 'data-driven decision-making' pillar.The review concludes with a research agenda emphasising longitudinal, mixed-method investigation of the TQM-IQAC linkage across India's diverse institutional landscape.

papers.title: CHARLES: Continuous Homeostatic Adversarial Resilience through Learning and Epistemic Sifting
papers.authors: Ishma Deshmukh Britton
papers.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and reinforcement learning (RL) in cybersecurity introduces the possibility of autonomous cyber agents capable of observing an environment, learning from interaction, and selecting sequential actions with limited human intervention.This development creates a challenge for conventional defensive strategies, which frequently depend on relatively stable system configurations, predefined detection rules, and human-led response processes.Cyber deception and moving target defense (MTD) provide mechanisms for increasing uncertainty and changing the environment encountered by an attacker, while game theory and reinforcement learning provide mathematical and computational approaches for modelling adaptive attacker-defender interactions.This paper proposes CHARLES (Continuous Homeostatic Adversarial Resilience through Learning and Epistemic Sifting), a conceptual defensive architecture designed to continuously manage the information and environmental conditions available to an autonomous attacker.Rather than attempting only to detect an attack after malicious activity has occurred, CHARLES proposes a feedback-based approach consisting of epistemic sifting, adaptive state transformation, adversarial learning estimation, and adversarial utility management.The framework aims to investigate whether controlled environmental variability and strategically deployed deception can reduce the stability of an attacker's learned policy, increase uncertainty, and alter the expected utility of attack strategies.The paper develops a simple mathematical model for representing attacker utility, environmental uncertainty, and defensive transformation.A simulation-based methodology is proposed to compare static and adaptive defensive environments against learning-based attackers.The work does not claim that continuous transformation universally defeats autonomous attackers; instead, it establishes a testable framework for investigating the relationship between defensive environmental adaptation and autonomous attacker learning.

papers.title: User-Generated Content and Responsible Tourism Destination Branding: A Conceptual Framework for Kerala
papers.authors: Faslu Rahman, Sharath AP, Muhammed Irfan V.P, Resha Basheer Pattupara
papers.abstract: User-generated content (UGC) has restructured how destination brands are formed, but the tourism-marketing literature has largely theorised this shift in the context of mainstream, high-volume destinations, leaving the branding dynamics of responsible tourism (RT) destinations under-conceptualised.This paper addresses that omission by developing an integrative conceptual framework explaining how UGC contributes to destination branding in Kerala's RT destinations.Rather than treating relevant theories in isolation, the framework fuses Source Credibility Theory, electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) theory, destination branding theory, and brand co-creation theory into a single explanatory chain.It positions UGC credibility and UGC authenticity as the qualities that make peer-generated eWOM persuasive; it treats responsible tourism attributes -community participation, cultural authenticity, environmental sustainability, local products, and ethical tourism practices -as the contextual brand meanings that credible, authentic content renders believable in a domain otherwise vulnerable to greenwashing scepticism; and it models destination brand image as the mediating asset that converts co-created content into travel intention.Six propositions specify the relationships among these constructs and are justified through the integrated theoretical logic.The paper contributes a theory-grounded account of how tourist-authored content co-creates a responsible destination brand, extends credibility and co-creation reasoning into the sustainability domain, and offers destination management organisations guidance on curating authentic advocacy rather than manufacturing it.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Changing Patterns of English Language Use: An Applied Linguistic Perspective
papers.authors: Monica Nnenne Okafor, Innocent Njoku Nweze
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is redefining the structure, practice, and evolution of English use in the twenty-first century.Generative AI technologies have been rapidly adopted in various fields as the educational tool of choice, language constructor for professional correspondence and creative writing assistance.Although artificial intelligence has gained increasing attention in the academic community, there is a surprising lack of studies focused on practical implications that center around language use, communication and changing discourse practices, especially from applied linguistic perspectives.This article explores the impact of artificial intelligence on modern English usage, including how it has influenced writing and speaking as well as our vocabulary processes and modes of communication in a digital age.It examines, in particular, how AI opens new avenues for language acquisition and communication, the new linguistic and pedagogical issues that arise with such AI-mediated language production, and what it may mean for future English.A qualitative research design based on documentary analysis, discourse analysis and perspectives of recent academic literature was adopted to enrich the study.The analysis is rooted on the Adaptive Linguistic Ecology Framework (ALEF), which proposes an original theoretical model positing that human linguistic creativity, sociocultural context, and algorithmic intelligence constantly co-evolve to give rise to language.It outlines that although artificial intelligence contributes to higher communicative efficiency, improved accessibility and language learning it also promotes linguistic homogenization and less stylistic diversity.The article, therefore, argues that AI should enhance, not replace, linguistic creativity through human agency, and advocates for language education to embrace AI literacy alongside critical language awareness and the preservation of linguistic diversity in digitally mediated communication.

papers.title: Design and Implementation of an AI-Based Email Filtering and Prioritization System for Polytechnic Administration Efficiency
papers.authors: Komolafe I.A., Fabiyi A.O., Fasoyiro S.O.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of electronic communication within higher education institutions has significantly increased the volume of emails processed by administrative personnel.Consequently, critical institutional communications are often overlooked among routine messages, promotional content, and spam, resulting in communication delays, reduced productivity, and administrative inefficiencies.This study presents the design and implementation of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based email filtering and prioritization system tailored for polytechnic administrative environments.The proposed framework integrates Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised machine learning algorithms to classify incoming emails into Urgent, Actionable, Routine, Promotional, and Spam categories.Multiple classification algorithms, including Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, and DistilBERT, were evaluated to determine optimal performance for institutional communication datasets.The system incorporates contextual prioritization mechanisms, role-based access controls, audit logging, and a web-based dashboard for real-time communication management.Findings indicate that intelligent email prioritization can significantly improve communication responsiveness, reduce email overload, and support digital transformation initiatives in tertiary institutions.The study contributes to a scalable framework suitable for deployment across Nigerian polytechnics and other public-sector organizations.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Tuned and Untuned Machine Learning Models for Cybersecurity Intrusion Detection
papers.authors: Kun Wang, Jinlei Gu
papers.journal: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Green Manufacturing
papers.abstract: This study benchmarks tuned and untuned machine learning models for intrusion detection across a 63-class attack taxonomy using the Cybersecurity Attack and Defense Dataset ($n=14{,}133$). A leakage-safe pipeline is designed, fitting all encoders and scalers exclusively on training data. Nine models are evaluated: five classical methods (Random Forest, Histogram-based Gradient Boosting, Extra Trees, SGD-based SVM, and Logistic Regression), two boosting frameworks (XGBoost and LightGBM), and two hybrids (soft-voting ensemble and two-level stacking with a LightGBM meta-learner). All models are systematically tuned via stratified randomized search and assessed on twelve metrics. XGBoost performs best, achieving a weighted $F_1$ of 0.8062, accuracy of 0.8094, MCC of 0.8030, and Cohen's $\kappa$ of 0.8028, outperforming Random Forest ($F_1=0.7062$), LightGBM ($F_1=0.7925$), linear classifiers, and hybrid models. LightGBM shows the largest tuning gain ($+0.755$ $F_1$). The proposed protocol offers a reproducible, bias-controlled benchmark for high-cardinality intrusion detection.

papers.title: Predicting Indie Game Success: A Diverse Stacking Ensemble Approach for Consumer Demand Forecasting
papers.authors: Tongyuan Zhang, Bin Hu
papers.journal: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Green Manufacturing
papers.abstract: As consumer expectations escalate across the video game market, accurately understanding player preferences is crucial for maximizing profitability and long-term retention. This is particularly challenging for independent (indie) developers who lack the resources of AAA studios. However, forecasting game ownership using the vast, heavy-tailed data from digital distribution platforms remains a significant hurdle. To address this gap, we propose a specialized, robust machine learning framework exclusively tailored for the indie market segment. Our approach utilizes a Diverse Stacking Regressor ensemble—integrating Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost algorithms alongside a Huber meta-learner—to predict game ownership based on comprehensive SteamSpy data. Compared to standalone baselines, such as a traditional Random Forest which achieved an $R^2$ score of 0.69 and a Median Absolute Error (MedAE) of nearly 100,000, our stacking approach demonstrates superior accuracy. It yields an $R^2$ score of 0.72, lowers the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) to approximately 20\%, and reduces the MedAE from approximately 100,000 to under 5,500. Ultimately, this predictive framework empowers indie developers to systematically interpret large-scale consumer data, facilitating optimized resource allocation and data-driven game design.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN EDUCATION FOR SUSTAINABILITY: ALIGNING AI-ENHANCED EDUCATION WITH THE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS
papers.authors: Amienseifa Sunny Yobolo
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATION SOCIAL AND MANAGEMENT SCIENCES
papers.abstract: This study examined the extent to which artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced educational practices in Bayelsa State universities align with, and contribute to, the attainment of Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4), which commits to inclusive, equitable, and quality education. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and Connectivism, the study adopted a correlational (ex post facto) survey design involving 350 respondents, comprising 75 lecturers and 275 students, drawn through a multistage sampling procedure from five universities. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the AI-Enhanced Education and SDG Alignment Questionnaire (AIESAQ), and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson Product Moment Correlation, Simple Linear Regression, and Hierarchical Moderated Regression. Findings revealed a moderate, positive, and statistically significant relationship between AI tool adoption and indicators of educational access and equity (r = 0.533, p < .001). AI literacy was also found to significantly and positively predict the perceived quality of AI-enhanced learning outcomes (β = 0.481, p < .001), accounting for approximately 23.2% of the variance. Furthermore, institutional readiness and infrastructural support significantly moderated the relationship between AI-enhanced education and SDG-aligned sustainability outcomes (ΔR² = 0.015, p = .021), although this construct recorded the weakest overall rating among the three variables examined. The study concludes that AI adoption and literacy are advancing ahead of institutional and infrastructural readiness, and that this lag constitutes the principal constraint on realising AI's full sustainability potential within Nigerian universities. Recommendations include the development of clear institutional AI-use policies, targeted infrastructural investment, and structured AI literacy training for lecturers and students.

papers.title: CHATGPT AS A TOOL FOR PLANNING SECONDARY EDUCATION: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: Gabriel Odobi Odey
papers.journal: INT’L JOURNAL OF EDUCATION MANAGEMENT SCIENCES AND PROFESSIONAL STUDIES
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of ChatGPT in planning secondary education in Nigeria, emphasizing both its opportunities and challenges in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Secondary education serves as a critical bridge between primary and tertiary levels, equipping learners with knowledge, skills, and values essential for personal development and national progress. However, the system continues to face persistent challenges, including inadequate funding, poor infrastructure, declining teacher performance, and low learning outcomes, which undermine its effectiveness and sustainability. In response to these challenges, AI has emerged as a transformative tool for strengthening educational planning. Specifically, ChatGPT holds significant potential in improving planning processes, facilitating evidence-based decision-making, enhancing communication, streamlining administrative functions, and supporting both teaching and learning. Despite these opportunities, the study recognizes major barriers to effective integration. These include financial constraints, infrastructural deficits, limited digital literacy among teachers and administrators, ethical and data privacy concerns, and resistance to adoption due to fears of eroding professional autonomy. To address these barriers, the study recommends phased funding models, targeted infrastructural investment, continuous professional development programs, robust data protection measures, and collaborative change management strategies. Effective implementation of these measures can ensure that ChatGPT serves as a complementary tool, strengthening rather than diminishing educational standards. The findings highlight that, with strong policy frameworks and sustainable practices, ChatGPT has the potential to foster a more efficient, equitable, and future-ready secondary education system in Nigeria.

papers.title: Continuance Intention Towards AI-Enabled Fintech Services in India: Examining the Roles of Trust and Perceived Privacy Risk Method
papers.authors: Mrs. Surabhi R, Dr. Shivakumar ., Mr. Ramesha K
papers.journal: Journal of Asia Entrepreneurship and Sustainability
papers.abstract: With India’s rapid digital transformation driven by the Unified Payments Interface ecosystem and widespread adoption of AI-powered fintech services, such as Google Pay, PhonePe, and Paytm, understanding the determinants of users’ continuance intention has become increasingly critical. Despite extensive research on fintech adoption, post-adoption behavior and continuance usage of AI-enabled fintech services in emerging economies like India remain underexplored. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a comprehensive model integrating parasocial relationship theory, trust-commitment theory, UTAUT2, and the Service Robot Acceptance Model (sRAM). Survey data from 624 fintech AI users across Karnataka, India, provide rich insights into AI-enabled fintech service continuance in a rapidly digitizing economy. The findings reveal that performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, and social influence positively impact engagement and continuance intentions, with perceived intelligence and perceived accuracy also playing significant roles. The study establishes the moderating effect of perceived privacy risk on several key relationships, advancing the understanding of AI-enabled fintech service continuance in the Indian context.

papers.title: AN ADAPTIVE COMPETENCY-BASED METHODOLOGICAL SYSTEM FOR TEACHING INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY IN GENERAL EDUCATION SCHOOLS
papers.authors: Raxmatilla Mamajanov
papers.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies and artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming the educational environment and changing the requirements for contemporary schooling [13, 7]. Schools are increasingly expected not only to provide students with basic computer literacy but also to develop broader digital competencies, including information and data literacy, digital content creation, problem solving, and computational thinking [22, 6, 16]. At the same time, the growing integration of artificial intelligence into everyday life requires students to develop AI literacy and learn to engage with AI technologies critically and responsibly

papers.title: Students’ Perspectives on Generative AI Usage Policies at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia
papers.authors: M. Maulana, Riana Irawati, Ronny Mugara, Bagja Nugraha, I Ketut Widhi Adnyana, Enjang Yusup Ali, Rina Munawaroh
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Practice and Policy
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education offers learning benefits but raises concerns about academic integrity, transparency, and students’ independent thinking. This study examined students’ perspectives on GenAI usage policies and their needs regarding policy implementation. A descriptive survey design was employed, involving 187 students who were familiar with or had used GenAI for academic purposes. Data were collected through a questionnaire comprising closed- and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, item–total association and internal consistency analyses, the Kruskal–Wallis test, and Spearman’s correlation. Qualitative responses were analyzed thematically, with both data strands integrated during interpretation. The overall mean score was 4.03 (80.57%). Relevance and learning support received the highest score (83.24%), whereas clarity and understanding of policies received the lowest (77.46%). No statistically significant differences in students’ perspectives were found across GenAI usage-frequency groups. The qualitative findings highlighted students’ needs for clearer guidelines on acceptable AI use, improved AI literacy, transparent disclosure practices, appropriate monitoring and consequences for violations, and policies responsive to technological developments. Overall, students viewed GenAI as a supportive learning tool rather than a substitute for independent thinking and academic responsibility. These findings underscore the need for clear, transparent, and adaptable higher education policies that facilitate responsible GenAI use while safeguarding academic integrity and student autonomy.

papers.title: Trends in 21st-Century Learning Technology Research: Digital Transformation, AI, and Adaptive Learning
papers.authors: Lucie Nicole Addison, Lynn Elizabeth, Fatqurhohman Fatqurhohman
papers.journal: JINEA Journal of Innovation in Education and Learning
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive learning is reshaping 21st-century education, yet their interrelationships and research trajectories remain fragmented. This study systematically reviews research published from 2020 to 2026 to examine the evolution, dominant and emerging themes, and conceptual relationships across digital transformation, AI, and adaptive learning. Using a systematic literature review with thematic synthesis, relevant studies were analyzed temporally and thematically to identify shifts in research orientation and emerging directions. The findings reveal a progressive transition from technology integration and digital learning environments toward intelligent tutoring, personalization, adaptive learning, and, more recently, generative AI and human–AI collaboration. Conceptually, digital transformation functions as the enabling ecosystem, AI as an intelligent capability, and adaptive learning as a learner-responsive application. Importantly, AI-enabled personalization does not necessarily constitute adaptive learning; meaningful adaptation requires continuous responsiveness to learner performance, needs, feedback, and learning trajectories. The synthesis further indicates that technological advancement alone is insufficient, highlighting teacher agency, learner autonomy, organizational readiness, data governance, and ethical accountability. The study proposes a human-centered and responsible orientation in which AI augments pedagogical judgment rather than displacing it.

papers.title: Predictors of Anesthetic Augmentation in Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.authors: Derya İpekçioğlu, Ceyhan Oflezer, Numan Konuk, Özge Canbek, Yusuf Ezel Yıldırım, Zümrüt Ela Arslan Kaşdoğan, Melih Avcı, Yusuf Besim Sıkar, Nihal Begüm Yılmaz, Mustafa Nuray Namlı
papers.abstract: Background: Anesthetic augmentation with aminophylline and/or remifentanil is commonly used to prolong seizure duration when propofol-based electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) results in inadequate seizures. We aimed to identify independent predictors of subsequent augmentation use and develop an exploratory risk score.Methods: This retrospective cohort study (January–December 2015, single center) included 527 patients (4,016 ECT sessions) who received propofol anesthesia. Patients were categorized as propofol-only (n=357) or augmentation (n=170) group. Multiple logistic regression was used to identify predictors of augmentation. ANCOVA compared the effect of different adjunctive agents on post-adjunct seizure duration.Results: Shorter first-session electroencephalography (EEG) seizure duration (OR = 0.968, P < .001) and higher first-session seizure-inducing energy (OR = 1.044, P < .001) independently predicted augmentation, while age was not significant (P = .120). All three augmentation strategies significantly prolonged seizure duration; although, the sample sizes for individual agents (aminophylline n=85, remifentanil n=44, combination n=41) precluded a definitive comparative analysis; the ANCOVA revealed no significant differences between agents (F=0.967, P = .382). CGI scores were comparable between groups at baseline (P = .412) and discharge (P = .321). An exploratory risk score based on the two significant predictors showed good discriminative ability (AUC = 0.786).Conclusion: First-session EEG seizure duration and stimulation energy are practical predictors of subsequent augmentation use, whereas age is not independently predictive. No statistically significant difference in post-adjunct seizure duration was detected among the three adjunctive strategies and augmentation is associated with comparable clinical improvement. External validation of the proposed risk score is required before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Algorithmic Determinism vs. Executive Agency: A Theoretical Examination of Strategic Management in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Chen Wei
papers.abstract: Strategic management settled its dispute between environmental determinism and managerial choice by treating constraint as arriving from outside the firm. Artificial intelligence unsettles that arrangement, because the algorithms that filter markets, rank acquisition targets and evaluate strategic alternatives are installed by executives themselves. This conceptual paper asks where executive agency goes when strategic decisions pass through algorithmic systems. Drawing on upper echelons and managerial discretion research, sociomaterial accounts of technology and evidence on how decision-makers respond to algorithmic outputs, it develops a framework of configured discretion. Algorithmic determinism is theorized as an endogenous, cumulative constraint operating through attention, evaluation and capability. Executive agency is relocated into three practices: framing objectives, contesting outputs and reconfiguring decision architecture. The central argument is that delegation is self-binding. Each act of delegation can erode the capabilities executives need to contest the system later, so formal authority persists while real latitude shrinks. Seven propositions follow, with a state-transition model of four adaptation states (algorithmic capture, governed hybridity, executive voluntarism and fragmented drift) that recasts the two-continua model of organizational adaptation for firms whose constraints are partly self-made. The framework reconciles conflicting findings on algorithm aversion and appreciation and on the value of human override. Governance regimes moderate the loop: fiduciary duties of care and oversight, audit-committee benchmarks against core models and party-state oversight each shape how far effective discretion can fall below formal authority.

papers.title: Relationship between Financial Stress and Young Adults’ Psychological Distress
papers.authors: Eileen Pak
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that approximately 1 in 3 young adults experience significant financial stress which leads to heightened anxiety levels prompting us to test this growing relationship between economic instability and young adults’ mental health. Understanding how economic instability, insecurity, and debt contribute to the rising anxiety that is commonly observed among young adults and explores its psychological effects is very crucial for preventing financial stress on them. By analyzing existing research on income, socioeconomic class, and mental health outcomes this review demonstrates how financial pressure correlates to chronic stress, uncertainty about futures in both young adults which can lead to physical problems as well. The paper further highlights young adults as a particularly vulnerable group to impacts of financial anxiety because of their limited financial independence, debts from colleges and universities, and uncertain future which can lead to psychological distress. Not only do these burdens cause psychological distress but also, early socioeconomic stress is associated with long-term mental and physical health consequences, including elevated BMI, hypertension, and eating disorder symptoms into adulthood.

papers.title: Synapse AI: A Multimodal Machine Learning Framework for Early Seizure Prediction Using Wearable Physiological Signals
papers.authors: Anna Suherman
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent seizures that often occur without warning, posing significant risks to patient safety and quality of life. While current treatments reduce seizure frequency for some individuals, reliable early seizure prediction remains a major challenge. This study developed Synapse AI, a prototype machine learning framework for early seizure prediction using electroencephalography (EEG) signals, intended to serve as the foundation for a future multimodal seizure prediction system integrating wearable physiological signals. EEG recordings from five cases in the publicly available CHB-MIT Scalp EEG Database were segmented into 10-second windows and labeled as preictal (5–30 minutes before seizure onset) or interictal. Statistical, time-domain, and frequency-domain features were extracted from each EEG window and used to train and compare three supervised machine learning models: XGBoost, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Model performance was evaluated using grouped train-test splitting, grouped cross-validation, and the metrics accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and ROC-AUC. Among the models evaluated, XGBoost achieved the strongest overall performance, obtaining an accuracy of 76.2%, recall of 84.6%, F1 score of 78.0%, and ROC-AUC of 85.2% on held-out test cases. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using machine learning to identify preictal EEG patterns for early seizure prediction. Overall, this study establishes a proof-of-concept and provides a foundation for the development of more effective and accessible seizure prediction systems.

papers.title: The role of AI in the primary sector
papers.authors: Thainara Rafaela Luís Rosa
papers.abstract: Increased reliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) has intensified patterns of sectoral dependency in the global economy, a trend that dates back to the Industrial Revolution. While the adoption of AI in the secondary and tertiary sectors has greatly expanded, its integration remains uneven for the primary sector. This paper assesses the advantages and disadvantages of AI in the agriculture, fishing and forestry industries. The current literature also adds to this, highlighting that smaller firms face particularly significant barriers, ethical and regulatory concerns surrounding inequality and job displacement, among other barriers. Overall, this paper suggests the need for stricter regulations, and tailored planning for each industry, through government initiatives that integrate Environmental Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) and AI developers. Moreover, it suggests that technological progress promotes efficiency, equity, and sustainability.

papers.title: Perceptions of AI and Patterns of Use among Attorneys in Richmond, Virginia
papers.authors: Aaiza Rassiwala
papers.abstract: This study examines how attorneys in Richmond, Virginia, perceive and use artificial intelligence (AI) within legal practice. As AI tools become further integrated in legal workflows, questions have emerged about accountability, transparency, bias, and professional responsibility in regards to AI. A mixed-methods approach was used to collect data from 32 legal professionals, and a semi-structured interview was conducted with a legal expert to evaluate patterns of AI use and perceptions of the existing regulatory framework. Findings indicate that AI has been moderately integrated into most legal practices through primarily low-risk tasks like document drafting and research, though general trust in large language model systems remains low. The study identifies patterns suggesting that attorneys selectively integrate AI based on perceived professional risk, relying on informal self-regulation in the absence of clear oversight. These findings contribute to the emerging research on behavioral responses to AI in legal practice and suggest the need for future studies examining how professional beliefs shape AI adoption patterns.

papers.title: Words as Value: The Market Premium of AI Disclosure
papers.authors: Nathan Wang
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly reshaped the business landscape. Now, firms are not only adopting this novel tool but also publicizing their AI efforts through official filings and third-party media coverage. While extensive research has examined the benefits of internal AI usage, little is known about how communication on this usage affects investor perception and consequently market valuation. This study examines the relationship between Dual AI Signaling (annual 10-K reports and AI news coverage) and firm market performance. We hypothesize that heavier signaling corresponds with stronger performance, particularly in the Financial sector and among larger companies. Our data sample comprises 5,643 firm-year observations covering 503 point-in-time S&P 500 constituents from 2015-2025, drawn from SEC EDGAR filings and RavenPack news analytics accessed through Wharton Research Data Services. Employing Tobin’s Q as the performance outcome, with year fixed effects and controls for R&D intensity, leverage, and size, we find that firms with higher Dual AI Signaling Scores (lagged by one year) demonstrated significantly stronger market performance (β = 0.70, p < 0.001). The positive relationship is strongest in the Consumer Staples and Consumer Discretionary sectors and intensifies as firm assets rise (β = 0.24, p < 0.001). Independently, formal disclosures tended to be far more favorable than media attention in achieving greater market performance. For firms and investors, these findings suggest that increased AI communication itself is not a homogeneous advantage but depends considerably on sector and size.

papers.title: How Accurately and Creatively Can Generative AI Produce Music Across Genres? A Mixed-Methods Evaluation of ACE-Step 1.5
papers.authors: Flora Wu
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence music tools such as Suno, Udio, and ACE-Step can now create full songs with vocals, instrumentation, and production quality convincing enough to sound like human-made music. However, musical "quality" is not a single measurable property, and treating "AI music" as one category by itself risks missing details on how performance varies by genre. This study asks: how accurately and creatively can generative AI produce music across different genres? Two hundred tracks were generated using the open-source model ACE-Step 1.5 across ten genres (Pop, Hip-Hop & Rap, Classical, EDM, Rock, Latin, Country, R&B, Jazz, and Metal), using five human-written lyric sets to isolate genre as the main variable. Each track was evaluated through two complementary methods: a computational audio analysis using Essentia's Discogs-trained genre classifier, and a human evaluation using a five-criterion rubric assessing harmonic language, melodic development, rhythmic integrity, dynamics, and emotional fidelity. Results suggest that AI-generated music performance is uneven and genre-dependent instead of uniform: genres that relied on standardized and rhythmic structures were classified and rated more consistently than genres that needed more sophisticated harmonies or improvisation and creativity. Genre-classification confidence and rubric-based creativity scores did not always align, which may mean the model can recreate surface-level genre traits without capturing the expressions and qualities associated with human musicianship. The study also brings a methodological finding to light: the genre classifier's own training taxonomy assigns subgenre labels unevenly across genres, which can distort genre-accuracy independent of the audio itself.

papers.title: Shifting the Balance of Stability: The Automation Gap, AI-Defense, and the Transition to First-Strike Cyber Exploitation
papers.authors: Ezra Matiwos Wesenie
papers.abstract: Historically, state-sponsored cyber operations operated within a 'grey zone'—defined here as an operational and diplomatic sanctuary of sub-threshold conflict, where low-intensity digital intrusions remain below the threshold of conventional armed conflict or formal military response. However, autonomous, AI-driven cyber defense platforms (such as automated, enterprise-wide AEGIS security architectures) have closed the "Automation Gap," which represents the traditional time delay between an attacker exploiting a vulnerability and a defender deploying a patch. Operating at machine speed, automated defenders instantly detect and neutralize low-intensity intrusions. This capability systematically dismantles the stabilizing temporal buffer that once protected peacetime statecraft, forcing cyber operations out of the grey zone. Applying three core theoretical frameworks, this paper examines how defensive AI dominance paradoxically destabilizes international relations. First, it uses the Security Dilemma 2.0, where a state installing powerful defensive AI makes neighboring states feel threatened, driving them to prepare aggressive counter-attacks. Second, it incorporates the Deception-Detection Dichotomy, which highlights the structural divide between AI’s high proficiency in pattern-based threat detection and its weakness in executing creative, stealthy attacks. Third, it applies the Subversive Trilemma, the strategic constraint holding that a cyberattack can never maximize speed, intensity, and stealth simultaneously. Automated defense renders gradual digital subversion ineffective. Consequently, it incentivizes revisionist states—those seeking to alter the geopolitical status quo—to bypass traditional escalation ladders entirely. These states are driven to launch high-stakes "first-strike" cyberattacks that cause physical destruction (cyber-kinetic campaigns). Their goal is to achieve an unalterable victory (a fait accompli) before automated defenses can adapt or human diplomats can intervene. This study demonstrates how competing strategic paradigms accelerate escalation. It compares the offensive, proactive "Persistent Engagement" model of the United States with the defensive, denial-oriented "Digital Fortress" model of Singapore. The analysis leverages case studies from Operations Epic Fury, Roaring Lion, and Cyber Guardian. Furthermore, the paper shows how these technological gaps force small states to surrender digital control to superpower-led "AI-Defense Blocs." Meanwhile, international governance efforts—such as the UN permanent Global Mechanism launched in March 2026—remain constrained by enforcement gaps in international law (the "Legal Trilemma"). Finally, the study highlights how automated cyberattacks on dual-use conventional and nuclear command networks risk triggering preemptive nuclear escalation under "use-it-or-lose-it" pressures. To restore strategic stability, this paper proposes three critical policy interventions: cryptographic machine- speed hotlines to exchange automated tokens of intent during high-velocity network events, mandatory human-in-the-loop agentic AI guardrails to require explicit human authorization for high-risk operations, and decentralized AI-defense capacity-building to democratize security tools for developing nations.

papers.title: The Era of Super intelligence (SI) and the Indian Education System: Challenges, Opportunities, and Future Directions
papers.authors: Satya Narayan Yadav
papers.journal: The Paradigm Chronicle Journal of Academic Inquiry and Critical Thought
papers.abstract: This research paper presents a serious and comprehensive analysis of how the emerging and rapidly changing era of 'Super intelligence' (SI) is fundamentally transforming the fabric of global and Indian society. In the history of modern technological revolutions, this turning point is the most unprecedented, where the traditional boundaries of artificial intelligence have been shattered and intellectual capacity is moving far beyond the scope of human control. Basic sectors such as education, health, employment, and industries are being affected the most by this technological leap. Focusing on these broad, complex, and far-reaching effects, this research paper closely examines the current preparedness of the Indian education system, the emerging trends of the younger generation, the serious challenges encountered along the way, and a comparative study with the foreign perspective of developed countries. In the next phase of the study, this research explores ideological paths to save Indian identity, culture, and originality amidst globalization and the blind race of technology. For this, the provisions of the National Education Policy (NEP 2020), modern technological requirements, and the support of our rich Indian philosophical tradition and 'Indian Knowledge Systems' (IKS) have been made the basis. The main objective of the research is to emphasize that in this race for the future, only technical proficiency is not enough; rather, the inclusion of moral values, character-building, and human sensitivities is equally essential. Finally, this research paper presents practical and policy suggestions to make the future direction robust, inclusive, self-reliant, and balanced, so that this torrential era of super intelligence does not become a cause of destruction for the Indian education system and society, but rather proves to be a great boon. This study will serve as an important document for policy-makers, academicians, and researchers in preparing the framework for the future.

papers.title: Depression, Stigma, and Social Support Among Patients with Epilepsy at King Abdullah Medical City, Makkah: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Sami Yahya A. Saad, Omniah Andijani, Alhanouf Alharthi, Hayfa Al-Alfard, Bayan Fatani, Turki M Al-Shehri, Hanadi Abualela
papers.abstract: Background: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder frequently complicated by psychiatric comorbidities, particularly depression, which substantially impairs quality of life. In addition to its clinical burden, epilepsy remains highly stigmatized, especially within culturally conservative societies such as Makkah, Saudi Arabia. This study aimed to assess perceived stigma and examine its association with depression among patients with epilepsy. Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted among adults with electroencephalography (EEG)-confirmed epilepsy. A total of 68 adult patients with epilepsy were included after providing informed consent. Depression was assessed using the Neurological Disorders Depression Inventory for Epilepsy (NDDI-E), the Oslo Social Support Scale (OSSS-3), and stigma was measured using the Epilepsy Stigma Scale (ESS). Univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to examine associations with stigma scores. Results: The prevalence of depression was 35.3% (95% CI: 25.0%-47.2%). Most participants were female (58.0%), aged 30–40 years (40.6%), unemployed (76.8%), and had focal temporal seizures (65.2%). The mean stigma score was 34.37 (SD = 12.57). In univariable analysis, depression was not significantly associated with stigma (β=2.27, p=0.482). In multivariable linear regression adjusting for age, gender, education, seizure focus, and social support, depression remained unassociated with stigma (β=2.50, p=0.455). However, poor social support independently predicted higher stigma scores (β=10.83, p=0.022), and high school education was independently associated with lower stigma scores (β=-7.16, p=0.042). Conclusion: Depression and perceived stigma are prevalent among patients with epilepsy. Although no independent association was observed between depression and stigma, some factors, such as social support and educational level, significantly influenced perceived stigma. These findings underscore the need for integrated psychosocial interventions, enhanced social support systems, and targeted educational strategies to improve mental health outcomes among epilepsy patients in Makkah, Saudi Arabia.

papers.title: Democratization or Digital Enclosure? Socio-Economic Disparities in Access to AI and Digital Learning Tools in Higher Education
papers.authors: Sharma M. K.
papers.journal: Wisdom Vortex International Journal of Social Science and Humanities
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is widely heralded as an equalizer in higher education, yet emerging evidence suggests that tiered monetization and computational requirements may reproduce existing inequalities. Anchored in Pierre Bourdieu’s theory of cultural capital and Jan van Dijk’s digital divide framework, this study investigates socio-economic disparities in student adoption of GenAI tools. Utilizing a cross-sectional survey of university students (N=450) across public and private institutions, bivariate and hierarchical regression analyses were conducted. Findings indicate significant institutional (χ2 = 44.18, p<.001) and income-based (χ2 = 68.92, p<.001) divides in access to premium AI tiers. Furthermore, "Digital Cultural Capital" (prompt literacy and critical auditing) and paid subscription access independently predicted significant variance in academic self-efficacy (ΔR2 = .234, p<.001). The study concludes that paywalled algorithmic tools risk instituting a modern digital enclosure, necessitating policy interventions such as institutional licensing consortia and standardized prompt literacy curricula.

papers.title: Talenta Society 5.0 dan Transformasi Kerja: Tantangan dan Peluang Pengembangan Sumber Daya Manusia di Era Digital
papers.authors: Brilliant Jagad Satrio, Jofite Maulana Rohman, Ahmad Faizal Afandi, Mochammad Isa Anshori
papers.journal: Journal of Business Economics and Management
papers.abstract: The development of Society 5.0 has transformed talent management and the characteristics of work through the increasing use of digital technology and artificial intelligence. These changes require organizations to develop not only digital competencies but also adaptability, creativity, innovation, communication, and continuous learning capabilities. This study aims to analyze changing talent requirements and human resource development in addressing work transformation in the Society 5.0 era. The research applies a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach by identifying, selecting, and synthesizing relevant scientific articles concerning talent, Society 5.0, digital transformation, competency development, AI, and changes in work. The findings indicate that organizational readiness is strongly influenced by the ability to develop talent capable of integrating digital and human competencies. Upskilling, reskilling, AI utilization, adaptive leadership, and human-centered approaches are important elements in responding to changes in the world of work. These findings emphasize that talent development should be positioned as a strategic component of organizational transformation to support an adaptive, innovative, and sustainable workplace. .

papers.title: A Scientometric and PCA-Based Structural Mapping Study Identifying Research Fragmentation and Gaps in Agentic AI
papers.authors: Long N Nguyen, Trang P Chau
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Studies
papers.abstract: Although Agentic AI has emerged rapidly as a distinct, goal-pursuing paradigm within artificial intelligence, its scholarship remains fragmented and conceptually unsettled. Most extant literature conflates functional AI agents with system-level Agentic AI and relies heavily on qualitative surveys lacking empirical structural validation. To address this gap, this study develops a data-driven scientometric and structural mapping framework using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Analyzing $N = 170$ peer-reviewed publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus between 2024 and 2026, text data across titles, abstracts, and keywords were standardized and coded into five primary themes: Technology & Architecture (T1), Ethics & Trust (T2), Governance & Policy (T3), Human–AI Interaction (T4), and Applications & Domains (T5). PCA reveals that three principal components capture 98.17% of the total variance. The thematic space is governed by two prominent orthogonal bipolar axes: PC1 (43.33% variance) contrasts deployment and interaction (T4, T5) with normative and policy dimensions (T2, T3), while PC2 (37.98% variance) sharply opposes core technical architectures (T1) against ethical governance (T2, T3). These findings expose systemic structural fragmentation, demonstrating that Agentic AI is predominantly investigated as isolated technical or normative problems rather than an integrated socio-technical system. By pinpointing critical research gaps at the intersection of agentic architecture, oversight mechanisms, and institutional accountability, this paper proposes a future research agenda centered on governance-aware agent architectures and cross-disciplinary research designs.

papers.title: Comparación de modelos estadísticos y aprendizaje automático para predecir rendimiento académico universitario con datos abiertos
papers.authors: Johnny Gerardo Barriga-Arizabala, Rosman José Paucar Córdova, Nelson Marcelo Aldaz Herrera
papers.abstract: Predicting academic performance using statistical models and machine learning algorithms may provide useful information for the early identification of university performance patterns. However, meaningful comparisons require homogeneous validation protocols and control of information leakage. This study aimed to compare the performance of one statistical model and three machine learning algorithms for predicting university academic performance before the final examination. A quantitative, observational, analytical, comparative, and predictive study was conducted using 560 open academic records. The target variable was Categories, comprising five performance levels. Seven predictors available before the final examination were used: Quiz, Midterm, Assignment_1, Assignment_2, Assignment_3, Project, and Presentation. Multinomial logistic regression, decision tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting were compared using an 80/20 stratified split and five-fold stratified cross-validation. Macro-F1 was the primary metric. Random Forest showed the best overall profile, with a Macro-F1 of 0.7360 in cross-validation and 0.7633 on the test set, followed by Gradient Boosting with 0.7099 and 0.7477, respectively. Random Forest achieved an Accuracy of 0.7768 and an F1 score of 0.8571 for Fail. Midterm showed the highest permutation-based predictive importance. Ensemble-based models showed a predictive advantage over the statistical reference model, although the findings are limited to the analyzed dataset and require external validation.

papers.title: Explaining FOMO Symptoms Based on Maladaptive Perfectionism and Emotional Loneliness with Emphasis on the Mediating Role of Artificial Intelligence Dependency among Female High School Adolescents
papers.authors: Zohre Rajabzade Dezfouli, Saeed Moshtaghi,  Shahram Noori Samarein
papers.journal: Journal of Adolescent and Youth Psychological Studies (JAYPS)
papers.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to explain FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) symptoms based on maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness, with a particular focus on the mediating role of artificial intelligence dependency among female high school adolescents. Methods and Materials: This correlational study employed a structural equation modeling approach to investigate the relationships among maladaptive perfectionism, emotional loneliness, artificial intelligence dependency, and FOMO symptoms. The statistical population consisted of all female students enrolled in secondary high schools in Dezful, Iran, during the 2025–2026 academic year. A total of 250 students were selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected using the Fear of Missing Out Scale developed by Przybylski et al. (2013), the Multidimensional Perfectionism Questionnaire by Hewitt and Flett (2004), the Social and Emotional Loneliness Scale by DiTommaso et al. (2004), and the Artificial Intelligence Dependency Questionnaire developed by Huang et al. (2024). Data analysis was conducted using descriptive and inferential statistics in SPSS and AMOS software packages. Path analysis and structural equation modeling were utilized to evaluate both direct and indirect relationships among the study variables and to assess the overall model fit. Findings: The results demonstrated that maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness significantly predicted FOMO symptoms both directly and indirectly through artificial intelligence dependency. Maladaptive perfectionism showed a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.411, p < .01), while emotional loneliness also exhibited a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.506, p < .01). Furthermore, maladaptive perfectionism had a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.267, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect through artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.124, p < .01). Similarly, emotional loneliness exerted a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.259, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect mediated by artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.152, p < .01). Artificial intelligence dependency itself significantly and positively predicted FOMO symptoms (β = 0.301, p < .01). Model fit indices indicated a satisfactory fit of the proposed structural model to the observed data. Conclusion: The findings suggest that adolescents with higher levels of maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness are more likely to develop dependency on artificial intelligence technologies, which in turn intensifies FOMO symptoms. Artificial intelligence dependency functions as a significant psychological mechanism linking individual vulnerabilities and social-emotional difficulties to heightened fear of missing out. These results highlight the importance of addressing maladaptive perfectionistic standards, strengthening real-world emotional relationships, and promoting healthy patterns of AI use in interventions designed to reduce FOMO among adolescents.

papers.title: THE LOGIC, DILEMMAS, AND PATHWAYS OF AI-EMPOWERED TEACHING REFORM IN HIGHER VOCATIONAL TOURISM MANAGEMENT
papers.authors: Jing Su
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the form of the tourism industry. The in-depth development of smart tourism imposes new requirements on tourism management professionals in higher vocational colleges, demanding a combination of digital technology application, cross-boundary integration, and humanistic service capabilities. Based on an analysis of the internal logic of AI empowering teaching reform in higher vocational tourism management, this paper examines the realistic dilemmas currently facing higher vocational tourism management teaching in terms of curriculum systems, faculty digital literacy, practical training conditions, and evaluation mechanisms. Accordingly, it proposes systematic pathways that include reconstructing an integrated “AI + Tourism” curriculum system, innovating human-machine collaborative teaching models, upgrading practical training conditions, cultivating a digitally literate faculty, building an intelligent evaluation mechanism, and deepening industry-education integration and digital ethics education, with a view to providing a reference for the digital transformation of tourism management programs in higher vocational colleges.

papers.title: Implementation Strategies to Improve Adherence to Sports Injury Prevention Programs: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Ishu verma, Divya Midha, Mr. Jatin, Dr. Navneet Kaur
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: Exercise-based sports injury prevention programs (IPPs), such as the FIFA 11+, reduce injury incidence when performed as intended 1,2, yet real-world adherence and program fidelity remain inconsistent across athlete populations. Whereas prior reviews have largely quantified program efficacy or examined implementation among adolescents specifically 3 , no review has systematically synthesized comparative evidence on which implementation strategies are associated with improved adherence, compliance, and fidelity to sports injury prevention programs across the full spectrum of athletes. Objective: To systematically review and synthesize evidence on implementation strategies used to improve adherence to sports injury prevention programs among youth, collegiate, elite, and recreational athletes in team and individual sports. Methods: This review followed PRISMA 2020 reporting guidance 10. Eligible studies evaluated an implementation strategy (eg, coach or player education, digital reminders, behavior change techniques, feedback and monitoring systems, leadership or organizational support, stakeholder co-creation, audit and feedback) against a standard-practice, no-strategy, or alternative-strategy comparator, and reported adherence, compliance, program fidelity, or implementation success as a primary outcome, with injury incidence, burden, severity, training availability, completion, acceptability, feasibility, or sustainability as secondary outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for randomized designs 11 , ROBINS-I for non-randomized comparative designs 12, and Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists for crosssectional, survey, and qualitative designs 13. Given substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity across programs, strategies, outcome definitions, and study designs, findings were synthesized narratively rather than pooled statistically. Results: Twenty-four studies met inclusion criteria, spanning youth, high-school, collegiate, semi-professional, amateur, and professional/elite populations across soccer, rugby union, and team handball, predominantly evaluating the FIFA 11+ and related neuromuscular training programs. Implementation strategies clustered into seven overlapping categories: coach education and workshops; behavior-change-theory-informed delivery (particularly the Health Action Process Approach); stakeholder co-creation; scheduling and dosing adjustment; feedback and monitoring systems; RE-AIM-guided dissemination; and national or organizational governance programs. Theory-informed, practically delivered coach education combined with on-field supervision or simplified feedback showed the most consistent favorable association with adoption and adherence. Passive, information-only dissemination (eg, website-only access) and, in one recent trial, a co-created multilevel program layered onto standard practice, were not associated with meaningfully higher adherence than comparators. Certainty of the evidence was low to moderate, limited by reliance on self-reported adherence, absence of blinding inherent to coach- and player-mediated interventions, and heterogeneous outcome measurement. Conclusion: Active, theory-informed implementation strategies that combine practical coach education with ongoing feedback, supervision, and organizational backing are associated with better adherence to sports injury prevention programs than passive or purely informational dissemination, although the certainty of this evidence remains limited. Multifaceted, contextadapted strategies with organizational-level support appear more promising than single-component approaches, but rigorous hybrid effectiveness-implementation trials with objectively measured fidelity are needed to strengthen this evidence base.

papers.title: Indirect Prompt Injection in Autonomous LLM Agents
papers.authors: Zohaib Muaz
papers.abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in external data sources manipulate agent behavior without direct user input. These external data can originate from user documents, web retrieval results, or API outputs, leading to unauthorized compliance, sensitive information disclosure, identity spoofing, and cross-agent propagation of unsafe practices. This review synthesizes current research on IPI vulnerabilities and proposed mitigation strategies. Key attack vectors include manipulating webpage HTML via adversarial triggers for web agents, poisoning agent skills with tampered content, and injecting malicious commands into cloud logs processed by debugging agents. Covert attacks, which execute malicious actions without user-perceptible traces, pose a particularly insidious threat. Existing defenses, such as SecAlign's preference optimization, StruQ's structured queries, and multi layered zero-trust architectures, show promise. More advanced frameworks like ClawGuard enforce user-confirmed rule sets at tool-call boundaries, while ZEDD detects semantic shifts in embedding space for zero-shot detection. However, current guardrails often fail against sophisticated, adaptive attacks, and frameworks like AgentVigil and MUZZLE demonstrate high success rates in red-teaming exercises. The UReCoM attack further highlights vulnerabilities where benign users unknowingly relay adversarial content, bypassing existing defenses. The pervasive nature and increasing sophistication of IPI necessitate robust, behavior-grounded evaluation metrics and unified defense mechanisms to secure autonomous LLM agents in complex, untrusted environments.

papers.title: SOCIO-TECHNICAL ADAPTATION AND CUSTOMER VALUE CO-CREATION: THE HUMAN ELEMENT IN IOT-ENABLED CRM DEPLOYMENTS GROUP
papers.authors: Moin Khan, Saeed Hassan, Muhammad Adnan Aziz
papers.abstract: The hyper-acceleration of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies within corporate infrastructures has shifted customer relationship management (CRM) from a historical ledger of static touchpoints to an automated, real-time diagnostic pipeline. However, empirical enterprise outcomes reveal a widespread paradox: multi-million-dollar sensor-infrastructure deployments frequently stall or fail to generate strategic market returns. This comprehensive study builds upon Socio-Technical Systems (STS) Theory and Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic to explore the critical human elements modulating this technology gap. We introduce a formal mathematical layer mapping data streaming volumes against frontline interpretive capabilities and customer trust thresholds. Using structural equation modeling and multi-stage ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regressions on a primary dataset of N = 250 enterprise business-to-business (B2B) organizations, this paper proves that internal employee data literacy and socio-technical adaptation (beta = 0.410, p < 0.001) exert a far more powerful influence on customer value co-creation (VCC) than baseline technical architecture capacity alone (beta = 0.261, p < 0.001). Furthermore, customer trust is shown to act as a pivotal structural gatekeeper, where systemic privacy violations eliminate any operational dividend from predictive telemetry. The paper concludes with a comprehensive multi-horizon implementation framework to help executive leaders design balanced, human-centric Industry 4.0 engagement strategies.

papers.title: The Extended UTAUT Model in Predicting ChatGPT Adoption: Analyzing the Influence of Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, Self-Efficacy, Social Influence, and Facilitating Conditions on Actual Use by Biology Education Students
papers.authors: Diva Musyaffa, Robi Hendra, Ali Sadikin
papers.journal: IJOEM Indonesian Journal of E-learning and Multimedia
papers.abstract: Background: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI), particularly ChatGPT, has emerged as a revolutionary learning tool that can improve academic efficiency in Biology education. However, the factors driving student acceptance in this discipline need to be explored further.Aims: This study integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Usage of Technology (UTAUT) model with the Self-Efficacy (SE) variable to investigate the intention and behavior of using ChatGPT.Method: Using a quantitative approach, data were collected from 235 valid participants enrolled in Biology Education programs across two public universities in Indonesia and analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS software.Results: Performance expectancy, social influence, and self-efficacy significantly influence behavioral intention, with self-efficacy as the strongest predictor (β = 0.392, p = 0.000). Conversely, effort expectancy and facilitating conditions have no significant influence on behavioral intention (R^2=0.708). Critical findings reveal a severe gap between intention and action, where behavioral intention fails to significantly influence actual use (β = 0.075, p = 0.471), supported by a very low R^2 value for actual use (0.006).Conclusion: This significant gap indicates that contextual barriers such as academic ethics policies prevent students' intentions from translating into actual behavior. Implications are provided for educators to improve AI literacy and align policies to optimize the integration of GAI in Biology education.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and its Role in Mitigating Foreign Language Speaking Anxiety
papers.authors: Emad Alwreikat, Nizar Al-Qpilat, Rashad Alhasan, Marwan Alqaryouti
papers.abstract: The technology of GenAI has become an important instrument in the learning process for language acquisition and more specifically for helping students overcome FLSA. Providing an environment free of judgment and social threats, GenAI helps students to feel psychologically safe and boosts the efficacy of the teaching process. Using Convergent Parallel Mixed-Methods designs gives strong scientific backing to the findings of this paper, making sure that the reduction in anxiety is not just a number but also reflects students’ real experiences. By combining hard data—like scores from the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS)—with personal stories, this study can pinpoint the exact "micro-moments" during AI interactions that bring real psychological relief. Numerous studies have proven that artificial intelligence technology helps boost the education process and improve the effectiveness of learning thanks to the personalized approach, real-time feedback and increased motivation and autonomy. However, one should pay attention to some issues associated with the credibility of such interaction and its motivational value. It should be noted that difficulties associated with digital literacy, ethical questions, and learner preference for human evaluation remain relevant challenges in this regard. Combining all the above-mentioned strategic imperatives into one leads to the conclusion about the necessity of introducing a bimodal instructional strategy. Overall, GenAI will undoubtedly become a powerful instrument in helping to achieve this goal and change learning dynamics.

papers.title: Digital Media Literacy in the Age of AI: Exploring the Comfort–Competence Gap Among University Students in the
papers.authors: Layal Halawani, Farah Saboune, Barakat S. Alzyoud, Rania Abdallah
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates how citizens access information, making digital media literacy a condition for informed participation. This exploratory study conceptualizes a comfort–competence gap, whereby students report confidence and ease in using AI tools but a weaker capacity to evaluate what those tools produce, and examines it among 300 university students in the United Arab Emirates. The gap is advanced provisionally, and all measures are self-reported perceptions rather than demonstrated performance. Cross-sectional questionnaire data (twelve four-point ordinal items) were analyzed with ordinal-appropriate methods. Students generally reported greater confidence and comfort in using AI than capacity to evaluate it critically. Every operational item mean (2.51–2.55) exceeded every critical item mean (2.39–2.44), and the within-person contrast between the composite indices was small but statistically significant (difference = 0.12, p = 0.027, dz = 0.13), a pattern shown by 44.7% of individuals. No item-level contrast reached significance and 36.0% showed the reverse pattern, so the difference is read as an exploratory tendency rather than evidence of a general gap. The contrast is also sensitive to the composition of the operational index: with comfort removed, it retains its direction, but not conventional significance (p = 0.056). Digital confidence was the only correlate of comfort in AI-mediated communication (ρ = 0.131; OR = 1.29), a weak association in a model with minimal explanatory power (McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.012); communication competence and demographic characteristics showed no detectable associations, and parallel analysis retained no factors. Interpreted cautiously, the pattern bears on responsible AI use, since comfort unmatched by evaluative capacity is a weak basis for human oversight. The study’s clearest contribution is methodological: single-item self-report batteries can profile levels and detect aggregate differences, but they cannot show whether AI literacy is one capacity or several, cannot separate real capability from what respondents are willing to claim, and cannot support strong conclusions from null results. It therefore specifies the multi-item and performance-based measurement agenda a confirmatory test would require.

papers.title: Individualized English Language Learning for Students with Disabilities through Adaptive Educational Technologies
papers.authors: Malika Ergasheva
papers.abstract: The integration of adaptive educational technologies into language education creates new opportunities for providing individualized learning experiences for students with disabilities. Traditional approaches to English language teaching may not always adequately address the diverse cognitive, sensory, communicative and learning needs of such students. The development of flexible and accessible learning environments is therefore becoming increasingly important, particularly in home-based education. This study explores the potential of adaptive educational technologies for individualizing English language learning for students with disabilities. Particular attention is given to the adaptation of learning materials, instructional pace, task complexity, communication formats and assessment strategies. The study argues that digital resources, multimedia tools, interactive exercises, speech technologies and applications based on artificial intelligence can facilitate differentiated instruction and increase students’ engagement and autonomy. At the same time, technology should not be regarded as a substitute for pedagogical interaction. Its effectiveness depends largely on the teacher’s ability to select and adapt technological tools according to the learner’s individual educational needs. The findings suggest that a combination of individualized instruction and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more accessible, flexible and learner-centred approach to English language education.

papers.title: Sustainable AI Governance: A Theoretical Framework for Legal Compliance and Environmental Accountability A Systematic Conceptual Review
papers.authors: Samta Kathuria, Rajesh Singh, Shyamal M. Dave, Mahima Chaudhary, Parth Makwana, Dixita Suthar, Pradeepto Pal
papers.journal: International Journal for Global Academic & Scientific Research
papers.abstract: The fast increase in artificial intelligence (AI) in vital points in society has created significant governance issues at the interface of environmental sustainability and legal responsibility. Although there is a rich literature on AI ethics, technical safety, and standalone regulatory compliance, a cohesive theoretical framework that encompasses both legal compliance and environmental responsibility conditions under one governance framework have not existed yet, seemingly conspicuously in the literature. The review thus poses the question of how legal compliance requirements and environmental accountability requirements for AI systems can be incorporated in one, theoretically coherent governance architecture, and what are the structural gaps in existing regulatory instruments in this context? This gap is filled in this paper, by introducing the Sustainable AI Governance Framework (SAGF) a conceptual model, three pillars in theory which integrates regulatory coherence, environmental accountability and legal compliance architecture. A systematic conceptual review of studies published in the period 2021–2025 and indexed in Scopus, WoS and PubMed (search on 3–10 March 2026) was carried out after PRISMA 2020. For empirical studies, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool was used to assess the quality of the studies and for doctrinal and conceptual studies, a five-item checklist was used. To develop the SAGF, 58 articles in sustainability science, environmental law, governance theory and AI regulation were selected fulfilling the inclusion criteria. The article outlines seven key global regulatory tools, seven research gaps (six corpus-derived and one framework-level), and presents a policy roadmap plan that includes mandatory carbon disclosures by AI, legal harmonization across jurisdictions, and tiered organizational standards of compliance. The results have shown that current regulatory frameworks are methodically ineffective in uniting environmental and legal aspects of AI regulation and expose structural gaps, which are inadequately addressed by technical norms and soft-law tools. The paper adds a theoretically sound and practically feasible model to help legislators, regulatory bodies, AI creators, and legal professionals negotiating the twin demands of both sustainable and legally responsible AI use on a globally scale.

papers.title: Smart AI-Based Waste Segregation System
papers.authors: Vignesh Kumar M, Loga Ratcheni R, Subhaharini K, Tejaswini S
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: The Smart AI-Based Waste Segregation System is an intelligent waste management solution designed to automatically identify and segregate different types of waste using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and image processing technology. The proposed system uses an ESP32-CAM module to capture an image of the waste item placed in front of the camera. The captured image is transmitted through Wi-Fi to an AI-based image analysis system integrated with OpenAI for intelligent waste classification. Based on the visual characteristics of the captured waste, the system categorizes it into predefined classes such as wet waste, dry waste and metal waste. After classification, the control unit activates the appropriate segregation mechanism to direct the waste into the corresponding collection bin. This automated approach reduces the need for manual waste sorting and improves the efficiency and accuracy of waste segregation. The system combines IoT, embedded systems, computer vision and Generative AI to provide a smart and scalable solution for modern waste management, and can be implemented in smart cities, educational institutions, industries, public places and residential environments.

papers.title: The uncanny valley effect and the creepiness of ai generated advertising: a study on customer trust and loyalty
papers.authors: Pradeep Kumar Patnaik, Sadhvika Reddy Mallidi
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
