papers.title: NeuroCrown AI: A Voice-Interactive, EEG-Informed, USB-C Rechargeable Learning Crown
papers.authors: Begüm Yıldırım
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes NeuroCrown AI, a minimal, flat-crown wearable learning assistant that integrates scalp electroencephalography (EEG), miniature contact and wear-state sensors, wireless communication, hands-free speech interaction, artificial-intelligence-assisted lesson capture, and adaptive retrieval practice. The user-defined design is intended to recognize authorized spoken educational content, organize it into a revisitable knowledge library, support voice-driven topic switching, ask retrieval questions, and report remaining battery charge on request. A rechargeable battery is supplied through a concealed USB Type-C receptacle. A safety-critical charging interlock prohibits wired battery charging whenever the crown is worn and defaults to the non-charging state under ambiguous wear detection. At a measured state-of-charge threshold of 5%, the assistant issues an automatic spoken warning; optional earlier alerts and graceful shutdown are specified. The article contributes a requirements traceability framework, layered architecture, conceptual mechanical and electrical partition, computational pipeline, learning-policy formulation, power and safety-state models, threat model, staged verification plan, and executable reference-state logic. The educational core is informed by evidence for spaced practice and retrieval practice [1–4]. EEG is treated as an uncertain, low-dimensional auxiliary indicator rather than a method of reading semantic learning content from the brain [6–8]. The proposed system does not claim direct neural information upload, clinical benefit, measured learning gains, certification, or validated battery runtime. These remain separate development questions. The manuscript establishes a technically explicit foundation for prototyping and controlled evaluation.

papers.title: Critical Literacy as Leadership Praxis: Reading, Recognising, Re-purposing and Re-designing Value in Higher Education
papers.authors: Nadia Maria Vassallo
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Higher education institutions must sustain purposes that cannot be reduced to a single measure: educational quality, student development, regulatory and professional obligations, staff capability and financial viability. In private and hybrid institutions, these demands are especially visible because educational provision and organisational sustainability are tightly coupled. Existing scholarship offers rich resources for understanding such tensions, yet the organisational mechanism through which competing definitions of value become embedded in everyday institutional life remains under-theorised. This conceptual paper argues that institutional texts and organisational design constitute that mechanism. Strategic plans, key performance indicators, quality frameworks, learning outcomes, assessment regulations, appraisal systems, workload models and participation formats do not simply describe institutional priorities; they produce and reproduce them by making some forms of value visible, measurable and rewardable while rendering others difficult to evidence. Drawing on institutional logics and Bourdieusian field theory, Janks' critical literacy, recognition theory and ethics of care, and MacIntyrean accounts of practice and purpose, the paper reconstructs critical literacy as a praxis of senior institutional leadership. It proposes a framework of four mutually correcting practices (Reading, Recognising, Re-purposing and Re-designing) and tests it against assessment and generative artificial intelligence, which together expose the gap between what institutions claim to value and what their evidence systems can actually establish. Five propositions are advanced to guide an empirical research programme.

papers.title: Opportunities and Challenges of AI-Based Educational Assessment Tools
papers.authors: Aili Cui
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MULTIDISCIPLINARY RESEARCH AND ANALYSIS
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the integration of artificial intelligence in educational evaluation tools, focusing on both opportunities and challenges. It assesses how AI can enhance educational assessments through innovative features such as personalized feedback, adaptability, and immediate response capabilities. Additionally, the study critically addresses pressing concerns surrounding data privacy, equity in education, and ethical implications, proposing future directions and potential solutions to navigate these complexities in the evolving educational landscape.Simultaneously, the research examines strategies for leveraging AI technology to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of educational assessment. This exploration may yield valuable insights and guidance for the integration of AI within educational evaluation practices, thereby expanding the potential for innovation in this area.

papers.title: INTELLIGENT INFORMATION SYSTEMS FOR EDUCATIONAL MANAGEMENT: A FRAMEWORK FOR DATA-DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING IN NIGERIAN COLLEGES OF EDUCATION
papers.authors: Onyenweuwa Basil Onyeogaziri, Agwu Monica E., Agba Favour O.
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The increasing volume of digital information generated by Colleges of Education creates opportunities for evidence-based educational management, yet institutional data are often distributed across separate administrative systems and are not adequately transformed into actionable intelligence. This study developed an Intelligent Information Systems (IIS) framework for data-driven decision-making in Nigerian Colleges of Education. The study adopted a Design Science Research (DSR) approach, focusing on the identification of the educational-management problem, definition of system requirements, framework design, conceptual demonstration and evaluation. The proposed framework integrates institutional data sources, data integration and quality management, an institutional data repository, Business Intelligence and analytics, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, decision-support mechanisms, management dashboards, and governance, security and human oversight. The framework demonstrates how data relating to students, academic programmes, examinations, personnel, institutional resources and other administrative functions can be transformed from operational records into information and intelligent insights for management decisions. The study argues that integrating heterogeneous institutional data with appropriate analytical and intelligent technologies can strengthen evidence-based planning, monitoring, resource allocation, academic administration and institutional performance management. The framework also emphasises that Artificial Intelligence should complement rather than replace professional judgement, with privacy, security, data quality, transparency and human oversight incorporated into institutional implementation. The study contributes a Computer Science-oriented framework for addressing educational-management information challenges in Nigerian Colleges of Education and provides a conceptual foundation for subsequent prototype development and empirical evaluation.

papers.title: What a language model does when you poke it: the clinical map of the Perturbational Complexity Index, pre-registered and reproduced in Pythia-410m
papers.authors: Werner Baumgarten
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) decides whether a human is conscious without asking them: a brief transcranial pulse, and the EEG tells whether the response is long and complex (wakefulness) or short and simple (anaesthesia, deep sleep). This record applies the same logic to an open language model that nobody built for the purpose. Pythia-410m is run in a closed loop over its own text (soft feedback: the expectation over words is fed back — an input the model never saw in training, so the apparatus is a system of its own and says nothing about deployed models; the sampled loop of ordinary generation was measured separately, and its calibration against the weight null models failed — its stage is open); a single pulse is injected into the residual stream at one block; under a running noise field the apparatus records, at six blocks, how many units still deviate from the unperturbed run at each step. The duration τ of the response (in words) and its form (uniformity across noise repetitions, noise sensitivity of the unperturbed run) were calibrated in advance against the null models chaos and freezing at three model sizes and then never changed; the healthy value was reproduced fifteen times. Interventions were translated by biological function — damping of all weights (anaesthesia), amplification (psilocybin), unit loss (neurodegeneration), context masking (amnesia), activation threshold (GABA), gain adaptation (fatigue), preamble (state), truncated prompt (sensory deprivation), rounding (substrate change), a bridge between two models (conjoined twins), common firing of all units (seizure) — in 36 experiments, each pre-registered before the first number with predictions, probabilities and tipping conditions. Of 190 bound predictions 93 were met and 25 tipping conditions were triggered, each with a pre-stated meaning. The clinical map appears in the model in the same order as in humans. A second readout, the fingerprint (Spearman of τ-profiles over 40 prompts), identifies the individual: repeat 0.99, siblings of identical architecture 0.32, states 0.4–0.7; in three unrelated interventions the person is lost before the stage. A third readout, the boundary: a transformer is one stage, and whether two models are one is decided by the speed of the return path, not the strength of the bridge. What the model cannot do — split-brain, half-brain sleep, deep sleep by a per-unit switch, hysteresis after a seizure — has a named, retrofittable architectural cause. Thirty-four predictions for human TMS-EEG follow. All failures are reported. Files: the measurement paper (version 1.0), the reproduction package (all scripts, batch files, seeds, 379 expected values and a checker; MIT licence), the pre-registration documents with their result sections appended unchanged (CC BY 4.0), all logs and result files (CC BY 4.0), the consistency report v7 (assignment to the theory Process-Identity Theory, PIT), the Phase 1 and Phase 2 reports, and a statement on what this work contributes to the question of model welfare — and what it does not. Hardware: one consumer GPU (RTX 4070 Super, 12 GB); a full re-run takes about 60 GPU-hours. AI involvement: Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, wrote the apparatus code, the pre-registration documents, the evaluations by wording and the drafts of all reports under the author's decisions; this is declared in every document, and no self-report of the model enters any result. Models: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) for the model-network programme, the calibrated re-measurements and the first language-model branch (September 2026), and for two external readings of the final drafts; Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic) for the pre-registered language-model experiments, the measurement paper, the theory paper and the deposited packages (October 2026). Theory: Process-Identity Theory (PIT): theory paper, canon document and the model-network programme are a separate record, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23280480.

papers.title: Nonfreeness for rational two-parabolic groups with numerator 24
papers.authors: Ziheng Wang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This preprint presents a proof of nonfreeness for rational two-parabolic matrix groups with numerator 24. For every integer denominator r with |r| > 6, the groups at parameter 24/r are nonfree over both the rational and complex numbers, in SL(2,Q) and SL(2,C). For each such parameter, the proof provides a nonempty, freely reduced relation with at most 64 alternating nonzero generator-power syllables. For |r| > 17, the parameter is a two-step relation number. The mathematical results are accompanied by a Lean 4 and Mathlib formalization. This record includes the manuscript PDF and LaTeX sources, the complete Lean project with pinned dependencies, finite certificate data, an exact Python certificate verifier, and verification scripts and logs. The included verification documentation specifies the scope and provenance of the checks. Author: Ziheng Wang.AI assistance: GPT-6-Astra. The manuscript and its LaTeX/PDF sources are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0). The software and Lean sources are licensed separately under the MIT License. Source repository: https://github.com/wingsyuyi-satori/nonfree-G24r

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE OF SMEs IN ANAMBRA STATE, NIGERIA
papers.authors: KACHIKWULU ANASTECIA (PhD) ODINANWA
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The growing accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies presents new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve efficiency, customer engagement, decision-making and competitiveness. However, the level of AI adoption among SMEs remains uneven, particularly in developing economies where financial, technological and infrastructural constraints may limit effective utilization. This study examined the extent of AI adoption, its relationship with organizational performance, and the major constraints affecting adoption among SMEs in Anambra State, Nigeria, with particular focus on the Onitsha and Nnewi business clusters. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was employed. From a population of 1,200 registered SMEs, a sample of 300 owner-managers and managers was determined using Taro Yamane's formula and selected through proportionate stratified sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression with SPSS version 27 at the 5% level of significance. The findings revealed a moderate overall level of AI adoption, with relatively higher use of AI-supported customer communication and generative AI applications for marketing and content creation, while advanced applications for sales analysis, inventory management and personalization recorded lower usage. The regression results showed that AI adoption was positively associated with organizational performance (B = 0.576, β = .518, R² = .268, p < .001), indicating that higher levels of AI adoption corresponded with improved organizational performance. The major constraints to AI adoption were high implementation cost, inadequate AI and digital literacy, unreliable electricity supply, lack of technical expertise and poor or expensive internet connectivity. The study concludes that although AI adoption among SMEs in Anambra State remains moderate and uneven, its effective integration into business activities is associated with improved organizational performance. It therefore recommends practical AI-literacy programmes, affordable digital-financing support and improved electricity and internet infrastructure to facilitate wider and more effective adoption among SMEs.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED TOOLS AND ENGLISH LANGUAGE PROFICIENCY AMONG UNIVERSITY STUDENTS IN UZBEKISTAN: A PRISMA-GUIDED SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
papers.authors: Ermatova Guljakhon
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping English language education through generative chatbots, automated writing evaluation, intelligent tutoring systems, speech-recognition applications, adaptive learning environments, and AI-supported feedback. This PRISMA-guided systematic review synthesizes recent international and Uzbekistan-specific evidence on the effectiveness of AI-based tools in improving English language proficiency among university students. The review focuses on writing, speaking, reading, listening, vocabulary, feedback, motivation, engagement, and learner autonomy. Meta-analyses and systematic reviews generally report positive effects, particularly for productive skills and individualized feedback, but they also reveal substantial heterogeneity across technologies, intervention duration, learner profiles, and research designs. Evidence on ChatGPT and related generative AI tools suggests benefits for idea generation, revision, conversational practice, and autonomous learning, while highlighting risks related to inaccurate information, overreliance, academic integrity, privacy, and uneven AI literacy. Emerging studies from Uzbekistan confirm strong interest in AI-supported language learning and indicate potential benefits for writing and vocabulary development, although local evidence remains smaller and methodologically less mature than the international literature. The review concludes that AI is most effective when integrated into structured pedagogy, combined with teacher guidance, and supported by explicit AI literacy and ethical-use practices.

papers.title: Study of Phase Synchronization and Network Structures in Complexes of Physiological Activity in Cardiovascular Pathologies
papers.authors: Руннова Анастасия Евгеньевна, Maksim О. Zhuravlev, Natalya S. Akimova
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common sleep-disordered breathing disorder associated with hypoxemia, sleep fragmentation, and significant changes in functional brain activity. This study analyzed polysomnography recordings from 548~patients, including groups with varying OSA severity and healthy volunteers. Wavelet bicoherence was used to assess functional connectivity, and network structure was analyzed using the betweenness centrality index. Synchronization changes in OSA were found to be frequency-specific: in the Δ band (1 -- 4 Hz), a significant decrease in interhemispheric coherence was observed, with significant negative correlations with the apnea-hypopnea index (r = -0.77 to -0.81), while in the high-frequency band (12 - 30 Hz), a relative increase in intrahemispheric connections was observed. Restructuring of network characteristics is significantly evident only during REM sleep, with changes predominantly localized in the occipital leads. The obtained data are consistent with the visceral theory of sleep and indicate a compensatory restructuring of integrative brain processes under conditions of chronic hypoxia, opening up the possibility of using quantitative EEG markers to assess the severity of OSA and associated cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Minimal Recurrence Orders for Rationally Weighted Binomial Sums
papers.authors: Stephen Lamb
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: For a positive integer r and a rational function R regular at the origin, this preprint studies a_n(R) = [z^n] R(z)(1-z)^(-rn-1). An elementary specialization of Hermite reduction produces a residual space of dimension s+1, where s is the number of distinct finite poles of R other than 1, irrespective of their multiplicities. The manuscript proves that coefficient extraction is injective on this residual space, so that the first linear dependence among shifted kernels gives the minimal recurrence of the coefficient sequence rather than only a sufficient telescoping relation. A sharpness theorem gives order exactly s+1 under stated hypotheses on the pole images under z(1-z)^r and on the value of R at the critical point. Applications recover the order-one classification for geometric weights and give a uniform third-order recurrence, with a proof of minimality for every positive integer r, for the family sum_k binom((r+1)n-k, n-2k). A Lucas-number identity supplies compact certificates. Explicit applications include OEIS A371742, A371743, A371744 and A385632. The paper situates the construction within established Hermite-reduction and creative-telescoping methods. Companion code, exact rational certificates and a recorded verification log are supplied. AI-assisted research preprint; not independently peer reviewed. The manuscript discloses assistance in mathematical development, literature searching, code construction and English drafting. Computational checks support the displayed identities but do not replace independent review of the analytic proofs or establish first-discovery priority. No claim is made that the work resolves a previously recognized unsolved OEIS conjecture.

papers.title: ENHANCING ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR TEACHERS IN UZBEKISTAN
papers.authors: Juraeva Maftuna Komilovna
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities for English language teaching through personalized learning, interactive practice, automated feedback, and instructional material development. However, its effective integration requires pedagogical planning, digital competence, and attention to ethical considerations. These issues are particularly relevant to English language education in Uzbekistan, where teachers work in diverse educational settings.

papers.title: TEACHING GRAPHIC SUBJECTS IN THE CONTEXT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: T.V. Nesterova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article examines the problem of teaching students using artificial intelligence (AI). Students find ready-made papers on subjects and submit them instead of their own. This process is facilitated by the introduction of graphics programs, which makes it possible to purchase finished work inexpensively. The experience of conducting classes in mechanical engineering drawing suggests ways to solve this problem. The article provides recommendations on the use of tests for the operational verification of knowledge and the degree of independence of performing household routine calculation, graphic and term papers.

papers.title: AI in Business Intelligence and Entrepreneurship
papers.authors: Hakikur Rahman
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern business environments, fundamentally reshaping how organizations collect information, generate knowledge, make decisions, and create value. The convergence of AI and Business Intelligence (BI) enables enterprises to move beyond descriptive reporting toward predictive and prescriptive decision-making frameworks. Simultaneously, entrepreneurs and startups increasingly employ AI-powered analytics, intelligent automation, and machine learning to identify market opportunities, optimize operations, and develop innovative products and services. This article examines the evolving relationship between AI, Business Intelligence, and entrepreneurship, highlighting how organizations leverage data-driven intelligence for sustainable competitive advantage and organizational innovation. Drawing upon contemporary research and practical examples, the article explores technological foundations, leadership implications, entrepreneurial opportunities, global and local applications, and future challenges. The discussion emphasizes that successful adoption of AI requires not only technical capabilities but also strategic leadership, ethical governance, and a culture of continuous innovation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Finance: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Benefits and Challenges
papers.authors: Dr. Basukinath G Jha
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the financial sector has fundamentally transformed the way financial institutions operate, manage risk, and deliver services to customers. Despite the growing adoption of AI technologies across banking, insurance, and investment management, there remains a limited understanding of how the perceived benefits and perceived challenges of AI collectively shape the adoption behavior of finance professionals and organizations. This study addresses this gap by developing and empirically testing a conceptual model that examines the influence of perceived benefits (PB) and perceived challenges (PC) on AI adoption (AD) in the financial services industry. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this research employs a quantitative survey methodology. A structured questionnaire was administered to 100 respondents working in or associated with the financial sector. The instrument comprised 24 items distributed across three constructs: Perceived Benefits of AI (8 items, α = 0.922), Perceived Challenges of AI (8 items, α = 0.931), and AI Adoption in Finance (8 items, α = 0.911). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. The results of the multiple linear regression analysis revealed that the model explained 38.9% of the variance in AI adoption (R² = 0.389, F(2,97) = 30.87, p < .001). Perceived benefits emerged as a strong and statistically significant positive predictor of AI adoption (β = 0.580, p < .001), while perceived challenges had a statistically significant but weaker negative effect (β = -0.162, p < .05). The regression equation was: AI Adoption = 0.884 + 0.617(PB) - 0.162(PC). These findings underscore that while perceived benefits are the primary driver of AI adoption, perceived challenges exert a modest inhibiting effect, suggesting that organizations can accelerate AI adoption by strategically emphasizing tangible benefits while proactively addressing recognized challenges. Keywords: artificial intelligence, AI adoption, financial services, perceived benefits, perceived challenges, Technology Acceptance Model, multiple linear regression

papers.title: MODERN MODELS OF INNOVATION-DRIVEN TOURISM DEVELOPMENT: A HYBRID FRAMEWORK FOR UZBEKISTAN
papers.authors: Dilnoza Safarovna Umirova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study systematises and comparatively evaluates contemporary models of innovationdriven tourism development and develops an integrated framework adapted to the context of Uzbekistan. The analysis encompasses six complementary models: smart tourism destinations, digital platform ecosystems, experience and creative tourism, sustainable (green) innovation, open innovation and tourism clusters, and AIand data-driven management. A mixed analytical design combining a systems approach, comparative analysis, descriptive statistical analysis, structured content analysis, and SWOT analysis is applied to international and national evidence covering the period 2024–2026. The study identifies a methodological gap in existing approaches that tend to examine these models separately and proposes a hybrid framework that links innovation inputs and capabilities with destinationlevel mechanisms and measurable tourism outcomes. The findings indicate that Uzbekistan's recent tourism development has been supported substantially by institutional and market-access innovations, while opportunities for the next stage of development are increasingly associated with enhancing quality, productivity, diversification, and sustainability alongside continued tourism growth. The proposed framework integrates digital infrastructure, smart-destination governance, experience design, AI-enabled decision-making, green transformation, and collaborative innovation, linking each component to specific implementation stages and performance indicators. The study provides an applied methodological basis for selecting and combining innovation mechanisms according to destination-specific conditions and offers practical policy recommendations for advancing innovation-driven tourism development in Uzbekistan.

papers.title: AIMLS: standardized graphic labeling to disclose the use of artificial intelligence in scientific-academic manuscripts
papers.authors: Freddy Alexander Chinchilla Serrano, Carolina Seas, Steven Segura Jiménez
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: English translation of the Spanish-language preprint (original version): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23273378 Introduction: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific-academic writing continues to grow steadily, with and without editorial policies regulating it. A disclosure drafted without standardized vocabulary is not standardized, comparable, or itemized, and therefore does not produce a datum that can be counted. Objective: To develop an open-access tool that generates, based on what the author declares, a standardized graphic label accompanied by its textual disclosure in prose, to communicate the use of AI in the preparation of manuscripts in a clear, explicit, and visible way. Methods: We adopted a classification of eight declarable AI use activities according to the STM Association, and we added an optional four-grade ordinal scale of the extent of each use (minimal, partial, majority, and total) with respect to each task. We designed a monochrome label with fixed-rule alphanumeric notation, always generated in English, with the codes ordered according to the classification and a QR code that links to the system’s documentation. We developed the software, verified the consistency between the label and the prose through 1,337 automated tests, and illustrated its operation with an example case. Results: We obtained AIMLS (AI Manuscript Labelling System), an HTML application that runs in any browser, requires no installation or registration, and does not store or transmit the declared information. It generates a matching label and draft textual disclosure, whose notation allows the declared use of AI to be compared and counted. Its limitations include dependence on editorial adoption, visual accessibility, the voluntary and unverifiable nature of disclosures, and the need to update the taxonomy. Conclusion: The tool converts the disclosure of AI use into a visible, standardized, and portable label that complements, without replacing, editorial policies and prose disclosure; it constitutes a mechanism for communication, not certification or detection. As future work, we propose its integration into editorial platforms such as Open Journal Systems and scientific metadata standards, as well as its validation with users and periodic updating.

papers.title: Obligations and Optionality: Strategy Retired Preferred Stock, BitMine Bought Back Common
papers.authors: Giorgio Elia
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: When the shares of a crypto treasury company trade below the value of the crypto assets it holds, buying back shares seems like the textbook remedy. In 2026, Strategy Inc. (MSTR) did not use it. It sold bitcoin in five sale windows, left a $1.0 billion common stock buyback unused, and repurchased no common stock; it repurchased only one series of preferred stock (STRC) and one convertible note issue. This short working paper argues that, in this case, fixed-yield obligations came first in how Strategy used its funds, and that how the discount is measured decides whether a common buyback is the remedy at all. Measured gross, as bitcoin value per diluted share before debt and preferred stock, Strategy sold $5.2 billion of common stock from July 6 to August 30, 2026 at 9% to 28% below gross NAV and spent only 7.2% of the proceeds on bitcoin. Measured net of debt and preferred stock, as Strategy has defined mNAV since July 23, 2026, the same stock traded at or slightly above NAV (the company reported 1.01x to 1.06x). As a contrast, BitMine (BMNR), whose fixed charges are small, bought back about 21 million common shares from July 14 to August 17, 2026. The paper states predictions that would falsify the argument. It rests on one main case and one contrast, so its findings illustrate the argument and do not test it. Working paper (version 1.0), not peer reviewed. Disclosure: the author holds a large, concentrated long position in Strategy (MSTR), including call options, and holds BitMine (BMNR) common stock. This paper was AI-assisted in parts of the data extraction, calculation and drafting; the author is responsible for the content. Nothing in this paper is investment advice.

papers.title: The Tower We Build: Human Ambition, Technological Power, and the Limits of Transcendence
papers.authors: Evans Otse'agbenu Obande
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Human beings have always sought to exceed the limits of their finitude. From the biblical builders of Babel to contemporary projects of technological enhancement, humanity repeatedly transforms its desire for security, knowledge, permanence, and power into structures that promise to overcome creaturely limitations. This article reconsiders the Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) not simply as a story about disobedience, but as a theological account of the limits of human self-transcendence. It argues that the central issue in Babel is not human creativity or technological construction itself, but the attempt to convert human capacity into a substitute for dependence upon God. The argument is developed through biblical-theological analysis and philosophical reflection on technology, transhumanism, human dignity, and the doctrine of creation. The article distinguishes legitimate technological creativity from technological absolutism: technology may extend human agency, but it cannot transform finite creatures into autonomous sources of ultimate meaning, immortality, or divine authority. The discussion engages classical and contemporary perspectives, including Augustine, Aquinas, Heidegger, Ellul, Tillich, Jonas, and recent scholarship on artificial intelligence and transhumanism. The article concludes that the enduring theological significance of Babel lies in its diagnosis of a recurring human temptation: to mistake increased power for increased being. Authentic transcendence, from a Christian theological perspective, is therefore not achieved by abolishing creaturely limits but by rightly inhabiting them in relation to God, other human beings, and creation.

papers.title: Token-Generation-Control-Deterministic-Logical-Timeline
papers.authors: Yong Qiu, Zhehao Wang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Text generation by large language models is essentially a probabilistic sampling process: the model computes a probability distribution over the next token based on the input context, and then samples a token from that distribution. This probabilistic design gives large models creativity but also introduces a fundamental engineering problem: the same input may produce different outputs at different times, in different environments, or on different hardware. For AI agents (automated trading, code generation, industrial control) that require stability and reproducibility, this non-determinism is fatal. This paper proposes a token generation control method based on a deterministic logical timeline. The method uses the logical state S(n) output by a Protocol Security State Machine (PSSM) as the initialization seed of a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG), replacing random sources based on physical time or hardware noise, thereby transforming the token sampling process from "physical non-determinism" to "logical determinism". The paper provides the complete token generation flow, two working modes (deterministic mode and divergent-but-reproducible mode), a cryptographically bound record format, and, building on the independent verification and replay mechanism disclosed in the applicant's prior patent, an auditing method for token generation records. The method does not change the model's native probability distribution (intelligence representation); it only controls the token sampling path, achieving cryptographic-level determinism across environments, hardware, and frameworks.

papers.title: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority
papers.authors: Nicholas Cott
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An institution can issue a determination in seconds and take months to reconsider it. Now put a conversational AI in front of that institution. In the book's fictional test case, an insurer's AI appeals agent tells a policyholder, in the first person: "I have reconsidered my decision. I have reversed it and will honor this correction in future cases." Nothing happens. The insurer's claims and recovery systems reject any stay or reversal the agent proposes unless the corporate appeals office separately signs it, because the agent never held the power to grant one. Who, exactly, answered? The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority is a book-length answer. It argues that automated decisions can scale faster than institutions' capacity to justify, reconsider, correct, or repair them, and it gives conceptual tools for saying precisely where that failure lies. Is the interface a bearer of commitments at all? Does the institution behind it own the position? Was adopting it justified? Can anyone actually sustain the answering at that scale? These are separable questions, and the book's central claim is that evidence for one does not by itself settle another. The central thesis Presumptive institutional authority requires effective Answerability at the grain and scale of its exercise. Accuracy, fluency, attribution, and nominal human oversight are not substitutes. What matters is whether there are routes through which reasons can actually change institutional commitments and their consequences, and whether they can do so in time. A route that can vindicate an objection only after its consequences have run gives the person relying on the institution no protection while it matters. What the book builds Discursive ontology and Answerability. Defines commitment-bearing as the conjunction of four public relations (attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence, and standing-consequence), argued to be necessary for the role and, defeasibly, sufficient. It distinguishes Actual, Residual, Prospective, and Empty Occupancy: a role's present, historical, developing, and missing bearership. It defends the axiom that missing bearership is not defective ownership: an institution cannot escape ownership of its commitments by pointing to an interface that never bore them, and its own failure to answer is not evidence that it never owned them. It gives a three-part test (Evidential Independence, Adversarial Defeatability, Normative Effectiveness) for when an automated review counts as genuine reconsideration, and traces these questions through model succession and agentic chains. Testimony without a testifier. Separates what a hearer can learn from a machine output from who owns the claim. On assurance-based accounts, outputs can exercise testimonial force without constituting testimony. Reliability, fluency, and conversational memory do not by themselves make an interface the owner of a commitment. Normative Sponsorship. Five conditions for warranted institutional adoption (epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection, repair power) and an opacity threshold set at contestation grain, so institutions need not achieve complete transparency. It separates technical opacity from organizational capture, where reasons are knowable but cannot bind. Deontic Debt and Institutional Insolvency. Derives a service requirement from the defeasibility of presumptive authority, and argues that defeasibility must be timely: eventual redress or compensation does not make earlier reliance warranted if no material objection could alter the claim while it operated. Deontic Debt is matured obligations deficiently serviced, not just a backlog. Institutional Insolvency is a scale-indexed finding that no credible service plan exists under a specified lawful architecture and horizon. Its consequence is the targeted loss of presumptive authority, not automatic legal invalidity and not release from ownership and repair duties. Institutional stewardship. Three levels of force (tool, advisory, operative). An operative use whose sponsorship conditions cannot be met is prohibited, not treated as a fourth kind of force. The levels are tied to protective review, binding reconsideration, effective repair, and staged resumption after failure. The book also maps intersections with administrative-law principles in Australia, with comparative EU, UK, and US material. Tested against the record Public-record analyses of Robodebt, Moffatt v. Air Canada, A.M.C. v. Smith (TennCare), the Post Office Horizon scandal, the Dutch childcare-benefits affair, and a press-based DPD chatbot episode show what the framework can and cannot establish from documents. Robodebt yields a determinate finding on the documentary record: a Deontic Debt at the level of the shared income-averaging premise. By 30 May 2017 about 29 tribunal decisions had rejected averaging as a sufficient basis for the asserted debts, yet the method continued to generate demands. Accountability in the actor–forum sense was present case by case, through individual appeals and tribunal scrutiny and later a Royal Commission. It does not settle whether the matured common-premise obligation was serviced when it was due. The book claims a Deontic Debt verdict only; whether the scheme was institutionally insolvent remains indeterminate on the selected record. The Air Canada and DPD records leave the decisive questions about interface standing indeterminate, and the book says so. An explicitly fictional comparator, the Meridian–Aster appeals case, supplies the determinate Empty Occupancy verdict: the AI agent Aster is an Empty Occupant, and its insurer, Meridian, remains the actual bearer who owns the refusal. That pair of findings is the book's distinctive payoff. It is not empirical evidence, and it settles neither sponsorship nor serviceability. Built to be challenged A full chapter of objections takes on synthetic agency, status-function constructivism, intentionality, the human–machine double standard, scarcity, strategic contestation, and the charge that insolvency is trivially curable. It closes with explicit conditions under which the book would be wrong. Appendices provide a conceptual glossary, a proposed public-marker and obligation audit specification, and a worked obligation ledger. The ledger makes missing evidence explicit rather than filling it in with theory. Scope. This is philosophical reconstruction with bounded public-record analysis, not an empirical evaluation of model capabilities or a survey of deployments. Seven standing limits, stated once in Chapter 1, govern every claim: no legal consequence follows from the terminology; the equations are uncalibrated; stipulated cases test whether the criteria discriminate, not how often the cases occur; documentary codes are local to their record; constitutive absence requires affirmative evidence; the audit specification is unvalidated; the role criterion does not settle personhood, consciousness, or moral status. Who it is for Philosophers of language, testimony, assertion, and responsibility; social epistemologists and social ontologists. AI-governance researchers and administrative lawyers. Public-sector auditors, regulators, and anyone who has been told by a machine that their problem was "resolved." 124 pages. Open access under CC BY 4.0. What's new in this version A new section, "Why Defeasibility Must Be Timely," defends the service requirement against the objection that eventual redress or compensation preserves defeasibility. A new section, "A Determinate Divergence from Actor–Forum Accountability," identifies the Robodebt common-premise Deontic Debt finding that case-level accountability does not settle. Scope limits are consolidated into seven numbered standing limits. Terminology is streamlined: fewer coined terms, and the former "Level 4" is restated as unsponsorable operative use. The weighted reporting index moves to Appendix B. Prose is tightened throughout. papers.title: Leveraging Custom AI "Gems" for Personalized Student Support
papers.authors: Jessica Kohlschmidt
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The integration of generative AI in education has transitioned from general-purpose chatbots to specialized, task-oriented assistants. This study explores the efficacy of Google Gemini "Gems"-customizable AI personas-in enhancing student learning and academic productivity. Unlike standard models, Gems allow students to interact with a persistent "expert" assistant tailored to my specific course. As an instructor, I can tell the Gem the tone that I would like and instruct it be a Socratic tutor for my students. I would like my students to use a Gem about the syllabus to answer their questions instead of emailing me first. My students continuously want more 'practice' to prepare them for the exam. This gives me the opportunity to leverage AI and provide support that students request. Key benefits include grounding AI responses in specific course materials through long-context uploads, automating study-guide generation, and fostering self-regulated learning. Customizing the Gem's tone and methodology encourages students to move beyond passive answer-seeking toward active, inquiry. This tool serves as an evolving digital companion designed to support students.

papers.title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation
papers.authors: Leydi Yojanna Higidio Henao
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.

papers.title: Tensors Beyond the Array: A Teaching Note on Karras's Account, Set Against Abstract Geometry and Fractal Algebra
papers.authors: Syed Muntasir Mamun
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This note isolates the claims in Dimitrios A. Karras's short professional exposition of the tensor, and reads them against two bodies of theory that a research student is liable to conflate with it: the abstract-geometric theory of tensors, from the absolute differential calculus to the modern language of multilinear maps and tensor bundles; and the several programmes gathered, loosely, under fractal algebra and non-integer geometry. Karras is right on the point that matters for a first encounter. A tensor is not a multidimensional array. It is an object whose components transform by a definite rule, so that the quantity represented does not depend on the coordinates used to write it down. That criterion is the classical one of Ricci and Levi-Civita, and it correctly separates the geometric object from the storage format used in computation and in machine learning. The account is nevertheless incomplete as a definition, and it is silent on the setting in which the definition can fail. It counts indices rather than distinguishing covariant from contravariant slots; it treats a change of basis and a change of coordinates as one operation; it does not say that a tensor field is a section, nor that the coefficients of a connection fail the tensor test. Abstract geometry takes the multilinear map, or the element of a tensor product, as primary, and derives the transformation law. Fractal and fractional geometries suspend the hypothesis on which that law depends: a tangent space of integer dimension, with a Jacobian at a typical point. The teaching consequence is sharp. Karras is the right door into the component calculus. It is the wrong place to stop if the student is to understand curvature, or to understand why a snowflake curve does not carry an ordinary stress tensor. KSCCN teaching note, 10 October 2026. Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

It gives an irreducible 68-state finite model with positive usual stationary entropy production, and exact growing-cardinality finite models of the SAME entire real-time observation law whose actual stationary entropy production tends to zero while departure rates remain at most 5. VERSIONE ITALIANA (RELEASE v3.3) SOMMARIO (ITALIANO)La Release v3.3 (Audit-Master Unificato) del METODO DEMARIA™ formalizza il definitivo cambio di paradigma epistemologico nello studio dei corpora simbolici storici non decifrati, con applicazione primaria al Manoscritto Voynich (Beinecke MS 408). papers.title: A four-qubit counterexample to first-excited parity in phase-shifted EPR-like Hamiltonians
papers.authors: Shunpei Shimizu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This source-only preprint gives a four-qubit counterexample to the arbitrary-phase extension of the first-excited parity conjecture discussed in Wong, Bravyi, Gosset and Liu, Lee-Yang tensors and Hamiltonian complexity, arXiv:2602.03605v1, Section 5.6. For an unweighted four-cycle with phase pi on one edge and a common parameter 0 <= s < 1, it derives the complete 16-dimensional spectrum and an exact parity threshold. The rational value s = 2/3 is an explicit witness; a specified fixed-witness robustness interval is also proved. The original zero-phase conjecture and the general all-graph gap problem remain open. Ground-state uniqueness and the non-strict gap bound are known inputs, explicitly credited to Wei, arXiv:2609.26802v2, Corollary 5.8 and Section 5.4, and Bravyi, Gosset, Liu and Wong, arXiv:2607.14401v1, Theorem 1. The concrete phase counterexample, complete spectrum and threshold are distinguished from these known results. The primary-source comparison is dated and bounded; worldwide priority is not certified. papers.title: An infinite family of non-star trees admitting Laplacian peak state transfer
papers.authors: Shunpei Shimizu

papers.abstract: Unrefereed AI-assisted preprint, version 0.2.2, 9 October 2026. No author affiliation is given. For each m >= 1, set q = m^2 + m + 1. Attach q intermediate vertices to a root and q - 1 leaves to each intermediate vertex. This produces infinitely many pairwise nonisomorphic non-star trees of order q^2 + 1, with root Laplacian spectral support {0, m^2 + 1, (m + 1)^2 + 1}. The symbolic argument establishes Laplacian peak state transfer at time pi from the root to an intermediate vertex for odd m and to a leaf for even m, addressing Open Problem 7.1 of Coutinho, Guo and Schmeits, arXiv:2505.11986v4. The ten-vertex m = 1 member is their known Figure 10 example. Phase alignment is an application of their Lemma 5.2 and Corollary 5.3; the general peak-time classification follows their Theorem 5.4 and Corollary 5.5. The contribution presented here is the explicit infinite family and its spectral coefficients, targets and gcd calculation. For the specified pairs, all positive peak times are odd multiples of pi/g, where g = 5 when m = 2 mod 5 and otherwise g = 1. Novelty and priority are not certified. Peak transfer means attaining the mutual-projector absolute-sum bound, not unit amplitude. The probabilities tend to zero along both parity subsequences. This does not establish perfect transfer, efficient long-distance quantum communication or a classification of all trees. Exact standard-library reruns check actual full-tree Laplacians for m = 1..5, quotients for m = 1..1000, and gcd/phase regressions for m = 1..10000. papers.title: Paying for Nutrition: A Mechanism-Design Approach to the Nutrient Density Standard
papers.authors: Mayone Maha Rajan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Can a voluntary farm-gate payment improve the nutritional quality of food crops at a defensible cost? This paper proposes a Nutrient Density Bonus for verified protein, zinc, and iron in harvested wheat, alongside existing income protection. It compares three payment architectures: direct lot assays, contracts for specified practices, and evidence-backed claims subject to independent audits. A capped, volume-adjusted payment rule makes the unit of reward explicit; a simplified deterrence condition identifies the recovery and enforcement assumptions behind the audit mechanism. The proposed evaluation begins with a measurement season in western Kansas and northern Oklahoma, followed, only if feasible, by a controlled comparison over multiple harvests. Reference assays remain the basis for mineral verification unless predictive methods meet prespecified payment-relevant error tolerances. The policy must demonstrate additional crop-quality improvement, affordable verification, fair access, and acceptable effects on yield, income, food safety, and the environment. Higher grain mineral concentration is distinguished from nutrient output, bioavailability, and health benefit. The contribution is a policy-design framework and prospective evaluation plan; no pilot results or national cost estimate are reported. Status: Policy working paper, version 1.0; not peer reviewed. No new dataset, completed pilot, or national cost estimate is reported. Provenance: A revised archival adaptation of the June 2026 web proposal. Disclosure: The author is affiliated with Maha Strategies and wrote the commercially available book. ChatGPT assisted with adaptation, source checking, drafting, and formatting. The author remains responsible for the content.

papers.title: The Digital Pillbox: Evaluating the Impact of Digital Health on Medication Compliance
papers.authors: Piyush Y. Patil
papers.abstract: Medication adherence is veritably important for reaching the stylish possible treatment results, especially when dealing with long- term health conditions. Indeed, thought there have been numerous advancements in chancing new drugs, a lot of cases still don't follow their specified drug plans. This can make their condition worse, lead to further sanitarium visits, and indeed increase the threat of death. This composition looks at how digital health tools can help ameliorate drug adherence by offering new ways like mobile apps, telehealth services, wearable bias, and remote monitoring. These tools, which include AI and machine literacy, offer substantiated monuments, support, and real- time shadowing, which help cases stay more involved and harmonious with their treatment. Traditional healthcare styles for diagnosing and keeping track of conditions are generally expensive and not veritably accurate. Lately, wearable health technology grounded on flexible electronics has come veritably popular because of its numerous benefits, similar as lower costs, easier access to patient health information, capability to work in tough surroundings, storing data at normal temperatures, being non-invasive, and the capability to be made in large amounts. papers.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Decision Support System for Student Tuition Fee Reduction: Integrating Tree-Based Ensemble Models and SHAP-Based Justification
papers.authors: Riyadi Purwanto, Fajar Mahardika, Dwi Novia Prasetyanti, Cahya Vikasari, Rostika Listyaningrum, Raden Bagus Bambang Sumantri
papers.abstract: Tuition fee reduction (Uang Kuliah Tunggal, UKT) is a key affordability instrument in Indonesian higher education, yet its assessment still relies largely on manual verification, producing decisions that are slow, inconsistent between reviewers, and difficult to justify to applicants. This study develops and evaluates an explainable machine learning decision support system that classifies the eligibility of tuition fee reduction applications and accompanies every prediction with a human-readable justification. Four tree-based ensemble models (Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and LightGBM) were trained on 5,000 application records from Politeknik Negeri Cilacap (2022–2024) described by socio-economic, academic, and administrative attributes, and benchmarked against a Logistic Regression baseline using hold-out testing, 10-fold cross-validation, and the Friedman test. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was then applied to the best-performing model to quantify global feature contributions and generate per-application explanations. XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy (0.822) and F1-score (0.850), while Random Forest obtained the highest ROC-AUC ([≈0.89]); however, all models remained within approximately 2.6 percentage points of accuracy, and the Logistic Regression baseline attained the highest precision (0.838). The SHAP analysis revealed that number of dependents and document completeness dominated the decision function, far exceeding parental income, indicating that the historical decision process encoded an administrative gate alongside genuine economic need. These findings support deploying the system as a human-in-the-loop screening aid rather than an autonomous decision maker, and demonstrate that explainability is essential for accountable financial aid decisions.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Based Large Language Model with Formative Feedback and Traditional Instruction in Learning Fraction
papers.authors: Ida Bagus Indrabudhi Kusuma, Dade Nurjanah
papers.abstract: Learning fractions poses challenges for students, and while traditional one-on-one tutoring is effective, it faces human resource limitations. While generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable personalized support, large language models (LLMs) risk generating hallucinations, leading students to misconceptions. To address these challenges, this study evaluates the effect of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) integrated with formative feedback on students' learning performance in fraction arithmetic, comparing it to traditional instruction. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 56 7th grader students, divided into an experimental group (N=26) utilizing the ITS and a control group (N=30) receiving regular classroom instruction. The ITS employed GPT-4o and RAG grounded with fraction educational content to deliver personalized, step-by-step formative feedback based on the Mason and Bruning framework. Students’ learning performance was measured through pre and post-test and were analyzed using ANCOVA. The experimental group outperformed the control group with higher learning gain of 47.02% compared to the control group’s 31.54%. ANCOVA results confirmed the significant main effect (p = 0.002) suggesting that the RAG-based tutor improved the mathematical comprehension and reduced knowledge variance among students. These results underscore the grounded LLM integrated with formative feedback demonstrates potential to improve students learning performance. This study provides a comparative evaluation of RAG-based ITS integrated with formative feedback and traditional classroom instruction in improving student learning performance in fraction. Furthermore, this study advances AI-supported tutoring by introducing an LLM-based ITS that combines RAG-grounded generation, formative feedback, and LLM-based judgment for dynamic and adaptive student modelling.

papers.title: Optimizing Diabetes Complication Prediction Using Adaptive Boosting With Naive Bayes, Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique, And Information Gain Feature Selection
papers.authors: Farid Fitriyadi, Erna Indriastiningsih, Indriyati Indriyati
papers.abstract: Primary healthcare facilities often face significant technical challenges in the early detection of diabetes complications due to their heavy reliance on micro-datasets characterized by extreme class imbalances. Such data constraints typically make standard single-prediction models prone to overfitting and low sensitivity, which are critical issues in clinical decision-making. This study proposes a multi-level optimization framework to overcome these limitations by integrating Information Gain for dimensionality reduction, Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) to handle class imbalance, and Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) with Categorical Naive Bayes as the base learner. To address the critical aspect of model validity on a highly limited dataset (n=20), this methodology employs a stratified cross-validation scheme to ensure reliable performance estimation and minimize prediction bias. The integration of Information Gain effectively optimized the model by reducing the predictor variables from seven to four optimal features, thereby decreasing computational complexity. Based on rigorous testing, the proposed ensemble architecture achieved a robust average accuracy of 87.00% and, more importantly, a high Recall (Sensitivity) of 90% in identifying positive complication cases. This research provides a significant scientific contribution to machine learning development by demonstrating that the systematic integration of SMOTE and AdaBoost offers a stable, precise, and computationally efficient solution for predictive modeling in data-constrained clinical environments. These findings suggest that the proposed model can serve as a reliable early warning system to improve patient outcomes in primary care settings.

papers.title: Fake News Detection on Social Media Based on Indonesian Public Opinion Sentiment Analysis Using Naïve Bayes and Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Nuril Lutvi Azizah, Ade Eviyanti, Mochamad Alfan Rosid, Julia Atmaranti
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of social media in Indonesia has intensified the spread of fake news, posing serious threats to public opinion, social stability, and democratic processes. This research proposes a fake news detection model based on sentiment analysis of Indonesian public opinion using Naïve Bayes and Deep Neural Network (DNN) classification methods. Textual data were collected from 4,990 records across Instagram (1,298), Twitter/X (2,004), and Facebook (1,690), with fact-checking verification conducted using TurnBackHoax (MAFINDO). After preprocessing — including normalization, tokenization, stopword removal, and stemming — 4,548 records were retained. Sentiment analysis was applied to capture public emotional tendencies, followed by TF-IDF feature extraction. The Naïve Bayes classifier achieved 87.25% accuracy, with macro recall of 0.5633 and macro F1-score of 0.6382. The DNN model achieved higher accuracy at 90.99%, with macro recall of 0.7204 and macro F1-score of 0.7951, demonstrating better performance across minority sentiment classes. These findings confirm that integrating sentiment analysis with machine learning and deep learning approaches significantly enhances fake news detection on Indonesian social media, with DNN models showing strong potential for deployment in automated detection systems driven by public opinion, thereby supporting more effective misinformation mitigation and national digital literacy initiatives in Indonesia.

papers.title: A Stacking-Based Ensemble Learning Framework for Disease Severity Classification Using Electronic Medical Records
papers.authors: Edi Ismanto, Abdul Fadlil, Anton Yudhana
papers.abstract: The increasing availability of Electronic Medical Records (EMR) presents significant opportunities for improving clinical decision-making through data-driven approaches. Nevertheless, the intricacy, heterogeneity, and high degree of dimensionality of EMR data pose challenges for conventional statistical techniques and single machine learning (ML) models in accurately predicting patient conditions, particularly disease severity. This study aims to develop and evaluate a stacking-based framework for ensemble learning for disease severity classification using EMR data. The proposed approach integrates multiple ML models, including LR, SVM, K-NN, RF, and NB, using a meta-learner to enhance predictive performance. The dataset comprises 4,412 patient records with clinical and laboratory features, and the assessment is carried out using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. The findings of the experiment demonstrate that the stacking-based ensemble model outperforms all individual models, achieving an accuracy of 0.790, a recall of 0.660, a precision of 0.770, and an F1-score of 0.710. The model also demonstrates improved capability in identifying severe cases while maintaining a balanced performance across evaluation metrics. These results verify that ensemble learning, particularly stacking, provides a more robust and generalized solution for handling complex EMR data. This research helps the development of ML in healthcare by demonstrating the efficiency of stacking-based ensemble frameworks in improving disease severity classification, thereby supporting more reliable and accurate clinical decision-making systems.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and business performance among small and medium enterprises in Tanzania
papers.authors: Angela Richard Mkindi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied in business operations, yet empirical evidence on its adoption and performance implications among small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Tanzania remains limited. This study assessed the level of AI adoption and examined its relationship with business performance among Tanzanian SMEs. The study was anchored in the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV). A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed. Data were collected using a structured, self-administered questionnaire from 320 SME owners and managers in Dar es Salaam, Arusha, Mwanza and Dodoma. AI adoption and business performance were measured using five-item reflective constructs on a five-point Likert scale. Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results revealed a relatively high level of AI adoption (M = 3.45, SD = 0.82). AI adoption had a positive and statistically significant relationship with business performance (β = 0.533, p < 0.001), explaining 28.4% of its variance. The findings support the RBV perspective that AI can function as a valuable technological resource. SMEs should integrate AI into relevant operations while strengthening employee skills and data practices, while policymakers should improve training, digital infrastructure and affordable AI access.

papers.title: The Right Child, the Right Treatment, the Right Time: Rethinking Referral in Pediatric Drug-resistant Epilepsy
papers.authors: Ranjith Kumar Manokaran, Pearl Judith Raju
papers.journal: Journal of the Indian Medical Association
papers.abstract: Review ARticleManagement extends beyond optimizing ASMs.Rational pharmacotherapy remains important, but unnecessary polytherapy often increases adverse effects without improving seizure control.Dietary therapies, particularly the ketogenic diet and its variants, are valuable options in selected epilepsy syndromes and younger children.Neuromodulation, including vagus nerve stimulation, offers meaningful seizure reduction when curative surgery is not feasible.7,8 However, epilepsy surgery remains the most effective treatment for appropriately selected children with focal DRE. 4 Resective and disconnective procedures can achieve sustained seizure freedom Despite remarkable advances in pediatric epileptology, nearly onethird of children with epilepsy continue to have seizures despite appropriate antiseizure medication (ASM) therapy. 1 Drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) is associated with substantial neurodevelopmental, cognitive, psychosocial, and mortality burdens during childhood.Yet, many of these children have potentially effective treatment options.The challenge today is no longer simply controlling seizures-it is ensuring that children are identified early and receive the right treatment at the right time.The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) defines DRE as the failure of two appropriately selected, tolerated, and adequately dosed ASMs, used either sequentially or in combination, to achieve sustained seizure freedom. 1 Beyond this point, the likelihood of achieving sustained seizure freedom with further ASM trials decreases substantially, underscoring the need to reconsider the treatment strategy rather than continuing prolonged sequential medication trials.Drug-resistant epilepsy is not merely a failure of medications-it is the point at which the treatment strategy must change.[2][3][4] Pediatric DRE encompasses a heterogeneous group of disorders, including focal cortical dysplasia, developmental brain malformations, perinatal brain injury, tuberous sclerosis complex, Rasmussen encephalitis, genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, and metabolic disorders.5,6 Advances in high-resolution epilepsy protocol magnetic resonance imaging, prolonged video-electroencephalography, molecular genetics, and functional neuroimaging have improved etiological diagnosis, enabling individualized treatment and better prognostication.

papers.title: Functional Dissociative Seizures in Children: From Diagnostic Dilemma to an Integrated, Inclusive Model of Care
papers.authors: Satyesh Chowdary Muppavarapu, Lokesh Lingappa
papers.journal: Journal of the Indian Medical Association
papers.abstract: Diagnosis also requires assessment of developmental history, learning and neurodevelopment, mood and anxiety, family context, school functioning, bullying, trauma, recent loss, and major life changes.A specific psychological trigger is common but not required.2,3 Diagnosis a n D ManageMentThe diagnostic and management approach is summarized in Table 1.• Functional dissociative seizures and epilepsy can coexist; confirmation of one must not automatically exclude the other.• Management begins with a clear, nonjudgmental explanation shared by neurology and mental health teams: the diagnosis is known, the symptoms are genuine, and recovery is possible.• Treatment combines a multidisciplinar y approach: psychoeducation, individualized psychological therapy, management of comorbidities and stressors, family participation, school reintegration, and restoration of normal activity. CliniCal overviewFunctional/dissociative seizures (FDS), previously termed psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES), are paroxysmal episodes of altered movement, sensation, awareness, responsiveness, perception, or behavior that resemble epileptic seizures but are not generated by epileptic ictal discharges.The events are real and involuntary.Delayed recognition can expose children to unnecessary antiseizure medication, repeated emergency visits and investigations, school absence, restricted activity, and escalating family anxiety.The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) term FDS avoids defining the condition only by what it is not and reduces the implication that symptoms are fabricated or purely psychological. 1 The current pathophysiology model integrates brain-network functioning with attention, emotion, memory, arousal, prior experience, development, and environmental context.FDS should therefore be diagnosed positively, using characteristic history and semiology, rather than solely after excluding every disease.A careful description should document onset, duration, evolution, motor pattern, eye state, responsiveness, fluctuation, triggers, recovery, injury, and whether events are stereotyped.Eyewitness accounts and smartphone videos are useful.When available, video-electroencephalography (video-EEG) capture of the child's habitual event, showing typical clinical behavior without an epileptic ictal correlate, provides the highest diagnostic certainty.If video-EEG is unavailable, graded certainty may be based on clinician-witnessed events, reliable video, semiology, and appropriate EEG data. 2 Rigid semiology labels may be less useful than describing the event using a three-dimensional axis: motor activity, responsiveness, and change over time.Events may be nonmotor or hypermotor, with preserved or impaired responsiveness, and may fluctuate or transition during a single episode.

papers.title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
papers.authors: Jiawei Xiong, Cheng Tang, Hong Jiao, 최한나
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.

papers.title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
papers.authors: Mykhailo Kopytskyi, Jianhua Yang, Mir Seyedebrahimi
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.

papers.title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
papers.authors: Josef Habdank
papers.abstract: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.

papers.title: Trust Hinders Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment
papers.authors: Michaela Benk, Kacper Sokol
papers.abstract: Trust calibration remains the dominant framing of AI-assisted decision making: the goal is to close the gap between perceived and actual trustworthiness of AI systems so that users rely on them appropriately. We argue that this approach, while useful for decision problems that are well-defined and clearly scoped, overly restricts what it means to make a decision with AI support. To overcome this limitation, we develop three dimensions of AI-assisted decision making. First, trusting AI is only one of several possible strategies for managing uncertainty. Second, trust calibration is often misapplied when AI models large-world decision problems, i.e., ill-defined situations where goals and states are only partially known or unknowable. Third, in such settings human-AI alignment requires addressing higher-order decision processes. We conclude by reflecting on the implications of our observations on the design of process-oriented human-AI coupled systems that jointly identify and negotiate uncertainty throughout the decision-making task.

papers.title: To Defer or Not to Defer? Online Learning with LLMs and Congested Experts
papers.authors: Vasileios Saketos, William Réveillard, Alexandre Proutière, Sebastian Dalleiger, Ming Xiao
