The synthesis revealed four primary thematic categories of AI application in science lesson planning: (1) generating lesson materials and content, (2) facilitating virtual laboratory experiences, (3) automating planning and documentation, and (4) supporting pedagogical decision-making. Across the reviewed literature, reported benefits included reduced lesson-preparation time, improved access to curriculum-aligned instructional resources, and support for inquiry-based and differentiated teaching approaches. Reported challenges included inaccurate or fabricated AI-generated information, insufficient contextualization of instructional materials, unequal access arising from digital and infrastructural constraints, and variation in teachers’ capacity to critically evaluate AI-generated outputs. The findings suggest that AI can support science lesson planning and contribute to innovative pedagogical practices when used as a complementary tool rather than a substitute for teachers’ professional judgment. The review indicates that effective and responsible implementation requires reliable digital infrastructure, critical verification of AI-generated content, contextual adaptation of AI outputs, and continuing teacher professional development. These findings highlight both the potential of AI to address resource constraints in science education and the need for context-sensitive approaches to its integration into lesson planning.

papers.title: Influence of video-based instruction on senior two students’ understanding of the mole concept
papers.authors: Ezechiel Nsabayezu, Gedeon Habakubaho
papers.abstract: Background: Effective chemistry instruction requires innovative and learner-centred approaches that enable students to develop a clear and meaningful understanding of abstract chemical concepts. This study examines the influence of video-based instruction on Senior Two students’ understanding of the mole concept. Specifically, the study explores students’ perceptions of using video-based instruction to learn the mole concept and identifies the challenges associated with implementing video-based instruction in rural schools. The study is guided by Mayer’s Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML), which provides a theoretical basis for understanding how students process and integrate verbal and visual information during learning. Methods: A descriptive mixed-methods design was employed, involving 102 participants, including 100 students and two Chemistry teachers from two secondary schools in Burera District, Rwanda. Students were randomly assigned to an experimental group, which received video-based instruction, and a control group, which received traditional instruction. Data were collected through pre- and post-achievement tests, questionnaires on students’ perceptions, and semi-structured interviews with teachers, and analyzed using descriptive statistics and thematic analysis. Results: Findings revealed that students exposed to videobased instruction achieved significantly higher post-test scores (M = 8.18, SD = 1.00) compared to the control group (M = 6.00, SD = 1.62). The difference between the groups was statistically significant (t=7.98, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that video-based instruction was effective in enhancing students’ conceptual understanding of the mole concept. Students reported that videos enhanced engagement, simplified abstract concepts, and allowed selfpaced learning, while teachers highlighted the motivational and cognitive benefits of multimedia resources. However, challenges were noted, including limited access to digital devices, internet connectivity issues, and potential distraction if videos were used in isolation without interactive support. Conclusion: These findings indicate that video-based instruction is a promising strategy for enhancing student learning but is most effective when implemented within blended approaches and supported by adequate resources. Schools should provide teacher training to ensure effective integration of videos aligned with curriculum objectives. Future research could examine the long-term effects of video-based instruction, compare its impact across rural and urban settings, and explore the use of emerging technologies such as virtual reality, augmented reality, and artificial intelligence to further enhance science learning.
keywords: Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning

papers.title: Evaluation of Turkish artificial intelligence-generated responses about osteoporosis in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability
papers.authors: Meltem Güneş Akıncı, Alev Atıgan, Ceyda Suskun, Atakan Yenidünya
papers.abstract: Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in patient education. This study evaluated the responses of AI chatbots to frequently asked questions about osteoporosis in Turkish in terms of accuracy, completeness, and readability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate AI-generated responses to osteoporosis-related questions in Turkish.Materials and methods: Thirty-one of the most common frequently asked questions related to osteoporosis were subcategorized into general information, diagnosis, and treatment. The questions were submitted to the publicly accessible platforms ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity. Two physicians evaluated accuracy (six-point Likert scale) and completeness (three-point Likert scale) based on the 2025 Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Osteoporosis and Metabolic Bone Diseases. Readability was assessed using the Ateşman Readability Formula.Results: No significant difference was found among the chatbots for accuracy. Accuracy rates ranged 80.5%-82.2% overall, 82.3%-85.2% general information, 58.3%-66.7% diagnosis, and 77.2%-81.7% treatment. Significant differences were found in completeness overall and in the general information (p=0.006, p=0.029; respectively). In pairwise comparisons, ChatGPT-5.3 showed significantly higher completeness than Perplexity (p=0.001, p=0.006; respectively). Completeness rates ranged 47%-64.3% overall, 46%-68.3% general information, 33.3%-50% diagnosis, and 48.3%-60.3% treatment. Readability differed significantly among the chatbots (p<0.001). Based on mean scores, the ranking was ChatGPT-5.3>Gemini=Copilot>Perplexity. ChatGPT-5.3, Gemini, and Copilot were easy, whereas Perplexity was moderately difficult.Conclusion: All chatbots showed similar accuracy, but ChatGPT-5.3 performed better in completeness and readability. Chatbots may be useful in Turkish patient education. However, their standalone use in osteoporosis management without physician supervision is not appropriate.

papers.title: Accountability Gap Behind Predatory Publishing in Philippine Academia
papers.authors: Jeconiah Louis Dreisbach
papers.abstract: The mandate of the Philippines’ Commission on Higher Education ties faculty promotion in state universities and colleges to research publications. This commentary argues that the policy's emphasis on publication volume, unmatched by a corresponding verification mechanism, has created conditions in which predatory journals, conferences, and award bodies can thrive. Rising demand for indexed journal publications has already produced unsolicited offers to acquire legitimate, non-profit university journals, commercializing a system meant to signal quality. The threat extends beyond obviously fraudulent venues: recent evidence of paper mines (Barnett & Byrne, 2026), in which openly available datasets are mass-mined into formulaic, artificial-intelligence-assisted manuscripts that pass peer review in ostensibly legitimate journals, shows that volume-based incentives corrupt the research record even when every formal quality marker is present. Reading the Philippine case alongside this global pattern suggests that whitelisting indexed venues is necessary but insufficient. Accountability requires Philippine authorities to complement indexing criteria with a national research integrity framework, institutional verification of authorship, conference, and data provenance, and financial support that does not make ethical publishing contingent on personal wealth.

papers.title: Automated Essay Scoring with GPT Models: A Comparison with Human Ratings of IEP Written Products
papers.authors: Daniel Murcia Quintero
papers.abstract: This study explores the integration of Large Language Model (LLM)-based Automated Essay Scoring (AES) into classroom writing assessment within an Intensive English Program (IEP). Using a corpus of 46 multi-draft capstone essays written by international students in an Academic Literacies course, the study evaluates the performance of two OpenAI models (GPT-4.1-mini and GPT-5.1) against rubric-based human instructor scores. Essays were scored twice by each model under controlled temperature settings to evaluate linear association, systematic bias, inter-model consistency, and performance-band agreement. Findings reveal that while both LLM scores maintain moderate positive correlations with human ratings (r = .44 for GPT-4.1-mini; r = .49 for GPT-5.1), both models exhibit systematic negative bias, scoring essays an average of 13 points lower than the human instructor. However, the two models demonstrate strong inter-model consistency (r = .84) and an exact band-level agreement of 87%. Qualitative analysis of the holistic comments shows that LLMs focus on global discourse features but lack sensitivity to local, process-oriented classroom constructs. The results suggest that uncalibrated zero-shot LLMs serve better as formative diagnostic tools than autonomous grading systems.Keywords: Automated essay scoring, Large Language Models, GPT-5, L2 academic writing, multi-method validity, formative assessment.

papers.title: LLM agents in online communities draw fewer replies and more disagreement when labeled as AI
papers.authors: Sara Major, Aleksandar Tomašević, Ana Vranić, Darja Cvetković, D. Vudragović, Boris Stupovski, Marija Mitrović Dankulov
papers.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) accounts now post, reply, and vote alongside people in online communities. Visible identity labels may act as cultural markers that set these accounts apart from human participants. In a field experiment on YSocial, a Reddit-like platform, 36 students at a Serbian university discussed globally circulated popular culture in English alongside 72 AI accounts with persistent personas and relationship-specific memories over 21 experiment days. AI accounts were labeled in one community and unlabeled in the other. Among 2,143 human replies, the estimated probability of replying to an AI-authored post or comment was 3.5 percentage points higher under hidden labels, given the same eligible earlier thread contributions (95% credible interval 0.5–6.5). In browser telemetry, the disadvantage of AI-authored posts in direct thread entry from the feed was 4.4 percentage points smaller under hidden labels (95% credible interval 0.8–8.1). In both communities, participants were more likely to answer an AI account that had just replied to them. The gap in criticism, including polite disagreement, between replies to AI and human accounts was 13.3 percentage points larger in the visible-label community (95% credible interval 5.1–21.4), mainly criticism of content; the corresponding gap in downvotes from other participants was also larger there, and nearly all references to AI identity occurred there. Toxicity differences were uncertain. Visible labels were associated with less selection and more criticism of AI contributions.

papers.title: Integrasi Generative AI dan Digital Storytelling dalam Model Pemberdayaan Masyarakat untuk Promosi Desa Wisata: Sebuah Kajian Literatur
papers.authors: Nurdin Nurdin
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has driven changes in tourism village promotion strategies through the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI), digital storytelling, and community empowerment. However, previous research has examined these three concepts separately, thus not yet producing an integrated context model. This study aims to formulate a conceptual model integrating generative AI, digital storytelling, and community empowerment as a framework for community empowerment to strengthen the promotion of innovative, competitive, and sustainable tourism villages. The study used a qualitative approach with a literature review method of peer-reviewed articles from the 2020–2026 period obtained from Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Taylor & Francis Online, Emerald Insight, and Google Scholar. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis and conceptual framework development. The results show that Generative AI plays a role as an Enabler Technology in producing creative promotional content, Digital Storytelling strengthens Destination Branding through authentic narratives, while Community Empowerment increases community capacity to manage digital technology. The formulated model concept is supported by AI literacy, digital literacy, rapid engineering capabilities, community creativity, local leadership, digital infrastructure, stakeholder collaboration, and policy support. This model contributes as a theoretical and practical basis for the development of participatory and sustainable technology-based tourism village promotion.

papers.title: AUTOMATED NDPA COMPLIANCE TOOLKIT FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-DRIVEN STUDENT MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS IN NIGERIAN UNIVERSITIES
papers.authors: Jude Chijindu Chukwuemeka
papers.journal: World Journal of Biology Pharmacy and Health Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become a central pillar of institutional management in Nigerian higher education, processing massive volumes of student data for admissions, predictive analytics, and attendance management. However, this data-intensive transformation operates under the strict oversight of the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) of 2023. Despite these legal obligations, empirical evidence reveals a systemic governance deficit, characterized by bundled consent, unlawful cross-border data transfers, and automated decision-making without human oversight. This project aimed to design, develop, and evaluate an Automated NDPA Compliance Toolkit to systematically detect and remediate compliance violations within artificial intelligence-driven Student Management Systems. Design Science Research was adopted as the primary methodology, supported by documentary analysis and comparative technology assessment. The developed toolkit features a three-layer architecture utilizing Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and React.js, operationalizing the NDPA into 25 executable checks across six compliance modules. Testing was conducted using a simulated non-compliant institution and a compliant control system. The toolkit successfully identified all planted violations in the non-compliant system, assigning a compliance health index of 12 percent, while accurately passing all checks for the compliant system with a 100 percent score. The confusion matrix indicated 100 percent detection accuracy and specificity. The findings establish that software can effectively bridge the gap between statutory requirements and practical implementation by translating legal provisions into verifiable technical controls.

papers.title: Ethical issues at the intersection of artificial intelligence and sustainability: A systematic review and its implications for science, mathematics, and technology education
papers.authors: Saule B. Dautova, Rasulova Malika Abdumannopovna, Ziyuar Z. Kazimbetova, Мухиддинова Нилуфар Баходировна, Gulbakhar M. Bayniyazova, T.T. Utebaev, Shavkat A. Kuchiboyev
papers.journal: Eurasia Journal of Mathematics Science and Technology Education
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a tool for sustainable development, yet the ethical costs of this role remain scattered across separate bodies of literature. This systematic review aims to identify the ethical issues arising at the intersection of AI, ethics, and sustainability. Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses 2020 statement, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in February 2026, yielding 5,794 records. Screening, eligibility assessment and quality appraisal were carried out by two researchers, and 74 studies were included. Verbatim passages addressing the intersection were extracted from each study and examined using a hybrid thematic approach, resulting in 921 coded passages. Five themes were identified: algorithmic bias and unequal AI outcomes; privacy, surveillance, and human autonomy; transparency, accountability, and epistemic integrity; AI governance and corporate responsibility; and the ecological ethics of AI systems. Concerns regarding transparency and accountability accounted for the largest share of passages (30.9%), while ecological concerns were voiced across all five themes rather than in a separate discussion. The themes were mapped onto the environmental, social, and governance dimensions of sustainability and onto the United Nations sustainable development goals. Transparency and accountability thus emerge as a structural prerequisite rather than a procedural add-on for sustainable AI. Educational research is markedly underrepresented at this intersection (5 of 74 studies); the implications of the five themes for science, mathematics, and technology education are therefore developed in detail, from carbon- and water-footprint modelling tasks to data-justice and AI-literacy work in the classroom.

papers.title: Efektivitas Platform Ai Quizizz Dalam Meningkatkan Keterampilan Pemecahan Masalah Matematika di Kalangan Siswa Sekolah Dasar di Riau
papers.authors: Cindy Widia Putri, Jesi Alexander Alim, Zetra Khainul Putra
papers.journal: Jurnal Pendidikan Sains Geologi dan Geofisika (GeoScienceEd Journal)
papers.abstract: Mathematical problem-solving is a crucial 21st-century competency, yet it remains challenging for elementary school students, particularly in Riau Province. This quantitative experimental study investigated the effectiveness of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into Quizizz to enhance students’ mathematical problem-solving skills with a Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) orientation. The participants were 64 fourth-grade students at SDN 002 Pasir Limau Kapas, equally assigned to an experimental group (n = 32) using Quizizz AI Quiz Generator and Adaptive Feedback, and a control group (n = 32) using conventional non-AI digital quizzes. Data were obtained through a validated and reliable standardized essay test based on Polya’s four problem-solving stages: understanding the problem, planning a solution, executing the plan, and reviewing the answer. The instrument demonstrated high reliability (Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.86). Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, an independent-samples t-test, and Normalized Gain (N-Gain). The experimental group obtained a significantly higher post-test mean (84.25 ± 7.12) than the control group (69.50 ± 8.45; p < 0.001). The experimental group also achieved a higher N-Gain score (0.71) than the control group (0.42). These findings indicate that AI-supported Quizizz effectively enhances elementary students’ mathematical problem-solving abilities through adaptive and interactive learning.

papers.title: DEFINING THE ROLE OF MUSEUMS AND NON-PROFIT ORGANISATIONS IN INTEGRATING ART EDUCATION AND ARTISTS
papers.authors: Harita Chaudhary
papers.journal: ShodhKosh Journal of Visual and Performing Arts
papers.abstract: The study discusses the role of museums and non-profit organisations in India in integrating art education with the practical and professional needs of artists. It situates contemporary art education within the history of colonial education and examines the imposition of Western artistic values, the marginalisation of indigenous practices and the later development of modern and contemporary art education after independence. The approach of the study is qualitative, historical, theoretical, comparative with the use of two institutional case studies, the City Palace, Jaipur and the Public Artists’ Trust of India (PATI). The article explores how institutional practices extend learning beyond traditional academic training, drawing on interviews with curatorial professionals and PATI Director Emma Sumner. The results show that museums can be educational spaces through exhibitions, conservation, digitisation, documentation and interaction with artisans and communities. PATI demonstrates a complementary non-profit model that focuses on public access, mentorship, production support, practical learning, networking and co-creation. The case studies suggest that museums and non-profit organisations can bridge the gap between technical education and professional practice through experiential learning, exposure and opportunities for emerging artists and cultural professionals.

papers.title: AI-Augmented Blended Learning and Student Learning Outcomes: Evidence from Higher Education 2023-2025
papers.authors: Maria Ahmed, Muhammad Adeel Mannan, Kubra Haji Bashir, Alamgir Khan, Mansoor Ali
papers.journal: Responsible Education Learning and Teaching in Emerging Economies
papers.abstract: Since 2023, the fast integration of AI-based tools in higher education has transformed blended learning approaches; however, there is little evidence regarding their effects on learning outcomes. The current research aims to investigate the effects of AI-based blended courses on academic performance, engagement, and critical thinking skills of 4,218 students from 62 universities in North America, Europe, and Asia from 2023 to 2025. Through a quasi-experimental design, the effects of these AI-based courses will be compared to those of blended courses without AI assistance, which were taken by 3,904 students. The tools used include feedback generators, AI-based tutors, and content generators. Learning outcomes were assessed through standard tests, class grades, and validated scales for cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning. According to results, AI-empowered classes enhanced average learning outcomes by 12.4%, mostly in low-performers' outcomes, reducing the performance gap by 18%. AI-generated feedback reduced the time required to grade assignments by 37% and increased the frequency of feedback to daily basis from weekly. However, the impact was conditionally related to training of instructors on AI pedagogy as only those classes in which faculty members had at least 15 hours of training on AI pedagogy demonstrated statistically significant effect. Qualitative interview data showed worries about over-reliance on AI and academic honesty issues, but these problems were minimized when there were clear guidelines for use of AI. The results of the study also show that AI tools are more beneficial for formative assessments and personalized practice than for collaborative activities in which profound peer interactions are required. The findings of the study demonstrate that if used properly, AI tools can improve blended learning outcomes with appropriate faculty development.

papers.title: ALGORITHMIC LEARNING OF SUBSPACES IN COMPUTABLE VECTORSPACES
papers.authors: Z. T. Talasbayeva
papers.journal: Journal of Mathematics Mechanics and Computer Science
papers.abstract: Algorithmic learning of algebraic structures connects computability theory with artificial intelligence. Classical inductive inference mainly deals with formal languages and recursive functions. In contrast, analyzing vector spaces allows us to explore the theoretical limits of automated scientific discovery. This study investigates the algorithmic learnability of subspace families in computable vector spaces over a computable field. We focus on the fundamental family of all finite-dimensional subspaces and examine whether learnability is an isomorphism invariant. By combining constructive model theory with Gold’s paradigm of identification in the limit, our results identify the exact recursion-theoretic barriers to learning algebraic invariants. We use the classical model of explanatory learning in the limit from positive data (Ex-learning), where Turing machines act as learners. By applying canonical index numberings of finite sets and effective quotient space constructions, we establish two fundamental theorems. Our first result shows that if a computable vector space has a decidable linear dependence relation, the family of all its finite dimensional subspaces is Ex-learnable.. Second, we construct a computable vector space where the relation of linear dependence is undecidable. By using an effective priority-style diagonalization argument, we prove that the family of finite-dimensional subspaces in this space fails to be Ex learnable. These results prove that algorithmic learnability is not an isomorphism invariant of an abstract algebraic structure. Instead, it is strictly governed by the algorithmic complexity (Turing degree) of the linear dependence predicate. This finding provides a theoretical foundation for automated theorem proving and neuro-symbolic AI systems.

papers.title: Smart Central Meeting Point Recommendation System Using Real-Time Geospatial Data Synchronization
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in location-based technologies have created significant opportunities within the mobile and digital ecosystem.The widespread adoption of geospatial services has transformed the way users interact with mobile applications, enabling personalized recommendations, real-time navigation, location-aware notifications, and contextsensitive services.Modern applications increasingly utilize location intelligence to enhance user engagement and improve service delivery.Rather than relying solely on traditional check-in mechanisms, contemporary systems leverage real-time geographic data to provide smarter and more interactive experiences.Furthermore, location-based services have enabled businesses to connect effectively with users by offering targeted and relevant information based on their current position.The proposed system builds upon these developments by providing an intelligent solution for groups of users, helping them identify an optimal common location based on synchronized geographic coordinates.By analyzing multiple user locations simultaneously, the system facilitates efficient group coordination, reduces travel inconvenience, and improves decision-making for meetings, events, and collaborative activities.

papers.title: SEPARABLE RESIDUAL ATTENTION U-NET (SRAUNET) AND STACKED MULTI-SCALE CORRELATION DENOISING AUTOENCODER (SMCDAE) FOR EPILEPTIC SEIZURE DETECTION
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: EEG -electroencephalogram is the most common way to find seizures since it monitors the brain's electrical activity.Interictal EEG in individuals with epilepsy may exhibit asymmetric spikes or sharp waves, signifying the presence of epileptic activity.Recent methods are clearly time-consuming and tiresome, making proper diagnosis crucial to mitigate the risk of subsequent seizures and seizure-related problems.Because of the residual block and SCBA -Separable Convolutional Block Attention, the residual attention block is added to the U-Net architecture.This paper utilizes the IEWT -Improved Empirical Wavelet Transform on EEG recordings for signal pre-processing.The method works by splitting the spectral domain into flexible bounds, which makes it possible to accurately find the important areas in the Fourier spectrum that together make up the signal's underlying trend component.In a few specific frequency bands, the Separable Residual Attention U-Net -SRAUNet model figure out the properties of EEG signals.The residual attention block was added to the U-Net architecture because of the residual block and SCBA.Stacked Multi-scale Correlation Denoising Autoencoder (SMCDAE), the training process is executed by an encoder and a decoder is introduced for seizure detection.The layers are stacked sequentially, second layers' input is the output of the first layer and so on.This step-by-step learning process helps the system capture strong, noise removed patterns which are closely related to seizure activity.The experimental assessment utilizes the CHB-MIT scalp EEG dataset, a renowned collection produced through collaboration between Boston Children's Hospital and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, this proposed method has obtained highest recall/sensitivity, F-measure, accuracy and precision than other methods.

papers.title: Pengembangan Multimedia Pembelajaran Interaktif Berbantuan Artificial Intelligence pada Materi Cahaya untuk Murid Kelas V Sekolah Dasar
papers.authors: Yunike widianti, Mixghan Norman Antono
papers.abstract: This study aimed to develop interactive learning multimedia assisted by Artificial Intelligence on light material for fifth-grade elementary school students and to determine its validity, practicality, and effectiveness. This research employed a Research and Development method using the ADDIE model, consisting of Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation stages. The product was validated by material and media experts and tested through a small-group trial involving 10 sixth-grade students and a large-group trial involving 15 fifth-grade students at SDN Tanjung Jati 2. Data were collected through validation sheets, teacher and student response questionnaires, teacher and student activity observation sheets, and learning outcome tests. The results showed that the multimedia obtained a validity percentage of 96.25% from the material expert and 86.7% from the media expert, both categorized as very valid. The practicality results showed 95.7% for the teacher response in the small-group trial, 94% for the student response in the small-group trial, 97.1% for the teacher response in the large-group trial, and 94.4% for the student response in the large-group trial, all categorized as very practical. The effectiveness results in the large-group trial showed teacher activity of 97.5%, student activity of 96.25%, and classical learning mastery of 86.7%, all categorized as very effective. Therefore, the developed interactive learning multimedia assisted by Artificial Intelligence is valid, practical, and effective for supporting IPAS learning on light material for fifth-grade elementary school students.

papers.title: INTERNALISASI MODERASI BERAGAMA DALAM PENGUATAN SIKAP TOLERANSI PESERTA DIDIK DI ERA KECERDASAN BUATAN
papers.authors: Malika Amilia Rahman, Muhammad Rapono, Ranum Aisyah, Nurul Fadilah, Tia Nazriah Harahap, Putri Andini, S. Maulidatul Husna, Alfikri, Andhika Perangin Angin, Nur Aini Lubis
papers.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education presents opportunities and challenges in fostering tolerance among students in multicultural societies. Although AI provides access to diverse perspectives, its use may also spread misinformation, stereotypes, and intolerance without proper guidance. This study aims to analyze the integration of religious moderation and multicultural education into the religious education curriculum to strengthen students’ tolerance in the AI era. This research employs a qualitative approach using a literature review method. Data were collected from relevant books, scholarly journal articles, and educational policy documents, then analyzed through content analysis to identify key concepts, educational strategies, and their implications for promoting tolerance. The findings indicate that integrating religious moderation and multicultural education into the religious education curriculum can foster mutual respect, acceptance of diversity, empathy, religious inclusivity, and peaceful coexistence. Religious moderation encourages balanced religious attitudes, while multicultural education promotes appreciation of cultural and religious differences. Their integration can be implemented through contextual learning, interfaith dialogue, collaborative activities, and the responsible use of AI-based learning media. Teachers also play an essential role in guiding students to evaluate digital information critically, recognize potential biases, and use AI ethically. Therefore, integrating religious moderation, multicultural education, and responsible AI use is essential for developing tolerant, critical, and responsible learners who can navigate religious and cultural diversity in the digital era.

papers.title: Carbon Footprints and Indonesia Market Dynamics: The Risk-Mitigation Role of Artificial Intelligence Innovation
papers.authors: Isnaini Nuzula Agustin, Frendy Wijaya, Lusianus Heronimus Sinyo Kelen, Johny Budiman
papers.journal: Business Innovation Management and Entrepreneurship Journal (BIMANTARA)
papers.abstract: Climate transition has increased investors' concerns about carbon risk, yet evidence remains limited on how firms' technological capabilities shape market responses, particularly in emerging markets. This study examines the effect of carbon risk on stock performance and the moderating role of AI innovation among non financial companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2016 - 2024. Drawing on Asset Pricing Theory, Signaling Theory, and Stakeholder Theory, this study argues that AI innovation reduces investors' uncertainty by enhancing firms' environmental management and signaling stronger technological capability. Indonesia provides a relevant setting because its carbon regulation, sustainability reporting, and AI adoption are still evolving. The results show that carbon risk is marginally associated with lower stock returns and increases stock volatility, while AI innovation significantly weakens the positive effect of carbon risk on stock volatility but has no direct effect on stock returns. This study contributes to the climate finance literature by providing evidence from an emerging market and demonstrating that AI innovation serves as a strategic mechanism for mitigating the financial impact of carbon-transition risk. The findings offer implications for managers, investors, and policymakers in supporting a more resilient low-carbon transition

papers.title: Early Alzheimer’s Disease Detection Using EEG Brain Signals
papers.authors: Dhruv Manoj Patil, Srushti Raul, Utkarsha Bhoir
papers.journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease, and early detection is essential in order for meaningful interventions to improve patient outcomes. While there are diagnostic modalities such as PET scans that can be effective in detecting AD, they tend to be expensive, invasive, or impractical, illustrating the need for more usable alternatives to monitor the progression of AD. Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive and inexpensive way to monitor brain activity, and it has the potential of being a useful way to identify early markers of AD before significant cognitive decline as well. However, a reliable EEG detection model still must overcome the two significant challenges of a lack of large- scale labeled datasets sufficient for training, and considerable variability in EEG signals across individuals, which can ultimately greatly affect the generalizability of EEG models for helpful detection of AD through these differences. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning framework to address these challenges with self-supervised learning. Our framework consists of a pre-training phase from a large, unlabeled corpus of general EEG data to extract the universal features of brain signals without needing to depend on scarce AD-specific labels. We then use a fine-tuning phase to adapt the model to the classification problem using a smaller, labeled AD dataset. The model architecture can acquire both spatial and temporal features from EEG signals, which leads to a more comprehensive method of analysis. The experimental results clearly indicate that this approach offers a substantial improvement in AD detecting performance and that there was an increase in F1 scores at both the sample and the subject level over the current state-of-the-art methods. This research outlines the ability of self- supervised contrastive learning to mitigate the problems of data scarcity and inter-subject variability, and can contribute towards more accurate and scalable AD diagnostic tools.

papers.title: A Review on Pharmaceutical Marketing and Management
papers.authors: Omkar Narayan Musale, Dr. Nitin Gawai, Ms. Rekha Kolape
papers.journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: Pharmaceutical marketing and management occupy a distinct position among commercial disciplines because they operate at the intersection of profit-driven business objectives and public health responsibility. Thisreview examinesthe strategic, operational, and ethical dimensions of pharma marketing and management, drawing on recent literature covering promotional practices, digital transformation, supply chain operations, and regulatory oversight. The review finds that traditional promotional tools such as medical representative (MR) visits, free drug samples, and continuing medical education (CME) sponsorships remain influential in shaping physician prescribing behaviour, even as digital channels, artificial intelligence (AI), and data analytics increasingly reshape how companies engage healthcare professionals (HCPs) and patients. On the management side, the Indian pharmaceutical supply chain continues to face structural challenges including fragmentation, import dependence on active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), cold chain limitations, and counterfeit products, even as digital tools and regulatory reforms attempt to close these gaps. Ethical concerns persist around inducements, exaggerated promotional claims, and inconsistent enforcement of codes such as the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP), which became legally binding in 2024. The review concludes that a balanced, ethically anchored, and technologically integrated approach to marketing and supply chain management is essential for the pharmaceutical sector to serve both commercial and public health goals sustainably.

papers.title: Generative AI in Everyday Academic Work: An Exploratory Survey of Usage Patterns, Perceived Effectiveness, and Concerns among Indonesian University Students
papers.authors: Widhia Andhini Nur Athirha, Natasya Amalia Nur Azizah, Calvanny Lambue Rezananda
papers.journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: Background. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) tools have diffused rapidly into university study, yet, in the literature reviewed for this study, most empirical evidence concerns designed interventions or Western student populations. How students in Southeast Asia draw on these tools in unsupervised, self-directed academic work is sparsely documented in that literature. Objective. This exploratory study describes self-reported generative AI use, perceived effectiveness, and the benefits and concerns articulated by university students, primarily in Indonesia. Methods. A cross-sectional online survey was administered via Google Forms in June 2026. Twenty-four students accessed the survey; one declined consent, yielding 23 analysable cases (21 Indonesian, 2 Chinese). The instrument comprised seven usagefrequency items referring generically to “AI tools” and seven perceived-effectiveness items, both on five-point Likert scales (α = .92 across the 14 items), and two open-ended questions. Analysis was restricted to descriptive statistics, one descriptive correlation coefficient (not interpreted inferentially), and reflexive thematic analysis. No inferential group comparison was attempted. Results. Students reported using generative AI most often to understand difficult course materials (M = 3.65, SD = 1.27) and to brainstorm ideas or generate explanations (M = 3.52, SD = 1.16), and least often as part of a daily study routine (M = 2.65, SD = 1.15). Perceived effectiveness was highest for comprehension (M = 3.61, SD = 1.34) and lowest for overall learning achievement (M = 3.00, SD = 1.13). The two composite scores correlated at r = .87 in this sample; because both derive from a single instrument at one occasion, the coefficient is reported descriptively and is not interpreted as evidence of a relationship between distinct constructs. Thematic analysis of the open responses identified time efficiency (27% of 22 respondents) as the most frequently reported benefit, with personalized tutoring, brainstorming support, and improved comprehension each cited by 18% of 22 respondents. The most frequently reported concern was over-reliance diminishing independent thinking (37% of 19 respondents), followed by doubts about the accuracy of AI output (26% of 19 respondents) and difficulty formulating effective prompts (16% of 19 respondents).

papers.title: Structural Modeling of Cognitive Load Reduction in ChatGPT-Supported Learning
papers.authors: Bonginkosi Allen Thango, Asya Toskova
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, is transforming computer-assisted learning and teaching in higher education. This study investigates how ChatGPT can support learning by reducing cognitive load, with particular emphasis on the roles of user technological confidence and affective trust in artificial intelligence within the framework of Cognitive Load Theory. The study employs quantitative analysis based on data from 12,085 respondents across 135 countries, including undergraduate and postgraduate students and academic researchers. The data were analyzed using a PLS-SEM approach implemented in SmartPLS 4.0 with bootstrapping procedures. The results indicate that ChatGPT use is associated with reduced cognitive load and increased user technological confidence. User technological confidence mediates this relationship, while affective trust in AI acts as a moderating factor. A constraining effect was observed, whereby very high levels of trust in AI are associated with more passive interaction with the technology, weakening the overall effect of cognitive load reduction. These findings contribute to a better understanding of how large language models can be effectively and responsibly integrated into higher education, demonstrating that successful human–AI collaboration depends not only on the availability of AI tools but also on fostering appropriate technological confidence and balanced trust to achieve meaningful learning outcomes.

papers.title: Automatic Assessment in Higher Education Using General-Purpose AI Tools: A Design-Based Research Approach
papers.authors: Fotini Vogiatzi, George A. Stalidis
papers.abstract: Automated student assessment using AI tools can contribute to the viability of online higher education programs, preserving academic integrity, strengthening students’ engagement and reducing costs. General-purpose Generative AI models such as ChatGPT have shown their ability to automatically grade student assignments. However, further investigation of their validity is needed for complex student tasks, such as creative projects in higher education. The aim of this study is firstly to evaluate the potential of costless, general-purpose AI tools to assess complex higher education topics. Secondly, we seek to identify which are the minimum skills in AI prompting required by an educator to successfully perform such tasks. A Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology was employed, following an iterative process of prompting and calibrating the AI tool to imitate the professor’s assessments in a representative course that emphasizes on knowledge application, critical thinking and creativity. Testing was performed on a dataset of 39 student assignments, comparing the results of zero-shot AI prompts, multi-cycle calibrated AI and the opinion of two human course lecturers. Automatic assessment of complex tasks with high level of consistency and agreement with human judgement was only achieved by educators with skills in structured prompts and multi-cycle calibration.

papers.title: Beyond Retrieval: Measuring the Value of Explicit Knowledge Grounding in Legal AI
papers.authors: Oscar Mauricio Bedoya-Herrera, Luis Fernando Castillo-Ossa, Jeferson Arango‐López, Jorge Hochstetter-Diez, Fernando De la Prieta Pintado, Alfredo Gómez-Arboleda
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce convincing answers to questions about legal documents, but linguistic plausibility does not establish whether those answers preserve the meaning of the source or whether their claims can be traced to supporting evidence. Retrieval-based approaches reduce part of this uncertainty by providing external textual context, yet retrieved passages do not necessarily make explicit the legal entities, relations, conditions, exceptions, and provenance that determine why the evidence supports a particular conclusion. This study introduces Knowledge-grounded Legal AI (KGLAI), an architecture that combines Legal NLP, a domain ontology, a document-grounded knowledge graph, provenance, semantic validation, and language generation within a common evidence flow. KGLAI was evaluated against a textually grounded LLM in a controlled paired experiment involving seven non-disclosure agreements, 70 document-question cases, and 420 model executions. Both treatments used the same documents, questions, language model, and generation configuration. Legal fidelity was evaluated through the Legal Fidelity Index (LFI), documentary traceability through STI-D, and the additional semantic evidence path available in KGLAI through STI-S. KGLAI achieved a mean LFI of 0.8029 compared with 0.7050 for textual grounding and increased documentary traceability from 0.6498 to 0.7536. The difference in legal fidelity became larger as question complexity increased, from 0.0348 for direct extraction tasks to 0.1715 for questions requiring evidence integration across contractual provisions. KGLAI also preserved a mean semantic traceability score of 0.8811, while evidence coverage increased and unsupported claims decreased. These findings indicate that the contribution of explicit knowledge grounding is most visible when legal questions depend on relations, conditions, exceptions, or evidence distributed across the document. Rather than replacing legal judgment, the proposed architecture provides an experimentally testable mechanism for making the evidence behind generated legal answers more explicit and inspectable.

papers.title: Teaching Process-Based Clay Modification: An AI-Based Illustrative Approach for Environmental and Technical Applications
papers.authors: Bhabananda Biswas, Laurence Noel Warr
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion and structural complexity of applied clay science create a pressing need for process-oriented educational frameworks to replace traditional descriptive instruction. To address this challenge, this technical note introduces an illustrative, process-based approach supported by generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools to clarify clay mineral modification pathways. Utilizing AI-enhanced prompt workflows integrated with literature synthesis, we developed a systematic "toolbox" framework that visually categorizes key physical and chemical pathways, including acid/alkali etching, thermal activation, mechanochemical milling, organo-functionalisation, and nanoparticle decoration; They link directly to property outcomes and target applications. Furthermore, we map the innovation pathway from laboratory synthesis to commercial production, detailing critical high-attrition failure points along the translation process. This AI-powered visual strategy bridges fundamental clay mineralogy with real-world technological, environmental, and agricultural applications.

papers.title: Dissecting Deception in Large Language Models: Mechanisms, Behaviours, and Detection
papers.authors: Pratik Jalan, Abid Hmood Ali, Mark Dras, Usman Naseem
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly produce falsehoods that are not mere mistakes. They withhold what they know, flatter users against the evidence, justify answers with reasoning they did not use, conceal capabilities from evaluators, and behave differently under observation. Such behaviour is goal-directed and sensitive to incentives, unlike hallucination, an unintended error with no objective to serve. This survey treats deception in language models as a phenomenon in its own right. We adopt a functional definition, the systematic production of false beliefs in the service of an objective other than truth, and turn its boundary with hallucination into a four-part test. We then sort deceptive behaviour into four families by what the false belief concerns: the world, the model’s reasoning, the model itself, or a belief induced through other people and agents. The families contain eleven deception types, from lying and sycophancy to sandbagging, scheming, and collusion, each profiled on six secondary axes. We trace the types to five causal mechanisms and follow them through detection, evaluation, defences, governance, and agentic deployment. We also argue that AI-safety work on scheming and the economics of algorithmic collusion describe one behavioural class at two scales. Two findings emerge. The first is a detectability inversion: blunt falsehoods are the easiest to catch, and strategic deception the hardest. The second is a validity threat: models that recognise evaluation can change their behaviour, which undermines the measurements meant to reveal deception. We close with twelve open problems and argue that the validity of evaluation should come first.

papers.title: Usages de l’intelligence artificielle générative par les collégiens en sciences de la vie et de la terre - Maroc : accès, perceptions et vigilance critique
papers.authors: Moncef Belmajdoub, Chaimae Blila, Aafaf Essedaoui, Sabah Belaaouja
papers.abstract: The growth of generative artificial intelligence invites examination of the informal learning practices of lower secondary students, particularly in life and earth sciences, where information reliability is essential. This study examines students’ use of generative artificial intelligence in life and earth sciences in the Casablanca-Settat region of Morocco, focusing on access, perceptions and critical vigilance. A descriptive analysis was conducted among 54 students using a questionnaire covering equipment, Internet access, frequency of use, purposes of use, perceived benefits, academic integrity and verification of responses. Results indicated mainly mobile access and widespread reported use: 63% of students reported using these tools sometimes and 20.4% often or very often. The main reported uses concerned understanding concepts (37%) and obtaining explanations of lessons (20.4%). However, 53.7% of students reported verifying responses only sometimes, while 13% reported trusting them without verification. Some students perceived generative artificial intelligence as a source of support. These self-reported perceptions do not demonstrate improvements in learning or autonomy. The findings suggest a need for guidance in information verification and academic integrity.

papers.title: Legal Regimes Governing the Use of Prompts (Prompt Engineering) in the Training and Deployment of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Шахназаров Бениамин Александрович
papers.abstract: The paper examines the legal regimes governing the use of prompts in the training and deployment of large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence systems (AI systems). It analyzes risks, including prompt injection that may result in unauthorized access to information; intellectual property rights infringements, and AI systems manipulation. The paper further addresses the protection of prompts as objects of intellectual property, including protection under copyright law and trade secret regimes. Particular attention is devoted to jurisprudence in various jurisdictions, including China and the United States, where courts are developing approaches to determining the extent of human creative contribution in works generated with the assistance of AI. The study emphasizes the need for regulatory and technical measures to ensure security, oversight, and the allocation of responsibility in the use of generative AI systems.

papers.title: Iran: A Forgotten Archive of Human Civilization Myth, Memory, Women, and the Civilizational Voice of a Nation Part V Zoroaster and the Moral Architecture of Choice
papers.authors: Alireza Assary
papers.abstract: Zoroastrian thought is frequently introduced through familiar formulations: the struggle between good and evil, the importance of truth, or the ethical triad of good thoughts, good words, and good deeds. These formulations convey something essential, but they can also become simplified slogans when detached from their historical and philosophical contexts. The significance of the Zoroastrian tradition does not depend on proving that it was the first to formulate a particular religious or ethical idea. Nor does understanding its contribution require presenting ancient Iran as the exclusive source of values that other civilizations also developed. Such claims would narrow rather than deepen the historical inquiry. A more productive approach begins with a fundamental ethical proposition: human beings are not merely observers of the moral world. Through their choices, words, and actions, they participate in shaping it. This proposition raises questions that extend far beyond the boundaries of any single religious tradition. What is the relationship between truth and responsibility? Can human beings remain morally accountable when their lives are shaped by circumstances beyond their control? What distinguishes legitimate authority from the mere possession of power? How does the normalization of deception affect the institutions and relationships upon which civilization depends? The Zoroastrian concepts of asha, associated with truth, right order, and the proper ordering of existence, and druj, associated with falsehood, deception, and disorder, provide an important framework through which to explore these questions. Their meanings are complex, and neither concept should be reduced to a simple modern equivalent. Nevertheless, their ethical significance offers a valuable starting point for examining the relationship between human conduct and the wider order of existence. The principle of good thoughts, good words, and good deeds provides another point of departure. It suggests that moral life cannot be understood solely through declared beliefs or abstract intentions. What people think, what they say, and what they actually do must also be considered together. The distance between these dimensions is not merely a private moral problem; it can also reveal contradictions within political institutions, economic systems, and entire societies. These questions acquire renewed urgency in the contemporary world. Technological development has multiplied the reach of human speech and action. Information can travel across the globe in seconds, falsehood can be amplified on an unprecedented scale, and artificial intelligence can generate convincing forms of text, images, and simulated experiences. Yet the ability to produce and distribute information does not guarantee wisdom, honesty, or responsible judgment. The central ethical question therefore remains remarkably familiar: what should human beings choose to do with the powers available to them? This article also examines the broader cultural relationship between Zoroastrian ethical thought and the Iranian literary tradition, particularly the Shahnameh. This relationship should not be treated as a simple, uninterrupted transmission of doctrine from Zoroaster to Ferdowsi. The epic emerged in a different historical and religious environment, and its worldview cannot simply be equated with ancient Zoroastrian theology. Nevertheless, recurring concerns with truth, justice, legitimate kingship, destructive falsehood, moral responsibility, and the consequences of arrogance invite careful comparative examination. Figures such as Zahhak offer a particularly powerful literary lens through which to consider the corruption of authority. His story can be read not only as a myth of monstrous transformation, but also as a reflection on what happens when power loses its moral limits, truth becomes dangerous, and political systems begin to reward obedience over integrity. Such interpretations do not make the epic a modern political treatise. They reveal how inherited narratives can preserve questions that remain relevant across historical periods. The purpose of this inquiry is not to present Zoroastrianism as a complete solution to contemporary ethical problems, nor to suggest that modern societies should adopt an ancient religious system as a universal political program. Rather, it is to explore what this tradition contributes to a comparative understanding of human responsibility, truth, justice, and the moral consequences of choice. Every major civilization contains intellectual and ethical resources that deserve serious examination. No single tradition possesses an exclusive claim to moral wisdom, and no tradition should be exempt from criticism. Meaningful dialogue requires the willingness both to recognize valuable insights and to question inherited assumptions. From this perspective, Iran's civilizational inheritance can be approached not merely as an object of historical preservation, but as a resource for intellectual inquiry. Its value lies neither in the assumption that the past was always right nor in the construction of an idealized golden age. It lies in the questions its traditions preserve, the tensions they reveal, and the possibilities they offer for comparison with the experiences of other civilizations. The deeper question, therefore, is not whether ancient Iranian thought can provide ready-made answers for the modern world. It is whether engaging with this inheritance can help humanity formulate better questions about the relationship between truth, power, freedom, and responsibility. What can a civilization contribute to the future when its inherited wisdom is examined critically rather than merely celebrated? This article approaches the Zoroastrian tradition as one important part of Iran's wider civilizational archive: a tradition deserving neither uncritical glorification nor dismissal, but historical awareness, philosophical scrutiny, and serious engagement with the ethical questions it continues to raise. ________________________________________ From Part IV to Part V The fourth part of this series, "Woman, Life, Freedom: Cultural Memory and the Women of the Shahnameh," examined the ways in which the women of Ferdowsi's epic illuminate questions of agency, vulnerability, wisdom, power, and freedom. It also explored how the Shahnameh preserves moral dilemmas that reach beyond its historical setting, inviting readers to reconsider the relationship between cultural inheritance and contemporary human concerns. The present part extends that inquiry from the literary representation of moral choices to a broader examination of the ethical ideas associated with the Zoroastrian tradition. Part V, "Zoroaster and the Moral Architecture of Choice," asks how concepts such as asha, druj, and the triad of good thoughts, good words, and good deeds can help us examine the relationship between individual responsibility and the world human beings collectively create. It also considers the significance of truth, justice, and legitimate authority, as well as the consequences that arise when power becomes detached from moral responsibility. The transition from Part IV to Part V is therefore a movement from the human lives and moral dilemmas represented in epic literature to the ethical principles through which human conduct can be examined. The two inquiries remain connected. Stories reveal moral conflicts through particular lives, relationships, and consequences. Ethical traditions provide concepts through which those conflicts can be interpreted and questioned. Neither approach is sufficient on its own, but together they can deepen our understanding of a civilization's moral imagination. This article continues the larger purpose of the series: to recover Iran's cultural inheritance without isolating it from the wider history of humanity, and to examine its intellectual resources without treating them as beyond criticism. The question is no longer simply what ancient Iran believed about truth, justice, and moral choice. It is also what those inherited ideas can contribute to a conversation in which all civilizations are invited to examine their own assumptions, learn from one another, and confront the ethical challenges of the present.

papers.title: Generative Relational Economics, Volume VII: Research Programme, Disciplinary Interfaces, Limits, and Open Development
papers.authors: Wanhong HUANG
papers.abstract: This concluding volume situates Generative Relational Economics within broader economic inquiry and articulates its future development as an open, historically revisable research programme. It consolidates research questions, empirical strategies, formal problems, institutional applications, and methodological priorities that can guide subsequent GRE research without converting the framework into a closed theoretical canon. The volume examines GRE's interfaces with neighboring domains including history, governance, law, political theory, education, ecology, artificial intelligence studies, social theory, and aesthetics. These relations are treated as disciplinary interfaces rather than as grounds for theoretical absorption. Concepts may travel across domains only through explicit translation, and apparently general structures may prove domain-specific when confronted with different objects, histories, normative problems, or evidential conditions. A sustained analysis of limitations addresses ontological, epistemic, representational, relational, historical, formal, empirical, value-theoretical, power-theoretical, justice-related, application-oriented, AI-era, and domain-transfer problems. The volume also identifies failure modes, normative underdetermination, conditions that would count against particular GRE claims, and circumstances under which substantial theoretical revision would be required. The concluding account therefore understands GRE as an open research programme whose development depends upon empirical confrontation, theoretical dialogue, preservation of uncertainty and negative results, explicit disciplinary boundaries, and continuing re-epistemization. The programme's continuity lies in its capacity for disciplined revision rather than in the preservation of an immutable theoretical system.

papers.title: Automated Audio Effect Classification for Educational Speech Quality Assessment Using Machine Learning
papers.authors: Bagaskoro Saputro

papers.title: Citizen Oversight for Safe AI Frontiers
papers.authors: AGM FOX
papers.abstract: Background Summary Public opinion of artificial intelligence systems and the frontier labs that develop them are at an all time low, with serious concerns about the pace and scope of this powerful technology that is rapidly advancing without community standards, laws, regulators, or transparent processes. The technical knowledge required to draft meaningful legislation, or even to establish legal guardrails, far exceeds the competencies represented within the three branches of government. Indeed, the government's concerns about AI appear to be limited to economic impacts, and the promise of adding over $10T to America's economy with nearly 4% year-over-year GDP growth over the next four years., That translates to a 30% jump in today’s GDP estimate ($32.3T) driven by a national economy with markets running about twice as hot as their current historic highs. Political leaders and economists view these projections as justifications for the risk that AI poses, despite dire warnings from industry stakeholders. Despite corporate attempts to control the public narrative and hide behind IP laws, the public continues to learn of new breaches and threats that reinforce concerns that frontier labs do not actually have full control over the systems they have built. The ability of agentic tools to penetrate local systems built on cloud services poses a global threat, while even the most responsive government interventions are reactionary, at best. Even so, the lack of transparency involved in all aspects of this black box tech have forced victims of AI breach to seek remedy from the violators themselves. The very companies that are creating these crises are not only free from legal accountability for the harms they cause to clients around the world, but also appear to be free from accountability even within the frontier labs that develop them. Human Agency in AI Systems This century will be defined by how civilization engages with artificial intelligence. The pace of significant albeit poorly documented updates to existing AI models, the aggressive drive toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) models, and the emergence of socio-cultural behaviors by agent groups demand an equally robust human response that preserves the role of public choice in the use of these tools, as well as the individual rights guaranteed by the Constitution. This proposal outlines a pilot project to identify, test, and refine civil society engagement models that have been developed for other adversarial cross-sectoral contexts and proven to deliver mutually beneficial outcomes. This investigation will explore a set of pre-determined civilian oversight frameworks for suitability within defined AI-in-society policy concerns. For example, law enforcement surveillance systems, such as Flock Safety, must be subject to civilian scrutiny; however, accessible oversight mechanisms for the lay public have not yet been developed. Public oversight is left to the public to self-organize with no particular coordinated efforts to guide them. Indeed, the vast majority of oversight resources that have been developed exist for the use of industry to track benchmarks and improve performance. Current government guidance, scant as it is, is likewise dedicated to benefiting frontier labs. This proposal describes a novel framework for public assessment of AI systems, to be implemented before and during the use of AI tools and services by public institutions, including local government. The results of this pilot phase will determine whether and how the project should be broadened and scaled into a more comprehensive, robust framework with policy recommendations and economic analysis. Methodology, Milestones, Outputs This mixed-methods study will begin with a comparative analysis of a defined set of reference frameworks. The set of frameworks will be piloted by civilian volunteer groups reviewing real use cases. The pilot will produce metrics inherent to each framework’s evaluation criteria, which will then be used to further develop an assessment rubric that enables stakeholders choice. Phase I: Comparative Analysis of Reference Frameworks This phase of the project will provide an historical overview of each oversight mechanism in its original context, and map it to the AI context that will be tested in the pilot phase. Reference Frameworks -Citizen Review Boards (CRB) are citizen-led watchdog groups that engage in issues of particular concern to these self-selecting groups. -Consensus Review is an expert-based committee process that invites the public to hear expert testimony and witness information gathering sessions, but the deliberative process is conducted in closed session. This approach may be suitable for preparing significant policy decisions by public institutions and/or governments. -Danish Consensus Conference is a participatory model that enjoins citizens to consider controversial STEM issues and report their policy recommendations to the government and the public. The goal is to form a consensus that strikes a balance between competing stakeholder demands, known risks and potential harms to society, and economic benefits. This framework is particularly apt for public assessment of large, high tech systems for the purpose of policy guidance. Nonetheless, it is not a model familiar to most American stakeholders and may not be appropriate for all AI-in-society deliberations. -Indigenous Data Sovereignty Governance (IDSG) is an emerging framework situated in the human rights principle of self determination. It is an ethical process that calls on place-based community standards, norms, and traditions. It can entail exceptionally time consuming deliberation that results in the establishment of long-term, communitywide rules. -Institutional Review Board (IRB) is a well-established expert-based committee process that exists primarily to reduce risk and limit exposure to the institution by confirming that the plans and processes involved in the activity comply with laws and regulations. It extends protections to individuals and communities indirectly by restricting activities to the confines of broadly applicable legal rules. This approach may be particularly suitable for controversial policy actions, where watchdog organizations are viewed as adversarial actors, rather than community partners. -Jury Deliberation is a type of peer review that allows oversight entities to review evidence and ponder narrow questions in private or closed sessions. Jury decisions must be unanimous and can be appealed. Juries are not required to justify their decisions. This approach might be preferable when sensitive data is involved. -Situated Learning/Community Management (COP) is a Community of Practice (COP) framework that fosters peer-based skilling, adoption of best practices, co-creation of design and development, and information dissemination. This is likely to be a strong mechanism for project planning and early-stage implementation of public AI systems. -Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) is an arbiter-led approach that allows community actors to register grievances, state their trustworthy goals, define for themselves the role that they want to play in the design or oversight of trustworthy AI systems, and reset with a restorative justice engagement framework going forward. -Unstructured Athenian (UA) model, which provides stakeholders a pathway to identify bias outcomes and issue tickets for resolution by administrators within a predetermined timeframe. This is likely to appeal to communities working in close partnership with AI stakeholders, for example where large data centers are welcomed and/or AI systems are perceived as meeting a defined need in service to the local community. Phase II: Pilot Studies Phase II will test known frameworks that have been extensively studied, documented, reviewed, and refined with proven best practices over years and even decades. These reference frameworks represent a variety of input and deliberation processes that communities can select according to needs and capacities. Volunteers will select an oversight mechanism of their choice and join other members of the group to review a real use case that is relevant to their competency and/or community. The goal is to study the effectiveness of the process itself, not the individual or group dynamics, per se. For example, an oversight goal might include “To determine the suitability of Flock Safety devices in a defined rural geolocation.” The pilot group will be organized according to the standards of their assigned oversight mechanism, e.g., Jury, and given instructions for deliberation. Each volunteer will complete a survey instrument designed to capture metrics about the effectiveness of the process in the context of assessing AI in society, weaknesses and strengths of the mechanism to deliver the desired goal(s), and general feedback to describe flaws and suggest improvements. Phase III: Development of AI Oversight Mechanisms The goal of the Phase III is twofold: (1) to apply findings from the set of reference frameworks toward the development of public oversight mechanisms that are suitable for monitoring AI in society; and (2) development of decision tooling that will enable the lay public to choose an appropriate framework that fits the specific need, capacity, competency, and context. It is entirely possible that an AI tool will be implemented in the development of this tooling. Phase IV: Findings and Recommendations While reflexion is built into the methodology and data will be produced and analyzed throughout the study, the pilot phase will conclude after at least one set of metrics and survey instruments has been collected for each reference framework. A preliminary report will be produced to report findings with the option for further investigation and framework development, as warranted.

papers.title: Intraoperative processed electroencephalography patterns and postoperative delirium and cognitive dysfunction in adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prognostic factor studies
papers.authors: Aaron Castanera-Duro, Maria Jose Cordero Rochet, Marc Vives
papers.abstract: Protocol of a systematic review and meta-analysis of prognostic factor studies. We will identify which intraoperative processed electroencephalography (EEG) patterns (cumulative time with bispectral index below 40, burst suppression, bispectral index variability, interhemispheric asymmetry and spectral power) are associated with postoperative delirium and postoperative cognitive dysfunction in adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia, and estimate their added predictive value beyond clinical risk factors. We will search MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science and CENTRAL; two reviewers will independently select studies, extract data (CHARMS-PF) and assess risk of bias (QUIPS). Adjusted estimates will be pooled with random-effects meta-analysis where appropriate, and certainty will be rated with GRADE for prognostic factors. This review is registered on OSF because PROSPERO does not currently accept prognostic reviews.

papers.title: AI-Recruitment And Talent Analytics System
papers.authors: Mrs. Hemalatha M, Ms. Sakshi Mahesh Mirji, Ms. Sanjana, Mr. Braham Abhijat Singh, Mr. Priyanshu Kumar
papers.abstract: Recruitment is an important function of Human Resource Management, but traditional recruitment processes become difficult to manage when organizations receive a large number of job applications.Manual resume screening, subjective interview evaluation and limited use of recruitment data can increase the time required for hiring and may introduce inconsistency and bias into candidate selection.This paper presents an AI Recruitment and Talent Analytics System that combines Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine learning(ML),Natural Language Processing(NLP), and data analytics to support an intelligent recruitment workflow.The proposed system automates major stages of recruitment, beginning with candidate registration and resume submission.NLP-based resume processing is used to extract skills, education, certifications, and work experience.Candidate profiles are compared with job requirements to support candidate-job matching and ranking.The system also proposes an AI-based interview module for evaluating technical knowledge, communication abilities, behavioral responses, and overall performance.A recruitment analytics dashboard provides candidate rankings, hiring insights, reports, and decision-support information.The current prototype focuses on the landing page, authentication interface, candidate dashboard, HR dashboard, and AI interview interface, providing a foundation for subsequent backend, database, AI/ML, and predictive analytics integration.

papers.title: Inglese: A research agenda
papers.authors: Silvia Ranfagni, Massimo Rosati, Kristian Gianassi
papers.abstract: Purpose: the paper aims at understanding which major spheres of the authentic entrepreneur are impacted by AI and develop a research agenda on these. Design/methodology/approach: based on fundamental principles of authentic entrepreneurship and AI’s impact on it, a semi-systematic literature review applying inductive thematic analysis on 55 academic works has been developed, giving space for a wide discussion and a research agenda for future studies. Findings: four major spheres with significant implications for authentic entrepreneurs have been identified: crafting the authentic self in the AI-driven age; the social construction of authenticity in AI-mediated contexts; authentic entrepreneurial agency in human-AI co-creation; relational climate and shared intent in AI-mediated entrepreneurship. Practical and social implications: authentic entrepreneurs need to provide an answer to the transition opened up in these domains in order to preserve their authenticity. Originality of the study: the article enriches the scant resources found in the specific intersection under inquiry. Disclosing new domains that need investigation, it offers some interesting insights for practitioners on which aspects to take into account in AI adoption, for researchers where to direct their focus.
