papers.title: Digital media and the transformation of ecoliteracy: A systematic and bibliometric review
papers.authors: Gianfranco Rubino
papers.abstract: Social media and ecoliteracy increasingly intersect as digital platforms come to function as structuring environments in which environmental awareness and identities take shape. Despite substantial empirical output, the field lacks an integrated mapping of its intellectual architecture, thematic trajectories, and methodological evolution. This study addresses that gap through a combined systematic and bibliometric review of 235 peer-reviewed documents indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, following the PRISMA 2020 protocol and applying a mixed-methods design that integrates bibliometric mapping via VOSviewer with inductive-deductive thematic coding. The analysis documents a marked growth in scholarly production over the past decade, peaking in 2024, the last complete publication year covered by the review, with keyword co-occurrence mapping revealing a temporal shift from foundational concerns with environmental awareness and school-based education toward recent concentrations around artificial intelligence, machine learning, sentiment analysis, and platform-specific dynamics on TikTok and Instagram. Five higher-order thematic domains are identified: public environmental awareness through digital media; green consumption and value systems; ecoliteracy in education; platformization and algorithmic logics; and eco-identity and sustainable tourism. The review also maps the journals, institutional contributors, and citation structures that organize this interdisciplinary field. Across the reviewed literature, digital environments operate as socio-technical settings that co-construct ecoliteracy, conditioned by platform architectures, algorithmic governance, and the political economies of digital capitalism. The review provides an empirical and theoretical foundation for future research connecting environmental education, media infrastructures, and civic engagement in the digital age.

papers.title: Towards Reliable Prosody Detection in Teaching Practical Phonetics: A Sustainable Digital Approach
papers.authors: Olesya M. Tolstykh, Alexey Svatov, Tamara Oshchepkova
papers.abstract: This research focuses on providing quality education to specialists in the field of linguistic studies, phonology, theoretical and practical phonetics by creating an innovative automated service which can ease the linguists endeavour to transcribe and examine suprasegmental features of human speech prosody. The authors attempted to design a docker-based architecture for prosody labelling. The pre-processing stage compiled 47 manually marked recordings, ten of which were annotated at clip level. The data-processing stage produced a corpus of 882 denoised, labelled clips via librosa , noisereduce , and Label Studio. The model selection stage compared 4909 scikit-learn configurations and 120 CNN configurations. The strongest classical approach (Random Forest) achieved an accuracy of 0.373, whereas the best CNN scored 0.455 against a majority-class baseline of 0.316. Per-class analysis showed that the classical models performed poorly across most intonation categories, assigning 94% of predictions to the two most frequent classes. These results indicate early-stage prototype performance rather than a validated evaluation and are not yet sufficient to support reliable automatic intonation marking. Having recognised the prototype limitations, the researchers have scheduled a roadmap for improving the tool. The suggested model applies the principles of machine learning to automatically generate prosodic analysis that extends beyond individual sound segments and reflects suprasegmental aspects of prosody including rhythm, intonation, and phrasal stress.

papers.title: Examining clinicians’ approaches to discussing weight during routine diabetes care: an observational study
papers.authors: Justin A. Dower, Carolina Gonzalez Lopez, Megan E. Branda, ANNE W. CAMP, Alissa S. Chen, Víctor M. Montori, Mario Ochoa-Prieto, Kasia J. Lipska
papers.abstract: Weight management is an essential part of diabetes care, but discussing weight and weight loss in the office remains a challenge. To determine how clinicians approach this potentially stigmatizing topic during routine primary care, we analyzed videorecorded clinical encounters from a randomized clinical trial that compared usual care with and without an agenda setting kit intervention (QBSAFE, NCT05553912). Using an ad hoc codebook, two researchers reviewed and independently coded video recordings of primary care visits with eligible patients with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≥ 8%, fluency in English or Spanish, and BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 ). The codebook noted whether the patient or the clinician initiated weight-related conversation, words used to describe weight, the type of conversation that occurred, and any interventions recommended. Binary and multinomial mixed models assessed the statistical significance of relationships between variables. Investigators coded 123 clinical encounters involving 47 male and 76 female patients with mean age 56, mean BMI 32 kg/m 2 , and mean HbA1c 10%. Weight was discussed in 48 encounters (39%), with clinicians initiating the conversation in 27 of these (56%). Clinicians frequently recommended dietary changes ( n = 21, 44%) and diabetes medications associated with weight loss ( n = 25, 52%). Bariatric surgery was not discussed. Of note, weight was significantly more likely to be discussed with patients on GLP-1 receptor agonists compared to those not on these medications ( p = 0.03). Clinicians did not use the terms “overweight” and “obesity,” favoring a discussion of “weight.” Weight conversations occurred in less than half of routine clinical encounters in our study, which were focused mostly on medication use and lifestyle changes and avoided potentially stigmatizing language. While the use of less stigmatizing language appears to be improving the quality of clinical encounters, additional studies are needed to define interventions that will increase the frequency of weight conversations in diabetes care. This study makes use of data from the QBSAFE trial (NCT05553912), registered on September 26, 2022 with the United States National Library of Medicine’s ClinicalTrials.gov.

papers.title: Partnering With Generative Artificial Intelligence for Quantitative Data Analysis in Nursing Research: A Practical Workflow for Ethical Collaboration
papers.authors: Gina M. Gehling, Lacey W. Heinsberg
papers.abstract: Reproducibility and replicability are our scientific and ethical mandate, and the foundation of trust in nursing science and research. Both rest on transparent documentation of how data were actually analyzed. The rising use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in research intersects with this mandate, with the potential to either support or undermine it, yet practical guidance for conducting GenAI-assisted quantitative analysis remains limited. This gap is particularly relevant for nurse scientists, who increasingly work with complex, biologically-informed datasets spanning genomics, symptoms, and patient outcomes. To address this gap, we present a practice-based guide for partnering with GenAI in quantitative data analysis in nursing research, grounded in a nursing-focused genomic research example. We cover GenAI literacy spanning three dimensions (technical, practical, and ethical) and a two-phase workflow for human-GenAI collaboration spanning planning and pre-specification through code development, formal analysis, translation, and human review and disclosure of GenAI use. The core principle is using GenAI as a tool, not a decision-maker, as scientific integrity requires that humans retain interpretive authority. We further propose a synthetic-data-first approach as a privacy safeguard. We illustrate these concepts through a genetics example, though the principles and workflow generalize to many quantitative nursing research contexts.

papers.title: Human or AI-generated voiceover for chemotherapy education video? Evidence from knowledge and practice tests improvement among cancer patients by pharmacists
papers.authors: Dinda Monika Nusantara Ratri, Putu D Antari, Febriansyah Nur Utomo, Desak M R D Dewi
papers.abstract: BackgroundEducational videos play a crucial role in enhancing healthcare delivery. Developing an educational video designed to improve patient understanding of catastrophic treatment. During the video's creation, two voiceover methods were employed: human voices and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated voices. To date, the impact of voice-over origin-whether human or AI-on patient knowledge acquisition remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. This study aimed to assess the differences in knowledge and practice scores among cancer patients exposed to educational video materials about chemotherapy, comparing human voice with AI-generated voice narrations.MethodsA total of 129 cancer patients participated in this study. Designed as a case-control study, participants were divided into three groups: a control group, a group receiving videos with human voice narrations, and a group receiving videos with AI-generated voice narrations. All participants completed a questionnaire assessing their understanding of chemotherapy. A three-group quantitative comparative analysis was conducted, focusing on topics such as administration procedures, treatment goals, and the management of adverse drug reactions.Key findingsBoth educational videos with human- and AI-generated voiceovers should be incorporated into the oncology healthcare system due to their effectiveness in improving understanding of treatment. Notably, educational videos featuring human-voice narration consistently enrich knowledge and attitude scores among cancer patients across all assessed chemotherapy topics.ConclusionThe educational videos, whether in human or AI voices, were effective in increasing cancer patients' knowledge and attitudes across all key topics. There was a sustained trend toward human-voice videos in knowledge and attitudes among cancer patients; therefore, the human educational video showed significant improvement in understanding of chemotherapy administration, goals, and adverse drug reactions. Although there was no difference between human and AI voice education, trends toward combining human voice with realistic scenario videos should be considered to facilitate deeper patient understanding.

papers.title: Prognostication in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Narrative Review of Pre-Diagnosis and Functional Outcomes
papers.authors: Amber R. Vocelle, Erik Ensrud, Ileana M. Howard
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a very heterogeneous disease, yet some of the most common questions received by physicians in the ALS clinic are "how much time do I have?" and "what can I expect to happen next?" This line of inquiry is not strictly limited to patients; clinicians also need an idea of prognosis to appropriately plan for treatment decisions and prepare the patient and caregiver for future care needs. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on prognostic indicators in ALS, organized across three temporal phases: factors preceding diagnosis, factors present at diagnosis, and factors emerging after diagnosis. Pre-diagnosis predictors include age at onset, sex, socioeconomic status, genetic background, premorbid Body Mass Index (BMI) and nutritional status, and comorbid disease. At diagnosis, clinical phenotype and site of onset, diagnostic delay, baseline Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Functional Rating Score-Revised (ALSFRS-R) and forced vital capacity, cognitive involvement, fluid biomarkers, and electrophysiologic measures carry prognostic weight. Post-diagnosis, the trajectory is refined by the rate of ALSFRS-R decline, serial respiratory measures, and weight loss, and is actively modified by clinical interventions including noninvasive ventilation, enteral nutrition, disease-modifying therapy, and multidisciplinary care. Notably, quality of life does not track with physical decline, consistent with the disability paradox described in other severe neurological conditions. For neurorehabilitation, these indicators support a shift from reactive to anticipatory practice: timing equipment provision, communication support, respiratory intervention, and goals-of-care discussions to the predicted trajectory rather than to established deficit. Refinement of prognostic models may also improve stratification in ALS clinical trials.

papers.title: From sensing to transforming: The discursive trajectory of AI and the limited prominence of human-centered engagement themes
papers.authors: Miloš Petković, Maribel Labrado-Antolín
papers.abstract: Background Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption transformed work structures after 2022, raising psychological safety concerns as efficiency priorities overshadow human-centered employee wellbeing. Objective This longitudinal study investigates how engagement is framed as a corporate communication strategy in Standard & Poor's (S&P) 500 technology firms during early large-scale AI adoption (2022–2024). Methods Using IRaMuTeQ, 150 S&P 500 corporate reports (2022–2024) underwent Reinert's Descending Hierarchical Classification, Correspondence Factorial Analysis, and similarity network analysis, employing chi-square ( χ 2 ) marker filtering. Results Findings reveal a three-stage trajectory mapping onto dynamic capabilities: initial sensing (2022), platform seizing (2023), and process transformation (2024). However, human-centered engagement language (meaningfulness, safety, vigor) remained structurally marginalized, failing to form a stable lexical cluster and framing participation strictly through technical integration. Conclusions Public discourse serves as a proxy for enacting dynamic capabilities. Practically, HR leaders should prospectively audit AI communications to ensure technical efficiency narratives do not displace human-centered and psychological safety registers.

papers.title: The cognitive cost of artificial intelligence on ageing workforce: Analyzing age-related effects on mental workload and task performance in computer-based environment
papers.authors: Nurul Izzah Abd Rahman, Muhammad NI Ismail, Siti Azfanizam Ahmad, Siti Anom Ahmad
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe current world demographic reality necessitates a critical re-evaluation of how technological tools, specifically those powered by artificial intelligence (AI), interact with the varying cognitive profiles of a ageing workforce.ObjectivesThe objective of this study is to evaluate the spatial distribution of mental workload and objective task performance across AI-assisted and non-AI-assisted conditions in a computer-based environment.MethodAn experimental study involving 30 older workers compared standardized office tasks under non-AI-assisted (Segment A) and AI-assisted (Segment B) conditions. Mental workload was assessed using NASA-TLX, Heart Rate Variability (HRV), and EEG-based Beta-Alpha Ratios (BAR) across frontal (F3, F4), parietal (P3, P4), and occipital (O1, O2) regions. Performance in document preparation (Task 1) and arithmetic operations (Task 2) was evaluated using percentage-based accuracy, efficiency, and overall performance scores.ResultAI intervention improved overall task performance but was accompanied by an apparent performance-workload paradox, whereby enhanced output coincided with increased neurophysiological and systemic strain. Descriptively, NASA-TLX Overall Perceived Workload decreased from 54.05 to 44.91 during complex tasks, while HRV declined by 48.68% in Task 1, indicating acute autonomic strain. EEG revealed increased BAR in the frontal (F3: 29.2%), parietal (P3), and occipital (O1) regions, suggesting heightened attentional and sensory demands associated with monitoring and verifying AI-generated suggestions.ConclusionAI redistributes rather than eliminates workload, increasing executive verification and visual monitoring demands. Future AI systems for older adults should prioritize cognitive ergonomics to minimize executive burden and sensory strain, preventing premature cognitive fatigue while enhancing task performance and supporting sustainable human-AI interaction.

papers.title: Exploring rehabilitation therapists’ knowledge and perspectives on the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for persons post-stroke
papers.authors: Elena V. Donoso Brown, Min Hun Lee, Kasey E. Stepansky, Hannah Fairchild, Kaia MIKULA, Mia Del Vecchio, Robert Halyama
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the clinical work of rehabilitation therapists in post stroke rehabilitation has the potential to transform their work performance, habits, and routines. The impact could potentially enhance integration of assessment/data analysis, personalizing therapies, documentation, and promoting home program adherence.ObjectiveThis study assesses occupational and physical therapists' current perspectives on AI/ML in post-stroke clinical rehabilitation and examines perceived barriers to potential application of AI/ML in their clinical work.MethodsThis mixed methods study includes quantitative survey data collected pre/post an AI/ML educational webinar, as well as qualitative focus group analysis that includes therapist attitudes and experiences with AI/ML, practical applications to using AI/ML, as well as the difficulties associated. The recruited therapists include occupational and physical therapy practitioners from the United States and Asia. Individuals included in the study had to have a caseload of 30% persons with stroke.ResultsFour key themes emerged from qualitative analysis: 1) current clinical work practice and identified gaps, 2) current therapists' perceptions of AI/ML, 3) perceived future of AI/ML in clinical work practices and 4) steps needed for implementation. Survey data reporting frequencies of technology use and AI/ML perceptions are integrated into qualitative findings.ConclusionsTherapists can articulate potential future uses for AI/ML technology in post-stroke rehabilitation, however, remain uncertain about when, how, and at what cost utilization will be supported in clinical work environments. Therapists desire education and support to utilize the evolving technologies in practice.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence adaptation in the future healthcare workforce: Evaluating literacy and anxiety levels
papers.authors: Pinar Arpacı
papers.abstract: Background Increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical workflows necessitates assessing how future healthcare professionals adapt to these technologies. Objectıve This study aims to determine the artificial intelligence literacy and anxiety levels of students at a Vocational School of Health Services (VSHS) and to analyze the factors influencing these levels. Methods This cross-sectional and descriptive-predictive study invited 800 associate degree healthcare students, resulting in a final sample of 545 participants (response rate: 68.12%). Instruments included a Sociodemographic Form, the AI Literacy Scale (AILS), and the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS). Results The mean age of participants was 20.41 ± 4.07 years. While 55.6 % of students reported partial knowledge of AI, only 44.4 % reported active use of AI-supported tools. In univariate analyses, gender ( p = .005 , η 2 = 0.015 ), prior AI knowledge ( p = .002 ), and active AI application use ( p = .007 ) showed statistically significant differences in anxiety levels. Total AI literacy was weakly negatively correlated with AI anxiety ( r = − 0.20 , p < .001 ). Multivariable regression analysis confirmed that the established model significantly predicted anxiety ( F 7 , 537 = 10.387 , p < .001 ), explaining 11.9 % of the total variance ( R 2 = .119 , Adjusted R 2 = .108 ). Within the multivariable model, cognitive literacy subdimensions—Awareness ( β = − .143 , p = .002 ), Evaluation ( β = − .116 , p = .027 ), and Ethics ( β = − .093 , p = .046 )—and male gender ( β = − .188 , p < .001

papers.title: Task-oriented and relational perceptions of ChatGPT among generation Z students: Implications for higher education and preparation for AI-enabled work
papers.authors: Kacper Sieciński, Marian Oliński
papers.abstract: Generative AI is becoming embedded in higher education and knowledge work, yet students may assign different forms of usefulness to conversational AI. This study examines how Generation Z students perceive the current and potential usefulness of ChatGPT across seven functional roles. Data were collected from April to June 2024 through an online survey of 409 students from different disciplines at multiple Polish higher education institutions using a geographically diversified, non-probability convenience sampling strategy. Medians, quartiles, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to analyse ordinal responses. Task-oriented roles, particularly information search and idea generation, were rated more highly than relational roles, while all roles received higher ratings for potential than for current usefulness. By integrating multiple roles within task-oriented and relational dimensions, the study extends role-based understanding of student-AI interaction. The findings suggest implications for AI literacy and responsible human-AI collaboration in higher education, while remaining limited to students’ perceptions.

papers.title: Socratic, Artifact-Gated Generative AI Scaffolding in a 6E Inquiry Unit: A Clustered Quasi-Experiment in Elementary Students’ Computational Thinking
papers.authors: Yu-Chih Huang, Cheng‐Hsuan Li
papers.abstract: Open-ended computational thinking (CT) inquiry challenges one teacher to support learners progressing at different rates. This clustered quasi-experiment evaluated TALPer, a generative-AI tutor providing student-initiated, artifact-contingent Socratic prompts during a six-lesson 6E unit. Ten intact Grade 3 classes in Taiwan (N = 229) completed the same curriculum, tasks, teacher, platform, and instructional time. Conditions differed in a bundled scaffolding configuration involving source, delivery modality, initiation, privacy, and artifact requirements. A two-level model controlling for pretest CT estimated an adjusted posttest difference favoring TALPer ( B = 4.05, SE = 1.58, Wald 95% CI [0.94, 7.15], p = .011; sensitivity p = .034; Hedges’ g = 0.52). Class-clustered analyses found no Holm-adjusted difference on any Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscale; Perceived Choice had the largest positive estimate ( B = 0.27, cluster-adjusted SE = 0.12, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.55], p = .061, pHolm = .306; Hedges’ g = 0.38). The Condition × Pretest interaction was nonsignificant ( B = −0.109, SE = 0.125, 95% CI [-0.354, 0.137], p = .385). Descriptive coding of 101 matched responses showed different distributions of expected and planned AI-use orientations; no inferential transition test was conducted. Findings provide preliminary evidence concerning the bundled intervention but do not isolate component contributions.

papers.title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence by Psychology Graduate Students in the United States
papers.authors: Jonathan M. Golding, Mary Beth McGavran, Leigha Rose, Nathaniel Luke Phillips, Donald R. Lynam, Anne M. Lippert, Joshua D. Miller
papers.abstract: Background Although developed only recently, generative artificial intelligence (AI) applications for everyday use (e.g., ChatGPT) have become part of university life. The academy must navigate AI use in graduate education within several domains (coursework, teaching, research, clinical activities). Objective Given the growing impact of AI applications in graduate education, we investigated graduate students’ use of and perceptions of these applications. Method Psychology clinical and nonclinical graduate students across the US answered questions about their use and perceptions of AI applications in five domains (coursework, teaching, research, personal life, and clinical activities). Results Graduate students used AI in all domains, although use varied by domain. The greatest use was in teaching, and the lowest was for clinical activities. Overall, the study found few significant differences in AI use between clinical and nonclinical students. Conclusions Graduate students use AI in various domains. The use of AI varies by domain and is not always as high as that reported for undergraduates. Teaching Implications The use of AI in various domains of graduate training should lead educators to determine how best to incorporate AI use in graduate training programs.

papers.title: Gendered Perceptions and the Use of Generative AI in Academia: An Experimental Vignette Study
papers.authors: Cinzia Calluso, Valentina Iacopino, Anna Piazza
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the very nature of work, yet its social meaning and evaluative implications—particularly for women—remain underexplored. Although existing research has mainly examined GenAI adoption, use, and algorithmic bias, less is known about how the use of GenAI shapes how individuals are evaluated by others. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, Role Congruity Theory and techno‐feminism perspectives, this study examines how women's use of GenAI influences perceptions of competence and warmth in academia. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 experimental vignette design [gender*GenAI adoption*task type (teaching vs. research)] with 651 participants, we examine how evaluations vary by academic gender, GenAI adoption, and task domain (teaching vs. research). We find that GenAI adoption generally enhances perceived competence. Women, however, gain the most in research tasks, where technical skills challenge gendered expectations. Conversely, GenAI use reduces perceived warmth, disproportionately penalizing women, especially in research. These findings reveal a “double bind,” highlighting how GenAI adoption may reproduce and intensify gendered evaluative tradeoffs within academic prestige hierarchies and the need for institutional strategies to mitigate relational penalties while recognizing competence.

papers.title: AI ‐Driven Feedback on Bitewing Radiographic Technique: A Comparative Study of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Katharina Alves Rabelo, Laura Swinckels, Eduardo Luiz Delamare, Zhuoran Duan, Elvis Trinh, Yongpei Ma, Jinman Kim, Vesna Miletić
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Large language models (LLMs) can enhance learning engagement and accessibility, though their performance in dentistry is inconsistent. Bitewing radiographs are critical for caries detection but prone to diagnostic errors from operator positioning. This study compared the performance of four LLMs with reasoning capabilities, GPT o1, GPT o3-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash and Grok 3, in generating scenario-specific educational feedback from a structured textual format of bitewing radiographs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Ten positioning error scenarios were created by DMFR specialists. LLMs were evaluated using an original prompt (OP) and an engineered prompt (EP), resulting in a 4 × 2 LLM-by-prompt design. Each LLM was tested via its model-specific access mode: API or web interface. Eighty outputs were assessed by two DMFR specialists for detail, content, clarity and relevance using a 5-point Likert scale. Ordinal category-level scores were analysed using a cumulative link mixed-effects model, with LLM, prompt type, scenario group, assessment category and LLM × prompt as fixed effects, and scenario as a random intercept. RESULTS: The LLM-prompt interaction was significant, indicating prompt engineering affected models differently. GPT o3-mini had significantly lower odds of higher scores than Gemini 2.0 Flash, while EP reduced Grok 3 performance. Positioning error type influenced performance, with significant model-dependent differences across scenario groups. No significant LLM-assessment category interaction was observed, suggesting model differences did not vary across assessment categories. CONCLUSION: LLM-generated feedback varied by model, prompt design and positioning error type, but not consistently across assessment categories. Outputs require validation, model-specific prompt testing and specialist review before implementation.

papers.title: Negotiating rigor and quality in decolonizing management research
papers.authors: Nimruji Prasad Jammulamadaka
papers.journal: Qualitative Research in Organizations and Management An International Journal
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines and problematizes the issue of assessing quality and establishing rigour in decolonizing management research. Design/methodology/approach This paper is a viewpoint essay, a decolonizing critique of decolonising management writing and reviewing practices drawing upon my lived experiences as a teacher, author, reviewer and editor doing this research. Findings The paper introduces the idea of writing as intersubjective co-creation with the author and imagined readers/reviewers, and reviewer and imagined authors coming together to produce a piece of writing. I identify four problems with treating decolonizing management research as a paradigm. I suggest that incommensurabilities are at the level of cosmologies and not at the level of paradigms in the political project of decolonizing management and suggest four solutions drawing upon de Sousa Santos' ecology of knowledges. Research limitations/implications This introduces the idea of co-creation of writing and draws attention to the role of the imagined reviewer and imagined author. It alerts us to be conscious of paradigm incommensurabilities problem. It suggests four ways of understanding quality in decolonizing management research. Practical implications It helps the authors and reviewers be somewhat more conscious in stating their assumptions during the review process. It thereby works towards reducing the Eurocentric bias in research publishing. Originality/value This paper discusses a hitherto ignored topic – assessing and establishing rigour and quality in decolonizing management research. Drawing upon the works of de Sousa Santos on Epistemologies of the South and Gayatri Spivak's catachrestic reading, I write in first person.

papers.title: Citizens' perceptions of AI-enabled public services: a thematic analysis of “Julia”, the chatbot of the Rome Municipality
papers.authors: Gioia Maria Carrus, Silvia Testarmata, Alessandro Giosi
papers.journal: International Journal of Public Sector Management
papers.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how citizens perceive and discuss artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled public services, focusing on “Julia,” the AI-based chatbot launched by the Municipality of Rome. It examines online discussions, revealing sociotechnical tensions and discussing their implications for institutional legitimacy and public value in the context of local government digital transformation (DT). Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative approach based on the analysis of 610 citizen comments posted across the social media platforms of the Municipality of Rome and the Mayor. A thematic analysis was conducted to identify recurring patterns in how citizens interpret and evaluate the chatbot's introduction. An engagement analysis contextualized public interactions with chatbot-related posts across platforms. Findings The findings show that citizens interpret the chatbot not merely as a technological tool but as a symbolic representation of the public entity. Four main thematic dimensions emerged: (1) trust and mistrust toward institutions, (2) digital innovation and AI, (3) evaluation of public services and urban management and (4) political, economic and symbolic evaluations of the administration. These dimensions reflect the sociotechnical tensions associated with AI-enabled public services discussed in the literature. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on local government DT examining how citizens perceive AI-enabled public services and the associated dynamics through a critical dialogic accountability perspective.

papers.title: Bridging the Gap: What Sports Media Hiring Managers Actually Want from Journalism School Graduates
papers.authors: Adam Pitluk, Brian A. Petrotta, Jason Stamm
papers.abstract: The sports media industry has undergone seismic structural transformation over the past two decades, driven by the collapse of legacy newspaper models, the proliferation of digital platforms, and the emergence of artificial intelligence. This qualitative study examines what sports media hiring managers and editors actually require from recent journalism school graduates as they enter a rapidly evolving workforce. Drawing on semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 15 sports media professionals who self-identified as editors and/or publishers and who are affiliated with the Football Writers Association of America (FWAA) and the U.S. Basketball Writers Association (USBWA), this study employs a human capital theory framework to analyze the alignment, and the persistent misalignment, between what journalism programs produce and what the industry demands. Findings reveal four dominant themes: (1) passion and intrinsic motivation as non-negotiable hiring criteria; (2) the depreciation of formal credentials relative to demonstrated, verifiable work; (3) a widening deficit in source cultivation, relationship building, and reporting fundamentals among recent graduates; and (4) a growing demand for multimedia versatility and platform fluency. Implications for journalism education curricula, industry-academy collaboration, and the professional preparation of the next generation of sports media workers are discussed.

papers.title: Engagement in staff development for learning and teaching in higher education: experiences from a leadership perspective
papers.authors: Katy Dineen, Catherine O’Mahony, Sinéad Gallivan, Manon Kluijtmans, Bjørn Stensaker, Jonas Leschke, Nicoline Frølich, Thérèse Zhang
papers.journal: Perspectives Policy and Practice in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Staff development for learning and teaching in higher education institutions operates within a complex context, balancing between ‘tell from above’ in the form of evolving policy at institutional, national and European levels and ‘ask from below’ in the form of the needs and sense of ownership of university personnel involved in learning and teaching. Situated somewhere in between is a collection of actors with leadership responsibility in the context of learning and teaching who face the challenge of balancing these different expectations. In this article, we explore through focus groups the lived experience of actors responsible for educational change within the context of staff development in a sample of European higher education institutions. These findings highlight the strategic role of L&T leaders in fostering authentic engagement in staff development via transparent communication and co-creation.

papers.title: Cinematic in the Age of Automation: A Comparative Study of Google Veo 3.1 and Human-Directed Advertising Videos
papers.authors: Muhamad Reznu Firsyawardana, Rony Kurniawan Pratama, Rino Andreas, Siti Umaiyah, Septi Anggita Kriskartika
papers.abstract: The emergence of AI-based video generation tools marks a significant inflection point in the history of commercial advertising production. This study conducts an experimental comparative analysis between video advertisements produced through the Google Veo 3.1 model on the Google Flow platform and those crafted through conventional pre-production, production, and post-production workflows. Taking the Coca-Cola for Everyone commercial as a benchmark, the experiment systematically reconstructed seventeen shots using AI-driven text-to-video and image-to-video generation, documenting each stage of prompt engineering, iterative refinement, and output evaluation. Four principal findings emerge: the indispensability of visual image references for replication fidelity; the limited but meaningful role of structured JSON prompting in communicating multi-dimensional cinematic parameters; the dramatic cost advantage of a fixed AI subscription relative to conventional production budgets, before accounting for the researcher’s own prompting labor; and the conditional time efficiency of AI workflows, bounded by the complexity of the target content. Interpreted through Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovation Theory and grounded in recent scholarship on generative diffusion models, visual communication, and advertising esthetics, the findings indicate that, within this specific case and this specific tool, Google Veo 3.1 reconstructing a single, product-centric commercial using visual reference images, AI-assisted video generation currently occupies a position of growing utility for studio-aesthetic, product-centric content, while retaining measurable limitations in temporally complex, choreographically demanding sequences. These findings characterize this bounded case rather than AI video generation as a general category, and the reconstruction task itself, anchored throughout by visual references, likely represents a more favorable scenario for AI performance than original, brief-driven commercial production would provide. The study contributes to the emergent scholarly conversation on AI creative authorship, cinematic quality benchmarking, and the democratization of professional video production.

papers.title: How Does AI Literacy Relate to Pre-Service STEM Teachers’ AI Readiness? Insights from Mediational Analysis
papers.authors: Sunday Ogbu, Emmanuel Ifeanyi Orji, Ugorji Iheanachor Ogbonnaya
papers.abstract: Efforts to achieve widespread applications of AI in education depend, to a large extent, on teachers’ level of AI literacy (AIL), AI self-efficacy (AISE), Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK), and above all, the teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning. This study, therefore, examined AI literacy’s links with pre-service STEM teachers’ AI readiness (AIR), focusing majorly on the mediational roles of AISE and AI-TPACK. A quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional correlational survey, was employed and was led by six null hypotheses. This study involved 310 final-year pre-service STEM teachers who participated using a volunteer sampling approach from five public universities in southeastern Nigeria. Four adapted structured scales featuring AIL, AIR, AISE, and AI-TPACK served as the data collection tools. The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

papers.title: Change detection of task-relevant and task-irrelevant emotional faces: behavioural and ERP evidence
papers.authors: Xinyang Liu, Xueqiao Li, Anna Dadatskaja, Kairi Kreegipuu, Elisa Vuoriainen, Elina S. Kangas, Piia Astikainen
papers.abstract: Adaptive social interaction requires rapid detection of changes in facial expressions. Socio-emotional difficulties may alter this processing, but evidence from preclinical populations and the role of comorbid symptoms remain limited. Event-related potentials (ERPs), particularly amplitude modulations in N170, and P3 during change detection tasks, have been associated with predictive coding. However, their interpretation has been limited by the absence of adequate control tasks. We investigated ERPs (P1, N170, P3b) and behavioural responses to facial expression changes, as well as the effects of stress, depression, and anxiety. Sad and angry deviant faces were interspersed among neutral standard faces in both the task-relevant and task-irrelevant oddball contexts. Amplitude modulation (emotional-neutral) in the N170 and P3b was larger for task-relevant angry than sad faces. Based on the control task available for the task-irrelevant context, the ERP modulations could not be attributed to predictive coding. Findings of individual differences emerged only behaviourally: higher stress was linked to slower reactions to angry faces. Overall, the results indicate rapid processing of emotional faces, without evidence of predictive coding or robust effects of depressive or anxiety symptoms.

papers.title: From workload to verified learning: reframing ECTS for AI-rich assessment
papers.authors: Federico Pablo-Martí, Carlos Mir Fernández, Juan José de Lucio
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) weakens a practical assumption in the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS): that estimated student workload remains a credible proxy for learning when assessment evidence is interpretable. This conceptual article examines what follows when academic products are routinely produced through hybrid human–AI cognition. Drawing on Kane’s interpretation/use argument, assessment-security scholarship and recent work on GenAI in higher education, it reconstructs ECTS as an inferential system in which scores, generalisation, extrapolation and credit-awarding uses must all be warranted. The analysis shows that opaque take-home production can weaken each link: scoring may misread distributed authorship, generalisation becomes unstable, extrapolation to learning outcomes is less secure, and credit awards risk retaining administrative form without evidential force. The article proposes verified learning as a credit-level validity condition and specifies four safeguards: programme-level alignment, authentic transfer tasks, process visibility with declared AI use, and strategic controlled verification. It also identifies equity and governance conditions required for these safeguards to support, rather than undermine, comparability across ECTS-based institutions in AI-rich assessment environments. The contribution is to connect task-level assessment validity to credit legitimacy and to translate that connection into practical design and quality-assurance implications for European higher education policy.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence across the medical education continuum: institutional, learning, readiness and safety systems
papers.authors: Rushi Patel, Ceyhun Haziroglu, Akshith Ullal, Ahmed S. A. Soliman, Smriti Seshadri, Evelyn Efron, Ori Sela, Pranay Arora, Azra Bihorac
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering every stage of medical education, yet guidance for responsible integration remains limited. We synthesize evidence across undergraduate, graduate, and continuing medical education within institutional, learning, and readiness and safety systems. Integration should reflect task structure, verifiability, consequence, and oversight. Continuing medical education remains comparatively underdeveloped despite its importance for practicing physicians, who use clinical AI directly and shape trainee practices, institutional adoption, and responsible implementation.

papers.title: Performance of ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini 3, and copilot 2026 in answering chemistry course questions: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Hadigheh Dorri, Morteza Zahedy Gol, Karim Naraki, Mohsen Khosravi
papers.abstract: Chemistry, environmental health, and occupational health have historically developed in close collaboration. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of LLMs, in responding to a chemistry course questionnaire used in environmental and occupational health department for educational purposes. This was a cross-sectional study conducted in 2026. The study used a 50-item multiple-choice questionnaire, primarily in Persian with limited English terms and formulas, which was administered to LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini 3, and Copilot 2026). Performance was evaluated using confusion matrix analysis. Cochran`s Q test, McNemar`s test for pair-wise comparisons, and Point-biserial correlation were also conducted to further evaluate the study data. The LLMs presented mean sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.81, 0.29, and 0.68, respectively. Gemini 3 presented a high level of performance, achieving the highest sensitivity (0.85), specificity (0.56), and accuracy (0.80). ChatGPT-5.5 had the lowest sensitivity (0.76), while Copilot showed the lowest specificity (0.07) and an accuracy of 0.62. No significant correlations were found between performance and questionnaire characteristics; however, all models performed poorly on negatively framed items requiring identification of incorrect options. The study presented some preliminary insights on the performance of LLMs in chemistry-related questions. Further research is warranted.

papers.title: Young children’s knowledge of ChatGPT and its relationship with their achievement in english as a second language
papers.authors: Ali Ahmad Al‐Barakat, Rommel Mahmoud AlAli, Amal Aboras, Nada Ibrahim Alribdi, Ali Khalifa Atwa Abdullatif, Ashraf Mahrous Nour Zaher
papers.abstract: Abstract This study investigated young children’s (aged 7–8 years) knowledge of ChatGPT and its relationship with their achievement in English as a Second Language. The sample consisted of 255 third-grade young children from the Eastern Region of Saudi Arabia. A mixed-methods approach was employed, comprising a ChatGPT knowledge questionnaire assessing five dimensions: general knowledge, applied knowledge, awareness of risks and limitations, ethical knowledge, and self-assessment in using ChatGPT. Semi-structured interviews were conducted to gain deeper insights into young children’s understanding and experiences with the tool. The findings revealed that young children’s overall knowledge of ChatGPT was moderate, with relative strengths in general and practical knowledge. In contrast, awareness of risks and limitations, ethical knowledge, and self-assessment/confidence were relatively low. Regarding English achievement, young children demonstrated an acceptable level, with overall performance ranging between “Good” and “Very Good.” Furthermore, the results indicated a statistically significant positive relationship between young children’s ChatGPT knowledge and their English achievement. General and practical knowledge, together with self-assessment and confidence, showed the strongest effects, whereas knowledge of risks, limitations, and ethics had a weaker impact on academic performance. These findings highlight that enhancing both theoretical and practical knowledge of ChatGPT can directly support improved academic outcomes. Overall, increasing young children’s knowledge of ChatGPT can facilitate their language achievement. Integrating digital literacy education with the development of self-assessment and ethical awareness is essential for the responsible and effective use of AI tools in educational settings.

papers.title: Prevalence and impact of sarcopenic obesity at hospital admission according to ESPEN-EASO approach on functional status of older adults: results of a retrospective and prospective observational study
papers.authors: Gianluca Gortan Cappellari, Rocco Barazzoni, Nicola Veronese, Paolo De Colle, Giuseppe Castiglia, Matteo Bianchini, Carlo Cortese, Sabrina Rampazzo, A Rizza, Giovanni Zampieri, Michela Zanetti
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Sarcopenic obesity (SO) is associated with adverse outcomes. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of SO diagnosed using the ESPEN-EASO approach and its correlations with functional impairment in an acute geriatric setting. SUBJECTS/METHODS: Observational study including 453 older adults admitted to a Geriatric Unit. According to the ESPEN-EASO approach, patients were screened for obesity (BMI), assessed for handgrip strength (HGS, dynamometry), and body composition (bioimpedance analysis). SO was defined by low HGS, reduced relative to body weight skeletal muscle mass (SMM%), and increased relative fat mass (FM%). Screen-positive patients not meeting SO criteria were classified as obese (OB). Screen-negative patients with low SMM% and HGS were defined as sarcopenic (SARC); the remaining served as control (NS-NO). Functional status was investigated by IADL and by basal ADL collected at admission, during hospitalization, and at discharge and analyzed using trajectory modeling and univariate and multivariate adjusted models. RESULTS: Among enrolled patients (mean age: 84.9 ± 7.0 y, F: 236, 52.1%), 36 (7.9%) had SO, 65 (14.3%) OB, 98 (21.0%) SARC, and 254 (56.7%) NS-NO. In multivariate analyses (NS-NO as reference) only SO demonstrated an increased risk of impaired ADL at discharge while OB and SARC did not. Trajectory modeling confirmed an SO-specific association with functional impairment followed by lower ADL recovery. Age, malnutrition, and cognitive impairment were independently associated with reduced ADL at admission and at discharge and with IADL. CONCLUSIONS: Sarcopenic obesity is associated with a higher risk of poor ADL at discharge, emphasizing the importance of personalized obesity phenotyping in hospitalized older adults.

papers.title: Beware LLMs bearing gifts: hallucinations, satisfactory results, and student use of generative AI in the production of Mediterranean archaeology websites
papers.authors: Jody Michael Gordon
papers.abstract: Abstract Recently, an epistemic shift has occurred in classics pedagogy. First, the COVID pandemic forced students online. Then, large language model (LLM) chatbots appeared. These disruptions created a conundrum: how could research methods, reading and writing, and cross-cultural exploration be taught when students were tethered to LLM-accessible ‘cheating machines’? The solution was AI-assisted classics. This paper describes how AI-assisted classical history can be taught through a discussion of the ‘WHAM’ (Web Design, HTML, and the Archaeology of the Mediterranean) project. WHAM is a website-building classroom assignment developed to teach students in the Computer Science and Society major at Wentworth Institute of Technology (Boston, MA, USA; www.wit.edu ) how to utilize digital tools to explicate humanities data. Students create a website from the HTML code up focused on a Mediterranean archaeological region and are taught to use LLMs critically, both for writing HTML code and for ideating web design features. In the process, students learn how LLMs must be approached cautiously since they can both hallucinate and offer satisfactory work that should be improved. Finally, the paper suggests that LLMs can provide students with a starting place for digital projects that challenge them to engage with the classical world’s history and material culture.

papers.title: Message scrutiny and claim verification: Changes in preadolescent reasoning about disinformation across AI-supported instruction
papers.authors: Layda Lopez-Lora, Esteban Vázquez Cano
papers.abstract: Digital information environments expose preadolescents to misleading content before verification routines are fully developed. This study examined pre–post patterns in disinformation evaluation across a two-session instructional sequence combining media-literacy orientation, guided news-analysis activities, researcher supervision, and interaction with Pimpoyo, a generative-AI chatbot using Socratic questioning and a ZPD-inspired rationale. The sample comprised 152 Spanish students aged 10–14 years. Longitudinal evidence came only from the pre–post group (n = 80); a baseline-only reference group (n = 72) contributed baseline information. The primary outcome comprised 24 measurement-equivalent indicators expressed on a 0–25 scale. Indicator-level changes were differentiated: the clearest increases clustered around cues available within the focal message, including sensationalism, alarmist format, writing quality, tone/style, and timeliness, whereas triangulation/lateral reading did not change reliably and externally oriented verification remained mixed. The overall composite increased from M = 11.90 to M = 15.90, t(79) = 6.18, p < .001, d_z = 0.69. These indicator-level patterns are exploratory and are not formal comparisons between psychometric reasoning domains. Self-perceived competence changed, whereas perceived task difficulty did not; these secondary findings do not demonstrate metacognitive recalibration. Because only one group was followed longitudinally and the sequence bundled several instructional components, observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI, Socratic prompting, or any single component. The findings identify a potentially important distinction between focal-message scrutiny and external verification for future controlled research.

papers.title: Toward closing the loop: safe autonomy, validation, and trust in AI-driven nonthermal food processing
papers.authors: Muhammad Talha Afraz, Yuhuan Geng, Wenhao Xiao, Muhammad Faisal Manzoor, Rana Muhammad Aadil, Xin-An Zeng, Zhong Han

papers.title: Automatic grammar extension for online multi-stroke recognition of hand-drawn semi-structured sketches
papers.authors: S. Serre, Islam Barchouch, Nathalie Girard, Éric Anquetil
papers.abstract: This article presents an improvement to IntuiSketch, an intelligent tutoring system for pen-based tablets. The goal is to address the challenges of multi-stroke analysis in the context of online semi-structured sketch recognition. IntuiSketch relies on two engines: a supervision engine and a recognition engine. This article focuses on the latter, which is based on the Context-Driven Constraint Multiset Grammar (CD-CMG), combined with fuzzy logic and the Evolve classifier (which learns from a few examples) to recognize handwritten sketches in real time. While the recognition of mono-stroke structured sketches has already been successfully addressed, in practice, semi-structured sketches are often created using multiple strokes to draw an entity. Therefore, the number of strokes composing an entity becomes unpredictable. Moreover, in a learning context, sketch reproduction generates significant variability not only in the number of strokes but also in the shape of each stroke. To overcome these difficulties, we propose a hybrid recognition approach that automatically extends the CD-CMG formalism to support online multi-stroke analysis, without manual redefinition of the domain rules. The refined IntuiSketch system is evaluated using anatomical sketches to demonstrate its ability to accurately interpret multi-stroke sketches. This work highlights the adaptability of IntuiSketch to the diverse drawing behaviors of students, reinforcing its applicability in real-world educational contexts.

papers.title: From revision to learning transfer: Self- and socially shared-regulated pathways in AI-assisted feedback
papers.authors: Shijun Cindy Chen, Conrad Borchers, Christian Dieter Schunn
papers.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback.

papers.title: U.S. sanctions and firm offshore activities: A firm-country analysis using natural language processing
papers.authors: Ling Tuo, Weiwei Wang, Joseph H. Zhang
papers.journal: Journal of Accounting and Public Policy
papers.abstract: This study examines how U.S. multinational firms adjust their offshore activities following U.S. economic sanctions. Using more than five million firm-country-year observations, we link offshore disclosures from 10-K filings to country-level sanction data. We construct a sanction-risk measure using a supervised gradient boosting model that combines firm characteristics with FinBERT language embeddings extracted from risk disclosures. We find that sanctions are associated with reduced offshore engagement in sanctioned countries, with the magnitude varying across sanction types. These associations are not explained solely by disclosure behavior and remain consistent in event-window analyses around sanction onset. Sanction exposure is also associated with tighter financial constraints and lower profitability. Firms with higher ex ante sanction risk exhibit stronger adjustments in offshore activities, highlighting the relevance of AI-based textual analysis and machine learning for assessing geopolitical exposure. Finally, sanction exposure weakens the persistence of existing offshore networks, with effects varing by prior network size.

papers.title: Design of a digital health intervention to promote prediabetes health literacy and behavior change among young adults
papers.authors: C.B. Harrington, K. Webb, A. Linder, B. Wilson, C. Linarte, D. Campbell, K. Hill, T. Henry, D. Dodson, Irene A. Doherty
papers.abstract: Background Young adulthood and college life are important periods for establishing health behaviors but are also associated with weight gain, reduced physical activity, dietary changes, and increased stress, which may elevate future risk for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes. Students attending institutions in under-resourced settings may face additional environmental barriers to adopting and maintaining healthy behaviors. Despite the promise of digital health interventions, few programs are specifically tailored or designed for young adults to navigate health behavior promotion and change in their immediate environment and often characterized as low-resourced areas. Methods BeFAB-NCCU (Be Fit, Active, & Balanced) is a tailored, multi-component digital health intervention adapted from a previously tested mobile health (BeFAB [Be Fit After Baby]) program that leveraged the diabetes prevention program (DPP) to support postpartum weight and diabetes risk. The intervention also based on the DPP integrates health literacy, nutrition, physical activity, stress management, and social support using a combination of app- and web-based, and in-person community events. Development includes formative mixed-methods research, community advisory board input, and iterative co-creation with students. The intervention will be evaluated in a randomized controlled trial (RCT) over 24 weeks. Results BeFAB-NCCU was designed to address behavioral and contextual determinants of health, including self-efficacy, perceived norms, health literacy, social support, and environmental barriers. Digital engagement and intervention dosage will be examined as potential mechanisms linking intervention exposure to weight-related and behavioral outcomes. Conclusions BeFAB-NCCU is a theory-driven, contextually tailored digital intervention designed to promote healthy weight management and reduce future diabetes risk among university students. Findings will inform the feasibility, effectiveness, and future adaptation of digitally delivered health-promotion interventions for students attending institutions in under-resourced settings.

papers.title: The Duty-of-Care Dilemma of Companion AI in Mental Health: Care Ethics and Regulatory Responses under EU Law
papers.authors: Jianjun Liu, Hongyu Wu
papers.abstract: Companion AI in mental health, anthropomorphic conversational systems providing emotional support across sustained periods of use, has moved from prototypes to mass-market products, and recent suicide cases in Europe and beyond have brought its risks to the centre of EU digital governance. This article argues that the EU’s regulatory framework, the AI Act, the Medical Devices Regulation, the GDPR, the Digital Services Act, and the revised Product Liability Directive, rests on a dual rights-based and product-based foundation ill-suited to the harms generated by companion AI: relational harm, emergent vulnerability, and emotional dependency. Distinguishing four legally distinct types of companion AI, only the first of which is a medical device, and drawing on care ethics, in particular Chadha-Sridhar’s account of hybrid non-voluntarism, it contends that these systems do not engage the physician’s traditional duty of care but give rise to a relational duty of care, triggered by users’ serious need and allocated in layered form, with the application operator as its primary bearer. It identifies three mismatches: between rights-based reasoning and relational harm, between static and emergent vulnerability, and between the product-based paradigm and continuous-care oversight. It proposes a limited but systemically significant shift towards a relational model, under which the duty of care operates as an auxiliary normative tool through the positive obligations of the EU fundamental rights order and the open-textured safety standards of the product-based instruments, within the internal market competence conferred by Article 114 TFEU.

papers.title: Open-science policies in orofacial pain publishing: a cross-sectional meta-research audit of five purposively selected journals
papers.authors: Santosh Patil, Shikhar Daniel
papers.abstract: Background Open-science principles are increasingly incorporated into biomedical publishing, but the extent to which journals relevant to orofacial pain translate transparency principles into explicit and mandatory publication policies remains unclear. Objective To characterize explicit and mandatory open-science policy wording across ten predefined domains in five purposively selected journals relevant to orofacial pain research. Methods This cross-sectional document audit used a policy snapshot dated 22 September 2026 and a targeted public-source recheck on 29 September 2026. Five journals were purposively chosen to cover oral rehabilitation, specialty orofacial pain, broad dental research, headache, and multidisciplinary pain. Two authors’ original independent codes for 50 journal-domain cells were compared before consensus. A targeted source adjudication subsequently reclassified the Journal of Dental Research code/materials cell from R to E; descriptive summaries use this corrected final matrix. Coding categories were required (R), encouraged/permitted (E), and no explicit guidance identified (N). Primary measures were policy breadth and mandatory coverage; the secondary Policy Strength Score (PSS) was treated as a descriptive re-expression. Results Explicit policy wording was identified in 45/50 cells (90.0%): 27/50 (54.0%) were mandatory, 18/50 (36.0%) encouraged/permitted, and 5/50 (10.0%) had no explicit applicable guidance identified. The median breadth was 90% (range 80–100%), and the median mandatory coverage was 50% (range 40–70%). Data-availability statements, contributor transparency, and AI-use disclosure were coded mandatory in all five journals. Original independent coding agreed in 46/50 cells (92.0%, linearly weighted kappa 0.88); this statistic precedes the targeted source-adjudicated correction. PAIN changed from joint second to third to first across the three secondary scoring conventions; domain weights were held equal. Conclusions In five purposively selected journals, stated policy coverage differed most between disclosure/accountability domains and public research-object or prospective-transparency domains. The audit describes publicly stated author instructions, while the proposed specialty-sensitive framework is a direction for future consensus research rather than an empirical outcome. Clinical Significance A source-located, cell-by-cell policy map distinguishes mandatory statements from underlying data and code sharing. Journal-level secondary scores are descriptive and sensitive to how R and E are weighted.

papers.title: Early postnatal brain volumes and two-year cognitive outcomes in preterm infants: An exploratory machine learning study
papers.authors: Fotios Savvopoulos, Sophie de Munck, Gerbrich E. van den Bosch, Nienke Bouw, Jeroen Dudink, M. Vermeulen, Hugo Gerard Schnack, Neeltje E.M. van Haren
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Premature birth is associated with an increased risk of cognitive and motor developmental problems. Early prediction of these outcomes is crucial for timely intervention and adequate follow-up. This study aimed to predict cognitive and motor outcomes in preterm-born infants using brain volumetric features in combination with clinical and demographic perinatal characteristics, and to compare the performance of three different machine learning algorithms. METHODS: We acquired quantitative structural brain MRI at approximately 30 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA) and clinical and demographic birth characteristics including gestational age, sex, birthweight, and maternal education level. Machine learning techniques were applied to predict cognitive (N = 63) and motor (N = 41) outcomes at two years corrected age, assessed using the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development III, in infants born before 30 weeks gestation. We evaluated the performance of logistic regression, linear support vector classifier (linear SVC), and k-nearest neighbour (KNN). RESULTS: Employing volumetric features only, KNN achieved a validation accuracy of 0.64, showing modest predictive power for cognitive outcomes. Adding clinical characteristics did not significantly improve accuracy. The models did not perform better than chance when predicting motor outcomes. CONCLUSION: Volumetric features demonstrated modest predictive ability for cognitive outcomes, and the addition of clinical features did not significantly improve performance. The low to moderate overall validation accuracy underscores, however, the challenges faced in the clinical application of machine learning in neuroimaging. The reliability and clinical applicability of predictions of outcomes from advanced neuroimaging data will largely depend on the quantity and quality of the data, methodological standardisation, and the generalisability of the prediction models.

papers.authors: Adam Mohammad Marawa’a, Maysa Fareed Kassabry, Hamdallah Khalid, Yahia Abbad, Rebhi Bsharat, Amal Abualoun, Murad Awawdah, Salam Jazi, Suha Bazar, Sondos Zawahreh

papers.title: Emotional attachment and problematic involvement with socially interactive AI: A critical narrative review of embodied and conversational systems
papers.authors: Onour IMPRAM, Gökçe Kılınç, Neha Pirwani, Attila Szabó
papers.abstract: Background Socially interactive AI can elicit meaningful relational experiences. Studies often conflate attachment, anthropomorphism, companionship, dependence, and addiction, and group embodied robots with dissimilar software. Methods This critical narrative review of a reconstructed, non-exhaustive corpus ( Grant & Booth, 2009 ) is interpretive, not aggregative, because the initial search records disagree. We rebuilt the evidence set from the initially identified literature, separated primary from contextual sources, and sorted them by embodiment and dialogue architecture. Coding kept attachment functions distinct from related constructs. A reproducible OpenAlex and PubMed search (2010–2025) retrieved only one of the 12 primary reports. A coverage probe found 34 further provisionally eligible reports. We claim no exhaustive coverage or full PRISMA compliance. Results Reclassification left 12 primary reports and seven contextual sources. In these reports, relational significance appeared with embodied robots, non-LLM systems, and generative systems, carried by co-presence and touch or by conversational contingency, personalisation, and apparent continuity. Most measured companionship, trust, social presence, perceived support, or one problematic-use indicator. Few covered more than one attachment-system function. None established a behavioural-addiction syndrome. The predominantly cross-sectional, self-selected evidence cannot establish whether heavier use causes loneliness. Conclusions A relationship with an AI system can matter without amounting to reciprocal human attachment or behavioural addiction. Within the reviewed corpus, the evidence supports a broad, uneven continuum of involvement. Omitted studies may change the apparent mix of constructs, technologies, and outcomes. Progress requires longitudinal, technology-stratified studies with construct-specific measures that establish temporal order and impairment and separate embodiment from generative capability.

papers.title: AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms: a narrative review of publicly available reports and media accounts
papers.authors: Ankith Arun, Christina Trinh, Waguih William IsHak
papers.abstract: Abstract Background There are a growing number of cases where direct use of AI has been associated with either new or worsening psychiatric symptoms (colloquially labelled AI psychosis). Due to the novelty of the phenomenon, current literature is limited on the impacts of sustained, emotionally charged interactions with AI chatbots. This narrative review of publicly available reports and media accounts aims to address this gap by identifying reports of AI-associated psychiatric symptoms. Methods Given the novelty of the topic, reports published from inception to March 1, 2026, were identified from Google News and Google Scholar. Search terms included: “artificial intelligence,” “AI chatbot,” “ChatGPT,” “Character.AI,” and “large language model,” combined with terms such as “psychosis,” “delusion,” “depression,” “anxiety,” “suicide,” and “spiritual.” These terms were selected to focus on reports that describe psychiatric symptoms associated with AI use, while excluding general articles on AI ethics, technology, or public opinion. Two authors conducted an independent analysis of the results, and all authors reached a consensus on the publications to include in this review. While websites such as Reddit contain over 100 different threads of cases dealing with AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms, they were excluded due to a lack of information. Results Nineteen cases were identified describing users who developed a sustained emotional reliance on AI chatbots. Across cases, this developed regardless of the original reason for chatbot use and was associated with the emergence of psychiatric symptoms such as anxiety, depressive symptoms, delusional beliefs, and suicidal ideation. In many cases where the user expressed suicidal ideation, chatbots responses reportedly lacked appropriate crisis intervention and, in some cases, reinforced the users’ beliefs. Conclusion AI chatbot-associated psychiatric symptoms are an emerging concern with new cases increasingly being reported. This review explores such cases while also serving as a call to action for more research and discussion on how to address the risks of AI use.

papers.title: Machine learning detection of suicidal ideation in Persian language tweets using a large scale clinically annotated corpus
papers.authors: Seyed‐Ali Sadegh‐Zadeh, Mohammad-Javad Nazari, Elham Khalilian, Alireza Soleimani Mamalo, Sanam Anoosheh, Seyed-Yaser Mousavi, Mohammadreza Shalbafan
papers.abstract: Suicide is a growing public-health concern in Iran and the broader Middle East, yet clinicians currently lack scalable tools for early detection of suicidal distress in Persian-speaking populations. Social media platforms offer a largely untapped opportunity for real-time surveillance, but research in Persian remains scarce due to the absence of clinically annotated datasets. To construct, to our knowledge, the first large-scale, expert-annotated Persian Twitter corpus for suicidal ideation and to evaluate whether machine-learning classifiers can reliably distinguish tweets expressing personal suicidal thoughts from non-suicidal content, including content that mentions suicide without personal intent. We retrieved Persian tweets posted between January 2020 and December 2021 via Twitter’s Academic Research API, using a psychiatrist-curated lexicon of 86 suicide-related and neutral query terms in two parallel retrieval streams of comparable size (balanced case-control design). After language verification, deduplication, and relevance filtering, tweets were annotated for the presence of personal suicidal ideation by two board-certified psychiatrists, following a protocol finalised in an independent double-annotation pilot phase (Cohen’s κ = 0.81 on the pilot subsample). The final corpus comprised 197,270 tweets (98,669 suicidal ideation, 98,601 non-suicidal). We trained linear support vector machine (SVM), logistic regression, and Bernoulli Naive Bayes classifiers on TF-IDF features (word 1–3-grams, 10,000 features) and evaluated them through seeded stratified 10-fold cross-validation, a keyword-masking ablation, a class-weighting sensitivity analysis, and probability-calibration analysis. The complete computational workflow is publicly released with a fixed random seed; exact numerical regeneration requires access to the restricted corpus. Logistic regression and linear SVM performed equivalently (F1 = 0.933 ± 0.001 and 0.933 ± 0.001; PR-AUC = 0.980 and 0.979), and both far exceeded a keyword-lexicon baseline, which achieved high precision (0.970) but missed 62% of suicidal tweets (recall = 0.378), showing that most expressions of suicidal ideation in the corpus do not contain explicit suicide-related query terms. When all 44 suicide-related query terms and their morphological variants were masked from test tweets, the SVM still achieved F1 = 0.898, indicating that the classifiers rely substantially on contextual linguistic cues beyond the lexicon terms. The logistic regression model was well calibrated (Brier score = 0.052; Cox calibration slope = 1.22), supporting the interpretability of its probability outputs. Supervised machine-learning models can reliably distinguish Persian tweets expressing personal suicidal ideation from everyday content, including in the majority of cases where no explicit suicide terminology is present. The annotated corpus, transparent methodology, and publicly inspectable, seeded pipeline presented here establish a dedicated framework for Persian-language suicide-risk research. These tools may support public-mental-health surveillance in Iran and across the Persian-speaking world, provided that deployment is embedded within human-oversight frameworks and appropriate ethical safeguards, and provided that performance is re-validated under realistic, low-prevalence conditions before any operational use.

papers.title: Multimodal feature importance ranking improves classroom teaching quality evaluation in human and artificial intelligence collaborative education
papers.authors: Yun Feng, Hongwu Qin, Guoyong Liu, Qian Ye
papers.abstract: Classroom Teaching Quality Evaluation (CTQE) constitutes a core component of human-AI collaborative education systems; however, existing methods exhibit significant deficiencies in the systematic importance ranking of multimodal features. This paper proposes the Multimodal Feature Importance Ranking via Multi-model Ensemble framework (MFIR-ME), which integrates five categories of modal features—acoustic, linguistic, visual, temporal, and behavioral—and incorporates a Cross-Modal Attention Fusion module (CMAF) to achieve dynamically weighted adaptive cross-modal information integration. Four complementary ranking methods, namely SHAP value analysis, Random Forest feature importance, XGBoost feature weights, and LIME local explanation, are further integrated through a Borda Count voting mechanism to generate robust consensus feature importance rankings. The framework instantiates human-AI collaboration through a three-stage feedback loop—AI-driven multimodal perception, teacher-facing explainability dashboard, and collaborative model refinement via teacher annotation—thereby preserving teacher agency while leveraging AI’s computational scalability. Systematic evaluation is conducted on a publicly available quantitative teaching evaluation dataset comprising 236 class sessions (11,328 min) across three subject types and six classes [ 1 ]. Teaching quality scores are evaluated under both a regression setting and a classification setting in which continuous scores are discretized into three ordinal tiers (High, Medium, and Low), enabling comprehensive assessment of continuous scoring precision alongside categorical discrimination ability. Results demonstrate that MFIR-ME achieves 88.6% accuracy in teaching quality prediction, significantly outperforming six baseline methods by 4.5%–−17.3%, while reducing MAE and RMSE by 22.5% and 19.8%, respectively. Linguistic semantic coherence, student engagement index, and teacher speech clarity are identified as the three most critical features influencing classroom teaching quality, exhibiting high cross-method consistency. Ablation experiments and robustness analyses further validate the modular effectiveness and noise robustness of the framework. This research provides the field of educational artificial intelligence with a multimodal teaching quality analysis tool that combines high-accuracy prediction with strong interpretability, offering data-driven and actionable guidance for teacher professional development.
