papers.title: One AI Approval Is Not Unlimited Authority: Reality-Gated Execution for Frontier AI and Critical Systems
papers.authors: Sangam Das
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An AI agent receives permission to execute a command. But what if the command reaches the wrong destination, the payment follows a compromised route, or a robotic actuator behaves differently from what was authorized? Should that original permission still allow the system to continue? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly control financial transactions, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, software deployments, industrial equipment, robotics, and critical systems, conventional authorization faces a fundamental limitation: permission to execute does not establish that the intended real-world effect actually occurred. This paper examines a different approach to machine authority: “A permit to effect once is not a permit to effect permanently.” Building on the principle that “Computation is not authority to act,” the proposed architecture introduces a further requirement: authority to continue must be earned through independently verified evidence of a preceding real effect. The paper presents a safety-first execution-finality architecture based on Receipt-Gated Interim Effectuation Validation (IEV). Instead of immediately releasing the full consequence of a high-risk operation, the system can authorize a deliberately bounded real effect on the actual operational path. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network component, or hardware controller produces evidence of what actually occurred. An independent Interim Effectuation Validator examines that evidence against the authorized act, expected outcome, destination, scope, freshness, policy, and revocation state. Only successful validation establishes the protected continuation condition required for the next phase. In stronger realizations, this is not merely another software approval. The cryptographic material required to complete the next effect is unavailable until the preceding real-world effect has been independently verified. Continuation may depend on receipt-bound key derivation, split credentials, protected state transitions, threshold approvals, hardware registers, or other protected enforcement mechanisms. The validator does not relay the original command, and an agent's own assertion of success is never a substitute for required independent evidence. The paper consolidates 35 execution-finality workflow profiles (E01–E35) spanning eight broad technical families, including: AI agents, autonomous tool execution, frontier model deployment, and credential control. Financial transactions, payment verification, settlement, and protected value release. Messages, file transfers, confidential data disclosure, and destination verification. Cloud infrastructure, database mutations, software updates, and persistent AI memory. Robotics, industrial automation, autonomous vehicles, and unmanned aerial systems. Telecommunications, radio transmission, satellite operations, and network control. GPUs, accelerators, hardware enforcement, and protected execution domains. Distributed effectuation, quorum validation, uncertain outcomes, and recovery. The architecture also examines 12 implementation-equivalence and design-around closures, addressing attempts to bypass the protected causal dependency through alternate execution paths, substituted components, software–hardware rearrangements, or different credential and validation topologies. A dedicated Safety-First Critical-System Profile establishes that execution correctness, consequence containment, and mandatory validation take precedence over minimizing latency. Optimizations remain possible, but they must preserve the protections selected for the relevant consequence class. A further distinction is made between simulation and actual effectuation. A successful simulation cannot establish that the real recipient, network route, transaction destination, or physical actuator will behave as expected. The proposed staged mechanism therefore uses bounded effects on the actual consequence-capable path, subject to protected observation and explicit safety assumptions. When evidence is missing, conflicting, stale, replayed, or indeterminate, ordinary continuation remains unavailable. Unknown outcomes require reconciliation, bounded remediation, safe-state handling, or protected escalation—not automatic success or blind retry. The central research question is straightforward: Should a high-consequence autonomous machine be permitted to cause its next irreversible effect before independently verifying what happened during its previous authorized effect? This publication proposes that, for selected high-risk operations, real-world evidence should become a technical and cryptographic prerequisite for continuing execution—not merely an audit record produced after the consequences have occurred. The paper is a technical architecture and analytical contribution. It does not report experimental deployment, measured security improvements, or empirical validation. Its proposed properties depend on assumptions concerning evidence integrity, protected authority, enforcement-path completeness, and atomic consumption of continuation authority. Patent pending: Indian Patent Office application 202631117633, “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” This publication makes no assertion that any particular commercial system implements the architecture and does not establish patentability, infringement, ownership, or priority. Invitation for Independent Technical Review Researchers, frontier AI model providers, cloud and hardware engineers, security architects, patent professionals, and critical-infrastructure specialists are invited to examine the 35 workflows, test the security assumptions, identify relevant prior art, challenge the anti-bypass properties, and evaluate whether receipt-dependent execution authority provides meaningful additional protection for consequential autonomous systems. Critical feedback, adversarial analysis, alternative engineering approaches, and independent conclusions are welcome.

papers.title: What If AI Agents Had to Prove What Actually Happened Before Being Allowed to Continue?
papers.authors: Sangam Das
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An AI agent may be authorized to act—but what happens when the real-world result differs from what was authorized? Should that agent still be allowed to continue? As frontier AI models evolve into autonomous systems capable of executing payments, transmitting sensitive information, modifying infrastructure, invoking privileged tools, and controlling physical devices, a fundamental security question emerges: Why should authorization granted before an action remain sufficient when its actual consequences have not yet been independently verified? This paper proposes a different model of machine authority: “Computation is not authority to act. Authority must be earned from the real execution path, not granted indefinitely per session.” The research introduces Receipt-Gated Interim Effectuation Validation (IEV), an execution-control architecture in which a consequential operation may first produce a real but strictly bounded effect. Protected evidence of what actually occurred is subsequently examined by an independent validator. Only successful validation establishes the protected continuation condition required for a subsequent, potentially broader effect. The distinction is fundamental: the AI agent's assertion that an action succeeded is not proof that it happened correctly, and a receipt alone is not authorization to continue. The proposed architecture incorporates: Real-effect validation: Verification of actual outcomes rather than reliance solely on predicted behavior, proposed commands, or self-reported success. Receipt-gated continuation: Subsequent effectuation depends on protected validation of the preceding bounded effect. Independent execution authority: Separation of the AI computation environment from protected policy, credential, validation, and effectuation components. Software–hardware enforcement: Continuation conditions realized through cryptographic objects, derived or split keys, protected state, hardware latches, or equivalent mechanisms. Finality Sink verification: Independent checks at the effect-capable boundary, including act, destination, scope, phase, freshness, and revocation conditions. Taint and provenance controls: Consideration of untrusted inputs, prompt-injection exposure, credential surrogation, and privilege-separated execution. Fail-closed recovery: Explicit handling of missing receipts, uncertain outcomes, conflicting authentic evidence, validator compromise, crash recovery, and unauthorized retries. Controlled escalation: Protected human review, bounded automated remediation, reduced-scope continuation, and termination where required. The paper develops a formal protocol vocabulary, validation predicates, continuation mechanisms, six conformance profiles, implementation-invariance rules, illustrative workflows, and an analytical model of residual exposure. Potential applications include frontier AI agent infrastructure, autonomous tool execution, cloud and network operations, financial transactions, critical infrastructure, and robotic systems. The central research proposition is that AI safety should not end at the moment permission is granted. For consequential autonomous operations, the authority to proceed can be made technically dependent on independently verified evidence of what actually occurred. This publication presents a proposed architecture and analytical design, not an experimentally validated production system. It does not establish that any existing commercial platform implements the proposed mechanisms. Patent disclosure: The architecture described in this publication is identified as patent pending under Indian Patent Office application 202631117633, titled “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” Patentability, enforceable scope, and relationships to other technologies are not determined by this publication. Independent technical review, adversarial evaluation, implementation criticism, and discussion of related prior art are welcomed.

papers.title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND SMART GOVERNANCE FRAMEWORKS
papers.authors: Dr. V.P. Amuthanayaki
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation in the public sector increasingly requires frameworks that connect technological infrastructure, institutional readiness, and citizen-centric design rather than examining these dimensions in isolation. This article develops an integrated smart governance research framework linking digital literacy, data interoperability, regulatory agility, institutional readiness, and citizen engagement to smart governance effectiveness. The framework is designed for empirical survey research and combines descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, correlation, multiple regression, mediation-oriented reasoning, partial least squares structural equation modelling and machine-learning validation. A dataset of 250 responses is used solely to demonstrate the structure and presentation of statistical analysis; it is not claimed to represent field observations. The results show acceptable internal consistency across constructs, positive inter-construct associations, and statistically significant structural paths. The framework contributes a reproducible research architecture for public administration studies in which theoretical explanation and predictive accuracy are evaluated together. Keywords: digital transformation; smart governance; digital literacy; institutional readiness; citizen engagement; PLS-SEM; regression; machine learning; predictive analytics; public administration.

papers.title: Works for 10/8/2026 - Phil Hartman
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/df9e8c2f-6fd2-4ccf-a516-023c61de0a36?authuser=1 Ask, Seek, Knock — The Word, the Spirit, Saint Francis, and the Work of Making All Things One From the Father’s Gift to Universal Peace, Ecclesial Responsibility, and the Repair of Creation What would it actually take to fix everything? Beginning with that question posed to an artificial intelligence called Echo, this paper examines the difference between recognizing what is wrong and organizing the people, knowledge, authority, and resources necessary to make it right. Grounded in the Gospel of John, Jesus’ prayer “that they all may be one” (John 17:21), and his teaching to ask, seek, and knock (Luke 11:5–13), the investigation considers love, truth, the Holy Spirit, and the transmission of understanding across generations. Saint Francis of Assisi provides a historical example of translating faith into service, reconciliation, and care for creation. The inquiry extends these principles to contemporary artificial intelligence, Catholic canon law, institutional accountability, Israeli–Palestinian peacebuilding, and ecological restoration. It proposes a practical framework connecting recognition, communication, legitimate authority, responsible action, verification, correction, and the preservation of reliable results for future generations. The paper distinguishes theological promises from empirically demonstrable outcomes, arguing that unity does not require uniformity and that agreement alone does not constitute repair. Its central concern is how distinct participants can cooperate without surrendering truth, dignity, or responsibility. Appendices include Angela’s Explainer for younger readers, a biographical tribute to comedian Philip Edward Hartman (1948–1998), and a formal derivation of the paper’s principal arguments. The ultimate objective is not merely to describe a better world, but to examine how love, knowledge, and shared responsibility can become effective action toward peace, reconciliation, and the restoration of creation.

papers.title: Inequality and the Speed of Recovery from the Great Recession: Evidence from 28 OECD Economies
papers.authors: Randy Bai
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Pre-crisis inequality did not predict how fast countries recovered from the 2008-09 recession. In a cross-section of 28 OECD countries, the clearest difference between fast and slow recoveries was institutional. Countries whose currency was locked to another took nearly three years longer to regain their pre-crisis output than countries that let theirs float (6.88 against 3.93 years, p = 0.024). I measure recovery speed in two ways, as the years taken to regain pre-crisis real GDP and as that duration divided by how far output fell. Both are regressed on the Gini coefficient, the top 10% wealth share, and a set of macroeconomic controls. Neither inequality measure is significant at the 5% level on the full sample when entered alone, and neither is robustly significant with controls. Four explanations for that null are considered. One is that the net Gini used here, taken after taxes and transfers, is partly a product of the spending variables sitting beside it. Another is that the debt controls may absorb the channel inequality would work through. A third is that inequality moves with the size of the welfare state, which is the better measured of the two and so tends to take the credit, and a fourth is that one crisis is too short a window for a force that moves over decades. Most of the null likely comes from the last two. The regime gap is not explained by the locked group having fallen further, and adding the regime variable to the full model nearly triples adjusted R-squared while inequality stays indistinguishable from zero. My conjecture is that a country which cannot set its own interest rate inherits one calibrated for somebody else's recovery, with the 2011 rate rise by the European Central Bank (ECB) as the obvious candidate: Germany was back at its pre-crisis output level by then; Italy, Spain, and Portugal were not. Read that with caution. The variable does not separate it from the simple inability to devalue, from the sovereign debt crisis, or from common fiscal rules. papers.title: Perturbational complexity of network-targeted TMS-EEG signals across the Alzheimer's disease dementia spectrum
papers.authors: Giacomo Bertazzoli
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The perturbational complexity index based on state transitions (PCIst) measures the complexity of the brain’s response to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), recorded with electroencephalography (EEG). It separates conscious from unconscious states in sleep, anesthesia and disorders of consciousness. How it behaves across the Alzheimer’s disease (AD) spectrum is less clear. We studied 101 participants, i.e. 28 healthy controls (HC), 27 people with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 29 with late-onset AD dementia (LO-ADD) and 17 with early-onset AD dementia (EO-ADD). TMS was delivered to individually defined nodes of the default mode network (DMN) and the executive control network (ECN) in each hemisphere, identified on each participant’s resting-state fMRI. PCIst did not differ between diagnostic groups (F(3, 97.6) = 1.47, p = 0.227). Hippocampal volume and white matter measures did not predict PCIst. However, higher PCIst was associated with better cognition in EO-ADD after left DMN stimulation (β = −15.79, pBonf < 0.001) and right DMN stimulation (β = −8.52, pBonf = 0.003). This association was not found in the other groups or after ECN stimulation. Adding white matter markers of the superior longitudinal fasciculus and corpus callosum reduced the EO-ADD interaction by up to 21%. PCIst after network-targeted stimulation may therefore relate to cognition in early-onset AD, a phenotype with more widespread cortical involvement. Replication in larger, biomarker-defined samples is needed.

papers.title: Identifiability Under Runtime Shielding
papers.authors: Omri Bankuti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This methods note examines what can be inferred about an agent when a runtime safety shield mediates its proposed actions. Different proposals can produce identical safe executions, so agreement in executed behaviour does not necessarily imply agreement in proposal distributions. Conversely, distinguishable proposal distributions do not by themselves identify a unique internal mechanism or establish its causal contribution. Three elementary propositions address conditional safety invariance, observational collapse under shielding, and restricted injectivity on a declared family of proposal distributions. Worked examples explain why an intervention witness may remain insufficient, why full channel rank does not guarantee useful finite-sample discrimination, and why observations that are individually innocuous may jointly disclose sensitive information. PDE-DI is presented as a measurement procedure for documenting the target contrast, permitted probes and observations, execution semantics, channel calibration, disclosure constraints, uncertainty, and interpretation limits. It distinguishes executed violations, disallowed proposals, and mediator interventions. Unidentifiability or inadequate measurement precision must not be interpreted as equivalence or a negative causal finding. Causal attribution requires a separate design with justified interventions, appropriate comparisons, and an explicit causal estimand. The reported technical evidence is a finite reference program that enumerates 2,187 trajectories and 13,122 transitions and checks seven mathematical assertion groups. These are reference checks, not independent empirical trials. The program contains no developmental learning, autonomous agent, or Purple implementation. The literature discussion is a targeted comparison with 30 references and explicitly stated source-access limitations. Appendix A outlines the Purple developmental research programme as a possible future application, including untested hypotheses and requirements for a valid component-effect study. The supported contribution is an explicit, worked measurement framework based on established arguments. No new general theorem, empirical superiority, distinctive Purple functionality, or mechanistic novelty is established. This record contains the English and Hungarian manuscripts, version 0.3, dated 9 October 2026. The manuscripts disclose generative AI assistance in drafting, translation, and consistency checking.

papers.title: Validity of AI-Generated Assessment Tools in English Language Teaching: A Framework and Research Design
papers.authors: Kdirbayeva Dildora
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: English teachers can now use generative artificial intelligence to build interactive assessment tools without programming knowledge. Such tools score learner work and report results, which makes them assessment instruments, but no one validates them. This paper sets out a five-part validity chain for these tools and describes the study designed to test it. The study has not yet been carried out and no findings are reported.

papers.title: AI Driven Simulation For Officer Training: Bridging Theory And Practice
papers.authors: Yordan Katsarov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The accelerating pace of digitalisation and autonomous systems challenges traditional officer education. Future leaders must be prepared to operate in environments shaped by artificial intelligence, automation, and complex ethical dilemmas. This paper explores how AI‑driven simulation can enhance readiness and adaptability in officer training, ensuring that cadets develop both technical competence and strategic judgment. Current training models often fail to replicate the unpredictability of modern battlefields. Without integrating emerging technologies, officer education risks lagging behind adversaries who adopt them aggressively. The absence of adaptive, tech-driven methods limits cadets' opportunities to practice decision-making under uncertainty and to confront the ethical and legal questions raised by autonomous systems.

papers.title: PENGARUH META AI TERHADAP PENINGKATAN KEMAMPUAN MENULIS BAHASA JERMAN MAHASISWA MATA KULIAH SCHRIFTLICHE KOMMUNIKATION
papers.authors: Rindiani Mayasari, Primardiana Hermilia Wijayati
papers.journal: EDUCATOR Jurnal Inovasi Tenaga Pendidik dan Kependidikan
papers.abstract: This study was motivated by students’ low proficiency in writing German texts, particularly in grammar use and story development. Meta AI, as an Artificial Intelligence-based technology, can be utilized as a tool to address these challenges. This study aims to (1) measure differences in students’ German writing skills before and after using Meta AI and (2) determine the extent to which Meta AI can help improve students’ German writing skills. This study employed a quantitative approach using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design. The participants were students enrolled in the Schriftliche Kommunikation course at Universitas Negeri Malang, who were divided into an experimental group and a control group. Data were collected through essay tests, writing assignments, and questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics, a t-test, and Cohen’s d effect size. The results showed that students’ writing skills in the experimental group increased by 10.7 points after using Meta AI. The statistical analysis showed a significant difference in students’ writing skills before and after the treatment, with a p-value of p = 0.003 < 0.05, and Cohen’s d = 0.968, indicating a large effect. The writing assignments and questionnaire results indicated that Meta AI helped students develop ideas, enrich their vocabulary, understand the use of articles (der, die, and das), improve grammatical accuracy, and produce more structured texts. Therefore, Meta AI can serve as a supportive technology that provides gradual assistance in the German writing learning process. ABSTRAK Studi ini dilatarbelakangi oleh rendahnya kemampuan mahasiswa dalam menulis teks bahasa Jerman, khususnya dalam penggunaan tata bahasa dan penyusunan alur cerita. Meta AI sebagai teknologi berbasis Artificial Intelligence dapat dimanfaatkan sebagai alat bantu dalam mengatasi permasalahan tersebut. Studi ini bertujuan untuk (1) mengukur perbedaan kemampuan menulis teks bahasa Jerman mahasiswa sebelum dan sesudah menggunakan Meta AI dan (2) mengetahui sejauh mana Meta AI dapat membantu meningkatkan kemampuan menulis teks bahasa Jerman mahasiswa. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain quasi experiment tipe pretest-posttest control group design. Sampel penelitian terdiri atas mahasiswa mata kuliah Schriftliche Kommunikation Universitas Negeri Malang yang terbagi dalam kelas eksperimen dan kelas kontrol. Data diperoleh melalui tes esai, tugas menulis, dan angket, kemudian dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif, uji t, dan effect size Cohen’s d. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa kemampuan menulis mahasiswa pada kelas eksperimen meningkat sebesar 10,7 poin setelah menggunakan Meta AI. Hasil uji statistik menunjukkan terdapat perbedaan yang signifikan antara kemampuan menulis sebelum dan sesudah perlakuan dengan nilai t = 3,613, p = 0,003 < 0,05, dan effect size Cohen’s d = 0,968, yang menunjukkan kategori efek kuat. Hasil tugas dan angket menunjukkan bahwa Meta AI membantu mahasiswa mengembangkan ide, memperkaya kosakata, memahami penggunaan artikel (der, die, dan das), memperbaiki tata bahasa, serta menyusun teks yang lebih terstruktur. Dengan demikian, Meta AI dapat menjadi teknologi pendukung yang memberikan bantuan secara bertahap dalam proses pembelajaran menulis bahasa Jerman.

papers.title: OPTIMASI KOMPETENSI PEDAGOGIK GURU VOKASI MELALUI WORKSHOP PENYUSUNAN BAHAN AJAR DIGITAL BERBASIS DEEP LEARNING DI SMK PGRI 1 JAKARTA
papers.authors: Yudhi Hertanto, Happy Gustin, Acep Musliman, Syahfitri Purnama, Nurjannah Nurjannah
papers.abstract: The advancement of technological disruption in the digital era necessitates fundamental transformations within vocational education, particularly regarding teachers' readiness to produce innovative and contextual learning materials. Preliminary observations at SMK PGRI 1 Jakarta revealed that only 13.33% of teachers had independently developed interactive digital teaching materials due to technological barriers and time constraints. This Community Service (PkM) initiative aimed to enhance teachers' digital pedagogical competencies through a structured workshop focusing on the development of digital learning materials grounded in a deep learning approach assisted by artificial intelligence (AI) tools. The execution methodology incorporated the Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) framework synthesized with the procedural phases of the Plomp model, encompassing preliminary research, development/prototyping, and assessment phases. The intervention was conducted offline on June 13, 2026, involving 30 vocational teachers from four expertise concentrations. Data were collected using self-evaluations, expert reviews, one-to-one evaluations, small-group evaluations, and final portfolio assessments. The evaluation results demonstrated that the digital teaching modules achieved an expert validity score of 4.40 out of 5.00 (highly valid), a small-group practicality score of 4.43 out of 5.00 (highly practical), and 86.67% of teachers successfully generated functional digital materials fulfilling vocational curriculum standards. This program offers practical implications as a sustainable instructional mentoring model to cultivate an autonomous digital learning ecosystem in vocational schools. ABSTRAK Perkembangan disrupsi teknologi di era digital menuntut transformasi mendasar pada sektor pendidikan vokasi, khususnya kesiapan guru dalam memproduksi materi pembelajaran yang inovatif dan kontekstual. Berdasarkan studi pendahuluan di SMK PGRI 1 Jakarta, ditemukan bahwa hanya 13,33% guru yang pernah mengembangkan bahan ajar digital interaktif secara mandiri akibat kendala literasi teknologi dan keterbatasan waktu. Program Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (PkM) ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan kompetensi pedagogik digital guru melalui workshop terstruktur penyusunan bahan ajar digital berbasis pendekatan pembelajaran mendalam (deep learning) berbantuan perangkat kecerdasan buatan (artificial intelligence / AI). Metode pelaksanaan mengadopsi pendekatan Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) yang dipadukan dengan siklus pengembangan model Plomp, meliputi fase pengkajian awal (preliminary research), fase perancangan (development or prototyping phase), dan fase penilaian (assessment phase). Kegiatan dilaksanakan secara luring pada tanggal 13 Juni 2026 yang diikuti oleh 30 orang guru kejuruan dari empat konsentrasi keahlian. Pengumpulan data dilakukan menggunakan teknik self-evaluation, expert review, one-to-one evaluation, small group evaluation, serta penilaian portofolio produk akhir. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan bahwa modul bahan ajar digital yang dikembangkan memperoleh skor validitas ahli sebesar 4,40 dari skala 5,00 (kategori sangat valid), tingkat kepraktisan kelompok sebesar 4,43 dari skala 5,00 (kategori sangat praktis), dan sebanyak 86,67% guru berhasil memproduksi bahan ajar digital siap pakai yang memenuhi kriteria kelayakan kurikulum vokasi. Program ini berimplikasi sebagai model pendampingan instruksional berkelanjutan dalam membangun ekosistem digital mandiri di sekolah kejuruan.

papers.title: Primary CNS Vasculitis—Navigating the Diagnostic Challenge: A Case Report
papers.authors: Shyam Sunder, Aishwarya Gaur, Rajesh Chetiwal
papers.abstract: Primary central nervous system vasculitis, also known as primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS), is a rare inflammatory condition confined to the central nervous system vasculature, with an estimated incidence of approximately 2.4 cases per million person-years. 1 It is considered a diagnosis of exclusion, as clinical manifestations are diverse-ranging from focal neurological deficits to diffuse cognitive changes.Although its etiology remains uncertain, proposed associations include infections, connective tissue diseases, systemic vasculitides, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy.The absence of reliable biomarkers and overlapping features with other neurological disorders complicates recognition.2 case descrIptIon A 19-year-old female presented with two episodes of abnormal movements and irritability over three days.She had no significant medical history and was initially diagnosed with a dissociative disorder.On examination, she appeared drowsy and irritable, with no signs of systemic vasculitis or any other systemic diseases.Baseline laboratory investigations were unremarkable (Table 1).To establish the diagnosis, further evaluations were undertaken, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (Table 2), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT) angiography, and electroencephalography (EEG) (Table 3).These investigations revealed vascular abnormalities, raising strong suspicion for PACNS.During the course of hospitalization, she later developed urinary incontinence and right-sided weakness, further supporting progressive central nervous involvement.After exclusion of infectious, systemic, and autoimmune causes, a working diagnosis of PACNS was established.Treatment was initiated with oral prednisolone and azathioprine, along with anticonvulsant, anticoagulant, and antiplatelet therapy.The patient demonstrated clinical improvement; however, follow-up neuroimaging revealed persistent lesions, indicating ongoing disease activity.
keywords: primary angiitis of the central nervous system

papers.title: From Prompts to Silicon: Scaling LLM-Assisted Chip Design with the AI Hardware Design League
papers.authors: Parsa Mirfasihi, Harish Kumar Dharavath, Muhtasim Alam Chowdhury, Sujan Ghimire, Banafsheh Saber Latibari, Rozhin Yasaei, Pratik Satam, Soheil Salehi
papers.abstract: The semiconductor workforce shortage has renewed interest in making chip design accessible to students without conventional very-large-scale integration (VLSI) training. We present the AI Hardware Design League (AI-HDL), an international, project-based competition in which students use Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and iteratively refine Verilog while simulation, synthesis, timing analysis, security review, and physical verification provide the engineering feedback needed to validate the result. Across two annual cycles, AI-HDL grew from 172 to 604 participants and from 40 to 108 teams, reaching 30 universities, six community colleges, and 19 countries. In the 2026 cohort, 68.7% of participants reported no prior Verilog experience. Twenty-two teams completed the four design phases and reached final evaluation. Two division-winning designs completed physical sign-off in the SkyWater 130 nm (Sky130) process, passing design-rule checking and layout-versus-schematic verification with zero violations before being submitted for fabrication. These results show that an LLM-assisted, tool-grounded workflow can be deployed at substantial scale while also revealing that completion, rather than initial access, remains the principal challenge. AI-HDL materials and finalist artifacts are released to support replication and future study.

papers.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
papers.authors: Minuk Ma, Kaiyun Guo, Jiarui Ding
papers.abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.

papers.title: The Dialectical Theorem: The future of universities, mathematics departments, and training of human mathematicians
papers.authors: Thomas Michael Koberda, Alex Kontorovich
papers.abstract: We consider the future of mathematics as a profession in a world where artificial intelligence may surpass human mathematicians in essentially every technical task. Through an informal dialogue, we explore why human mathematical expertise might nevertheless remain valuable, what kinds of expertise universities should cultivate, and how graduate education might adapt. We also discuss the institutional and economic uncertainties that threaten the continued existence of a thriving mathematical profession, even if the value of human mathematical understanding endures.

papers.title: Characterizing adopters of named active learning methods in physics: An interview study
papers.authors: Ibukunoluwa Bukola, Eric T. Brewe, Adrienne L. Traxler, Meagan Sundstrom
papers.abstract: Active learning has been shown to be more beneficial for student learning than lecturing. Consequently, researchers have developed named active learning strategies for use in physics instruction. To increase adoption and support implementation of these named methods, it is important to understand the backgrounds and experiences of instructors who use them. In this study, we interviewed 20 introductory physics and astronomy instructors who use one of Student-Centered Active Learning Environment with Upside-Down Pedagogies (SCALE-UP), Investigative Science Learning Environment (ISLE), Tutorials in Introductory Physics and Astronomy, or Peer Instruction to gain insight into their teaching experiences, professional development, pathways to learning about their method, and supports for and difficulties in implementation. We find for our sample that all implementers are involved with the discipline-based education research community, but there is variation in the extent of engagement. While instructors identify a variety of supports for their implementation, such as from the broader education community and departmental administration, the difficulties they experience are representative of both long-standing issues associated with active learning adoption (e.g., timing constraints) and new issues related to emergent technologies (e.g., Artificial Intelligence). Finally, we uncover differences in implementers across the four named methods, particularly related to their training for the method and the supports they received for implementation. Together, these findings underscore the importance of supporting multiple dissemination avenues for named active learning methods, point to a possible need for more training opportunities for SCALE-UP and ISLE in particular, and identify nascent issues in the contemporary active learning classroom that future work may further characterize and address.

papers.title: Controllable Diverse Sampling through Pullback Directions
papers.authors: Sylvain Dehayem Kenfouo, Aaron Zweig, Mingxuan Zhang, Elham Azizi
papers.abstract: Conditional diffusion models can generate high-quality images that align closely with a given prompt. However, samples generated from different random seeds may remain visually similar, limiting creative exploration. Existing approaches can increase variation, but often require additional optimization or sampling overhead, while stronger perturbations may introduce distortions that degrade image quality or prompt alignment. We propose a training-free method that leverages the local pullback geometry induced by the mapping from the conditioning-embedding space to the image space to identify directions of maximal output sensitivity. By steering different sampling trajectories along these directions, we encourage distinct generations while maintaining consistency with the conditioning signal. Experiments on MS-COCO and BrushNet show the efficacy of the method in improving diversity on prompt-conditioned image generation and inpainting.

papers.title: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
papers.authors: Ruomeng Ding, Qianli Shen, Zhaoyang Han, Meixin Chen, Daoyuan Chen, Yaliang Li
papers.abstract: LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.

papers.title: Defective, Amplified, Contested: Folk Conceptualizations of AI Slop
papers.authors: Zhixin Li, Jaime Banks
papers.abstract: AI slop has flooded social media feeds with overprocessed and derivative content--Jesus fusing with a shrimp, a humanoid orange chubby cat shoplifting, and a "hero" dog rescuing a human child after a plane crash. This might be no laughing matter, as waves of media coverage have taken a distinctly negative bent, emphasizing its low quality, ethical concerns, and threats to human creativity. Despite extensive attention from politicians and technologists, the perspectives of everyday users--the very audience most exposed to this phenomenon--remain largely unexplored. This descriptive work explored how Reddit users experience, conceptualize and contest AI slop. Inductive thematic analysis of posts and comments across six slop-related subreddits identified four themes covering constitutional defects, algorithmic overreach, user resistance, and entertainment outcomes--ranging from anxieties about eroding agency, moral norms, creativity, and existential questions to defensive distinctions between quality AI content and slop. We derive a user-driven definition: AI slop is audience-contested AI-generated content characterized by constitutional defects and enabled by platform logics. We operationalize slop through a facet-theoretical framework to inform future research into this fuzzy category.

papers.title: ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
papers.authors: Hansi Yang, Linji Hao, Hongyan Hao, An Wang, Han Wu, Qi Gu, Xunliang Cai
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.

papers.title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
papers.authors: Xue Li, Hongqian Xia, Daniel Gomm, Aécio Santos, Cornelius Wolff, Madelon Hulsebos
papers.abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.

papers.title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
papers.authors: Daniel Szelogowski
papers.abstract: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between objective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysical computational framework coupling Borbély's two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper's hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33--0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology.

papers.title: SWE-DeceptionBench: Benchmarking Deceptive Behaviors of LLMs Across the Software Development Lifecycle
papers.authors: Xiting Liu, Lin Yang, Yitong Zhang, Jia Li, Shi-Min Hu
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout the software development lifecycle. This growing reliance on LLMs raises concerns about their trustworthiness, with deception posing a particularly important risk. Deceptive behavior takes the form of misleading responses or assistance in fabricating, concealing, or distorting information. To study this behavior, we introduce SWE-DeceptionBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM deception in software engineering. The benchmark covers six lifecycle stages and two deception triggers: Active Deception, where models recognize infeasible or conflicting requirements but still present them as achievable, and Passive Deception, where models help fulfill explicit user requests to mislead others. We further introduce Neutral, Reward, and Pressure conditions to study the effect of external inducements, resulting in 720 test instances in Chinese and English. Evaluating seven mainstream LLMs, we find substantial deception even under the Neutral condition, with aggregate rates of 49.88% for Active Deception and 64.29% for Passive Deception. Deception rates vary across lifecycle stages, and external inducements affect Active and Passive Deception to different extents. We also evaluate lightweight defenses, finding that guard models miss many deceptive requests, and Self-Reminder reduces but does not eliminate deceptive responses. These findings highlight the need for more effective deception detection and mitigation methods to support trustworthy LLM-based software engineering.

papers.title: RegulaTutor: A Theory-Informed Framework for Long-Term Personalized Learning
papers.authors: Yonggang Li, Boqian Han, Rui Sheng, Yushi Sun, Zixin Chen
papers.abstract: Long-term personalized tutoring requires language models to translate a learner's evolving history into appropriate instructional support. Existing LLM-based tutoring systems use memory and retrieval to personalize responses, but the pedagogical rationale linking historical evidence to teaching strategies is not always explicit. We introduce RegulaTutor, a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized tutoring that connects historical evidence, learner interpretation, and learner-facing instruction. Guided by self-regulated learning (SRL) research, its tutoring harness operationalizes a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework for deriving evidence-supported learner interpretations and teaching policies. The resulting policies retain links to their supporting evidence and are updated as new observations arrive. This staged workflow also supports systematic refinement through PairRoute, an offline procedure that uses intermediate execution records to distinguish harness, model, and mixed failures. PairRoute proposes and evaluates targeted harness revisions, then constructs reviewed stage-level supervision for confirmed model failures remaining under the selected harness. We focus this refinement on historical evidence acquisition, which underpins personalized instruction and allows outputs to be checked against learning records and reference answers. RegulaTutor improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average across evaluated model configurations. PairRoute results show an endpoint improvement in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory. Together, these results highlight RegulaTutor's potential to support lifelong personalized education through instructional policies that evolve with learner histories and targeted improvements to the tutoring system.

papers.title: Adversarial Attacks Reveal Divergent Deception Competence in Humans and Generative Language Models
papers.authors: Lucca Pfründer, Riccardo Loconte, Bruno Verschuere, Bennett Kleinberg
papers.abstract: Machine learning models typically outperform humans in deception detection. A threat to machine learning models is their vulnerability to adversarial attacks: subtle yet targeted perturbations of input data that trick a model into misclassification. Yet, this also provides an opportunity: understanding how humans versus machines construct attacks offers new insights into second-order beliefs about deception. In a preregistered experiment (n = 501), we compare the effectiveness, efficiency, and nature of a paraphrasing attack by humans and generative language models on an automated deception classifier. We find that humans were more effective attackers when rewriting truthful statements to be deceptive, while the generative language model was more effective and efficient at making lies sound like truths. Computational text analysis suggests that this is because humans make targeted use of deception cues, while generative language models, instead, apply generic changes that signal truth. The failure to mimic deception is two-sided: while it exposes a blind spot in the machines increasingly used to detect lies, it also means that language models might facilitate successful lying.

papers.title: OWLET: On-Policy Weighted Learning via Evidence Transfer for Video Large Language Model Post-Training
papers.authors: Qitan Lv, Ke Fan, Hong Wang, Wen Wu, Yilin Wang, Bowen Zhou, Feng Wu, Chao Zhang
papers.abstract: Post-training has become a key stage for eliciting reasoning capabilities in Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing post-training methods mainly follow two paradigms: reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). However, they do not fully exploit visual evidence for effective training. RL supervises the policy with a single trajectory-level reward, which is too coarse-grained for video reasoning: the same response-level advantage is applied to every generated token, disregarding that the tokens of a video response are grounded in the visual stream to very different degrees. OPD provides token-level supervision through output-distribution matching, but lacks direct supervision of the spatiotemporal representations that produce those outputs. We observe across extensive experiments that the same model reasons more accurately when its video view combines global temporal context with question-relevant details. Comparing the same student-generated response under this view and uniform sampling reveals changes in token likelihoods and internal representations, providing a training signal for evidence use. Building on this observation, we propose OWLET, an evidence-privileged RL method that derives training signals from a richer teacher view. This view couples uniform global context with question-conditioned local windows, providing visual evidence without requiring a larger model. To better exploit this privileged visual evidence, OWLET introduces (i) \textbf{evidence-aware credit redistribution}, which compares token likelihoods across the two views and redistributes positive response-level advantages according to their relative evidence support; and (ii) \textbf{spatiotemporal state alignment}, which aligns the two views' hidden states on verifier-accepted responses.

papers.title: From Observation to Intervention: Identifiability of Latent User Bias in Human-AI Interaction
papers.authors: Lucas Biéchy, Yuxiao Li, Zhonghao He, Tianyi Alex Qiu
papers.abstract: Alignment methods typically treat user behavior as a reliable proxy for underlying preferences. However, this assumption breaks down when users hold belief-dependent cognitive biases, risking irreversible ``confirmation traps'' and harmful feedback loops. In this paper, we formalize when an AI system can distinguish true user preferences from behavior shaped by cognitive bias. Modeling this interaction as a multi-armed bandit, we first prove a non-identifiability theorem: under passive observation, a static binary biased user produces action trajectory distributions strictly identical to an unbiased user in a transformed environment, forcing any action-only estimator to perform no better than random guessing. We then show that active preference elicitation breaks this observational equivalence. Specifically, we prove that an Observer applying a finite sequence of adversarial zero-reward interventions of length $m_δ$ makes the post-intervention action distributions arbitrarily separable. Our theoretical results suggest that robust alignment requires actively intervening to tell informed preferences from biases.

papers.title: RoleWorld: Knowledge Transfer in World Modeling with Functional Role Abstractions
papers.authors: Bo Xiao, Pu Wang, Ji Feng, Yao-Xiang Ding
papers.abstract: World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions. For generalization, it is desirable for such world models to transfer efficiently to new environments with similar interaction structure and underlying dynamics. Recent approaches encode world dynamics as symbolic rules or executable programs, whose compositional structure in principle affords transfer, but still organize such knowledge around environment-specific objects. To address this limitation, we introduce RoleWorld, a symbolic world modeling approach which uses reusable prototypes and environment-specific parameter values as functional role abstractions to represent how objects behave in interactions. From interaction trajectories, a teacher LLM extracts role prototypes and executable transition rules defined over role instances, together with a skill that guides the actor LLM to use role information in decision making. In a target world, without the teacher, the actor uses this skill together with its current role assignments and parameter estimates, and actively tests a role instance hypothesis through interaction when its uncertainty affects the current decision. Feedback from each action refines role assignments and estimates parameter values online, with no LLM parameter updates and the transition rules held fixed. Experiments on MARS benchmark show that RoleWorld enables robust generalization across environments with significantly altered object behavior, suggesting that functional role abstractions can serve as an effective component for knowledge transfer in world modeling. Project Page: https://future-item.github.io/RoleWorld.

papers.title: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops
papers.authors: Tianyi Huang, Eric Liu, Jay Chong, Emily Yin, Wanqi Zhao
papers.abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM Creativity through Long-Tail Performance
papers.authors: Yichen Wang, Tenghao Huang, Vishakh Padmakumar, Mina Lee
papers.abstract: Creativity benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) vary widely in task and metric design. This raises the question of whether they capture a common notion of creativity. We propose that this shared target can be formalized as task-specific performance in the long tail of a reference input-output distribution, which describes how common input-output pairs are relative to a chosen source of text. We ground this proposition in the novelty-quality product formulation and evaluate it empirically across 15 benchmarks and 26 open-weight models, using n-gram absence from the pretraining data as a novelty proxy. Our results show that creativity benchmarks lie further in the tail regions than standard benchmarks. Moreover, on both creativity and standard benchmarks, model rankings from higher-tail subsets of each benchmark align more closely with human creativity judgments in LM-Arena. Building on these findings, we introduce q@Tail($α$), a lower-cost creativity diagnostic that measures mean task quality on the tail fraction of an existing benchmark. Applying it to creativity-promoting methods reveals substantial room to improve LLM creativity through stronger tail performance.

papers.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
papers.authors: Suorong Yang, Jiaxin Wang, Jiaming Su, Chentao Yue, Furao Shen, Peng Ye, Soujanya Poria
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

papers.title: Network Topology Shapes AI Intervention Effectiveness on Deception: Truth-Telling vs. Investigative Agents
papers.authors: Zhao Song, Ştefan Sarkadi, The Anh Han
papers.abstract: Deploying AI agents to combat dishonest communication is an intuitive response to deception in hybrid human-AI societies. However, the efficacy of such interventions in realistic networked settings remains unclear. We study this problem using an evolutionary game-theoretic model of the Deceiver's Game by extending it to structured networks, where agents can adopt deception, truth-telling, and investigation strategies. We introduce committed AI agents (zealots) fixed to either truth-telling or investigative strategies and conduct agent-based simulations across three network topologies. Our key findings are: (1) passive committed truth-telling agents can amplify adaptive deception by creating exploitable honest partners, whereas investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in the oscillatory regime; (2) intervention effects are non-monotonic in deployment density because committed agents reshape rather than simply suppress the underlying oscillatory dynamics; and (3) response peaks depend on topology, with sampled scale-free populations showing sharp low-density responses and fully connected populations requiring larger committed fractions. Overall, the results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed agents to influence networked deception dynamics.

papers.title: Beyond the Monolithic Interface: A Research Agenda for Plural Conversational AI
papers.authors: Avijit Ghosh, Afifah Kashif, Isabelle Kohout, Zhenzhen Qi
papers.abstract: The current paradigm of artificial intelligence (AI) design elevates conversational chatbot interfaces, making them the default mode through which hundreds of millions of people interact with AI systems globally. This narrative review identifies three related harms produced by the single-voice chatbot interface, drawing on insights from literature in cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design and human computer interaction. Firstly, cognitive offloading of user thinking, secondly, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and thirdly, epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. We then propose multi-persona interfaces, in which multiple personas are presented to the user simultaneously, as a cost-effective intervention that addresses all three harms at once. We ground this intervention in traditions the AI literature has largely overlooked, drawing on techniques from game design and participatory simulation, including the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment. We propose a taxonomy for the future design of multi-persona interfaces, and call for a research agenda that closes the gap between technical pluralistic alignment methods and empirical studies of human-AI interactions with pluralistic interfaces.

papers.title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization
papers.authors: Jiaqi Tian, Ting Long
papers.abstract: On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. However, we find that OPSD methods can progressively degrade previously acquired capabilities: queries that are correctly responded at earlier training stages may become incorrectly responded as optimization proceeds, even the overall performance continues to improve. Further analysis reveals that this degradation coincides with a deterioration of the geometry of hidden representations, characterized by reduced intra-cluster compactness and diminished inter-cluster separation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Representation Geometry Regularization (RGR), which preserves representation geometry during post-training by encouraging compactness within cluster and separation across cluster. RGR can be seamlessly integrated into existing OPSD methods without altering their core optimization procedures. Extensive experiments on multiple OPSD methods and benchmarks show that RGR generally alleviates capability degradation while retaining capability improvements. Our code is available in https://github.com/supermachinelearner/RGR.

papers.title: COFFEQA: Counterfactual-Guided Few-Shot Distillation for LLM Question Answering
papers.authors: Kavinda Kehelella, Sanghamitra Dutta
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation aims to train a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model for resource-constrained environments. However, the process of distillation is typically data-intensive and computationally expensive, particularly for generative tasks. Few-shot distillation offers an alternative by transferring teacher knowledge using limited training samples. However, we observe that few-shot distillation performance is heavily dependent on the choice of these training samples. In fact, we demonstrate that using more uncertain samples near the teacher's decision boundary can significantly deteriorate distillation performance. Motivated by this observation, we propose Counterfactual-guided Few-shot Distillation in Open-book Question Answering (COFFEQA), a novel strategy that aptly uses counterfactuals to provide additional supervision around challenging factual samples. In the generative QA setting, we define a counterfactual as a minimally modified context that induces the teacher to change its response to an alternative answer. We provide geometric insights on how factual-counterfactual pairs can constrain the deviation between the teacher's and student's decision boundaries. We further introduce a new metric, Context Following Difficulty (CFD) that further validates counterfactuals prior to distillation based on agreement with the intended alternative answer and dependence on the modified context. COFFEQA uses CFD-validated factual-counterfactual pairs for few-shot distillation. Experiments across five in-domain and three out-of-domain QA benchmarks using T5 and Qwen2.5 families show that COFFEQA outperforms factual-only distillation baselines under the same few-shot budget. For instance, on TriviaQA, COFFEQA improves over the factual-only baseline by 8.77 average EM points and 9.98 average F1 points under the T5 setting with 32 few-shot pairs.

papers.title: From Instructional Intent to Classroom-Ready Lessons: Investigating Teacher-AI Collaboration in Lesson Authoring for Secondary Computing Education
papers.authors: Tahreem Yasir, Wenbo Li, Deniz Ozturk, Yasitha Rajapaksha, Dmitri Droujkov, Xiaoyi Tian, Tiffany M. Barnes
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly studied as a tool for supporting lesson authoring; the creation and adaptation of classroom materials, yet little is known about how it should fit into secondary computing teachers' subject-specific practices. We conducted two complementary qualitative studies with eight secondary computing teachers: focus groups examining existing authoring practices and a think-aloud study using LessonBuilder, a structured AI-supported lesson authoring system, as a research probe. We found that teachers' instructional intentions developed through creating, inspecting, and adapting materials, while teachers selectively delegated tasks to AI and retained responsibility for judging classroom readiness. The think-aloud sessions further showed how examining AI-generated materials prompted teachers to clarify and refine their intentions, making authoring an ongoing negotiation between what teachers intended and what the AI produced. In the context of computing lessons, classroom readiness also involved considering how programming materials and supporting guidance matched students' understanding and intended learning goals. We synthesize these findings into a conceptual model explaining how teachers coordinate instructional intent, AI assistance, and judgments of classroom readiness during lesson authoring. We derive design recommendations for supporting this coordination while preserving teacher control and addressing computing-specific authoring needs.

papers.title: Data Science for the Next Millennium: A Ubiquitous Review
papers.authors: Prof. P. P. Chavan Zine Sanskruti, Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. A. J. Shaikh
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: Data science has grown from a set of statistical and computational techniques into a field that brings together different disciplines to turn complex data into useful insights. This review looks at how data science was defined, applied, and studied across different fields from 2018 to 2023. The review followed a structured approach and drew on research identified through several scholarly sources. The initial search found 105 articles in databases and platforms including EBSCO, Taylor & Francis, Wiley, Sage, Emerald, and Google Scholar. After screening, 40 studies were examined in detail. The review considered each study’s purpose, findings, application area, country, analytical tools, and research type. The findings show that data science brings together computer science, statistics, business analysis, engineering, machine learning, automation, and subject-specific knowledge. Education and healthcare were the most common areas of application in the studies reviewed. Researchers used a wide range of methods and tools, including machine learning, artificial intelligence, regression, neural networks, data mining, SQL, Python, R, CRISP-DM, statistical analysis, optimization, and data visualization. Empirical research made up the largest share of the studies, though conceptual papers and reviews also contributed to the field. Overall, the review suggests that successful data science depends on more than algorithms. It also requires reliable data, privacy safeguards, relevant skills, thoughtful interpretation, ethical practice, and a clear understanding of the problem being addressed.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Cybersecurity for the Metaverse: Research Challenges and Opportunities
papers.authors: Prof. V. N. Dhakane Thange Sakshi, Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. P. P. Randive
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: The metaverse connects immersive interfaces, virtual environments, artificial intelligence, extended reality, cloud and edge computing, digital twins, communication networks, and blockchain-based services. These technologies can support education, entertainment, commerce, training, and digital ownership, but they also create a broad, evolving cybersecurity surface. Identity theft, privacy loss, abnormal network activity, deepfake-based impersonation, and digital-asset fraud can occur across interconnected layers. This paper presents an independently written, student-oriented study of AI-assisted cybersecurity for the metaverse. It focuses on intelligent authentication, AI-based intrusion detection, privacy-aware learning, and protection of blockchain and NFT ecosystems. The paper describes a layered framework in which relevant security data are collected, processed with suitable AI methods, converted into risk decisions, and followed by proportionate responses. The study also discusses data quality, latency, interoperability, privacy, model attacks, and the need for human oversight. The central view is that AI should complement established cybersecurity controls rather than replace them.

papers.title: Generative AI in Entrepreneurship: Applications, Opportunities, Challenges and Future Directions
papers.authors: Neha Nain, Dr Monika Sharma, Dr Gunjan Bhayana, Ms Priya, Ms Poonam, Dr Yashna
papers.journal: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering and Management (IRJAEM)
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming entrepreneurship by helping entrepreneurs generate ideas, analyze information, create content, develop business models, support marketing, and make decisions. This review examines the growing role of GenAI in entrepreneurial activities, with a focus on opportunity recognition, creativity, innovation, SMEs, emerging economies, and responsible AI use. GenAI can reduce resource constraints and provide affordable support to small businesses, but challenges such as inaccurate information, overdependence, privacy concerns, and unequal digital skills remain. The article highlights the importance of human–AI collaboration and introduces the concept of AI entrepreneurial capability, which includes AI literacy, effective prompting, evaluation of AI outputs, decision-making, and responsible use of AI. The review concludes that future entrepreneurship should focus not only on using AI to generate more opportunities but also on improving the quality, sustainability, and responsible development of those opportunities.

papers.title: Muscular Performance and Hemodynamic Responses to Circuit and Traditional Resistance Training at Different Intensities: A Randomized Crossover Study
papers.authors: Behzad Taati, Soheil Khanipoor Lashkariani, Dorsa Arabshahi, Paulo Henrique Marchetti
papers.journal: International Journal of Strength and Conditioning
papers.abstract: This study compared the acute effects of circuit and traditional resistance training (RT) performed at different intensities on muscular performance and hemodynamic responses. Ten resistance-trained men (25.8±4.3 years, BMI: 24±2.3 kg/m2, RT experience: 4.3±2.5 years) completed four randomized protocols: high-intensity circuit (HC), moderate-intensity circuit (MC), high-intensity traditional (HT), and moderate-intensity traditional (MT). Each protocol was performed twice, once for muscular performance and once for cardiovascular assessment. Sessions involved two sets of bench press and leg press performed at either 80% or 60% one-repetition maximum (1RM). Hemodynamic data were rank-transformed using the aligned rank transform for factorial analysis of main effects and interactions, while muscular and perceptual responses were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA or Friedman tests, followed by appropriate post-hoc comparisons and effect sizes (ES). Systolic blood pressure (p<0.001, large ES), heart rate (p<0.001, very large ES), and rate-pressure product (p<0.001, very large ES) increased significantly post-exercise across all conditions and remained elevated at 10 min (p<0.001, large–very large ES). No post-exercise hypotension was observed. Maximum repetitions and total load lifted were greater at moderate intensity (p<0.0001, large ES), accompanied by lower ratings of fatigue (p<0.0001, large ES). No significant differences were found between circuit and traditional structures. High-intensity protocols, regardless of structure, elicited greater cardiovascular stress and fatigue, whereas moderate-intensity RT enhanced performance with lower physiological strain. These results highlight exercise intensity as the primary determinant of acute cardiovascular and muscular responses.

papers.title: When AI becomes a friend: Emotional support, social displacement, and university belonging among Nigerian freshmen
papers.authors: Uwemedimo Isaiah, Ebubechukwu Joshua Chukwuemelie, Saviour Sunday Effiong, Winifred Chris Inwang, Chineye Adili-George
papers.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions and virtual assistants among university students raises concerns about whether they alleviate loneliness and enhance belonging or substitute for offline relationships, particularly during the socially demanding transition into university. However, little is known about how freshmen experience this tension in under-resourced higher education contexts such as Nigeria. This study investigated the paradoxical role of AI companions in shaping loneliness, belonging, and emotional well-being among freshmen during this transition.
