Using a qualitative case study within an interpretivist paradigm, semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with 36 participants: 30 freshmen at the University of Uyo, Nigeria, reporting daily relational AI use exceeding 30 minutes, and 6 student affairs counsellors. Five themes emerged: (a) AI companions as emotional scaffolding, (b) the displacement dilemma, (c) the authenticity paradox, (d) institutional belonging in the age of algorithmic companionship, and (e) the conditional role of offline social capital. Critically, even minimal offline social anchors like a roommate, religious fellowship, or study partner appeared to determine whether AI use remained supplementary or became substitutive. This resembled a contextual "digital Matthew effect" where students with stronger offline social resources used AI more complementarily, whereas those with fewer offline anchors described more substitutive use. The study concludes that relational AI can complement or substitute for offline social relationships among university freshmen, depending on their offline social resources and patterns of use. It recommends digital literacy, early identification of substitutive AI use, and strengthened opportunities for meaningful offline connection

papers.title: Mapping the new frontier: Current perspectives on evolving gastrointestinal pathophysiology
papers.authors: Gautam Ray
papers.abstract: With rapid advancement in cutting edge basic research in genetics, multi-omics, bioengineering and artificial intelligence focusing on improvement in precision medicine, the study of gastrointestinal (GI) pathophysiology has transitioned from describing GI conditions as isolated structural disorders to a systems-biology approach which recognize them as a complex network of interconnected systemic and functional diseases.It emphasizes the "interactome" -the complex crosstalk between the gut microbiome, the enteric nervous system, the mucosal immune system, and the enteroendocrine system -with associative effects on distant organs, metabolic, and immune function of the body.The gut is thus a central regulatory hub for metabolic health, immune education, and possibly neurocognitive function.Current perspectives emphasize three primary pillars in disease pathogenesis, namely the role of low-grade chronic inflammation and the integrity of the epithelial barrier (leaky gut), the metabolic influence of the microbiome, and its effect on functioning of distant organs.This narrative review will broaden the above perspectives highlighting the effect of smouldering inflammation affecting the epithelial barrier (its causative metabolomic signatures, the resulting epithelial plasticity, and its involvement in local and systemic diseases), the gut-microbiomedistant organ axis, the gut-metabolic axis (contributing to systemic inflammation and atherosclerosis), immuno-gastroenterology (related to GI cancers and other diseases), and advances in bioengineering (three dimensional in vitro modelling like organ-on-a-chip and personalized organoids) for better delineation of disease pathogenesis, biomarkers and precision therapeutics.Further, the utility of artificial intelligence in precision diagnostics (radiology, histology, multi-omics) and in shaping future therapies will be discussed as also the present limitations.

papers.title: Neurophysiology of first- vs third-person moral decision-making
papers.authors: Roberta  Antonia Allegretta, Laura Angioletti, Michela Balconi
papers.abstract: Despite extensive research on moral dilemmas, little is known about how perspective (first- vs. third-person) shapes neural dynamics during interpersonal communication. This study investigated the electrophysiological underpinnings of moral reasoning during an interaction by comparing discussions of third-person and first-person moral dilemmas. 28 participants discussed two moral dilemmas: one involving a fictional decision-maker (third-person perspective) and one requiring participants to take a personal stance (first-person perspective). Electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was simultaneously recorded from each participant. Power spectral density analyses focused on delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands across frontal, temporo-central, and parieto-occipital regions. Results indicated that delta and theta oscillations were significantly higher in frontal and temporo-central regions compared to posterior sites, highlighting their role in emotional regulation, attentional allocation, and socio-cognitive integration during moral communication, regardless of the perspective. Also, gamma activity was enhanced in parietooccipital areas, reflecting attentional modulation to socially salient information. Crucially, beta power increased specifically during first- compared to third-person discussions, suggesting heightened self-referential processing and emotional engagement when participants directly evaluated their own moral choices. These findings reveal distinct EEG oscillatory dynamics underlying moral reasoning in social interaction, emphasizing perspective-specific beta activity linked to personal involvement, alongside perspective-invariant mechanisms of emotional and cognitive coordination. The study contributes to a deeper understanding of how interpersonal communication shapes moral decision- making at the neural level.

papers.title: Emerging Technologies for Employment Competence Development in Vocational Education
papers.authors: Yu Lei, Yuen Choo
papers.journal: International Journal of Web-Based Learning and Teaching Technologies
papers.abstract: This study explored how emerging technologies, including big data and AI, are reshaping employment competence development in technical and vocational education and training. Drawing on publications from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus databases between 2015 and 2025, the research applied bibliometric and qualitative analysis to examine knowledge evolution and research trends. The findings indicated a steady increase in scholarly output, with China and several Asia-Pacific countries playing leading roles, although international collaboration remained limited. The field shifted from early adoption of immersive technologies to more integrated, data-driven, and intelligent approaches. Key application models and implementation challenges were also identified. The study highlighted the need for balanced skill development, industry-responsive curricula, and more inclusive digital environments to support sustainable advancement in vocational education.

papers.title: Mobile Generative AI Literacy and English Writing Self-Efficacy: The Role of AI Feedback Engagement in Higher Education
papers.authors: Liu Dan, Zuwati Hasim, Jia Wei Lim
papers.journal: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
papers.abstract: This study examines the relationship between mobile Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) literacy and English writing self-efficacy (EWSE) among university students, with AI feedback engagement (AFE) proposed as a mediating mechanism. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 312 university students in China through validated self-report measures. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test the proposed relationships and mediation effects. The results show that mobile GenAI literacy (MGL) significantly predicts AFE (β = 0.563, p < 0.001) and EWSE (β = 0.182, p = 0.003), while AFE significantly predicts writing self-efficacy (β = 0.478, p < 0.001). AFE partially mediates the relationship between MGL and writing self-efficacy, accounting for approximately 59.6% of the total effect. The model explains 41.2% of the variance in writing self-efficacy. These findings indicate that the educational value of MGL extends beyond technological competence, with active engagement in AI-generated feedback serving as an important mechanism for strengthening writing confidence. The study highlights the importance of pedagogical approaches that promote critical evaluation, reflective use, and meaningful engagement with AI feedback.

papers.title: AI-Powered Personalised Mobile Learning Using Large Language Models: Design, Implementation, and a Simulation-Based Feasibility Evaluation
papers.authors: S. Murugaanandam, J. Nithyashri, Partheeban Nagappan, M. Jamuna Rani, Neeththi Aadithiya Balakrishnan
papers.journal: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies (iJIM)
papers.abstract: The significance of mobile learning (m-learning) has been greatly highlighted by the advent of technology due to its flexibility, accessibility and capability of being used to learn at any time and place. The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers great potential for creating adaptive, conversational and content-aware learning experiences via mobile apps. Most existing mobile-learning systems, however, still provide largely static content and shallow personalisation, which limits sustained learner engagement and adaptive support. This paper presents the design and implementation of an Android-based, LLM-powered personalised m-learning platform that integrates four components: a conversational tutoring agent, an Item-Response-Theory (IRT)-based adaptive quiz engine, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) content-recommendation module, and an analytics-driven feedback loop. We describe the system architecture, the prompt-orchestration and knowledge-tracing pipelines, and a rigorous quasi-experimental evaluation protocol (pre-/post-test, System Usability Scale (SUS), and engagement analytics) designed for a controlled classroom deployment. To validate the core algorithmic contributions prior to human-subject trials, we conduct two simulation-based feasibility studies: (i) a synthetic-learner simulation comparing the adaptive difficulty engine against a static item sequence and (ii) a retrieval-precision benchmark comparing RAG-based content recommendation against keyword-matching on a synthetic tagged corpus. The adaptive engine delivered quiz items within the optimal challenge zone (0.4 < P(correct) < 0.8) for 77.8% of interactions, compared with 40.8% for the static baseline, while the RAG recommender achieved substantially higher retrieval precision at every cut-off (P@10 = 0.845 versus 0.483 for keyword matching). These results provide algorithmic evidence that the proposed adaptive and retrieval components behave as intended and motivate the full-scale classroom evaluation described in the protocol. The paper concludes with a discussion of design implications, limitations, and a concrete plan for the human-subject study and future extensions of the platform.

papers.title: The AI Divide in Academic Libraries: A Comparative Bibliometric Analysis of Technological Determinism vs Information Equity (2010–2025)
papers.authors: Sudhanshu Shekhar Mishra
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
papers.abstract: Background: While the exponential growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries is extensively documented, existing bibliometric scholarship has largely treated the global research landscape as a monolith. This oversight has led to a saturation of "generalist" reports that fail to address critical regional and thematic disparities.  Methods: This study analyzes 512 Scopus-indexed publications (2010–2025) using a dual-methodological approach: quantitative science mapping via VOSviewer (1.6.20) and qualitative thematic critique. We specifically contrast the research priorities of dominant geopolitical producers (China and the USA) against the emerging narrative from the Global South, with a primary focus on India.  Results: The analysis reveals a fundamental "two-speed" adoption model. The Global North prioritizes high-tech interventions—including robotics, advanced machine learning for metadata automation, and generative models—aimed at enhancing operational efficiency. In contrast, the Global South, led by pivotal recent insights from India (Mishra, 2026), emphasizes AI as a strategic survival mechanism for bridging information literacy gaps and democratizing access in resource- constrained environments.

papers.title: From ChatGPT to Classroom Practice: A Visualized Protocol for Generative AI-Supported Feedback, Critical Thinking, and EFL Writing Instruction
papers.authors: Liling Liao, Qu Liu, Ziyue Lin
papers.abstract: This study examined associations between Visualized Protocol-guided ChatGPT Writing Instruction (VP-CGWIP), writing-score trajectories, critical-thinking dispositions, and post-intervention feedback judgment in an English as a foreign language (EFL) course. Two intact second-year university classes completed a ten-week intervention and four-week follow-up. The complete-case sample included 43 experimental and 42 control participants. Writing was assessed using the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) Task 2 criteria, and dispositions using the Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory-Chinese Version (CTDI-CV). The judgment task was administered only at the immediate (T1) and delayed (T2) posttests. The experimental-minus-control differences in overall-writing change were 0.48 points at T1 (pointwise 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.26-0.70) and 0.44 at T2 (0.22-0.66). The overall score and all four writing dimensions had interaction p values below 0.05 after post hoc Holm adjustment across 18 tests. Among seven disposition dimensions, only analyticity had an adjusted interaction p value below 0.05; the total score also met this threshold. Judgment accuracy was higher in the experimental class at both posttests, whereas the adjusted p values for perception-gain correlations exceeded 0.05. Log and journal summaries provided descriptive context. Because one class represented each condition, participant-level models cannot separate condition from class. These exploratory findings describe observed associations over the four-week follow-up; measurement limitations constrain their interpretation.

papers.title: Towards Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: A Review of Perturbation and Backpropagation-Based Methods
papers.authors: Abir Hamrouni, Thuraya N.I. Alrumaih, Mahmoud Ltaeif, Monia Hamdi, Hela Elmannai, Ridha Ejbali
papers.abstract: Machine and deep learning algorithms have been proven their efficiency in the medical domain. This is particularly noticeable in medical imaging, where these algorithms have demonstrated exceptional capabilities, often surpassing human experts in detecting diseases, segmenting anatomical structures, and in aiding diagnosis. However, despite their high performance, the non-transparency of these models has raised concerns about trust and explainability, especially in critical domains, such as healthcare. Explainable AI (XAI) has emerged as a promising field that, aims to make the decision-making processes of AI systems more interpretable and understandable to humans. By offering clear, human-understandable justifications, XAI enhances clinicians' trust in AI-assisted decisions, and supports the safe integration of these technologies into clinical workflows. This paper focuses on perturbation-based and backpropagation-based explainability methods that are widely adopted for convolutional neural networks in medical imaging. We intend to provide deeper insight into the relevance of XAI methods in medical imaging. We propose a structured taxonomy that categorizes these methods into perturbation and backpropagation-based approaches. For each category, we highlight their respective strengths, limitations, and areas of applicability. Furthermore, we discuss the key challenges hindering the adoption of XAI and identify promising research directions to bridge the gap between high-performance AI models and their responsible deployment in real-world healthcare environments.

papers.title: AI Adoption, AI Literacy, and Employee Performance: The Mediating Role of Work Autonomy in MSMEs
papers.authors: Arif Tirtana, Sudarmiatin Sudarmiatin, Agus Hermawan, Wening Patmi Rahayu
papers.abstract: This study aims to examine the effects of AI Adoption and AI Literacy on Employee Performance and to investigate the mediating role of Work Autonomy in the MSME context. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed using questionnaire data from 300 respondents, analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 3. The measurement model was assessed through reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while the structural model was evaluated using path coefficients and indirect effects. The results indicate that AI Adoption and AI Literacy are positively and significantly associated with both Work Autonomy and Employee Performance, and Work Autonomy is positively and significantly associated with Employee Performance. Work Autonomy also partially mediates the relationships between AI Adoption and Employee Performance and between AI Literacy and Employee Performance. This study contributes to the literature by integrating AI Adoption, AI Literacy, and Work Autonomy into a single framework to explain Employee Performance in MSMEs. The findings highlight Work Autonomy as an important mechanism through which employees’ AI adoption and literacy can translate into improved performance, offering a more nuanced understanding of the human and organizational implications of AI in the workplace.

papers.title: The dynamic bodily self across lifespan: Agency, ownership, and the plasticity of internal body models
papers.authors: Amir Jahanian Najafabadi, Matthew R. Longo, Roman Liepelt
papers.abstract: Two fundamental aspects of research on bodily self-consciousness, agency and body ownership, have recently seen exponential growth. The seminal paper of Botvinick and Cohen in 1998 provided a vital psychophysical tool for studying the bodily self - the rubber hand illusion, in which one feels as if an external object becomes a part of one's body. Recent motor control views of ownership highlight the influence of agency, the sense that one is in control of one's movements. Technological advancements have facilitated more ecologically valid experimental paradigms, such as virtual versions of the rubber hand illusion, furthering our understanding of the mechanisms through which the brain generates agency and ownership sensations. Recent findings suggest that agency and ownership can interact while remaining dissociable, as one may experience agency over an object that is not embodied or ownership of an object that cannot be controlled. Understanding the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying agency and ownership is critical for addressing the challenges of healthy aging. As sensory-motor precision declines across the lifespan, maintaining a coherent sense of body and control becomes essential for mobility, the successful adoption of assistive technologies, and overall cognitive resilience. This review synthesizes current findings on the agency-ownership interaction, discusses its neurobiological substrates, and explores its transformative potential for the design of "self-inclusive" prosthetics and brain-machine interfaces. We conclude by outlining a framework showing how optimization of these processes can support functional independence and psychological well-being in an aging population.

papers.title: Can artificial intelligence produce lawyers or merely law graduates? The crisis of competency in South African legal education
papers.authors: Melisa Mutsa Chawaremera
papers.journal: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education is fundamentally reshaping how students access and present knowledge. Within legal education particularly, AI tools increasingly enable students to generate summaries, conduct research, draft legal content and retrieve information with minimal engagement in traditional legal reasoning processes. At the same time, South African law faculties remain tasked with cultivating industry ready candidate legal practitioners who possess critical thinking abilities, ethical judgment, persuasive communication skills as well as strong legal research competencies. This creates an important pedagogical tension. While AI may enhance efficiency and technological fluency, its uncritical use may simultaneously undermine the intellectual rigour required for competent legal practice. This paper critically examines whether the growing integration of AI in legal education supports or compromises the cultivation of graduate attributes required within the South African legal profession. Using a doctrinal and conceptual methodology, the study analyses the graduate competency frameworks advanced by the Council on Higher Education and the South African Qualifications Authority. It further interrogates whether AI tools meaningfully contribute toward the development of legal reasoning, ethical sensitivity, drafting proficiency and contextual interpretation, all of which remain central to professional legal readiness. The paper argues that although AI presents significant opportunities for enhancing legal research efficiency and technological competence, overreliance on these tools risks producing graduates who are technologically capable yet jurisprudentially underdeveloped. It contends that AI cannot replace the human processes of critical engagement, ethical reflection and contextual legal interpretation that define legal education within a constitutional democracy. The study concludes that responsible AI integration in legal education requires careful pedagogical design and ethical oversight to ensure that innovation does not come at the expense of professional competence and intellectual integrity.

papers.title: AI-Powered Digital Transformation in Mathematics Education as a Strategic Business Ecosystem: A Systematic Review of Governance, Capability and Equity Conditions
papers.authors: Thabisa T. Maqoqa
papers.journal: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
papers.abstract: This systematic review examines artificial intelligence (AI)-powered digital transformation in mathematics education as a strategic business ecosystem issue rather than only a classroom technology concern. The objective is to synthesise how AI-supported pedagogies create educational value, what ecosystem risks accompany adoption, and which organisational capabilities and governance conditions enable responsible implementation. Guided by PRISMA 2020 principles, peer-reviewed empirical and conceptual studies published between 2018 and 2025 were identified from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, Education Source and Google Scholar. A total of 3,241 records were initially retrieved; after duplicate removal, screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 203 studies were included for structured extraction, quality appraisal and thematic synthesis. The evidence was analysed through a business ecosystem lens focusing on value co-creation, stakeholder interdependence, digital governance, teacher capability, infrastructure readiness and equity. The findings show that AI tools can strengthen adaptive practice, formative feedback, diagnostic analytics, multimodal representation and teacher decision-making when they are embedded in coherent institutional strategies. However, strategic value is weakened by digital inequality, data privacy risks, algorithmic opacity, cognitive offloading, platform dependence, weak curriculum alignment and insufficient teacher capability. The study contributes an ecosystem strategy framework that positions AI as a pedagogical and organisational mediator within a network of learners, teachers, institutions, technology providers, policy bodies, infrastructure actors and communities. It concludes that AI adoption in mathematics education should be strategy-led, ethically governed and capability-driven. Sustainable value creation requires inclusive infrastructure, teacher professional development, data governance, assessment redesign, transparent procurement and partnerships that protect educational equity while enabling innovation in resource-constrained and digitally uneven contexts.

papers.title: A TPACK–Bloom’s Taxonomy Hybrid Framework for Integrating Technology in Accounting Education in Sub-Saharan African Countries
papers.authors: Emmanuel Kojo Oseifuah
papers.journal: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital technologies necessitates a transformative approach to accounting education, particularly in developing countries. Building on Mishra and Koehler’s (2006) foundational assertion that there is no universally accepted method for integrating technology into the educational curricula, this study proposes a TPACK-Bloom’s Taxonomy framework to articulate how technology enhances learning in accounting education. TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) offers a multidimensional lens for aligning technological tools with pedagogical strategies and disciplinary content, ensuring that emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and data analytics are contextually and instructionally relevant. Bloom’s Taxonomy complements this by structuring cognitive development across six hierarchical levels, ranging from remembering to creating, within technology-enhanced learning environments. Together, these two frameworks provide a versatile tool for designing curriculum interventions that foster digital literacy, critical thinking, and professional competence. This study makes three key contributions to the literature. First, it bridges the gap between technology adoption and pedagogical effectiveness by linking digital tools to cognitive learning outcomes. Second, it contributes to human capital development by promoting the integration of technical, cognitive, and digital competencies. Third, it supports organisational transformation by offering a practical, scalable approach to technology-enhanced learning in resource-constrained contexts.

papers.title: Governing Academic Integrity in AI-Enabled Higher Education Ecosystems: A Systematic-Narrative Review of Assessment Technology, Risk and Strategy
papers.authors: Thabisa T. Maqoqa
papers.journal: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
papers.abstract: AI-enabled assessment technologies are increasingly used by higher education institutions to protect academic integrity, scale online assessment and respond strategically to generative artificial intelligence. This paper examines how online proctoring, automated scoring, AI writing detection, and learning analytics risk flagging reshape institutional governance, stakeholder trust, and assessment strategy in higher education business ecosystems. Using a systematic-narrative review approach informed by PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, the study synthesises peer-reviewed literature and authoritative policy guidance published between 2015 and 2025. The analysis is organised around an integrated theoretical framework that combines assessment validity, academic integrity values, algorithmic accountability, and ecosystem strategy. The findings show that AI-enabled assessment can support identity verification, monitoring capacity, workflow triage and timely feedback when deployed as human-governed decision support rather than automated adjudication. However, over-reliance on surveillance and detection creates strategic risks: false positives, bias against linguistically diverse students, privacy intrusion, opaque decision-making, weakened due process and construct distortion when assessments measure surveillance compliance instead of intended learning outcomes. The review further shows that institutional legitimacy depends less on the technical promise of tools and more on governance capability, including proportionality, transparency, contestability, equity auditing, privacy protection and authentic assessment redesign. The paper contributes to business ecosystem and strategy scholarship by positioning academic integrity technology as a strategic governance issue within higher education service ecosystems. It recommends integrity-by-design, cross-functional AI governance, vendor accountability and assessment strategies that preserve fairness, validity and stakeholder trust.

papers.title: Exploring The Role of AI and Educational Factors in Shaping Academic Performance in Accounting Education in South African Universities: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: Nokuthula Ngobese
papers.journal: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming teaching and learning in accounting education. While AI technologies offer opportunities to enhance learning outcomes, academic performance is also influenced by broader educational factors such as teacher competence, institutional support, curriculum design, and student engagement. This study investigates the role of AI and educational factors in shaping academic performance in accounting education through a systematic literature review of studies published between 2020 and 2025. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a structured search of major academic databases yielded 168 initial records. After screening and eligibility assessment, 28 studies were retained for final analysis. The review synthesizes empirical evidence on AI applications in accounting education and identifies key factors influencing student performance. The study is grounded in Human Capital Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, which provide insights into how technological and educational investments influence learning outcomes. The findings reveal that AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI tools, predictive analytics, and automated assessment platforms enhance academic performance through personalized learning and data-driven feedback. However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends on teacher digital competence, student motivation, curriculum alignment, and institutional support. The study proposes an integrated conceptual framework linking AI adoption and educational factors to academic performance in accounting education. The findings provide implications for educators, policymakers, and curriculum developers seeking to improve accounting education in the digital era.

papers.title: Electroencephalography Based Analysis of Brainwave Responses During I Kuan Tao Three Treasures Practice
papers.authors: Ying-Chin Chang, Yung-ching Lai, Chung-Yen Liao, Hendry Hendry
papers.abstract: I-Kuan Tao emphasizes spiritual cultivation through the practice of the Three Treasures, which is believed to influence physical, mental, and spiritual well-being through changes in brain wave activity. The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of Tao-receiving of I-Kuan Tao and the practice of the Three Treasures on brain wave patterns. To achieve this, 32 volunteers were recruited, and their brain waves were measured using an electroencephalograph developed by Neurosky Company. Brain wave data were collected under various conditions. Initially, brain waves were measured for 3 minutes in the natural state with 32 samples. After Tao-receiving, brain waves were measured again in the natural state for 3 minutes with 15 samples. Subsequently, brain waves were measured for another 3 minutes during the practice of the Three Treasures, with 32 samples collected. After one month of practicing the Three Treasures, participants were invited back for a second round of testing. In the natural state, brain waves were measured for 3 minutes with 4 samples. Following the Three Treasures practice, brain waves were measured again for 3 minutes with 4 samples. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and paired-sample t-tests. The results showed a very significant difference (p < 0.001) in attention improvement and fatigue reduction. The δ wave showed a very significant difference (p < 0.01), while the relaxation index (Meditation) and pressure index (Pressure) demonstrated a significant difference (p < 0.05). In other words, after participating in the Tao-receiving of I-Kuan Tao, there was an immediate improvement in attention, meditation, δ and θ waves, along with a reduction in fatigue and pressure, contributing positively to the coordination of body and mind. Furthermore, after one month of practicing the Three Treasures, significant changes were observed in brain wave patterns in the natural state, including reduced fatigue and increased intensity of the δ wave. This indicates that sustained practice of the Three Treasures enhances the production of δ waves, facilitating deeper sleep and effectively reducing fatigue.

papers.title: A Human-Centered Web Technology for Reproducible Statistical and Machine-Learning Analysis of Heterogeneous Data
papers.authors: Mariano Vargas-Santiago, Diana A. León-Velasco, Sergio Quezada García, Ricardo Isaac Cázares Ramírez, E.-G. Espinosa–Martínez
papers.abstract: The analysis of heterogeneous tabular datasets remains challenging for non-specialist users because data preparation, statistical diagnostics, algorithm selection, model evaluation, and result interpretation are frequently distributed across separate software environments. This manuscript presents a reproducible web-based technology that integrates data ingestion, automated data-quality assessment, statistical validation, transparent rule-based analytical guidance, supervised and unsupervised machine learning, and interactive visual analytics within a unified workflow. The platform supports commonly used tabular formats and employs a modular, containerized architecture to support portability and reproducible analytical execution. Rather than autonomously selecting a supposedly optimal model, the recommendation mechanism identifies the analytical task, screens incompatible methods, detects semantic ambiguity, generates methodological warnings, and prioritizes compatible candidate models using explicit and inspectable rules. Final supervised-model selection is based on empirical cross-validation within the training data. The technology is evaluated through functional tests on heterogeneous health and financial datasets, predictive and clustering experiments, controlled recommendation-engine and schema-robustness experiments, computational benchmarks, and a usability study involving users with limited programming experience. In a COVID-19 dataset containing 95,839 records, the platform supported two-code and three-code patient-classification experiments, descriptive clustering, and data-quality analysis while transparently identifying class imbalance, predictor missingness, repeated predictor profiles, and performance limitations. A grouped-profile sensitivity analysis further showed that the principal classification results did not deteriorate when identical selected predictor configurations were prevented from occurring in both the training and held-out partitions. Controlled schema-robustness experiments correctly identified all prespecified unambiguous analytical tasks, detected all prespecified semantic ambiguities, rejected incompatible supervised configurations, and produced no silent acceptance of ambiguous or invalid cases. The recommender-specific evaluation also showed that the highest-ranked rule-based candidate does not necessarily coincide with the cross-validation-best model, reinforcing its role as a decision-support mechanism rather than an autonomous model-selection procedure. An exploratory laboratory usability evaluation with twelve non-specialist participants produced an average task-success rate of 95.3% and a mean System Usability Scale score of 86.7±5.2. These values correspond to aggregate results recorded during the original laboratory experiment. Because the participant-level observer logs and individual SUS responses were not retained in the available study materials, the usability results are interpreted descriptively and are not presented as population-level estimates. The results indicate that the proposed architecture can reduce technical barriers while preserving analytical traceability, methodological transparency, and user control. The platform therefore provides an extensible foundation for human-supervised, reproducible analysis of heterogeneous tabular data rather than an autonomous statistical or machine-learning decision-making system.

papers.title: An Exploratory Pilot Study of Cognitive Factors Influencing the Adoption of AI Coding Agents in Agile Development Teams
papers.authors: Paschal Ugochukwu, Aisha Kazeem, Angela Bland, Brian Black, Lesley J. Strawderman
papers.abstract: This study considers the cognitive factors influencing the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents among software engineers in Agile development environments. In this context, Transparency refers to the degree to which an AI system’s decision processes are clear or understandable to its users, while Trust denotes the confidence developers place in the reliability and correctness of AI-generated code. Specifically, it analyzes the roles of Transparency and Trust as predictors of developers’ Behavioral Intention to deploy AI-generated code. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design administered to 19 Agile software professionals, this study uses descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and simple and multiple linear regression to test a mediation model based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). In this exploratory pilot sample, Trust emerged as the strongest predictor of Behavioral Intention (β = 0.64, p = 0.007), though findings should be interpreted cautiously given the limited sample size. Trust demonstrated the strongest association with Behavioral Intention, while Transparency showed a non-significant positive association with Trust. The observed pattern is consistent with a possible indirect relationship, although mediation was not confirmed in this sample. This evidence suggests that organizations seeking to improve AI adoption in development teams should prioritize the reliability and accuracy of AI tools, conditions that encourage trust, over transparency features alone. This study adds to the cognitive engineering literature on human–AI interaction in high-cognitive-demand work environments.

papers.title: Ecological Invisibility in Classroom AI Use: Rethinking Pedagogical Efficiency, Sustainability and Teacher Agency
papers.authors: Hilal Uğraş, Mustafa Uğraş
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in everyday teaching, yet its environmental costs remain largely absent from how educators reason about its use. This study examines how 22 teachers working in public schools in Türkiye, each with at least one academic year of experience integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom, interpret and navigate these technologies at the intersection of pedagogical effectiveness, professional responsibility, and ecological sustainability. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed through Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis within a generic interpretive qualitative design. Five themes were developed. The first three show teachers actively mediating AI through pedagogical judgment, a restructured professional agency, and a renewed relational and epistemic role. The study’s central contribution lies in the final two: for almost all participants, AI’s ecological cost was not unknown but rendered invisible in everyday practice—a professionally produced ordering of attention enacted through the very pedagogical agency that makes teachers effective. When this cost surfaced, teachers managed rather than resolved the tension through pedagogical rationalization and self-reported intentions toward ecologically motivated restraint, while extending their moral concern to students’ cognitive dependence. Ecological invisibility thus emerges not as a knowledge deficit but as a by-product of professional attention—one that teacher education and policy should address through a critical AI literacy integrating ethical, ecological, and pedagogical dimensions.

papers.title: How Multi-Actor Resource Exchange Enables Sustainable Rural Tourism: Value Co-Creation in Zhushan Village, China
papers.authors: Jiaqi Zhang, Qing Hu
papers.abstract: Rural tourism sustainability depends on economic returns, community participation, cultural continuity, and ecological stewardship. This study uses a resource exchange perspective to explain how multiple actors co-create value in rural tourism and how institutional coordination and service interaction transform resources. Drawing on more than 90 days of fieldwork in Zhushan Village, western Hunan, China, between July 2021 and July 2025, the case study uses 96 semi-structured interviews, participant observation, and supplementary sources. Qualitative content analysis combined deductive and inductive procedures. The findings show that actors form exchange relationships around heterogeneous resources, including capital, land, dwellings, skills, knowledge, information, affect, reputation, and institutional support. Resource complementarity and cost–benefit assessments shape relationship formation, while reciprocity and fairness sustain cooperation. Institutional coordination stabilises resource commitment through arrangements for participation, rights, responsibilities, and benefit allocation; service interaction expands resource use through joint practice. New uses and related claims for participation and benefits then prompt institutional adjustment. Feedback between the two mechanisms connects dispersed resources in tourism operations and collaboration over public affairs, producing economic, social, cultural, emotional, and ecological value manifestations.

papers.title: Between Pressure and Coping: Stress Management Strategies and Social Support as Predictors of Abnormal Eating Behaviours in Young Polish Judo Athletes
papers.authors: Paulina M. Baran, Katarzyna Szczepanik, Łukasz Kapica, Piotr Mamcarz
papers.abstract: Background: Young athletes in weight-category sports such as judo may experience pressure related to body weight, which can be associated with unhealthy eating. Building on two earlier studies of young Polish judo athletes, this study examined whether ways of coping with stress, weight-related pressure from the social environment, and perceived availability of nutritional support are associated with abnormal eating behaviours. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 142 judo athletes aged 12–17 years (48 girls, 94 boys) completed questionnaires assessing eating behaviours (the Test of Eating Situation Style and the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire), coping with stress (the How Do You Cope? inventory, JSR), and a study-specific questionnaire on weight-related pressure and perceived availability of nutritional support. Results: Girls reported higher emotion-focused coping in several sex-by-age subgroup comparisons. After accounting for sex, age, and BMI-for-age z-score, coping styles and weight-related pressure were significantly associated with dietary restraint and emotional eating. Critical comments about an athlete’s weight or body shape and pressure to maintain a specific competition weight were among the most consistent the strongest predictors, whereas BMI-for-age z-score was not. Athletes who perceived broadly defined nutritional support as available reported less eating in response to external cues than those without such support. Conclusions: In this sample of young Polish judo athletes, weight-related comments and pressure, together with coping strategies, are associated with abnormal eating behaviours. Careful coach communication about weight, evaluation of structured nutritional-support provision, and coping-skills training are candidate prevention targets that should be tested in longitudinal and intervention studies.

papers.title: Balancing Efficiency and Human Oversight in AI-Driven ESG Audits: The Roles of AI Automation and Decision Making
papers.authors: Ioannis C. Ploumpis, Nikolaos Eriotis, Apostolos G. Christopoulos, Dimitris F. Kenourgios, Theodoros Kounadeas
papers.journal: Journal of risk and financial management
papers.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) audits has created new opportunities to enhance corporate governance through faster and more consistent assurance processes. However, concerns remain regarding accountability, transparency, and the role of human oversight in AI-assisted auditing. Prior research has predominantly examined AI adoption in traditional financial auditing, leaving its role in the more qualitative and judgment-intensive context of ESG assurance comparatively underexplored, particularly with respect to how AI decision-making authority should be balanced against human oversight. This study examines the effects of AI automation and AI decision making on audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency, while assessing the mediating role of human oversight. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were collected from 150 professionals involved in ESG audit-related functions (including ESG auditors, compliance officers, sustainability managers, and AI governance analysts) across private, public, and non-governmental organizations, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling via professional networks, audit forums, and LinkedIn ESG groups. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI automation significantly improves audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency. Similarly, AI decision making within governance structures exerts positive effects on all three outcome dimensions. Furthermore, human oversight partially mediates these relationships, strengthening the overall impact of AI on ESG audit outcomes. These results suggest that AI enhances ESG auditing effectiveness, but its benefits are maximized when supported by strong governance and human supervision. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled ESG assurance by demonstrating the importance of balancing technological efficiency with accountability and transparency in corporate governance.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence: Risks, Governance, and the Path from Privacy Paradox to Digital Inevitability
papers.authors: Ioannis Stylios, Spyros Kokolakis, Dimitris Damopoulos, Alexandros T. Tzallas, Stefanos Gritzalis
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs), is reshaping digital services while raising ethical, legal, cybersecurity, privacy, and alignment challenges. This narrative review provides an interdisciplinary synthesis of these challenges, examining GenAI-related risks, the evolving European Union regulatory landscape, including the AI Act, cybersecurity threats to AI systems, and core principles for trustworthy AI. Beyond this synthesis, the paper’s central contribution is a reconceptualisation of the privacy paradox: where data collection is structurally entrenched, non-participation is costly, and viable lower-data alternatives are lacking, the gap between privacy attitudes and disclosure behaviour can reflect structural constraints on participation as well as individual decisions, a conditional account we term “digital inevitability” (DIGINEV). GenAI does not create this condition but can intensify it by inferring sensitive information from indirect signals. We develop this into a conceptual framework that proposes how constraints on participation may interact with user resignation and identifies possible responses through regulation, design, collective action, and viable alternatives. The paper further discusses AI alignment as a supporting consideration in the governance of GenAI systems. The findings offer an integrated perspective for future research, regulatory development, and responsible AI deployment, anchored in the DIGINEV framework.

papers.title: Do-It-with-AI Framework for Invention: A Kundt’s Tube Case Study
papers.authors: Thammarong Eadkhong, Pakamat Attachaiya, Surapong Luanghiranpusit, Jittiporn Chimtab, Punsiri Dam-O, Sorasak Danworaphong, Chitnarong Sirisathitkul
papers.abstract: This exploratory case study examines the feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) into a low-cost Kundt’s tube activity in pre-service science teacher education. The proposed Do-It-With-AI framework comprises four phases: conceptual exploration, design development, troubleshooting, and extension to real-world applications. Scopus AI was used to support the literature-oriented conceptual exploration, while ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-5 supported the generation of design alternatives, troubleshooting hypotheses, and possible extensions. Three pre-service teachers constructed and tested the apparatus, and successive configurations were evaluated through resonance measurements and estimation of the speed of sound. The case illustrates how AI-generated suggestions can be incorporated into an iterative design–test–verification process in which proposed modifications are examined against physical principles and experimental evidence. The four-phase sequence is therefore presented as a feasible framework for integrating generative AI with hands-on experimentation, with instructor-guided verification serving as an essential component. Because the present study focuses on feasibility and process rather than educational outcomes, further investigation with larger cohorts and explicit measures of student reasoning, learning, collaboration, and AI literacy is required. The principal contribution of the Kundt’s tube case is to demonstrate a structured and empirically grounded use of generative AI in low-cost experimental development within pre-service science teacher education.

papers.title: Students’ Perceptions of the Professional Orientation of a Probability and Statistics Course: A Multidimensional Gap Analysis for Curriculum Improvement
papers.authors: Yessenkeldy Tuyakov, Alma E. Abylkassymova, G.А. Rysbekova
papers.abstract: Professional orientation has become an essential objective of higher education because university courses are increasingly expected to prepare students for professional practice as well as academic achievement. This study examined students’ perceptions of the professional orientation of a university Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics course using a seven-dimensional framework. Data were collected from 242 undergraduate students enrolled in the Artificial Intelligence and Data Analysis bachelor’s program at a university in Kazakhstan using a 37-item questionnaire that measured both the current and the needed levels of professional orientation. The instrument demonstrated good-to-excellent reliability and confirmatory factor analysis provided support for the proposed multidimensional measurement structure. Linear mixed-effects models, importance–performance priority analysis, and repeated-measures marginal models were used for data analysis. Students evaluated the needed level significantly higher than the current level across all seven dimensions, showing a consistent professional-orientation gap. Descriptively, Software and Digital Tools showed the largest observed gap, while Assignments and Learning Activities was classified as a curriculum-improvement priority using the sample-specific priority matrix. Students without previous statistics coursework, first-year students, and those with lower mathematical confidence reported significantly larger gaps than their counterparts. Students with previous statistical-software experience also reported greater unmet needs across all dimensions. The findings illustrate a potentially useful multidimensional framework for evaluating professionally oriented statistics courses and offer practical direction for curriculum redesign through stronger addition of authentic learning activities, software-supported data analysis, and professionally relevant applications.

papers.title: Sampling-Frequency-Aware Wavelet-Statistical Features for Fault Diagnostics in Inverter-Integrated Medium-Voltage Networks
papers.authors: Samuel Nnamdi Onyedikachi, Omowunmi Mary Longe
papers.abstract: Inverter-based resources (IBRs) alter fault behaviour in medium-voltage (MV) networks, while heterogeneous monitoring devices operating at different sampling rates provide different bandwidths and representations of fault transients, complicating consistent feature formulation for data-driven fault diagnostics. This study develops a sampling-frequency-aware wavelet–statistical framework for fault detection, classification and location (FDCL). Voltage and current signals from 1800 simulated cases spanning six fault categories on a 33 kV radial feeder were sampled at 120 kHz, with anti-aliased decimation producing datasets at 12 and 1.2 kHz. Six Nyquist-valid feature families were extracted at each sampling rate, from which compact subsets were formulated using minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance (MRMR) and ReliefF feature selection. Four supervised machine-learning (ML) models—decision tree, k-nearest neighbour (KNN), bagged-tree ensemble and neural network—were evaluated for classification and regression using an 80/20 train–test split. Classification remained comparable across sampling tiers, with best test accuracies of 94.9%, 95.1% and 94.9% at 1.2, 12 and 120 kHz, respectively. Regression was more configuration-dependent: the 12 kHz full-feature neural network achieved the lowest unseen-location root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 2.603 km, with mean absolute error (MAE) = 1.845 km and coefficient of determination (R2) = 0.992, while MRMR-20/KNN retained a comparable RMSE of 2.659 km. Selected features shifted from predominantly wavelet descriptors at lower rates towards high-frequency band-energy descriptors at 120 kHz without improved prediction. The results show that increasing sampling bandwidth expands the observable frequency content but does not guarantee improved diagnostic accuracy; predictive performance depends on sampling frequency, physically valid feature formulation, feature selection and learner choice.

papers.title: Curriculum Design and Evaluation of Data Science Track for Management Students
papers.authors: Anna Khalemsky
papers.abstract: The growing demand for data science competencies across professional fields creates a need for curricula that enable management students to develop analytical skills while navigating increasingly complex technological environments. This study examines the design and evaluation of a three-year Data Science track embedded within an undergraduate management program. The curriculum integrates statistics, programming, data management, visualization, artificial intelligence, and project-based learning within a progressively structured, multi-tool environment. A multi-cohort, multi-method design combined longitudinal academic performance data from two independent cohorts with graduates’ attitudes toward data science, career adaptability, course perceptions, and qualitative feedback. Academic performance showed cohort-specific patterns: variability decreased progressively across the three years in Cohort 1, whereas in Cohort 2 it decreased in the second year but increased in the third year. Graduates reported high perceived utility and interest in data science, relatively high career adaptability, and positive perceptions of applied and project-oriented courses, although self-efficacy varied in technically demanding areas. Qualitative findings highlighted authentic projects, progressive learning, and multi-tool exposure, alongside challenges related to technical complexity. The study provides program-level evidence for designing accessible yet rigorous data science curricula and highlights the potential value of progressive curricular integration and applied multi-tool learning for management students.

papers.title: From Individual Chatbot Interaction to the Virtual Tutor with Physical Presence: Comparing Educational Interaction Models with Conversational AI
papers.authors: João Braga Santos, Flávio Almeida, Ernesto Filgueiras
papers.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can provide individual study support, but the educational significance of its responses depends on how they are examined and used. We develop a conceptual framework comparing Individual Chatbot Interaction and Standard Classroom Interaction, then specify a Virtual Tutor with Physical Presence as a situated implementation of shared AI inquiry. The framework draws on selected scholarship concerning mediated learning, educational dialogue, self-regulation, cognitive engagement, pedagogical agents, and AI literacy. We define the unit of analysis as an interaction episode and distinguish private consultation, shared instruction, and hybrid activities through observable criteria. The tutor is specified as an animated avatar projected by video-mapping onto a static volumetric surface in the classroom; perceived presence and learning are treated as outcomes requiring measurement. The proposed contribution is a design specification linking public AI responses, teacher orchestration, evidence-based scrutiny, and individual reflection. An explanatory pathway connects these conditions to possible cognitive and metacognitive processes, with four propositions and matched comparisons for future evaluation. A projected avatar is neither necessary nor sufficient for collective verification, and its incremental value must be tested against simpler shared interfaces. No empirical effectiveness is claimed. The framework provides a basis for investigating when a situated conversational tutor supports disciplinary understanding and critical AI use.

papers.title: The Impact of AI on Game Development: A Scoping Review of Transformations, Career Implications, and Emerging Challenges
papers.authors: Yongkang Xing, Jethro Shell, Tracy G. Harwood, Conor Fahy, Hongji Yang, Shengxiang Yang, Kun Chen, Guokai Feng
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the game industry by reshaping development processes, production workflows, and career structures. In this study, we present a scoping literature review examining the impact of AI on game development and employment within the industry, with particular attention to the perspectives of displacement, task transformation, and productivity effects. Drawing on academic research and industry reports published between 2020 and 2026, while retaining earlier foundational literature where relevant, this study analyzes how AI technologies such as generative AI, machine learning, procedural content generation, and large language models are integrated across major stages of game production, including game art, production management, programming, and live operations. Our findings indicate that AI can support efficiency, accelerate development cycles, and enable new forms of personalization and creative experimentation. At the same time, AI adoption may alter workforce dynamics by increasing the automation potential of routine and entry-level tasks, especially in areas such as asset creation and quality assurance. Rather than fully replacing workers, however, AI more commonly reconfigures job roles and increases demand for hybrid skill sets that combine technical knowledge, creativity, and AI literacy. Our study also identifies emerging opportunities in AI-assisted design, data analytics, and machine learning integration. Despite these benefits, AI adoption introduces important challenges related to employment polarization, intellectual property, workforce adaptation, ethical governance, and market concentration. We conclude that AI is fundamentally reshaping the game industry and highlight the need for balanced strategies that support innovation while preserving creative diversity, sustainable career pathways, and equitable access to technological opportunities. Overall, the strongest evidence concerns AI capabilities, workflow changes, and task-level transformation, whereas direct evidence of actual employment outcomes and long-term occupational change remains limited and uneven.

papers.title: Fostering Scientific Skill Development Through Interactive Classification of Celestial Bodies
papers.authors: Ilham Bouisaghouane, Joanna Holt, Bert Bredeweg A, Patricia Kruit, Pedro Russo, Tom van Eijck
papers.abstract: Developing scientific literacy in primary education can be challenging. Teachers often lack the time, scientific domain knowledge, and capacity to provide individualised support and guidance during hands-on science activities. As a result, students may struggle to interpret observations and draw accurate conclusions. To address this, we designed a feedback-enhanced lesson and investigated students’ performance and engagement with optional feedback while developing classification skills using the Solar System as context. Developed within the Minds-On application, the lesson combines hands-on activities with a knowledge-based artificial intelligence approach in which encoded domain knowledge enables automated checking of students’ classifications and error-triggered feedback. Students classify celestial bodies by shape, composition, and orbit using a three-level classification tree. A classroom evaluation with 164 students (ages 10–12), using student-performance and interaction-log data, showed that most successfully engaged with the tasks and navigated their increasing complexity. Performance and interaction data indicated that task difficulty peaked at Level 2, while error rates and engagement decreased at Level 3. Although feedback was available to 89 students following an error, only 25 consulted it at least once, and use was fragmented across classification levels. The small and inconsistent feedback-user subgroup therefore does not allow strong conclusions about feedback effectiveness but provides insight into patterns of feedback uptake and interaction.

papers.title: LLM-Based Waypoint Authoring via Augmented Reality for Human–Robot Interaction
papers.authors: Mohammad Hashemi, Kasra Mojallal, Saeed Mozaffari, Shahpour Alirezaee
papers.abstract: Augmented reality (AR) can make robot programming more intuitive by letting users set motion parameters directly in the workspace. This paper extends AURaPath, an AR system for interactive 6-DoF waypoint determination on a UR10 collaborative robot using HoloLens2, with a voice modality for hands-free authoring. The voice layer follows a two-tier design: an on-device keyword recognizer handles the safety-critical verbs behind a two-step confirmation gate, and a large language model (LLM) maps the resulting transcript to the system’s structured command set so that operators need not memorize fixed phrases; the deployed pipeline takes spoken microphone input, while the benchmark below evaluates the transcript-to-command mapping stage in isolation. We evaluate the mapping layer on an objective benchmark of 169 labeled utterances that isolates language-to-command mapping from speech recognition and robot execution, and we compare a deterministic keyword baseline, four local models on a single consumer GPU, and free-tier cloud backends. The keyword baseline cannot express parameterized authoring commands and scores zero on every authoring field, while a free-tier cloud model reaches 95.3% exact-match results, averaged over 10 runs. The reject analysis shows that the ability to decline out-of-scope input, rather than raw accuracy, determines whether a model is suitable for the language-mapping tier of our safety-gated architecture, in which a deterministic layer and a preview-before-execute gate remain responsible for execution, which supports keeping the safety-critical verbs on the deterministic layer. The benchmark selects the backend that the deployed system uses, on the same physical UR10 demonstrated in the base system. The project code, the evaluation harness and dataset, and the base-system demonstration are available on GitHub (Please see Data Availability Statement section).

papers.title: A Scoping Review of Vibe Coding and AI-Assisted Programming in University Computing Education
papers.authors: Jing Tian
papers.abstract: Background: Generative AI coding tools are increasingly used in university computing education, including emerging practices commonly described as vibe coding. However, evidence on their educational effects is scattered across studies that differ in interaction patterns, instructional designs, assessment practices, and learning contexts. Methods: We conducted a scoping review using a PRISMA-guided process and synthesized 37 studies published between 2022 and July 2026. Five research questions examined student–AI interaction patterns, learning outcomes, task-level instructional strategies, assessment and academic integrity, and curriculum alignment with emerging professional practice. Results: The reviewed articles reported that students commonly relied on debugging-oriented prompts, common-case testing, and short edit-run cycles, while stronger performance was associated with more exploratory and evaluative interactions. Reported outcomes included conceptual learning, programming productivity, and affective benefits. Emerging instructional strategies included planning with hints, adaptive scaffolding, dual-mode assignments, and process visibility. Conclusions: The educational value of AI-assisted coding appears to depend less on tool access than on how student interaction is scaffolded, assessed, and connected to emerging competencies in specification, verification, testing, and critical evaluation. Therefore, computing education should treat AI-assisted programming not simply as accelerated code generation, but as a practice requiring deliberate reasoning and responsible oversight.

papers.title: QuizTools: Question Generation with Explanations
papers.authors: Andreea Dutulescu, Răzvan Păroiu, Denis Iorga, Micah Watanabe, Ştefan Ruşeţi, Mihai Dascălu, Danielle S. McNamara
papers.abstract: Automated generation of multiple-choice questions (MCQs) represents a viable strategy for scalable assessment and instructional support, but current systems exhibit persistent limitations in distractor quality, reasoning validity, and deployment accessibility. Building on our earlier short paper, YMCQ: Reasoning-Enhanced MCQ Generation, this journal article extends that work by providing a more detailed presentation and explanation of the MCQ generation and multi-stage filtering method introduced there. The method integrates reasoning-based answer generation with misconception-aware distractors, using open-source LLMs fine-tuned on publicly available corpora augmented with synthetic explanations for correct answers and distractors. These augmentations enable the generation of MCQs that are structurally valid, semantically coherent, and pedagogically aligned. The extended presentation further details the method and its implementation in QuizTools, a publicly available platform that supports automated MCQ generation from source materials and enables human-in-the-loop refinement. The pairwise performance evaluation of the generated questions was reported in the short paper; this journal article additionally includes an individual-question quality evaluation, analysis of user edits, and a usability study of QuizTools. The models, datasets, and source code, including over 300,000 quiz items with annotated explanations, are publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research in educational NLP.

papers.title: Adoption decision-making of AI digital humans for agricultural regional public brands in short videos
papers.authors: Rong Wu, Jin Xiao, Jiaqi Chen
papers.abstract: Introduction This study examines the adoption of AI digital humans (AI-DHs) by agricultural regional public brands in short-video promotion. Methods A complex network evolutionary game model is developed in which brands interact on a scale-free network and update their strategies through the Fermi rule. The model considers AI-DH production and generation costs, real-human promotion costs, consumer preference, recommendation priority, and network size. For each parameter scenario, 100 stochastic simulation runs are conducted, and mean adoption trajectories with 95% simulation intervals are reported. Results Higher AI-DH-related costs reduce the relative payoff of AI-DH promotion and suppress adoption, whereas higher real-human promotion costs make AI-DH promotion comparatively more attractive. Consumer preference produces the most pronounced change in the evolutionary outcome, with higher preference shifting the system toward broader AI-DH adoption. Higher recommendation priority helps sustain AI-DH adoption during the evolutionary process but does not independently determine the final adoption state. Network size has limited influence on long-run average adoption, although larger networks reduce stochastic variation in the evolutionary process. Discussion These findings extend digital-human research from post-adoption consumer responses to the dynamic adoption decisions of agricultural regional public brands and highlight the roles of relative payoffs, platform conditions, and inter-brand learning.

papers.title: The impact of encouraging utterances by a human partner and a conversational robot on older adults’ subjective well-being: a 6-week sustained interaction
papers.authors: Lingxuan Xiang, Hideaki Kikuchi
papers.abstract: Introduction In human–human communication, encouragement has been closely associated with subjective well-being (SWB). However, the long-term effects of encouragement in human–robot interaction remain unclear, particularly in comparison with human-delivered encouragement and across different encouragement strategy types. SWB comprises both affective well-being (AWB) and cognitive well-being (CWB). This study investigated whether sustained verbal encouragement from a human partner and a conversational robot could enhance older adults’ SWB. Methods A two-phase design was adopted. First, a preliminary online survey with 55 older Japanese adults (aged 65–74) was conducted to select encouragement strategies for the main experiment, identifying offering specific actions (high-efficacy) and distraction (low-efficacy) as two encouragement strategies that differed significantly in participants’ perceived effectiveness (p < 0.05). Based on this survey, 18 older Japanese adults (aged 62–90) were recruited for an exploratory 6-week longitudinal experiment. Participants interacted with either a human partner or a conversational robot once per week and were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: human partner or social robot (RoBoHoN) crossed with high- or low-perceived-efficacy encouragement strategy. SWB was assessed using questionnaires, while post-session open-ended responses, diary entries, and post-experiment interviews provided qualitative data on encouragement experience, perceived SWB changes, and participants’ perceived sources of SWB change. Results Results suggested that high-efficacy verbal encouragement may positively influence older adults’ SWB, possibly with a stronger effect than low-efficacy encouragement, with a crossover-like pattern emerging: for AWB, the advantage of high-efficacy over low-efficacy encouragement tended to be more pronounced in the robot condition (Δ gap = 2.8) than the human condition (Δ gap = 0.5), whereas for CWB, it appeared to be more pronounced in the human condition (Δ gap = 2.0) than the robot condition (Δ gap = 0.2); these crossover trends should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size. Qualitative findings further suggested that the conversation itself may have contributed to participants’ perceived emotional support in the Japanese cultural context. Discussion These preliminary longitudinal findings suggest that social robots and human partners may both contribute to supporting older adults’ SWB and may play complementary roles.

papers.title: Case Report: An MDT-guided multimodal protocol for large-area stroke plateau — integrating neuromodulation with multimodal assessment
papers.authors: Xiao-li Wu, Xiao-qian Xia, Chang-qing Ye, Yun-lei Wang, Xing-Zhu Li, Lixu Liu, Fu-biao Hang, Jing-song Liu, Yichuan Song, Yue Zhang, Xiao-xia Du
papers.abstract: Objective This case report investigates the feasibility and potential value of an individualized precision rehabilitation protocol for large-area stroke, integrating multimodal neuromodulation under the guidance of a multidisciplinary team (MDT) and dynamic assessment. Methods A 38-year-old male with right hemiplegia and global aphasia following large left hemispheric infarction underwent an 8-month MDT-managed program. A closed-loop “assess-decide-intervene-re-assess” framework was implemented, featuring periodic multimodal evaluations (clinical scales, DTI, fMRI, EEG, 3D gait analysis). The intervention dynamically combined conventional therapy with staged neuromodulation: repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) for aphasia and intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation (iTBS) for motor disorder, Brain-Computer Interface (BCI)-robotic training and task-oriented Virtual Reality (VR) for upper limb function, and biomechanical correction with custom insoles based on gait analysis. Results Notable functional improvements were observed: LOTCA increased by 16 points, CRRCAE subscale improved by 60%–90%, FMA increased from 20 to 56, FMA-B reached 12, and MBI improved from 40 to 91. Neuroimaging revealed increased fractional anisotropy (FA) in the corpus callosum and right corticospinal tract, and elevated ALFF/ReHo in right frontal-temporal areas. Event-related desynchronization (ERD) decreased during BCI training, and gait parameters improved. Conclusion In this patient with large-area stroke who showed limited response to conventional rehabilitation, an MDT-guided, dynamically adjusted multimodal intervention was temporally associated with concurrent recovery across cognitive, language, motor, and daily living domains. The concomitant neural changes suggest possible trans-hemispheric network reorganization. These observations are hypothesis-generating and, while limited by the single-case design, provide a preliminary rationale for future investigations into precision neurorehabilitation approaches in similar complex cases. Clinical trial registration ChiCTR2300069203.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and small-business competitiveness in an emerging economy
papers.authors: Navruz-Zoda Layli Baxtiyorovna, Fayzullayev Nurulla Bakhromovich, Кахрамон Мадрахимов, Aajaz Ahmad Hajam, Razzaqbergan Jumaniyozov, Dilora Saydamenova, Inomjon Yusubov
papers.abstract: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the driving force of developing economies, yet they remain limited in resources to implement artificial intelligence (AI), and there is little empirical evidence that AI adoption is associated with small business growth in the region, particularly in Central Asia. This research makes two contributions. First, we propose a concise framework that links classes of AI technologies to SME competitiveness features and identifies machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI as low-cost, quick-return priority areas for resource-constrained firms. Second, using 16 years of data (2010–2025) for the Bukhara region of Uzbekistan, we estimate ARIMA models for each indicator and forecast eight small business indicators to 2030. Small business output is projected to grow at a steady rate of approximately 16% by 2030, with digital adoption and preferential credit support emerging as indicators associated with long-run growth. Forecast accuracy is high for the human-capital indicator and acceptable for output. The evidence is associational rather than causal: the framework and the forecasts converge on a single, cautiously formulated proposition—the adoption of low-cost AI is measurably associated with the sustainable competitiveness of SMEs, providing a practical, evidence-based starting point for regional AI policy in developing countries.

papers.title: Between policy and pedagogy: writing teachers' perspectives on institutional AI policies and expectations
papers.authors: Mohammed Alzahrani, Faris A. Aldubayyan, Ibrahim Alshabi
papers.abstract: Despite the growing interest and rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) within higher education, English language teachers remain in a constant state of interpreting, implementing, and negotiating institutional policies and expectations. While rapidly developed AI policies have started to emerge and evolve, little is known about how writing teachers understand, evaluate, and negotiate these policies, especially in relation to their everyday pedagogical practices. This qualitative study is set to explore how 10 writing teachers viewed and navigated their institutional AI policies in Saudi Arabia. Utilizing a case-study design, data were collected from narrative frames and semi-structured interviews. The results revealed that the teachers expressed a lack of clear institutional guidance, leading them at times to navigate AI-related issues on their own. Additionally, the teachers underlined their partial exclusion from AI policy design, which mainly followed a top-down institutional approach. Despite that, teachers perceived AI adoption as an inevitable development within higher education and a necessity that they need to adapt to in the future. The study underscores the importance of designing clear AI policies, tailored specifically to help writing teachers working in higher education settings. It also highlights how a bottom-up approach, where teachers are involved in the policy-drafting and implementation phases, could have a fundamental and constructive effect on their pedagogical practices.

papers.title: Large language models as sources of diabetic retinopathy patient education: a comparative evaluation of safety, health information quality, and readability
papers.authors: Zhiqi Chen, Wen Liu, Jing Zhang, Tian Zheng, Yan Li, Qing Bao, Pingting Ji, Hongmei Yao, Ying He
papers.abstract: Background Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to seek medical information, but their performance in answering diabetic retinopathy (DR) questions remains insufficiently characterized. Objective To evaluate the safety, accuracy, patient-centered communication, information quality, transparency, and readability of diabetic retinopathy information generated by widely accessible large language models. Methods Fifty standardized DR patient questions were submitted to ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Doubao, Copilot, and Perplexity. Responses were independently evaluated by five raters using guideline-based reference answer elements. Rater-based outcomes included Safety, Accuracy, Empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and Global Quality Score (GQS). Readability was assessed using the Automated Readability Index, Coleman–Liau Index, Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog Index, SMOG, and Flesch Reading Ease Score.
