papers.title: CAPACITY-BUILDING WORKSHOP ON AI LITERACY AND ADAPTIVE LEADERSHIP FOR PRE-SERVICE TEACHERS
papers.authors: Roni Faslah, Wahyuning Darwati, Devi Desianti Pritasari, Suryo Adrianto, Listiyaning Handayani, Widya Arti Anggraini, Soni Wandrial, Muhammad Ikhwan
papers.abstract: Digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping how schools are managed and led, widening the competencies expected of those who will run tomorrow’s schools. Beyond pedagogical expertise, prospective leaders increasingly need adaptive leadership, digital literacy, ethical judgment, and the ability to act on data. This community service program set out to strengthen these future-leadership competencies among pre-service teachers at Johor Business School, Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia (UTHM). Delivered on 22 June 2026 within the ELEVATE 2026 program, the workshop used a participatory design that combined seminars, interactive discussion, case studies, reflective learning, and collaborative problem-solving. Its effect was gauged through paired pre-test and post-test assessments, participant observation, and reflective discussion. Average understanding rose from 60.6% to 87.8%, a gain of 27.2 percentage points, or 44.9% in relative terms, across five competency areas, with AI literacy improving most. Participants grew more confident in adaptive leadership, ethical AI use, data-informed decision making, and collaborative school culture. The program also deepened academic collaboration between Universitas Negeri Jakarta and UTHM. Pairing leadership development with digital literacy offers a workable route to preparing future school leaders for the AI era.

papers.title: The Mathematics of Deception: A Unified Framework for AI-Driven Honeypot Systems
papers.authors: Yoothana Suansook
papers.abstract: Honeypots occupy a peculiar place in the security landscape: they are among the few mechanisms whose value is defined by their failure. A firewall that is never tested, an intrusion detection system that never alarms—these are successes. A honeypot that is never attacked is useless. This inversion of the usual security logic gives honeypots an unusually clean signal, but it has also kept their theoretical foundations fragmented. Game theorists model deception in isolation; information theorists treat intrusion detection generically; queuing theorists model traffic separately; and the recent wave of AI-driven honeypots—powered by Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning—has proceeded largely without formal mathematical treatment.This paper attempts a synthesis. We develop a unified mathematical framework for AI-driven honeypot systems, building on six pillars: stochastic processes (the honeypot as a continuous time Markov chain), game theory (the honeypot as a Bayesian signaling device), detection theory (the honeypot as a near-ideal hypothesis test), information theory (the honeypot as a channel for intelligence), optimization (the honeypot as a constrained POMDP), and AI integration (LLM as observation kernel, RL as policy optimization).Along the way, we derive equilibrium conditions, detection thresholds, optimal deployment fractions, information-theoretic bounds, and LLM deception limits. We prove that the mixed strategy equilibrium is unique and Lyapunov stable, solve the POMDP for a reduced state space to obtain a threshold policy, and show that in the myopic case this threshold coincides exactly with the game-theoretic equilibrium under consistent payoff specifications. We generalize the Poisson detection assumption to a Weibull hazard model and derive a bound on the mutual information achievable under LLM-generated observations via the data processing inequality.We accompany the analytical development with numerical Monte Carlo experiments based on exact Gillespie simulation of the CTMC, replicator dynamics for the game-theoretic component, and parametric sampling for the detection and information-theoretic components. These experiments validate the closed-form predictions and expose the qualitative behavior of the system in transient and steady state. All quantitative claims are analytical; the simulations serve as numerical illustrations, not as empirical validation of real-world deployments.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: Perceptions, Challenges and Opportunities Among Medical Students
papers.authors: Pietra Atencia Crunfle, Rogério Leone Buchaim, Daniela Vieira Buchaim, João Paulo Mardegan Issa, Vinícius Rodrigues Silva, Vinícius Barroso Hirota, André Antonio Pelegrine, Peter Karyen Moy, Daniel Gimenez da Rocha, Victor Augusto Ramos Fernandes, Ronny Rodrigues Correia, Marcel Fernado Inácio Cardozo, Marcelo Rodrigues da Cunha
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming medical education and clinical practice, requiring digital, critical, and ethical competencies. This study aimed to assess medical students’ attitudes toward AI, including perceived benefits, risks, and use in medical training. Methods: A mixed-methods, descriptive study used an electronic questionnaire comprising sociodemographic data and 13 items adapted from the authorized Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale, with reverse-coding of negative items. Total and subscale scores for benefits, risks/threats, and use were calculated. Participants were medical students from the 1st to 6th years at the School of Medicine of Jundiaí (FMJ). Results: Among 436 students, attitudes toward AI were generally favorable. No significant gender difference was observed (p = 0.291), whereas scores differed significantly across training years (p = 0.025), with higher scores among advanced students. Despite recognizing AI’s benefits, students reported concerns regarding reliability, clinical autonomy, ethical implications, and gaps in practical knowledge. Conclusions: AI is positively perceived by medical students, particularly those in advanced years. These findings support structured AI integration into medical curricula to promote critical, ethical, and responsible use in medical education and future clinical practice.

papers.title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Generative AI in Clinical Diagnosis and Prognosis
papers.authors: Noura Aqeeli, Munib Mesinovic, Tingting Zhu
papers.abstract: Generative AI increasingly supports clinical diagnosis and prognosis, but safe deployment into clinical practice requires standardized evaluation. Evaluation practices from 2022 to 2025 are surveyed, and a five-dimensional framework is introduced: (I) Factual and Contextual Correctness, (II) Safety, Alignment, and Robustness, (III) Reasoning Quality, (IV) Calibration and Uncertainty, and (V) Clinical Anthropomorphism. Current automated and human evaluation methods rely heavily on accuracy, lack multimodal assessment, and are not aligned with human judgment. Emerging benchmarks are assessed and linked to our framework. A hybrid evaluation approach combining automated scalability with expert clinical judgment is recommended for safe and effective deployment.

papers.title: Understanding AI Use at Work: Trust, User Experience, and Basic Psychological Needs in U.S. and Chinese Workers
papers.authors: Tianxin Zhang, Victoria K. Lew, Christina M. Frederick
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the workplace, yet less is known about how workers experience AI and whether these experiences differ across countries. The present work compared workplace AI use and attitudes in 225 workers in China and 198 workers in the United States. Participants completed measures describing their work practices, attitudes and motivation toward AI (GAAIS; Schepman & Rodway, 2020, 2023; TENS-Life; Peters et al., 2018; Schrepp et al., 2017; Jian et al., 2000). Using Self-Determination Theory, we also examined whether autonomy, competence, and relatedness were associated with weekly AI use through trust and mistrust in AI. Chinese workers reported using AI more hours per week and reported greater organizational support for AI use than U.S. workers. They also reported more positive and more negative attitudes toward AI, as well as greater mistrust. Chinese workers reported lower AI-supported autonomy and competence but greater AI relatedness than U.S. workers. Mediation analyses indicated that relatedness was indirectly associated with greater weekly AI use through greater trust in AI in both samples. The findings suggest that understanding workplace AI use requires attention not only to the technology itself, but also to workers’ psychological and social experiences with AI.

papers.title: Learning to Distrust Correct Answers: The Effect of Deliberate AI-Induced Ambiguity on Conceptual Reasoning in Electrical Engineering Students
papers.authors: Amirhossein Rezaeian
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly becoming part of engineering students’ learning environments, particularly in quantitative problem solving, explanation generation, and formative feedback. The educational value of these systems, however, depends not only on output accuracy but also on whether learners can evaluate claims that appear authoritative. This paper proposes Deliberate Ambiguity Verification (DAV), an instructional framework in which electrical engineering students compare two AI-generated solutions that are mathematically plausible and professionally presented but differ in a consequential assumption, boundary condition, or physical interpretation. Students must identify the point of divergence, verify each response against an independent engineering principle, justify a decision, and report confidence before and after verification. The framework integrates epistemic vigilance, trust calibration, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive engagement, productive failure, and discipline-specific AI literacy. A randomized four-condition design is proposed for students in circuit analysis, contrasting no-AI problem solving, a single AI answer, a plausible-but-incorrect AI answer, and deliberate ambiguity. Primary outcomes are conceptual reasoning, verification behavior, confidence calibration, and AI-free transfer. The paper argues that the goal should not be generalized distrust of AI, but calibrated skepticism: the capacity to determine when an AI response should be accepted provisionally, when it requires independent verification, and when disciplinary reasoning should override the apparent authority of the system. The framework is intended to provide a testable pathway for studying epistemically responsible human-AI collaboration in engineering education.

papers.title: Guided AI integration model (GAIIM): Effects of verification-oriented generative AI-supported learning on undergraduate students’ algebraic problem-solving
papers.authors: Isaac Davor, Ernest Larbi, Francis Ohene Boateng, Michael Osei Tawiah
papers.journal: Journal of Interdisciplinary Research in Artificial Intelligence and Society
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education; however, most instructional applications emphasizeanswer generation rather than mathematical reasoning and critical verification of AI-generated mathematical solutions. The current study examined the effectiveness of the Guided AI Integration Model (GAIIM), a verification-oriented instructional framework that utilizes AI for verification of students’ algebraic problem-solving within a problem-solving context. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 86 undergraduate mathematics education students using a randomized pretest-posttest control group classroom design. During the 12-week intervention, students in the experimental group engaged in GAIIM-based instruction involving independent problem-solving, AI-generated solution comparison, error detection and justification, error resolution, and reflective verification, while the control group received conventional algebra instruction. Qualitative data were subsequently collected from 10 purposively selected students through semi-structured interviews and analyzed thematically to explain and elaborate on the quantitative findings. Students in the GAIIM group demonstrated significantly higher posttest performance in algebraic problem-solving, error detection, and error resolution after controlling for pretest scores. Qualitative findings further revealed stepwise verification, iterative engagement with AI feedback, conditional trust in AI-generated responses, and difficulties interpreting and correcting AI-generated mathematical reasoning. The findings suggest that structured AI-supported verification can support students’ algebraic problem-solving and error-verification performance.

papers.title: Experiencia Docente con Tecnologías Educativas: El Modelo SAMR en la Era de la IA
papers.authors: Flavia Del Pup, Leticia Castro, Natalia Moreira
papers.abstract: La incorporación de tecnologías digitales en la educación superior no garantiza por sí sola transformaciones pedagógicas significativas si no está acompañada de una reflexión didáctica crítica sobre sus finalidades y modos de uso. En este marco, esta investigación analiza la incorporación de materiales didácticos interactivos autoadministrados, diseñados con apoyo de inteligencia artificial (IA), según el modelo de sustitución, aumento, modificación y redefinición (SAMR) y en clave problematizadora, en comparación con clases presenciales tradicionales, en el curso introductorio de la Facultad de Información y Comunicación (FIC) de la Universidad de la República (Udelar) de Uruguay. Este curso es obligatorio para todo el estudiantado de ingreso, tiene como propósito ofrecer información sobre la oferta formativa de la FIC, su estructura académica, instalaciones y espacios de referencia institucionales. La intervención, dirigida a 1254 estudiantes inscritos de las licenciaturas en Comunicación, Archivología y Bibliotecología, consistió en sustituir las presentaciones presenciales iniciales de las unidades curriculares del primer semestre por un módulo virtual interactivo que integró múltiples lenguajes, navegación condicionada, un espacio colaborativo asíncrono y una encuesta de retroalimentación. El diseño promovió un recorrido autónomo y progresivo del contenido, habilitando la reflexión individual y colectiva. Se recogieron 831 respuestas a la encuesta (66.3 %) y 628 publicaciones en el espacio colaborativo (50.1 %). Esto permitió evaluar percepciones, niveles de apropiación conceptual y evidencias de autorregulación. Los resultados sugieren que la propuesta contribuye a fomentar la autonomía estudiantil y a enriquecer los procesos de enseñanza en educación superior mediante el uso crítico y pedagógico de tecnologías digitales.[The integration of digital technologies in higher education does not automatically lead to meaningful pedagogical transformation unless it is guided by critical reflection on their educational purposes and uses. This research analyzes the integration of self-paced interactive learning materials designed with the support of artificial intelligence (AI), following the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition (SAMR) model and framed from a problematizing approach. It compares these materials with traditional face-to-face classes within the introductory course at the Faculty of Information and Communication (FIC), Universidad de la República, Uruguay (Udelar). This mandatory course is aimed at all first-year students and seeks to provide information about the FIC’s academic offerings, academic structure, facilities, and institutional reference spaces. The intervention, targeting 1,254 enrolled students from the Communication, Archival Science, and Library Science programs, involved replacing the initial in-person presentations of first-semester courses with an interactive virtual module. This module incorporated multiple media, conditional navigation, an asynchronous collaborative space, and a feedback survey. The design encouraged a self-guided and progressive exploration of content, enabling both individual and collective reflection. A total of 831 responses to the survey (66.3%) and 628 posts in the collaborative space (50.1%) were collected, allowing for the evaluation of perceptions, conceptual appropriation levels, and evidence of self-regulated learning. The results suggest that this initiative helps foster student autonomy and enriches teaching processes in higher education through the critical and pedagogical use of digital technologies].

papers.title: Regulation in the Digital Information Space
papers.authors: Bolormaa Battsogt, Dagiimaa D
papers.journal: The Journal of Communication and Media Studies
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) tools and digital platforms become embedded in everyday communication, governments face growing pressure to regulate misinformation, hate speech, and other harmful online content while protecting freedom of expression. This study examines regulatory debates in Mongolia’s digital information space and argues that regulatory acceptance and legitimacy cannot be explained through an individual-centered perspective alone. It first organizes Mongolia’s digital governance challenges through four interrelated forms of uncertainty: cultural, ethical, institutional, and relational. This approach highlights Mongolia’s hybrid cultural environment, where collectivist traditions intersect with expanding individualism, and where public judgments about regulation are shaped by relationships and trust. Drawing on a quota-sampling survey of two hundred and seventy respondents from urban and rural Mongolia, the study employs Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and multi-group analysis to examine the direct, mediating, and moderating effects of four trust dimensions: strong-tie trust, weak-tie trust, institutional trust, and platform trust. The findings show that institutional trust is the strongest positive predictor of regulatory acceptance, followed by platform trust, strong-tie trust, and weak-tie trust. Relational trust statistically mediates the relationship between freedom-of-expression concerns and regulatory acceptance, suggesting that concerns about censorship are interpreted through broader trust environments. Urban-rural and generational differences further condition the effects of trust. The Mongolian case illustrates broader challenges faced by small democracies and platform-dependent societies, where domestic regulatory capacity remains limited while global platforms shape the public sphere. The study demonstrates the need to understand regulatory legitimacy through relationships, trust, and cultural context, not solely legal systems or individual literacy alone.

papers.title: Digital Readiness for Technology-Enhanced Undergraduate Research
papers.authors: Hau Trung Ho
papers.journal: The International Journal of Technologies in Learning
papers.abstract: As undergraduate research increasingly relies on digital databases, analytical software, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled technologies, research learning is potentially mediated through digital infrastructures that enable students to engage in knowledge construction. However, disparities in technological access and institutional support may constrain these learning opportunities. Guided by van Dijk’s digital divide model and Ragnedda’s concept of digital capital, this study employed interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) to examine how undergraduate students experienced digital readiness during the research process. Data were generated through three rounds of in-depth interviews with each of the eight undergraduate researchers at a Vietnamese public university. Analysis revealed that limited access to scholarly databases and research software usually restricted students’ engagement with technology-enhanced research learning. In addition, the absence of clear institutional policies and guidance regarding AI technologies potentially generated uncertainty about acceptable AI practices and contributed to uneven development of students’ digital competencies. These technological constraints influenced many students’ academic self-efficacy and reduced their ability to transform digital resources into meaningful learning and research outcomes. The effectiveness of technology-supported undergraduate research might depend not only on the availability of digital tools but also on equitable access, AI literacy development, and institutional support structures. The study contributes to the field of technologies in learning by demonstrating how digital infrastructure and technology governance may shape students’ participation in research-based learning. Implications are offered for the design of inclusive technology-enabled learning environments that support equitable undergraduate research engagement.

papers.title: The Moderating Effect of Gender on the Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence Usage, Behavioral Intentions, and Academic Engagement in Mathematics Education
papers.authors: Oluwanife Segun Falebita, Olubunmi Kayode Ayanwoye, Lukman Shina Akinola, Godwin Audu, Olukemi Oluranti Ayoola
papers.journal: The International Journal of Technologies in Learning
papers.abstract: In the age of technology, where the educational sphere and strategic advancements drive development, it is essential to understand the complex nature of gender and implement innovative tools to foster an inclusive learning environment and empower every learner. This study examines the moderating effect of gender on the relationships among Artificial Intelligence (AI) use, behavioral intentions, and academic engagement in mathematics education. Using a cross-sectional design, the study sampled 328 mathematics undergraduates from public universities in southwestern Nigeria. A structured online questionnaire hosted on Google Forms was used to collect data. The data collected were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicated that AI actual usage has a significant positive impact on behavioral academic engagement (BAE), and AI behavioral intention positively influences AI actual usage. Additionally, AI behavioral intention does not significantly influence BAE. Furthermore, AI social norms exerted large positive effects on actual AI use and behavioral intentions. In addition, gender moderates the relationship between AI behavioral intention and BAE, AI behavioral intention and AI actual usage, and AI actual usage and BAE. Therefore, educators should create specialized interventions that are responsive to the motivational and demotivational factors affecting both male and female students.

papers.title: Technical and Emotional AI Labor
papers.authors: Emma Duester
papers.journal: The International Journal of Social Political and Community Agendas in the Arts
papers.abstract: Chinese digital-first policies have accelerated artificial intelligence (AI) integration across the cultural and creative industries (CCIs). While AI is promoted as enhancing creativity, productivity, and efficiency, the labor required to create with AI remains underexamined. Artistic labor scholarship recognizes networking, self-promotion, and entrepreneurial work, while AI-assisted creativity research emphasizes collaboration, authorship, and outcomes. Neither adequately conceptualizes the continual labor embedded in AI-integrated artistic production. Drawing on surveys and semi-structured interviews with independent contemporary visual artists in China conducted in 2023–2024, alongside systematic analysis of international Status of the Artist (TSOTA) policy recommendations published between 2018 and 2025 by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers (CISAC), and the International Federation of Coalitions for Cultural Diversity (IFCCD), this article develops the concept of technical and emotional AI labor. Findings demonstrate that AI redistributes artistic labor into continual cycles of software learning, prompt engineering, experimentation, technical maintenance, platform coordination, and emotional self-management. These activities are integral to artistic production rather than external professional development. Although international policy increasingly recognizes digital skills, lifelong learning, copyright, and AI governance, it continues to frame technological adaptation as education rather than labor. Reconceptualizing this adaptation as artistic labor extends artistic, digital, platform, and AI labor scholarship and identifies the need to update international TSOTA policy recommendations.

papers.title: The New European Union Legal Framework on Defective Digital Medical Devices: Alleviating the Patient’s Burden of Proof
papers.authors: Maja Proso
papers.abstract: Digitalisation has changed the medical sector, introducing sophisticated digital medical devices (such as software as a medical device and devices assisted by Artificial Intelligence systems). Innovations in medicine present potential for improving diagnosis and treatment. Simultaneously, they raise certain questions about civil liability and the legal position of the patient who has suffered harm caused by a defective digital product. This paper examines whether the modernized EU liability rules for defective digital medical devices can alleviate the evidentiary burden patients face in civil litigation, thus strengthening their position. The author focuses on the adequacy of the new rules on disclosure of evidence and burden of proof. The key findings show that the new rules strengthen patients' position by alleviating the burden of proof and imposing an obligation to disclose relevant evidence. The author proposes drafting guidelines to resolve existing ambiguities, ensuring the new evidentiary framework is applied consistently and effectively.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Operations: A Foundational Framework of Emerging Research and Practice
papers.authors: Dai T., Swaminathan J.M.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to reshape operations across industries. Yet its real-world impact reveals a jagged and uneven implementation frontier. To make sense of this emerging landscape, we develop a foundational framework that synthesizes research and practice at the intersection of AI and Operations Management (OM), anchored in three interdependent pillars: (1) AI for OM, (2) OM for AI, and (3) Human–AI Interaction. First, AI for OM analyzes how AI enhances core operational processes, including design, procurement, production, and delivery. Second, OM for AI argues that scaling AI safely and effectively stands to benefit from core OM principles, including workflow design, capacity management, process control, drift detection, and continuous improvement, all of which are central to AI development and deployment. Third, Human–AI Interaction emphasizes the role of trust, incentives, and organizational design in mediating how humans and machines learn from and collaborate with each other. This triadic framework provides a foundation for organizing research on AI and OM and offers practical guidance for integrating AI into business and societal systems.

papers.title: Generative Relational Economics, Volume VI: Artificial Intelligence, Domains, and Economic Order
papers.authors: Wanhong HUANG
papers.abstract: This volume examines the implications of artificial intelligence and radical capability asymmetry for economic relations and extends Generative Relational Economics across a range of substantive domains before developing an integrated account of economic order. Artificial intelligence is analyzed as a potential source of large and persistent asymmetries in productive, epistemic, symbolic, and organizational capability. The volume considers artificial productive capacity, labor, ownership, surplus, redistribution, participation, subjecthood, epistemic dependence, research orientation, governance, and long-horizon human–AI relations. Capability asymmetry is not treated as intrinsically equivalent to domination; the analysis instead asks how asymmetry becomes coupled to ownership, dependence, institutional authority, access, exclusion, or generative participation. The framework is then translated into domains including education, research and knowledge institutions, work and organizations, development and humanitarian practice, welfare, communities and commons, platforms, public infrastructure, migration, ecology, and symbolic economy. Domain translation is used to test both the usefulness and the limits of GRE rather than to absorb neighboring disciplines into economics. Comparative domain inquiry provides the basis for an analysis of generative relational economic order. Economic order is examined through institutional capacity, allocation, value circulation, dependency, participation, contestability, temporal sustainability, epistemic conditions, and revisability. The volume thereby connects technological transformation and domain-specific analysis to broader questions concerning the constitution and governance of economic order.

papers.title: A Dialogic Cognitive System With Externally Persisted State: A New Architecture of Human–AI Joint Thinking
papers.authors: Dmitry Kozhevanov
papers.abstract: The article proposes the concept of a dialogical cognitive system with an externally persistent state as a distinct architecture of joint thinking between humans and generative artificial intelligence. It examines situations in which an evolving reasoning process is preserved in an external dialogue and can be resumed after a temporal interruption without reconstructing the process from the beginning. The preserved state includes not only information, but also hypotheses, arguments, objections, connections, intermediate conclusions, and unresolved questions. Within such a system, generative AI functions not merely as a tool for obtaining or processing information, but also as a participant in the subsequent transformation of the preserved state of reasoning. The concept is related to research on extended and distributed cognition, cognitive offloading, transactive memory, and human–AI co-creativity. The article defines the principal elements of the proposed architecture and outlines directions for its further empirical investigation.

papers.title: AIDA - Artificial Intelligence for Digital Alcohol interventions
papers.authors: Marissa de Vries, Matthijs Blankers, Reinout W. H. J. Wiers
papers.abstract: This research project aims to improve adherence to a Dutch digital self-help program designed to support individuals in reducing or stopping alcohol consumption. Digital self-help interventions are increasingly recognized as accessible and cost-effective preventive tools that prevent people going seek for help at traditional addiction care. However, their effectiveness is strongly dependent on sustained user engagement. Within the current Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program, approximately 2,200 individuals create an account annually, yet only about 20% progress to the third phase of the intervention, indicating substantial dropout and limited adherence. The central objective of this study is to enhance adherence by introducing a conversational agent (CA) that provides personalized, motivational, and informational support throughout the intervention. The CA leverage a large language model (LLM) to generate tailored messages and is designed to simulate supportive guidance, without replacing professional treatment. Its use is optional and it does not serve a therapeutic or diagnostic function. In addition to the CA, AI-driven personalized reminder messages will be sent to participants throughout the intervention to encourage continued engagement with the program. This adaptation of the intervention is a responds to previously identified user needs, including a desire for more personalization, feedback on progress (e.g., alcohol registration), and motivating reminders comparable to those used in digital learning platforms. Participants who enroll in the Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program and meet the predefined inclusion criteria, including be adult (18 years or older), an AUDIT score ≤20, no current treatment for alcohol-related problems, no pregnancy or breastfeeding, and no reported suicidal ideation during screening will be asked to participate in research. After providing informed consent, participants complete baseline assessments of alcohol use, substance use, psychological distress, and quality of life. Follow-up assessments are conducted four weeks after the start of the intervention and twelve weeks after baseline. The study uses a non-randomized sequential A/B design. Participants who enroll during the first half of the study period receive the standard self-help intervention, whereas those enrolling during the second half receive an AI-enhanced version that includes a conversational agent and AI-driven personalized reminder messages. The primary outcome is adherence to the intervention, assessed using platform-based usage data, including the number of completed modules and exercises, time spent using the intervention, and number of logins. Secondary outcomes include alcohol consumption and alcohol-related problems, other substance use, psychological distress, quality of life, and program usability/satisfaction. Fort the participants who could use the conversational agent, additional questionnaires about the acceptibility, feasibility and usability of the conversational agents will be asked. These outcomes are measured using validated instruments, including the TLFB, AUDIT, MATE, DASS, MANSA, SUS, AIM, IAM, FIM, CUQ and CSQ. This study aims to evaluate whether the addition of a conversational agent and AI-driven personalized reminder messages is associated with improved adherence to the Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program. In addition, the study will examine whether participants using the AI-enhanced version of the intervention show different outcomes in alcohol use, psychological distress, quality of life, and program usability compared with participants using the standard version of the program. The findings will provide insight into the potential added value of AI-supported features within digital alcohol interventions and inform the further development and optimization of the Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program. If the AI-enhanced version is associated with higher adherence, this may indicate that conversational support and personalized reminders can help users remain engaged with online self-help interventions for a longer period of time.

papers.title: Predicting a clinically meaningful decline in walking speed at 48 months in the Osteoarthritis Initiative: a comparison of a simple rule, logistic regression and machine learning
papers.authors: Bismah Zainab
papers.abstract: Prognostic prediction study using public-use data from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI), a longitudinal cohort of adults with or at risk of knee osteoarthritis. Baseline measures (age, sex, race, BMI, knee pain and function, walking speed, chair-stand time, radiographic grade, comorbidity, depression, physical activity, education, income) are used to predict a decline of at least 0.10 m/s in 20 m walking speed from baseline to the 48-month visit. A calibrated 0–3 point rule, a compact logistic model, a full logistic model, elastic-net logistic regression, random forest and gradient boosting are compared with identical preprocessing by repeated 5-fold cross-validation, using AUROC with bootstrap intervals for paired differences, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Machine learning is pre-defined as better only if it exceeds logistic regression by a stated AUROC margin (0.02) with an interval excluding zero. One Python pipeline runs the full analysis from the OAI files. Sensitivity analyses cover the decline threshold, non-linear terms, missing follow-up and death. Reporting follows TRIPOD+AI. Status: this registration documents an analysis plan made after a first run of the pipeline, with the results of that run seen before registering; it is not a preregistration of unseen data (see Knowledge of Data). The author chose the question, outcome and threshold and ran all code. No participant-level data are shared. Data and/or research tools used in the preparation of this manuscript were obtained and analyzed from the controlled access datasets distributed from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI), a data repository housed within the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). OAI is a collaborative informatics system created by the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute of Arthritis, Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) to provide a worldwide resource to quicken the pace of biomarker identification, scientific investigation and OA drug development. Dataset identifier(s): NDA Study DOI 10.15154/ybhc-me02. This work reflects the views of the author and does not imply endorsement by the NIH, NIMH or NIAMS.

papers.title: Development of an Intelligent Educational Platform Module using LLM and RAG Technologies
papers.authors: Anastasia O. Berezina, A. V. Medvedev, K. S. Schneider, Maksim A. Mitrokhin
papers.abstract: The article discusses the design and implementation of an intelligent assistant for the "PROPS" educational platform based on the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. The relevance of the transition from static learning management systems (LMS) to adaptive environments using large language models (LLM) to form individual educational trajectories is substantiated. The technological cycle of the "AssistenPROPS" assistant is described, including the use of the Llama 3.1 model, vector databases, and semantic matching mechanisms. Special attention is paid to the method of dynamic generation of prompt templates that take into account the student's cognitive load, the context of the dialogue, and pedagogical goals. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the implementation of the principle of dynamic thematic granularity of content, which provides automatic branching of thematic nodes within competencies without pre-setting rigid hierarchies. The authors show that the integration of the RAG framework allows minimizing the risk of generative "hallucinations" and ensuring the factual accuracy of educational materials. The results of the study confirm the effectiveness of using RAG architectures to create scalable intelligent educational systems of the next generation.

papers.title: Behind the AI policies: A critical examination of the underlying conceptions of assessment in higher education
papers.authors: Mònica Feixas i Condom, Georgeta Ion, Liana Pirovino, Mireia Barrobés
papers.journal: Journal of Adult Learning Knowledge and Innovation
papers.abstract: Abstract The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to develop policies regulating its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Little empirical research has examined how they conceptualise assessment, and the assumptions underpinning their normative frameworks. This study addresses this gap through a comparative analysis of GenAI-related policy documents from 14 universities in Switzerland and Spain. Drawing on Chan's AI Ecological Education Policy Framework and Bacchi's problematisation theory, we use collaborative consensus-based coding to examine pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions alongside problem representations, assumptions, subject positions, and silences. The findings reveal coexisting and sometimes competing representations of GenAI. Concerns about academic integrity, authorship, transparency, and data protection coexist with calls for AI literacy, assessment redesign, formative feedback, and critical engagement with AI. Assessment emerges as a key site of this tension, with policies combining AI-resistant approaches with attempts to integrate GenAI into educational processes. The analysis also reveals asymmetrical subject positions: teachers and institutions generally define legitimate AI use, whereas students are positioned as accountable users expected to disclose, justify, or verify their use of AI. AI literacy and evaluative judgement are likewise framed mainly as students competencies, leaving teachers corresponding needs less examined. Current GenAI policy therefore represent an important but incomplete response to AI-driven change. Future policy development should move beyond regulating acceptable use towards participatory and pedagogically grounded frameworks that involve students more actively in shaping AI-mediated assessment and support human agency, evaluative judgement, and meaningful learning.

papers.title: Revisiting post-stimulus theta activity: evidence for a broadband rather than narrowband spectral origin
papers.authors: Théo Vanneau, Michaël Quiquempoix, Bradley Voytek, Máté Gyurkovics, Sophie Molholm
papers.abstract: The aperiodic, 1/f-like component of electrophysiological activity is increasingly recognized as a meaningful feature of neural function rather than background noise. Meanwhile, many EEG studies interpret transient post-stimulus changes in oscillatory power as signatures of attention, salience, or cognitive control. Such interpretations typically depend on baseline normalization, which assumes aperiodic activity remains stable from pre- to post-stimulus periods. Using high-density EEG from typically developing children, we tested this assumption across two paradigms: an audiovisual simple reaction-time task (n = 36, 19 males and 17 females) and a visual oddball task (n = 38, 20 males and 18 females). In each, conventional spectral analyses were compared with analyses that explicitly modeled and removed aperiodic activity in both windows. Across tasks, stimulus onset produced robust increases in aperiodic exponent and offset, indicating systematic 1/f changes. In the audiovisual task these were modality-specific, with central, parieto-occipital, or combined topographies by stimulus type. They diminished but persisted after ERP removal, suggesting they were not fully explained by phase-locked activity. Critically, once aperiodic activity was accounted for, the apparent theta increase was largely abolished in both tasks, including the canonical fronto-central enhancement to infrequent targets. The conventional method also overestimated beta desynchronization, especially in the induced signal, indicating a spurious consequence of spectral slope steepening. By contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust and was enhanced, reflecting genuine suppression. Together, these findings suggest many conventional time-frequency effects, particularly apparent theta synchronization, may reflect stimulus-driven aperiodic changes rather than robust narrowband changes, challenging core assumptions of these analyses. Significance statement Frequency-domain neural activity comprises both narrowband oscillations and broadband aperiodic activity. Conventional time–frequency analyses use baseline normalization to isolate oscillatory responses, implicitly assuming that aperiodic activity remains stable following stimulus onset. Across two EEG paradigms, we show that stimulus presentation systematically alters aperiodic activity in a sensory- and attention-dependent manner. These changes can produce apparent increases in theta-band power that do not reflect genuine narrowband oscillations and can exaggerate beta desynchronization. In contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust after accounting for aperiodic activity. These findings demonstrate that stimulus-related aperiodic changes can substantially influence conventional time–frequency measures and should be explicitly considered when interpreting post-stimulus oscillatory responses.

papers.title: Die vergangene Zukunft der Literaturtheorie. Zur temporalen Dimension disziplinärer Arbeitsteilungen
papers.authors: Charlotte Coch
papers.abstract: Abstract The essay departs from the so-called »end of theory« and relates it to transformations of temporal horizons: the loss of an emphatic conception of the future, ecological crises, and artificial intelligence. It engages in conversation with two developments, each starting from the past of (literary) theory: first, the demand for a return to the object of study; second, the historicization of formerly emphatic theory, which is now regarded as a cultural event of former generations. The essay proposes to connect these various directions in a productive way: the literary studies division of labor between theory, method, and object is interpreted temporally with reference to proposals by, among others, the theoreticians of science Mary Hesse and Niklas Luhmann. The role of the object is to represent the constructed past of scientific arguments. Method secures the future in an operative sense: it generates probable possibilities for continuation. Theory, then, is the mediation of reconstructed past and operative continuation. Building on Gayatri Spivak’s concept of future anteriority, the third section of the essay develops an understanding of literary theory in the mode of the future perfect. Theory as textual practice keeps the future open. It makes its own historicity visible, thereby keeping contingent paths open. This meaningful textuality of theory is indispensable especially against algorithmic constructions of reality. The essay advocates, in both research and teaching, an understanding of literary theory that relates it to media-ecological infrastructures and practices of reading and writing. The proposed conceptual differentiation between theory, method and object has concrete implications for research and teaching: in teaching ›methods and theories of literature‹, these could be reflected in relation to concrete architectures of writing and reading instead of ordering them according to big names. In research, concrete projects can use the reflection on the relationship between object, method, and theory to keep the spatio-temporal location of speaking and writing recognizable.

papers.title: Integrating large language model-generated culturally adapted verbal suggestions into music therapy for university students: A pilot randomized exploratory study
papers.authors: Wen Li, Guoqing Wang, Pravina Manoharan, Xuerong Cui, Lu Dai, Li Huang
papers.abstract: Previous research has suggested that culturally mismatched interventions may cause resistance and reduce the effectiveness of music-based interventions. This pilot randomized exploratory study examined the implementation and preliminary outcomes of a music-based intervention incorporating large language model (LLM)-generated, culturally adapted verbal suggestions among Chinese undergraduate students. A total of 113 participants were randomly assigned to three multicomponent conditions: (1) Chinese film music accompanied by LLM-generated verbal suggestions involving Eastern imagery, (2) a standardized music therapy recording with conventional verbal guidance, or (3) piano music without verbal guidance. Following a 40-minute cognitively demanding task, participants completed pre- and post-intervention measures of state anxiety, positive and negative affect, and heart rate. Baseline-adjusted ANCOVAs showed no group differences in positive affect, F(2, 109) = 1.03, p = .360, ηp2 = .019, or state anxiety, F(2, 109) = 0.68, p = .511, ηp2 = .012. A significant group effect was found for negative affect, F(2, 109) = 4.60, p = .012, ηp2 = .078; the Eastern imagery group had lower adjusted post-intervention scores than both comparison groups (Holm-adjusted ps = .026). Heart rate also differed across groups, F(2, 109) = 10.56, p < .001, ηp2 = .162, with lower adjusted values in the standardized therapy group than in the other two groups. The findings identify potentially meaningful response patterns but do not establish efficacy or the independent effect of culturally adapted verbal suggestions because the conditions differed in musical material and duration. Larger, controlled trials are required. (ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07359950).

papers.title: Factors associated with the unmet need for spacing and limiting family planning: Evidence from a national survey
papers.authors: Muhammad Khairul Alam, Rumana Rois
papers.abstract: Traditional binary frameworks tend to combine the various aspects of unmet family planning needs into one general category. This study evaluates unmet family planning needs by first using conventional multinomial logistic regression to determine baseline demographic risk profiles. It then applies machine learning methods such as Random Forest and XGBoost to see if they can provide further insights into non-linear patterns and complex interactions between features that standard regression might miss. Using data from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS 2022), we built a multivariable multinomial logistic regression model. Additionally, we applied sophisticated ensemble classifiers such as Random Forest and XGBoost, paired with a synthetic hybrid resampling technique (SMOTE) to address severe class imbalance. Feature selection was conducted using the Boruta algorithm, and we used Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to visualize complex global patterns and interaction effects. Bivariate analysis showed significant associations between unmet needs and maternal age, parity, wealth, residence, and decision-making power (p < 0.05). Multivariable logistic regression confirmed that having more children (4 or more) greatly increased the likelihood of unmet needs for spacing (aOR = 20.60) and limiting (aOR = 2.24). Wealth was notably protective against unmet needs for limiting, especially for the richest quintile (aOR = 0.48). Although SHAP analysis offered exploratory insights into complex, non-linear interactions between residence and factors such as parity and education, the predictive accuracy of tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost) was only moderate, with macro-averaged AUCs comparable to those of traditional regression. Therefore, population-level conclusions are most reliably drawn from the MLR model. The limitations of cross-sectional survey data as a diagnostic tool show that spacing needs are often fluid, transient, and shaped by relationships. Addressing the unmet need gap involves moving away from broad media campaigns toward localized counseling, ensuring stable rural spacing supplies, and involving husbands and mothers-in-law to turn reproductive healthcare into a shared household conversation.

papers.title: Performance of large language models in the Chinese National Medical Licensing Examinations and Beyond: Scoping review
papers.authors: Hui Zong, Jiao Wang, Jiaxue Cha, Rongrong Wu, Shanshan Hu, Yan Zhao, Bairong Shen
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and DeepSeek have shown potential in medical education and assessment. In China, the Chinese National Medical Licensing Examination (CNMLE) has become a critical benchmark for evaluating LLMs' professional knowledge and reasoning ability in non-English contexts. This scoping review aims to synthesize research evaluating LLM performance on the CNMLE and related Chinese medical examinations, identifying performance trends, methodological gaps, and future directions. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed and Web of Science were searched on June 12, 2025, using terms related to LLMs and Chinese medical examinations. Studies were included if they evaluated any LLM on national-level Chinese medical exams and reported performance metrics. Two reviewers screened and extracted data. Study quality was assessed using a 12-item checklist covering dataset characteristics, LLM setup, and evaluation methods. Fisher's exact test was used to assess differences in the passing rates of different LLMs. 14 studies were included, covering 51 evaluation records across 8 types of Chinese medical examinations, including CNMLE and specialty exams such as critical care, radiation oncology, and ultrasound medicine. Exam years ranged from 2017 to 2024, with a shift toward using recent exams. A total of 9 LLMs were evaluated, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, ERNIE, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen-72B, Baichuan2-7B, Baichuan2-13B and DISC-MedLLM. GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 achieved the highest scores of 552 (92.00%) and 523 (87.20%) in the 2024 CNMLE, respectively, both surpassing the passing threshold. In an exploratory comparison, GPT-4 achieved a higher pass rate than GPT-3.5 with a statistically significant difference, although inconsistencies in datasets, model transparency, and evaluation criteria persist across the included studies. LLMs show improving performance on Chinese medical exams, especially newer models. Nevertheless, future research should prioritize standardized benchmarks, multimodal capabilities, and transparent evaluation to ensure meaningful clinical relevance and educational value.
