The analysis focuses on how language models not only reflect existing cultural structures but also actively participate in the formation of new social practices, forms of interaction, and conceptions of intelligence. Through an anthropological perspective, the study traces the transformation of language as a primary vehicle of culture in the context of digitalization and algorithmic mediation. The paper ex- amines the applications of language models in education, the media, business, and everyday communication, as well as the ethical and social challenges associated with their proliferation. In conclusion, it is argued that artificial intelligence should be viewed not only as a technological tool but also as a cultural agent that changes the way people create, interpret, and share knowledge.

papers.title: IMPROVING STATISTICAL LITERACY AND THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN RESEARCH AMONG NUTRITION STUDENTS THROUGH EDUCATIONAL ACTIVITIES
papers.authors: Dela Riadi
papers.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in health education and research provides opportunities to support learning and statistical understanding, but also raises concerns regarding information accuracy, data privacy, and academic integrity. This community service program aimed to strengthen statistical literacy and responsible AI use in health research among nutrition students through interactive education. The participants were eight undergraduate students with a nutrition specialization from a health education institution in Jakarta. The activity was conducted online on September 19, 2026, through interactive presentations, practical demonstrations, discussions, and question-and-answer sessions covering statistical literacy, AI-assisted research, prompt formulation, statistical output interpretation, information verification, data privacy, and research integrity. Evaluation used a 12-item questionnaire consisting of eight closed-ended and four open-ended questions. Descriptive and thematic analyses identified four main themes: AI as a learning and research support tool, AI-assisted statistical understanding, awareness of AI-related risks, and human responsibility and critical thinking. Participants recognized AI as useful for understanding statistical concepts, interpreting outputs, searching for information, and supporting research activities, while emphasizing verification, data anonymization, and avoiding excessive dependence on AI. The activity strengthened participants’ conceptual understanding of statistical literacy and responsible AI use in health research.

papers.title: Atribución de género en inteligencia artificial generativa: estudio comparativo e implicaciones para la educación superior
papers.authors: Lorena Rodríguez-Calzada, Antonio Julio López Galisteo
papers.journal: Revista de Investigación en Tecnologías de la Información
papers.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education requires examining how these systems represent gender. This study analyses gender attribution in the responses of five systems (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok and Perplexity) to 16 controlled prompts about professional roles, organised into eight categories. In 40 responses to prompts without gender cues, we examined whether systems assigned a gender to the professional referent; in 39 responses to explicitly gendered prompts, we analysed differential treatment and the reproduction of stereotypes. Coding followed an explicit protocol, was assisted by a language model, and was validated through independent human coding of a subsample (κ = 0.87 between human coders). For gender-neutral prompts, 55.0 % of responses attributed no gender, but when gender was marked, masculine marking predominated (40.0 %), mainly through the generic masculine, compared with a single feminine attribution (2.5 %). Differences between systems did not reach statistical significance with this sample size. In gendered scenarios, no system favoured the male candidate, three responses recommended the female candidate, and one system gave contradictory assessments depending on the prompt version. The results reveal patterns consistent with an androcentric default and highlight the need for critical AI literacy in higher education.

papers.title: An Analysis of How TVET Colleges in South Africa Can Help Mitigate Future Global Pandemics : Insights from the Experiences of Students with Disabilities
papers.authors: Precious Muzite, Samuel Dumazi Khoza
papers.abstract: Background: The potential of Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) colleges in the Global South to mitigate the impacts of future global pandemics is critically examined, using a theoretical perspective that understands learning continuity as shaped by instructional design and institutional capacity, social recognition and support, and the competence-generating logic of vocational learning. Aims: The project intended to determine implications for TVET preparedness in future emergencies and investigate how the COVID-19 pandemic impacted educational continuity for students with physical and cognitive disabilities in the TVET sector in Johannesburg, South Africa. Methods: The data came from a qualitative study done in Johannesburg, South Africa, that examined the experiences of forty students during the COVID-19 pandemic, paying particular attention to the ways in which TVET learning practices and disability-related needs interacted. Results: The results demonstrate that learning in TVET colleges often relies on in-person instruction, practical demonstrations, and apprenticeship-style training components that mainstream universities can frequently convert more easily to online formats so students in these institutions face unique challenges during pandemics. According to students' accounts, the pandemic exacerbated structural barriers that already existed for students with disabilities, interfering with educational continuity beyond temporary curricular modifications. Conclusion: The report contends that TVET colleges are still crucial for addressing labour shortages during emergencies despite these difficulties. To enhance meaningful participation and the development of competence, it suggests preparatory techniques focused on enhancing accessible e-teaching skills and using artificial intelligence into TVET courses.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

papers.title: HUMAN-CENTRED ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN INDIAN SPORT AND PHYSICAL EDUCATION: A FIVE-LAYER FRAMEWORK FOR TALENT, TRAINING AND GOVERNANCE TOWARDS 2036
papers.authors: Tushar Dhar Shukla
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering sport, from talent identification and training-load monitoring to injury-risk prediction and technique analysis.India has begun to adopt these tools at scale: the Khelo India Rising Talent Identification (KIRTI) programme uses AI-assisted assessment of school-age children, and the Khelo India Mission announced in the Union Budget 2026-27 explicitly integrates sports science and technology.Yet the adoption of AI in Indian sport is running ahead of the frameworks needed to make it valid, fair and safe, particularly where the data subjects are children.This conceptual paper synthesises international evidence, the IOC Olympic AI Agenda ( 2024), India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 and Rules 2025, the India AI Governance Guidelines, and the National Sports Governance Act 2025.It proposes the Human-Centred AI Sport Ecosystem (HAISE) Framework, a five-layer model comprising (1) data foundation, (2) analytics and models, (3) Tushar Dhar Shukla https://iaeme.com/Home/journal/IJSAPES23 editor@iaeme.comapplications, (4) capacity and people, and (5) governance and ethics, held together by two cross-cutting principles: human-in-the-loop decision-making and continuous validation.The paper argues that the main risks for India are not technological but institutional: unvalidated models applied to children, bias against rural, tribal and female athletes, weak data protection in sport bodies, and a shortage of sports scientists and AI-literate coaches.It offers a phased roadmap to 2036, a risk-mitigation matrix and specific roles for universities, which are well placed to act as regional sportsscience and AI hubs.The framework is intended to guide policymakers, sports federations, universities and physical education institutions.

papers.title: When Nobody Knows What Is Real: Associations Between AI-Generated Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance
papers.authors: Zoran S. Pavlović, Borislav Bojić, Marija Stanković, Đorđe Sančanin, Aleksandra Vujko
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified concerns regarding misinformation, identity fraud, privacy, and public trust in AI governance. This study examines the associations among perceived exposure to AI-generated manipulation, fear of AI fraud, privacy protection behavior, and trust in AI governance. Informed by Protection Motivation Theory, a theoretically specified sequential model of associations among Exposure to AI Manipulation, Fear of AI Fraud, Privacy Protection Behavior, and Trust in AI Governance was evaluated. Data were collected from 2683 respondents across ten countries using Prolific. The measurement model was assessed through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, while the proposed associations were examined using covariance-based structural equation modeling and bootstrap analysis of specific indirect associations. Perceived exposure to AI manipulation was positively associated with fear of AI fraud, which was positively associated with privacy protection behavior. Privacy protection behavior was positively associated with trust in AI governance. However, exposure was not directly associated with privacy protection behavior or trust, while fear was not directly associated with trust. Significant specific indirect and sequential indirect associations were identified within the specified model and should be interpreted as model-dependent statistical associations. Interpreted through the lens of Protection Motivation Theory, the findings identify a theoretically consistent pattern of associations among perceived technological exposure, AI-related fear, privacy-protective behavior, and institutional trust. Because the data are cross-sectional, these associations do not establish temporal or causal ordering among the constructs.

papers.title: Digital Media Literacy in the Age of AI: Exploring the Comfort–Competence Gap Among University Students in the United Arab Emirates
papers.authors: Farah Saboune, Layal Halawani, Barakat Alzyoud, Rania Abdel-Qader Abdallah
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates how citizens access information, making digital media literacy a condition for informed participation. This exploratory study conceptualizes a comfort–competence gap, whereby students report confidence and ease in using AI tools but a weaker capacity to evaluate what those tools produce, and examines it among 300 university students in the United Arab Emirates. The gap is advanced provisionally, and all measures are self-reported perceptions rather than demonstrated performance. Cross-sectional questionnaire data (twelve four-point ordinal items) were analyzed with ordinal-appropriate methods. Students generally reported greater confidence and comfort in using AI than capacity to evaluate it critically. Every operational item mean (2.51–2.55) exceeded every critical item mean (2.39–2.44), and the within-person contrast between the composite indices was small but statistically significant (difference = 0.12, p = 0.027, dz = 0.13), a pattern shown by 44.7% of individuals. No item-level contrast reached significance and 36.0% showed the reverse pattern, so the difference is read as an exploratory tendency rather than evidence of a general gap. The contrast is also sensitive to the composition of the operational index: with comfort removed, it retains its direction, but not conventional significance (p = 0.056). Digital confidence was the only correlate of comfort in AI-mediated communication (ρ = 0.131; OR = 1.29), a weak association in a model with minimal explanatory power (McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.012); communication competence and demographic characteristics showed no detectable associations, and parallel analysis retained no factors. Interpreted cautiously, the pattern bears on responsible AI use, since comfort unmatched by evaluative capacity is a weak basis for human oversight. The study’s clearest contribution is methodological: single-item self-report batteries can profile levels and detect aggregate differences, but they cannot show whether AI literacy is one capacity or several, cannot separate real capability from what respondents are willing to claim, and cannot support strong conclusions from null results. It therefore specifies the multi-item and performance-based measurement agenda a confirmatory test would require.

papers.title: Fear-EEG-AI: A Conceptual and Operational Framework for Designing EEG-AI Systems for the Inference of Fear-Compatible Neurophysiological States
papers.authors: Bladimir Serna, Ricardo Salazar, Gustavo Adolfo Alonso-Silverio, Rosario Baltazar, Elías Ventura-Molina, Antonio Alarcón-Paredes
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and artificial intelligence (AI) are central tools in affective computing, yet fear-related inference remains constrained by a gap between experimental performance and deployable evidence: high accuracy on controlled datasets guarantees neither neurobiological specificity, nor robustness across users, nor traceable inference. EEG does not measure fear directly; it captures cortical dynamics compatible with threat processing, arousal or vigilance. This paper introduces the Fear-EEG-AIFramework, a technology-independent architecture for designing, validating and deploying EEG-AI systems targeting fear-compatible neurophysiological states. Building on a prior systematic review, it organizes development into three hierarchical levels-neurobiological foundation, neuroelectric correlates and computational modeling-governed by six cross-cutting principles, and makes them evaluable through eight observable dimensions, the Fear-EEG-AI Alignment Index (FAI) and five validation evidence levels. Applied to the eight eligible studies of that corpus by two raters who had not drafted the instrument, with adjudication by a third, the rubric reached 67.2% exact agreement (quadratic-weighted κ=0.741; ICC(2,1) =0.744). Under 10,000 admissible weightings the equal-weight ordering survived in 10.1% of draws, and one of 56 ordered pairs met a stability criterion fixed before the pairwise results were tabulated. The index is therefore reported as a descriptor of methodological documentation and not as a ranking of implementations.

papers.title: The Ethical Challenges of Artificial Intelligence: The Role of the Catholic Church in Shaping a Personalist Framework for AI Ethics
papers.authors: Przemysław Janowski, Andrzej Janowski
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is generating unprecedented technological opportunities while raising profound ethical, anthropological, and social challenges. This article examines the role of the Catholic Church in shaping AI ethics within the tension between technological progress and a personalist understanding of the human person. The study employs a hermeneutical approach and critical analysis of the scholarly literature and key documents of the Church’s Magisterium, including Gaudium et Spes, Laudato si’, Laudate Deum, and the Rome Call for AI Ethics. It also compares Catholic ethical reflection with selected secular frameworks, namely the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, and the European Union AI Act. The findings indicate that Catholic reflection on AI is grounded in an integral personalist anthropology that emphasises human dignity, the common good, moral responsibility, and the relational nature of the person as fundamental criteria for evaluating technology. While secular regulatory models primarily focus on safety, transparency, and accountability, the Catholic perspective contributes a deeper anthropological and theological dimension rooted in the concept of imago Dei. The article proposes a model of ‘personalist ethics of co-creation’ that integrates contemporary AI ethics standards with a Christian vision of human responsibility. Such an approach may complement existing legal and technical regulations and promote a more human-centred development and use of AI.

papers.title: The Social Intelligence Reliance Halo: Perceived Social Understanding, Epistemic Trust, and Reliance Quality in Human–AI Decision Making
papers.authors: Filiz Mızrak, Ayça Can Kırgız, Hatice Gokce Demirel
papers.abstract: As generative AI systems become more socially responsive, personalized, and perspective-aware, a central question is whether such features improve human–AI decision quality or simply make AI advice more influential. This study introduces the Social Intelligence Reliance Halo as a proposed social-to-epistemic spillover pattern in which perceived social understanding functions as a non-diagnostic cue for epistemic evaluation: an AI that appears to understand the user may also be granted greater epistemic authority or reliability even when the relational cue provides no evidence of factual accuracy. A randomized two-condition experiment was conducted with 462 working adults with recent generative-AI experience. Participants interacted with either a High Social-Intelligence (High-SI) relational framing package or a Neutral AI across six repeated decision trials. Post-interaction measures assessed perceived social intelligence, epistemic authority, epistemic reliability, suspension of critical judgment, verification behavior, and AI literacy; trial-level behavioral reliance was analyzed with generalized estimating equations. The randomized High-SI package increased perceived social intelligence and increased advice-taking both when participants were initially correct and the contingent AI recommendation was wrong (OR = 1.507, p < .001) and when participants were initially incorrect and the recommendation was correct (OR = 1.800, p < .001). The Condition × participant-dependent advice-correctness interaction was nonsignificant (OR = 1.195, p = .289), providing no reliable evidence that the randomized treatment effect differed across these two states. Because recommendation correctness was mechanically determined by participants’ initial accuracy rather than independently randomized, this interaction is interpreted as exploratory treatment heterogeneity across participant-dependent correctness states rather than evidence that the High-SI package altered sensitivity to AI accuracy. Post-interaction perceived social intelligence was positively associated with epistemic authority and reliability, and AI literacy was associated with lower suspension of critical judgment and greater verification; these associations do not establish temporal or causal mediation. The study therefore provides experimental evidence that a bundled relational framing package can amplify both beneficial and harmful reliance, while the proposed social-to-epistemic pathway and accuracy-sensitive reliance remain questions for stronger future designs.

papers.title: From Pattern Recognition to Abstract Representation: Visual Search and Neural Mechanisms of Structured Pattern Processing in Skilled Basketball Players
papers.authors: Na Xu, Xiaoqin Wang, Xiuying Miao, Juntong Song, Xin Zhang, Pengfei Ren, Yue Zhang, Lizhong Chi
papers.abstract: Objective: This study employed eye-tracking and ERP to investigate structured pattern processing in basketball players of different skill levels. Methods: A skill-level comparison (skilled vs. less-skilled) was adopted. Participants viewed static point-light displays depicting basketball half-court configurations, with structured (typical tactical formations) and unstructured (random positions) conditions randomly presented. Participants predicted offensive actions while behavioral, eye-tracking, and ERP data were simultaneously recorded. Results: Skilled players showed higher decision accuracy than less-skilled players under structured conditions but not under unstructured conditions, whereas they responded significantly faster under both conditions, with a larger group difference under structured conditions. For pupil diameter, skilled players showed smaller pupil diameters than less-skilled players under both conditions, while within the skilled group pupil diameter was larger under structured than unstructured conditions. Eye-tracking revealed fewer total fixations and a distinct gaze distribution in skilled players—more fixations on opponents and the ball, fewer on open space—along with larger pupil diameters under structured conditions, suggesting enhanced cognitive engagement. ERP data showed that skilled players exhibited larger P300 and LNC amplitudes under structured conditions, reflecting enhanced semantic mapping and schema-based retrieval. Conclusions: These findings are consistent with a theoretical perspective in which expertise may involve a shift from “pattern recognition” toward “abstract representation,” rather than a reduction in neural activity. However, abstract representation, neural information density, and semantic encoding were not directly measured in the present study. The Transformer architecture is therefore offered as a conceptual analogy—its multi-head self-attention corresponds to skilled players’ hierarchical visual sampling, its encoder to semantic mapping (P300 enhancement), and its memory integration to schema-based retrieval (LNC enhancement). These findings provide a basis for structured situational training in sport decision-making.

papers.title: A Knowledge-Distilled Conformer Framework for On-Device Sleep Assessment
papers.authors: V. Geetha Lekshmy, Simi Surendran
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are prevalent across the population and, in older adults, are associated with cognitive decline, reduced functional capacity, and diminished quality of life. While polysomnography (PSG) provides detailed neurophysiological information for sleep assessment, its reliance on specialized expertise and high computational cost prevents the scalable, continuous monitoring needed in home and long-term care settings. We propose an edge-deployable, Conformer-based multimodal PSG framework for automated sleep staging. A high-capacity teacher model encodes electroencephalogram (EEG), electrooculogram (EOG) and electromyogram (EMG) through per-channel Conformers, a graph transformer and cross-attention fusion, with a temporal transformer capturing inter-epoch dynamics. To enable low-power operation, a dual knowledge-distillation strategy combining feature and logit-level transfer compresses the teacher into a compact, EEG-only student. The framework is evaluated across two clinical cohorts, the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) and the Cleveland Family Study (CFS). The teacher achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods on both cohorts, but distillation retention is cohort-dependent. On CFS, the student retains 92.7% of the teacher’s macro-F1, with above 90% retention for Wake, N1, N2, and N3, though REM retention is limited to 79.7%. The distilled student reduces parameters by 38.5× and latency by 11.3×, processing a 30-s epoch in 6.64 ms using 0.64 MB on an edge-class CPU. On the older, sparser MESA cohort, retention falls to 78.1% of the teacher’s macro-F1, with REM retention dropping to 52.1%. These results show that resource-efficient multimodal sleep staging is feasible for on-device deployment, while identifying robust minority-stage retention on sparser, older cohorts as the key remaining challenge for reliable cross-cohort operation.

papers.title: Hygiene 4.0: Proposing a Conceptual Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Hygiene Management
papers.authors: Daniela Haluza
papers.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into hygiene management is offering new opportunities to strengthen infection prevention in healthcare. From real-time environmental monitoring to predictive risk assessment, AI may support proactive, continuous, and data-driven approaches to hygiene practice. Building on the concepts of Industry 4.0 and Health 4.0, this Opinion article introduces the term Hygiene 4.0 as a conceptual framework for the integration of AI with digital, automated, and data-driven technologies into hygiene management. Applications include AI-supported hand hygiene surveillance, automated robotics-assisted disinfection, and machine learning for identifying patterns associated with healthcare-associated infections. While these technologies may augment human decision-making and improve the efficiency of hygiene processes, important ethical, legal, and operational challenges remain, including data governance, algorithmic transparency, and the risk of over-reliance on automated systems. A human-centered and interdisciplinary approach is essential to ensure that AI systems are trustworthy and aligned with evidence-based hygiene practices and regulatory standards. As a proposed conceptual framework, Hygiene 4.0 requires further empirical evaluation to determine its potential impact on infection prevention, patient safety, and public health.

papers.title: Mediterranean Diet Adherence and Cardiometabolic, Inflammatory, Hormonal, Body Composition, and Behavioral Health Profiles in Physically Active Young Adults: An Analytical Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Nour Amin Elsahoryi, Huda Awni Al-Ramahi, Omar A. Alhaj, Haitham Jahrami
papers.abstract: Background: The Mediterranean Diet (MD) is linked to better cardiometabolic and inflammatory health, but its relationships with appetite-related hormones, body composition, and behavioral health remain unclear in physically active young adults from understudied Arab settings. Objective: To examine associations between MD adherence and cardiometabolic, inflammatory, hormonal, body-composition, and behavioral-health profiles, including sleep quality, physical activity, perceived recovery, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL), among physically active young adults in Jordan. Methods: Eighty adults aged 18–35 years (44 men and 36 women) were recruited from fitness centers and campuses in Amman. MD adherence was assessed using the validated Moroccan Arabic version of the 14-item Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener (MEDAS; adherent ≥ 8). Fasting lipid profile, C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), leptin, and ghrelin were measured using enzymatic and ELISA methods. Anthropometric and body-composition measures were assessed using stadiometry and multifrequency bioelectrical impedance analysis. Sleep quality, physical activity, perceived recovery, and HRQoL were assessed using validated questionnaires. Results: 60% of participants were non-adherent to the MD. In exploratory analyses, non-adherence was associated with higher odds of abnormal triglycerides (adjusted OR = 9.17, 95% CI: 2.08–40.38). After additional adjustment for percent body fat, the association with abnormal CRP remained significant (adjusted OR = 5.39, 95% CI: 1.34–21.61), whereas the association with abnormal leptin was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (adjusted OR = 3.47, 95% CI: 0.75–16.07). The leptin finding was sensitive to adjustment for adiposity, while residual confounding remains possible for the CRP association. Non-adherent participants had higher BMI, body fat mass, and percent body fat, and lower physical HRQoL. No statistically significant associations were detected for ghrelin, resting blood pressure, or resting heart rate. The IL-6 findings were inconclusive because 62.5% of measurements were below the assay detection limit. Conclusions: Greater MD adherence was associated with a more favorable cardiometabolic and body-composition profile in this exploratory cross-sectional sample. These hypothesis-generating findings highlight the importance of considering dietary quality alongside physical activity and require confirmation in larger prospective studies with more comprehensive confounder adjustment.

papers.title: Machine Learning for Digital Instruction: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and Ensemble-Based Off-Task Detection
papers.authors: Huei‐Chi Chou, Hui-Chen Yang, Yen-Wen Chung
papers.abstract: Digital tutoring systems require real-time modeling of learners’ hidden states. In this study, we develop a unified machine learning model that integrates Bayesian knowledge tracing (BKT) with ensemble-based off-task detection to address latent state estimation and class imbalance. BKT, optimized with Expectation-Maximization, achieved 82.8% accuracy and strong probability calibration, ensuring interpretable mastery prediction. For anomaly detection, a hybrid random forest-lite and threshold-tuned logistic regression improved Cohen’s Kappa to 0.521, outperforming a decision tree baseline. These results demonstrate that this model provides a scalable engineering solution that combines accuracy, interpretability, and efficiency, advancing data-driven instructional decision-making in real-world education.

papers.title: Beyond Agentic Translation: A Design-Based Framework for Human-AI Collaboration in Translator Education
papers.authors: John Qiong Wang
papers.abstract: Agentic translation systems, autonomous multi-agent architectures capable of planning, tool orchestration, and end-to-end translation, increasingly perform routine translation tasks that translator education programmes were historically designed to teach. Without reform, programmes risk producing graduates for occupational categories that are projected to be increasingly automated. This design protocol paper proposes a framework for human-AI collaboration in translator education, redirecting training from routine translation skills toward four competencies: cross-disciplinary knowledge, AI orchestration competence, higher-order strategic judgement, and critical AI evaluation. The framework is grounded in distributed cognition, task-based automation theory, human-AI collaboration theory, AI literacy, and the EMT competence framework. We specify (a) a translation-task displacement inventory mapping 18 translation sub-tasks to current AI capability and remaining human role, (b) the four-dimensional competence framework with draft assessment rubrics, and (c) a 12-month design-based research (DBR) protocol with a 5-person co-design team and five separately recruited pilot participants, with pre-registered evaluation criteria on the Open Science Framework (OSF). The study contributes (a) a theoretically grounded four-dimensional competence framework, (b) a reproducible small-team co-design methodology, and (c) a transferable design protocol for institutions facing similar redesign challenges. Positioned within the Special Issue’s three pillars of new epistemologies, pedagogies, and research methodologies, the framework complements existing Special Issue contributions on AI curriculum design and educator-AI workflow design by addressing the learner-competence layer. The empirical evidence on the framework’s feasibility, acceptability, and educational effects will be reported in a subsequent paper following the pilot’s completion; the present paper’s contributions are the framework (whose operationalisation is developed through a co-design process rather than the framework structure itself), the reproducible co-design methodology, and the transferable design protocol.

papers.title: Eating-Disorder Psychopathology in Children and Adolescents with Chronic Diseases Requiring Dietary Management: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Maria Konstantinidi, Foivos Zaravinos-Tsakos, George Giannakopoulos, Vassiliki Benetou, Ioanna Loukou, Alexandra Papadopoulou, Christina Kanaka‐Gantenbein, Gerasimos A. Kolaitis
papers.abstract: Chronic diseases (CDs) requiring dietary management, including type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), cystic fibrosis (CF), and gastrointestinal diseases (GIDs), often require sustained dietary management and may be associated with an increased risk of disordered eating and eating-disorder psychopathology. However, factors associated with eating-disorder psychopathology in children and adolescents with CDs requiring dietary management remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to examine the psychosocial characteristics of children and adolescents with CDs requiring dietary management, compare different diagnoses, and identify factors associated with eating-disorder psychopathology in a Greek pediatric sample. The study included 90 children and adolescents aged 9–17 years (63.3% girls) diagnosed with T1DM, CF, or GIDs along with their parents. Participants were recruited from specialized units of “Aghia Sophia” Children’s Hospital, Athens, Greece. Eating-disorder psychopathology was assessed using the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire-6.0 (EDE-Q 6.0), while emotional and behavioral difficulties, health-related quality of life, and parental psychopathology were evaluated using the SDQ, KIDSCREEN-27, and DASS-21 questionnaires, respectively. Eating-disorder psychopathology above the screening cutoff was identified in 14.4% of participants, all of whom were girls. No significant differences in psychosocial indicators were found across diagnoses. In exploratory multivariable analyses, female sex, higher BMI, and lower psychological well-being were associated with higher EDE-Q global scores. These exploratory findings identify candidate correlates that require confirmation in larger, longitudinal studies and may inform the future development of age-appropriate and disease-sensitive screening approaches.

papers.title: Multimodal Feedback-Enhanced Soft Hand Rehabilitation Robot: System Development and Preliminary Clinical Evaluation
papers.authors: Jianwei Lai, Aiguo Song, Xuemei Fan, Guangyu Sun, Yaxuan Di, Ting Wu
papers.abstract: Soft robotic systems have attracted increasing attention for hand rehabilitation because of their compliance, adaptability, and potential for comfortable human–robot interaction. However, the clinical translation of soft hand rehabilitation robots remains limited by insufficient integration of interactive training, user feedback, and practical wearability. This study presents a multimodal feedback-enhanced soft hand rehabilitation robot based on lattice-structured soft pneumatic actuators (LSPAs), together with a preliminary clinical evaluation. The system integrates a fabric-based soft glove, pneumatic actuation, fingertip force sensing, hand-motion tracking, and interactive virtual rehabilitation tasks to provide coordinated visual, auditory, force-related, and mirror-visual feedback. Material characterization was first conducted to compare three TPU materials with different mechanical properties, followed by system-level evaluation of usability, wearability, and actuator durability. A four-week robot-assisted rehabilitation intervention was then conducted in nine stroke survivors. Participants completed five one-hour sessions per week, including passive training and multimodal interactive training. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Brunnstrom motor recovery stage, Fugl–Meyer Assessment of the upper extremity (FMA-UE), National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scale, while usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUS). After four weeks, the mean Brunnstrom stage increased from 2.44±2.07 to 3.67±2.12, FMA-UE increased from 18.33±25.63 to 32.67±23.11, NIHSS decreased from 5.67±4.36 to 3.22±2.99, and ADL increased from 49.78±39.53 to 66.67±22.50. The mean SUS score was 74.4. TPU420D provided the best durability among the tested configurations, with more than 30 h of recorded use without failure during the experimental period. These findings support the feasibility and usability of the proposed system and provide preliminary evidence for its application in stroke hand rehabilitation. Because of the small sample size, heterogeneous post-stroke status, short intervention period, and absence of a control group, the clinical findings should be interpreted as preliminary rather than confirmatory evidence of therapeutic efficacy.
keywords: Fugl-Meyer Assessment of the Upper Extremity

papers.title: From ICT to Intelligent Education: A Many-Objective Topic-Modeling Systematic Review of the Artificial Intelligence–ICT Intersection in Higher Education
papers.authors: Agostino Marengo, Vito Santamato, Alessandro Pagano, Jenny Pange
papers.abstract: The diffusion of information-and-communication technologies (ICT) and, increasingly, artificial intelligence (AI) across higher education—the transition from ICT-supported teaching toward intelligent, data-driven, and sustainable educational applications—has produced a large but fragmented literature, and no systematic account yet maps the thematic structure of this AI–ICT intersection quantitatively. This study addresses that gap with a systematic literature review coupled to a reproducible topic-modeling pipeline. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, we searched six bibliographic databases and screened the results down to a corpus of 126 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2021 and 2026. The corpus was analyzed with a Latent Dirichlet Allocation model whose number of topics and hyper-parameters were selected by a many-objective NSGA-III optimization that jointly balances topic coherence, separation, distributional equity, generalization, and stability, complemented by an overlap-aware soft assignment that quantifies cross-cutting studies. The analysis recovers three comparably sized themes—institutional adoption and digital transformation; generative AI, instructional design, and critical thinking; and AI for teaching quality, performance, and intelligent systems—each accounting for a comparable share of the corpus. Interpreted through an ICT–AGI framework used as an analytical lens, scholarly attention spreads across the framework’s administrative, generative-AI, and learning-facing dimensions rather than concentrating on any one, and about a quarter of the studies bridge more than one theme; the strongest coupling links institutional adoption to teaching quality and the weakest links generative AI to teaching quality, a difference that a null-model test shows is not statistically robust, so we report it as suggestive rather than as a firmly established gap. The study offers an evidence-based thematic map of the AI–ICT intersection in higher education and a transferable, many-objective methodology for machine-assisted evidence synthesis.

papers.title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented LLM Tutoring with Synthetic Learners: A Factorial Simulation of Newtonian Misconception Revision
papers.authors: Semih Yumuşak, Güngör Keskinkılıç Yumuşak
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is increasingly used to ground large language model (LLM) tutors, but comparing tutoring architectures is expensive, because every design decision ordinarily requires a fresh study with students. We present a reproducible simulation harness that evaluates tutoring architectures against LLM-based synthetic learners, and we use it to run a full factorial comparison. Five learner profiles, parameterized from Conceptual Change Theory and the Force Concept Inventory literature, were crossed with four tutoring conditions (knowledge-graph-augmented RAG, BM25 RAG, a vanilla LLM without retrieval, and a non-LLM template baseline) across 30 deterministically seeded replications, giving 600 fully logged sessions on GPT-4o-mini, plus a 58-session cross-provider sensitivity run on Claude Sonnet 4. Two findings were robust to every check we applied. First, the learner-profile effect (ηp2=0.315) resolved into two clusters rather than a ranked gradient, and a Condition × Profile interaction (ηp2=0.097) showed that no architecture lifted the low-engagement, low-prior-knowledge profile. Second, every LLM-based condition exceeded the non-LLM floor under the simulator’s rule, under two independent LLM judges from different model families, and under a binomial generalized linear model with Holm-corrected inference. A third finding is measure-dependent and we report it as such: under the simulator’s keyword-triggered revision rule, the Misconception Revision Rate followed a monotonic retrieval gradient across the LLM-based conditions (M=0.40 for KG-RAG, 0.33 for RAG and 0.24 for the vanilla LLM; ηp2=0.099), but this gradient was not reproduced by either LLM judge (Cohen’s κ with the simulator =0.12 and 0.07) and was not reproduced in the Claude Sonnet 4 sensitivity run. A re-scoring ablation over the fixed dialogue logs shows that the gradient survives leave-one-keyword-out, IDF-weighted and independently authored vocabularies, and that the simulator’s numeric constants can be perturbed by ±50% without changing any ordering, so the gradient is a stable property of keyword-based measurement rather than of one keyword list, while its absence under the judges bounds how far it should be read as evidence about learners. All architectural findings are reported as simulator-internal results and as pre-registerable hypotheses for human-subject testing. The full pipeline, all session logs, both judges’ outputs and the analysis code are released.

papers.title: Access before literacy: reframing conversational AI in health self-management for low-resource contexts
papers.authors: Ahmed Saad, Joshua S. Yudkin
papers.abstract: Qama's [1] editorial on health self-management with conversational artificial intelligence (AI) makes a compelling case that the usefulness of tools such as ChatGPT for chronic condition management depends on prompt literacy: a user's ability to frame effective queries and critically interpret AI outputs. The editorial frames prompt literacy as an extension of digital health literacy and a source of disparity: users who prompt effectively can shape a plan suited to their situation, whereas weaker prompting tends to return advice too generic, or too inaccurate, to act on. This is a valuable observation, but it rests on an assumption that limits its applicability: that the user has access to a healthcare system as an alternative or complement to AI. Where this assumption does not hold, the disparity that matters most may not be a gap in skill but a gap in access. This condition arises across a range of low-resource settings, including low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), as well as under-resourced populations within high-income countries (HICs).Prompt literacy, as Qama [1] defines it, addresses what may be understood as a second-order inequality. It concerns differences among users who have a choice between AI and professional care. It asks how well a person navigates AI as one option within a broader information ecosystem. This fits much of the empirical literature. Alon and Levkovich's [2] scoping review of 27 studies on generative AI and health information seeking found that credibility and trust concerns were the most commonly reported barriers to AI use, appearing in 48.1% of included studies. The same review found AI was typically part of a broader information routine rather than a replacement for other sources. Similarly, patients with low back pain used AI-generated information but sought professional oversight as perceived stakes increased [3]. These patterns fit a prompt-literacy-style framework because they describe populations for whom professional care remains reachable.A first-order inequality is different. It concerns whether any accessible guidance exists at all. Where professional care is unaffordable, distant, or otherwise unavailable, the comparison is not AI versus a clinician but AI versus nothing. Under that comparison, even an imperfect AI response may represent an improvement over the counterfactual. Framing AI as preferable to no guidance should not be mistaken for endorsing AI as a substitute for health-system investment. Rather, it highlights the need to evaluate AI tools under the actual counterfactual conditions users face: rather than displacing prompt literacy, access constraints alter its function. In settings where AI is used as a substitute rather than a supplement, the consequences of low prompt literacy are amplified, but the appropriate intervention cannot rely only on user training. (Table 1)The evidence on AI-mediated health information seeking is itself geographically narrow. In Alon and Levkovich's [2] review, the largest shares were conducted in the United States (n = 8), Saudi Arabia (n = 3), the United Kingdom (n = 3), and China (n = 3). The authors explicitly note "a concentration of evidence from English-speaking and high-income settings, with limited representation from low-and middle-income countries, sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and South and Southeast Asia." Only one study was conducted in an African country: Adeyemi et al.'s [4] study in Nigeria. The study's own authors caution that their convenience sample of university students, recruited online, likely overrepresented those with greater internet access and digital literacy. This matters not only for representativeness but also for theory. In under-resourced populations within high-income countries, several studies suggest that cost, convenience, stigma, and reduced social friction -not literacy alone -shape AI use. Ayo-Ajibola et al. [5] found that U.S. ChatGPT users were more likely than nonusers to report lower income and lower educational attainment and also scored lower on a validated eHealth literacy scale. Other studies find that chatbots may reduce embarrassment when users seek information about sensitive symptoms, an effect most pronounced for embarrassing sexual symptoms specifically [6,3]. Yet acceptance cannot be assumed: McLeod et al. [7] found that underserved UK participants valued immediacy and privacy in online support but often rejected chatbots specifically, citing scripted responses and a preference for a live human. Studies with older Black adults further show that credibility, cultural tailoring, and historic mistrust shape responses to health chatbot design [8,9]. Together, this literature suggests that access-adjacent and structural factors, not literacy, explain most of this pattern.If access rather than skill is the binding constraint for many users, the policy problem changes. The harm attributed to low prompt literacy in an access-constrained setting is not only the harm of using AI less effectively than a skilled peer. It is also the harm of having only one channel of guidance, used imperfectly. These are not equivalent problems. The former can be addressed primarily through user training. The latter requires improving what the AI channel offers by default, including uncertainty signaling, red-flag escalation, and safer design for users with no route to verification. This distinction also matters for equity. Qama's [1] argument assumes a shared floor of care access below which literacy differences operate. Where that floor does not exist -because of geography, cost, and/or local health system capacity -the more consequential inequality may be binary rather than graded: whether a person has any accessible source of guidance at all. Treating both situations as the same literacy gap risks under-weighting the more severe access disparity.The same issue applies to intervention design. Prompt literacy workshops embedded in rehabilitation curricula or delivered through existing care programs presuppose contact with a healthcare system. Where that contact is scarce, these interventions may fail to reach the people who need them. An access-sensitive intervention agenda should therefore supplement, and in some settings precede, user-facing prompt literacy training. Safety cannot depend solely on the user's ability to ask the right question; it must also be built into the tool and its surrounding delivery infrastructure. (Figure 2)Alon and Levkovich [2] call for research on generative AI health information seeking in "higher-stakes and underserved contexts, where verification burdens, literacy demands, and access constraints may be especially consequential." We endorse and extend this call. Access constraint should not be treated as one barrier among many, but as a variable that changes the meaning of outcomes already being measured. Intention to use, verification behavior, and downstream escalation to a clinician mean something different for someone who can see a doctor tomorrow than for someone who cannot see a doctor at all. Future research should therefore stratify AI adoption and reliance by baseline access, including insurance status, affordability, geographic distance, provider-patient concordance, and whether AI was used before, instead of, or after professional care. Research should also evaluate which access-sensitive design and delivery strategies reduce harm, improve appropriate escalation, and narrow disparities in real-world self-management contexts.Prompt literacy remains a useful construct. Better-formed queries can produce more useful outputs, and critical interpretation remains essential. Our claim is narrower: prompt literacy describes a second-order inequality among users who have a baseline choice, while access describes a first-order inequality over whether that choice exists. Extending Qama's [1] disparities argument to populations across both LMICs and HICs for whom that first-order question is not settled requires treating access, not only literacy, as a primary axis of analysis.

papers.title: Digital information manipulation, AI readiness, and security outcomes in Africa: evidence from Africa’s most populous countries
papers.authors: Tersoo Solomon Shaminja, Merlyn Barkhuizen
papers.abstract: Introduction The advent of generative AI has reduced costs, scaled up operations, and made it more difficult to identify disinformation and manipulated content, leading to new governance and security challenges in Africa. This paper analyses the nexus among the manipulation of digital information, governments’ readiness to adopt AI, digital connectivity, and security outcomes in Africa’s five most populous countries, namely Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, for the period from 2023 to 2026. The research attempts to fill a gap in the existing literature by addressing the lack of empirical research on the relationship between digital information manipulation and government AI readiness, and on its consequences for security issues in Africa. Methods The paper draws on the theoretical frameworks of Social Learning Theory and Routine Activity Theory and uses seven credible datasets, including ACLED, UCDP/PRIO, V-Dem, GSMA, ITU, the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, and Afrobarometer, to construct a country-year panel. Correlation analyses were conducted to test three hypotheses regarding the relationship among digital manipulation, digital connectivity, institutional readiness for AI adoption, and conflict fatalities. It utilises a verified multisource panel dataset spanning five countries and operationalises AI readiness as an institutional capability distinct from digital exposure. Results Digital manipulation was found to have a weak positive correlation with fatalities ( r = 0.23), a moderate negative correlation with digital connectivity ( r = −0.56), and a weak negative correlation with institutional readiness to adopt AI ( r = −0.42). These findings show that correlations between digital exposure and security consequences may be distorted by underlying conflict contexts. Discussion It can therefore be deduced that although digital manipulation is becoming an emerging security challenge, conflict and other structures are more significant predictors of security outcomes. This study offers an initial cross-national empirical assessment of AI-related security vulnerabilities in Africa and calls for stronger AI governance and longitudinal, event-level research.

papers.title: Explainable AI and ESG analytics for sustainable investment decision: the roles of ESG forecast credibility and trust in AI-generated information
papers.authors: M. Vijayananth, R. Muthu Sundari, N Saravanabhavan
papers.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming sustainable investing, yet limited evidence explains how AI capabilities influence investors stated preferences and willingness toward sustainable investment. Methods This study develops and empirically tests a sequential behavioural framework explaining how AI-related characteristics influence investors stated sustainable investment preferences through perceived ESG forecast credibility and trust in AI-generated ESG information, using survey data from 566 middle-income retail investors across four Indian metropolitan cities. Results The findings reveal that explainable AI and ESG analytics capability significantly enhance perceived ESG forecast credibility, which sequentially strengthens trust in AI-generated ESG information and is associated with stronger stated preferences and willingness toward sustainable investment. Perceived Greenwashing Risk weakens the positive relationship between Perceived ESG Forecast Credibility and Trust in AI-generated ESG Information, while the interaction between Human-AI Interaction Competency and Trust in AI-generated ESG Information is statistically significant but negligible in practical magnitude (f 2 = 0.012) in relation to Sustainable Investment Decision. Discussion The study provides actionable guidance for AI developers, financial institutions, and policymakers to enhance transparency, credibility, investor trust, and responsible AI-enabled sustainable finance.

papers.title: AI chatbots for health information-seeking and self-diagnosis among Saudi university students: patterns of use, predictors, attitudes, and trust
papers.authors: Haitham Alzghaibi, Manahil Mohammed Alfuraydan
papers.abstract: Background The diffusion of large-language-model (LLM) chatbots such as ChatGPT has introduced a new layer to the digital health information ecosystem, alongside search engines, social media, and national mobile-health (mHealth) platforms. The actual prevalence of AI chatbot-based self-diagnosis among Saudi university students, the ecosystem of tools they choose, and the factors that predict use are not well characterised. Objectives To estimate AI chatbot use for self-diagnosis among Saudi university students, map the ecosystem of tools used, characterise attitudes and perceived superiority over traditional search, identify predictors through logistic regression, and surface qualitative themes. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 511 Saudi university students between April and May 2024. Instruments included a binary item on prior self-diagnosis use, a multi-response item on AI tools used, an 8-item AI Chatbot Perceived Superiority scale, a 15-item AI Doctor Chatbot Attitudes and Trust scale, five multi-response items, and three open-ended items analysed thematically. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, multivariable logistic regression, Mann–Whitney U/Kruskal-Wallis tests, tool co-use analysis, and latent class analysis. The study received IRB approval from Qassim University (No. 23-19-02). Results ChatGPT was the dominant tool ( n = 355), followed by Google Gemini ( n = 197), Microsoft Copilot ( n = 166), and the Ministry of Health’s Sehhaty AI chatbot ( n = 154). Multivariable logistic regression identified three independent predictors: gender [female vs. male, adjusted OR = 0.32, 95% CI (0.20, 0.52), p < 0.001], age (per step OR = 1.24, p = 0.080), and specialty (Health vs. Education OR = 6.71, p < 0.001). AI was rated easier and faster than search engines ( M = 3.51) and more comprehensive (M = 3.43). Privacy concerns were prominent ( M = 3.69); 65.1% endorsed institutionally verified AI chatbots. Tool co-use analysis showed the seven AI tools were used largely independently (max phi = 0.12). Conclusion AI doctor chatbots have already become mainstream tools for self-diagnosis among Saudi university students, with ChatGPT dominating but the Sehhaty AI chatbot already in active use. Male students and those in Health, Management, Social Science, and Engineering are substantially more likely to use AI. The strong endorsement of institutionally verified chatbots provides a clear policy signal for embedding safe, MOH-aligned LLM tools within Sehhaty under Vision 2030.

papers.title: Cognitive flexibility, technostress, and mathematics teachers' acceptance of ChatGPT: a cross-sectional indirect-effect analysis
papers.authors: Baris Demir, Rümeysa Beyazhançer
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering mathematics classrooms, yet little is known about how teachers psychologically adapt to its use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an organizing framework and the transactional theory of stress and coping as a process account, this study examined whether general technology-related technostress statistically accounted for part of the association between cognitive flexibility and ChatGPT acceptance. Methods This cross-sectional correlational study included 127 in-service middle-school mathematics teachers from 30 public schools in the Marmara Region of Türkiye. Validated self-report instruments assessed cognitive flexibility and general technology-related technostress. ChatGPT acceptance was calculated from perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward use, and pedagogical AI self-efficacy; actual use was excluded. A regression-based indirect-effect analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples) controlled for gender. Results Cognitive flexibility was negatively associated with general technology-related technostress (B = −0.243, p < 0.001), which was negatively associated with ChatGPT acceptance (B = −0.620, p < 0.001). Cognitive flexibility was positively associated with ChatGPT acceptance after technostress was included (B = 0.355, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (B = 0.151, SE = 0.043, 95% CI [0.074, 0.241]). Discussion Teachers reporting greater cognitive flexibility also reported lower general technology-related technostress and greater ChatGPT acceptance. Because all variables were measured concurrently by self-report, the indirect effect is statistical and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. The findings identify psychological adaptation as a relevant complement to technology-centered accounts of GenAI acceptance and motivate longitudinal research with practicing teachers.

papers.title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
papers.authors: Xuming Shang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

papers.title: The structural pathways from AI attitude to AI literacy among university students: considering the serial mediators of AI self-efficacy and AI motivation
papers.authors: Xu Wang, Jinpeng Niu
papers.abstract: Background In the digital era, university students' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has increasingly received considerable scholarly attention. However, the existing literature predominantly focused on extrinsic supportive conditions that influence AI literacy development, and very rare research has examined how subjective AI attitudes relate to AI literacy acquisition. In view of this, the current study aims to explore the structural relations between AI attitude, AI self-efficacy, AI motivation, and AI literacy among contemporary university students. Methods A chain mediation model was employed as the statistical technique, and the participants were 1,323 college students selected from two universities in Shandong, China. Results The results demonstrated that AI attitude is positively associated with AI literacy both directly and indirectly through the single mediation of AI self-efficacy, the single mediation of AI motivation, and the serial mediations of AI self-efficacy and AI motivation. Nevertheless, due to the limitations of unrecorded classroom-level clustering, the statistical findings should be treated as exploratory associations. Conclusion The research underscores the importance of addressing AI-related psychological factors, rather than solely focusing on external supports, in order to effectively promote students' AI literacy in higher education system. Additionally, this exploratory study suggests that the preliminary associations among AI attitude, AI self-efficacy, AI motivation, and AI literacy may require more rigorous replication using hierarchically structured data with recorded cluster identifiers in the future.

papers.title: The association between generative AI acceptance and college students’ career preparation: the serial mediating role of AI trust and career confidence and the moderating role of intrinsic motivation
papers.authors: Juan Jiang, Shuang Liang, Jiachun Chen
papers.abstract: Against the backdrop that artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market and occupational ecosystem, how college students build career preparation amid technological uncertainty has become a pressing question. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study constructs a research model in which AI acceptance is associated with career goal setting through AI trust and career confidence, and it examines the moderating role of intrinsic motivation. This study surveys undergraduate students in Chinese universities, obtaining 539 valid responses. The results show that (1) both performance expectancy and effort expectancy are positively associated with AI trust, with a stronger association for performance expectancy; (2) AI trust is positively associated with career confidence; (3) career confidence is positively associated with career goal setting; (4) AI trust and career confidence play a serial mediating role between performance expectancy, effort expectancy and career goal setting; (5) intrinsic motivation positively moderates the relationship between AI trust and career confidence, such that this association is stronger at higher levels of intrinsic motivation. These findings reveal how AI acceptance relates to college students’ career preparation and offer evidence for universities to implement AI literacy education and career counseling.

papers.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on students’ metacognition: a systematic review
papers.authors: Chunyu Ji, Qi Tan
papers.abstract: Given the critical role of metacognition in academic achievement and the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings, understanding the interplay between the two has become essential. In recent years, a growing number of studies have examined their relationship, creating a pressing need for a systematic review to synthesize the accumulating evidence. This review adhered to the PRISMA guidelines, involving the search and screening of papers from three major databases (Web of Science, Scopus, EBSCOhost). A total of 22 empirical studies were included in the final synthesis. Data extraction and thematic analysis were employed to identify key impacts and underlying interaction patterns. This review distinguishes between Learning-Oriented AI (LAI) and General-Purpose AI (GAI) to organize the evidence. The findings suggest that LAI was more often associated with Guided Interaction, in which AI provides guiding feedback without directly supplying answers, whereas GAI was more commonly associated with Direct Feedback Interaction, in which AI provides answers or explicitly corrects errors. Across both categories, positive findings were reported for several metacognitive outcomes, including regulation, awareness, and shared metacognition. However, some GAI studies also reported that students relied excessively on AI, particularly when they accepted direct answers from AI without sufficient reflection. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of interaction design and teacher guidance in shaping how AI supports students’ metacognitive development.

papers.title: Altered body representation in chronic non-specific low back pain: a testable framework linking body-schema-related disturbance, corticomotor alterations, and altered pain processing
papers.authors: Zhifei Xie
papers.abstract: Low back pain is a leading contributor to disability worldwide; in chronic non-specific low back pain (CNSLBP), the processes sustaining pain and disability in the absence of identifiable structural pathology remain incompletely understood. Three partially overlapping research lines have documented altered body representation, corticomotor alterations of trunk musculature, and altered pain processing in this population, but these domains have rarely been measured concurrently within the same cohort. This Hypothesis and Theory article proposes that, once the measurement structure of candidate indicators has been established, body-representation-related measures will provide reproducible incremental explanatory information for prespecified corticomotor and pain-processing outcomes beyond relevant clinical, psychological, and nociplastic-feature variables. Within this multidimensional domain, body-schema-related sensorimotor disturbance is examined as one candidate interacting mechanism that may be coupled to corticomotor and pain-processing abnormalities; it is not assumed to be a privileged or causally primary organizer. Currently available assessments do not directly measure body schema but rely on indirect and theoretically heterogeneous proxies, including self-reported back perception, tactile acuity, and implicit laterality or motor-imagery processing. We synthesize evidence from neuroimaging, transcranial magnetic stimulation, psychophysical pain assessment, and behavioral paradigms, using predictive coding as a heuristic framework for deriving testable predictions concerning trunk-state estimation, motor regulation, and pain-processing indices. The proposed framework suggests that altered trunk-state representation may interact with altered motor regulation and altered pain processing in a mutually reinforcing loop. However, the directional architecture remains untested; models in which altered pain processing, corticomotor alteration, or a shared upstream process contributes to representational disturbance remain viable. The framework specifies a construct-validity prerequisite and four predictions concerning incremental cross-domain association, nociplastic-feature enrichment, intervention-linked cross-domain change, and temporal ordering and model comparison. Current evidence supports several measurable body-representation-related phenomena associated with clinical features in CNSLBP; however, the incremental explanatory value of the broader domain and the mechanistic independence of the narrower body-schema-related component remain empirical questions requiring discriminant, longitudinal, and experimental validation.

papers.title: Embolization of jugular bulb diverticula in the management of pulsatile tinnitus
papers.authors: Timothy G. White, Cassidy Werner, Brianna M. Donnelly, Varun Sridhar, Kadir Ozler, Justin Turpin, Kelly Hannsgen, Shyle H. Mehta, Athos T Patsalides
papers.abstract: Introduction Pulsatile tinnitus (PT) caused by a high riding jugular bulb or prominent diverticulum can negatively impact quality of life. This study evaluates the effectiveness of endovascular treatments, including stenting, coiling, and Woven EndoBridge (WEB; Terumo Neuro, Aliso Viejo, CA) devices, for managing jugular bulb diverticula (JBD)-induced PT. Methods A retrospective review was conducted from September 1, 2020 to April 30, 2026, identifying twelve patients diagnosed with JBD. Data extracted included demographics, PT characteristics, treatment details, and outcomes. Endovascular interventions were pursued after in depth work-up, often including balloon test occlusion. The outcomes and techniques of various interventions are described. Results Twelve patients (eight females and four males) underwent endovascular treatment for JBD, with a median age of 40.5 years and a median BMI of 25.8 kg/m 2 . Balloon-test occlusion (BTO) showed at least moderate improvement in 7/8 patients (87.5%). Stent-assisted coiling for the JBD was performed in eleven cases (91.7%), and placement of a WEB was successful in one patient. There were two unsuccessful attempts in placing a WEB device, and treatment was converted to stent-assisted coiling. At an average last follow-up of 7.25 months, nine patients (75%) had complete resolution and three (25%) had significant improvement (25%) of their symptoms. Conclusion Endovascular interventions are safe and effective for treating JBD-related PT. BTO is an important intraprocedural tool that may help predict treatment success. Further investigation into optimal patient selection and the role of specific devices in treating JBD is warranted.

papers.title: Immediate anxiety-reducing effects of multisensory virtual reality reminiscence therapy in older adults with a wide range of cognitive functions: a pilot study using electrophysiological measures
papers.authors: Keita Ueno, Kazuyuki Niki, Hiroyuki Tanaka, Takeshi Okuda, Daisuke Iwai, Kosuke Sato, Yasuo Naito, Toshinori Ito, Ryouhei Ishii
papers.abstract: Introduction Anxiety is a prevalent behavioral and psychological symptom of dementia (BPSD) in older adults with cognitive impairment, severely diminishing their quality of life. Although reminiscence therapy (RT) is a promising non-pharmacological intervention, objective neurophysiological methods to evaluate its immediate emotional impact remain unexplored. This pilot study proposed “Smart Reminiscence Therapy (SRT)” – a novel virtual reality (VR) system integrated with synchronized multisensory stimuli – and evaluated its immediate anxiety-reducing effects and the utility of electrophysiological measures. Methods A single-session, single-arm pre-post exploratory design was adopted. Twenty older adults (aged 65 years or older) at a day service center, with Mini-Mental State Examination-Japanese (MMSE-J) scores of 11–30, participated. The intervention consisted of a 10-min SRT session featuring a 1960s Japanese townscape. The primary outcome was objective resting-state eye-closed frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) via a wearable EEG device, while subjective state anxiety via the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) was evaluated as a secondary outcome. Results After excluding three participants with excessive artifacts, 17 participants (mean age: 85.9 ± 5.9 years; mean MMSE-J: 23.8 ± 3.8, with 64.7% clustered in the MCI-to-mild-dementia range) were analyzed. Subjective STAI scores showed a non-significant decreasing trend with a moderate effect size ( p = 0.088, r = 0.414). Conversely, the FAA index significantly increased post-intervention ( p = 0.038, Cohen’s d = 0.55). No significant correlation was found between changes in STAI and FAA (r = −0.15, p = 0.562). Conclusion A single session of SRT was associated with an increase in FAA; however, the uncontrolled design precludes causal attribution to the intervention. The dissociation between subjective reports and neurophysiological changes suggests that FAA may complement self-reported measures by capturing aspects of acute emotional change that may be difficult to verbalize in people with cognitive impairment. The non-significant but moderate-sized reduction in STAI scores warrants confirmation in larger controlled studies.
keywords: behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia

papers.title: Neurexin-3α IgG-mediated autoimmune encephalitis with psychiatric manifestations and choreiform movements: a case report and literature review
papers.authors: Han Yao Shen, Xin Chen, Run Ze Yu, Wei Jie Wu, Xing Ying Dou, Xing Juan Fan
papers.abstract: Objective To summarize the clinical manifestations, ancillary examination findings, treatment course, and prognosis of a patient with neurexin-3α IgG-mediated autoimmune encephalitis presenting with prominent psychiatric disturbances and choreiform movements, and to review the literature on the clinical spectrum of this disease. Case summary A 52-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and biopsy-proven podocytopathy with a “full-house” immunofluorescence pattern showing diffuse positivity for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q, diagnosed in February 2026; however, a definitive diagnosis of lupus podocytopathy remained uncertain, as the patient lacked systemic lupus erythematosus manifestations. She was admitted on April 3, 2026, with a 5-day history of psychiatric disturbances and involuntary choreiform movements in all four limbs, preceded by significant psychological stress (bereavement). Neurological examination revealed slowed responses and impaired calculation. Cranial MRI showed only bilateral periventricular small ischemic foci (Fazekas grade 1) with normal SWI. Initial EEG demonstrated sharp waves and spike-and-wave complexes in the left parietal, occipital, and temporal regions. CSF analysis revealed leukocytosis (21/μl, 90% mononuclear cells), protein of 0.4 g/L, elevated IgG index of 0.76, and elevated 24-hour intrathecal IgG synthesis rate of 5.63 mg/dl. CSF mNGS detected 453 EBV sequences (RPM) with a relative abundance of 97.48%. Serum EBV VCA-IgG and EBNA-IgG were elevated with negative IgM. Autoantibody testing followed a stepwise approach: initial screening for conventional autoimmune encephalitis, paraneoplastic, and demyelinating antibodies was negative; subsequent tissue-based assay (TBA) of CSF revealed strong positive immunoreactivity, prompting expanded antibody panel testing, which ultimately detected anti-neurexin-3α antibodies in serum (titer 1:30) and CSF (titer 1:100), confirmed by both cell-based assay (CBA) and TBA. The patient’s condition progressively deteriorated, requiring endotracheal intubation on April 21 and tracheostomy on April 30. She received methylprednisolone pulse therapy at 500 mg/day for 5 days followed by a stepwise taper, intravenous immunoglobulin at 0.4 g/kg for 5 days, and five sessions of plasma exchange from April 30 to May 8 due to poor initial response. Choreiform movements gradually resolved after plasma exchange. She was weaned from mechanical ventilation on May 19 and decannulated on May 27. During the ICU course, she developed pulmonary infection with carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, which was controlled after antibiotic adjustment. Repeat EEG normalized on June 1. She was discharged from rehabilitation on June 9 on oral methylprednisolone 32 mg/day. On June 26, 2026, follow-up serum TBA showed weakly positive immunoreactivity, with the serum antibody titer remaining at 1:30. She subsequently received four infusions of efgartigimod at 400 mg each for consolidation immunotherapy and was transitioned to ofatumumab for long-term maintenance. At follow-up on August 6, 2026, the patient had no residual psychiatric symptoms or choreiform movements, with muscle strength recovered to 4+ in all limbs, full independence in daily activities, ambulation without assistance, and only mild gait instability. Conclusion Neurexin-3α IgG-mediated autoimmune encephalitis is a rare but treatable condition. Choreiform movements expand its clinical spectrum. The coexistence of podocytopathy raises a hypothesis of shared antigenicity between renal and neuronal neurexin family members, though this remains purely speculative. CSF EBV reactivation may represent a bystander phenomenon or epiphenomenon of severe immune dysregulation rather than a confirmed trigger. Tissue-based assay provides crucial diagnostic direction when conventional screening is negative. Early recognition, comprehensive immunotherapy, and meticulous ICU management are important determinants of favorable outcomes. Given the inherent limitations of a single case report, these findings warrant confirmation through larger cohort studies.

papers.title: When hybrid (ChatGPT and teacher) feedback does not outperform teacher-only feedback: evidence from A2 EFL writing in Ecuador
papers.authors: Rony Monteros Campues, Alexis Contreras-Falcones
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether hybrid (ChatGPT-generated and teacher-provided) feedback could yield greater gains in grammatical accuracy than teacher-only feedback among on-site A2-level English as a foreign language (EFL) students at a technical higher education institute in Quito, Ecuador. A six-week quasi-experimental study involved 41 students from two intact classes: teacher-only ( n = 18) and hybrid feedback ( n = 23). Both groups completed six handwritten writing tasks. Initial feedback was provided in English by the teacher or ChatGPT. Students in both groups reviewed this feedback using the textbook, class notes, and teacher clarification in English and Spanish as needed before rewriting their sentences. All students completed the same 18-item Grammar Accuracy Writing Test before and after the intervention. The test assessed verb tense usage, word order, subject-verb agreement, articles, prepositions, and conjunctions. Both groups improved from pretest to posttest. Teacher-only scores increased from M = 7.17 to M = 9.61 and hybrid scores from M = 9.17 to M = 10.78. The unadjusted gain difference (hybrid minus teacher-only) was −0.84 points [95% confidence interval (−2.68, 1.00), p = 0.364].
