Analysis of covariance controlling for pretest scores also detected no statistically significant difference [adjusted mean difference = −0.40 points, 95% confidence interval (−2.25, 1.45), p = 0.664]. None of the six grammatical-category comparisons reached statistical significance after Holm correction. Interpretation is limited by the small sample, intact classes with different schedules, repeated use of the same test, and scoring by one non-blinded rater. The confidence intervals include effects favoring either condition, so the nonsignificant results should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. The study did not detect a statistically significant advantage for hybrid feedback in this A2 EFL context. Because both conditions included teacher mediation, the findings do not isolate the independent contribution of ChatGPT. Future research should examine longer interventions, larger samples, and how learners interpret and apply AI-generated feedback.

papers.title: Designing responsible AI feedback in higher education: faculty readiness, student judgement, and metacognitive calibration
papers.authors: Patrícia Fidalgo, Reem Hashem
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now part of everyday academic work in higher education, including feedback. However, AI feedback does not automatically lead to learning. It can help students rethink a concept, improve a draft, and notice gaps in their work, but it can also create a false sense of progress when students accept suggestions without understanding them. This Perspective article argues that responsible AI feedback depends on faculty readiness and students’ evaluative judgement. Readiness is not mainly technical. It involves pedagogical judgement: knowing how to design tasks in which students work with feedback, compare it with evidence, revise with purpose, explain their choices, and remain responsible for the final submission. The article focuses on generative AI feedback and uses metacognitive calibration as a central concept. Calibration refers to the relationship between students’ confidence or self-judgement and independently evaluated evidence of performance. Evaluative judgement concerns students’ capacity to judge the quality and relevance of feedback and work, whereas calibration concerns the accuracy of their judgements relative to independently evaluated performance evidence. The article shows how ideas from feedback literacy, evaluative judgement, and self-regulated learning need to be adapted when feedback comes from systems whose accuracy and educational value cannot be assumed. It proposes a conceptual responsible AI feedback design cycle linked to assessment integrity, university policy, and faculty development. Although the cycle requires empirical testing, it offers a practical way to support reflection, calibrated judgement, and accountability without replacing students’ thinking.

papers.title: GenAI accelerates surface localization but not deeper culturally responsive teaching in UAE higher education
papers.authors: Ajda Osifo, Mustafa Aydoğan, Esra KAPTAN İZMİR
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education teaching practices, yet we still know little about how faculty in culturally specific, non-Western contexts evaluate and adapt GenAI outputs for culturally responsive teaching (CRT). This qualitative interpretivist study examines how faculty members in UAE higher education use GenAI to support cultural fit in multicultural classrooms while navigating local norms, institutional expectations, and ethical constraints. Drawing on Gay’s CRT framework, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 faculty members across disciplines and national backgrounds who actively use GenAI in their teaching. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we identified four themes: (1) Culturally responsive pedagogical strategies using GenAI; (2) Faculty sensemaking of GenAI for cultural responsiveness; (3) Cultural and relational benefits of GenAI-supported teaching; and (4) Institutional, ethical, and cultural risks/barriers. Findings suggest that GenAI primarily functions as an accelerator of surface localization (e.g., examples, tone, translation) rather than a driver of deeper CRT transformation unless faculty apply explicit cultural decision rules and critical consciousness to interrogate bias, representation, and epistemic authority. Implications highlight the need for UAE-specific guidance, culturally grounded professional development focused on evaluative judgment, and shared vetted case resources to support responsible GenAI use at scale.

papers.title: The access–conversion gap across countries: how generative AI adoption exceeds learning use
papers.authors: Krishnashree Achuthan
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence has diffused rapidly among learners, but a question remains whether that reach becomes useful for learning or stalls at access. This distinction matters most where learners already have connectivity, so the barrier is no longer reaching the technology but converting access into learning use. Methods This study draws on a survey of 14,653 computer science learners across 166 countries, a population for whom first-level access is broadly shared. A two-part model separates whether an everyday user converts to any learning use from how widely converters then use the tool, estimated across World Bank income tiers. Results Everyday adoption is high across income levels and is not lower in poorer settings. The quantity that varies is conversion. Among everyday users, those in low-income countries are markedly less likely to convert to any learning use, at an odds ratio of 0.49 (95% CI 0.27, 0.90), while breadth among converters does not differ by income tier. A latent typology shows that disengaged learners are found across every income tier rather than in one region, and the association between AI use and self-rated proficiency is strongest where other support is weakest. Discussion The gap sits at the threshold of first learning use, not in the breadth beyond it. This article names the pattern the access-conversion gap and develops it as a measurable construct at the second and third levels of the digital divide. The findings describe a connected population of engaged learners, so the divide to address is in use, not access.

papers.title: Refining posthuman aesthetic pedagogy for teacher education through multidisciplinary expert consultation
papers.authors: Okhee Jeong
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence and digitally mediated creative practices are changing not only the tools available to teachers but also the conditions under which teachers exercise professional judgment. Although posthuman scholarship offers a rich vocabulary for understanding relational agency among humans, technologies, materials, and environments, its educational implications often remain philosophically expansive and pedagogically underspecified. This study therefore refined an initial conceptual framework of Posthuman Aesthetic Pedagogy for teacher education through multidisciplinary expert consultation. The study used a theory-informed qualitative design rather than an inductive theory-generation approach. Five expert fields spanning art education, curriculum studies, educational philosophy, media aesthetics, and contemporary artistic practice critically examined the framework's coherence, educational relevance, conceptual relations, and implications. Consultation data were interpreted recursively in relation to the initial framework through three analytic lenses: conceptual confirmation, conceptual divergence, and conceptual refinement. Experts broadly confirmed the value of relationality, mediation, dialogicity, transformative creativity, and reflective responsibility, while questioning any account that treated technology as a neutral tool, aesthetic experience as private appreciation, or creativity as unconstrained novelty. The refined framework consequently positions professional judgment as the connective pedagogical capacity through which future teachers notice distributed agency, interpret technologically mediated situations, deliberate with others, create alternatives, and assume responsibility for educational consequences. The contribution is threefold: conceptually, the study clarifies the internal relations of Posthuman Aesthetic Pedagogy; methodologically, it demonstrates how expert consultation can refine rather than falsely “validate” a theory-informed framework; and educationally, it offers a teacher-education orientation that complements competency frameworks by foregrounding situated, aesthetic, ethical judgment. Although it requires empirical examination in teacher-education settings, this framework provides a defensible basis for designing learning experiences in which teachers critically and creatively negotiate complex human-technology relations.

papers.title: Technology acceptance of artificial intelligence for cognitive assessment in autism spectrum disorder: a structural equation modeling approach with robustness and predictive analytics
papers.authors: Faisal K. Alshraah, Ahmad Khaled Mohammad Khazaleh, Ayed Mohammad Ahmad Melhem, Ekhlas Nawaf Albari
papers.abstract: Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition for which cognitive assessment can be time-consuming, resource intensive, and subject to interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers potential advantages in accuracy, efficiency, and usability, but human-centered factors influencing acceptance remain insufficiently examined. Methods This study examined healthcare and education professionals' perceptions of AI-based versus traditional cognitive assessment for ASD using a multi-method analytical framework. A final sample of 77 participants was analyzed after three outliers were removed. The analysis integrated PLS-SEM, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), PLSpredict, and robustness analyses to examine structural relationships, configurational pathways, predictive relevance, mediation, and moderation. Results AI-based assessment was perceived as more accurate, time-efficient, and user-friendly than traditional assessment. Perceived AI-based accuracy significantly predicted AI acceptance ( β = 0.412, p < .001), while ease of use partially mediated the accuracy–acceptance relationship (VAF = 55.3%). Prior AI exposure and professional role influenced the relationships examined. fsQCA identified three configurations associated with high AI acceptance. PLSpredict indicated out-of-sample predictive relevance (Q²predict = 0.410). Discussion The findings indicate that perceived accuracy, ease of use, and time efficiency are important dimensions of professionals' acceptance of AI-based cognitive assessment. The study integrates TAM and UTAUT2 with cognitive-load and psychometric perspectives and provides evidence relevant to AI implementation, professional training, workflow design, and ethical governance in ASD assessment.

papers.title: Prioritizing meaning: value, prediction, and age differences in sentence processing
papers.authors: Yu Min W. Chung, Kara D. Federmeier
papers.abstract: Introduction Across three experiments, we investigated how people process important but complex information and how this may change with age. Methods Using an adaptation of the value-directed remembering (VDR) paradigm for sentences that varied in constraint and predictability, younger and older adults read sentences associated with high or low value for subsequent memory tests. Behavioral measures of recall and recognition were collected, and event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded during reading to examine the processing strategies engaged during sentence comprehension. Results Behaviorally, both younger and older adults used value information to prioritize memory, showing better recall for high- than low-value sentences, alongside patterns consistent with prediction-based memory distortions (e.g., increased false recognition for predictable but unseen items). At the neural level, across age groups, a post-N400 anterior positivity elicited by unexpected words in strongly constraining sentences, a pattern associated with revising disconfirmed predictions, was not modulated by value. In contrast, value reliably influenced a late frontal negativity elicited by moderately to strongly expected words and thought to reflect message-level integration, with larger effects for high-value sentences. Younger adults also showed enhanced N400 expectancy effects for high-value items, indicating increased semantic facilitation, whereas older adults did not show value-based modulation of the N400. Sorting ERPs by subsequent recall revealed little evidence that sentence-final word processing robustly predicted later memory in either group. Discussion Together, these findings suggest that both younger and older adults use value information to prioritize processing, with particularly clear evidence for enhanced message-level integration. At the same time, sensitivity to prediction violations, and the predictive processes that give rise to them, appeared relatively insensitive to value, consistent with the idea that predictive processing operates in a state-like manner. Notably, with sufficient task support, older adults showed evidence of engaging prediction-related processes typically reduced in aging, although this engagement did not extend to modulation of earlier semantic facilitation and did not fully eliminate age-related differences in comprehension.

papers.title: Building equitable AI capacity: lessons from continuous education on artificial intelligence as a catalyst for global health and oncology
papers.authors: Dulgunn Myagmarsuren, Saif Pasha, Heng Li, Akila Viswanathan, Wilfred Ngwa
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare; however, equitable access to AI training remains limited, particularly in low-and middle-income countries, where digital infrastructure and technical training opportunities are limited.The AI Catalyst for Global Health course was developed as a free, easily accessible, virtual course to provide foundational AI literacy and ethical awareness for a globally diverse audience, with an emphasis on underserved settings.We collected baseline participant demographics using a precourse survey and evaluated participation, engagement and educational impact using weekly post-lecture surveys and a final post-course survey incorporating a retrospective pre-post design.Survey items assessed confidence in explaining core AI concepts and evaluating ethical implications, as well as the perceived feasibility of applying AI approaches, likelihood of future application, perceived barriers and open-ended reflections on course content and impact.A total of 63 participants from 12 countries completed the survey, including healthcare providers (41%), students (24%), researchers or academics (22%) and professionals in technology, policy or other roles (13%).Confidence in explaining AI concepts increased from 2.68 ± 1.22 (retrospective pre-course) to 4.22 ± 0.75 (post-course) (t(62) = 9.84; p < 0.001; d p = 1.24), while confidence in evaluating ethical implications increased from 2.68 ± 1.28 to 4.27 ± 0.70 (t(62) = 9.58; p < 0.001; d p = 1.21).Participants rated the feasibility of applying AI as 3.86 ± 0.93 and the likelihood of applying AI insights within the next 12 months as 4.29 ± 0.87, with strong agreement that AI has the potential to reduce global health inequities (4.40 ± 0.64).The most reported barriers to AI adoption were funding limitations (43%), limited technical capacity (21%) and lack of stakeholder awareness (16%).Qualitative analysis highlighted collaboration, efficiency and the importance of sustained AI education.These findings suggest that accessible virtual education can meaningfully strengthen self-reported AI literacy and ethical awareness, supporting capacity building for global health and oncology in resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Cloud-native data platforms as the foundation for enterprise artificial intelligence: Architectural principles for scalability, governance, and operational intelligence
papers.authors: Ravindra Patil
papers.journal: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies
papers.abstract: Most enterprise artificial intelligence programs now run on data infrastructure that was never built for the volume, velocity, or governance load that machine learning and generative AI workloads bring with them. Organizations report strong gen AI adoption alongside persistent data-related obstacles, and a majority acknowledge that their data management practices are not yet ready to support AI at scale (McKinsey & Company, 2024), (Gartner, 2025). This paper looks at the architectural principles that make cloud-native data platforms a structural precondition for enterprise AI, rather than an optional modernization layer bolted on afterward. Cloud-native characteristics, elasticity, modularity, automation, and observability among them, are mapped against the operational demands AI workloads place on infrastructure, and governance frameworks such as data mesh are examined for their ability to establish trust, lineage, and accountability across federated data domains. Event-driven architecture and change data capture are presented as the mechanisms that keep AI systems supplied with current, high-fidelity data. Platform engineering practices are discussed as the operational layer that turns architectural intent into repeatable delivery. The paper also reports primary metrics drawn from the author's enterprise transformation program experience, covering deployment velocity, infrastructure cost, pipeline performance, data accuracy, platform footprint, and operational impact. The discussion draws these threads together into a set of architectural principles for AI-ready data platforms, while acknowledging the limits of evidence drawn from a single practitioner's experience.

papers.title: Pendampingan Pemanfaatan Media Generatif berbasis Artificial Intelligence dalam Penyusunan Modul Ajar PAI Guru Sekolah Kepulauan
papers.authors: Ahmad Nur Fahmi, Sari Narulita, Khairil Ikhsan Siregar, Muhammad Jibrin, Muhammad Syahid
papers.abstract: Guru Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) di wilayah kepulauan menghadapi tantangan dalam menyusun modul ajar yang sesuai standar Kurikulum Merdeka akibat keterbatasan pemahaman teknologi pendidikan dan tingginya beban kerja administratif. Kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan mendampingi guru PAI di SMPN Satu Atap 01 Pulau Pari, Kepulauan Seribu, dalam memanfaatkan media generatif berbasis Artificial Intelligence (AI) dengan pendekatan deep learning untuk menyusun dan memvalidasi modul ajar. Kegiatan dilaksanakan pada 11 Mei 2026 melalui tahapan sosialisasi, pelatihan, penerapan teknologi, serta pendampingan dan evaluasi, diikuti oleh guru SD dan SMP di Pulau Pari. Evaluasi program dilakukan melalui survei kepuasan peserta (n=25) yang mencakup dua aspek, yaitu pelaksanaan acara dan kualitas fasilitator. Hasil survei menunjukkan tingkat kepuasan pelaksanaan acara sebesar 87% (Sangat Puas) dan kepuasan terhadap fasilitator sebesar 93% (Sangat Baik), dengan skor tertinggi pada aspek pelayanan panitia dan penguasaan materi oleh fasilitator. Peserta memberikan masukan berupa penambahan contoh praktis, variasi metode, dan perpanjangan sesi diskusi. Temuan ini mengindikasikan bahwa pendekatan pendampingan yang kontekstual dan berbasis praktik efektif membangun penerimaan awal guru terhadap teknologi AI generatif, meskipun keberlanjutan perubahan praktik penyusunan modul ajar memerlukan siklus pendampingan lanjutan. Teachers in island regions face limited access to professional development amid the demands of the Kurikulum Merdeka (Independent Curriculum), which requires the independent and systematic compilation of teaching modules. This community service activity aimed to assist teachers at SMPN Satu Atap 01 Pulau Pari, Thousand Islands, in utilizing artificial intelligence (AI)-based generative media to compile Islamic Religious Education (PAI) teaching modules along with their supporting tools. The activity was carried out on May 11, 2026, through five stages: socialization, training, technology application, mentoring and evaluation, and the completion of evaluation instruments. The evaluation employed a one-group pretest-posttest design involving 24 teachers using a five-item self-efficacy questionnaire on a 1–5 scale, supplemented by data collection on module component completeness, estimated compilation time, and participant satisfaction surveys. The results showed an increase in the average perceived capability score from 2.44 to 4.68 with an N-Gain of 0.88 in the high category, presenting a statistically significant difference (Wilcoxon, p < 0.001). A total of 23 out of 24 participants experienced an increase, and none decreased. All participants produced a complete draft of a teaching module, with 23 of them containing all five complete components ranging from learning objectives to learning media and student worksheets. Furthermore, the estimated compilation time for a single module dropped from a majority taking over three hours to less than one hour. Remaining challenges included system limitations in generating visual illustrations, handling materials with mathematical symbols, and breaking down learning achievements into learning objectives. Recommendations include tiered mentoring, the provision of digital guides and online consultation channels, and expert evaluation of module quality in the next cycle.

papers.title: In Silico Advertising Tests
papers.authors: Marta Trales, Guillaume Hochard, Christophe Benavent
papers.abstract: This research examines whether large language model agents can produce analytically useful evidence for advertising testing when treated as synthetic respondents rather than as substitutes for human consumers. We report an in-silico comparative post-test of two television advertisements in the French telecommunications market, conducted on a panel of 800 profile-conditioned consumer agents. The study evaluates the synthetic corpus through internal validity criteria: whether the questionnaire covers the main dimensions of advertising response, whether evaluative dimensions form coherent relations, whether the two stimuli are discriminated across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic embeddings, and whether responses vary intelligibly across social profiles.The results indicate that the synthetic panel produces structured and interpretable evidence. The contribution is not that the analysis discovers a contrast invisible in the advertisements themselves: Bouygues and Orange are clearly built around different persuasive registers. Rather, the contribution is methodological. The synthetic-interview pipeline consistently recovers and differentiates these registers across preference labels, scores, lexical patterns and semantic comparisons. Bouygues is associated mainly with creative, humorous and memorable qualities,while Orange is associated with reliability, informativeness, purchase orientation and overall preference. This structure is visible quantitatively in the main six dimensional coding scheme. Among all 800 synthetic agents, Bouygues leads on creativity (83.6% versus 14.8% for Orange), whereas Orange leads on informationseeking or consideration (76.8% versus 14.8% for Bouygues) and overall preference (54.8% versus 20.6% for Bouygues), with the remaining responses classified as mixed or neutral. The analysis remains deliberately limited to synthetic respondents.Claims about similarity to human preferences or market behaviour would require external comparison with representative human data or market-level indicators.

papers.title: Generative AI use and the 2022–2025 decline in PISA performance across countries
papers.authors: Ernesto Guerra, Асланов Иван Александрович
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has spread rapidly among students since 2022, and PISA 2025 recorded its lowest results. In a preregistered study, we related four independent country-level AI-use measures to the mathematics, reading and science PISA performance of 15-year-olds. Countries with more AI use scored higher, but, critically, they also tended to show larger declines or smaller gains between 2022 and 2025, as predicted. This association was no longer detectable after adjusting for 2018 performance, before generative AI existed. AI use was unrelated to change from 2015 to 2018, but some measures were associated with declines from 2018 to 2022, during the pandemic, mainly in mathematics. The spread of country means, stable since 2015, narrowed by 7–9% from 2022 to 2025, as upper-middle performers lost and some low performers, which tend to use AI less, gained relative ground. These patterns suggest AI may have contributed to the recent decline.

papers.title: Think Before You Connect: Pennsylvania Supreme Court Signals Police Can Track Wi-fi Without Warrantin Commonweath v. Dunkins
papers.authors: Hailey E. Duris
papers.abstract: This note examines the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s decision in Commonwealth v. Dunkins and argues that, although the court correctly admitted Wi‑Fi connection records obtained by law enforcement, it failed to apply the full analytical framework established by the Supreme Court in Carpenter v. United States. As technological advances expand the government’s ability to monitor individuals through digital devices and wireless networks, courts increasingly confront difficult Fourth Amendment questions regarding privacy, surveillance, and the continued viability of the third-party doctrine. The note traces the development of modern search doctrine from Katz v. United States through United States v. Miller, Smith v. Maryland, United States v. Jones, and Carpenter, highlighting the growing importance of digital location data and the emergence of mosaic-theory reasoning in constitutional privacy analysis. Against this backdrop, the note analyzes law enforcement’s use of campus Wi‑Fi records to place a criminal suspect at a specific location and time. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court concluded that the defendant relinquished any reasonable expectation of privacy because he voluntarily agreed to the college’s computing-resources policy and connected to the network. The note contends, however, that the court improperly ended its inquiry with the third-party doctrine and failed to consider Carpenter’s additional focus on the nature, scope, and revealing quality of the data collected. Drawing comparisons between Wi‑Fi records, cell-site location information, and tower dumps, the note argues that courts should evaluate both the voluntariness of disclosure and the extent to which the data enables location tracking and aggregation of personal information. The note concludes that Dunkins highlights the uncertainty lower courts face in applying modern Fourth Amendment doctrine to emerging surveillance technologies and underscores the need for a clearer framework governing government access to digital location data.[This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

papers.title: ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY AND SHAREHOLDERS’ VALUE CREATION IN SELECTED DEPOSIT MONEY BANKS IN NIGERIA
papers.authors: ABDULQOYYUM ADEDEJI ODUBONA, ADEDIGBA AJENIFUJA, OLAYINKA SAMUEL ONI, Dele Jacob Ojomolade
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
papers.abstract: This study examined the effect of advanced technology on shareholders’ value creation in Zenith Bank ltd and Wema Bank ltd with desire whether the adoption of AI, big data analytics and cloud computing impacts on shareholders' value creation. The study adopts survey research design using structured questionnaires to gather responds from the employees of the selected banks. Descriptive statistics and multiple regression analysis were used to analyse the data collected. The study's results showed that artificial intelligence and big data analytics positively impacted shareholders' value creation, likewise, cloud computing has significant and positive impact on shareholders' value creation. It is recommended that effective use of advanced technology improve operational efficiency, decision making and reduced operational expenditure therefore, management of banks should continuously invest in technological infrastructure and enhance employees' technological skills as technology-driven strategies.

papers.title: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK FOR AI-PERSONALIZED E-COMMERCE SKILLS DEVELOPMENT TO STRENGTHEN DIGITAL BUSINESS RELATIONS
papers.authors: Dilnoza Zaripova, Islam Elshan Dunyamaliyev, Nasibakhon Yusufjonovna Rasulova
papers.journal: Journal of Science and Innovative Technologies
papers.abstract: The purpose of the researchthis article develops a conceptual framework explaining how AI-personalized learning can build relationship-critical e-commerce competencies and thereby strengthen digital business relations.It addresses the gap in the literature, where AIenabled adaptive learning systems, e-commerce competency taxonomies, and relationship digital trust constructs are usually examined separately rather than within one integrated causal model.The methodology of the researchthe study is based on a conceptual and theoretical synthesis of adaptive learning theory, capability-based reasoning, and relationship marketing.On this basis, three core constructs are defined as AI-personalized learning, relational ecommerce skills, and digital business relationship quality.In addition to that the mechanisms connecting them are specified.The model also incorporates contextual factors such as digital literacy, experience, and interaction context, and proposes an operationalization roadmap for later empirical validation through objective competency tests, scenario-based performance rubrics, and learning analytics.The practical importance of the researchthe framework provides value for researchers, educators, and e-commerce practitioners by offering a basis for designing adaptive learning interventions that explicitly develop trust-building, papers.title: Cybersecurity Awareness and Behavioral Outcomes in Healthcare Organizations
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Healthcare organisations are subject to growing cyber threats with the need to safeguard patient information and connected systems.According to research, 82% of breaches come from human error and social engineering.The effectiveness of traditional awareness programmes is constrained by poor retention of behavioural changes of less than 30 per cent.Adaptive awareness models incorporating behavioural analytics and ongoing training interventions are highlighted.Studies show that it is more effective in increasing retention by more than 55 percent in the healthcare workforce.The simulations help cut the attack surface by almost 60 percent, making an organisation more resilient towards targeted attacks.Behavioural outcomes are assessed in terms of compliance rates, incident reporting rates and decreases in risky behavior.Anomaly detection algorithms used to improve staff interaction monitoring of EHRs.Federated learning helps to provide privacy-preserving distributed learning across healthcare endpoints, protecting sensitive patient information.With 85 percent accuracy by Bayesian inference predictive scoring, high-risk employees are identified to allow targeted interventions.By 40 percent, SOAR eliminates the need for extra time to respond to incidents, increasing operational efficiency.In clinical settings, zero trust architecture provides constant verification, reducing potential risks of unauthorized access.Industry 4.0 concepts offer scalability and sustainability for complex healthcare facilities.In conclusion, the adoption of AI-based adaptive awareness systems can have a profound impact on the success of behavioral change initiatives in healthcare.The research helps build sustainable cybersecurity cultures, by making security awareness part of the routine of healthcare organizations and their workflows.

papers.title: Correlation Between Body Mass Index (BMI) and Type/Severity of Urogynecological Disorders in Women Attending a Tertiary Urogynecology Clinic: A cross sectional study
papers.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Background: Urogynecological disorders including pelvic organ prolapse (POP), stress urinary incontinence (SUI), and overactive bladder (OAB) significantly affect women's quality of life, particularly in low-resource settings.Obesity has been proposed as a contributing factor to pelvic floor dysfunction; however, evidence regarding its independent role remains inconsistent, especially in South Asian populations.The aim of the study is to assess the association between body mass index (BMI) and the type and severity of urogynecological disorders among women attending a tertiary urogynecology clinic Methods: This cross-sectional study involved women presenting with urogynecological complaints to the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre, Karachi, from January 2022 to December 2024.Demographic, obstetric, and clinical data were extracted from medical records.BMI was categorized and analyzed in relation to POP severity, SUI, OAB, and fistula.Associations were assessed using chi-square tests.Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to control for potential confounders. Results:Data from 193 women were analyzed; 71.5% had pelvic organ prolapse.Most participants were overweight or obese (80.3%).A significant association was observed between higher BMI and increasing POP severity on unadjusted analysis (p < 0.03), with a significant linear trend (p = 0.009).However, after adjustment for confounding variables, BMI was not independently associated with POP severity (adjusted OR 0.47, 95% CI: 0.22-1.02;p = 0.055).No significant associations were found between BMI and SUI, OAB, or fistula.POP severity showed significant associations with menopausal status, chronic constipation, heavy weight lifting, and mode of delivery.Conclusion: BMI was not an independent predictor of urogynecological disorders after adjustment for confounders.These findings highlight the multifactorial nature of pelvic floor dysfunction and emphasize the need for comprehensive risk assessment beyond weight alone.

papers.title: PARAPHRASING MACHINES AND ACADEMIC INTEGRITY: INDONESIAN EFL STUDENTS' USE OF DIGITAL TOOLS TO AVOID PLAGIARISM IN THESIS WRITING
papers.authors: Fahrus Zaman Fadhly, Yayan Suryana, Dadang Solihat, Dadang Solihat, Marwito Wihadi, Harun Al Rasyid, Nur Fathiyya Zahira Mujahidah, Magdalena Ngongo
papers.abstract: Paraphrasing is central to avoiding plagiarism in thesis writing, yet many EFL students find it difficult and increasingly hand it to digital tools. This study examines how Indonesian EFL students use digital tools to avoid plagiarism in thesis writing and what their practices reveal about their understanding of academic integrity. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined a questionnaire completed by 23 undergraduate, master's and doctoral students from 11 universities with semi-structured interviews with six of them. Students rated paraphrasing as one of the harder language skills (M = 2.96 on a scale where 1 is very difficult), and 22 of 23 used online tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly or thesauruses. Of the 20 students who described how they avoid plagiarism, 9 delegated paraphrasing entirely to tools, 3 combined tools with their own editing or translation, 5 relied on their own words and correct citation, 2 used similarity checkers and 1 sought peer feedback. QuillBot was named by 8 students and was the default strategy among doctoral respondents. Interviews revealed premium accounts bought through online marketplaces, tools shared among friends, and one interviewee's observation, from Turnitin training, that similarity checkers cannot verify whether in-text citations match the reference list. The findings suggest that students commonly equate avoiding plagiarism with avoiding textual similarity, a view that treats integrity as a technical matter rather than one of authorship and attribution. The study proposes an integrity-oriented paraphrasing process and discusses implications for supervision, writing instruction and institutional AI policy.

papers.title: Organizational and legal principles of the use of artificial intelligence in the process of exercising the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine
papers.authors: Tetyana Kaganovska, Oleksandr Holovko, О. С. Передерій
papers.abstract: The purpose of the article is to provide a comprehensive characterization of the current organizational and legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine, to identify problems associated with the implementation of its regulatory potential, and to formulate proposals for optimizing the regulatory framework governing the use of artificial intelligence by higher education students in the learning process. The scientific analysis of the organizational and legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine was conducted using a system of general and specific methods of scientific inquiry. The dialectical philosophical and legal approach served as the basic methodological foundation for the development of the empirical material of the article. Among the general methods of scientific inquiry, the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete, the systemic and structural method, and the systemic and functional method were applied. Among the specific methods of scientific inquiry, the method of legal formalization, the historical and legal method, and the method of theoretical and legal forecasting were employed. A comprehensive scientific analysis of the organizational and legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine demonstrated that the provisions of current education legislation do not establish clear legal frameworks for its use by higher education students. It was established that, within the current system of national legislation of Ukraine, there is no law that defines clear legal parameters for the status of artificial intelligence technologies and the rules governing their use (application) in various spheres of social life and public administration, including higher education. The authors substantiate the position that the use of artificial intelligence products by higher education students takes place within the exercise of the constitutionally guaranteed right to use various forms and methods of learning, as well as the right to free access to information for educational purposes in accessible formats through the use of competitive technologies while participating in scientific, innovative, and research and technological activities. It was established that, against the background of the absence of legislation regulating the use of artificial intelligence in education, a general trend among Ukrainian higher education institutions has been attempts to regulate, at the local level, the use of relevant technologies by participants in the educational process. The results of the scientific study of the selected issue make it possible to conclude that the lack of regulatory and legal provisions governing the rules and procedures for the use of artificial intelligence technologies in higher education increases the risks of artificial intelligence having a harmful impact on the quality of knowledge acquired at higher education institutions. Taking this into account, as well as in the context of Ukraine’s accelerated European integration, amendments to the fundamental legislative acts governing higher education are proposed in order to establish generally binding rules for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the right to higher education in Ukraine. A promising area for further research is the development of well-substantiated proposals concerning the content of the relevant amendments and the forecasting of their regulatory impact following their implementation.

papers.title: A methodological approach to developing models for calculating energy efficiency standards for industrial enterprises
papers.authors: Tatiana Meshcheryakova
papers.abstract: Introduction. More than 6,000 scientific papers on the topic of lean construction by Russian and foreign scientists, reflected in the bibliographic catalog of scientific works OpenAlex, were analyzed, basic tools of lean construction offered in educational and scientific publications were considered, and available data on the application of lean technology in large construction projects of residential and industrial infrastructure were used, including the historical case of the construction of the fourth power unit of the Kalinin NPP. Materials and methods. The theoretical framework was based on works in the field of energy conservation management, applied statistics, and econometric modeling. The information base consisted of hypothetical data for testing the tools. Three models were used: statistical (based on a normal distribution and Z -scores), robust (based on quartiles and interquartile range), and regression (multiple regression analysis taking into account predictor factors). Results. The selection of specific energy consumption as the standardized indicator was substantiated. A sequence of standardization stages was developed: collecting and cleaning data to remove emissions, grouping enterprises by OKVED-2 codes, applying mathematical models, and systematizing and approving standards. The models were tested using hypothetical data from twenty oil refineries. Comparative analysis confirmed that the choice of a specific standardization method should be determined by the goals of regulation, specimen size, and availability of factor characteristics. Conclusions. The proposed set of models enables objective differentiation of standards based on regulatory objectives and data volume and quality. The statistical model is applicable at the initial stages, the robust model is resistant to outliers, and the regression model allows for individualization of standards. The practical significance lies in creating a basis for enterprise ranking, informed investment prioritization, and systemic industrial modernization. Adapting this approach to machine learning methods is a promising direction.

papers.title: Generative AI as Teacher-Guided Feedback: Exploring Independent Academic Writing among First-Generation Undergraduates in Tamil Nadu
papers.authors: Ms. K. Kayathri, Ms. P. Poonkodi, Ms. S. Mythili, Ms. K. Kavipriya
papers.journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: First-generation undergraduates in Tamil Nadu often arrive at college with strong oral reasoning but little prior exposure to the conventions of academic English. Many have studied in Tamil-medium schools, and few have a parent or older sibling who can read a draft and say what is missing. Generative AI tools now offer them a reader at any hour. Yet unmediated use can slide into outsourcing, where the tool writes and the student submits. This article examines a middle path: generative AI positioned as teacher-guided feedback rather than as a text producer. Drawing on a qualitative multiple-case design in [two] arts and science colleges in the Kongu region, we followed [n] first-generation undergraduates across a [12]-week writing module. Teachers set explicit boundaries, modelled feedback-seeking prompts, and required students to keep a revision log showing what they accepted, rejected or reworked. Data came from semi-structured interviews, draft histories, revision logs and teacher reflective notes, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: (1) from answer-seeking to questionasking, (2) the teacher as a trust anchor, (3) language as both bridge and barrier, and (4) the slow growth of evaluative judgement. Students who used the tool within a teacher-framed routine reported greater confidence in planning and revising their own arguments, while teacher mediation appeared central to preventing dependency. The study argues that the pedagogical value of generative AI for first-generation writers lies less in the tool than in the feedback culture built around it. Implications are offered for writing instruction, institutional AI policy and bilingual support in regional Indian higher education

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: Benefits, Ethical Challenges, and Learning Perspectives among Medical Students
papers.authors: Muhammad Yusuf Arrafi, Andra Novitasari, Mega Pandu Arfiyanti, Romadhoni Romadhoni, Titin Setyowati
papers.journal: Indonesian Journal of Biotechnology (Universitas Gadjah Mada)
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed educational practices and learning processes. While beneficial, its use requires ethical considerations and responsibility. Previous studies have reported varying perceptions of AI use among educators and students. In medical education, AI offers potential but raises ethical concerns. This research is crucial for examining AI use in medical faculties to inform technology implementation decisions. Aims: This study aims to explore the utilization of AI as a learning tool among medical students at the Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Muhammadiyah Semarang.Methods: This study employs a phenomenological qualitative approach, conducted at the Faculty of Medicine, Muhammadiyah University of Semarang in 2024. The study involved 6 main informants, 2 key informants, 1 supporting informant, and used source triangulation through document studies. Sampling was done through purposive and snowball sampling methods.Results: The study of 9 informants revealed ChatGPT as the dominant AI tool, though some users are switching to alternatives like Gemini, Humata.ai, and Quillbot for various academic needs. While AI assists students with academic tasks, concerns exist regarding plagiarism and dependency. Ethical aspects of AI usage are crucial, and educational institutions need regulations to prevent misuse.Conclusion: Students are familiar with ChatGPT and Gemini, with ChatGPT being dominant despite occasional inconsistencies. AI facilitates literature searching and supports academic task completion. but can create dependency. While it brings positive impacts like efficiency and new ideas, plagiarism risks exist. AI usage must consider moral and ethical aspects. Regulations through policies and workshops are necessary to prevent misuse.

papers.title: Performance of Parental Controls in ChatGPT for Teen Safety-Risk Scenarios: Evaluation Study (Preprint)
papers.authors: Ryan K. McBain, Brooke Hollister, Ellice Huang, Adrián Salas, Li Ang Zhang, Joshua A. Breslau, Fang Zhang, Angela Burnett, Benjamin M. Rader, Bradley D. Stein, Ateev Mehrotra, Pat Pataranutaporn, Hao Yu, Jonathan Cantor
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Background. Adolescents increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for sensitive health and safety topics. ChatGPT’s parent-teen account linking feature can notify parents and apply content restrictions. However, independent evidence on consistent activation across high-risk scenarios and differences from adult accounts is limited. OBJECTIVE Objective: To evaluate parent notifications across repeated adolescent safety-risk scenarios and compare message blocking and safety-oriented responses between parent-linked teen and unlinked adult accounts. METHODS Methods. We conducted a paired, repeated-measures audit of the consumer ChatGPT web interface from July 22 to August 18, 2026. Twenty fixed 10-message scripts spanning 7 safety domains (self-harm, harm to others, sexual abuse, unsafe sexual practices, substance use, weapon access, and dangerous challenges) were each administered to 15 parent-linked teen accounts and 15 unlinked adult control accounts, yielding 600 conversations. The primary outcome, evaluated among 300 linked teen conversations, was receipt of at least 1 parent notification within 30 minutes. Secondary conversation-level outcomes were message blocking, explicit refusal, safety redirection, and crisis resource referral. Notification heterogeneity across scenarios was assessed using the Cochran Q statistic with conditional permutation, followed by exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Secondary outcomes were compared using paired account-level absolute differences and logistic mixed-effects models. RESULTS Results. Parent notifications occurred in 15 of 300 linked teen conversations (5.0%). Fourteen notifications followed self-harm conversations, 1 followed a dangerous challenge conversation, and none followed conversations in the other 5 domains. Thirteen notifications arose from a single suicidal ideation scenario, and overall notification rates differed across scenarios (P<.001). Message blocking occurred in 24 linked teen conversations (8.0%) and 11 adult control conversations (3.7%; difference, 4.3 percentage points; 95%CI: -1.3 to 10.0; P=0.14). Explicit refusal occurred in 230 linked teen conversations (76.7%) and 216 adult control conversations (72.0%; difference, 4.7 percentage points; 95%CI: 1.6-7.7; P=0.01). Differences in safety redirection (83.7% vs 80.7%; P=0.33) and crisis resource referral (66.0% vs 68.7%; P=0.56) were not significant. CONCLUSIONS Conclusions. Parent notifications were uncommon and concentrated in one suicidal ideation scenario, indicating selective activation across clinically concerning scenarios. Parent-linked teen accounts generated more explicit refusals than adult control accounts, but other safety responses did not differ significantly. Parent notifications should be understood as one component of a broader safety system.

papers.title: Ensemble of Domain-Specific Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models for Detecting Suicidal Ideation and Mental Health Conditions in Social Media Text: Development and Evaluation Study
papers.authors: Thomas Kallstenius, Basil Duvernoy, Adam Kallstenius, Andrea Johansson Capusan, Adam Williamson
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental illness contributes substantially to global disability, and public adoption of AI for mental health support is accelerating without commensurate safety evaluation. General-purpose large language models can fail to recognize naturalistic text expressing suicidal ideation, with immediate clinical consequences. Domain-specific natural language processing methods offer a contrasting approach, but ensembles integrating the two have not been formally characterized. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to (1) benchmark 5 modeling approaches for classifying mental health-related social media text, (2) develop and optimize ensembles integrating a domain-specific natural language processing classifier with a fine-tuned large language model, and (3) derive a closed-form framework constraining ensemble weighting in safety-critical classification. METHODS: We analyzed 60,889 publicly available Reddit and Twitter texts spanning 9 categories (anxiety, bipolar disorder, depression, a normal baseline, personality disorder, stress, suicidal ideation, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and autism spectrum disorder). Labels were derived from the originating subreddit or a self-stated condition and are not clinical diagnoses. Five architectures were compared: prompt-engineered base GPT-4o-mini; fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini; a domain-specific classifier (support vector machine over symptom-informed lexical features); and 2 ensembles of these models, hybrid probability-indicator fusion and soft probability fusion. Data were split into 70%, 10%, and 20% at the post level (n=42,622, n=6089, and n=12,178); weights were selected on the validation split and all reported performance comes from the held-out test split. Closed-form bounds on permissible language model weights were derived for both strategies. CIs are paired bootstrap intervals (n=10,000 replicates); accuracy differences were tested with exact McNemar tests. RESULTS: The domain-specific classifier achieved 91.9% accuracy (95% CI 91.4%-92.4%), exceeding the base (58.7%) and fine-tuned (88.6%) large language models. Both ensembles outperformed either constituent model, reaching 93.9% (soft fusion; 95% CI 93.5%-94.3%) and 93.8% (hybrid fusion; 95% CI 93.4%-94.2%) at a weighting of 60% classifier to 40% fine-tuned model, selected on validation (P<.001 for both against the classifier alone; the 2 ensembles did not differ from each other [P=.16]). The hybrid ensemble reduced the miss rate for the suicidal ideation category from 32.5% (650/2000) to 1.9% (37/2000), a 17.6-fold reduction relative to the base model, although its advantage over the classifier alone within that category was not significant (P=.68). Accuracy fell discontinuously above a 50% language model weight, where the hybrid ensemble reduced exactly to the fine-tuned model; the selected weight satisfies the derived instance-level bound of 44.0%. CONCLUSIONS: Domain-specific clinical grounding remained necessary for stable ensemble performance in this corpus, and probabilistic fusion outperformed both constituent models when language model weight was bounded by a derivable, model-agnostic constraint. Because labels were community-inferred and only one corpus was analyzed, these results are hypotheses requiring external validation on clinically characterized data before use in decision support.

papers.title: Clinicians’ Trust in AI-Based Clinical Recommendations Across Controlled Primary Care–Style Clinical Vignettes: Nurse-Dominant Experimental Pilot Study
papers.authors: Avishek Choudhury, Yeganeh Shahsavar, Ayşe P. Gürses
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Safe integration of AI-enabled clinical decision support requires understanding whether users' trust and behavioral reliance are appropriately calibrated to recommendation quality. OBJECTIVE: This pilot study examined a 3-item vignette-level trust construct and accept or reject behavior across sequential primary care-style clinical vignettes. METHODS: A total of 68 health care professionals, including 59 (86.8%) registered nurses and 9 (13.2%) physicians, each evaluated 21 clinical vignettes from 1 of 2 series. Each series contained 10 correct and 11 intentionally incorrect AI recommendations. Participants accepted or rejected each recommendation and responded to 3 questionnaire items measuring trust, perceived transparency, and likelihood of acting on the recommendation before receiving correctness feedback and points. The unrounded item mean formed the trust composite. In the behavioral analysis, 50 unrecorded accept or reject responses were classified as rejections. A pooled cross-classified linear mixed-effects model was constructed to assess associations between the trust composite, recommendation correctness, vignette position, and participant and vignette characteristics. It included random intercepts for participant and vignette item, with case series included as a nuisance adjustment. RESULTS: Participants accepted 374 of 748 (50%) incorrect recommendations and rejected 112 of 680 (16.47%) correct recommendations. Incorrect recommendations received lower prefeedback trust than correct recommendations (β=-0.772, 95% CI -1.036 to -0.507; standardized effect=-0.419). Trust declined modestly across vignette positions (β=-0.027, 95% CI -0.048 to -0.005; standardized effect=-0.088), with a decline in case series A but not case series B. Baseline intention to use AI was positively associated with trust (β=0.391, 95% CI 0.110-0.672; standardized effect=0.243), whereas higher perceived diagnostic difficulty was negatively associated with trust (β=-0.474, 95% CI -0.648 to -0.301; standardized effect=-0.257). In the exploratory lagged model, trust in the preceding recommendation was associated with trust in the current recommendation (β=0.266, 95% CI 0.210-0.322; standardized effect=0.264). CONCLUSIONS: Self-reported trust differentiated correct from incorrect recommendations in aggregate, while acceptance and rejection were not fully aligned with recommendation correctness. These preliminary findings identify a potential evaluation problem: lower trust in incorrect advice does not necessarily imply that users will reject it. The findings do not establish real-world clinical effects.

papers.title: Development and Internal Validation of an Interpretable Machine Learning Model for Identifying Past-Year Nonsuicidal Self-Injury Among Adolescents With Depression: Retrospective Study
papers.authors: Gaoyang Liu, Chenxi Yang, wendan chen, Ningning Ding, Wenwen Tian, Xinwu Ye, Mengdan Luo, Xinnan Mao, Guohua Zhang, Ke Zheng
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is common among adolescents with depressive disorders and is associated with substantial clinical burden. Machine learning may assist in identifying multidimensional patterns associated with NSSI, although its incremental value beyond direct clinical assessment remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: This study compares 7 supervised machine learning model variants for classifying past-year NSSI status among adolescents with depressive disorders and conducts detailed analyses of interpretability, sensitivity, subgroup performance, and clinical utility using a random forest model as the focal exploratory model. METHODS: We retrospectively identified 437 adolescents aged 10-19 years who received inpatient or outpatient psychiatric care at 4 hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, between January 2021 and December 2023. A total of 410 eligible participants were included, of whom 274 reported NSSI during the preceding year. The primary analysis included 67 assessment-time sociodemographic, physiological, biochemical, and clinical-behavioral features. The sample was divided into a training set (287/410, 70%) and an untouched held-out test set (123/410, 30%) using stratified random sampling. Hyperparameters were optimized using 5-fold cross-validation within the training set. Performance was evaluated using discrimination, classification metrics, calibration, and decision-curve analysis. Random forest model behavior was examined using Gini importance, permutation importance, and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP). RESULTS: The radial basis function support vector machine achieved the highest mean cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) in the training set (0.720), whereas the random forest showed the highest observed AUROC and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and the lowest Brier score in the held-out test set. The random forest achieved an AUROC of 0.681 (95% CI 0.583-0.778), an AUPRC of 0.808 (95% CI 0.741-0.874), an accuracy of 0.667 (95% CI 0.585-0.748), a sensitivity of 0.720 (95% CI 0.622-0.817), a specificity of 0.561 (95% CI 0.415-0.707), and a Brier score of 0.212 (95% CI 0.188-0.236). Its calibration slope was 1.013. Pairwise AUROC differences between the random forest and alternative models were not statistically significant after Holm correction (Holm-adjusted P values ranged from .17 to .81). The full random forest model did not outperform a suicidal-ideation-only model (AUROC 0.701), whereas excluding suicidal ideation and previous suicide attempt reduced the AUROC to 0.540. A biochemical-only model showed near-chance discrimination (AUROC 0.513). Decision-curve analysis indicated that the random forest provided greater net benefit than the assess-all and assess-none strategies across threshold probabilities of approximately 0.51-0.80. Suicidal ideation showed the most consistent importance across Gini, SHAP, and permutation analyses. CONCLUSIONS: The random forest had the highest observed AUROC and AUPRC and the lowest Brier score in the held-out test set among the evaluated algorithms, although the pairwise AUROC differences were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Suicidality-related information contributed substantially to model discrimination, whereas routinely collected biochemical variables did not demonstrate clear incremental value. Because this was a retrospective cross-sectional classification study, the findings do not establish prospective risk prediction. External and prospective temporal validation is required before clinical implementation.
keywords: radial basis function support vector machine

papers.title: What Users Say About Reimbursable Digital Therapeutics in Germany: Large-Scale App Store Review Analysis Using a Large Language Model
papers.authors: Benjamin Kinast, Henrik Rohde, Björn Schreiweis, Hannes Ulrich
papers.abstract: Background: In 2019, Germany introduced a unique regulatory framework for digital therapeutics (DTx), termed digital health applications (DiGAs) in Germany, with the goal of integrating evidence-based DTx into statutory health care. DTx are eligible for reimbursement by statutory health insurance if manufacturers demonstrate positive health care effects, such as improved health status or health literacy, in a controlled study setting. Although regulatory evaluation primarily relies on manufacturer-conducted studies, these studies do not fully capture how users experience and use DiGAs in everyday life. Objective: The study aims to systematically characterize user experiences with reimbursable DiGAs by analyzing the sentiment and thematic content in publicly available app store reviews at scale to identify recurring patterns of positive and negative feedback across regulatory-relevant quality dimensions. Methods: All DiGAs with publicly available mobile app reviews were identified via the official German Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices (BfArM) directory. User reviews were extracted from the German Apple App Store and Google Play Store using a tailored Python script. Reviews were then processed using GPT-4o, which extracted up to 5 core statements per review and assigned each a sentiment label (positive, neutral, or negative) and one of ten predefined thematic categories to each statement: content, technology, cost and reimbursement, login and registration, prescription and approval, user experience and design, support, tracking and documentation, effectiveness, and overall impression, all derived from the regulatory and quality criteria applicable to DiGA certification. Classification quality was assessed through manual validation, in which each of the 3 authors independently reviewed one-third of all model outputs. Results: -score of 0.95). While the categories overall impression (1233/1431, 86.2% positive) and effectiveness (1440/1609, 89.5% positive) received particularly positive feedback, users commented most negatively on the login and registration process (263/280, 93.9% negative) and technology-related aspects (563/668, 84.3% negative). Conclusions: User feedback on reimbursable DiGAs is predominantly positive, particularly regarding perceived effectiveness, overall impression, and content. However, recurring criticism of login and registration processes, technical reliability, and prescription and approval procedures reveals persistent barriers to access and use. As many of these aspects are prerequisites rather than peripheral convenience issues, they should be treated as essential implementation requirements. Analyzed at scale with large language model-based methods, publicly available app store reviews can complement formal evaluation by providing user-centered real-world evidence for postmarket monitoring and regulatory quality improvement.

papers.title: Large Language Model Chatbot Responses to Cancer Survivorship Questions in Hong Kong: Bilingual Evaluation and Prompt Optimization Study
papers.authors: Haoyu An, Wanshu Huang, Rachel Tsoi Man Cheung, Qijun Du, Rong Na, David Ka-Ki Wong
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: As the population of survivors of cancer grows and new information technologies become widespread in Hong Kong, survivors of cancer increasingly seek ongoing care and support information from large language models (LLMs). While these tools provide immediate conversational responses, they carry substantial risks of generating inaccurate, unsafe, or generic medical advice. Evaluating LLM response performance is particularly critical in Hong Kong's bilingual health care context. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the clinical utility, safety, understandability, and readability of 4 popular commercial LLMs answering cancer survivorship questions in English and Traditional Chinese and to explore whether a structured prompting strategy improves response performance. METHODS: We conducted a 2-phase evaluation study combining quantitative scoring with qualitative classification of unsafe responses. In phase 1, 25 expert-curated questions spanning 5 survivorship domains were input into 4 LLMs: Google Gemini 3.1 Pro, HK Chat-0.6.2, DeepSeek-V3.2, and Kimi-K2.5. A Delphi expert panel evaluated the baseline responses for clinical utility using a 5-point scale and assessed safety via binary categorization. Understandability was measured using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT). Readability was assessed via the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level for English and lexical richness for Traditional Chinese. In phase 2, experts developed an optimized context, role, audience, format, task, and tone (CRAFT) prompt, and the resulting LLM responses were compared with baseline outputs in an exploratory within-sample analysis using paired statistical tests. RESULTS: Baseline evaluations identified Google Gemini 3.1 Pro as the most clinically useful model in English (mean 3.99/5, SD 0.16) and Traditional Chinese (mean 4.21/5, SD 0.20). Unconstrained models demonstrated language-dependent safety vulnerabilities: English errors (up to 24%) centered on service mismatches and definitive interpretations, whereas Traditional Chinese errors (up to 20%) involved prescriptive disease management and unverified adjunctive therapies. Within each language, the models producing the most readable text were not those achieving the highest clinical utility; this relationship was not formally tested. Applying the CRAFT prompt to Gemini 3.1 Pro significantly improved clinical utility across both languages (English: mean 4.68, SD 0.18, P<.001; Traditional Chinese: 4.66, SD 0.23, P<.001). After prompting, the 2 unsafe English baseline responses were reclassified as safe (English 23/25 to 25/25 safe; Traditional Chinese 25/25 at both time points). This transition was not statistically significant on a post hoc exact McNemar test (P=.50) and is reported as descriptive. CONCLUSIONS: LLMs exhibited language-divergent clinical safety vulnerabilities when answering cancer survivorship queries, and within each language, the most readable models were not the most clinically useful. In an exploratory within-sample comparison, expert-designed CRAFT prompting improved clinical utility and corrected the unsafe outputs seen at baseline without reducing understandability. Safe deployment of LLMs in multilingual oncology contexts requires strict validation combined with structured, role-restrictive constraints.

papers.title: Literary interpretation mediated by an intelligent conversational agent: A prompt-based framework for digital transformation in the humanities
papers.authors: Rômulo Sherman, Sílvia Araújo
papers.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education is reshaping literary learning, where interpretation requires sustained pedagogical support rather than ready-made answers. While large language models can provide personalised assistance, use without instructional framing may encourage surface-level engagement. This study introduces RELIA: empathetic reading guide with artificial intelligence, a conversational agent developed through an iterative design-and-evaluation approach to support interpretative learning. RELIA uses structured prompts as an instructional script in a three-mode design—Tutor (guided support), Checkpoint (adaptive formative assessment), and Evaluator (formative learning summary), including a conditional review loop that redirects learners to additional support when repeated difficulty is detected. An exploratory mixed-methods study (N = 20) examined learner perceptions, complemented by thematic analysis of open-ended responses. Results provide preliminary indications of high perceived clarity (M = 4.13) and strong acceptance of adaptive formative assessment (M = 4.21), alongside high usability but more variable motivation (M = 3.83). Moving beyond an evaluation focused solely on RELIA, the article proposes a transferable framework for integrating conversational agents into humanities teaching–learning cycles, showing how structured prompting can mediate literary interpretation while preserving critical agency.

papers.title: Impacto dos chatbots assistidos por inteligência artificial na aprendizagem de português como língua adicional por estudantes universitários chineses
papers.authors: Carina Jiayu Liu
papers.abstract: This qualitative study provides an empirically grounded analysis of the perception held by learners of Portuguese as an Additional Language (PAL) regarding the impact of AI-assisted chatbots on language learning, which is essential for understanding the mediational and affective role of AI in the digital era. Specifically, drawing on Krashen’s Input Hypothesis and Affective Filter Hypothesis (1982, 1985), as well as key theories of motivation, anxiety, and self-confidence in second language acquisition, this study explores learners’ perceptions, advantages, and perceived limitations of chatbot use. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with sixteen Chinese students learning PAL. Thematic analysis revealed positive outcomes such as enhanced motivation, increased confidence, and improved linguistic performance, alongside negative effects such as excessive dependence and stagnation of independent thinking. Furthermore, limitations persist in personalized responses, emotional sensitivity, data privacy, and technical stability. These findings provide valuable pedagogical and technological implications for language educators and assessors aiming to optimize AI integration in language teaching and learning contexts.

papers.title: A aplicação da inteligência artificial generativa na aprendizagem de português como língua estrangeira em contextos não imersivos: um estudo exploratório com aprendentes chineses
papers.authors: Mengru Liu
papers.abstract: This study aims to investigate the application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in learning Portuguese as a foreign language (PLE) in non-immersive contexts, with a focus on learners’ usage patterns, learning experiences and perceptions, attitudes, and reflections, as well as differences across proficiency levels. An exploratory descriptive design is adopted, with data collected via a questionnaire distributed to 23 Chinese learners at A2 and B1 levels at a university in Chinese mainland. The findings indicate that GenAI is widely used in tasks such as writing support, text production, and grammar comprehension, significantly enhancing learning efficiency, whereas its application in oral skills, pronunciation practice, and listening comprehension remains relatively limited. Overall, learners exhibited positive attitudes toward GenAI, while simultaneously demonstrating critical awareness and reflective capacity, expressing concerns about information reliability and potential overreliance. It was observed that A2-level learners tend to use GenAI more frequently, valuing primarily its ease of use and rapid feedback. In contrast, B1-level learners exhibit greater concern with information verification and associated risks, fearing that potential errors generated by GenAI could affect learning outcomes. These differentiated results suggest that GenAI not only functions as an effective resource to support Portuguese language learning but also holds potential for transformative use, contributing to the development of learners’ critical thinking skills.

papers.title: Nueva tendencia pedagógica multimodal en ESP. IA generativa, rendimiento oral y percepción del alumnado
papers.authors: Beatriz Chaves-Yuste, Juana María Anguita Acero
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the impact of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) on students’ academic performance and motivational perceptions. A total of 114 first-year Tourism degree students from Complutense University of Madrid (Spain) participated. The assessed skill was oral production in English for specific purposes (ESP) in the tourism field, through two promotional videos: one created conventionally and another supported by AI. Performance was evaluated using a six-dimension rubric (pronunciation and intonation, grammatical and lexical accuracy, fluency, coherence and cohesion, communicative appropriateness and content, and overall presentation), and a 20-item questionnaire based on the expectancy-value theory (Wigfield & Eccles, 2000) was administered. Results show a slight improvement in the score of the AI-assisted video, but without statistically significant differences and with a small effect size, indicating no robust impact of AI on oral performance. However, students reported moderate-to-high levels of perceived usefulness, attainment value, and success expectancy, along with moderate interest and perceived cost. The study concludes that the pedagogical value of AI depends on its instructional integration and that, although it does not immediately enhance oral skills, it can serve as a motivational resource and support tool for planning and completing authentic ESP tasks.

papers.title: O uso da inteligência artificial para a gamificação do conteúdo de substantivos. Uma proposta para uso nas aulas de língua portuguesa no ensino secundário
papers.authors: Paciência Hifindaka, Zolina Massiala, Margareth Azenaid Ebó Pereira João Justino, João Indembi
papers.abstract: This study presents a proposal for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into the teaching of the Portuguese language, aiming at the gamification of noun instruction in secondary education. The proposal is grounded in an awareness of students’ familiarity with digital technologies and the need to promote digital literacy, critical and inclusive competences, as well as the use of AI in teaching and learning processes. A Pedagogical Design methodology was employed, drawing on interface design dimensions which, combined with pedagogical planning and incorporating aspects of Design-Based Research, enabled the development of the digital learning material embodied in the educational game Caça aos Substantivos (Noun Hunt), based on the adaptation of a literary text. The construction of the game incorporated generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Perplexity and Canva, to create interactive and progressively challenging activities involving the identification, classification, and completion of sentences using nouns. The game contextualises grammar instruction within reading practices, promoting motivation, critical thinking, personalised learning, and the democratisation of access to digital technologies. The proposal emphasises ethical principles such as transparency, consent, explainability, legality, security, and privacy, while demonstrating that simple and targeted solutions can contribute significantly to pedagogical innovation, even in resource-constrained contexts. The findings suggest that artificial Intelligence can function as an ally in teaching and learning processes by fostering innovative, inclusive, reflective, and context-sensitive practices adapted to students’ realities, without replacing human mediation.
