Interviews were guided by Jacobson et al.'s Knowledge Translation Framework, and were analyzed thematically using a hybrid inductive-deductive approach with MAXQDA software. Triangulation, member-checking, and reflexivity were employed to ensure analytical rigor and validity. RESULTS: The findings reveal that evidence uptake is influenced by leadership priorities, institutional structures, and alignment with policy windows. While formal platforms such as the National Technical Expert Group and Health Technology Assessment India facilitate evidence appraisal for clinical decisions, non-clinical areas such as communication and strategy lack systematic review processes. A disconnect persists between researchers and implementers, with limited co-creation of research questions. Operationally relevant evidence is often missing or inadequately disseminated, and global models are frequently adopted without sufficient local adaptation, reflecting isomorphic mimicry. The credibility of evidence producers and strategic brokering by intermediaries plays a significant role in determining policy influence. Participants emphasized the need for locally grounded, policy-aligned, and practically useful evidence. CONCLUSION: Improving evidence used in the National Tuberculosis Elimination Program requires co-creation, strategic dissemination, and alignment with institutional priorities, leadership timing, and contextual realities. SPANISH ABSTRACT: https://links.lww.com/IJEBH/A701.

papers.title: A Structured Framework for Translation of the ACNS Standardized Critical Care EEG Terminology Into Spanish
papers.authors: Clio Rubiños, Daniel San‐Juan, Carlos Alva‐Díaz, Maritza Beato, Juan Enrique Bender del Busto, Paloma Balugo, Saskia Bermudez R, Sixto Bogantes-Ledezma, Yamille Calle-Lopez, Lucía Cibils, Guilca Contreras, Jose Carlos Cordero, Victoria Fernandez, Cynthia Florentín, Henry Hugo Galvez, Iván Gaona, María del Carmen García, Nicolás Garófalo Gómez, Rosaly Gonzalez, Alfonso Gutierrez, Laura Hernandez, Mariana Legnani, Angélica Lizcano, Daniel Magos, Nancy Malpartida, Jorge A. Mateos, Laura Mendoza, Anna Milan, Ramiro Montenegro López, Guillermo Martín-Palomeque, Elma M. Paredes-Aragón, Mónica Beatriz Perassolo, Eunice Ramírez, Ana Ramos, Víctor Rivas, Natali Sánchez Ortiz, Oscar Servin, Sebastián Silva-Soto, Humberto Su, Arnold Thompson, Vanessa Thonon, Adriana Ulate-Campos, Reinaldo Uribe-San-Martín, Jean Paul Vergara, Manuel Vides-Rosales, Ivan Viñan Vazquez, Álvaro-Alejandro Zavala-Reina, Jessica Daily, Jessica Grant, Rosemary Frasso, Andres Fernandez, Maria Bruzzone, on behalf of Consorcio Hispano de Monitoreo Electroencefalográfico
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: The American Clinical Neurophysiology Society (ACNS) Critical Care EEG Terminology provides standardized language for describing electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns in critically ill patients but has not been formally translated into Spanish. We aimed to develop a consensus-based Spanish translation of the ACNS Critical Care EEG Terminology using a multi-phase methodology involving physicians from Spanish-speaking countries. METHODS: This qualitative study aimed to establish a standardized Spanish ACNS Critical Care EEG terminology through a three-phase process: Phase 1: Initial iterative translation by 14 Spanish-speaking physicians working in subgroups. Discrepancies were documented for further discussion. Phase 2: Focus groups with specialists practicing in Spanish-speaking countries, guided by qualitative research experts. Sessions explored terminology preferences, implementation challenges, and regional variations. Phase 3: Qualitative analysis and final consensus using a modified Delphi methodology. Ranked choice voting analysis to achieve ≥75% consensus was used and when needed, a two-option runoff determined the final selected term. RESULTS: Forty-five physicians from all Spanish-speaking countries except Nicaragua participated in 10 focus groups to review 25 terms. Seven terms generated two possible Spanish translations, four generated three, five generated four, and nine generated five. A consensus-based Spanish terminology was established, prioritizing semantic fidelity to the ACNS terminology while also accounting for terms already in wide regional use. Examples of final consensus terms included: Generalized Periodic Discharges → Descargas Periódicas Generalizadas (98%, Round 1); Lateralized Rhythmic Delta Activity → Actividad Delta Rítmica Lateralizada (100%, round 1); and Sharp Wave → Onda Aguda (82%, round 1). The outdated term periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges remained widely used because of familiarity among intensivists. CONCLUSIONS: This effort provides the first structured Spanish adaptation of the ACNS Critical Care EEG terminology. The resulting lexicon reflects linguistic diversity across regions and supports consistent communication, training, research, and broader adoption of evidence-based continuous EEG practices.

papers.title: Application of deep learning and explainable AI-supported medical decision-making for facial phenotyping in genetic syndromes
papers.authors: Ömer Sümer, Tobias Huber, Jiayi Cheng, Dat Duong, Suzanna E. Ledgister Hanchard, Cristina Conati, Elisabeth André, Benjamin D. Solomon, Rebekah L. Waikel
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly employed in clinical genetics to assist in diagnosing genetic conditions by assessing photographs of patients. For medical uses of AI, explainable AI (XAI) methods offer a promising approach by providing interpretable outputs, such as saliency maps and region relevance visualizations. XAI has been discussed as important for regulatory purposes and to enable clinicians to better understand how AI tools work in practice. However, the real-world effects of XAI on clinician performance, confidence, and trust remain underexplored. This study involved a web-based user experiment with 31 medical geneticists to assess the impact of AI-only diagnostic assistance compared to XAI-supported diagnostics. Participants were randomly assigned to either group and completed diagnostic tasks with 18 facial images of individuals with known genetic syndromes and unaffected individuals, before and after experiencing the AI outputs. The results show that both AI-only and XAI approaches improved diagnostic accuracy and clinician confidence. The effects varied according to the accuracy of AI predictions and the clarity of syndromic features (sample difficulty). While AI support was viewed positively, users approached XAI with skepticism. Interestingly, we found a positive correlation between diagnostic improvement and XAI intervention. Although XAI support did not significantly enhance overall performance relative to AI alone, it prompted users to critically evaluate images with false predictions and influenced their confidence levels. These findings highlight the complexities of trust, perceived usefulness, and interpretability in AI-assisted diagnostics, with important implications for developing and implementing clinical decision-support tools in facial phenotyping for rare genetic diseases.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Training for Informatics Students and Pharmacy Residents
papers.authors: Julie A. Pawola, Kevin T. Fuji, Catherine Palmer
papers.abstract: Julie Pawola, PharmD, Kevin T Fuji, PharmD, MA, Catherine Palmer, PharmD; Artificial Intelligence Training for Informatics Students and Pharmacy Residents,

papers.title: Theory-informed redesign of clinical reasoning education in the era of generative artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Verity E. Schaye, Andrew S. Parsons, Andrew P. J. Olson, Raja-Elie  Edward Abdulnour, Michelle M. Daniel
papers.abstract: Clinical reasoning is a foundational competency that develops over the course of training and comprises two sub-components. Diagnostic reasoning classifies a patient's condition and assigns a diagnostic label, whereas management reasoning weighs multiple defensible plans with consideration of patient preferences and contextual constraints. Clinical reasoning education has historically emphasized "in-the-head" cognitive processes, such as information gathering, hypothesis generation, problem representation, and differential prioritization, over "out-in-the-world" contextualized processes, such as system navigation, use of tools, and interprofessional management. Generative artificial intelligence (GAI), itself a tool "out-in-the-world," is changing where, with whom and what, and how trainees learn to reason. The unit of reasoning educators must attend to shifts from the individual learner to the learner-AI dyad. This shift creates opportunities for upskilling alongside risks of never-skilling, mis-skilling, and deskilling. Drawing on "in-the-head" information processing theories and "out-in-the-world" situativity theories, the authors propose a redesign of clinical reasoning education. They share learner vignettes to illustrate the upskilling potential and skilling risks most concerning at each stage of training before proposing five cross-cutting strategies for redesign: introduce GAI tools early in the curriculum, preserve reasoning-first GAI-assisted workflows, promote graduated autonomy for GAI use in clinical care, equip faculty to supervise GAI-assisted reasoning, and rethink clinical reasoning assessment. If GAI is integrated deliberately in a theory-informed way, the next generation of learners can be better prepared to incorporate GAI skillfully and responsibly into clinical reasoning.

papers.title: A Dual-Path CNN-GRU Framework with Seizure Activity Scorebased Channel Attention for Multichannel EEG Seizure Detection
papers.authors: Swathy Ravi, Ashalatha Radhakrishnan
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate detection of seizures from electroencephalography (EEG) remains a critical challenge due to the inherent complexity and the limited generalizability of existing models. This study proposes an interpretable seizure-detection framework for classifying EEG segments and highlighting channel indices exhibiting seizure-related characteristics. The model follows a dual-path design that integrates temporal and spectral EEG representations with clinically inspired seizure features. The temporal pathway employs depth-wise 1D convolutions and bidirectional gated recurrent units (GRU) to capture temporal dynamics, whereas the spectral pathway uses 2D convolutional neural networks (CNN) on EEG spectrograms to extract frequency domain patterns. A novel channel attention mechanism, modulated by seizure activity scores derived from spike count, beta power, wavelet-based delta theta power, and rhythmicity measures, adaptively emphasises the most discriminative channels. The framework was evaluated on the CHB-MIT and SCTIMST datasets using leave-one-patient-out cross-validation. The proposed framework achieved 90.72% accuracy, 94.23% precision, 87.81% sensitivity, 93.64% specificity, 90.47% F1 score on CHB-MIT with a false positive rate of 0.06 and 90.72% accuracy, 93.33% precision, 88.18% sensitivity and 93.25% specificity and F1 score of 90.14% with false positive rate of 0.07 on SCTIMST. Beyond performance, the model enhances interpretability by highlighting channel indices exhibiting physiologically plausible ictal characteristics. By integrating seizure-specific activity scores with channel attention, the proposed framework improves accuracy, strengthens cross-patient generalisability, and supports physiologically meaningful interpretation of seizure-related patterns.

papers.title: Practice Makes Human: AI Conversation and Simulation as Deliberate Practice for Human Connection in CPD
papers.authors: Michael Burke, Jeffrey L. Drezner
papers.abstract: Future-ready continuing professional development (CPD) must integrate artificial intelligence without eroding the human relationships, empathy, and teamwork that underpin quality care. This brief report describes an immersive interactive AI-driven conversational simulation model that supports non-scripted encounters with lifelike avatars, followed by structured scoring and feedback, and repeated practice opportunities to rehearse difficult conversations with both colleagues and patients before they occur. Grounded in deliberate-practice theory, the approach is examined through the five Key Themes central to future-ready CPD as specified for the Journal of CME Special Collection: lifelong learning and wellbeing; quality-driven leadership; equitable and sustainable community health; responsible innovation and digital empowerment; and global equity through collaborative CPD. The report considers adaptive expert-tutor and patient-avatar interactions, individualised Socratic questioning, formative assessment of observable communication behaviours, multilingual and locally configurable scenarios, and auditable governance, including the absence of a formal learner utilisation survey and the early state of evidence linking simulation to patient outcomes. It reviews emerging literature and defines important boundaries: simulated experience is not the entirety of clinical experience; observable empathic behaviour is measurable while empathy itself is more complex; AI feedback can enable deliberate practice but is not infallible; and scalability does not create universality. AI-driven rehearsal is best understood as a scalable complement, not a substitute for traditional clinical supervision, mentorship, standardised patient training, and authentic patient care.

papers.title: AI governance and digital transformation in hospitality firms: a PRISMA-based systematic review and bibliometric analysis
papers.authors: Ashutosh Parhi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital transformation are reshaping hospitality operations, yet governance mechanisms ensuring accountability, transparency, data stewardship, and responsible innovation remain fragmented. This study systematically reviews literature on AI governance and digital transformation in hospitality firms and develops a sector-specific governance architecture. A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 principles using Scopus as the sole database, resulting in a final corpus of 162 peer-reviewed articles published through August 2026. The selected literature was examined through bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer and Biblioshiny, alongside qualitative thematic synthesis to identify major research patterns and emerging governance concerns. Findings indicate rapidly expanding scholarly attention to AI-enabled hospitality, increasingly connecting artificial intelligence and digital transformation with sustainability, governance, smart tourism, and organisational decision-making. Thematic synthesis identifies five core areas: AI and algorithmic governance, data governance and cybersecurity, strategic governance of digital transformation, ethical and responsible AI, and fintech and decentralised governance. Building on these findings and established governance perspectives, the study proposes the ADAPT-H Framework, comprising seven interconnected pillars: Accountability, Data Stewardship, Algorithmic Transparency, People-Centred Governance, Technology–Strategy Alignment, Regulatory Harmonisation, and Ecosystem and Vendor Governance. The framework addresses hospitality-specific challenges and supports responsible, transparent, and strategically aligned AI adoption.

papers.title: From prohibition to curriculum judgment: a critical integrative review of generative AI in higher education
papers.authors: Jason Zagami
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has shifted from a peripheral educational technology to a central problem for higher education curricula. Early responses have often focused on prohibition, detection and academic integrity, yet these approaches are insufficient for preparing students to learn, work and act responsibly in AI-mediated professional environments. This critical integrative review synthesises recent literature on generative AI, higher education curriculum, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy and graduate capability. The review identifies seven recurring but often disconnected themes: Academic integrity and prohibition; Student uncertainty; AI literacy; Human-AI collaboration; Assessment reform; Fluency and dependency; and Ethics and employability. It argues that these themes can be brought together through curriculum judgment, defined as students’ capacity to decide when, why, how and with what limits AI should be used in disciplinary and professional practice. Six curriculum design principles are proposed: explicit AI-use conditions, disciplinary authenticity, human-AI division of labour, process-rich assessment evidence, metacognitive calibration and ethical-professional accountability.

papers.title: AI acceptance in religious literacy: educational implications for epistemic verification and scholarly authority in higher education
papers.authors: Tedi Supriyadi, Julia Julia, Cucu Surahman, Muhammad Arif Yahya, Suxrob Saitov Djumaydillayevich, Usmonova Mahliyo Sobirjon Kizi
papers.abstract: This study examines cross-national differences in students’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) for religious literacy, epistemic verification, and perceptions of religious authority. A cross-sectional, quantitative-dominant embedded mixed-methods design involved 348 Muslim undergraduates from Indonesia (n=120), Malaysia (n=96), and Uzbekistan (n=132). An online questionnaire collected Likert-scale responses and open-ended answers. Quantitative analyses employed descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis tests, Dunn–Bonferroni comparisons, and epsilon-squared effect-size estimates, while 876 statements underwent thematic analysis. Both strands were analyzed separately and integrated during interpretation. Significant cross-national differences with large effect sizes emerged across all three constructs. Indonesian students reported the highest AI use, Malaysian students demonstrated the strongest epistemic verification, and both samples showed comparable perceptions of religious authority. Uzbekistani students reported lower and more variable scores. Qualitative findings suggest that AI primarily served as an initial cognitive assistant, with outputs subject to verification and negotiation with established religious scholarship. The findings highlight the need for context-sensitive higher education that strengthens epistemic literacy, source evaluation, and responsible engagement with AI-generated religious knowledge. These educational priorities may inform broader discussions of quality education relevant to SDG 4.

papers.title: Envisioning Norwegian teacher education for public good professionalism: a curriculum policy analysis
papers.authors: Ciara Solheim, Tobias Christoph Werler
papers.journal: Nordic Journal of Studies in Educational Policy
papers.abstract: Teacher education (TE) policy is often caught between preparing teachers as agents of social change and a narrow ‘teacher effectiveness’ paradigm. This article examines this tension in Norway, where egalitarian traditions meet global neoliberal accountability discourses. Analysing the pivotal Norwegian TE curriculum policy document, Stortingsmelding nr. 11 (Minstry of Education and Research, 2008–2009), the study uses the Public Good Professionalism (PGP) framework as an analytical lens to assess the extent to which the policy enables the development of teachers as transformative public good professionals. We employ an AI-assisted deductive content analysis using a multi-coder ensemble of nine GPT-4 assistants configured with diverse parameters (temperature and top_p) to provide a parametric stress-test of the coding scheme. Findings reveal a significant discrepancy between stated social equality goals and substantive content. Capabilities explicitly addressed in policy (e.g. Informed Vision) show high ensemble convergence but are instrumentally reframed, stripped of their transformative potential. Conversely, capabilities essential for social justice (e.g. Social and Collective Struggle) show the lowest convergence, reflecting their marginalization. The study concludes that the policy prioritizes a ‘proficient technician’ over a ‘public good professional’, revealing a fundamental structural barrier to socially just teacher education in Norway.

papers.title: Co-creating and testing a bibliotherapy e-storybook for children coping with parental complex post-traumatic stress disorder
papers.authors: Marg Rogers, Victoria Williamson, Einar Thorsteinsson, Neil L. Greenberg, Michelle Gossner, Amy Johnson, Yonggang Ren, Margaret Sims, Philip Siebler, Michèle L. Hébert, Dominic Murphy
papers.abstract: Background: Children living with a parent with complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD) may struggle to understand and respond to parental behaviours, increasing their risk of distress and mental health difficulties. Despite this, few evidence-informed narrative resources exist to support these children.Method: A free bibliotherapy e-storybook was co-created with over 30 participants from the affected communities and partners, including individuals with lived experience, service providers, clinicians, and an international interdisciplinary research team. Public feedback on a draft version informed further refinement. A cross-sectional online survey of additional community members and partners assessed the e-storybook. Twenty-two additional participants completed closed-ended and six open-ended survey questions.Results: Findings indicated that the co-creation approach was effective in developing a targeted and relevant resource for children.Conclusion: The e-storybook was perceived as a useful bibliotherapy tool to support child and family outcomes and to facilitate meaningful conversations about family experiences.

papers.title: The AI of attractions: hype and performance of artificial intelligence in contemporary theatre
papers.authors: Federico Mattioli
papers.journal: International Journal of Performance Arts and Digital Media
papers.abstract: Since the public release of ChatGPT in 2022, generative AI has attracted considerable public attention and impact in manifold areas of application, including theatre and the performative arts. Drawing on the concept of the cinema of attractions developed to describe the peculiarities of early cinema, this article introduces the notion of ‘AI of attractions’ to illustrate a key way in which theatre responds and participates in the hype around this new technology. I suggest the term ‘AI of attractions’ to describe the mode in which artists rely on the explicit and self-referential use of AI as a form of attraction for the audience. I argue that the AI of attractions is characterised by the exhibition of the technological medium, by an interactive dynamic with the audience, and by a looping textual structure that oscillates between revelation and suspicion. Through the analysis of six European shows employing AI tools, I examine a distinctive arrangement of technology, spectatorship and text that makes up the attraction dispositif (Kessler, F. 2006. “The Cinema of Attractions as Dispositif.” In The Cinema of Attractions Reloaded, edited by W. Strauven, 57–70. Amsterdam University Press). While the article focuses on the performing arts, the concept of AI of attractions illuminates dynamics that are common to multiple artistic and creative fields.

papers.title: Trending use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools in K–12 school settings
papers.authors: Nicholas Shirlaw, Jihyun Lee
papers.abstract: This study examined AI tool use trends by analysing messages in the Facebook group ‘AI & ChatGPT for Australian School Leaders and Teachers’ using a mixed-methods approach built upon the ‘Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD)’ framework. Results revealed a rapidly evolving landscape with 72 AI tools mentioned across two years, but only 14 referenced in both. While ChatGPT remained popular, tools such as Canva, Curipod, Bing, Turnitin and Bard, mentioned in 2023, were absent in 2024. Teachers consistently used AI tools for generating ideas across both years. The discussion shifted from general topics to specific classroom applications, such as worked examples and lesson hooks/starters. This study offers insights for educators, schools and policymakers, to guide more informed decisions on AI use in K–12 schools.

papers.title: Occupational exposure to generative AI and worker wages in Korea
papers.authors: Seungil Lee, Suyeon Kim
papers.abstract: This paper examines the wage changes associated with occupational exposure to generative AI in Korea by matching an occupation-level LLM exposure measure to worker-level panel data for 2018–2024. Using a continuous difference-in-differences framework and an event-study design, we find statistically significant relative declines in real hourly wages among workers with higher baseline occupational LLM exposure in 2023 and 2024. These results indicate that wage changes were relatively more negative among workers with greater occupational LLM exposure during the early diffusion of generative AI. The estimates reflect potential occupational exposure rather than the causal effect of actual AI adoption.

papers.title: Verification and task performance in teacher-guided AI-supported EMI: an SDT-informed multisection study in Taiwan
papers.authors: Stanley Y. B. Huang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in higher education, but access does not by itself establish educational value. This cross-sectional multisection study examined how teacher-guided AI use was associated with motivation, self-regulation, self-reported verification practice, and performance in Taiwan’s English-medium instruction (EMI) and bilingual higher education. De-identified records came from 684 students in 30 course sections at nine universities. The design combined questionnaire measures with an embedded, independently rated task in which students evaluated and revised an AI-assisted academic response. Standardized regressions used course-section-clustered CR1 standard errors and t(29) inference. Adaptive feedback quality, AI dialogic scaffolding, and student-rated teacher orchestration were positively associated with need satisfaction. Need satisfaction was associated with autonomous motivation, and autonomous motivation was associated with AI-supported self-regulated learning. Self-reported verification practice was associated with self-regulated learning, need satisfaction, and section-level verification climate. In the task-performance model, self-reported verification practice had the largest conditional association (β = .484), followed by AI-supported self-regulated learning (β = .172) and section-level EMI/bilingual task challenge (β = .140); the model explained 38.7% of the variance. The design does not establish temporal mediation or causal effects. The results offer a bounded conceptual distinction between conversational AI support, actionable feedback, and evidence-facing learner regulation in a linguistically demanding context.

papers.title: AI literacy and self-regulated learning: variable- and person-centred evidence from pre-service English language teachers
papers.authors: Meral Şeker, BANU İNAN KARAGÜL
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, making Artificial Intelligence Literacy (AIL) an important competence for critical and responsible engagement with AI technologies. Although previous research has extensively examined how AI-supported environments foster self-regulated learning (SRL), less is known about how learners’ SRL strategies and broader profiles are associated with AIL. The study examined the relationship between SRL and AIL among 301 pre-service English language teachers. Data were collected using the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) and the Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS) and analysed using correlation analysis, multiple regression, and latent profile analysis with Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars (BCH)-adjusted comparisons. The results showed that the five SRL strategy dimensions were significantly associated with AIL, explaining 21.9% of its variance. Rehearsal, elaboration, and critical thinking made significant unique contributions to AIL, whereas metacognitive self-regulation and organisation did not. LPA identified three profiles characterised by low, moderate, and high SRL. The profiles differed significantly in overall AIL and most dimensions, with higher SRL profiles generally reporting higher AIL. Overall, the findings indicate that AIL is associated with both specific SRL strategies and broader patterns of SRL engagement, highlighting the value of integrating SRL-oriented approaches into AIL education within teacher education.

papers.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into K-12 school education through self-determination theory from a longitudinal study: opportunities, challenges, and future direction
papers.authors: Thomas K. F. Chiu
papers.abstract: Successful integration of artificial intelligence into K-12 school education depends on teacher motivation. This motivation can be explained by the three basic psychological needs (i.e. autonomy, competence, and relatedness) proposed by self-determination theory (SDT). This study used SDT to investigate how teachers experience psychological need satisfaction and frustration during AI integration. Using a two-year longitudinal qualitative design, seventy-four K-12 school teachers were interviewed, and data were analyzed via deductive thematic analysis. Findings revealed that the three SDT needs satisfaction fostered pedagogical innovation, efficiency, and professional community. Conversely, needs frustration undermined high-quality integration, which is caused by external control, skill gaps, isolation, and ethical disengagement. These results demonstrate that AI integration is fundamentally a motivational challenge, not merely a technical one. Implications call for needs-supportive environments that honor teacher agency, build genuine AI competence through sustained professional learning, and strengthen collaborative professional communities. Schools must move beyond tool-centric mandates to human-centered implementation strategies that proactively address teacher psychological needs. This transforms AI from a source of resistance into a catalyst for sustainable educational change.

papers.title: Learning effectiveness in AI-supported higher education: examining the roles of AI feedback quality, human-AI collaboration, self-Directed learning, and digital readiness
papers.authors: Chiao‐Chen Chang
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed higher education by reshaping learning processes, instructional practices, and human-AI interactions. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines associations among AI feedback quality, human-AI collaboration, self-directed learning, learning performance, learning effectiveness, and digital readiness. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 164 undergraduate students who had prior experience using generative AI tools in university learning activities, and the proposed associations were examined using structural equation modeling. AI feedback quality, human-AI collaboration, and self-directed learning were positively associated with learning performance, which was positively associated with learning effectiveness. Statistically significant indirect associations through learning performance and interaction effects involving digital readiness were also observed. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because learning performance and learning effectiveness were assessed with highly overlapping self-report items concerning the perceived benefits of AI-supported learning. The direct and indirect associations may therefore partly reflect semantic redundancy and shared method variance rather than distinct educational processes. Moreover, the cross-sectional, single-source design does not establish temporal mediation or causal effects. Subject to these limitations, the findings suggest that technological support, learner agency, and digital readiness are jointly relevant to students’ perceptions of AI-supported learning.

papers.title: How does conversation unfold? analyzing learner–LLM dialogues through multiple analytical lenses
papers.authors: Luciano Hidalgo, Mar Pérez‐Sanagustín, André Câmara Alves do Nascimento, Jorge Muñoz-Gama
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models increasingly permeate educational scenarios, understanding the dynamics of learner-LLM collaboration has become a priority for learning analytics research. Existing approaches, however, tend to rely on surface-level metrics or single perspective coding schemes, limiting insight into the multifaceted nature of these exchanges. This study introduces an analytical framework that combines three theoretically grounded coding schemes with process mining techniques to analyze learner-LLM collaboration in a metacognitive learning task. We applied the framework to 159 conversations from 78 higher education students interacting with a Socratic LLM-based chatbot deployed in a Thermodynamics course, identifying patterns in dialogue structure, epistemic contribution, and conversational balance. For each coding scheme, cluster analysis identified distinct interaction profiles, capturing meaningful variability beneath aggregate patterns. Results reveal that dialogue was structurally dominated by the LLM, yet epistemic contributions were similar in proportion between agents despite pronounced asymmetry in utterance volume. Cross-scheme comparison showed that the three schemes produced related but non-equivalent partitions, each capturing a complementary dimension of the same conversations. Furthermore, learners and the LLM assumed clearly differentiated interactive roles, consistent with a tutor-student dynamic. These findings illustrate the value of multi-perspective, process-oriented frameworks for studying learner-LLM dialogues.

papers.title: Assessing Extraneous and Intrinsic Cognitive Load of Teleoperation: A Physiological-Performance Study with Cognitive Load Theory
papers.authors: Xiaonan Yang, Haonan Fang, Yan Zhao, Yaoguang Hu, Yahui Wang, Chaoran Wang, Hongwei Niu
papers.abstract: Teleoperation is critical in high-risk environments such as space missions, where operators face substantial cognitive demands.Existing studies often assessoverall cognitive load (CL) without distinguishing between intrinsic (ICL) and extraneous (ECL) components. This study examinedphysiological-performance correlates of ICL and ECL during space robotic arm teleoperations. A 2 × 2 experiment manipulated task difficulty (high/low) and operation mode (joystick/key), while measuring CL via subjective scales, attention allocation, electroencephalography (EEG) and pupil diameter. Results revealed that higher task difficulty significantly increased ICL, whereas joystick control elevated ECL. EEG spectral changes in frontal and occipital regions and pupil diameter variations provided complementary physiological evidence, but these measures should be regarded as exploratory correlates rather than validated source-specific biomarkers. These findings suggest that multimodal monitoring may support teleoperation interface design and adaptive assistance, while further validation is needed before physiological measures can reliably distinguish ICL and ECL.

papers.title: AI-Driven Kiosk Support for Older Adults Through Nonverbal Behavior Recognition
papers.authors: Gayoung Kim, Hyun K. Kim
papers.abstract: Older adults experience difficulties using digital kiosks because of low digital literacy, perceived social pressure, and low self-efficacy, and often encounter confusion and negative interactions when errors occur. Additionally, because of the challenges associated with seeking help from nearby individuals, an automated system that detects difficulties and provides support is needed. This study proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) kiosk that automatically detects difficulties experienced by older adults by analyzing their nonverbal behaviors and facial expressions from video data and provides real-time voice and video guidance. Considering that older adults typically require more time to process visual information, a multimodal guidance system combining visual and auditory cues was designed. The concept of “kiosk literacy” was introduced to define five types of guidance: location, task, input, feedback, and screen narration. Furthermore, 16 major pain points experienced by older adults were identified and systematically mapped to their corresponding literacy levels and guidance types to generate appropriate voice and video feedback. A user test with older adults demonstrated that the difficulty detection performance of the proposed AI kiosk achieved 82.35% accuracy, 93.33% precision, 87.5% recall, and an F1 score of 90.32%. Furthermore, the AI kiosk scored significantly higher than conventional kiosks across several user experience dimensions, including ease of use, usefulness, enjoyment, satisfaction, and personalization. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides both a technical and practical foundation for improving accessibility and helping bridge the digital divide among older adults.

papers.title: User–AI–Physician Collaboration in Self-Medication: Decision Weight Allocation and Continuance Intention
papers.authors: Guyue Tang
papers.abstract: Self-medication increasingly involves artificial intelligence (AI) and healthcare professionals, yet how users distribute decision authority among AI, physicians, and themselves remains insufficiently understood. This study examined decision-authority allocation and continuance intention in user–AI–physician self-medication systems among 1136 participants. Measures included perceived eHealth literacy, AI use, perceived AI risk, trust, self-medication behavior, and fixed-sum authority allocations. Participants assigned the greatest authority to physicians, followed by AI and themselves, and preferred joint AI–physician systems over either single-agent configuration. Higher eHealth literacy was associated with more frequent AI use, lower perceived risk, greater trust, more authority allocated to AI and users, and less physician-reliant behavior. Trust in AI and physicians showed distinct associations with authority allocation and system preference, while autonomous self-medication behavior was related to authority allocation. These findings conceptualize digital self-medication as a triadic process and support adaptive designs that coordinate roles, preserve user agency, and mitigate AI overreliance.

papers.title: Determinants of Perceived Source Credibility in Generative AI: The Roles of Information Source Type, Information Accuracy, Information Type, and Presentation Modality
papers.authors: Hongjin Shim, Eunyi Kim
papers.abstract: This study examines how information source type, information accuracy, information type, and presentation modality shape perceived source credibility in generative AI settings. A four-way factorial experiment (N = 960) revealed that information accuracy was the dominant determinant of source credibility, while source type (human, AI) and presentation modality (text, video) produced no significant effects. The credibility penalty for factual inaccuracy was nearly four times larger than the penalty for counter-attitudinal opinion content, consistent with Expectancy Violations Theory: higher baseline accuracy expectations in verifiable domains amplify the credibility penalty for error. A significant three-way interaction further showed that human sources incurred larger penalties for factual errors than AI sources, suggesting that individuals apply unequal accuracy standards depending on source identity. The credibility consequences of accuracy violations are thus context-dependent, varying by information type and source identity. These findings offer theoretical and practical insights for AI literacy education and generative AI design.

papers.title: When AI Challenges the Manager: From Technostress and Identity Threat to Leadership Resilience in Design Management
papers.authors: Haoyang Zhang, Zhang Luokuan, Tongxi Ye, Le Yi
papers.abstract: As AI increasingly handles managerial tasks, it undermines some design managers while encouraging others. To explain this divergence, we surveyed 556 Chinese design managers, linking five technostress dimensions to professional identity threat, adaptive learning, and leadership effectiveness. Results show that all technostress dimensions—especially technological invasion and overload—heighten professional identity threat. However, this threat positively drives adaptive learning, which strongly enhances leadership effectiveness. Perceived organizational support and growth mindset strengthen this threat-to-learning conversion, whereas general self-efficacy does not. Machine learning confirmed adaptive learning as the strongest predictor of effectiveness. Ultimately, this study shifts the focus from initial AI adoption to reconstructing human leadership as AI becomes routine, highlighting system explanation, support visibility, learning scaffolds, and boundary-preserving workflows as critical system-design levers.

papers.title: Emotional Comfort at a Cost: The Dynamic Role of Social Chatbot Use in Daily Loneliness, Well-Being, and Interpersonal Interaction
papers.authors: Yun Chen, Yue DING, Linxin Wang, Yu Kou
papers.abstract: As generative AI chatbots increasingly serve as emotional companions, understanding their implications for users’ emotional and social lives is critical. This 14-day diary study involving 97 social chatbot users examined how daily loneliness relates to chatbot engagement and subsequent psychosocial outcomes. Bayesian multilevel models showed that on days when participants felt lonelier than usual, they reported longer chatbot use and stronger emotional engagement. Notably, these two forms of engagement showed distinct associations with daily outcomes. Emotional engagement was associated with higher daily subjective well-being but shorter interpersonal interaction duration, whereas longer usage duration was associated with lower interpersonal interaction pleasure. Mediation analyses reflected the same patterns. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing behavioral from emotional engagement with social chatbots and suggest that emotional benefits and interpersonal costs may coexist in everyday human–AI interaction, informing the responsible design and balanced use of social AI companions.

papers.title: Syringic acid improves cognitive impairment in palmitic acid-induced obesity model: an in vitro and in vivo study
papers.authors: Amina Khatun, Jayasree Saha, Priti Garai, Susovan Chowdhury, Surendra Patra, Ritobrata Goswami, Shrabani Pradhan, Kuntal Ghosh, Sudipta Chakrabarti
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Obesity-mediated cognitive impairment is increasingly known as high levels of saturated fatty acid intake and accumulation in the body. Saturated fatty acids, mainly palmitic acid (PA) is recognized as the leading cause of oxidative stress, metabolic dysregulation, and neuronal degeneration in obesity. METHOD: The current study investigated the neuroprotective effects of syringic acid (SA) against PA-induced neuronal injury in N2a neuronal cells, as well as in a high-saturated-fat-induced obese mouse (DIO) model. RESULT: The study demonstrated that PA significantly reduced cell viability, increased lactate dehydrogenase release, nitric oxide generation, lipid peroxidation, reactive oxygen species, and intracellular lipid accumulation, following a decrease in the levels of glutathione, superoxide dismutase, catalase, and downregulation of synaptic plasticity-related molecules, including NR2a, PSD-95, and GluR1, in N2a neuronal cells. In high-saturated-fat-diet-induced mice, metabolic data showed a significant increase in body weight, basal metabolic rate, fasting blood glucose, and triglyceride levels, along with downregulation of synaptic plasticity and diminished behavioural activity. In contrast, SA treatment was able to restore cell viability and redox homeostasis by decreasing lipid peroxidation, LDH release, and NO generation, along with increasing GSH, SOD, and Catalase activity. It decreased ROS and lipid overload while maintaining neuronal morphology and synaptic molecule expression. The PPAR-α plays the main regulatory role in synaptic plasticity. DISCUSSION: study revealed that SA markedly decreased body weight, BMI, metabolic alteration, and upregulated synaptic plasticity. It improved spatial learning and memory in high-saturated-fat-induced mice. Together, these results illustrate that SA protects from neuronal dysfunction linked to obesity by means of antioxidant, anti-lipotoxic, and synaptic-plasticity-preserving mechanisms. Thus, SA might be a potential therapeutic target for cognitive impairment related to obesity and neurodegenerative disorders caused by overconsumption of saturated fats.

papers.title: The role of generative AI in doctoral research: Business students’ experiences in a bilingual, resource-limited context
papers.authors: Pedro Julián Barrera Bolívar, Téofilo Ozuna
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI (GenAI) is transforming doctoral education, yet limited research has examined how students in bilingual, resource-constrained settings integrate these tools into their research workflows. This mixed-methods study investigated the use, perceptions, and impacts of ChatGPT among 35 business doctoral students at a leading private university in Mexico. Survey data were analyzed descriptively, and open-ended responses were examined using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal extensive GenAI use, with most students employing it for research tasks. Students reported significant productivity benefits, particularly for writing refinement, idea generation, and literature synthesis. However, students simultaneously expressed substantial concerns about academic integrity, potential inaccuracies, over-reliance, and the erosion of critical thinking. Crucially, students explicitly called for structured GenAI literacy initiatives and clearer supervisory guidance, highlighting the need for institutional frameworks to support responsible integration. By situating this study in a bilingual, resource-limited context, we demonstrate how linguistic and structural factors shape GenAI adoption and identify implications for doctoral program design, research supervision, and institutional policy in non-Anglophone settings.

papers.title: A duoethnography of recognition in AI-mediated academic writing
papers.authors: T. L. Le, Phạm Trút Thùy
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can produce fluent prose without revealing the writer’s underlying reasoning. We examine how two multilingual academics interpret the relationship between AI-mediated fluency and judgements of academic competence. A duoethnographic reanalysis of a six-month inquiry draws on reflective accounts and dialogue alongside selected ChatGPT traces. Four curated scenes explore reported praise, relief from writing difficulty, the normalisation of a professional voice, and contrasting responses to fluency. Reciprocal questioning and comparison with material that challenged our initial explanations informed the analysis. Our interpretations concern experienced and anticipated judgements. We develop relational literacy as the situated capacity to interpret and take responsibility for the relations through which AI-mediated writing is produced and judged. Connecting AI literacy with academic literacies, we examine how textual qualities become grounds for attributing competence. We propose teaching and assessment activities that make composing decisions discussable without treating polished prose as sufficient evidence of learning.

papers.title: Care and pastoral provision within a distance-based postgraduate learning in initial teacher education (ITE): a research review
papers.authors: Jillian Duncan, Caroline Walker‐Gleaves, Laura Mazzoli Smith
papers.abstract: The concept of care as an underpinning pedagogical agent of support to students is a complex yet under-researched matter in higher education. Similarly, under-researched and institutionally undervalued is the pivotal role that the caring academic fulfils in imbuing pastoral care within postgraduate distance learning provision to enable successful learning and positive outcomes. This article examines the conceptual basis of care within face‑to‑face and virtual learning and teaching within postgraduate initial teacher education (ITE). The theoretical basis of the paper rests on care as a set of relational practices that may foster mutual recognition, growth and holistic development, positioning it within the context of distance learning and therefore placing a distinct value on the importance of human connection and belonging in a virtual world, a much under-theorised phenomenon. The significant and original contribution of this paper is through, the application of theory to distance-based initial teacher education (ITE) and used as a basis for arguing and interrogating the application of care theory to care practice.

papers.title: Use of generative Artificial Intelligence tools in medical student research projects: An activity system analysis
papers.authors: Joanne Louise Hart, Ali Makki, Kellie Charles
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Little is known about how medical students use generative AI in research training or how supervisors respond. Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), this study aimed to characterise how generative AI is reshaping the activity of learning to do research within a mandatory medical student research project, and to identify the contradictions driving that change. METHODS: = 10) at an Australian medical school, were coded inductively by an independent analyst. Themes were mapped onto CHAT elements and examined for contradictions. RESULTS: Reported AI non-use fell from 44% to 19% between cohorts, a difference not explained by project type, enrolment or location. Verification of AI output was the most prominent practice in both cohorts, treated as the condition of AI use. Efficiency was the most consistently stated rationale for AI use, often alongside reports that output was unreliable. Prompt refinement emerged as a competence acquired informally but dependent on disciplinary knowledge. Most supervisors felt unprepared, not only to use the tools but to judge when student use was legitimate, and the two most confident had funded that competence themselves. The primary contradiction lay within the object-motive: the written report, historically a workable proxy for research capability, no longer reliably evidences it. DISCUSSION: Students generated norms for AI use that lacked institutional standing and were invisible to supervisors, while the programme, responding to student AI use rather than those norms, began remodelling how capability is evidenced, including through oral assessment. Connecting these two processes is the central curricular task, requiring discipline-based AI literacy, forums in which student practice and the rationale for assessment changes are shared, equitable supervisor development, and assessment of reasoning over text production.

papers.title: Thinking AI: How Artificial Intelligence Emulates Human Understanding
papers.authors: Russell L. Herman
papers.abstract: Over fifty years ago, when some of us joined the MAA, the main technology in the classroom was a slide rule. We learned to use slide rules, as well as tables of logarithms and trigonometric functio...

papers.title: From Automation to Coevolution: A Systematic Review of Human–AI Interaction Hierarchies and Professional Implications in the Construction Industry
papers.authors: Maruoyan Shi, Mingxuan Liang, Bon‐Gang Hwang
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping the construction industry, creating increasing reliance on human–AI interaction across project processes. Although previous research has made significant progress in applying AI across construction workflows, existing literature reviews lack a systematic analysis of human–AI interaction patterns, coupling depths, and the implications for professional competence. To close this gap, this study aims to (1) systematize the hierarchical levels of human–AI interaction in construction applications; and (2) identify the professional competence requirements corresponding to different interaction levels. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided systematic review was conducted, covering 57 peer-reviewed studies from 2016 to 2025, complemented by bibliometric mapping and thematic synthesis to identify patterns of interaction and competence demand in construction contexts. The review proposes a four-layer hierarchical framework of human–AI interaction: AI automation (Layer 1), AI assistance (Layer 2), AI–human coordination (Layer 3), and adaptive coevolution (Layer 4). Layers 1–3 emerged from empirical analysis of construction practice, and Layer 4 represents an emergent stage informed by nascent construction technologies and cross-domain coevolution frameworks. Each layer reflects distinct coupling intensity, interaction dynamics, and competence requirements. Building on these insights, this study proposes a human–AI interaction literacy matrix that systematically maps distinct levels of interaction depth to evolving professional competence requirements across technical-operational, analytical-evaluative, collaborative-interactional, and reflective-adaptive dimensions. These findings provide actionable guidance for construction organizations to design role-differentiated training programs aligned with interaction depth, assess workforce readiness for AI integration at specific project phases, and develop career pathways as human–AI interaction evolves from automation-dominant to collaboration-intensive configurations. The framework redefines AI adoption as a competence-driven progression rather than a purely technological implementation.

papers.title: Integrating LLM-based tutor into digital game-based learning for Chinese as a foreign language: impacts on language acquisition, motivation, and learning behaviours
papers.authors: Lu Zhang, Lu Fang, Yuhan Huang, Tim Pelton, Jun Oshima
papers.abstract: Although Digital Game-Based Learning (DGBL) has been widely recognized as an effective approach for foreign language learning, its feedback mechanisms are often predefined and limited in adaptivity. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to provide adaptive support within DGBL environments. This study investigates the impact of integrating an LLM-based tutor into a DGBL environment for Chinese as a foreign language (CFL) learning, focusing on language acquisition, motivation, and process-oriented learning behaviours. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 66 CFL learners, who were randomly assigned to either a DGBL + LLM-based tutor group or a DGBL-only group. Participants completed six 20-minute gameplay sessions across a two-week intervention. The LLM-based tutor provided real-time corrective feedback, metalinguistic explanations, and free-form Q&A. Results showed that, after controlling for baseline performance, learners in the DGBL + LLM-based tutor group achieved significantly higher discourse comprehension and motivational intensity than those in the DGBL-only group. Within the LLM-based tutor group, learners also showed significant improvements in extrinsic motivation, intrinsic motivation, and self-confidence over the intervention. Behavioral sequence analysis further showed that learners in the DGBL + LLM-based tutor group were more likely to transition from error correction to subsequent correct responses, exhibited fewer voluntary gameplay interruptions, and alternated between asking questions and reviewing previous tutor explanations. Together, these findings suggest that integrating an LLM-based tutor into DGBL can strengthen discourse learning while supporting learner motivation and more adaptive learning behaviours in CFL learning.

papers.title: The antecedents of value co-creation behavior among audiobook creators in the creator economy
papers.authors: Li Yu, Na Hou, Deyan Zhao
papers.abstract: Abstract In the context of the creator economy, audiobook anchors have become essential agents in platform-based value co-creation, yet the psychological and structural factors driving their sustained content production remain underexplored. Guided by the Motivation–Opportunity–Ability (MOA) framework, this study employs fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to analyze 460 valid responses from anchors on the Himalaya platform. The results reveal three distinct configurations associated with high-value co-creation: economy-and-interest-driven, socially embedded support-driven, and self-efficacy-driven types. Complex substitution patterns among antecedent conditions are identified, with economic benefits playing a particularly pivotal role. In contrast, lack of intrinsic interest is a key factor contributing to non-high-value co-creation behavior. These findings underscore the configurational nature of content production behavior and offer theoretical and practical insights for enhancing platform incentives and sustaining creator engagement.

papers.title: Novel Approaches to Language Assessment Part 1: Artificial Intelligence–Automated Scoring of a Sentence Recall Task for School-Age Children
papers.authors: Dancheng Liu, Jason Yang, Carol Miller, Pamela A. Hadley, Sean M. Redmond, Jinjun Xiong
papers.journal: Language Speech and Hearing Services in Schools
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have the potential to enhance the delivery of speech-language pathology services. One area of practice that could benefit from AI is automated screenings for developmental language disorder (DLD) in early elementary students. This report presents the elements and processes involved in evaluating an AI-based automated scoring system using archival recordings. METHOD: A total of 947 audio samples of children completing the Redmond Sentence Recall (RSR) task, representing cases with and without DLD, were used. We developed an automated version of the RSR (AutoRSR), employing automated speech recognition (ASR), natural language processing, and machine learning models, to automate the tasks of transcribing recordings, tracking the number of errors children produced, scoring production accuracies based on RSR criteria, and generating pass/fail decisions based on age-referenced expectations against a reference standard (i.e., Core Language scores from the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals-Fourth Edition for a subset of 130 children). Different speech recognition models (Whisper and Reverb ASR) were applied to examine potential trade-offs. The accuracy of the AutoRSR was compared to human scoring. RESULTS: AutoRSR with Whisper speech recognition yielded sensitivity = .768 and specificity = .784, whereas Reverb speech recognition yielded sensitivity = .873 and specificity = .730. While AutoRSR had some mismatches with human evaluators and tended to produce lower scores, it converged more closely with the reference standard than human-scored protocols. CONCLUSIONS: AI technologies have become powerful enough to automate the scoring of recordings of children's sentence recall with similar accuracy levels as human evaluators. Next steps are discussed. SUPPLEMENTAL MATERIAL: https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34050876.

papers.title: Novel Approaches to Language Assessment Part 2: Evaluating Measures of Effort in a Sentence Recall Task for School-Age Children
papers.authors: Tracy Preza, Dancheng Liu, Carol Miller, Abdlrahman Alabdallah, Jinjun Xiong, Sean M. Redmond, Pamela A. Hadley
papers.journal: Language Speech and Hearing Services in Schools
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Children with developmental language disorder (DLD) produce more speech disruptions and have a slower speech rate than their peers. This study validated measures of effortful sentence production by examining their association with general language ability and differences between groups of children with DLD and typical language development (TLD). Measures of effort were expected to be related to general language ability, and children with DLD were expected to produce more stall-type disruptions (i.e., repetitions, filled pauses, and unfilled pauses) and use fewer words per minute (WPM) than their peers with TLD. METHOD: = 90.64 months) were transcribed, aligned to the audio, and coded for sentence disruptions using the Codes for the Human Analysis of Transcripts form from TalkBank. A custom-made Python script computed measures of stall rate, nondisrupted rate (e.g., the percentage of utterances with no disruptions), and WPM and were examined relative to child performance on the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals-Fourth Edition. RESULTS: When controlling for age, stall rate and nondisrupted rate were moderately correlated with general language ability, and WPM was strongly correlated with general language ability. The DLD group used significantly more stalls and fewer WPM and nondisrupted utterances than did the TLD group. CONCLUSIONS: The findings demonstrate that measures of effortful sentence production are systematically associated with language ability. Future directions for leveraging artificial intelligence to automate these measures and exploring their utility as value-added indicators of DLD are discussed.

papers.title: Governing cognitive labor delegated to AI in scholarly writing and medical education
papers.authors: Zhicheng Lin
papers.abstract: Abstract Across scholarly communication and medical education, AI-assisted writing redistributes cognitive labor. Mapping publishing policies from 2023 through 11 August 2026 finds governance centered on permitted uses, human authorship and accountability, disclosure, verification, and confidentiality. Five sociotechnical domains—agency and development, epistemic quality, fairness, rights and governance, and economy and culture—inform tiered oversight of editing, drafting, surrogate reading, and methodological use, with safeguards for learning and assessment.

papers.title: Comparison of the performance of large language models (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1, and Claude 4.6) in answering pharmacology questions
papers.authors: Mohsen Khosravi, Kobra Naseri, Zahra Kiani, Fatemeh Khosravi, Karim Naraki
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced a fundamental transformation in healthcare and medical education. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of LLMs in answering pharmacology questions. This quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted in Iran in 2026. A 50-item Persian multiple-choice questionnaire assessing pharmacology knowledge was administered to ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1, and Claude 4.6. Data were analyzed using confusion matrix methods, Cochran’s Q, McNemar, and point-biserial tests. Sensitivity values were 1.00 for ChatGPT-5.5, 0.94 for Gemini 3.1, and 0.90 for Claude 4.6. Specificity values were 0.43, 0.50, and 0.35, respectively. Accuracy was 0.82 for both ChatGPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1, and 0.72 for Claude 4.6. Overall, the mean sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy across all LLMs were 0.95, 0.43, and 0.78, respectively. The analysis further revealed a statistically significant decline in performance of ChatGPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 when addressing quantitative questions (φ = −0.286, p < .05). LLMs have potential to support professionals in educational/knowledge contexts of pharmacology, provided ethical considerations are addressed, though further research is needed to better understand their performance and limitations.

papers.title: A hybrid AHP–PID framework balancing structural stability and behavioral adaptivity for 5G-enabled innovation and entrepreneurship education
papers.authors: Chuanqi Cheng, Mazita Binti Mokhtar, Zarith Sufia Azlan, Jinxia Huang
papers.abstract: Ultra-low latency and high-frequency interaction in 5G-enabled learning environments pose engineering challenges to quality evaluation, as existing static and dynamic models cannot effectively balance structural stability and real-time responsiveness. This challenge is particularly pronounced in innovation and entrepreneurship education (IEE), where intensive interaction, rapid feedback, and heterogeneous learning behaviors are integral to instructional effectiveness. This study develops and validates a hybrid AHP–PID dynamic evaluation framework grounded in an integrated Structure–Behavior–Regulation perspective that synthesizes Complex Systems Theory (CST), the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and Digital Control Theory (DCT) to reconcile structural stability and behavioral adaptivity. Based on a rigorously constructed 4–12–36 hierarchical indicator system incorporating pedagogical, behavioral, and 5G-specific metrics (e.g., 5G-supported AR/VR immersion and network latency), the framework uses high-frequency behavioral observations collected in 5G-enabled environments to support periodic re-weighting of the evaluation indicator set in an open-loop scoring design that does not actuate pedagogical intervention, while preserving structural consistency through expert-derived static weights. Using data from 200 participants (100 teachers and 100 students) across comprehensive universities, applied undergraduate institutions, and vocational colleges, the hybrid model achieves higher predictive accuracy than the traditional static Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), standalone dynamic models, and machine-learning benchmarks on the present cohort. It achieves an AUC of 0.94 and a Pearson r of 0.76 against an expert-specified multi-source gold standard. The results further indicate that an empirically optimized fusion coefficient β of 0.65 underpins these performance gains by effectively balancing institutional comparability and behavioral adaptivity, while exploration subgroup analysis across institutional types and course categories revealed no significant performance degradation ( p = 0.18). The comprehensive‑university subsample ( n = 34, 17%) is underpowered, so these subgroup generalizability results should be regarded as preliminary. Theoretically, this study advances a coherent Structure–Behavior–Regulation logic that clarifies how systemic structure, learner behavior, and adaptive regulation interact in digital educational evaluation. Practically, the framework supports a shift from post hoc assessment toward timely quality governance and offers a replicable and adaptive evaluation template for 5G-enabled IEE and similar technology-intensive learning environments.

papers.title: Improved detection of email and SMS spam using a hybrid deep and shallow learning model
papers.authors: Amin. Hadi, Mahdi Mosleh, Keyvan Mohebbi
papers.abstract: This study addresses the critical challenge of detecting sophisticated spam in digital communications by developing an advanced hybrid machine learning framework. The primary objective is to enhance detection accuracy through the synergistic integration of traditional and deep learning approaches, thereby overcoming the limitations of existing single-method systems. Our methodology combines shallow linguistic features (BoW, TF-IDF, lexical statistics) with deep contextual embeddings from a fine-tuned BERT model, processed through a novel Deep-Shallow Hybrid Model (DSHM) architecture. The system employs a multilayer perceptron for feature fusion and a Gradient Boosting meta-learner to ensemble predictions from five baseline classifiers (GBAM, RL-SPAM, HMAM, SSHM, MSSL) with DSHM outputs. The research uses the SMS Spam Collection v.1 dataset, containing 5,574 messages, to evaluate the proposed framework under a realistic imbalanced spam distribution. Data collection followed standard preprocessing protocols, including tokenization, normalization, and stratified sampling to maintain dataset balance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid ensemble consistently outperforms the individual baseline models on the SMS Spam Collection v.1 dataset. The final ensemble achieves an accuracy of 98.8%, a ROC-AUC of 0.993, and an F1-score of 0.956 for the spam class while maintaining a low false positive rate (0.0058). The proposed Deep-Shallow Hybrid Model (DSHM) also demonstrates strong standalone performance, confirming that combining shallow linguistic features with contextual BERT embeddings substantially improves spam detection robustness. These findings indicate that the proposed hybrid feature-fusion and ensemble-learning strategy provides an effective and scalable solution for real-world spam detection.

papers.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into higher education balances student learning benefits and cognitive overload
papers.authors: Mohammad Nurul Alam, Tareq Faisal Alharbi, Md. Aminul Islam, Mohammad Bin Amin, Zainun Mustafa, Zaiba Ali, Sotiris Zygiaris, Mohammad Abul Kalam Azad
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, reshaping how students access information, complete academic tasks, and engage with learning. Despite its growing educational role, the implications of AI-supported learning for students’ psychological well-being remain insufficiently understood, particularly in developing-country contexts. This study examines how Perceived Usefulness of AI Tools in Learning (PUAITL) and Frequency of AI Tool Usage in Academic Activities (FAITUAA) are associated with Student Mental Health (SMH), while investigating Cognitive Overload (CO) as a mediating mechanism and Digital Self-Efficacy (DSE) as a moderating factor. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 390 undergraduate and postgraduate students from public and private universities in Bangladesh and analyzed using PLS-SEM with Smart-PLS 4.0 and bootstrapping procedures. The findings indicate that both perceived usefulness and frequency of academic AI use are positively associated with SMH. Importantly, both PUAITL and FAITUAA are associated with lower cognitive overload, whereas greater cognitive overload is associated with poorer student mental health. CO partially mediates both relationships, indicating that AI-supported learning is associated with psychological well-being both directly and indirectly through reduced cognitive burden. DSE significantly strengthens the positive relationship between PUAITL and SMH, whereas its moderating effect on the relationship between FAITUAA and SMH is not statistically significant. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Technostress Theory, the study provides an integrated explanation of the cognitive, resource-related, and psychological mechanisms underlying AI-supported learning. The findings emphasize the importance of responsible AI integration, cognitive-load management, digital capability development, and context-sensitive institutional support for promoting psychologically sustainable AI-enabled learning environments in higher education.

papers.title: Improving employee performance rating prediction using ANN probability-enhanced ensemble learning
papers.authors: Xuanming Chang
papers.abstract: Employee performance rating prediction is an important task in human resource management. It helps organizations identify high-performing employees, improve training programs, and support decisions regarding promotions and workforce allocation. However, employee performance is influenced by multiple factors such as job position, work experience, job satisfaction, overtime, department, and managerial environment. These factors are typically nonlinear and interrelated, making accurate prediction challenging. To address this issue, this study proposes an ANN probability-enhanced ensemble learning framework, in which the soft class-probability outputs generated by multiple ANN base learners are used for both weighted prediction fusion and feature enhancement by combining them with the original employee features for second-stage classification. First, multiple ANN base learners with different hidden layer structures are trained to obtain diverse predictive information. Then, the output probabilities of these base learners are utilized in two ways: weighted ANN ensemble and probability-enhanced feature construction. The probability-enhanced features are further combined with various meta-classifiers, including Random Forest, ExtraTrees, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, HistGBDT, AdaBoost, Logistic Regression, and Linear Support Vector Machine (LinearSVM). Experiments were conducted on the IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition and Performance dataset from Kaggle. Results show that the proposed ANNProb-AdaBoost model achieves the best macro F1 score of 0.4885 and an accuracy of 0.8265. Compared to individual ANN models and traditional machine learning models, this approach delivers more balanced classification performance. Additionally, sensitivity analysis and feature importance analysis based on feature deletion were performed to evaluate the model's robustness and interpretability.

papers.title: A wearable device data-driven artificial intelligence framework for personalized training guidance and its application in physical education teaching
papers.authors: 政雄 戴
papers.abstract: Wearable sensing creates an opportunity to tailor physical education (PE), but a deployable system must reconcile heterogeneous sampling rates, individual physiological variation, safety constraints, and classroom-scale latency. This study presents a scenario-oriented, full-chain framework that links multi-source sensing, edge preprocessing, spatiotemporal feature fusion, multi-task assessment, and multi-objective Actor-Critic decision support. Its distinguishing design is the coupling of individual baseline calibration with explicit objectives for training effectiveness, injury-risk control, and plan adaptability; the contribution is therefore an integrated PE-specific design rather than a new learning paradigm. Wearable inputs are acquired at different sampling rates, including 1, 50, and 100 Hz. On the self-built campus dataset, the framework achieved an ability-assessment MAE of 2.18 (R 2 = 0.962), risk-warning recall of 95.8%, and plan adaptability of 94.7%. The system supported 200 concurrent users with a mean response time of 185 ms. In an 8-week controlled teaching study (n = 120), the intervention group showed larger improvements than the control group across the reported fitness outcomes (P < 0.05), including a 32.4% higher overall improvement efficiency; injury incidence was 1.7% versus 13.3%. These findings support the feasibility of the integrated framework in the evaluated university PE setting. Teacher awareness of allocation and the single-institution design limit causal interpretation and generalizability.

papers.title: A hybrid deep learning and ensemble approach for accurate prediction of hepatocellular carcinoma from sequence variants of hepatitis B virus (HBV) X gene
papers.authors: Sadia Ejaz, Syed Ali Nawaz
papers.abstract: The current study presents a hybrid framework combining deep learning and ensemble learning models to predict hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) based on sequence variants of the hepatitis B virus (HBV)-X gene. In contrast to traditional single-model approaches, the proposed framework integrates deep learning architectures with data balancing and ensemble learning strategies to enhance predictive robustness and generalization. The dataset comprises 3,360 distinct DNA sequences categorized into HCC and Non-HCC classes, with a significant class imbalance favoring the Non-HCC group. To address this issue, the Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied to reduce classification bias and improve minority class learning. Two sequence encoding strategies, One-Hot encoding and K-mer encoding (K = 3 and K = 6), were employed to capture nucleotide composition and sequence dependencies. A range of machine learning models, including Multinomial Naive Bayes (MNB), Support Vector Classifier (SVC), Nu-Support Vector Classifier (NuSVC), Logistic Regression (LR), XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), and AdaBoost, as well as deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM), were systematically evaluated. To further enhance predictive performance, a hybrid stacking ensemble framework was developed, integrating a CNN–BiLSTM architecture and Random Forest as base learners, with Logistic Regression serving as the meta-classifier to combine their predictions. All methodological steps, model configurations, and evaluation strategies were explicitly defined to ensure reproducibility and facilitate verification. The proposed hybrid stacking ensemble model demonstrated superior performance compared to individual machine learning and deep learning models. One-Hot encoding consistently outperformed K-mer encoding across most models. The best-performing hybrid stacking ensemble achieved an accuracy of 0.9139 and an F1-score of 0.9126, indicating a strong balance between classification performance and generalization. The application of SMOTE further improved model stability and reduced classification bias. These results highlight that the integration of hybrid deep learning models with ensemble learning and class imbalance correction provides a significant improvement over conventional single-model approaches for HBV-related HCC prediction. The proposed framework has potential applications in clinical diagnostic systems for early and accurate detection of HCC. Future work will focus on external validation using independent datasets and further optimization of encoding strategies and advanced deep learning architectures.

papers.title: Systematic benchmarking of oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid sampling techniques using SMOTE-CCU+ with statistical validation and ablation analysis
papers.authors: Khaled Mahmud Sujon, rohayanti  binti hassan, Manal A. Othman, Kwonhue Choi, Md Abdus Samad
papers.abstract: Abstract The persistent challenge of class imbalance continues to hinder predictive accuracy and fairness in Educational Data Mining (EDM), particularly in modelling academic performance and student behaviour. In this study, we present a comprehensive benchmark of resampling strategies encompassing oversampling, undersampling, and hybrid approaches to evaluate their effectiveness in improving classification performance across diverse educational contexts. We trained and evaluated five machine learning classifiers (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Support Vector Classifier) on two complementary datasets: a structured academic performance dataset and a publicly available heterogeneous behavioral dataset.
