To address imbalance-induced bias, we propose a novel hybrid resampling technique, SMOTE-CCU + (Synthetic Minority Oversampling and Cluster Centroid Undersampling Plus), which integrates DBSCAN-based minority filtering, distance-weighted synthetic sample generation, adaptive centroid undersampling (CCU), and Tomek Link boundary refinement. This multi-stage pipeline enhances minority representation while preserving decision-boundary integrity, thereby improving model generalisation. Our experimental results demonstrate that SMOTE-CCU + consistently outperformed established methods (SMOTE, ADASYN, ENN, and CCU) across all evaluation metrics, particularly in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), the most reliable indicator of discriminative performance under imbalance. Notably, while tree-based models achieved near-perfect performance even without resampling due to their inherent robustness to class imbalance, SVC’s MCC improved dramatically from 0.000 to 0.986 when paired with SMOTE-CCU + , demonstrating its critical role for classifiers sensitive to imbalance. To ensure rigorous statistical validation, we applied three complementary frameworks: the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test with effect size estimation ( $$r = Z/\sqrt{N}$$ ), the Friedman test for multi-group comparison, and Nemenyi post-hoc analysis with critical difference diagrams. The Friedman test confirmed statistically significant differences among sampling strategies on both datasets (primary: $$\chi ^2 = 11.50$$ , $$p = 0.042$$ ; secondary: $$\chi ^2 = 14.07$$ , $$p = 0.015$$ ), while 24 out of 25 pairwise Wilcoxon comparisons yielded large effect sizes ( $$r \ge 0.50$$ ), confirming practical superiority independent of sample size constraints. Our ablation study revealed that DBSCAN filtering is the critical differentiator of the pipeline, while CCU and Tomek Links provide structural refinement most pronounced under noisy, heterogeneous conditions. Computational time analysis further confirmed that SMOTE-CCU + is the most efficient resampling method evaluated (0.036s on the secondary dataset training partition), faster than SMOTE, ENN, ADASYN, and CCU, confirming its suitability for practical deployment. By systematically evaluating our proposed hybrid method alongside standard resampling techniques on both datasets, supported by multi-group statistical validation, effect size reporting, component-level ablation analysis, and computational cost comparison, we provide one of the most comprehensive benchmarks of imbalanced learning in EDM to date. Our findings demonstrate that SMOTE-CCU + is a robust, computationally efficient, and generalisable solution for imbalanced educational data, particularly valuable for institutions deploying diverse classifier portfolios where resampling must benefit all model architectures simultaneously. Through this work, we establish a reproducible and statistically validated benchmark for imbalanced learning in EDM, offering a concrete pathway toward fairer and more reliable predictive systems for student performance monitoring and early intervention.

papers.title: Machine learning-based multiclass classification of cognitive decline using ACE-III assessment data: a comparative study with SHAP explainability
papers.authors: Mohamed Sherif N. Abd Rabou, Heba M. Tawfik, Nabil A. Ismail, Gamal Attiya, Gamal A. El-Sheikh, Salah Eldin S. E. Abdulrahman
papers.abstract: Abstract Dementia and its earlier stages mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and subjective cognitive decline (SCD) are increasingly common, yet automated tools that distinguish all four cognitive states simultaneously remain rare. Most published models address a simpler binary problem; the four-class case, which is what clinicians actually face, has attracted far less attention. We developed and benchmarked twelve machine learning classifiers spanning linear, kernel-based, tree-based, boosting, probabilistic, distance-based, and ensemble meta-learning paradigms for four-class cognitive stratification (Cognitively Normal, SCD, MCI, Dementia) using ACE-III assessment-derived clinical and demographic data ( n = 140, 28 features). Class imbalance was mitigated through pipeline-integrated Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE), with model evaluation conducted via stratified five-fold cross-validation. All performance metrics (accuracy, macro F1-score, ROC-AUC, balanced accuracy, Cohen’s Kappa, Matthews Correlation Coefficient) were computed across folds and reported as mean ± standard deviation. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was employed to quantify global and local feature contributions across all model types. LightGBM achieved the highest macro F1-score (0.723 ± 0.114), ROC-AUC (0.944 ± 0.030), and Cohen’s Kappa (0.729 ± 0.138) among the twelve classifiers, with a balanced accuracy of 0.716 ± 0.121. Voting Classifier attained a near-identical balanced accuracy (0.716 ± 0.068) and the highest single-model MCC (0.734 ± 0.091), closely matching LightGBM’s own MCC (0.733 ± 0.139), and ranked second by macro F1-score (0.714 ± 0.058). k-NN and SVM ranked third and fourth by macro F1-score (0.640 ± 0.136 and 0.631 ± 0.095, respectively), while Gaussian Naïve Bayes performed least favourably (F1: 0.480 ± 0.143). A paired t-test found LightGBM’s macro F1-score advantage statistically significant against one of the eleven remaining classifiers, Logistic Regression (t = 6.783, p = 0.0025, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0271), while differences from the other ten classifiers — including its closest competitors, Voting Classifier, k-NN, and Extra Trees — did not reach significance at this sample size. SHAP analysis identified age, health-condition status, educational attainment, depression, blood pressure, and family history of MCI/Alzheimer’s disease as the most consistently influential predictors across model types. LightGBM classifier trained on Egyptian Arabic ACE-III data classifies patients into four cognitive categories with accuracy that is promising for pre-screening or triage role, though external validation on independent cohorts is needed before any claim of clinical utility can be made, and SHAP makes its reasoning transparent. The framework requires no specialist equipment and runs on data already collected in routine Egyptian encounters, making primary care deployment in Egypt and the MENA region practical pending that validation.

papers.title: Limits of questionnaire-based prediction of oral health-related quality of life in non-smokers
papers.authors: Gowri Sivaramakrishnan, Mariam Abdulla Alselait, Jaber Emad Basri, Bushra F Althawadi, Sufyan Ansari, Samah Ebrahim Alalawi, Kannan Sridharan, Mohammed Abdulla AlMuharraqi
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) reflects the perceived impact of oral health on daily functioning, psychosocial well-being, and social interaction. While clinical symptoms strongly influence OHRQoL, it is unclear how well OHRQoL can be estimated using only non-clinical information, particularly in non-smoking populations. This study evaluated whether sociodemographic, behavioral, and self-perceived health variables can predict OHRQoL in non-smokers. METHODS: This cross-sectional study recruited 130 adults. Participants completed a questionnaire capturing demographics, behavioral habits, and self-rated health. OHRQoL was measured using the OHIP-14. Bayesian regression was used to examine associations between these variables and OHIP-14 scores. Additional analyses were performed to identify the variables contributing most to predictions and examine predictions at the individual level. Predictions were compared with 14 machine learning (ML) models to evaluate whether algorithmic complexity could overcome model limitations. RESULTS: The Bayesian model explained 30% of variance in OHIP-14 scores (Bayesian R² = 0.30, 95% CrI: 0.20-0.39). Educational level, gender, and self-rated oral health were the strongest predictors. Simulated changes in self-rated oral health and dental attendance produced the largest reductions in predicted population-level OHIP-14 scores. The model performed reasonably well for individuals with mild-to-moderate impairment but systematically underestimated individuals with severe impairment (OHIP-14 > 30). ML methods did not substantially improve identification of severe cases. CONCLUSIONS: Non-clinical questionnaire information can provide moderate estimation of OHRQoL, particularly among individuals with mild-to-moderate impairment, but has limited ability to identify severe burden. These findings suggest that digital or questionnaire-based screening should incorporate a small number of symptom- or clinically relevant questions when the goal is to detect individuals with severe OHRQoL impairment. However, given the modest sample size, convenience sampling, and absence of cross-validation and external validation, the generalizability and robustness of these findings require confirmation in larger studies with independent external validation.

papers.title: Factors influencing the digital competence of preschool teachers in Vietnam: Insights from boosted regression analysis
papers.authors: Tieu Thị My Hong, Vũ Thị Mai Hường, Nguyen Thi Bich
papers.abstract: This study investigates the key factors influencing the digital competence of preschool teachers in Vietnam using a machine learning-based approach. A large-scale quantitative dataset was collected from 1237 early childhood educators across diverse regions. The boosted regression results indicate that institutional and policy-related requirements emerge as the strongest predictors within the modeled relationships, while individual-level characteristics show comparatively limited incremental predictive contribution. Demographic characteristics such as teaching experience and geographic location were included for descriptive and group comparison purposes but demonstrated minimal predictive influence in the machine learning model. The application of machine learning allows a more nuanced examination of non-linear patterns and the relative contributions of multiple contextual factors without relying on strict parametric assumptions. The findings highlight the dominant influence of institutional and regulatory requirements - such as school-level expectations, local authority mandates, parental requirements, and participation in digital transformation-related initiatives-on predicted digital competence outcomes. In contrast, individual-level characteristics, including teacher motivation and professional roles, showed limited predictive influence once institutional factors were taken into account. Overall, the results provide data-driven insights into how digital competence is shaped within a highly standardized policy environment, highlighting dominant contextual influences rather than causal effects and underscore the potential of machine learning methods to inform targeted, evidence-based policy considerations relevant to discussions on strengthening digital capacity in early childhood education.

papers.title: Optimising shallow and deep learning for emotion recognition with small EEG data
papers.authors: Sivaraj Nimishan, Selvarajah Thuseethan, Shanmuganathan Vasanthapriyan, Roshan Ragel
papers.abstract: Emotion recognition through electroencephalography (EEG) is an important part of passive brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), yet its practical implementation is often hindered by the challenges of limited data availability. Modern deep learning architectures, while powerful, typically require extensive datasets, leaving a significant research gap regarding the comparative robustness of shallow versus deep learning models in small-data conditions. In particular, existing literature has not systematically examined how model performance changes as the available training data is progressively reduced. This study addresses the gap by investigating the optimisation of learning architectures for EEG-based emotion recognition under scarce training data. Two novel evaluation frameworks are proposed: the variable test data scheme, which dynamically adjusts train-test ratios to assess generalization, and the static test data scheme, which isolates the impact of training data reduction. Ten widely used shallow (SVM, DT, RF, LR, KNN) and deep (MLP, CNN, LSTM , GRU, KAN) models were evaluated across three benchmark datasets, namely the EEG Brainwave, GAMEEMO, and LUMED datasets. The models are evaluated at training sizes ranging from 95% down to 5% of the available data. Key findings indicate a shallow advantage, where Random Forest and K-Nearest Neighbour consistently outperformed deep models in low-data conditions, maintaining accuracies above 90% even at 5% training capacity. Conversely, Recurrent Neural Networks exhibited extreme instability and performance collapse as data decreased. However, Convolutional Neural Networks demonstrated competitive resilience when training data exceeded 50%. These results provide the first systematic, data volume-based evidence of model performance with the available training data. This has important implications for BCI design, suggesting that model selection must be strategically aligned with data volume, specifically labelled data, rather than being driven solely by model complexity. This research contributes a foundational guide for developing efficient emotion recognition systems. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/Nimishan/small-labelled-data .

papers.title: Studying trust in AI in sports: An interdisciplinary primer
papers.authors: Fabian Wunderlich, Moritz Reis
papers.abstract: The increasing use of AI in daily life has not only changed society, but also research on AI. The focus has broadened from methods and problem-solving ability towards consideration of legal, ethical or psychological aspects, investigating how AI is perceived, used and affects human behavior. Rapid developments in AI technology and conflicting theories on the extent of human trust in AI-based decision aid have made trust in AI a much-discussed topic. Inspired by the increasing importance of AI-tools in sports and the role of sports as a well-established environment to study psychological phenomena, we review the current state of research on trust in AI in sports. Moreover, drawing on existing research from other domains, we explore the potential of sport to expand our theoretical understanding of trust in AI. Through a literature search, we find that sport has been mainly ignored in the literature so far. At the same time, reviews from other domains have highlighted open research questions, for which sports would be the predetermined research environment. We particularly identify sports as a domain where behavioural measures are easy to assess, where field studies are possible, where reliable and objective skill assessments exist and with high availability of individual-level data. This article intends to serve sports psychologists as a starting point to assess existing evidence in this large, interdisciplinary and rapidly growing research field and to stimulate more studies on trust in AI in sports.

papers.title: Radiosurgical capsulotomy for treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder through a network neuroscience lens
papers.authors: Paolo Tini, Flavio Donnini, Salvatore Chibbaro, Mario Ganau, Mario Pinzi, Andrea M. Fagiolini, Alessandro Cuomo
papers.abstract: Severe, treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) remains disabling despite optimized pharmacotherapy and exposure and response prevention (ERP). Radiosurgical capsulotomy is an irreversible ablative intervention reserved for highly selected patients. This narrative review examines evidence from structural MRI, diffusion imaging, functional connectivity, electrophysiology, and radiobiology. The search was supplemented by a reproducible PubMed search across eight prespecified modules (856 records before and 739 after deduplication), with an audited 102-record core SRS/OCD set. Structural lesion mapping and a small longitudinal diffusion study support investigating pathway involvement alongside lesion volume, but do not establish a validated network mechanism or individualized targeting biomarker. Functional MRI and EEG findings in OCD and connectivity studies of other interventions provide complementary evidence but require cautious cross-modality extrapolation. Single-session irradiation must be distinguished from thermal capsulotomy; dose, prescription isodose, irradiated volume, and delayed toxicity require joint interpretation. We use "functional disconnection" as a hypothesis concerning downstream effects of tissue injury, not evidence of a nonablative or reversible treatment. Priorities include harmonized longitudinal imaging, dose-volume-connectivity analyses, cognitive and behavioral surveillance, and controlled evaluation of ERP timing. Current evidence supports a network-informed research framework without establishing a post-radiosurgery plasticity window or superiority of connectivity over conventional planning variables.

papers.title: Exploring trainees’ proficiency with fall arrest systems for effective design of personalized behavioral feedback using machine learning and augmented reality
papers.authors: Kwonsik Song, EunHae Grace Park, Jonghoon Kim, Matt Ray
papers.abstract: Introduction: The integration of machine learning (ML) and augmented reality (AR) into fall arrest system (FAS) training permits the creation of accurate personalized behavioral feedback in a non-invasive and timely manner. However, trainees’ physical interaction with FAS during training is not well understood, limiting the design of effective technology-driven behavioral feedback. Therefore, this research explored trainees’ FAS-related behaviors and provided useful insights for effective design of personalized behavioral feedback. Method : FAS training regarding the usage of safety harnesses was conducted with 37 college students majoring in construction management. Training subjects were asked to answer survey questionnaires before the training and recorded using three monocular cameras during their interaction with five safety harnesses. The collected data were then analyzed using multiple statistical methods. Results and Conclusions : Four key findings were observed from the analysis. First, trainees demonstrated an average safety harness usage accuracy of 22.3%, and only two out of the 37 participants successfully completed all harness-related tasks. Second, participants were less likely to succeed in inspecting and donning safety harnesses than in adjusting them. Third, trainees did not perform safety harness–related tasks differently based on trainees’ prior work experience or previous training. Fourth, trainees’ proficiency varied depending on the type of safety harness used (i.e., condition of safety harnesses, number of buckle-connected straps, and type of buckles). Practical Applications : The training results highlight the need for AR-assisted personalized behavioral feedback to address trainees’ deficiencies in inspection postures, visual attention, strap connections, and adjustment behaviors. By leveraging ML–based object detection, action recognition, and eye-tracking technologies, AR-guided feedback can enhance safety skill acquisition and support effective FAS training across experience levels.

papers.title: Machine learning-based diagnosis and health monitoring of solid oxide fuel cells using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy under multiple failure modes
papers.authors: Zeynab Salehi, Sayedabbas Sobhi, Saeed Hanifi, Daniel J. B. Smith, Amir Reza Hanifi, Mahdi Shahbakhti
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of failure modes is essential for predictive maintenance of hydrogen-fueled solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs). This study presents an electrochemical impedance-based failure mode diagnosis framework trained on experimentally generated degradation trajectories from twelve SOFCs subjected to four high-impact failure conditions: redox cycling, fuel starvation, short circuit, and thermal shock. Frequent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy measurements are converted into diagnostic signatures using distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis, and the resulting DRT-peak features and ohmic resistance are organized into labeled multivariate time-series windows for classification. The extracted DRT features are linked to underlying electrochemical phenomena within the cell, enabling failure modes to be interpreted through their impedance signatures rather than only through global power degradation. To benchmark diagnostic capability across different modeling paradigms, six classifiers are evaluated, including feature-based Random Forest (RF), XGBoost (XGB), and RF+XGB ensemble models, as well as sequence learners including Long Short-Term Memory, Temporal Convolutional Network, and an adapted attention-based Informer. Results demonstrate that temporal deep models provide improved balanced performance, with Informer achieving the strongest overall performance (Macro-F1 = 0.98). A sensitivity analysis further evaluates the repeatability of the impedance-derived features across repeated experiments for each failure mode. Finally, a computational cost analysis quantifies the performance-efficiency trade-off across model families.

papers.title: Subjective and objective image quality evaluation of a scatter correction algorithm applied to hip radiographs
papers.authors: Hoi Ching Cheung, Robert M. Meertens, Fay Manning, Richard P. McWilliam, Ben Lopez
papers.journal: Journal of medical imaging and radiation sciences
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hip radiographs are common examinations but are technically challenging because of variable patient body habitus and anatomy. Physical anti-scatter grids improve contrast but increase radiation dose and introduce practical limitations, particularly in trauma and mobile imaging. Software-based scatter correction offers a potential alternative; however, evidence for musculoskeletal applications remains limited. AIM: To evaluate the impact of a software-based scatter correction algorithm on hip radiograph image quality using objective image quality metrics and subjective observer assessment. METHODS: Hip radiographs without a physical grid obtained from a volunteer research study were retrospectively processed with and without IBEX TrueView scatter correction. Objective analysis of 63 images assessed contrast, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) across regions of interest, stratified by body mass index (BMI) and bone density. Seven radiographers of varying experience subjectively assessed 24 images for diagnostic acceptability, overall image quality, anatomical visibility, and windowing behaviour under controlled viewing conditions. RESULTS: Scatter-corrected images showed consistently higher contrast and CNR across BMI and bone density categories than uncorrected images. A reduction in SNR over bone regions was observed following scatter correction, consistent with removal of background scatter signal. Subjectively, scatter-corrected images were more frequently rated as diagnostically acceptable and achieved higher median image quality scores. Anatomical visibility scores favoured scatter-corrected images for all assessed structures. Scatter-corrected images also required less windowing, indicating improved baseline image presentation. CONCLUSION: Software-based scatter correction improves contrast and perceived diagnostic image quality in hip radiographs, despite an associated increase in visible noise. Reduced reliance on windowing suggests potential workflow and reporting efficiency benefits. These findings support further evaluation of scatter correction as an alternative to physical grids in musculoskeletal radiography, particularly in mobile and trauma settings. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Hip X-rays can be hard to perform because unwanted radiation scatter can reduce image quality. This study compared hip X-rays with and without a software tool that removes some of this scatter. This study found that the software improved image contrast, made anatomy easier to see, and increased overall image quality, although images showed slightly more noise. This matters because software-based image improvement may help produce clearer X-rays and could offer an alternative to equipment that can increase radiation dose or be difficult to use in some situations.

papers.title: From academic integrity to credential integrity: What does management education certify once artificial intelligence can produce the work?
papers.authors: Weng Marc Lim
papers.journal: The International Journal of Management Education
papers.abstract: The debate on generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in management education has centered on whether students may use AI, yet the larger question is what student work can still prove. Once AI can draft and polish a case analysis, an essay, or slides, polished work stops being strong evidence of what a student can do. This article calls the resulting problem credential integrity (i.e., whether a business school can defend what its degree certifies when AI may have produced the graded work). Policies on detection, disclosure, and originality cannot solve this problem, given that all three ask who produced the work and leave intact the assumption that good work proves a capable student. In response, this article draws on assessment scholarship, policy research, and validity theory to propose a verified-judgment architecture in which high-stakes certification rests on unaided command of core concepts and methods, reasoning defended when questioned, positions reconsidered when challenged, learning transferred to changed conditions, and accountable decision making. The architecture is translated into program-level responsibilities for school leaders and redesigned assessments for teachers, neither of which requires a ban on AI or the false belief that an AI-free submission proves learning. A reality check of 84 business schools shows how far practice is from this standard, given that schools describe AI access, curriculum integration, and faculty development more fully than any proof of what the degree certifies and only one school in seven reports a safeguard (e.g., a defended capstone or work kept free of AI).

papers.title: Exploiting latent contextual knowledge for high-performance lightweight large language models: A framework for children’s language
papers.authors: Hyerim Park, Sean-Daniel Buddingh, 전은비, Junghye Lee
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are effective at generating and simplifying text, but they lack the ability to adjust the level of simplification and associated semantics for specific audiences, such as children, and implementing these adjustments is expensive. This limitation leads some approaches to avoid actively utilizing LLMs and instead rely on human intervention for effective simplification, which restricts their scalability and practical application. To resolve this challenge, we propose a framework for developing a lightweight LLM specifically designed to automatically transform complex texts into a format suitable for children, ensuring appropriate vocabulary, semantics, sentence structure, and simplicity. Central to our framework is a novel method called Teacher–Student Task Separation inspired by offline distillation, which smartly addresses the cost issue of directly tuning LLMs for this purpose. We use an LLM as a teacher model to generate children’s language based on prompt engineering with a beginner’s dictionary and children’s stories, without any learning. Then, we train a lightweight LLM as a student model using an advanced dictionary and the data generated by the teacher model. This method, referred to as offline distillation through data, employs task separation to allow the lightweight student model to efficiently capture latent contextual knowledge tailored for children’s language and even outperform the LLM, the base for the teacher model, in quantitative and qualitative evaluations including a new target-specific comprehension metric. Our work provides a cost-effective solution using LLMs to enhance children’s comprehension of diverse content and has the potential for adaptation to other purpose-specific LLMs. 1

papers.title: Implementing AI-supported, educator-led simulation to support motivational interviewing practice in pharmacy students
papers.authors: Caroline Welles Sasser, Amna C. Mazeh, Peter Koval, Emily Stokes, Cady Thomas, Philip Rodgers
papers.journal: Currents in Pharmacy Teaching and Learning
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Motivational interviewing is an important skill taught to student pharmacists, however providing adequate practice and quality feedback in the didactic curriculum is challenging. Generative artificial intelligence (AI)-supported simulations may address some of these issues. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the impact of an educator-led, AI-supported simulation (ATLAS) on pharmacy students' confidence in motivational interviewing (MI) skills, and to determine the optimal timing for its integration, either before or after peer-based MI practice, to maximize impact of MI learning interventions. METHODS: Students were divided into two groups: Pathway A used ATLAS after doing practice interviews with peers; Pathway B used ATLAS before doing practice interviews with peers. Surveys measured MI confidence and attitudes at baseline and at key timepoints before and after ATLAS use and peer interviews, enabling comparison of confidence trajectories across both pathways. RESULTS: Students in Pathway B, who completed ATLAS followed by a peer interview, demonstrated gains in MI confidence (P = 0.0063). In contrast, Pathway A who completed a peer interview followed by ATLAS, did not show robust improvements in confidence (P = 0.68). These findings suggest that using ATLAS prior to peer interaction may better support confidence in MI skill acquisition. Qualitative feedback revealed that among students who commented on practice preferences, most favored ATLAS over peer interviews, citing its low-stakes environment and flexibility. CONCLUSION: Educator-led, AI-supported simulation using ATLAS offers scalable, time-efficient and a pedagogically sound approach to enhancing MI training. Students who engaged with ATLAS prior to peer interviews reported the highest confidence gains, suggesting that early exposure to AI-supported practice may enhance learners' confidence and preparedness for MI conversations. These findings support the integration of structured, low-stakes simulation tools as valuable precursors to peer-based learning, enhancing confidence development during MI training in pharmacy students.

papers.title: Robot gaze-timing combinations and the uncanny valley
papers.authors: Te-Yi Hsieh, Pai-He Hsiao, Sin-Cheng Ciou, Chia-Hui Pan, Tzu-Chun Chen, Chia-Chun Tsai, Yu Fang, Su‐Ling Yeh
papers.abstract: Anthropomorphic robots are increasingly prominent technologies, yet how variations in robot gaze are associated with human perception and visual engagement remain poorly understood. We examined this with a multi-method design spanning three complementary levels: subjective ratings assessed whether an uncanny-valley pattern was present across the tested gaze combinations, individual-difference measures tested moderation effects by personality and attitudes, and eye movements characterized how the robot's face is visually explored. We presented a virtual robot across nine gaze conditions, systematically varying direct-to-averted gaze ratios and durations within a storytelling scenario. Participants ( N = 61) rated each robot's anthropomorphism, likability, and perceived empathy while their eye movements were recorded, and their personality traits and attitudes toward robots were assessed. Results showed that (1) the relationship between perceived anthropomorphism and likability followed an uncanny-valley pattern (a significant cubic relationship), whereas perceived empathy increased monotonically with anthropomorphism; (2) exploratory analyses showed that extraversion and negative attitudes toward robots moderated the relationship between anthropomorphism and likability, while neuroticism moderated the relationship between anthropomorphism and perceived empathy; (3) Eye Movement analysis with Hidden Markov Models (EMHMM) identified two viewing patterns (analytic and holistic) and participants higher in openness viewed the highest-rated robot gaze more analytically and the uncanny robot gaze more holistically. These findings indicate that an uncanny valley pattern was observed across the tested gaze-timing combinations and that individual differences may be associated with variation in robot evaluations and visual attention patterns.

papers.title: The invisible signature: Top-down bias in aesthetic evaluation of visual and textual AI-generated art
papers.authors: Cinzia Di Dio, Federico Manzi, Giulia Peretti, Federico Longoni, Vittorio Gallese M. D, Davide Massaro, Gabriella Gilli, Antonella Marchetti
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of generative AI has blurred the boundaries between human and machine art making, raising questions about how authorship information shapes the evaluation of creative products. This study extends previous research by examining how attributed authorship influences the evaluation of genuinely AI-generated art by directly comparing expressive modalities, namely prose (ChatGPT) and images (DALL·E), while also accounting for participant- and stimulus-related characteristics. Participants (N = 121 Italian adults) first evaluated stimuli under a blind baseline condition and then a different, balanced set accompanied by an explicit human- or AI-attribution label. Mixed repeated-measures GLMs examined whether evaluations changed from baseline to disclosure as a function of attributed authorship; educational level and perceived complexity were then entered stepwise as covariates to assess whether the observed pattern was sensitive to participant- and stimulus-related variability, respectively. Across models, evaluations decreased following AI attribution, whereas they remained stable following human attribution. Before covariate adjustment, the baseline-to-disclosure decrease was stronger for texts than for images and varied across evaluative dimensions, with the largest decreases observed for subjective and objective aesthetic judgments, a smaller near-threshold change for emotion, and comparatively stable originality. After educational level and perceived complexity were taken into account, modality- and dimension-related differences were no longer evident in the final model, suggesting that these effects were partly intertwined with characteristics of the participants and stimuli. By contrast, the differential response to attributed authorship persisted after adjustment. These findings confirm that source attribution exerts a robust top-down influence on the appraisal of AI-generated creative products, while differences across expressive modalities and evaluative dimensions provide a more fine-grained account of how this influence is expressed within aesthetic evaluation.

papers.title: Integrating artificial intelligence into medical laboratories: A structured implementation framework
papers.authors: Avi Peretz, Hanoch Goldshmidt, Sari Peretz, Marielle Kaplan, Orna Schwartz, Ronit Marco, Maya Azrad
papers.abstract: This article presents a structured framework for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into medical laboratory workflows. As laboratories face increasing demands, workforce shortages, and technological complexity, AI offers promising solutions to enhance efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and predictive capabilities. The paper outlines key benefits of AI, including automation, quality assurance, and administrative optimization, while also addressing critical challenges such as bias, legal and ethical concerns, workforce disruption, and over-reliance on automated systems. A multi-level implementation strategy is proposed, spanning international, national, and organizational domains, with emphasis on standards, guidelines, training, and oversight. Importantly, the article underscores that AI is a supportive tool, not a replacement for laboratory professionals, whose expertise remains essential for validation and interpretation. The framework aims to guide responsible AI adoption while safeguarding quality and patient safety.

papers.title: The brain before the herd: Pre-Decision EEG prediction of herd-consistent investment choices among bilingual investors
papers.authors: Ooi Kok Loang, Jiyang Hu, Ali Sorayyaei Azar
papers.abstract: This study examines whether pre-decision electroencephalographic (EEG) activity provides incremental information for explaining and predicting herd-consistent investment choices when social and fundamental signals conflict. A controlled 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 within-participant factorial experiment involving 80 English-Mandarin bilingual Chinese investors who met a predefined English-proficiency threshold equivalent to IELTS 6.5 or TOEFL iBT 80 and had prior experience in U.S. equity markets manipulated language, information format, social-media sentiment, and information consistency. Herd-consistent choice was conservatively defined as alignment with the social signal when it contradicted fundamental information. Behavioural and single-trial EEG responses were analysed using mixed-effects models, while machine-learning models were evaluated through nested participant-disjoint validation. The findings indicate that Mandarin-language presentation and short-form financial information are associated with greater conformity to social signals under informational conflict. Conflict between social and fundamental information also elicits stronger frontal-midline theta activity, consistent with heightened demands on cognitive control and conflict monitoring before choice. Pre-decision P300 and theta provide distinct predictive information beyond contextual and participant characteristics, indicating that attentional updating and conflict processing contribute differently to subsequent herd-consistent decisions. These findings support a process-based account of investment conformity in which information architecture, social influence, and pre-decision neurocognitive processing jointly shape herd-consistent choices.

papers.title: Imagining joint action is more cognitively demanding than imagining individual action: Evidence from a dual-task paradigm
papers.authors: Molly Brillinger, Timothy N. Welsh
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI), the mental simulation of movement without physical execution, engages neural and behavioral mechanisms that are similar to those engaged in physical movement. Although extensive research has examined how individuals engage in MI when they act alone, little is known about MI of joint actions when an individual imagines themselves coordinating with a partner. Recent evidence suggests that joint MI is shaped not only by one's own motor plans, but also representations of a partner's assumed action capabilities. The present study investigated whether imagining a joint action is more cognitively demanding than imagining the same action performed alone. The task involved transferring 4 discs onto a post. Participants (n = 28) physically executed this task alone and imagined performing the task alone and with an imagined partner. This task was performed and imagined on its own (single-task) and with a concurrent mental calculation task (dual-task). Results showed that the physically executed and imagined movement times (MTs) were larger in the dual-task condition than in the single-task condition; an effect that was larger in imagined than physical movements. Critically, the dual-task had a greater impact on imagined MTs in the joint MI task compared to imagined MTs in the alone MI task. Motor overflow, unintended micromovements during MI that might index inhibitory control during imagery, also increased under dual-task conditions, but did not differ between alone and joint MI tasks. These findings suggest that imagining joint actions is a more cognitively demanding process than imagining alone tasks.

papers.title: Predicting cybersecurity knowledge and behavior among Somaliland university students using machine learning
papers.authors: Shuaib Jama Hassan, Abdisalan Ahmed Osman
papers.abstract: This study assesses cybersecurity knowledge and online behaviors among university students in Somaliland. Data were collected from 1,026 participants through a structured survey to evaluate cybersecurity awareness, digital practices, and factors associated with safe online behavior. Although more than 85% of students recognized the importance of cybersecurity, risky practices were commonly reported, including password reuse (65%), lack of two-factor authentication use (48%), and interaction with suspicious or phishing links (30%). To identify the key determinants of cybersecurity awareness, the study employed both statistical analysis and machine learning techniques, including Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Decision Tree, Naive Bayes and K-Nearest Neighbors models. Among these, the Random Forest model achieved the strongest predictive performance (F1-score = 0.83), indicating that prior ICT training, password management practices, and institutional support were the most influential predictors of cybersecurity awareness and behavior. The findings demonstrate that cybersecurity awareness is influenced not only by knowledge but also by behavioral practices, educational exposure, and institutional support. This study provides rare large-scale empirical evidence on digital safety within Somaliland’s higher education sector and highlights the need for targeted interventions, practical cybersecurity training, and stronger institutional policies to improve students’ cybersecurity resilience.

papers.title: Human-centred Artificial Intelligence and Learning Analytics in emerging higher education: a critical scoping review
papers.authors: Abdullah Feraih Alenezi
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Learning Analytics (LA) are increasingly being adopted by higher education institutions (HEIs) to support student learning, institutional decision-making, and student success. However, most published evidence originates from high-income countries, and comparatively little is known about how these technologies are implemented within the institutional, governance, and socio-cultural contexts of emerging economies. This critical scoping review synthesises the current evidence on AI and LA implementation across emerging higher education systems, with particular attention to educational outcomes, implementation contexts, equity, and institutional readiness. The review followed the methodological framework of Arksey and O’Malley [ 2 ] and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Peer-reviewed and selected grey literature published between 2019 and 2025 were systematically searched across major education, computer science, and multidisciplinary databases. Nineteen primary studies met the eligibility criteria, together with one contextual background study retained to inform interpretation of the historical development of AI and LA implementation. The evidence comprised empirical investigations, systematic and scoping reviews, policy reports, bibliometric analyses, and conceptual studies. The reviewed evidence indicates considerable regional variation in both the maturity and emphasis of AI and LA implementation. Studies from Latin America primarily describe collaborative institutional capacity-building initiatives, while evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa focuses on ethical governance, data justice, and responsible implementation. Studies from South Asia predominantly examine predictive modelling with comparatively limited evaluation of pedagogical impact, whereas evidence from East Asia and the Middle East remains exploratory and reflects early stages of institutional implementation. Across the reviewed literature, predictive early-warning systems, adaptive learning platforms, institutional analytics dashboards, and generative AI applications demonstrate potential to support educational decision-making when implemented alongside appropriate human oversight, educator involvement, and governance arrangements. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous, with relatively few longitudinal investigations, limited causal evaluation, and substantial variation in methodological quality. The review identifies algorithmic myopia as a recurring pattern within the current literature, whereby research frequently prioritises predictive performance over educational effectiveness, learner experience, equity, and long-term institutional impact. Building on this synthesis, the paper proposes a Human-Centred and Contextually Responsive AI Framework that integrates responsible AI, equity by design, educator participation, and contextual governance to support sustainable implementation in emerging higher education systems. The review concludes with evidence-informed recommendations for higher education institutions, policymakers, technology providers, and international development partners, together with a future research agenda aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4.

papers.title: Explainable artificial intelligence driven dynamic evaluation framework for Industry 4.0 oriented talent cultivation in higher education
papers.authors: HaiMei Liu, Xiangqian Liu
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of Industry 4.0 technologies has created an urgent demand for highly skilled graduates equipped with competencies in artificial intelligence, data analytics, Internet of Things (IoT), cloud computing, cybersecurity, digital manufacturing, and innovation management. To address this challenge, this research proposes an Explainable AI (XAI)-Driven Dynamic Evaluation Framework for assessing and optimizing Industry 4.0 talent cultivation in higher education institutions. The proposed model utilizes the College Student Placement Factors Dataset containing 10,000 student records with attributes such as academic performance, communication skills, internships, and project experience, to evaluate talent cultivation outcomes. Min–Max normalization is applied to standardize heterogeneous educational attributes, ensuring data consistency and balanced feature contribution during model training. Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA) is employed to extract informative nonlinear competency representations, reducing feature redundancy and enhancing predictive learning capability. Subsequently, a hybrid deep learning model combining Chaotic Dragonfly Algorithm-tuned Attention-Based Long Short-Term Memory (CDA-Attention-LSTM) is developed to dynamically evaluate students' Industry 4.0 competency levels and predict talent cultivation effectiveness. To enhance transparency and trustworthiness, SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) is used to identify key factors influencing evaluation results and provide interpretable recommendations for educators and administrators. Experimental evaluation is conducted using Python-based tools. Results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior prediction accuracy (98.92%), strong evaluation reliability, and high adaptability compared with conventional assessment approaches. The proposed model offers an effective decision-support tool for curriculum optimization, educational quality enhancement, and sustainable Industry 4.0 workforce development, thereby strengthening the alignment between higher education outcomes and evolving industrial requirements.

papers.title: The association between AI usage and critical thinking in AI contexts: examining the mediating roles of automation bias and cognitive offloading
papers.authors: Eyüp Yurt, İsmail Kuşci
papers.journal: Journal of Computing in Higher Education

papers.title: Long-Term Satisfaction with the Choice to Complete Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery: The Hindsight 20/20 Study
papers.authors: Alexandra Burtea, Jaime P. Almandoz, Marielle Nagele, Sunil Mathew, Luyu Xie, Kathleen Esselink, Jeffrey N. Schellinger, Sarah Elizabeth Messiah, Ildiko Lingvay
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Despite proven benefits, metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) remains underutilized. This study assessed long-term satisfaction among individuals after MBS and identified predictors of sustained satisfaction. RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS: In this cross-sectional survey with retrospective EHR linkage, adults with prior MBS identified through electronic health records at a large academic medical center completed a satisfaction survey. LASSO regression was used for variable selection, followed by an exploratory multivariable logistic regression model. RESULTS: Among 2,385 respondents (mean age 55.1 +/- 12.2 years; 84.7% female; mean 12.0 +/- 7.5 years post-MBS), 74.2% would choose MBS again, 7.3% were unsure, and 18.5% would not. Overall health benefit was the most commonly reported reason for willingness to choose MBS again, whereas weight recurrence was the most commonly reported reason for uncertainty or unwillingness. In the exploratory adjusted model, greater pre-MBS BMI and maximum percent total weight loss were associated with higher odds of choosing MBS again, whereas longer time since MBS and higher current BMI were associated with lower odds. Percent recurrence of lost weight was not independently associated with the outcome. CONCLUSIONS: Most respondents remained satisfied long-term with their decision to undergo MBS. Time since surgery and current and historical weight measures were associated with willingness to choose MBS again, although these exploratory, mutually adjusted associations should not be interpreted as independent causal effects. These findings may inform counseling about the long-term benefits and limitations of MBS.

papers.title: Lightweight seizure detection with channel attention and multilayer gated recurrent unit for cross-patient EEG analysis
papers.authors: Priyanka Soni, Linesh Raja, Vaibhav Bhatnagar, Rajendra Kumar Sureka, Amitabh Dube
papers.abstract: Real-time epileptic seizure detection from multichannel EEG signals remains a challenging clinical problem due to high inter-patient variability, severe class imbalance, and complex multi-scale ictal dynamics. Existing deep learning approaches predominantly rely on computationally intensive architectures such as Bidirectional GRU (BiGRU), increasing model complexity. This paper proposes SE-TCN-MGRU, a novel lightweight framework integrating three modules: a Squeeze-and-Excitation Network (SE-Net) for adaptive channel-wise recalibration; a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) with dilated causal convolutions for multi-scale temporal feature extraction; and an enhance Multilayer GRU (MGRU) with residual connections and Layer Normalization as a parameter-efficient, unidirectional replacement for BiGRU. A strict cross-patient LOOCV protocol with an independent validation strategy is applied on the CHB-MIT dataset to evaluate the proposed model. SE-TCN-MGRU achieves an accuracy 95.82%, sensitivity of 88.72%, specificity of 97.24%, F1-score of 87.83%, MCC of 86.17%,ROC-AUC of 0.9659 $$\pm$$ 0.0659, and PR-AUC of 0.9314 $$\pm$$ 0.1133. The proposed framework contains only 345,330 trainable parameters, corresponding to a 47.8% reduction compared with the reproduced SE-TCN-BiGRU baseline, while maintaining competitive seizure detection performance. These results demonstrate strong cross-patient generalization and computational efficiency, highlighting the potential of SE-TCN-MGRU for real-time wearable EEG-based seizure monitoring. This work supports United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG-3: Good Health and Well-being) by promoting accessible and automated monitoring of neurological disorders in epilepsy patients globally. Not applicable. This study is not a clinical trial.

papers.title: Conversational artificial intelligence and children’s social-emotional development: a scoping review

papers.authors: Christophe Stammet

papers.title: Constructing Selves in AI ‐Mediated Apprenticeship Learning: Students of Colour's Narratives of Agency, Recognition and Negotiation
papers.authors: Eugene Kwasi Gyekye
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming computer‐assisted learning, yet little is known about how students of colour engage with AI within authentic educational settings. Existing research has focused primarily on academic integrity, efficiency and technological adoption, with comparatively less attention to students' own experiences of AI‐mediated learning. Objectives This study examined how students of colour in online apprenticeship programs constructed narratives of agency, recognition and negotiation while engaging with generative AI and what these experiences reveal about AI‐mediated learning within apprenticeship education. Methods A qualitative narrative inquiry was conducted over 9 months with five secondary school apprentices participating in online placements across healthcare, government, finance, technology and public service. Data comprised repeated narrative interviews, classroom observations, digital artifacts and field notes, which were analyzed using manual narrative coding. Results Three interconnected patterns emerged. First, students exercised agency by strategically using, refusing, verifying, revising and disclosing AI in ways that maintained authorship and credibility. Second, participants viewed AI as procedurally fair while also recognizing that generic responses often overlooked their cultural and linguistic identities. Third, students negotiated tensions between AI‐generated outputs and institutional expectations through continual verification and adaptation, while proposing design features that would better support transparency, learning and equitable participation. Conclusions The findings suggest that effective AI‐mediated learning extends beyond technical proficiency to include learners' capacity to exercise agency, establish legitimate authorship and experience meaningful recognition within educational contexts. The study introduces Institutional AI Literacy and Recognition Bandwidth as interpretive concepts for understanding how students of colour navigate AI within apprenticeship learning and highlights the importance of designing AI systems that support transparent, equitable and culturally responsive learning experiences.

papers.title: Trustworthy AI Is Not Valuable
papers.authors: Jeehyun Lim
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT ‘Trustworthy AI’ is a buzzword in AI research, with scores of scholars discussing whether AI systems can be trustworthy. This demand for trustworthy AI is intuitive, especially when AI is used in healthcare or criminal law, where the stakes are incredibly high. In this article, I push back on calls for trustworthy AI. Even if trustworthy AI can be developed, it will not offer people any benefits over AI that is reliable, transparent, non‐discriminatory, and safe. As a result, we should discuss AI in terms of those more specific properties, and think about how the people and institutions that use AI systems can be trustworthy. I offer two sets of arguments. On one hand, many theories of trustworthy AI reduce trustworthy AI to systems that possess other desirable traits, like reliability, transparency, and so on. Thus, the value of trustworthy AI is similarly reducible to the value of those traits. On the other hand, other theories define trustworthiness as reliability combined with some mental property, like goodwill. On those theories, the goods of trust – that is, the reason trust is distinctly valuable – are goods that are enjoyed within interpersonal relationships. They cannot be realized, or need not be realized, in human–AI interactions. Thus, we do not gain any distinct value from having trustworthy AI.

papers.title: Understanding Weight Change in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Adults With Eating Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis
papers.authors: Jessica Ellingham, Glenn Waller
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective To examine body mass index (BMI) change during and following cognitive behavioural therapy for eating disorders (CBT‐ED), separately for underweight and non‐underweight participants. Method Random‐effects meta‐analyses synthesised 55 studies. Pre‐to post‐treatment and follow‐up BMI changes were analysed by baseline weight status. Treatment setting was examined among underweight participants. Results BMI increased substantially in underweight participants ( g = 1.15, 95% CI [0.43, 1.88], k = 26) and slightly in non‐underweight participants ( g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.10, 0.65], k = 43) from pre‐to post‐treatment. Heterogeneity was very high (I 2 = 98.90% and 96.05%, respectively). Among underweight participants, effects were positive in inpatient ( g = 1.53) and community settings ( g = 0.84), with no significant between‐setting difference ( p = 0.168). At follow‐up, BMI remained higher than baseline in underweight participants ( g = 0.91, 95% CI [0.39, 1.43]) but not in non‐underweight participants ( g = 0.11, 95% CI [−0.11, 0.33]). Conclusions BMI change following CBT‐ED differs by baseline weight status and should be interpreted in relation to treatment goals. However, the conclusions should be considered cautiously, given the low quality of the research, and future studies should be more attentive research quality.

papers.title: General‐purpose agents in human‐machine teams: Can we preserve meaningful human control?
papers.authors: Karel Van den Bosch, Peter-Paul van Maanen, Jurriaan van Diggelen
papers.abstract: Abstract As General‐Purpose AI (GPAI) grows more capable of cross‐domain reasoning and multi‐agent coordination, it reshapes the design space of military human‐machine teams and introduces new opportunities for adaptability as well as new risks for Meaningful Human Control (MHC). The paper presents an integrated delegation framework for preserving MHC in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams. It combines play‐based task structuring, normative constraints, LLM‐mediated interaction, and an exploratory empirical evaluation with military professionals. Part of this framework is DIALOG, an LLM‐mediated interaction component that translates natural language into doctrine‐aligned plays, and builds up a context with ethical, legal, and operational constraints. We evaluate this framework in TNO's vehicle simulation facility, where five military professionals executed tactical missions using closed play, open play, and goal‐based delegation modes. Findings reveal a nuanced autonomy‐control trade‐off: operators initially favored higher‐autonomy modes but reverted to more structured control when confronted with unexpected or non‐doctrinal agent behaviors. The results highlight implications for MHC, transparency, and trust calibration, and point toward research directions for enhancing tactical competence, communication fidelity, and verifiability in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams.

papers.title: Co-creating adapted high-genetic-diversity cultivars for organic agriculture through a European network of Living Labs
papers.authors: Isabelle Goldringer, Véronique Chable, Francesca Gori, Kostas Koutis, Barbara Pipan, Adrián Rodríguez‐Burruezo, Mariateresa Lazzaro
papers.journal: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
papers.abstract: Organic production systems require cultivars with specific traits that are often absent in varieties developedfor conventional, high-input agriculture. The prevalent use of these conventional varieties in organic farmingleads to suboptimal performance, particularly in traits like nitrogen use efficiency, weed competitiveness, andresistance to soil-borne diseases. There is proof that selection under organic farming and breeding for higherlevel of diversity improves local adaptation and buffering capacity to various stresses. A breeding processbased on greater genetic diversity between and within the populations is therefore essential to developlocally adapted, resilient, and productive cultivars for organic and agroecology-oriented farming systems.This research leverages the Living Lab approach, bringing together a multi-stakeholder network for co-creation, to accelerate innovation in organic seed systems. Agroecology-oriented Living Labs include farmers,researchers and other stakeholders in the food system for collaborative learning and design processes, makingthem a suitable framework for participatory plant breeding (PPB). Through the LiveSeeding project, 17Living Labs across Europe are implementing dynamic management of plant genetic resources (PGR) anddeveloping Organic Heterogeneous Material (OHM) and Organic Varieties (OV), new cultivar typespromoted by EU Regulation 2018/848, which are characterized by high genetic diversity.This presentation will provide a systematic overview of the breeding methodologies employed across 20 cropspecies within the OHM and OV breeding programmes. We will analyze exemplary cases for OHMdevelopment, comparing the initial genetic diversity, parental material, selection environments, and thedegree of actor involvement. The outcomes are intended to provide evidence-based best practices forbreeding high-diversity cultivars for organic and agroecological seed systems, contributing to the transitionto a more sustainable and resilient food system.

papers.title: Healthy skepticism in AI: a data visualization research agenda
papers.authors: G. Elisabeta Marai, Marc Baaden, Michael Behrisch, Michael Krone, Pere‐Pau Vázquez
papers.journal: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
papers.abstract: Research in data visualization of artificial intelligence (AI) models has historically focused on enhancing trust through visual explanations of AI. The trustworthiness line of work was built at least partially on an assumption that humans were critical users unlikely to adopt AI technology. It is increasingly clear that human trust levels in AI span, in fact, a wide range from critical to over-reliant. There is an urgent need to support both trust and healthy skepticism in AI solutions. We argue that it is healthy for humans to adopt a skeptical view both on the results of AI models and on the use of such AI models. We share our thoughts on the rising phenomenon of over-reliance on AI models, the risks and opportunities in using AI models, and the role of data visualization in over-reliance situations where humans are not motivated to engage in critical thinking.

papers.title: TraceableAI:An Open-Source Agentic Framework For Prisma-Compliant Literature Synthesis
papers.authors: Philip Lau, Nidhi; id_orcid 0000-0001-5861-9752 ..
papers.abstract: Systematic literature reviews are slow and hard to reproduce, because screening and knowledge extraction are manual and rarely documented. Large language model (LLM) survey generators speed up the work, but their reasoning and citations are hard to audit, and deep research agents add fluent-yet-unfaithful synthesis and run-to-run variability. We present TraceableAI, an open-source agentic framework for PRISMA 2020-compliant literature review that treats auditability as its primary objective. The tool writes the review protocol before it searches, keeps the raw response of every source query, and records every model decision with its knowledge in a machine-readable research-ledger, captured by a manifest of SHA-256 fingerprints. It searches open sources (arXiv, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref) and, with a key, Scopus and IEEE Xplore, and extends the result set by citation chaining. Each record is screened twice by independent prompts and the agreement is reported as Cohen’s ; included studies are extracted and appraised with MMAT, and every cited sentence in the synthesis is checked against a word-by-word quote from its source. In a pilot with three master’s students on an earlier version, the agent reduced about five hours of screening and synthesis to 4 minutes, and its reviewer caught five of seven hallucinated citations. In a final run of the current version, the two screening passes agreed with = 0.81, and the citation check judged 37 of 48 cited statements supported or partly supported and flagged 9 as unsupported. The tool is fast and auditable, but not a substitute for human judgement. We argue that traceableAI could make AI-assisted reviewing ethically defensible, and release the tool under the Apache 2.0 licence.

papers.title: "This Is an AI Assistant": Disclosure and Consent Duties
papers.authors: Shivam Tiwari

papers.title: ТРАНСФОРМАЦІЯ СОЦІАЛЬНИХ КОМУНІКАЦІЙ У БЛОГОСФЕРІ ПІД ВПЛИВОМ ГЕНЕРАТИВНОГО ШТУЧНОГО ІНТЕЛЕКТУ: ЕТИКО-ПРИКЛАДНИЙ АСПЕКТ (2024–2025)
papers.authors: Людмила ЮРСА, Людмила ЮРСА
papers.journal: Naukovì zapiski Nacìonalʹnogo unìversitetu «Ostrozʹka akademìâ» Serìâ «Fìlologìâ»
papers.abstract: This research aims to perform a systemic analysis of the transformational processes in the modern blogosphere caused by the mass integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools and the emergence of virtual influencers. The study focuses on identifying changes in media consumption structures, reimagining the concept of authenticity, and evaluating the ethical and legal challenges facing social communications in 2024–2025. Special attention is paid to the Ukrainian segment of social networks and the adaptation of domestic media professionals to algorithmic innovations within the context of global trends.The methodological framework of the study is based on a comprehensive approach, including general scientific methods of analysis, synthesis, and generalization to process the theoretical foundation of social communications. A comparative analysis of empirical data (including Reuters Institute 2025 reports and IMI 2024 monitoring) was applied, alongside sociological research (based on secondary data regarding age differentiation in media consumption) and content analysis of digital platforms (YouTube, Instagram, TikTok). To study audience interaction with AI subjects, the parasocial relationships (PSR) model and the Mind Perception Theory were utilized.It was established that the blogosphere has evolved into a hybrid communication system where AI acts as both a technical assistant and an independent producer of meaning. According to 2025 data, 88% of marketers use AI daily, with 83% indicating a significant increase in content volume due to generative models. A "comfort gap" was identified: only 12% of users feel comfortable consuming fully generated news, while 62% prefer the human factor. In the Ukrainian media space, 63% of professionals recognized AI as the main innovation of 2024. It is proven that virtual influencers, despite high engagement (e.g., Lu do Magalu with 6.7 million followers), evoke lower levels of trust compared to humans due to a deficit in perceived "experience" and "agency."It is proven that digital ethics and radical transparency are becoming fundamental conditions for the survival of professional blogging. The successful transformation of the blogosphere requires the implementation of AI content labeling standards and verification of expert qualifications in critical sectors (finance, health). The future of social communications lies in the plane of human-centered AI, where technology enhances rather than replaces human uniqueness. It is determined that the Ukrainian blogosphere demonstrates high resilience, adapting AI to counter disinformation and increase communication efficiency under martial law.

papers.title: AI-Augmented logistics and strategic evaluation: an extended ELECTRE Tri-Neutrosophic framework for DHL’s global transformation
papers.authors: Fadoua Tamtam, Amina Tourabi
papers.journal: Brazilian Journal of Operations & Production Management
papers.abstract: Goal: The objective of this research is to evaluate DHL’s transformation into an AI-augmented logistics provider. The study aims to determine how strategic initiatives can be prioritized under uncertainty, ensuring resilience, scalability, sustainability, and workforce adaptation in global logistics operations. Design / Methodology / Approach: The study applies the Extended ELECTRE Tri method enriched with neutrosophic uncertainty modeling. Techniques include entropy-based weighting, neutrosophic closeness, outranking flows, and Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis. Expert judgments were collected and modeled using Interval-Valued Neutrosophic Sets to capture hesitation, divergence, and indeterminacy in evaluations. Results: The analysis classified cybersecurity platforms, autonomous orchestration, and sustainability routing as high-priority initiatives, demonstrating stability under uncertainty and alignment with operational and ecological goals. Predictive workforce augmentation and agentic AI communications were assessed as moderate priority, reflecting contextual dependence and variability in expert judgments. Limitations of the investigation: The study focuses exclusively on DHL, limiting generalizability across the logistics sector. Reliance on expert judgments introduces potential bias, and the criteria set reflects DHL priorities rather than evolving conditions. Proprietary data constraints restricted empirical validation, and classification outcomes remain sensitive to threshold selection despite robustness checks. Practical implications: The findings provide DHL and similar operators with a structured framework to selectively scale robust initiatives while cautiously adapting those with weaker stability. The approach supports evidence-based decision-making for digital transformation strategies in logistics under uncertainty. Originality / Value: This research contributes to logistics literature by advancing multi-criteria decision-making through the integration of neutrosophic uncertainty modeling. It demonstrates the applicability of the Extended ELECTRE Tri framework to real-world logistics transformation, offering a replicable model for global operators navigating AI adoption and digital resilience.

papers.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
papers.authors: Leyou Deng, Christian Carl Ruff, Shuting Mei, Ya Zheng, Gökhan Aydogan
papers.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

papers.title: Tecnologías en electricidad. Revisiones bibliográficas y aplicaciones sostenibles
papers.authors: Juan Valentín Cedeño-Mendoza
papers.journal: Directory of Open access Books (OAPEN Foundation)
papers.abstract: Electrical systems are undergoing a technological transformation that is redefining how energy is generated, distributed, monitored, protected, and used. The expansion of renewable energy sources, distributed generation, energy storage, microgrids, and connected devices is converging with advances in sensors, automation, digital communications, data analytics, and artificial intelligence, creating infrastructures with new capabilities for monitoring, coordination, and management. Against this backdrop, this book offers a comprehensive perspective that connects the essential principles of electrical engineering with the advances shaping the evolution of the sector. Its contents cover the fundamental concepts required to understand electrical phenomena and components before progressing to the study of modern power grids, protection systems, power quality, digitalization, monitoring, automation, and energy efficiency. Drawing on recent scientific literature, the book examines developments in fault detection, protection coordination, disturbance diagnosis, grid monitoring, the integration of distributed energy resources, and intelligent energy consumption management. This analysis is complemented by technological development proposals that integrate the knowledge examined into architectures suitable for subsequent processes of design, implementation, and validation. Intended for students, faculty, researchers, and professionals, the book goes beyond conventional explanations of how electrical systems operate to provide an understanding of their evolution and the challenges associated with their increasing complexity. Throughout its pages, technical knowledge, scientific evidence, and innovation converge to interpret an increasingly distributed, digitalized, and dynamic energy landscape, in which the challenge lies not merely in having access to electricity, but in developing the capabilities required to monitor, protect, manage, and use it efficiently, safely, and sustainably.

papers.title: UMUMTA’LIM MAKTABLARIDA TA’LIM SIFATINI BOSHQARISHNING INTELLEKTUAL TIZIMI
papers.authors: Shonazar G'aybullayev
papers.abstract: Abstract. The article analyzes contemporary challenges in managing the quality of education in general education schools in the context of digital transformation and the development of artificial intelligence technologies. It substantiates the insufficient integration of existing management systems, electronic gradebooks, EMIS, and monitoring and assessment platforms due to their largely isolated operation. The main purpose of the study is to develop a concept of an intelligent ecosystem for managing the quality of education in general education schools and to provide a scientific justification for its structural components, principles, conceptual model, and operational mechanism. As a result of the study, an original definition of the concept of an “intelligent ecosystem for education quality management” was developed, a conceptual model was proposed, the institutional, technological, analytical, and managerial components of the ecosystem were systematized, and a data-driven management mechanism was recommended.

papers.title: A Tribute to Cynthia Adams
papers.authors: Peter K. Cramer
papers.abstract: I have known Cynthia Adams for over twenty-five years now.At the beginning, I knew Cynthia as the "Legal Writing Prof," and someone who was very dedicated to working with international students, but that was about all.Later, when I decided to get an LLM from IU Bloomington, her name started to become more familiar to me.It was in 2005, though, that I met Cynthia in person at the first Global Legal Skills Conference

papers.title: KERENTANAN STATUS GIZI PADA STROKE ISKEMIK AKUT: DAMPAK GABUNGAN DISFAGIA DAN GANGGUAN KOGNITIF
papers.authors: Amriani Amriani, Ika Marlia X, Nasrul Musadir
papers.journal: Majalah Kedokteran Neurosains Perhimpunan Dokter Spesialis Saraf Indonesia
papers.abstract: Introduction: Malnutrition, dysphagia, and cognitive impairment frequently occur after acute ischemic stroke and may interact to influence clinical recovery.Aim: This study aimed to examine the association between dysphagia, cognitive function, and nutritional status in patients with acute ischemic stroke.Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted at Dr. Zainoel Abidin Hospital, Banda Aceh, Indonesia, involving 79 adult patients with acute ischemic stroke.Nutritional status was assessed using body mass index (BMI) and the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST).Dysphagia was evaluated using the water swallow test, and cognitive function was measured using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).Results: Median BMI differed significantly across dysphagia groups, with higher BMI observed in patients without dysphagia compared with those with mild and severe dysphagia (p<0.001).Dysphagia was associated with a lower BMI (β=-5.19;95%CI: -6.88--3.50;p<0.001) and higher MUST score (β=1.168;95%CI: 0.863-1.473;p<0.001).Cognitive impairment was associated with lower BMI (β=-2.61;95%CI: -4.57--0.65;p=0.010) and higher MUST score (β=0.554;95%CI: 0.172-0.935;p=0.005).MoCA scores also differed significantly across nutritional risk groups based on MUST (p=0.015).Discussion: Dysphagia and cognitive impairment are associated with poorer nutritional status in patients with acute ischemic stroke.Early identification of swallowing dysfunction and nutritional risk may support timely intervention and improve clinical management after stroke.

papers.title: СУЧАСНІ ІНТЕРАКТИВНІ РЕСУРСИ ДЛЯ ЗАБЕЗПЕЧЕННЯ ЕФЕКТИВНОЇ ІНШОМОВНОЇ ПІДГОТОВКИ ЗДОБУВАЧІВ ОСВІТИ
papers.authors: Olha Shum, Levishchenko Mariia, Olha Shum, Levishchenko Mariia
papers.journal: Naukovì zapiski Nacìonalʹnogo unìversitetu «Ostrozʹka akademìâ» Serìâ «Fìlologìâ»
papers.abstract: The following article examines possibilities and mechanisms of integrating AI technologies into the educational process in order to intensify foreign language training of students, in particular, professional orientation. The study considers theoretical approaches of domestic and foreign researchers to the transformation of linguistic education under the influence of AI. Particular attention is paid to the functionality and didactic potential of modern digital resources, namely: Roshi.ai, Site123, Trello and Talkpal.ai. The study describes the results of the experimental implementation of a voice AI simulator. It is proven that regular interaction in the “student – ​​AI” system provides a high level of personalization, provides instant feedback, develops the autonomy of education seekers and significantly reduces the language barrier. The leading role of the teacher as the coordinator of this process is emphasized. It is important to understand that AI does not replace the teacher, but serves as a tool for expanding didactic opportunities. This approach ensures a harmonious combination of advanced technologies with the humanistic values ​​of modern higher education. However, the prospects for further research lie in the development of comprehensive methodological recommendations for the effective use of artificial intelligence with strict adherence to the principles of academic integrity and digital responsibility.

papers.title: From Consumers to Makers: A Community-Based Model of the DIY Food and Beverage Kit Ecosystem
papers.authors: Mark Mitchell, Martin Richard, Sheila Mitchell
