papers.journal: DigitalCommons - Kennesaw State University (Kennesaw State University)
papers.abstract: The market for do-it-yourself (DIY) food and beverage kits continues to expand as consumers seek experiences that combine convenience, learning, creativity, and participation. This conceptual paper proposes a four-community ecosystem model consisting of consumers, makers, marketers, and consumption communities. Drawing on value co-creation, prosumption, experiential consumption, and diffusion of innovation theories, the model suggests that participation in DIY production transforms consumers into makers, fosters a maker identity, and encourages engagement in product-category consumption communities. Through sharing experiences and outcomes, participants attract new consumers into the marketplace, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of growth. The framework extends value co-creation theory by explaining how interconnected stakeholder communities collectively contribute to the expansion of the DIY food and beverage kit marketplace.

papers.title: Sosislisasi Dampak Penggunaan Artificial Intelligence (AI) Untuk SMA YPK Oikumene Manokwari
papers.authors: Joice Pangulimang, Irmawati Leppang, Levina Marthina Rumaropen, Yammes Jonas Batkunde, Narzisca Angga Dewy, Sherly Febriani
papers.abstract: The advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has brought significant convenience to human tasks, including in the field of education. High school students, in particular, find it increasingly easy to access information through various platforms and AI-based applications; however, misuse can sometimes lead to a decline in critical thinking skills. Therefore, a proper understanding is essential to ensure that AI usage does not result in negative consequences. This Community Service (PKM) activity aims to enhance the understanding of students at SMA YPK Oikumene regarding the benefits and potential impacts of AI usage. The implementation methods employed included awareness-raising sessions, lectures, Q&A discussions, and case studies. The activity was conducted over the course of a single day, from 08:00 to 15:00. The program was deemed successful based on the evaluation of students' comprehension, evidenced by their enthusiastic and correct responses to questions posed by the team regarding the impacts of AI and the appropriateness of its use.

papers.title: Students' Experiences with Artificial Intelligence Tools in English Language Learning: A Descriptive Study
papers.authors: Ridwan Vienendra, Hustarna, Failasofa
papers.journal: IDEAS Journal on English Language Teaching and Learning Linguistics and Literature
papers.abstract: Research on AI in language education has mostly examined perceptions, acceptance, and effectiveness, leaving students' lived experiences insufficiently understood. This study explores students' experiences in using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, namely ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, which are commonly used to support language learning, in English language learning. Employing a qualitative descriptive design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews and document analysis. Five participants, consisting of Master's students in English Language Education, one of whom is also an active English teacher, participated in the study. The data were analysed using the six-phase thematic analysis procedure of Braun and Clarke (2006). The findings reveal that students' experiences with AI can be understood through five interrelated dimensions: cognitive, affective, social, technological, and overall experience. Cognitively, AI supported material comprehension, language-skill development, and academic writing. Affectively, participants reported increased comfort and confidence associated with AI use, alongside persistent anxiety and mistrust toward the accuracy of AI-generated content. Socially, AI both facilitated and reshaped peer and lecturer interaction through additional verification practices, while raising ethical concerns about dependency and academic honesty. Technologically, ease of use was closely tied to digital literacy and prompting skill, and was constrained by internet connectivity and subscription costs. Overall, participants evaluated their experience as positive but conditional, cautioning that overreliance on AI risks shallow understanding and reduced critical thinking. The study contributes a multidimensional understanding of students' experiences with AI and points to practical implications for AI literacy training, ethical AI use, and teacher guidance.

papers.title: An Artificial Intelligence-Based Framework for Automated Research Gap Identification in COVID-19 Literature
papers.authors: Şahinde Ünal İlhan, Fatma Ozge Ozkok
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Natural Sciences and Engineering Researches
papers.abstract: The surge in COVID-19 scientific publications has complicated the process of identifying research gaps through traditional literature reviews, necessitating automated analysis methods. This study presents a framework to identify and classify these gaps using BERTopic and large language models (LLMs). From the CORD-19 dataset, 84,964 abstracts indicating potential literature gaps were filtered for analysis. The text-processing pipeline vectorized abstracts with SBERT, performed dimensionality reduction with UMAP, and clustered the data with HDBSCAN. To increase interpretability, the generated micro-topics were grouped into 29 main themes, and the Gemini LLM was implemented to generate descriptive labels for each research gap. Hyperparameter optimization via a Genetic Algorithm (GA) improved the model's coherence score to 0.7518. The method was effective for processing large medical datasets and successfully identified different research gaps, including seroconversion in immunosuppressed patients and socioeconomic and educational issues.

papers.title: Human-AI Conversational Behaviors Predict Unassisted Task Performance
papers.authors: Li Siyan, Federico Bianchi, James Zou, Kaitlyn Zhou
papers.abstract: Assistance from AI tools has supported and improved human performance across domains. However, recent research suggests that these immediate benefits may entail future costs, including diminished performance when AI assistance is no longer available. We study how human-AI interaction behaviors correlate with immediate and future unassisted task performance across two game-based problem-solving user studies ($n=139$ and $n=111$), using a \textit{dialogue act} framework adopted from a tutor-student dialogue taxonomy. In our studies, verbalizing thought processes correlates with higher unassisted outcomes, whereas directly requesting solutions correlates negatively. Similar to these participant-side patterns, assistant explanations of the current problem state are associated with better subsequent unassisted performance, whereas directly providing the next action is associated with worse performance. Qualitative and subtype analyses further show that ostensibly similar reasoning turns can elicit different assistance. Our findings suggest that preserving users' cognitive participation in problem-solving may support performance beyond AI-assisted interaction.

papers.title: Intentional Forgetting of Autobiographical Memories: Current Neuroimaging Evidence and Moving Towards an Integrationist EEG-fMRI Approach
papers.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal, Palmer Smith
papers.abstract: Intentional Forgetting (INF) is one of many human memory processes which has gathered academic intrigue in emergent literature. Understood as a conscious and voluntary cognitive effort to suppress the recall of, or remove certain memories, INF has been extensively studied in associative paradigms. However, its application to autobiographical memory (AM) remains under-investigated, especially within neuroimaging studies. First, we summarize existing neuroimaging literature on intentional forgetting of autobiographical memories (INF-AM). Upon reviewing, we found evidence to be fragmented, providing no clear consensus around the neural bases of INF-AM. We argue this fragmentation is, in part, a result of a reliance on single-modality applications of electroencephalograph (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) methodology. EEG and fMRI, however, are complementary in their respective temporal and spatial superiority. Subsequently, we propose the application of an EEG-fMRI integrationist approach to INF-AM. We discuss how its application may help address conceptual, paradigm-level, and methodological concerns. Since human AM and the process of forgetting are inherently longitudinal, we contrast the popular cross-sectional design with a longitudinal alternative. We then present the application of the integrationist approach to longitudinal INF-AM designs. Though cognizant of the limitations that may accompany such an approach, we present the integrationist approach as a much needed and promising way forward in decoding the neuroscience of INF-AM. Keywords: intentional forgetting, autobiographical memory, neuroimaging, EEG-fMRI, integrationist

papers.title: Neural signatures of creative idea generation and evaluation in bilinguals.
papers.authors: Guillaume Thierry, Ali Asgari, Patryk Andrzej Maciejewski, Rafał Jończyk, Maciej Behnke, Michał Klichowski
papers.abstract: Creative problem-solving relies on two interlinked processes: idea generation, the production of candidate solutions, and idea evaluation, the selection of the most original and appropriate among them. While idea generation has received considerable neuroscientific attention, comparatively little is known about the neural basis of idea evaluation and how the neural mechanisms that control generation and evaluation interact during problem-solving. Comparing bilinguals' performance across their two languages offers a promising, underexploited route to dissociating these processes. Language of operation has been shown to shape cognition beyond communication, modulating emotional processing, decision-making, and meta-cognition, particularly through inhibitory control. If generation and evaluation draw on inhibitory control to different degrees, operating in the first (L1) versus second (L2) language should affect them differently; thus, language offers a new opportunity to dissociate their underpinning neural mechanisms. We address these questions in three studies reported in two Stage 2 articles: Output 1 will report the norming study (Study 1) and the EEG evaluation study (Study 2), and Output 2 will report the EEG study combining generation and evaluation (Study 3). In Study 1, we develop and validate 100 everyday mini-problem scenarios (e.g., To fix a wobbly chair, …), each with common, creative, and implausible solutions, in English and Polish, with an aim to select 80 scenarios for the EEG studies. In Study 2, we record EEG while Polish–English bilinguals evaluate solutions in L1 and L2, in a within-subject design and using hierarchical modeling of single-trial EEG. We hypothesised that evaluating solutions of increasing unusualness (common < creative < implausible) elicits graded modulation of ERP components (N2, N400, LPP) and oscillatory power (theta, alpha, beta), and that language of operation modulates these effects such that operating in L1 may suffer greater semantic interference and thus call for inhibitory mechanisms to optimise task performance. In Study 3, participants complete a novel paradigm combining idea generation (across three successive cycles) and idea evaluation. We predicted that the neural signatures of generation and evaluation covary across trials and that language of operation modulates both processes: L1 should recruit greater inhibitory control during generation, whereas L2 should reduce affective reactivity and self-critical appraisal during evaluation. This programmatic Registered Report identifies the neural signatures of creative idea generation and evaluation in a controlled, ecologically valid problem-solving task, characterizes their neural coupling, and tests how language of operation modulates these processes.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Digital Transformation in Higher Education: A Data-Driven Framework for Addressing Learning Inequalities, Administrative Inefficiencies, and Barriers to Institutional Innovation
papers.authors: Tahira  Khalid, Syed Ahmed Raza, Asad Ullah, Abid Hussain, Laiba Riaz, Zeeshan Hassan Saeed
papers.journal: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
papers.abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly adopt digital technologies, yet learning inequalities, administrative delays, and organizational barriers continue to restrict their transformative potential. This study develops an artificial intelligence enabled framework for integrating equitable student support, administrative optimization, and institutional innovation at the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST), Pakistan. The dataset comprises 120,000 student learning records, 18,000 administrative service requests, and survey responses from 2,400 students and 360 staff members collected over three academic years. Recorded variables include academic performance, socioeconomic circumstances, digital accessibility, learning engagement, service processing times, technology adoption, and institutional readiness. The proposed framework integrates XGBoost to identify students requiring additional academic support, natural language processing to classify administrative requests, and interpretable clustering to characterize institutional innovation barriers. Data from earlier academic periods are used for training and validation, while the latest period supports independent testing. Student identifiers are separated across partitions to minimize information leakage. Evaluation considers predictive discrimination, classification accuracy, subgroup sensitivity, administrative processing time, and institutional readiness, using logistic regression and conventional service routing as comparative baselines. Experimental results show that XGBoost achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.91 and a macro F1 score of 0.86, exceeding logistic regression values of 0.82 and 0.76, respectively. Following targeted academic support, the completion gap between digitally disadvantaged and advantaged learners decreases from 14.2 to 9.1 percentage points. Automated administrative request classification achieves 92.4% accuracy, while median processing time declines from 6.8 to 4.3 days. Clustering identifies inadequate infrastructure, limited staff capabilities, and fragmented governance coordination as principal barriers to institutional innovation. Following coordinated interventions, the institutional readiness index increases from 58.6 to 72.3 on a normalized scale. The findings indicate that integrated artificial intelligence can support institutional decisions concerning educational inclusion, administrative responsiveness, and innovation planning. However, observed changes require cautious interpretation because predictive performance and intervention outcomes do not independently establish causality. The framework incorporates data minimization, explainable predictions, human oversight, and subgroup auditing. Its contribution is a practical analytical architecture linking student needs, operational performance, and organizational readiness within higher education.

papers.title: Role of Innovative Technologies for Enhancing Sustainability in Higher Education of Afghanistan: A Review Paper
papers.authors: Abdul Baseer Safi, Hamza Atifnigar
papers.journal: Kunduz University International Journal of Islamic Studies and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Innovative technology is a dire need of contemporary education society in bringing paradigm changes in higher education by ameliorating learning experiences, improving accessibility, and reinforcing sustainability. In Afghanistan, a country confronting different educational challenges, the application of technologies such as Adaptive Learning Technologies, Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence, Mobile Learning the Internet of Things, and Gamification can address such issues and contribute to the sustainable development of higher education. Hence, this paper aims to investigate the role of these technologies in the higher educational sector of Afghanistan, particularly exploring their utility, potential advantages, challenges, and implications to further support educational sustainability. To support this research, the investigators collected keywords related to the innovative and digital technologies in higher education and their effects on sustainability form different international reliable databases such as Scopus, Web of Science, Science Direct, Taylor and Francis. After critically synthesizing various research papers, it is concluded that ALT, CC, ML, IoT, AI, Blockchain, and Gamification offer promising solutions to many concurrent challenges toward higher education of Afghanistan. Finally, this provides suitable recommendations for policy makers, teachers, and higher educational institutions on the integration of these technologies to achieve sustainable education improvement in Afghanistan.

papers.title: Educomunicación en educación inicial, primaria y secundaria en Iberoamérica (2020-2025): un análisis bibliométrico
papers.authors: Diana Caridad Ruiz-Onofre, Rodrigo Marcelo Criollo Burbano
papers.abstract: This study analyzes scientific production on educommunication in early childhood, primary, and secondary education in Ibero-America during the period 2020–2025. Using a descriptive and relational quantitative approach, and applying the criteria of the PRISMA 2020 statement, a sample of 255 publications retrieved from the Scopus, SciELO, and Redalyc databases was consolidated and processed using VOSviewer software. The results show a significant increase in publications between 2021 and 2022, driven by the health crisis, followed by a marked decline in 2025. Scientific articles overwhelmingly predominate, mainly focusing on experiences and practical cases related to digital competence and digital literacy, which reveals limited conceptual discussion. Geographically, Spain and Mexico lead scientific output within predominantly small-scale and individual collaboration networks, reflecting asymmetries in the circulation of knowledge around a concept that originated in Latin America. Finally, the keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies five thematic clusters and an evolution of the research agenda from ICT toward social media and computational thinking, revealing a complete lack of attention to artificial intelligence up to 2025

papers.title: THE ROLE AND SIGNIFICANCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN IMPROVING ACCESS TO PRIMARY MEDICAL CARE
papers.authors: Nilufar Rasulova, Rukhsora Mamaraimova
papers.journal: Eurasian Journal of Medical and Natural Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming an important component of digital transformation in healthcare, with particular potential to improve access to primary medical care. Primary care is the first point of contact between individuals and healthcare systems and plays a fundamental role in prevention, early diagnosis, health monitoring, referral, and continuity of care. However, geographical distance, shortages of healthcare professionals, increasing patient demand, limited diagnostic capacity, and unequal distribution of healthcare resources continue to restrict access to primary medical services. This article examines the role and significance of AI in addressing these barriers and evaluates the principal mechanisms through which AI can improve accessibility, efficiency, continuity, and equity in primary care. A narrative analytical review of scientific literature and international health-policy documents was conducted. Particular attention was given to AI-supported symptom assessment, clinical decision support, risk prediction, automated patient triage, remote monitoring, personalized prevention, administrative automation, and multilingual digital health services. The analysis demonstrates that AI can expand the effective capacity of primary care by supporting healthcare professionals, enabling earlier identification of health risks, reducing unnecessary visits, and facilitating remote access to preliminary medical guidance. At the same time, AI implementation introduces significant challenges related to algorithmic bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, explainability, digital exclusion, clinical responsibility, and unequal technological infrastructure. Therefore, AI should not be regarded as a substitute for primary healthcare professionals but as an augmentative technology integrated into a human-centred primary care model. The study proposes a conceptual framework in which AI improves access through five interconnected mechanisms: availability, affordability, timeliness, geographical reach, and continuity of care. Responsible governance, clinical validation, interoperability, digital literacy, and equitable infrastructure are identified as essential conditions for sustainable implementation.

papers.title: The Ethical Limitations of AI
papers.authors: Parth Manoj Purandare
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovations in Science Engineering and Management.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into the decision-making process of corporations across various industries, including finance, healthcare, marketing, supply chain management, cybersecurity, and human resources. Although AI has proven to be highly efficient, automated, and data-driven in its strategic decision-making, its increasing autonomy in high-stakes strategic decisions raises important ethical concerns. This paper discusses the ethical constraints of AI in corporate decision-making, especially in terms of accountability gaps, algorithmic bias, transparency issues, privacy risks, and the loss of human judgment and moral reasoning. This paper is aimed at critically assessing whether AI systems should be allowed to make autonomous strategic business decisions without meaningful human control and also exploring the impacts of these ethical constraints on stakeholders such as employees, consumers, executives, and policymakers. This study is a synthesis of interdisciplinary academic literature, industry reports, and real-world case studies in relation to AI governance and corporate ethics using a qualitative conceptual research approach. The results indicate that despite the fact that AI can be used to increase the efficiency of operations and assist in making informed decisions, fully autonomous AI systems are ethically unreliable in situations that require empathy, situational understanding, and responsibility. The experience in the fields of hiring systems, cybersecurity, advertising, and data governance proves that AI may unintentionally support discrimination, introduce transparency in decision-making, and expose organizations to considerable ethical and reputational risks. This paper concludes that AI must be used as a decision-support tool and not an autonomous corporate decision-maker and that human oversight, transparent governance structures, and ethical regulation are necessary to ensure responsible AI adoption in corporate settings.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Language Education: Pedagogical Applications, Representative Platforms, and Human Oversight
papers.authors: Sema Mehdi, Turkan Mehraj Ismayilli
papers.journal: EuroGlobal Journal of Linguistics and Language Education.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping language education through automated feedback, speech recognition, adaptive practice, dialogue systems, machine translation, learning analytics, and generative language models. This article critically reviews the principal pedagogical uses of these technologies and examines representative AI-assisted language learning platforms. It adopts an integrative review design that prioritizes peer-reviewed research from established indexed journals, supplemented by international guidance and current platform documentation. The synthesis shows that AI can expand opportunities for repeated practice, individualized feedback, formative assessment, and access to multilingual resources. Evidence is strongest when AI supports a clearly defined task and learners remain responsible for interpreting and revising the output. Important limitations include recognition errors, fabricated or culturally narrow responses, opaque scoring, privacy risks, unequal access, academic-integrity concerns, and excessive dependence on automated correction. A comparison of representative platforms demonstrates that products differ substantially in target skills, feedback, adaptivity, and data demands; they should not be treated as interchangeable. The article proposes a six-stage teacher-guided integration cycle covering learning outcomes, tool selection, accountable interaction, verification, assessment, and impact review. The central conclusion is that effective AI-assisted language education depends less on the novelty of a platform than on pedagogical alignment, human oversight, and learners’ developing capacity to evaluate automated output.

papers.title: Social networks as a tool for civic activism and international communications in Tajikistan
papers.authors: Kateryna Serbina, Inna Voloshenko, Oleksandr Alekseychenko, Anatolii Humenchuk, Oleh Deneha
papers.abstract: The aim of the research was to evaluate the effectiveness of social networks as a tool for transforming the public sphere. The methodology was based on a comprehensive approach combining structural-functional analysis of quantitative data, a detailed case study method (the court cases of journalists, the Tell Me Sister and Pamir Inside initiatives), content analysis of communication strategies (the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, the Embassy of the United States of America) and secondary analysis of reports from the CIVICUS Monitor and the RSF World Press Freedom Index. It was established that Tajikistan practises hybrid digital authoritarianism, where counter-extremism legislation is used as a productive mechanism for outsourcing censorship to society, leading to mass self-censorship. It was proven that digital platforms (Facebook, Instagram, Telegram, TikTok) initiated a transformation of the traditional public sphere, becoming a medium for counter-hegemonic discourse that bypasses socio-cultural silencing of taboo topics. It was clarified that digital inequality and gender asymmetry (76.1% male in the social network audience) act as a non-institutional form of censorship. Case analysis confirmed the emancipatory potential within social networks. A comparative analysis of strategies revealed that independent activism (Tell Me Sister) and citizen journalism (Pamir Inside) rely on engagement algorithms (utilisation of emotional quotient and visual operability), where Pamir Inside functions as a critical digital hub for covering high-risk events (Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region). Concurrently, state/international structures utilise financial support to legitimise social networks, counterposing preventive content to critical dissent. It was clarified that technological asymmetry (low media literacy) combined with generative artificial intelligence creates a threat of “hyperreal” deepfakes. To improve the situation, a number of recommendations were proposed (specifically, developing digital obscurity programmes, investing in fact-checking of artificial intelligence content, and international pressure for compliance with Digital Services Act standards) to enhance the resilience of the civic space and minimise risks for activists. The research results can serve as a theoretical and empirical basis for comparative studies of digital authoritarianism mechanisms in other countries of Central Asia and the Global South

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Scientific Research Instrument: Productivity, Discovery, and the Risk of Illusions of Understanding
papers.authors: Shabnam Eshmonova
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming embedded across the scientific research pipeline, from literature discovery and data analysis to hypothesis generation, simulation, and experimental design. This paper examines AI as a research instrument rather than merely a productivity application, with particular attention to the relationship between increased research throughput and scientific understanding. A structured literature synthesis was conducted using recent empirical and conceptual studies of AI in science together with the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science. Evidence indicates that AI use and its potential benefits are widespread across scientific fields and have expanded rapidly since 2015, while a persistent mismatch remains between AI education and its application in research. At the same time, recent scholarship identifies an epistemic risk: researchers may produce more outputs while developing weaker causal, conceptual, or methodological understanding of the phenomena under study. The analysis therefore distinguishes operational productivity from epistemic quality. It proposes a research-governance framework in which AI-generated hypotheses, analyses, and interpretations remain traceable, reproducible, critically evaluated, and integrated with open scientific practices. The paper concludes that the scientific value of AI depends not simply on model capability but on the design of human–AI research workflows, verification procedures, and institutional norms for transparency and reproducibility.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Adaptive Learning in Education: Evidence, Teacher Competency, and Implementation Conditions
papers.authors: Diyor Tursunov, Mushtariy Narkulova
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into educational technologies that personalize practice, generate feedback, and support teachers’ instructional decisions. This paper examines the conditions under which AI-assisted adaptive learning is most likely to improve educational outcomes without weakening teacher agency or learner autonomy. The study uses a structured evidence-synthesis design based on recent international guidance, a 2026 World Bank systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, and the OECD TALIS 2024 country evidence for Uzbekistan. The synthesis indicates that adaptive and AI-enabled interventions are associated with a positive average learning effect of 0.125 standard deviations, while AI-powered tutoring or instruction shows an average effect of 0.12 standard deviations; however, the evidence base remains limited and does not establish that generative AI is superior to earlier adaptive technologies. Uzbekistan provides a particularly relevant implementation case: 62% of surveyed teachers reported using AI in their work, while substantial shares identified infrastructure and skills as constraints. The paper proposes an implementation model that combines evidence-based tool selection, teacher AI competency, formative assessment, human oversight, and continuous evaluation. The main conclusion is that AI should be deployed as a pedagogical augmentation layer rather than as a substitute for teachers, with effectiveness judged by learning outcomes and equity rather than by technology adoption alone.

papers.title: A SIMULATION STUDY OF INDONESIAN SENTIMENT CLASSIFICATION FOR A WHATSAPP STUDENT SUPPORT CHATBOT
papers.authors: Dian Dwi Lestari, Anggi Rizky Windra Putri, Tasiu Abdullahi Yusuf
papers.abstract: Short Indonesian messages may help institutions organise student support requests, but sentiment polarity does not directly measure psychological well-being. This study evaluates a text-classification component intended for a WhatsApp student support chatbot through a fully synthetic, reproducible simulation. A constructed corpus contains 360 messages from 60 scenario families across six support domains. Families, including their positive and negative variants, are separated into training, validation, and test partitions of 216, 72, and 72 messages. A further 48 synthetic messages test negation, abbreviations, language mixing, and explicitly mixed sentiment. Term frequency–inverse document frequency features and multinomial Naïve Bayes are compared with a constant baseline and logistic regression. On the held-out synthetic test set, Naïve Bayes achieves accuracy of 0.875 and macro-F1 of 0.875, matching logistic regression on both aggregate metrics. On the challenge set, its accuracy decreases to 0.813 and macro-F1 to 0.806. Negation is the weakest scenario, with six correct predictions out of twelve; all six positive negation examples are misclassified. Feature inspection links selected errors to polarity-bearing words and unseen abbreviations. The results establish a reproducible computational baseline and expose limitations obscured by aggregate scores. They do not validate real student conversations, live WhatsApp integration, stress detection, or improvements in well-being.

papers.title: From foresight to implementation: building collaborative ecosystems for distribution grid planning
papers.authors: Helena Lindquist
papers.abstract: Extended abstract 5-210-26 The energy transition is increasingly shaped at the local and regional level, where electrification, DERs, and climate mitigation and adaptation intersect with territorial development. This work presents findings from a global co-creation project within ISGAN, an IEA Technology Collaboration Program, involving participants from 15 countries. The work forms part of the ISGAN Lighthouse Project and builds on a sense-making framework for long-term planning of smart distribution grids under uncertainty developed in an earlier project phase. The framework conceptualises grid planning as a multi-actor process spanning five phases, from foresight to implementation, underpinned by three essential framework conditions. One of these, effective actor collaboration and coordination, is the focus of this work. Taking a system innovation perspective, we explore the characteristics of a well-functioning actor ecosystem and how these can be developed and maintained to improve the quality and speed of distribution grid planning, drawing on complementary governance, relational, and operational perspectives, including multi-level coordination between top-down steering and bottom-up initiatives, and interfaces with spatial and cross-sector planning processes. Particular attention is given to the foresight phase, where actors need to develop a shared understanding of and agree on the long-term direction of the energy system and the role of the distribution grid within it. The analysis focuses on three actor groups influencing distribution-grid planning across governance levels: DSOs; local and regional government actors with territorial planning responsibilities; and energy policy makers and regulators, typically operating at the national level. We examine interdependencies across the planning process, including flows of data, information and decisions, and related coordination and sense-making challenges. Informed by insights from different national contexts, we show how inadequate collaboration can undermine effective grid planning and local energy transitions while also suggesting practical pathways towards more effective collaboration, strengthening multi-level governance. Read the full abstract. Download presentation.

papers.title: Lactate Promotes Tunneling Nanotube Formation and Reduces Temozolomide Sensitivity in Glioblastoma Cells
papers.authors: Sambhavi Pattnaik, Subashree Anand, Ganeshini P, Amal Kanti Bera
papers.abstract: Abstract Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) mediate intercellular communication and contribute to cancer progression. Tumour cells produce excess lactate through increased glycolysis, but whether lactate regulates TNT formation has not been studied. Here, we show that lactate promotes TNT formation in U-87 MG glioblastoma (GBM) cells under both glucose-restricted and glucose-replete conditions, with a similar effect in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. This effect depends on lactate uptake and metabolism rather than receptor-mediated signalling: inhibition of monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) or lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) reduced TNT formation, while exogenous lactate restored TNT formation during LDH inhibition. 3-chloro-5-hydroxybenzoic acid, an agonist of the plasma membrane-localized lactate receptor (GPR81/HCAR1), did not reproduce the effect of lactate. Lactate also increased intercellular mitochondrial transfer, attenuated temozolomide (TMZ)-induced growth suppression of GBM spheroids, and increased expression of the TNT-associated genes CDC42 , MYO10 and FSCN1 . Inhibition of p300/CBP-mediated lactylation with A-485 reduced both protein lactylation and TNT formation, implicating lactylation in TNT biogenesis. Lactate increased basal and ATP-linked respiration that persisted during MCT1 inhibition and reduced on LDH inhibition, indicating that the effects of lactate on respiration and on TNT formation are at least partly separable. Together, these findings identify lactate as a regulator of TNT formation and link tumour metabolism to intercellular connectivity and TMZ response, highlighting lactate metabolism and lactylation as potential therapeutic targets. Highlights Lactate promotes tunneling nanotube (TNT) formation in glioblastoma and breast cancer cells. MCT1-dependent uptake and LDH-dependent metabolism, rather than GPR81 signalling, mediate lactate-induced TNT formation. p300-mediated protein lactylation contributes to lactate-induced TNT formation. Lactate enhances intercellular mitochondrial transfer and attenuates temozolomide-induced growth suppression of glioblastoma spheroids. Graphical abstract

papers.title: Feature-Engineering Strategies for EEG-Based ADHD Classification in Children: A Controlled Benchmark of Expert, LLM-Guided and Full-Space Comparators
papers.authors: Faezeh Rohani, Hasan Alhatab, Mohamed Jarrud, Nour Salous, Salman Kasimoğlu, Andreas Mueller
papers.abstract: Abstract EEG-based machine-learning studies of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are vulnerable to optimistic performance estimates when feature selection or model choice is informed by data outside the training fold. We compared expert-reconstructed, large language model (LLM)-guided and full-space feature strategies under leakage-controlled subject-level validation in a frozen cohort of 77 children (45 ADHD, 32 controls) represented by 1,185 gamma-free EEG features. Four classifiers (SVM, GMM, random forest [RF] and XGBoost) were evaluated with nested leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOOCV), with all data-dependent operations restricted to outer-training subjects. Across 100 repetitions of stratified 10-fold cross-validation, RF/expert achieved mean accuracy 62.8% (SD 3.5%; empirical 95% interval 55.8%–69.5%), mean balanced accuracy 62.3% and mean AUC-ROC 0.618. The corresponding LOOCV point estimate was 71.4% accuracy and 71.0% balanced accuracy (AUC-ROC 0.673). GMM/expert achieved the highest AUC-ROC (0.699), indicating metric-dependent model ranking. The expert-reconstructed strategy achieved the highest accuracy and balanced accuracy for every classifier, whereas the LLM-guided strategy showed no consistent advantage over the full feature space. Pairwise classifier differences were not significant after Holm correction. A pre-specified 200 µV artifact gate reduced RF/expert accuracy to approximately 55.8%, below the 58.4% no-information rate; this drop may reflect removal of artifact-related signal and/or reduced epoch counts leading to noisier feature estimates. These findings support cautious benchmarking and external validation rather than claims of algorithmic or LLM superiority.

papers.title: HealthFound: a health world model for quantitative reasoning on longitudinal health profiles
papers.authors: Hongcheng Guo, Lingran Song, Peng Ren, Jinghong Han, Yuxin Wang, Haoran Li, Jiebi Deng, Jiali Wang, Weikang Gong, Jianfeng Feng, Wei Cheng
papers.abstract: Abstract Medical large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in medical knowledge retrieval and clinical reasoning. However, their capacity for quantitative reasoning over dense, longitudinal health data remains limited, largely due to the lack of effective training strategies that leverage large-scale, natural-language-based prospective cohorts. To address this, we present HealthFound, a medical LLM trained on 12.4 million self-constructed examples. These include 15-year longitudinal biomedical records from 501,936 participants, as well as datasets for medical knowledge and general reasoning. We propose a novel three-stage training framework comprising progressive curriculum supervised fine-tuning, rejection-sampled retention fine-tuning, and task-verifiable policy optimization. This enables the model to effectively parse heterogeneous quantitative follow-up data and perform robust quantitative reasoning. HealthFound achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple newly constructed benchmarks. It attains the highest accuracy on eight public medical benchmarks for general medical competence. On 1,162 UK Biobank tasks predicting future disease onset from biomedical measurements, it outperforms the second-best model by over 10 percentage points on average. In two independent external validations (MIMIC-IV and NHANES), it demonstrates superior zero-shot generalization, achieving improvements of over 6% across 484 disease endpoints. The model also achieves top results on novel tasks for literature-derived question answering and quantitative indicator imputation. Furthermore, HealthFound generates interpretable reasoning rationales that are consistent with established biomedical knowledge. Collectively, our results demonstrate that HealthFound enables medical LLMs to evolve from static knowledge repositories into dynamic quantitative reasoning engines over longitudinal health data.

papers.title: Exploring Students’Critical Thinking through Interaction with Generative AI: A Constructivist Perspective
papers.authors: Allifatur Rohma, Ahsan Hakim
papers.journal: Al-Hikmah International Journal of Islamic Studies
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence expands students’ access to information while raising questions about how they evaluate, verify, and construct knowledge. This study explores students’ critical thinking through interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence from a constructivist perspective, focusing on interaction patterns, information verification, and knowledge construction. A qualitative multisite case study was conducted at two secondary schools, involving students experienced in using Generative Artificial Intelligence and teachers who observed or facilitated its use. Data were collected through observations, interviews, documentation, and field notes, then analysed thematically using within-case and cross-case analysis. Findings indicate that students interacted with Generative Artificial Intelligence in situational, iterative, and dialogical ways, treating it as an additional learning resource. Critical thinking emerged when students encountered uncertainty, contradictions, or inadequate explanations, prompting them to question, compare, verify, and reassess responses using textbooks, teachers, peers, digital sources, prior knowledge, and practical testing. These processes enabled students to connect new information with knowledge, resolve inconsistencies, and reconstruct understanding through reflection and application. The study identifies critical thinking as a cognitive process linking AI interaction with constructivist knowledge construction. Its findings suggest that educational value depends on pedagogical practices supporting inquiry, verification, reflection, and knowledge reconstruction rather than access to generated information.

papers.title: GENERATIVE AI DEPENDENCY AND DECISION-MAKING STYLES: A PREDICTIVE STUDY OF ADULTS IN PAKISTAN
papers.authors: Umara Hafeez, Samreen Arshad, Fatima Afzal, Zara Shafiq, Zeba Nazeer
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized how people access information, get things done, and make decisions in their daily lives. With the growing use of AI-powered technologies, questions have arisen about the psychological impact of such tools, especially when linked to decision making behavior. This study explored the correlation between Generative AI usage dependency and Decision making styles among adult population (N = 102; 51 Male & 51 Female aged 20-40) who were purposively selected from Rawalpindi and Islamabad, Pakistan. AI dependency was measured by the Generative AI Dependency Scale (Goh et al., 2025) while the decision-making styles of vigilance, hypervigilance, buck-passing and procrastination were measured by the Melbourne Decision Making Questionnaire (Mann et al., 1997). Results indicated that there was significant and negative relationship between AI dependency and both buck-passing and procrastination, and there was significant prediction of both these variables by AI dependency, but there was no significant relationship between AI dependency and vigilance or hypervigilance. Women expressed significantly higher dependence upon the AI than men. The results indicate that AI dependence is selectively correlated with decision making and the discussion is based on cognitive offloading, S.D.T. and educational context of Pakistan. The term "buck-passing" is becoming more common when discussing generative AI's impact on decision-making styles, as well as the risk of overreliance on generative AI, which can cause procrastination. Keywords: Generative AI dependency, decision-making styles, buck-passing, procrastination, cognitive offloading

papers.title: Телеологічні та некоректні причинні пояснення у шкільних підручниках з біології: потенційні ризики для формування наукового мислення учнів
papers.authors: Mariia Dovha
papers.abstract: The article examines teleological and scientifi cally problematic causal explanations in three Ukrainian biology textbooks for Grade 7 and discusses their potential implications for the development of students’ scientifi c thinking. Particular attention is paid to the distinction between pedagogically acceptable functional or anthropomorphic simplifi cations and formulations that distort the causal structure of biological and evolutionary explanations. The initial screening of textbook content was performed with the assistance of a large language model and was followed by expert verifi cation of all identifi ed cases. A total of 150 problematic or potentially problematic formulations were retained for analysis. They were classifi ed using a five-level scale ranging from acceptable personifi cation and functional shorthand to explicitly teleological, Lamarckian, progressivist, and intentional explanations of evolutionary change. Most identifi ed cases belonged to the intermediate level of causal and logical distortion, while nearly one quarter of the sample consisted of the most serious categories, in which biological traits were explained through organismal needs, environmental demands, intended outcomes, or purposeful evolutionary change.The fi ndings indicate that textbook quality should be evaluated not only in terms of factual accuracy but also in terms of the causal models conveyed to students. The study also highlights the potential value of large language models as tools for largescale preliminary screening of educational texts when combined with expert validation. The results do not establish a direct causal eff ect of particular textbooks on students’ reasoning; however, they support the need for further experimental research on how diff erent explanatory formulations infl uence the acquisition of evolutionary concepts and the development of scientificreasoning. The fi ndings also point to the need to update textbook development and review procedures by including explicit assessment of causal coherence, evolutionary accuracy, and the epistemic quality of scientifi c explanations.

papers.title: Who Is Responsible When AI Shapes Corporate Decisions? Director Duties and Corporate Accountability under Indian Company Law
papers.authors: Ashutosh Mani Pathak
papers.journal: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
papers.abstract: A company is deciding whether to acquire another business. An artificial intelligence system examines financial records, market data and compliance risks, and recommends that the deal should proceed. The directors approve it. Months later, the acquisition causes serious loss. The board signed the resolution, but the model shaped the information and the choice. Who was really responsible? This article examines that question through section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013. It argues that directors may use AI, just as they use lawyers, auditors and other advisers, but they must not allow assistance to become substituted judgment. The relevant legal question is not whether the model was perfect. It is whether the directors understood its purpose, considered its limits, questioned important assumptions and retained the practical ability to reject its recommendation. The article distinguishes routine assistance, decision support and decision substitution. It then explains how opacity, automation bias, defective data and fragmented vendor arrangements may weaken accountability. Drawing on Indian company law and comparative principles reflected in the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and Indian financial regulation, the article proposes five safeguards: disclosure of material AI use, board-level competence, governance-level explanation, records and continuing model review, and non-delegable human responsibility. Corporate governance may become algorithmically informed, but it cannot become algorithmically unaccountable.

papers.title: Detecting anomalies in LMS user behaviour using machine learning
papers.authors: Vitalii Yanishevskyi
papers.abstract: The study aimed to develop a theoretical-analytical model for the interpretation of atypical digital user traces in learning management systems, covering capabilities of machine learning, structure of LMS logs, and the limits of pedagogical interpretation of algorithmic signals. The methodological framework encompassed an analysis of standards and specifications for digital learning environments, event-based descriptions of learning activity, the quality of software systems, information security, privacy, and decision-making based on artificial intelligence. The study utilised theoretical analysis, a classification approach, feature-based generalisation, comparative analysis, structural-logical modelling and critical generalisation. The study established that users’ digital traces are not a homogeneous array of technical records, but reflect temporal, navigational, resourcerelated, task-related, testing, communicative and technical interactions with the learning environment. The study demonstrated that anomalies may manifest as temporal, navigational, resource-related, task-related, testrelated, communicative, technical and mixed deviations. The study determined that machine analysis requires the transformation of activity logs into features related to login frequency, session duration, transition sequences, task completion, test attempts, communicative activity and technical access parameters. The study established that the choice of machine learning methods depends on the type of anomaly, the availability of labelled data, the structure of events, and the need for interpretability. The sequence of steps from activity logs to data cleaning, refinement of the context of learning resources, feature extraction, determination of a typical profile, selection of an algorithmic approach, detection of an anomaly signal, and its pedagogical or administrative interpretation is demonstrated. The study also argued that an anomaly signal cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence of a violation, as its significance depends on data quality, user history, course structure, technical access conditions, and human verification. The practical significance of the results includes possible use of the proposed scheme to build systems for analytical support of learning, where an anomalous signal is considered as a basis for contextual verification

papers.title: BrightPath AI: A Privacy-Preserving Edge-AI Framework for Early Warning of Classroom Engagement, Safety, and Student Well-Being
papers.authors: Mostafa Elshahat, Ahmed Sami, Mustafa Mohamed, Mahmoud Atef, Mohamed Elsayed, Ibrahim Nabil, Ahmed Hossam
papers.abstract: Schools increasingly use digital tools to support learning, yet continuous observation of individual engagement and safety remains difficult in large classrooms, while continuous cloud video analytics raises substantial privacy concerns. This paper presents BrightPath AI, an edge-first educational early-warning framework that combines open-set face identity routing, classroom-behavior classification, facial-expression category detection, violence detection, a questionnaire-based well-being risk screen, and role-specific mobile reporting. Raw classroom video is processed on a local edge unit and discarded after inference; downstream services receive only derived metadata and alerts. The framework was evaluated using the project datasets and implementation logs supplied for five analytical modules. At a cosine-similarity threshold of 0.5, the face-verification module produced 0 false acceptances among 46,548 impostor comparisons and 27 false rejections among 862 genuine comparisons, corresponding to 99.94% pairwise accuracy, 96.87% recall, and an observed false-acceptance rate of 0%. The classroom-behavior model achieved 98.69% test accuracy across seven classes. The YOLOv8m facial-expression detector obtained mAP@0.50 of 0.877 and mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.697. The MobileNet-BiLSTM violence detector achieved 90% accuracy on the reported 40-video test subset, with no false-positive violence alerts in that subset and 110.55 ms inference time per 15-frame sequence. The binary well-being screening classifier achieved 95% accuracy and 0.92 recall for the needs-support class. The scientific contribution is the integration of heterogeneous school-safety and well-being signals within a privacy-minimizing, human-in-the-loop architecture, together with explicit operational boundaries that prevent facial-expression or questionnaire outputs from being treated as autonomous clinical diagnoses or disciplinary decisions.

papers.title: Catalyst: A Human-Supervised AI Framework for End-to-End Handwritten Assessment and Personalized Learning Support
papers.authors: Mohamed Ahmed, Abdullah Samir, Mostafa Zaki, Mahmoud Khaled, Mohamed Wael, Abdelrhman Fathy
papers.abstract: Artificial-intelligence applications in education are increasingly expected to support assessment, feedback, and learning analytics, yet many prototypes evaluate a single model without showing how it can be embedded in a coherent educational workflow. This paper presents Catalyst, an integrated educational platform that connects handwritten-answer processing, assessment management, teacher verification, learner feedback, and performance-oriented support within a modular client-server architecture. The system uses a Flutter mobile client, a Spring Boot backend, PostgreSQL persistence, a two-stage document-processing pipeline that combines Differentiable Binarization-based text detection with TrOCR recognition, and a T5-based text-to-text service for content summarization and explanation. The principal technical evaluation focuses on handwriting recognition because it provides an objective, ground-truth-based measure. Word Error Rate (WER) is used throughout without converting WER into an artificial “accuracy” score. The reported evaluation yields WER = 0.0090 for single-line handwriting and WER = 0.1925 for multi-line document processing, showing that layout analysis and line extraction are the dominant sources of degradation at page level. In the recorded model comparison, TrOCR-Large and TrOCR-Base produced substantially lower WER than Tesseract, EasyOCR, and Donut under the project evaluation configuration. Beyond model performance, Catalyst separates machine transcription from final academic authorization: objective items may be scored automatically, whereas written responses remain teacher-verifiable before publication. The resulting contribution is an end-to-end, human-supervised architecture that links document AI to actionable educational workflows rather than treating recognition, grading, analytics, and learning support as disconnected functions.

papers.title: An AI-Enabled Integrated Framework for Diabetes Risk Screening, Self-Management, and Care Navigation
papers.authors: EL-Sayed Ramy, Esraa Mohsen, Rana Sameh, Romisah Osama, Farouk Mohamed, Youssef Emad, Walid Abdullah
papers.abstract: Diabetes management applications commonly emphasize logging and reminders, whereas machine-learning studies often evaluate prediction models outside the workflow in which users act on their outputs. This paper presents Diabetes, a mobile platform that integrates tabular risk screening, self-management support, Arabic-language educational assistance, and location-aware care navigation within one deployable architecture. The system combines a Flutter client with Node.js/Express services, hybrid Firebase/PostgreSQL persistence, three task-specific classifiers, and OpenStreetMap/OSRM-based doctor routing. The predictive layer is evaluated on three public tabular benchmarks. On the archived internal test splits, the Random Forest general-risk model achieved 94.10% accuracy, 90.11% sensitivity, 98.10% specificity, and ROC-AUC 0.9916; the SVC women-focused risk model achieved 90.29% accuracy and ROC-AUC 0.95; and the XGBoost health-indicator model achieved 94.99% accuracy, 95.00% sensitivity, 94.98% specificity, and ROC-AUC 0.9900. The publication version deliberately distinguishes risk screening from clinical diagnosis. In particular, the 1,000-record women-focused benchmark contains pregnancy-count and metabolic variables but does not constitute a gestational-diabetes cohort; it is therefore not presented as evidence of gestational-diabetes diagnostic validity. The study’s contribution is an end-to-end digital-health architecture that couples model outputs to monitoring, educational support, and clinician navigation while making evaluation boundaries explicit. Because the reported results arise from public benchmark data and internal development splits, they should be interpreted as proof-of-concept performance rather than prospective clinical validation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Teaching Uterine Fibroids to Medical Students.
papers.authors: Zulfiya Dekhkambaeva, Дехкамбаева Зулфия Абубакировна, Evgeniya Bolunts, Kobiljonova Madina Ulugbek qizi, Mokhina Mirzayeva
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in medical education, but task-level guidance on when learners should engage with AI during clinical reasoning remains underdeveloped. This Special Article presents a literature-informed conceptual proposal, not an evaluated educational intervention, using uterine fibroids as an illustrative teaching context. A targeted narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE and the Spanish Journal of Medical Education website identified literature on AI-supported medical education, clinical reasoning, case-based learning, cognitive load, reflection, assessment, and recent AI-integration frameworks and approaches. We propose a five-step supervised sequence: prepare, reason, interact, verify, and reflect. The conceptual contribution is an AI-specific temporal sequencing principle: learners commit to an independent problem representation before AI exposure; AI is then used as a fallible comparator or feedback source; its claims are checked against an external authoritative source; and discrepancies are closed through reflection. The sequence is designed to address AI-specific risks of answer substitution, uncritical acceptance, and closure without reflection while preserving established case-based and feedback-rich learning. It is intended to be transferable to other specialties when tasks require contextual reasoning, source verification, and professional judgement. The framework has not been implemented or empirically evaluated; its feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, workload implications, and effects on learning, clinical reasoning, and competency development require prospective study.

papers.title: Krisis Kepercayaan terhadap Citra Digital: Semiotika Visual, Deepfake, dan Negosiasi Kebenaran dalam Media Digital
papers.authors: Andi Banus Achir, Zaldy Handi Aditia, Susie Sugiarti, Yunidyawati Azlina, Mety Titin Herawaty
papers.journal: SABER Jurnal Teknik Informatika Sains dan Ilmu Komunikasi
papers.abstract: The development of generative artificial intelligence has transformed the digital visual communication ecosystem by enabling the production and manipulation of increasingly realistic images, thereby challenging the assumption that what is seen can immediately be trusted as evidence. This study aims to analyze the relationship between visual signs, deepfakes, digital verification, visual trust, and the construction of truth in digital media. This study employs an interpretive qualitative approach through visual semiotic, multimodal, and reflexive thematic analyses of a corpus of digital visual materials, including deepfakes, AI-generated images, visual manipulation, misinformation, and debates concerning authenticity. The analysis focuses on denotative and connotative aspects, the relationship between visual representation and textual framing, circulation context, and verification processes through source tracing, reverse image search, comparison with independent sources, metadata, and provenance. The findings show that visual realism still shapes initial credibility but is no longer sufficient to guarantee authenticity because deepfakes can preserve strong iconic resemblance while weakening the indexical relationship with reality. Awareness of deepfakes also creates a paradox of distrust in which both synthetic and authentic content may be questioned. Authenticity is also determined by the consistency among images, claims, sources, time, location, and circulation context. Digital verification therefore becomes an important epistemic mechanism for linking images with sources, context, and external evidence. This study concludes that visual truth is increasingly contextual, conditional, and negotiated, shifting the paradigm from seeing is believing to seeing requires verification, while emphasizing the importance of visual literacy and evidence triangulation in building trust.

papers.title: AI-Driven Business Intelligence for Managerial Decision-Making: The Roles of Prediction Accuracy, Response Speed, Transparency, Explainability, and User Trust
papers.authors: Ika Rosalika, Ibnu Akil, Muhamad Harun, Wahyu Indrarti, Linggar Kiki Zakaria
papers.journal: SABER Jurnal Teknik Informatika Sains dan Ilmu Komunikasi
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has accelerated the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with Business Intelligence (BI) to support faster, more accurate, and data-driven managerial decision-making. This study examines the effects of Prediction Accuracy, Response Speed, Transparency, and Explainability on Managerial Decision Quality, with User Trust positioned as a mediating variable. A quantitative explanatory design was employed involving 190 respondents who had experience using AI-based systems, Business Intelligence, data analytics, or digital applications for work-related decision support. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale and analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that Prediction Accuracy, Response Speed, Transparency, and Explainability have positive and significant effects on User Trust. User Trust also has a positive and significant effect on Managerial Decision Quality. In addition, all four AI-driven Business Intelligence characteristics directly influence Managerial Decision Quality. Mediation analysis confirms that User Trust significantly mediates the relationships between Prediction Accuracy, Response Speed, Transparency, and Explainability and Managerial Decision Quality, indicating partial mediation. Among the examined relationships, User Trust demonstrates a particularly strong contribution to decision quality, highlighting the importance of appropriate reliance on AI-supported recommendations. These findings indicate that effective AI-driven Business Intelligence requires not only accurate predictions and rapid responses but also transparent processes and understandable explanations. Organizations should therefore develop AI-BI systems that balance technical performance with user understanding and trust to improve the quality, relevance, timeliness, and consistency of managerial decisions. This approach strengthens human-AI collaboration while preserving informed managerial judgment in organizations.

papers.title: Demography and Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Nigerian Higher Institutions: Implication on the Needs for Policy Implementation
papers.authors: Dangana-Onuche,, Gloria Ojonoka, Maha, Emaojo Blessing, PhD & Alhassan, Aladi Deborah, Unekwu Grace Oguche, Onoja Emmanuel
papers.journal: International Journal of Scientific Research Studies
papers.abstract: Demography plays a crucial role in understanding the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Nigerian Higher institutions as different demographic factor can influence the rate and extent of the adoption. This paper analyzed Demography and adoption of AI in Nigerian Higher institutions with the focus of examining the factors influencing the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Nigerian Higher Institutions and the needs for policy on its adoption. The paper relied on secondary sources of data such as documented Journals, articles and books written in the area of Demography and adoption of AI in Nigerian higher institution for its analyses. Drawing from the Social Learning Theory the article argued that graduate students' self-efficacy is correlated with their beliefs about their capacity to use and benefit from AI-powered technologies, and outcome expectations are correlated with their beliefs about the possible consequences and outcomes of using AI. Findings suggest that AI adoption in Nigerian Higher institutions is still in its early stage, with many participants recognizing both the potential benefits and the challenges associated with AI integration. More importantly, interactions with artificial intelligence (AI)-based educational tools might be influenced by various demographic factors, including age, gender, marital status, prior technology experience, learning preferences, the type of academic programs, level of education, urban / rural location of the institutions, and socio-economic status of students. The paper recommends among others that policy makers and educators should address potential disparities and ensure equitable access to AI education considering factors like age, gender, location of the institution and socio-economic status in order for Nigerian to prepare its students for the digital age and foster economic growth and development.

papers.title: How generative artificial intelligence tools support self-directed learning: Implications for students’ learning motivation and design thinking
papers.authors: Basant A. Alakabawy, Esam S. Elzok, Ahmed S. Elattar, Mohamed Hozaifa, بسمة عبد المحسن العقباوي
papers.journal: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have introduced promising opportunities for enhancing learning and automated assessment. Self-directed learning (SDL) and a design thinking mindset (DTM) have also been recognized as promising pedagogical approaches that support and contribute to advancing the Sustainable Development Goals. Although prior research has suggested that components of SDL may influence motivation and that motivation may be associated with DTM ability, there remains a noticeable gap in empirical studies examining the interrelationships among these variables. Grounded in the principles of SDL, the present study investigates the use of GenAI tools in assessing students’ DTM. A quantitative study was conducted with a sample of 379 university students, and the data collected through validated measurement instruments were analyzed using structural equation modeling to test and verify the proposed structural model. Empirical findings revealed that the use of GenAI tools for assessment significantly influenced all components of SDL, ultimately leading to enhanced learning motivation. Furthermore, awareness, learning strategies, learning activities, and interpersonal skills were found to mediate the relationship between the use of GenAI tools in assessment and students’ learning motivation. Interestingly, students’ self-assessment did not significantly affect learning motivation and did not play a mediating role between GenAI tools-based assessment and motivation. A particularly noteworthy finding is the absence of a significant relationship between motivation and DTM. This study highlights the role of GenAI tools in relation to students’ learning motivation and the development of their DTM, offering important implications for policies governing virtual learning environments and for instructional practices.

papers.title: The potential of large language models for the assessment of cognitive engagement in informal online communities
papers.authors: Simon Krukowski, H. Ulrich Hoppe, Daniel Bodemer
papers.journal: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
papers.abstract: Studying the cognitive engagement shown in forum messages of informal online communities can help to associate discussion behaviour with underlying learning processes. The ICAP framework can serve as a theoretical lens for labelling forum messages by distinguishing different levels of cognitive engagement, yet requires time-consuming, high-inference human coding, which is not feasible at scale. Although this can be mitigated by supervised classification models, these rely on large amounts of labelled training data, and their decision-making often remains opaque. In contrast to this, Large Language Models (LLMs) work “out-of-the-box” for qualitative coding tasks via natural language instruction and can produce reasoning traces and explanations for their judgments. In this study, we explore this potential by integrating the ICAP framework into natural-language prompts for few-shot in-context classification, comparing LLM judgments and explanations with those of human raters. Results indicate that LLM judgments generally align with the human ratings, while their reasoning traces and variations offer additional insight into where the coding scheme invites ambiguous interpretations. This suggests that LLMs could serve as cognitive proxies that help diagnose and improve high-inference coding processes. Finally, we apply our approach to large-scale forum data, revealing cross-platform differences in expressed cognitive engagement.

papers.title: Proficiency informed knowledge tracing: Leveraging large language models to enhance predictive methods in mathematics learning
papers.authors: Kannan Nataraj, Charles Y.C. Yeh, Chih-Yueh CHOU, Tak-Wai Chan
papers.journal: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
papers.abstract: Predictive methods play a key role in learning systems to enable effective interventions. However, most existing approaches emphasize concept-level suggestions and pay limited attention to cognitive constructs aligned with instructional goals. For instance, in mathematics, mastery depends on the integrated and balanced development of multiple interwoven proficiency strands. When predictive outputs do not reflect instructional objectives, educators may struggle to trust or utilize the insights generated by these models. To address this, we propose a predictive framework that incorporates cognitive construct-aligned features into the modeling process. The research focuses on elementary mathematics, where proficiency strands represent fundamental cognitive dimensions of learning. Since manually labeling these strands is time-intensive for experts, large language models (LLMs) are used to classify semantic features. These features are integrated into the proposed Proficiency-informed Knowledge Tracing (PKT) model as auxiliary signals to enhance mastery estimation. PKT is evaluated on the XES3G5M dataset, which contains elementary mathematics problems, and is compared with established deep learning models. The results indicate that PKT achieves overall competitive performance and surpasses base models, demonstrating a capacity to capture latent mastery patterns. Further experiments reveal that integrating LLM-generated features improves model calibration, as measured by Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), compared to base models. PKT ranked first overall when predictive performance and calibration were considered together, followed by AKT and sparseKT. Additionally, the model generates interpretable diagnostic profiles at both cognitive and concept levels. These findings underscore the value of incorporating cognitively relevant constructs into knowledge tracing.

papers.title: Implementasi Kecerdasan Buatan (Artificial Intelligence) dalam Manajemen Pengambilan Keputusan Kepala Madrasah untuk Peningkatan Mutu Pendidikan Islam: Sebuah Kajian Konseptual
papers.authors: Yahya Nurul Haq, Kholis Lisdawati, Mistiah Basir, Syaidi Huzan, Muhamad Faisal Zindan, Sukmo Danu Tirto
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is developing rapidly and beginning to enter the domain of educational management, including the decision-making processes carried out by madrasah principals. This article aims to conceptually examine how AI can be implemented in the decision-making management of madrasah principals to support the improvement of Islamic education quality, while also identifying supporting and inhibiting factors and their implications for madrasah leadership practice. This study employs a qualitative approach using a literature review method, conducted through systematic searching and analysis of journal articles, books, and prior research relevant to AI, Islamic education management, and madrasah principal leadership. The findings indicate that AI implementation can strengthen the functions of planning, organizing, and evaluating education quality through more evidence-based decision making. However, the success of its implementation strongly depends on the principal's digital literacy, the availability of technological infrastructure, institutional policy support, and readiness to integrate AI use with Islamic ethical values. This study formulates a conceptual framework linking principal readiness, AI implementation in managerial functions, contextual factors, and Islamic education quality outcomes, serving as a theoretical foundation for further field research.

papers.title: Effect of Artificial Intelligence Tools on Teaching Effectiveness of Geometry in Tertiary Institutions in Benue State
papers.authors: Benjamin Tavershima Ako
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: This study examined the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on teaching effectiveness of geometry in tertiary institutions in Benue State, Nigeria. A cross-sectional survey design was adopted. The study involved 235 respondents comprising 60 mathematics lecturers and 175 undergraduate students selected from state-owned tertiary institutions across the three educational zones of the State. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics and multiple regression at the 0.05 significance level. Findings showed a moderate-to-high extent of AI tool usage in geometry instruction (Grand Mean = 3.08). AI tool usage significantly predicted effective teaching of geometry (β = .612, p < .001), student engagement (β = .641, p < .001), and assessment and feedback practices (β = .628, p < .001). The models explained 45.0%, 42.8% and 42.1% of the respective variations. Major challenges included inadequate infrastructure, insufficient lecturer training and unclear institutional policies. The study concludes that AI tools can strengthen geometry teaching, student engagement, and assessment practices when appropriately integrated with lecturers’ professional judgement. It recommends improved ICT infrastructure, continuous lecturer training, clear institutional AI policies, and responsible integration of AI into geometry instruction.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Academic Libraries in Nigeria: Opportunities, Challenges and Prospects
papers.authors: Hussaini Isa
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries remains at nascent stages, particularly in developing economies. Understanding librarians' adoption patterns, institutional readiness, and perceived opportunities and challenges is crucial for strategic planning. Purpose: This study examines the level and extent of AI adoption in academic libraries, identifies key AI applications, explores perceived opportunities and challenges, and assesses librarians' readiness for AI integration. Method: A quantitative descriptive survey design was employed. The study population comprised librarians and library professionals from 15 academic libraries across Nigeria's North-East geopolitical zone (n = 127, 89.4% response rate). Data were collected using a structured questionnaire with eight sections (Likert-scale items, Section A–H) and analysed using descriptive statistics (frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation) and inferential statistics (Pearson correlation, independent t-tests, one-way ANOVA). Instrument validity was established through expert validation and content validity index (CVI = 0.89); reliability was confirmed using Cronbach's alpha (α = 0.81). Results: Current AI adoption rates remain low (mean = 2.34/5.0), with limited AI applications in catalogue management (mean = 2.41/5.0) and reference services (mean = 1.98/5.0). Significant positive correlations emerged between librarians' AI skills and adoption willingness (r = 0.67, p < 0.001) and between institutional support and adoption rates (r = 0.58, p < 0.001). Major opportunities identified include enhanced information retrieval (mean = 4.23/5.0) and improved user experience (mean = 4.18/5.0); critical challenges included inadequate infrastructure (mean = 4.41/5.0), limited funding (mean = 4.37/5.0), and insufficient AI skills (mean = 4.29/5.0). Conclusion: Strategic institutional investment, targeted capacity-building programmes, and supportive institutional policies are essential to accelerate AI adoption.
