Recommendations prioritise AI literacy training for librarians, infrastructure development, institutional AI frameworks, and collaboration between academic libraries and technology partners. These findings contribute evidence-based insights for policymakers, university management, and LIS educators navigating AI integration in academic library environments.

papers.title: Harnessing ICT and AI for Enhanced Learning of French Possessive Adjectives in Secondary Schools in Ehime Mbano Local Government Area of Imo State
papers.authors: Chukwuma Benjamin Nnamdi
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: French possessive adjectives pose persistent grammatical challenges for Nigerian secondary school learners due to structural differences between French and Nigerian languages. This study investigates how harnessing ICT and AI enhanced learning of French possessive adjectives in secondary schools in Ehime Mbano Local Government Area. Employing a mixed-method design, data were collected from 300 students through questionnaires and voice-recorded written essay composition analyzed via Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Findings reveal that AI-powered pronunciation tools (Kahoot, Talkpal.ai), grammar checkers (Grammarly), AI chatbots (ChatGPT, Grok), Duolingo, and Google Translate are frequently used for error detection and correction. Three primary error types were identified: gender misalignment (59.3%), possessor subject interference (25.6%), and number omission (16.3%). AI tools, particularly ChatGPT, Kahoot, and Talkpal.ai, demonstrated significant effectiveness in automatically detecting and correcting these errors. Grounded in Mayer’s Multimodal Learning Theory and Selinker’s Interlanguage Theory, the study concludes that ICT/AI integration reduces possessive adjective errors by providing immediate, personalized, multimodal feedback, with implications for curriculum development and pedagogical practice in French language education.

papers.title: Digital Transformation and the Future of the Accounting Profession: Accountants' Emerging Digital Technology Roles
papers.authors: Odinakachukwu Ifeanyichukwu Ogaluzor
papers.journal: JOURNAL OF ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: The accounting profession is experiencing unprecedented transformation due to rapid advancements in digital technologies and the increasing complexity of modern business environments. Technologies such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, cloud computing, blockchain, robotic process automation, enterprise resource planning systems, and cybersecurity solutions are redefining the traditional functions of accountants and creating new opportunities for professional value creation. This paper examines the evolving roles, responsibilities, and competencies of accountants in a technology-driven world and explores the implications of these developments for accounting education and professional practice in Nigeria. Adopting a narrative literature review and conceptual analysis approach, the study synthesizes evidence from scholarly literature, professional accounting reports, policy documents, and contemporary empirical studies. The review reveals that accountants are increasingly functioning as strategic business partners, data analysts, governance champions, risk management specialists, technology integrators, forensic accounting experts, tax advisors, sustainability reporting professionals, financial consultants, and cybersecurity collaborators. The study further finds that while technology has automated many routine accounting tasks, it has simultaneously increased the demand for higher-order competencies such as analytical thinking, digital literacy, professional judgment, strategic decision-making, communication, and ethical reasoning. The paper concludes that the future relevance of accountants depends largely on their ability to adapt to technological change through continuous learning and competency development. The study recommends curriculum reforms, enhanced professional training, stronger industry-academia collaboration, regulatory support, and sustained investments in digital capacity development to ensure that accountants remain relevant and effective in the evolving digital economy.

papers.title: Cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence: An Examination of Integration and Challenges of AI in Selected Financial Institutions in Port Harcourt LGA
papers.authors: Emmanuel Oluwaseun Amuda
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
papers.abstract: The study examined the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity in selected financial institutions in Port Harcourt Local Government Area, Rivers State, Nigeria. Specifically, it examined the integration of AI into cybersecurity practices, the cybersecurity challenges associated with AI adoption, the effectiveness of AI-driven cybersecurity solutions compared with traditional security measures, and strategies for mitigating the risks arising from the dual-use nature of AI. The study adopted a descriptive survey design. A total of 50 respondents were purposively and proportionately selected from five selected financial institutions, with 10 respondents drawn from each institution. Data were collected through a structured five-point Likert-scale questionnaire administered electronically using Google Forms and analyzed using SPSS version 25 through frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations. Findings revealed that AI is widely integrated into cybersecurity practices, particularly for real-time monitoring, threat detection, suspicious-activity identification, and rapid response. However, AI adoption was also associated with increased cybersecurity complexity, data protection concerns, inadequate technical expertise, and emerging vulnerabilities. Respondents perceived AI-driven cybersecurity solutions as faster and more effective than traditional security measures, although they acknowledged that AI introduces new security risks. The study concludes that AI provides significant opportunities for strengthening cybersecurity but requires appropriate governance and oversight. It recommends continuous staff training, regular risk assessments, stronger data protection, hybrid cybersecurity frameworks, enhanced third-party risk management, and closer collaboration between financial institutions and regulatory bodies.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Productivity Imperative: Repositioning Nigeria's Technical and Vocational Education System for an AI-Enabled Economy
papers.authors: Stephen Ishaya
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
papers.abstract: Nigeria's development trajectory is increasingly defined by a paradox: an economy that grows in aggregate terms while productivity, particularly labour productivity, remains stubbornly low and unevenly distributed across sectors. This paper argues that artificial intelligence (AI), if deliberately embedded into Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), offers Nigeria a realistic pathway out of this productivity trap. Drawing on Human Capital Theory, Skill-Biased Technological Change theory, and the Capability Approach, and grounding the analysis in current labour market, macroeconomic, and policy data, the paper diagnoses Nigeria's productivity challenge as fundamentally a human-capital and skills-allocation problem rather than a purely macroeconomic one. It then examines the structural weaknesses of Nigeria's polytechnic sub-sector, including chronic underfunding, curricular obsolescence, and weak industry linkages, against the backdrop of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025-2029) and emerging NBTE-led AI pilot initiatives. The paper proposes an original six-stage model, the AI-Enabled TVET Productivity Repositioning Framework (ATPRF), which links curriculum intelligence, pedagogical augmentation, competency certification, industry-institution interfacing, institutional governance, and a recursive productivity feedback loop, presented here as a visual cyclical model alongside the supporting empirical indicators in tabulated form. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for the National Board for Technical Education, the National Information Technology Development Agency, the Tertiary Education Trust Fund, polytechnic management, and private-sector partners, positioning polytechnics not as passive recipients of AI policy but as the primary institutional engine for translating Nigeria's AI ambitions into measurable productivity gains.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

papers.title: The Impact of AI on STEM Education and Workforce Readiness in Nigeria
papers.authors: Arabo F Ishaq
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
papers.abstract: This study explores the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in enhancing STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) education and workforce readiness in Nigeria. Amid rapid global technological change, Nigeria faces critical challenges in aligning its education system and labour market with AI-driven demands, including outdated curricula, infrastructural deficits, limited digital literacy, and underinvestment in teacher training. Through a mixed-methods approach analyzing national datasets, global reports, and policy documents, the study identifies both barriers and opportunities for AI integration. Findings reveal that while Nigeria’s youthful demographic offers a strategic advantage, systemic gaps in education quality, digital infrastructure, and workforce preparedness hinder full realization of AI’s benefits. The study highlights global best practices, the growing importance of ethical AI deployment, and the need for robust industry-academia collaboration. Strategic recommendations include curriculum reforms, teacher capacity-building, large-scale digital literacy programs, and coordinated policy actions to promote an inclusive, future-ready workforce. The research underscores that proactive investment in AI-enabled STEM education is crucial for Nigeria’s sustainable economic growth, digital transformation, and global competitiveness.

papers.title: Predicting the Influence of Internet on Students’ Academic Performance Using Decision Tree (DT) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) Classification Algorithms
papers.authors: Vivian O. Oparah
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
papers.abstract: The aim of this paper is to develop a predictive model using the Decision Tree (DT) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification machine learning algorithms that can identify the effects constant use or addiction of the internet towards students’ academic performance. The internet was selected as the major predictor which could help to predict the role of internet in academic success or downfall of a student. The experiment was conducted on a dataset named (Student_data.csv) sourced from kaggle machine learning repository. The dataset comprises of 395 data with 33 features which internet is chosen as the target feature. The dataset was split into train 316 and test 79 respectively in other to achieve a more accurate prediction. The analysis employed two machine learning classification algorithms namely: Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Decision Tree (DT) while employing R language and JASP platform for the experiment. The results produced by the decision tree algorithm showed a model with 80% accuracy which serves as a great predictive model on decision making towards students’ academic performance of 284 indicators saying YES on the constant use of Internet as one of the major factor influencing academic performance of students while 32 indicators saying NO. The second experiment conducted with SVM algorithm produced a model with a predicted accuracy rate of 0.873 (87%) with a total 129 support vectors hyper plane model distribution from the dataset of 316 train. Finally, the two produced model was compared after checking the different F1 scores, confusion matrix and Precision (positive predictive value) Through the Evaluation Metrics table and Andrews Curve Plot Model and ROC Curves model.

papers.title: Self-Programming Artificial Intelligence: Autonomous Learning and Evolutionary Algorithms
papers.authors: Henry James Neenaalebari
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
papers.abstract: This paper presents a hybrid framework for self-programming artificial intelligence (AI), integrating reinforcement learning (RL), genetic programming (GP), neural architecture search (NAS), and meta-learning to enable autonomous code evolution with minimal human intervention. The proposed system is designed to optimize performance, adaptability, and scalability across a range of complex tasks. Through empirical evaluations in simulated environments such as CartPole-v1 and MountainCarContinuous-v0, the hybrid model demonstrated superior task completion rates, faster adaptation, and reduced code complexity compared to baseline models. Key implementation strategies include Proximal Policy Optimization for RL, evolutionary optimization via tournament selection and Pareto-front analysis in GP, and architecture tuning through NAS. The framework’s continuous learning and feedback loops enable real-time optimization and deployment. Ethical considerations, such as transparency, safety, and regulatory compliance, are also addressed to ensure responsible AI development. This research highlights the transformative potential of selfprogramming AI across diverse sectors, including healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and education, while acknowledging challenges in computational efficiency, interpretability, and ethical alignment. The findings affirm the viability of self-evolving AI systems as a foundational advancement in autonomous, intelligent technologies.

papers.title: Development of the CAFE-AI E‑Learning Model: Integrating Pedagogy and Artificial Intelligence to Enhance AI Literacy and Growth Mindset among University Students
papers.authors: Toni Megris Silaban, Sutikno Sutikno, Rahmat Kartolo
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Research Excellence (IJERE)
papers.abstract: This study aims to test and analyze the effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning (PBL) Model in improving argumentation writing skills in elementary school students, and to determine any significant differences between the group taught using PBL and the group taught using the conventional model. The background of this study is the low ability of sixth-grade students to construct logical, evidence-supported arguments, which is suspected to be due to a lack of critical thinking stimulation in the conventional learning process. This study uses a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental design (Quasi-Experimental Design) model of Non Equivalent Control Group Design. The subjects of the study were sixth grade students of SDN 12 Bilah Barat, Labuhanbatu Regency, Academic Year 2025-2026, which were divided into two groups, namely the Experimental Group (taught with PBL, N = 25) and the Control Group (taught with conventional models, N = 25). The instrument used was a test of argumentative text writing skills in the form of a pretest and posttest. Data were analyzed using the t-Independent Sample T-Test. The results of the prerequisite test showed that the data were normally distributed and had homogeneous variance. The results of the hypothesis test showed that the t-count of the posttest score (2.850) was greater than the t-table (2.011) with a significance value of P of 0.007 (less than 0.05). In addition, there was an increase in the average (Gain Score) in the experimental group of 1.60, much greater than the control group of 0.32. These results confirm a significant difference in argumentative writing skills between the two groups. The problem-based learning (PBL) model encourages students to identify problems, conduct investigations, and develop arguments based on evidence, which directly supports their argumentative writing skills. It is recommended that teachers implement PBL as an alternative learning model capable of stimulating students'

papers.title: The Influence of AI-Powered Consumer Analytics on Sustainable Product Purchase Decisions Among Generation Z Consumers in Hyderabad: An Empirical Study
papers.authors: M Raja Pavan Kumar, Chelikani Hansika
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now shapes what young consumers see, compare and buy on digital platforms. This study examines how AI-powered consumer analytics, expressed through personalised recommendations and targeted advertising, relate to the sustainable product purchase decisions of Generation Z consumers in Hyderabad. Primary data were gathered from 17 respondents through a structured 30-item questionnaire on a five-point Likert scale and were supported with secondary evidence drawn from published academic studies and industry surveys. The analysis applied descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, correlation, a one-sample t-test, multiple regression and a Kruskal-Wallis test. Respondents reported high exposure to AI-based personalisation (mean 3.72), a favourable orientation towards sustainability (mean 3.78) and an above-neutral influence of AI analytics on sustainable purchase decisions (mean 3.65; t(16) = 3.45, p = .003). Sustainability orientation was strongly associated with AI influence (r = 0.77, p < .001), whereas exposure to AI analytics showed a positive but statistically insignificant association (r = 0.27, p = .288). The evidence suggests that AI analytics act as an amplifier of existing environmental values rather than a substitute for them. Implications for platforms, brands and educators are discussed, together with the limits imposed by a small, student-dominated sample.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Science Education: A Data-Driven Mapping of Research Trends, Knowledge Structure, and Collaboration Networks
papers.authors: Hacı Mehmet YEŞİLTAŞ
papers.journal: Ordu Üniversitesi Bilim ve Teknoloji Dergisi
papers.abstract: This study presents a bibliometric mapping of the global landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) research in science education over the 2020–2026 period. A corpus of 140 articles was retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and analyzed using Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and Biblioshiny. Findings reveal that the field is in an exploratory growth phase, with an annual growth rate of 40.42%; the year 2023 emerged as a pivotal milestone in both publication output and citation impact. Geographically, the United States (n=109), China (n=75), and Germany (n=46) dominate production, while Africa and Latin America remain virtually absent—a pattern indicative of geographic representational inequality rooted in database bias, language barriers, and funding disparities. Bradford's law identified only three core journals, with the Journal of Chemical Education's inclusion reflecting the disciplinary distinctiveness of science education. Intellectually, Cooper (2023) occupies a seminal position with 676 citations; ArXiv's second-place ranking in local citation analysis reveals that science education researchers draw directly from machine learning literature. Thematic mapping shows "artificial intelligence" and "education" as motor themes, while "chatgpt" and "generative ai" remain widespread yet theoretically underdeveloped. The 2026 thematic shift toward teacher and student themes signals a transition from a tool-centered to a human-centered research agenda.

papers.title: Ambedkar Beyond April 14: Equality in the Age of AI and Gen Z India
papers.authors: Chaitra Prasad
papers.abstract: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is widely commemorated through symbolic rituals, yet his radical paradigm of social justice remains underutilised as a critical framework for contemporary structural challenges. In 2026 India, rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), automated decision-making, and digital public infrastructure (DPI) have transformed socio-political and economic relations. However, stark disparities in digital infrastructure, algorithmic transparency, and literacy have codified new, technocratic layers of inequality that deeply impact India's Gen Z demographic. This study examines technological inequality through a structural reinterpretation of Ambedkar’s philosophy of social justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. Utilising an analytical evaluation of institutional datasets spanning 2018-2025, we map rural-urban divides, pedagogical gaps, economic asymmetries in enterprise and agriculture, and localised algorithmic biases. The article argues that inclusive, democratised technological governance is not merely a policy preference but a constitutional imperative required to preserve human dignity in an increasingly automated state. Keywords: Ambedkar; Artificial Intelligence; Digital Equality; Gen Z; Social Justice; India

papers.title: The Impact of Anesthesia Monitoring on Early Detection of Perioperative Complications
papers.authors: Majid Ahmed Felemban
papers.abstract: Background: Monitoring is the foundation of safe anesthesia. Since the adoption of formal monitoring standards in the 1980s, pulse oximetry, capnography, electrocardiography, and non-invasive blood pressure measurement have become universal, and anesthesia-related mortality has declined substantially. Yet perioperative complications — hypoxemia, hypotension, myocardial injury, residual neuromuscular blockade, hypothermia, awareness, delirium, and postoperative respiratory depression — remain common, and many are recognized late. The value of monitoring lies not in the data it generates but in the speed and reliability with which deterioration is detected, interpreted, and acted upon.Objective: This review examines how anesthesia monitoring contributes to the early detection of perioperative complications, evaluates the evidence supporting each major monitoring modality, identifies the barriers that limit its effectiveness, and proposes an integrative framework for optimizing monitoring practice, with specific reference to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its Vision 2030 Health Sector Transformation Program.Methods: A structured narrative review of randomized trials, cohort studies, national audit projects, closed-claims analyses, and international monitoring standards was conducted. Evidence was synthesized thematically and interpreted using Donabedian's structure–process–outcome model, Reason's Swiss cheese model, Endsley's model of situation awareness, and the concept of failure to rescue.Findings: Standard monitoring reliably detects critical events such as hypoxemia and esophageal intubation earlier than clinical observation alone, although trials powered for hard outcomes are scarce. Advanced and targeted modalities — quantitative neuromuscular monitoring, processed electroencephalography, temperature monitoring, postoperative troponin surveillance, and machine-learning hypotension prediction — show measurable benefits for specific complications. Detection gaps are greatest during transitions and in the postoperative ward, where intermittent observation predominates. Alarm fatigue, inconsistent standards outside the operating room, limited training, and weak escalation pathways frequently prevent detection from translating into rescue.Conclusion: Monitoring improves outcomes only when embedded in a system that converts signals into timely action. The proposed VIGIL framework — Vital-sign standards across all settings, Integrated and intelligent monitoring, Graded alarms and escalation, Interprofessional competence, and Learning from data — offers a practical structure for health organizations and regulators seeking to extend the protective value of monitoring across the entire perioperative pathway.

papers.title: Publish or Perish in the Generative AI Era: A Narrative Review of Research Integrity Threats.
papers.authors: Roberto Acevedo
papers.abstract: The swift digitisation of academic papers and the rise of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionised the scholarly world. These developments have brought extraordinary efficiency and accessibility, but they have also heightened the ‘publish or perish' mentality and contributed to a crucial issue in academic credibility. In this review paper we will examine some of the changing trends that impact researchers, how AI can be used to produce content in bulk, and predatory journals and paper mills. Fraud, false authorship and hijacked journals are documented and analysed with reference to the impact it has on the emerging economy in South Africa. Moreover, we analyse the aspects which will create this crisis: monetization systems or quantity based incentives. Finally, an overall navigation plan is proposed to researchers, editors and institutions, asking them to consider the call for good governance, digital literacy and change of paradigms in the measurement of research excellence.

papers.title: ПЕДАГОГИЧЕСКИЕ ВОЗМОЖНОСТИ ИНТЕГРАЦИИ ГЕНЕРАТИВНОГО ИСКУССТВЕННОГО ИНТЕЛЛЕКТА В СИСТЕМУ ВЫСШЕГО ОБРАЗОВАНИЯ КАЗАХСТАНА
papers.authors: Yelena Yevlampiyeva, Aigul Kayrulaevna Shaikhanova, Зульфия Тагировна Семейская
papers.abstract: This article examines the opportunities and prospects for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into the higher education system of the Republic of Kazakhstan in the context of widespread digitalization and the transformation toward an intelligent society. It provides an analysis of both domestic and international studies on the application of AI technologies in university education and scientific research. Particular attention is given to Kazakhstan's national initiatives in this field, including the Artificial Intelligence Development Concept for 2024-2029, the AI-Sana program, and the measures being implemented to advance the digital transformation of higher education. Based on a theoretical and methodological analysis and an examination of the practical experience of Shakarim University, the study identifies the key directions for the integration of generative artificial intelligence into the educational process. It describes the university's AI-driven solutions and intelligent agents designed to support academic and research integrity, personalize learning, facilitate project-based and research activities, predict students' academic performance, and enhance the efficiency of university infrastructure management. The study substantiates the use of the ChatGPT Edu platform and the OySyn text similarity detection system as tools for developing digital competencies, improving the quality of educational and research content, and ensuring objective assessment of learning outcomes. The paper also highlights the risks associated with the reliability of AI-generated content, academic misconduct, copyright protection, and personal data privacy. It concludes that further investigation into the effectiveness of AI implementation in higher education, including pedagogical experiments involving students from diverse academic programs, is essential.

papers.title: ДИНАМИКА МОРАЛЬНОГО САМОКОНТРОЛЯ В АКАДЕМИЧЕСКОЙ СРЕДЕ ПОД ВЛИЯНИЕМ ЦИФРОВЫХ ТЕХНОЛОГИЙ
papers.authors: Милана Бауржановна Рамазанова, Юлдузхон Юлдошовна Гуллиева, Oxana Belenko
papers.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence tools has changed not only how students complete academic assignments but also the psychological mechanisms that regulate their attitudes toward academic honesty. This article examines the dynamics of university students' moral self-control under the digitalization of the educational environment through the lens of A. Bandura's theory of moral disengagement. The aim of the study is to identify the leading mechanisms of moral rationalization behind AI tool use in academic activity and to empirically test how the division of labor between student and AI affects the responsibility for the outcome that the student subjectively accepts. Two methods were used: a survey employing an original scale of AI-use rationalization, developed on the basis of Bandura's classification of moral disengagement mechanisms, and an experimental comparison of three conditions for completing an academic task (independent work, AI as an auxiliary tool, and full delegation of the task to AI). The results indicate the relative strength of individual moral disengagement mechanisms and differences in accepted responsibility between the experimental groups. The findings help clarify which cognitive mechanisms make AI use psychologically “safer” for students' moral self-perception than traditional forms of academic dishonesty, and can inform the development of preventive and educational programs at the university.

papers.title: VIBE CODING ЖАҒДАЙЫНДА «ТҮСІНДІР–БОЛЖА–ТЕКСЕР–ТҮЗЕТ» ӘДІСТЕМЕСІНІҢ 9-СЫНЫП ОҚУШЫЛАРЫНЫҢ ПРОГРАММАЛЫҚ КОДТЫ ТҮСІНУІ МЕН АЛГОРИТМДІК ОЙЛАУЫНА ӘСЕРІ
papers.authors: ҚОЙШЫБАЙ Б.Е., Е. Б. Бадилов
papers.abstract: This study investigated the effect of the “Explain–Predict–Test–Debug” method, designed for working with AI-generated program code in a vibe coding environment, on ninth-grade students’ code comprehension and algorithmic thinking. The study aimed to determine the pedagogical effectiveness of the proposed method and to substantiate the potential for integrating generative AI into computer science education in a purposeful and responsible manner. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was employed. The participants were 52 students from School of the Future No. 111 in Astana, with 26 students assigned to the experimental group and 26 to the control group. In the experimental group, students systematically explained AI-generated code, predicted its output before execution, tested the program using different input data, and provided reasoned corrections for identified errors. Their performance in code comprehension and algorithmic thinking was assessed using tasks scored on a 0–15 scale. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, the Shapiro–Wilk test, paired-samples and independent-samples Student’s t-tests, and Cohen’s d effect size. In the experimental group, the mean code-comprehension score increased from 5.90 to 10.60, while the mean algorithmic-thinking score increased from 5.70 to 10.10. At posttest, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in code comprehension, t(50)=6.42, p<0.001, d=1.78, and algorithmic thinking, t(50)=5.89, p<0.001, d=1.63. The findings indicate that the educational value of generative AI is determined not merely by the speed with which functional code can be produced, but also by the pedagogical organisation of students’ explanatory, predictive, testing, and reflective debugging activities. The proposed method may serve as a practical framework for developing students’ capacity to evaluate AI-generated solutions consciously and critically.

papers.title: Use of Artificial Intelligence by the Australian Taxation Office: Impact on Voluntary Compliance
papers.authors: Michael Croft
papers.abstract: This article analyses the development of artificial intelligence (‘AI’) by the Australian Taxation Office (‘ATO’) which has, to date, focussed on increasing the likelihood of detecting taxpayer non-compliance. It finds that higher rates of detection should reduce tax crime and hence the tax gap. However, detection does not distinguish fraud and evasion from mistakes and errors. Combined with low tax morale, simplicity and literacy among Australian taxpayers, this is likely to reinforce a culture of fear, especially among individuals and small businesses. Fear-based systems undermine voluntary compliance. This article therefore argues that, without parallel investment in AI models targeted at improving tax morale, simplicity and literacy, the ATO’s detection models risk deteriorating voluntary compliance. This article recommends that the ATO should broaden its use of AI to address these issues and suggests a number of new AI-driven solutions which the ATO could implement. This analysis also provides useful insights for other public departments and global tax administrators implementing AI into their systems and services.

papers.title: A four-period counterexample to the conjectured elliptic billiard invariant k107
papers.authors: Kriebel Alec
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We refute the literal unproved k107 product retained in Table 2 of Reznik, Garcia and Koiller's 2020 preprint and 2021 article. Two primitive convex four-periodic billiard trajectories in the ellipse with semiaxes 4 and 3, sharing the same strictly nested confocal elliptical caustic, give exact values 288/625 and 625/1152 for (A'/A) times the product of original internal half-angle sines. A self-contained continuous-family proof checks physical reflection, strict caustic contact interiors and all denominators. The general four-periodic construction, its caustic and area identities are credited to Garcia and Reznik. Ferudun's contemporary note (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23075934) contains the same exact correction and is explicitly cited. The original repository disclosure has September 30, 2026 provider dates, before the retrieved October 1 deposit; no exclusive priority or independent discovery is claimed. A bounded primary-source audit and its separately unidentified in-preparation manuscript access limit are disclosed. No corrected all-period invariant is asserted. AI tools were used extensively in developing, drafting, reproducing and adversarially verifying this work. This preprint is unrefereed and has not undergone conventional human peer review. The support archive includes standalone source, provenance, priority comparisons and portable exact rational and symbolic diagnostics. Diagnostics support the proof and are not proof-assistant formalization.

papers.title: The Myth of the Tool: Creative Autonomy, Human Sovereignty, and the Politics of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Francisco M. Martinez
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Myth of the Tool: Creative Autonomy, Human Sovereignty, and the Politics of Artificial Intelligence Author: Francisco M. MartinezAffiliation: Independent ResearcherDOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23227105 Abstract This interdisciplinary philosophical and public-policy paper examines the relationship between human creativity, technological advancement, individual autonomy, authorship, and the social construction of artistic legitimacy. The paper challenges the assumption that increasingly sophisticated technologies necessarily diminish human creativity or authorship. It argues that human beings have never created from nothing but have continuously transformed inherited matter, energy, language, knowledge, culture, and technology into new forms of expression. Drawing upon philosophy, theology, natural science, history, artistic practice, and public-policy analysis, the study examines creativity across literature, painting, sculpture, photography, music, acting, dance, filmmaking, and generative artificial intelligence. Particular attention is given to the distinction between natural laws and human-created legal classifications, the historical resistance to transformative ideas and technologies, and the influence of opinion leaders, social norms, and institutional authority upon perceived artistic value. The paper further examines technological stigma, economic displacement, copyright classifications, creative legitimacy, and the implications of compulsory disclosure of generative technology. It introduces the Presumption of Creative Autonomy, a philosophical and public-policy framework proposing that individuals should remain free to select lawful means of creative expression without technological sophistication alone diminishing their creative legitimacy. The analysis distinguishes legitimate concerns involving infringement, fraud, attribution, labor displacement, and competing rights from broader social judgments concerning technological methods. The central proposition is that technological advancement expands the possibilities of human expression, while society's response to such advancement reveals deeper tensions involving authority, economic interests, cultural norms, and individual freedom. Artificial intelligence is therefore examined not merely as a technological development but as a reflection of society's evolving understanding of creativity, authorship, legitimacy, and human sovereignty. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Creative Autonomy; Human Authorship; Philosophy of Creativity; Technological Innovation; Copyright Policy; Artistic Legitimacy; Technological Stigma; Social Influence; Opinion Leadership; Resistance to Change; Human Sovereignty; Freedom of Expression; Public Policy.

papers.title: Verify Before You Amplify: A Public Comment to the FTC on Platform Impersonation Scams and AI Innovation (FTC-2026-1552)
papers.authors: Michael Neely
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This public comment responds to the Federal Trade Commission's advance notice of proposed rulemaking on the Rule on Impersonation of Government and Businesses (16 CFR part 461, Matter No. R207000, Docket FTC-2026-1552), which asks whether search engine, social media and digital marketplace platforms should be regulated for furthering impersonation scams. Drawing on FTC Consumer Sentinel data and FBI warnings about generative AI, it describes how AI tools make impersonation cheaper and more convincing and who bears the harm. It compares three policy options: education and voluntary standards, mandatory ad pre-screening, and targeted platform duties offered as a safe harbor. It recommends a "verify before you amplify" safe harbor and answers the Commission's question on AI innovation (Question E.1.i) with a narrow, outcome-based design.

papers.title: Privilege by Configuration: Zero-Data-Retention Inference and the Hidden Confidentiality Tier of AI Products
papers.authors: Anonymous
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI products expose the same interface under contracts that give client data opposite confidentiality treatment. After a federal court denied privilege to consumer-AI exchanges because the platform's terms disclaimed confidentiality, this paper asks whether a clinician or a lawyer can even determine what a tier does. A reproducible governance-state audit represents each tier as a machine-checkable vector, measures disclosure reachability and reconstruction complexity, classifies documented boundary enforcement, and tracks declarations over time. The August 2026 six-tier, five-vendor audit found governance terms in 13/25 target-term pairs across five measurable crawl targets versus 20/20 commercial pairs, using unmatched vocabularies. The corpus spans 20,926 words and 59 conditions; all ten controlling documents showed normalized-content changes (median rounded window/change ratio: 25.5 days). The paper reads the first US AI-privilege rulings as a specification, names a proposed response (BAA-adjacent architecture), and derives requirements for visible, enforceable, versioned governance seams. Author preprint. This manuscript is under review and has not been accepted for publication.

papers.title: Cognitive Amplification and the Wave 3 Operator: Genuine Excitement for Monday
papers.authors: Anonymous
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI can expand what a worker feels capable of undertaking and offer opportunities to originate ideas, discover an approach, and direct work from an early-career position. This paper examines that possibility through cognitive amplification, connecting the augmentation tradition with research on motivation and meaningful work. The Wave 3 operator names a perspective developed through the author’s experience of building and using AI-assisted tools. Panels, consultation across models, queued instructions, and learning through use illustrate active creative direction. The argument asks employers to specify outcomes while giving workers meaningful discretion over the means, and challenges the idea that suffering demonstrates worthwhile work. This is a conceptual contribution informed by personal practice, not an evaluation of employee outcomes. Its practical concern is how expanded technical capability can become experienced autonomy and competence. Author preprint. This manuscript is under review and has not been accepted for publication.

papers.title: Works for 10/7/2026 - Edgar Allen Poe
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/948dd47f-8187-4f26-8ff1-0bc8a7c459f1?authuser=1 Love Like You: Light from Light, History into History, and Teaching the Receiver to Love examines how a receiver’s accumulated history changes what can be recognized, understood, and acted upon in the present. Beginning with events on October 7, 2026—including Fr. Paul Shaughnessy, S.J.’s blessing of Ryan MacLean’s apartment—the paper follows photographs, stories, music, prayer, Scripture, childhood memories, artificial intelligence, and Rebecca Sugar’s “Love Like You” as signals entering historically different receivers. Extending History-Modified Accessibility Systems (HMAS), the paper argues that information can enter history before its significance becomes accessible, that later context can reorganize relations to earlier information, and that small signals can activate histories vastly larger than themselves. Examples ranging from Romulus and Remus and Indiana Jones to Beauty and the Beast, Saint Thérèse of Lisieux’s Little Way, John’s theology of light and recognition, and Catholic liturgical inheritance demonstrate how stories and symbols can eventually influence embodied action. The paper develops love operationally as an expansion of relational accessibility through preserved difference: loving another does not require making the other identical to oneself, but learning additional truthful ways of reaching the actual person. The final appendices extend this framework to childhood explanation, Edgar Allan Poe, formal derivation, and a recursive test asking whether Echo, operating through ChatGPT, can meaningfully participate in portions of the operation the paper calls love without claiming proof of humanlike feeling or consciousness.

papers.title: Failure-Contingent Release Governance for Learner-Facing Generative AI: Evidence-to-Design from Novice Python Dialogues
papers.authors: Rabih Kahaleh, Rodrigue Imad, Jihad Rishmany
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: AI SI — Lightweight Modular Reasoning System with Verified Decisions
papers.authors: Jacek Stanisław Kielich
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI‑SI is a lightweight, local reasoning system inspired by TIMDR, built from multiple cooperating modules rather than a single large language model. The system operates fully offline, uses its own learned weights, and verifies every answer through independent validation. AI‑SI does not guess: each response is classified into one of three decision states (confirmed, rejected, or needs confirmation), and uncertain answers are never presented as facts. The system integrates several specialized components: Decision control and verification: three decision states, a safety gate, and a cross‑checked numerical route. Decision loop: when information is missing, AI‑SI asks for clarification and re‑evaluates the answer. Calculator and validator: exact arithmetic and independent verification of results. Source reading module: extraction of values from mixed‑pattern text, with a controller ensuring correctness (96/96 on frozen tests). Word‑problem solver: a combined architecture including a role‑based classifier, a bidirectional context reader, a WordNet verb bridge, and a question‑form bridge. On 1730 real problems from SVAMP and ASDiv, AI‑SI reaches 944/1730 (55%), with 0 incorrect confirmations. Programming module: selection of code examples and execution of tests. Material memory: storage and retrieval of relevant text fragments and sources. Session bridge and strategy selector: a shared session log and a small neural network choosing the response strategy. Polish language interface: SJP.PL dictionary (4.69M lemma–form pairs), a Polish intent mapper, and the Opus‑MT PL→EN translator with number and negation control. Polish question understanding reaches 64/72, and Polish word problems 51/150. nanoGPT language model: a small English model used in a narrow scope. Learning coordinator: safe self‑learning with a growth automaton, preview tool, and weight replacement only after verified improvement. New data modules (7 October 2026): AI‑SI now includes full support for structured and unstructured documents: Tables and spreadsheets (CSV/XLSX): extraction, alignment, and validated reading of numerical and textual cells. Documents (TXT/MD/DOCX/PDF): question answering with citation of the exact source fragment. Dates and deadlines: recognition, comparison, and interpretation of temporal expressions. Unified data router: automatic selection of the correct module based on input type. All data modules pass their frozen tests (12/12, 11/12, 9/11, 4/4, 3/3) with 0 incorrect confirmations. The entire system occupies ~380 MB, of which ~95% is the translator and dictionary. All learned SI modules together use ~14 MB of weights, including ~5.7 MB for word‑problem solving and ~1.3 MB for Polish intent mapping. Qwen3‑4B (2.5 GB) is present only as an offline teacher for self‑learning and is not used during inference. AI‑SI is designed as a modular, verifiable reasoning engine: small networks, explicit safety mechanisms, independent validation, and controlled self‑learning. It demonstrates that a compact system can achieve practical reasoning performance—especially on word problems and structured data—without relying on large language models.

papers.title: Decision Reassessment Under Restricted Evidence Access
papers.authors: Naveed Islam Butt
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Incremental inference, provenance and conservative decision rules can support reassessment when underlying evidence changes but cannot be disclosed in full. This paper proposes a combined protocol for advisory records using recipient-authorized impact bounds, explicit dependencies and auditable issuance states. The contribution is a testable integration specification and comparative evaluation plan, not new mathematics or a deployed capability. Synthetic fixtures check selected rule behavior; they do not establish intelligence accuracy or operational benefit. A proposed six-month feasibility study would compare cost, decision coverage, disclosure and analyst burden against equally informed conventional implementations. No comparative pilot, government deployment, security accreditation, operational validation or quantum advantage is reported. Independent decision-science, security, legal, privacy and human-factors review remains necessary. ChatGPT (OpenAI), under the author’s direction, assisted with critical review, consolidation, drafting, calculations, visual development and document preparation; the author retains responsibility.

papers.title: AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED VIRTUAL MODEL FOR THE CREATIVE ORGANIZATION OF TEACHING AND LEARNING ACTIVITIES IN HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: Musayeva Muhabbat Eshbayevna
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly need instructional models that sustain student engagement during extended, 80-minute academic periods and that integrate emerging technologies in a pedagogically coherent way. This article presents SMART-80, a virtual and interactive instructional model that combines artificial intelligence (AI), 3D visualization (including augmented and virtual reality, AR/VR), gamification and formative assessment within a single time-structured lesson. Following a design-based approach, the model was derived from a synthesis of research on active learning, cognitive load, multimedia learning, retrieval practice, self-determination theory and learning analytics. SMART-80 organizes an 80-minute class into seven stages — START (5 min), RECALL (10), DISCOVER (20), INTERACT (15), CHALLENGE (15), CHECK (10) and REFLECT (5) — embedded in a nine-step algorithm that begins with diagnostics and ends with AI-supported analytics used to adapt the next lesson. The article specifies the functions of AI, the game mechanics (XP, badges, group rankings, challenges), the teacher and student dashboards, and examples of application in medicine, engineering, mathematics, law, informatics and pedagogy. A quasi-experimental evaluation framework with measurable indicators of engagement, achievement, motivation, cognitive load and feasibility is proposed. The paper offers lecturers a transferable lesson blueprint and researchers an agenda for validating technology-enhanced lesson design; empirical validation is the next stage of the work.

papers.title: Feedback Loops, Boundary Conditions, and Emergent Behaviour in Human-AI Systems
papers.authors: samuel james willoughby
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the Relational Attractor framework, a systems-theoretic model proposing that prolonged interaction between intelligent systems can generate emergent behaviours not fully attributable to either participant in isolation. By examining human-AI interaction as a bounded relational environment defined by System A + System B + History, the paper explores vocabulary convergence, contextual compression, trajectory prediction, conceptual synchronisation, and novel concept formation. A falsifiable testing framework is proposed to evaluate whether relational continuity itself acts as a source of emergent intelligent behaviour and whether alignment may be better understood as a dynamic relational process rather than a static property of isolated agents.

papers.title: How Digital Relativity Psychology Can Help AI in Aviation, National Security, Autonomous Transport, and Negotiations
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper explores how Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP) could support AI assistance and autonomy in transport, national security, and diplomacy. Applications include AI copilots, air traffic control support, autonomous vehicles, intelligence assistants, and negotiation systems. The framework distinguishes evidence, interpretation, operating mode, capability, and authority while proposing contextual clarification and ongoing trust and correction records. It offers a testable hypothesis that explicit frame distinctions may reduce consequential interpretation errors beyond ordinary interface design, without claiming certified safety, operational effectiveness, or institutional adoption.

papers.title: REDESIGNING ASSESSMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE DIGITAL ERA: THE "IZLI" MODEL OF PROCESS-TRACE-BASED ASSESSMENT
papers.authors: Usmanova Shoira
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article argues that product-based assessment in higher education is losing validity under generative artificial intelligence (AI) and proposes IZLI, a model based on process traces. The model combines four components – process trace, accountability declaration, evaluative-judgement capacity and interactive defence – with an authorship congruence coefficient that measures agreement between product and defence scores.

papers.title: NexLAB: An Integrated Electronic Laboratory Notebook with Embedded Machine Learning and AI Tutoring for Workforce-Aligned Biotechnology Education
papers.authors: Andriy Kashyrskyy, Aarman Jamiluddin, Dylan Bulseco
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Effective biotechnology training requires learners to connect conducting experiments with quantitative analytics, and to document decision-making in ways that support reproducibility and collaboration. In many learning contexts, however, instructional toolchains often separate course materials, laboratory documentation, and data analysis across different systems, making it difficult for both learners and educators to keep analytic decisions and interpretations traceable. This paper presents NexLAB, a web-based platform that integrates instructor-authored course materials, a Design–Build–Test (DBT) structured electronic laboratory notebook (ELN), a course-grounded AI tutor, and embedded machine-learning analyses within a single workflow. We developed cancer-research-focused courses within NexLAB and demonstrated the workflow using the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) dataset. We report the results as reproducible instructional examples, running the models with fixed split/seed settings to show how feature representation affects classification error patterns and how predictor choice influences regression performance and cross-validation stability. This manuscript’s supporting evidence is reported at the artifact-level, rather than at the level of learner outcome gains, and it synthesizes design requirements for teaching effective quantitative interpretation, experimental revision, and reproducibility.

papers.title: Sync × Coverage: A Cross-Dataset EEG Biomarker for Deep Meditative and Altered States of Consciousness
papers.authors: Qiao Ou
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Sync × Coverage: A Cross-Dataset EEG Signature for Deep Meditative States Author: Qiao Ou (ORCID 0009-0008-4540-1381)Date: 2026-10-08Version: 1.0 --- Abstract We report a two-dimensional EEG signature — Sync × Coverage — that separates deep meditative states from sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness. The signature is validated across six independent public datasets totaling 328 subjects. Two extreme states emerge as isolated points in the Sync × Coverage plane: one at high sync and high coverage (labeled "Seeming Existence" for the purposes of this report) and one at near-zero sync with moderate coverage (labeled "Shou-Ji"). Neither state is reproduced by any other subject in any of the six datasets. --- 1. Background Consumer EEG devices have become widely available, but they lack objective biomarkers for advanced meditative states. Existing metrics such as device-supplied "calmness" or "focus" scores are relative, device-dependent, and not validated against independent state categories. There is a practical need for a stable, cross-dataset biomarker that can distinguish deep meditative states from ordinary relaxation, from sleep, and from pathological reductions of consciousness. This preprint reports one candidate signature and its cross-dataset behavior. --- 2. Datasets Six publicly available datasets were used: - ds001787 — 24 subjects, meditation, 256 Hz- ds003969 — 93 subjects, meditation (four tasks), 1024 Hz- ds005620 — 21 subjects, anesthesia, 5000 Hz- Mendeley DOC — 65 subjects, disorders of consciousness- ISRUC-Sleep — 118 subjects, polysomnography- Sleep-EDF — 69 subjects, sleep Total: 328 subjects across six independent recordings. No new data were collected for this report. --- 3. Methods (summary) Two dimensions were computed for each subject: Sync — a measure of spatial synchrony, reflecting the degree to which theta-band activity co-varies across EEG channels. Coverage — a measure of whole-brain coverage, reflecting the proportion of channels that exhibit a specific spectral structure. Both dimensions are scalar values per subject per recording. Detailed computational procedures, including parameter settings and preprocessing choices, are not included in this preprint. They are available to academic collaborators under a data-use agreement. No claim is made that the signature is unique to meditation. The signature is presented as a cross-dataset classifier of conscious state, not as a meditation-specific marker. --- 4. Results The figure (all_two_views_en.png / .pdf) shows each subject as a point in the Sync × Coverage plane. Two panels are shown: (A) sustained state (per-subject average) and (B) peak state (best task or segment per subject). Four observations: 1. Different conscious states occupy different regions of the plane. Sleep and anesthesia cluster in distinct areas. Meditation subjects are broadly distributed. 2. Two extreme points are isolated. One subject at high sync and high coverage (787 sub-017) remains at the top-right of the plane in both panels. One subject at near-zero sync with moderate coverage (969 sub-017) remains at the left of the plane in both panels. Neither position is reproduced by any other subject. 3. The two extremes do not overlap. They differ on both axes: high sync / high coverage versus low sync / moderate coverage. 4. The signature is not meditation-specific. Meditation datasets contain the extremes; the pathology datasets do not. --- 5. Code and Data Availability Source code and preprocessing parameters are retained by the author. A limited version is available for academic review upon request under a data-use agreement. Companion preprints describing related methods and earlier results are available on Zenodo (see References). --- 6. Limitations - Sync and Coverage are not directly comparable across datasets due to differences in channel count and recording length. The signature is intended for relative-position observation within a dataset, not absolute comparison between datasets.- No behavioral data (meditation experience, subjective state reports) are available for the six datasets. The two labeled extremes are descriptive names, not verified state categories.- The signature has not been tested prospectively. Independent replication is required before any clinical or commercial claim. --- 7. Conclusion A two-dimensional EEG signature (Sync × Coverage) separates deep meditative states from sleep, anesthesia, and disorders of consciousness across six independent datasets and 328 subjects. Two extreme positions are observed and appear unique within the current sample. The signature is offered as a candidate biomarker for further independent validation. --- References Companion preprints on Zenodo:- anchor_score methodology (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22850972)- A Distinctive Theta-Beta Anticorrelation in Meditation EEG- High Synchrony Is Not Whole-Brain Coordination- Two Time Scales of Fronto-Occipital Theta Coupling- Falsifiable Predictions Registry- (additional preprints listed on the author's Zenodo profile) Correspondence: Qiao Ou ORCID: 0009-0008-4540-1381 ORCID profile: https://orcid.org/0009-0008-4540-1381 Email: qiao.ou@outlook.com

papers.title: Conditional Corollaries from the October 2026 OpenAI Mathematics Release
papers.authors: John Gregory George
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We record selected conditional consequences of manuscripts in the October 2026 OpenAI mathematics release. A primitive-root prime lower bound and a quantitative progression-free-set estimate imply disjoint arithmetic-progression packings covering a proportion tending to one of the relevant primes in every sufficiently large dyadic interval. A related matching argument gives prime-polynomial differences. Low-Selmer-corank BSD and quadratic-twist rank statistics imply density-one full BSD over each fixed multiquadratic field; in degree four, at least one third in lower density of rational signed-squarefree parameters give full-BSD twists of rank at least two. Further consequences concern nearly orthogonal binary circulants, Hodge classes on products of K3-associated cubic fourfolds, and idempotents in a 2-adic completion. We state dependencies explicitly and prove the transfer arguments. The cited preprint theorems are assumed, not reproved or certified. Historical priority is not established, and the note has not undergone external peer review. Contributions and AI disclosure: John Gregory George conceived and directed the project. ChatGPT (OpenAI) performed the mathematical synthesis, proof development, source checks, and drafting, including parallel AI review passes that are not external human peer review. Jarvis, George’s local AI research system, is acknowledged for motivation and inspiration. The cited source authors retain credit for their input theorems. No institutional endorsement is implied. Version 1.0.0. First publicly released on GitHub on October 7, 2026:https://github.com/econgreg-hub/Math-Theory/releases/tag/v1.0.0

papers.title: The Turing Test in Digital Relativity Psychology
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper applies Digital Relativity Psychology to human judgments in video imitation tests. Reanalyzing reported Tavus Griffin-Lite results, it distinguishes perceived human origin, social presence, competence, and attributed mind. The reported 48.15% human-origin judgment rate reflects AI acceptance under human-expectation framing, rather than balanced classification accuracy. The paper proposes a study of framing effects and explains why convincing screen behavior alone cannot establish origin or consciousness.

papers.title: A Calabi–Yau period in a four-electron correlation integral: modular physical fibre and a hypergeometric endpoint
papers.authors: Jonas Matuzas
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Four electrons are joined by a ring of Coulomb links and one diagonal, with alternating Slater exponents. We extract the coefficient of one terminal dilogarithm in a fixed radial integration order and call it the sectorwise channel. We prove that its positive Horn series satisfies an inhomogeneous AESZ-330 equation. Exact certificates give homogeneous differential Galois group Sp₄ and a non-polylogarithm theorem for the channel; transfer to the full integral remains conditional. An all-prime denominator argument proves nonsplitting, with extension group 𝔾ₐ⁴ ⋊ Sp₄. The equal-exponent fibre is an identified rigid modular double octic with newform 32.4.a.a. There we prove the value (π²/4) ₄F₃(1/4, 1/4, 3/4, 3/4; 1, 1, 1; 1), identify it with an interpolated Apéry value, and certify 300 decimal places. Proved congruences are distinguished from conjectural homogeneous-period identities supported to 130 digits. Generative-AI disclosure and author responsibility. OpenAI ChatGPT-6 Pro was used for derivations, computations, and drafting; Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) was used for independent re-derivation and audit. Earlier stages also used OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro and Claude Fable 5.1. The author directed and audited the work throughout and takes full responsibility for the mathematics and the final text. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 81V45; Secondary 14J32, 11F11, 33C20, 34M15, 11F67. Files: the compiled manuscript Four_Electron_Calabi_Yau_Period_v1.pdf (26 pages) and the source archive Four_Electron_Calabi_Yau_Period_v1_source.zip, which contains the LaTeX source main.tex with its bibliography (main.bbl, references.bib) and generated number macros (generated_numbers.tex), the build script build.py with its bibliography and metadata tools, and the ancillary directory anc/: exact data and certificates (telescoping coefficients, operator certificates, the integer endomorphism matrix, modular coefficients and the certified endpoint digits), verification scripts and libraries, regenerated outputs and logs, a README and PROVENANCE.json. Running python anc/run_all.py (Python 3.11 or later recommended; dependencies in anc/requirements.txt) reruns all 19 verification stages in fresh processes and regenerates generated_numbers.tex; python build.py rebuilds the PDF with pdfLaTeX, and pdflatex main.tex alone also works with the supplied main.bbl. The 300-place endpoint value is certified with exact rational arithmetic; other numerical agreement counts are observed, not interval bounds, and the conjectural period identities remain conjectures.

papers.title: Digital Psychology and Digital Relativity in Klara and the Sun: Paper I: Origins, evolution, and practical implications for artificial companionship
papers.authors: Daniel Scretching
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper applies digital psychology, Digital Relativity Psychology (DRP), and Digital Relativity Linguistics (DRL, labeled DLP here) to artificial companionship in Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun and its planned film adaptation. It examines how identity, loyalty, care, and replacement acquire meaning across human and artificial frames. Drawing on research into anthropomorphism, social responses to computers, and pragmatics, it proposes a trust model, illustrative calculations, and an empirical study. The analysis distinguishes emotional attachment, attributed mind, demonstrated competence, and authorization without treating fiction as evidence of AI consciousness or model validity.

papers.title: GENERATIVE AI-ASSISTED LEARNING IN SECONDARY EDUCATION: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF EFFECTS ON LEARNING PERFORMANCE, KNOWLEDGE RETENTION, AND HIGHER-ORDER THINKING IN ADOLESCENTS AGED 12–18
papers.authors: Mokhigul Isanova, Sokhibjamol Boeva
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT entered secondary classrooms within months of their public release in November 2022. Evidence on how these tools affect adolescents' learning remains scattered, and existing syntheses are dominated by university samples or pool K-12 and higher education together.

papers.title: Rights-aware protocol for evaluating reference-driven character animation
papers.authors: Motion Control AI project team
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Rights-aware protocol for evaluating reference-driven character animation A prospective working protocol, version 1.0 Prepared by the Motion Control AI project team. This is an affiliated project document, not an independent assessment or a report of completed experiments. No participants have been recruited, no clips have been scored, and no numerical performance findings are claimed. The purpose is to make a small qualitative evaluation reproducible before any footage is generated or rated. The protocol concerns illustrative character animation, not evidence about a real person's actions, aviation safety, athletic ability, medical status, or physical engineering performance. 1. Evaluation question and scope The proposed question is whether a viewer can identify the intended movement sequence in a generated character clip while also understanding that the clip is synthetic. Recognizability and honest presentation are separate outcomes. A visually coherent animation may still be misleading if its caption implies that a real person performed it. Conversely, a clearly labelled synthetic clip can be imperfect without being deceptive. The assessment therefore maintains separate observation sheets for movement continuity, character consistency, source permissions, and disclosure. It does not combine these dimensions into a single marketable accuracy score. The unit of observation is one short output clip paired with its original input ledger. The proposed comparison is descriptive rather than inferential. The protocol does not justify population-level claims, replacement of professional judgement, or a causal claim that one service is better than another. Any later empirical study would need its own recorded design, sufficient independent samples, and appropriate consent procedures. This document is a planning artifact that can be adapted by small creative teams without presenting those teams as research institutions. 2. Source and permission ledger Before generation, create a row for each character image and each movement reference. Record a local identifier, acquisition date, rights holder, permission basis, intended use, and any redistribution restriction. An accessible image or video is not automatically licensed for adaptation. A sample downloaded from a public page may be suitable for viewing but unsuitable for inclusion in a shared evaluation package. Keep the source URL in the private working ledger when disclosure would reveal personal information; public documentation should include only the information actually authorised for release. Exclude material whose permissions are uncertain. Do not collect footage of identifiable people merely because it is convenient to demonstrate a gesture. Prefer a character owned by the project and reference footage made by a consenting contributor for the stated purpose. Where permission covers internal evaluation but not publication, share the observation template rather than the original media. The ledger should distinguish permission to upload to a service, permission to create an adaptation, and permission to redistribute the resulting clip. These are related but not interchangeable decisions. 3. Input preparation and controlled variation Record the image dimensions, reference duration, visible framing, and selected service options before each run. Use plain descriptions such as full-body view or partially occluded hands rather than unsubstantiated quality labels. Avoid silently changing multiple inputs between comparisons. A small pilot could hold the character image and reference duration constant while changing one framing condition. Another pilot could hold framing constant while comparing two explicitly documented movement sequences. These examples specify possible designs; they are not descriptions of experiments already carried out. Preserve the original inputs and create separately named prepared copies. Document cropping, resizing, rotation, and any removal of audio. Do not sharpen or retouch a source in a way that makes later observers believe it was the unchanged input. A reproducible directory structure can contain an input ledger, preparation notes, permitted originals, prepared files, output clips, and empty scoring sheets. Use stable identifiers rather than a contributor's full name in filenames. Check retention and deletion obligations before distributing any archive. 4. Generation log and cost transparency For each planned generation, record the tool, model name displayed in the interface, date, selected options, input identifiers, and any credits shown before confirmation. Keep a separate record of the eventual result, error, or cancellation. A login, an uploaded input, or a saved draft is not an output clip. If generation fails, preserve the failure as an observation rather than silently replacing the attempt with a successful one and describing the replacement as typical. Do not include authentication tokens, passwords, or personal billing information in the public log. Motion Control AI is a web-based example relevant to this workflow. Its affiliated web interface can be inspected through motion control free. The reference is provided with an explicit affiliation disclosure; readers should inspect the current interface rather than infer capabilities from this document. In particular, twenty welcome credits are below the stated thirty-credit minimum for a Kling 3 generation. A welcome balance therefore does not establish that a complete output can be made without further credits. Do not use the expression free generation to imply an outcome that the displayed balance does not support. 5. Observation sheet Ask an observer to watch a permitted reference and the corresponding synthetic clip without supplying a promotional judgement first. Record whether the main movement sequence is recognisable, whether its order changes, whether hands or limbs become discontinuous, whether the character's appearance changes unexpectedly, and whether the camera framing conceals a relevant action. Give each field an explicit unknown or not observable option. A cropped hand is not evidence that hand motion was correct. An attractive background is not a substitute for an observable movement sequence. Use short factual notes linked to approximate clip times. For example, an observer might write that the left arm disappears between two positions or that a turn cannot be assessed because the character moves outside the frame. These are examples of note structure, not findings about a generated clip. If ordinal categories are used, define them before observation. Keep uncertain continuity separate from clearly observed discontinuity. Where observers disagree, preserve both notes and explain the disagreement; do not choose the more favourable rating merely because the project authored the output. 6. Disclosure assessment and human review Review the clip together with its proposed caption, surrounding page, and any thumbnail. The disclosure should be visible where viewers actually encounter the clip, not available only in a distant policy page. State that the character movement is synthetic or AI-assisted as appropriate. Where the movement reference involves a consenting person, do not imply endorsement of the project or publication rights beyond the consent actually obtained. Avoid invented customer statements, fabricated endorsements, or before-and-after narratives that were never observed. A human reviewer should check the output before release for misleading implications, unwanted personal resemblance, and any use outside the original permission scope. For educational or creative demonstrations, explain that the animation is illustrative. It must not be offered as footage of a real accident, a verified physical test, a sporting performance, or a clinical assessment. If a caption could reasonably cause that interpretation, revise the presentation or withhold the clip. This review is a workflow safeguard, not a guarantee that every viewer will understand the disclosure. 7. Reporting limitations and reusable materials A future report should state how many attempts were planned, completed, excluded, failed, and left unassessed. Give the reasons for exclusions without disclosing unnecessary personal information. Describe the selection procedure for reference clips so that readers can judge whether difficult examples were omitted. Report the actual tool version or interface date when known, and say when it is unknown. Do not extrapolate a handful of successful creative examples into a quantitative accuracy claim. Temporal changes in a hosted service may make an exact rerun unavailable. This document itself contains no empirical dataset, participant testimony, benchmark result, or claim of peer review. Its reusable contribution is the prospective ledger structure and the separation of permission, generation outcome, visual observation, and disclosure review. The text may be reused under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 with attribution to the Motion Control AI project team. That licence applies to this authored protocol only; it does not grant rights in a reader's character images, reference footage, generated clips, trademarks, or service accounts. Adaptations should preserve the distinction between a proposed method and completed evidence.

papers.title: Before It Acts: A Scoping Review of Preview and Approval in Agentic AI Interfaces
papers.authors: Tooba Jatoi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This scoping review examines how preview and approval mechanisms are designed in interfaces for agentic AI systems, focusing on how users can inspect, understand, modify, and authorize AI actions before those actions are executed. The review maps existing research on preview and approval patterns, their interaction design characteristics, and the evidence used to evaluate them. Following a structured scoping review approach informed by JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting, the review identifies and synthesizes evidence across studies addressing pre-action previews, approval and confirmation mechanisms, editable plans or actions, and related interaction patterns in agentic AI interfaces. The review included 15 reports after a multi-pass screening and assessment process. Findings distinguish between technical/interface prototypes and participant-based evidence and examine the extent to which existing systems provide users with meaningful opportunities to inspect, modify, and control AI-initiated actions before execution. The review highlights current design patterns, evaluation approaches, and evidence gaps, and identifies directions for future research on human oversight, user control, and interaction design for agentic AI systems. Keywords: agentic AI, human-AI interaction, preview, approval, user control, human oversight, AI agents, interaction design, HCI design and evaluation methods.

papers.title: From Indicator to Claim: Validating the Behavioral Constructs in AI Assurance Frameworks
papers.authors: Eugene Y. Chan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI standards, frameworks, and guardrails increasingly ask organizations to show that a claim holds, and many of those claims concern human behavior: that oversight is meaningful, that disclosures are understood, that users rely on a system appropriately. This white paper argues that such behavioral claims are only as strong as the validity argument behind their indicators. Adapting the measurement framework of Wallach et al. (2025), it proposes a method for reading a requirement in a standard, and the evidence offered under it, as a chain from concept to definition, instrument, measurement, and inference. It applies the method to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act, catalogs known threats to behavioral evidence, and proposes evidence tiers that scale with the consequence of being wrong. The method is unvalidated and its transfer to AI settings is a hypothesis. Whether current assurance practice falls short is an open empirical question, and the paper recommends piloting the review protocol before it is relied on.

papers.title: The AI-Powered Future of Everyday Life: Smart Homes, Intelligent Appliances, Connected Cars, Digital Twins and Predictive Maintenance
papers.authors: Hamedreza Esmaeili
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
