Across all three models, truth-directed responses elicited fewer reasoning tokens than both lie-directed and truth-indifferent responses. In addition, in one model, untruthful instructions increased the likelihood of reasoning at all. These findings show that explicitly prompted untruthful response policies can produce robust group-level differences in test-time reasoning-token use. While not yet establishing reasoning-token count as a detector of spontaneous deception or general misalignment, our results are a proof of concept that it can serve as a simple, content-independent black-box candidate signal for differentiating untruthful from truthful model behavior when raw reasoning traces are unavailable or unreliable. Future work should test instance-level detection rates, out-of-distribution generalization, learned deceptive policies, hidden objectives, and robustness under adversarial pressure.

papers.title: DuoSketch: How Pairs Navigate Challenges in AI-Supported Collaborative Design Ideation
papers.authors: Weiyan Shi, Darryl Lim, Geraldine Quek, Kenny Tsu Wei Choo
papers.abstract: Generative AI offers new resources for collaborative design ideation, yet how designers work with it as a shared concept develops remains underexplored. We developed DuoSketch, integrating a shared canvas and live transcripts with a separate AI for each member of a pair. An exploratory qualitative study with 12 pairs identified three challenges: unresolved fit between AI proposals and shared design purposes, shared meanings not expressed in AI responses, and agreed changes missing from later outputs. We found that pairs navigated these challenges through bridging work in two directions: AI -> Shared Design (reworking features, developing uses, and assessing fit with shared requirements) and Shared Design -> AI (supplying materials, explaining meanings, and communicating decisions). We discuss how future AI systems can support the joint exploration and articulation of design ideas.

papers.title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
papers.authors: Kamile Dementaviciute, Julija Vaitonyté, Tijl De Bie
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $ρ= 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

papers.title: Generative AI in Publishing: An Editors' Panel on Ethics and Policies
papers.authors: Jun Yan, Mark E. Glickman, Paul S. Albert, Yulin Hswen, Lan Wang, Minge Xie
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping scholarly research faster than journals have developed stable norms for its use. This article presents an edited thematic account of a 2026 Joint Statistical Meetings panel that brought together editorial perspectives from mathematical statistics, data science, biomedical statistics, and general statistical scholarship. The discussion examines journal policies, disclosure, authorship and research integrity, peer-review confidentiality, researcher training, editorial workload, access, and possible future models of scholarly publishing. Panelists shared commitments to human accountability, the protection of confidential submissions, and disclosure of consequential assistance, while offering different recommendations on assistance with research ideas and proofs, disclosure requirements, automated review, and policy enforcement. By distinguishing shared principles from unresolved implementation questions, the article clarifies the choices facing statistical publishing and outlines an agenda for evaluating policies and practices as GenAI evolves. The account seeks to foster continued discussion of GenAI in scientific communication and encourage statistical organizations to develop more robust operational standards.

papers.title: EEG and Eye-Tracking Evidence That AI Disclosure Shapes Face Evaluation
papers.authors: Teodora Mitrevska, Luise Donat, Andreas Martin Butz, Thomas Kosch, Abdallah El Ali, Francesco Chiossi
papers.abstract: AI-generated faces can be difficult to distinguish from real ones, leaving viewers to rely on source labels when judging an image. Yet prior work has made it difficult to separate the effects of what an image actually is from what viewers are told it is. We validated faces as AI-generated or human in an online study (N=169), then crossed actual source (AI, human) with label (none, Made with AI, Made by a human) in a lab study $N=30), recording event-related potentials (ERPs) and gaze. ERP responses were equivalent for AI-generated and real faces, but varied with the label: labels drew early attention (N2), while labels that conflicted with the face's actual source prompted re-evaluation of the face (P3). Affective processing and initial gaze orienting were unchanged, but labels altered visual exploration. We provide a validated stimulus set and evidence that attributed origin shapes face processing, with implications for disclosure design.

papers.title: A Scale For Value Alignment In Human-AI Interaction
papers.authors: Lena Hegemann, Steeven Villa, Hyemin Bang, Mitchell Gordon, Antti Oulasvirta, Robin Welsch, Patrick Ebel
papers.abstract: Value alignment is a central objective in AI and HCI research, yet no validated instrument measures how users perceive it. This gap hampers the comparison and accumulation of findings and limits the effectiveness of applications, where understanding users' viewpoints is critical. We construct and evaluate a 13-item psychometric scale that measures perceived value alignment across two components: value understanding and value manifestation. It is based on a large item pool drawn from prior empirical studies, filtered by experts, and finally assessed by users (N=607) across diverse AI scenarios. Confirmatory factor analysis on an independent sample (N=259) confirmed the two-factor structure and high internal consistency for both subscales. Using optimization, we also derived a 6-item short form for quick administration. The scale is a reliable measure, providing HCI researchers with a common evaluation metric across contexts.

papers.title: Love for Believable AI: Artificial Partiality and Relationship Persistence as an Engineerable Stance
papers.authors: Sebastian Cochinescu
papers.abstract: We study a behavioral mechanism for artificial partiality in conversational agents. The paper reports no human-subjects data and makes no claim about attachment, trust, perceived mind, or machine interiority. Partiality has two components: caring, defined as allocation of a finite interaction surplus above a guaranteed per-user service floor, and particularity, defined as a per-user state estimate accumulated from relationship history on fixed inference machinery. We implement both as a persistence layer over one open-weight base model and evaluate them on constructed multi-session relationships with known hidden-state schedules. A four-channel divergence compares known-user and stranger conditions on identical probes with paired generation seeds; the stranger prompt is not length-matched, and one channel (initiative) is an allocator output rather than generated behavior. The full mechanism reproduces the ordinal shape, but not the magnitude, of an analytically specified curve and is the only arm satisfying the protocol-defined joint signature on the calibrated battery. The initial mechanism fails probe-quality equivalence because relationship content reduces topical relevance. A guarded revision satisfies equivalence on the calibrated battery but not on a second battery not used in calibration, where it scores higher than the unmodified baseline. On that second battery, the specificity margin is 0.0198, below the 0.02 protocol threshold. The paired mean right-user--wrong-user estimation-accuracy contrast is 0.375 but is not positive in every run. The mechanism is therefore a candidate for a later perception study, not evidence that users perceive love. The versioned protocol record is not independently time-stamped and is not described as a preregistration. Ethical constraints include a stranger-treatment floor, a bounded surplus, disclosure, and de-intensification.

papers.title: A Proof-of-Concept Study of Weakly Supervised Labeling of Fine-Grained EEG Components for Artifact Attenuation
papers.authors: Lu Wang-Nöth, Hai Huang, Philipp Heiler, Shuqiong Wu, Liyun Zhang, Helmut Mayer
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is highly susceptible to electromyographic (EMG) artifacts, whose temporal heterogeneity and spatial-spectral overlap with neural activity can leave mixed sources after blind source separation. Existing artifact-removal methods are further limited by scarce reliable component-level ground truth: expert annotations are costly and subjective, while no established method provides realistic simulation-based ground truth for EMG contamination in multichannel scalp EEG. To address these limitations, we propose a framework combining a frequency-aware high-dimensional representation with Multi-Instance Learning. The representation unfolds separated components into frequency-resolved intra-components, creating a space in which mixed neural and muscular activity becomes more separable, while the weakly supervised learning formulation enables artifact-likelihood scores for individual intra-components to be learned from epoch-level labels without finer-grained ground truth. The resulting intra-component classifier supports fine-grained EMG artifact detection and score-guided attenuation. Experiments on held-out subjects show that the framework learns informative intra-component scores and reduces artifact-related spectral deviations most clearly for jaw tension, with moderate effects for raising eyebrows and limited effects for frowning.

papers.title: Healthy skepticism in AI: a data visualization research agenda
papers.authors: G. Elisabeta Marai, Marc Baaden, Michael Behrisch, Michael Krone, Pere‐Pau Vázquez
papers.abstract: Research in data visualization of artificial intelligence (AI) models has historically focused on enhancing trust through visual explanations of AI. The trustworthiness line of work was built at least partially on an assumption that humans were critical users unlikely to adopt AI technology. It is increasingly clear that human trust levels in AI span, in fact, a wide range from critical to over-reliant. There is an urgent need to support both trust and healthy skepticism in AI solutions. We argue that it is healthy for humans to adopt a skeptical view both on the results of AI models and on the use of such AI models. We share our thoughts on the rising phenomenon of over-reliance on AI models, the risks and opportunities in using AI models, and the role of data visualization in over-reliance situations where humans are not motivated to engage in critical thinking.

papers.title: Rubric Spans are Label Representations: Joint LLM Encoding for Short Answer Scoring
papers.authors: Zhifan Sun, Sebastian Gombert, Fabian Zehner, Leon Camus, Longwei Cong, Hendrik Drachsler
papers.abstract: Automatic Short Answer Scoring (ASAS) requires models that can score student responses against question-specific criteria while remaining efficient and transferable across rubric sets. We propose RUSPAN, a rubric-conditioned ASAS framework that treats rubric descriptions as semantic label representations. RUSPAN serialises the question context, student answer, and all candidate rubric levels into a single sequence, then scores the levels listwise from the rubric-span and whole-sequence representations produced in a single LM pass. We further introduce RUSPAN-RIM, in which a Rubric-Independent Mask prevents rubric spans from attending to one another, making rubric representations depend only on the answer and question context and preventing overfitting to rubric patterns during training for zero-shot transfer. On six ASAS benchmarks spanning English, German, and Portuguese, RUSPAN improves mono-benchmark scoring over discriminative and generative baselines, while RIM with position reindexing delivers consistent and substantial gains on PT-ASAG, the held-out benchmark with the strongest combined language and rubric-structure shift.

papers.title: Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss
papers.authors: Genki SHIKADA, Kazuki Osamura, Masaru Ide, Tetsuya Ogata, Kanata Suzuki
papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. Through real-robot evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we show that under vision loss the success rate of the baseline policy drops substantially, whereas TMD sustains task execution. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.

papers.title: A multi-scenario EEG dataset for auditory attention decoding in naturalistic multi-talker environments
papers.authors: Shu Peng, Rui Liu, Yufei Zhang, Wenlong You, Zhige Chen, Jiachen Xi, Qiyuan Sun, Yan Liu, Kay Chen Tan, Jibin Wu
papers.abstract: Understanding how the brain selectively follows relevant speech amid competing voices is a central challenge in auditory neuroscience and a key step toward neuro-steered hearing technologies. However, most open-source Electroencephalography (EEG) datasets for Auditory Attention Decoding (AAD) use idealized single-competing-talker paradigms that oversimplify the acoustic, spatial, and semantic structure of everyday communication. To capture this ecological complexity, we introduce the SoundBubble-EEG dataset: a high-density 128-channel EEG resource comprising more than 25 hours of recordings from 30 participants. The paradigm requires listeners to selectively attend to a dynamic target speaker group, a designated "sound bubble", amid competing multi-speaker distractor bubbles across three realistic scenarios: a restaurant, a home TV viewing, and a meeting discussion. By bridging the gap between constrained laboratory protocols and real-world auditory scenes, this dataset enables investigations of multi-talker speech comprehension, neural speech tracking, and cross-scenario generalization. It also provides a benchmark for AAD algorithms under realistic acoustic and semantic variability and may support auditory neuroscience and the development of neuro-steered hearing technologies.

papers.title: ActiveLang: Active Open-Vocabulary 3D Mapping with Semantic-Uncertainty-Guided Exploration
papers.authors: Liyan Chen, Hairong Yin, Huangying Zhan, Yi Xu, Raymond A. Yeh, Philippos Mordohai
papers.abstract: As robots increasingly assist humans with diverse tasks, they need both geometric and semantic understanding of their surroundings. Moreover, robots often operate in unfamiliar environments and take on new tasks without knowing the relevant concepts ahead of time. This motivates language-annotated 3D maps that support open-vocabulary scene understanding and human-robot interaction. We introduce ActiveLang, an autonomous system for active open-vocabulary 3D mapping with semantic-uncertainty-guided exploration. ActiveLang performs online language-feature adaptation on a compact dual-Gaussian representation to jointly reconstruct scene geometry, appearance, and open-vocabulary semantics with modest memory overhead. Its planner efficiently selects informative viewpoints, enabling effective mapping with fewer observations and lower computational cost. Experiments on Replica and ScanNet++ demonstrate substantial improvements in 2D and 3D open-vocabulary segmentation over both online and offline baselines, highlighting that actively exploring scenes builds language-annotated 3D maps more efficiently.

papers.title: RT-DETR-World: Transferring Rich LLM Semantics to Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Detection
papers.authors: Yupeng Zhang, Ziyi Zhao, Juntao Cheng, Sheng Wang, Ningnan Guo, Ruize Han, Liang Wan
papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary detection (OVD) recognizes categories unseen during training through textual category queries, yet achieving strong generalization with real-time efficiency remains challenging. Beyond vocabulary scaling, zero-shot generalization may benefit from reusable visual--semantic cues learned from seen data, including attributes, actions, states, and contextual relations. Existing real-time OVD methods primarily emphasize vocabulary coverage and efficient region/query--text matching; under strict efficiency constraints, compact detectors may struggle to absorb rich instance semantics and scene context. We propose RT-DETR-World, a compact DETR-style detector that transfers the rich semantics conveyed by descriptions during training while retaining lightweight query--text matching at inference. We construct GroundingCapv2 with three levels of supervision: category names for standard OVD, object descriptions conveying instance-level semantics, and image descriptions conveying object relations and scene context. These descriptions serve only as training-time semantic supervision. To help the compact detector absorb these semantics, we propose Dual-Path Description Alignment (DDA), combining a deployment-consistent MiniLM pathway with a training-only LLM teacher. MiniLM provides query--category supervision and object-description alignment, while offline teacher features supervise matched queries and global visual representations at the object and image levels, respectively. All teacher features are precomputed, and the teacher-side modules are removed after training. We further propose Relation-Aware Negative Relaxation (RNR), which uses teacher-derived semantic similarities to relax related negatives while preserving exact positives. Experiments demonstrate competitive zero-shot accuracy and a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off. The code will be released.

papers.title: Beyond Score Accuracy: Examining the Diagnostic Quality of LLM-Generated Structured Assessment in Higher Education
papers.authors: Xi Zhao, Xinyue Jiao, Zhen Xu
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted for automated grading and feedback in higher education, their structured outputs, including multi-dimensional rubric scores, detailed feedback comments, and improvement suggestions, create an appearance of thorough analytic evaluation. This study examines whether these outputs deliver what they appear to offer. Using the JorGPT dataset of 3,041 student responses to 50 open-ended computer science questions, scored by both human instructors and three commercial LLMs, we identify three systematic discrepancies between the apparent and actual quality of LLM-generated grading and feedback. The sub-dimension scores are highly correlated (r = 0.82-0.99, VIF up to 45), providing redundant rather than independent diagnostic information. The textual feedback rarely detects student misconceptions (5-7% vs. 15-31% for teachers), functioning as a coverage checklist rather than a diagnostic instrument. The feedback tone remains uniformly positive regardless of response quality, lacking the severity modulation observed in human feedback. Additionally, grading accuracy varies significantly by knowledge domain, with procedural topics most reliable. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance on which aspects of LLM-generated grading and feedback can be relied upon and which require continued human oversight.

papers.title: TutorLoop: Regulating Student Learning Behaviors via Sensor-in-the-Loop Generative Feedback
papers.authors: Songlin Xu, Xinyu Zhang
papers.abstract: We present TutorLoop, a sensor-in-the-loop system that regulates student learning behaviors by delivering adaptive feedback based on real-time cognitive states. Unlike prior large language model (LLM) tutors that directly depend on scenario-specific content, TutorLoop operates on sensor-derived signals captured via webcams. Moreover, unlike direct cognitive-to-feedback mappings that are short-sighted, the system employs a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent to optimize the feedback type across the entire learning process. Finally, another LLM tutor refines feedback into human-like, context-aware messages. We evaluate TutorLoop in a large-scale user study (N=187), where a model trained offline is directly applied to a new learning task without retraining. Results show that TutorLoop provides less frequent yet more effective interventions, improving attention, reducing workload, increasing engagement, and ultimately enhancing learning outcomes. These findings highlight the potential of closed-loop, sensor-driven feedback for scalable human-AI integrated systems to support learning.

papers.title: Multimodal LLMs Can Learn to Read Brain Signals: A Vision--Language Model for Unified Multi-Task EEG Decoding
papers.authors: Parastoo Azizeddin, Omid Sharafi, Maryam Modir Shanechi
papers.abstract: Learning EEG representations that generalize across cognitive tasks, subjects, and recording conditions remains a key challenge in electroencephalography (EEG) decoding. Recent advances in foundation models have improved EEG decoding performance, yet a fundamental open question remains: how to effectively interface neural signals with these models to enable multi-task learning across datasets. To investigate this question, we introduce BraVista, a visual-language framework that encodes multichannel EEG signals as structured images and enables multi-task learning through instruction-conditioned vision-language models (VLMs). Our approach relies on continued post-training of a general-domain VLM, leveraging its visual and linguistic priors to adapt to neural signals without a separate large-scale EEG-specific pretraining stage. We evaluate BraVista on four datasets spanning sleep staging, emotion recognition, cognitive workload classification, and abnormal EEG detection, showing strong performance across these tasks. Further analyses show that the choice of EEG-to-image representation is critical to performance. Moreover, through controlled perturbations of the EEG signal, we observe a gradual performance degradation under increasing noise, suggesting that the model relies on EEG-relevant information rather than superficial visual patterns. Together, these findings establish structured visual representations as an effective and scalable interface between neural signals and general-domain foundation models for unified multi-task EEG decoding.

papers.title: Multidisciplinary Research on Social Media, Artificial Intelligence and Mental Well-Being
papers.authors: Ms. Deepti Udyavar Kirthi Nair, Dr. Harvinder Singh Daisy Mangla
papers.journal: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
papers.abstract: Social media and artificial intelligence increasingly occupy the same space in everyday emotional life. People encounter algorithmically selected content, discuss personal difficulties online, and may seek support from conversational systems. Yet these activities are often examined in separate academic fields. This paper develops a multidisciplinary critical review connecting social media research, psychological measurement, computational inference, and digital mental health interventions. A purposive selection of verified publications from 2020 to 2026 provides the evidence base. No primary survey, clinical experiment, or participant-level dataset is reported. The synthesis distinguishes three roles of artificial intelligence: organizing digital exposure, inferring possible mental health signals, and providing interactive support. Evidence on social media emphasizes variation between individuals and the limits of time-based measures. Research on conversational agents suggests potential benefits for selected symptoms, while broader well-being, sustained effectiveness, and safety require separate evaluation. These findings motivate an original conceptual framework linking digital experiences with social comparison, perceived support, emotional regulation, and personal agency. Four propositions specify relationships for future testing. The paper argues that a technically accurate model cannot establish the psychological value of an intervention without valid outcomes, appropriate comparison conditions, and attention to consequences. It proposes collaborative research practices for psychology, computer science, communication studies, education, and public health. The contribution is a structured explanation of how these disciplines can investigate the same digital experience without treating prediction, engagement, and well-being as interchangeable outcomes.

papers.title: Large Language Models (LLMs) for Generating Personalized Educational Feedback: Architecture, Methods, and Perspectives
papers.authors: Ridouane Oubagine, Ibtissam Azzi, Loubna Laaouina, Adil Jeghal, Hamid Tairi
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-4 and LLaMA, have opened new opportunities for personalized learning support in intelligent educational environments. Feedback matters for how students stay motivated, how they study, and how well they do, but giving each of them personalized feedback in real time is rarely workable: someone, or something, has to answer thousands of students at once. We propose SIGFE (Smart Intelligent Generation of Feedback for Education), a modular framework that produces such feedback with LLMs. It has six components: data collection and preprocessing, learner profile analysis, content-to-goals mapping, LLM-based feedback generation, personalization and adaptation, and an evaluation loop that combines human assessment with usage logs. We tested it in domain-independent LLM-based settings on six real learner-record datasets taken from a Learning Management System. On both quantitative and qualitative measures, the feedback produced by SIGFE was more accurate, more informative, better contextualized, and more personalized than the output of a rule-based system. Learner modeling and prompt engineering turned out to matter most for how well the LLM performs in this setting. For AI in Education, the work offers a personalized feedback mechanism that scales and deals with bias, transparency, and learner agency, and it sets out what remains to be done on real-time and multimodal delivery. Received: 7 June 2026 | Revised: 17 August 2026 | Accepted: 23 September 2026 Conflicts of Interest The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest to this work. Data Availability Statement The data that support the findings of this study are openly available in GitHub at https://github.com/riiid/ednet. Author Contribution Statement Ridouane Oubagine: Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Validation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing, Visualization. Ibtissam Azzi: Conceptualization, Software, Validation, Writing – review & editing, Supervision. Loubna Laaouina: Methodology, Formal analysis, Writing – original draft, Supervision, Project administration. Adil Jeghal: Conceptualization, Methodology, Validation, Investigation, Resources, Data curation, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration. Hamid Tairi: Software, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.

papers.title: Navigating the Digital Transformation of Islamic Education: Authority, Verification, and the Problem of Unsourced Religious Content
papers.authors: Fathorrahman Fathorrahman, Mustopa Mustopa, Miki Suprianto, Ambo Tang, Carlos Lazaro Prawirosastro
papers.abstract: Digital platforms have become a primary route through which Indonesian students encounter religious knowledge, and teachers of Islamic education increasingly meet classroom questions whose answers students have already obtained from sources carrying no chain of transmission. This study examines how the digital transformation of Islamic education reconfigures the relationship between teacher, text, and learner, and asks what verification practice becomes possible when the volume of accessible religious content exceeds any teacher’s capacity to authenticate it. The study is a conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed literature, policy documents, and institutional reports, selected purposively and analysed thematically across accessibility, content authenticity, pedagogical innovation, teacher role, ethics, and institutional readiness. The analysis finds that digitalisation expands access decisively but redistributes interpretive authority in ways existing teacher preparation does not address; that content generated by artificial intelligence intensifies rather than creates this problem, since fluency without sanad is already characteristic of much online religious material; and that blended learning models developed for school-age learners transfer poorly to the adult and para-professional audiences that dominate Islamic non-formal education without andragogical adjustment. The study argues that the practical task facing institutions is not the adoption of technology but the design of verification competence, and proposes three design principles: teaching provenance rather than conclusions, making the limits of teacher authority explicit, and building institutional review of digital content into curriculum governance rather than leaving it to individual discretion.

papers.title: Early Prediction of At-Risk MCA Students Using Machine Learning-Based Classification Models
papers.authors: Mrs Arati Patil, Dr Prashant P Patil, Dr S V Deshmukh
papers.journal: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering and Management (IRJAEM)
papers.abstract: Student academic performance prediction has become an important area of educational data mining due to its potential to improve learning outcomes through timely intervention. Early identification of academically at-risk students enables educational institutions to provide personalized academic support, thereby reducing failure rates and improving student retention. Master of Computer Applications (MCA) programmes present unique challenges because students come from diverse academic backgrounds and are expected to acquire advanced technical competencies within a limited duration. Consequently, identifying students who may experience academic difficulties at an early stage is essential for enhancing educational quality and student success. This paper proposes a machine learning-based methodology for the early prediction of MCA students' academic performance using multiclass classification. The proposed framework categorizes students into three performance groups: At-Risk, Average Performer, and High Performer. The methodology integrates student demographic information, academic history, attendance records, continuous assessment scores, laboratory performance, assignment completion, learning management system engagement, and classroom participation as predictive features. A systematic pre-processing pipeline consisting of data cleaning, feature encoding, normalization, missing value treatment, and feature selection is incorporated to improve data quality before model training. The proposed methodology recommends the implementation and comparative evaluation of several supervised machine learning algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbour, Naïve Bayes, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). Model performance is assessed using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, Confusion Matrix, and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis. Greater emphasis is placed on Precision, Recall, and F1-score since these measures provide more reliable evaluation in educational datasets where class imbalance frequently exists. The proposed framework is expected to support higher education institutions in establishing an intelligent early warning system capable of identifying academically vulnerable students before the final examinations. Such predictive systems can facilitate timely counselling, personalized mentoring, remedial instruction, and data-driven academic decision-making, ultimately contributing to improved student retention and academic excellence.

papers.title: HIGH-SCHOOL STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS OF CHATGPT AS A SUPPORT TOOL FOR LEARNING MATHEMATICS
papers.authors: Verica Milutinović, Ivana Obradović, Suzana
papers.abstract: Генеративна вештачка интелигенција се све више препознаје као значајно средство за подршку процесима учења. Циљ овог истраживања био је да се испитају ставови ученика гимназије о коришћењу ChatGPT-а као подршке учењу математике, са фокусом на улогу мотивационих оријентација, индивидуалних потреба и услова коришћења у обликовању њихових ставова и намере употребе овог алата. Истраживање је спроведено на узорку од 99 ученика једне гимназије у Србији, применом упитника заснованог на интеграцији модела прихватања технологије и мотивационог модела саморегулисаног учења. Резултати истраживачке факторске анализе указали су на постојање шест латентних димензија: ставови према коришћењу ChatGPT-а, намера коришћења, унутрашња и спољашња оријентација ка циљу, индивидуалне потребе ученика и олакшавајући услови. Налази регресионе анализе показују да ставови ученика имају кључну улогу у формирању намере употребе ChatGPT-а, док унутрашња мотивација, индивидуалне потребе и олакшавајући услови значајно доприносе развоју позитивних ставова. Добијени резултати указују на значај педагошких и мотивационих услова за смислену и одговорну примену генеративне вештачке интелигенције у настави математике.

papers.title: AI-Powered Customer Experience in Sustainable Retail: Bridging Technology and Conscientious Consumption
papers.authors: M Rinki, R Sunitha, N Chethan Kumar
papers.journal: REST Journal on Banking Accounting and Business
papers.abstract: This research investigates the strategic integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enhance the customer experience (CX) within the sustainable retail sector. As consumer demand shifts towards ethical and environmentally friendly products, retailers face the dual challenge of delivering personalised, technologically advanced experiences while also communicating their sustainability credentials authentically. This study employs a descriptive research design, synthesising insights from a comprehensive review of current literature and primary data from a survey of 100 retail professionals and environmentally conscious consumers in Bangalore. The analysis reveals a significant gap between consumer expectations and retail execution. While 75% of consumers prioritize sustainability in their purchase decisions, only 32% feel retailers effectively use technology to communicate these efforts. The most desired AI application was ’AI-powered tools for supply chain transparency and product footprint analysis’ (42%), yet the primary barrier to adoption is ’Fear of AI-powered greenwashing’ (38%). The paper concludes with a strategic framework for retailers, recommending a shift from using AI solely for sales personalisation to employing it for "sustainability storytelling," supply chain verification, and empowering consumer choice.

papers.title: Why does human oversight remain essential in the age of AI?
papers.authors: L.P. Jayatissa
papers.journal: Journal of the National Science Foundation of Sri Lanka
papers.abstract: Biological evolution required millions of years for primates to evolve into Homo sapiens, acquiring advanced cognitive abilities along the way. Among all species, humans stand out for their superior intelligence—specifically, the capacity to perceive information, store it as knowledge, and apply it adaptively within complex environments. Today, similar processes can be simulated artificially through Artificial Intelligence (AI) without direct human intervention. However, this raises a crucial question: as AI advances, can human input be discarded? The answer is clearly no. Human intelligence encompasses another vital dimension: creative imagination, the ability to generate genuinely original and valuable ideas. While intelligence forms the foundation of creative thinking, true human creativity involves semantic understanding, intentionality, and contextual reasoning that current generative AI models lack. ...............

papers.title: Professional Development for Artificial Intelligence Integration
papers.authors: Yuyang Yan, Yanchun Zou
papers.abstract: This systematic review synthesizes 56 empirical studies from 2022 to 2026 on AI-focused professional development and reveals that most initiatives prioritize technical competencies while neglecting pedagogical application, ethical assurance, and sustained support. The findings identify AI literacy, self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, ethical guidance, and institutional support as critical determinants of adoption readiness, leading the study to conceptualize AI readiness as a multidimensional capability encompassing literacy, continuous learning, motivational engagement, and enabling structures. Beyond pedagogy, the review frames AI professional development as both an intervention and a strategic managerial tool that strengthens information governance, aligns human competencies with organizational needs, and supports evidence-based decision making. For policymakers and leaders, the insights guide embedding ethics and pedagogy, integrating training with digital strategies, and securing support, linking AI development to capacity, information management, and sustainable oversight.

papers.title: Generative AI-Driven Personalized English Writing Feedback
papers.authors: Yunying He, Hong Xiao
papers.abstract: This study constructed a closed-loop governance framework integrating learning behavior and academic performance big data with generative AI writing feedback. This was done because existing intelligent feedback tools focus on surface-level text generation and ignore learning behaviors, failing to explain differentiated outcomes across student ability levels. The research analyzed 1,248 sophomores in a 16-week online English writing course, utilizing behavior storage, diagnosis, scheduling, and calibration modules to dynamically adjust feedback granularity based on revision lag and absorption rates. It found an inverted U-shaped relationship between feedback length and score improvement, showing that tailoring intervention frequency and text length to specific student abilities significantly enhances writing performance. This means generative AI must evolve beyond a simple text correction tool into a standardized teaching component governed by risk thresholds to provide sustainable, personalized support.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Audit Performance and Ethical Risk Governance in Financial Fraud Identification
papers.authors: Xiaojian Liu, Jiannan Yu, Hailian Yu
papers.abstract: This study constructs a dual-cycle framework integrating financial fraud identification and ethical governance for artificial intelligence-assisted audit. It uses financial indicators, text features, and corporate governance variables to build multi-dimensional detection models. Traditional models and machine learning models including tree ensemble, explainable, and review-adjusted models are compared. Empirical results show that machine learning models outperform traditional models in fraud identification accuracy and stability. The explainable module and manual review can effectively reduce ethical risks such as opacity, bias amplification, over-reliance, and responsibility ambiguity. This work balances technical performance and ethical compliance, reveals ethical challenges of intelligent audit applications, and provides a governance path for the standardized application of artificial intelligence in auditing.

papers.title: Metadata in the Disciplines: Social Justice Through Infrastructural Literacy
papers.authors: Lynne Stahl, Michelle Elaine Colquitt
papers.abstract: Lynne Stahl, PresenterMichelle Colquitt, Recorder At a time when academic libraries face pressure to compete for limited funding and status in both the public and institutional eyes, one thing every discipline has in common is metadata. It is through the information infrastructures within academia, which are often underexamined by non-librarians, where inequities exist: troublesome subject headings and taxonomic practices, dubious data privacy practices, and the ongoing insinuation and commoditization of generative artificial intelligence (AI). Library workers are uniquely positioned to call out the political aspects of inequitable information infrastructures. Many librarians in the classroom attempt to address information inequality but are limited by time constraints and competing priorities associated with one-shot information literacy sessions. Drawing on examples from the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, this talk illuminates how collaborations across public services, technical services, and departmental faculty can promote a deeper understanding of the component pieces of research and scholarship while combating structural biases.

papers.title: From Models to Workflows: Communicating Agentic AI in Asset Management
papers.authors: Mike Chen
papers.abstract: Agentic AI creates a new communication problem for asset managers: stakeholders need to understand not only what a model produced, but how the workflow around it was built, checked, and signed off. As access to foundation models becomes less differentiated across large institutions, sophisticated stakeholders increasingly ask not only whether a model is accurate, but what evidence the analysis rests on, what checks were run, and where accountability sits. A fluent AI-supported output can hide that entire chain. This article proposes three workflow controls—grounding, stability, and permissioning—and a compact disclosure record that travels with each AI-supported investment output, keeping what the model produced separate from what the firm approved. Operationally, these controls help keep unsupported, unstable, or unauthorized AI-supported outputs from entering the investment process. Communicatively, they give a firm a concrete language for explaining its AI-supported investment processes: what the workflow read, whether its conclusions are repeatable, what it could and could not do, and where human judgment entered. This is a framework for explaining and supervising AI-supported investment workflows, not a performance claim or a certification: it makes the process auditable, and accountability for investment decisions stays with the people who make them.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Early Childhood Education in Nigeria: A Critical Inquiry into Pedagogical Opportunities, Systemic Challenges and Policy Imperatives
papers.authors: Onyung Sandra Effiong, Orji Cyrus Ebere MCPN, Agu Mercy Oluchi, Ugwu John-Jerry Tochukwu, Ajagu Kingsley Onyeka
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
papers.abstract: Introduction: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Early Childhood Education (ECE) represents a transformative paradigm shift globally, yet Nigeria's ECE sector remains critically underexplored in this domain.  Problem: Despite AI's demonstrated potential to enhance foundational literacy, numeracy, and personalized learning, Nigerian ECE faces systemic barriers including inadequate infrastructure, low teacher preparedness, ethical concerns, and the absence of comprehensive policy frameworks.  Significance: This inquiry critically examines the pedagogical opportunities, systemic challenges, and policy imperatives for AI integration in Nigerian ECE, addressing a significant gap in empirical and theoretical literature.  Method: Adopting a critical analytical methodology grounded in constructivist theory, critical rationalism, and African humanism, this study synthesizes peer-reviewed literature, policy documents, and empirical studies published between 2015 and 2026, drawing extensively from verified Nigerian-focused research.

papers.title: Integración de métodos ágiles e IA generativa en la formación en gestión de proyectos: Un estudio de métodos mixtos sobre competencias digitales
papers.authors: Ciro Martínez Oropesa
papers.abstract: Los programas de gestión de proyectos de posgrado necesitan cada vez más equilibrar la instrucción tradicional con el rápido crecimiento de los métodos ágiles y la IA generativa (GenAI). A diferencia de estudios anteriores que tratan la adopción de tecnología como una condición binaria de presencia o ausencia, este estudio es uno de los primeros en modelar la intensidad de la integración como una variable gradual de dosis-respuesta en un contexto de posgrado latinoamericano. Evaluamos un rediseño curricular en la Universidad Autónoma de Occidente (Cali, Colombia) que incorporó progresivamente prácticas ágiles y herramientas de GenAI a lo largo de tres semestres académicos en un solo año, utilizando un diseño cuasiexperimental de dosis-respuesta con métodos mixtos (Shadish, Cook y Campbell, 2002). Comparamos a 160 estudiantes de posgrado y 18 instructores en dos niveles de integración pedagógica: un grupo fundamental (Scrum introductorio y herramientas digitales básicas) y un grupo avanzado (Scrum completo, Disciplined Agile, plataformas de nivel industrial y uso sistemático de herramientas GenAI, específicamente ChatGPT para la resolución iterativa de problemas y la redacción de contenido, y GitHub Copilot para la planificación asistida por código). La competencia digital se midió con un instrumento DigComp 2.2 validado y adaptado, aplicado como pruebas previas y posteriores, complementado con entrevistas y grupos focales. Ambos grupos mejoraron significativamente en las cinco áreas de DigComp 2.2, pero el grupo de integración avanzada mejoró sustancialmente más, con un gran tamaño del efecto (d = 0,84, IC del 95 % [0,51, 1,17]), especialmente en la creación de contenido digital y la resolución de problemas. Los hallazgos cualitativos muestran que los estudiantes que interactuaron con GenAI como un socio de pensamiento, en lugar de una simple herramienta de automatización, desarrollaron un pensamiento crítico y una adaptabilidad más sólidos. Estos resultados indican que los programas que ya imparten formación ágil fundamental pueden lograr avances desproporcionadamente mayores en competencias digitales al avanzar hacia una integración más completa de la metodología ágil con la IA de última generación, lo que ofrece un modelo replicable y basado en la evidencia para los programas de gestión de proyectos de posgrado que buscan adaptarse a la transformación digital.

papers.title: Application of Electroencephalography for Assessing Adaptation Processes in Humans (Review)
papers.authors: М Н Панков, А. Б. Гудков, Yakov S. Pestov, О. Н. Попова, Ирина Сергеевна Кожевникова
papers.journal: Journal of Medical and Biological Research
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography is an informative method for recording the electrical activity of the brain, which is widely used in physiological and clinical studies to assess the functional state of the body. In general, electroencephalography allows to identify characteristic adaptive changes and helps understand the general patterns of compensatory and adaptive responses. This review examines the use of electroencephalography to assess adaptation processes during stress, and cognitive and physical exertion. Currently, neurophysiological diagnostics of stressful conditions is based on the analysis of the main electroencephalogram rhythms: delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–14 Hz), beta (14–30 Hz), and gamma (>30 Hz), with an assessment of their spectral characteristics (amplitude, dominant frequency, index). Modern research has identified three key electrophysiological correlates of stress: decreased mediofrontal theta activity, modified delta oscillations, and frontal alpha asymmetry. Adaptation to cognitive loads is a crucial mechanism for maintaining mental performance and preventing cognitive fatigue. Electroencephalography allows for an objective assessment of the functional state of cognitive processes, tracking the dynamics of changes in fundamental brain rhythms, and identifying key neurophysiological mechanisms of central nervous system adaptation to various types of mental exercise. This is of significant importance for both fundamental research on cognitive functions and applied aspects of optimizing mental performance. The review shows that the neurophysiological mechanisms of adaptation to physical loads include various complex changes that are clearly reflected in the electroencephalogram. Thus, electroencephalography is an effective tool for assessing not only changes in the brain’s bioelectrical activity, but also the processes of adaptation and recovery during stress, and cognitive and physical exertion.

papers.title: Perceptions of Socio-Technological Shifts and Ethical Risks among Next-Generation Emirati IT Specialists: An Empirical Assessment
papers.authors: Dimitrios Xanthidis, Anang Judaya Muhamad Amin, Ourania Koutzampasopoulou Xanthidou, Moataz Salhab, Abdelrahman Altigani, Alya Yousef Abdulla Alhammadi
papers.journal: WSEAS Transactions on Information Science and Applications archive
papers.abstract: The accelerating evolution of digital infrastructures and cognitive technologies has fundamentally reshaped contemporary social fabrics; a complex matrix of systemic opportunities and ethical challenges. However, while the socio-economic dividends of automation abound, the swift and uncoordinated spread of these tools poses significant disruptions to traditional socio-cultural norms, ethical paradigms, and long-standing religious values. For highly advanced governmental and judicial technical frameworks in a rapidly growing economy like the United Arab Emirates, this digital transformation happens during a critical transition through legacy infrastructure disparities, often termed the digital divide, that exist in tandem with advanced governmental and judicial technical frameworks. While sophisticated solutions, including automation and artificial intelligence, such as intelligent legal informatics, predictive machine learning, and nuanced digital forensics, play a substantial role in optimizing security frameworks, compliance architectures, and compliance processes, they also introduce new sources of exploitation for automated bias, algorithmic manipulation, and the erasure of cryptographic evidence. At the same time, rampant deepfakes, organized disinformation schemes, and generative AI systems undermine trust, necessitating strict legal and operational scrutiny of content authenticity, platform accountability, and user cognitive health. This paper provides a systematic empirical analysis of next-generation Emirati IT professionals’ levels of awareness about these sociotechnical vectors. Using an extensive questionnaire-level survey given to about 200 upper-level computer information sciences students, our initial empirical results suggest a rather sophisticated awareness baseline. The participants express considerable critical awareness of the structural, ethical, and socio-psychological dangers of these new paradigms and show a strong cultural and occupational capability to imaginatively think, govern, and steer future technologies responsibly.

papers.title: AI IN TAXATION, GST AND TAX ADMINISTRATION: TRANSFORMING COMPLIANCE, REVENUE COLLECTION AND TAXPAYER SERVICE
papers.authors: Nagaveni .
papers.journal: EPRA International Journal of Environmental Economics Commerce and Educational Management
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the way governments design, administer and enforce tax systems. Tax administration is particularly suitable for AI because it involves large volumes of structured and unstructured data, repetitive compliance processes, risk assessment, fraud detection and continuous interaction with taxpayers. In India, the digital transformation of taxation has progressed through income-tax e-filing, faceless assessment, the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN), e-invoicing, e-way bills, automated return processing and data analytics. These systems create an extensive digital information environment in which AI and machine learning can support tax compliance, identify anomalous transactions, improve taxpayer services and assist tax authorities in allocating limited administrative resources. This paper examines the role of AI in taxation, with particular emphasis on GST and Indian tax administration. It analyses major applications including fraud detection, input tax credit verification, risk-based scrutiny, taxpayer assistance, automated document processing, predictive analytics and compliance management. The paper also evaluates the benefits and limitations of AI, including privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, explainability, data quality and the danger of excessive automation. International evidence indicates rapid adoption of AI by tax administrations, while India's expanding digital tax infrastructure provides a substantial foundation for further AI-enabled administration. The paper argues that AI should primarily function as a decision-support and risk-management technology, with appropriate human oversight rather than completely replacing statutory decision-making. A governance framework based on transparency, accountability, data protection, human review and continuous auditing is therefore essential for trustworthy AI-enabled taxation.

papers.title: AI-INDUCED ACADEMIC DEVIANCE: A CRIMINOLOGICAL STUDY ON CHANGES IN STUDENTS’ LIFE ACTIVITIES AND CONDUCT
papers.authors: Angelica B. Ngojo, Queen E. Mabilog
papers.journal: EPRA International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research (IJMR)
papers.abstract: This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) affects academic deviance among criminology students at the University of the Visayas. Using a quantitative research design, it gathered data from 278 randomly selected respondents to assess how AI tools affect students’ study habits, academic integrity, and ethical decision-making. The results show that AI can make learning more efficient and effective, but it also brings risks such as academic dishonesty, overreliance on technology, and reduced independent thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. ChatGPT is the AI tool respondents use most often, showing that conversational AI is becoming more popular in academic settings. The study also finds that students with some experience using AI understand its benefits and challenges, but they do not have advanced skills or a strong understanding of ethics. Gender and year level play important roles in how students use AI. Even though institutions try to encourage ethical use of AI, there is still a gap between what policies say and what actually happens. The study suggests adding AI literacy, ethical guidelines, and monitoring systems to academic programs. This approach supports responsible AI use, protects academic integrity, and helps future criminology professionals think independently. These findings are meant to guide educational strategies and policies as digital learning becomes more common.

papers.title: Who Is Responsible for the Findings? Researcher Agency and Expertise in Quantitative Educational Research in the Age of AI
papers.authors: Jihyun Hwang
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are transforming how quantitative research is conducted. This essay reflects on how four core practices—method selection, coding, result interpretation, and reproducibility—have shifted in the age of AI, and its implications for researcher expertise and accountability. Quantitative expertise was forged through generative resistance: encounters that force deeper engagement with methods, data, and theory, forming professional judgment. AI removes much of this resistance while demanding a new form of expertise—the capacity to judge what AI produces. Current institutional responses address knowing-that and knowing-how but say nothing about knowing-why and knowing-whether: the layers that determine whether a study is trustworthy. Shifting from disclosure to accountability requires structural responses from training programs, journals, and research communities.

papers.title: Future Education with Augmented Reality and Deep Learning
papers.authors: Wahid Sadique Koly, Homaira Adiba, Shah Murtaza Rashid Al Masud
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel system that combines deep learning-powered image classification with augmented reality (AR) to enhance educational visualization. The system uses advanced image recognition to scan textbook images, classify them, and generate AR markers in real-time to render relevant 3D models, animations, and other educational content. It offers a dynamic and adaptable learning experience, allowing seamless integration and expansion of instructional material without client-side modifications. Utilizing real-time streaming and rendering technologies ensures efficient data transfer and exceptional performance. The dynamic AR markers improve personalization and context-awareness, offering significant improvements over traditional static AR systems. This approach enhances student engagement and comprehension, setting a new benchmark for integrating AR and machine learning in education.

papers.title: The Effect Is in the Specification: Wording Sensitivity, Grader Blind Spots and the Validity of Pass Rates in LLM-Graded Programming Practice
papers.authors: Hon-Ren Lin
papers.abstract: LLM-graded pass rates are increasingly used as outcomes when evaluating AI feedback, yet they may measure conformity to a grading specification rather than student correctness. We audited one such system, in which GPT-4o graded Python function-interface designs and, in one of two practice modes, also gave detailed advice (43 novices, AB/BA crossover, 899 submissions; two independent human coders). The grader was not invariant to construct-preserving lexical change: replacing one reference name with a human-acceptable synonym failed 47 of 100 otherwise unchanged passing variants, against 7% for unchanged copies, and in two problems the grader rejected the wording of the problem statement itself. Its errors were systematic rather than random: false passes concentrated on answers whose only defect was a type the grading prompt had been told to accept (24–39% vs 6–8% for substantive defects). Measured by the system’s own pass rate, detailed feedback outperformed pass/fail feedback (OR 4.6); measured by a uniform re-grader or by human judgement, it did not (OR 1.5 and 1.4). Which arm the system mis-measured depended on whether the human standard adopted the grader’s type rule. Effects measured by an LLM grader are properties of the specifications — problem statement, reference answer, grading prompt and human standard — as much as of the instruction. We provide an audit checklist and release the procedure, coding manual and scripts.

papers.title: Ethical Epistemic Collaborative Output Dialogue (EECOD): A Practical Solution Providing Visible Thinking in an Era of AI-Assisted Educational Teaching and Learning
papers.authors: Mary Beth Herron
papers.abstract: The Ethical Epistemic Collaborative Output Dialogue (EECOD) is a structured classroom protocol designed to support AI fluency and make student thinking visible throughout the learning process. Developed from Further Education and Training (FET) practice, EECOD guides students through a standardised interaction with large language models (LLMs) that is transparent, assessable, and teacher-verifiable. Students explain the task in their own words, receive one constrained LLM suggestion at a time, and accept or reject each with a stated reason. This visible chain of reasoning is captured in a Protocol Score Card that evidences both student engagement and teacher intervention without adding to workload. The framework is mapped against Irish National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) and Quality and Qualifications Ireland (QQI) standards using Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. Worked examples and a proposed assessment rubric are provided. The paper argues that EECOD represents a replicable, subject-transferable model for process assessment in an era when AI use in education is unavoidable but largely unmediated.Keywords: AI fluency; visible thinking; assessment for learning; Teacher in the Loop; large language models; academic integrity

papers.title: Student Co-Construction of Evaluation Criteria for AI-Generated Responses: A Research Protocol for Developing Evaluative Judgment in Engineering Education
papers.authors: Amirhossein Rezaeian
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has created new challenges for engineering education by making it increasingly difficult to distinguish fluent outputs from reliable engineering reasoning. This paper presents a research protocol that investigates whether student co-construction of evaluation criteria for AI-generated responses can support the development of evaluative judgment, self-regulated learning, and conceptual understanding in engineering students.The proposed intervention shifts students from passive acceptance of AI-generated answers toward active evaluation of claims, evidence, assumptions, procedures, and limitations. The protocol integrates perspectives from evaluative judgment, formative assessment, self-regulated learning, assessment co-design, and AI literacy. It specifies research questions, hypotheses, instructional procedures, measurement instruments, and an analysis plan for a mixed-methods classroom study.The proposed study does not assume that GenAI automatically improves learning; instead, it examines the mechanism through which students may learn to judge the quality of AI-supported engineering work. The protocol is designed to generate evidence about how criteria construction, verification practices, and reflective activities influence students’ ability to evaluate AI-generated engineering responses. Limitations, including external validity, variation across engineering disciplines, and the complexity of measuring cognitive processes, are discussed.This work contributes a testable framework for designing human-centered AI pedagogy in engineering education and provides a foundation for future empirical investigations.

papers.title: SMAP-ST: Smart MBTI-Adaptive Public Speaking Tutor
papers.authors: Leonardo Mogianesi, Stelios Kapetanakis, Giacomo Nalli
papers.abstract: Up to 80% of graduate students in the UK struggle to speak confidently in front of an audience, whether during class presentations, seminars, assessments or interviews. A major reason for this is the lack of a consistent support during their school education for developing strong public speaking skills whilst most teachers do not feel confident, with the tools they have, to support learners in developing these skills. Consequently, many primary and secondary school students do not have enough opportunities to develop their public speaking skills. Beyond institutional gaps, individual differences such as personality traits can significantly impact a student’s confidence and ability to speak in public. For some students, public speaking can trigger overwhelming anxiety or cognitive overload. Students with more introverted or sensitive traits, for example, may feel intense discomfort when asked to perform in public. Personality patterns can create a range of barriers that traditional classroom environments rarely accommodate. These patterns affect more than just academic performance; they also limit opportunities after graduation. Without targeted support, many students may miss out on opportunities simply because there is a lack of effective support for their diverse communication needs. SMAP-ST (Smart MBTI-Adaptive Public Speaking Tutor) is an intelligent tutoring system powered by AI. It is designed to support oral presentation training in an online environment that combines text and voice-based interactions with a virtual tutor. Thanks to interaction with SMAP-ST, students can rehearse presentations on selected topics through guided interaction and receive immediate, personalized feedback on their communication skills. The system’s distinctive feature is its MBTI-based personalisation, whereby the tutor adapts the tone and structure of the feedback to suit different personality types. This helps students to identify their own weaknesses during speech, boost their confidence and fluency, and be effective at the same time because it fits with their personality traits. The system is evaluated by analysing collected data during user interaction with the SMAP-ST to identify the effectiveness of the response generated for each personality trait.

papers.title: Beyond Audio: An Empirical Assessment of AI-Generated Podcasts and Videocasts in Business Education
papers.authors: Gokhan Egilmez, Karolina Schneider
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is opening new possibilities for personalized, engaging instructional content in higher education. Extending our earlier work on AI-generated podcasts, this study examines the addition of AI-generated videocasts (video overviews) alongside podcasts in an undergraduate business analytics course, asking whether a multimodal (audio + video) approach improves students' learning experience beyond audio alone in a subject area that is conceptually dense and data-intensive. The study takes a quasi-experimental approach, comparing two consecutive sections of the same course: one with access only to AI-generated audio podcasts (Fall 2025, n = 24), and one where the same podcasts were supplemented with companion AI-generated videocasts (Spring 2026, n = 20). Student-perceived academic performance, engagement, and satisfaction were measured through a 15-item survey covering prior podcast experience, AI familiarity, usage patterns, perceived impact on quiz preparation and comprehension, effectiveness relative to traditional study methods, and open-ended feedback. Results showed a consistent, though modestly powered, advantage for the multimodal condition: students in the audio + video section rated the materials more favorably than the audio-only section on nearly every measured dimension, with a statistically significant increase in willingness to recommend the format for other courses (84.2% vs. 47.6% favorable, p = .026). Qualitative responses reinforced this pattern, with audio + video students more often citing improved comprehension and valuing multiple ways to engage with material, while a smaller subset preferred less synthetic-sounding narration. Across both sections, most students rated podcasts as at least as effective as traditional study methods, and roughly half had never used podcasts as a learning tool before the course. These findings offer preliminary but encouraging evidence that integrating AI generated video and audio content strengthens students' learning experience and engagement in business analytics education, while underscoring the need for larger, multi-term samples and objective performance measures to confirm the effect. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enhanced instructional design by identifying student-reported benefits and design considerations relevant to integrating generative AI tools into business education curricula.

papers.title: AI and Academic Integrity: Student Perceptions of Plagiarism and Ethical Use at the University of Fort Hare
papers.authors: Bongo Mqukuse, Nathunathi Mvunge
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education is transforming how students engage with learning, research and academic writing, while raising concerns about plagiarism, authorship, originality and academic integrity. This study explored undergraduate students' perceptions of plagiarism and the ethical use of generative AI at the University of Fort Hare. A mixed-methods, interpretive design was used, drawing on pre-workshop responses from 347 students and post-workshop responses from 127 students. Quantitative items were analysed descriptively, while open-ended responses were analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke's approach. The findings show that students entered the workshop with substantial prior exposure to AI but uneven understanding of ethical use. Among post-workshop respondents, 96.9% rated their understanding of responsible AI use as good or excellent, while 86.6% agreed or strongly agreed that they understood when AI use could become plagiarism or academic misconduct. The study highlights the need for continuous AI literacy development, clear institutional guidance and assessment practices that promote responsible AI use while preserving student authorship and independent thinking.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Learning: Opportunities, Tensions, and Transformation in Higher Education.
papers.authors: Nathunathi Mvunge, Bongo Mqukuse
papers.abstract: The growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education globally, with increasing relevance for institutions such as the University of Fort Hare (UFH), which are navigating digital transformation within resource constrained contexts. At UFH, the emergence of AI tools presents both exciting opportunities to enhance teaching and learning, and complex challenges related to ethics, academic integrity, and digital readiness. While AI has the potential to support more flexible and personalized learning, there remains uncertainty about how it is being used and experienced by both students and lecturers. This study explores the use and implications of AI in teaching and learning at UFH, with a specific focus on students. It aims to examine the extent of AI adoption among students, how they engage with these tools in their everyday academic practices, and the implications of this engagement for the future of teaching, learning, and assessment within the institution. A mixed methods case study design was employed. Quantitative data was collected through survey questionnaires administered to students to identify patterns of AI use, perceived benefits, and levels of digital competence. This was complemented by qualitative data from semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions, which provided deeper insights into participants’ experiences, concerns, and expectations. The study is informed by the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework. The findings reveal that while students are increasingly turning to AI tools for academic support such as idea generation, summarization, and content clarification. Participants expressed optimism about AI’s potential to enhance learning and concern about issues such as over reliance, plagiarism, and the erosion of critical thinking. The study also highlights gaps in institutional policy and development related to AI. The study concludes that AI can play a meaningful role in advancing learning at UFH, but its successful integration depends on fostering a shared `z understanding of ethical use, strengthening digital literacy, and providing ongoing support for both staff and students.

papers.title: Challenges and Opportunities for Applying Artificial Intelligence to Learning in Secondary Schools
papers.authors: Ioannis Lappas
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is gradually becoming part of everyday practice in secondary education. Teachers now encounter AI-based tools in different aspects of school work, from feedback and classroom organisation to adjusting learning activities to fit individual student needs. As the use of such technologies expands, their educational role and practical value in schools require closer examination. This becomes particularly relevant in classrooms with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in learning pace, participation, learning needs, and overall educational readiness. In such settings, AI technologies can support the adaptation of instructional material, provide more individualised feedback, and offer additional forms of participation in the learning process. Their educational value, however, depends on professional judgement and on the way these tools are used within everyday classroom practice. The present paper addresses opportunities and challenges connected with the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. It focuses on teachers’ perspectives and on their experiences with the educational use of AI tools in school practice. This doctoral work adopts a primarily qualitative approach. Data will be collected through semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers and later analysed through thematic analysis. Through interview responses, the analysis will examine how AI is perceived in relation to lesson preparation and student support, as well as the practical limits of its implementation in schools. Special attention will be given to professional preparedness and to the everyday classroom conditions that affect the responsible use of AI. The analysis will also consider how participants understand the educational value of AI tools and the ways these technologies are applied in secondary school classrooms. The paper therefore approaches AI not as an independent solution, but as a tool whose usefulness depends on teachers’ judgement and the pedagogical context in which it is used.

papers.title: Digital Learning Environments and Student Satisfaction: A Learning Analytics Perspective
papers.authors: Sarmite Mickevica, Signe Bāliņa
papers.abstract: Higher education is increasingly characterised by heterogeneous student populations, digitally mediated learning environments, and the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI). This study examines how student complexity, digital readiness, learning-environment preferences, and perceived employability may inform the development of AI-enabled Student Relationship Management (SRM). The conceptual framework integrates relationship marketing, the Industrial Marketing and Purchasing (IMP) network perspective, the Nordic School’s value co-creation logic, and learning analytics. Using EUROSTUDENT 8 data, the study combines a comparative descriptive analysis of six European higher education systems with exploratory correlation analysis across all countries for which comparable indicators are available. The findings reveal a pronounced “working student” profile among mature learners, characterised by substantial employment alongside continued academic commitments. Digital access and self-assessed professional digital skills are comparatively well-established across age groups, while high digital readiness shows no meaningful association with high perceived employability. Most importantly, greater online-learning intensity does not automatically produce stronger alignment with student preferences. Higher employment intensity is associated with stronger preferences for online learning, yet some mature student groups experience more online provision than they would ideally prefer. The findings therefore highlight a critical distinction between digitalisation and flexibility. AI-enabled SRM may contribute by supporting adaptive alignment between institutional delivery models, student circumstances, and differentiated support needs rather than by increasing digital intensity alone. The study contributes to educational technology and relationship-management literature by demonstrating that the strategic necessity of AI-enabled SRM arises primarily from growing student complexity and institutional adaptability challenges rather than from deficiencies in baseline digital readiness.

papers.title: An AI-Supported Simulation-Based Serious Game in Digital Health Management Education: Design and Formative Evaluation
papers.authors: Annika Hering, Gülsen Otman, Annika Viedenz, Jan-David Liebe
papers.abstract: Background Teaching digital transformation in healthcare management requires students to address complex organizational challenges, multiple stakeholder perspectives, and decision-making under uncertainty. Traditional case-based teaching provides limited experience of real-world decision-making complexity and feedback. Objectives This study presents the design and formative evaluation of the first version of an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported digital serious game (DSG) in Digital Health Management (DHM) education. It examined students’ evaluations of the integrated management methods, generative AI (GenAI)-supported stakeholder interactions, educational design, and AI-generated model solutions. Methods Design of the DSG was informed by the co.LAB generic framework and resulted in a scenario-based learning environment integrating management methods, collaborative problem-solving, GenAI-supported stakeholder interactions, and AI-generated model solutions. The formative evaluation used an embedded mixed-methods design across bachelor’s and master’s degree courses at two higher education institutions. Twenty-one students participated in the DSG, of whom 15 completed the interim evaluation, while the number of method-specific evaluations varied across learning activities. Qualitative reflections were collected at group level. Results The browser-based DSG combined healthcare digitalization case scenarios, sequential management methods, GenAI-supported stakeholder interactions, collaborative problem-solving, and AI-generated model solutions. The management methods received consistently positive ratings (M = 4.19–4.55/5).
