Students also positively evaluated the GenAI-supported stakeholder interactions (M = 5.95/7), their usability (M = 4.18/5), the teaching-learning experience (M = 4.98/6), and the AI-generated model solutions (M = 3.98/5). Internal consistency ranged from acceptable to excellent (α = .72 to .91), while Spearman-Brown coefficients for two-item subscales ranged from .66 to .92. The qualitative findings suggest that the AI-generated model solutions supported validation, extension, and critical comparison of students’ own analyses. The Net Promoter Score (NPS) was 40. Discussion The findings suggest that GenAI can support scenario-based learning in DHM when GenAI-supported stakeholder interactions and feedback are embedded in a coherent, collaborative learning design. Future studies should use a prospectively defined evaluation framework to compare different forms of AI-generated feedback and assess reflection, objective learning outcomes, competency development, and transfer in larger samples. Conclusion The study provides an initial design and empirical basis for the further development of AI-supported DSGs in DHM education. The findings indicate that the AI-supported components may support perspective taking, comparison, reflection, and method-based decision-making within a coherent learning design.

papers.title: Societal Transformation Related to Emerging Technologies in Industry Through Bi-Lateral Collaboration
papers.authors: Rico Marisol, Mikael Ericsson, Prakruthi Hareesh, PB Venkataraman, Kerstin Johansen, Lennart Malmsköld
papers.abstract: Emerging Industry 4.0 technologies—such as automation, additive manufacturing, and artificial intelligence—are accelerating the need for continuous upskilling in industrial workforces. While upskilling is not a new societal phenomenon, the current pace and breadth of technological change interact with national education systems, industrial structures, and funding models in ways that differ substantially across countries. This creates both challenges and opportunities for international collaboration in lifelong learning and work-integrated learning (WIL). This paper examines societal transformation related to emerging technologies through a bilateral lens, focusing on learning initiatives and institutional practices in Sweden and India. Drawing on observations and interactional collaboration between higher education institutions in both contexts, we illustrate how upskilling demands are shaped by differing national trajectories. For example, historical Swedish adult education initiatives—such as evening studies undertaken to respond to increasing internationalization—can be contrasted with contemporary patterns in India, where engineers often engage in weekend-based learning to meet rapidly evolving industrial competence needs. Despite the global nature of industrial markets, priorities regarding who funds upskilling (industry, academia, individuals, or the state), how learning time is allocated, and how competence development is evaluated vary across contexts. We benchmark a WIL-oriented model associated with Indian experiences against Swedish experiences of WIL and educational quality enhancement, including structured follow-up with participants (e.g., focus groups) to iteratively improve course design. Based on this comparative analysis, we propose an initial conceptual framework to support bilateral collaboration in upskilling emerging technologies. The framework highlights critical dimensions to align across contexts, including technology maturity, competence capability, and resource conditions such as time and financial support in both industry and academia. The paper concludes with a gap-oriented discussion of how virtual laboratories and shared e-learning platforms could enable scalable bilateral collaboration for work-integrated upskilling.

papers.title: Integrating ChatGPT into University English Teaching: Linguistic Performance, Autonomy, and Learning Experience
papers.authors: Jeany Liseth Argueta Villalobos, Gisela Espinoza, Víctor Sandoval
papers.abstract: This study examines how the planned integration of ChatGPT influences English language development, student autonomy, and the overall learning experience in a university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) Intermediate English II course in El Salvador. The aim is to analyze both quantifiable changes in language proficiency and students' interactions with artificial intelligence as a learning support tool, particularly in relation to self-regulation and independent learning processes. Furthermore, the study sought to understand how students perceive the usefulness and limitations of AI in academic contexts. A convergent mixed-methods case study design was implemented with twenty-three undergraduate students enrolled in an Intermediate English II course. Quantitative data were collected through TOEFL ITP simulation tests administered before and after the intervention to assess changes in language proficiency. Qualitative data were collected through a focus group of four participants, where students shared their perceptions, attitudes, and experiences interacting with ChatGPT during the learning process. Both datasets were analyzed separately and then integrated to provide a comprehensive interpretation of the findings. The quantitative results reveal a positive, though not statistically significant, trend in TOEFL ITP scores after the intervention. While quantifiable improvements in test performance were limited, the qualitative findings offer a clearer understanding of the learning process. Students reported using ChatGPT as an accessible and ongoing learning partner to practice language skills, clarify doubts, generate examples, and receive immediate feedback. This consistent interaction contributed to increased confidence, greater autonomy, and the development of self-regulated learning strategies. However, participants also expressed concerns about potential over-reliance on AI and occasional inaccuracies in the generated responses, underscoring the importance of maintaining critical awareness. This standalone study highlights the pedagogical potential of AI tools when intentionally integrated into language teaching and underscores the need to foster critical AI literacy so that such technologies enhance, rather than hinder, meaningful learning.

papers.title: Beyond Engagement: A Human Flourishing Framework for Emotion-Aware AI in Education
papers.authors: Spyros Kontis, Sofia Anastasiadou
papers.abstract: Emotion-aware artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to infer learners' affective states, such as frustration, confusion, or engagement, and to adapt instruction in response. These capabilities may make learning environments more responsive, but they also raise questions about privacy, surveillance, bias, and the treatment of emotional experience as data. Evaluation has therefore moved beyond accuracy alone. Trustworthy AI stresses transparency and oversight; AI Ethics adds fairness and harm prevention; Human-Centred AI foregrounds learner agency. These perspectives are necessary, yet they do not fully settle a further educational question: against what longer-term human purpose should emotion-aware AI be judged? This conceptual paper proposes the Human Flourishing Framework (HFF) as a normative evaluative perspective for addressing that question. It is not presented as a computational layer or a causal model. Instead, it examines the conditions created around AI-mediated learning within a wider educational ecosystem. The framework organises five dimensions, Emotional Autonomy, Psychological Safety, Transparency and Data Dignity, Fairness and Inclusion, and Human Flourishing, across Foundation, Empowerment, and Outcome layers. Its purpose is to examine whether the design and use of emotion-aware AI support or constrain learners' longer-term development, without attributing flourishing to the technology itself. The paper clarifies the framework's epistemological and theoretical positioning, distinguishes flourishing from related concepts such as capability, agency, and self-regulation, and translates the HFF dimensions into indicative system requirements. The contribution is conceptual rather than empirical. The framework has not yet been validated or operationalised as a measurement model; future work will therefore require longitudinal, multi-level, and cross-cultural research capable of studying AI-mediated learning within its wider educational context.

papers.title: Student Ambassadors for Sustainable AI EdTech Knowledge Sharing in Higher Education
papers.authors: Hyein Cho, Min Soo Lee, Ko Young Woong, Yong Geun Kim, Jion Kim, Minho Kim, Tae Il Yoon
papers.abstract: This conceptual paper develops a framework for appraising institutional knowledge assets produced through AI EdTech dissemination. Knowledge mobilisation research emphasises dissemination, interpretation, usefulness, uptake and context, but does not typically isolate representational quality as a distinct asset-level appraisal dimension. This gap is especially consequential when verification asymmetry and promotional incentive co-occur: claims may exceed inspectable evidence, overstate attribution or omit material conditions and risks even when assets remain visible, accessible and reusable. The paper therefore conceptualises representational quality through four criteria: claim traceability, attribution restraint, condition disclosure and risk representation. It further specifies a student ambassador model in which case-linked direct-user knowledge is combined with evidence access, expert review and revision rights across a governed production-and-maintenance lifecycle. Production-stage verification constrains distortion before dissemination, while post-hoc fidelity audit supports correction after publication; engagement analytics substitute for neither. Five falsifiable propositions address construct distinctness, verification, direct-user informational advantage, conditional diagnostic value and maintenance after material change. The paper reports no empirical findings. Its contribution is to position representational quality as an explicit property of AI EdTech knowledge assets and to specify the conditions and governance mechanisms under which it should be appraised.

papers.title: Prompt-as-Lesson: Authoring AI-Delivered Lessons for Fidelity and Observability
papers.authors: Lefevre David
papers.abstract: This paper reports the development of the prompt-as-lesson: a lesson encoded as a single prompt and run in the student’s own LLM tool, with the model cast throughout as a tutor delivering the teacher’s lesson, and the session closing with a report of the dialogue returned to the teacher. The purpose of the prompt-as-lesson is to enable students to pursue teacher-specified learning outcomes through tutorial dialogue with an LLM. The interactive, conversational nature of an LLM makes Laurillard’s Conversational Framework the natural interpretive lens. Under this lens, the paper argues, the LLM is the first single medium capable of enacting the iterative teacher–learner dialogue the framework holds essential to formal teaching, yet this dialogue is frequently lacking in higher education. Introducing LLM activities into the formal learning environment risks inconsistency as, left to its defaults, the model teaches from its own conception and constructed learning environment rather than the teacher’s. The prompt-as-lesson is a response. Utilising the prompt-as-lesson within the teacher’s formal environment makes three demands: consistency, so that what is taught is drawn from the teacher’s conception and pedagogy; adherence, so that the enacted lesson remains the authored one; and reporting, so that the dialogue is not opaque to the teacher. Design-based iteration on two contrasting modules to address these demands yielded two primary findings: contemporary LLMs struggled to adopt the learner’s perspective and would not reliably hold to an unstructured lesson. The format that emerged seeks to address both issues and comprises three artefacts: a control surface of fourteen dimensions; an eight-section structure; and a four-phase authoring method. The paper claims no effect on learning; its contribution is a control surface, a structure and an authoring method. A formal evaluation of the format’s fidelity of implementation begins in September 2026.

papers.title: Integrating Generative AI in Assessment and Feedback in Higher Education in Albania
papers.authors: Xhensila Sinanaj, Ervis Sanço, Erion Selimi, Doris Madhi, Elvira Fetahu
papers.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming assessment and feedback practices in higher education, creating both opportunities and challenges for teaching and learning. This empirical study, situated within Aleksandër Xhuvani University investigates how GenAI is integrated into assessment and feedback practices in higher education. The study investigates 57 educators’ and 128 students’ perceptions, experiences and expectations regarding the use and feedback with the aim of informing evidence-based pedagogical innovation. It seeks to answer five research questions. (1) What GenAI tools are integrated in assessment and feedback activities? (2) What do educators and students need for GenAI integration? (3) How to integrate GenAI tools in pedagogical practice? (4) What are the experienced and desired impacts of GenAI tools? and (5) What are the foreseeable pitfalls of using GenAI tools? Methodologically, the study applies a mixed-method, qualitative exploration through open-ended questions and a quantitative survey based research design administered to higher education educators and students. The findings indicate that currently the most commonly used GenAI tools are large language models and plagiarism detection tools by both groups of respondents. The main reason for using these tools appears to be for research purposes such as essays or scientific papers. The respondents provided almost identical answers regarding the perceived risks of using AI tools and gave valuable information about their needs and the integration of GenAI into higher education institutions. Concerns persist regarding plagiarism, over-dependence on AI-generated content and the absence of clear regulatory frameworks in Albanian universities. The results contribute to Albanian educational research by identifying priority areas for institutional policy development, capacity building, and the design of ethical and inclusive GenAI-supported assessment frameworks. They offer transferable insights for higher education institutions and policymakers seeking to integrate GenAI responsibly and effectively into assessment and feedback practices across Albanian context and beyond.

papers.title: From Technology to Teaching Practice: A Didactic Roadmap for Emerging Tech in Education
papers.authors: Gunver Majgaard, Regina Lamscheck-Nielsen, Maria Skougaard Andersen , Rasmus Ploug
papers.abstract: This article presents the tech-didactic model DigiDidactics as a didactic roadmap for educators seeking to integrate emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and robotics into teaching practice. While these technologies offer new pedagogical possibilities, their rapid development creates uncertainty in how to design, implement, and evaluate meaningful learning activities. DigiDidactics addresses this challenge by providing a stable, non‑prescriptive framework that supports educators in aligning technological use with pedagogical purpose. The model builds on earlier work with ROBOdidactics and has been further developed through collaboration between researchers and educators. It comprises five interconnected dimensions: (1) Teaching Design, focusing on learning objectives, activities, and evaluation; (2) Digital Production, emphasizing students’ active creation and reflection; (3) Digital Literacy, including critical thinking, ethics, and responsible engagement with technology; (4) Environment, highlighting collaboration with external stakeholders and career learning; and (5) Sustainability, integrating long‑term societal, environmental, and educational perspectives. The article demonstrates how DigiDidactics functions both as a design and evaluation framework. It provides concrete examples of its application in practice. The model is currently being used in the Interreg project MYREcross (myre.tech), in which 110 teaching modules for learners in secondary education, as well as in higher education are being designed and implemented with the model as the guiding didactic framework. These cases illustrate how the model supports educators in navigating the complexities of emerging technologies while maintaining pedagogically sound and reflective teaching practices. By combining DigiDidactics with action research, educators are positioned as co‑designers and co‑researchers who iteratively experiment with and refine their teaching practices. The model thus supports pedagogically grounded innovation and helps shift focus from technological novelty to meaningful learning. The article concludes that a structured, reflective didactic framework is essential for ensuring that emerging technologies contribute to educational quality, student engagement, and sustainable development.

papers.title: Ruwad Al-Mustaqbal System: A Knowledge-Behavior Gap-Aware Framework (KBG-Ruwad) for Personalized Responsible AI Education among Omani Undergraduates
papers.authors: ArunaDevi Karuppasamy, Samah Alzidi, Aseel Al Shizawi
papers.abstract: The use of generative AI among undergraduate students has surpassed structured instruction in responsible use of generative AI, and this gap is documented, with students' awareness of and knowledge of AI ethics not matching with their ability to apply it in academic contexts. This has been identified as a critical issue in Oman, with Vision 2040 stating AI adoption as a visionary goal, and most Omani HEIs lack formal AI governance, along with faculty AI literacy falling short of visionary goals. AI ethics are structured into progressive levels in competency frameworks like UNESCO's, and adaptive systems already personalize content. This paper proposes a conceptual framework, KBG-Ruwad, that introduces a novel measure of the knowledge-behavior gap (KBG). The framework assesses, for each student and across each dimension, the discrepancy between self-reported ethical knowledge and behavior demonstrated in scenario-based tasks. In addition, it measures students' level of ethical knowledge, their confidence in that knowledge, and the misconceptions they hold. The framework further extends the existing seven-dimensional model. Building on these measures, KBG-Ruwad extends the seven-dimension Responsible AI Competency Vector with discipline-specific, misconception-aware adaptive scenarios, and with a guidance function sensitive to gap, confidence, discipline and learning history; it further introduces a student-owned Learning Passport and a privacy-protected institutional dashboard. The paper reviews the AI-competency, AI-ethics pedagogy and Omani AI-readiness literature; argues for integration over invention; critically analyzes the components and flow of the proposed framework; and identifies gaps in the current specification and challenges for its operationalization

papers.title: Beyond AI Use: Understanding University Students’ Acceptance of AI-Assisted Academic Misuse
papers.authors: Basil Alzougool, Sumayya A. Banna
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new learning opportunities while raising concerns about academic integrity and students’ acceptance of AI-assisted academic misuse. This study examined factors associated with such acceptance among 304 university students in Kuwait using a cross-sectional online survey and non-probability convenience and snowball sampling. The three focal constructs—general academic-integrity awareness, policy and AI-plagiarism awareness, and acceptance of AI-assisted academic misuse—were measured using 15 dichotomous Yes/No items coded 0 = No and 1 = Yes. Acceptance of AI-assisted academic misuse was operationalised as the mean of three misuse-acceptance items (Y12-Y14), producing a composite ranging from 0 to 1 that was analysed as a continuous outcome. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, principal-axis exploratory factor analysis with varimax rotation, KR-20 reliability analysis, correlations, and ordinary least squares regression with HC3 robust standard errors. The regression model was significant (F = 2.579, p = .010, R² = .067). Policy and AI-plagiarism awareness was positively associated with misuse acceptance (B = .193, p = .013), contrary to the hypothesised negative direction, and Kuwaiti nationality was also associated with higher acceptance (B = .103, p = .039). General academic-integrity awareness and prior AI use were not significant. Because the study is cross-sectional and the misuse-acceptance scale had modest reliability (KR-20 = .587), the findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The results support clearer, context-specific AI policies and guidance that distinguishes legitimate AI-supported learning from academically inappropriate use

papers.title: The Prisoner's Dilemma of AI: Cognitive Offloading Among Future Mathematics Teachers
papers.authors: Otto Suchánek, Tomáš Javorčík, Tatiana Havlásková, Magdaléna Závodná
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into education has introduced substantial opportunities as well as challenges related to students’ cognitive processes and professional development. For pre-service teachers, generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) creates a professional paradox. While AI systems can increase efficiency, support learning processes, and provide rapid access to information, excessive reliance on such systems may lead to cognitive offloading, automation bias, and gradual weakening of critical thinking and professional autonomy. Within educational contexts, this tension may be interpreted as a conflict between short-term individual gains and long-term consequences for human expertise and independent reasoning. This study compares pretest and posttest perceptions of generative AI among first-year pre-service mathematics teachers following a targeted educational intervention focused on principles of AI functioning and related cognitive risks. The Prisoner's Dilemma is used as a conceptual and pedagogical lens for framing the tension between the immediate benefits of AI use and its possible long-term educational consequences; it is not empirically operationalised or tested as a game-theoretic model. Within this framework, delegating cognitive activities to AI may represent a rational strategy at the individual level while simultaneously producing undesirable outcomes for broader educational development. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design without a control group was employed. Participants consisted of undergraduate students enrolled in a Mathematics Teacher Education programme at the University of Ostrava (pretest n = 18; posttest n = 14). Data collection was conducted using a semantic differential instrument consisting of sixteen bipolar dimensions measuring students’ perceptions of AI characteristics. The intervention included instructional activities explaining principles of large language models, cognitive offloading, automation bias, and ethical implications of excessive dependence on AI systems. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and non-parametric methods, specifically the Mann–Whitney U test. The results did not reveal statistically significant differences between pretest and posttest measurements across any of the analysed dimensions. Several mean scores differed descriptively between the measurements, particularly for transparency, predictability, and the role of AI in deeper learning, but these differences were not statistically significant. Given the small, unmatched samples and the absence of a control group, they cannot be interpreted as evidence of an intervention effect. These results highlight the importance of integrating critical AI literacy into teacher education programmes.

papers.title: From “AI is Supi” to “Democracy is in Danger”: Users’ Perceptions About AI
papers.authors: Dagmar Monett
papers.abstract: Educational institutions worldwide have introduced courses, training, guidelines, and similar documentation which range from allowing unlimited use of artificial intelligence (AI)-based products to their complete ban in specific settings. Tangentially, and with the spread of chatbots and similar software programs for fast producing textual and other types of information, there are also increasing concerns regarding how and what students actually learn or should, as well as whether outsourcing reading comprehension, academic writing, critical thinking, and other cognitive skills, once paramount in educational contexts, are enhanced or atrophied with the help of AI, and how academic integrity might be devalued as a result of the latter. Tangentially, because the harms are often acknowledged but the use of AI is simultaneously promoted, which is known as responsible realism and is a form of ethics washing. This paper presents part of an empirical, exploratory study whose goals include the analysis of users’ perceptions about the use of AI and their awareness of possible harms. To gather opinions on these and related topics, a survey was conducted to which a total of 535 university members participated. All responses were scrutinized using qualitative content analysis. This allowed for the extraction of categories that depict the whole spectrum of their stances regarding AI. The results contribute to understanding users’ awareness, opinions, concerns, and needs regarding the use of this technology. They also help in uncovering common tropes that might be preventing university members from assessing generative AI harms critically.

papers.title: From Cognitive Overload to Individualized Learning: AI Tutoring in Electrical Engineering
papers.authors: Jens Müller, Annalena Meier, Matthias Heinz, Kilian Göller, Alexander Alfred Zyla
papers.abstract: First-year students in electrical engineering often encounter significant challenges in their undergraduate programs, particularly due to heterogeneous prior knowledge in mathematics and physics, as well as difficulties in managing their own learning processes. These issues frequently result in cognitive overload, poor exam performance, and high dropout rates. Traditional teaching methods, especially in large cohorts, struggle to address these challenges effectively, as excessive tutorial time is spent on basic calculation steps rather than fostering deeper, subject-specific understanding. To address this, a domain-specific AI tutor was piloted during the winter semester of 2025/2026 in the first-semester course "Fundamentals of Electrical Engineering". The AI, based on the Google Gemini 2.5 Pro language model, was enhanced with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to integrate tailored teaching materials, such as annotated lecture transcripts and detailed solution manuals. Configured as a Socratic tutor, the AI provided individualized, asynchronous support by guiding students through tutorial preparation, verifying their calculation steps, and assisting with step-by-step troubleshooting. This tool was tested with a seminar group of 18 students who got access to the AI tutor via the platform you.com. The pilot project included continuous data collection throughout the semester. Weekly online reflection forms captured students' usage patterns, perceived task difficulty, and feedback on the AI's usefulness or limitations. These data were complemented by two comprehensive surveys conducted at midterm and end of semester. The study presents the technological configuration and didactic applications of the AI tutor, analyzing its impact across different student performance levels. The results indicate high acceptance of the AI tutor, particularly for verifying calculations and resolving short-term learning obstacles. However, the analysis also revealed limitations, especially in handling subject-specific visual and topological contexts. The findings underscore the importance of fostering critical AI literacy among students and highlight the need for future multimodal AI models to better support engineering education. In addition, the use of AI in undergraduate studies serves to build competencies within the context of a potential core curriculum.

papers.title: Integrating AI-Generated 3D/360° Content into VR-Based Secondary Education
papers.authors: Vasile-Ioan-Grigore Avram, Ovidiu Cosma, Nadia Barkoczi
papers.abstract: This paper presents a pedagogical framework for integrating AI-generated educational content into Virtual Reality (VR)-based teaching within SmartLab-supported secondary education. The framework addresses the limited classroom adoption of AI and immersive technologies by combining AI-assisted content generation, VR integration, interdisciplinary SmartLab activities, and evaluation of learning outcomes into a structured teacher-centred workflow. The framework was implemented during the second semester of the 2025–2026 academic year in a Romanian technological high school, involving 702 secondary school students and 35 master's students who collaboratively designed and delivered 11 interdisciplinary SmartLab lessons. The evaluation combined classroom observations, Kahoot assessments, discussions, and an anonymous questionnaire completed by 550 students. The results indicate increased student engagement, motivation, interdisciplinary understanding, and positive perceptions of AI-assisted immersive learning. The study demonstrates that integrating AI-generated educational resources with VR technologies enhances classroom interaction while supporting the preparation of future teachers through interdisciplinary practice. The proposed framework provides a scalable model for the digital transformation of secondary education and can be adapted to different educational contexts.

papers.title: From Potential to Practice: Challenges of Integrating Artificial Intelligence Technologies in School Classrooms
papers.authors: Norah Almusharraf, Muhammad Imran
papers.abstract: This study investigates the integration of Artificial Intelligence Technologies (AIT) into classroom teaching, focusing on three factors: teachers' access to AIT tools, the frequency of their use, and the key challenges and barriers to integrating AIT for e-learning. A quantitative, survey-based approach was employed to address the study's research questions. A 25-item questionnaire was administered to 90 elementary and secondary school teachers, and the data were analyzed descriptively and correlationally using SPSS (version 23). The findings reveal that teachers have limited access to various AIT applications, receive inadequate training, and face infrastructural challenges. More than half of the teachers (54%) reported using the Internet to prepare lessons and carry out other teaching activities. Despite recognizing AIT's potential to enhance teaching effectiveness, educators reported attitudinal and systemic barriers to its integration. This study offers original evidence on AIT integration in elementary and secondary classrooms, a context that remains underrepresented in the literature, by examining teachers' actual access, usage patterns, and the systemic barriers they face, and by situating these findings within established technology-adoption frameworks to offer policy-relevant insights.

papers.title: The Use of Generative AI in Higher Education Student Assessments: A Synthesis of Empirical Studies
papers.authors: Chun Meng Tang
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become increasingly common among higher education students as an aid for completing assessments. Although previous studies have examined the implications of GenAI use in assessments, there is a need to synthesise existing findings to better understand how students use GenAI and how it affects their experiences. This study aimed to synthesise empirical research on higher education students’ use of GenAI in assessments. Guided by the Population, Exposure, and Outcome (PEO) framework, the study adopted a hybrid deductive and inductive codebook thematic analysis of 14 empirical studies identified through a search of the Education Resources Information Center (ERIC) database. The analysis identified four main themes: uses of GenAI in assessments, perceived benefits of GenAI, challenges and limitations of GenAI, and academic integrity and ethical implications of GenAI. The findings suggest that students use GenAI for writing and content development, research and information support, idea generation and planning, and feedback and assessment support. Participants also perceived several benefits associated with GenAI use, including improved assessment performance, increased efficiency, and enhanced learning support. However, the use of GenAI also presents challenges and limitations, including ineffective use, concerns about accuracy and reliability, and effects of over-reliance on learning skills. In addition, participants expressed concerns about plagiarism and academic misconduct, fairness and academic equity, and the need for transparency and ethical GenAI use. The findings suggest that effective and responsible GenAI use requires institutional guidelines and adequate proficiency in GenAI competencies. This study contributes to the growing literature on GenAI in higher education assessments and provides insights for students, educators, and policymakers on the integration of GenAI into assessment designs.

papers.title: Designing Meaningful AI Learning Activities in Pre-Service Teacher Education
papers.authors: Antonín Jančařík, Kateřina Jančaříková, Martina Šmejkalová
papers.abstract: This article examines how artificial intelligence can be meaningfully integrated into pre-service teacher education through a case study approach. Rather than treating AI as a general technological innovation or a universal tool for increasing efficiency, the article focuses on three concrete teaching interventions in the subject didactics of Czech language, mathematics, and biology. Each case was designed and implemented in university courses for future teachers and illustrates a different way in which AI can support students in professionally demanding areas where they often experience uncertainty, anxiety, or lower self-efficacy. The study is grounded in the assumption that the educational value of AI does not lie in the mere use of a digital tool, but in its integration into subject-specific and pedagogically meaningful activities. In Czech language education, AI supports work with authentic language data, particularly when formulating corpus queries, interpreting corpus results, and didactically transforming language material for school use. In mathematics, AI functions as a consulting partner in the design of empirical investigations and the statistical processing of data in students’ final theses, helping students understand the relationship between research questions, data, methods of analysis, and interpretation. In biology, AI-based applications facilitate the identification of plants and animals using visual and audio inputs, thereby allowing students to focus not only on correct species naming but also on observation, comparison, verification, and argumentation. Across the three cases, the analysis shows that AI can serve as didactic scaffolding. It lowers the entry barrier to complex activities that student teachers might otherwise avoid, while still requiring them to check, refine, interpret, and critically evaluate AI outputs. The aim is therefore not to replace expert judgement, but to make it more visible and to support its development. The cases also show that AI-supported activities become educationally meaningful only when they are clearly connected to future classroom practice and when students are guided to reflect on the limits and responsible use of AI. The article formulates common principles for designing AI-supported activities in teacher education: subject-didactic anchoring, orientation toward professionally demanding areas, critical work with AI outputs, explicit links to future work with pupils, development of AI literacy, and support for students’ professional confidence. In this sense, AI can contribute not only to technological competence but also to subject reasoning, pedagogical judgement, and the didactic transformation of knowledge.

papers.title: Embedding Responsible AI in a Technical Machine Learning Course
papers.authors: Stefania Zourlidou, Frank Hopfgartner
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) courses in higher education usually emphasise mathematical foundations and algorithmic methods, while ethical and societal questions are often treated as separate or optional topics. This paper reports a small-scale practice-based evaluation of a blended design that embedded responsible AI within a Master’s-level ML and Data Mining course at a German university in winter semester 2025/26. The design combined fifteen on-campus lectures on core ML topics, including one lecture on fairness as a technical topic, fifteen optional weekly assignments discussed in tutorials, and an eight-module microlearning course on AI literacy and responsible AI. Completion of at least half of the microlearning and a mandatory practical assignment were required for exam eligibility. The study analyses an anonymous end-of-course survey, using only responses from students who explicitly consented to research use (n=35). Student perceptions were generally positive: 78% reported a good balance between theory and practice, 75% found the weekly assignments important for understanding, and 59% judged the microlearning to fit well with the on-campus lectures. For responsible AI, around two thirds reported greater confidence in identifying fairness issues, feeling better prepared to discuss ethics professionally, or perceiving ethics as integrated rather than added on. 75% intended to consider fairness and ethical implications in future ML projects, with no respondent disagreeing. Open responses suggested perceived transfer, with students naming hiring systems, facial recognition, student-risk prediction and credit or loan decision-making, and often using technical vocabulary such as training data, optimisation objectives and evaluation metrics. The paper does not claim causal impact, and findings should be interpreted in light of the small voluntary sample, the single-cohort single-institution setting, and the possibility of social-desirability bias on an end-of-course survey on ethics. Instead, it offers descriptive evidence that a lightweight microlearning layer, combined with a technical fairness lecture, can be a feasible way to connect technical ML learning with ethical reflection in practice. It also identifies revisions for the next iteration: reduce workload tension, add explicit ethical-reflection prompts to assignments, and include more practical coding work.

papers.title: Pre-Service Teachers’ Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence within the UTAUT Model
papers.authors: Dilara Arzugül Aksoy, Elif Polat
papers.abstract: This study aims to examine pre-service teachers’ perceptions of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in their learning processes and their intentions to utilize these technologies as future teachers within the framework of the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model. Adopting a qualitative approach, the participants of this research consist of education faculty students studying at a public university in Türkiye. In this context, data were collected from 109 pre-service teachers via written opinion forms and from 6 pre-service teachers through semi-structured interviews. Descriptive findings indicate that all participants reported using AI tools, and half of them reported using these tools a few times a week. Content analysis was employed to derive codes from the data. Codes derived from both written responses and interview data were organized under the themes of performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, behavioral intention, and risks and concerns. The findings reveal that students primarily associate the performance expectancy of AI tools with "fast and easy access to information" and "simplified understanding." In terms of effort expectancy, most students found AI tools easy to use, while some students also reported expending effort to verify the accuracy of AI responses. Regarding social influence, participants reported that their AI awareness and usage are shaped significantly by their social environment, particularly by peers and social media. Concerning facilitating conditions, despite the widespread adoption of AI across all fields today, participants emphasized the need for training and curriculum integration to support informed AI use. Although pre-service teachers most frequently intend to use AI for content generation and activity/task design in their future teaching, they expressed significant concerns. These include the potential for AI to promote cognitive laziness, disseminate inaccurate or biased information, negatively affect creativity, and pose risks to data privacy and security. The study concludes that while future educators utilize AI and are willing to integrate it into their practice, they remain cautious, particularly regarding the risk of cognitive laziness. Consequently, it is recommended that AI literacy be integrated into education programs to better prepare future educators for AI-enhanced classrooms.

papers.title: Beyond the Standalone AI: Embedding Educational Chatbots through Scaffolded Pedagogical Design
papers.authors: Colin Loughlin
papers.abstract: Generative AI chatbots are rapidly being introduced into higher education as institutional learning technologies. However, much current implementation assumes that educational value emerges primarily through access to the technology itself. This paper argues that AI chatbots are pedagogically weak when deployed as standalone resources and that meaningful educational impact depends upon deliberate integration into learning design, teaching practice, and assessment structures. The paper presents a case study from a UK university initiative involving BrunOwl, an institutionally supported AI chatbot embedded within the virtual learning environment. Rather than positioning the chatbot as a generic student support tool, the initiative adopts a scaffolded pedagogical integration model led by a central Digital Education team. Academic staff complete an online curriculum-design form capturing disciplinary context, learning challenges, threshold concepts, assessment relationships, cohort characteristics, and intended uses of AI within teaching. These submissions are then used collaboratively to develop structured implementation plans tailored to specific modules and programmes. The paper examines how this process reframes AI adoption from technological deployment to educational design. Drawing on concepts from constructive alignment and socio-technical approaches to educational change, the study explores how academic partnership, contextualisation, and structured scaffolding mediate the effectiveness of AI-supported learning. Early findings from institutional implementation suggest that staff are more likely to integrate AI meaningfully when supported through iterative pedagogical dialogue rather than technical training alone. Similarly, students appear more likely to engage critically and productively with AI when chatbot activities are explicitly aligned with learning outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment expectations. The paper contributes a transferable institutional model for embedding generative AI within higher education curricula while also offering a critical perspective on the prevailing “provision-led” discourse surrounding AI in education. It will be of relevance to researchers, educational developers, learning technologists, and institutional leaders seeking sustainable and pedagogically grounded approaches to AI-enabled learning.

papers.title: Alternative Higher Education Assessment Framework in Generative AI Era: Project Proposal and Pitch Approach
papers.authors: Naghmeh Aghaee, Daniel Lindvall, Christina Keller
papers.abstract: Technological advancements are reshaping higher education (HE) by challenging the traditional non-proctored assignments. These formats have historically supported learning are increasingly vulnerable to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) assisted content generation, raising concerns about authorship, academic integrity, and assessment of higher-order thinking. This study investigates the Project Proposal and Pitch (PPP) approach as an alternative assessment framework, combining a written project proposal with a structured oral pitch. A mixed-method pilot case study was conducted at a university in Sweden. Data sources include design narrative reflection on the assessment design process, and survey responses from undergraduate students with open-ended qualitative reflections. The analysis focuses on how students perceived the PPP format to shape learning practices and support assessment authenticity and students’ learning motivation. Findings indicate generally strong student support and satisfactions for the PPP approach. Students report that it enhances idea development, problem-solving, and engagement with course content, while also improving communication and learning organization. The combined proposal and pitch format was perceived as more engaging than traditional project-based assignments and effective for demonstrating learning in a concise and reflective way. The results suggest that PPP shifts GAI use toward supportive, process-oriented engagement rather than output production. The findings contribute to discussions on assessment innovation by demonstrating how the PPP approach can strengthen reasoning, articulation, and situated meaning-making in GAI-augmented learning environments.

papers.title: How Gaming Activities Shape Lower Secondary School Pupils' Understanding of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Magdaléna Závodná, Hana Ulrichova, Kateřina Kostolányová
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into everyday life, there is a growing need to develop not only technical skills among lower secondary school pupils, but above all an understanding of how AI works and the ability to use it critically and effectively. The aim of this study was to determine whether incorporating selected game-based activities, specifically escape rooms and activities focused on “learning” a simple artificial intelligence model related to ocean cleanup and the creation of fake news in the Canva app using AI tools, leads to a better understanding of how AI works and improves pupils’ ability to use these technologies effectively. The research was conducted as a pedagogical experiment at a lower secondary school in the Czech Republic. A total of 56 pupils aged 14 to 15 were involved in the study, divided into one control group and two experimental groups. The experiment took place over three class periods as part of the computer science curriculum, with data collected through pre-tests and post-tests, analysis of pupils’ outputs, and a self-evaluation questionnaire in which pupils assessed individual activities and the extent of their impact on their understanding of the subject matter and motivation to learn. The results show that the pupils in the experimental group achieved significant improvement compared to the control group. These pupils demonstrated a greater understanding of the basic principles of how artificial intelligence works, as well as an improved ability to effectively use AI tools when solving problems. At the same time, a higher level of motivation to learn was observed. The strongest motivation was identified in the activity focused on creating fake news. The findings suggest that the implementation of game elements into computer science instruction represents an effective approach to developing AI literacy in lower secondary school. The study thus contributes to expanding knowledge about the possibilities of didactically utilizing game-oriented activities in the field of artificial intelligence education and offers insights for further research and pedagogical practice.

papers.title: Pedagogical Innovation through Generative AI: Benefits, Challenges, and Responsible Use in Higher Education
papers.authors: Muhammad Imran, Norah Almusharraf
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) into higher education has transformed how students engage in learning and educational activities, including personalized learning, creativity, and knowledge production. This study aims to explore the adoption patterns, perceived benefits, and challenges of using GAI tools such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Google Gemini in higher education. A quantitative survey was conducted with 102 students from higher education institutions across various disciplines and degree levels. Findings revealed that 77.5% of participants reported using GAI daily, master’s students reported the highest benefit perception scores, while ethical and accuracy concerns were identified as the most pressing challenges; PhD students adopted a more critical stance. Findings further suggest that GAI has a positive influence on academic engagement and creativity; however, concerns about the ethical implications, responsible use, and originality remain critical challenges. This study, by highlighting both opportunities and challenges, provides actionable insights for teachers, learners, policymakers, and technology developers. It emphasizes the need for artificial intelligence AI literacy and responsible integration to ensure that GAI fosters sustainable and meaningful pedagogical innovation in higher education.

papers.title: Toward Intersectionally Fair Educational AI for Learning Analytics and Student Guidance
papers.authors: Stefania Zourlidou, Quy Tai Le, Resmin Hossain, Frank Hopfgartner
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in learning analytics dashboards, adaptive learning environments and student-guidance tools. These systems do more than personalise learning: they rank, filter and prioritise educational opportunities in ways that shape learner visibility, access and future pathways. Fairness evaluations, however, often remain organised around single protected attributes such as gender, ethnicity, socio-economic status or disability. This paper argues that such evaluations are insufficient for educational contexts because they can obscure harms experienced by learners located at the intersection of multiple demographic positions. It therefore advances intersectional fairness auditing as a human-centred requirement for responsible educational AI. The argument is informed by a motivating adjacent-domain case: a study of a transformer-based job-recommendation system found that a system appearing fair attribute by attribute can still conceal substantial unfairness for intersectional subgroups, and that common mitigation methods do not necessarily improve all subgroups evenly. Drawing on recent scholarship on human-centred AI in education, learning analytics auditing, educational recommendation and intersectional fairness, the paper proposes an audit framework for educational AI. The framework extends existing learning analytics audit work by making subgroup visibility, ranking effects, demographic data governance, contestability and post-deployment monitoring explicit. The paper concludes that educational AI should be judged not only by predictive accuracy or personalisation, but also by whether it supports equitable learner futures across intersecting differences and enables learners and educators to question, interpret and contest AI-mediated guidance.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use Among Students: A Cross-National Comparison Between Türkiye and England
papers.authors: Merve Kara Kara, Zeynep Cömert, Kubra Kaymakci Ustuner
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly present in children’s everyday digital lives, yet research on primary school students remains limited. This study examines how students in Türkiye and England conceptualise and use GenAI, and whether family AI use is associated with students’ own use. A quantitative cross-national survey was conducted with 359 students in Türkiye and 98 students in England. The questionnaire included open-ended and closed-ended items on AI conceptualisations, frequency of use, purposes of use, and family AI use. Open-ended responses were coded thematically, and chi-square tests were used to examine group differences and associations. Findings showed that students in Türkiye more often described AI in technological and functional terms, whereas unclear understanding was more common among students in England. GenAI use frequency did not differ significantly between countries, with most students reporting occasional use. However, purposes of use varied: students in Türkiye reported more diverse and creative uses, while students in England more often used GenAI for information seeking or reported unclear/non-use. In the England sample, family AI use was strongly associated with students’ own use frequency. The study highlights the need for developmentally appropriate AI literacy initiatives involving both schools and families.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Mediating Tool in Higher Education: An Exploratory Study in Quantitative Methods
papers.authors: María Teresa García Florentino
papers.abstract: This study investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI), with a focus on generative tools such as ChatGPT, in higher education through the lens of pedagogical mediation. The analysis contends that the educational impact of AI is not direct or automatic, but rather depends on instructional design, teaching practices, assessment structures, and instructor guidance. An exploratory mixed-methods approach was employed in a Quantitative Methods I course involving undergraduate students from Real Estate and Construction programmes. A questionnaire was administered to 89 students, resulting in 24 valid responses and a response rate of 27%. Data from both closed- and open-ended questions were analysed using descriptive and interpretive methods, reflecting the voluntary and self-selected nature of the sample. The findings reveal that students primarily use AI to clarify concepts, assist with solving exercises, and organise their study routines. A significant proportion also reported encountering incorrect or misleading outputs, underscoring the necessity for validation, critical interpretation, and explicit pedagogical guidance. The results suggest that AI functions mainly as a complementary learning resource rather than a replacement for cognitive engagement, especially when integrated into self-regulated learning processes (Kasneci et al., 2023; Panadero et al., 2023). This study introduces a Pedagogical Mediation Framework to analyse how AI use is shaped by the interplay among curriculum, assessment, teaching mediation, and students’ critical engagement.

papers.title: The use of artificial intelligence in the education in lyceums with enhanced military and physical training
papers.authors: Bohdan Revenko
papers.abstract: Purpose. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has changed how teachers prepare lessons, how learners complete tasks and how institutions assess results. Ukrainian schools now operate under a new legal framework that treats the undisclosed use of AI outputs as a distinct violation of academic integrity. Lyceums with enhanced military and physical training work under conditions that existing guidance does not address: intensive academic study, heavy physical and military-applied loads, and a strict statutory regime. The purpose of this article is to systematise approaches to the use of AI in the educational process of such lyceums and to define the forms of its application. Methodology. We conducted a qualitative document analysis combined with comparative analysis. The corpus comprised six normative and methodological documents and fifteen research publications, selected by relevance, currency and full-text availability. We extracted statements that define spheres of AI application, principles of responsible use, levels of permitted use, attribution requirements, risks and mitigation measures. We coded these statements, compared them across the general secondary and higher education documents, and transferred the resulting categories to the conditions of a military lyceum. The study involved no human participants and produced no quantitative data. Results. The analysis identified five spheres of AI application, eight principles of responsible use shared across the documents, and a five-level scale of permitted use with graded attribution requirements. The documents converge on human oversight, transparency, privacy, non-discrimination and accountability. They diverge on pedagogical expediency and on societal well-being. We formulated four conditions for the use of generative AI in a military lyceum and a seven-step sequence of teacher actions. Conclusions. International and national documents rest on a shared human-centred approach in which AI supports rather than replaces the teacher. Their transfer to a military lyceum does not require a separate set of principles, but it changes the priority of organisational conditions. Verification of generated content becomes a safety requirement, not only an academic one, because errors in load dosage or tactical provisions threaten learner health. The proposed conditions require empirical testing in such institutions.

papers.title: Didactic potential and limitations of generative artificial intelligence in university German language teaching: A comparison of German as a first and second/foreign language
papers.authors: Ivan Paroviak
papers.abstract: Purpose. The study aims to determine and systematize the didactic potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in university German language teaching and to compare its functions and limitations in teaching German as a first language and as a second/foreign language. Methodology. The study employs qualitative didactic analysis and comparative analysis. The analytical material consists of self-developed, didactically modelled instructional scenarios representing typical university German language tasks. The examples cover grammar, vocabulary, writing, communication, stylistic revision, register differentiation, genre transformation, and critical analysis of AI-generated texts. No human participants or statistical procedures were involved. Results. The analysis demonstrates a functional asymmetry in the pedagogical use of GenAI. In second/foreign language teaching, GenAI primarily functions as linguistic scaffolding. It can provide contextualised grammar practice, lexical differentiation, corrective feedback, communicative simulation, and support for successive stages of writing. In first-language teaching, its dominant function shifts towards linguistic and metalinguistic reflection. GenAI can support academic writing, stylistic differentiation, register awareness, genre transformation, argumentation, and critical evaluation of alternative formulations and AI-generated texts. In both contexts, the pedagogical value of GenAI increases when learners evaluate, modify, and justify AI suggestions rather than merely reproduce generated content. Conclusions. GenAI should not be treated as a uniform instructional technology whose functions remain identical across language-learning contexts. Its didactic value depends on the linguistic status of the target language and on the degree of learner agency built into the task. For second/foreign language instruction, GenAI is particularly valuable as a scaffold for language production and practice. For first-language instruction, it is more productive as an instrument of linguistic reflection, text development, and critical language awareness. Responsible implementation therefore requires teacher mediation, explicit task design, and activities that preserve the learner's role as the primary linguistic decision-maker.

papers.title: Developing an adaptive educational environment model to meet the needs of Generation Alpha learners in general secondary education: A case study of a private lyceum
papers.authors: Maryna Salun, Larysa SAVYTSKA
papers.abstract: Aim. The aim of this article is to identify and substantiate approaches to adapting the educational process of a private lyceum to the Generation Alpha learners' needs, through the systematisation of current theoretical and methodological approaches to the digital transformation of education and the analysis and synthesis of the results of learners’ survey. Methodology. The study employed theoretical analysis of the relevant scholarly literature, questionnaire-based surveying, quantitative and qualitative interpretation of the survey findings, synthesis of pedagogical experience, and pedagogical modelling. The empirical basis of the study consisted of a survey of 64 learners in Years 9–10 at the Private Lyceum ‘Kharkiv Collegium’, Kharkiv, Ukraine. The questionnaire addressed high school students’ perceptions of the educational process, digital learning practices, academic workload, attention and concentration, communication, psychological well-being, learner autonomy, critical thinking and career orientation. The interpretation of the findings was based on theoretical and methodological approaches to digital learning, multimedia learning, self-regulated learning, formative assessment, social-emotional learning, Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and career guidance discussed in the literature review. Particular attention was paid to the school context of the private lyceum, characterised by greater potential for flexible organisation of learning, individualised support and the integration of digital and supplementary educational practices. The findings are therefore interpreted primarily as evidence of the specific educational needs and adaptation priorities of learners in the lyceum under study, rather than as representative of general secondary school education as a whole. Findings. The findings indicate that learners generally perceive the lyceum’s educational environment positively, particularly in terms of learning comfort, teachers’ explanations and communication with teachers. At the same time, several priorities for adaptation were identified. These include establishing a more coherent digital learning environment and providing structured online revision materials; optimising academic workload; developing learner’s autonomy and self-regulated learning; strengthening social-emotional support and formative feedback; increasing the practical orientation of learning; expanding career guidance; and developing critical thinking and responsible use of generative AI. The findings demonstrate that adaptation to Generation Alpha learners should not be limited to increasing the use of digital technologies, but should involve the coordinated development of digital, cognitive, self-regulatory, social-emotional, assessment, career-guidance and AI-literacy components of the educational environment. Conclusions. The study substantiates a practice-oriented model of an adaptive educational environment for a private lyceum, grounded in empirically identified learners’ needs and contemporary approaches to educational transformation. Its effectiveness should be assessed through repeated diagnosis of learners’ needs, changes in academic stress, satisfaction with the digital learning environment, learner autonomy, and clarity of educational and career trajectories. The proposed approach provides a basis for further empirical validation and adaptation across different educational contexts.

papers.title: Responsible use of generative artificial intelligence in teacher education: Implications for academic integrity in Zimbabwe
papers.authors: Florence Sebele, Phumuzani Mpofu, Georgina Chauke
papers.abstract: Purpose. This study examined the awareness, use, and ethical implications of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in Zimbabwean teacher education. Although tools such as ChatGPT are widely accessible, their pedagogical integration and ethical use remain underexplored in resource-constrained contexts. Methodology. Guided by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study employed a convergent mixed-methods design involving 30 participants (25 student teachers and five teacher educators). Data were collected through surveys, semi-structured interviews, and document analysis. Results. Findings revealed moderate awareness of generative AI tools, with 52% of participants reporting awareness and 40% indicating frequent use. However, AI use was predominantly limited to academic support tasks, such as assignment completion and content generation, with minimal integration into pedagogical activities, including lesson planning. TPACK analysis indicated moderate technological knowledge but weak translation into pedagogical practice. Document analysis also identified instances of AI-generated content in student submissions with limited or no attribution. Although participants recognised ethical concerns related to plagiarism and academic integrity, responsible AI practices were applied inconsistently. Conclusions. The study concludes that the adoption of generative AI in Zimbabwean teacher education remains largely operational rather than pedagogically transformative. It recommends strengthening AI literacy, developing institutional policies, and embedding AI competencies within teacher education curricula to promote responsible, ethical, and contextually relevant integration of generative AI.

papers.title: CHATBOT MARKETING EFFORTS, COMMUNICATION QUALITY, USAGE MOTIVATION : DAMPAK TERHADAP SATISFACTION, REUSE INTENTION, PURCHASE INTENTION, DAN E-TRUST
papers.authors: Ratna Pinasti, Adma Sari Sitepu
papers.abstract: The use of chatbots on e-commerce platforms is increasingly expanding as a means to enhance customer service quality. Consequently, it is crucial to understand the factors influencing user satisfaction and their impact on user behavior regarding chatbot usage. This study aims to analyze the influence of Chatbot Marketing Efforts on Chatbot Communication Quality; the influence of Chatbot Communication Quality and Motivation for Chatbot Usage on Satisfaction; and the influence of Satisfaction on Reuse Intention, Purchase Intention, and E-Trust. A quantitative approach was employed using purposive sampling involving 530 Shopee users who were at least 17 years old, had used the chatbot feature, and possessed shopping experience on Shopee. Data analysis was conducted using Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The results indicate that all path coefficients show a positive direction and all tested relationships between variables are significant. Chatbot Marketing Efforts positively influence Chatbot Communication Quality; Chatbot Communication Quality and Motivation for Chatbot Usage positively influence Satisfaction; and Satisfaction positively influences Reuse Intention, Purchase Intention, and E-Trust. This study contributes to the development of chatbot service strategies for e-commerce platforms. It is recommended that Shopee optimize its knowledge base, improve chatbot response quality, and periodically evaluate the user experience to enhance user satisfaction.

papers.title: Organisational Capacities Relevant to OGD-Driven Co-Creation in Smart Public Governance: Evidence from Slovenian Public Administration
papers.authors: Petra Vujković, Tina Jukić, Sanja Vrbek
papers.abstract: Although open government data (OGD) and co-creation are increasingly recognised as important components of smart public governance (SPG), less is known about the organisational capacities relevant to the development of OGD-driven co-creation. This study examines the extent to which Slovenian ministries, as central government organisations responsible for policymaking, possess selected OGD-related and co-creation-related organisational capacities that may represent potential preconditions for OGD-driven co-creation. This study draws on a focused re-analysis of semi-structured interview material collected in eight Slovenian ministries and examines seven capacities: data stewardship and institutional data governance, data-driven policymaking and decision-making, monitoring of data reuse, sensitive-data awareness and responsible openness, stakeholder participation, feedback mechanisms, and co-creation practices. Based on participants’ accounts, data stewardship arrangements and awareness of sensitive-data requirements were reported across all eight ministries, while data-driven policymaking and decision-making and monitoring of data reuse showed greater variation. Stakeholder participation was reported in all eight ministries, although its extent and form varied, while feedback mechanisms were well established across the ministries. At the same time, reported co-creation practices were predominantly at lower or intermediate levels of the co-creation ladder. Participation practices primarily reflected stakeholder input, while feedback mechanisms mainly reflected institutional responsiveness rather than co-creation in themselves. This study provides an empirical assessment of the reported presence and extent of seven selected organisational capacities relevant to OGD-driven co-creation in the participating Slovenian ministries.

papers.title: From Youth Learning Needs to AI-Supported SDG/ODA Education Design: Evidence from Ukraine and a Cross-National Benchmark
papers.authors: Khrystyna Lipianina-Honcharenko, Diana Zahorodnia, Sergiy Nadvynychnyy
papers.abstract: Education for Sustainable Development requires learning approaches that are accessible, context-sensitive, and responsive to learners’ actual needs. This study investigates the educational needs of Ukrainian youth regarding the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Official Development Assistance (ODA) and examines how these needs can inform AI-supported educational design. A cross-national mixed-methods survey was conducted within the YouthSOFTPOWER project, involving 498 respondents (374 youth and 124 youth workers/educators). Ukraine served as the primary analytical case (n = 99), while respondents from other countries (n = 399) formed a pooled international benchmark. Quantitative analyses compared awareness, previous learning experience, willingness to participate in SDG/ODA education, learning barriers, and preferred learning formats. Open-ended responses were analyzed using LLM-assisted thematic coding followed by researcher validation. Ukrainian respondents demonstrated lower SDG awareness, less previous participation in SDG/ODA-related training, and lower willingness to engage in future learning than the international benchmark, whereas ODA awareness was low across both groups. Qualitative findings highlighted the need for plain language, authentic ODA case studies, concise visual materials, project-based learning, and interactive educational formats. These findings were translated into evidence-informed AI-supported design priorities that emphasize understandable explanations, localized case-based learning, microlearning, experiential learning, and interactive engagement. The study provides a human-centred framework for AI-supported SDG/ODA education grounded in empirically identified learner needs and researcher-validated evidence.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Improvement in Total-Factor Carbon Productivity: Evidence from China’s Heavily Polluting Enterprises
papers.authors: Qiang Ma, Yanming Bai, Wanshu Yu, Tiemin Liu, Sa Li
papers.abstract: Against the backdrop of intensifying global low-carbon transition and digital technologies’ profound empowerment of the real economy, widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) provides critical technical support that can help heavily polluting enterprises with high energy consumption and emissions overcome the bottlenecks in green development and improve total-factor carbon productivity (TFCP). Using panel data on Chinese listed heavily polluting enterprises from 2013 to 2024 as the research sample, this study investigates artificial intelligence’s impact on firms’ total-factor carbon productivity. The results show that AI has a significant positive impact on TFCP, with mitigating financing constraints, promoting green innovation, and strengthening corporate governance serving as underlying mechanisms. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that such a promotive effect is more pronounced for heavily polluting enterprises in Eastern China, firms with high R&D investment, state-owned enterprises, large-scale firms, and enterprises with low levels of environmental information disclosure. Furthermore, environmental regulation, digital infrastructure, and human capital can amplify artificial intelligence’s productivity-enhancing effect on total-factor carbon productivity. On the basis of these findings, we propose policy suggestions focusing on attaching importance to artificial intelligence technologies, strengthening financial support, and advancing digital infrastructure construction so as to address the low-carbon-transition predicament pertaining to heavily polluting industries and achieve the coordinated development of economic growth and carbon emission reduction.

papers.title: Generative AI Literacy and Research Self-Efficacy in Relation to Attitudes Toward Scientific Research Among Health Sciences Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Carmen Raquel Guzman Damian, Persi Vera Zelada, Jorge Alejandro Tejada Carrera, Julio Roberto Izquierdo Espinoza, Margot Isabel Herbias Figueroa, Alexander Fernando Haro Sarango
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered undergraduate research training, yet its relationship with research self-efficacy and attitudes toward scientific research remains underexplored among Health Sciences students. This cross-sectional study examined how self-reported GenAI literacy and research self-efficacy are associated with attitudes toward scientific research, separately and when modelled together. Of 101 submissions from undergraduate Health Sciences students enrolled in research courses at a private Peruvian university, 91 were analysed after 10 invariant response patterns were excluded. Students completed a 36-item self-report questionnaire whose items had been reviewed for content relevance and clarity by three experts. Analyses combined Spearman correlations, multiple regression with HC3 standard errors, a bootstrapped indirect-effect model and exploratory fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). Reliability computed from the three dimension scores of each construct was α = 0.861 for GenAI literacy, 0.927 for research self-efficacy and 0.790 for attitudes. GenAI literacy correlated with attitudes (ρ = 0.475, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), but in the female–male regression model (n = 90), research self-efficacy was the only one of the two capability scores that retained a statistically significant adjusted association (b = 0.353, 95% CI 0.087 to 0.619, p = 0.010; GenAI literacy b = 0.088, 95% CI −0.214 to 0.389, p = 0.564; R2 = 0.405). The indirect term through research self-efficacy (0.313, 95% CI 0.092 to 0.536) is a statistical decomposition of overlapping, contemporaneous scores rather than evidence of a mechanism. Discriminant validity between GenAI literacy and research self-efficacy was not established (HTMT = 0.912), and parallel analysis favoured two factors rather than three. Under the primary calibration (theoretical anchors 2-3-4 with crossover memberships assigned to 0.501), functional knowledge and the critical–ethical evaluation of GenAI appeared in both terms of the intermediate fsQCA solution (consistency = 0.913, coverage = 0.741), but the minimised solutions changed with alternative anchors and with the handling of cases at the crossover. The findings describe associations among self-reported measures; whether developing both capabilities jointly improves research attitudes remains a question for future evaluation.

papers.title: Governing the Privacy-Personalization Tension in AI-Driven Marketing Platforms: An Integrative Framework for Customer Data Platforms
papers.authors: Zhulieta Mihaylova
papers.abstract: Customer data platforms (CDPs) are increasingly positioned as the data and decision infrastructure of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven marketing. Yet the academic literature has not adequately explained when a CDP can reconcile privacy compliance with hyper-personalization, nor how this reconciliation depends on platform governance, consumer trust, data quality, and responsible AI controls. This article develops an integrative conceptual framework through a structured interdisciplinary literature review. The review covers marketing, information systems, platform studies, consumer behavior, data governance, privacy engineering, and AI ethics. A structured integrative review with a systematic search component and concept-centric synthesis produced a final analytical corpus of 70 sources, comprising 60 peer-reviewed publications, one book, eight authoritative legal, policy, or standards documents, and one industry source used only for descriptive context. The synthesis identifies CDP governance capabilities as the central antecedent of two complementary mechanisms: privacy assurance and customer-data quality. Privacy assurance strengthens consumer trust and willingness to disclose first- and zero-party data, while governed identity resolution, provenance, interoperability, and data minimization improve the reliability of inputs available to machine learning, recommendation systems, generative AI, and autonomous agents. The resulting personalization effectiveness influences customer and marketing outcomes, but the relationships are conditional on responsible AI controls, platform ecosystem governance, regulatory intensity, data sensitivity, consumer privacy orientation, and organizational maturity. Seven direct-effect propositions and a decomposed family of path-specific moderation and boundary propositions specify theoretically expected relationships without implying causal identification by the review itself. The article contributes by conceptualizing the CDP not as a neutral database or stand-alone compliance tool, but as a governed platform control plane that coordinates data rights, AI decisioning, and multi-actor accountability. The framework offers a research agenda and practical design principles for privacy-preserving, transparent, and accountable AI-driven marketing ecosystems.

papers.title: Rethinking Giftedness in the Age of Generative AI: A Relational Epistemic Agency Model for Advanced Learners
papers.authors: Çiğdem Nilüfer Umar
