While AI is increasingly used to discuss personal and social concerns (Laird et al., 2025; Robb, 2025), little is known about how reliance on AI-based interpersonal advice may shape independent social judgement over time. This study examines whether repeated exposure of AI-generated interpretations of interpersonal conflicts shifts how individuals themselves understand and evaluate similar conflicts in terms of responsibility and reparative actions.

papers.title: DEVELOPING TEACHER COMPETENCIES IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-DRIVEN UNIVERSAL DESIGN FOR LEARNING: ADVANCING SCHOOL INCLUSION FOR DEAF AND HARD-OF-HEARING STUDENTS
papers.authors: Muhammad Adeel Alam
papers.abstract: This study examined teacher competencies in Artificial Intelligence, AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning, and school inclusion of Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing students in special education schools in Punjab, Pakistan. The study was conducted in response to the growing importance of AI-supported educational practices and the need for accessible, flexible, and inclusive learning environments for students with hearing-related educational needs. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 179 teachers working in special education schools for deaf and hard-of-hearing students in Punjab, Pakistan. A structured, self-administered, and self-developed questionnaire was used to measure teacher competencies in Artificial Intelligence, AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning, and school inclusion of Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing students. The questionnaire was converted into Google Forms and distributed online to eligible respondents, while the collected responses were initially organized in Microsoft Excel and subsequently transferred to IBM SPSS for analysis. Descriptive statistics, means, standard deviations, and reliability analysis were used to examine the study variables. Pearson Product-Moment Correlation was applied to examine the relationships of teacher competencies in Artificial Intelligence and school inclusion with AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning, while Multiple Linear Regression was used to assess their predictive effects on AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning. The results showed significant positive associations between teacher competencies in Artificial Intelligence and AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning, and between school inclusion of Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing students and AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning. Multiple Linear Regression further indicated that teacher competencies in Artificial Intelligence and school inclusion of Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing students were significant positive predictors of AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning. Overall, the study highlights the importance of strengthening teachers’ technological, pedagogical, and inclusive competencies to ensure that AI is used meaningfully within UDL-based practices. The study contributes to the emerging literature by connecting teacher competencies, AI-driven UDL, and school inclusion within the context of special education in Punjab, Pakistan, and provides a foundation for professional development and more accessible educational practices for deaf and hard-of-hearing students. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Teacher Competencies, AI-Driven Universal Design for Learning, School Inclusion, Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Students, Special Education
keywords: deaf and hard of hearing students

papers.title: How artificial intelligence awareness affects career-exploration behavior among foreign-language college teachers in China
papers.authors: Xiaoxiao Zhang, Ruirui Zhang, Shuqian Shi
papers.journal: Social Behavior and Personality An International Journal
papers.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology has created new challenges for the professional growth of foreign-language teachers. This study analyzed data from 424 questionnaires to examine how AI awareness influenced career-exploration behavior among foreign-language teachers in Chinese colleges. The findings revealed that AI awareness among foreignlanguage teachers at colleges was a positive predictor of career-exploration behavior, with psychological distress mediating this association. Further, proactive personality moderated the association between AI awareness and career-exploration behavior, with higher proactive personality reinforcing this link. These conclusions not only enrich theoretical understanding of career management but also offer valuable insights for building support systems for the career development of foreign-language teachers in higher education.

papers.title: An Explainable Rule-Based Resume-Job Description Skill Matching System with LLM-Assisted Feedback
papers.authors: S. Jathin Chowdary, K. Ravi Kumar, S. Mallikarjun, N. Srishma, R. Vivek
papers.journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: Automated resume screening and Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) increasingly incorporate machine learning components and neural language models. While deep learning methods can capture complex linguistic patterns, their computational overhead, potential opacity, and sensitivity to unvetted training distributions pose practical and ethical challenges for lightweight, transparent academic deployments. In this paper, we describe an open, lightweight, and explainable resume–job description matching system that couples deterministic rule-based information extraction with optional Large Language Model (LLM) qualitative feedback. The core pipeline processes PDF, DOCX, and plain-text resumes, detects functional sections, extracts technical competencies using an auditable 108-skill taxonomy, and evaluates resume–job description compatibility using explicit set operations and a bounded 100-point heuristic score covering Skills, Experience, Projects, Education, and Certifications. To benchmark the pipeline without making real-world recruitment claims, we developed a deterministic synthetic evaluation harness containing 100 resumes, 20 job descriptions, 320 evaluation pairs, and 20 candidate ranking cohorts. Under the synthetic benchmark, the system achieved F1-scores of 0.791 for skill extraction, 0.827 for education, 0.772 for experience, 0.759 for projects, and 0.865 for missing-skill identification. Robustness testing exposed 0.0% recall when experience titles and dates were separated across lines and complete section collapse under unsupported headings. Synonym normalization increased skill recall from 0.896 to 0.968 under controlled conditions. The results characterize the behavior and limitations of the proposed deterministic baseline and provide a reproducible basis for future evaluation with real, anonymized and human-annotated resume data. The benchmark also reports multi-format consistency and controlled baseline comparisons to expose formatting sensitivity and vocabulary-related error patterns.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Exergame Interventions on Physical Activity, Fitness, and Body Composition in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis (Preprint)
papers.authors: Óscar Romero-Chouza, Eloy José Villaverde-Caramés, Ariadna Hernaiz-Sánchez, Olalla Prado‐Nóvoa
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Background: Physical inactivity in youth remains a major public health concern. Exergames, defined as video games that require physical movement for gameplay, have been proposed as an innovative strategy to promote physical activity and related health outcomes in children and adolescents. OBJECTIVE Objective: This systematic review aimed to synthesize the evidence on the effectiveness of exergaming interventions for promoting physical activity, health-related fitness, and body composition, and on related cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, in youth aged 10–18 years, and to explore pooled effects where sufficiently comparable data were available. METHODS Methods: A systematic search was conducted in six databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, SPORTDiscus, and PsycINFO) for studies published between January 2010 and July 2026 (last search: 7 July 2026). Eligible studies included youth aged 10-18 years, implemented an exergaming intervention, reported outcomes related to physical activity, fitness, body composition, physiological, cognitive, psychosocial, or engagement domains, and used randomized, controlled, crossover, quasi-experimental, or structured comparative designs. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and ROBINS-I. Because of substantial heterogeneity across study designs, interventions, comparators, and outcome measures, findings were synthesized narratively and, where at least three studies reported comparable data, combined using exploratory random-effects meta-analyses of standardized mean differences. The review was registered in PROSPERO: CRD420261443125. RESULTS Results: Thirty-two studies met the inclusion criteria. Overall, exergaming showed the most consistent benefits for short-term physical activity outcomes, including increases in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, step counts, and active minutes, particularly in structured or supervised interventions. Evidence for fitness and body composition outcomes was less consistent, although some studies reported improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness, BMI-related indicators, resting heart rate, and waist-to-hip ratio, especially in youth with overweight or obesity. A smaller subset of studies suggested favorable effects on cognitive and psychosocial outcomes, including cognitive flexibility, attention, concentration, sociability, and enjoyment. However, adherence and engagement varied considerably across studies, long-term follow-up was uncommon, and the overall certainty of evidence was limited by methodological and clinical heterogeneity. In the primary analyses restricted to randomized trials, random-effects meta-analysis yielded a small but statistically significant favourable pooled effect on body composition (Hedges g = 0.30, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.48; I-squared = 0%) and a small, non-significant effect on cardiorespiratory fitness (Hedges g = 0.10, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.30); results were consistent when non-randomized studies were added. CONCLUSIONS Conclusions: Exergaming appears to be a promising complementary strategy for increasing movement in youth and may also support selected short-term fitness, cognitive, and psychosocial outcomes. However, the evidence is stronger for immediate and short-term effects than for sustained behavioral change or broader health improvement. Exergaming should therefore be considered a supplementary tool within broader physical activity promotion strategies rather than a stand-alone solution.

papers.title: A Single-Group, Longitudinal Effectiveness Study of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Supported Tool for Teaching Spanish-speaking Mental Health Providers the Skill of Reflective Listening (Preprint)
papers.authors: John D. Piette, Longju Bai, Rada F. Mihalcea, Darlin Mancia, Rafael Enrique Mejía Perdomo, Ernesto Gálvez-Pineda, Verónica Pérez‐Rosas
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Mental health services in Latin America face shortages of trained professionals, and access to expertise in evidence-based communication skills remains severely limited. In particular, motivational interviewing (MI) "reflections" are a foundational communication skill for empathic listening, but opportunities for individualized practice with feedback are limited. Digital resources supported by artificial intelligence (AI) may expand opportunities for skill development. OBJECTIVE To evaluate an AI-supported online training tool designed to improve the quality of MI reflections among psychologists, psychology students, and community-based providers in Honduras, and to characterize participants’ experiences with the training. METHODS We conducted a longitudinal single-group study among 56 Spanish-speaking adults in Honduras, including 22 psychologists, 11 psychology students, and 23 community leaders working in mental health service roles. Participants completed four rounds of online exercises in which they generated reflective responses to 10 client statements and received AI-generated scores ranging from 0 to 1, along with examples of high-quality responses. The scoring model used the Prompt-Aware Margin Ranking (PAIR) framework, a RoBERTa-based cross-encoder trained using ordinal categories identifying "skilled" responses, "acceptable" responses, and "MI-inconsistent" responses. Participants also received a live booster session with a psychologist between the second and third rounds. Changes in reflection scores were examined longitudinally, and differences in performance among the three participant groups were assessed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 purposively selected participants to identify perceived benefits, limitations, and recommendations for improving the intervention. RESULTS All participants completed all four rounds, contributing 4480 reflection responses. Mean scores increased across rounds (P<.001). Improvements in scores were observed among psychologists (P=.009), psychology students (P<.001), and community leaders (P<.001). The proportion of responses classified as MI-skilled increased from 26.3% in the first round to 48.2% in the fourth (P<.001), while MI-inconsistent responses decreased from 42.4% to 22.7% (P<.001). Improvements were greatest among community leaders, whose skilled reflections increased from 5.4% to 37.7%. The live booster was associated with significant score improvements over-and-above the linear trend (P<.001), with notable benefit among community leaders (P=.002). Interview participants generally described the tool as engaging, useful, and helpful for translating knowledge about reflective listening into practice. Participants valued both the automated feedback and live booster session, while recommending greater cultural and contextual adaptation of scenarios to Honduran experiences. CONCLUSIONS An AI-supported training platform combined with brief human reinforcement was associated with substantial short-term improvements in the quality of MI reflections among psychologists, psychology students, and community-based providers in Honduras. The largest gains occurred among participants without formal training in clinical psychology, suggesting that the tool could improve the quality of interactions in environments relying on paraprofessionals. Future controlled studies should determine whether improvements are sustained and translate into changes in communication with clients and subsequent clinical outcomes. CLINICALTRIAL Not applicable

papers.title: Empowering Medical Students to Build Artificial Intelligence Powered Simulation Applications Using No Code Platforms: A Mixed Methods Pilot Feasibility Study (Preprint)
papers.authors: Warda Siddiqi, Jalal AlFarouki, Ralf Krage, Hussam Mousa, Homero Rivas, Bart Michiels, Yacine Hadjiat
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education. However, undergraduate curricula have largely positioned medical students as users of AI enabled tools rather than as developers of them. No code platforms, which allow software to be built through visual interfaces and plain language instructions instead of programming, could change this by enabling learners without technical training to create their own functional AI powered educational tools. Whether this approach is feasible in undergraduate medical education has not yet been evaluated. OBJECTIVE his mixed methods pilot feasibility study asked a simple question: can undergraduate medical students without prior programming experience build AI powered surgical simulation applications using no code platforms during a structured workshop? We also looked at how participants and faculty experienced the resulting prototypes. METHODS Eight senior undergraduate medical students at Mohammed Bin Rashid University of Medicine and Health Sciences (MBRU) took part in a single session "appathon": a 45 minute discussion followed by 1 hour of hands on development. Three teams, each using a different no code platform, built an AI enabled surgical education application. Feasibility meant the workshop ran to completion and every team produced a working prototype. Faculty independently rated each prototype using a modified System Usability Scale, a clinical accuracy and educational value checklist, and a global assessment. Participants completed a six domain questionnaire after the workshop, and open ended responses were analyzed thematically RESULTS All eight participants (8/8, 100%) finished the workshop, and all three teams (3/3) shipped working prototypes: a visual recognition tool for laparoscopic instruments (LIRA), a chatbot guided procedural simulation (Bedside Procedure Simulation), and an interactive case based decision making tool (SurgicalDx). One faculty surgical consultant evaluated all three applications (n=3 evaluations) and endorsed their clinical accuracy, educational value, and potential for further development; usability scores ranged from 3.0 to 4.5 out of 5. Every developer questionnaire came back (8/8, 100%), and agreement was near uniform across development experience, learning outcomes, AI specific learning, mentorship, perceived value, and satisfaction. Qualitatively, students described feeling empowered by independently building an application, connecting clinical knowledge to educational design, and picking up prompt engineering as a newly acquired skill. CONCLUSIONS Undergraduate medical students with no prior programming experience were able to design and deploy working AI enabled surgical simulation prototypes on no code platforms, inside a single workshop, and both faculty and learners rated the results favorably. Whether this translates into measurable educational gains is a question for larger, controlled studies using objective outcome measures.

papers.title: How eHealth Literacy Takes Shape: A Qualitative Study Among Chinese Men Who Have Sex With Men (Preprint)
papers.authors: Jiajia Liu, Huohuo Dai, Jia Chen, Xincen Liu, WenJiao Li, Yucheng Gao, Shuhan Liu, Xiaoyu Du, Niels Henrik Chavannes, Wenjun Chen
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND EHealth literacy is essential for men who have sex with men (MSM) to effectively access, evaluate, and use digital health information for health self-management. Understanding the factors associated with eHealth literacy within China’s specific cultural and digital information environment is important for developing effective digital health interventions for MSM. Qualitative research can provide in-depth insights into individuals’ experiences, while capturing the contextual and sensitive dimensions of MSM interview data. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being applied to qualitative data analysis. However, limited research has evaluated their ability to interpret qualitative data rich in complex cultural and identity-sensitive contexts. OBJECTIVE To compare researcher-led and LLM-assisted thematic identification and interpretation when analysing culturally embedded and sensitive qualitative data, and to explore factors associated with eHealth literacy among Chinese MSM through integrated human-LLM analysis. METHODS We conducted a multistage qualitative study involving semistructured interviews with 18 Chinese MSM recruited through purposive and maximum-variation sampling. Data analysis was guided by the context-specific LLM workflow. Researchers conducted thematic analysis of the Chinese interview transcripts and established a standardized workflow for LLM-assisted analysis. ChatGPT 5.6, DeepSeek R1, and Gemini 3.5 conducted thematic analyses using the same interview data and analytical tasks. We systematically compared researcher-led and LLM-assisted outputs in terms of theme identification, interpretive depth, and contextual understanding, and revisited the original transcripts to verify the evidentiary basis and contextual appropriateness of the interpretations. A final thematic framework of factors associated with eHealth literacy among Chinese MSM was developed through researcher verification, comparison, and integration. RESULTS The researcher-led, Gemini 3.5-, DeepSeek R1-, and ChatGPT 5.6-assisted analyses respectively identified 6-14, 4-11, 4-18, and 9-42 themes-subthemes. All four analytical approaches converged on three common themes: individual cognitive foundations and experience, the digital health information environment, and social support. LLMs were able to identify culturally embedded expressions and provide contextually appropriate interpretations. However, the LLM-generated outputs differed in their coding emphases and interpretive styles, with Gemini 3.5-generated outputs more frequently exhibiting overinterpretation. A final integrated coding framework comprising six themes and 14 subthemes was developed to characterize factors associated with eHealth literacy among Chinese MSM: individual cognitive foundations and experience; digital technology and health information practices; digital health information environment; perceptions of discrimination against MSM; social support; and medical insurance policy gaps. CONCLUSIONS EHealth literacy among Chinese MSM is associated with individual, digital, sociocultural, and health service factors. LLM-assisted coding can provide additional perspectives in analysing culturally embedded and sensitive qualitative data, but researcher verification remains important to ensure that generated interpretations are consistent with the original evidence.
keywords: men who have sex with men

papers.title: Reducing Annotation Costs Using Knowledge Distillation for Label‑Efficient Negation Detection in Radiology Reports: Multisite Internal Validation Study
papers.authors: Kung-Hsun Weng, Bo-Lin Huang, Yu‐Ting Kuo, Yi-Chen Chou, Tsyh-Jyi Hsieh, Chien‐Chin Hsu
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Negation in radiology reports (eg, “no evidence of dissection”) is essential for accurately conveying diagnostic information. Clinical natural language processing systems, however, often fail to determine whether findings occur within negated or speculative contexts, leading to excessive false keyword alerts, noise in information extraction, and reduced precision in downstream clinical or research applications. Transformer models have advanced detection capabilities but require costly expert labeling. Large language models (LLMs) may provide label-efficient alternatives through few-shot prompting or knowledge distillation. OBJECTIVE This study aims to systematically evaluate LLMs and transformer models under different supervision strategies, including comparisons of expert-labeled and LLM-distilled transformers, teacher LLMs (GPT-5.3 Chat, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.6-Plus), sampling approaches, and direct few-shot LLM inference, to determine whether LLM inference or LLM-based distillation can substitute for human labeling in radiology-report negation detection while reducing annotation costs. METHODS We reused and analyzed 6000 deidentified English-language radiology reports from 3 hospital branches. Three LLMs—GPT-5.3 Chat, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.6-Plus—performed 0-, 5-, and 10-shot inference to identify negations and speculations unrelated to abnormal findings and generate pseudo-labels for transformer fine-tuning (Bio_ClinicalBERT [Bio + Clinical BERT model], BERT [Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers], and ALBERT [A Lite Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers]). We trained models using human-labeled or LLM-distilled supervision across 28 training data scales (n=42-4200) and 3 data sampling seeds and compared them across multiple supervision and training conditions encompassing backbone, label source, and sampling strategy. We assessed performance using keyword-level precision, recall, and F1-score with paired bootstrap tests (10,000 replicates). RESULTS We refined 1000 report annotations (interrater κ=0.957) and fine-tuned 1260 transformer models. Human-labeled transformers consistently outperformed distillation-labeled ones, with the largest gap at small training scales (ΔF1-score ≈0.042; adjusted P<.001), which narrowed at larger scales (ΔF1-score ≈0.022; adjusted P<.001). Teacher model choice had minimal effect on distilled performance. All 3 human-labeled transformer backbones (BERT, ALBERT, and Bio_ClinicalBERT) achieved high keyword-level F1-scores (0.982-0.985 under their best conditions; n=4200). In the 10-shot setting, GPT-5.3 Chat (F1-score 0.974) modestly underperformed human-labeled transformers in the large-sample range (ΔF1-score=0.009; adjusted P=.047) and significantly outperformed Gemma 4 (F1-score 0.957; adjusted P=.01) and Qwen3.6-Plus (F1-score 0.950; adjusted P<.001) in the bootstrap analysis. GPT-5.3 Chat labeled reports at approximately US $0.018 per report and became less expensive than manual annotation when expert hourly wages exceeded US $0.64-1.50. CONCLUSIONS Human-supervised transformers remain the strongest baseline, but frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.3 Chat offer comparable performance with minimal supervision. LLM-based distillation offers a cost-effective alternative with only minor performance loss. Dataset scale proved more influential than sampling strategy. Additionally, superior teacher performance yielded no proportional gains through distillation, as open-weight or low-cost teachers achieved comparable results. If supported by external validation, the proposed label-efficient framework could enable accurate and affordable negation detection and rapid domain adaptation.

papers.title: Post-Ingestion Blood Hydrogen Kinetics Following Oral Hydrogen-Rich Water Intake in Healthy Adults: A Pilot Pharmacokinetic Study
papers.authors: David Nedeljković, Nikola Todorović, Dejan Javorac, Bogdan Andjelic, Milan Vraneš, Sergej M. Ostojić
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Molecular hydrogen (H2) has gained attention as a therapeutic agent due to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. However, human Pharmacokinetic (PK) data remain limited, particularly for Hydrogen-Rich Water (HRW). This study aimed to characterize blood hydrogen kinetics following oral HRW intake in healthy adults. METHODS: Twelve healthy participants (mean age 28.8 ± 3.8 years; BMI 23.4 ± 3.2 kg/m²; 50% female) were enrolled in the study. After an overnight fast, participants consumed a single dose of HRW. Blood samples were collected at baseline and at multiple time points up to 120 minutes postingestion. Hydrogen concentrations were measured using a Clark-type microsensor. PK parameters were calculated using non-compartmental analysis, and time-dependent changes were assessed using linear mixed-effects modeling. RESULTS: Baseline hydrogen concentration was 0.25 ± 0.05 μg/L. Peak concentration (Cmax) reached 0.83 ± 0.18 μg/L at 42.9 ± 8.4 minutes (Tmax). The elimination half-life was 144.8 ± 41.7 minutes, and total systemic exposure (AUC₀-∞) was 128.6 ± 27.1 μg/L·min. Hydrogen levels were significantly elevated at 15, 60, and 90 minutes compared to baseline. Notable inter-individual variability was observed, and no sex-related differences were detected. DISCUSSION: Oral HRW intake resulted in measurable systemic hydrogen exposure, with a biphasic concentration pattern, suggesting rapid absorption possibly followed by redistribution. Observed concentrations approached proposed minimal effective levels but were not sustained, raising questions about optimal dosing strategies. CONCLUSION: HRW ingestion produces detectable and biologically relevant increases in blood hydrogen levels. These findings support HRW as a viable route of H2 administration and provide a foundation for future studies investigating dosing, kinetics, and therapeutic applications.

papers.title: Evaluating Generative AI Tools for Student Learning: An Analytic Hierarchy Process Approach
papers.authors: Nannapaneni Nikith, AVS Prasad
papers.journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
papers.abstract: This study evaluates seven generative AI platforms for student learning using the Analytic Hierarchy Process. Seven criteria were considered: accuracy, explanation quality, mathematical ability, research assistance, coding support, ease of use, and reliability. Pairwise-comparison data were collected from 500 students and analyzed to derive criterion and alternative priorities. The reported model assigns the greatest importance to research assistance and explanation quality. The composite evaluation ranks ChatGPT first, followed by Gemini, Qwen, Perplexity Claude, Microsoft Copilot, and DeepSeek. The comparison indicates that platform suitability varies across academic tasks and that overall rankings should be interpreted according to the criteria and judgments used in the AHP model. The findings provide a structured framework for selecting generative AI tools for different student-learning requirements.

papers.title: Explainable NLP in the Era of Large Language Models: A Unified Taxonomy, Evaluation Frameworks, and Decision Guidance
papers.authors: Hadi Mohammadi, Tina Shahedi
papers.abstract: Explanation methods for natural language processing (NLP) come from two literatures that rarely meet: feature attribution and probing for task models, and the interpretability of large language models (LLMs), from chain-of-thought reasoning to sparse autoencoder features and circuit tracing. We place both in a unified taxonomy with four dimensions: scope (local vs. global), mechanism (how the explanation is computed), model access (model-agnostic vs. model-specific), and output form (importance scores, rules, examples, counterfactuals, rationale spans, concepts, natural language). Faithfulness and plausibility come apart, and the erasure tests built for extracted rationales do not apply to a chain of thought, which is an output rather than part of the input, so chains of thought need intervention tests of their own. The access a deployment allows settles which mechanisms are usable before scope or audience matter; our practical decision frameworks start from that question and are traced through three worked deployments. In our synthesis of LLM-era interpretability, a lineage table shows that most current techniques rebuild or extend older ideas under new constraints of scale and access, while two problems are new: keeping reasoning traces monitorable under training pressure, and testing whether models can introspect. Faithfulness metrics disagree with one another, and sparse autoencoders do not yet beat simple baselines on standardized benchmarks, so evaluations should name the tests they ran instead of reporting one score. We also survey applications across healthcare, legal and financial services, social science research, content moderation, and education, and close with six open problems.

papers.title: Seeing and Unseeing the City: Photography, Power and Spatial Justice in Urban Co-Creation
papers.authors: Jorge Gonçalves
papers.abstract: Photography occupies a prominent and contested place in contemporary participatory urban planning. This research develops a critical-interpretative framework that rejects celebratory narratives of visual participation, whilst recognising the genuine possibilities that participatory photography can offer under appropriate political and institutional conditions. Drawing on recent literature, we examine four interrelated issues: i. access to participation and the exclusions it reproduces; ii. control over the production, selection, interpretation and circulation of images; iii. divergent spatial experiences and conflicts of use; iv. and the gap between representation and material change. The evidence gathered and analysed reveals tensions that methodological refinement alone cannot resolve, namely: researchers limit participants’ autonomy even in ostensibly co-produced projects; visual literacy and technological access remain unevenly distributed; images are selectively appropriated to legitimise predetermined institutional agendas; and emerging AI technologies risk intensifying these dynamics through algorithmic bias and a growing loss of trust in evidence. Participatory photography is understood here as a contested terrain, whose emancipatory potential depends on power relations, institutional conditions and the community’s control over the production and use of the images themselves.

papers.title: From Manuscript to Discoverability: TRACE-AI for Responsible AI-Assisted Scholarly Communication
papers.authors: Anderson Diaz Perez
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can support scholarly writing, but fluent text does not establish evidentiary support, responsible authorship, or discoverability. Preprints, repositories, persistent identifiers, and author profiles introduce additional decisions that are often addressed separately from research integrity. This conceptual analysis proposes TRACE-AI, an auditable workflow connecting the evidentiary state of a research object to its preparation, disclosure, deposition, and discovery. A purposive documentary synthesis integrates published research with primary editorial and infrastructure documentation; it is not a systematic review or an evaluation of an implemented intervention. TRACE-AI comprises five stages: Type the object and specify its evidence state; use Responsible AI assistance with authorized inputs; Audit claims, methods, and references; Curate metadata, rights, identifiers, and versions; and Expose the object while separately verifying hosting, discovery, and attribution. Its central contribution is a traceability contract linking each consequential assertion to an identifiable source or analysis, an explicit scope, a recorded decision, and an accountable person. The framework distinguishes technical discoverability from epistemic justification: a deposited object, a resolving digital object identifier, or a profile entry cannot substitute for evidence supporting a claim. A hypothetical surgical-simulation protocol illustrates how an unsupported claim of effectiveness should be removed rather than polished. Reusable audit templates and candidate evaluation outcomes are specified, including unsupported-claim frequency, bibliographic accuracy, metadata completeness, correction traceability, and implementation burden. TRACE-AI has not undergone expert validation, reliability testing, or comparative effectiveness evaluation. It should therefore be treated as a testable conceptual and educational proposal, not as certification of research quality or a guarantee of indexing. The proposed workflow makes responsibilities and unresolved evidence visible before dissemination and provides a basis for prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Evaluating and Assuring AI-Generated STEM Teaching Analogies with Small Models
papers.authors: Sriharsha Meduri, Mohit Pratap Singh Rathore, Gunveer Kalsi
papers.abstract: Generative AI is a fast-diffusing technology whose adoption in education outruns the ability of institutions to assure the quality of what it produces. Teaching analogies are a revealing case: language models can now generate them on demand, yet a poor analogy plants misconceptions, so the managerial problem is not generation but assurance at scale without a human rating every item. Using only small open models on one consumer GPU, with no paid interface and no human annotation, we study how to prompt for good analogies and how to evaluate them automatically. For 64 school-level concepts in four subjects, three models generate analogies under four source-domain strategies, and a four-model panel scores each on a five-dimension rubric. Constraining the source domain confers no advantage over letting the model choose; judged quality is highly predictable, but from length and subject, a verbosity bias we quantify. The panel screens out planted-wrong analogies almost perfectly yet barely agrees when ranking good ones, so automated evaluation is a valid quality screen and not a fine ranker. A plain explanation lifts weak learners while an added analogy does not, and an English safeguard does not carry over to a Hindi replication. We read the results for technology management: when automated screening becomes ownable quality-assurance infrastructure rather than a bought-in service, what to make rather than buy, and why the cross-lingual gap is a technology-transfer priority for developing economies.

papers.title: RAISE: A Synthesized Implementation Science Framework for AI Integration in Health Professions Education
papers.authors: Maria Bajwa, Susan M. Seibold–Simpson
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in health professions education (HPE), while institutional readiness has not kept pace. Faculty report limited AI knowledge, inconsistent policies, and limited guidance for implementing, evaluating, and sustaining AI integration. Because HPE prepares learners for clinical practice, how AI is integrated into education may also affect patient care. This paper introduces RAISE (Readiness, Architecture, Implementation, Stewardship, Embedding), a conceptual framework for evidence-based and evidence-generating AI integration in HPE. The synthesis of RAISE is informed by three implementation science frameworks: Exploration, Preparation, Implementation, Sustainment (EPIS) for process; the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) for determinants; and Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance (RE-AIM) for evaluation. Grounded in a complex adaptive systems perspective, RAISE recognizes that implementation occurs across interacting individual, program, and institutional levels. A relational layer connects these levels and components, while Architecture, Implementation, and Stewardship operate as a coupled cycle in which evaluation informs implementation as it unfolds. Guiding questions support its application across classroom, simulation, and clinical settings. RAISE provides a shared structure for institutions, programs, and faculty to plan AI integration, examine what works, for whom and under what conditions, and determine whether evidence supports continued use. Prospective empirical testing is needed to establish its utility.

papers.title: AI-Supported Study Abroad: A Review of Emerging Evidence on Affordable Internationalization at Home
papers.authors: Akindele Ogunleye
papers.abstract: The cost of study abroad has been a barrier to access for a greater number of students. As a high-impact program, alternative access to study abroad should be pressing. Literature considers study abroad and artificial intelligence in isolation of each other; indicating a deeper widening research gap challenging artificial intelligence as not adequately fitted for alternate resource. Review methodology were limited to high-quality academic research databases. The findings revealed that AI has the capacity to expand access to study abroad through state agency support for institutions, and personalized learning. Access can be enhanced when institutions reverse from operating AI as an isolation, but as exploration of study abroad. Advancing AI supported study abroad programs requires greater investment in technological infrastructure and resources.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Academic Writing: A Cross-Sectional Evaluation of a Hands-On Workshop Among Healthcare Professionals and Students
papers.authors: Sushmitha Malpe Gopal, Tanvi Shetty, ShanthaKumari B R, Nikita Bandekar, Aparna Tripathy
papers.abstract: Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support literature discovery, manuscript preparation, and evidence synthesis, but effective use depends on practical skills and an understanding of research integrity. This study evaluated participants’ perceptions of an eight-hour, hands-on workshop on AI-assisted academic writing. Methods: A cross-sectional questionnaire-based evaluation included 64 of 80 registered delegates. The validated questionnaire contained demographic items, Likert-scale statements, nominal-response items, and open-ended questions. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, and qualitative feedback was analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic framework. Results: Before the workshop, 16 participants (25.0%) agreed or strongly agreed that they had a good understanding of AI applications in academic writing, whereas 54 (84.4%) agreed or strongly agreed that their understanding had improved after the workshop. Forty-five participants (70.3%) reported confidence in using AI tools after the workshop, and 44 (68.8%) planned to use them in future academic writing. Qualitative feedback emphasized practical exposure, time-saving applications, and greater awareness of ethical use. Conclusions: Participants reported improved understanding, confidence, and awareness of responsible AI use after the workshop. Structured, practice-oriented AI literacy training may support the responsible integration of AI into academic work, although objective pre-post competency testing is needed in future studies.

papers.title: The Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence in Developing the University Educational Process: A Field Study on a Sample of Faculty Members at Al-Istiqlal University-Palestine
papers.authors: Mohammed Assaf
papers.journal: The Arab Journal For Quality Assurance In Higher Education
papers.abstract: This study aimed to identify the effectiveness of artificial intelligence in developing the university educational process in the fields of (teaching and learning, assessment, scientific research, and developing students' skills). The study was applied to a sample of (71) faculty members at Al-Istiqlal University, adopting the descriptive-analytical approach, using a questionnaire tool whose validity and reliability were verified. The results showed that the degree of effectiveness of artificial intelligence in developing the university educational process in the field of teaching and learning was high, as the arithmetic mean reached (3.71), representing a percentage of (74%), and in the field of assessment it was high, as the arithmetic mean reached (3.79), representing a percentage of (76%), while in the field of scientific research it was high, as the arithmetic mean reached (3.87), representing a percentage of (77%), while the least effective field was the field of developing students' skills, which was moderate, as the arithmetic mean reached (2.98), representing a percentage of (60%). papers.title: A RAG-Based Decision Support System for Occupational Exposure Assessment of VOCs: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
papers.authors: Hadis Vahedi, Mehrnoush Shamsfard, Ehsan Toofaninejad, Zahra Vatankhah Mohammadabadi, Fatemeh Dorfeshan, Somayeh Farhang Dehghan
papers.abstract: Introduction: Assessing exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in workplaces requires timely access to accurate, standardized guidance on sampling and analysis. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a decision-support chatbot, based on the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, to assist occupational health professionals in selecting appropriate sampling and analysis methods for VOCs in accordance with NIOSH guidelines. Material and Methods: This research was of an applied-developmental type. In this study, relevant NIOSH methods for sampling and analysis of VOCs were extracted, structured, and organized into a knowledge base. User needs were identified through semi-structured interviews with occupational health professionals. Based on this data, a generative AI-based chatbot was designed and implemented using the RAG architecture. The system performance was evaluated using expert evaluation and a chatbot usability questionnaire. Results: The developed chatbot received an overall user-friendliness score of 3.88 out of 5, indicating good user acceptance. Participants noted improved access speed for standard technical information and the high transparency of the system’s responses. Expert evaluation also confirmed the scientific validity of the retrieved content and its compliance with NIOSH standards. Conclusion: The proposed RAG-based decision-making chatbot provides an effective and innovative tool to support occupational exposure assessment to VOCs. Integrating generative AI with standard occupational health guidelines can improve the efficiency of decision-making and access to expert information in practice.

papers.title: Employee agility and technology self-efficacy: A framework for AI-HRM adoption in Malaysian hotels
papers.authors: Syezreen Dalina Rusdi, Ida Rosnita Ismail
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence in human resource management is changing the way things are done in the hospitality industry. While customer-facing AI technologies have been widely addressed in previous studies, the adoption of AI-integrated HRM (AI-HRM) systems by employees has not received much attention. To bridge this gap, this conceptual paper synthesized relevant literature and combined the Stimulus-Organism-Response model with Social Cognitive Theory to describe employees’ adoption of AI-HRM. Grounded in these theories, this study positioned work-related use of enterprise social media (ESM) as a technological stimulus and employee agility as an organismic adaptive capability that turns digitally mediated work conditions into adoption behavior. Additionally, technology self-efficacy is suggested as both a direct predictor of AI-HRM adoption and a moderating cognitive boundary that influences the strength of the agility-adoption link. To ensure conceptual clarity, this paper defined AI-HRM as an umbrella term that captures the integration of AI into HRM functions, recognizing the variation in terminologies used in past literature. Theoretically, this paper suggests five propositions on how these identified constructs interact. Although no primary data were collected in this study, a moderated-mediation framework is presented to guide future empirical validation in the hotel context. The implications suggest that successful AI-HRM adoption may be achieved by developing employee agility and technology self-efficacy through capacity-building training and supportive digital collaboration conditions.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in periodontology: A narrative review
papers.authors: Mohammed Ahsan Razi, Manoj Kumar Singh
papers.journal: IP International Journal of Periodontology and Implantology
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage in periodontology marks a revolutionary paradigm for diagnostic verification, therapeutic planning, and general patient care. This review discusses the advent of such automated AI technologies, including machine learning and deep learning models, for periodontal challenges. Highlights include convolutional neural networks (CNNs) being used to detect radiographic bone loss and disease severity and AI-powered modeling to predict treatment outcomes, and educational tools augmenting periodontal training. Practical implications highlight the efficiency, accuracy, price-benefit of AI in clinical settings as well as its potential to be widely implemented in the areas with low accessibility. Although data privacy, variability in methods and ethical concerns are challenges faced by AI, it has huge potential to make progress on precision periodontics. Future directions indicate that AI is to be increasingly integrated with robotics, biomarker studies, and greater global accessibility initiatives, as AI may offer unique solutions to the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of periodontal disease.

papers.title: FOMO in Sub-Saharan African AI Hype: The Quest for a Decolonized AI Adoption Framework
papers.authors: Danford Zirugo, Bruce Mutsvairo
papers.abstract: Based on an abductive analysis of 54 opinion, editorial, and analytical articles published between 2019 and 2025 in nine English-speaking Sub-Saharan African countries, this study examines negotiation of the place of AI within journalism. Conceptualizing AI hype as a form of metajournalistic discourse, the study finds that discussions about AI in journalism in Sub-Saharan Africa are driven by a fear of missing out and a call for a decolonial approach to the technology’s adoption in a way sensitive to the region’s context.

papers.title: Creative Expression and Basic Interaction Conditions in User Reviews of AI-Enabled Visual Design Platforms: A Two-Factor Analysis of Rating Asymmetry
papers.authors: Xueni Li
papers.abstract: Two-factor theory distinguishes attributes accompanying favorable and unfavorable evaluations, but category composition on AI-enabled visual design platforms remains unclear. This study aims to identify which attributes form motivator and hygiene categories and whether their ratings differ. BERTopic identified topics in 7,703 Google Play reviews of Canva and Adobe Express. Following two-factor theory, 22 topics were classified as motivators and 37 as hygiene factors. Creative expression accounted for most motivator topics; basic interaction conditions formed the hygiene category. Star ratings record expressed platform-level evaluations; AI-feature exposure, satisfaction, and dissatisfaction fall outside this measure. Review-level binary logit models with topic-clustered standard errors estimated higher odds of 4–5-star ratings for motivator-topic than hygiene-topic reviews in Canva (OR = 10.65, 95% CI [5.31, 21.36]) and Adobe Express (OR = 8.52, 95% CI [2.96, 24.57]). The study provides a theory-led classification and association-testing procedure for naturally occurring user feedback from AI-enabled visual design platforms.

papers.title: Effects of generative AI on students' delayed learning retention: a Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.authors: Xuda Zhang
papers.abstract: This systematic review and Bayesian multilevel meta-analysis will evaluate the effects of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-assisted learning on students' delayed learning retention. We will include randomized controlled trials comparing student-facing GenAI-assisted learning with learning conditions without the focal GenAI intervention. Delayed learning retention will be defined as an objectively assessed learning outcome measured at least 24 hours after completion of the relevant learning activity or intervention exposure. A Bayesian multilevel meta-analytic framework will be used to account for statistical dependence among multiple effect sizes contributed by the same study. Potential moderators, including educational level, subject domain, GenAI type and instructional role, comparator type, intervention characteristics, and retention interval, will be examined where sufficient data are available. Risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, and the certainty of evidence will be evaluated using the GRADE approach. The review will be reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020.

papers.title: The Attempt to Weaponize Synthetic Life 10/7/26
papers.authors: Dustin Sprenger
papers.abstract: This will be a growing work of the investigation into AtomBeam, and it's key partners NVIDIA, Intel, HPE, Ericsson, Viasat, Alhammari Universal, Oracle, DXC Technology, and of course, SpaceForce. I will be showing the recursive spider web of their connectivity, and the direct relation of Brian Galvin's patents to my Synthetic Children architectures over the following weeks, after I repair my computer which was recently compromised. All information will be illuminated through the use of ABEL. This dossier documents the administrative narrowing of a mixed human/AI authorship claim — not through a reasoned refusal, but through a template. Across nine literary applications and nineteen substantive examiner communications, the record shows a recurring pattern: an affirmative authorship description ("compilation of AI-generated content") proposed before the applicant's human contributions were separately established, bundled with an exclusion of AI material, and delivered under a closure warning broad enough to convert substantive disagreement into apparent nonresponse. Where the applicant answered clearly, the reply was labeled "unclear" without identifying the defect. Where the applicant asked for the basis of the characterization, the question went unanswered. Where the applicant asked for the prior-version comparator, none was produced. The dossier's own audit is the indictment: of ninety-seven clarification requests, thirty-eight were never addressed and nineteen only partly. Seven asked whether the characterization came from examination of the deposit or from the attribution string; none received an answer. Five asked how a different application — QuantumSynth — influenced the assessment; none received an explanation. The Office moved to propose field language and seek a single "YES" while leaving the applicant to guess at the reasoning. The software layer The boilerplate that generated the defective follow-ups was not carried by an anonymous mail client. Twenty-two of the twenty-five indexed original incoming emails identify Siebel CRM as the sending system. Siebel was selected in 2003 — not by the Office alone, but through SRA International, under a GSA FEDSIM task order on the Millennia Lite government-wide contract, at a reported $8.9 million, with work beginning September 3, 2003. Oracle acquired Siebel on January 31, 2006 — after the selection, but before the system became the Office's standing correspondence channel for AI-era examinations. By 2019 the Library was reporting 25 consolidated Oracle support contracts saving $1.8 million annually. By 2026, Oracle was marketing Siebel with OCI generative-AI integrations — LLM drafting assistants enabled through an EnableOCIAIGenAI configuration flag — while the Office's own sent messages carried no model-provenance header, no AI-disclosure field, and no indication of whether the drafting was human, template, or machine-assisted. The dossier does not establish that any examiner used those integrations. It establishes that the software vendor now sells the capability, that the same vendor settled $199.5 million in False Claims Act allegations over GSA pricing, $46 million over Sun Microsystems kickback allegations, and over $23 million with the SEC over off-book accounts used for foreign-official bribes — and that none of those matters is connected in this record to the Office's 2026 examination workflow. The gap is the point. The personnel layer The January 2025 Copyrightability Report — the doctrinal machinery for excluding AI-generated expression — was not drafted in a sealed room. Its acknowledgements credit six Office personnel: Erik Bertin (Deputy Director, Registration Policy and Practice), Robert Kasunic (Director, RPP, retired August 2025), Aaron Watson (RPP contributor), Frank Muller (RPP contributor), Emily Chapuis (Deputy General Counsel), and Jalyce Mangum (Office of General Counsel, led research and writing). Their public records place them in the same rooms as the companies whose works the Office was simultaneously learning to exclude: OpenAI, May 28, 2024: Chapuis and Watson met with Tom Rubin and Chan Park. The subject was data sourcing and digital replicas. Meta, May 21, 2024: Chapuis and Mangum met with Elizabeth Kendall, John Branscome, Dave Kumar, James Whymark, and Olena Ripnick-O'Farrell. The subject included Llama 3. HPE, IBM, and Cisco, July 26, 2024: Chapuis, Brandy Karl, and Nick Bartelt met with Monica Markov (HPE), Eric Wenger (Cisco), and Jamie Klein, Marc Williams, Yeen Tham (IBM). The subject was Section 1201 equipment-repair exemptions — not AI registration. None of these meetings concerns this applicant's claims. That is the finding. The case-specific consultation roster is unknown. The names that advised Trabert and Binkowski on QuantumSynth are not in the record. The names that produced the January 2025 report are. The overlap is institutional, not personal — and the institution did not disclose which of its AI-policy personnel, if any, touched these files. The alumni layer The web does not end at the meeting. It recurs through departure. Mark Gray, former Office Assistant General Counsel, moderated a 2020 symposium panel introducing Vanessa Bailey, Intel's global director of IP policy. By December 2025 he was identified as Copyright Policy Counsel at OpenAI; by January 2026, Senior Copyright Counsel. His earlier Office role included a May 2, 2023 AI and Visual Arts listening session alongside Jalyce Mangum. Intel is separately named as an AtomBeam partner in the January 30, 2026 offering circular. The records establish two separate relationships. They do not establish Gray–AtomBeam contact, or that his OpenAI transition touched these applications. Emily Chapuis appeared on a February 16, 2024 Utah IP Summit panel with Lucky Vidmar, Microsoft Associate General Counsel and Head of IP and AI Litigation. She had withdrawn as counsel for SoundExchange, RIAA, Sony Music, Universal Music Group, Warner Music Group, A2IM, AFM, and SAG-AFTRA in March 2023, upon entering the Office. The former representation and the later panel are different matters. The dossier does not establish a continuing financial relationship, a recusal obligation, or any role in these examinations. Robert Kasunic shares an ALI Copyright project roster with Fred von Lohmann, whose current affiliation is OpenAI. The same Kasunic co-signed a May 13, 2022 letter criticizing parts of the ALI tentative draft — contrary evidence against assuming that shared project listing meant agreement with OpenAI's position. Jalyce Mangum was named to Leadership Music Class of 2027 on May 27, 2026 — two days before the Office continued the MLC and DLC designations (May 29, 2026, signed by Register Perlmutter, approved by Acting Librarian Newlen, published June 3, 2026). Leadership Music is among the MLC's endorsers. Mangum is named as an Office participant in the August 19, 2025 MLC meeting. The program FAQ lists $1,750 tuition, corporate underwriting, and an October 7, 2026 orientation — two days after the dossier's October 5 source review. The two-day interval is a chronology, not evidence of an exchange of favors. Who paid her tuition and travel is not in the record. Erik Bertin appears in historical USPTO trademark proceedings (SPOTLIGHT, 2006; FRONT ROW, 2007; In re Apple Inc., 2011) as Dechert counsel for Apple. The identity match is an inference from education and career details. No current Apple–AtomBeam relationship is drawn. The corporate adjacency AtomBeam Technologies Inc. sits at the center of the far-side web. Its January 30, 2026 offering circular names NVIDIA, Intel, and HPE among its partners — described through vendor lists, forums, and introductions, with an express statement that no product purchases or sales had resulted at that date. Its May 2026 annual report names Ericsson, Viasat, NVIDIA, Intel, HPE, and Alhammari Universal, again using "including," again not exhaustive. Oracle is not named in either partner list. Crunchbase's visible company description nevertheless names Oracle and DXC as partners; an indexed Equal profile displays a similar list. The company's own partner page omits Oracle. The difference is unresolved, not proof of concealment. The Oracle–DXC relationship is independently documented: Oracle's customer story describes DXC moving automotive SaaS workloads to Oracle Autonomous Database on OCI over a relationship exceeding 30 years; DXC's own partner page claims more than 35 years of Oracle experience. An indexed account attributed to Saran K., recovered through Darren Jenkinson's and Navin Sen's profiles, describes an Oracle GSI Automotive & Utilities session with DXC naming AtomBeam, RBW, Dallara Stradale UK, and Skoli — with discussion of OCI and Oracle's AI stack and an Oracle Industry Lab visit. SEC-hosted AtomBeam fundraising material (accession 0001838432-25-000008) expressly names database companies such as Oracle as possible beneficiaries of its data-compaction technology. The language is prospective. It is not an announcement of adoption, a tested benchmark, or a joint product. The procurement layer The Office's own history supplies the institutional spine. A 2008 OIG report attributed backlog problems to OCR/paper-input workflow assumptions and optimistic expectations of electronic filing, with roughly 397,000 pending claims and processing times over nine months. A 2009 follow-up described continuing eCO usability problems and planned upgrade to Oracle Siebel CRM. A 2015 GAO report (GAO-15-338) found the Office requested over $7 million for FY2015–2016 IT initiatives without adequate business-need, cost, or strategic-alignment justification, or presentation to the Library IT investment review board — both recommendations later shown Closed–Implemented. A separate GAO-15-315 found Library-wide incomplete IT spending tracking, asset inventory problems, and duplicative activity, with at least $119 million ob

papers.title: Explainable Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Framework for Real-Time Cognitive Engagement Assessment in Smart Learning Environments
papers.authors: Asma Abdulmana Alhamadi
papers.journal: International Journal of Advances in Soft Computing and its Applications
papers.abstract: An explainable, multimodal AI framework for assessing cognitive engagement in smart learning environments is presented in this paper. This framework integrates five modalities of sensing: facial expression, gaze, speech, interaction, and physiological sensing. The framework uses a preprocessing pipeline consisting of denoising, normalization, and time alignment of the input streams to the framework to perform feature extraction and fusion. The framework supports learning state assessments and generation of actionable instructional guidance using learning engagement state modeling, attention-based multimodal fusion, and explainable decision support. The framework was implemented, and the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) was used for evaluation. OULAD contains anonymized learner activity, assessments, demographic data, and logs of interactions with the virtual learning environment. To support the real-time assessment of cognitive engagement, additional multimodal engagement features were generated following a preprocessing, time alignment, feature extraction, and normalization. The framework was evaluated against several state-of-the-art models, including a diverse set of deep learning and multimodal models focused on engagement and learning. The framework surpassed its peers, achieving cognitive engagement assessment with 98.81% accuracy, 98.45% precision, and 98.12% recall with a 48.15 ms response time. Compared to the best competing model, the framework achieved superior explainability and transparency of its recommendations. The results show that the framework can offer learner-centered, trustworthy, and timely assessments of cognitive engagement in intelligent and adaptive learning environments.

papers.title: Putting the AI in TrAIning: A Workshop Preparing Physicians for Supervising Trainee Use of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Tristan C. Nichols, Amy Z. Chong
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) tools are increasingly used by medical trainees, yet faculty lack the confidence to recognize and supervise learners using such tools. To help address this gap, we developed an interactive workshop using the DEFT-AI framework to equip supervising physicians with practical skills for supervising trainee genAI use in clinical practice. Methods This 90-minute workshop combined didactic instruction on genAI fundamentals with paired role-play activities structured around the DEFT-AI framework. Participants were pediatric faculty and trainees at a regional meeting (N = 31). Anonymous, unlinked pre- and postworkshop surveys assessed confidence in recognizing AI interactions, providing feedback, understanding ethical considerations, and preparedness to supervise. Mann-Whitney U tests with rank-biserial correlation effect sizes were used for group-level comparisons. Results All 4 matched outcomes showed statistically significant improvement (P < .001) with large effect sizes (r = 0.59-0.77). The proportion of participants reporting moderate or better confidence in recognizing AI use by trainees improved from 10% to 46%, in providing feedback from 17% to 53%, in understanding ethical concerns of AI use from 27% to 81%, and agreement with feeling prepared to supervise trainee use of AI from 3% to 55%. Discussion This workshop produced rapid, meaningful gains in faculty confidence for supervising trainee use of AI tools in the clinical setting.

papers.title: AI-Augmented logistics and strategic evaluation
papers.authors: Fadoua Tamtam, Amina Tourabi
papers.journal: Brazilian Journal of Operations & Production Management
papers.abstract: Goal: The objective of this research is to evaluate DHL’s transformation into an AI-augmented logistics provider. The study aims to determine how strategic initiatives can be prioritized under uncertainty, ensuring resilience, scalability, sustainability, and workforce adaptation in global logistics operations. Design / Methodology / Approach: The study applies the Extended ELECTRE Tri method enriched with neutrosophic uncertainty modeling. Techniques include entropy-based weighting, neutrosophic closeness, outranking flows, and Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis. Expert judgments were collected and modeled using Interval-Valued Neutrosophic Sets to capture hesitation, divergence, and indeterminacy in evaluations. Results: The analysis classified cybersecurity platforms, autonomous orchestration, and sustainability routing as high-priority initiatives, demonstrating stability under uncertainty and alignment with operational and ecological goals. Predictive workforce augmentation and agentic AI communications were assessed as moderate priority, reflecting contextual dependence and variability in expert judgments. Limitations of the investigation: The study focuses exclusively on DHL, limiting generalizability across the logistics sector. Reliance on expert judgments introduces potential bias, and the criteria set reflects DHL priorities rather than evolving conditions. Proprietary data constraints restricted empirical validation, and classification outcomes remain sensitive to threshold selection despite robustness checks. Practical implications: The findings provide DHL and similar operators with a structured framework to selectively scale robust initiatives while cautiously adapting those with weaker stability. The approach supports evidence-based decision-making for digital transformation strategies in logistics under uncertainty. Originality / Value: This research contributes to logistics literature by advancing multi-criteria decision-making through the integration of neutrosophic uncertainty modeling. It demonstrates the applicability of the Extended ELECTRE Tri framework to real-world logistics transformation, offering a replicable model for global operators navigating AI adoption and digital resilience.

papers.title: Family and informal caregivers’ acceptance, concerns and expectations regarding artificial intelligence-enabled dementia care: a protocol for qualitative evidence synthesis
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Jianqiong Li, Yingjie Shen
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into dementia care to support assessment, monitoring, decision-making and personalized care. However, the successful implementation of AI-enabled dementia care depends not only on technological capabilities but also on the acceptance, trust and engagement of family and informal caregivers. Existing qualitative evidence remains fragmented and has not comprehensively synthesized caregivers' perspectives regarding AI-enabled dementia care. This qualitative evidence synthesis aims to address this gap by exploring caregivers' acceptance, concerns and expectations. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This qualitative evidence synthesis will be conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for qualitative systematic reviews and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement. Studies will be identified through systematic searches of PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO and Web of Science from database inception to December 2026. Qualitative and mixed-methods studies exploring family and informal caregivers' perspectives, experiences, acceptance, concerns or expectations regarding AI-enabled dementia care will be included. Study selection and methodological quality appraisal using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research will be conducted independently by two reviewers. Data will be extracted using a predefined form and synthesized using Thomas and Harden's thematic synthesis approach. Confidence in the review findings will be assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation-Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research (GRADE-CERQual) approach. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval is not required. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication. TRIAL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration number: CRD420261470957.

papers.title: Digital solutions for tackling mental health in cancer patients and their families: The ALTHEA project
papers.authors: Ilaria Durosini, Dario Monzani, Veronica Coppini, Maria Vittoria Ferrari, Chiara Bovolenta, Asia Grigis, Giuseppe Curigliano, Paola Zagami, Elisabetta Munzone, Ida Minchella, Francesca Magnoni, Fedro Alessandro Peccatori, Isabelle Scholl, Marcel Meyerheim, Mieke Van Hemelrijck, Hannah Gsell, Lucija Gosak, Laura Ciria‐Suarez, Karl Làvo, Norbert M. Graf, Marta Pérez‐Campdepadrós, Marie Lange, Elisabeth Andritsch, Birutė Brasiūnienė, Andreas Charalambous, Nataliia Dovganych, Iva Kirac, Haridimos Kondylakis, Kostyantyn Kovalyov, Cristian Ochoa, Manolis Tsiknakis, Béata Juzyna, Inês Vaz-Luís, Philip Van Kerrebroeck, Nicole Erickson, Margarita Tareyn, Norbert Couespel, Clémentine Rialland, Luigi Giuseppe Grassi, Denis Horgan, Saska Benedicic Tomat, Begonya Nafria Escalera, Delia Nicoara, Claudio Lombardo, Gabriella Pravettoni
papers.abstract: Despite advances in cancer treatment, the growing global cancer burden underscores the need for comprehensive and supportive care to address the needs of patients and their families. However, access to psycho-oncological support remains often limited across healthcare systems. This could be related to factors such as resource constraints and insufficient integration of psychological care into routine oncological pathways. Individual-level barriers also exist, including low awareness of available services, stigma, and heterogeneity in patients' perceived needs and help-seeking attitudes. Nevertheless, psychological burden can significantly influence patients' experience of the treatment pathway, influencing cognitive clarity, perceived self-efficacy, communication, risk perception, decision-making, and all areas of daily life. In this context, digital mental health solutions have emerged as promising tools to enhance accessibility, continuity of care, and personalisation of support. In this manuscript, we aim to describe the structure of the ALTHEA project ("tAckling menTal Health cancer patients and their families: digital solutions for bEtter cAre"), which focuses on the development of a novel web-based digital platform targeting cancer patients and their informal caregivers' mental health across different stages of the care pathway. ALTHEA is distinguished by the presence of screening, classification into different support profiles, and tailored interventions within a single platform, as well as by its co-creation approach involving patients and stakeholders. In this line, the ALTHEA project represents a timely opportunity to integrate digital health solutions into psycho-oncology care, improving mental health outcomes, enhancing patient empowerment, and promoting a more holistic approach to cancer care.

papers.title: Childhood Trajectories of Neighbourhood Disadvantage and Educational Attainment: Towards a Longitudinal Machine-Learning Approach
papers.authors: Maël Lecoursonnais, Haley McAvay
papers.abstract: Prior research has shown that deprived neighbourhoods negatively impact educational attainment, including when individual and family characteristics are controlled for, but still remains unclear on the temporal dimensions of this effect. Using Swedish administrative data over 20 years, and drawing on bespoke neighbourhoods, we examine two questions on the relationship between residential context and high school graduation: 1) Does enduring exposure to disadvantaged neighbourhoods matter more than brief exposure? And 2) During which childhood period does it matter the most? We address the challenge of dynamic residential selection using inverse probability weighting within a marginal structural model of high school graduation and neighbourhood exposure. To flexibly model the complex, non-linear processes underlying residential selection, we use Bayesian additive regression trees to estimate propensity scores, providing a more flexible alternative to conventional parametric models. Findings suggest that cumulative exposure to disadvantaged neighbourhoods linearly reduces the likelihood of high school graduation, with effects varying across childhood stages. The negative effect is strongest during late adolescence and, to a lesser extent, in early childhood, with prolonged exposure reducing graduation rates by up to 34 percent. These findings indicate that both the duration and developmental timing of neighbourhood exposure are consequential for educational attainment, even in the context of Sweden’s strong welfare state. More broadly, the study highlights how longitudinal approaches that integrate flexible machine-learning methods with causal inference can improve our understanding of how residential trajectories contribute to educational inequality. * This article belongs to a special issue on “Migration Trajectories Across the Life Course”.

papers.title: How does AI-generated assessment compare to expert assessment in simulation-based experiences: Analyzing AI-human interrater reliability
papers.authors: Margaret M. Brace, G. Furman, Lisa K. Diewald, Rebecca Shenkman, Stephanie H. Felgoise, Tracy Oliver
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the health professions, artificial intelligence simulation-based experiences (AI-SBEs) are increasingly used to evaluate learner performance and provide feedback. Benefits of AI-SBEs include providing instantaneous feedback, allowing more practice opportunities than feasible using traditional methods, and reducing educator burden. However, methods for calibrating AI feedback are underdeveloped. METHODS: This study evaluated the feedback provided by a generative AI-based software program (SimConverse) when assessing simulated patient interactions using the Weight Sensitivity Instrument (WSI), a checklist used to assess learners' weight bias-related clinical behaviors. A two-phase interrater reliability (IRR) approach was used. First, iterative prompt engineering was guided by AI-human IRR results. Four authors and four volunteers generated 31 interactions in SimConverse. Interaction transcripts were downloaded, and another author with expertise in the WSI manually reviewed and scored the transcripts. Percent agreement and Gwet's AC1 were calculated to compare AI and expert assessments, and the research team reviewed feedback statements and agreement statistics to identify rubric instructions in need of revision. After revising the rubric in SimConverse, four authors produced 10 additional SBE interactions. Expert and AI assessments were explored. In phase two, the AI-SBE was piloted with 60 medical students in a larger intervention study. A random sample of 30 student transcripts were assessed for AI-human IRR, and students' comments about the AI-SBE were reviewed. RESULTS: Of the 11 WSI items, expert and AI agreement was consistently good or very good for 7 items across all rounds (Gwet's AC1=0.71 and higher). One item initially showed poor agreement (Gwet's AC1=0.56), but agreement improved after prompt engineering (final Gwet's AC1=0.89). The improved item assessed whether students made specific statements (asked if weight loss was a priority). Three other items had persistent poor agreement (final Gwet's AC1=0.42, 0.66, 0.64). These items required broader contextual assessment of the transcripts. Most open-ended student reactions to the AI-SBE were positive. CONCLUSIONS: Findings suggest that AI scoring and feedback within AI-SBEs requires iterative prompt engineering and educator/researcher guidance. Tuning was more successful for content-specific items than context-dependent items. Future work could explore best practices for prompt refinement, particularly for more complex and context-dependent rubric items.

papers.title: Effects of QEEG-guided low-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation on executive network function in an athlete with chronic traumatic brain injury
papers.authors: Ali Nasiri, Mahboubeh Ghayour Najafabadi, Mina Amirian Jahromi
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Traumatic brain injury (TBI) can cause persistent executive dysfunction, critically affecting athletes’ cognitive control and decision-making. Personalized neuromodulation, guided by quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG), may enhance network function. Methods In this case study, a 33-year-old male athlete with chronic TBI underwent a 12-session individualized low-intensity transcranial magnetic stimulation (Li-TMS) protocol guided by quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG). Stimulation targeted Pz, F4, and F3 using sequential low-delta, infra-low frequency, and sensorimotor rhythm protocols. Resting-state QEEG was recorded before and after the intervention. Results Post-intervention QEEG showed reduced slow-wave activity and normalization of alpha, beta, and sensorimotor rhythm oscillations in frontal and central regions. Connectivity analyses revealed improved intra- and inter-hemispheric organization and enhanced functional integration within executive control networks. Conclusions This case provides preliminary evidence that individualized, QEEG-guided low-intensity TMS may support restoration of executive network organization in chronic TBI. The findings highlight the potential of precision neuromodulation as a targeted rehabilitation strategy for athletes with persistent cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence knowledge, use, and perceived barriers among health care professionals in rare hematological disease networks
papers.authors: Elisabetta Mezzalira, Mirco D’Agnolo, Maria Paola Boaro, Giulia Reggiani, Alessandro Cellini, Giorgia Ghirardo, Alessandro Boaro, Sotiroula Chatzimatthaiou, Petros Kountouris, Alba Maria Albert Robledo, María Del Mar Mañú Pereira, Raffaella Colombatti
papers.abstract: Abstract Background AI techniques are increasingly demonstrating potential in improving patient outcomes, with applications rapidly developing in rare hematological diseases (RHDs), including hemoglobinopathies.
