The low p ‐value of 0.001205 ( p < 0.05) of the educational facilities utilised indicates a statistically significant result, proving the association between educational quality and improved water facilities. All of the variables under evaluation, including the respondents' vehicle type, landholding type, and house type, have large and positive chi‐squared values, suggesting that the ‘before’ and ‘after’ distributions for each of these variables differ. Principal Component Analysis is used to summarise correlated livelihood indicators and reveals that income growth and livelihood improvement is multi‐dimensional. Multiple pathways to income change are identified through Partial Least Squares Regression, including agriculture and market‐linked channels. A Random Forest Regression Model is utilised to assess the relative importance of livelihood channels and baseline characteristics. Results indicate that improvement in irrigation access, crop diversification, housing quality, livestock ownership and female literacy are strongly associated with higher income gains. Hence, it may be said that the groundwater recharge as a result of construction of check dams must have improved agricultural activity or agricultural output in a material manner, and accordingly all capitals for Raleras have improved.

papers.title: Knowledge on trial: AI, trust and the future of decision-making
papers.authors: Saleeq Ahmad Dar, Hilal Ahmad Dar
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of the paper is to highlight that while they may be in a hurry to feed the growing giant of AI, they must also thoughtfully consider the consequences. The black-box nature of AI raises concerns about transparency and trust and as long as they do not fully understand how AI reaches its conclusions, questions about the reliability of AI-driven decision-making will continue. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative secondary research approach, using content analysis of evidence collected from newspapers, research papers and recent books to critically compare AI-driven and traditional approaches to knowledge and decision-making. Findings The findings reveal that AI-driven decisions cannot be trusted blindly, as they may reinforce existing vulnerabilities and discrimination in society. Therefore, AI must be used mindfully, with continuous human oversight, transparency and accountability, to reduce rather than exacerbate disorder and inequality in the information society, while building public trust instead of creating fear. Originality/value The paper is original, offering a critical perspective on AI-driven decision-making, trust and the need for mindful human oversight in the information society.

papers.title: AI research in libraries (2017–2025): a scoping review with bibliometric mapping across the COVID era
papers.authors: Efren Torres, Janice Peñaflor
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how research on artificial intelligence (AI) in libraries evolved between 2017 and 2025, with specific attention to changes before, during and after the COVID-19 period. It seeks to identify shifts in publication trends, geographic participation, thematic emphases and methodological approaches and to assess what these shifts suggest about the changing focus and maturity of AI research in library scholarship and practice. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a scoping review methodology following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, supported by PRISMA-ScR-based screening and selection procedures. A structured search of the Scopus database retrieved AI-related library research published between 2017 and 2025. The final dataset of 373 documents was analyzed using bibliometric profiling and author keyword co-occurrence mapping. Records were grouped into three periods – pre-COVID (2017–2019), during COVID (2020–2022) and post-COVID (2023–2025) – to enable comparative analysis of publication output, citation patterns, geographic distribution, thematic clusters and study designs across phases. Findings The results show a sharp increase in AI-related library research after 2020, with sustained high output after 2023 and an expected citation lag for the most recent year. Geographic participation broadens substantially over time, although publication output remains concentrated in a small number of countries and journals. Thematic analysis reveals a clear shift from early exploratory and infrastructure-linked research in the pre-COVID period, to service continuity, automation and operational concerns during COVID and toward post-COVID consolidation around governance, adoption, generative AI and AI-related literacies, alongside continued interest in service technologies. Methodologically, the literature becomes more diverse across periods, with growing use of quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods, although non-empirical studies remain the largest category overall. Originality/value By explicitly treating pre-COVID, COVID-period and post-COVID literature through 1 August 2025, this study extends earlier bibliometric work by examining publication trends, geographic participation, thematic clusters and methodological change within a single three-period framework. This makes visible changes that are less apparent in aggregate bibliometric analyses of AI-in-libraries research.

papers.title: AI recommendation agent autonomy and tourists’ adoption intention: the boundary role of occupational type
papers.authors: Guohao Pan, Andrew Z. A. Jin, Yueli Tang, Qiang Wang, Yuchen Wang
papers.journal: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Technology
papers.abstract: Purpose Drawing on compensatory control theory, this study aims to examine how AI recommendation agent type (autonomous AI vs. collaborative AI) influences tourists’ adoption intention. It further investigates the moderating role of tourists’ occupational type and the mediating role of perceived control. Design/methodology/approach Three scenario-based experiments were conducted. Experiment 1 tested the general effect of AI recommendation agent type on adoption intention. Experiment 2 examined the moderating role of occupational type (manual labor vs. mental labor) and the mediating role of perceived control in the relationship between AI recommendation agent type and adoption intention. Experiment 3 manipulated participants’ temporary control state, namely, control deprivation versus control affirmation, to provide causal evidence for the proposed control-based mechanism. Findings When tourists’ occupational type was not differentiated, tourists were generally more willing to adopt recommendations from autonomous AI than from collaborative AI. Occupational type significantly moderated this relationship. Manual laborers were more willing to adopt recommendations from collaborative AI, whereas mental laborers were more willing to adopt recommendations from autonomous AI. Perceived control in the AI recommendation interaction mediated the interaction effect of AI recommendation agent type and occupational type on adoption intention. Experiment 3 further showed that the temporary control state changed individuals’ preferences for autonomous versus collaborative AI. Originality/value This study extends tourism AI adoption research by shifting attention from AI-generated content and tourists’ general perceptions of AI technologies to the autonomy of AI recommendation agents. It also enriches compensatory control theory by applying it to AI-enabled tourism recommendation contexts and distinguishing different sources of perceived control provided by autonomous and collaborative AI.

papers.title: Embracing artificial intelligence in European auditing: the role of familiarity, motivation, organizational support and education in shaping perceived effectiveness
papers.authors: Sandra Khalil, Samer Murshid
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how familiarity with artificial intelligence (AI), motivation and organizational support for AI, and demographic characteristics influence the perceived AI effectiveness among a sample of European auditors, as well as the moderating role of education on these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Data collected from a developed survey were analyzed using multiple and moderated hierarchical regressions. Findings The results reveal a positive association between auditors’ familiarity with AI and their perception of AI effectiveness. Similarly, auditors’ motivation and organizational support enhance their perception of AI effectiveness. Female auditors perceive AI as less effective than males. Education is negatively associated with perceived effectiveness but positively moderates the relationship between auditors’ familiarity with AI and their perception of AI effectiveness. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by its sample size and focus on the European context, which may restrict the generalizability of findings to regions with different resource constraints. Practical implications The findings suggest that audit firms should enhance AI adoption by investing in targeted training programs that build familiarity, emphasize benefits and improve auditors’ confidence and perceptions toward AI. In addition, fostering organizational support, motivation, inclusive initiatives and long-term strategic integration of AI further strengthen the effective utilization of AI in auditing. Originality/value This study contributes to literature by providing insight into how familiarity, motivation and organizational support, gender and education are associated with the perceived AI effectiveness of a sample of European auditors.

papers.title: AI readiness and digital pedagogical competence as enablers of innovations in environmental management within higher education institutions: evidence from Vietnam
papers.authors: Phi Dinh Khuong, Duong Lam Thuy
papers.journal: International Journal of Sustainability in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) readiness and digital pedagogical competence (DPC) are associated with lecturers’ perceptions of digital environmental governance innovation (DEGI) and perceived environmental performance in higher education institutions (HEIs). Moving beyond isolated green technologies, the study adopts a governance-oriented perspective to explain how individual digital capabilities among academic staff are linked to perceived sustainability-related outcomes through digitally enabled environmental governance innovation. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 1,525 academic staff working in Vietnamese HEIs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed capability–governance–perception framework and to examine both direct and indirect relationships among the constructs. Findings The findings indicate that AI readiness (artificial intelligence readiness) is positively associated with DPC and lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI. DPC is also positively associated with governance innovation. Most importantly, lecturers’ perceptions of DEGI are strongly associated with perceived environmental performance and indicate a statistically significant indirect association between AIR and perceived environmental outcomes within the specified model. Research limitations/implications This study is based on cross-sectional, self-reported survey data from a single national context, which limits causal inference and statistical generalisability. The findings should therefore be interpreted as perception-based associations rather than evidence of objectively measured institutional environmental improvement. Future research could adopt longitudinal, comparative, multi-source or objective-indicator designs. Practical implications The findings suggest that HEIs should move beyond technology adoption alone and invest in human digital capabilities, sustainability dashboards, environmental data reporting systems and governance structures. Strengthening AIR and DPC among academic staff may support digitally mediated governance innovations for environmental management. Social implications By highlighting governance innovation as a perception-based pathway linking digital capabilities to perceived environmental performance, this study offers insights for HEIs seeking to strengthen their sustainability responsibilities. Digitally enabled environmental governance may support broader sustainability transitions, provided it is embedded within accountable institutional practices. Originality/value This study offers empirical evidence linking individual digital capabilities to perceived environmental management outcomes in higher education through governance innovation. It extends sustainability and digital transformation research by positioning AIR and DPC as enablers of perceived digitally driven environmental governance, particularly within a Global South context.

papers.title: The donkey and the algorithm: cultivating judgement infrastructure for AI literacy in higher education
papers.authors: Tori Anne Langill, Maarten Matheus van Houten
papers.journal: Education Innovations Systems and Future Learning
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper reframes artificial intelligence (AI) literacy in higher education as a problem of judgement formation rather than tool fluency alone. It asks how students can be supported not only to use generative AI, but also to evaluate, limit, disclose or refuse its use responsibly under conditions of uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach This paper develops a conceptual and pedagogical argument through engagement with AI literacy scholarship, evaluative judgement, information judgement and educational theory. Rhetorical literacy, informal logic and argumentation, and ethical reasoning/phronesis are used as a pragmatic framework for analysing the judgement capacities required for meaningful AI engagement. Findings This paper proposes a judgement-infrastructure account of AI literacy. It argues that student suspicion, selective use, uncritical reliance and refusal can be read as sites where judgement is practised, bypassed or left unarticulated. The Judgement-Infrastructure Gap Model is offered as a diagnostic heuristic for examining where judgement is supported or neglected across curricula, assessment, institutional policy and technological platforms. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual paper, the argument and model require empirical and design-based testing. Future research should examine how students justify AI use, limited use, disclosure and refusal across disciplines, and how programme-level scaffolding, assessment design, institutional policy and technological platforms support evaluative judgement. Practical implications AI literacy initiatives should include assessable activities that make reasoning visible, such as claim-evidence mapping, annotated AI outputs, oral defences, AI-free checkpoints, ethical decision logs and justified decisions about AI use, limitation, disclosure or refusal. These practices should be supported at programme and institutional levels rather than placed only on individual teachers or students. Originality/value This paper contributes a judgement-infrastructure account of AI literacy that treats both use and non-use as teachable and assessable forms of evaluative judgement. It extends existing AI literacy frameworks by linking student suspicion, refusal, assessment design, programme-level scaffolding and educational ecosystem conditions to responsible AI engagement.

papers.title: Code-driven planning in grid worlds with large language models
papers.authors: Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan, Zhisheng Tang, Mayank Kejriwal
papers.abstract: We propose an iterative programmatic planning (IPP) framework that solves grid-based tasks by using large language models (LLMs) to synthesize interpretable, executable programs that act as agent policies mapping environment states to action sequences, rather than relying on traditional search or reinforcement learning. Alongside prompting strategies such as direct code generation, pseudocode conditioned refinement and curriculum-based prompting, IPP centres on an iterative refinement mechanism that updates code from coarse, task-level feedback. We evaluate our approach using six leading LLMs and two challenging grid-based benchmarks (grid-based reasoning for assessing spatial planning (GRASP) and MiniGrid). Our IPP framework demonstrates improvements over direct code generation for five of the six models, with net energy gains ranging from a few per cent to roughly threefold and, for Gemini-2.5-Pro, a sign flip from a negative baseline to a strongly positive score, establishes a new state-of-the-art result for GRASP and significantly outperforms direct elicitation from GPT-o3-mini (by 43% on the hardest MiniGrid task to 116% on GRASP). While code generation has a higher initial prompting cost compared to direct solution elicitation ($0.08 per task versus $0.002 per instance for GPT-o3-mini), the code can be reused for any number of instances, making the amortized cost significantly lower (by 400 times on GPT-o3-mini across the complete GRASP benchmark). Beyond performance gains, IPP produces reusable, human-readable policies that support transparent inspection and modification, underscoring the advantages of planning as program synthesis over per-instance inference. The code and results can be found at http://github.com/Mystic-Slice/LLM-Planning-CodeGen.

papers.title: Moral echoes: do morality and humanness affect emotional and aesthetic responses to music?
papers.authors: Abbigail Marie Fleckenstein, Mariola Paruzel‐Czachura, Katarzyna Pypno‐Blajda, Henna‐Riikka Peltola, Jonna K. Vuoskoski
papers.abstract: Abstract When listening to novel music, extra-musical information about the musician may influence a listener's evaluations of the music. Here, we studied the extent to which information about the musicians’ Humanness, Morality and Sex, conveyed by their vocal timbre and tessitura, affected listeners’ emotional and aesthetic responses to their music. This online, pre-registered experiment followed a 2 (Humanness: Human vs. AI model) × 2 (Vocalist Sex: Male vs. Female) × 3 (Morality: Moral, Immoral, Neutral) mixed factorial design. Participants (n = 400) were randomly assigned to one of four groups, differing in Humanness and Vocalist Sex. Participants read three descriptions depicting a Moral, Immoral and Neutral behaviour and listened to three unfamiliar songs pseudorandomly paired with a description. Emotional and aesthetic responses to each song were measured using validated measures (GEMS-9 scale) and additional items assessing feelings of being Moved, Connected, perceived Beauty, Liking and perceived Creativity. As predicted, linear mixed-effects models revealed significant main effects of Morality for all dependent variables, with Immoral descriptions consistently yielding more negative ratings. Contrary to predictions, we observed no differences in responses to songs based on Humanness, no significant interaction between Morality and Humanness and no effect of Vocalist Sex on responses.

papers.title: The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation
papers.authors: PAOLO BARBIERI, Jacopo Frascaroli, Greta Varesio, Francesca Piovesan, Ludovico Bechis, Pietro Sarasso, Irene Ronga
papers.abstract: A century-old tradition characterizes aesthetic experiences as intense contemplative moments in which we suspend practical concerns and devote our full attention to the object at hand. In line with this tradition, recent theories suggest that aesthetic experiences involve heightened sensory processing accompanied by a suppression of motor activity. Yet, while the link between aesthetic appreciation and perceptual enhancement has received considerable attention, the role of motor inhibition remains largely unexplored. The present study addressed this gap by investigating whether the aesthetic appreciation of images can modulate behavioral and electrophysiological markers of motor inhibition. In Experiment 1, significantly slower reaction times following the observation of preferred images were found. In Experiment 2, EEG responses associated with motor preparation and execution were significantly reduced in trials involving preferred compared with non-preferred images. Time-frequency analysis revealed significantly decreased alpha power (associated with attentional engagement toward visual perception) and increased beta power (associated with inhibited motor preparation) for preferred than non-preferred images. Overall, our results provide new evidence for the existence of a relationship between aesthetic appreciation and motor inhibition and position aesthetic experience as a valuable case study for exploring the adaptive coordination of sensory and motor systems in response to environmental demands.

papers.title: Deploying Meaningful Medical Informatics and Artificial Intelligence Solutions in the Clinical Field: A Call to Action for Researchers in Cardio-Oncology Informatics
papers.authors: Jacob Krive, Aarti H. Asnani, Paaladinesh Thavendiranathan, Marianna Krive, Teresa López‐Fernández
papers.abstract: Abstract Rapid advances in oncology care have resulted in a growing population of cancer survivors, many of whom suffer from short- and long-term cancer therapy related cardiovascular toxicities (CTR-CVT). Cardio-oncology aims to diagnose and manage these cardiovascular conditions, but part of the challenge pertains to finding such individuals among the millions of cancer survivors. Medical informatics may help identify patients eligible to receive cardio-oncology care, assess the risk of cardiovascular complications, and predict toxicity by employing artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms. Uncoordinated development of the medical informatics solutions for cardio-oncology has produced disparate algorithms aiming to predict CTR-CVT by analysing features of patient records in the context of clinical guidelines developed by organizations such as the American Heart Association, the American College of Cardiology, and the European Society of Cardiology. These algorithm development efforts emphasize narrowly-defined clinical goals, rather than integrating an entire array of the applicable data elements to provide medical professionals with comprehensive analyses resembling care delivery in community settings and translatable into clinical workflows. The resulting mismatch between solutions developed by informaticists and the needs of practicing clinicians has led to difficulty with external validation and practical application of these informatics solutions. Additionally, the latest AI and medical device developments, such as digital twins and wearables, enable new solutions to support clinical decision making and patient education in cancer survivorship care. We aim to describe, summarize, and evaluate these developments in a cohesive vision and call to action for medical informaticists to develop relevant translatable solutions for cardio-oncology.

papers.title: Adaptive Threshold-Based Logistic Regression Using Metaheuristic Optimization for Enhanced Binary Classification
papers.authors: Morukurthi Sreenivasu, Kumaran Kumar. J
papers.abstract: Abstract Logistic regression (LR) operated with fixed threshold for binary classification produce suboptimal results particularly for real-time scenarios expressed with imbalanced and noisy datasets. To improve the classification attributes of LR model in such scenarios, an adaptive threshold-based logistic regression (AT-LR)_ mechanism is proposed in this work. The threshold value of LR model is opted as decision parameter of the classification process and its optimal value evaluates with a popular metaheuristic algorithm known as teaching learning-based optimizer (TLBO). In the proposed AT-LR mechanism, the threshold adjusted dynamically according to data distribution characteristics with an objective of improving the classification accuracy. The performance of AT-LR model investigates on numerical, text and image datasets to check its applicability in different domains and the results presents with metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The extensive results with various datasets reveals the effectiveness of the AT-LR model over classical LR model operated with fixed threshold. In addition, comparisons provides with other machine learning classifiers to show the advantages of the AT-LR model offers a flexible and efficient solutions for complex binary classification problems.

papers.title: Higher education transformation through artificial intelligence: an empirical study in Saudi Arabia
papers.authors: HAYAT GHUNAIM, Mahmoud Masoud
papers.abstract: This study examines associations between AI awareness, readiness, ethical perceptions, attitude, and actual AI usage.Survey data from 424 students at King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals (KFUPM) were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Two structural models were compared: one specifying direct effects and a second in which attitude served as a partial mediator. In Model 1 (direct effects), only readiness and attitude were significantly associated with AI usage. In Model 2 (mediation), readiness retained both direct and indirect associations with usage via attitude; ethics displayed a competitive mediation structure, simultaneously building positive attitudes that supported usage while directly restraining use when ethical concerns remained unresolved ; and awareness remained non-significant across all paths. These findings advance adoption theory by repositioning awareness as a distal antecedent in high-penetration contexts, elevating readiness to a central dual-pathway antecedent, and providing the first structural evidence of competitive mediation for ethical perceptions in a higher education AI adoption model. For institutions, the findings indicate that building structured student capability and embedding transparent ethical governance are the two essential conditions for AI adoption that are not only widespread but also responsible and sustainable.

papers.title: Mind the gap: capability, policy and uncertainty in the adoption of generative AI within post-compulsory education
papers.authors: Paul Lees, Naomi Davis-Crane, Chris Taylor
papers.abstract: This qualitative, interpretivist study explores perceptions of Generative AI (GenAI) adoption among academic staff and Level 7 senior leader apprentices within a UK business school. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with sixteen participants, inductive thematic analysis revealed three interrelated themes: engagement under uncertainty, the capability gap, and the policy gap. Findings indicate that whilst participants recognise the potential utility associated with embracing GenAI, adoption is constrained by ethical sensitivity, limited application literacy, and the opacity of governance frameworks across the tripartite apprenticeship relationship. This study contributes to emergent debates on AI literacy and technological acceptance by surfacing how uncertainty is socially and structurally produced, offering practical recommendations for education providers seeking to embed GenAI both effectively and ethically.

papers.title: Different forms of interaction with generative AI in higher education: a latent profile analysis
papers.authors: Marcos Pascual‐Soler, Luca Delbello, Alejandro de Vega de Unceta, María Dolores Frías Navarro
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming how students interact with digital systems in learning contexts, although students differ substantially in how and why they use these technologies. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and adopting a person-centered approach, this study examined latent profiles of students’ interaction with generative AI based on autonomous motivation, amotivation, AI self-efficacy, and academic self-concept, and their associations with behavioral and attitudinal variables. A sample of 422 undergraduate students completed the study measures. Latent profile analysis identified four distinct user profiles: moderate functional users, self-determined and competent users, low-motivation users, and active competent users. Multinomial logistic regression indicated that AI user identity consistently differentiated the more adaptive profiles, whereas perceiving AI as a form of academic plagiarism was associated with the low-motivation profile. Positive expectations regarding the professional impact of AI were also associated with the self-determined and competent profile. Overall, the findings suggest that students’ relationships with generative AI reflect heterogeneous configurations of motivational regulation, perceived competence, and academic self-perceptions, associated with differences in AI-related identity, ethical beliefs, and professional expectations. These results highlight the importance of motivational heterogeneity in students’ use of generative AI.

papers.title: Examining measurement properties of AI literacy instruments in the era of generative artificial intelligence: a review study
papers.authors: Zhenghong Du, Tianle Dong, Bing Wei
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes embedded in interactive learning environments, measurement of AI literacy is central to instructional design and policy. Valid and reliable instruments are essential for capturing what AI literacy entails in the GenAI era, yet existing reviews have not systematically evaluated the quality of evidence for their measurement properties. This review applied the COSMIN methodology to assess the methodological quality and measurement properties of AI literacy instruments developed in the GenAI context. A search across five databases yielded 37 eligible empirical studies covering four populations, including students, teachers, employees, and the general public. Instrument development was concentrated in East Asian and Western regions and predominantly targeted university students. Self-report scales outnumbered performance-based assessments, with Likert-type formats dominating. The included instruments drew on a range of theoretical sources, with earlier AI literacy concepts often reframed, reorganized, or extended to fit different contexts and emerging assessment needs. Structural validity and internal consistency were the best-supported measurement properties, whereas evidence for several other applicable properties was limited or uncertain. Based on these findings, this review provides guidance for instrument selection according to assessment purpose while considering population and context.

papers.title: Teaching English language learners to prompt effectively: examining effects on prompt literacy, AI self-efficacy, and self-directed English learning readiness
papers.authors: Rahavi Murugesan, P Madhumathi
papers.abstract: Prompt literacy, Artificial Intelligence (AI) self-efficacy and self-directed learning (SDL) are increasingly recognized as essential skills and competencies for learners in the AI era, regardless of discipline. However, developing these key competencies in AI-assisted language learning contexts has received limited scholarly attention. This study examined whether structured instruction in prompt literacy could enhance learners’ prompt literacy, AI self-efficacy (AISE), and self-directed English learning readiness (SDELR) in GenAI-assisted learning contexts. 82 undergraduate English as a Second Language (ESL) learners were randomly assigned to a control group (CG), which received AI-assisted language instruction and an experimental group (EG) that additionally incorporated structured prompt literacy instruction. The results revealed that structured prompt literacy instruction significantly enhanced students’ prompt literacy and AISE. However, there were no marked differences between the two groups in SDELR. The study highlights the value of prompt literacy instruction in AI-based language learning contexts to promote equitable development of digital competencies essential for the AI era alongside language instruction. The findings have important implications for language learners, language educators, teacher educators and researchers.

papers.title: The AI-Provided Social Support Scale: Development, Psychometric Properties, and Its Relationship to Mental Health
papers.authors: Xinglu Shen, Sufen Chen, Sang Min Lee
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly functions as a source of social and emotional support, yet existing measureswere developed for human-human interactions.This study introduces the AI-Provided Social Support Scale (AISS), providing initial validation evidence. Using a split-sample of 684 adults, we examined its psychometric properties through exploratoryand confirmatory factor analysis. Results suggested a three-factor, 11-item structure comprising emotional support, social companionship, and functional support, reflectingAI’s blend of informational and instrumental assistance. The AISS showed moderate positive correlations with human-provided online social support. However, unlike human support being negatively associated with psychological distress, AI-provided support was not significantly related to depression, anxiety, or stress in this sample. These findings suggest that although users perceive AI as supportive, such interactions may function as a functional supplement or emotional companion in this sample, rather than showing the same associations with psychological distress typically associated with human-provided online support.

papers.title: How Agent-Driven Creative Trace Mining Reshapes Design Behavior in a Deployment Study of Intent-Aligned Multimodal Design
papers.authors: Seung Won Lee, Jiin Choi, Yejin Yun, Semin Jin, Yugyeong Jang, Geunmin Hwang, Sang Woon Park, Seonghoon Ban, Kyung Hoon Hyun
papers.abstract: Designers continuously capture inspirations across media, yet these creative traces remain underutilized in computational design support. We present DesignJournal, an agent-driven system that mines multimodal creative traces and transforms them into intent-aligned image generation. The system consolidates artifacts into a unified workspace and employs an agentic pipeline for structured grouping, belief-guided prompt refinement, and iterative intent updates. We developed a framework that classifies sequential design actions, deriving a hierarchical action taxonomy from interaction logs. We used it to examine how agent affordances reshape design behavior. A 10-day deployment study with eight professional designers compared baseline and agent-supported conditions across 5838 classified actions. Agent support significantly reduced the frequency of spatial repositioning actions, particularly small-distance movements, while sequential transition structures shifted from extended repositioning chains toward relational encoding sequences. Awareness of agent interpretation shaped upstream recording behavior, and agent-mediated collaboration extended designers’ creative reach beyond independent exploration.

papers.title: Activating Social Responses in Human–AI Interaction: The Effects of Reciprocal Self-Disclosure and Social Role Framing
papers.authors: Xuejiao Chen, Shuining Wang, Chen Chen, Yiming Zhao, Guoming Yu
papers.abstract: As chatbots become increasingly embedded in everyday communication, understanding when they elicit social responses is important. We conducted an experiment in which 169 participants interacted with LLM-based chatbots in a 2 (reciprocal self-disclosure: yes vs. no) × 3 (social role: mentor, companion, or assistant) between-subjects design. Self-esteem was measured before the interaction as an individual-difference factor. Factorial analyses showed that reciprocal self-disclosure increased users’ disclosure but did not significantly increase trust or perceived support; enjoyment was lower in the reciprocal-disclosure condition. Social role interacted with self-esteem in predicting self-disclosure quality, with favorable responses to the mentor role among participants with higher self-esteem. These findings suggest that chatbot social cues elicit different behavioral and evaluative responses and that role framing should account for user characteristics. The study offers a conditional account of social responding in human–AI interaction and implications for chatbot design in relational contexts.

papers.title: Deep fusion for multimodal subtype classification of major depressive disorders based on TSCANet
papers.authors: Yuchen Liang, Xuelin Gu, Jun Wang, Xiaoou Li, Lihong Pan
papers.journal: Computer Methods in Biomechanics & Biomedical Engineering
papers.abstract: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) represents a major global health burden, characterized by high recurrence rates and an increased risk of suicide. Traditional clinical diagnoses rely primarily on subjective scales, which limits their objectivity in accurately distinguishing MDD subtypes.To address these challenges, this study introduces a multimodal assessment framework that integrates EEG functional connectivity with clinical scale data.We developed TSCANet (Transformer Local-Global Graph Neural Network Scales Cross-Attention Network), a deep learning multimodal model designed to address the complexity of psychiatric data. TSCANet achieved classification accuracies of 82.62% and 81.36% in visual and auditory paradigms, respectively, outperforming single-modality models.

papers.title: Feminist Crip Co-Making with Speech-to-Text Accessibility Software
papers.authors: Amy Gaeta
papers.abstract: This creative-academic essay explores the use of speech-to-text software as a site of feminist crip practice and critical technological reflection. Blending insights from disability studies, feminist theory, personal narrative and AI ethics, the piece situates accessibility technology within broader histories of extraction, surveillance and disability. In light of this, it asks what it means to rely on speech-to-text software in creative practice and how it transforms ideas of authorship and resulting artistic outputs. By treating transcription errors, bodily interruptions and software failures as meaningful traces of co-composition, the essay develops an account of creative practice grounded in technological interdependence, willed passivity and reflexivity. It includes a critical overview of disability and technology, an account of the author's poetic practice and original poems co-written with a speech-to-text software. These poems all mediate themes central to the author's theoretical provocation: passivity, accessibility and artificiality.

papers.title: Research on ChatGPT in higher education: shifting from exploration to policy development
papers.authors: Baomin Qi, Mark Ching‐Pong Poo, Chengbo Wang, Bing Wang
papers.journal: Journal of Further and Higher Education
papers.abstract: The Covid-19 outbreak has brought the digital transformation of the higher education sector to a new level. Technologies like ChatGPT have significantly impacted learning and teaching, raising concerns about academic integrity and the effects on students’ critical thinking ability. Research on ChatGPT in higher education has garnered substantial attention from academics and practitioners, with various facets explored in the literature. However, given its recent emergence, systematic reviews and holistic views of the research landscape in this field remain scarce. Using a bibliometric analysis approach, our research retrieved and analysed 461 publications using VOSviewer and Dimensions. Through citation and keyword co-occurrence network mapping, four research trends with accompanying sub-themes emerged in the academic literature: ChatGPT as an educational application, its integration into the higher education system, learners’ perspectives on ChatGPT, and its Challenges of implementation. Additionally, our study revealed an evolutionary shift in research attention within the domain, from earlier studies focusing on the use of ChatGPT in higher education (HE) to recent concerns about HE policies and regulations. Our study’s results offer insights into the research landscape of ChatGPT in HE and help inform future research directions.

papers.title: AI-mediated teaching of oral interpreting: professional judgment, teacher agency, and human oversight
papers.authors: Lixuan Sun, Weize Sun
papers.journal: British Journal of Guidance and Counselling
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in the teaching of oral interpreting, where university students practise spoken-language mediation across languages, such as listening to a source-language speech and orally rendering it into another language. This qualitative study examines how twelve higher education teachers engaged with large language models, automated speech recognition, and machine translation in oral interpreting courses. Semi-structured interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings suggest that participants positioned AI as a pedagogical resource rather than a substitute for professional expertise. Teacher agency was enacted through boundary-setting, instructional redesign, and human oversight, while professional judgment centred on evaluating, contextualising, and regulating AI-generated outputs. The study argues that AI-mediated oral interpreting education reconfigures, rather than replaces, professional practice. It recommends teacher development and institutional guidance that support critical evaluation, calibrated reliance, ethical boundary-setting, and human oversight.

papers.title: Between caution and adaptation. Artificial intelligence in Polish social work practice
papers.authors: Ryszard Necel
papers.abstract: This article examines how Polish social work practitioners perceive artificial intelligence (AI), the extent of its adoption, and the hopes and concerns linked to its use. In December 2025, a nationwide Computer-Assisted Web Interview (CAWI) survey was conducted with 1,243 social workers and managers employed in social assistance centres. Findings show adoption is at an early stage: some respondents use generative tools, but for many AI remains marginal or absent from everyday practice. Perceived benefits focus on back-office support – saving time, organising and synthesising information, improving documentation quality – and thus freeing staff for relationship-based work with clients. Assessments of potential applications form a clear hierarchy: text support, translation, summarisation and information management are rated highest, whereas tools affecting direct client interactions (e.g. chatbots, automated diagnosis or needs assessment) raise the greatest concern. Key barriers are institutional and competence-related, including unclear rules, limited organisational readiness, and gaps in knowledge and training across diverse local welfare contexts.

papers.title: Different lenses on human-AI collaboration: towards a comprehensive view on hybrid intelligence in education
papers.authors: Anne Horvers, Inge Molenaar, Karcie Snoeijen, Oana Costache, Joep van der Graaf, Anne‐Wil Kramer, Susanne M. M. de Mooij, Paraskevi Topali, Zowi Vermeire, Peter J. C. Sleegers
papers.abstract: This paper aims to deepen our understanding of hybrid intelligence in education by investigating human-AI collaboration in four real-world educational use cases. We argue against the simple view of automation and augmentation as distinct processes and foreground the automation-augmentation paradox. This paradox proposes a comprehensive view of automation and augmentation as co-occurrent processes that drive task allocation between humans and AI. We use this paradox as an analytical lens to examine patterns of task changes in human-AI collaboration across four educational use cases. This study approaches teacher-AI collaboration as emerging from task-level changes when AI tools are implemented in educational settings, and these task-level changes are conceptualised as replacement, complementation, and transformation. Across cases, the analysis suggests that automation and augmentation are distributed across different stages in the instructional process. Replacement was primarily situated in bounded analytical subtasks, whereas complementation emerged when teachers interpret, validate and enact AI-generated output. Transformation was most visible in the planning and reflection phases. The cases illustrate how AI may redistribute tasks between teachers and AI systems without displacing teachers’ pedagogical judgement. These findings suggest that the automation-augmentation paradox can serve as a useful analytical lens for analysing meaningful patterns of human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: Using a theory-based approach to explore medical students’ engagement with exemplar-based feedback and self-reflection for communication skills
papers.authors: Thea G. Musselman, Kendra Hester, Jason Snyder, Angelo E. D’Addario, Anastasiya A. Lipnevich, Krista Mattern
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Patient-Centered Communication (PCC) is essential to quality medical care and a crucial skill in medical education. While prior studies have focused on communication skills training in medical education, less is known about how learners engage in self-reflection when learning and practicing communication skills. The current study investigates levels of learner cognitive and reflective engagement with exemplar-based feedback and guided self-reflection to inform best practices for integrating self-regulated learning (SRL) supports in medical education. METHODS: Participants consisted of medical students in years one through three. Participants watched video vignettes depicting patients asking a question or making a statement, recorded verbal responses to the patients, reviewed their response alongside two exemplar responses, and completed a self-evaluation checklist aligned with defined communication learning objectives, and responded to three structured reflection prompts comparing their responses to the exemplars. Using an AI-assisted, human-in-the-loop coding process, participant engagement was evaluated using the ICAP taxonomy and Kember categorizations, each coded on a 1-4 scale reflecting framework-specific criteria. SRL strategies were coded as a separate unit of analysis that informed engagement. RESULTS: (Kember) engagement at least once, along with widespread use of SRL strategies. Engagement varied between reflection prompts and across vignettes, with the third prompt and certain vignettes consistently eliciting deeper engagement. DISCUSSION: Results indicate that learners engaged meaningfully with exemplar-based feedback and self-reflection. Deeper engagement emerged with prompts that required comparison or improvement planning. While engagement varied by vignette and prompt, learners employed SRL strategies in nearly every reflection. These findings indicate that the use of exemplar responses and enhanced prompt design may support broader conceptual and deeper future learning.

papers.title: An integrated model of executive function, AI literacy, and Chinese L2 reading comprehension among ethnic minority adolescents in Hong Kong
papers.authors: Zheng Liang Sun, Yau Yu Chan
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in second language (L2) learning, yet the cognitive demands of AI-mediated environments, particularly for logographic languages such as Chinese, remain underexplored. This study investigated the interrelationships among executive function (EF), reading-related linguistic skills, AI literacy, and Chinese L2 reading comprehension in 155 Form 4 Southeast Asian ethnic minority students in Hong Kong. Using a quantitative design, we validated a three-factor EF model (working memory, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control) and examined how these components, together with orthographic and morphological skills, relate to L2 reading outcomes. Structural equation modeling showed that all three EF components significantly predicted reading comprehension, underscoring the importance of executive control for processing a complex logographic script. AI literacy significantly supported both foundational reading skills and overall reading comprehension. A key finding of the integrated model is that cognitive flexibility significantly predicted AI literacy, which in turn significantly predicted reading comprehension, indicating an indirect pathway from EF to reading via AI literacy. This pattern highlights the cognitive underpinnings of digital engagement in L2 learning. The study extends the Reading Systems Framework by positioning AI literacy as an external scaffold that interacts with learners’ cognitive resources, and offers practical implications for designing cognitively supportive, AI-enhanced Chinese L2 instruction for ethnic minority learners.

papers.title: Large Language Models versus Expert Response: A Comparative Analysis of Patient Education Quality after Skull Base Surgery
papers.authors: Mahmood Manavi, Noel Ayoub, Arifeen S. Rahman, Jacquelyn Callender, Lirit Levi, David Tianxiang Liu, Axel Eluid Renteria, M. Fieux, Matei A. Banu, Juan Carlos Fernandez-Miranda, Peter Hwang, Jayakar Nayak, Zara M. Patel, Michael T. Chang
papers.journal: Journal of Neurological Surgery Part B Skull Base
papers.abstract: Abstract Patients undergoing endoscopic skull base surgery (ESBS) often seek postoperative guidance. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly accessible resources, but their quality in this setting remains poorly studied. This study compared LLM-generated responses with expert responses for common postoperative ESBS questions. Eight common postoperative questions were answered by seven LLMs (ChatGPT-o1, Gemini, Claude, Meta, GROK, DeepSeek, Copilot) and expert surgeons. Eight blinded raters evaluated responses for understandability and actionability using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), while accuracy was graded on a 5-point Likert scale. Readability was assessed using Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) and Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES). ANOVA with Tukey's honestly significant difference (HSD) tested group differences. Most LLM-generated responses showed accuracy comparable to expert responses (p > 0.05), except ChatGPT-o1, which scored lower (p = 0.006). Significant differences were found in understandability (F(7, 56) = 23.42, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.75) and actionability (F(7, 56) = 21.06, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.72). Gemini, GROK, Meta, and DeepSeek achieved the highest PEMAT scores. Expert responses scored lowest on PEMAT. Expert and Claude required college-level reading, whereas ChatGPT-o1 and Copilot produced grade school–level content. Gemini, GROK, Meta, and DeepSeek produced high school–level text. LLMs generated responses that were more understandable, actionable, and readable than expert responses while maintaining comparable accuracy. LLMs may improve postoperative counseling after skull base surgery, though expert oversight remains essential.

papers.title: Preface
papers.authors: Lik Yin Ng, Bee Lin Chua, Kin Wai Cheah
papers.abstract: The Symposium of Malaysian Chemical Engineers (SOMChE) is an established annual event that provides a platform for researchers, academics, industry practitioners, professionals and students to share research findings, exchange knowledge and establish collaborations across the chemical engineering community.The 2026 symposium marked the 35th edition of SOMChE and continued its longstanding role in bringing together the Malaysian and international chemical engineering communities.The theme of SOMChE 2026, "Intelligent and Integrated Chemical Engineering for Global Challenges," reflects the rapidly changing role of chemical engineering in addressing increasingly complex and interconnected global issues.Challenges associated with sustainability, climate change, energy transition, resource efficiency, environmental protection, food and pharmaceutical production, advanced materials, process safety and industrial transformation require solutions that extend beyond conventional disciplinary boundaries.At the same time, developments in artificial intelligence, digitalisation, advanced modelling, smart manufacturing and data-driven engineering are creating new opportunities for the design, optimisation and operation of chemical processes and products.Against this background, SOMChE 2026 provided a forum to explore how intelligent technologies, integrated engineering approaches and sustainable practices can be combined to address these challenges.The symposium encouraged interaction among researchers from different disciplines and between academia and industry, with emphasis on translating scientific and engineering advances into practical and sustainable solutions.The scientific scope of SOMChE 2026 encompassed key areas of contemporary chemical and biochemical engineering, including Bioprocess Engineering and Biotechnology; Polymer Science and Engineering; Chemical Engineering Education and Professional Development; Process and Product Synthesis and Design; Computational Methods in Chemical Engineering; Process Intensification and Optimisation; Environmental Impact and Green Chemistry; Process Safety and Risk Management; Food and Pharmaceutical Engineering; Renewable Energy and Biochemical Engineering; Materials and Corrosion Science; Smart Manufacturing and Industry 4.0 in Chemical Engineering;
