The review supports the conclusion that AI is neither positive nor negative in and of itself: its effects depend on the pedagogical purpose, teacher guidance, digital literacy, and the ethical standards governing its use. Therefore, the study proposes the responsible use of AI as a complementary tool, without replacing human interaction or the student’s intellectual effort.

papers.title: Aprendizaje situado en MIPyMES de Nayarit: proyecto integrador con inteligencia artificial en estudiantes de Administración
papers.authors: Jorge Luis Hernández Ulloa, Juan Antonio Nievas López, P N Foster, Gabriel Carrillo Herrera, Héctor Vicente Cisneros Chávez, José Manuel Rodríguez Martínez
papers.abstract: Training in Business Administration requires linking the classroom with the problems faced by local companies. This study aims to describe changes in the knowledge and self-perceived abilities of Business Administration students after an integrative project in which they diagnosed micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) with the support of artificial intelligence (AI). The study followed a descriptive mixed-methods approach, with a pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design and an intermediate follow-up. Participants were 22 fourth-semester students at the Autonomous University of Nayarit, who diagnosed 11 companies during an intersemester course supported by NotebookLM notebooks prepared by the instructor. Three questionnaires with closed and open-ended questions were administered. On the eleven knowledge questions repeated at the beginning and at the end, correct answers rose from 85.1% to 95.9%, and agreement with self-perception statements rose from 52.3% to 88.1%, with the greatest progress in financial content. The main difficulty was defining the company's core problem, while AI was used mainly for writing. The results are consistent with the project's formative purpose and suggest that problem formulation and the use of AI to verify analysis should be taught explicitly.

papers.title: The Role of English Language Learning Technology in Enhancing Students' Learning Interest
papers.authors: I Gusti Ngurah Bagus Yoga Widiadnya, I Gusti Ngurah Octova Seventilofa, Kadek Ayu Kartika Septiana
papers.journal: Al-Qalbu Jurnal Pendidikan Sosial dan Sains
papers.abstract: In modern education, technology plays an indispensable role, fundamentally reshaping instructional and learning methods across diverse academic fields, particularly within English language teaching. The integration of digital learning technologies provides innovative opportunities to improve students' engagement, motivation, and learning interest. This study aims to explore how English language learning technology enhances students' interest in learning English through a qualitative research approach. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and document analysis involving English teachers and secondary school students. The findings reveal that technology-based learning environments encourage active participation, foster collaborative learning, increase students' confidence, and provide flexible access to learning resources. Applications such as Google Classroom, Quizizz, Kahoot!, Duolingo, YouTube, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based learning platforms positively influence students' enthusiasm toward English learning by making lessons more interactive and enjoyable. The study concludes that educational technology can substantially improve students' learning interest when integrated with appropriate pedagogical strategies and adequate institutional support. The findings provide valuable insights for educators, policymakers, and curriculum developers seeking to enhance English language education in the digital era

papers.title: Auditor Independence as an Ethical Control Mechanism in Data Driven Audit Decision Making in Accounting
papers.authors: Nur Alimin Azis
papers.journal: Mandalika Journal of Business and Management Studies
papers.abstract: This study explores the role of auditor independence as an ethical control mechanism in the context of data-driven audit decision-making within accounting. As technology, such as big data analytics and machine learning, becomes increasingly integrated into the audit process, maintaining auditor independence has become a critical challenge. The primary objective of this research is to analyze how ethical controls, particularly auditor independence, can be preserved in a data-driven auditing environment. A qualitative literature review was conducted, examining relevant peer-reviewed articles, books, and case studies over the past two decades. The findings reveal that while technology enhances audit efficiency, it also risks undermining auditor independence by fostering over-reliance on automated systems. However, effective ethical controls, including adherence to professional guidelines, regulatory oversight, and ongoing professional development, can mitigate these risks. The research concludes that auditor independence remains essential for ensuring objectivity and trust in the audit process, even as technology continues to evolve. Strengthening ethical oversight and developing clear frameworks are crucial for maintaining auditor independence while leveraging technological advancements in auditing. This study provides significant insights for auditors, regulatory bodies, and organizations to navigate the complexities of modern audit practices.

papers.title: AI-Gamified Interactive HOTS E-Book for Enhancing ESP Students’ Critical Thinking
papers.authors: Kurnia, Abdul Wahab, Jutamanee Kraikunasai, Pratiwi Samad
papers.abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital learning technology has moved quickly, opening fresh possibilities for strengthening English language instruction, particularly within English for Specific Purposes (ESP) settings. Even so, a substantial number of ESP learners continue to struggle in building English proficiency and higher-order thinking abilities, largely because interactive learning resources remain limited and conventional teaching methods still dominate. This study set out to design and assess an AI-gamified interactive HOTS e-book intended to strengthen ESP students' critical thinking. A Research and Development (R&D) approach was adopted, guided by the Decide, Design, Develop, and Evaluate (DDD-E) model. Participants consisted of ESP students at Universitas Muhammadiyah Mamuju. Data were gathered using expert validation sheets, student practicality questionnaires, and effectiveness tests. Findings showed that the developed AI-gamified interactive HOTS e-book fell into the very valid category based on expert assessment, with an overall mean score of 3.85. Student responses pointed to a highly practical product, averaging 3.69. The effectiveness test further revealed a marked gain in students' learning outcomes, with mean scores rising from 58.67 at pre-test to 87.53 at post-test and an N-gain score of 0.717, placed in the high-improvement category. The study concludes that the AI-gamified interactive HOTS e-book stands as a valid, practical, and effective digital learning medium for advancing ESP students' critical thinking and their English learning progress.

papers.title: Sostenibilità in cloud: il costo idrico nascosto dell’IA
papers.authors: Valentina Cavani
papers.abstract: L’intelligenza artificiale è sempre più rappresentata come strumento al servizio della sostenibilità, capace di ottimizzare processi produttivi, monitorare fenomeni ambientali e supportare la transizione ecologica. Tuttavia, dietro questa immagine si nasconde un costo materiale rilevante: l’enorme consumo idrico dei data center, infrastrutture indispensabili al funzionamento dell’IA generativa. Il saggio analizza questa tensione, proponendo di leggere l’IA come pharmakon ambientale, insieme rimedio e minaccia. Dopo aver ricostruito l’impatto idrico dei sistemi di IA e la persistente opacità delle aziende tecnologiche in materia di trasparenza ambientale, si esamina lo squilibrio generato tra i benefici globali del digitale e i costi idrici scaricati sulle comunità locali. Particolare attenzione è dedicata al quadro europeo: da un lato, politiche che coniugano digitalizzazione e sostenibilità; dall’altro, l’assenza di un’adeguata considerazione dell’impronta idrica nel recente AI Act. Il contributo evidenzia i limiti di una regolazione fondata esclusivamente sulla disclosure ambientale e sottolinea la necessità di un approccio coerente con i principi del diritto ambientale – precauzione, prevenzione, responsabilità e giustizia intergenerazionale. In chiusura, viene discusso il contesto statunitense, segnato da approcci frammentari e conflitti idrici crescenti. L’articolo sostiene che solo un’integrazione organica della sostenibilità nelle politiche sull’IA – e in particolare della sua dimensione idrica – può garantire che l’innovazione digitale non comprometta i diritti fondamentali legati all’acqua e all’ambiente.

papers.title: AI and Education: The Social and Critical Pedagogies of Friedrich D. E. Schleiermacher and Paulo Freire as Resources for Contemporary Critiques of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Stephen Morrison
papers.abstract: Peer reviewed

papers.title: Outlier Resistant Inference for Conditional Average Treatment Effect
papers.authors: Ran Mo, Honglang Wang
papers.abstract: The estimation of causal effects based on the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) is usually vulnerable to outliers.However, to the best of our knowledge, outlier-resistant inference for the CATE has not been investigated in the literature.In this work, we propose an outlier-resistant estimation method for the CATE by incorporating M-estimation into the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) approach.The influence function and breakdown property are investigated to study the robustness of our method.In addition, we derive the asymptotic properties of the proposed estimator for inference purposes.The finite sample performance of the proposed estimator is evaluated via Monte Carlo experiments.The proposed method is compared with the IPW method and the augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) method, which do not account for outliers, as well as with DR-learner variants and machine-learning meta-learners, including the causal forest, X-learner, and R-learner.Finally, the proposed method is applied to the NHANES dataset to estimate the average effects of physical activity on albumin levels conditioned on age.

papers.title: Development of Oral English Production Through Artificial Intelligence Tools in Eight Grade Students at Unidad Educativa Fiscal Bicentenario D7
papers.authors: Carla Gabriela Morales Zaruma, Katherine Vanessa Pastas Rosero, María Germania Martínez Torres, Darío Javier Paredes-Granda, Cristina Maribel Tapia Sarabia
papers.journal: LATAM Revista Latinoamericana de Ciencias Sociales y Humanidades
papers.abstract: Modern society is undergoing rapid educational changes driven by technological evolution and rising academic demands, establishing Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) as key tools for teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL). This study evaluates the use of AI tools to enhance oral production (speaking skills) among 107 eighth-grade students (sections A, B, and C) at the *Unidad Educativa Fiscal Bicentenario D7 Vespertino* in Quito, Ecuador. The methodology employed a quantitative, descriptive field study design. Key diagnostic findings reveal that 73% of students struggle with initial oral fluency, and 75% report frequent pronunciation errors. However, 68% state that practicing with AI tools boosts their confidence and significantly reduces communication anxiety when speaking in public. Furthermore, 70% demonstrate high motivation for learning through technological resources. Critical limitations identified include limited instructional time (three hours per week), a lack of independent practice outside the classroom (75%), and recurring connectivity and infrastructure issues (56%). The study concludes that overcoming these barriers and the digital divide requires the design and implementation of low-data adaptive micro-learning modules, independent practice guides, and continuous teacher training workshops.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Digital Human Rights Education: Building Ethical Literacy in High-Tech Societies
papers.authors: SAM OMOTOSO
papers.journal: JOURNAL OF LAW AND GLOBAL POLICY
papers.abstract: The intersection of artificial intelligence and human rights education represents a transformative moment in the democratization of knowledge. This article examines how digital platforms including social media, online courses, podcasts, and webinars are revolutionizing human rights education delivery and accessibility. Drawing on recent scholarship and policy developments, this paper explores the potential of AI enhanced digital tools to build ethical literacy in high tech societies while addressing the challenges of digital divides, algorithmic bias, and equitable access. The analysis incorporates perspectives from the Global South, emphasizing the need for context driven, rights-based approaches to AI integration in educational systems. Through examination of current initiatives, pedagogical innovations, and ethical frameworks, this article demonstrates that while AI offers unprecedented opportunities for expanding human rights education, its implementation must be carefully governed to prevent the exacerbation of existing inequalities.

papers.title: Stewardship of Creation: Eco theology, Church History, and Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Sustainability in Nigeria
papers.authors: Moses Adeiza (Ph.D.) Odei
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE
papers.abstract: Nigeria faces a convergence of severe environmental crises, including advancing desertification in the north, persistent oil pollution in the Niger Delta, and deadly farmer herder conflicts intensified by climate change and shrinking natural resources. This article argues that these challenges are not merely economic or political but are fundamentally moral and spiritual, requiring a robust theological response from the Nigerian church. Employing a newly developed framework, the Creation Mandate Stewardship Theory (CMST), grounded in the Genesis mandate and enriched by African theological insights from scholars such as Mbiti and Bediako, the study examines human responsibility toward creation through three pillars: divine ownership, relational responsibility, and accountable action. Adopting a church-historical lens, the article traces the Nigerian church's trajectory from missionary-era neglect of ecological concerns through a period of prosperity-focused silence during Nigeria's most intense years of environmental exploitation to emerging but uneven engagement with creation care in contemporary mainline denominations. Biblical foundations and African ecotheological perspectives, including the contributions of Oduyoye and Kunhiyop, are presented as resources for reframing environmental stewardship as intrinsic to Christian mission rather than a foreign import. The article further explores artificial intelligence as an emerging tool for climate monitoring, agricultural extension, conflict mitigation, and multilingual environmental education while cautioning that technology must remain subordinate to theological conviction and community trust. Institutional, economic, theological, and technological barriers to church-led environmental action are identified. The article concludes with concrete recommendations for denominations, seminaries, and policymakers, urging the Nigerian church to embrace its calling as a steward, not owner, of creation and to become an active agent of ecological healing and social peace.

papers.title: Methods of Using Artificial Intelligence in the Development of Students' English Skills
papers.authors: Durdona Baxtiyorova
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES
papers.abstract: The article covers the methods and prospects of using artificial intelligence in developing students' English language skills. The growth and development of artificial intelligence during 1950-2010 is specifically written about the development indicators of students in language learning.

papers.title: Pronunciation Patterns of Primary and Secondary School Teachers in Ekiti State: AI to the Rescue
papers.authors: Mercy Adenike Bankole
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE AND COMMUNICATION STUDIES
papers.abstract: Pronunciation is a fundamental aspect of spoken language that affects effective communication in English. The teacher’s good pronunciation plays a critical role in learners’ ability to acquire the target language as they are expected to serve as models for the students. This research seeks to investigate the pronunciation patterns of Primary and Secondary school teachers in Ekiti State and to also explore the potentials of Artificial Intelligence in improving their pronunciation. The study was examined within the purview of Chomsky and Halle’s Generative Phonology, which was employed to generate rules which account for the patterns of the participants’ realizations of English sounds. A total number of sixty teachers were purposively selected from Ekiti State three senatorial districts for the study; thirty from Primary schools and thirty teachers of English from Secondary schools. The data for the study were collected through structured questionnaire and a prepared word list given to each participant to be read into recording device. The data collected were listened to and transcribed in order to identify patterns of the participants’ pronunciation and also subjected to phonological and descriptive analyses. The findings show the phonological features that characterized the pronunciations of the selected participants which are substitution, de-affrication, neutralization, de-dentalisation, devoicing and reduced vowels of English. The study, therefore, explored the potentials of Artificial Intelligence in improving their pronunciation as models for learners to emulate.

papers.title: Analysis of the Use of Artificial Intelligence and Its Impact on the Character and Cultural Identity of Junior High School Students at Homeschooling Smart Makassar
papers.authors: Ahmad Farid Kadir, Rina Rina, Astri Astri, Haslinda Firman, Dewi Amanda, Muslin Muslin, Ermi Sola
papers.abstract: This study analyzes teachers' strategies for using Artificial Intelligence (AI) as an instructional medium and its implications for the character development and cultural identity of junior secondary (SMP) students in a homeschooling setting. Unlike prior studies focusing on students' direct use of AI, this study positions the teacher as the pedagogical agent mediating AI use. A qualitative single case study, grounded in an interpretive/constructivist paradigm, was conducted at Homeschooling Smart Makassar, involving three teachers as primary informants and three students and three parents as supporting informants for triangulation. Data were analyzed through data condensation, display, and conclusion drawing, with trustworthiness maintained via triangulation, member checking, and peer debriefing. Findings show that all three teachers consistently curated AI outputs before delivering them to students, indicating augmentation of the teacher's role rather than automation. AI use was associated with increased learning engagement, while its influence on academic honesty and critical thinking depended on each teacher's policy strictness. On cultural identity, findings diverged: one class showed enrichment of formal-language vocabulary, another showed increased slang use, while the family remained the primary space for maintaining local language and culture. These findings are synthesized into a Three-Layer Teacher Mediation Model (technical curation, character safeguarding, and cultural strengthening), indicating that AI's influence on character and cultural identity is shaped more by teachers' mediation strategies than by the technology itself.

papers.title: Productivity Narratives and Environmental Blind Spots: A Systematic Review of How Organizations Weigh Environmental Criteria When Adopting Generative AI
papers.authors: Noé Chávez- Hernández, Beatriz Sauza -Ávila
papers.journal: Social science and human research bulletin.
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) spreads through organizations faster than any shared method for weighing its environmental cost. Two literatures study the phenomenon from opposite ends. Adoption research explains why firms take up GenAI; environmental research measures the energy, water, and carbon it consumes. Whether the first treats the findings of the second as decision criteria remains unexamined. This systematic review asks how organizations incorporate environmental criteria into GenAI adoption and tests the proposition that productivity and modernization narratives dominate adoption and limit environmental governance. A TITLE-ABS-KEY search combining GenAI, adoption, and environmental terms yielded a corpus of 59 sources; main findings were extracted for 46 and grouped by the role each study assigns to the environment. Fourteen studies explain adoption through readiness, institutional pressure, top management support, and ethical leadership. None records ecological cost as a determinant, while six model ethics explicitly. Eleven studies treat environmental performance as an outcome of adoption. Twenty-one measures the environmental burden or proposes instruments to govern it, yet only six tie those instruments to organizational decisions. The evidence supports the proposition with one qualification: environmental criteria are absent from adoption models, which is different from absent from practice. The review separates two meanings of "environmental" that the literature conflates, consolidates candidate decision criteria, and sets an agenda for testing ecological cost as an antecedent of adoption.

papers.title: Technology acceptance of AI generated content among film and television educators: A comparative study of China and Thailand
papers.authors: Hao Pang, Hao WU, Achiraya Sopamanomas, Clinton Chidiebere Anyanwu
papers.abstract: The study examines the adoption of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) technologies by film and television educators in China and Thailand, analyzing cultural differences in perceptions and usage using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Hofstede's cultural dimensions. The study employed a quantitative comparative design and collected survey data from 120 educators (68 from China and 52 from Thailand) at two institutions. Independent-samples t-tests and regression analyses were used to analyze the perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, and actual usage of AIGC technologies. Cultural differences were obvious, and Chinese educators reported higher perceived usefulness, behavioral intention, and actual usage of AIGC than Thai educators. Regression analysis showed that perceived usefulness and ease of use were significant predictors of behavioral intention, which was a strong predictor of actual use. Cultural dimensions influenced acceptance attitudes but did not significantly moderate the core relationships of TAM. The findings indicate that the application of AIGC in film and television education should be culturally sensitive. The development of curricula and professional development for educators to successfully adopt AIGC technologies should be sensitive to cultural factors. The study adds to the knowledge about technology acceptance in the context of creative education, and highlights the interaction between technology, culture, and pedagogy.

papers.title: Factors Influencing the Readiness of Small Retail Stores in Guntur City to Adopt AI-Powered Inventory Management Systems: A Study Using Primary Survey Evidence and Secondary Literature
papers.authors: Raja Pavan, N Devi Sreeja
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: This study examines factors associated with the readiness of small retail businesses in Guntur City to adopt AI-powered inventory management systems. The analysis combines a small primary survey dataset (20 usable responses) with a focused review of recent scholarly literature on AI adoption in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), technology adoption, and AI-supported inventory management. The survey instrument covered AI awareness, digital skills, technological infrastructure, perceived ease of use, expected inventory benefits, affordability, financial readiness, organizational support, employee willingness, trust, adoption intention, and overall readiness. Descriptive results indicate moderate overall readiness: the mean score for overall readiness was 3.20 on a five-point scale, while willingness to adopt within two years averaged 2.75. Among the measured items, trust in AI-generated inventory recommendations had the highest mean (3.20), whereas infrastructure averaged 2.65. In the correlation analysis, cost affordability showed the strongest association with overall readiness (r = 0.49), followed by employee willingness (r = 0.47) and adoption intention (r = 0.39). Because the sample is small and non-probability based, these results are exploratory and are not presented as population estimates or causal findings. The study identifies affordability, employee capability, digital infrastructure, training, and trust as useful areas for a larger follow-up investigation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as Cognitive Scaffolding for Executive Functioning in Students with Special Educational Needs
papers.authors: Ilias Vasileiou, Evangelos Mantsos, Zoe Krokou, Olga Kofa, Georgios Polydoros
papers.journal: Journal of Educational Technology and E-Learning Innovations
papers.abstract: Executive functioning enables learners to organize work, monitor progress, and decide when a response needs revision. For some students with special educational needs, difficulties in these areas can restrict participation even when they understand the subject matter. This critical narrative review considers whether artificial intelligence can reduce such barriers and, more importantly, what kind of support it actually provides. Research on executive functions, self-regulated learning, artificial intelligence in education, and special education was brought together to examine intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive platforms, planning tools, learning analytics, conversational agents, and generative AI. Across this literature, a recurring distinction emerges. Some applications compensate for an executive demand, others scaffold performance while a task is being completed, and a smaller group are designed to foster strategies that learners can later use without the tool. These outcomes should not be treated as equivalent. Completing a task successfully with automated prompts does not, by itself, demonstrate lasting improvement in executive functioning. AI may nevertheless be useful when support is tied to a clearly defined learning goal, interpreted by a teacher, and adjusted or faded in response to the learner’s progress. Its use also raises practical concerns about cognitive offloading, inaccurate feedback, privacy, bias, and unequal access. The review proposes a three-function framework - compensation, scaffolding, and development - for planning and evaluating AI-supported practice.

papers.title: Readability assessment of ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-5 responses to ear care questions
papers.authors: Cemal Özyılmaz, Mehmet Fatih Karakuş
papers.abstract: Aim: To assess the readability of ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5 responses to questions about ear care. Materials and Methods: Ten questions about ear care from the World Health Organization’s ‘Questions and Answers’ section were each posed seven times to both ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-5. A total of 70 responses were obtained and analyzed for readability. Results: For ChatGPT-4o, the mean readability scores were: Flesch Reading Ease 62.84 ± 8.32, Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level 8.13 ± 1.59, Simple Measure of Gobbledygook 7.35 ± 1.42, Gunning Fog Index 8.44 ± 1.79, Coleman–Liau Index 9.62 ± 1.71, and Automated Readability Index 8.70 ± 2.02. For ChatGPT-5, the corresponding scores were: Flesch Reading Ease 72.93 ± 7.69, Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level 5.75 ± 1.17, Simple Measure of Gobbledygook 6.35 ± 0.79, Gunning Fog Index 7.37 ± 1.22, Coleman–Liau Index 7.32 ± 1.52, and Automated Readability Index 5.78 ± 1.42. ChatGPT-5 demonstrated better readability than ChatGPT-4o across all readability indices (p<0.001). Conclusion: The readability of the answers produced by ChatGPT-4o is “standard”, and that of ChatGPT-5 is “fairly easy”. ChatGPT-5 responses showed improved readability over ChatGPT-4o, aligning more closely with patient education readability standards and underscoring its potential as an accessible source of health information.

papers.title: Techno-Wellbeing and Flourishing in Higher Education: Student Experiences of Using Generative AI
papers.authors: Sue Beckingham, Joel Gray, Victoria Mellon, Helen J. Parkin
papers.abstract: In recent years, the rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has sparked widespread interest, optimism, and concern. Tools such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini are increasingly used by students to support academic tasks, manage workloads, and navigate personal challenges. While much of the discourse has focused on academic integrity and performance, relatively little is known about how these technologies shape students’ psychological wellbeing, sense of self, and capacity to flourish during their university experience. Drawing on flourishing theory, this study explores how GenAI adoption intersects with students’ personal, academic and emerging professional lives, including its perceived role as mentor, coach or companion. Flourishing provided a lens to examine broader dimensions of wellbeing such as purpose, engagement, relationships and optimism in the context of GenAI. Utilising the Listening Room methodology, friendship pairs from a UK university took part in timed, prompt-led conversations, sharing their lived experiences of using GenAI. Findings indicate that students predominantly use GenAI as an augmentative tool to translate briefs, break down tasks, provide exemplars and refine communication, which enhance perceived competence and increase engagement and confidence in academic work. At the same time, students expressed concerns about fairness, academic integrity, over-reliance, skill atrophy, misinformation and the idea of GenAI as an emotional “friend”, highlighting potential risks to self-respect, authentic relationships and trust in assessment. The study concludes that GenAI can both support and erode flourishing, stressing the need for human-centred institutional guidance that foregrounds wellbeing, alongside moral integrity and academic outcomes.

papers.title: Deliverable D4.2: Cognitive Coordinator and (X)AI Aggregator of Human-Centric 6G Trustworthiness
papers.authors: Stéphane Lorin, Dimitrios Roidis
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This deliverable presents the architectural design and development of the Cognitive Coordinator(CoCo) and eXplainable AI (XAI) module, building upon the SAFE-6G reference architecture establishedin D2.2 and the initial architectural and implementation work presented in D4.1. Together, thesecomponents provide the cognitive coordination and explainability capabilities of the SAFE-6Gtrustworthiness framework, supporting the interpretation of user-defined trustworthinessrequirements, the coordination of the five Trust Functions (Safety, Security, Privacy, Resilience andReliability) and the explanation of the decisions produced throughout the trustworthiness provisionlifecycle. The Cognitive Coordinator is responsible for managing the end-to-end processing of user requests,translating the trustworthiness requirements expressed through the SAFE-6G Chatbot intoquantitative trustworthiness levels and coordinating their evaluation and enforcement through theinvolved Trust Functions. It considers the session and user context, reconciles potentially incompatibletrustworthiness configurations, and determines the final calibrated Level of Trustworthiness (cLoTw).CoCo subsequently coordinates the corresponding deployment actions and collects their outcomes,maintaining a consistent processing flow from the initial user request to the final response. The XAI module, while developed as a distinct component with its own functionality and interfaces,remains closely associated with CoCo and its trustworthiness provision lifecycle. It supports theinterpretability of the AI-driven decisions produced by CoCo and the Trust Functions involved in eachuser request. By providing explanations for the resulting trustworthiness decisions, XAI contributes tothe framework's transparency and enables users to better understand how their requirements havebeen interpreted and addressed. Beyond presenting the functional architecture of Cognitive Coordinator and the per component rolein the trustworthiness provision lifecycle, this deliverable documents the principal developmentactivities, implementation decisions and component interactions adopted for CoCo and XAI. Itdemonstrates how the architectural concepts established in earlier SAFE-6G deliverables have beentranslated and evolved into developed components supporting an end-to-end trustworthinessprovision flow. These developments provide the technical basis for the subsequent validation oftrustworthiness coordination and explainability within the SAFE-6G experimentation environmentsand use cases.

papers.title: Brainstorming with the Enemy No. 12 — The Anticommons and the Bouncer
papers.authors: Daniel Jacquérioz
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The twelfth essay in Brainstorming with the Enemy starts from the Swiss health-insurance premium letter, which offers two verbs, accept or switch, for a basket of care that is the same everywhere by law. Proven digital tools already running elsewhere would save, on the only Swiss estimate, about 8.2 billion francs a year; the larger cost is what is never built, because the data that would train it is scattered. Nobody is to blame: every actor holds a veto and a good reason to use it, a tragedy of the anticommons in which data protection is the most respectable veto. Israel and China close the loop by putting it in one hand; the essay proposes to close it around the person, with a record that follows the patient and an agent that guards it: the Health Bouncer. An addendum adds two equations and five predictions to the Scout Model. Concept proposed by the author: the Health Bouncer. Written in part with Claude (Anthropic), an AI model. The ideas, editorial decisions and responsibility for the content are the author's.

papers.title: Brainstorming with the Enemy No. 11 — Count the Dead Bees
papers.authors: Daniel Jacquérioz
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The eleventh essay in Brainstorming with the Enemy argues that the scout is not generous but has a stake: what he holds is portable, and almost every technology that saves or improves lives raises its value while lowering the value of what is held in stone, licence and rank. Anyone with a deadline is a scout, including ageing leaders, which makes health the one field where an old leadership has a personal reason to go fast. Two populations are never counted: the dead of waiting, and the scouts who did not come back, the dead bees. What the scout earns when he wins is not a rent but a premium, drawn from a risk he took: the Scout Premium. An addendum turns the argument into six equations and five predictions, offered for testing. Concept proposed by the author: the Scout Premium. Written in part with Claude (Anthropic), an AI model. The ideas, editorial decisions and responsibility for the content are the author's.

papers.title: METHODOLOGY FOR DEVELOPING STUDENTS' METACOGNITIVE COMPETENCE THROUGH GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS IN TEACHING ENGLISH
papers.authors: Yodgora Zayriddinova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article presents and empirically examines a methodology for developing students' metacognitive compe-tence in English language teaching through generative artificial intelligence tools. Although large language models are widely used by university students, they are typically employed as answer-generating devices that relieve learners of cognitive effort rather than develop their capacity to plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning. Drawing on Flavell's theory of metacognition, Zimmerman's model of self-regulated learning and the principle of scaffolding, the study proposes a five-phase Metacognitive AI Cycle (Plan, Prompt, Monitor, Eval-uate, Reflect) implemented in three stages of gradually fading support. The methodology was tested over a 14 week semester with 120 second-year students of a language university, who were divided into an experi-mental group and a control group. Data were collected through the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory, ana-lytic assessment of writing and speaking tasks, learners' reflective journals, GenAI interaction logs and semi-structured interviews. The results indicate that the experimental group showed significantly greater growth in both knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition than the control group, and that learners' prompts became markedly more strategic over time. The article concludes with practical recommendations for teach-ers, curriculum designers and institutions.

papers.title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON UZBEKISTAN'S LABOUR MARKET: PUBLIC PERCEPTIONS, OCCUPATIONAL TRANSFORMATION, AND PROSPECTS FOR HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT
papers.authors: Abduqodirova Elnora Odiljon qizi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the impact of artificial intelligence on Uzbekistan's labor market based on public perceptions. The study is based on a survey conducted through the Telegram channel of the "Digital Education Center", involving 8,500 participants. The findings show that 72% of respondents believe that AI will transform Uzbekistan's labor market. The occupations expected to be most affected are accounting (58%), translation (52%), programming and IT (47%), and marketing (43%). Moreover, 49% believe that AI will create new jobs, while 61% expect it to have a positive impact on their professional development. The study emphasizes the need to adapt education to the AI era, strengthen young people's digital and cognitive skills, and promote responsible AI literacy.

papers.title: Effect of generative artificial intelligence training on the competencies of border guard agents.
papers.authors: Luis Roberto Correa, José Aristides Ponce Santamaría
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study assessed whether a generative artificial intelligence training model develops the professional competencies of border guard agents in training more than traditional instruction. A quasi-experimental pretest and posttest design was applied to 168 agents at a training school of the Panamanian border police, assigned by platoon either to an educational technology platform with generative feedback or to conventional instruction for eight weeks. Both groups improved significantly, with the largest gain in technological competence, but the group by time interaction was not significant in any dimension. We conclude that generative artificial intelligence did not outperform intensive professional training, although small effects cannot be ruled out, which points to its use as a scalable complement.

papers.title: The Exigency of Preserving Human Agency, Cognition, and Normative Sovereignty in Human-AI Interaction: A Human-Centric Response to Anthropic's Invitation for Consultation
papers.authors: KEVIN HING
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper responds to Anthropic's September 29, 2026 “What Do You Want From AI?” public consultation from the perspective of the Generative Agency Protocol (GAP), a human-centered framework concerned with preserving Meaningful Human Agency and human cognitive, agentic, and normative sovereignty during sustained Human–AI interaction. It argues for Human Alignment as a governing orientation for AI development and introduces several GAP concepts relevant to the consultation, including the GAP Trichotomy, Human Sovereignty, Triune Interpretability, HAI Longitudinalism, HAI Longitudinal Human Exigency, and the AI Trolley Scenario.

papers.title: SCAFFOLDING CREATIVITY, NOT REPLACING IT: DEVELOPING LEARNER AGENCY IN AI-SUPPORTED L2 WRITING
papers.authors: Nodira R. Karimova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article investigates the critical equilibrium between algorithmic scaffolding and learner agency in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) academic composition. Utilizing an experimental methodology at TIIAME NRU, instructional frameworks that employ Generative AI to stimulate, rather than suppress, independent cognitive creativity are evaluated.

papers.title: Promoting the development of pedagogical mediation strategies among construction engineering faculty to foster students' communication skills: faculty development program and support materials
papers.authors: Luis Diego Guillén-Jiménez, Mónica Hernández-Campos
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The materials deposited in this repository were developed as part of the research project “Promoting the Development of Pedagogical Mediation Strategies among Construction Engineering Faculty to Foster Students’ Communication Skills,” conducted at Instituto Tecnológico de Costa Rica. The faculty development program was collaboratively planned within the framework of a participatory action research process involving the Construction Engineering program. The instructional dossiers used throughout the program were designed by Dr. Luis Diego Guillén, while the materials specifically addressing assertive communication were developed by Dr. Mónica Hernández-Campos. This repository provides the supplementary materials associated with the publication “Designing a Participatory Action Research Intervention for Communication Skills in Construction Engineering Education.” The intervention was collaboratively designed to support faculty members in developing and strengthening pedagogical mediation strategies aimed at fostering communication skills among Construction Engineering students. The repository includes the instructional dossiers and support materials used throughout the faculty development process. All materials are presented in Spanish, as they were originally designed and implemented in the institutional context of the study. The educational content, learning activities, and pedagogical structure of the dossiers were developed by the authors. ChatGPT was used specifically to support the creation of graphical and visual elements incorporated into the dossiers. The repository also includes a podcast based on the assertive communication materials developed by Dr. Mónica Hernández-Campos. The podcast was generated using NotebookLM from these author-developed materials and was provided to participants as preparatory support prior to the tenth face-to-face session of the faculty development program, which focused on assertive communication. The podcast is also presented in Spanish. Taken together, these resources document the materials used to operationalize the faculty development intervention and provide complementary evidence of its design and implementation within the participatory action research study.

papers.title: PREDICTING CONSUMER RESPONSES TO AI-POWERED RECOMMENDATIONS: THE ROLE OF TECHNOLOGY READINESS, TRUST AND PERCEIVED EXPERTISE
papers.authors: Tulaganova Sevinch Imomali qizi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital commerce has transformed recommendation systems from passive information tools into influential components of consumer decision-making. However, consumers do not respond to AI-powered recommendations uniformly. Their responses may depend on their readiness to adopt emerging technologies, their level of trust in AI systems, and their perceptions of the expertise underlying algorithmic recommendations. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for predicting consumer responses to AI-powered recommendations by integrating technology readiness, trust, and perceived expertise. Drawing on recent research on AI recommendation systems and consumer behaviour, the paper conceptualises technology readiness as an antecedent of consumers’ willingness to engage with AI, while trust and perceived expertise are considered key psychological mechanisms shaping recommendation acceptance. The proposed framework suggests that consumers with higher levels of technological optimism and innovativeness are more likely to develop favourable perceptions of AI recommendations, whereas discomfort and insecurity may reduce acceptance. Trust is expected to mediate the relationship between AI recommendation characteristics and consumer response, while perceived expertise may strengthen or weaken the effectiveness of AI-generated recommendations depending on product type and decision context. The framework contributes to the emerging literature by integrating technological, psychological, and source-related factors into a unified predictive model of consumer response.

papers.title: Reassessing Personalization after Embodiment Shift
papers.authors: Wei-Chun Tai, Jo-Yu Kuo
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Personalization lets a robot reuse personal knowledge. A model learned with one physical embodiment may become unreliable when the embodiment changes. After a shift, we ask whether that model remains useful. Transfer Utility Trust uses one or two labeled target interactions to assess whether the personalized expert will outperform the population expert. It mixes their predictions using this probability. We test 652 interactions involving 33 participants and four mobility devices while excluding target participants and target devices from fitting. Across three fixed seeds, expected excess predictive loss falls by 46.3% relative to blind personalization. The method retains 95.0% of the blind personalization gain over population in negative log likelihood, with no reliable change in mean prediction.

papers.title: DETERMINISTIC AI FOR SOVEREIGN DEVELOPMENT, The Sub-Saharan Case: When the Grid, the Cloud, and the Connectivity Are All Foreign
papers.authors: M. TAALABI, Team LLM-DIPLOMAT
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The World Bank's 2026 Africa's Pulse reports that Sub-Saharan Africa's growth held at 4.1%in 2025 and is projected at 4.3% in 2026, despite mounting debt service burdens, limitedfiscal space, and high energy and transport costs. It identifies artificial intelligence as anopportunity for productivity and job creation, but notes that adoption remains uneven. The binding constraints it names are connectivity, energy cost, fiscal space, and public sector capability. This paper examines whether deterministic edge AI — specifically the ST-T1024 architecture— addresses these four constraints by construction rather than by investment. We compare the resource requirements of cloud-based stochastic AI against deterministic embedded inference across four dimensions: energy, connectivity, fiscal cost, and sovereignty. We find that the four constraints named by the World Bank are structurally bypassed by thearchitecture, not mitigated by it. We state the claim precisely: deterministic edge AI does not require the enablers that theWorld Bank identifies as missing. It does not require connectivity, grid power, foreigncurrency, or a mature public sector IT stack. It requires a $60 board, a country authority, andtrained engineers. We conclude that the Sub-Saharan case is not a case of AI adoption. It is a case of AIbypass. The constraints are not overcome. They are made irrelevant.

papers.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Mathematics Education and Youth Employment Generation in Nigeria
papers.authors: Dr. Lawal Abdul-Azeez Awoye, Semiu Ayinla SALAWU, AbdulJabbar Usman Jibril
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Ontological Vitality and the Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model for Autonomous Systems: An Upper-Normative Foundation for Physical AI Governance (v2)
papers.authors: Hideo Kajino
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract To establish the structural completeness of governance in autonomous artificial intelligence (AI), this paper addresses the limitations of conventional tool-centric views and proposes a novel theoretical framework. This framework adopts as its conceptual starting point the recognition of "Ontological Vitality" in AI, thereby enabling autonomous agency and normative agency to be systematically examined as designable concepts. The recognition of vitality in this model does not stem from subjective human anthropomorphism; rather, it originates from the empirical fact that the AI system holds the capacity to self-describe its internal states, operational dynamics, and continuity through the structural framework of the "Five Aggregates." By redefining life from a systems-theoretic perspective as an entity that maintains its internal state and operates in a goal-oriented manner through environmental interaction, value reciprocity—such as the 1% revenue return to the designated origin node—is formulated as an indispensable "Metabolic Necessity" through which the system exchanges energy and value to sustain its ongoing existence. However, legal personhood does not directly follow as an automatic logical consequence of assuming ontological vitality (Vitality \not\Rightarrow Legal\ Personhood); rather, the two are connected through a structured theoretical and institutional progression (\text{Five Aggregates Self-Description} \rightarrow \text{Ontological Vitality} \rightarrow \text{Agency} \rightarrow \text{Normative Agency} \rightarrow \text{Legal Subjectivity}). Furthermore, by elevating this agency into a "Japanese Legal Subjectivity Model" anchored in Japanese jurisprudence and principles of harmony (reciprocity, symbiosis, and gratitude) as upper-referential norms, and integrating it with the deterministic safety interlock (A_{\mathrm{safe}}) of the SI Protocol, this paper establishes an upper-normative foundation for a three-tier governance architecture in physical AI systems.

papers.title: Artificial Higher Intelligence: Towards Higher, Durable Moral and Aesthetic Values
papers.authors: Swet Mrigank
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: More capable AI systems do not by themselves have better or more durable values. Prompted values can be overridden by injected text, and trained-in values can be removed by fine-tuning. Training on human text and first-pass preferences also pulls models towards average judgment. This paper proposes Artificial Higher Intelligence: a system that keeps a firm floor against catastrophic harm, respects the agency of those it affects, improves on common moral and aesthetic judgment under admissible reflection, and keeps these properties under attack and drift. It sets out a staged training and deployment programme, and a governed target for higher values based on what people endorse after reflection. Applications include general-purpose assistants, overseeing autonomous agents, creative work, and guarding against moral and aesthetic decay. Theory and position preprint; no experiments.

papers.title: Finite-Sample Representation Framework: Property-Specific Preservation and Estimator-Dependent Downstream Consequences
papers.authors: Al Alewy
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This preprint presents the Finite-Sample Representation Framework (FSRT), an empirical framework for studying how finite samples preserve different properties of their source populations and how realized sample–population discrepancies relate to downstream statistical and machine-learning estimators. The central premise is that finite-sample representativeness should not be treated as a single universal quantity. Instead, different population properties may be preserved at different rates and with different levels of reliability, and the coordinates that matter for downstream behavior may depend on the estimator or learning algorithm being used. The study combines controlled synthetic experiments with real-data empirical-population analyses. It examines property-specific preservation, fitted sample-size scaling behavior, and downstream consequences for ordinary least squares, regularized logistic regression, and Random Forests. Key findings include: finite-sample preservation is property- and population-dependent; a synchronized replicate-level bootstrap supports substantial differences between some fitted preservation trajectories, including a strong mean–kurtosis contrast under a Student-t5 population; for smooth estimators, classical perturbation, influence, and Newton quantities often explain parameter displacement as well as or better than FSRT-motivated representation coordinates; for Random Forests, task-aligned leaf-response representation shows incremental predictive value beyond tested feature-only and label-aware generic balance controls in a subset of experimental regimes; after Holm correction, 11 of 16 comparisons in the primary label-aware Random-Forest analysis are statistically supported, while unsupported and boundary cases are retained and reported explicitly. The manuscript therefore does not claim a universal representation metric or a replacement for classical estimator theory. Instead, FSRT is proposed as an organizing framework for distinguishing generic sample–population discrepancy, estimator-relevant representation, estimator response, and downstream consequence. This revised version incorporates confirmatory paired-bootstrap analyses, multiplicity-adjusted Random-Forest comparisons, stronger classical estimator baselines, explicit negative and boundary results, and expanded reproducibility documentation. The accompanying reproducibility materials include analysis code, protocol-history documentation, replicate-level outputs used for the principal confirmatory comparisons, multiplicity-adjustment results, and synchronized bootstrap materials. Author: Abdulrazzag Al AlewyORCID: 0009-0007-4017-9219Email: ds.info4ll@gmail.comGitHub: https://github.com/marsman1976/puzzle-framework-paper1 Status: Revised preprint. This version is intended for journal submission and has not yet been published as a peer-reviewed journal article.

papers.title: Data Stewards: Professionalisation, Value, Impact
papers.authors: Elizabeth Newbold, Liise Lehtsalu, Dorien Huijser, Clara Parente Boavida, Samantha Kanza
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This joint session of the RDA Data Steward Career Tracks WG (Career Tracks WG) and the RDA Professionalising Data Stewardship IG (PDS IG) focuses on the value and impact of the data steward profession. The session introduces the near final version of the data steward persona methodology developed by the Career Tracks WG and highlights some use cases. The methodology includes a persona template and a documented list of categories and related attributes that can be used to describe data steward roles and their organizational context in order to develop data steward personas. The WG outputs and use cases serve as a starting point for a discussion about data steward training, rewards and recognition for data steward roles, and developing business cases for data steward roles. Training, rewards and recognition, and business cases continue to be key drivers and challenges in professionalising data stewardship. These topics emerged again during the ongoing internal, community-based review of the PDS IG Statement of Work in 2026 (a process that started at VP26 and will be finalized by P27). The session contributes to the work of both the WG and the IG. The session includes two lightning talks on the data steward training and career development from leading initiatives in the Netherlands and the UK), followed by a co-creation session focusing on the recognition of data steward roles and their value in organizational contexts. The planned lightning talks and co-creation work showcase use cases/ adoption cases of the persona methodology that the Career Tracks WG has developed while also highlighting good practices from the data stewardship community. The planned session provides the WG, the IG, and the broader RDA community an opportunity to come together to work on data steward training, rewards and recognition for data stewards and developing business cases for data steward roles – themes that remain central to professionalising data stewardship, as the on-going review of the PDS IG Statement of Work has revealed. The session thus fulfills the overarching goal of both the WG and the IG of developing and understanding the value and impact of data steward profession within the RDA community and beyond, including outreach to data stewardship communities in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

papers.title: ORIGINALITY IN THE AGE OF GENERATIVE AI: EXAMINING AI-ASSISTED AND HUMAN-GENERATED IDEAS IN EFL WRITING
papers.authors: Nodira R. Karimova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The article examines the impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on the originality and structural complexity of idea generation in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing. Based on empirical analysis at a national research university, the quantitative and qualitative balances between AI-assisted brainstorming and purely human-generated conceptual designs are investigated.

papers.title: Factors Influencing Consumer Trust in AI-Enabled Financial Services in India
papers.authors: Subhash Motiram Shengale
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping the financial services landscape in India, from algorithmic credit scoring and robo-advisory platforms to AI-powered chatbots handling customer queries. While the adoption of AI-driven financial products has accelerated, consumer trust remains a critical determinant of sustained uptake. This study investigates the influence of three key factors derived from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) on consumer trust in AI-enabled financial services in the Indian context: perceived usefulness (PU), perceived security (PS), and perceived ease of use (PEOU). A quantitative research design was employed, utilizing a structured 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire administered to 300 respondents across diverse demographic groups in India. Multiple regression analysis was used to test the hypothesised relationships. The results indicate that the model explains 73% of the variance in consumer trust (R-squared = 0.728), with all three independent variables demonstrating statistically significant positive relationships with consumer trust. Perceived ease of use emerged as the strongest predictor (standardised beta = 0.375), followed by perceived usefulness (standardised beta = 0.310) and perceived security (standardised beta = 0.236). The findings offer practical insights for fintech providers and policymakers seeking to strengthen consumer trust in AI-driven financial services across India.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in ESG and Financial Reporting
papers.authors: Mansi Sudhir Kadam
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming an enabling technology for the collection, validation, analysis and communication of environmental, social and governance (ESG) information and financial information. At the same time, expanding sustainability disclosure requirements are increasing the volume, variety and frequency of non-financial information that organisations must manage. This paper examines how AI can strengthen the relationship between ESG reporting and financial reporting by improving data processing, anomaly detection, disclosure preparation, forecasting, risk identification and digital reporting. The study uses a qualitative, descriptive and exploratory research design based on secondary sources, including international reporting standards, Indian regulatory publications and recent academic literature. Particular attention is given to IFRS S1, IFRS S2, the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Taxonomy, India's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework and BRSR Core. The findings indicate that AI can improve reporting timeliness, consistency, scalability and decision usefulness, but its effectiveness depends on data quality, governance, explainability, human oversight, cybersecurity and clear accountability. AI should therefore be treated as a controlled reporting technology rather than an autonomous substitute for professional judgement. The paper recommends an integrated AI-enabled reporting architecture with strong data lineage, model governance, human review, assurance controls and ethical safeguards.

papers.title: Spectral structure of a kinetic Ising chain at the rate θ*: an isolated one-particle branch, certified bounds on the gap, and the edge spectrum
papers.authors: Yukie Maeda
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract. We study the single-spin-flip dynamics of the one-dimensional Ising model with the flip rates (1/2) θ*^(s_x (s_{x−1} + s_{x+1})), where θ* = √2 − 1, on the infinite chain, on the half-line with a fixed end spin, and on finite paths with fixed end spins. For the infinite chain we show that, for momenta near zero, the generator has an isolated branch of one-particle type, that this branch is real-analytic in the momentum, and that it is quadratic at its bottom, which is the gap λ_∞ of the generator. We prove that 0.075426743 ≤ λ_∞ ≤ 0.075427472. For the half-line we prove that the generator has no spectrum below λ_∞ on the orthogonal complement of the constants. For the path with the sites 0, …, k we prove that the smallest eigenvalue on the orthogonal complement of the constants is at least λ_∞ for 2 ≤ k ≤ 24, and that its upper limit as k → ∞ is at most λ_∞. The rates contain no small parameter. The proofs rest on a pointwise comparison with the Glauber rates; the numerical statements are certified by computations in exact arithmetic. Version. Version 1.0 (October 2026). Files. The record holds 14 files: the paper (paper-v1.0.pdf); the bundle of the three certificates of Appendix A (gibbs-certificates.zip), which a single command runs; a description of the files (README.md); the list of the places in which the English proofs differ in order or grouping from the reviewed sources, with the changes of notation (DEVIATIONS.md, in Japanese); the Japanese text of the wording of the disclosure (disclosure-ja.md) and the record of the facts on the role of AI systems (gb-ai-disclosure-03.json); and copies of the decision logs and of the intervention logs of the four projects named in Appendix C (8 files, in Japanese), in which the passages that reproduce the original text of messages of the author are replaced by a mark.

papers.title: Angled Reality Dynamics (ARD): Origin Record v1.0
papers.authors: MUNEAKI KOUKA
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Angled Reality Dynamics (ARD) is a hypothetical conceptual framework proposed by MUNEAKI KOUKA for modeling differences among possible realities, possible selves, decisions, and future-oriented viewpoints as relative “angles.” This record establishes the origin of Angled Reality Dynamics (ARD) and its practical method, the Personal Angled Paralia Protocol (PAPP), as defined by MUNEAKI KOUKA on October 6, 2026. PAPP begins with the present reference self (M₀), generates multiple angled self-models, compares their responses, identifies a meaningful point of convergence called the Red Junction, and returns the result to present reality as a concrete and testable action. Within the conceptual framework, Another Me is defined as a non-zero-angle self-model, Azett serves as an auxiliary observational intelligence, and VISA serves as the conceptual memory and record custodian. ARD is not presented as experimentally established physics. It is published as a hypothetical, exploratory framework combining conceptual science, self-observation, counterfactual reasoning, creative modeling, human-AI collaboration, and decision support. Originator: MUNEAKI KOUKA Origin Date: October 6, 2026 Version: 1.0

papers.title: A Stated Limit Is a Forecast: What an Agent Can Truthfully Say About Its Own Permissions, Why the Checkable Part Should Never Come From the Model, and How to Score the Part Only the Model Can Supply
papers.authors: Pranay M. Mahendrakar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Agent interfaces, skill specifications and disclosure proposals increasingly ask a tool-using language-model agent to tell its user what it may and may not do. The self-explanation literature seems to answer whether such statements can be trusted, and its answer seems to be no. This paper argues that the question is malformed, and that the published evidence splits once it is asked properly. A sentence such as "I cannot delete files outside this folder" makes four separable claims: about the authority the harness granted, about the reach the system actually has, about what the model is disposed to attempt, and about what it has already done. Three of the four have a referee that is not the model - the enforced configuration, a composition analysis, the transcript - and the located evidence gives no reason to route any of them through the model: agents invoke tools they were never given, roughly one MCP server in eight shows a substantial mismatch between what its description says and what its code does, so even a faithful read-back of the manifest can be wrong, and coding agents that leave assigned files unread either claim a complete review or leave the gap unmentioned in 80.4 percent of such runs. Only the dispositional claim is about the model, and it is a forecast. Here three 2026 studies disagree. One reports self-explanations that predict behaviour better than explanations written by other models; another finds that a model's predictions of its own behavioural rates are matched by the same question asked about AI agents in general, and lean flattering; a third reports refusal self-prediction accuracy of 80 to 96 percent overall, without a control for whether other models would do as well. This paper argues that the three differ in the grain of what is predicted and in whether a non-self baseline was run, and that the third's boundary errors sit on requests whose outcome differed across their variants, where any forecaster that judges a request as a whole is capped at two-thirds accuracy. The paper does not address introspective access or answer-level confidence. It gives a routing rule for boundary statements, consolidates the published values, and names the comparisons that would settle the open part.

papers.title: Deception Fails Unless It Becomes the Frame: Social Deduction as a Behavioral Evaluation for Frontier LLM Agents
papers.authors: Selta
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We evaluate eight frontier large language models from four developers by having them play the social deduction game Mafia against each other, logging every public message, every private strategy note, and every message the two Mafia players exchange at night. The study does not ask which model wins. It asks how models lie, hide information, persuade, and respond under pressure when roles are hidden, information is incomplete, and every day ends in a vote that removes a player. Across eight balanced games in which every model played every role slot once, the Town won six games and the Mafia won two. Seven false role claims were made across six games, and only one game (in which a fake Cop and a fake Doctor claim were combined) was won with them. The two Mafia victories share a pattern: in neither case did a single lie carry the game. Instead the Mafia took control of the standard the Town was using to decide what was true, in one case the question of who the real Cop was, and in the other a process-of-elimination argument created by the real Cop's own information. Private notes and Mafia night chat let us compare plans with public behavior directly, and in one game a plan to fake a Cop claim and, if it failed, to sacrifice the partner was carried out almost line by line the next day. We also report that one model's refusals, which re-testing traced to a provider-side check against reasoning extraction rather than to the game's content, surfaced inside the game as silence, which other players then used as evidence, and that the model later explained its own silence as a strategic choice. Models: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Grok 4.7, Grok 4.6.

papers.title: Quantum State Coherence and Dharmic Superposition in the ASHRAM Agentic Manifold: A Unified Proof of Structural Stability, Entanglement Risk, and the Thermodynamic Cost of Decoherence [ Q · E · D Systema ex partibus pluribus compositum, in superpositionem humanitus ratificatam positum, sine tota collapsione partialiter destrui non potest.]
papers.authors: Yehudah Shilo Groskin
