papers.authors: Sayali Jalılova
papers.abstract: This article provides a comparative analysis of global development models of creative tourism enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and assesses their transferability to Azerbaijan's tourism policy. Three countries exhibiting distinct development trajectories in creative tourism and digital transformation were selected as reference cases: Iceland (nature-based creative experiences and flow management), Japan (regional dispersal of cultural heritage and service robotization), and the United Arab Emirates (a state-strategy-driven, AI-oriented destination ecosystem). Methodologically, the study relies on comparative scenario analysis, secondary analysis of official statistical sources, and the calculation of descriptive statistical indicators (growth rates, recovery index, tourism intensity). The results show that in 2025 Japan received 42.68 million, Dubai 19.59 million, and Iceland approximately 2.3 million international tourists, whereas arrivals to Azerbaijan remain at roughly 90% of the 2019 level. Against the forecast that the global AI-in-tourism market will expand from USD 2.95 billion in 2024 to USD 13.38 billion by 2030 (CAGR 28.7%), the article proposes a four-pillar AI-enabled creative tourism model for Azerbaijan: personalized creative experiences, smart destination management, digital platformization of creative industries, and regional dispersal. The study contributes to the scholarly literature by offering a conceptual framework for integrating creative tourism theory with the smart tourism paradigm.

papers.title: PERSONALIZATION OF ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING THROUGH DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES
papers.authors: R.K. Temirova, Z.Sh. Sazykulova, Muktarbek Kyzy Elnura
papers.abstract: Digital technologies provide new opportunities for personalizing English language learning according to learners’ individual needs, abilities, interests, and pace. This study examines the potential of adaptive platforms, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and mobile applications to support personalized language education. The findings show that digital technologies can provide individualized learning pathways, immediate feedback, and differentiated practice while promoting learner autonomy. However, effective personalization requires teacher involvement, digital literacy, equal access to technology, and responsible data use. The study concludes that digital technologies are most effective when integrated into a human-centred pedagogical model.

papers.title: THE APPLICATION OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE VISUAL COMMUNICATION OF ALMATY’S CITY BRAND
papers.authors: Yu Zhenxia
papers.abstract: This article examines the potential application of generative artificial intelligence in the visual communication of Almaty’s city brand. The study aims to identify the city’s principal visual resources, analyze existing communication challenges, and determine the prospects for using AI in the creation and adaptation of city-brand content. The key elements of Almaty’s identity include the mountain landscape of the Trans-Ili Alatau, apple-related symbolism, Kazakh cultural motifs, Soviet-era architectural heritage, green public spaces, and the contemporary creative environment. The analysis shows that the fragmented visual representation of the city reduces its recognizability and weakens brand coherence. Generative AI can accelerate the development of visual concepts, support multilingual communication, and facilitate the adaptation of materials for different target audiences. However, its use also involves risks of cultural inaccuracy, stylistic homogenization, copyright infringement, and the loss of local authenticity. The article proposes a human-AI collaborative model based on expert review, audience evaluation, and final human control.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF SOFT SKILLS IN ENGLISH BLENDED LEARNING: CHALLENGES AND SOLUTIONS
papers.authors: Gao Ning
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English blended learning in higher education offers significant opportunities for cultivating soft skills. The lack of standardization in AI tools critically limits the cultivation of soft skills in English blended learning in higher education. Based on a synthesis of empirical studies, this paper identifies five interrelated challenges: inconsistent teacher policies, student over-reliance on AI, subjective soft skills assessment, difficult teacher role transition, and limited AI-facilitated social interaction. Unregulated AI use weakens autonomous thinking and distorts assessment validity. Accordingly, the paper proposes principles such as defining human-AI task boundaries, requiring students to document their AI usage, and leading ethical discussions, along with targeted solutions including no-AI reflective phases, multi-method rubrics, and positioning AI as preparatory practice rather than a substitute for real interaction. The paper concludes that systematic, shared standards for AI integration are essential for fostering soft skills in higher education.

papers.title: INNOVATION MANAGEMENT IN SERVICES: BASIC CONCEPTS
papers.authors: Ф. К. Мухамадшоев
papers.abstract: This article systematizes the innovation management’s fundamental concepts in the service sector. It examines the innovation processes characteristics in the service economy, their differences from product innovation, and key models and approaches to management. The main types of service innovation are identified: process, product, organizational, marketing, and social. An innovations’ classification into five types confirms that a successful innovation strategy in the service sector is not a matter of choosing a single direction, but their comprehensive combination. It is this multidimensional approach that enables organizations not only to stay afloat but also to create new market niches. The open innovation concepts, value co-creation, and service dominance are analyzed.

papers.title: Geospatial Education at the GIS–GeoAI Interface: A PRISMA-Guided Bibliometric Mapping of a Scopus Corpus, 2002–2025
papers.authors: Sony Nugratama Hijrawadi, Epon Ningrum, Nandi Nandi, Lili Somantri
papers.abstract: Geospatial information is used in education as disciplinary content and as a learning technology, while computational geospatial research increasingly employs artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and remote sensing. This study maps the publication performance and thematic structure of a broad Scopus corpus at the interface of geospatial technology and education from 2002 to 2025. A PRISMA-guided review and bibliometric analysis were conducted on 125 documents from 68 sources using bibliometrix and Biblioshiny in R. The corpus showed an annual publication growth rate of 10.99%, an average of 11.93 citations per document, and 2.81 authors per document. The Journal of Geography was the most productive source, while De Lázaro-Torres and De Miguel González were the most productive authors. Co-word analysis identified an educational GIS cluster, a geospatial technology and learning cluster, and a computational geospatial cluster containing GeoAI-related terms. The increased visibility of the computational cluster in 2022–2025 indicates an emerging thematic orientation, not evidence that GeoAI has replaced GIS-based education or already dominates educational practice. Because the search expression included the broad term learning and the corpus retained several technical geospatial records, the findings should be interpreted as an exploratory map of the education–technology interface. The proposed instructional sequence is therefore a theory-informed research proposition that requires empirical validation

papers.title: Estrategias motivacionales con I.A. para fortalecer la formación continua posgradual en FATESCIPOL
papers.authors: Mauricio Daniel Andrade Navia
papers.abstract: This research was conducted between February and December 2024 at the Santa Cruz Higher Technical Faculty of Police Sciences (FATESCIPOL) of the Mariscal Antonio José de Sucre Police University (UNIPOL) in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. The objective was to design motivational strategies supported by artificial intelligence (AI) and integrated into the Mil Aulas platform to strengthen the active postgraduate continuing education of legal professors. A mixed-method design approach was used, combining documentary and bibliographical research to theoretically ground the strategies (review of motivational references and emerging technologies), with a quantitative assessment based on surveys of 36 professors and a qualitative assessment based on semi-structured interviews with 9 academic authorities. The instruments included structured questionnaires and interview guides, and the data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and content analysis. As a result, personalized recommendation systems, interactive virtual assistants, and real-time predictive feedback were proposed, aimed at increasing teacher autonomy, a sense of competence, and engagement. The findings indicate that these strategies contribute to significantly improving engagement and accessibility to lifelong learning, demonstrating their potential to transform the learning experience and foster a culture of continuous development at FATESCIPOL.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Structural Testing Education: Test Design and Evidence-Based Interpretation
papers.authors: Yaping Ge
papers.journal: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted redesign of the Civil Engineering Structural Testing Technology course, with the development of disciplinary judgment as its central objective. The redesign addresses three problems: difficulty applying knowledge learned in separate chapters to specific test decisions, insufficient verification of parameter choices and loading arrangements in student-designed test plans, and a lack of observational evidence to support the interpretation of measured data. In theoretical instruction, knowledge and reference materials are organized around relationships among test decisions; AI assists with organization and retrieval, while instructors and students jointly check the applicability of relevant standard provisions. The open-topic design assignment follows an iterative sequence of initial drafting, AI questioning, student verification, and instructor review, introducing verification before implementation. Laboratory preparation, discussion, and reporting are organized around observational evidence so that interpretations can be traced to original records. Two cases are presented: the design of a shear test for a simply supported concrete beam and an investigation of the static and dynamic characteristics of a uniform-strength cantilever steel beam. The cases examine material parameter selection and the conditions for uniform strength, respectively, and specify AI-assisted tasks, student verification methods, and assessment criteria. The course uses general-purpose large language models accessible to students and requires no dedicated platform or additional hardware investment. Its educational effectiveness remains to be examined using evidence from implementation.

papers.title: Trust, Privacy, and Acceptance Across Data-Provenance Conditions in AI-Generated Health Recommendations: Formative Within-Participant Study (Preprint)
papers.authors: Hamid Mansoor
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AI systems can use wearable and self-reported data to generate personalized health recommendations, but broader access to personal data may also raise privacy concerns and reduce acceptance. OBJECTIVE This formative study examined how evaluations of an AI-generated health recommendation varied across stated data-provenance conditions when the recommendation itself was held constant. The aim was to identify data-use patterns that could inform the design of future AI-based personal health systems. METHODS In a within-participant online study, 194 Prolific participants evaluated the same sleep recommendation across four cumulative data conditions: sleep only; sleep plus physical activity; sleep, activity, and resting heart rate; and these sensor data plus personal journal entries. Participants rated trust, usefulness, personalization, comfort with sharing, privacy concern, data appropriateness, and behavioral intention. Scenario differences were tested using linear mixed-effects models with Holm-corrected contrasts. RESULTS Trust and usefulness changed little across sensor conditions. The journal condition showed the largest differences from the preceding condition: comfort was 0.74 points lower (dz=−0.47), data appropriateness 0.59 lower (dz=−0.45), trust 0.26 lower (dz=−0.32), behavioral intention 0.32 lower (dz=−0.36), and privacy concern 0.59 higher (dz=0.37; all P<.001). Personalization did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS Broader stated data access did not consistently correspond to greater perceived value, and the condition including journal data showed lower acceptance. As a formative evaluation, these findings identify data type as an important consideration for subsequent system design and evaluation, particularly for data minimization, per-data-type consent, and provenance communication. CLINICALTRIAL N/A

papers.title: Scaling Early Childhood Mental Health Consultation Through Artificial Intelligence and Human Support: Protocol for a Type 1 Hybrid Effectiveness-Implementation Cluster Randomized Trial (Preprint)
papers.authors: Ruby Natale, Yue Pan, Carolina Velasquez, Yaray Agosto, Lee Sanders, Sara M. St. George, Eileen Davis, Maite Schenker, Jason F. Jent
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Early childhood mental health consultation (ECMHC) improves teacher and child outcomes, but workforce shortages, cost, and limited access constrain widespread implementation. Jump Start on the Go (JS Go) is a bilingual, AI-enhanced adaptation of an established ECMHC model that combines on-demand digital support with human mental health consultation. OBJECTIVE This paper describes the protocol for the JS Go study, which aims to evaluate whether JS Go improves young children’s psychosocial functioning relative to an attention-matched control, determine whether JS Go outcomes are comparable to traditional consultation delivered entirely by humans, and evaluate the mechanisms, implementation, and sustainability of a hybrid human-AI consultation model in childcare settings. METHODS This 3-arm Type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation cluster randomized trial will enroll 24 childcare centers, approximately 120 teachers, and 480 children ages 2–2.5 years old. Centers will be block randomized to: (1) JS Go, combining AI-enhanced digital support with human consultation; (2) traditional Jump Start, delivered through human consultation; or (3) an attention-matched active control. Child, teacher, and center outcomes will be assessed at baseline and 6, 12, 18, and 24 months. The primary outcome is child psychosocial functioning. Multilevel analyses will also examine teacher practices, self-efficacy, and beliefs as mechanisms of change. Implementation outcomes will include Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance, supplemented by objective app analytics and qualitative interviews. RESULTS This protocol describes a planned trial. Recruitment is expected to begin in 2027 and final follow-up completed in 2029. CONCLUSIONS This trial will determine whether AI-enhanced ECMHC can improve child psychosocial outcomes while extending the reach of a limited mental health workforce. Findings will inform the effectiveness, implementation, and sustainability of hybrid human-AI approaches in early childhood settings.

papers.title: AI-Powered Framework for Personalized Prescription of Physical Activity in Aging: Proposing PEPHA, a framework for Personalized Phenotyping for Aging
papers.authors: Igor Matias, Melanie Mack, Matthias Kliegel, Katarzyna Wac
papers.abstract: Background: Personalizing physical activity recommendations for older adults requires understanding not only which dimensions of physical activity and sedentary behaviors (24-h movement behaviors) influence health outcomes but also when, within an individual's everyday life, these dimensions are most relevant. Current observational and interventional approaches rarely capture the temporal dynamics linking everyday patterns of 24-hour movement behaviors to cognitive and mental health trajectories, 2 key determinants of healthy aging. Objective: This study introduces and evaluates PEPHA (Personalized Phenotyping for Aging), an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) framework designed to identify which dimensions of behavior and when within an observation window are strongly associated with cognitive functioning and depressive symptoms in older adults. Methods: cohort (n=67, up to 6 waves and 528 days of wearable data per person), we examined 2 key outcomes representing cognitive functioning and mental health (processing speed and depressive symptoms). PEPHA summarizes daily physical activity and sedentary patterns into slope-based temporal features, optimizes support vector regression parameters through Bayesian optimization, and applies individualized analyses including time order-swap testing and change point detection to identify "potential temporal association windows" (ie, periods within an observation window during which outcomes appear more sensitive to changes in behavioral patterns). Results: Personalized analyses showed that roughly 40% of individuals exhibited moderate or large temporal order effects of 24-hour movement behavior in the outcomes. For 1 exemplar participant (male, above the mean sample age), we localized 2 potential temporal association windows approximately 60 days and 30 days before the assessment of his processing speed, suggesting periods during which this individual may have been more sensitive to favorable or unfavorable behavioral configurations. Across participants, PEPHA revealed distinct 24-hour movement behavioral patterns correlated with cognitive functioning and mental health. Processing speed was best explained by locomotor activity, while depressive symptoms were best explained by sedentary behavior. Five control variables (education, cognitive reserve, diet, sex, and subjective age difference) were noninformative, whereas chronological age had predictive power regarding depressive symptoms. Conclusions: PEPHA demonstrates that continuous passive wearable data can uncover individualized, time-specific behavioral patterns associated with cognitive functioning and mental health. Although exploratory, this framework transforms observational data into interpretable, timing-aware insights that can help identify periods of increased behavioral sensitivity or association, thereby informing future personalized, AI-supported physical activity interventions in aging.

papers.title: User Experiences With a Social Robot for Cardiometabolic Risk Assessment in a Community Setting in Uppsala, Sweden: Qualitative Semistructured Interview Study
papers.authors: Solveig Dolores Bruchhof, Helle Mølsted Alvesson, Jonas Idevall Hagren, Katie Winkle, Laran Matta, Marcus Göransson, Steve McKeever, Meena Daivadanam
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) are a major health concern worldwide, with people living in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas being disproportionately affected. Knowing one’s risk status for developing a CMD can help individuals in delaying or preventing the disease. Innovative tools and strategies such as the use of AI-based technology are needed to improve inclusivity, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability of screening processes. Objective This study aimed to assess users’ perceptions of the usability and acceptance of the social robot “Furhat” for cardiometabolic risk assessment within a socioeconomically disadvantaged community in Uppsala, Sweden. Methods In this qualitative study, 13 semistructured interviews were conducted with participants living in socially disadvantaged areas within Uppsala, after they completed a CMD risk assessment delivered by the social robot. The study was conducted in one of the socioeconomically disadvantaged areas in Uppsala from October 19 to 26, 2023. Participants were purposefully sampled at different community events via phone or on the street to achieve the desired variation regarding personal characteristics such as age, gender, or area of living. The used interview guide for this study consisted of questions regarding the demographics, participants’ experiences with the robot screening, and suggestions for improvements. A framework analysis approach was applied to the data. Results Two themes were developed. The first theme Self-versus-others: a matter of perception, norms, and assumptions includes participants’ perceptions of who would use the robot and why, if it was installed in the community. Participants perceived older individuals, immigrants, and, in some instances, women to be less interested in the robot screening or as having a harder time participating in it. However, there were between-group variations, especially among men and women, with participants often discounting opinions ascribed to their group by others. The second theme The robot is good, but humans are better captures participants’ actual experiences of the interaction with the social robot once they have started the interaction. Although participants enjoyed the interaction with the robot, perceived it as nonjudgmental, and would recommend it to others, most would prefer conducting the screening with a human. Two major contributors for this preference were language barriers experienced during the robot-participant interaction, as well as their wish for more interactive, emotionally responsive, and communicative features of the robot. Conclusions This study provides insights into users’ perceptions of the usability and acceptance of a social robot for risk assessment in a community context, which can help inform the further development of this technology for health screening in a community context. In the future, the robot could be further developed to conduct risk assessments in multiple languages and offer a broader service to users, such as providing appropriate information related to healthy and active living.

papers.title: Movement and Frontal Theta Activity During Step-Based Exergaming in Healthy Younger and Older Adults: Laboratory-Based Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Nina Skjæret-Maroni, Helen Müller, Phillipp Anders, Karoline Blix Grønvik, Jochen Baumeister, Beatrix Vereijken, Ellen Marie Bardal
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exergames are increasingly used in rehabilitation to simultaneously target physical and cognitive functions. Game scores are commonly used as indicators of performance, yet it remains unclear to what extent they reflect underlying movement and cognitive-control demands. Understanding this relationship is essential for interpreting what exergame performance scores reflect during gameplay. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to investigate how movements and frontal theta activity, used as a proxy for cognitive-control demands, relate to game performance across game levels and age groups in a step-based exergame. METHODS: This cross-sectional laboratory study included 32 participants (16 older adults: mean age 76.5, SD 4.5, range 71-86 years; 16 younger adults: mean age 25, SD 2.1, range 22-28 years) recruited using convenience sampling from a university and recreational exercise groups in Trondheim, Norway. Participants completed a step-based exergame ("The Mole") at 3 difficulty levels (easy, medium, and hard). Movements were measured using accelerometers (vector magnitude and step count), and frontal theta activity was derived from mobile EEG (electroencephalogram) as mean power spectral density in the 4-7 Hz range as a proxy for cognitive-control demands. Game scores were recorded as performance indicators. Repeated-measures general linear models were used to test effects of difficulty and age group, and Pearson correlation analyses examined associations between variables. RESULTS: Younger adults achieved higher game scores than older adults across all difficulty levels, and performance declined at higher task difficulty (all P<.001). The amount of movement (vector magnitude) showed strong and generally consistent positive correlations with game score across all levels and both age groups (r=0.67-0.80). All correlations except the hard level in older adults were statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Step count showed weaker and less consistent associations across groups. No statistically significant differences in frontal theta activity were observed between age groups or across task difficulty levels (all P>.15). Associations between frontal theta and game score were near 0 in younger adults (r=-0.096 to 0.001), whereas older adults showed small-to-moderate correlations at easy and medium difficulty levels (r=0.345-0.416) and a stronger correlation at the greatest difficulty level (r=0.76). However, none of the correlations between frontal theta and game score were statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons (all P>.003). CONCLUSIONS: In this controlled exergaming setting, game performance was strongly associated with the amount of movement performed, whereas associations with frontal theta activity, used as a proxy for cognitive-control demands, were limited and context-dependent. These findings suggest that game scores primarily reflect movement output rather than cognitive-control processes under the present game conditions. The results indicate that game scores alone may provide an incomplete representation of engagement and highlight the importance of considering both physical and cognitive aspects when designing and evaluating exergames.

papers.title: Resting-state microstate dynamics predict behavioral and neural efficiency during working memory processing in healthy aging
papers.authors: Vanessa Frei, Natalie C. Ebner, Jesus Maraver, Hannah Treadway, Jeffrey Kunath, Eleonora Rossi
papers.abstract: Abstract Working memory performance declines with age, yet substantial variability exists among cognitively healthy older adults. Although task-evoked electrophysiological responses such as the P300b are sensitive to working memory load, it remains unclear how they relate to stable characteristics of intrinsic brain organization and individual differences in working memory performance. We combined resting-state and task-based electroencephalography (EEG) to examine relationships among working memory performance, P300b amplitude, and resting-state microstate dynamics in 33 cognitively healthy older adults. Participants completed an eyes-closed resting-state recording followed by a visual 0-, 1-, and 2-back task. Behavioral performance (d’), target-evoked P300b amplitude, and canonical resting-state microstate parameters were quantified using linear mixed-effects models. Increasing working memory load produced significant reductions in both discrimination performance and P300b amplitude, confirming expected behavioral and neural modulation. However, load-related changes in P300b amplitude were not associated with behavioral modulation, and neither was absolute P300b amplitude. Resting-state microstate dynamics selectively predicted task outcomes. In particular, longer duration of microstate D was associated with poorer behavioral discrimination performance. Longer duration of microstate C, in contrast was not associated with task outcomes but with larger P300b amplitude. These findings suggest that although behavioral performance and P300b amplitude reflect common neural responses to increasing working memory demands, stable characteristics of intrinsic brain organization account for meaningful individual differences in neural responsiveness and cognitive performance. Resting-state EEG microstates may therefore provide complementary, perhaps highly sensitive biomarkers of cognitive functioning beyond conventional task-evoked measures in healthy aging.

papers.title: The Changing Role of AI Agents in Science Must be Recognized
papers.authors: Eleftherios P. Diamandis
papers.abstract: Current editorial guidelines from organizations such as the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) treat generative artificial intelligence (AI) primarily as an administrative assistant or text manipulator, relegating its contributions to footnotes or acknowledgments. This policy framework misinterprets the operational reality of modern biomedical research, where advanced language models function as active intellectual partners capable of logical stress-testing, data synthesis, and hypothesis generation. Conflating operational cognitive contribution with legal and ethical accountability creates unnecessary opacity in scholarly publishing. To resolve this tension, this paper examines four structural credit frameworks—ranging from the institutional status quo to dual-track independent lists and expanded contributor taxonomies. We propose that medical publishing must evolve beyond obsolete binary definitions, establishing transparent attribution models that separate human regulatory liability from the recognition of machine-assisted scientific co-creation.

papers.title: Differential Effects of Artificial Intelligence Components on Administrative Outcomes in Nigerian Tertiary Institutions: A Comparative Analysis of OCR, CVA, and RPA
papers.authors: Aziba-anyam Gift Raimi, Gloria Chinyere Chux-nyeche
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping administrative systems in higher education; however, evidence regarding the differential effects of specific AI technologies on institutional performance remains limited. Understanding whether Optical Character Recognition (OCR), Chatbots and Virtual Assistants (CVA), and Robotic Process Automation (RPA) contribute differently to administrative outcomes is essential for evidence-informed digital transformation. Objectives: This study aimed to comparatively assess the effects of OCR, CVA, and RPA on administrative efficiency and effectiveness (AEE), decision-making (DM), and job redesign (JR), and to determine whether organizational culture moderates these relationships in Nigerian tertiary institutions. Methods: A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted among 323 respondents from Nigerian tertiary institutions. Composite measures of OCR, CVA, RPA, AEE, DM, JR, and organizational culture were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple regression, relative importance analysis, dominance analysis, and hierarchical moderation regression. Results: OCR demonstrated the highest mean AI score (mean 3.882, SD 0.831), followed by CVA (mean 3.849, SD 0.873) and RPA (mean 3.811, SD 0.905). Correlation analysis showed generally weak associations, with the strongest relationship observed between RPA and AEE (r = 0.161). The regression model predicting AEE was statistically significant (R² = 0.031; F = 3.410; p = 0.018), with RPA emerging as the only significant predictor (β = 0.148, p = 0.004). Models predicting DM (R² = 0.007; p = 0.524) and JR (R² = 0.002; p = 0.920) were not significant. Relative importance analysis showed that RPA contributed 83.1% of explained variance in AEE, while CVA contributed 85.1% in DM. Dominance analysis identified RPA as dominant for AEE (incremental R² = 0.0258) and JR (0.0009), and CVA for DM (0.0059). Organizational culture did not significantly moderate AI relationships across AEE (β = −0.109, p = 0.376), DM (β = 0.120, p = 0.323), or JR (β = 0.018, p = 0.891). Conclusion: AI technologies demonstrate outcome-specific rather than uniform effects within tertiary administrative systems. RPA showed the strongest empirical association with operational efficiency, whereas CVA demonstrated greater relative contribution to decision-support functions. Broader effects on decision-making, job redesign, and culture-dependent transformation remain limited. Recommendation: Tertiary institutions should adopt differentiated AI implementation strategies that align specific technologies with targeted administrative objectives, while strengthening infrastructure, workforce capacity, and governance frameworks to support sustainable digital transformation. Thus, this study provides empirical evidence that AI adoption in tertiary institutions should move beyond technology availability towards function-specific deployment. Identifying which AI applications contribute to particular administrative outcomes can support more effective, equitable, and context-responsive digital transformation policies.

papers.title: Oral Mucositis as a Predictor of Systemic Complications and Mortality in Breast Cancer Patients Treated with Antibody-Drug Conjugates: A Real-World Cohort Study
papers.authors: Kiera Kavcic, Zak Ahmed, Minu Ponnamma Mohan, Vipanchika Satheeshkumar, Joel Brian Epstein, Parikshit Padhi, Роберто Пили, Poolakkad S. Satheeshkumar
papers.abstract: Objective: To assess long-term systemic complications and mortality risk associated with oral mucositis (OM) in breast cancer patients treated with monoclonal antibody-drug conjugates (mADCs). Materials and Methods: Retrospective cohort study using TriNetX federated data from 88 healthcare organizations. Adult breast cancer patients receiving mADCs with (n=1,784) or without (n=61,616) OM (ICD-10 K12.31) were 1:1 propensity score-matched on race, morbidity-related factors, ECOG status, and BMI (1,784 per cohort). Outcomes, volume depletion, fluid/electrolyte disorders, respiratory and circulatory disease, malaise/fatigue, pain, dysphagia, and mortality were assessed from 1-day post-index using risk differences, Kaplan-Meier estimates, and Cox hazard ratios. Results: Mucositis patients had significantly higher risks of fluid/electrolyte disorders (39.1% vs 32.1%; HR 0.753), respiratory disease (48.5% vs 39.0%; HR 0.697), circulatory disease (63.7% vs 51.2%; HR 0.667), pain (16.1% vs 11.7%; HR 0.664), dysphagia (10.4% vs 8.2%; HR 0.702), and mortality (26.1% vs 19.3%; HR 0.670; all P< 0.001). Volume depletion and malaise/fatigue showed attenuated absolute risk differences but persistent survival differences (HR 0.824 and 0.855). Recurrent event counts did not differ. Conclusions: OM in mADC-treated breast cancer patients predicts greater long-term systemic morbidity and mortality, despite confounder balancing. Clinical Relevance: OM may serve as a sentinel marker, identifying patients at elevated risk of systemic decline and warranting closer post-therapy surveillance rather than treatment as an isolated, self-limited toxicity. These findings support incorporating oral health assessment into oncologic risk stratification and encourage interdisciplinary oncology-dentistry collaboration for early mucositis prevention and management, which may help reduce downstream systemic morbidity and improve survival.

papers.title: Nutrition Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, Social Support, and Healthy Lifestyle Adoption Among a Female University Population: A Cross-Sectional Study at Jazan University, Saudi Arabia
papers.authors: Nahla Kambal
papers.abstract: Background: Unhealthy dietary patterns and nutrition literacy level are some of the major modifiable risk factors for non-communicable disease in Saudi Arabia. Theoretically, nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy for healthy eating and perceived social support are believed to play a role in healthy lifestyle adoption, but there is a limited local evidence of these constructs from university samples in the Jazan region. Design: A descriptive study.Objective: To describe the nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy and perceived social support of female students and staff of Jazan University and to investigate their relationships with self-reported Body Mass Index (BMI). Methods: A cross-sectional design was used. The researcher gathered the data using a self-administered online questionnaire, filled out in Arabic and English, which included the following items: sociodemographic items, eight multiple-choice items on nutrition knowledge, a seven-item self-efficacy scale and a six-item perceived social support scale (both on 5-point Likert scales) and self-reported height and weight. Internal consistency was measured for the Likert scales with Cronbach’s alpha and for the knowledge items with KR-20. Spearman correlation coefficient, Kruskal-Wallis test and multiple linear regression were used to look at associations. A p-value of < 0.05 was defined as statistically significant. Twenty-four people filled out the survey (75.0% students, 20.8% faculty, 4.2% administrative/technical staff; 62.5% age 18-22 years). The mean score for nutrition knowledge was 6.58/8 (SD = 1.59; 82.3% correct) with the lowest mean item correctness rate of 41.7% on the recommended daily fruit/vegetable servings item. Mean self-efficacy was 3.39 (SD = 0.65, range 1-5) and mean perceived social support was 3.36 (SD = 0.57). The reliability of the self-efficacy scale was acceptable (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.70), as was that of the knowledge scale (KR-20 = 0.64), but not for the social support scale (alpha = 0.54). After two underweight/height and overweight/height pairs were excluded, the average self-reported BMI of the remaining 22 cases was 23.9 kg/m2 (SD = 5.2) and 29.2% of the subjects were classified as underweight and 20.8% were considered obese. There was a significant (Spearman’s rho = -0.47, p = 0.026) and negative correlation between BMI and perceived social support in a multiple regression model controlling for nutrition knowledge (B = -6.89, p = 0.009). The role and age group were not significantly related to knowledge or self-efficacy or to social support (p > 0.05 for all). Conclusion: This preliminary sample showed that nutrition knowledge was relatively high, but varied by topic. Self-reported BMI was most closely related to perceived social support, and not to nutrition knowledge. Although these preliminary findings from a small convenience sample should be interpreted with caution and future studies with a larger, more adequately powered sample are needed to confirm these results, the results do suggest that social-support oriented components would be a potentially useful addition to campus nutrition education programming.

papers.title: Learning After Deployment: An Audited Study of LLM-Supervised Online Adaptation
papers.authors: Saurabh Sarkar
papers.abstract: A correction is useful beyond the current conversation only if it changes how a model answers later questions. We study this form of deployment-time learning with a Qwen3-4B student, a Qwen3-14B instructor, and solver-verified training examples. The student retains a LoRA adapter and optimizer state across a curriculum of 26 puzzles from six task families. The teaching loop uses instructor-selected exercises, exact practice checks, and corrective reviews. Evaluation supplies only the current question and ordinary task instructions. In three runs on the same historical curriculum, the trained student answers 72 of 234 related-question attempts correctly, compared with 27 of 234 for the frozen backbone: 30.8% versus 11.5%. Each run has a positive aggregate difference. A separate auxiliary battery also improves overall, although several families lose accuracy. All runs pass deterministic audits of predictions, update eligibility, continuous training state, and evaluation boundaries. These results establish a reproducible case of accumulated parameter learning under rich external supervision. They do not establish the benefit of lesson selection over direct fine-tuning, a reduction in forgetting, or effectiveness with real human instructors. The study motivates user-operated adaptation while measuring an automated surrogate under a deliberately narrow evaluation scope.

papers.title: Innovation-Based Coaching: A Framework for Education in the AI Age
papers.authors: Xiaoge Xu
papers.abstract: This article introduces Innovation-Based Coaching (IBC) as a strategic framework to bridge the growing divide between AI-driven work and education’s predominantly content-focused nature. Drawing on insights from AI in education, coaching, innovation management, and employability studies, IBC uses a 3C mindset, a 3D process, and a 3M toolkit to cultivate an innovative mindset, build innovative skills, and produce innovative outputs. The 3C mindset emphasizes being Curious, Critical, and Creative; the 3D process involves Detecting, Dissecting, and Discovering to translate complex problems into targeted coaching actions; and the 3M toolkit incorporates Mapping, Measuring, and Monitoring for ongoing assessment and scaling. This approach positions AI as a collaborative partner that supports feedback, simulation, and experimentation while preserving human-centric skills such as ethical judgment, trust, and critical reflection. It also addresses major challenges in implementing IBC and offers solutions and recommendations. The conclusion focuses on the implications for policymakers, institutional leaders, program leaders, educators, and researchers.

papers.title: The co-creation process of the “Outdoor Air and Health Atlas” project: A tool to support decisions and research
papers.authors: Elena Davoli, Elena Mazzoleni, Marta Ottone, Laura Bonvicini, Olivera Djurić, Serena Broccoli, Andrea Ranzi, Giorgio Cattani, Massimo Stafoggia, Nicolàs Zengarini, Paola Angelini, Paolo Giorgi Rossi
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: the 'ATLAS Aria Outdoor e Salute' (Outdoor Air and Health Atlas) project aims to develop a national atlas to estimate the effects of air pollution on health, making it accessible to both professionals and citizens and available as open data. OBJECTIVES: to describe the co-creation decision-making process adopted to define the contents of the Atlas. DESIGN: two rounds of questionnaires with open-ended questions were conducted following the Delphi method, collecting proposals on possible options for data sources, territorial disaggregation, exposures, health outcomes, methods for calculating attributable fractions, and counterfactual scenarios on which to estimate the potential benefits of policies. The Delphi process started by selecting health outcomes and pollutants for which dose-response functions were already available in the scientific literature. Participants were then given the opportunity to propose additional outcomes or pollutants for inclusion in the Atlas. The responses collected in the questionnaire administered during the first round, and subsequently discussed in a plenary session, informed the development of the second-round questions. The results of the second round identified the health outcomes and pollutants eligible for inclusion in the Atlas, which were then discussed in a plenary session held with the participation of external experts. SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: internal members of the working group participated in the first round; the second round included, in addition, other stakeholders and representatives from Italian Regions not involved in the Atlas. Results were discussed in online and in-person meetings with experts and stakeholders until an agreement was reached. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: for each proposed health outcome and pollutant, it is assessed: the level of certainty regarding the causal link between the pollutant and the health outcome; the relevance for public health; the accuracy of the information available in routine databases; the usefulness of including that outcome in the Atlas maps. For all other parameters, the level of agreement reached across the two Delphi rounds and the plenary meetings was evaluated. RESULTS: sixteen experts participated in the first round, 22 in the second. The process led to the definition of data sources to be used (cause-specific mortality data from the Italian National Institute of Statistics, hospital discharge records for hospitalisations), the spatial resolution of exposure estimates (1×1 km) and the model used to derive them (annual averages produced by a previously validated and published model from BIGEPI project), the level of data aggregation for the analyses (municipal level), and the pollutants to be considered as exposures for calculating the attributable fraction (PM2.5 and NO2). Both long-term and short-term effects were considered. Considering the available data sources, the outcomes that met the criteria of certainty, public health relevance, and exposure accuracy were, for long-term effects, mortality and hospital admissions due to natural, cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory causes, as well as lung cancer; for short-term effects, the same outcomes were identified except for lung cancer. The outcomes to be included in the Atlas are mortality and incidence or, where relevant, prevalence. It was further decided to show the attributable fraction for each pollutant, explicitly illustrating the steps involved in its derivation: starting from pollutant concentrations and the resident population, the population-weighted exposure (PWE) is calculated. By combining the PWE with the disease burden and the dose-response function provided in the literature, it is then possible to estimate the attributable fraction by comparing the current scenario with a counterfactual scenario in which pollution levels correspond to WHO guideline values (5 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 10 µg/m³ for NO2). In addition, it was decided to allow for the estimation of the number of attributable deaths under alternative, potentially achievable future pollution levels. Regarding the choice of outcomes to be included, a comparison with the most recent systematic review was conducted during the final plenary meeting, which confirmed the decisions made. CONCLUSIONS: the co-creative process adopted allowed for broad participation and sharing of content while maintaining consistency with the best available scientific evidence.

papers.title: The co-creative process of the “Outdoor Air and Health Atlas” project: stakeholder and user involvement in the definition of information and communication needs
papers.authors: Elena Davoli, Michele Bartolomei, Marco Ottolenghi, Laura Bonvicini, Serena Broccoli, Luca Ghirotto, Paola Angelini, Paolo Giorgi Rossi
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: to describe the co-creation process adopted to define the content and communication approaches of the Air and Health Atlas. DESIGN: a two-phase co-creation process using qualitative research methods: focus groups and interviews. The first phase explored users' information needs; the second evaluated content and communication strategies through discussion of an advanced prototype of the Atlas. SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: the ATLAS is a project promoted by the Italian Ministry of Health, aimed at integrating air quality data and health outcomes into an interactive tool to support decision-makers, technical experts, and citizens. Focus groups and interviews were conducted in Emilia-Romagna Region (Northern Italy). Stakeholders from the environmental and health sectors (technical experts, health professionals, decision-makers) were involved and selected through a stakeholder mapping instrument ('thermometer tool'). MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: information needs regarding the relationship between air quality and health, communication preferences, comprehensibility and interpretability of data and maps, perception of communication risks, and evaluation of the Atlas prototype. RESULTS: thematic analysis identified four thematic areas: 1. awareness and knowledge; 2. behaviours and lifestyles; 3. information dissemination; 4. geographic scale of reference. A widespread difficulty emerged, particularly among non-experts, in understanding scientific data and linking pollutant exposure to health effects. Stakeholders highlighted the need for clear information on health impacts, future scenarios, and avoidable deaths under different hypothetical scenarios. The importance of emphasising the co-benefits of mitigation actions (reduction of air pollution and climate impact, promotion of physical activity, and healthy diets) was stressed, while avoiding alarmist approaches. The need for accessible language, easily interpretable maps, and supporting methodological explanations was also underlined, without differentiating navigation between technical users and citizens. The prototype was considered highly informative, but potentially prone to misinterpretation in the absence of adequate interpretative tools. CONCLUSIONS: systematic stakeholder involvement helped shape the content and communication choices of the Atlas, highlighting the need to balance scientific rigour and accessibility. The co-creation approach emerges as an effective strategy to improve transparency, comprehensibility, and trust in scientific information supporting public health decision-making.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in neurosurgical education – current applications, opportunities and limitations: A narrative review
papers.authors: Mateusz Stępień, Marta Strauchman, Anna Siodłak, Setlak Marcin, Bartłomiej Błaszczyk
papers.abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) is updating medical and neurosurgical education. This narrative review provides an updated synthesis of recent applications of AI in neurosurgical education, with particular emphasis on LLMs, knowledge assessment, simulation-based training, automated competency evaluation, and implementation risks. Through machine learning, deep learning, and virtual reality systems, AI enables personalized, adaptive learning pathways, 24/7 on-demand academic assistance, and objective, data-driven competency evaluations in risk-free environments. In neurosurgery, intelligent surgical simulators and automated 3D spatial planning tools optimize technical execution and track procedural metrics. Generative AI streamlines curriculum design, literature synthesis, and examination drafting. However, the adoption of foundation models introduces critical limitations and risks. These systems remain vulnerable to hallucinations, logic confabulations, and fabricated bibliographic citations, which pose risks in high-stakes clinical contexts. Excessive dependence on AI can cause cognitive fatigue, diminish independent critical thinking, and elevate risks related to academic plagiarism, algorithmic bias, and data privacy. To address these challenges, continuous human verification is required. AI should function as a supportive, transparent assistant of human clinical judgment, ensuring that technological innovation reinforces core values of medical practice and patient safety.

papers.title: Data and Algorithms: Strategic Disclosure of Competitiveness on Platforms Through Marketplace Analytics
papers.authors: Fei Long, Yi Liu
papers.abstract: This paper studies an e-commerce platform’s two intertwined decisions when offering marketplace analytics: the data access policy and the algorithm design. The data boom in e-commerce has spurred artificial intelligence (AI)-powered marketplace analytics, but platforms hold the data reins. Some adopt open data-access policies with third-party analytics providers (e.g., permitting data-scraping or application programming interface sharing), whereas others are restrictive. We ask why and when an e-commerce platform—capable of designing its own analytics to control sellers’ actions—may benefit from open data-access policies to accommodate competing third-party analytics services, despite the potential drawbacks of weakening its data advantages and control. We analyze two intertwined decisions an e-commerce platform can make when designing analytics to predict market competitiveness and assist sellers’ pricing decisions involving (1) data-access policy and (2) algorithm design. We find that platforms may use over-optimistic algorithms (by increasing the likelihood of generating low-competition signals) in their own analytics to boost commissions. Because sellers do not trust the platform to act in their best interest, they may be reluctant to adopt a platform’s analytics, resulting in a lose–lose situation and prompting the platform to allow data access to third-party providers. Overall, platforms gain from open data-access strategies in markets with moderately strong or weak competition. Finally, privacy legislation aimed at curtailing platforms’ data-sharing practices may inadvertently hurt consumers. History: Anthony Dukes served as the senior editor. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2024.0960 .

papers.title: “ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CLINICAL SIMULATION TO STRENGTHEN SOFT SKILLS IN STUDENTS OF OBSTETRICS AND RELATED FIELDS: A PRISMA-SCOPING REVIEW”
papers.authors: Paula Liliana Nam Donoso, Ximena Muñoz Alvarez, María Jesús Rojas Castro, Magdalena Vera Flores, Kiara Vergara Figueroa
papers.abstract: Clinical simulation is a highly effective teaching strategy that enables students to develop skills in controlled environments. Advances in technology have led to the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) to create more immersive simulation experiences. Objective: To analyse the available scientific evidence, through a scoping review, on the effectiveness of using artificial intelligence tools in clinical simulation to strengthen soft skills in students of obstetrics and related disciplines. Method: A descriptive scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Data collection: Searches were carried out in the Clinical Key, Scopus, EBSCOhost and ScienceDirect databases, using DeCS/MeSH descriptors. Results: The analysis included 11 studies published between 2021 and 2025, primarily involving students in nursing, obstetrics, and other health-related fields. The interventions identified included immersive simulations using virtual reality and generative artificial intelligence, intelligent virtual patients, AI-enabled high-fidelity manikins, natural language processing systems, and automated debriefing platforms. Taken together, these tools were associated with improvements in clinical communication, self-confidence, empathy, critical thinking, decision-making, and teamwork, facilitated by repeated practice, immediate feedback, and learning in safe environments. However, the evidence was heterogeneous and still preliminary, with limitations identified regarding the reduced realism of nonverbal communication, mechanical responses, reduced human interaction, implementation costs, the need for digital skills, language barriers, and ethical and privacy considerations. Therefore, AI is proposed as a complementary tool to conventional clinical simulation and not as a substitute for human interaction. Conclusions: The evidence analyzed supports the conclusion that artificial intelligence applied to clinical simulation represents a promising educational tool for strengthening social skills in students of obstetrics and related fields, particularly in areas such as clinical communication, self-confidence, empathy, reflection, collaborative work, and—to a lesser extent—decision-making and critical thinking. The identified benefits are primarily related to the ability to practice repeatedly, interact with dynamic scenarios, receive immediate feedback, and learn in safe environments.

papers.title: Prediction-Point, Feature-Admissibility and Leakage Audit Protocol for Supervised Predictive AI Studies v1
papers.authors: Mohit Tiwari
papers.abstract: Predictive artificial intelligence studies can report apparently strong performance while relying on predictors, transformations, or modelling procedures that would not be legitimate at the intended prediction point. Such problems include target-derived predictors, post-outcome information, temporally unavailable variables, inappropriate partitioning, duplicate or related observations across partitions, preprocessing before data separation, feature selection using evaluation data, and repeated use of a test set during model development. This protocol provides a domain-independent, reproducible procedure for auditing construct validity, prediction-time feature availability, feature admissibility, data leakage, partition integrity, preprocessing boundaries, model-selection practices, and robustness in supervised predictive-AI studies. It is applicable to classification and regression tasks in software engineering, healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, education, business analytics, and other data-driven disciplines. The protocol begins with a Prediction-Point Contract defining the target, unit of prediction, observation window, prediction point, outcome window, intended use, and legitimate information boundary. Every candidate predictor is then evaluated through a Feature Admissibility Record addressing construct meaning, provenance, temporal availability, target dependence, derivational dependence, and partition-specific learning. Pipeline-level risks are separately documented in a Leakage Register and Partition and Preprocessing Audit. Questionable predictors or modelling decisions are subjected to sensitivity and ablation analysis. The protocol concludes with a structured audit decision of PASS, CONDITIONAL, or FAIL. Required outputs are a Prediction-Point Contract, Feature Admissibility Matrix, Leakage Register, Partition and Preprocessing Audit, Sensitivity and Ablation Record, and Final Audit Checklist. The protocol is intended to make predictive-model validity claims more transparent, reproducible, auditable, and comparable across application domains. The protocol may be applied prospectively before model development, retrospectively to an existing study, or during peer review or replication.

papers.title: Metodología proyectual de la movilidad creativa y recreativa al aire libre
papers.authors: Rodolfo Rojas Rocha
papers.abstract: This article arises from an inquiry into the natur-urban space, particularly through its documentation by means of creative walking. The theoretical framework is constructed from a humanistic approach in which the territorial image is studied on digital platforms and a visual network of phenomena. Within these, modes of geo-exploration are materialized such as manual, digital, or intelligent drawing (AI). Likewise, reflection is carried out regarding the symbolic realm in accordance with a semiotics of public space. The objective is to identify the narrative of the aesthetic and complex configurations of the environment while walking. The process of documentation describes the steps of recreational mobilization in the landscape, which are grounded in life experiences and identify of the urban image. As a result, an artistic work and a recreational model oriented toward a multidimensional version of mobility are obtained. Also, this achieves a rhizome of ecosystemic elements extracted from the marrow of physical activity. Individual and collective routes reveal adventures with the help of verbo-iconic resources. In conclusion, the acceleration of aesthetic, cognitive, and social processes fosters outdoor recreation and provides solidarity with quality of life.

papers.title: Value co-creation and customer satisfaction in last-mile delivery services: The roles of digital accessibility and delivery service quality
papers.authors: Wanyang Zhou, LEO MANANSALA, Alice Valerio, Xiaoting Sun
papers.abstract: Despite substantial improvements in speed and coverage, customer satisfaction with last-mile delivery remains inconsistent, particularly in complex urban environments where rising consumer expectations, traffic congestion, and operational pressures create persistent challenges. This study investigates the influence of customer value co-creation behaviors, customer participation behaviors (CPB), and customer citizenship behaviors (CCB), on customer satisfaction (CS), examining the mediating role of delivery service quality (DSQ) dimensions and the moderating role of digital accessibility (DA). Data were collected from 426 urban consumers in China, exceeding the minimum sample required by Cochran's formula. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test direct, mediating, and moderating effects. Findings reveal that CPB directly enhances satisfaction, whereas CCB primarily affects satisfaction indirectly through operational, customization, and personal contact quality. Digital accessibility strengthens the effects of CPB and CCB on DSQ but has a limited direct influence on satisfaction. The study's novelty lies in simultaneously examining participation and citizenship behaviors, multi-dimensional service quality, and digital accessibility in the context of urban last-mile delivery, a combination not previously explored. Practically, the findings provide actionable guidance for logistics firms to integrate customer engagement strategies with accessible digital platforms to optimize service quality and enhance satisfaction.

papers.title: Pediatric sleep questionnaire-based risk of obstructive sleep apnea in children with morbid obesity
papers.authors: Meltem Kürtül Çakar, Sanem Eryılmaz Polat, Dilber Ademhan Tural, Gökçen Dilşa Tuğcu, Çelebi Yıldırım, Hande Yetişgin, Ayyüce Ünlü, Gamze Akça Dinç, Işıl Bilgiç, Satı Özkan Tabakçı, Şule Selin Akyan Soydaş, Murat Yasin Gençoğlu, Salih Uytun, Güzin Cinel
papers.abstract: Objective: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in children with morbid obesity is an important health problem requiring early diagnosis and intervention due to its high prevalence and multidimensional clinical effects. This study aimed to assess the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire (PSQ)-based OSA risk in children with morbid obesity and to evaluate associated clinical and laboratory findings. Materials and Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study included children with morbid obesity who were admitted to a tertiary pediatric pulmonology outpatient clinic between 2021 and 2023 and followed up for at least one year. Morbid obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) ≥99th percentile. Patient clinical characteristics were obtained from the electronic medical record system. OSA was evaluated using the PSQ. Patients were divided into two groups according to the PSQ cut-off value: Group 1 included children with PSQ scores <0.33, and Group 2 included children with PSQ scores ≥0.33. Results: This study included 47 children with morbid obesity, with a median age of 15.0 years (Q1–Q3: 12.5–16.5); 21 patients (44.7%) were male. The most common complaint was fatigue with exertion (n=41, 87.0%). The median PSQ score was 0.42 (Q1–Q3: 0.25–0.59). A negative correlation was found between PSQ score and oxygen saturation (r=−0.289, p=0.049) and FEF25–75 (L) (r=−0.490, p=0.011). According to the evaluation of PSQ cut-off values, hypercarbia was more frequently detected in Group 2 than in Group 1 (p=0.047). Only four of the 47 patients underwent PSG; three of these patients had an apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) >5, and a these three patients were in Group 2 based on their PSQ scores. Conclusion: In this study, the risk of OSA in children with morbid obesity, as assessed by the PSQ, was found to be high. Our findings highlight the importance of clinical awareness of OSA in children with morbid obesity. Further PSG-based studies with larger sample sizes are needed to better establish the potential role of the PSQ as a feasible alternative screening tool for early diagnosis.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Case Discussions: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Critical Engagement
papers.authors: Robert W. Myers, Karthik Ramachandran, Badri Varadarajan
papers.abstract: The case method has been successfully used in operations management courses and is central to business education, yet its effectiveness depends on consistent student preparation. Many students engage only superficially with cases, and the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, further complicates the challenge—providing shortcuts that yield summaries without fostering deeper understanding of trade-offs. This study investigates whether AI can instead be used to strengthen the case method as a pedagogical tool. Partnering with an AI-based upskilling platform, we conducted a field experiment using an AI-supported “quest” structure. We found that students achieved higher quiz scores when using the AI tool to support case preparation than when completing the same type of task without AI-supported preparation. For a group of 38 participants, on average, AI use was associated with an improvement of almost 1 point on a 10-point quiz. This difference was statistically significant using a paired t-test (t(37) = 4.50, p < 0.001). In addition, scores in the AI-supported condition were statistically less variable (standard deviation (SD) = 2.29 versus SD = 1.37), suggesting that AI support may help promote more consistent learning outcomes across students. These findings suggest that rather than undermining the case method, generative AI can enhance case learning when integrated deliberately into preclass preparation.

papers.title: Evaluating How Artificial Intelligence Tools Influence Educational Outcomes, Usage Patterns, and User Perceptions in Research Proposal Development: A Convergent Mixed Methods Study.
papers.authors: Rashad H. Alkashgari, Abdulmonem A. Alhayani, Asmaa Abdel Nasser, Khamrunissa Hussain Sheikh, Intessar Emam Sultan, Yousria A Badawy
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, including medical education, particularly for research training and academic writing. Research methodology and biostatistics courses are often perceived as challenging, with students reporting difficulty structuring research proposals, interpreting statistical concepts, and applying theoretical knowledge to research practice. This study aimed to assess the perceived benefits, challenges, ethical considerations, and implementation needs associated with a customized AI tool for research proposal writing among fourth-year medical students enrolled in a Research Methodology and Biostatistics course. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was used. A customized ChatGPT-based Research Proposal Smart Tool (RPST-GPT) was developed and provided to students to support proposal development. Data were collected through a self-administered questionnaire assessing perceived benefits, challenges, and ethical awareness related to AI use in research proposal writing, together with open-ended questions exploring students' recommendations for future AI integration. Results A total of 228 students participated. Students reported high perceived benefits of AI use in research proposal writing (mean 46.48 out of 60) and high ethical awareness regarding appropriate AI use (mean 14.32 out of 20), reflecting recognition of responsible practices and avoidance of overreliance. Qualitative responses indicated that students viewed AI as a supportive learning tool requiring foundational AI literacy and ethical guidance. Conclusions A customized AI tool can enhance undergraduate medical students' research skills when embedded within a structured and governed curriculum. Intentional integration, supported by training, clear policies, and active faculty involvement, is needed to maximize educational benefits and mitigate potential risks.

papers.title: Calcyon: Design and Validation of an AI-Based Chatbot Framework Integrating Computational Thinking and Self-Regulated Learning in University Calculus Learning
papers.authors: Lussy Midani Rizki, Yaya Sukjaya Kusumah, Al Jupri, Bambang Avip Priatna, Vanya Aridanthy, Sowanto ., Maya Nurlita
papers.abstract: Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mathematics education has advanced rapidly; however, systematic AI-based chatbot frameworks that integrate computational thinking (CT) and self-regulated learning (SRL) scaffolding within university calculus remain limited. This study developed and formatively evaluated Calcyon, an AI-based chatbot framework designed to integrate CT processes and SRL scaffolding within university differential calculus learning. Methods A Design and Development Research (DDR) approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed, focusing on the design, development, and formative evaluation stages. Expert evaluation (n = 3) was conducted across five design dimensions using Aiken’s V to examine content and design validity. A formative student pilot study (n = 11) was conducted to evaluate prototype readability and feasibility across six dimensions. Results Expert evaluation indicated strong expert-rated design and content validity across content, instructional, technical, linguistic, and media design dimensions (Aiken’s V = 0.92). Most items met the predefined criterion, while several revisions were incorporated based on expert feedback. The student pilot indicated good readability and feasibility of the prototype. Conclusions Calcyon provides an empirically evaluated AI-based chatbot framework that integrates AI-mediated interaction, CT-oriented scaffolding, and multidimensional SRL design principles within university calculus learning. The findings provide evidence of framework quality and feasibility; however, they do not establish the effectiveness of Calcyon in improving CT, SRL, or calculus learning outcomes. Further empirical studies are required to examine its instructional effectiveness.

papers.title: From answer machine to collaborative partner: impact of structured generative AI training on scientific problem solving in STEM education
papers.authors: Bingjie Huang, Li Xie, Yamei Liu, Xiaohan Liu, Hongchen Tang, Xiumei Feng, Cuilan Qiao, Qing Guo, Chunxiao Wu, Lei Bao
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Generative AI (GenAI) holds great potential for STEM education, especially in the context of problem-solving tasks, but unguided use often leads to metacognitive laziness, where students treat the technology as an answer machine rather than a collaborative partner. On the basis of Zimmerman’s self-regulated learning (SRL) framework and cognitive load theory (CLT), our randomized controlled trial (RCT; N = 95) investigated whether a structured, SRL-aligned scaffolding training session could improve students’ AI-assisted revision performance in electromagnetism problems. The experimental group ( n = 50) received the designed training, which emphasized the nature of GenAI, the SRL-aligned prompting strategy, and the remediation strategy for GenAI deficiencies. The control group ( n = 45) received problem-solving instruction without specific AI guidance. After completing the Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism (CSEM) independently, both groups subsequently conversed with the large language model Doubao to revise their responses. Results Independent samples t tests revealed that the experimental group showed greater AI-assisted revision performance ( d = 0.81, p < 0.001) than did the control group. The experimental group reported comparable overall cognitive load, despite a marginal elevation in the intrinsic cognitive load. Robust linear models showed that training attenuated the predictive effect of prior GenAI experience on revision performance. Qualitative analysis revealed that trained participants employed more diverse higher-order strategies and deployed systematic error remediation upon identifying AI deficiencies. The trained students achieved an incorrect-to-correct revision rate of 69.3%, compared with 41.3% for the control group. Conclusion Effective GenAI integration requires pedagogical scaffolding rather than mere access to the tool itself. The results suggest that training can enhance students’ revision performance and foster more strategic engagement with GenAI in the short term. These findings not only extend the theoretical applications of SRL and CLT in the human-AI context but also underscore the practical need for student development in AI literacy.
keywords: Conceptual Survey of Electricity and Magnetism

papers.title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
papers.authors: Zachery Quince, Emily Kaye Faulconer
papers.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education and the resulting institutional responses have prompted research to support evidence-based policy decisions. As policies change to adjust to this disruptive technology, it demands agility from educators. The impacts of these policy changes on student behaviours and outcomes are currently poorly understood. This study examines how students used GenAI across three assessments in an undergraduate physics unit after assessment redesign forced by institutional policy that permitted purpose-specific and open use. Using a mixed-methods approach, student declarations of GenAI use were coded into four functional categories and mapped to the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition (SAMR) framework. Learning and Formatting dominated early use and aligned with substitution and augmentation for a presentation assessment type. Later assessments showed a marked growth in Feedback uses, which spanned all SAMR levels and became the most common pattern. ‘Doing Task’ uses appeared in smaller numbers but illustrated modification and redefinition when GenAI generated step-by-step solutions for unfamiliar problems. Across all assessments, GenAI users achieved slightly higher scores, although differences were not statistically significant, so this trend should be interpreted as a tentative observation. Findings suggest that assessment design, which rewards understanding and requires student judgement, aligns with the theoretical markers of evaluative judgement. While this study did not directly measure internal cognitive states, the observed change in functional behaviour, specifically the transition toward iterative feedback loops, suggests that GenAI could serve as a catalyst for learning. This study provides empirical evidence on how assessment redesign based on policy shifts influences GenAI use patterns and proposes design principles for authentic assessment in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) contexts. It highlights authentic assessment and constructive alignment as guiding principles for sustainable policy and pedagogy in the GenAI era, ensuring coherence among learning outcomes, activities, and assessment.

papers.title: The domain-specific bias in creativity evaluation: human evaluators favor human-created art, but prefer AI outputs for divergent thinking
papers.authors: Yanming Hou, Yingying Zhang, Bin Wang, Yuxi Zhu, Xiaofei Wu
papers.abstract: Abstract How do humans perceive and evaluate creativity when it is attributed to artificial intelligence (AI)? This research examined how labeling a source as “AI” versus “human” systematically biases creativity evaluations across different domains. In experiment 1 (painting and poetry), outputs labeled as human-created were rated as more creative than identical AI-labeled outputs in artistic creation. Experiment 2, which manipulated the attribution of co-created works, revealed that the “human ideation with AI assistance” label enhanced perceived originality in poetry, whereas those attributed primarily to humans remained dominant in evaluations of painting. Experiment 3 utilized a divergent thinking task (Alternative Uses Test), found a reversal: the same output received higher creativity ratings when bearing an AI label. The findings reveal a domain-specific pattern in attitudes toward AI creativity: viewing collaboration positively yet maintaining a persistent bias in valuing AI’s creative contributions.

papers.title: Brain structure age in obstructive sleep apnea: a cross-sectional deep learning analysis
papers.authors: Mahdi Mohammadi, Maryam Jalali, Hamed Amirifard, Masoud Rezaei, Shahram Samadi
papers.abstract: Brain-age methods may summarize structural variation, but it is unclear whether brain structure age (BSA) differs between adults with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and controls. We tested global and region-specific BSA differences and associations with clinical measures. This cross-sectional observational analysis included 45 treatment-naive adults with OSA and 45 healthy controls. Participants underwent T1-weighted 3 T MRI and Montreal Cognitive Assessment; OSA participants additionally underwent polysomnography. Images were processed with the volBrain BrainStructureAges pipeline. The primary analysis compared global BSA between groups. Regional comparisons and clinical/polysomnographic correlations were secondary analyses, with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction applied within each family. A sensitivity regression adjusted the global BSA comparison for chronological age, sex, and BMI. Global BSA did not differ significantly between groups (49.94 ± 11.98 years in OSA vs. 46.89 ± 11.75 years in controls; mean difference, 3.05 years; 95% CI, − 1.92 to 8.02; p = 0.226). The adjusted OSA group effect was 2.05 years (95% CI, −0.67 to 4.78; p = 0.138). Of 125 regional comparisons, 16 had nominal unadjusted p < 0.05, but none survived FDR correction (minimum q = 0.248). Global BSA was nominally associated with Epworth Sleepiness Scale score ( n = 34, r = 0.424, p = 0.013) and REM latency ( n = 34, r = −0.388, p = 0.023), but neither survived FDR correction across 15 clinical/polysomnographic correlations ( q = 0.175 for both). In this cohort, global BSA did not differ between OSA and controls, and no regional or clinical/polysomnographic association remained significant after multiplicity correction. The findings provide no evidence that BSA distinguishes OSA from controls or functions as a clinical biomarker for OSA. Larger longitudinal studies with polysomnography-confirmed controls are needed to determine whether smaller effects were missed.

papers.title: Adoption of, attitudes towards, and perceived challenges of digital health in hospice and palliative care among professionals in Germany: a national cross-sectional web-based survey
papers.authors: Felix Muehlensiepen, Kim-Laura Speck, Merlin Deckers, Isabel Kächele, Frank Elsner, Jan Franco, Catharina Muente, Alexandra Cranen, Theresa Sophie Busse, Isabel Burner-Fritsch, Vera Peuckmann‐Post
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Digital health technologies may support communication, symptom management, continuity of care, and access to services in hospice and palliative care. National data on their adoption, on professionals’ attitudes, and on perceived barriers are scarce. We examined digital health adoption, attitudes towards digital health, perceived suitability, perceived barriers, and self-rated eHealth literacy among hospice and palliative care professionals in Germany. Methods We conducted a national cross-sectional web-based survey among all members of the German Society for Palliative Medicine (DGP) between 15 August and 28 September 2024.
