The questionnaire covered current use of digital devices and services, perceived suitability and impact of digital health, perceived usefulness across care domains, perceived barriers, use of and willingness to use artificial intelligence (AI), and self-rated eHealth literacy using the German Revised eHealth Literacy Scale (GR-eHEALS). We analyzed data descriptively and with bivariate tests. We report the study according to the CHERRIES and CROSS checklists. Results In total, 618 professionals completed the survey (completion rate 88%; 9.6% of all invited members). Established tools were used by most respondents (computers 99%, email 98%, electronic patient documentation 73%), whereas patient-facing and newer technologies were used less often (electronic health card 39%, mobile health apps 29%, video consultation 20%). In 2024, 69% reported no regular AI use; 12.7% selected the maximum score for willingness to use AI regularly at work. Respondents rated digital health as less suitable for hospice and palliative care than for general healthcare (M = 3.53 vs. 4.00 on a 1–5 scale; Cohen’s d = 0.59). Digital tools were rated as most useful for coordination with external professionals, advance care planning, and communication with relatives, and as least useful for nursing care, therapies, and pastoral care. The most frequently perceived barriers were inadequate technical infrastructure (75%) and perceived limited digital literacy among patients (67%) and relatives (62%). Self-rated eHealth literacy was high (GR-eHEALS M = 4.31 on a 1–5 scale). Conclusions Hospice and palliative care professionals in Germany broadly use established digital tools, whereas patient-facing technologies are used less. Acceptance is context-specific: digital support is welcomed for coordination, advance care planning, and communication, and viewed more cautiously where personal presence is central to care. Implementation should prioritize technical infrastructure and context-sensitive design that preserves relational, person-centered care.

papers.title: Machine learning-based analysis of factors influencing maximum tongue pressure in patients after cardiac surgery: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Aimin Shao, Run Huang, Tingting Zhang, Jia Xin Wan, Haiou Xia, Yilei Zhu
papers.abstract: A low postoperative maximum tongue pressure (MTP) reflects diminished tongue muscle strength, which can compromise oral-phase swallowing function and lead to adverse clinical outcomes. However, the specific perioperative determinants of MTP in cardiac surgery patients remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify the independent clinical predictors of postoperative MTP using a hybrid machine learning approach. In this cross-sectional study conducted at a teaching hospital in Shanghai from April 2025 to January 2026, a total of 470 adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery were included. MTP was assessed 8–24 h post-extubation, and comprehensive perioperative data were systematically extracted. To overcome multicollinearity and prevent model overfitting, a dual-algorithm feature selection was employed. Variables were ranked by a Random Forest (RF) algorithm, and optimal feature subsets were selected using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression with 10-fold cross-validation. The overlapping core variables were subsequently incorporated into a multivariable stepwise linear regression model. A total of 470 patients were included. Based on the RF and LASSO models, 12 core features were extracted from 18 candidate variables. Multivariable linear regression confirmed five independent predictors. According to the variable importance ranking and standardized coefficients, prolonged endotracheal intubation duration ( β = -0.254, p < 0.001) emerged as the strongest independent predictor of postoperative MTP, followed by older age ( β = -0.167, p < 0.001) and higher log-transformed NT-proBNP levels ( β = -0.111, p = 0.011). In contrast, greater handgrip strength ( β = 0.221, p < 0.001) emerged as the strongest independent positive predictor of postoperative MTP, followed by higher body mass index ( β = 0.133, p = 0.001). Prolonged endotracheal intubation, advanced age, and diminished physiological reserves (low handgrip strength, elevated NT-proBNP, and lower BMI) are independent predictors of lower postoperative tongue pressure. Although extubation timing is dictated by overall clinical status, close monitoring of tongue strength and early rehabilitative support are essential for patients experiencing prolonged intubation. Furthermore, preoperative physical and nutritional optimization are key strategies to preserve postoperative tongue pressure and facilitate oral-motor recovery in vulnerable cardiac surgery patients.

papers.title: Multidimensional evaluation of generative AI chatbots for public consultation on sudden cardiac death: safety, accuracy, empathy, reliability, quality, and readability across six models
papers.authors: Youyou Chen, Hui Ma, Huimin Wang, Duoxue Chen, Haiyan Wang, Rongyan Jiang
papers.abstract: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for health information, but their performance in safety-sensitive sudden cardiac death (SCD) consultation remains insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated six publicly accessible chatbots on SCD-related public questions involving symptom triage, emergency response, CPR/AED use, inherited risk, myocarditis-related concerns, return to exercise, screening, and ICD decision-making. This cross-sectional, comparative, text-level study evaluated ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, Doubao, and Perplexity. A standardized set of 56 SCD-related public consultation questions was developed from Google Trends, online forums, public question-answer platforms, clinical guidelines, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and qualitative interviews. Each question was submitted once to each chatbot between May 10 and May 16, 2026, yielding 336 model-response items. Five blinded senior cardiology raters assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS. Readability was calculated using six formula-based indices. Between-model comparisons were performed using Cochran’s Q test and Friedman tests, with Kendall’s W reported as the effect size. Responses containing potential safety concerns were additionally examined qualitatively. Inter-rater agreement was high across all manually assessed metrics, with Fleiss’ kappa of 0.856 for Safety and ICC values ranging from 0.801 to 0.887 for other domains. Safe responses predominated across all models, although responses containing potential safety concerns occurred in every chatbot. ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking and Perplexity had the highest observed safety proportions during this query window, whereas Doubao had the lowest. Qualitative analysis identified recurrent concerns involving delayed emergency activation for chest pain, syncope, or post-viral symptoms; over-reassurance about prevention; fixed return-to-exercise timelines after infection or COVID-19; pulse-check instructions that could delay CPR; and oversimplified screening, electrolyte, or ICD-related advice. Most flagged responses contained a single potential safety concern. The qualitative severity distribution was concentrated in low and low-to-moderate concerns, whereas higher-severity concerns were less frequent. Accuracy differed significantly across models ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.864), with ChatGPT Plus 5.5 thinking, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot smart, DeepSeek-V4-pro, and Perplexity achieving similar median scores and Doubao performing lower. Empathy also differed significantly ( P < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.531), with DeepSeek-V4-pro having the highest observed score. Significant differences were observed for DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA, GQS, and all readability indices (all P < 0.001). Within this dataset, DeepSeek-V4-pro had the highest DISCERN and EQIP scores and the most favorable readability profile, Gemini 3.5 Flash showed comparable EQIP performance, and Microsoft Copilot smart had the highest JAMA score. However, transparency remained limited overall, and all models produced responses with relatively high reading-grade requirements. In this multidimensional evaluation of six generative AI chatbots for SCD-related public consultation, most responses were safe and clinically relevant, but potential safety concerns occurred across all models. Important limitations involved emergency escalation, CPR/AED guidance, return-to-exercise advice, individualized risk interpretation, transparency, and readability. These tools may support general SCD education, but they should not replace emergency medical services or clinician assessment. Because each question was sampled once during a defined week and all prompts were submitted in English through public interfaces accessed in China, the findings should be interpreted as a time-, language-, and access-specific snapshot rather than a stable ranking of the underlying models. Future development should prioritize evidence-linked content, clear red-flag escalation, plain-language communication, and ongoing expert review.

papers.title: Health literacy and metabolic syndrome in Korean adults: a nationwide cross-sectional analysis of KNHANES 2023–2024
papers.authors: Sena Hwang, Hyun Min Kim
papers.abstract: Health literacy (HL) is a social determinant of health, yet its independent, population-level association with metabolic syndrome (MetS) remains unclear, particularly in Asian populations. Using data from the first Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cycles to include a validated, multidimensional HL instrument, we examined the association between HL and MetS, including variation by sex and associations with individual MetS components. We performed a nationally representative cross-sectional analysis of 11,142 adults using the 2023–2024 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, applying complex survey weights. HL was measured using a validated 10-item instrument (range, 10–40); a score ≥ 30 was considered adequate. MetS was defined using harmonized criteria. We used sequential logistic regression, with age and sex adjustment followed by socioeconomic adjustment as the primary model, and conducted sensitivity analyses additionally adjusting for lifestyle factors and body mass index (BMI). Restricted cubic splines and prespecified subgroup and domain-specific analyses were also performed. Prevalence ratios were estimated using survey-weighted modified Poisson regression. The weighted prevalence of MetS was 31.1%. In the primary model, adequate HL was inversely associated with MetS after adjustment for sociodemographic factors (prevalence ratio, 0.903; 95% CI, 0.848–0.962; P = 0.002; OR, 0.843). The association persisted after additional adjustment for lifestyle factors (PR, 0.917; 95% CI, 0.859–0.978) and was modestly attenuated after BMI adjustment (PR, 0.928; 95% CI, 0.874–0.986). An exploratory restricted cubic spline suggested a nonlinear pattern that was not significant under a design-based test ( P = 0.084). The association differed by sex ( P for interaction < 0.001) and was observed in women but not in men. Domain- and component-specific findings were exploratory; the four HL domains were highly intercorrelated and not distinguishable in mutually adjusted models. In Korean adults, adequate HL was inversely associated with prevalent MetS. The stronger association observed in women warrants prospective confirmation. Although separate exploratory models suggested inverse associations for the Healthcare and Technology & Resources domains, these domains were highly intercorrelated and not distinguishable in mutually adjusted analyses.
keywords: Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey

papers.title: Predictors of clinical pregnancy after IVF in women with ovarian endometriomas: a propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study
papers.authors: Y. Lynn Wang, Yuqing Zhang, Xinzhe Wang, Na Duan, ZhenGao Sun, Ruihua Zhao, Yanyun Yin
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Ovarian endometrioma (OMA) is associated with reduced in vitro fertilization (IVF) success rates. Therefore, the purpose of the study is to investigate risk factors associated with pregnancy outcomes following IVF in women with OMA and assess the predictive utility of maximum OMA diameter. Methods This propensity score-matched retrospective cohort study enrolled 2416 women who underwent IVF between December 2020 and November 2025. A total of 248 transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS)-confirmed OMA patients who underwent IVF were allocated to the OMA group. Conversely, 2,168 concurrently enrolled patients without ultrasonographically confirmed OMA who underwent IVF were assigned to the non-OMA group. A sample size of 738 was calculated to achieve a statistical power of 99.9% and a two-sided α of 0.05. Age, body mass index (BMI), and controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) protocols were adjusted between the two groups using propensity score matching (PSM) at a 1:3 ratio. After PSM, 248 OMA patients were matched to 738 patients without OMA who underwent IVF. Additionally, 248 OMA patients were stratified into pregnant and non-pregnant groups according to clinical pregnancy outcome, and factors associated with clinical pregnancy among these patients were identified. Results After PSM, multivariate logistic regression revealed that type of infertility, number of abortions and cesarean deliveries, and level of sex hormones were independent factors for OMA, and OMA independently influenced clinical pregnancy and early miscarriage rates ( P < 0.05). In the OMA group, multivariate logistic regression identified age, miscarriage number, COH protocols, and maximum OMA diameter as independent predictors of clinical pregnancy outcomes. The integrated predictive model exhibited an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.857, with optimal predicted cutoff values of 32.5 years for age and 21.25 mm for maximum OMA diameter. Conclusions The retrospective analysis delineated infertility type, obstetric history, and sex hormone profiles as independent risk factors for ovarian cysts. OMA subgroup analysis demonstrated age, miscarriage count, COH protocols, and maximum OMA diameter as key predictors of IVF outcomes. Registry : the Ethics Review Committee of the Jiangsu Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, approval number:2021NL-045-03, Registration date: 16 January 2021.

papers.title: Neural Representations of Perceptual Reorganization in the Musical Scale Illusion
papers.authors: Ahyeon Choi, Jusung Ham, Kyogu Lee, Inyong Choi
papers.abstract: The auditory system organizes complex acoustic input into coherent perceptual streams, yet how neural responses relate to physical stimulus structure and reported perception when the two diverge remains unclear. We investigated perceptual reorganization using the scale illusion, in which interleaved tone sequences presented separately to the two ears are typically heard as continuous melodic streams.Thirty participants listened to illusory, zigzag, and continuous sequences during EEG recording and reported whether each sequence sounded continuous or zigzag. Temporal response function models characterized neural encoding and reconstruction of amplitude-envelope (envelope) and pitch-change magnitude features. We tested whether neural responses during illusory listening corresponded more closely to reference patterns associated with the physical zigzag structure or reported continuous organization. Illusory sequences were predominantly categorized as Continuous and elicited longer RTs than non-illusory sequences. Encoding models revealed delayed pitch-change magnitude responses in the illusory condition, whereas envelope latencies remained comparatively stable. For pitch-change magnitude, reconstruction correlations computed over the full sequence exceeded chance levels estimated separately for each reference, with higher correlations for the continuous reference. Envelope correlations exceeded neither chance level, despite a small relative preference for the zigzag reference. These findings show that neural response timing and relative correspondence with the tested reference patterns depend on the modeled feature during the scale illusion. The reconstruction result concerns correlations across complete sequences and does not establish continuous tracking of the perceived melody.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play Dramaturge: A Divide-and-Conquer Approach for Iterative Narrative Script Refinement via Collaborative LLM Agents
papers.authors: Wenda Xie, Chao Guo, Yanqing Jing, Junle Wang, Yisheng Lv, Fei–Yue Wang
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
papers.abstract: Although LLMs have been widely adopted for creative content generation, a single-pass process often struggles to produce high-quality long narratives. How to effectively revise and improve long narrative scripts like scriptwriters remains a significant challenge, as it demands a comprehensive understanding of the entire context to identify global structural issues and local detailed flaws, as well as coordinating revisions at multiple granularities and locations. Direct modifications by LLMs typically introduce inconsistencies between local edits and the overall narrative requirements. To address these issues, we propose Dramaturge, a task and feature oriented divide-and-conquer approach powered by hierarchical multiple LLM agents. It consists of a Global Review stage to grasp the overall storyline and structural issues, a Scene-level Review stage to pinpoint detailed scene and sentence flaws, and a Hierarchical Coordinated Revision stage that coordinates and integrates structural and detailed improvements throughout the script. The top-down task flow ensures that high-level strategies guide local modifications, maintaining contextual consistency. The review and revision workflow follows a coarse-to-fine iterative process, continuing through multiple rounds until no further substantive improvements can be made. Comprehensive experiments show that Dramaturge significantly outperforms all baselines in terms of script-level overall quality and scene-level details. Our approach is plug-and-play and can be easily integrated into existing methods to improve the generated scripts.

papers.title: Humanoid AI with Humanity Modeling: Bridging Humans and Virtual–Physical Humanoids
papers.authors: Longbing Cao
papers.journal: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
papers.abstract: The seventy-year AI is now entering another major resurgence, the era of Generative AI (GenAI), characterized by the rapid advancement of large multimodal models (LMMs). GenAI and LMMs are fundamentally transforming sixty-decade-old humanoid robots, advancing them from human-looking and humanlike embodiments toward human-level AI and robotics, and inspiring a new era of AI-robotics symbiosis: humanoid AI . Humanoid AI develops humane AI-driven humanoids (AI humanoids) that go beyond traditional human-looking robots, which typically exhibit little or no humanity and intelligence due to their dedication to predefined and limited AI functions and exteriors. By contrast, AI humanoids undertake real-time, situated, and interactive mind-to-action, perception-to-behavior, and vision-to-emotion transformations, achieving an unprecedented degree of replicating human characteristics and intelligence. Realizing this vision requires systematic humanity modeling, ensuring that AI humanoids are shaped, guided, and governed by robust frameworks of AI and robotic humanity. We then propose human-virtual-physical humanoid transform and alignment and human-metaverse-humanoid ecosystem for open, complex human-digital-machine-cooperative methodology and problem-solving, followed by general principles and frameworks for building actionable humanoids and evaluating humanoid quality.

papers.title: Reframing Museum Intelligence: A Survey of Large Language Models in Museums
papers.authors: Fan Bu, Zhan Li, Yu Jiang, Ziyao Liu
papers.journal: Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a transformative technology for museums, enabling a shift from static content delivery toward interactive and intelligent systems. However, existing studies and deployments remain fragmented, with a lack of systematic analysis of how LLM capabilities align with the unique goals, constraints, and values of museum contexts. This gap motivates the need for a unified survey that views LLM-based systems not only as technical tools, but also as components embedded within cultural, educational, and institutional settings. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of how LLMs are being integrated into museums, covering both interactive intelligence for visitor-facing applications and backstage intelligence that supports curatorial and governance processes. By synthesizing prior work and emerging practices, we aim to offer valuable insights into research challenges, future directions, and practical considerations for developing LLM-enabled museum systems that are robust, responsible, and aligned with long-term cultural heritage objectives. CCS Concepts: • General and reference → Surveys and overviews; • Social and professional topics → Cultural characteristics; • Human-centered computing → Empirical studies in interaction design; • Computing methodologies → Artificial intelligence.

papers.title: MiKid-QA: construction and performance evaluation of a paediatric myopia education question-answering model
papers.authors: Zixun Wang, Jingtao Yu, Tingyu Zhang, 鹿大千, Yifan Li, Yabin Hu, Jun Zhou, Liqin Huang, X. J. Zhang, Xiaoxue Hu, Xueshuo Xie, Xu Yan, Jing Yang, Bei Du, Ruihua Wei
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The surging prevalence of paediatric myopia has overwhelmed clinical education services. While general-purpose large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for medical information, they often lack the domain-specific precision required for specialised care. This study aimed to develop and evaluate Myopia in Kids Question-Answering (MiKid-QA), a paediatric myopia education question-answering model fine-tuned to support standardised patient education. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional evaluation study. MiKid-QA was developed by fine-tuning the Qwen2.5-32B model using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on curated professional datasets (2015-2025), including textbooks and expert consensus. Performance was assessed against DeepSeek and GPT-4 through a multicentre, single-blind expert evaluation of 25 standardised clinical scenarios. A panel of specialists rated responses across five dimensions (correctness, completeness, readability, helpfulness and safety) using a 5-point Likert scale. RESULTS: MiKid-QA demonstrated superior automated performance compared with its base model (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy: 0.1423 vs 0.0967). In expert evaluations, MiKid-QA achieved significantly higher scores for correctness (4.43±0.63) and safety (4.38±0.59) compared with DeepSeek and GPT-4 (all p<0.001). While completeness and helpfulness were comparable (p>0.05), MiKid-QA produced more concise responses and lower reading difficulty than GPT-4 (p<0.001), suggesting a potentially favourable balance between information accuracy and patient accessibility in standardised educational scenarios. CONCLUSION: Specialised fine-tuning on curated myopia-related datasets was associated with higher expert-rated correctness and safety in standardised myopia education scenarios. MiKid-QA may serve as an auxiliary educational tool to support patient communication in myopia care, although further external validation and prospective clinical studies are required before clinical deployment.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence ( AI) ‐enhanced journal club: integrating podcasts, AI , and social media in medical education
papers.authors: Mohamed Abouelenein, Muhammed Arif İbiş, Molly M Nichols, Azhar Khan, Maria Satchi, Nicholas Tobias Johannes Raison, Kawa Omar, Francesca Kum, Tet Yap, Edward James Bass, Kalyan Gudaru, Shyaw Mahmood Ahmed, Sanjith Gnanappiragasam, Fabio Castiglione, Ömer Onur Çakır
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted, multimedia journal club model that improves accessibility by transforming scientific articles into on-demand educational formats distributed through digital platforms. SUBJECTS AND METHODS: This prospective single-centre educational evaluation was conducted at King's College Hospital (London). Six AI-enhanced journal club sessions were implemented between June and September 2025. Peer-reviewed urology articles were processed using AI-assisted tools to generate podcasts, slide presentations, short-form video summaries, question-and-answer materials, and visual infographics. Content was distributed through clinician-facing platforms including YouTube, Spotify, and social media. Two surveys evaluated educational impact: a format-specific survey completed by 48 participants and a second survey assessing overall perceptions of the AI-enhanced journal club completed by 19 participants. RESULTS: The AI-generated podcast was the most preferred format (62.5%), followed by video summaries (16.7%) and slide presentations (8.3%). Participants reported greater engagement compared with traditional journal clubs, with 54.2% selecting the response option 'much more engaged'. Format-specific ratings were consistently high, particularly for podcasts (mean [standard deviation, SD] score for engagement 4.6 [0.6] and for clarity 4.8 [0.5]). In the second survey, overall ratings of the AI-enhanced journal club were high across all domains, including engagement (mean [SD] score 4.8 [0.4]), clarity (mean [SD] score 4.8 [0.5]), time efficiency (mean [SD] score 4.7 [0.6]), and overall preference (mean [SD] score 4.9 [0.3]). CONCLUSION: An AI-assisted, multimodal journal club integrating podcasts, slides, and digital dissemination was associated with improved participant-reported engagement and accessibility. This scalable model supports asynchronous learning and may complement traditional journal club formats in postgraduate medical education.

papers.title: Awareness and Perception of Artificial Intelligence in Diagnostic Imaging: A Cross‐Speciality Survey of Indian Medical Practitioners
papers.authors: Mwanajuma Yahya Kassim, Dolly Anil Sharma, Shreeni Shah, M. Panda, Santosh Ojha
papers.journal: Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is one of the rapidly evolving areas of diagnostic imaging; however, the extent to which medical professionals are willing to apply these tools to routine care in India has not been thoroughly researched. This is a cross-sectional descriptive study that evaluated awareness, perceptions and perceived impact of AI among radiologists, orthopaedic surgeons and physicians practising in Gujarat. METHODS: A questionnaire, designed according to Scheetz et al., was completed by 102 practitioners in a structured manner. Frequency distributions, percentage analysis and descriptive statistics were performed. RESULTS: It was also found that 88.2% were aware of AI, with only 47.1% identifying their knowledge as average, and 13.7% as above average. Although AI is not used regularly, 52.9% reported never using AI. Most respondents had a favourable view of AI: 66.7% indicated willingness to implement AI-supported clinical workflow, and 60.8% believed AI would positively affect their area. The issues raised were data security (67.6%), less dependence on specialists (62.7%) and confidence in the black-box systems. Most of the respondents (64.7%) felt that AI would have a significant effect on clinical practice in the next 1-10 years. CONCLUSION: Radiologists expressed relatively more acceptance, and physicians expressed more concern with workforce implications. The results show that there is a significant interest, but unequal readiness, in the specialties. Enhancing AI-specific training and developing governance models can help make the safe and ethical adoption of AI-enabled diagnostic imaging.

papers.title: Positive psychology for executives in the wake of AI
papers.authors: Michael J. Provitera, Mostafa Sayyadi, Hamid H. Kazeroony
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to integrate positive psychology and artificial intelligence (AI) into leadership development by proposing a six-dimensional model for preparing executives to lead effectively in AI-intensive organizational environments. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2000 and 2026, the authors develop the Positive Psychology for Executives (PPE) model − a six-sign, six-dimensional framework that integrates strengths-based development, self-awareness, high-quality connections and AI-supported decision-making. Sources were identified through searches of Business Source Complete, PsycINFO and Google Scholar using terms including positive organizational scholarship, strengths-based leadership, reflected best self, mindfulness-based leadership and AI-enabled leadership. Credibility, accuracy and relevance were the key criteria used to select sources that ultimately informed the model. The resulting framework is conceptual and propositional; the authors explicitly distinguish between established empirical findings and the model’s forward-looking propositions. Findings This paper translates PPE into pedagogical practices for management educators, including learning outcomes, classroom exercises and assessment strategies. Proposed linkages between PPE dimensions and organizational outcomes are framed as researchable propositions rather than established causal claims. Practical implications PPE offers a theoretically grounded, pedagogically actionable approach to preparing leaders to thrive in the social, emotional and ethical complexities of the AI era. Originality/value AI is reshaping executive work, organizational design and the competencies required for effective leadership. Yet, management education has not fully integrated the psychological, relational and developmental capacities that leaders need to navigate AI-intensive environments. This paper introduces the PPE model, a strengths-based framework grounded in Positive Organizational Scholarship, the Reflected Best Self-Exercise and contemporary research on AI-enabled leadership. The model addresses a gap in existing frameworks by explicitly coupling human-centered positive psychology constructs with the technological realities of AI-enabled organizations.

papers.title: Are HR professionals insecure? AI, job insecurity and the re-wiring of workplace learning
papers.authors: Federica Polo, Kousay Abid, Amel Ahmed
papers.abstract: Purpose The expediting adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across organizations is fundamentally reconfiguring human resource management functions, raising substantive questions about the psychological experience of the HR professionals who perform them. Building on conservation of resources theory, this study aims to explore how HR professionals experience and interpret AI-driven changes to their roles, how these changes shape perceptions of job insecurity and whether workplace learning helps in mitigating these effects. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted, based on semi-structured interviews with HR professionals. The interview data were analyzed thematically to identify recurring patterns and themes. Findings Findings reveal that HR professionals experience AI-driven role changes as incremental and task-restructuring, broadly interpreting AI as a complementary tool that redistributes work toward more strategic and relational responsibilities. These changes nonetheless generate job insecurity that manifests predominantly in qualitative form, expressed as uncertainty over evolving role expectations, instead of an immediate fear of job loss. The perceived irreducibility of human judgment and relational expertise emerged as a stabilizing identity resource, while engagement in workplace learning, particularly through self-directed strategies, functioned as the primary mechanism through which participants restored professional agency, rebuilt adaptive capacity, and in some cases reframed AI disruption as an opportunity for career development rather than a threat to occupational continuity. Research limitations/implications This study presents several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, we used a qualitative design, which enabled the collection of rich and contextually grounded insights but limited the generalizability of the findings. The interpretations are based on a relatively small sample and reflect subjective accounts, which may not capture the full diversity of experience across the broader HR population. Second, the inclusion of participants from different sectors introduces variability in organizational practices and levels of AI adoption. While this enhances the breadth of perspectives, it may also reduce comparability, as sector-specific dynamics can shape how GenAI is experienced and interpreted. Third, the data were collected in 2025 and adopt a cross-sectional design. Given the rapid evolution of AI technologies, future research could adopt longitudinal designs to examine how HR roles, job insecurity perceptions, and learning behaviors evolve as AI becomes more deeply embedded in organizational practices. Further, future research could advance this line of inquiry by quantitatively measuring workplace learning as a mediating or moderating mechanism of job insecurity during technological transitions. Originality/value The novelty of this study lies in shifting the literature’s focus toward the subjective experience of job insecurity among insiders (HR professionals), offering a psychologically grounded perspective on how such insecurity is interpreted and managed through adaptive strategies, particularly workplace learning. Contextually, it provides rare empirical evidence from the Gulf region, extending the predominantly Western scope of research on AI.

papers.title: School-to-work transitions into hospitality and tourism for people with intellectual disabilities: a sustainable career perspective
papers.authors: YunYing Zhong, Alan Fyall, Juliana Rodrigues Vieira Tkatch, Karen C N Tavares, Charles E. Hughes
papers.journal: Journal of Organizational Effectiveness People and Performance
papers.abstract: Purpose This exploratory study examines the employment of people with intellectual disabilities (PwIDs) in the hospitality and tourism (HT) industry through a sustainable career lens incorporating multiple-stakeholder perspectives. It explores convergent and divergent views of educators, HT employers and PwIDs on school-to-work transition, addressing gaps in prior research that have largely focused on workplace experiences. Design/methodology/approach Using an exploratory qualitative design, 22 semi-structured interviews were conducted with a convenient and purposive sample of special education faculty and administrators, PwIDs and HT employers and policymakers. Content analysis identified key themes regarding job positions, needed competencies, motivations, challenges and resources. The findings were synthesized into a framework based on the sustainable career perspective, illustrating the dynamic and interrelated transition process and potential pathways for collaboration. Findings Findings show stakeholders, including educators, PwIDS and HT employers, agree on the diversity and employability of PwIDs and the importance of person–job fit, transferable soft skills and available multi-level supports. However, persistent barriers such as stigma, limited paid internships, workplace integration challenges and post-graduation constraints in housing, transportation and advancement undermine long-term career sustainability, highlighting the limits of short-term placement-focused approaches. Practical implications Three practical collaboration directions were identified: (1) raising awareness about PwIDS and improving transition process through joint training and coalitions; (2) strengthening organizational capacity to support PwIDs at work by developing initiatives like buddy systems and artificial intelligence job coaches and addressing transportation, affordable housing issues and (3) partnering with HT colleges to educate future industry leaders and engage HT partners. Originality/value This study presents a more holistic framework by integrating multiple stakeholders, context, time, and outcomes and redefining employment as a dynamic process of human capital transfer and life course development, rather than a static outcome of workplace experience. It offers fresh insights to support cross-sector collaboration in facilitating the school-to-work transition for PwIDs.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and green collaborative innovation: knowledge-based channels and governance conditions
papers.authors: Yang Xu, Qilong Zhou, Qi Fan, Xuanming Zhang
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether and how firm-level artificial intelligence (AI) adoption promotes green collaborative innovation. It focuses on two knowledge-based capability channels, namely, knowledge learning capability and green governance capability, and investigates the organizational and institutional conditions under which the innovation effect of AI varies. Design/methodology/approach This study uses panel data on Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2023. AI adoption is measured by per-capita machinery and equipment book value, and green collaborative innovation by jointly filed green patents. The analysis applies two-way fixed-effects models, robustness tests, instrumental-variable estimation and propensity-score matching. Findings AI adoption significantly promotes green collaborative innovation in both invention and utility model patents, and the results remain robust across multiple tests. It strengthens knowledge learning and governance capabilities, while internal green strategy and external media coverage amplify its effect. The effect is stronger among firms with broader patent knowledge bases, high-technology and heavily polluting firms, and those located in cities with better digital infrastructure. Originality/value This study shifts attention from AI as an efficiency-enhancing technology to its role in reshaping firm knowledge processes. It identifies knowledge learning capability and green governance capability as two pathways through which AI supports green collaborative innovation, and uses knowledge-distance governability to explain how strategic commitment, media scrutiny, knowledge endowments, industry characteristics and digital infrastructure shape AI’s innovation returns. Using knowledge-distance governability, this study explains how AI makes distant knowledge more visible, interpretable and applicable to green innovation.

papers.title: Beyond the tech neutrality myth: integration and resistance to ethics and gender equality in Portuguese AI higher education
papers.authors: Rosa Filomena Brás Lopes Monteiro, Camila Marques, Nuno Lourenço, Fernando Paulo Belfo
papers.journal: Journal of Information Communication and Ethics in Society
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the extent to which ethics and gender equality are integrated into artificial intelligence (AI) and data science (DS) pedagogies within Portuguese higher education institutions (HEIs). It aims to identify the pedagogical approaches, specific contents and structural barriers that shape how future professionals are prepared to address the societal impacts of AI. Design/methodology/approach Using a three-phase mixed-methods design, the research includes: a desk survey of 37 university programmes (undergraduate, master’s and doctoral levels); an online questionnaire for program coordinators and lecturers (n = 13; 25% response rate among coordinators); and 10 semi-structured interviews with AI educators and experts. Findings Results reveal that only 24% of AI-related programmes incorporate a gender perspective, often implicitly through recommended bibliographies or broad concepts such as “fairness” and “bias.” The study identifies a significant disconnect between institutional equality rhetoric and participants’ reported teaching practices. This gap is exacerbated by a masculinised academic culture, in which 73% of programmes are coordinated by men and by emerging forms of resistance to gender-related perspectives, which may further contribute to the marginalisation of gender-related knowledge in AI education. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first systematic study in Portugal to map the integration of gender equality in AI education, offering critical insights into the persistence of the “tech neutrality” paradigm and the need for a transition towards socio-technical and feminist pedagogies.

papers.title: Perception of artificial intelligence and intrinsic work motivation: evidence from Vietnam
papers.authors: Nguyễn Ngọc Lan, Yueru Ma, Oluwole Nurudeen Omonijo, Farhan Hussain, Tanyuan Xing
papers.journal: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how sales staff’s perceptions of AI (i.e. perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) drive their intrinsic work motivation through AI use experience (AUE) and how internal training (IT) moderates this process within tourism and hospitality business. Design/methodology/approach Rooted in the technology acceptance model (TAM), flow theory and self-determination theory (SDT), this study used exploratory sequential mixed-method design. Scale purification (EFA) and scale validation (CFA) were conducted using SPSS and AMOS and hypothesis testing results were validated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results revealed that PU and PEOU positively influence AI-specific intrinsic work motivation (AI-IWM) indirectly, through the mediating role of AUE. Furthermore, IT positively moderates the relationships between perception of AI and AUE, which ultimately improves AI-IWM. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insight into service and hospitality management sectors aiming to enhance work motivation among sales staff through AI. Given the significant influence of intrinsic motivation among sales staff in tourism and hospitality businesses, organization with a focus on AI adoption at workplace must be mindful of negative influence of AI on employees’ work motivation and outcome. Originality/value This study enriched the understanding of the motivations underlying the perception of AI and intrinsic work motivation by integrating insights from the TAM, SDT and flow theory. This study provided valuable implication for research and practices in the service business sector.

papers.title: A Unified Approach to the Correction of Male Torso Deformities After Massive Weight Loss: A 443-Patient Consecutive Series
papers.authors: Murat Diyarbakırlıoğlu, Yunus Dogan, Fatih Çınar
papers.abstract: Although numerous techniques have been described, standardized approaches for comprehensive male torso reconstruction remain limited. This study presents a unified approach integrating circumferential planning, chest reshaping, and abdominal contouring. A retrospective review was performed of 443 consecutive male MWL patients treated between 2018 and 2024. All patients underwent a standardized protocol combining posterior body lift, chest reduction/mastopexy, and either standard or fleur-de-lis (FDL) abdominoplasty. Preoperative planning incorporated Pascal's Rule of 16 for circumferential marking, while chest management utilized a pedicle-length-based decision pathway. Closure techniques and postoperative management, including compression therapy and lymphatic massage, were standardized. Outcomes were assessed using BODY-Q patient-reported outcome measures and prospectively recorded complications. Mean BMI was 29.6 (range, 22.4-34.3), and mean follow-up was 7 months. Mean tissue resection weights were 1006 g for posterior body lift and 2148 g for abdominoplasty, with approximately 240 g removed per breast. Complications included 13 (2.9%) breast hematomas, 16 (3.6%) abdominal hematomas, 8 (1.8%) partial nipple-areola complex necroses, 1 T-junction necrosis requiring grafting, 4 (0.9%) hypertrophic scars, and 52 (11.7%) seromas. Revision surgery was required in five patients. Significant improvements were observed across all BODY-Q domains, with satisfaction scores increasing from the low 40s preoperatively to above 80 postoperatively (p < 0.001). A unified approach to male MWL torso reconstruction provides safe, reproducible, and reliable outcomes. Standardized planning, objective chest management criteria, consistent closure techniques, and structured postoperative care contribute to low complication rates and high patient satisfaction. Level of Evidence: IV.

papers.title: Teaching With AI: A Practical Guide to a New Era of Human Learning—2nd Edition
papers.authors: Jacqueline Sivahop
papers.journal: The Journal of Physician Assistant Education
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: Over the past decade, physician assistant/associate education has experienced significant changes, most notably in the implementation and reliance on technology. The impact of the use and necessity for technology in our everyday lives as educators, leaders, and clinicians is also felt by our learners as they navigate new learning and practice expectations that are evolving quicker than most expected. Perhaps the most robust technologic advancement has been in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in all facets of the educational and clinical environments. With AI's imminent emergence and implementation, many educators are seeking resources to better understand its role and utilization in their learning environments with direct transference to the professional setting. In the second edition of their fundamental book, Teaching with AI: A Practice Guide to a New Era of Human Learning, Jose Antonio Bowen and C. Edward Watson expand on new information and emerging topics and provide many examples to encourage fresh ideas and help guide educators, leaders, and clinicians as they navigate AI in the educational and professional settings. This is a book that new and experienced educators will reference over the coming years as they are met with the needs of our ever-changing profession and the future of learning, education, and healthcare.

papers.title: Exploring the use of technology in menopause education for patients: a scoping review of the literature
papers.authors: Angella Appah, Supriya Jain, Maria Elena Cunningham, DeAshley Smith, S Manvi, E. Britton Chahine, Selen Bozkurt, Azra Ismail, Nadi Kaonga
papers.journal: Menopause The Journal of The North American Menopause Society
papers.abstract: IMPORTANCE AND OBJECTIVE: Menopause is an underaddressed topic in the lives of women. Patient education initiatives can play a significant role in menopause care by improving patient awareness and self-advocacy, which can impact quality of life and symptomatology. This scoping review was conducted to identify and characterize menopause patient education initiatives, with a specific focus on how technology has been used in their provision. METHODS: A scoping review following the JBI method was conducted, with the following databases searched: PubMed, Embase, SCOPUS, Web of Science, and AAMC MedEd Portal. Studies included described curricula related to menopause education for patients. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION: This review identified 50 publications that described patient-facing menopause education interventions. These interventions were diverse in their teaching methods and educational content, but few studies leveraged analogue and digital technology. Future research should explore how to further leverage technology-especially digital technology such as artificial intelligence-to potentially improve menopause education.

papers.title: Transparency features alone are insufficient for trust calibration in artificial intelligence diagnostic support
papers.authors: Cassiopeia AC Frank, Alexander Stevens, Yea‐Jen Hsu, Guodong Gordon Gao, Michael Blake Streiff, Lilly D. Engineer
papers.journal: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Clinician trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is a frequently cited barrier to adoption, yet there is limited empirical evidence on how transparency features influence trust. This study aimed to address this evidence gap. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a randomized controlled experiment in which 220 clinicians were randomized to 1 of 3 conditions: no transparency (control), numeric confidence scores, or narrative explanations with citations, using simulated AI diagnostic assistance across clinical case vignettes. RESULTS: Transparency did not influence tool-specific trust [F(2, 214) = 0.38, P = .68], global trust [F(2, 217) = 0.13, P = .88], or perceived information credibility [F(2, 210) = 0.42, P = .66]. Confidence increased following any AI assistance (+6.7%), but narrative explanations were associated with greater change in confidence compared with both control (P = .024) and numeric confidence (P = .0051). Participants changed or refined diagnoses after reviewing AI output 45.8% (SD 23.4%) of the time, with participants in the control group demonstrating higher levels of behavioral influence than transparency conditions (P = .0006). DISCUSSION: Trust, confidence, and behavioral influence represent distinct constructs and are impacted differently by transparency methods. The difference in these contributions to clinician-AI partnerships should be considered when designing for safe trust calibration, with particular consideration for the dissociation between trust and confidence. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest common interface transparency features alone failed to produce a detectable, meaningful shift in clinician trust in AI assistance and that changes may instead alter behavioral influence and confidence without a corresponding change in trust.

papers.title: Digital innovation enablers in sustainable banking and insurance: a systematic review of business model transformation factors
papers.authors: Sonny Supriyadi, Mohammad Hamsal, Asnan Furinto, Pantri Heriyati
papers.abstract: Banking and insurance institutions face increasing pressure to transform their business models through digital technologies while advancing sustainability objectives, yet existing research remains fragmented in explaining how digital innovation is translated into sustainable outcomes. This systematic review applies PRISMA guidelines to synthesize 168 peer-reviewed articles published between 2002 and 2026 from Scopus and Web of Science, using systematic screening, structured coding, and thematic analysis to examine the links among digital transformation, business model innovation, and sustainable performance in banking and insurance. The review identifies an evolutionary trajectory from basic digitalization and financial inclusion models toward AI-enabled, ecosystem-based, and sustainability-integrated business model transformation. More importantly, the synthesis develops a mechanism-based explanation of sustainable transformation by showing that business model innovation functions as an enabler, amplifier, mediator, moderator, and boundary spanner through five mechanisms: technology-enabled inclusion, ecosystem orchestration, revenue model transformation, risk resilience engineering, and stakeholder value co-creation. The review further proposes a four-archetype framework comprising The Reinventors, The Mavericks, The Adapters, and The Adventurers, each reflecting different combinations of innovation impetus, organizational focus, sectoral logic, and sustainability orientation. By translating these findings into concrete and testable propositions, this review contributes a parsimonious research agenda for examining when, how, and under what conditions digital business model innovation produces sustainable transformation in banking and insurance.

papers.title: Prompting for justice: generative AI, translanguaging, and the equity imperative in bilingual education
papers.authors: Kidega Charles
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is entering bilingual and dual language classrooms faster than theoretical and pedagogical frameworks can respond. Trained predominately on English-dominant data, large language models encode linguistic hierarchies that contradict equity-oriented bilingual education stands for. Drawing on translanguaging theory, critical AI literacy research, and empirical studies of language bias, this paper proposes Equity-Centered Prompting Framework (ECPF). ECPF comprises five principles spanning prompt design, output evaluation, student participation, instructional function, and epistemic authority. Unlike existing critical AI literacy frameworks that address technology broadly, or culturally sustaining pedagogies that do not engage AI specifically, ECPF targets the linguistic structure of GenAI and its consequences for bilingual learners, positioning AI interaction itself as an act of equity-oriented pedagogy. The framework was developed through a four-stage systematic theoretical synthesis: construct identification, literature search and selection, thematic synthesis, and principle formulation and validation based on 20 core sources. The contribution is threefold: a translanguaging-based critique of how GenAI architectures. five actionable principles for equity-centered prompting in actual bilingual classrooms, and a research and policy agenda for linguistically just AI integration.

papers.title: Perceptions of artificial Intelligence use in online graduate coursework: a Q methodology study
papers.authors: Michelle Bartlett, Suzanne Ehrlich, James Bartlett, Rakesh Kumar Maurya
papers.journal: Journal of Research on Technology in Education
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming educational practices across all levels, bringing new possibilities and challenges to online graduate programs. With AI tools integrated into coursework, providing automated feedback, personalized resources, and organizational support, graduate students are increasingly engaging with AI throughout their learning experiences. However, subjective viewpoints on AI integration, including its effectiveness, and ethical implications, vary significantly among students. This study uses Q methodology to explore and categorize the unique viewpoints of online graduate students regarding AI integration in their coursework. By understanding these perspectives, educators and program designers can better address student needs, improve AI tool implementation, and foster a supportive online learning environment that aligns with graduate student viewpoints.

papers.title: ‘ChatGPT can make mistakes’: pedagogically problematic discourses on generative AI in higher education
papers.authors: Elizabeth M. Olsson, Evelina Johansson
papers.abstract: Fill in the blank: Generative AI (genAI) is a ________. This seemingly simplistic exercise reveals more than you might think, especially if you are a teacher. While most agree that words have implications, few have interrogated the pedagogical consequences of the dominant genAI discourses circulating in higher education. This Point of Departure argues that these discourses – often originating from big tech companies – shape how teachers and, ultimately, students understand and engage with genAI. Drawing on a poststructuralist view of discourse analysis and Lea and Street’s [1998. Student writing in higher education: An academic literacies approach. Studies in Higher Education 23, no. 2: 157–72] Academic Literacies framework, we argue that dominant utopian and dystopian framings focus on technological capabilities at the expense of pedagogical consequences. In response, we propose a human-centred model of discursive engagement that foregrounds discourses of curiosity, criticality, and collaboration. Ultimately, we aim to help teachers appreciate how the discourses they use to describe genAI affect how their students learn.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Development and the maturity mismatch between investment and financing: evidence from China
papers.authors: Yi Li, Danhui Fang, Zhixiang Yin, Lingqing Dong
papers.abstract: Using China’s National New Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation Development Pilot Zones as a quasi-natural experiment, this study examines the relationship between the AI pilot policy and firms’ investment–financing maturity mismatch. Based on a sample of Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2009 to 2024, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach. The results show that the pilot policy significantly reduces firms’ investment–financing maturity mismatch. Mechanism analysis indicates that information asymmetry and operating volatility play relatively important mediating roles, whereas the indirect effect through short-term debt dependence, although statistically significant, explains only a small proportion of the overall effect and serves mainly as a supplementary transmission channel. The effect is stronger among firms facing more intense product market competition, lower agency costs, and managers with overseas educational experience. This study provides empirical evidence on the relationship between AI development and firms’ financing maturity structure.

papers.title: Disciplinary Perspectives on the Relevance of AI Research Assistants for Scholarly Article Discovery
papers.authors: Sanja Gidakovic
papers.abstract: This study explored artificial intelligence (AI) research assistants through the lens of scholars from different disciplines as they interacted with the tools. The goal was to determine whether AI tools provide relevant scholarly literature or prioritize surface-level relevance at the expense of disciplinary depth, and to examine how scholars perceive the usefulness of the tools in teaching and learning. The study used a multiple-phase, qualitative design in which ten scholars from several disciplines completed structured search tasks in each AI research assistant (Consensus, Elicit, SciSpace), followed by semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using qualitative coding techniques, with themes developed through thematic analysis approach. Analysis involved data familiarization, memoing, iterative first and second cycle coding, and the generation and refinement of themes. The findings revealed six themes from the search task diaries and interviews with participants: article coverage varied across disciplines; discipline specific information needs and resource mismatch; a complementary resource for scholarly article discovery; AI summaries technically correct but generic; faculty perceptions on AI tools in student learning; usability and cognitive load considerations. The findings indicate that while most tools surfaced additional research from scholarly journals, they often did not consistently identify seminal literature across the sampled disciplines. AI summaries on the literature were perceived as factually correct but generic. Lastly, participants expressed varied perceptions about the ways in which the tools could be used in teaching and learning contexts.

papers.title: The User Agency Trap in Media Literacy Chatbots: Interactive Evaluation Format, Imperfection Disclosure, and Visual Misinformation Discernment
papers.authors: Jiyoung Lee, Suhyun Kim, Hakjun Lee, Jiwon Hwang
papers.abstract: Although media literacy interventions are increasingly used to counter misinformation, many remain text-centered and non-interactive, limiting engagement during real-time evaluation. This limitation is particularly consequential for visual misinformation, where realistic synthetic images can encourage intuitive judgments. This study examines how two chatbot design features—interactive evaluation format and chatbot (im)perfection disclosure—shape perceived user and AI agency and, in turn, truth discernment. In an online experiment (N = 348), participants evaluated visual misinformation in a chatbot-supported task varying these two features. Interactive evaluation increased perceived user agency but decreased perceived AI agency, whereas imperfection disclosure modestly increased user agency without affecting AI agency. Critically, interactive evaluation indirectly reduced truth discernment through increased perceived user agency. These findings reveal a potential user agency trap: chatbot interactivity can make users feel more empowered while paradoxically undermining their ability to discern visual misinformation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Personalization in Business: A Two-Layer Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
papers.authors: Quan Le, Truong Thi Hue
papers.abstract: Despite the rapid growth of research on artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalization in business, there appears to be a lack of comprehensive syntheses integrating both performance analysis and framework-based content analysis. This study conducts a two-layer systematic literature review of AI-driven personalization in business. First, a performance analysis of 302 Scopus-indexed articles published between 2001 and 2026 examines the field’s intellectual development. Second, the TCCM (theory-context-characteristics-methodology) framework is applied to 113 articles published in ABDC-ranked A*, A, and B journals to provide an in-depth assessment of the field. The findings reveal substantial growth in research output since 2022, driven by advances in generative AI, recommender systems, and data-driven marketing. China and the United States emerge as the leading contributors in both productivity and scholarly impact. The literature is primarily grounded in Stimulus-Organism-Response Theory, Uses and Gratifications Theory, and the Elaboration Likelihood Model, with a strong concentration in e-commerce, tourism, media, and entertainment contexts. Existing studies mainly focus on outcomes such as purchase intention, trust, and engagement, while negative consequences and long-term effects remain underexplored. Based on these findings, the study identifies key knowledge gaps and proposes a TCCM-based future research agenda to advance AI-driven personalization research.

papers.title: Irreplaceable human educators in moral and character education during the era of artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Hyemin Han
papers.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence technology (AI) have significantly impacted education in practice. Such a trend is also becoming prevalent in moral and character education. In this paper, I will argue whether moral and character educators will remain as irreplaceable educational agents in the era of AI. For the discussion, I will examine whether AI agents will be able to become sole teachers or mentors while considering three aspects of ethics education: (1) Phronesis cultivation; (2) Promotion of moral and positive youth development; and (3) Development of autonomy and agency for the wise and ethical use of AI. I will refer to relevant theoretical and empirical studies on moral development and education to examine AI’s potential capacity related to the three aspects of moral education. Finally, I will briefly discuss how the role of human moral and character educators needs to be reshaped during the era of AI.

papers.title: Tactile perception of fabrics based on fMRI and EEG
papers.authors: He Zhang, Shengjie Bai, Meimei Zhang, Wei Tang, Chunfeng Hu
papers.abstract: The tactile perception of fabrics determines consumer acceptance and satisfaction with the fabrics. This study investigated the tactile perception of three woven fabrics made from linen, cotton, and silk fibers using friction, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG) methods. The results showed that the surface roughness of these fabrics was significantly negatively correlated with the friction coefficient and significantly positively correlated with the maximum Lyapunov exponent of the vibration signal. The larger the adhesive friction was, the higher the stickiness feeling of the fabric. The larger the fluctuation amplitude of the vibration signal was, the higher the roughness feeling of the fabric. Moreover, the main regions activated during tactile perception of the three fabrics were the primary somatosensory cortex and postcentral gyrus. Both the large friction and the large vibration generated by touching the fabrics evoked a larger activation area and intensity in the brain, resulting in a lower comfort feeling. Furthermore, the fabrics that produced larger friction or vibration during tactile perception evoked smaller Lempel-Ziv complexity (LZC) and approximate entropy of EEG signals. These findings revealed that mechanical stimulation during fabric perception can affect subjective evaluations and brain responses.

papers.title: Why overtrust in social robots is inevitable
papers.authors: Kerstin Fischer
papers.abstract: Abstract When robots enter our social spaces, we may view them from three different perspectives: as machines, as artefacts with specific affordances (like ‘seeing’, ‘speaking’, ‘dancing’), or as nonstandard characters, which people construct based on the features of the robot depicted, the way it is framed by others, and influenced by their own needs and dispositions. People can switch seamlessly between the three perspectives, for example, offering polite assistance in one minute and turning it off for cleaning in the next. However, when robots are construed as characters, they become social actors, and with this sociality, also expectations concerning trust apply. The fact that they participate in activities that rest on human social interaction mechanisms is likely to lead to overtrust in these characters since it evokes general pragmatic principles, like recipient design, grounding and drawing on common ground. In this paper, I present experimental evidence that it is possible to block overtrust to some extent, but that regulating people’s trust in social robots remains challenging.

papers.title: Dissecting AI discourse
papers.authors: Feng Kevin Jiang
papers.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the discourse characteristics of AI-generated argumentative essays designed to simulate student writing, comparing them with human-authored texts to explore linguistic variation and its implications for academic discourse. While large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT demonstrate impressive fluency and coherence, questions remain about their capacity to engage in nuanced argumentation and the critical reasoning expected in academic contexts. Employing Biber’s (1988) multidimensional (MD) analysis, this study examines systematic differences between LLM-generated and human-written essays across dimensions of register variation, informational density, syntactic complexity, and persuasion. The results reveal that ChatGPT essays are markedly more informationally dense, context-independent, and abstract, yet exhibit reduced interpersonal engagement and overt persuasion compared with student essays. The paper concludes by reflecting on broader pedagogical and ethical implications for the integration of AI tools into academic writing and corpus-based research.

papers.title: Cybernetics, the Anthropocene, and education: student learning in conjunction with AI
papers.authors: David Robert Cole, Pegah Marandi
papers.abstract: This article develops a speculative and empirically inflected account of how university students are learning in conjunction with artificial intelligence (AI). It brings together three interlocking fields: cybernetics, the Anthropocene and education. Cybernetics is central because the communicative and control processes through which students engage AI for research, writing and study raise fundamental questions about agency, authorship and the capacity to think otherwise within machine-mediated capitalism. The Anthropocene provides a second axis of analysis, naming the planetary consequences of human technological development, economic acceleration and ecological damage. Education forms the third axis, because universities are key sites in which these cybernetic and Anthropocene dynamics are materialised through everyday practices of study, assessment and writing. The article combines philosophical analysis with empirical data from education students learning with AI. These data are organised as “data portals”: analytic thresholds that interrupt, extend and test the conceptual argument. Drawing on Deleuze’s transcendental empiricism, the article argues that students do not encounter AI as an external tool alone, but as part of a wider student-AI-university assemblage. The article concludes that agency persists in this assemblage, but is increasingly modulated by feedback, acceleration, assessment pressure, economic precarity and machinic cognition.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal encoding signatures of covert speech revealed by source-localized EEG and fMRI
papers.authors: Wei Zhang, Muyun Jiang, Kok Ann Colin Teo, Raghavan Bhuvanakantham, Zhiwei Guo, Shuailei Zhang, Chuan Huat Vince Foo, Victoria Leong, Jia Lü, Balázs Zoltán Gulyás, Cuntai Guan
papers.abstract: Covert speech, the silent production of words without overt articulation, is fundamental to human cognition and a potential target for restoring communication in speech-impaired populations. Yet where, when, and how the human brain represents specific phrase content during covert speech remains largely unresolved. Here, we combine source-localized EEG (n = 57) with fMRI validation in the same cohort (n = 49) to map the encoding of five covert command phrases. Phrase-discriminative activity is concentrated before estimated articulation onset, peaking at 200–400 ms and strongest in the theta band. Cross-modal representational similarity analysis reveals convergent EEG–fMRI phrase representations in left sensorimotor cortex, while phase-lag connectivity identifies left postcentral gyrus as a phrase-sensitive functional hub within a parietal-somatosensory-temporal sequence during the speech planning period. Beyond these group-level signatures, individual-specific encoding patterns substantially exceed group-average effects. These findings provide a temporally precise, cross-validated cortical map of covert speech and identify targets for speech neuroscience and non-invasive brain-computer interfaces. Source-localized EEG with fMRI validation in the same cohort maps where and when the cortex encodes covert speech. Phrase information peaks 200-400 ms after the cue in left sensorimotor cortex, and individual-specific patterns exceed group effects.

papers.title: A legal and ethical architecture for a surgical video data registry in England
papers.authors: Mindy Duffourc, Andrew J. Yiu, Kyle Lam
papers.abstract: Surgical video is an emerging, high-value data source for quality improvement, education, and AI-enabled innovation, yet existing legal and ethical frameworks have not been designed with its distinctive properties in mind. In this perspective we propose a governance architecture for a surgical video data research registry in England that clarifies how surgical video should be classified across health law and data protection law, and how these regimes intersect over the data lifecycle. Firstly, we analyse the legal status of surgical video and associated metadata at key processing stages, highlighting when it constitutes confidential patient information, personal data, and special category health data. Secondly, we outline a two‑tier pathway for registry development differentiating between retrospective and prospective inclusion. Thirdly, we describe a registry model that relies on pseudonymisation, accredited secure data environments, independent oversight, and proportionate access controls to enable EHR linkage while minimising re-identification risk and preserving public trust. While developed in the context of the English National Health Service, this architecture offers a transferable template for health systems globally seeking to responsibly harness high-dimensional intraoperative data for AI development and learning health-care, while maintaining robust protections for privacy, confidentiality, and accountability.

papers.title: A data-driven cognitive feature–based model for english text readability assessment to support college english instruction
papers.authors: Jing Zhao, Congrong Zou
papers.abstract: Abstract Text readability assessment is essential for effective college English teaching and instructional material selection. Traditional readability models mainly rely on surface linguistic features and often fail to reflect the cognitive processes involved in reading comprehension. To address this limitation, this study proposes a cognitive feature–based approach for English text readability assessment, aiming to support data-driven English teaching evaluation. The proposed method incorporates cognitive features related to lexical rarity, logical complexity, and comprehension difficulty, and integrates them with conventional linguistic features. Multiple machine learning models are employed and evaluated on four benchmark datasets, including CEFR, CLEC, OneStopEnglish, and RACE. Experimental results show that models combining cognitive and linguistic features consistently outperform those using linguistic features alone across multiple evaluation metrics. The findings indicate that cognitive features provide complementary information for readability assessment and enhance the discriminability of readability levels. This study offers practical implications for college English teaching by enabling more accurate matching between reading materials and learners’ proficiency levels, thereby supporting personalized and data-driven instructional decision-making.

papers.title: Interrupting prolonged sitting in classrooms for healthcare students: classroom movement breaks acceptability and perceived benefits
papers.authors: Reem Basuodan, Shaima Alothman, Reem A. Albesher, Bodor H. Bin Sheeha, Kholood Matouq Shalabi, Wafa Saeed Alahmari
papers.abstract: Sedentary time among university students has risen over the past decade and is associated with adverse health outcomes, while its relationship with academic performance remains unclear. Although Classroom Movement Breaks (CMB) are beneficial, evidence among healthcare students is limited. This study examined female healthcare students’ acceptability and perceived benefits of introducing CMB into classrooms, sedentary behaviour, and its relationships with sedentary behaviour, pain/discomfort, and perceived benefits of a CMB. A cross-sectional online survey-based study design involved healthcare students. The survey was administered via a learning management system in classrooms, including sociodemographic information, acceptability of implementing CMB in lectures lasting ≥ 2 h, perceived benefits in health, academic, and physical and mental status, sedentary behaviour (measured by RADI), and pain/discomfort (the Corlett and Bishop diagram). Data from 481 students age (17.9 ± 0.8 years) were analyzed where 96% (463/481) considered CMB is acceptable. The mean Rapid Assessment Disuse Index (RADI) score was 23.1 ± 7.5, 43.9% scored ≥ 26, and 64.7% reported sitting for 100% of classroom time. A total of 85.2% of students reported multi-site pain/discomfort, with a median pain intensity of 4.6 (IQR = 3.05). Higher sedentary behavior of the RADI was significantly associated with lower perceived academic benefits (β = -0.11, p = 0.02). Similarly, greater pain intensity was associated with reduced perceived academic benefits (β = -0.18, p < 0.001). No significant associations were observed for sitting time, BMI, age, or prior CMB exposure. The model predicting physical/fatigue outcomes was also statistically significant (F = 3.08, p = 0.01), with R² = 0.04. Pain intensity was negatively associated with perceived physical benefits (β = -0.14, p = 0.001), indicating that students with greater discomfort perceived fewer benefits. Interestingly, prior exposure to CMB was also associated with lower perceived physical benefits (β = -0.12, p = 0.01). No significant associations were observed for sedentary behavior (RADI), sitting time, BMI, or age. The study revealed that CMB is highly accepted among university students in healthcare. Students with greater sedentary behaviour and higher pain/discomfort levels perceived lower CMB benefits. Future studies should assess the implementation of CMB in classrooms at medical and health colleges to reduce sedentary behaviour in educational settings.

papers.title: An AutoML-based stacked ensemble framework for early prediction of maternal health risks
papers.authors: S. Anitha Auxilia, Mythili Thirugnanam
papers.abstract: Abstract Predicting maternal health risks is a major clinical challenge. Early and precise predictions can reduce maternal deaths and complications. AI applications in maternal healthcare play a vital role in predicting risk and improving diagnoses. However, conventional machine learning approaches to maternal risk prediction require extensive manual effort during model design, algorithm selection, training, and tuning, which causes delays and is prone to human error. This study overcomes these challenges by implementing an automated machine learning (AutoML) approach based on the H2O framework in predicting pregnancy risks. The dataset used is a publicly available MHRD consisting of 1014 observations and six clinical variables. In total, 52 different ML models based on six different algorithms were automatically trained and tested in one unified pipeline. These algorithms include XGBoost, random forest, generalized linear model, and stacked ensembles. The stacked ensemble model demonstrated superior predictive performance on all other base models. Also, this model showed an area under the curve value of 0.9539, LogLoss of 0.4093, and root mean square error value of 0.3638 when applied to a holdout test set. The model achieved 96.2% sensitivity for high-risk pregnancies, which is an essential characteristic in clinical practice. These results outperform all individually trained base learners and previously reported results from manually tuned models in the literature. This work demonstrates that the AutoML-based framework for maternal risk prediction is capable of automatically selecting the best machine learning models from clinical data. The framework also enhances predictive accuracy, decreases development effort, and facilitates prompt clinical decision-making in maternal healthcare.

papers.title: A placebo-controlled randomized cross-over lovastatin trial in neurofibromatosis type 1 reveals Ras/MAPK modulation of dynamic emotional face processing
papers.authors: Diana Costa, Teresa Sousa, Ana Espírito, Ana Dionísio, Marco Simões, Inês Bernardino, Ricardo Martins, Miguel S. Castelo-Branco
