papers.abstract: Abstract Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by cognitive and socioemotional processing deficits, associated with dysregulation of the Ras/MAPK pathway and alterations in neural inhibition and the GABA system. This study examined the effects of lovastatin, a Ras/MAPK pathway modulator with a direct influence on excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance, on neural responses during an emotional recognition task using a randomized, triple-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design. Electroencephalography (EEG) oscillatory responses were recorded pre- and post-intervention, focusing on parietal theta rhythms previously shown to be associated with inhibitory processing and to index dynamic facial emotion recognition. In this within-subject cross-over design, fifteen individuals with NF1 were pseudorandomly assigned to both the placebo (3 doses of 60 mg) and the lovastatin (3 doses of 60 mg) intervention. Data were collected at pre-intervention, post-placebo and post-lovastatin administration and analyzed using event-related spectral perturbations (ERSP) computed with Morlet wavelets. Lovastatin selectively modulated theta band power (5–6 Hz) during emotional recognition, as reflected by a significant intervention × task interaction and a significant within-session reduction in centroparietal theta oscillations following lovastatin. No significant effects were observed in alpha (8–11 Hz) or beta (13–20 Hz) bands, nor in theta power during a visual control condition. Given the established role of theta oscillations in face emotion processing, the observed reduction suggests lovastatin influences task-specific oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, these findings provide a mechanistic link between parietal theta oscillations, emotion recognition, and inhibitory regulation. This novel neurophysiological effect identifies a potential treatment target for NF1 and related neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism (NIH Trial Registration #NCT03826940).

papers.title: Post quantum federated authentication framework for Industrial Internet of Things using FALCON threshold signatures and zero knowledge verification
papers.authors: Majed Alsanea, Ashit Kumar Dutta, Jung Taek Seo, Yousef Ibrahim Daradkeh, Mohd Anjum, Sana Shahab, Hong Min
papers.abstract: Abstract Distributed authentication techniques enable edge device trust in smart manufacturing and energy infrastructure Industrial Internet of Things contexts. Existing blockchain-based authentication schemes mostly use the elliptic curve digital signature algorithm, which can be exploited by quantum adversaries using harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks to record authenticated communications for cryptanalysis. CIPHER-QNL, a post-quantum federated authentication framework, integrates three complementary mechanisms: (1) FALCON threshold signature aggregation with federated polynomial key sharding over NTRU lattice rings for distributed multi-party authentication without centralized private-key exposure; and (2) zk-STARK-based privacy-preserving verification for blockchain consensus authentication proof validation without credential disclosure. Through threshold confidentiality, reduction-based reasoning, and computational complexity analysis, the proposed framework’s security is assessed under Module-SIS and NTRU lattice hardness assumptions. Controlled harvest now, decrypt adversarial authentication scenarios are used to evaluate TON-IoT communication performance. Scalable, privacy-preserving, post-quantum authentication for distributed Industrial Internet of Things environments is shown by 99.1% authentication integrity, 98.7% threshold signature aggregation latency reduction, and 0.29% false rejection rate.

papers.title: Satiety does not always silence attention to high-calorie foods: BMI modulates food-related attentional bias
papers.authors: Marc Ballestero‐Arnau, Borja Rodríguez‐Herreros, Toni Cunillera B

papers.title: AI and the PI: Infinite Generation, Finite Understanding
papers.authors: Toni Giorgino A
papers.journal: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) produces code and prose quickly, apparently enabling a principal investigator (PI) in a computational group to do more. Assessing this gain must also account for the laboratory’s role in training scientists who understand, maintain, and own their work. AI creates a generation–verification asymmetry: it reduces the effort of producing plausible code and prose without similarly reducing the expertise needed to evaluate them, potentially leaving groups with technical and epistemic debt while obscuring the reasoning needed for supervision. I argue that AI adoption should therefore be judged by whether it builds sustainable laboratory capacity, with assistance adjusted to task purpose and verifiability and human ownership retained for every consequential artifact.

papers.title: Transforming a Physical Card Game into a Browser-Based Learning Tool: AI-Assisted Digitization of Compound Chain
papers.authors: Kaisar Tursyngozhayev, Nusret Kavak, Nurlan K. Akhmetov
papers.abstract: Abstract This study reports the AI-assisted transformation of Compound Chain, a validated physical inorganic chemistry card game, into a browser-based learning application. The development used a “vibe coding” approach, in which educators describe functionality in natural language while an LLM generates and refines the code. We propose a five-step Pedagogical System Architect framework, intended for chemistry educators without programming experience, that covers architectural planning, data design, incremental implementation, AI-assisted debugging, and version control. The digital version extends the original game through automated rule enforcement, a zoom interface, and single-player mode, in a manner consistent with reduced extraneous cognitive load, and supporting self-regulated practice beyond class. In an exploratory classroom deployment, voluntary out-of-class usage (a self-reported approximation of 4.5 sessions per student) suggests that the digital format can transform a classroom activity into an intrinsically motivated practice resource. This exploratory evaluation documents engagement, usability, and voluntary practice; establishing conceptual learning gains from the digital version remains a question for future controlled study.

papers.title: Functional seizures: care experiences of U.S. Veterans and their care partners
papers.authors: Samin Panahi, Diana E. Naranjo, Andrea Kalvesmaki, Sarah Matson, Robert T. George, Hamada Hamid Altalib, Anna Emilia Blanken, Stephan J. Eisenschenk, David McCarthy, Kristen L. Mordecai, Maria Lopez, William Curt LaFrance Jr, Mary Jo Pugh
papers.abstract: Functional seizures (FS) present substantial diagnostic and treatment challenges, particularly for Veterans with multiple medical and psychiatric comorbidities including post traumatic stress disorder, mood disorders and traumatic brain injury. To more effectively care for Veterans with FS and neuropsychiatric comorbidities, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) neurology program office developed an interdisciplinary Mind Brain Program (MBP) to bridge the gap between neurology and mental health care for Veterans. In the context of expandeding MBP program development targeting Veterans with FS and complex comorbidities, this quality improvement project explored Veterans' lived experiences navigating FS diagnosis and treatment to identify opportunities for enhancing seizure care. Between April and July 2024, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 participants: 10 Veterans and 9 care partners. Using rapid qualitative analysis, we coded data into predefined themes to identify opportunities for improving care. Three major themes were identified within the predefined framework, with emergent subthemes. First, diagnostic challenges included clinicians' limited FS knowledge resulting in delayed video-EEG monitoring, and patient stigma, delaying diagnostic clarity. Second, limited access to specialty care was shaped by geographical barriers, lack of local expertise, scheduling difficulties, and reliance on community care referrals. Third, communication gaps within and between VA and community clinicians contributed to fragmented care, duplicated testing, and increased care partner burden. Findings are limited by a small sample from a single health system and by reliance on interview notes. Despite these limitation, findings highlight opportunities to improve FS care through standardized diagnostic pathways, enhanced clinician and patient education, strengthened communication within and between VA and community, and formal inclusion of care partners. These results can inform ongoing efforts to optimize FS care across the VA system.

papers.title: From threat to reconfiguration: How content creators reshape occupational identity in AI-driven creative practices
papers.authors: Mingsheng Wang, 杨永忠

papers.title: Hybrid graphene-MXene heterostructure for ultra-sensitive optomechanical sensors with multi-modal robotic sensing capabilities
papers.authors: Arash Vaghef‐Koodehi, Mahmoud Nikoufard, Hossein Karamitaheri, Elham Samadpour
papers.abstract: This work presents a computational investigation of a hybrid graphene-MXene heterostructure designed as an optomechanical sensor for robotic applications, integrating photonic detection with mechanical sensing in a unified platform. All results reported herein are derived exclusively from multi-scale simulations; no experimental validation has been performed. The proposed architecture exploits the broadband optical absorption of graphene and the plasmonic response of Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene in the visible spectrum. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations coupled with finite element modeling (FEM) predict a photoresponsivity of 1.2 A/W at 550 nm, detectivity exceeding 1012 Jones, and spectral coverage across 400–800 nm. Simulated optical and mechanical response times are 2.1 ms and 2.8 ms, respectively, enabling concurrent multi-modal operation. Dual-gate voltage control allows independent tuning of photonic and piezoresistive channels. Predicted pressure sensitivity reaches 4.2 kPa⁻1 in the low-force regime (0.05–1 kPa), with additional environmental responsivity of 0.18%/°C (temperature) and 0.3%/RH (humidity, 20–90% range). Iterative FEM simulations over 50,000 loading cycles suggest minimal performance degradation under idealized conditions. The heterostructure’s multi-modal capability—decoupled through differential material responses—enables simultaneous optical transparency analysis, texture recognition via combined optical-mechanical signatures, and low-light navigation. This theoretical framework establishes performance benchmarks for integrated optomechanical sensors in autonomous robotics, human-robot interaction, and industrial automation, while highlighting the necessity of experimental validation to assess practical feasibility, interface stability, and environmental robustness.

papers.title: Unrecognized burden: Determinants of malnutrition among critically ill adults in tertiary hospitals of addis ababa
papers.authors: Misrak Woldayohannes Menchamo, Zelalem Yilma Debebe, Zeweter Abebe
papers.abstract: Identifying nutritional status of patients at admission aids in determining the extent of care needed, predicting problems, and allocating limited resources where they are most needed. The aim of this study was to identify the nutritional status of ICU patients at admission in recourse limited settings. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among adult patients admitted to 3 specialized hospitals of Addis Ababa intensive care units (ICU). validated subjective global assessment tool (SGA) was used to assess the nutritional status of ICU patients at admission. Comparison of SGA categories (well, moderately, and severely malnourished) with clinical characteristics' was made with Kruskal–Wallis test for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Spearman's rank correlation was used to compare correlation between other nutritional indicators and SGA classification. The ordered logistic regression model (OLOGIT) was utilized to identify factors associated with the nutritional status of ICU patients. Comparison was taken as statistically significant when the P -value was less than 0.05. Results: There were 218 study participants who are admitted in the 3 ICUs. The mean age was 45.22 years (SD ±18.68), and the age range was between 18 and 92 years. The prevalence of malnutrition, according to the SGA, was 79.35%, with 128 patients (58.71%) categorized as moderately malnourished and 45 patients (20.64%) categorized as severely malnourished. In the multivariable ordinal logistic regression model, increasing age (AOR = 1.02, 95% CI: 1.00–1.04), APACHE II score (AOR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.03–1.11), and the presence of diagnosed infection (reference: yes; no vs. yes, AOR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.21–0.80) were associated with nutritional status at ICU admission. On the other hand, higher BMI (AOR = 0.79, 95% CI: 0.72–0.88), higher hemoglobin concentration (AOR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.78–0.99), and trauma as the primary admission diagnosis (AOR = 0.11, 95% CI: 0.01–0.84) were associated with lower odds of more severe malnutrition. Conclusion: Malnutrition at ICU admission was associated with older age, greater illness severity, and the presence of infection, while higher BMI and higher hemoglobin concentration, were protective against worse nutritional status. These findings highlight the importance of early nutritional screening and targeted nutritional interventions, particularly among older, severely ill, and infected critically ill patients at the time of ICU admission.

papers.title: From exploration to application: A scoping review of stand-alone generative AI tool use in undergraduate nursing education and its impact on learning outcomes
papers.authors: Mathew Ellis, Samantha Jakimowicz, Lorraine Rose, Shanna M. Fealy
papers.abstract: AIM: To review the applied, student directed use of stand-alone Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) tools in undergraduate nursing education, with consideration given to pedagogical structure, learning outcomes, usability and student experience, to inform meaningful integration of these tools within undergraduate nursing curricula. BACKGROUND: The application of stand-alone Gen-AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) continues to rapidly reshape educational discourse and knowledge production. Within undergraduate nursing education, understanding how these tools are actively applied to support student learning, usability and the student experience when implemented in educational practice is an emerging area of research. DESIGN: A scoping review guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). An a priori review protocol was registered with Open Science Framework (OSF). METHODS: N = 5 electronic databases were searched (MEDLINE, Scopus, CINAHL, ProQuest Nursing & Allie Health, Cochrane Library); Conducted in May 2025 and updated in March 2026, studies were screened against pre-defined inclusion criteria. RESULTS: N = 26 full-text articles were included for review. Synthesis indicates that highly structured implementation of Gen-AI demonstrates more consistent improvements across learning outcomes among nursing students compared with less structured implementation approaches. CONCLUSIONS: The educational benefits of stand-alone Gen-AI in undergraduate nursing education are shaped primarily by how the technology is integrated into learning. Structured pedagogical approaches that actively support prompting, verification and critical reflection appear to maximise higher-order learning, highlighting the importance of educator-guided implementation rather than technology adoption alone.

papers.title: AI-mediated informal digital learning of English in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan: The roles of L2 motivational selves and learner resilience
papers.authors: Guangxiang Liu, Xinyan Jojo Zhou, Lihang Guan, Farhad Ghorbandordinejad, Muhiddin Nizomiddinovich Esirgapov, Temirbolat Kenshinbay, Hongqiang Zhu
papers.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped informal digital learning, yet most research has focused on well-resourced contexts and often treats AI-mediated learning as a standalone phenomenon. This leaves a limited understanding of how learners in underrepresented regions adopt AI-supported practices and how such practices are connected to established forms of informal learning. Addressing this gap requires examining both the developmental relationship between IDLE and AI-IDLE and the psychological factors that shape learners’ participation. This study investigates how L2 motivational selves and learner resilience are associated with learners’ participation in IDLE and AI-mediated informal learning across two Central Asian contexts. Drawing on proactive language learning theory, the study employed a cross-sectional survey design with 997 university students from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. A structural equation modelling (SEM) approach was used to examine the relationships among ideal and ought-to L2 selves, learner resilience, IDLE, and AI-IDLE, alongside a multigroup analysis to test cross-context variation. The findings showed that L2 motivational selves significantly predict resilience and IDLE, while resilience supports AI-mediated learning primarily through indirect pathways. IDLE emerged as the strongest predictor of AI-IDLE, suggesting a close connection between established informal digital learning practices and learners’ use of AI-supported tools. Although the overall model was broadly stable, several relationships varied across contexts, highlighting the role of sociocultural and institutional conditions in shaping AI-mediated informal learning in Central Asian contexts.

papers.title: Humour, academic labour, and researcher identity: A multimodal discourse analysis of PhD memes on Instagram
papers.authors: Juhi Yasmeen, Md. Tauseef Qamar, Abdur Rahman

papers.title: The prompt-response paradox: A cybernetic perspective of generative artificial intelligence usage and corner-cutting behavior
papers.authors: Bin Zhang
papers.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
papers.abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. While existing GenAI literature has largely focused on the scale, frequency, and operational patterns of its application, it has largely overlooked the inherent imbalances within these P-R cycles. Building on control theory, this study investigates how and when GenAI usage is related to employees’ corner-cutting behavior (CCB). Using a scenario-based experiment and a three-wave field survey, we demonstrate that: (i) performance pressure mediates the nonlinear relationship between GenAI usage and CCB, such that this nonlinear indirect effect shifts from positive to negative as GenAI usage intensifies; (ii) workplace status moderates the inverted U-shaped relationship between GenAI usage and performance pressure. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. By conceptualizing GenAI usage through the dual lenses of expectation induction and cognitive friction operating within P-R cycles, our findings extend and refine traditional perspectives on human-AI interaction in the workplace.

papers.title: Granular incremental learning for uncertain data streams: A unifying conceptual and methodological overview
papers.authors: Leite Daniel
papers.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual and methodological synthesis of incremental machine learning under uncertainty. It connects the foundations of incremental learning with granular computing through interval, probabilistic, and fuzzy-possibilistic representations as canonical forms of information granules. A unified framework is introduced to organize existing approaches according to data representations, model structures, locally valid functions, information fusion mechanisms, and underlying optimization principles. The resulting classifiers, predictors, or controllers account for input-output, parametric, structural, and representational uncertainty. At their core, granular incremental learners balance multiple regularization criteria—including prediction error, interpretability, coverage-specificity equilibrium, structural compactness, stability, and semantic coherence—that guide how granules and local models are created, adapted, merged, and removed over time. Their outputs are combined through aggregation operators that allow cooperation among localized models without fully interconnected architectures. By systematizing the relationships among granular and structure-adaptive learning methods, this work provides a foundation for extending incremental learning toward interpretable, safe, and autonomous systems operating in complex and multimodal environments.

papers.title: Neurodiversity and generative AI in higher education: A sequential multi-method qualitative study of students’ interactions, motivations, and strategies
papers.authors: Anne‐Laure Le Cunff, Eleanor Jane Dommett, Martin Compton
papers.abstract: Neurodivergent students have been largely overlooked in research examining student experiences with generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, creating critical knowledge gaps about inclusive educational technology use. This sequential multi-method qualitative study examined how neurodivergent students (NDS) and neurotypical students (NTS) interact with and experience GenAI in academic contexts. Using a sequential design, we employed a virtual revisit think-aloud protocol with 24 university students (12 NDS, 12 NTS) completing an academic task using Microsoft Copilot, followed by focus groups with 14 participants (7 NDS, 7 NTS) to contextualise these task-based behaviours through broader GenAI perceptions. A neurodivergent research advisory board co-designed all procedures. Three themes emerged: approaching the task efficiently, evaluating and refining output, and maintaining academic integrity. While both groups demonstrated strategic GenAI use, neurodivergent participants in this sample explicitly described their cognitive processing needs, using GenAI to manage energy, and humanising some AI interactions. In the neurodivergent focus group, students described GenAI as essential scaffolding for managing academic demands, though this created complex tensions around authenticity and over-reliance. Interface design challenges seemed to particularly disadvantage users with executive function differences. As institutions rapidly integrate these technologies, inclusive design principles and empirical evidence regarding diverse student needs are essential to ensure equitable access to AI-supported education.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning framework for predicting childhood polio vaccination in Somalia: Comparative performance of multiple algorithms and SHAP-based interpretation
papers.authors: Mohamed Abdilahi Mohamed, Hamse Arab Ali, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nuh, Hamse Adam Abdi, Abdisalam Hassan Muse, Abdirashid Muhumed Guled, Omran Salih
papers.abstract: Background Polio remains a critical threat in fragile states where routine immunization systems are frequently disrupted. In Somalia, protracted conflict and nomadic mobility create significant hurdles for vaccine delivery. This study aimed to predict polio vaccination status (Polio3) among children under five years of age and identify socio-demographic predictors through an explainable machine learning framework. Methods Data from 1,527 children aged 0–59 months from the 2020 Somali Health and Demographic Survey was analyzed. Eight supervised algorithms were evaluated using an 80:20 train-test split executed prior to preprocessing to prevent data leakage. Synthetic Minority Over-sampling (SMOTE) was applied to the training set to address class imbalance. Model transparency was achieved through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). A survey-weighted multivariate logistic regression served as the baseline for performance comparison. Results The national prevalence of completed polio vaccination among the cohort was 55.73%. The Gaussian Naive Bayes model demonstrated the highest classification accuracy (66.6%), while the Random Forest model reported the highest discriminative power (AUC: 0.714). SHAP interpretation identified administrative region (Togdheer and Woqooyi Galbeed), child age (0–59 months), and administrative region, child age, and maternal education were the primary predictive determinants of uptake. Geographic factors significantly outweighed the predictive importance of household wealth and child gender. Conclusion The optimized ensemble models provide actionable risk-stratification tools for health authorities. Findings suggest that a transition toward residence-aware and region-specific strategies is necessary to address immunization gaps. The implementation of mobile clinics in high-risk geographic zones and the enhancement of maternal information networks is recommended to improve population immunity. This framework facilitates the systematic identification of under-vaccinated sub-populations to optimize resource allocation.

papers.title: Transparency fallacy: insights from healthcare professionals on the safe use of medical AI
papers.authors: Tatiana de Campos Aranovich, Rita Matulionytė, Farah Magrabi
papers.abstract: As medical Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in clinical care, transparency is widely promoted as a means to support safety, accountability, and trust. In this paper, 'transparency' refers to the provision of meaningful information about an AI system, conceptually distinct from 'explainability'. We examine the policy and regulatory dimensions of transparency in medical AI, drawing on semi-structured interviews with twelve healthcare professionals in Australia and New Zealand, jurisdictions whose regulatory frameworks align with those of other International Medical Device Regulators Forum members. The study explores what information clinicians require and how it should be conveyed for AI transparency to achieve its intended goals. Participants primarily supported clear disclosure to health professionals of AI use and key instructions for safe operation of the technology. Yet, the findings reveal a 'medical AI transparency fallacy': the assumption that more information alone ensures safe and responsible use. In practice, clinicians often overlook labels, face low AI literacy, and experience information overload, all of which undermine transparency's effectiveness. The article proposes a four-step, holistic approach to ensure safe use of AI which integrates improved information design and supply chain, and greater regulatory disclosure to enable external scrutiny. This approach aims to inform regulators, policymakers, and industry in ensuring the safe implementation of medical AI.

papers.title: No added benefit of VR and neurofeedback-enhanced VR for trait mindfulness in long-term mindfulness training
papers.authors: Yuqin Liu, Weitao Zhang, Yilin Wang, Chen Wu, Sha Zhao, Gang Pan, 胡宇正
papers.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) and neurofeedback (NF) are increasingly promoted to enhance mindfulness meditation, yet it remains unknown whether these externally engaging technologies confer lasting benefits for trait mindfulness over sustained practice. This longitudinal randomized controlled trial compared three conditions over a 4-week program (eight sessions) with a three-month follow-up: screen-based audio-guided mindfulness (Non-VR), mindfulness in an immersive VR environment (VR), and mindfulness in VR with real-time EEG neurofeedback (VR-NF). Ninety-four meditation-naïve participants completed the study. Trait mindfulness (Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire, FFMQ) was assessed at six time points, EEG signal was recorded during all sessions, and subjective presence (Igroup Presence Questionnaire, IPQ) in VR was measured. Linear mixed models and Bayesian analysis revealed comparable FFMQ increases across all three groups, indicating that VR and VR-NF did not confer added behavioral benefit for trait mindfulness development. Higher IPQ presence scores showed a modest negative correlation with long-term FFMQ gains at three-month follow-up. Exploratory EEG analyses described a numerically steeper theta trajectory in the Non-VR group relative to the VR and VR-NF groups, whereas alpha trajectories were comparable across groups. However, because the two EEG systems were not equivalent across conditions and recordings were obtained from frontopolar sites, these patterns are descriptive only and cannot be interpreted as evidence of group differences. Taken together, these findings suggest that VR and VR-NF did not confer added benefit for trait mindfulness in long-term mindfulness training.

papers.title: Human–AI interaction in cybersecurity: An SOR model approach to users' intention to adopt AI-based authentication systems
papers.authors: Md. Solaiman Chowdhury, Shafiyatur Maria, Md. Rabiul Awal, Raiyan Jannat Sohana
papers.abstract: Cyber-attack poses potential threats and challenges for both individuals and organizations. Although strong security systems can protect against the destructive outcomes of cybercrime victimization, this is comparatively feasible in the current era of Artificial Intelligence. Therefore, the current study aims to unlock users’ intention to adopt AI-based authentication systems (AAI), prioritizing the role of attitude toward AI (AT) as a key direct predictor, while investigating prior cybercrime victimization experience (CVE), perceived severity (PS), and fear of cybercrime victimization (FCV) as antecedent psychological factors determining users’ adoption-related perceptions. Employing a cross-sectional research design, the current study uses convenience sampling with a quantitative method to examine the inner, outer, and structural models. PLS-SEM was applied to conduct both descriptive and inferential statistics by using a total of 453 screened responses. The findings explore that users’ AT, compared to CVE, FCV, and PS, has the strongest impact on users’ AAI. The outcomes also indicate that CVE, FCV, and PS have a positive association with AAI, but all the paths are statistically insignificant. Moreover, FCV has a positive and statistically significant relationship with users’ PS, while CVE has a positive interaction with FCV. By integrating the SOR model into AI-based technology adoption for cybersecurity, this empirical study offers a robust understanding of how AT shapes individuals’ AAI through human-AI interaction. This study uniquely identifies users’ AAI as a key factor in promoting cybersecurity, whereas previous studies emphasized traditional authentication systems.

papers.title: Native relation learning for cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition
papers.authors: Zhenwei Cao, Yonghua Lu, Xinyu Di, Tim Xiao, Weiguo Zhou
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition is widely used in affective computing, brain–computer interfaces, and mental-state assessment. Its performance, however, often drops when a model is transferred across subjects or datasets because EEG recordings vary with individual neural responses, elicitation paradigms, acquisition settings, and emotion-label definitions. Public EEG emotion datasets also differ in the number of categories and in how labels are obtained. Collapsing these datasets into a single output space may simplify training, but it can also remove the native category relations that define the decision boundaries of each target dataset. This study proposes NativeRelation, a native relation learning framework for cross-dataset EEG emotion recognition. During multi-dataset joint pre-training, NativeRelation keeps each dataset in its own emotion label space while sharing an EEG encoder across datasets. Dataset-specific prediction heads, class prototypes, native relation geometry constraints, and subject-level few-shot adaptation are used to shape frozen representations that can be read out from a small number of labeled target-subject samples. Experiments are conducted under a leave-one-dataset-out, subject-independent protocol on five public EEG emotion datasets: SEED, SEED-IV, SEED-V, SEED-VII, and DEAP. NativeRelation achieves 79.89%, 55.74%, 66.13%, 48.42%, and 72.47% accuracy on the five target datasets, respectively, with a macro-average accuracy of 64.53%. Under the evaluated protocol, the results suggest that preserving native emotion relations supports target readout under heterogeneous label spaces and yields a more traceable representation structure for EEG emotion recognition.

papers.title: Anticipated relevance prepares visual processing for efficient memory-guided selection
papers.authors: Lasse Dietz, Christoph Strauch, Kabir Arora, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Samson Chota, Surya Gayet
papers.abstract: Finding an object typically involves using working memory to select relevant visual information at the right time. Using EEG, we investigated how predictable changes in stimulus relevance influence top-down visual selection. Participants memorized an oriented grating, followed by a cue indicating which of two sequentially presented probes was relevant for a memory-match/-mismatch judgment. Consistent with earlier work, relevant probes evoked stronger univariate responses than irrelevant probes. Furthermore, responses to (memory-matching and memory-mismatching) probes were more distinct when they were relevant compared to irrelevant. Crucially, using rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT), we found that visual responses to the (empty) probe location were enhanced even before the presentation of relevant (compared to irrelevant) probes. Predictable changes in stimulus relevance, therefore, induce both pro-active and re-active changes in visual processing. We conclude that anticipating the (ir)relevance of upcoming visual events enables the visual system to prepare for efficient memory-guided visual selection.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence driven framework for enhancing sustainability and resilience in communal cattle insurance in Lupane District Zimbabwe
papers.authors: Nyasha Nyakuchena, Joseph P. Musara, Emmanuel Zivenge
papers.abstract: Communal cattle farming in Sub-Saharan Africa continues to face destabilization from non-linear climate variability, yet insurance penetration remains negligible. In Lupane District, Zimbabwe, uptake is exceptionally low at approximately 0.01%, despite recurrent droughts that threaten household livelihoods. This study aimed to develop an AI-driven framework to enhance sustainability and resilience in communal cattle insurance within the district. A positivist research philosophy guided the study, and a quantitative approach was adopted. The Kothari sample size determination formula was applied to derive a statistically representative sample of 219 households from a population of 49,841 communal cattle farmers distributed across four villages in 23 wards. Data were collected through KoboCollect, transmitted to secure servers, and analyzed using JAMOVI version 2.6.44. Descriptive statistics indicated that the majority of farmers were male (62%), with an average age of 47 years and herd sizes ranging from 3 to 25 cattle. Education levels were generally low, with 54% reporting primary schooling and only 12% having secondary or higher qualifications. Income sources were largely subsistence-based, and 71% of respondents relied on cattle as their primary asset. Binary logistic regression revealed that affordability (β = 1.25, p < 0.01) and awareness (β = 0.99, p < 0.01) were the strongest determinants of adoption, while institutional trust (β = 0.74, p < 0.05) emerged as a significant direct predictor of adoption willingness. The study was theoretically anchored in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which explains how perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use influence uptake. Informed by findings from Objectives 1 and 2, the study proposes the Tri-Modular AI Resilience Engine (TMAIE). TMAIE integrates Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for biometric cattle identification, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) for satellite-derived NDVI index triggers, and Transformer-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) localized in IsiNdebele and ChiShona for inclusive voice-based access. The study findings suggest that adoption is not a linear process but an adaptive evolution requiring both technological and social mechanisms. The proposed framework reflects these relationships through the integration of technological precision and community-based mediation. Overall, the findings provide empirical evidence on the determinants of cattle insurance adoption and inform the development of a conceptual AI-driven framework that may support future climate-resilient livestock insurance innovations, subject to further validation and testing.

papers.title: Perceptions of AI-assisted learning and learner development among Moroccan secondary school students
papers.authors: Rajae Kandirou, Safaa El Youssfi, Mohamed EL Atlassi, Abdeghni Dahman, Mohamed Merouane El Hammoumi
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in education has fundamentally altered traditional learning paradigms, presenting both unprecedented opportunities for personalized support and novel academic challenges. This study aims to examine secondary school students’ perceptions of the influence of AI-assisted learning on perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, while also exploring the perceived benefits and challenges associated with AI use in the Casablanca-Settat region of Morocco. Employing a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were collected via a structured questionnaire completed by 150 secondary school students, while qualitative data were collected separately through online semi-structured interviews with 12 students and analyzed thematically. The findings suggest that ChatGPT was the most frequently used AI tool, primarily accessed on students’ personal mobile devices as a complementary learning resource. Quantitative results indicated positive perceptions of AI-assisted learning across perceived learning outcomes, motivation, self-regulated learning, and digital literacy, with a significant positive association between perceived learning outcomes and motivation. Qualitative findings identified four major themes: perceived learning benefits (clearer explanations and reduced academic stress), conditional trust in AI outputs through cross-checking with traditional learning resources, concerns about AI hallucinations in STEM subjects, and the "laziness paradox," reflecting reduced cognitive effort associated with excessive reliance on AI. The findings highlight the importance of promoting responsible AI integration in schools rather than relying solely on restrictive approaches. Pedagogical implications emphasize the need for responsible AI use, subject-specific prompting frameworks, and the redesign of traditional homework into AI-supported critique activities that foster students’ intellectual autonomy and critical thinking.

papers.title: Research-informed tools as a science-practice interface for mediating multifunctional design: reflections from a collaborative design research studio
papers.authors: Yue Zhu, Jing Wang, Ye Zhang, Yun Hye Hwang, Dengkai Chi, Yeshan Qiu, Xinyu Chen, Chenyu Feng, Zuyuan Zhou, Jianxiang Huang, Paolo Burlando, Puay Yok Tan
papers.abstract: Abstract Urban design is under growing pressure to accommodate multiple ecological and socio-economic functions, yet translating the multidisciplinary scientific knowledge needed to support this goal into practical design solutions remains a persistent challenge. This challenge largely arises from the complex and often non-linear relationships between urban spatial patterns and multiple dimensions of urban functional performance. This study examines how research-informed tools may serve as a science-practice interface for supporting designers’ perception and integration of urban multifunctionality within a collaborative design studio. The study draws on a project-based design studio as an empirical setting, involving student participants from architecture and landscape design backgrounds who used a tool package comprising written guidelines and a machine-learning-based assessment tool. Questionnaire surveys, semi-structured focus group discussions, and model-estimated performance of selected design proposals were used to examine disciplinary starting points, patterns of tool use, and engagement with trade-offs and synergies. Across the studio, participants’ reported priorities and perceptions of influential urban form indicators changed, while the two tool components were described as serving complementary roles in conceptual framing and iterative evaluation. Overall, the study showcases a practical approach to translating scientific insights into design guidance, demonstrating its potential to broaden designers’ perspectives, moderate disciplinary predispositions, and support data-informed consideration of urban multifunctionality in design outcomes, thereby providing a basis for deepening understanding of the interface between science and design in sustainable urban landscape planning.

papers.title: Designing Teacher-Centered Interfaces to Elicit Pedagogical Context for LLM-Based Content Generation
papers.authors: Abdolali Faraji, Mohammadreza Tavakoli, Mohammad Mahdi Moein, Mohammadreza Molavi, Gábor Kismihók
papers.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) can help teachers generate and adapt educational materials, but most interactions still rely on free-form prompting, making instructional intent difficult to express and reuse. In this paper, we study how teacher-facing interfaces can elicit pedagogically meaningful contextual information and reduce ad hoc prompt engineering. We first conducted a requirement analysis with $$N=100$$ N = 100 teachers across 17 contextual fields. We measured importance and introduced fill deficit to identify “friction points” (i.e., information teachers consider important but are less likely to provide). Based on this analysis, we implemented a context-rich interface with targeted supports for important and friction-point fields. In a separate user study with a different sample of $$N=100$$ N = 100 teachers, the interface achieved high usability (SUS mean $$=80.33$$ = 80.33 ), low perceived workload, and increased willingness to provide contextual information, particularly for friction-point fields. For further validation, we conducted a comparative pilot with $$N=10$$ N = 10 experienced teachers; participants reported a greater tendency to use content generated with our context-rich interface (72.2%) than content generated with a baseline GPT interface (37.0%).

papers.authors: Rotimi-Williams Bello, Roseline Oluwaseun Ogundokun, Pius Adewale Owolawi, Chunglin Du, Etienne Van Wyk

papers.abstract: The advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a critical technology has facilitated the attainment of United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In the context of South Africa, this paper examines the impact of AI on SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure). The adoption of AI and policy landscape in South Africa is reviewed, including the assessment of advantages and disadvantages of AI to the SDG 9 (and intersecting goals like education, energy, and economic growth), and the presentation of case studies of AI applications in infrastructure development. The paper analyzes the key barriers, such as the digital divide, skills shortages, and regulatory gaps. Finally, evidence-based policy and investment recommendations are offered by the paper to harness AI for innovation, infrastructure, and sustainable industry in South Africa.

papers.title: From scores to causality and confidence: operational acceptance of AI weather forecasts
papers.authors: Steven Ramsdale
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that the operational value of machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) cannot be assessed through verification skill alone. Instead, acceptance depends on support for the core functions of operational meteorology: understanding, translating and communicating. Current MLWP systems show strong performance but lack the interpretability, diagnostic depth and stability required for trust in safety‐critical contexts. The paper highlights the need for closer collaboration between developers and operational users and identifies a key future role for artificial intelligence (AI) in supporting data triage and human decision‐making.

papers.title: Observer‐Based Adaptive Sliding Mode Control for Fuzzy Markov Jump Systems Subject to Deception Attacks: A Q‐Learning Event‐Triggered Communication Protocol
papers.authors: Mourad Kchaou, Rabeh Abbassi, Muhammed Syed Ali, Houssem Jerbi
papers.journal: International Journal of Robust and Nonlinear Control
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article addresses the secure control problem for nonlinear Markov jump systems subject to communication constraints and false data injection attacks. The Takagi–Sugeno (TS) fuzzy model is employed to describe the systems under consideration, and the Q‐learning concept is utilized to enhance the dynamic event‐triggered mechanisms (DETM) and reduce network load without compromising control performance. The main contribution of this work lies in designing an adaptive fuzzy sliding mode observer (SMO) with mismatched premise variables to estimate compromised system states and in synthesizing a sliding mode controller (SMC) to maintain the stochastic stability of the closed‐loop system while guaranteeing the reachability of the sliding‐mode dynamics. Moreover, a feasible solution algorithm based on a Real‐Valued Genetic Algorithm (RVGA) is proposed to synthesize the controller and observer gains and to optimize system performance. Finally, extensive simulations on the Chua chaotic system are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy.

papers.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI)‐Supported Removable Partial Denture Design Tools in Dental Education
papers.authors: Shixin Chen, Lavanya Ajay Sharma, Steve An
papers.abstract: PURPOSE/OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning tool can enhance students' confidence, understanding, and overall experience in removable partial denture (RPD) design. The study also explored student perceptions of AI within dental education. METHODS: A mixed-methods study was conducted involving Undergraduate Dental Technology and Prosthetics students and Undergraduate and Postgraduate Dentistry students with prior training in RPD design. Of the 40 students invited to participate, 35 completed the study. Participants independently completed conventional RPD designs before using an AI-assisted RPD design tool that generated design suggestions based on prosthodontic design principles for comparison and reflection. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires containing Likert-type items and open-ended questions were administered using Qualtrics. Quantitative data were analyzed using non-parametric tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to assess pre- and post-survey differences within participants, while the Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare post-survey responses between Dentistry and Dental Technology and Prosthetics students and between clinical-based and laboratory-based student groups. Analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS. Qualitative responses from the open-ended questions were reviewed and grouped into four thematic categories to identify recurring perspectives and experiences related to the use of the AI-assisted RPD design tool. RESULTS: Students showed significant improvements in confidence and understanding following use of the AI tool. Items related to the tool's effectiveness, design experience, and visualization received positive ratings, with median scores of 4 (interquartile range [IQR] 3-4), 4 (IQR 4-4), and 4 (IQR 4-5), respectively. Willingness to use AI and perceived helpfulness remained stable, likely due to high baseline attitudes. Qualitative findings supported the quantitative results, with participants highlighting the tool's value for visualizing RPD frameworks and guiding design decisions, while also identifying usability challenges and limitations in design flexibility. CONCLUSION: The findings indicate that the AI-supported tool contributed positively to RPD design learning by enhancing student confidence and conceptual understanding. While it does not replace manual or clinical skill development, the tool shows clear potential as a complementary educational resource that helps bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application. Further research involving larger cohorts is recommended to confirm and expand upon these findings.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Systems vs. Clinicians in Fetal Echocardiography: A Structured Knowledge‐Based Comparative Assessment
papers.authors: Uğurcan Zorlu, H. İbrahim Altınsoy, Mehmet Utku Başarır, Şükrü Bakırcı, Eda Özden Tokalıoğlu, Özgür Kara, Fatma Doğa Öcal, Dilek Şahın
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Fetal echocardiography requires systematic anatomical assessment, segmental interpretation, and high-level clinical reasoning. This study aimed to compare the performance of contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems and clinicians with different levels of expertise in a standardized fetal echocardiography knowledge-based assessment. METHODS: This cross-sectional comparative assessment study used a 60-item, single-best-answer multiple-choice examination covering eight fetal echocardiography subdomains: general principles of fetal echocardiography, general fetal cardiac anatomy, left-sided cardiac pathologies, conotruncal anomalies, isomerism and heterotaxy syndromes, fetal arrhythmias, anomalies of venous return, and pulmonary malformations/right-sided cardiac pathologies. The same examination was administered to seven publicly accessible AI systems and three clinicians: one senior perinatologist, one junior perinatologist, and one junior obstetrician. All AI systems were accessed during the same predefined evaluation period in January 2026. The primary outcome was response correctness. Secondary analyses included total accuracy, domain-specific performance, and AI-clinician group comparisons. RESULTS: A total of 600 group-question response entries were analyzed, comprising 420 AI-generated responses and 180 clinician responses. The senior perinatologist achieved the highest total score among all participants, with 53 correct responses out of 60, followed by GPT-5 with 52 correct responses. Overall accuracy was 78.8% for AI systems and 73.3% for clinicians. The mean domain-level score was 5.91 for AI systems and 5.50 for clinicians, without a statistically significant difference using either unequal-variance t-test or Mann-Whitney U-test. AI systems showed higher mean performance in general fetal echocardiography principles and general fetal cardiac anatomy, whereas the senior perinatologist performed best in complex integrative domains, particularly conotruncal anomalies and isomerism/heterotaxy syndromes. CONCLUSIONS: In a structured text-based fetal echocardiography knowledge assessment, AI systems achieved overall performance comparable to clinicians, particularly in standardized knowledge domains. However, the senior perinatologist retained the strongest performance in complex fetal cardiac categories requiring integrative clinical reasoning. These findings support the potential role of AI as an adjunctive educational and structured decision-support tool in fetal echocardiography, while emphasizing that performance in a multiple-choice format should not be interpreted as equivalent to autonomous real-world fetal cardiac diagnosis.

papers.title: DIGITAL LEARNING AND EDUCATIONAL EQUITY: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES IN HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: Kamlesh Kumar Tewari
papers.journal: ACCENT JOURNAL OF  ECONOMICS ECOLOGY  & ENGINEERING
papers.abstract: Digital learning has emerged as a significant component of higher education, transforming teaching methodologies, learning environments, academic collaboration, and access to educational resources. The integration of digital platforms, learning management systems, virtual classrooms, open educational resources, and artificial intelligence has created new opportunities for flexible, inclusive, and learner-centred education. However, the expansion of digital learning has also highlighted persistent inequalities associated with internet connectivity, access to digital devices, socioeconomic status, geographical location, disability, language, and digital literacy. These disparities can prevent disadvantaged students from benefiting equally from technology-enabled education. This research paper examines the relationship between digital learning and educational equity in higher education, focusing on its major opportunities, structural challenges, and potential policy interventions. The paper adopts a qualitative, descriptive, and analytical approach based on a review of relevant literature, international policy documents, and educational frameworks. It argues that digital learning can promote educational equity only when supported by affordable infrastructure, accessible learning materials, inclusive pedagogical practices, faculty development, and institutional accountability. The paper concludes that technology should be treated as an instrument for educational inclusion rather than as a substitute for equitable educational policies and meaningful human interaction. Keywords: Digital learning, educational equity, higher education, digital divide, inclusive education, online learning, digital literacy.

papers.title: Feasibility and effects of a multimodal EEG-fNIRS neurofeedback platform for motor imagery
papers.authors: Camille Muller, Isabelle Corouge, Thomas Prampart, Élise Bannier, Pierre Maurel
papers.journal: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
papers.abstract: Neurofeedback (NF) promotes neuroplasticity by enabling users to self-regulate their brain activity in near real-time through sensory representations. In rehabilitation contexts, motor imagery (MI), i.e. the mental simulation of movement, offers a promising approach to stimulate motor-related brain regions without any movement. To optimize NF for MI, current research turns toward the combination of neuroimaging methods that are both ecologically feasible and neurophysiologically accurate. The integration of various portable recording techniques, such as electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), respectively based on electrical and hemodynamic activity, could enhance the characterization of brain responses and subsequently improve NF performance. Multimodal EEG-fNIRS systems could address this need by combining complementary signals. To our knowledge, no study has yet combined EEG and fNIRS within a NF paradigm targeting upper-limb MI for post-stroke motor rehabilitation. This study evaluates the feasibility and the effects of a multimodal EEG-fNIRS NF system for upper-limb MI.A custom platform was developed for real-time signal processing of both EEG and fNIRS recordings in order to provide continuous unimodal or multimodal NF scores via a visual gauge. Following an initial baseline calibration block used to determine individual regulation thresholds, thirty healthy participants (15 women, 25 ± 4 years) completed three randomized MI-NF conditions: EEG-only, fNIRS-only, and multimodal EEG-fNIRS. Each condition comprised two runs of 10 blocks alternating 15 s of rest and 15 s of active NF task. The NF score was derived from the right primary motor cortex (M1) activity during left-hand MI. The EEG feature was the alpha-band event-related desynchronization (ERD, 8–13 Hz;), while the fNIRS feature was the change in oxyhemoglobin concentration (ΔHBO₂). To evaluate the effect of the NF-MI session, brain activity was computed offline as the average ERD and ΔHBO₂ across conditions and participants. Following each condition, participants also assessed their subjective feeling of success and the mental strategies used to modulate the feedback. All variables were compared using repeated measures ANOVAs (significance level of α = .05).The average online NF scores (mean scores: EEG-NF = 45.88%, fNIRS-NF = 44.30%, EEG-fNIRS-NF = 48.00%) significantly exceeded the threshold set during calibration, confirming successful online regulation. No significant difference in displayed NF scores was observed across the three conditions. Offline analysis of brain activity at the level of right M1 revealed no significant difference in EEG-ERD or fNIRS-ΔHBO₂ between conditions (all p > .05). Participants reported a higher perceived sense of control over the feedback in the EEG and EEG-fNIRS conditions compared to fNIRS-only (p < .05).All participants successfully modulated their NF score across every condition relative to calibration, confirming the overall validity of the paradigm. However, under the current protocol, the EEG-fNIRS combination offered no measurable advantage over unimodal approaches, either at the level of brain activity or perceived control. The lower subjective sense of control in the fNIRS-only condition may reflect the inherently slower hemodynamic response compared to electrophysiological signals, but will require further investigation. Future work will also explore additional brain regions beyond M1 and investigate the use of repetitive sessions of multimodal NF training on motor learning. Such a platform holds strong clinical potential, particularly for post-stroke upper-limb motor rehabilitation.

papers.title: The Law of the Digital Smokestack: Regulating the Dual-Use Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Climate Crisis
papers.authors: Walters Nsoh, Talal Abdulla Al-Emadi, Eduardo G. Pereira, Timothy Alfonso, Jiangyan Fu
papers.journal: University of Birmingham Research Portal (University of Birmingham)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a cornerstone of the global climate transition, enabling advances in renewable energy integration, emissions monitoring, and environmental governance. Yet the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure – including energy-intensive data centres, large language models, and computationally demanding machine learning systems – is generating substantial greenhouse gas emissions, water consumption, and resource extraction, thereby creating a fundamental regulatory paradox. Existing legal frameworks largely treat AI as an enabler of climate action while overlooking its growing environmental footprint. This article examines the dual environmental character of AI within the climate governance framework. The central research question is how climate, environmental, and related regulatory regimes must be redesigned to govern AI as both a tool of climate action and an emergent driver of climate risk. The article argues that the existing corpus of environmental, energy, and technology law is structurally inadequate to address this paradox. Employing a doctrinal-institutional methodology combined with comparative regulatory analysis across EU, US, and international frameworks, it identifies critical lacunae in Environmental Impact Assessment law, the Polluter Pays Principle, and corporate disclosure regimes. Three original contributions are advanced: first, the reconceptualisation of computational load as a digital smokestack under environmental law; second, the proposal of CAFE-analogy computational efficiency standards that directly internalise the externality of algorithmic waste; and third, a burden-shifting tort mechanism to address the responsibility gap created by the opacity and transnational diffusion of AI harms. The article further distinguishes its framework from Le Goff (2025) by extending that analysis into concrete operational proposals and a phased international roadmap. A sui generis 'Sustainable AI' legal framework grounded in mandatory transparency, corporate accountability, and the precautionary principle is proffered as both necessary and achievable.

papers.title: Can we trust AI research in education? Introducing the Reporting AI Studies in Education (RAISE) framework
papers.authors: Jordan Allison

papers.title: Salesperson Adaptability and Career Sustainability in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Review of Sales Task and Role Transformation
papers.authors: Damar Kristanto, Vivi Rodliyatuz Zulfa, Edwin Fiatiano
papers.journal: Journal of Innovation Research and Knowledge
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital transformation are reshaping sales tasks, roles, and competency requirements, raising questions about how salespeople adapt and whether such adaptation supports career sustainability. This study examines the relationship between technological transformation, salesperson adaptability, task and role transformation, and career sustainability in the AI era. A Critical Literature Review (CLR) was conducted on 48 scholarly articles, comprising 30 studies on salesperson adaptability and 18 on sales career sustainability. The analysis combined proposition development, cross-examination of the two literature groups, and critical synthesis across individual, job/role, and career/profession levels. The findings indicate that AI is better understood as driving task transformation and redistribution rather than direct salesperson replacement. Adaptability is supported by resilience, change agility, technology readiness, learning, and psychological resources, while technology may also generate job demands through technostress, technological uncertainty, and job insecurity. Adaptation further contributes to role transformation toward consultative selling, relationship management, complex problem solving, and value co-creation. However, direct evidence linking salesperson adaptability to career sustainability remains limited. Career sustainability therefore extends beyond job retention to encompass employability, professional relevance, well-being, and the capacity to maintain professional value as work structures evolve. The findings position adaptability as both adaptive protection and adaptive transformation in sustaining the salesperson profession in the AI era.

papers.title: End-to-End Safe Social Navigation via Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning and Probabilistic Perception
papers.authors: Tommaso Van Der Meer, Andrea Garulli, Antonio Giannitrapani, Renato Quartullo, Alberto Vaglio, Alexandre Alahi
papers.abstract: Autonomous social navigation requires balancing efficiency, physical safety, and social compliance. Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods provide a viable and effective solution but often rely on unrealistic assumptions, such as the knowledge of humans' position and velocity. In this paper, we introduce JESSI (JAX-based E2E Safe Social Interpretable navigation), a lightweight end-to-end RL framework that maps raw LiDAR scans directly to kinematically feasible control commands. JESSI enhances safety via Dirichlet-parameterized continuous action spaces and deterministic bounding, while an integrated attention-based perception module extracts probabilistic human states for interpretable, socially aware decision-making. Through extensive simulations and real-world deployment on a differential-drive robot, we demonstrate that jointly optimizing the RL policy with a supervised perception signal in a multi-task paradigm enhances social behavior. Ultimately, JESSI is able to balance high navigation success rates and superior social behaviors compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Oltre le parole: immagini, corpo e narrazione come dispositivi embodied di comunicazione generativa nei processi identitari e interculturali
papers.authors: Paola Cortiana, Farnaz Farahi
papers.journal: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: Il contributo si colloca nel quadro teorico dell'Embodied Education che interpreta apprendimento e conoscenza come processi incarnati in cui corpo, emozione e cognizione si intrecciano nell'esperienza.Integrando pedagogia esperienziale, approccio socioculturale, narrazione e fenomenologia del corpo, il lavoro richiama gli sviluppi dell'embodied cognition, paradigma che supera la dicotomia mente-corpo e riconosce il ruolo di azione, percezione e interazione nella costruzione della conoscenza.In tale prospettiva, le immagini attivano risonanza emotiva, memoria corporea e simbolizzazione, favorendo la costruzione identitaria di sé.Sul piano applicativo, viene presentata un'esperienza laboratoriale narrativa centrata sulla conoscenza di sé attraverso immagini evocative riferite a corpo ed emozioni.A partire da un brainstorming, viene costruita un'agenda di domande-stimolo che orienta il lavoro in piccoli gruppi come comunità di discorso e pratica, fino alla realizzazione di artefatti nati dalla riflessione su incertezze, desideri e vissuti emotivi dei partecipanti.Particolare attenzione è data ai contesti interculturali, nei quali immagini, corpo e narrazione possono favorire incontro con l'alterità, la decostruzione di stereotipi e la gestione trasformativa del conflitto.Il contributo evidenzia il potenziale dell'integrazione tra corpo, emozione, narrazione e relazione nel promuovere processi di apprendimento inclusivi, orientati alla costruzione di comunità educanti.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Language Analytics for Student Development in Higher Education: Evidence from Longitudinal Academic Records
papers.authors: Weiqi Lyu, Ke Yu, Yuchun Lu, Jianhui Yang, Xiaoxiao Wu, Dehua Ye
papers.abstract: In higher education, standardized entry scores provide an important but incomplete basis for understanding students’ subsequent development. This study explores whether AI-assisted language analytics can provide complementary information about student development beyond standardized academic measures. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, we examine the relationship between National College Entrance Examination (NCEE) scores, language-based indicators from students’ self-introductions, and academic performance across four semesters. The study involved 72 undergraduate students majoring in mathematics education who provided free-form self-introductions describing their interests and experiences. Interest types were categorized, and linguistic features were extracted and analyzed using an artificial intelligence (AI)-based model. Results show that the association between NCEE scores and academic performance weakened across successive semesters, whereas students expressing more autonomous interests tended to achieve higher academic performance. An exploratory AI classification analysis further indicated that linguistic features could distinguish developmental profiles within this sample. These findings suggest that AI-assisted language analytics may offer a complementary source of information for understanding student development and informing formative advising and student support. Given the single-institution sample, the findings should be interpreted as exploratory and require validation in larger and more diverse populations.

papers.title: Oltre il tecnocentrismo: l’intelligenza artificiale tra embodied education e cognizione distribuita. Una prospettiva pedagogica critica.
papers.authors: Roberta Marsicano
papers.journal: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: The pervasive integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into contemporary educational and training contexts is leading to a profound metamorphosis, not only of teaching practices and methodological tools, but of the very ways in which the learning experience is perceived, organized, and lived. This paper aims to critically analyze this scenario, overcoming the sterile polarizations that characterize the current academic and public debate, often oscillating between uncritical technosolutionism-which sees AI as the automatic response to the fragilities of educational systems-and alarmist perspectives, which view digital innovation exclusively in terms of human loss and cognitive impoverishment. The paper analyzes digital technologies and generative AI as socio-material mediators that reconfigure and influence complex learning processes such as attention, agency, and meaning-making. Therefore, through a critical pedagogical perspective that draws inspiration from the theories of F. Varela, E. Thompson and A. Clark, the risks of an educational disembodiment, of cognitive delegation and technocentric drift. This reflection, however, does not fail to highlight the opportunities offered by AI as a distributed learning engine and support for metacognitive processes. Finally, through the lens of the «extended mind», learning is reread as a situated, embodied, and distributed experience, in which cognition emerges from the dynamic interaction between body, environment, tools, and relational networks. In conclusion, the paper outlines the need for an AI pedagogy that is not limited to defining operational skills, but is capable of interrogating the anthropological and relational transformations introduced by technologies, promoting a critical awareness aimed at preserving the relational and corporeal complexity of teaching-learning processes.

papers.title: The digital poster as a multimodal artefact in teacher education: an exploratory study
papers.authors: Agnese Vezzani
papers.journal: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: This study examines the digital poster as a multimodal artefact commonly used in academic contexts for research dissemination, reinterpreted within an educational and professional framework. Digital posters have been adopted as a form of final documentation for both direct and indirect internship experiences of fifth-year students in the Primary Education degree programme at the University of Xxxx, since the 2022–2023 academic year. The affordances of the poster have been analysed, to deepen its role within the training pathways for students (future teachers) and their tutors (in-service teachers). The poster represents both an opportunity to present internship experiences to peers and an authentic task transferable to professional contexts, fostering transversal skills in content selection and visual representation, also through the use of multimedia and AI tools. Data collected via questionnaires administered to trainees (96) and a convenient sample of tutors (39) focused on the technologies used, metacognitive value, and perceived communicative effectiveness. Findings highlight strengths and weaknesses of digital posters: as tools integrating creativity, digital technologies, and multiple languages, they effectively support embodied reflections; however, they may not fully capture experiential complexity, suggesting the need to integrate them within broader documentation and reflective practices.

papers.title: Oltre il Tecnocentrismo: Ambienti Ibridi, Mente Estesa e Centralità dell’Umano nei Processi Formativi
papers.authors: Giovanna Amendola, Monica Di Domenico, Fortunata Romano, Pio Alfredo Di Tore
papers.journal: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: The growing diffusion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence systems within educational contexts is reconfiguring spaces, practices and cognitive processes, redefining the contours of contemporary educational experience. Such a transformation calls for pedagogical reflection to critically interrogate the meanings, limits and potential of technological mediation, counteracting technocentric tendencies and reaffirming the centrality of the person, the body and the relational dimension within learning processes. This paper examines the role of physical, digital and hybrid environments in shaping educational experience, with particular attention to school contexts, community-based educational services and the continuing professional development of educators. The proposal is situated within the framework of Embodied Education and It is theoretically grounded in the integration between the extended mind thesis (Clark & Chalmers, 1998) and the enactive and embodied paradigm of cognition (Varela, Thompson & Rosch, 1991). From this perspective, learning is understood as a situated, distributed and relational process, emerging from the dynamic interaction between mind, body, environment and devices, all of which contribute to knowledge construction (Gomez Paloma, 2013). In dialogue with a critical perspective on educational technologies (Selwyn, 2016), this paper argues that the design of learning environments should be understood as an intentional pedagogical act, capable of shaping attention, participation and the quality of relationships. Digital technologies and AI are thus understood as mediators whose role remains subordinate to human centrality (Floridi, 2022), in the service of an equitable, inclusive and sustainable education. Within this framework, the classroom is configured as a generative ecosystem in which the physical and the digital dimensions are integrated to support meaningful learning, reflective professional practice and educational communities capable of critically interpreting contemporary complexity.

papers.title: Embodied learning in the era of Artificial Intelligence and immersive technologies: corporeality, digital mediation, and cognitive artifacts for an innovative teaching process.
papers.authors: Angelo Cappello
papers.journal: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: The current projection of technological infrastructures leads us to analyze how the emergence of embodied education as a pedagogical paradigm is redefining the interactions and inferential methods through which students relate to knowledge, in the construction of artifacts, and in learning environments themselves. Processing knowledge by shifting it from a neutral to an "embodied" position allows us to think of our body not as a simple sensory vehicle, but as an epistemic mediator that structures attention, perception, and the construction of meaning (Habrahanson et al. 2023). From this scenario, the growing diffusion of immersive technologies such as virtual reality, augmented reality, phygital environments, and AI-based systems give rise to new opportunities for experiential educational design in which corporeality becomes a lever for engagement, conceptual understanding, and the personalization of educational paths (Farina, 2021). From this perspective, digital artifacts take on significant significance precisely because of their role. Indeed, when designed according to principles of digital mediation, they facilitate the transition from concrete experience to abstract representation, supporting deep and situated learning processes. Consider how essential it is to preserve the corporeal dimension of learning, seeking to avoid deviations from corporeality by promoting a balanced approach between automation, human agency, and teacher mediation. This paper aims to analyze the relationship between corporeality, emerging technologies, and digital artifacts, outlining implications for instructional design, teacher training, and the development of dynamic, inclusive, and cognitively satisfying learning environments. (Ciccarelli, Tafuri, 2024).

papers.title: Body, reflexivity and educational citizenship: embodied practices for the dialogic construction of meaning
papers.authors: Antonio Balestra, Daniela Maggi, Michele Marangi
papers.journal: Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching
papers.abstract: The contribution is situated within a line of research that understands the body as a mediator of knowledge, identity and the educational relationship. The hypothesis that guides it is that bodily experiences do not in themselves generate ethical-civic learning, but can foster reflexivity, mutual recognition and citizenship where they are intentionally designed and supported by dialogic practices of re-elaboration. The body is not assumed here as an instrument or support for learning, but as an original condition through which the subject perceives, acts, interprets and communicates. Movement, gesture, posture and interaction with space, both physical and digital, acquire pedagogical value insofar as they convert experience into awareness, speech and responsibility. From this perspective, the dialogic dimension does not arise as an additional moment in relation to action, but operates as a device that gives form to bodily experience and makes its meanings shareable, even when the educational relationship is mediated by digital environments or by Artificial Intelligence. On this basis, the contribution proposes a model founded on the body-reflexivity-citizenship triad, articulated in three interdependent dimensions. The first, experiential, links the body to situated access to knowledge; the second, reflective-dialogic, entrusts its elaboration to sharing; the third, ethical-civic, concerns responsibility, listening, belonging and participation. What emerges is a contribution to that common grammar of Embodied Education in which the educational quality of bodily practices depends on intentional design, capable of enabling the student to recognise themselves as an embodied, relational and responsible subject. Embodied Education is therefore not positioned as an alternative to the digital, but as an experiential anchor that restores bodily depth to technologically augmented learning.

papers.title: Strengthening the Capacity and Competitiveness of MSMEs in Talang Beringin Village Through Guidance on Digital Marketing, Branding, and Business Finance
papers.authors: Trufi Murdiani, Rikha Dewi Natalia, Zida Nadhifah Aulia Kencana Zida, Yuda Raja Reza
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the transformation of the community’s role from beneficiaries into drivers of the digital economic ecosystem through collaboration with MSMEs. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of 30 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2026, with the selection process based on PRISMA 2020 and the analysis conducted using the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that digital empowerment develops through the stages of digital inclusion, digital literacy, digital capability, community participation, community–MSME collaboration, digital value co-creation, and the formation of a local digital economic ecosystem.
