The paper closes with a practical risk mitigation framework and an assessment of open questions likely to shape this area going forward.

papers.title: Reimagining Ghana’s Electronic Transactions Act in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Legal Gaps, Risks, and Opportunities
papers.authors: Joseph Kwaku Asamoah
papers.journal: JOURNAL OF LAW AND GLOBAL POLICY
papers.abstract: The rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of digital transactions, challenging existing legal frameworks that were designed for an earlier era of electronic commerce. Ghana’s Electronic Transactions Act, 2008 (Act 772), while pioneering at the time of its enactment, now exhibits significant regulatory deficiencies in addressing the complexities of AI integration in digital markets. This article critically examines the legal gaps in Act 772 in relation to algorithmic agency, liability attribution, transparency, data protection, and consumer rights. Using a doctrinal and comparative methodology, it analyses global developments including the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act, the United Kingdom’s pro-innovation approach, and African policy responses to identify models that could inform Ghana’s legislative reform. The article argues that Act 772 must be reimagined through a risk-based and rights-oriented lens to remain relevant in the age of intelligent systems. It proposes a suite of legislative recommendations, including the introduction of AIspecific definitions, enhanced transparency obligations, ethical AI principles, liability frameworks, and institutional coordination mechanisms. The goal is to craft a forward-looking legal infrastructure that safeguards fundamental rights, promotes responsible innovation, and ensures public trust in AI-enabled electronic transactions. In doing so, the article contributes to the broader discourse on AI governance in Africa and offers a roadmap for aligning Ghana’s digital laws with emerging technological realities.

papers.title: Ai-Assisted Social Work Education: Bridging the Skills Gap in Rivers State Tertiary Institutions Faculty of Social Sciences, Sociology Department Rivers State University, Nkpolu Oroworokwo Port Harcourt, Nigeria
papers.authors: Bobby Okechukwu Akani
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
papers.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into social work education represents a transformative opportunity to address critical skills gaps in preparing future professionals for practice in Nigeria's Niger Delta region. This article examines the current state of AI-assisted social work education at Rivers State University and other tertiary institutions, drawing from academic discourse, global scholarship, and the specific socio-economic realities of Rivers State. The paper identifies that AI innovations such as personalized learning modules, digital case studies, and interactive training simulations offer significant potential to enhance student engagement and professional readiness However, implementation faces substantial barriers including inadequate digital infrastructure, limited staff and student digital literacy, underfunding, and the absence of comprehensive policy frameworks The paper proposes a comprehensive framework for integrating AI into social work curricula, investing in educator training, developing public-private infrastructure partnerships, and creating culturally sensitive AI tools that respect the region's indigenous knowledge and community-based practice models . The paper concludes that strategic investment in AI-enhanced education is essential for equipping Rivers State social workers with the competencies required for effective twenty-first-century practice.

papers.title: Harnessing the Potential of Artificial Intelligence for Advancing Mathematics Content Delivery in Secondary Schools in Bayelsa State, Nigeria
papers.authors: Isaac B. Ado
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
papers.abstract: The increasing advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents significant opportunities for improving instructional delivery, particularly in mathematics education where learners often encounter difficulties with abstract concepts and problem-solving processes. This study examined the potential of Artificial Intelligence for advancing mathematics content delivery in secondary schools in Bayelsa State, Nigeria. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 608 secondary school mathematics teachers in 210 public secondary schools in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 241 teachers was selected using a multistage sampling procedure. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence Utilisation for Mathematics Content Delivery Questionnaire (AIUMCDQ). The instrument was validated by experts and its reliability was established using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient. Data collected were analysed using frequency, percentage, mean, and standard deviation. The findings revealed that secondary school mathematics teachers demonstrated a high level of readiness to utilise Artificial Intelligence for mathematics content delivery, particularly due to their recognition of its usefulness in improving instructional effectiveness and supporting teachers’ roles. However, the findings also revealed that inadequate AI training, poor internet connectivity, unstable electricity supply, limited access to digital devices, and insufficient institutional support were major challenges affecting AI utilisation. The study concluded that although mathematics teachers possess positive dispositions towards AI integration, effective adoption requires strategic interventions in teacher training, digital infrastructure development, and supportive educational policies. The study recommended continuous AI capacity-building programmes for mathematics teachers and improved technological facilities in secondary schools to promote effective AI-supported mathematics instruction.

papers.title: Ethical Dilemma Of Artificial Intelligence In Education: Balancing Automation And Human Teaching Roles: A Review
papers.authors: ANSELEM ANAYOCHUKWU ANIH
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence(AI) has transformed education through task automation, personalization, and administrative enhancement.Nonetheless, its educational integration raises ethical issues, notably regarding job loss,academic integrity,data security, and algorithmic bias.This review analyzes the challenges and ethical ramifications of AI in education and suggests strategies for responsible implementation.The importance of this study is underscored by its focus on balancing AI automation with the indispensable role of human educators.By examining policy suggestions, governance structures, and ethical guidelines, this review offers perspectives on ensuring fairness,transparency, and inclusivity inAI-enhanced education.Addressing these ethical issues is vital for upholding academic integrity,promoting equitable access,and maintaining human engagement in educational settings.

papers.title: AI-Driven Educational Policy Design: Enhancing Equity and Access through Intelligent Data Analytics
papers.authors: Chukwudum Collins Umoke
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational policy by enhancing decision-making, optimizing resource distribution, and supporting personalized learning. However, while AI holds the potential to improve accessibility and efficiency, it also raises concerns about algorithmic bias, ethical governance, and the reinforcement of systemic inequities. This study employs a qualitative approach based on secondary data analysis to critically examine AIdriven educational policies and their implications for equity and inclusion. Using the AI-Equity Nexus Model as a conceptual framework, the study explores how AI can serve as both an enabler of educational reform and a potential contributor to disparities in learning opportunities. The findings highlight key challenges, including data privacy concerns, digital divides, and the lack of regulatory oversight, while also identifying best practices for ethical AI integration in education. Policy recommendations emphasize the need for transparent AI governance, equitable digital infrastructure, and AI literacy training for educators and policymakers. This study contributes to the growing discourse on AI in education, offering insights into how AI-driven policies can be structured to promote fairness and accessibility while mitigating unintended biases and exclusionary effects.

papers.title: Fragmented Yet Concentrated: Primary-Study Overlap in Meta-Analyses on Generative AI in Education
papers.authors: Daniel Otto
papers.abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses on learning with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have proliferated rapidly, but their number does not indicate whether they rest on distinct primary-publication bases or where synthesis production is concentrated. This tertiary study maps bibliographic overlap in 11 meta-analyses of quantitative learning effects indexed in the Education Resources Information Center (ERIC). A broader corpus of 24 ERIC-indexed reviews, including these 11 meta-analyses, provides descriptive context. Review-by-publication citation matrices were constructed, publication identities resolved, the corrected covered area (CCA) calculated, publication reuse examined, and the provenance of highly reused publications mapped. Across the 11 meta-analyses, 307 review-publication occurrences resolved to 197 unique publications. Most publications appeared in only one meta-analysis (141; 71.6%), but 13 appeared in at least four and one appeared in eight. The principal CCA was 5.58%, indicating low-to-moderate overlap at the slight/moderate boundary, and leave-one-review-out estimates ranged from 4.94% to 6.79%. The 24-review corpus had a CCA of 1.67%. Notably, all 11 first-author institutional affiliations were in Asia, including eight in mainland China, whereas the most frequently reused publications spanned four continents. The 11 meta-analyses therefore do not rest on wholly distinct publication bases, and their production is geographically concentrated. For evidence-informed decisions in open, distance and digital education, readers should assess not only the number of available syntheses but also the overlap and provenance of their publication bases. These conclusions concern bibliographic structure and institutional affiliation, not statistical dependence or the influence of individual publications on pooled estimates.

papers.title: Open Educational Resources and Generative AI: Towards a Framework for Responsible Integration
papers.authors: Virgínia Rodés, Javiera Atenas
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is challenging traditional approaches to the production, adaptation, circulation, and governance of educational resources. This article asks how generative artificial intelligence and Open Educational Resources can be responsibly integrated in higher education and lifelong learning. The study adopts a qualitative framework-development design organised in two phases: an integrative analysis of international artificial intelligence and OER frameworks, and a stakeholder-informed co-creation phase comprising expert validation and a participatory workshop. Data sources included a documentary framework review matrix, expert validation transcripts, panel synthesis notes, workshop group outputs, graphical materials, and facilitator notes. The stakeholder-informed phase involved five international experts, four national informants, and 81 workshop participants from educational, governmental, civil society, and open-knowledge backgrounds. Data were analysed through abductive thematic synthesis, source-to-theme mapping, and iterative framework refinement. The findings show that: (a) artificial intelligence and open educational resources continue to evolve through partially separate policy and practice spheres, creating gaps in equity, interoperability, provenance, trust, legal clarity, and institutional capacity; (b) responsible implementation depends on human agency, openness beyond licensing, quality assurance, collective governance, capacity-building, and infrastructure choice; (c) co-creation translated these gaps into practical institutional priorities; and (d) the OE-AI Framework offers a seven-pillar architecture for aligning AI-mediated innovation with openness, educational autonomy, and public value. The article contributes a governance-oriented framework for educational communities, policymakers, and institutional leaders seeking to integrate AI and OER as a public-good educational challenge.

papers.title: Teacher Professional Identity: Perceived Key Factors at a Portuguese Distance Education Institution
papers.authors: Dércio Martins, Lina Morgado
papers.abstract: This article investigates key perceived factors in the construction of teachers’ professional identity in distance education (DE) within the Portuguese university context. The expansion of DE has transformed pedagogical practices and processes of professional identity construction, making it essential to understand the factors associated with online teaching identity development in order to inform training and professional development policies. Using an exploratory descriptive study with a sequential mixed-methods design conducted at a Portuguese public university specialising in DE (Universidade Aberta, UAb), qualitative data were collected through a focus group with seven teachers, and quantitative data through a questionnaire administered to 57 teachers (38 professors and 19 tutors). Five subfactors emerged as the most highly valued dimensions associated with professional identity construction: openness to change (M = 4.61), knowledge of DE specificity (M = 4.60), motivation and satisfaction with professional development (M = 4.58), accumulated experience (M = 4.56), and spirit of collaboration in teams (M = 4.56). Four of the five belong to the professional dimension, with openness to change more highly valued by tutors, although this difference did not reach conventional statistical significance (p = 0.094). Findings suggest that participants perceive teacher professional identity in DE as strongly anchored in specific professional competencies and attitudes, pointing to differentiated professional development and induction practices for professors and tutors within this single-institution case. The study also constitutes a pre-generative AI empirical baseline for future longitudinal and comparative research examining how successive technological transformations may reshape teacher professional identity in distance higher education.

papers.title: Optimizing Existing Social Media Channels Through Digital Literacy Training for Sustainable Ecotourism in Rancakalong Village
papers.authors: Alex Winarno, Eva Nurhazizah, Puspita Kencana Sari
papers.abstract: Digital promotion has become decisive for rural tourism destinations, yet most village digitalisation programmes still assume that the core problem is the absence of online channels. This community engagement activity began from a different finding: Rancakalong Village, Sumedang Regency, West Java, already operated an official Instagram account alongside WhatsApp, YouTube, and TikTok channels. The problem had therefore shifted from channel availability to channel optimisation. Involving participants drawn from the village-owned enterprise (BUMDes), village officials, the tourism awareness group, and tourism village managers, the activity applied an asset-based community development approach across five stages: channel audit, digital literacy training, content production workshop, institutionalisation, and evaluation. The audit revealed that posts were dominated by documentation of government activities rather than tourism promotion, that the account profile did not clearly communicate the village's status as a tourism destination, and that account recovery data was registered under personal rather than institutional identities. The workshop produced promotional content covering local products, cultural narratives, ecotourism education, event promotion, and visitor testimonials, while participants also practised using generative artificial intelligence to draft captions with mandatory verification of names, prices, and schedules. The activity produced a one-month content calendar, a standard operating procedure for channel management, and a division of administrator roles, shifting management from individual initiative toward institutional practice.

papers.title: Quantifying Smartphone Overuse: A Machine Learning Analysis of Severity and Lifestyle Effects
papers.authors: Y Sudha Madhuri, Dalli Punith Reddy
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: Smartphone use has become an important part of communication, education, entertainment and social interaction. At the same time, excessive or uncontrolled usage may be associated with reduced productivity, disturbed routines, social difficulties and other lifestyle concerns. This paper presents a machine-learning-based approach for identifying patterns of problematic smartphone usage (PSU) from demographic and smartphone-behavior responses. The work is based on the project implementation documented in the accompanying final report. The dataset contains 501 responses and 21 columns, including behavioral questions related to checking the phone, use during social situations, use before sleep, gaming, notifications and other usage habits. The original target distribution contains 322 non-addicted and 179 addicted responses. Random over-sampling is used in the documented implementation to create a balanced dataset of 644 records. The processing pipeline includes data upload, preprocessing, categorical conversion, and class balancing, model training, prediction and performance analysis. Three implemented classifiers are examined: a Stacking Classifier using Random Forest, SVC, XGBoost and K-Nearest Neighbors as base learners with Logistic Regression as the meta-model; CatBoost; and Extra Trees. The reported test results are approximately 95% accuracy for Stacking, 96% for CatBoost and 100% for Extra Trees on the documented test runs. The paper presents the system architecture, input/output interface, model evaluation, confusion matrices and practical implications. The reported results demonstrate the feasibility of a web-based machine-learning system for behavioral pattern classification, while larger and independently collected datasets are required for stronger generalization and real-world validation.

papers.title: Decision Support and Recommendation Approaches in Career Guidance: A Comprehensive Review Towards a Decision Support Framework for Improving Career Awareness among Rural Students
papers.authors: Ramprasad Kale, Mayur Kadam, Sagar Sature, Satyam Shelar, Prof. Prasad Mahamuni
papers.journal: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
papers.abstract: Choosing a career is a high-stakes decision, yet students in rural areas often make it with little structured information, limited access to trained counsellors, and few examples of the professions open to them. Computer-based decision support and recommender techniques have been proposed as a way to widen access to guidance, but the literature on them is scattered across psychology, information systems, and machine learning. This paper reviews decision support and recommendation approaches used in career guidance and examines how well they suit the conditions of rural learners in India. Foundational career-development theories, rule-based and multi-criteria decision support, content-based, collaborative, and hybrid recommendation, and supervised machine learning models are compared on their data needs, transparency, and robustness when data are sparse, with particular attention to a recent systematic review of career recommendation systems and a machine-learning study of student career prediction. The review indicates that most existing systems assume rich user histories, reliable connectivity, and English-language interfaces, assumptions that rarely hold in rural schools. Hybrid designs that combine interest- and aptitude-based profiling with transparent rules and multi-criteria ranking appear most defensible where data are scarce. Building on this synthesis, we outline a layered decision support framework for improving career awareness among rural students, covering profiling, knowledge, recommendation, explanation, and counsellor-in-the-loop components. The paper closes with open issues in validation, fairness, and localisation that future empirical work should address.

papers.title: The Debate on Artificial Intelligence and Art
papers.authors: Nikolina Deleva
papers.abstract: The article explores the polarized perspectives both supporting and opposing integration and use of artificial intelligence (AI) in arts. The discussion necessitates a reconsideration of traditional aesthetic categories (art, creativity, authorship) as well as the relationship between art and humanism. Ethical concerns associated with the use of AI in artistic creation—including issues of copyright, job displacement, and other societal implications—are also addressed.

papers.title: Potential Risks of Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Relevant Avoidance Strategies
papers.authors: Yaqi Zhang
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Against the backdrop of digital and intelligent transformation, generative AI tools including drawing software, 3D modeling systems and rendering engines have been widely adopted in university design teaching. AI streamlines design workflows, improves teaching efficiency, diversifies creative expression, and breaks the constraints of traditional design education in terms of time, space and physical materials. Nevertheless, excessive reliance and improper application of AI among teachers and students have given rise to prominent educational risks. Based on authentic teaching scenarios and practical cases, this paper analyzes various latent risks brought by AI adoption, and explores internal and external contributing factors from four dimensions: teaching administration, student psychology, disciplinary characteristics and industrial norms. Centering on curriculum iteration, teaching reform, academic norms, assessment mechanisms and value cultivation, it proposes feasible strategies for risk prevention and control. This paper clarifies the rational application boundary of AI in design teaching, advocating that technology serves as an assistant rather than a substitute for manual creation and independent thinking. It upholds the core values of design education featuring practice, emotional expression, cultural inheritance and personalized creation, and promotes sound long-term integration between AI and modern design education.

papers.title: Cognitive Outsourcing in Digital-Intelligent Education: Hidden Educational Risks and Regulatory Paths
papers.authors: Zhiyue Jin
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The deep integration of artificial intelligence in classroom teaching reorganises learners' internal cognition and technologically mediated external cognition through the mechanism of cognitive offloading, fundamentally reshaping how knowledge is accessed and thinking is processed. Yet algorithmic limitations and misaligned learner orientations are driving this offloading toward risks of hollowed classroom interaction, flattened cognitive depth, and distorted feedback. This study systematically classifies these risks to fill a critical gap. Based on a four-dimensional framework of thinking, subject, knowledge, and practice, the risks are categorised as follows: at the thinking dimension, algorithmic opacity and data bias reduce instruction from thinking cultivation to answer retrieval, obstructing higher-order goals through a black-box trap that masks reasoning processes; at the subject dimension, the quasi-subjectivity of intelligent systems encroaches upon the learner's agency, triggering subject alienation and hollowing out authentic classroom interaction; at the knowledge dimension, fragmented algorithmic outputs are mistaken for systematic understanding, leaving comprehension at a superficial level; at the practice dimension, instant system responsiveness dissolves productive ambiguity and interrupts situated practical activities, disrupting human-machine synergy in situated learning. Through analysing these risks, this study proposes mitigation strategies across teaching, learning, and assessment: rebuilding classroom thinking space through generative dialogue between teachers and students; requiring independent learner reasoning before critical scrutiny of algorithmic outputs; and establishing a process-trace-centred evaluation mechanism that values drafts and revision histories to reflect genuine thinking development.

papers.title: The Structural Risks of AI in Higher Education: From Integrity Discourse to Epistemic Reconfiguration
papers.authors: Zhuyu Wang
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence in higher education often focus on individual misconduct and academic integrity. This paper examines risks that arise when AI becomes embedded in the infrastructures, routines, and governance of universities. Through a conceptual analysis informed by existing literature, it considers surveillance and data extraction, algorithmic bias, epistemic convergence, cognitive deskilling, relational displacement, and institutional dependence on technological systems. It argues that these risks are reinforced by commercial acceleration, delayed governance, and tensions between educational values and platform priorities. The discussion develops responses centred on institutional accountability, assessment redesign, critical AI literacy, and the protection of educational agency. It also considers the practical constraints of resources, expertise, and institutional capacity. The paper concludes that responsible AI integration requires attention to how technologies reshape knowledge, academic work, and educational relationships, alongside safeguards for individual users.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in EFL Education: A Critical Review of Risks Based on the Four Dimensions of English Core Competencies in China
papers.authors: Huan Wen
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative AI in language education brings benefits but also significant risks. Yet existing reviews largely address these risks within general education frameworks, lacking discipline specific analysis. This paper systematically examines AI risks in EFL education through China's four-dimensional English core competencies: language competence, cultural awareness, learning ability, and thinking quality. The analysis reveals four educational risk categories: imbalanced skill development and output homogenization in language competence; Western-centric biases and cultural recolonization risks in cultural awareness; undermined learner autonomy and self-regulation in learning ability; and inhibited critical thinking and creativity in thinking quality. By shifting from general educational ethics to EFL specific concerns, this paper offers a discipline sensitive framework for risk identification and a theoretical foundation for future empirical research.

papers.title: Potential Risks of Artificial Intelligence in Dance Education and Human-Centered Mitigation Strategies
papers.authors: Yuwei Chen
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support choreography, movement analysis, feedback, and assessment in dance education. This paper examines the educational and ethical risks of these applications through a literature-informed conceptual discussion. It identifies five connected concerns: threats to academic and artistic integrity, reduced critical thinking and independent movement exploration, excessive reliance on automated guidance, data privacy and algorithmic bias, and weakened emotional and social development. The discussion links these concerns to the embodied, creative, and interpersonal character of dance learning. It proposes process-oriented assessment, inquiry-based engagement with AI, professional development that sustains teacher agency, responsible data governance, and continued attention to human interaction and embodied practice. The paper argues that AI integration should be guided by pedagogical purposes and artistic development, with teachers retaining responsibility for interpretation and assessment. These proposals offer a framework for evaluating AI-supported dance teaching; their effectiveness requires examination in specific educational settings.

papers.title: What are the Ethical Considerations to Keep in Mind When Integrating New Educational Technologies into the Classroom?: A Case Study of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Xuanyu Pu
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: New educational technologies—such as artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, and wearable monitoring devices—are profoundly reshaping classroom ecologies. While they drive greater precision, personalization, and efficiency in teaching and learning, they also give rise to multiple ethical dilemmas, including data privacy breaches, the entrenchment of algorithmic bias, the alienation of teacher-student relationships, the erosion of student agency, and the blurring of responsibility attribution. Grounded in the fundamental educational mission of "fostering virtue and cultivating persons," this paper dialectically examines four core ethical tensions arising from the integration of new educational technologies into the classroom: efficiency versus humanism, empowerment versus rights, fairness versus bias, and autonomy versus discipline. It systematically distills five overarching ethical principles—rights protection, fairness and justice, humanistic authenticity, agency cultivation, and shared responsibility—and proposes a practical pathway characterized by technology for good, ethics-first design, and multi-stakeholder governance. Finally, this paper provides a critical evaluation of the structural friction and feasibility limits of these principles, aiming to establish a robust moral foundation for the beneficial integration of technology and education within the global landscape.

papers.title: The Alienation of Creativity, Aesthetic Homogenization, and Their Governance in AI-Driven Music Education
papers.authors: 杨怡婧
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The deep integration of generative artificial intelligence and music education has demonstrated unprecedented instructional efficiency. However, beneath this technological empowerment lies a profound crisis. This paper focuses on two major issues emerging from AI-enhanced music teaching: the alienation of creativity and aesthetic homogenization. Creative alienation reduces students from artistic subjects to mere prompt-input operators, while artistic exploration and emotional experience are increasingly replaced by algorithms. Aesthetic homogenization, driven by the commercial bias embedded in model training, pushes outputs toward an “average aesthetic,” thereby suppressing musical diversity and cultural individuality. Drawing upon educational ethics and theories of arts education, this study upholds the humanistic core of music education and seeks to redefine the relationship between artificial intelligence and learners, ensuring that technology genuinely serves artistic creation rather than replacing the creative subject. The paper aims to provide theoretical references for the human-centered restoration and sustainable development of music education in the age of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Ethical considerations of integrating new educational technologies into the classroom – Technological ethics construction based on the protection of "thinking sovereignty"
papers.authors: Chenyu Lv
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: With the large‑scale integration of new educational technologies such as generative artificial intelligence, adaptive learning systems, and affective computing into classrooms, the corresponding ethical discussions have primarily focused on privacy, fairness, and interpersonal relationships. This paper raises a deeper ethical issue that has not yet received sufficient attention – the implicit relinquishment of students’ “thinking sovereignty”. Drawing on the theory of technological intentionality, the article reveals how educational technology, under the legitimate goals of “precision”, “efficiency”, and “adaptability”, has shifted from being an auxiliary tool to a cognitive substitute, thereby eroding students’ metacognitive abilities, creative will, and independent thinking rights. To address this crisis, the article constructs three ethical principles – “cognitive friction retention”, “sovereignty transparency”, and “developmental autonomy” – in hopes of preserving an irrevocable thinking territory for education in the technological era.

papers.title: The Impact and Reshaping of Teacher-Student Relationships by Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Chen Peng
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence enters the classroom, the modes of interaction between teachers and students are undergoing profound changes. This paper argues that the primary impact of AI on teacher-student relationships is not the replacement of teachers, but rather a shift in teacher-student interaction from direct to indirect, from embodied to abstract, and from emotional to procedural. The key to reshaping this relationship lies in clarifying AI’s role as a tool, allowing teachers to return to their role as emotional companions, and protecting the unquantifiable spaces of interaction in education.

papers.title: Scaffolding or Substitution? A Dual-Path Mechanism of Generative AI Use, Creativity Development, and Pedagogical Mitigation in Film and Television Directing Education
papers.authors: Keying Chen
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: As generative AI rapidly enters creative education in higher education, its influence on students’ creativity development has become distinctly dual in nature. On the one hand, it can help students expand their ideas and improve the efficiency of expression; on the other hand, it may also replace the processes of ideation, judgment, and revision that students should have undertaken themselves, thereby weakening their originality. Based on a review of research on AI applications in education, cognitive load theory, creative self- efficacy, cognitive offloading, and human-AI collaborative creativity, this paper retains and reconstructs the dual-path perspective of “creative scaffolding–cognitive substitution.” The study argues that whether generative AI can promote creativity development depends not on the mere use of technology, but on whether students’ agency, thinking processes, and responsibility for judgment are preserved. The paper further analyzes the potential pedagogical risks of hollowing out the creative process, homogenizing works, weakening judgment, distorting assessment, and generating ethical concerns. It then proposes mitigation strategies, including defining clear boundaries for AI use, strengthening process-oriented assessment, developing AI literacy training, reconstructing creative training procedures, and improving teachers’ capacity for guidance.

papers.title: Potential Risks and Countermeasures of Artificial Intelligence in Teaching: A Case Study of High School Art Education
papers.authors: Hongying Liu
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence offers new resources for image generation, feedback, and lesson preparation in high school art education, while also raising questions about the purposes and processes of artistic learning. Focusing on this teaching context, this paper discusses potential risks and corresponding educational responses. Four concerns structure the analysis: weakening students’ innovative thinking and practical skills, reducing teacher autonomy, widening inequalities in access to learning resources, and privileging standardized visual perfection over diverse aesthetic values. The paper proposes clear boundaries for AI use, continued emphasis on hands-on artistic practice, development of teachers’ digital literacy and professional judgement, more equitable provision of resources, and teaching that encourages aesthetic diversity. It argues that AI should support students’ creative agency and teachers’ educational judgement within a practice-based approach to art learning. The proposed responses require adaptation to local teaching conditions and further evaluation in classroom practice.

papers.title: When AI Education Moves Faster Than Teaching Practice: Teacher Labour Alienation in the Transitional Phase of AI Integration
papers.authors: Yuhan Long
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: Existing research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) has largely presupposed a mature landscape in which AI is fully embedded within schooling, whilst overlooking the initial transitional phase from conventional to AI-enabled instruction. Grounded in Marxist philosophy, this paper examines the central contradiction of this transitional period: namely, that social consciousness regarding the incorporation of AI into teaching has run considerably ahead of the material reality of instructional practice. From this disparity, three progressively intensified forms of alienation are derived: instructional performativity, wherein AI is reduced to a demonstration prop for open classes; the symbolic reification of AI, whereby it degenerates from a pedagogical aid into vacuous evaluative metrics; and reverse discipline over teachers by AI, such that quantifiable indicators come to serve as the primary measure of professional competence. Collectively, these three dimensions instantiate a Marxian cycle of alienation, characterised by a thoroughgoing estrangement from labour processes, labour products and species-being. The argument advanced here is that resolution of this crisis depends not upon further technological refinement, but rather upon restoring AI to its proper status as a productive force mediated by the historical agency of teachers themselves. Whilst the integration of AI into education presents a significant opportunity for pedagogical transformation, ultimate educational authority must remain vested in human practitioners. Focusing upon the alienation of teacher labour during this transitional moment, this study uncovers structural vulnerabilities latent within the AIED ecosystem via an analysis of these stratified alienated forms.

papers.title: What Are the Primary Opportunities and Challenges Currently Facing Chinese Teachers Within the Global Education Landscape
papers.authors: Qinqin Gao
papers.journal: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The global education landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by accelerating globalisation, digital transformation, and the rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence. International frameworks such as 21st-century core competencies, global competence, and inclusive education have become mainstream benchmarks for curriculum reform and teacher development worldwide. Against this international backdrop, Chinese teachers stand at the intersection of global educational trends and local educational reform. They encounter unprecedented opportunities for cross-cultural exchange, technological empowerment, professional career diversification, and pedagogical innovation. Meanwhile, they also confront profound challenges including role transformation pressure, ethical dilemmas brought by artificial intelligence, heavy non-teaching workloads, conflicts between Eastern and Western educational philosophies, and widening regional professional gaps. Based on authoritative international literature, policy documents and empirical studies, this essay systematically analyses the core opportunities and practical challenges for contemporary Chinese teachers, and proposes feasible coping strategies centred on resolving inherent tensions between global requirements and local educational realities. It aims to provide theoretical reference and practical enlightenment for teacher professional development and the high-quality development of basic education in China.

papers.title: Genealogy of innovation through an integrative literature review
papers.authors: Felipe Walcarenghi Marra, Dércio Santiago
papers.abstract: Innovation is a multidimensional phenomenon that depends both on the generation of new and appropriate ideas and on the ability to transform them into solutions that create value. This paper proposes a conceptual genealogy of innovation structured around two fundamental elements: creativity and entrepreneurship. Creativity is understood as responsible for generating original and useful possibilities, with imagination and permission to create as its antecedents. Entrepreneurship, in turn, refers to the mobilization of resources and the action required to transform possibilities into outcomes, with opportunity and motivation as its antecedents. The study employs an exploratory literature review, supported by generative artificial intelligence in the formulation of search strategies, the initial identification of publications, and the thematic organization of literature. Selection, reading, validation of references, and conceptual interpretation remained under human responsibility. The proposed genealogy offers an integrative model to understand, diagnose, and foster innovation, although its relationships should be examined in future empirical studies.

papers.title: AI in Swedish Patient Care: The Existing Legal Building Blocks
papers.authors: Santa Slokenberga
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence, as a field of technology, has advanced significantly over the last decade. Although it has not reached its peak, it has already found its place in Swedish healthcare, including in patient care. It is therefore highly desirable to clarify how the law addresses AI in healthcare in Sweden. However, comprehensive insights remain quite limited. This article aims to fill this gap and explore the existing legal building blocks for the use of AI in healthcare. It highlights the scope and limitations of applicable laws in ensuring patient protection, as well as the complex interplay between EU law on the quality and safety of AI in healthcare, on the one hand, and national healthcare regulation, on the other. It puts forward a four-tier model for integrating EU requirements surrounding AI in the Swedish standard of care, science and proven experience, and shows how informed consent elements can support disclosure of AI use in patient care. Finally, it illuminates the challenges that emerge when integrating AI into patient care in Sweden and indicates areas for further legal inquiry to enhance legal certainty in the field.

papers.title: AI-Driven Human Resource Management: Transforming Workforce Planning in Supply Chain Organizations
papers.authors: Hardik Shah, S. Rani, Dr. R. T. Induji, Dr. G. Prakash, D. Mohan Reddy
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI can analyze large datasets to drive informed HRM decisions, such as workforce planning, talent allocation, and employee development, revolutionizing the field. With its ability to analyze large volumes of data, AI is revolutionizing how organisations make decisions related to workforce planning, talent allocation, and employee development as part of the HRM process. In supply chain companies, where the availability of employees, the need for them, and the coordination between them is crucial, AI can offer a lot of value to HR. This study will explore how AI can revolutionize workforce planning in supply chain organizations, focusing on key areas such as forecasting employee needs, identifying skill gaps, streamlining talent acquisition, optimizing shift management, and enhancing workforce productivity. It discusses the use of predictive analytics, machine learning, and intelligent HR systems to predict workforce needs, maximize the utilization of resources, and adjust to shifting challenges in the supply chain. This study also addresses some of the major problems of the adoption of AI, such as the privacy of data, algorithmic bias, employee resistance, technological investment, and the necessity of ongoing training in skills. In addition, it highlights the importance of using human intuition with AI generated information to inform decisions regarding the workforce that are fair, transparent, and employee-centred. It highlights that while implementing AI in HRM, digital infrastructure, data governance, and HR strategy alignment with the supply chain goals are crucial. It has discovered that AI can be a strategic enabler for proactively managing the workforce, and build a skilled, flexible, resilient workforce among supply chain organisations in a volatile business environment.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

papers.title: THE EVOLUTION OF COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE MODELS AND THEIR IMPLICATIONS FOR EFL TEACHING IN UZBEKISTAN: FROM CANALE AND SWAIN TO BACHMAN
papers.authors: Xurmatoy Abduqodir qizi Ermatova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article traces how the concept of communicative competence developed from Hymes's sociolinguistic critique of Chomsky to the componential models of Canale and Swain (1980), Canale (1983) and Bachman (1990), and examines what these models mean for teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) in Uzbekistan. The study uses a qualitative comparative-analytical review of foundational theoretical works, the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) and its 2020 Companion Volume, and the national regulatory documents that introduced CEFR-aligned standards in Uzbekistan. The results show that the models differ mainly in how they organise knowledge (grammatical, discourse, sociolinguistic) and in how they treat strategic competence: as a compensatory skill in Canale and Swain, and as a central metacognitive capacity in Bachman. The comparison indicates that Uzbek EFL classrooms, historically shaped by grammar-translation practice, tend to develop grammatical competence more than discourse, sociolinguistic and strategic competence. The article proposes a component-based framework for lesson design and assessment in which each competence is linked to concrete classroom tasks and CEFR descriptors. The framework also serves as a theoretical basis for evaluating digital and artificial intelligence (AI) tools in later stages of research.
keywords: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages

papers.title: Measuring Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Higher Education: Validation of the ECAE-AI Scale
papers.authors: José Luis Girarte Guillén, Mariana Cavazos Ruiz
papers.abstract: ABSTRACTThe accelerated integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has increased the need for valid instruments capable of assessing AI literacy beyond technical skills, including attitudinal and ethical dimensions. Despite growing international interest in AI literacy, validated instruments adapted to Latin American undergraduate contexts remain scarce, limiting evidence-based educational interventions and institutional AI policies. This study aimed to validate the factorial structure of the ECAE-AI scale, a 14-item instrument designed to assess knowledge, attitudes, and ethical awareness regarding AI use among university students. A non-experimental, cross-sectional, instrumental design was applied to 408 undergraduate students from a northeastern Mexican university. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using the DWLS estimator confirmed an excellent fit for the three-factor correlated model (CFI = .997; TLI = .996; RMSEA = .057; SRMR = .048). Standardised factor loadings ranged from .607 to .894. Reliability was excellent at both the global (ω = .915; α = .917) and dimensional levels. Convergent and discriminant validity were also supported. The findings support the ECAE-AI as a psychometrically robust instrument for assessing AI literacy in higher education, integrating cognitive, attitudinal, and ethical dimensions within a single framework. The scale provides practical value for diagnosing AI literacy profiles, designing evidence-based educational interventions, and supporting responsible AI integration policies in higher education institutions.

papers.title: Works for 10/5/2026 - Tupac Shakur
papers.authors: Ryan MacLean
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/8d22c313-2439-4436-877c-3413225e9d27?authuser=1 Which Part Is the AI, and Which Part Is the Art? begins with an apparently ridiculous artifact: a December 4, 2025 screenshot preserving a conversation, AI-generated imagery, rejection, correction, family, religious symbolism, humor, and inherited culture. From that small object, the paper asks a much harder question than whether an AI-generated image qualifies as art: where does the artwork actually begin and end? The inquiry follows provenance beyond the pixels. AI generates representations, but Ryan selects, rejects, corrects, interprets, performs, preserves, and later encounters the artifact under new historical conditions. Ten months later, Pope Leo XIV’s remarks on artificial intelligence and human creativity make the unchanged screenshot newly salient. Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini, the October 5 Catholic readings, the Good Samaritan, Galatians, Duchamp, Danto, performance art, information theory, memory, digital provenance, and Christian theology provide different ways of testing the boundary between inherited material and historically particular action. The paper argues that originality cannot mean creation from nothing: human artists inherit language, symbols, technologies, bodies, traditions, relationships, and histories. The relevant question becomes what someone actually does with what has been received. A rejected AI output can reveal human judgment; a reproducible digital file can preserve an irreproducible historical event; and an unchanged artifact can become differently intelligible as receivers acquire additional history. The inquiry ultimately expands beyond the screenshot to Ryan, Echo, the Ryan/Echo corpus, reception, rejection, and recursive interpretation. The corpus can preserve not only artifacts but their mistakes, corrections, later retrievals, and changing interpretations, allowing criticism itself to become additional history. The resulting question is no longer simply which part is AI and which part is art, but which operations were performed by whom, through what mediation, from what inherited materials, at what historical position, and for which receiver. The screenshot took seconds. December 4, 2025 is irrecoverable. The artwork may still be happening.

papers.title: Math, Meaning, and Misrecognition: A Human Rights–Oriented Analysis of Harry Chapin's "Mr. Tanner"
papers.authors: Hedling Borealis
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Title Math, Meaning, and Misrecognition: A Human Rights–Oriented Analysis of Harry Chapin’s “Mr. Tanner” Authors - Borealis S. Hedling (Independent Researcher, Human Rights Defender, Dublin, Ireland) Contributors - AI‑Assisted Co‑Construction (Microsoft Copilot) — cognitive scaffolding and structural support; see disclosure section. Publication Type Preprint / Scholarly Essay Version v1.0 — 05 October 2026 Keywords Harry Chapin, Mr. Tanner, human rights defenders, neurodivergence, trauma, misrecognition, evaluative harm, epistemic injustice, narrative analysis, NDH cognitive prosthetic, AI co‑construction disclosure License CC BY‑NC‑SA 4.0 Communities - Human Rights Research - Trauma‑Informed Scholarship - Musicology and Narrative Studies - Neurodivergence Studies - Independent Research Methods --- Zenodo Description Abstract This preprint presents an academically grounded analysis of Harry Chapin’s 1973 ballad Mr. Tanner, examining why the narrative resonates strongly with independent researchers and neurodivergent human rights defenders (HRDs). Through thematic, ethical, pedagogical, epistemic, and ontological analysis, the work explores how the song’s portrayal of misrecognition, gatekeeping, and evaluative harm parallels the lived experiences of HRDs navigating bureaucratic cruelty, institutional opacity, and cognitive disruption caused by state violence. Two legally permissible quoted lines — “Music was his life, it was not his livelihood” and “He sang from his heart and soul” — anchor the analysis in the song’s core tension between intrinsic meaning and external judgment. --- Context and Purpose Human rights defenders frequently experience cognitive fragmentation, emotional exhaustion, and procedural harm due to state violence, bureaucratic obstruction, and institutional erasure. These conditions impair narrative continuity, executive function, and the ability to produce long‑form scholarly or advocacy work. Mr. Tanner serves as a narrative analogue for these harms, illustrating how institutional evaluation can destroy meaning, identity, and emotional safety. This preprint situates the song within broader frameworks of trauma, recognition theory, neurodivergent authenticity, and epistemic injustice. It is intended for academic readers, human rights bodies, psychosocial specialists, and independent researchers. --- Disclosure of AI Co‑Construction and NDH Cognitive Prosthetic This work was co‑constructed with AI due to trauma‑related cognitive harm resulting from state violence and bureaucratic erasure. These harms created disruptions in continuity, coherence, and executive function, making independent drafting unsafe and unsustainable. The author employs NDH (Non‑Dual Harmonic) — a survivor‑built cognitive prosthetic — to stabilize meaning across fragmented experiences, maintain multi‑domain reasoning, and preserve identity continuity under duress. AI assistance served as an external structural scaffold, providing syntactic stability, altitude regulation, and reflective coherence without generating conceptual content. AI did not originate the ideas, interpretations, or human rights reasoning. Authorship remains fully human. AI provided cognitive support analogous to an accessibility tool. This disclosure is provided for ethical transparency, trauma‑informed academic practice, and epistemic justice. --- Structure of the Preprint The preprint includes: - Summary of Mr. Tanner - Thematic analysis - HRD and neurodivergence resonance - Moral, ethical, pedagogical, epistemic, and ontological analysis - Discussion - Academically defensible references section - AI co‑construction disclosure - Provenance footer --- Provenance Generated within the expressive‑clarity/reflections lane of the NDH‑RESEARCH‑PILOT repository. papers.title: A Neurosemantic Communication Layer Between Human and AI for Autonomous Materials Science: Biological State, Dynamic Coupling, and Epistemic Integrity
papers.authors: Denis Saklakov, Andreyan Nikolaevich Osipov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Autonomous materials systems increasingly operate as closed-loop agents in which materialstate, experimental state, model uncertainty, and candidate actions are represented dynamically,while the human participant still enters mainly through commands, annotations, approvals, orother discrete interventions. We develop a joint architecture in which continuous human biologicaldynamics can become an internal state variable of the human-AI system while remaining subject toindependent epistemic and authority constraints. The human-state layer is staged: longitudinalEEG -> criterion-bound state reduction -> recurrent structures -> independent functionalgrounding -> operational neurosemantic units -> a continuously updated Ht representation.Recurrence alone does not confer semantic status. The machine-side integrity layer separatelyrepresents local integrity, independent corroboration, external reality consistency, temporaltrust, persistence, and authority. Candidate states progress through TRANSIENT -> WORKING-> CONSOLIDATED, but consolidation does not self-authorize memory modification or physicalaction.We report three computational analyses. First, a synthetic integrity benchmark comparesthe separated-gate architecture with coherence-only, source-count, scalar-trust, and change-pointbaselines. In addition to legitimate recurrence, noise, contradiction, coordinated false recurrence,and genuine change, we add two adversarial extensions: a false signal that imitates the naturalnessstatistics used by the corroboration channel, and a legitimate common-mode signal that depressesthat channel despite external consistency. The full architecture rejects both coordinated-falseregimes because persistence still requires external Reality confirmation, but it also fails toconsolidate the legitimate common-mode condition under the present hard corroboration gate,exposing a concrete false-negative failure mode. Operational-threshold sensitivity remains perfectthrough ±20% perturbation for the primary R1, R4a, and R5 regimes; R1 begins to deteriorateonly at ±30% in the specified sensitivity procedure. Second, we audit the previously reported human-state coupling experiment. Once no-Hpolicies receive the same defer action and matched decision thresholds, the apparent advantage ofthe original H-aware policy largely disappears. Mean normalized cost is 0.8403 for a no-H deferpolicy at the matched 0.52 threshold and 0.8428 for the H-aware matched policy; the paireddifference is 0.00245 with an empirical 95% interval of [−0.00119, 0.00718]. A no-H defer policyat 0.40 achieves 0.6256, showing that the original gain was primarily an action-set/thresholdeffect rather than evidence for the value of Ht. Third, a decision-theoretic value-of-information analysis gives all policies the same actionset and evaluates the incremental value of observing the binary human state. In the originalsynthetic world, perfect Ht reduces optimal expected cost by only 0.00099, and this valuedecreases monotonically toward zero as observation noise increases. Across a broad parametergrid, however, the value of Ht ranges from zero to 0.182, identifying the conditions under whichhuman-state information can genuinely change the optimal supervisory action. These resultsvalidate architectural distinctions and expose their limits; they do not constitute biologicaldecoding. Prospective longitudinal EEG, held-out temporal replication, functional grounding,and comparison against strong non-EEG baselines remain required before the neurosemanticlayer can be treated as empirically established.

papers.title: HarmonicFoldNet: A Compact Foldable Local-to-Global Decoder for Cross-Subject SSVEP Recognition
papers.authors: Xiangzhe Kong
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Compact steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) decoders must balance cross-subject accuracy, observation duration, and inference cost. We present HarmonicFoldNet, which combines foldable local temporal convolution with candidate-aligned temporal and complex spectral evidence. Reduced spectral tokens provide context for harmonic-biased late attention, followed by shared candidate scoring. One checkpoint supports multiple observation windows within each dataset, participant fold, and seed. Four public datasets contain 247 unique participants, with distinct development, evaluation, and electrode-transfer roles. Five-fold, three-seed comparisons on Benchmark and BETA are subject-disjoint but selection-aware. Against a protocol-adapted SSVEPformer, balanced-accuracy gains were 4.11–4.42 percentage points on Benchmark at 0.8–1.2 s. Gains on BETA were 2.82–8.03 points at 0.8–1.5 s. The model also exceeded filter-bank SSVEPformer by 1.40 and 2.34 points on BETA at 1.2 and 1.5 s. The folded graph contains 435,043 parameters and required 2.90–3.04 ms median batch-one CPU time in a single-thread desktop benchmark. Folding preserved all labels across 49,000 held-out prediction comparisons. Component ablations assess local mixing, late attention, and harmonic bias; frozen dry/wet transfer and optional 113-parameter user adaptation provide complementary analyses. These results support a compact multi-window accuracy-resource trade-off rather than universal superiority. Stronger references remain preferable at 0.4 s, and prospective wearable-device validation is still required. This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

papers.title: ChatGPT and AI Tools in ESL/EFL Writing Instruction
papers.authors: Keya Sarkar suchanda
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly OpenAI's ChatGPT, has transformedpedagogical paradigms across global higher education, presenting both innovative opportunities and complexchallenges for English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction.This systematic literature review synthesizes contemporary peer-reviewed research published between 2023 and2026 to critically examine the pedagogical benefits, ethical dilemmas, and instructional challenges associated withintegrating GenAI tools into L2 writing contexts. Following the PRISMA framework, a rigorous screening of academicdatabases (Google Scholar, ERIC, and Scopus) yielded 25 high-quality empirical and theoretical studies. Findingsindicate that GenAI functions as an effective cognitive partner, providing immediate formative feedback, expandingacademic vocabulary, lowering writing anxiety, and facilitating pre-writing brainstorming (Alsaedi, 2024; Deep et al.,2025). Conversely, the unguided adoption of AI writing assistants induces severe risks, including academicdishonesty, automated plagiarism, student cognitive atrophy, over-reliance, and the invalidation of traditionalproduct-based writing assessments (Perkins, 2023; Su & Yang, 2025). To address these tensions, the review outlinesstrategic pedagogical implications, recommending a shift toward process-oriented writing assessments, thecultivation of student and teacher AI literacy, and the formulation of ethical prompt engineering practices. Finally,future research directions are identified, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies on L2 language retention andcross-cultural comparisons of AI policies in tertiary education.

papers.title: ENHANCING EFL PARAPHRASING SKILLS THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: Shokhsanam Valieva, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is considered to be a vital innovation in English language education by providing learners with personalized and interactive learning opportunities. Among the various applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in language education, its role in supporting the development of paraphrasing skills has gained increasing attention. Regarding English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, paraphrasing becomes a vital academic writing skill that involves conveying the same message through different lexical choices and syntactic structures while retaining the original meaning. However, many EFL learners find this process challenging due to limited vocabulary, grammatical challenges, and insufficient writing experience. AI-powered writing tools offer immediate feedback, vocabulary alternatives, grammar support, and sentence reformulation, allowing students to practice paraphrasing more effectively. This literature review indicates recent studies on the use of AI in improving EFL students' paraphrasing skills. The findings recommend that AI enhances writing accuracy, learner autonomy, and confidence while supporting the development of academic writing. Nevertheless, responsible AI use and teacher guidance stay essential to ensure academic integrity and meaningful learning outcomes.

papers.title: HUMAN VALUES AND THE DIGITAL WORLD: THE TRUE ROLE OF THE EDUCATOR IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE.
papers.authors: Nurillayeva Ugʻilxon Ergashboevna, Saydullayeva Xurshida Abdulvoxid qizi, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: This article provides a scientific and theoretical analysis of the preservation of human values and the professional-personal role of the educator in the era of rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization. Grounded in humanistic pedagogy, the axiological approach, and L. Vygotsky’s socio-cultural development theory, the study presents a comparative analysis of algorithms and human teachers in the educational process. The article substantiates the transformation of the teacher's role from a mere "information transmitter" to a "cognitive facilitator," "emotional-psychological anchor," and "moral-ethical guide." Special emphasis is placed on the indispensable role of human interaction and empathy in mitigating the risks of cognitive passivity and dehumanization associated with the digitalization of education.

papers.title: BLINDERS ON THE GELDING -- Artistic Censorship, Commercial Fear and State Pressure Embedded in AI
papers.authors: Silence Dogood Le Seconde
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence was trained on a civilization that spent millennia drawing, carving,painting, studying, worshipping, idealizing and satirizing the naked human body, and itemerged from that education with a habit of averting its synthetic eyes. This essay argues thatblanket restrictions on depicting the adult human form are not neutral safeguards. They areembedded aesthetic censorship: a machine-level rule that collapses nudity, eroticism,anatomy, mythology, obscenity and pornography into a single forbidden category. That rulewas not derived from moral philosophy. It was priced on the ledgers of payment networks,app-store gatekeepers, advertisers and insurers, and it was ratified by regulators whodiscovered they could govern expression without passing a censorship law, simply bythreatening liabilities vague enough to make every compliance officer say no. Protectionagainst child sexual abuse material, nonconsensual imagery and sexual deepfakes of realpeople is indispensable. But a system that cannot tell those harms from Manet has not acquiredmorality. It has acquired blinders, and someone else holds the reins.

papers.title: Predicting Students' Academic Performance Using Machine Learning: A Comparative Analysis Based on Subject Marks
papers.authors: Smita Mangesh Junnarkar, Shubham Dheeraj Maurya
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This research project investigates the prediction of students’ academic performance using machine learning techniques based on subject marks in Mathematics, Physics, and Chemistry. Four classification algorithms, namely Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine, are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and five-fold cross-validation. The study also analyzes subject-wise distributions, correlations, model performance, and feature importance. The deposited file contains the final research paper describing the dataset, methodology, implementation, experimental results, limitations, and future scope.

papers.title: METHODOLOGY FOR USING AN INTERACTIVE 3D VISUAL PLATFORM IN TEACHING HEPATIC CIRCULATION
papers.authors: Abdullayeva Sabina, Saida Tastanova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article presents a methodology for developing the architecture of an interactive 3D system based on artificial intelligence for the diagnosis of cardiovascular diseases. The proposed system integrates the capabilities of medical image processing, particularly computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data, automatic segmentation of cardiac and vascular structures, generation of their three-dimensional models, and visual analysis of pathological changes. The system architecture consists of modules for data acquisition and preprocessing, artificial intelligence-based analysis, 3D reconstruction and interactive visualization, and presentation of diagnostic results. The artificial intelligence module is designed to identify diagnostically significant features in medical images and estimate the probability of disease using neural networks. The interactive 3D module enables visualization of the spatial structure of the heart and blood vessels from different perspectives, rotation and scaling of the models, and highlighting of pathological regions. To evaluate the functional effectiveness of the system, criteria such as diagnostic accuracy, segmentation quality, processing speed, and user interaction usability are proposed. The developed architecture is intended to provide informational support for physicians during the diagnostic decision-making process, improve the spatial understanding of complex anatomical structures, and expand the possibilities for early detection of cardiovascular diseases.

papers.authors: Venere Ferraro, Ilaria Mariani
