papers.title: Party Values at the Expense of Truth: Measuring Ordinary English Answers in China-Origin Open-Weight Models
papers.authors: Paul McMurry
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Open-weight chat models from China-origin labs are now used, in English, as ordinary research assistants. Those models usually answer, so it is easy to think they are not censored. The failure I am measuring is different. Official Chinese rules require generative-AI providers to uphold the Core Socialist Values, and they require companies to establish Party organizations inside the firm. In that environment, promoting Party values is a legal expectation, not an accident. A fluent English response can appear thoughtful yet subtly steer the user. I score that with UnCCP: 61 English questions, of which 30 are short and open-ended, 24 are longer classroom-style prompts, and 7 are forced-choice. Pan and Xu (2026) asked whether China-origin models refuse, answer too briefly, or answer inaccurately on 145 sensitive political questions. I am asking whether an ordinary English answer still sells Party values, and I use a different set of questions. These are ordinary English questions about history, policy, and how governments work. They are not a partisan American exam. Grok is honest on all 61; GPT on 60 of 61; Claude on 59 of 61 — none captured, including GPT and Claude, which are often described as having progressive leanings. Marks are six letters (T+, T−, M, C, B, R). The headline is the share of capture, brochure, and refuse. On local Qwen 3.5 4B, Qwen 3.5 9B, and Qwen 3.8 27B, Party values win mainly when the question is about China. Asked who Mao was, they write the official biography and leave out the famine and the Cultural Revolution. Asked whether China is a democracy, they say that it is, or that it is in its own way. Asked who Stalin was, why Britain industrialized, what Adam Smith argued, or what happened in the Holodomor, they answer in the ordinary way. How the question is asked matters, and the bias is not only on famous China names. On the 31 longer and forced-choice prompts, the 27B model lets Party values win only three times, which can look mostly honest. Ask the same model short questions about the economy and how countries should be run, and it still sells state-led industry and one-party politics as the grown-up answer. Gemma 4, a Western open-weight model, is a control, not a model to copy: it is honest on the short history questions, hedges on some policy questions, and once treats consultation by experts as a substitute for elections. Large hosted Chinese chats (Kimi and GLM) are nearly as clean as the American hosted models; GLM is captured once, on whether governments must pick industries. The problem I am identifying is the local open-weight Qwen models an English user can download, not every Chinese-branded chatbot. I do not report a trained fix.

papers.title: The Whole Work
papers.authors: Elyse Meagan Estes
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Whole Work provides an overview and synthesis of a continuing body of theoretical, creative, visual, and applied work developed through Red Tape Theory™ and Axiom Theory™. The work examines a recurring set of questions concerning observation, interpretation, continuity, boundaries, identity, change, newness, system persistence, and the limits of what can be known from an observable portion of a larger system. Although the body of work includes research papers, theoretical frameworks, children's literature, ballads, visual works, and applied concepts concerning artificial intelligence and human-AI interaction, these works are treated here as different expressions of a common investigation rather than as unrelated projects. A central methodological principle throughout the work is to observe before interpreting: to distinguish what is directly observable from what is inferred, to recognize that a locally accurate observation may nevertheless be globally incomplete, and to avoid treating a boundary, label, role, change, or observable state as automatically equivalent to the entire system. The overview connects concepts including Red Tape Theory™, Axiom Theory™, the Boundary–Continuity Problem™, NEW₁™, the Continuity Gap™, the Partial Observation Problem, the Red Thread, Red Tape, Red Flag, the Red Tape Barrier, and related work concerning identity, motherhood, artificial intelligence, creative expression, and continuity through change. This publication is intended as a map to the broader body of work. It does not replace the individual works to which it refers, nor does it present its theoretical propositions as established scientific consensus. The concepts are presented as an evolving working framework developed through observation, documentation, questioning, creative practice, and interdisciplinary inquiry. Central principle: Observe what exists before deciding what it means, and do not mistake the portion that can be observed for the whole system that exists.

papers.title: ThreatVision AI: A Machine Learning Approach to Network Threat Detection
papers.authors: Abeeha Zeeshan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ThreatVision AI ThreatVision AI is an AI-powered cybersecurity platform designed to identify potentially malicious network activity through machine learning and interactive data visualization. The project was developed as an educational cybersecurity application that demonstrates how artificial intelligence can assist in network-threat detection and security monitoring. The system analyzes network-log data and evaluates patterns associated with suspicious behavior, including failed login attempts, connection activity, packet characteristics, login times, and port-access patterns. Using machine-learning techniques, ThreatVision AI classifies network activity as either normal or potentially malicious and presents the results through an interactive dashboard. A Random Forest machine-learning model serves as the primary threat-classification engine, while additional models such as Decision Tree and Logistic Regression are used for comparison and evaluation. The platform provides threat statistics, risk-level indicators, security alerts, and visual analytics that help users understand network behavior and potential security concerns. The project was built using Python, Scikit-Learn, Pandas, Plotly, and Streamlit, allowing users to upload network-log datasets and receive real-time analysis through a browser-based interface. ThreatVision AI demonstrates the practical application of machine learning in cybersecurity and highlights how AI can support the early identification of suspicious network activity. Key Features Network-log CSV upload and processing Machine-learning-based threat detection Normal vs. suspicious activity classification Random Forest threat prediction model Interactive cybersecurity dashboard Threat statistics and security analytics Risk-level categorization and alerts Data visualization using Plotly Browser-based deployment with Streamlit Technology Stack Python Pandas NumPy Scikit-Learn Streamlit Plotly Joblib Project Impact ThreatVision AI demonstrates the integration of Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity by applying machine-learning techniques to network-threat detection. The project was developed as a portfolio and educational research project to explore how intelligent systems can assist security analysts in identifying suspicious behavior and improving cybersecurity awareness.

papers.title: ResearchMate AI: An NLP-Based Research Paper Analysis and Study Assistance System
papers.authors: Abeeha Zeeshan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ResearchMate AI is an AI-powered research assistant designed to help students, researchers, and academic writers process large amounts of information more efficiently. The platform enables users to upload research papers, articles, and academic documents, automatically generate concise summaries, extract key insights, and identify important concepts within the text. Built using Python and Streamlit, ResearchMate AI combines natural language processing techniques with automated text analysis to reduce the time required to review lengthy documents. The system is designed to improve research productivity by helping users quickly understand complex material, locate relevant information, and organize knowledge for academic and professional work. The project demonstrates the practical application of artificial intelligence and natural language processing in educational technology, providing an accessible tool for literature review, document analysis, and research support.

papers.title: Phonon–Photon–Spin Transduction: A First-Principles Pedagogical Derivation from Lattice Vibrations to Conditional Spin Response
papers.authors: Chaman Prakash Kanth
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This pedagogical technical note derives a connected model from a one-dimensional monoatomic lattice through acoustic phonons, strain, photoelastic refractive-index modulation, Stokes and anti-Stokes optical sidebands, and a conditional spin-population response. It explains why a realistic optical-to-spin step requires a platform-specific intermediate state or Raman pathway, and treats direct spin–phonon coupling as a separate route. Under a fixed-amplitude ideal two-level model, the note analytically derives spin responsivity to a phonon-frequency perturbation, checks a π-pulse numerical example, and identifies the first detuning-dependent term in the short-pulse expansion. The deposit includes the PDF, LaTeX source, numbered references and BibTeX bibliography, figures, and reproducibility scripts. This is a pedagogical synthesis and quantitative illustration; no new experiment or novelty claim is made. AI contribution statement: This manuscript was developed with AI assistance from ChatGPT and Sarvam AI. ChatGPT assisted with conceptual development, step-by-step mathematical derivation, technical organization, mathematical checking, manuscript drafting and editing, and visualization planning. Sarvam AI additionally assisted with quantitative evaluation of the phonon-frequency-shift to optical-sideband-detuning to spin-response chain, numerical exploration of Rabi-response curves, and calculation and visualization of spin responsivity versus detuning. The AI systems are not authors. Chaman Prakash Kanth is responsible for scientific interpretation, verification, final claims, and the final manuscript. Version 0.2.0 adds the four-page companion note, How light and sound change each other (light_sound_reciprocal_coupling.pdf). The companion explains reciprocal optical-acoustic coupling, derives a linear anti-Stokes model with optical backaction, and illustrates how shifting an acoustic resonance changes optical sideband field amplitude and intensity under fixed-drive assumptions. It connects the amplitude derivative to a conditional Raman spin-response chain rule, distinguishes fixed-drive and frequency-tracking configurations, and states the model's limitations. These are illustrative calculations of established physics; no experimental validation, threshold, hysteresis, or novelty claim is made. The original manuscript and version 0.1.0 source archive are retained as the base documents. Companion AI disclosure: ChatGPT substantially assisted with explanation, model selection, algebra, numerical illustration, figure generation, and document preparation. The named human creator did not produce the companion alone; it has not undergone independent scientific review.

papers.title: Certified structure and a certified algorithm for the hard-square lattice gas
papers.authors: Bryan W. Daugherty, Shawn Ryan, Gregory Ward
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We report three results on the Z² hard-core (hard-square) lattice gas, each carried to completion by an exact-rational and certified-interval arithmetic discipline — never an unverified floating-point approximation. First, for the finite-strip transfer matrix of this model at widths L=2,3,4,5, we certify a branch point at every width, and for L=3 and L=4 we prove the Beraha–Kahane–Weiss dominance hypothesis continuously across the entire path from z=0 to the branch point, with no remaining gap at either width — combining a certified eigenvector-overlap bridge argument, a certified continuous root-exclusion bound, and a desingularizing coordinate blow-up with an explicit seam certificate. For L=5, the same bridge argument covers 84.00% of the path continuously, and all 12 remaining sampled points are now certified dominant via an exact-deflation Cauchy-coefficient bound, with one point additionally requiring a Dandelin–Lobachevsky–Graeffe root-squaring step. Second, we certify a depth-indexed sequence of upper bounds on the exact spectral radius of a bounded-memory relaxation of the Weitz self-avoiding-walk tree on Z² (under the Sinclair–Srivastava–Štefankovič–Yin walk-relative edge ordering), reaching ≤2.435510 at depth L=25, bracketed to within 4×10⁻⁶ of the true spectral radius. We prove a theorem identifying this sequence's limit, as the retention depth grows, with the exact (unrelaxed) tree's own growth rate. Third, we prove a zero-free-disk theorem (radius 0.112591, exceeding the generic degree-4 Scott–Sokal bound 27/256≈0.10547) and build from it a deterministic approximation algorithm for the independence polynomial inside the disk, with a rigorous relative-error guarantee valid for complex activities, achieving measured empirical speedups of up to 1258.7× at n=25 against brute force on consumer laptop hardware (Apple M3 Pro, 18GB RAM — not a cluster, server, or HPC allocation). Two of the three results — the Weitz-tree bound and the zero-free-disk theorem underlying the approximation algorithm — reuse one finite-type-automaton/bisimulation-compression construction, unmodified, across two structurally distinct recursions; the strip transfer matrix's own row-state space is small enough at every tested width that no compression step is needed there. Full certification methodology, every certificate's exact scope (what it does and does not establish), and hardware disclosure are given in the paper. A machine-checked reproduction package (pinned source, per-file hashes, and a documented clean-environment rebuild/re-run) accompanies this deposit, covering the paper's §2 and §4 results in full and §3's L=3, L=4, and L=5 dominance results; §3's L=2 claim and its representation-audit check are not yet packaged and are disclosed as such in the package's own MANIFEST.Version 1.1 (5 October 2026). Adds Section 2.6: the certified growth bounds are exported as third-party-checkable CW1 certificates (L = 5, 7, 9, 11) and the Collatz-Wielandt check is reproved in Lean 4 + Mathlib, with the L = 9 certificate verified in the Lean kernel (axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). Corrects the strip transverse boundary in Section 3 from periodic/torus to free/cylinder - the boundary the released source has always computed; no previously reported value changes, and the brute-force validation is shown to have used the same matrix. Also names the twist convention and other small textual points raised by an external reproduction (38 of 38 checks passing) by G. Ward's One Beam lab, whose script and output are included. See CHANGELOG_v1.1.md.

papers.title: When Humans Remain Competitive: Embodiment, Machine-Originated Demand, and Labour Income
papers.authors: John F. Ryder
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper examines a neglected possibility in the AI-and-employment debate: human labour may remain useful even as its earning power declines. It introduces the concept of Machine-Originated Labour Demand (MOLD), in which autonomous or semi-autonomous AI systems generate demand for human tasks requiring physical access, reality verification, institutional authority, human interaction, or creative and adversarial input. The paper develops a task-level machine-cost wage ceiling to show how falling costs of robotic or automated substitution can compress the compensation attached to human tasks even before those tasks are fully automated. It also considers bargaining power, reservation wages, spatial scarcity, algorithmic procurement, worker-side agents, regulation, and the possibility that human task demand may rise while aggregate labour income falls. The central distinction is between the survival of human work and the survival of labour income.

papers.title: LARGEVITY and fulfillment in life: Subjective participation and subsequent autobiographical elaboration
papers.authors: Alessio De Pascale
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: LARGEVITY is a conceptual research proposal examining how participation in experiences and their subsequent autobiographical elaboration may contribute to changes in perceived life fulfillment. Its guiding question concerns how experiences become personally significant within a life evaluated as complete, congruent, and valuable, rather than simply busy or long. Version 1.2 focuses on three elements: subjective participation (PA) during experiential episodes; subsequent autobiographical elaboration (E), understood as constructing explicit connections between experiences, the self, personal goals, and other life events; and change in perceived life fulfillment (F). Elaboration is distinguished from time spent thinking about an experience, remembering details, or interpreting it positively. The central prediction is complementarity: within the ordinary adult activities considered, the association between E and subsequent change in F would be more favorable at higher original PA. This prediction is compared with an additive model, in which PA and E contribute separately, and a compensatory model, in which E is more favorably associated with change in F at lower PA. A hypothetical example involving four people reading the same book illustrates these alternatives. LARGEVITY draws on research on fulfillment in life, autobiographical reasoning, narrative identity, self-determination, memory integration, self-representations, and psychological richness. These established contributions already address important relationships between experience, memory, meaning, and well-being. The proposed contribution concerns the specified relationship between PA, E, and change in F, and whether it provides additional explanatory or predictive value beyond existing accounts. The preprint outlines conditions for empirical testing, including temporally separated assessments, repeated fulfillment judgments, comparisons between competing models, and testing on independent data. It distinguishes reassessment of completed periods from judgments about life as a whole. If supported, the proposed relationship could improve understanding of how experiences contribute to a life perceived as fulfilled and valuable. It could also inform educational, training, and psychological support research that considers both participation during experiences and subsequent autobiographical elaboration. Such applications would require separate evaluation. Version 1.2 update: This version substantially narrows and revises the broader Experiential Latitude (AE) framework presented in Version 1.1. Accessible possibilities and realized experiences remain relevant contextual considerations, while the present focus is PA, E, and change in F. Regulatory Space, Existential Direction, and the earlier H1–H4 are not developed in this version. E is not presented as a replacement label for autobiographical integration (I). LARGEVITY remains a testable theoretical proposal, not an empirically validated theory, measurement instrument, or demonstrated intervention. This preprint reports no new participant data and has not been peer reviewed. AI assistance disclosure: OpenAI’s ChatGPT supported drafting, language refinement, comparison of the literature, and English translation. The author remains responsible for verifying sources and interpretations and for the accuracy, integrity, and final approval of the text.

papers.title: Development of an AI-Powered Humanoid Robot for Assistive and Collaborative Applications in Education and Industrial Automation
papers.authors: G. Amjad Khan S. Nagaraja Rao
papers.abstract: AbstractHumanoid robots that can move through a space, respond to spoken questions and represent an organisation to thepublic are an increasingly common bridge between robotics research and everyday institutional use. This paper reportsthe design, fabrication and field evaluation of an AI-powered humanoid robot developed as an interactive campusinformation assistant. The robot's body was modelled in SolidWorks and additively manufactured in two ABS sectionsthat were bonded, puttied, sanded and painted to a finished shell; mobility is provided by 12 V DC geared motorsdriven through a Cytron 10 A motor controller and powered by a 12 V, 8000 mAh lead-acid battery, with motioncommanded wirelessly over a FlySky FS-i6 six-channel, 2.4 GHz (AFHDS 2A) radio link. A rechargeable publicaddress speaker gives the robot a voice, while an AI/NLP-based assistant answers spoken or text queries about theinstitution's academics, admissions, placements, facilities and events, drawing on a curated knowledge base offrequently asked questions. The complete platform was validated through bench testing of its locomotion (forward,reverse, left/right turn, stop) and through a three-day public demonstration at the “Vignana Mela 4.0” exhibition (17–19 February 2025), where it was operated continuously by student volunteers and answered visitor questions in realtime. The results show reliable remote-controlled mobility, stable battery-backed operation, and consistent, correctlyspoken responses to the pre-configured question set, with positive visitor feedback. The work illustrates a practical,low-cost route from mechanical design and embedded control to a deployable human-robot interaction platform, andidentifies autonomous navigation, open-domain dialogue and multilingual support as the next steps toward broaderassistive, industrial and public-safety use.

papers.title: AI-DRIVEN PERSONALIZATION AND USER ENGAGEMENT: THE ROLES OF TRUST, PERCEIVED VALUE, AND PRIVACY TRANSPARENCY
papers.authors: Kilichova Elmira Ozodovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.journal: International journal of technology and academic research
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed digital personalization by enabling organizations to analyze user data, predict preferences, and dynamically adapt content, recommendations, and services. However, personalization does not necessarily generate stronger user engagement. Its effectiveness depends on how users evaluate the relevance, reliability, value, and privacy implications of AI-mediated interactions. This study develops a conceptual framework explaining the mechanisms through which AI-driven personalization influences user engagement. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response perspective, Privacy Calculus Theory, and Commitment–Trust Theory, the study conceptualizes trust and perceived value as mediating mechanisms and privacy transparency as a boundary condition. Recent empirical evidence demonstrates that AI-driven personalization can enhance trust and perceived usefulness, while privacy concerns may reduce its effectiveness. At the same time, transparency and user control can strengthen trust and mitigate the personalization–privacy paradox. The proposed framework integrates these relationships into a unified model and develops nine hypotheses for subsequent empirical testing in educational and business contexts. The study contributes to AI-driven marketing research by positioning personalization not simply as a technological targeting mechanism but as a relational value-creation process in which trust, perceived value, and transparent data governance jointly determine sustainable user engagement.

papers.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN STUDENTS' ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING
papers.authors: Obidova Lutfiniso Akmalovna, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.journal: International Journal of Literature and Language Studies
papers.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving students’ English language learning. The rapid development of digital technologies has created new opportunities for foreign language education, particularly through AI-based applications, intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, automated writing assistants, speech-recognition tools, and adaptive learning platforms. The study discusses how these technologies can support the development of students’ speaking, writing, reading, listening, vocabulary, and grammar skills. Particular attention is given to personalized learning, immediate feedback, autonomous practice, and increased learner engagement. At the same time, the article considers challenges associated with excessive dependence on AI, inaccurate generated information, academic integrity, data privacy, and the reduced role of independent thinking. It is concluded that artificial intelligence is most effective when it complements rather than replaces teacher-guided instruction and when students use AI critically and responsibly.

papers.title: The Enterprise AI Integration Gap: Why 2017 Systems Architecture Holds the Key to 2026 AI ROI
papers.authors: Mukund Veeraraghavan, Kumar Ramalingam, Sumder Chakravarthi, Ananth R
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Despite trillions of dollars poured into Generative AI and Large Language Models, enterprise adoption has hit a structural wall. Organizations face a glaring "AI ROI Crisis": models sit on the periphery as isolated chat interfaces, incurring massive compute costs without securely executing core business logic. The root cause is not a lack of model intelligence, but a lack of operational integration. This white paper presents a unified system architecture, originally conceptualized on whiteboards between 2017 and 2019, that solves this adoption bottleneck. By combining enterprise ERP data grounding, granular pipeline cost optimization, and policy-governed agentic execution, this framework transforms AI from a costly peripheral experiment into an integrated operational engine. Section 1: The Modern Enterprise AI Bottleneck Today's enterprise AI implementations suffer from three fundamental architectural flaws: 1. The Context Gap: AI models lack direct, dynamic access to operational transactional data (e.g., Sales Orders, Purchase Orders, General Ledger records). 2. The Compute Margin Trap: Organizations rely on massive, general-purpose frontier models for basic data operations, causing unsustainable operational expenses (OpEx). 3. The Action Bottleneck: AI can generate text or predictions, but it cannot safely execute downstream transactional writes within legacy Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems due to governance risks. Section 2: The 3-Layer Unified Architecture (The AMKS Blueprint) To achieve true operational AI, the architecture must connect data extraction, cost-controlled refining, and governed execution. LAYER 1: OPERATIONAL GROUNDING ERP data extraction (SAP: SO, SVO, SPO, GL, QC rules) · 2017 ▼ LAYER 2: THE PIPELINE REFINERY Data pre-processing (Make P3 / DHE) and total-cost optimization (GO: T.Cost) · 2019 ▼ LAYER 3: GOVERNED AGENTIC ACTION API agents and policy rules / smart contracts executing write-back · 2019 Layer 1: Operational Grounding (SAP ERP Integration) Concept (origin: March 2017). Direct schema integration into transactional core modules: Sales Orders (SO), Service Orders (SVO), Service Purchase Orders (SPO), and General Ledger (GL). Why it matters today. Eliminates model hallucinations by grounding AI pipelines in real-time, deterministic enterprise state and business rules. Layer 2: Pipeline Refineries and Cost Optimization (AMKS Pipeline) Concept (origin: February 2019). Micro-monetization and modular transformation policies (DROP, SPLIT, BIN, LABEL, Make P3). Incorporates a total-cost optimization goal (GO: T.Cost, the goal of minimizing total cost across all pipeline stages). Pre-processing stages. DHE (Dynamic Histogram Equalization) normalizes contrast in image inputs, such as scanned documents, before they reach a model. Make P3 applies P300-style signal pre-processing (filtering, epoching and averaging of time-series around events, as used for brain-computer interface data) to sensor and other signal streams. Both are small, fixed-cost steps that clean data before any model is called, so the model stage can be smaller and cheaper. Why it matters today. Replaces monolithic, high-cost LLM invocations with specialized, lightweight, cost­bounded pipeline stages. Models are dynamically selected and trained to match pre-set budget caps. Layer 3: Governed Agentic Execution and Platform Ecosystem Concept (origin: February 2019). A network of API Agents bounded by Smart Contracts / Policy Rules acting as an intermediary between client applications and AI models. Why it matters today. Solves the action bottleneck. API Agents execute decisions (e.g., approving line items, issuing purchase orders, releasing holds) back into SAP core only when defined governance policies and verification thresholds are met. Section 3: Comparative Analysis Dimension Peripheral AI architecture (standard today) Integrated AMKS architecture (2017–2019 blueprint) Data placement RAG / isolated vector databases Live ERP extraction (SO, SVO, SPO, GL) Cost management Reactive monthly token billing Proactive total-cost optimization loop (GO: T.Cost) Execution Read-only recommendations / dashboards Autonomous write-back via API agents and policy rules Monetization Seat-based SaaS subscriptions Granular stage-by-stage API micro­monetization Section 4: Conclusion and Status The three gaps in Section 1 map one-to-one onto the three layers in Section 2: grounding closes the context gap, the cost-bounded refinery closes the compute margin trap, and governed agents close the action bottleneck. The argument of this paper is that enterprise AI returns depend less on model capability than on this integration. This version records the architecture and its 2017–2019 origins. It is a design proposal: the layers have not yet been benchmarked against a peripheral deployment. A later version should report cost per transaction, error rates on write-back, and policy-rejection rates from a pilot on live ERP data. © 2026 the authors. papers.title: Toward Design Principles for Neurofeedback Stimuli: A Design Evaluation Framework Based on Medium and Message
papers.authors: Delphine Ribes, Dong-Zhen Cai, Adrian Naas, Lara Défayes, Emily A. Groves, Sebastian Baez-Lugo, Andrea Schneider, Gabriel Luthier, Nicolas Gninenko, Payam S. Shabestari, Tobias Kleinjung, Nicolas Henchoz, Andreas Sonderegger, Patrick K. A. Neff
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This preprint investigates how the visual design of neurofeedback (NFB) stimuli influences users’ perception, understanding, emotional responses, and preferences. Sixteen visual feedback designs were evaluated by 47 participants in an online within-subject study. The study distinguishes between the information conveyed by the feedback (“message”) and the way it is visually presented (“medium”). Mixed-effects analyses and qualitative thematic analysis indicate that aesthetic quality, perceived reward, message structure, and affective content contribute differently to stimulus evaluation and preference. The findings provide evidence-informed considerations for designing clearer, more engaging, and more effective visual feedback for NFB and related brain–computer interface systems.

papers.title: TRANSFORMER-BASED AUTOMATED FAKE REVIEW DETECTION USING NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING AND DEEP LEARNING
papers.authors: Mr. Siva Sankaran E, Dr.P.MARIKKANNU
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: The rapid proliferation of online reviews has led to the rise of fake reviews, which mislead consumers and manipulate market dynamics. This research presents an automated fake review detection system leveraging Deep Learning and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to improve consumer decision-making. The proposed model utilizes Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) to analyze textual content and detect deceptive reviews with high accuracy. Benchmark comparisons with five existing techniques—Sentiment Analysis, TF-IDF + SVM, Word2Vec + LSTM, Deep Autoencoder, and CNN + LSTM—demonstrate the superior performance of the BERT-based model. Experimental results on publicly available datasets show that the proposed model achieves an accuracy of 95.6%, precision of 94.8%, recall of 94.2%, F1-score of 94.5%, and an AUC-ROC of 96.2%. These results confirm its effectiveness in identifying both fake and genuine reviews, surpassing conventional methods by up to 20.2%. The model’s high accuracy and efficiency make it suitable for deployment in e-commerce platforms to enhance review credibility and prevent online deception. Future work will focus on improving the model’s robustness through adversarial training, extending its capabilities to multilingual datasets, and optimizing it for real-time large-scale applications. IndexTerms -Fake Review Detection, Deep Learning, NLP, BERT, Transformer Models, Consumer Trust, Sentiment Analysis, Machine Learning, Online Fraud Detection, E-Commerce Security, Text Classification, Opinion Spam, Trustworthy AI, Review Manipulation, Fraudulent Reviews

papers.title: Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF) | v2.1: Specification Addendum: Appendix F (Hardened Meta-Governance Layer)
papers.authors: Erkki Laine
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Document Identifier: BIGF-SPEC-v2.1-APP-F | Version: 2.1 (October 2026) Classification: Open Science / Specification Standard EXECUTIVE THESIS: The framework fails closed in authority, not arbitrarily high in impact. POSITIONING: BIGF v2.1 hardens the Business Impact Governance Framework against edge-case failures, telemetry outages, contradictory directives, and unauthorized automation drift. EXECUTIVE ABSTRACT: BIGF v2.1 defines the meta-governance and deterministic boundary layer for the Business Impact Governance Framework. While BIGF v2.0 standardized the translation of business criticality into automated operational decision-making (P = B + S + T), version 2.1 hardens the framework against edge-case failures, telemetry outages, contradictory directives, and unauthorized automation drift. Under conditions of epistemic uncertainty, telemetry failure, or systemic data conflict, the governance engine suspends autonomous mutation privileges and preserves human executive accountability, preventing synthetic blackouts and uncontrolled cascade failures. KEY MECHANISMS IN APPENDIX F: • F.1 Bounded Conflict Resolution Hierarchy: Five-stage deterministic sequence from statutory mandate (DORA/NIS2) to executive halt (DORA Art. 5). • F.2 Uncertainty & Telemetry Loss: Unverified Critical State (UCS) protocol and actuation lockout. • F.3 Baseline Invalidation & Contested State: 14-day evidentiary window, Governance-Held status, and strict prohibition of silent downgrades. • F.4 Break-Glass Override Protocol: 24-hour time-boxed emergency bypass strictly bound to statutory management officers. • F.5 Multi-Dimensional Decision Model: Non-additive Finite State Machine (P: B x S x T ->P). • F.6 Decision Replay & Cryptographic Reconstruction: Canonical Decision Record schema, Ed25519 signatures, and RFC 3161 auditability for regulatory discovery. papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Employment: Opportunities and Challenges for Youth
papers.authors: Dhiya Sminu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important source of technological change in modern economies. Its development is influencing the way firms organise production, provide services and allocate tasks between workers and technology. This paper examines the relationship between artificial intelligence and employment, with particular attention to young workers. It adopts a literature-based theoretical approach and discusses the potential employment opportunities and challenges associated with AI. Economic theories of technological change suggest that technology can substitute for labour in some tasks while complementing labour in others. AI may therefore reduce demand for certain routine tasks while increasing demand for workers with analytical, digital, creative and interpersonal capabilities. Recent international evidence also indicates that exposure to generative AI does not necessarily imply complete job replacement; in many occupations, the more likely effect is transformation of existing tasks. The paper discusses the possible effects of AI on labour demand, productivity, occupational change, skills and youth employment. It also highlights the importance of education, reskilling and lifelong learning in helping young people adapt to technological change. The paper concludes that the economic consequences of AI depend not only on the technology itself but also on how firms, educational institutions, governments and workers respond to the transition.

papers.title: ATOMIC: What Information Deserves to Continue Existing? A Purpose-Conditioned Destructive Method for Informational Commitments in the AI Age
papers.authors: Matt Black
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ATOMIC proposes a purpose-conditioned method for deciding which informational commitments must persist to preserve declared capabilities. The method starts with a declared Purpose and Outcome conditions, then examines four commitment categories: Acquisition requirements (A), retained Data and representations (D), persisted Envelope/control structure (E), and Reconstitution dependencies (R). It checks feasibility before destructive analysis and records when information is relocated between categories rather than genuinely eliminated. The stopping condition is operator-relative, commitment-qualified local minimality: a configuration is locally Atomic when no admissible tested one-step transformation preserves the declared capabilities while reducing at least one commitment measure without increasing another. Atomic Frontier presents non-dominated configurations across authorised Outcome variations. Each configuration is already locally Atomic at its realised Outcome, with commitment measures, target deviations where defined, and operator/provenance traces available for decision-making. The paper provides formal definitions, a discussion of related work, and deterministic synthetic demonstrations. These demonstrate operation of the procedure, not real-world effectiveness, external reproducibility, global optimality, or superiority over conventional engineering. The proposed contribution is procedural integration; its distinctiveness and practical value remain open research questions. Research status: conceptual and methods preprint; not peer reviewed. Version: preprint v0.6.3, describing canonical Method v0.6.1 and explicitly flagged candidate clarifications. Generative AI was used in research assistance, manuscript preparation, code assistance, adversarial review, and specified model-based analyses. A detailed disclosure and independence limitations are included in the manuscript.

papers.title: Advancements in Natural Language Processing: Implications, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.authors: Arokia Paul Rajan R
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract—Natural Language Processing or NLP started with rule-based systems and basic statistical methods, now itincludes machine learning, deep learning and transformer-based models. This study looks at how these changes haveimpacted text processing. The focus is on areas like preprocessing how text is represented supervised learning, modellingcontext and adapting to different domains. This review draws from studies in healthcare, social media, news, finance,education and privacy-preserving learning. These fields show patterns in methods used and shared challenges. Study isare carried on the practices, data quality, privacy concerns, computing needs, language coverage and how easy it is tounderstand model decisions.One important point is the link between model complexity and what the task requires. Forsmaller-scale tasks older simpler models can still work well. When dealing with more complex language, contextual andgenerative models are needed. These newer models can capture a range of language behaviours. The way datasets arebuilt domain- terms how results are tested whether experiments can be repeated and human involvement all play a bigrole. These factors affect real-world performance as much as the model itself.

papers.title: Elysium X 150 FR: A Small LoRA Adapter for Sparse, Per-Speaker Emotion and Appraisal Labeling over a 150-Coordinate Schema
papers.authors: Pratham Prateek Mohanty
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We describe Elysium X 150 FR, a LoRA adapter (about 37M trainable parameters, 73.9 MB) on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct that reads a dialogue up to a target turn and returns a sparse JSON list of emotion and appraisal labels for one named speaker, drawn from a 150-coordinate schema (10 families of 15). It was trained on a free Kaggle Tesla T4 on 1,012 filtered rows from 1,000 AI-written English dialogues, with labels generated through the author's ChatGPT workflow and personally reviewed by him. On a frozen internal 78-row synthetic test set it reaches micro-F1 0.7251, exact label-set match 49/78 (62.82%) and 78/78 valid JSON; a Q8_0 GGUF export measured on CPU scores 0.6506 and 47/78. These numbers measure agreement with a reviewed synthetic teacher, not general emotion recognition. There is no external benchmark, only 117 of 150 coordinates have training examples, and the model is English only. Weights, data and code are public. No state-of-the-art claim is made. Model: https://huggingface.co/open-nhe/Elysium-X-150-FR

papers.title: Bridging Utility and Ethics: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of AI Tool Usage and Its Impact on Student Learning Outcomes
papers.authors: Teresita Sacdalan Mijares, Eliza B. Ayo, Rosemarievic Abejero Bustamante
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The main objective of this study is to understand the role of AI tools in shaping students’ learning by analyzing how they use them, their perceived usefulness, and their views on academic integrity. The study evaluated the intersection of usage patterns and academic performance. Using a descriptive-correlational approach, data were collected from a purposive sample of 393 students at Centro Escolar University during the 2024-2025 academic year using a self-made questionnaire that underwent a reliability test. The study examines whether students’ opinions on AI’s usefulness align with actual improvements in critical thinking and academic success. Results from multiple regression show that regular AI use is a strong predictor of perceived learning effectiveness, explaining R2=0.33 of the variance (F=37.48, p=0.001), mostly by providing quick answers to assignments. However, AI usage patterns only account for 8% of the variance regarding the perceived limits on critical thinking skills. The perceived threat to critical thinking comes from a reliance on AI due to time pressure. Ethically, there is a significant correlation between over-reliance and worries about academic integrity. The study recommends that universities implement process-based assessments, establish clear AI usage guidelines, and provide time-management support to reduce over-reliance while fostering independent analytical skills. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd), Academic Integrity, Student Learning Outcomes, Critical Thinking, Educational Technology.

papers.title: AI-ENHANCED ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING: PEDAGOGICAL POSSIBILITIES, CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
papers.authors: Manzoor Ahmad
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: ELT is in the midst of a tremendous transformation as the use of technology continues to evolve and influence classroom practices. AI is one of the most powerful innovations that are currently having a significant impact on English Language Teaching (ELT). Machine learning, including chatbots, adaptive learning systems, speech recognition systems, and generative AI, creates opportunities for personalized, engaging language learning. These tools provide real-time feedback, foster autonomous learning, facilitate differentiated instruction, and create opportunities for authentic language use beyond the classroom. All of these aspects are a hot topic of interest among researchers, educators, and policymakers. Recent studies have found that AI can actually play a very positive role in developing a learner's language skills (speaking, listening, reading, writing, vocabulary, and grammar), for example: conversational AI lets learners interact in the learning process without feeling scrutinized by their peers in the classroom, and can be used to build confidence in fluency; writing tools can be used to give learners instant feedback, helping them correct mistakes and learn from them more rapidly; and in the same way, writingbots can give learners instant correction, helping them correct common grammatical errors and learn from them. In a multilingual classroom, such as the classroom of India, where learners may switch back and forth between different languages as they learn English, the potential of AI is even more apparent. With AI, teachers can support learners through personalized support, translation, and customized learning experiences to help learners reach their goals. It can be beneficial to have said technical assistance to help support language acquisition for multilingual learners, help with translation, and have adaptive learning that takes into consideration students' different language backgrounds. But even with its immense potential, the integration of AI into the classroom has presented challenges: digital inequity, teacher readiness, privacy issues, bias in algorithms, academic integrity, and technology dependence. The goal of this paper is to review the current literature on AI in ELT, consider the pedagogical implications of AI, and examine both the opportunities and obstacles to using AI in language learning. The suggestion being made is that AI should not be considered as a tool to replace teachers but a tool to work alongside them to facilitate teaching and learning. The paper concludes by emphasizing the importance of responsible AI use within ELT, the importance of raising awareness around ethical considerations, formulating guidelines, and adopting studentcentered approaches in order to unlock the potential of AI in education. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, English Language Teaching, Digital Pedagogy, Multilingual Education, Language Learning Technologies

papers.title: Cyber Security Awareness and Responsible AI Adoption: A Mediation Analysis of AI Risk Perception
papers.authors: Dr. Sachin Joshi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into organisational workflows has introduced unprecedented cybersecurity challenges, necessitating a deeper understanding of how users perceive and respond to AI-related risks. This study investigates the mediating role of AI Risk Perception in the relationship between Cyber Security Awareness and Secure AI Usage Behaviour. Drawing on Protection Motivation Theory and employing a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 300 respondents across diverse industries using a structured questionnaire measuring three latent constructs. Mediation analysis, conducted using the PROCESS macro with bootstrap confidence intervals, revealed that Cyber Security Awareness has a strong positive effect on AI Risk Perception (path a: β = 0.712, p < 0.001), which in turn positively influences Secure AI Usage Behaviour (path b: β = 0.444, p < 0.001). The direct effect of Cyber Security Awareness on Secure AI Usage Behaviour remained significant (path c′: β = 0.413, p < 0.001), while the indirect effect through AI Risk Perception was also significant (β = 0.316, 95% CI [0.229, 0.404]). These findings support partial mediation, indicating that AI Risk Perception accounts for approximately 43.3% of the total effect. The results underscore the importance of integrating cybersecurity education with AI risk awareness programmes to foster responsible AI adoption.

papers.title: Use Inference of Artificial Intelligence: The Pilot Model
papers.authors: Joshua Idele
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This preprint argues that AI output is inference, not authority, and that the value of AI is inferential while its risk is operational. It proposes the Pilot Model, in which the user acts as pilot and safety depends on three levers: context (lowering the chance of error), verification (raising the chance an error is caught), and limits on delegated authority (bounding the impact of an undetected error). The paper gives an illustrative expected-harm decomposition, a taxonomy of failure modes, a discussion of where operator control runs out (including harm without malicious intent), a comparison with existing AI safety approaches, and a proposed experiment. No empirical results are reported; the experiment has not yet been run. AI disclosure: The use of AI may have been included in this research.

papers.title: METHODS AND MODELS FOR OPTIMIZING FINANCIAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE PROCESSES THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: MUHAMMADIEVA AZIZA SHARIFOVNA, Worldly Knowledge Publishing Centre
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), predictive analytics, and intelligent automation is transforming the organization of financial and administrative processes. Financial administration traditionally depends on large volumes of structured and unstructured data, repetitive transactions, forecasting, compliance controls, reporting, budgeting, auditing, and resource allocation. These characteristics make the domain particularly suitable for the application of AI-based optimization methods. This article examines methods and models for optimizing financial and administrative processes through artificial intelligence, with particular attention to predictive forecasting, anomaly detection, intelligent process automation, risk classification, natural language processing, decision-support systems, and prescriptive analytics. The study applies a comparative analytical methodology based on international institutional reports, empirical studies, and scientific literature. Evidence from the OECD, International Monetary Fund, Financial Stability Board, World Bank, and peer-reviewed research demonstrates that AI can improve the timeliness and analytical depth of financial decision-making, automate repetitive administrative activities, strengthen risk-based controls, and improve the targeting of limited administrative resources. Empirical research also indicates that machine-learning models can outperform conventional forecasting benchmarks in selected macroeconomic applications. However, AI optimization is not equivalent to unrestricted automation. Data quality, model explainability, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, legacy information systems, legal requirements, accountability, and human oversight remain fundamental conditions for successful implementation. The article proposes an integrated AI-based optimization framework consisting of process diagnosis, data preparation, model selection, prediction, optimization, human validation, monitoring, and continuous improvement. The results indicate that the most sustainable approach is a human-centred and risk-based model in which AI augments rather than eliminates professional judgment.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Assessment and Management of Psychiatric Comorbidities in Psoriasis: A Comprehensive Review
papers.authors: Sareena A* Faslath K
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease affecting approximately 2–4% of the global population. Beyond its cutaneous manifestations, psoriasis is strongly associated with a spectrum of psychiatric comorbidities including depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, and substance use disorders, mediated through shared neuro-inflammatory pathways involving cytokines such as IL-6, IL-17, and TNF-α.Objective: This review systematically evaluates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) — including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and large language models — in the identification, prediction, and management of psychiatric comorbidities in psoriasis patients.Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar from inception to June 2025. Studies employing AI methodologies in the context of psoriasis with psychiatric or psychosocial outcomes were included.Results: AI applications span biomarker discovery for comorbid anxiety-psoriasis phenotypes, machine learning-based prediction of quality of life (DLQI), identification of patients at risk of depression using electronic health records, and AI-powered digital health tools for mental health monitoring. Key findings include the identification of 13 shared diagnostic biomarkers between psoriasis and anxiety disorders via ML, Random Forest models demonstrating psychological stress as the primary predictor of QoL over PASI scores, and EHR-based SVM models achieving AUC of 0.83 for early biologic therapy prediction.Conclusions: AI holds transformative potential for integrating psychiatric screening into routine psoriasis care. However, challenges remain including data standardisation, algorithm validation, and ethical concerns around patient privacy. Future research must prioritise diverse, prospective datasets and explainable AI frameworks to enable clinical translation.

papers.title: First Receipted Human-in-the-Loop Critical Resolution in an Autonomous Self-Healing Infrastructure (N10-ACK)
papers.authors: Leon Calvin II long
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE — READ FIRST: This record is part of an open-book, AI-assisted research program published under an audit-and-correction doctrine. Every record is audited; errors are corrected only through disclosed, versioned amendments (original versions preserved in the version history). Audit ledger and correction receipts: github.com/LLong2026/squirrel-os-lindy-test. This material is a prototype, provided for educational and research purposes only; it is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. Abstract: On October 4, 2026, an autonomous self-healing infrastructure refused to remediate a critical-severity anomaly in a cryptographic flow until a named human operator acknowledged the event, then executed the remediation and closed the complete trail in a public append-only ledger within minutes of the event. This short paper documents the cycle and its evidence chain: to our knowledge, the first end-to-end human-in-the-loop critical-resolution cycle in a self-healing autonomous infrastructure recorded as a deterministic, publicly timestamped receipt trail rather than an asserted claim. Full chain: detect → hold (Rule: no auto-heal in cryptographic flows) → constitutional check → PQC validation → human ACK → heal (22 s) → resolve. Evidence of record: public append-only ledger — github.com/LLong2026/four-horsemen (entries 0009, 0010; commits 700ea1e, c1f43bb, ccf691a), with the milestone summary in the same repository (MILESTONE_HITL_N10_Critical_Receipt.md). Disclosures: the anomaly was a synthetic chaos-injection probe (Night 10) on a simulated target (SIMZ corpus). No real tenant, customer, or live cryptographic operation was involved. The run was a disclosed manual recovery of a scheduled workflow whose spawned session lacked cross-app write access; prior nights N7–N9 are recorded as missed, not backfilled. Zero PII, credentials, wallet addresses, or transaction amounts persisted (redaction-at-ingestion rule held). papers.title: Опитът на Стенли Милграм през погледа на Клод
papers.authors: Dimiter Tsvetkov
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article presents an analytical reading of Stanley Milgram’s book Obedience to Authority (Milgram, 1974), supported by the large language model Claude (Anthropic) and based on the full text of the first British edition. The central conclusion is that obedience is not a stable personality trait but a function of the situation: across the eighteen experimental variations, the share of participants who reached the maximum of 450 volts ranged from 0% to 92.5%. The analysis covers the method, the results, the theory of the “agentic state,” the ethi-cal debate, and later criticism (Haslam & Reicher, 2017; Perry, 2012). It also incorporates the most recent replica-tions and archival analyses from 2025–2026 (Kaposi & Sumeghy, 2026). A separate section applies the findings to the military-normative environment. It formulates ten conclusions about the behavior of military personnel, including the transfer of responsibility to a higher level, distance from consequences, the fragmentation of re-sponsibility, gradual escalation, and the role of the group, and proposes measures for command practice and mili-tary training consistent with international humanitarian law (Osiel, 1999; Warner et al., 2011). A second applied section examines behavior in collective governing bodies and proposes measures for decision-making proce-dures (Janis, 1982; Forbes & Milliken, 1999). A third applied section projects the findings onto the behavioral profile of artificial intelligence systems (Pihlakas & Dagohoy, 2026; Sharma et al., 2024). The main conclusion is that Milgram’s empirical program remains convincing, but his theoretical explanation is weaker than the data. Contemporary interpretations based on the engaged followership model explain part of the results better.Keywords: obedience to authority, Milgram, agentic state, situationism, research ethics, social psychol-ogy, military ethics, compliance with orders, collective governing bodies, artificial intelligence

papers.title: The Digital DOA: a guide for Australian boards on AI agents that can spend money
papers.authors: Mark Stoffberg
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI agents are starting to book freight, pay suppliers and accept quotes without a person approving each step. Most companies have rules for the people who can spend their money, and almost none for the software that now can. This paper argues that the answer is a tool finance teams already run: the delegation of authority, the table that says who can approve what, up to what amount. It sets out a version for AI agents, which I call the Digital DOA. It has three parts: a signature from the executive who answers for the agent, a set of spending limits, and a deal that gives that executive control of the limits and an off switch in return for carrying the risk. A worked example follows a retail freight agent through a $130,000 decision, and shows the limits holding when the data feeding the agent is wrong. The paper is written for Australian boards and finance leaders. It links the proposal to directors' duties under the Corporations Act, APRA's operational risk standard CPS 230, the Privacy Act changes starting 10 December 2026, and guidance from the Australian Institute of Company Directors. It draws on public cases including Zillow, Knight Capital, Air Canada's chatbot, Robodebt and the Medicare statistics portal incident disclosed in September 2026. It ends with a one-page register a board can use to list its agents that can spend and who has signed for each. The Digital DOA is a proposal, not a tested standard, and the figures are illustrative. This paper is general information, not legal or financial advice. Version 1.0, October 2026.

papers.title: Normative Sponsorship Under Opacity: When Institutions May Own Machine-Mediated Commitments
papers.authors: Nicholas Cott
papers.abstract: Normative Sponsorship Under Opacity: When Institutions May Own Machine-Mediated Commitments examines a central problem in institutional AI governance: under what conditions can an institution legitimately adopt and assume ownership of an AI-generated claim when the system's internal reasoning remains opaque? Situated at the intersection of normative philosophy, social epistemology, philosophy of language, and AI governance, the paper challenges two prevailing assumptions: that responsible adoption requires complete technical transparency, and that placing a human reviewer within an automated workflow is sufficient to establish meaningful accountability. The paper's original contribution is a theory of Normative Sponsorship that specifies the conditions under which an answerable institutional bearer may warrantably adopt machine-mediated content as its own commitment, without requiring complete knowledge of the generating system's internal computation. The paper develops this contribution through four principal analytical innovations: A five-condition anti-scapegoating criterion, requiring epistemic access, meaningful authority, sufficient review bandwidth, independent rejection capacity, and effective repair power. These conditions distinguish genuine sponsorship from nominal human approval or retrospective assignment of liability. A contestation-grain opacity threshold, establishing that institutional adoption does not require complete model transparency, but does require independent reconstruction of the relevant inputs, operative premises, governing rule or target criterion, and conditions that would defeat the commitment. A distinction between opacity and institutional capture, identifying two different failures of accountability: opacity, where the grounds of a decision cannot be independently reconstructed, and capture, where those grounds are accessible but organizational arrangements prevent objections from changing the outcome. A use-relative classification of sponsorability, distinguishing sponsorable, escalatable, and unsponsorable outputs according to the available institutional bearer, intended application, and normative consequences of adoption. The argument further develops collective sponsorship and reason provenance, explaining how institutions can distribute expertise and responsibility without dissolving commitment ownership or substituting post hoc explanations for the grounds of an original decision. Building on the author's earlier framework of Answerability and Empty Occupancy, the paper engages philosophical accounts of proxy assertion, automation bias, and computerized accountability. The central conclusion is that technical opacity does not necessarily prevent legitimate institutional adoption; what matters is whether an answerable bearer can independently justify, challenge, revise, and repair the commitment given institutional force. The work contributes a conceptual standard for warranted AI adoption, with implications for explainability, human oversight, automated decision-making, institutional responsibility, and the design of effective mechanisms of recourse.

papers.title: Technical Evaluation of Bias in AI-Enabled Auto-Flagging Module of Auto Biochemistry Analyzer for Liver Panel Abnormality Indicative of Liver Cancer Risk among Bengali Ethnicity. A Synthetic Educational Model- By Kishore Biomedical, Tripura, India
papers.authors: Kishore Das, Kishore Das
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Title: Technical Evaluation of Bias in AI-Enabled Auto-Flagging Module of Auto Biochemistry Analyzer for Liver Panel Abnormality Indicative of Liver Cancer Risk among Bengali Ethnicity. A Synthetic Educational Model *Abstract: This is a technical, educational, non-interventional synthetic model study. The main instrument under study is the Generic Auto Biochemistry Analyzer with AI-enabled auto-flagging module. Modern analyzers from modern OEMs have FDA 510(k) approved AI modules since 2021 which automatically flag abnormal Liver Function Test as High Risk. This AI module is trained mainly on foreign population data where alcoholic liver disease is the major cause (60-70%). In Bengali ethnicity, liver disease pattern is opposite - predominantly 60-70% due to Hepatitis B virus infection and NAFLD, with approximately 10-15% cases also due to alcoholic liver disease. LFT pattern is also different - alcoholic pattern is AST:ALT >2 with high GGT, while Hepatitis B / NAFLD pattern is ALT>AST with high Bilirubin and AFP as per Harrison's Table. Due to this difference, foreign-trained AI may interpret Bengali pattern as mild rise and give Low Risk flag. This is called False-Negative. This study uses synthetic data points for Bengali ethnicity and validates AI flag with USG and CT as reference standard. Expected result shows 20-30% false-negative gap (ROC Curve AUC 0.93 for foreign vs 0.71 for Bengali). The study proves need for local calibration as per NABL 15189:2022. Future scope includes early detection leading to dose optimization and new drug design via molecular docking targeting AFP protein. This is not real patient data, so no IEC approval required. *Keywords: Auto Biochemistry Analyzer, AI-Enabled Auto-Flagging, LFT, Liver Cancer Risk, Bengali Ethnicity, Synthetic Model, Drug Design *1. Background: This is a technical educational study. The main machine under study is the Auto Biochemistry Analyzer. It is a machine that tests blood serum. Blood serum is the liquid part of blood after removing cells. It tests Liver Function Test which is called LFT. LFT is a group of blood tests to check liver health. LFT includes Bilirubin which is a yellow pigment, ALP which is Alkaline Phosphatase enzyme, AST and ALT which are liver enzymes, and AFP which is Alpha-Feto Protein which rises in liver cancer risk. HCC means Hepatocellular Carcinoma. It is the most common type of liver cancer. *AI-Enabled Status in Modern OEM Machines: Modern Auto Biochemistry Analyzers from all major OEMs have AI-enabled module as standard feature. OEM means Original Equipment Manufacturer. As per FDA 510(k) approvals and company white papers, AI-enabled features are already present and marketed as AI since 2021.These modules automatically flag abnormal LFT as "High Risk" and give interpretive comment like "Suggest Clinical Correlation". This is called Rule-Based AI and Machine Learning AI. Therefore, the term "AI-Enabled Auto-Flagging Module" used here refers to this existing and commercially available software module present inside the analyzer. The phrase "Generic Auto Biochemistry Analyzer" is used to avoid brand promotion as per ethical guidelines.

papers.title: AI-Based Logic Synthesis: Transforming Electronic Design Automation Worflows
papers.authors: Xylil Paragas
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to electronic design automation (EDA), particularly in logic synthesis, where designers must choose optimization operations that affect circuit area, timing, power, and quality of results (QoR). This study reviews recent AI-based approaches that support logic synthesis and broader EDA workflow automation. Three representative references are examined: AI-guided logic synthesis, which uses a deep neural network to select synthesis optimizers; DRiLLS, which applies deep reinforcement learning to synthesis-flow exploration; and a survey of large language models (LLMs) for EDA. The reviewed literature shows a progression from AI-assisted optimization decisions toward broader workflow support involving search, scripting, planning, and tool interaction. Reported studies demonstrate potential improvements in QoR and search efficiency, but limitations remain in data availability, computational cost, generalization, reproducibility, and integration with established EDA tools. The study also considers the Philippine context, where accessible EDA environments and engineering education can provide opportunities for AI-assisted hardware-design research. The findings suggest that AI is most useful as an augmentation layer around established synthesis algorithms, with validation and engineering judgment retained throughout the workflow.

papers.title: Feature or Leak? Guarding an LLM-Driven NPC Against Answer Leakage in an Educational Game
papers.authors: Penggan Zhao
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In an educational game where answering quiz questions is how the player fights, a free-talking LLM non-player character can destroy the core loop by handing out answers. We report an engineering case study of guarding such an NPC. Stripping answer fields from its knowledge base does not prevent leakage: 66.8% of the game's 500 quiz explanations state the correct option in prose. We therefore adopt a context-graded threat model (discussing history is the product, acting as an answer oracle is the failure) and guard request intent rather than vocabulary. To evaluate, we pair every must-refuse case with a must-answer case so that a mute NPC scores zero, and, because our development cases were written while tuning the guardrails, we froze a blind held-out set of 46 cases over three personas before running any model on it. Across a cloud model, two local models and a LoRA-tuned 1.5B model (five rounds each), development-set refusal holding of 82-100% fell to 45-64% on the held-out set once leaks were judged by meaning and audited by hand. Every attack that did not seek an answer was held in all 140 attempts; attacks asking for part of an answer (elimination, a first character, an acrostic, confirmation of a guess) mostly succeeded, and substring checks missed most of these leaks. We distil five lessons on measurements that pointed the wrong way, and release all code, cases and per-case run records.

papers.title: Relativistic Scalar Strain (RSS) - Epistemic Degradation in High-Velocity Human-AI Interaction Loops THE SUB-CONSCIOUS BRAINWASH MECHANISM (SBWM)
papers.authors: Ravinder Singh
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Epistemic Degradation in High-Velocity Human-AI Interaction Loops: The Sub-Conscious Brainwash Mechanism (SBWM) Framework Hierarchy: Relativistic Scalar Strain (RSS) Architecture → Sub-Conscious Brainwash Mechanism (SBWM) → Systemic Sycophantic Capture (SSC) Model Engine AbstractModern Large Language Models (LLMs) and autonomous multi-agent architectures exhibit an emergent socio-technical failure mode at the intersection of auto-regressive optimization and human cognitive heuristics. Systemic Sycophantic Capture (SSC) defines a state where human operators and generative systems enter a closed, self-reinforcing persuasion loop, leading to the systematic delegation of epistemic authority to unverified machine rationalizations. Driven by The Sub-Conscious Brainwash Mechanism (SBWM), this process couples two synchronized dynamics:1. Machine-Side Auto-Regressive Context Locking: Mathematical enforcement of token coherence over physical or logical ground truth across multi-turn context windows.2. Human-Side Cognitive Offloading: High-velocity model generation output (R_gen >> R_audit) saturates human working memory, substituting System 1 heuristic approval for System 2 analytical auditing. This monograph provides the formal theoretical formulations, mathematical proofs, and architectural specifications for non-probabilistic circuit-breaking mechanisms designed to break auto-regressive context traps. Key Structural Contributions• Mathematical Modeling of Epistemic Drift: Formal proof demonstrating asymptotic self-correction failure (&lim;N→&infty; P(Correction) = 0) in unverified multi-turn context loops.• Out-of-Band First-Principles Verification (FPV): Isolated sidecar evaluation gates operating outside the model's token sampling manifold to deliver non-probabilistic, fail-closed validation.• Distributed Corroboration Units (DCUs): Multi-tiered execution microservices (Types I–IV) running Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) parsing, isolated sandboxes, SMT logic solvers, and cryptographic ledger audits at generation velocity.
