papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Components and Job Redesign in Nigerian Tertiary Institutions: Does Organizational Culture Matter
papers.authors: Aziba-anyam Gift Raimi, Gloria Chinyere Chux-nyeche, Viola Nwanyisunday Ndukwu, Ifiaobebh Agnes Ita
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into administrative work, yet evidence remains limited on whether specific AI components translate into measurable job redesign and whether organisational culture conditions this relationship. This study examined the relationships between optical character recognition (OCR), chatbots and virtual assistants (CVA), robotic process automation (RPA), organisational culture and job redesign. Objectives: To assess the associations of OCR, CVA and RPA with job redesign and determine whether organisational culture moderates these relationships among administrative personnel. Methods: A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted among 323 respondents. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, multiple linear regression, and hierarchical moderation regression were used. Statistical inference was based on regression coefficients, F tests, P values and explained variance. Results: Respondents reported relatively favourable levels of OCR (M = 3.882, SD = 0.831), CVA (M = 3.849, SD = 0.873), organisational culture (M = 3.819, SD = 0.849), RPA (M = 3.811, SD = 0.905) and job redesign (M = 3.730, SD = 0.868). Correlations among variables were minimal. Collectively, OCR, CVA, and RPA explained only 0.2% of variance in job redesign, and the regression model was not significant (F(3,319) = 0.165, P = 0.920). None of the predictors was independently significant: OCR (β = 0.014, P = 0.797), CVA (β = 0.021, P = 0.708), and RPA (β = 0.031, P = 0.582). Organisational culture did not significantly moderate the AI–job-redesign relationship (β = 0.018, P = 0.891). Conclusion: AI-component adoption was not associated with measurable job redesign in this sample, and organisational culture did not significantly alter these relationships. AI implementation may therefore enhance specific administrative processes without necessarily restructuring jobs. Recommendation: Institutions should complement AI deployment with task redesign, workflow integration, employee capability development and implementation-readiness strategies rather than assuming that technology adoption alone will transform jobs. Significant statement: These findings challenge a simple technology-deterministic assumption that AI adoption automatically produces job redesign and highlight the importance of examining the organisational and task-level mechanisms through which AI becomes consequential for work.

papers.title: Design and Preliminary Validation of a ROS2-Based Autonomous Mobile Robot for AI-Assisted Airport Security and Terahertz Screening
papers.authors: Mahmood Nurul Hossain, Mahmood Nurul Hossain, Fawaz Mustafa, Mohammed Nurul Hossain, Mohammed Nurul Hossain, Hamad Khalid, Avent Rao, Khaled Goher (11878018)
papers.abstract: Airport security screening is largely concentrated at fixed checkpoints, leaving limited opportunities for continuous monitoring within terminal areas. This paper presents the design and preliminary validation of a ROS2-based autonomous mobile robot intended to provide an additional security layer through real-time object detection, tracking, mapping, navigation, and future integration of non-ionizing terahertz-(THz) imaging. The prototype integrates an NVIDIA Jetson Orin, Intel RealSense D415 camera, RPLidar-A1, Arduino-based motor control, and a mobile platform. ROS2, RViz2, Navigation2, and YOLOv11 were used to combine perception, visualization, motion control, and system monitoring. Laboratory tests demonstrated live indoor mapping, detection of people and objects, persistent tracking identities, target tracking, motor operation, and wireless access. A survey of 54 respondents examined passenger acceptability; half expressed comfort with mobile robotic scanning, while 75.9% believed it could improve airport security. Acceptance depended strongly on non-ionizing operation, privacy protection, transparency, and human oversight. Because the THz camera was not experimentally integrated owing to budget constraints, concealed-object detection remains a proposed capability. The study establishes a functional foundation for future THz-RGB-D-LiDAR fusion, quantitative performance evaluation, cybersecurity assessment, and controlled airport trials. It also identifies key technical, ethical, regulatory, and human-factor requirements for responsible deployment in crowded, safety-critical airport terminal environments.

papers.title: Human Factors in AI-Assisted Interpreter Training: A Design Science Approach to Human-Centred Educational Technology
papers.authors: Adrián Valledor, Francisco Calles-Esteban, Josefa Gómez, Abdelhamid Tayebi
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education creates opportunities to support learning, but its educational value depends not only on technological capabilities but also on human–AI interaction. This issue is particularly relevant in interpreter training, where learning involves high cognitive demands, contextual decision-making, and time-sensitive activities. This study investigates how Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI) principles can guide the design of AI-assisted educational environments for interpreter training. A Design Science Research (DSR) methodology was adopted to develop and evaluate an AI-assisted learning environment integrating AI capabilities across the interpreter training cycle. Drawing on literature on Computer-Assisted Interpreting, HCAI, human–AI interaction, technology acceptance, and interpreting cognition, five design principles were derived: learner agency and human control, transparency and calibrated trust, protection of cognitive resources, contextualised assistance, and AI as a support for learning. These principles were operationalised in the artefact and evaluated through heuristic evaluation and a technology acceptance study involving 42 professional interpreters. Results show that perceived usefulness alone is insufficient to explain technology acceptance, with trust, reliability, ease of use, latency, workflow integration, and cognitive demands also shaping adoption. The study contributes a human-centred framework for aligning AI capabilities with learners’ needs and educational objectives.

papers.title: Learning from Adaptive Oscillatory Modes: An Interpretable Synchrosqueezing Transformer for Patient-Independent Seizure Detection
papers.authors: Afrah Alanazi, Kais Khaldi, Sarah Almaghrabi, Hamed Alshammari
papers.abstract: Transformer-based analysis of physiological signals depends critically on how input tokens are constructed, yet conventional tokens derived from raw temporal windows or spectrogram patches may overlook the intrinsic oscillatory organization of electroencephalographic (EEG) activity. To address this limitation, we propose AMST-Former, an adaptive mode-wise synchrosqueezing Transformer for patient-independent epileptic seizure detection. Each EEG channel is first decomposed into oscillatory modes using Adaptive Local Iterative Filtering (ALIF), after which the Synchrosqueezing Transform (SST) is applied independently to each mode. This decomposition-before-synchrosqueezing strategy reduces cross-component interference in instantaneous-frequency estimation while preserv- ing mode-specific time–frequency dynamics. The resulting time–frequency patches are embedded together with channel, mode-frequency, and positional information. A hierarchical factorized-attention mechanism then models token relevance across time–frequency regions, oscillatory modes, and EEG channels before a Transformer encoder captures their interactions. Evaluation using a repeated patient-independent five-fold cross-validation protocol on the CHB-MIT database (22 subjects) yielded an F1-score of 70.76% and an area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.870. At the event level, AMST-Former achieved a sensitivity of 81.4% at one false detection per 24 h. Ablation experi- ments showed that mode-wise SST provided more effective representations than direct SST, per-mode Hilbert spectra, and fixed filter-bank decomposition. Furthermore, the factorized-attention mechanism provides mode, time–frequency, and channel-level explanations, whose faithfulness was assessed through deletion analysis. These results support adaptive mode-wise time–frequency tokenization as a promising strategy for interpretable, patient-independent EEG seizure detection.

papers.title: Pemberdayaan Guru TK Melalui Pemanfaatan Generative AI Gratis untuk Inovasi Pembelajaran Anak Usia Dini
papers.authors: Setio Basuki, Mahar Faiqurrahman, Zeedan Mustami Argani, Rahmatun  Nikmah, Elga Putri Tri Farma
papers.journal: IJCOSIN Indonesian Journal of Community Service and Innovation
papers.abstract: The presence of digital technology in supporting early childhood education (PAUD) is considered increasingly important. This is in line with the development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology. One technology that teachers can utilize is Generative AI (GenAI), which is capable of generating text, images, audio, and learning ideas. Situational analysis at partners shows that many teachers have not yet adapted to GenAI to create innovative learning materials. Free access to GenAI technology allows teachers to save time, expand the variety of learning media, and create more engaging learning experiences. This mentoring activity aims to improve the competency of PAUD teachers through practical activities implementing AI, namely ChatGPT, Gemini, Bing Image Creator, Canva, and Narakeet. The results of the activity achieved an average increase in AI understanding (13.96%), AI utilization practices (48.18%), and understanding of AI tools (71.93%) in creating PAUD learning materials. This proves that PAUD teachers can develop creative learning media independently without relying on paid resources, while simultaneously increasing the interactivity and quality of early childhood learning experiences.

papers.title: AI-MEDIATED FEEDBACK AND IELTS SPEAKING PERFORMANCE: AN INVESTIGATION INTO STUDENT PROGRESS AND PERCEPTIONS
papers.authors: Duong Thu Ha
papers.abstract: This study examines the potential impact of a human-AI collaborative feedback system on the IELTS speaking abilities of upper-intermediate English majors at a university in Vietnam. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used, with the research focusing on the students’ oral performance over a 4-week formative assessment period. The quantitative findings, derived from a pre-test and post-test conducted with a single group as a quasi-experimental study and from a 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire completed by the participants (N = 76), were supplemented by the qualitative responses to three open-ended survey questions. The quantitative data indicated a statistically significant improvement only in the area of Lexical Resource, whereas the overall band scores did not show a significant change, likely due to a temporary compromise between linguistic complexity and oral spontaneity. The survey results revealed that the learners regarded score breakdowns based on criteria as highly valuable and also placed importance on justifications of their transcripts that were supported by evidence in order to encourage self-regulated learning. At the same time, the qualitative responses emphasized that ongoing involvement by human experts is still necessary for overcoming affective barriers and for ensuring evaluative reliability. The study therefore proposes a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) framework that combines the accuracy of automation with the guidance of pedagogy and thus complements standalone AI evaluation tools in the context of language assessment.

papers.title: Development of an AI-Based Assessment Analytics Model for Transformative Teacher Professional Education
papers.authors: Didah Nurhamidah, Muhammad Ridhwan, Nuryani Nuryani
papers.journal: Jurnal Pendidikan Teori Penelitian dan Pengembangan
papers.abstract: Transformative Teacher Professional Education (PPG) requires an assessment system that not only produces scores, but is also able to map competency achievements, identify risks, and provide data-driven follow-up recommendations. This research aims to develop an artificial intelligence-based assessment analytics model to support the monitoring of academic development and intervention of PPG UIN Syarif Hidayatullah Jakarta students. The research uses a Research and Development approach with the ADDIE model which includes the Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, and Evaluate stages. Data was obtained through needs analysis, document review, interviews, observations, expert validation, system tests, user questionnaires, and assessment data in the form of tryout results and reflective essay responses. The results of the analysis showed that 91.6% of students needed automatic learning recommendations and 94.1% needed individual competency weakness mapping. The product developed is a web-based platform that contains a tryout dashboard, reflective essay analysis, risk mapping, essay forms, an administration panel, data filtering, and report export. The results of expert validation obtained an average score of 4.94 with the very feasible category, while the implementation results obtained an average score of 4.91 with the very feasible category. This model is considered very practical, operationally effective, and beneficial for supervisors and PPG managers. These findings suggest that AI-based assessment analytics have the potential to strengthen diagnostic assessments, achievement monitoring, and data-driven academic interventions, although their impact on graduation improvement still requires longitudinal testing.

papers.title: Technology-assisted interventions for second language speaking anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: huan wang
papers.abstract: 1. Administrative information 1a. Title Technology-assisted interventions for second language speaking anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis of component-level and technology-type effects. Original-language title: 技术辅助干预对二语口语焦虑的影响：按焦虑分量与技术类型拆解的系统评价与元分析 1b. Registration To be registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at osf.io (registration DOI issued on submission). INPLASY (inplasy.com) is the fallback. PROSPERO is not used because it is oriented to health-related outcomes and this review addresses language-learning anxiety. 1c. Authors and contributions Flora Genius — conception, screening, data extraction, analysis, writing. Reviewer 2 — independent screening and risk-of-bias assessment (to be recruited; see §7 selection process). 1d. Amendments Amendments to this protocol after registration will be logged on the OSF project wiki with date, rationale, and the affected section; deviations will be reported in the final manuscript under "Differences between protocol and review". 1e. Support Funding: [to be declared] Competing interests: none declared. 2. Introduction 2a. Rationale Foreign language speaking anxiety (FLSA) is among the most prevalent affective barriers in second-language (L2) learning, impairing oral production, classroom participation, and persistence (Horwitz, Horwitz, & Cope, 1986). Technology-assisted speaking practice — immersive virtual reality (VR), AI chatbots/conversational agents, and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback — has become the dominant contemporary remedy. Yet reported effects are inconsistent: immersive VR both reduces anxiety (Kaplan-Rakowski & Gruber, 2023) and, in some contexts, increases it by heightening perceived realism (Pertaub, Slater, & Barker, 2002). A prior meta-analysis of technology interventions on foreign language anxiety (24 studies, 2016–2021) found that fewer than half of the interventions reduced anxiety, but did not decompose FLSA into its components. A 2025 systematic review (Huang et al., Humanities and Social Sciences Communications) explicitly notes that prior reviews "failed to link specific technologies systematically to the three anxiety components — communication apprehension, fear of negative evaluation, and test anxiety." No published meta-analysis to date has (a) decomposed FLSA into components and (b) linked each technology affordance to a specific component. A scoping search (OpenAlex, 2026-10-05, five PICO-aligned queries) returned 120 deduplicated records, confirming a sufficient and rapidly growing body of empirical intervention studies across all three core technology types plus adjacent technologies (synchronous computer-mediated communication [SCMC], mobile-assisted language learning [MALL], telecollaboration). This supports the feasibility of a component- and technology-type-stratified synthesis. 2b. Objectives Primary objective. To estimate the pooled effect of technology-assisted speaking interventions on FLSA (overall and by anxiety component) compared with traditional or lower-immersion instruction, in L2/EFL/ESL learners. Secondary objectives. To test whether the effect differs by (i) technology type (VR / AI chatbot / ASR / other technology), (ii) anxiety component (communication apprehension / fear of negative evaluation / test anxiety), (iii) educational level, and (iv) intervention duration. Research question (PICO). In second/foreign language learners, do technology-assisted speaking interventions (immersive VR, AI chatbot, ASR feedback, or other technology) compared with traditional instruction reduce foreign language speaking anxiety, and does the effect differ across anxiety components and technology types? 3. Methods 3a. Eligibility criteria (PICO) Population. L2/EFL/ESL learners at any educational level (primary, secondary, tertiary) and any first-language background; classroom and out-of-class contexts; no proficiency exclusion (proficiency coded as a moderator where reported). Intervention. Technology-assisted speaking practice via one of four categories: Immersive virtual reality (head-mounted display); AI chatbot / conversational agent (including large-language-model–based tutors); Automatic speech recognition–based speaking/pronunciation feedback; Other technology (synchronous computer-mediated communication, mobile-assisted language learning, telecollaboration). Comparator. Traditional non-technology instruction (teacher-led speaking practice, textbook drill, or no speaking practice), or a lower-immersion technology control (e.g., desktop VR, video watching). Outcomes. Primary: overall FLSA (FLCAS total or equivalent validated scale); communication apprehension; fear of negative evaluation. Secondary: test anxiety; speaking proficiency/oral performance. Study designs. Randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies with a control/comparison group (pretest–posttest or between-groups). Single-group pre–post designs and correlational studies are excluded. Other eligibility. Language: English and Chinese. Time: inception to search date. Publication status: peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, theses, and preprints (grey literature included to reduce publication bias; sensitivity analysis excludes grey literature). 3b. Information sources PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, CNKI (Chinese); supplemented by ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, conference proceedings (CALL/EUROCALL/AACL), and backward/forward citation chasing of included studies and prior reviews. An updated rerun of all searches will be performed within three months of submission. 3c. Search strategy The full PubMed strategy is reproduced in the protocol package (Part 2.1). Each database uses the same three concept blocks — (technology) AND (anxiety) AND (L2 population) — adapted to its syntax: Database Adaptation PubMed MeSH + [tiab], as in protocol package §2.1 Scopus TITLE-ABS-KEY with the same three blocks Web of Science TS= field; filter to Linguistics / Education & Educational Research categories ERIC descriptors + free terms (Second Language Learning, Anxiety, Computer Assisted Instruction) CNKI Chinese boolean equivalent Grey literature ProQuest, conference archives, OpenAlex Search records (date, database, query, hits) will be logged per PRISMA-S. 3d. Study records Data management. Deduplication in EndNote/Zotero; screening in a shared spreadsheet (Rayyan or Covidence if a licence is available). Selection process (two stages). Title/abstract screening by two independent reviewers against eligibility criteria. Full-text screening by two independent reviewers; disagreements resolved by discussion, with a third reviewer arbitrating. Pilot screening on a 10% sample precedes full screening; inter-rater agreement reported (Cohen's κ or percentage agreement). Data collection process. Two independent extractors using a standardized form (protocol package Part 3: study-level and effect-level sheets); discrepancies resolved by consensus. 3e. Data items See the coding sheets (protocol package Part 3). Study-level: design, technology type, immersion level, country, educational level, target language, sample sizes, duration, sessions, anxiety instrument and validation status, control type, funding, RoB ratings. Effect-level: outcome, means/SDs/Ns (or reported Hedges' g), direction of scoring, and reporting status (reported/computed/imputed). Where component subscale scores are not reported, authors will be contacted; if unavailable, the study contributes to the total-score synthesis only, and this is reported as a limitation. 3f. Outcomes and prioritisation FLSA total is the anchor outcome. Component scores are extracted whenever reported. Speaking proficiency is a secondary outcome analysed separately. Effect size is Hedges' g (continuous outcome, between-groups or pretest–posttest), computed such that negative g = intervention reduces anxiety (higher anxiety score = worse outcome). 3g. Risk of bias in individual studies RCTs → Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2). Quasi-experimental studies → ROBINS-I. Two independent raters; disagreements resolved by consensus. 3h. Data synthesis Effect size: Hedges' g with 95% CI; between-groups and pretest–posttest designs computed separately and combined with appropriate variance corrections. Model: random-effects (restricted maximum likelihood, REML), given expected heterogeneity. Dependence: multiple effect sizes per study (multiple components, technology arms, timepoints) handled with robust variance estimation (RVE) or a three-level model. Heterogeneity: I², τ², and Q; I² > 50% triggers subgroup/meta-regression analysis. Software: R (metafor), aligned with the installed meta-analysis-r skill. 3i. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses Prespecified subgroups. (1) technology type (VR / AI chatbot / ASR / other technology); (2) anxiety component (communication apprehension / fear of negative evaluation / test anxiety); (3) educational level (school vs university); (4) intervention duration (≤4 weeks vs >4 weeks). Prespecified sensitivity analyses. (1) excluding high-risk-of-bias studies; (2) retaining only controlled designs; (3) excluding non-validated anxiety instruments; (4) fixed-effect model as a robustness check; (5) excluding grey literature. 3j. Meta-bias(es) Publication bias assessed by funnel plot and Egger's test when ≥10 studies are available, plus trim-and-fill. Selective-outcome reporting noted during extraction; small-study effects interpreted cautiously given expected heterogeneity. 3k. Confidence in cumulative evidence Overall certainty rated with GRADE (downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias), reported as a summary-of-findings table. 4. Timeline Milestone Target Protocol registration (OSF) 2026-10-15 Search completion + dedup 2026-11-01 Screening (title/abstract → full text) 2026-12-15 Data extraction + RoB 2027-02-01 Analysis 2027-03-15 Manuscript 2027-05-01 Updated rerun search

papers.title: Adaptive strategies of the history of Russian philosophy
papers.authors: A.V. Malinov
papers.abstract: This article explores possible areas of integrating the history of Russian philosophy into the contemporary educational environment, its place in the cultural situation of our time and philosophy as a whole. It is noted that the history of Russian philosophy as an academic discipline began to fully develop only in the second half of the 20th century, and the formation of a community of historians of Russian philosophy was completed only in the first decade of the 21st century. Both the process of institutionalization of the history of Russian philosophy (the formation of departments, research centers, seminars, etc.) and an example of its deinstitutionalization are considered. The issues of the degree of integration of the history of Russian philosophy into the teaching of the general course of philosophy in higher education, the possibilities of conducting individual classes as electives or optional courses and their effectiveness as means of transmitting Russian philosophy to the public environment are discussed; the relationship between the history of Russian philosophy and other national studies is discussed. Possible negative consequences for the discipline itself are noted in the event of its adaptation to political expediency. Adaptive strategies for the implementation of the discipline of the history of Russian philosophy are analyzed. In this regard, the opportunities offered by the digital environment and artificial intelligence are highlighted. Commemorative practices and the prospects of philosophical regional studies are also considered.

papers.title: i-Sihat 2026
papers.abstract: Breast cancer remains one of the most prevalent health challenges affecting women worldwide, yet gaps in breast health literacy continue to hinder early detection and informed healthcare decision-making.In the era of Society 5.0, where technology is increasingly designed to serve human needs, artificial intelligence presents new opportunities to transform health education into a more accessible, engaging, and empowering experience.This plenary session introduces the Breast Imaging Education Bot (BieBot), a human-centric artificial intelligence (AI) initiative developed to enhance breast health literacy and promote proactive health behaviours among communities.Designed as a bilingual conversational chatbot, BieBot provides evidence-based information on breast cancer awareness, risk factors, screening options, and breast self-examination through an interactive and user-friendly digital platform.By integrating educational content, multimedia resources, instructional videos, and direct access to screening-related services, the initiative seeks to bridge knowledge gaps while improving access to reliable health information.The presentation will showcase the development journey of BieBot, highlighting how human-centred design principles, stakeholder engagement, and healthcare expertise were combined to create a meaningful digital health solution.Community evaluation findings reveal high levels of user acceptance, demonstrating the chatbot's effectiveness in supporting self-directed learning and increasing awareness of breast health practices.Furthermore, the initiative illustrates the potential of AI-powered health education to extend beyond awareness campaigns by fostering empowerment, informed decision-making, and greater participation in preventive healthcare.By sharing the BieBot experience, this session offers a practical example of how human-centric AI can be leveraged to create inclusive, scalable, and impactful healthcare innovations.The discussion will provide valuable insights for healthcare professionals, educators, researchers, and policymakers seeking to harness emerging technologies to improve health literacy and strengthen community wellbeing in the digital age.

papers.title: Impact of generative AI on Teaching and Learning Processes
papers.authors: Manjusha Gundale, Priya Porwal, Ms. Usha V
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has become a highly transformative technology with the capacity to reshape teaching and learning in schools and other educational institutions.Since it can facilitate intelligent content generation, adaptive learning, automated assessment, and personalized instructional support, Generative AI provides numerous opportunities for improving the quality of education, increasing learner engagement, and boosting instructional efficiency.This paper gives a critical look at the effect of Generative AI on teaching and learning by looking at its applications, advantages, challenges, and future potential in the education sector.The study looks at major opportunities such as personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, content creation, and collaborative learning environments, while also tackling important issues like algorithmic opacity, explainability, data privacy and security, bias and fairness, academic integrity, and the reliability of content produced by AI.The paper also examines ways of responsibly introducing Generative AI by creating transparent and ethical AI frameworks, establishing strong data governance mechanisms, setting up appropriate regulatory policies, and using high-quality training datasets.It stresses the need to give teachers the necessary AI skills through ongoing professional development so that they can effectively incorporate AI-based teaching methods.Lastly, the study highlights some of the new trends in AI-driven education, such as intelligent tutoring systems, immersive virtual learning environments, adaptive assessment, and collaborative human-AI learning ecosystems.The results show that although Generative AI offers great potential for enhancing educational accessibility, personalization, and learning outcomes, its successful implementation relies on ethical governance, responsible use, and continued cooperation between educators, researchers, policymakers, and technology developers.

papers.title: AI-Powered Autonomy: Reforming Digital Privacy in Dominant Markets Through Consumer Protection Framework
papers.authors: Moch. Marsa Taufiqurrohman, Tarsisius Murwadji, Helza Nova Lita, Vicko Taniady
papers.journal: Journal of Law and Legal Reform
papers.abstract: This research examines how artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems deployed by dominant digital platforms, particularly in Indonesia’s e-commerce, undermine consumer autonomy through extensive data harvesting and preference manipulation. The study aims to analyze these AI-driven mechanisms against the consumer protection principles set out in Law No. 8/1999, particularly regarding consumers’ rights to accurate information and protection from deceptive practices. The research problem centers on the interpretive legal analysis of whether AI-powered personalization and opaque algorithmic decision-making violate consumer protection obligations, specifically transparency requirements and honest business practices mandated by Indonesian Consumer Protection Law. This study employs a doctrinal legal analysis methodology, incorporating a comparative assessment of Indonesian consumer law against the European Union’s regulatory framework, examining consumer protection frameworks, and conducting comparative case studies from global jurisdictions to develop comprehensive regulatory solutions. The research proposes an AI-Consumer Protection Framework requiring dominant platforms to provide clear, comprehensible information about algorithmic processes affecting consumers, ensuring compliance with transparency obligations under Articles 4 and 7 of the Consumer Protection Law. Findings reveal that current AI practices by digital platforms often violate consumer rights through manipulative algorithms and insufficient disclosure mechanisms. The study concludes that implementing mandatory algorithmic transparency and explainable AI practices would effectively safeguard consumer autonomy while ensuring fair business practices in digital markets. The proposed framework establishes governance structures that uphold consumer rights, promote algorithmic accountability, and support equitable digital commerce while balancing technological innovation with fundamental consumer protections required by Indonesian law.

papers.title: Metric Improvement of Single Image Hand Reconstruction by 3D NIR Active Stereo and Model Based Surface Reconstruction
papers.authors: Yan ZHANG, Roland Ramm, Wang LIAO, Chen ZHANG, Gunther Notni
papers.abstract: Metric hand reconstruction can support human-robot interaction and geometric annotation of signlanguage datasets.However, current mainstream hand reconstruction methods rely on monocular images, and their predictions remain uncertain in absolute size and camera-relative position.We present a method that combines patten-projection-based near-infrared (NIR) active stereo with WiLoR (image-based hand reconstruction) for initialization and MANO (a parametric hand model) for surface fitting to reconstruct articulated hands in a calibrated camera coordinate system.WiLoR estimates an initial hand model from an unpatterned NIR image without NIR-specific fine-tuning.Scale initialization using a thumb-segment prior preserves the predicted image projection, and perspective-n-point fitting adapts the model to the calibrated camera intrinsics.Geometric optimization then aligns the hand with the measured point cloud through rigid registration followed by joint refinement of articulation, shape and global pose.Evaluation uses recordings across 23 acquisition conditions, covering hand motion, challenging orientations, gloves and two image-binning modes.Across 12,001 paired hand reconstructions, the point-weighted mean surface distance decreases from 68.985 to 3.286 mm, a reduction of 95.24%.Exploratory motion analysis characterizes surface errors across estimated-speed intervals.The results demonstrate improved agreement with measured hand surfaces.

papers.title: The Effects of High-Intensity Functional Training With a Respiratory Muscle Training Device on Performance, Mood, and Ventilatory Function
papers.authors: Alexa J. Chandler, Chimaobim E. Martin-Diala, Gianna F. Mastrofini, Sten O. Stray-Gundersen, Ryan Artsinger, Noah Nakagawa, Shawn M. Arent
papers.journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
papers.abstract: Abstract Chandler, AJ, Martin-Diala, C, Mastrofini, GF, Stray-Gundersen, S, Artsinger, R, Nakagawa, N, and Arent, SM. The effects of high-intensity functional training with a respiratory muscle training device on performance, mood, and ventilatory function. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2026—Respiratory muscle training (RMT) may enhance exercise performance by delaying respiratory muscle fatigue. This study examined the effects of performing an RMT protocol during high-intensity functional training (HIFT) on pulmonary function, exercise performance, and psychometrics. Twenty-six volunteers (age = 22.4 ± 1.9 years, BMI = 23.8 ± 3.0 kg·m −2 ) were randomized into an RMT or control group and completed three 30-minute HIFT sessions per week for 6 weeks. Each session included 4 rounds of 6 exercises using a 30:30-second work-to-rest ratio, with 2.5 minutes of rest between rounds. Pretesting and posttesting occurred across 3 days. On day 1, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Positive and Negative Affect Scale, Profile of Mood States, spirometry, body composition, and V̇ o 2 max testing were completed. On day 2, countermovement jump testing and the Wingate Anaerobic Test were performed. On day 3, an 18-minute HIFT-specific test was administered. Repeated-measures analyses of variance and analysis of covariance with baseline V̇ o 2 max as a covariate were used to determine time and group main effects and group-by-time interactions with significance set at p < 0.05 for all analyses. Analysis of covariances revealed group-by-time interaction for forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity approached significance ( p = 0.06; = 0.05). Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores improved, % body fat decreased and fat-free mass increased, V̇ o 2 max improved, and HIFT performance improved over time for both groups ( p < 0.05), with no differences between groups. These results suggest no additive benefits of the RMT device when used during HIFT sessions. Future research should investigate if RMT sessions completed outside of exercise provide benefits beyond those seen with exercise alone.

papers.title: Designing generative AI–powered reflective learning dashboards for enhancing self-regulated learning in higher education
papers.authors: Thacha Lawanna
papers.abstract: A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. Using a quasi-experimental design, 180 undergraduate students participated in a 12-week intervention comparing traditional instructor feedback with AI-generated reflective feedback. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in self-regulated learning behaviours, time on task, login frequency and academic performance (p < .001), indicating strong effects on both cognitive and behavioural dimensions of learning. In addition, students reported high levels of perceived usefulness, trust, personalisation and positive attitudes towards AI-generated feedback, supported by qualitative insights highlighting increased motivation and learner agency. The findings demonstrate that combining generative AI with learning analytics transforms feedback into a dynamic, dialogic process that enhances reflective thinking and adaptive learning. This study contributes a scalable, human-centred and ethically grounded model for improving both learning outcomes and learner experience in digital education environments. Implications for practice or policy: University administrators should implement transparent AI dashboards ensuring ethics, privacy and accountability. Educators can enhance reflective learning by integrating adaptive AI feedback that supports metacognitive development. Policymakers should promote AI literacy and self-regulated learning within higher education frameworks. Technology developers need to design user-centred and interpretable AI systems aligned with pedagogical objectives. Higher education leaders should foster AI-supported reflection, professional development and evidence-based innovation for sustainable transformation.

papers.title: The Teacher-Guided Generative AI for Sustainable EFL Writing Development: Longitudinal Validation of the AI-MWD Framework
papers.authors: Jargal Tugsuu, Sainzaya Sumiya
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing instruction by providing immediate, individualized, and context-sensitive feedback. Despite these advantages, increasing evidence suggests that unguided interaction with GenAI often overwhelms learners' cognitive capacity, encourages passive dependence on AI-generated revisions, and weakens the development of long-term writing autonomy. This study addresses this challenge by proposing and empirically validating the AI-Based Metacognitive Writing Development (AI-MWD) Framework, a teacher-guided instructional framework that integrates macro-pedagogical scaffolding with AI-enabled micro-scaffolding to promote sustainable writing development. A 14-week longitudinal quasi-experimental study was conducted with forty undergraduate EFL learners assigned to either an experimental group receiving the AI-MWD intervention or a control group using the same GenAI tools without structured teacher guidance. Independent-samples t-tests examined differences in cognitive load and metacognitive writing autonomy, while 2 × 3 mixed-design ANOVAs evaluated longitudinal changes in Complexity, Accuracy, and Fluency (CAF) across pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test measures. The findings revealed that teacher-guided AI significantly reduced learners' extraneous cognitive load while substantially enhancing metacognitive writing autonomy. Although both groups demonstrated comparable improvements in writing accuracy immediately after the intervention, only the AI-MWD group maintained these gains six weeks later, indicating significantly stronger long-term retention of linguistic knowledge. Unlike previous AI-assisted writing studies that primarily report immediate performance improvements, this study demonstrates that teacher-guided scaffold fading is the critical mechanism through which AI-supported feedback becomes internalized as learners' metacognitive writing strategies. The proposed AI-MWD Framework therefore reconceptualizes generative AI not as an autonomous instructional agent, but as a pedagogically mediated cognitive scaffold capable of supporting sustainable second-language writing development. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence, Teacher-Guided Instruction, Metacognitive Writing, Cognitive Load, Scaffolding, Writing Autonomy, Longitudinal Learning, EFL Writing

papers.title: The Somnogenesis System
papers.authors: Mouhammad Ousmane Ndiaye
papers.abstract: For more than 150 years, since the idea that mental illness is rooted in the brain first emerged in the mid-1800s, psychiatry has searched for a reliable biological system to anchor its understanding of mental illness. This paper proposes a candidate for that system, starting from a striking observation. Almost every major psychiatric disorder shows three things together: REM sleep disturbance, altered default mode network (DMN) activity, and emotional dysregulation. The DMN is independently known to play a central role in emotional regulation and emotional memory, which is what suggests these three recurring findings are not coincidental but are manifestations of a single, previously unidentified biological system. The Somnogenesis System hypothesis states that the DMN's three principal hubs, the medial prefrontal cortex, the posterior cingulate cortex and precuneus, and the bilateral inferior parietal cortices, reactivate in a specific, ordered sequence during every REM period, and that this order is identical across the large majority of healthy individuals. Each hub carries an established, distinct function, and the evidence suggests these functions operate as a dependency chain rather than as independent, parallel contributions, consistent with the proposed existence of a genuine biological system rather than three regions coincidentally active at the same time. This hypothesis can be tested without collecting new data. A protocol is proposed using an existing public dataset of simultaneous EEG-fMRI sleep recordings, in which the three hubs are anatomically defined using a standardized cortical atlas and each REM period's activation order is estimated from onset latency rather than raw BOLD timing, controlling for each region's own hemodynamic response. Confirming the hypothesis would reframe REM sleep as the physiological interface of an underlying biological system, with implications for conditions including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy, and major depressive disorder, where a disrupted system rather than a disrupted stage may be the more precise marker of pathology. The hypothesis is directly falsifiable, a failure to find a consistent, shared order would refute it outright.

papers.title: EEG emotion recognition via multilevel entropy analysis: The power of entropy of entropy on phase dynamics
papers.authors: Morteza Jafari Malali, Sepideh Zolfaghari, Raheleh Davoodi
papers.abstract: Emotion recognition from EEG signals has become a central task in affective computing, offering non-invasive insight into human emotional states. Due to the nonlinear and nonstationary nature of EEG, entropy-based features have gained prominence as reliable indicators of brain complexity. However, traditional entropy metrics-such as Shannon entropy (ShanEn) and its variants-often lack sensitivity to transient dynamics and multiscale irregularities in the brain's electrical activity. This study introduces a novel application of Entropy of Entropy (EoE) to EEG phase series (EoE - phase), aiming to enhance the detection of emotional states by capturing second-order variability in signal complexity. Unlike conventional measures, EoE quantifies not just signal unpredictability, but also the fluctuation of that unpredictability over time, offering a more dynamic representation of neural information flow. Using the GAMEEMO dataset, which includes EEG recordings from 28 participants during four emotion-evoking game scenarios (funny, boring, horror, calm), we computed and compared four feature sets: Phase Entropy, EoE - phase, ShanEn, and EoE applied to EEG amplitude time series. These features were classified using six machine learning models, including AdaBoost, SVM, and Random Forest. Our results demonstrate that EoE applied to phase dynamics significantly outperforms other entropy-based features, achieving a classification accuracy of 71.7% and AUC of 0.869 using the RF classifier with mixed PhaseEn and EoE-phase features, while traditional Shannon-based features reached only ~59% accuracy. This study provides the first systematic evaluation of EoE on EEG phase signals for emotion recognition, revealing its strong discriminative power and potential for integration into next-generation brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: From Systems Map to Systemic Actions: Co-creating actions to promote physical activity with adolescents and adult stakeholders in YoPA Denmark
papers.authors: Line Madsen, Elise Rivera, Jasper Schipperijn, Charlotte Skau Pawlowski, Teatske M. Altenburg, Mai J. M. Chinapaw
papers.abstract: Aim Physical inactivity among adolescents remains a major public health challenge, particularly among those in vulnerable life situations. Systems thinking and co-creation are promising approaches for intervention development, yet limited evidence exists on how system insights can be translated into concrete actions. This study aimed to co-create actions targeting systems change to promote outdoor physical activity among adolescents. Methods An 8-month participatory, systems-informed co-creation process was conducted in two Danish youth clubs, involving 24 adolescents, 11 staff members, two researchers, and a facilitator. Across nine co-creation sessions, participants built on a previously developed systems map to translate system insights into concrete actions. Results The co-creation process resulted in four context-specific actions aimed at improving opportunities for outdoor physical activity. Together, the actions addressed the physical environment, maintenance practices, organisational routines, adult facilitation, peer relationships, self-expression, and adolescents’ sense of ownership and belonging. Using the Action Scales Model, the actions primarily targeted system structures through changes to environments, routines, maintenance practices, facilitation, and opportunities for activity. Several actions also addressed system goals and beliefs related to adolescent participation and outdoor physical activity. Conclusion The four actions illustrate how locally identified systemic constraints can be translated into concrete actions addressing multiple aspects and levels of the youth club system. The study provides practical insights into translating system insights into contextually grounded actions. Further research is needed to examine their implementation, interactions with the wider youth club system, and potential influence on adolescents’ outdoor physical activity.

papers.title: EEG-Based Inner Speech Decoding Using Phase-Locking and Spatial Features with a Dual-Branch Deep Learning Model
papers.authors: Hussna Elnoor Mohammed Abdalla, Hamidon Basri, Ishak b. Aris, Abdul Hanif Khan Yusof Khan, Sureshkumar Natarajan, Muhammad Shaufil Adha, Wurood Fadhil Abbasa, Siti Hajjar Zakaria, S. A. R. Al-Haddad
papers.abstract: Background Decoding inner speech from electroencephalogram signals presents a promising direction for advancing brain-computer interface technologies. However, this remains a highly challenging task because of factors such as the inherently low signal-to-noise ratio, significant inter-subject variability, and the complex, non-stationary nature of neural activity captured in EEG data. Methods This study presents a novel classification framework that combines instantaneous phase-locking value and common spatial patterns for feature extraction. The dimensionality of the instantaneous phase-locking features was reduced using principal component analysis. The two feature types are processed independently using Recurrent Neural Networks and Deep Neural Networks and then concatenated for the final classification. The model was evaluated under both subject-dependent (S-d) and subject-independent (S-Ind) settings on two publicly available EEG dataset. The first dataset includes imagined speech from five individuals in two categories: social and numerical, while the second dataset includes inner speech from ten participants performing four Spanish-word commands. Results The proposed model demonstrated strong performance in the S-d setting, achieving average accuracies of 95.16 ± 3.50% for social words and 95.96 ± 2.40% for numerical words, with macro F1-scores exceeding 95.19%. For the second dataset, the mean S-d accuracy was 90.23 ± 10.61%, while S-Ind accuracies were 64.09 ± 3.20% and 52.19 ± 2.64% for the second and first datasets, respectively, highlighting the challenge of cross-subject generalization in EEG-based inner speech decoding. Notably, the proposed method outperformed previously reported approaches on both datasets, achieving relative improvements of up to 226.21%. Conclusion The proposed approach shows strong performance in subject-dependent inner speech decoding and provides additional validation across two publicly available EEG datasets with different participants and task configurations. While the method shows practical potential, the results also highlight the ongoing challenge of generalizing across individuals, motivating further evaluation on larger, more diverse, and multi-session datasets.

papers.title: Agency, Cognition and Mathematical Learning in Agentic Human–AI Ecosystems
papers.authors: Ruhit Bardhan, Suman Das, Gamachu Adugna Ganati, Fikadu Tesgera Tolasa, Ayoub Alsarhan
papers.abstract: Background The rise of artificial intelligence systems that can make their own goals plan several steps and take initiative in tasks that involve people is changing how students learn math. Earlier technology was mostly a tool thatwaited for instructions. Currently, agentic AI systems are becoming increasingly popular. They share the initiative to negotiate goals and help manage parts of learning with the student. This change raises several questions. How is agency shared? What does this mean for thinking? How good is the math understanding that comes from the long-term collaboration between humans and AI? Methods This article introduces an idea called the agency-cognition–mathematics (ACM) model. The model blends theories on agency, ideas on distributed and situated thinking, and research on how people learn math. It also examines research on agentic AI in education. Results This study shows how agency can be seen in a spectrum. On one end AI is a tool for this purpose. Finally, AI is a delegate who helps make decisions. It also explains how using AI to think and regulate learning changes how students practice metacognition. This article discusses how a student’s math identity and the power to know what they can do are either strengthened or weakened in environments where humans and AI work together. Conclusion This article offers design rules for teachers, thoughts on ethics, and ideas, for studies. These suggestions aim to carefully and responsibly bring AI into math classrooms.

papers.title: SICAPS COMMUNITY-BASED AI PLATFORM FOR SCABIES SCREENING IN ISLAMIC BOARDING SCHOOLS: A CASE STUDY
papers.authors: Erlina Wijayanti, Ummi Azizah Rachmawati, Mufid Farhan Muhana, Chandra Prasetyo Utomo, Muhammad Wildan Pratama, Nashuha Insani, Sofa Inayatullah, Widjayanti Widjayanti, Dylan Alam Fadilah, Eriska Arlia Widyastuti, Bayu Saputera
papers.abstract: Background Scabies is a neglected disease and has the risk of reducing the quality of life due to disturbing symptoms and the risk of transmission. Islamic boarding school (pesantren) students are a risky population because they live in densely populated locations. Cadres as an extension of health workers have the potential to help detect scabies, especially assisted by artificial intelligence (AI). This study aims to describe the application of the SICAPS model with cadre empowerment and the use of AI in the detection of scabies in Islamic boarding schools. Method We started from cadre training for empowerment. Cadres were trained to be competent in detecting scabies and providing education on the use of topical treatment. We also added an alternative to scabies screening with artificial intelligence (AI). Cadre competence was measured by skill observation in standard patient settings, then followed by screening in real cases. AI chatbot was tested by measuring user experience and accuracy. Results The cadre training was attended by 29 people (mean age 18.3 years) and 93.1% were competent in screening or education. User experience feedback from 45 chatbot users showed positive scores in all six aspects, namely attractiveness, perspicuity, efficiency, dependability, stimulation, and novelty. The results of the accuracy test in cadre’s scabies detection were 89.0% (95% CI 79.5% – 95.1%) and chatbot 84.9% (95% CI 74.6% – 92.2%). Conclusion The results of scabies screening in trained cadres are slightly higher than chatbots. In conditions of limited number of cadres, chatbots can be used as an additional screening. Further validation with larger sample sizes is recommended.

papers.title: Guideline-grounded retrieval versus unconfigured generation in obstructive sleep apnea: a pilot comparison of notebookLM and ChatGPT for AASM v3.0 PSG scoring-rule questions
papers.authors: Volkan Tekin, Mehmet Koçer, Rukiye Oktay Tekin
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in sleep medicine, but their reliability for polysomnography (PSG) scoring-rule tasks that require up-to-date guideline knowledge remains uncertain. This pilot study compared response quality when identical AASM v3.0 PSG scoring-rule questions were answered by NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook)—a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant configured with the AASM Scoring Manual v3.0 as its sole source—and ChatGPT (GPT-5.3), an unconfigured generative model without uploaded source documents. The task assessed guideline-based scoring knowledge, not interpretation of raw PSG signals or automated sleep staging. Thirty questions were developed across five PSG content domains: Technical ( n = 7), Sleep Staging ( n = 6), Respiratory Scoring ( n = 11), Movement ( n = 4), and Arousal ( n = 2). The AASM Manual v3.0 was uploaded to NotebookLM; no files were uploaded to ChatGPT. Identical question wording was used as the sole prompt (Appendix 1), without custom system prompts (prompting protocol in Appendix 3). Three board-certified sleep medicine physicians independently scored de-identified responses presented as Response A and Response B in randomized order using a binary rubric (0/1) across four evaluation domains—Accuracy, Evidence Reasoning, Additional Information, and Information Integration (720 ratings total). Accuracy was anchored to a pre-specified gold-standard answer key (Appendix 1). Analyses used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, exact McNemar test with Holm correction, Fleiss’ kappa, and Cochran’s Q (Python 3.11; SciPy 1.13.1, statsmodels 0.14.2, and NumPy 1.26.4). NotebookLM received more favorable overall ratings (76.1% vs. 66.9%). Median total score per question was 9.5 versus 8.0 (mean matched difference + 1.10; Wilcoxon Z = 2.62, p = 0.0089; post-hoc power ≈ 83%). This difference derived entirely from Additional Information (46.7% vs. 23.3%; McNemar χ² = 12.60, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0020; odds ratio 4.0). No significant differences emerged in Accuracy (88.9%–90.0%), Evidence Reasoning, or Information Integration after correction. Inter-rater agreement was fair overall (Fleiss’ kappa 0.347 ChatGPT, 0.297 NotebookLM) but unreliable for Information Integration (kappa − 0.111 and − 0.023). Systematic rater effects appeared for ChatGPT (Cochran’s Q = 13.89, p = 0.0010) but not NotebookLM (Q = 1.61, p = 0.447). Under unequal resource allocation, guideline-grounded RAG provided clinically valuable supplementary PSG-scoring information more consistently than an unconfigured generative model. This likely reflects source grounding rather than intrinsic model superiority and does not establish RAG as universally preferable across all clinical AI use cases. AI may serve as a complementary educational and reference aid for PSG scoring rules, not as a substitute for expert clinical judgment or autonomous guideline surveillance in patient care.

papers.title: Seeing what students learn: assessing cognitive representations and academic outcomes via EEG image reconstruction
papers.authors: Zhu Su, Zhiqing Ouyang, Xiaoxuan Shao, Xinchen Huang, Sannyuya Liu, Zhi Liu
papers.journal: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding how humans process visual information during learning remains a central challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Traditional approaches typically rely on behavioral observations or indirect neural measures, which limits direct insight into learners' internal cognitive representations. Recent advances in brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) and deep learning have enabled image reconstruction from electroencephalography (EEG), providing a promising pathway to decode latent cognitive states. In this study, we investigate how EEG-based image reconstruction relates to students' learning. While students watched educational videos, we recorded EEG signals and used an image reconstruction model to generate images reflecting their perceived visual representations. We assessed reconstruction quality using semantic similarity between reconstructed and original images. First, we examine whether semantic similarity predicts overall academic performance and find a strong positive association. Second, we evaluate item-level effects and show that questions answered incorrectly correspond to significantly lower semantic similarity than correctly answered questions. Third, we analyze the temporal dynamics of reconstruction and demonstrate that temporal misalignment patterns---quantified through dispersion-related measures---are associated with learners' performance. Overall, these results suggest that EEG-based image reconstruction captures both the strength and the temporal evolution of learners' cognitive representations, offering a novel tool for studying learning mechanisms and supporting more personalized, data-driven educational interventions.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence self-efficacy among iranian medical sciences students: academic, behavioral, and socioeconomic correlates
papers.authors: Neda Gilani, Ahmad Pourabbas, Rouhollah Haghshenas, Gholamali Dehghani
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare and medical education. This study assessed AI self-efficacy and its associated factors among medical sciences students with prior self-reported AI use. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 550 students from Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Iran, were recruited using convenience sampling through an online questionnaire distributed via university social media channels and student networks. The questionnaire covered demographic, academic, socioeconomic, and digital media use characteristics, as well as the Persian version of the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale (AISES). Prior self-reported AI use was assessed using a Likert-scale item; students selecting “not at all” were excluded. Univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses were used to examine factors associated with AI self-efficacy. Results The mean AISES score was 69.80 ± 13.34 on a standardized 0–100 scale. Educational level was associated with AI self-efficacy, with bachelor’s (β = 15.34, 95% CI: 8.05–22.64), master’s/PhD (β = 12.63, 95% CI: 6.88–18.48), and professional-doctorate students (β = 18.63, 95% CI: 13.71–23.55) having higher scores than residents. Higher GPA (β = 3.62, 95% CI: 2.44–4.80) and employment (β = 5.25, 95% CI: 1.03–9.49) were also associated with higher AI self-efficacy. Compared with < 1 h/day, educational digital-media use of ≥ 3 h/day was associated with higher AI self-efficacy, whereas recreational use of ≥ 3 h/day was associated with lower scores. Age and gender were not independently associated with AI self-efficacy. Conclusions AI self-efficacy was associated with academic, socioeconomic, behavioral, and educational characteristics among medical sciences students. These cross-sectional associations do not establish causality; longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal direction.

papers.title: Lifestyles, psychological well-being, and mental health: A cross-sectional study in a higher education sample
papers.authors: Inês Conceição, Raquel Simões de Almeida, Raquel Simões de Almeida
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The transition to higher education represents a critical developmental stage during which lifestyle behaviours and psychosocial factors interact to influence well-being and mental health. Understanding these dynamics is essential to prevent adverse health outcomes and support academic success. This study aimed to (i) describe lifestyle patterns among Portuguese higher education students, (ii) examine their associations with well-being and mental health, and (iii) assess the influence of sociodemographic and contextual variables. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 1,159 students from the Polytechnic of Porto, Portugal. Participants completed the FANTASTICO Lifestyle Questionnaire, the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21), and the CORE-18 to assess lifestyle behaviours and mental health indicators. Descriptive analyses were performed, and one-way ANOVA and independent Student’s t-tests were used to compare lifestyle and psychological variables across sociodemographic groups. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated to examine associations with age, body mass index (BMI), and self-rated health. A multiple linear regression model using a stepwise method identified explanatory variables of lifestyle scores. Results The mean age of the sample was 21.51 (± 2.65) years; most participants were women (69.70%) and lived with their families (71.00%). Students reported overall favourable lifestyle profiles and relatively low psychological distress. However, mild symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were present, approaching the threshold for moderate severity. Higher self-rated health, absence of depressive symptoms, lower stress levels, lower BMI, female gender, younger age, and enrolment in the School of Health Sciences were significantly associated with healthier lifestyle scores. Fourth-year students also reported better lifestyle and mental health indicators than those in earlier years. An unexpected positive association emerged between the CORE-18 problems/symptoms subscale and lifestyle scores, possibly reflecting compensatory health behaviours among students more aware of psychological symptoms. Conclusions These findings highlight the complex interplay between psychological well-being, lifestyle, and sociodemographic factors in higher education students. Future research should include more diverse samples, consider additional factors such as social support, economic pressures, and physical context, and adopt longitudinal designs with objective measures to better capture the relationships between lifestyle and mental health.

papers.title: Sex differences in mortality risk profiles across the life course in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: a machine learning analysis of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
papers.authors: Cindy Xin Wen, Wei Tu, Giada Sebastiani, Jessica Burnside, Carmela Rapino, Alnoor S. Ramji, Mark G. Swain, Keyur Patel, Erica E. M. Moodie, Jennifer A. Flemming, Sahar Saeed
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Prognostic models for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) are largely ‘one-size-fits-all’ and do not collectively account for sex differences and social determinants of health (SDoH). To address this gap, we trained and developed sex-specific machine learning models that incorporated SDoHs to examine important predictors of all-cause mortality among adults with MASLD. Methods Using the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, MASLD was defined as the presence of hepatic steatosis, at least one cardiometabolic risk factor, and low levels of sex-specific alcohol consumption (females: < 140 g/week, males: < 210 g/week). Three machine learning models were examined in sex and age-specific subgroups (middle-age: 45–64 years vs. older age: $$\:\ge\:$$ 65 years). Based on the literature, expert input, and data availability, 25, clinical, sociodemographic, and lifestyle predictors capturing upstream, intermediate, or surrogate factors associated with MASLD progression and mortality were considered. The cohorts were split into 75% training and 25% testing, and 5-fold cross-validation was used for hyperparameter tuning. Evaluation was performed in the held-out test set using the Concordance index (C-Index), integrated Brier score (iBS), time-dependent area under the curve (AUC(t)), and visual calibration plots. Important predictors were described based on global importance and directionality of Shapley additive explanation values. Results Of 30,097 participants, we identified 8,429 with MASLD (35.3% female) followed for a median of 7.67 years (IQR: 6.84, 8.45), of which 631 (7.5%) died. Using a random survival forest model, all-cause mortality risk prediction demonstrated meaningful stratification across the follow-up period (Females: C-Index 0.73, iBS 0.032, mean AUC(t) 0.78; Males: C-Index 0.79, iBS 0.035, mean AUC(t) 0.82). Risk prediction profiles for females and males differed. Alongside clinical factors such as albumin and cardiometabolic multimorbidity, female risk was impacted by income, education, and lifestyle, particularly in middle-age. Comparatively, metabolic parameters such as waist circumference, blood pressure, albumin, and body mass index were important predictors for males. Conclusion Our findings describe how mortality risk prediction profiles for people with MASLD vary by sex and age. This highlights the potential value of integrating SDoHs into sex-specific prognostication, bridging social and precision medicine to enable more equitable, individualized risk prediction in MASLD.

papers.title: Proceedings from the VIII International Symposium on Orofacial Clefts and Related Anomalies – Bauru Medical School, University of São Paulo (FMBRU-USP)
papers.authors: Bruno Mariano Ribeiro Braga, Vinícius Contrucci Dantas Segarra, Adélia Ferraz Daher Miranda, Ana Carla Pasquini Abu-yaghi Nogueira, Ana Carolina Canuto Minozzi, Ana Laura Herrera Farha, Cristiane Sabino Vianna de Oliveira Domingues, Denicia Stefane Rodrigues Queiroz, Franciane da Silva Nascimento, Gabriel Bispo Botari, Gleisieli Baessa-Cardoso, Henrique Regonaschi Serigatto, Maria Carolina Neves, Nayara Tomazi Batista, Rosemery Aparecida Ferreira, Tatiane Aparecida da Silva, Verônica de Abreu Francisco, Marielena Layuno Matos, Christian Friederich Poets, Adriano Fernandes, Cristiano Tonello, Ivy Kiemle Trindade‐Suedam, Sérgio Henrique Kiemle Trindade
papers.abstract: The VIII International Symposium on Orofacial Clefts and Related Anomalies, organized by the Graduate Program in Rehabilitation Sciences at the Bauru Medical School, University of São Paulo (FMBRU-USP), brought together clinicians, researchers, students, and healthcare professionals to discuss recent advances in craniofacial rehabilitation. Held with the I FMBRU-USP Graduate Program Pre-Symposium, the scientific program comprised a keynote lectures on Robin Sequence management protocols, six thematic panels, and a poster session. The panels explored topics on Robin Sequence, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, velopharyngeal insufficiency, rehabilitation outcomes, translational research, and professional training. Across these themes, the symposium reinforced the value of multidisciplinary collaboration, evidence-based practice, emerging technologies, and international partnerships in advancing patient care and scientific innovation. This proceedings paper summarizes the principal discussions and key messages presented during the meeting, providing an overview of current advances, persistent challenges, and future directions in research, education, and the multidisciplinary management of individuals with orofacial clefts and related craniofacial anomalies.

papers.title: Investigating care outcomes and experiences of adults with Long COVID through patient-reported indicators (PROMs and PREMs) in Belgium
papers.authors: Sarah Moreels, Reindert Ekelson, Pierre Smith, Niko Speybroeck, Sherihane Bensemmane, Robrecht De Schreye, D Annaert
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Long COVID, with its multisystemic manifestations, poses a substantial burden on health systems. Nevertheless, evidence regarding Long COVID patients’ perspectives, perceived health outcomes and care experiences in Belgium remains limited. Methods: OECD’s Patient-Reported Indicator Surveys (PaRIS) collected patient-reported outcome and experience measures (PROMS and PREMs) from individuals aged 45+ with chronic conditions. In Belgium, 4,687 primary care patients provided self-reported data between March 2023 and January 2024. This study explores the associated clinical and sociodemographic factors, care outcomes and experiences of adults with Long COVID in Belgium, by comparing respondents with and without Long COVID. Multivariate models were used to examine the clinical and sociodemographic determinants of Long COVID, and mixed-effects models were applied to compute the 10 key PROM and PREM indicators following the PaRIS10 methodology, accounting for the hierarchical structure of the data (patients nested within GP practices). Results: Overall, 50% (N=2,359) had a previous COVID-19 infection diagnosis, and over one in four (26%) of them reported Long COVID-related symptoms lasting 2 months or longer after COVID-19 infection (N=605, 12.9% overall prevalence). Higher risk of Long COVID was associated with being female, aged 45-54, lower educated, having multiple chronic conditions and higher BMI. Long COVID adults reported significant lower PROM scores for general health, wellbeing, physical and mental health compared to non-Long COVID respondents. Those with Long COVID symptoms lasting at least 1 year reported even poorer outcomes, particularly in general health, wellbeing and physical health. PREMs showed no significant differences between Long COVID and non-Long COVID respondents overall. However, trust in healthcare system and person-centred care was significant lower when Long COVID patients still had these long-term symptoms at survey time. Conclusions: In Belgium, adults with Long COVID report poorer health outcomes and less positive care experiences compared with those without Long COVID. These findings point to the substantial burden associated with Long COVID and to gaps in the current healthcare response to this emerging condition. Strengthening dedicated care pathways, improving coordination across services, and ensuring clear communication and support for patients will be essential to better address the needs of people living with Long COVID.

papers.title: Applications, advantages, and limitations of artificial intelligence in medical education assessment: a systematic review
papers.authors: Murat Polat, Engın Karadağ
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being integrated into medical education, where assessments are high-stakes and intricately linked to clinical competence, professional judgment, and patient safety. Although several recent reviews have broadly explored the use of AI in medical education, a focused, methodologically transparent synthesis of AI applications in assessment and evaluation remains limited. This systematic review aimed to (i) identify and classify AI tools and methods used in medical education assessment; (ii) examine their advantages, limitations, and ethical implications; (iii) map AI use to established assessment frameworks (Assessment of Learning [AoL], Assessment for Learning [AfL], Assessment as Learning [AaL], validity, and reliability frameworks); and (iv) clarify the evolving role of medical educators. A systematic review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines [1]. Six electronic databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, ERIC, and Cochrane Library) were searched for English-language records published between January 2019 and February 2026. The search combined terms related to artificial intelligence, generative AI, machine learning, assessment, evaluation, and medical education. Two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts against pre-specified PICOS criteria. The methodological quality was appraised using the Medical Education Research Study Quality Instrument (MERSQI). The findings were thematically synthesized. After deduplication, 1,247 records were screened; 187 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 62 studies met the inclusion criteria. Six themes emerged: (i) AI-supported assessment tools and platforms; (ii) AI use across AoL, AfL, and AaL; (iii) validity, reliability, and feasibility considerations; (iv) medical-education–specific applications including written examinations, objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs – standardized, station-based assessments of clinical competence), simulation-based assessments, and workplace-based assessments (WBAs); (v) limitations including algorithmic bias, transparency, equity, and data privacy; and (vi) the redefined role of medical educators. The strength of the available evidence, judged descriptively on the basis of MERSQI scores, was variable: most studies were small-scale feasibility or proof-of-concept reports, and few were high-quality validation studies. AI has the potential to improve the efficiency, individualization, and timeliness of feedback in medical education assessment, particularly in large-scale written examinations, OSCE grading, and longitudinal competency tracking. However, evidence of improved validity or reliability is limited to narrowly bounded tasks, current evidence is heterogeneous and dominated by feasibility studies, and concerns regarding bias, transparency, equity, and the irreplaceable role of professional human judgment persist. AI should be positioned as a complement, not a substitute, for expert human evaluation. Medical educators, institutions, and regulators must develop validation, governance, and AI literacy frameworks before AI tools can be safely deployed in high-stakes assessments.

papers.title: Predicting subsequent-year physical fitness assessment failure in university students using longitudinal data and explainable machine learning
papers.authors: Lan Luo, Fawei Huang, Baixia Li
papers.abstract: Annual university physical fitness assessments are primarily used to describe students’ current fitness status, but their value for predicting failure in the subsequent year remains unclear. This study evaluated whether routinely collected physical fitness measurements could predict subsequent-year failure using a temporally separated modeling framework. This retrospective longitudinal prediction study used annual physical fitness assessment records from a university in China collected from 2023 to 2025. We developed models using 11,430 linked 2023–2024 student-year pairs and evaluated them on an out-of-time test dataset of 11,427 linked 2024–2025 student-year pairs. We defined subsequent-year failure as a total physical fitness score below 60. Predictors from the preceding year included body mass index, vital capacity, 50 m sprint time, standing long jump distance, sit-and-reach distance, endurance run time, and sex-specific muscular strength. We compared logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost using discrimination, calibration, and classification metrics at a prespecified probability threshold of 0.50. We used SHapley Additive exPlanations to characterize feature contributions within the fitted XGBoost model. Subsequent-year failure occurred in 6.39% of the model-development dataset and 6.30% (720/11,427) of the out-of-time test dataset. Logistic regression showed the highest discrimination and recall (ROC-AUC = 0.8167; PR-AUC = 0.3227; recall = 0.7569). Random forest showed the highest accuracy (0.9320), F1 score (0.3573), and the lowest Brier score (0.0578), but its recall was 0.3000, and its calibration slope was 0.4985. XGBoost achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.7935 and a recall of 0.5458. In the XGBoost SHAP summary plot, BMI, endurance run time, standing long jump, and vital capacity showed the largest overall contributions to model output. Sensitivity analyses showed lower predictive performance under percentile-based definitions of subsequent-year failure. Although predictor measurements preceded the outcomes, the predictors and subsequent-year total fitness score were derived from the same physical fitness assessment framework; therefore, persistence of the underlying fitness construct and conceptual predictor–outcome overlap may have contributed to the observed performance. Routinely collected physical fitness measurements provided useful discrimination for subsequent-year failure, although model performance varied by evaluation metric and outcome definition. We conducted the out-of-time evaluation within a single university, and it should not be interpreted as independent external validation. External validation, local calibration, threshold assessment, and prospective evaluation are required before using the models for routine student monitoring or intervention.

papers.title: Cardiovascular and psycho-emotional changes among completers of a medical student cohort with high loss to follow-up
papers.authors: Jaime A. Cespedes-Londono, Elizabeth Sanchez-Sanchez, Tatiana Camacho-Carvajal, Maria J. Rosero-Chamorro, Sara J. Guerrero-Leon, Gustavo Tovar, Erika V. Ladino-Marin, Germán Briceño, Alejandra Tordecilla‐Sanders, Andrea-Catalina Trompetero-González, Juan David Rodriguez-Parra, Diana Marcela Ramos‐Caballero
