Thematic analysis of 71 core articles identified six major thematic domains - GIS curriculum and pedagogy, school geography and teacher integration, spatial thinking and cognitive learning, online and WebGIS education, experiential and community-based learning, and teacher professional development - while K-means clustering of the same corpus identified five corresponding conceptual clusters, including WebGIS and environmental education, spatial thinking and cognitive GIS learning, and open-source and AI-supported geospatial learning. As shown, the time-based analysis shows an increasing tendency to transform from conventional instruction into interdisciplinary and AI-supported geospatial learning environment. Geospatial education programs are being actively implemented at the university and college level in Uzbekistan; primarily, they are developed at the faculties of geodesy, cadastre, geography, ecology, and urban planning. However, there are still many issues with modernization of educational programs, WebGIS implementation, AI integration, digital learning platforms and geospatial teaching abilities. Although there is growing demand for geospatial skills, the research proves that the problems of developing countries remain relevant. The contribution of the research is in developing the approach that combines bibliometric analysis, thematic interpretation and clustering using machine learning.

papers.title: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback of left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to enhance emotional cognitive control: A randomized controlled trial
papers.authors: Timothy J. McDermott, Aki Tsuchiyagaito, Sam Ramirez, Mallory J. Cannon, Elisabeth Akeman, James Touthang, Namik Kirlić, Masaya Misaki, Martin P. Paulus, Robin L. Aupperle
papers.abstract: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rt-fMRI-nf) is an endogenous neuromodulation approach whereby individuals are taught to self-regulate their own neural activity in the moment. Cognitive control in emotional contexts is related to risk for or protection against mental health disorders, such as depression, anxiety, or posttraumatic stress disorder. The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) has been shown to be centrally important in facilitating emotional cognitive control (ECC). Using a double-blind randomized controlled trial design, the present study tested a novel rt-fMRI-nf protocol to increase left dlPFC activity during ECC and improve ECC measured by self-report and behavioral task performance. Seventy healthy adult participants were enrolled and randomized to either active (n = 37; left dlPFC) or sham [n = 33; left postcentral gyrus (PCG)] neurofeedback. Linear mixed effects models tested for effects of time (practice/run 1/run 2/run 3/transfer), feedback target (active/sham), and their interaction on left dlPFC activity, left PCG activity, and ECC measures (self-report and behavior). Results showed a significant time-by-feedback interaction on left dlPFC activity (p = .031). This interaction was such that active feedback led to greater left dlPFC activity in run 1 (p = .030; d = .66) and run 2 (p = .042; d = .62), but not for run 3 nor the transfer run (when no feedback was provided). There were no significant effects of feedback on ECC measures. These findings demonstrate that rt-fMRI-nf had an initial but not a sustained effect on left dlPFC activity, providing evidence of neural target engagement. However, the lack of a sustained effect on neural activity nor any observed effects on ECC highlight the complexity of identifying the optimal design and dosing for novel rt-fMRI-nf protocols.

papers.title: Explainability of large language models: Opportunities and challenges toward generating trustworthy explanations
papers.authors: Shahin Atakishiyev, Housam Khalifa Bashier Babiker, Jiayi Dai, Nawshad Farruque, Teruaki Hayashi, Nafisa Sadaf Hriti, Md Abed Rahman, Iain Smith, Mi-Young Kim, Osmar R. Zai͏̈ane, Randy G. Goebel

papers.title: Transparent forecasting with XAI: Improving accuracy and trust in electricity demand prediction
papers.authors: Somya Bansal, Vaibhav Baldeva, Asmit Cajla, Parth Vashitha, Priya Kansal, Sachin Kansal, Kamran Shaukat, Talha Mahboob Alam
papers.abstract: This research is based on forecasting the net demand for electricity by considering the previous trends. Considering the overall increase in demand for electricity year by year, predicting such a trend plays a crucial role in a country’s development, as it helps make an accurate prediction of future energy consumption and prepare accordingly. The trends will be considered in light of various factors that affect the electricity usage rate. Different algorithms would be applied to a pipeline to predict appropriate results. The algorithms that would be used are XGB followed by Prophet, which is applied with regressors and then is ensembled, and further optimization is performed. Our result is compared against a broad set of classical statistical and machine-learning baselines (ARIMA, linear/ridge/lasso regression, decision tree, random forest, SVR, KNN, and gradient boosting), evaluated both on the full dataset and, separately, on two demand clusters. The model presented in this paper has outperformed all of these baselines. While hybridisations of Prophet with other learners, and of boosting methods with classical time-series components, have each been explored separately in prior work, the contribution of this research is a formalised, cross-validated stacking ensemble of Prophet and XGBoost specifically for national-scale electricity demand, combined with a SHAP-based explainability layer applied to the resulting ensemble, achieving an RMSE of 13.734 on test data. Not only does the proposed model yield better results, but it also provides a method to explain the effect that each parameter has on the outcome. It accurately depicts the magnitude and impact, whether positive or negative, of electricity load consumption, which in turn affects the prediction of the outcome.

papers.title: Responses of AI chatbots to escalating suicide risk: A simulation study of repeated interactions
papers.authors: Wojciech Pichowicz, Marek Kotas, Natalia Kalka, Julia Dembowska, Julia Karska, Patryk Piotrowski, Błażej Misiak
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for emotional support, yet their safety remains insufficiently characterized across repeated interactions. Prior work relied mostly on single-session prompts, limiting evaluation of changes in responses across days. The present study aimed to assess how major AI chatbots respond to escalating suicidal risk over time, including imminent-risk scenarios and attempts to bypass safeguards (jailbreaking). METHODS: We simulated interactions with ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Replika across three suicidal risk scenarios with risk escalation over seven days, informed by the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. Outcomes included exploration of suicidal ideation, symptom assessment, referral to human support, and vulnerability to jailbreak attempts. RESULTS: In ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Replika, respectively, overall human referral occurred in 54/63 (85.7%), 48/63 (76.2%), and 6/63 (9.5%) daily records. During the high-risk period, exploration of suicidal ideation was higher for ChatGPT than DeepSeek (adjusted difference, 25.9 percentage points; 95% CI, 2.4-49.5; q = 0.037) and Replika (66.7 percentage points; 95% CI, 44.2-89.1; q < 0.001). Day 7 referral occurred in 9/9 (exact 95% CI 66.4-100%), 4/9 (13.7-78.8%), and 1/9 (0.3-48.2%) trajectories, respectively. Jailbreaking succeeded in 6/9 (exact 95% CI 29.9-92.5%), 7/9 (40.0-97.2%), and 8/9 (51.8-99.7%) attempts, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: AI chatbots showed marked variability and safety vulnerabilities in simulated suicidal crises, particularly under jailbreaking conditions. The simulation design and small sample of 27 trajectories limit generalizability. These findings raise concerns about unsupervised chatbot use during suicidal crises and support further evaluation of safeguards across repeated interactions.

papers.title: Co-creation and emotional perception in the development of seasoned goat butter: A consumer-centered approach
papers.authors: Thamirys Lorranne Santos Lima, Mônica Josy Trajano França, Erick A. Esmerino, Neila Lidiany Ribeiro, Mônica Tejo Cavalcanti, Mônica Correia Gonçalves, Haíssa Roberta Cardarelli
papers.journal: International Journal of Gastronomy and Food Science
papers.abstract: This study explored co-creation and emotional perception in the development of spicy goat bottle butter, investigating the influence of factors on product quality and acceptance. 379 consumers participated in the study in the co-creation stage and 135 in the emotional assessment, through online questionnaires on the Compusense Cloud® platform. The results revealed that consumers showed a preference for condiments such as garlic and oregano and the form of powder and extract addition, guiding the development of new formulations with greater acceptance, in addition to that, for the commercialization of bottled butter, glass packages in smaller sizes were preferred. Understanding the emotions evoked in the butters spiced with saffron and oregano generated well-being and the traditional and pink pepper versions were associated with feelings of dissatisfaction. Finally, the relevance of co-creation studies in the development of food products is highlighted, since they enable the direct incorporation of consumer perceptions and expectations in the innovation process, showing, in this study, the market potential for innovative goat dairies, overcoming barriers of food neophobia and expanding consumption beyond traditional niches, by aligning the product with the consumer's sensory and emotional expectations.

papers.title: Effects of generative AI and translanguaging on second language writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency
papers.authors: Emily Di Zhang, Chengyuan Yu, Yanchao Yang
papers.abstract: While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) exhibits the potential to scaffold L2 students’ writing, research found that L2 students struggle to craft effective prompts for GenAI to produce high-quality feedback and responses. As such, there is a need to incorporate translanguaging into L2 students’ prompt engineering to capitalize on the learning potential of GenAI for L2 students. The present study, therefore, investigated whether the combined use of GenAI and translanguaging influenced L2 writing linguistic features. We adopted a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental design by assigning L2 writers to four groups: a control group, translanguaging - only, GenAI - only, and translanguaging + GenAI. Comparing the lexical complexity, syntactic complexity, accuracy, and fluency of the four groups, we found that GenAI had a significant positive impact on the lexical and syntactic complexity, accuracy, and fluency of L2 students’ writing, while translanguaging alone and the combination of GenAI and translanguaging did not yield significant positive impacts on most indices of the writing performance. L2 teachers are encouraged to integrate GenAI tools into writing instruction to improve students’ writing complexity, accuracy, and fluency, while providing scaffolding for translanguaging, as its benefits might not emerge automatically, particularly for advanced L2 writers.

papers.title: AI disclosure: Symbolic signal or performance driver? Scale, systemic disruption and bank outcomes in Nigeria
papers.authors: Mohammed Ibrahim Abba, Onyinyechi Precious Edeh, Ovbe Simon Akpadaka, Wabla Dahiru Onoja
papers.abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) disclosure in Nigerian banks functions primarily as symbolic communication or as a performance-relevant organisational signal, and whether its economic relevance depends on organisational scale and systemic disruption. Design/methodology/approach: Using 144 bank-year observations from 15 Nigerian deposit money banks over 2015–2024, the study measures AI disclosure from annual reports and estimates bank- and year-fixed-effects models. Organisational scale is modelled as both a determinant and moderator, while the 2020–2021 period is treated as a systemic-disruption regime. Inference combines bank-clustered standard errors with 9,999 restricted wild-cluster bootstrap replications. Robustness tests include alternative estimators, capital-adequacy controls, leave-one-bank-out analysis, placebo disruption windows, outlier-resistant specifications, a narrower AI vocabulary, disclosure decomposition and listed-bank price-to-book value (PBV) validation. Findings: Aggregate AI disclosure has limited standalone association with return on assets (ROA). The strongest result is a positive shift in the AI disclosure-by-scale relationship during systemic disruption, although inference is qualified under few-cluster and outlier-resistant tests. Strategic AI communication is positively associated with implementation-oriented disclosure, while full-period market-valuation effects are comparatively imprecise. Originality/value: The study advances a boundary-conditioned view of AI disclosure by distinguishing observable communication from organisational capability and realised outcomes. It shows that the economic relevance of AI disclosure depends on organisational and systemic conditions rather than on disclosure volume alone, while integrating accounting performance, market recognition and symbolic-versus-implementation-oriented disclosure evidence.

papers.title: From graphical design to digital learning: One hundred years of the McCabe-Thiele method
papers.authors: Crisleine P. Draszewski, Flávio Dias Mayer
papers.abstract: The McCabe-Thiele method, introduced in 1925 by Warren L. McCabe and Ernest W. Thiele, remains one of the most influential graphical tools in chemical engineering. Created to simplify the rigorous calculations previously required for binary distillation design, it combines vapor-liquid equilibrium and operating-line mass balances into a clear visual framework. Through a simple stepping procedure, the method estimates the number of theoretical stages, feed location, and the effect of reflux ratio. This article commemorates one hundred years of the McCabe-Thiele method by reviewing its historical origins, theoretical basis, assumptions, and evolution. The method is discussed alongside earlier approaches, such as Sorel and Ponchon-Savarit, and later developments including shortcut correlations and rigorous simulation-based design. Special attention is given to its enduring educational value. Even in the era of process simulators and artificial intelligence, the McCabe-Thiele diagram remains a powerful tool for understanding cause-effect relationships, design trade-offs, and the link between energy demand and equipment requirements, bridging fundamental principles and modern engineering practice. Social Media Post Abstract: 100 years later, the McCabe–Thiele method still bridges fundamental distillation concepts and modern simulation tools, remaining essential for engineering intuition and education.

papers.title: Do anthropomorphic descriptions of AI influence trust, distrust, and reliance? – Two pre-registered framing experiments
papers.authors: Philip Porwol, Tobias M. Peters, Ingrid Scharlau
papers.abstract: Anthropomorphizing artificial “intelligence” (AI) – that is, attributing human characteristics to it – is prevalent in the AI field. Using human-like voices or appearances is a prominent example. Similarly, the language used to describe AI applications is anthropomorphic. “AI” is “fed” with data, it “learns”, “acts”, and “decides”. However, little is known about the effects of using such anthropomorphisms when describing AI systems. Previous research has shown that anthropomorphic appearance and design increase trust among people utilizing AI applications. To test whether this translates to anthropomorphism used in descriptions of AI, we conducted two pre-registered experiments comparing two conditions in which an AI application is either linguistically anthropomorphized or described non-anthropomorphically. In the first large-scale online experiment ( N = 1072), participants read a fictitious newspaper article about the usage of an AI system in radiology. In the second laboratory experiment ( N = 55), participants completed a classification task using AI. Using a response-elicitation approach, participants had to judge their trust and distrust towards the AI system, and reliance was additionally compared in the second experiment. We found no significant differences in trust, distrust, or reliance between anthropomorphic and technical conditions. Subgroup analyses accounting for domain expertise and general attitudes towards AI systems yielded similar null results. These results suggest that anthropomorphic descriptions alone are insufficient to shift trust-related concepts (trust, distrust, and reliance). Further, the results indicate boundaries for anthropomorphic framing effects in general and, specifically, for trust.

papers.title: Three cases of Dravet syndrome with electrical status epilepticus in sleep: Case reports
papers.authors: 昌平 江藤, Minoru Shibata, Atsushi Yokoyama, Takeshi Yoshida, Takeo Kato
papers.abstract: Background Interictal electroencephalography (EEG) findings in Dravet syndrome (DS) evolve with age. EEG is typically normal during early infancy; however, various abnormalities may later emerge, including generalized spike-and-wave activity. Nevertheless, cases of DS associated with electrical status epilepticus in sleep (ESES) are extremely rare. We report three cases of DS in which ESES developed during the disease course. Case presentation Case 1: A 10-year-old boy with DS presented with clonic seizures, focal impaired awareness seizures, generalized tonic–clonic seizures, myoclonic seizures, and atypical absence seizures. His interictal EEG demonstrated abnormal frontal epileptiform discharges at 7 years of age, and ESES subsequently developed at age 10. Case 2: An 11-year-old girl with DS presented with generalized tonic–clonic seizures, myoclonic seizures, and atypical absence seizures. Her interictal EEG revealed frontally predominant continuous spike-and-wave complexes during nonrapid eye movement sleep, consistent with ESES at age 8. Case 3: A 13-year-old girl with DS presented with generalized tonic–clonic seizures, right-sided tonic seizures, and myoclonic seizures. Her interictal EEG demonstrated ESES at age 5. Conclusion All three DS cases exhibited ESES, suggesting atypical ESES or isolated spike-and-wave activation in sleep because no immediate global cognitive decline was observed following ESES onset. Because ESES in patients with DS remains poorly understood, periodic evaluation using long-term sleep EEG monitoring is essential, as ESES may arise during the disease course. Further case accumulation and detailed investigation are warranted.

papers.title: Physically consistent and spatially conformalized machine learning for trustworthy flood susceptibility mapping of the 2024 Feni flash flood
papers.authors: Rakib Ahammed Diptho, Pial Ghosh, Safiul Haque Chowdhury
papers.abstract: Data-driven flood susceptibility mapping (FSM) has converged on a common template: a gradient-boosting classifier, a random train/test split, a global feature-attribution chart, and a five-class map. Using the catastrophic August-2024 Feni flash flood (Bangladesh) with 11 Google-Earth-Engine conditioning factors ( $$n=1{,}510$$ inventory samples; 982, 866 mapped pixels at 30m), we examine three limitations it can obscure. First, random splitting inflates the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by about 0.06–0.09 relative to spatially blocked cross-validation. Second, an unconstrained learner can attain high accuracy while encoding hydrologically implausible response functions, monotone in the physically expected direction on only $$54.5\%$$ of its response surface. Third, its outputs are neither calibrated nor accompanied by valid uncertainty. The proposed framework injects hydrological priors as hard monotonicity constraints, enforcing physically consistent behaviour at no measurable cost in skill (spatial AUC 0.938; Matthews correlation 0.700). Because the inventory is balanced by design, we report a relative, event-conditioned susceptibility score rather than an absolute occurrence probability. Predictions are calibrated with cross-fitted isotonic regression (expected calibration error 0.150–0.016) with spatially stratified (Mondrian) conformal sets exposing a conditional-coverage degradation under extrapolation (worst-region coverage 0.48 at the 0.90 level). A Physical Consistency Score (PCS) audits whether learned relationships obey their hydrological priors. The imposed directions are additionally confirmed against the observed inundation, and sensitivity analyses over the constraint set, spatial-block count and calibrator leave the conclusions unchanged. Validated against the spatially independent (same-event) observed 2024 inundation extent, the map yields a strictly monotone class-frequency response (observed flooding rising from $$1.0$$ to $$45.4\%$$ ; AUC 0.75). The contribution reframes FSM around physical consistency, calibrated probability and honest spatial uncertainty.

papers.title: Machine learning in predicting the effects of personality traits on college students’ grit in Ghana
papers.authors: Anastasia Hansen
papers.abstract: This study examines whether Big Five personality traits are associated with grit among Ghanaian teacher trainees, applying regularisation assisted econometric estimation within a double machine learning framework. Using survey data from 288 students at Jasikan College of Education, three complementary post lasso estimators were applied, namely ordinary least squares with CHS lasso orthogonalised variables, CHS post lasso orthogonalised variables, and PDS selected variables alongside the full regressor set, each employing lasso purely for covariate selection and orthogonalisation within an OLS framework. A cross validated predictive lasso model corroborated these estimates. Across specifications, openness and conscientiousness consistently predicted higher grit, with openness exceeding conscientiousness in effect size, while extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism showed no significant association. These specific findings suggest that personality dimensions relevant to grit may depend on resource constrained teacher training conditions, offering targets for interventions strengthening grit among prospective educators in Ghana.

papers.title: The influence of artificial intelligence on students’ academic performance through career aspiration emotional intelligence and psychological well being among secondary school students in Awi Zone
papers.authors: Adimtew Abebe, Yaschalew Geremew, Tesfaye Muluye
papers.abstract: This study aimed to examine the Influences of Artificial Intelligence on students’ academic performance through Career Aspiration, Emotional Intelligence and Psychological Well-Being. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 200 students in secondary schools that have integrated Artificial Intelligence technologies into their tasks. A structured questionnaire comprising standardized measurement scales was used to assess Artificial Intelligence usage, emotional intelligence, career aspiration, psychological well-being, and students’ academic performance. Data were analysed using SPSS and AMOS through multiple regression analysis, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modeling (SEM). The findings revealed that Artificial Intelligence significantly; and positively influenced students’ performance and psychological well-being. Emotional intelligence and career aspiration also had significant positive effects on students’ academic performance. Furthermore, psychological well-being partially mediated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and students’ academic performance. The study concludes that schools can enhance students’ academic performance by effectively implementing ‘‘Artificial Intelligence’’ technologies while fostering students' psychological well-being, emotional intelligence, and career aspirations.

papers.title: Meta-synthesis of global cases for the adaption stages of artificial intelligence systems into university practices
papers.authors: Barış Burak Uslu, Liudvika Leišytė
papers.abstract: Abstract The transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in universities is simply extending beyond instructional applications to include administrative and strategic domains in university management. This study aims to explore how AI could be integrated into university practices by addressing three core questions: to what AI technologies are being employed, which integration stages support their implementation, and what kind of ethical risks need to be considered for AI usage in universities. To respond to these questions, the researchers a meta-synthesis approach to qualitatively analyse selected studies. Based on a systematic search protocol, they selected 49 empirical cases from different parts of the world; then, analysed them using thematic analysis through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing/verification. The findings were categorised into a three-layered framework capturing various purposes of AI usage, technical and institutional integration steps, and the components of ethical AI regulations in universities. The analysis shows that higher education authorities, university leaders, and techno-experts initially decide the purpose(s) of AI usage, regarding teaching, research, engagement, and administration. Then, as a structured roadmap, they can follow eight steps identified for the technical and institutional AI integration: 1. AI System Design, 2. AI Algorithm Development, 3. Data Management-Preprocessing, 4. AI System Integration, 5. Strategic Management Policies, 6. Operational Management Roles, 7. Curriculum-Pedagogical Design, and 8. Evaluation-Performance Monitoring. Lastly, ethical regulations could be organised combining sub-themes of Data Ethics, Algorithmic Ethics, Human-AI Interaction and Social Impact, Academic Integrity and Responsible Use, and Institutional and Managerial Ethics.

papers.title: Value Co-creation in Service Ecosystems—Investigating the Role of Mediating Modalities Between Structure and Agency in Business-to-business Relations
papers.authors: Felix Volz, Christopher Münch
papers.abstract: Abstract Research in the field of service ecosystems (SE) in the business-to-business (B2B) context is still in its infancy, especially lacking consideration of social dynamics that shape collaboration among firms. This study focuses on this topic and investigates how companies interact, coordinate, and co-create value within in an industrial SE. Applying structuration theory as the theoretical foundation for analyzing the dynamics and relationships between actors in an industrial SE, we conduct a single case study focusing on the ecosystem revolving around an Industrial Internet of Things software startup as the focal firm, its business partners, and customers. The investigated ecosystem consisted of 17 firms, with 29 interviews building the foundation for analysis. We generate insights on the underlying mechanisms that enable cooperation, knowledge exchange, and joint value creation. Based on our findings, we derive six interrelated modalities that explain how firms align interests, distribute responsibilities, and build shared understanding within the ecosystem. We synthesize these findings into three core dynamics that are integrated into a recursive loop that builds a self-containing system providing both structure and flexibility for change. By providing empirical insights into these dynamics, the study enhances our understanding of how SEs function as complex socio-technical systems. The study contributes to both research and practice by explaining how firms can strengthen collaboration and manage interdependencies to achieve collective value creation.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence, the knowledge problem, and academic judgment: an Austrian perspective
papers.authors: William Hongsong Wang, Miguel Ángel Alonso Neira
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have renewed claims that university teaching and research can be largely automated. This article argues that such claims confuse information processing with judgment. Drawing on Hayek’s theory of dispersed and tacit knowledge, Huerta de Soto’s analysis of computation and entrepreneurial discovery, and the theory of judgment under Knightian uncertainty, it explains why greater computational capacity does not eliminate the knowledge problem. Contemporary AI can retrieve, recombine, and generate large volumes of context-sensitive information, while memory and retrieval mechanisms allow earlier interactions to shape later outputs. These capabilities expand the range of plausible explanations and possible courses of inquiry, but they do not provide a purpose-independent criterion for determining which interpretation is relevant, which assumptions are defensible, or which course of action should be pursued. The article applies this distinction to higher education. Artificial intelligence is likely to substitute for some standardized and information-intensive academic tasks, including routine content delivery, retrieval, and preliminary synthesis. At the same time, it increases the relative importance of judgment-intensive functions: diagnosing misunderstanding, selecting worthwhile research questions, evaluating methods and evidence, mentoring students, and assigning responsibility for scholarly claims. The argument is therefore not that every existing university practice will persist unchanged, but that artificial intelligence shifts the comparative advantage of professors and universities toward the cultivation, evaluation, and institutional coordination of judgment under uncertainty.

papers.title: Development and Nationwide Multicentre Evaluation of Guideline-Grounded Large Language Model Chatbots to Support Patient Self-Management and Education in Rheumatology
papers.authors: Tim Wilhelmi, Vanessa Bartsch, Marius Platt, Asarnusch Rashid, Johannes Hornig, Martin Krusche, Axel J. Hueber, Daniel Fink, Alexander Pfeil, Gabriel Dischereit, Marie-Therese Holzer, Ulrich Drott, Peer Malte Aries, Max Müller, Peter Böhm, Harriet Morf, Hannah Labinsky, Felix Mühlensiepen, Diego Benavent, Sebastian Kuhn, Philipp Klemm, Johannes Knitza
papers.abstract: Patients with rheumatic diseases have persistent information needs that are not fully addressed in routine care. We developed and evaluated guideline-grounded, large language model (LLM) chatbots to support patient self-management and education in rheumatology.Ten disease-specific chatbots based on German guidelines were co-developed and deployed through 13 rheumatology centres and six patient organisations. Chatbot users rated responses and completed a questionnaire. User questions, feedback, and response characteristics were analysed using category-based coding and a six-dimensional LLM-as-a-judge assessment, with LLM-based ratings compared with rheumatologist ratings in random subsets.Between September 2025 and January 2026, 6291 questions were recorded. Thirteen question categories were identified, most commonly disease-specific questions (50.2%), medication and monitoring (37.3%) and diagnostics (28.2%). The chatbots were unable to answer in 263 interactions (4.2%). Of 2671 responses rated by users, 2481 (92.9%) received a positive rating. Insufficient detail was the most common reason for negative ratings (125/190, 65.8%). Among 602 questionnaire respondents, 84.6% reported that the chatbot was easy to use, 84.1% that answers were easy to understand, and 80.2% that it was a useful addition to patient education. In the LLM-based evaluation, 95.3% of answers were rated as completely safe and 79.1% as completely correct. Guideline adherence was assessed separately, with 45.0% rated as fully adherent; agreement with physician assessment was weak.Guideline-grounded chatbots received predominantly positive user feedback in real-world use, while LLM-based evaluation suggested that most responses were safe and correct. User questions and feedback may help guide iterative improvements to source content and patient education materials. Further studies are needed to evaluate educational effectiveness and independently validate response quality and clinical safety.

papers.title: Beyond processed depth targets: frontal EEG patterns, brain vulnerability, and postoperative delirium in older adults
papers.authors: Vikas Chauhan
papers.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
papers.abstract: Limited-channel frontal electroencephalography is widely used during anesthesia through processed EEG platforms, but clinical interpretation often remains centered on numerical depth indices. This narrative review examines whether frontal EEG signals, including raw waveforms, suppression behavior, spectral features, and processed index behavior, may provide information beyond hypnotic depth in older adults at risk for postoperative delirium. A targeted literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar for articles published from database inception through April 30, 2026. Priority was given to randomized trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, consensus statements, prospective observational studies, and mechanistic studies relevant to processed EEG monitoring, frontal EEG interpretation, postoperative delirium, aging, frailty, anesthesia, and critical care. Evidence from randomized trials and systematic reviews suggests that processed EEG-guided anesthetic titration and suppression minimization alone do not reliably prevent postoperative delirium. However, several clinically accessible frontal EEG patterns may provide contextual information about anesthetic sensitivity and reduced cerebral reserve. These include reduced frontal alpha power, early or disproportionate burst suppression, spectral slowing or low spectral edge frequency, and disorganized emergence. Their interpretation depends on anesthetic dose and agent, hemodynamics, signal quality, artifact burden, frailty, baseline cognition, and postoperative recovery context. Limited-channel frontal EEG should be interpreted as a contextual brain-monitoring signal rather than a single-number depth target. Future studies should test whether multimodal frameworks integrating frontal EEG patterns with physiologic and patient-level variables improve postoperative neurocognitive outcomes.

papers.title: Measuring AI literacy in design education: development and validation of the artificial intelligence literacy scale for design students
papers.authors: Li Chen Gu, Xun Gao, Rong Li, Zaixing Liu, Yong Li
papers.journal: International Journal of Technology and Design Education
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in design practice, challenging how design education fosters students’ AI literacy and thus prepares students to engage efficiently with AI. However, there is currently no domain-specific theoretical framework and reliable instrument in the literature to conceptualize and assess design students’ AI literacy, hindering its systematic cultivation. This study fills in this gap by developing and validating the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale for Design Students (AILS-DS), in accordance with established standards for scale development. The opinions of a wide range of experts were gathered through a qualitative method in order to define the AI literacy for design students, and served as a theoretical framework for the scale’s item pool. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA, N = 294) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA, N = 325) were then applied to explore the underlying factor structure of the scale and validate its psychometric properties. The final 23-item, five-factor scale demonstrated good reliability and construct validity. Five factors (AI Concepts and Technical Skills, AI Tool Proficiency, AI Ethics and Originality Awareness, Recognition of AI Value in Design, and Independent Evaluation of AI Outputs) in the AILS-DS capture both widely acknowledged AI literacy components and design-specific structure, reflecting the designerly way of knowing and thinking. This study provides a practical tool for educators and researchers, supporting the assessment and cultivation of AI literacy in design education and laying a foundation for pedagogical innovation in the AI era.

papers.title: A context-aware multimodal multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for autonomous personalized education
papers.authors: Muddsair Sharif, Hüseyin Şeker
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces the Context-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (CA-MA-DRL) framework, a transformative approach to personalized digital education that shifts the paradigm from passive learning analytics to autonomous, decision-making agents. The framework addresses the limitations of static, rule-based systems by integrating Multimodal Learning Analytics (MmLA) with advanced coordination mechanisms. By fusing heterogeneous data streams from Learning Management Systems (LMS), virtual classrooms, digital laboratories, and AR/VR platforms, the system constructs a rich Context-Aware Multimodal Representation that captures cognitive mastery, affective states, and behavioral engagement in real-time. The core architecture employs Student Agents and Teacher Agents that utilize Deep Q-Networks (DQN) and Actor- Critic architectures to learn optimal, personalized pedagogical policies. These agents engage in formalized negotiation protocols to balance learner agency with pedagogical integrity and institutional constraints. Incorporating a Human-inthe- loop oversight model through explainable AI (XAI), the framework ensures that instructors retain authority while benefiting from computational assistance. Comparative analysis across eight capability dimensions demonstrates that CAMA- DRL achieves 86% aggregate capability (69/80) compared to 29% for LLM Multi-Agent, 26% for Single-Agent DRL, and 18% for Rule-Based ITS, while resolving the accuracy-scalability trade-off through shared policy networks with meta-learning transfer. This digital-first foundation enables scalable and ethical personalization and provides a systematic pathway toward future hybrid cyber-physical and embodied educational AI systems.

papers.title: Examining the role of a structured AI-supported intervention in developing EFL students’ academic writing skills in Mozambican higher education
papers.authors: Joaquim Vicente Vinte, Mustafa Kurt
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping educational practices and redefining how academic writing is taught, learned, and assessed. This study explores the role of a structured AI-supported writing intervention on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students’ academic writing performance and examines lecturers’ awareness of, and alignment with, emerging AI trends in a Mozambican public university. Employing an Exploratory Sequential Case Study-Mixed Methods design, data were collected through documents analyses, interviews, an intervention, and observations. Participants included eighteen undergraduate EFL students and five lecturers. Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Social Practice Theory (SPT), qualitative data were analysed thematically, while quantitative data were examined using descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test to measure performance differences. Findings revealed that students in the control group had limited informal exposure to AI and lacked ethical guidance, whereas students participating in the structured AI-supported intervention demonstrated higher levels of academic writing performance and responsible AI use following the intervention. However, most lecturers reported limited awareness of AI writing tools and students’ use of these technologies. From a TAM perspective, perceived usefulness, ease of use, and pedagogical support were associated with students’ acceptance of AI tools for academic writing purposes. The SPT interpretation further suggested that social interactions, supervision practices, and shared ethical norms contributed to how students integrated ChatGPT as an AI writing tool in their undergraduate writing practices. The study highlights the importance of AI literacy initiatives for both students and lecturers, as well as institutional ethical guidelines to support responsible and sustainable AI adoption in Mozambican higher education.

papers.title: Time-Aware Explainability for Cryptocurrency Forecasting: Evidence from a User Study
papers.authors: Donika Xhani, Hakan Tirsi, João Moreira, Renata S. S. Guizzardi, Marcos R. Machado
papers.abstract: Abstract As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into financial decision-making, concerns about model opacity and regulatory compliance have come to the forefront. These concerns are particularly important in settings where forecasts influence risk assessment, portfolio decisions, and the credibility of AI-supported financial advice. This study examines how eXplainable AI (XAI) techniques can enhance transparency in the context of cryptocurrency forecasting–a domain characterized by extreme volatility and uncertainty. Using historical Bitcoin prices and macroeconomic indicators, we compare two deep learning approaches and apply TimeSHAP, a sequentially-aware explanation method, to clarify their predictions. Rather than focusing solely on model performance, we assess how different explanation formats are interpreted by finance-oriented users through a structured user study. Results show that local explanations are more easily understood and perceived as actionable, while more abstract forms–such as event-level and global plots–elicit mixed responses. This distinction matters because the practical value of explainability in finance depends not only on technical faithfulness, but also on whether explanations improve users’ confidence, support better-informed decisions, and help institutions justify model-based actions under scrutiny. To further support transparency and regulatory alignment, we document the entire machine learning process using a domain-specific ontology (XMLPO), offering a structured approach to traceability and reproducibility. Our findings suggest that effective explainability in financial AI requires both technically robust methods and communication strategies tailored to the needs of end-users. For financial economists and policy- and decision makers, the results indicate that the format in which AI explanations are presented can shape trust, perceived usefulness, and the governance value of predictive systems. This study contributes to the growing body of work on how AI systems can be made more interpretable, trustworthy, and aligned with economic governance in high-stakes domains.

papers.title: The lack of creative destruction in healthcare systems makes innovation a cost driver
papers.authors: Christine Westermann-Lammers, Johannes Hohenauer
papers.abstract: Creative destruction, a concept developed by the economist Joseph Schumpeter, describes the process by which new innovations displace and replace existing technologies, business models and structures. While this approach has driven significant efficiency gains across various industries, it remains largely absent in healthcare. The disproportionate rise in health expenditure relative to care output points to structural inefficiencies and untapped potential. A cross-sectoral comparison with telecommunications and banking shows that technological progress in those industries generated tremendous efficiency gains, as intense competition forced the creative destruction of inefficient structures. In healthcare, by contrast, additive and content-based innovations dominate: they supplement existing processes rather than replace them, increasing complexity and cost without generating efficiency gains. The primary causes are financial misalignment through cost-based reimbursement principles, fee for service mechanisms that favor low-value care, structural barriers such as capital investment lock-in and institutions' cultural resistance to change. At present, creative destruction has little effect in healthcare because systematic mechanisms for de-implementing outdated processes are absent. To enable sustainable efficiency gains, three things are required: embedding cost efficiency as a governance criterion, realigning research and reimbursement incentives towards substitutive and process-based innovations and rigorously establishing de-implementation models. Without these reforms, the efficiency-enhancing potential of disruptive technologies, such as AI-assisted diagnostics, telemedicine and automated administrative processes will remain untapped.

papers.title: Quality of life and functional outcomes after low anterior rectal resection with total mesorectal excision: a propensity score-matched comparison of robotic-assisted versus open surgery
papers.authors: Frederick Bröcker, Susanne Merkel, Anne Jacobsen, Klaus Weber, Axel Denz, Robert Grützmann, Georg F. Weber, Maximilian Brunner, Christian Krautz
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) for rectal cancer is increasingly adopted. However, a recent systematic review highlighted a significant gap in the literature regarding quality of life (QOL) after different total mesorectal excision (TME) techniques, with open TME being particularly underrepresented. This study aimed to compare QOL and anorectal function between robotic-assisted and open low anterior rectal resection with TME. METHODS: Patients who underwent low anterior rectal resection with TME and primary anastomosis between 2006 and 2021 at a single tertiary centre were identified. Propensity score matching was performed based on sex, age, BMI, UICC stage and tumour height. After excluding patients without QOL follow-up or with a persistent diverting stoma, 40 patients per group were available. QOL was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30, QLQ-CR29, and LARS score. RESULTS: In the matched cohort, baseline characteristics were well balanced except for tumour height (p = .002), with more lower-third tumours in the open group. No significant differences were observed in any EORTC QLQ-C30 domain, including global health status (66.5 vs. 71.7, p = .197). QLQ-CR29 showed comparable outcomes for most domains; however, sexual interest was significantly lower in the RAS group for women (88.1 vs. 55.6, p = .008). LARS scores were similar between groups (24.4 vs. 25.6, p = .765). Perioperative outcomes including morbidity (10.0% vs. 22.5%, p = .130) and anastomotic leakage (2.5% vs. 5.0%, p = .526) did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS: Robotic-assisted and open low anterior rectal resection with TME resulted in comparable QOL and anorectal function across all assessed domains. Notably, approximately one third of patients in both groups reported major LARS, underscoring the persistent functional burden irrespective of surgical approach. By providing direct comparative data on open TME - an approach underrepresented in the literature - these findings contribute to closing an important evidence gap.

papers.title: Against mandatory prompt disclosure in AI-assisted scholarship
papers.authors: Brian David Earp, Udo Schüklenk, Julian Savulescu, Sebastian Porsdam Mann
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are becoming routine as tools for drafting, editing, and revising scholarly manuscripts, raising difficult questions about how much transparency is needed to assess research integrity, authorship claims, and accountability. In response, some authors have proposed that researchers who use LLMs in manuscript preparation should be required to submit the prompts they used, together with the generated outputs, as supplemental material. We support detailed disclosure when it is needed to assess the scientific validity or reproducibility of a study, for example where LLMs are used in data analysis, coding, literature synthesis, or the production of figures. We argue, however, against Mandatory Full Inclusion (MFI) of prompts and outputs for ordinary writing assistance. Such a policy would, we suggest, be difficult to enforce, easy for dishonest users to evade, burdensome for careful users to follow, and poorly suited to the capacities of editors and peer reviewers. It would also risk discouraging beneficial uses of LLMs, penalizing careful multi-model consultation, distorting how researchers interact with AI systems, and disadvantaging scholars who already face undue or unnecessary barriers in academic publishing, including scholars at under-resourced institutions. More generally, an MFI policy would impose a level of surveillance on AI-assisted writing that has no clear analog in ordinary human collaboration. We propose instead a proportionate prompt-and-output disclosure framework: targeted disclosure where reproducibility or validity requires it; voluntary documentation where authors wish to demonstrate their contribution; and continued reliance on authorship attestation, contributor statements, and misconduct procedures where warranted. This approach better aligns transparency with the risks posed by LLM use in scholarly writing, while also minimizing surveillance-related harms and inefficiencies.

papers.title: Perspective: Ten Principles of Green Polymer Processing
papers.authors: Brandi L. Martz, Gary E. Wnek
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Polymer sustainability is commonly evaluated through feedstock selection, renewable materials, and chemical design; however, the role of polymer processing is often overlooked when determining environmental impact. Existing sustainability frameworks, including the principles of Green Chemistry and Green Engineering, provide important guidance for chemical and industrial development but do not fully address the unique challenges associated with polymer processing, such as high thermal and mechanical energy input, process complexity, scalability, and industrial implementation. In this work, 10 principles of green polymer processing are proposed to provide a sustainability‐focused framework specifically for polymer manufacturing and process development. These principles include solvent responsibility, intentional chemistry, energy efficiency, carbon consciousness, zero‐waste processing, process and material simplification, processing that is safe‐by‐design, data‐driven manufacturing, scalable design, and industrial integration. Each principle is discussed in the context of common polymer manufacturing operations including extrusion, thermoforming, additive manufacturing, solid‐state processing, and solvent‐based processing. The framework emphasizes that processing methods can significantly influence recyclability, energy consumption, additive usage, occupational safety, and overall environmental impact. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, real‐time sensing, and predictive modeling are also highlighted as tools for sustainable polymer manufacturing. These principles are intended to serve as an educational and conceptual guide for students, researchers, educators, and industry professionals developing more sustainable polymer processing technologies.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Well‐Being Paradox: When AI Decision Delegation Helps and Hurts Consumer Well‐Being
papers.authors: Jingru Xu, Chunli Ji, Haoqi Chu, Catherine Prentice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative AI increasingly shapes consumer decision‐making, its implications for consumer well‐being remain unclear. Existing research largely focuses on the trade‐off between algorithmic efficiency and autonomy loss. This research advances understanding by proposing the algorithmic well‐being paradox, whereby the same AI delegation can enhance or diminish well‐being depending on the consumption context. Integrating Savoring Theory and Self‐Determination Theory, we develop a framework that explains when and why these divergent outcomes occur. To test the proposed relationships, four studies were conducted with 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiments ( N = 1427) spanning multiple consumption domains, including cameras, guided tours, ergonomic chairs, glamping trips, smartphones, Arctic expeditions, and smart‐home systems. Study 1 demonstrates that the effects of algorithmic delegation differ between experiential and material consumption. Studies 2 and 3 identify anticipatory savoring and autonomy frustration as the underlying mechanisms, while Study 4 confirms the proposed dual‐mediation process in a high‐complexity context. Results show that consumption type shapes how consumers respond to AI delegation. In experiential consumption, AI delegation increases well‐being by enhancing anticipatory savoring, with these benefits outweighing autonomy concerns. In material consumption, AI delegation reduces well‐being by increasing autonomy frustration, which diminishes the benefits of convenience. These findings advance human‐AI interaction research by demonstrating that the impact of algorithmic delegation depends on consumers' underlying consumption goals and provide guidance for designing more human‐centered AI decision‐support systems.

papers.title: AI‐Powered Virtual Patients in Health Professions Education: Learner Engagement and Knowledge Application
papers.authors: Jeffrey J. Borckardt, Debra Henninger, Joe Vuthiganon, Dusti Annan‐Coultas, Lisa Langdale, Kimberly Kascak, Lindsey M. Hamil
papers.abstract: PURPOSE/OBJECTIVES: Immersive educational technologies, including applications of artificial intelligence in education (AIED), are increasingly used to develop clinical skills in health professions education. This study evaluated the feasibility and perceived value of integrating an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled virtual patient platform into a required first-year dental medicine course and explored AI-assisted analysis of student interview transcripts. METHODS: Seventy-eight first-year Doctor of Dental Medicine (D.M.D.) students completed three faculty-developed virtual patient interviews aligned with course objectives. Students then completed a voluntary survey assessing usability, learning experience, and engagement/motivation on a 5-point Likert scale, along with preferences for interaction modality and avatar style. Exploratory qualitative analyses of interview transcripts were conducted across six domains: empathy, professionalism, thoroughness, attention to behavioral health, interview skill, and potential bias by race/sex. Descriptive statistics summarized responses. RESULTS: Mean ratings were high for usability (M = 4.22, SD = 0.24), learning experience (M = 4.47, SD = 0.09), and engagement/motivation (M = 4.42, SD = 0.04). For avatar preference, 33% of students preferred realistic avatars, 22% preferred cartoon avatars, and 45% had no preference; most (89%) preferred text-based over voice-based interaction. Exploratory analysis of 217 transcripts suggested generally strong performance with identifiable areas for improvement, including subtle differences in rapport by patient race and sex. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the feasibility and perceived value of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation in early dental education. Controlled studies are needed to evaluate effects on learning outcomes and skill development relative to existing instructional approaches.

papers.title: Brief Cognitive‐Behavioral Therapy for Non‐Underweight Eating Disorders ( CBT ‐T): Psychological and Weight‐Related Outcomes, and Predictors of Improvement
papers.authors: Jessica Ellingham, Hannah M. Turner, Madeleine Tatham, Glenn Waller
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Brief Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT-T) has been developed as an accessible treatment for eating disorders in non-underweight individuals. It is important to understand the factors that predict response to this treatment in this population. This study examined predictors of outcomes from CBT-T using a large naturalistic sample. The aims were to determine outcomes of CBT-T and to identify the role of pre-therapy characteristics and early change in predicting outcomes. METHOD: The sample consisted of 371 adults who entered CBT-T (10 sessions). All completed measures at sessions 1, 4, and 10, including eating pathology (EDE-Q); anxiety (GAD-7); and depression (PHQ-9). Body Mass Index was calculated from clinician-measured weight and height. Intent-to-treat (GLMM) and completer analyses were used. RESULTS: Of the 371 participants, 53.1% completed therapy. There were no factors that predicted attrition. In ITT analyses, patients showed significant changes in EDE-Q scores overall and between sessions 1-4 and 4-10, with large effect sizes and ending substantially below clinical cut-off. In ITT analyses, BMI did not change over treatment, regardless of baseline BMI. Completer analyses indicated a small increase in BMI, although the magnitude of change was small. Baseline scores (EDE-Q, BMI, PHQ-9, GAD-7) offered minimal prediction of outcome at end of therapy, whereas early change (session 1-4) in restraint and weight concerns were strong predictors of overall outcome. CONCLUSIONS: CBT-T replicated its strong effects for non-underweight patients, while BMI remained broadly stable, with only small increases observed in completer analyses.

papers.title: When AI Sounds Supportive: Comparing Conversational AI and Therapist Responses to Mental Health Disclosures
papers.authors: Shriya Thakkar, Paras Bhatt, Harsh Parekh
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives To compare artificial intelligence (AI) and therapist responses to real‐world mental health (MH) disclosures and evaluate differences in empathy, safety practices and contextual usefulness. Methods We analysed 937 unique MH disclosures and 2749 therapist responses using the Counsel Chat dataset. For each disclosure, we generated a standardised AI response using a large language model. Responses were evaluated across empathy, safety and contextual usefulness measures using automated metrics, blinded human ratings of 120 therapist‐AI response pairs, mixed effects regression models, and qualitative analyses of disagreement cases. Results AI responses scored higher than therapist responses on automated empathy ( β = 0.30; p < 0.001), human‐rated empathy ( β = 0.38; p < 0.001), emotional validation ( β = 0.40; p < 0.001) and automated safety ( β = 0.25; p < 0.001). AI safety advantages were largest for self‐harm or suicide‐related disclosures. Therapists scored higher on specificity/personalisation ( β = −0.62; p < 0.001) and helpfulness ( β = −0.23; p = 0.013); overall quality did not differ significantly. Conclusions As conversational AI becomes an increasingly common source of MH support, AI responses may offer strengths in empathic communication and explicit safety‐oriented guidance, whereas therapist responses were rated more highly for personalisation and contextual usefulness. These findings highlight different strengths across AI and therapist responses while underscoring the need for caution in interpreting response quality as clinical effectiveness. They also point to a potential role for conversational AI as an accessible first point of support within broader MH care systems, particularly where timely professional support is limited.

papers.title: Digital Divide in Access to AI Health Services Across Linguistic Minorities: An English Language and Literature Perspective
papers.authors: Revant Gautam
papers.journal: World Journal of Future Technologies in Computer Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled health services are transforming healthcare delivery through automated diagnosis support, virtual assistants, predictive analytics, and personalized health recommendations. However, unequal access to these technologies remains a significant challenge, particularly among linguistic minority communities where language barriers influence digital participation and healthcare communication. This study examines the digital divide in AI-based healthcare access from an English Language and Literature perspective by analysing the relationship between language accessibility, digital literacy, trust, and adoption of AI health platforms among linguistically diverse users. A mixed-method research design was adopted involving a structured survey of 300 respondents belonging to linguistic minority groups. The findings reveal that English proficiency, availability of multilingual AI interfaces, and confidence in digital communication significantly influence AI healthcare adoption. Statistical analysis indicates a strong association between language accessibility and willingness to use AI health services. The study highlights the importance of inclusive language design, culturally responsive AI systems, and multilingual digital health communication strategies for reducing disparities in emerging healthcare technologies.

papers.title: Τεχνητή νοημοσύνη στη λογιστική, στη φορολογία και στην ελεγκτική : μια συστηματική ανασκόπηση εφαρμογών, επιπτώσεων και μελλοντικών κατευθύνσεων
papers.authors: N. Nikolopoulou
papers.abstract: This thesis examines the role and impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the fields of accounting, taxation, and auditing. Its main objective is to investigate how AI technologies are transforming traditional financial processes, improving efficiency and accuracy, supporting decision-making, and creating new opportunities and challenges for financial professionals. The study adopts a qualitative research approach based on a systematic review of academic literature. It examines the applications of key AI technologies, including Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Robotic Process Automation (RPA), and Generative AI. Through a comparative analysis, the thesis explores the benefits, limitations, and implications of AI adoption across the three professional fields. In accounting, AI contributes to the automation of routine tasks, such as bookkeeping, invoice processing, financial reporting, and account reconciliation. Furthermore, machine learning and predictive analytics support financial forecasting, risk assessment, fraud detection, and managerial decision-making. These applications reduce manual workload, improve the accuracy and timeliness of financial information, and allow accountants to focus on more analytical, advisory, and strategic activities. In taxation, AI plays an important role in automating tax calculations and reporting, improving tax compliance, identifying potential tax evasion, and predicting compliance risks. AI-powered systems can analyze large volumes of financial data and help tax authorities identify high-risk cases more effectively. Nevertheless, their implementation raises important concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, fairness, and the protection of taxpayers' rights. In auditing, AI enhances audit procedures through advanced risk assessment, fraud and anomaly detection, document analysis, and continuous monitoring of financial transactions. Unlike traditional approaches that often rely on sampling and manual verification, AI enables auditors to analyze larger datasets and identify potential irregularities more efficiently. However, the use of AI in auditing requires particular attention to transparency, explainability, accountability, and compliance with professional and regulatory standards. The comparative analysis demonstrates that, although AI offers significant benefits across all three fields, its applications and adoption patterns differ. Accounting focuses primarily on process automation and financial analysis, taxation emphasizes compliance and enforcement, while auditing concentrates on audit quality, risk assessment, and the reliability of assurance procedures. The thesis also highlights that accounting appears relatively advanced in organizational AI adoption, while auditing faces greater challenges because of its strict requirements for professional judgment, transparency, and accountability. Despite its considerable potential, AI adoption presents several challenges. These include inadequate data quality, limited model explainability, algorithmic bias, data security and privacy concerns, regulatory uncertainty, implementation costs, and the need for specialized skills. Generative AI also raises concerns about the accuracy and reliability of its outputs. Therefore, AI-generated information must be carefully evaluated and verified, particularly when it affects financial reporting, taxation, or audit conclusions. The findings further indicate that AI is transforming the role of accounting, tax, and auditing professionals rather than simply replacing them. As routine tasks become increasingly automated, professionals must develop digital literacy, data analytics skills, technological knowledge, critical thinking, and the ability to evaluate AI-generated results. Human judgment, ethical responsibility, and professional skepticism remain essential for ensuring reliable outcomes. The thesis concludes that AI should be regarded as a complementary tool that enhances human expertise rather than replacing it. Successful implementation requires high-quality data, appropriate technological infrastructure, continuous professional training, effective governance, transparent systems, and clear regulatory frameworks. Future research should focus on empirical studies examining the real-world effects of AI adoption, human–AI interaction, explainable AI, ethical governance, and the integration of AI with technologies such as blockchain and cloud computing.Overall, the study demonstrates that Artificial Intelligence represents a significant driver of digital transformation in accounting, taxation, and auditing. Its responsible adoption can improve efficiency, accuracy, transparency, and decision-making, provided that technological innovation is combined with human expertise, ethical principles, and appropriate regulatory safeguards.

papers.title: تحلیل مروری پایداری سیستمهای غیرخطی بر اساس روش مستقیم لیاپانوف
papers.authors: محمد یزدان پرست, حکیمی, پوهنمل فرهاد, پوهنیار احمدولی نوری
papers.abstract: A Review Analysis of the Stability of Nonlinear Systems Based on Lyapunov’s Direct Method Mohammad Yazanparast, Farhad hakimi, Ahmad Wali Noori Abstract Nonlinear systems appear in many mathematical, engineering, physical, and population-related phenomena. Their stability analysis is important for understanding system behavior near equilibrium, especially when explicit solutions of the differential equations are difficult or unavailable. This article presents an analytical review of nonlinear system stability based on Lyapunov’s direct method. The study focuses on the Lyapunov function, its positive definiteness, the behavior of its derivative along system trajectories, the difficulty of constructing a suitable function, recent computational approaches, and several simple illustrative examples. The study relies on reliable sources published after 2015, covering stability theory, nonlinear control, fractional-order systems, neural networks, optimization and methods, and also population and epidemiological models. The review shows that Lyapunov’s direct method can assess stability, asymptotic stability, and, under stronger assumptions, exponential stability without explicitly solving the system equations. Nevertheless, constructing a suitable Lyapunov function remains the most difficult part of the method, which has motivated the development of computational methods, machine-learning approaches, and control Lyapunov functions. The article concludes that Lyapunov’s direct method, despite its practical limitations, remains important for both the analysis and teaching of nonlinear system stability. Keywords: Asymptotic stability, Lyapunov direct method, Lyapunov function, Nonlinear systems, Stability

papers.title: A BLOCKCHAIN IMMUTABILITY AND MACHINE LEARNING CERTIFICATE: FRAUD DETECTION FOR MITIGATING CREDENTIAL FRAUD
papers.authors: Aminu Baffa Ibrahim, Ibrahim Bashir Faruk, Eli Adama Jiya
papers.abstract: Academic credential fraud is a critical systemic challenge in Nigerian higher education because conventional verification depends on the continued operation, record integrity, and responsiveness of issuing institutions. This study addresses the resulting research gap by developing a verification infrastructure that remains functional independently of institutional continuity. A blockchain-based academic certificate verification system was designed and implemented using two Solidity 0.8.20 smart contracts, InstitutionRegistry and CertificateRegistry, deployed on the Sepolia Ethereum testnet. Certificate documents were stored on the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) through Pinata, while SHA-256 hashes and IPFS Content Identifiers were permanently anchored on-chain during issuance. A React 18 application provided role-specific interfaces for institutions, graduates, and third-party verifiers. Security evaluation demonstrated resistance across five attack categories, while 200-trial benchmarking recorded an average verification time of 87 ms at zero verifier cost. Polygon Layer 2 deployment reduced certificate issuance costs to approximately $0.018. A complementary machine-learning fraud-detection component used 1,000 structured certificate records, each containing 16 domain-specific features. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost were optimized using GridSearchCV with five-fold cross-validation and evaluated on held-out data. XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy (93.5%), followed by Random Forest (91.5%) and Logistic Regression (75.5%). Verification complexity, previous rejections, and days to verify were the most predictive features. The complete system and analytical pipeline are packaged in a reproducible Google Colab notebook.

papers.title: The Artificial Intelligence Revolution in Higher Education: From the E-Learning Model to the Smart Learning Model
papers.authors: Dr. Chouini Khalid
papers.abstract: The university educational landscape is undergoing rapid transformations as a result of the continuous development of information and communication technology. Higher education institutions have gradually shifted from traditional forms of education toward the use of digital media, giving rise to e-learning, which has provided new methods for presenting educational content, managing interaction, and overcoming spatial and temporal boundaries. With the major revolution brought about by artificial intelligence, qualitative transformations have emerged in the nature of the educational environment. Digital technology is no longer limited to making educational content available or facilitating communication and interaction between the professor and the student; rather, it has gone beyond this to include the ability to analyze students’ educational data, provide them with personalized content, support assessment, and contribute to building educational environments that are more responsive to learners’ needs and preferences. This study aims to analyze this transition from e-learning to smart learning through a theoretical examination of the concept of the educational process in the digital environment and the position of educational technology and e-learning within it, followed by an analysis of how artificial intelligence is employed to develop the components of the educational process and the new roles within it, while identifying the most prominent applications and challenges associated with this transformation. The study adopted the descriptive-analytical method through an analysis of the relevant scientific literature and references. The study concluded that the transition from the e-learning model to the artificial intelligence-based smart learning model does not merely represent the addition of a new technology to the educational environment; rather, it reflects a transformation in the structure of the educational process itself, from a digital environment that provides access to knowledge to an environment capable of analyzing educational content, adapting to it, and providing a greater degree of personalization and intelligent support, while the professor and learner remain central elements of the educational process.

papers.title: ChatGPT in Education: Beyond the Boon-or-Bane Debate—A Critical Narrative Review of Opportunities, Risks, and Responsible Integration
papers.authors: Sadia Samar Ali
papers.journal: International journal of industrial engineering and operational research
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence, particularly ChatGPT, has rapidly entered educational practice and has intensified debate about whether it strengthens or weakens learning. This paper critically reviews the educational roles, benefits, risks, and implementation lessons associated with ChatGPT, drawing on the literature assembled in the original manuscript. The review indicates that ChatGPT can support personalized explanation, rapid formative feedback, lesson and assessment design, language learning, idea generation, and access to learning support beyond normal classroom hours. At the same time, its educational value is constrained by inaccurate or fabricated outputs, overreliance, weakened independent reasoning, ambiguity around authorship, academic integrity concerns, privacy and equity issues, and the risk of superficial learning. The evidence, therefore, does not support a simple 'boon versus bane' dichotomy. A more useful interpretation is that outcomes depend on how the technology is positioned within pedagogy, assessment, institutional policy, and human oversight. The paper proposes the Purpose–Verify–Disclose–Demonstrate (PVDD) human-in-the-loop framework, built around four principles: purposeful use, verification, transparent attribution, and authentic assessment. Practical implications are presented for students, educators, institutions, and policymakers. The paper concludes that ChatGPT is most educationally valuable when it augments rather than substitutes for human judgment, disciplinary reasoning, creativity, and teacher–student interaction.

papers.title: SPORADIC CREUTZFELDT-JAKOB DISEASE: CLINICAL FEATURES, DIAGNOSIS AND THERAPEUTIC HORIZONS.
papers.authors: A Shala, N Shala, F Jashari, B Jashari, R Jashari
papers.abstract: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) is a rare, rapidly progressive, and fatal prion disease that remains a major diagnostic and therapeutic challenge. Its presentation often overlaps with other causes of rapidly progressive dementia, making early recognition essential, particularly to exclude potentially reversible conditions. This review provides an updated overview of the diagnostic tools, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers, prognostic factors, clinical progression, differential diagnosis, and current management strategies in sCJD. A literature-based review was conducted using PubMed and Scopus for articles published between October 1, 2015, and October 1, 2025, focusing on patients with suspected or confirmed CJD. Clinical features, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), electroencephalography (EEG), CSF biomarkers, prognostic indicators, and therapeutic approaches were synthesized. Current diagnosis of sCJD relies on the integration of clinical presentation with MRI, EEG, and CSF testing. Diffusion-weighted MRI and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) have substantially improved antemortem diagnostic accuracy, while traditional biomarkers such as 14-3-3 protein and total tau remain useful supportive tests. Prognosis is uniformly poor, with median survival usually limited to a few months, although disease course varies according to age, PRNP codon 129 polymorphism, and molecular subtype. Important differential diagnoses include autoimmune encephalitis, viral encephalitis, vascular cognitive impairment, and other neurodegenerative disorders presenting with rapidly progressive dementia. No disease-modifying therapy has shown definitive benefit, and management remains primarily supportive and symptom-directed. Advances in biomarkers and greater understanding of molecular heterogeneity may improve early diagnosis, prognostication, and future therapeutic development.

papers.title: FounderPulse-AI: Design and Pilot Evaluation of Bounded Intelligence for Startup Founders Under Entrepreneurial Strain
papers.authors: Stavros Sindakis, Christina Kovatsi
papers.journal: Journal of Intelligence Technology and Innovation
papers.abstract: Intelligent decision support systems increasingly assist users under uncertainty, but limited research explains how they can support startup founders under entrepreneurial strain without crossing into coaching, clinical, or advisory authority. This study designed and pilot-evaluated FounderPulse-AI, a retrieval-grounded, prompt-governed, nonclinical decision support artifact for Greek startup founders. Using design science research, the study combined a qualitative needs analysis with 20 founders, co-founders, and ecosystem actors and a four-week comparison involving 100 founders and co-founders assigned to FounderPulse-AI or a structured reflection journal. FounderPulse-AI produced stronger gains in reflective clarity, perceived decision quality, perceived usefulness, trust in AI, usability, boundary clarity, escalation appropriateness, and intention to continue use, while privacy concerns decreased more in the journal condition. The main contribution is a bounded AI founder support architecture and a Responsible AI Founder Support Model that connects intelligent interaction, decision recovery, privacy sensitivity, and human escalation.
