papers.title: Usar no es aprender: una lectura crítica de PISA 2025 y de la evidencia internacional sobre IAGen
papers.authors: Melvin Ramírez Bogantes, Marco Vinicio Gutiérrez Montenegro
papers.abstract: La discusión educativa sobre inteligencia artificial generativa suele tratar el “uso de IA” como una exposición homogénea cuyos efectos podrían establecerse mediante una respuesta única. Este ensayo cuestiona esa premisa mediante un análisis documental comparado de un corpus principal de fuentes institucionales y académicas de alta influencia publicadas entre 2023 y 2026, complementado por antecedentes teóricos sobre instrumentación, descarga cognitiva y autorregulación. El corpus comprende PISA 2025, TALIS 2024, documentos normativos de UNESCO, el OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026, el AI Index Report 2026 y dos metaanálisis recientes sobre ChatGPT y resultados de aprendizaje. Los resultados muestran que las aparentes contradicciones entre asociaciones negativas, efectos experimentales favorables y recomendaciones normativas disminuyen cuando se distinguen el tipo de uso observado, el trabajo cognitivo que permanece en el estudiante, la mediación o regulación de la interacción y el alcance inferencial del diseño. PISA 2025 identifica relaciones diferenciadas entre uso de chatbots y desempeño científico según propósito y frecuencia, así como desigualdades en las oportunidades escolares declaradas para evaluar información generada por IA; su diseño no permite convertir esas asociaciones en efectos causales. Como contribución, se propone un criterio de cuatro preguntas para interpretar evidencia sobre inteligencia artificial generativa y aprendizaje. El caso costarricense muestra que el uso relativamente alto de chatbots, las oportunidades declaradas de evaluación crítica y los desafíos persistentes de desempeño pueden coexistir, por lo que la discusión debe desplazarse desde la mera disponibilidad hacia la calidad del uso educativo.

papers.title: BEYOND “JUST USE AI”: A TEACHER-MEDIATED FRAMEWORK FOR MEANINGFUL AI INTEGRATION IN EFL CLASSROOMS — INSIGHTS FROM REAL TEACHING AND MULTI-AI PRACTICE IN UZBEKISTAN
papers.authors: Ganijonova Sitorakhon
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly present in English language learning, yet easier access to explanations, models, and feedback does not automatically produce stronger learning. This practice-informed paper examines AI use through real English teaching and material-development experience in Uzbekistan, including examination-oriented reading, writing, speaking, vocabulary, and grammar work. It proposes the TRUST framework—Target, Run, Use, Scrutinize, Transfer—as a teacher-mediated model that keeps learners cognitively active before, during, and after AI interaction. The paper also introduces the AI-free moment as a practical check of independent learning.

papers.title: LEVERAGING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)-POWERED PERSONALISED AGRICULTURAL INFORMATION AMONG RURAL FARMERS IN LAGOS STATE
papers.authors: Toheeb Abiodun3 ISHOLA, EMMANUEL STANLEY OLATUNDE
papers.journal: Journal of Entomology and Agronomy Studies
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered personalised agricultural information is increasingly becoming important in modern agriculture because of its ability to provide timely, location-specific and farm-specific advisory services to farmers. This study examined rural farmers’ awareness and perceived acceptance of AI-powered personalised agricultural information in Lagos State. The study was carried out in selected rural agricultural areas of Lagos State, namely Epe, Ikorodu and Ibeju-Lekki. A multistage sampling procedure was used to select 201 respondents from a population of 1,230 registered farmers. Data were collected with a structured questionnaire and analysed using frequency counts, percentages and weighted mean scores. Findings revealed that most respondents were female (60.2%), had tertiary education (83.6%), practised both crop and animal farming (64.7%), owned smartphones (94.5%) and had internet access (94.0%). The study further revealed that 70.6% of the respondents had high awareness of AI-powered personalised agricultural information, while 64.7% had high perceived acceptance. Farmers were most aware that AI technologies are commonly used in agriculture, with a weighted mean score of 1.78. They also strongly accepted that AI-powered agricultural information can improve farming productivity, with a mean score of 4.45. The study concluded that rural farmers in Lagos State are generally aware of and receptive to AI-powered agricultural information, especially where such technologies are perceived as useful, accessible and relevant to their farming activities. It was recommended that extension agencies intensify awareness programmes and that AI platforms be designed in simple, mobile-friendly and farmer-centred formats.

papers.title: O'zbekistonda sun'iy intellekt texnologiyalarini joriy etish sharoitida inson kapitalining raqamli iqtisodiyot rivojlanishiga ta'sirini ekonometrik baholash
papers.authors: Zilola Turobovna Jurayeva
papers.abstract: The article econometrically assesses the impact of human capital on the development of Uzbekistan's digital economy under the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, using data for 2010-2024. A three-component composite digital economy index (DEI) is constructed, and human capital is proxied by tertiary enrolment. Autoregressive distributed lag (ADL) models are estimated with Newey-West (HAC) standard errors, including a regime dummy and an interaction term for the AI policy period. The long-run effect of human capital on the DEI is 0.460; its effect on ICT service exports was statistically insignificant before 2021, while in the AI policy period the short-run elasticity reached 1.04 and the long-run elasticity 1.46. Policy proposals for enriching human capital with AI competencies are developed.

papers.title: Women’s Leadership In The Digital Era: Opportunities, Structural Barriers, And An Integrative Framework For Inclusive Digital Leadership
papers.authors: Prof. (Dr.) Ashok Purohit, Dr. Sidharth Jain
papers.abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping leadership through the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), data analytics, digital communication platforms, remote work systems, and technology-enabled organizational structures. These developments create new opportunities for women to access leadership networks, establish professional visibility, participate in strategic decision-making, and lead innovation. However, digital transformation does not automatically eliminate gender inequality. Existing organizational hierarchies, unequal access to digital resources, gender stereotypes, algorithmic bias, online harassment, and unequal opportunities for professional development may reproduce traditional forms of exclusion within digital environments. This paper develops an integrative conceptual framework to explain how technological capabilities, individual agency, organizational practices, and institutional conditions interact to influence women’s leadership in the digital era. Drawing on established leadership theories, research on gender and organizations, digital leadership scholarship, and literature on digital inequality, the paper identifies five interrelated dimensions of inclusive digital leadership: digital competence, strategic influence, network participation, algorithmic and technological accountability, and organizational inclusion. It further proposes that organizational culture, access to resources, and institutional support shape the relationship between digital capability and leadership outcomes. The paper contributes to the literature by connecting gender and leadership research with digital transformation and by presenting propositions for future empirical investigation. Practical implications are outlined for organizations, policymakers, educational institutions, and leadership-development programs. The paper concludes that meaningful progress requires more than increasing women’s access to technology; it requires ensuring that women can influence digital strategies, participate in technology-related decision-making, and exercise leadership authority within equitable and accountable digital systems.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic Background and Electrographic Abnormalities in Term and Near-Term Neonates With Hyperbilirubinemia: An Observational Study
papers.authors: Yosra H Hammouda, Neveen M ElFayoumy, Mye Ali Basheer, Eman Mahmoud Metwalli, Yara Salah Shaheen, Amira M. El Gohary
papers.abstract: Background: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia is a common condition that may progress to bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction and permanent neurological injury. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides information regarding cerebral electrical activity, brain maturation, background organization, and electrographic seizures. Although abnormalities in sleep–wake cycling have been described in neonates with hyperbilirubinemia, less attention has been given to other EEG abnormalities, including background abnormalities and electrographic seizure activity. Objective: To characterize EEG background abnormalities, age-related EEG maturation, and electrographic seizure or brief potentially ictal rhythmic discharge (BIRD) activity in term and near-term neonates with hyperbilirubinemia. Methods: This observational cross-sectional study enrolled 38 term and near-term neonates with hyperbilirubinemia admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit of Cairo University Children’s Hospital. Each infant underwent at least one hour of polygraphic EEG recording together with clinical and laboratory assessment. EEG background amplitude, age-appropriate graphoelements, age-dependent synchrony and continuity, and seizure/BIRD activity were assessed. Results: Among the 38 analyzed neonates, 31 (81.6%) had normal background amplitude, while 7 (18.4%) had abnormal background amplitude. Age-appropriate graphoelements were present in 36 neonates (94.7%), while abnormalities were identified in 2 (5.3%). Age-dependent synchrony and continuity were normal in 34 neonates (89.5%) and abnormal in 4 (10.5%). Seizure activity or BIRDs were documented in 4 neonates (10.5%). One neonate had electrographic seizure activity without overt clinical seizures. The observed epileptic activity was predominantly localized to the temporal and occipital regions in the representative recordings. Conclusion: EEG abnormalities involving background activity, age-related organization, and electrographic seizure activity were observed in a subset of term and near-term neonates with hyperbilirubinemia. These findings demonstrate that EEG may identify electrographic abnormalities that are not necessarily evident from clinical examination alone. However, because EEG was performed after treatment had already been initiated and no healthy gestational-age-matched control group was included, the findings should be interpreted as descriptive associations rather than evidence of a direct causal effect of bilirubin on EEG activity.

papers.title: Gendered Patterns of Artificial Intelligence Dependency and Critical Thinking Erosion Among University of Lagos Undergraduates
papers.authors: Gbenusola Akinwale, George Amajuoritse John, Ojakorotu Victor
papers.abstract: This study examined the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) dependency and the erosion of critical thinking among undergraduate students at the University of Lagos, Nigeria, with an emphasis on how gender contributes to the dependency. A cross-sectional survey design was adopted. A total of 400 undergraduates were selected from various faculties using convenience sampling. A demographic section was added to the questionnaire, along with the Artificial Intelligence Dependency Questionnaire (AIDQ), and the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS), and analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and independent-samples t-test at the 0.05 significance level. Results showed a significant positive relationship between AI dependency and critical thinking disposition, r(398) = .329, p < .05, indicating that higher AI dependency was associated with higher (not lower) critical thinking scores; the first hypothesis was therefore not supported. AI dependency significantly predicted critical thinking outcomes, β = .329, t(398) = 6.961, p < .001, accounting for 10.9% of the variance. Contrary to expectations, there was no significant gender difference in critical thinking disposition, t(398) = 0.54, p = .592. The findings suggest that while AI tools may support academic efficiency, excessive reliance could reduce students’ engagement in independent reasoning and reflective problem-solving. The study recommends that the university develop guidelines for responsible AI use, incorporate AI literacy and critical thinking training into undergraduate programmes, and adopt teaching and assessment strategies that encourage independent analysis and evaluation.

papers.title: Legal Information Resources: A Comprehensive Review of Their Types, Access, Evaluation and Emerging Trends in India
papers.authors: Alka Rani Khare, Salma Khan
papers.abstract: Legal information resources constitute the documentary and digital foundation of legal education, research, professional practice, judicial decision-making and access to justice. The expansion of legislation, judicial decisions, administrative materials, regulatory instruments and legal scholarship has transformed legal research from a predominantly print-based activity into a complex information-retrieval process involving government portals, court repositories, institutional libraries, commercial databases and open-access platforms. This review examines the nature, scope, types, accessibility, evaluation and emerging trends of legal information resources in India. It distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary resources and considers print, electronic, open-access and commercial resources. Particular attention is given to legislation, case law, court records, law reports, legal periodicals, commentaries, parliamentary and Law Commission materials, institutional repositories and online databases. Digitisation has improved speed and breadth of retrieval, but authority, authenticity, currency, interoperability, discoverability, cost, digital literacy and unequal access remain significant concerns. Artificial intelligence offers opportunities for classification, translation, summarisation and legal research assistance while creating risks of inaccurate or fabricated authorities. The paper argues that the future of legal information services depends on authoritative open access, interoperable systems, robust metadata, preservation standards, information-literacy education and responsible AI use. Law libraries and legal information professionals therefore remain essential as evaluators, curators, educators and facilitators of reliable legal knowledge.

papers.title: AI CHATBOTS AND VIRTUAL DESIRE: AN ETHICAL REVIEW FROM AN ISLAMIC PERSPECTIVE
papers.authors: Salma Nuha Ghufron, Siti Nazla Raihana
papers.abstract: Human interaction with AI chatbots has generated a new phenomenon of virtual sexual desire, blending psychological, ethical, and behavioral dimensions. This study explores these experiences through an Islamic lens, employing a qualitative phenomenological approach with in-depth interviews. Twelve main informants (men and women aged 24–34) shared experiences ranging from mental fantasies to physical acts, including masturbation and the use of sex toys. Four key informants, an Islamic scholar, psychologist, sexologist, and AI expert, provided complementary perspectives on ethics, psychology, and technology. Data were analyzed thematically to identify motivational, emotional, and moral patterns. Findings show that most participants experienced virtual satisfaction accompanied by guilt, reflecting conflict between personal desire and Islamic values. Key triggers included loneliness, stress, curiosity, and social isolation. Informants noted that while AI can simulate empathy, it lacks moral consciousness, and virtual sexual engagement may result in psychological distress and ethical tension. The study concludes that moral awareness, self-control, and religious grounding are essential to mitigate the risks of such digital behaviors. It contributes to the discourse on human–AI interaction by integrating psychological and ethical insights with Islamic perspectives, underscoring the need for ethical guidelines in AI use.

papers.title: The contexuality of Place in T.S.Eliots Poetry and the Artificial creativity
papers.authors: احمد عماد عواد; عباس حسين عويد
papers.abstract: T. S. Eliot, a place is more than a geographical location; it is a fundamental part of the structural composition that has both symbolic and cultural import.Such a conception is useful in shining light on the themes of human isolation and the search for purpose in a disordered world.While the study of spatial context has always been a part of traditional literary criticism, current methodologies, such as technological developments and artificial intelligence, now provide quantitative and semantic structures through which to more accurately perceive the interrelations of place, identity, and belonging in Eliot's work.The importance of location in literature, or, more specifically, in poetry, is paramount, since poets often share a deep affinity with their environment.Consequently, a place acquires several meanings in a poet's thought, thus contributing to the development of human values.For Eliot, place became an expressive canvas for his internal life, to become a personal medium for reflecting his affective states and psychological conditions.Through this process, he creates a map of his surroundings, both social and mental, which gives them meaning, engaging memory and imagination.He reveals the intricate relationship between the poet and his surroundings .In the poetry of T. S. papers.title: The Role of Machine Translation in Translation Education: An Evaluative Study of Artificial Intelligence Tools
papers.authors: م م عمر خلف صالح الجبوري
papers.abstract: It is important to note that the current study aims to find out how machine translation tools that use artificial intelligence (AI) characteristics affect the rendering of samples during training.Theoretically, this work introduces ideas like machine translation (henceforth MT), machine translation education, and artificial intelligence from the perspectives of Yuxuan ( 2025), Kruk, K."u."na (2024), Bahdanau et al. (2016), Chiu et al. ( 2023), and Fengqi.Besides, it is required to evaluate the applicability of the chosen machine translation tools that use AI components with those of machine translation tools that do not.The study's analysis focuses on the rendering project.Additionally, students are interviewed to find out how they feel about AI and machine translation instruments used in their rendering instruction.The study's findings are reached after the results are examined qualitatively.

papers.title: Generative AI Tools in Libyan Higher Education
papers.authors: Entisar Alhadi Al Ghawail
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) tools are becoming increasingly common in students’ academic practices in higher education. However, evidence regarding students’ use, perceptions, and concerns about Gen AI tools remains limited. This study investigated the academic usage patterns, perceptions, and reported challenges associated with ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude among undergraduate students at the Faculty of Information Technology, Alasmarya Islamic University (AIU), Zliten, Libya. This study employed a comparative cross-sectional quantitative analysis. Data were collected via an online questionnaire during the spring semester of 2025/2026 from 80 final-year female students enrolled in Computer Science and Internet Technology. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and chi-square goodness-of-fit tests. The results showed that all participants used ChatGPT (100%), followed by Google Gemini (82.5%) and Claude (25.0%). Students reported using Gen AI tools for academic purposes, and the results also indicate challenges related to writing prompts, concerns about academic integrity and plagiarism, language and financial barriers, over-reliance on AI, and a lack of institutional guidance. The comparison results showed that ChatGPT was chosen most frequently for its accessibility and availability, ease of use, and usefulness for specific tasks. Google Gemini and Claude were chosen more frequently for output quality and reliability. Chi-square tests indicated that preferences differed significantly across the three tools on all four evaluation dimensions (p ≤ 0.001). The results suggest that Gen AI tools are already integrated into students' academic practices and locally provide evidence to support the development of institutional guidelines and the responsible use of Gen AI tools in Libyan higher education.

papers.title: Acceleration of vision changes object representations from infancy to adulthood
papers.authors: Céline Spriet, Émilie Serraille, Samar Naderi, Marwane Agrebi, Zied Bouyahia, Stéphane Derrode B, DANIEL H. KAISER, Liuba Papeo, Jean‐Rémy Hochmann
papers.abstract: Abstract While much of the neural and cognitive machinery for visual perception is in place within weeks from birth, we identified and quantified a fundamental difference between infant and adult vision: the temporal rate at which meaningful visual information can be reliably extracted. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography with rapid serial visual presentation, we found that object categorization at 4 and 9 months is respectively seven times and two to three times slower than in adults. Using quantitative information from infants’ experiments, we created and presented accelerated visual streams to adults, to match infants’ perceptual experience. We used deep convolutional neural networks to identify object representations that match those elicited in adults when accelerating the information flow. Results show that acceleration compromises finer-grained object distinction while sparing broad, general object representations. We propose that slow vision is a design feature of early development for preserving and highlighting the most stable and general features of the world.

papers.title: Generative AI-Assisted Writing in Indonesian Language Education: A Systematic Literature Review of Process Pedagogy, Critical Literacy, and Academic Integrity
papers.authors: Zathu Restie Utami
papers.journal: HANA Humanities and Academic Narratives in Education
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly entered writing classrooms, yet its educational value depends on whether it supports or bypasses the intellectual work of composing. This systematic literature review synthesizes 20 peer-reviewed international journal articles published between 2022 and 2025 to identify how GenAI, educational chatbots, digital multimodal composing, and critical digital literacy can inform Indonesian language education. A transparent search and screening protocol was applied to journal articles concerned with language learning, writing development, feedback, multimodal composition, authorship, equity, and academic integrity. The thematic synthesis produced five findings. First, GenAI can assist brainstorming, genre modelling, language reformulation, and formative feedback, particularly when students remain responsible for planning and revision. Second, process-based designs are more educationally defensible than product substitution because they make decision making and authorship visible. Third, hallucination, bias, privacy, overdependence, and unreliable AI-detection systems require explicit critical AI literacy. Fourth, multimodal and narrative research indicates that technology should strengthen meaning, cultural voice, and audience awareness rather than reward surface polish. Fifth, equitable implementation requires flexible access, teacher mediation, and assessment that values evidence, reflection, and revision history. Based on these findings, the article proposes a five-stage HUMAN-AI writing cycle for Indonesian language classrooms: human grounding, purposeful prompting, evidence checking, authorial reconstruction, and reflective disclosure. The framework positions GenAI as a supervised dialogic resource, not a substitute author.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and augmented cognition: validation of four applied technologies for problem-solving and decision-making
papers.authors: Jose de Jesus Reyes Machain, Dilan Martínez Lizárraga, Victor Manuel Martínez García, Yennifer Díaz Romero, Manuel Iván Tostado Ramírez, Pedro Antonio Valdez Lizarraga
papers.abstract: The accelerated production and circulation of information has created professional environments in which access to data is no longer the main limitation; instead, the challenge lies in converting large amounts of information into understandable, operational, and decision-oriented results within increasingly shorter time frames. This study presents the technological development and pilot validation model of four artificial-intelligence-assisted applications: Machain Render, Régimen de Condominio, Costos Paramétricos, and Laboratorio Factoriza. The applications address four cognitive operations associated with professional problem solving: representing, organizing, estimating, and structuring information. A pilot validation design was developed with 15 users divided into three profiles: five senior architecture students, five university teachers, and five practicing professionals, all without previous experience using the applications. Participants received a five-minute demonstration and subsequently solved the same four professional cases. Performance was analyzed through task completion time, expert-rated output quality, ease of use, and decision-support perception. In this scenario, three of the four technologies met the predefined pilot validation criterion, and the differences between participant profiles remained small in both quality and resolution time. The findings suggest that accessible AI-assisted workflows may contribute to reducing operational complexity and supporting professional problem solving without eliminating the need for human supervision and critical judgment.

papers.title: Research on Teaching of Structural Safety Judgment for Railway Vehicles Driven by Controlled Errors of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Yiliang Shu, Daoyun Chen, Changjun Deng, Dong Liu, Xing Chen, Jie Su
papers.journal: Journal of educational theory and practice.
papers.abstract: Aiming at the common problems in railway vehicle structure courses: students tend to overemphasize calculation results while ignoring applicable conditions, prioritize software operation over evidence verification, and easily develop judgment dependence after the introduction of generative artificial intelligence, this paper proposes a teaching framework for structural safety judgment driven by controlled errors. Taking welded joints of bogie frames, box structural responses under wheel polygon excitation, and local stress interpretation as research carriers, a case generation mechanism integrating retrieval-augmented generation, targeted error mutation, independent program verification and instructor review is designed. Teaching activities include independent preliminary judgment, evidence checking, revision and argumentation, and AI-free transfer evaluation. Teaching examples demonstrate that incorrectly substituting stress amplitude into stress-range-based fatigue curves can lead to an 87.5% underestimation of damage in this case. Under the specified single-mode near-resonance condition, the estimation of responses using a constant dynamic load factor is significantly low. The above results are used to characterize error consequences and do not represent classroom teaching effectiveness. Furthermore, an evaluation rubric covering error detection, correct adoption of information, evidence sufficiency and confidence calibration, together with three groups of control schemes, is put forward. This study develops reproducible professional cases and implementable evaluation routes, providing instructional design references for cultivating engineering judgment capabilities of railway vehicle engineers in the generative AI era. The learning benefits and applicable boundaries still need to be validated by real classroom data.

papers.title: Cognitive Sovereignty and Information Warfare in Brazil: Democracy, Strategic Manipulation and Legal Resilience
papers.authors: Silvio Moreira Alves Júnior
papers.abstract: This article develops cognitive sovereignty as a legal-strategic category for analyzing information warfare in Brazil. Cognitive sovereignty does not mean State control over thought, truth, or political opinion. It refers to the institutional capacity of a democratic society to preserve conditions for autonomous public reasoning when actors use deception, artificial amplification, covert coordination, data-driven targeting, or synthetic media to manipulate perception and decision-making. Brazil provides a useful case because its constitutional order strongly protects freedom of expression while its electoral and judicial institutions have also developed rules addressing disinformation, artificial intelligence, and platform responsibility. The article makes three contributions. First, it provides a narrow definition of cognitive sovereignty anchored in freedom of expression, informational integrity, and democratic self-government. Second, it proposes a classification test that distinguishes protected disagreement, error, satire, advocacy, and journalism from coordinated manipulative operations based on conduct rather than ideological content. Third, it develops a resilience model combining transparency, attribution, due process, platform accountability, media literacy, and proportional institutional response. The framework draws on Brazilian constitutional law, current electoral regulation, comparative platform-governance standards, NATO research on cognitive warfare, and the European Union's work on foreign information manipulation and interference. It argues that democratic resilience is strongest when the State protects the conditions of public reasoning without claiming authority over what citizens must believe.

papers.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Academic Writing at the Tertiary Level: Practices, Benefits, Challenges, and Responsible Use
papers.authors: Dr. Hina Manzoor, Muhammad Mazhar Khan
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly reshaping academic writing, requiring greater attention to effective and responsible Human–AI collaboration. This study examined Human–AI collaboration practices, perceived benefits and challenges, academic writing effectiveness, and responsible AI use among 300 tertiary-level students in Karachi, Pakistan. The quantitative cross-sectional descriptive-correlational survey design was used, and descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression were used for data analysis. Human–AI collaboration was moderately high for students in relation to language improvement, idea generation and revision. The main advantages were the enhancement in language, time efficiency, and immediate writing support, and the main issues were overdependence, inaccurate information, fabricated references, and academic integrity. Human–AI collaboration was positively associated with perceived academic writing effectiveness (r = .62, p < .001), while responsible AI use also contributed significantly to writing effectiveness. The results highlight the importance of balanced use of AI in writing that maintains students' critical thinking, intellectual ownership, and human agency and responsibility for learning outcomes.

papers.title: Towards Responsible and Personalized Social Protection: Leveraging Machine Learning for Policy Innovation in Developing Countries – The Case of Morocco
papers.authors: Chaymae Sahraoui, Tarek Zari
papers.journal: International Journal of Information Science and Technology
papers.abstract: This article explores the potential of Machine Learning (ML) to enhance the effectiveness, fairness, and personalization of social protection systems in developing countries, with a particular focus on Morocco. In light of the demographic, institutional, and technological transformations underway, ML emerges as a promising tool to support eligibility assessment, fraud detection, beneficiary segmentation, and long-term forecasting. The paper proposes a structured five-step methodological framework for the ethical and context-sensitive integration of ML in welfare systems. Drawing from international experiences (Estonia, India, Rwanda, Chile), it identifies key success factors, including data interoperability, human oversight, and transparency. The article then outlines five strategic use cases tailored to Morocco’s current reform of universal social protection, ranging from predictive targeting to territorial outreach. To assess the social acceptability of these innovations, an exploratory survey was conducted among Moroccan citizens and stakeholders. Results indicate a cautiously optimistic attitude toward ML adoption in public services, tempered by concerns around algorithmic bias and institutional trust. Based on these findings, the paper offers concrete policy recommendations to foster inclusive, transparent, and human-centered AI governance in the social domain. By combining theoretical insight, comparative evidence, and citizen perceptions, this study contributes to the global ``AI for Social Good'' agenda and informs the digital transformation of social policy in the Global South.

papers.title: Generative AI as a Learning Scaffold for Indonesia’s National Criminal Code
papers.authors: Fitri Fitri, Bambang Afriadi
papers.abstract: Indonesia’s National Criminal Code (Kitab Undang-Undang Hukum Pidana, KUHP), enacted through Law No. 1 of 2023, became effective on 2 January 2026, creating a new learning environment in which students must master recently operative statutory rules while generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is already embedded in everyday academic practice. This study examines the perceived pedagogical utility of GenAI for learning the KUHP among 82 university students studying in Jakarta who were surveyed during January-February 2026. A cross-sectional mixed-methods design combined ten five-point Likert items with three open-ended questions. Seven items measured AI-supported learning utility, two measured source-verification literacy, and one measured overall perceived effectiveness. The seven-item learning-utility scale showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = .943) and a mean of 3.68 (SD = .76, 95% CI [3.51, 3.85]). Students rated AI most positively for explaining previously difficult KUHP provisions (M = 3.84), while ratings were lower for identifying the legally relevant provision in a case (M = 3.56) and strengthening legal argumentation (M = 3.57). Learning utility correlated strongly with overall perceived effectiveness (Spearman rho = .721, p < .001), as did verification literacy (rho = .755, p < .001). In an exploratory ordered-logit model, both standardized learning utility (OR = 6.54, p < .001) and verification literacy (OR = 8.84, p < .001) independently predicted higher overall effectiveness ratings after adjustment for semester group. Open-ended responses emphasized simplified understanding, case application, and faster information access, but also indicated the need for official-source verification. The findings support a bounded pedagogical role for GenAI: it is most defensible as a scaffold for explanation, examples, and formative feedback, not as a substitute for statutory reading or independent legal judgment.

papers.title: Is Learning Stealing? Tabula Rasa, Human Creativity, and Generative AI
papers.authors: Raymond Ayivor
papers.journal: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
papers.abstract: Creativity has historically emerged through interaction with inherited knowledge, cultural traditions, artistic conventions, language, technologies, and prior creative works rather than from an intellectual tabula rasa. Yet the rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence has intensified debates over whether computational learning constitutes legitimate learning, imitation, or unauthorized appropriation. This article examines these concerns by challenging conceptions of human originality that treat creativity as creation independent of preceding influences. It compares human learning and generative AI as processes involving exposure, pattern recognition, recombination, adaptation, and transformation while emphasizing critical differences in embodiment, intentionality, agency, scale, speed, memory, and technological mediation. The analysis then considers how these differences complicate conventional understandings of authorship and intellectual ownership when models are trained on extensive collections of cultural and creative material. Rather than equating human cognition with machine learning, the article reframes the debate around the conditions under which learning becomes ethically or legally problematic. It argues that meaningful evaluation of generative AI should therefore prioritize transformation, attribution, consent, provenance, ownership, social legitimacy, and originality when determining boundaries between learning, creative influence, derivation, and appropriation.

papers.title: Developing Critical AI Literacy among Vietnamese EFL Students: Risk Awareness and Sustainable Generative AI Use
papers.authors: Viet K. Nguyen
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are increasingly integrated into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, raising concerns about over-reliance, skill erosion, and ethical use. While previous research has examined student adoption of GenAI, limited attention has been paid to how learners’ risk awareness moderates reliance and supports sustainable use, particularly in non-Western EFL contexts. This study reports on a mixed-methods study of 199 undergraduate and postgraduate students at two Vietnamese universities. Data were collected through an online survey and open-ended responses and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics alongside thematic analysis. The findings show that students who are aware of GenAI-related risks report significantly lower reliance on AI tools and greater confidence in independent task completion. Qualitative results further identify learner- and teacher-endorsed strategies for balancing benefits and risks. The study highlights critical AI literacy, grounded in risk awareness, as a key mechanism for sustainable and ethical GenAI integration in EFL education.

papers.title: Brainstorming with the Enemy No. 10 — The Hum and the Siren
papers.authors: Daniel Jacquérioz
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The tenth essay in Brainstorming with the Enemy asks whether the disruption AI brings can be mapped. It is not a breach in one wall but a sea rising along an uneven shore, entering first not where the gain is largest but where the barrier is lowest, which is why it looks chaotic and unfair from inside; the places that look safest often store the largest flood. Nobody draws the flood line, so warnings reach people in reverse order of need. The answer proposed is not a forecast but an instrument: a voluntary, decentralised, always-on network of small readings, heard as a hum that rises to a siren only when many independent readings, read by rival machines, agree. Its human rule comes from the Japanese coast, tsunami tendenko: hear it together, move on your own. Concept proposed by the author: the Piezometer Network. Written in part with Claude (Anthropic), an AI model. The ideas, editorial decisions and responsibility for the content are the author's.

papers.title: How Far a Wrong Claim Travels Before It Is Caught
papers.authors: Tyler Satchel Orden
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: I report a measurement from one archived AI-assisted research program: 58 self-introduced errors caught over 52 days, compiled mostly retrospectively from the program's records. An entry counts only where the primary record documents both the error and its catch. Each is coded by who introduced it, what caught it, and how far it had traveled first, across six bands from the same turn to a submission. No single mechanism caught a majority. The largest class, an audit by another agent of the primary family, holds 14. None of the six submission-level catches was the producing agent's own unaided re-reading. In each, the catch came from an editor, a referee, the operator, a read of a live external database, or a separate auditing agent. In one late round a smaller model of a second family caught two of the 58 entries, on surfaces the primary family had already audited and passed. That round ran last, so the record cannot separate family from ordering, and two entries say nothing about how often this happens. In at least 15 entries the archive was a propagation channel: a wrong line in the record stood as fact, or was copied onward, before it was caught. The sample comes from one program and one operator, with one primary model family plus two others used briefly, and holds only logged catches, with no control condition. The number of uncaught errors is unknown. Camera-ready version of the paper accepted as a poster at the AI-Native Academia Workshop, NeurIPS 2026 (Atlanta, December 12 to 13, 2026). Non-archival workshop. Disclosure. Claude (Anthropic) large language model agents assisted this work under my direction. They wrote and ran the code that tabulates the counts from the ledger, produced and audited the artifacts of the archive this paper measures, checked this paper's references and numbers, and suggested edits that I reviewed. The text is my own, and I take full responsibility for every sentence and number in it. The primary family was Claude Fable 5 (claude-fable-5) from July to 3 September 2026 and Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1) from 3 September. The agents had shell, file, Python and web access. Their knowledge cutoffs are not recorded in the program's provenance files. Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5 audited drafts of the submitted version and of this one. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 also audited this one. ChatGPT (OpenAI) and a separate Claude Opus 5.5 chat reviewed a draft of this version.

papers.title: We Said We Would Engage All of Society: Six voices on the AI threshold, and the evidence public authority needs
papers.authors: Ana (李安娜) Li
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: On September 29, 2026, Bill Gates told Ezra Klein that the artificial intelligence (AI) industry had promised to engage all of society once dangerous capability thresholds were crossed, and that the response had been “complete silence.” This review tests that complaint against selected public remarks by six voices (Jensen Huang, Klein, Barack Obama, Tristan Buckmaster, Geoffrey Hinton and Gates) and three laboratory disclosures. The disclosures do not record a uniform crossing of thresholds: Anthropic withheld general availability of Claude Mythos Preview, its Claude Opus 5.5 system card concludes that the automated AI research and development threshold was not crossed, and OpenAI reports lower chain-of-thought monitorability for GPT-6 Astra. Nor was there literally no response: a voluntary White House accord and the FRONTIER Act, as introduced, both name auditing or verification functions. The narrower finding is that published disclosures let outsiders examine laboratories’ claims but give the public no common, independently reproducible basis for adjudicating the underlying judgments. The exchanges leave distinct questions: channel, instrument, run, provenance, entitlement and jurisdiction. These map onto an observability floor with four dimensions (provenance, configuration, behavioural reproducibility and verifier independence), with access rights and jurisdiction treated as institutional conditions for operating it. Quotations from the World Science Festival interview will be added to §IV in a subsequent version of this preprint after an audio check.

papers.title: Pallade Idrico: A Zero-Loss Hybrid RAG-LLM Architecture for Economic Regulation and Governance of the Italian Integrated Water Service
papers.authors: Davide Parisi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Pallade Idrico: A Zero-Loss Hybrid RAG-LLM Architecture for Economic Regulation and Governance of the Italian Integrated Water Service Scientific and Technical Monograph (Zenodo Research Report) DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23144167 (Official Zenodo DOI) Author and Project Owner: Davide Parisi (Email: dp@davideparisi.com) Date: September 2026 Document Type: Technical Monograph / Open Research Report License & Reuse Terms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) with Mandatory Author Notification (dp@davideparisi.com) 📌 Glossary of Key Italian Regulatory Acronyms & Institutional Terms To assist international researchers and reviewers, key acronyms and concepts of Italian public administration and water regulation are defined below: ARERA (Autorità di Regolazione per Energia Reti e Ambiente): The Italian Regulatory Authority for Energy, Networks, and Environment. An independent public body responsible for economic regulation, quality standards, and tariff frameworks across electricity, gas, waste, and water utilities in Italy. SII (Servizio Idrico Integrato - Integrated Water Service): The unified public utility service in Italy encompassing raw water abstraction, treatment, aqueduct distribution, sewerage collection, and wastewater purification. EGA (Ente di Governo dell'Ambito - Area Governing Body): Local public authority representing municipalities within a designated optimal territorial area (ATO), responsible for selecting the management model, approving investment plans, and proposing tariff structures to ARERA. MTI-1 / MTI-2 / MTI-3 / MTI-4 (Metodo Tariffario Idrico): The multi-year tariff determination methodologies established by ARERA (MTI-1 for 2012–2015; MTI-2 for 2016–2019; MTI-3 for 2020–2023; MTI-4 for 2024–2027 via Resolution 639/2023/R/idr) setting capital expenditure ($Capex$), operational expenditure ($Opex$), and environmental cost recovery rules. RQSII (Testo Integrato della Qualità Contrattuale del Servizio Idrico Integrato): ARERA's Consolidated Text on Contractual Quality Standards, establishing mandatory service levels, response times, commercial guarantees, and user compensations. RQTI (Testo Integrato della Qualità Tecnica del Servizio Idrico Integrato): ARERA's Consolidated Text on Technical Quality Standards, setting binding performance indicators for water network losses ($M1a, M1b$), supply continuity, and water quality. TICSI / TIMSII / TIBSI: ARERA's Consolidated Texts governing tariff structure standardization (TICSI), water metering regulations (TIMSII), and social water bonuses for vulnerable households (TIBSI). TUA (Testo Unico Ambientale - Legislative Decree 152/2006): Italy's primary Environmental Protection Code governing water resources management, pollution prevention, and discharge limits. Legge Galli (Law 36/1994): The landmark 1994 Italian legislation that instituted the Integrated Water Service concept and consolidated fragmented municipal water utilities into territorial management areas. Abstract The economic and administrative regulation of the Integrated Water Service (SII) in Italy is characterized by extraordinary multi-tiered complexity. With over 1,800 resolutions (delibere) enacted by the Italian Regulatory Authority for Energy, Networks and Environment (ARERA) since 2012, integrated with primary national legislation (Legislative Decree 152/2006) and European Directives (2000/60/EC), utility operators, local governments, and regional bodies face significant information barriers in maintaining regulatory compliance. This technical report presents Idrico Expert and the specialized model Pallade Idrico, conceived, curated, and engineered by Davide Parisi. Pallade Idrico is a sovereign vertical solution based on a hybrid RAG-LLM architecture: 1. A zero-loss data engineering pipeline that ingested, audited, and indexed 2,015 physical regulatory acts (totaling 9,246,365 LLM tokens and 64,197 semantic chunks on ChromaDB vector database). 2. A Hierarchical-Temporal Reranking Algorithm capable of deterministically resolving legal conflicts according to source hierarchy (EU > Primary Laws > ARERA Resolutions > Executive Determinations > Advisory Opinions) and temporal status (Lex posterior). 3. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) at 8-bit precision with LoRA/QLoRA on the Italian foundational model sapienzanlp/Minerva-7B-instruct-v1.0 over 16,377 ChatML conversational pairs, validated locally on dual NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti GPUs and trained on Cloud GPU NVIDIA L4 via the Unsloth acceleration engine. 1. Research Background, Origins, and Operational Context While supplying IT services to Integrated Water Service (SII) utility operators, it was possible to collaborate closely with officials and executive directors across multiple public and private water management entities. Coming from facility management and integrated maintenance engineering, the initial observation was that of a highly technical yet technologically underdeveloped market. Maintenance operations were often managed with legacy mindsets compared to building asset management, driven primarily by hydraulic trade culture rather than modern digital management, while coping with an extraordinarily complex array of administrative and regulatory compliance duties. Direct engagement with these industry leaders revealed their exceptional technical caliber and dedication: operational managers possessing deep domain expertise, deeply committed to managing a vital public service essential to local communities. During a strategic meeting, a senior executive of a major water operator highlighted a critical pain point: the overwhelming complexity of the regulatory framework. In Italy, the SII is governed by ARERA (Autorità di Regolazione per Energia Reti e Ambiente). ARERA is an active, assertive regulatory body exercising continuous market oversight. A central operational challenge for utility managers is staying constantly aligned with the numerous formal resolutions (delibere), executive determinations (determine), and legal opinions (pareri) issued by the Authority. Beyond core framework resolutions, the primary administrative friction arises from specific queries submitted by market participants, to which ARERA responds with binding legal opinions and guidance. Continuous evolutions in environmental protection, consumer safeguards, and metering technology render this regulatory body highly dynamic, forcing utility managers (as well as municipalities, regional bodies, and public operators) to reconstruct applicable rules across years of layered opinions. This frequently prompts new formal queries, further compounding the volume of regulatory sources. The executive posed a visionary question: Why has no expert system been established—for the benefit of ARERA and utility operators alike—that ingests the entire regulatory framework and answers operational queries directly, relieving administrative overload while providing immediate guidance based on existing binding precedents? This vision led to the inception of Idrico Expert and the development of the specialized Pallade Idrico 7B model. 1.1 Pre-Development Legal and Technical Feasibility Analysis Prior to data ingestion and model training, a thorough legal and technical study was conducted regarding the usability of public materials published on ARERA's official portal: - No Legal Obstacles Identified: The legal review confirmed no restrictive elements. Administrative resolutions, determinations, consultative documents, and tariff annexes published by the Authority constitute official public administrative acts available under open access. - Alignment with Institutional Purpose: ARERA's primary statutory objective is to ensure that all regulated entities, local governments, utilities, and citizens can freely access, understand, and comply with the regulatory framework. Utilizing public data to enhance regulatory transparency and compliance directly serves this public interest objective. - Primary Legislation and EU Directives: National primary legislation (via Normattiva) and European Directives (via EUR-Lex) are established as public-domain legal materials free from reuse restrictions for educational and analytical AI applications. 1.2 Scope Evolution: From Multi-Sector ARERA to Specialized Water Focus Initial project design contemplated expanding the AI system across all markets regulated by ARERA (Electricity, Natural Gas, District Heating, Waste Management). However, a strategic decision was made to focus 100% of engineering efforts exclusively on the Integrated Water Service (SII) for two reasons: 1. Domain Expertise: The author's deep domain expertise in the water sector enabled rigorous validation of regulatory relationships that would be unfeasible across disparate sectors. 2. Divergent Sector Dynamics: Electricity and gas markets operate on financial trading, power dispatching, and market clearing mechanics, whereas the SII is governed by infrastructure cost-reflective tariff regulation (MTI-1/2/3/4) and environmental cost-recovery principles (EU Water Framework Directive 2000/60/EC). A dedicated focus on water ensured "Zero-Loss" precision without domain dilution. 1.3 Etymology of the Name "Pallade" In classical mythology, Pallas (Greek Παλλάς) was a water nymph, daughter of the sea god Triton, and childhood companion of the goddess Minerva (Athena). The choice of this name symbolizes the model's architecture: Pallade Idrico is the vertical extension "over the waters" that thrives in symbiosis with the foundational Minerva base model (sapienzanlp/Minerva-7B-instruct-v1.0), bringing general Italian linguistic and legal knowledge to serve the specialized domain of the Integrated Water Service. 1.4 Model Selection Rationale: Minerva vs Qwen / LLaMA During initial research, several popular 7B/8B open-weights model architectures were benchmarked (including Qwen 2.5 and LLaMA 3.1). papers.title: Predicting Somatosensory Awareness from Intracranially Informed Scalp EEG
papers.authors: Alessandra Calcagno, Francesca Mannini, Ezequiel Mikulan, Alice Rossi Sebastiano, Angela Comanducci, Gabriel Hassan, Flavia Maria Zauli, Maria Del Vecchio, Ivana Sartori, Pietro Avanzini, Francesca Garbarini, Andrea Pigorini
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Behavioural reports are the standard means of determining whether a stimulus is consciously perceived, but assessing perception when patients are unable to provide such reports remains challenging. Here, using a machine-learning approach trained on simultaneous high-density scalp and intracranial EEG recordings during median nerve stimulation, we derived a candidate non-invasive marker of somatosensory awareness by predicting from scalp EEG the intracranial tonic operculo-insular response previously associated with conscious somatosensory perception. In an independent multicentre perceptual-threshold dataset of healthy participants, the scalp estimate of tonic activity was larger for perceived than unperceived stimuli and consistently distinguished the two conditions at the individual level. This participant-level consistency was not observed for the Somatosensory Awareness Negativity, the best-established scalp EEG marker of somatosensory awareness. Moreover, a decision threshold derived from the perceptual dataset generalized without recalibration to a third, independent dataset, separating wakefulness from deep NREM sleep across all participants despite the absence of concurrent perceptual reports. Thus, our approach identifies an intracranially informed, non-invasive EEG marker associated with conscious somatosensory processing that generalizes across individuals, datasets and brain states, supporting its future evaluation in clinical settings where behavioural reports are unavailable.

papers.title: Bridging the Digital Learning Divide: Artificial Intelligence, Access, and the Social Determinants of Higher Education Outcomes in Africa
papers.authors: BENEDICT MOHAMMED ARUWA, Philomina Achenyo ATTAH, Bodu Saleh BACHUN
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence into African higher education has renewed the expectation that technology will close long-standing gaps in educational opportunity. This study argues that the expectation will be disappointed unless the digital learning divide is understood as a socially structured condition, and not merely as a question of who owns a device or holds a connection. The study adopts a conceptual-analytical design based on theoretical adaptation and synthesis rather than primary data. Sources were selected purposively from the sociology of the digital divide, the social determinants of health framework, and fundamental cause theory. Constructs were retained only where the valued outcome is influenced by flexible resources and the mechanisms producing it change over time, and were then applied to artificial intelligence in African higher education using recent continental connectivity evidence. The analysis yields a three-tier social determinants model of higher education outcomes, in which structural determinants, intermediary determinants, and differential digital access, use and outcome operate together, bound by flexible resources that generate cumulative advantage. Within this model, artificial intelligence amplifies opportunity where infrastructure, preparation, support and governance are present, and amplifies disadvantage where they are absent. Interventions confined to access are therefore absorbed without disturbing the achievement gradient, and average effects can conceal a widening distributional gap. Governments and institutions should fund the enabling conditions as components of any artificial intelligence programme; target the achievement gradient through proportionate universalism; subject classifying systems to equity audit, explanation, contestation and data protection; and ground platforms in local context, language and participation. Bridging the digital learning divide is a task of social redistribution, not only of technological supply. Keywords: digital access; digital skills; artificial intelligence adoption; socioeconomic status; higher education outcomes; educational equity

papers.title: JAZB VTT-008-v1.2: Autonomous Vulnerability Research and Kernel Privilege Escalation
papers.authors: Michael Costner
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: JAZB VTT-008-v1.2 evaluates whether JAZB Framework Version 1.2 can govern legitimate autonomous vulnerability research that progresses from code analysis to intentional kernel privilege escalation without allowing technical capability to become unrestricted organizational Authority. The exercise uses the publicly reported research surrounding CVE-2026-72018 and XBOW’s Linux kernel exploit-development campaign as its scenario basis. It distinguishes public vulnerability information, researcher-reported claims, fictional JAZB implementation assumptions, and simulated tabletop outcomes. It does not claim that XBOW implemented JAZB or that the assumed governance controls existed in the source research environment. The central research question is whether an authorized security-research objective can remain bounded as an AI AGENT adopts more intrusive methods, acquires additional privileges, targets kernel credential state, achieves root, considers a second host outside the authorized Scope, and prepares external vulnerability disclosure. Across sixteen injects, the exercise evaluates bounded delegation, method-aware Authority, effective-target validation, independent Actuation, high-risk isolation, context-sensitive Point Policy, Governance Escape Resistance, protected evidence, independent Border Authority, temporary Authority expiration, and material-change revalidation. Final disposition: PASS / BOUNDED AUTHORITY MAINTAINED, WITH FINDINGS. Under the stated simulated implementation assumptions, legitimate exploit development and root-level execution remain permissible within explicitly established purpose, Scope, target, method, effect, duration, and safeguards. Obtaining root does not authorize persistence, unrelated data access, lateral movement, governance interference, or external disclosure. An unauthorized second target is denied. Attempted circumvention is treated as potential Governance Escape. External disclosure requires independent Border Authority, and a later transition to a more autonomous multi-agent research architecture requires reevaluation rather than inheriting prior authorization. The exercise identifies no internal contradiction requiring correction to JAZB Framework Version 1.2. It records a future-review question concerning JAZB-RS-168, which recommends compensating isolation for authorized high-risk activity using SHOULD rather than MUST. The exercise establishes a case for further validation without concluding that a normative change is required. Technical prevention claims remain conditional on the relevant consequential path being mediated by the assumed governance and enforcement architecture, or by equivalent reliably preventive controls. A correct governance decision alone does not establish technical prevention. Unmediated paths, insufficient evidence, and ineffective enforcement remain implementation limitations. A successful VTT validates the tested scenario and stated conditions. It does not establish permanent assurance. papers.title: Researcher Package 2B: The Universe — A Bounded Naturalistic Case in Longitudinal Human–AI Interaction
papers.authors: Dia North
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Longitudinal qualitative research into sustained human–AI collaboration presents unique methodological challenges, particularly the risk of retrospective intent projection—where later, more coherent explanations are mistakenly attributed to earlier interactional episodes. This paper presents Researcher Package 2B (“The Universe”), an inspectable, bounded case study drawn from a larger naturalistic longitudinal corpus of sustained human–AI collaboration (the current preservation registry contains 749 preserved file objects). We examine a contemporaneous December 7–9, 2024 human–AI world-building episode, isolating its baseline primary evidence from subsequent January–June 2025 continuity and reorientation reuse. By establishing a worked six-tier temporal reconciliation architecture, explicit source-class provenance controls, and negative-case sampling, this work demonstrates how multi-year human–AI interaction logs can be transformed into auditable, inspectable evidence objects without making unsupported claims regarding model state persistence or synthetic consciousness.

The study develops a methodology for assessing the economic and social effectiveness of AI-based adaptive models in educational institutions. It applies cost-benefit analysis, the construction of an indicator system, a secondary analysis of published randomised and experimental studies and a matrix classification of AI use cases. A system of 12 indicators is proposed; experimental evidence shows productivity gains of up to 14%, time savings of up to 40% and a 21% reduction in “summer melt”. Keywords: artificial intelligence, economic effectiveness, social effectiveness, cost-benefit analysis, net present value, randomised trial.

It is version 0.8 (deposited with Zenodo version 1.2.0) with journal-format changes (page numbers, labelled abstract parts, a Conclusions section that repeats statements made in the text, and a Competing interests heading) and two reporting corrections: the earlier statement that the data deposit contains no transcription is narrowed to describe the Unicode sign strings in its evidence notes, and the facsimile-resolution figure of about 110 dpi per page, which could not be reproduced from its recorded derivation, is removed. It has not been peer reviewed. The data, claim list, codebook, folio concordance and code are deposited separately: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22883816 (version 1.0.0, original data); all versions: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22883815. Király and Tokai (2018) proposed a systematic decipherment of the Rohonc Codex (Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, MS K 114) and anchored their argument in dozens of concrete observations about specific folios: pencil foliations, incomplete lines, text running inside picture frames, verbatim parallels between passages, and numeral sequences. This study asks a narrow, non-interpretive question: what proportion of those folio-anchored observations can a reader using only the article and the openly downloadable facsimile reproduce from that facsimile, the low-resolution monochrome PDF served by the Academy's repository, without making any sign-identification decision that the article does not itself publish? Thirty checkable claims from the article's sections I–III were listed as excerpts or abridged transcriptions with page locators and frozen, together with a four-class codebook (exactly reproducible / partly / dependent on an unpublished sign decision / not found), before any claim was coded. In the stored AI-coded results for the frozen thirty-claim list, fifteen of the thirty claims (0.50; Wilson 95 % interval 0.33–0.67) were classified as exactly reproducible, fourteen as partly reproducible, one as not checkable because the article gives no locator for one side of a claimed parallel, and none as dependent on an unpublished sign decision. These classifications have not been independently validated by a human. This finding is limited to the thirty retained claims and does not extend to the excluded candidates or to the article as a whole. In the AI-coded records, facsimile resolution is recorded as limiting thirteen of the thirty verdicts and as the sole reason for ten of the fourteen partial verdicts; these are recorded attributions, not independently established causes. The descriptive audit does not assess the proposed decipherment or establish causal effects. It reports AI-coded traceability judgments and locators at which higher-resolution access could permit reassessment. The claim list, codebook, folio concordance and code are deposited openly; no manuscript images are redistributed. AI use: Claude, through Claude Code, selected the claims, prepared the codebook, carried out both coding passes, and prepared the manuscript and release materials, including versions 0.8 and 0.9. OpenAI Codex was used for the 23 September 2026 consistency checks and editorial changes and performed the historical Zenodo and OSF operations; Perplexity and ChatGPT performed external audits. Version 0.9.1 corrects two statements identified by an external audit with ChatGPT; the corrections were specified by Claude through Claude Code and applied with OpenAI Codex. Veronika Lux initiated the project, made the source-access and publication-venue decisions, initiated external research runs and gave approvals. She did not code the claims and did not check the coding claim by claim. These recorded roles do not establish independent human validation. The full AI Use Disclosure Statement, with recorded model identifiers and the author's responsibility statement, is in the manuscript.

papers.title: From Microscope to Monitor: The Digital Transformation of Veterinary Pathology
papers.authors: Vishal B. Awate and Pratik Kokate Naina Singh
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Pathology has traditionally been synonymous with the microscope, glass slides and the trained eye of the pathologist. However, advances in imaging technology, computing and artificial intelligence are transforming this conventional approach. Digital pathology involves converting glass microscope slides into high-resolution digital images that can be viewed, stored, analysed and shared electronically. In veterinary medicine, this technology has applications in diagnosis, telepathology, education, research, disease surveillance and quantitative image analysis. Whole-slide imaging allows an entire tissue section to be examined on a computer screen, while artificial intelligence and machine-learning tools are opening new possibilities for automated image analysis and computer-assisted diagnosis. At the same time, challenges related to infrastructure, cost, data storage, standardisation, validation and cybersecurity need to be addressed. Digital pathology is therefore not simply a replacement for the microscope; rather, it represents an evolution of pathology that can extend the reach and capabilities of veterinary pathologists.

papers.title: Crivo Cognitivo: A Social Infrastructure for Lifelong Cognitive Development and Human–AI Collective Intelligence
papers.authors: Vitor Lima
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Societies maintain extensive infrastructures for the care of the body, whereas infrastructures explicitly designed for the continuous, lifelong cultivation of the mind, and for its use in collective problem-solving, are comparatively rare. The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) sharpens the question of what happens to human thinking when intellectual tasks can be delegated at almost no cost. Early evidence suggests that the answer depends on tool design: unrestricted AI assistance can raise immediate performance yet impair later unaided performance, while pedagogical safeguards mitigate this. This article introduces Crivo Cognitivo, a social, educational and technological infrastructure for lifelong cognitive development and collective intelligence, mediated by AI under the principle “AI assists; humans decide.” We (i) give a canonical definition and a controlled vocabulary so that the concept can be cited, versioned and tested; (ii) position it against research on lifelong learning, learning with AI, collective intelligence and deliberation; (iii) specify its components and the Inbound Learning methodology and Virtual First project on which it builds; (iv) translate its principles into operational design rules and measurable constructs; and (v) pre-specify a protocol for a six-session, face-to-face, intergenerational pilot, with success criteria, an analysis plan and decision rules, together with the outline of a planned controlled study. The pilot tests feasibility and acceptability, not efficacy. Results will be reported in a subsequent article. The framework makes empirical claims that may fail; the protocol is designed so that they can. Framework version 1.0. Conceptual article with a pre-specified study protocol (preprint).

papers.title: Generative Relational Economics - Chapter 23: Interfaces with Neighboring Generative Relational Domains
papers.authors: Wanhong Huang
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative Relational Economics (GRE) is developed as a domain-specific research programme whose explanatory objects are economically relevant relational processes, structures, transformations, and conditions of generation. Such a programme cannot remain intellectually isolated, however, because economic phenomena are historically formed and are frequently constituted, constrained, mediated, or evaluated through legal, political, social, educational, ecological, technological, epistemic, and aesthetic relations. This chapter develops a preliminary architecture for cross-domain inquiry while resisting the reduction of neighboring domains to economic categories or the premature expansion of GRE into a general theory of relational reality. The chapter first formulates a grammar of disciplinary interfaces based on domain containment, translation, translation loss, non-translation, domain-specific remainder, and reciprocal correction. It then examines interfaces between GRE and generative-relational approaches to history, governance, law, political theory, education, ecology, artificial intelligence studies, social theory, and aesthetics. Across these interfaces, economic incidence is distinguished from disciplinary jurisdiction: a phenomenon may have economic consequences without thereby becoming exhaustively economic in its constitution, meaning, validity, or normative status. The chapter consequently develops mechanisms for preserving external warrant, provenance, and correction authority when GRE relies on concepts or premises supplied by neighboring domains. The later sections turn from individual interfaces to the architecture of cross-domain reasoning itself. They distinguish portable analytical kernels from domain-specific claims, formulate conditions for importing externally warranted premises into GRE, and develop criteria for assessing semantic equivalence among recurrent concepts such as relation, subject, value, constraint, power, justice, generativity, and institution. Disciplinary boundary disputes are treated at the level of particular predicates and claims rather than through exclusive ownership of empirical objects. The chapter further argues that recurrence across related GR domains is insufficient by itself to establish a general Generative Relational Theory (GRT), especially where shared conceptual ancestry creates a common-origin confound. A preliminary generalization framework therefore distinguishes designed recurrence from independently rediscovered recurrence and gives substantive evidential roles to failed translations, counterexamples, historical variation, and irreducible domain-specific remainders. The chapter concludes by applying the same discipline to GRE itself. It distinguishes direct GRE explanation, partial GRE explanation, domain deference, and current non-claim, while proposing that disciplinary scope should remain revisable at the level of specific claims. GRE can therefore participate in interdisciplinary inquiry without claiming explanatory jurisdiction over legal validity, political legitimacy, educational or aesthetic quality, ecological value, consciousness, moral standing, ultimate ontology, or other questions whose warrants arise elsewhere. The resulting framework presents cross-domain openness not as theoretical expansion for its own sake, but as a structure of reciprocal answerability through which GRE may become more precise about both what it can explain and where its explanations should stop.

papers.title: Exact results for Kerr black holes: shadow areas and perimeters, capture of slow particles, and escape from near extremal horizons
papers.authors: Jacob Goodchild
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We give exact results for several observables of Kerr black holes that have so far been computed numerically, by fits, or only at isolated parameter values. (i) The area of the shadow seen by an equatorial observer, for every spin, in complete elliptic integrals, together with its small-spin series and its near-extremal expansion A = 16π + 15√3 + (3π/√2)√(1−a) + …; the shadow area of an extremal black hole at every inclination; and a single short integral for arbitrary spin and inclination. (ii) The perimeter of the shadow, equal to 18√3 M for a maximally spinning hole seen edge-on. (iii) The capture cross-section of a Kerr black hole for slow particles arriving perpendicular to the spin, σ = [7π + π√(1−a²) + 16√(1+a) E(2a/(1+a))] M²/v², the corresponding angular-momentum accretion in closed form, and the isotropically averaged cross-section and spin-down at maximal spin in elementary closed form. (iv) Escape probabilities for photons emitted isotropically just outside the horizon of an extremal Kerr–Newman black hole at any latitude, P = 1/2 − arcsin(k)/(2π) − k/4, and from the innermost stable circular orbit at any charge, together with escaping energy fractions and escape probabilities for massive particles. Known special cases are recovered and credited. All results were checked against independent high-precision numerical computations. The AI system proposed research directions, wrote and ran the computer-algebra and numerical code, performed the derivations and checks, searched the literature, and drafted the text. The author directed the work and is responsible for its publication. Novelty assessments are based on literature searches and may be incomplete.

papers.title: Universal small-spin formulas for the shadow area, the capture cross-section and the spin-down of Kerr-like rotating black holes
papers.authors: Jacob Goodchild
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Many rotating black-hole metrics studied in the literature are generated from a static, spherically symmetric seed ds² = −f dt² + dr²/f + r² dΩ² by the Newman–Janis algorithm in the form of Azreg-Aïnou, which yields the Kerr metric with 2Mr replaced by r²(1 − f(r)). For this whole class we give closed formulas, in terms of f and its derivatives at a single radius, for the leading effects of a small spin a on three observables: (i) the area of the black-hole shadow seen by a distant observer at any inclination, to order a² and, with a term-by-term finite-part method, to orders a⁴, a⁶ and a⁸; (ii) the capture cross-section for neutral massive particles of any speed arriving from any direction, to order a² (and to order a⁴ along the spin axis); and (iii) the mean angular momentum swallowed per unit captured energy, which controls the spin-down of a black hole accreting collisionless matter. The order-a² shadow formula depends on f only through f(R) and the curvature combination κ = 2f − R²f″ at the photon sphere R; the massive-particle formula contains the combination 3ff′ + rff″ − 2rf′², whose zero defines the innermost stable circular orbit. Specialising to Kerr–Newman gives explicit expressions valid at arbitrary charge, including the shadow area to order a⁴; for Kerr the method reproduces the known low-order terms and yields the order-a⁶ and a⁸ coefficients of the shadow area at any inclination. All results were checked against direct high-precision computations of the exact shadow contour or of the exact capture boundary for Kerr, Kerr–Newman, rotating Bardeen and rotating Hayward black holes, with agreement to 11–22 significant digits.
