papers.authors: Galina Ilieva, Tania Yankova, Margarita Ruseva, Stanislava Klisarova-Belcheva, Penyo Georgiev, George Totkov
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used in higher education for explanation, content generation, feedback, and personalized learning. However, conventional prompt-response chatbots may provide insufficient support for complex academic tasks requiring planning, evidence organization, comparison, justification, verification, and reflection. This study proposes the Agentic GAI-Supported Learning Framework for Higher Education (AGAI-HE), which positions GAI agents as bounded, human-supervised learning partners rather than substitutes for students or instructors. The framework compares traditional e-learning, GAI-chatbot-supported learning, and GAI-agent-supported learning. Agentic support covers task contracting and interpretation, decomposition and planning, evidence organization, alternative generation, comparison and decision, feedback and refinement, and learner verification and reflection. It also incorporates human supervision, academic integrity, privacy safeguards, and instructor validation. An exploratory perception-based validation involving 130 students in an e-commerce learning context found that both AI-supported conditions were rated more positively than traditional e-learning for learning enhancement, personalization, decision-making support, and workflow organization. However, the difference between GAI agents and GAI chatbots was not statistically significant for the matched composites. The findings provide initial perception-based support for agentic GAI but do not demonstrate superior learning outcomes. Its educational value depends on making multi-step reasoning more structured, visible, verifiable, and accountable.

papers.title: Data Governance as a Decision Variable: A Model-Driven Decision Support System for Budget Allocation in Generative AI Adoption
papers.authors: Almudena Recio-Román, Manuel Recio-Menéndez, María Victoria Román-González
papers.abstract: Corporate adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is routinely managed as a problem of technological scaling: firms decide how much to use the tool while treating the quality of the underlying knowledge base as a given feature of the environment. This paper shows that such a formulation is structurally incomplete and yields systematically biased recommendations. We present a model-driven decision support system (DSS) that endogenises data governance through an explicit budgetary variable and jointly solves the allocation between investment in information quality and the intensity of algorithmic use. The formal core is a non-linear, two-variable optimisation model in which data quality simultaneously modulates the value production function and the cost structure, through a variable cost coefficient and a convexity exponent that captures the agency cost of human oversight—the Babysitting Tax. We prove the existence of a scissor effect, whereby data degradation shifts marginal value downwards and marginal cost upwards at once; we characterise the Marginal Profit Destruction Zone, in which the firm remains profitable while destroying margin on every additional query; and we establish a viability corridor for governance investment bounded both from below and from above. We further prove that, for firms with severely fragmented data architectures, conditional optimal profit is non-monotonic, which gives the decision the character of a big push rather than of a marginal adjustment. On this core we build a five-layer artefact—telemetry, estimation, optimisation, policy, and interface—whose policy layer materialises in three executable budgetary decision rules. We show that these rules decentralise the centralised optimum between the Finance function and the Data function through the exchange of two scalars only, and that the convergence condition of the protocol coincides exactly with the second-order condition of the problem. The two-variable problem reduces to a scalar search of logarithmic cost, which makes the artefact computable in real time. Simulation over 10,000 replications and two calibrated organisational profiles quantifies the value of the artefact: a firm with fragmented data that applies the conventional static model over-uses the technology by 27.8%, believes it is obtaining a profit of +32.0 monetary units and in fact realises a loss of 36.7, whereas the DSS solution places it at +8.4.

papers.title: Preservice Special Education Teachers’ Acceptance of an AI-Based Microteaching Evaluation and Feedback System: A Pre–Post UTAUT Mixed-Methods Study
papers.authors: Gayoung Lee, Youngjin Yoo, Seolhee Lee
papers.abstract: We examined preservice special education teachers’ acceptance of an AI system that supports the evaluation of, and feedback on, their own teaching demonstrations. The system analyzes recorded demonstrations against a structured rubric with time-stamped behavioral evidence, allows users to review and revise the AI evaluation through chatbot dialogue, and then generates personalized feedback. We used a convergent mixed-methods design informed by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and interpreted through an expectation-confirmation lens. Undergraduate students at a private university in South Korea completed a 23-item UTAUT-based questionnaire before and after a semester of use of the system in two required courses (valid pre-use responses N = 42; posttest N = 65; matched pairs n = 33), and 20 students were interviewed across the semester’s two demonstration cycles. Acceptance was uniformly high before use (composite means 4.22–4.63 on a 5-point scale) and did not decline after a semester of use; post hoc, exploratory one-sided non-inferiority tests rejected a decline of d = −0.35 or larger for every factor (all p ≤ 0.007). Performance expectancy increased modestly (d = 0.36; t-test p = 0.047, Wilcoxon p = 0.055, Holm-adjusted p = 0.282), a change that is best read as suggestive rather than established. At posttest, a regression of intention on the four UTAUT factors accounted for 62% of the variance, but effort expectancy (β = 0.37) showed the most consistent evidence of association with intention across classical, heteroscedasticity-robust, bootstrap, and influence-adjusted specifications; the association for social influence (β = 0.39 under classical estimation) was not robust to the estimator, performance expectancy was significant only when one influential case was excluded, and facilitating conditions were nonsignificant throughout. Facilitating conditions were, as the original model specifies, strongly associated with use behavior (β = 0.65) rather than with intention. In interviews, participants described their sustained acceptance in terms of evidence-grounded, time-stamped feedback, score discrepancies that prompted questioning and reflection, uptake into lesson planning and re-teaching, and the system’s role as an accessible complement to scarce instructor feedback, and they located the limits of that acceptance in context-recognition errors, feedback inconsistency, and interface friction. Taken together, the findings suggest that high pre-use expectations of AI-supported evaluation need not erode over a semester of sustained use when the system continuously displays the grounds of its judgments, and that ease of use, rather than perceived usefulness, is the factor showing the most consistent evidence of association with continued-use intention.

papers.title: Student-Reported Cognitive Engagement with Structured Generative-AI Questioning: Differentiated Associations with AI, Teacher, and Peer Questions
papers.authors: Yuqiang Liu, Zehua Ji, Siguang Zhang
papers.abstract: Generative AI can sustain follow-up questioning, but questions do not constitute engagement by themselves. This qualitative-dominant mixed-methods study examined student-reported cognitive engagement around AI, teacher, and peer questions in a Chinese university critical-thinking course. Seven reflection points produced 1034 matched submissions, including 648 substantive texts. A structured source item provided an implementation check for 399 responses at two common reflection points, and two human coders independently analyzed a stratified sample of 120 reflections. Sampling-weighted and reflection-stratified checks assessed sensitivity to unequal stratum sizes. Within this structured intervention, AI-salient accounts more often concerned assumptions, criteria, evidence, uncertainty, and reason organization; teacher-salient accounts made situated clarification more visible; and the smaller peer-salient set highlighted comparison and counter-positioning. These patterns changed little after weighting, although the AI prompt explicitly requested several of the functions later observed in AI-salient reflections. Across sources, reason organization was clearer than low-pressure participation. The reflections did not establish inherent source effects, complete interaction sequences, critical-thinking gains, or a consistently stronger hybrid pattern. They support a testable proposition: question sources may contribute complementary reasoning resources when students remain responsible for evaluating and revising their judgments.

papers.title: Chronic Proton Pump Inhibitor Use and Glycemic Control in Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Safiye Kübra Çetindağ Karatlı, Hatice Ergin, Merve Duygu Yurtbay, Meva Esra Doğan
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Evidence regarding the effects of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) on glucose metabolism is conflicting, and real-world data on the association between chronic PPI use and glycemic control in older adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are limited. This study aimed to evaluate the association between chronic PPI use and glycemic control in patients with T2DM aged 65 years or older. Methods: This single-center, retrospective cross-sectional study included 462 T2DM patients attending the Family Medicine Outpatient Clinic of Ankara Bilkent City Hospital between April 2025 and April 2026. Patients with regular PPI use for ≥6 months before the index HbA1c were classified as chronic PPI users. Suboptimal glycemic control was defined as HbA1c ≥ 8.0%. Associations were evaluated using logistic regression for suboptimal control and linear regression for HbA1c level. Results: Of the 462 patients, 316 (68.4%) were chronic PPI users. Mean HbA1c (7.11 ± 1.21% vs. 6.23 ± 0.99%; p < 0.001) and fasting plasma glucose (148.70 ± 64.87 vs. 116.23 ± 43.54 mg/dL; p < 0.001) were higher among PPI users. In multivariable logistic regression, chronic PPI use was independently associated with suboptimal glycemic control (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 3.416; 95% CI: 1.572–7.422; p = 0.002). This association remained significant in a sensitivity model additionally adjusted for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), smoking status, diabetes duration, insulin use, metformin use, and heart failure/coronary artery disease (aOR = 3.834; 95% CI: 1.734–8.478; p = 0.001). In multivariable linear regression, chronic PPI use was independently associated with a 0.793-percentage-point higher HbA1c level (95% CI: 0.570–1.016; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Chronic PPI use was independently associated with higher HbA1c levels and suboptimal glycemic control in older adults with T2DM. Because of the observational design, causality cannot be established. Prospective studies accounting for PPI indication, agent-specific effects, dose, and duration of exposure are needed to clarify the nature of this association.

papers.title: A Topology-Aware Graph Learning Framework for Occlusion-Robust Skeleton-Based Human Action Recognition
papers.authors: Haoxin Lyu, Suk-Hwan Lee, Soo-Yol Ok, Jiyoung Oh, Yang Liu
papers.abstract: Skeleton-based human action recognition is attractive for practical vision systems because it represents motion compactly, but occlusion and pose-estimation failures can remove spatially adjacent joints for extended periods and degrade graph-based recognition. We propose a Topology-Aware Graph Learning (TAGL) framework that couples three mechanisms: Neighborhood Expansion Masking generates spatially correlated, sequence-level joint loss during training; Adaptive Multi-Hop Graph Learning reweights information from different graph distances when local neighborhoods become unreliable; and Holistic Topological Mapping provides complementary global structural cues through persistent topology. TAGL achieves 93.3%/97.9% top-1 accuracy on NTU RGB+D 60, 90.4%/91.6% on NTU RGB+D 120, 97.0% on Northwestern-UCLA, and 47.2% on UAV-Human. Across six heterogeneous skeleton corruptions, its average accuracy reaches 85.8%, compared with 79.3% without NEM and 84.5% with random masking, while requiring 1.78 M parameters and 2.58 GFLOPs. These results show that TAGL improves tolerance to incomplete and structurally degraded skeleton observations without excessive computational overhead. Its compact and corruption-aware design is therefore promising for skeleton-based monitoring systems operating under imperfect pose observations, including safety surveillance, human–robot interaction, and rehabilitation-oriented motion analysis.

papers.title: Autistic Trait Dimensions and Resting-State Neural Markers: A Multimodal EEG/fNIRS Study in Non-Clinical Adults
papers.authors: Elena Flores-García, Dominika Z. Wojcik, Silvia Huelmo, Emiliano Díez Villoria
papers.abstract: Autistic traits are continuously distributed in the general population, but whether this variation is reflected in resting-state brain activity remains unclear. We recorded simultaneous EEG and fNIRS during alternating eyes-open and eyes-closed rest in 51 non-diagnosed young adults, 44 of whom had complete EEG and questionnaire data. Total and subscale scores on the Abridged Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ-28) were related to electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and multimodal measures, with adjustment for age and sex, FDR correction within each analytic family, and sensitivity analyses across EEG preprocessing choices. No association survived correction in any family: global and dynamic connectivity, regional spectral power, microstates, fNIRS amplitude measures, or the multimodal canonical correlation. The only regularity was directional: greater self-reported social difficulty was associated with lower theta power across regions, but this pattern was neither significant after correction nor specific to theta. In a secondary analysis, the change in right frontal beta power between eyes-closed and eyes-open conditions varied with the AQ total; this interaction depended on channel handling and remains provisional. The results do not support a stable resting-state neural marker of autistic traits in this sample. Larger, preregistered studies are needed to establish whether these patterns replicate.

papers.title: Pedagogical Scaffolding for Generative AI-Supported Self-Directed Learning: A Qualitative Study of the CRAFT Framework
papers.authors: Alwyn Vwen Yen Lee, Timothy Cheng, Joo Seng Melvin Chan
papers.abstract: This study investigates how generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can scaffold self-directed learning (SDL) in secondary classrooms. Focusing on the interaction between teacher facilitation and AI affordances, it examines and refines the Content–Response–AI&peers–Fusion–reflecT (CRAFT) framework as a practitioner-informed pedagogical scaffold for operationalizing aspects of the Process dimension of the Person–Process–Context (PPC) model. The study addresses a persistent gap between SDL theory and classroom practice by examining how learner agency can be cultivated within AI-supported learning environments. Adopting a qualitative multi-case study design, the research analyzed instructional practices, lesson artifacts, and reflective accounts from six experienced educators from a secondary school in Singapore across one academic year. Data were analyzed using a theoretically informed, hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis, enabling cross-case examination and iterative refinement of CRAFT in relation to the PPC model. Findings indicate that while generative AI supports goal setting, idea generation, and iterative feedback, the metacognitive and reflective dimensions of SDL remain underdeveloped without deliberate teacher mediation. Teachers remain critical orchestrators of AI and peer interactions, supporting disciplinary sense-making and learner autonomy rather than positioning AI as a standalone instructional aid. Overall, this study integrates a practitioner-informed and empirically refined pedagogical scaffold with an established theoretical model, offering a theoretically grounded, context-sensitive pedagogical guide for designing learning experiences that support opportunities for student agency.

papers.title: Boards in the Age of AI: Antecedents, Decisions, and Outcomes of Board-Level Artificial Intelligence Governance—A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Darko Tipurić, Domagoj Hruškа, Elena Perić
papers.abstract: The article deepens understanding of artificial intelligence on corporate boards by systematically reviewing the literature using the ADO (Antecedents, Decisions, Outcomes) and TCM (Theories, Contexts, Methods) frameworks, following established systematic review guidelines and PRISMA. The findings integrate theoretical, contextual, and methodological perspectives to identify key antecedents, decisions, and outcomes. Organizational, structural, individual, and external antecedents are crucial in shaping board-level decisions on structural adjustments, technology integration, human capital and education, strategic communication, and operational adaptation. These decisions influence the quality of supervision, the effectiveness of decision-making, as well as resilience, legitimacy, accountability, and behavioral outcomes. The research provides three distinct contributions. First, a synthesis contribution: a systematic taxonomic mapping of the construct space represented in the included corpus, comprising 30 antecedent, 15 decision, and 27 outcome constructs specific to board-level AI governance. Second, a conceptual contribution: the first integrative application of the combined ADO-TCM framework to the board-AI intersection. Third, a theoretical contribution: the identification of an emerging pattern in the reviewed literature favoring engaged augmentation over full automation as an approach to human–algorithm collaboration in board oversight.

papers.title: DEVELOPING AN ETHICAL-PEDAGOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR AI-ASSISTED MAH?RAH KIT?BAH LEARNING: A WAHDATUL ‘UL?M PERSPECTIVE
papers.authors: Neli Dian Rahmawati, Syamsul Maarif, Inayah, Muhammad Miftah Al Aufa
papers.journal: JALIE Journal of Applied Linguistics and Islamic Education
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed Arabic language learning, particularly Mah?rah Kit?bah (writing skills). Generative AI enables students to receive immediate assistance in translation, text composition, grammatical correction, and academic writing. However, its integration into learning also raises pedagogical and ethical concerns, including cognitive dependency on AI, diminished authenticity of students’ academic work, weakened critical thinking, and challenges to academic integrity. This study develops an ethical-pedagogical framework for AI-assisted Mah?rah Kit?bah learning from the perspective of the Wahdatul ‘Ul?m paradigm. Employing a qualitative library research design, the study adopts philosophical, pedagogical, and ethical-normative approaches. Data were collected from scholarly literature on AI in education, Arabic language pedagogy, academic integrity, and the Wahdatul ‘Ul?m paradigm, and analyzed using content analysis. The findings indicate that AI should function as a learning support tool rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual processes. The study proposes an ethical-pedagogical framework that integrates academic integrity, the authenticity of students’ academic work, critical thinking, lecturers’ pedagogical supervision, and academic adab to support the ethical implementation of AI in Mah?rah Kit?bah learning based on the Wahdatul ‘Ul?m paradigm.

papers.title: INOVASI MEDIA LAYANAN PSIKOSOSIAL: PELATIHAN PEMBUATAN VIDEO ANIMASI BERBASIS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) BAGI GURU BK
papers.authors: Ulvina Rachmawati, Agus Triyanto, Widya Juwita Sari, Ismarini Bekti Setiani, Sugiyana Sugiyana
papers.abstract: Abstrak: Perkembangan teknologi dan tingginya penggunaan media sosial pada remaja Gen Z meningkatkan risiko cyberbullying. Guru BK berperan sebagai garda terdepan dalam pencegahan, namun mitra MGBK SMP Kabupaten Gunungkidul masih terkendala keterbatasan literasi dan kompetensi digital; 83% belum memanfaatkan AI dalam media BK dan 76% kesulitan menyusun media BK yang menarik. Pengabdian ini bertujuan meningkatkan literasi dan kompetensi teknis guru BK dalam membuat video animasi berbasis AI sebagai media layanan psikososial untuk pencegahan cyberbullying. Kegiatan diikuti 41 guru BK (10 laki-laki dan 31 perempuan) dengan tahap pelaksanaan melalui 4 sesi: pemaparan dan diskusi, workshop dan pendampinga penyusunan prompt dan produksi video dengan Google Gemini dan Google Veo 3.1, editing CapCut, penugasan mandiri, presentasi dan umpan balik. Evaluasi menggunakan pretest–posttest dan wawancara. Hasil menunjukkan rerata skor literasi meningkat dari 16,2 menjadi 18,9; 85,7% peserta mengalami peningkatan, melampaui indikator 75%; tidak ada peserta di kategori rendah dan 85,4% berada di kategori tinggi setelah pelatihan. Dari kompetensi teknis, 90% peserta mampu menyusun prompt, membuat video animasi, dan editing, melampaui indikator 80%. Sebanyak 41 video animasi berhasil dikembangkan dan siap digunakan. Dengan demikian, pelatihan ini berhasil meningkatkan literasi digital dan kompetensi teknis guru BK dan menghadirkan inovasi media layanan psikososial yang relevan dengan Gen Z.Abstract: The high number of cyberbullying cases among adolescents has not been matched by the digital competence of school counselors in developing AI-based psychosocial service media. This community service program aimed to improve school counselor’s literacy and technical competence in developing AI-based animation videos for cyberbullying prevention. The program partner was MGBK SMP Kabupaten Gunungkidul with 41 school counselor as participants (10 male, 31 female). The training was conducted in a blended format across four sessions, including material presentation, a workshop and mentoring in animation video production, assignments, and presentation of participants’ work with feedback. Evaluation used a pretest-posttest questionnaire containing 10 questions about literacy understanding and interviews. The results showed an increase in the average total literacy score from 16.2 to 18.9. Participants in the high literacy category increased significantly from 21.9% (9 people) to 85.4% (35 people), while the low literacy category decreased to 0%. All participants also successfully produced contextual, ready-to-use AI-based animation videos for psychosocial services in scThe development of technology and the high use of social media among Gen Z adolescents increase the risk of cyberbullying. Guidance and counseling (BK) teachers serve as the frontline in prevention, but the partner, the Junior High School Guidance and Counseling Teacher Working Group (MGBK) of Gunungkidul Regency, still faces limited digital literacy and competence; 83% have not used AI in BK media, and 76% have difficulty creating attractive BK media. This community service program aims to improve BK teachers’ literacy and technical competence in creating AI-based animated videos as psychosocial service media for cyberbullying prevention. The activity was attended by 41 junior high school BK teachers (10 men and 31 women) and was carried out in four sessions: presentation and discussion; workshop and mentoring on prompt writing and video production using Google Gemini and Google Veo 3.1; editing with CapCut; independent assignments; and presentations and feedback. Evaluation used a pretest–posttest and interviews. The results showed that the average literacy score increased from 16.2 to 18.9; 85.7% of participants improved, exceeding the 75% success indicator; no participants were in the low category, and 85.4% were in the high category after training. In terms of technical competence, 90% of participants were able to write prompts, create animated videos, and perform editing, exceeding the 80% indicator. A total of 41 animated videos were successfully developed and are ready for use. Thus, this training successfully improved BK teachers’ digital literacy and technical competence and provided innovation in psychosocial service media relevant to Gen Z.

papers.title: CHATBOT-DELIVERED COGNITIVE BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY: A STRUCTURED REVIEW OF EFFICACY, USER ENGAGEMENT, AND EQUITY OF ACCESS
papers.authors: Krzysztof Konopka, Michalina Justyna Kozłowska, Eliza Zofia Kabat, Maryan Liasota, Zuzanna Julia Komin, Mateusz Lis, Jakub Juskowiak, Alicja Kwiatkowska, Faustyna Magdalena Kołodziej, Maciej Kamil Majchrzak
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science
papers.abstract: Background: Chatbots are increasingly used to deliver cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) via mobile and web applications. Many mental health systems cannot meet demand with face-to-face care alone. CBT chatbots have therefore been introduced in app form, but data on outcomes, dropout, and unequal uptake remain limited. Objective: This review evaluates whether CBT chatbots reduce anxiety and depression symptoms, which user- and design-related factors are linked to engagement and dropout, and which structural barriers limit who can practically use these tools. Methodology: Peer-reviewed studies from 2018 to 2026 were identified through searches in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar. Included studies examined automated CBT chatbots (e.g., Woebot, Wysa, Youper, Limbic Care) and reported clinical outcomes, engagement or dropout, and/or access-related findings. Twenty-four publications were synthesised thematically. Results: Short-term trials and observational studies reported reductions in anxiety and depression symptoms, with small-to-moderate effects1. Generative conversational designs were linked to higher engagement than static digital programmes in at least one RCT, which reported roughly 2.4 times the use frequency of a generative CBT app relative to workbook controls3. Attrition remained notable; one meta-analysis estimated intervention-arm dropout at 21.84%5. Unequal access persisted because of connectivity, device availability, and digital literacy, despite the privacy and round-the-clock availability of app-based care23. Conclusion: CBT chatbots may serve as useful low-intensity interventions, but their public health value depends on improved retention and fairer access. Implementation should address digital literacy, culturally appropriate design, and governance that does not restrict validated tools to already advantaged users.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND CLINICAL PRACTICE: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
papers.authors: Anna Bociąg, Łukasz Ptach, Rafał Marciniak, Konrad Kowalski, Aleksandra Milewska
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Technologies in Social Science
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping medicine, influencing clinicians’ training and patient care. Despite growing enthusiasm for AI-enabled diagnostics and digital learning tools, integration of these technologies into medical education and clinical practice remains uneven. Objective: This narrative review synthesises recent literature on the role of AI in medical education and clinical practice, mapping current applications, stakeholder perceptions, and the conditions that determine successful adoption. Methods: Relevant articles were identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, and EMBASE, prioritising literature from the last decade. Empirical studies, methodological reviews, and authoritative commentaries addressing AI, machine learning, or digital health technologies in clinical or educational settings were included and organised thematically. Findings: AI-powered tools are embedded across medical training, spanning augmented and virtual reality simulations, bedside mobile learning, and a range of clinical specialties, with performance matching expert levels on narrowly defined diagnostic tasks. Stakeholder attitudes are positive but conditional: medical students expect digital health technology to feature in their curricula yet many consider their own competencies inadequate, and very few physicians-in-training report familiarity with AI. Patients express willingness to engage with AI for self-management while preferring human contact in sensitive clinical domains. Persistent barriers remain, including limited availability of curated data, algorithmic bias, difficulties reproducing published models, and underdeveloped regulatory and workflow structures. Conclusion: AI delivers its greatest value when deployed as a collaborative instrument that augments rather than replaces clinical judgment. Realising this potential depends on sustained investment in digital literacy, explainable systems, clinician involvement in design, and equitable institutional infrastructure.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and occupational medicine
papers.authors: Roko Žaja, Begoña Martínez‐Jarreta, Hana Brborović, Milan Milošević
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping occupational medicine through applications in automation, smart monitoring, extended reality training, algorithmic management, and digital work arrangements. The EASOM Summer School 2025 examined how AI technologies enhance occupational health systems by enabling real-time risk identification, predictive surveillance, and targeted interventions to prevent work-related accidents and diseases. Practical applications include smart personal protective equipment, wearable sensors, augmented reality training systems, and predictive diagnostics exemplified by noise-related hearing loss risk assessment. However, significant challenges accompany these opportunities: data quality concerns, new technological hazards, psychosocial risks including surveillance-related stress and work intensification, algorithmic bias, and accountability gaps. Implementation requires comprehensive governance frameworks emphasizing early worker involvement, privacy-by-design approaches, phased pilot programs, and human-centered practices that complement rather than replace traditional occupational safety measures. Professional responsibility and education demand new competencies in digital literacy, algorithmic critical thinking, and applied ethics while maintaining essential clinical judgment and empathy. AI offers unprecedented potential for protecting workers' health and safety when responsibly implemented within transparent frameworks, but poor management risks deepening inequalities and eroding established protections. Successful integration depends on multidisciplinary research, international cooperation, stakeholder engagement, and a commitment to human-centered occupational medicine that prioritizes worker dignity and wellbeing.

papers.title: Towards an AI-augmented, human-centred smart digital ecosystem in occupational health and safety
papers.authors: Martina Padovan, Veronica Traversini, Andrea Romani, Giuseppe D'avino, Emanuela Tomasini, Alessandro Palla, Stefano Dugheri, Nicola Mucci, Antonio Baldassarre
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping occupational health and safety (OHS), shifting prevention models, risk assessment, and organisational processes. While traditional safety systems rely on reactive approaches and post‑event analyses, AI enables predictive, adaptive, and data‑driven prevention based on continuous monitoring and machine learning. The integration of sensor technologies, computer vision, and intelligent personal protective equipment supports early detection of biomechanical risks, fatigue, unsafe behaviours, and environmental hazards. Furthermore, AI enhances the structuring and linkage of occupational electronic health records, integrating biometric, behavioural, and environmental information while ensuring compliance with privacy‑by‑design principles through advanced Privacy Enhancing Technologies. A human‑centred digital ecosystem is proposed, founded on three pillars - technical‑predictive, organisational‑decision‑making, and ethical‑social - to ensure transparency, fairness, and sustainability in AI adoption. The role of occupational physicians is reassessed considering emerging digital competencies and ethical requirements, emphasising that AI should augment, rather than replace, professional expertise. A successful digital transition requires continuous dialogue among stakeholders, updated ethical frameworks, and robust interdisciplinary cooperation to place human health, dignity, and rights at the core of technological innovation.

papers.title: Beyond the algorithm
papers.authors: Lovela Machala Poplašen, Hana Brborović
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into occupational health medicine practice, offering potential improvements in diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, their implementation introduces novel challenges, including algorithmic bias, lack of transparency in decision-making processes, and risks of over-reliance on automated outputs without appropriate clinical judgment. As occupational health decisions directly affect both individual worker protection and broader workplace public health, professionals must develop advanced information literacy that extends beyond traditional source evaluation to include a critical understanding of AI systems themselves, including their underlying data sources, technical limitations, and potential biases. This study evaluated AI information literacy among 16 occupational health professionals (specialists and residents) participating in the EASOM Summer School 2025. A five-item knowledge-based assessment adapted to occupational health contexts evaluated participants' competencies in identifying biased research questions, selecting evidence retrieval strategies, assessing the accuracy of AI-generated content, applying ethical AI use practices, and understanding proper citation protocols. Overall mean quiz performance was 2.56/5 points (SD = 1.09), indicating substantial gaps in AI information literacy. Questions assessing biased research design yielded the poorest performance (12.5% correct), while questions on ethical AI use in academia (81.2% correct) and citation practices (68.8% correct) demonstrated higher competency. Age showed significant negative correlation with quiz scores (ρ = −0.511, p = 0.043), suggesting younger professionals are better prepared for AI-integrated practice. These findings, although comprised from a small sample, demonstrate the need for targeted educational interventions addressing algorithmic bias recognition, critical question formulation, and responsible AI integration in occupational health medicine practice and worker protection.

papers.title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
papers.authors: Yuying Tang, Lin Gao, Haotian Li, Baiqiao Zhang, Rebecca A. Fiebrink, Sebastian Deterding, Xiaojuan Ma, Huamin Qu
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

papers.title: Conocer a Picasso en Educación Primaria a través de la Gamificación e Inteligencia Artificial Generativa
papers.authors: Ana Manzano León, Paula Rodríguez-Rivera, José M. Rodríguez-Ferrer
papers.journal: Etic net Revista científica electrónica de Educación y Comunicación en la Sociedad del Conocimiento
papers.abstract: In recent years, the integration of innovative methodologies, such as gamification and generative artificial intelligence (AI), has opened up new possibilities in art education. This study examines the impact of a gamified intervention incorporating AI-based activities on the creative development of primary school students, evaluating its effectiveness in enhancing artistic and narrative expression. A quasi-experimental single-group design with pre- and post-intervention measures was implemented using the Prueba de Imaginación Creativa – Niños (PIC-N). The intervention was structured around a gamified narrative, in which students assumed the role of artistic explorers tasked with rescuing Picasso. The findings reveal a significant increase in both graphic and narrative creativity, accompanied by enhanced fluency, flexibility, and originality. Moreover, no gender differences were found, indicating that the intervention had an equitable impact. The results reinforce the effectiveness of gamification and generative AI as strategies to enhance creativity in the classroom. The importance of avoiding pointsification and promoting meaningful experiences is emphasized. Despite the benefits, several challenges were identified, including the risk of technological dependence and the need to strike a balance between digital experimentation and the development of manual skills.

papers.title: INTELLIGENT CAD/CAM INTEGRATION FOR ADAPTIVE MANUFACTURING: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF AI AND IOT FRAMEWORKS IN INDUSTRY 4.0
papers.authors: MADIBA Krista Kundai, MADZIMURE Tatenda, MAFUKIDZE Liberty, MAFUKIDZE Trinity, MAKASI Farai
papers.journal: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
papers.abstract: The union of Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming the way Computer-Aided Design (CAD) and Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) systems are used in the Industry 4.0 production process. Based on the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework (Page et al., 2021), this report is a systematic literature review on the intelligent integration of CAD and CAM technologies in adaptive manufacturing. Based on a structured search of major scientific databases, a curated list of peer-reviewed studies was analysed thematically to address five research questions related to designing with AI, toolpath optimisation using AI, IoT/IIoT architectures for real-time adaptive control, interoperability standards and barriers to AI adoption in specific sectors. AI models, especially deep learning, graph neural networks and reinforcement learning, have led the way in recent research and development on automatic feature recognition and toolpath generation, while digital twins, edge computing and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensor networks are more and more being used to implement predictive maintenance and closed-loop adaptive control in the shop floor. The design phase is also starting to change with Generative AI to enable manufacturability constraints to be built in earlier in the CAD process. The literature, however, shows that there are still significant gaps that need to be addressed: AI models deployed outside of the simulation environment are not adaptable in real-time, training datasets are not standardized and openly shared, and there are interoperability protocols that are still quite disjointed, and resources for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) looking to use these technologies are still limited. To situate these gaps in a particular developing-economy context, this review is also supplemented by a series of recently published empirical studies. The review suggests that interoperability standards, Human Safety for Industry 5.0 design principles, cybersecurity, and sustainable practice are the key factors that need to be coordinated for the intelligent CAD/CAM-IoT integration to be fully realised, and it presents a roadmap of future research directions for adaptive and connected manufacturing ecosystems.

papers.title: Subject-independent evaluation of mental fatigue detection models using limited-channel EEG in construction operations
papers.authors: MAA Imran, Farnad Nasirzadeh, Chandan Kumar Karmakar
papers.abstract: Mental fatigue is a significant risk in hazardous industries such as construction. EEG-based neural markers offer a promising means of fatigue monitoring, but practical deployment remains limited by the discomfort of multi-channel devices and their high computational demands. This study examines limited-channel EEG configurations for detecting mental fatigue in a crane operation simulation. Statistical, frequency, and entropy features were extracted and four classical classifiers compared under subject-independent evaluation. Random Forest achieved the most balanced performance. Under Leave-One Subject-Out, the best limited-channel configuration (AF3+T8) attained 61% accuracy, while the best single channel (AF3) attained 58%. Notably, under a subject-mixed ten-fold protocol, the same pipeline yielded substantially higher scores, with the T7 channel reaching 95% accuracy and F1 score. This highlights that subject-mixed validation used in past studies may potentially inflate model performance and overestimate generalisability. These findings emphasise that subject-independent evaluation is essential to prevent data leakage. These early results indicate that limited-channel EEG is a promising and practical direction for monitoring mental fatigue in construction, and that validation with professional operators on site is a natural next step.

papers.title: Pelatihan Pemberdayaan Kecerdasan Buatan Sebagai Asisten Pintar Guru di SDN 163 Buahbatu Bandung
papers.authors: Feri Sulianta, Viddi Mardiansyah, Azizah Zakiah, Fitrah Rumaisa, Yan Puspitarani, Sriyani Violina, Ai Rosita
papers.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi Kecerdasan Buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) menawarkan peluang besar dalam meningkatkan efisiensi administrasi dan kualitas pedagogis di institusi pendidikan dasar. Namun, banyak guru Sekolah Dasar (SD) masih menghadapi tantangan literasi digital serta kecemasan terhadap miskonsepsi bahwa AI akan menggantikan peran pendidik. Kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (Abdimas) ini bertujuan untuk membekali guru-guru di SDN 163 Buahbatu Bandung dengan keterampilan praktis dalam memanfaatkan ekosistem AI, seperti ChatGPT, Google Gemini, dan NotebookLM, guna mendukung administrasi pembelajaran, pembuatan media visual, dan evaluasi interaktif. Metode pelaksanaan program meliputi pemaparan materi teoretis berbasis kerangka TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge), demonstrasi langsung teknik penyusunan instruksi (prompting), serta pendampingan praktik intensif. Hasil pengabdian menunjukkan peningkatan pemahaman guru secara signifikan terhadap fungsionalitas AI serta eliminasi mitos negatif mengenai teknologi tersebut. Melalui pelatihan ini, peserta berhasil menyusun draf Rencana Pelaksanaan Pembelajaran (RPP) berdiferensiasi, materi ajar berbasis visual (Canva/Gamma), dan instrumen penilaian otomatis (Quizizz AI) yang valid, akurat, dan tetap memegang kendali penuh atas kendali guru (teacher agency).

papers.title: Deepfake News as Artificial Intelligence-Based Disinformation in Kompas.com
papers.authors: Gina Sonya Pane, Nurfitriani M Siregar
papers.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed digital communication while simultaneously introducing new challenges through the spread of AI-based misinformation, including deepfakes, voice cloning, and digitally manipulated content. This study aims to analyze how Indonesian online media frame the phenomenon of AI-generated misinformation and examine their role in raising public awareness of its associated risks. The study employs a qualitative approach using a library research method by collecting and analyzing relevant scholarly articles, books, government reports, and publications related to Artificial Intelligence, digital misinformation, online media, and digital literacy. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify patterns, themes, and perspectives presented in the selected literature. The findings indicate that online media predominantly frame the misuse of AI as a serious threat to information security, personal privacy, and public trust. Media coverage extensively highlights cases involving deepfakes, AI-assisted digital fraud, and gender-based digital violence resulting from manipulated content. Beyond their informative function, online media also serve as public educators by promoting digital literacy, information verification, and public awareness regarding the risks associated with AI misuse. This study emphasizes the importance of collaboration among government institutions, media organizations, academics, technology companies, and society in establishing ethical, secure, transparent, and accountable AI governance to safeguard the integrity of information in the digital era.

papers.title: Visualizing a decade of machine translation research (2016–2025): A VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis
papers.authors: Na Tang, Mohamed Abdou Moindjie, Zhennan Lyu, Shuo Wu
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose: Machine translation has undergone rapid transformation over the past decade, driven by advances in neural machine translation and large language models, yet systematic attention to the field’s overall intellectual structure during this critical transition remains limited. This study aims to visualize the evolution of machine translation research from 2016 to 2025, with particular attention to its interdisciplinary development and trends in the post-2022 era of large language models. Methodology: This study presents a bibliometric analysis of machine translation research from a language and translation perspective, based on 582 journal articles published between 2016 and 2025 and indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection. Using VOSviewer, it examines the main characteristics of machine translation publications and key research themes. Findings: The findings show a steady rise in machine translation research output, reflecting growing scholarly interest alongside technological advances. Research is globally distributed but concentrated in Europe and Asia, particularly in Spain and China. Journals in translation studies and computational linguistics account for the largest share of publications and receive the most scholarly attention. However, the field has yet to form a stable core author group, indicating a dispersed and evolving research structure. Five major research themes are identified: technological development and model innovation; human-machine collaboration and application contexts; machine translation quality evaluation; translation studies and industry-related research; and language education with ethical considerations. Contributions: By mapping research trajectories and key contributors, this study offers a solid foundation for advancing future research, emphasizing the need for cross-regional and interdisciplinary collaboration and a balanced integration of technological, human, and ethical dimensions. Keywords: Bibliometric analysis, machine translation, translation studies, visualization, VOSviewer. Cite as: Tang, N., Moindjie, M. A., Lyu, Z., & Wu, S. (2026). Visualizing a decade of machine translation research (2016–2025): A VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis. Journal of Nusantara Studies, 12(1), 1-19. http://dx.doi.org/10.24200/jonus.vol12iss1pp1-19

papers.title: AI detectors, academic freedom, and scientific communication: A transition from prohibition to regulated disclosure
papers.authors: Elvira Pocheshkhova, Natalia G. Popova, Serik D. Nurbaev, Nurbiy Aslanovich Pocheshkhov
papers.abstract: The turbulent integration of generative language models into the research cycle has prompted an institutional response, including stricter editorial policies and ubiquitous AI detection tools. This article analyzes the statistical limitations of automated detectors and their effect on academic freedom and cognitive diversity in scientific discourse. Recent empirical data (2023–2026) indicate that the false-positive rate is approximately 16% when testing a single detector using texts written by native English-speaking students. However, this figure rises to 61.3% for texts written by non-native English speakers when testing seven detectors, indicating a systemic bias in these tools. Bayesian statistics suggest that, due to the low prevalence of violations, even a moderate proportion of false positives can lead to a high false discovery rate (FDR) in sanction decisions. Legitimate scenarios for AI application during the stages of literature review, hypothesis formalization, methodological design, and linguistic preparation of the manuscript for publication are considered. Approaches to regulating the use of AI in scientific research and the presentation of research findings in the form of scientific texts have been systematized using official statements from COPE, WAME, Nature Portfolio, American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS), Elsevier, Springer Nature, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Association for Computing Machinery (ACM), and the International Federation of Translators (FIT), as well as a review of relevant publications. The authors argue the need to transfer from a culture of detection and prohibition to that of transparent disclosure, cryptographic traceability, and verification of the research process. Particular attention is given to the Russian context, including the implementation of an AI-detection module in the Antiplagiat system and the absence of a unified stance by the Higher Attestation Commission (VAK) and the White List operators. The applicability of Western quality metrics for plagiarism detectors to Russian-language texts is also discussed. Another focus is the transformation of scholarly text creation and the peer-review system, the global inequality of access to language tools, as well as the “arms race” between detection tools and circumvention technologies.

papers.title: The utility of point-of-care haemoglobin A1c tests in a very remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community: an agreement analysis with routine laboratory testing
papers.authors: Dissanayake, Braat, Gurruwiwi, Gulamanda, Tynan, Marlow, Harrap, Gongnini, Wentworth, Sanderson, Biggs, CLAN study group
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Optimal blood glucose control is critical to the prevention of diabetes complications. Point-of-care testing (POCT) provides a flexible alternative to conventional approaches that rely on laboratory processing of venous blood samples, with variable time to receiving results. We determined the level of agreement between the A1CNow+ glycated haemoglobin POCT system and routine laboratory haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) testing in a remote Aboriginal Australian community. METHODS: HbA1c was measured in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults using capillary blood and the point-of-care device and venous blood using standard laboratory procedures. Agreement between the point-of-care and laboratory results was examined using a modified Bland-Altman analysis and diagnostic agreement for type 2 diabetes using Cohen's kappa coefficient. Capillary and venous blood collection were conducted in a clinical setting. RESULTS: Participants (n=49) were on average age of 43±10 years, 65% were female, and with mean BMI of 30±5 kg/m2. Median HbA1c was 5.7% (39 mmol/mol) for both methods of measurement. The mean difference between the A1CNow+ point-of-care test and laboratory HbA1c measurement was 0.03% (0.34 mmol/mol), with limits of agreement of -0.75 to 0.81% (-8.15-8.83 mmol/mol). Diagnostic agreement for type 2 diabetes (HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol)) was moderate (Cohen's kappa statistic 0.70), with minor discrepancies observed at higher HbA1c levels. DISCUSSION: These findings support the clinical usefulness of portable HbA1c point-of-care testing beyond traditional clinic settings. While clinic-based models have improved diabetes care, they do not reach all remote communities effectively. Home-based outreach health care utilising A1CNow+ point-of-care testing may improve access to care, strengthen family engagement, and reduce cultural and logistical barriers. Despite sparse data at HbA1c levels greater than 55 mmol/mol, overall benefits appear meaningful. CONCLUSION: Capillary measurement of HbA1c using a portable point-of-care device demonstrated promising agreement with routine laboratory-tested venous blood HbA1c. This supports the development of novel outreach models of diabetes care that meet remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community needs.
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

papers.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence Feedback in College English Writing Assessment
papers.authors: Jun Chen
papers.abstract: In the fast-changing digital education and the rapid development of artificial intelligence, AI-generated feedback has been widely used in college English writing assessment as a valuable teaching support. The traditional manual marking is typically characterized by a heavy workload, slow feedback, and subjective judgment, making it difficult to meet students’ individual needs for writing improvement. AI feedback can detect surface-level language errors and improve the efficiency of assessment because it can provide immediate feedback, follow standard correction procedures, and offer detailed diagnostic guidance, thereby helping students to revise their writing autonomously. In this study, the analysis of student essays titled “The Impact of Influencer Culture on Youth Consumption Patterns” will be done to evaluate the utility of feedback provided by artificial intelligence. Additionally, rule-based AI correction and a more detailed review by teachers considering the practical value and importance of the learning process will be applied. It is proved that AI is quite efficient when dealing with language mistakes, yet it is insufficient in the logical development of an essay, in-depth interpretation, and critical thinking that are still the responsibility of teachers. From the author’s teaching experience, a new model that combines the efforts of AI and teachers can be proposed, according to which AI makes surface-level corrections and teachers concentrate on developing the higher-order skills of students.

papers.title: Bias, Benefit, or Both?: Surveying Perceptions of AI in Healthcare (Preprint)
papers.authors: Ela Adhikari, Li Shiyin, Anitza Lopez, Lifeng Lin, Elaine Situ-LaCasse
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare, presenting new opportunities in diagnostics, clinical decision support, workflow optimization, patient engagement, and population health. Yet important concerns remain about trust, transparency, bias, privacy, and the adequacy of existing regulatory frameworks. OBJECTIVE The objective of this study was to compare the perspectives of Healthcare Professionals (HCPs) and non-HCPs on the integration of AI in healthcare, with a focus on identifying perceived benefits, risks, ethical concerns, and barriers to adoption. METHODS We conducted a cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18, sampling both HCPs and non-HCPs. The questionnaire assessed perceived benefits and risks of AI, trust in AI systems, health bot applications, privacy and ethical concerns, regulatory priorities, and views on AI’s role in clinical decision-making. Responses from HCPs and non-HCPs were compared using descriptive statistics and group-level difference testing. RESULTS A total of 297 participants completed the survey, including 189 HCPs and 108 non-HCPs. Both groups expressed strong agreement that AI can improve efficiency, enhance access to care, support diagnosis, reduce medical errors, and aid early disease detection. However, trust in AI systems remained limited: nearly two-thirds of respondents expressed no confidence in AI’s ability to ensure privacy, safeguard data, or make unbiased ethical decisions. HCPs demonstrated greater emphasis on safety, accountability, transparency, and regulatory oversight, particularly in high-risk clinical environments, whereas non-HCPs were more likely to endorse shared responsibility when AI causes harm. Across groups, the majority believed that AI should serve primarily as an assistive tool, with humans retaining decision-making authority. Concerns about cost, infrastructure, and digital literacy were prominent barriers to equitable AI adoption. CONCLUSIONS Despite recognizing AI’s potential benefits, both clinicians and the public remain cautious about its risks and ethical limitations. These findings highlight the need for robust governance, transparent design, targeted education, and human-centered approaches to promote trustworthy, safe, and equitable AI integration in healthcare.

papers.title: Enhancing Stroke Patients’ BCI Performance: A Transfer Learning Framework Based on Jensen-Shannon Divergence to Reduce Calibration Time
papers.authors: Mohamed Nabil Nabil, Ahmed Awadallah, Ahmed Mohamed Azab, Mohamed Eldosoky
papers.journal: Journal of Engineering Science and Military Technologies /Journal of Engineering Science and Military Technologies
papers.abstract: The clinical utility of motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) is limited by lengthy calibration procedures required to address the non-stationarity and low signal-to-noise ratio of EEG signals. While transfer learning (TL) is a promising way to reduce this burden, models trained on small datasets often fail to generalize well. To overcome these issues, this paper introduces a novel subject-to-subject TL framework designed to improve classification accuracy while minimizing training requirements. The proposed framework integrates a 10-fold cross-validation scheme for hyperparameter optimization with a Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD) similarity metric, which measures the statistical divergence between target and source domains to select the most similar subject-specific or trial-specific models, thereby improving transfer performance. The EEG data were preprocessed using filtering and artifact removal techniques to enhance signal quality prior to feature extraction. A Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier was employed for classification due to its effectiveness in handling high-dimensional EEG feature spaces. Empirical testing on 50 subjects shows that the JSR-subjects model reaches mean accuracies of 86.80% using 10 trials and 85.33% using 5 trials. Additionally, the JSR-trials version maintains a robust accuracy of 83.90% with just one trial. These results represent an approximate 13% improvement over standard subject-specific benchmarks, demonstrating that JSR-based TL can enable fast, high-quality MI-BCI use in stroke neurorehabilitation, where reducing cognitive fatigue and calibration time is essential.

papers.title: Preparing the Healthcare Workforce for Digital Transformation: Artificial Intelligence Readiness, Attitudes, and Ethical Perceptions
papers.authors: Hyem Khiari, Najet Mahjoub, Khouloud Saadani, Nesrine Hamdi, Emna Arfaoui, Ahlem Fourati, Emna Gara Bach Ouerdian, Hind Bouguerra, Alia Methnani, Saida Sakhri, Khaoula Meftah
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Healthcare professionals have shown different perceptions regarding the safety, validity, trust, and expectations associated with the implementation of medical AI in the world. This study aimed to assess the knowledge, attitudes, and practices concerning artificial intelligence (AI) among healthcare professionals at Jendouba Hospital, northwest Tunisia. Methods: This was a cross-sectional study realized between September and December 2025, targeting all medical healthcare workers in Jendouba Hospital. Data were collected through a well-structured questionnaire. Results: A total of 224 healthcare workers responded (response rate: 90.6%). Most participants were unable to differentiate between core AI concepts. Over half supported integrating AI into formal training programs, while 61.5% strongly disagreed that teachers could be replaced by AI. Additionally, 60.5% believed AI cannot function without human assistance, and 52.2% disagreed that clinical AI will outperform human professionals. Although more than half found AI often useful, over a quarter reported being misled by it at times. In research, AI was mainly used for grammar and spell-checking. A majority (88.3%) believed that AI should always be supervised by physicians. Concerning ethics, nearly half felt that AI could compromise the doctor–patient relationship, while 42.4% did not consider its use a breach of medical confidentiality. Mean attitude and practice scores were significantly higher among professionals in non-clinical specialties compared to clinical ones. Conclusion : While healthcare staff favor AI integration despite limited technical knowledge, ethical concerns highlight the need for targeted training. These findings offer vital baseline data to foster equitable AI implementation in developing healthcare systems.

papers.title: Seven Questions Before Every Prompt: A Pre-Use Checklist for LLM-Assisted Academic Work
papers.authors: Shuaitong Liang
papers.abstract: Background: The rapid diffusion of AI-generated content (AIGC) tools has shifted the central question for university teachers and students from whether to use large language models (LLMs) to how to use them. Yet institutions face a structural gap: policy documents specify what is permitted or prohibited, while technical literature describes what models can do — and neither tells an individual user what concrete actions to perform before each use. In high-reliability domains such as surgery and aviation, precisely this gap is closed by a checklist.Objective: This paper introduces the first systematic pre-use checklist for LLM-assisted academic work — a seven-item verification instrument that translates regulatory requirements and technical constraints into executable actions, bridging the policy layer and the technology layer.Methods: To derive the checklist, we combine a structured review of Chinese legislation, ministerial regulations, and university AIGC policies (consolidated into a three-norm compliance model: Permitted / Prohibited / Disclosure) with an analysis of five structural limitations of LLMs documented in the technical literature (mapped to four countermeasure strategies and an Ask–Plan–Craft tri-layer interaction model). Checklist design follows the evidence-based methodology of high-reliability domains: items are short, binary-verifiable, and target the steps most often skipped. The instrument is validated through a documented case study — the development of a local text-to-speech workbench (qwen-tts-app) with a commercial agentic tool.Results: The checklist comprises seven pre-use gates spanning task scoping, plan-before-execution, task decomposition, auditable computation, mandatory output verification, data isolation, and AI-use disclosure; each item maps explicitly onto institutional and regulatory requirements. In the case study, every checklist item corresponded to a concrete, auditable action, and six of ten documented iteration failures were directly attributable to structural LLM limitations — confirming that mandatory output verification is indispensable.Conclusion: Compliance first, boundary awareness second, method third. The seven-item checklist operates as an actionable bridge between what institutions require and what individuals do, reducing individual cognitive load and institutionalizing tacit best practices. We offer it as a protocol awaiting its outcome study.
