papers.title: ChatMIT: A university recruitment chatbot based on zero-shot self–retrieval augmented generation
papers.authors: Michał Błaszczykowski, Magdalena Jastrzębska, Magdalena Paśnikowska-Łukaszuk
papers.journal: Advances in Science and Technology – Research Journal
papers.abstract: This study presents ChatMIT, a domain-specific conversational system designed to support undergraduate recruitment at the Faculty of Mathematics and Information Technology at Lublin University of Technology.Three Retrieval-Augmented Generation architectures, namely Naive RAG, Hybrid RAG, and Self-RAG, were implemented and evaluated across three levels of question complexity using three large language models of varying parameter scales: Gemma 3 (27B), Llama 3 (70B), and gpt-oss (120B).Response quality was assessed by independent domain experts according to two criteria: factual correctness and linguistic quality, each evaluated using a five-point scale developed by the authors.The results indicate that the choice of RAG architecture is the primary factor influencing response quality, exerting a greater impact than model scale.Self-RAG substantially outperformed both Hybrid RAG and Naive RAG across all levels of question complexity, achieving mean factual correctness scores of 4.67/5, 2.77/5, and 2.33/5, as well as linguistic quality scores of 4.90/5, 4.37/5, and 4.33/5, respectively.Furthermore, the adoption of a zero-shot variant of Self-RAG constitutes a methodological contribution of this study, demonstrating that the adaptive properties of the original architecture can be preserved while significantly reducing deployment complexity, without the need for supervised training of a dedicated critic model.The findings confirm that RAG-based conversational systems represent an effective approach to automating information access in academic environments and offer considerable potential for deployment across diverse institutional domains and faculties.

papers.title: Integrating ChatGPT into 5E inquiry-based learning to scaffold EFL academic research writing
papers.authors: Ying-Hsueh Cheng
papers.journal: Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education
papers.abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in education, yet evidence on how to integrate them systematically into EFL academic writing pedagogy remains limited. This study examined a 16-week undergraduate EFL composition course at a national university in Taiwan that embedded ChatGPT within the 5E inquiry-based learning (IBL) cycle (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate). Students completed sequenced research-writing tasks (outline, questionnaire design, initial findings, abstract/introduction, and a full research report) with ChatGPT used as a dialogic scaffold. Using an exploratory classroom-based mixed-methods design, the study collected pretest and posttest writing scores, peer-discussion transcripts, writing artifacts, ChatGPT interaction logs, and reflective journals. Descriptive statistics and paired-samples t -tests examined score change, while qualitative content and thematic analyses triangulated engagement patterns across phases. Results showed a modest, non-significant increase in timed argumentative writing performance, while qualitative findings suggested process-oriented development in inquiry-based academic research writing practices. Students used ChatGPT throughout the 5E cycle for higher-order inquiry work, including topic framing, instrument refinement, and data interpretation as well as for drafting and language polishing. Across the semester, they developed phase-sensitive prompt literacy and critical filtering by selectively adopting, revising, or rejecting AI suggestions to maintain authorial control. An illustrative case further demonstrated how this phase-sensitive ChatGPT engagement unfolded across the five inquiry phases. Overall, the 5E IBL structure appeared to channel AI use toward purposeful inquiry and responsible academic writing development.

papers.title: When Safety Claims Fail Silently: A Modelling Approach to AI Assurance
papers.authors: Kalvin Thuan-Phong Khuu
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Problem. The rapid deployment of large language models (LLMs) into safety-critical roles, including mental health support, education, and professional guidance, has created a gap between the safety claims AI developers publish and the behaviors their systems exhibit in practice. Current documentation practices, primarily model cards and system cards, describe safety properties in natural language which is unstructured by nature, lack proper validation mechanisms, and are rarely maintained across the lifecycle of a deployed system. Proposal & Approach. This paper presents my doctoral research project that addresses this gap through a modelling language and semantics to present AI safety claims as dynamic, reusable models. It will be developed through two phases. First, we propose to model AI safety claims with a structured argumentation notation that makes the logical dependencies between evidence and claims explicit and exposes precisely where a safety argument breaks down. Second, we propose a guidance system built on top of JPipe, an open-source modelling tooling platform, that allows practitioners to query a curated library of modeled safety claims and receive contextually relevant, personalized guidance for their own AI systems. Current Status. The first phase is substantially complete: five publications establish the empirical and tooling foundations of the project, including the extraction and categorization of 32 recurring safety patterns from major provider model cards, an in-depth model-based analysis of the GPT-5 system card, and the development of composition operators within JPipe that enable decomposition and reuse of sub-models. The remaining work focuses on completing the models library, building the guidance system, and evaluating both phases through expert review, case studies, and a user study with ML practitioners and safety-critical systems engineers.

papers.title: On the Non-Interchangeability of Deterministic and LLM-Based UML Evaluators
papers.authors: Giacomo Garaccione, Riccardo Coppola, Luca Ardito
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Automated assessment of UML class diagrams is essential for scaling software engineering education, with educators adopting both deterministic evaluators and, in recent years, emerging solutions based on Large Language Models. Existing comparisons between the two approaches conflate differences in format and reasoning, making it difficult to identify the causes of disagreement and, consequently, to understand whether the two approaches can be used interchangeably. The goal of this study is to analyze the agreement between a fuzzy-matching deterministic evaluator and an evaluator based on Claude Sonnet (4.6 model) in a scenario where both evaluators consume the same format for diagrams and the same type of evaluation criteria and reference solution, and produce output in the same format, to identify whether reasoning differences affect score reliability and error sensitivity, while also discussing the implications related to deployment costs. We conducted our analysis by having the two evaluators assess 50 student diagrams taken from two different exam sessions from the Software Engineering course at Politecnico di Torino, measuring aggregate correlation related to diagram correctness, agreement across reported errors, and estimating LLM performance scaling in terms of time and cost. Results showed a strong aggregate correlation on the combined dataset; however, it also dropped substantially within each exercise, revealing that the overall correlation is inflated by the separation between exercise clusters rather than by within-exercise-agreement. Furthermore, agreement on error types showed divergences, showing that the deterministic evaluator flagged structural anti-patterns more frequently than the LLM-based one, which in turn flagged completeness violations more frequently. These findings, together with the cost and time analysis, point to the fact that deterministic and LLM evaluators are complementary rather than interchangeable, and that per-type agreement analysis should be performed to understand where each approach is preferred, and in which cases one is more suited than the other.

papers.title: When AI Assistance Becomes High‑Risk: EU AI Act Compliance for Digital Twin in Critical Infrastructure
papers.authors: Римма Джусупова, Mark van den Brand
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly used to engineer and operate critical infrastructure, and general-purpose AI tools are gradually entering the front-end specification work that shapes those twins. Under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, some AI systems used as safety components in the management and operation of critical infrastructure qualify as high-risk, yet many AI-assisted engineering activities are still treated as low-risk office automation. This paper examines how general-purpose AI participates in digital-twin engineering workflows and identifies when such participation remains ancillary versus when it becomes sufficiently compliance-sensitive to require formal high-risk classification review. Based on a legal–technical reading of the EU AI Act and prior empirical work on industrial AI, we develop a workflow-centred compliance-by-design framework structured around three indicators: degree of reliance on AI output, role in binding design decisions, and downstream embedding of AI-shaped artefacts. The framework provides a lightweight way for engineering teams to record AI provenance, distinguish compliance-sensitive situations, and trigger stronger review and documentation before AI-assisted content propagates into safety-relevant configurations of critical-infrastructure digital twins.

papers.title: A Pedagogy-Aware Model-Driven Engineering Approach for AI Literacy
papers.authors: Riccardo Belliato, Antonio Bucchiarone, Juri Di Rocco, Alfonso Pierantonio, Antonio Cicchetti, Judith Michael, Michael Mittermaier, Andrea Vázquez‐Ingelmo, Jo Tondeur, Thibaut Cromphaut, Sarah K. Howard
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy is becoming an essential competency across disciplines and stakeholders. However, AI-related education poses important difficulties, as it combines many concerns such as technical skills, ethical/legal issues, critical thinking, etc. These difficulties, combined with the variety of learners background, push towards customizable learning support. Such needs could be better addressed through machine processable representations, as those enable distribution, reuse, and automation mechanisms both from Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) and Generative AI techniques.

papers.title: Enhancing Software-Design Learning by Combining UML and LLM-Assisted Feedback in a Learning Platform
papers.authors: Reenu Maria Jerry, Jacob Krüger, Michel R. V. Chaudron
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Software design is an important part of software engineering. In contrast to some parts of software engineering that are dominated by mathematical logic and analytical thinking, software design is based on judgment and there is rarely a single right software design. Instead, software design involves selecting one out of a number of “reasonable” solutions, all of which satisfy the functional requirements but vary in structure and thereby affect non-functional properties such as maintainability. To account for this “it-depends” situation, software-design education must focus on training students to evaluate decisions with respect to design concepts and their trade-offs. In this paper, we present our work on a web-based learning platform that helps students learn about this diversity of software design. Our platform offers a series of software-design assignments that focus on understanding and applying design concepts. The assignments are supported by interactively editable UML diagrams. We use Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide automated formative feedback on students’ designs, aiming to automatically generate detailed and actionable first guidance. By combining a level-based learning approach, interactive UML editors, and LLM-powered feedback, we aim to help students understand software-design concepts and improve their design decisions. To evaluate the ideas of our platform, we conducted a user study with 15 students. The results show strong engagement and underpin the usability of our platform across all learning-experience dimensions. In our evaluation, we found that LLM-generated feedback explaining why a design decision violates a concept correlates with self-reported improvements on successive attempts. Thus, our contributions and insights can help improve students’ learning experiences.

papers.title: Teaching UML Modeling in the Age of Generative AI: Combining Manual Modeling, Prompt Engineering and Model Evaluation
papers.authors: Oksana Ņikiforova
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming software engineering practice, including the creation of Unified Modeling Language (UML) artifacts. While Large Language Models can generate UML diagrams from natural language descriptions, their implications for software modeling education remain insufficiently understood. This paper presents an educational framework for AI-supported UML modeling developed based on 25 years of experience teaching the Object-Oriented System Analysis course, analysis of student UML projects, and insights obtained by the author from projects investigating AI-assisted software artifact generation. The framework combines four complementary learning activities: manual UML modeling, (meta)prompt engineering, AI-assisted model generation, and systematic model evaluation. Rather than treating AI as a replacement for modeling activities, the framework positions AI-generated artifacts as objects of comparison, reflection, and critical assessment. The paper concludes by outlining directions for future classroom deployment and empirical evaluation of the framework in software engineering courses.

papers.title: Teaching the Development of Software Agents in Higher Education: First Insights from a European Initiative
papers.authors: Lukas Sebastian Hofmann, José Ignacio Requeno, Elena Gómez-Martínez, Daniel Braun, Gabriele Taentzer
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing software engineering by enabling autonomous software agents. This shift requires new educational approaches that prepare students to design and realise such systems. We present first experiences from an exploratory seminar in which students developed software agents using three open-source frameworks: n8n, OpenClaw, and LangChain/LangGraph. Through project-based learning, students explored agent development, prompt engineering, and the use of software models as exchange artefacts. Our observations indicate that the different frameworks offer distinct educational benefits while highlighting common challenges, including ensuring reliable software model outputs and maintaining human oversight. These preliminary results provide insights into integrating model-driven agent development into higher education and identify directions for future curricula.

papers.title: Domain Knowledge Debt: Why Metamodeling Still Needs Elicitation
papers.authors: Alfonso Pierantonio, Davide Di Ruscio, Zakaria Hachm, Massimo Tisi, Hugo Brunelière, Théo Le Calvar
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: We teach metamodeling because building a metamodel forces a student to understand a domain: its concepts, classifications, relations, and constraints are acts of abstraction, and abstraction is where domain understanding forms. The models, transformations, code generators, and modeling environments built on a metamodel all presuppose that understanding, so any deficiency propagates to every artifact derived from it. Generative AI is by now an accepted aid across software activities, and metamodeling is no exception: a large language model (LLM) can return a valid, often plausible metamodel in a single shot, so the artifact appears while the decisions that would have produced it do not. The metamodel can be correct, yet the modeler may lack the conceptual competence it presupposes. We call this gap domain knowledge debt, a debt of the learner rather than the artifact, invisible at delivery and paid later, when the metamodel must be extended, justified, or transferred. Building a metamodel step by step is itself knowledge elicitation that grows the modeler’s understanding, assimilating and accommodating cognitive schemas in Piaget’s sense, whereas one-shot generation extracts the same domain knowledge at once without the modeler acquiring it. Our position is pedagogical: however the LLM enters the workflow, teaching must keep the abstraction decisions with the student, preserving the incremental elicitation a normal modeling process induces rather than avoiding the tool. We instantiate this as Socratic, step-by-step construction, a scaffold that elicits each abstraction decision rather than an oracle that supplies it, illustrated through a five-phase sequence. This is a position paper; an empirical study is future work.

papers.title: Towards LLM-Driven Transformation of Goal Models for AI-Enabled Socio-Technical Systems
papers.authors: Ahmed Hassine, Jameleddine Hassine
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Organizations are increasingly transforming traditional software systems into AI-enabled socio-technical systems. While goal models are widely used to capture stakeholder intentions, organizational objectives, and system requirements, existing approaches provide limited support for systematically evolving these models to reflect AI capabilities and the governance concerns they introduce, such as explainability, fairness, and accountability. This paper presents AI-Oriented Goal Model Transformation (AIGMT), an approach for transforming Goal-oriented Requirement Language (GRL) models of traditional systems into GRL models for AI-enabled socio-technical systems. AIGMT combines an AI Readiness Assessment, a catalog of AI transformation patterns, and Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted reasoning to identify candidate tasks for AI augmentation and generate corresponding model transformations. The methodology systematically introduces AI-enabled tasks, supporting resources, and governance requirements while preserving the original stakeholder intentions and goal-model structure. The approach is evaluated using three representative GRL models from the insurance, education, and healthcare domains, namely Insurance Claim Processing (the running example), University Course Registration, and Hospital Patient Intake and Triage. Together, these examples demonstrate the domain-independence of AIGMT and its ability to systematically evolve existing goal models into AI-enabled systems.

papers.title: Bridging Social and Technical Compliance in Autonomous Systems through a Standardized Pattern Catalog
papers.authors: Luca Brodo, Giuseppe Scalora, Lukas Walter, Stefan Henkler
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: As autonomous systems move into human-centered environments, their correctness can no longer be defined in purely technical terms. Beyond safety and liveness, these systems must comply with social norms: the implicit, context-dependent rules that govern acceptable conduct, such as yielding to pedestrians or avoiding noise near residential areas. Temporal logics such as TCTL and CTL are well established for technical properties, but engineers have no systematic way to verify social norms alongside them: encoding such norms in (T)CTL by hand is error-prone, hard to trace back to requirements, and not reusable. We address this gap with a standardized catalog of reusable observer patterns spanning both families of social norm: regulative norms, which constrain behavior (permission, prohibition, obligation, exceptions, role-based authority, and graded compliance), and constitutive norms, which create institutional facts. Each pattern couples a natural-language template, a (T)CTL formalization, and an observer automaton for integration into existing workflows. We evaluate the catalog on smart-farming and autonomous-transport scenarios, showing how engineers formalize social requirements, resolve norm conflicts, and quantify compliance–performance trade-offs.

papers.title: From Complex Ecosystems to Understandable Models – Evaluating a Domain-Specific Modeling Language for Digital Ecosystem Governance
papers.authors: Taija Kolehmainen, Gabriella Laatikainen, Juha‐Pekka Tolvanen, Tommi Mikkonen
papers.journal: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS)
papers.abstract: Designing governance in digital ecosystems, such as software and platform ecosystems, requires a shared understanding of the ecosystem structures, governance mechanisms, and value co-creation. To support description, analysis and communication of ecosystem governance, we developed a domain-specific modeling language called Ecosystem Governance Compass (EGC). This paper evaluates the EGC by examining which language characteristics support understanding and learning when modeling ecosystem and their governance. The evaluation was conducted through two empirical experiments involving 38 participant groups in an educational setting. The first one assessed model interpretation through sense-making tasks, while the second evaluated designing and constructing governance models using a graphical mock-up. The findings provide preliminary insights into how users understand and apply modeling languages at the ecosystem level. The participants were generally able to understand the basic concepts and notation of EGC and communicate their ideas using the language. The main challenges emerged when moving beyond individual concepts and interactions toward complete ecosystem governance representations, particularly when interpreting relationship semantics, maintaining consistency across multiple ecosystem layers, and reasoning at the ecosystem level. These findings suggest a need for support in semantic clarity, ecosystem-level modeling, and keeping the models consistent across different layers in addition to providing domain-specific concepts and notation. Further research is needed to evaluate EGC in industrial settings and to examine broader language quality aspects.

papers.title: How Brokers Enable Collective Identity Formation in Fragmented Industry Groups: The Case of Franciacorta Wineries
papers.authors: Alessandra Zamparini, Ileana Stigliani, Kevin Corley
papers.abstract: Abstract This study illuminates the role of brokers, that is, actors spanning inter‐organizational boundaries, in the process of collective identity formation in fragmented industry groups. Through an in‐depth longitudinal analysis of the Franciacorta wineries from the 1960s to the 1990s, we uncover how technical consultants acting as brokers facilitated collective identity formation by interacting with wineries through three mechanisms: translation, cross‐pollination, and integration. Our grounded model of collective identity formation reveals a distributed and co‐creative pathway to cohesive identity understandings built from the interstices of fragmented industry groups, through the co‐creation of practices, the weaving of social connections, and the facilitation of an optimally distinctive collective identity via inward adaptation and outward alignment between broader industry domains and local contexts. Our study advances theory by foregrounding the more inconspicuous practice‐level and social work that precedes, and ultimately determines the success of, the more visible identity‐defining moments that happen via symbolic representation or institutional codification.

papers.title: Making Ethical AI Teachable: Distributed Accountability in Language Teacher Education
papers.authors: Lucas Kohnke
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Discussions of ethical generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use in language education are often disconnected: whether by focusing on practical concerns (classroom dos and don'ts around disclosure, academic integrity, the boundaries of acceptable assistance) or through broader critical questions concerning surveillance, platform power, data extraction, linguistic bias and unequal participation in AI development. This split has practical consequences for language teacher education because it associates ethics with teacher compliance while leaving GenAI's structural conditions unexamined. This viewpoint article proposes distributed accountability as a conceptual and teachable framework for ethical AI praxis. It provides a language‐education‐specific framework that highlights how responsibility is shared by learners, teachers, institutions, AI developers and vendors. The distributed accountability model supports the implementation of three practice‐informed heuristics: a stakes‑and‐harm filter, an authorship receipt and a linguistic justice check, which are offered as adaptable prompts for professional judgement rather than universal compliance procedures. The article clarifies the framework's limits, including the need for empirical testing, workload‐sensitive implementation, learner‐centred framing and institutional support.

papers.title: Public involvement in the Brazilian Cerebral Palsy Register: An exploratory, sequential, mixed‐methods study
papers.authors: Luana Cristina da Silva, Claire Kerr, Israt Jahan, Raphael Fagundes Figueira Pinho, Aline Lincoln Silveira, Nadia A. Badawi, Gulam Khandaker, Gabriela Lorençoni Pauletti, Egmar Longo, María de las Mercedes Ruiz Brünner, Paula Silva de Carvalho Chagas, Hércules Ribeiro Leite
papers.abstract: AIM: To describe the implementation of a public involvement strategy based on the UK Standards for Public Involvement in Research within the Brazilian Cerebral Palsy Register (BrCPR). METHOD: We conducted a participatory, exploratory, sequential, mixed-methods study. Eleven partners (five adults with cerebral palsy and six mothers) from different Brazilian states participated in a four-phase online process: partner integration; knowledge building; exploring public involvement standards and identifying barriers and facilitators; and action plan development and co-creation of an implementation process of a public involvement group. RESULTS: Partners selected WhatsApp as their primary communication method and were satisfied with meeting the dynamics and content, except meeting duration (1 hour 30 minutes). Reported barriers included language inaccessibility, researcher attitudes, limited family empowerment, time constraints, and lack of researcher flexibility. Facilitators included researcher flexibility, varied knowledge-sharing formats, plain language use, qualitative impact measures, governance council creation, and revised public involvement implementation steps. Partners proposed a seventh standard: continuous review (of standards, co-responsibility, and research aspects). A 26-action implementation plan and a 6-stage public involvement implementation model for cerebral palsy registries were co-created. INTERPRETATION: The UK Standards for Public Involvement in Research proved an adequate guide for the BrCPR public involvement group. Identified barriers and facilitators guided group actions, leading to a public involvement implementation process grounded in partners' needs and perspectives.

papers.title: Multidimensional engagement effects of generative AI adoption among minority ethnic international students in UK higher education
papers.authors: Olatunji David Adekoya, Hakeem Adeniyi Ajonbadi, Chima Mordi
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has become a prevalent tool in higher education, yet little is known about how its use affects the learning experiences of minority‐ethnic international students (MEIS). Drawing on an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and a four‐strand engagement model, this quantitative study surveyed 273 MEIS across UK business schools and analysed the data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS‐SEM). The findings suggest that performance expectancy, effort expectancy and social influence predicted intention, and facilitating conditions and intention were also positively associated with self‐reported GAI use frequency. GAI frequency positively predicted cognitive, behavioural, emotional and, most strongly, agentic engagement. Multigroup analysis revealed that female students showed stronger effects of effort expectancy, performance expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions on intention than males; low‐experience students were more sensitive to effort expectancy than high‐experience peers; and postgraduate students exhibited stronger facilitating conditions, performance expectancy and social influence effects than undergraduates. The study highlights both theoretical and practical implications by linking GAI adoption with multidimensional student engagement, with the strongest association observed for agentic engagement, and calls for equity‐focused policy, curriculum interventions and institutional support targeted at individual access gaps among MEIS. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic? Generative AI (GAI) technologies are increasingly used by students in higher education for learning support. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) has been widely applied to examine technology adoption in educational contexts. What this paper adds? It extends UTAUT to an under‐researched population (MEIS), who often face heightened academic, technological and cultural challenges in UK higher education. GAI use by MEIS is strongly associated with cognitive, behavioural, emotional and especially agentic engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy Institutions should consider embedding GAI literacy and access support into orientation and academic skills programmes for MEIS. Educators who integrate GAI into teaching may consider structured questioning, verification and reflection activities while evaluating rather than assuming their effects on engagement. Policymakers should develop equity‐oriented strategies that support the digital and cultural integration of disadvantaged student groups.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence as enabler and object of strategic foresight: a theoretical framework for digital organisational transformation
papers.authors: Eduardo Carlos Dittmar, Martin Sposato, Jenny Patricia Vargas Portillo
papers.abstract: Purpose Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in organisations has concentrated on operational efficiency and automation. This study aims to reposition AI as both a constitutive element and a strategic object of foresight, a dual role the literature has noticed but not theorised. Design/methodology/approach A narrative literature review draws peer-reviewed work from foresight studies, socio-technical systems theory and organisational change into an integrated analytical framework. Selection prioritised conceptual contribution, transparency of reasoning and relevance to AI in strategic futures thinking. Findings AI strengthens environmental sensing, complex modelling and scenario work under uncertainty. The framework has four components: inputs, AI systems, human–AI interaction and outcomes, and yields five propositions for empirical testing. Research limitations/implications As a theoretical contribution, empirical validation remains a priority. Findings should be tested across sectors and organisational contexts before generalisation. Practical implications Organisations must cultivate digital foresight literacy, restructure around cross-functional foresight teams and implement agile governance capable of auditing AI-generated outputs. The framework provides guidance for navigating algorithmic bias, transparency obligations and power asymmetries. Originality/value This study makes four contributions. It reconceptualises AI as constitutive of organisational foresight instead of an instrument applied to it, introduces and differentiates anticipatory co-evolution as a novel construct, integrates Rohrbeck’s (2010) maturity model with Ivanov’s (2023) configuration taxonomy and sets out ethical governance requirements specific to AI-enabled foresight.

papers.title: Modulating stress and sleep through a multi-compound dietary supplement: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
papers.authors: Gianna F. Mastrofini, Riccardo F. Romersi, Maria G. Lombardi, Katelynn T. Persaud, Monica M. Ryan, Katie R. Hirsch, Amy L. Fraley, Jay J Dawes, Sten O. Stray-Gundersen, James W. Hardin, Shawn M. Arent
papers.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
papers.abstract: Background Stress and poor sleep are prevalent public health concerns that negatively impact well-being and daily functioning. Although adaptogens and sleep-focused supplements have separately demonstrated potential benefits, few studies have examined combined effects, particularly in healthy populations. Therefore, this study evaluated the impact of morning adaptogens, evening sleep-focused supplements, and their combination on stress, mood, and subjective and objective sleep quality.Methods Using a double-blind, placebo-controlled design, 103 healthy physically active adults (F = 53; age = 34.8 ± 9.6 yrs; BMI = 24.0 ± 2.7 kg/m2) were randomized to one of four treatment groups: 1) AMPM (n = 25): active morning (AM) and active evening (PM); 2) AM (n = 26): active AM and placebo PM; 3) PM (n = 25): placebo AM and active PM; and 4) PL (n = 27): placebo AM and placebo PM). The AM group contained 600 mg ashwagandha and 300 mg Rhodiola rosea (R. rosea). The PM group contained 2 g Magnesium L-threonate (MgT) (delivering 145 mg of magnesium), 200 mg L-theanine, and 50 mg apigenin. The total study duration was four weeks, consisting of one baseline week, two weeks of supplementation, and one washout week. Participants completed daily stress questionnaires and weekly questionnaires on perceived stress, affect, and subjective sleep (Patient-Reported Outcome Measurement Information System (PROMIS), and monthly subjective sleep (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline and post-washout. Objective sleep data were collected nightly using a wearable sleep monitoring device. Data were analyzed using baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models with alpha set at 0.05. Tukey-adjusted post hoc comparisons were performed, and effect sizes are reported as partial eta squared (η2) and Cohen's d (d).Results The AM group showed a decrease in weekly perceived stress (p = 0.034; η2 = 0.020), whereas there were no differences in daily stress (p < 0.05). For positive affect, there was a significant effect in the AM group at the end of the cessation period (p = 0.003; d = 1.68), which continued to increase, whereas the AMPM group showed a decrease (p = 0.009; d = 0.16). The AM group showed a decrease in subjective sleep-related impairments (p = 0.032, d = 2.74) and in objective wake after sleep onset (p = 0.047, η2 = 0.020). PSQI subjective sleep quality was significantly improved in the AM group compared with the AMPM group (mean difference = 0.66 AU, p < 0.001, d = 1.45).Conclusions Morning supplementation with adaptogens (ashwagandha and R. rosea) was associated with improvements in subjective stress, sleep quality, and positive affect following 14 days in healthy physically active adults as compared to the placebo product. Minimal effects on other outcomes may reflect limited benefits in healthy individuals over a short supplementation period. Future research should investigate longer interventions and populations with greater baseline stress and sleep disturbance.

papers.title: Crafting the future of drinks: a TAM and Jd-R perspective on bartenders’ AI adoption
papers.authors: Mohammad Alimohammadirokni, Nafas Emadlou
papers.journal: Journal of Human Resources in Hospitality & Tourism
papers.abstract: As AI transforms hospitality, its role in creative areas like bartending is underexplored. This study uses the Technology Acceptance Model and Job Demands-Resources theory to examine bartenders’ adoption of AI tools for drink creation. A survey of 384 U.S. bartenders analyzed the impact of ease of use, usefulness, job demands, and resources on AI attitudes, job strain, motivation, and turnover. Results from Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) indicate that both TAM variables significantly shape attitudes toward AI, while job demands increase strain and reduce retention. Although job resources reduce strain, they do not significantly enhance motivation. Additionally, positive AI attitudes and intrinsic motivation reduce turnover intentions, while job strain increases them. Findings extend theory and offer insights for encouraging AI adoption and staff retention.

papers.title: Does artificial intelligence impact employment in the medium-skilled labor force? Evidence from China’s National AI Innovation and Application Pilot Zones
papers.authors: Zhui Liu, Shengyue Wang
papers.journal: Journal of the Asia Pacific Economy
papers.abstract: Rapid artificial intelligence diffusion in China, shaped by government initiatives, is reshaping labor markets and raising questions about medium-skilled employment. Using a 2015–2023 panel of 287 Chinese prefecture-level cities, we examine how policy-induced artificial intelligence diffusion affects medium-skilled employment. Identification exploits the staggered establishment of China’s National AI Innovation and Application Pilot Zones as a quasi-natural experiment in a staggered difference-in-differences design. The estimated policy effect is negative and statistically significant for treated cities. This result remains robust across multiple robustness checks and estimators that accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects. Dynamic estimates show persistent but non-monotonic negative effects and significant differences across treatment cohorts. Following policy implementation, education expenditure and industrial upgrading increase, but neither coincides with improved medium-skilled employment over the same period. A stronger pre-policy industrial base is associated with a less negative policy effect, whereas greater pre-policy public attention to AI is associated with a more negative effect.

papers.title: Does CEO AI literacy curb ESG greenwashing? Evidence from China
papers.authors: Yanqiu Hu, Hongmin Chun, Jae Yeon Sim
papers.abstract: This study examines whether CEO AI literacy curbs or amplifies ESG greenwashing. Using 10,820 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2019 to 2022, we construct CEO AI literacy from resume-based evidence of AI-related education, work experience, and executive background. We find that CEO AI literacy significantly reduces ESG greenwashing, suggesting that technological cognition promotes substantive ESG practices rather than symbolic disclosure. This effect is stronger in high-tech industries, where digital infrastructure enables CEOs’ AI capabilities to translate more effectively into ESG monitoring and transparency. The findings remain robust to PSM and entropy balancing. This study contributes by identifying CEO-level AI literacy as a micro-foundation of ESG authenticity.

papers.title: Value Co-Creation Outcomes Under Multi-Level Drivers: Case Study of Agricultural E-Commerce Ecosystems
papers.authors: Yian Chen, Fu-Tien Hsu, Chun-Liang Chen, Yung-Chih Lien
papers.journal: Journal of Organizational Computing and Electronic Commerce
papers.abstract: The aims of this article were to explore value co-creation outcomes in agricultural e-commerce service ecosystems and to identify the domains of ecosystem actors and their roles. We adopted a multiple-case analysis approach, focusing on four small agribusinesses in Taiwan which can be considered low-resource actors. We found that outcomes of value co-creation include customer experience, ecosystem identity, delivery, profit-sharing, and increasing overall ecosystem momentum. We conceptualized these outcomes using a multi-level driving force framework, with focal firms serving as facilitators and governments acting as enablers to co-create value. Within this framework, there are two pathways to value co-creation: the market-driven path and the policy-guided path. The government plays the roles of trigger, supervisor, and inclusive development enhancer. Our findings contribute to the conceptualization of value co-creation in e-commerce service ecosystems, particularly for the context of low-resource actors.

papers.title: A review of open-vocabulary semantic mapping and navigation with foundation models for mobile robots
papers.authors: Yoshinobu Hagiwara, S. Hasegawa
papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots that coexist with humans must construct not only geometric maps but also semantic maps that can be accessed through natural language. Conventional semantic mapping has mainly focused on assigning labels from predefined closed vocabularies to metric maps, limiting its ability to handle novel objects, open-ended linguistic expressions, and flexible human-robot interaction. Recent advances in large-scale foundation models, particularly LLMs and VLMs, have accelerated research on open-vocabulary semantic mapping. In parallel, generative 3D representations such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting have enabled dense, continuous spatial representations associated with language-derived features. Together, these developments allow robots to acquire spatial semantic representations that connect perception, language, and action. This paper reviews this rapidly evolving field through a four-part taxonomy: (i) fusion of semantic features into 3D metric maps; (ii) object-centric open-vocabulary representations; (iii) hierarchical scene graph representations; and (iv) continuous generative 3D language fields. We also revisit the history of open-vocabulary semantic mapping and provide an overview of foundation model-based navigation using language-accessible maps, ranging from object-goal navigation to LLM-based hierarchical task planning. Finally, we introduce evaluation datasets, simulators, robot platforms, and evaluation metrics, and summarize seven open challenges.

papers.title: Trustworthy healthcare AI for wellbeing: how AI characteristics and information sensitivity shape privacy disclosure
papers.authors: Jungwon Kim, Yongjun Sung
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into healthcare, understanding how AI characteristics and data sensitivity influence users’ disclosure behaviour is critical for designing trustworthy and emotionally safe AI systems. This study investigates how two types of AI trust cues (i.e. technical vs. psychological securities) and the type of personal information requested (i.e. demographic vs. digital footprint) interact to shape perceived trust, disclosure intention, and actual disclosure behaviour in the course of AI interaction. We conducted a 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with 146 participants using a Wizard-of-Oz healthcare chatbot. Results showed a significant interaction effect on disclosure intention. Participants showed higher intention to disclose demographic information to psychologically secure AI, while technical security framing increased disclosure intention for digital footprint information. Trust significantly mediated these effects. Although AI characteristics did not affect the amount of disclosed data, psychological security led to significantly deeper, more emotionally intimate disclosures. These findings extend trust and privacy research by revealing that AI trust cues operate differently depending on information sensitivity. The interaction demonstrates that effective trust-building strategies must be tailored to the specific disclosure context.

papers.title: High-optimized crash severity prediction: a calibrated, leakage-aware ensemble stacking framework for deployment-ready decision making
papers.authors: Mona Saleh Alzahrani, Eslam Hamouda, Mayada Tarek, Ayman Mohamed Mostafa
papers.abstract: Abstract Predicting traffic crash severity is essential for emergency management, roadside infrastructure deployment and safety policy. The current machine learning (ML) approaches concentrate on accuracy, while overlooking the operational costs of false negatives (severe crash incidents missed) versus false positives (false alarms) and the associated higher societal cost of false negatives. In this paper, we propose a five-step enhancement process to advance a baseline, reproducible crash severity model into a calibrated, cost-sensitive, and operationally tested decision-making system. Our approach includes first: feature space locking for reproducibility and drift-free feature sets. Second: leakage-aware interaction mining using second-order multiplicative features and separation of training and testing dataset. Third: Bayesian hyper-parameter tuning with Optuna and stability selection using multiple seeds. Fourth: a leakage-aware ensemble stacking of four diverse base learners including Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), Histogram GB (HGB), and cost-sensitive Extra Trees (ET) using out-of-fold meta-learning. Fifth: The calibration metrics were computed on the validation partition using 5-fold out-of-fold cross-validation, so that no sample was used to both fit and evaluate its own calibrated probability. Pre-calibration ECE was 0.0637 (Brier score = 0.0742); following isotonic regression, post-calibration ECE decreased to 0.0004 (Brier score = 0.0648), both comfortably within the target of ECE < 0.03. The approach also introduces a feature-cost mapping framework, which segments the 37-feature space into six comprehensible clusters and explicitly links each cluster to cost-reduction strategies. The approach is validated on a large-scale crash database of 2,263,315 records, showing significant gains across all performance metrics, with a macro F1-score of 97.67% and an AUC-ROC of 99.85%. More importantly, the pipeline achieves a 42% reduction in false negatives for the severe class while reducing false positives for the non-severe class by 36%, resulting in an increase of 54,000 more correctly predicted crashes over the baseline. This study provides a robust, replicable, and actionable framework that bridges the gap between statistical performance of a model and operational constraints for real-time traffic safety systems and emergency dispatch systems.

papers.title: DHCBT: a digital human psychological counseling system with a CBT multi-agent framework
papers.authors: Litun Tan, Zongze Li, Yitian Huang, Jun Liu, Mao Ni, Shaoying Wang, Junlin Che, Keliang Chen
papers.abstract: Academic stress is a major risk factor for mental health problems among college students. Existing online counseling systems often face three limitations: limited user trust in virtual interactions, insufficient adaptation to academic-stress scenarios, and inconsistent professional quality in single-agent counseling. To address these issues, we developed DHCBT, a digital human counseling system based on a hierarchical CBT multi-agent framework. Coordinated by a meta-agent and specialized expert agents, the framework structures counseling into two stages: establishment of an initial intervention framework and execution of the CBT core process. We evaluated the framework through benchmark testing on CBT-BENCH Level II, response-quality assessment on academic-stress counseling cases, and a controlled user study comparing DHCBT with a text-based chatbot. In benchmark testing, the framework showed strong performance on cognitive distortion and core-belief understanding tasks. In counseling-response evaluation, it outperformed baseline models in safety, adherence to CBT process, problem comprehension, and empathy. In the user study, DHCBT was associated with lower cognitive load and higher social presence, usability, and intention to continue use than the text-based control. These findings provide preliminary evidence that combining a digital human counseling interface with a CBT multi-agent framework is feasible for supporting college students with mild-to-moderate academic stress.

papers.title: Brains on copy-paste mode? A mixed-methods study on the relationship between generative artificial intelligence use and students’ critical thinking skills
papers.authors: Héctor Galindo‐Domínguez, Lucía Campo, Nahia Delgado, María Victoria Urruzola
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools, such as ChatGPT, into higher education has raised important questions about their relationship with students' critical thinking (CT) skills. This study explored these associations among 398 undergraduate students using a mixed-methods design. Quantitatively, participants completed validated measures of critical thinking and a survey assessing frequency of AI use in academic contexts. Correlation analyses indicated a significant negative association between AI use and Analyzing/Organizing skills. Moderation analyses revealed that academic achievement moderated this relationship for Analyzing/Organizing and Evaluating, with higher achievers showing a stronger negative association. No significant effects emerged for gender and age on the remaining CT dimensions. Likewise, qualitative analyses of 200 open-ended responses identified three user profiles: (1) instrumental/uncritical, comprising younger low-achieving male students emphasizing AI speed and utility while reporting reduced verification effort; (2) stable/complementary, comprising older high-achieving students perceiving little change in their evaluative practices; and (3) ambivalent/skeptical-trusting, comprising women with medium achievement, divided between increased skepticism and greater reliance on AI outputs. Supplementary analyses linking Analyzing/Organizing and Evaluating scores to these profiles showed that lower development of both skills consistently aligned with the instrumental/uncritical profile. The interpretive consistency between both analytical strands suggests that the relationship between generative AI use and CT skills is nuanced and profile-dependent, limited in scope to specific dimensions and student groups rather than reflecting a broad negative impact, while highlighting the risks of uncritical reliance and the potential of AI as a complementary academic tool when used reflectively.

papers.title: A pragmatic approach to a computational model of human intention applied to human-robot interaction
papers.authors: J. E. Domínguez-Vidal

papers.title: AI vs. human authorship in paintings: Differential impacts on consumers' perceived value
papers.authors: Dan Zhang, Peiyao Chen, Yixuan Wu, Xiaolin Li, Yutong Wang
papers.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) art generators has introduced algorithmically created paintings into mainstream consumer markets, yet consumers consistently assign lower value to AI-generated works than to human-created equivalents. This paper proposes perceived creative authenticity---consumers' subjective perception that an artwork reflects a genuine creative process characterized by human-centered values of originality, craftsmanship, and uniqueness---as a theoretically distinct mechanism explaining this value differential. Conceptually differentiated from perceived creativity, which concerns the novelty of the artistic output, perceived creative authenticity addresses the genuineness of the creator-work relationship. Drawing on authenticity theory and Psychological Ownership Theory, we develop a moderated mediation framework hypothesizing that (H1) human authorship elicits higher perceived value than AI authorship, (H2) perceived creative authenticity mediates this effect, while the indirect effects through perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs are not significant, establishing perceived creative authenticity as the primary explanatory mechanism within the tested model, and (H3) non-fungible token (NFT) authentication attenuates the mediated pathway by providing verifiable creative provenance. Across five studies, results support this framework: Study 1 conceptually replicates the human-AI value gap among Chinese consumers; Studies 2a—2c demonstrate the mediating role of perceived creative authenticity: Study 2a establishes the basic mediation pathway; Study 2b shows through parallel mediation that perceived creative authenticity uniquely mediates the effect while perceived creativity, perceived effort, and anthropocentric creativity beliefs do not exhibit significant indirect effects; and Study 2c provides causal evidence through a moderation-of-process design; and Study 3 shows that NFT authentication narrows the authenticity gap between human and AI art. These findings advance the literature on human-computer interaction by identifying process-based authenticity judgments as a key psychological mechanism shaping consumer responses to algorithmic creative products, with implications for artists and platforms navigating digital art markets.

papers.title: The circular economy, explained by AI
papers.authors: Piero Morseletto, Nancy M. P. Bocken
papers.abstract: Abstract Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the circular economy (CE) has largely examined how AI can improve circular operations. Much less attention has been paid to AI tools widely used to understand and reason about the CE, particularly large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT. Researchers, practitioners, students, and decision-makers use these tools to seek explanations and support reasoning about circularity. This paper examines what is at stake when LLM-generated accounts enter CE inquiry. As a conceptual contribution, it develops a framework for analysing how AI-supported CE knowledge is formed, how it may influence action, and what ethical implications follow. The Content dimension concerns the construction and credibility of CE knowledge, focusing on pattern-based generation, opaque and heterogeneous sources, and fragmentation within CE scholarship. The Transformative dimension considers how such knowledge may influence innovation and entrepreneurship, including whether familiar, optimisation-oriented approaches overshadow systemic alternatives. The Moral dimension addresses the risks of relying on LLM outputs, including operational indifference to truth, AI assertiveness, the absence of moral agency, and the need for human judgement and accountability. The paper argues that LLMs can widen access to CE knowledge and support inquiry, but cannot independently determine which interpretations are better supported, exercise the judgement required to challenge linear assumptions, or decide how environmental, social, and economic values should be balanced. It identifies governance priorities concerning transparency, expert scrutiny, human agency, and epistemic humility. The framework can also guide future empirical research on how LLM-generated accounts vary across models, prompts, languages, and user contexts.

papers.title: Pre-service teachers’ interactions with generative AI for creating culturally grounded visual teaching resources
papers.authors: Macharious Nabang, Harry Barton Essel, Akosua Tachie-Menson, Prosper Setsoafia, Charles Atta Koduah, Julliet Appiah-Kubi, Edmund Boamah Acheampong, George Attah Aboagye, Matthew Nyaaba
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for developing instructional resources, but evidence remains limited on how technological confidence, cultural responsiveness and system experience relate to the quality and instructional use of AI-generated visuals in teacher education in sub-Saharan Africa. This study examined these relationships among 201 final-year pre-service teachers at Bagabaga College of Education, Ghana, after they had gained practical experience with the Culturally Responsive Visual Aid Generator (CReVAG) during teaching practicum. A post-exposure cross-sectional explanatory survey assessed Self-Efficacy, Culturally Responsive Teaching Self-Efficacy, Perceived System Usability, AI Tool Acceptance, Visual Resource Quality and Lesson Delivery Effectiveness. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was complemented with Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) and robust subgroup comparisons. The model explained 39.9% of the variance in AI Tool Acceptance, 39.3% in Visual Resource Quality and 61.6% in Lesson Delivery Effectiveness, with an SRMR of 0.077. The largest structural associations were between System Usability and AI Tool Acceptance (β = 0.330, p = .004, 95% CI [0.118, 0.564]) and between Visual Resource Quality and Lesson Delivery Effectiveness (β = 0.309, p < .001, 95% CI [0.151, 0.478]). NCA identified Visual Resource Quality as the strongest statistical necessity condition for high Lesson Delivery Effectiveness (d = 0.190, p = .002), followed by AI Tool Acceptance (d = 0.158, p = .0015). Programme differences were most defensible for System Usability and Lesson Delivery Effectiveness, while gender differences were generally small, although males reported higher AI Tool Acceptance (d = 0.40, p = .006). The findings suggest that meaningful GenAI-supported instructional design involves more than favourable technology appraisal; it also requires usable systems, culturally informed teacher judgement and careful evaluation of generated visual resources. Because the constructs were measured once after exposure to CReVAG, the findings represent explanatory associations rather than causal effects.

papers.title: A human-centred artificial intelligence and learning analytics framework for equitable personalised higher education enrolment
papers.authors: Abdullah Feraih Alenezi
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are increasingly deployed within higher education to support admissions decision-making, student success initiatives, and personalised learning. However, most AI-enabled admissions systems remain narrowly focused on efficiency, prediction, and institutional optimisation, with limited attention to learner agency, educational equity, transparency, and human-centred support. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than merely a selection or gatekeeping process. The study adopts a conceptual and integrative literature review approach, synthesising scholarship from human-centred artificial intelligence, learning analytics, personalised learning, educational equity, explainable AI, generative AI, responsible AI governance, learner agency theory, and value-sensitive design. To strengthen transparency during revision, the integrative synthesis was supplemented by a targeted ERIC search and bibliographic verification using publisher and authoritative policy repositories. Drawing upon these interdisciplinary perspectives, the paper develops the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF), a governance-oriented model for ethical and transparent AI adoption in higher education admissions and enrolment management. The framework comprises five interconnected dimensions: learner profiling and contextual understanding; explainable AI decision support; equity and inclusion auditing; human oversight and shared decision-making; and personalised transition and success support. Together, these dimensions provide a governance architecture for evaluating how admissions might be connected to personalised educational pathways while making explicit the trade-offs among equity, privacy, explainability, accuracy, human oversight, and learner agency. The framework identifies governance mechanisms required to address algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, accountability, and learner autonomy. A five-stage Human-Centred AI Ecosystem extending governance across the full student lifecycle — from admissions through to graduate development — provides a further organising contribution. The study advances existing literature by integrating admissions analytics, learning analytics, personalised learning, learner agency, and responsible AI governance within a unified framework. Unlike conventional admissions models that prioritise institutional efficiency, HCPAF positions admissions as the foundation of a personalised learning ecosystem and conceptualises trust as a relational, calibrated, and empirically contingent construct connecting transparency, fairness, learner agency, and AI adoption. The framework contributes to emerging debates concerning ethical and human-centred AI in education and identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4, 10, and 16, while emphasising that any contribution to those goals requires empirical validation. Introduces the Human-Centred Personalised Admissions Framework (HCPAF) for equitable and personalised higher education enrolment. Repositions admissions as the beginning of a personalised learning journey rather than a terminal selection mechanism. Integrates human-centred AI, learning analytics, educational equity, explainable AI, learner agency, and responsible governance. Introduces trust as a central mediating construct linking transparency, fairness, and AI adoption in education. Provides a governance roadmap for ethical, transparent, and accountable AI adoption across the student lifecycle. Identifies normative alignments with Sustainable Development Goals 4 (Quality Education), 10 (Reduced Inequalities), and 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), subject to empirical validation. Establishes a multi-dimensional research agenda for human-centred AI in higher education.

papers.title: An integrated scientometric and BERTopic-based analysis on examining the role of artificial intelligence in achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
papers.authors: Reetu Verma, Ashok Kumar, Kavita Pabreja, Saurabh Kumar
papers.abstract: This study investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through a comprehensive scientometric analysis. It explores the evolution of scholarly research, identifies leading contributors, maps thematic trends, examines how AI technologies contribute to advancing sustainability across multiple domains, and identifies latent semantic themes. A total of 3262 unique scholarly records published between 1989 and 2025, after deduplication and screening, were finalized from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The dataset was analysed using Biblioshiny (R-based Bibliometrix) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, citation impact, collaborative networks, thematic evolution, and conceptual structures. Indicators such as Relative Growth Rate (RGR), Doubling Time (DT), h-index, g-index, and Lotka’s Law were applied to evaluate research productivity and scholarly influence. In addition, BERTopic-based abstract-level topic modelling was applied to identify latent semantic themes, SDG-linked thematic domains, temporal evolution and potential research gaps. Results reveal a significant growth in AI-SDG research, particularly after 2015, with an accelerated increase post-2020. India, USA, and China emerged as the most productive contributors, while countries like USA, India, United Kingdom and Australia lead in research impact and citation quality. Thematic evolution analysis reveals a transition from foundational themes such as AI, machine learning, climate change, and decision support systems toward more integrated and sustainability-oriented research themes, including sustainable development and SDGs. Thematic linkages further demonstrate the persistent foundational role of AI and machine learning, alongside the growing centrality of climate change and sustainable development, reflecting the increasing convergence of AI research with global sustainability priorities. BERTopic analysis further revealed eleven interpretable abstract-level thematic domains after excluding one heterogeneous outlier category. The dominant themes included digital transformation and green innovation, AI-enabled education, digital health, smart agriculture, renewable energy systems, clean water and sanitation, remote sensing, NLP-based decision support, sustainable construction, tourism, and sustainable chemistry/pharmaceutical applications. This study maps the AI–SDG research landscape by integrating bibliometric indicators with thematic evolution, conceptual analysis, and abstract-level semantic topic modelling. The findings provide insights into the development and thematic orientation of AI-related research in the context of sustainable development. The use of BERTopic complements conventional bibliometric approaches by examining semantic patterns within publication abstracts alongside keyword and citation-based analyses.
