The research was conducted at SDN Cijengkol 02, Bekasi Regency, involving fourth-grade students. Data were collected through observation, interviews, expert validation questionnaires, teacher and student response questionnaires, and problem-solving tests administered as pretests and posttests. The results showed that the media obtained feasibility scores of 95% from the material expert, 95% from the media expert, and 97.5% from the language expert, categorized as highly feasible. Teacher responses reached 100%, while student responses in the large-scale trial reached 92.88%, both categorized as highly practical. The average N-Gain score was 0.61 in the experimental class and 0.17 in the control class. The Mann-Whitney test showed a significance value of <0.001, indicating a significant difference between the two groups. Therefore, the AI-based Digital Spinning Wheel is feasible, practical, and effective for improving students’ problem-solving skills in IPAS learning

papers.title: The influence of AI-powered investment recommendations on individual investors: A mixed-methods study from the perspective of persuasive communication
papers.authors: Gül Dilek Türk
papers.abstract: This study examines how individual retail investors receive AI-generated investment advice from the perspective of persuasive communication. Arguing that large language models (LLMs) create a persuasion dynamic different from that of traditional media, it combines in-depth interviews with a content analysis of AI outputs in a mixed-methods design. Interviews with 18 investors who use AI for investment decisions were analyzed through Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, and the responses of four models to six standardized scenarios were coded with the AI Investment Advice Evaluation Scale (AIIAES), a researcher-developed instrument of eight dimensions and 24 items. The findings show how framing, the machine heuristic and sycophancy shape user decisions, and they indicate that financial literacy differentiates responses without protecting users evenly. No model produced a complete disclaimer in any scenario, and Gemini displayed a scenario-dependent sycophancy pattern. On the theoretical side, the study describes a deliberate form of user-induced sycophancy, in which users steer a model over repeated interactions toward confirming their own preferences. On the methodological side, it offers an instrument that turns the suitability and disclosure standards of investment regulation into criteria for conversational AI outputs. The study concludes with policy recommendations for user protection.

papers.title: Early Evidence on Employer Responses to College Student Use of Generative AI
papers.authors: Casey Boyd-Swan, C. Lockwood Reynolds

papers.title: The Benefits of ChatGPT in Supporting Students’ Thesis Writing: A Qualitative Case Study
papers.authors: Santi Safitri, Mukhlash Abrar, Tubagus Zam Zam Al Arif
papers.journal: IDEAS Journal on English Language Teaching and Learning Linguistics and Literature
papers.abstract: This study explores the perceived benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT in supporting students during the thesis writing process. Using a qualitative case study design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews with three master’s students who used ChatGPT in writing their theses. Five themes emerged: supporting research idea and topic development, organizing thesis structure and content, supporting literature exploration and conceptual understanding, supporting academic language and writing development, and supporting revision and writing efficiency. Participants perceived ChatGPT as helping them generate research ideas, organize their thesis structure, understand theory and methodology, revise drafts, overcome ideation barriers, and improve their academic writing and writing efficiency. However, participants also reported challenges, including the need to verify AI-generated references and citation information, repetitive responses, and language output that sounded overly complex or machine-generated. The study concludes that, based on these participants’ experiences, ChatGPT can serve as a valuable academic writing support tool when used critically and responsibly in higher education contexts.

papers.title: Beyond Digital Government: Examining Indonesia's Readiness for Artificial Intelligence-Driven Public Sector Transformation
papers.authors: Danang Kurniawan, Sunituti, Agustiyara, Nurul Hidayati, Somnuek Worawiset
papers.abstract: This study aims to analyze Indonesia's level of institutional readiness to support public-sector transformation through Artificial Intelligence (AI) using the Government AI Readiness Index. This study uses a descriptive quantitative approach, analyzing secondary data on the Index for Indonesia AI publication trends in the public sector, the global Government AI Readiness Index, and the Government AI Readiness Index for Indonesia for the 2021–2025 period. The results show that research on AI in the public sector has increased significantly in recent years, peaking at 195 publications in 2025. The United States, the United Kingdom, and China dominate the field, reflecting strong global interest in AI-driven government transformation. Globally, countries are assessed based on their Government AI Readiness scores. Higher scores indicate a stronger capacity in policy, governance, digital infrastructure, and AI adoption, providing a foundation for AI implementation in the public sector. Government AI Readiness: Indonesia's score increased from 58.14 in 2021 to 65.85 in 2024, then declined to 59.87 in 2025, indicating that the improvement in AI readiness has not been sustained. Indonesia performed relatively well on the AI dimension. Policy Capacity (77.00) and public sector adoption(73,77), but still weak at development and diffusion (44.09) and resilience (58.27). At the indicator level, Indonesia's strengths lie in e-government delivery, data quality, and policy vision, whereas compute capacity, AI sector maturity, and human capital become the main challenges.

papers.title: Event-Aware Predictive Route Recommendation Using Random Forest and A* Search
papers.authors: S Sandhiya
papers.journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
papers.abstract: Urban traffic conditions can change considerably during peak hours and around public events. Conventional route selection generally reacts to the traffic condition observed at the time of travel, whereas a predictive approach can estimate likely travel duration before a journey begins. This paper presents a student-level prototype for event-aware route recommendation that combines supervised learning with graph-based path search. A Random Forest regression model is used to estimate travel duration from route origin, destination, distance, travel hour, and an event indicator. The predicted duration is then used as the cost of road segments in an A* search procedure. A small urban road graph representing selected locations is used for demonstration. The implementation consists of a Python-based machine-learning module, a Flask backend, and a React user interface. The project report records an R? value of 0.9687 for the main modeling experiment, while a separately generated event-focused dataset produced an R? value of 0.9291. These results indicate that the prototype can learn useful relationships in the prepared dataset and can translate predicted travel time into route-selection decisions. The work is intentionally presented as an academic prototype rather than a live city-scale navigation system; real-time traffic feeds, geographical coordinates, larger datasets, and extensive field validation remain future work.

papers.title: Russian youth policy in the field of digitalization: current trends
papers.authors: L. V. Korobitsyna
papers.journal: Professional education in the modern world
papers.abstract: Introduction . Digitalization and modern media are an integral part of the daily lives of young people and their natural environment for communication, self-expression, and personalized consumption. Therefore, the issue of state youth policy in the field of digitalization is extremely relevant, affecting both the training of young highly qualified personnel and the transformation of the education system. Purpose setting . The article aims to analyze the mechanisms for integrating state youth policy and informatization in the context of the formation of a «digitally mature» society. To achieve this goal, the following tasks are addressed: analysis of the regulatory framework; identification of specific forms and methods of interaction with young people within the framework of national and federal projects; analysis of the integration of digital achievements into the education and upbringing system. Methodology and methods of the study . The author of the article relies on a systemic-institutional approach and uses such methods as legal analysis, content analysis, systems analysis, secondary analysis of statistical data, monitoring of internet communications, as well as the case study method. Results . A comprehensive regulatory framework has been identified, including the «Strategy for the Development of the Information Society in the Russian Federation for 2017–2030,» as well as the national projects «Youth and Children» and «Data Economy and Digital Transformation of the State.» This framework represents an interconnected system in which technological infrastructure enters into a symbiotic relationship with educational practices. At the same time, risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence and neural networks in the educational process have been identified, requiring administrative decisions. Conclusion . Russian youth policy in the field of information technology is creating a successful technological infrastructure for developing digital competencies and patriotic education, and it also facilitates the career advancement of young people, ensuring the achievement of «digital maturity» of society and technological sovereignty. However, the widespread implementation of artificial intelligence and neural networks requires the development of systemic legal and regulatory frameworks that would prevent intellectual passivity and the diminished cognitive capabilities of young people.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in foreign language teaching: cultural alienation as a pedagogical problem of the semi‑periphery
papers.authors: Н. ХИШИГДУЛАМ
papers.journal: Professional education in the modern world
papers.abstract: The article examines cultural alienation arising from the use of AI tools in foreign language teaching in a semi-peripheral educational context, drawing on data from the Mongolian National University of Education. The study is motivated by the rapid spread of Anglo-centric language models (ChatGPT, DeepL, Grammarly) in academic settings where no local AI alternatives exist. The theoretical framework synthesizes the global language system concept (A. de Swaan), world-systems analysis (Wallerstein), hybrid identity theory (Bhabha, Hall), postcolonial EFL pedagogy (Canagarajah, Pennycook), and a socio-axiological approach to language education. This article is conceptual-theoretical in nature; empirical data collected through student surveys (n = 82) and qualitative interviews (n = 6) serve an illustrative function and do not claim to verify theoretical propositions in a strict sense. Cultural alienation is differentiated into two structural subtypes: content distortion, whereby AI substitutes culturally specific concepts with neutral equivalents, and rhetorical normalization, whereby Western discursive conventions are imposed at the level of text style and structure. Sub-scale data show that 78.1 % of students noticed content distortion and approximately 80 % experienced rhetorical normalization. Three differentiated pedagogical strategies are proposed in response: cultural anchoring, targeting content distortion; critical analysis of AI suggestions, addressing rhetorical normalization; and reflective writing as a comprehensive tool for developing conscious AI use. Findings are most directly transferable to post-Soviet and Central Asian semi-peripheral educational systems; their extension to other semi-peripheral contexts requires dedicated comparative research.

papers.title: Cognitive base of personal educational
papers.authors: N. E. Gorbacheva, A. N. Dakhin
papers.journal: Professional education in the modern world
papers.abstract: Introduction . This article examines the cognitive foundations of personalized learning based on networked information blocks (chunks). The authors develop the classical pedagogical model of N. V. Kuzmina, adapting it to the modern conditions of digitalization in education. The proposed personalized learning system includes five interrelated components: gnostic, design, constructive, organizational, and communicative. Purpose setting . The study aims to address the mismatch between traditional linear formats of presenting educational materials and the individual cognitive characteristics of learners, as well as to explore new approaches to organizing the educational process in the digital age. The research task is decomposed as follows: 1. Theoretical justification and design of a personalized learning model by modernizing the classical five-component functional model of N. V. Kuzmina, incorporating advances in cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence technologies. 2. Development of a structure for information blocks (chunks) as fundamental units of educational content with properties of self-sufficiency, compactness, connectivity with other blocks, and measurability of mastery. 3. Design and implementation of personalization algorithms for educational trajectories based on collaborative and content-based filtering, hybrid approaches, deep learning methods, and reinforcement learning. 4. Development and testing of a digital Assistant based on large language models to implement autodidactic principles in personalized learning. 5. Experimental validation of the developed system’s effectiveness in the process of professional development for educators in the field of digital competencies. The widespread integration of information and telecommunication technologies in education and the evolving demands of the labor market necessitate changes not only in the content but also in the educational process itself for all categories of learners. Therefore, it is essential to consider new cognitive opportunities for personalized learning based on networked information blocks, which can ensure effective learner-centered education for both students and participants in additional education programs. Methodology and methods of the study. The methodological foundation of the study is a functional five-component model adapted by the authors to the modern conditions of digitalization in education. The research employs an interdisciplinary approach, integrating cognitive psychology, educational design principles, and neural network theory. The theoretical basis includes: G. A. Miller’s research on short-term memory («Miller’s Wallet»), H. A. Simon’s studies on «chunking» as a mechanism for developing expert competence, J. Sweller’s cognitive load theory, and R. Mayer’s multimedia learning theory. The research methodology includes designing a personalized learning system based on networked information blocks (chunks). Results . This study has developed and implemented a «digital Assistant» for autodidactic learning based on large language models. An experimental pilot program for professional development was conducted with the participation of 100 educators. The development of key digital competencies was monitored through a system of regular assessment activities. A statistical analysis of the effectiveness of the proposed personalization algorithms for educational trajectories was presented. As part of the study, diagnostic tools were modified to assess educators’ digital competencies, identify professional deficiencies, and determine individual educational needs. The results of the pilot program were evaluated using a vector-based assessment model that considers navigation patterns in educational content, the semantic density of material comprehension, and the temporal dynamics of learning. Conclusion . The proposed personalized learning system based on networked information blocks (chunks) effectively enhances the classical pedagogical model by adapting it to the digital education environment. Structuring educational materials as a network of interconnected chunks aligns with the psychological characteristics of cognitive processes. Developed personalization algorithms include collaborative and content-based filtering, hybrid approaches, deep learning, and reinforcement learning methods. The integration of a digital Assistant based on large language models facilitates the implementation of M. Montessori’s autodidactic principles in a modern digital format, enabling learners to construct their own educational trajectories. Experimental validation of the professional development model for educators confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed system. The proposed vector-based assessment model considers navigation patterns, semantic density, and temporal dynamics of learning.

papers.title: Ethical boundaries of artificial Intelligence in military education: developing cybersubjectivity as a psychological and pedagogical task
papers.authors: A. V. Saburov
papers.journal: Professional education in the modern world
papers.abstract: Introduction . The digital transformation of military education actualizes the problem of ethical use of artificial intelligence (AI), which cannot be solved within the framework of traditional restrictive approaches based on external control and limitations. Purpose setting. The research aims to develop the concept of cybersubjectivity as a psychological and pedagogical alternative to external regulation and to identify practical ways of its formation in the educational environment of a military university. Methodology and methods of the study. The methodological basis was the subjective approach and the concept of psychological safety; methods of theoretical modeling, conceptual analysis and structural-functional design were used. Results . A structural-dynamic model of cybersubjectivity has been developed and presented as an integrative personality quality, including critical-reflexive, value-semantic, regulatory-volitional and constructive-activity components that ensure conscious and responsible interaction with AI. Conclusion . The necessity of transitioning from a control paradigm to a development pedagogy is substantiated, where the purposeful formation of cybersubjectivity becomes a key condition for the ethical use of technologies in military education. Practical guidelines 9for integrating the model into the educational process are defined.

papers.title: A study of students’ reflective strategies when using generative artificial intelligence in project‑based activities
papers.authors: M. M. Zaitseva, T. N. Rogovenko
papers.journal: Professional education in the modern world
papers.abstract: Introduction . Higher education is being transformed under the influence of the widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), which creates risks of reduced criticality and reflective skills among students. In contrast to previous studies focusing on workload and implementation algorithms, this research focuses on students’ reflective strategies. Purpose setting . The aim is an in-depth analysis of students’ reflective practices when using GenAI in project-based activities, including self-assessment of responsibility, editing strategies, and differentiated content quality evaluation. Methodology and methods of the study . The study is based on a mixed post-experience methodology using an adapted NASA-TLX questionnaire and an author-designed survey. The sample consists of 64 students who completed a business «packaging» project using GenAI. Results . A gap was identified between declared responsibility (92 %) and the actual depth of content revision (32 % make less than 30 % changes). The main reason for editing (75 %) was the AI’s inability to account for specific contextual nuances. Only 25 % of students use metacognitive strategies. Conclusion . The pedagogical task is to organize a learning environment where GenAI enhances learning but does not replace students’ reflective and critical thinking.

papers.title: Advertising in the Age of Inflation and Artificial Intelligence: Examining Cost Efficiency, Consumer Perception and Advertising Effectiveness
papers.authors: Sandip Deore, Kamal Srivastava, Manisha Sanchihar, Mahendra Potdar, Ashish Sheje
papers.abstract: The global advertising system is increasingly shaped by two concurrent pressures: persistent inflation and the rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into advertising production and media management. This study examines the trade-offs between advertising cost efficiency, consumer perceptions, and downstream communication effectiveness using Transaction Cost Economics, the Persuasion Knowledge Model, Signaling Theory, and Mental Accounting Theory. Study 1 applies panel econometric modeling to data from 184 advertising agencies and marketing enterprises to assess production and media-placement efficiency across different Consumer Price Index (CPI) regimes. Study 2 employs a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment (N = 512) comparing Human-Created and Disclosed GenAI advertisements under neutral and high-inflation salience conditions. Study 1 shows that GenAI adoption reduces production costs by 44.6%, although higher inflation weakens the acquisition-efficiency benefits of predictive advertising. Study 2 shows that AI disclosure increases perceived manipulative intent and reduces perceived authenticity, particularly when inflation salience is high, with adverse effects on brand trust and purchase intention. Overall, the findings provide an AI-enabled managerial decision-support perspective for balancing production efficiency, acquisition performance, and consumer trust when making advertising resource-allocation and human–AI deployment decisions.

papers.title: ПРО ДЕЯКІ МЕТОДОЛОГІЧНІ ОСОБЛИВОСТІ ВИКЛАДАННЯ МАТЕМАТИЧНИХ ДИСЦИПЛІН МАЙБУТНІМ ФАХІВЦЯМ З ІНФОРМАЦІЙНИХ ТЕХНОЛОГІЙ
papers.authors: Tetiana Anatoliivna Oleshko, Олена Вальтерівна Карупу, Валерія Пахненко
papers.journal: Problems of a systemic approach to the economy enterprises (National Aviation University, Ukraine, Kyiv)
papers.abstract: The article explores the transformation of approaches to teaching higher mathematics for students of IT specialties. Based on empirical data from a survey of students of the educational program «Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence», key cognitive and motivational factors influencing the quality of learning have been identified.

papers.title: ІНТЕГРАЦІЯ ШТУЧНОГО ІНТЕЛЕКТУ У ВИКЛАДАННЯ АНГЛІЙСЬКОЇ МОВИ
papers.authors: Olena Kononova
papers.journal: Problems of a systemic approach to the economy enterprises (National Aviation University, Ukraine, Kyiv)
papers.abstract: The article explores the possibilities of using artificial intelligence in teaching English in higher education. It outlines the role of AI in personalizing learning, differentiating educational content, and increasing learners’ motivation.

papers.title: ПОЗАШКІЛЬНЕ ОСВІТНЄ СЕРЕДОВИЩЕ ЯК ДЕТЕРМІНАНТА УСПІШНОЇ ПРОФЕСІЙНОЇ САМОДЕТЕРМІНАЦІЇ ТА АКСЕЛЕРАЦІЇ ОБДАРОВАНОСТІ
papers.authors: Анна Гончарова-Тисляцька
papers.journal: Problems of a systemic approach to the economy enterprises (National Aviation University, Ukraine, Kyiv)
papers.abstract: The article examines extracurricular education as an innovative educational environment that acts as a factor in the acceleration of giftedness and the formation of young people’s professional self-determination in the context of global technological transformations. The expediency of implementing a life-creation approach is substantiated, within which the learner is positioned as an active subject in designing their own educational and professional trajectory. The results of an empirical study conducted on the basis of an extracurricular educational institution are presented, including psychodiagnostic identification of giftedness and the implementation of an innovative STEAM case using artificial intelligence tools.

papers.title: Social Acceptability and Continuance Intention Toward AI-Augmented Reality in Higher Education: The Roles of Trust, Privacy Concerns, Perceived Usefulness, and AI Literacy)
papers.authors: Ahmed Mahmoud Fakhry
papers.journal: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
papers.abstract: AI-augmented reality (AI-AR) combines real-world overlays with intelligent adaptation, interaction, and content generation. Its educational value therefore depends on more than technical performance: students must regard its use as legitimate, beneficial, safe, and compatible with academic norms. This conceptual paper develops an integrated model of social acceptability and continuance intention toward AI-AR in higher education. The model combines technology-acceptance logic with trust-risk reasoning and AI-literacy perspectives. It proposes that perceived usefulness increases both social acceptability and continuance intention; trust operates as a central affective and relational mechanism; privacy concerns reduce acceptability and continuance, partly by weakening trust; and AI literacy functions as a competence-based antecedent that strengthens usefulness perceptions and enables calibrated trust. The model distinguishes initial acceptance from post-adoption continuance and treats social acceptability as a bridge between individual evaluation and the perceived legitimacy of AI-AR within the university community. Existing augmented-reality studies support the importance of usefulness and attitude for continued use, while recent AI-in-education studies show that literacy, trust, privacy, and perceived usefulness are interdependent rather than isolated predictors. The paper offers testable propositions, measurement guidance, and design implications. No original survey or experimental dataset was supplied; consequently, the paper does not report empirical Methods or Results and should be treated as a literature-grounded conceptual manuscript pending validation.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Developmental Assessment in Early Childhood Education: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Rui Zhang
papers.abstract: This scoping review aims to map the research landscape of artificial intelligence–enabled developmental assessment in early childhood education. It will examine the developmental domains assessed, AI technologies and data sources used, assessment contexts, validation evidence, and the role of educators in AI-supported assessment. It will also identify research gaps and implications for educational practice. The review will be reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Literature searching and screening have been completed and extraction is under way; the registration transparently documents the stage reached and the methods established at the time of registration.

papers.title: Learning in the Wild: GenAI as a Dialogic OER – open materials
papers.authors: Eyal Rabin
papers.abstract: Analysis plan, codebooks, AI-coder instructions, scripts, coded data (with each coder's stated reasons), raw coder outputs and results for a coding study of 3,000 English-language WildChat conversations. All coding was done by two large language models; no human coded the data. Conversation text is not included; it is available from the WildChat corpus (ODC-BY).

papers.title: O custo ambiental da inteligência artificial generativa (IAGen): aplicação de uma sequência didática em Física para estudantes do Ensino Médio
papers.authors: Andréia Ramos Comin, Heydrian Freitas Ferreira, Marcelo Franco Leão
papers.abstract: This article analyzes the results of applying a Didactic Sequence (DS), grounded in the Science, Technology, Society, and Environment (STSE) approach, with first-year high school students in Physics classes. The topic focused on the environmental cost of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), seeking to demystify its apparent immateriality and relate resource consumption to the concepts of energy and power. The objective was to analyze how the implementation of the DS raised students’ awareness of the socio-environmental impacts of GenAI. The qualitative and applied research involved 17 students and used a diagnostic questionnaire, written records, group productions, and discussions. The results indicated that, initially, AI was understood mainly through its practical functionality. Throughout the intervention, students identified water and energy consumption and distinguished the energy cost of simple and complex tasks. It was concluded that the articulation between the DS and the STSE approach fostered awareness of the relationships between technology and the environment and a critical analysis of GenAI implications.

papers.title: Recommendations for the Development and Implementation of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools in Pediatric Clinical Care: Policy Statement
papers.authors: Srinivasan Suresh, Ryan Brandon Hunter, Barbara Periard, Juan Espinoza, Eli M. Lourie, Srinivasan Suresh, Juan D. Chaparro, Kathryn Cheek, Kevin R. Dufendach, Rachel L. Goldstein, Marvin B. Harper, Lauren M. Hess, Christina Jung, Brandan P. Kennedy, Naveed Rabbani, Sonja S. Short, Lindsay A. Stevens, Melissa S. Van Cain, Section on Innovation in Therapeutics and Technology, Amy Molten, Alyssa M. Abo, Gwenyth Anne Fischer, Janene H. Fuerch, Karen M. Kaplan, Vasum Peiris
papers.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into pediatric health care offers exciting opportunities alongside critical challenges. GenAI tools, like large language models (LLMs), show promise in several health care applications, including but not limited to clinical decision support, documentation, and medical education across a wide range of pediatric subspecialties. However, real-world validation remains limited, and concerns persist around accuracy, bias, reliability, sustainability, and durability. Studies indicate that LLMs, when applied to pediatrics, often underperform compared with adult medical specialties, raising questions about their readiness for use in the care of children and adolescents. Moreover, the risk of exacerbating health disparities among patients of various races, ethnicities, genders, languages, abilities, and socioeconomic statuses because of biased or nonrepresentative training data underscores the need for rigorous oversight and accountability. This policy outlines recommendations for the safe, equitable, and effective use of GenAI in pediatric settings. Developers should prioritize diverse pediatric data sets, proactively address bias, and implement strong data privacy and security safeguards. Health care institutions must establish rigorous validation protocols, ensure compliance with privacy regulations, and maintain clear human oversight. Relevant regulatory and oversight bodies should enforce pediatric-specific evaluations and require postmarket surveillance. Governance frameworks must support interdisciplinary collaboration, transparency, and education initiatives to equip pediatricians with GenAI literacy. Reasonable disclosure of GenAI involvement in patient care is essential to establish and strengthen trust. GenAI policies pertaining to the care of children and adolescents must remain adaptive to ensure ethical, equitable, and evidence-based implementation. Despite these numerous challenges, GenAI holds transformative potential to improve pediatric health outcomes, and this policy seeks to empower developers, researchers, and clinicians to responsibly build and harness this technology.

papers.title: The role of GenAI in learning Chinese as a foreign language: perspectives from university students in Ireland
papers.authors: Weiming Liu, Françoise Blin
papers.journal: Journal of China Computer-Assisted Language Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping language education and continues to shape how learners access, produce and evaluate knowledge. Its application in learning Chinese as a Foreign Language (CFL) in Ireland, however, remains limited and underexplored. This study investigates how university students in Ireland engage with GenAI tools to support their CFL learning. As a small-scale exploratory study, an anonymous online questionnaire was distributed across five Irish universities between May and June 2025, yielding 19 valid responses from students across four year groups. Quantitative data show the distribution of GenAI use while thematic analysis of open-ended responses provides insights into learners’ experiences, orientations and ethical perspectives. The findings reveal three preliminary learner personas, namely pragmatic users, critical users and principled non-users. Overall, GenAI emerges as a conditional learning partner that offers both pedagogical benefits and challenges. By offering empirical evidence from an underrepresented context, this research helps inform CFL curriculum design, language teacher education and policy development to ensure the responsible use of GenAI in higher education.

papers.title: What Should Teachers Upload to GenAI? A Privacy- Aware Framework for Language Education
papers.authors: Locky Law
papers.journal: The Asian Journal of Applied Linguistics
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly intertwined with language education, teachers are expected to integrate AI-supported materials development into their pedagogical practice. However, discussions of GenAI in the field have largely focused on pedagogical innovation and student use, while giving comparatively little attention to the protection of student data and the responsible handling of educational resources. This article argues that data privacy and security should be regarded as core components of teacher GenAI literacy. Adopting a conceptual and practice-oriented approach, it proposes a privacy-aware decision framework for GenAI use that helps teachers align the level of data sensitivity with appropriate GenAI environments, including public cloud-based platforms, institutionally supported services, and offline local GenAI tools. Drawing on research from computer science, cybersecurity, and platform governance, the article suggests practical strategies for reducing privacy risks, including removal, masking, and splitting, before discussing how key considerations relating to student data protection, network security, institutional confidentiality and copyright restrictions may influence teachers’ decisions when selecting GenAI tools. Using examples from language materials development, the article illustrates how educators can use GenAI to adapt disciplinary texts, create differentiated learning materials, and generate pedagogical resources while reducing unnecessary disclosure of sensitive information. The article concludes by advocating a more balanced approach to GenAI integration in language education, one that combines pedagogical innovation with informed and responsible data practices.

papers.title: Customized chatbot for patient education in vitreoretinal diseases
papers.authors: Enrico Bernardi, Lorenzo Ferro Desideri, Carla Troyas, Janice Roth, Shakib Ba-Ali, Yousif Subhi, Martin Sebastian Zinkernagel, Rodrigo Anguita
papers.journal: International Journal of Retina and Vitreous
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose To develop and evaluate the accuracy and safety of a customized, domain-restricted chatbot providing postoperative patient education after vitreoretinal surgery. Methods We evaluated a domain-restricted GPT-4 chatbot accessed through the OpenAI API and implemented with retrieval-augmented generation, a curated vitreoretinal postoperative knowledge base, a persistent system prompt, and rule-based safeguards. Nineteen frequently asked postoperative questions were each submitted in three independent fresh sessions, generating 57 responses. Each response was rated by one of three retinal specialists as accurate and sufficient, partially accurate and sufficient, or inaccurate, and screened for hallucination. Results Across 57 reviewer ratings, 53 (93.0%; 95% CI 83.0–98.1) were rated accurate and sufficient and 4 (7.0%; 1.9–17.0) partially accurate and sufficient; none was inaccurate. Sixteen of 19 questions (84.2%; 60.4–96.6) received unanimous accurate-and-sufficient ratings. Disagreement was confined to three activity-related questions: lifting, exercise, and driving. Hallucinations occurred in 3 of 57 ratings (5.3%; 1.1–14.6), all in activity advice and each flagged by a single reviewer; none arose in red-flag symptom responses. Inter-rater agreement was high (pairwise agreement 89.5%; Gwet’s AC1 0.88). Conclusion A customized, domain-restricted chatbot is a feasible and safe approach to postoperative vitreoretinal patient education, with the only residual inconsistencies arising in areas where clinical practice itself varies between surgeons.

papers.title: Technological frontiers in neuropsychological rehabilitation: a bibliometric-systematic literature review of AI applications for pediatric, adult, and geriatric populations
papers.authors: Diego D. Díaz‐Guerra, Marena de la C. Hernández-Lugo, Jennifer Obregón, Anai Guerra Labrada, Carlos Ramos-Galarza, Yunier Broche‐Pérez
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into neuropsychological rehabilitation represents an expanding technological frontier, yet no study has systematically mapped this field across the lifespan. This bibliometric-systematic review analyzed 4336 Scopus-indexed publications (2020–2025) across pediatric ( n = 366), adult ( n = 883), and geriatric ( n = 3,087) populations using Bibliometrix. Results reveal an overwhelming disparity: research on older adults exceeds that on children and adults by eightfold. Geriatric research shows sustained annual growth (≈ 18.5 articles/year), while pediatric and adult corpora exhibit volatile, non-linear patterns (R²=0.0515 and 0.0087), indicating lack of research consolidation. Virtual reality emerged as the central cross-cutting technology, yet with marked specialization: in pediatrics, associated with executive functions training; in older adults, combined with machine learning for cognitive assessment (highest impact: 4.250). Thematic foci align with epidemiological priorities—neurodevelopmental disorders in children, acquired conditions in adults, neurodegenerative diseases in older adults—while revealing methodological stratification: geriatric research integrates neuroimaging with AI; pediatric research emphasizes behavioral interventions. High-impact niches identified include AI-integrated neurofeedback in pediatrics (impact 2.052) and VR with machine learning for mild cognitive impairment in gerontology (impact 4.250). Working-age adults with acquired brain injuries emerge as a persistently underserved population. This first comparative cartography of AI-enabled neuropsychological rehabilitation across the lifespan offers actionable insights for strategic resource allocation and identifies critical gaps requiring urgent attention.

papers.title: Effect of carnitine supplementation on quality of life: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.authors: Mahdi Honardoust, Rahil Ranjbar, Afsane Ahmadi, Sahar Foshati, Mohammad Ali Mohsenpour
papers.journal: Health and Quality of Life Outcomes
papers.abstract: The quality of life (QoL) is a multidimensional concept that its enhancement is a key goal in clinical and public health interventions. Evidence for the effect of carnitine on QoL is still contradictory. Therefore, the present study aims to systematically review the current evidence from randomized controlled clinical trials (RCTs) and quantify the effect through a meta-analysis. Online databases were searched for relevant RCTs published until 9th November 2025, without any restrictions on publication date or language. The random-effect model was carried out to calculate effect size (Hedges`s g) from extracted mean change values and standard deviations (SD) of RCTs. Pre-planned subgroup analyses were conducted based on region, target population, mean age and BMI, and dose, formulation, and duration of intervention. Screening the database search results led to find 20 eligible RCTs with 21 study arms including 1878 participants. Results indicated that the carnitine supplementation could improve general health (Hedges’ g = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.33, 1.68), bodily pain (Hedges’ g = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.15, 1.50), vitality (Hedges’ g = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.32, 1.30), and social functioning (Hedges’ g = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.31, 1.13). Lower effects were observed for emotional functioning and global QoL. This is while, no significant effect was observed for mental health and physical functioning. Subgroup analyses indicated the dosage and formulation of intervention, target population, and region could possibly affect the observed results. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of findings, though substantial residual heterogeneity highlights variability in measurement instruments and study designs. Carnitine supplementation especially when tailored by formulation and dose appears to enhance multiple aspects of QoL, particularly bodily pain, general health, vitality, and social functioning. Clinicians should individualize supplementation strategies. Large, well-designed RCTs that evaluate dose, duration, formulation, and long-term outcomes are proposed to refine clinical recommendations. This systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251162350).

papers.title: Co-developing women-centered strategies to improve HIV self-testing and PrEP uptake among adolescent girls and young women in Ghana: Findings from the WISE WOMAN study
papers.authors: Gloria A. Aidoo-Frimpong, Winfred Kofi Mensah, Daniel Selase Anyidoho, Yaa Adutwumwaa Obeng, Abass Tando Abubakar, Maame Araba Oduro
papers.abstract: Abstract Background : Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in Ghana face persistent barriers to HIV prevention, including limited uptake of HIV self-testing (HIVST) and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). While national policies support these tools, implementation gaps remain, particularly among young women navigating socio-cultural and structural constraints. This study aimed to identify multilevel barriers to HIVST and PrEP uptake and to co-design contextually grounded implementation strategies through participatory engagement. Methods : We conducted a co-creation workshop with adolescent girls and young women (n=10) and community stakeholders (n=5) from Greater Accra and Eastern Regions of Ghana. Data sources included audio-recorded discussions, facilitator field notes, Nominal Group Technique rankings, and intervention prototypes. Transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis with iterative coding and consensus refinement. Identified barriers were mapped across individual, interpersonal, socio-cultural, and structural levels. Co-created strategies were synthesized and aligned with the manifestations of barriers. Results : Four higher-order barrier domains were identified: (1) cultural and religious norms that moralized female sexuality and framed HIV prevention as inappropriate behavior; (2) limited actionable knowledge and procedural uncertainty regarding HIVST and PrEP; (3) fear and stigma operating through anticipatory emotional distress, relational scrutiny, and confidentiality concerns; and (4) structural constraints, including inconsistent service availability, financial barriers, geographic inequities, and health system practices. Participants co-designed multilevel implementation strategies, including culturally grounded storytelling, faith-leader engagement, peer-led WhatsApp-based education, anonymous digital support mechanisms, and decentralized community-based service-delivery pathways. Conclusions: HIVST and PrEP uptake among AGYW in Ghana is shaped by intersecting socio-cultural, interpersonal, and structural determinants. The co-developed strategies will inform a pilot phase to evaluate feasibility and acceptability and to refine approaches for broader scale-up. By grounding intervention design in lived experiences and structural realities, this study offers contextually specific guidance for strengthening HIV prevention implementation in Ghana.

papers.title: Construct and concurrent validity of the Navigator patient segmentation service: cross-sectional study among diabetic patients in Finnish primary care
papers.authors: Riikka Riihimies, Elina Tolvanen, Mika Helminen, Elise Kosunen, Tuomas Koskela
papers.abstract: Patient segmentation aims at recognizing groups of patients with similar needs in health care. Targeting appropriate services and care resources to each group reduces care costs. Navigator is a Finnish patient segmentation service based on questionnaires for patients and professionals. Navigator considers the patient’s individual values and functional ability, and therefore this service may supplement data-based segmentation methods. Knowledge concerning Navigator’s validity is lacking. Nurses ( n = 16) used Navigator with diabetic patients ( n = 304) at a health center. We performed an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) of Navigator’s data, and we derived factor scores to test hypotheses of smaller differences between the genders and greater differences between younger (< 75 years) and older (≥ 75 years) groups when responding to Navigator (construct validity). We correlated (using Spearman’s rho) Navigator’s dimension of the patient’s ability to function with measures of disability (WHODAS 2.0), self-rated health (SRH), health-related well-being (EQ-VAS), and general well-being (WBQ-12), as well as the dimension of the patient’s health status with patient-reported chronic conditions, all medication and diabetes care values (glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), blood pressure (BP), smoking, and body-mass index (BMI). Both EFAs were successful as we identified the “patient’s mood” and “patient’s enablement” factors in the patient’s questionnaire, and the “fulfilling care” and “patient’s health status” factors in the professional’s questionnaire. Significant differences in most factor scores emerged in the comparison of age groups. Significant correlations were noticed between the patient questions and WHODAS 2.0 ( p < 0.001), SRH ( p < 0.001), EQ-VAS ( p < 0.001), and WBQ-12 ( p < 0.001), as well as between the professional questions and the number of chronic conditions ( p < 0.001), all medication ( p < 0.001), HbA1c ( p < 0.001), UACR ( p < 0.001), smoking ( p < 0.044), and BMI ( p < 0.027). The factors successfully identified in the EFAs support the dimensions of Navigator. It also differentiated between people on the basis of age when the features of patient enablement, fulfilling care, and health status were considered. In respect of these appropriate construct validity results and preferable concurrent validity, Navigator seems to be valid in measuring the dimensions of patients’ coping in everyday life and health status. Therefore, Navigator may supplement data-based patient segmentation by adding to the understanding of individuals in patient groups.

papers.title: Development and structural validation of the Artificial Intelligence Competency Scale for Nurse Educators (AI-CSNE): a three-domain measure of perceived AI competency
papers.authors: Mona Gamal Mohamed, Zahra Abdirahman Mahmoud, Marwa Samir Sorour
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare and nursing education has created new competency requirements for nurse educators. Despite this growing demand, there is a notable lack of rigorously developed and psychometrically validated instruments specifically designed to assess AI-related competencies among nursing faculty. This gap limits the ability to systematically evaluate nurse educators’ perceived preparedness for AI integration and hinders evidence-based curriculum development in nursing education. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically validate the Artificial Intelligence Competency Scale for Nurse Educators (AI-CSNE). A methodological cross-sectional study was conducted among 470 nurse educators from multiple nursing faculties in Egypt between mid-October 2025 and February 2026. The scale was developed based on the UNESCO Artificial Intelligence Competency Framework for Teachers and relevant literature. Content validity was established through expert evaluation and pilot testing. The total sample ( N = 470) was randomly divided into two independent subsamples. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted using the first subsample ( n = 235) to identify the underlying factor structure, followed by confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using the second independent subsample ( n = 235) to validate the proposed measurement model. Internal consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficients. Exploratory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure representing Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application, Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use, and AI-Supported Professional Growth. Factor loadings ranged from 0.661 to 0.822, and the three factors explained 56.10% of total variance. Internal consistency reliability was satisfactory, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients of 0.842 for Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application, 0.810 for Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use, and 0.697 for AI-Supported Professional Growth in the EFA subsample, with comparable estimates in the CFA subsample. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the three-factor structure of the AI-CSNE, with excellent model fit (CFI = 0.989, TLI = 0.986, RMSEA = 0.023, SRMR = 0.046). The Foundational AI Knowledge and Instructional Application domain demonstrated the highest standardized factor loadings (ranging from 0.626 to 0.785), while the Ethical and Human-Centered AI Use domain showed comparatively lower but still acceptable loadings (0.570 to 0.734). The near-zero inter-domain correlations indicate that the three subscales are empirically distinct and should be interpreted separately. The AI-CSNE demonstrates initial evidence of structural validity and internal consistency as an instrument comprising three distinct subscales for assessing perceived AI competency among nurse educators. The near-zero inter-domain correlations indicate that the three subscales should be interpreted separately rather than combined into a single total score. As the scale measures perceived rather than objectively demonstrated competency, it is best suited for exploratory group-level needs assessment, research comparisons, program evaluation, and self-reflective development rather than for individual appraisal, certification, or high-stakes evaluation. Convergent, criterion, and known-groups validity were assessed and demonstrated no significant differences across subgroups, though further validation is required. The scale provides a foundation for research and self-reflective faculty development but should be used with appropriate caution until comprehensive validation is established. Not applicable.

papers.title: Exploring the experiences of medical sciences faculty members and students in using artificial intelligence applications: a qualitative descriptive study
papers.authors: Leila Homayouni, Zahra Karimian
papers.abstract: Abstract Background The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical education worldwide. However, existing studies are predominantly quantitative and Western-centric providing limited empirical evidence regarding how medical sciences faculty members and students experience and interpret the use of AI within constrained educational and socio-cultural contexts. This study aimed to explore the experiences of medical sciences faculty and students regarding AI use at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted from November 2024 to April 2025. A total of 16 participants (eight faculty members and eight students) from diverse medical disciplines with prior AI experience recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi‑structured, in‑depth interviews (50–60 min) supported by field notes and continued until data saturation was achieved. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using Graneheim and Lundman’s qualitative content analysis with MAXQDA 24. Trustworthiness was ensured through qualitative rigor criteria, following COREQ guidelines. Results Five overarching themes with 16 subthemes emerged from the study: 1) functional and practical value of AI; 2) human oversight, ethics and authenticity; 3) perceived capacity building and institutional readiness; 4) cognitive, emotional, and behavioral influence; and 5) socio-cultural dynamics and future transformation. However, participants’ experiences varied based on their roles: faculty members used AI strategically for routine tasks preserving cognitive effort for more complex ones, whereas students exhibited a more relational reliance on AI, which appeared to increase their vulnerability to automation bias. Both groups expressed concerns about potential "intellectual deskilling" and infrastructure barriers, conceptualized as a geopolitical algorithmic divide that limits equitable access. Conclusions The experiences of AI use among medical sciences faculty and students are context-dependent and conditional rather than uniformly positive or negative. Its sustainable integration into medical education involves a complex negotiation between efficiency and significant ethical, cognitive and institutional challenges. these findings highlight the potential need for a pedagogical shift toward evaluative judgment and institutional support to bridge the geopolitical digital divide, alongside human-in-the-loop supervision to help mitigate the risk of educational deskilling. Future longitudinal research is recommended to explore how perceptions, ethical concerns, and usage patterns evolve as AI becomes more embedded in medical education.

papers.title: Nutritional risk and life satisfaction in older adults: a cross-sectional analysis using the NUFFE-TR scale
papers.authors: Emine Merve Ekici, Pınar Göbel, Neslihan Arslan
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between nutritional risk and life satisfaction in community-dwelling older adults. A cross-sectional web-based survey was conducted with 779 adults aged ≥ 65 years. Nutritional status was assessed using the Turkish version of the Nutritional Form for the Elderly (NUFFE-TR), a 12-item screening tool (score range: 0–24) where higher scores indicate greater malnutrition risk. Life satisfaction was evaluated using the 20-item Life Satisfaction Scale (LSS) (score range: 0–20), with higher scores indicating better life satisfaction. Descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed. Life satisfaction was negatively correlated with NUFFE-TR scores ( r = − 0.47, p < 0.001). In the regression model, higher nutritional risk significantly predicted lower life satisfaction (β = − 0.341, 95% CI: − 0.438 to − 0.294, p < 0.001). Age, BMI, and NUFFE-TR collectively explained 12.7% of the variance in life satisfaction (R2 = 0.127). Higher nutritional risk may be associated with lower life satisfaction in older adults. Incorporating nutritional screening into geriatric care may support early detection and promote healthy aging, although longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causality.

papers.title: A Pilot Study on Facial Expression Recognition by Autistic Children of a Social Robot
papers.authors: Irina Kondaurova, Jeremy Gaskins, Riten Mitra, Ali Ashary, Robert C. Pennington, Dan O. Popa
papers.abstract: This study investigates the accuracy of recognition of four basic facial expressions (Angry, Happy, Sad, and Surprised) on a social assistive robot's face by children with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Human-robot interaction experiments (HRI) were conducted with Milo, an expressive social robot. A total of 60 children aged 8–12 took part in the study: 41 non-autistic children and 19 children who met DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for ASD. Milo displayed four basic facial expressions in a randomized order across two consecutive attempts. Participants identified the expressions, allowing for a quantitative analysis of potential differences between groups.The proportion of correct answers was used for validity and reliability ratings. A logistic mixed-effect regression model was employed to analyze the relationship between accuracy, demographic variables, emotion type, and ASD status. Our results suggest that although overall differences in facial expression recognition between autistic and non-autistic participants may be subtle, more detailed emotion-specific analyses are necessary to identify and characterize these differences. Results indicated that overall group differences in labeling accuracy were modest, whereas emotion-specific analyses identified a significant group difference for Milo's Angry facial expression. The number of repeated attempts showed a marginally significant effect in overall accuracy in both groups, with the recognition accuracy decreasing on the second attempt, particularly among autistic children. However, this decline was sensitive to the treatment of “None of the above” responses. Therefore, the attempt effect should be interpreted cautiously. These findings highlight the importance of considering specific emotions, task structure, and response options when evaluating children's interpretations of robot-generated facial expressions.

papers.title: When Recruiters Meet Algorithms: Advice Taking and Bias in AI‐Assisted Recruitment
papers.authors: Alain Lacroux, Christelle Martin‐Lacroux
papers.journal: International Journal of Selection and Assessment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examined whether professional recruiters revise their hiring decisions after receiving external advice under cognitive conflict, that is, when advice contradicts their initial evaluation. In a between‐subjects experiment, 1,208 recruitment professionals evaluated two candidates, made an initial hiring decision, and then received advice whose source (human expert vs. algorithmic recruitment system, ARS), accuracy (accurate vs. inaccurate), and number of advisors (one vs. two) were manipulated across eight conditions. Results revealed widespread egocentric advice discounting. Although trust predicted advice utilization, a trust–reliance paradox emerged: recruiters reported lower trust in the ARS yet were behaviorally more influenced by it. Convergent advice was most influential, and exploratory analyses suggested that inaccurate advice degraded decision quality more than accurate advice improved it. Findings underscore the need for calibrated reliance in AI‐assisted selection.

papers.title: AI ‐Mediated Multimodal Reading Education for EFL Learners: Effects on Students' Enjoyment and Engagement
papers.authors: Lei Pan, Hangbo Zhao, Mehmet Şengül
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly reshaped educational practices by expanding opportunities for adaptive, multimodal and learner‐centered instruction. While growing attention has been paid to AI‐supported language learning, less is known about how multimodal AI technologies may support the emotional and behavioural dimensions of education among at‐risk students, particularly in second/foreign language reading contexts. Addressing this gap, the present study examined whether AI‐mediated multimodal reading education could enhance at‐risk English as a foreign language (EFL) learners' enjoyment and engagement during reading instruction. Using an interventional pre‐test/post‐test design, 80 at‐risk EFL students were assigned to either a control group ( n = 40) or an experimental group ( n = 40). Over two semesters, students in the experimental group received reading instruction supported by multimodal AI reading bots and AI chatbots, whereas those in the control group received conventional reading instruction. Enjoyment and engagement questionnaires were administered at the beginning and end of the intervention. ANCOVA results showed that students in the AI‐mediated education group demonstrated significantly higher levels of enjoyment and engagement than their counterparts in the control group. These findings suggest that multimodal AI technologies can contribute to more inclusive and emotionally supportive reading education for at‐risk learners. The study offers implications for educational researchers, teachers and policymakers seeking to integrate AI technologies into equitable and engaging language education.

papers.title: Prevalence of binge eating disorder symptoms and associated characteristics in Danish adults with type 2 diabetes: A cross‐sectional study
papers.authors: Pernille Fiil Nybo, Sidsel Louise Domazet, Michael Einar Røder, Jakob Linnet
papers.abstract: Abstract Aims Coexistence of binge eating disorder (BED) and type 2 diabetes is linked to poor health outcomes, but data on the prevalence and clinical profile of BED symptoms remain limited and inconsistent. We estimated the prevalence of BED symptoms and examined their associated clinical characteristics in Danish adults with type 2 diabetes. Methods We conducted a cross‐sectional study within the Danish Centre for Strategic Research in Type 2 Diabetes (DD2) cohort. Adults with type 2 diabetes completed the Binge Eating Disorder Questionnaire (BED‐Q) to determine the presence of BED symptoms. Data on well‐being, comorbidities, treatment and biomarkers were retrieved from national health registers. Associations between participant characteristics and BED symptoms were examined using Poisson regression to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs). Results Among 2459 individuals, 72 (2.9%) screened positive for BED symptoms, and 76 (3.1%) showed subclinical BED symptoms. Individuals with BED symptoms had an earlier age at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (median 51.8 years, IQR: 41.3–57.6) than adults without BED symptoms (median 59.5 years, IQR: 52.1–66.2). BED symptoms were also associated with severe obesity (BMI ≥35 kg/m 2 ) (PR 11.37, 95% CI: 2.78–46.49), female sex (PR 1.54, 95% CI: 1.12–2.10), and lower well‐being (PR 1.83, 95% CI: 1.15–2.92). Conclusions BED symptoms were associated with a distinct clinical and psychosocial profile in Danish adults with type 2 diabetes. These findings support clinical awareness of BED symptoms in this population, particularly among women, individuals with obesity, those with lower well‐being and those diagnosed with diabetes at a younger age.

papers.title: How can empowering leadership foster employee–AI collaboration? A multilevel analysis of AI trust and psychological safety
papers.authors: Thao Nguyen, Trung Quang Nguyen, Giang Truong Hoang, Alvedi Sabani
papers.abstract: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the workplace underscores the urgent need to understand how employees collaborate effectively with AI systems. Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study investigates the impact of empowering leadership on employee–AI collaboration. Furthermore, we examine the mediating roles of psychological safety and AI trust. Design/methodology/approach To test the research model, we utilized a multilevel design data from 418 employees across 103 teams in AI-integrated organizations in Vietnam. Findings Our findings indicate that empowering leadership is positively related to employee–AI collaboration, with this relationship mediated by both psychological safety and AI trust. Originality/value This study contributes to the leadership and technology management literature by establishing a multilevel link between empowering leadership and employee–AI collaboration. It identifies key mediating mechanisms (AI trust and psychological safety), offering a more integrated understanding of leadership influence in AI-enabled settings. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for practitioners navigating the dynamics of employee–AI collaboration, highlighting the importance of empowering leadership in building AI-ready workforces.

papers.title: How conversational AI shapes the readability of 10-K reports
papers.authors: Junru Zhang, Zheng Chen, Grantley Taylor, Xuequn Wang
papers.abstract: Purpose We investigate whether the adoption of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) translates corporate complexity into clearer financial narratives. CAI, representing AI-driven innovation, can bolster operational efficiency and performance, thereby leading to better financial transparency and readability of financial statement information. Design/methodology/approach We construct a firm-level CAI measure from CAI-related disclosures in 10-K filings using Sent-latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA)-variational expectation maximization (VEM) topic modelling. Our measure captures CAI applications related to service and operations, and decision-making and governance. We also use patent-based measures based on natural language processing and speech-recognition technologies as alternative proxies in robustness tests. Findings We find that CAI adoption is associated with lower Bog Index scores, indicating more readable 10-K reports. Mediation tests show that financial performance and operational efficiency partially mediate this relationship. The results remain robust after addressing endogeneity concerns and using alternative specifications. Originality/value Using unsupervised machine learning topic modelling, we observe that CAI is predominantly employed in corporate operations, notably in service-related activities, decision-making processes and corporate governance.

papers.title: Negotiating generative AI in online and distance higher education: lecturers' task-selective adoption in Yogyakarta, Indonesia
papers.authors: Rendra Widyatama, Tawar Tawar, Shuhui Sophy Cheng
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how lecturers in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, adopt and negotiate the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic work, focusing on perceived usefulness, task-selective use, ethical ambivalence and institutional readiness. Design/methodology/approach A convergent mixed-methods design combined an online survey of 120 lecturers from public and private universities in Yogyakarta with semi-structured interviews with eight lecturers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and compared across age, academic rank and institution type using the Kruskal–Wallis H test; interview data were analyzed thematically. The strands were merged during interpretation. Findings All respondents (100%, n = 120) agreed that generative AI improves academic efficiency (M = 4.47). However, agreement declined across presentations (56.7%), teaching material preparation (53.3%), disciplinary understanding (51.7%), scholarly articles (48.3%), research (46.7%) and academic books (46.7%), indicating task-selective adoption. None of the task-specific usefulness ratings differed significantly by age or academic rank (all p > 0.05), but perceived training need differed significantly by age and rank, with a large effect for age and a moderate effect for academic rank (both p < 0.001). Institution type was associated with attitudes toward AI for academic books and toward AI possibly replacing lecturers (both p < 0.05). Interviews revealed the same task-selective logic, alongside ethical ambivalence about plagiarism and dependency and a perceived absence of institutional guidance. Research limitations/implications The study used purposive convenience sampling in one Indonesian province, with an unequal public-private institutional ratio, a cross-sectional self-report survey and eight interviews. The findings therefore cannot support causal claims or represent all Indonesian lecturers, higher education institutions, or open and distance learning (ODL) systems. Negotiated professional adoption remains an emergent interpretation that requires further testing. Future research should use multisite, more balanced and longitudinal designs to examine institutional differences and changes in lecturers' AI practices as policies and technologies evolve. Practical implications Universities should issue task-specific policies that distinguish legitimate AI assistance from inappropriate substitution, especially in scholarly writing and research. They should establish authorship-disclosure rules, verification procedures and clear academic-integrity mechanisms. Lecturers need guidance on checking AI-generated content and preserving professional judgment. ODL administrators should provide differentiated training based on seniority and need rather than uniform programs. National bodies should set minimum standards, while institutions should adapt operational policies to their own contexts. Social implications Clear institutional guidance can support responsible generative AI use while protecting academic integrity, professional accountability and trust in higher education. Differentiated training can reduce uneven preparedness across age groups and academic ranks. Transparent rules on authorship, verification and acceptable use may help lecturers and students understand the boundaries between assistance and substitution. These measures can encourage fairer, more consistent and more trustworthy use of generative AI in digitally mediated and open and distance higher education. Originality/value The study proposes negotiated professional adoption as an emergent, contextually grounded conceptual interpretation that extends the Technology Acceptance Model with professional, ethical and institutional dimensions specific to generative AI in open and distance higher education.

papers.title: Cross-subject electroencephalography-based emotion recognition using source-constrained graph representation learning
papers.authors: Yuxuan Zhu, Meng Xun, Nan nan Wang, Xulong Liu
papers.abstract: Abstract Cross-subject emotion recognition from electroencephalography remains challenging because inter-subject variability alters spectral characteristics and spatial relationships across electrodes. This paper proposes a source-constrained graph representation learning method based on static differential entropy features. A band-aware encoder first refines the multi-band descriptor of each electrode, after which direct, local-graph, and global-graph paths capture complementary spatial information. For transductive adaptation to an unlabeled target subject, labeled source data remain the supervisory reference, while multi-source distribution alignment and source-prototype-referenced target alignment reduce cross-subject discrepancy. Gradient projection further limits transfer updates that conflict with source supervision. The method is evaluated on the SEED and SEED-IV datasets under leave-one-subject-out protocols, with all three recording sessions evaluated independently and experiments repeated using three random seeds. Averaged across sessions, the method achieves accuracies of 82.42% and 68.69% and macro-averaged F 1 scores of 82.21% and 68.18% on SEED and SEED-IV, respectively.

papers.title: Development and implementation of an AI-based handwriting recognition tool for math education: improving students’ attitudes and computational thinking
papers.authors: Sejun Oh
papers.abstract: Handwriting recognition for mathematical expressions remains challenging in educational settings, especially when solutions combine Korean text and symbolic notation. This study reports the design and classroom implementation of an AI-based handwriting annotation tool that uses the Mathpix OCR API to convert handwritten solutions into LaTeX and allows students to correct errors. An eight-session program integrated mathematics for AI (functions, loss functions, gradients, and neural networks) with data annotation and human-in-the-loop debugging. Eighty-three 12th-grade students at a high school in Incheon, Korea, completed pre- and post-tests of mathematics attitude and computational thinking. Paired-samples analyses showed small-to-medium gains in mathematics confidence and interest and significant improvements in algorithmic thinking, creativity, cooperativity, and critical thinking; lower raw problem-solving difficulty scores indicated fewer self-reported difficulties. Open-ended responses suggested that students viewed AI as mathematically grounded, recognized stronger links between school mathematics and real-world technologies, and gained confidence despite challenges with OCR errors and LaTeX editing. Although the single-group, short-term design in one school limits causal inference and generalizability, the findings suggest that human-in-the-loop handwriting tools can support mathematics engagement and computational thinking.

papers.title: Playful leadership as a catalyst for transformation in higher education
papers.authors: Susannah Quinsee
papers.journal: Perspectives Policy and Practice in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Higher education in the UK and globally is under severe pressure; one could argue that it is in crisis (Cartland Citation2026). AI, financial challenges, changing student needs, and geopolitics have all created a perfect storm around the higher education system. To survive, we need radical change. Enter playful leadership. Playful practices inspire us to think differently, and playful leadership requires us to lead in a different way. It is based on engagement, inclusivity, creativity and autonomy; many of the characteristics we need in turbulent times. This article proposes a framework for playful leadership which uses the lens of crisis leadership to demonstrate how this approach can support the radical rethinking required to transform higher education (Moseley Citation2020; Walsh Citation2022). Examples are given as to how to create specific opportunities to enact playful leadership practice to foster the new thinking we need to reshape universities for a changed world.

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Advertising Measurement in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Shuba Srinivasan, Yuping Liu–Thompkins, Edward Carl Malthouse, Ewa Masłowska
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling large-scale creative automation, dynamic personalization, and AI-mediated consumer decision journeys. Existing measurement systems were developed for human-authored and relatively stable communication environments and do not capture how GenAI systems cocreate brand touchpoints with advertisers or mediate consumer evaluations of brands. In this study, we develop an integrated triadic framework for understanding the GenAI-mediated advertising landscape and reconceptualizes the action–mindset–behavior–finance measurement architecture to reflect an advertising process that is increasingly recursive, nonlinear, and adaptive. In doing so, we distinguish between traditional metrics that remain relevant but require reconceptualization and novel metrics unique to GenAI-assisted advertising systems. In addition, we extend the framework beyond firm-centered outcomes to incorporate stakeholder-oriented metrics relevant to employees, regulators, investors, and society. The framework offers guidance for scholars and managers seeking to evaluate GenAI advertising while maintaining transparency, trust, and competitive integrity. The study concludes with a future research agenda and crosscutting priorities addressing measurement, governance, accountability, and methodological challenges associated with GenAI-assisted advertising.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among EFL learners: a structural equation modelling approach
papers.authors: Mohammad Hamad Al-khresheh, Mayez Almayez
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in English as a foreign language (EFL) learning, yet its cognitive implications depend on how learners engage with it rather than on its use alone. This study examined the structural relationships among differentiated patterns of AI use, creative thinking disposition, and metacognitive awareness among undergraduate EFL learners. Using a quantitative cross-sectional correlational design, data were collected from 713 learners and analysed through structural equation modelling. AI use was conceptualised as cognitive-support use, creative-extension use, reproductive or substitutive use, and ethical and critical awareness. The findings indicate that the use of cognitive-support and creative-extension AI is positively associated with both creative thinking disposition and metacognitive awareness. In contrast, reproductive or substitutive use is negatively associated with these outcomes. Creative thinking disposition demonstrates a strong positive relationship with metacognitive awareness and mediates the effects of constructive AI use on regulatory awareness. Ethical and critical engagement with AI moderates these relationships, strengthening the positive associations between constructive AI use and both creative and metacognitive outcomes. The results clarify that the cognitive value of AI in EFL learning is shaped by learner agency, reflective judgement, and responsibility for meaning-making. The study advances a cognitively grounded account of AI-mediated EFL learning and provides empirical support for differentiating AI engagement patterns in both research and instructional design.

papers.title: AI-enabled marketing analytics for SMEs: multimethod evidence on application potential and adoption conditions
papers.authors: Anita Talitha Parsegyan, Manuel Muth, Michael Lingenfelder
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming marketing analytics by enabling advanced data processing, predictions, and decision support. However, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often face substantial barriers to AI adoption due to limited organizational, technological, and human resources. To bridge theoretical and practical perspectives, this study employs a hybrid approach combining a systematic literature review of 49 studies with an empirical survey of more than 100 SMEs. The findings identify organizational, technological, and user-related conditions, as well as AI application potential, that shape AI adoption in SMEs. Based on these insights, a conceptual framework is proposed that differentiates between opportunistic, operational, strategic readiness, and strategic AI use. The framework translates SMEs’ AI application potential and adoption conditions into practice, thus structuring AI-enabled marketing analytics, which provides SMEs with new opportunities for data-driven operations despite resource constraints.

papers.title: Development and preliminary validation of a machine learning model for forward head posture in university students
