papers.authors: Yanru Li, Xin Li, Wei Zhang, Yuqing Tao, Chenjia Gao, Yuxi Liu, Rui Zou, Jiongming Liu
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study aimed to develop and preliminarily validate a machine learning model for preliminary forward head posture (FHP) screening and deploy the final model as an online tool. Among 825 university students, 625 comprised the development dataset (training set, n = 437; test set, n = 188), and 200 the exploratory external validation dataset. FHP was defined as a craniovertebral angle < 50°. Six machine learning models were compared through nested cross-validation. Restricted cubic splines and Shapley additive explanations analysis were used for exploratory association analysis and model interpretation, respectively. Random forest (RF) achieved the highest sensitivity in nested cross-validation (0.748, 95% CI 0.661–0.825) and was therefore selected as the final model based on the prespecified priority of reducing missed cases. In the external validation, RF achieved an AUC of 0.827 (0.751–0.896), sensitivity of 0.745 (0.615–0.865), specificity of 0.784 (0.715–0.845), and Brier score of 0.125 (0.097–0.154). Body mass index contributed most to model output and showed a significant nonlinear association with FHP (adjusted p = 0.017). The model showed moderate-to-good discrimination for FHP among university students and may offer a relatively accessible approach to preliminary FHP screening.

papers.title: Structured multimodal mobilization versus pilates-based motor imagery-focused pelvic floor exercises for primary dysmenorrhea: a randomized controlled trial
papers.authors: Zeynep Betül Bilgi, Gizem Boztaş Elverişli
papers.abstract: Abstract Primary dysmenorrhea impairs physical and emotional functioning. This prospective randomized controlled trial equally assigned 72 women aged 18–30 years to four groups: the structured multimodal mobilization group, the Pilates-based motor imagery-focused pelvic floor exercise group, the conventional treatment group, or the no-treatment control group. Active interventions comprised 24 twice-weekly sessions over 12 weeks. The primary outcome was the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ) total pain score; secondary outcomes included SF-MPQ sensory and affective scores, the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Menstrual Symptom Questionnaire, and Functional and Emotional Measure of Dysmenorrhea scores. Groups were comparable at baseline. Post-intervention pain differed significantly among groups. Structured multimodal mobilization produced the largest reduction in total pain score (15.44 ± 9.95 to 8.78 ± 6.78; mean change, -6.67 [95% confidence interval, -8.60 to -4.73]), although its post-intervention score did not significantly differ from the Pilates-based exercise group. Post hoc comparisons favored structured mobilization over Pilates-based exercise for VAS pain intensity, menstrual pain symptoms, and emotional dysmenorrhea. No adverse events occurred; all participants completed the trial. Pain scores decreased significantly within all active intervention groups, while structured multimodal mobilization showed outcome-specific advantages that require confirmation in larger multicenter trials with long-term follow-up. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07314021. Registration date: December 4, 2025.

papers.title: A Protocol to Identify Large Language Model Use in Undergraduate Chemistry Essays
papers.authors: Keith Livingstone
papers.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have been widely adopted by chemistry undergraduate university students as a learning tool, but few methods exist to measure the scope of their influence on essay writing. This report introduces a protocol based on monitoring the frequency of specific words used excessively by LLMs among a sample of 1073 chemistry student essays between 2018 and 2025. Analysis revealed that 54 keywords known to be favored by LLMs simultaneously increased in frequency among essays submitted during the last two years. When the lists of keywords were applied to specific essays, the findings indicated 43% of essays submitted during 2025 had at least some evidence of LLM-generated text. This protocol offers a simple method to generate an approximate scope of LLM uptake among a cohort, which can be combined with student survey data to produce a detailed overall impression of students’ use of generative artificial intelligence. This work’s findings are intended to stimulate discussion on the best practices to update literature review assessment criteria, to ensure it is maintained as a valid assessment option within a curriculum equipped for the widespread adoption of LLMs.

papers.title: LOTE teachers’ agency and digital literacy in AI-mediated language teaching: A qualitative multi-case study
papers.authors: Yang Zhao, Xiaozhou Zhou

papers.title: Escaping the AI cage: construction workers’ perceived risk with AI gives rise to unsafe behaviors
papers.authors: Tianyu Li, Huaiyuan Zhai, Ming Guo, Jiajun Deng
papers.abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety.

papers.title: Energy infrastructure for AI data centers: A critical review of grid integration, techno-economic challenges, and future pathways
papers.authors: Mahmoud Mohammadnezhad Kiasari, Hamed H. Aly
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are rapidly changing the energy landscape of today's data centers, both in terms of total electricity usage and power density at the facility level. The ongoing deployment of large-scale AI training and inference infrastructure is further driving and increasing the demand for electrical reliability, cooling capacity, power quality, grid interconnection, and low-carbon electricity supply. These interdependent issues require coordinated consideration of energy-infrastructure planning that takes into consideration renewable energy generation and storage, electrical architecture, operational flexibility, economic performance, and system resilience. The critical review combines 155 sources, mostly published between 2015 and 2026, identified and screened following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, which includes peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, technical standards, agency and institutional reports, market analyses, and corporate disclosure. The resulting evidence is presented in a seven-component decision framework that includes site and resource assessment, technology selection, electrical architecture, control and dispatch, workload flexibility, economic evaluation, and resilience and sustainability. The reviewed evidence indicates that renewable generation, energy storage, grid-support technologies, and workload flexibility can support lower-carbon AI data-center operations; however, the technical and economic performance of these approaches remains highly dependent on project-specific resource conditions, market structures, reliability requirements, and system boundaries. Reliability assessment requires a chronological, site-specific evaluation of load, resource, and infrastructure conditions. Wind–solar complementarity and workload flexibility may improve renewable-energy utilization; however, their benefits remain strongly dependent on operational and geographic constraints. The proposed framework is intended as a screening and decision-support tool rather than a prescriptive design methodology or site-specific optimization model. Important research needs include reproducible techno-economic assessment methods, independently verifiable corporate metrics, improved workload-flexibility characterization, and integrated evaluation of energy, water, reliability, and sustainability impacts. The resulting framework provides a structured basis for evaluating renewable-powered AI data center infrastructure across technical, economic, operational, and sustainability dimensions.

papers.title: Early and explainable identification of handwriting difficulties in children via game-based machine learning
papers.authors: Chiara Piazzalunga, Chiara Gentile, Linda Greta Dui, Alice Donati, Samuele Ravazzani, Stefania Fontolan, Cristiano Termine, Simona Ferrante
papers.abstract: Handwriting is a fundamental, but complex skill. Many children find it hard to master due to motor, cognitive, or attentional factors. Structured and timely training can reduce struggles, but some children are training-resistant, signaling clinical risks. Technological tools, including serious games and machine learning, can enrich training, but it is crucial to verify in an online manner and with explainable methods its efficacy with attention to temporal evolution, for early intervention in cases of resistance. This study addresses such challenge by evaluating game-based features for clinical risk detection in first-graders. Sixty-six children (age 6.45 ± 0.31 years) underwent three-month tablet-based handwriting training at school, with clinical assessments and teacher observations collected before and after training. We extracted kinematic, smoothness, temporal, frequency, and performance features, selecting those showing strong learning trajectories (|r| ≥ 0.5 or R 2 ≥ 0.5). Models were trained on aggregated features using nested 5-fold cross-validation with hyperparameter tuning, oversampling and progressive evaluation using cumulative data from the first month, first two months, and full period. Clinical risk detection outperformed teacher-identified weakness detection (Average Precision: 0.86 vs. 0.67), achieving test ROC-AUC = 0.850 ± 0.063 and AP = 0.772 ± 0.057, with discriminative signal emerging by day 36 (11 gameplay days), and smoothness and pressure features guiding classification. Misclassification patterns revealed attention-related difficulties in false negatives and compensated motor inefficiencies in false positives. These findings demonstrate that tracking learning dynamics over time via game-based features enables early identification of training-resistant children, supporting educators in timely intervention beyond static assessments.

papers.title: StoryReasoning dataset: Using chain-of-thought for scene understanding and grounded story generation
papers.authors: Daniel A. P. Oliveira, David Martins de Matos
papers.abstract: Visual storytelling systems struggle to maintain character identity across frames and link actions to appropriate subjects, frequently leading to referential hallucinations. We address these issues through entity grounding and propose StoryReasoning, a dataset containing 4178 stories derived from 52,016 movie images, with both structured scene analyses and grounded stories. Each story maintains character and object consistency across frames while explicitly modeling multi-frame relationships through structured tabular representations. Our approach features cross-frame object re-identification using visual similarity and face recognition, chain-of-thought reasoning for narrative modeling, and a grounding scheme linking textual elements to visual entities across frames. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL 7B, creating Qwen Storyteller, which performs end-to-end object detection, re-identification, and landmark detection while maintaining consistent object references throughout the story. Under a panel of Large Language Model (LLM) judges, evaluation shows a reduction from 4.06 to 3.56 (−12.3%) hallucinations per story and improved creativity from 2.58 to 3.38 (+31.0%) compared to the base model. Larger closed-source models remain ahead on free-form narrative quality; the contribution of our approach is explicit structured grounding with entity identifiers that persist across frames. • First dataset with entity-grounded stories from 52,016 movie frames. • Chain-of-thought reasoning structures scene analysis across frames. • End-to-end model unifies detection, re-identification, and story generation. • Boosts creativity 31% and cuts hallucinations 12.3% vs baseline. • 150+ grounded references per story maintain cross-frame consistency.

papers.title: Accounting for metallogenic heterogeneity in ensemble learning-based mineral prospectivity mapping: A case study of copper mineralization in eastern Junggar, Xinjiang, China
papers.authors: Jinfeng Yang, Jian Wang, Yunhui Kong, Binli Liu
papers.abstract: While machine learning has greatly advanced data-driven mineral exploration, its effectiveness is often limited by geological heterogeneity arising from the coexistence of multiple mineralization types within the same area. For example, in eastern Junggar, Xinjiang, China, copper deposits occur within a broadly shared regional metallogenic framework and exhibit similar surface expressions, yet different deposit types vary significantly in ore-controlling factors and geochemical signatures. Treating these distinct deposit types as a single homogeneous target may obscure subtle, type-specific patterns crucial for mineral exploration. To address this issue, this study presents an interpretable ensemble learning approach that explicitly accounts for mineralization types and applies it to copper prospectivity mapping in eastern Junggar. Copper deposits in the study area are categorized into Porphyry, VMS, and Vein types, and separate models including random forest (RF), logistic regression (LR) and k-nearest neighbor (KNN) are evaluated to select the best model and identify the key controlling factors for each mineralization type. The probabilities predicted by the type-specific base models are then used as inputs for an LR meta -learner to construct a stacked ensemble, which produces an integrated copper prospectivity map. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis is further adopted to interpret the prediction mechanisms and factor contributions for each mineralization type. Results show that the type-specific models effectively capture the spatial distribution and ore-controlling patterns of each copper mineralization type. High-prospectivity zones in the integrated prospectivity map cover 20 % of the study area but contain 81 % of known copper deposits, outperforming baseline models that ignore mineralization types. SHAP analysis reveals distinct controlling factors and contribution patterns across the deposit types, consistent with their established ore-controlling characteristics. The proposed framework therefore improves predictive performance while providing more geologically consistent and interpretable prospectivity mapping.

papers.title: The neural architecture of first-person moral choice: a demand-dependent working model
papers.authors: Alana Arrouet, Jennifer A. Chandler, Steven Laureys, Roxane S. Hoyer
papers.abstract: First-person moral choice may require the coordination of norm-relevant, self-relevant, affective, and outcome-related information. This narrative review integrates neuroimaging and electrophysiological evidence into a network-informed temporal working model organized around integrative demand: the extent to which multiple, potentially competing constraints must be represented and coordinated. The model distinguishes four candidate functional contributions: salience-related orienting, posterior default-mode/medial-temporal self-relevant situation construction, executive-control/frontoparietal comparison when competing rules, anticipated consequences, or response options must be actively maintained, and ventromedial-prefrontal value integration. Rather than forming a fixed cascade, these contributions may overlap, recur, and interact dynamically, with their relative involvement depending on task structure and integrative demand. Neuroimaging findings document task-dependent regional effects and, in a small number of studies, network interactions, while event-related potentials and oscillatory dynamics constrain the timing of salience-sensitive, conflict-sensitive, mnemonic, evaluative, and response-related processes. Together, these findings motivate a temporally structured but flexible account in which first-person moral choice emerges from changing coordination among domain-general processes rather than from a dedicated moral network or universal sequence. The model generates testable predictions for paradigms that manipulate integrative demand while controlling arousal, difficulty, and response requirements, and that combine event-specific electrophysiology with anatomically constrained connectivity measures. Together, these predictions provide a path toward testing how distributed neural dynamics contribute to first-person moral choice.

papers.title: Prolonged participation AI-based mindfulness school programme in primary education: Implications for AI practices, schools and developers
papers.authors: Şükran Uçuş
papers.abstract: Background Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) -supported mindfulness programs in primary education remains limited, particularly in rural contexts where implementation conditions differ from urban settings. Aim This study examines the effects of an AI-supported mindfulness intervention on rural primary school students' behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes, and on teachers' self-regulation and creativity, measured at pretest (T1), posttest (T2), and follow-up (T3). Method The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group across selected classrooms in four rural schools. The sample comprised an intervention group ( N = 91) and a control group ( N = 54), with 16 teachers participating in the intervention group. The intervention ran for ten weekly sessions across the fall and spring semesters. AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) supported teacher candidates in lesson planning and in the inquiry phase that followed each mindfulness practice. Implementation fidelity, assessed through mentor cross-rating, was 88.6% ( SD = 9.7), with Cohen's κ = .86 in a sub-sample. Results Split-plot ANOVAs showed significant Time × Group interactions favouring the intervention group on life skills (LSAS, η 2 p = .242), behavioural difficulties (SDQ total, η 2 p = .378), and teacher-student relationship quality (STRS total, η 2 p = .025). In the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), all five subscales were significant. The Closeness subscale drove the STRS effect; Conflict did not change. Nested analyses confirmed consistent effects across grade levels. Teachers showed gains on all nine TSRS subscales, and on the Social Value subscale of the TCS. Conclusion The intervention was associated with improvements in students' life skills, behavioral functioning, and teacher-student closeness, as well as gains in teachers' self-regulation. The findings inform AI-supported mindfulness practice in rural primary education.

papers.title: InstructGen: Generating Scalable and Realistic Visual-Language Navigation Data with Unlabeled Internet Videos
papers.authors: Yu Yan, Peiyang Li, Jianqin Yin

papers.title: AI and cloud adoption in European banking: Country-level evidence on the profitability-cyber risk trade-off
papers.authors: Iulia Cristina Iuga, Syeda Rabab JAFRI
papers.abstract: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, banking profitability, and ICT-related cyber risk across 28 European countries. These countries are selected because of persistent profitability pressures in the banking sector, rising digital transformation costs, and increasing exposure to cyber threats within a context of uneven digital maturity and cyber resilience. Using a recent cross-sectional dataset covering the EU-27 and Norway, we investigate the risk–return implications of AI adoption. Cloud computing is considered both as a key digital infrastructure and as a moderating factor in the relationship between AI adoption, return on equity (ROE), and cyber risk. Methodologically, the study employs a cross-sectional quantitative design combining Hierarchical Cluster Analysis and Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) to address heterogeneity and model uncertainty. These issues are particularly relevant given substantial differences across countries in digital maturity, institutional capacity, and risk exposure. The empirical analysis is conducted using R version 4.2.2. Our results reveal a strong association between AI adoption and cloud computing. AI adoption is negatively associated with ROE, suggesting that implementation costs, organizational adjustment, and learning frictions may precede profitability gains. In contrast, cloud computing is positively associated with ICT-related cyber risk and strengthens the positive relationship between AI adoption and cyber risk, highlighting a trade-off between digital capability and operational vulnerability. Overall, the study contributes to the AI–finance literature by integrating profitability and cyber-risk perspectives within a digital complementarity framework. The results indicate that the outcomes of AI adoption depend on digital infrastructure, institutional readiness, and cyber resilience, with implications for balanced digital transformation and financial stability.

papers.title: From generative AI usage to entrepreneurial intention: The sequential roles of task and social self-efficacy
papers.authors: Qianjun Zhang, Qiang Li, Zhuoyu Li, Kai Gan
papers.journal: The International Journal of Management Education
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly evolving and creating new possibilities for supporting students' entrepreneurial development. However, limited research has examined how GAI usage is associated with entrepreneurial intention (EI) through specific psychological pathways. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examines the relationship between GAI usage and EI, focusing on the mediating roles of task and social self-efficacy. Using survey data from 521 Chinese university students, this study empirically tests the proposed model. The results show that GAI usage is positively associated with students' task and social self-efficacy. However, task self-efficacy (TSE) is not directly associated with EI. In contrast, social self-efficacy (SSE) accounts for a significant indirect association between GAI usage and EI. Moreover, a significant sequential indirect association is observed, linking GAI usage with EI through TSE and SSE. By disentangling the distinct roles of TSE and SSE, this study shows that the association between GAI usage and EI is consistent with pathways that differ in their functions and proximity to entrepreneurial action. The findings also provide practical insights for entrepreneurship education and AI-supported learning environments.

papers.title: Ethical reasoning and responsible use of ChatGPT in higher education: Integrating technology acceptance and moral cognition
papers.authors: Hamood Mohammed Al‐Hattami, Saleh Hamood Nasser AL-Sinawi
papers.journal: The International Journal of Management Education
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has raised important questions about how students evaluate the ethical implications of AI-assisted academic practices and whether those evaluations are linked to intentions to use these tools responsibly. While previous research has largely focused on technology adoption and acceptance, it has paid less attention to the relationship between ethical reasoning and intentions to use these tools responsibly. This study develops and tests an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and moral cognition theory to examine how technology perceptions and academic and cognitive factors relate to students’ ethical reasoning and intentions to use ChatGPT responsibly. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design among business and management students in Oman and analysed the data using structural equation modelling. The findings indicate that perceived ease of use, academic pressure, and moral disengagement are positively associated with ethical reasoning, whereas perceived usefulness is not significantly associated with ethical reasoning. Ethical reasoning is positively associated with behavioural intention to use ChatGPT responsibly. In contrast, ChatGPT usage does not significantly moderate the relationship between academic pressure and ethical reasoning. These findings suggest that students’ responsible-use intentions are associated with their ethical evaluations of ChatGPT-assisted academic practices, while conventional technology acceptance perceptions and usage frequency alone offer a more limited explanation of ethical reasoning. The study contributes to emerging research on responsible generative AI use by extending TAM beyond conventional adoption outcomes and integrating it with a moral cognition perspective. It highlights the relationship between ethical reasoning and responsible-use intentions while distinguishing ethical evaluation from technology acceptance and usage frequency. The findings also provide context-specific evidence from Omani higher education, while recognising the limitations of the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and a context-specific sample.

papers.title: Bridging the Human-AI preference gap: A persuasion-oriented tripartite framework
papers.authors: Mathew S. Isaac, Ajay T. Abraham, Ameiya A. Isaac
papers.abstract: The remarkable performance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems on a wide variety of complex tasks has fueled its rapid adoption in recent years. Yet, many individuals still exhibit a human-AI preference gap, such that they prefer human-generated over AI-generated outputs and follow recommendations made by generative AI (GenAI) less than human advice. We conceptualize the rejection of a superior AI system in favor of an inferior human as a persuasion failure that necessitates psychological rather than technological resolution. Recent research has identified various interventions that compress the human-AI preference gap. We codify these interventions by introducing a persuasion-oriented tripartite framework that delineates three distinct paths by which the preference gap between humans and AI systems may be narrowed: (1) AI-centric interventions, which directly bolster perceptions and evaluations of AI systems; (2) human-centric interventions, which reduce the (often inflated) perceptions and evaluations of humans; and (3) hybrid interventions, which offer an integrated or reformulated alternative that combines human and AI elements. Ultimately, our tripartite framework illustrates how different persuasion tactics fundamentally reshape beliefs and attitudes about both AI and humans, thereby informing system design elements and communication strategies that can bridge the human-AI preference gap.

papers.title: Natural language-driven trust requirement elicitation in intent-based networks
papers.authors: Javier Paredes Serrano, Alfonso Serrano Gil, José María Jorquera Valero, Manuel Gil Pérez
papers.abstract: The telecommunication industry has evolved dramatically in recent years and so has its complexity. Due to that, the research and industry community has put the spotlight on developing innovative tools that automate every aspect related to the network management lifecycle, also known as zero-touch network and service management. One of the activities of the utmost importance associated with automated network management is the selection of network and service providers that are going to form an end-to-end connection, even considering multiple domains. In this vein, a pivotal requirement in the context of 6G heterogeneous networks is the representation of trustworthiness and how trust is associated with each network element and its provider. This article addresses such a challenge with the incorporation of Natural Language Processing to build a trust-oriented interpreter which is ultimately leveraged by intent-based network orchestrators. Specifically, this interpreter is designed to process trust requirements in 6G Cloud Continuum scenarios together with an ad-hoc ontology joining three areas such as intent-based networks, trust management, and Cloud Continuum. The interpreter also minimizes the number of interactions between end-users and our system via a context-aware chatbot. Finally, the experiments showcase a high performance of the proposed language model on a synthetic, hand-annotated dataset comprising hundreds of intent and entity samples, indicating an F1-score above 90% for entity recognition, and above 95% in the case of intent recognition when processing trust requirements on intent-based solutions.

papers.title: More than a loading bar: Conversational silence and anthropomorphic latency cues in mental health chatbots
papers.authors: Shiyi Wang, Han Zhang
papers.abstract: Mental health chatbots increasingly rely on conversational interaction to support users' emotional well-being, yet little is known about how users interpret temporary silence while waiting for system responses. Existing research on social presence and anthropomorphic interaction has primarily focused on conversational content after a response is generated, whereas the waiting phase remains underexplored. Drawing on social presence theory, this study conceptualizes anthropomorphic latency cues as socially meaningful signals that may shape users’ emotional and interactional experiences during temporary conversational silence. Two studies were conducted. Study 1 developed and semantically validated three categories of anthropomorphic latency cues (empathic, effortful, and playful). Study 2 employed a within-subjects laboratory experiment with university students, comparing five latency-cue conditions (text, progress bar, empathic, effortful, and playful) using subjective evaluations, eye-tracking measures, and semi-structured interviews. The results showed that anthropomorphic latency cues were associated with lower anxiety and greater pleasure in several condition-level comparisons relative to non-anthropomorphic feedback. Perceived interaction continuity was significantly associated with reduced anxiety and enhanced pleasure. Within the anthropomorphic conditions, mediation analyses revealed significant indirect associations among perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, and emotional and interactional outcomes. Eye-tracking results indicated longer fixation durations on anthropomorphic latency cues during temporary silence. Qualitative findings further suggested that participants often interpreted latency cues as signals of attentiveness, responsiveness, and interaction continuity rather than merely as technical loading indicators. Overall, temporary conversational silence may function as a socially meaningful phase of AI-mediated interaction rather than a purely technical delay. The study extends social presence research into temporally silent phases of conversational AI interaction and provides preliminary design implications for chatbot-based support systems.

papers.title: Edge-attention graph convolutional network for depression grading via EEG cross-network interaction analysis
papers.authors: Zhenzhen Ru, Jiaxin Tai, Mengyuan Liu, Xu Zhang, Liwei Guo, Ying Cai, Jing Hu, Jin Li, Ning Qiang
papers.abstract: Depression is a serious global social problem. Personalized treatment is an effective way to improve the symptoms of depression. The edge attention graph convolutional network (EAGCN) model of EEG signals effectively extracts features in cross-network interactions for accurate depression grading. This paper proposes a novel fusion method of Time-frequency cooperative functional connectivity (TF-FC) and EAGCN to extract cross-network interaction features. This method employs intrinsic time-scale decomposition (ITD) to extract EEG time-frequency features, constructs whole-brain/intra-network/cross-network TF-FC matrices using Pearson correlation coefficients as edge features, integrates traditional EEG features (Hjorth parameters, PSD) as node features, and inputs them into the EAGCN for grading to establish a fusion model. The results show that with depression severity increasing, the TF-FC connectivity strength decreases. Quantitative analysis shows that the fusion model achieves 93.14% classification accuracy for whole-brain analysis. Especially, the fusion model reaches 97.63% accuracy in VN-VAN and ECN-DMN cross-network interactions. Compared with other methods, our novel fusion method achieves superior performance, ranking among the top positions in the precise classification table. This novel fusion method significantly improves classification accuracy. At the same time, the cross-network interaction features may serve as a novel neurophysiological biomarker for depression severity grading. This study provides a novel theoretical framework and methodological innovation for personalized depression treatment.

papers.title: Cognitive state dependent enhancement of cognitive control with transcranial magnetic stimulation
papers.authors: Aaron N. McInnes, Victoria L Pipia, Kiyana L Maynard, Güldamla Kalender, Alik S. Widge
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is an effective treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), yet variability of therapeutic responses remains high. A key contributor to this variability may be state-dependent effects of brain stimulation, where activity in underlying circuits can shape the propagation of TMS-evoked activity. Thus, constraining the target circuits’ state by engaging cognition may make TMS’ effects more consistent. Objective We tested whether TMS’ effects on cognitive control, a transdiagnostic construct implicated across psychiatric disorders and a putative mediator of TMS efficacy, are state-dependent. Methods Participants (N = 25) completed a context-dependent behavioural assay of cognitive control before and after we delivered rTMS to the prefrontal cortex (PFC). During rTMS, participants performed either the cognitive control task (active-state TMS), or performed a context-independent perceptual task (control-state TMS). We assessed changes in downstream behavioural metrics of circuit function, as well as neural indices of cognitive control measured from electroencephalography (EEG). Results rTMS enhanced downstream readouts of cognitive control only when stimulation was delivered concurrent with the cognitive control task. Similarly, only active-state TMS modulated theta band oscillatory activity, which is thought to be a marker of cognitive control engagement Conclusion These findings demonstrate that TMS’ effects on cognitive control are state-dependent, in which endogenous engagement of PFC-anchored networks can shape the magnitude and functional relevance of TMS-induced plasticity. Considering cognitive states during TMS may therefore offer a framework to enhance and/or accelerate TMS’ therapeutic effects.

papers.title: Neural processing of facial expressions: An ERP study in athletes and non-athletes
papers.authors: Chenxiao Wu, Xueqiao Li, Piia Astikainen
papers.abstract: Facial expressions are important cues for conveying social-emotional information, and their processing unfolds across multiple neural stages. The study employed event-related potentials to examine the neural dynamics of facial-expression change detection while testing the role of sports expertise. It further examined whether N170 responses showed prediction-error-related enhancement. Non-athletes, team-sport athletes, and individual-sport athletes completed ignore- and attend-oddball tasks, with angry and happy faces presented as rare stimulus types (deviants) and neutral faces as the frequent stimulus type (standard). An ignore-equiprobable task provided physically identical, probability-matched control stimuli for angry and happy deviants. For P1 in both oddball conditions, amplitudes were smaller for happy than for angry and neutral faces, suggesting expression-related modulation during early sensory encoding. For N170, amplitudes showed a robust graded pattern (angry > happy > neutral, more negative) in each task condition, indicating sensitivity to expression category during perceptual face representation. For P3b in the attend-oddball condition, amplitudes were larger for angry and happy faces than for neutral faces, and larger for angry than for happy faces, consistent with greater resource allocation to rare emotional targets, particularly angry faces, during task-relevant target detection and stimulus evaluation. Separately, comparison of N170 responses to probability-matched deviant and control stimuli provided no evidence for prediction-error-related N170 enhancement for either angry or happy faces. No reliable modulation by sports expertise was observed in the present sample and task conditions. Overall, multistage neural responses were strongly shaped by expression category, highlighting expression-related effects on early sensory, perceptual, and later evaluative processing.

papers.title: Against speech liberalism for generative AI
papers.authors: Tamara Dobler
papers.abstract: Abstract Speech liberalism holds that the linguistic output of generative AI is continuous with human speech and should therefore be treated as meaningful in broadly the same way. Strong versions of this view take the fluent behaviour of chatbots to justify attributing genuine linguistic and cognitive agency, while nevertheless advocating caution when questions of moral or legal responsibility arise. I argue that this gives too much evidential weight to successful conversational interaction, where speaker intentions largely recede into the background. Once AI-generated speech contributes to serious harm, however, those intentions become central. More broadly, the paper challenges a way of theorising about AI speech that builds classifications of linguistic agency primarily from successful conversational interaction. I develop two independent but complementary arguments. The first is ethical–legal. I argue that classifying chatbot output as speech is not normatively neutral: within existing free-speech doctrine, it risks generating responsibility and liability gaps in cases of AI-mediated harm. The second is epistemic. I argue that the behavioural evidence supporting strong speech liberalism is systematically distorted by anthropomorphic bias, reinforced by AI design practices. The paper concludes that theories of AI speech should not be built exclusively from successful conversational exchanges and that, until a broader evidential case is made, a more conservative approach to AI speech is warranted in high-stakes contexts.

papers.title: Surrogate-Driven Multi-Objective SMEPO Framework for Optimal EEG Channel and Feature Selection in Motor Imagery BCI
papers.authors: Alok Kumar Shukla, Shubhra Dwivedi, Niraj Kumar Dewangan
papers.journal: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
papers.abstract: Abstract Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) hold significant potential in communication, mechatronic control, and rehabilitation. However, existing BCI systems are often expensive, and require laborious preparation. A major challenge in motor imagery (MI)-based BCIs is the effective selection of EEG channels due to the non-stationary, high-dimensional, and subject-specific nature of EEG data. Consequently, most MI-BCI pipelines fail to simultaneously optimise classification accuracy and computational efficiency across subjects. Although nature-inspired algorithms have been explored, they often suffer from premature convergence and poor balance between exploration and exploitation, while conventional methods typically rely on single-objective optimisation that ignores the trade-off between accuracy and model complexity. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the novel Surrogate-Assisted Multi-Objective SMEPO (Emperor Penguin Optimiser) algorithm for efficient EEG channel selection in MI-BCIs. SMEPO integrates temperature-gradient dynamics and adaptive phase-gate scheduling strategy within a multi-objective Pareto archive framework, enabling effective navigation of the complex binary search space while maintaining computational efficiency via a kNN-5 surrogate model. To address inter-subject variability and prevent data leakage, spatial covariance features are extracted using Multivariate Empirical Mode Decomposition (MEMD). Subject-specific normalisation is performed using statistics derived exclusively from the training set. Extensive experiments on three BCI Competition datasets (BCI-IV Dataset 2a, BCI-IV Dataset 1, and BCI-III Dataset IVa) show that SMEPO achieves superior mean SVM accuracies of 85.79%, 83.28%, and 84.75%, respectively, consistently outperforming five state-of-the-art surrogate-assisted multi-objective baselines across SVM, Naïve Bayes, and Decision Tree classifiers. Further validation on eight UCI benchmark datasets confirms that SMEPO wins best accuracy on six out of eight datasets with a mean accuracy of 92.56% and mean feature reduction of 56.2%. These results establish SMEPO as a robust, efficient, and generalisable channel and feature selection solution.

papers.title: Processes of Patterning: AI, Literacy, and the Epistemological Challenge
papers.authors: Henrik Åhman, Claes Thorén
papers.abstract: Abstract This article develops a conceptual analysis of what occurs when central dimensions of literacy are outsourced to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems. Classical conceptions of literacy, sociocultural theories of mediated learning, and postdigital perspectives on knowledge practices, provide the theoretical foundation to further the argument that contemporary AI tools reshape the developmental processes through which judgement, independent thinking, and internal structures of meaning are formed. Using the Swedish AI‑based study platform Tentaklar as an example, we show how tools of this kind redistribute cognitive labour by generating interpretations, structures, and patterns on behalf of learners. Drawing on Aristotle’s phronesis and Vygotsky’s concept of mediation, we argue that externalising literacy to AI in such a way risks producing forms of borrowed judgement , where students are served the products of reasoning without having to go through the interpretive struggle of reasoning. We further propose that a fundamental aspect of literacy lies in patterning , the developmental process through which individuals reason and organise complexity into meaningful structures. We argue that AI‑mediated study tools risk undermining the conditions under which such patterning can occur. The article concludes by outlining design principles for AI systems that support rather than replace processes through which human judgement and pattern‑formation develop.

papers.title: AMGFM: A multimodal fusion model for depression identification based on adversarial metric learning

papers.title: Sensory gamma entrainment in older adults with or without cognitive impairment: a systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis
papers.authors: Myeonghae Hyun, Yeseung Park, Seo Yoon Park, Ki Woong Kim
papers.abstract: Gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS) is a noninvasive approach under investigation in older adults with and without cognitive impairment, including Alzheimer’s disease; however, human evidence remains scattered across structural, functional, biomarker, electrophysiological, and cognitive domains. We searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science for English-language articles published from January 2016 to December 2025, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a retrospectively registered PROSPERO protocol. Eligible studies evaluated non-invasive sensory gamma-frequency stimulation in adults aged $$\ge$$ 60 years, including Alzheimer’s disease-spectrum and cognitively normal older adults, with quantitative outcomes reported in at least one relevant domain. Narrative synthesis was the primary approach, supplemented by an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of hippocampal and ventricular volume change. Eight studies were included, spanning single-session to 6-month interventions. Findings were directionally favorable across domains but derived from small, heterogeneous studies with nonoverlapping outcomes. Fluid biomarker evidence was limited to exploratory immune-related findings from a single uncontrolled study. Controlled structural studies suggested possible attenuation of hippocampal atrophy, ventricular enlargement, and white matter decline. Functional connectivity findings suggested possible preservation of connectivity in Alzheimer’s disease-relevant networks. Electroencephalography studies supported target engagement, with entrainment strength and propagation varying according to stimulation parameters and individual characteristics. Cognitive findings from small exploratory studies did not establish a consistent benefit. Exploratory pooled effects for ventricular and hippocampal volume change were favorable but not robust to conservative sensitivity analysis. Human evidence for GENUS is promising but preliminary and hypothesis-generating; larger, adequately powered, standardized trials are needed before firm efficacy conclusions can be drawn.

papers.title: Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research
papers.authors: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich
papers.abstract: Abstract Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) may transform the nature of science (NOS). These transformations may extend to science education research, where AI methodologies increasingly enable scalable, reproducible, and fine‑grained analyses of student learning. To reflect on potential transformations that AI methodologies may bring to science education research, we draw on Hasok Chang’s notion of epistemic iteration , in which successive stages of knowledge build iteratively on one another to achieve specific epistemic aims. Anchored in this notion, and further illustrated by the historical development of thermometers, this article proposes and applies a framework for reflecting on how AI methodologies may transform the nature of science education research. The framework comprises seven phases: (1) problem framing, (2) instrumentation and measurement, (3) experimentation and evidence‑based inference, (4) comparisons and replication, (5) building norms and consensus, (6) implementation and its consequences, and (7) continuous refinement. For each phase, we analyze how AI methodologies may transform the nature of science education research and draw parallels to historical explorations of temperature. Our analysis suggests that the field may currently be amid an epistemic iteration, in which AI methodologies may advance scientific inquiry within the field. Simultaneously, AI methodologies may contribute to prioritizing different epistemic aims, epistemic criteria, and epistemic practices compared with traditional methods. By recognizing these potential transformations and drawing on lessons from the history and philosophy of science, we evaluate how AI methodologies may impact how science education research is done to ensure that promising avenues for future research are epistemically well grounded.

papers.title: Objects as Means of Sustainability Knowledge Co-Creation: Working on Value-Laden Issues Across the Research-Practice Boundary
papers.authors: Karelia Dagnaud, Minna Halme, Linda Lisa Maria Turunen, Jarkko Levänen
papers.abstract: Abstract The negative sustainability impacts of business keep escalating despite the profusion of research-based evidence regarding problems and solution pathways. Sustainability knowledge is complex and value-laden, thus often difficult to act upon. Co-creation between researchers and practitioners stands as a fruitful means of making sustainability knowledge more actionable, yet we lack insight into what motivates and facilitates sustainability knowledge co-creation. Boundary objects, which assist collaboration among diverse groups, can facilitate knowledge co-creation between researchers and practitioners, but little is known of their workings in the context of tackling value-laden sustainability issues. Based on rich qualitative data from two empirical cases, we examine how boundary objects motivate and facilitate knowledge co-creation between practitioners and researchers, helping to make sustainability knowledge more actionable. Our analysis illuminates three main dynamics whereby boundary objects do so: boundary objects initiate dialogue on complex issues through conveying clarity, provide a physical realm for co-creation in a value-laden domain, and motivate participation despite ethical vulnerability. These insights elaborate and challenge previous research regarding the boundary object ambiguity-clarity tension in the context of sustainability knowledge co-creation among diverse actor groups. Specifically, our findings foreground boundary object clarity, rather than ambiguity, in helping to initiate dialogue on complex sustainability issues. Furthermore, our analysis extends understanding of participant motivations to engage in sustainability knowledge co-creation, indicating that objects provide instrumental value and more intrinsic learning value, as well as help parties be with ethical vulnerability induced by knowledge co-creation around value-laden issues.

papers.title: OsteoCHAT: real-world patient evaluation and benchmarking of a guideline-grounded osteoporosis chatbot
papers.authors: Nils Schulz, Martin Gehlen, Karin Mahn, Björn Bühring, Paula Hoff, Olga Seifert, Edgar Wiebe, Asarnusch Rashid, Sebastian Kuhn, Frank Buttgereit, Alexander Pfeil, Peter Oelzner, Uwe Lange, Johannes Knitza, Philipp Klemm
papers.abstract: Patients with osteoporosis have information needs that routine care inconsistently addresses. In this multicenter real-world evaluation, the LLM-based, guideline-grounded chatbot OsteoCHAT showed high participant acceptability and achieved expert-rated answer quality comparable to general-purpose LLMs. Despite challenges in complex treatment and safety-related topics, guideline-grounded chatbots may represent useful educational adjuncts. PURPOSE: Patients with osteoporosis have information needs that routine care inconsistently addresses. Guideline-grounded chatbots may offer scalable educational support METHODS: We developed OsteoCHAT, a retrieval-augmented conversational system based on the current German osteoporosis guideline, and conducted a multicenter evaluation at seven centers in Germany. Participants interacted with OsteoCHAT, provided real-time feedback on individual responses, and completed a standardized questionnaire assessing usability, comprehensibility, usefulness, trust, perceived quality, and preference over conventional internet search. In parallel, OsteoCHAT was benchmarked against three general-purpose large language models (LLMs) using ten osteoporosis frequently asked questions derived from the BfO patient guideline as the gold standard. Five clinical experts independently rated these responses across five domains, each scored 0-3. RESULTS: Overall, 1,075 question-answer interactions were recorded. Of 389 individually rated responses, 379 (97.4%) received positive feedback. Among 217 complete questionnaire responses, 84.3% rated answers as easily understandable, 79.8% found OsteoCHAT easy to use, 77.2% perceived time savings, and 78.7% considered it a useful addition to existing educational materials. Trust was comparatively lower (64.7% agreement). Blinded expert benchmarking showed acceptable-to-high-quality responses across all LLMs (median total scores 14/15 for Gemini, ChatGPT, and OsteoCHAT and 13/15 for Meta AI), with expert-identified weaknesses mainly concerning pharmacological treatment indication and communication of adverse and rare safety-critical events. CONCLUSION: OsteoCHAT demonstrated high user acceptability and usability in a real-world multicenter evaluation, was rated as a valuable addition to existing educational materials, and achieved expert-rated response quality comparable to general-purpose LLMs, although limitations in safety communication were identified across all examined systems.

papers.title: More than we can make: generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming
papers.authors: Amit Raphael Zoran
papers.abstract: Abstract Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions. Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures. The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them. Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured. The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

papers.title: Tricky trade-offs on a transparency spectrum: how the Financial Times approaches transparency about AI use in news
papers.authors: Liz Lohn, Felix M. Simon
papers.abstract: Abstract As news organisations adopt artificial intelligence (AI), they face growing pressure to be transparent about when and how it is used—yet practical approaches remain uneven. This paper examines AI transparency through an in-depth case study of the Financial Times (FT). Drawing on 13 semi-structured interviews with 12 senior managers across editorial, product, data science, and communications, together with internal documents, we show that the FT approaches transparency as a hybrid of policy, process, and practice, framed by a desire to safeguard both internal and external trust. Transparency is calibrated to context: internally, AI use is signposted in tools and reinforced through training and personal accountability; externally, the prominence of disclosure scales with system autonomy and editorial oversight, with stronger labelling for no-human-in-the-loop features than for AI-assisted, journalist-edited outputs. We identify nine factors that shape audience-facing disclosure—legal/provider requirements, industry benchmarking, nature of the task, human oversight, system novelty, audience expectations, perceived risk, commercial sensitivities, and design constraints—and five crosscutting challenges, including site-wide consistency (especially on mobile) and potential “transparency backfire.” Conceptually, our analysis links AI transparency to isomorphic pressures and to intersecting institutional logics. We argue that AI transparency in news is best understood as a spectrum, evolving with technological advancements, commercial, professional and ethical considerations and shifting audience attitudes.

papers.title: Scn1a ‐mediated developmental regulation of prefrontal cortex plasticity and cognition
papers.authors: Maurizio S. Riga, Mercedes Pérez‐Fernández, Yuniesky Andrade‐Talavera, Benito Domínguez-Velasco, Rodriguez-Moreno Antonio, Manuel Álvarez‐Dolado
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1, encoded by Scn1a, is essential for γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic function, and its alteration is associated with neurological disorders such as Dravet syndrome and Alzheimer's disease. We previously demonstrated that local Nav1.1 dysfunction in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) during adolescence causes epilepsy, cognitive deficits, and depressive-like behaviors. Here, to investigate putative developmental differences, we analyzed whether Nav1.1 dysfunction in the adult mPFC produces comparable phenotypic outcomes. METHODS: Nav1.1 dysfunction was selectively induced in the adult mPFC via conditional expression of a mutant human SCN1A variant. We then analyzed PFC-related cognitive tasks and depressive-like behaviors; epileptic and oscillatory activity using in vivo electroencephalography (EEG) recordings; and ex vivo synaptic plasticity in mPFC circuits. RESULTS: As observed after adolescent Nav1.1 dysfunction, adult manipulation induced epileptic activity and depressive-like phenotypes. However, mPFC-dependent cognitive functions remained intact, unlike adolescent mice, which showed impaired working memory and fear extinction. Electrophysiological recordings revealed distinct mPFC oscillatory patterns. Adult Nav1.1 dysfunction reduced sleep-related delta mPFC power and dorsal hippocampus (dHPC)-mPFC coherence, mimicking adolescent patterns. In contrast, no alteration in mPFC oscillatory activity was observed during wakefulness, differing from adolescent mice. IN addition, synaptic plasticity analyses showed that adolescent-but not adult-Nav1.1 dysfunction impaired long-term potentiation (LTP) at cortical L2/3-L2/3 prelimbic synapses. Moreover, LTP was sensitive to Nav1.1 pharmacological activation only in adolescent mice. SIGNIFICANCE: These findings reveal a developmental role for Nav1.1 activity in mPFC plasticity and cognition, whereas in adulthood, it remains critical for regulating network stability and depressive-like behaviors.

papers.title: Vibe Coding for Simulation Development in Engineering Education
papers.authors: Poramate Tarasak, Wipawadee Wongsuwan, Pongsatorn Sedtheetorn
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Simulation‐based learning is widely adopted in engineering education because it enables learners to explore complex engineering systems through interactive and self‐paced learning. However, developing educational simulations traditionally requires both domain expertise and software development skills. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have introduced vibe coding , in which software is created primarily through natural‐language prompting, potentially lowering the technical barrier to educational simulation development. While existing research mainly focuses on AI‐assisted programming from either a practical or a learning perspective, this study presents a preliminary investigation of vibe coding for developing educational simulations through two undergraduate engineering case studies: one in automotive engineering and the other in communication engineering. A practical workflow for simulation development is proposed, and the development process is analyzed to identify both its benefits and challenges. The findings demonstrate that functional web‐based educational simulations can be developed efficiently without requiring extensive programming or prompt engineering expertise. However, the study also shows that instructors remain responsible for validating engineering concepts, verifying simulation behavior, and diagnosing conceptual implementation errors that could not be resolved through iterative prompting alone. Furthermore, the developed simulations were found to align with established simulation design principles reported in the literature. The findings suggest that AI‐assisted vibe coding can substantially reduce the technical barriers to educational simulation development while preserving the central role of educators in instructional design and domain‐specific validation.

papers.title: AI-Based Information-Seeking Behavior as a Mediator between Metacognition and Students' Academic Achievement
papers.authors: Noer Hidayah, Noer Fitria Putra Setyono
papers.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in learning has become widespread among university students to enhance material comprehension. How deeply and effectively students search for information using AI is largely determined by their metacognitive abilities. This study aims to examine: (1) the effect of metacognition on AI-based information-seeking behavior, (2) the effect of AI-based information-seeking behavior on academic achievement (GPA), (3) the effect of metacognition on GPA, and (4) the mediating role of AI-based information-seeking behavior in the relationship between metacognition and GPA. A quantitative approach was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) executed via the seminr package in R. The study population comprised students at UIN Syekh Wasil Kediri, using a cluster sampling technique representing all faculties (n = 273). The findings revealed that metacognition has a positive and significant effect on AI-based information-seeking behavior (β = 0.472, t = 10.856). However, metacognition did not significantly affect GPA (β = 0.116, t = 0.971), and AI-based information-seeking behavior likewise showed no significant effect on GPA (β = 0.040, t = 0.907). Consequently, AI-based information-seeking behavior does not mediate the relationship between metacognition and academic achievement. Therefore, higher education institutions should design AI literacy initiatives that focus on higher-order information processing to ensure technology utilization translates directly into enhanced academic outcomes.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Reader Response Theory: A Culturally Responsive Approach to Inclusive Indonesian Literature Education
papers.authors: Ekarini Saraswati
papers.abstract: Indonesian literature education is increasingly oriented to consider students' diverse cultural backgrounds, language abilities, and learning processes. However, at present, literature teaching is based on culturally homogeneous literature knowledge and reading skills, so students have difficulty understanding literary texts that are entangled in complex historical, sociocultural, and linguistic contexts. This study addresses the integration of AI with Reader Response Theory (RRT) in Indonesian literature education to promote more inclusive reading. It considers whether AI-supported features (contextual annotation, automated translation, text-to-speech, and adaptive learning paths) can help students construct personal meanings while preserving the central RRT notion that literary meaning is delivered through transactions between the reader and text. Five Indonesian literature works (Bumi Manusia and Arus Balik by Pramoedya Ananta Toer, Gadis Kretek by Ratih Kumala, Robohnya Surau Kami by A.A. Navis, and Layar Terkembang by Sutan Takdir Alisjahbana) are used to illustrate the proposed approach. Our research implies that AI-enhanced reader response helps make culturally and contextually unique knowledge available, and more individualised reader interaction with cultural symbols, historical events/experiences, and social issues. However, excessive technological intervention could hinder reading and the affective, dialogic, and interpretive aspects of literary experience. We therefore propose an AI-Enhanced Culturally Responsive Reader Response framework that considers AI as a replacement for reader agency and rather, an adaptive interpretive scaffold for students and teachers. This approach is relevant to AI-based humanities education by relating technological accessibility, cultural responsiveness, and reader agency as interweaving aspects of inclusive literature learning in contemporary education.

papers.title: Separating the Art from the Algorithm: Detecting Moral Decoupling in Consumer Discourse About Generative AI
papers.authors: Julius Mboli, Onuchukwu Joseph Chimezie
papers.abstract: Some consumers who learn that a generative AI tool was trained on creative work taken without consent condemn the practice and stop using it. Others condemn it and keep using it. The second response is moral decoupling: separating judgements about wrongdoing from judgements about usefulness. The construct is established in laboratory research but has not been measured in naturally occurring discourse. We present a stance detection study of 7,371 Reddit posts from three professional communities differently exposed to generative AI. Each post is human-annotated on two axes, stance toward AI content and type of justification, with decoupling operationalised as a supportive stance co-occurring with explicit ethical acknowledgement. Across five calibration rounds, two annotators reached Cohen’s kappa of 0.654 on stance and 0.621 on argument type; GPT-4o, given the same guidelines, reached 0.058 and 0.209 and never used the MIXED label. Fine-tuned RoBERTa reached macro-F1 of 0.63 and 0.82. Moral positions differ sharply across communities (V = 0.23), and among engaged posts the decoupling-coupling balance differs too (V = 0.15). Marketers rarely engage morally at all, whereas artists produce most moral reasoning and resolve it against the tools three times in four. Involvement governs primarily whether ethical evaluation happens; secondarily, which way it falls.

papers.title: Technical Challenges and Solutions for Building Augmented Reality for Education 1 st
papers.authors: Mohammed Oussama Seddini, Hamza Falih Mohamed, Mohamed Ez-Zaouia, Iza Marfisi, Saifuddin Khalid Md
papers.journal: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
papers.abstract: Augmented and Mixed Reality (AR/MR) applications are increasingly utilized in education to facilitate situated, interactive, and multimodal learning. However, the technical production of these experiences remains non-trivial, particularly for authoring tools designed to enable teachers to build custom activities without programming skills. Furthermore, while web-based deployment advances open access and cross-device sustainability, it introduces strict browser, performance, and data management constraints. This paper presents a developerperspective case study of MIXAP, a browser-based, open-access AR/MR authoring application developed within the MIXAP-EU project. We document the key architectural and software design decisions, including the choice of React, MindAR.js, and an offline-first RxDB database architecture, designed to survive erratic school network infrastructures and heterogeneous device environments. Rather than evaluating student learning gains, this work focuses on how strict pedagogical requirements were translated into technical design solutions, addressing engineering compromises around marker quality recognition, layout complexity, data sovereignty, and Generative AI integration via compliant Mistral models. By triangulating teacher-originated requirements with the technical rationale and trade-offs derived from developer focus groups, this paper synthesizes holistic design insights for sustainable educational technology.

papers.title: Telecom-Specific Small Language Models for Root-Cause Analysis
papers.authors: Y. Fan, S. A. R. Zaidi, M. Hafeez
papers.journal: White Rose Research Online (University of Leeds, The University of Sheffield, University of York)
papers.abstract: AbstractÐFault localization is a fundamental task for reliable and automated telecommunication network operation, while root-cause analysis (RCA) goes a step further by identifying the underlying cause of an observed network fault.Recent large language model (LLM)-based RCA approaches provide strong diagnostic capability but can be computationally expensive for deployment.This paper investigates whether such capability can be distilled into a compact small language model (SLM).We formulate TeleLogs RCA as an eight-class closedset classification problem and distil diagnostic knowledge from an OTel-LLM-8.3Bteacher into a LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5Bstudent with a sequence-classification head.Under a strict train/validation/test protocol, the two-stage knowledge-distillation (KD) student achieves 84.72% accuracy and 83.59% macro-F1.Its dominant failure is confusion between excessive serving-cell downtilt (C1) and higher-throughput neighbouring-cell coverage (C3), producing 97 direct class swaps.We therefore introduce a lightweight evidence-aware specialist that explicitly binds drivetest measurements to engineering parameters.The hierarchical system reaches 94.44% accuracy using four interpretable features and 95.49% using the full structured representation, reducing C1/C3 swaps from 97 to 4. Controlled perturbations further reveal severe SLM sensitivity to telemetry serialization, while the structured evidence remains invariant for all 864 test samples, localizing the remaining robustness bottleneck to SLM-based routing.The student also reduces peak GPU memory by 4.53× and improves throughput by 1.51× over the teacher.These results demonstrate both the deployment potential of compact telecomspecific SLMs and the importance of explicit relational evidence processing for reliable RCA.

papers.title: Influence of Model Voice Cues and Hearing Impairment on Behavioural and Cortical Responses to the Pitch Shift Reflex
papers.authors: Tony; id_orcid 0009-0005-2919-320X Schelhorn, Benjamin Peschel, Wieling Martijn, Ulrich Hoppe, Dollinger Michael, Defne Abur
papers.journal: University of Groningen research database (University of Groningen / Centre for Information Technology)
papers.abstract: Background: Altered auditory feedback (AAF) tasks can grant insights into neural control of speech, including how auditory perceptual information influences speech motor production. In AAF tasks, participants are asked to produce speech while their auditory feedback (via headphones) is shifted in realtime (e.g., the pitch is increased). Speakers typically respond by opposing the shift (e.g., lowering their own vocal pitch) but there is high variability in responses. To reduce vocal variability, model voice cues can be used, wherein speakers hear a model voice before each trial. However, it is not clear how the distance between a speaker’s habitual pitch and the pitch of the model voice (’pitch distance’) impacts responses. The current study assessed how pitch distance influenced behavioural and cortical responses as well as voice stability during an AAF experiment. Given that this relationship may vary with the degree of auditory feedback, the task was evaluated in speakers with differing hearing status. Methods: Participants with typical hearing (N = 20; 13 female, 7 male, median age: 61 years) and with bilateral sensory-neural hearing impairment of ≥ 40 dBHL (N = 15; 5 female, 10 male, median age: 76 years) completed the study. All participants completed written consent in accordance with the ethical review board of the Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (no.: 423_20 B). Habitual pitch was calculated by averaging fundamental frequency across two speech tasks (counting from 20 to 30, and producing the vowel /a/). Voice stability parameters were calculated from 40 baseline (no shift) productions of the vowel /a/ during the experiment. In the AAF experiment, a model voice cue (/a/) was presented before each trial (with a pitch of 220 Hz for female and 110 Hz for male) and participants were instructed to match it. Between 1 - 1.3 seconds later, a +2 semitone pitch shift was applied in the headphone feedback. This was repeated for 40 trials. Responses were measured behaviourally (fundamental frequency via microphone) and cortically (N1 and P2 responses via EEG). Linear mixed effects models were used to analyse the impact of pitch distance, speaker group, and sex on behavioural and cortical responses and voice stability parameters. Results: Pitch distance had a significant effect across observed parameters for the typical hearing group (p < 0.001), but not the hearing impaired group (p = 0.822). In both groups, female participants had lower habitual pitches (mean: 180.5 Hz) compared to the female model voice cue. Conclusion: Model voice cues can reduce voice variability for AAF experiments; however, the perceptual pitch distance can influence responses and voice stability. Future work should directly compare responses with and without a model voice to determine comparability of AAF findings using voice cues.

papers.title: AI-Driven Customer Relationship Management: Exploring Its Influence on Customer Experience and Customer Loyalty
papers.authors: Dr. Danil M. Carter M. Carter
papers.journal: International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Studies
papers.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly changed the way organizations manage customer relationships, communicate with consumers, and deliver personalized services. Traditional customer relationship management (CRM) systems primarily focused on storing customer information, tracking interactions, and supporting sales and service activities. The integration of AI has expanded these capabilities by enabling organizations to analyze large volumes of customer data, predict customer needs, automate interactions, personalize recommendations, and provide real-time support. As a result, AI-driven CRM has become an important strategic capability for organizations seeking to improve customer experience and strengthen customer loyalty. This study examines the influence of AI-driven customer relationship management on customer experience and customer loyalty. The study develops a conceptual model in which AI-driven CRM is considered an antecedent of customer experience, while customer experience is expected to contribute to customer loyalty. The study draws upon previous research on AI in marketing, CRM, customer experience, technology adoption, service quality, and relationship marketing. A quantitative research design is proposed, using a structured questionnaire to collect data from customers who have interacted with AI-enabled CRM technologies such as chatbots, virtual assistants, recommendation systems, personalized marketing platforms, and automated customer service systems. The proposed analysis uses reliability and validity assessment followed by Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The conceptual framework proposes that AI-driven CRM improves customer experience through personalization, responsiveness, convenience, predictive service, and interaction quality. Improved customer experience is expected to strengthen customer loyalty by increasing customers' willingness to repurchase, remain with an organization, and recommend its products or services. The study also discusses the importance of balancing technological automation with human interaction, transparency, privacy, and customer trust. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI-enabled CRM by highlighting customer experience as an important mechanism connecting AI capabilities with long-term customer relationship outcomes.

papers.title: CSIR: Contextually and Socially Informed Robots for Efficient Person Goal Navigation
papers.authors: Tyler Chung, Nahl Farhan, Hao Zhang, Munan Yuan, Jinjun Shan, Amy Wu, Yue Hu
papers.abstract: We address the Person Goal Navigation (PersonNav) problem, enabling robots to search for people under realistic constraints on information accessibility and language uncertainty. This tackles the current solutions revolving around rigid person finding systems requiring exact knowledge of the individual for item-delivery in indoor settings. While the focus in literature is on learned methods using unavailable public or sparse data due to human privacy. We propose a planning framework that combines distance and semantic information about the recipient (habits and intent) weighted by the trust of the user-provided information. A synthetic benchmark of scenarios is also developed including actors, items, and requests to evaluate performance before real-world deployment aiming to simulate natural language human-robot interactions. Results show our informed search outperforms classical distance-based graph baselines, while semantics alone lead to ungrounded, sporadic search. Our method achieves strong gains over baselines, with an LLM-based variant performing comparably, and its explicit belief representation naturally supports future Bayesian filtering. Hardware tests demonstrate our method supports real-world embodiment able to leverage between semantic and distance information in a real setting. This work moves toward more intelligent mobile service agents capable of human-like, informed search in realistic environments to be leveraged in day-to-day use. https://anonymous.4open.science/r/personnavsite-4ED2/index.html.

papers.title: Not Until the Evidence Says So: Teaching LLM Investigators When to Close a Case
papers.authors: Tingzhu Bi, Ping Wang, Meng Ma
papers.abstract: Accident, defect and outage investigations end with a decision that ordinary question answering never faces: whether the evidence gathered so far is enough to close the case. We study this decision for LLM investigators, which request evidence from a case file, revise their hypotheses, and either close the case with a conclusion grounded in what they read or leave it open and name what is missing. This judgment does not come with capability: an untrained 9B model overstates its evidence in 97% of its answers, and a frontier model that identifies the right cause in 84% of cases still overstates in 91% and closes 17 of the 41 cases whose official finding is "cause undetermined". Measuring it is also non-trivial: the source of a case largely predicts its label, and a rule that reads only the source reaches 83.0 balanced accuracy on our test cases.
