papers.authors: ‎ Humairoh, S. Asriah Immawati, Eni Suharti
papers.abstract: Utilizing information technology is crucial for enhancing the competitiveness of MSMEs. An emerging innovation is the utilization of chatbots, which facilitate automated communication between businesses and customers. The objective of this study is to assess the impact of ease perceptions, usefulness perceptions, information quality, and chatbot implementation on the revenue growth of MSMEs) in Banten Province. The objective of this study is to provide empirical evidence demonstrating the positive impact of chatbots on customer service, operational efficiency, and ultimately the income of MSMEs. The study’s sample consisted of 230 participants from eight cities within the Banten Province region. The data collection method involved sending G Forms to MSME business actors who utilize chatbots, using nonprobability sampling techniques. Based on the gathered MSMEs that used chatbots experienced a 24% increase in their revenue within one month. The findings indicate that perceived ease, perceived usefulness, and information quality significantly influence the adoption of chatbots, leading to a subsequent increase in income for MSMEs. This study is expected to enhance the growth of MSMEs in Banten Province, particularly in the utilization of AI chatbot digital technology.

papers.title: Obesity-related social stigma and its social, psychological, and health implications among Saudi women in clinical settings: A cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Saleh Bin Al-Rumaih, Nahlah Ali R Alsulami
papers.abstract: Obesity-related social stigma is increasingly recognized as a structural psychosocial determinant of health, yet empirical evidence from Middle Eastern clinical settings remains limited. This study aimed to examine the associations between obesity-related social stigma and social, psychological, and health-related implications among Saudi women attending bariatric and obesity medicine clinics in Jeddah. A cross-sectional correlational design was employed. Data were collected from 220 Saudi women with overweight or obesity (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m²) attending obesity medicine clinics in two governmental hospitals in Jeddah between January and December 2025. Validated and researcher-developed scales were used to assess obesity-related stigma, negative social identity, selective social withdrawal, engagement in stigmatizing behaviors, psychological security, self-criticism, binge eating, and adoption of extreme weight-loss methods. Internal consistency reliability ranged from α = 0.766 to α = 0.945. Pearson correlation coefficients and multiple linear regression models with HC3 robust standard errors were estimated, controlling for BMI, age, education level, income, and employment status. Stigma was significantly and positively associated with adverse outcomes across all social, psychological, and health-related domains (all p < 0.001). Following adjustment for BMI and sociodemographic covariates, stigma remained a statistically significant independent predictor of all outcome dimensions, with standardized coefficients ranging from β = 0.733 to β = 0.799 and explained variance ranging from 59% to 72%. These findings indicate that obesity-related stigma functions as an independent psychosocial risk factor among Saudi women in clinical settings. Obesity-management programmes should integrate stigma-reduction strategies, psychological screening, and stigma-sensitive healthcare training alongside standard biomedical treatment.

papers.title: Human–AI Collaboration in Academic Writing Instruction: Calibrated Feedback Model for EAP
papers.authors: Reza Farzi
papers.abstract: This study adopts a mixed-methods design to compare the feedback generated by a human instructor and ChatGPT-3.5 on student essays. It analyzes scoring consistency, students’ perceptions of feedback usefulness, and the extent to which each form of feedback aligns with instructional objectives. The dataset comprises 30 first-year students enrolled in a Canadian English for Academic Purposes (EAP) course. Each student submitted two argumentative essays, which were evaluated independently by both the instructor and ChatGPT-3.5 across three calibration stages. The findings suggest that while ChatGPT-3.5 consistently identified surface-level issues and demonstrated close alignment with human scoring, it was less effective in addressing rhetorical structure and contextual nuance. Student responses indicated a clear preference for a hybrid feedback model, which combines the immediacy of AI-generated comments with the depth and pedagogical value of instructor feedback. Through calibrated prompts and pedagogical (re-)framing, GenAI can supplement human feedback effectively but will not replace it. This study puts forward a hybrid model of feedback provision in which language instructors can leverage GenAI to support formative assessment while maintaining pedagogical oversight. The findings offer guidance for integrating GenAI into academic writing instruction in ways that preserve instructional quality and student agency.

papers.title: The Potential Impacts of Artificial Intelligence on Preoperative Optimization and Predicting Risks of Morbidity and Mortality: A Narrative Focused Review
papers.authors: Tetsuro Sakai, James Harvey Jones
papers.abstract: Preoperative optimization clinics enhance surgical outcomes by optimizing patients' health, reducing unnecessary tests, and minimizing cancellations. Artificial intelligence (AI) now promises to further advance these efforts by improving predictive modeling, automating risk assessments, and enabling personalized care strategies. AI models have shown particular strength in predicting postoperative complications, such as cardiovascular events. Tools like natural language processing (NLP) have also improved risk detection for conditions like alcohol misuse. The historical development of preoperative clinics-from Dr. J Alfred Lee's initial concept in 1949 to modern models like Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) and Anesthesia Preoperative Evaluation Clinic (APEC)-laid the groundwork for today's integration of electronic health records (EHRs) and decision-support systems, now evolving toward AI-driven care. Machine-learning algorithms have proven superior to traditional models for predicting postoperative anemia, opioid dependence, diabetes complications, and mortality risks, thus offering precise stratification and resource optimization. Specific applications include AI-assisted anemia management, penicillin allergy delabelling, and opioid use prediction after major surgeries. AI also enhances patient education through tools like ChatGPT and improves smoking cessation efforts using conversational AI. NLP has demonstrated better accuracy than standard International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes in identifying risky alcohol use (>2 standard drinks per day before surgery). However, barriers to widespread adoption include data privacy, algorithmic bias, and clinician skepticism. Future studies should focus on validating AI models across diverse populations and integrating AI recommendations within clinical workflows while adhering to evolving regulatory standards. Ultimately, AI's incorporation into preoperative assessments could significantly boost the efficiency and impact of clinic resources, potentially shifting outcomes more favorably by improving the slope of resource utilization versus patient outcome curves. Continued research and refinement are essential for AI to achieve its full potential in perioperative medicine.

papers.title: Regulating the Self, Orchestrating Interaction, and Acting Responsibly: A Positive Computing Perspective on Digital Wellbeing in GenAI-IDLE
papers.authors: Xiaoqi Wang
papers.abstract: This project examines digital wellbeing (DW) in generative artificial intelligence-mediated informal digital learning of English (GenAI-IDLE). Drawing on the positive computing framework, the study investigates the roles of GenAI-supported self-regulated learning, student–student interaction, student–teacher interaction, student–GenAI interaction, and perceived GenAI responsibility in shaping DW among Chinese EFL learners. Data were collected from 281 participants and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) to examine both predictive relationships and necessary conditions. The project materials include the English and Chinese versions of the measures used in the study and related analytical results. These materials are made openly available to support transparency, reproducibility, and future research on GenAI-mediated informal language learning and digital wellbeing.

papers.title: Performing With AI, Learning Without It? A Cross-Domain Meta-Analysis of the Gap Between AI-Assisted Performance and Unassisted Learning in Generative AI Experiments
papers.authors: Song Zhou
papers.abstract: Learning research distinguishes performance during practice from learning - the durable change that supports later independent performance. Generative AI can raise performance while it is available, but cognitive offloading, the generation effect, desirable difficulties, and metacognitive laziness all predict that this gain will not carry over, and may reverse, when AI is withdrawn. This registered systematic review and multivariate three-level meta-analysis codes, for every eligible experiment, whether AI was available during the outcome test. It pools (a) effects on assisted performance (g_A) and (b) effects on unassisted learning (g_U: immediate, delayed retention, near transfer, far transfer), estimates the within-experiment performance-learning gap (Delta = g_A - g_U) using experiments that report both outcomes, and tests theory-derived moderators: AI design (unrestricted answer-giving vs. guardrailed/tutoring vs. attempt-first), mode of use (substitutive vs. complementary), retention interval, and prior knowledge. Domains span mathematics, programming, writing, reading, reasoning, and professional skills; adult laboratory and crowdsourced experiments are included alongside student samples. The design supports later living updates every 6 months. Coded data and R scripts will be posted on OSF.

papers.title: Blamed Less for Acting, More for Failing to Act? A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Third-Party Blame, Responsibility, and Punishment for Human Versus AI Agents
papers.authors: Song Zhou
papers.abstract: People increasingly evaluate actions taken by AI systems, robots, algorithms, and automated vehicles, and theories of moral judgment make opposing predictions about how such agents are judged relative to humans: mind-perception theory predicts LESS blame, responsibility, and punishment for AI agents; norm-expectation accounts predict no overall difference but a specific asymmetry whereby AI agents that fail to act are blamed MORE than humans who do the same; and blame theory predicts larger human-machine differences for blame-type judgments than for norm judgments. This registered systematic review and three-level meta-analysis synthesizes third-party judgment experiments that hold the act or outcome constant and vary only the agent (human vs. AI/robot/algorithm/automated vehicle), across paradigms (transgressions, accidents and errors, discrimination, service failures, moral dilemmas). Judgment type (norm vs. blame vs. responsibility vs. punishment) is the primary moderator; the agent x action/inaction interaction is tested directly with interaction contrasts; intentionality, outcome severity, moral domain, agent type, anthropomorphism manipulations, and cultural region are further moderators. The literature is covered through 2026, including Chinese-language studies and marketing, public-administration, and transport literatures. The dilemma-permissibility subset that overlaps with the prior meta-analysis by Hill-Cousins et al. (2026) is reported separately and compared with their estimate.

papers.title: Old Tales, New Skills: Exploring the Influence of Fables on EFL Writing Performance
papers.authors: Verónica Espinoza-Celi, Gina Camacho-Minuche, Eva Ulehlova
papers.journal: Theory and Practice in Language Studies
papers.abstract: This quasi-experimental mixed-methods study investigated the efficacy of integrating fables into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction to enhance high school students’ writing proficiency and critical thinking. Conducted with 65 A1-level learners aged 15–16, this research employed pre- and post-tests to evaluate improvements in paragraph structure, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary range, and critical problem-solving skills. At the outset, participants demonstrated difficulties with verb tense consistency, sentence construction, and the logical organization of ideas. Thus, an eight-week intervention was implemented, using a series of fable-based activities that included moral interpretation, character analysis, and narrative reconstruction, providing repetitive and contextualized input and opportunities for meaningful writing practice. Results showed that this scaffolded approach significantly softened initial problems, leading to marked gains in writing coherence, cohesion, lexical diversity, syntactical precision, and expansion of vocabulary. Furthermore, the tasks were effective in enhancing critical thinking, students learned to formulate and justify arguments, interpret implicit messages, analyze narrative structures, and consider alternative perspectives. Students also strengthened their ability to evaluate information and recognize biases, producing more well-supported written responses. These findings affirmed fables as a powerful tool that effectively harmonizes linguistic development with critical reasoning. The study suggests further research into integrating AI with story-based writing activities to promote creativity and differentiated instruction.

papers.title: Plataforma da Diversidade Linguística Brasileira: repositório de dados linguísticos para uma inteligência artificial soberana
papers.authors: Márcia dos Santos Machado Vieira, Raquel Meister Ko. Freitag, Juliana Bertucci Barbosa
papers.abstract: Objective: To present the proposal of the Brazilian Linguistic Diversity Platform, an initiative of the Brazilian Association of Linguistics (ABRALIN) and the Sociolinguistics Working Group of the National Association of Postgraduate Studies and Research in Letters and Linguistics (ANPOLL), and to discuss its contribution to the development of Portuguese language models foreseen in the Brazilian Artificial Intelligence Plan (PBIA) 2024-2028. Methods: Theoretical and propositional essay, based on documentary analysis of the PBIA and on studies of linguistic bias in language models and of the management of sociolinguistic data collections in Brazil. Results: The language models currently available are trained on data dominated by English, in which Portuguese appears mostly in written, formal, and urban registers, which results in the reproduction of biases, stereotypes, and the invisibility of underrepresented varieties and speakers; meanwhile, linguistic data collections produced by specialists remain fragmented and regionally and institutionally concentrated. The Platform is proposed as a national repository of linguistic data collections, guided by the FAIR principles and supported by a collaborative network of laboratories. Conclusions: The Platform represents a strategic bridge between linguistic science, data science, information science, and technological development, with impacts on education, language policies, and Brazilian digital sovereignty.

papers.title: “Can you hear me, ChatGPT?”: interaction patterns, challenges, and learner perceptions in out-of-class EFL speaking practice
papers.authors: Wenzheng Huang, Hao Zhou
papers.journal: Journal of China Computer-Assisted Language Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract As Generative AI (GenAI) expands voice interaction capabilities, it offers new possibilities for foreign language speaking practice in more realistic interactional environments. This study investigates EFL learners’ interaction patterns with ChatGPT as an out-of-class language partner and examines how these patterns and learner perceptions evolve over time. Over a 15-week semester, thirty EFL students at a Japanese university used their smartphones to converse with ChatGPT on six designated topics. Data were collected through recordings, transcripts, and pre- and post-surveys. Content analysis revealed that students relied mainly on reactive strategies, mostly responding to ChatGPT’s questions, while demonstrating fewer proactive behaviors, such as steering the conversation or asking questions. Task design also influenced interaction patterns. Over time, increases in conversation length and proactive output suggested greater interactional engagement and growing familiarity with AI-mediated speaking practice. However, recurring technical issues, particularly interruptions, often disrupted conversational flow, leading to disengagement, as also reflected in open-ended survey responses. The tension between potential benefits and practical limitations challenges uncritical technological optimism. Although GenAI offers valuable practice opportunities, its limitations mean it complements rather than replaces human interaction. Rather than assuming technology alone transforms learning, educators must develop frameworks that address technical constraints, scaffold learner autonomy, and cultivate critical AI literacy.

papers.title: From centralised AI to distributed intelligence: implications for bioinformatics
papers.authors: Erik Bongcam‐Rudloff
papers.abstract: This article examines a possible transition in artificial intelligence from centralised, cloud-based systems toward smaller, specialized models operating locally on personal devices, laboratory instruments, medical equipment, and industrial machinery. Drawing on the historical shift from mainframe computers to personal computing, it argues that local AI may complement, and in some applications partly replace large centralized models by providing lower latency, greater privacy, reduced operating costs, and less dependence on cloud connectivity. Although hyperscale data centers will remain essential for training frontier models and addressing complex problems, the growth of local.AI could challenge current infrastructure-focused business models and lead to market consolidation and repricing. The article further explores the implications of this transition for bioinformatics and the life sciences. It argues that bioinformatics should become an integral part of life-science education and research, enabling scientists not only to use AI tools but also to understand, validate, and develop them. Universities and research institutions should therefore support interdisciplinary training and research environments in which specialised AI solutions can be designed and deployed for biotechnology, medicine, agriculture, food production, and environmental monitoring. The article concludes that bioinformatics can serve as a vital bridge between AI and biology, allowing the life sciences to actively shape the transition from centralised, general-purpose AI to distributed, specialised local intelligence.

papers.title: Digital technologies for adaptive climate governance: a systematic literature review with implications for policy innovation in South Africa
papers.authors: Human Sciences Research Council
papers.abstract: Climate change governance in developing countries continues to face persistent implementation challenges arising from uneven institutional capacity, weak data infrastructure, and limited stakeholder participation. Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, blockchain, and digital participation platforms, have been proposed as potential enablers of adaptive climate governance. However, evidence on how these technologies contribute to adaptive governance and policy innovation in developing-country contexts remains fragmented. A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Literature published between January and March 2026 was identified through searches of five electronic databases. After screening and quality appraisal, 44 studies were included in the review. Data were analysed using qualitative thematic synthesis in ATLAS.ti 25 through a hybrid deductive -inductive coding approach. Five themes emerged from the analysis: (1) AI and predictive climate analytics, (2) IoT and real-time environmental monitoring, (3) digital platforms for stakeholder engagement, (4) blockchain for transparent climate governance, and (5) big data and policy learning. The review demonstrates that digital technologies support anticipatory governance, adaptive policy learning, accountability, and collaborative decision-making when supported by appropriate institutional conditions. It also introduces the Digital Adaptive Governance Framework (DAGF), which proposes five governance pathways linking digital technology inputs to policy outcomes: anticipatory governance, feedback loops, adaptive policy learning, accountability-triggered reform, and collaborative governance. The findings indicate that digital technologies are governance-contingent rather than inherently transformative; their effectiveness depends on institutional capacity, policy coordination, digital literacy, and inclusive governance arrangements. For South Africa, the review highlights opportunities to strengthen climate governance by improving digital infrastructure, enhancing transparency in Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) implementation, addressing water governance challenges, and promoting inclusive digital participation. Institutional reform and capacity development should precede large-scale technology procurement. The proposed DAGF provides a conceptual foundation for future empirical research on digital technologies and adaptive climate governance in developing-country contexts.

papers.title: Comprehensive Multimodal Diagnostics and Rehabilitation in Persistent Post-Concussion Syndrome Following Motor Vehicle Collision
papers.authors: Kenneth Jay, Mary Shaya, Jonathan Walker
papers.abstract: Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) are among the most common mechanisms of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), and a meaningful proportion of affected individuals develop persistent post-concussion syndrome (PPCS) characterized by prolonged multidomain dysfunction. Conventional neuroimaging frequently fails to capture the underlying pathophysiology, leaving clinicians without objective diagnostic evidence. We describe a 57-year-old woman who sustained mTBI in a rear-end MVC in March 2023. Head computed tomography (CT) performed at the emergency department and a subsequent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were both unremarkable. Despite normal structural neuroimaging, comprehensive multimodal functional assessment identified functional abnormalities across eight domains: vestibular function (videonystagmography (VNG)), cortical electrophysiology (quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG)), pupillary autonomics (automated infrared pupillometry), postural stability (computerized dynamic posturography (CDP)), oculomotor control (saccadometry), cardiac autonomic regulation (24-h heart rate variability (HRV)), olfaction (University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT)), and computerized concussion assessment (C3 Logix). Standardized psychological assessments confirmed moderate depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) = 14), moderate anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) = 12), clinically significant post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms (PTSD Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) (PCL-5 = 38)), and substantial headache impact (Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) = 58). The patient underwent a 10-modality individualized rehabilitation program. Concussion Symptom Checklist (CSC) scores declined from 92 at initial presentation to 0 by July 2023 (17 weeks post-injury), with near-complete re-resolution to 8 by February 2024 following a transient stress-related exacerbation. When conventional neuroimaging is unremarkable, comprehensive multimodal functional testing may provide evidence consistent with mTBI pathophysiology and help guide targeted rehabilitation. This case illustrates the potential value of a systematic, multimodal approach in PPCS management, while acknowledging that definitive attribution of findings to the index injury is constrained by the single-case design and absence of a pre-injury functional baseline.

papers.title: 6th International Mobile Brain-Body Imaging Conference
papers.abstract: The Mobile Brain/Body Imaging (MoBI) Conference brings together researchers from various fields using mobile brain imaging from around the world. Using portable methods such as EEG and fNIRS, MoBI brings neuroscience closer to embodied and naturalistic states that we experience in real life. The 6th International Mobi conference was hosted by the Berlin Brain-Body Imaging Lab at the Technical University of Berlin between August 25-28. We foster scientific communication, networking, and good scientific practices related to MoBI research. All abstracts in this book were reviewed by members of the scientific committee and approved by authors.

papers.title: GEN-AI and CEFR-C1 Compliance under a Mandatory Language Policy An Explanatory Case Study of an In-Service Teacher in Malaysia
papers.authors: Warid Mihat

papers.title: Promoting flexibility, inclusivity and innovation within advanced practice education: part 2
papers.authors: Sadie Diamond-Fox
papers.abstract: This article, the second in a three-part series, explores the integration of immersive technologies and experiential learning in advanced practice education. It examines how innovations such as virtual reality, artificial intelligence and blended learning models can address global disparities in education, enhance clinical reasoning and support equitable access to advanced training. It also emphasises the need for robust evaluation frameworks to assess the effectiveness of digital education tools.

papers.title: Effects of velocity-based and traditional resistance training on physical performance, anaerobic capacity, and perceptual responses in trained male football players
papers.authors: Ahmet Mor, Hakkı Mor, Gürkan Selim Çelgin, Zehra Kargın, Erkal Arslanoğlu, Fatih KARAKAŞ
papers.journal: BMC Sports Science Medicine and Rehabilitation
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Velocity-based resistance training (VBRT) has emerged as a prominent method for optimizing neuromuscular adaptations by accommodating daily fluctuations in athlete performance. Despite its growing popularity, comparative evidence on VBRT versus traditional resistance training (TRT) across multiple performance and perceptual outcomes in trained football players remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the effects of two 8-week, strength-focused resistance-training programs, VBRT and TRT, on explosive performance, anaerobic capacity, balance, football-specific performance, and perceptual responses in trained male football players. Methods Sixteen trained male football players (age: 19.60 ± 1.26 years; height: 174.75 ± 5.49 cm; weight: 73.49 ± 5.24 kg; body mass index (BMI): 24.09 ± 2.35 kg/m²; training age: 10.10 ± 1.37 years) were randomly assigned to a VBRT group ( n = 8) or a TRT group ( n = 8). Both groups completed two resistance training sessions per week for 8 weeks. Performance assessments, including vertical jump (VJ), running anaerobic sprint test (RAST), 30-m sprint, T-change of direction (T-CoD), balance, ball speed, and perceptual measures (rating of perceived exertion (RPE), visual analogue scale (VAS)), were conducted before and after the intervention under standardized conditions. Results No significant group x time interactions were observed for any outcome ( p > 0.05). Significant time effects were observed for VJ performance ( p = 0.013, η² p = 0.56), estimated anaerobic power ( p = 0.018, η² p = 0.53), balance ( p = 0.003, η² p = 0.70), fatigue index ( p = 0.042, η² p = 0.42), and muscle soreness assessed using the VAS ( p = 0.014, η² p = 0.55). A significant group effect was observed for estimated anaerobic power ( p = 0.004, η² p = 0.67); however, the groups already differed at baseline for this outcome ( p = 0.013). Conclusions No significant group x time interactions were observed for any outcome, providing no clear evidence that training adaptations differed between VBRT and TRT over the 8-week intervention. Velocity-based load autoregulation may still provide a practical approach to adjusting resistance-training loads based on current performance capacity in trained football players. Trial registration The randomized controlled trial was retrospectively registered on 11/06/2026 at ClinicalTrials.gov, under the registration number NCT07652307 ( https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07652307 ).

papers.title: The mediating role of AI anxiety between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI in nursing students: a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Liping Wang, 聂曼华, Yanchao Xiao, Sai Liu
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: AI is a key driver in the Fourth Industrial Revolution, significantly impacting healthcare. Nursing students' acceptance and readiness to use AI are crucial for its successful integration. Understanding their perceptions is vital to prepare them for the intelligent healthcare era. AIM: To examine the mediation effect of AI anxiety between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI in college nursing students. DESIGN: A cross-sectional study. METHODS: Nursing students from 10 universities across 7 provinces in China were recruited using convenience sampling from May to June 2025. The data collection tools included the Self-Designed Demographic Questionnaire, the General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale and the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. Data were collated and analyzed using SPSS Statistics 26.0 software and AMOS 29.0 software. RESULTS: The study found that nursing students possess moderate levels of AI literacy and AI anxiety, while generally maintaining positive attitudes towards AI. Mediation analysis indicated that AI anxiety statistically mediated the association between AI literacy and nursing students' attitudes towards AI. CONCLUSIONS: AI literacy was significantly associated with nursing students' attitudes towards AI, and AI anxiety statistically mediated this association. Therefore, nursing education may benefit from a dual-path approach, designed to simultaneously enhance cognitive competencies (AI literacy) and manage affective responses (AI anxiety).

papers.title: “We cannot sit and wait for these things to happen by themselves”: a qualitative study of barriers and enablers for active patient involvement in Norwegian undergraduate nursing education
papers.authors: Catrine Buck Jensen, Bengt Karlsson, Frank Oterholt, Kim Fangen, Åsne Knutson de Presno
papers.abstract: Scientific abstract Background Active patient involvement in health professions education (HPE) is increasingly recognized to enhance patient-centered care and improve healthcare outcomes. However, in Norway, there are no formal requirements for patient involvement in nursing education, and its implementation remains inconsistent. The study aims to explore the enablers and barriers to active patient involvement in Norwegian undergraduate nursing education, as perceived by nursing students, nurse educators, and patients/family members. Methods A collaborative research methodology was employed, involving three digital workshops and one co-creation workshop with six educators, three senior nursing students, and six patients/family members. Data were analyzed using an iterative qualitative framework to identify key themes. Findings Three main themes were generated: (1) Hesitance toward experiential knowledge were identified as a fundamental barrier, with participants highlighting a perceived hierarchy that undervalues patient expertise. (2) Lack of formal requirements, systems, and structures was seen as a significant limitation, leaving patient involvement dependent on individual educators’ initiatives. (3) Training and competency development were identified as both enablers and barriers, with participants emphasizing the need for training both patients and educators to ensure meaningful and effective involvement. Conclusion The study underscores the need for structural changes, including formal requirements for patient involvement in nursing education, faculty development programs, and training for patient contributors. Addressing epistemic injustice and fostering a culture that values experiential knowledge is critical for advancing patient involvement in HPE.

papers.title: Double machine learning analysis identifies heterogeneous patterns in Ethiopian fertility intention: cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Ye Jun Kim, Eun Woo Nam, Haftu Hailu Berhe, Hocheol Lee
papers.abstract: Ethiopia’s stagnating fertility transition has exposed the limitations of generalized public health strategies. This study aimed to move beyond national averages by identifying context-dependent determinants and evaluating the adjusted conditional associations of reproductive knowledge and media exposure on fertility preferences across distinct socioeconomic archetypes. Using cross-sectional data from the Small, Happy, and Prosperous Family in Ethiopia (SHaPE2) survey ( n = 16,322), we applied k-means clustering to stratify regional data into Rural, Transitional, and Urban archetypes. To adjust for high-dimensional confounders and capture non-linear heterogeneity, we utilized Double Machine Learning (DML), integrating LightGBM-based Linear DML and Causal Forest DML. Additionally, Robustness Values were calculated to quantify the threshold of omitted variable bias. The associations of these information interventions were context dependent. In the Rural cluster, Knowledge Depth ( \(\:-0.051;p<.001\) ) and Media Exposure ( \(\:-0.063;p=.009\) ) were correlated with reduced fertility preferences. Conversely, in the Transitional cluster, Knowledge Depth ( \(\:+0.067;p<.001\) ) and Media Exposure ( \(\:+0.101;p<.001\) ) were correlated with higher fertility preferences. In the Urban cluster, Knowledge Depth ( \(\:+0.048;p=0.002\) ) demonstrated a positive association, whereas Media Exposure ( \(\:-0.075;p=0.005\) ) correlated with lower fertility preferences. Causal Forest DML indicated that the association of media exposure depends on pre-existing knowledge in rural and transitional settings but operates structurally independently in urban environments. The assumption that information interventions are uniformly associated with reduced fertility demands has been flawed. In transitional clusters, increased reproductive knowledge and media exposure correlate with higher fertility preferences. Although the cross-sectional nature of our data restricts these findings to conditional associations rather than causal effects, they suggest that public health policies could benefit from shifting to cluster-specific precision strategies. This includes the persistence of foundational education in rural areas, prioritizing economic structural shifts over information campaigns in transitional zones and leveraging standalone mass media for normative reframing in urban centers.

papers.title: INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTO MEDICAL EDUCATION AND FUTURE PRACTICE: STUDENTS’ EXPERIENCES, RISKS, AND PERSPECTIVES
papers.authors: Inna V. Korda
papers.abstract: The article examines the features, priority goals, and risks of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into medical education. The work examines how future doctors implement digital tools in their training and assess their role in future practice. A survey of 79 4th and 6th year students of the Ternopil National Medical University named after I. Ya. Horbachevsky, who study “Obstetrics and Gynecology”, revealed a paradox. On the one hand, AI has become a part of daily routine for 67.1 % of respondents, another 31.6 % turn to it several times a week. The main advantage is the optimization of time spent: 97.5 % of respondents confirmed significant resource savings. However, the implementation is superficial, as 100 % rely on general-purpose text language models (ChatGPT, Claude) rather than specialized medical software. Expert assistants (UpToDate, Glass AI) are integrated by only 8.9 % of respondents, and image generation programs by 6.3 %. It was found that 83.5 % of students turn to AI to search for clinical protocols; 67.1 % to prepare for the KROK/OSKI exams; 67.1 % to solve clinical problems or write case histories, and only 17.7 % to translate articles. An important aspect was the analysis of self-assessment of prompting skills on a 5-point scale: 12.7 % of students rated them 5 points, 36.7 % rated them 4 points, 46.8 % rated them 3 points, and 3.8 % rated them 2 points. Despite high confidence, 93.7 % of respondents personally encountered AI “hallucinations” – the generation of non-existent facts. Future doctors are clearly aware of the risks of degradation of clinical thinking (63.3 %, n = 50), getting used to “easy answers” (65.3 %, n = 52), and unconscious assimilation of false information (43.0 %, n = 34). The introduction of mandatory discipline in medical AI was fully supported by 23.4 % (n = 18) of respondents, actively supported with reservations by 18.2 % (n = 14), and taken in a neutral position by 45.5 % (n = 35). Based on the data obtained, it is concluded that medical students demonstrate a high intensity of AI use against the background of a critical shortage of work with profile software and a high frequency of encounters with neural network errors. The results justify the need for a strategic transformation of higher medical education – a transition from ignoring technology to the implementation of systematic training in medical prompting, data verification methodology, and digital hygiene for the safe use of AI in future practice.

papers.title: Vulnerability Trends across Open-Source AI-Attributed Code
papers.authors: Clarisa Caballero-Ignacio, Lucas Stephens, Josiah Sage, Manish Motwani, Zane Ma
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to widespread adoption of AI-coding tools and increasing deployment of AI-assisted code. While AI’s potential for programming productivity is becoming evident, the security of AI-attributed code is still poorly understood. In this work, we collect the largest set of in-the-wild AI-attributed code to date, examining 253,390 files containing AI-assisted code from seven tools and 9,544 human-written files from public GitHub repositories. Our analyses reveal significant differences in security-relevant CWE prevalence across programming languages and AI tools, with tool-specific differences varying by language. Additionally, human-written Python exhibited significantly higher security-relevant CWE prevalence than AI-attributed Python (21.08% vs 11.15%) and higher file-level CVSS severity. Ultimately, our results extend prior work showing that vulnerable AI-assisted code is making it into public repositories, indicating a need for stronger review practices and greater developer security awareness when using these tools.

papers.title: Curated Semantic Mutants: Multi-purpose Artifacts for Grading and Hinting Student Test Suites
papers.authors: Earle Rebecca, Jonathan Bell
papers.abstract: Mutation testing can evaluate a student's test suite, but traditional mutation tools do not encode which generated faults a course rubric should weight or what feedback should be delivered to students that do not detect a mutant. We report a human-LLM workflow that pairs each curated semantic mutant with an instructor-approved seed phrase for an on-demand LLM expansion. Deployed across two semesters of CS 3100, an introductory software-engineering course (N=1,893 submissions), the workflow provided automated per-submission feedback about undetected curated faults. In a deployment with on-demand hint expansions, 46% of students requested at least one, at roughly three cents each. At the failing submission--unit-pair level, requested expansions were associated with improvement on the next submission at 1.62 times the rate of pairs with no request, though because requests were self-selected this is not a causal estimate. A same-code comparison also shows that the curated semantic-mutant set contains a fraction of the mutants a traditional mutation engine produces. We do not compare this LLM-assisted approach with an instructor curating and writing mutants and hints by hand; whether it is cheaper or better remains an open question.

papers.title: Adaptive Human-AI Collaboration: A Review of Multimodal Context Modeling, Uncertainty-Aware Intervention, and Longitudinal Co-Adaptation
papers.authors: Mahyar Tourchi Moghaddam, Mina Alipour
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is shifting from a static decision-support tool to an adaptive collaborator that must sense context, decide when and how to intervene, and improve through repeated interaction with humans individually and in groups. Yet meta-analytic evidence shows that human-AI combinations often fail to outperform the best of either partner alone, and the enabling literature remains fragmented across multimodal sensing, uncertainty quantification, reliance and delegation, facilitation, and teaming. This paper reports a review of adaptive human-AI collaboration literature through a closed-loop lens. Following iterative identification, staged selection against explicit criteria, structured extraction, taxonomy-driven synthesis, and snowballing, we analyze 50 reviewed works. We contribute i) a taxonomy of multimodal context modeling, from individual states to collective states such as group engagement and participation equality; ii) a taxonomy of uncertainty-aware intervention, covering uncertainty sources, estimation and calibration mechanisms, an intervention repertoire that ranges from explanation modulation and deferral to group facilitation, and intervention policies; and iii) a taxonomy of longitudinal co-adaptation and synergy-oriented evaluation. We integrate the three taxonomies into MCAL, a dual-timescale Multimodal Co-Adaptation Loop reference model, and instantiate it on a mixed human-robot workspace, walking every stage of the loop through one concrete setting to show what each taxonomy cell holds in practice.

papers.title: PlainHealth: A Multimodal Service Suite for Cognitively Accessible Healthcare Communication
papers.authors: Lourdes de la Rosa Moreno, Paloma Martı́nez, Jesús M. Sánchez-Gómez
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Health information is often difficult for patients, relatives, and caregivers to understand because of technical language, limited health literacy, and cognitive interface barriers. This paper presents PlainHealth, a work-in-progress multimodal service suite that uses generative AI and task-specific language technologies to support accessible healthcare communication in clinical consultations, residential care, and home settings. The suite offers reusable services for audio capture, multi-recipient report generation, plain-language and easy-to-read adaptation, accessible infographic generation, and assistive care. It also includes a quality-status service that communicates output quality, traceability, and human-review status for AI-generated content. Services are delivered through cognitively accessible interfaces designed in accordance with relevant standards. The service-oriented implementation selects models and resources according to communication goals, accessibility requirements, and safety risks. The paper presents the architecture, implementation strategy, interaction design, and quality-control mechanisms, with particular attention to cognitive accessibility, human oversight, explainability, traceability, and responsible use.

papers.title: A Modular Reference Architecture for Patient-Facing Generative AI Health Coaches in Chronic Self-Management
papers.authors: Leon Paul Mondrian Munz, Ana Müller, Christopher Joachim Kania, Tim Fellerhoff, Anja Richert
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Patient-facing generative AI is increasingly proposed for chronic self-management support, but trust-relevant properties such as source verification, safety boundaries, traceability, bias monitoring, and escalation are difficult to inspect when treated as emergent properties of a dialogue model. This paper presents LUCID, a modular conceptual reference architecture for non-diagnostic, patient-facing generative AI health coaching grounded in Therapeutic Patient Education (TPE). It separates curated knowledge, controlled health-context integration, analysis and personalization, response generation through an internal large language model (LLM) Gateway, safety, explainability, audit, and staged evaluation. The architecture mediates patient requests, preferences, symptom reports, wearable summaries, educational goals, source-linked explanations, and escalation notices through explicit responsibility boundaries. Six design requirements are derived from a related-work synthesis, and key decisions are documented through Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). A runtime walkthrough and staged evaluation plan show how the architecture can be tested from architecture readiness to human-centered feasibility. By making curated sources, released context fragments, competency targets, model and prompt versions, safety and release decisions, and escalation paths explicit, LUCID enables developers and evaluators to inspect and compare how individual patient-facing responses are produced.

papers.title: From Wizard-of-Oz to Autonomous: A Hybrid Rule and LLM Backchannel Architecture for a Silent Listening Agent
papers.authors: Emmanuel Ayedoun
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: We present a working autonomous system that replaces the human wizard in a previously validated listening-agent architecture for second-language (L2) production support. The system streams learner speech through cloud ASR and runs two parallel rule-based policies, one for content-driven facial affect and one for rhythm-driven head motion, alongside a third LLM-mediated meta-policy that supplies a slow coherence signal over a 15-second window. Facial expressions are grounded in FACS Action Units and rendered on a 158-morph ARKit-mapped avatar. From two real pilot sessions we identify concrete failure modes of a unified, priority-ordered classifier (1 nod in 44 decisions on a monologue) and show that the parallel policy split rebalances it (19 nods of 34 decisions on the follow-up session). We frame these two-session results as a preliminary technical evaluation of system behaviour: they characterise what the architecture does, not yet how it is perceived, and a controlled human-centred study is left as the immediate next step. Full per-session event logs and a demo video are released as an artifact for the GENEA Reproducibility Award.

papers.title: Modeling Conversation as a Prompt Planning Problem for Adaptive Human–Robot Interaction
papers.authors: Giulia Berettieri, Anna Allegra Bixio, Lucrezia Grassi, Carmine Tommaso Recchiuto, Antonio Sgorbissa
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Adaptive behavior is a fundamental requirement for social robots operating in real-world environments, where interactions must dynamically respond to both observable actions and inferred user states. In this work, we propose a novel framework that models human–robot interaction as a planning problem, where adaptive conversational behavior is driven by a symbolic planner based on the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL).

papers.title: Making Videos Accessible for Blind and Low Vision Users Using a Multimodal Agent Video Player
papers.authors: Anoop K. Sinha, Adriana Olmos, Renelito Delos Santos, Ruben Rodriguez Rodriguez, James A. Landay, Sam Sepah, Philip Nelson, Shaun K. Kane
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Video content remains largely inaccessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. To address this, we introduce a prototype that leverages a multimodal agent — powered by a novel conversational architecture using a multimodal large language model (MLLM) — to provide BLV users with an interactive, accessible video experience. This Multimodal Agent Video Player (MAVP) demonstrates that an interactive accessibility mode can be added to a video through multilayered prompt orchestration. We describe a user-centered design process involving 18 sessions with BLV users that showed that BLV users do not just want accessibility features; they desire independence and personal agency over the viewing experience. A subsequent study with 8 participants indicated that the MAVP's conversational interface fosters collaboration, trust, and a sense of personal agency. Notably, even when the model produces hallucinations, meta-conversational dialogues regarding the AI's limitations can effectively repair and maintain trust.

papers.title: Conceptual Alignment to Promote Discussion and Empathy towards Disability in Teenagers: a Protocol Proposal
papers.authors: Marco Mores, Simone Ciciliano, Rosella Gennari
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: With the growing use of digital technology in the healthcare and rehabilitation sectors, there is an emerging need for future developers and policy-makers to genuinely understand People with Disabilities (PwD). However, the diffuse misconceptions and misrepresentations of PwD can prevent an appropriate understanding of PwD and mislead technological development. Empathy can be a relevant tool for developers and policy-makers to achieve a genuine understanding of the needs of PwD. This paper proposes a protocol for a Future Design workshop involving teenage students that addresses communication-related disabilities and how students describe future technologies to be used by PwD. The protocol proposal outlines activities, tools (including an LLM-based interface) and data analysis strategies to assess the workshops’ success.

papers.title: SMILE: A Hybrid Memory-Driven Dialogue Manager for Social Companion Robots
papers.authors: Mariacarla Staffa, Salvatore M. Anzalone, Lorenzo D’Errico
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: This paper presents SMILE (Social Memory-Integrated Language Environment), a memory-augmented dialogue system designed for social companion robots. Current LLM-based conversational agents are stateless by design, creating a fundamental tension between their apparent linguistic intelligence and the persistent, structured memory required for long-term social interaction — a limitation particularly critical in assistive contexts involving older adults or individuals with cognitive impairments. SMILE addresses this gap through a controlled, locally-run architecture combining real-time face recognition, offline speech processing, and a three-layer memory structure comprising working, semantic, and episodic memory, in which the LLM serves exclusively as a linguistic realizer while memory retrieval and dialogue control remain deterministic. Rather than introducing a new memory algorithm, SMILE contributes an explainable system architecture that separates deterministic memory management from neural language generation, providing a practical foundation for trustworthy long-term human–robot interaction.

papers.title: CreaRobot - Improving creativity using a social robot
papers.authors: Claudie Cuveillier, Marco Grandclaude, Maria Valentina Cavarretta, Sudapa Chompunuch, Béatrice Biancardi, Stéphanie Buisine A, Isis Truck, Jean‐Marie Burkhardt, Todd Lubart, Salvatore M. Anzalone
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Supporting children’s creativity in educational settings remains a key challenge, which generative AI-powered social robots may help address. This paper presents CreaRobot, a study in which children performed a standardized drawing task while interacting with a social robot driven by a vision-language model. We compared two conditions: a generic feedback condition, in which the robot produced pre-recorded generic compliments, and a contextualized feedback condition, in which the robot engaged in structured interaction phases grounded in a real-time visual analysis of each child’s drawing. Results from 49 participants show that contextualized feedback significantly improved the value of the creative product (M = 21.52 vs. M = 13.85; Cohen’s d = 1.34), with a large effect size. These preliminary findings suggest that grounding a social robot’s feedback in real-time perception of the creative process is a promising direction for AI-supported creativity in educational settings.

papers.title: Can Vision-Language Models Extract Relevant Multimodal Cues for Post-Inference Cue Integration? A Comparison of Affective Judgments on Adult and Child Interaction Data
papers.authors: Xiajie Zhang, Sharifa Alghowinem, Hae Won Park, Cynthia Breazeal
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Inferring human affective states from multimodal behavioral cues is essential for socially aware AI and human-robot interaction. Conventional research practice either relies on hand-crafted behavioral detectors or end-to-end deep learning models that often lack interpretability and contextual adaptation. Recent work suggests that vision-language models (VLMs) may serve as informative priors for affective inference; however, their ability to extract and reason over behavioral cues in naturalistic human-human interactions remains unclear. We propose EPIC, a three-stage framework to delineate VLMs’ affective inference into testable sub-processes: multi-modal cue extraction, cue-level affect prediction, and cue integration. Applying the framework, we conduct a case study with one VLM on affective inference tasks with a real-world dyadic interaction dataset. Preliminary results show that explicit cue integration improves performance when cue quality is high, reaching up to a 14% gain. However, VLM’s cue extraction shows strong visual bias and underuses speech and paralinguistic information, leading to weaker performance when inferring arousal and children’s states. Overall, our results suggest VLM might provide promising interpretable priors for affective reasoning but remain limited in modality balance, context sensitivity, and demographic robustness.

papers.title: Is Bad Handwriting Really Bad? Multimodal Human–AI Interpretation of Illegible Handwriting in Palliative Care
papers.authors: Zhigang Ni, Lei Yang
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: In palliative care, severe physical and cognitive decline renders patients’ handwritten notes highly degraded, transforming intention reconstruction into a multimodal interaction problem. Because static images lack sufficient evidence and AAC or sensor-rich systems impose unbearable physical burdens, we propose passively capturing and fusing static ink with dynamic kinematics (e.g., stroke order, pauses), family context, and low-effort patient gestures. Drawing on three co-design workshops (N=14) and scenario-based interviews with four family caregivers, we contribute three design requirements: (1) capture should preserve familiar pen-and-paper expression while moving sensing and computation to the back end; (2) the system should externalize uncertainty as evidence-ranked Top-N hypotheses, process-cue evidence, and confirmable questions rather than emit a single answer; and (3) disclosure controls should support tiered access, expiration, and withdrawal so families can recruit help without exposing patients’ dignity. This work contributes early ICMI design evidence for organizing multimodal fusion under high ambiguity, where multimodal evidence and human confirmation jointly resolve meaning rather than the system claiming autonomous recognition.

papers.title: A Multimodal Latent State-Space Framework Reveals Spontaneous Interpersonal Synchrony Dynamics
papers.authors: Yubraj Gupta, Stefanie Suttkus, Steffen Schulz, Feliberto de la Cruz, Maria Geisler, Karl‐Jürgen Bär, Andy Schumann
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony reflects the temporal coordination of behavioural, physiological, and neural processes between interacting individuals. Existing synchrony-analysis methods quantify signal similarity but provide limited insight into recurring coordination states and their temporal organization across modalities. We propose a multimodal latent state-space framework that integrates EEG, body movement, facial expression, and eye-gaze signals into a unified dyadic divergence representation. Following dimensionality reduction, Gaussian mixture modelling identifies recurring synchrony states, whose temporal organization is characterized by measures of occurrence, persistence, and long-range stability. The framework was evaluated using a publicly available dataset of 23 dyads who passively observed one another under Near and Far Vision conditions without communication or an explicit shared task. Five latent synchrony states were identified, spanning highly synchronized to highly desynchronized interaction patterns. Near Vision interactions exhibited greater occupancy of the highest synchrony state (22.0% vs. 17.3%), longer persistence (d = 0.59, p =.004), and greater long-range stability (d = 0.56, p =.007). Surrogate analyses further showed a substantial disruption of the recovered state architecture when interpersonal temporal dependencies were removed. These findings demonstrate that recurring multimodal synchrony states can emerge under minimally constrained social conditions and highlight latent state-space modelling as a complementary approach for characterizing dynamic interpersonal coordination.

papers.title: Benchmarking Prompt Extension and Image Generation Models for Automotive Instructional Imagery
papers.authors: Yuval Zak, Eli Tzirkel
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: Generative image models can support instructional visual content, but safety-relevant automotive imagery requires more than photorealism: generated scenes must preserve cockpit geometry, human-machine-interface (HMI) iconography, and physically plausible vehicle behavior. We evaluate a two-stage pipeline in which large language models (LLMs) extend technical owner-manual descriptions and reference-image constraints into downstream image-generation prompts, across four Cadillac LYRIQ advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) scenarios. Using a factorial design over prompt-extension LLM, thinking mode, injected Chain-of-Thought (CoT) source, prompt style, scenario, and image generator, we collect N = 18, 551 manually rated images (Excellent/Good/Fair/Poor). The downstream generator was the dominant quality determinant: Nano Banana Pro and Nano Banana 2 produced 16.9% and 14.3% usable images, whereas GPT-Image-1.5 produced 0.5% and collapsed to near-uniform failure. Within the viable Google generators, LLM and CoT effects were generator- and scenario-dependent; because both viable generators are Google, the CoT-source effect reflects trace–generator alignment (Google-aligned CoT helped, OpenAI-sourced CoT hurt) rather than a general CoT benefit. A robustness analysis further reveals a trade-off between high-performing specialist and lower-variance generalist configurations. Domain-constrained instructional image generation should therefore be evaluated as a coupled system spanning generator, prompt-extension model, reasoning trace, prompt template, and scenario.

papers.title: "Nobody Told me Farming is not Only Farming": A Conversational AI Agent for Causal Loop Reasoning with Japan Farmers
papers.authors: Tomohide Mizuuchi, Eduardo Feteira, Liuru Nan, Mami Yoda, Wan Jou She, Panote Siriaraya
papers.journal: Companion Publication of the International Conference on Multimodal Interaction (ICMI Companion)
papers.abstract: As the agricultural industry becomes more interconnected and shaped by globalized markets, smallholder farmers face mounting challenges in navigating an increasingly complex and highly competitive business landscape. This paper reports a study in which a conversational AI system, Seseragi was used to help synthesize systemic knowledge through participatory causal loop diagramming with four farmers who possessed extensive lifelong experience in local agricultural practice. Despite some technical limitations posed by latency, the farmers provided promising feedback and acknowledged the benefits of reflective brainstorming guided by our system. Our findings and design implications offer valuable insights into co-designing AI agents that support individuals navigating complex systemic problems that exceed the scope of their own professional expertise, as exemplified by the agricultural context.

papers.title: Collective States in Multimodal Interaction
papers.authors: Teruhisa Misu, Giovanna Varni, Koji Inoue, Zhaobo Zheng, Chikara Maeda
papers.abstract: Collective states, such as group emotion, engagement, rapport, coordination, and team functioning, emerge from interactions among participants and cannot be understood by simply aggregating individual behaviors. This paper presents the motivation, program, and expected outcomes of CSMI 2026, the first workshop on Collective States in Multimodal Interaction. Through two invited keynotes, eight research presentations, and interdisciplinary discussion, the workshop examines multimodal methods for sensing, modeling, and supporting collective states in multiparty human-human and human–AI interaction. The contributions address topics including group emotion recognition, affect sensing, conversational backchannels, team outcomes, speaker roles, reciprocal coordination, and adaptive human–AI collaboration. CSMI aims to connect individual- and group-level perspectives, identify shared methodological and evaluation challenges, and foster collaboration toward AI systems that can understand and appropriately support group dynamics.

papers.title: HeMAI 2026: Multimodal Interaction with Generative AI Health Applications
papers.authors: Lisa Raithel, Stefan Hillmann, Roland Roller, Sebastian Möller, Catherine Pélachaud
papers.abstract: This workshop explores the potential of multimodal interaction for generative AI health applications. Healthcare is an inherently multimodal setting, combining language, speech, vision, gesture, physiological signals, and interactive visualizations, and one in which transparency, reliability, and trust are prerequisites for deployment. The workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from multimodal interaction, natural language processing, generative artificial intelligence, affective computing, human-computer interaction, and clinical practice to examine how generative and multimodal systems can support interactive, collaborative decision-making in clinical and patient-facing scenarios. Through paper presentations, invited talks, and posters, the workshop aims to identify shared methodological challenges, promote responsible design, and foster cross-disciplinary collaboration.

papers.title: Inclusive AI: Rethinking AI-based Multimodal Interaction for Diverse and Underrepresented Users
papers.authors: Giulia Barbareschi, Nataliya Kosmyna, Maristella Matera, Anoop K. Sinha, Shruti Sheth, Micol Spitale, Alessandro Vinciarelli
papers.abstract: Socially interactive AI systems increasingly shape how people access information, services, and support. However, many of these systems are designed around normative assumptions about communication, behavior, and social interaction, creating barriers for people with disabilities and other underrepresented populations. As a result, social AI technologies risk excluding users whose communicative styles diverge from dominant norms, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, employment, and autonomous systems. This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners from HCI, HRI, AI, and related fields to explore the challenges and opportunities of designing inclusive social AI. Discussions will address disability bias, limitations of current datasets and models, methodological challenges in capturing diverse interaction behaviors, and ethical considerations in the development of socially interactive technologies. Through participatory activities, attendees will identify research gaps and future directions. Outcomes include a community-authored white paper, shared resources, and the establishment of a multidisciplinary research network to advance inclusive social AI.

papers.title: ERR@HRI 3.0 Challenge: Multimodal Detection of Errors and Anticipation in Human-Robot Interactions
papers.authors: Maria Teresa Parreira, Micol Spitale, Maia Stiber, Shiye Cao, Amama Mahmood, Chien-Ming Huang, Hatice Güneş, Wendy G. Ju
papers.abstract: As robots become increasingly integrated into human environments, their ability to detect and respond to errors remains critical for maintaining user trust and interaction quality. While recent advances in machine learning have improved error detection capabilities, most approaches are limited to specific contexts, controlled settings, or pre-extracted features, limiting their generalizability and applicability to real-world conditions. To address this challenge, the third edition of the ERR@HRI Challenge (ERR@HRI 3.0) provided researchers with two complementary datasets that enable end-to-end innovation in methods for both detecting and preventing errors in human-robot interaction. The challenge offered raw, non-anonymized video data from naturalistic settings: (1) the Bystander Affect Detection (BAD) dataset, containing webcam recordings of 45 participants’ spontaneous reactions to robot and human failure scenarios; and (2) the Bad Idea dataset, featuring 29 participants’ anticipatory facial responses while predicting action outcomes before failures occur. Both datasets were collected via crowdsourcing, capturing the inherent variability of real-world conditions—diverse lighting, camera angles, participant positioning, and environmental contexts. This naturalistic variability, while challenging, provides an authentic testbed for developing robust error detection systems. Participants developed multimodal machine learning models for bystander reaction detection (Track 1) and anticipatory outcome prediction (Track 2), with an optional cross-dataset generalization track (Track 3). Three teams submitted valid models, all of which surpassed our convolutional neural network baselines. This paper describes the datasets, tasks, baselines, and results of ERR@HRI 3.0, and discusses implications for building generalizable, context-aware, and anticipatory error detection systems for human-robot interaction.

papers.title: Emotional Echoes: A Spatialized VR Gallery for Revisiting and Reinterpreting Emotional Memory
papers.authors: Yao Liu, Marina Carulli, Monica Bordegoni
papers.abstract: Emotional Echoes is an interactive VR installation that reimagines emotional journaling as an embodied, multimodal, and ritualized practice. Spoken reflections are captured through a custom hardware interface and represented in VR as interactive bubbles whose color and animated visual behavior are driven by a creative, non-diagnostic mapping of provisional emotional metadata derived from the spoken reflection. The reflections are then further explored through dialogue with an AI conversational agent. Each session generates an AI-composed image that is archived in a personal VR gallery and physically printed as a tangible keepsake. Rather than presenting emotion as objective data to be measured, Emotional Echoes treats it as a lived experience that can be constructed, revisited, and reinterpreted over time. We propose a VR demonstration in which conference attendees record a short reflection, converse with the AI agent, explore the resulting memory gallery, optionally experience an associated olfactory cue when approaching a gallery artwork, and receive a printed keepsake.

papers.title: Embodying Luca Giordano: A RAG-Grounded Context-Aware Robot for Cultural Heritage Storytelling
papers.authors: Mario Barbato, Marco Grazioso, Martina Di Bratto, Azzurra Mancini, Valentina Russo, Silvia Rossi
papers.abstract: This demo presents a context-aware Furhat robot that impersonates Luca Giordano, the Neapolitan Baroque painter, and engages visitors through first-person cultural heritage storytelling. The system combines a RAG-based language model, grounded in a validated art-domain document store, with a separate vision-language component that extracts contextual cues such as audience configuration and room features. These cues are used to adapt the robot’s responses to the interaction setting. The demo shows how modular multimodal architectures can support grounded and culturally situated storytelling in human-robot interaction.

papers.title: Context-Aware Student Engagement Detection with MLLM
papers.authors: Andreas Naoum, Mario Barbato, Lily-Cannelle Mathieu, Imadaldin Berika Ismail, Raffaella Esposito, Diego Veneruso, Luigi D’Arco, Alessandra Rossi, Silvia Rossi
papers.abstract: Student engagement detection is an important component of adaptive learning systems, yet it remains challenging because observable behaviours can have different meanings depending on the context. Most existing approaches primarily infer engagement from visual cues, while other contextual information is less frequently incorporated. This work investigates whether a Multimodal Large Language Model can estimate student engagement through prompt-based reasoning without task-specific training. Using the CASED dataset, we propose a structured prompting architecture that jointly processes student and instructor key frames, a slide snapshot, and textualized facial and head-behaviour descriptors extracted with MediaPipe. The model is guided through a fixed question-answering schema that first characterizes the teaching context, then analyses the student’s observable behaviour, and finally integrates both sources of information to assess engagement. Although the engagement classification results are not fully satisfactory, our analysis suggests that vision-language models appear promising for this task.

papers.title: Detecting and Anticipating Robot Failures from Human Behavioral Signals
papers.authors: Eunyoung Hwang, Francesco Longobardi, Mahmoud Wael Aly, Luca Raggioli, Pradip Pramanick, Raffaella Esposito, Imadaldin Berika Ismail, Alessandra Rossi, Silvia Rossi
papers.abstract: Detecting robot failures from human behavioral responses is a challenging problem in human-robot interaction, due to the high inter-subject variability of overt reactions and the influence of contextual factors on their expression. In this work, we address two complementary formulations of this problem within the ERR@HRI 3.0 Challenge: detecting failure reactions from bystander videos; and anticipating perceived failures before they occur. For the former, we propose a decoupled two-stage framework in which a one-class deep metric learning model performs subject-calibrated pseudo-labeling of anomalous temporal windows, which are then used to supervise a spatio-temporal Graph Attention Network for fine-grained reaction classification. For the latter, we introduce a multimodal late-fusion Transformer that independently models visual appearance via a frozen EfficientNet-B0 backbone and facial landmark dynamics via frame-to-frame delta features, further fused with a Voice Activity Detection based audio score. Both approaches outperform the official challenge baseline across most primary evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of our methods for detecting subtle behavioral signals in human-robot interaction. Code is available at https://github.com/eunyhwang/ERRHRI-3.0-PRISCA/.

papers.title: Guided Temporal Modeling for Perceived Failure Detection in Human–Robot Interaction
papers.authors: Bahram Salamat Ravandi, Neziha Akalın, Maria Riveiro
papers.abstract: Robot failures are often expected when operating in dynamic human environments. Robot actions may be technically correct from the system’s perspective yet still violate users’ expectations, resulting in confusion, uncertainty, and interaction breakdowns. Detecting such perceived failures is therefore important for supporting effective human–robot collaboration, as it can enable adaptive explanations and interaction repair when expectation violations occur. In this paper, we address Track 1, Bystander Affect Detection (BAD), of the ERR@HRI 3.0 Challenge, which aims to detect whether participants are observing a failure or non-failure scenario from webcam recordings collected under naturalistic conditions. We propose a guided temporal framework that models facial behavior using a bidirectional LSTM with attention-based pooling. Here, ‘guided’ refers to auxiliary frame-level supervision derived from manually annotated temporal segments. The proposed temporal model for robot failure detection jointly performs frame-level and sequence-level prediction while incorporating consistency loss and temporal smoothness regularization to capture coherent behavioral dynamics over time. Evaluated on the BAD dataset, the proposed model achieved a macro F1-score of 0.567 and a balanced accuracy of 0.557 on the held-out test set, representing improvements of 6.5 and 5.3 percentage points over the official baseline in macro F1-score and balanced accuracy, respectively. These findings suggest the value of temporal facial modeling for detecting behavioral responses associated with user-perceived robot failures and may serve as one component of future adaptive explanation systems in human–robot interaction.

papers.title: A Multimodal Cross-Attention Framework for Robot Error Detection from Bystander Reactions
papers.authors: Paul Gering, Ruyi Tian, Samiulhaq Chardiwall, Yuchen Wang, Alessandro G. Di Nuovo, Chaona Chen, Zhixiang Chen, Roger K. Moore
papers.abstract: To detect human-robot interaction errors, existing approaches have primarily focused on behavioural responses from individuals directly involved in the interaction, whereas reactions from external observers have received comparatively little attention. Similarly, these approaches have been limited to interactions in controlled environments with little variability in lighting, camera angles, and background noise. Addressing these gaps, the ERR@HRI 3.0 challenge focuses on bystander error detection in unconstrained, real-world environments. Our primary submission is a time-aware multimodal fusion framework that combines facial and acoustic representations via bidirectional cross-attention. Two versions of this framework, with different encoding approaches, are evaluated against a bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) classifier with simple concatenation. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this cross-fusion approach for capturing errors and generalising to unseen real-world data. Our cross-fusion and BiLSTM models achieved the top-three positions on Track 1, outperforming the challenge baseline and other competing submissions. Feature importance analysis further revealed that smile-related action units and their temporal dynamics serve as primary discriminative cues for error detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/chardiwall/SHEF-HRI.

papers.title: Towards Gaze-Informed AI Disclosure Interfaces: Eye-Tracking Attentional and Cognitive Load While Reading AI-Assisted News
papers.authors: Pooja Prajod, Hannes Cools, Thomas Röggla, Pablo S. Cesar, Abdallah El Ali
papers.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated into journalism, designing effective AI-use disclosures that inform readers without imposing unnecessary burden is a key challenge. While prior research has primarily focused on trust and credibility, the impact of disclosures on readers’ attentional and cognitive load remains underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 3 × 2 × 2 mixed factorial study manipulating the level of AI-use disclosure detail (none, one-line, detailed), news type (politics, lifestyle), and role of AI (editing, partial content generation), measuring load via NASA-TLX and eye-tracking. Our results reveal a significant attentional cost: one-line disclosures resulted in significantly higher fixation durations and saccade counts, particularly for AI-edited content. Detailed disclosures did not impose additional burden. Drawing on Information-Gap Theory, we argue that brief labels may trigger increased visual scrutiny by alerting readers to AI use without providing enough information. NASA-TLX scores and pupil diameter showed no significant differences across conditions, suggesting that AI-use disclosures do not impose cognitive burden regardless of the detail level. Interview insights contextualize these findings and reveal a strong preference for detailed or “detail-on-demand” designs. Our findings inform the design of gaze-informed adaptive disclosure interfaces that dynamically adjust transparency levels based on readers’ attentional patterns and news context.

papers.title: SENSE: Efficient EEG-to-Text via Privacy-Preserving Semantic Retrieval
papers.authors: Akshaj Murhekar, Christina Liu, Abhijit Mishra, Shounak Roychowdhury, Jacek Gwizdka A
papers.abstract: Decoding brain activity into natural language is a major challenge in AI with important applications in assistive communication, neurotechnology, and human–computer interaction. Most existing Brain–Computer Interface (BCI) approaches rely on memory-intensive fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) or encoder–decoder models on raw EEG signals, resulting in expensive training pipelines, limited accessibility, and potential exposure of sensitive neural data.
