We introduce SENSE (SEmantic Neural Sparse Extraction), a lightweight and privacy-preserving framework that translates non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) into text without LLM fine-tuning. SENSE decouples decoding into two stages: on-device semantic retrieval and prompt-based language generation. EEG signals are locally mapped to a discrete textual space to extract a non-sensitive Bag-of-Words (BoW), which conditions an off-the-shelf LLM to synthesize fluent text in a zero-shot manner. The EEG-to-keyword module contains only ∼ 6M parameters and runs fully on-device, ensuring raw neural signals remain local while only abstract semantic cues interact with language models. Evaluated on a 128-channel EEG dataset across six subjects, SENSE matches or surpasses the generative quality of fully fine-tuned baselines such as Thought2Text while substantially reducing computational overhead. By localizing neural decoding and sharing only derived textual cues, SENSE provides a scalable and privacy-aware retrieval-augmented architecture for next-generation BCIs.

papers.title: An Explainable Neurosymbolic Multimodal Deepfake Detection with A Comparative Study of Cross-Dataset Generalization
papers.authors: Md Shafiqul Baten Sumon, Fatma Najar
papers.abstract: Deepfake detection methods have reported near-perfect performance on standard benchmarks, with many models exceeding \(98\%\) accuracy under conventional in-distribution evaluation protocols. However, such results largely rely on dataset–specific train–test splits and fail to characterize robustness under distribution shift, where deepfakes are generated by previously unseen synthesis pipelines. Moreover, most existing detectors operate as black box classifiers with limited interpretability, making their decisions difficult to understand and trust for practitioners outside the machine learning community. Our primary contribution is XNeuro-MDeep, an Explainable Neurosymbolic Multimodal DeepFake detection framework that explicitly exhibit inter-modality extracted from visual, acoustic, and linguistic modalities using physiological and a neurosymbolic reasoning architecture. We contrast this approach with DeepGuard, a strong unimodal baseline that relies solely on visual embeddings extracted by an EfficientNet-B4 backbone trained with a progressive curriculum. In this work, we evaluate cross-dataset generalization in deepfake detection by benchmarking two systems on datasets constructed using disjoint generation methods. While XNeuro-MDeep achieves \(98.25\%\) accuracy when evaluated on FakeAVCeleb v1.2—the dataset used for training—its performance drops to \(48.00\%\) under zero-shot evaluation on Celeb DF v2, approaching chance level classification. This sharp degradation under distribution shift highlights the brittleness of detectors trained on narrow visual artifacts and motivates multimodality integration as a principled direction for improving generalization to unseen deepfake generation methods. All code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/mdshafiqulbaten.

papers.title: Beyond Surveys: Predicting Student Well-being from Open-ended Video Responses using LLMs
papers.authors: Thu Bui, Minjun Choi, Shifa Somji, Hillary Merzdorf, Nan Kong, Louis Tay, Sooyeon Jeong
papers.abstract: Traditional well-being assessment relies on infrequent self-report questionnaires (e.g., PHQ-9), which provide only sparse, retrospective snapshots of well-being and may miss everyday fluctuations. This creates an opportunity for low-burden, lightweight assessments embedded in everyday interactions, such as open-ended conversations with AI systems, to complement existing approaches and enable more natural, potentially more reliable monitoring of well-being over time. However, it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can predict self-reported psychological well-being from naturalistic multimodal data. As a first step toward such an AI-based informal assessment system, we recruited N=228 college students to collect self-reported well-being responses paired with corresponding open-ended video responses. Using this dataset, we conducted four studies to examine the effects of input modalities, model architectures, contextual inputs, and prompting strategies. Our results show that LLMs leveraging multimodal features outperform regression baselines without task-specific fine-tuning, and that retrieval-augmented chain-of-thought prompting with contextual inputs yields the most robust performance. These findings show the promise of multimodal LLM-based approaches for scalable, low-burden well-being assessment and offer design guidance for integrating conversational AI into real-world affective computing systems.

papers.title: HARMONI: Multimodal Personalization of Multi-User Human-Robot Interactions with LLMs
papers.authors: Jeanne Malecot, Hamed Rahimi, Jeanne Cattoni, Marie Samson, Mouad Abrini, Mahdi Khoramshahi, Maribel Pino, Mohamed Chétouani
papers.abstract: Existing human-robot interaction systems often lack mechanisms for sustained personalization and dynamic adaptation in multi-user environments, limiting their effectiveness in real-world deployments. We present HARMONI, a multimodal personalization framework that leverages large language models to enable socially assistive robots to manage long-term multi-user interactions. The framework integrates four key modules: (i) a perception module that identifies active speakers and extracts multimodal input; (ii) a world modeling module that maintains representations of the environment and short-term conversational context; (iii) a user modeling module that updates long-term speaker-specific profiles; and (iv) a generation module that produces contextually grounded and ethically informed responses. Through extensive evaluation and ablation studies on four datasets, as well as a real-world scenario-driven user-study in a nursing home environment, we demonstrate that HARMONI supports robust speaker identification, online memory updating, and ethically aligned personalization, outperforming baseline LLM-driven approaches in user modeling accuracy, personalization quality, and user satisfaction.

papers.title: IntentVLM: Open-Vocabulary Intention Recognition through Forward–Inverse Modeling with Video-Language Models
papers.authors: Hamed Rahimi, Clémence Grislain, Adrien Jacquet Crétides, Olivier Sigaud, Mohamed Chétouani
papers.abstract: Improving the effectiveness of human–robot interaction requires social robots to accurately infer human goals through robust intention understanding. This challenge is particularly critical in multimodal settings, where agents must integrate heterogeneous signals including text, visual cues to form a coherent interpretation of user intent. This paper presents IntentVLM, a novel two-stage video-language framework designed for open-vocabulary human intention recognition. The approach is inspired by forward-inverse modeling in cognitive science by decomposing intention understanding into goal candidate generation followed by structured inference through selection, effectively reducing hallucinations in latent reasoning. Evaluated on the IntentQA and Inst-IT Bench datasets, IntentVLM achieves state-of-the-art results with up to 80% accuracy, notably surpassing the baseline performance by 30% and matches human performance. Our findings demonstrate that this structured reasoning approach enhances open-vocabulary intention understanding without catastrophic forgetting, offering a robust foundation for human-centered robotics.

papers.title: Explanation Needs Emerge Before Explicit Requests in Human-Robot Interaction
papers.authors: Dimosthenis Kontogiorgos, Joakim Gustafson, Julie Shah
papers.abstract: Enabling proactive robot explanations requires recognising when users need an explanation before they explicitly ask for one. In human–robot interaction, such needs may emerge implicitly through facial, bodily, and vocal behaviour, making early detection a temporal and highly imbalanced problem. We compare temporal learning methods across multiple observation windows using multimodal behavioural features. Short-term modelling provides the strongest overall predictive performance, whereas longer windows support earlier detection, revealing a trade-off between discrimination and warning time. Multimodal fusion yields the best results, achieving precision–recall performance over five times the prevalence baseline while maintaining practical false-alarm rates. Attribution shifts from vision and pose in raw scores to robot-state and context after normalisation. Overall, explanation needs appear to emerge through short-horizon behavioural dynamics rather than isolated static cues, supporting robots that can anticipate misalignment and provide timely explanations proactively.

papers.title: DatasetOS: An Agentic Framework For Multimodal Dataset Construction
papers.authors: Bashayer Alsreidi, Ghaleb Aldoboni, Lobna Nassar, Fakhri Karray
papers.abstract: Constructing multimodal video datasets remains a labor-intensive process requiring manual content discovery, viewing, annotation, and feature extraction, a bottleneck that limits progress in multimodal interaction research. We present DatasetOS, the first open-source, prompt-driven multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end construction of multimodal video datasets from web sources. Given a natural-language prompt describing the desired dataset, DatasetOS autonomously discovers relevant videos, applies multi-stage filtering, including format verification via face detection and identity clustering, performs semantic labeling using large language models, and extracts time-aligned multimodal features across visual, audio, and textual modalities. The framework comprises five specialized agents (Content Discovery, Relevance Filtering, Feature Extraction, Dataset Validation, and Supervision) orchestrated through a pip-installable command-line interface. We evaluate DatasetOS on depression detection from personal vlogs, which requires semantic disambiguation between experiential and educational content, verification of the single-speaker format, and synchronized multimodal feature extraction. Across three V/LLM configurations, automated labeling achieves up to 95.5% accuracy against clinician-verified ground truth with zero false positives. A model trained exclusively on automatically curated data reaches within 3.70 percentage points of the expert-labeled baseline, and augmenting the baseline with curated samples improves F1-score by +5.96 pp and +7.30 pp over the published D-Vlog benchmark. DatasetOS is released as an open-source tool for the research community.

papers.title: Investigating Foundation Models, Disentanglement and Latent Alignment for Subject-Independent EEG Learning
papers.authors: Lia Schmid, Jacopo Burger, Alessandro D’Amelio, Raffaella Lanzarotti
papers.abstract: Brain–Computer Interfaces (BCIs) require models that generalize across subjects, yet EEG signals exhibit strong inter-subject variability and non-stationarity, leading to performance degradation on unseen users. This limitation is particularly critical in interactive and multimodal systems, where reliable, calibration-free decoding is essential for real-time interaction, and even minor errors can directly affect user experience. To address this challenge, several paradigms have been explored: foundation models leverage large-scale pretraining, disentangled representation learning aims to separate subject, task, and noise factors, and alignment methods focus on reducing distribution shifts in the feature space. Despite their promise, a systematic comparison of these approaches is still lacking. In this work, we propose a modular framework for the unified evaluation of these paradigms in subject-independent learning. We conduct extensive experiments on Motor Imagery (MI) and Event-Related Potential (ERP) datasets, representative of interactive BCI scenarios spanning both oscillatory (MI) and event-related (ERP) paradigms, to analyze their relative effectiveness and practical trade-offs. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/phuselab/eeg_subj_indep_learning.

papers.title: Multimodal Rapport Estimation in Real-World HRI
papers.authors: Akihiro Sakuramoto, Takato Hayashi, Ryo Miyoshi, Yuki Okafuji, Shogo Okada
papers.abstract: Evaluating interaction quality in real-world HRI is an important challenge. If interaction quality can be estimated reliably, the results can be used to improve dialogue strategies and ultimately enable robots to adapt their behavior autonomously. However, existing automatic evaluation methods have been developed primarily in controlled laboratory settings, and it remains unclear whether they can be directly applied to real-world environments, where users are free to disengage and multi-party participation may arise naturally. In this study, we investigate the automatic estimation of third-party-rated rapport scores using 62 sessions of multimodal recordings collected in a Japanese drugstore. We compare zero-shot LLMs, pretrained text, audio, and visual models, and their prediction-level fusion. The results show that, in real-world HRI, zero-shot LLMs achieve strong performance, while audio and visual models tend to provide complementary information. In particular, Gemini 2.5 Flash performs strongly as a single model, and a fusion model combining Gemini (text) with HuBERT and V-JEPA performs best overall. Further analyses showed that estimation performance varied across interaction-duration and group-size conditions. These findings suggest that rapport estimation in real-world HRI requires evaluation and model design that account for contextual variability beyond that assumed in laboratory settings.

papers.title: Multimodal Learner-State Analytics: Cross-Modal Insights from Motor-expressions and EEG for Instructor-Facing Visualization Platform
papers.authors: Qi Song, Gaoyuan Zhang, Chengchen Lyu, Xurong Xie, Naiming Yao, Hui Chen, Feng Tian
papers.abstract: Remote video lectures expand educational access but limit instructors’ ability to observe how students engage with instructional content. To address this challenge, we explore how insights from portable electroencephalography can enrich visual analytics for computer-based learning environments. In our study, sixteen middle school students watched a mathematics video lecture while we collected and temporally aligned their gaze data, video recordings of motor expressions, and physiological indices of attention, valence, and arousal. By comparing these measures, we developed models to estimate internal learning states from accessible motor-expression data alone. We then applied changepoint detection to identify critical learning moments and integrated these alongside the estimated trends into a visualization platform designed for educators. An evaluation with thirty teachers revealed that observing these critical moments helped them identify specific lecture segments warranting closer inspection, allowing educators to reflect deeply on pacing, explanation quality, and overall slide design. These findings highlight a practical path toward scalable visualization platforms for digital education, equipping educators with profound pedagogical insights through accessible sensing alone.

papers.title: Beyond Rhythm and Prosody: Inter-Utterance Silence Predicts Drone Movement Duration in Spontaneous Vocal Guidance
papers.authors: Allan HENRY, Solange Rossato, Christian Graff, Sylvain Huet, José-Ernesto Gomez-Balderas
papers.abstract: Most existing voice-controlled robot systems in human-robot interaction (HRI) rely on fixed or predefined movement durations, or on explicit quantity markers in spoken commands, with no direct link between the spontaneous acoustic signal and the amount of movement produced. Prosodic features such as fundamental frequency, energy, and speech rate have been proposed as potential carriers of such information, but their validity in naturalistic, spontaneous speech remains largely untested. This paper investigates whether several acoustic and rhythmic parameters, including inter-utterance silence duration, are more strongly associated with drone movement duration than classical prosodic features. Using N = 1, 592 spoken instructions from spontaneous French speech collected during real human-drone teleoperation, we evaluate this relationship through correlation and regression analyses. Silence duration substantially outperforms all prosodic features, yielding the strongest correlation with movement duration (r =.498, p <.001) and accounting for approximately 80% of the variance explained by the full model (R2 =.226 univariate vs. R2 =.283 multivariate). These findings question the assumption that prosody encodes motor intent in continuous-control HRI, and suggest that when a speaker talks may matter more than how they sound.

papers.title: Framing the Formless: A Xing–Qi–Shen Framework for Culturally Aware Multimodal Human–AI Co-Creation
papers.authors: Conggang Yu, Shudan Tan, Yuxing Zhang, Lin Yu
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has significantly lowered the technical threshold for visual creation. However, current systems frequently exhibit a lack of cultural context and aesthetic flattening when applied to Chinese-style scene generation. Existing models commonly offload control responsibilities to prompt engineering, making it difficult for non-expert users to consistently articulate Chinese aesthetic intentions, which require spatial order, atmospheric hierarchy, and semantic depth. This paper reframes this limitation as a human-computer interaction (HCI) problem of "cultural operability." The core objective is not merely to prompt the model to output more cultural symbols, but to translate tacit cultural knowledge into interaction dimensions that users can directly manipulate. Based on the aesthetic logic of Chinese classical gardens, we propose the Xing-Qi-Shen (Form-Atmosphere-Spirit) interaction framework. This framework is operationalized into spatial relational control, atmospheric condition regulation, and semantic guidance within a generative system. Subsequently, we developed the proof-of-concept prototype to manifest abstract cultural structures as actionable interface controls. A within-subjects experiment involving 53 participants demonstrated that the framework significantly outperformed the baseline condition across four dimensions: compositional rationality, atmospheric expressiveness, resonance and imagination, and cultural consistency. The aggregate comparison yielded a baseline mean of 2.946 versus a framework mean of 3.857 (t(52) = 6.981, p < 0.001, Cohen's dz=0.959). These findings provide initial evidence that culturally structured representations can improve the perceived quality of generated outputs.

papers.title: Han-Vibe: Culturally-Situated Multimodal Interaction for AI-Mediated Live Music Performance
papers.authors: Zhengyang Ma
papers.abstract: We present Han-Vibe, a terminal-based multimodal system for live electronic music performance that unifies direct manipulation, live DSP editing, AI-mediated natural-language control, offline voice triggers, and community resource sharing in a culturally situated workflow we term vibe performing. The design draws on hanmai (喊麦), a Chinese internet music tradition in which an MC’s voice modulates a live-streamed performance. Han-Vibe organizes three input modalities (tactile, linguistic, vocal) into four interaction paradigms: TuneTouch (keyboard parameter control), LiveForge (hot-reloadable Faust DSP editing), VibeLink-Text (LLM-mediated typed intent), and VibeLink-Voice (offline keyword-to-scene mapping). The PulseHub (脉冲社) resource layer supplies reusable DSP and scenes through VibeLink-Text. We report component-level latency measurements as a necessary technical characterization, not an evaluation of usability or creative value. Completed asynchronous commands are scheduled at the first subsequent bar boundary, preserving grid alignment while leaving the performer’s waiting time variable. We discuss the contribution and limits of this culturally situated design case.

papers.title: Memory-Driven Self-Disclosure and Relational Turning Points: A Longitudinal Multimodal Study of Human-AI Interaction
papers.authors: Ryuichi Sumida, Mao Saeki, Masaki Eguchi, Sadahiro Yoshikawa, Koji Inoue, Tatsuya Kawahara, Yoichi Matsuyama
papers.abstract: As conversational AI systems are designed for repeated use, a central question is how a series of interactions becomes a relationship. We present a longitudinal multimodal study of a memory-augmented conversational agent (24 participants × 10 sessions), in which participants rated five relational constructs—familiarity, self-disclosure, perceived memory, conversational quality, and enjoyment—after each session. Two complementary dynamics emerge. First, conversational quality strongly shapes how enjoyable a session feels in the moment but does not carry forward across sessions, whereas perceived memory is relationally conditioned—predicted by prior relational state rather than reflecting system capability alone—and it shapes later enjoyment indirectly, via subsequent self-disclosure. Second, relationships are punctuated by discrete turning points—crashes and surges—that are partially traceable in multimodal behavior and open different intervention windows: surges are more behaviorally detectable in the moment, enjoyment surges persist more reliably than enjoyment crashes recover, and some crashes are better forecast from person-specific behavioral drift than detected after they have already occurred. Together, the findings suggest that longitudinal human-AI relationships are built through both slow accumulation and abrupt turning points.

papers.title: How YouTube Frames ChatGPT Use in Education: An Epistemic Network Analysis with Supporting Multimodal Metadata
papers.authors: Shayla Sharmin, Mohammad Al-Ratrout, Mohammad Fahim Abrar, Roghayeh Barmaki
papers.abstract: We examine educational YouTube videos through multimodal metadata, such as transcripts, titles, thumbnails, and viewer comments, to investigate how ChatGPT is framed across creator groups and how those framings relate to audience response and platform reach. Little is known about how large language models are presented to learners in informal, creator-driven public discourse. Following PRISMA, we selected 52 videos for analysis. We identified three structurally distinct discourse groups: (G1) videos that positioned ChatGPT as a conceptual scaffold for thinking, (G2) videos oriented toward retrieval practice and skill-building, and (G3) videos that framed ChatGPT as a tool for output generation. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed statistically significant group differences with large effect sizes. Multimodal metadata consistently reflected these distinctions across transcript discourse, titles, and thumbnails. Viewers of learning-oriented content described ChatGPT as a thinking partner or tutor, whereas viewers of output-oriented content raised concerns about over-reliance, surface-level learning, and cognitive offloading. G3 achieved comparable platform reach to G2, yet with substantially weaker learning-oriented framing. This may suggest that output-oriented content competes for visibility despite lower pedagogical depth. These findings reveal a structural tension in self-directed AI learning: content that prioritizes quick outputs reaches far more learners than content that promotes deep engagement. This gap raises critical questions about whose vision of AI literacy scales and what learners are actually left with.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Spatiotemporal EEG and Self-Supervised Audio Fusion: A Mixture-of-Experts Approach to Continuous Affect
papers.authors: Ali Amini, Sarmad Maqsood, Irfan Abbas, Muhammad Abdullah Sarwar, Rytis Maskeliūnas, Robertas Damaševičius
papers.abstract: Emotion-aware human–computer interaction increasingly relies on continuous emotion recognition (CER) to track affective states over time. This paper investigates continuous valence prediction on the MAHNOB-HCI database using a multimodal EEG+audio framework. The proposed model combines (i) a hierarchical spatiotemporal EEG encoder that captures per-channel temporal dynamics and inter-channel dependencies and (ii) self-supervised audio embeddings extracted from SSLAM in a feature-based transfer setting. To integrate modalities robustly, we introduce a modality-sensitive mixture-of-experts (MoE) fusion module with modality-specific experts and a learned gating network that dynamically weights EEG and audio contributions. Under session-preserving partitioning with 5-fold cross-validation, the proposed approach achieves strong agreement with ground-truth valence trajectories (PCC=0.778, CCC=0.742, RMSE=0.034), comparing favorably with representative prior results reported under broadly related MAHNOB-HCI protocols. Finally, we provide interpretability evidence by linking the EEG encoder’s alpha-band saliency asymmetry to classical alpha-band power asymmetry patterns, thereby supporting the neurophysiological plausibility of the learned representations.

papers.title: The Person Multimodal AI Cannot Finish
papers.authors: Mohammad Rashedul Hasan
papers.abstract: The signals that matter most in clinical, educational, and counseling interactions are often the ones current multimodal AI is designed to remove. A topic that disappears between sessions becomes missing data the pipeline tries to repair. When a face contradicts the words spoken, the fusion architecture integrates the contradiction away. Silence shaped by cultural prohibitions becomes a single confident label. Multimodal large language models build on encoders pretrained via contrastive cross-modal alignment, which compresses modality-specific information away and biases the architecture toward agreement. This architecture of certainty must be replaced in systems that interact with people. Drawing on Paul Cézanne’s unfinished portraits, in which the painter refused to invent the part of another person that perception does not reach, we propose productive uncertainty as the design stance that multimodal interaction has been missing. We sketch the architecture and the evaluation it requires.

papers.title: What Matters Over Time: Temporal Properties of Non-Verbal Signals for Intent Recognition in Human–Robot Interaction
papers.authors: Eunyoung Hwang, Alessandra Rossi, Silvia Rossi
papers.abstract: Multimodal fusion systems for human–robot interaction predominantly rely on snapshot-level features that capture what nonverbal signals are present at a given moment, ignoring when they occur, how long they last, and in what order they unfold. Nevertheless, the temporal dynamics of human behaviour may convey communicative intent beyond the presence of individual cues. This paper investigates the temporal properties of nonverbal signals including onset timing, duration, ordering, and cross-modal coordination across gaze, gesture, and speech for intent recognition in human-robot interaction. We empirically characterise how these properties differ across 30 communicative intent classes in MIntRec 2.0, finding that speech timing features are the strongest discriminators, that speech act function governs nonverbal temporal patterns more than valence or arousal, and that cross-modal ordering follows a consistent intent-modulated hierarchy. Our work argues that the bottleneck in current multimodal fusion lies not in the architecture but in a feature space that discards the temporal structure most relevant to social understanding. Future work will incorporate these features into a multimodal fusion model and evaluate their effect on robot intent recognition in real HRI settings.

papers.title: Structured Representations For Human-Robot Interaction with Non-Expert Users
papers.authors: Valerie K. Chen
papers.abstract: A prerequisite for deploying robots alongside people is the ability to exchange information fluidly across multiple modalities: robots must interpret implicit social signals, receive explicit instructions, and communicate back in ways non-experts can understand. A key challenge is that humans naturally exchange information through multiple modalities, requiring computational systems to consider heterogeneous signals to be fully fluent, interactive partners. My key insight is that structured intermediate representations can serve as a common backbone across modalities, grounding both understanding and communication without requiring specialized user input. I develop two such representations: a topological formalism for reasoning about multimodal social signals in human environments, and a motion descriptor framework that translates natural language stylistic intent into steerable robot behavior, supporting bidirectional refinement through grounded feedback. Together, these contributions advance a vision of robot systems that that fluently share spaces and interactions with any user.

papers.title: Generic modeling of Human-Machine Interaction
papers.authors: lykong un
papers.abstract: Human interaction understanding is usually studied separately for Human-Human Interaction (HHI), Human-Object Interaction (HOI), and Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), which limits progress toward more general interaction models. This paper investigates whether explicit structured interaction cues can support a shared multimodal representation across interaction settings. The proposed framework encodes pose, object, relation, and temporal cues into interaction tokens and aligns them with a multimodal backbone through a lightweight trainable interface. The current study evaluates this formulation on coarse-grained dyadic interaction understanding in two complementary settings: video-based HHI on the mutual-action subset of NTU RGB+D 120 and image-based HOI on HICO-DET. Preliminary results show that the framework can generate interaction-aware outputs in both settings, with substantially stronger performance on NTU RGB+D 120 than on HICO-DET. These findings suggest that making interaction structure explicit is a promising direction for multimodal interaction understanding and provides a basis for future extension toward more complex multi-party and human-robot interaction scenarios.

papers.title: Towards Memory-Aware Adaptive Agents
papers.authors: Deborah van Sinttruije
papers.abstract: Human memory is dynamic and uncertain, yet adaptive systems often overlook how it shapes interaction. This PhD investigates how agents can model and adapt to human memory by treating it as a latent, time-varying process. In this work we develop adaptive models that progress from estimating how much a user can remember, to inferring which information is retained, to identifying factors that influence forgetting, and finally to modeling individual differences shaped by prior knowledge and biases. Through simulation and user studies, this research examines whether agents can accurately infer memory states and provide targeted support. The goal is to enable more effective human-AI interaction through memory-aware adaptive systems that personalize behavior based on dynamic and individual cognitive characteristics.

papers.title: Multi-Domain Representation Learning For Enhanced EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
papers.authors: Yuanyuan Gao, Shuhui Liu, Jiye Zhan, Shiliang Shao, Ting Wang, Zhenpeng Gao
papers.journal: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
papers.abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in EEG-based emotion classification using convolutional neural networks; however, effectively leveraging multi-domain EEG features to improve emotion recognition accuracy remains challenging. To address this, we propose a dual-branch feature fusion architecture that integrates complementary EEG features. Specifically, the Global Temporal Branch uses a Transformer to capture long-range dependencies, while the Local Multi-domain Branch employs a bidirectional gated recurrent Unit (BiGRU) to extract local temporal dynamics from multi-domain features. Their collaboration enables effective exploitation of complementary EEG information. Finally, experiments on the public SEED and SEED-IV datasets show that the proposed model outperforms existing methods.

papers.title: AN INTELLIGENT SLEEP STAGING FRAMEWORK FOR SLEEP-QUALITY CHARACTERIZATION AND DIGITAL INTERACTION DESIGN FOR OLDER ADULTS
papers.authors: Zhiwei Chen, MINNING ZHOU, Yunyi Ma, Xiang Chen
papers.journal: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
papers.abstract: Advancing age is commonly accompanied by a decline in sleep quality, while objective clinical sleep assessment often relies on polysomnography (PSG), which is costly and burdensome for older individuals. To address this issue, we develop an age-adaptive framework using single-channel EEG for automatic sleep staging, staging-derived sleep characterization, subsequent sleep quality index (SQI) calibration, and digital interaction. The proposed framework consists of three successive stages. First, single-channel EEG is acquired using a low-burden sensing configuration. Second, sleep stages are predicted using a multi-scale CNN, channel-wise feature recalibration, and a BiLSTM model optimized with focal loss and age-adaptive fine-tuning. Finally, sleep-architecture and continuity measures derived from the predicted hypnogram, including total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency (SE), wake after sleep onset (WASO), N3 proportion, REM proportion, and fragmentation index (FI), are organized as candidate variables for subsequent SQI calibration. Evaluation on older-adult recordings from Sleep-EDF yielded an accuracy of 87.6% for five-stage classification and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.83, while ablation experiments further demonstrated the effectiveness of the individual design components. Correlation and multicollinearity analyses showed physiologically meaningful associations among the staging-derived variables without severe multicollinearity, with variance inflation factor (VIF) values ranging from 1.31 to 3.48. Because Sleep-EDF does not provide concurrent subjective sleep-quality references, no SQI regression weights or categorical sleep-quality cut-offs are estimated in the present study. Instead, the SQI is formulated as a calibration framework whose weights and clinically meaningful interpretation require subsequent external calibration and validation using datasets with appropriate subjective sleep-quality reference scores.

papers.title: Approaches used in Canadian academic institutions to keep nursing students safe during clinical placements: a systematic review protocol of policy and expert opinion.
papers.authors: Rose M. McCloskey, Patricia Morris, Alexis McGill, Richelle L. Witherspoon, Emily Gregg, Lisa Keeping‐Burke, Elizabeth Pavlovic, Kim Lauzier, Julia Payne, Taylor Copeland, Martha Jane Paynter
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This review will synthesize the available evidence on approaches used by Canadian academic institutions to keep nursing students safe during clinical placements. INTRODUCTION: The safety of health care workers is a global priority, with growing concern for pre-licensure students. Nursing students face heightened physical, psychological, and professional risks as they provide direct, sustained patient care within complex clinical environments. Academic institutions play a critical role in safeguarding students by creating protective learning environments. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: The phenomenon of interest is approaches used by academic institutions to promote nursing student safety during clinical placements. The population is Canadian academic institutions delivering pre-licensure nursing programs leading to a registered nurse designation, across all provinces and territories. Eligible sources may include policies, directives, guidelines, curriculum documents, clinical requirements, and other text-based materials produced by accredited nursing programs, regulatory bodies, occupational health and safety organizations, and recognized experts in nursing education or student safety. METHODS: This review will follow JBI methodology for systematic reviews of textual evidence: narrative, opinion, or policy. The review will evaluate the feasibility of using a large language model (Claude AI) to support gray literature retrieval by comparing its performance with the Google search strategy on a sample of nursing education programs. Two independent reviewers will screen records, extract data, and critically appraise eligible sources using JBI critical appraisal tools for text and opinion evidence. The findings will be synthesized using JBI meta-aggregation for textual evidence and the results will be presented in both tabular and diagrammatic formats. REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420251268176.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence use and personalized learning in higher education: pathways toward sustainable development goals and student mental health
papers.authors: Yuhao Su, Irum Zeb, Aashiq Khan
papers.journal: International Journal of Sustainability in Higher Education
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence use (AIU) and personalized learning contribute to SDG-4 quality education (QE) and students’ mental health (MH) in higher education, and the study also investigates whether AIU statistically mediates the relationships between personalized learning and QE and MH. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 460 students at a Chinese university. The hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings Open learning was positively associated with both queality education and mental health, information management was positively associated with mental health but not with quality education, and knowledge creation was positively associated with quality education but not with mental health. None of the three personalized-learning dimensions were significantly associated with artificial intelligence use. In turn, artificial intelligence use was positively associated with both quality education and mental health. Artificial intelligence use showed significant indirect effects only between open learning and quality education and between open learning and mental health. No significant indirect effects were found for information management and, knowledge creation. Because the study used cross-sectional self-reported data, these findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal relationships. Practical implications The findings suggest that higher education institutions consider creating open and knowledge-rich learning environments, integrating AI tools that provide adaptive support and strengthening students’ information management (IM) skills. These factors were positively associated with quality education and mental health. However, the results should be interpreted cautiously because the study does not establish causal relationships or directly measure institutional progress toward SDG-4. Originality/value This study examines OL, IM and KC separately and tests their direct and indirect associations with QE and MH through AIU. The findings reveal dimension and outcome specific associations, with significant indirect effects only for the OL–QE and OL–MH relationships. Thus, AIU is not a common statistical pathway linking all personalized-learning dimensions with student outcomes.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning for the classification of prevalent cardiovascular disease using clinical and nutritional factors in United States adults: a cross-sectional analysis of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011–2018
papers.authors: Le Huu Nhat Minh, Han H. Huynh, Phat K. Huynh, Thanh-Huy Nguyen, Mai Anh Vu, Dang Nguyen, Tien Truong, Thomas Duong, Chenyu Sun, Chi L K Nguyen, Nguyen Cung Que Truong, Thanh T Nguyen, Tu Ngoc Nguyen, Truong Quang Dang Khoa, Yayoi Natsume‐Kitatani, Phu Nguyen, Thach Nguyen, Nguyen Quoc Khanh Le, Ulaş Bağcı, Chi N Duong, Tuan Vinh, Vu Thien
papers.abstract: Abstract Background and aims Machine learning (ML) is increasingly applied to the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) to classify cardiovascular disease (CVD), but whether it outperforms logistic regression, and whether dietary intake adds information beyond clinical variables, is uncertain. Because NHANES is cross-sectional, such models classify prevalent disease rather than predict future risk. We developed and internally validated explainable ML models for prevalent, self-reported CVD in US adults using a leakage-safe pipeline, compared six algorithms against conventional logistic regression, and compared clinical-only, dietary-only and combined predictor sets. Methods We analysed 19,404 adults aged ≥20 years from NHANES 2011–2018 with complete self-reported CVD status (heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina, myocardial infarction or stroke), at least one 24-hour dietary recall, and examination data. The sample was split 80:20 before any data-dependent processing. Within the development set, multivariate imputation, correlation filtering, LASSO selection and 1:1 down-sampling were nested inside repeated 5-fold cross-validation (2 repeats) to tune six algorithms (elastic-net logistic regression, random forest, naive Bayes, support-vector machine, XGBoost, LightGBM). Performance was assessed once on the test set using ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Brier score, calibration intercept/slope, and decision-curve analysis, with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). Predicted probabilities were corrected for down-sampling. SHAP values were computed for the final LightGBM models. Results Prevalent CVD was reported by 2,117 participants (10.9%). The combined LightGBM model discriminated well (ROC-AUC 0.843 [0.825–0.861]; PR-AUC 0.409 [0.364–0.462] vs. a 0.109 prevalence baseline) and, after down-sampling correction, was adequately calibrated (intercept 0.043 [−0.074–0.151], slope 0.989 [0.906–1.086], Brier 0.078 [0.072–0.084]), with net benefit over classify-all/none across thresholds of 1–50%. Cross-validated and test ROC-AUC were similar (0.862 and 0.843), and discrimination was similar across sex, race/ethnicity, education and income groups but lower within age strata. In the unweighted test set the six algorithms did not outperform conventional logistic regression (LightGBM minus conventional: 0.009 [−0.000 to 0.020]), and clinical predictors carried nearly all discriminative information (combined minus clinical: −0.0004 [−0.004 to 0.003]); dietary-only discrimination was poor (0.587 [0.558–0.615]). Age, hypertension, total cholesterol, poverty-income ratio, kidney function and red-cell distribution width had the largest SHAP attributions. Conclusions Explainable gradient-boosting models classified prevalent, self-reported CVD with good discrimination but not clearly better than logistic regression, and dietary intake added little beyond clinical measures. Cross-sectional design, self-reported outcome and lack of external validation limit these models to epidemiological description and hypothesis generation, and support simple clinical models as the starting point for prospective analyses.

papers.title: ASAS-NANP SYMPOSIUM: MATHEMATICAL MODELING IN ANIMAL NUTRITION: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models
papers.authors: John Gottula
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of scientific literature and other unstructured materials has made agricultural decision support increasingly complex. Students, extension agents, inspectors, and private sector researchers increasingly rely on large language models (LLM). These models can produce incomplete, overly cautious, or erroneous responses. We outline how LLM offers a possible opportunity for the animal science discipline, describe what LLM do well and where they fall short, and explain how retrieval-augmented generation reduces fabrication and improves relevance. We present a case study that builds a compact index from the United States Department of Agriculture Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) inspection narratives for Agricultural Research Service bird facilities and show how those passages ground concise answers for nutritionists in that audience. We propose an integrated system in which frontline decision makers gain access to LLM while accessing sound information through a lens of subject-matter expertise.

papers.title: Customer Innovativeness and Customer Value Co-Creation Behaviours’ Impact on Well-Being: The Moderating Role of Insurance Premium
papers.authors: Setsoafia-Tukpeyi Godwin, Ibrahim Mohammed, Nana Owusu‐Frimpong
papers.abstract: Ensuring customer well-being is vital for the long-term viability and market penetration of private health insurance firms. Grounded in service-dominant logic and cognitive dissonance theory, this study examines how customer innovativeness (CIV) and customer value co-creation behaviors (VCB) comprising participation behavior (PB) and citizenship behavior (CCB) influence customer well-being (happiness) in Ghana’s private health insurance sector. It also investigates the moderating role of insurance premiums (price) on these relationships. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey, data was collected via convenience sampling from private health insurance customers in Ghana and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The findings reveal that CIV positively influences CCB but has no significant effect on PB. Furthermore, PB significantly enhances customer well-being, whereas CCB shows no significant relationship with well-being, highlighting the distinct roles of different co-creation behaviors. Crucially, insurance premiums exert a negative moderating effect, weakening the positive impact of PB on well-being. Overall, the study demonstrates that higher premiums dampen the well-being gains derived from customer participation. These insights underscore the critical importance of strategic pricing considerations for insurers aiming to foster effective co-creation and optimize customer well-being in private healthcare markets.

papers.title: Reconfiguring faculty agency in the age of generative AI: Authorship, pedagogical judgement, and autonomy in Palestinian higher education
papers.authors: Zuheir N. Khlaif, Bilal Tawfiq Hamamra, Hani Khalil Farran, Wejdan Awadallah Alkouk
papers.journal: Innovations in Education and Teaching International
papers.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly transforming higher education, yet existing research has concentrated on adoption, literacy, efficiency, and ethics, leaving faculty agency underexamined. This study explores how Palestinian faculty members negotiate AI-mediated teaching through authorship, pedagogical judgement, autonomy, and responsibility. Using a qualitative descriptive design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 30 faculty members from two Palestinian universities and analysed thematically. The findings show that generative AI supports teaching, academic writing, communication, and workload management while raising concerns about blurred authorship, dependency, and reduced reflection. Faculty agency was reconfigured through critical mediation: educators evaluated, adapted, and contextualised AI-generated outputs before use. Pedagogical judgement emerged as the mechanism through which educators maintained responsibility and control, while AI-enabled cognitive offloading became educationally responsible only when governed by Critical AI Literacy and situated professional judgement.

papers.title: Students’ conceptions of artificial intelligence and machine learning in K–12 education: a systematic review
papers.authors: Moritz Kreinsen, Meleknur Mercan, Sandra Schulz
papers.abstract: Background and context Knowing students’ conceptions of computer science phenomena is essential for the design of teaching–learning settings and instruments. They are particularly interesting in teaching artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) concepts. Therefore, a comprehensive synthesis focused on K–12 is essential to provide educators with actionable conceptions for curriculum design and assessment.Objective We investigate common conceptions of AI/ML in K–12 and to which curricular concepts these can be assigned. We also examine how conceptions vary across age/grade groups and the data collection/evaluation methods employed. This study uniquely synthesizes fragmented research on students’ conceptions of AI/ML into a unified snapshot, offering a systematic mapping that informs curriculum recommendations.Method A systematic literature review according to PRISMA is used to identify the relevant studies. We analyzed the selected literature, extracted the student conceptions, and classified them according to the curricular concepts.Findings We identified 27 relevant studies (from 2007 to 2024) including the conceptions of 1,077 K–12 students from 30 different countries. In addition, our data includes further information on the type of school, age/grade levels, genders and nationalities, the availability of the collected data, and the survey and evaluation methods used. We took a closer look at 29 of the 409 resulting, highly prevalent conceptions, which stand out due to their frequent occurrence.Implications Our findings may be useful for determining in which grade levels interventions targeting specific concepts would be most effective. This could also be used to study the development of these conceptions or developing assessments.

papers.title: Integrating Behavioral Interventions into the Routine Immunization System in Chad: Implementation Lessons from a Fragile Setting
papers.authors: Fauzia Aman Malik, Rachel Lang-Baldé, Hannah Camille Melchinger, Esias Bedingar, Abdoulaye Annour Idriss, Anastasie Bananeh, Hadje Ache Abakar, Tiandjé Béré Didier, Youssouf Foki, Eric John Cummings, Fatima Rahim, Abdoulaye Youssouf Addoum, Mbailamen Demian Antoinette, Mahamat Allamin Tadjadine, Margaret Anderson, Sten H. Vermund, Choua Ouchemi, Ali Mahamat Moussa
papers.abstract: Despite global progress, COVID-19 pandemic disruptions increased immunization inequities, particularly in fragile contexts like Chad. In 2022-2023, Chad reported 124,544 zero-dose children, in addition to 122,935 children who were classified as under-vaccinated. Low immunization uptake reflects persistent barriers related to access, knowledge, misinformation, and hesitancy. Behavioral interventions, adapted to low-resource settings, can help address these challenges. Anchored in the WHO Behavioral and Social Drivers (BeSD) framework and aligned with the Immunization Agenda 2030 (IA2030), we designed a multi-partner initiative to build government capacity, strengthen the national immunization system, and integrate a package of culturally grounded behavioral interventions into routine immunization delivery. Partners at the Institut National de la Santé Publique du Tchad (INSAPT), the Ministère de la Santé Publique du Tchad (MSP), Yale University, UT Southwestern, and the Université de N'Djaména co-developed a package of vaccine messages, champions, and reminder-and-recall activities implemented across four field sites. This paper presents a qualitative implementation-focused process evaluation, assessing the feasibility, acceptability, and integration into routine immunization practices. We conducted four site visits at each health center, field observations, and 48 qualitative interviews with community members, health center staff, and MSP staff. Team-based thematic analysis provided key insights into community ownership, integration into daily life, perceived trust, and reported shifts in engagement around vaccination. Participants consistently described the co-creation process and inclusion of active vaccine champions as central to acceptance and participation. Despite early interruption, the initiative highlighted mechanisms through which embedding community-led behavioral interventions within routine immunization systems can support trust, facilitate vaccine engagement, and support IA2030 priorities of locally owned, context-responsive delivery.

papers.title: EEG-based mental workload recognition during multi-tasking scenarios: the role of resting-state normalization and brain region of EEG features
papers.authors: Yuchen Ji, Zongqi Liang, Jiaqi Huang, Da Tao
papers.abstract: EEG-based mental workload (MWL) recognition is challenged by inter-individual variability and limited model interpretability. This study investigated MWL recognition in long-term multi-tasking scenarios using resting-state EEG normalisation and regional feature analysis. Participants performed multi-tasking operations at three difficulty levels, while resting-state and task-state EEG, behavioural performance, and NASA-TLX ratings were collected. The best whole-brain model achieved 93.78% ± 0.45% accuracy under standard normalisation, while the parietal configuration retained substantial recognition capability with fewer electrodes. Resting-state normalisation changed EEG feature-importance patterns, but its effects on classification were classifier-dependent rather than uniformly beneficial. SHAP analysis identified prominent frontal and parietal contributions. The findings support interpretable and lightweight EEG-based MWL monitoring in complex operational environments.

papers.title: A hybrid human-AI collaborative workflow for digital heritage interpretation: a case study on the “Dongdong Push” Nuo mask
papers.authors: Unknown Xiao��Xin��https://orcid.org/0009-0006-4091-3965, Qingxin Liu, Jinfeng Wang, Jing Feng
papers.abstract: Abstract With the development of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC), its application in human–AI collaborative design has attracted increasing attention. However, in the process of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) digital revitalisation and cultural product design, systematic research on balancing traditional cultural characteristics with contemporary market aesthetics while avoiding AI-generated cultural bias and visual homogenisation remains limited. Taking the “Dongdong Push” Nuo mask of the Dong ethnic group in China as a case study, this paper proposes an AIGC-assisted ICH IP design workflow based on human–AI collaboration. By integrating the Double Diamond design model, large language models, and AI image-generation tools, the study reconstructs the traditional ICH IP design process. Consumer preference analysis and cultural feature extraction are employed to establish semantic constraints for AI generation, while an AHP-FCE-based multi-stakeholder evaluation framework is constructed to assess design effectiveness through questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. The results indicate that the proposed workflow supports efficient trend extraction, style exploration, and visual ideation while achieving overall performance comparable to traditional manual design. The quantitative comparison revealed only small differences across evaluation dimensions, while the qualitative findings highlighted potential benefits of AIGC in visual exploration and iterative ideation. At the same time, the application of AIGC remains subject to challenges such as visual homogenization, AI hallucinations, and aesthetic inertia. These findings suggest that the value of AIGC in ICH design lies not in replacing human designers, but in supporting and expanding their cognitive and creative exploration through human–AI collaboration.

papers.title: Development and preliminary evaluation of a GenAI-supported ethics learning platform for interprofessional healthcare education
papers.authors: Liam Rankine, Jennifer Van Bussel, Sheila Moodie, Andrews Kwabena Tawiah
papers.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can generate realistic clinical scenarios on demand and deliver immediate, individualized feedback, yet practical guidance on how to design and vet such content for teaching ethical reasoning, as opposed to addressing the ethics of AI itself, remains scarce in interprofessional healthcare education. Aim This pilot study describes the development of a GenAI-supported interactive learning platform for ethical decision-making across physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, and audiology, and reports students' preliminary perceptions of the platform. Methods The platform was developed through a five-step pipeline: defining requirements, generating 20 case scenarios with a large language model through iterative prompting, faculty review and revision of each case, implementation as a self-paced interactive module, and deployment within the institutional learning management system. Each case required students to classify a scenario as ethical uncertainty, dilemma, or distress and provided immediate feedback. Students then completed an optional post-activity survey, analyzed descriptively alongside content analysis of open-ended responses. Results Among the ten respondents, perceptions of the platform's usefulness and usability were broadly positive, particularly its immediate feedback and variety of scenarios, while perceptions regarding comparisons to traditional classroom learning were more mixed. Conclusions The main contribution of this work is a transparent, replicable pipeline for creating instructor-vetted, GenAI-generated ethics cases. Early perceptions were encouraging, but the small sample means findings are preliminary and best used to inform future development and evaluation.

papers.title: Assessing inter-rater agreement among large language model judges: Evidence from persona evaluation across varying educational risk contexts
papers.authors: Danial Amin, Joni O. Salminen, Bernard J. Jim Jansen
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as automated judges for evaluation, yet their reliability remains unclear. This study examines the inter-rater agreement of three LLM judges (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro) when evaluating fairness, lack of stereotypicality, and diversity in user personas across varying educational risk contexts. We analyzed 60 individual personas and 12 persona sets to assess whether these judges demonstrate sufficient consistency to function as reliable evaluators. Although inter-rater agreement was moderate at the individual persona level, three critical limitations emerged. At the set level, agreement ranged from .39 to .63 across persona generators and therefore did not show a uniform decline relative to individual-level agreement. Mean dimension-support scores were 41% to 61% lower, although the individual- and set-level tasks are not directly comparable. Second, non-compliance rates, where judges could not provide textual justification for their ratings, ranged from 9.6 to 26.7% at the individual level and increased to 34% to 49% at the set level. Third, agreement differed across the three educational scenarios classified by risk: individual-level agreement declined from the lower- to higher-risk scenarios, while set-level agreement showed no monotonic pattern. We conclude that, under the tested protocol, current LLM judges demonstrate poor-to-moderate inter-rater agreement for persona evaluation. These findings contribute a descriptive characterization of LLM evaluation behavior across risk contexts and provide a foundation for future validation studies comparing LLM agreement against human judgment.

papers.title: Can LLMs effectively annotate learner writing? Prompting strategies and proficiency effects in annotating L2 learner argumentative essays
papers.authors: Detong Xia, J. Elliott Casal, Erick Purwanto, Natasha Atmadja
papers.abstract: Recent research has demonstrated promising performance of large language models (LLMs) in genre-based discourse annotation. However, most existing work has focused on academic research genres, with less attention paid to the annotation of learner writing, where argumentative elements may be realized in diverse and linguistically variable ways. This study investigates LLM-based annotation of argumentative elements in L2 English argumentative essays drawn from the Yonsei English Learner Corpus. The dataset consists of 780 timed argumentative essays (390 beginning-level essays and 390 intermediate-level essays) written by first-year university students. We evaluate model performance under zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning conditions, and analyze residual human–LLM disagreement patterns using human annotations as a reference. Results reveal a clear performance hierarchy, with the fine-tuned model substantially outperforming zero-shot and few-shot prompting conditions in overall annotation performance. However, systematic human–LLM disagreements persist even under the fine-tuning condition, particularly in Claim identification. Qualitative analysis shows that these disagreements are not random inconsistencies but reflect tensions between the argumentative patterns captured by the model and the diverse ways argumentative functions are realized in learner writing. This study advances theoretical understanding of automated discourse analysis in learner corpora and highlights implications for methodological design and pedagogical integration in genre-based writing instruction.

papers.title: How patient-operated AI tools are reshaping patient perceptions and the patient-clinician relationship: A narrative review
papers.authors: Dmitry Beylin, Rachel KORNHABER, Michelle L. Cleary
papers.abstract: Objectives To examine how patient-operated AI tools influence patient perceptions and the patient-clinician relationship, including their role in supporting health literacy and the risks of misinformation, algorithmic bias and cyberchondria. Methods This narrative review synthesises published literature examining how patients use AI tools to enter symptoms, obtain assessments and judge the urgency of seeking care, and how these tools shape communication, trust and interaction during clinical encounters. Findings were organised around empowerment, anxiety, safety, bias, demographic differences and clinical workload. Author-developed illustrative examples were included to support the narrative synthesis and were distinguished from empirical findings. Results Patients value the convenience, immediacy and sense of control provided by AI tools. However, concerns about accuracy, inconsistent triage, hallucinations, privacy and the potential for increased health anxiety are common. Cyberchondria is reported when AI-generated information amplifies worry or leads to unnecessary escalation of care. Trust in clinicians remains central, and disclosure that AI contributed to a diagnosis can reduce confidence in medical advice. Clinicians report challenges in correcting misinformation, preserving empathy and managing increased workload. Engagement varies by age, education, digital literacy and cultural context, with lower literacy and marginalised groups more vulnerable to misunderstanding or inequitable AI performance. Conclusions Patient-operated AI tools are reshaping early help-seeking and expectations during consultations. They can improve preparedness and health literacy but also introduce new pressures on trust, safety and communication. Effective integration requires transparency and continued emphasis on the human elements of care. Practice implications Clinicians should ask whether patients have used AI tools, encourage them to share the advice received and explain how AI outputs differ from clinical assessment. They should correct unsafe or inaccurate information and reinforce shared decision-making. Services adopting these AI tools should support clinicians with guidance on communication, privacy, bias and digital literacy to maintain trust and person-centred care.

papers.title: Altered neural prioritization of auditory information during cross-modal attention in children with ADHD
papers.authors: Letian Yang, Chen Dang, Weizhen Yin, Xinru Xu, Xuye Yuan, Han Yang, Shanping Zhang, Shuai Jiang, Yuanjie Guo, Yao Wang, Chanjuan Yang, Yanlin Zhou, LI Dongwei, Yan Song, Cai-Ping Dang
papers.abstract: Efficient auditory attention requires prioritizing target over nontarget information. Although attention deficits are a core feature of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the neural mechanisms underlying auditory prioritization during cross-modal attention remain unclear. We examined neural differentiation between target and nontarget auditory information in children with ADHD. Ninety-five school-aged children (mean age = 10.81 years), including 46 children with ADHD and 49 typically developing (TD) children, performed a visually cued auditory spatial attention task during electroencephalography (EEG) recording. Auditory selective attention was assessed using the N2-anterior-contralateral (N2ac) component and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA). TD children showed enhanced MVPA decoding of target locations and reduced decoding of nontarget locations. Greater target-nontarget neural differentiation was associated with larger N2ac amplitudes. In contrast, children with ADHD showed reduced target lateralization, smaller N2ac amplitudes, weaker target decoding, and enhanced decoding of nontarget locations, resulting in diminished neural differentiation between relevant and irrelevant auditory information. Reduced target-related lateralization was associated with greater response-time variability, whereas reduced target decoding accuracy was linked to more severe hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms. Together, these findings indicate that children with ADHD show altered neural prioritization of auditory information within a visually cued attention context. Altered neural prioritization was associated with behavioral variability and symptom severity, providing new insights into the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying attentional dysfunction in ADHD.

papers.title: From fragmentation to integration: Rethinking the measurement of responsible management education
papers.authors: Stephen Thomas Homer
papers.journal: The International Journal of Management Education
papers.abstract: Responsible Management Education (RME) has become a central agenda within business schools, as institutions seek to prepare graduates capable of addressing complex sustainability and societal challenges. Despite its growing prominence, approaches to evaluating RME remain fragmented, with studies measuring diverse educational, institutional and societal outcomes using inconsistent conceptualisations and indicators. This study systematically reviews the contemporary literature to examine how RME is currently measured and develop a more coherent conceptual framework for evaluation. Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature review of 62 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2016 and 2026 using the Scopus database—an AI-assisted, human-in-the-loop thematic synthesis identified and consolidated 328 measurement-related concepts. The synthesis identified five complementary measurement domains: implementation, learning, behaviour, performance and impact, alongside five stakeholder groups: students, educators, institutions, industry and society. Building on these findings, the study proposes the Integrated Responsible Management Education Measurement Framework (IRMEF) as a multidimensional conceptual evaluation architecture that organises these domains and stakeholder perspectives. Rather than representing an empirically validated measurement model, the IRMEF provides a common conceptual vocabulary for organising existing approaches and guiding future evaluation and empirical validation. It provides a foundation for greater theoretical coherence and methodological consistency while supporting business schools, accreditation bodies, and policymakers seeking more balanced, multidimensional, and contextually appropriate approaches to RME evaluation.

papers.title: Application of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Large Language Models in Stomatology: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: junshengLao , Yiteng Liang, Linyong Xu
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been gradually applied to tasks such as specialized question answering, educational assistance, clinical decision support, and knowledge integration in stomatology. However, general-purpose LLMs still suffer from critical limitations, including outdated knowledge, hallucinatory generation, untraceable information sources, and inadequate clinical adaptability. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) offers a core solution for improving the accuracy, interpretability, and evidential traceability of model outputs by integrating external authoritative knowledge sources. Despite the rapid growth of relevant research, a systematic review on the application status of RAG-enhanced LLMs in the field of stomatology remains lacking. This is a scoping review reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A systematic search was performed in the PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore databases from January 2023 to August 2026. Original studies that developed, applied, or evaluated RAG-enhanced large language models in the field of stomatology were included. Literature screening and data extraction were independently conducted by 2 researchers. Extracted items included research scenarios, subspecialties, knowledge sources, RAG technical characteristics, evaluation design, and main findings. A narrative synthesis approach was used to integrate the results. A total of 20 studies were included, most of published between 2025 and 2026, covering many subspecialties of stomatology. Application tasks included specialized question-and-answer and evidence-based support, clinical decision making and diagnostic assistance, treatment or prescription recommendation, as well as education and training support. Existing studies consistently demonstrated that RAG-enhanced LLMs significantly improved knowledge relevance, evidential traceability, and task adaptability in oral specialty settings, and outperformed unenhanced generic LLMs in multiple comparative evaluations. However, current evidence remains dominated by prototype development, simulated scenario assessments, and small sample studies, with substantial heterogeneity across studies in knowledge base construction, retrieval methods, evaluation metrics, and the extent of clinical validation. RAG-enhanced LLMs show preliminary potential in stomatology, particularly in task scenarios requiring specialized knowledge grounding, evidence-based support, and traceable information sources. However, the field remains at an early stage of development, and current evidence is largely based on prototype systems, benchmark datasets, simulated scenarios, and limited validation settings. Further studies are needed to strengthen real-world validation, multimodal knowledge integration, standardized evaluation frameworks, and safety governance mechanisms before this technology can be responsibly translated into stomatological practice.

papers.title: Higher weight suppression in eating disorder patients with provisional PTSD admitted to residential treatment
papers.authors: Timothy D. Brewerton, Joel Jahraus
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Measures of weight suppression (WS) are recognized indicators of ED severity and outcome. Concurrent posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is also associated with higher symptom severity in patients with ED + PTSD. Those with ED + PTSD may engage in more ED behaviors, including dietary restriction, to regulate their emotions and counteract weight gain. Whether WS is associated with ED + PTSD has not been previously explored. METHODS: Participants included 2529 patients (91% female) admitted to residential care for DSM-5 defined EDs who gave written informed consent for use of their anonymized data. Patients completed self-report assessments for weight history, including highest and lowest non-pregnant weight at current adult height, and symptoms of EDs and PTSD. Provisional diagnoses of PTSD (PTSD+) were found in 45% of the sample and were made using the Life Events Checklist for DSM-5 and the PTSD Symptom Checklist for DSM-5. Groups with and without PTSD+ were compared in unadjusted analyses (t-tests) and in adjusted analyses using multivariate analyses of variance with age, admission BMI, age of ED onset, gender, ED diagnosis, and Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire Restraint subscores as covariates. RESULTS: In the adjusted model, patients with PTSD+ demonstrated significantly higher measures of WS regardless of measurement used, i.e., traditional WS, relative WS and WS at lowest weight (p ≤ .001). CONCLUSION: This is the first known report of significantly higher measures of WS in ED patients with PTSD+, which reinforce findings indicating PTSD as a marker of higher severity of illness. Potential mechanisms, such as glucocorticoid alterations and mitochondrial dysfunction, are discussed.

papers.title: Malnutrition and related nutritional classifications in patients undergoing pancreatic surgery: A systematic review of assessment methods and associated factors
papers.authors: Yin JiaLi, Ronglin Liu, Zhouqing Yu, Li Ji, FangYan Lu
papers.abstract: AIMS: To summarize study-specific reports of malnutrition and related nutritional classifications across nutritional assessment methods in patients undergoing pancreatic surgery and to synthesize the available evidence on associated factors. METHODS: Multiple databases were searched for studies reporting malnutrition or related nutritional outcomes in patients undergoing pancreatic surgery. Study-specific nutritional outcomes were summarized descriptively according to the assessment method and outcome construct. Associated factors were synthesized narratively, with adjusted estimates prioritized when available. RESULTS: A total of 13 studies involving 1890 patients were included. Nine studies reported malnutrition or related nutritional classifications using GLIM, PG-SGA, SGA, MNA, or PNI. Among four studies applying GLIM criteria, the proportion of patients classified as malnourished ranged from 48.6% to 70.0%. Results based on PG-SGA, SGA, MNA, and PNI were summarized separately according to the classifications used in the original studies. No overall prevalence estimate was calculated because these assessment approaches represented non-equivalent nutritional constructs. Older age, smoking exposure, BMI, preoperative serum albumin, primary disease type and surgical characteristics were examined in individual studies, but the evidence was limited by heterogeneous outcome definitions, follow-up periods, and adjustment models. CONCLUSION: Malnutrition and related nutritional impairment are frequently reported among patients undergoing pancreatic surgery, although reported estimates vary across nutritional assessment methods and clinical contexts. Heterogeneity in assessment constructs and methods precluded estimation of a clinically meaningful overall prevalence. Evidence on associated factors remains limited and inconsistent. Greater standardization of nutritional assessment methods and outcome reporting may improve comparability among future studies.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence and commercial sexual exploitation of children: Implications for healthcare providers
papers.authors: Paulette Orhii, Kara Shannon, Cayla Hari, Frances Recknor, Jennifer Martin, Phuong Thanh Nguyen, John Coverdale, Mollie Gordon
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has created new avenues for the commercial sexual exploitation of children through the creation or manipulation of sexually explicit images using a child's likeness. Such images constitute a form of child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including when they are generated or manipulated without physical contact with the child. Because this abuse may occur without the child's awareness, it can complicate recognition, disclosure, and intervention while contributing to ongoing psychological harm. When such content is produced, distributed, or monetized in exchange for anything of value, it may also constitute commercial sexual exploitation of children (CSEC), a term commonly used to describe child sex trafficking. Healthcare providers play an important role in identifying possible GAI child sexual abuse material (GAI-CSAM), supporting affected children and caregivers, and incorporating digital safety into routine care. This article highlights clinical considerations for pediatric, primary care, and mental health settings, including developmentally appropriate assessment of online experiences, caregiver education, trauma-informed response, and multidisciplinary collaboration. As generative technologies evolve, clinician awareness is essential to strengthen prevention, early intervention, and responses to technology-facilitated exploitation.
