papers.title: EEG-based analysis of driver cognitive load in subsea tunnel vs. open road: A hybrid machine learning and statistical modeling approach
papers.authors: Yirun Qu, Ke Wang, Pengyu Zhao, Mengting Cao, Kaixun He, Xin Song, Wei Wang
papers.abstract: Driver cognitive load significantly impacts traffic safety, particularly in high-risk environments such as subsea tunnels. However, the complex effects of environmental factors and individual characteristics on cognitive load remain inadequately understood. To address this gap, this study employed a two-stage research framework to estimate cognitive load and examine its contributing factors. First, a standardized auditory N-back task was used to develop an EEG-based cognitive-load calibration model using features spanning the time domain, frequency domain, nonlinear dynamics, and functional connectivity. Subject-independent leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation yielded an accuracy of 87.2 %. Out-of-fold SHAP analysis identified cross-channel functional-connectivity and multiscale-complexity features as leading contributors to the model predictions. The calibrated model was then applied to real-world driving data to derive cognitive-load estimates in two driving environments: an open road and a subsea tunnel. The model-derived cognitive-load estimate was highest at the subsea tunnel exit. Mixed-effects ordered logit models showed that, within the tunnel, illuminance variability was associated with higher odds of assignment to a higher model-derived load category, OR = 1.147. Greater upslope grade was also associated with higher odds in both violation groups. This association was stronger in the higher-violation group, with conditional ORs of 1.630 and 1.181, respectively, and an interaction OR of 1.380. The upslope association was curvilinear and became steeper above approximately 2 %. These findings provide essential theoretical and empirical support for the development of context-sensitive intelligent driver-assistance systems and targeted infrastructure safety measures.

papers.title: Controlled flexibility for agronomic and natural-science research embedded in Living Labs safeguarding scientific rigor under adaptive conditions
papers.authors: Beatrix Waechter Alsanius, Liselot Bourgeois, Saskia Buysens, Thibault Cloet, Christina Elshoff, Lisa Heyman, Jérôme Lambion, Anne‐Violette Lavoir, Mira Lehberger, Anna Karin Rosberg, Denise Sewkaransing, An Van De Walle, Elien Van den Bossche, Hélène Védie, Gerben Messelink
papers.abstract: CONTEXT Living Labs (LLs) bring agricultural research into real-world settings where researchers and practitioners co-create, test and adapt solutions as conditions change. This flexibility is valuable, but creates a less visible problem: if reference conditions (comparators), sampling, measurements or research questions change during the process, the scientific claim may no longer be supported in the same way. OBJECTIVE We propose controlled flexibility as a framework for keeping evidence scientifically interpretable while preserving the adaptiveness and co-creation that make LLs useful. METHODS This Perspective focuses on quantitative, experimental and structured observational research embedded within LLs. It distinguishes two questions that are often conflated: did the LL generate useful learning or change, and can the resulting data support a specific scientific claim?, thus differentiating between “evaluation for impact” and “evidence for publication”. Systems thinking helps match the measurements to the claimed level of change. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS The framework separates a protected evidential core (research question and claim, analytical unit, comparator or case-selection logic, core indicators, sampling rules, metadata, analysis plan and model of change) from elements that may be adapted locally. Decision logs, deviation records, shared scientific rationale and data audits make adaptations visible. If a change affects the evidence supporting the claim, a new claim version is defined before further analysis. SIGNIFICANCE Controlled flexibility offers a practical way to remain adaptive without weakening scientific credibility. It helps LLs produce evidence that is transparent, proportionate to the claim and publishable, without sacrificing co-creation and situated learning.

papers.title: Eating disorder-related content in Reddit suicidal ideation posts: an LLM-assisted analysis of mental health comorbidities, substance use, and demographic patterns
papers.authors: Salim Sazzed
papers.abstract: Eating disorders are severe psychiatric conditions characterized by a markedly elevated risk of suicidal ideation and behavior. Although prior research has documented these associations in clinical settings, the underlying psychosocial and behavioral dynamics of such co-occurrence remain underexplored in non-clinical contexts, such as social media health narratives. This cross-sectional study examines the prevalence, demographic characteristics, and patterns of co-occurring mental health conditions and substance use among individuals who self-identify as having eating disorders and express suicidal ideation on Reddit’s r/SuicideWatch community. Using a validated keyword-based filtering framework informed by large language model–generated keyword expansion, we identified 688 eating disorder–related posts from a corpus of 27,434 suicidal ideation posts, representing a co-occurrence prevalence of 2.5% (95% CI: 2.33%–2.70%). Among posts with self-reported gender (n=75), females were the largest group (42.7%); among posts with self-reported age (n=170), individuals aged 18–20 were most represented (28.8%). Co-occurring mental health conditions were referenced in 79.0% of posts (95% CI: 75.8%–81.9%), particularly depression (43.9%) and anxiety (31.5%), alongside alcohol as the most prominent substance. These findings illustrate how social media discourse can complement clinical research in characterizing high-risk populations, with potential implications for the design of targeted digital mental health interventions for adolescents and young adults at the intersection of eating disorders and suicide risk.

papers.title: Psychological Outcomes and Correlates Associated with Over-Reliance on Artificial Intelligence Tools: An Integrative Review
papers.authors: Batoul Fneich, Navidreza Ahadi, Jamshid Ali Turi, Farah Alkadhimi
papers.journal: International Journal of Mental Health and Addiction
papers.abstract: Abstract The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) has raised concerns about over-reliance and its psychological implications. This integrative review synthesised psychological outcomes and correlates associated with AI over-reliance and examined its conceptualisation and measurement. The review included 28 studies identified through database and citation searching. AI over-reliance was associated with depression, anxiety, psychological distress, and cognitive disengagement, while findings concerning well-being and self-related functioning, including self-efficacy and autonomy, were mixed and context-dependent. Evidence concerning social or relational functioning was particularly limited, with only one included study directly examining this domain as an outcome. Most evidence was cross-sectional and therefore did not establish temporal direction or causality. Notably, the only longitudinal study found that depression and anxiety predicted subsequent AI dependence, whereas dependence did not predict later depression or anxiety, suggesting that psychological distress may precede dependence. No consensus definition or measure emerged; studies examined reliance, psychological dependence, problematic or compulsive use, and addiction-like engagement. AI over-reliance is therefore best understood as an overarching, multidimensional concept. These findings highlight the need for clearer conceptual boundaries, standardised measurement, and longitudinal and experimental research. PROSPERO CRD420251038303.

papers.title: xAutoGA: an automated deep learning software to educate users
papers.authors: Seyed Mojtaba Mohasel, Alireza Afzal Aghaei
papers.abstract: Abstract Automated deep learning (AutoDL) has emerged as a promising approach to simplify model development for non-experts. However, existing automated tools often lack critical domain-specific features, such as automatic sliding window optimization and subject-wise data splitting, and they remain opaque, which limits their adoption in scientific applications. This study introduces xAutoGA (for E x plainable Auto DL based on a G enetic A lgorithm), designed to address these limitations for multivariate time-series data. The software automates subject assignment to the training, validation, and test sets and jointly optimizes windowing hyperparameters and model architectures in both time and frequency domains. To address the black-box issue, the software guides users through an interactive interface that allows them to configure hyperparameters for the genetic algorithm and neural networks. In addition, it employs a natural selection analogy to explain the selection of specific hyperparameters by visualizing the optimization trajectory. To further enhance interpretability, a rule-extraction method identifies the hyperparameters contributing to top-performing models, which are then synthesized into educational insights using a Large Language Model (LLM). The proposed software is benchmarked against two existing AutoDL systems (McFly and DRAGON) for activity recognition and movement disorder detection tasks. Feedback on the educational component and software usability was collected from 19 university students and two machine learning experts. Statistical tests demonstrated superior performance on three of the five public datasets compared to existing tools ( p -value< 0.05), and user feedback supported the educational value of the proposed software.

papers.title: AiDER: Auditing and Document Evaluation via Rule Compilation and Small Language Models – An Education Case Study
papers.authors: Valerio Crocetti, Elia Pacioni, Aldo Franco Dragoni, Michael Schumacher, Davide Calvaresi
papers.abstract: Abstract Reviewing documents against natural-language requirements is hard when those requirements demand interpretation, contextual evidence, and non-trivial judgment. It is even harder when the review is to be automated reliably and made auditable. In domains like education, where teaching materials must align with pedagogical models and evolving expectations, including the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), such decisions cannot be reduced to mechanical checks. When an LLM assigns a verdict directly, interpretation, evidence selection, and judgment collapse into a single opaque step, making errors hard to localize and outcomes hard to audit. AiDER separates interpretation from judgment under a deliberate 2B–4B parameter constraint. Each natural-language requirement is compiled into an executable Common Expression Language (CEL) rule, and static analysis of that rule produces a bounded-evidence scaffold that constrains what the model may extract from the document. The verdict is then computed deterministically by applying the rule to the extracted evidence (no LLM call at this step), yielding an inspectable trace from requirement to rule, rule to evidence, and evidence to verdict. We evaluate AiDER on four small models (Gemma 4 and Qwen3.5, at 2B and 4B) under three compilation strategies: human-written reference rules, direct compilation, and validation-loop repair. The evaluation uses 200 requirement-document pairs from a higher-education course pack. Across three performance dimensions (syntactic validity, semantic fidelity, and document-level agreement), direct compilation often yields valid but semantically divergent rules, whereas validation-driven repair substantially improves both validity and fidelity across all four models. An ablation shows that the static scaffold alone encodes most of the extraction intent: LLM-generated extraction contracts add little when the rule is well-specified, but matter more when it is ambiguous.

papers.title: Generative AI ‐Supported Creative Writing Among Primary School Students: A Study of Creative Writing Performance, Writing Self‐Efficacy, and Flow State
papers.authors: Xin Liu, Yi Wen, Xiaozhe Yang, Yihe Gao
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing is a growing trend. However, few studies have examined primary school students' interactions with GenAI alongside their writing experiences and resulting writing products. Objectives This study compared creative writing performance, writing self‐efficacy, and flow state across GenAI‐supported, peer‐collaborative and individual writing conditions. It also descriptively examined patterns of student–AI interaction during the writing activity. Methods An experiment involved 78 primary school students in China assigned to three conditions: GenAI‐supported writing ( n = 20), peer collaboration ( n = 38; 19 pairs), and individual writing ( n = 20). Results and Conclusions Students in the GenAI‐supported writing group obtained higher creative writing performance scores than those in the peer‐collaborative and individual writing groups. Interaction analysis showed that students mainly used GenAI to generate and elaborate ideas. Among episodes with observable uptake, adapted or selective incorporation was more common than direct incorporation, and no complete GenAI response was reproduced verbatim. In addition, students in the GenAI‐supported writing group also reported higher writing self‐efficacy than those in the individual writing group, although the difference from the peer‐collaborative writing group was not significant. However, they reported the lowest flow state. Writing self‐efficacy was positively associated with creative writing performance, whereas no significant association between flow state and creative writing performance was observed in this sample. These findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a resource for developing ideas in primary school creative writing.

papers.title: A Software Platform for Orchestrating, Monitoring, and Evaluating Distributed Actor–Learner Urban Routing Systems
papers.authors: Daan Schram, Alberto Garcia‐Robledo, Mahboobeh Zangiabady
papers.abstract: Adaptive, learning-based vehicle routing is a promising alternative to static navigation, but at city scale it must run as a distributed system, and deploying, operating and evaluating one raises software-engineering problems largely separate from routing: sequencing the startup of heterogeneous layers, queuing experiments, monitoring across machines and comparing runs. General-purpose Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) tools manage a training job, not a deployment of interdependent services. We present a software platform for this class of system: each layer exposes a uniform control agent through a small REST API and starts only after the layers it depends on report ready, routing algorithms plug in through a descriptor-based contract, and every run is recorded in a versioned result schema. A browser-based dashboard drives the research lifecycle, from configuration and live monitoring through Grid Search and Simulated Annealing tuning to post-run comparison. The case-study workload is a four-layer Actor–Learner routing system on seven virtual machines, with static Dijkstra, dynamic Dijkstra and Deep Double Q-Routing as interchangeable routers. The evaluation shows routing stays off the simulation’s critical path, and finds no measurable effect of the platform’s telemetry on mean decision latency at the lighter of two traffic loads.

papers.title: Measuring AI Fluency Among Business Students: A Technology Acceptance Model Approach for Digital Transformation in Indonesian Higher Education
papers.authors: Risno Arief Abuyahman, Antonius Felix, Andy Chandra, Syahrul Ramadan Abdurrahman, Selly Swandari, Akbar Lufi Zulfikar
papers.journal: Indonesian Interdisciplinary Journal of Sharia Economics (IIJSE)
papers.abstract: This study examines AI fluency among business students in Indonesian higher education by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with AI literacy, digital self-efficacy, and institutional support. Using a quantitative survey of 385 business students at Universitas Bunda Mulia, data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that AI literacy significantly predicts perceived usefulness (beta = 0.521, p < 0.001), perceived ease of use (beta = 0.486, p < 0.001), and behavioral intention to use AI tools (beta = 0.412, p < 0.001). Attitude also predicts behavioral intention (beta = 0.328, p < 0.001), while digital self-efficacy strengthens the relationship between AI literacy and behavioral intention (beta = 0.256, p < 0.001). Institutional support positively influences both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, although with smaller effect sizes. The model explains 52.3% of the variance in behavioral intention. The study contributes by clarifying the conceptual boundary between AI literacy and AI fluency within an extended TAM framework and by showing how individual confidence and institutional support condition AI adoption among Indonesian business students. Because the study uses cross-sectional self-reported data from a single institution, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of perceived and intention-based AI fluency rather than objective AI performance or causal development over time.

papers.title: A Post-Humanist Ethical View of Truth: Human–Grok Interactions on X in Times of Crisis
papers.authors: Javad; id_orcid 0000-0001-8263-8769 Imani, Arul; id_orcid 0000-0002-3833-8889 Chib
papers.abstract: Truth, as a social practice, depends on trusting the testimonies of particular reference groups. This epistemically social process has been technologically disrupted as users’ agency in establishing trust relationships becomes increasingly constrained by social media infrastructures, where algorithms govern the circulation of (mis)information and shape social networks, contributing to fragmented public spheres. The emergence of generative AI comment bots intensifies this disruption, as nonhuman actors now intervene directly within social media interactions. Unlike epistemic trust networks grounded in social relations, these bots produce “truth” through probabilistic reasoning while offering limited transparency. This raises ethical concerns about the extent to which comment bots prescribe deliberation and remain open to contestation in knowledge construction regarding power asymmetry between genAI and human users. Research Approach: Addressing the issue, we first propose a post-humanistic conception of truth that enables an examination of how the traceability of claims is negotiated within human-nonhuman interactions. Building on this framework, the study investigates the tensions emerging in users’ engagements with Grok comment bot on X during political conflicts. While extensive scholarship has examined the role of manipulative campaigns and social media algorithms in sensitive contexts, we focus on how epistemic practices are reshaped when users rely on Grok to verify information that is both imperative and doubtful. Findings and Conclusion: Examining the 2025 DFRLab dataset of tweets shared during the war, we find that the comment bot operates in a fundamentally disruptive manner: it challenges users’ preexisting trust networks, including journalists and public officials as reference groups, while simultaneously reinforcing unequal relations with users through authoritative forms of communication that lack sufficient transparency and accountability mechanisms. In this sense, tracing nonhuman claims through techno-social practices becomes increasingly difficult. The findings highlight the risks accompanying the rapid expansion of comment bots across social media platforms.

papers.title: Цифровая готовность и информированная тревожность студентов среднего профессионального образования: социологическое исследование паттернов освоения технологий искусственного интеллекта
papers.authors: Roman Yu. Cherkashnev, Р. Ю. Черкашнев
papers.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence is reshaping the professional competence landscape; nevertheless, the patterns of its adoption among vocational education and training students remain largely unexamined. An anonymous online survey was administered to 535 students representing four fields of study (IT, economics and law, medicine and pedagogy, and creative specialties). The study identifies an “informed anxiety” paradox: technologically most engaged students exhibit heightened concerns regarding professional displacement, whereas the correlation between self-assessed digital proficiency and positive attitudes toward AI proves statistically non-significant. The findings provide empirical grounds for integrating AI literacy into VET curricula in a field-specific manner and advocate for a transition from prohibition-based policies toward a regulated-use framework

papers.title: Philosophical Foundations and Pedagogical Approaches to Artificial Intelligence in Algerian Higher Education
papers.authors: Fazilet Alachaher, Nadjima Tabheriti
papers.abstract: This study examines the pedagogical and philosophical implications of artificial intelligence (AI) use at four Algerian university sites. It combines a survey of 200 students, interviews with 20 faculty members and a review of institutional documents. Humanism, constructivism, pragmatism and critical pedagogy provide the interpretive framework. The reported student indicators show more use for writing and translation than for activities labelled critical analysis. Faculty accounts identify both practical uses and concerns about academic integrity, while participants also describe difficulties with access, training and institutional guidance. These findings concern the participating sample and perceptions of AI; they do not establish national adoption rates or measured improvements in learning. Incomplete reporting of recruitment, item-level denominators and institutional documentation limits the analysis. The article proposes that institutions evaluate AI through explicit educational aims, support for human judgement and attention to equitable access. The philosophical framework is an analytical proposal whose effectiveness requires further study.

papers.title: Project Activities in Education in the Context of Exploring the Possibilities of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Art
papers.authors: M. G. Smolina, Р. С. Вологодский, С. В. Степанов, Maya G. Smolina, Ruslan Vologodskiy, Sergey V. Stepanov
papers.abstract: В статье рассмотрена специфика проектной деятельности, касающейся возможностей искусственного интеллекта и цифрового искусства. При этом указанные возможности могут быть как самоцелью проекта, так и средством достижения цели. Приведен обзор реальных проектов студентов и школьников, осуществлен кейс-анализ. Привлекается материал из сферы образования высшей и средней школы на примере проектной практики Красноярского края. В итоге представлена возможная типология и тематика для таких проектов, отмечены необходимые включения, совершенствующие проектные документы и презентационные материалы: такие как процессный анализ генераций ИИ, систематизация запросов и прозрачный алгоритм использования определенных инструментов. Проекты должны рефлексировать применение ИИ для создания качественного работающего на свои задачи продукта. Цифровое искусство предоставляет субъекту проектной деятельности большое проблемное поле в связи с обогащением ИИ, задает эталоны для творческого моделирования

papers.title: Navigating the AI Era: How Perceived Organizational Support Shapes Employees’ AI-Related Anxiety via AI Self-Efficacy
papers.authors: Alsudays HA, Alsudays S
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Hind A Alsudays,1 Sultanah Alsudays21Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Majmaah University, Al Majmaah, 11952, Saudi Arabia; 2Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi ArabiaCorrespondence: Sultanah Alsudays, Department of Business Administration, College of Business, Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Email Smalsudays@imamu.edu.saPurpose: This quantitative study examined the relationships between perceived organizational support (POS), Artificial intelligence self-efficacy (AISE), employees’ artificial intelligence learning anxiety (AILA), and AI job replacement anxiety (AIJRA) in private sector employees; it examined the potential direct effect of POS on both AILA and AIJRA, and the indirect effect via AISE by drawing on social cognitive theory and using structural equation modeling (SEM).Participants and Methods: Convenience and snowball sampling techniques were used to recruit 311 employees from the private sector in the Saudi context. Data were collected using an online survey and analyzed using Mplus to conduct confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and SEM.Results: In the total sample, POS influences AI learning anxiety only via AI self-efficacy (β = - 0.073; p ≤ 0.01). However, AI job replacement anxiety was influenced only directly by POS (β = − 0.184; p ≤ 0.01). These findings suggest that the relative importance of organizational and individual factors varies based on the type of AI anxiety. Finally, Age has a significant and negative relationship with AIJRA (β = − 0.121, P ≤ 0.05).Conclusion: The Study’s findings underscore the importance of individual factors such as AISE in enhancing the role of POS on AILA. Furthermore, These findings suggest that the relative importance of organizational and individual factors varies based on the type of AI anxiety.Keywords: perceived organizational support, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, artificial intelligence learning anxiety, artificial intelligence job replacement anxiety, social cognitive theory, Saudi private sector

papers.title: Preserving Clinical Reasoning in ChatGPT-Integrated Medical Education: From AI Use to Cognitive Engagement
papers.authors: Khajeali N, Amini M, Javaheri F
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Nasrin Khajeali,1 Mitra Amini,2 Fateme Javaheri31Medical Education, Education Development Center, Ahvaz Jundishapur University of Medical Sciences, Ahvaz, Iran; 2Clinical Education Research Center, Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Shiraz, Iran; 3Department of Anesthesiology, School of Allied Medical Sciences, Alborz University of Medical Sciences, Karaj, IranCorrespondence: Fateme Javaheri, Alborz University of Medical Sciences, Karaj City, Alborz Province, Iran, Tel +989381104656, Email javaherifateme1377@yahoo.comKeywords: ChatGpt, generative artificial intelligence, medical education, clinical reasoning, cognitive offloading, AI literacy

papers.title: Transformando la educación desde la inmunología
papers.authors: Sebastián García-Ortega
papers.abstract: Accelerated digital transformation demands a reconfiguration of pedagogical models in medical education to adapt training processes to emerging technological environments. Digital literacy among faculty and students is decisive for the critical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in classrooms, optimizing learning personalization and academic management. In health sciences education, intelligent tutoring systems, virtual environments, and conversational assistants (chatbots) have shown capacity to monitor student progress, assess competencies, and provide immediate feedback. However, the effective adoption of these tools requires continuous strengthening of teachers' digital and pedagogical skills. This article analyzes an educational innovation experience based on using generative AI image tools to create digital comics on complex immunological concepts. Through this transdisciplinary and visual approach, students illustrated intricate immunological dynamics, stimulating creativity, critical thinking, and conceptual retention. The evaluation of scientific comics, grounded in criteria of scientific rigor, narrative coherence, and attainment of pedagogical goals, demonstrated a deeper understanding of the subject. It is concluded that generative AI, when pedagogically mediated, constitutes a powerful didactic resource for teaching biomedical sciences, although technical challenges such as text editing within images must be addressed, alongside mitigating the risk of technological dependency

papers.title: Leveraging AI Learning Analytics to Support CRT-Based Creative Writing Strategies for Quality Education
papers.authors: Ernalida Ernalida, Hani Atus Sholikhah, Izzah Izzah, Zahra Alwi, Chrisnatama Tangguh Prasetyo
papers.abstract: Creative writing instruction in multicultural classrooms requires balancing inclusive, culturally grounded pedagogy with timely, individualized feedback. Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT) validates students' cultural identities in narrative expression, yet its assessment has traditionally relied on subjective, time-consuming teacher judgment. Advances in AI Learning Analytics, including natural language processing (NLP) and automated writing evaluation (AWE), offer the capacity to monitor writing processes and outcomes at scale. This study employs a qualitative library research design, a form of systematic literature synthesis, to examine how AI Learning Analytics can be conceptually integrated into CRT-based creative writing strategies and how this integration may contribute to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education). Data comprised peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, and policy documents published between 2015 and 2025, with emphasis on recent work, analyzed through thematic synthesis. Three converging themes emerged. First, AI Learning Analytics provides linguistic, structural, and affective indicators that can approximate students' cognitive engagement, although cultural expression remains difficult to measure automatically. Second, AI-generated feedback mediated through CRT principles can enhance rather than homogenize culturally diverse voices. Third, this synergy supports equity-oriented, data-informed instruction aligned with SDG 4. The review also identifies risks of algorithmic bias, reduced human interaction, and contextual insensitivity. The study offers a conceptual framework for educators and policymakers designing culturally responsive, AI-supported creative writing pedagogy, while underscoring the continued necessity of human pedagogical judgment.

papers.title: [Clinical reasoning in the age of artificial intelligence: the urgent need for formal education].
papers.authors: Moshe Y. Flugelman, Arieh Riskin
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical reasoning remains the cornerstone of medical practice, yet unlike anatomy or physiology, medical curricula rarely teach it explicitly. This omission has significant consequences, as diagnostic errors account for up to 15% of adverse events in healthcare. RESULTS: Theoretical models such as Dual Process Theory (System 1 intuitive vs. System 2 analytical reasoning), illness scripts, and metacognition highlight both the strengths and vulnerabilities of clinical cognition. The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical practice intensifies the need for structured reasoning education. While large language models demonstrate impressive diagnostic capabilities, risks such as automation bias and AI confabulations threaten safe decision-making. CONCLUSIONS: Consequently, this review calls for a paradigm shift: clinical reasoning must become a formal, longitudinal core subject across all stages of medical education. In the AI era, clinical reasoning is not diminished; it is indispensable.

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs for Cervical Cancer Across the Care Continuum: From Vaccination and Screening to Personalized Therapy
papers.authors: Leng J, Wei W, Wen X, Lu S, Liu Y
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Jiyan Leng, Wenzhi Wei, Xiaohua Wen, Shan Lu, Yanru LiuDepartment of Health Medicine, Bethune International Peace Hospital, Shijiazhuang, Hebei, 050082, People’s Republic of ChinaCorrespondence: Yanru Liu, Department of Health Medicine, Bethune International Peace Hospital, No. 398, Zhongshan West Road, Qiaoxi District, Shijiazhuang, Hebei, People’s Republic of China, Email 13126829469@163.comAbstract: Cervical cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related death among women worldwide, with a disproportionately high burden in low- and middle-income countries. Infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) is the central etiological factor. Although HPV vaccination and standardized screening can substantially reduce incidence and mortality, major bottlenecks persist in real-world settings, including inadequate coverage, loss to follow-up, data silos, and limited interpretability of algorithms. Knowledge graphs (KGs), characterized by their core "entity–relation” structure, can integrate electronic medical records, HPV genotyping, pathology/imaging, multi-omics, and public health data within a unified semantic framework, and provide traceable evidence chains and reasoning pathways to support clinical decision-making. KGs may become an important enabler. This review summarizes the potential mechanisms and application paradigms of KGs along the full continuum of cervical cancer prevention and care, including primary prevention (vaccination strategies and health education), screening and diagnosis (multimodal data integration, explainable AI, and clinical decision support systems, CDSS), as well as therapeutic decision-making and follow-up management (molecular subtyping, drug associations, and recurrence monitoring. We further highlight key challenges such as ontology standardization, cross-institutional interoperability, dynamic knowledge updating, and reliability of automated knowledge extraction. Future work should focus on establishing reusable, engineering-oriented pathways for the synergy of "KG + large language models (LLMs)/multimodal AI”, the development of explainability evaluation metrics, privacy-compliant frameworks, and deployable solutions for primary care settings, in order to accelerate progress toward the global cervical cancer elimination goal.Keywords: knowledge graph, cervical cancer, HPV, vaccine, personalized treatment, explainable artificial intelligence

papers.title: Indonesian Language Learning Strategies In The Digital Era: Implications For The Preparation Of Adaptive Pedagogy-Based Semester Learning Plans
papers.authors: Elen Nurjanah, Dinda Listiana Awali*
papers.abstract: Digital transformation has changed the practice of Indonesian language learning with the presence of various technologies, such as Learning Management Systems (LMS), digital media, collaborative platforms, and Artificial Intelligence (AI). These conditions require learning strategies that not only utilize technology as a medium but are also able to adjust learning to the needs, characteristics, and abilities of students. This study aims to analyze and synthesize digital technology-based Indonesian language learning strategies as a foundation for preparing adaptive pedagogy-based Semester Learning Plans (RPS). The research uses a qualitative descriptive approach with a literature review method of 18 research articles published between 2020–2026. Data were analyzed through stages of reduction, grouping, comparison, interpretation, and synthesis based on learning strategies, technologies used, competencies developed, learning activities, assessments, and the application of adaptive pedagogical principles. The results show five main patterns of learning strategies: digital literacy integration, digital media-based multimodal learning, digital collaborative learning, project-based learning and digital content production, and the utilization of adaptive technology and AI. Digital technology no longer simply functions as a medium for delivering material, but has become part of a pedagogical strategy that supports the development of language competence, digital literacy, creativity, communication, collaboration, critical thinking, and independent learning. The synthesis results also indicate that adaptive pedagogy is realized through differentiated learning, the use of multimodal media, digital feedback, technology-based personalization, and authentic assessments based on digital products and portfolios. These findings provide implications for the development of adaptive, multimodal, student-centered, and responsive RPS to digital transformation by considering educator readiness, student digital competence, infrastructure, and technology integration with learning objectives.

papers.title: The Effectiveness of Using ChatGPT in Teaching Writing Skills for Vocational High School Students
papers.authors: Ignosia Adi Irawan, Sri Wahyuni
papers.abstract: The present study aims to examine the effectiveness of ChatGPT in teaching writing skills for vocational high school students. This study employed a quantitative research method with a quasi-experimental design to investigate the effectiveness of ChatGPT in teaching writing skills. The subjects of this study were the eleventh-grade students of SMK AL Huda Kota Kediri. The sample consisted of two classes: the experimental group, which used ChatGPT during the learning process, and the control group, which used peer-correction. The data were collected through writing tests in the form of pre test and post-test. The students’ writing was assessed based on content, organization, grammar, vocabulary, and mechanics. The collected data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 27, due to the data were not normally distributed, Mann Whitney U test was used. The results revealed a significant difference in writing achievement between the experimental and control groups. The significance value of the Mann–Whitney U test was 0.036 (p < 0.05), indicating that the use of ChatGPT had a positive effect on students’ writing skills. The experimental group achieved higher post-test scores compared to the control group. This finding indicates that students who used ChatGPT improved their writing more effectively through instant feedback, corrections, and suggestions provided during the writing process. In conclusion, the study highlights that ChatGPT is effective at enhancing students’ writing skills and can serve as a supportive learning tool in English writing classes at vocational high school level.

papers.title: Green Nanoparticles in Precision Agriculture: A Critical Review of Smart Crop Management, Nano-Enabled Delivery Systems, and Sustainable Farming
papers.authors: Marshal Williams AM, Dennison MS, Bukke SPN, Ashwin BCMA
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Abisha Meji Marshal Williams,1 Milon Selvam Dennison,2 Sarad Pawar Naik Bukke,3 Bosco Christin Maria Arputham Ashwin41Department of ETC Engineering, School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Kampala International University, Western Campus, Ishaka-Bushenyi, Uganda; 2Department of Mechanical Engineering, School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Kampala International University, Western Campus, Ishaka-Bushenyi, Uganda; 3Department of Pharmacy, Faculty of Health Sciences, Victoria University, Victoria Towers, 1-13 Jinja Road, Kampala, Uganda; 4PG Department of Chemistry, Pioneer Kumaraswamy College, Nagercoil, Tamil Nadu, IndiaCorrespondence: Abisha Meji Marshal Williams, Email abisha.meji@kiu.ac.ug Bosco Christin Maria Arputham Ashwin, Email b.mashwin@yahoo.comAbstract: Sustainable agricultural production requires approaches that improve resource-use efficiency while limiting environmental burdens. This critical review examines green-synthesized Nanoparticles (NPs) in precision agriculture, covering sustainable synthesis, smart crop management, nano-enabled delivery systems, nano-biosensors, plant-nanoparticle interactions, environmental risks, circular agriculture, and digital technologies. The NPs derived from Plant, microbial, biomolecule, and waste shows potential for targeted nutrient delivery, crop protection, stress management, and improved monitoring. However, reported performance varies with NP size, surface properties, concentration, formulation, crop type, soil, and environmental conditions. The review therefore critically considers both benefits and risks, including phytotoxicity, effects on beneficial microorganisms, persistence, bioaccumulation, and long-term ecosystem impacts. Waste-derived NPs and circular nanomanufacturing offer opportunities for resource recovery and agricultural waste valorization, but their scalability and economic feasibility remain uncertain. The integration with Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoTs), Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), remote sensing, and smart decision-support systems may improve site-specific management. The review also examines technology readiness, commercialization pathways, manufacturing consistency, cost, and regulatory requirements. The green NPs shows promise for sustainable precision agriculture, but wider adoption requires stronger field validation, standardized characterization, environmental risk assessment, reproducible manufacturing, economic evaluation, and responsible regulatory development.Keywords: circular agriculture, green nanoparticles, nano-biosensors, nano-enabled delivery systems, nano-fertilizers, nano-pesticides, plant-nanoparticle interactions, precision agriculture, smart crop management, waste-derived nanoparticles

papers.title: Application of Machine Learning Models to Predict Tigecycline Exposure in Critically Ill Patients Using Different Limited Sampling Strategies
papers.authors: Dai A, Liu H, Yang B, Zheng F, Guan Y, Liu J, Zhu J, Liang G, Yang Y, Yu LH, Zhao Y, Yu Z
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Anran Dai,1,2,* Hao Liu,3,* Bo Yang,4,* Feiyue Zheng,1 Yan Guan,1 Jieqiong Liu,1 Jianping Zhu,1 Gang Liang,1 Yi Yang,1 Lingyan Yu,5 Yuhua Zhao,6 Zhenwei Yu1,21Department of Pharmacy, Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, People’s Republic of China; 2Research Center for Clinical Pharmacy, College of Pharmaceutical Science, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, People’s Republic of China; 3State Key Laboratory of Natural Medicines, Key Laboratory of Drug Metabolism, China Pharmaceutical University, Nanjing, People’s Republic of China; 4Department of Pharmacy, Zhejiang Academy of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Tongde Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou, People’s Republic of China; 5Department of pharmacy, Second Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, People’s Republic of China; 6Department of Pharmacy, Affiliated Xiaoshan Hospital, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, People’s Republic of China*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Yuhua Zhao, Email zhaoyuhua1987@126.com Zhenwei Yu, Email yzw_srrsh@zju.edu.cnBackground: The high variability in the pharmacokinetics of tigecycline may impact therapeutic efficacy, particularly in critically ill patients. This study introduces machine learning (ML) methods, aiming to clarify their effectiveness in individualized drug exposure prediction and determine the optimal modeling strategy.Methods: The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) method was used to screen the covariates. Four ML models, random forest, extreme gradient boosting, multilayer perceptron, and long short-term memory network (LSTM), were trained and tested using 751 concentrations from 98 patients in the pharmacokinetic dataset to predict the area under the steady-state plasma concentration-time curve within 24 hours (AUC0-24h) of tigecycline. Furthermore, on the internal test set, we evaluated the accuracy of the published tigecycline Population Pharmacokinetics (PopPK) models.Results: Seven covariates were screened out by LASSO method, including total bilirubin, creatinine clearance, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, body mass index, serum creatinine, age, and prothrombin time. Internal validation showed that, among the four ML models, the LSTM model performed the best, with the combination of covariates and the plasma concentration feature "C0 + C0.5 + C6” exhibited the optimal predictive performance (R2: 0.887, RMSE: 2.496 mg·h/L, F20: 75%). In comparison, the model combining covariates with C0 was the most concise and better suited to practical computational conditions; its LSTM model was comparable to some PopPK models in terms of overall trend fitting and systematic bias control (R2: 0.818, RMSE: 3.164 mg·h/L, F20 = 60%).Conclusion: The LSTM model established in this study enables an accurate estimate of tigecycline AUC0-24h. Three-point sampling provided the lowest prediction error, whereas C0 alone reduced the sampling burden. These findings provide an effective modeling reference for tigecycline therapeutic drug monitoring.Keywords: tigecycline, machine learning, trough concentration, area under curve, precision medicine

papers.title: Architectural and Pedagogical Affordances of Mobile Systems for Problem-Based Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: I Ketut Agus Muliana
papers.abstract: The integration of mobile systems in higher education has transitioned from static content delivery to dynamic, ubiquitous learning ecosystems. While Problem-Based Learning (PBL) demands high cognitive engagement and collaboration, there is a systemic gap between the architectural capabilities of mobile applications and their actual pedagogical effectiveness in facilitating PBL syntax. This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) aims to map and evaluate the interaction between the architectural configurations and pedagogical affordances of mobile systems in supporting PBL within higher education. Following the PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search was conducted on the Scopus database, supplemented by snowballing techniques, covering the last decade (2016–2026). A total of 32 empirical studies met the rigorous inclusion criteria and were analyzed using thematic synthesis. The findings reveal three dominant architectural spectrums: bespoke native/hybrid apps, mobile-optimized LMS integrations, and cloud-based collaborative architectures. Pedagogically, mobile systems distribute cognitive load through system-embedded and socio-collaborative scaffolding. Consequently, this socio-technical interaction significantly enhances Meaningful Learning and fosters Mindful and Joyful learning experiences. Mobile systems act as vital cognitive partners in PBL. Future research must pivot to domain-specific, customized M-PBL architectures integrating a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approach.

papers.title: Student Assessment Quiz: Artificial Intelligence and Global Law — Professional Responsibility, Legal Verification and Responsible AI Practice
papers.authors: Marta Gonzalo Quiroga
papers.abstract: Instrumento académico de evaluación elaborado por la profesora Marta Gonzalo Quiroga, de la Universidad Rey Juan Carlos, en colaboración con la profesora Halima Bensouda, de la Université Mohammed V de Rabat, en el contexto de las actividades de formación académica desarrolladas en Rabat (Marruecos) en 2026. El cuestionario está dirigido a estudiantes de Derecho y de doctorado y tiene como finalidad evaluar la comprensión de los principales riesgos, obligaciones y criterios de actuación profesional asociados a la utilización de inteligencia artificial en el ámbito jurídico. La prueba consta de quince preguntas de opción múltiple, con cuatro alternativas de respuesta y una única respuesta correcta por pregunta. Cada respuesta correcta equivale a un punto, se propone una puntuación de diez sobre quince para superar la evaluación y se establece un tiempo estimado de realización de entre diez y quince minutos. Incluye una hoja individual para registrar las respuestas y una escala de interpretación que diferencia entre dominio excelente, buen dominio, comprensión parcial y necesidad de revisión adicional. El contenido aborda, en primer lugar, la responsabilidad profesional en el uso de inteligencia artificial generativa para la investigación jurídica y la elaboración de escritos. A través de cuestiones vinculadas a casos como Mata v. Avianca y Ayinde / Al-Haroun, se evalúa la capacidad para reconocer la necesidad de comprobar independientemente las autoridades jurídicas generadas mediante IA, verificar su existencia y contenido en fuentes autorizadas y determinar si respaldan efectivamente la proposición jurídica para la que se invocan. Asimismo, se examina la diferencia entre la fluidez lingüística y la fiabilidad jurídica, así como el riesgo de considerar acreditada una afirmación por el mero hecho de que esté formulada con seguridad y precisión aparente. La responsabilidad organizativa constituye otro eje relevante mediante el análisis de Moffatt v. Air Canada. Se examina la utilización de sistemas conversacionales dirigidos al público y la imposibilidad de presumir que la automatización o la externalización tecnológica eliminan las obligaciones de la organización que despliega esos sistemas. Las preguntas promueven la comprensión de la necesidad de establecer controles, mecanismos de corrección y procedimientos de supervisión para reducir los riesgos derivados de información incorrecta proporcionada por herramientas automatizadas. El cuestionario evalúa también la capacidad para aplicar criterios de verificación proporcionados a la naturaleza de la tarea y a las consecuencias potenciales del error. Se diferencia entre usos de bajo impacto, como la organización formal de documentos, y aplicaciones que pueden influir directamente en derechos, intereses jurídicos o decisiones profesionales relevantes. Se destaca así la necesidad de adaptar la intensidad de la revisión humana y las salvaguardias al nivel de riesgo de cada utilización. Un bloque específico se dedica a la confidencialidad, la protección de datos y la seguridad de la información. Mediante situaciones prácticas relacionadas con expedientes de clientes, se evalúa la capacidad para identificar las precauciones que deben adoptarse antes de incorporar documentación a una plataforma de IA, incluyendo la delimitación de la finalidad, la clasificación y minimización de los datos, la protección de información sensible y la comprobación de las garantías técnicas y contractuales del entorno utilizado. La dimensión internacional se concreta mediante cuestiones sobre el trabajo jurídico transfronterizo y la organización de un procedimiento de actuación bajo presión temporal. La evaluación destaca la importancia de definir primero la cuestión jurídica antes de utilizar una herramienta de IA, así como la necesidad de comprobar las fuentes primarias, contrastar los resultados, identificar incertidumbres y mantener el juicio profesional independiente. También considera la interacción entre los deberes profesionales, la protección de datos, la confidencialidad y las obligaciones jurídicas aplicables en distintas jurisdicciones. El material incorpora asimismo cuestiones sobre el enfoque regulatorio basado en riesgos, la utilización de inteligencia artificial en la preparación de negociaciones y mediaciones y las particularidades del contexto marroquí. Se evalúa la comprensión de que la IA puede contribuir a generar argumentos alternativos y simular la perspectiva de la contraparte, sin reemplazar el conocimiento de los hechos, la estrategia ni la responsabilidad del profesional. En relación con Marruecos, se destaca la coexistencia de un marco de protección de datos personales con el desarrollo de iniciativas de gobernanza digital y de inteligencia artificial responsable. Finalmente, la evaluación integra un principio transversal de responsabilidad: la inteligencia artificial puede transformar los instrumentos y métodos de trabajo jurídico, pero no transfiere automáticamente las obligaciones profesionales o institucionales a la tecnología. La utilización responsable exige verificación independiente, protección de la información, reconocimiento de la incertidumbre, supervisión humana y rendición de cuentas por las decisiones y actuaciones realizadas. En conjunto, este cuestionario constituye un instrumento de evaluación, apoyo a la docencia y formación jurídica avanzada en inteligencia artificial y Derecho global. Su enfoque práctico permite comprobar la adquisición de conocimientos, reforzar las competencias de análisis y verificación y fomentar una utilización jurídicamente fundamentada, ética y responsable de la inteligencia artificial en el ejercicio profesional y en contextos de colaboración internacional. Palabras clave Inteligencia artificial; Derecho global; evaluación académica; cuestionario de evaluación; responsabilidad profesional; ética jurídica; inteligencia artificial generativa; verificación de fuentes jurídicas; confidencialidad; protección de datos; gobernanza de la IA; regulación basada en riesgos; supervisión humana; responsabilidad institucional; negociación; mediación; práctica jurídica transfronteriza; Derecho internacional privado; formación doctoral; Marruecos.

papers.title: Students’ Acceptance of Generative AI Tools and Their Perceived Learning Effectiveness in Higher Education: The Mediating Role of AI Literacy
papers.authors: Ahmed Siddique
papers.journal: J-STAR: Journal of Social & Technological Advanced Research
papers.abstract: Although the use of generative AI tools is rapidly spreading among university students, little is known about why these tools might bring positive learning experiences to university students. This study investigates whether the perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of generative AI tools is mediated by AI literacy with the perceived learning effectiveness of the students.This study aims to explore the mediation of AI literacy between students' acceptance of generative AI tools as perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use with the ones' perceived learning effectiveness. The survey will be a quantitative, cross-sectional online self-administered instrument that will be completed by a sample of about 270 university students (with a sampling target of about 300) who have used generative AI for academic purposes, using methods of purposive and convenience sampling. Items of the adapted technology acceptance model will be used to measure the acceptance, items from validated AI literacy scales will be used to measure the AI literacy, and items from a pilot-tested self-report scale that is explicitly different from an objective measure of learning effectiveness will be used to measure perceived learning effectiveness. Data screening, reliability assessment and confirmatory factor analysis will be performed, followed by testing the hypotheses with regression-based mediation procedures (PROCESS Model 4) with 5,000 random bootstrap resamples, with latent variable based structural equation modelling as a robustness check. A Monte Carlo power analysis revealed that there was approximately 80% power to detect indirect effects in this study of size a = b = .20 at a sample size of N = 250. The study aims to better understand the relationship between technology acceptance and perceived learning through competence-based mechanisms and to provide insights for AI-literacy programs in higher education.

papers.title: Assessment of Perceptions, Trust, and Adoption of Clinical Artificial Intelligence Tools Among Physicians and Dentists, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
papers.authors: Alghofaily JM, Alghofaily MM, Elhadi FEM, Alturki DM, Alshommemri AE, Dawria A, Aldrees SS, Alzoheri MA, AlGhamdi JM, Ahmed MH, Mohammed MEA
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Jawaher M Alghofaily,1 Maha M Alghofaily,2 Fatima Elshikh Mohammed Elhadi,3 Deema M Alturki,4 Amjad E Alshommemri,5 Adam Dawria,6 Shorouq S Aldrees,7 Malak A Alzoheri,8 Jihan M AlGhamdi,9 Mariam H Ahmed,10 Mazahir Elhadi Abdallah Mohammed111Medical Consultations Department, Seha Virtual Hospital, Ministry of Health, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 2Restorative Dental Sciences, College of Dentistry, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 3Department of Public Health, College of Health Sciences, Saudi Electronic University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 4ECHO Cardiovascular Technology, King Faisal Specialist Hospital & Research Center, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 5Dental Department, Ram Clinics, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 6Department of Public Health, College of Applied Medical Sciences, Khamis Mushait Campus, King Khalid University, Abha, Saudi Arabia; 7Dental Department, Durma General Hospital, Third Health Cluster, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 8Quality Management and Patient Safety, King Saud Medical City, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 9Department of Biochemistry, College of Science, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia; 10Department of Public Health, Health Science College, Saudi Electronic University, Riyadh City, Saudi Arabia; 11Department of Public Health, College of Applied Medical Science, Khamis Mushait Campus, King Khalid University, Abha City, Saudi ArabiaCorrespondence: Fatima Elshikh Mohammed Elhadi, Email f.elhadi@seu.edu.saPurpose: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly integrated into healthcare; however, their acceptance varies across professional groups. Understanding clinicians’ familiarity with and perceptions, trust, and adoption of clinical AI tools is essential for safe and effective implementation. This study assessed physicians’ and dentists’ perceptions, trust, and intention to adopt clinical AI tools in governmental university hospitals in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.Participants and Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 400 clinicians selected from three major governmental university hospitals in Riyadh (King Saud University Medical City, King Abdulaziz Medical City-National Guard, and King Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz University Hospital), which serve as large tertiary academic centers at the forefront of digital health and AI implementation in Saudi Arabia. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire assessing familiarity, usage patterns, perceptions, trust, and adoption intention. The instrument demonstrated high reliability across subscales (Cronbach’s α: 0.880– 0.952). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, non-parametric tests, and multivariate linear regression.Results: Familiarity with AI was high (89.5%), with physicians reporting greater familiarity than dentists. Overall perceptions were moderate (mean 3.2– 3.8 on a 5-point scale), with physicians showing more positive views. Trust was generally low (mean 3.1– 3.6), particularly among physicians; dentists reported moderate trust. Intention to adopt was moderate (mean 3.5– 3.9), with physicians demonstrating higher adoption intention than dentists. Residents, physicians, and those in digitally advanced hospitals had significantly higher perceptions, trust, and adoption intention scores (p < 0.05). Multivariate regression identified work setting, resident status, and physician specialty as the strongest predictors of higher scores across all domains.Conclusion: Despite high awareness, perceptions of clinical AI tools and intention to adopt them remain moderate and constrained by low trust. Targeted training, transparent systems, and regulatory support are essential for enhancing integration into practice.Keywords: artificial intelligence, clinical decision support systems, technology adoption, trust, physicians, dentists, Saudi Arabia

papers.title: Supporting Social Engagement in Long-Term Care Through Paired Socially Assistive Robot-Virtual Reality Activities for Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment and Apathy
papers.authors: Migovich M, Ghosh R, Khan N, Maxwell CA, Newhouse PA, Scharre DW, Tan A, Tate JA, Mion LC, Sarkar N
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Miroslava Migovich,1 Ritam Ghosh,2 Nibraas Khan,3 Cathy A Maxwell,4 Paul A Newhouse,5 Douglas W Scharre,6 Alai Tan,7 Judith A Tate,7,* Lorraine C Mion,7,* Nilanjan Sarkar1– 3,*1Department of Mechanical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA; 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA; 3Department of Computer Science, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, USA; 4College of Nursing, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA; 5Center for Cognitive Medicine, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, USA; 6Department of Neurology, The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, Columbus, OH, USA; 7College of Nursing, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH, USA*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Miroslava Migovich, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Vanderbilt University, 2400 Highland Ave, Room 107, Nashville, TN, 37212, USA, Email miroslava.migovich@vanderbilt.eduIntroduction: Older adults living in long-term care settings, particularly those with cognitive impairment and apathy, frequently experience reduced social engagement. Socially assistive robots and virtual reality systems may help support engagement, but little is known about whether they can sustain engagement during real-world deployment while also facilitating interaction between older adults. This study examined whether socially structured socially assistive robot-virtual reality (SAR-VR) systems could sustain engagement and support human-human interaction during repeated use in long-term care settings.Methods: This analysis focused on the SAR-VR intervention arm of a larger eight-week study and included 60 older adults with cognitive impairment from 23 long-term care sites. Participants were exposed to two SAR-VR systems featuring different robot embodiments (dog-like and humanoid), roles, and activities. Across 756 repeated intervention sessions, engagement was observationally assessed using observed ratings of attention, activity attitude, robot attitude, and conversational targeting.Results: Sustained attention and activity attitudes remained consistently positive across both SAR-VR systems over repeated exposure. Peer-to-peer and research-staff directed speech occurred across both systems. While robot-directed speech was more common in the dog-like condition, partner-directed communication remained stable, indicating that increased human-robot interaction did not occur at the expense of human–human interaction. Baseline cognitive functioning was associated with attentional engagement but not with attitudinal evaluations. Baseline technology acceptance did not strongly predict post-interaction impressions. Participants who anthropomorphized the robots at baseline demonstrated more positive engagement during sessions.Discussion: These findings suggest that socially structured SAR-VR systems can sustain meaningful engagement while preserving peer interaction in naturalistic dementia care. The results also support the feasibility of designing SAR-VR activities around shared goals and coordinated actions to promote reciprocal human engagement, while recognizing that the study design does not allow definitive conclusions about clinical efficacy or the effects of specific robot features.Keywords: collaborative technologies, multimodal intervention, human-centered design, dyadic activities, cognitive impairment, apathy

papers.title: Listening, partnering, designing: SMU Libraries’ journey towards human-centered wellness
papers.authors: Vincent ONG, Devika Sangaram, Zhenyan Li
papers.journal: Singapore Management University Institutional Knowledge (InK) (Singapore Management University)
papers.abstract: As student wellness emerges as one of the most pressing concerns facing academic institutions today, libraries are uniquely and powerfully positioned to reimagine their spaces and services as holistic, human-centered environments that nurture the whole person.This paper presents three initiatives by the Singapore Management University (SMU) Libraries that embody this vision, collectively affirming the library's evolving role as a human-centered wellness hub and its commitment to actively shaping a more inclusive and people-first future.The first initiative repurposed a vacated collection space into a wellbeing-centered quiet study environment, incorporating user experience (UX) design principles and longitudinal survey evidence, to provide students with a calm, conducive, and thoughtfully refurbished space for focused learning.The second initiative expanded the entire library building into a quiet area during examination periods, leveraging behavioural nudges guided by the EAST Framework to foster a shared sense of responsibility and mutual respect.The third initiative, the Library Calm Space, represents community co-creation -a holistic wellness sanctuary designed with students for students -engaged over 200 participants during a roadshow and drew a pulse survey response in which approximately 80% of students welcomed the Space and expressed a likelihood of using it.Together, this evidence confirms that user-centered, evidencebased design offers a practical and replicable pathway for positioning the library as a central partner in the holistic student experience.As education continues to evolve, library spaces must also adapt to meet changing user needs.By leveraging data and adopting a usercentered approach, SMU Libraries aim to ensure that library spaces not only support academic growth, but also serve as a sanctuary for wellness and mindfulness.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence Competencies Across the Six ACGME Core Competencies: A Proposed Framework for Graduate Medical Education
papers.authors: Kabbash MS, Loftus TJ, Morrow J, Dent D, Rodriguez R
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Michel S Kabbash,1 Tyler J Loftus,1 Jason Morrow,2 Daniel Dent,3 Ronald Rodriguez41Department of Surgery, University of Florida College of Medicine, Gainesville, FL, USA; 2Department of Medicine, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA; 3Department of Surgery, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USA; 4Department of Medical Education, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, San Antonio, TX, USACorrespondence: Ronald Rodriguez, Department of Medical Education, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, Floyd Curl Dr, San Antonio, TX, 7703, USA, Tel +1 210 567 7000, Email rodriguezr32@uthscsa.eduAbstract: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical practice and Graduate Medical Education (GME), AI-specific competencies are not yet explicitly represented as a distinct domain within the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education’s (ACGME) six core competency framework. The ACGME’s ongoing consideration of AI in its Common Program Requirements revision process signals an emerging recognition of the need to address this gap. Over 1200 FDA-authorized AI medical devices, unregulated generative AI tools in clinical workflows, and a proliferating state legislative landscape create urgent educational needs. We conducted a purposive narrative review of literature addressing AI adoption, documented failures and litigation, regulatory developments, and bioethical frameworks to develop AI-specific learning objectives, milestone language, and assessment strategies mapped to each ACGME competency. We propose the SHARED ethical framework - Stewardship, Humanity, Accountability, Responsiveness, Equity, and Disclosure - as the moral foundation for AI education. We map AI-related capabilities and representative developmental descriptors across the six existing ACGME competency domains and propose corresponding curricular content and assessment approaches. The alternative to systematic, integrated AI training - informal adoption without standards or assessment - poses unacceptable risks to patients, trainees, and the profession. The proposed framework provides a structured foundation for further development and evaluation of AI education within competency-based GME.Keywords: artificial intelligence, ACGME competencies, graduate medical education

papers.title: Development and Real-World Evaluation of an Interpretable Machine Learning Framework for Predicting COPD-Related Healthcare Costs
papers.authors: Chen YL, Liu GH, Li CL, Yang CY, Shih FJ, Guo SE, Liu SF
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Yi-Li Chen,1,* Guan-Heng Liu,2,* Chin-Ling Li,1 Chih-Yuan Yang,2 Fu-Jong Shih,3 Su-Er Guo,4 Shih-Feng Liu1,5,61Department of Respiratory Therapy, Kaohsiung Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Kaohsiung, Taiwan; 2Department of Artificial Intelligence, Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan; 3Department of Gerontology and Health Care Management, Chang Gung University of Science and Technology, Taoyuan, Taiwan; 4Department of Nursing, College of Medicine, National Sun Yat-Sen University, Kaohsiung, Taiwan; 5Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, Kaohsiung Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Kaohsiung, Taiwan; 6Medical Department, College of Medicine, Chang Gung University, Taoyuan, Taiwan*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Shih-Feng Liu, Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, Kaohsiung Chang Gung Memorial Hospital, Kaohsiung, Taiwan, Tel +886 7 7317123 (ext. 8199), Email liuphysico@yahoo.com.twBackground: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) imposes a substantial economic burden. While machine learning (ML) enables data-driven cost prediction, real-world benchmarking comparing algorithms, data-splitting strategies, and feature optimization on continuous, skewed healthcare expenditures remains limited.Objective: To develop an interpretable ML framework for predicting annual COPD-related healthcare expenditures, assessing the impact of algorithm selection, train–test split ratios, and feature optimization.Methods: We analyzed a retrospective cohort of 396 COPD patients from a Taiwanese medical center. Annual healthcare costs were log-transformed and standardized due to extreme skewness. Five ML regression algorithms were benchmarked across four train–test split ratios. Recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV) applied within training sets identified an optimal predictor subset. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Performance was evaluated using R-squared (R2) and mean absolute error (MAE).Results: The 80:20 split yielded the most stable generalization performance. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest accuracy (test R2=0.365; MAE=0.258 on log-transformed scale, ~NTD 82,400 raw scale), outperforming baseline models. RFECV identified six key predictors—Age × BMI, malignancy, exacerbation frequency, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and DOSE index—retaining > 95% of full-model performance. SHAP analysis confirmed their clinical relevance.Conclusion: Gradient Boosting provides robust predictive performance for COPD healthcare costs. A parsimonious six-feature set enhances interpretability without compromising accuracy. This explainable ML framework supports cost-aware healthcare management, pending future multi-center validation.Keywords: COPD, healthcare cost prediction, explainable artificial intelligence, recursive feature elimination, RFE, machine learning

papers.title: EEG-Derived Pain Threshold Index-Guided Remifentanil Titration During Laparoscopic Abdominal Surgery: A Randomized Trial
papers.authors: Cao B, Qi Z, Zhao YY, Xue Q, Ren JJ, Xu WW, Fan YN, Nan ZH, Sun PP, Li HJ, Zhang J, Yang JJ
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Bin Cao, Zheng Qi, Ying-Ying Zhao, Qiong Xue, Juan-Juan Ren, Wei-Wei Xu, Yu-Ning Fan, Zhen-Hua Nan, Pei-Pei Sun, Hui-Juan Li, Jie Zhang, Jian-Jun YangDepartment of Anesthesiology, Pain and Perioperative Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou, Henan, 450052, People’s Republic of China*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Jian-Jun Yang; Jie Zhang, Department of Anesthesiology, Pain and Perioperative Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, 1 Jianshe East Road, Zhengzhou, Henan, 450052, People’s Republic of China, Tel/Fax +86-371-66271657, Email jianjunyangzzu@hotmail.com; joannyzh@163.comObjective: To determine whether remifentanil titration guided by the pain threshold index (PTi), an electroencephalography-derived proxy for nociceptive tolerance rather than subjective pain, reduces intraoperative remifentanil infusion during laparoscopic abdominal surgery.Methods: In this prospective, single-center, assessor-blinded randomized trial, adults undergoing elective laparoscopic abdominal surgery with propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion were assigned 1:1 to PTi-guided or conventional hemodynamic-guided remifentanil titration. The primary endpoint was intraoperative remifentanil infusion rate. The principal analysis used the full-analysis set and covariate-adjusted linear regression with heteroskedasticity-consistent robust standard errors.Results: Among 200 randomized patients, 195 were analyzed (98 PTi-guided; 97 control). The primary endpoint was neutral: mean (SD) remifentanil infusion rate was 7.44 (1.43) versus 7.63 (1.41) μg kg− 1 h− 1; adjusted mean difference, − 0.06 μg kg− 1 h− 1 (95% CI, − 0.44 to 0.32; P=0.758). Per-protocol results were similar. Median (IQR) NRS at post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) admission was 2.0 (2.0– 3.0) versus 3.0 (2.0– 4.0), and Ramsay score was 2.0 (2.0– 2.0) in both groups. In exploratory secondary analyses, rescue opioid was used in the PACU by 18/98 (18.4%) versus 31/97 (32.0%) patients and any rescue opioid through 48 h by 29/98 (29.6%) versus 44/97 (45.4%). Any postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) through 48 h occurred in 17/98 (17.3%) versus 29/97 (29.9%) patients. Total postoperative opioid exposure through 48 h was not reduced.Conclusion: PTi-guided remifentanil titration did not reduce intraoperative remifentanil infusion. PACU pain and sedation scores were not materially different. Lower early rescue-opioid use and fewer PONV events through 48 h were exploratory secondary findings, were not accompanied by lower postoperative opioid dose, and require prospective confirmation.Keywords: electroencephalography, laparoscopic surgery, nociception monitoring, pain threshold index, postoperative analgesia, remifentanil

papers.title: Development, Validation, and Deployment of an Interpretable Machine Learning Model for In-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Critically Ill Patients with COPD and Sepsis: A Multicenter Cohort Study
papers.authors: Ju J, Chen J, Li G, Wang JJ, Yang L
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Jianjie Ju,1– 4,* Jingjing Chen,1– 4,* Gaojin Li,1– 4,* Jingting Wang,1– 3 Limei Yang1– 31Department of Pharmacy, Fuzhou University Affiliated Provincial Hospital, Fuzhou, Fujian, People’s Republic of China; 2Department of Pharmacy, Fujian Provincial Hospital, Fuzhou, Fujian, People’s Republic of China; 3Department of Pharmacy, Provincial Clinical College of Fujian Medical University, Fuzhou, Fujian, People’s Republic of China; 4School of Pharmacy, Fujian Medical University, Fuzhou, Fujian, People’s Republic of China*These authors contributed equally to this workCorrespondence: Jingting Wang; Limei Yang, Department of Pharmacy, Fuzhou University Affiliated Provincial Hospital, Fuzhou, Fujian, People’s Republic of China, Email jitiwang210@163.com; yanglimei214@fzu.edu.cnBackground: Critically ill patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and sepsis are at high risk of in-hospital mortality because of respiratory and organ dysfunction. Early risk assessment may be useful for clinical decision-making. This study aimed to develop an interpretable machine learning model for this population.Methods: Data were extracted from MIMIC-IV and the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD). The MIMIC-IV cohort was split in a 7:3 ratio into training and internal test sets. Features were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression and Boruta. Eight models were trained using 10-fold cross-validation and grid search. The best-performing model was externally validated using eICU-CRD, interpreted using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), and compared with the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score.Results: Among 4,900 MIMIC-IV patients, in-hospital mortality was 19.2%. In the internal test set, the naive Bayes (NB) model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.743 (95% CI, 0.711– 0.775), outperforming the SOFA score (AUC, 0.696, 95% CI, 0.663– 0.730, P < 0.001). In external validation, AUC decreased to 0.681 (95% CI, 0.607– 0.755), an absolute reduction of 0.062. SHAP identified Simplified Acute Physiology Score II and SOFA as predictors, followed by the anion gap and urine output. The model was deployed across web, desktop, and mobile platforms.Conclusion: An NB model was successfully developed to predict in-hospital mortality in critically ill patients with COPD and sepsis. Further prospective multicenter validation is warranted before routine clinical use.Keywords: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sepsis, machine learning, naive bayes, in-hospital mortality

papers.title: Teaching, coding, learning: Using AI to unlock patterns in learner language
papers.authors: Robin Couture-Matte, Maura Cruz Enríquez, François Pichette
papers.abstract: In second language acquisition (SLA), analyzing learner production data provides valuable insights into language development and informs pedagogical practices. However, processing large corpora of student assignments can be time-consuming and technically demanding. Although advances in natural language processing have made automated analysis more accessible, programming expertise remains a barrier for many applied linguistics professionals. In this context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising solution for researchers with limited coding experience (Kim, 2023). This study examined how AI tools can support linguists and language teachers in automating corpus analysis. Specifically, we explored whether ChatGPT and Copilot could be integrated across the research workflow to assist researchers with limited coding knowledge with data manipulation, library selection, code generation, troubleshooting, and output verification. The dataset consisted of a Spanish corpus of more than 350,000 words drawn from the assignments of 219 learners (A1–A2: 77; B1–B2: 62; C1–C2: 80) and an English corpus of over 45,000 words from 98 learners (A2: 50; B1: 49). All participants were adult francophone learners at a Canadian university. The analysis examined patterns in learner writing, focusing on gender assignment in Spanish and the use of gerunds and participles in English.
