papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has transformed the creation of literary, artistic, musical, dramatic and audiovisual works.Unlike conventional computer-assisted creativity, Generative AI systems independently produce sophisticated outputs after processing vast datasets and responding to human prompts.This development challenges copyright law at its foundation, because traditional regimes are constructed around a human author, originality, ownership and exclusive rights.The central legal question is whether an output generated substantially or entirely by an AI system attracts copyright and, if so, who is to be recognised as its author and owner.The difficulty intensifies where the user supplies only a prompt, where the user undertakes extensive creative selection and modification, or where the system autonomously produces the final expression.The Copyright Act, 1957 contains no dedicated framework for Generative AI, although Section 2(d)(vi) on computergenerated works, Section 13 on subsistence, Section 17 on first ownership and Sections 18 and 19 on assignment supply the governing principles.The order of the Registrar of Copyrights of 31 August 2026 in the DABUS matter holds that an artificial intelligence system, having no legal personality, cannot be the statutory author, although its output may satisfy originality.The United States requires human authorship, the United Kingdom protects computergenerated works by statute, and the European Union regulates providers of general-purpose AI models through copyright and transparency obligations.This paper examines the Indian framework and the relevant comparative developments, the first Indian judicial ruling on model training, and the contemporary controversies concerning authorship, ownership, training data, infringement and accountability.It argues that neither unrestricted copyright for autonomous AI outputs nor the complete exclusion of AI-assisted works is adequate.

papers.title: MALICIOUS USE OF DEEPFAKES IN INDIA: LEGAL, TECHNOLOGICAL AND SOCIO-ECONOMIC CHALLENGES AND THE NEED FOR AN EFFECTIVE REGULATORY FRAMEWORK
papers.authors: Nilam Navanath Pawar
papers.journal: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.
papers.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has transformed the creation, manipulation and dissemination of audio-visual information.Deepfakes, broadly understood as synthetic or manipulated audio, images and videos capable of presenting fabricated persons, statements or events as authentic, have consequently become a significant legal and socioeconomic concern.Although synthetic media has legitimate applications in education, entertainment, accessibility, research and creative expression, its malicious use can facilitate impersonation, financial fraud, defamation, misinformation, electoral manipulation, identity theft, non-consensual intimate imagery and child exploitation.This paper examines a central research question: whether India's existing legal and regulatory framework adequately addresses the distinct harms caused by malicious deepfakes while preserving constitutionally protected expression.It adopts a doctrinal and analytical approach to the Information Technology Act 2000, the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021 as amended in 2026, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, constitutional guarantees under Articles 14, 19 and 21, and relevant judicial developments concerning personality rights.The analysis finds that India now has an express regulatory framework for synthetically generated information, including intermediary obligations relating to unlawful synthetic content, prominent labelling and technical provenance mechanisms.However, legal protection remains dispersed across criminal, civil, evidentiary, data-protection and sector-specific regimes.Significant gaps persist in relation to electoral deception, cross-border investigation, attribution, authenticity of electronic evidence, rapid

papers.title: RETHINKING AUTHORSHIP: A DOCTRINAL ANALYSIS OF COPYRIGHT PROTECTION FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-GENERATED WORKS
papers.authors: Divyanshu Tiwari
papers.journal: LawFoyer International Journal of Doctrinal Legal Research.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges a foundational assumption of copyright law: that protectable expression is attributable to a human author who exercises creative judgment.This article examines how copyright law should treat works generated or materially assisted by AI, with particular attention to authorship, originality, ownership, and the threshold of human creative contribution.Using a comparative doctrinal method, it analyses statutory provisions, judicial decisions, administrative practice, and ongoing reform initiatives in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, and India.The analysis considers, inter alia, Thaler v. Perlmutter and U.S. Copyright Office guidance; section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 and the United Kingdom's reform debate; the Court of Justice of the European Union's "author's own intellectual creation" jurisprudence and the transparency framework under Article 53 of the EU AI Act; and India's section 2(d) of the Copyright Act, 1957 together with the RAGHAV/Suryast registration episode.The comparison reveals substantial convergence around the need for identifiable human creative input, notwithstanding significant differences in legal technique and the continued existence of statutory provisions for computer-generated works in the United Kingdom and India.The principal unresolved question is not whether human contribution matters, but how much creative control, selection, arrangement, modification, or other expressive intervention is sufficient to support authorship in AI-assisted works.The article argues that neither categorical exclusion nor unrestricted protection adequately addresses this intermediate zone.It therefore proposes a disclosure-based rebuttable presumption under which claimants identify the nature and extent of AI 1 5th-Semester B.A. LL.B. Student at

papers.title: Designing for Predictability: How Mental Models of AI Error Boundaries Shape Human-AI Team Performance in High-Stakes Decision Making
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed to advise human decision-makers in high-stakes domains—including healthcare, criminal justice, and financial services—organizations face a critical but often overlooked challenge: the accuracy of an AI system alone does not determine the performance of the human-AI team. This article examines the role of human mental models of AI capabilities, specifically mental models of AI error boundaries, in shaping collaborative decision-making outcomes. Drawing on foundational experimental research demonstrating that properties such as the parsimony and stochasticity of an AI's error boundary significantly influence whether humans can learn when to trust or override AI recommendations, this article translates those findings into actionable organizational strategies. Evidence-based interventions are presented across interface design, model selection, training protocols, and governance structures, illustrated with examples from healthcare, surgery, criminal justice, and AI research and development. Forward-looking pillars for building long-term human-AI collaboration capability—including psychological contract recalibration, continuous learning systems, and distributed oversight—are proposed for practitioners seeking to maximize the return on AI-augmented decision systems.

papers.title: From Breaking Point to Breakthrough: How AI Is Reinventing Assessment in Higher Education and Corporate Learning
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has fundamentally disrupted traditional assessment practices in higher education and corporate learning and development. This article examines how AI has simultaneously destabilized century-old assessment methods while enabling more authentic, scalable alternatives. Drawing on recent empirical evidence and organizational case examples across education and industry, we analyze four major shifts reshaping assessment design: process-oriented evaluation, AI-enhanced oral examinations, AI personas for situated skill assessment, and continuous behavioral assessment. Rather than representing assessment's demise, AI has exposed the inherent limitations of conventional methods while dramatically reducing the cost barriers to implementing more valid alternatives. We synthesize evidence-based organizational responses and propose a framework for building assessment systems that leverage AI to better measure learning, skill development, and performance. The findings suggest that AI has not broken assessment—it has broken the economics of inadequate assessment, creating unprecedented opportunities to align evaluation methods with learning outcomes that matter.

papers.title: The Creative Advantage: How Organizations Can Future-Proof Their Workforce by Investing in Creativity
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: This article examines the relationship between occupational creativity and resilience to automation, drawing on a landmark study by Bakhshi, Frey, and Osborne (2015) which found that 86–87 percent of workers in highly creative occupations face low or no risk of computerization. The article situates these findings within the broader landscape of workforce disruption, including recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, and explores both organizational and individual consequences of the accelerating automation trend. Five evidence-based organizational responses are identified—creative skills development, human–AI collaboration models, design-thinking integration, creative industry ecosystem investment, and workforce transition support—each illustrated with practitioner examples spanning technology, entertainment, and professional services. The article concludes by articulating three forward-looking pillars for building long-term creative resilience: continuous creative learning systems, adaptive organizational design, and purpose-driven talent strategies. Implications for leaders seeking to future-proof their organizations against technological displacement are discussed throughout.

papers.title: Different Speeds, Different Strategies: Mapping AI Adoption Across Career Areas to Prioritize Workforce Preparation
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: Public debate about artificial intelligence often treats the labor market as if it were changing all at once. Job postings data suggest otherwise. A Lightcast analysis of U.S. postings for the first half of 2026 plots career areas by their current level of AI adoption and by how quickly that adoption grew from 2025, revealing four distinct "climates": AI hotspots, emerging frontiers, established AI hubs, and AI cold zones (Lightcast, 2026). This article uses that map as a starting point for workforce strategy. Integrating labor economics, technology diffusion research, and field evidence on generative AI in customer support, finance, software development, healthcare, and education, it argues that organizations and individuals have more time to prepare than the prevailing narrative implies, provided their strategies match where each career area actually stands. Five evidence-based responses are presented, each tailored to a different adoption climate and illustrated with organizational examples, followed by three long-term capabilities for navigating an uneven, multi-speed transition.

papers.title: Navigating the Evolving Landscape of Human Reliance on Generative AI
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence into workplace and personal contexts has created substantial uncertainty regarding how individuals rely on these systems over time. This article examines longitudinal patterns in AI delegation and disclosure behaviors, drawing on evidence from a six-wave study spanning ten months with over 1,000 U.S. participants. Contrary to expectations of increasing familiarity breeding greater reliance, findings reveal declining willingness to delegate tasks and disclose information to AI systems, particularly for personally meaningful activities. Professional writing contexts maintained relatively stable delegation patterns, while personal contexts showed pronounced declines. Trust, anthropomorphic perceptions, and positive attitudes toward AI emerged as consistent predictors of both delegation and disclosure behaviors. These patterns suggest that human-AI interaction reflects a calibration process rather than simple habituation, with important implications for organizational AI adoption strategies, training programs, and technology design. Organizations must recognize that sustainable AI integration depends less on repeated exposure and more on cultivating well-calibrated trust, contextually appropriate applications, and meaningful transparency mechanisms.

papers.title: Cognitive Polarization in the AI Era: Organizational Strategies to Prevent a Mental Underclass
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: David Brooks's cautionary framework on cognitive polarization—wherein individuals with high need-for-cognition leverage AI to amplify capacity while others outsource thinking entirely—presents organizations with an urgent strategic imperative. This article synthesizes research on workplace AI adoption, employee development, and organizational psychology to examine how enterprises can prevent the emergence of a "mental underclass" while capturing AI's productivity benefits. Evidence demonstrates that cognitive engagement patterns are shaped less by innate traits than by organizational design, learning culture, and job architecture. Organizations that frame AI as an augmentation partner rather than a substitution tool, embed reflective practice into workflows, democratize access to cognitively enriching tasks, and cultivate psychological safety around experimentation show measurably higher workforce capability development alongside productivity gains. Through examination of interventions spanning interface design, learning infrastructure, work redesign, and leadership communication across manufacturing, professional services, healthcare, and financial sectors, this article provides actionable guidance for HR leaders, learning officers, and executives navigating the dual mandate of technological adoption and human capital development. The conclusion emphasizes that organizational choices—not individual cognitive disposition—will largely determine whether AI widens or narrows capability gaps within the workforce.

papers.title: Digital Transformation, AI, and Inclusive Education: Creating Equitable Learning Ecosystems
papers.authors: Jonathan Westover
papers.abstract: This article examines the complex interrelationship between digital transformation, artificial intelligence adoption, and inclusive education in creating more equitable learning environments. Through mixed-methods research combining systematic literature review, survey data from 412 educational practitioners, and 37 semi-structured interviews with diverse stakeholders, the study explores how these three forces collectively reshape educational access, engagement, and outcomes for diverse learners. Statistical analyses reveal significant correlations between implementation patterns and equity outcomes (r=0.57, p<.001), with institutional commitment to inclusion (β=0.42, p<.001) emerging as the strongest predictor in regression models. Findings identify five key implementation patterns that significantly influence equity outcomes, including intentional design approaches, comprehensive integration strategies, continuous evaluation practices, stakeholder participation models, and balanced innovation-support frameworks. The study identifies critical barriers to equitable implementation, including persistent digital divides, algorithmic biases, professional development gaps, and governance challenges. The research contributes an empirically grounded Education Equity Technology (EET) model conceptualizing the interaction zones where these domains converge, while providing evidence-based recommendations for educational leaders and policymakers. These findings have important theoretical implications for understanding sociotechnical systems in education and practical applications for creating more inclusive digital learning environments.

papers.title: Machine Learning for Predicting Student Academic Performance: A Case Study at a Public University
papers.authors: Habibrahman Habibi, Abdul Wajid Fazil, Kefayatullah Khairkhah
papers.journal: Frontiers in Sustainable Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Predicting how well a student will perform before, rather than after, a semester goes wrong is one of the more practical promises that machine learning has brought to higher education. This study reports a case study conducted at a public university, in which academic records, attendance logs, and a small set of socio-demographic indicators were used to build classification models that sort students into low, average, and high performance categories well before final examinations. Seven algorithms were trained and compared on the same dataset: logistic regression, decision tree, k-nearest neighbors, support vector machine, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and a multilayer perceptron artificial neural network. After cleaning the data, encoding categorical fields, and selecting the ten most informative features through a correlation-based filter, the models were evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and the area under the ROC curve, with a stratified 80/20 train-test split and five-fold cross-validation. XGBoost produced the strongest results, reaching 90.1% accuracy and an AUC of 0.95, followed closely by random forest and the neural network, while logistic regression and k-nearest neighbors trailed behind. Prior GPA, midterm score, and assignment performance emerged as the three most influential predictors, consistent with findings reported in comparable studies. The paper closes by discussing what these results mean for early-warning systems and academic advising at resource-constrained public universities, and where the approach still falls short. By turning data that public universities already collect into an early, actionable signal for advisors, this work speaks directly to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education), particularly its emphasis on equitable learning opportunities and student retention.

papers.title: Digital Readiness, Artificial Intelligence Use, and Student Learning Outcomes in Indonesia: Evidence from PISA 2025
papers.authors: Debora Nuraini, Sri Nurfitrianty, Andry Steven Manongga, Dian Aprilia Manase, Ahmad Suhendra
papers.journal: Indonesian Journal of Multidisciplinary on Social and Technology
papers.abstract: Teknologi digital dan kecerdasan artifisial (AI) semakin mengubah praktik belajar siswa, tetapi peningkatan akses terhadap teknologi tidak selalu meningkatkan capaian belajar. Penelitian ini mengkaji hubungan antara kesiapan digital sekolah, penggunaan AI oleh siswa untuk kegiatan sekolah, kesempatan untuk mengevaluasi secara kritis informasi yang dihasilkan AI, kondisi sosial ekonomi, dan capaian belajar siswa di Indonesia berdasarkan data PISA 2025. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif berbasis data sekunder dengan analisis deskriptif, komparatif, dan interpretatif yang berfokus pada Indonesia. Siswa Indonesia melaporkan keterlibatan yang relatif tinggi dalam penggunaan teknologi digital dan AI, termasuk penggunaan perangkat digital untuk belajar di sekolah selama 2,5 jam per hari dan 53% siswa yang menggunakan chatbot AI setiap minggu. Namun, capaian rata-rata tetap berada di bawah rata-rata OECD dalam sains (389 dibandingkan 482), matematika (364 dibandingkan 463), dan membaca (365 dibandingkan 461). Penggunaan AI tidak secara konsisten berkaitan dengan capaian yang lebih tinggi, sehingga manfaat pendidikannya bergantung pada tujuan dan intensitas penggunaan. Kesempatan mengevaluasi informasi secara kritis dan kesiapan digital sekolah menjadi dimensi kontekstual penting, sementara perbedaan sosial ekonomi menunjukkan ketimpangan kesempatan dalam mengembangkan kompetensi AI. Tantangan Indonesia kini bergeser dari akses teknologi menuju penguatan kapabilitas digital dan AI. Penguatan kesiapan sekolah, kapasitas pedagogis guru, literasi AI kritis, dan akses yang setara terhadap pembelajaran berbantuan AI yang berkualitas menjadi penting. Mengingat bukti bersifat potong lintang dan observasional, hubungan yang ditemukan harus ditafsirkan sebagai asosiasi, bukan hubungan sebab-akibat.

papers.title: Assessing the Artificial Intelligence Training Needs of Primary School Teachers in Punjab: A UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers-Based Study
papers.authors: Sidrah Hanif, Ishtiaq Hussain
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming educational practice, creating new professional competency requirements for teachers. This study assessed the perceived AI training needs of primary school teachers in Punjab, Pakistan, using the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers as the guiding framework. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed with a targeted sample of 500 primary school teachers from nine districts representing northern, central, and southern Punjab. Data were collected through a 25-item structured questionnaire covering five UNESCO-aligned domains: human-centered mindset, ethics of AI, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and professional learning. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Welch independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and descriptive analysis of open-ended responses were conducted. The 25-item scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = .957). Overall, teachers reported a moderately high level of perceived AI training need (M = 6.88, SD = 1.96). Professional learning emerged as the highest-rated domain (M = 7.01), followed by AI foundations and applications (M = 6.91) and ethics of AI (M = 6.90). The highest-priority individual needs were fair AI access for rural schools, maintaining teacher authority when using AI, multimedia resource generation, AI certification, professional learning networks, and AI-integrated lesson planning. No statistically significant differences were found in overall training needs by gender, district, school location, academic qualification, or teaching experience. Open-ended responses further emphasized the need for practical AI training, lesson-planning support, time-saving applications, ethical guidance, and improved digital infrastructure. The findings indicate that AI professional development for primary teachers in Punjab should be continuous, practical, human-centered, ethically grounded, and supported by adequate infrastructure and professional learning opportunities.

papers.title: Presumptive Taxation in India: Balancing Simplified Taxation with Enhanced Financial Disclosure
papers.authors: Asfar Ibrahim J
papers.journal: Journal of Law and Legal Research Development.
papers.abstract: Digital transformation is the incorporation of novel technologies across all facets of an organization. This technology integration will need a transformation of conventional business models. Likewise, artificial intelligence has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies of recent decades, possessing significant potential to affect both businesses and individuals. Cognitive methodologies that replicate human behaviour and cognition are yielding sophisticated analytical models that assist firms in enhancing sales and customer engagement, optimizing operational efficiency, refining offerings, and ultimately generating pertinent insights from data. These decision-making methods rely on descriptive, predictive, and prescriptive analytics. This requires a legislative framework that uniformly controls all digital changes across countries and facilitates an effective digital transformation process under defined regulations. Conversely, it is imperative that this digital disruption is not impeded by the regulatory structure. This study will illustrate that AI and digital transformation will be integral to numerous applications and hence will be universally implemented. Nonetheless, this implementation must adhere to established regulations and align with the current circumstances.

papers.title: A Machine Learning-Based Student Dropout Risk Prediction and Early Warning System
papers.authors: Kritanat Chungnoy, Tanatorn Tanantong, Naphat Jakkraphatcharakul, Nongnapat Sunontanam, Supada Boonyavattanavijit, Thanyaluck Tungthananithirath, Surasit Uypatchawong
papers.journal: Asian Health, Science and Technology Reports
papers.abstract: Student dropout rates in higher education have become a significant problem for universities worldwide, impacting both student academic achievement and institutional stability. To address this problem, this research proposes the Student Dropout Risk Prediction and Early Warning System (SDRP-EWS), a machine learning framework designed to predict the risk of eventual student dropout. Utilizing multi-semester academic performance data from 20,919 undergraduate students at Sakon Nakhon Rajabhat University, Thailand (2014–2024), the study developed logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost models. To support early and continuous monitoring, these models were evaluated at three distinct prediction horizons: following the first semester, after the second semester, and after three or more semesters. Cohen's d effect size analysis compared ROC-AUC distributions across engineered feature sets, confirming the practical advantage of the selected model configurations. The results show that XGBoost consistently outperformed other models across all prediction stages, achieving F1-scores for the dropout class ranging from 0.65 in the early stages up to 0.93 in later semesters with comprehensive academic histories. This study's primary contribution is integrating the top-performing multi-semester model into a functional, web-based prototype dashboard tailored for Thai higher education. By providing academic advisors with intuitive risk scores and key contributing factors, the system demonstrates strong potential as an evidence-based decision-support tool to facilitate proactive, targeted institutional interventions.

papers.title: AI Literacy for Teachers: An Ethical Imperative
papers.authors: Neelima G S
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing lesson planning, learning support, assessment, and teachers’ professional work. These possibilities also create concerns involving accuracy, bias, privacy, transparency, academic integrity, inclusion, and overdependence on automated systems. This review discusses AI literacy as a professional and ethical competency for teachers. It uses a narrative review approach, drawing on selected scholarship on AI in education, AI literacy, and international guidance for teachers. The discussion is organised around the meaning of AI literacy, its pedagogical value, major ethical concerns, and implications for teacher education. The literature indicates that responsible AI use requires more than operational familiarity with digital tools: teachers need to understand the limits of AI outputs, check information against reliable sources, protect learners’ data, identify possible bias, and make context-sensitive decisions about when AI is appropriate. International guidance also emphasises human agency, ethics, AI foundations, AI pedagogy, and professional learning as connected dimensions of teacher competence. Accordingly, teacher education should combine practical experimentation with case-based ethical discussion, assessment redesign, privacy awareness, and continuing professional development. This paper argues that AI should support rather than replace teachers’ professional judgement and relationships with learners. As a narrative review, it does not report original survey data or claim to provide an exhaustive systematic review. It concludes with recommendations for integrating AI literacy into pre-service and in-service teacher education.

papers.title: İş Sağlığı ve Güvenliği Eğitiminde Görsel İletişim, Dijital Teknolojiler ve Güvenlik Kültürü: Güncel Yaklaşımlar Üzerine Bir Derleme
papers.authors: İlyas Güngör, Sevinç Güngör
papers.journal: Journal of Management and Educational Sciences
papers.abstract: Occupational safety and health (OSH) training plays a fundamental role in helping employees identify risks, develop safe behaviors, and foster a sustainable safety culture. With the digital transformation, visual communication tools, e-learning, mobile learning, artificial intelligence, virtual and augmented reality, simulation, and other digital technologies are increasingly being used in OSH training. The purpose of this study is to examine the relationships between visual communication, digital educational technologies, and safety culture in OSH training from a holistic perspective and to present a conceptual framework that integrates these areas. The study was conducted using an integrative review approach; empirical, theoretical, and conceptual studies in the national and international literature were evaluated comparatively. The literature was synthesized under four main themes: the theoretical and behavioral foundations of OSH training; visual communication and risk communication; digital technologies and technology-enhanced learning; and safety culture and safe learning environments in vocational and technical education. The findings indicate that visual communication tools support the recognition of risks and the understanding of safety information, while digital technologies expand opportunities for interactive, experiential, and personalized learning. However, the ability of these tools to translate into safe behavior depends on their integration with appropriate pedagogical design, administrative support, and a strong safety culture. The conceptual framework proposed in this study demonstrates that the integration of visual communication and digital technologies within the foundation of a safety culture can support safe learning environments, safe behavior, and vocational competence.

papers.title: Secondary school teachers’ attitude towards learning AI technology and their professional development in District Khushab, Punjab
papers.authors: Nimra Qasim, Nargis Abbas
papers.journal: Journal of Emerging Trends in Social Sciences and Humanities
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the future of learning environments, paving the way for personalization, creativity, and immersive experiences. Research objectives of the study were to examine secondary school teachers’ attitudes towards adopting and learning AI technology in their teaching practices and also identify the challenges secondary school teachers face in integrating AI technology into their professional growth. The study followed quantitative approach to evaluate the attitude of secondary school teachers (SSTs) in Tehsil Khushab.The descriptive correlational survey design was utilized to investigate the relationship between Attitude of SSTs and their professional development (PD). Quantitative data were collected using a structured questionnaire incorporating scales adopted. A stratified random sampling technique was used to select the sample. Out of the total population of the 404 teachers (228 females and 176 male), 30 percent of the teachers were sampled. In line with this, 122 teachers (79 females and 43 male teachers) were selected in 20 high schools in Tehsil Khushab. The findings revealed that SSTs showed positive attitude towards learning AI technology. The results indicated that the attitude of secondary school teachers toward AI significantly influence their professional development. It is recommended that further researchers investigate various district of Punjab to understand teachers’ attitude towards learning AI technology in diverse teaching settings.

papers.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Academic Libraries: Advancing Research, Teaching, and Societal Development in the Digital Age
papers.authors: Mohammed Abubakar Abdullahi, Maihadishi Aisha Abubakar
papers.journal: Azman University International Journal of Management and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed information management, education, and knowledge dissemination across the globe. Academic libraries, as critical support systems for teaching, learning, and research, are increasingly integrating AI-driven technologies to improve service delivery and user experiences. This study examined the role of Artificial Intelligence in academic libraries with particular emphasis on its contributions to research, teaching, and societal development in the digital age. The study adopted a quantitative survey research design and was conducted at the University Library, Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. A total of 200 questionnaires were administered to library users, drawn from undergraduate students, postgraduate students, academic staff, and librarians selected through stratified random sampling, of which 187 were properly completed and returned, representing a response rate of 93.5%. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analysed using frequency counts, percentages, and mean scores. The findings revealed that Artificial Intelligence significantly enhances research productivity, facilitates teaching and learning activities, and improves access to information resources. The study also found that users generally possess positive perceptions regarding AI-driven library services. However, inadequate funding, poor ICT infrastructure, lack of technical expertise, and concerns relating to data privacy and security remain major challenges affecting the successful integration of AI into academic libraries. The study concludes that AI has enormous potential to transform academic libraries and contribute to educational and societal development, and recommends increased investment in technological infrastructure, continuous training for library personnel, and the establishment of policies to guide the ethical deployment of AI technologies.

papers.title: Price, Sentiment, and Activity in Bitcoin and U.S. Equities: A Comparative Machine-Learning and Predictive-Inference Framework, 2014 to 2026
papers.authors: Arnav Aggarwal
papers.journal: Student Journal of Business and Economics
papers.abstract: Bitcoin and U.S. equities are forecast in largely separate literatures, which leaves open whether the two markets respond to different forces or whether researchers simply study them differently. This paper imposes one framework on both: four feature blocks (Price/Technical, Sentiment/News, Activity/On-chain-or-Volume, Cross-market) evaluated across six classifier families under a walk-forward design, giving 114 model-block-asset comparisons for Bitcoin (4,346 daily returns) and for Tesla and the S&P 500 (2,338 common-calendar observations each). No comparison exceeds its majority-classbase rate by a statistically significant margin after Benjamini-Hochberg correction, so daily directional predictability is not detectable for either asset class. The fitted models nevertheless draw on different information. SHAP attribution assigns 60.3% of Bitcoin's fitted signal to activity and on-chain features and 5.6% to sentiment, against price and technical dominance for Tesla (55.0%) and the S&P 500 (53.5%). Bitcoin's largest single feature is a trading-volume-based illiquidity proxy rather than a blockchain-native metric, so the model's predictions rely on trading activity broadly rather than narrowly on on-chain metrics, and the shares are inconsistent with the claim that cryptoasset prices are driven mainly by hype; because SHAP describes a fitted model rather than the price process, this is evidence about predictive reliance, not causation. A HAC-robust, false-discovery-rate-corrected Granger battery finds that Bitcoin and Tesla returns predict next-day changes in the Crypto Fear & Greed Index (F = 157.72 and F = 15.34, p < 0.001) with no reverse effect. Since volatility and momentum carry half the weight of that index, the Bitcoin result is partly mechanical; the Tesla result cannot be, and is therefore the informative one, although a Granger test establishes predictive precedence rather than the underlying mechanism. GARCH(1,1) estimates place Bitcoin's volatility persistence (α+β = 1.000) and tail thickness (Student-tν = 3.20) above both equities.

papers.title: INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL GENERATIVA NA EDUCAÇÃO BÁSICA: POSSIBILIDADES, RISCOS E DESAFIOS PARA A FORMAÇÃO DOCENTE
papers.authors: Italo Gregório Carvalho Ferraz
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: This article analyzes the possibilities, risks and challenges associated with the incorporation of generative artificial intelligence into basic education, emphasizing teacher education and teaching work. The qualitative, exploratory, bibliographic and documentary study combines Brazilian legislation, UNESCO guidance, documents from the Brazilian Ministry of Education and academic studies published mainly between 2023 and 2026. Findings indicate that systems capable of producing texts, images, code and summaries may support planning, accessibility, differentiated instruction and formative assessment, provided that outputs are verified and subordinated to curricular goals. Responsible integration requires institutional governance, protection of children and adolescents, transparent assessment criteria, equitable infrastructure and continuing education combining technical foundations, ethics, pedagogy and inquiry into practice. Generative AI does not replace human mediation, but changes the conditions under which teaching, learning and assessment take place, making it essential to strengthen teachers’ professional autonomy and students’ critical AI literacy. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; basic education; teacher education; assessment; digital ethics.

papers.title: APRENDER A JULGAR: DÉDALO, O LABIRINTO E A FORMAÇÃO ÉTICA DIANTE DA INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL
papers.authors: Narda Telles
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: This article analyzes the formation of ethical judgment in the educational use of artificial intelligence. The investigation begins with Jatobá's (1992) essay on Daedalus and the labyrinth, acknowledged as the initial interlocution for connecting myth, technique and ethics, and shifts this reading toward an educational question: how can one learn to judge when answers and decisions are mediated by systems whose functioning and consequences are not entirely under human control? This qualitative, bibliographical and interpretive study is developed as a theoretical essay. It brings together Aristotle's (2014) account of practical wisdom, Arendt's (2004) reflections on thinking and responsibility, the discussion by Pinheiro and Valente (2024), and UNESCO (2021) guidelines on the ethics of artificial intelligence. The analysis identifies five nuclei in the myth: Daedalus's technical power, Minos's authority, the opacity of the labyrinth, Icarus's loss of measure, and the orientation offered by Ariadne's thread. The results indicate that principles and rules are necessary but insufficient unless education develops the ability to examine circumstances, purposes and consequences. The article concludes that ethical education for artificial intelligence must preserve human authorship of decisions, make affected persons visible and teach learners to answer for the paths they choose. Keywords: ethical judgment; artificial intelligence; education.

papers.title: Risks Associated with the Use of Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Review
papers.authors: Sujal Mutgekar, Sanika More Sanika, Vipul Zope, Vedant Bhangale Bhangale
papers.journal: International Research Journal of Innovation in Science and Technology
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adopted across healthcare, finance, manufacturing, cybersecurity, education, and other sectors because of its ability to support prediction, automation, pattern recognition, and decision-making. However, the growing use of AI also introduces technical, security, economic, ethical, and social risks. This study examines the major risks associated with AI and classifies them into data privacy and security, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency and explainability, cybersecurity threats, economic and employment effects, and ethical and social concerns. A qualitative review-based methodology is used to examine relevant research and established AI risk-management frameworks. The study further discusses how these risks can affect different industries and reviews mitigation approaches including data governance, explainable AI, cybersecurity controls, human oversight, continuous monitoring, and governance mechanisms. The findings indicate that AI risk management should be addressed throughout the AI lifecycle rather than only after system deployment. A coordinated approach involving technical safeguards, organizational practices, human oversight, and appropriate governance can support more responsible and risk-aware deployment of AI systems.

papers.title: Số hóa di sản văn hóa Phật giáo Việt Nam: cơ hội và thách thức
papers.authors: Thích Chân Định
papers.journal: Tạp chí Dân tộc học và Tôn giáo học
papers.abstract: In the context of national digital transformation and the Fourth Industrial Revolution, the digitization of Buddhist cultural heritage has become an essential strategy for preserving, promoting, and disseminating the cultural, historical, and spiritual values of Vietnamese Buddhism. Employing an interdisciplinary approach that integrates cultural studies, Buddhist studies, and information science, this paper examines the theoretical foundations, opportunities, and challenges associated with the digitization of Buddhist heritage. The study argues that digitization extends beyond the simple conversion of physical materials into digital formats; it encompasses data standardization, governance, preservation, and utilization, thereby contributing to the development of a sustainable digital heritage ecosystem. The application of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), big data, and digital platforms enhances the preservation of heritage, facilitates academic research, supports Buddhist education and Dharma propagation, and promotes sustainable cultural and spiritual tourism. Nevertheless, the digitization process continues to face significant challenges, including inadequate digital infrastructure, the lack of standardized and interoperable data, shortages of interdisciplinary human resources, and issues related to copyright, cybersecurity, and data governance. To address these challenges, the paper proposes several strategic solutions, including the formulation of a national strategy for digital Buddhist heritage, the establishment of centralized digital repositories and digital libraries, the development of standardized data frameworks, the cultivation of interdisciplinary expertise, and the strengthening of international collaboration. These measures are expected to ensure the sustainable preservation of Buddhist cultural heritage while enhancing its contribution to digital transformation and international integration.

papers.title: Effect of Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning on Metacognitive Skills and Performance in Geometry among Secondary Students in Kaduna State, Nigeria
papers.authors: Emmanuel Yohanna, Yusuf Feyisara Zakariya, Aliyu Suleiman Aliyu
papers.journal: Journal of Studies in Science and Mathematics Education
papers.abstract: This study examined the effect of Process-Oriented Guided Inquiry Learning (POGIL) on metacognitive skills and performance in geometry among secondary school students in Kaduna State, Nigeria. A quasi-experimental design was employed, involving 131 SS2 students from two public senior secondary schools in Zaria Educational Zone. The experimental group (n=62) were taught geometry using POGIL, while the control group (n=69) were taught lecture method. Data were collected using the Geometry Performance Test (GPT) and Metacognitive Skills Inventory (MSI), validated and tested for reliability (α = 0.84 and 0.85 respectively). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) at 0.05 significance level. The experimental group showed significantly post metacognitive skills scores (M=57.29, SD=15.20) than in the control group (M=42.97, SD=9.52). Similarly, the experimental group reveals a significantly higher post-test scores (M=55.29, SD=19.06) compared to the control group (M=39.12, SD=13.61) in geometry performance. POGIL demonstrates positive effects on students' geometry performance and metacognitive skills at F(1, 128) = 40.21, p < .001. In addition, the findings reveals a significant effect of POGIL on students' Post-Performance scores, at F(1, 128) = 31.061, p < .001. The findings, reveals no significant gender differences were found in either metacognitive skills, or performance scores. This results shows that POGIL is gender friendly. The findings support the adoption of inquiry-based pedagogical approaches.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION-MAKING IN UNIVERSITY SPORTS MANAGEMENT IN RIVERS STATE, NIGERIA
papers.authors: Daniel Chinonso Ochor, Chijoke Frank, Bassey Udeme
papers.journal: INT’L JOURNAL OF HUMANITIES ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT AND CONTEMPORARY STUDIES
papers.abstract: This study found that AI adoption significantly predicted administrative decision-making and sports management efficiency among university sports administrators in Rivers State, Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional correlational research design. The study involved sports administrators from the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State University, Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, and Federal University of Environment and Technology. The estimated population was 160 sports administrators, from which a sample of 114 respondents was selected using the Taro Yamane formula. Eighty-nine completed questionnaires were retrieved, representing a 78% return rate. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring AI adoption, administrative decision-making, and sports management efficiency. Descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, were used to answer the research questions, while simple linear regression was employed to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 significance level. The findings showed that AI adoption had a strong perceived influence on administrative decision-making (grand mean = 3.03). Regression analysis further indicated that AI adoption significantly predicted administrative decision-making, R = .614, R² = .377, β = .614, F(1, 87) = 52.61, p < .001. AI adoption also demonstrated a strong perceived influence on sports management efficiency (grand mean = 3.06) and significantly predicted management efficiency, R = .638, R² = .407, β = .638, F(1, 87) = 59.72, p < .001. The study concludes that AI adoption represents a promising mechanism for improving decision quality and operational efficiency in university sports management. The study recommended, among other things, that university sports management adopt AI-supported administrative systems for planning, scheduling, information management, resource allocation, and monitoring of sporting programs.

papers.title: Perceptions of Paramedical Students Regarding Artificial Intelligence in Paramedical Education: A Cross-Sectional Questionnaire-Based Study
papers.authors: Niraimathi P R, Mrs. Gnana Nisha Juliet, Madhumathi A, Hepzhibah S
papers.journal: INDIAN JOURNAL OF ALLIED HEALTH SCIENCE
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing healthcare education, but evidence regarding its integration into paramedical curricula remains limited.The objective was to assess paramedical students' perceptions and attitudes towards integrating AI into paramedical education.

papers.title: Key Concepts Regarding the Ethical Implications of Artificial Intelligence: A Review
papers.authors: Oluwatosin ADEMIJU
papers.journal: Journal International Review of Research Studies
papers.abstract: This study presents a review of relevant literature on key concepts related to the ethical implications of artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the historical evolution, conceptual foundations, classifications, and ethical frameworks. Furthermore, it adopts the Responsible AI Framework, which emphasises fairness, accountability, transparency, and human-centred design as articulated by global institutions such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), United Nations Education Scientific Cultural Organization (UNESCO), and the European Commission. These frameworks were found to integrate ethical theory and policy and governance perspectives. Finally, the concepts reviewed provide the analytical foundation for understanding the ethical implications of AI in public policy decision-making, particularly within the Nigerian context.

papers.title: AI-Enabled automated feedback and debriefing in simulation-based healthcare education: a systematic review of educational effectiveness
papers.authors: Saeed Abdullah Alzahrani
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into healthcare simulation to deliver individualized feedback and support reflective learning. Educational evaluations include procedural coaching, virtual patient encounters, and facilitator development. This review examined educational effectiveness while distinguishing observed performance from perceived competence and feedback feasibility. Original research published to May 2026 evaluating artificial intelligence enabled feedback or debriefing in healthcare simulation was reviewed. Comparative educational studies and complementary feedback validation or feasibility investigations were synthesized narratively. Outcomes included technical performance, clinical reasoning, communication, perceived competence, cognitive workload, and debriefing utility. Ten original reports comprised seven randomized trials and three prospective, pilot, or qualitative investigations. Surgical trials show improvements in selected performance measures, with benefits dependent on feedback timing, instructional design, and human participation. Personalized expert instruction informed by artificial intelligence exceeded artificial intelligence tutoring alone in practice and transfer tasks. Virtual patient feedback improved clinical reasoning in a small trial, while nursing simulations demonstrated gains in communication and perceived competence. Artificial intelligence enabled feedback offers benefits for simulation outcomes. Data for autonomous team debriefing is less developed than data for individualized coaching. Integration with educators, independent assessment, and longitudinal evaluation provides the strongest direction for educational implementation.

papers.title: Decolonising AI in Higher Education: A Transcultural Ethics of Knowledge and Participation
papers.authors: Edmore Mashungu, Gilbert Karombo, Taddious M Pasipanodya, Joyce Mudzamiri, J. Sangano, Elizabeth Nyamukusa
papers.journal: PJ Palgo Journal of Education Research
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education presents what scholars term a "colonial paradox" for the Global South: a tool positioned as a force for development and inclusion, yet whose underlying infrastructure, governance, and epistemological foundations remain concentrated within a few developed nations and resource corporations.This paper examined the imperative to decolonise AI in higher education through a transcultural ethics framework that centers epistemic justice, Indigenous knowledge systems, and equitable participation.Drawing on the Ubuntu-Ẹ̀kọ ́ framework, which synthesises the communal ethics of Southern African Ubuntu with the West African Yoruba educational philosophy of Ẹ̀kọ ́, we argued that the uncritical adoption of AI systems built on Western, individualistic definitions of intelligence risks perpetuating digital colonialism and enabling deep epistemological capture.We proposed an alternative conceptualisation: AI as Augmented Collective Wisdom (ACW), reframing AI as a socio-technical vehicle designed to enhance and sustain a community's collective wisdom and ethical fabric.Through critical examination of empirical research documenting representational harms and the application of African ethical frameworks including Ubuntu and Ọmọlúàbí, we articulated transcultural ethical principles of relationality, community benefit, context sensitivity, and virtue cultivation.The paper concluded with actionable recommendations for policymakers, educators, and researchers to build equitable, sovereign, and sustainable AI futures in higher education.

papers.title: Administration Digital Support System (ADSS)
papers.authors: Samuella Shyka B. Escolta, April Rose B. Flores
papers.journal: International Journal of Sustainable and Integrated Studies
papers.abstract: This study developed and evaluated the Administration Digital Support System (ADSS), a web-based platform designed to support the generation, storage, retrieval, review, visualization, downloading, and printing of selected school administrative reports. The system was anchored in Data Quality Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Human-Computer Interaction and Usability Theory. Developmental and descriptive research designs were employed, with the Agile System Development Life Cycle guiding system development. Twenty respondents, consisting of five school heads and fifteen designated office heads from five public high schools in Kibawe and Damulog, Bukidnon, were purposively selected. A structured survey questionnaire incorporating the Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire and technology acceptance and acceptability measures was used, while data were analyzed using frequency count, percentage distribution, and mode. The ADSS provided role-specific dashboards and centralized the management of BMI, incident, bullying, child mapping, and Curriculum Management Support System reports. Results showed that the system was Highly Acceptable in user interface, data storage and retrieval, report generation, and overall acceptability. The study concluded that the ADSS performed well in the evaluated areas and was suitable for routine administrative tasks. Recommended improvements include standardized report formats, enhanced report content, offline functionality, additional report types, stronger security mechanisms, continuous user feedback and evaluation, and broader system implementation. The study supports SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). The ADSS contributes to educational, technological, and institutional sustainability by supporting organized reporting, accessible records, monitoring, and data-informed school administration.

papers.title: How AI Listens to Neurodivergence - A Comparative Study of Advice Responses Generated by Four Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jacob M. Gao
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to provide advice on a wide range of areas in life, yet little is known about how their advice changes when users supply neurodivergence-related context.Drawing on the author's positionality as a student with autistic experience, this study examines a fixed body of 180 responses generated with ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and DeepSeek.to 15 adolescent-oriented advice questions under three conditions: 1) no additional context, 2) a broad neurodivergent label, and 3) specific executive-function and sensory-overload difficulties.Archived lexical indicators and close reading show that the broad neurodivergent label primarily changed tone and explanation, while framing with specific difficulties produced more concrete support strategies, with increased scripts and more concrete support strategies for task scaffolds, sensory adjustments, routines and accommodations.Variations between AI systems also appeared; however, responses spanning the data body were not generated under identical conditions or under a singular protocol, so these contrasts are descriptive and observational rather than controlled estimates of model performance.Overall, the findings suggest that specific prompts make access needs more visible than identity labels alone, potentially helping neurodivergent users obtain more targeted advice from generative AI.

papers.title: Autism Spectrum Disorder Screening Through Behavioral Gaze Trajectories and Electroencephalography Signal Classification
papers.authors: Joseph Park
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that needs accurate early screening for early intervention.Early diagnosis is crucial for infants when their neuroplasticity allows treatment that could effectively hinder long-term developmental outcomes.Indeed, traditional methods are employed such as the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT), Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R), and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS).Yet, these approaches are subjective, which makes them susceptible to bias and misdiagnosis.Therefore, this research aims to identify an objective and accurate non-invasive biomarker for early diagnosis of ASD.

papers.title: Aberrant Structural and Functional Signatures of the Social-Cognitive Brain Network in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Multi-Site ABIDE Investigation of Theory-of-Mind Circuitry and Amygdala Morphometry
papers.authors: vihan choudhary
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is characterized by persistent impairments in social reciprocity and communication, therefore linked to atypical development of the "social brain".It is a distributed network anchored by the temporoparietal junction (TPJ), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and the amygdala.Diagnosis of ASD remains purely behavioral, with no validated biomarker of this circuitry to complement clinical assessment.The aim of this study is to ask whether structural and functional signatures of amygdala-centered mentalizing circuitry differ between ASD and typically developing individuals, and whether such differences track clinical severity.Using multi-site neuroimaging data from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE), the circuitry was characterized in a large, clinically phenotyped cohort (N = 1112; 539 ASD, 573 controls), combining amygdala surface morphometry, voxelwise general linear modeling of whole-brain effect-size and statistical parametric maps, and dimensional phenotyping via the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) and Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS).Group-level contrasts revealed reduced signal in the left mesial temporal cortex encompassing the amygdala and parahippocampal gyrus in ASD relative to controls, alongside subtle morphometric deviation in amygdala surface topology.SRS scores were markedly elevated in ASD (t = 24.1,p < 0.001), but categorical ADOS severity and dimensional SRS scores were not significantly correlated within the ASD group (r = -0.07,p = 0.51), indicating partially dissociable clinician-and caregiver-rated measures.These findings implicate amygdala-centered mentalizing circuitry in ASD social cognition and motivate a planned EEG extension examining mu rhythm suppression during action observation.

papers.title: Combined population and patient-specific brain networks predict electrical stimulation propagation
papers.authors: Sarah B. Lavelle, William K.S. Ojemann, Marc Jaskir, Zican Zou, Carlos A. Aguila, Katherine G. Walsh, Odile Feys, Daniel J. Zhou, Kathryn A. Davis, Brian Litt, Erin C. Conrad, Nishant Sinha
papers.abstract: Objective: Cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) are used during intracranial EEG (iEEG) monitoring to probe effective connectivity and guide epilepsy surgery. However, the factors governing spatial distribution and variability of stimulation-evoked responses across patients remain incompletely understood, making it difficult to distinguish physiological variation from pathological responses. We aimed to develop interpretable models of CCEP responses that integrate normative and patient-specific features, and to assess how these relationships are influenced by distance, brain-state, and epileptogenicity. Methods: We analyzed single-pulse stimulation data from 34 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy undergoing stereo-EEG monitoring. Significant CCEP responses were defined using N1 peak amplitude. For each stimulation-response pair, we derived multimodal features capturing Euclidean distance, effective connectivity priors from F-TRACT, a published population atlas of CCEP response probabilities, normative structural connectivity and communication metrics, and patient-specific functional connectivity estimated from iEEG during baseline and pre-stimulation periods. Lasso-regularized logistic regression models were trained to predict response using leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, and feature importance was examined across spatial scales and seizure onset zone (SOZ) involvement. Results: Performance to predict stimulation-evoked responses improved with the integration of multiple feature domains, with the full model achieving the highest accuracy (median AUC = 0.84). Feature relevance varied with spatial scale: short-range responses were dominated by distance and normative priors, whereas long-range responses depended strongly on patient-specific functional connectivity, especially when measured from pre-stimulation periods. Prediction errors were significantly higher for stimulation-response pairs within the SOZ, indicating deviations from normative connectivity-response relationships in epileptogenic networks. Significance: CCEP responses reflect an interaction between spatial constraints, network architecture, and patient-specific brain state. Multimodal modeling of CCEPs provides a principled framework to interpret stimulation responses and may offer complementary markers for identifying epileptogenic networks during presurgical evaluation.

papers.title: EEG mu rhythms and trait empathy during observation of a romantic partner’s pain with and without consoling touch
papers.authors: Sarah Love, Lauren Rowden, Bryten Ballenger, Amber L. Harris Bozer
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction Observation of a partner in pain elicits empathy-related cortical responses and social support can modulate pain. Objective The aim of this study was to investigate empathy and the cortical response during observation of a romantic partner in pain with and without consoling touch. Methods A total of 40 participants (20 couples) completed validated measures of handedness, pain and empathy. Each member of the couple was randomly assigned to be either the recipient of cold pressor pain or the consoling partner undergoing EEG. EEG activity was recorded from the consoling partner during baseline and pain conditions (with and without consoling touch) to investigate how observation of a partner in pain could alter mu rhythms. Results Observing a romantic partner in pain significantly enhanced mu at electrodes C4 and Cz, yet addition of consoling touch did not significantly change mu rhythms. Personal Distress was positively associated with mu rhythm enhancement at electrode C4 during pain without consoling touch ( r = .576, p = .008). Conclusion Viewing a romantic partner in pain significantly increased mu rhythms, that was not further changed by offering consoling touch. The association between increases in mu rhythms and Personal Distress in the current study suggests that self-oriented distress may be especially relevant to sensorimotor cortex responses when witnessing a partner in pain, particularly when consoling touch is not possible.

papers.title: STAMP-LME: A spatiotemporal surface-mapping framework for population-level iEEG
papers.authors: Alejandro Omar Blenkmann, Sabine Liliana Leske, Robert Thomas Knight, Anne‐Kristin Solbakk, Robert Oostenveld
papers.abstract: Abstract Intracranial EEG (iEEG) affords a unique opportunity to assess human neural activity with millisecond temporal resolution and millimeter spatial precision. However, group-level statistical analyses remain challenging due to sparse and heterogeneous electrode coverage, anatomical variability, and the difficulty of integrating spatiotemporal responses across individuals. Most iEEG studies therefore define brain regions of interest for the group analysis, sacrificing a spatial resolution strength of iEEG and excluding data outside those regions of interest. Here, we present a spatiotemporal analysis and mapping with permutation-based linear mixed-effects models (STAMP-LME), a cortical-mapping framework for population-level iEEG analysis independent of predefined cortical regions of interest. STAMP-LME is a complete processing pipeline spanning electrode localization, mapping to a standardized surface of the cortical mantle —including medial, orbitofrontal, and insular regions— and statistical inference at the cortical level. Electrode-level data from each participant is mapped to a standardized cortical surface using weights that account for electrode-to-cortex distance and confidence in cortical sampling. Brain signals are then combined with a spatial smoothing kernel and entered into LME models at each vertex-node and time point. Data-derived null distributions are generated through controlled permutations and used for spatiotemporal inference with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) or false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction. We validated STAMP-LME using simulations with known cortical ground truth while varying effect size, interparticipant source-location variability, electrode coverage, and spatial smoothing. The framework reliably detected simulated effects and recovered their spatiotemporal distribution while maintaining low localization error and limiting false-positive detections across different sampling conditions. We then applied the method to intracranial recordings from nine individuals performing an auditory oddball task. The empirical analysis revealed distributed auditory cortical responses consistent with conventional channel-level analyses, while providing more fine-grained group-level activation maps across sampled cortical regions. STAMP-LME provides a flexible, open-source framework for data-driven population-level cortical iEEG analysis that preserves the spatiotemporal strengths of intracranial recordings while accounting for sparse and heterogeneous electrode coverage. The structured workflow enables reproducible and anatomically precise group-level inference on a standardized cortical surface and facilitates comparison with surface-based fMRI and source-localized M/EEG results, therefore providing a practical tool for cognitive and clinical neuroscience research. Highlights STAMP-LME generates population-level cortical maps from sparse SEEG recordings. Projection weighting accounts for electrode-to-cortex distance and confidence in cortical sampling. Mixed-effects models capture participant- and channel-level variability. Data-derived permutations enable ROI-free spatiotemporal inference using TFCE or FDR correction. Simulations quantify detection, spatial recovery, and robustness to reduced electrode coverage.

papers.title: Impact of Daily Physical Fatigue on Inter-Limb Load Asymmetry and Joint Loading Rates During Daily Living Tasks in Unilateral Knee Osteoarthritis
papers.authors: Muhammad Hassan Bari, Ghulam Abbas, Abdullah Abid, Atta Rasool
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is characterized by progressive joint degradation and altered gait biomechanics. Inter-limb load asymmetry during daily living tasks may accelerate joint deterioration, particularly when combined with physical fatigue. This study investigates the relationship between daily physical fatigue and inter-limb load asymmetry patterns during functional activities in individuals with unilateral knee OA. Objective To evaluate the impact of fatigue on inter-limb load asymmetry and joint loading rates during daily living tasks in patients with unilateral knee osteoarthritis, and to identify biomechanical and clinical factors associated with load distribution patterns. Methods One hundred eighteen participants with unilateral knee OA (mean age 62.6 (SD 7.4) years, BMI 29.9 (SD 4.2) kg/m 2 ) completed biomechanical assessments during non-fatigued and fatigued conditions. Ground reaction force measurements were obtained during functional tasks including stair climbing, sit-to-stand transitions, and level walking. Load asymmetry was quantified as the inter-limb difference in peak vertical ground reaction forces. Statistical analysis was conducted using Python (v3.9), including paired t-tests, analysis of variance, and linear regression modeling. Results Participants demonstrated significantly increased load asymmetry under fatigue conditions (mean difference 8.7% (SD 12.3) %, p < 0.001). Fatigue-induced asymmetry was task-dependent, with stair negotiation showing the greatest increase (11.2% (SD 14.1) %). Peak loading rates on the affected knee were inversely correlated with time-to-peak load during fatigued conditions ( r = -0.68, p < 0.001). Disease severity (WOMAC score) and age significantly predicted asymmetry changes (R 2 = 0.52, p < 0.001). Conclusions Physical fatigue exacerbates inter-limb load asymmetry in unilateral knee OA, potentially accelerating joint degeneration. Task-specific interventions targeting fatigue management and load redistribution may improve long-term outcomes. Future longitudinal studies should examine the temporal relationship between acute biomechanical changes and progressive structural joint damage.

papers.title: Toward A Whole-Brain Interface Enabled by High-Resolution Surface Electrophysiology
papers.authors: Elton Ho, Katrina J. Barth, Jacqueline Dister, Aneil Srivastava, Adam J. Poole, Federico Claudi, Molly V. Lucas, Joshua S. Miller, Mark Hettick, Yoon Woo Byun, Ramin Anushiravani, Mark Murphy, Peter E. Konrad, Sanjay Bhatia, Geoffrey Adams, Steven Carte, Dominique Ottonello, Joshua B. Bederson, Ignacio Sáez, Christopher Paul Kellner, Gelana Tostaeva, Brian Harris Kopell, Daniel D. Cummins, Sedat Ulkatan, Saadi Ghatan, Iahn Cajigas, Bijan Pesaran, Pedro G. Borges, Qasim Qureshi, Jarl Haggerty, Zhengjia Wang, Crone Nathan, Chetan Bettegowda, Kurt Lehner, Steve Luo, Miguel Angrick, Rebecca Greene, Youssef G. Comair, Joshua P. Aronson, Michael T. Lawton, Prashanth Prakash, Tianhao Lei, Joon Hei Lee, Marc W. Slutzky, Matthew Tate, Angelique Christine Paulk, Gavin P. Dunn, Benjamin L. Grannan, Mijail Demian Serruya, Kevin Hines, Chengyuan Wu, Robert Rosenwasser, Assaf Berger, Elad I. Levy, Adnan Hussain Siddiqui, Jonathan Riley, Jason M. Davies, Jayme Strauss, Michael J. Mager, Craig H. Mermel, Benjamin I. Rapoport
papers.abstract: The goal of building a whole-brain interface-capable of generating a real-time digital representation of the state of the entire central nervous system-has long been framed as a hardware challenge of recording simultaneously from ever-larger numbers of microelectrodes. Advances in high-resolution neural interfaces now enable electrophysiologic interaction with the human nervous system at spatial and temporal resolutions previously unattainable without disrupting tissue architecture or physiology. These capabilities create new opportunities for mechanistic neuroscience, neuroprosthetics, and precision-guided neurosurgery. With the advent of modern microelectrode array technology, however, the whole-brain interface has also become a data challenge. Rather than pursuing large-scale human brain recording purely through a single device placed in a single patient, we demonstrate here that systematic multi-subject aggregation, across brain regions and behavioral paradigms, in a common anatomical framework, can achieve something functionally similar to a whole-brain interface. Here we present an approach to a functional atlas of the human central nervous system derived from high-resolution surface electrophysiology recordings obtained in the first 70 patients implanted with an anatomically conformal, thin-film neural interface positioned in more than 100 locations. The atlas comprises >100,000 electrode deployments and catalogs placement across a broad range of neuroanatomic targets spanning the motor, sensory, language, auditory, and associative domains, as well as brainstem and spinal cord structures that have historically been difficult to access at high electrophysiologic resolution. Across participants, aggregated recordings reveal somatotopic organization, including digit representations that follow a lateral-to-medial ordering consistent with classical homuncular maps, with transitions between adjacent representations occurring over spatial scales of approximately 0.8-2.0 mm; canonical frequency-band signatures, such as movement-related beta-band suppression and focal high-gamma (70-200 Hz) increases during motor and speech behaviors; and task-modulated population dynamics in both evoked and spontaneous activity across cortical, brainstem, and spinal cord regions. These findings yield insight into patterns of mesoscale electrophysiological dynamics conserved across the entire human central nervous system, suggesting that fine-scale functional organization is preserved across individuals when aligned to common anatomical landmarks. We further demonstrate several applications of these high-resolution recordings, including real-time neural decoding from upper extremity motor cortex to enable real-time neuroprosthetic control, and from ventrolateral cortex to decode cortical correlates of spoken language, facial movements, and complex facial expressions of emotion, supporting initial feasibility of combined verbal and nonverbal communication interfaces. Together, these results establish a paradigm for approaching large-scale interfaces with the human brain, as well as a starting point for a scalable, extensible atlas of human electrophysiologic function designed to accelerate discovery across basic neuroscience, translational research, and clinical neurotechnology.

papers.title: Efficacy of AI-Based Wearable EEG Devices in Detecting Psychological Distress and Monitoring Relaxation Interventions in Active-Duty Armed Personnel.
papers.authors: Monisha M, Mahesh A. Tripathi
papers.journal: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology
papers.abstract: High-stress workplaces, such as active-duty armed forces, make objective, continuous assessment of distress difficult.Smart wearables embedded with AI would provide an ideal alternative to self-reporting.To assess the ability of a commercially available AI-based EEG device, to compare the effectiveness of these techniques, and to compare their effectiveness on stressrelated neurophysiological biomarkers over the duration of a 12-session protocol for armed staff.A withinsubject repeated-measures design was employed with 200 active-duty armed personnel (mean age= 34.2 years, SD= 8.7).Participants completed 12 structured experimental sessions and incorporated five relaxation techniques, which are pranayama, dhyana, nadayoga, visual meditation, and mantra chanting.EEG band recordings measured pre-and post-session measured alpha (8-13 Hz), and beta (13-30 Hz) band power, which were measured as primary biomarkers of psychological arousal.The Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-14 (DASS-21) was administered at baseline and follow-up.Paired-samples t-tests and repeated-measures ANOVA were used for multiple comparisons.All five interventions showed statistically significant pre-to-post changes in both Alpha power and Beta power (all p< 0.001).Alpha power increased significantly (M_pre = 10.03Hz, M_post = 10.34Hz, Δ = +0.31Hz, t (199) = -12.02,p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.85; 95% CI [0.67, 1.03]), indicating cortical relaxation.Beta power decreased significantly (M_pre = 20.01Hz, M_post = 17.30Hz, Δ = -2.71Hz, t (199) = 56.46,p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 3.99; 95% CI [3.75, 4.23]), indicating reduced cortical arousal.When comparing efficacy, mantra chanting produced the largest beta reduction (Δ = -0.36Hz each, d = 1.28), and pranayama and dhyana produced the largest alpha augmentation (Δ = +0.36Hz each, d= 0.92 and d= 0.91, respectively).Total DASS-21 scores decreased 54.4% from baseline (M= 16.74, SD= 8.23) to post-protocol (M= 7.62, SD= 4.15), t (199) = 15.37,p< 0.001, d= 1.09; 95% CI [0.91, 1.27], suggesting a clinically meaningful change in psychological distress.This is the strongest empirical evidence to date of an objectively measurable neurophysiological signature of reduced psychological distress from AI-enabled wearable EEG devices in armed personnel.When objectively measurable biomarkers of reduced neurophysiological stress converge with reduced psychological distress, this offers converging evidence of the neural correlates of these reductions and, in this way, confirms the neurophysiological meaningfulness of the reduction and, in such a context, can form the robust basis for the deployment of wearable EEG platforms into military occupational health surveillance systems as stigmareducing, deployable alternatives to subjective-only assessment paradigms.

papers.title: Generative AI influences on political attitudes and suffrage behavior: Democratic resilience as an analytical framework in the United States
papers.authors: Steven B. Madison, Nicol I. Jane, Mariam Awad Abdulla Aljeaidi
papers.journal: Al-Biruni Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences
papers.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced new challenges to democratic governance by transforming political communication, voter engagement, and information dissemination. Despite growing concerns about deepfakes, synthetic media, and AI-enabled persuasion, scholars have paid limited attention to how these technologies collectively influence voter attitudes and electoral behavior in contemporary United States elections. This study investigates the impact of generative AI technologies, including Large Language Models (LLMs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), conversational bots, and synthetic media, on political persuasion and democratic resilience during the transition from the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election cycle to the 2026 Midterm Election cycle. Using a qualitative doctrinal and policy-analysis methodology supported by election-related case studies, regulatory documents, platform policies, and emerging empirical evidence on AI-generated political content, the study evaluates how AI reshapes electoral communication. The findings reveal three significant trends.
