papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: The study determined Artificial Intelligence Tools Utilized by Postgraduate Business Education Students for Effective Research-Based Learning in Rivers State Universities. Three specific objectives, research questions and hypotheses were posed and answered in the study. Descriptive survey research design was adopted for this study. The area covered by this study was Rivers State University (RSU) and Ignatius Ajuru University of Education (IAUE). The population of the study consist of One-hundred and thirty-three (133) Business Education postgraduate students of 2023/2024 academic session, in the two universities offering Business Education. The sample size for this study was the entire population and census was adopted as sampling techniques. Data for the study were collected by means of questionnaire titled “Artificial Intelligence Tools utilized by postgraduate Business Education students for effective Research Based learning in Rivers State universities (AITUPBESERBL)”. The instrument adopted a four point rating scale of Very High Extent, High Extent, Moderate Extent and low Extent (LE). The research instrument was face and content validated by three experts two in the Business Education and one expert in Measurement and Evaluation. The reliability of the instrument was determined by using test re-test method. The set of scores was collected and computed using Pearson Pearson's Product Moment Correlation Coefficient(r) and the correlation yielded a score of 0.86 which was considered appropriate for this study. One-hundred and thirty-three (133) copies of the questionnaire were administered to the respondents, which One-hundred and thirty-three (133) was retrieved for the analysis. Mean and Standard Deviation were used to answer the research questions and Independent Sample t-test Analysis was used to test the null hypotheses at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that Quill Bot as an Artificial Intelligence tool utilised by postgraduate Business Education students to a very high extent promotes effective research-based learning in Rivers State University and Ignatius Ajuru University of Education. It was concluded that Quillbot, Research Rabbit, and Scholarcy Artificial Intelligence tools utilized by postgraduate Business Education students to a high extent promote research-based learning. Based on the findings and conclusion made, it was recommended amongst others that Universities should formally integrate training on AI tools like QuillBot, Research Rabbit, and Scholarcy into postgraduate curricula. Workshops, seminars, and practical sessions should be organized to familiarize students with the functionalities and ethical use of these technologies in research writing and data analysis. Academic staff should be trained to understand and evaluate AI-supported research outputs effectively. Equipping supervisors and lecturers with knowledge about AI tools will enable them to guide students appropriately and integrate AI-assisted approaches into research supervision

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Learner Roles: Student Co-Creation and Participatory Dynamics in AI-Driven Business Education Ecosystems
papers.authors: Alfred-Jaja Stella Wellignton-Igonibo Wellignton-Igonibo
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has redefined pedagogical practices and necessitated a critical reconceptualization of learner roles in higher education. This paper titled reconceptualizing learner roles in student co-creation and participatory dynamics in AI-driven business education ecosystems examines how AI technologies are transforming learning from teacher-centred instruction to learner-driven engagement. The study begins examine major concepts such as AI-driven business education, learner roles in contemporary education, student co-creation in AI-enabled business education and students’ participatory dynamics in AIenabled learning environments. The study integrates these components into an AI-Based Integrative Process that combines adaptive pedagogy, intelligent tutoring, and automated assessment to enhance engagement and improve academic outcomes. Finally, the conclusion stress the need for redefined learner agency and institutional adaptability, while it was recommended to advocate for policy-driven adoption of AI tools, faculty retraining, co-design learning platforms, and equitable access to AI resources.

papers.title: Exploring the Integration of Emerging Technologies in Promoting Inclusive Learning Environments in Accounting Education in Nigerian Schools
papers.authors: Hannah Ore-Ofe Williams
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: This study investigated the integration of emerging technologies in promoting inclusive learning environments within Accounting Education in Nigerian secondary schools. A descriptive survey research design was employed, involving a sample of 462 accounting teachers selected from inclusive secondary schools across Bayelsa State using stratified and simple random sampling techniques. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Emerging Technologies and Inclusive Education Questionnaire (ETIEQ), validated by experts and tested for reliability using Cronbach’s Alpha (0.70). Data were analyzed using mean, standard deviation, Pearson Product Moment Correlation (PPMC), independent t-test, and Chi-square (χ²). Findings revealed that accounting teachers demonstrated moderate utilization (Mean = 3.01) of emerging technologies, primarily limited to multimedia and online collaborative tools, while the use of advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Virtual Reality (VR) remained low. Teachers exhibited a high level of awareness and moderate competence (Mean = 3.70), but faced major challenges including inadequate infrastructure, insufficient training, and poor internet connectivity (Grand Mean = 4.16). The study concluded that effective integration of emerging technologies in inclusive accounting education depends on teachers’ digital literacy, institutional support, and infrastructural development. It recommended continuous professional development, improved resource provision, and curriculum reform to enhance inclusive and technology-driven accounting instruction.

papers.title: Transforming Entrepreneurial Education through Artificial Intelligence in Nigerian Tertiary Institutions
papers.authors: Najeem Olawale Adelakun
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: The teaching of entrepreneurship in the tertiary institutions in Nigeria is still trapped in the traditional mode of teaching, low level of digitalization and innovation culture. With the world economy shifting to automation and knowledge-driven business, artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is an effective solution to re-brand the process of teaching entrepreneurial skillsets. The paper is a critical assessment of AI-based educational models and their applicability to the Nigerian case. AI offers a good chance to update the entrepreneurship training. Institutions can equip students with the latest information on a fast-evolving job market by altering the ancient paradigms with AI-powered problems. The paper will examine the available AI models, and how they will be applied in higher education in Nigeria. Based on a hybrid conceptual framework that integrates Technology Acceptance Model and Experiential Learning Theory. the paper examines the potential of artificial intelligence applications like generative language models, adaptive learning systems, virtual incubators, recommender algorithms, and machine learning based assessments to boost creativity, innovation, employability, and business readiness among students. The discussion concurs with the National Policy on Education of Nigeria and recent projects such as the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and digital projects supported by TETFund. These policy frameworks depict the national interest in incorporating AI in the learning environments. Based on the comparative lessons of international best practice, the paper outlines the key institutional barriers, including infrastructural gaps, data privacy issues, and resistance to change, and outlines scaled opportunities of digital transformation in entrepreneurship education. The research concludes that educational models that are enabled by artificial intelligence together with proper strategizing have the potential to be used as a catalyst in developing a robust and innovation oriented entrepreneurial ecosystem in tertiary institutions in Nigeria

papers.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) On the Performance and Efficiency of Retail Business Operations in Enugu Metropolis, Enugu State
papers.authors: Ukamaka Roseline Azubuogu
papers.journal: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
papers.abstract: This project seeks to investigate the growing influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the performance and efficiency of retail business operations in Enugu Metropolis, Enugu State, Nigeria. In today’s fast evolving digital economy, AI technologies are becoming essential tools in driving innovations, automating routine tasks, improving decision-making and enhancing customer satisfaction across various sectors including retail. However, in many developing regions, including Enugu, the level of AI adoption and its direct impact on business performance remain under-researched. The proposed study will utilize a mixed methods research design. Quantitative data will be gathered using structured questionnaires distributed to business owners, managers and selected employees within Enugu Metropolis. Qualitative data will be obtained through semi-structured interviews to gain deeper insights into the experiences, perception and challenges faced by retailers in adopting AI tools. Data analysis will involve descriptive statistics, correlation analysis and multiple regression techniques using software such as SPSS or STATA. The anticipated outcome of the research is to provide data-driven recommendations for retail businesses seeking to improve operational performance through AI, and to inform policy makers and technology stakeholders on how to support digital transformation in the local retail sector

papers.title: EVOLUTION OF THE EDUCATIONAL PARADIGM: DIASPORA AND KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER UNDER THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
papers.authors: Alina Ardeleanu, Viorel Buța
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: The analysis addresses the structural reconfiguration of educational systems, highlighting the strategic dimension of diaspora within the process of curricular reform. Under the impact of artificial intelligence, the scientific community abroad constitutes a fundamental vector in the dynamics of knowledge transfer and advanced digital competencies toward the domestic environment. The mechanisms through which external expertise facilitates the integration of best practices and innovative methodologies are evaluated, optimizing the convergence between the foundations of classical pedagogy and contemporary technological imperatives. From this perspective of global interconnectivity, the text formulates strategic benchmarks to transform the phenomenon of brain drain into a bidirectional circuit of shared intelligence, capable of substantiating future national educational policies.

papers.title: D-MNR: Dynamic Malevolent Node Recognition in VehicularCommunications — A Machine Learning Approach
papers.authors: Sarada Yaddanapudi, M. Roopa
papers.abstract: For Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs) to be secure and private, it is essential to identify hostile activity. The problem of detecting black hole attacks, which seriously jeopardize the Dynamic Source Routing (DSR) protocol, is discussed in this study. While effective for static data, traditional machine learning-based approaches find it difficult to adjust to the constant stream of real-time data in VANETs. We use incremental classifiers, which can analyze data dynamically for prompt attack detection, to get around this issue. In particular, we assess how well Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) and K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) identify black hole attacks. In order to capture important characteristics that define black hole behaviour, the data used for attack detection is simulated under controlled conditions. Key performance parameters, such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and training/testing timeframes, are used to evaluate the classifiers. Despite requiring longer training and testing durations, the results reveal that ARF performs better than KNN across all criteria, indicating greater detection capabilities for black hole attacks. The results emphasize the usefulness of ARF for enhancing security in dynamic network environments and demonstrate the potential of incremental online learning techniques for continuous and real-time threat detection in VANETs. This study suggests a scalable approach for real-time cyber security in automotive networks and provides fresh insights into improving threat detection techniques.

papers.title: Psychological Perspectives on the Transition to Learner-Centred Environments: Analysing the Impact of Artificial Intelligence and Personalised Learning on Student Engagement
papers.authors: Sreeja P.G., Mekhala Venkatesh
papers.journal: International Journal of All Research Education & Scientific Methods

papers.title: Students’ Experiences of an Artificial Intelligence-Supported Virtual Learning Environment in Science Lessons: A Case Study
papers.authors: Kazim Atag, Harun Çelik
papers.journal: Journal of Education in Science Environment and Health
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine students’ learning experiences and their awareness of AI literacy during the instruction of the Energy Transformations and Environmental Science unit in the eighth-grade Science course through an AI-supported virtual learning environment. This study employed a qualitative embedded single-case study design. The study group consisted of 20 students (12 girls and 8 boys) selected through criterion sampling. Data were collected using an open-ended questionnaire following a 16-class-hour instructional implementation and analyzed through content analysis. The findings revealed that the AI-supported virtual learning environment facilitated students’ understanding of abstract concepts through instant feedback and interactive learning materials while also enhancing their motivation toward the Science course. Furthermore, the students developed a critical awareness of AI by recognizing not only its benefits but also its limitations, including the potential to generate hallucinated responses and conceptual errors. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-supported virtual learning environments are not only effective instructional support tools but also valuable learning environments that contribute to the development of students’ AI literacy.

papers.title: AI-Powered Verbal Intelligence Games: Academics’ Views on Open-Ended and Verifiable Inquiry, Problem-Solving, and Scientific Reasoning Skills
papers.authors: Bekir Yıldırım
papers.journal: Journal of Education in Science Environment and Health
papers.abstract: Today, artificial intelligence is making its impact felt in education, as in all other fields. The use of artificial intelligence in education is becoming an increasing priority. The purpose of this study was to examine academics' views on the implications of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported verbal intelligence games for open and confirmatory inquiry, problem-solving, and scientific reasoning skills in education. The study group consisted of 13 academics. Convenience sampling was employed to select the participants. A phenomenological research design, one of the qualitative research methods, was adopted in this study. Qualitative data were collected through a semi-structured interview form. The collected qualitative data were analyzed using the inductive content analysis method. The findings revealed that the participants held positive views regarding AI-supported verbal intelligence games. Furthermore, the participants stated that AI-supported verbal intelligence games had positive implications for open and confirmatory inquiry, problem-solving, scientific reasoning, and reasoning skills in education. Based on these findings, recommendations were made for educators and policymakers.

papers.title: Pedagogical Applications of Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Disciplines: A Systematic Review for Higher Education
papers.authors: Zhenhong Huang, Ying‐heng Fei, Gang Song
papers.journal: Journal of Education in Science Environment and Health
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with teaching activities has become a hotspot in education, offering transformative potential for improving learning outcomes. This review aims to examine the pedagogical integration of AI within environmental disciplines for higher education, analyzing its practical scenarios, merits and drawbacks. Literature was retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus, with 10 qualified studies selected covering environmental science and engineering disciplines. Building upon this synthesis, supplemented with analogous cases from related disciplines (e.g., basic chemistry and engineering courses) that are also transferable to environmental education, the expanded discussion identified typical AI applications covering virtual assistants, adaptive learning, virtual experiments and intelligent evaluation. Though limited by insufficient empirical data and publication bias, findings suggest that AI holds transformative potential for environmental education, especially in enhancing personalized learning experiences, boosting teaching efficiency, increasing student engagement, and enabling data-driven instructional decision-making. However, limitations such as insufficient data quality, ethical and academic integrity concerns, uneven technical accessibility, and lack of long-term empirical validation were also consistently reported. More rigorous, longitudinal, and discipline-specific research is required to validate the observed benefits. Corresponding suggestions are put forward to better balance generic technological advancement and deep integration with discipline-specific teaching practice.

papers.title: Domain-Specific Cyberchondria and AI-Assisted Health Information Seeking among Pre-Clinical Medical Students in South India: A Two-Wave Longitudinal Study
papers.authors: Jaideep Rao M, Sridhar D, Kiranmai B.
papers.abstract: Background: Generative AI is widely used for health information seeking, but its longitudinal relationship with specific cyberchondria domains has not been examined. The objective was to examine domain-specific associations between AI-assisted health information seeking and cyberchondria among medical students, and to assess within-person change after AI adoption or discontinuation. Methods: Prospective two-wave study of 100 pre-clinical MBBS students at a single South Indian government medical college (January-April 2026; 100% retention). The Cyberchondria Severity Scale (CSS-15) was administered at both waves. Students were classified by AI-use status across waves into persistent non-users, new adopters, discontinued users and persistent users. Cohen’s d effect sizes, paired t-tests and Spearman rank correlations were applied. Results: AI use was reported by 81% at Wave 1 and 83% at Wave 2. AI users scored higher than non-users on Excessiveness (d=0.96), Distress (d=0.55) and Reassurance (d=0.53); Compulsion and Mistrust differed minimally. In a small, underpowered subgroup of new adopters (n=12), Distress increased significantly (Δ=+0.39, d=0.69, p=0.036); this within-person result is exploratory. Search frequency correlated with Excessiveness (ρ=0.47), Reassurance (ρ=0.57), Compulsion (ρ=0.35) and Distress (ρ=0.32). Pre-consultation symptom searching had a large effect on Excessiveness (d=1.04). Conclusion: AI users showed higher Excessiveness, Distress and Reassurance; only Distress rose significantly, and only within a small new-adopter subgroup, where it should be read as exploratory. Search frequency was the most consistent and most modifiable correlate.

papers.title: Driving Sustainable Engagement: The Role of AI-Driven HRM and Ethical AI in Digital Transformation
papers.journal: International Journal of Business and Technology Management
papers.abstract: While digital transformation (DT) is widely recognized to enhance agility, resilience, and competitiveness and as a strategic resource, its translation into employee social sustainability and employee engagement remains underexamined. To address this gap, the current study seeks to investigate two primary objectives by integrating the RBV and DCT. Firstly, how AI-driven HRM practices (AIHRMP) as dynamic capabilities mediate DT’s impact on employee engagement (EE) and employee social sustainability (ESS); secondly, how ethical AI implementation (EAI) affects these relationships. The study adapted a structured questionnaire to gather responses from 308 professionals working on DT initiatives from the top ten Banks of Pakistan. PLS-SEM is used to test the proposed moderated mediation model to evaluate the measurement and structural models. Results suggested that DT significantly drives AI adoption and enhances both EE and ESS. AIHRMP partially mediates DT’s effects on EE and SS, with a stronger indirect influence on SS. EAI moderates these relationships negatively, suggesting that stricter ethical constraints can temper DT’s immediate benefits. Findings further reveal that DT’s full impact emerges when AIHRMP is effectively integrated, while EAI acts as a boundary condition shaping the extent of organizational outcomes in engagement and social sustainability. The three original contributions of this work are as follows: firstly, the integration of RBV (static resources) and DCT (adaptive capabilities) fills the gap in the previous literature in the field of HRM digitalization, where resources and capabilities are considered as separate entities. This two-lens approach demonstrates the way AI-HRM practices can be turned into a sustainable engagement of employees through DT resources. Second, it changes priorities towards sustainable people practices in digital transformation instead of technological efficiency. Lastly, it offers recommendations on how to design ethical AI systems and governance models to align the digital strategies with the long-term social welfare of employees.

papers.title: Vision-Based Tracking Turret using ESP32-CAM and YOLO
papers.authors: KARTHIK BALAJI
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Autonomous pan-tilt tracking platforms are widely used in surveillance, robotic guidance and human-robot interaction. Commercial Pan-Tilt-Zoom (PTZ) trackers run video decoding, tracking and motor control on one resource-limited processor, which causes control-loop delays of 200–500 ms and limits them to rudimentary detectors such as frame differencing. Running a deep neural network on a microcontroller is not practical either, since it takes hundreds of milliseconds per frame. To overcome this, we propose a vision-based tracking turret with a decoupled architecture. An ESP32-CAM streams live MJPEG video over Wi-Fi to a host PC. The PC runs a You Only Look Once (YOLO) detector through OpenCV, computes the centroid of the detected target and converts the pixel error into pan and tilt servo angles. These angles are sent as short serial commands to an ESP32 board, which drives two SG90 servos and a laser indicator. The prototype costs about INR 1,940. It achieves person-detection confidence of 0.85–0.98 at 0.5–2 m and an end-to-end latency of about 80–150 ms using only a CPU.

papers.title: ERA of Students: A Class-Wise Virtual Electronics and Microcontroller Learning Platform with an AI Tutor for Classes 8–10
papers.authors: Prof. Divya Meshram, Vaijavi Choudhari, Vrushali bobade, Achal Lende, Apurva Doifode
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: The cost of the kit, lack of lab time, supervision and damaged components limit the hands-on approach to electronics teaching in schools. This paper describes ERA of Students, an LMS implemented using a web-browser interface which allows students in classes 8, 9 and 10 to learn sensors, actuators and microcontrollers with the help of virtual experiments. After logging-in with their names and classes, the students get access only to the material pertaining to their classes: 30 different experiments per class (totally 90 experiments), lessons and notes, quizzes and their individual progress history. The students design their circuits by dragging-and-dropping the components on the board and connecting the wire between the component pins and the microcontroller pins. They can select from the five available boards (Arduino UNO, NodeMCU, ESP32, ESP8266 and PIC18F47Q10) with their pin layouts shown and run a threshold-based simulation with live graphs and auto-generated Arduino code. The features include context aware AI tutor accessible from every page, animated video lectures that have their scripts generated using AI technology, four ten question quizzes based on questions specific to the learner and do not repeat until they have been used up, badges for experiment and quiz and finally a certificate upon completion of all the experiments. The software is built in the form of a single page web application which requires neither installation nor any hardware component. This research paper will talk about the design and functionality of this project and discuss its limitations as well.

papers.title: PPN – Pedagogy Pathfinder Network: A Multi-Agent, Retrieval-Augmented AI Framework for Automated Academic Administration Plan Generation
papers.authors: Kirtana Singh, Pradnya Khanse, Pooja Divekar
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Preparing an Academic Administration Plan (AAP) for each course in each semester is a heavy documentation task for engineering faculty working under Outcome-Based Education (OBE), NEP 2020 and National Board of Accreditation (NBA) requirements; faculty-reported estimates exceed 40 hours per course. This paper surveys 17 studies published between 2020 and 2026 that bear on automating such documentation with large language models (LLMs). The studies were drawn from arXiv, IEEE Xplore, the ACL Anthology, the ACM Digital Library and SpringerLink and grouped into four themes: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), LLM-based multi-agent orchestration, AI-assisted Bloom’s taxonomy and CO–PO mapping, and AI-assisted lesson planning, assessment and grading. Each study is compared by technique, dataset or domain, strengths and limitations, and related to the Pedagogy Pathfinder Network (PPN), a three-layer, 17-agent framework proposed by the authors. The comparison shows that the individual components are well studied, that outcome-mapping work has concentrated on classifying text that already exists rather than generating it, and that none of the reviewed studies combines document-grounded generation, agent orchestration and automated compliance checking for Indian accreditation documents. Open gaps concern integration and compliance validation, small single-institution datasets, error propagation and scalability, and the lack of measured review effort. The survey does not experimentally validate PPN, and figures reported for it are treated as unverified estimates. Future directions include shared multi-institution benchmarks and comparison with manually prepared plans.

papers.title: Generative AI in Cloud Computing: Applications, Security Challenges, and Future Research Directions
papers.authors: Ruchita Bharat Konde, Mrs. Asmita Mohan Phatangare
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is increasingly delivered through cloud platforms, where scalable infrastructure, managed model services, and application programming interfaces (APIs) lower the barrier to adoption. This integration also changes the security and privacy risk profile of cloud systems. This paper presents a preliminary, literature-based review that aims to identify major applications, characterize security and privacy risks, compare reported mitigation approaches, and highlight unresolved research questions. Peer-reviewed papers, conference papers, preprints, and authoritative guidance were collected through web-based searches and compared by objectives, methods, findings, and limitations. The reviewed evidence shows concrete uses in cloud incident analysis and code assistance, together with recurring risks involving prompt injection, sensitive-data disclosure, retrieval-data leakage, and excessive permissions granted to AI agents. Reported mitigations, such as provenance marking, execution isolation, and least-privilege design, are promising but are generally evaluated against limited attack sets, and none is presented as a complete solution. The review identifies gaps in cloud-specific security evaluation, agent authorization, and joint analysis of security, performance, and cost.

papers.title: Constitutional Resilience in the Age of Synthetic Politics: A Comparative Study of AI-Driven Electoral Governance
papers.authors: Lakshdeep Singh
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how political campaigns communicate, how voters consume information, and how electoral institutions manage allegations of manipulation. Generative AI can now produce incredibly convincing audio, images, and video; automated tools can instantly translate and tailor campaign messages; and recommendation algorithms can dictate which political claims reach massive audiences. While these advancements can boost participation—particularly for those who benefit from accessible formats or local-language content—they also lower the barrier for fabricating evidence, impersonating candidates, hiding the true sponsors of political messaging, and spreading disinformation faster than it can be corrected. This paper explores the constitutional and legal consequences of AI-driven electoral communication by comparing India’s parliamentary system with the United States’ presidential system. It examines the tension between voter autonomy, freedom of speech, privacy, electoral fairness, and the independence of election administrators. The Indian legal landscape is analyzed through the lens of the Constitution, the Representation of the People Act of 1951, the regulatory powers of the Election Commission of India, and judicial precedents regarding digital speech. The U.S. offers a contrasting model, defined by the First Amendment, federal election laws, a decentralized administrative structure, and diverse state-level regulations. Additionally, the European Union’s frameworks on political advertising transparency and AI provide a useful comparative benchmark. The paper contends that "constitutional resilience" should not be defined as a government's authority to decide which political opinions are valid. Instead, it should represent the capacity of democratic institutions to safeguard meaningful voter choice while maintaining a space for open debate. Achieving this requires a balanced approach: mandating the disclosure of synthetic campaign content, increasing transparency in paid advertising, preventing invasive micro-targeting, creating rapid yet reviewable complaint processes, preserving digital evidence, and establishing remedies for deceptive impersonation. Ultimately, the analysis suggests that India and the United States should prioritize transparency and procedural accountability over broad, sweeping powers to remove content. The core democratic goal must be to protect a voter's ability to evaluate political claims without granting the state the unchecked power to act as the final arbiter of truth.

papers.title: campus bot - ai college enquiry assistant
papers.authors: Amouse nijanthan j, sham s
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: CampusBot is an intelligent, full-stack educational technology solution engineered to bridge the communication and information latency gaps prevalent in higher education admissions and campus operations. Traditional college helpdesks suffer from severe query backlogs, restricted operational hours, and high manual staff overhead during admission cycles. CampusBot addresses these bottlenecks by deploying a lightweight, high-performance conversational AI engine built upon a hybrid NLP architecture combining tokenized Jaccard similarity, weighted multi-intent keyword categorization, and pluggable Large Language Model (Google Gemini / OpenAI) hooks. The system provides an end-to-end web portal featuring interactive academic course catalogs, 4-stage admissions tracking roadmaps, interactive placement analytics powered by Chart.js, accessibility-compliant voice interaction via the Web Speech API (STT/TTS), and a secure administrative dashboard for real-time lead monitoring, FAQ CRUD lifecycle, and conversation telemetry. Empirical testing demonstrates a 96.4% intent recognition accuracy with sub-15ms local response latencies, proving CampusBot to be an efficient, scalable, and resilient assistant for modern institutions.

papers.title: Determinants of Customer Adoption of Generative AI-Enabled Banking Services in India: An Empirical Study
papers.authors: GRANDHI JAYALAKSHMI, Meda Srinivasa Rao
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: While GenAI is transforming the customer interface in banking, there is limited empirical evidence that offers insights into why customers in India may or may not embrace GenAI. This study explores the effects of perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), security and privacy (SP) and perceived risk (PR) on customers' intentions to use GenAI capabilities in Indian banking, examines trust in GenAI as a mediator between the two, and examines differences in intention across groups of respondents. A structured online questionnaire (five-point Likert scale) was used to gather data, which was subsequently analysed in MS Excel using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, chi-square tests of independence, one-way ANOVA and regression-based mediation (Sobel test) and moderation (interaction terms) models. Together, the four perceived characteristics accounted for 34.2% of the variance in adoption intention (F(4, 126) = 16.35, p < .001); and, when examined individually, only perceived usefulness was found to be a statistically significant predictor (B = 0.226, p = .017). All four characteristics were robust predictors of trust in GenAI (R² = .739) but failed to mediate the influence of the four on the adoption intention (all Sobel p > .42). There were four significant moderation effects (interaction p < .05) for digital literacy. In the chi-square tests, intention was not significantly different across gender or prior use or frequency of use of the AI features, and in the ANOVA, intention was significantly different across usage frequencies (F(4, 126) = 4.68, p = .001), and was linked to age group. The study provides a preliminary evidence basis for banks and policymakers in India around the adoption of GenAI by customers.

papers.title: Human Values and Ethical Education in the Digital Age: Challenges, Opportunities and a Human-Centered Approach
papers.authors: Dr.Kavita Arora
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: The rapid development of digital technologies, social media platforms, and artificial intelligence has significantly transformed the educational environment. While these technologies provide opportunities for flexible learning, wider access to information, and innovative teaching practices, they also raise important concerns regarding ethical responsibility, human values, privacy, academic integrity, empathy, and social relationships. Education in the digital age must therefore extend beyond the acquisition of technological skills to include the development of responsible, thoughtful, and socially conscious individuals. This paper examines the role of human values and ethical education in contemporary digital learning environments through a qualitative secondary-data-based conceptual analysis. The study draws upon academic literature, educational philosophy, international policy documents, and publications concerning digital citizenship and artificial intelligence in education. The analysis focuses on five dimensions: ethical digital behaviour, critical thinking, privacy and academic integrity, empathy and social responsibility, and inclusive human-centered learning. The paper identifies a need to integrate ethical reflection into digital literacy programmes rather than treating ethics as a separate or optional educational component. It proposes a Human Values and Ethical Digital Education Framework that connects digital competence with moral reasoning, responsible participation, respect for diversity, and human well-being. The study concludes that technology can contribute meaningfully to education when it supports human development instead of replacing independent judgement, meaningful relationships, and ethical decision-making. The proposed framework offers implications for curriculum design, teacher preparation, institutional policy, and future research in higher education.

papers.title: AI-Resume Analyzer and Job Matcher
papers.authors: Sudiksha Somanth Jadhav, Asmita Mohan Phatangare
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: The AI Resume Analyzer and Job Matching System is an intelligent solution designed to streamline recruitment by using artificial intelligence and natural language processing (NLP) to extract, interpret, and evaluate information from resumes and job descriptions, enabling more accurate and efficient candidate–job matching. Such an instrument extracts vital skills, including education, experience, technical, and other qualifications, and compares them with targeted vacancies, examining the degree of match between the applicants’ credentials and the job requirements. t then scores and ranks the best positions that are suitable for the applicants based on their competencies and skill set. Thus, the tool is valuable for enhancing the screening process because it reduces the amount of work when manually reviewing resumes. As a result, it can save time for the recruiters by analyzing hundreds of documents and narrowing the options for the best candidates for the vacancies. analyzing hundreds of documents and narrowing the options for the best candidates for the vacancies. The applicants benefit from the tool in identifying the best opportunities and skills to improve their qualifications further. In general, the proposed solution is ideal for recruitment processes that intend to adopt a smart and organized manner in screening and providing recommendations for both the recruiters and the applicants. The system can be used to screen multiple resumes against a job description to identify the best candidates or the best opportunities for an applicant based on the experience and qualifications required

papers.title: IMPACT OF AI-DRIVEN DECISION-MAKING ON STRATEGIC PERFORMANCE IN THE IT SECTOR: THE ROLE OF ORGANIZATIONAL READINESS AND HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION
papers.authors: YERRA MANI SHANKAR, Dr. D. Praveena Devi
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organizational decision-making within the IT sector, yet empirical evidence linking AI-driven decision-making to strategic performance remains limited, particularly regarding the roles of organizational readiness and human–AI collaboration. This study examines AI-driven decision-making and its relationship with strategic performance among respondents with academic, internship, or professional exposure to the IT sector in India. Primary data were collected using an online questionnaire developed on a 5-point Likert scale. 158 responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, chi-square tests, one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlation, and linear regression. AI-driven decision-making (M = 3.80), strategic performance (M = 3.99), organizational readiness (M = 4.07), and human–AI collaboration (M = 4.03) were all rated high. Chi-square tests revealed significant associations between AI familiarity, IT exposure, and gender with perceived importance of AI-driven decision-making. ANOVA showed significant differences in all constructs by IT sector exposure and AI familiarity. AI-driven decision-making was a strong positive predictor of strategic performance (R² = 0.401, β = 0.514, p < .001). In the combined model, organizational readiness and human–AI collaboration jointly explained 32.1% of the variance in AI-driven decision-making effectiveness, though organizational readiness was the only statistically significant individual predictor (β = 0.77, p = 0.003), reflecting high collinearity between the two factors (r = 0.921). These results should be interpreted with caution, as the sample is predominantly composed of undergraduate students with limited direct IT work experience, and approximately 24.7% of respondents gave identical ratings across all statements.

papers.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Operational Efficiency in the Insurance Industry
papers.authors: Bommisetty Gnana Deep, Dr. Podile Venkateswararao
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has become a buzzword across industries, and insurance is no exception, with applications in customer service, claims processing, underwriting and fraud detection. However, many existing studies focus on individual applications. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and perceived operational efficiency in the insurance industry, considering AI chat bots, claims automation, AI underwriting, fraud detection and AI-based customer service. Operational efficiency is measured through processing speed, accuracy and response time, among other dimensions. The research design was quantitative and cross-sectional, and data were gathered with a structured questionnaire on a five-point Likert scale. Convenience sampling was used to reach college students and insurance policyholders; 400 questionnaires were distributed and 78 completed responses were returned. Microsoft Excel was used for descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson correlation, chi-square tests, one-way ANOVA and linear regression. The findings show a strong positive relationship between AI adoption and operational efficiency, with AI adoption accounting for 64.6% of the variance in operational efficiency; the null hypothesis was therefore rejected. Among the individual applications, fraud detection was the strongest predictor once it and AI-based customer service were added to the model, which increased explanatory power. Familiarity with AI and age were associated with perceptions of operational efficiency, whereas gender and prior insurance use were not. The main barriers to adoption were data privacy and security, lack of AI skills, and cost. Overall, the study provides empirical evidence from Indian respondents on the relationship between AI adoption and perceived operational efficiency. The results should be interpreted with caution given the small, non-probability sample, the predominance of young undergraduate respondents, and the use of perception-based measures from a single questionnaire.

papers.title: RETHINKING CONSTITUTIONALISM IN THE DIGITAL AGE Digital Rights, Technology and Global Internet Governance
papers.authors: Aditya Tripathi
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence, algorithmic decision-making, biometric surveillance, social-media platforms and digital infrastructure has altered the location and exercise of constitutional power. Classical constitutionalism was principally designed to restrain the State through the rule of law, separation of powers, fundamental rights and judicial review. In the digital environment, however, power is increasingly exercised through data systems, algorithms and private platforms as well as traditional public institutions. This paper examines whether classical constitutionalism can adequately respond to these developments or whether a complementary framework of digital constitutionalism is required. It studies privacy, freedom of expression, equality, Internet shutdowns, AI surveillance, platform power and global Internet governance, with particular reference to India. Contemporary examples include the 2026 Jantar Mantar student protests and reported use of AI-assisted facial recognition and targeted Internet restrictions, the 2024 Manipur student protests and Internet suspension, and the 2026 Jharkhand student movement concerning alleged recruitment-examination irregularities. Comparative reference is made to the European Union and United States. The paper argues that digital constitutionalism should not displace classical constitutionalism; rather, it should extend constitutional principles of legality, proportionality, transparency, accountability, equality, privacy, due process and human oversight to digital spaces and technologically mediated public and private power.1

papers.title: Java-Based System for Personalized Study Tracking and Performance Prediction
papers.authors: Nikhil kailas Gambhir
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Students often find it difficult to maintain consistent study habits and evaluate their learning progress over time. Manual study records do not provide sufficient information about subject-wise effort, study consistency, or possible future performance. This research proposes a Java-Based System for Personalized Study Tracking and Performance Prediction that records and analyzes students’ daily study activities. The proposed system is developed using Java and Java Swing, with CSV-based storage for maintaining study records. It collects information such as study date, subject, study duration, and study description, and uses this data to generate date-wise and subject-wise summaries. The system further analyzes historical study behavior, including study duration, active study days, subject-wise effort, and consistency, to generate a performance estimate. A weighted scoring approach is used to provide personalized performance guidance based on the student's previous study patterns. The proposed system provides a lightweight and low-cost solution for students to monitor their learning activities without requiring a complex database environment. Experimental evaluation on 38 study-log records covering 35 active study days showed a total study duration of 148 hours across five subjects, with an estimated performance score of 86.80 out of 100 (High level). The results indicate that structured study tracking and historical analysis can help students identify their study patterns and areas requiring additional attention. The proposed framework can be further enhanced using machine learning algorithms, larger datasets, graphical dashboards, and web or mobile interfaces.

papers.title: Eduvision Ai: An offline, syllabus-driven system for generating narrated animated video lessons In computer science
papers.authors: Dr. Nandish M, Sanjana R, T G Chinmay, Thulasi B K, Ullas P
papers.journal: INTERANTIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH IN ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT
papers.abstract: Revising a Computer Science topic such as Quick Sort or Binary Search is difficult with the resources students normally have: a textbook is accurate but static, generic videos online rarely match a specific syllabus, and text-based AI chatbots cannot produce a visual explanation at all.This paper presents Proposed Eduvision AI model, a system that converts the name of a Computer Science topic into a narrated, animated teaching video, generated entirely on a single laptop with no paid API, no user account and no internet connection required after installation.The system accepts a topic name, verifies that it belongs to a fixed syllabus of 286 Computer Science topics, generates a fresh numerical example for the run, uses a locally hosted large language model to draft a lesson script, subjects that script to six automated correctness checks, re-creates the algorithm's execution in code to drive the animation, converts the narration to speech, aligns every spoken word to an exact timestamp, renders the diagrams as code-generated images rather than AI-generated images, and finally assembles a subtitled MP4 video.The central design decision of the model is that no step which requires factual precision -arithmetic, counting, or text rendering inside a diagram -is delegated to a generative AI model; such steps are performed by verifiable Python code instead, while the AI model is used only for the parts of the task that are genuinely creative, namely prose.The resulting pipeline is fully reproducible, produces a different worked example on every run, and has been validated using 808 automated tests.

papers.title: Professional Identity of Graphic Designers in the Age of Generative AI: Threats, Adaptation, and a Conceptual Typology
papers.authors: Bahaa Mustafa, A Hasan Ibrahim
papers.journal: American Journal of Arts and Human Science
papers.abstract: Generative AI tools such as Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, and DALL-E are changing how graphic designers work and putting pressure on how they see themselves professionally. Prior research has looked at GenAI’s technical capabilities, its effects on creative industries broadly, copyright questions, and design pedagogy, usually one at a time; few studies connect these threads to ask what GenAI means for graphic designers’ professional identity specifically, and that is the gap this review addresses. The review draws on 33 peer reviewed sources published between 2021 and 2026, from design studies, human computer interaction, organizational psychology, and legal scholarship, located through keyword searches of Consensus, Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, and the ACM Digital Library. Sources were grouped around three areas, authorship and creative ownership, skill acquisition, and career prospects, and read against functional identity theory, professional role identity research, and work on human AI collaboration. Out of this comes a typology of three ways designers respond to GenAI: Resisters, Adapters, and Integrators, running from human centered to AI centered practice. GenAI unsettles familiar ideas about authorship, expertise, and creative ownership, and speeds up changes already underway in design workflows. Early career designers appear to face a higher risk of skill loss than experienced ones, who tend to treat GenAI as a complement to their existing competencies rather than a replacement for them. The typology extends functional identity and professional role identity theory into the creative professions, giving other researchers something concrete to test. It should also help in practice: design educators can use it to build GenAI literacy and skill retention into curricula, and designers and professional associations can use it to think through positioning, ethical concerns, and copyright as generative AI becomes part of everyday practice.

papers.title: AI Literacy Is Not Enough: Faculty Strategies for Teaching Students to Evaluate AI-Supported Information
papers.authors: Monica Sava
papers.journal: Journal of Educational Practice and Technology
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has moved quickly into higher education, and faculty are now making instructional decisions in real time. Many early conversations have focused on course policies, academic integrity, and acceptable use. Those conversations matter, but they do not fully address the teaching challenge faculty face. Students may know how to use AI tools to brainstorm, summarize, draft, organize, or study, but they may not know how to judge the quality of the information those tools produce. This article argues that faculty need practical, teachable strategies for helping students evaluate AI-supported information before they rely on it in academic work. The focus is on helping students question claims, verify sources, examine evidence, recognize uncertainty, and notice weak or misleading data-based conclusions. Rather than treating AI only as a compliance issue, faculty can use this moment to strengthen critical thinking, information literacy, evidence evaluation, statistical reasoning, and responsible academic judgment. The article offers practical strategies that can be adapted across disciplines, course levels, and instructional formats.

papers.title: econdary Teachers' Perceptions of Utilizing AI-Facilitated Small Groups
papers.authors: Daisy Cabler
papers.journal: Journal of Educational Practice and Technology
papers.abstract: This mixed methods study focused on the perceptions of secondary math and English teachers of the use of artificial intelligence to facilitate differentiated small groups in the post-pandemic learning environment. The researcher collected the teachers’ reflections, conducted interviews, and examined Likert-scale data to form a comprehensive view of their perceptions of the pedagogical practice after delivering a professional development (PD) workshop on how to use AI tools to effectively deliver small group learning in a variety of secondary contexts. After collecting the data and analyzing it, the researcher found that the secondary teachers had overall positive perceptions of AI’s ability to aid in the differentiation of learning. However, when comparing both qualitative and quantitative data, the researcher found that teachers require ongoing coaching in areas like prompting and output refinement in order to feel completely confident in their abilities. In all, the results of the study suggest a need for further training and that the professional should always remain the cornerstone in classroom decision making.

papers.title: An Educational Model Based on Digital Projects Enhanced by Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Impact on Developing Creative Thinking and Reading Comprehension Skills among Preparatory and Secondary School Students in Upper Galilee
papers.authors: Akbal Badawi, Yasera Hijazi
papers.abstract: سعت دراستنا الحالية إلى تحليل نموذج تعليمي يقوم على المشاريع الرقمية المدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي (GenAI)، وبيان صلته بالتفكير الإبداعي وبقية كفايات التعلم المعاصرة لدى طلبة الصفوف من السابع حتى الثاني عشر في منطقة الجليل الأعلى. اعتمدت الدراسة تصميم بحثي كمي وصفي-ارتباطي ومقطعي (عرضي). وتكوّنت عينة الدراسة من 300 طالب تتراوح أعمارهم بين 13 و18 عاماً، وقد استكملوا استبانة مقننة تقيس استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي، والمشاريع الرقمية، والتعاون والعمل الجماعي، والتفكير الإبداعي، والدافعية، والتواصل الرقمي، وحل المشكلات واتخاذ القرار، والتعلم الذاتي والاستقلالية، والرضا عن النموذج التعليمي. جرى تحليل البيانات من خلال الإحصاءات الوصفية، ومعامل «ألفا كرونباخ»، واختبار (Mann–Whitney U)، واختبار (Kruskal–Wallis)، ومعامل ارتباط الرتب لسبيرمان، والتحليل العاملي الاستكشافي. أظهرت النتائج مستويات وسيطة مرتفعة عبر الأبعاد التي تم فحصها. كما تبين وجود فروق ذات دلالة إحصائية في درجات التفكير الإبداعي تبعاً للجنس، والخبرة السابقة في مجال الذكاء الاصطناعي، والمستوى الدراسي، والعمر، ونوع المدرسة، والكفاءة الرقمية؛ في حين لم تُسجَّل فروق ذات دلالة تبعاً لامتلاك جهاز شخصي، أو توفر الإنترنت في المنزل، أو مدة استخدام التكنولوجيا يومياً. وقد ارتبطت الخبرة السابقة في مجال الذكاء الاصطناعي بمستويات أعلى من التفكير الإبداعي. كذلك، ظهرت علاقات ارتباطية إيجابية ودالة بين التفكير الإبداعي وكل من: استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي، والمشاريع الرقمية، والتعاون والعمل الجماعي، والدافعية، والتواصل الرقمي وحل المشكلات واتخاذ القرار، والتعلم الذاتي، والرضا. وأوضح التحليل العاملي الاستكشافي أن البيانات ملائمة للتحليل العاملي، مع الحاجة إلى مزيد من الفحص من أجل التحقق من البنية العاملية. لذا، تشير النتائج إلى وجود ترابط بين التعلم الرقمي المعزز بالذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي والتفكير الإبداعي وكفايات التعلم الأخرى.

papers.title: Разработка системы мониторинга безопасности информационных систем с применением анализа данных
papers.authors: А.М. Кумратова, Е.И. Счетчикова
papers.journal: Вестник Адыгейского государственного университета серия «Естественно-математические и технические науки»
papers.abstract: Разработана и экспериментально проверена облегченная система мониторинга безопасности, предназначенная для образовательных и малых корпоративных информационных систем, где применение дорогостоящих и сложных SIEM-платформ нецелесообразно. Предложена компактная модульная архитектура системы, включающая этапы сбора и предобработки логов, анализа данных и визуализации результатов. Для выявления аномалий использованы алгоритмы машинного обучения. Работоспособность системы протестирована на синтетическом наборе данных, имитирующем логи реальной информационной системы (время события, идентификатор пользователя,тип события, IP-адрес, статус операции). В ходе эксперимента система продемонстрировала высокую эффективность, корректно идентифицировав все заранее заложенные в данные аномалии (точность 100 %).Наибольшую угрозу представляли события с нетипичными IP-адресами. Разработанный подход позволяет автоматизировать мониторинг безопасности, обеспечивая обнаружение подозрительных событий и генерацию отчетов. Система является практичной альтернативой для организаций с ограниченными ресурсами и может быть использована в учебных целях. A lightweight security monitoring system has been developed and experimentally tested for educational and small corporate information systems, where the use of expensive and complex SIEM platforms is not feasible. A compact modular system architecture has been proposed, which includes the stages of log collection and preprocessing, data analysis, and result visualization. Machine learning algorithms have been used to detect anomalies. The system's performance has been tested on a synthetic dataset that simulates the logs of a real information system (event time, user ID, event type,IP address, and operation status). During the experiment, the system demonstrated high efficiency, correctly identifying all anomalies that were predefined in the data (100 % accuracy). The events with atypical IP addresses posed the greatest threat. The developed approach allows for the automation of security monitoring, enabling the detection of suspicious events and the generation of reports. The system is a practical alternative for organizations with limited resources and can be used for educational purposes.

papers.title: Disciplined Integration: AI and the Legal Profession’s Existing Duties
papers.authors: Pouya Lajevardi
papers.abstract: Abstract This article argues that the legal profession’s existing duties of competence, supervision, candour, confidentiality, and procedural fairness provide the necessary framework for integrating generative AI into legal practice, without requiring a wholly new regulatory paradigm. Narrowing its focus to transformer-based large language models, the article examines the ‘fake law’ phenomenon, where models generate plausible but non-existent authorities, and traces its implications for miscarriages of justice, particularly where adversarial safeguards are thinnest: self-represented litigants, resource-constrained parties, and off-record settlements. It then considers AI in adjudication, arguing that transparency, contestability, and human-authored reasons remain non-negotiable for judicial legitimacy. The central recommendation is disciplined augmentation, not automation: AI should operate within the profession’s existing load-bearing beams through auditable workflows, clear disclosure norms, and continuous education. Used with discipline, AI can strengthen practice; used without it, it risks eroding the trust and outcomes the profession exists to protect.

papers.title: Designing Homework for the AI Era
papers.authors: Excellent Educator
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines how generative AI is changing the role of homework and the distinction between using AI as support and using it as a substitute for learning. It proposes assignments that emphasise reasoning, metacognition, evaluation, personal interpretation, and reflection rather than simply producing answers.

papers.title: Global AI Adoption: From Experimentation to Real-World Impact
papers.authors: Marianna Olefyrenko
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines the global adoption of artificial intelligence as it moves from experimentation toward practical, measurable impact across businesses, governments, industries, and workforces. It explores the current state of AI adoption, regional differences, key market drivers, infrastructure requirements, governance challenges, and the human capability needed to turn AI tools into trusted value. The article discusses how AI adoption is expanding across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Australia, and emerging markets, with attention to investment trends, enterprise use cases, responsible AI frameworks, workforce transformation, and the growing importance of AI literacy. Australia is integrated into the global context as an example of applied AI adoption, particularly in sectors such as professional services, mining, software, finance, and small business enablement. A central argument of the article is that the next phase of AI adoption will not be determined only by model performance, infrastructure investment, or technological capability. It will depend on whether organizations can build the skills, governance, trust, data foundations, and practical workflows required to use AI responsibly and effectively. The article also highlights the role of AI trainers, educators, and workforce facilitators in supporting responsible AI adoption. It positions AI training as an important bridge between technological potential and real-world implementation, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, professionals, and non-technical users. This publication is intended for business leaders, policymakers, educators, AI trainers, entrepreneurs, researchers, and professionals interested in understanding how AI adoption is evolving globally and what is required to translate experimentation into sustainable value.

papers.title: The Accessibility of Compositional Thinking: Artificial Intelligence and Special Educational Needs
papers.authors: Francesco Scagliola
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This publication presents an author-edited transcript of a conference presentation examining the relationship between artificial intelligence, cognitive accessibility, and inclusive music education. The contribution explores how artificial intelligence, multimodal interfaces, and computational approaches to musical composition may support the accessibility of compositional thinking, particularly in educational contexts involving students with specific learning disorders (SLD) and special educational needs (SEN). Particular attention is given to cognitive mediation, the representation and manipulation of musical structures, and the role of explicit rules in designing accessible learning environments. The original presentation was delivered during the Fourth Conference on “Specific Learning Disorders and Disabilities: Inclusion in the Higher Education System for the Arts, Music and Dance (AFAM)”, held at the Conservatorio di Musica “Niccolò Piccinni”, Bari, Italy, on 15–17 October 2026. This document is an edited and revised transcript of an oral presentation, not a peer-reviewed research article or a paper published in conference proceedings. The publication contains the English translation followed by the original Italian version.

papers.title: The Silent Heart in Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis
papers.authors: Brahim ABDELOUAEB
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: English translation of the French original published in Cardioimmunology Review, issue 1 (October 2026). This critical reading examines cardiac involvement in ANCA-associated vasculitis through the 2026 French national diagnostic and care protocol, observational studies and treatment trials. It distinguishes prognostic associations, the limits of screening evidence, and questions that remain untested in cardiac outcomes. The deposit contains the full English article, including the French abstract, references, educational questions, disclosure of interests and declaration of artificial intelligence use. This is an independent critical review, not a clinical guideline or an original clinical trial. Author and editor: Brahim Abdelouaeb, MD. ORCID : 0009-0002-7690-9993. English online edition: https://cardioimmunologyreview.org/revue/n1-the-silent-heart.htmlFrench original, retained as the reference text: https://cardioimmunologyreview.org/revue/n1-le-coeur-silencieux.html The archived reprint retains the author name as it appeared in the original issue (Brahim S. Abdelouaeb); the current bibliographic author name is Brahim Abdelouaeb, linked to the same ORCID. Editorial resources: Brahim Abdelouaeb — author profile · Cardioimmunology Review.

papers.title: A Study on the Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in School Education
papers.authors: Rashmi Shukla
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Mobile phones have become an important part of students’ daily lives and educational experiences. With the rapid development of digital technology, mobile phones are increasingly being used as tools for accessing educational resources, attending online classes, communicating with teachers, participating in academic activities, and developing independent learning skills. The present study focuses on examining the impact of mobile phones on students’ learning, considering both their educational benefits and potential challenges. Mobile phones provide students with convenient access to e-books, digital libraries, educational videos, online assessments, and learning applications. These resources can support conceptual understanding, encourage self-directed learning, and facilitate communication and collaboration beyond the traditional classroom. However, excessive or inappropriate mobile phone use may also contribute to distraction, reduced concentration, poor time management, and interruptions in academic activities. The educational impact of mobile phones may vary according to students’ usage patterns, learning objectives, digital literacy, and the guidance provided by teachers and parents. The study aims to understand how mobile phone usage relates to students’ learning experiences, study habits, classroom engagement, and academic performance. It also highlights the importance of responsible digital practices and the effective integration of mobile technology into educational settings. A systematic investigation of these factors can help teachers, parents, and educational institutions develop appropriate strategies for promoting productive mobile phone use. The study emphasizes that mobile phones should be considered neither entirely beneficial nor entirely harmful; rather, their educational value depends largely on how, why, and under what conditions they are used. The findings of such an investigation may contribute to a better understanding of technology-supported learning and encourage a balanced approach to mobile phone use in education.

papers.title: AI as CEO: Why AI's Next Productivity Gains Depend on Managing Work, Not Doing It
papers.authors: Meinhaj Hussain
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: AI is now cheap for companies. Ramp's AI Index, which tracks card and bill-pay spending at more than 70,000 US businesses, shows the median adopter spends $11.95 per employee a month on AI, while the top 1% spend more than $7,400 (Ramp, 2025). Against an average fullyloaded employee cost of about $8,500 a month, AI pays for itself if it makes a worker 0.15% more productive—about three extra productive minutes a week (Palihapitiya, 2025). The production evidence is strong: in a field experiment at Procter & Gamble with 776 professionals, individuals using AI matched the performance of two-person teams without it (Dell'Acqua et al., 2025). MIT economists explain why some deployments pay far better than others. In their theory of AI chaining, a human checks only the final output of a chain of AI steps, so the cost of checking stays fixed however long the chain gets (Demirer et al., 2024). The same paper points to the central problem. Firms design jobs by weighing the gains from specialization against the coordination costs that come with splitting work more finely (Becker & Murphy, 1992; Coase, 1937). Coordination—meetings, alignment and sign-offs—is where most of the corporate week goes. AI can return the three minutes, but it cannot decide how they are used. If they disappear into another meeting, the return is zero. This article argues that the next stage of AI productivity will come from AI taking over management and coordination, not just production. The article applies chaining logic to the organization itself. Every approval, handoff and status meeting is a human checkpoint that breaks the chain. An AI operating layer could run allocation, routing and approvals from start to finish, making all those hours of meetings largely redundant. Humans would check outcomes rather than steps and give consent periodically. The company starts to work like an operating system; taken further, the AI becomes the company itself. This can happen at any scale, and small firms may gain the most, as coordinating capacity that once required layers of managers would cost the price of software. Ramp's spending gap hints at the divide ahead: the leaders are not buying different tools; they are reorganizing around them. The transformation runs into law at two points. First, corporate law: Delaware requires every board member to be a natural person under DGCL §141(b), though scholars have shown that an algorithm can gain legal personhood by controlling an LLC (Bayern, 2016; LoPucki, 2018), and Wyoming briefly allowed algorithmically managed DAO LLCs (Wyoming Legislature, 2021). Second, professional licensing hard-codes human checkpoints into the firm. Sarbanes-Oxley requires the CEO and CFO to personally certify every quarterly and annual report (Sarbanes-Oxley Act, 2002), audits rest on individual CPA licenses, FINRA requires a firm's chief compliance officer to be a registered person who has passed qualification exams (FINRA, 2025), tax representation is limited to CPAs, attorneys and enrolled agents, and legal advice requires bar admission. Even Utah's regulatory sandbox has approved no lawyer-free models (Utah Office of Legal Services Innovation, 2026). Each rule is a mandatory human checkpoint that breaks the AI chain. This article asks where productivity disappears between employee and P&L, what a firm run by AI would look like, and which laws would need to change.

papers.title: METHODOLOGY AND PRINCIPLES FOR THE APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ADAPTIVE ECONOMIC MODELS OF HIGHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: O'lmasxo'jayev Zoirxo'ja Abbos o'g'li
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The study develops a methodology and principles for applying artificial intelligence (AI) in the adaptive economic models of higher education institutions. It conducts a normative comparative analysis of the OECD AI Principles, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI and Uzbekistan's AI strategy, adapts the CRISP-DM process model to higher education economics, and classifies model families. Seven principles and their practical requirements are substantiated, and a six-stage methodological cycle and a model-selection map are proposed.

papers.title: Adopting Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Building Supply Chain Resilience in Uncertain and Disrupted Global Environments
papers.authors: Amedu Peter JACOB
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study investigates how agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be leveraged to enhance supply chain resilience in increasingly uncertain and disruption-prone global environments. Motivated by recent systemic shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical conflicts, and climate-induced disruptions, the study argues that traditional efficiency-driven supply chain models are insufficient for contemporary volatility. Drawing on Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, the research conceptualises agentic AI as an autonomous, goal-directed system capable of sensing disruptions, making independent decisions, and executing real-time corrective actions across supply chain operations. A mixed-methods sequential explanatory design was employed, combining qualitative interviews, a structured survey analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM), and thematic analysis. Quantitative results reveal that agentic AI adoption significantly improves supply chain responsiveness and adaptability, while organisational readiness strengthens these effects. Qualitative findings further highlight key adoption conditions, including leadership commitment, skills gaps, trust in autonomous systems, and the critical role of digital infrastructure, particularly in emerging economies such as Nigeria. The study finds that agentic AI functions not merely as a technological tool but as a strategic capability that enhances dynamic sensing, seizing, and transformation processes within supply chains. However, its effectiveness is contingent upon robust socio-technical alignment and enabling infrastructure. The study concludes that resilient supply chains are built not only through technological advancement but through deliberate organisational preparation, making agentic AI most effective when embedded within well-prepared, adaptive organisations

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Social Sciences and Humanities: Opportunities, Challenges, Ethical Issues, and Future Perspectives
papers.authors: Hemlata Rathod
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the intellectual, educational, cultural, and institutional environment in which knowledge is produced and communicated. Its development has moved beyond conventional automation toward systems capable of processing large collections of text and data, recognizing patterns, generating language, supporting translation, and assisting decision-making. These capabilities create new possibilities for social sciences and humanities, disciplines that frequently work with complex information about people, societies, languages, cultures, institutions, and historical records. At the same time, the adoption of AI raises questions about privacy, bias, academic integrity, intellectual property, unequal access, transparency, and the continuing role of human judgement. The significance of AI becomes greater when its applications are considered in relation to sustainable development. AI-supported systems may contribute to education, inclusion, public services, cultural preservation, research efficiency, and evidence-informed decision-making. In education, for example, AI can support adaptive learning, feedback, language assistance, learning analytics, and teacher professional development. However, these benefits cannot be separated from questions of equity and responsible governance. UNESCO has emphasized that AI in education and research should follow a human-centred approach, with attention to data protection, ethical validation, inclusion, and meaningful educational use (Miao & Holmes, 2023). UNESCO's broader Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence also places human dignity, human rights, fairness, transparency, diversity, privacy, and human oversight at the centre of AI governance (UNESCO, 2021). This conceptual paper reviews relevant literature and policy documents to examine the emerging role of AI in social sciences and humanities. It discusses disciplinary applications, research opportunities, educational implications, ethical challenges, the Indian context, and future directions. The paper argues that the value of AI in these fields should not be judged only by computational efficiency. Its long-term contribution will depend on whether institutions can combine technological capability with critical thinking, disciplinary expertise, ethical responsibility, digital inclusion, and meaningful human oversight.
keywords: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

papers.title: True You: A Behavioral Congruence Framework for Human, Artificial, and Human–AI Alignment
papers.authors: Daniel Hedberg
papers.abstract: True You: A Behavioral Congruence Framework for Human, Artificial, and Human–AI Alignment proposes a framework for measuring whether an intelligent agent’s observed behavior corresponds to its declared or required behavioral profile over time. The framework is developed in three stages. For humans, True You is voluntary and is intended to support self-knowledge, behavioral self-assessment, interpersonal alignment, and evidence relevant to trust while recognizing substantial privacy and surveillance concerns. For sufficiently capable artificial intelligence systems, the paper proposes that True You should become compulsory: AI systems should maintain explicit behavioral alignment specifications, continuously self-report compliance, undergo independent evaluation, assess other AI systems, and track alignment drift over time. For humans substantially augmented with AI, the paper proposes a compulsory composite alignment framework that evaluates the behavior of the combined human–AI agent, including emergent behavior, attribution of actions, preservation of human autonomy, and prevention of “alignment laundering” across the human–AI boundary. Version 1.1 expands the human True You model by introducing the concept of behavioral concept-boundary profiles.
