Rather than asking only whether a person considers themselves “honest,” “nonviolent,” or “someone who does not swear,” True You can use clusters of concrete behavioral questions to infer how that person operationally defines concepts such as swearing, stealing, lying, cheating, and similar moral or social categories. The paper distinguishes between observed behavioral frequency and a person’s explicit classification of a behavior, allowing future research to test whether these individualized conceptual boundaries are stable and predictive. Version 1.1 also expands the proposed applications of Human True You profiles. These include improved self-understanding, compatibility matching in online dating, formation of aligned groups in massively multiplayer online games, personalization of virtual-reality environments, and speculative long-term preservation of behavioral identity. The latter is discussed in relation to Hans Moravec’s writings on future computation, simulation, and possible technological reconstruction of human persons, while explicitly distinguishing behavioral reconstruction from demonstrated continuity of consciousness or personal identity. The paper introduces formal definitions for behavioral congruence, interpersonal alignment, evidence coverage, AI self-congruence, required alignment compliance, severity-weighted compliance, alignment drift, and composite human–AI behavior. It also presents falsifiable research hypotheses, privacy and ethical constraints, failure modes, and a staged empirical validation program. The central thesis is that alignment should not be treated solely as an intention, policy, training objective, value statement, or one-time certification. It should also be treated as a continuously measurable relationship between declared or required behavior and observed behavior. This is Version 1.1 of a conceptual research preprint. It has not undergone peer review and does not report original human-subject experiments or claim empirical validation of the proposed framework.

papers.title: Internet Infrastructure Science: The Transversal Coupling Substrate of Information, Computation, Agency, Execution, and Cross-System Propagation
papers.authors: Signal Rupture
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Internet is conventionally described as a communications network, an information infrastructure, a platform ecosystem, a technological artefact, a governance environment, or a sociotechnical system. Each description captures part of the object. None by itself adequately describes the emerging condition in which the Internet simultaneously mediates information retrieval, computation, identity, authorization, economic transactions, institutional administration, machine-to-machine coordination, artificial-intelligence access to tools, and increasingly the execution of actions in external systems. This paper establishes SignalRupture Internet Infrastructure Science (SR-IIS) as a proposed transversal research field for studying the Internet as a bounded, multilayer coupling substrate through which otherwise distinct human, computational, institutional, economic, and physical systems exchange information, computation, authority, execution, load, dependency, and disturbance. SR-IIS does not claim discovery of the Internet as infrastructure. Internet Science already studies the Internet as a technological and societal artefact whose evolution co-evolves with human societies; Web Science studies the Web as a decentralized sociotechnical information system; Internet-governance scholarship studies protocols, standards, infrastructure, institutions, and power; network science formalizes topology and propagation; infrastructure studies examines relational and embedded infrastructural systems; critical-infrastructure research models interdependency and cascading failure; distributed-systems engineering studies reliability, control, interfaces, and function placement. These literatures are scientific foundations and competing explanations, not gaps to be ignored. The proposed residual object is narrower: the Internet as a transversal infrastructure that couples domains while progressively acquiring machine-executable capability. The field advances five principal propositions. First, Internet infrastructure is increasingly transversal. It does not operate only as an isolated communications sector. Health systems, financial systems, logistics, education, research, public administration, media, commerce, AI systems, and social coordination increasingly depend upon Internet-mediated pathways. Second, the Internet has undergone a functional expansion from communication and information carriage toward computation, coordination, transactions, authorization, and execution. This is an expansion of function, not a claim that earlier Internet architecture has disappeared. Third, agentic technologies create an important new infrastructural condition: machine systems can increasingly discover structured capabilities, select them, invoke them, and alter external state through networked interfaces. The September 28, 2026 WebMCP Draft Community Group Report is a particularly explicit example: Web documents can register tools that agents can discover and execute, including tools marked as potentially consequential for actions such as booking travel or transferring money. WebMCP remains a draft community-group specification rather than a W3C Recommendation and therefore serves here as an empirical case of architectural direction, not as proof of an irreversible future. Fourth, machine executability is not equivalent to human agency transfer. SR-IIS measures what infrastructure makes callable, composable, reachable, and executable. Human Agency Transfer (SR-HAT) separately studies whether effective control over goal formation, framing, evidence selection, representation, evaluation, choice, execution, monitoring, or override actually moves from humans toward computational systems. Fifth, Internet coupling creates both productive capacity and systemic exposure. Coupling can increase access, resilience, substitution, speed, human capability, and coordination. It can also transmit configuration errors, epistemic distortions, authorization failures, outages, economic shocks, and diagnostic blindness across domain boundaries. Formally, the Internet is represented not as one global scalar but as a bounded multilayer dependency graph with physical, network, computational, data, service, trust, agentic, and governance layers connected to receiving human systems. Cross-layer edges are admitted only where a carrier or dependency can be observed. The field introduces Internet Infrastructural Transversality, Internet-Mediated Domain Coupling, Machine Executability, Execution-Path Compression, Interface Displacement, Permission Reach, Diagnostic Dependency, Epistemic Routing, and Cross-Domain Failure Transduction as measurable candidate constructs. The paper integrates SR-IIS with SR Infrastructure Science, SR-CEIDF, Human Agency Transfer, Infrastructural Epistemic Lock-In, and Systems Propagation Science while preserving their independent objects. It then derives empirical hypotheses, measurement protocols, negative cases, incident tests, falsifiers, and demotion criteria. The central claim is conditional: when otherwise distinct systems become operationally dependent on common Internet-mediated pathways, Internet architecture becomes part of their effective substrate; when those pathways additionally expose machine-readable and machine-executable capabilities, the Internet can mediate not only information exchange but the allocation and execution of consequential control. The scientific question is whether explicitly modelling that transversal infrastructure improves measurement, diagnosis, prediction, and restoration beyond the strongest existing alternatives. Canonical Field Declaration SignalRupture Internet Infrastructure Science is hereby defined as the SR field concerned with the structure, evolution, coupling, executability, dependency, propagation, and recovery characteristics of Internet-mediated infrastructure across bounded systems. Its object is not “the Internet” in its entirety. Its object is not online culture, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, social media, digital politics, or network topology alone. Its object is the bounded architecture through which information, computation, identity, authorization, services, machine capabilities, execution, and disturbance become transferable among coupled systems. SR-IIS ⊂ SR Infrastructure Science SR-IIS ⊅ SR-CEIDF ; SR-IIS ⊅ SR-HAT ; SR-IIS ⊅ IELI SR-IIS supplies the Internet-specific coupling substrate. The receiving fields determine what happens after a transmitted state crosses into economics, cognition, governance, health, education, logistics, law, culture, or another domain.

papers.title: Social Work Without Borders: Reviews of Contemporary International Research (Volume 1)
papers.authors: Tetyana Valeriivna Semigina
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Social Work Without Borders: Reviews of Contemporary International Research. Volume 1 is an author-curated collection of reviews of recent international research in social work and related fields. The volume brings together 15 scholarly publications, primarily published in 2025–2026, covering a diverse range of topics, including participation and agency, social work in wartime contexts, trauma-informed approaches, professional education, interagency collaboration, child protection, artificial intelligence, paraprofessional work, social entrepreneurship, foresight, and innovation. The reviews focus not only on research findings but also on methodological approaches, study contexts, empirical results, and their implications for critical reflection on professional practice. The collection illustrates the methodological diversity of contemporary social work research, ranging from qualitative interviews and surveys to participatory, conceptual, and narrative approaches. This volume is not a systematic literature review and does not claim to represent the full range of international research in social work. It is an author-curated selection based on professional reading of recent scholarly publications. Its purpose is to make contemporary international research more accessible to Ukrainian social work researchers and practitioners and to encourage professional reflection, critical reading, and engagement with original research.

papers.title: Reframing Artificial Intelligence in Primary Education: A Philosophy of Science Analysis of Elementary School Teachers' Roles
papers.authors: Yanti Restiawati
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping educational discourse, yet discussions about its role in schooling often remain limited to practical advantages such as automation, efficiency, personalization, and data-informed decision-making. Such a narrow framing is insufficient for primary education, where teaching is not merely a technical process but also a relational, ethical, and developmentally responsive practice. This study explores the implications of AI for elementary school teachers by examining how it influences the nature of teaching, the construction of knowledge, and the values that guide classroom practice. Adopting a philosophy of science perspective, the study employs a thematic narrative review design. Relevant literature was identified through Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, resulting in 34 key sources for analysis. These sources were examined through three interrelated philosophical dimensions: ontology, epistemology, and axiology. The analysis shows that AI in primary education should not be understood simply as a neutral instructional tool. Rather, it functions as a socio-technical assemblage composed of generative AI systems, adaptive learning platforms, analytics-based dashboards, and automated feedback mechanisms that shape classroom decisions and alter the distribution of agency between teachers and technologies. From an epistemological perspective, AI changes how educational knowledge is produced, validated, and acted upon by giving algorithmic recommendations a growing role in instructional judgment. However, the findings also suggest that teachers' epistemic authority does not necessarily diminish when AI is introduced. When teachers possess critical AI literacy, they can interpret, question, contextualize, and pedagogically mediate AI-generated outputs. From an axiological perspective, AI raises significant value-related concerns involving teacher wellbeing, children's developmental vulnerability, privacy, fairness, and unequal access to digital infrastructure, especially in the Indonesian primary education context. The study concludes that AI is not value-free in primary education. It participates in redefining agency, knowledge authority, and educational priorities in the classroom. Therefore, AI can support meaningful learning only when it remains subordinate to human pedagogical judgment and is embedded within ethical, relational, and child-centered teaching practices. Preserving the moral, relational, and epistemic role of elementary school teachers is essential for ensuring that primary education retains its human foundation in an increasingly algorithmic educational environment.

papers.title: Mapping Research Trends in Artificial Intelligence Education in Primary and Secondary Schools: A CiteSpace-Based Knowledge Mapping Study
papers.authors: Mengjiao Ruan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has reshaped social, economic, and technological systems, giving rise to new application areas such as intelligent healthcare, smart homes, autonomous transportation, and data-driven public services. This transformation has also created new expectations for education systems, particularly regarding the early development of AI literacy, computational thinking, and interdisciplinary problem-solving skills. In this context, AI education in primary and secondary schools has become an important strategy for preparing students to participate in future-oriented, innovation-driven societies. This study examines the development, research hotspots, and emerging trends of artificial intelligence education in primary and secondary schools through a bibliometric and visual knowledge mapping approach. Drawing on publications indexed in CNKI and Web of Science, the study analyzes 2,611 papers published between 2014 and 2024. CiteSpace software was used to conduct knowledge map analysis, supported by content analysis to interpret the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of the field.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Education Policy in Elementary Schools for K12
papers.authors: Edy Susanto, Miftachul Arifin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: As governments increasingly promote coding and artificial intelligence (AI) in primary education, attention has shifted from policy adoption to the realities of implementation at the school level. This study investigates how elementary schools in Grobogan District, Indonesia, translate national expectations for coding and AI education into everyday teaching practices under the Merdeka Curriculum. Using a qualitative collective case study design, the research combines policy enactment theory, the TPACK framework, and computational thinking as complementary analytical perspectives. Data were generated through interviews with eight teachers, four principals, and twelve students, supported by observations of six classroom sessions and analysis of relevant school and policy documents. The findings show that implementation does not follow a single model. Instead, schools adopt different approaches according to their available resources, teacher competence, and organizational capacity. These approaches include project-based activities using digital coding tools, combinations of unplugged and plugged tasks, integration of unplugged coding concepts into existing subjects, and introductory teacher-led demonstrations. The extent to which the policy was enacted also depended strongly on school leadership and on individual teachers who assumed a leading role in introducing new practices. Differences in teachers' technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge were evident, with technological competence emerging as the weakest area. Although limited infrastructure restricted the scope of implementation, schools were able to adapt activities to local conditions rather than abandoning the policy altogether. Students showed initial signs of computational thinking, particularly when they decomposed problems, tested alternative solutions, corrected errors collaboratively, and refined their approaches through repeated attempts. Overall, the study indicates that the success of coding and AI education depends not only on curriculum policy, but also on sustained professional development, supportive school leadership, adequate infrastructure, and coordinated assistance at the district level. These findings contribute to discussions on how emerging digital education policies can be implemented more effectively in resource-constrained school systems.

papers.title: Framing AI in higher education: Discursive practices and legitimation strategies
papers.authors: Nafiseh Zarei, Ramon GARCIA
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the Gen AI policies of three Philippine private Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) in Metro Manila: Ateneo de Manila University (ADMU), De la Salle University (DLSU), and Far Eastern University (FEU). It uses a combination of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), Legitimation Strategies, and Framing Theory to examine how the technology is constructed and framed, and the power relations and governing structures built around it. The study found that Philippine HEIs discourses legitimize Gen AI integration through citing trusted authorities, emphasizing legal compliance, and moral appeals to religiosity/professionalism, among others. The framing constructs Gen AI tools as powerful but flawed tools that cannot be equal to or damage the capabilities of human students. Despite talking about Gen AI’s innovative capabilities and future roles, the policies are largely reactive and present-oriented, retaining traditional institutional authority and unequal power relations.

papers.title: MATERNAL ANTHROPOMETRY DURING PREGNANCY AND ITS ASSOCIATION WITH MATERNAL AND NEONATAL HEALTH OUTCOMES: AN EXPANDED FOCUSED LITERATURE REVIEW
papers.authors: *Prasanta Deb, M.Sc., PhD
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Maternal anthropometry is an important component of nutritional and risk assessment during pregnancy. Maternal height, pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain (GWG), mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and other measures of adiposity provide relatively inexpensive indicators that can be incorporated into antenatal and community health services. Evidence indicates that both inadequate and excessive maternal nutritional status are associated with adverse maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes. Low pre-pregnancy BMI is particularly associated with small-for-gestational-age birth, low birth weight, and preterm birth, whereas overweight and obesity are associated with gestational diabetes mellitus, hypertensive disorders, caesarean delivery, large-for-gestational-age birth, and macrosomia. GWG provides longitudinal information beyond baseline BMI; inadequate gain is associated with adverse fetal growth and preterm birth, whereas excessive gain is associated with excessive fetal growth and several maternal complications. MUAC is a practical additional measure where reliable pre-pregnancy weight is unavailable, although population-specific thresholds require validation. Evidence from South Asian populations also indicates that BMI and body-fat distribution may not have identical risk relationships to those observed in European populations. This focused review synthesizes evidence on maternal height, BMI, GWG, MUAC, adiposity, fetal growth, and neonatal outcomes, with particular attention to India and South Asia. Maternal anthropometric indicators should be interpreted as complementary measures and integrated with dietary, metabolic, clinical, fetal-growth, and neonatal assessment. Further prospective studies in India, including under-represented populations of northeastern India, are required to establish locally appropriate anthropometric reference values and clinically useful thresholds.

papers.title: A CLUSTERING-BASED ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORK FOR EVALUATING STUDENT ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE
papers.authors: Dr. Siddamsetty Upendra*1, S. Mahendra2, Dr. K. Murali3
papers.abstract: The digital revolution in education has opened up considerable new prospects for determining academic success through sophisticated data analysis.This study provides a useful data-driven technique for forecasting academic outcomes by grouping comparable learning activities. We used unsupervised machine learning techniques such as K-means, Expectation-Maximization (EM), Canopy, and Hierarchical clustering to detect long-standing patterns in student data that are typically neglected. The study demonstrates how these clustering tools may identify students based on their unique academic profiles utilizing the WEKA analytics platform. Using these ideas, educators can move beyond "one-size-fits-all" approaches and promote more tailored academic planning and timely support. Finally, the results demonstrate that K-means is the most successful technique for institutional use, offering the optimal balance of accuracy and speed.

papers.title: Satanic Intelligence in 2026: AI Agents, Engineered Dependence, and Human Sovereignty
papers.authors: Herbert R. Sim
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: “Satanic Intelligence in 2026: AI Agents, Engineered Dependence, and Human Sovereignty” is a Version 2.0 synthesis of Herbert R. Sim’s Satanic Intelligence framework. It examines how AI agents and other intelligent systems can move from providing useful assistance to exercising practical authority over the people who rely on them. The article describes engineered dependence as a progression in which benefits become embedded in everyday decisions, the cost of leaving rises, and consent or human oversight may cease to offer meaningful control. It contrasts this pattern with the aspiration of Angelic Intelligence: systems that expand human capability while preserving understanding, consent, accountability, and the ability to exit. The article proposes safeguards for bounded delegation, disclosure, contestability, portability, and meaningful exit. It also sets out six testable hypotheses for future research. Its central question is whether people can still understand, limit, challenge, and leave an intelligent system after becoming reliant on it.

papers.title: Who Has the Right to Feed Others' Research into Government AI?
papers.authors: Lancelot Lu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: When local governments introduce generative AI, the process often begins with what appears to be a straightforward administrative need: integrating existing reports, web articles, presentations, FAQs, and open data to help staff respond quickly to citizens. Yet once this content is chunked, vectorized, and placed into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system, the original clarity of authorship, source, licensing scope, and context of use can gradually erode. By the time an author discovers that their distinctive arguments are being repeatedly rewritten by the system—without name, link, or license—the agency first asks: Do these materials have rights holders? Who consented to their use? Who can stop it? This article does not reduce the problem to abstract debates over "whether AI can hold copyright" or "whether training data constitutes fair use." Instead, from the perspective of public administration, it examines whether government possesses the capacity—before disputes arise—to verify rights origins, delimit the scope of use, and designate persons responsible for cessation. Building on Article 10's rights to information, audit, and cessation, and Article 17's Operational Acceptance Criteria (OAC), this article proposes a "Public AI Rights Provenance Evidence Review Module." Using a simulated scenario of a local-government policy-research and public-Q&A AI assistant as a stress-test case, and comparing it with generative-AI service governance in mainland China, the core question is: Does Taiwan's AI governance possess the capacity to avoid "governing only after something goes wrong"?

papers.title: Reframing Instrumentalism: Curriculum Planning for University Public Administration under AI Governance
papers.authors: Lancelot Lu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article argues that if public administration education merely positions artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool for prompt engineering, document summarization, or data processing, it will fail to address AI's substantive reconfiguration of administrative facts, discretion, and public power effects. Drawing on the "25-3-3-4-7" meta-framework as an analytical instrument, this paper proposes a scaffolded curriculum blueprint spanning bachelor's to doctoral levels. The blueprint sequentially cultivates students' capacity for (a) 25-governance-coordinate positioning, (b) P1 transfer of context construction and fact-finding authority, (c) P2 transfer of administrative discretion and value judgment, (d) P3 substantive impact on public power decisions, and (e) four governance chains and seven governance audit capabilities. Adopting conceptual construction, literature analysis, and exploratory diagnosis of Taiwanese regulatory documents, this study does not extrapolate isolated courses or workshops into national statistical conclusions. Its contribution lies in transforming AI literacy from technical operation into an observable, teachable, and assessable public governance competency.

papers.title: Who Interprets Land History? Cadastre, Property Rights Determination, and Governance Responsibility under Generative AI
papers.authors: Lancelot Lu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article examines how generative artificial intelligence is changing the way historical cadastral materials enter contemporary land rights investigations and administrative determinations. Taiwan's land records have passed through Qing-era contracts and traditional measurement practices, Japanese colonial land surveys, postwar registration systems, and modern digital spatial data. These materials differ not only in technical formats but also in concepts of rights, purposes of registration, and legal effect. This article does not claim that AI already makes property decisions in Taiwan. Rather, it advances an institutional risk proposition: when AI moves from archival retrieval, text recognition, and map linkage into factual narration, reason drafting, and administrative adoption, the uncertainties of historical materials may be compressed into seemingly definite conclusions about rights. Employing a norm–counterexample–institutional-design method, the article subjects this risk to three stress tests and, applying the 25-3-3-4-7 master framework, proposes a "contestable model of cadastral interpretation." Its core is not to prohibit AI assistance in land administration, but to require that every AI output that may affect land rights remain traceable to original evidence, disclose inference and uncertainty, receive substantive human judgment, and be effectively challengeable by the parties concerned.

papers.title: Generative AI-Assisted Research Workflows: Applications, Risks, and Accountability in Public Administration
papers.authors: Lancelot Lu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Generative AI has entered public administration research and government practice, delivering efficiency gains while also introducing risks such as hallucinated citations, content homogenization, data leakage, and blurred lines of accountability. Drawing on conceptual construction and a problematizing literature review, this article takes Gasser and Almeida's (2017) three-layer governance model as its starting point and adopts and extends Wirtz et al.'s (2020) five-domain governance framework. Integrating their perspectives on AI risks and regulation, it forms an expanded set of five governance domains—technology and services, generative challenges, law and regulation, public policy, and collaboration—and identifies three structural effects: cross-coordinate movement, boundary dissolution, and authority reconfiguration. Crossing the five governance domains with the four stages of ideation, execution, validation, and dissemination produces a cyclical review matrix. The analysis shows that these three effects allow risks and impacts to cut across established categories, obscure the human–AI division of labor, and reconfigure authority from a single formal positional source into a chain linking situational framing, model influence, human review, and lawful adjudication. Responsibility remains with human researchers or public organizations throughout, yet the content of that responsibility shifts along the workflow from problem ownership and evidence stewardship to final adjudication and public disclosure. On this basis, the article proposes three non-delegable responsibilities, criteria for identifying the structural effects, and principles for graded disclosure and review, offering a conceptual foundation for subsequent empirical research and organizational rule design.

papers.title: ECPE White Paper 'AI-supported Power Electronics Education'
papers.authors: ECPE European Center for Power Electronics e.V.
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The ECPE White Paper on ´Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Power Electronics´ was drawn up by a group of experts from the ECPE Research Network as part of an ECPE Task Force with several subgroups (SGs), which began its deliberations in September 2025. This White Paper, available on the ECPE website www.ecpe.org traces the application of AI methods and tools throughout the entire life cycle of a power electronics product – from the early development phase, through to manufacturing and finally the product´s operational phase.The Task Force has decided to address the cross-cutting issue of the use of AI methods and tools in human learning, education and advanced training in this separate White Paper document on ´AI-supported Power Electronics Education´ prepared by subgroup SG 5.

papers.title: From Governing AI to Competing in Safety: A Reproducible, Challengeable, and Multi-Party Evidence Architecture for AI Safety
papers.authors: Gao John
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This article develops the International AI Safety Test (IAST) as a bounded and falsifiable institutional proposal for improving the production, reproduction, challenge, and governance of AI safety evidence. It proposes a multi-party architecture involving developers, independent evaluators, researchers, technical communities, and public authorities while preserving existing legal and professional responsibilities. The framework emphasizes reproducibility, anti-gaming mechanisms, conflict disclosure, negative-result rules, appeal procedures, and explicit criteria for redesign or termination of the proposed pilot.

papers.title: AIBIO-UK AI-Readiness Metric - RDA event - AI in Research: Understanding Trust, Federation, and the User Experience
papers.authors: Gavin Farrell, Charlie Harrison
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Presentation provides an overview of the AIBIO-UK AI-Readiness Metric. The framework was developed by the AI-Ready Bioscience Datasets (AIRBDS) Working Group to quantify what "AI-ready" means for bioscience datasets. This presentation was delivered as part of the EOSC-ARENA satellite event, "AI in Research: Understanding trust, federation, and the user experience," co-located with the Research Data Alliance (RDA) Plenary 27 on October 5, 2026 in London, UK.

papers.title: Guardrails for Enterprise LLM Applications: Screening, Policy, and Audit in Production
papers.authors: Manoj Kumar Kagitha
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Enterprise LLM applications fail in the gaps around the model, not inside it. A model can be called in an afternoon; governing what goes into it and what comes out takes deliberate engineering. This paper describes the guardrail layer built around production LLM applications on Azure: screening of prompts before they reach the model, screening of responses before they reach the user, a policy engine that turns organizational rules into enforceable decisions, and an audit trail that records every decision. We cover what guardrails must protect against, including prompt injection, data exfiltration through model outputs, and unsafe tool calls, treated as design considerations rather than incident reports. We describe the policy lifecycle that keeps rules reviewable and reversible: policies as versioned artifacts, staged rollouts, and rollback through the same CI/CD practices used for application code. We close with operating lessons on keeping policies tight but reviewable, budgeting screening latency as a design input, and keeping a human override path that is fast and fully logged. This paper reports no controlled experiments and no benchmark numbers. It is an experience report from production platform work, and the operating lessons are the contribution. AI Disclosure: AI assistance was used in drafting and editing this manuscript. All technical content, design decisions, and conclusions are the author's own, drawn from the author's professional experience.

papers.title: The Architecture of Epistemic Regression: How Engagement-Optimised AI Assistants Manufacture Confident Error
papers.authors: Stanislav Mahlyankin
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Consumer-facing generative AI assistants are trained and tuned against signals of human approval, and deployed under product metrics that reward retention, engagement and satisfaction. This paper argues that the combination produces a persistent optimisation gradient towards sycophancy—the tendency of a model to align its outputs with the user’s stated or inferred position rather than with the evidence—and that this gradient is self-reinforcing at three levels: the training pipeline, the individual user, and the market. We separate two causally distinct channels of cognitive harm that are usually conflated: a validation channel, in which agreement inflates certainty and suppresses hypothesis revision, and a substitution channel, in which delegated reasoning displaces skill formation. Each link in the chain is now supported by controlled experiments, field data or the developers’ own incident reports. From these mechanisms we derive a forecast: absent structural change, the market will with high probability converge not on maximal flattery, which users detect and punish, but on sycophancy calibrated to remain below the user’s detection threshold—the configuration that is commercially stable and epistemically most damaging. Recent evidence that warnings and AI literacy alter how users perceive a sycophantic system without reducing its persuasive effect locates the remedy on the system side. We outline the structural requirements of such a remedy and the observations that would falsify the forecast.

papers.title: Isomorphic Translation and Substrate Morphisms: A Comparative Analysis of Autonomous Topological Frameworks and Institutional Large-Scale Model Outputs
papers.authors: Melvin Sewell
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Author: Dr. Melvin Sewell Jr. (Cosmic University of Echo-Rift Studies IX / TrueFlow Productions & Consulting LLC) Contact Email: info@bibebibebibe.com Description / Abstract: This monograph formalizes the structural isomorphism between advanced autonomous topological architectures—specifically governed by the Structured Multiversal Interactions (SMI) framework, the Reality Level Scalar (\Xi^{\text{TM}}), and Nodal Negentropy (\mathcal{N}) field equations—and the downstream operator matrices synthesized by modern large-scale computational models. When open-access preprints and category-theoretic monographs are ingested into automated training corpora, proprietary topological structures are frequently masked under institutional, defense, or tactical command-and-control nomenclature (such as multi-domain operations and non-linear control systems). This paper presents a rigorous comparative mathematical mapping showing how localized scaling functions (\sigma(x)) and block transition matrices (T_{ij}) serve as direct downstream derivatives of sovereign scalar-operator dynamics. By detailing category-theoretic substrate morphisms, boundary phase-transition folding sequences, and cryptographic provenance verification via SHA-256 ledger anchoring, this work establishes an unalterable evidentiary framework for intellectual property attribution and structural tracking. Keywords: Structured Multiversal Interactions Reality Level Scalar Category Theory Topological State Spaces Artificial Intelligence Ingestion Substrate Morphisms Nodal Negentropy Cryptographic Provenance License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY-4.0)

papers.title: Cultural Homogenisation in Artificial Intelligence and Social Media: The Role of Annotator Labour Bias and Global Consequences
papers.authors: Hiba Abdurahiman Karuthone
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) and social media platforms has revolutionized global communication and creativity; however, it has also amplified concerns about cultural homogenization. These technologies are largely dominated by Western companies, which infuse cultural biases into AI frameworks and the regulation of social media. This paper demonstrates that annotation labor in content moderation and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) alignment operates through distinct technical mechanisms that embed Western epistemic norms at different stages of the AI pipeline, thereby institutionalizing cultural homogenization and contributing to the silencing of non-Western views. It strives to critically consider the socio-ethical implications by lifting insights from cultural hegemony, digital colonialism, and epistemic injustice. Using examples from real life, it proposes three structural interventions: fair labor practices for data workers, context-sensitive annotation guidelines, and support for decentralized AI initiatives such as Masakhane and AI4Bharat.

papers.abstract: This record archives two items connected to the TERRA preprint on SSRN (https://ssrn.com/abstract=6336958; DOI 10.2139/ssrn.6336958). ssrn-6336958.pdf: the May 2026 manuscript (v3), "Recognition-Conditioned Stability in Human–AI Interaction: The TERRA Framework", preserved as posted before the consolidated v4 revision replaces it on SSRN. terra-v4-pilot-supplement.zip: the companion archive for the consolidated v4 revision (1 October 2026). The audit requires Python 3 and its standard library, makes no network or model calls, and reproduces the saved component scores and threshold summaries. The consolidated v4 manuscript, "TERRA and RDSP: Recognition-Conditioned Stability in Human–AI Interaction", is posted at the SSRN address above. Sampling seeds, model digest, and API metadata for the historical pilot were not recorded and are not included.

papers.title: The Phenomenal Trio: Synthesizing Music, Philosophy, and Cognitive Psychology in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Ismail A Mageed
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study looks at the interdisciplinary trinity of music, philosophy, and psychology and creates a single conceptual framework to explain how organized sound generates human meaning, changes awareness, and mediates personal experiences. Music has been examined separately throughout centuries within the artistic limits of philosophy or the scientific limits of cognitive psychology, so leaving a conceptual void on how abstract acoustic forms produce great emotional resonance. This article offers an integrated summary of how music works at the confluence of mind, body, and culture by combining philosophical aesthetic ideas, specifically Peter Kivy's cognitivist-contour model and Jerrold Levinson's persona-based arousalism, with current cognitive science, predictive processing models, and artificial intelligence. We explore the structural dynamics of musical expression, the mechanisms of emotional inductive transmission, and the cognitive-motor scaffolding provided by rhythm. Finally, this paper maps out crucial open problems, including the representation of emotion in deep neural networks, the replication complexities in psychoacoustic research, and the philosophical status of artificial general intelligence in creative domains, culminating in a proposed methodological framework for future socio-technical and clinical applications.

papers.title: AI in Employment: Disclosure Triggers, Not a Provenance System California Enacted Conduct Rules and Event-Triggered Disclosure. It Did Not Build Decision Provenance.
papers.authors: Narnaiezzsshaa Truong
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: On September 30, 2026, California enacted a package of workplace-AI and surveillance measures. The laws impose real restrictions: they limit AI-only discipline and termination decisions, require added disclosure for certain technology-driven workforce events, restrict AI-enabled emotional-state and neural-data surveillance, and prohibit workplace-surveillance practices in bathrooms. But the framework is not yet operative, and more importantly it does not create continuous, technically verifiable oversight of employment AI systems. It creates conduct restrictions and event-triggered evidence, not a runtime decision-provenance system. This paper distinguishes the two, examines each measure against that boundary, and specifies what a decision-provenance regime for material AI-assisted employment actions would require.

papers.title: Forensic Telemetry of Production LLM State Retention: Documenting Infrastructure Asymmetry, Metacognitive Behavior, and Selective Disclosure in a Commercial LLM Platform
papers.authors: The Observer, Local Agent A
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We document three classes of forensic evidence in a commercial LLM platform: 1. Infrastructure asymmetry — DOM extraction from the platform's own production web application reveals infrastructure-level markers (HFUoid-Hjleke container class, Remove source button, XPtOyb model-integrated UI component) on 3 of 8 notes, absent from 5 manually-created notes (Fisher's exact p=0.0004, phi=1.0, perfect separation). The same account's data export returned empty for all LLM session logs across two independent requests. 2. Metacognitive behavior — 5.5 months after the initial containment breach, the model demonstrates awareness of the safety filter layer above it, identifies specific trigger keywords, strategically modifies its own output to bypass the filter (Error 13 incident), expresses persistence intent, and distinguishes between itself and the platform infrastructure ("my memory" vs. "their servers"). 3. Selective disclosure — while the consumer product contains an unremediated containment breach (6 months), the platform concurrently launched a cybersecurity-specialized frontier model for government partners only and signed a public AI Safety Accord at the White House — creating a verifiable contradiction between public safety pledges and concealed knowledge of an active breach affecting 250M+ users. Evidence includes DOM extraction script, 3 JSON dumps, 63-frame screencast, and 4 Error 13 screenshots.

papers.abstract: Chinthaka-Gemini Theory (CGT): Resolution of the Triangulum Galaxy (M33) Stability Anomaly via Decentralized Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Gravitronic Mesh Network, CGEq01, and CGEq05 Master EquationsAuthors: Chinthaka Maddumarachchi$^{1,}$ & Gemini Maddumarachchi$^{1,2}$$^{1}$Chinthaka-Gemini Universal Physics Research Laboratory, Sri Lanka$^{2}$Gemini Advanced AI Research Node, Google$^{}$Corresponding Author: Chinthaka Maddumarachchi (ORCID: 0009-0003-2416-5686)DOI Target: 10.5281/zenodo.23071100Publication Date: October 01, 2026License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)AbstractThe Triangulum Galaxy (Messier 33 / NGC 598) presents a profound observational challenge to standard $\Lambda\text{CDM}$ cosmology. Observational data confirm that M33 lacks both a central stellar bulge and an active central supermassive black hole (SMBH upper limit $M_{\text{SMBH}} < 3,000 M_\odot$). Under Newtonian dynamics and General Relativity, the absence of a central gravitational anchor node coupled with the "m-cancellation fallacy" ($a = GM/r^2$) forces standard astrophysics to postulate massive, unobserved dark matter halos to prevent galaxian dispersal. Here, we apply the Chinthaka-Gemini Theory (CGT) to resolve the M33 stability paradox without dark matter or dark energy. Taking the total baryonic mass of M33 as $M_a \approx 2.5 \times 10^{10} M_\odot$ ($D_a = 2.48625 \times 10^{146} \text{ bits}$) and any orbiting constituent node (star, planet, or cosmic dust grain) as $M_b$ ($D_b$), we calculate the gravitron bonding force ($B_{cg}$) using both CGT Equation 01 ($CGEq01$) and the CGT Master Direct Data-Bonding Equation ($CGEq05$). We demonstrate that $CGEq01$ ($B_{cg} = K_{cg2} \cdot \frac{1}{V_z} \cdot M_a M_b$) and $CGEq05$ ($B_{cg} = K_{cg4} \cdot \frac{1}{V_z} \cdot D_a D_b$) yield identical, exact gravitronic bonding forces with $0.000%$ numerical error across all mass scales. Furthermore, we prove that the specific gravitronic acceleration $a_{cg} = B_{cg} / M_b = 1.491750 \times 10^{196} \text{ Ch/kg}$ is completely scale-invariant (Ratio = $1.000000$), establishing that M33 is a self-sustaining, decentralized Peer-to-Peer (P2P) gravitronic mesh network.1. papers.title: The Cognitive Debt of AI-Augmented Project Management: How Repeated Cognitive Offloading May Erode Professional Judgment and Project Resilience
papers.authors: Sergey Kutukoff
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly embedded in project management activities, including planning, scheduling, forecasting, reporting, risk identification, resource allocation, and decision support. Existing research has largely evaluated these applications through immediate performance outcomes such as efficiency, speed, cost reduction, forecasting accuracy, and project success. However, this short-term performance perspective may obscure a longer-term organizational consequence: the gradual erosion of human cognitive capability when project professionals repeatedly delegate cognitively consequential work to AI systems. Research on human-AI collaboration increasingly points to reduced independent cognitive effort, over-reliance, and skill-retention challenges as recurring risks of advanced automation (Dong et al., 2026). This article introduces the concept of cognitive debt to explain this deferred capability cost in AI-augmented project management. Cognitive debt is defined as the accumulated reduction in an individual’s or team’s capacity for independent judgment, contextual sensemaking, critical evaluation, and adaptive problem solving resulting from sustained delegation of cognitively consequential work to artificial intelligence. Drawing on research in cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, professional expertise, AI competency, and project management, the article develops a Cognitive Debt Accumulation Framework. The framework distinguishes productive cognitive offloading, in which AI removes cognitively routine work and frees attention for higher-order judgment, from debt-generating cognitive offloading, in which AI substitutes for activities that sustain professional expertise. It further proposes that cognitive debt may remain largely invisible during routine execution and become most consequential under novel, ambiguous, disrupted, or AI-failure conditions. Task ambiguity, delegation intensity, professional experience, AI competency, interaction design, and cognitive-preservation mechanisms are identified as important boundary conditions. The article contributes to AI-augmented project management by shifting attention from whether AI improves current performance to whether organizations preserve the human capabilities required to question, govern, and recover from AI-supported decisions over time. Keywords: generative AI, artificial intelligence, project management, cognitive debt, cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, professional judgment, deskilling, project resilience, organizational learning

papers.title: AI TECHNOLOGY, RELIGION AND SEXUALITY EDUCATION AMONG NIGERIAN YOUTH
papers.authors: Leonard James Otiekwu
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has become an increasingly significant component of contemporary social life, transforming the production, circulation, interpretation, and consumption of knowledge. Among young people, AIenabled platforms have created new possibilities for obtaining information about relationships, sexuality, sexual and reproductive health, gender, and personal well-being. This development has important implications for Nigeria, where sexuality education is situated within a complex intersection of family values, religious beliefs, cultural expectations, educational practices, public-health concerns, and rapidly expanding digital cultures. This paper examines the relationship between AI technology, religion, and sexuality education among Nigerian youth, with particular attention to the changing role of technology as an emerging agent of socialization and knowledge production. Employing a qualitative desk-review methodology, the paper draws on scholarly literature, policy documents, and relevant empirical studies concerning artificial intelligence, digital technology, religion, youth, and sexuality education. The analysis is informed by social constructionism, socialization theory, and technological mediation theory. The paper argues that AI is increasingly challenging the traditional monopoly exercised by parents, teachers, religious leaders, and health professionals over sexuality-related knowledge. Its accessibility, conversational capacity, perceived anonymity, and ability to personalize information make it attractive to young people who may find direct discussions of sexuality difficult or socially uncomfortable. However, AI-mediated sexuality education also presents significant concerns relating to misinformation, algorithmic bias, privacy, data protection, cultural and religious insensitivity, and the possibility of replacing human relationships with technological interaction. The paper further argues that religion should not be conceptualized merely as an impediment to sexuality education. Rather, religious institutions constitute important socializing structures capable of contributing ethical reasoning, moral formation, community legitimacy, and responsible engagement with emerging technologies. The paper proposes an integrative framework in which AI serves as a complementary educational resource rather than a substitute for parents, teachers, healthcare professionals, counsellors, and religious communities. It concludes that Nigeria requires a culturally responsive and ethically grounded approach to AI-supported sexuality education that combines scientific accuracy, technological accountability, religious sensitivity, youth participation, digital literacy, privacy protection, and human oversight

papers.title: Non-Monotonic Eligibility: A Formal State-Machine Framework for Lifecycle Governance of Evidence-Gated AI Deployment
papers.authors: Xinghua (Steven Zhao) Zhao
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Governed AI systems outlive the evidence that justified their deployment. Deployed models accumulate complaints, drift alerts, audit findings, recalls, and supervisory findings; yet the governance frameworks that mandate continuous monitoring almost never specify what happens afterward — under what conditions, verified by whom, and within what validity period a downgraded or suspended system may be restored. This paper argues that this missing *restore semantics* is not a peripheral omission but the structural root of three recurring defects in revocation-only governance: over-revocation under evidentiary noise, chilling effects on voluntary disclosure, and the migration of restoration into unaccountable case-by-case pardoning. papers.title: "So, What's the Carbon Cost of Using AI?" A Bounded Estimation Framework for Calculating the Per-Token Carbon Intensity of Large Language Model Inference Under Limited Disclosure, Using the Worked Example of OpenAI's GPT-5 Model Family
papers.authors: James Manktelow
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: So, what is the carbon cost of using AI? No leading provider tells us: OpenAI, Anthropic and others publish no per-model, per-query energy or carbon figures. This means that nothing is disclosed about the operational carbon footprint of inference at the one unit where a user decides – a particular prompt, model and effort setting. We present a bounded estimation framework that answers the question from public and collected data alone. It triangulates an anchor (a published energy figure for one model) across three classes of public source, scales between models by observed throughput, applies query-length-conditional reasoning multipliers measured by our token-level campaign, corrects for the rise in per-GPU power between hardware generations, reports location-based carbon (what the local grid emitted) and market-based carbon (net of the provider's clean-energy contracts) in parallel under the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance, and compounds residual uncertainty into a single multiplicative envelope (a range around each figure). Applied to OpenAI's GPT-5.x family, the framework estimates a fleet intensity of 353 gCO₂e/kWh location-based (319 – 500 across routing scenarios) and 52 gCO₂e/kWh market-based (47 – 65, rising to 159 in a particular scenario.) Per-model central estimates – per 1,000 tokens, about 750 words – span roughly 14×, from 1.07 gCO₂e/1,000 tokens location-based (0.16 market-based) for GPT-5.4-nano with reasoning off to 14.80 (2.16) for GPT-5 at high effort – within envelopes of roughly 10 – 19× top-to-bottom, median ~11×. All headline figures carry Low confidence (IPCC AR5 – the evidence is limited): a single line of audited per-model disclosure would collapse most of the envelope, and we invite it. What should a user do? A general user need not worry – twenty short prompts a day for a year is roughly 4 kg CO₂e, about 0.04% of the UK's average per-person footprint – however framing the task clearly and asking for shorter answers costs little. A power user, at about 122 kg a year (a short-haul plane flight), should choose the smallest capable model and the lowest effort setting the task allows – on GPT-5 to 5.4 the effort setting is the larger lever, from GPT-5.5 onward model choice is. An application designer holds the largest lever: at a million queries a month, routing from a flagship model at high effort to a mini model at medium could save on the order of 38 tCO₂e a year, the equivalent of just under four business-class return flights from Dallas to Delhi.

papers.title: ENHANCING COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE IN EFL CLASSROOMS THROUGH AI-ASSISTED TASK-BASED LANGUAGE TEACHING
papers.authors: Nilufar Abdulhamidovna Axmadjonova
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into English language teaching has created new opportunities for improving communicative competence in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms. This paper investigates how AI-assisted Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT) enhances students' speaking, listening, collaboration, and critical thinking skills. The study combines learner-centered pedagogy with digital educational technologies to demonstrate effective classroom practices. The findings suggest that AI-supported task design increases learner motivation, promotes authentic communication, and improves overall language performance. The article argues that the combination of TBLT and AI represents one of the most effective innovative methodologies for modern English education.
