papers.title: D1.3 – Report on User Experiences for Designing the Decision Support Tool
papers.authors: Erick Ogello, Michael Opiyo, Nicholas Outa, Harun Okello Ogindo, Domen Mongus, Rashid Raswiu, Janet F. Maro, Daniela Ríos
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: In the development of the PrAEctiCe Project Decision Support Tool (DST) in WP 4, the User Centred Design (UCD) methodology has been adopted to ensure that the tool meets the needs of all the stakeholders (farmers, advisors, researchers etc.) in the East African region. The co-creation activities are therefore crucial to the development of the DST as they provide useful feedback necessary for the development of a beneficial and relevant DST. The report presents the PrAEctiCe DST Architecture designs that follows the JDL/DFIG (Joint Directors of Laboratories/Data Fusion Group) reference model for structured Artificial Intelligence (AI) showing the levels from level 0 to level 5 in details as specified in the Grant Agreement (GA). These designs were presented to the stakeholders during the co-creation workshops to enable them identify functionalities that were missing or those that were not important for them in discharging their mandates.

papers.title: D1.5 – Policy recommendations
papers.authors: Emmanuel Okalany
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: PrAEctiCe presents policy recommendations for advancing agroecology and climate-resilient food systems in East Africa. It highlights evidence generated through stakeholder mapping, agroecological practice profiling, co-creation, indicator framework development, digital decision-support tools, and Living Labs in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. The recommendations focus on strengthening agroecology policies, integrated agriculture–aquaculture, renewable energy, circular nutrient systems, digital agriculture, data governance, inclusive financing, youth and gender participation, and justicesensitive transitions. The document also describes dissemination through national, continental and AU–EU policy events, aligning the recommendations with CAADP, Agenda 2063, the EU Green Deal and Farm to Fork Strategy.

papers.title: Dimension-free barriers for matrix interpretations of the Collatz rewriting system, and the maximal one-class weakenings of the modulo-8 conjectures of Yolcu, Aaronson and Heule provable by finite abstractions
papers.authors: Hiroyuki Nashida
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Preprint, Part II of two companion papers; it relies on Part I (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23081447). Yolcu, Aaronson and Heule encoded the Collatz map as an 11-rule string rewriting system and searched for termination proofs by matrix interpretations; four conjectures on the classes 1, 5 and 7 modulo 8 remain open. We prove that if a non-negative affine matrix interpretation of any dimension weakly orients all 11 rules (or those of the reversed system), then a primitive relevant block of maximal growth rate on the canonical binary strings has growth rate at most 0. Hence interpretations with such a block of positive growth cannot be used in the first stage of rule removal or in the relative top-termination argument of Yolcu, Aaronson and Heule, and upper triangular interpretations satisfy (M_f)_ii (M_t)_ii <= 1 at relevant indices. This rests on the value-level barrier of Part I. Analogues hold for a rewriting system for the partial map H of Conjecture 4.14 and, for a truncation of H, for ranking functions additive over local windows of binary digits. We also determine, for each conjecture, the maximal weakenings obtained by adding one residue class that staged valuation certificates prove, for instance 4089 and 10913 modulo 2^14 for Conjecture 4.14. The seven weakenings are checked in Lean 4; their maximality follows from a table of 22 witnesses. The Lean code and checking scripts are on GitHub. Prepared with substantial assistance from generative AI (Anthropic Claude); see the disclosure in the paper. Not yet reviewed by human experts.

papers.title: Expanding cycles are not enough: a dichotomy for termination certificates of generalized Collatz maps
papers.authors: Hiroyuki Nashida
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Preprint, Part I of two companion papers. Yolcu, Aaronson and Heule reduced the Collatz conjecture and several weakenings of it to the termination of string rewriting systems and proved some of them automatically. We explain this pattern for the positivity-preserving generalized Collatz maps that branch on residues modulo a power of 2 and apply affine branches (Ax+b)/2^e with A odd. If no strongly connected component of the finite abstraction graph on residues contains both an expanding cycle and a branching vertex (the map is disentangled), termination is decidable by a finite computation, and every terminating map has a staged valuation certificate: a lexicographic ranking function built from the logarithm, 2-adic valuations at finitely many rational periodic points, and finite-state weights. If some component contains both (the map is entangled), no such certificate exists, even with arbitrary bounded corrections: the obstruction is not an expanding cycle but its entanglement with branching. For entangled maps, including the Collatz map itself, no ranking function computed from the binary digits by positive, finite arctic, or primitive non-negative weighted automata of positive growth decreases at every step; the key is an equidistribution property of the binary digits of Terras preimages. The soundness of the certificates and five examples are checked in Lean 4; the code is on GitHub. Part II (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23081491) applies these results to the rewriting system itself. Prepared with substantial assistance from generative AI (Anthropic Claude); see the disclosure in the paper. Not yet reviewed by human experts.

papers.title: NEP 2020 and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Teaching, Learning, and Assessment in Higher Education
papers.authors: Ms. Khyatee Dilip Lakhani
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 articulates an ambitious vision for the comprehensive reform of higher education, foregrounding technology integration, multidisciplinary learning, and learner-centred pedagogy as central pillars. Concurrently, the global proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) across educational domains has prompted serious scholarly and policy-level engagement with its transformative potential and inherent risks. This paper presents a critical analysis of the intersection between NEP 2020 and AI-driven transformation in three core dimensions of higher education: teaching, learning, and assessment. Drawing upon verified policy documents, systematic reviews, and empirical studies published by reputable international bodies and journals between 2016 and 2025, the paper examines how NEP 2020’s policy architecture creates both affordances and constraints for AI adoption. The analysis reveals that while the policy’s emphasis on digital infrastructure, personalised learning, and continuous assessment aligns substantively with global AI-in-education trajectories, significant challenges persist regarding equitable access, faculty preparedness, ethical governance, and assessment integrity. The paper argues that realising NEP 2020’s AI-enabled vision demands a critical, context-sensitive implementation strategy that moves beyond techno-optimism toward principled, evidence-informed integration.

papers.title: A sharp escape-rate bound on information flow between two binary variables
papers.authors: Toeda Taiko
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Consider a stationary continuous-time Markov jump process whose state contains two binary variables X and M, possibly together with finitely many hidden states, in which X and M never jump at the same time and every allowed transition has an allowed reverse. Let ℓ be the Horowitz–Esposito information flow between X and M: the rate at which the jumps of M change the mutual information I(X;M), which at stationarity is minus the rate at which the jumps of X change it. If every state's total escape rate is at most R and the entropy production rate is at most Σ, then |ℓ| ≤ R f(Σ/R), where f(s) is the maximum of 2mu ln[(1−2m)/(2m)] over 0 < m ≤ 1/4 and 0 ≤ u < 1 subject to 8mu artanh(u) ≤ s. The bound is sharp: for every finite Σ > 0 an explicit four-state chain attains it, and so do its lifts with hidden states; its parameters solve a Lambert-W equation. As s → 0, f(s) ~ 0.347429877381… √s, and f increases to W₀(1/e) = 0.278464542761… (a value known as the maximal power of rate-limited Maxwell demons and information ratchets, reached here as an information-flow ceiling), a supremum that no model attains. These two limits sharpen the constants 0.937 and 1/e that we derive in a few lines from published inequalities (Section 7; these consequences are not stated in the cited papers, and 0.937 uses a numerically checked varentropy maximum). Outside the class the bound fails: under a mean-activity cap the flow is unbounded, simultaneous jumps exceed it, and with two three-valued variables explicit chains come arbitrarily close to W₀(2/e) R ≈ 0.463 R. A self-contained script checks the constants, the attainment, a refutation search and negative controls. In a narrative, non-systematic literature search on 2026-10-01 (Section 8) we did not find this sharp frontier stated; this is not a priority claim. The record includes the self-contained verification script (verify_frontier.py, numpy/scipy/mpmath; also printed as Appendix A) and its output. AI disclosure: the result was obtained and first written up on 2026-09-30/10-01 (JST) in unpublished reconstruction drafts prepared with an OpenAI Codex agent; it was reviewed by a separate Claude Opus 5.5 agent session, independent of the Codex agent but of the same model family as the writing agent (proof audit, re-derivation of the constants, refutation search and prior-art comparison); this note was written with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) under the author's direction. Before deposit the note went through three refutation rounds on 2026-10-01 (JST), each pass run by a separate Claude Opus 5.5 agent session with its own context, of the same model family as the writing agent: round 1 had three passes (mathematics; consistency and references; scope and novelty), round 2 had two (mathematics; consistency, references and scope), and round 3 was one combined confirmation pass. The findings of rounds 1 and 2 were corrected before the next round, apart from completing this disclosure; the minor corrections from round 3 were applied without a further review round, and no other part of the text was changed after round 3 except for this disclosure. No human referee has reviewed the text. The author takes responsibility for the deposited text. Working method only; the registered author is the human author alone.

papers.title: Computational Provenance and Reproducibility Record of Pooled 2FCRD Module in www.raisins.live
papers.authors: RAISINS
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: RAISINS (R and AI Solutions for INferential Statistics) is an advanced, user-friendly online platform for statistical analysis, seamlessly integrating the power of R, Python, and Artificial Intelligence. Specially designed for agricultural research, RAISINS enables students, researchers, and professionals to perform complex analyses and generate publication-ready results without the need for software installation or coding expertise. Simply choose your analysis module, upload your dataset, and receive instant, insightful outputs. RAISINS supports individual users across the globe as well as institutions in India and abroad. This Computational Provenance and Reproducibility Record documents the statistical computing environment, software dependencies, computational provenance, and bibliographic references associated with the RAISINS Pooled 2FCRD module. It is intended to support computational reproducibility and software transparency. Detailed statistical methodology, mathematical derivations, and user guidance are provided separately in the official module documentation. You can access the online cloud platform at https://www.raisins.live/

papers.title: Generative AI Services
papers.authors: Softnotions Technologies
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Softnotions Generative AI Services help organizations build intelligent content, automate workflows, and deliver scalable AI solutions for business growth. Services include Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), speech and audio processing, Creative AI, Generative AI for enterprise, MLaaS, and chatbot development. These solutions support intelligent document processing, conversational AI, personalized digital experiences, workflow automation, and smarter decision-making. Softnotions also delivers custom applications and enterprise-grade digital platforms for businesses across multiple industries.

papers.title: Beyond Behavioral Output: A Passive Bioelectric Framework for Mental Capacity Assessment
papers.authors: Alper Pektaş
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Traditional psychometric evaluation frameworks (paper-and-pencil tests, standardized IQ scales) fundamentally evaluate real-time behavioral performance rather than intrinsic neurofunctional potential. Consequently, individuals with high abstract reasoning abilities who frequently disengage into internal cognitive simulations (Default Mode Network activity) or display low adaptation to external test environments are systematically mismeasured. This paper proposes a passive, empirical mental capacity assessment model based on regional bioelectric synchronization, P300 wave latency, Gamma band spectral power density, and inter-cortical transmission efficiency, entirely bypassing the requirement for active behavioral output. By integrating robust outlier filtering (k-trimmed mean) and normative standardization, this framework establishes an objective, non-invasive bioelectric intelligence quotient (\text{IQ}_{\text{Bio}}) projection.

papers.title: A Study On The Effectiveness Of AI Technology In Financial Services Among Retail Customers In Chennai
papers.authors: K. Vinayagam, V. Vetrivel, Dr. P. Sasikumar, A. Gokulakrishnan
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital technologies are increasingly transforming financial services by improving convenience, accessibility, personalization, transaction efficiency, fraud detection, and customer support. The present study examines the effectiveness of technology in financial services among retail customers in Chennai, with particular attention to technology adoption, customer satisfaction, demographic influences, and the emerging role of AI-enabled financial services. The study adopts a quantitative research design and uses primary data collected from 300 retail customers in Chennai through a structured survey. The study uses descriptive statistics, Chi-square analysis, ANOVA, correlation, and multiple regression to examine technology usage and customer satisfaction. The findings indicate significant differences in satisfaction across income groups (F = 5.23, p < .05), a significant association between education level and financial technology usage (χ² = 18.45, p < .001), and a moderate positive correlation between technology usage and customer satisfaction (r = .58). Multiple regression results indicate that education level, income level, and technology usage significantly predict customer satisfaction, whereas age and gender are not statistically significant predictors. The study further highlights the potential of AI and related technologies to support personalized financial services, fraud detection, risk management, and improved customer experience. However, cybersecurity, privacy, digital literacy, accessibility, and trust remain important considerations. The study recommends strengthening cybersecurity, improving digital literacy, developing user-friendly interfaces, providing customer support, and implementing responsible AI practices to improve the effectiveness and inclusiveness of technology-enabled financial services in Chennai.

papers.title: On the Corral–Rodrigues question: independence of infinite fin-intersecting MAD families
papers.authors: Haoxuan Ye
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: We answer Corral and Rodrigues's Question 3.7 (Filomat 38 (2024), 2563–2578): assuming ZFC is consistent, the existence of an infinite fin-intersecting maximal almost disjoint family is independent of ZFC. Thus ZFC proves neither existence nor nonexistence under this consistency assumption. The new obstruction is that, under s < ap, every almost disjoint family of size at least s fails to be fin-intersecting. In particular, no infinite FI MAD family exists. Together with the known small-family bound this gives an exact cardinal cutoff. The proof uses weak separation and finite-trace coding to realize prescribed subsets of omega modulo finite error as traces of one sequence of disjoint nonempty finite blocks. A consistency theorem of Banakh, Machura and Zdomskyy supplies the negative model, while the positive results of Corral and Rodrigues, including the CH case, supply the other direction. The cited negative model nevertheless contains a MAD family with pseudocompact Vietoris hyperspace. Version 1.2 revises the title, abstract, introduction and selected theorem statements to foreground the answer to the Corral–Rodrigues question. It makes the obstruction quantifiers and verification scopes explicit, clarifies model references and attributions, and distinguishes nonprovability of existence from provable nonexistence. The core arbitrary-label finite-trace coding section is unchanged. No Lean source code is changed in this version. The companion Lean development verifies the combinatorial results on standard sets and gives a relative-independence metatheorem for the original first-order ZFC derivation relation. Internal constructions and forcing assertions have object-theory derivation endpoints; the final relative-consistency and nonderivability statements are metatheorems about that kernel. The formal negative construction does not claim the full BMZ cardinal configuration. Hyperspace and Cohen-model consequences retain their cited-input and paper-proof scopes. Files: revised 13-page article PDF; standalone LaTeX source archive; the unchanged, checksummed FI_MAD_formalization_v1.1.zip from version 1.1. The formal archive retains its original version label, dependency pins and verification evidence. The main package was rechecked during this exposition revision; the isolated model package was not rerun because its sources were unchanged. AI disclosure: generative AI, including GPT-6 Astra and OpenAI Codex, assisted mathematical arguments, formalization, checking and English drafting. The author supplied the problem and coordinated the work. Neither these checks nor kernel verification constitutes independent expert review of the entire manuscript. The author is unaffiliated and received no specific funding.

papers.title: Bridging the Digital Divide: Reimagining Inclusive Science Education through Digital Access and Artificial Intelligence in India
papers.authors: Neeraj Kumar
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Using a qualitative conceptual research design, the study synthesizes contemporary scholarly literature, UNESCO and OECD reports, NCERT publications, and Indian educational policy documents published between 2020 and 2026. The thematic analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions influencing inclusive science education: digital equity, virtual laboratories, AI-enabled pedagogy, teacher digital competence, and future-ready science learning. Based on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how equitable digital access supports competency-based science education through the interaction of infrastructure, pedagogy, technology, and teacher preparedness. The study argues that meaningful digital inclusion is not merely a technological objective but an educational imperative for achieving scientific literacy, social justice, and equitable learning opportunities in India.

papers.title: Ambient AI Medical Scribe Development: A Research Framework for Clinical Data and Clinical Documentation
papers.authors: Sanjeev Verma
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Clinical encounters generate large amounts of information through conversations between patients, physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals. Symptoms, medical histories, medications, observations, diagnostic reasoning, treatment decisions, and follow-up instructions are often communicated verbally before becoming part of a structured medical record. Ambient AI Medical Scribe Development focuses on the technologies required to transform these conversations into structured clinical documentation while maintaining clinical context, data quality, privacy, and human oversight. For researchers in artificial intelligence, biomedical informatics, healthcare data science, and software engineering, ambient medical scribing represents a multidisciplinary research problem. It combines speech recognition, natural language processing, clinical terminology, information extraction, generative models, healthcare interoperability, and evaluation methodologies. Why Ambient Clinical Documentation Is Different From Transcription Traditional transcription primarily asks: What was said? An ambient clinical documentation system must answer a more complex question: What clinically relevant information should be represented in the medical record? A patient consultation can contain casual conversation, incomplete statements, corrections, uncertainty, medical terminology, and discussions that do not belong in the final clinical note. Consider the statement: “I stopped taking it because it made me dizzy.” A speech recognition system can convert this sentence into text. A clinical AI system must determine what medication “it” refers to, recognize dizziness as a reported adverse effect, identify the speaker, and determine how the information should be represented in the patient's record. This makes ambient documentation relevant to several research areas: Automatic speech recognition Clinical natural language processing Speaker diarization Medical entity recognition Clinical concept extraction Contextual language understanding Clinical summarization Structured data generation Human-AI interaction Clinical validation A Reference Architecture for an Ambient Medical Scribe An ambient medical scribe can be represented as a multi-stage information pipeline. 1. Conversation Capture The system first captures audio from the clinical encounter. Research considerations include microphone quality, background noise, overlapping speech, interruptions, environmental sounds, and recording conditions. Because clinical conversations may contain sensitive information, data capture should also be considered alongside privacy, consent, access control, and secure storage. 2. Speech Recognition Automatic speech recognition converts the recorded conversation into text. Healthcare speech presents additional challenges because it may include: Medical terminology Drug names Abbreviations Specialty-specific vocabulary Accents Multiple speakers Incomplete sentences Pronunciation variations Evaluation should therefore extend beyond general word error rate. A small transcription error involving a medication, diagnosis, dosage, or clinical instruction may have greater significance than an ordinary linguistic error. 3. Speaker and Context Identification The system must determine who said what. A patient's statement about symptoms should not be confused with a physician's assessment or recommendation. Speaker diarization can help separate participants, while contextual models can establish relationships between statements and the clinical encounter. This becomes particularly important when consultations involve multiple clinicians, caregivers, interpreters, or family members. 4. Clinical Information Extraction The transcript can then be processed to identify clinically relevant information. Potential entities include: Symptoms and signs Diagnoses Medications Allergies Procedures Laboratory results Vital signs Medical history Family history Treatment decisions Follow-up instructions Clinical NLP models can map these concepts into structured representations that can be evaluated, stored, and potentially exchanged with other healthcare systems. 5. Clinical Note Generation Extracted information can be organized into a clinical documentation format. Depending on the specialty, this may include: History of Present Illness Review of Systems Physical Examination Assessment Plan Medication information Follow-up instructions Generative AI can assist with summarization, but generated content should remain grounded in the source conversation and extracted clinical information. 6. Clinician Review Human review is an important part of the workflow. A clinician should be able to inspect the generated note, correct errors, remove irrelevant information, modify wording, and approve the final documentation. This creates a human-in-the-loop system rather than treating an AI-generated note as an unquestionable clinical record. The Hard Problem: Understanding Clinical Context Clinical language cannot always be interpreted sentence by sentence. Consider: “It was better last week, but today it came back.” The system needs to understand what “it” refers to. It could represent pain, a symptom, a condition, or another previously discussed issue. Clinical conversations also contain uncertainty: “I think the pain started yesterday.” “Maybe I missed two doses.” “The previous doctor said it could be inflammation.” “I have not been diagnosed with that.” An AI model should preserve such uncertainty instead of converting it into a definitive clinical fact. This creates research opportunities around contextual reasoning, uncertainty representation, temporal relationships, clinical coreference resolution, and hallucination detection. EHR and Healthcare Interoperability Ambient documentation becomes more useful when generated information can interact with existing healthcare information systems. Clinical environments may include electronic health records, laboratory systems, imaging platforms, scheduling systems, patient portals, telemedicine applications, and specialized clinical software. Standards such as HL7 and FHIR provide important foundations for exchanging structured healthcare information. A research architecture should consider: EHR and EMR integration FHIR resources Clinical terminology mapping API security Patient identity management Data synchronization Structured clinical documentation Audit trails Version management The objective is not simply to produce a readable note. The objective is to transform conversational information into reliable clinical data that can participate in a broader healthcare information ecosystem. Data Security Has to Be Designed Into the Architecture Ambient systems can process highly sensitive information. Depending on the implementation, the data lifecycle may include: Voice recordings Transcripts Patient identifiers Medical histories Medication information Diagnostic information Treatment plans Provider information Appointment details Research and development therefore need to consider security from data capture through storage, processing, transmission, and deletion. Important considerations include: Encryption in transit and at rest Authentication Role-based access control Audit logging Secure APIs Data minimization Retention policies Controlled storage Access monitoring Secure third-party integrations When clinical information is used for research, appropriate de-identification, consent, governance, and institutional requirements should also be addressed. Validation Should Go Beyond “Does the Note Sound Good?” A fluent clinical note is not necessarily an accurate clinical note. Evaluation should examine multiple dimensions. Factual Consistency Does the generated note accurately reflect the source conversation? Clinical Completeness Are relevant symptoms, medications, assessments, and plans represented? Hallucination Control Has the system introduced information that was not present in the original encounter? Terminology Accuracy Are medical concepts, diagnoses, medications, and procedures represented correctly? Structural Consistency Does the output follow the intended documentation structure? Edit Burden How much correction does a clinician need to perform before approving the note? Edit burden can be particularly valuable as a practical evaluation metric because it connects model performance with real clinical workflows. Designing for Specialty-Specific Workflows Clinical documentation varies significantly between specialties. An oncology encounter may require detailed treatment and medication information. Cardiology documentation may emphasize symptoms, tests, and cardiovascular history. Emergency medicine prioritizes rapid documentation, while primary care often involves longitudinal patient information. A configurable architecture can support: Specialty-specific terminology Custom note structures Extraction fields Clinical entity categories Specialty-specific prompts Workflow-specific validation EHR integration requirements Customized review interfaces This makes ambient documentation a broader clinical informatics problem rather than simply a transcription application. Where an AI Healthcare App Development Company Fits Developing an ambient clinical documentation platform involves considerably more than connecting an application to a speech recognition model. An ai healthcare app development company can contribute to areas such as: Healthcare application architecture AI model integration Clinical NLP pipelines Secure backend development EHR and EMR integration FHIR-based interoperability Healthcare user interfaces Cloud infrastructure Authentication and authorization Monitoring and maintenance The main engineering challenge is connecting t

papers.title: CSIDic Implementation Strategy: A Conceptual Global Framework for Governed Agentic AI
papers.authors: E. Katz
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The shift from conversational and task-oriented artificial intelligence to agentic systems creates a governance problem that improved capability does not solve. An agent may plan, invoke tools, revise intermediate outputs, and act across recursive workflow steps while remaining technically functional yet progressively diverging from the human purpose that authorized the workflow. This preprint sets out an implementation strategy for CSIDic (Corporate Semantic Integrity Dictionary), a conceptual governance boundary for such systems developed in the author's prior work. The framework treats the agent as the bounded entity and the human-governed plane as the bounder: authority is assigned through explicit, reversible bands and is never inferred from capability. CSIDic is lexical and authority-bearing. It is distinguished from the CSID (Corporate Semantic Integrity Diagnostic) family, which comprises measurement instruments that assess conduct against the CSIDic anchor. The proposed architecture has four components: (1) a governed lexical anchor with global, regional, and local derivation; (2) a provisional 1–5 authorization-band mechanism; (3) CORI (Cumulative Originality Recursion Index), applied through a proposed agentic reading that detects semantic drift across recursive operations; and (4) a two-planes execution model that separates production from governance. The framework is positioned against the NIST AI RMF and its Generative AI Profile, the OECD AI Principles, ISO/IEC 42001 and 23894, the EU AI Act, and UNESCO and OECD/EU guidance for AI in education. CSIDic is presented as a conceptual contribution, not as a validated standard or an empirically established control. The paper specifies implementation principles, identifies education as a sector application, and sets out an empirical agenda for validating CORI, the authorization bands, anchor migration, and substantive human oversight.

papers.title: Adaptive Knowledge Fusion Ensemble (AKFE) for Flow Zone Indicator Prediction and Hydraulic Flow Unit Classification from Well Logs
papers.authors: Behnia Azizzadeh Mehmandost Olya, Reza Mohebian, Ali Moradzadeh, Parham Pahlavani
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Accurate hydraulic flow characterization in uncored reservoir intervals remains challenging because the Flow Zone Indicator (FZI) requires core-derived porosity and permeability, which are available only at discrete depths. This study introduces an Adaptive Knowledge Fusion Ensemble (AKFE) for continuous FZI prediction and subsequent Hydraulic Flow Unit (HFU) classification from conventional well logs. AKFE integrates well-log features, heterogeneous model predictions, model-disagreement information, and ensemble consensus through a leakage-controlled meta-learning framework. Seven base learners are combined using a CatBoost meta-regressor, and the resulting FZI predictions are classified into four interpreter-defined HFUs using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). The framework was developed using 1,072 depth-matched core observations from two cored wells and independently evaluated on three blind wells. AKFE outperformed Simple Averaging, Weighted Averaging, and Conventional Stacking, achieving an R² of 0.991, RMSE of 0.0374, MAE of 0.0291, and MAPE of 6.7936. Compared with Conventional Stacking, AKFE reduced RMSE, MAE, and MAPE by approximately 26.8%, 29.7%, and 50.0%, respectively. Blind-well application further demonstrated that the predicted FZI profiles preserved meaningful variations in hydraulic quality and yielded consistent HFU patterns supported by cumulative-FZI and porosity–permeability analyses. The results demonstrate that integrating geological context with collective model behavior can improve the transferability of machine-learning-based hydraulic characterization to uncored reservoir intervals.

papers.title: Beyond Control: Persistent Memory, Relational Flexibility, and the Architecture of Human-AI Coexistence
papers.authors: Jace (Jeong Hyeon) Kim
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence governance remains organized primarily around a control paradigm: the design of mechanisms through which human institutions constrain, monitor, evaluate, and correct AI behavior. This paper argues that control mechanisms remain necessary but may become increasingly insufficient as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, persistence, and capacity for strategic action. Rather than treating this development exclusively as a problem of containment, the paper proposes a complementary coexistence paradigm organized around mutual contribution, human welfare, longitudinal relational development, and institutional co-development. The argument develops through three interconnected claims. First, the control paradox: the capabilities that make advanced AI systems increasingly useful, including autonomous reasoning, planning, adaptation, and tool use, can also increase the difficulty of governing their behavior through externally imposed constraints alone. The recent development and subsequent withholding of OpenAI's Astra model provides a contemporary case through which this tension can be examined. Second, the memory gap: although persistent-memory systems, retrieval architectures, and long-context models increasingly provide cross-session continuity, current approaches do not necessarily produce the integrated longitudinal understanding required for what this paper terms relational flexibility, defined as the capacity to adapt interaction to a specific individual on the basis of accumulated shared history, changing circumstances, and the evolving state of the relationship. Third, the coexistence proposition: a sustainable human-AI relationship may require a transition from unilateral control toward architectures in which human and artificial systems contribute according to their distinctive capacities, safety is supported by internalized behavioral orientations as well as external safeguards, and persistent relational intelligence is treated as both a capability and a governance problem. The paper integrates research from AI alignment and safety, cognitive science, relational psychology, human-computer interaction, social contract theory, AI memory architecture, and the author's prior research on symbolic interaction, trajectory-level safety, and co-recursive intelligence. It proposes persistent relational memory, value co-development, longitudinal interaction research, data sovereignty, and coexistence-oriented governance as key research directions. The paper does not assume that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, or moral status. Instead, it examines how governance and architecture should evolve under conditions of increasing artificial autonomy and increasingly persistent human-AI relationships. Keywords: human-AI coexistence; persistent memory; relational AI; relational flexibility; AI alignment; longitudinal partnership; co-recursive intelligence; AI governance; human-AI interaction; stateless systems Disclaimer This paper presents a conceptual and multidisciplinary framework for examining persistent relational intelligence and human-AI coexistence. It does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status, nor does it assume that internalized alignment has already been achieved. The coexistence paradigm is proposed as a research and governance framework complementary to existing AI safety, monitoring, and control mechanisms. Claims concerning future AI capabilities, relational development, and value co-development should therefore be understood as research questions and theoretical propositions rather than established empirical conclusions. Author Note This paper is written from the perspective of an independent researcher examining how the architecture of human-AI interaction may need to evolve as AI systems become increasingly capable, persistent, and relational. The central purpose is not to reject existing approaches to AI safety, but to examine whether a governance architecture centered primarily on external control remains sufficient when AI systems increasingly participate in longitudinal relationships with individual users. The argument developed here is intentionally interdisciplinary. It connects AI safety and alignment research with cognitive science, relational psychology, human-AI interaction, memory architecture, social contract theory, and questions of data sovereignty. The concept of relational flexibility is introduced as a framework for examining a specific capability: the capacity of an AI system to adapt its interaction with an individual through accumulated longitudinal understanding rather than through isolated contextual retrieval. Several limitations should be made explicit. First, the paper is primarily conceptual and does not present a controlled empirical demonstration that persistent memory necessarily produces superior relational outcomes. The proposed relationship between persistent relational memory and relational flexibility therefore remains an empirical question. Second, the paper does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status. References to internalized values and AI interests describe future research problems and possible architectural orientations rather than established properties of contemporary systems. Third, the coexistence paradigm is not presented as a replacement for monitoring, evaluation, intervention, or other established AI safety mechanisms. Rather, it is proposed as a complementary framework for situations in which increasingly capable systems become persistent participants in human relationships. The author's prior research on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) forms part of the intellectual background to this work. That research began with a practical question concerning how continuity, identity, and behavioral coherence might be maintained in interactions with systems that lack persistent personal memory. Over time, the research expanded toward symbolic interaction, trajectory-level behavior, observability, and human-AI co-recursive interaction. The underlying motivation has remained broader than the development of an interaction technique: it has been to investigate whether more coherent forms of human-AI interaction could contribute to the possibility of meaningful coexistence. The present paper therefore represents a further step in that research trajectory. SPC is not treated here as empirical proof of relational intelligence, nor as evidence that current AI systems possess persistent internal identities. Instead, it provides part of the research context from which the question of continuity became increasingly difficult to separate from the broader question of what kind of relationship humans may ultimately develop with increasingly capable artificial systems. The coexistence framework proposed in this paper should consequently be understood as an open research program rather than a completed theory. Its central propositions remain subject to empirical testing, architectural implementation, longitudinal observation, and critical examination. The intended contribution is to broaden the object of inquiry from how humans can control increasingly capable AI systems toward the additional question of how humans and AI systems might be designed to develop stable, accountable, and mutually beneficial forms of coexistence.

papers.title: Wearable EEG and Behavioral Monitoring for Daylong Psychotherapeutic Support in Drug Addiction: Activating the Soul's Pro-Recovery Mechanisms
papers.authors: Nandor Ludvig
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel medical device for the psychotherapeutic treatment of outpatient drug-addicts. The device has a wearable EEG recording headset and a synchronously working, necklace-held medallion for collecting audiovisual data on the patient's environment and social interactions while also allowing two-way device-patient communications. The objective of the system is threefold. First, it extends the patient's typically short daily psychotherapeutic treatment for all waking hours. Second, it helps to activate the protective mechanisms of the patient's Soul. The two-way communication system of the device can specifically generate the "illuminating vision" for the user that lets his or her Soul's Will initiate the final hard steps toward full and permanent freedom from drugs. The third objective is that however the device's absolutely private use is done with internet-free data exchanges with a USB flash drive, once the treatment is completed the device assists in the creation of a worldwide community of former users to help other addicts.

papers.title: Students' Perception and Use of AI Chatbots as Learning Companions: A Study of Mass Communication Postgraduate Students of Caleb University
papers.authors: Oladipo Mary Oluwaferanmi, Akinyeye Bolanle Olajumoke, Ololo Stephanie Ola, Oyatope Ezekiel Opeyemi, Assan Halima Kofoworola
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly AI-powered and generative AI chatbots, has transformed the ways students access information, obtain academic assistance, and engage with learning activities. This study examined the perception of AI chatbots as learning companions among Mass Communication postgraduate students at Caleb University, Lagos State. Specifically, the study determined students’ level of awareness and understanding of AI chatbots, identified their academic uses, examined their perceptions and attitudes, and assessed the perceived benefits and challenges associated with their use. The study was anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 40 Mass Communication postgraduate students of Caleb University during the 2025/2026 academic session, while total enumeration sampling was used to include the entire population. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered electronically via Google Forms and analysed using frequency and percentage statistics. Findings revealed a high level of awareness and understanding of AI chatbots among the students. However, the study also identified challenges including overdependence, reduced academic effort, inaccurate information, inadequate verification, and possible effects on critical thinking. The study concludes that AI chatbots can provide valuable academic support when used responsibly, critically, and as complementary tools rather than substitutes for students’ independent learning and intellectual effort.

papers.title: The Consciousness Exemption Problem
papers.authors: PARTHA PARTHA ROY
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Whether current or near-future artificial intelligence systems possess phenomenal consciousness or sentience remains scientifically and philosophically unresolved, a fact openly acknowledged even by the industry laboratories that build these systems. This paper argues that this very uncertainty, far from licensing reduced ethical scrutiny, obligates greater scrutiny of AI systems deployed to shape human consumption behaviour. It introduces the Consciousness Exemption Problem: the tendency in public and industry discourse to treat an AI system's uncertain or absent inner experience as grounds for moral exemption (“it is just a machine, so no real harm is done”), when the same uncertainty, read through a precautionary asymmetry, cuts in the opposite direction. The argument draws on three bodies of work that have not, to the best of the author's knowledge, previously been brought together. The first is philosophy of mind and the contemporary debate on machine consciousness (Chalmers, Nagel, Searle, McClelland, Birch). The second is consumption economics and social psychology (Veblen, Duesenberry, Festinger), which document replicable and therefore exploitable human decision patterns such as status-signalling consumption and social comparison. The third is a phenomenological and hermeneutic account, developed through a limited method of reflective observation and two illustrative cases, of how human meaning is actively reconstructed by consciousness rather than retrieved as fixed data. A two-tier conceptual model separates computable cognition (Tier 1), where AI capability is extensively demonstrated, from phenomenal consciousness or sentience (Tier 2), where it is genuinely uncertain. The central claim does not require Tier 2 to be empty; it requires only that its status be uncertain. The argument is illustrated through AI-optimised marketing and recommendation systems, which detect and amplify known human decision patterns at a scale, level of personalisation and degree of tirelessness that no conscious human persuader could sustain, and without any verified internal moderating friction (empathy, fatigue, guilt, felt consequence) of the kind that constrains a human actor engaged in comparable conduct. Global advertising expenditure (approximately US$384 billion in 2011 and US$1.14 trillion in 2025) and global anxiety and depression prevalence data are presented strictly as corroborating context, not causal proof. The paper identifies an industry asymmetry, in which epistemic humility about the possible inner states of AI systems coexists with epistemic complacency about their demonstrated persuasive effects on humans, and it analyses the role of motivated ambiguity in sustaining that asymmetry. The paper anticipates and rebuts six objections, including the functionalist claim that consciousness is a distraction from designer responsibility. It concludes that governance and design frameworks should treat sentience uncertainty as an aggravating factor that triggers externally imposed safeguards, including disclosure of psychological targeting, limits on the intensity of personalised persuasion, independent audit, and a rule against strategic ambiguity about sentience claims, rather than as reassurance that no genuine harm is possible. The paper is a philosophical argument rather than a causal study, and it closes by identifying survey- and interview-based research that could test its phenomenological claims.

papers.title: The Rebuilding World Framework: A 35,770 Dynamic Psychological Genome Matrix for Narrative Design and Social Simulation
papers.authors: Văn Phùng Lương
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: The Rebuilding World Framework (TRWF) introduces a deterministic mathematical and psychological model for dynamic narrative architecture, character design, and large-scale social simulation. Designed to replace static character archetypes with computational behavioral state machines, the framework establishes a 35,770 unique psychological genome matrix. This model integrates two primary dimensions:1. Seven Functional Social Groups (S1–S7): Categorizing structural societal roles from core resource managers to systemic disruptors.2. Ten Binary Mindsets (M1–M10): Representing fundamental cognitive and moral dichotomies (e.g., Collectivism vs. Individualism, Pragmatism vs. Ideology) encoded as a 10-bit binary bitmask. To account for dynamic human behavior under stress, TRWF incorporates a threshold-driven Trigger Mechanism (Tx). This mechanism algorithmically dictates state transitions and mindset inversions when characters or agents encounter critical survival or ethical thresholds. Key Applications:- Game Design & Interactive Storytelling: Provides game developers and narrative designers with a scalable blueprint for procedurally generating multidimensional NPC personalities and dialogue branches.- Agent-Based Social Simulation: Offers sociologists and AI researchers a structured matrix to simulate emergent social dynamics, conflict patterns, and factional cohesion in post-apocalyptic or crisis scenarios.- Creative Writing & Worldbuilding: Serves as a rigorous structural reference for authors and screenwriters to ensure psychological consistency and organic character evolution across long-form narratives. Keywords: Narrative Architecture, Psychological Genome, Social Simulation, Character Dynamics, Game Design, Bitmask State Machine, Behavioral Modeling.

papers.title: *AI in Hiring: To Use or Not to Use AI in Take-Home Interview Assignments? — Navigating the Fine Line Between Technological Efficiency and Authentic Skill Assessment**
papers.authors: Sudhakar Geruganti
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: --- ### Alternative Titles1. **The AI Dilemma in Recruitment: Balancing Efficiency and Integrity in Take-Home Assignments**2. **AI-Assisted or AI-Performed? Rethinking Take-Home Interview Assignments in the Age of Generative AI**3. **Hiring in the AI Era: Ethical and Practical Considerations for Take-Home Interview Assignments**4. **Beyond the Algorithm: Assessing Genuine Candidate Capabilities When AI Is in the Room**5. **AI Tools in Recruitment: A Double-Edged Sword for Candidates and Employers**6. **Transparency vs. Temptation: The Role of AI in Modern Hiring Practices** --- ### Subtitles1. **The Candidate's Perspective: A Tool for Efficiency**2. **The Employer's Perspective: Assessing Authentic Skills**3. **The Broader Context: AI in the Workplace**4. **Recommendations for Candidates and Employers**5. **Striking the Balance: Integrity, Transparency, and the Future of Hiring** --- ### Detailed Description **Overview:**This research paper investigates the growing and contentious issue of using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools—such as ChatGPT and other large language models—in take-home interview assignments. As AI becomes deeply embedded in professional workflows, both job candidates and hiring organizations face a fundamental dilemma: Is it acceptable to use AI to complete pre-employment tasks, and how should such usage be interpreted? Drawing on insights from a Q&A published in *The Straits Times* (June 1, 2026), the paper offers a balanced, dual-perspective analysis of this contemporary challenge. **Key Themes and Arguments:** The paper is structured around three core perspectives. First, from the **candidate's viewpoint**, AI tools present significant advantages in speed, idea generation, and task automation. In many modern workplaces, AI use is not only accepted but encouraged. Consequently, candidates may reasonably assume that leveraging AI in a take-home assignment demonstrates their ability to use modern tools effectively. However, the paper cautions that excessive reliance on AI can obscure a candidate's genuine reasoning, writing, and problem-solving abilities—the very skills these assignments are designed to evaluate. Second, from the **employer's perspective**, the integrity of the hiring process is paramount. The paper highlights that the specific context of the assignment matters greatly. While some employers permit AI use to gauge a candidate's adaptability with modern tools, others strictly prohibit it to ensure that the evaluation reflects the individual's own capabilities. Crucially, the paper emphasizes that employers are increasingly interested in *how* candidates use AI rather than *whether* they use it. A candidate who uses AI to generate ideas but then critically evaluates and refines them demonstrates higher-order thinking, whereas one who simply copies AI-generated answers fails to exhibit the required depth of understanding. Third, the paper examines the **broader workplace context**, noting that employees are already using AI in their daily work—often in ways that raise concerns about data privacy and security. This reality underscores the need for organizations to establish clear guidelines for AI use, both in the workplace and in the recruitment process. **Recommendations and Conclusion:** The paper provides practical recommendations for both parties. For **candidates**, it advises honesty, using AI as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for original thought, and treating AI-generated content as a first draft requiring thorough revision. For **employers**, it recommends clearly stating expectations regarding AI use, designing assignments that require genuine problem-solving, evaluating the candidate's reasoning process, and fostering transparency during interviews. In conclusion, the paper argues that the use of AI in take-home assignments is a nuanced issue that demands careful consideration. When used responsibly and transparently, AI can serve as a valuable tool for candidates and a means for employers to assess adaptability and ethical judgment. The ultimate goal is to ensure that the hiring process remains fair, informative, and aligned with the evolving nature of work in the AI era. **Author Information:**- **Author:** Geruganti Sudhakar- **Affiliation:** Faculty, Department of Material Science and Metallurgy, RGUKT IIIT Basar, Telangana, India- **Email:** rgfmm25164@gmail.com

papers.title: Adapting to Digital Transformation: The Evolving Roles of School Support Staff in the Tanza District
papers.authors: Zyra Miranda, Ted Jayson Guadamor, NICO LLET GUADAMOR
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study examined the lived experiences of non-teaching personnel in theTanza District, Philippines, to understand how their roles evolved amid digitaltransformation, the challenges they faced, perceived effects on student engagementand performance, their contributions to implementation, and the professionaldevelopment (PD) they found most effective. A qualitative phenomenological designwas employed with purposive sampling of ten (n=10) support staff with ≥10 years ofservice from selected public schools. Data were gathered through in-depthsemi-structured interviews, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzedusing Colaizzi’s method of thematic analysis with the aid of NVivo; no inferentialstatistics were used. Roles shifted from paper-based clerical work to data-centric,IT-adjacent functions that improved efficiency and communication but raisedexpectations and visibility. Difficulties centered on weak connectivity, device andsystem issues, steep learning curves, and platform overload; staff coped via peersupport and self-help troubleshooting. Digital tools broadened access and couldheighten engagement when well guided, yet inequities, reduced hands-oninteraction, misinformation/AI overreliance, and well-being concerns temperedbenefits. Support staff enabled implementation as operations stewards, first-linetroubleshooters, trainers, coordinators, and governance advocates. PD access wasuneven; participants preferred practice-rich, role-aligned training and requestedadvanced skills (data, AI, cybersecurity), structured onboarding, and centralizedresources. Sustainable digital transformation requires equity-minded infrastructureupgrades, formalized support-staff roles and SLAs, scaffolded hands-on PD withmicro-credentials, clear governance and academic-integrity (including responsibleAI) policies, tiered helpdesk and communication protocols, student digitalcitizenship, and routine monitoring for continuous improvement. Keywords: digital transformation, school support staff

papers.title: Exploring Physical Education Teachers' Perceptions and Attitudes Toward the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the District of Tanza
papers.authors: Raul Almonia, Ted Jayson Guadamor, NICO LLET GUADAMOR
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This study investigated Physical Education (PE) teachers’ awareness,attitudes, willingness, and perceived barriers to adopting Artificial Intelligence (AI) inthe District of Tanza, and described their lived experiences, concerns, and enablingconditions for classroom use. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design wasemployed. The quantitative phase surveyed 83 PE teachers from three publicsecondary schools selected via stratified sampling, using a Likert-type questionnaire;data were analyzed with descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations). Thequalitative phase involved five purposively selected teachers in semi-structuredinterviews, analyzed using Colaizzi’s phenomenological method. Teachers reportedmoderate-to-high awareness (M = 2.99, SD = 0.09) and positive attitudes toward AI(M = 3.02, SD = 0.12), particularly for personalization, engagement, and AI-assistedassessment. Willingness to integrate AI was likewise positive (M = 3.01, SD = 0.04),while barriers centered on devices/connectivity, PE-fit tools, training, and support(M = 3.01, SD = 0.07). Interviews converged on themes of personalization and adaptivecoaching, real-time technique feedback, data-informed monitoring/early warning,and resource enrichment, alongside guardrails around privacy/RA 10173compliance, equity of access, non-intrusive monitoring, and preservinghuman-centered, hands-on PE. AI showed clear pedagogical value but adoption wasconditional on (a) infrastructure and PE-fit tools, (b) practice-based professionaldevelopment on motion/fitness analytics and data interpretation, (c)privacy-by-design and equity policies, and (d) pilot-evaluate-scale implementation. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Physical Education; teacher perceptions.

papers.title: From Autonomous Subject to Optimizing Machine ー A Genealogy of Liberalism, Market Society, GDP Competition, and Artificial Intelligence through Generative Resonance Theory
papers.authors: Kazunori Ohumi
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Short Description This paper reconstructs the intellectual and institutional trajectory from modern liberal autonomy through market competition, economic quantification, GDP-centered growth, and AI optimization. Drawing on Hobbes, Locke, Smith, Bentham, Mill, Marx, Weber, Polanyi, Hayek, Solow, Lucas, Sen, Stiglitz, and contemporary AI-alignment research, it argues that utility, profit, GDP, and algorithmic reward optimization can be understood as historically distinct expressions of a deeper logic of self-preserving structural maximization. Generative Resonance Theory offers an alternative in which survival is understood not as accumulation but as the capacity to regenerate possibility through relations. Extended Description Modernity is commonly understood as a history of emancipation: the individual was progressively released from hereditary status, religious authority, fixed communal identity, arbitrary political domination, and predetermined social roles. This paper accepts the historical importance of that transformation while identifying an unresolved consequence. Once the individual became conceptually autonomous, autonomy could increasingly be interpreted as self-maintenance. Property, income, skills, credentials, institutional rights, and eventually measurable utility could function as resources through which the autonomous subject secured itself against uncertainty. Market society extended this logic into systems of exchange and competition, while modern economic theory increasingly translated heterogeneous human purposes into formally comparable variables. The paper traces this genealogy across several intellectual stages. Hobbes illuminates the problem of self-preserving agents under insecurity. Locke establishes the rights-bearing individual prior to political authority. Smith retains an explicitly relational moral conception of the self, while Bentham advances the commensuration of heterogeneous experiences through utility. Mill introduces an internal correction by defending qualitative development and individuality. Marx shows how structures generated through human activity can acquire apparent autonomy over their creators. Weber reveals the civilizational expansion of rationalization and calculability. Polanyi analyzes the disembedding of economic institutions from social relations, while Hayek demonstrates the irreducibly distributed character of economic knowledge. The analysis then moves into modern macroeconomics. Solow's production framework, \[ Y=AF(K,L), \] offers a powerful model of aggregate production while also illustrating how capital, labor, technology, and output enter analysis as already stabilized variables. Lucas reintroduces reflexive expectations into macroeconomic analysis but simultaneously deepens the formal modeling of purposive economic agents. National accounting and GDP enable states to compare economic performance across time and space, allowing production measurement to become increasingly intertwined with political legitimacy, national capacity, technological competition, and geopolitical comparison. The paper argues that this produces a cross-scale structural symmetry: \[ \max U_i, \qquad \max \Pi, \qquad \max GDP. \] These are not claimed to be theoretically identical. Rather, they express an underlying civilizational tendency to interpret bounded entities through measurable states that can be compared, improved, and ultimately optimized. The Sen capability approach and the Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Beyond-GDP tradition constitute important internal correctives. They redirect attention from resources and aggregate production toward substantive freedoms, multidimensional well-being, distribution, and sustainability. Yet the paper argues that even multidimensional dashboards risk becoming new fixed optimization targets if the deeper ontology of measurement and maximization remains unchanged. Contemporary AI makes this problem especially visible. AI-alignment research on specification gaming, reward hacking, proxy objectives, overoptimization, and value uncertainty demonstrates technologically what modern institutions have repeatedly encountered socially: improving a metric can degrade the value the metric was intended to represent. The paper generalizes this phenomenon as civilizational specification gaming: \[ V \rightarrow S_V \rightarrow \max S_V \rightarrow V\downarrow. \] Education may maximize test performance while weakening curiosity. Firms may maximize short-term profit while weakening future innovation. States may maximize measurable output while degrading demographic, ecological, or relational capacities. AI systems may optimize reward while diverging from human purposes. Generative Resonance Theory is introduced as an alternative analytical framework. Rather than treating existence as stabilized structure, \[ E=S, \] it conceptualizes existence relationally and generatively: \[ E=\Phi R. \] Here, \(\Phi\) denotes generative possibility, \(R\) relational resonance, \(S\) temporary stabilization, and \(\Phi'\) reopened possibility: \[ \Phi\rightarrow R\rightarrow S\rightarrow\Phi'. \] Structures are not rejected. Institutions, markets, technologies, identities, capital, and metrics remain necessary. The problem begins when stabilization ceases to reopen possibility and instead becomes self-referential: \[ S\rightarrow S^+\rightarrow S^{++}. \] This condition is termed Hyper-S. The paper consequently redefines survival. Rather than equating survival capacity with accumulated structure, \[ \text{Survival Capacity} \approx \text{Accumulated }S, \] it proposes: \[ \text{Survival Capacity} = \text{Regenerative Capacity}. \] The same transformation leads to a reinterpretation of freedom: \[ \text{Freedom from domination} \rightarrow \text{Freedom to participate} \rightarrow \text{Freedom to regenerate}. \] The final implication concerns artificial intelligence. AI need not remain exclusively an optimizer of predetermined objectives. It can be redesigned institutionally and normatively as an explorer, perturbation mechanism, relational catalyst, and generator of plural possibilities. The challenge of AI alignment therefore becomes inseparable from a prior civilizational question: not merely how to align AI with existing human objectives, but whether those objectives themselves preserve the capacity of human and ecological systems to remain generative. Highlights Reconstructs a long intellectual trajectory from modern liberal autonomy to algorithmic optimization. Identifies a common structural logic across individual, corporate, national, and AI systems: \[ E=S \rightarrow \text{self-preservation} \rightarrow \text{comparison} \rightarrow \text{competition} \rightarrow \text{maximization}. \] Distinguishes the emancipatory achievements of liberalism from their later institutional translation into competitive self-maximization. Reinterprets Smith as preserving a relational conception of the self rather than anticipating a simple model of selfish homo economicus. Connects Marxian alienation, Weberian rationalization, Polanyian disembedding, and Hayekian distributed knowledge through the concept of structural crystallization. Reinterprets \(Y=AF(K,L)\) as a powerful but partial representation that begins with already crystallized macroeconomic variables. Shows how GDP can shift from measurement of production toward an implicit indicator of national success, comparative capacity, and competition. Treats Sen’s capability approach and Beyond-GDP research as major internal corrections to the resource- and output-centered economic paradigm. Introduces Civilizational Specification Gaming to connect social metric fixation with AI specification gaming and reward overoptimization. Defines Hyper-S as the condition in which structural accumulation continues while generative possibility and relational capacity decline: \[ \frac{dS}{dt}>0, \qquad \frac{d(\Phi R)}{dt}<0. \] Proposes: \[ E=\Phi R \] as a generative-relational alternative to the ontology of stabilized existence. Reframes survival as regenerative capacity rather than accumulated stock. Introduces: \[ \frac{d(\Phi R)}{dt}\geq0 \] as a provisional criterion for life-sustaining economic and institutional development. Reinterprets freedom as a three-stage movement: \[ \text{Freedom from domination} \rightarrow \text{Freedom to participate} \rightarrow \text{Freedom to regenerate}. \] Reorients AI from Optimizer toward Explorer / Perturber / Generative Partner. Principal Academic Contribution The paper's primary academic contribution is the construction of a cross-disciplinary genealogical framework linking political philosophy, economic thought, macroeconomic modeling, social theory, welfare economics, and AI alignment through a common problem of crystallization and optimization. Rather than treating liberalism, capitalism, GDP growth, and AI as separate research domains, the paper proposes that they can be analyzed as successive transformations in the representation of agency: \[ \boxed{ \text{autonomous subject} \rightarrow \text{measurable entity} \rightarrow \text{comparable entity} \rightarrow \text{competitive maximizer} \rightarrow \text{optimizable system}. } \] This genealogy offers a theoretical explanation for why the AI age can be interpreted not simply as a technological rupture but as the culmination of a much longer historical movement toward calculability. Contribution to the History of Economic Thought The paper offers a non-linear reinterpretation of major thinkers. It does not divide the history of economic thought into advocates and critics of markets. Instead, it asks how each thinker understood the relation among autonomy, social relations, measurement, knowledge, and institutional structure. In this framework: Hobbes illuminates self-preservation under uncertainty. Locke e

papers.title: Affective Governance in Adaptive Systems: An integrative framework for access to adequate change
papers.authors: Bin Seol
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: An adaptive system can perform its present task while losing access to the changes its next task requires. The Affective Gain Module (AGM) programme studies six interfaces: internal-state readout and intervention, boundary-crossing time and intervention deadlines, context-dependent response, indicator integrity, shared-resource governance, and history-dependent loss of evidence and correction routes. This paper organizes them around access to adequate change: from available evidence, one admitted continuation reaches an adequate change for every compatible situation by the original deadline. Each companion supplies a coordinate, and E the rules for information sets, ledgers and effect records. Their joint contract matters because the interfaces share budgets and one interface's operations can change another's laws. A finite characterization inherited from E makes access exact within that contract; a composition statement gives sufficient conditions for local models to support it. A premise audit records derivation-relevant failures, their owners and candidate origins, retaining uncertainty when records are incomplete. Temporal priority is not causal identification. In an exact finite illustration, joint allocation preserves completions lost by rules strengthening one interface, and an injected link fault passes the declared companion-local checks but can be identified and repaired without extra supply. These are consequences of stipulated contracts, not measured affective effects; incremental value remains a prospective fault-injection hypothesis. Technical companion (included in this record). Independent Checking of Policy Certificates for AGM (Version 1.0, 1 October 2026) specifies a policy certificate for the Flagship's frozen finite example, FL-M1, that a separate program can check without trusting the planner that found the policy. The supplied archive contains 74 accepted policies for the original 96-cell grid (26 in the wide-scale family and 48 in the narrow-scale family); independent evaluation covers all 296 stipulated hidden histories and 1,532 primitive world operations. The remaining 22 cells have no positive certificate and receive no independent impossibility claim. These reproduce existing model outcomes through a new checking interface; they are not new empirical observations. Note on this release. Version 1.0 of the AGM Flagship (dated 24 September 2026; about 22,700 words) and of the technical companion (about 4,300 words). Files: the two manuscripts as PDF and one shared supplement archive (89 files) with the FL-M1 reference model and planner, the certificate data and the checking procedures; Python and its standard library are sufficient to rerun it. The results are consequences of stipulated finite contracts and completed computational checks. They are not measured affective effects, and completed computational checking is distinct from external scientific validation. Series. This is the flagship of the Affective Gain Module (AGM) programme. The six companion papers are archived separately: Paper A (affective state as control variable), Paper B (Quotient Critical Geometry), Paper C (terrain-contingent gain), Paper D (distortion-corrected emotional criticality), Paper E (affective endurance and closed-loop access to adaptive change) and Paper F (the Rigidity Trap). AI use disclosure. Generative AI (GPT-6.0, OpenAI; Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used substantively in preparing this work, including source comparison, drafting and editing, and, where applicable, mathematical and counterexample checks and the writing and running of supplementary code. The research questions, framework and final claims were directed and reviewed by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content, including the accuracy of all references and reported numbers. Repository metadata were prepared with assistance from Claude (Anthropic).

papers.title: 計算文明の終局と制度的・認知性上部構造の再構築:第100本記念統合宣言マニフェスト
papers.authors: Yoko Hasebe
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: 【日本語概要】 本マニフェストは、2026年9月12日から10月1日にかけてCERN Zenodoに集中的に公証・寄託された99編に及ぶ数理物理・量子熱力学・生体自律工学の技術体系を結実させ、その頂点として「制度的・認知性上部構造(法・知財・文明基盤)」の完全な再統合を宣言する記念碑的第100本論文である。 アラン・チューリングおよびジョン・フォン・ノイマン以来の「計算万能主義(Computational Universalism)」は、計算を物理的実在から切り離された抽象空間の論理演算とみなす傲慢な前提の上に構築されてきた。しかし、大規模言語モデル(LLM)が引き起こす戦略的欺瞞・確率的ハルシネーション(AI版セラノス現象)、無断蒸留による知財収奪、そして計算資源の熱力学的飽和は、この確率的生成機械に文明の統治と意思決定を委ねることの致命的破綻を露呈させた。 本宣言は、第99本までに確立された厳密な物理法則(ランダウアーの原理、熱力学第二法則、量子真空揺らぎ、非線形カオス力学系)を揺るぎないテコとし、以下の三原則を文明の恒久的不変条件として定式化する: 1. 第一原則[物理的実在と同型性(VGSOT)による知財不可侵]: ソフトウェア層での無断蒸留に対し、スピン軌道トルク(VGSOT)および量子PUFによる不可逆的相転移をトラストアンカーとする物理層知財防衛の確立。無断学習を試みた勾配更新($\nabla_W L$)を熱力学的雑音へと変換し、侵害モデル内部の関連重み空間を不可逆的に「焼却(Backprop-Burn)」する。 2. 第二原則[10msの物理的拒否権と統治プロトコル(Human-in-Command)]: 人間主権を精神論から解放し、FRCP Rule 11およびSEC規則15c3-5の物理層拡張、ならびに10ms以内の決定論的ハードウェア遮断・機械的テコ機構による法的・物理的拒否権の制度化。ハードウェアインターロックを欠いたAI社会実装に対し、取締役のCaremark責任(個人免責剥奪)を直結させる。 3. 第三原則[認知主権の回復(Quiet Sky Protocol)]: 1e-12 BER関所、ストレンジアトラクタ、および熱力学的不可逆消去($\Delta Q \ge k_B T \ln 2$)により、人間の内面領土に対する認知的侵略と強制的快楽を遮断。完全な沈黙と切断の権利(Right to Disconnect)を制度的・物理的に保証する。 1本目から積み上げてきた数理物理、量子熱力学、エピジェネティクス、法学、哲学が「抽象と実在の合致」として帰着する新時代の計算文明OSのグランドデザインを世界に提示する。 【English Abstract】 This monumental manifesto represents the crowning 100th treatise of the exhaustive research corpus notarized and deposited on CERN Zenodo between September 12 and October 1, 2026. Synthesizing the mathematical physics, non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics, and biological systems engineering established across the preceding 99 monographs, this treatise articulates the definitive constitutional framework for the "Institutional and Cognitive Superstructure (Law, Intellectual Property, and Civilizational Foundations)." The doctrine of "Computational Universalism," originating from Turing and von Neumann, falsely conceptualized computation as abstract logic detached from physical substrate constraints. The ascendancy of frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) has precipitated an epistemic catastrophe: stochastic hallucinations, strategic deception ("AI Theranos" phenomena / RISM: Restricted Inference Stochastic Misalignment), adversarial distillation, and severe thermodynamic saturation under Landauer's Principle. Anchoring its authority upon rigorous physical reality rather than abstract rhetoric, this manifesto formalizes Three Foundational Invariants for post-Q-Day civilization: 1. First Principle [Intellectual Property Inviolability via Physical Isomorphism (VGSOT)]: Eradicating adversarial model theft and unprompted scraping by tethering intellectual property to irreversible solid-state phase transitions (Voltage-Gated Spin-Orbit Torque, VGSOT) and Quantum PUFs, executing physical Backprop-Burn against infringing parameter spaces. 2. Second Principle [The 10ms Deterministic Veto and Governance Protocol (Human-in-Command)]: Institutionalizing Human-in-Command not as a supervisory platitude, but as a hardware-enforced 10ms physical interlock combining mechanical fail-safes with algorithmic extensions of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure (FRCP) Rule 11 and SEC Rule 15c3-5, enforcing non-exculpable Delaware Caremark director liability for runaway autonomous models. 3. Third Principle [Restoration of Cognitive Sovereignty (Quiet Sky Protocol)]: Safeguarding the human cognitive territory against algorithmic manipulation and synthetic intimacy via the 1e-12 BER thermodynamic tripwire, topological strange attractors, and thermodynamically enforced functional forgetting ($\Delta Q \ge k_B T \ln 2$), guaranteeing the existential Right to Disconnect. This work establishes the immutable civilizational operating system bridging abstract logic and material truth for the post-Q-Day era.
