papers.title: A rubric landscape for evaluating clinical reasoning in large language models: what exists, what is missing, and what needs to be combined
papers.authors: Zhangshu Joshua Jiang, Zina M. Ibrahim, James Teo
papers.abstract: Exam-style accuracy does not establish whether large language models (LLMs) reason well over clinical records. We define clinical reasoning as integrating and updating evidence across time and sources to form, revise and justify a patient's problem representation and a defensible plan. This structured narrative review maps three literatures: medical education assessment instruments, clinical LLM benchmarks published from 2023 onwards, and general-domain methods for evaluating long-form generation. We examine six dimensions: problem representation, temporal synthesis, differential and management reasoning, counterfactual reasoning, calibrated uncertainty, and reasoning faithfulness. Preprints are included and flagged. No single instrument covers all six dimensions. Problem representation and differential or management reasoning are reasonably covered, although reliability varies by instrument and setting. TIMER-Eval targets temporal synthesis, and ER-Reason assesses sequential diagnostic belief updating. Dedicated uncertainty and counterfactual evaluations are emerging, but their applicability to longitudinal free-text reasoning remains limited. Factual completeness is well theorised in general-domain evaluation, with early clinical evidence of important omissions. Faithfulness remains the weakest dimension, with one identified clinical causal-ablation study on multiple-choice questions. Existing tools should be combined through binary rubric items, separate completeness and correctness scores, case-specific importance weighting with non-compensable safety caps, temporal order-consistency checks, and chance-corrected reliability reporting. Further design work is needed for calibrated uncertainty, counterfactual reasoning and faithfulness over longitudinal free-text records. This review provides a design rationale, not a validated instrument.

papers.title: The Innocent Courier: Covert Exfiltration Through Legitimate LLM Web Fetching
papers.authors: Alessandro Pegoraro, Daryan Merx, Phillip Rieger, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi
papers.abstract: With the increasing capabilities of Large-Language-Models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents, users are increasingly using them to solve everyday problems, such as answering e-mails or providing programming support. Existing work has extensively investigated security and privacy risks, such as prompt injections and the disclosure of sensitive data to chatbot providers. While various solutions were developed to address these risks, including input structuring to prevent prompt injections or deploying local LLMs to avoid sharing confidential data with chatbot operators, LLMs also pose the risk of leaking confidential data to third parties. In this paper, we demonstrate with LLMLeak a novel attack vector where malicious software that runs locally but cannot communicate directly with the internet abuses LLMs to establish a covert channel. While inputs that instruct the LLM to send data directly via generated code are easy to detect and network libraries are typically restricted, LLMLeak relies only on the LLM's tool to fetch websites for further information. A malicious software component on the client side embeds a secret into a URL. It presents the referenced website as providing information required for a benign task, such as migrating a software library. When the LLM accesses the URL, the attacker receives the encoded secret through an attacker-controlled DNS or web server. We perform an extensive evaluation on eleven open-parameter models, observe an attack success rate of 79.7%, and also conduct a case study on real-world chatbots, demonstrating the relevance of LLMLeak.

papers.title: Teaching LLMs to Hear Who Spoke What: Metadata-Supervised Pretraining for Encoder-Free Speech-LLMs
papers.authors: Mohan Shi, Ruchao Fan, Sunit Sivasankaran, Keqi Deng, Jinyu Li
papers.abstract: Encoder-based speech large language models (Speech-LLMs) commonly employ pretrained speech encoders that prioritize linguistic content but may discard fine-grained acoustic cues essential for speaker discrimination and paralinguistic understanding. Encoder-free Speech-LLMs instead map Mel-spectrogram features directly into the LLM input space through lightweight embedding layers, enabling the LLM to learn from low-level acoustic features. However, systematic pretraining strategies for encoder-free Speech-LLMs remain underexplored, limiting their ability to compensate for the absence of large-scale pretrained speech encoders. We propose metadata-supervised pretraining (MSP), which leverages speech attributes such as speaker identity and emotion to develop speaker-discriminative and paralinguistic capabilities. We further introduce speaker-aware utterance composition (SAUC) to strengthen speaker discrimination and apply random span masking to regularize pretraining. We primarily evaluate our approach on joint ASR and speaker diarization in multi-speaker conversations, complemented by experiments on paralinguistic speech-understanding tasks. Under matched training-data conditions, our encoder-free model outperforms its randomly initialized encoder-based counterpart. With limited metadata-annotated data, it is competitive with models using speech encoders pretrained on substantially larger corpora, outperforming them in several settings. These results demonstrate the potential of encoder-free architectures for building native multimodal LLMs that acquire diverse speech capabilities.

papers.title: Gacha Decoding: Eliciting Diverse Generations Through Instruction Following
papers.authors: Scott Geng, Yufei Zhang, Joseph Lee, Jerry Zheng Li, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Pang Wei Koh
papers.abstract: We introduce Gacha Decoding, an inference-time method for eliciting diverse language model generations that scales with model capability. Across open-ended domains (in-the-wild chat, creative writing, planning for image generation, and protein design), Gacha Decoding significantly outperforms existing generation diversity approaches at equal quality (up to 2.4x Vendi over the next-best prior approach), reaching the same number of high-quality modes with over an order of magnitude fewer samples (11.0x) and discovering novel modes that no other approach surfaces. Our key insight is to treat diversity as an instruction-following problem: rather than relying on the LM's token entropy, we combine its instruction-following capability with randomness from an external RNG tool to scalably identify and realize distinct modes of the response space. This approach of "planning with dice" enables Gacha to invert the long-observed tension between diversity and model capability. As the underlying LM becomes a better instruction follower, diversity under Gacha Decoding consistently improves--even as its token entropy and diversity under prior approaches decline. Together, our results highlight that instruction following, rather than token entropy alone, can drive generation diversity.

papers.title: A High-Density EEG Dataset for Stimulus-Driven Auditory Attention
papers.authors: Ruofan Yan, Na Lu, Shu Peng, Wenlong You, Zhige Chen, Yuxuan Yan, Yan Liu, Kay Chen Tan, Jibin Wu
papers.abstract: Stimulus-driven auditory attention determines which sound gains priority when multiple sources compete without an explicit listening goal, yet most computational studies focus either on acoustic salience or on decoding predefined attended targets. This study investigates instruction-free auditory competition using the Stimulus-driven Auditory Attention (SAAD) paradigm and develops a neurophysiologically informed framework that integrates stimulus-derived sound priority with trial-specific EEG evidence. Behavioral analysis using a Bradley--Terry model showed that sound priority estimated from previous competitions generalized to unseen sound pairings, improving held-out prediction from an AUC of 0.577 to 0.718. EEG analysis further revealed mid-to-late centro-temporal lateralization associated with the reported selection side, with neural information remaining predictive beyond acoustic asymmetry. Guided by these findings, the proposed model first estimates a latent priority for each competing sound and forms relative stimulus evidence from their difference. A multi-scale EEG pathway with complementary signed and power-based readouts then extracts trial-specific neural evidence, which is incorporated through gated decision-level integration. The framework is evaluated using mirror-constrained and pairing-held-out protocols, together with representative acoustic, EEG, multimodal baselines, and systematic ablations. The results support a computational account in which spontaneous auditory selection reflects the interaction between generalizable stimulus priority and trial-specific neural variability.

papers.title: Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class
papers.authors: Lili Chen, Gavin Buskes, Yuxin Ren, Chin Tong Leong
papers.abstract: Timely and specific feedback is one of the strongest influences on student learning, yet it is difficult to sustain in large electrical engineering classes where the ratio of students to demonstrators is high and a learner who is stuck may wait days to find out why an approach was wrong. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers a way to scale conversational feedback, but using it to grade assessed work raises trust and accountability concerns, and keeping a human in the loop to assure its judgements reintroduces the very delay that erodes the value of feedback. The result is a tension between the immediacy that makes feedback so impactful and the human oversight that makes it trustworthy. In this work, we set out to resolve that tension in practice by designing and piloting a GenAI practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice. This relocates human oversight from real-time grading to the upfront verification of solutions. Our goal was to understand how students engaged with the tool, how they perceived the value and reliability of its feedback, and what lessons transfer to other engineering subjects.

papers.title: Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields
papers.authors: Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Yoonje Lee, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Margaret Ellis, Naren Ramakrishnan
papers.abstract: This research full paper examines how undergraduate students use large language models (LLMs) across computer science subfields. As LLMs become increasingly integrated into computing education, understanding how their use varies across technical and pedagogical contexts is essential for designing effective, subfield-aware instruction. This paper presents a cross-subfield analysis of LLM usage among 211 undergraduate students in a problem-solving course intentionally designed to support responsible and effective LLM use through structured instruction and reflection. Using post-assignment reflection data collected across seven instructional modules spanning multiple computer science subfields, we examine prompt counts, LLM role conceptualization, and verification behavior. Results show that LLM adoption varies substantially by assignment, with higher usage in algorithms and web development and lower usage in software engineering. Students predominantly treat LLMs as assistive tools rather than authoritative sources, and verification is common across all subfields, with most students using multiple strategies. Verification behavior also varies by assignment context, with testing more common in structured tasks and web search more common in open-ended tasks. These findings suggest that assignment characteristics play a central role in shaping how students interact with and evaluate LLM outputs, even under a single, consistently applied instructional design. This work contributes empirical evidence on how LLM adoption, role conceptualization, and verification behavior vary across computer science subfields, extending our prior work on structured, reflective LLM instruction to show how its effects differ by task rather than only in aggregate.

papers.title: Virtual Global Collaboration in Data Analytics and Machine Learning Education: A Mixed-Methods Study of Asynchronous Cross-Border Teamwork
papers.authors: Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Saad Nizamani, Khyati Goyal, Sarwat Nizamani, Zannah Zeiw
papers.abstract: This innovative practice full paper examines a structured Virtual Global Collaboration (VGC) activity between undergraduate computing courses in the United States and Pakistan. The project was designed to support technical and intercultural skill development through asynchronous international teamwork in data analytics and introductory machine learning. Students worked in mixed-institution teams through a six-phase project including cultural orientation, dataset selection, data cleaning, analysis, introductory machine learning, and structured reporting. Using shared computational tools, teams coordinated across time zones to complete a joint data-driven project. Survey and qualitative reflection data were analyzed to examine collaborative experience, communication and cultural dynamics, learning outcomes, perceived value, and global readiness. Results show consistently positive student experiences across both cohorts, with collaborative processes strongly associated with learning and perceived value, and cross-cultural communication emerging as the primary driver of global readiness. These findings demonstrate how short-term, structured VGC can be effectively integrated into computing courses to support both technical learning and global competence.

papers.title: Classical Hardness of Learning Functions of Hamiltonians
papers.authors: Sota Hashimoto, Akinori Kawachi
papers.abstract: Morohoshi, Nakayama, Manabe, and Mitarai proposed a physically motivated quantum machine learning problem in which the goal is to predict quantities of the form $\operatorname{Tr}[f(H)ρ]$ from classical descriptions of a Hamiltonian $H$ and a quantum state $ρ$, where $f$ is an unknown function. We call this problem Hamiltonian function learning in this paper. They constructed an efficient quantum learning algorithm under suitable conditions, while leaving a rigorous proof of average-case classical hardness open. In this paper, we rigorously prove the average-case classical hardness for two distribution-specific Hamiltonian function learning problems for $f_{\cos,π}(λ)=\cos(πλ)$ and $f_{\exp,β}(λ)=e^{-βλ}$ discussed in the paper of Morohoshi et al. under the assumption of the average-case hardness of factoring random RSA moduli. More specifically, we show that an efficient classical randomized learner under squared loss whose output hypotheses are evaluable in classical polynomial time for either problem would yield a classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm for factoring random RSA moduli.

papers.title: GeoFWI3D: Large-scale 3D Velocity Model Dataset for Deep Learning-assisted Seismic Imaging
papers.authors: Sujith Swaminadhan, Yiran Shen, Chao Li, Kai Gao, Ting Chen, Sergey B. Fomel, Tolulope Agbaje, Yang Cui, Lianjie Yang, Jaewook Lee, Robin Dommisse, Umair Bin Waheed, Mrinal K. Sen, Yangkang Chen
papers.abstract: We introduce GeoFWI3D, a large-scale open-source benchmark dataset of geologically plausible 3D subsurface models designed to accelerate deep learning (DL) assisted seismic imaging and full waveform inversion (FWI). FWI is a physics-driven, wave-equation-based optimization technique used in seismic imaging to estimate the subsurface properties. However, traditional FWI is highly non-linear, non-unique, and ill-posed. The iterative process often converges to local minima when the starting model is insufficiently accurate. Most importantly, 3D FWI is prohibitively expensive. With the advent of DL, a direct mapping between the shot gathers and subsurface properties can be established by training a network on realistic models. The primary bottleneck for such approaches is the lack of large-scale, realistic training datasets. GeoFWI3D addresses this gap with 10,000 geologically diverse velocity models at 96x96x96 resolution, spanning four structural complexity classes: pure stratigraphy, faulted networks, salt diapirism, and complex coupled fault-salt systems. Each model is accompanied by co-registered multi-modal labels including compressional velocity (Vp), zero-offset seismic reflectivity, relative geologic time (RGT), and semantic fault/salt masks. To facilitate systematic evaluation, we introduce benchmark tasks covering fault detection, joint salt body segmentation and chronostratigraphy prediction, FWI, wavefield and traveltime surrogates using neural operators, and generative modeling with a 3D diffusion model. We present baseline results for each task to establish reference performance metrics for future users. The dataset is publicly available under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International.

papers.title: Scaling and Distilling Text Embeddings for Better Diffusibility
papers.authors: Zekai Zhang, Yunjie Tian, Yanjin He, Xiaoyan Zhang, DongDi Zhao, Qing Qu, Di Fu
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive (AR) language generation. Recent advances in continuous DLMs, which apply latent diffusion to continuous text embeddings, raise a practical question: which embedding makes the best latent space, i.e., the most diffusible? To answer this, we search through different embeddings and find that scaling the embedding model to stronger ones within the same family (T5 to T5Gemma-1 to T5Gemma-2) greatly improves generative performance. But the raw T5Gemma-2 embeddings are still not optimal. They are so discriminative that even the embeddings of plausible alternative words are separated, which makes the generation vulnerable to imperfect sampling. Consequently, continuous diffusion often fails to reach any of them and ends up at an invalid embedding instead. To address this, we distill T5Gemma-2 into a student encoder that learns the teacher's decoded probabilities as soft labels. Learning from such soft labels makes the student pull the alternative embeddings closer while maintaining the encoding-decoding mechanism. The distilled embeddings form a more connected and diffusible latent space, improving over the vanilla T5Gemma-2 embeddings. As a result, our medium-sized DLM achieves Gen. PPL 17.8 (against real-text PPL 15.4) at real-text entropy on OpenWebText, outperforming GPT-2-M on Gen. PPL.

papers.title: RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation
papers.authors: Jingtan Wang, Sirajul Salekin, Young mok Jung, Javier R. Movellan, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low, Manjot Bilkhu
papers.abstract: Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning. Beyond rubrics' usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes. Together, these components form RISED. Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

papers.title: Towards Fast and Disentangled Counterfactuals for Visual Foundation Models
papers.authors: Sidney Bender, Benedikt Kunz, Ahmed Zeid, Shinichi Nakajima, Klaus-Robert Müller, Marco Morik
papers.abstract: Foundation models remain vulnerable to spurious correlations and ``Clever Hans'' strategies. Explainable machine learning can find and remove such strategies for classifiers without metadata. For foundation models, no such option exists yet. We propose Disentangled Diffusion Autoencoders (DiDAE). DiDAE wraps a frozen foundation model in a conditional diffusion decoder. A counterfactual is one closed-form edit along a direction of a disentangled dictionary, followed by decoding. The dictionary can be supervised (Procrustes) or unsupervised (Singular Value Decomposition, Sparse Autoencoders). No gradients are needed, so DiDAE is up to 2000 times faster than the state of the art. We evaluate on six datasets, two synthetic and four real-world. In a desiderata-driven benchmark on three of them, its counterfactuals are on par with or better than the state of the art, and they repair downstream classifiers through Counterfactual Knowledge Distillation (CFKD), where they beat metadata-based correction. The same machinery can rank a pretrained dictionary against a trained classifier. It returns the few directions the classifier actually reads, each causally verified by a counterfactual that flips the decision, and repairs the classifier along those a teacher marks spurious. The workflow is plug-and-play in our open-source Peal library we publish alongside the paper. With a public dictionary and a pretrained decoder, all that remains is a cheap linear distillation of the classifier and its own fine-tuning.

papers.title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
papers.authors: Sara Riazi, Pedram Rooshenas
papers.abstract: We present an educator-guided LLM pedagogical agent for scaffolded feedback in conceptual database design. Integrated into an entity--relationship diagram (ERD) editor, the system grounds feedback in the student artifact, assignment requirements, educator-authored rubrics, and instructional resources. Its architecture separates hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis from the workflow that controls the form and disclosure level of student-facing support. We instantiate the architecture as a four-stage workflow progressing from concept checks and guided application to low-detail feedback and localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. In a deployment spanning three ERD environments and 383 feedback episodes, 71.1\% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after Stages~1--2. Qualitative analysis showed that staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, or allowed later recovery, though some errors still shaped revisions. Survey responses from a self-selected sample favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

papers.title: Correctness, Convergence, and AI-Generated Code Detection: A Longitudinal Study of Student and Large Language Model Code in Introductory Programming
papers.authors: Runlong Ye, Jing Fan, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Oscar Karnalim, Paul C. Denny, Juho Leinonen, Michael Liut
papers.abstract: Large language models can generate plausible solutions to programming assignments, making it tempting to detect their use by matching student code against a reference bank of generated solutions. Yet similar code can also arise when an assignment admits only a few natural implementations, which leaves open what a match actually shows. We investigate generated-reference matching using 29,970 student submissions from ten Python labs offered in 2021, 2023, and 2025, together with 90,000 solution attempts generated retrospectively by three frontier LLMs. We validate the generated solutions using hidden instructor tests, compare code with MOSS after excluding the starter code, and examine the exact abstract syntax tree (AST) forms of selected functions. The models usually produced correct solutions and, across most assignments, converged on similar implementations. Student submissions matched the generated references more often in later cohorts, including among submissions that passed every hidden test. On tightly specified functions, the models converged on a few exact abstract-syntax-tree forms, and the number of distinct student forms also declined across cohorts, whereas open-ended functions remained diverse in both sources. Most reported overlaps were short, making the minimum match length an important choice when reviewing students' code. Finally, we discuss how instructors can build a reference bank of generated solutions before releasing an assignment to identify tasks on which generated solutions converge, decide how much review a match warrants, and redesign tasks to elicit tests, reasoning, and intermediate work. These findings support tracking population-level changes in submitted code, while attributing AI use to an individual submission would require additional evidence about how it was produced, such as prompts, revisions, intermediate code, and student disclosures.

papers.title: COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE IN THE ERA OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: TOWARDS DIGITAL LANGUAGE EDUCATION
papers.authors: A.M. Ibrayeva, R.A. Skakova, К.Т. Медеубаева, A. Oka
papers.abstract: The digital environment is increasingly influencing the development of communication skills. Interaction often takes place through platforms where human input is combined with algorithmic processing. In these circumstances, traditional models of communicative competence do not fully explain how students interpret, develop, and coordinate meaning. The purpose of this research is to identify and conceptualize the key components of digital communicative competence necessary for modern language education in the era of artificial intelligence. To achieve this goal, the study analyzes classical theories of communicative competence, the foundations of digital competence and literacy in the field of artificial intelligence. These sources were studied taking into account the changes introduced by initiatives on trilingual education and digital transformation in Kazakhstan. The research uses a theoretical and analytical approach based on the synthesis, comparison and interpretation of modern and classical research in the field of language education. The analysis revealed four interrelated components of digital communication competence: linguistic resources, digital information processing skills, intercultural mediation, and adaptability to technological advances. These components collectively describe how students interact with texts, messages, and communication tasks in an environment mediated by artificial intelligence. Communicative competence arises as a multi-layered structure formed by both language knowledge and digital influences. The results provide a conceptual framework for rethinking communicative competence in a technologically mediated educational context and highlight the importance of integrating digital technologies and artificial intelligence-related abilities into the training of foreign language teachers and curriculum development. The integration of digital technologies and artificial intelligence capabilities facilitates more accurate interpretation of machine-modified content and more effective participation in multilingual digital communication.

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED PEDAGOGICAL STRATEGIES FOR ENHANCING LINGUODIDACTIC COMPETENCE IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE TEACHER EDUCATION
papers.authors: I.F. Assankhojayeva, Д.М. Джусубалиева
papers.abstract: The digital transformation of modern education has positioned Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a key catalyst in reshaping both teaching and learning processes. Within the sphere of foreign language teacher education, AI technologies are driving significant methodological changes by promoting more individualized, adaptive and data-informed approaches to instruction. The emergence of intelligent tutoring systems, automated evaluation tools, voice and speech recognition applications, and advanced generative language models provides innovative pathways for developing linguodidactic competence, that is, the professional ability of future language educators to design, implement, and assess effective language teaching within technology-enhanced learning environments. Linguodidactic competence represents an integration of linguistic proficiency, pedagogical knowledge, and methodological flexibility. Traditionally, this competence has been developed through direct classroom practice, observation, and reflective teaching. However, contemporary AI-powered pedagogical methods extend these opportunities by offering instant feedback, creating realistic communicative simulations, and supporting adaptive learning tailored to individual students’ needs. Consequently, programs preparing foreign language teachers must reconsider their curricula, emphasizing the acquisition of digital literacy and AI-related competencies as essential components of professional qualification. Beyond improving the efficiency and personalization of instruction, the incorporation of AI into linguodidactic practices also raises important ethical, cognitive, and communicative considerations. Therefore, it is crucial to understand how AI-based strategies can be purposefully and responsibly embedded in pedagogical design. This research aims to examine innovative AI-driven teaching approaches that enhance linguodidactic competence among pre-service and in-service foreign language teachers, focusing on theoretical foundations, practical applications, and long-term implications for sustainable professional growth in the era of intelligent education.

papers.title: Responsible AI Governance in Organizational Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework of Calibrated Trust, Ethical Acceptability, and Decision Legitimacy.
papers.authors: Mohamed Hamza Bennani, Driss Helmi
papers.abstract: By functioning in an advisory capacity, AI systems are playing an increasingly central role in organizational decision-making, yet their value cannot be assessed based solely on predictive performance. This article describes the governance-centered conceptual model of how technological governance capability and organizational governance capability jointly shape decision quality and decision legitimacy, both of which are distinct outcomes of AI-augmented decision-making. Our proposal not only considers calibration of trust in AI but also ethical acceptability (ecological validity) as parallel mechanisms rather than a fixed serial sequence. Calibrated trust is whether a decision-maker can count on AI at the level that it claims to perform, and ethical acceptability whether AI-supported decisions are justifiable in fairness, safety, privacy, human oversight, traceability & accountability. Learning culture is suggested as an organizational boundary condition by which the influence of organizational governance capability (with a positive sign) on calibrated trust and ethical acceptability is enhanced, while regulatory institutional pressure is proposed to strengthen (with a positive sign) the link between ethical acceptability and decision legitimacy. The framework also differentiates formative higher-order governance capabilities from evaluative mechanisms at the individual level and clarifies their levels of analysis. An example conceptual application to AI-enabled credit decisions is provided to demonstrate how the framework can be connected to verifiable governance evidence without claiming empirical validation. The model provides a unified explanation of the ways in which AI-governance capabilities can influence sound and institutionally justifiable organizational decisions across levels.

papers.title: The Role of ESG Governance and Internal Control in Preventing Corporate Tax Fraud: Expert Perspectives
papers.authors: Zineb El Idrissi, Hafsa EL KADIRI, Tabyaoui Hajar, Anas Azenzoul, Nacer Mahouat
papers.abstract: Corporate tax fraud is a growing phenomenon not only in terms of legal control and audit but also in terms of corporate responsibility and stakeholder control. This study aims to describe how Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) governance and internal control mechanisms could work together to prevent companies’ tax fraud and improve tax behavior. The research was conducted using a qualitative methodology. The study involved 15 semi-structured interviews with experts in corporate taxation, auditing, control, and governance. The interviews were analyzed using Nvivo software. The results of the study revealed that ESG governance could improve the situation if it is integrated with tax responsibilities through the development of appropriate control mechanisms. They also showed that there is a significant decoupling risk between ESG goals and actual tax behaviors due to competing financial and managerial incentives. The analysis also revealed that the prevention of corporate tax fraud requires an ethical and accountable governance system, whistleblower policies, ESG disclosure mechanisms, and digital technologies. Such technologies as artificial intelligence could be used to improve monitoring and detect tax fraud in a timely manner. The research provides theoretical and practical contributions to the understanding of how to prevent corporate tax fraud by transforming ESG governance mechanisms and internal control systems. It also provides several suggestions for practitioners and policymakers in the field.

papers.title: METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TRAINING FOR FUTURE COMPUTER SCIENCE TEACHERS
papers.authors: Анаргул Нариманова, Maira D. Koshanova, Кажиакпарова Жадыра Сериковна
papers.abstract: This article is devoted to the development and experimental verification of a scientific and methodological model for teaching generative artificial intelligence to future computer science teachers. The relevance of the research lies in the rapid integration of artificial intelligence technologies into educational systems and the growing need to develop digital competencies among future teachers. The study used a mixed-methods approach, including theoretical analysis, pedagogical experiments, surveys, observations, and statistical data processing. The proposed model is purposeful, includes substantive, technological, and evaluative components and is aimed at the systematic introduction of generative artificial intelligence tools into the educational process. The purpose of the research is to develop and scientifically substantiate a methodological model for teaching generative artificial intelligence to future computer science teachers. The study was conducted at the Khoja Ahmed Yasawi International Kazakh-Turkish University and the West Kazakhstan Innovative and Technological University, which 75 students attended. The level of students' artificial intelligence competence in the experimental group showed a significant increase compared to the control group, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed model. The results show that the introduction of generative artificial intelligence tools into the educational process has a positive impact on the development of professional, digital and creative competencies of future teachers. The proposed scientific and methodological model can serve as a practical basis for improving artificial intelligence education in universities.

papers.title: HYBRID EDUCATIONAL ECOSYSTEMS IN UPPER SECONDARY EDUCATION: A SYSTEMIC AND ETHICAL APPROACH TO AI DISRUPTION
papers.authors: Victor Alfonso Crispin Castrejon
papers.abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in upper secondary education is transforming teaching and learning processes beyond the physical classroom and contributing to the formation of digitally mediated educational ecosystems. This study examines the impact of AI integration on student behavior, ethical attitudes, academic performance, and critical thinking at High School No. 7 of the University of Guadalajara. The aim of the study is to identify the relationship between the frequency of AI use and changes in students’ behavioral, academic, and ethical patterns, as well as to assess whether AI functions primarily as a learning-support tool or risks becoming a substitute for independent thinking. Using a systemic ecosystem approach, the research considers not only technological adoption but also its cognitive and ethical implications in the context of the Sustainable Development Goals. Methodologically, a quantitative diagnostic study was conducted to examine the relationship between the frequency of AI use and behavioral changes among students, considering both personal interests and required curricular content. The findings reveal a complex relationship between AI use and educational outcomes. Although frequent use is associated with time-saving practices and a potential risk of cognitive dependence, a weak positive association was identified between intensive AI use and academic integrity. Contrary to assumptions about increased passivity, frequent AI users demonstrated higher levels of source verification and informed skepticism. The results suggest that sustained interaction with AI may contribute to the development of algorithmic literacy when its use occurs within an educational environment that prioritizes ethics, critical thinking, and responsible engagement over speed and convenience.

papers.title: Turkish Adaptation of the AI Motivation Scale (AIMS): A Self-Determination Theory Approach
papers.authors: Şahin Gökçearslan, Hatice Yıldız Durak, Nebi Yılmaz
papers.journal: International Journal of Studies in Education and Science
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has underscored the need to better understand students’ motivation to learn with AI. Motivation is a key determinant of students’ engagement and effective use of AI-supported learning environments; however, there is a scarcity of validated instruments grounded in robust motivational theory and adapted to different cultural contexts. Recently, the Artificial Intelligence Motivation Scale (AIMS), based on Self-Determination Theory, was developed to assess university students’ motivation to learn with AI across five dimensions: intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, and amotivation. The present study aims to adapt the AIMS into Turkish and to examine its validity and reliability among Turkish university students. The study sample consisted of 221 undergraduate and graduate students from 10 universities in Türkiye. Following a translation and back-translation procedure, the Turkish version of the AIMS was administered online. The factorial structure of the scale was examined using first- and second-order confirmatory factor analyses, and internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha coefficients. The results supported the original five-factor structure and demonstrated acceptable model fit and satisfactory reliability coefficients. The second-order analysis provided partial support for a higher-order AI motivation construct. Overall, the findings indicate that the Turkish version of the AIMS is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing university students’ motivation to learn with AI in the Turkish education context.

papers.title: The Role of Generative AI in Supporting Students’ Group Work in Flipped Law Courses
papers.authors: Mikko Hyttinen, Ville Isomöttönen
papers.journal: International Journal of Studies in Education and Science
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but its role in supporting group work in flipped classroom settings remains underexplored. This study examined how students used AI to support group work in a flipped law course and how they perceived its role in collaboration. The participants were 86 international business students, and the data were collected through a survey and analysed using qualitative content analysis. The findings show that students primarily perceived AI as a learning tool rather than as a tutor, teacher, or group member. Students viewed AI as useful for dividing and structuring tasks, helping groups begin their work, and enabling the teacher to focus on groups requiring additional support. They also perceived AI as helpful in navigating culturally diverse perspectives in international groups. However, students emphasised that AI could not replace the emotional support, physical presence, and personalised guidance provided by a teacher. They also expressed concern that overly comprehensive AI-generated responses could reduce further group discussion and limit collaboration and critical thinking. The study contributes to research on AI-supported collaborative learning by showing that AI can support the initiation and organisation of group work in flipped classroom settings. However, its pedagogical value depends on clear guidance that ensures AI support, rather than replaces, meaningful collaboration.

papers.title: Shaping the Future: The Use of Machine Learning in Predicting Students’ University Admissions
papers.authors: Ali TAŞ, Furkan ŞİMŞEK, Burak Şimşek, Gülşah Taşçı
papers.journal: International Journal of Research in Education and Science
papers.abstract: This study aims to predict the university admission status of students using machine learning algorithms. In this context, support Vector Machines, K-Nearest Neighbors, and Random Forest algorithms were used for prediction. The models were evaluated using students' data, employing accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score metrics. The overall best results came from Support Vector Machines because it achieved 82.80% accuracy and 89.23% F1 score which demonstrates its effectiveness with high-dimensional datasets. The K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm achieved its best results through sensitivity (96.52%) and specificity (80.95%) which helped it separate different classes effectively. The interpretability of Random Forest proved to be its main benefit despite its lower overall performance. The research demonstrates that machine learning algorithm success depends on the characteristics of the dataset and the specific classification objectives. This study was conducted in the context of the feature of 785 students aged 18-20. The research was carried out using three different machine learning algorithms. For future studies, it is recommended to use more student features, additional algorithms, and expanded sample sizes to improve prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Exploring Secondary Teachers’ Perceptions of AI Integration in Teaching and Learning
papers.authors: Melissa Daggett, Casey Kirk
papers.journal: International Journal of Research in Education and Science
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) presents both opportunities and challenges for secondary education. Our qualitative study focused on secondary teachers' perceptions of AI integration in the classroom, examining their beliefs, experiences, and concerns. Drawing on Transformative Learning Theory, our research investigated how teachers conceptualize AI, their willingness to adopt AI-driven tools, and the perceived risks related to time, academic integrity, and student learning. The case study approach utilized semi-structured individual interviews and focus groups with secondary educators to provide insights into their evolving attitudes and factors influencing AI adoption. The promises and perils of AI outlined can inform professional development, policy considerations, and pedagogical strategies to support ethical and effective AI use in education.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Avatars in Competency-Based Education: Human Oversight for Personalised and Ethical Learning
papers.authors: Caleb Chin Poh Or
papers.journal: International Journal of Research in Education and Science
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence avatars are increasingly proposed as scalable tutors, coaches, and assessors within competency-based education (CBE). While these systems promise personalised learning pathways, adaptive feedback, and fine-grained evidence of mastery, their use in high-stakes educational contexts raises fundamental questions about accountability, pedagogical integrity, and professional judgement. This conceptual opinion article argues that AI avatars should not be treated as autonomous instructional or assessment agents but as mediating systems whose outputs must remain subject to human oversight and professional interpretation. Drawing on scholarship in CBE, learning analytics, and AI ethics, the article proposes a human-oversight-centred design framework in which the AI avatar–learner interaction is embedded within explicit structures for ethical governance, moderation and calibration, pedagogical integrity, and professional judgement. By reframing AI avatars as bounded pedagogical partners rather than decision-making authorities, the article contributes a principled model to guide institutions experimenting with AI-enhanced competency-based learning while safeguarding educational values, equity, and human agency.

papers.title: Navigating Uncertainty: Urban Teacher Agency in an AI-Mediated Educational Landscape
papers.authors: Mina Min, Sejin Lee, Songhee Kim
papers.journal: International Journal on Social and Education Sciences
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in educational settings, yet how teachers develop agency toward AI adoption remains underexplored. This study examines how Korean teachers working in the Seoul metropolitan area experience AI integration by focusing on contextual factors they navigate, benefits and challenges encountered, and how they reconstruct professional agency. Guided by grounded theory, semi-structured interviews with 17 Korean teachers were analyzed using constant comparative methods. Findings indicated teachers experienced AI integration through intersecting influences including policy discourses, media narratives, institutional expectations, and resource constraints that both enabled participation and intensified normative pressures. Despite strong state coordination, teachers’ agency varied: some viewed AI as a tool requiring oversight, others as a professional partner, and others as a transformative force reshaping professional identity. These patterns reflect strategic responses to uncertain conditions rather than competency hierarchies. Implications for teacher educators, school leaders, and policymakers emphasize recognizing teachers as professional agents navigating uncertainty rather than passive implementers of technological change.

papers.title: Scaffolded Lexical Performance and Self-regulated Vocabulary Learning: Examining ChatGPT in University ESL/EFL Settings
papers.authors: Promethi Das Deep, Miao Li, İ̇smail Şahi̇n, Nitu Ghosh, Md. Shiblur Rahaman
papers.journal: International Journal on Social and Education Sciences
papers.abstract: Research on ChatGPT in ESL and EFL higher education is expanding rapidly, yet the evidence remains conceptually and methodologically fragmented across vocabulary development, academic writing performance, motivational modelling, and learner autonomy. This study employed a qualitative synthesis of peer-reviewed journal articles to systematically examine and integrate empirical findings on the pedagogical use of ChatGPT in tertiary ESL and EFL contexts. Drawing on heterogeneous research designs, including experimental, mixed-method, and survey-based studies, the review identifies patterns across outcome measures and theoretical frameworks. The literature indicates that ChatGPT enhances scaffolded lexical performance, writing fluency, and learner engagement when embedded within structured instructional environments. Most studies, however, assess performance on AI-supported tasks rather than on independent vocabulary retrieval, which limits claims about durable lexical internalization. The findings indicate that ChatGPT primarily functions as a mediational scaffold and sustained self-regulated vocabulary development depends on deliberate instructional sequencing, critical engagement, and the gradual withdrawal of AI support to strengthen autonomous language control.

papers.title: Digital Literacy for Adopting Artificial Intelligence in University’s Leadership Roles
papers.authors: Chunting Guo, Alan Robert White, Supot Rattanapun
papers.journal: International Journal on Social and Education Sciences
papers.abstract: The rapid application of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has increased the relevance of digital skills and basic AI skills for university leaders. However, there is limited actual information regarding the correspondence between existing leadership competencies and AI change competencies. This quantitative study examined the extent to which university leaders in Henan Province, China currently possess digital and AI skills and the extent to which they want to be proficient. Eight skill areas were included in a questionnaire distributed to 400 leaders in public and private universities. Priorities and skill gaps were identified using simple statistics and the Priority Needs Index (PNI Modified). The findings indicate that leaders perceive their digital and AI skills to be at a medium to high degree, but gaps exist between the current and desired levels in all aspects. The use of AI in research and university management, as well as online communication and collaboration, are the most significant areas needing improvement. The study provides evidence to inform the development of leadership skills and institutional regulations that would enhance the inclusion of AI in higher education in a sustainable and ethical manner.

papers.title: Thinking about originality: creativity in legal research
papers.authors: Chris Dent
papers.journal: Queen Mary Journal of Intellectual Property
papers.abstract: With the rise of AI, there has been an increase in legal interest in what it means to be creative. The approach taken here is to focus on an area of endeavour – academic legal research – that is well-known to the law. This form of research, specifically the practices of both doctrinal and socio-legal research, will be assessed against a range of understandings of ‘creativity’, drawn from disciplines that include psychology. The analysis will demonstrate that our work is, in fact, creative. This conclusion will be the basis for an assessment of the role of ‘authority’ in legal research, as well as a consideration of its intersection with the test of ‘originality’ in current copyright law. That said, there is no need to see legal research as creative; however, there may be value in the use of the term for students and junior academics – to allow them to explore the possibilities of the discipline.

papers.title: Warhol v Goldsmith and the shrinking canvas of fair use: a comparative critique of artistic expression in US and UK copyright law
papers.authors: W Oshada Rodrigo
papers.journal: Queen Mary Journal of Intellectual Property
papers.abstract: The landmark Warhol v Goldsmith decision has catalysed a doctrinal recalibration of transformative fair use in the United States, tightening judicial scrutiny and elevating market substitution as a dominant criterion. This shift narrows the interpretive scope previously afforded by cases like Campbell and Cariou, constricting expressive latitude for remix culture, digital reappropriation and emerging artistic practices, including AI-generated works. Parallel trends in UK copyright law, marked by restrictive interpretations of fair dealing exceptions such as parody and pastiche post-Deckmyn and Shazam, similarly constrain creative freedom by demanding explicit critical engagement and limiting tolerance for nuanced homage or intertextuality. Against the backdrop of evolving participatory artistic ecosystems and algorithmic creativity, these converging jurisprudential trajectories risk ossifying copyright law into a gatekeeping mechanism privileging proprietary control over cultural dialogue. This paper argues for a doctrinal evolution towards an ‘expressive pluralism’ framework that embraces medium sensitivity, layered communicative functions and contextual transformation beyond overt market impact or explicit critique. Through a proposed Four-Step Expressive Reuse Test, the study offers a comparative judicial roadmap for recalibrating fair use and fair dealing to better align copyright law with contemporary modes of creativity, fostering a sustainable cultural commons that balances authorial rights with the imperative of artistic innovation in the digital age.

papers.title: Systematic literature review, bibliometric analysis, and future research framework
papers.authors: Chetanya Singh, Manoj Kumar Dash, Rajendra Sahu
papers.abstract: This chapter provides a systematic literature review, bibliometric analysis, and a future research framework for digital assistant acceptance in online shopping. The first covers the introduction and the three-way method to the review, including a systematic literature review, a bibliometric overview, and a critical review. The second section includes the flowchart of the systematic review and details of the review data. It emphasizes yearly publications, top journal publications, and country-wise publications. The third section covers the findings of the bibliometric evaluation, including authorship analysis, keyword co-occurrence analysis, citation analysis of institutions, and bibliographic coupling of publications. It also explores the primary research clusters and develops a future research framework. The fourth section covers the critical review of literature on online shopping acceptance, digital assistant acceptance in online shopping, factor citations, and multi-criteria decision-making. The fifth section concludes the chapter.

papers.title: To Authors: Verify and Read Your References!
papers.authors: Gail M. Sullivan, DEBORAH E. SIMPSON
papers.abstract: An author makes a strong statement in an article and cites a reference in support.A reviewer checks the reference, which they know very well as they are a co-author.In fact, the cited article says the opposite of the statement it is used to support.The reviewer is perplexed: How could this happen? Scenario 2A reviewer is reading an assigned manuscript in their area of expertise.As the reviewer toggles between the manuscript and references, they are puzzled that recent, pertinent references are missing.Most references are more than 10 years old, yet there are important new developments in this area.The reviewer thinks: Are these authors knowledgeable about the field? Scenario 3An author cites articles to support key statements in the introduction.The journal editor, interested in the topic, looks up some of the referred articles from familiar medical education journals.The editor is surprised to find that several articles do not exist; they are fabricated or AI-hallucinated.Yet, in their disclosure statements, the authors state there was "no use of generative AI."The editor wonders: How did AI infiltrate the manuscript?Are the authors' disclosures false? Scenario 4Journal staff carefully check each cited reference in an accepted article to determine if it has been accurately cited in the required format.Many references are incomplete or have incorrect issue numbers or pages, and some journal names are abbreviated incorrectly.It takes time to correct the references so that they are accurate, findable by readers, and support the statements to which they are attached.Staff ask: Why does this keep occurring?Journal of Graduate Medical Education (JGME) reviewers, editors, and editorial staff are increasingly experiencing these scenarios in submitted articles.Yet references are an essential aspect of scholarship.Providing a reference citation demonstrates that an evidence source exists and that it has been read, understood, and appropriately integrated into the manuscript's thesis.Inaccurate references create a cascade of concerns and may delay a manuscript's decision or publication.

papers.title: Development of two‐phase framework for driver behavior classification and representative motion prototyping for a reliable simulation‐based driver monitoring system
papers.authors: Kezia Amanda Kurniadi, Woojin Kim, Daesub Yoon
papers.abstract: Abstract Driver monitoring systems (DMS) are critical for safe autonomous driving, which requires accurate behavior recognition and reliable simulation environments for validation. This study proposes a robust two‐phase framework that combines a classification model and a prototype selection procedure to automatically generate realistic motion baselines from the acquired 3D skeleton data. Phase 1 uses a spatial temporal graph convolutional network to classify driver behaviors, and Phase 2 leverages class‐wise mean trajectories to interpret motion prototypes and select the closest real sequence, creating a verifiable motion trajectory library for simulation‐based safety testing. Our approach addresses DMS challenges through prototype visualization, robustness via discriminative embeddings, and standardized simulation scenarios, making it suitable for human–AI interactions in automotive safety systems. This framework produces a motion library of a real recorded sequence that can be directly used for simulation scenario generation and demonstrated through Metahuman retargeting and visualization in Unreal Engine.

papers.title: HASHIMOTO’S ENCEPHALOPATHY: A FORGOTTEN CAUSE OF ACUTE ALTERED SENSORIUM
papers.authors: Patel Rushikumar Piyush, Dr. Ankit Notwani, V. Ramachandran
papers.abstract: Introduction: Hashimoto’s encephalopathy (HE), or steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT), is a rare, underrecognized autoimmune neuro-endocrine disorder. It presents with acute or subacute neuropsychiatric features, ranging from altered sensorium and stroke-like episodes to status epilepticus. Because patients are frequently euthyroid, diagnosis is often delayed. Case Report: A 48-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of acute onset altered sensorium, visual hallucinations, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Physical examination revealed an agitated patient with fluctuating consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale 11/15) and hyperreflexia. Routine metabolic panels, toxicological screens, and contrast-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated elevated protein (68 mg/dL) with normal cellularity and negative infectious PCR panels. Electroencephalography (EEG) showed diffuse bi-frontal theta-delta slowing. Thyroid function testing revealed euthyroid status (TSH 2.10 mIU/L), but serum anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies were markedly elevated at >1,000 IU/mL. Results: After excluding infectious, metabolic, toxic, and vascular etiologies, a diagnosis of HE was established. High-dose pulse methylprednisolone (1 g/day intravenously) was initiated for 5 consecutive days. The patient exhibited rapid neurological recovery within 48 hours, regaining baseline orientation with resolution of seizure activity. An oral prednisone taper was maintained, and follow-up at 3 months confirmed complete cognitive recovery without recurrence. Conclusion: HE remains a forgotten differential diagnosis in acute altered sensorium. Normal thyroid function does not rule out the disease. Early recognition and prompt administration of high-dose corticosteroids yield remarkable clinical recovery, preventing unnecessary invasive interventions and permanent neurological damage.

papers.title: Assessing medical interns’ perception regarding the use of artificial intelligence on critical thinking and clinical reasoning
papers.authors: Abeer Ahmed Kassem, Sally F. Mohamed, Azza Awad Aboraya, Amel Hashish
papers.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots have made medical education more efficient. However, many medical students and residents are unaware of AI. Since a major reason for diagnostic errors is a lack of higher cognitive abilities, integrating AI may help enhance critical thinking (CT) and clinical reasoning (CR). Aim This study aimed to explore medical interns’ perceptions of AI in relation to CT and CR. Patients and methods This study adopted an exploratory qualitative design using focus group discussions to collect qualitative insights from the medical interns at Tanta University Hospitals who studied the Integrated Medical Bachelor Program. Results Analysis of the focus group discussion revealed that the interns showed general awareness of CT and CR and recognized their importance. But they lacked the structured approach and practical application of these skills. Similarly, while they understood the concept of AI, especially chatbots, they had a limited understanding of its practical applications in healthcare and education. Despite this, they expressed a strong willingness to learn about and adopt AI. Conclusion These findings highlight the need for targeted educational interventions to strengthen interns’ structured use of CT and CR, as well as to enhance their practical understanding of AI applications in medicine.

papers.title: Prompt engineering for academic and clinical writing: A practical guide for clinicians
papers.authors: Alessandro DE CASSAI, Elisa Pistollato, Tommaso Pettenuzzo, Burhan Dost, Nicolò Sella, Annalisa Boscolo
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, offering potential benefits ranging from literature synthesis and clinical decision support to patient education and documentation assistance. However, the quality of LLM output is highly dependent on the quality of the instructions provided, a process known as prompt engineering. This article introduces clinicians to the foundational principles and advanced techniques of prompt engineering, enabling clinicians to extract accurate, contextually relevant, and clinically safe responses. Key strategies discussed include role prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, few-shot learning, and output constraint specification. The paper also addresses domain-specific considerations, including hallucination risk, the importance of clinical verification, and ethical obligations when using artificial intelligence-generated content in patient care contexts.

papers.title: Correlation of Emotional Maturity and Physical Activity in Adolescents of Working and Non-working Mothers
papers.authors: Mehreen Bandmaster, Megha Basavaraj Logavi, Mona Kishan Vachhani
papers.journal: Medical Journal of Dr D Y Patil Vidyapeeth
papers.abstract: Background: Adolescence is a critical developmental phase during which emotional maturity (EM) and physical activity (PA) significantly influence overall well-being. The former supports emotional regulation and interpersonal development, while the latter benefits both mental and physical health. Given the central role of mothers in child development regardless of their employment status, this study explores how maternal employment correlates with adolescents’ EM and PA. Methodology: A cross-sectional study was conducted from February to August 2025 among 600 adolescents aged 14–17 from high schools and pre-university colleges (PUCs) in Belagavi city, India. EM was assessed using the Emotional Maturity Scale (EMS) by Dr. Tara Sabapathy, and PA was measured with the Physical Activity Questionnaire for Adolescents (PAQ-A). Data were analyzed using SPSS software (SPSS Inc.; Chicago, IL) version 29.0.10. Result: There was no statistically significant difference in the age, height, weight, or body mass index (BMI) of both groups. Adolescents of non-working mothers had higher EM, while those of working mothers were more physically active. An inverse correlation was found between the two. Conclusion: Maternal employment status influences adolescent development: adolescents of working mothers tend to be more physically active, while those of non-working mothers exhibit higher EM. The inverse relationship suggests a potential trade-off, highlighting the need for balanced developmental strategies.

papers.title: A comparative cross-sectional study on the accuracy, readability, and understandability of AI-generated (ChatGPT and Google Gemini) versus traditional patient information sheets for labor epidural analgesia
papers.authors: Michell Gulabani, Geetanjali T Chilkoti, Medha Mohta, Swati Jain
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated tools are being studied in diverse areas of anesthesia. A labor analgesia (LA) patient information sheet (PIS) forms the foundation to include “a pain free delivery experience” in a parturient’s obstetric plan. The present study was planned to compare and evaluate the accuracy, readability, and understandability of the two AI-generated PISs on labor epidural from ChatGPT and Google Gemini (GG) with the human-made, traditional PIS. Ten experts in the field of obstetric anesthesia evaluated the accuracy and completeness of each PIS on labor epidural, both the AI-generated versions, and the traditional PIS based on a Likert scale (from 1 to 10). The readability of each PIS was evaluated by the Flesch Reading Ease. The Patient Materials Education Assessment Tool analysis was performed by all experts for the three drafts. Descriptive statistics were used to calculate the mean scores for accuracy and completeness. A one-way ANOVA followed by post hoc comparisons using the Tukey test was performed to assess statistical differences between the drafts. Inter-rater reliability across the 10 raters was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient. A statistically significant mean difference for both accuracy and completeness was found on comparing the traditional PIS versus GG (P = 0.012). Readability ease and understandability were comparable between drafts. ChatGPT and GG were both more actionable than traditional PIS (P = 0.001). Google Gemini was more accurate, complete, and actionable than traditional PIS but at par with ChatGPT. AI-generated PISs must be reviewed and validated by clinical experts.

papers.title: Investigating the Health Implications of Asymptomatic Obesity through Clinical and Epidemiological Metrics in the Population of Lucknow and Adjoining Areas
papers.authors: Arti Yadav, Satyendra Kumar Sonkar, Vikas Bharti, Suchit Swaroop
papers.abstract: A BSTRACT Background: Even when there are no obvious chronic illnesses present, obesity can cause hidden health issues. Obese people who are asymptomatic may have early, frequently undetectable physiological and clinical alterations. For prompt prevention and management, it is important to comprehend these early consequences. Objectives: To evaluate the early physiological and clinical effects of asymptomatic obesity in adults without diagnosed chronic illness and to explore the role of anthropometric indicators in timely identifying hidden health risks. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional study in which 90 asymptomatic obese subjects of both sexes, aged 18–60 years, who attended outpatient department, were included. Anthropometric, demographic, and clinical parameters were recorded. Results: The study found a higher obesity rate among asymptomatic obese subjects in the age groups 40–49 and 50–60 (28%) with a body mass index (BMI) of 25–29.5, and in the 30–39 age group (35%) with a BMI of 30–45. A significant positive correlation was found between hip circumference (HC) and waist–height ratio (WHtR) ( r = 0.396, P = 0.000). In addition, differences in WHtR and systolic blood pressure were noted ( P < 0.05 for both genders). In the BMI range of 25–29.9, approximately 15.5% of subjects experienced joint-related pain, whereas 20% faced both stress and sleep-related issues along with joint pain. About 16.6% subjects in the BMI range of 30–45 had stress and sleep-related issues with joint-related pains. Conclusion: Asymptomatic obesity in adults aged 30–49 years shows early signs of physical and psychological strain despite the absence of diagnosed chronic illness. Significant correlations among BMI, waist circumference, and HC support their role in early risk detection. Joint pain, stress, and sleep disturbances were common, indicating hidden health impacts. These findings highlight the need for early screening and preventive care to reduce long-term risks.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in medical education: Assessing knowledge and perception of faculty at College of Medicine, Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Dammam
papers.authors: Ethar M. Sewaket, Fatima H. Alali, Shahd W. Alusaimi, Ruqayyah M. Albahrani, Zahra A. Aleid, Sara A. Hashim, Farhat Nadeem Saudagar, Mohammad Ayub Zeeshan
papers.journal: Journal of Family and Community Medicine
papers.abstract: Abstract: BACKGROUND: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical education is rapidly increasing, so faculty members’ knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions may influence how effectively it is integrated into teaching and assessment. This study aimed to assess the knowledge, perceptions, and implications of AI in medical education among faculty members at College of Medicine, Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among faculty members using a structured validated questionnaire. Information sought included demographic characteristics, faculty's knowledge and perception about AI, its impact in medical education, its ethical implications and institutional policy on AI, and the AI tools used by the faculty. The questionnaire was disseminated to all medical faculty electronically via institutional email and WhatsApp messages. Data were entered and analyzed using SPSS, Version 26, and P ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. RESULTS: A total of 114 faculty members participated in the study; 89.5% acknowledged awareness of the concept of AI, and 66.7% were familiar with its applications. However, only 55.3% acknowledged its practical use in medical education. Most participants (86%) viewed AI as a useful tool for improving learning, content creation, and academic efficiency, but concerns were raised about accuracy and ethical issues (92.1%). Awareness of the institutional AI policy was limited, reported by only 50.9% of participants. CONCLUSION: Faculty members generally demonstrated positive perceptions of AI in medical education; however, gaps in knowledge, practical experience, and policy awareness highlight the need for targeted faculty development and institutional guidance to support its safe and effective adoption.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of transvaginal ultrasound versus endometrial histopathology in women with abnormal uterine bleeding: A single-center experience from Saudi Arabia
papers.authors: Ahmed A. Alsayyah, Ahmed Alessa, Osama H Alghamdi, Omar Mohammed Alghamdi, Haifa S. Al-Ghamdi, Mostafa H. Alyousif, Abdulraheem K. Alshenqiti, Tajammal Mustafa
papers.journal: Journal of Family and Community Medicine
papers.abstract: Abstract: BACKGROUND: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is a prevalent gynecological complaint that affects women’s quality of life and requires accurate diagnostic evaluation. Although transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is a noninvasive first-line imaging modality, endometrial biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis. However, there is no substantial evidence in Saudi Arabia of any discussion of the correlation between the endometrial biopsies of AUB and TVUS findings. Therefore, this study’s aim was to explore this gap and uncover the subtle relation between TVUS and the findings of endometrial histopathological samples. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted at King Fahd Hospital of the University, a tertiary referral center in Al Khobar, Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia, from November 2022 to November 2025. The medical records of women with AUB who had undergone TVUS and endometrial biopsy were retrospectively reviewed. Clinical, radiological, and histopathological data were extracted and analyzed using SPSS. Histopathology was used as the gold standard for assessing TVUS diagnostic accuracy and as a guide to the appropriate management. RESULTS: Of the 249 participants (mean age 47.5 years), histopathology identified endometrial polyps in 38.6%, malignancies in 4.4%, and hyperplasia in 2.8%. TVUS diagnostic sensitivity was low: 24.0% for polyps, 0.0% for hyperplasia, and 9.1% for malignancy, giving slight overall agreement with histopathology (κ =0.189). Notably, 40.0% of the normal scans yielded missed abnormalities, including 4 of 11 reported malignancies (36.4%). In multivariable regression, age was the only independent predictor of significant endometrial pathologies (adjusted odds ratio 1.14 per year, P < 0.001), while no significant association was seen in BMI and parity with the outcome of the biopsies. CONCLUSION: TVUS shows low sensitivity and poor agreement with histopathology, leading to missed significant lesions such as malignancies. Thus, as normal TVUS cannot rule out disease safely, histopathology remains the gold standard.

papers.title: Getting your publication right – Part 4 structuring a research manuscript: A guide to understanding, detecting, and preventing plagiarism
papers.authors: Aditya Mitra, R. S. Mohan Kumar, Velmurugan Natanasabapathy, Sonali Sharma, Geeta Asthana, Sonali Taneja, Suparna Saha, Shishir Singh
papers.journal: Journal of Conservative Dentistry and Endodontics
papers.abstract: Abstract Plagiarism is one of the most persistent ethical problems in academic and scientific publishing. Once limited to copying sentences from books, it has grown into a far more complicated challenge, driven by the internet, intense research competition, and the rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools. This article provides a thorough overview of plagiarism – definition, historical roots, types, contributing factors, detection tools, and regulatory frameworks with particular focus on recent developments through 2025/2026. The article pays special attention to India’s regulatory approach under the University Grants Commission 2018 Regulations, the global role of the Committee on Publication Ethics, and the newly published Generative AI Transparency 2024 guidelines. The central argument is that addressing plagiarism today demands a combination of good ethical education, clear institutional policies, honest AI disclosure, and a genuine commitment to original thinking.

papers.title: Parasites and Skin: Complex Interactions and Innovative Solutions
papers.authors: Falah Hasan Obayes Al-Khikani
papers.abstract: Abstract Parasitic skin infections, caused by organisms such as lice, scabies mites, and helminths, represent a significant clinical and research challenge due to their diverse clinical manifestations and potential to cause severe health complications. The skin, as the body’s primary barrier, provides an ideal environment for these parasites, which exploit its immune interactions and surrounding microbial ecosystem. This review synthesizes recent advances in understanding the epidemiology, pathogenesis, and management of these infections, while introducing novel hypotheses to guide future investigations. Current diagnostic tools include microscopic examination and molecular testing, while treatments range from topical agents like permethrin to oral medications such as ivermectin. However, these approaches often fall short in addressing issues such as drug resistance, recurrent infections, and the complex life cycles of parasites. Three hypotheses are proposed: The skin microbiome may modulate parasite virulence through microbial competition, epigenetic changes induced by parasitic infections could influence chronic inflammation and immune evasion, and skin-specific immune memory might be harnessed to prevent reinfection. Looking ahead, the integration of advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-based interventions, and multi-omics approaches holds transformative potential for improving diagnostics, treatment, and prevention. Drawing on recent studies to bridge current knowledge with innovative, evidence-based ideas, this article emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary strategies to overcome existing limitations. By exploring these emerging insights and future directions, the review aims to inspire researchers and clinicians to address the persistent burden of parasitic skin infections with renewed focus and creativity.

papers.title: Efficiency vs. safety in AI-enabled medical education: an ethical analysis of AI as a bridge or a wedge
papers.authors: Liu Yanling, Liu Huanhuan, Gao Jie
papers.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing medical education, promising faster workflows and richer learning resources while quietly reshaping how future clinicians think and act. This paper examines the central tension between efficiency and safety in AI-enabled medical education, asking when AI functions as a bridge that strengthens training and when it becomes a wedge that undermines it. Drawing on a targeted review of 1,266 pieces of literature on clinical decision support, diagnostic algorithms, and generative AI, we identify three interlocking ethical tensions: clinical efficiency versus health equity, cognitive convenience versus clinical judgment, and data-driven personalization versus professional integrity. Using role conflict theory, we demonstrate how these tensions manifest in the daily work of learners and clinical educators, who must simultaneously prioritize patient safety, promote independent reasoning, and adapt to AI-mediated workflows. We argue that medical education should treat AI not only as a technical tool but as a curricular and ethical problem: learners must be trained to question, calibrate, and sometimes refuse AI outputs. Framed this way, the task is not to decide for or against AI, but to design conditions under which it reliably acts as a bridge rather than a wedge.

papers.title: Impact of AI Exposure on the Development of English Language Skills: A Single-Participant Case Study-Based Investigation
