papers.title: Precisión y limitaciones de los chatbots de IA para responder a las preguntas de los pacientes sobre la cirugía de escoliosis
papers.authors: GuÓngör Alibakan, Yusuf SuÓlek
papers.abstract: Objective: The aim of this study was to analyze the accuracy, reliability, and quality of the content of responses provided by artificial intelligence (AI)-based chatbots to frequently asked questions related to scoliosis surgery. Methods: A set of 25 questions related to diagnosis, treatment options, surgical risks, and recovery was developed based on clinical experience. The responses were anonymized and evaluated by two orthopedic surgeons using a 4-point scale to rate accuracy, clarity, and consistency. Cohen's kappa coefficient was used for interrater reliability, and the Kruskal-Wallis test was used for statistical analysis. Results: ChatGPT 4o performed best, with 60% of responses rated as excellent. Gemini Advanced 1.5 Pro followed with 56%, while Microsoft Copilot performed poorly, with 76% of responses requiring moderate clarification. The differences between the chatbots were statistically significant (p < 0.001). ChatGPT 4o and Gemini did not differ significantly from each other (p = 0.850), but both outperformed Copilot (p < 0.001). Conclusions: AI chatbots show great potential for patient education in scoliosis surgery. ChatGPT 4o was the most effective, although complex queries still require medical supervision.

papers.title: Hardware implementation of AI-based fuzzy logic for real-time sign language interpreter robotic control using FPGA
papers.authors: Kshitij Shinghal, Amit Saxena, Avnesh Verma, Rajul Misra
papers.abstract: Abstract Communication barriers between hearing-impaired individuals and non-sign language users remain a significant challenge in modern society. Existing sign language recognition systems primarily focus on unidirectional communication and are often limited by high latency, excessive power consumption, and lack of robustness in uncertain environments. This paper proposes a novel FPGA-based Bidirectional Robotic Sign Language Communication System (BRSLCS) integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI), fuzzy logic, and robotic control for real-time assistive communication. The proposed architecture supports both forward communication, where sign language gestures are translated into text or speech, and reverse communication, where text or speech is converted into robotic sign language gestures through an actuated robotic hand. In the forward communication flow, gesture images captured using a camera are processed through preprocessing, feature extraction, AI-based classification, and fuzzy inference stages. In the reverse communication flow, speech or textual inputs are interpreted using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and mapped into robotic sign gestures controlled using FPGA-based actuation logic. The integration of fuzzy logic improves classification robustness and interpretability under uncertain conditions such as illumination variation, gesture ambiguity, and motion blur. FPGA implementation provides deterministic timing, low latency, hardware parallelism, and energy efficiency suitable for embedded real-time systems. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed system achieves 92-95% recognition accuracy with latency between 10-25 ms while consuming only 4-6 W power, outperforming conventional CPU and GPU-based implementations. The proposed BRSLCS provides a scalable and practical framework for inclusive communication systems in healthcare, education, public services, and human-robot interaction environments.

papers.title: Analisis faktor penerimaan pengguna terhadap adopsi Artificial Intelligence di Perguruan Tinggi melalui Extended UTAUT2
papers.authors: Jessica Nathania Kho, Hindriyanto Dwi Purnomo, Yessica Nataliani
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increasingly been used to support scientific writing, offering various benefits while simultaneously raising ethical challenges for higher education institutions. This situation highlights the need for targeted AI integration based on a comprehensive understanding of students’ acceptance and actual use. This study investigates the factors influencing users’ acceptance and actual use of AI in research and scientific writing using the Extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) framework and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected through a survey of 129 respondents from the Faculty of Information Technology, Satya Wacana Christian University (SWCU). The results indicate that Trust has the strongest influence on Behavioral Intention, followed by Habit and Social Influence. Meanwhile, Habit is the strongest predictor of Use Behavior, whereas Facilitating Conditions and Behavioral Intention do not significantly influence actual use. These findings provide evidence of an Intention–Behavior Gap, suggesting that actual AI use in scientific writing is influenced more strongly by established usage habits than by conscious behavioral intentions alone.

papers.title: Different Paths to Authenticity: Vision Transformers and ResNet Learn Distinct Cues for Real vs. Generated Image Classification
papers.authors: Sharon Arandia, Maria Fernanda Cortes, John Brown, Steven Cai
papers.abstract: Advances in AI-based image generation have enabled the creation of creative asset prototypes that are more cost-effective, faster to produce, and highly personalized; however, this also erodes trust in visual evidence. In this study, we train two deep learning architectures—ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16—to classify real images versus AI-generated images (AIGI). We utilize the MS COCOAI dataset (stripped of metadata), which includes AIGI from five generators: Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, Stable Diffusion 3, DALL-E 3, and MidJourney v6. We conclude that these architectures are highly efficient at the task; specifically, we find that: (1) transferring weights pre-trained on ImageNet increases the F1-score by over 20% compared to models trained from scratch; (2) applying techniques to address class imbalance yields negligible benefits; (3) these architectures exhibit generalization issues when trained on images from a single generator; and (4) ResNet-50 relies primarily on high-frequency texture cues, whereas ViT-B/16 depends on low-frequency color signals for detection.

papers.title: Student Perception of Artificial Intelligence-Generate Child Sexual Abuse Material: A Qualitative Content Analysis
papers.authors: Paige Horton, Amanda Isabel Osuna
papers.journal: Dignity A Journal of Analysis of Exploitation and Violence
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative AI and deepfake technology, has introduced new challenges in the production and dissemination of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). While existing research has examined the technological and legal implications of AI-generated child sexual abuse material, less is known about how the public, especially young adults who are most likely to use AI technologies, perceive these developments. The present study addresses this gap by examining undergraduate student perceptions of AI-generated child sexual abuse material at a medium-sized private university in the Southeastern United States. Using data from a Qualtrics survey, this study employed a qualitative content analysis of the open-ended responses to explore how students define AI and deepfake technology, perceive associated risks, and identify potential prevention strategies. Three themes were uncovered: 1) understanding AI’s foundations, capabilities, and societal impacts, 2) perceptions of the blurred boundaries between human and AI-generated content, and 3) proposed preventive measures involving both individual responsibility and institutional regulation. Findings suggest that while students demonstrate a general awareness of AI’s risks, there is variability in their depth of understanding and proposed solutions. These findings have implications for educational initiatives, policy development, and broader discussions of ethical AI use and the prevention of technology-facilitated exploitation.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-powered visual simulation in basketball training and competitive performance among collegiate basketball students in China
papers.authors: Ge Linna
papers.abstract: This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence-powered visual simulation in basketball training and competitive performance among collegiate basketball students in China. Specifically, it assessed artificial intelligence-supported training in terms of data capture through cameras and sensors, recognition and analysis of player movements, visual simulation and interactive training scenarios, performance analytics and coaching decision support, and training monitoring, workload control, and practical integration. Competitive performance was examined through game performance indicators, efficiency and context-adjusted evaluation, decision-making and perceptual-cognitive ability, physical performance and training responsiveness, psychological quality and mental functioning, and system-level and developmental conditions. The study employed a quantitative, comparative-correlational research design and involved 169 collegiate basketball students from Yancheng Institute of Technology. Data were gathered using a researcher-made four-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed through frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson product-moment correlation. Results showed that the respondents generally agreed with the implementation and usefulness of artificial intelligence-powered visual simulation, with an overall mean of 2.92 and a standard deviation of 0.73. Data capture through cameras and sensors obtained the highest composite mean of 2.95, while training monitoring, workload control, and practical integration received the lowest mean of 2.88. Competitive performance recorded an overall mean of 2.85 and a standard deviation of 0.70. Efficiency and context-adjusted evaluation ranked highest at 2.99, whereas decision-making and perceptual-cognitive ability registered the lowest mean of 2.76. No significant differences were found in the overall assessments when respondents were grouped according to year level and playing position. Playing years, however, produced significant differences in training monitoring, decision-making and perceptual-cognitive ability, physical performance and training responsiveness, psychological quality and mental functioning, and overall competitive performance. Most importantly, artificial intelligence-powered visual simulation was strongly and positively correlated with competitive performance, r = .760 r = .760 r = .760, p < .001 p < .001 p < .001. The findings suggest that greater exposure to coordinated visual simulation, movement analysis, performance feedback, and workload monitoring is associated with higher perceived competitive performance. Still, because the study relied on self-reported data from a single institution, the results indicate association rather than direct causation. A structured artificial intelligence-supported basketball training program is recommended to strengthen tactical decision-making, individualized feedback, physical responsiveness, and psychological preparation among collegiate players.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of body mass index, physical activity, sleep and stress levels among IVF and non-IVF pregnant women during the second trimester
papers.authors: M Pravalika
papers.journal: Journal of Current Research in Food Science
papers.abstract: Background: Pregnancy is associated with major physiological, nutritional and psychological changes. Body mass index (BMI), physical activity, sleep and stress are relevant components of maternal well-being. Women who conceive through in vitro fertilization (IVF) may experience a pregnancy requiring particular attention to nutritional and lifestyle factors. Objective: The study aimed to compare BMI and selected lifestyle and psychological factors, including physical activity, sleep and stress levels, among IVF and non-IVF pregnant women during the second trimester. Methods: A comparative cross-sectional study was conducted among 80 pregnant women aged 20–45 years, consisting of 40 IVF and 40 non-IVF pregnant women. Purposive sampling was used. Only second-trimester singleton pregnancies were included. Data were collected using a structured and pre-tested questionnaire through personal interviews. Anthropometric measurements, physical activity, sleep and stress information were obtained. Frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, independent t-test and chi-square test were used for analysis. Results: The mean BMI was 27.79 ± 5.82 kg/m2 among IVF women and 23.90 ± 3.91 kg/m2 among non-IVF women. The difference was statistically significant (t = 3.51, p < 0.05). Physical activity frequency also differed significantly between the groups (χ2=30.44, p < 0.05). Sleep duration did not differ significantly (χ2=3.32, p > 0.05). The mean stress score was 16.23 ± 2.98 among IVF women compared with 6.95 ± 2.18 among non-IVF women. Conclusion: The study observed differences between IVF and non-IVF pregnant women in BMI, physical activity and reported stress levels, whereas sleep duration did not differ significantly. These findings indicate the relevance of individualized nutritional, lifestyle and psychological support during pregnancy following IVF.

papers.title: AI ethics and digital governance: Principles, challenges and frameworks for responsible artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Dr.Rajeshwari Mishra, Shailendra Kumar
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology influencing governance, education, healthcare, finance, communication, public administration, and social life. The increasing integration of AI into decision-making processes has created significant opportunities for efficiency, innovation, accessibility, and economic development. However, it has simultaneously raised critical ethical and governance concerns relating to privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, human autonomy, cybersecurity, and digital inequality. AI ethics provides a normative foundation for ensuring that intelligent systems respect human dignity, fairness, justice, and fundamental rights, while digital governance establishes the institutional, legal, and technological mechanisms required to regulate their development and deployment. This paper examines the conceptual relationship between AI ethics and digital governance, identifies major ethical challenges associated with contemporary AI systems, and analyses international frameworks, including UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, OECD AI Principles, the European Union AI Act, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It further examines the relevance of responsible AI governance in India, particularly in relation to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and emerging digital governance structures. The study adopts a qualitative, descriptive and analytical approach based on secondary sources, policy documents, scholarly literature, and international regulatory frameworks. It argues that effective AI governance requires a human-centred, risk-based, transparent, inclusive, and accountable approach supported by institutional oversight, ethical impact assessment, public participation, and continuous monitoring. The paper concludes that ethical governance should not be treated as an obstacle to technological advancement but as an essential condition for sustainable, trustworthy, and socially beneficial AI.
keywords: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

papers.title: Scientometric Analysis of Research Trends in Smart and Sustainable Architecture in Educational Environments: With an Emphasis on Green Schools and Campuses
papers.authors: Milad Olfat, Faezeh Asadpour, Amir Hossein Shirdel
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research trends in sustainable and smart architecture within educational environments, with a particular focus on green schools and university campuses, during 1990 to 2025. Educational spaces, as crucial settings for knowledge development and social interaction, play a pivotal role in shaping sustainable behaviors among future generations. In recent decades, accelerated technological transformations, the global environmental crisis, and the necessity of aligning with sustainable development goals have highlighted the need for rethinking the design of educational facilities. Against this backdrop, this research aims to identify the intellectual structure, thematic clusters, and evolutionary trajectory of scholarly output in this field. Additionally, it seeks to determine the most influential authors, institutions, and countries contributing to the advancement of knowledge in sustainable and smart educational architecture.Methodology: The study employs a bibliometric and science-mapping approach. Data were collected from the Web of Science (WoS) Core Collection, one of the most authoritative international scientific databases, ensuring comprehensive coverage of high-quality scholarly works. A total of 736 documents—including research articles, review papers, and conference proceedings—published between 1990 and August 2025 were retrieved. After eliminating duplicates and cleaning metadata using Zotero, the data were processed with VOSviewer version 1.6.20. The analysis involved co-citation, co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and bibliographic coupling techniques, enabling the identification of research fronts, intellectual foundations, and emerging topics. This multi-stage procedure ensured a systematic, transparent, and reproducible analysis of the field.Findings: The temporal analysis revealed a relatively stable research output until the mid-2000s, followed by a significant surge beginning around 2010. This growth accelerated markedly post-2015, coinciding with the establishment of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This trend highlights the growing global recognition of sustainable educational environments as a critical research area. Citation analysis further identified highly influential works that established the theoretical foundations of the field, particularly those addressing biophilic design, environmental psychology, and international green building standards such as Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) and the Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method (BREEAM). Conceptual mapping indicated six interconnected domains of inquiry that collectively shape the intellectual structure of the field: Sustainable and Environmental Design; User Experience and Spatial Quality; Energy Efficiency and Green Buildings; Health and Sustainable Urban Development; Environmental Participation and Education; and Architectural Education with a Socio-Cultural Approach. Research on sustainable architecture and environmental design emphasizes integrating ecological and biophilic principles into school and campus planning, while studies on human experience and spatial quality explore comfort, perception, and well-being, with particular attention to children and students. Another important stream focuses on energy efficiency and building performance, highlighting the role of advanced digital tools such as Building Information Modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and smart energy systems in enhancing resilience and resource management. A further cluster links health, learning, and urban sustainability, examining how educational spaces contribute to public health, urban green infrastructure, and the broader sustainability agenda. In parallel, investigations into participation, education, and environmental behavior underscore the importance of cultural, social, and behavioral aspects in achieving long-term sustainability. Finally, research on architectural pedagogy and socio-cultural sustainability stresses the responsibility of architectural education and design studios in embedding cultural identity, social equity, and participatory practices into sustainable design processes. International collaboration analysis revealed that the United States, China, Australia, and several European countries are the leading contributors, forming robust scientific networks and advancing global standards. In contrast, developing countries in Asia and the Middle East are increasingly present in this field but face persistent challenges in adapting universal sustainability frameworks to their specific socio-cultural and climatic conditions. The findings also highlight a prevailing imbalance between technically oriented quantitative studies and the relative scarcity of qualitative, user-centered research that captures the lived experiences of students and communities within sustainable educational environments.Conclusion: The study concludes that research in sustainable and smart educational architecture has evolved from a narrow, technology- and energy-focused perspective to a multidimensional, interdisciplinary framework that integrates environmental, social, cultural, and psychological dimensions. Future directions are expected to be shaped by the convergence of advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twins, alongside participatory and biophilic design approaches. This paradigm shift will require bridging the gap between global frameworks and local conditions, ensuring that sustainable educational environments not only optimize energy performance but also promote well-being, equity, and a sense of place for students and communities. By providing a systematic mapping of the field over three and a half decades, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the intellectual landscape and future opportunities in sustainable and smart architecture for educational settings. The insights can guide policymakers, architects, and researchers in developing integrated strategies to design schools and campuses that serve as models of resilience, innovation, and ecological responsibility.

papers.title: Bibliometric Analysis and Co-word Mapping: The Field of Knowledge Graphs
papers.authors: Ameneh Shenavar, Saeed Rezaei Sharifabadi, Molouksadat Hosseini Beheshti, Akram Fathian Dastgerdi
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Purpose: The rapid expansion of research in the field of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) over the past decade has positioned The field as a dynamic area at the intersection of computer science, artificial intelligence. Following Google’s introduction of the KG in 2012, scholars and industry stakeholders have increasingly explored the conceptualization, development, and application of KGs across a wide range of disciplines. KGs, as structured representations of entities, relationships, and semantic information, enable machines to process heterogeneous data in a contextually meaningful and interpretable manner. Beyond traditional knowledge representation, new directions such as ontology modeling, semantic web integration, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are driving innovation. Despite these advances, large-scale, systematic, and global evaluations of the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and thematic clusters in the field of KGs remain limited. This study addresses this gap by examining the evolution of research in the field of KGs between 2013 and 2025 using bibliometric and scientometric approaches. The overarching purpose is to uncover research trends, identify leading contributors and institutions, explore co-authorship and co-word networks, and highlight conceptual clusters shaping the KG landscape. Methodology: This applied descriptive bibliometric study was conducted using the co-word analysis method. Data were collected from the Scopus citation database, covering outputs published between January 2013 to July 2025 that included the keyword "knowledge graph" in titles, abstracts, or author keywords. Keyword normalization reduced 19,141 initial keywords to 19,058 unique terms. After removing duplicates, excluding irrelevant records, and normalizing author, institution, and country names, a curated dataset of 9,000 articles was obtained. To enhance the accuracy of the analysis, keywords and knowledge graph-related concepts were carefully categorized and standardized. Data analysis and visualization were performed using VOSviewer, mapping collaboration networks and co-occurrence clusters. The study examines temporal publication and citation trends, prolific countries, funding bodies, influential authors, highly cited works, and thematic clusters, with particular focus on knowledge graph embedding, recommender systems, semantic web applications, and natural language processing. Findings: Results indicate that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has grown substantially, reaching a publication peak in 2024 with 2,541 articles and 33,701 citations. Asia contributes the majority of publications (83.7%), with China accounting for 6,889 articles (76.5% of the total). The United States ranks second with 987 publications, followed by the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia. This trend reflects strong investment by Chinese funding bodies—particularly the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) and the National Key Research and Development Program. Leading publication outlets include IEEE Access (345 articles), Knowledge-Based Systems (293 articles), and Applied Sciences Switzerland (248 articles), with many top journals in the Q1 quartile of Scopus. At the author level, Markus Kraft (University of Cambridge) leads with 48 publications, while Chinese researchers dominate the top ten. Co-authorship analysis revealed seven author clusters (42 nodes, 62 links) and broad participation from 136 countries, with China, the US, and Germany serving as central hubs of international collaboration. Co-word analysis identified six major clusters, including graph neural networks, deep learning, ontology, KG embeddings, question answering, and large language models (LLMs). Highly cited works include comprehensive surveys on KGs published between 2017 and 2022 in leading computing journals, which have shaped the understanding of KG construction, refinement, and applications. . Emerging contributions, such as roadmaps on unifying LLMs and KGs, along with applications in digital twin systems and scientific entity recognition, illustrate the field’s ongoing shift toward integrating advanced AI paradigms. Conclusion: The bibliometric analysis reveals that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has rapidly emerged as a dynamic interdisciplinary area, characterized by strong publication growth, a high geographic concentration in Asia, and expanding international collaboration networks. Chinese institutions and scholars play a leading role, supported by significant policy and funding initiatives, while Europe and North America remain important contributors. Thematic clustering highlights both the consolidation of established domains—such as ontology, the semantic web, and knowledge representation—and expansion into cutting-edge areas, including graph neural networks, embeddings, digital twins, recommender systems, and large language model (LLM) integration. These findings provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure and evolving dynamics of research in KGs, offering valuable insights for future studies. Scholars can use this mapping to identify promising areas of inquiry, foster international collaborations, and navigate the funding and publication landscape. Ultimately, KGs play a pivotal role in advancing intelligent systems, semantic technologies, and digital transformation across sectors such as healthcare, education, natural language processing, and recommender systems. The integration of bibliometric analysis with scientometric evaluation further underscores the maturity of this field and its potential to shape next-generation knowledge-driven applications.

papers.title: Futures Studies of Takaful Accounting in Iran
papers.authors: Mohammad Javad Zare Bahnamiri, Mohammad Hasan Maleki, Amirabbas Salemi
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: In recent decades, the Takaful industry has experienced a rapid growth in Islamic countries as a Shariah-compliant alternative to conventional and Western insurance. With the increasing demand for transparency and compliance with Shariah principles, the need for specialized accounting frameworks for this industry has become prominent. The introduction of Takaful into Iran’s formal insurance system has created multiple challenges in the areas of recognition, measurement, and financial disclosure, necessitating a future-oriented approach. The primary objective of this research is to identify and analyze the key driving forces shaping the future of Takaful accounting in Iran, to prioritize these drivers, and to develop plausible scenarios for this future. Accordingly, the findings of this study can provide a scientific and policy-oriented roadmap for insurance companies, regulators, and professionals.METHODS: This research is applied in terms of purpose and adopts a mixed-methods approach in terms of methodology. To achieve the research objectives, a combination of two quantitative methods—the Fuzzy Delphi Method and the MARCOS multi-criteria decision-making method was depolyed. The number of experts participating in this study was 15, considered appropriate and acceptable for judgment-based and expert-centered methods. The expert evaluation questionnaire was developed based on a literature review, and to assess its validity, the Content Validity Ratio (CVR) and Content Validity Index (CVI) of Lawshe were applied. The research process was conducted during 2024–2025. This study was conducted in four stages. In the first stage, the drivers influencing the future of Takaful accounting were identified through a literature review. In the second stage, expert evaluation questionnaires were distributed among selected experts to screen the identified drivers using the Fuzzy Delphi Method. In the third stage, the key drivers affecting the future of Takaful accounting in Iran were prioritized to extract the final drivers via the MARCOS multi-criteria decision-making method. In the fourth stage, the plausible Takaful accounting scenarios in Iran were mapped using the final drivers, with focus group interviews as the primary tool.FINDINGS: In the first stage, an initial list of drivers influencing the future of Takaful accounting in Iran was prepared through a review of previous studies. In this stage, 25 drivers were identified and classified into five main categories: socio-cultural, technological, regulatory, market-related, and economic drivers. In the second stage, the Fuzzy Delphi Method was employed to screen these drivers and identify the key ones. For this purpose, a questionnaire was designed and distributed among a group of experts. As a result of this process, 17 drivers were excluded due to not meeting the required criteria, and 8 drivers were selected for final ranking. The Content Validity Ratio (CVR) and Content Validity Index (CVI) of Lawshe were calculated for the drivers in this study, confirming that all retained drivers possessed acceptable validity. In the next stage, these 8 drivers were further evaluated using the MARCOS method to rank and prioritize them based on multiple criteria. According to the scores, the drivers “competitiveness of Takaful against conventional insurance” and “development of Islamic financial culture” received the highest priority. In the final stage, future scenarios for Takaful accounting were developed based on these two high-priority drivers and focus group interviews. Each driver consisted of two contrasting states. The contrasting states for the first driver are: low competitiveness of Takaful against conventional insurance versus high competitiveness of Takaful against conventional insurance. The second driver also has two contrasting states, which are: significant development of Islamic financial culture versus weak development of Islamic financial culture. Overall, four plausible future scenarios for Takaful accounting in Iran were derived, reflecting different combinations of these two drivers, including significant development of Islamic financial culture alongside low competitiveness of Takaful, significant development of Islamic financial culture alongside high competitiveness of Takaful, weak development of Islamic financial culture alongside low competitiveness of Takaful, and weak development of Islamic financial culture alongside high competitiveness of Takaful.CONCLUSION: Considering the four plausible scenarios for the future of Takaful accounting in Iran, it is essential for policymakers and insurance companies to adopt a set of coordinated measures to enable the sustainable and competitive development of Takaful. These measures should contribute both to the expansion of Islamic financial culture and to strengthening the competitiveness of Takaful against conventional insurance. The following recommendations are structured around five key areas. Key areas for action include establishing a legal and regulatory framework for the formation of Takaful companies, providing tax incentives, formulating Shariah-based regulations, and creating specialized regulatory bodies to enhance transparency and accountability; developing diverse, simple, and competitive insurance products tailored to societal needs while standardizing schemes to increase trust; conducting public awareness campaigns, promoting Islamic financial culture, and training specialized human resources; utilizing artificial intelligence, blockchain, and data analytics to improve processes, transparency, and efficiency; and expanding Takaful reinsurance, establishing Shariah-compliant guarantee funds, and employing Islamic financial instruments within company structures.

papers.title: From Legislation to Underwriting: A Regulatory Analysis of the Insurability of Artificial Intelligence and The Internet of Things in the European Union
papers.authors: Fatemeh Najibzadeh Vamegh Abadi, Sayyed Mohammad Hadi Ghabooli Dorafshan, Hosein Naseri Moghaddam
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) systems, characterized by data-dependence, learning capabilities, continuous updating, and multi-actor interaction across supply and operational chains, has challenged classical models of liability allocation and the logic of insurability with new forms of uncertainty. Because AI and IoT systems often evolve after deployment, operate through interconnected hardware and software layers, and distribute control across manufacturers, developers, deployers, operators, importers, and service providers, they complicate the identification of the legally relevant act, the responsible person, and the causal path linking malfunction to damage. These characteristics challenge the assumptions on which traditional civil liability and insurance have long relied, namely relative stability of product configuration, clearer boundaries between product and service, and a more direct relationship between conduct, fault, defect, and harm. In the European Union, the consolidation of risk-based regulation under the Artificial Intelligence Act and the redesigning of product-defect liability under the revised Product Liability Framework have strengthened the capacity to translate technological risk into legally auditable and actuarially priceable risk. Yet this transformation is not linear. The same reforms that clarify certain duties may also broaden the circle of potentially liable actors, expand recoverable damage, and intensify disputes over evidentiary access, causation, and allocation of loss in complex socio-technical ecosystems. This article therefore assesses the extent to which the emerging legislative architecture enhances liability predictability and supports the insurability of AI-IoT-related risks, while identifying the points at which interpretive and enforcement heterogeneity, together with aggregated and correlated risks, may undermine insurability. The article also asks whether the EU’s current model merely improves ex ante risk governance, or whether it can also sustain ex post compensation through insurance markets under the conditions of technological opacity, cross-border litigation, and systemic exposure.METHODs: Adopting a legislative-interpretive approach and a normative analysis of the core EU instruments, the study proceeds along three axes: (1) the construction of risk and compliance obligations in the AI Act; (2) the redefinition of “product,” “liable person,” the scope of compensable harm, and related evidentiary mechanisms in the revised Product Liability regime; and (3) the implications of the absence of an EU-wide harmonized layer of proof in fault-based liability following the abandonment of the AI liability initiative. On the first axis, the analysis focuses on how the AI Act turns technical and organizational requirements into legally reviewable obligations, including data governance, documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, post-market monitoring, and traceability across the system lifecycle. On the second axis, it examines how the revised Product Liability Framework accommodates software-intensive and update-dependent technologies by extending the concept of product, broadening the category of accountable economic operators, and facilitating the production and disclosure of evidence in disputes involving technical opacity. On the third axis, it evaluates the legal and insurance consequences of leaving fault-based claims subject to divergent national procedural and evidentiary regimes, especially regarding standards of proof, access to information, judicial timing, and causation analysis. These legal elements are then mapped onto the technical variables of insurance underwriting, including data and model auditability, the control of moral hazard and adverse selection, aggregation-risk management, premium differentiation, the design of compliance-based policy conditions, deductibles, limits of liability, exclusions, and the structuring of reinsurance responses to low-frequency and high-severity events.FINDINGS: Clearer liability boundaries and measurable obligations, particularly in high-risk domains, enable insurers to rely more heavily on external compliance benchmarks, reduce dispute costs over causation and fault, and support more realistic risk-based pricing and contractual design. The AI Act contributes to this outcome by transforming broad expectations of safe and trustworthy AI into verifiable legal duties that can function as underwriting signals, policy conditions, and claims-handling reference points. The revised Product Liability Regime likewise improves legal intelligibility by clarifying the status of software and digitally integrated systems, by extending possible liability beyond the narrow figure of the traditional manufacturer, and by facilitating evidentiary access in contexts where defect and causation would otherwise remain difficult to establish. From an insurance perspective, these developments improve observability, reduce some information asymmetries, and create a more structured basis for calibrating premiums, exclusions, deductibles, and coverage triggers. Nevertheless, the findings also show that the same architecture generates new pressures on insurability. The expanded set of potentially liable actors, the rise of multi-defendant litigation, and the difficulty of quantifying certain data-related and non-pecuniary losses, combined with divergence in evidentiary standards and adjudicatory timelines across Member States, introduce divergent legal risk into pricing functions and place market capacity under strain, especially in low-frequency, high-severity, and highly correlated scenarios such as update shocks, security incidents, and systemic failures. This is particularly important where a single defect, update, model error, or cyber event may affect large numbers of devices or users simultaneously, thereby turning what appears to be isolated liability into accumulated exposure. The absence of a harmonized evidentiary layer for fault-based liability means that legal uncertainty remains unevenly distributed across jurisdictions, increasing reserve volatility, claims administration costs, and the difficulty of maintaining consistent underwriting standards across the internal market.CONCLUSION: Effective insurance responses to AI-IoT risks depend on three concurrent linkages: (1) lifecycle traceability and auditability of data and models; (2) tying coverage to compliance-based conditions and robust incident-logging and event-recording obligations; and (3) a minimum degree of interpretive and institutional coordination to reduce evidentiary fragmentation and cross-border transaction costs. Absent these linkages, fault-shifting within ecosystemic chains and correlated risks may destabilize premiums and constrain market capacity. Accordingly, standardizing baseline disclosure and event-recording requirements, periodically reviewing regulatory regimes against insurability metrics, and strengthening reinsurance mechanisms and risk pools are central to sustaining insurability and ensuring continuity of compensation in an evolving technological environment.

papers.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence in Predicting Banking Crises: Analysis of Audited Data in Accordance with National Standards in Iran’s Banking System
papers.authors: Bashar Qasim Tuaib, Ali Ashtab, Pari chalaki
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: This study aims to develop and validate an artificial intelligence-based early warning system for predicting banking crises in Iran by integrating audited financial data, audit quality indicators, and macroeconomic variables, thereby improving the accuracy and interpretability of crisis forecasting for regulatory and supervisory applications. A comprehensive dataset of 792 bank-year observations from 22 Iranian banks over the period 2004–2023 was analysed. The study employed multiple predictive models, including XGBoost, Random Forest, LSTM, Transformer, and classical logistic regression. Key variables included the capital adequacy ratio (CAR), non-performing loans (NPL), return on assets (ROA), liquidity ratios, audit opinion types, audit tenure, disclosure quality, GDP growth, inflation, and exchange rate volatility. Model performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation and accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR metrics. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was used to ensure model interpretability and to identify key risk drivers. XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy (96.10%), AUC-ROC (0.982), and F1-score (0.96), outperforming logistic regression by reducing Type I errors by 59.8% and Type II errors by 61.1%. SHAP analysis showed that CAR (20.8%), NPL (17.6%), and ROA (15.6%) were the most influential predictors, while audit quality variables contributed 13.5% to overall model performance. The NLP module achieved 93.2% accuracy in classifying audit opinions and an AUC-ROC of 0.947 using textual features alone. Artificial intelligence, particularly XGBoost combined with SHAP interpretability and NLP-enhanced audit analysis, provides a robust and actionable framework for predicting banking crises in Iran, offering significant improvements over classical statistical methods for proactive regulatory intervention.

papers.title: Evaluating Expressed Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Model Outputs: A Viewpoint on a Proposed Assessment Framework (Preprint)
papers.authors: Zhangshu Joshua Jiang, Zina M. Ibrahim, James Teo
papers.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical documentation, information synthesis, health communication, and decision-support tasks. Evaluation must address the quality of their outputs in clinically meaningful terms, not only whether a response reaches an expected answer. Endpoint correctness can conceal important failures in problem representation, differential prioritisation, response to new evidence, temporal synthesis, uncertainty, and safety. Existing clinical benchmarks address overlapping aspects of these qualities through physician-authored criteria and task-specific scoring, but organise them in different ways. Medical education offers established approaches to making selected aspects of clinical reasoning observable for assessment. Its instruments were developed for human learners: their validity does not transfer automatically to LLMs, and a generated explanation does not establish how a model produced its answer. We therefore use medical-education assessment traditions as sources of constructs and task-design logic, not as prevalidated scoring tools for model outputs. We propose a provisional seven-domain framework for evaluating expressed clinical reasoning: the clinically defensible organisation, interpretation, and updating of available patient information in a generated response. The domains cover accuracy and grounding, validity and completeness, diagnostic and management reasoning, temporal reasoning, uncertainty and updating, clinical safety, and communication. They are organised into an evidential foundation, an expressed-reasoning core, and clinical guardrails. Proposed five-point behavioural anchors are applied only to relevant domains and components. Case-specific reference criteria permit defensible alternatives, and judgements are made using evidence available at the specified decision point. Prespecified safety-critical breaches are flagged separately and cannot be compensated for by strong scores elsewhere. The framework is intended for offline evaluation, error analysis, and benchmark design. It is not a validated measurement instrument, a measure of internal model reasoning, or evidence of readiness for clinical deployment. We outline priorities for independent content review, feasibility testing, domain-level agreement assessment, and evaluation of automated judging before stronger measurement claims are made.

papers.title: A Tutor(bot) for Every Student: Tutorial on Building and Deploying Customized Large Language Model Instructional Assistants (Preprint)
papers.authors: Conan MacDougall, Carrie Evans, Katherine Gruenberg, Janice Jiang, Queenie Leung, Elizabeth Gatewood
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND Students and educators are interested in the potential of generative artificial intelligence (gAI) large language models (LLMs) to provide individualized instruction, but commercial LLMs are not optimized for pedagogically sound student-instructor interaction. The configuration of expert systems to act as tutors has historically been technically complex. Now, with widespread access to LLMs, configuration is broadly accessible. OBJECTIVE To develop and perform early evaluation of no-code LLM-based course-specific customized generative pretrained transformer (cGPT) models (“tutorbots”) in health professions settings. METHODS We developed tutorbots using the cGPT function of ChatGPT to support courses in infectious diseases pharmacotherapy (School of Pharmacy; SOP) and symptom recognition and management (School of Nursing; SON). Content experts rated cGPT interactions for accuracy and teaching behavior. Students in the courses were invited to complete a survey on the usability and value of the tutorbots. Feedback was also gathered via focus group discussion. RESULTS Experts gave favorable ratings on the tutorbots’ accuracy (83-100%), identification of learners’ mistakes (75-95%), answer-withholding behavior (75-80%), provision of appropriate direction (80-95%), and tone (100%). Among survey respondents (SOP: 58/114 [51%], SON: 12/33 [36%]), about three-quarters reported using the tutorbot at least once during the course. Common themes for not using the tutorbot included a lack of time, a lack of confidence in using AI, and an unclear value relative to other study methods. Users generally viewed the tutorbots as engaging and accurate; 63% (SON) - 75% (SOP) rated them as very valuable for learning, and 72% (SON) – 92% (SOP) would definitely recommend tutorbots for other courses in the curriculum. Themes from qualitative analysis of respondent comments included use for self-assessment and explanation, the right balance between withholding and revealing answers, factual accuracy versus clinical judgment, and calibration of question difficulty. Step-by-step processes for constructing and deploying tutorbots were compiled into a how-to document and an interactive cGPT to enable other faculty to deploy tutorbots in their courses. CONCLUSIONS Development and customization of tutorbots on a commercial LLM platform was achievable without technical expertise, and students had favorable views of their usability and value for learning.

papers.title: Effects of Generative AI–Supported Virtual Reality Dental Skill Training on Learning Performance, Visual Behavior, and Cortical Activation Among Dental Students: Stratified Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.authors: Yuting Wen, Chang Wen, Siyu Huang, Yufei Chong, Yang Dong
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The rapid advancement of AI, particularly generative AI (GenAI), is reshaping educational paradigms. However, its utility in preclinical digital medical skills education remains insufficiently explored. OBJECTIVE: This study aims to investigate whether GenAI‑assisted training yields superior performance relative to traditional instruction in virtual reality (VR)-supported preclinical dental skill education. METHODS: A total of 123 eligible students from a top‑tier Chinese university completed the trial. Participants were stratified by baseline theoretical scores and randomly assigned within each stratum into two arms: the GenAI-assisted group (n=62) received ChatGPT guidance without human tutoring, with research assistants monitoring AI outputs solely for safety and error checking; the teacher-led control group (n=61) received on-site instructor guidance. Both groups underwent standardized VR-based dental skill training for 7 days. Assessments included dental operative skill examinations, functional near-infrared spectroscopy recording, continuous eye-tracking monitoring, visual-spatial ability tests, and questionnaires measuring self-regulated learning, learning emotions, and engagement. RESULTS: =3.88, Cohen d=0.70; P<.001). For secondary outcomes, the GenAI‑assisted group also demonstrated significantly lower cognitive‑load indicators (mean 0.180, SD 0.136) than the control group (mean 0.346, SD 0.150; P<.001), accompanied by more efficient visual attention allocation patterns and stronger activation in prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, visual association cortex, and temporoparietal junction brain regions. The GenAI‑assisted group showed better performance across low (P=.003), medium (P=.004), and high (P=.004) level visual-spatial ability tests. Among low-achieving participants, the largest between-group difference in self-regulated learning was found in favor of the GenAI-assisted group (P=.02). Better scores were also observed for the GenAI‑assisted group in learning enjoyment, as well as behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. CONCLUSIONS: Students randomized to GenAI-assisted training had higher immediate operative scores than students receiving teacher-led instruction. Secondary cognitive, behavioral, and neurophysiological findings were exploratory and pointed toward a link between GenAI exposure and variations in skill‑acquisition metrics among dental students receiving VR-based training. The results offer preliminary insights regarding the potential integration of GenAI into preclinical dental skill education. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ChiCTR2500110063; https://tinyurl.com/2hkv5wt9.

papers.title: Integrating AI-assisted design thinking in citizenship education: Enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills
papers.authors: Novia Wahyu Wardhani, Eni Rahmawati, Ganda Febri Kurniawan
papers.abstract: This study aims to analyse the implementation of an AI-assisted design thinking learning model in enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills in Citizenship Education programmes. The study employed a qualitative approach involving undergraduate students from several Citizenship Education programmes at universities on Java Island, Indonesia. The learning implementation integrated artificial intelligence (AI) to assist students in exploring information, generating ideas and reflecting on solutions to civic and social issues. Research data were collected through observations of the learning process, analysis of students’ assignment documents, AI-assisted interaction records and group discussions conducted during the implementation of the model. Data were analysed descriptively to identify the dynamics of the learning process at each stage of design thinking. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design thinking encouraged students to engage actively in social problem analysis and problem-solving. During the empathise stage, students identified social issues through digital information exploration, AI use and group discussions, enabling them to understand problems from multiple perspectives. In the define stage, students formulated problems more systematically by identifying causal relationships and the underlying social contexts. The ideate stage encouraged students to generate alternative solutions creatively and collaboratively through group discussions and AI-supported idea development. In the prototype and test stages, students developed solution designs in the form of programmes or simple policy models and evaluated their effectiveness through reflection, feedback and AI-assisted analysis. The study concludes that AI supports, but does not replace, students’ critical reasoning, the quality of which depends on reflective pedagogical design.

papers.title: AI-HRM Adoption and HR Performance in Egyptian Banks: The Mediating Role of Digital Literacy and HR Analytics Capability
papers.authors: د. هشام رمضان عيسى حسان
papers.journal: Mağallaẗ Rāyaẗ Al-Dawliyyaẗ Lil ʿulūm Al-Tiğāriyyaẗ
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), especially generative AI, is rapidly revolutionizing how organizations attract, develop and retain talent within human resource management (HRM) (Venugopal et al., 2024). However, empirical studies on the adoption of AI-HRM in the banking sectors of emerging markets are scarce, and the pathways through which AI investments translate into tangible HR performance improvements are not well-understood (Prikshat et al., 2023; Singh & Pandey, 2024). This study addresses both limitations by developing and testing a structural model of AI-HRM adoption antecedents and performance outcomes in the Egyptian banking sector — a strategically important yet empirically underexplored context undergoing CBE-mandated digital transformation. The study explores the impact of Organizational Readiness, AI Adoption Level and Regulatory Compliance on Recruitment Efficiency and Employee Retention, supported by the theoretical basis of Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV), and with the mediating mechanisms of Digital Literacy and HR Analytics Capability. A quantitative cross-sectional survey (N=134 target; HR professionals across Egyptian public, private, foreign and Islamic banks) is analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Organizational Readiness does not consistently improve recruitment or retention when considering capabilities. However, its positive impact on HR outcomes is fully mediated by Digital Literacy and HR Analytics Capability and before these capabilities are fully developed, readiness may even be negatively related to recruitment efficiency. AI Adoption Level demonstrates two different roles: it influences Employee Retention both directly and indirectly via HR Analytics Capability, while its effect on Recruitment Efficiency is completely mediated by Digital Literacy, suggesting that improvements in front‑end efficiency rest on the HR staff's capacity to shape and interpret AI solutions. Regulatory Compliance rises as an uneven institutional driver, positively affecting Recruitment Efficiency but having no measurable effect on retention. The proposed study reproduces the frameworks of TOE and RBV within the setting of AI‑HRM not just in Egypt but in a regulated developing-market financial sector and provides concrete recommendations to both HR leaders and regulators who want to implement digital technologies while ensuring compliance and good HR outcomes.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

papers.title: The impact of AI-Based Recruitment on Quality of Hiring: The mediating role of Candidate Experience
papers.authors: رانیا سقراط, جاكلين دميان, تامر سيد كامل خليفة
papers.abstract: By increasing organizational effectiveness and decision-making, quick adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has significantly altered recruitment procedures. This study examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI) affects hiring results, with a particular emphasis on the mediating role of candidate experience. Data were gathered from Egyptian human resource (HR) professionals using a quantitative research design. The findings show that hiring quality and candidate experience are positively impacted by AI adoption, with candidate experience acting as a key mediator in this relationship. The proposed conceptual framwork was examed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with AMOS and the Bootstrap Bias-Corrected Percentile Method to assess both direct and indirect relationships among the study variables. The results reveal that AI in Recruitment has a significant positive effect on enhanced candidate experience (β = 0.880, p < 0.05), explaining 71.2% of its variance (R² = 0.712). Enhanced candidate experience also exerts a significant positive influence on the quality of hires (β = 0.886, p < 0.05; R² = 0.745). Furthermore, AI implementation directly improves the quality of hires (β = 0.945, p < 0.05; R² = 0.777). The research contributes the theoretical understanding of candidate experience as an additional concept. In order to improve recruitment results, practical implications include the necessity of transparent AI systems, frequent feedback, and cultivating an innovation-oriented culture. The cross-sectional approach and the concentration on a single nation are limitations that point to potential avenues for further investigation into cross-cultural comparisons and longterm impacts.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management
