papers.title: Evaluation of Post-Mastectomy Patients for Eligibility of Autologous Breast Reconstruction by Extended Latissimus Dorsi Flap
papers.authors: Hedayat Khaled Zaky Mansour, Amr Magdy Mahmoud, Dina Mohamed Hanafy, Lina Salah
papers.abstract: Introduction: The extended latissimus dorsi (LD) flap provides a pedicled autologous option for post-mastectomybreast reconstruction. Its main limitation is the amount of tissue available relative to the volume required for breastreconstruction.Aim of work: To evaluate post-mastectomy patients eligibility for autologous breast reconstruction using theextended LD flap and to assess the ability of preoperative anthropometric and imaging measurements to predictpostoperative volume.Patients and methods: Prospective cohort study was conducted at Ain Shams University Hospitals over 12months. Women aged 20–60 years after unilateral mastectomy, with A–C cup breasts and no stated contraindicationto surgery, underwent clinical anthropometric assessment, mammographic estimation of contralateral breastvolume using the Kalbhen formula, and superficial ultrasound assessment of donor-site tissue thickness. The thesisreports 30 patients screened, 15 meeting the reconstruction criteria, 10 selected for detailed assessment, and fiveunderwent surgery. Postoperative assessment was done at 3 months.Results: The 10-patient selected cohort had a mean age of 38.4 years and mean BMI of 30.8 kg/m². Estimatedtotal flap volume in the 10 assessed patients ranged from 456.0 to 1020.0 cm³, with a reported volumereplacementratio of 58.0–86.0%. In the five operated patients, preoperative estimated flap volume predicted3-month postoperative volume with 88.0–94.6% accuracy. BREAST-Q scores in the five operated patients werefavorable, with reported mean breast satisfaction, donor-site satisfaction, and donor-site function scores of 54, 61,and 74, respectively.Conclusion: Combined anthropometric and imaging-based assessment may assist in selecting patients in whoman extended LD flap can provide meaningful autologous breast volume.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Single-Anastomosis Gastric Bypass with Cruroplasty in Managing Patients with Reflux Symptoms and Weight Regain after Sleeve Gastrectomy
papers.authors: Mohamed Diaa Mohamed Abdelmohsen, Mohamed Magdy Abdelaziz, Mohamed Atef El Azazy, Mohamed Fared Ahmed
papers.abstract: Introduction: Obesity is a major global health challenge, with prevalence rising dramatically over the pastdecades. Bariatric surgery is considered one of the most effective strategies for achieving sustained weight lossand improving obesity-related comorbidities.Aim of work: To evaluate the effectiveness of single-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB) with cruroplasty inmanaging gastroesophageal reflux symptoms and weight regain in patients after sleeve gastrectomy.Patients and methods: This combined cohort study (prospective and retrospective) was conducted over oneyear at the General Surgery Department, Ain Shams University Hospitals, Cairo, Egypt. Ethical approval wasobtained, with informed consent for prospective participants and anonymized data for retrospective cases. Thestudy included a convenience sample of patients with prior sleeve gastrectomy who developed GERD, experiencedweight regain, failed medical therapy, and were scheduled for one-anastomosis gastric bypass with cruroplasty.Results: Revisional OAGB with cruroplasty after SG was performed in predominantly female patients (76.7%) witha mean age of 38.6 ± 9.2 years and BMI of 41.3 ± 4.8 kg/m². The mean interval from SG was 5.1 ± 1.9 years,with refractory GERD (93.3%) and weight regain (86.7%) predominating. Operative time averaged 128.4 ± 24.6minutes, hospital stay 2.8 ± 0.9 days, GERD resolution reached 86.7%, PPI use significantly declined, and excessweight loss reached 68.4% at follow-upConclusion: Revisional single-anastomosis gastric bypass (OAGB) with cruroplasty represents an effective andcomprehensive surgical approach for patients with refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease and weight regainfollowing sleeve gastrectomy

papers.title: Abdominoplasty After Weight Loss Post Bariatric Surgery
papers.authors: Hagar Magdy Mahmoud
papers.journal: Al-Azhar International Medical Journal /Al-Azhar International Medical Journal
papers.abstract: Background: Massive weight loss after bariatric surgery often leads to excessive skin in the abdominal area, causing restriction of functions, hygiene-related issues, and psychological problems for many patients. Abdominoplasty is a common surgical option for these problems; however, there are no studies on post- bariatric patient-reported outcomes and complications. Objective: To assess patient satisfaction with abdominoplasty procedures for patients who have had massive weight loss after undergoing bariatric surgery. Patients and Methods: In this prospective observational study, a total of 25 post-bariatric abdominoplasties were conducted in patients who had achieved a stable weight following a bariatric procedure. Demographic, clinical, and surgical data were recorded. We used a six-month follow-up period with a BODY-Q questionnaire, which measures abdominal satisfaction and psychological well-being, along with a four-point scale to determine satisfaction. Post-operative complications were also investigated statistically. Results: The study participants were predominantly female with a mean BMI of 29.98 kg/m². The most used modality in abdominoplasty was full abdominoplasty. The complication rate in the postoperative period among participants was 32%, predominantly for wound reasons, with no venous thromboembolic complications. Significant improvements in abdominal satisfaction and psychological well-being were shown using the BODY-Q, measuring an increase from 14 to 90 at 6 months postoperatively. Patient satisfaction in the postoperative period was generally high at 72%. The only predictor of complications in the postoperative period was BMI. Conclusion: Abdominoplasty after bariatric surgery has distinct benefits, including improvement of abdominal appearance, psychological state, and patient satisfaction, with a satisfactory safety profile.

papers.title: Evaluation of Serum Homocysteine Level in Type II Diabetes Mellitus for Diagnosis of Diabetic Nephropathy
papers.authors: Fatma Ahmed Sayed Mourad, Eman Roshdey Mohamed, Dalia Mohmoud Eldewi, Aya Ahmed Abdelrahman Mohamed
papers.journal: Al-Azhar International Medical Journal /Al-Azhar International Medical Journal
papers.abstract: Background: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a common microvascular complication of type 2 diabetes(T2DM), leading to progressive renal damage. This study evaluates serum homocysteine (Hcy) as a potential biomarker for early identification of diabetic nephropathy. Aim: To assess the clinical importance of blood Hcy as a diagnostic biomarker for diabetic nephropathy in cases having T2DM. Patients and method: This comparative research has been performed at Al-Zahraa University Hospital on 60 subjects: twenty type II DM cases with DN, 20 type II DM patients without nephropathy, and twenty healthy age- and sex-matched controls (30 males, 30 females). Subjects were recruited after oral and written consent, with ethical approval, between November 2022 and January 2024, and have been separated into 3 groups: Group I—healthy controls, Group II—DM without nephropathy, and Group III—DM with nephropathy. Results: Groups were comparable in age and sex, while BMI, diabetes duration, blood glucose, renal function, and lipid profile differed significantly, with the worst values in Group III. Serum homocysteine was highest in Group III and showed excellent diagnostic performance in distinguishing diabetic nephropathy from diabetes without nephropathy (AUC = 0.981). Conclusion: Homocysteine is elevated in type 2 diabetes, especially with nephropathy, and serves as a potential early biomarker.

papers.title: Neuropedagogical Alpha Training Technology: Integrating EEG Analysis into Correctional and Developmental Practice
papers.authors: Miklyaeva Natalya
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: This article introduces a neuropedagogical alpha-training technique implemented through interdisciplinary collaboration among specialists in special education, speech therapy, psychology, and neurophysiology. The technique utilizes electroencephalogram (EEG) analysis to personalize the correctional and developmental process for children with disabilities. Rather than a highly specialized medical procedure, this alpha-training is a scientifically grounded, systematic technology suitable for special education environments, relying on cooperation between medical professionals, educators, and neuropsychologists. The method is based on the principles of neuroplasticity and operant conditioning. A detailed training algorithm ranges from baseline EEG monitoring to practical sessions using biofeedback hardware and software systems. Systematic alpha-training promotes psycho-emotional stabilization, optimizes cognitive rhythms, and facilitates the development of stable neural networks, thereby establishing a solid foundation for the effective schooling of children with disabilities. The viability of the approach was verified through a systematic literature review conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 protocol. The results confirmed the high efficacy of the method and its significance for modern neurodefectology.

papers.title: Human creativity and artificial creativity: an exploration through the “Titan 2358” project
papers.authors: Olivier Moreau
papers.abstract: This paper explores the dynamics between human creativity and artificial creativity, drawing on a personal approach at the crossroads of art and science, as well as on the Titan 2358 project, a hybrid work combining art, science, fiction, history, philosophy and artificial intelligence. Human creativity is analysed through the theoretical frameworks of Margaret Boden (Novelty, Surprise, Value and Combinational, Exploratory, Transformational) and Mark A. Runco (the four Ps: Person, Process, Product, Potential). Artificial Creativity (a concept forged by Runco) is analysed by an Artificial Intelligence in response to a very lengthy prompt written after researches by the author. Three visions are compared con-cerning AC in general (it is possible, it is not yet possible, it is impossible). The discussion comments on that analysis and tries to explain why AC is impossible using the theory of Antonio Damasio who highlight the importance of affects, emo-tions, sentiments, consciousness and homeostasis in the creative process. Ray Kurzweil contradicts this point of view and affirms that computers are, or soon will be, far more intelligent and creative than humans. But can a computer decide to create art to please other computers or to increase its chance of survival? Can AC be a revolutionary tool for artists, just as photography was at one time? In appendix a conversation between the author and the AI provides some interesting insights on the Human versus Artificial creativity.

papers.title: Any Artificial Intelligence Tool Use Experience and Depression–Anxiety Symptom Profiles Among Rural University Students in China
papers.authors: Keren Zhou, Yi Zhang, Yuxin Yang, Zhuang Bian, Zhenxing Lin
papers.abstract: Purpose: Associations of artificial intelligence (AI) tool use with concurrent depressive and anxiety symptoms among rural university students remain uncertain. We explored associations of any AI tool use experience with depression–anxiety symptom profiles. Methods: This cross-sectional survey included 1529 students with rural household registration from three universities in Zhejiang, China. GAD-7 and PHQ-9 scores informed latent profile analysis; five conceptually ordered multinomial models compared profile membership with the low-symptom profile. Results: The profiles comprised low symptoms (n=896; 58.6%), anxiety-predominant symptoms (n=587; 38.4%), and depression-predominant symptoms (n=46; 3.0%). In the reported fully adjusted model, AI use experience was associated with lower odds of anxiety-predominant membership (OR=0.764, 95% CI 0.654– 0.893) and depression-predominant membership (OR=0.239, 95% CI 0.101– 0.566) compared with low-symptom membership. Conclusion: AI use experience and symptom patterns were associated in this exploratory sample. These observations warrant longitudinal assessment with more detailed measures of AI engagement. Keywords: artificial intelligence, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, rural university students, latent profile analysis

papers.title: Effects of the Integration of Medical Treatment and Prevention on Glycaemic Control Among Patients with Diabetes in Qianjiang District, China: A Difference-in-Differences Study
papers.authors: Huawei Tan, Xiaochong He
papers.abstract: Background: The Integration of Medical Treatment and Prevention (IMTP) is one approach to integrated disease management within China's primary healthcare system. Evidence on its association with glycaemic control and potential behavioural pathways among patients with diabetes remains limited. Methods: We conducted a retrospective quasi-experimental study of 5676 adults with diabetes in Qianjiang District during 2023Q1-2024Q4. Four primary healthcare (PHC) facilities implemented IMTP in January 2024 (treatment group), while 26 formed the control group. Patient-level propensity score matching via the Super Learner machine learning algorithm (PSM-SLMLA) at the 2023Q4 baseline retained 1240 patients per group (19,840 patient-quarter observations). Weighted difference-in-differences (DID) models included facility and quarter fixed effects with facility-clustered inference. Results: IMTP was associated with a 3.73% relative reduction in HbA1c (95% CI, 0.04%-7.29%; β = -0.0380; 95% CI, -0.0757 to -0.0004; P = 0.048), equivalent to approximately 0.27 HbA1c percentage points at the pre-intervention mean. Pre-intervention coefficients were not jointly significant (P = 0.857), and sensitivity estimates remained negative. Exploratory indirect associations were -0.0021 through active follow-up behaviour (95% bootstrap CI, -0.0037 to -0.0007; P = 0.004) and -0.0006 through staple-food intake behaviour (95% bootstrap CI, -0.0026 to -0.0001; P = 0.014); the exercise adherence estimate included zero. Formal interaction tests did not identify heterogeneity (all P for interaction > 0.05). Conclusion: IMTP was associated with modest short-term glycaemic improvement. Active follow-up behaviour may be a potential pathway. Increased staple-food intake raises a dietary-compensation hypothesis, but concurrent behavioural and HbA1c measurements preclude causal interpretation.

papers.title: EEG-Derived Pain Threshold Index-Guided Remifentanil Titration During Laparoscopic Abdominal Surgery: A Randomized Trial
papers.authors: Bin Cao, Zheng Qi, Yingying Zhao, Qiong Xue, Ren Juan-juan, Wei-Wei Xu, Yu-Ning Fan, Zhen-Hua Nan, Pei-Pei Sun, Huijuan Li, Jie Zhang, Jian-Jun Yang
papers.abstract: Objective: To determine whether remifentanil titration guided by the pain threshold index (PTi), an electroencephalography-derived proxy for nociceptive tolerance rather than subjective pain, reduces intraoperative remifentanil infusion during laparoscopic abdominal surgery. Methods: In this prospective, single-center, assessor-blinded randomized trial, adults undergoing elective laparoscopic abdominal surgery with propofol-remifentanil target-controlled infusion were assigned 1:1 to PTi-guided or conventional hemodynamic-guided remifentanil titration. The primary endpoint was intraoperative remifentanil infusion rate. The principal analysis used the full-analysis set and covariate-adjusted linear regression with heteroskedasticity-consistent robust standard errors. Results: Among 200 randomized patients, 195 were analyzed (98 PTi-guided; 97 control). The primary endpoint was neutral: mean (SD) remifentanil infusion rate was 7.44 (1.43) versus 7.63 (1.41) μg kg − 1 h − 1 ; adjusted mean difference, − 0.06 μg kg − 1 h − 1 (95% CI, − 0.44 to 0.32; P=0.758). Per-protocol results were similar. Median (IQR) NRS at post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) admission was 2.0 (2.0– 3.0) versus 3.0 (2.0– 4.0), and Ramsay score was 2.0 (2.0– 2.0) in both groups. In exploratory secondary analyses, rescue opioid was used in the PACU by 18/98 (18.4%) versus 31/97 (32.0%) patients and any rescue opioid through 48 h by 29/98 (29.6%) versus 44/97 (45.4%). Any postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) through 48 h occurred in 17/98 (17.3%) versus 29/97 (29.9%) patients. Total postoperative opioid exposure through 48 h was not reduced. Conclusion: PTi-guided remifentanil titration did not reduce intraoperative remifentanil infusion. PACU pain and sedation scores were not materially different. Lower early rescue-opioid use and fewer PONV events through 48 h were exploratory secondary findings, were not accompanied by lower postoperative opioid dose, and require prospective confirmation. Keywords: electroencephalography, laparoscopic surgery, nociception monitoring, pain threshold index, postoperative analgesia, remifentanil

papers.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence as a Link in Dementia Patient Education: Bridging Transparency, Trust and Understanding
papers.authors: Mohammad Sharif, Mobin Mottahedi, Fatemeh Hesami
papers.abstract: Abstract: Dementia is a growing global health burden, and artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded across dementia diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring. Because many of these systems are opaque, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, such as Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME), and gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM), have been developed to make model reasoning inspectable, and they have been applied extensively to dementia diagnosis. Far less attention has been given to whether, and how, such explanations should reach the people whose lives the predictions describe. We advance this as a conceptual proposition and an underexplored opportunity, not as a finding of a systematic review. In this commentary, XAI in patient education means the third of three related but distinct things: model-level explainability, which makes a system’s computation inspectable; clinician-facing interpretability, which supports professional judgment; and patient-facing explanation, which is written to be understood by the person the prediction is about. Greater model interpretability does not by itself produce greater patient understanding. We examine what would have to be true for the proposition to hold. Explanations are only as truthful as the data that feed them, so patient-facing XAI presupposes sound data governance. Explanations can mislead, increasing trust without increasing truth. Dementia is heterogeneous, so explanation must be matched to an individual’s cognitive and communicative profile and retained abilities rather than to a general cognitive level. Explainability may support comprehension, but it cannot establish decision-making capacity, which is decision-specific. We therefore frame dementia education as a relational process among the person living with dementia, care partners, and clinicians, with AI in a supporting role, and outline what a deployable, governed, workflow-integrated system would require. Keywords: cognitive impairment, shared decision-making, health literacy, human-computer interaction, caregiver support

papers.title: Assessment of Perceptions, Trust, and Adoption of Clinical Artificial Intelligence Tools Among Physicians and Dentists, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
papers.authors: Jawaher M Alghofaily, Maha M. Alghofaily, Fatima Elshikh Mohammed Elhadi, Deema M Alturki, Amjad Ebrahim Alshommemri, Adam Dawria, Shorouq Shaker Aldrees, Malak A Alzoheri, Jihan Mesfer Alghamdi, Mariam H Ahmed, Mazahir E. Abdallah Mohammed
papers.abstract: Purpose: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly integrated into healthcare; however, their acceptance varies across professional groups. Understanding clinicians’ familiarity with and perceptions, trust, and adoption of clinical AI tools is essential for safe and effective implementation. This study assessed physicians’ and dentists’ perceptions, trust, and intention to adopt clinical AI tools in governmental university hospitals in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Participants and Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 400 clinicians selected from three major governmental university hospitals in Riyadh (King Saud University Medical City, King Abdulaziz Medical City-National Guard, and King Abdullah Bin Abdulaziz University Hospital), which serve as large tertiary academic centers at the forefront of digital health and AI implementation in Saudi Arabia. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire assessing familiarity, usage patterns, perceptions, trust, and adoption intention. The instrument demonstrated high reliability across subscales (Cronbach’s α: 0.880– 0.952). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, non-parametric tests, and multivariate linear regression. Results: Familiarity with AI was high (89.5%), with physicians reporting greater familiarity than dentists. Overall perceptions were moderate (mean 3.2– 3.8 on a 5-point scale), with physicians showing more positive views. Trust was generally low (mean 3.1– 3.6), particularly among physicians; dentists reported moderate trust. Intention to adopt was moderate (mean 3.5– 3.9), with physicians demonstrating higher adoption intention than dentists. Residents, physicians, and those in digitally advanced hospitals had significantly higher perceptions, trust, and adoption intention scores ( p < 0.05). Multivariate regression identified work setting, resident status, and physician specialty as the strongest predictors of higher scores across all domains. Conclusion: Despite high awareness, perceptions of clinical AI tools and intention to adopt them remain moderate and constrained by low trust. Targeted training, transparent systems, and regulatory support are essential for enhancing integration into practice. Keywords: artificial intelligence, clinical decision support systems, technology adoption, trust, physicians, dentists, Saudi Arabia

papers.title: From Consultation to Partnership: Leadership for Patient, Family, and Community Engagement in People-Centred Health Systems in LMICs: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Mohamed Abubakar Ahmed
papers.abstract: People-centred health systems depend on more than inviting patients, families, and communities to provide feedback. Meaningful engagement requires opportunities for people to influence decisions and healthcare organizations that can respond to their priorities. This structured narrative review used targeted searches of PubMed-indexed literature and World Health Organization sources to identify relevant reviews, health-systems studies, and recent evidence. The synthesis focused on leadership approaches that support a shift from one-way consultation to meaningful partnership in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), drawing on literature on community participation, patient and public involvement, co-creation, social accountability, and people-centred care. The literature indicates that partnership is more credible when leaders create inclusive representation, share decision-making, allocate time and resources, clarify accountability, and close feedback loops by showing how community input affects services. Common barriers include hierarchical decision processes, limited institutional capacity, unequal opportunities to participate, communication gaps, and poor follow-through on feedback. Drawing these findings together, this review proposes the LISTEN leadership framework: Listen, Include, Share Decisions, Train and Resource Participation, Establish Accountability Loops, and Notice Equity and Outcomes. The framework is presented as a practical synthesis rather than a validated instrument. People-centred leadership should therefore be assessed not only by whether patients and communities are invited to participate, but also by whether their involvement influences decisions, strengthens trust and responsiveness, and contributes to more equitable and higher-quality health systems.

papers.title: How Implementation Context Shapes Clinician Acceptance and Engagement with Guideline-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Primary Care: A Qualitative Study
papers.authors: Purvi Mehta, Pavani Rangachari, Alvin H. Tran, Susan Lambrecht-Smith
papers.abstract: Background: Guideline-based clinical decision support (CDS) tools have become central to promoting evidence-based, high-quality primary care. Despite widespread implementation, clinician adoption and sustained use remain inconsistent. Existing research has typically examined technological usability or organizational implementation factors separately, providing limited understanding of how these influences interact in real-world primary care settings. This study examined how organizational implementation context and clinician technology acceptance jointly shape adoption and sustained use of guideline-based CDS tools in US primary care using an integrated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) perspective. Methods: A qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis was conducted with 13 US primary care clinicians, including physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and pharmacists with prescribing authority. Participants were purposively recruited from diverse ambulatory settings. Semi-structured interviews explored experiences with CDS usability, workflow integration, organizational support, trust, cognitive burden, and implementation processes. Data were analyzed iteratively using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, informed by CFIR and TAM. Results: Six interrelated themes emerged. Clinician acceptance and sustained use of CDS were shaped by (1) workflow integration, (2) organizational legitimacy and leadership support, (3) preservation of clinical judgment, particularly with emerging AI-enabled CDS, (4) social reinforcement and team-based implementation, (5) cognitive and resource constraints, and (6) clinician role, experience, and digital comfort. Across themes, acceptance was driven less by technological capability than by the interaction of workflow design, organizational context, implementation climate, trust, and clinician perceptions. Conclusion: Guideline-based CDS implementation is fundamentally a sociotechnical process requiring alignment between technology, workflow, organizational context, and clinician acceptance. Integrating CFIR and TAM provides a comprehensive framework for understanding these interactions. The findings informed the TRUST framework, which offers practical implementation guidance emphasizing tailored workflow integration, reinforced organizational legitimacy, usability, social reinforcement, and transparent, trustworthy AI-supported CDS to support sustainable implementation in primary care.

papers.title: Development and Validation of a Machine Learning-Based Model for Elevated Depressive Symptom Risk in COPD Patients: A Multi-Cohort Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Zewen Cheng, Jian Wu, Xiaokun Yan
papers.abstract: Background: Depression is a common yet underrecognized comorbidity in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Existing prediction models often lack external validation, limiting cross-population generalizability. We aimed to develop and externally test machine learning models for predicting concurrent elevated depressive symptoms in COPD using three international aging cohorts. Methods: We included COPD patients from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS, USA, n=1,899) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, China, n=2,206) for model development, and the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA, UK, n=538) for external testing. Elevated depressive symptoms were defined using harmonized cutoffs (CES-D‑8≥ 3 for HRS/ELSA; CES-D‑10≥ 10 for CHARLS). Following recursive feature elimination, seven machine learning algorithms were trained and assessed for discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was employed for model interpretability. Results: Eight variables were used to build the seven models. The XGBoost model achieved the best internal performance (training AUC 0.824, 95% CI: 0.809– 0.838; validation AUC 0.757, 95% CI: 0.731– 0.783) and maintained robust external validity in ELSA (test AUC 0.785, 95% CI: 0.748– 0.824). Calibration and decision curve analyses supported clinical utility. SHAP analysis identified functional dependency, self‑rated health, and life satisfaction as predominant predictors. Higher dependency and poorer self-rated health had positive SHAP contributions, indicating higher model-predicted risk, whereas higher life satisfaction had negative contributions, indicating lower model-predicted risk. BMI exhibited a U‑shaped association. Conclusion: The XGBoost model generalized to an independent cohort and was deployed as a research prototype web application for risk stratification. SHAP analysis identified important model contributors for risk stratification in COPD, but these explanations describe model predictions and do not establish causal intervention targets. Prospective studies are needed to evaluate clinical utility. Keywords: chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, elevated depressive symptoms, prediction model, machine learning, external validation, SHAP

papers.title: Supporting Social Engagement in Long-Term Care Through Paired Socially Assistive Robot-Virtual Reality Activities for Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment and Apathy
papers.authors: Miroslava Migovich, Ritam Ghosh, Nibraas Khan, Cathy A. Maxwell, PAUL A. NEWHOUSE, Douglas W. Scharre, Alai Tan, Judith Ann Tate, Lorraine C. Mion, Nilanjan Sarkar
papers.abstract: Introduction: Older adults living in long-term care settings, particularly those with cognitive impairment and apathy, frequently experience reduced social engagement. Socially assistive robots and virtual reality systems may help support engagement, but little is known about whether they can sustain engagement during real-world deployment while also facilitating interaction between older adults. This study examined whether socially structured socially assistive robot-virtual reality (SAR-VR) systems could sustain engagement and support human-human interaction during repeated use in long-term care settings. Methods: This analysis focused on the SAR-VR intervention arm of a larger eight-week study and included 60 older adults with cognitive impairment from 23 long-term care sites. Participants were exposed to two SAR-VR systems featuring different robot embodiments (dog-like and humanoid), roles, and activities. Across 756 repeated intervention sessions, engagement was observationally assessed using observed ratings of attention, activity attitude, robot attitude, and conversational targeting. Results: Sustained attention and activity attitudes remained consistently positive across both SAR-VR systems over repeated exposure. Peer-to-peer and research-staff directed speech occurred across both systems. While robot-directed speech was more common in the dog-like condition, partner-directed communication remained stable, indicating that increased human-robot interaction did not occur at the expense of human-human interaction. Baseline cognitive functioning was associated with attentional engagement but not with attitudinal evaluations. Baseline technology acceptance did not strongly predict post-interaction impressions. Participants who anthropomorphized the robots at baseline demonstrated more positive engagement during sessions. Discussion: These findings suggest that socially structured SAR-VR systems can sustain meaningful engagement while preserving peer interaction in naturalistic dementia care. The results also support the feasibility of designing SAR-VR activities around shared goals and coordinated actions to promote reciprocal human engagement, while recognizing that the study design does not allow definitive conclusions about clinical efficacy or the effects of specific robot features.

papers.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence Competencies Across the Six ACGME Core Competencies: A Proposed Framework for Graduate Medical Education
papers.authors: Michel S Kabbash, Tyler John Loftus, Jason Morrow, Daniel Dent, Ronald Rodriguez
papers.journal: Advances in Medical Education and Practice
papers.abstract: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in clinical practice and Graduate Medical Education (GME), AI-specific competencies are not yet explicitly represented as a distinct domain within the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education's (ACGME) six core competency framework. The ACGME's ongoing consideration of AI in its Common Program Requirements revision process signals an emerging recognition of the need to address this gap. Over 1200 FDA-authorized AI medical devices, unregulated generative AI tools in clinical workflows, and a proliferating state legislative landscape create urgent educational needs. We conducted a purposive narrative review of literature addressing AI adoption, documented failures and litigation, regulatory developments, and bioethical frameworks to develop AI-specific learning objectives, milestone language, and assessment strategies mapped to each ACGME competency. We propose the SHARED ethical framework - Stewardship, Humanity, Accountability, Responsiveness, Equity, and Disclosure - as the moral foundation for AI education. We map AI-related capabilities and representative developmental descriptors across the six existing ACGME competency domains and propose corresponding curricular content and assessment approaches. The alternative to systematic, integrated AI training - informal adoption without standards or assessment - poses unacceptable risks to patients, trainees, and the profession. The proposed framework provides a structured foundation for further development and evaluation of AI education within competency-based GME.

papers.title: Transmedia as a three-dimensional model: a metatheoretical synthesis of narratology, media ecology, and a performative approach
papers.authors: S. A. Kucharina
papers.abstract: The article is devoted to a meta-theoretical analysis of transmedia storytelling as the dominant form of cultural production in the 21st century. In the context of the evolution of communication systems from simple transmission of messages to the creation of complex narrative ecosystems, the author substantiates the need to integrate three complementary theoretical perspectives: transmedia narratology, media ecology and the performative approach. Transmedia narratology is seen as an extension of traditional narrative theory, focusing on the «narrative potential» and specific capabilities of various media. The ecology of media provides a macroscopic view of the media environment as the habitat of culture, where transmedia projects act as an evolutionary response to the atomization of the audience. The performative approach, which goes back to the concept of the «culture of participation» by G. Jenkins, emphasizes the active role of the audience as a co-author and a full participant in the transmedia worlds. The article also examines the principles of transmedia design, the role of artificial intelligence and metaverses, as well as the challenges associated with maintaining canonical integrity and developing transmedia literacy. The conclusion is drawn about a fundamental shift in the media landscape: stories are turning into spaces that the audience jointly creates and performatively experiences.

papers.title: Machine Learning Provides Reliable ESP-Condition Monitoring
papers.authors: Chris Carpenter
papers.abstract: _ This article, written by JPT Technology Editor Chris Carpenter, contains highlights of paper SPE 229219, “Translating Physics Into Intelligence: Machine Learning For Reliable ESP-Condition Monitoring,” by Temirlan Zharkynbek, Sergio A. Caicedo, SPE, and Cristina Hernandez Labrador, AIQ, et al. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. _ This research focuses on combining physics-based expert rules with machine learning (ML) to improve the detection of failure-related events in electrical submersible pumps (ESPs). The goal is to create a generalized framework for abnormal-event detection that addresses the challenge of limited labeled data and sensor data, providing a practical solution for ESP management and maintenance planning. By using ML as a denoising layer over the physics rules, the method bridges rule-based and data-driven approaches. Introduction ESP reliability remains a decisive lever for production uptime, yet unplanned shutdowns still account for a significant share of lifting costs. Years of field digitalization have turned each pump into a high-frequency data source, but limited ground-truth failure labels and heterogeneous sensor layouts still hinder the move from reactive maintenance to predictive decision-making. This study tackles that constraint by treating physics knowledge as a source of weak supervision. A library of expert rules—encapsulating known degradation signatures—runs continuously on sliding windows of normalized sensor trends, producing numeric scores that act as soft labels. Rather than stopping at these rule outputs, the authors trained a model-agnostic supervised learner to denoise and generalize the aggregated scores across wells with varying sensor availability and operating envelopes. The resulting model serves as a single, field-deployable anomaly index that requires no manual labeling while retaining the interpretability of its physics roots. Methodology Previous work introduced a two-stage hybrid pipeline for ESP-failure-related abnormal-event handling. The two stages were as follows: 1. Semisupervised detection: A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on expert-labeled “normal” periods flags any reconstruction-error spikes as abnormal events. 2. Physics-rule-based classification: A library of physics-inspired rules diagnoses each flagged event. That workflow proved accurate but labor-intensive because subject-matter experts had to annotate large “normal” spans initially. The current contribution is to invert the sequence such that the following takes place: - Physics rules are run continuously (on every sliding window, not only alarms). - Numeric scores are treated as weak labels. - A supervised model is trained to denoise and generalize these scores, eliminating the need for manual “normal” tags. The result is a label-efficient, physics-guided ML framework that delivers earlier, cleaner abnormal-failure-related event detection. Motivation for Physics‑Based Diagnostic Rules. Early alarm systems successfully highlighted operational changes, such as pump-speed adjustments or choke-setting shifts that affect wellhead pressure, and revealed issues beyond the pump, enabling comprehensive monitoring of the entire well system rather than focusing solely on the ESP. For each predefined alarm category, the rule engine calculates a similarity score that quantifies how closely the current sensor-trend pattern aligns with that category’s signature. The category with the highest score is flagged as the primary diagnosis for the window. Ranking alarms in this way surfaces the most-probable root cause while still preserving secondary scores for additional context, thereby reducing ambiguity when different failure mechanisms share overlapping symptoms.

papers.title: Is there an app for that? Can a free app to promote physical activity be inclusive of inner-city children?
papers.authors: Mohamed Ghamry, Fakeha Masood, Cadina Powell, Yossef Alnasser
papers.abstract: Background: Mobile health (mHealth) tools may offer accessible, affordable and safe option to be physically active at home. Children living in urban settings and dealing with many poor social determinants of health (SDoH) are considered inner-city children. The study aims to assess feasibility of implementing mHealth based free application to promote physical health among inner-city school-aged children. Similarly, accessibility, acceptance and applicability were assessed. Methods: A 3-week feasibility study using Exercise for Kids at Home, a free multilingual mHealth application for school-age children was conducted. Children aged 7–12 years were stratified by BMI into obese and non-obese groups. Weekly follow-up assessed acceptance, accessibility, feasibility, and applicability. Results: The study was able to recruit 34 inner-city children (mean age 9.6 years; 50% female; 44% obese) to participate in three weeks feasibility study. Families were primarily African American (53%) and Hispanic (38%). Acceptance of using a free multilingual mHealth application was higher among obese children (3.1 vs. 0.6; P=0.01). Similarly, the acceptance was higher among non- English speakers (4.1 vs. 0.9; P=0.01). Accessibility was greater for non-English–speaking families (2.7 vs. 0.7; P=0.003) and families of obese children (2.0 vs. 0.5; P=0.004). The mean feasibility was 2.31. Still, children with obesity reported higher feasibility (2.9 vs. 1.8; P=0.05). The applicability score was 2.59. Gender, age group (7–9 vs. 10–12 years), insurance type, and health literacy level did not significantly contribute to acceptance, accessibility, feasibility, or applicability. Conclusions: A free, multilingual mHealth application was found to be acceptable and accessible among targeted inner-city children in the South Bronx. However, the use of a free application to promote physical activity was not feasible nor applicable to inner-city children at this current time.

papers.title: Analysis of the 2021 PIRLS Data for Türkiye Using Cognitive Diagnostic Modeling
papers.authors: Nihal Burçin Bircan Çubuk, Sedat Şen
papers.journal: Eğitimde ve Psikolojide Ölçme ve Değerlendirme Dergisi
papers.abstract: This study examines the Turkish PIRLS 2021 data through the lens of cognitive diagnostic modeling (CDM). Türkiye last participated in the PIRLS exam in 2001, prior to 2021. Türkiye’s participation in this international assessment after a twenty-year hiatus is of great significance. The analysis was restricted to responses to one publicly released PIRLS 2021 literary passage (“The Empty Pot”) administered to 667 students in the Turkish sample. Applying CDM to these assessment data makes it possible to identify students’ specific reading-related strengths and limitations and to generate more fine-grained feedback. Additionally, CDM can provide insights into the approach needed to better develop students’ reading skills during the educational process. In this study, the text “The Empty Pot” was selected for analysis, and data from 667 students in Türkiye who completed this text were included in the analysis. First, with input from subject matter experts, the PIRLS attributes “Interpreting and integrating ideas/information” was divided into “Interpretation” and “Using personal knowledge and experiences.” The final Q-matrix includes the attributes “Making inferences,” “Interpretation,” “Using personal knowledge and experiences,” and “Examination and Evaluation.” Additionally, a Q-matrix validation step was applied to correct possible classification errors. The analyses involved estimating and comparing six CDMs: G-DINA, DINA, DINO, A-CDM, LLM, and R-RUM. The fit evidence indicated that G-DINA provided the most adequate representation of the observed response data. The results indicated that 39 students (5.85%) were classified as experts (1111) in all attributes. Another notable result is that 69 students who took the exam were not proficient in any attributes (0000), indicating that under the selected model, nearly 10% of the students was assigned to the non-mastery profile. Results also showed that making inferences showed the highest estimated mastery probability in this analysis among the four, using personal knowledge and experience was identified as the most difficult. Because the study used a retrofitted CDM design based on a single released passage and a validated Q-matrix with some remaining interpretive limitations, the findings should be interpreted as passage-specific diagnostic evidence rather than nationally generalizable estimates of reading proficiency.

papers.title: Decolonising higher education in the Global South: A student–staff partnership approach to equitable co-created pedagogy
papers.authors: D. Govender, S. Pillay, I. Moosa, Jaisubash Jayakumar
papers.journal: South African Journal of Higher Education
papers.abstract: Decolonising higher education in the Global South requires addressing entrenched colonial epistemologies, hierarchical structures, and Eurocentric curricula that limit equitable participation and critical engagement. This article examines how student–staff partnerships can serve as a practical mechanism for advancing socially just and contextually relevant pedagogy within a preclinical medical curriculum at a South African research-intensive university. Using reflective engagement with a partnership initiative, the methodology involved collaborative workshops and iterative dialogue between three students and one staff member to explore perceptions of power, experiences of engagement and exclusion in lecture-based teaching, and the co-creation of inclusive pedagogical practices. Findings demonstrate that partnership facilitates the redistribution of pedagogical authority, amplifies student voice, and transforms teaching and learning from hierarchical and prescriptive processes into collaborative, co-constructed experiences. Key insights include enhanced student agency, negotiation of authority between students and staff, and the development of co-created guidelines for inclusive teaching that are responsive to local contexts and diverse epistemologies. By situating student–staff partnership as a vehicle for decolonial praxis, this work contributes both conceptual and practical guidance for higher education institutions seeking to embed equity, dialogue, and co-creation into curriculum and pedagogy. It illustrates that participatory approaches can disrupt hierarchical norms, foster critical reflexivity, and generate contextually grounded learning environments, providing a replicable model for advancing socially just and inclusive higher education across the Global South.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Development: From Molecular Design to Clinical Pharmacometrics
papers.authors: M. R. Galyamova, Olga V. Valieva, Kirill V. Peskov, Artur Kadurin, K. M. Kravtsov
papers.abstract: The aim was to demonstrate the potential of using artificial intelligence (AI) in pharmacology and the development of new drugs. This study reviews the key technological drivers shaping the market for generative design and AI applications in medicine, the dynamics of the global AI drug discovery market, the activities of leading players and startups, and the regulatory and legal aspects governing the industry. Particular focus is placed on the Russian market, including its maturity, growth barriers, and AI adoption case studies from 2022 to 2025.

papers.title: An Agentic AI Framework for ESG Disclosure Monitoring and Governance Evidence
papers.authors: Amit Aylani, Madhuri Rao
papers.journal: Indonesian Journal of Sustainability Accounting and Management
papers.abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure is increasingly important for sustainability assessment, compliance review, and managerial decision-making. However, existing AI-based ESG applications are often task-specific and provide limited support for longitudinal indicator harmonisation, missing-data handling, adaptive rule updates, and auditable decision trails. This study develops and evaluates an Agentic ESG Integration Framework (AEIF), a four-agent decision-support architecture for ingesting disclosures, mapping and aligning ESG indicators, detecting anomalies, and generating governance-oriented decision trails. The study harmonises 43 ESG indicators across 480 firm-year reports from 24 listed firms in four countries and six sectors over 2005–2024. AEIF is compared with a rules-based baseline using 60 retrospective monitoring scenarios and missing-data stress levels of 10%, 20%, and 30%. AEIF reduced mean compliance-update latency from 47.2 to 12.4 days and remediation time from 16.2 to 3.5 hours. Precision increased from 0.62 to 0.89 and recall from 0.58 to 0.86. At 30% missingness, detection accuracy was 84% versus 42% for the baseline. The findings indicate that governed agentic workflows can improve ESG monitoring while supporting comparability, traceability, human review, and assurance readiness.

papers.title: Current status and perspectives on earthquake science popularization under the technological innovation of the new era
papers.authors: Lei Li, Xu Chen, Da Zeng, Jin Ma
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Earthquake science popularization serves as a vital bridge between scientific research and public understanding. This study reviews the current status on earthquake science popularization in China, pointing out the limitations, such as the outdated knowledge system, limited dissemination formats, and insufficient audience targeting. To address these issues, three development paths are proposed: ① building an integrated knowledge framework that links fundamental theories，engineering applications，and technological frontiers; ② adopting new technologies such as artificial intelligence and virtual/augmented reality to enhance immersive and interactive communication; ③ establishing tiered and localized strategies to meet the diverse needs of different age and regional groups, by making full use of authoritative materials. The findings suggest that modern earthquake science popularization should shift from emergency-focused education toward comprehensive emergency knowledge dissemination and scientific understanding, leveraging innovation and intelligent technologies to elevate public literacy, strengthen collaboration among earthquake agencies, schools, media outlets, and research institutions, promote the joint development and sharing of science communication resources, support the national disaster prevention strategies.

papers.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Technologies on Creativity: An Examination in the Context of Intention to Adopt AI, AI Self-Efficacy, Perceived Quality, and Performance Expectation.
papers.authors: Engincan YILDIZ
papers.journal: Gümüşhane Üniversitesi İletişim Fakültesi Elektronik Dergisi
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has impacted knowledge generation, problem-solving, and content development processes in numerous fields, from education to media and creative industries. These impacts raise the question of how AI tools influence the creative performance of university students in particular.This study aims to examine the effects of perceived quality, AI self-efficacy, and perceived usefulness on willingness to use AI and creativity, and to test the mediating role of AI adoption intention in these relationships. The research involved a survey of university students over 18 years of age studying communication in Turkey. 385 valid data points were obtained using simple random sampling and analyzed. After completing reliability and validity analyses of the measurement tools, structural equation modeling was used to test the relationships between variables. The findings show that perceived quality, self-efficacy, and perceived usefulness have positive effects on creativity; furthermore, AI adoption intention plays a partial mediating role in these relationships. In conclusion, the study showed that students' perception of artificial intelligence as a reliable, useful, and manageable tool supports their integration of this technology into their creative processes and leads to higher creative performance. The results offer significant theoretical and practical contributions to both educational policies and AI-assisted learning designs.

papers.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND THE VALIDITY CRISIS OF ASSESSMENT IN MEDICAL EDUCATION: AN INTEGRATIVE REVIEW
papers.authors: Viviane Canhizares Evangelista de Araújo, Márcia Abusio, Percyleine Pelegrine Herculiani, Fábio Augusto Freiria Barbosa, Adriana Porto Nunes Gazetta, Josiane Ramos Garcia Rodrigues, Eleny Rosa Guimarães Gonçalves, João Paulo Galletti Pilon, Gustavo Pereira Mais, Ana Glaucia Paulino Lima, Mara Flávia Mamédio Avallone, Igor Soares Gianini Grecca, Silvia Helena Soares Gianini, Cristiano Machado Galhardi, Cintia Gisele de Andrade Pozenato, Wilson Bernardo Silva, Lisete Horn, Fabiane Lopes Toledo, Marcus Vinicius Tenuta Araújo, Tawana Pascon Lopes, Samantha Santos, Thaís dos Santos da Silva, Rodolfo de Oliveira Medeiros
papers.journal: Veredas do Direito Direito Ambiental e Desenvolvimento Sustentável
papers.abstract: Introduction: The rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence tools based on large language models has challenged the assumptions that support assessment in medical education. When a chatbot can answer licensing-style questions, write reflective narratives, generate test items, and score clinical performance, the interpretations drawn from assessment results may no longer correspond to the competencies they are intended to represent. Objective: To examine the scientific evidence on the effects of generative artificial intelligence on the validity of assessment in medical education, considering its roles as examinee, item writer, and assessor. Method: An integrative literature review was conducted, grounded in the principles of evidence-based practice. The review question was structured using the PICo strategy. The search was carried out in the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC databases. Included studies were characterized in terms of their methodological features and levels of evidence, and the findings were subjected to interpretive thematic synthesis. Results: Eleven studies were included in this review. The literature indicates that generative artificial intelligence performs at or above the level of students in knowledge-based and written tasks, that educators show limited ability to identify texts produced by these tools, that automatically generated items require expert review to preserve content validity and cognitive level, and that AI-based scoring shows limited agreement with human judgment and may introduce linguistic bias against specific groups of students. Conclusion: The validity crisis associated with generative artificial intelligence does not stem from the technology alone, but from assessment formats that depend on unsupervised written products and isolated measurements. Programmatic assessment, supervised performance-based methods, transparent institutional policies, and qualified human oversight of AI-supported processes are needed to preserve the credibility of assessment decisions.

papers.title: Developing a Machine Learning Platform-Enhanced Deep Learning Model (MLP-DLM): Effects on Conceptual Understanding, Digital Literacy, and Higher-Order Cognitive Engagement in Islamic Boarding Schools
papers.authors: Muchammad Ibnu Muzakir, Mahmun Mahmun, Muhammad Romadhona Kusuma
papers.journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
papers.abstract: Many pesantren (Islamic boarding schools) still rely on teacher-centered instruction, and available digital technology is rarely designed to support deep learning. This study developed and evaluated the Machine Learning Platform-Enhanced Deep Learning Model (MLP-DLM), which combines deep learning pedagogy (6C), machine learning platform features, and core pesantren values. Following the ADDIE model, the product was validated by three experts, field-tested with 30 students, and evaluated in a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design involving 60 students in two intact classes. Analyses used t-tests, N-gain, ANCOVA, and Cohen's d. The model scored 4.72 out of 5.00 in expert validation and 87.5% in usability, with response scores of 89.5% from students and 92.8% from teachers. With equivalent pretest scores, the experimental group improved significantly more than the control group in conceptual understanding (d = 1.83), digital literacy (d = 1.86), and higher-order cognitive engagement (d = 1.85). N-gain was moderate in the experimental group and low in the control group. ANCOVA supported these differences, although for digital literacy and higher-order cognitive engagement it counts only as supporting evidence. MLP-DLM is valid and practical and shows promise in this context. It should be replicated in more pesantren with longer interventions before wider adoption.

papers.title: DEVELOPMENT OF THE EDUCATIONAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USE CONCERNS SCALE
papers.authors: Erdem Erdoğdu, Mustafa Doğuş, Gizem Yıldız, Yusuf Levent Şahin
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has brought pedagogical opportunities to the fore, but it has also made students’ affective responses, particularly concern related to AI usage, more visible. The aim of this study is to develop the Educational Artificial Intelligence Use Concerns Scale within the framework of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and AI concern and anxiety literature. The scale development process was conducted using the classical test theory approach and included the following stages: item pool creation, content validity through expert opinion, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and reliability-validity analyses. Data were collected from higher education students enrolled at [name of university / universities] in [city, country] through an online survey distributed via [institutional e-mail / classroom announcements / learning management system / social media], and separate samples were used for EFA (n = 300) and CFA (n = 129). CFA results yielded a two-factor structure, explaining 57.99% of the total variance. CFA findings revealed that the twofactor structure showed acceptable/excellent fit (χ²/df=1.88; CFI=.98; TLI=.98; RMSEA=.08; SRMR=.01). The scale’s internal consistency was found to be high (total α = .90), and convergent validity was supported by AVE values. The results indicate that the scale is a valid and reliable tool for measuring concerns related to AI use in higher education contexts. The scale can contribute to studies explaining the acceptance and integration of AI in education, particularly when used in conjunction with TAM variables, by examining the role of affective determinants in technology acceptance processes.

papers.title: CLASSROOM DYNAMICS OF AI-SUPPORTED AUTOMATED WRITING EVALUATION IN AN EFL HYBRID FEEDBACK LOOP
papers.authors: Dila Süzan, Sezin Eşfer
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: This action research study examined how an AI-supported automated writing evaluation (AISAWE) tool can be integrated into EFL writing instruction through a hybrid AI+teacher feedback loop. Because classroom use of AISAWE can introduce feedback overload, interpretation problems, and concerns about learner agency, we implemented an eight-week exploratory action research (EAR) cycle to adapt instructional routines while documenting classroom uptake in a naturalistic setting. Data were primarily qualitative (field notes, teacher focus group data, and student reflections), supplemented by quantitative indicators (pre–post rubric scores, self-report scales, and the System Usability Scale) to contextualize patterns of change. Findings address three research questions. First, uptake was shaped by three recurring practices: managing feedback load, clarifying AI feedback through teacher mediation, and regulating reliance on AI feedback. Second, indicators showed gains in micro-level linguistic accuracy alongside stability in rhetorical structure across the cycle. Third, while students valued speed and coverage, engagement was constrained by usability friction, digital fluency gaps, and motivational and voice-related concerns. Overall, results suggest that AISAWE can support micro-level revision when teacher mediation structures dense feedback and protects learner authorship.

papers.title: EQUALITY, DIVERSITY, AND INCLUSION IN OPEN AND DISTANCE EDUCATION: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS
papers.authors: Rudi Susilana, Gema Rullyana
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: Equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) have become central to educational discourse, particularly within the context of open and distance education (ODE), where digital environments demand inclusive and equitable approaches. Despite increased scholarly attention, research on EDI in ODE remains uneven, with limited interdisciplinary integration and geographic representation. This study addresses these gaps through a bibliometric mapping analysis of 1,013 publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus between 2015 and 2025. Using the Biblioshiny interface of the Bibliometrix package in R, the study systematically identifies key contributors, influential publications, core research domains, and emerging trends in EDI research within ODE. Findings reveal a significant rise in EDI-related research since 2020, driven by the global shift to digital learning. However, four critical gaps persist: a research bias toward learners, with limited attention to educators’ roles in inclusive pedagogy; minimal integration of ethical technologies, including artificial intelligence and emotion-aware tools, into EDI frameworks; a geographic imbalance favoring high-income countries, with limited representation from the Global South; and a predominance of descriptive and correlational methodologies, which limits causal inference. This review contributes to the body of knowledge by providing a comprehensive overview of the field and offering practical and theoretical directions for developing inclusive and equitable digital education systems.

papers.title: EXPLAINABLE AI IN HIGHER EDUCATION ASSESSMENT: A BIBLIOMETRIC EXPLORATION OF AN EMERGING RESEARCH DOMAIN
papers.authors: Flavio Manganello, Alberto Nico, G Boccuzzi
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: This study employs bibliometric analysis following GLOBAL recommendations to systematically map the emerging research landscape on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in higher education assessment, pursuing five objectives: quantifying research productivity, assessing geographic distribution, identifying collaborative networks, uncovering thematic evolution, and mapping intellectual foundations. We analyzed 72 peer-reviewed publications from Scopus spanning 2019-2025 to address a critical gap in systematic knowledge about AI transparency in educational contexts, particularly in response to regulatory frameworks such as the GDPR and the EU AI Act. The analysis reveals accelerating research activity, with publication output growing from single contributions in 2019-2020 to 26 documents in 2024 (R² = 0.7666). Geographic distribution shows China leading in productivity (8 documents) while Sweden demonstrates exceptional citation efficiency (25.50 citations per document), with European institutions collectively accounting for 35.4% of contributions. The field generates moderate but growing scholarly impact with 655 total citations, achieving an h-index of 13 and g-index of 24. Science mapping identifies four primary thematic domains: AI transparency methodologies, educational analytics applications, machine learning implementations, and student performance prediction systems. Author collaboration analysis reveals Dragan Gasevic as the most productive researcher (5 documents, 61 citations) alongside a highly integrated four-author cluster (Afzaal, Fors, Nouri, and Zia) achieving exceptional impact with 101 citations each from 3 joint publications. Cocitation analysis identifies Adadi and Berrada’s XAI survey (2018) as the primary theoretical anchor. The temporal evolution indicates progression from fundamental XAI concepts toward practical educational applications, with innovative South-South partnerships emerging among developing economy institutions. The findings provide systematic preliminary evidence for growing academic attention to AI transparency in educational contexts, highlighting critical needs for terminological standardization and longitudinal investigation of regulatory drivers shaping this emerging field.

papers.title: GOVERNANCE BY DESIGN: AN AI–IOT READINESS AND EQUITY FRAMEWORK FOR LOW-RESOURCE SCHOOLS
papers.authors: Muyideen Dele Adewale
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: The rapid convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) promises more intelligent, connected, and personalised learning environments, yet deployment in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains uneven and weakly governed. Much of the available evidence derives from campus-based and comparatively well-resourced educational settings, while existing studies often treat AI and IoT separately and give insufficient attention to equity, environmental sustainability, and institutional readiness. This study advances a Governance by Design perspective and proposes an AI–IoT Readiness and Governance Framework for low-resource schools and open and distance learning (ODL) systems, including open universities, dual-mode institutions, school-based distance programmes, and community or non-formal initiatives. It addresses three research questions: what enabling conditions are required for AI– IoT readiness in ODL; how AI–IoT-rich ODL environments can be governed to balance personalisation, security, and equity; and what transferable lessons can be generalised from early deployments in low-resource contexts. Conceptualising AI and IoT as a layered ecosystem spanning devices and sensors, connectivity and platforms, analytics and AI services, applications and pedagogy, and governance and values, the framework operationalises six readiness dimensions with maturity levels: infrastructure and IoT ecosystem; data governance, privacy, and security; AI-driven personalisation and learning analytics; staff capacity and change management; equity and inclusion; and environmental sustainability. A structured evidence review of Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, yielded 57 studies that were analysed through a two-cycle conceptual synthesis. The resulting framework is a conceptual planning and reflection tool rather than a validated measurement or certification instrument. The synthesis identifies proposed readiness conditions, governance considerations and design constraints to inform phased adoption, yielding a structured, privacy-aware, and inclusive pathway for AI–IoT implementation in low-resource education.

papers.title: WHEN CHATGPT “FEELS LIKE FAMILY”: SERIAL MEDIATION PATHWAYS TO RELIANCE AND CRITICAL USE
papers.authors: Muhammad Rifa’ie
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: This study aims to test the serial mediation pathway based on the expanded Affective–Behavioural–Cognitive (ABC) model to explain Reliance on ChatGPT (RC) and Critical Use of ChatGPT (CU) in an academic context. A cross-sectional quantitative survey study was conducted among multi-ethnic students in the coastal region of Southeast Sulawesi, Indonesia, in two stages: a pilot study (n = 72) to test the instruments and a main study (n = 287) to test the model. The analysis used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) based on CB-SEM to validate the measurement model, and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) to test the structural model through 5,000 bootstrap resamples (CI 95%). The results showed that the indirect serial effect from PCU to CU via EA/AIS-ST-RC was significant, whereas the direct path from ST to CU was not. These findings confirm that attachment to ChatGPT is not directly related to a decrease in CU. CU practices are primarily formed when User Stickiness (ST) has a positive and significant effect on RC, which is functional in completing academic tasks. Thus, RC acts as a proximal mediator in the relationship between ST and CU.

papers.title: MAPPING THE DIGITAL LITERACY OF INDONESIAN TEACHERS FOR PEDAGOGICAL READINESS
papers.authors: Wachidatul Linda Yuhanna, Puguh Jayadi, Raras Setyo Retno, Much Fuad Saifuddin
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a catalyst for educational transformation, underscoring the need to increase teachers’ digital literacy to utilize technology pedagogically. Although important, AI literacy as a teacher’s competence is still rarely studied empirically, especially in Indonesia. This study maps the level of AI literacy of Indonesian teachers and its relationship with pedagogical readiness, using a survey of 220 teachers from various regions. The instrument covers three dimensions, namely Digital technical competence, Ethical and critical awareness, and AI-based pedagogical practices. This dimensional structure is used consistently throughout the study. The descriptive analysis showed that the highest average score was in the AI in Pedagogical Practice dimension (Mean = 4.33), followed by Digital Competence (Mean = 4.29) and Ethical Awareness (Mean = 4.27). The correlation between Digital competence and Pedagogical practice was strong (r = 0.854). Multiple regression showed that digital competence significantly influenced pedagogical readiness (β = 0.7031, p < 0.001), accounting for 75.5% of the variance (R² = 0.755). SEM structural modeling showed good model fit (CFI = 0.946; RMSEA = 0.062). Two teacher clusters were successfully identified, namely the high (M ≥ 4.7) and medium (M ≈ 4.0) clusters. These results confirm the importance of AI literacy training that balances technical skills and ethical awareness in supporting teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning.

papers.title: THE EFFECTS OF CHATBOTS-BASED INTERVENTIONS ON FOREIGN LANGUAGE SPEAKING PERFORMANCE: A META-ANALYSIS STUDY
papers.authors: Nurbanu Kansızoğlu, Selvanur Kayhan
papers.journal: Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education
papers.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine the effect of chatbot-based interventions on foreign language speaking performance through a meta-analysis. Studies investigating the effects of chatbots on speaking performance were retrieved from various databases (e.g., ERIC, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis) using a range of keyword phrases. Following the inclusion and exclusion criteria, this meta-analysis included 16 experimental studies (k = 17) that implemented chatbot-based interventions to enhance learners’ foreign language speaking performance. All statistical data were collected and transferred to the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) software to compute Hedges’ g values. The overall effect size of the intervention studies on foreign language speaking performance was 1.035, indicating a large effect. Intervention duration and education level were examined as moderator variables, but they did not significantly affect foreign language speaking performance. This study offers a theoretical basis for using artificial intelligence tools in language teaching by emphasizing chatbots’ potential to improve speaking.

papers.title: African Community Media, AI, and the Question of Community Participation in the Disruptive Era
papers.authors: Lyton Ncube, Allen Munoriyarwa, Albert Chibuwe, Refilwe Whitney Mofokeng, Antonette Kakujaha- Murangi
papers.abstract: In this article, we examine the nexus of Southern African community newspapers’ sceptical AI integration and grassroots democracy. The sceptical approach to AI integration in marginalised media markets of Southern African community newspapers’ news ecosystems is interrogated. We respond to the questions: In what ways is the integration of AI tools in everyday news production routines within Southern African community media institutions defined by scepticism? What is the basis of scepticism amongst Southern African community media journalists? What are the implications for grassroots democracy in these communities? The Southern African community media under study are drawn from South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled journalists and editors from these newsrooms. Findings show that the sceptical approach to AI adoption among Southern African community newspapers is largely driven by fears and concerns about AI’s documented mass production of misinformation and disinformation. In addition, the sceptical approach to AI adoption in these newsrooms is rooted in a lack of technical proficiency with AI tools and financial limitations occasioned by the decline in philanthropic funding.

papers.title: Human-Centered Design as a Tool for Advancing Culturally Responsive Research
papers.authors: Emma Barnard, Jessica Otero Machuca, Paul Mihas, Suzanne Maman, Elizabeth S. Chen, Vivian Romero
papers.abstract: Human-centered design is a participatory approach that centers those encountering a challenge to develop solutions that are desirable, feasible, and contextually grounded. Increasingly, health researchers are adopting HCD to advance equity by elevating lived experience and community knowledge. This brief report explores how HCD can be understood and operationalized as a form of culturally responsive research in participatory research. CRR is characterized by the culturally responsive tenets of transformation, specificity, and expansion. To understand how this has been done, we conducted an exploratory review of peer-reviewed studies applying HCD in qualitative health research to examine how methods such as Conversation Starters, Card Sorts, Rapid Prototyping, Co-Creation, and Journey Mapping reflect these tenets. Through iterative team analysis, we identified illustrative examples and, as a byproduct of the synthesis process, developed a Culturally Responsive Journey Map, a flexible reflexive tool, to help researchers visualize and document transformation, specificity, and expansion in their research projects. Findings suggest that while HCD naturally aligns with culturally responsive principles, intentionality is required in its selection and application. We also identify challenges related to training, time, resources, and participant readiness. We conclude with recommendations for researchers, institutions, and funders to expand access to high-quality HCD training, develop user-friendly tools, and embed iterative, participatory processes into qualitative health research design.

papers.title: Data and materials for perceptions of generative AI in language education
papers.authors: Kaiyuan Chen

papers.title: Scoping Review Protocol: Cognitive Skills, Pedagogical Barriers, and Usage Guidelines of Artificial Intelligence in Education.
papers.authors: Carlos Daniel Camacho Trelles
papers.abstract: Objective: To establish a standardized methodological protocol for systematically mapping and characterizing the available scientific evidence on changes in cognitive abilities, pedagogical barriers, and guidelines for the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in formal education. Introduction: The emergence of generative AI models creates a dialectical tension between cognitive offloading and critical thinking, confronting teachers with a profound crisis in authentic assessment and curricular mismatches. Inclusion criteria: Studies in formal education (Population: higher education and secondary education) focused on AI (Concept) that address cognitive skills, pedagogical barriers, or usage guidelines (disjunctive logic), in face-to-face, hybrid, or virtual settings (Context). Time period: 2021–2026; Spanish and English. Methods: The review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI 2024 Manual for systematic reviews and will be reported using the PRISMA-ScR extension. Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar will be consulted. The process will include a two-phase screening (title/abstract and full text) and data extraction using a standardized form with 12 variables. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; higher education; cognitive skills; teacher barriers; ethical guidelines; scoping review.
