Our execution-grounded, rationale-driven training aligns with transition-aware execution semantics at the statement level, enhancing prediction accuracy. Our experiments show that T-REX enables Reasoner to outperform much larger GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini models across multiple dimensions of runtime behavior prediction, while also aiding in static detection of runtime errors as well as in debugging. Finally, we discuss how T-REX can be generalized to static emulation of any dynamic analysis through such a teacher-student distillation, illustrating with the specific case of dynamic program slicing in Python.

papers.title: How Safe Is Your Screen? Understanding and Detecting Privacy Leaks in Sensitive Activities
papers.authors: Youngseok Kim, Sungho Lee, Sungjae Hwang
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on software engineering.
papers.abstract: Android apps handle sensitive data, often displayed on screens (i.e., Activities), and protecting these activities is vital for ensuring user privacy. Several studies have demonstrated the risk of private data leakage via screen capture and identified malware exploiting this vulnerability. To mitigate such threats, Google introduced FLAG_SECURE, an activity-level security feature that protects an Activity when set by blocking screen capture and restricting display on non-secure devices. Proper usage of this security feature could significantly reduce data leakage risks. However, to the best of our knowledge, its adoption across diverse Android apps has not been systematically studied. In this work, we present a large-scale empirical study of screenshot-based vulnerabilities in Android apps using a systematic static analysis pipeline, ASSA. The pipeline automatically constructs UI models of activities and fragments by leveraging a customized version of Frontmatter, and combines them with a Large Language Model (LLM) to infer runtime context and identify sensitive user data rendered on screens. We apply ASSA to 5,667 popular real-world Android apps and find that 19.8% contain at least one activity that displays sensitive information without screen-capture protection, while 87.2% of apps do not apply FLAG_SECURE to any activity, exposing credentials, financial information, and location data to screenshot attacks. Beyond quantifying prevalence, we analyze FLAG_SECURE usage patterns and establish a taxonomy that captures diverse factors influencing developers’ decisions to adopt or omit screen protection, including intentional privacy protection, intellectual property safeguarding, and unintentional inheritance from base activities. To assess real-world impact, we further conduct in-depth case studies on 200 vulnerable apps and responsibly disclose our findings to the affected vendors, receiving 6 confirmed patches and 20 acknowledgments, including 11 vendors who reported ongoing efforts toward mitigation. These findings indicate that screenshot-based vulnerabilities are not only widespread but also systematically overlooked in practice, highlighting the need for greater awareness and more careful handling of sensitive on-screen information by developers.

papers.title: On Behavioral Alignment of Model-Code and Human-Code Understandability via Behavioral Proxies
papers.authors: Xiaokai Rong, Aashish Yadavally, Hridya Dhulipala, Anh H. N. Nguyen, Tien N. Nguyen
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on software engineering.
papers.abstract: Code understandability is a critical aspect of software quality. Prior research has largely focused on this attribute from a human-centric or code-centric perspective, while it should be viewed as a relational property arising from the interaction between a reader and the code. With the increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs) in software engineering, we posit that the notion of “reader” should be generalized to encompass both humans and models. Building on this relational perspective, we extend the concept of code understandability to distinguish between human and model code understandability, aiming to investigate the behavioral alignment between the two. To this end, we use a dataset from a prior study containing human-rated judgments of understandability across diverse participant groups, and evaluate multiple open and closed-source LLMs. To operationalize such behavioral alignment, we introduce four behavioral proxies of model-code understandability (BPMU): P0, based on program comprehension-focused question answering; and P1–P3, based on program intent summarization (derived from our proposed semantic self-consistency). Our findings show that LLMs exhibit stronger behavioral alignment with general human code understandability than previously used shallow machine learning baselines. Stratified analyses further reveal that model code understandability aligns most closely with professional developers, but significantly less with other student groups. Role-conditioned prompting does not improve the alignment for the latter, suggesting that current LLMs cannot accurately mimic the perspectives of human readers with varying expertise. Finally, we demonstrate that semantic self-consistency is a reliable and extensible measure to be used as a behavioral proxy for quantifying model code understandability, with broad implications in both software engineering research and practice.

papers.title: HELO-APR: Enhancing Low-Resource Program Repair through Cross-Lingual Knowledge Transfer
papers.authors: Zhipeng Wang, Boyang Yang, Yidong Wan, Liuye Guo, You Lv, Tao Zheng, Zhuowei Wang, Tieke He
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on software engineering.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on automatic program repair (APR) for high-resource programming languages (HRPLs), but their effectiveness drops sharply in low-resource programming languages (LRPLs) due to the lack of sufficient verified buggy–fixed pairs for APR training. To address this challenge, we propose HELO-APR ( H igh-resource E nabled LO w-resource APR), a two-stage APR framework that enables cross-lingual transfer of repair knowledge from HRPLs to LRPLs. HELO-APR (1) constructs high-quality LRPL training data by synthesizing LRPL buggy–fixed pairs from their HRPL counterparts, preserving defect-type consistency while ensuring that the synthesized code is idiomatic; and (2) adopts a curriculum learning strategy that progressively performs HRPL repair learning, cross-lingual repair alignment, and LRPL repair adaptation, thereby improving repair effectiveness in LRPLs. Using C++ as the source HRPL and Ruby and Rust as the target LRPLs, experiments on xCodeEval show that HELO-APR achieves the best macro-average Pass@k results and outperforms strong baselines in most settings. It increases Pass@1 from 31.17% to 48.65% on DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B and from 1.67% to 11.97% on CodeLlama-7B, while improving syntactic validity by raising the macro-average target compilation rate on CodeLlama from 49.77% to 91.98%. On Defects4Ruby, HELO-APR increases BLEU-4 from 61.20 to 66.79 and ROUGE-1 from 76.76 to 83.59 on CodeLlama-7B, indicating higher similarity to developer patches in real-world settings. Finally, we conduct ablation studies to assess the necessity of each core component. These results suggest that verified cross-lingual supervision provides a reusable approach for improving LLM-based repair in low-resource programming languages.

papers.title: Evaluating the Impact of Explainable AI on Trust in AI-Assisted Code Review
papers.authors: Zhenhan Gao, Marvin Muñoz Barón, Umm-e- Habiba, Daniel Graziotin, Stefan Wagner
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on software engineering.
papers.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) for automated code review has brought significant change to a time-consuming part of software engineering. Prior work has shown that LLM-based code tools can improve code quality and enable more robust software development processes. As the tools get more powerful, the explanations behind their decisions remain hard to understand. Developers struggle to assess the validity of LLM-generated code reviews, making it difficult to gauge how much trust they should place in them. While the application of automated code review with LLMs has been extensively investigated, the inclusion of Explainable AI (XAI) for transparency in code reviews and its impact on trust are yet to be explored. We aim to address this research gap by studying the influence of XAI on the trust of software developers in AI-assisted code reviews. We conducted a within-subjects user study with 34 participants from diverse programming backgrounds, comparing three experimental LLM-based automated code review systems with varying levels of XAI support: Condition A (detailed explanation and review feedback), Condition B (review feedback only), and Condition C (no explanations). Participants were shown a series of real-world code change requests along with the AI-generated code reviews. During the study, we measured trust perceptions for each system using a questionnaire, agreement with the AI recommendation, the reasoning for accepting or rejecting the code change, and the time taken to review the code change. Our quantitative results show that the level of explanation significantly influences both the level of trust of software developers and their agreement with AI recommendations, but in different ways. Full explanations (Condition A) yield the highest perceived trust (M = 3.99/5) but not the highest agreement with AI recommendations, whereas moderate explanations (Condition B) achieve the highest agreement with AI (89.22%). This could suggest that more explanations prompt developers to question AI recommendations more frequently. In contrast, providing no explanations (Condition C) results in the lowest levels of trust and agreement. We also find that the level of explanation did not significantly impact the time taken to accept or reject a code change. Across all conditions, the most commonly cited reasons for code change decisions were changes in code readability and the correctness of the implementation. Overall, these findings indicate that incorporating XAI into the code review process significantly changes the trust perceptions and agreement with AI recommendations for software developers. These results provide insights for the design and evaluation of trustworthy AI-based code review systems, and support researchers in the design of studies on the human factors of AI-assisted software development.

papers.title: SWE-PDB: Teaching LLMs to Leverage Debugging Tools via Agentic Training
papers.authors: Jiaxing Liu, Xing Hu, Xin Xia
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on software engineering.
papers.abstract: Interaction with debugging tools enables large language models (LLMs) to reason over concrete runtime states, rather than relying solely on static analysis of source code. Specifically, with the help of a debugger, an LLM-based agent can observe actual program execution by inspecting intermediate variable states and stepping through the control flow. These runtime observations enable the model to better understand program behavior and identify the root causes of bugs. Despite these advantages, using debuggers correctly and effectively remains challenging for many models because debugger interaction is inherently stateful and requires executing complex, long-horizon action sequences. As a result, models often exhibit unproductive interactions in which the debugger is underutilized or even disrupts the debugging process. To address this challenge, we propose SWE-PDB , the first training-based framework that teaches LLMs to leverage debuggers for interactive debugging and program repair. Our approach constructs large-scale buggy Python instances with verified failing tests from diverse sources and synthesizes multi-turn interactive debugging trajectories that follow structured debugging workflows. To ensure data quality, we apply multi-stage trajectory filtering and refinement, and train models using agentic supervised fine-tuning to learn effective debugger behaviors, followed by agentic reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards to improve generalization and promote more strategic debugger usage. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate substantial gains. In particular, SWE-PDB-14B achieves 38.0% accuracy on SWE-bench Verified with complete test suites, more than tripling the base model’s performance, while improving interaction efficiency and exhibiting robust, meaningful debugger usage.

papers.title: E4R-Reviewer: Effective and Explainable Automated Code Review via End-to-End Reasoning-Guided Alignment
papers.authors: Yifei Liu, 侯熙智, L Yang, Huan Liu, Chen Zhu, Fengjun Zhang, Chun Zuo
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on software engineering.
papers.abstract: Code review is a key practice for ensuring software quality and maintainability. Despite progress in Automated Code Review (ACR), existing methods face two core challenges: (1) Isolated Task Modeling. Current approaches often model and optimize subtasks in ACR independently, ignoring the inherent logical order and internal dependencies among them which affects the effectiveness of ACR. (2) Lack of Explainability. At the task level, the absence of explanatory information in review comments increases developers’ cognitive load; at the model level, the black-box nature fundamentally undermines developer trust. To address these challenges, we propose E4R-Reviewer, which improves the E ffec­tiveness and E xplain­ability of ACR through E nd-to- E nd R easoning-guided alignment. For effectiveness , E4R-Reviewer unifies multiple fine-grained ACR subtasks into a single end-to-end reasoning process, enabling cross-task knowledge sharing and allowing the model to explicitly complete a reasoning chain that covers quality estimation, issue localization, issue classification, issue description, fix suggestion, and code refinement in one generation. Meanwhile, we adopt a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)-based reinforcement-learning alignment, treating the reasoning steps as optimizable intermediate objectives. We design subtask-specific rewards and integrate them via curriculum-inspired, multi-stage reward fusion that follows the real-world review workflow. For explainability , E4R-Reviewer produces reasoning process and structured review results covering all fine-grained ACR subtasks, improving the transparency and explainability of the review results. Extensive evaluations on public, real-world datasets demonstrate that E4R-Reviewer significantly outperforms existing methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance: a 74.61% F1-score in quality estimation and +22.96% CodeBLEU in code refinement. Furthermore, Large Language Model (LLM) and human evaluation further confirm the superiority of E4R-Reviewer in terms of effectiveness and explainability.

papers.title: Regulatory pathways for neurointerventional devices: narrative review of FDA clearance trends in the AI and robotics era
papers.authors: Sardar Umer Irshad, Syeda Mishkat Ismail, Noor-ul-Eman Haider, Shah Mir, Muhammad Hanzala, Muhammad Shaheer khan, Irfan Ullah, Ali Mumtaz
papers.abstract: Neurointerventional devices are entering an era of rapid innovation, driven by advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics. However, the US regulatory framework governing their approval was largely established before these technologies emerged. Bhenderu et al provided a comprehensive overview of two decades of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulatory files for endovascular neurosurgical devices. However, their analysis preceded the FDA’s 2024 final guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) for AI-enabled device software. This review builds on the work of Bhenderu et al by focusing on the AI- and robotics-driven era (2022–2026). We examine FDA clearance patterns across AI/software-enabled triage and decision-support systems, robotic and computer-assisted thrombectomy platforms, and next-generation flow diverters, while assessing whether the 510(k), De Novo, and PMA pathways remain appropriate for devices capable of post-clearance evolution. Examples such as Viz.ai’s predicate lineage and Penumbra’s THUNDERBOLT platform highlight the strengths of the current framework for iterative hardware development, as well as its emerging limitations for adaptive AI/machine learning(ML) technologies. As of mid-2025, only 26 AI/ML-enabled devices had received authorization with a PCCP, while the FDA’s 2025 request for public comment on evaluating real-world AI device performance underscores continuing uncertainty regarding post-market oversight. This review argues that although the predicate-based regulatory framework has adapted well to incremental hardware innovation, it has not kept pace with continuously evolving AI and robotic technologies. We conclude by recommending that FDA formalize binding PCCP eligibility criteria, require predicate recall-history disclosure, and adopt a public–private post-market surveillance registry for higher-risk devices.

papers.title: P75 Diet influences systemic inflammation in cirrhosis
papers.authors: Yevedzo Ntuli, Abigail Bernardo, Maria Nehme Ibrahimi, Ellis Kobina Paintsil, Victoria Tatiana Kronsten, Debbie Lindsay Shawcross
papers.abstract: Background Systemic inflammation is a well-recognised feature of decompensated cirrhosis and interleukin-6 (IL-6) is associated with the transition from a compensated to decompensated state.1 Gut-derived translocation of pathogen-associated molecular patterns and microbes through a dysfunctional intestinal epithelium drive this, with gut microbiome perturbations implicated in disease progression.2 Gut microbiota-targeted diets modulate the systemic immune response in healthy participants,3 and there is evidence supporting the immune modulatory effects of diet in patients with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy.4 The limited availability of simple efficacious interventions for cirrhosis presents an opportunity to enhance current treatment options. Aim To investigate the impact of dietary habits and consumption of foods considered to exert influence on the gut microbiome, on systemic inflammation and intestinal barrier integrity. Methods Patients with stable cirrhosis secondary to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), abstinent alcohol-related liver disease (ArLD) and overlap of both, (Met-ALD) were consecutively recruited in a cross-sectional study. An investigator administered, study-specific dietary questionnaire assessed general dietary patterns, with focus on fermented foods, fruit, vegetables and dairy. Plasma inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, IL-21, IL-22, IL-17, IL-10 and IL-1β) were measured using mesoscale discovery electrochemiluminescent assay. Plasma D-lactate and intestinal fatty acid binding protein 2 (FABP2) were measured as surrogate markers of intestinal barrier dysfunction. Dietary associations with cytokines and barrier markers were assessed using linear regression adjusted for presence of diabetes, MELD-Na and aetiology with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction applied to all analyses. Spearman correlation was used to assess association between continuous variables. Results Sixty-nine patients were included: median age 62 years (IQR 56-71); 71% male (n=49); 55% ArLD (n=38); 32% MASLD (n=22), and 7% Met-ALD (n=5). Median MELD-Na was 9 (8-11). Dietary patterns included lactose free (1%), vegetarian (3%), pescatarian (3%), gluten free without coeliac disease (3%), low carbohydrate (10%) and red meat-free (15%) diets. No significant observations were found between overall dietary pattern and systemic inflammation or barrier dysfunction. However, patients consuming 2-3 portions of fermented food per day (n=5) had lower plasma IL-6 than those consuming none. (p=0.012, adjusted p=0.042). The MELD-Na score was positively correlated with D-lactate (r=0.333, p=0.023), adjusted for age, diabetes, aetiology and BMI. Conclusion Dietary habits may influence gut-derived systemic inflammation in cirrhosis, through specific foods rather than overall dietary pattern. The association between fermented food consumption and lower IL-6 is limited by small group size (n=5) and this should be considered as an exploratory finding. References investigators from the E-CC, Grifols C, European Foundation for the Study of Chronic Liver F, Arroyo V, Angeli P, Moreau R, et al. The systemic inflammation hypothesis: Towards a new paradigm of acute decompensation and multiorgan failure in cirrhosis. Journal of Hepatology 2021;74(3):670–85. Bajaj JS, Heuman DM, Hylemon PB, Sanyal AJ, White MB, Monteith P, et al. Altered profile of human gut microbiome is associated with cirrhosis and its complications. J Hepatol. 2014;60(5):940–7. papers.title: P18 Enhancing recruitment to alcohol-related liver disease clinical trials through the use of a regional data repository: a site-led project (Manual search versus the West of Scotland SafeHaven database for pre-screening adults with steatohepatitis on a background of alcohol-related liver disease for the GlaxoSmithKline-Starlight phase 2 clinical trial)
papers.authors: Mohamed Zarroug, Katherine Burrows, Rachael Swann
papers.abstract: Introduction Liver disease is the 3rd leading cause of premature death in the UK, with alcohol-related liver disease (ARLD) being the most common aetiology. However relatively few interventional clinical trials target this group. The GSK-Starlight study is a dose-finding, double-blinded, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial evaluating the efficacy and safety of GSK4532990 in adults with steatohepatitis on a background of alcohol-related liver disease (ARLD), recruiting across compensated, decompensated and intermediate cohorts. Identifying eligible candidates is resource-intensive; we therefore compared a conventional manual search with the West of Scotland SafeHaven electronic data repository for pre-screening within NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde (NHSGGC). Methods Key inclusion criteria were age 18-70, ARLD, with participants demonstrating liver stiffness above a specific threshold as assessed by FibroScan (Vibration-Controlled Transient Elastography, VCTE). Key exclusions were alternative liver disease, prolonged QTcF, BMI >35, prohibited concomitant medications and haematological, hepatic and renal laboratory thresholds. The manual approach interrogated the NHSGGC liver database, prior ARLD-cirrhosis study lists, ward discharge summaries, clinic lists and consultant referrals. SafeHaven was automated to identify NHSGGC adults with ICD-10 K70 codes (since 01/01/2000) and/or thiamine prescriptions (since 01/09/2024), filtered by liver clinic/FibroScan attendance, living status, age and blood parameters from 01/01/2024. Results Over 13 months, manual search identified 119 potential participants; 25 (21%) were initially eligible. Of these, 16 (64%) declined and 9 (36%) attended screening visit 1, yielding 2 randomisations and 7 screen failures (mainly due to liver profile and FibroScan outside of trial parameters). SafeHaven search, completed in 2 weeks, identified 33,447 patients (20,111 ICD-10 K70-coded and 13,336 thiamine-dispensed). Of these patients, 1,200 had liver clinic/FibroScan attendance; further restricting to alive status, age and blood parameters yielded 105 potential participants. Fourteen (13.3%) were initially eligible. Of these, 13 were to be approached and 1 had attended screening visit 1 and was randomised. Pre-screen failures were mainly due to FibroScan results outside of trial parameters, alternative aetiology of liver disease and cognitive impairment. Discussion SafeHaven generated a comparable pre-screening pool to manual search while substantially reducing the pre-screening time from months to weeks and providing up-to-date laboratory data filterable against trial-specific thresholds. The two approaches identified largely complementary patients, supporting a combined strategy to optimise recruitment in a complex trial. A modified SafeHaven query incorporating FibroScan values, a key inclusion criterion currently not searchable, would further streamline identification of eligible candidates. References Williams R, Aspinall R, Bellis M, et al. Addressing liver disease in the UK: a blueprint for attaining excellence in health care and reducing premature mortality from lifestyle issues of excess consumption of alcohol, obesity, and viral hepatitis. Lancet. 2014;384(9958):1953–1997. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(14)61838-9 Rady ED, Anouti A, Mitchell MC, Cotter TG. Current clinical trials for alcohol-associated hepatitis. Am J Pathol. 2026;196(1):182–191. doi:10.1016/j.ajpath.2025.03.009

papers.title: P142 The utility of conventional non-invasive liver assessment tools in cystic fibrosis: analysis of a single centre cohort
papers.authors: Sara Elsaadany, Zoe Constantinou, Farjana Enayathulla, Yannis Kallis, N. Shafi, Danie Watson
papers.abstract: Introduction Cystic fibrosis-related liver disease (CFLD) affects 30–40% of people with cystic fibrosis (CF), with 5–10% developing advanced fibrosis or portal hypertension. It is the third leading cause of CF-related mortality, more than double that of non-CFLD.1–4 UK registry data show rising adult prevalence from 14% to 19% between 2019 and 2024.3 Standard liver function tests (LFT) lack sensitivity to detect the development of CFLD,1 and whilst ultrasound and annual elastography are recommended for surveillance in CFLD inter-modality agreement in real-world cohorts remains poorly characterised.5–7 Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 96 (39.0%) patients with CF that had undergone vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE), out of a total CF cohort of 246 patients in a single tertiary CF centre. Inter-modality agreement between VCTE, ultrasound, and serum markers was assessed alongside genotype associations and Baveno-VII applicability. Results Median age was 30 years [IQR 23–37], 54.2% male, 77.1% White ethnicity; 87.5% on cystic fibrosis transmembrane receptor modulators, 76% were on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor-based regimens. Median BMI 23.1 kg/m2, 59.4% had diabetes and 89.6% were pancreatic insufficient. Of the 96 patients, 49.0% had homozygous F508del, 35.4% heterozygous F508del, and 15.6% other genotypes. Median Liver Stiffness Measurement (LSM) (5.04, 5.40, and 4.50 kPa; p=0.138), prevalence of cirrhosis (12.8%, 17.6%, 13.3%; p=0.819) and portal hypertension (12.8%, 17.6%, 6.7%; p=0.571) did not differ significantly by genotype. Ultrasound determined steatosis was identified in 21.3%, 23.5%, and 6.7%, respectively, with nodular appearances in 31.9%, 35.3%, and 26.7% respectively (figure 1) Of patients with CFLD, 91.7% had APRI <1.5 and 33.3% had FIB-4 <1.3, meaning the majority would not reach thresholds warranting further investigation. No patient without liver disease had APRI >1.5, and only 10.7% had FIB-4 >1.3 (p<0.001). Applying the Baveno-VII CSPH rule-out criterion (LSM <15 kPa and platelets ≥150×109/L), 87 patients (90.6%) were classified as low risk; however, 4 (4.6%) had confirmed portal hypertension (NPV 95.4%). All 9 patients (9.4%) not meeting rule-out criteria had confirmed portal hypertension (sensitivity 69.2%, specificity 100%, PPV 100%, p<0.001). Conclusion In this CF cohort, VCTE outperformed serum markers and ultrasound in detecting the presence of significant liver disease, with APRI and FIB-4 lacking the sensitivity to identify liver disease in CF. Genotype was not associated with severity of hepatic disease . Baveno-VII criteria performed well to ruling in CSPH but may be less reliable at excluding it. Further prospective validation of the applicability of these non-invasive assessment modalities in CFLD is warranted. References Debray D, Kelly D, Houwen R, Strandvik B, Colombo C. papers.title: Exploring emotion identification and categorisation in simulated central vision loss: an event-related potential study
papers.authors: Gopinath Madheswaran, Ramesh S Ve, Shonraj Ballae Ganeshrao, Rajiv Raman, Hari Prakash Palaniswamy
papers.abstract: Objective This study investigated how simulated central vision loss (SimCVL) affected emotion identification and categorisation in individuals with normal vision.Methods and analysis The study recruited 29 healthy volunteers, including young adults (YA: 20–35 years) (n=10), mid-aged (MA: 40–55 years) (n=10) and older adults (60–75 years) (n=9). The participants were presented with human faces displaying three emotions, neutral, happy and sad, as stimuli. SimCVL was simulated using custom-made MATLAB programming. The study developed two experiments to investigate emotion identification (experiment 1: oddball design) and categorisation (experiment 2: equiprobable design). The behavioural responses and event-related potential (ERP) waveforms were analysed using E-prime and electroencephalogram laboratory toolbox in MATLAB, and the data was analysed using SPSS V.20.Results Emotion identification was present for both happy and sad in the Oddball (P300) paradigm. However, reduced amplitudes and delayed latencies were observed in OAs, particularly in simulated conditions (p<0.01). OAs had delayed reaction times and reduced accuracy in the simulated condition compared with MA and YA (p<0.01). No or minimal differences in amplitudes and latencies were found for early visual processing (P100) and encoding of facial features (N170) across age groups in simulated conditions. Delayed latencies and reduced amplitudes were observed in OAs when decoding (N250) facial features.Conclusion Emotion identification and categorisation are affected in older individuals with SimCVL compared with young and MA adults. Negative emotions had reduced performance index than happy across age groups, and this effect was maximum in OAs. The study suggests that further research is needed to explore the neural basis of emotional processing in patients with CVL using event-related potentials.

papers.title: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised clinical trial on flexible doses of escitalopram and naltrexone in the treatment of men with compulsive sexual behaviour disorder: study protocol presentation
papers.authors: Michał Lew‐Starowicz, Małgorzata Draps, Kacper Wilk, Paweł Wiśniewski, Mateusz Kazimierz Gola
papers.abstract: Background Recent research has led to a better understanding of biological and psychosocial correlates of compulsive sexual behaviour disorder (CSBD). Psychotherapy is considered a first-line treatment strategy, while evidence on the use of pharmacotherapy is still scarce. This study aimed to provide new data on the efficacy of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an opioid receptor antagonist used as monotherapy or in combination in CSBD. Methods and analysis 410 adult men seeking treatment due to perceived loss of control over sexual behaviour and its negative consequences, meeting the ICD-11 diagnostic guideline of CSBD and scoring ≥50 on the Compulsive Sexual Behavior Disorder Scale, used for assessment of CSBD according to ICD-11 guidelines (CSBD-19) questionnaire, will be randomised to 24-week, double-blind treatment with either escitalopram 10–20 mg, naltrexone 25–50 mg, combined treatment or placebo (fixed- and flexible-dosing for the first and subsequent 12 weeks, respectively) with a 12-month follow-up after completing the medication. Men with relevant psychiatric or neurological comorbidity or cognitive impairment, with current psychoactive substance dependence or compulsive gambling, already using psychotropic medications, with positive drug test or significant blood lab test abnormality, or any medical or concomitant treatment-related contraindications for use of any of the investigated medications will be excluded from participation in this clinical trial. Patients will be assessed using structured clinical interviews, validated questionnaires, ecological momentary assessment and functional electroencephalography. Pharmacovigilance and lab tests will be provided throughout the active treatment phase to monitor its safety and tolerability. Main outcome measure will include changes in the severity of symptoms of compulsive sexual behaviours operationalised using CSBD-19 and Brief Pornography Screen (BPS) questionnaires as well as diary assessments. A mixed multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) model will be applied with three measurements (before therapy initiation, after 12—primary endpoint and 23 weeks of treatment—secondary endpoint) in the four treatment arms. Regression models will be used in the search of predictors of clinical outcomes and correlation analyses to measure the relationship between psychometric outcomes, diary variables and neuronal biomarkers. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval was granted as part of the Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS) Part II assessment in Poland on 17 February 2025. The trial was authorised in Poland on 24 February 2025 (EU CT approval reference: 2024-514490-22-01). The results of the study will be presented during conferences and published in peer-reviewed journals. Trial registration number EUCT: 2024-514490-22-01.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled mental health applications for adolescents: a scoping review of safety, effectiveness and clinical implementation
papers.authors: Meita Dhamayanti, Susaldi Susaldi, Fanni Hanifa, Yova Agustini, Hardinsyah, Hardinsyah, Salma Widya Azhari
papers.abstract: Objectives To map artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled mental health applications for adolescents and distinguish the available evidence on clinical functions, predictive or diagnostic performance, symptom-level effectiveness, safety, governance and implementation readiness. Design Scoping review conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) extension for Scoping Reviews. Data sources PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, the Cochrane Library and ScienceDirect were searched from 1 January 2014 to 17 June 2026. Eligibility criteria English-language peer-reviewed sources addressing AI-enabled screening, prediction, assessment, monitoring, therapeutic support, care navigation, safeguarding or implementation for adolescents or school-aged youth were eligible. Adult-only studies, non-AI digital tools, protocols without results and unverifiable or promotional sources were excluded. Charting and synthesis Primary studies and evidence syntheses were analysed separately. 95 primary studies were mapped using mutually exclusive principal AI-modality and clinical-function categories; effectiveness, safety and implementation domains were non-mutually exclusive. Results The database searches identified 11 167 records, and 1 additional evidence synthesis was identified and assessed during revision; 103 sources were included, comprising 95 primary studies and 8 evidence syntheses. Structured-data machine learning was the dominant modality (42/95, 44.2%), and risk prediction or prognosis was the leading clinical function (45/95, 47.4%). Predictive or diagnostic performance was reported in 83 studies (87.4%), but symptom-level effectiveness in only 1 (1.1%). No primary study provided a dedicated prospective AI-safety evaluation. Implementation evidence focused on bias or equity monitoring (28/95, 29.5%), privacy or data governance (26/95, 27.4%), human oversight (19/95, 20.0%), acceptability (18/95, 18.9%) and feasibility (15/95, 15.8%). No study evaluated sustained routine-care scale-up or implementation cost as a principal outcome. Conclusions Within the retrieved evidence base, adolescent mental-health AI research was concentrated in technical development, with limited prospective evidence of clinical benefit, safety and routine implementation. The field is dominated by prediction and internal validation, whereas symptom-level benefit, prospective safety, workflow integration, scale-up and sustainability remain largely untested. Future applications should be evaluated as supervised, human-in-the-loop systems with explicit safeguards for consent, privacy, fairness, accountability and crisis escalation.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of a DenseNet-121 deep learning algorithm for chest radiograph triage in health assessment applicants: a prospective shadow-mode validation study in Nepal
papers.authors: Lochan Shrestha, Dinesh Maharjan, Uttam Bista
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of a publicly available DenseNet-121 convolutional neural network (TorchXRayVision) for triaging chest radiographs of health assessment applicants at a tertiary hospital in Nepal. DESIGN: Prospective, single-centre, shadow-mode diagnostic accuracy validation study. Reported in accordance with the Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) 2015 checklist and STARD-Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Developmental and Exploratory Clinical Investigations of DEcision support systems driven by Artificial Intelligence (DECIDE-AI) guidelines. SETTING: Department of Radiology and Imaging, Patan Academy of Health Sciences/Patan Hospital, Lalitpur, Nepal. PARTICIPANTS: 826 consecutive health assessment applicants (foreign employment predeparture medical examination and student migration) undergoing chest radiography from 5 June 2026 to 20 June 2026 inclusive (16 days). Two cases were excluded due to Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine technical failure. INDEX TEST: DenseNet-121 algorithm (TorchXRayVision library, densenet121-res224-all pretrained weights). A maximum aggregated pathology probability score was derived per radiograph and compared against a post hoc derived threshold of 0.6258 (selected as the highest threshold achieving the prespecified ≥95% sensitivity criterion). REFERENCE STANDARD: Single-reader-per-case review by one of three radiologists-two board-certified radiodiagnosticians (LS: 276 cases; DM: 275 cases) and one radiology resident (UB: 275 cases)-each blinded to AI output, using a standardised data collection worksheet capturing binary classification (abnormal/normal) and free-text findings. RESULTS: Of 826 radiographs, 41 (4.97%) were classified as abnormal by the reference standard. At the post hoc derived threshold of 0.6258, the DenseNet-121 algorithm achieved: sensitivity 95.12% (95% CI 83.9% to 98.7%), specificity 77.2% (95% CI 74.1% to 80.0%), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.9583 (95% bootstrap CI 0.9225 to 0.9843), negative predictive value (NPV) 99.67% (95% Wilson CI 98.8% to 99.9%), positive predictive value 17.89% (95% Wilson CI 13.4% to 23.5%) and Cohen's κ 0.237 (95% bootstrap CI 0.174 to 0.304). Brier score was 0.3621 (null Brier 0.0472) and expected calibration error was 0.564, confirming calibration failure due to score compression (range 0.52-0.72) despite preserved discrimination. The sensitivity estimate should be interpreted with caution given the relatively small number of reference-standard positives (n=41); the Wilson CI width of 14.8 percentage points (83.9-98.7%) reflects substantial uncertainty around this point estimate. CROSS-VALIDATED RESULTS: 10-fold cross-validation yielded bias-corrected sensitivity 95.12% (95% Wilson CI 83.9% to 98.7%; optimism 0.00 pp) and specificity 75.80% (95% Wilson CI 72.7% to 78.7%; optimism+1.40 pp), confirming by internal validation that primary metrics are not materially inflated by circular optimisation; independent external validation was not performed. CONCLUSIONS: The DenseNet-121 algorithm demonstrated high point-estimate sensitivity and excellent discrimination for chest radiograph triage in a Nepali health-assessment population, supporting its potential as a radiographic abnormality rule-out triage tool (NPV 99.67%); this does not constitute microbiological exclusion of active pulmonary tuberculosis. Systematic score compression-preserved discrimination despite calibration shift-is a quantifiable marker of low- and middle-income country distributional shift. Prospective local calibration studies and independent external validation are warranted before operational deployment.

papers.title: Sub-clinical eating behaviours in Celiac disease: a scoping review
papers.authors: Marina Francesca Gattoni, Eleonora Volpato
papers.abstract: Objectives Coeliac disease (CeD) is an autoimmune disorder caused by the ingestion of the gluten allergen, leading to damage to the small intestine and nutrient malabsorption. Currently, the only safe treatment is the gluten-free diet (GFD), whose dietary restrictions may affect people with CeD (PwCeD)’s relationship with food and increase the risk of subclinical eating behaviours. This scoping review aimed to identify the presence and diversity of subclinical eating behaviours among PwCeD. Design The scoping review observed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines to select studies, with two independent reviewers conducting all the phases of the review. Data sources Eligible articles were retrieved from the following databases from inception to September 2025: PubMed (NCBI platform), Psycinfo (APA PsycNet), Web of Science (Clarivate), Scopus (Elsevier), Cochrane Library (Wiley). Eligibility criteria English, peer-reviewed full-text papers regarding quantitative studies focusing on PwCeD and subclinical eating behaviours that do not reach significance for a full eating disorder diagnosis were included in the present review. Studies involving individuals with non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, qualitative designs, reviews, grey literature and non-English publications were excluded. Data extraction and synthesis The main outcomes involved eating behaviours that did not reach significance for a full eating disorder diagnosis and that might be related to emotional regulation. Results From 1805 records, 13 predominantly cross-sectional studies met inclusion criteria involving 3724 subjects in total. Participants were predominantly female (M: 595/F: 3129; age: 35.14±8.37, BMI: 22.50±2.48), mostly referring to a moderate adherence towards GFD. The identified subclinical eating behaviours included: maladaptive eating attitudes, disordered eating, food insecurity, hypervigilance and body dissatisfaction. In addition, nine studies investigated their associations with GFD, quality of life (QoL), social anxiety and psychiatric comorbidities. Conclusion Subclinical disordered eating behaviours may impair QoL, mental health and adherence to GFD in PwCeD. Further studies are needed to enhance patients’ psychological state.

papers.title: Multidimensional evaluation of AI for integrated panvascular disease management: benchmarking against consensus guidelines on lipid, metabolic and antithrombotic therapy (2024–2025)
papers.authors: Zhaozhi Zhang, Yangyang Tan, Hao Chen, Jiayuan Song, Jiuhua She, Zhaoying Li, Tiebiao Liang
papers.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the performance of large language models (LLMs) in the comprehensive management (CM) of panvascular disease (PVD) across dimensions of language complexity, comprehensibility, actionability and information reliability. Design A cross-sectional benchmark evaluation study using a standardised clinical question bank derived from Chinese expert consensus statements on PVD management. Setting Four mainstream LLMs (DeepSeek-V.3.2, Doubao-1.8, Kimi-K2 and Qwen3-Max) were evaluated using 50 standardised clinical questions covering dyslipidaemia management, metabolic regulation, antithrombotic therapy and CM. The evaluation was conducted using the publicly available versions of the models in January 2026. Primary and secondary outcome measures The primary outcomes were differences among LLMs in nine validated readability metrics, including the Automated Readability Index, Flesch Reading Ease Score, Gunning Fog Index, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Coleman-Liau Index, SMOG Index, Linsear Write, Dale-Chall Readability Score and Spache Readability Formula. Secondary outcomes included understandability, actionability and overall scores assessed using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), information quality assessed using the DISCERN instrument, and correlations between readability and core evaluation metrics. Results A total of 200 artificial intelligence (AI)-generated responses were included in the analysis. Significant differences were observed among the AI models across all four evaluation metrics (PEMAT-Understandability Score (PEMAT-U), PEMAT-Actionability Score, PEMAT-Total Score (PEMAT-T) and Mean DISCERN Score (M Dis Score); all p<0.001). Qwen3-Max achieved the highest median scores for PEMAT-U and PEMAT-T, whereas DeepSeek-V.3.2 achieved the highest median M Dis Score. Content category had a limited influence on evaluation outcomes, with an overall difference initially observed only for PEMAT-U; however, this difference was no longer significant after Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction (FDR-adjusted p=0.136). Stratified analyses showed that intermodel differences were generally consistent across content categories, although the difference in PEMAT-U for the CM and cross-cutting issues category was no longer significant after FDR correction (FDR-adjusted p=0.052). Overall, model type was associated with substantial differences in PEMAT-P and DISCERN scores, whereas content category exerted a comparatively limited effect. Conclusions Mainstream LLMs generate structured management recommendations with varying characteristics across readability, understandability, actionability and information quality. As this study focused on structural and linguistic attributes rather than clinical accuracy, the conclusions are limited to instrument-based assessments. Future research should validate real-world clinical utility and patient comprehension to ensure safe AI integration.

papers.title: Association between the triglyceride-glucose-waist circumference index and obstructive sleep apnoea: a hospital-based case–control study in China and the development of machine learning models
papers.authors: Chuan Guo, Tiangu Yang, Yong Liu, Li Zhang, Youzhuang Zhu, Lili Jiang, Yuanfang Jia, Fang Sheng, Lin Wang
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We aimed to examine the association between the triglyceride-glucose-waist circumference (TyG-WC) index and obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and to develop machine learning (ML) models to identify OSA. DESIGN: Case–control study and development of six ML models. SETTING: A sleep medicine centre at a tertiary hospital in China. PARTICIPANTS: 534 patients with OSA diagnosed by polysomnography between 2017 and 2025, matched with 534 OSA-free individuals. PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the association between TyG-WC and OSA, assessed using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, education, marital status, hypertension, diabetes, smoking and alcohol use. Secondary outcomes were the dose-response and threshold effects, subgroup interactions, external consistency testing in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), sensitivity analyses and development of ML models (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbours, Naive Bayes) incorporating TyG-WC and the same clinical variables, evaluated for discrimination, calibration and clinical utility, interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). RESULTS: TyG-WC was linearly associated with OSA (adjusted OR=1.067, 95% CI 1.055 to 1.079; p<0.001; p for non-linearity=0.827), and this association remained robust in NHANES and sensitivity analyses. Significant interactions were observed by age and hypertension status. In the test set, six ML models demonstrated good predictive performance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)=0.732–0.803). XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination (AUC=0.803, 95% CI 0.755 to 0.851), with no evidence of miscalibration (Brier score=0.183; Hosmer-Lemeshow p>0.05) and positive net benefit across threshold probabilities. SHAP identified TyG-WC as the most influential predictor across all ML models. CONCLUSIONS: TyG-WC was associated with OSA. ML models incorporating TyG-WC and clinical variables achieved good performance, supporting TyG-WC’s potential as an accessible risk marker. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

papers.title: Determination of central pain modulation biomarkers to characterise patients with cancer and refractory pain: protocol for a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Lara Rubal‐Otero, Natalia Martínez Rodríguez, Margarita Álvarez-Rodríguez, Alberto González-Villar, M. T. Carrillo‐de‐la‐Peña
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pain is one of the most prevalent and disabling oncological symptoms, but its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Most research has focused on peripheral mechanisms, while central pain modulation has been poorly explored. Quantitative sensory testing (QST) and electroencephalography (EEG) provide non-invasive approaches to assess central pain processing but the evidence using those approaches in patients with cancer is limited. This study protocol aims to identify and validate central biomarkers of pain perception and modulation (QST and EEG) and the role of moderator variables to better characterise patients with cancer pain. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This study protocol describes a multicentre, cross-sectional, case-control study that will include a minimum of 470 ambulatory patients with cancer, including 313 with oncological pain and 157 without pain. Participants will be recruited taking into account age, sex and cancer type (lung, breast, pancreas, prostate and colon). All participants will perform a single face-to-face assessment that will include sociodemographic and clinical data, QST (pain modulation and inhibitory pain mechanisms, temporal summation and pain thresholds) and EEG (at rest and in response to thermal nociceptive stimuli) assessment and administration of questionnaires (pain, quality of life, fatigue, sleep, mood, etc). Statistical modelling and machine learning approaches will be used to investigate pain modulation biomarkers, their association with age and sex and to characterise patients with cancer pain. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study has received approval from all local ethics committees of the participating clinical sites. Results will be disseminated through high-impact peer-reviewed journals, international conferences and open data repositories, in compliance with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles, and following the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) statement for observational case-control studies. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ISRCTN35887998.

papers.title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence Health Education Accurately Linking System (AI-HEALS) for the intervention of chronic kidney disease: a randomised controlled trial protocol
papers.authors: Xin Zhao, Yajuan Wang, Min Liu, Difei Duan, Xinyue Chen, Yunhua Li, Dengyan Ma
papers.abstract: Introduction Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health challenge with high morbidity and socioeconomic burden. Despite medical advances, long-term prognosis remains poor, highlighting the need for sustained self-management and health education. Traditional face-to-face care is limited by inefficient follow-up and insufficient attention to psychosocial and behavioural determinants, making it inadequate for long-term support. Artificial intelligence and mobile health offer personalised sustainable health education interventions. Accordingly, we developed the Artificial Intelligence Health Education Accurately Linking System (AI-HEALS) to support CKD self-management. Methods and analysis This is a single-centre, randomised, assessor-blinded, parallel-group controlled trial. A total of 74 adults with stages 1–5 CKD will be randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to either the control group, receiving standard care or the intervention group, receiving standard care plus the AI-HEALS programme for 3 months. The primary outcome is health-related quality of life, assessed using the physical component summary (PCS) score of the 12-item Short Form Health Survey (SF-12). The primary endpoint is the between-group difference in change in SF-12 PCS score from baseline to the end of the 3-month intervention. Secondary outcomes include serum creatinine levels, urinary protein creatinine ratio, anxiety, depression, quality of sleep, self-efficacy, dietary behaviour and eHealth literacy. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, at the end of the intervention and at 3, 6 and 9 months after completion of the intervention. Linear mixed-effects models will be used to analyse repeated measurements over time. The findings of this study will provide evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI-HEALS in improving health-related quality of life and supporting self-management among patients with CKD. Ethics and dissemination This study protocol has been approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of West China Hospital of Sichuan University (Ethics Approval Number: 2024–2106). The findings are expected to be disseminated through peer-reviewed journal publications, academic conference presentations and other forms of scholarly communication. Trial registration number ChiCTR2500099413.

papers.title: Glow Up: a single-centre observational study protocol to develop digital biomarkers for prediabetes screening and digital phenotyping
papers.authors: Victoria Brügger, Magdalena Fuchs, Qiuhan Jin, Benjamin Wirth, Stefan Bilz, Michael Brändle, Tobias Kowatsch, Mia Jovanova
papers.abstract: Introduction Prediabetes, a key precursor to type 2 diabetes, is highly prevalent and underdiagnosed, particularly among adults aged ≥45 years with elevated body mass index (BMI). Early detection is critical because lifestyle interventions can delay or prevent progression to type 2 diabetes. The Glucose Observation and Wearable Use for Prevention (Glow Up) study aims to (1) test the feasibility of a digital biomarker for pre-diabetes screening using wearable- and smartphone-derived lifestyle factors (eg, sleep, physical activity and nutrition patterns) in daily life and to (2) characterise individual- and metabolic subgroup-level variability in lifestyle factors and glycaemic control. Specifically, we aim to examine how lifestyle factors relate to glycaemic status and identify personalised predictors of early metabolic dysregulation. Methods and analysis Glow Up is a prospective, single-centre, observational case-control study conducted in Switzerland. Adults (n=200) aged ≥45 years with body mass index (BMI) ≥25 kg/m² will be recruited, including n=100 individuals with pre-diabetes and n=100 age- and sex-matched normoglycaemic controls. Participants will undergo 4 weeks of continuous monitoring using a blinded continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and commercial- and medical-grade wearables; for example, capturing physical activity, sleep and physiological markers (heart rate variability, heart rate and skin temperature), in addition to completing daily image-based meal logs using smartphones. Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and body anthropometrics will be collected at the enrolment visit (T0) and repeated at follow-up (T3), approximately 5 weeks apart. The primary outcome is glycaemic status at T3, classified from HbA1c and FPG using prespecified thresholds. Secondary outcomes include CGM metrics, lifestyle profiling (sleep, physical activity, stress and nutrition) and adherence to image-based meal logging. Ethics and dissemination The study received ethics approval from the Ethics Committee of Eastern Switzerland on 15 May 2025 (BASEC ID: 2025–00972). Written informed consent is obtained from all participants before any study procedures are performed. Findings will be disseminated as articles in international peer-reviewed journals and as posters and oral presentations at national and international conferences. Summaries will be provided to funders and collaborators, and personalised reports to participants. Trial registration number NCT07373418.

papers.title: Risk assessment and prediction of myopia among school-age children in South China: protocol for a longitudinal follow-up study
papers.authors: Jingfeng Mu, Haoxi Zhong, Huimin Zhu, Qingting Pan, Mingjie Jiang
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT: INTRODUCTION: Myopia among children and adolescents has become an important public health concern. The pathogenesis of myopia remains unclear, and myopia may be associated with various ocular complications. Although myopia is preventable and controllable, established myopia is currently irreversible. Therefore, early and comprehensive strategies for myopia prevention and control are needed. This study aims to longitudinally assess fundus images, ocular biometric parameters, and environmental and behavioural factors in children and adolescents and to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-based model for dynamically assessing the risk of myopia. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a school-based prospective longitudinal study that will be conducted in four administrative districts in Shenzhen, China, including two economically developed and two economically underdeveloped districts. One primary school will be randomly selected from each district, and all first-grade students in the selected schools will be recruited as study participants. The study will be conducted over the project period from April 2024 to November 2026, with follow-up assessments scheduled every 6 months after enrolment. During the follow-up period, participants will undergo fundus photography, ocular biometric measurements, myopia screening, including visual acuity and non-cycloplegic refraction, and questionnaire assessments of environmental and behavioural factors. AI technology will be used to interpret and quantify findings from bilateral fundus images. A DeepSurv model for predicting myopia risk will be developed using multimodal AI combined with ocular biometric parameters, environmental and behavioural factors, and other relevant indicators. The model will estimate the 1-, 2- and 2.5-year risks of developing myopia. The primary outcome of the study will be the incidence of myopia. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Shenzhen Eye Hospital (2024KYPJ023) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent will be obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all participants. The study findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and presentations at academic conferences. Key findings relevant to myopia prevention and control will also be communicated to participating schools, parents and other relevant stakeholders through appropriate educational and public health communication channels, with the aim of supporting evidence-based strategies for myopia prevention and control. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: ChiCTR2400082680.

papers.title: Psychological and anthropometric outcomes in preschool children exposed to antenatal maternal obesity: modelling of early life risk factors
papers.authors: Julie Nihouarn Sigurðardottir, Kathryn V. Dalrymple, Mary Rutherford, Lucilla Poston
papers.abstract: Background Maternal obesity is associated with increased risk of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes and obesity in offspring, yet their comorbidity among preschoolers and underlying mechanisms remain unclear.Objective To examine associations between maternal obesity in pregnancy and offspring preschool psychopathology, focusing on clinical and biological pathways.Methods In a cohort of 462 women with obesity in pregnancy (body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m²) from the UK Pregnancies Better Eating and Activity Trial, followed up with their children at 3–4 years postpartum (49% boys), structural equation models assessed effects of antenatal exposures (measured at three visits) on child risk of psychopathology: maternal inflammation (by interleukin-6), glycaemia (by random glucose or gestational diabetes diagnosis), placental function (by placental growth factor) and depressive symptoms. Child outcomes were derived from the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire scores and psychological phenotypes from latent class analysis (LCA). Child adiposity and eating behaviours were compared across phenotypes.Findings High-risk of psychopathology was identified in 11.3% of children (boys 14.7%, girls 8%). Higher antenatal maternal depression and lower placental function predicted increased risk of psychopathology, while inflammation and glycaemia were not associated (R 2=44.5%). LCA identified externalising (8%) and internalising (4.1%) phenotypes. An externalising phenotype was associated with higher BMI, weight-for-age z-scores and waist circumference; both phenotypes showed greater food fussiness than well-adjusted children.Conclusions One in 10 children of women with obesity showed early risk of psychopathology, which was linked to adiposity. Antenatal maternal depression emerged as the primary risk factor, with a novel role for placental dysfunction.Clinical implication Screening for maternal depression and placental function in pregnancies affected by obesity may help reduce adverse neurodevelopmental and metabolic outcomes in offspring.

papers.title: Public perspectives on artificial intelligence in healthcare in the USA: a cross-sectional survey
papers.authors: Vishnu Nair, Rebecca Handler, Megha D. Tandel, Yingjie Weng, Laura M. Holdsworth, Ethan Goh, Roger W. Sands, Natasha Z. R. Steele, Laura Trollinger Derry, Robert Downey Boutin, Matthew DeBell, Tamara Scott, David Svec, Neera K. Ahuja, Fátima Rodríguez, Roxana Daneshjou, Akshay Sanjay Chaudhari, Sigall K. Bell, Jonathan H. Chen, Andre D. Kumar, Adam M. Rodman, Jason Hom
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate public perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare in the USA and assess variation in trust, comfort and perceived fairness across demographic groups. Methods and analysis: This cross-sectional survey of US adults was conducted between 21 November and 4 December 2025, via YouGov, a private public opinion research firm, using a non-probability-based online panel. The sample included 500 general population respondents and an oversample of 750 adults aged 60+. Survey weights were applied to approximate the US adult population. Responses were measured using Likert-type or categorical scales and analysed using survey-weighted statistical tests with false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons. Primary outcomes included comfort with healthcare providers using AI, attitudes towards AI-generated second opinions, prior use of AI for healthcare, relative trust in AI versus clinicians for health information, preference for AI chatbots versus providers in explaining care plans and perceived effects of AI on healthcare fairness. Results: Among weighted respondents (n=500), 34.0% reported prior healthcare AI use, which was more common among college graduates than those without a high school diploma (46.5% vs 22.9%). Only 25.4% reported being comfortable or very comfortable with their provider using AI, while 43.0% were uncomfortable and 31.5% were neutral. Regarding information trust, 44.5% trusted AI much less than clinicians; 88.4% reported a provider would better help them understand their care plan than a chatbot. Prior AI use was associated with more favourable attitudes towards laboratory/imaging interpretation and AI-assisted referrals. Differences by political affiliation, insurance, health status and age were not statistically significant after FDR correction. Conclusions: AI implementation appears to be outpacing public trust. Higher educational attainment was the most consistent predictor of favourable attitudes. Notably, one-third of respondents were neutral across outcomes, suggesting public attitudes are potentially modifiable. These findings underscore the need for transparent deployment and targeted trust-building strategies to support equitable AI adoption in healthcare.

papers.title: Interhemispheric EEG Coherence in Young Children during Situations Involving Helping Behavior
papers.authors: Anna Mikhailova, T. P. Makaryina, A. A. Petrushina, V. B. Pavlenko
papers.journal: Journal of Evolutionary Biochemistry and Physiology
papers.abstract: Abstract We analyzed interhemispheric coherence of mu/alpha and beta EEG rhythms in 40 typically developing children aged 1.5 to 3.5 years. EEG was recorded from 19 electrodes during sustained visual attention and in experimental situations involving helping behavior (HB). The child’s emotional and altruistic HB was scored on a point scale. Interhemispheric EEG coherence was analyzed in eight symmetrical electrode pairs. We found that in young children, altruistic HB was more pronounced than emotional HB across the studied situations. Moreover, the higher the children’s cognitive development, the faster they shared their resources. During altruistic HB, a significant increase in interhemispheric EEG coherence was found compared to the baseline condition of sustained visual attention in the frequency ranges studied. These coherence changes are consistent with the hypothesis that interhemispheric connections are involved in HB. However, further research is needed to confirm the specific neural mechanisms involved.

papers.title: EEG-Guided Sensory Stimulation in the Correction of Mild Cognitive Impairment and Functional Disorders
papers.authors: Alexander I. Fedotchev
papers.journal: Journal of Evolutionary Biochemistry and Physiology
papers.abstract: Abstract Early detection and effective therapy of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and functional disorders is a pressing challenge in modern neurology. The aim of this work is to analyze the potential for alleviating MCI and psychogenic disorders using low-intensity transcranial and sensory (auditory, visual, audiovisual) stimulations automatically modulated by feedback signals derived from the patient’s electroencephalogram (EEG). The review addresses the outcomes of successful applications of EEG-guided transcranial interventions for the non-pharmacological correction of diverse cognitive impairments and adverse functional states in humans. Therapeutic effects of EEG-driven auditory, visual, and audiovisual stimulation modalities are discussed, alongside the advantages of combining multimodal EEG-controlled approaches. The developmental trajectories, key features, and current limitations of EEG-based technologies, as well as promising directions for their further advancement, are also analyzed.

papers.title: Augmented reality displays: from fundamentals to AI integration
papers.authors: Yuge Huang, Yizhou Qian, Yefu Zhang, Ziyang Shen, Po-Sheng Chiu, Chih-Lung Lin, Shin-Tson T. Wu
papers.abstract: In this tutorial, we introduce the key components of augmented reality (AR) glasses, an emerging platform for information display and artificial intelligence (AI) assistants that benefit users across daily life, education, healthcare, and manufacturing. We begin with perceptual metrics as key considerations in AR glasses design and then introduce light engines for image generation, including mainstream liquid crystal on silicon microdisplays and emerging micro-LED displays, as well as their driving methods. Next, we discuss display system architectures for delivering images from the light engine to the human eye, covering widely used waveguide systems as well as emerging retinal projection approaches. We also explore supporting optics for beam steering, smart dimming, and eye tracking. Finally, we highlight the integration of AI methods to enhance AR display performance, including applications in materials discovery and optical component optimization.

papers.title: Distinct Visual Pathways of Threat Retrieval in Fear‐Conditioned Faces
papers.authors: Enya M. Weidner, Marlene Götze, Adrian Taday, Johanna Maria Kissler
papers.abstract: Many have demonstrated rapid (< 100 ms) visuo-cortical differentiation of threat-associated faces. This may go back to low-spatial frequency (LSF) visual information originating from magnocellular pathways. Yet it remains unknown whether potentially magnocellular fear signals extend beyond evolutionarily prepared emotional faces. If so, spatial frequency characteristics should modulate visual processing of faces with newly acquired threat-relevance. Furthermore, it is unclear whether sub-bands of the visual spectrum are associated with autonomic arousal. Using a differential fear-conditioning paradigm (n = 68), this study tested whether early visual attentional capture, indicated by the P1 event-related potential component, face encoding, indicated by the N1 component, and autonomic arousal, indicated by skin conductance responses (SCR), prioritizes LSF information of threat-associated faces with neutral expressions during fear retrieval. Additionally, correlations tested whether the same subcortical system underlies the P1 and SCR. Stimulus ratings and N1 amplitudes confirmed successful fear acquisition. During fear retrieval, the P1 showed a selective left-hemispheric enhancement in response to LSF threat-faces. By contrast, the N1 was sensitive to spatial frequency but not fear-relevance. CS-differentiation in the SCR was not modulated by spatial frequency but longer CS presentations resulting in larger fear differentiation. Amplitudes of P1 and SCR were positively correlated only for safety faces. Data support the notion that magnocellular-cortical pathways adapt quickly to novel threat-associations and facilitate rapid threat retrieval in early visual attention, but not face encoding, even for perceptually neutral faces. At least in the present paradigm, subcortical fear pathways do not associate with anticipatory arousal in SCR.

papers.title: Inducing Interpersonal Closeness: Effects on Inter‐Brain Synchrony and Collaborative Performance
papers.authors: Laura Fornari, Tieme W. P. Janssen, Ido Davidesco, Lydia Krabbendam M. A, Nienke van Atteveldt
papers.abstract: Feeling close to another person is widely assumed to facilitate collaboration. However, causal evidence that interpersonal closeness improves collaborative behavior remains limited, and it is unclear whether any such influence is accompanied by increased synchrony at the neural level. Previous studies comparing inter-brain synchrony (IBS) and collaborative performance across relationship types (e.g., friends vs. strangers) have reported better collaboration and higher IBS in closer relationships, but these effects are confounded by familiarity and shared interaction history. To address these limitations, we experimentally manipulated interpersonal closeness in 123 dyads of strangers (N = 246) to test its causal influence on IBS and collaborative performance. Dyads were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: No Interaction, Small Talk, or a closeness-generating conversation. After the manipulation, dyads completed a collaborative task while undergoing mobile EEG hyperscanning. The manipulation was effective: perceived closeness increased significantly between the No-Interaction, Small-Talk, and closeness-generating conversation conditions. However, induced closeness did not affect collaborative performance or IBS during collaboration. These findings suggest that the better collaboration and higher IBS often reported for pre-existing relationships in previous studies may originate from factors beyond momentary feelings of closeness, such as familiarity derived from prior interaction. Interestingly, across all dyads, we observed a negative association between central delta IBS and collaborative performance, with IBS explaining unique variance beyond self-reported measures. This negative link is consistent with the idea that, in this context, IBS reflects speech-tracking and increased cognitive demands during coordination, rather than coordination efficiency.

papers.title: Emotional Context Modulates Neural Prediction‐Error Encoding
papers.authors: Darin R. Brown
papers.abstract: Emotional experiences are closely intertwined with reinforcement learning, yet the extent to which emotional context influences the neural encoding of learning signals remains unclear. The present study examined whether emotional context modulates trialwise neural prediction error (PE) encoding during reinforcement learning. Fifty-six participants completed a drifting three-armed bandit task while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Choice options were consistently paired with positive, neutral, or negative emotional images that were presented during feedback processing. Trial-by-trial PEs were estimated using a computational reinforcement-learning model and related to feedback-locked EEG activity using hierarchical linear mixed-effects modeling. Traditional condition-averaged analyses revealed robust feedback-related ERP responses to reward outcomes but minimal effects of emotional context on overt behavior or mean reward positivity (RewP) amplitude. In contrast, trialwise analyses demonstrated that emotional context significantly moderated the relationship between PE and feedback-locked neural activity. The relationship between trialwise PEs and EEG amplitude was strongest in neutral contexts, whereas it was attenuated in positive emotional contexts during the early RewP interval and in negative emotional contexts during a later posterior stage of feedback processing. Consistent with this temporal pattern, scalp topographies revealed a corresponding shift from early frontocentral to later posterior activity over the course of feedback processing. Together, these findings suggest that emotional context does not substantially alter overt learning performance or condition-averaged reward responses, but instead subtly shapes the neural encoding of PEs during reinforcement learning. More broadly, the results highlight the value of computationally informed trial-level analyses for identifying affective influences on learning signals that may be obscured by traditional condition-averaged approaches.

papers.title: EEG Signatures Support a Shrinking Spotlight of Attention After Errors
papers.authors: Mark Lavelle, Alexander Fengler, Andrew Zhang, James F. Cavanagh
papers.abstract: Errors inhibit attainment of our goals, but there are many ways to get back on track: from increased caution to heightened attention. In this report we examined EEG signatures of control and perception in 21 participants who completed a luminance-varying flanker task. Hierarchical Sequential Sample Modeling with a shrinking spotlight model was used for algorithmic decomposition of post-error adjustments. Control-related changes included a relationship between frontal midline theta power and raised decision threshold, as well as faster drift rate. Yet contrary to our hypothesis, these relationships were not significantly modulated following an error. Perceptual changes elicited by the luminance manipulation scaled with posterior alpha/beta power; both these extrinsic and intrinsic features loaded on an enhanced drift rate. Most importantly, after an error, this relationship between alpha/beta power and drift rate was enhanced. These findings support separate roles of neural systems in adaptive control: midfrontal regions were linked to generic control, whereas sensory-specific mechanisms of attentional adjustment were specifically recruited to boost evidence accumulation when control is needed.

papers.title: Blunted Neural Error Monitoring Amplifies the Adverse Effect of Childhood Maltreatment on Depressive Symptoms: Time‐Domain and Time‐Frequency Analysis
papers.authors: Jun Yang, Linghui Yang, Cong Cao
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Performance monitoring (PM) has been suggested as a promising cognitive factor to explain individual differences in the association between early maltreatment and depression, yet evidence remains limited. From a monitoring vs. executive perspective, this study thus comprehensively examined whether and how the neurophysiological (ERN and its time‐frequency decomposition components) and behavioral (posterror accuracy) indicators of PM interacted with childhood maltreatment on young adult depressive symptoms. A total of 192 Chinese university students ( M age = 21.08 ± 1.91 years; 59.4% girls) completed self‐report questionnaires and an Eriksen Flanker task while EEG activity was recorded. The results showed that blunted vs. heightened ERN and error‐related delta were more likely to amplify the adverse effect of childhood maltreatment, especially emotional neglect, on young adult depressive symptoms. However, error‐related theta and posterror accuracy did not show such interaction effects. The findings showed strong robustness across a series of sensitivity analyses. The results provide preliminary evidence that blunted error monitoring but not executive ability, reflected by ERN and error‐related delta, may be a neurobiological moderator that underlies maltreatment‐related depression, which deepens the cognitive control underpinnings of depression. However, given the high‐functioning sample, caution is warranted when generalizing these findings in high‐risk clinical samples.

papers.title: Value Sovereignty and the Limits of Democratic Delegation
papers.authors: Kwangyong Park
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Why do some forms of delegation to non‐majoritarian institutions generate persistent democratic controversy while others, equally insulated from political control, do not? The Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, for instance, are alike on the standard measures—authorization, accountability, expertise, and performance—yet are judged differently in democratic terms, a difference those measures cannot explain. This paper argues that the missing factor is who retains the authority to revise the criteria by which an institution resolves value conflicts. I call this condition value sovereignty, and treat it not as something a delegation simply has or lacks but as a matter of degree: the further the power to revise an institution's operative criteria has moved from ordinary political reach, the less value sovereignty it retains. This yields a single scale, delegation depth, on which the two banks fall at different points—the Federal Reserve's mandate, revisable by ordinary legislation, near one end, and the European Central Bank's treaty‐entrenched objective further along—and on which systems built to govern open‐ended domains, including advanced artificial intelligence, mark the far limit, where the authority to revise the criteria passes to the delegated system itself. The framework thus supplies a criterion that authorization, accountability, and performance leave unnamed, and orders both established institutions and emerging ones. Related Articles Agoba, Abel Mawuko, Yakubu Awudu Sare, Ebenezer Bugri Anarfo, and Christian Tsekpoe. 2023. “The Push for Financial Inclusion in Africa: Should Central Banks be Wary of Political Institutional Quality and Literacy Rates?” Politics & Policy 51, no. 1: 114–136. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12514 . Asongu, Simplice A., Joseph Nnanna, and Vanessa S. Tchamyou. 2021. “Finance, Institutions, and Private Investment in Africa.” Politics & Policy 49, no. 2: 309–351. https://doi.org/10.1111/polp.12395 .
