papers.title: Entrepreneurial leadership, AI adoption, and innovation performance: evidence from Indian entrepreneurial ventures
papers.authors: Rubee Singh, K. Raghuveer, Akshay Singh, Prof Vikas Kumar, Tuong Vi Thi Tran
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to explore the effect of Entrepreneurial Leadership (EL) on Innovation Performance (IP) with the mediation of Organizational Learning Culture (OLC) and the moderation of Artificial Intelligence Adoption (AIA). There is little empirical evidence encompassing the complex elements of EL and OLC in the context of Indian companies. The authors believe that this study can support leaders in implementing the right strategies to foster a learning culture and drive innovation. Design/methodology/approach An empirical study of 241 employees working in entrepreneurial ventures across India was conducted using a survey questionnaire. Structural Equation Modeling was used to examine the mediation and moderation effects using the SPSS AMOS statistical package. Findings The findings of this study align with existing research in that EL does affect the OLC, and AIA plays a moderator role in this effect. However, OLC is not found to affect IP. The authors suggest that future researchers in this field can take into account other organizational features to examine the effect more closely. Research limitations/implications This study’s findings are limited by contextual factors and sample demographics. Future research should explore additional organizational traits and technological readiness for a deeper understanding of innovation performance enablers. Originality/value The findings of this study can be useful for practitioners, i.e. entrepreneurial leaders, in implementing strategies to drive a continuous learning and innovation culture throughout the firm to mitigate the effects of dynamism in external business environments.

papers.title: Becoming-with GenAI: reconfiguring agency and authorship in science curriculum development
papers.authors: Denis Dyvee R. Errabo
papers.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the entanglement of researcher’s agency and authorship in curriculum development mediated by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Despite growing enthusiasm for GenAI’s transformative potential, little is known about the process of becoming-with AI in the epistemic and ethical labor of design. Guided by the research question – what forms of agency and authorship emerge through the process of becoming-with AI in AI-mediated curriculum design? Design/methodology/approach Employing a hermeneutic autoethnographic methodology, the researcher documented a lived experience through iterative interactions with GenAI across curriculum planning, sequencing, mapping, alignment and implementation. Data sources included structured prompting protocols, reflective analytic memos and Photovoice artifacts capturing critical decision points in AI-assisted design. Findings Qualitative content analysis has revealed five configurations in curriculum work: GenAI as a mediator of curricular coherence, an architect of sequencing learning, a cartographer of curricular alignment, a curator of contextualized learning experiences and an orchestrator of aligned and active learning. Originality/value Findings indicate that agency and authorship are not diminished in AI-mediated contexts but reconstituted as distributed and ethically intensified practices. GenAI redistributes cognitive labor while amplifying the need for disciplined discernment in evaluating alignment, coherence and epistemic integrity. Curriculum development thus emerges as a negotiated sociotechnical practice in which professional judgment remains the locus of accountability.

papers.title: Navigating ethical perceptions and relationship quality in social commerce-based AI-chatbot continuous usage
papers.authors: Saleh Bazi, Doa’a Hajawi, Zainah Qasem
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how consumers' ethical perceptions and relationship quality influence chatbot adoption in social commerce, using an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) model. The study specifically emphasizes the role of ethical considerations and relationship dynamics in shaping users' continuous intention to use chatbots. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through an online survey targeting social commerce customers in the United States and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings The results reveal that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, hedonic motivation, habit and ethical perception significantly influence relationship quality. Relationship quality and consumers' ethical perception significantly influence continuous intention to use chatbots. Facilitating conditions showed a negative impact on relationship quality, while social influence demonstrated no significant effect. Research limitations/implications The study's focus on US customers may limit its generalizability to other cultural contexts and geographical regions. Practical implications Social commerce businesses can utilize these insights to enhance chatbot implementation, foster customer engagement and address ethical concerns, ultimately improving continuous usage intention. The findings have broader social implications for understanding the acceptance of technology and ethical practices in contemporary society. Originality/value This study extends the consumers' ethical theory model by incorporating relationship quality and technology usage as key factors in understanding chatbot adoption in social commerce, addressing a gap in the existing literature regarding the integration of artificial intelligence chatbots and social commerce platforms.

papers.title: AI-generated content in personalized learning and intelligent tutoring systems: a bibliometric analysis
papers.authors: Chengxuan Liu, Walton Wider, Hao Wu, Leilei Jiang, Jingjing Li
papers.abstract: Purpose This study maps the intellectual structure and emerging thematic trajectories of research on AI-generated content (AIGC) in personalized learning and intelligent tutoring systems (ITS). It addresses the limited understanding of how AIGC-enabled personalization reorganizes learner observation, instructional communication, feedback, pedagogical mediation and institutional accountability. Design/methodology/approach A bibliometric science-mapping design was applied to 511 English-language journal articles retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection on January 30, 2026. Bibliographic coupling identified contemporary research fronts, while co-word analysis examined emerging themes and future-oriented research directions. The mapped findings were interpreted through a cybernetic and social systems lens focused on feedback, adaptation, learner agency, pedagogical communication and organizational governance. This lens informed the interpretation of the bibliometric results; it did not constitute an additional empirical test. Findings Publications and citations increased sharply from 2023 onward. Bibliographic coupling identified five research fronts: cognitive and pedagogical infrastructure; large language model-driven adaptive architectures; human agency and learner experience; adoption, ethics and governance; and stakeholder readiness. Co-word analysis revealed five thematic trajectories: large language model-centered tutoring ecosystems, institutional integration, real-time adaptive learning, pedagogical integration in digital learning contexts, and ethical and creative personalization. Together, these patterns suggest a shift beyond technology-centered automation toward recursive educational regulation, in which technical generation, pedagogical interpretation, learner response, and institutional correction remain interdependent. Originality/value The study provides a focused bibliometric mapping of AIGC in personalized learning and ITS and offers a theory-informed integrative framework. The framework distinguishes AIGC and ITS as technical systems from pedagogical communication, learner meaning-making, organizational decision premises, and reflexive governance. It positions responsible personalization as dependent on feedback quality, educator oversight, learner agency and institutional capacity to review and correct AI-supported instructional decisions.

papers.title: Using artificial intelligence to mitigate global teacher shortage
papers.authors: Rollin D. Nordgren
papers.journal: Journal of Research in Innovative Teaching & Learning
papers.abstract: Purpose This viewpoint addresses the systemic global teacher crisis – driven by burnout, unsustainable workloads and administrative attrition – and explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to reduce non-academic tasks. This piece argues that by using AI to help with administrative burdens, education systems can improve teacher retention, enhance individual student engagement and even support democracy. Design/methodology/approach This piece uses a conceptual and synthesis-based approach, combining a review of current literature with the author's firsthand narrative reflections as a veteran educator and teacher trainer. Findings The piece identifies the root causes of the teacher shortage: the overwhelming volume of non-instructional work. The analysis of the literature supports the use of AI tools to unburden teachers from non-instructional work gaining time to build robust relationships with students, increase the individualization of instruction, all of which can lead to better meeting the learning needs of their students. Finally, it allows for a better life–work balance that can mitigate teacher attrition and attract more quality candidates. Research limitations/implications This is a viewpoint article, and although it is supported by a robust review of relevant literature, it does not put forward new empirical evidence. Practical implications The practical implications of the piece focus on reforming the daily operations of educators' work by integrating AI to eliminate up to six hours of administrative workload per week, thereby reducing teacher burnout and mitigating the global shortage. Social implications The social implications center on safeguarding democratic foundations by stabilizing an endangered education system. Restoring work–life balance through AI helps attract and retain qualified teachers, preventing the systemic collapse of public schooling. Originality/value The originality of this piece is in its unique view of how to mitigate the teacher shortage by embracing AI tools rather than fear them. By using relevant national and international literature in conjunction with the authentic, lived perspective of a veteran educator, the piece provides a fresh approach to combatting the teacher shortage.

papers.title: When and how anthropomorphic AI avatars relate to user engagement intentions: roles of emotional connection, perceived authenticity and technological familiarity
papers.authors: Usman Ahmad Qadri, Alsadig Mohamed Ahmed Moustafa
papers.journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines when and how anthropomorphic AI service avatars shape user engagement intentions in digital commerce. Drawing primarily on computers are social actors (CASA) theory and using parasocial interaction (PSI) as a bounded interpretive lens, it examines emotional connection as an encounter-specific affective mechanism and perceived authenticity and technological familiarity as theoretically focal contingencies operating at different stages of the engagement process. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 employed a between-subjects experiment that manipulated higher versus lower levels of bundled visual-form anthropomorphism. Study 2 used a three-wave survey of online shoppers to re-examine the focal relationships in prior AI-avatar service encounters. Mediation, moderation, and conditional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Findings Study 1 shows that higher visual-form anthropomorphism increases user engagement intention, with emotional connection accounting for a meaningful but partial share of the effect. Study 2 provides associative support for the core relationships, although the association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection is comparatively modest. Perceived authenticity strengthens the theoretically focal association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection, while technological familiarity strengthens the association between emotional connection and engagement intention. The findings indicate that emotional connection represents one mechanism among multiple affective, cognitive and evaluative pathways linking anthropomorphic AI avatars with engagement intentions. Originality/value This study advances interactive marketing research by identifying emotional connection as a meaningful but partial encounter-level mechanism linking AI-avatar anthropomorphism with engagement intentions. It further demonstrates that perceived authenticity and technological familiarity condition the theoretically focal stages of this process, while the dominant direct component highlights the need for a multiple-pathway, rather than exclusively affective, account of AI-avatar engagement.

papers.title: The dark side of AI disclosure: can family buffer the profitability backfire?
papers.authors: Safaa M. Ahmad, Huthaifa Al-Hazaima, Sajead Mowafaq Alshdaifat, Ibrahim Alnohoud, Basma Khoja
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) disclosure and bank profitability, and to assess whether family ownership plays a moderating role in this relationship. It takes into account the trade-off between increased disclosure and near-term profitability pressure, as well as how family ownership reduces that effect. Design/methodology/approach The study utilizes a balanced panel data of 14 banks included in the Amman Stock Exchange (ASE) for the period 2015–2024, which provides a total of 140 bank-year observations. Ordinary least squares regressions are employed to explore the association between AI-related disclosure and bank profitability, measured by return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE), and the moderating effect of family ownership. In order to mitigate the potential endogeneity concerns and evaluate the robustness of the results, two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimations are conducted. Findings AI-related disclosure is negatively and significantly associated with bank profitability (ROE and ROA), showing that greater disclosure does not necessarily imply positive financial outcomes. Instead, increased disclosure of AI could signal more aggressive investment, implementation, and organizational change, which can have high upfront costs in the short term before financial gains are seen. Notably, the negative relationship is weaker in family-owned banks, indicating that better monitoring, longer investment time horizon, and greater resource discipline can help mitigate the short-term financial pressures of banks going through transformation due to AI. Originality/value This study extends the emerging AI disclosure literature by documenting a potential contemporaneous profitability penalty associated with greater AI-related disclosure. To the best of the authors' knowledge, it is among the first studies to examine the adverse profitability implications of AI-related disclosure in the banking sector while simultaneously investigating family ownership as a moderating governance mechanism. It also contributes to the family-business and corporate-governance literature by identifying family ownership as a buffering condition in the AI disclosure–profitability relationship. The findings provide new evidence from an emerging-market banking context that the financial consequences of AI-related transformation depend partly on ownership structure.

papers.title: Can GenAI be an ally for sustainable income generation through community-based tourism?
papers.authors: Sankalp Srivastava, Parijat Upadhyay, Dibyendu Nandy
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how Generative artificial intelligence (AI) based tools and technology supports skill development and capability enhancement for indigenous community-based tourism (CBT) practitioners. Emerging tools can serve as an ally in promoting sustainable income generation, economic empowerment and social inclusion for communities offering tourism services in remote locations. The study focuses on indigenous populations in Northeast India, a region renowned for its cultural and ethnic diversity but facing significant socio-economic challenges. Design/methodology/approach The researchers implemented a qualitative constructivist grounded theory method to collect data through literature reviews and interviews and surveys which included indigenous stakeholders and CBT operators and policymakers as research participants. The researchers used MAXQDA software to analyze data through thematic and axial coding methods which enabled them to discover main dimensions and their related occurrences. Findings The results show that GenAI can effectively address digital skill deficiencies while enabling indigenous practitioners to work independently. The study presents an updated Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) framework which introduces “Challenges” as a new element and shows how “Community Support” functions as a vital moderator of individual motivation. The research results demonstrate that GenAI can effectively close digital skill gaps while enhancing indigenous people’s skills through CBT and promoting their independence and social connections. The system becomes inaccessible to users because digital infrastructure limitations and public knowledge deficiencies combine with policy development shortcomings. Practical implications Successful integration requires policy interventions which need to address digital infrastructure and literacy and regulatory trust. GenAI-mediated CBT through its ability to create sustainable communities (Sustainable Development Goal [SDG] 11) and reduce poverty (SDG 1) helps preserve tribal values and their cultural heritage. The research shows that targeted skill development programs need to exist together with policy measures which will help communities achieve their optimal GenAI benefits for sustainable income generation and employment. Originality/value This research addresses a severe dearth of literature regarding GenAI integration into indigenous homestay operations. The study presents an original theoretical framework which demonstrates through empirical evidence how advanced AI technologies link to environmental sustainability objectives in rural areas. There is very limited published literature on GenAI technology integration into homestay operations amongst indigenous communities. The findings of this study present unique insights which have not been documented in previous research.

papers.title: Statistical multi-objective evaluation of human–robot interaction modes for collaborative robot control
papers.authors: Pratiksha Prakash Jawale, Shantipal Suresh Ohol, Kamalesh Arun Sorate
papers.journal: Industrial Robot the international journal of robotics research and application
papers.abstract: Purpose Human–robot interaction (HRI) modalities have been extensively investigated in recent years; however, limited research has quantitatively compared different interaction modes within a unified experimental and statistical framework. The effectiveness of such interactions depends not only on the interface design but also on the operating conditions that influence both accuracy and efficiency. Design/methodology/approach This study presents a statistical analysis and multi-objective optimization framework to evaluate three modes of operation – voice, gesture and joystick – implemented on collaborative robot systems. Experiments were conducted using a replicated full factorial design with the speed scaling factor, operating distance and payload selected as control parameters. The positional error and task execution time were used as response variables to represent accuracy and efficiency, respectively. A general linear model-based ANOVA was performed to see the significance of the main factor and their interaction. Main effect and interaction analyses further studied to quantify the performance characteristics of each interaction interface. To minimize the positional error and execution time simultaneously, a multi-objective optimization framework based on response normalization and a comparative performance index (CPI) was developed. Findings The statistical analysis revealed that interaction modality, speed scaling factor and operating distance significantly influence system performance, while significant interaction effects are also observed among the operating parameters. Joystick-based interaction exhibited the highest overall CPI, followed by voice and gesture modes. The optimized condition was obtained for joystick operation at a speed scaling factor of 0.5, an operating distance of 100 mm and a payload of 4.5 kg, with a composite desirability of 0.9344. Practical implications This study provides practical insights for implementing multimodal control systems in collaborative robotic environments. By evaluating voice, gesture and joystick-based interaction using performance metrics such as positional error, task completion time and CPI, the research identifies suitable operating conditions for improved human–robot collaboration. The findings can assist industrial practitioners in selecting appropriate control modalities for tasks involving varying payloads, distances and speed factors. The proposed evaluation framework can support. Originality/value The proposed statistical evaluation and CPI-based optimization framework provide a practical methodology for selecting optimal HRI configurations for collaborative robotic applications.

papers.title: Enhancing the manufacturing processes and productivity in Industry 5.0 with the integration of machine learning and cyber-physical systems
papers.authors: Venkatesh Naik, Soma Das, M N Vinay, H Manikandan, K Mohan Kumar
papers.journal: International Journal of Intelligent Unmanned Systems
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine the synergistic integration of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Machine Learning (ML) as a foundational enabler for Industry 5.0, focusing on creating human-centric, sustainable and resilient manufacturing ecosystems. Design/methodology/approach The study utilizes a synthesis and review approach, analyzing recent advances in ML-driven CPS applications such as workflow optimization and predictive maintenance, alongside enabling technologies like 5G and digital twins. Findings The findings show that the integration of ML in multi-tier Edge-Fog-Cloud CPS brings significant operational advantages for the shop floor, such as sub-millisecond real-time control, more efficient human–robot interaction and a 10–20% reduction in energy used by the shop floor. But, the benefits of such physical manufacturing solutions rely on the need to work through a number of operational challenges. These include formally verifying non-deterministic ML policies, reducing IT/OT cybersecurity threats, including data poisoning and signal spoofing, reducing data heterogeneity in Federated Learning (FL) and lowering high deployment costs for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Research limitations/implications Future implementation requires addressing the need for Explainable AI (XAI) for transparency, FL for privacy and reinforcement learning for human-in-the-loop control. Practical implications The proposed paradigm is applicable in smart factories, autonomous production lines and supply chain optimization, helping manufacturers maximize asset output and reduce environmental impact. Originality/value This paper highlights the essential shift from “technology-driven” (Industry 4.0) to “value-driven” (Industry 5.0) manufacturing, identifying the CPS-ML convergence as the critical engine for this transition.

papers.title: Arts and the market: an ethnography of their complex contemporary relationships
papers.authors: Paul G. Barretta
papers.abstract: Purpose An in-depth understanding of how art is valued in the market using photography as context. Changes in how photography is produced and consumed warrant a contemporary understanding of the contributions of artistry and commercialism. Design/methodology/approach A seven-year ethnography explored the current state of the relationship between arts and the market through four phases – education and training; initial fieldwork; in-depth interviews; confirming and clarifying findings through additional fieldwork. Findings Analysis of ethnographic data reveals eight inter-related categories of findings – artistry; commercialism; contrariety of artistry and commercialism; credibility of photographer (producer); shared vision; value co-creation; control of access; collaboration and coordination. As these categories progress, there is a shift in control over identifying and creating value from artistry to commercialism. Research limitations/implications The relationship between artistry and commercialism has a history of contrariety, culminating in a contemporary situation that favors the contributions of commercialism. Recommendations are made for how the definition of value can begin to shift back in the direction of artistry. Practical implications Improved collaboration and coordination among artists and arts management organizations is recommended to better represent artistry in defining and creating value. Originality/value Interaction with members of arts markets enables the researcher to investigate the contemporary relationship between arts and the market from the inside. Findings reflect the current state of the relationship and inform differences in power dynamics between the influences of commercialism and artistry in defining value.

papers.title: Testing the validity of embedding-based similarity and clustering for handwritten physics solutions
papers.authors: Maike Tauschhuber, Gerd Kortemeyer
papers.abstract: Text embeddings are increasingly used in physics education research to organize, compare, and cluster large collections of written text. Their appeal is clear: once student responses have been mapped into a vector space, similarity comparisons and clustering become computationally inexpensive. However, in assessment contexts, the relevant question is not merely whether clusters can be produced but whether the geometry of the embedding space preserves grading-relevant distinctions. We tested this premise using 992 handwritten student-problem solutions from a high-stakes engineering thermodynamics exam, transcribed into five textual representations and embedded using nine embedding mechanisms. We compared embedding similarity and embedding-based hierarchical clusters against human-assigned scores. Across models, representations, and clustering choices, embedding similarity showed a consistent but modest relationship to score similarity, and the resulting clusters were score-enriched but not score-equivalent. Experiments with a synthetic dataset suggest that this may be due to embeddings behaving like novices when categorizing physics-problem solutions; that is, their similarity geometry is strongly influenced by surface features rather than conceptual, semantic structure. These findings suggest that rubric-blind transcription and out-of-the-box, state-of-the-art embeddings can support exploratory organization and human-in-the-loop review of physics solutions, but they do not provide an unsupervised basis for grading without external validation against the assessment construct of interest.

papers.title: Denario Project: Deep Knowledge Artificial Intelligence Agents for Scientific Discovery
papers.authors: Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, Boris Bolliet, Pablo Villanueva-Domingo, Adrian E. Bayer, Aidan Acquah, Chetana Amancharla, Almog Barzilay-Siegal, Pablo Bermejo, Camille Bilodeau, Pablo Cárdenas, Miles Cranmer, Urbano L. França, ChangHoon Hahn, Yan-Fei Jiang, Raúl Jiménez, Jun-Young Lee, Antonio Lerario, Osman Mamun, Thomas Meier, Anupam Anand Ojha, Pavlos Protopapas, Shimanto Roy, David N. Spergel, Pedro Tarancón-Álvarez, Ujjwal Tiwari, Matteo Viel, Digvijay Shivaji Wadekar, Chi Wang, Bonny Y. Wang, Licong Xu, Yossi Yovel, Shuwen Yue, Wen-Han Zhou, Qiyao Zhu, Jiajun Zou, Íñigo Zubeldía
papers.abstract: We present , an Artificial Intelligence (AI) multiagent system designed to serve as a scientific research assistant. can perform many different tasks, such as generating ideas, checking the literature, developing research plans, writing and executing code, making plots, and drafting a scientific paper. The system has a modular architecture, allowing it to handle specific tasks, such as generating an idea or carrying out near end-to-end scientific analysis using as a deep-research backend (end-to-end except for the novelty assessment, which is intentionally left for the user to inspect). In this work, we describe in detail and its modules, and illustrate its capabilities by presenting multiple AI-generated papers generated by it in many different scientific disciplines such as astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, material science, mathematical physics, medicine, neuroscience, and planetary science. can also produce work that combines ideas from different disciplines, which we illustrate with a single ( N = 1 ) example: a paper that applies methods from quantum physics and machine learning to astrophysical data. We report the evaluations performed on these papers by domain experts, who provided both numerical scores and reviewlike feedback. These papers were scored by domain experts on our team; we report these scores as an indicative self-assessment rather than an independent evaluation, and we flag the resulting conflict of interest explicitly. Most drafts were rated above the midpoint of a 0–10 scale, with several rated 8–9, indicating that the generated papers reach the level a good undergraduate or early graduate student could achieve after weeks or a few months of work. They should be regarded as first drafts that require expert development, not publication-ready papers. We also document an important failure mode in which, when the input data cannot be read, the system may silently generate synthetic data, which we flag explicitly as a key limitation. We then highlight the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of the current system. Finally, we discuss the ethical implications of AI-driven research and reflect on how such technology relates to the philosophy of science. We publicly release the code at . A demo can also be run directly on the web at , and the full app will be deployed on the cloud.

papers.title: Determinants of hypertensive retinopathy among non-diabetic adults in comprehensive specialized hospitals of the Amhara region, northwest Ethiopia: a case-control study.
papers.authors: Sewunet Ademe, Tigist Feleke, Zewdu Bishaw Aynalem, Alamrew Enyew, Aynetaw Abawa, Kelemework Gashinet Ferede
papers.abstract: Background: Hypertensive retinopathy is a common microvascular complication of hypertension associated with visual impairment and increased cardiovascular risk, but evidence regarding its associated factors in Ethiopia is limited. This study aimed to identify factors associated with hypertensive retinopathy among adult hypertensive patients in northwest Ethiopia. Methods: < 0.05. Results: (AOR = 7.9; 95% CI: 2.6-24.2), diastolic BP > 90 mmHg (AOR = 25.3; 95% CI: 3.1-212.1), poor self-care (AOR = 5.6; 95% CI: 2.1-15.9), and lack of social support (AOR = 5.1; 95% CI: 2.1-12.4). Conclusion: Urban residence, elevated BMI, uncontrolled diastolic blood pressure, poor self-care, and lack of social support independently increase the odds of hypertensive retinopathy. Comprehensive management that integrates retinal screening, self-care education, and social support is needed, especially in urban areas.

papers.title: Body Mass Index: Does It Really Matter for Breast Reductions?
papers.authors: John S. Mayo, Michelle Frees, Allison J. Kehren, Omar Cespedes-Gomez, Nicole Garrett, Warren Schubert, Minh-Doan T. Nguyen
papers.abstract: Background: Multiple studies have demonstrated higher complication rates for patients undergoing reduction mammoplasty who have high body mass index (BMI). As a result, some insurance companies and providers have used a BMI limit to deny coverage of this procedure to patients seeking surgery. Still, few studies have examined whether higher complication rates affect patient satisfaction. This study further explores the relationship between BMI, complications, and patient satisfaction in reduction mammoplasty. Methods: A total of 899 consecutive patients at a single institution underwent reduction mammoplasty by 8 surgeons for symptomatic macromastia from 2016 to 2021. This cohort was queried using the BREAST-Q survey postoperatively. Kruskal-Wallis H-test was used to evaluate patient satisfaction and complication rates for 4 BMI groups, that is, normal (18.5–24.9 kg/m 2 ), overweight (25–29.9 kg/m 2 ), obese (30–39.9 kg/m 2 ), and morbidly obese (>40 kg/m 2 ). Results: Two hundred fifty patients completed surveys. The mean BMI was 32.4 kg/m 2 (range 20.3-50.5 kg/m 2 ). Mean survey responses were highly favorable in all BMI categories, including 90% stating they “definitely agree” they “would do it again.” There was no statistical difference between the 4 BMI categories for patient satisfaction or complications. Conclusions: Patients with high BMI may have similar postoperative BREAST-Q satisfaction scores when compared to those with lower BMI.

papers.title: EP8.15 Increasing BMI associated with poorer predicted post-operative patient-reported outcome measures following peri-acetabular osteotomy for developmental dysplasia of the hip – A national registry study
papers.authors: William Cawley, Mr Richard Holleyman, Vikas Khanduja, The NAHR Board, Marcus J.K. Bankes, Johan D. Witt, Mr Callum McBryde, Oliver R. Marin-Peña, Professor Ajay Malviya
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction This study aimed to assess the impact of body mass index (BMI) on post-operative patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) from periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). Materials and Methods All PAO performed for DDH were identified in the UK Non-Arthroplasty Hip Registry (NAHR) between January 2012 and November 2025. PROMs utilised were iHOT-12, EQ-5D Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and EQ-5D Index. Multiple linear regression (MLR) and ANOVA, as well as Tukey’s Highly Significant Difference (HSD) were used to assess trends in absolute PROM score and score improvement from baseline on a continuous and categorical basis, utilising World Health Organisation (WHO) BMI categories. Results 718 PAO with BMI data were identified. The majority of patients were either “Healthy” (53.8%, n=386) or “Overweight” (27.7%, n=199) BMI categories. Obese Class III (BMI ≥40) patients were excluded due to low numbers (n=3). Increasing BMI was associated with poorer predicted absolute iHOT-12 score at 12 months post-operatively (-0.65 [SE 0.27], p=0.0174) and a non-significant trend towards poorer predicted outcomes was noted at 12-months for EQ-5D VAS (-(-0.31 [SE 0.18], p=0.0883) and EQ-5D Index (-0.0040 [SE 0.0024], p=0.0939). ANOVA demonstrated a significant association between BMI and absolute outcome at 12-months post-operatively for iHOT-12 (p<0.0001), EQ-5D VAS (p=0.0182) and EQ-5D Index (p=0.0003) as well as at 6-months post-operatively for EQ-5D Index (p=0.0205). ANOVA for WHO BMI category showed a statistically-significant association between BMI and iHOT-12 (p=0.0017), EQ-5D VAS (p=0.001765) and EQ-5D Index (p=0.0020) at 12-months post-operatively. Increasing BMI was associated with greater predicted EQ-5D Index 0.0058 [SE 0.0025], p=0.0216), score improvement from baseline at 6 months post-operatively. ANOVA for effect of WHO BMI category on outcomes was significant for EQ-5D VAS (p=0.01623) and EQ-5D Index (p = 0.0499) at 6 months. Conclusions This study demonstrates a modest, statistically-significant association between increasing BMI and poorer iHOT-12 scores at 12 months post-operatively, as well as trends towards poorer iHOT-12 scores at 12 months for EQ-5D VAS and EQ-5D Index. Patients with increased BMI demonstrated greater PROM score improvement at 6 months post-operatively compared to Healthy weight patients, but these improvements were lost by 12 months.

papers.title: EP4.9 Comparing Artificial Intelligence Performance to Hip Preservation Experts on Consensus-Based Hip Preservation Questionnaire
papers.authors: Mr Karter Morris, Felix Conrad Oettl, James A. Pruneski, Balint Zsidai, Michael Tobias Hirschmann, Kristian Samuelsson, Matthew John Kraeutler
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly utilized in medical education and clinical contexts, yet few studies compare the newest large language models (LLMs) to subspecialized experts on guideline-based medical knowledge. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the performance of three AI platforms versus a panel of international hip preservation experts in answering guideline-based questions related to femoroacetabular impingement syndrome, hip dysplasia, and microinstability of the hip. Methods A 21-item multiple-choice questionnaire was developed, each containing a single correct answer based on published consensus guidelines. The survey was distributed to a panel of hip preservation specialists, and 10 expert responses were included for analysis. Three LLMs (ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3, and Claude 4.5 Sonnet) were prompted using the same questionnaire, with each LLM performing 3 runs per item. Outcomes included overall accuracy, percent agreement, Fleiss’ Kappa, generalized linear mixed-effects modeling, and qualitative assessment of AI answer justifications. Results Expert accuracy was 90.5% (95% CI 87.1 – 93.9), compared to 100% (p = 0.004) for Gemini, 98.4% (p = 0.016) for ChatGPT, and 96.8% (p = 0.053) for Claude. Expert percent agreement was 42.9% and Fleiss’ Kappa was 0.769; alternatively, AI intra-item percent agreement was 100% (Gemini) and 95.2% (ChatGPT and Claude), and Fleiss’ Kappa could not be accurately calculated due to high consistency. ChatGPT and Claude provided thorough justifications for even incorrect responses, and Gemini demonstrated consistent formatting deviations despite 100% accuracy. Conclusion Although human performance was good, all 3 LLMs demonstrated high accuracy and consistency when answering the questionnaire and outperformed the expert panel. In structured, verifiable question sets, it is evident that the knowledge of AI is rapidly approaching and/or exceeding that of medical subspecialists. LLMs are likely to serve as an effective adjunct in medical education, and limitations to AI’s implementation into clinical practice should be explored.

papers.title: EP1.24 Midterm Outcomes of Revision Hip Arthroscopy in Patients with Borderline Dysplasia: A Propensity-Matched Comparison to a Nondysplastic Control Group
papers.authors: Shahar R. Barda, Ady H. Kahana-Rojkind, Talha Syed, Roger Quesada-Jimenez, Benjamin Domb
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Hip arthroscopy for borderline hip dysplasia (BHD) remains controversial, particularly in the revision setting. Limited data exist on mid-term outcomes in this population, and few studies have compared them with patients without dysplasia undergoing revision arthroscopy. The purpose of this study is to report minimum 5-year patient-reported outcomes (PROs) and survivorship in patients with BHD who underwent revision hip arthroscopy and to compare these outcomes with those of a propensity-matched control group without dysplasia. Methods Prospectively collected data were reviewed. Inclusion criteria were revision hip arthroscopy, lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) 18°–25°, capsular plication, labral treatment of any kind, and minimum 5-year follow-up with available PROs. Exclusion criteria included prior hip conditions, preoperative Tönnis grade >1, and LCEA <18°. Controls had normal coverage (LCEA 26°–40°) and met identical surgical and follow-up criteria. Groups were matched 1:2 for age, sex, BMI, and follow-up. Rates of minimal clinically important difference and reoperations were recorded. Results 31 patients with BHD (LCEA 22.4° ± 2.0) were matched to 62 controls (LCEA 31.3° ± 3.5), with comparable age, sex, BMI, and follow-up time (79.6 ± 29.1 vs 83.2 ± 27.4 months). Both groups demonstrated significant improvement from preoperative to latest follow-up in all PROs (p < 0.001). Postoperative PROs, magnitude of improvement, MCID, and satisfaction were comparable between groups (p > 0.05). The BHD group demonstrated a lower arthroplasty free survival rate (64.5% vs 88.7%, p = 0.005), while tertiary arthroscopy rates were comparable (12.9% vs 14.5%, p > 0.99). Conclusion At minimum 5-year follow-up, patients with borderline dysplasia undergoing revision hip arthroscopy achieved significant and durable improvements in PROs, with MCID and PASS rates comparable to those of a matched control group without dysplasia. Although the borderline dysplasia group demonstrated higher rates of conversion to THA, overall outcomes and patient satisfaction remained favorable.

papers.title: FP15.6 Increasing BMI associated with poorer predicted post-operative patient-reported outcome measures at 12 months following hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement – A national registry study
papers.authors: William Cawley, Richard James Holleyman, Moksh Sachdeva, Mr Antonio Andrade, Vikas Khanduja, The NAHR Board, Mr Callum McBryde, Marcus J.K. Bankes, Professor Ajay Malviya
papers.abstract: Abstract ICLB15 - The Preservation Scorecard: Fundamentals of Tracking Outcomes and Standardizing Recovery, Session Room 12 (BMCC Level 3), October 9, 2026, 14:00 - 16:00 Introduction This study aimed to assess the impact of body mass index (BMI) on post-operative patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) from hip arthroscopy (HA) for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI). Materials and Methods All HA performed for FAI were identified in the UK Non-Arthroplasty Hip Registry (NAHR) database between January 2012 and November 2025. International Hip Outcome Tool (iHOT)-12, EuroQol- 5 Dimension (EQ-5D) Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and EQ-5D Index scores were captured pre-operatively and at 6- and 12-months post-operatively. Multiple linear regression (MLR), adjusting for age, sex and baseline score, ANOVA and Tukey’s Highly Significant Difference (HSD) pairwise models were used to assess trends in absolute PROM score as well as score improvement from baseline on a continuous and categorical basis, utilising World Health Organisation (WHO) BMI categories. Results 2845 HA with available BMI values were identified. The majority of patients were “Healthy” BMI (50.2%, n=1427) or “Overweight” (34.7%, n=986). Increasing BMI was a predictor for poorer absolute outcomes at 12-months post-operatively for iHOT-12 (-0.49 [SE 0.19], p=0.0096), EQ-5D VAS (-0.68 [SE 0.15], p<0.0001) and EQ-5D Index (-0.0043 [SE 0.0016], p=0.0064). A non-significant trend was also noted at 6-months post-operatively for EQ-5D VAS (-0.23 [SE 0.13], p=0.0796). ANOVA of BMI groups demonstrated significant associations of BMI with outcome at 6- and 12-months post-operatively for all PROMs (all p≤0.015). Increasing BMI predicted greater post-operative EQ-5D Index score improvement at 6-months (0.0033 [SE 0.0015], p=0.0270), but was not demonstrated at 12-months (p=0.5130) on continuous analysis. No association between iHOT-12 or EQ-5D VAS was demonstrated. No association between WHO BMI category and PROM score improvement were demonstrated on ANOVA. Conclusion This study has demonstrated a modest but significant association between increasing BMI and poorer absolute post-operative PROM scores at 12-months, as well as a significant association between WHO BMI category and absolute post-operative PROM scores in patients undergoing HA for the management of FAI. Patients with increased BMI demonstrated greater EQ-5D Index score improvement at 6 months post-operatively compared to Healthy weight patients, but these improvements were lost by 12 months.

papers.title: FP12.4 Impact of Squeaking on Substantial Clinical Benefit After Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Ten-Year Follow-up
papers.authors: Giovanni Provenza, Doctor Beatriz Martin Velez, Student María Hornero-Vázquez, Doctor Miguel Cañones-Martin, Doctor Jorge Martin-Lozoya, Doctor Claudia Santafe, Doctor Ricardo Larrainzar-Garijo, Doctor Oliver Marin-Pena
papers.abstract: Abstract ICLA12 - The Chondral Masterclass: Advanced Scaffolds, Orthobiologic Realities, and Young THA, Auditorium B (BMCC Level 1), October 9, 2026, 10:30 - 12:30 Objectives To analyze whether the phenomenon of squeaking following ceramic-on-ceramic (CoC) total hip arthroplasty (THA) affects long-term clinical outcomes, by evaluating the achievement of the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) and Substantial Clinical Benefit (SCB). Materials and Methods A retrospective study was conducted including 68 patients (40 men, 28 women; mean age 49.5 years; mean BMI 24.58) with a mean follow-up of 11.45 years (range 10–14). All patients underwent CoC THA using the same stem and acetabular component design, with femoral head sizes of 36 mm (n=53) and 32 mm (n=15). Functional outcomes were assessed using the iHOT-33 and HOS (Activities of Daily Living and Sports subscales). Comparative analysis between cohorts with and without squeaking was performed using Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables (MCID/SCB) and Student’s t-test for continuous variables, with statistical significance set at p<0.05. Results Squeaking occurred in 23 patients (33.8%), being mostly episodic and associated with extreme ranges of motion. No infections or revision surgeries were recorded. At 10 years, the clinical success rate (MCID) exceeded 90% for both iHOT-33 and HOS-ADL in the overall cohort. No statistically significant differences were observed in SCB achievement at 10 years between patients with and without squeaking: iHOT-33 (SCB): 83% vs 86% (p=0.74) HOS-ADL (SCB): 83% vs 86% (p=0.74) HOS-Sports (SCB): 50% vs 60% (p=0.44) One patient requested information regarding revision due to acoustic discomfort but ultimately declined given excellent functional outcomes. Overall satisfaction remained high, with no correlation between noise and implant failure. Conclusions At 11-year follow-up, squeaking in CoC THA does not compromise functional outcomes or the achievement of substantial clinical benefit. It represents an activity-dependent mechanical phenomenon that does not predict bearing failure. Surgeons can reassure patients that implant survival and clinical success are independent of the presence of this acoustic phenomenon.

papers.title: ‘The Opportunity to Catch Up’: From Emergency Response to Immunization Sustainability in Cameroon
papers.authors: Jean Christophe Fotso, Adalbert Tchetchia, Ferdinard Ngong, Victoria Ngako, Elihou Adje Olaïtan
papers.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic severely disrupted routine immunization globally and across Cameroon, causing a surge in 'zero-dose' (ZD) children and exacerbating 'missed opportunities for vaccination' (MOV). This necessitated accelerated recovery initiatives like the Big Catch-Up (BCU). This study explores BCU's operationalization, implementation and sustainability in Cameroon, assessing how vertical funding interacted with national health systems to reach ZD and under immunized (UI) children. Focusing on four districts (urban, conflict-affected, isolated island, and remote rural), we triangulated data from 34 document reviews (e.g., national policies, operational plans, budget frameworks, and EPI reports), 37 key informant interviews across all health system levels, and 11 Focus Group Discussions (FGD) with 86 community stakeholders, including caregivers. Thematic analysis reveals that while BCU remained a campaign-style intervention with parallel reporting structures, its funding acted as a critical accelerator to operationalize Cameroon's pre-existing but under-implemented 2021 National Policy and Guidelines on Catch-up Immunization. However, centralized financial control created top-down pressures that were mitigated through bottom-up co-creation during local micro-planning. Operationally, reducing MOV required a shift from passive screening to active 'Catch and Vaccinate' models, necessitating context-specific delivery adaptations in conflict zones and island populations. Despite these operational successes, stakeholders expressed deep concern regarding the long-term institutionalization due to an impending fiscal cliff. The system's heavy reliance on external donor financing threatens the sustainability of Community Health Workers' (CHW) incentives essential for demand generation. Furthermore, while the parallel IASO digital platform enabled real-time geolocation of missed children, it created double-reporting burdens, highlighting the structural challenge of synchronizing campaign tools with the national routine health information system. Ultimately, while recovery funding can successfully catalyze national policies and drive immediate equity gains, sustained resilience requires an urgent transition to domestic financing, the embedding of adaptive service delivery models into routine primary care, and the harmonization of digital tracking systems.

papers.title: Thinking out of distribution: what a PhD must train in the age of AI
papers.authors: Juan Ezequiel Gago, Rocco Di Tella, Joy Shi
papers.abstract: Abstract The production of scientific knowledge, as well as the skills required for research, is undergoing profound changes in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI) assisted research. At the same time, the use of AI assistants has been linked to the atrophy of some skills among students at different levels. Doctoral students are in a particular position: in previous levels of higher education, students’ role is based on acquiring skills; doctoral education, however, is centered on mastering knowledge in a given field as well as on being able to produce novel scientific research. In this new scientific landscape, this means balancing learning fundamental skills (e.g., formulating interesting scientific questions, articulating assumptions) with learning how to work proficiently and reliably using modern tools. While the tools that are used will keep changing, we believe that the core objective of doctoral training remains unchanged: preparing the next generation of scientists to continue the human scientific endeavor.

papers.title: CT protocol optimization for oncologic surveillance imaging: phantom-based comparison of multi-scan and single-scan acquisition strategies
papers.authors: Desislava Z. Kostova-Lefterova, P Simeonov, Desislava Hitova-Topkarova, Angel Danchev Yordanov, Virginia Payakova
papers.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) plays an important role in oncologic surveillance after treatment of gynecological malignancies, including patients treated with vaginal electronic brachytherapy. This phantom study evaluated CT acquisition strategies for oncologic surveillance, focusing on radiation dose reduction and objective image quality in the cranial, thoracic, and upper abdominal regions assessed quantitatively. CT acquisition protocols were investigated using an anthropomorphic Kyoto Kagaku phantom. Two acquisition strategies were analyzed: a multi-scan approach with separate acquisitions for the head, neck, thorax, and abdomen-pelvis, and a single-scan head-torso acquisition with region-specific reconstructions. Different exposure parameter settings and reconstruction kernels were evaluated. Objective image quality was assessed using semi-automated region-of-interest measurements with a custom FIJI/ImageJ macro. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and Artifact Index (AI) were calculated for cranial, thoracic, and abdominal regions. For the single-scan protocols, CTDIvol decreased from 4.21 mGy in the standard protocol to 2.97-3.99 mGy in the optimized protocols, while DLP decreased from 410 mGy.cm to 287-388 mGy.cm. Across all anatomical regions, SNR and CNR remained comparable with the standard protocol. Thoracic CNR ranged from 2.68 to 3.01, abdominal CNR remained stable in both liver and aortic regions, and AI demonstrated only moderate variability across the optimized protocols. Optimized CT acquisition protocols reduced radiation dose while preserving the evaluated objective image quality metrics in the cranial, thoracic, and upper abdominal regions. Among the evaluated configurations, a reduced dose single scan head-torso acquisition using reduced tube voltage and tube current modulation showed a favorable balance between radiation dose reduction and objective image quality under the investigated phantom conditions and was identified as a candidate protocol for subsequent clinical and reader performance validation.

papers.title: Design and Analysis of a Variable Stiffness Cable-driven Upper Limb Rehabilitation Robot*
papers.authors: Xiangxu Qu, Xiaojie Lv, Guanli Fang, Yuanbo Yang, Gang Wang, Cui Liu
papers.abstract: Abstract To enhance the compliance and environmental adaptability of rehabilitation robots in complex human-robot interaction scenarios, a hybrid passive-active variable stiffness mechanism incorporating linear springs was designed. Based on this mechanism, a flexible cable-driven upper limb rehabilitation system was developed, and its dynamic model was constructed. By introducing screw theory, a three-dimensional kinematic model was established, and the coupled dynamics of the multi-flexible-body system were further derived using the Lagrangian method, enabling coordinated modeling and regulation of cable tension and stiffness. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed system exhibits favorable workspace coverage and tension distribution coordination under multi-degree-of-freedom motion. The end-effector’s reachable workspace shows adaptive extensibility, while the stiffness distribution exhibits a spatial gradient structure, with higher stiffness at the top and lower stiffness at the bottom. The proposed approach provides a theoretical foundation for the modeling, control strategy development, and structural optimization of compliant rehabilitation systems.

papers.title: Involuntary facial muscle activity during imagined vocalisation contaminates EEG and enables emotion decoding
papers.authors: Yichen Tang, Paul Michael Corballis, Luke E. Hallum
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Decoding imagined speech from electroencephalography (EEG) recordings is potentially useful for brain-computer interfaces. Previous studies have focused on decoding semantic information from EEG, leaving the decoding of emotion – an important component of human communication – largely unexplored. Approach . Here, we report two experiments involving participants tasked with overt (n = 14) or imagined (n = 21) emotional vocalisation in five different categories: anger, happiness, neutral, sadness, and pleasure. Throughout, we recorded 64-channel EEG; we computed time-frequency features and used a logistic-regression classifier to evaluate emotion decoding accuracy. In five participants, we also recorded facial surface electromyography (sEMG) during imagined vocalisation, and studied the contamination of EEG by sEMG. Main results . Our results show that emotion can be decoded from single-trial EEG recordings of both overt (78.1%, chance = 20%) and imagined vocalisation (36.4%). The high-gamma band (50 to 100 Hz) and lateral EEG channels (T7, T8, and proximal) were important for decoding. sEMG analysis indicated that involuntary facial muscle activity contributed to these spectral and spatial patterns during imagined vocalisation. We identified a prominent muscle-induced pattern over lateral EEG channels – the railroad cross-tie pattern – showing greater activation during imagined happy vocalisations. We conclude that involuntary facial muscle activity is associated with certain emotion categories (i.e., happiness) and contributes to the decoding of emotion from single-trial EEG recordings. Significance . This study provides converging EEG and sEMG evidence demonstrating that involuntary facial muscle activity occurs during imagined vocalisation and is modulated by emotion, producing emotion-specific EEG contamination patterns. Although we focused on imagined vocalisations, the EMG patterns we observed closely resembled EEG patterns commonly reported in emotion decoding studies, raising concerns about involuntary facial muscle activity in such work.

papers.title: Spectrally-resolved transfer entropy in resting-state SEEG reveals epileptogenic and non-epileptogenic communication in adults and children with refractory epilepsy
papers.authors: Francois Okoroafor, Ghassan S. Makhoul, Bruno Hidalgo Monroy Lerma, Anas J. Reda, Zekai Qiang, Addison C. Cavender, Kate Wang, Emily Liao, Ajai Chari, Rory J. Piper, Timothy Denison, Rod C. Scott, Victoria L. Morgan, Torsten Baldeweg, Martin M. Tisdall, Dario J. Englot
papers.abstract: Abstract Objective . To characterise directed, frequency-resolved communication between seizure onset zone (SOZ) and non-involved zone (NIZ) regions in resting-state stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) from adults and children with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE). Approach . We analysed retrospective SEEG from 21 adults and 18 paediatric patients who underwent focal resective surgery. Channels were grouped into four link classes (SOZ → SOZ, NIZ → SOZ, SOZ → NIZ, NIZ → NIZ). Signals were decomposed into delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma, and broadband bands, and transfer entropy (TE) was estimated with a Gaussian estimator. For each source–target channel pair, an optimal temporal delay was selected by scanning delays from 2–200 ms and choosing the delay that maximised broadband TE. Significance testing used 100 phase-randomised surrogates per source and per target; Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction ( α = 0.05) was applied within each band-to-band TE grid (separately for source- and target-surrogate p -values). Main results . In NIZ → SOZ links median communication delays were longer in adults than children (median 87.9 ms vs 68.0 ms; Mann–Whitney p < 1 × 10 −10 ; Kolmogorov–Smirnov p < 1 × 10 −10 ). Across most link classes, dominant source frequencies were broadband, delta, and theta. A distinct SOZ → SOZ pattern emerged: adults showed broadband, alpha, and beta source dominance with prominent broadband → gamma transfer, whereas children showed broadband, delta, and theta dominance while retaining broadband → gamma contribution. Cross-link-class source and target frequency distributions differed significantly in both cohorts ( p < 0.05). While intra-regional SOZ–SOZ communication revealed unique multiplex signatures, inter-regional NIZ → SOZ interactions did not show a distinct spectral profile from non-involved connectivity. Significance . Resting-state SEEG communication in DRE exhibits multiplex, cross-frequency directed interactions. Spectrally resolved TE reveals conserved and cohort-specific shifts in SOZ-NIZ communication motifs. While these differences are confounded by pathology and site variations, they provide a frequency-specific characterization of the epileptogenic network that may support grounded interpretation of resting-state dynamics.

papers.title: A classroom experimental demonstration of AI water consumption
papers.authors: Barun Raychaudhuri
papers.abstract: Abstract This work presents an inexpensive laboratory model of introductory physics level for the massive consumption of water, an often-overlooked environmental issue caused by artificial intelligence (AI) hardware. The experiment comprises a power resistor serving as a miniature, table-top model of AI data centre. The electrical current passing through the resistor generates heat, while a continuously moistened cloth covering the resistor cools it by evaporation. The water lost by evaporation is refilled continuously from a reservoir kept on a sensitive balance. The rate of mass loss of water over time, and the electrical power consumed are measured independently. When magnified to the same extent of 10 8 times or more, these values reach the scale of the reported data on real-world power and water consumptions of AI hardware. The model serves two purposes: it imitates the huge water loss in actual AI data centres, and provides a hands-on practice on thermodynamic parameters involving conversion of electrical work to thermal phase change, thermal dissipations, and entropy enhancement.

papers.title: Where free chatbots fail in school physics: an evaluation across 780 Uzbek-language textbook problems
papers.authors: Bahodir Bahromovich Akhmedov, Mirjalol Yuldashev
papers.abstract: Abstract Pupils in Uzbekistan now consult free generative chatbots as a routine part of their physics homework, but the reliability of these systems on Uzbek-language K-12 problems has not been measured. We tested the free chat interfaces of ChatGPT (the GPT-5 family) and DeepSeek (the V3 family) on 780 worked exercises from the four current Uzbek state physics textbooks for grades 7–10. Each problem was submitted in its original Latin-script form, with textbook figures uploaded when referenced. Testing was carried out grade by grade between September 2025 and March 2026; the two systems were administered and graded by different researchers, with a 20% subsample ( n = 156) cross-checked for rubric consistency. Of the 772 problems scoreable for both models, ChatGPT solved 575 correctly (74.5%) and DeepSeek 600 (77.7%). The difference between the two systems was small and not sufficiently robust to support a pedagogical preference for one platform. More important for classroom practice, both systems failed on the same 119 problems (15.4%), and these joint failures were concentrated in identifiable textbook sections: fuel calorimetry and reference-value retrieval in grade 7, molecular-kinetic theory in grade 9, and inclined-plane dynamics with friction and temperature-dependent resistance in grade 10. Grade 8 showed a much lower joint-failure rate (4.1%). Across the main failure clusters, recurring demands included textbook-specific value retrieval, unit tracking and multi-step quantitative reasoning. The teaching implication is therefore not to choose a ‘better’ chatbot, but to teach pupils where verification is most necessary; we provide a section-by-section recommendation table for this purpose.

papers.title: Role of AI in physics problem-solving skills
papers.authors: Athira Ramaswamy, Mahima Chhabra
papers.abstract: Abstract The utilisation of artificial intelligence (AI) is increasing rapidly among students, specifically at the higher education level. However, its integration in teaching is comparatively gradual. Although the policies on education across the world are supporting the incorporation of AI in teaching and learning, it is worth understanding how its use would affect the problem-solving skills of students when the threat of AI taking over the job market is becoming progressively real. In this context, the present study investigates the role of AI (ChatGPT) in students’ physics problem-solving skills. We analysed and compared the responses from two groups of physics undergraduates—one who practised problem-solving using AI and the other who practised without AI—to three problem-solving tasks. Findings indicate that the group that practised without AI outperformed the group that used AI. Our study highlights the necessity of broader, large-scale investigations before implementing policy changes concerning the use of AI in education.

papers.title: Atypical late neurosyphilis presenting as status epilepticus: diagnostic and screening implications
papers.authors: Sacha Pollet, Ludovic Ernon, Joris Meeuwissen, Hélène Boogaerts, Xavier Willaert, Els Oris, Tom Fivez, Ives Hubloue, Willem Boer
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: invasion of the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from silent infection to severe neurological deficits. Despite progress in diagnostics and treatment, the diagnosis is frequently missed because it is not considered, particularly in atypical presentations and in patients with no evident risk factor. . METHODS: A 45-year-old man presented with confusion, speech difficulties, and left-sided weakness following subtle behavioral changes. In the emergency department, he had a witnessed focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure starting with head deviation to the left and tonic posturing of the left arm. Brain CT was normal, while MRI revealed right thalamic and bilateral temporal FLAIR hyperintensities with diffusion restriction in the thalamus. CSF showed mild pleocytosis (17 WBC/µL) and raised protein (67.6 mg/dL). Serum treponemal screening was positive with an RPR titre > 1:32. Neurosyphilis was confirmed by a reactive CSF non-treponemal test (RPR 1:2) in a patient with compatible clinical and CSF findings; the CSF TPHA titre was >1:10,240, which is supportive but not in itself a diagnostic criterion.Levetiracetam was started on admission and intravenous penicillin G on day 2, after the diagnosis was confirmed. Because EEG and MRI suggested possible focal status epilepticus, valproate and phenytoin were added. The patient developed respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation and deep vein thrombosis. After extended ICU stay and rehabilitation, he recovered with mild residual critical illness myopathy and cognitive deficits. CONCLUSION: Neurosyphilis is not intrinsically difficult to diagnose, provided it is considered, including outside the classically recognised risk groups such as men who have sex with men.
keywords: men who have sex with men

papers.title: Neuroimaging and neurophysiological changes following structured interventions in children with developmental coordination disorder: a scoping review
papers.authors: Francisca Domke, Mauricio A. Lopez-Espejo
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Longitudinal neuroimaging and neurophysiological studies can indicate whether structured interventions in developmental coordination disorder (DCD) are accompanied by neurobiological change, but this literature has not been synthesized across modalities, follow-up intervals, and analytic approaches. OBJECTIVE: To map longitudinal neurobiological outcomes after structured interventions in children and adolescents with DCD or probable DCD and the analytic approaches used, including neurobiological-clinical/functional linkage analyses. METHODS: We conducted a scoping review following JBI methodology, reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S. Eligible sources included participants aged 0-18 years with confirmed or probable DCD, a structured intervention, and neurobiological assessment at baseline and ≥1 post-intervention time point. Two reviewers independently screened records and charted data. We searched six databases, two trial registries, and preprint platforms on January 10, 2026 (updated August 21, 2026), without date or language restrictions. Formal critical appraisal was not undertaken; methodological and reporting features were charted descriptively. RESULTS: Of 747 records identified, 13 sources (eight independent cohorts) published between 2012 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Neurobiological sample sizes ranged from 20 to 88 (median 49). Designs included randomized controlled, non-randomized controlled, and quasi-experimental pre-post studies. Interventions clustered into Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance (CO-OP; 6 sources), exercise/motor-learning programs (4), and neuromuscular/biomechanical approaches (3). Modalities included diffusion tensor imaging, resting-state functional MRI, structural MRI/voxel-based morphometry, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, electroencephalography/event-related potentials, and surface electromyography. MRI-based longitudinal outcomes were reported exclusively in CO-OP cohorts, with several publications arising from shared registered trials and partial cohort overlap. Six sources included neurobiological follow-up beyond the immediate post-intervention assessment. Analytic approaches varied in pre-post versus group-by-time contrasts, region-of-interest versus whole-brain analyses, and correction for multiple comparisons. Seven sources reported neurobiological-clinical/functional linkage analyses; five tested change-based associations, and statistically significant findings were limited to individualized movement-quality outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and unevenly distributed across intervention categories and modalities. Priorities include independent replication, longitudinal neuroimaging of non-CO-OP interventions where scientifically justified, more consistent follow-up, and prespecified, adequately powered linkage analyses.

papers.title: Development and Student Perceptions of a Custom AI Agent for Asynchronous Construction Education
papers.authors: Shadi Alathamneh, Wesley Collins
papers.journal: International Journal of Construction Education and Research
papers.abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly used in education; however, most applications position them as supplementary tools rather than central instructional systems. This study develops and evaluates students’ perceptions of a custom AI agent designed to serve as an instructional interface for an asynchronous learning activity focused on BIM-based quantity takeoff (QTO). The agent was developed using a structured dialogue tree and a curated knowledge base to provide guidance through technical workflows. A classroom implementation was conducted with 114 senior-level undergraduate construction management students across eight course sections, with no direct instructor intervention during the activity. Because most participants had limited prior exposure to Autodesk Assemble and BIM-based QTO, the study examined whether students could use the AI-guided environment to support task completion and confidence in learning. Results from a mixed-methods post-activity survey indicated that students perceived the agent as useful, accurate, and effective in supporting model navigation, data extraction, and QTO tasks. Students also reported low reliance on instructor assistance, moderate confidence after the activity, and willingness to use similar tools in future learning. Qualitative responses emphasized the value of self-paced learning, immediate support, and structured, step-by-step guidance, while also identifying limitations in specificity of responses and conversational flexibility.

papers.title: Exploring User Attitudes and Brand Loyalty in AI Chatbots: The Roles of Service Quality, Perceived Ethics, and Self-Efficacy
papers.authors: Chun Shao
papers.abstract: With the growing prevalence of AI technologies, chatbots have become integral to online experiences. While prior research has made considerable progress in understanding factors influencing chatbot adoption, limited attention has been paid to the antecedents of user attitudes and brand loyalty. Grounded in self-efficacy theory and the SERVQUAL framework, this study adopts a SEM-ANN approach to examine: (1) how self-efficacy, system quality (e.g., service quality and social presence), and trust factors (e.g., perceived ethics and credibility) relate to users’ attitudes toward AI chatbots, and (2) how these attitudes subsequently predict brand loyalty. Using survey data from US chatbot users, the study identifies perceived credibility as the strongest predictor of user attitudes, followed by service quality, perceived mastery, perceived ethics, and social presence. Additionally, the relationships between user empowerment, system evaluations, and attitudes toward chatbots differ based on perceived ethics and credibility. Implications for chatbot design and consumer loyalty are discussed.

papers.title: Preference and decision difficulty in AI-generated architectural facade stimuli: evidence from spatial design students in Taiwan
papers.authors: Yu-Chao Chen, Lucky Shin-Jyun Tsaih
papers.journal: Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering
papers.abstract: Understanding how design students evaluate architectural visual cues is complicated by real-world building variation. Generative AI can produce comparable facade alternatives from a common baseline, though it transforms multiple visual attributes simultaneously rather than isolating pure “style”. This study examines visual preference and decision difficulty among spatial design students in Taiwan using AI-generated transformations based on seven architect-style prompt categories applied to familiar campus buildings. A cohort of 106 students completed a pairwise forced-choice task, yielding 3,298 valid judgments. To address the methodological challenges of comparative research, preferences were analyzed using a Bradley–Terry-style logistic model, and the AI stimuli were validated through an independent expert recognition task, which confirmed high category recognizability (81.3% accuracy) despite geometric drift. The model revealed a structured preference hierarchy, with the Zaha Hadid, Richard Meier, and Oscar Niemeyer categories receiving the highest estimated utilities. Furthermore, mixed-model analysis of reaction times demonstrated that decisions were significantly faster when the overall preference gap between the two architectural options was larger. While adopting a cautious approach to claims of pure style isolation, this study contributes to architectural education by offering a rigorous, audited framework for using generative AI imagery to investigate visual judgment and design cognition.

papers.title: Root tourism marketing: a conceptual framework
papers.authors: Luca Giraldi, Guido Capanna Piscè, Simone Splendiani
papers.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual framework for root tourism marketing. Drawing on push-pull theory, service-dominant logic, the experience economy, and post-COVID destination-resilience thinking, it explains how diaspora motivations shape value co-creation, experience design, sustainable destination positioning. A central theoretical contribution aligns strategic marketing levers with distinct diaspora clusters,categorized by their genealogical proximity and emotional engagement. This equips destination management organizations (DMOs) with a rigorous tool to move beyond generic promotion toward efficient, culturally sensitive marketing strategies. Furthermore, the framework integrates the role of digital technologies across the visitor journey, from ancestry research to AR/VR on-site interpretation and AI-enabled post-visit storytelling. Finally ethical responsibilities and operational barriers are incorporated as critical conditioning variables for strategic decision-making.

papers.title: DMSPC: A novel approach for meta learner selection in stacked ensemble to enhance speech emotion recognition
papers.authors: Astha Tripathi, Poonam Rani
papers.journal: International Journal of Computers and Applications
papers.abstract: Speech emotion recognition plays a vital role in human–computer interaction. In this research work, we propose a Dynamic Meta-Selection approach in Stacked Ensemble. The proposed model is structured with two distinct layers. In the first layer we select the datasets, perform pre-processing and extract handcraft features. In the second layer we selected different machine learning classifiers, as base learners. Further, we introduce a novel meta-selection approach DMSPC, which dynamically selects the most suitable base classifier as the meta-classifier. To validate the results we have taken into account four distinct datasets: SUBESCO, RAVDESS, EMOVO, and EMODB. The results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves promising accuracy across multiple datasets – 79.39% on RAVDESS, 91% on SUBESCO, 84.44% on EMOVO, and 84.55% on EMO-DB – showing superior performance when compared to various traditional ML classifiers.

papers.title: GOVERNING AI-ASSISTED ASSESSMENT IN MARKETING EDUCATION: A ROLE-BASED TYPOLOGY AND PRATICAL GUIDELINES
papers.authors: Roberto Bello
papers.abstract: This article examines how marketing educators and programs can govern artificial intelligence (AI) used for assessing student work. AI denotes the broader category of computational systems that predict, classify, interpret, or support decisions; generative AI (GenAI) denotes the subset of those systems that produces new content, such as feedback, rubric interpretations, assessment summaries, and grade rationales. The distinction matters because governance requirements follow from the authority an output is permitted to exercise rather than from whether the system is generative. Marketing provides a particularly revealing context because its assessments often require students to integrate analytical evidence, creative choice, audience-sensitive communication, and defensible managerial judgment. Drawing on research on marketing education, assessment, legitimacy, procedural justice, and algorithmic judgment, the article develops a role-based typology of AI-assisted assessment. The typology distinguishes five roles (Assistant, Evaluator, Arbiter, Monitor, and Governor) according to the authority AI exercises over assessment judgment and the scope across which its consequences extend. Legitimacy determines the governance burden associated with each role, including requirements for explanation, oversight, evidence, accountability, and contestability. The article then provides practical guidelines for classifying AI uses and determining whether a particular role is defensible given the learning objective, assessment stakes, and institutional context.

papers.title: From AI innovation to educational inclusion: comparative perspectives on AI-enabled personalized learning and transformative skill development across developed and developing country contexts
papers.authors: Shouket Ahmad Tilwani, Anas Alhur, Isa Spahiu, Yalalem Assefa, Bekalu Tadesse Moges, Huda Majeed
papers.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education offers significant potential to enhance personalized learning and workforce development. However, AI adoption varies widely between developed and developing countries due to differences in digital infrastructure, socio-economic conditions, and institutional capacity. This study employs a meta-synthesis approach following PRISMA guidelines to systematically synthesize empirical studies on AI’s role in reshaping personalized learning and skill development in higher education across developing and developed country contexts. The study findings reveal that while AI can improve educational outcomes globally, equitable benefits depend on context-sensitive implementation. In developed countries, AI integration in higher education has advanced to an innovation–optimization phase, featuring adaptive learning platforms, generative instructional tools, and strong governance structures.
