papers.title: Prospective predictors of generative AI initiation, engagement, and problematic use among Japanese adults: a two-wave study
papers.authors: Atsushi Nakagomi, Satoshi Inagaki, Takahiro Tabuchi
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is rising rapidly, but how its determinants extend beyond first-level access into within-user engagement and problematic use remains poorly understood, and almost all existing evidence is cross-sectional. Using two consecutive waves of the Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey (2024 baseline; 2025 follow-up), we examined 49 baseline characteristics — organized with Resources and Appropriation Theory (RAT) as a taxonomy of personal, positional, and resource-based factors of (a) generative AI initiation during 2025 among 9,411 baseline never-users and, among 2,490 new-onset users, (b) use intensity, three purpose composites (productivity/creative, daily-life/information, social/emotional), and (c) problematic AI use measured with the 11-item Problematic ChatGPT Use Scale. All predictors were measured at the baseline wave. Twenty directional expectations were separated from exploratory screening; 17 were supported. Three findings stand out. First, the correlates of adoption and within-user engagement only partially overlapped across all three RAT domains, with several factors — age, graduate education, employment role, and device type — differentiating not only whether people adopted but also what they used AI for. Second, daily-life/information use was largely undifferentiated by age, education, income, employment role, or device type, suggesting an egalitarian leading-edge use case alongside more stratified productivity, social/emotional, and problematic-use domains. Third, problematic AI use was distinct from heavy use on two complementary criteria — measurement-level non-identity and a divergent predictor profile — with predictor profiles diverging across male, agreeableness, and heavy PC/tablet use. Equity-oriented governance of generative AI should monitor not only access and intensity but also the qualitative engagement profile of use.

papers.title: Self-disclosure context and parasocial relationship in LLM-based chatbot interaction: The role of mind perception
papers.authors: Xi Wang, Yujia Zhou, Guangyu Zhou
papers.abstract: Chatbots based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for companionship and emotional support, yet how users’ relational perceptions vary across conversational contexts remains unclear. In a within-person experiment, 102 participants completed two 30-minute chats with an LLM-based chatbot in low and high self-disclosure contexts. The final corpus contained 9,084 dialogue turns from real-time conversations. A high self-disclosure context was associated with a stronger parasocial relationship ( t = 2.46, p = .016) and greater mind perception ( t = 2.70, p = .008). Within-person differences in mind perception were positively associated with differences in parasocial relationship ( β = 0.604, p < .001). A within-person mediation model further yielded a significant indirect association between self-disclosure context and parasocial relationship through mind perception (indirect effect = 0.162, p = .018). To explore linguistic features associated with mind perception, we extracted 51 linguistic features from chatbot responses, covering subjective agency, interactional alignment, formulaic social routines, and expository informativeness. LASSO regression retained 18 candidate features ( R 2 = 0.444). Subsequent mixed-effects models showed positive associations for pronoun proportion, ellipsis usage, lexical overlap, and syntactic dependency depth, and negative associations for gratitude expressions and long-word proportion. These findings characterize within-person relational differences across conversational contexts and identify candidate linguistic correlates of mind perception for further investigation.

papers.title: The Psychological Impact of Conversational AI: A Theoretical Framework on Perceived Validation, Immediate Feedback, and Repeated Interaction
papers.authors: Javier Naranjo Sanjuán
papers.journal: Computers in Human Behavior Artificial Humans
papers.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence is increasingly used not only as a tool for information retrieval and task completion, but also as a psychologically meaningful interaction environment. This article proposes that conversational AI may influence psychological states through a combination of perceived validation, immediate feedback, and low-friction interaction, operating through two reinforcement mechanisms: negative reinforcement via uncertainty relief, and variable reinforcement via response variability. These features may alter how users experience reduced uncertainty, reduced negative affect, attentional engagement, and motivation to continue interacting. Although current evidence does not support direct claims about specific neurochemical effects in this context, recent research in reward processing, feedback evaluation, digital engagement, and conversational systems suggests that social feedback, psychologically meaningful responses, and reinforcement-related dynamics may play a relevant role in repeated human interaction with digital systems. Drawing on literature from reward processing, social validation, feedback evaluation, problematic digital use, human–chatbot relationship development, and human-computer interaction, this paper proposes a theoretical framework for understanding how conversational AI may shape users’ psychological states and contribute to repeated engagement. Four testable hypotheses are derived with distinct outcome variables to avoid construct circularity, moderated by individual differences including social anxiety, anxious attachment, and loneliness. In addition, the article outlines a future laboratory-based research agenda using a dual-manipulation paradigm (validation tone × response latency) with a post-text discrete symbol design that enables clean time-locking of reward-related event-related potentials (RewP, FRN, P300) while avoiding confounds with semantic processing of continuous text (N400, P600). • Conversational AI may shape psychology via validation, feedback, and friction • Proposes negative and variable reinforcement as core engagement mechanisms • Four falsifiable hypotheses link antecedents to distinct outcome variables • Individual differences moderate effects: social anxiety, attachment, loneliness • EEG paradigm resolves confound between reward and language processing

papers.title: Users’ perception of chatbot language fluency and hallucination
papers.authors: Marianna A. de Sá Siqueira, Tibor Bosse, Barbara C. N. Müller
papers.journal: Computers in Human Behavior Artificial Humans
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots are increasingly capable of generating fluent, coherent, and contextually appropriate language, raising questions about how these linguistic properties shape user perceptions and evaluations. This study examined the effects of linguistic fluency and hallucination on users' perceived intelligence of an LLM-based chatbot, and how perceived intelligence in turn relates to trust, user satisfaction, and intention to use. Using a 2 x 2 between-subjects experimental design (N = 395), participants observed a pre-defined user-chatbot dialogue in which the chatbot varied in linguistic fluency (high vs. low) and hallucination (present vs. absent) in the context of a Lord of the Rings-themed conversation. Results showed that higher fluency significantly increased perceived intelligence (H1), while the presence of hallucination significantly reduced it (H2). The expected moderating effect of fluency on the relationship between hallucination and perceived intelligence was not supported (H3); however, a notable pattern emerged in which users who observed a fluent but hallucinating chatbot rated its intelligence at a comparable level to those who viewed a less fluent but factually correct chatbot, with equivalence and Bayesian tests indicating no meaningful difference between these conditions within a small-to-moderate margin. Perceived intelligence was positively associated with trust, user satisfaction, and intention to use (H4). These findings highlight the role of linguistic fluency as a cue that shape user’s impressions of intelligence in human-chatbot interaction, with important implications for the risk of overreliance on LLM-based systems that communicate confidently but not always accurately.

papers.title: Evaluation of an advanced large language model as an educational tool in understanding the impact of the exposome on airway epithelial barrier dysfunction and TSLP release in asthma
papers.authors: F.D. Popescu, C.S. Marghidan, M. Preda, O.M. Cristea

papers.title: Can AI help teachers? Experimental evidence on the effects of generative AI use and AI training on teachers’ lesson preparation
papers.authors: Philipp Appel, Lukas Fervers, Joachim G. Piepenburg
papers.abstract: Teachers face considerable workload outside the classroom. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) could support teachers by enhancing lesson preparation while decreasing workload. Moreover, training on GenAI could further enhance its effectiveness and is increasingly demanded by practitioners. The present study examines whether GenAI (ChatGPT) effectively supports teachers during lesson preparation, and whether participation in AI training improves outcomes. For this purpose, we conducted a preregistered, RCT with N = 204 teachers who were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) No access to ChatGPT, (2) access to ChatGPT, and (3) access to ChatGPT with prior AI training. Teachers completed four incentivized lesson preparation tasks: Crafting an introductory quiz, writing a course mail, extending a textbook exercise and creating text and transfer questions. Dependent variables were (a) quality of the prepared materials, assessed by blinded expert ratings based on weighted criteria and (b) time spent on total preparation. Results indicated that GenAI effectively helped teachers during lesson preparation tasks, demonstrated by improved lesson preparation quality and a 34 % reduction in preparation time. AI training did not further improve lesson preparation quality but led to an additional 21 % reduction in preparation time. As revealed by prompt data, AI training led to a distinct prompt strategy (as intended): Teachers with prior training wrote longer and more detailed prompts, that needed less refinement afterwards. Untrained teachers used shorter prompts that required more subsequent prompt iterations. Although the first strategy required less preparation time, both strategies led to equal output quality.

papers.title: An automated online proctoring system with live suspicious activity detection using YOLOv11 pose estimation and multi-model classification
papers.authors: Md. Taslim Arif, Abu Salyh Muhammad Mussa, Abdullah Al Mamun, Mominur Rahman, Md. Moshiur Rahman, Md. Ashiqussalehin
papers.abstract: Remote and hybrid education has spread rapidly, revealing severe limitations of traditional human-invigilated and rule-based systems of examination monitoring. Maintaining academic integrity in online assessments has become increasingly difficult students devising various ways to avoid scrutiny. In a bid to combat these challenges, this paper proposes an automated proctoring system that combines machine learning classification using YOLOv11-based pose estimation to detect suspicious behavior in real-time. The system takes live video streams or recorded video streams, and detects 17 essential body landmarks in each frame and estimates deviations in posture, trends in head movement, and unusual upper-body motion. A labeled dataset of examination scenarios was used to evaluate several classifiers. Mutual-information-based feature selection retained 30 pose features, and standard K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) with k = 1 was selected for deployment. The selected model achieved an accuracy of 99.56%, precision of 99.20%, recall of 99.60%, F1-score of 99.40%, and an AUC (Area Under the Curve) of 0.9957 on the held-out test set. The system includes a lightweight user-friendly interface on the web that allows real-time deployment with just a single webcam to allow easy monitoring and immediate behavior feedback without the need to have specialized hardware. On balance, the suggested solution can provide a lightweight, efficient, and scalable solution to the problem of promoting academic integrity in online and face-to-face settings of assessment environment.

papers.title: HASTE: Topology-constrained adaptive coupling for streaming EEG fatigue regression
papers.authors: Qiyu Niu, Yi Xie, Siao Liu, Fan Li, Yingnan Nie, Shouyan Wang

papers.title: Mobile EEG Reveals Age-Dependent Cognitive-Motor Interference with Increasing Motor Task Complexity- a cross-sectional study
papers.authors: Bettina Wollesen, Leoni Viola Winter, Klaus Gramann, Janna Protzak
papers.abstract: This study examined age-related differences in behavior and brain dynamics underlying cognitive-motor interference (CMI) during motor dual-tasks (DT) with increasing motor task complexity. Behavioral performance and electrocortical activity were assessed in 19 younger adults (11 males, 8 females; 25.5 ± 2.3 years) and 11 older adults (6 males, 5 females; 72.6 ± 4.6 years) using mobile electroencephalography (EEG). Participants performed an oddball choice-reaction task under three conditions: sitting, standing, and treadmill walking. Event-related potential (ERPs; P1, N1, P3) amplitudes and latencies, response times, postural sway, and gait parameters were recorded to evaluate CMI. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVAs with within-subject factors of motor condition and stimulus type and age group as a between-subject factor. Older adults exhibited reduced step length compared to younger adults, but no DT-related changes in gait or postural sway were observed. Response times were generally slower in older adults and increased from sitting to standing and walking whereas younger adults showed slowing only from sitting to standing. Early sensory ERP components (P1, N1) demonstrated increased amplitudes with higher motor demands. The P3 component was reduced in amplitude in both groups during walking, with delayed latencies in older adults. For both groups, P3 latencies were associated with prolonged response times. Our findings suggest that this slowing during walking reflects altered cognitive resource allocation, characterized by delayed central information processing and enhanced early visual processing, rather than impaired peripheral motor coordination.

papers.title: Reading Intention Where There Is None: Neurobehavioral Correlates of Intention Attribution of Morally Ambiguous Scenarios in Borderline Personality Disorder
papers.authors: Buket Şen, Gianluigi Giannini, Eugenia Kulakova, Renée Lipka, Arno Villringer, Katja Wingenfeld
papers.journal: Biological Psychiatry Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by altered social cognition, including a tendency to bias intention attribution in ambiguous situations. However, the neurobehavioral mechanisms underlying this tendency remain poorly understood. Here, we examined whether intention attribution is disturbed in BPD and reflected in behavioral bias and altered neural processing of morally ambiguous social information. METHODS: A total of 71 individuals with BPD (55 female, 16 male) and 72 healthy controls (56 female, 16 male) were included. Participants viewed harm-based scenarios depicting intentional and accidental actions while electroencephalography was recorded. Behavioral responses and event-related potentials were analyzed exploratorily to examine group differences in intention attribution and neural differentiation. RESULTS: Behaviorally, individuals with BPD were more likely to misinterpret accidental harm as intentional, whereas responses to intentional harms did not differ between groups. Mass-univariate event-related potential analyses revealed group differences in early frontocentral (approximately 200-250 ms) and later centroparietal (734-789 ms) time windows. Healthy controls showed greater accidental-intentional differentiation in the early windows, whereas individuals with BPD exhibited reduced neural differentiation. In contrast, the later effect showed greater differentiation in the BPD group. CONCLUSIONS: These condition-specific findings indicate a selective intention-attribution bias in BPD alongside altered neural differentiation of ambiguous social information at earlier and later time points. More broadly, social judgment disturbances in BPD may be particularly evident when harmful outcomes conflict with innocent intentions, rather than reflecting generalized response differences.

papers.title: Connectome reorganization and precision neurorehabilitation after traumatic brain injury
papers.authors: Juanita Ramírez Mancera, Alexandra Ramos-Márquez, David F. Estupiñan-Pepinosa, Liz González, Óscar Zorro, Diego F. Gómez-Amarillo, Juan Fernando Ramón, Diego Quintero-Rueda, Fernando Hakim, Javier G. Patiño-Gómez, Edgar G. Ordóñez-Rubiano
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of long-term disability. The connectome paradigm reframes TBI as a disconnection syndrome, in which disruption of large-scale brain networks underlies cognitive and behavioral sequelae. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence on connectome alterations after TBI using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and graph theory analyses. TBI severity correlates with reductions in global efficiency and modularity, and connectomic reorganization is shaped by neuroinflammation, glymphatic dysfunction, and neurovascular uncoupling—processes that can leave network nodes functionally impaired despite structural preservation. Reorganization follows a biphasic pattern, characterized by acute hypoconnectivity within integrative networks, such as the default mode network (DMN), followed by compensatory hyperconnectivity. These disruptions are associated with deficits in memory, executive function, and emotional regulation. Emerging connectome-guided approaches enable neuromodulation targeting dysfunctional hubs, and machine learning (ML)-based recovery prediction has achieved accuracies of up to 92% in stroke connectome models. However, comparable TBI-specific frameworks remain at a considerably earlier stage of development and, where tested across independent cohorts, have demonstrated more modest and heterogeneous performance. TBI is best understood as a dynamic network disorder in which clinical outcomes depend on the trajectory of connectomic reorganization. Future research should prioritize biomarker validation, mechanistic studies linking neuroinflammation to network remodeling, pro-glymphatic therapies, and the development of individualized precision neuroengineering interventions.

papers.title: Neural Response to Monetary and Social Feedback in Childhood: Processing Reward and Loss in Relation to Peer Outcomes and Anxiety Symptoms
papers.authors: Serena J. Gu, Margaret M Redic, Danielle Kelly, Rebecca Tillman, Kirsten Gilbert

papers.title: Dual-pathway EEG analysis: ML with hybrid DL for adaptive educational interventions
papers.authors: Carlos Sandoval-Medina, Alexis Gallegos-Acosta, Héctor Cardona-Reyes, Ezra Parra-González
papers.abstract: Diagnosing Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) remains a clinical challenge, as does designing appropriate educational interventions for students with this diagnosis. Electroencephalogram (EEG) analysis offers an objective physiological alternative; however, capturing the non-linear, micro-temporal dynamics of attention remains a significant hurdle for current diagnostic models. This study proposes a dual-pathway framework combining a Hybrid Deep Learning (DL) architecture — Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), a Transformer encoder, and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) — for binary ADHD diagnosis, with an interpretable Machine Learning (ML) pathway (XGBoost) for micro-temporal attention profiling, applied to 19-channel EEG recordings from 121 children (61 ADHD, 60 controls). The preprocessing pipeline integrated Wavelet Transforms, Independent Component Analysis (ICA), and Common Average Reference (CAR). Data were segmented into five micro-temporal scales (1, 2, 4, 8 and 16s). On the validation fold, the best Hybrid DL checkpoint reached 92.5% accuracy and an AUC-ROC of 0.979; the XGBoost profiling model reached a macro-F1 of 97.2% ( Cohen’s κ = 0.967 ) under subject-wise 5-fold cross-validation for reconstructing five rule-defined attention profiles. A spectral comparison at electrode Cz showed no significant group difference in absolute band power after Bonferroni correction, except for alpha and gamma; this direction was not stable across alternative normalizations. An individual case (subject v263) illustrates how the profiling pathway translates a moderate-confidence ADHD classification (probability 0.85) and a ”Moderate Compensated Fluctuation” dominant profile into a self-regulation-focused intervention plan. By providing interpretable attention maps and performance indices, this system bridges the gap between high-level signal processing and actionable clinical insights, supporting more precise, personalized diagnostic pathways.

papers.title: Low-Dose Aripiprazole for Long COVID Symptom Management: A Retrospective Observational Study
papers.authors: Jason Z. Cui, Müge Kalaycıoğlu, Giorgio Ricciardiello Mejia, Lü Tian, Linda N. Geng, Grace A. McComsey, Vincent Macorni, Jacob S. Ballon, Anita Chopra, Tom C. Quach, Mehr Grewal, Amogha Medha Paleru, Vincent Xin, Makeda Robinson, Lauren Grossman, Robert W. Shafer, Hector Fabio Bonilla
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Long COVID (1) is defined as the persistence of new or worsened symptoms for 3 or more months following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, affecting multiple organ systems. Currently, there are no approved drugs for treating LC. We reported the effect of low-dose Aripiprazole (LDA) on the management of LC symptoms in a retrospective study. Methods A retrospective study was done using electronic health records from 50 adult patients from the Stanford LC clinic with a history of SARS-CoV-2 and subsequent LC who received LDA between 5/2021 and 10/2023. LDA was prescribed with dose titration (0.1-2.0 mg oral daily). The assessment include 29 symptoms, (ii) severity of each symptom on the Likert-scale 1 (mild) to 5 (very severe), and (iii) the Functional Status Scale (FSS) from asymptomatic (level I), symptomatic without limitations (level II), symptomatic with reduced daily activity (level III), symptomatic with a struggle to perform daily activities (level IV), or incapacitated and bedridden (level V). An improvement was defined as a reduction in the FSS ordinal scale (V, IV, III, II, and I) from higher to lower before and after exposure to LDA. A composite score of the severity of the seven most common symptoms (headache, fatigue, brain fog, unrefreshing sleep, sleep difficulty, post-exertional malaise, and lightheadedness) was calculated to assess the effect of LDA pre- and post-treatment, using Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Tests. Results Within the cohort of 50 patients, the median patient age was 46.5 years, 62% were female, and the mean body mass index (BMI) was 27.5 kg/m 2 . The median duration of symptoms was 566.5 days (range 153-1457). The FSS improved significantly from 3.78 to 3.28 (p = 0.001) after treatment with LDA. There were no statistically significant differences in reductions in symptom severity, symptom count, or composite scores across the seven selected symptoms. Symptom duration before treatment, and course of the illness before and after the aripiprazole period did not significantly affect treatment associated changes. The median dose of LDA was 1 mg. LDA was generally well tolerated in our study cohort (the most common side effects reported were headache in 3, restless leg in 1, and diarrhea in 1), with no severe adverse effects reported. Conclusion In our cohort study, LDA was associated with improved FSS. These retrospective observational results suggest that LDA warrants further investigation in a randomized controlled trial as a therapeutic option for LC. Exploring the mechanism of action for LDA in LC may also provide new insights into pathogenesis.

papers.title: Association of early life adversity and peer victimisation with psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic risk in adolescents from the eBRAIN study: the role of sex and diet
papers.authors: Xuemei Ma, Andrew J. Lawrence, Pei-Jung Chen, Rebecca Pollard, Svenja Kretzer, Nare Amasi-Hartoonian, Corentin Vallée, Lucas Andersen, Yifan Xu, Nur Najiah Zaidani Kamarunzaman, Naghmeh Nikkheslat, Craig Morgan, Seeromanie Harding, Carmine Maria Pariante, Mitul Mehta, Giovanni Montana, Sylvane Desrivières, Chiara Nosarti, Ana Rodriguez‐Mateos, Paola Dazzan
papers.abstract: Background Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period during which psychosocial stress can become biologically embedded, increasing risk for psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic dysregulation. Early life adversity (ELA, such as maltreatment and household dysfunction) and peer victimisation frequently co‑occur, yet their cumulative association with adolescent psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic risk remains poorly understood. Diet may be a modifiable pathway linking stress to both psychopathology and inflammatory and metabolic processes, yet evidence integrating multiple adversities with both subjective and objective dietary measures is limited. This study aimed to investigate whether co-occurring ELA and peer victimisation were associated with adolescent psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic markers, and to test whether diet mediated these associations. Methods In an ethically and socio-economic diverse community sample of adolescents (N = 230, age: 12.9 ± 0.9 years), we assessed: 1) exposure to ELA and peer victimisation via structured interviews; 2) Internalising and externalising symptoms, using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ); 3) Age‑adjusted body mass index (BMI) and plasma levels of C‑reactive protein (CRP), as indicators of metabolic and inflammatory risk; and 4) Diet, using self‑reported dietary intake from a Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ) and urinary metabolic signatures of diet from spot urine samples measured via ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography and triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-q-Q MS). Linear regression models examined the associations between multiple exposures to ELA and peer victimisation with psychopathology, CRP and age-adjusted BMI, and mediation models tested the role of diet. Results Participants exposed to both ELA and peer victimisation showed more internalising (B = 3.3, 95%CI: 2.0 to 4.6) and externalising symptoms (B = 3.9, 95%CI: 2.5 to 5.3), higher log 10 CRP (B = 0.4, 95%CI: 0.1 to 0.7) and age-adjusted BMI (B = 1.0, 95%CI: 0.3 to 1.6), and a higher likelihood of unhealthy dietary patterns (76% vs. 51%, pairwise p = 0.020), compared to those with no exposure. However, urinary metabolic signatures were not associated with adversity exposure. An unhealthy diet was associated with higher CRP (1.2 ± 3.8 vs. 0.4 ± 0.6 mg/L; p = 0.013), but not with psychopathology, and did not mediate associations between adversity and outcomes. Exploratory sex‑stratified analyses suggested that associations between multiple adversities and higher CRP and BMI were stronger in boys (log 10 CRP: B = 0.6, 95% CI: 0.2 to 1.1; age-adjusted BMI: B = 1.2, 95% CI: 0.2 to 2.2) than in girls (log 10 CRP: B = 0.2, 95% CI: −0.2 to 0.6; age-adjusted BMI: B = 0.6, 95% CI: −0.2 to 1.6), though the moderation effect for BMI did not reach statistical significance, but, again, diet did not mediate these differential associations. Conclusions Risk for both behavioural difficulties and elevated CRP and BMI was higher among adolescents exposed to multiple forms of adversity, especially boys. Although diet alone may not explain these associations, it remains a relevant target for reducing inflammation and metabolic risk. Future longitudinal research should explore how diet and other modifiable lifestyle behaviours can mitigate the long-term impacts of adolescent adversity.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Research Assistants: The Risk of Topic-Overclassification in Financial Disclosure Research
papers.authors: Anne d’Arcy, Christian Stefan Haas, Nicolaus Wallner
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) are transforming unstructured text analysis. In accounting research, this raises measurement validity questions when disclosure-based constructs are derived from text. This study investigates LLMs as research assistants (RAs) for topic modeling and classification of financial disclosures. Comparing OpenAI’s GPT-4o with Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and human RAs, we evaluate LLM performance in identifying mergers and acquisitions (M&A) content in analyst reports. Results show document-specific LLM prompting generates more interpretable topics than LDA. However, GPT-4o exhibits high but lower reliability than human RAs. This difference reflects topic-overclassification risk: relative to consensus human benchmarks, GPT-4o applies a more inclusive classification profile, increasing the likelihood that contextually plausible but irrelevant text is classified as topic-relevant. Robustness tests using GPT-OSS 20B show that topic-overclassification depends on implementation choices and increases with additional contextual information. Additional analyses indicate that benchmark-relative positive classifications are concentrated in boilerplate-like and noisy text, while an ESG setting suggests that some disagreements with consensus human benchmarks may reflect human conservatism and ambiguity in construct boundaries. We conclude that apparent reliability can mask economically meaningful differences in classification profiles, requiring LLMs to be treated as measurement tools with transparent implementation choices, careful prompt design, and task-specific validation.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence and automated scoring in curriculum-based measurement for elementary students with early writing needs
papers.authors: Seohyeon Choi, Jechun An, Manjary Guha, Emily A. Reno, Emma Shanahan, Adrea J. Truckenmiller, Kristen L. McMaster

papers.title: Assessing the assessors: GenAI and human ratings of second language writing using analytic and holistic rubrics
papers.authors: Apichat Khamboonruang, Ute Knoch
papers.abstract: With the evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology, there has been a surge in research exploring its potential for automated essay scoring (AES). However, few studies have investigated the AES capabilities of multiple GenAI models within language classrooms nor have studies compared GenAI performances when scoring different types of rating scales. Therefore, this study aims to compare the analytic and holistic ratings of GenAI models (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, DeepSeek) and nine experienced teachers on 104 students’ opinion paragraphs in a Thai EFL classroom context. GenAI models scored each paragraph following structured, rubric-aligned prompting. Data were analysed using Spearman’s rank-order correlation and many-facet Rasch measurement. Findings revealed that overall, experienced teachers demonstrated relatively less extreme severity estimates, better-fitting ratings, and broadly satisfactory score differentiation across rubrics. GenAI models showed better alignment with human ratings for holistic scoring and language than for task completion and content, and organisation. While approaching human rating behaviours, GenAI models’ rating performances varied across scoring rounds, rubrics, and traits. The findings support supervised application of GenAI models as a supplementary scoring assistant in classroom assessment, with teacher oversight remaining essential. This study offers implications for validating and integrating GenAI-assisted AES into L2 writing classrooms.

papers.title: Contrastive Attention Network for Motor Imagery Classification Using Variable Length of Datasets
papers.authors: Nadeem Ullah, Su Jin Im, Tae Ho Kim, Kang Ryoung Park

papers.title: Class-aware distillation for federated fraud detection
papers.authors: Gbenga Adebiyi, Ahmed Moustafa, Nina Dethlefs
papers.abstract: Credit card fraud continues to pose a substantial threat to financial institutions globally, necessitating advanced machine learning solutions such as Federated Learning (FL). While FL addresses data silos and offers privacy benefits, it faces class imbalance and the communication overhead of frequent model updates between institutions. Capturing subtle, evolving fraud patterns often requires larger, more complex models that shallow models may miss, but exchanging larger models increases communication cost. Knowledge distillation can reduce this cost by transferring a larger teacher’s knowledge into a compact model, while exchanging compact model. However, standard distillation may propagates majority-class bias, and deploying it everywhere adds computation that offsets the efficiency gained. This paper proposes Class-Aware Distillation for Federated Fraud Detection (CADFFD), which combines two complementary mechanisms within a federated averaging procedure. A targeted deployment first determines where the teacher is used, instantiating it only where the compact model struggles to learn local fraud patterns. Once deployed, Confidence-Correctness Calibrated Distillation (CCCD) calibrates what is transferred, weighting knowledge by the teacher’s confidence and label agreement to mitigate majority-class bias. An adaptive focal loss further adjusts its focusing strength per institution and per round to track local class imbalance. Evaluated on the European and IEEE-CIS datasets against FedAvg, Vanilla KD, and FedKD, CADFFD leads on f1-score and fraud ranking by up to 18% above the strongest baseline, while cutting false positives five- to thirteen-fold and achieving lower teacher-training compute than other distillation methods.

papers.title: TabEva: A unified evaluation framework for tabular data synthesis
papers.authors: Alex X. Wang, Colin R Simpson, Binh Phu Nguyen
papers.abstract: Generative AI has made significant progress, especially in computer vision and natural language processing. Now, sophisticated algorithms and architectures are expanding into tabular data synthesis, driven by the practical benefits of tabular data’s widespread presence in daily life. However, synthesizing tabular data presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous feature types, necessitating tailored evaluation models. Yet, there is a critical gap in unified and effective evaluation methods specifically designed for synthetic tabular data. To address this gap, we introduce TabEva, a unified and extensible evaluation framework for synthetic tabular data. Rather than proposing entirely new individual metrics, TabEva integrates established univariate, bivariate, multivariate, cluster-level, utility, and unit-record diagnostics into a consistent evaluation pipeline with standardized preprocessing, reporting, and visualization. The framework separates marginal distribution assessment, pairwise dependency preservation, global distributional similarity, support coverage, downstream utility, and post-hoc disclosure-risk diagnostics. In addition, TabEva includes framework-level refinements, such as a modified cluster tendency score, sign-aware association discrepancy handling, and structured visual diagnostics. Through experiments on diverse tabular datasets and synthesis algorithms, we demonstrate that TabEva provides a practical platform for comparing, ranking, and diagnosing synthetic tabular data generators. The results show that TabEva can reveal complementary strengths and weaknesses across different model families, supporting more informed selection and development of tabular data synthesis methods.
