papers.title: Transparency and Accountability in Graduate Education: Ensuring Financial Value and Gainful Employment
papers.authors: Kerry McGarr Empey, David Feola, Kimberly B. Garza, Qing Ma, Saisudha Koka, Surajit Dey, Sudip Das, Kenza E. Benzeroual, Peter M. Gannett, Om Perumal
papers.abstract: Graduate education in pharmaceutical sciences is undergoing rapid transformation driven by shifting student demographics, evolving workforce demands, and changing funding landscapes. As institutions increasingly develop tuition-bearing MS and certificate programs to offset declining research support, prospective students, many of whom are non-traditional adult learners, require clear, verifiable data on employment outcomes and financial return on investment to make informed decisions. This commentary argues that systematic transparency, shared accountability, and robust outcome measurement infrastructure are essential to responsible program growth. Three converging forces demand urgent attention: a projected demographic decline in traditional-age students intensifying competition for non-traditional learners; accelerating industry demand for graduates skilled in bioinformatics, regulatory science, and artificial intelligence; and institutional revenue pressures that risk outpacing genuine workforce demand. Despite substantial program proliferation (over 336 MS, PhD, and certificate programs nationally) standardized, publicly available outcome data for pharmaceutical sciences graduates remains scarce. Existing federal classification systems further impede meaningful analysis by misclassifying interdisciplinary and emerging programs. To address these gaps, this commentary proposes three pillars of action: systematic transparency through standardized national outcome surveys reporting employment rates, salary distributions, and career trajectories; shared accountability embedded in accreditation and program review cycles; and infrastructure reform including updated Classification of Instructional Programs (CIP) codes. Professional organizations such as AACP are well positioned to lead these efforts. Ultimately, transparency in financial value and gainful employment outcomes is not merely a regulatory requirement, it is an ethical imperative for institutions committed to student and societal welfare.

papers.title: Matching Artificial Intelligence and digital simulation to educational purposes in a competency-first pharmacy education framework
papers.authors: Yevhen Pruhlo, Amir Barzegar Behrooz, Ivan Iurchenko
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To synthesize pharmacy-education evidence across artificial intelligence (AI) and digital simulation technologies, compare modalities by educational function, evidence maturity, implementation requirements, and risk, and derive a competency-first framework for curricular selection, implementation, assessment, and governance. FINDINGS: A narrative search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science prioritized pharmacy-education studies and reviews published from 2018 through August 2026. Educational function, rather than AI status alone, provided the primary organizing principle. Simulation modalities mainly support standardized rehearsal, contextualized practice, feedback, visualization, and debriefing; adaptive systems and large language models (LLMs) can add personalization or generative dialogue; and AI-assisted assessment can support item development, feedback, and workflow. Evidence maturity differed substantially across modalities, but comparisons reflect the type and volume of literature identified rather than formal certainty grading. Across the literature, the strongest and most consistent outcomes were feasibility, engagement, satisfaction, and selected short-term knowledge or skill measures. Evidence for durable competence, transfer to clinical performance, patient outcomes, cost-effectiveness, and equity remained limited. SUMMARY: Pharmacy programs should use a competency-first, not technology-first, approach that defines observable learner outcomes before selecting tools. The proposed function-evidence-risk principle and ALIGN roadmap are author-derived syntheses intended to support curricular decision-making, not validated implementation instruments. AI literacy, output verification, transparent disclosure, privacy protection, and professional accountability should be developed longitudinally within existing pharmacy competency expectations, while faculty retain responsibility for curricular decisions, assessment validity, and patient-centered judgment.

papers.title: EFL teachers' emotional scaffolding strategies in AI-mediated L2 education: A descriptive qualitative study
papers.authors: Xin Lin, Akbar A. Jahanbakhsh
papers.abstract: Recently, the emotional aspects of using Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in second/foreign language (L2) education have been emphasized in the literature. Nevertheless, the way teachers may support their learners' emotional experiences via scaffolding practices has received comparatively limited attention in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts. To address this gap, the present descriptive qualitative research explored Chinese EFL teachers' perceived and reported emotional scaffolding strategies used to regulate learners' emotions in AI-mediated L2 education. The data were gathered through interviews with 20 Chinese EFL teachers. The results of thematic analysis revealed five common emotional scaffolding strategies, which were perceived by the participants as useful for regulating their learners' AI-induced emotions. Particularly, they had used 1) personal stories and narratives, 2) technical-emotional support, 3) scaffolded tasks with positive reinforcement, 4) friendly and collaborative atmosphere, and 5) immediate and constructive feedback to support their learners' emotions in AI-mediated classes. The study invites teacher education programs to focus on the psycho-affective aspect of AI integration in L2 education.

papers.title: Generative AI in K-12 creative writing instruction: A systematic review and narrative synthesis
papers.authors: Mátyás Turós, Norbert Beták, Tímea Vargáné Vincze, Vanessza Kapusi, Szabolcs Ceglédi, Zoltán Szűts
papers.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly entering writing instruction in public education; however, a systematic, quality-appraised synthesis of its effects on K-12 students' creative writing is lacking. This review synthesises and critically appraises the empirical evidence, using a scaffolding-versus-substitution framework to distinguish AI-assisted performance from the development of students' own writing. We searched seven databases without language restrictions for 2020-2026, following PRISMA 2020. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed with ROBINS-I, RoB 2 and CASP, the certainty of evidence with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual, and findings were synthesised without meta-analysis (SWiM), stratified by design. Seventeen studies met the criteria (total N = 736). All six comparisons of AI-supported with non-AI instruction favoured AI on text quality or creativity, but in every study the scored texts were produced with AI access or under unreported conditions; no study assessed AI-free or delayed writing performance. Effects on writing-related affect were mixed, and no intervention reported a planned withdrawal of AI support. Observational process data indicated that students used AI input to develop their ideas when they retained control, but that AI could also steer the narrative or supply text adopted with little reworking. No study was at low risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was very low for all quantitative outcomes. The evidence therefore describes what students produce with AI rather than what they learn to do without it; studies with AI-free post-tests, delayed transfer measures and planned fading of support are needed. The protocol was pre-registered (PROSPERO: CRD420261303257).

papers.title: Cognitively demanding motor exercise and subsequent inhibitory control: Behavioral and ERP Evidence
papers.authors: Lee-Xiang Lee, Shih‐Chun Kao, David Moreau, Cheng-Ta Yang, Chia-Chi Tsai, Chun-Hao Wang
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Acute exercise can influence executive function, yet conventional exercise prescriptions primarily characterize its physical dose and rarely specify the cognitive operations embedded within the exercise bout. Using a Motor-Cognitive Integrated Task (MCIT) with conditions differing in cognitive demand while involving comparable physical demands, this study examined whether cognitively demanding motor exercise was associated with differences in subsequent behavioral and neurophysiological indices of inhibitory control. METHODS: Forty healthy young adults completed two counterbalanced sessions separated by at least 24 h. In the experimental session, participants performed the MCIT, which required whole-body responses to flanker stimuli. In the control session, participants performed the same motor task in response to predictable single-arrow stimuli. Heart rate (HR), physical rating of perceived exertion (RPE), cognitive RPE, response time (RT), movement time (MT), and overall response time (RMT) were assessed during the MCIT. Immediately afterward, participants completed a computerized flanker task while electroencephalography was recorded. RESULTS: Cognitive RPE, RT and RMT of the MCIT were higher in the experimental session than in the control session, whereas HR, physical RPE, and MT of the MCIT were comparable across sessions. Following the MCIT, participants showed a smaller flanker interference in the experimental than in the control session, accompanied by differences in conflict-related modulation of the N2 and smaller overall P3 amplitude, with no between-session difference in accuracy. CONCLUSIONS: Cognitive demand may represent a manipulable characteristic of acute exercise prescription beyond physical intensity alone. Motor exercise incorporating greater cognitive demands was associated with reduced subsequent behavioral interference and differences in N2 and P3 modulation. Although these effects cannot be attributed exclusively to any specific cognitive operation, the findings highlight the potential importance of considering the cognitive characteristics of exercise when examining its acute neurocognitive effects.

papers.title: Social appearance anxiety and adult picky eating: Associations with sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and body mass index
papers.authors: Gülşen Delikanlı Akbay, Erdinç Karakullukçu
papers.abstract: Background Although adult picky eating has traditionally received limited attention, it is now recognized as a persistent eating behaviour with important psychosocial implications. However, its associations with sleep quality, depressive symptoms, body mass index (BMI), and social appearance anxiety remain insufficiently investigated, especially in non-Western settings. This study explored the relationships between adult picky eating and these psychological and health-related variables among Turkish adults. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 386 adults aged 18 years and older in Türkiye using an online snowball sampling method. Participants completed the Adult Picky Eating Questionnaire (APEQ), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), and the Social Appearance Anxiety Scale (SAAS). Sociodemographic information and BMI were also obtained. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests. Spearman's rank correlation and multiple linear regression analyses were used to examine the associations and independent correlates of picky eating. Results In multivariable linear regression analysis, social appearance anxiety showed a modest, independent positive association with picky eating ( B = 0.103, β = 0.201, p < 0.001), whereas BMI exhibited a weak inverse association ( B = −0.176, β = −0.121, p = 0.033). Depressive symptoms and sleep quality were not independently associated with total picky eating scores. The overall model explained 7.7% of the variance. Exploratory bivariate correlations indicated a modest positive relationship between social appearance anxiety and total APEQ scores ( ρ = 0.264, p < 0.001) with similar patterns observed across subscales, while associations involving depressive symptoms and sleep quality were largely weak or non-significant. Conclusions In this adult sample, picky eating showed a modest positive association with social appearance anxiety and a weak inverse association with body mass index, whereas depressive symptoms and overall sleep quality were not independently associated. These observational findings suggest that appearance-related concerns may be relevant to individual variations in adult picky eating. However, the cross-sectional design, the low explanatory power of the multivariable model ( R 2 = 0.077), and the modest internal consistency of the APEQ require cautious interpretation and preclude causal, physiological, or clinical inferences. Future prospective studies incorporating comprehensive assessments of sensory sensitivity, food neophobia, body image, and dietary intake are needed to clarify the temporal and contextual factors associated with adult picky eating.

papers.title: When vendor reputation does not matter: Trust decoupling and pragmatic trust in Generative AI adoption among university students
papers.authors: Achmad Nizar Hidayanto, Okky Putra Barus, Muhammad Arief Braja Putra, Muhammad Faris Umar Rahman, Kongkiti Phusavat, Rafif Naufal Rahmadika, Son Sulung Suryahatta Asnan, Dedi I. Inan, Zaenal Abidin
papers.abstract: Trust Transfer Theory predicts that trust in a reputable developer extends to its products, yet this assumption has rarely been tested for non-deterministic generative AI (GenAI) systems. This study examines how trust forms and transfers across conceptual (AI in general), institutional (vendor), and product (specific GenAI tool) levels, and how these trust layers relate to students' adoption intention. Survey data from 480 undergraduate students who actively use GenAI at a public research university in Indonesia were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by importance–performance map analysis and necessary condition analysis. Eight of ten hypotheses were supported. Attitude toward AI and social influence predicted trust in AI, which in turn predicted both vendor trust and trust in the specific GenAI tool. Trust in the tool was also predicted by problem-solving capability and user interface quality, and it predicted adoption intention (R 2 = 0.32). Two paths were not supported. AI anxiety was not associated with trust in AI (β = −0.02, p = 0.564), a result that applies to students who have already adopted GenAI. Vendor trust did not predict trust in the tool once the other antecedents were accounted for (β = 0.03, p = 0.450). We interpret this pattern as trust decoupling, in which product-level trust rests on direct performance evidence, termed pragmatic trust, rather than on vendor reputation. The findings suggest a boundary condition for trust transfer in GenAI contexts and inform how higher education institutions evaluate and integrate GenAI tools.

papers.title: Profiles of the Dark Tetrad and the frequency of GAI-related academic misconduct
papers.authors: Rongjian Sun, Nguyen Thi Thuy Loan, Cheng-Yen Wang
papers.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) presents new challenges to academic integrity, enabling students to engage in academic misconduct with reduced effort and risk of detection. While previous research has examined personality predictors of academic misconduct, very few studies have adopted a person-centered approach to explore how distinct Dark Tetrad personality profiles relate to GAI-related misconduct over time. A total of 781 university students in Taiwan completed the Time 1 survey and 760 completed the follow-up one month later. Latent Profile Analysis based on the Dark Tetrad classified students into three profiles: Narc-Psych-Sad, Machiavellian, and High Dark Tetrad. The profiles differed significantly in the total frequency of GAI-related academic misconduct: students in the Narc-Psych-Sad profile reported more frequent misconduct than those in the Machiavellian profile, whereas the small High Dark Tetrad profile showed the highest observed means but did not differ significantly from the other two.

papers.title: Socially prescribed perfectionism and graduate student burnout: Dual pathways via impostor feelings and generative AI anxiety, and via academic procrastination
papers.authors: Wendai Yang, Shuya Du
papers.abstract: Graduate students increasingly navigate sustained performance pressure alongside rapidly evolving norms around generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Drawing on stress and resource perspectives, this study examined whether socially prescribed perfectionism relates to academic burnout through two hypothesized pathways: an identity-threat route involving impostor feelings and GenAI anxiety, and a maladaptive coping route involving academic procrastination, while testing GenAI use frequency as a moderator. An anonymous cross-sectional survey of Chinese graduate students yielded N = 812 valid cases. Participants completed measures of socially prescribed perfectionism, impostor feelings, GenAI anxiety, academic procrastination, and burnout. Confirmatory factor analysis supported a five-factor measurement structure with good reliability and validity, and structural equation modeling with bootstrapped confidence intervals tested the hypothesized indirect associations. Socially prescribed perfectionism was associated with higher impostor feelings and procrastination; impostor feelings were linked to greater GenAI anxiety; and both GenAI anxiety and procrastination were positively related to burnout, with a larger statistical indirect association through procrastination. Multi-group analyses indicated metric invariance and showed that the impostor → GenAI anxiety association was stronger among higher-frequency GenAI users, whereas the procrastination → burnout association was stronger among lower-frequency users. These findings identify two distinct patterns of association linking perceived external evaluative demands with graduate burnout and indicate that the association between impostor feelings and GenAI anxiety differs by GenAI use frequency.

papers.title: ‘AI-Learner Partnership’: Psychological mechanisms and developmental trajectories of EFL learners’ writing agency in GenAI-assisted courses
papers.authors: Lei Zhang, 魏日宁, Chunli Jiang
papers.abstract: This study explores how EFL learners construct, negotiate, and develop writing agency through engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in second language writing courses. GenAI is conceptualized as a cultural mediational means within an integrated sociocultural and positive psychological framework. Eleven Chinese EFL university students were followed over a 16-week semester as they completed multiple academic writing tasks with GenAI support. Drawing on a qualitative multi-method design, data were collected through semi-structured interviews, screen recordings of writing sessions, and reflective journals. The analysis identified three interrelated, non-linear phases in learners' agency development: initial exploration (characterized by novelty-driven engagement, dependency on AI output, and emergent self-efficacy), strategic adaptation (marked by more selective, task-contingent tool use and the strengthening of writing-specific psychological capital), and deliberate appropriation (signaled by personalized integration of GenAI into writing workflows and the emergence of a more agentic techno-authorial identity). Across these phases, cognitive processes, affective experiences, positive psychological resources, and task design features jointly shaped how learners mobilized technological affordances to enact writing agency. The findings suggest that writing agency in human-AI collaborative writing is a dynamic, context-sensitive accomplishment rather than a fixed individual trait. By connecting sociocultural accounts of mediated action with positive psychological resources, the study offers a process-oriented account of how EFL learners negotiate assistance, authorship, and autonomy in GenAI-supported academic writing.

papers.title: Supporting bystander intervention through conversational AI: Experimental evidence from undergraduate samples
papers.authors: Seoyeon Bae, Marcus Trenfield, Mengyao Zhao, Grace Bauer, Liane Young
papers.abstract: Across campuses and workplaces, people are receiving bystander intervention training to empower them to support victims and mitigate situations of harm. But even after this training, many people remain insecure about their ability to intervene and hesitate to act when intervention is needed. One promising solution to bystanders' ongoing inaction is to provide a safe, judgment-free environment where people can repeatedly practice skills and receive personalized feedback. Here, we explore that solution through a chatbot-based bystander intervention practice tool, where an AI agent guides users through evidence-based training. Across two preregistered experiments with undergraduates-a pilot study conducted on a local college campus followed by a larger online study-we found preliminary evidence that chatbot-guided training may strengthen several motivational outcomes associated with bystander intervention, including bystander efficacy, attitudes, psychological safety, and norm perceptions. This work provides preliminary evidence of the impact of chatbot-guided bystander intervention training. The findings highlight the potential of AI as a pedagogical tool for supporting bystander intervention and provide an empirical foundation for future research on AI-assisted intervention training.

papers.title: Reconceptualizing learning sciences in the era of artificial intelligence: Toward hybrid intelligence and adaptive learning systems
papers.authors: Abdul Malik, Irfan Bashir
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming education through intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics, and large language models. However, research on Learning Sciences, AI in Education, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, and Hybrid Intelligence has largely progressed across partially separate research streams, resulting in fragmented theoretical perspectives and limited conceptual integration. This systematic review aims to synthesize the existing literature and develop an evidence-informed Hybrid Intelligence Framework that explains the relationships among Learning Sciences, AI technologies, learning analytics, and adaptive learning systems. DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: A qualitative systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature published between 2004 and March 2026 was retrieved through a focused, intersection-based search across seven databases: Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar. Following duplicate removal and eligibility screening, 32 studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were synthesized using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis. FINDINGS: Four interrelated themes emerged from the thematic synthesis: (1) epistemological fragmentation within Learning Sciences, (2) theory-technology contradictions between pedagogical theories and AI-supported educational systems, (3) the datafication of learning through learning analytics and adaptive technologies, and (4) Hybrid Intelligence as an emerging educational paradigm emphasizing collaboration among learners, educators, and intelligent systems. Building on these themes, the review proposes a Hybrid Intelligence Framework that integrates Learning Sciences, Artificial Intelligence, Learning Analytics, and adaptive learning systems into a coherent conceptual model for human-centred, ethical, explainable, and evidence-informed AI-supported education. ORIGINALITY/VALUE: This review advances the literature by moving beyond isolated examinations of AI technologies or learning theories to provide an integrative conceptual synthesis of their interrelationships. The proposed Hybrid Intelligence Framework offers a theoretically grounded foundation for future empirical research, instructional design, educational policy, and the development of adaptive learning environments that integrate human expertise with artificial intelligence while supporting learner agency and pedagogical integrity.

papers.title: Evaluating multimodal explainable adaptive learning in university EFL education: Learner outcomes, teacher oversight, and implementation conditions
papers.authors: Houda Boumediene, Abeer Aljohani, Mustapha Bouakkaz
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers substantial potential for personalized English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction, yet concerns remain regarding the transparency of adaptive recommendations, the fragmentation of learner data, and the preservation of teacher oversight. This study empirically evaluates the Multimodal Explainable Adaptive Learning Framework (MEALF), a pedagogical-computational framework operationalized through a prototype system that integrates textual, oral, visual, and behavioral learner information with explainable adaptive recommendations. Grounded in sociocultural theory, situated cognition, and human-centered AI, MEALF was designed to provide differentiated learning support while keeping pedagogical decisions interpretable and subject to teacher judgment. A 16-week partially randomized quasi-experimental mixed-methods study was conducted with 100 intermediate-level EFL learners and 15 teachers across three Algerian universities. Learners in the MEALF-supported condition showed larger proficiency gains and higher post-intervention engagement and metacognitive reading-strategy awareness scores than learners in the comparison condition. Exploratory multimodal analyses further revealed heterogeneous learner patterns that provided additional context for interpreting differences in learning needs and adaptive support. Teacher and qualitative evidence indicated that explanations and override mechanisms helped educators inspect and critically evaluate system recommendations, although teacher-level findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample. The findings provide preliminary, context-specific evidence that combining multimodal learner information with interpretable adaptive support may contribute to language development, engagement, and metacognitive reading-strategy awareness while preserving meaningful human oversight. However, the multi-component nature of MEALF, the quasi-experimental design, the small teacher sample, and the single-country context limit causal interpretation and broader generalizability. The study contributes an integrated empirical evaluation of multimodal, explainable adaptive learning by linking measurable learner outcomes with interpretable human-AI interaction and contextual implementation evidence in university EFL education.

papers.title: Silhouette-based body dissatisfaction and positive psychological functioning in Uruguayan adults
papers.authors: Mayda Alejandra Portela, Emilio Pericet-Caro, Julieta I. Sánchez-Bizama, Carla M. Pérez-Jaén, Cristian M. Olarte‐Sánchez
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to analyze the relationship between silhouette-based body dissatisfaction and positive psychological functioning (PPF) in Uruguayan adults, and to explore differences according to sex, body mass index (BMI), and body satisfaction status. METHOD: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 202 adults (M age = 35.44, SD = 12.69; 73.8% women). Participants completed the Stunkard Figure Rating Scale (SFRS), the Positive Psychological Functioning Scale (PPFS), the General Health Questionnaire-28 (GHQ-28), the Dutch Eating Behavior Questionnaire (DEBQ), and a sociodemographic survey. RESULTS: Body dissatisfaction was negatively correlated with PPF total score (r = -0.28, p < .001), as well as with several PPF dimensions, including self-esteem (r = -0.30), vitality (r = -0.29), autonomy (r = -0.18), and environmental mastery (r = -0.23). Body dissatisfaction was positively correlated with psychological distress, as measured by GHQ-28 total score (r = 0.30, p < .001). Participants classified as body dissatisfied had higher BMI and lower scores on several PPF dimensions at the uncorrected level. After Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, several PPF dimensions remained significantly lower among body dissatisfied participants, particularly self-esteem, vitality, environmental mastery, optimism, autonomy, resilience, and curiosity. No significant unadjusted sex differences were found in body dissatisfaction. In the adjusted logistic regression model, higher BMI, lower PPF total score, and sex were independently associated with body dissatisfaction status. CONCLUSIONS: Silhouette-based body satisfaction status was associated with higher positive psychological functioning and lower psychological distress. When age, sex, living situation, BMI, psychological distress, subjective socioeconomic level, and PPF were considered simultaneously, PPF remained independently associated with body dissatisfaction. These findings suggest that silhouette-based body satisfaction status is associated with psychological resources and may be relevant for understanding broader psychological functioning. Longitudinal research is needed to confirm causal directions.

papers.title: Navigating the N-shaped path: Nonlinear development of pre-service PE teachers' professional competencies in AI-driven STEAM instruction
papers.authors: TongKai Guan, Walton Wider, Xiaoman Wen, Qiang Song
papers.abstract: This study investigates the longitudinal developmental trajectories of pre-service physical education (PE) teachers' core competencies within a 16-week generative AI-driven STEAM basketball curriculum. Employing a parallel-group randomized controlled trial in which 80 participants were randomized and 75 completed the intervention (experimental n = 37; control n = 38), the study addresses the absence of longitudinal evidence on how Intelligent-TPACK develops over time by identifying a non-linear N-shaped trajectory across the three core competency domains, with two sub-dimensions (Professional Responsibilities, Ethics) as theoretically informative exceptions. Piecewise linear mixed-effects models show a Week-8 decline at peak instructional complexity followed by recovery; the between-group phase contrasts describing this pattern remain significant after correction for multiplicity. Two further patterns are reported as exploratory and hypothesis-generating: higher baseline AI proficiency was associated with a steeper Week-8 decline in classroom management (feature creep), and recovery co-occurred with reduced in-class AI activation (pedagogical simplification rebound). Intelligent-TPACK, interdisciplinary teaching ability and observed teaching practice were associated within persons, but because they were measured on the same occasions this is not evidence of a causal cascade. We offer the Generative AI-TPACK Fatigue Model as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than confirmed theory. The study offers preliminary, context-sensitive guidance for teacher education programs working in comparable settings, and identifies the conditions under which a mid-course performance decline might prove productive as a question for future work.

papers.title: “It is unfair!”: Exploring EFL students' perceived forms of AI-related assessment unfairness in coursework from a self-determination theory lens
papers.authors: Shuang Liu, Yanghaoze Qin
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of generative AI into foreign language education has reshaped how students complete coursework and how teachers assess. As students increasingly rely on AI to assist with coursework, teachers often cannot reliably distinguish AI-generated from human-authored work, which raises pressing concerns about assessment fairness. Yet how assessment unfairness is actually experienced and perceived, and how learners describe its psychological significance remain under-explored. Drawing on self-determination theory, this study investigates the forms of AI-related assessment unfairness perceived by students who reported experiencing such unfairness, and its perceived implications for students' basic psychological needs. Based on semi-structured interviews with 15 university EFL students, the findings suggest that perceived AI-related assessment unfairness takes the form of false suspicions about AI-generated coursework, unstable or opaque standards, and reward misalignment. Additionally, participants described experiences of frustration in their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness in relation to perceived AI-related assessment unfairness, though its perceived intensity varied with learners and contextual factors. The study offers practical implications for redesigning assessment, developing teacher capacity, and establishing institutional guidelines that support fairer, more motivationally sustaining practices.

papers.title: Explainable machine learning for identifying mild cognitive impairment in older adults with chronic diseases: Model development and temporal validation
papers.authors: Kun Ruan, Yuan Li
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning classification model for identifying MCI at the time of assessment among older adults with chronic conditions. We also evaluated model performance and the stability of TreeSHAP-based feature explanations across survey waves. METHODS: Data were obtained from the CHARLS. A total of 8222 participants from the 2018 wave were stratified by MCI status and randomly divided into a development set (n = 5754) and an internal validation set (n = 2468). Data from the 2020 wave (n = 5558) were used for temporal validation. LASSO regression was performed exclusively in the development set for feature selection, resulting in 27 retained predictors. Using the same feature set, seven classification models were developed: logistic regression, support vector machine, multilayer perceptron, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and k-nearest neighbors. Encoding, standardization, SMOTENC resampling, and hyperparameter tuning were performed within the training folds of 10-fold cross-validation to minimize information leakage, while the original class distributions were retained in both validation sets. Model performance was assessed using the AUROC, AUPRC, classification metrics, Brier score, calibration analysis, and decision curve analysis. TreeSHAP was then applied to the prespecified XGBoost model to characterize feature contributions and assess the stability of global feature importance across survey waves. RESULTS: In the 2018 internal validation set, the prespecified XGBoost model achieved an AUROC of 0.692 (95% CI: 0.660-0.724), an AUPRC of 0.282 (95% CI: 0.242-0.328), a sensitivity of 0.511, a specificity of 0.746, and a Brier score of 0.109. In the 2020 temporal validation set, the corresponding values were 0.702 for AUROC, 0.305 for AUPRC, 0.390 for sensitivity, 0.843 for specificity, and 0.137 for the Brier score. These findings indicate that discrimination remained broadly stable across survey waves, although sensitivity and calibration were limited. Decision curve analysis showed a positive net benefit for XGBoost mainly across low-to-moderate threshold probabilities. TreeSHAP analysis identified number of living children, sleep duration, educational attainment, activities of daily living (ADL), and age as the strongest contributors to model predictions. Global feature-importance rankings were highly consistent between the 2018 internal validation set and the 2020 temporal validation set (Spearman ρ = 0.996). CONCLUSION: This study developed an interpretable machine-learning framework for identifying current MCI status among older adults with chronic conditions. The prespecified XGBoost model showed moderate and relatively stable discrimination in both internal and temporal validation, while its TreeSHAP-based feature explanations were highly stable across survey waves. The model may serve as an adjunctive screening and preliminary risk-stratification tool before formal cognitive assessment, but it should not replace clinical diagnosis of MCI or be used to predict incident MCI or future cognitive decline. Further recalibration and external validation in independent populations are required before implementation.

papers.title: From Idea to Publication: A Step-by-Step Guide to Original Research in Radiology with AI-Integrated Workflow
papers.authors: Isabela Hernández, Daniel Souza, Cinthia Del Toro, Kristin Parker, Adriana Falcon, Gary H. Danton, Ty K. Subhawong, Francesco Alessandrino

papers.title: Examining Race-Based Puberty Information on Children’s Hospital Websites
papers.authors: Adeiyewunmi Osinubi, J. Reed Junkin, Sophia Austin, Christine Paula Lewis-de los Angeles, Lisa Swartz Topor
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In 2022, the American Academy of Pediatrics called for dismantling race-based medicine due to its harmful impact on patient care and education. Despite this, race-based guidance regarding pubertal timing persists in the literature and patient resources. Given the role of pediatric hospital websites as sources of information for families and as data for Artificial Intelligence, we examined the presence of race-based guidance on pubertal timing in girls across U.S. pediatric hospital websites. METHODS: Pediatric hospitals in the United States were identified, and each website was queried using the terms "puberty" and "precocious puberty." Information provided on pubertal timing in girls was recorded, along with any inclusion of race-based guidance. Descriptive statistics and qualitative analysis of pediatric hospital puberty information were performed. An analysis of variance (ANOVA) test compared the prevalence of race-based information across seven U.S. regions. RESULTS: Of 285 pediatric hospitals in the United States, 85 (29.8%) had patient-facing content on puberty, and 16 (18.8%) included race-based information. Half (8, 50%) of the pediatric hospitals that included race-based pubertal information included race as a "risk factor" for precocious puberty. Regional differences in the frequency of race-based pubertal information for patients on the hospital websites were not statistically significant (p=0.069). CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates the ongoing presence of race-based information about puberty on pediatric hospital websites. Updating the patient-facing websites of pediatric hospital to avoid race-based pubertal guidance may foster a more inclusive and equitable environment for patients and their families.

papers.title: A comprehensive review on recent pretrained multimodal deep learning models from architectures to future directions
papers.authors: Azhar A. Hadi, K. P. Supreethi
papers.abstract: In recent years, multimodal deep learning has made great progress, enabling artificial intelligence to learn across text, audio, images, video, and other data. Unlike earlier unimodal deep learning models trained on limited data, new multimodal models are trained on large collections of mixed media and achieve strong results. This review covers 13 recent pre-trained models from 2020 to 2025, including CLIP, GPT-4V, GPT-4o, SigLIP, ViT, BLIP, Flamingo, PaLI, LLaVA, Florence-2, PaliGemma-2, Gemma-3, and Llama-4, that help connect different types of information for tasks such as alignment, classification, and detection. Moreover, this paper provides a comparative analysis of recent pre-trained MMDL models, examining their specific applications, architectural designs, datasets utilized, and evaluation metrics used in current research. It highlights 120 articles on Multimodal Deep Learning (MMDL), including the challenges and limitations of each model. Additionally, this review covers 11 domains using recent pre-trained Multimodal Deep Learning (MMDL), including Healthcare, Education, Industrial and Manufacturing, Autonomous Systems and Transportation, and E-commerce, with dozens of applications across these domains. Although these models perform better, key problems remain, like data quality, high computational costs, model alignment, and the need for more efficient designs. This review also looks at future needs, such as making models faster, more robust, better at handling a wider range of data types, and more trustworthy. Our goal is to provide researchers and students with a clear view of current opportunities and capabilities in multimodal deep learning.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in orthodontics: clinical maturity, evidence gaps, and emerging applications—a narrative review
papers.authors: Kanza Ahmed Chandio, Laiba Iftikhar, Anum Shehzad, Ifrah Rao, Minahil Waseem, Muhammad Anas, Muhammad Farrukh, Ammar Al Shalabi, Sameh Talaat, Sinan Şen, Fatma E. A. Hassanein, Tarek M. Elshazly
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming orthodontics by enhancing diagnostic accuracy, supporting clinical decision-making, and facilitating digital workflows. This narrative review provides a comprehensive overview of current AI technologies and their applications in orthodontics, including diagnostic imaging, treatment planning, treatment monitoring, patient communication, education, and emerging generative AI tools. The available evidence indicates that automated cephalometric landmark detection and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) segmentation have among the most advanced technical and external-validation evidence bases in orthodontic AI, whereas digital-model analysis has demonstrated high technical performance but more limited independent validation. However, no application met the predefined criteria for higher clinical maturity because prospective clinical effectiveness remained insufficiently established. Other emerging or experimental applications include AI-assisted treatment planning, remote monitoring, large language models (LLMs), and robotic systems, for which evidence remains predominantly retrospective, technical, feasibility-based, or early clinical. However, much of the current evidence is derived from retrospective studies, technical validation investigations, and proof-of-concept reports, with limited prospective clinical data demonstrating improvements in treatment quality, efficiency, or long-term patient outcomes. Important challenges remain regarding data quality, algorithmic bias, external validation, explainability, patient privacy, and regulatory oversight. Overall, AI should currently be regarded as a clinician-supervised decision-support tool rather than a replacement for professional expertise. Future progress is likely to depend on robust prospective clinical trials, transparent reporting, and responsible integration of AI into evidence-based orthodontic practice and the broader digital transformation of dentistry.

papers.title: Determinants of artificial intelligence adoption in the Indian construction industry using the UTAUT model
papers.authors: Nuvotalu Ringa, Himmi Gupta, Harsh Vardhan Samalia
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been adopted in relatively few areas of construction industry, despite having the ability to make it more productive, efficient, and better informed. In this research, four additional constructs, namely, Awareness, Cost, Trust and Perceived Risk have been applied to the original Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) to explore the determinants of AI adoption in the Indian construction industry. This study utilized a quantitative design, surveying 121 construction professionals via an online platform. Analysis of the collected data was carried out in a structured sequence. This process began with frequency analysis, followed by reliability testing, calculation of descriptive statistics, and assessment of normality. Correlation analysis was first conducted to explore relationships between variables, followed by multiple linear regression to test their respective predictive effects. The findings suggest that Performance Expectancy, Social Influence, and Awareness have a significant impact on Behavioral Intention to adopt AI. Conversely, there are no notable impacts of Effort Expectancy, Cost, Trust, and Perceived Risk. Moreover, the effects of Facilitating Conditions and Behavioral Intention to predict actual Use Behavior are significant, and organizational and technical support appear to become a decisive factor of the implementation. The results indicate that the perceived performance benefits and social dynamics have a greater influence on AI adoption intentions as opposed to effort, cost, or risk concerns. The study builds on the UTAUT concept by introducing more constructs and offering practical values on how to enable successful AI adoption in construction industry.

papers.title: The evolution of American planning over four decades: professional change, institutional adaptation, and future directions
papers.authors: Sue Schwartz, Ruxia Bai
papers.journal: Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning
papers.abstract: Abstract Over more than four decades, American planning has evolved from a largely technocratic and regulatory practice into a more collaborative, interdisciplinary, and community-oriented profession. This featured interview traces Sue Schwartz’s reflections on her extensive experience in regional and local planning, including her service as Planning Director of Greensboro, North Carolina, and her leadership roles within the American Planning Association (APA) and the American Institute of Certified Planners (AICP). This interview-based perspective reflects on the major periods and turning points that have shaped the profession. It considers the development-led expansion of the 1980s, the influence of New Urbanism and Smart Growth, the transformation of public engagement, the lessons of the Great Recession, and the opportunities and risks associated with artificial intelligence and data tools. It also explores how professional certification, continuing education, ethical standards, and professional associations help sustain planning as an increasingly interdisciplinary field. Despite economic uncertainty, political change, and technological disruption, the interview highlights curiosity, public service, professional judgment, and optimism about the future as enduring foundations of the planning profession.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education assessment as an ecosystem of pedagogy governance and legitimacy
papers.authors: Joshua King Obeng-Nyarko
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping higher education assessment through applications such as automated feedback, adaptive testing, learning analytics, automated scoring, and generative support. Yet scholarship on AI-enabled assessment remains fragmented across technical, pedagogical, ethical, governance, and professional perspectives, limiting the field’s capacity to explain how these dimensions interact in practice and how misalignment among them affects educational legitimacy. This paper develops the AI-Assessment Ecosystem Model, a conceptual ecosystem framework for analysing AI in higher education assessment as a sociotechnical and institutional phenomenon rather than a discrete technical intervention. Drawing on a conceptual synthesis of literature published primarily between 2019 and 2024, and informed by foundational work on assessment validity, feedback, institutional legitimacy, organisational change, inclusive design, and computer-supported collaborative learning, the paper identifies five interdependent domains that shape AI-enabled assessment: technological innovation, pedagogical alignment and learner needs, institutional strategy and governance, faculty and professional readiness, and ethical and inclusive implementation. The paper theorises legitimacy as a relational and contested process through which AI-supported assessment must be justified to students, faculty, institutions, regulators, and other stakeholders as educationally valid, professionally defensible, ethically acceptable, inclusive, and organisationally accountable. The framework argues that AI in assessment cannot be adequately evaluated by technical capability, implementation success, or ethical compliance alone; it must be understood through the relations, tensions, and potential misalignments among educational purpose, organisational conditions, professional practice, student agency, and technological design. The model is offered as a conceptual ecosystem framework for guiding future research, critique, and institutional decision-making.

papers.title: Knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and utilization of artificial intelligence in higher education among university students in Mogadishu, Somalia
papers.authors: Ayan Mohamed Jama, Abdullahi Ahmed Tahlil, Ahmed Osman Ali, Mohamud Osman Hamud, Abdullahi Mohamud Hassan, Abukar Sheikh Mohamed
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming higher education through innovations in teaching, learning, assessment, and research. More than sixty countries have published national AI strategies, yet the overwhelming majority, over 70%, are developed nations. This geographic concentration of AI readiness reflects deeper structural inequalities: in 2024, more than 70% of AI-related job postings were concentrated in high-income countries, and generative AI vacancies surged ninefold from 2021 to 2024. Although global adoption of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Turnitin is accelerating, empirical evidence on AI awareness and use in fragile and low-resource settings, such as Somalia, remains limited. This study assessed the knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and use of AI among university students in Mogadishu, Somalia. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 1,690 undergraduate students at Somali National University. A structured, self-administered questionnaire collected data on sociodemographic characteristics, knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and AI utilization. Stratified random sampling ensured representation across all faculties. Data were analyzed in SPSS version 26 using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests to assess associations between sociodemographic factors and outcome variables. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The mean age of study participants was 23.5 ± 2.8 years. Most respondents (88.5%) had heard of AI, and 72.7% demonstrated good knowledge of it. Over half (51.5%) expressed positive attitudes toward integrating AI into higher education, and 58.1% held positive perceptions of its role in enhancing accessibility and learning quality. A large majority (82.2%) reported using AI tools, primarily ChatGPT (77.6%) and Grammarly (59.5%), mainly for assignments and language support. Age, faculty, and year of study were significantly associated with knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and utilization ( p < 0.001). Female students demonstrated significantly higher knowledge, perceptions, and AI utilization than male students. Our study found that university students demonstrate high awareness, positive attitudes and perceptions, and substantial use of AI tools despite limited formal training and policy guidance. These findings underscore the need for structured AI literacy programs, ethical frameworks, and institutional policies to ensure responsible and equitable integration of AI in Somalia’s higher education sector.

papers.title: The relationship between the uses of generative artificial intelligence and ethics and attitudes among student teachers in the faculties of education at Sana’a and Qatar Universities
papers.authors: عائشة فضل الكعبي, Yahya Abdulrazaq Qutran
papers.abstract: The study aimed to shed light on the relationship between the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) by student teachers in the Colleges of Education at Sana’a University and Qatar University, their awareness of its ethical aspects, and their attitudes toward its use. It also sought to identify the similarities and differences between the two groups of students. The researchers adopted a descriptive, analytical, and comparative methodology. Data were collected through a questionnaire designed to measure the levels of use and ethical awareness, and an attitude scale. The sample consisted of 388 male and female student teachers recruited from both colleges through a convenience sampling method. The findings revealed that ChatGPT was the most frequently used application. Although student teachers at Qatar University showed higher mean scores in both use and ethical awareness, these differences were not statistically significant. In contrast, student teachers at Sana’a University demonstrated a slightly higher mean score in attitudes toward generative AI, though this difference was also not statistically significant. A weak to moderate positive correlation was found between use and attitudes. Furthermore, there were no significant differences between male and female students across all dimensions, nor between specializations in the areas of use and ethics. However, significant differences were observed between specializations in attitudes, favoring students in scientific disciplines. The study recommended that both colleges adopt an institutional framework for integrating generative AI and align teacher preparation programs with contemporary technological advancements.

papers.title: AI integration in STEM learning in inclusive schools in Indonesia from teachers experiences and perspectives
papers.authors: I Wayan Sumandya, I Putu Pasek Suryawan, I Nyoman Bagus Suweta Nugraha, I Wayan Widana, Ni Wayan Widi Astuti
papers.abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in STEM learning within inclusive schools presents a significant opportunity to enhance personalized, adaptive, and equitable learning experiences for diverse learners. However, its successful implementation is constrained by complex pedagogical, technological, and human factors, where teacher perception plays a decisive role. This research aims to analyze the influence of AI integration and teachers’ professional experience on teacher perceptions regarding the use of AI in inclusive STEM education in Indonesia, a context characterized by heterogeneous student needs and varying levels of technological readiness. Employing a quantitative approach with an explanatory survey design, the study involved 1,000 teachers from inclusive primary and secondary schools selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model evaluation confirmed strong psychometric properties, with all indicators meeting validity and reliability criteria (outer loading > 0.70, composite reliability > 0.90, and average variance extracted > 0.50). Structural model results demonstrated that AI integration (β = 0.399, p < 0.001) and teachers’ experience (β = 0.512, p < 0.001) significantly influenced teacher perceptions, with teachers’ experience emerging as the more dominant predictor. The model exhibited moderate explanatory power (R² = 0.449) and excellent goodness of fit (SRMR = 0.045). Furthermore, PLS-Predict analysis indicated high out-of-sample predictive capability, confirming the robustness of the proposed model. These findings underscore that teachers’ lived pedagogical experiences, rather than technological availability alone, are central in shaping constructive perceptions of AI use. Consequently, this study recommends a strategic policy shift from infrastructure-centered initiatives toward sustained, experiential, and inclusive professional development programs to empower teachers in leveraging AI for effective and equitable STEM learning in inclusive educational settings.

papers.title: Pre-service science teachers’ anxiety levels about artificial intelligence applications
papers.authors: Cennet Çakir, Hasan Gökçe, İshak Afşin Kari̇per
papers.abstract: The objective of this study is to ascertain the levels of anxiety experienced by pre-service science teachers in relation to the utilization of artificial intelligence applications. A mixed research method was employed in the study. One of the mixed research method designs, the sequential explanatory design, was employed in the study. In the quantitative section of the study, a survey design was employed, while a case study design was utilized in the qualitative component. The population of the quantitative component, which constitutes the participants of the study, consists of 208 pre-service teachers enrolled in the science department of the faculty of education at a state university. The study sample consisted of 162 pre-service science teachers. The sample was selected through the use of simple random sampling. In the qualitative component of the study, eight prospective science educators, selected for their maximum diversity, were the subjects of investigation. In the course of data collection for the study, the scale was administered to 162 pre-service science teachers. Subsequently, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight pre-service science teachers. In the data analysis phase of the study, quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed separately. Descriptive statistics and inferential statistics were employed to analyze the quantitative data, while content analysis was utilized to analyze the qualitative data. The findings revealed that the level of artificial intelligence anxiety among the pre-service science teachers was moderate, as indicated by the scale administered to this group. The interviews revealed that pre-service teachers with high and low levels of artificial intelligence anxiety had similar responses. Both groups agreed that artificial intelligence cannot replace the teaching profession. Based on these findings, the research team proposed two recommendations: first, to provide pre-service teachers with the necessary training on artificial intelligence, and second, to offer an artificial intelligence course to all pre-service teachers.

papers.title: Spiking neural transformer based confidentiality preserving framework for breast cancer detection in histopathology images
papers.authors: Harish Kumar, Anuradha Taluja, N. Partheeban, Shashi Mehrotra
papers.abstract: Breast cancer diagnosis by medical imaging requires accuracy and high sensitivity to patient information. Even though artificial intelligence has made major progress in the field of histopathological image analysis, there are still limitations such as noise in the image, structural variability, and class imbalance, low interpretability of deep learning models, high computational complexity, and privacy risks. To overcome these limitations, this paper suggests a Confidentiality-Preserving Spiking Neural Transformer for Breast Cancer Detection (CP-SNT) to secure and robustly detect breast cancer. In initial phase Robust Double-Weighted Guided Image Filtration (RDWGIF) is applied to improve the quality of histopathological images and reduce noise, but not fine tissue borders. This is followed by the Discrete Quaternion Quadratic Phase Fourier Transform (DQQPFT) that obtains discriminative frequency and phase-domain features, allowing the representation of complex structural and textual patterns. The central classification layer is a Probabilistic Spiking Neural Network (PSNN) that is integrated with a Causality-Aware Transformer Network (CATN) spike-based uncertainty modeling and attention-directed learning, respectively. To maintain the privacy of data in training and inference, PrivTuner using Homomorphic Encryption allows the safe computation of medical data encrypted with the homomorphic encryption to avoid the disclosure of sensitive patient data. The proposed CP-SNT framework is evaluated on the publicly available BreakHis and Breast Histopathology Images (BHI) datasets of 16,116 images to validate classification performance across multi-scale and patch-level histopathological samples. Comprehensive experimental validation on the BreakHis and BHI datasets demonstrates that the proposed CP-SNT model achieves accuracies of 98.60% and 98.37%, respectively. The framework further records precision values above 98.1% and F1-scores near 98.2%, reflecting its strong capability to minimize both false positives and false negatives. Such outstanding performance highlights the effectiveness of the hybrid spiking-transformer architecture combined with encrypted-domain computation for secure and high-confidence breast cancer diagnosis.

papers.title: Navigating academic integrity in the Era of generative AI: a systematic literature review
papers.authors: Batool A. Hendal, Gobinda G Chowdhury
papers.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive overview of existing research on the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) within academic contexts. It aims to provide a nuanced understanding of the evolving role of GenAI in higher education institutions by identifying the dominant themes and emphasising the recommendations proposed by researchers. To achieve this purpose, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted, followed by an inductive thematic analysis to synthesise and interpret the findings. A convergent and divergent synthesis was subsequently undertaken to identify areas of agreement and debate across the reviewed literature. Based on 274 codes, six main themes were identified, including the potential benefits of GenAI, potential disadvantages of GenAI, GenAI and language, AI text detectors, policies and governance, and recommendations for responsible GenAI adoption. Grounded in the main recommendations identified across the literature, the study proposes an Academic GenAI Adaptation Framework, organised into two core dimensions: GenAI Governance and Infrastructure, and GenAI Education and Literacy. The framework provides higher education institutions with a practical roadmap for the strategic, ethical, and responsible integration of GenAI while safeguarding academic integrity.

papers.title: The psychology of machine intelligence: evaluating the necessity of artificial intelligence in everyday smart devices and automated systems
papers.authors: Swarnajit Bhattacharya
papers.abstract: Abstract The exponential rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has seamlessly woven intelligent systems into nearly every sphere of human life from smart homes and healthcare to transportation and entertainment. Yet, beneath this technological revolution lies a deeper psychological question: are humans truly benefiting from AI, or gradually examining the implications of increasing reliance on intelligent systems. Preliminary data suggests that over 78% of individuals in developed societies engage with AI-driven devices at least 12 times a day, while 62% admit to relying on automated systems for decisions once made intuitively. This study employs quantitative performance metrics and psychological dependency assessments across a diverse sample of 80 + participants to analyze the cognitive, emotional, and social implications of daily AI exposure. Comparative experiments between AI-assisted and manual task environments will measure productivity, satisfaction, and creative independence to determine whether constant AI support enhances or inhibits human potential. While the findings are expected to reveal fascinating insights into how humans psychologically adapt to machine intelligence, one crucial question remains unresolved does AI genuinely enrich human life, or subtly condition it for convenience at the cost of individuality. The answer, as the forthcoming analysis will uncover, may challenge the very foundation of our belief in progress.

papers.title: Generative AI utilization and employee productivity through digital skills with the moderating role of AI trust
papers.authors: Azatullah Zaheer, Yogeeswari Subramaniam, Nurul Mohammad Zayed, Munmun Shabnam Bipasha, Walid K. Alrawi
papers.abstract: Generative AI adoption has attracted considerable scholarly and managerial attention because of its potential to improve employee productivity. However, empirical evidence remains limited regarding how different dimensions of generative AI adoption relate to employee productivity, particularly in developing contexts. Drawing on Task–Technology Fit Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the associations between the frequency, depth, and purpose of generative AI adoption and employee productivity, with digital skills as a mediator and AI trust as a moderator. A cross-sectional survey of 404 employees from generative AI-enabled organizations in Kabul, Afghanistan, was analyzed using SEM. The findings show that the frequency and depth of generative AI adoption are positively associated with employee productivity, whereas the purpose of AI adoption has no significant direct association. Digital skills demonstrate significant indirect associations between generative AI adoption and employee productivity, while AI trust does not significantly moderate these relationships. The study contributes to the literature by conceptualizing generative AI adoption as a multidimensional construct and emphasizing the role of employees’ digital skills in AI-driven workplaces. Practically, the findings help identify ways to improve employees’ digital skills to ensure generative AI adoption and reap the associated benefits, supporting sustainable digital transformation. Thus, it contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure).

papers.title: Engaging with the heritage of Nazi persecution in the age of AI: ethical considerations and educational implications
papers.authors: Tobias Ebbrecht-Hartmann, Esther Rachow
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the ethical and educational implications of using AI in digital heritage environments dedicated to the Holocaust and Nazi persecution. Drawing on the Horizon Europe MEMORISE project, it argues that AI can support access to fragmented and multimodal heritage materials through tagging, linking, translation, recommendation, and personalization, but only if these functions remain embedded in a human-centered framework grounded in dignity, authenticity, transparency, provenance, and historical accuracy. The paper highlights the risks of algorithmic bias, decontextualization, hallucination, artificial empathy, and over-personalized “filter bubbles,” especially in relation to sensitive historical sources and marginalized victim perspectives. In response, it proposes an approach based on human-in-the-loop oversight, provenance by design, AI literacy, and experiential knowledge, showing how AI can enhance critical engagement with difficult histories without replacing human interpretation, educator responsibility, or the integrity of archival sources.

papers.title: Emotional chain reasoning-driven multimodal fusion for empathic humanoid robot interaction
papers.authors: Jie Fang, Feng Xiao, Xi Fang, Jun Nie, Yanjun Liu, Jie Gao
papers.abstract: As humanoid robots enter companion service, educational assistance, rehabilitation support, and public interaction, the central challenge is not only to recognize emotion but to convert multimodal human cues into coordinated language and action. The proposed Emotional Chain Reasoning-Driven Multimodal Fusion Network (ECDT-MFN) is not a separate alternative to vision-language-action (VLA) architectures. At the task and pipeline level, it is an emotion-aware VLA extension: visual observations and language context are mapped to social actions, while voice prosody, facial expression, body movement, and haptic feedback provide an auxiliary biometric-affective observation stream. The contribution lies in adding dynamic affective conditioning, explicit-to-implicit emotional chain reasoning, and empathy-conditioned action planning to this VLA-style perception-language-action loop. The model jointly produces empathic verbal responses and executable social behaviors such as gaze, head posture, interaction distance, waiting, assistance, and conflict avoidance. Evaluation is therefore organized at two levels. Participant-centered, end-to-end HRI outcomes—including perceived empathy, behavioral appropriateness, user satisfaction, interaction continuity, and long-term consistency—serve as the primary evidence of effectiveness; automatic emotion-recognition, semantic-similarity, module-ablation, and noise-retention measures are retained only as diagnostic evidence. Results show that the complete emotion-aware VLA pipeline improves the tested whole-interaction outcomes while maintaining the measured software-inference latency of the reference implementation. These findings support the value of affective conditioning for socially responsive VLA control, rather than claiming a new non-VLA control paradigm.

papers.title: HHEEG: Healthy Hybrid EEG-Based Mental Workload Assessment for Healthcare Using Integrated Spatial, Temporal Spectral Deep Learning
papers.authors: Vishal Sharma, Dipika Jain, Pallavi Ranjan, Nomesh Shourya Thakur, Saumya Srivastava, Aniket Raj
papers.abstract: Abstract Recognizing and understanding human mental workload while performing a task is extremely important for enhancing cognitive state monitoring, optimizing task design, and facilitating decision-making in complex environments. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive technique for monitoring brain activity patterns, albeit with challenges stemming from considerable noise and dimensional complexity that impact classification performance. In recent years, deep learning methodologies have demonstrated exceptional capability in extracting sophisticated spatio-temporal patterns from EEG signals during workload classification tasks. Expanding on these advancements, this paper proposes a comprehensive deep learning framework that combines one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (1D-CNN), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks, and attention mechanisms to simultaneously capture spatial, temporal, and contextual features directly from EEG signals’ raw data. Concurrently, a parallel spectral-processing path extracts frequency-domain features via Welch’s method to further boost performance in terms of spectral representation. The model was trained and tested on the publicly available STEW (Simultaneous Task EEG Workload) dataset, with a classification accuracy of 94.13% to separate low and high workload conditions. The fusion of multi-domain features and the model’s attention-driven focus on salient time windows is responsible for its better performance compared to single-stream neural models and classic machine learning. This work highlights the capability of hybrid deep architectures in real-time cognitive state monitoring and provides a basis for EEG-based adaptive systems.

papers.title: A Picture is Worth 1000 Words: Using Graphic Novels to Support Health Professions Education
papers.authors: K. Beth Marcellas, Melissa A Myers, Dina Kurzweil
papers.abstract: Abstract The article illuminates the communicative power of graphic novels and the instructional rationale for their use for health professions education (HPE), particularly for enhancing critical thinking, empathy, and interpersonal skills. The article also provides a methodological framework for creating graphic novels that incorporates Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for narrative codification and visual synthesis. It outlines a two-phase process: Phase I (Architecture), focused on conceptual design, and Phase II (Construction), which utilizes a "Human-AI-Human" (H-AI-H) workflow to streamline production while maintaining pedagogical integrity.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in mechanical engineering: foundations, opportunities, challenges, and responsibilities
papers.authors: Américo Cunha, Chandrasekhar Nataraj, Luciano M. Lorenzo, Hervé Panetto, Américo Scotti, JOSÉ VIRIATO COELHO VARGAS
papers.journal: Journal of the Brazilian Society of Mechanical Sciences and Engineering
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming mechanical engineering (ME) practice, influencing activities that range from modeling and simulation to optimization, diagnostics, design, and technical communication. This article consolidates perspectives discussed at a dedicated round-table during the 28th ABCM International Congress on Mechanical Engineering—COBEM 2025—and offers a structured reflection for the Brazilian and international ME communities. Rather than providing an exhaustive survey, the paper develops a coherent narrative around the conditions under which AI can strengthen—rather than dilute—engineering rigor. The article begins by clarifying how contemporary AI systems operate, distinguishing statistical learning from human cognition and outlining their capabilities, limitations, and emerging agentic AI systems. It then examines industrial adoption, workforce transformation, and the growing role of AI in scientific discovery and engineering workflows. Particular attention is devoted to the energy and infrastructure demands of AI-driven computation and their implications for sustainability, power systems, and thermal management. Building on these constraints, the paper discusses integrating physical knowledge, structured reasoning, and domain expertise into AI systems for safety-relevant engineering applications. Emphasis is placed on representative ME applications, physics-informed and hybrid learning frameworks, model development under physical constraints, validation, uncertainty quantification, and certification challenges. The paper also addresses the educational, epistemological, and ethical implications of AI, including curriculum modernization, human-agent collaboration, professional accountability, and the long-term sustainability of engineering knowledge. It concludes with a synthesis of principles for the responsible adoption of AI in ME, encompassing physical consistency, validation, awareness of uncertainty, energy sustainability, human oversight, and ethical responsibility. Our central message is that AI should be viewed not as a substitute for engineering judgment, but as a powerful tool whose value depends on disciplined integration with physical reasoning, scientific rigor, and professional responsibility.
