papers.title: Deep learning for evolving threat detection in online social networks: a PRISMA-based systematic review
papers.authors: Khouloud Alouani, Khaoula Bouazzi, Sadok Bouamama
papers.abstract: Social media platforms have become prime targets for disinformation, fake accounts, and cyberbullying. Deep learning approaches (CNN, RNN, LSTM, BERT) have demonstrated high performance in detecting these OSN threats, achieving over 90% accuracy on benchmark datasets. However, this performance is based on static, outdated data (2015–2018), while malicious actors may continuously modify their behaviors, tactics, and content in response to detection mechanisms. However, the extent to which these models remain robust under temporally evolving threat patterns is less systematically investigated. This systematic review follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines to analyze how deep learning approaches handle (or ignore) evolving OSN threats on social media. A search of five databases (IEEE, ACM, Scopus, Springer, Google Scholar) identified 450 records. After removing duplicates and screening titles, abstracts, and full texts, 35 studies published between 2020 and 2026 were selected for in-depth qualitative analysis. The results reveal three major findings. First, hybrid and transformer-based architectures are frequently represented among the reviewed approaches, with some studies reporting accuracy values above 90% on their respective benchmark datasets. Second, the distribution of the reviewed studies is concentrated on a limited number of OSN threat types. Fake news represents 31.43% of the corpus (11/35 studies), followed by cyberbullying (25.71%, 9/35) and social bots (14.29%, 5/35). Fake accounts account for 5.71% (2/35), while the remaining threat categories each represent 2.86% of the corpus. This distribution indicates that research attention is unevenly distributed across OSN threat types. Third, and most critically, explicit temporal validation and adaptation mechanisms remain limited and heterogeneous across the reviewed studies. None of the 35 studies explicitly reported a systematic chronological train/test validation protocol. Some studies nevertheless used newer datasets or considered evolutionary characteristics, which we coded separately from temporal validation. Overall, the extent to which researchers account for threat evolution varies considerably, ranging from indirect or partial consideration to more explicit evolutionary modelling. Similarly, mechanisms that enable models to adapt to changes over time remain limited and are not consistently reported. These findings highlight a methodological gap between conventional benchmark-based evaluation and the need to assess model robustness in OSN environments that continuously evolve. We refer to this gap as the Evolution Optimization Paradox (EOP), which is used in this review as a synthesis framework rather than as a machine-learning theory. To address this gap, we propose a research agenda structured around five directions: (1) collecting recent datasets (2024–2026), (2) systematically adopting temporal validation, (3) developing adaptive models (including concept drift detection and online learning), (4) evaluating cross-platform generalization, and (5) standardizing metrics for reproducibility. This review contributes to the literature by offering a novel critical analysis of existing approaches, identifying a fundamental gap that has been overlooked, and providing a roadmap for developing robust detection systems to address the rapid evolution of online OSN threats.

papers.title: Understanding Older Adults’ And Caretakers’ Attitudes Toward Social Robots Using Natural Language Processing and Thematic Analysis
papers.authors: Begüm Çonka, Burcu Aysen Urgen, Yasemin Afacan
papers.abstract: Abstract The present study aims to examine the role of social robots in enriching older adults’ environments and helping them cope with the problems that decrease their well-being and life quality. To understand how social robots can be integrated into older adults’ lives, we investigated both older adults’ and caretakers’ attitudes toward social robots. For this aim, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 participants. In these interviews, we showed them photos and videos of the three social robots with different looks, abilities, and degrees of resemblance to humans. Then, we asked them to answer some open-ended questions. These robots were the pet-like robot Aibo, the toy-like robot Paro, and the humanoid robot Pepper. We analyzed the answers using complementary quantitative and qualitative approaches. The quantitative approach included the Sentiment Analysis (SA) and the qualitative approach included the Thematic Analysis (TA). SA results indicate that caretakers approached negatively to Paro, and positively to Aibo and Pepper. On the other hand, older adults did not differ in the polarity of attitudes toward the three robots. The TA results yielded four overarching themes: I) Perceived and expected roles of the robot, II) Physical characteristics and design features of the robot, III) Factors influencing acceptance of the robot, and IV) Disadvantages of the robot. Under those, there were various themes and sub-themes diversified for each robot. Overall, our findings reveal significant insights into older adults’ and caretakers’ approaches to different types of social robots and enable researchers to use these robots more effectively.

papers.title: Weight Loss Measurements Under the Microscope: How Type and Baseline Definition Shape Clinical Response After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery — A 2-Year Follow-up Analysis of 17,568 Patients
papers.authors: Mira Fink, Geoffroy Andrieux, Stephan Herrmann, Ning Wei, Luisa Schäfer, Claudia Läßle, Andreas Tsouris, Jodok Matthias Fink, Goran Marjanović, Stefan Fichtner‐Feigl, Gabriel Seifert
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the era of modern metabolic-bariatric surgery, increasing attention is being paid to the assessment of clinical response after surgery. With the growing availability of multimodal obesity treatment, including preoperative pharmacological and lifestyle interventions, identification and optimization of factors associated with a suboptimal clinical response after metabolic-bariatric surgery (MBS) have become increasingly important. When considering weight loss specifically, two methodological factors substantially influence the interpretation of postoperative response: the metric used to quantify weight loss (percent total weight loss [%TWL] versus percent excess weight loss [%EWL]) and the baseline from which the weight-loss trajectory is calculated. OBJECTIVE: To illustrate how different weight-loss metrics and baseline definitions influence the interpretation of postoperative response and the apparent association between preoperative characteristics and suboptimal clinical response after MBS. METHODS: We analyzed 17,568 patients from the StuDoQ|MBE registry who underwent primary MBS and had complete 2-year postoperative follow-up data. Postoperative suboptimal clinical response was assessed using the 2024 IFSO reporting threshold of <20% TWL. Because the registry did not contain sufficiently standardized longitudinal information on improvement of obesity-related complications, the clinical component of the IFSO definition could not be incorporated. The historical threshold of <50% EWL was additionally analyzed as a surrogate criterion to facilitate comparison with previous literature. Multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models were used to evaluate the associations of preoperative BMI and preoperative weight loss with these weight-loss-based outcomes. Analyses distinguished between cumulative weight loss, calculated from the earliest documented weight before initiation of preoperative weight reduction, and postsurgical weight loss, calculated from weight at the time of surgery to follow-up. Partial-effects plots and heatmaps were used to visualize the modeled associations. RESULTS: The proportion of patients classified according to weight-loss-based criteria for suboptimal clinical response varied substantially according to the metric used, with more patients meeting the historical <50% EWL criterion than the IFSO-consistent <20% TWL threshold. Higher preoperative BMI was associated with a greater probability of meeting the historical <50% EWL criterion, whereas the association was reversed when suboptimal response was defined using <20% TWL. The definition of the baseline weight also substantially influenced the interpretation of preoperative weight loss. Greater preoperative weight loss was associated with a lower probability of weight-loss-based suboptimal clinical response when assessed cumulatively from the beginning of the preoperative treatment trajectory, whereas greater preoperative weight loss was associated with a higher probability of meeting the postsurgical suboptimal weight-loss criteria when weight at the day of surgery was used as the baseline. CONCLUSION: The choice of weight-loss metric and baseline definition substantially influences the classification of postoperative weight-loss response and the apparent association between preoperative characteristics and surgical outcomes. %EWL and %TWL are not interchangeable measures and can produce opposing interpretations of the association between baseline BMI and postoperative response. Consistent with the 2024 IFSO consensus, weight-loss assessment after MBS should use a baseline established before initiation of preoperative weight reduction where appropriate, particularly when evaluating the overall treatment trajectory. %TWL provides a more readily comparable metric for standardized reporting, whereas %EWL may remain useful for comparison with historical literature. Because clinical response after MBS is multidimensional, weight-loss thresholds should not be interpreted as synonymous with clinical treatment failure.

papers.title: Desflurane Increases Hippocampal RAF–MAPK–MSK1 Protein Levels and Reduces CLOCK Expression: Sorafenib Attenuates Cognitive Impairment in Aged Mice
papers.authors: Chenxu Chou, Yulong Jia, Xiaoyu Zhang, Jiali Bai, Xuying Shang, Xiaguang Duan
papers.abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) is common after anesthesia and surgery in older adults, yet no targeted therapy exists, and the mechanism linking volatile anesthetic exposure to circadian dysregulation in the aged hippocampus is undefined. Here we show that RAF manipulation bidirectionally alters CLOCK protein levels in HT22 hippocampal neurons, and that RAF-MAPK-MSK1 protein abundance is inversely related to CLOCK levels in the aged hippocampus after desflurane exposure. Aged C57BL/6 mice (18 months, both sexes) were exposed to 2% desflurane for 2 h, with or without pretreatment with the multi-kinase RAF inhibitor sorafenib (50 mg/kg), and phenotypes were assessed by Western blot, immunofluorescence, in vivo electroencephalography, whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of CA1 pyramidal neurons, and behavioral testing (righting reflex, contextual fear conditioning, Morris water maze). Parallel dissection in HT22 hippocampal neurons employed RAF knockdown, overexpression, and pharmacological inhibition. Desflurane increased total c-Raf, ERK1/2 (MAPK), and MSK1 protein levels-phosphorylation status was not assessed-while reducing CLOCK in both HT22 cells and aged hippocampus, accompanied by cellular senescence, impaired S-phase entry, increased hippocampal β-galactosidase and α-synuclein immunoreactivity, synaptic excitation-inhibition imbalance, and deficits in contextual fear memory and spatial learning. In HT22 cells, RAF knockdown normalized kinase abundance and restored CLOCK, whereas overexpression exacerbated these changes. In aged mice, sorafenib restored CLOCK, attenuated hippocampal β-galactosidase and α-synuclein immunoreactivity, and improved cognitive performance. These findings support a link between RAF-MAPK-MSK1 protein abundance and hippocampal CLOCK in desflurane-induced cognitive impairment and nominate RAF inhibition as a candidate strategy warranting further preclinical study.

papers.title: Pastoral AI ethics for chatbots in religious education
papers.authors: Christos Papakostas
papers.abstract: Abstract Religious Education faces new ethical challenges as AI-powered chatbots become capable of offering scriptural explanations, moral guidance, and personalized learning support. This theoretical article proposes a Pastoral AI Ethics framework for the responsible use of AI chatbots in Religious Education. The framework integrates AI ethics principles, including privacy, transparency, fairness, and accountability, with pastoral values such as confidentiality, doctrinal fidelity, human dignity, and communal trust. The article also presents a conceptual design for a religious learning chatbot composed of a Theological Knowledge Base, a constrained reasoning and retrieval engine, and a Moodle Integration Layer. The proposed model includes privacy-by-design, citation transparency, theological review, and human-in-the-loop escalation for sensitive questions. The article argues that AI chatbots may support Religious Education by improving access to learning resources and feedback, but they must not replace teachers, clergy, or human pastoral care. Further empirical research is required before classroom implementation.

papers.title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
papers.authors: Daiki Nakamura
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by treating the educational effect of GenAI not as a property of the tool but as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine. Integrating research on cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, and self-regulated learning, the framework holds that offloading augments learning when it discharges operations peripheral to the current learning goal, and risks erosion, whether of acquisition or of maintenance, when it bypasses the processing constitutive of that goal, unless the learner substantively processes the output or later reconstructs it. It supplies criteria for locating operations along a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum, specifies the comparison condition against which augmentation and erosion are defined, and states seven conditioned, testable propositions, each illustrated with a common example and paired with supporting and challenging patterns. On this basis, offloading regulation is proposed as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components: a competence comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization, enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners’ goals and motivation. The article closes with an intervention research program, a measurement strategy that triangulates interaction logs with process measures, and equity implications, using STEM learning as a strategically revealing case.

papers.title: A dermal backflow atlas of lymphatic dysfunction in breast cancer-related lymphedema with machine learning-based stage prediction
papers.authors: Lalida Sutejitsiri, Hiroo Suami, Poul MF Nielsen, Anthony R J Phillips, Hayley M. Reynolds
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: Breast cancer-related lymphedema (BCRL) is a chronic condition caused by impaired lymphatic drainage following cancer treatment, manifesting as fluid accumulation, adipogenesis, and lymph reflux to the skin (dermal backflow). The affected regions are diverse and therefore, improved understanding of the spatial distribution of lymphatic dysfunction may facilitate earlier detection and disease monitoring. This study aimed to develop a spatial atlas of dermal backflow in BCRL and apply machine learning (ML) models to predict disease severity. METHODS: Data from 282 female BCRL patients (289 affected limbs) were obtained from the Australian Lymphedema Education, Research and Treatment (ALERT) Centre Databank, including indocyanine green (ICG) lymphography studies and clinical information. A spatial atlas of dermal backflow prevalence in the upper extremities was constructed by co-registering and segmenting clinician-annotated ICG diagrams. Five ML models were developed to classify MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC) lymphedema stage, incorporating dermal backflow percentage and clinical features. RESULTS: The atlas revealed consistent spatial patterns of dermal backflow, with the highest prevalence in the wrist, forearm, and the olecranon region. Subgroup-specific heat maps stratified by MDACC stage, L-Dex ratio, limb volume difference, drainage regions, and hand dermal backflow further demonstrated distinct spatial variations with disease severity. The inclusion of dermal backflow percentage improved ML prediction of MDACC stage, with the best performance achieved by multinomial logistic regression and random forest models. CONCLUSION: Dermal backflow prevalence revealed non-uniform, region-specific patterns in BCRL patients, which can be visualized using spatial atlases. Integrating quantitative imaging features into ML models improves BCRL staging and supports objective, data-driven disease assessment.

papers.title: Pain outcomes in emergent versus elective ventral hernia repair: Propensity score matched analysis
papers.authors: Sidhant Kalsotra, Li-Ching Huang, Savannah Mackenzie Renshaw, Benjamin K. Poulose
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Whether emergent ventral hernia repair (VHR) compromises long-term patient-reported pain recovery compared to elective repair remains unknown. We compared Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Pain Intensity (PROMIS Pain 3a) outcomes between emergent and elective VHR using a multicenter registry after risk adjustment. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort analysis using the Abdominal Core Health Quality Collaborative (ACHQC) registry of adults undergoing VHR from 2013 to 2024 with complete baseline and 30-day PROMIS Pain 3a scores were included. Emergent and elective repairs were compared using 1:3 propensity score matching (PSM) across 31 covariates. The primary outcome was PROMIS Pain 3a T-score at one year postoperatively. RESULTS: Of 11,831 patients (94 emergent, 11,737 elective), emergent patients had higher baseline PROMIS Pain 3a T-scores (median 52 [IQR 46-58] vs. 44 [IQR 36-52], p < 0.001), BMI (median 36 [IQR 32-41] vs. 31 [IQR 27-36] kg/m², p < 0.001), and ASA class 3-4 rates (66% vs. 55%, p < 0.001). After PSM (71 emergent, 193 elective), baseline pain scores were equivalent (median 52 [IQR 44-58] vs. 49 [IQR 44-54], p = 0.2). At 30 days, pain scores did not differ (median 44 [IQR 40-52] vs. 46 [IQR 40-52], p = 0.6). At one year, emergent patients reported significantly lower PROMIS Pain 3a T-scores (median 31 [IQR 31-38] vs. 40 [IQR 31-46], p = 0.01) and greater improvement from baseline (median - 21 [IQR - 24 to - 11] vs. -8 [IQR - 16 to 0], p = 0.002). Complication rates and pragmatic recurrence through five years were equivalent between matched groups. CONCLUSION: Emergent VHR patients demonstrated superior patient-reported pain outcomes at one year compared to propensity-matched elective controls, with equivalent complication and recurrence rates. These findings challenge the notion that emergent repairs inherently lead to worse outcomes and suggest that surgical urgency may not negatively impact long-term pain recovery.

papers.title: A machine learning model for the prediction of the US news & world report ranking of the mechanical engineering graduate programs in the United States
papers.authors: Faeze Khademi, Nikith Rachakonda, Matias Salazar Ismodes, Houshang Darabi
papers.abstract: Abstract The U.S. News & World Report Ranking of the Mechanical Engineering Graduate Programs (USNWR–MEGP) plays a critical role in shaping reputation, attracting top-tier students and faculty, and strengthening research opportunities and partnerships. However, the ranking evaluation process functions as a black box, leaving programs with little clarity on how to improve their positions. Knowing how to uncover the hidden patterns by developing a simulated Machine Learning (ML) model can help programs take strategic actions towards ranking improvements. In this study, we obtained the Ranking of the Mechanical Engineering Graduate Programs (MEGP) for the years 2023, 2024, and 2025 from U.S. News & World Report (USNWR). The remaining variables were also gathered from mechanical engineering department websites, academic databases, and relevant reports. Using the data, we developed an ML model to predict the rank interval of the USNWR Mechanical Engineering Graduate Programs. The developed ML model successfully predicted the 2024 rank interval, demonstrating strong performance across accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC metrics. The developed ML model for the 2024 ranking was then used on the dataset for the following year. The results showed strong performance on the 2025 dataset as well, demonstrating both consistency and adaptability across consecutive academic years. Finally, we created a user-friendly website that leverages our developed ML model, allowing individuals to enter their specific input values and see which rank interval corresponds to their MEGP ranking. This website serves as a valuable resource, as it enables users to explore how alternative combinations of input values are associated with different model-predicted ranking intervals.

papers.title: Patient-independent EEG seizure detection using channel attention and dual-branch time–frequency features
papers.authors: Hrishikesh Tiwary, Arnav Bhavsar, H Muralikrishna
papers.abstract: Abstract We developed a patient-independent EEG-based seizure detection model that generalizes across subjects despite inter-subject variability in spatial seizure expression, electrode characteristics, and artifacts. Scalp EEG recordings from the CHB–MIT (18 channels) and the TUSZ v2.0.3 (20 channels) datasets were evaluated under strict subject-disjoint protocols, employing leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation for CHB–MIT and the official subject-disjoint train/dev/eval split for TUSZ. A channel-wise attention front end adaptively reweights EEG channels prior to feature extraction. The reweighted signals are processed through dual-branch time–frequency representations based on empirical mode decomposition (EMD) and discrete wavelet transform (DWT). Lightweight attention-augmented convolutional neural networks model each branch, and their embeddings are fused for seizure/non-seizure classification. Episode-level decisions are obtained by averaging window-level probabilities from short, overlapping segments. The proposed model demonstrated robust cross-subject generalization under strict subject-disjoint evaluation on both datasets. Ablation studies showed that the EMD and DWT branches provide complementary information and that the complete configuration, combining front-end channel attention with intra-CNN attention, achieved the highest accuracy, AUROC, F1-score, and recall on both datasets. These findings indicate that complementary EMD–DWT representations combined with channel reweighting enhance generalization for patient-independent seizure detection. The proposed framework may support scalable and robust seizure detection across unseen patients and heterogeneous EEG acquisition settings.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic complexity and cognitive decline: Insights from approximate entropy across aging and dementia
papers.authors: Alessia Cacciotti, Anna Fabbrocino, Chiara Pappalettera, Francesca Ginatempo, Nicola Loi, Damiano Sottana, Franca Deriu, Paolo Maria Rossini, Fabrizio Vecchio
papers.journal: Alzheimer s & Dementia Translational Research & Clinical Interventions
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Physiological aging involves gradual modifications of brain activity patterns sometimes leading to pathological outcomes. Understanding changes in brain signal complexity from healthy aging to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) may provide insights into cognitive decline and support early diagnosis. METHODS: = 85). Approximate entropy (ApEn) was computed for the total EEG spectrum and frequency bands. A random forest classifier with a one-versus-one strategy and recursive feature elimination (RFE) was used for group discrimination. Additionally, group comparisons and correlations with neuropsychological scores were performed to further investigate the functional relevance of these entropy changes by assessing their association with cognitive and functional performance. RESULTS: Significant group differences in total ApEn were found, particularly in central brain regions, with progressive decreases from HE to MCI and AD. Frequency-specific patterns emerged: (1) delta ApEn was increased in those with AD across the scalp; (2) alpha 1 ApEn showed frontal decreases and occipital increases in the AD group, with an intermediate pattern in MCI; (3) gamma ApEn was markedly reduced in those with AD compared to both HE and MCI groups, with central and frontal localization, and extended occipital differences in those with MCI versus AD. The classifier achieved 66.55% accuracy, with sensitivities of 78.90% (HE), 49.33% (MCI), and 65.88% (AD). Positive correlations were found between ApEn and cognitive scores in both the total EEG spectrum and gamma band; conversely, delta and alpha 1 ApEn showed negative correlations with cognitive and functional scores. DISCUSSION: The distinct entropy patterns observed across frequency bands and scalp/brain regions may help characterize electrophysiological changes associated with cognitive decline and AD.

papers.title: Cyclic Alternating Pattern as Adaptive Recalibration of Non‐Rapid Eye Movement Sleep: A Perspective
papers.authors: Maria Paola Mogavero, Giuseppe Lanza, Oliviero Bruni, Raffaele Ferri
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) is traditionally regarded as the electroencephalographic marker of unstable non‐rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. Although this interpretation has been highly useful, it may not fully capture the functional meaning of CAP. In this Perspective, we propose that CAP can also be interpreted as a recurrent microstructural recalibration cycle within NREM sleep. In this framework, CAP is viewed as a structured oscillation rather than solely as a sign of fragmentation. Through this oscillation, the sleeping brain may periodically test internal and external conditions, adjust arousability, redistribute network synchronization, coordinate autonomic and motor outputs and return toward a protected background state. The recalibrating function is likely subtype‐specific. A1 phases, dominated by slow‐wave activity and K‐complex‐like responses, may support sleep protection, deep NREM maintenance, instant sleep homeostasis and offline cognitive processing. A2 and A3 phases, characterized by increasing proportions of fast EEG activity and autonomic/motor activation, may represent arousal‐related recalibration events that restore responsiveness or terminate perturbations, but may become maladaptive when excessive. Phase B may provide the deactivation and integration interval through which NREM sleep returns toward stability. We integrate classical CAP physiology with evidence from arousal theory, slow‐wave and spindle biology, infraslow oscillations, autonomic regulation, sleep‐dependent cognition, sleep disorders, development, ageing and neurodegeneration. This framework is testable and may help distinguish adaptive from maladaptive NREM instability according to CAP subtype, sequence structure, integrity of Phase B, autonomic coupling and behavioural consequences.
